acuity.statement: And I’ve just heard Rawiri Waititi say, “Oh, that’s what money will do.” Well, let me tell Rawiri Waititi that a skin for a billboard or a hoarding costs about 30 bucks. It’s the volunteer labour of the people who got out and did that.
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes up the precise content of Waititi's interjection — that ACT's signage was a product of money rather than effort — and rebuts it directly, supplying the unit cost of a hoarding skin and attributing the rest to unpaid labour. The passage would not exist, and could not read as it does, had Waititi interjected something else; it is a point-for-point answer to the claim just made, not a mere naming of the interjector. Marked slightly below 1.0 because the rebuttal engages the cost half of the claim and then moves back to prepared thanks rather than pressing the inference further. Scored for engagement only: the jibe about hard work that follows and the accuracy of the $30 figure belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s what money will do." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: True; it’s true. But let me tell you two things: you’re heading for 54 years, if you’re on the Greens, of never having been in Cabinet if your party was formed in the first contest of 1972 under the name “Values”—54 years’ never being in Cabinet is a long time to wait.
acuity.explanation: He explicitly concedes the interjection's point ("True; it's true") before pivoting — that is a real, pointable engagement with what was just said, but he then leaves the claim behind for prepared material about the Greens' and Te Pāti Māori's futures rather than contesting it. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "We got back from Parliament, too. You’re not the only ones."

acuity.statement: Oh no. Unlike that member—she couldn’t fill a telephone booth. But we packed the halls—not enough chairs or anything.
acuity.explanation: He directly denies the interjection ("Oh no") and stays on the subject of meeting attendance, so the reply would be different had she said something else — but he substitutes a jibe about her own drawing power for any evidence on the point actually disputed, so the engagement stops at the denial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "They were there." (asserting journalists did attend his meetings)

acuity.statement: This is the high point. It’s going down now. I’ve been around—I’ve been around a long time. I know a bunch of losers when I see them.
acuity.explanation: The interjection offered a specific counter-example to his claim that the Greens never held meetings. He names Collins but engages no part of the claim, switching instead to a generic prediction of the Greens' decline that could have been delivered after any interjection whatever.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Fa’anānā Efeso Collins said "We had plenty in Ōtara" to rebut the claim the Greens held no public meetings, and this statement does not take up the Ōtara meetings at all.

acuity.statement: You’re asking us to compare CVs with somebody who’s been here 50 decades. You know, that’s a long, long time, and a long, long time in a House that has done a lot of damage, and he admitted to that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific challenge Peters had just thrown down — compare your authority and your record with mine — and inverts it, turning long tenure into a record of damage to tangata whenua. The opening would have to be rewritten if Peters had argued something else, which is the mark of genuine engagement; the garbled '50 decades' is a veracity/specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "He’s my authority. What’s yours? What’s your authority? They haven’t got one." — and his opening "having spanned six decades, I can give you a few examples"

acuity.statement: You have elected the largest Te Pāti Māori caucus in the history of this Parliament, and may I remind Winston: you only won five seats; we won six.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers Peters' challenge to Te Pāti Māori's mandate with a counter-figure — the seat count — rather than ignoring it. Partial rather than full engagement because it substitutes electorate seats for the party-vote share Peters actually cited and does not meet the 3 percent point on its own terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "How can they call themselves the Māori voice?" and "if they’re the Māori voice and they got only 3 percent of the vote most of the time"

acuity.statement: The Government’s agenda is a flashback to the 19th century. This Government’s agenda for the first hundred days is taking us back a hundred years. The coalition documents read like a manifesto of white supremacy and cultural genocide.
acuity.explanation: Prepared Speech from the Throne material on the subject under debate — the Government's agenda — but indifferent to what Peters had just argued. Nothing here would change if a different member had spoken before, and Peters' specific claims about the election being an inflection point and the coalition rescuing the economy go unanswered. On-topic, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters argued New Zealand First's return would end 'humbug' over the Treaty and that the coalition 'just got back in time' to save the country from becoming Venezuela or Myanmar; this passage and the policy list that follows it take up none of that

acuity.statement: I hope that you don’t continue to isolate yourself from the Generation T, because Generation Te Tiriti are here. Our kohanga generation has arrived and we’re as excited as heck.
acuity.explanation: Waititi's immediately preceding turn coined "generation Tiriti—'Gen T'" and built an argument around it (kotahitanga of tangata whenua and tangata Tiriti, a Tiriti-centric Aotearoa, self-determination by 2040). Ngarewa-Packer repeats the label back and asserts that the generation has arrived, but takes up none of the content: no engagement with his 2040 Matike Mai timeline, his referendum warning, or his claim about what Gen T will do. The address is also pivoted away from him to the Government benches ("you"), which the rubric treats as unresponsive. Her speech would read essentially unchanged had Waititi argued something else on the same topic, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the shared vocabulary is a visible gesture at the turn she follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The 21st century will be remembered for the rise of generation Tiriti—“Gen T”." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: This afternoon we saw the Leader of the Opposition, Chris Hipkins, lay out an amendment to the motion that was put that spelt out exactly what it is that we, as a Labour Opposition, will be holding this Government to account on. That is the job of an Opposition—it is to hold the Government of the day to account, and that is what we will be doing.
acuity.explanation: Woods follows Jackson in the same Address in Reply debate, so she is eligible, but her contribution engages no part of his argument about the Treaty principles. It is prepared material covering tax cuts, smokefree legislation, climate and housing, framed around her own leader's amendment rather than anything the previous speaker said. The speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Jackson had argued, though it is at least on the matter under debate (the Speech from the Throne), so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke immediately before, arguing that the Treaty principles review is an attack on Māori, that the principles exist to constrain the Crown, and that Māori will protest in the streets — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I know we’ve had different descriptions, haven’t we? That it was about theatre. We hear the brother over there—Shane—saying it was Matatini. No, it’s not; it’s about tikanga Māori—bringing tikanga into the House. This House was set up for us as Treaty partners. Māori have never had the opportunity to exercise our tikanga, and I mihi to Te Pāti Māori, because this is an evolving of our culture. This is an evolving of the House.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes up the strand of Ngarewa-Packer's turn about the standing of Māori culture in the House and endorses Te Pāti Māori's assertion of it, contesting the competing characterisation of their action as 'theatre'/'Matatini' and re-describing it as tikanga and Treaty partnership. That is a real engagement with the preceding turn's subject, and the passage would read differently had she argued something else. But he engages her framing rather than any specific claim she made — much of what he answers (the 'theatre'/'Matatini' descriptions) comes from outside her speech — and he then moves on to his own prepared material about the Speaker, his ministerial record on the reo and Nicola Willis. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "They destroy indigenous people’s culture. By what? By removing, demoting, and demonising their language." — her case that the Government is attacking Māori culture and te reo, and her closing tribute to reo speakers ("how the Government is targeting you is kino").

acuity.statement: Today, we’re here to discuss the Government’s agenda and what was said in the Speech from the Throne. I think there is as much being said when there is a speech where something is omitted, and something that was not said in the Speech from the Throne was anything in relationship explicitly to poverty. In fact, the words “poverty” and “inequality” did not get a single mention in today’s speech.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Henare's substantive turn immediately precedes it in the same Address in Reply debate. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate — it names the Speech from the Throne and the Government's agenda, and engages content from Christopher Luxon's speech — but it engages no part of Henare's argument. Nothing here would change if Henare had argued something different about Māori health or smokefree policy; the overlap is thematic only (both invoke evidence, both invoke Te Tiriti partnership). That is prepared material on the right subject with a clear gesture at the debate, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare spoke about the Government's "very regressive Māori policy agenda", Te Aka Whai Ora and the smokefree repeal, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Can I acknowledge the contribution she has made to Aotearoa over many, many years, the bravery, the vision, and the foresight she has had, and her tenacity, quite frankly, in dealing with what were some unprecedented attacks on her and her whānau throughout the previous term, which was distressing to witness.
acuity.explanation: Boyack follows a substantive turn by Bidois that made specific, contestable claims about crime, the PISA results, health waiting lists and transport costs — all of which she, as a Labour member, had every opportunity to rebut. Instead she opens with ceremonial acknowledgments: the Assistant Speaker, Nanaia Mahuta's record, and a personal tribute to Tim Costley. The passage would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before her and whatever they had said. It sits in the debate (an address-in-reply contribution, where acknowledgments are conventional), so it is not wholly adrift of the occasion, but it engages no part of the preceding argument. Scored only on responsiveness: the warmth, the generosity to a member opposite and the substance of the tribute are not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Bidois spoke immediately before, arguing that "Crime is up 50 percent in the last six years under this Government" and that there have been "20 years of educational decline in this country", and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I wanted to talk about my greater concern about that because of what I heard from Winston Peters today. He said—and I was listening to him carefully—that what Māori want is First World wages, and I wanted to say to him that that’s exactly what the people of Mt Albert want, too. That is a common need of people—we do want First World wages.
acuity.explanation: White takes up one identifiable strand of another member's contribution — Peters' claim about what Māori want — and does something with it, accepting it and universalising it to her own electorate rather than merely naming him as a target. But she does not engage the substance of the turn immediately before her (Boyack on Te Aka Whai Ora and the smokefree repeal), and the rest is prepared first-speech material on te reo and tikanga that would read identically whatever preceded it. Partial engagement, hence mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what Māori want is First World wages" — Winston Peters, as quoted by White from his earlier contribution; his turn is not in this window, so the engagement can only be pointed at through her own rendering of it. Rachel Boyack's immediately preceding turn argued the Government's canning of Te Aka Whai Ora will worsen Māori life expectancy, and White does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: We as a country have been a little slow in calling for a ceasefire. That is the very minimum, because until a ceasefire is imposed and people can sit down and talk, there can be no peace and there can be no prosperity; there can be no humanity.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific ceasefire clause of the motion just moved and argues it is both late and the bare minimum, which is the reasoning behind the amendment he moves to replace that exact wording. It engages the strand rather than the full argument of the motion, and then returns to general material about peace and prosperity, so it sits above a topical gesture but short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters moved: "call on all parties involved in the conflict, as well as countries with influence in the region, to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire"

acuity.statement: New Zealand has a proud history of an independent foreign policy. We have over the decades stood up for what is right. We set up a social welfare system. We supported the set-up of the United Nations and all its principles. We supported the World Trade Organization because we know of the importance of this.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on New Zealand's foreign-policy tradition, reaching as far as social welfare and the WTO. It is loosely within the subject area of the debate but would read identically whatever Peters had moved, so it belongs in the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters moved a motion on the Israel–Gaza conflict with specific clauses on condemning the 7 October attack, a ceasefire and Israel's right to self-defence, and this passage does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: This self-defence narrative, then: we utterly condemn all violence—I am a former prevention of violence Minister—of course, and have since the start condemned all violence, including the attacks by Hamas on 7 October. But it is intolerable and grotesque to suggest the actions of the Israeli Government are self-defence. This is retaliation against civilians, and the international community has a duty to not let it continue.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the self-defence clause of the motion just moved: it accepts the part condemning the 7 October attacks, then disputes the characterisation of Israel's actions as self-defence and supplies an alternative characterisation. This is the reasoning for the substitution she moves to that clause, and the passage would have to change if Peters' motion had been worded differently. Scored on engagement alone — the force of the language belongs to Civility and the truth of the characterisation to Veracity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters moved: "recognise Israel's right to defend itself, acting in accordance with international law, and that all civilians be protected from armed conflict"

acuity.statement: I'm pleased to see that the Deputy Prime Minister—the Minister of Foreign Affairs—has put up a ceasefire in this motion. I welcome it. I wish we as a country had put this pressure out to the world, given the many thousands of dead, innocent civilians, many, many weeks ago.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the ceasefire element of the motion just moved, accepts it explicitly, and then disputes its timing. That is partial acceptance plus a specific criticism of the thing moved, which is high responsiveness; it falls short of 1.0 only because it engages the timing rather than the substance of the clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters moved: "call on all parties involved in the conflict, as well as countries with influence in the region, to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The ACT Party supports this motion, but I would like to point out there are some real problems with the discourse that is being had in New Zealand over the past few months since 7 October.
acuity.explanation: Court follows a substantive statement by Todd McClay setting out the Government's position (ceasefire calls, Israel's right of self-defence, hostages, $10m aid, NZers exiting Gaza). He registers a position on the motion under debate — a gesture at the proceedings — but takes up no part of McClay's argument, pivoting instead to prepared material on domestic New Zealand discourse and anti-Semitism. The speech would read identically whatever McClay had said about the Government's response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd McClay set out the Government's response — "We've called on all parties, as well as countries with influence in the region, to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire" — and this statement supports the motion without taking up any part of it.

acuity.statement: We’re seeing the bombing of hospitals, the bombing of homes, refugee camps, schools, churches, for goodness’ sake. That’s not self-defence. The use of white phosphorous in densely populated areas is not self-defence. Collective punishment of civilians by cutting off food, water, and medical supplies is not self-defence.
acuity.explanation: This takes the self-defence justification McClay advanced on the Government's behalf and contests it directly, itemising conduct she says falls outside it. The passage only makes sense as a rebuttal of the preceding claim; had the Government framed its position differently, this would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: "The Government fully supports Israel's right to defend itself from the terrorist organisation Hamas."

acuity.statement: There is debate about who’s occupying who. From our perspective, Israel’s colonial occupation of Palestinian lands in Jenin by the British Empire has led to decades of pain, suffering, and bloodshed.
acuity.explanation: She names the disagreement Court opened — who is occupying whom — and reverses his characterisation, answering his framing of an occupation of Israeli land with a counter-account of occupation of Palestinian land. This is engagement with the specific contested premise of the preceding turn, not a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "What many have described as an occupation of the land of Israel, the Israeli people—Jewish people—call home."

acuity.statement: The conflict simply did not start on 7 October, and I will never ever accept this House normalising violent experiences and saying it’s OK and that we’ve had this happen here before.
acuity.explanation: Both preceding speakers dated the matter from 7 October, Court most heavily ("the trauma of 7 October", "in the past few months since 7 October"). She disputes that starting point explicitly, which is a direct correction of the chronological premise the earlier turns rested on rather than prepared material that happens to be on topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "The trauma of 7 October has reignited the worst memories of the Holocaust"

acuity.statement: What is stopping the Government right now from introducing an Israeli sanctions bill to Parliament, just as we did in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or creating a special visa category for Palestinians displaced by this war, as our allies in Australia have done, as we also did for Ukraine?
acuity.explanation: McClay's turn was substantially an account of what the Government has done — $10 million in aid, consular work on exits from Gaza, calls on all parties. This takes up that account and presses on what it omits, naming two specific further steps with precedents. It engages the topic of the Government's response rather than any particular figure McClay gave, and then runs into prepared Te Pāti Māori policy, so it is a partial rather than a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: "The Government has also contributed $10 million to address immediate humanitarian need."

acuity.statement: It requires a strong response, so I compliment the Minister for this initiative. But we think, as Phil Goff has said, we can go wider, we can be a bit stronger here, and we can stand up against the rest of the world.
acuity.explanation: Jackson follows Twyford and takes up one strand of his argument — that New Zealand's motion does not go far enough and the Government should use its voice more strongly — and makes it the ground of his own amendment, which adds words about the IDF's conduct. But he engages only that general strand, not any of Twyford's specific reasoning (the settlements, the 2016 Security Council resolution, the occupation's legal status), and the bulk of the speech is prepared material on Gaza and on Māori support for Palestine. He also misnames the member he is agreeing with, which weakens the claim that he is tracking the preceding turn closely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "New Zealand should now condemn the illegal occupation of Palestinian territory, demand that Israel immediately cease settlement activities"

acuity.statement: It matters that our Prime Minister and that our foreign Minister push back on that line of diplomacy that says we have to walk hand in hand with our allies and trading partners as they fail the children of Gaza.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns (Twyford, Jackson) precede this one in the same debate, so it is eligible. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and arrives at a point that converges with Twyford's — that officials' alignment with allies should not govern New Zealand's position — but it does not engage his claim, his evidence (the 2016 UNSC resolution, the settlements) or Jackson's amendment; it is prepared material about her own experience, the Green amendment's child-casualty figure, and New Zealand's standing. The gesture to colleagues in Te Pāti Māori names supporters rather than taking up any content, which the rubric counts as a mere reference. The speech would read almost identically whatever the two previous members had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Phil Twyford argued the Government should "resist the nervous and over-cautious advice of its foreign affairs officials who, as always, will be worried about being out of step with Canberra and Washington", and this statement makes a parallel point without taking up his argument

acuity.statement: When this outbreak of violence and mass murder occurred on 7 October, this Government was weeks from being formed—as the Government—despite some of the statements being made in this House today.
acuity.explanation: Closing the debate, Peters takes up one strand of what preceded him: Boyack's claim that Labour had spent weeks calling for a ceasefire carried the implicit charge that the Government had not, and Peters answers that strand directly by dating the Government's formation against 7 October. The engagement is real and pointable, but partial — he answers the timing imputation rather than any of the substance Boyack advanced (the casualty figures, the humanitarian position, the amendment's wording), and the rest of the speech moves to prepared material about virtue signalling, Keir Starmer and the Moriori that is largely indifferent to what Boyack actually argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "The New Zealand Labour Party has been for weeks urgently calling for a ceasefire in Gaza and Israel to put a halt to the appalling attacks and violence so that a journey to a lasting peace can begin."

acuity.statement: I've got a couple of questions. First, when can we expect to see copies of the bills? And, second, when the urgency motion is confirmed, can the Leader of the House confirm that there will be bills that are doing new things rather than just repealing other things?
acuity.explanation: Both questions are built out of the specific content of the statement he had just heard: he asks for the text of the very bills Bishop had named, and the second question draws out a feature of Bishop's own list — that the programme announced is an amendment and a repeal — and presses it. The speech could not have been delivered before Bishop spoke; substitute a different business statement and it would have to change. Short of 1.0 only because he engages the shape of the programme rather than anything in either named bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The legislation to be considered will include the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill and the Fair Pay Agreements Legislation Repeal Bill."

acuity.statement: In relation to the copies of the bills, as soon as they are available and the Government wishes to make them available to the Opposition. And in relation to the second part, it's always worth the House's time repealing dumb legislation.
acuity.explanation: He addresses both of McAnulty's questions in turn and in order, and the second reply engages the actual premise of the question — the suggestion that repeal is a lesser use of the House's time — by contesting it rather than sidestepping it. Scored on engagement alone: the answer is vague on timing and offers no detail, but vagueness and evasiveness belong to Specificity and Forthrightness, not here, and the reply is unmistakably shaped by what was just put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "can the Leader of the House confirm that there will be bills that are doing new things rather than just repealing other things?"

acuity.statement: We’ll get into that, keep asking supplementary questions—I’ve got it all worked out. And how the project can be brought back within the funding envelope that was originally agreed when somebody who was in charge knew what he was doing. We also have questions around Antarctica New Zealand’s management of the project and we intend to get answers to those questions in the weeks ahead, and also raise the issue of what happened to the private funding idea, or did the Minister of Finance just scare them off?
acuity.explanation: Peters picks up the one strand Robertson's interjection raised — the missing private funding — rather than ignoring it: he defers it ("We'll get into that"), then returns to it at the end of the answer and flips it back as a counter-question about whether the previous Minister of Finance frightened the sponsors off. You can point squarely at what is engaged, and the answer would read differently had Robertson interjected about something else. It is not a 1.0 because he supplies no figure or account of the $300 million, instead postponing it and resuming prepared material about Antarctica New Zealand's management.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You said you were going to get $300 million in private funding. What happened to that—what happened to that?" — Grant Robertson

acuity.statement: But we're here in the Address in Reply debate, and, look, it's been quite interesting this afternoon. I thought that speech before was more self-reflection than anything else, but someone whom I greatly respect on the other side of the House is the Hon Peeni Henare, who spoke yesterday.
acuity.explanation: Smith follows a substantive turn by Verrall in the same debate, so he is eligible. He gestures at the preceding speech with a one-line dismissal and then moves to prepared material about debating conduct — praise for Peeni Henare's point from the previous day and advice to Julie Anne Genter. Nothing in his speech engages Verrall's actual arguments; delete her turn and substitute any other Opposition speech and his remarks would stand unchanged. A bare reference is not engagement, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.2 for the gesture at the debate he had just heard.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "I was shocked, like many New Zealanders, to hear that the Government proposed to repeal these laws in order to fund their tax cuts." — Smith names her speech only to dismiss it as "self-reflection" and takes up none of its content (the smokefree repeal, health funding commitments, primary care, targets).

acuity.statement: I know. Look, members opposite have grown up in a car-dependent culture. They don’t understand that it’s possible to have economically rational investment that improves people’s options to alternatives, but the reality is—and we have 50 years of data on this if any of the members opposite would like to see it—that urban motorways do not reduce congestion; they make it worse; that the billions of dollars spent in central Wellington on an extra lane, an extra kilometre of lane is not going to make it easier to get to the airport; and that those billions of dollars spent in central Wellington and on the fringe of Auckland, and in Christchurch, are billions of dollars that this National-led Government will not be spending on the rural roads in the regions that actually need investment.
acuity.explanation: Genter stops her prepared line and takes up Bayly's interjection directly: he offers Auckland motorway congestion as the case for building motorways, and she answers that exact point with the claim that urban motorways increase congestion rather than reduce it, and that the money is drawn away from the rural roads his example implies. The passage would read differently had he interjected something else; it is not a 1.0 only because she does not engage the Pukekohe case specifically, generalising instead to 50 years of data.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Come to Pukekohe and see how you can get to Auckland Central." — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: Yeah, equality of opportunity cannot be achieved if you do not tax income from capital at the same rate that you tax income from work. You don’t believe that because you’re a bunch of landlords who want to keep getting richer at the expense of everyone else.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne interjects the opportunity/outcome distinction as a rebuttal, and Genter takes that exact distinction and argues it against her: she accepts the frame of equality of opportunity and contends it is unattainable without equal taxation of capital and labour income. This is engagement with the content of the interjection, not a mere mention of it. The second sentence is an insult, which bears on civility rather than on whether she listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Equality of opportunity, not equality of outcome." — Suze Redmayne

acuity.statement: Wow, that was an interesting speech, wasn’t it? I’ve got to say that is someone going back in time, I think, and I think I’d just say to the Hon Julie Anne Genter, maybe she should come up to Franklin, just south of Auckland, and try and get on the motorway and drive to work at 6.30 in the morning and tell all those people who are struggling to get on the motorway, let alone drive along the motorway, because it’s absolutely congested, that they are ignorant fools, because I’m not sure that they’re going to agree with you.
acuity.explanation: Bayly opens by taking up both Genter's "ignorant fools" charge and the substance behind it, turning the epithet back on the commuters whose congestion he says her position ignores. The speech is clearly shaped by what she said. It falls short of 1.0 because he answers her data claim (that motorways do not relieve congestion) with the existence of congestion rather than with the causal point, so the engagement is squarely aimed but partial; whether the counter reasons well is a rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They are ignorant fools, this Government" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: It’s interesting—I went back to the 2020 speech. Just to cast everyone’s mind back, Labour came in with this crushing absolute majority and the Governor-General said, on behalf of the Government, “Crises do not form an orderly line waiting to be addressed.”, then went on to wax lyrically about accelerating our economic recovery and to lay the foundations for a greater future. What a hash they made of it—what an absolute hash of it.
acuity.explanation: Having engaged Genter earlier, Bayly here moves to prepared material contrasting the 2020 Speech from the Throne with Labour's record. It is on the debate's subject — the Speech from the Throne — but engages no part of the argument immediately preceding it; the passage would be word-for-word identical whatever Genter had said, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued the Speech from the Throne was detached from the evidence on climate, tax and transport, and this passage does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The concern there about Onslow from the electricity companies that were half privatised by the previous National Government is that, actually, this is a lever to keep electricity prices down in the long term. Yes, it’s expensive. Yes, a lot of work is still to be done, but just tossing it out is handing to the existing electricity generators and gen-tailers, monopoly, monopsony rights to make super-profits—and we’ll wait and see.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific Onslow argument Smith had just made, concedes the cost point explicitly ("Yes, it’s expensive"), and disputes the conclusion by supplying a different rationale — Onslow as a price lever against the gentailers. The passage would have to be rewritten if Smith had argued something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because it leaves Smith's specific figures (the $15.7 billion and the 98 percent average overrun) unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "I think my colleague the Hon Simeon Brown neglected to mention that Lake Onslow is very expensive—there’s no doubt about that." (and the $15.7 billion / cost-overrun argument that follows it)

acuity.statement: Yes, we do appreciate the farmers—50 percent increase in export revenue in the primary sector when we were in office, through COVID and many other challenges.
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up Smith's closing claim that farmers were ground down and vilified under the previous Government and answers it with a counter-figure about primary sector export revenue in office. It engages the substance of the charge rather than merely naming it, but answers the broader proposition (we valued farmers) rather than Smith's specific complaints about piled-on costs, so it sits above the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "But it is the farming sector that is most relieved about what is going on. They have literally been ground down"

acuity.statement: But there’s one, of course—you know, there’ll be a ban on gang patches. Really interesting. How will you tell who are gangs? What will you say to the Ulysses Club? A bunch of guys get together, have a patch on—are you going to ban them? Are we going to ban people in rugby clubs who might have a patch on the back of their jersey? I’ll wait and see what happens in that area.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material working through a checklist of coalition policies. It is on the matter under debate — the Government's programme as set out in the Speech from the Throne — but engages no part of the argument Smith had just made, and would read identically whoever had spoken before. Scored in the 0.1–0.3 band because of the gesture at the debate's subject, not at its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Stuart Smith spoke about firearms regulation, fair pay agreements, Lake Onslow and the farming sector, and said nothing about gang patches; this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’ll just start with something else—accidentally and unexpectedly positive—that happened in the House today, which is that a Government in Aotearoa New Zealand quite unexpectedly recognised Palestine’s right to self-determination and Statehood.
acuity.explanation: Ghahraman follows a substantive O'Connor turn, so the turn is eligible, but she announces at the outset that she is starting on "something else" and delivers prepared material on Palestine and Gaza that engages no strand of what preceded her. Her one contact with the previous speaker's side — that "the Labour Government didn't do it for six years" — is a swipe at Labour's record, not an engagement with any claim O'Connor made, and the rubric treats a mere reference as unresponsive. It sits above 0.1 rather than at it because the speech is a genuine contribution to the debate on the incoming Government's direction and makes demands of that Government, which is the matter under debate; it is not 0.5 because nothing in O'Connor's turn can be pointed at as engaged. Substituting a different O'Connor speech on the same topics would not require a word of this to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O’Connor spoke about the Smokefree Environments amendments ("that misery from emphysema and cancer"), the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga, the Government's five health targets and infrastructure funding, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Now, I want to come to the proposals set out in the Speech from the Throne—in particular, those which relate to resource management reform and the need to deliver infrastructure in a more coherent and cost-effective way. This Government has made it clear, in the coalition agreement, we have a plan to do it, and we have some specific measures that will deliver that.
acuity.explanation: Court speaks immediately after a substantive Swarbrick turn, so he is eligible, but the speech engages no part of what she said. It is prepared material on resource management and infrastructure funding, pitched at the Speech from the Throne generally; the one comparison he draws is to a 2020 Throne speech by a former Labour Prime Minister, not to anything the previous speaker argued. Substituting a different Green critique on the same topic would not require a single word of this to change, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band; it earns 0.1 rather than 0.3 because there is not even a gesture at the preceding contribution. The speech is at least on the matter under debate, so it is not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chlöe Swarbrick argued that this Government is returning the country to the 1980s-90s 'trickle-down economics', and that 'you can negotiate with and you can change the rules of the economy, but you cannot negotiate with the laws of science', and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We heard from Grant Robertson, and the most interesting thing in his speech was that he said he made it to seventh form—not something I would have guessed—but I think we can be pretty sure that he didn’t do maths or economics, because he tried to argue that because Australia has a dual mandate and England doesn’t, and England had higher inflation than Australia at one point, the argument of removing the dual mandate is wrong. Now, no one that’s thought for a moment about these things would say that there’s a correlation from two data points.
acuity.explanation: Seymour restates Robertson's specific cross-country comparison and attacks its inferential basis — that a handful of data points cannot establish (or refute) a correlation. The rebuttal is aimed squarely at the argument just made and would have had to be different had Robertson argued something else, so acuity is high; the mockery of Robertson's schooling is a civility matter and the question of whether the rebuttal reasons well is a rigor matter, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent. So there’s no correlation there"

acuity.statement: I’d like to speak on behalf of New Zealand First in support of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill, and on that note, I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, so it is eligible, but the contribution engages no part of either argument. It is on the matter under debate (the bill is named) and nothing more; it would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, which places it at the bottom of the band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Grant Robertson argued the bill is not evidence-based and that inflation outcomes show no correlation with central bank mandates, and David Seymour argued price stability is monetary policy's sole job — this statement takes up neither

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I’m proud to stand on this side of the House as part of a Government which is totally committed to reducing the cost of living and reducing inflation. The commitment to beating inflation starts with ensuring the Reserve Bank is returning to a single mandate of keeping down inflation.
acuity.explanation: Wedd follows Waititi's substantive opposition speech, which made specific claims (Māori unemployment at 7.6 percent, double the general rate; no modelling for the inflation benefit of a single mandate) and put a direct challenge about evidence. Her speech engages none of it: it asserts the single-mandate commitment and then moves to prepared constituency material on Hawke's Bay growers, on-farm inflation and the cyclone rebuild. The speech is on the matter under debate — the bill and inflation — so it is not a 0.0, but it would have read word-for-word the same whatever Waititi had said, and there is not even a gesture at the preceding argument, so it sits at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band. Scored only for engagement: the fact that her material is on-policy and locally concrete belongs to Focus and Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that repealing the employment mandate will disproportionately hit Māori and Pasifika workers and asked "Where is the modelling? Where is the evidence that this repeal will have the material effect on inflation" — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: So it should not come as a surprise that a reasonable Government such as this National-led coalition Government has this bill as the first piece of legislation being introduced to the House in this term. It is a high priority to get the Reserve Bank’s focus back solely on getting inflation under control, but also maintaining it under control once you’re in the desired bandwidth.
acuity.explanation: Russell's immediately preceding speech made three specific arguments: the bill puts no money in pockets by Christmas, the same reordering could have been achieved under section 125 of the Reserve Bank Act without repeal, and the regulatory impact statement says Treasury would prefer the monetary policy remit. MacLeod engages none of them. He gestures at the 'first piece of legislation' theme she pressed — saying it should be no surprise this bill comes first — and then delivers prepared material on what inflation feels like, Milton Friedman and a Reagan quote. The speech would be nearly word-for-word identical had she argued something else about the bill, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is a recognisable glance at the point under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "One would think that the first piece of legislation that a Government put into the House—the very first piece of legislation—would make a tangible difference right from the start."

acuity.statement: There is no evidence that these two things do not work in alignment. There is simply no evidence, and the regulatory impact statement that the Minister saw made that incredibly clear.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod's central claim was that the dual mandate failed and caused the inflation New Zealanders are paying for. Woods takes up that exact strand — denying the two objectives are in conflict and citing the regulatory impact statement against him — so you can point at what is engaged. But she contests the conclusion by flat assertion rather than engaging his reasoning (the 2019 timing argument, the Reserve Bank 'struggling ever since'), and then returns to prepared material on Labour's DNA and Grant Robertson. Partial engagement: 0.5. Note the quality of the inference is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "Labour’s experiment of including an additional focus for the Reserve Bank has failed and we’re all paying for it—literally."

acuity.statement: I will take a moment as we’re hearing a chorus from the backbench of the Government benches that we don’t need regulatory impact statements because we had an election. Well, newsflash: elections don’t give you ultimate power. There still are requirements for you to do policy work, and our Government did all the way through.
acuity.explanation: This is unmistakably live engagement: she hears the interjection, names the proposition it carries (that an election mandate dispenses with the need for a regulatory impact statement), and rebuts it directly before returning to her argument. The passage could not have been written in advance and would not exist had Bidois stayed silent, which is the deciding test. Scored 0.9 rather than 1.0 because the thing engaged is a two-word interjection rather than a developed argument, so there is less content to take up. The combative, slightly mocking register ('newsflash') is a Civility matter and is deliberately not allowed to move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "The election!"

acuity.statement: We had a comment from the member Chlöe Swarbrick that the remit would still have reference to having regard to employment, and I want to clarify for that member that that is incorrect. We will have one operational objective in the remit, and, as has been the case in previous remits, it will be in pursuing that objective that will have regard to financial stability and other matters.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up one specific factual claim made by another member about the content of the remit, states that it is incorrect, and then supplies the substantive correction (one operational objective, with financial stability and other matters taken into account in pursuing it). The passage could not have been written without that prior claim, and would have to change if a different claim about the remit had been made. Scored on engagement only — not on whether the correction is true (veracity) or how the surrounding speech characterises the other side (focus/civility).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "the remit would still have reference to having regard to employment" — the claim as Willis restates it from the preceding debate on the same bill.

acuity.statement: Now, the member opposite says, “They had to water it down.” The member opposite needs to remember: she’s getting rid of it. She’s getting rid of it completely. The Reserve Bank of Australia, the Federal Reserve are both completely able to manage these two things together.
acuity.explanation: Robertson takes up the specific interjected claim about Australia watering down its employment mandate and does something with it: he concedes the premise implicitly and turns it into a contrast with the Minister's own bill, which removes the employment objective entirely, then cites both the RBA and the Fed as counter-examples. The passage would not exist if Willis had not interjected that line, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he does not dispute or examine the substance of the "watering down" claim itself, he pivots from it to the comparative point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "They had to water it down, you know that."

acuity.statement: Once again, we have there in black and white—as myself and the Minister, when she was previously a member of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, heard elucidated time and time again from the Reserve Bank Governor—that, ultimately, there was not all too much difference that was coming out of the monetary policy committee as a result of the dual mandate.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and is aimed at the Minister's earlier remarks rather than at the member who immediately preceded her, so it engages no part of Robertson's argument. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate puts it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band; the speech would read essentially identically had Robertson made a different argument about the dual mandate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Grant Robertson argued that the Reserve Bank's governors said the dual mandate "did not alter one iota their focus on inflation" and that the bill is "a solution in search of a problem", and this statement does not take up his argument — it arrives at an adjacent conclusion from the member's own material (the tabled remit review and her own select committee recollection) rather than engaging his.

acuity.statement: I think we’ve heard some fine contributions on the theory of inflation and Milton Friedman and the like. But essentially what we’re dealing with here is a real-world issue that, as Mr Stephenson just pointed out, families are hurting, cost of living is hurting, our business community and our farmers are hurting with record-high interest rates that’s driven as a result of the record-high inflation.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Stephenson's cost-of-living point — and explicitly sets aside his Friedman/theory material as 'fluff', extending the hardship claim to farmers and business. It engages the topic and a named element of the previous speech rather than any specific claim or figure in it, then moves straight to commending the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "that’s affecting households with increases in mortgages and petrol prices and grocery prices" (and his Milton Friedman quotation)

acuity.statement: By removing the dual mandate, will this Government push the official cash rate to an unachievable rate that the Governor can’t achieve, creating a forced recession? That’s a question that should be asked.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the removal of the dual mandate — and gestures at the interest-rate consequences the previous speaker raised, but engages no part of Patterson's or Stephenson's actual argument. The surrounding speech (job losses, rushed pre-Christmas legislation) would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Patterson spoke about record-high interest rates hurting families, farmers and business and about being persuaded by the Minister of Finance, and this statement does not take up either claim; it is prepared opposition to the bill's mechanism.

acuity.statement: If the inflation we experienced here in Aotearoa was a result only of Government spending as a result of the last Labour Government, why is it that the United States, Denmark, Australia, and virtually every other economy in the world experienced the same shape of inflation?
acuity.explanation: Directly takes the causal claim made two turns earlier — that the previous Government's spending and the dual mandate produced New Zealand's inflation — and tests it against cross-country CPI data, which she tables in the House. The speech would have to change if the preceding ACT contribution had attributed inflation to something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "this large increase in Government spending has had consequences" / "The last Government’s output certainly didn’t match the amount it was spending."

acuity.statement: I think we all know that the economic reforms of the 1980s did not lead to a giant increase in productivity.
acuity.explanation: Rebuts the specific historical warrant Stephenson built his case on — that the Douglas-era single-mandate reforms worked — by denying the productivity payoff rather than restating Green policy. It engages his premise squarely, though it answers the broader 1980s reform programme rather than the inflation-target claim itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "there’s actually nothing wrong with going back to 1989, when this was put in place and it worked"

acuity.statement: I just want to talk about what happens when you try and do two things and don't do either well. The interesting thing I will speak on is public transport. We want to try and reduce inflation. We are not going to do it by also focusing on the jobs. We need to reduce inflation first.
acuity.explanation: Nimon takes up the central strand of White's preceding speech — White's claim that the two objectives are complementary and not in competition — and asserts the opposite, that attempting two things means doing neither well, illustrated with a bus analogy. That is a real engagement with the topic of the claim, so it is not merely prepared material on the right subject. But she engages only the bare proposition and none of White's actual supporting argument (the dual-mandate versus single-mandate comparison, the absence of correlation, the wage-growth point), and the rest of the turn is repetition of the prepared "do one thing well" refrain that would be unchanged whatever White had said. Half marks: one strand engaged, then back to prepared material. Scored on engagement only — the weakness of the bus analogy as an inference belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So these things are not in competition." — Helen White, who argued at length that maximum sustainable employment sits alongside price stability rather than competing with it

acuity.statement: Well, I am mentioning the bill, Mr Speaker, because this bill—we’re shocked that they would repeal what we did to focus just on the material side of things for people in this country. If they’re really concerned about the cost of living, then they would follow what Grant Robertson has done.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the cost-of-living justification Wedd built her whole speech on and turns it back — if cost of living is the concern, the dual mandate should be kept. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding argument (the purpose of the mandate change), but it answers the theme rather than Wedd's specific claim that a single inflation mandate is what lowers prices, and the rest of the turn is prepared material praising the former Minister of Finance and attacking National. Partial engagement, hence mid-band; the weakness of the inference is a Rigor matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "It’s time we focus on hard-working New Zealanders and reducing the cost of living."

acuity.statement: Because no wonder it’s such a mess, and I tell you: I hear a number of members on the other side of the House talk about the problems that they believe this bill is going to present with employment, particularly for Māori in there. Well, it’s exactly the opposite. This is exactly what’s needed to actually get a great employment, great economy going throughout our country. This is exactly what is needed. It’s exactly the opposite of what they’ve been talking about.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific strand Jackson advanced — that the single mandate will cost employment, particularly Māori employment — and contradicts it directly, so the speech would have to change if Jackson had argued something else about the bill. It is engagement by flat assertion rather than by rebutting the figures Jackson cited, which keeps it below the top band; the absence of supporting reasoning is a Rigor failing and must not be scored again here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "he was certainly a supporter of what we were doing, and what we were doing was creating jobs" (and his unemployment figures for 2018)

acuity.statement: Some of the things we have heard from the other side tonight have just blown me away. They’re saying that the National Party or the coalition doesn’t care about employment, doesn’t care about people, etc. It’s complete and utter nonsense. In fact, those members might want to just have a look at some interesting comments made by, let’s say, the International Labour Organization.
acuity.explanation: Mooney directly names and takes up Russell's central charge — that removing the employment objective shows the Government does not care about employment — rejects it, and then mounts a substantive counter-argument that inflation itself is what harms low-income workers, quoting the ILO on the distributional cost of inflation. The speech would have had to change had Russell argued something else. It falls short of 1.0 because he does not engage her specific, pointable arguments (the Reserve Bank letter's use of "priority" rather than "exclusive", or the regulatory impact statement's alternative options that would have retained the maximum sustainable employment objective); he answers the broad accusation rather than the detailed case, then returns to prepared material on inflation and the 1980s.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government doesn’t care about employment. That’s what this bill is telling us." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: So I’d just like to back up those sentiments from the former Minister because, as we’ve well canvassed—and, actually, as is reflected in the monetary policy remit review from June 2023—it’s pretty clear in black and white from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand that there hadn’t been any meaningful impact or other decisions that would have been made had they not had that dual mandate and solely the focus on price stability.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Robertson's precise question — whether the dual mandate diluted the Reserve Bank's inflation focus — and does something with it, supplying the June 2023 monetary policy remit review as evidence for the negative before pressing the Minister for counter-evidence. The speech would have to change had Robertson asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "what advice, if any, has she received that there was less of a focus on inflation because of the dual mandate in the time that it has been in place?"

acuity.statement: As I’ve alluded to before, we haven’t had a select committee stage in this bill, but I have heard from a number of people, so I do want to bring some of those letters to the House so that they at least inform the discussions as we go through this part of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding turns — the absence of select committee scrutiny — and acts on it by substituting constituent correspondence for submissions. It engages nothing of the specific question about advice on the dual mandate, and the bulk of the turn is a letter read into the record, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "hasn’t gone off to a select committee, hasn’t had the ability to be scrutinised"

acuity.statement: The member prior to her asked why it is that we are amending the Act and whether we gave consideration to a change to the remit only. I would note that without amending the Act, the monetary policy committee (MPC) would still be required to have regard to maximum sustainable employment.
acuity.explanation: Identifies Swarbrick's specific alternative — amending the remit alone rather than the Act — and gives the reason it was rejected, that the statutory duty to have regard to maximum sustainable employment would survive a remit change. Directly engages the content of the question put, not merely its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "I wanted to ask the Minister if she meaningfully explored any of those other options, particularly on the monetary policy committee (MPC) remit only, or the Order in Council"

acuity.statement: It’s an important point, because the Minister has spent a significant amount of time in this debate telling us that we need to be crystal clear and laser-focused on inflation, and what we’ve heard consistently from the Reserve Bank Governor over the time that the dual mandate has been in place is that it has not caused him, or the monetary policy committee, or the Reserve Bank in general to take their eye off the ball of inflation.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated justification head-on, noting that she answered on the value of signalling clarity while leaving unanswered whether any advice showed the dual mandate actually compromised the Bank's inflation focus, and sets the Governor's repeated statements against it. The intervention is shaped entirely by what Willis had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we have received advice that there is value in amending the Act to signal a greater focus on price stability than that which could be achieved through a new remit alone"

acuity.statement: Because I totally appreciate—as she herself alluded to—that the remit review in June 2023 spoke to the need for prioritisation of explicitly that dual mandate and particularly the foreshadowing or the primacy of the price stability focus. But again, my point was that that could be achieved through a change to the remit, as again was recommended by her officials.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick follows Woods' line of questioning about what advice the Minister sought on alternatives to repeal, and takes up the same strand — that the policy aim could be achieved by another mechanism (a remit change rather than a statutory secondary objective). But she is mainly pursuing her own previously-put questions rather than engaging Woods' specific point about international best practice and the dual mandate comparators, so this is partial engagement with the topic and the adjacent strand, not with the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "did she ask for any advice around having employment as a secondary objective within the legislation"

acuity.statement: In answer to the member’s question: yes, I did receive advice that the dual mandate could affect monetary policy decisions, and in particular—as I have stressed—this is not just about the decisions the Reserve Bank makes but also the interpretation of those decisions. The Reserve Bank itself has supported the intention of clarifying its focus on inflation.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up one of the three questions just put to her — the evidence/advice on whether the dual mandate affected Reserve Bank decision making — and supplies a direct answer to it, adding the interpretation point and the Bank's own position. The speech would be different had the preceding turn not pressed on advice. But she leaves untouched the two strands Swarbrick flagged as outstanding (what the remit will contain, and whether employment or house prices feature in it), so engagement is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "the evidence that she has on whether there has been any meaningful impact on decision making by the RBNZ"

acuity.statement: When the Minister spoke before, she used the words “could” and “would be possible that it might happen”. That’s not, Mr Chair, with respect, what I asked. What I asked was whether or not the Minister had been advised that there had been some kind of impact, and the answer is no.
acuity.explanation: This takes the Minister's immediately preceding words and does something specific with them: it isolates her modal verbs ("could", "possible"), distinguishes an advised possibility from an advised actual effect, and draws the consequence that no evidence of actual impact was received. The speech is wholly contingent on what Willis just said — a different answer would have required a different reply. Scored on engagement only; the soundness of the inference and the truth of the characterisation are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "yes, I did receive advice that the dual mandate could affect monetary policy decisions"

acuity.statement: I just want to move, second, to the question of the content of the remit and the charter. I want to assure the member Chlöe Swarbrick that we will retain the flexible inflation targeting regime under which the response of the Reserve Bank to inflation is tempered by considering the impact on other factors in the real economy. I will publish an updated remit and charter upon passage of this Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Swarbrick's first question directly — what survives in the remit as opposed to the statute — and commits to publishing the updated remit, so the passage would read differently had she not asked it. But it answers the remit question only in general terms (flexible inflation targeting retained) without saying where employment or house price sustainability sit, and leaves her second and third questions (evidence of deprioritised price stability; who the market participants are) untouched. Partial, pointable engagement, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but the question still remains as to whether she thinks it should be within the broader monetary policy committee’s remit" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: But have they? That’s the question you’re not answering. Why don’t you answer the question—have they?
acuity.explanation: Pins the exact gap in the sentence just spoken: Willis moved from 'have they been in conflict' to the modal 'could move in opposite directions', and this interjection isolates that slip and demands the factual answer. It could not have been delivered against any other wording, which is the test. Short, and pointed at the content rather than the person.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "often the objectives of price stability and maximum sustainable employment will align. However, the objectives could move in opposite directions" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: So reducing the possibility of volatility—Mrs Woods—in future rates of inflation is actually a priority for this Government.
acuity.explanation: Woods asked whether the two objectives have in fact been in conflict. This acknowledges her by name and answers a different question — the Government's priorities — restating the general position rather than supplying the historical instance asked for. On the topic under debate, but engages no part of the challenge, which puts it in the low band rather than at a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But have they? That’s the question you’re not answering." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Finally, I want to note that there are a number of amendments that have been tabled and suggested by the member Hon Grant Robertson, who can’t seem to make up his mind what the purpose of the Reserve Bank Act has been, because I can count several different ideas he has, which is rather symptomatic of the member—that he couldn’t just land on one thing.
acuity.explanation: Names the amendments and their mover but engages the content of none of them — no clause, no mechanism, no reason any one of them fails. The count of 'several different ideas' is turned into a character observation and then a pivot to the Government's own line, which is the mere-reference pattern rather than engagement. Scored low for unresponsiveness only; whether the remark is fair or well-reasoned belongs to other attributes, which I have not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I still have a few points that I’d like the Minister to address" — the amendments referred to were tabled by Grant Robertson, whose only preceding turn in this window is a point of order; nothing in the preceding debate content is taken up.

acuity.statement: But this links back to why I’m standing in the Chamber and wanting to ask the Minister a question; it’s around perceptions. And so there is a perception, sometimes—by this Government, who has only just started—that there are a couple of failings in the rest of society. And yet when you go out into a community and you talk to these people within this society—both teachers and principals and families, and again, in some of the lowest socio-economic areas of the country—the perception that they might hold might actually be very different to the truth that is being held by those within that community.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds expressly picks up the previous speaker's turn and takes up one strand of it — White's argument that the Government should bust misconceptions rather than legislate to them. She develops the perception/truth distinction with her own material and later anchors it in paragraph 7 of the regulatory impact statement, but she does not engage White's central claim about maximum sustainable employment and the hierarchy inside that term, and most of the speech is prepared material (prize-givings, cross-country inflation comparisons) on her own chosen line of attack. Partial engagement: the strand engaged is pointable, the specific argument is not rebutted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I do take on board that there is an issue raised about the perception of others" — Helen White

acuity.statement: The amendment goes to the heart of what we object to in this bill. If I was to be really cynical, I’d say that the Government doesn’t care about people who don’t work, but they say they care about people who do work. The amendment restores the purpose of this monetary policy, and it would be to take out, remove in clause 7, the word “objective” and replace it with “welfare of working people”.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor follows two substantive turns but engages neither. He opens by noting he was absent the previous night and moves straight to his own tabled amendment to clause 7, delivering prepared material that would be word-for-word the same whatever Edmonds or White had argued. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the purpose clause of this bill — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but there is no point in it where the preceding argument is picked up, conceded, or rebutted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued that the evidence shows no relationship between a dual mandate and inflation, citing New Zealand, Australia and Sweden, and asked what evidence-based advice the Minister had received; this statement does not take any of that up.

The reply would have to change if O'Connor had argued something else; it is squarely aimed at his premise rather than at the topic in general. Brief and dismissive in tone, but tone is not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "then it must incorporate some reference to the people of New Zealand, not just to price stability"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued that the bill's purpose clause already promotes the prosperity and wellbeing of New Zealanders, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a prepared line of questioning on employment in Part 2 and refers back to unanswered questions from the Part 1 debate instead.

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, my colleague the Hon Grant Robertson, has indicated, the objective now has been changed through the passing of Part 1 of the bill, but in Part 2 there are a number of amendments, and given that now it is being narrowed down to that sole objective of the Reserve Bank, in Part 2 we have the opportunity—what measures are we going to put in place to ensure that employment is something that is still on the radar of the Reserve Bank?

acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "would the Minister consider that within those sections, there is scope to at least give the opportunity for the Reserve Bank to be able to speak more about employment"

acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question Woods asked — international best practice for a single-objective central bank, and the mechanism by which line of sight to employment survives — by naming flexible inflation targeting and the committee's continuing regard for the real economy. The content is determined by what was just put to her; a different question would have produced a different answer.

acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "has she received advice about international best practice when it comes to a central bank with a single objective—how it is that they can ensure that that line of sight is kept into employment?"

acuity.explanation: Russell follows Willis but engages no part of her argument — neither the Schedule 3 appointment provision, nor the charge that Labour has abandoned economic orthodoxy, nor the claim that the 2021 Act Robertson oversaw contradicts Woods' question. Her material is demonstrably prepared independently of it: a constituent's letter received over the preceding days, read in support of an Amendment Paper already tabled. Substituting a different Willis argument on the same topic would leave this speech word-for-word identical, which is the deciding test. It scores above 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it stays on the bill's actual subject, arguing for retaining both limbs of the dual mandate — the very question in contest — and so could not have been delivered in an unrelated debate. The lack of a select committee stage and the quality of the constituent's reasoning are not Acuity matters.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued that appointing a union rep would be "a significant departure from the Reserve Bank as it was presided over by the former Minister of Finance, the Hon Grant Robertson" and cited Schedule 3, clause 20 on appointment criteria; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The only answer we’ve had from the Minister has been to say, “Well, we’re not having a union member, because under your Government and under Grant Robertson, you wouldn’t have one either.” But the mere fact of the matter that we had a dual mandate made that not as necessary.

She engages one strand of what was said and then returns to her prepared amendment material, which puts her in the mid band rather than at the top.

acuity.responding_to: "we’re not having a union member, because under your Government and under Grant Robertson, you wouldn’t have one either" — Nicola Willis, the Minister's answer in the committee, quoted back by Woods

acuity.explanation: This gestures at the subject Woods raised (scrutiny and review) but engages no part of her argument about losing sight of employment; it pivots immediately to the record of the member's own government. A reference plus a counter-attack on the previous speaker's record is a glance at the debate, not an engagement with the claim.

acuity.responding_to: "My question for the Minister, if she is not going to support this amendment, is: what mechanisms will be in place to ensure that there can be scrutiny" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: In specific reference to member Woods’ proposal to review the Act, there is already a post-implementation review of the Act due by 2027.
acuity.explanation: This takes the specific amendment just moved and does something with it: it answers the proposed three-year independent review by stating that a post-implementation review is already due by 2027. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a new clause 14, to insert the following new section, which is a review of the Act" / "will be reviewed by an independent expert panel after three years of entry into force" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: So you’ll know that the Hon Megan Woods has proposed an amendment which would, effectively, allow someone with a focus on unemployment and the effect that would have on working people to contribute to monetary policy. And I think it’s relevant since this bill has not had a stage in select committee to turn to some of the submissions by people who would fit that bill—who have expertise and the experience of working people.
acuity.explanation: Robertson's immediately preceding turn argued that, with the dual mandate removed, Part 2 and the Woods amendment were the route to keeping a worker/employment voice in monetary policy. Mid-band, not top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that was the purpose of Dr Woods’ amendment, to find a way of doing that" — Grant Robertson

acuity.explanation: Robertson put a specific question: if not these amendments to section 131, what mechanism will ensure the Reserve Bank regularly reports the trade-offs of a single mandate. The reply would have had to be different had Robertson argued something else; it is aimed at his actual request rather than at the topic in general. Short of 1.0 because she does not engage his concrete example (Wheeler's 2013-14 tightening) or the particular trade-off/employment content his amendment would mandate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "So I ask the Minister again: if not these amendments, then what will she be doing to ensure that the Reserve Bank reports and reviews regularly the trade-offs that it's now going to have to make?"
