acuity.explanation: Edmonds' complaint was that passing the bill under urgency without a select committee removed her ability to scrutinise it and question the Governor on the mandates; Willis takes up that specific grievance and answers it with the ongoing Finance and Expenditure Committee avenue. It engages the scrutiny strand rather than the substantive flexibility question, so not a full 1.0, but it is clearly shaped by what Edmonds said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "Those are the types of assurance, in the absence of a select committee, that I would like to seek from the Minister."

acuity.statement: Let me say, again: the purpose of this Act is to give crystal clarity of the objective of the monetary policy committee (MPC), which is to ensure price stability. None of that precludes the matters that are set out in section 123 and section 125 whereby the remit may specify the matters the monetary policy committee has regard to in pursuing that one clear objective. So there are other matters that they can have regard to, but they must pursue the one clear objective. I will be publishing the remit upon passage of this Act.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds asked specifically where flexibility would come from once the dual mandate is removed, and when the remit would appear. Willis answers the mechanism question by name — sections 123 and 125 let the remit specify what the MPC has regard to while price stability remains the single objective — and commits to publishing the remit on passage. The reply would be different had Edmonds asked something else, which is the test; its accuracy and the strength of the inference are separate questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "what are the other ways in which the Minister, other than the remit, because I know the Minister has said that the remit will come after this legislation—but, actually, I want the Minister to provide some assurances now to the New Zealand public around how will the Minister continue to take that flexible approach"

acuity.statement: Really, this is simply an example of the Opposition attempting to fulfil the very thing that the Minister has said she supports. That is the idea that there should be flexibility in what the Reserve Bank does when it’s considering the setting of monetary policy. But we are adding to that some specificity about the kinds of things they can consider.
acuity.explanation: Robertson follows Helen White, who asked why the Minister is rejecting the employment-related amendments and what she means by "orthodoxy". He takes up one strand of that — he sets out and argues for the specific amendments she referred to, framing them as consistent with the Minister's own stated position on flexibility — but he engages nothing of her central question about orthodoxy, austerity and the role of monetary versus fiscal policy, and the bulk of the turn is prepared advocacy for two amendments that would read the same whatever she had argued. Partial engagement on the same strand, hence mid-low rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "why she seems to be rejecting these very important amendments which seek to commit to something which I think is a value we should universally hold"

acuity.statement: We believe that that is consistent with the purpose of the Act, in that, without price stability, all of the other good things that the Opposition seeks cannot be achieved. Price stability is the foundation on which employment and good economic conditions sits.
acuity.explanation: Willis directly takes up the specific claim Robertson had just made — that reducing the Reserve Bank to a single objective leaves the objectives unable to fulfil the Act's purpose — and rebuts it on its own terms, arguing a single price-stability objective is consistent with that purpose because price stability is the precondition for the employment outcomes the amendments seek. The reply would have to change if Robertson had argued something else; it is not a mere reference to him. Scored on engagement only, not on whether the economic premise is sound or on her separate point that nothing precludes these matters from the remit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "I think there is a serious issue now with the Act, which is that the objectives no longer fulfil the purposes of the Act"

acuity.statement: It would not be appropriate to add a new economic objective in the remit. This is not secondary legislation. Legislation is the proper place to set out the objectives, which this bill does. There was one objective: price stability.
acuity.explanation: Woods explicitly anticipated that the Minister would say the protection could go in the remit and challenged her to say what the legislative provisions would be. Willis takes that exact strand up and answers it on its own terms — the remit is the wrong instrument, legislation is where objectives sit, and the objective here is singular. The reply would be different if Woods had framed her challenge differently, so engagement is real and specific. It is held below the top band because Woods also asked, repeatedly, what advice she received and what options were accepted or discounted, and that part of the argument is left entirely untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m anticipating that the Minister may say that she’ll put it in the remit, but what about the legislation?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: We’ve usefully had from the Minister of Finance a contribution around the amendments that this side of the Chamber has put up to Part 2, which seek to clarify the role of the monetary policy committee in its view towards the effect of unemployment. However, the Minister has indicated that she will not be accepting those amendments, and I think that’s a problem, because we still have a purpose clause which was introduced in the 2019 amendment to the principal Act.
acuity.explanation: Willis had just asserted that legislation is the proper place for the objectives and that this bill does that job, with price stability as the single objective. Williams takes that claim and turns it against itself: if the amendments are refused, the 2019 purpose clause survives in the principal Act and the statute will carry two objectives at odds, so the bill does not in fact settle the objectives in legislation. That is engaging the content of the Minister's answer and drawing out its consequence, not merely naming her. Short of 1.0 because the turn then moves into prepared material on Graeme Wheeler and the global financial crisis that is indifferent to what Willis said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Legislation is the proper place to set out the objectives, which this bill does." — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: To save members their time, we will not be changing the commencement date. This is a Government that is getting on with it. After six years of dithering, delay, working groups, task forces, hot air, talk, good intentions, and no delivery, New Zealanders have elected a Government with a mandate to get the cost of living under control, to put price stability back as the core objective for the Reserve Bank. This bill does it, and we’re getting on with it.
acuity.explanation: Robertson explicitly asked the member in charge whether she would accept an amended commencement date, and Willis answers that one strand squarely and immediately — no, the date will not change. But she engages nothing of the substance he put: the contention that no evidence was produced that the dual mandate cost focus on inflation, the Governor's statements to the contrary, the offer of either an expert-review trigger or 1 December 2026. She pivots instead to prepared material on the previous government's record, which would have been identical whatever argument Robertson had made. One strand taken up, the reasoning untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "So I would like to hear from the member in charge of the bill whether or not she believes that this is something that would be sensible."

acuity.statement: I’m disappointed to hear from the Minister that she won’t be considering the amendments in the name of Grant Robertson to the commencement date. However, I have proposed in my name an amendment to the commencement date for a completely different reason, and I hope she’ll consider it.
acuity.explanation: Williams takes up the Minister's refusal in the turn immediately before hers and does something with it: she concedes it, distinguishes her own amendment as resting on a different ground (the lag between monetary policy committee decisions and effects in the real economy), and turns the Minister's own contention — that a further focus on fighting inflation is needed — into the thing a delayed commencement would test. The speech would have had to change had Willis accepted the amendment or argued for the date on other grounds. Short of 1.0 because much of what follows is prepared material on her clause 1 and clause 4 amendments rather than continued engagement with the Minister's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "To save members their time, we will not be changing the commencement date."

acuity.statement: Our job when we are in the House is to accurately describe legislation. If I was describing this piece of legislation accurately, I would say that this is the “Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Putting At Risk People’s Jobs) Bill”, because that is, essentially, what has happened here.
acuity.explanation: Williams' preceding turn argued that the bill's name matters and that she would have proposed changing it at select committee. Robertson takes up that one strand — the accuracy of the title — and supplies his own alternative titles, so the speech is shaped by what preceded it. But he engages none of her central argument (that elevating a secondary-legislation tool to primary legislation removed the only check and balance, and that debate was shut down), and the bulk of his call is prepared material on the 2019 amendment, Graeme Wheeler and the purposes clause. Partial engagement with the topic and one strand of the argument rather than the argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the name of this bill is really important and would have been important to the select committee's process if it were to have occurred" — Arena Williams

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued the commencement date should be delayed (18 months or 2026) on the strength of the Treasury regulatory impact statement's footnote about continuing monetary policy uncertainty and the absence of a statutory review, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: I want to recap on two questions I asked the Minister last night that I have not had an answer to. The first of those is a very specific question on whether or not the Minister has had advice that there was anything in the dual mandate that caused the Reserve Bank to take its focus off reducing inflation. I asked that question twice last night and I haven't had an answer.
acuity.explanation: Robertson follows a substantive turn by Williams on the very same point — whether the dual mandate affected the Reserve Bank's inflation focus — yet engages no part of what she said. He explicitly frames his call as a recap of his own two questions from the previous night and a pitch for his own Amendment Paper. The speech is squarely within the debate on Part 1 and clause 4, so it is not wholly unresponsive to the matter under debate, but it would have been word-for-word identical had Williams said something different, or nothing at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that "Had the Reserve Bank been operating under a straight inflation-targeting objective in recent years, it would not have had a different outcome" and put a specific question to the Minister about the November 2021 Monetary Policy Statement; this statement does not take up her contention or her question.

acuity.statement: And I have to say, was it a low point in Mr Robertson’s career when he used a filibuster in the House today to question whether the Governor-General should really be able to offer assent to bills at all? It felt like a bit of a low point to me.
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn was Robertson's argument that, given urgency and the absence of select committee scrutiny, clause 2's commencement date puts whoever grants Royal assent in a difficult position, and that amendments on the Table offer alternatives. Willis names that argument but does nothing with it: she neither defends the use of urgency, nor addresses the constitutional-importance point, nor engages the proposed commencement amendments. The reference is used as a springboard to an ad hominem ('a low point in Mr Robertson's career'), which the rubric treats as a mere reference rather than engagement. On topic, so not 0.0; no part of the content answered, so not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "The other matter that I believe would be given serious consideration as to whether Royal assent should be granted is the fact that this bill has gone through under urgency."

acuity.statement: There have been questions in this House about why we would amend the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. Confused questions, because some members have sort of been saying this is a terrible, awful bill—and we had the former member for Wellington Central waxing lyrical about the 1980s and 1990s; we got to occupy that part of his mind that lives in the past—but then we also had them saying that the bill would have no effect whatsoever. Well, the fact is this: without amending the Act, the monetary policy committee would still be required to have regard to maximum sustainable employment.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one strand of the opposition case running through the preceding turn — that the bill's stated purpose and reasoning are unsupported — and supplies an actual reason the amendment is needed: absent it, the monetary policy committee must still have regard to maximum sustainable employment. That is engagement with content, not just a reference. But it answers a different form of the objection ('the bill would have no effect') rather than the specific claim Robertson pressed, which was that no evidence was ever produced that the dual mandate took the bank's eye off inflation; on that she offers nothing, and the passage then returns to prepared material. Partial engagement, so mid-band rather than 1.0.

acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "we never heard evidence. So the actual purpose and reasoning of the bill is not supported with a commencement date as currently listed in clause 2."

acuity.statement: It is now many hours on from this legislation being introduced under urgency late last night, and I got to say I still am kind of left quite puzzled in the absence of any meaningful evidence as to the purpose of this very legislation.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick takes up one strand of the turn immediately before hers — Robertson's central charge that the Government produced no evidence that the bill is necessary — and carries it forward, later supplying the verbatim Adrian Orr select committee answer that Robertson had only gestured at ("The Reserve Bank Governor himself told us that"). That much is genuine engagement: the opening would read differently had Robertson argued something else about the bill. But it is explicitly prepared material — she announces she is restating "once again for the nth time the three reasons as to why the Green Party oppose this legislation" — and the bulk of the speech (GDP, Monopoly, Paul Hawken, the tax system, capital gains tax) engages nothing Robertson said. Partial engagement with a return to prepared content sits at ~0.5. Scored only on engagement: the quality of the inference, the truth of the Orr quotation and the drift onto tax policy belong to Rigor, Veracity and Focus respectively and are deliberately not reflected here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "no evidence has been presented that this piece of legislation is necessary"

acuity.statement: New Zealand First rises to support this bill in its third reading, probably in fewer words than the previous speaker, but we do endorse Mr Seymour’s comments.
acuity.explanation: Patterson follows a long, argument-dense speech by Seymour (the dual mandate as 'one lever pulled in two directions', the claim that markets will price in a credible single mandate, the charge that the Opposition's position is self-contradictory) and takes up none of it. He names the previous speaker, jokes about his length, and endorses him wholesale, then delivers prepared New Zealand First material on the cost of living, Governor Orr's 'monetary policy needs mates' remark and confidence in Minister Willis. The nearest echo — 'it's also a signal to the markets' — restates a theme Seymour raised without engaging his reasoning for it, adding nothing to and disputing nothing in it. Substitute a different pro-bill speech by any other coalition member before this and it would be word-for-word unchanged apart from the name; that is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.

acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Hon David Seymour argued that by making the monetary policy objective unambiguous, 'people are going to start pricing in, that a new sherrif is in town and inflation is going to the wall', and that the Opposition cannot square having introduced a dual mandate that it now says made no difference. Patterson endorses 'Mr Seymour's comments' as a bloc without taking up either strand.

acuity.statement: This bill is not likely to make any substantial difference to inflation in and of itself. There is absolutely no reason to believe it would make a difference to inflation.
acuity.explanation: Genter follows Waititi's third-reading speech and takes up one strand of it — his claim that there is no economic evidence linking the employment mandate to inflation — restating it as a claim about the bill and then supplying supporting material (the global CPI comparison, which she notes she had already presented the previous night). She does not engage his other arguments (urgency, widening the bank's mandate) and the bulk of the speech is prepared material on neoliberalism, donors and landlords that would have been delivered whatever Waititi said. Partial engagement on a pointable strand, then a return to prepared ground.

acuity.responding_to: "There is no economic evidence that the employment mandate has contributed to inflation over the past two years" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: I don’t buy into the rhetoric that exudes out of the Opposition members conveying that this bill will result in worse outcomes for Māori and Pasifika communities. I don’t see it as a cause of mass unemployment like they say. In fact, I strongly believe that this bill will deliver exactly the opposite.

He does gesture at the wider debate by naming an Opposition line (worse outcomes for Māori and Pasifika, mass unemployment), but only to dismiss it with assertion rather than engaging its content, and that line was not put in the turn he follows. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate: 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Catherine Wedd spoke about bringing back aspiration and confidence and the bill being a first step on the cost of living, and this statement does not take up any part of it.

acuity.statement: Now, one of the things with this bill that we’ve seen is that the Minister of Finance knows that this is not actually going to achieve that much. So when I hear some of those new members of Parliament saying that this is how they’re going to crack down on inflation, they’re going to be sorely let down.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the exact claim the two preceding new members made — that this bill is how inflation gets tackled — names it as theirs, and does something with it: she argues the Minister knows it achieves little, and goes on to supply the Reserve Bank's own forecast and the three alternative routes officials offered. Had the previous speakers argued something else about the bill, this passage would have had to change. Not a full 1.0 because she addresses the general inflation claim rather than any specific figure or reasoning either member gave, and she quickly rejoins prepared material about the three-bill package.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is a solid start to tackling inflation and reducing the cost of living for everyday Kiwis and businesses" — Catherine Wedd (and MacLeod's "this bill will deliver exactly the opposite" of unemployment)

acuity.statement: I am pleased to be speaking again on the third reading of this bill. I could speak at length about the benefits of this bill, but I’m not going to. The affirmative points have been plentiful, and all I need to say is that I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Directly follows a detailed critique — the forecast of inflation returning to 1-3 percent regardless, and the three options put to the Minister — and engages none of it, explicitly declining to argue at all. The words would be identical whatever Woods had said. It is at least tied to this bill's third reading rather than transplantable to any debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued the bill is virtue-signalling legislation that will not change the inflation track the Reserve Bank already forecasts, and that officials offered a remit or Order in Council instead, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: But I’m just going to make a very brief riposte to what we just heard. This bill is actually about fixing the economy, which is what we went into the election on and what people voted for the coalition Government to do. This is about helping all New Zealanders, particularly poor New Zealanders who inflation hits the hardest, and it’s the thief in the pocket.

acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "it is not the case that these population groups would be better off under a fair pay agreement"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just wanted to continue the train of thought that I was on when my last call ended, which was, similar to my colleague Ricardo Menéndez March, talking about some of the voices that we would’ve heard from, had we had a select committee process on this issue.
acuity.explanation: She follows a substantive turn by Menéndez March that put a specific question about overseas evidence for sector-wide bargaining and the absence of a transition period. Her speech names him and gestures at a shared theme, but it does not engage any part of his argument — it continues the prepared account of select committee submissions she was already delivering, and would read identically whatever he had said. On topic (Part 1 of the repeal) and so not 0.0, but a mere reference is not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "did she use international evidence and impact overseas of sector-wide bargaining to inform the arguments" — this statement names him but does not take up his evidence question; it resumes her own prepared material on submissions.

acuity.statement: I was very much enjoying the contribution of the member Camilla Belich, and if anyone was interested in the other submissions that came through, they can refer to my second reading speech; I don’t need to repeat those. But I also wanted to just touch on her earlier question about how we will improve conditions for people in our economy.
acuity.explanation: She identifies the preceding speaker's material and her earlier question, so something is pointable: she replies to the submissions point by directing listeners to her second reading speech, and acknowledges the conditions question. But she engages no content of the submissions Belich read out (disabled workers, health and safety, the impact on women) and answers the conditions question with a promise of future delivery rather than substance. Partial engagement that pivots to prepared assurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "it’s a pity, in my view, that they didn’t get the opportunity to submit again on this repeal bill" — and her earlier question about improving conditions, which van Velden names.

acuity.statement: So it’s not correct to say that there isn’t a regulatory impact statement. The regulatory impact statement from 2021 still well and truly applies, and within that regulatory impact statement they did not actually recommend that we had a fair pay agreements system.
acuity.explanation: She takes the specific factual premise of the question put to her — that there is no regulatory impact statement — reads the cover sheet and Treasury exemption wording that bears on it, and corrects the premise directly, then turns the document back against the questioner's position. The speech could not have been delivered against a different argument; it is built on the one made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford, as she states the question: "what evidence base we have for this bill given that we don’t have a regulatory impact statement".

acuity.statement: So what we are seeing here proposed is that instead of an organisation that employees and employers can associate to, they are proposing to replace it with the Labour Inspector. My concern being, of course, is that is one moving from organisations that are self-funded—through members; through associations—to one that is funded by the State.
acuity.explanation: He follows a substantive turn in which the Minister answered questions on the evidence base and on labour-market flexibility. His contribution engages neither: it is a self-contained clause-level reading of the replacement of section 224(1)(a) and the shift from member-funded bodies to a State-funded Labour Inspector. The material is squarely about Part 1, so not wholly out of place, but it would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, and there is no gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just argued that the 2021 regulatory impact statement still applies and that individual and collective agreements are more flexible than fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member Camilla Belich for asking why we are all here. What is the purpose for us being here tonight? It’s within the bill and it’s our reason for being here, which is that we are here to repeal the Fair Pay Agreements Act. She asks why that purpose is not explicitly written. The Parliamentary Counsel Office have advised that it’s not standard practice in drafting a repeal bill to include a purpose clause, because the purpose of a repeal bill is to repeal a bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific question — why the bill has no purpose clause — restates it accurately and supplies a substantive answer (PCO drafting advice that repeal bills do not carry purpose clauses). The speech would have had to be different had Belich raised a different objection, and it also picks up Menéndez March's amendment question raised in the same turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "The first is: why isn’t there a purpose clause in this document and why isn’t there more detail about what it seeks to achieve?"

acuity.statement: The reason why we have put in this specific amendment, which is to replace section 132(2) of the Employment Relations Act, is to return to the status quo from before we had the fair pay agreements. It was only during the process of the Fair Pay Agreements Act that this provision for overtime rate payments and the penalty rate payments was introduced into the law, and so, by removing this, we are going back to the status quo.
acuity.explanation: Engages the precise point just put — the replacement of section 132(2) and the loss of the overtime and penalty rate wording — and rebuts its premise by explaining the change is deliberate rather than a drafting error, since the wording was itself inserted by the Fair Pay Agreements Act. It leaves Belich's separate complaint about doing this under urgency untouched, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I think that the amendment that I’ve tabled corrects a mistake in the drafting of this bill."

acuity.statement: I wanted to follow up on the previous member’s contributions around analysis in relation to this bill, and specifically whether a child impact assessment was requested or had been considered at any point.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes up Webb's strand about the absence of analysis supporting the repeal and extends it to a specific missing document (a child impact assessment), tying it to child poverty targets. That is a real engagement with the preceding argument rather than a mere reference, but it uses Webb's point as a springboard into his own prepared material on child poverty and youth wages rather than engaging Webb's specific cost-benefit demand itself — so partial, not full, responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "by the ACT Party’s own principles of legislative quality, an analysis should be done of the costs and benefits of this legislation"

acuity.statement: We have absolutely no sight over them, so anything could be in them—and it really goes to the point of whether there’s been any analysis here, how much of the problem—of low pay, bad terms and conditions, unsafe conditions—do we really know exists.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the cost-benefit-analysis complaint made earlier in the debate and supplies a supporting reason for it — that no data on individual agreements is collected, so the scale of the problem is unknown and an analysis could not have been done properly. That is a pointable engagement with one strand of the preceding argument, but most of the turn is prepared material on her own new clause 8, the industries she has represented and her own union experience, which would read the same whatever had preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "What I want to know is what analysis has been done of the costs and the benefits of having fair pay agreements on the one hand"

acuity.statement: As I said before, under the previous system, they have not experienced better, and now, in 2023, they get to operate under another piece of legislation, which is about to be repealed by this House without even being given a chance to succeed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of van Velden's reasoning — she used the fact that no fair pay agreement was ever in effect to dismiss a review amendment, and Rurawhe turns that same fact against repeal, arguing the law is being removed before it could be tested. He also implicitly engages her "I will then focus my efforts on to next steps" by saying there is no vision for these workers' future. But the bulk of the speech is prepared material on clause 5 and Rosey Ngakopu that would stand unchanged whatever the Minister had said, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal of her argument's structure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Because there have not been any fair pay agreements in effect, it would be impossible to review what a system that had never been in place would look like after three years"

acuity.statement: My question goes to: what evidence does the Minister have that small-business owners do not want to sign up to something that is better than the minimum wage and that indeed sets minimum standards across their industries?
acuity.explanation: The question goes straight at the premise van Velden had just asserted — that industry-wide minimum standards harm businesses and therefore workers and families — and demands the evidence base for it, from the standpoint of a small-business owner. That is engaging the specific claim, not just the topic, and the question would have to be different had the Minister argued on other grounds. It falls short of 1.0 because the preceding material is a long prepared autobiographical passage, and her opening nod to Adrian Rurawhe is a reference rather than an engagement with his argument; the responsiveness is concentrated in the closing question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "I consider that the fair pay agreements system is a blunt tool that affects all employees and all employers within scope within a particular industry, and that would negatively impact on businesses"

acuity.statement: Now, if we talk about increasing productivity, this has been the rationale of those on the right for as long as anyone in this House can remember—for as long as anyone in this House can remember: if only we can increase productivity, then workers would be better off. The problem with that, of course, is that productivity is linked to wages, and there is a reason why Australia and other countries that follow what was in place in the Fair Pay Agreements Act—the Act that this bill, in Part 2, seeks to repeal—have higher productivity: the two go hand in hand. Since 1991, New Zealand’s productivity has not kept up with other countries that have maintained what is in the Fair Pay Agreements Act.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn in this window is Carmel Sepuloni's demand to know the productivity losses flowing from repealing fair pay agreements. McAnulty takes up that same productivity strand and develops it — arguing productivity and wages are causally linked and citing comparator countries — but he directs his engagement at the Minister's earlier answer to Adrian Rurawhe rather than at Sepuloni's specific cover-sheet question, and then moves into his own prepared material on deregulation and the Act's purpose clause. Partial engagement: one strand of the preceding contribution is clearly picked up and argued with, the specific demand put is not answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "I want to know what the productivity loss will be for those workforces because of the fact that we do not have fair pay agreements in place"

acuity.statement: Fair pay agreements (FPAs) are a key lever to reduce the gender pay gap. The new generation of women deserve equal pay for work. The gender pay gap will not close itself. We cannot become complacent, because the gap will not close without sustained and intentional actions. How will the Minister mitigate the disproportionate impact of stagnant lower wages for women without FPA?
acuity.explanation: This follows a substantive turn by Kieran McAnulty arguing that productivity and wages go hand in hand and that the Government has offered no tangible alternative to fair pay agreements. Carter's contribution is prepared material on the gender pay gap — Ministry for Women advice, historical gap figures, Kate Sheppard — ending in a question to the Minister. It is squarely on the matter under debate (the effect of repealing fair pay agreements on wages), but it engages no part of the argument immediately preceding it; the speech would read identically whatever McAnulty had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued that productivity is linked to wages and that the Minister has offered only "a theory and a loose promise" in place of fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: But, specifically, you asked what evidence I have that small businesses don’t actually want to sign up for this type of agreement. When the Fair Pay Agreements Bill went through Parliament, under the previous term of Government, there was quite a substantial select committee process, and many small-business owners did make submissions against the law change.
acuity.explanation: She names the specific question put to her and then supplies the evidence it asked for — the select committee submissions, one of which she goes on to quote. The reply would be different if a different question had been asked, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only; whether the submission actually supports the repeal is a veracity matter and whether the inference from one submitter to the sector holds is a rigor matter, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Darleen Tana, whose question the Minister reproduces in taking it up: "you asked what evidence I have that small businesses don’t actually want to sign up for this type of agreement" (the question was put in an earlier turn of the same committee debate, which is identified in this turn rather than reproduced in this window)

acuity.statement: But we don’t consider, as a Government, that we wish to have any exemptions to the repeal, because we believe that there is a better way to improve the conditions of workers, for business and employees, without having fair pay agreements, and that is through increased productivity; that is through reducing regulation.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific amendment — an exemption from the repeal for an industry already negotiating — and gives a reason for refusing it rather than restating the bill's purpose. Not a full 1.0 because she answers the class of exemption amendments generally and does not engage the security-guard case on its own terms; she concedes his premise about good employers and disputes the remedy. Agreement on part and disagreement on the rest is engagement, and the disagreement does not lower the score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe, whose amendment the Minister states and then answers: "He talked about proposing an amendment to allow for security guards to conclude the fair pay agreement" (moved in an earlier turn of this committee debate, identified here rather than reproduced in this window)

acuity.statement: It was very difficult to listen to the contribution from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, because I have to say it was rather patronising.
acuity.explanation: A reference to the preceding speaker that engages none of her content. The productivity-and-deregulation argument was squarely available to rebut and is left untouched; this sentence would read identically whatever the Minister had argued, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it at least gestures at the contribution just made in the same debate. Scored on responsiveness alone — the dismissive framing is a civility question and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden argued immediately before that no exemptions to the repeal are warranted because conditions are better lifted through increased productivity and reduced regulation, and this statement does not take up any part of that — it characterises the manner of her contribution and then turns to the amendments on the Table.

acuity.statement: Coming back to the member: because she’s asked for it to be specifically about statistical data in relation to those specific areas that we’d already touched on that does not actually exist, that question is not possible to answer.
acuity.explanation: Van Velden breaks off her prepared run-through to take up Sepuloni's interjected question directly, and gives a reason for her answer — that the underlying data for the sectors just discussed does not exist, so the question cannot be answered. The reply would not exist if Sepuloni had not interjected, which is strong evidence of engagement. It is short of 1.0 because she assimilates the productivity-loss question to the earlier coverage-statistics question rather than engaging the productivity point on its own terms, so one strand is answered and the specific claim is reframed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What's the productivity loss to not having fair pay agreements, is my other part of it." — Carmel Sepuloni (interjection)

acuity.statement: I live in Ōtepoti—Dunedin—and for years bus companies have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of wages, with drivers working split shifts and often engaging in second jobs just to put food on the table. Dunedin bus drivers have even had to pee behind bushes and limit their water intake—not like in the Chamber—so that they can keep at work because there are no toilets. So the Minister might argue that repealing fair pay is just tidying things up, but I'd argue that it's far tidier and healthier to provide good conditions and support bus drivers in Aotearoa rather than encouraging them to head to Australia.
acuity.explanation: Willis follows two substantive Opposition turns and takes up one strand of them: Jackson's claim that bus drivers are quitting because conditions are intolerable, and Andersen's "race to the bottom" framing, which he extends with Dunedin evidence of split shifts and no toilets. He does not engage Jackson's actual question (what consultation the Minister has had) or Andersen's specific clause 8 review proposal, and the second half moves to his own prepared question about Australian pay rates. Partial, pointable engagement rather than a rebuttal or direct answer, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's normal for four or five bus drivers to quit each week because the conditions are just too much for them." — Willie Jackson (Ginny Andersen immediately before also warned of a "race to the bottom")

acuity.statement: Well, just to pick up where I was likely to continue previously is that I’ve actually got another proposed amendment. There’s another proposed amendment, and that is a new clause 6, which has been presented to the House. So the new clause 6 that is proposed to amend this bill is that the Royal assent of the bill is contingent on a review by the International Labour Organization (ILO), ensuring that New Zealand is compliant with all international obligations including ILO conventions and free-trade agreements.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows the Minister's reply to her own amendment but engages none of its content: she neither contests the claim that the Minister will commission her own market advice nor the Minister's reason for refusing the amendment. She resumes her prepared sequence of amendments. It is squarely on the bill under debate, and there is a gesture at continuity ("pick up where I was likely to continue previously"), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just answered her directly — "I expect to do my own advice and information on the market, independent from the member, and that does not need to be in this bill" — and this statement does not take that refusal up, moving straight to a further amendment.

acuity.statement: I usually allow a range of members to speak before I respond, but I must respond to that statement. Nobody will be worse off this Christmas because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised. Nobody will be having lower wages because of the repeal of this Act.
acuity.explanation: She breaks her own stated practice of waiting in order to take up the specific claim Andersen had just made, and rebuts it on its own terms with the reason it fails — no fair pay agreement has been concluded, so no worker's pay is reduced by the repeal. The reply would be impossible had the preceding speech said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "that will be earning less this Christmas, that will afford less on their table, fewer Christmas presents"

acuity.statement: The other thing that I do want to ask the Minister again is what is the plan if it doesn’t work? Can we surely put aside the differences that we have fundamentally or philosophically tonight and look at why the Minister wouldn’t support our amendment to ensure that there is a review, that we continue to be proud to grow, as I said, good employers to be great employers; good employees, employees to be able to be looked after; and the most vulnerable are not targeted, because at times that’s how it’s coming across.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of the Minister's position — the commitment-based refusal to vary the repeal — and argues it should not block a review amendment, which does not continue the system for any sector. That is a real engagement with the Minister's stated reason. But she does not touch the claim in the turn immediately before hers (that nobody will be worse off this Christmas), and much of the surrounding material is prepared argument for her own new clause 8, so it is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Allowing the system to continue for one sector would go against the commitment that we brought to this House, but also our commitment to New Zealand voters"

acuity.statement: This is a clawback bill. This bill, to repeal the ground-breaking fair pay agreement legislation in New Zealand, is a clawback for workers, and I disagree wholeheartedly with the Minister’s statement earlier that workers will not be worse off.
acuity.explanation: Boyack follows a substantive turn by van Velden, who argued that a three-year review clause cannot work because no fair pay agreements were ever finalised, that employees need not join a union to be covered, and that repeal avoids engaging international obligations. Boyack takes up none of those three points. She gestures at the debate by contesting a ministerial claim that workers will not be worse off, but that claim was made 'earlier' and not in the turn she follows, and her speech is her prepared case for two amendments she had already tabled. If van Velden had made a different argument on the same clauses, this speech would read identically — hence the low band, with 0.3 rather than 0.1 for the gesture at the Minister's position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden argued 'there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised' and so a review of the repeal's sector impacts 'does not work in practice', and this statement does not take that up — it disputes a ministerial statement made earlier, outside the turn it follows.

acuity.statement: Speaking to the member’s question, no. The policy intent is quite correctly captured by the title of the bill. It’s pretty plain and simple and we have a coalition commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements by Christmas, which is what we intend to do.
acuity.explanation: Boyack put two direct questions to the Minister — will she support the retitling amendment, and will she support the three-year commencement amendment. Van Velden answers the title question squarely ('no') and gives her reason: the existing title captures the policy intent, and the coalition commitment is to repeal by Christmas, which also disposes of the three-year delay. The reply is unmistakably shaped by what was just said and would not exist without it. Short of 1.0 because she engages the amendments' framing rather than Boyack's substantive argument that three years of operation would supply the evidence the Government says it wants.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'will she support a proper title for this bill that properly reflects what the Government is doing here, which is a clawback' — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I would like to also support the amendments of my colleague Rachel Boyack, and, also, I have an amendment in my own name in relation to this part. My amendment really goes to the heart, I think, of the Government’s justification for this bill, which is, essentially, that we’ve had an election and the Government wants to implement their commitments from during the election.
acuity.explanation: Van Velden had just rested her refusal on an electoral mandate — a coalition commitment to repeal by Christmas. Belich names that exact justification as the thing her amendment is aimed at, and then offers a referendum threshold as the way to test whether the mandate is real. The speech is built on the reason the Minister had just given moments before, so substituting a different justification would force it to change. Not 1.0 because she characterises the mandate argument and pivots to her own amendment rather than rebutting its reasoning in detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we have a coalition commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements by Christmas, which is what we intend to do' — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: Just in regard to the title, I appreciate the amendments put by the Labour Party around the change of name. I would probably propose something around “Vibes-based Unfair Pay”. But, in relationship to the commencement, reflecting on some of the previous contributions from the Minister, I hear that she has been saying that this is part of the coalition agreement and that the intent is to pass it before Christmas.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the Labour amendment to the bill's title, which he acknowledges and offers his own alternative name for — and also engages the Minister's earlier stated reasons (coalition agreement, pre-Christmas passage) in order to test them. But it engages neither Belich's mandate amendment nor her GST question, and quickly returns to his own prepared argument about the absence of evidence. Partial engagement that you can point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I also wanted to support my colleague Rachel Boyack’s amendment to the change of the title, which I believe is more correct in the nature of the bill."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just wanted to support the last speaker but also my friend Rachel Boyack’s amendment which was to delay the bill coming into fruition. I think the point needs expanding a little bit because what we have in this situation is very, very little evidence, a lot of hunch about what will happen next.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the immediately preceding speaker's evidence argument and does something with it — converts the complaint about missing evidence into a positive case for a three-year delay as an evidence-gathering exercise, and concedes the Minister's scepticism while arguing the delay would settle it either way. She also takes up the Green speaker's bus-driver example by name and extends it with her own account. The speech would have had to be different had the previous turn argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "Throughout the debate there also has been a lack of ability to produce evidence as to why this must be repealed"

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich, there was a question about GST changes with the employment courts—once again, not relevant to this particular section. However, you might wish to note that while it’s not in the bill specifically in this section, we are retaining the provision. So we are reversing all other changes but retaining this one, so it’s not in the bill.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific answer the preceding turn asked for — explaining that the GST-exclusive provision is retained precisely because the bill is silent on it, which is why Belich could not find it. That is engaging the content of the question rather than merely referring to it. Marked down slightly because the answer is wrapped in a relevance objection rather than fully worked through.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I wonder if the Minister could point me to exactly where those retained amendments are."

acuity.statement: But to the point that was actually about this section, I heard a lot about delay, but this is not a Government that delays; this is a Government of action.
acuity.explanation: Names the topic the previous two speakers argued — delaying commencement to allow an evidence-gathering period — and engages no part of the reasoning for it. The slogan that follows would be identical whatever case for delay had been put, and could be delivered in any debate on any bill. A mere reference to the opponents' subject, not engagement with their claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "if we just did move your repeal out for three years and one day, we’d have time to find out whether it worked or not"

acuity.statement: I appreciate being able to speak on the name of this bill. It seems to me that the most appropriate name would be the “Poor Pay Promise Bill”, because it is indeed the fulfilment of a commitment to industry that they will be allowed to continue to exploit workers, continue to not guarantee basic wages—livable wages—and fair pay.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the preceding turn — having just been told the debate had drifted off the title, he pointedly addresses the title and proposes a name — but he engages none of the Minister's reasoning, and what follows is prepared material on disabled workers that would read identically whatever she had said. On the matter under debate, with a glance at it rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "the last three contributions have little to do with the title and commencement of this bill"

acuity.statement: I would like to know if the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety would consider a change to the name of the bill to “Back to the Status Quo”, because that is, essentially, what it does.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty follows Abel's proposed alternative title with a different proposed alternative title of his own. He is squarely on the matter under debate (what the bill should be called) and gestures at the state of the debate, but he engages no part of Abel's actual claim — that the bill is a commitment to exploitative industry — and the speech would read the same had Abel proposed any other name or none.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "The “Poor Pay Promise Bill”—that is the title."

acuity.statement: So the particular part that I’m talking to is clause 2, the “Commencement” in the new bill, which is the Act “[coming] into force on the day after Royal assent.” This is not a point about the commencement date, which my colleague Rachel Boyack has raised; it’s a point about the Royal assent itself. Those two things are different: the commencement and the place of the Royal assent in our constitutional framework.
acuity.explanation: Eligible because a substantive turn by another member precedes it, but the speech engages none of McAnulty's argument; it opens a separate line on clause 2 and the constitutional position of Royal assent. It stays within the same committee debate and situates itself against another member's earlier point, which lifts it off the floor, but it is prepared material that would be unchanged whatever McAnulty had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued at length that the bill should be renamed “Back to the Status Quo” because repealing fair pay agreements returns workers to the pre-FPA position, and this statement does not take that up — Williams opens by announcing it is “a brand new point”.

acuity.statement: My understanding is that Royal assent will happen as it does for all other bills that leave this House in the normal process, but I also want to make it very clear that my purpose in bringing this bill to the House is for all bargaining processes to stop and cease, and that the law itself ceases and the bargaining process thereunder ceases.
acuity.explanation: Van Velden takes up Williams' questions directly and answers the first (timing of Royal assent), and her second clause meets the premise of the rest head-on by confirming that extinguishing bargaining processes is the intended purpose rather than an oversight. Engagement is only partial: the questions on notification of parties, natural justice and compensation for costs already incurred go untouched, so one strand of a five-part argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: “when will the Royal assent be sought?” and “What natural justice issues does the Minister anticipate, given the Royal assent will cut across those proceedings?”

acuity.statement: I’ve heard the member Carl Bates interject repeatedly that people will have to join fair pay agreements even if they don’t want to. I ask the member to reflect on his time in the past, being an employee, if in fact that has been his experience. When you are presented with an employment contract, are you given an option of not accepting that employment contract? Most of the time you are not.
acuity.explanation: Belich names the interjector's claim — that fair pay agreements would bind workers who do not want them — restates it accurately, and then does something with it: she turns it into a comparison with ordinary individual employment agreements, which are also take-it-or-leave-it, and follows through to the point that a fair pay agreement sets a minimum that further negotiation can only improve on. The passage would not exist, and would have to be written differently, if Bates had interjected something else; that makes it near the top of the scale. Not a full 1.0 only because she answers the consent objection by analogy rather than engaging the coverage mechanism Bates was pointing at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Even if they don’t want to." — Carl Bates (repeated interjection during Belich's speech)

acuity.statement: They all think that individuals can all negotiate for themselves—no, no, here’s the thing: people go to work to do their mahi, to look after their family. They don’t go to work to negotiate with the boss.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford's immediately preceding interjection mocks Labour as claiming to know what is best for workers, i.e. asserts that individuals can speak for themselves. Jackson takes up exactly that premise and does something with it: he names it ('They all think that individuals can all negotiate for themselves') and argues against it on its own terms, that ordinary cleaners, security and hospitality workers go to work to do a job, not to act as their own bargaining agents. The passage would have to change if the interjection had been different, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because what he engages is a one-line jibe rather than a developed argument, so there is less specific content to rebut.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Yeah, 'I know what's best for us.'"

acuity.statement: Today is a day where a whole lot of New Zealanders lose a brighter future. What had been established over many, many years was that we had a problem. We had a problem of a low-wage economy where a whole lot of people were sinking, and we have the consequences of that, which we see every day.
acuity.explanation: White follows Jackson in the same debate and her opening is squarely on the matter under debate — the repeal and the low-wage economy — so it is not a 0.0. But it engages no part of what Jackson had just argued; the references she does answer ('the comment that we'd had earlier about bus drivers', 'when you talk about good employers') are to claims made earlier in the debate and not present in the preceding turn, so there is nothing in the immediately preceding contribution I can point at as engaged. This is prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, which the rubric puts at 0.3 and caps there because the engagement cannot be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke about Helen Kelly's work on fair pay bargaining, Jim Bolger's change of heart, and a Treasury warning that repeal would hurt Māori, Pasifika and women workers, and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: So I encourage those members—yeah, picture these workers. Because clearly the Minister chose to not engage with any of those workers when it came to the substance of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bates' claim that Government members are engaged with workers and turns it into a specific counter-charge that the Minister did not engage workers on the substance of the bill. It engages one strand of the interjection — the claim to be listening — rather than the food-bank evidence itself, and then returns to prepared material about submissions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I was at a food bank on Friday, food bank on Monday. Serving food on Monday. Don't tell me we're not looking at workers." — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: Today is a great day. It is the day of the liberation of New Zealand from the Fair Pay Agreements Act (FPA). The FPA is simply a mandated union bargaining tool and we will not stand for it.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate but indifferent to what preceded it. Substituting a different critique of the repeal in the prior turn would require no change to a word of this; there is no gesture at the consultation or coverage arguments just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the Government took no submissions and gave no reason for it, and that 200,000 to 300,000 workers would have benefited from fair pay agreements, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: New Zealand First supports the Fair Pay Agreements Act Repeal Bill for the reason that the Fair Pay Agreements Act is bad legislation—it’s the reason why we put the handbrake on it when we were last in Government and didn’t let it see the light of day. Despite the protestations of the members opposite, these are highly complex agreements that severely disadvantage regional employers.
acuity.explanation: Engages the opposition case in part: it answers the claim that the agreements would improve conditions by asserting they are too complex and disadvantage regional employers. But "the protestations of the members opposite" is a generic reference rather than engagement with a specific claim, and the speech then proceeds to prepared material and to a speech (Camilla Belich's) from outside this exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "fair pay agreements were one of the things in place to guarantee improvements to the working conditions of those workers" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Well, that’s the union’s problem; it’s not the Government’s problem to deal that out.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually put, and on its own terms: it concedes the gap and locates responsibility for it outside government rather than deflecting or changing the subject. Whether the answer is adequate is a separate question from whether it engages — on engagement it is squarely aimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "80 percent are not unionised. What about them?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: To be really clear, the repeal of this legislation is an absolute assault on workers. There are all sorts of guises and pretences based on belief—is what we keep hearing from the Minister: based on belief. It’s not; it is a direct assault on workers.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the subject under debate, addressed to workers and unions rather than to the argument just made. The glancing reference to what "we keep hearing from the Minister" is aimed at a framing from earlier in the bill's passage, not at Patterson's market-forces case, so the speech would be unchanged had he argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson argued the agreements were superfluous because low unemployment, employer demand and existing collective bargaining mean market forces already protect good workers, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: This year, I door-knocked and called over 9,000 people personally across the Whanganui electorate. It may surprise members opposite that this included thousands of workers and New Zealanders of every background.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the charge that Government members do not carry workers' voices and answers it with his own canvassing, with "New Zealanders of every background" picking up Davidson's groups. It answers the topic — who speaks for workers — rather than her specific claim about systemic inequities in low-paid sectors, and the rest is prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are bringing your voices into the halls of power" — Marama Davidson, whose speech claimed the repeal hits sectors overrepresented by Māori, Pasifika, women, young people and disabled people

acuity.statement: They’re all wrong, apparently—even business leaders, according to Simon Court. He just said they’re all wrong. So business leaders, economic leaders, Simon Court from ACT thinks you’re wrong.
acuity.explanation: She picks up Court's interjection and names it, but does nothing with its content: she restates it back and turns it into a label for ACT rather than defending the claim that commentators, business leaders and unions agree with her. The rest of the passage is prepared material on Australian enterprise bargaining that would have been delivered unchanged. A mere reference plus a pivot sits in the low band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They're all wrong." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Despite the rhetoric from the other side of the House over there, our business owners in the Wairarapa electorate take their responsibilities to their employees seriously, in good times and bad. If they’re forced to lay off staff, reduce production, or close their doors, everyone suffers, and the fair pay agreement will do nothing—nothing—to lift the productivity that New Zealand desperately needs.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of Boyack's preceding speech — her accounts of employers mistreating workers — with a direct counter-assertion that employers in his electorate treat staff responsibly, so the engagement is pointable. But it is a bare assertion rather than a reply to her actual case about sector-wide minimum standards (public holidays on a Tuesday-to-Saturday roster, bus drivers' split shifts), and the productivity line is prepared material that would stand whatever she had said. Partial engagement, hence mid-low rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just find it so offensive that people on the other side of this House actually think that stories about workers being mistreated in the workplace" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: We heard from the Minister that he’s had an opportunity to focus on this regressive and fiscally irresponsible piece of legislation, as it currently stands. He’s talked about fiscal irresponsibility. He has talked about how we would be taking the money from hard workers and, effectively, giving it to the rich. How fiscally responsible is it, then, for the Tesla-loving Prime Minister’s household to be able to access the very rebate that his Government seeks to remove?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific equity argument Brown had just built the case on (the 'reverse Robin Hood' claim that the scheme taxed workers to subsidise the wealthy) and turns it against him with the Prime Minister's own rebate. The speech would be different had Brown argued on different grounds — it is pegged to Brown's own framing and quotes his terms back in order to invert them. Short of 1.0 because it does not dispute the reasoning or the figures Brown gave; it answers the premise with a hypocrisy charge rather than engaging whether the distributional claim holds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this policy was taking from those who didn’t have a choice and giving it to people who could afford to pay for those vehicles" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: There was a market-based solution available. Now, to that member, Julie Anne Genter, heckling irrationally from the sidelines, the member said it’s time to confront reality. Well, it is. This wild scheme has led to a $300 million deficit, Julie Anne Genter—a $300 million deficit—between the amount of money recovered from long-suffering tradies, farmers, and big families who needed to replace a vehicle with a petrol diesel vehicle, and the amount of money paid out to people who receive subsidies for Teslas and other very expensive EVs.
acuity.explanation: Court picks up Genter's "confront reality" line and does engage one real strand of her case — she argued the scheme was fair because ute buyers help others into EVs; he contests the direction of that transfer with the deficit and the Tesla-subsidy figure. But his answer to her interjected question about industry support is a single unexplained assertion, and he leaves her other substantive points (the two megatons, the polling, the withheld regulatory impact statement) untouched in favour of prepared submitter material. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "The members in the Government are going to have to confront reality at some point." (and her interjection "Then why did the vehicle industry want the policy?")

acuity.statement: It shows a lack of understanding for the necessity of utes in particular, and the importance for our farmers and our tradies, and the critical roles that they play in our economy. They simply do not have the alternatives at the moment, as Simon Court has just outlined. Those alternatives are coming. The manufacturers are scaling up; they will become the tool of choice when they are available, but they simply are not at this moment.
acuity.explanation: Patterson takes up the preceding speaker's manufacturer-retooling claim by name and draws out its consequence — the alternatives are coming but are not here yet, so the scheme punishes people with no option. That is a pointable engagement with the previous turn, though it builds on an ally rather than testing the opposing argument, and the rest of the speech is prepared New Zealand First position that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "Vehicle manufacturers said, quite clearly, between 2025 and 2028 they’re going to completely retool manufacturing in Asia, South-east Asia, and Europe to produce almost nothing but EVs and hybrids."

acuity.statement: So I would say to you here now: farmers want to do their part to help with climate change. This is not one of them. This was unfair.
acuity.explanation: McCallum follows Kapa-Kingi's substantive opposition speech, which argued the repeal will raise emissions, cited the Climate Change Commission's halving target for transport emissions, and even made a rural-infrastructure point about EV viability. His speech is prepared material on the right subject: it asserts farmers' good faith on climate without taking up any part of her emissions or Commission argument, and his rural/Northland material does not engage her rural-infrastructure strand either. There is a gesture at the climate debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1; the speech would read identically had she argued something else on the same topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: 'Repealing this policy will increase carbon emissions and it will represent a backward step in terms of acting on climate change' — gestured at only to assert farmers want to help with climate change; the claim itself is not taken up.

acuity.statement: Because what members opposite cannot avoid is that this was an incredibly successful scheme. We’ve heard it being described as a scheme in deficit. This is a scheme that was set to be self-funding in 10 years. It needed a $300 million upfront cost, but its success is that it has overshot expectations, and for all New Zealanders that is a win.
acuity.explanation: Woods follows McCallum, whose case was that farmers and tradies had no choice and the tax was unfair. She does not engage that argument at all; her material is the COP agreement, the Commission's 2023 advice, Drive Electric's modelling and a demand for substitutions. She attempts to rebut a 'scheme in deficit' characterisation, which is real engagement in form, but that claim appears nowhere in the preceding turns in this window — I cannot point at it in what she had to respond to, which caps the score at 0.3. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate, hence 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable: Grant McCallum argued 'we have been punished by this ute tax, because we had no choice' and this statement does not take up the no-choice or unfairness argument; the 'scheme in deficit' line she rebuts was not said in any preceding turn here.

acuity.statement: Firstly, I’d like to commend the leadership of the Minister of Transport, the Hon Simeon Brown, for bringing this bill so quickly to the House to back the rural sector here in New Zealand, our hard-working farmers who that last member, Megan Woods, is out of touch with.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford immediately follows Woods and names her, but only as a target — 'out of touch', 'spending too much time here in Wellington'. None of the content of her turn is engaged: she asked what emissions measures would substitute for the scheme, down to megatonnes, and pre-emptively rebutted the deficit framing with the self-funding-in-10-years point, and he then simply reasserts the $302 million deficit without addressing that. Naming the previous speaker and pivoting to prepared praise of his own Minister is a mere reference, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because the pivot is at least aimed at her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: 'This is a scheme that was set to be self-funding in 10 years' (and 'What are those substitutions going to be?') — she is named as a target and the substance of both points is left untouched.

acuity.statement: I would like to invite that member, Julie Anne Genter, to nominate what kind of dinosaur she thinks I am. Some days I come to work, I fancy myself as a pterodactyl, soaring high above the forests of ancient New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Genter's preceding turn made a detailed, numerically specific case for the Clean Car Discount (186 g/km falling to 121 g/km, 2 megatonnes saved, the ETS/carbon-price consequence of repeal). Court picks up only her throwaway epithet 'dinosaur' and runs with it as a joke, engaging no part of the argument — the rubric's case of repeating an opponent's word back rather than engaging the content. It is a gesture at the preceding turn rather than prepared material delivered blind, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that National - ACT - New Zealand First dinosaur Government taking us back into the dark ages with their culture wars" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I rise in support of this bill and perhaps the biggest revelation this morning that we’ve heard has come from one of the most seasoned operators in the Labour Party, Megan Woods. She said in her call that this scheme was supposed to be self-funding in 10 years. Well, yesterday, the Minister of Transport revealed that the Clean Car Discount has become fiscally irresponsible, with taxpayers now footing a $302.5 million deficit.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the debate it follows — whether the scheme was a good investment — and answers it with a specific counter-figure, the $302.5 million deficit. But the claim he actually quotes and works on is Megan Woods's earlier "self-funding in 10 years" line, not anything in O'Connor's immediately preceding turn: O'Connor's arguments (the Euro5/Euro6 Ranger point, the M. bovis and agricultural-subsidy parallel, EV uptake as evidence of success) go untouched, and the rest of the speech is prepared material quoting the explanatory note. Engages the topic rather than the specific preceding claim, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the legislation for the Clean Car Discount we saw as a good investment in the future decarbonisation of our economy" — Damien O'Connor (the preceding turn, which argued the scheme was a sound investment)

acuity.statement: I’ve just been listening to the debate from the members opposite who have been trying to tell this House how amazing the scheme was, but they don’t have an answer to one of the key questions here: how are they going to pay for it?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly characterises the opposing speeches he has just heard ('how amazing the scheme was') and pushes back on the one strand of funding, putting a figure to it and then challenging the opposition to say what they would do instead — and he picks up Scott Willis's interjection in real time, which only a listening speaker could do. But he does not engage O'Connor's actual case: the agricultural-subsidy parallel (M. bovis, the billion-dollar Budget), the Euro6 emissions-profile point, or the 2030 carbon liability Woods raised. Much of the speech — the Greens 'hate the farmers' passage, the charging-network material, the coalition-agreement acknowledgement — would be identical whoever had preceded him. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the legislation for the Clean Car Discount we saw as a good investment in the future decarbonisation of our economy" — Damien O'Connor; also Scott Willis's "Yes" interjection, which Brown picks up directly ("the Greens say yes")

acuity.statement: In my first contribution on this bill I talked about the leadership aspirations of the Minister of Transport. They are well and truly down the road, gone, because that was just a pathetic attempt from the Hon Simeon Brown to justify this Government’s attempt to move in this particular direction.
acuity.explanation: This is a mere reference, not an engagement. Brown put a specific question to the members opposite and a specific number on the table; Utikere labels the speech a 'concession speech' and a 'pathetic attempt', then moves to prepared material about 'back to the future', a 'three-headed monster' and the use of urgency. Substituting a different argument on the same topic for Brown's would not require a word of this to change, but it is at least about the matter under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how are they going to pay for it?" and "a hole of $302.5 million for taxpayers—hard-working taxpayers—to foot the bill" — Simeon Brown. Named as a target but not taken up: no part of the funding challenge, the deficit figure, or the direct question put to Labour about what their plan would be is engaged.

acuity.statement: The last point that he made, and that’s been introduced to me since the first reading, is the $302 million fiscal hole that this scheme was running into. This is a time when we’ve got a $3.4 billion Budget deficit and a huge infrastructure crisis, but yet the Labour Government chose to subsidise Teslas—absolutely unbelievable.
