acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure from the immediately preceding speaker's closing argument and does something with it — sets it against the Budget deficit and the infrastructure shortfall — but it is adoption and extension of one strand rather than engagement with the substance of the dispute, and the rest of the turn is prepared material on electrify NZ and fast-track planning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "A $300 million deficit, now, between the revenue collected under the scheme and what was paid out to people to subsidise them to buy electric vehicles."

acuity.statement: When I come to the matter of costs, I’ve heard the kōrero from that side of the House that a loss or a fiscal hole of $300 million is there, and this is the reason why they are pulling the plug. The clean car rebates and fee scheme was designed to be reviewed and adjusted regularly, so that the fees could generate enough revenue to cover such costs. What I’ve also observed is that there was actually an implementation delay in the period between when rebates were granted and when the fees were applied. That’s an implementation issue.
acuity.explanation: Names the exact claim made by both preceding government speakers — the $300 million shortfall as the reason for repeal — and attacks its reasoning directly, arguing the gap is a timing artefact of rebates preceding fees under a scheme designed for fiscal neutrality over ten years. The speech would have to change if the earlier turns had not run the fiscal-hole argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "A $300 million deficit, now, between the revenue collected under the scheme and what was paid out" (and Mark Patterson's "$302 million fiscal hole")

acuity.statement: Now I hear that the Government is wanting to put everything back into the emissions trading scheme. But come on. Members on that side of the House: truly, we know this will not do anything or send any signals to the market. What it will do, though, is impose further costs on to the oil suppliers who will pass that on to the average people.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the central affirmative argument of the two preceding speakers — that the ETS is the simpler substitute for the discount — and contests it on its own ground, denying the market signal and identifying who bears the pass-through cost. Slightly short of the top because it asserts the rebuttal rather than engaging the specific per-tank pricing figure Court offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "There’s a much simpler solution: the emissions trading scheme."

acuity.statement: I’ve noticed with interest the amount of attacks that have been sent on the farming sector about our commitment to emissions reduction. Well, I’ll just point a couple of things out that a few people on the other side of the House might not be aware of, one of which is that Fonterra recently announced that we’re going to have a 30 percent reduction in our carbon intensity on-farm emissions by 2030.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right broad subject — emissions and the bill — with a gesture at unnamed 'attacks' on farming, but it takes up no part of the argument the preceding speaker actually made about implementation timing, designed fiscal neutrality or the two-megatonne saving. The speech would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said about the scheme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Darleen Tana argued the $300 million gap was an implementation-timing issue under a scheme designed for ten-year fiscal neutrality and that it saved two megatonnes of carbon dioxide, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I’m hearing about Resource Management Act (RMA) reform. Well, that’s interesting. That is an interesting interjection, because the RMA reform had a very full submission process. In fact, when submissions were open over Christmas, there was much debate from the Opposition about how it was so unfair to have a six-week submission process that was over the Christmas break. So, of course, that was extended time and time again to enable a very good process for some very fine legislation.
acuity.explanation: Meager interjects that Labour's own RMA reform used the same truncated process. Brooking takes that specific tu quoque and works on its content: she concedes the comparison is interesting, then argues the RMA reform had a full submission process that was extended repeatedly, and goes on to distinguish stage-by-stage urgency from all-stages urgency. The passage would not exist, and would have to be different, had the interjection been something else. Scored on engagement only — the strength of the analogy-breaking and the truth of the claim about extensions are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do RMA reforms ring a bell?" — James Meager

acuity.statement: Members opposite have asked for some specifics. Well, let me give you some. The tradies in my electorate, in Ōtaki, the good people of Horowhenua and Kāpiti—they don’t have another option. They don’t have another option. They don’t need to be forking out taxpayer dollars to support Tesla owners. The farmers that need to drive up the western faces of the Tararua Ranges, they don’t have an electric option and they don’t need another ute tax, and neither do the growers that are providing 30 percent of our leafy greens for New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Costley follows Brooking and takes up one strand of what she said — her claim that farmers should be worried about their carbon pollution — answering that the farmers and growers he represents have no electric option and need no further charge. He engages nothing of her central argument (the suspended regulatory impact statement, all stages under urgency, or that the scheme's problems could be fixed by regulation), and the rest is prepared electorate material. Partial engagement with a pointable strand, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If farmers are worried about the future of farming, they need to be worried about their carbon pollution and to reduce it as much as possible" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: We’re not engaging here, Mr van de Molen. This isn’t engaging; this is the start of an engagement. Usually this would be the very first thing we would do, and then we would send things off to a select committee and then we would look at the evidence and then we would respond.
acuity.explanation: Takes up van de Molen's interjection directly and disputes its premise, distinguishing an election mandate from parliamentary engagement and setting out what engagement would consist of (select committee, evidence, response). The passage would not exist, and could not be worded this way, had he not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We just engaged in an election." — Tim van de Molen

acuity.statement: What a great day for this coalition Government, that promised a 100-day action plan. We just heard “What is the urgency with this?” The urgency is this was one of our big campaign promises and over a million people supported it, and to think that in the first few days of this Government we’re coming out and backing businesses, small businesses, farmers, New Zealand taxpayers.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the specific question the preceding speaker put — why the urgency — and supplies an answer to it (an election commitment inside a 100-day plan), rather than merely naming her as a target. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the urgency question with mandate rather than engaging her argument that nothing else is ready to roll out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why is this so urgent? There are no roll-outs of other things at the moment." — Helen White

acuity.statement: The member over there, Megan Woods, asked for numbers and evidence. Well, if a $302 million deficit on taxpayers is not enough numbers, then let’s have a look at this. What did the subsidy do? What did the tax do to on-farm inflation? The year that it was introduced, on-farm inflation for sheep and beef farmers rose to 16.3 percent, up from 10.2 percent, and Dairy New Zealand says on-farm inflation for the last three years has been at 33 percent.
acuity.explanation: Engages the demand for evidence that the preceding speaker pressed, and offers figures in answer, which is more than a glance. But it answers a different question from the one asked: she asked for the regulatory impact statement on the repeal and the scheme's performance, and he supplies fiscal cost and on-farm inflation instead, then moves to prepared material on farm input costs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I challenge the Government to give us that impact statement so we can have a look" — Helen White

acuity.statement: I heard my friend the Hon Julie Anne Genter talking about the possibility of a compromise on things like utes so that there might be an exemption scheme in place. Has that been discussed, because I presume Drive Electric would have been one of the submitters in any process through a select committee and we would have heard from them?
acuity.explanation: White's turn is mostly her own prepared lines of inquiry (air quality, equity, dealer pricing), but she explicitly takes up one strand of Genter's preceding argument — the ute-exemption compromise — and converts it into a direct question to the Minister about whether such alternatives were discussed with Drive Electric. One identifiable strand engaged, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "you remove the fees on utes from the scheme and you could still have that financial incentive in the rest of the personal car market"

acuity.statement: Given that this is a bill that is not going through the select committee process and Part 1 of the bill is the part of the bill that does disestablish the legal basis for applying a Clean Car Discount, I have a question around the intersection of this bill with the Clean Car Standard and whether it’s the Minister’s intention to make any changes to the Clean Car Standard.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the clause 7 / Clean Car Standard territory Genter had just been probing — but it engages no part of either preceding argument; it is an independently framed question that would have been identical whatever Genter and White had said. The gesture at the debate (the select committee point) keeps it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Genter asked why the Government used legislation rather than regulation and whether tailpipe-emissions data will still be collected, and White asked about air quality and equity analyses; this statement takes up neither, though it touches the same Clean Car Standard subject matter Genter raised.

acuity.statement: So I’m really, really interested in how much of the fees were paid by people in urban areas for EVs, and what advice has he received regarding the proportion of fees and rebates paid by or received by rural dwellers, rural communities, and urban communities.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. Willis repeats the absence of a select committee (as Woods had) and aims his remarks at an off-window 'self-proclaimed dinosaur', but engages no content from the preceding turns by Genter, White or Woods; the speech would read identically whatever they had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Genter pressed why repeal was done by legislation rather than regulation and White asked for air-quality and equity analysis; this statement does not take up either, and instead introduces a rural/urban split question of its own.

acuity.statement: The Hon Julie Anne Genter asked about the scheme and talked about how we could make this somehow—she talked about fiscal neutrality and suggested we should exempt utes. But I don’t know whether she realised that would create an even bigger hole, and I’m not sure how the member suggests that that would be paid for, other than by borrowing more money.
acuity.explanation: Takes Genter's specific proposal — exempt utes, keep the rest of the scheme — together with her fiscal-neutrality claim, and draws out a consequence from it (a larger fiscal hole, requiring borrowing). The reply would have to change if she had proposed something else. Held below 1.0 because it leaves her central question (why legislate when regulation could achieve the same outcome) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "including taking the fees off utes and carrying on with the rest of the scheme—that would have been a possible option available to the Minister"

acuity.statement: My question is a very fundamental one for the Minister and goes to why we need any legislation at all. Of course, we could all think about what those reasons might be that we are here in the House under urgency when, of course, it is not mandatory to have these regulations.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Utikere's question about clause 5 and the repeal of section 167A — and develops it into a sharper version of the same point (that the repealed provision is permissive, so no primary legislation is needed). It engages the topic and that clause rather than any specific claim Utikere made, and most of the turn is her own prepared reading of the section, so it sits at the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether or not he is satisfied with clause 5, which, it seems to me, is the crux of it in terms of the repeal of section 167A of the Land Transport Act"

acuity.statement: The question I have for the Minister relates to the purpose of elevating some of these decisions to primary legislation. My colleague has touched on a more general point, but I want to focus specifically on the Minister’s views around making these decisions in primary legislation, and perhaps he can give us some guidance on his view around regulations within the transport sector as to whether this will be a trend of the Government to use primary legislation tools—indeed, within urgency or out of urgency—whereas the previous Government would have used the secondary legislation, or the regulations, to make those sorts of decisions.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up Brooking's point that the regulation-making power already suffices, marks it as the general case, and draws out a consequence she did not reach — whether using primary legislation here signals a standing approach to secondary legislation in transport. The turn would have to change if the preceding speech had argued something else, which is what high acuity looks like; it falls short of 1.0 because it extends rather than tests her reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "So it appears that there is no need to do any of this primary legislation and that we can just rely on the secondary legislation and the processes that the Minister can determine."

acuity.statement: The member Tangi Utikere asked a number of questions around whether other pieces of legislation require amendment. The answer is no. This bill includes all of the legislation that needs amending, and I note that he started talking about what’s in Part 2 and I look forward to him talking about that later when we get to that stage.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question put and supplies a direct answer to it, and additionally places Utikere's Part 2 material correctly in the debate's sequence. The reply could not have been given to a different preceding speech. Scored on engagement only — its brevity and lack of detail are specificity questions, not acuity ones.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether there may be other pieces of legislation that may subsequently require amendment"

acuity.statement: This piece of legislation needs to be repealed because this Government does not support the fees and charges which were put in place: the ute tax and the Clean Car Discount scheme. So we are removing the legislation off the books, and that is why we’re progressing it through the House in this method.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question at the level of the topic — a political reason for repealing — but engages no part of Brooking's actual argument, which was that section 167A is permissive throughout and the Minister's discretion over the regulations already achieves the result without primary legislation. Partial engagement: pointable, but aimed at the question's subject rather than its reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "why do we need any of this repeal legislation today?"

acuity.statement: The member Arena Williams asked exactly the same question, and I give exactly the same answer.
acuity.explanation: Names the member and declines to engage. Williams had expressly distinguished her question from Brooking's, asking about the Government's general approach to primary versus secondary legislation in the transport sector and the legal-risk consequences; treating it as identical takes up no part of that content. A mere reference to the previous speaker, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "whether this will be a trend of the Government to use primary legislation tools—indeed, within urgency or out of urgency"

acuity.statement: I’m not sure about that; I would like him to give a straight yes or no answer to it. But it is his preference to make the bold political call that the Government is opposed to Clean Car Discounts and that they are taking this down the primary legislative route, even though it is unnecessary, so this whole debate in urgency is unnecessary.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's own answer on why primary legislation rather than regulation is being used, treats it as a partial concession ('the answer is yes'), presses him for a straight yes/no, and draws the consequence that the urgency debate is therefore unnecessary. The speech would read differently had the Minister answered otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We actually don’t agree with keeping it on and using regulations instead. So we’re repealing the Act and repealing the regulation-making power." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I would like to seek a further response from the Minister in relation to the proportion of fees and rebates paid by or received by rural communities or urban communities.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the Minister's answer by identifying what it did not supply — the rural/urban split rather than the ute share — and presses for the precise figure, supplying his own modelling figure as the benchmark. Not a full 1.0 because it re-puts the question rather than contesting the reasoning of the reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m advised that about roughly half of the tax which has been received has been paid for by people buying utes." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I want to pick up on the contribution made by my colleague the Hon Rachel Brooking and the question to the Minister around an assurance—that he can assure the committee that the imposition of “make all … consequential amendments” is not considered as substantial, given that the House is in urgency and I’m yet to receive a response to my question around the nature of the work that officials have been undertaking.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific clause 9 point Brooking had just made about the scope of 'all necessary consequential amendments' and converts it into a demand for an assurance that the amendments are not substantial, tying it to the urgency context. Clearly shaped by the preceding turn, though it adds no new analysis of the clause itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m just interested in this phrase “make all necessary consequential amendments.”" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: So I’d love to ask the Minister, if I could: could the Minister explain what had been the fiscal costs of the Clean Car Discount—it would be good to get some clarification on that, and I think the opposite side would appreciate that—and, as laid out in clause 12, was this scheme actually sustainable at its time of implementation?
acuity.explanation: A fresh prepared question on the bill's fiscal costs and clause 12 that engages no part of the arguments immediately preceding it; the glance at 'the opposite side' is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with anything said in it, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Willis asked for the rural/urban split of fees and rebates and Rachel Brooking and Tangi Utikere asked about the scope of consequential amendments to Schedule 1, and this statement takes up none of those points.

acuity.statement: But just responding and kind of coming in on the question just raised by the member from the ACT Party—which I think is a great question—and the comments made by the Minister earlier that if you were to exclude utes, you’d have to raise more revenue, clearly the way that feebates are designed and used by successful countries all over the world is with that intention that it will be moving over time.
acuity.explanation: Takes Luxton's sustainability question and the Minister's revenue point and answers them on their own terms, explaining how narrowing rebate eligibility and escalating fees on high-emitting vehicles is how feebate schemes stay fiscally neutral. The contribution would have to change entirely had the preceding question been a different one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "was this scheme actually sustainable at its time of implementation?" — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: So in light of the fact that we have this legislation before us today—this bill—to repeal the policy mechanism of using a rebate for customers, I’d like to know further from the Minister whether he is thinking of bringing forward any review of the Clean Car Standard.
acuity.explanation: The turn follows a substantive ministerial answer, and it is squarely on the matter under debate — the repeal of the rebate mechanism. But it takes up no part of what the Minister had just said: not the section 167A drafting point, not the election-mandate account of engagement, not the $302.5 million net cost figure. It returns to a separate line of questioning about the Clean Car Standard and would have read identically whatever the Minister had just argued. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the bill before the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown's preceding turn addressed the repeal of section 167A, the election as the 'engagement' answer to Tangi Utikere, the scheme's fiscal costs for Cameron Luxton, and Julie Anne Genter's fee-change suggestion — this statement does not take up any of those.

acuity.statement: If you look at the label itself, if you look at new Schedule 2, inserted by Schedule 4, just to help the members, it’s quite clear that 5.5 refers to carbon dioxide; it states that—even I can read that—and the 29 figure is 29 grams of carbon per kilometre travelled.
acuity.explanation: Helen White's immediately preceding turn asked what the '29' on the label meant and complained she could not read the small print. Bayly takes that exact question and supplies the figure's meaning, pointing her to the schedule where it is defined — the textbook 'supplies the figure it asked for' case. The statement would be different had she asked about something else. Marked down from 1.0 only because it answers the narrowest of her questions while the turn leaves her efficacy and health-advice questions untouched; the engagement itself is squarely aimed. Scored on engagement only — whether '5.5 refers to carbon dioxide' is correct is a veracity question, and whether the detail is precise is specificity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So I can see that there is a level of emissions of “29”—29 out of what? What kind of emissions are we talking about?" — Helen White

acuity.statement: So I’d like to know whether the Government is willing to countenance that amendment to protect people so they don’t get caught in some tricky situations.
acuity.explanation: Bayly had just answered on the label figures, the amendment paper on clause 22A, and voluntary repayments to the Crown. Woods engages none of that: she opens a prepared line on clauses 18 and 19, the registration cut-off and Tangi Utikere's proposed new clause 28. It is squarely about the part of the bill under debate, so it is not a 0.0 — this passage would read identically whatever Bayly had just said, but it could not have been delivered in a different debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly explained the label figures and refused the clause 22A amendment paper, and this statement does not take either up — it raises the registration cut-off instead.

acuity.statement: I do have a further question around the label, and I appreciate that we will be getting blown-up copies of those labels so we can continue to debate this part of the bill. But my question is, given that the labels are going to continue to display the emissions from a particular vehicle, and given, under Part 1 of the bill, there were some very serious questions that the Minister never even addressed around emissions and reporting and advice, I’d like to know in terms of each of those labels displaying emissions information, what information more generally has the Minister received on emissions?
acuity.explanation: This takes up one strand of Bayly's turn — his undertaking to produce an enlarged label — acknowledges it, and then builds on his own framing that the labels will keep displaying emissions to press for the advice behind them. Partial rather than full engagement: she does not contest his substantive claim that the figures are 'pretty standard stuff' or that only the dollar sum is being removed, and the emissions-advice question is carried over from Part 1 rather than arising from what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "First of all, we are in the process of trying to get a blown-up version of the labelling." — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: You need to buy it and register it and make your application before 31 December—very clear rules. So just saying to people: don’t go and buy one that’s in the shipment; go and buy one that you can get straight away.
acuity.explanation: Woods put a specific scenario to him: a buyer whose vehicle has not made landfall and so cannot be registered before the cut-off. Bayly engages that exact scenario and answers it on its own terms — the vehicle in shipment is precisely the case she described, and his answer is that such buyers should not purchase at all. That is drawing out the consequence of her hypothetical rather than evading it, and the reply would be different had she raised a different problem. Below the top band because he leaves her second question, on what emissions advice he has received, entirely alone and never says directly whether the Government will support the Utikere amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They may be expecting receipt of their vehicle and its registration on, say, 29 December, 30 December, even 31 December, but there is a delay for some reason or another and it might not arrive until, say, 4 or 5 January." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: I note that this part relates to the administration of the scheme, in terms of how it will be executed and how it is followed through, and I wonder, in light of that, whether the Minister has any thoughts about implementing some sort of review process as part of that.
acuity.explanation: Follows Brown's exposition of what Part 2 does and is about the same part, but takes up none of the specific amendments or revocations Brown described; it introduces a prepared line of questioning about review mechanisms instead. On-topic without engaging the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This part deals, as you just said, with amendments, repeals, and revocations concerning other amendments" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Because we’re repealing the bill, you do not need a report back. It’s self-evident that no report back is required.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one real strand of the questions just put (the reporting mechanism) and answers it directly, but treats it as disposing of the review question too, which was the separate thing asked — partial engagement, and Utikere immediately has to correct the conflation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The other is whether there is a reporting mechanism back to the House—or it could be not to the House; it could be through some other mechanism" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I note that the Minister referred to a report-back opportunity. My question was not about report back; it was around whether or not a review would be signalled, which is not a requirement whether there’s legislation or not.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer and corrects it on its own terms: identifies that he answered report-back rather than review, and explains why the distinction matters (a review needs no statutory requirement). The contribution would be entirely different had Bayly answered the question actually asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The first one is the reporting-back requirement that the member asked about. Because we’re repealing the bill, you do not need a report back." — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: I just wanted to ask and seek some clarity from either the Minister, or maybe he can receive some advice, but it’s very difficult to read the labels in this proposed legislation.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's invitation to inspect the label templates and reports the result of doing so — that they are illegible as tabled — then does something with it by asking for a larger copy to be tabled before the committee stage ends. Not the immediately preceding turn, which holds it below 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "as members will see in their copy of the bill, there are some templates as to what the new labels will look like. I encourage members to take a look." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The first of those questions is to ask the Minister to confirm that in October 2022, KiwiRail wrote to Ministers noting “in a ‘worst case scenario’ the tagged contingency for the project would need to increase by $280m”.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise factual spine of the ministerial statement — when the previous Government was told of cost escalation — and puts a dated document to it. The question only makes sense as a reply to Willis's account of what was known and when; it could not have been pre-written for a different statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "We have been advised that the outgoing Government knew in February 2023 that the cost had blown out to $2.6 billion, but that was never made public"

acuity.statement: That information is new to me. I think what the member may be referring to is a pattern of cost escalation that occurred with this project while he was the key shareholder of KiwiRail.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific item put to her — she answers on the October 2022 letter rather than ignoring it — but having said it is new to her she pivots to the member's record as shareholder instead of engaging the substance of the date. Half engagement, half pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "to confirm that in October 2022, KiwiRail wrote to Ministers noting ‘in a worst case scenario’ the tagged contingency for the project would need to increase by $280m"

acuity.statement: So the timetable released by the Minister in her own press release yesterday includes the statement from October 2022 that KiwiRail noted that “in a ‘worst case scenario’ the tagged contingency would need to increase by $280m”. So I just note, for the member, the answer to the question I asked is contained in the time line she released yesterday.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the misstatement of fact just made, by showing the source of the quoted passage is the Minister's own released document. The whole intervention exists because of the preceding answer and would be meaningless after any other reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "That information is new to me."

acuity.statement: I want to address the member’s questions sincerely which is to say I am looking at the timetable I released yesterday and the date that the member has used, which is 2022—I’ve got dates on my time line of 2021 and 2023.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact artefact the previous turn invoked — the released timeline — and explains why she cannot find the date in it. It is a reply shaped entirely by the correction just made, though it resolves nothing of the substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "the answer to the question I asked is contained in the time line she released yesterday"

acuity.statement: To the second part of your question which regards my statement that the project had veered wildly from its original intent, I based that on the fact that as I understand it, when the Government first agreed to fund this project, it was in order to replace aging ferries, and that was to be the bulk of the infrastructure investment. As I have been advised, that now only comprises around 21 percent of the actual infrastructure project. The other 80 percent or so is for significant marine development and port-side development.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what the question asked for — the basis for the "veered away" claim — with the proportion of spend she relies on. The answer is tailored to the specific question rather than to the topic at large.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "can she please explain in what way the project ‘veered away from its core purpose’?"

acuity.statement: So it is absolutely clear that the statement that the Minister made—that this project had somehow “veered off course from its core purpose”—is incorrect. The core purpose of the project, agreed by the Labour Party and the New Zealand First Party, was for both the construction of new ferries and, indeed, portside infrastructure, as Mr Peters stated in his statement of 27 May 2020.
acuity.explanation: Attacks the premise of the answer just given — that the original purpose was ferries alone — with a dated contemporaneous release describing landside terminal infrastructure as part of the project. Rebuts the reasoning rather than merely rejecting the conclusion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "when the Government first agreed to fund this project, it was in order to replace aging ferries, and that was to be the bulk of the infrastructure investment"

acuity.statement: The first question that you asked was about whether or not the project had veered off. It is absolutely the case that the project today is four times what it was when the Government originally committed to it. And its core purpose was to replace an ageing ferry fleet, and yes there was an acknowledgment—not that the ferries would only be 20 percent of the project.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the strand that portside work was acknowledged in the original scope, which is the point just put to her, but then restates her own framing by proportion instead of dealing with the Peters release offered as evidence. Partial engagement, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "The core purpose of the project, agreed by the Labour Party and the New Zealand First Party, was for both the construction of new ferries and, indeed, portside infrastructure"

acuity.statement: So, to clarify, the Minister of Finance’s statement says that the project veered away from its core purpose when it hadn’t. The Minister’s statement also says that the cost had blown out to $2.6 billion under the Government’s watch when that money had not in fact been agreed.
acuity.explanation: Draws the two answers just given to their consequence, isolating the distinction the previous turn elided — that a requested escalation is not an agreed cost. It engages the specific content of both replies rather than the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "when the former Government learnt that the project had blown out to $2.6 billion, the Minister at the time then spent a significant number of months trying to work out what to do"

acuity.statement: I think if the point that the former Minister wishes to make is that this sorry saga dragged on for months under his watch, then, yes, that is correct and, yes, he did oversee multiple cost blowouts and, yes, there was engagement with KiwiRail about it. But, actually, what then happened was that he decided, four weeks out from an election, to put aside money for the project, knowing full well that in the form that he was choosing to fund it, KiwiRail had recommended it not proceed and that, for example, passengers would not have been able to get on the ferry unless they caught a bus on to the ferry.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the account of prolonged engagement with KiwiRail and then turns on the specific fact the previous turn offered in its own defence — the pre-election in-principle offer — recasting it as funding a scheme KiwiRail itself advised against. Shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "before we left Government we made an in-principle offer to KiwiRail for part of that construction cost"

acuity.statement: But if the member will just give me a moment of patience, I wish to apologise to the House, because when the member asked me about 2022, I had in front of me an old timetable, and not the one that I have released publicly. I regret that error.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the exact point pressed earlier in the exchange, identifies why her earlier answer was wrong and corrects it. Correcting a misstatement of fact in response to the other member's evidence is the strongest form of engagement available.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant Robertson: "in my first question I pointed out that in October 2022, KiwiRail told the then Government that the worst-case scenario would be a need to increase the tagged contingency we’d put aside by $280 million"

acuity.statement: I don’t need advice to know that New Zealand needs a reliable, safe ferry service between our two islands. Our Government is committed to ensuring that is the case and we are confident that that will be the case.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the 'advice' strand of Genter's question and rejects its premise, but substitutes a different proposition (that NZ needs ferries) for the one asked about (advice quantifying the risk of vessel failure). Engagement with one strand, then assurance — a partial, not a full, engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'Has the Government received any advice that quantifies the risk to New Zealand of not having replacement ferries if current vessels fail?'

acuity.statement: Notwithstanding that the chair of KiwiRail has mentioned that the choice that the Government has made to completely start over in this process will mean that there’ll be considerable delays, potentially, to the replacement ferries, how much of the cost that the Minister has been referring to is related to necessary upgrades to port infrastructure, particularly to address seismic risk?
acuity.explanation: The 'notwithstanding' clause directly counters the confidence the Minister had just asserted, citing the KiwiRail chair on delays, before moving to a new specific question. Engages the preceding answer's substance and would have read differently had the Minister said something else, though the engagement is a prefix to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: 'Our Government is committed to ensuring that is the case and we are confident that that will be the case.'

acuity.statement: The member will be aware that there are a number of options for how we proceed in terms of replacement ferries, and I’m confident that we can get a timely solution.
acuity.explanation: Answers the delay strand of the preceding turn (asserting a timely solution against the KiwiRail chair's warning) but engages no part of the question actually put about the port-infrastructure and seismic share of the cost. One strand taken up, the central claim left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'there’ll be considerable delays, potentially, to the replacement ferries'

acuity.statement: I don’t have that figure to hand, but I would note that the member herself said, on X, that the project had become too expensive.
acuity.explanation: Squarely addresses the question asked by conceding she cannot supply the figure, then engages the questioner's own stated position on the project. The turn is unmistakably shaped by what preceded it, though the second half pivots to the member rather than the costing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'how much of the cost is related to necessary upgrades to poor infrastructure, particularly to address seismic risk?'

acuity.statement: Yes, that’s true, and thank you for referring to my very reasonable comments, because I’ve long been a critic of Government spending in the transport sector inflating too fast and not being good value for money. But I guess the relevant point for the Minister that I’m interested in drilling down for the benefit of the House is whether or not the cost inflation is out of line with other cost inflation we’ve seen in infrastructure, particularly in the building space, because of changes made—I believe by a previous National Government—to earthquake standards and our awareness of the risk of seismic risk and whether in fact quadrupling of price is pretty standard certainly for the highways that this Government will be trying to deliver.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's gotcha outright, then turns it into the next question — whether the escalation is abnormal relative to other infrastructure cost inflation. Concession plus redirection built entirely on the preceding turn; it could not have been delivered had the Minister not quoted her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: 'the member herself said, on X, that the project had become too expensive'

acuity.statement: Well, a cost blowout of four times the size of the original project may have been pretty standard under the last Government, but it’s not going to be pretty standard under this Government. In fact, this project was an outlier, and the point I would make is this: the cost of the infrastructure that needed to be developed at port and on the land side and the marine side, I understand, was a lot more expensive because of the size of the boats—ships—that had been committed to. And that is relevant here because the pattern under the previous Government was that they would commission an infrastructure project without first doing the appropriate due diligence to fully understand the design implications and implications of it. Don’t take it at my word; read the Auditor-General’s report.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific proposition just put — that a quadrupling of price may be standard for infrastructure — denies it, gives a causal account of why this project's port costs were high (vessel size), and cites the Auditor-General as external support. Direct, substantive engagement with the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'whether in fact quadrupling of price is pretty standard'

acuity.statement: Two more quick questions: will energy efficiency and carbon emissions be a consideration in any new vessels that are commissioned, given that they do have ongoing implications for the cost of running the vessels?
acuity.explanation: Moves to a prepared new question without taking up the Minister's outlier argument, the vessel-size explanation or the Auditor-General reference. It is on the matter under debate and links loosely to the running cost theme, but engages no part of what was just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued the blowout was an outlier caused by the committed vessel size and cited the Auditor-General's report, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Yes, it’s my understanding that modern ferries are less emissions intensive than the ferries we are currently using.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked, in the affirmative, and supplies the reason the answer holds. Brief, but it engages the specific content put to her and would be different had a different question been asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'will energy efficiency and carbon emissions be a consideration in any new vessels that are commissioned'

acuity.statement: We will continue to want the ferries to support good freight connections between the North and South Island and we continue to support rail as a means for transporting freight around New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the rail-freight element of the question directly, affirming continued support, though it does not engage the port-side infrastructure half of what was asked. Clearly shaped by the question, partially complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: 'Will continuity of rail freight services be a consideration in the necessary port-side infrastructure?'

acuity.statement: Cabinet has made the right decision. KiwiRail’s project iReX was hugely wasteful, had already faced cost blowouts, and was facing larger significant cost blowouts. We are a Government that wishes to ensure that we deliver value for money for all New Zealand taxpayers. This move will also send a clear signal to the public sector that we will not tolerate cost blowouts and a lack of value for money.
acuity.explanation: Prepared endorsement of the decision that engages none of the preceding exchange — not the seismic and port-cost questions, not the comparison with general infrastructure inflation, not the emissions or rail-freight points. It is on the subject under debate but would be word-for-word identical whatever had been said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter had been pressing the Minister on what share of the cost was seismic port upgrades and whether a quadrupling is standard for infrastructure, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Tēnā tātou e te Whare. Look, just a couple of questions, please. We’ve been concerned—in fact, last night, we were debating how we protect small to medium sized businesses. So it’s a unique position Te Pāti Māori finds itself in, asking the Government about economic questions and, surely, productivity. So we’ve now got a decision that will axe and limit the economic ability within Te Wai Pounamu and its aspirations and ability to grow. We have been extremely concerned with the messages that we’ve had from businesses in Te Wai Pounamu. So we have a couple of questions.
acuity.explanation: Opens her party's own line of inquiry on the decision's effect on South Island businesses. It gestures at the value-for-money framing just advanced from the Government benches by setting a competing economic frame against it, but takes up none of the specific claims — not the waste argument, not the cost-escalation figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: 'KiwiRail’s project iReX was hugely wasteful' — engaged only as a general frame, not as a claim

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her question and her appreciation that, actually, the wellbeing of all New Zealanders is dependent on businesses being able to thrive, employ people, grow, and innovate. I can assure the member that our Government is committed to a range of policies to assist in that.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the member's framing about business wellbeing but engages none of the three things actually asked — how affected businesses are being contacted, what alternative is offered, what investment will follow. A restatement of the questioner's premise in place of a reply to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: 'what degree of investment is the Government going to provide so that the businesses, the very grassroots people who have been relying on this project and this solution to happen, will happen?'

acuity.statement: Tēnā koe. Can I seek clarity, please, on which businesses, which sector within the business sector have been communicated with or consulted, bar the release that came out?
acuity.explanation: Notices that the assurance just given contained no engagement detail and narrows the question to the specific gap, explicitly discounting the public release as the answer. Responsive to what the previous turn omitted, though it presses rather than rebuts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: 'we wish to reassure them that we remain 100 percent committed to reliable interisland ferry services'

acuity.statement: We have asked that KiwiRail engage its contract partners and stakeholders in communicating this information, and we anticipate further engagement in the days and weeks ahead.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the substance asked for — who has been asked to communicate with whom, and that further engagement is still to come. Directly keyed to the question, if less specific than the sector-by-sector answer sought.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: 'which businesses, which sector within the business sector have been communicated with or consulted'

acuity.statement: Can I please seek clarity: have Ngāi Tahu, Wakatū, the Māori business sector, who are extremely successful and prominent in Te Wai Pounamu—what has been the engagement with them and how are they being supported to realise their aspirations economically that they’ve had on hold for a very long time?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's generic answer about 'contract partners and stakeholders' and tests it against named entities, forcing the vague category to resolve. The follow-up exists only because of the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: 'We have asked that KiwiRail engage its contract partners and stakeholders'

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her question, and I would welcome further engagement with that group. I think the point here that we can agree on is that there are a number of stakeholders with an interest in ferry services across the Strait. Those stakeholders include businesses, the port, and KiwiRail itself. I wish to re-evaluate this project not just from the perspective of KiwiRail but actually from the perspective of all port users, ferry users, and freight users, to ensure that we’re coming up with a solution that best delivers value for all New Zealanders, not just for the KiwiRail business.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the named group and concedes a point of agreement on the breadth of stakeholders, which engages the question in part, but then generalises away from the Māori entities named and answers nothing about what engagement has occurred or how they are being supported.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: 'have Ngāi Tahu, Wakatū, the Māori business sector... what has been the engagement with them'

acuity.statement: We will be carrying out engagement with those entities in the coming days.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question put directly, conceding by implication that the engagement has not yet happened — which also disposes of the second half asking for their feedback. Plainly shaped by the specific question about councils.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: 'Have the regional and local government authorities been engaged, and what has been their feedback to the Government about this change of direction?'

acuity.statement: Does he agree with the National Party leader, Christopher Luxon, that “I can tell you we’re going to be straight with the New Zealand people, tell it as it is—the good, the bad and the ugly”; if so, what’s changed?
acuity.explanation: Takes the comfort-with-suspension Luxon has just expressed and sets it against his own transparency pledge, so the question depends on the answer it follows. It engages the stance rather than the specific reason given (that RISs add no value to repeal decisions), and the quoted pledge is clearly prepared material, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “We are very comfortable with suspending regulatory impact statements because we don’t think they’ll add value for decisions that we’re repealing legislation on.”

acuity.statement: Did he suspend regulatory impact statements before or after the regulatory impact statement for repealing fair pay agreements was leaked?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the suspension of regulatory impact statements — but it engages no part of the answer just given and would read identically had Luxon said something else. Prepared supplementary on the right subject, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Luxon answered about three of the last four quarters of declining economic growth and the $15 billion New Zealand Upgrade programme, and this question does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: In light of that answer, can we now expect that because of the election result, no pieces of legislation will be referred to a select committee?
acuity.explanation: Takes the electoral-mandate justification just offered and draws out its consequence, pressing whether the mandate logic extends to abolishing select committee scrutiny generally. The question could not exist without the answer it follows, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “We went to an election, we had a campaign, we made very clear what we were going to do, and we’re going to do it.”

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: has the Government just learnt, with respect to KiwiRail, the lack of impact that the impact statement had on the previous Government?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the subject under debate — regulatory impact statements — but engages no claim made in the preceding turns, instead pivoting to the previous Government's record on KiwiRail. A friendly supplementary that would be unchanged whatever had just been argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the preceding exchange concerned when regulatory impact statements were suspended and the mandate claimed from the election, and this question does not take up either.

acuity.statement: What reports has she seen on the outlook from here?
acuity.explanation: A pre-set follow-up in a prepared sequence; it moves the answer along chronologically rather than engaging anything in the answer it follows, including the direct challenge to an opposition member's claim. On topic, which keeps it above zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis had just said of the member for Remutaka's claims that “I have seen no evidence to confirm those reports”, and this question does not take that up.

acuity.statement: What other policies, then, does the Government have to reduce the 40.6 percent of New Zealand’s emissions that come from the energy sector, given that the Minister’s own officials advise that only 5.7 percent of New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions come from electricity generation and the Climate Commission advised complementary measures to the emissions trading scheme (ETS) are required to shift industrial and process heat from carbon sources?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the concession just made, using the two figures the Minister has accepted to show that the renewable-electricity answer addresses only a small share of energy emissions, and then asks what covers the rest. The question is wholly contingent on the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: “Well, as the member rightly knows, those are very good statistics and I’m sure she’s correct.”

acuity.statement: What is his plan to fix market imbalances in an electricity market dominated by four gentailers, which today’s Generating Scarcity 2023 report shows has stifled investment in renewable electricity generation and resulted in billions of excess dividends to shareholders, all while thousands of New Zealanders struggle to heat their homes?
acuity.explanation: Squarely within the energy debate but engages no strand of the answer immediately before it, opening an independent prepared line about gentailer market structure. It would have been asked word for word whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just argued the ETS is “a critically important market-based tool” and accused the former Government of subsidising profitable businesses, and this question does not engage either point.

acuity.statement: Can he confirm that for the ETS alone to shift industrial process heat to electrification, the price needs to be in excess of $200 a tonne, and can he advise New Zealanders what it will do to their electricity and petrol bills at that price?
acuity.explanation: Takes the single tool the Minister has nominated and tests it on its own terms, supplying the carbon price such a shift would require and asking for the consumer consequence. Aimed at the content of the answer rather than at the Minister; slightly short of 1.0 only because an intervening answer on Lake Onslow is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: “this Government will use the emissions trading scheme, which is a critically important tool—and a critically important market-based tool—to help move New Zealand and bend the curve of emissions down”

acuity.statement: I think the Hon Julie Anne Genter put it very well around whether or not that label that is covered off in this part is going to be enough to form that switch. We’ve already heard from the Minister that he thinks the mechanism for inducing people to do the switch will be the emissions trading scheme (ETS).
acuity.explanation: Woods picks up Genter's two specific questions — the unanswered emissions advice and whether a label can substitute for a price incentive — and does something with them: she notes they went unanswered in Part 1, then supplies the Climate Commission's EV registration pathway (11% to 67% by 2030, 100% by 2035) and prices out the Minister's stated alternative lever at $235 a tonne, or roughly 80c a litre of petrol. The speech would have to be different if Genter had argued something else; it is built on her strand and extends it with figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And what impact would a labelling scheme have on consumer behaviour?" — Julie Anne Genter, who asked the Minister whether the energy economy label could substitute for a price incentive and whether he had advice on the fiscal risk of missing the 2030 carbon budget

acuity.statement: I thank the Minister for some of those responses. It’s pleasing to see that that label has been provided because it did cause some concern prior—well, earlier in the day—that things couldn’t be seen.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's point about the new, larger labels and acknowledges it resolves the earlier legibility complaint, then pivots to a prepared line of asks (the RIS, amendment papers, price differential) that engages nothing further the Minister said. Partial engagement with one strand of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm very pleased to see the new labels, which I hope members have received. They're bigger. You can now read the labels." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: It has been a long day after another very long day, and yet I’m yet to get any answer to the question I’ve asked more than once to the Minister of Transport.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the Minister's answers on the scheme) but engages no part of the preceding speaker's argument; it restates his own previously-asked question and would read identically whatever Utikere had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere spoke immediately before about the regulatory impact statement, Camilla Belich's Amendment Paper and the EV price differential, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: I note member Tangi Utikere was referring to a tabled amendment in the name of Camilla Belich which suggested that there should be continued identification of what the rebate values would’ve been if the scheme had not been repealed. This adds no value as we’re discontinuing the scheme. We don’t support that tabled amendment.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific amendment the previous speaker raised, states its substance accurately, and gives a reason for rejecting it. The reply would have to change if Utikere had raised a different amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my colleague Camilla Belich has a tabled Amendment Paper that does seek to insert new clause 22A. It does relate to the ability for sellers and importers of vehicles to identify a value that would have been applicable had the scheme not been repealed." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I thank the member Scott Willis for his question. You know, this part that we’re dealing with here is dealing with amendments to the Land Transport (Motor Vehicle Registration and Licensing) Regulations 2011, amendments to energy efficiency labelling, revocation of land transport regulations. The question I don’t think fits within the part that we’re debating.
acuity.explanation: Names the question and rules it outside the scope of Part 2, but engages none of its content — the rural/urban split of fees and rebates goes unaddressed. A gesture at the preceding turn rather than engagement with its substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would like to hear from the Minister an understanding of the proportion of fees and rebates that are paid and received by rural communities" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: I have to say, if I had to choose between the colour and the black and white version, I’m going black and white. Blue’s not really my colour. The Minister asked us to state a preference in terms for the kind of copy we want, so when it comes for releasing the regulatory impact statement we’d quite like that, whichever way—colour or black and white will work.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own colour-preference remark about the labels and turns it back on him as a demand for the regulatory impact statement in any format. Directly built on what he said, though it then moves to prepared questions on marginal abatement cost.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I prefer colour as well—it's blue." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I note the Hon Julie Anne Genter continues to ask questions about her tabled amendment. I’ve already said we don’t support it.
acuity.explanation: Genter's immediately preceding turn set out a substantive case for her amendment — manufacturer transition timing, the gap to 2030, lock-in of 20 years of emissions per vehicle, the current-account argument, and the claim that the ETS will not deliver — and closed by asking directly how the gap to 2030 is closed and why the Minister refers only to budgets to 2025. This reply names the amendment and the fact that she keeps raising it, and engages none of its content: no answer on the 2030 gap, no response on the ETS point, no reason given for opposing. It is a reference to the previous speaker rather than engagement with her argument, so it sits in the low band; the gesture at the debate (acknowledging the amendment is live) lifts it slightly above 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "How do we close the gap between now and 2030?"

acuity.statement: But what we still want to know, despite asking multiple times and not hearing from the Minister, is what the impact will be on EB2 and EB3. I think they’re the ones that have the most consideration. Certainly EB2 is the focus of the Climate Change Commission’s advice that was released this week, which makes it abundantly clear that if we are going to see the uptake that we need to get baked into our emissions reduction plans—if we’re going to see that uptake, there do need to be supplementary measures. People aren’t going to make the shift of their own volition at the moment.
acuity.explanation: This takes up precisely the strand Genter left open in a preceding turn — that the Minister has spoken only to the budget period ending 2025 — and does something with it: it concedes the part that was answered (on track for EB1, "that is absolutely the case"), then presses the unanswered remainder on EB2 and EB3 and supplies supporting evidence, the Climate Change Commission advice released that week, for why supplementary measures are needed. Accepting part and disputing the rest, with the gap named specifically, is high responsiveness; it is short of 1.0 because the argument about to be rebutted (the Minister's EB1 answer) was given before this window, so the engagement is with a strand of the debate rather than a specific proposition quoted back and dismantled.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "The Minister’s only referred to meeting our emissions budgets to 2025, not beyond 2025."

acuity.statement: So I wonder whether the Minister has any comments on that. And I still haven’t quite received a response around whether or not there is some justification for having a purchase agreement reference in there. Again, we haven’t had an opportunity to hear from people about what they think about this bill as part of the parliamentary process, and so I would be grateful if the Minister could turn his mind to those questions.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — Part 2, clauses 22 and 25, and Schedule 2 of the bill before the committee — but it engages no part of any preceding turn's argument. It is a fresh line of prepared questioning on the administrative wind-up provisions, and the only backward reference is to the speaker's own earlier unanswered question, not to anything another member said. That places it in the low band: on topic, not responsive. The note that a response is still outstanding is enough of a gesture at the running debate to sit above a bare 0.1, but there is nothing here that would have had to change had the Minister or Genter said something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about the vehicle label, the New South Wales end date for EV subsidies and his refusal of Genter's amendment, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: We can link that target to the Climate Change Commission’s advice released just this week, which shows that the emissions trading scheme alone is insufficient to substantially move people away from fossil fuel - powered vehicles. So what then? What then is the actual plan and the vision for moving people to the solutions and supporting our communities and our people, moving to the way that the world is going to have to adapt rather than clinging with desperation to an old world with old energy and dirty energy?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one live strand of the preceding turn — the Climate Change Commission advice released that week and its finding that the ETS by itself will not shift people out of fossil-fuel vehicles — and carries it to a different target, the emissions reduction plan's 30 percent zero-emissions light fleet by 2035, then puts the consequent question to the Minister. That is a genuine partial engagement rather than a mere echo. It is not higher because the speaker opens by flagging an issue she says has not yet been explored, and the body of the turn is her own prepared line on the 2035 target rather than work on the specific claim Woods made about EB2 and EB3; the engagement is with the evidence Woods cited, not with her argument about substituting measures in an emissions plan.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "Certainly EB2 is the focus of the Climate Change Commission’s advice that was released this week, which makes it abundantly clear that if we are going to see the uptake that we need to get baked into our emissions reduction plans—if we’re going to see that uptake, there do need to be supplementary measures."

acuity.statement: I thank the member for the question. In regard to his tabled amendment, we don’t support it. The policy intention of the legislation is for the rebate and ute tax scheme to end at midnight on 31 December 2023.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise point Utikere pressed — what time on 31 December the scheme ends — and supplies the specific answer (midnight), plus a direct position on the named Amendment Paper. Not a full 1.0 because Utikere's other questions (officials' advice, efficiency gains and emissions budgets) are left untouched, but the reply would have been different had the preceding speech asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Does it mean that it’s going to be at 5 o’clock when the shop closes?" — and his tabled amendment on the transitional provision for vehicles purchased before the close of 31 December 2023

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I do have a question for the Minister about the vehicle emissions and energy economy label in Schedule 3, now that we have the larger version of it, and thanks to the officials for getting that, or whoever it is that provided that.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive ministerial answer immediately precedes it — but it engages no part of that answer, opening instead a self-contained new line of questioning about the Schedule 3 label. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, and the gesture at material obtained earlier in the committee stage keeps it above 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just said "The policy intention of the legislation is for the rebate and ute tax scheme to end at midnight on 31 December 2023" and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: He said—if I heard correctly—that it will be at midnight on 31 December 2023. I’m interested in why he’s saying it’s at midnight on 31 December 2023, because of course the Schedules refer to the close of 31 December 2023, and if the close is to mean midnight, I think it should say midnight.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's answer given minutes earlier and does something with it: contrasts "midnight" against the Schedules' "close of 31 December 2023" and asks him to confirm the former on the record. The contribution could not exist in this form had the preceding turn said anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The policy intention of the legislation is for the rebate and ute tax scheme to end at midnight on 31 December 2023"

acuity.statement: We heard a lot from the Minister of Transport recently around how this is a scheme that is fiscally unsustainable. Yet we know that with the changes that the Labour Government had put in place in July of this year, already the take of the rebate is $33 million higher than the actual cost.
acuity.explanation: Brown's third-reading speech rested centrally on the claim that the scheme was fiscally irresponsible, citing a $300 million deficit. Utikere takes up precisely that strand and contests it with a counter-figure about the post-July settings, i.e. he engages the content of the fiscal claim rather than merely naming the Minister. The passage would have had to change if Brown had argued on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the policy which was put in place by the prior Government was fiscally irresponsible—a $300 million deficit left behind by the previous Government"

acuity.statement: This is an interesting point because they have also talked about EV infrastructure, yet we haven’t heard from the Minister—although the Minister has had ample opportunity today to tell us about that, to address that issue. There have been no comments on the roll-out of EV infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the charging-infrastructure strand of Brown's speech, so it is pointed at something he actually said, but it engages it only as an absence rather than contesting the substance of the commitment, and then moves to a cost-benefit-analysis aside. Partial engagement with one strand. (Whether the characterisation of the Minister's silence is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "we will continue to invest in the electric vehicle charging infrastructure to support this uptake over time"

acuity.statement: It really is a sad day for this Parliament, which started on 12 December as the clocks in the Chamber do indicate, because this will, if successfully passed this evening, be the third piece of legislation that this new Government have brought to the House under urgency and it will make a huge difference in a negative way to families and communities all around Aotearoa, New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: The opening is on the matter under debate — this bill and its passage — but engages no part of the argument Brown had just made about fiscal cost, inequity or market uncertainty. It is prepared condemnation about the Government's use of urgency and would read identically whatever case the Minister had put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the scheme was fiscally irresponsible and inequitable and that EV uptake would continue regardless, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: No, that’s not choice. It’s the opposite of choice, I say to the member. It is the opposite of choice. If people don’t have the ability to walk, cycle, or take public transport, they don’t have a choice.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Meager's interjected claim that cars represent choice and directly inverts it, supplying the reasoning: choice requires available alternatives, so where walking, cycling and public transport are unavailable there is no choice. The passage could not exist if Meager had not made that specific interjection — it engages the content of the claim rather than merely naming him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s choice." — James Meager

acuity.statement: What I’ve just heard is—I mean, this has been an incoherent policy, as we’ve heard throughout the day. It’s unsustainable and it actually doesn’t make sense. What this Government is doing is actually restoring a sensible, coherent climate change policy that will actually work.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at having just listened and then labels the policy incoherent without engaging any part of the preceding argument — not the abatement-cost claim, not the point-of-purchase price-signal mechanism, not the Climate Change Commission advice. The speech is at least on the matter under debate, so not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically whatever Genter had argued; a label applied to a previous speech is not engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued the Clean Car Discount had the best marginal abatement cost and that Climate Change Commission and Ministry of Transport evidence shows a price signal at the point of vehicle purchase is required to meet the carbon budgets; this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: Sir Michael Hardie Boys was a man of firsts. He was, of course, our first MMP Governor-General, selected for that role because of his legal background and training and because of the new and potentially challenging circumstances that a Governor-General under MMP may face—or perceived challenges that a Governor-General under MMP may face—as they were envisaged back in 1996.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Luxon's tribute — that Hardie Boys 'guided New Zealand during its transition to an MMP electoral system' and was appointed in 1996 ahead of the first MMP election — and develops it, explaining what the perceived constitutional risk actually was and that he oversaw two government formations. Partial rather than full: much of the surrounding speech is prepared tribute material that would stand whatever Luxon had said, and a condolence motion gives limited scope to engage an argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: 'Sir Michael was appointed as New Zealand's 17th Governor-General in 1996, ahead of New Zealand's first MMP election.'

acuity.statement: As the Leader of the Opposition just pointed out, Sir Michael did believe that Governors-General actually had a duty to speak out about the community’s concerns, and he frequently did so on issues such as inequality, family violence, and child abuse, which, of course, are issues that we are continuing to grapple with in this Parliament and at this time.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Hipkins's claim that Hardie Boys 'did, as Governor-General, on occasion challenge the Government of the day' and does something with it — supplies the specific issues he spoke out on and draws the consequence for the present Parliament. More than a mere reference: the content of the preceding claim is extended, so the passage would read differently had Hipkins said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: 'He did, as Governor-General, on occasion challenge the Government of the day.'

acuity.statement: As others have mentioned, he helped New Zealand navigate what could have been, and what many thought would be, a tumultuous time in our constitutional history. Perhaps the fact that that period of uncertainty is such a distant memory, rarely if ever thought of or acknowledged, is actually a tribute to how well the Governor-General of the time was able to handle that situation and reassure the public.
acuity.explanation: Takes the earlier speakers' point about the feared constitutional crisis around the first MMP election and draws out a consequence they did not — that its having been forgotten is itself the measure of how well it was handled. That is engagement with the content, not just a nod to it, though the rest of the speech is generic tribute.
acuity.subject: speaker
