acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: 'there was concern back in 1996 about whether or not this would politicise the role of the Governor-General'

acuity.statement: I want to celebrate a little bit on behalf of New Zealanders who, thanks to the Clean Car Discount and Clean Car Standard, have a greater choice thanks to applying those mechanisms at the supply side so that the vehicle importers could bring a wider choice of electric vehicles into the country and at a faster rate.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's turn immediately before argued the scheme took no options away and that choice talk is an urban abstraction. Tana takes up the choice strand — arguing the scheme widened the choice actually available to buyers via supply-side obligations on importers — so she engages the topic Patterson raised rather than merely restating prepared material. But she answers the topic, not his specific claim: nothing here touches the rural/ute cost transfer that was the substance of his argument, and the passage reads as prepared celebration of the policy. Partial engagement, placed just below the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "It’s taking no options away for urban people. They can still buy their Teslas."

acuity.statement: There is nothing stopping them, you’re right, but the thing is it was too early to pull the plug.
acuity.explanation: A direct, unscripted reply to the interjection just made: she concedes the factual point Bates asserted (importers are not barred from bringing EVs in) and then disputes the inference he drew from it, that the scheme was therefore dispensable. The sentence could not exist if Bates had said something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because the counter is asserted rather than developed — but the quality of the inference is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "There’s nothing stopping them."

acuity.statement: Today is a good day. The Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Discount Scheme Repeal) Amendment Bill will get rid of the fiscally irresponsible and blatantly unfair Clean Car Discount scheme, also known as the “ute tax”.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows Tana's turn but engages no part of it — not the abatement figure, not the fiscal-neutrality question she explicitly put, not the overseas comparison. The speech would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before him. It is prepared material on the correct subject (this bill, by name), which keeps it off 0.0, but there is nothing to point at as responsive. Scored low for unresponsiveness only; whether the "reverse Robin Hood" framing is fair or accurate is not an Acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Darleen Tana argued immediately before that 2 megatonnes of carbon dioxide were saved by the policy and that repeal is premature pending the regulatory impact statement's finding on fiscal neutrality, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The Labour Party has made their position clear: that we should not be involved in this conflict. There’s no UN resolution in favour of such actions, and there are countries in Europe and Scandinavia that are against joining this conflict. We have to be very mindful about getting involved in such conflicts, and I don’t believe that the Government have made a clear case for it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the justification Collins had just advanced for the deployment and disputes its sufficiency, pointing to the absence of a UN resolution and to other states declining to join — a direct engagement with her stated rationale rather than a generic objection. The surrounding speech is substantially prepared material about his own time as defence Minister (Kabul, Ukraine), which pulls it below the top band, but the engagement is pointable and specific to what she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The decision to deploy NZDF personnel was made in response to Houthis’ actions which threaten commercial shipping, and it represents the commitment of the Government to defending our national interests and supporting our international partners." — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Thank you very much. Very happy to advise the member in the House that the deployment will be finishing before or on 31 July this year, so that’s when, after that, I’d expect families will be able to see their loved ones again, and the costing is around $500,000, and that’s being paid for within NZDF baselines.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the three things asked for — end date, cost, and funding source — in the order asked. The reply would be entirely different had the question been different; this is the clearest form of engagement, answering the specific content put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how long is this deployment intended for? Is it costed, and when can the families of these personnel expect them home; sooner or later?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: In light of those answers, the Minister in media statements today also said that “we are going to need money in the future.” Does this send an indication to New Zealanders, and indeed to the House, that further NZDF deployments in the Middle East will be in the pipeline in the future?
acuity.explanation: Builds off the funding answer just given, testing whether paying from baselines now implies more deployments later. It engages the strand of her answer about money, though the substance of the question is drawn from an outside media remark rather than from what she said in the House, so it is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the costing is around $500,000, and that’s being paid for within NZDF baselines" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: No, the member should not take it as being that. What he should take it as is being that the New Zealand Defence Force has been left in a very difficult position after six—well, actually, the last three years of neglect, and that, clearly, promises that were made by a previous Minister, himself, to Defence around capital funding have not been complied with.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question squarely at the outset ("No") and offers an alternative reading of the quoted remark about future money, which is genuine engagement with its content. It then turns to the questioner's own record as a Minister, which is prepared counter-attack rather than further engagement, so it sits mid-band: one strand taken up, then a pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does this send an indication to New Zealanders, and indeed to the House, that further NZDF deployments in the Middle East will be in the pipeline in the future?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: Given that the Minister raised that particular matter, is the Minister now, then, committing to all of the capital projects that this Government—the Labour Government in its time—committed to, in the past six years?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the capital-funding charge Collins had just levelled at him and turns it into a demand that she commit to those same projects, drawing out a consequence of her own criticism. This question could not have been asked had she not said what she said, which is the strongest test of responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "promises that were made by a previous Minister, himself, to Defence around capital funding have not been complied with" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Well, I’m sorry but there was so much noise coming from the other side that I actually missed the last part of the member’s question that might have actually related to the statement.
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of either question put to her, including the first part about capital projects, which she does not claim to have missed. It stays within the matter under debate only in the sense of gesturing at the ministerial statement, so it sits at the bottom band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is the Minister now, then, committing to all of the capital projects that this Government—the Labour Government in its time—committed to, in the past six years?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: Oh, right. Well, there are two options: one was to deploy a number of personnel, and the second was to deploy six, so those were the options and Cabinet agreed.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the question asked, naming the two options put to Cabinet and the outcome. The answer is thin in content — that is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one — but it addresses precisely the thing asked and would have been different had a different question been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what other options did the Minister present to Cabinet for consideration with respect and response to the US and the UK’s bombing of Yemen?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: In the Minister’s statement she talked with respect to adding hugely inflationary costs to New Zealanders. My question to the Minister is: what evidence does the Minister have to suggest that attacks in the Red Sea and Panama Canal are indeed adding to inflation and cost of New Zealanders, and, if that is the case, when can New Zealanders expect a relief in the cost of living that currently impacts this country?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the cost-to-New-Zealanders claim from the statement and demands the evidence base for it, which is engagement with the specific assertion rather than the topic at large. It loses ground because it characterises her words inaccurately and drifts to the Panama Canal, which she never mentioned — but misdescribing the claim is an accuracy failing, and the attempt to engage the claim is still real.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Disruptions to shipping in the Red Sea and Suez Canal mean higher costs for New Zealanders—in fact, nearly 15 percent of global trade flows through this shipping lane." — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Sorry, but the member clearly wasn’t listening to the statement I just read out. I didn’t actually make that statement. I’m happy to remind him that 15 percent of world trade goes through there, and if anyone really wants to know what happens when our shipping lanes and our supply chains are interrupted, just think back to what happened to New Zealanders and to their lack of buying power when we had the COVID-19 situation.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a misquotation of her own statement and then restates the trade-volume figure and the supply-chain analogy that bear on the cost question asked. Correcting a misstatement of fact in the preceding turn is squarely responsive; the dismissive framing is a civility matter and does not reduce the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In the Minister’s statement she talked with respect to adding hugely inflationary costs to New Zealanders." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: Yes, can I just tell the member and the House that the Defence Force are delighted to be trusted to undertake this deployment, that the morale seems to be improving, they are getting to do the work that they came to Defence to do, and they are so happy that they’ve got a Minister who’s on their side.
acuity.explanation: Answers the topic put to her — whether the deployment is a priority for the NZDF — with an affirmative and a reason (the Force welcomes the task, morale is improving), so the reply is shaped by the question. But it does not take up the strand Henare actually pressed, that her own statement concedes higher costs and that the NZDF faces challenges; it substitutes enthusiasm for the trade-off he raised and closes on an unrelated slogan. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister think that this is indeed the priority for the Defence Force?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: This Government’s denial—which will lead to some of our questions that I have—that this conflict in Yemen is connected to the war in Gaza is naive and dangerous—at best, wilfully ignorant—because we have seen, quite clearly across the world, that the Houthi have stated that their attacks on shipping are in response to Israel’s bombardment of Gaza and will only stop when a ceasefire is reached.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and clearly aimed at the Government's position, but it engages no part of the argument in the turn it follows. Nothing in it would change if Collins had said something different about the deployment; the content is set by the Greens' own prepared case rather than by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Judith Collins's preceding turn said "the morale seems to be improving" and that the Defence Force "are delighted to be trusted to undertake this deployment", and this statement does not take any of that up — it is prepared Green material on the Yemen/Gaza link, gesturing at the debate under way.

acuity.statement: I’d also remind the member that New Zealand has been involved in matters around the Red Sea since 2013. It’s been going on for quite a long time, and no matter what the Houthis may say is their reason for doing what they’re doing, there are 50 other nations that are affected by this.
acuity.explanation: Takes Davidson's central premise — that the Houthis' stated Gaza rationale makes the two conflicts one — and does something with it, conceding what the Houthis say and disputing its relevance by pointing to NZ's involvement since 2013 and the 50 affected nations. She goes on in the same turn to pick up her "independent foreign policy" strand and her reliance on global commentators as well. This speech would have to be written differently had Davidson argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Houthi have stated that their attacks on shipping are in response to Israel’s bombardment of Gaza and will only stop when a ceasefire is reached" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: What is the Minister’s end game? Does she believe that this deployment into the Red Sea is what is going to find enduring peace in the Middle East? Does the Minister believe that our association with the US and the UK—who are already seen to be meddling right around the world—will de-escalate violence, and does she believe that escalating violence is truly in the best interest of New Zealanders?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the answer just given — Collins's "best interests of New Zealanders" test — and turns it into a question about whether escalation can satisfy that test. But it leaves the substance of Collins's reply untouched (the 2013 involvement, the 50 affected nations, the shipping cost argument) and returns to her prepared de-escalation framing. Engages in part.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "decisions are made on the best interests of New Zealand and New Zealanders" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: I’m very happy to tell the member that I absolutely support the New Zealand Defence Force in what they’re doing. This is the right decision. New Zealand is not a freeloader.
acuity.explanation: Three questions were put — the end game, whether the deployment brings enduring peace, whether alignment with the US and UK de-escalates — and none is engaged. The reply asserts support for the NZDF and that the decision is right, then uses Davidson as a target by imputing support for the Houthis to her. Naming an opponent is not engaging her claim; this is a near-identical answer to whatever she had asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does she believe that escalating violence is truly in the best interest of New Zealanders?" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: Does the Minister support calls to end genocide and have a ceasefire and end further harm, and, on that, then, where was the public debate? If the Minister feels truly and confident that she has New Zealanders’ best interests at heart, where was the big debate?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and addressed to the Minister, but it leaves the charge just made against her unanswered and the freeloader argument untouched, reverting to prepared material about the absence of a public debate. A gesture at the exchange rather than engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Judith Collins had just said "the member may wish to, as she has today—express support for the Houthis" and "New Zealand is not a freeloader", and this statement takes up neither — it returns to the public-mandate point from her own opening.

acuity.statement: Look, I don’t think any of that has anything to do with the statement that I’ve made today. But I would say to that member that we all love world peace; we’d just like to see a bit more of it.
acuity.explanation: She identifies what was asked well enough to rule it outside the scope of her statement, which is a minimal form of taking it up, but she engages no part of its content — neither the ceasefire question nor the absence of public debate — and closes with a quip that would serve against any question Davidson might have asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does the Minister support calls to end genocide and have a ceasefire and end further harm, and, on that, then, where was the public debate?" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: We, as a country, cannot wish the evils of the world away. We must stand as a partner in a global society and play our important part in it.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive Green argument that the deployment risks escalation and lacks a public mandate, and glances at it with the line about not wishing the world's evils away. Everything else is a prepared ACT statement of support — trade volumes, freedom of navigation, the rules-based order — which would read identically whatever Davidson had argued. On the subject under debate, engaging none of the reasoning in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our long held values and tradition of focusing our efforts on peacekeeping and enduring justice" — Marama Davidson (gestured at only; the Green case for de-escalation and for a public mandate is not taken up)

acuity.statement: We cannot just sit in blissful ignorance and naivety and think that everyone else needs to protect us and protect our shipping lanes. We cannot sit back and wait for someone else to sort it out for us. So, for the benefit of members opposite, I’ll say it again: New Zealanders are not freeloaders; we are going to do our bit.
acuity.explanation: The closing speech inverts Davidson's charge of naivety and addresses itself explicitly to members opposite, so it is not indifferent to the debate. But it re-states the Government's prepared case — the Cape of Good Hope detour, supply chains, the freeloader line repeated — without engaging the escalation argument or the independent-foreign-policy objection that was put. A rhetorical turn on an opponent's word rather than engagement with her claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Government’s denial ... is naive and dangerous" — Marama Davidson (the word is turned back on her, but the argument behind it is not addressed)

acuity.statement: Could I ask the Prime Minister as to whether or not it’s axiomatic that if there is a dramatic decline, which is now the world’s leading decline in tobacco smoking, then it’s quite possible that the instance of tax will go down as well; and, second, that the legislation about which the Leader of the Opposition is talking was not constructed by him but by New Zealand First, which led to the dramatic fall in tobacco smoking in the first place? And that’s a fact.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact premise of Hipkins' line of questioning — that reverting the legislation raises tobacco tax revenue — and works on it directly, arguing that a falling smoking rate implies falling tax incidence, then disputes the authorship of the legislation Hipkins is relying on. The intervention would be different if Hipkins had pressed a different point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Will projected Government revenue from tobacco sales increase or decrease as a result of his Government’s decision to wind back changes to smoke-free legislation?"

acuity.statement: Does he, therefore, agree with Nicola Willis, who said, “Coming back to those extra sources of revenue and other savings areas that will help us to fund tax reduction, we have to remember that the changes to smoke-free legislation had a significant impact on the Government books - with about $1 billion there.”; if so, why does he think that more people smoking or smoking more is an acceptable way of funding tax cuts?
acuity.explanation: Builds on the answer just given rather than restating the prepared question: having been told revenue forecasts are Budget-sensitive and that the goal is lower smoking, he produces the Finance Minister's own quantified statement about the fiscal effect, which cuts against the answer's premise. The 'therefore' is doing real work.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "Revenue forecasts are Budget-sensitive, but we want lower smoking rates across this country—that’s what we’re going to do."

acuity.statement: How much revenue would the Government get from illegally smuggled and sold counterfeit cigarettes that are now dominating the Australian market, with organised crime taking over and the situation getting out of control?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the revenue strand of the exchange and redirects it to the black market, which engages the topic of the questioning without answering the specific claim about the Crown's tobacco take under the reverted legislation. Partial engagement: a recognisable response to the line of attack rather than to its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "why does he think that more people smoking or smoking more is an acceptable way of funding tax cuts?"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister please tell me why he is unable to answer how many people in Lower Hutt are presently on the social housing waiting list?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the matter under debate and glances at the wait-list figures the Minister had just cited, but engages no part of his argument about vacant homes; the substance is a pre-held grievance about an unanswered written question rather than anything in the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "with over 25,000 families on the social housing wait-list—20,000 more than six years ago—social housing homes should not be left empty for a day longer than absolutely necessary"

acuity.statement: Well, that was one of the stranger speeches I’ve heard; because whilst David Seymour strikes a knife into the heart of the Productivity Commission, he sings its praises. He tells us about the great reports that it’s done and names numerous people who have served with praise as he twists that knife.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact structure of Seymour's opening speech — the praise for the commission's reports and the named tribute to its commissioners — and turns it against the motion as a self-contradiction. The remark could not have been made had Seymour argued instead that the commission did poor work, so the speech is shaped by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is not, in any way, an indictment on the quality of the work of the Productivity Commission. The Productivity Commission has done some tremendous work over the past decade or so" — and the roll-call tribute to commissioners — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Have a look at clause 11 of the bill. What does it do? All employment contracts are terminated.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests Seymour's assurance about the treatment of commission staff by pointing to a specific clause of the bill he had just described in terms of savings provisions. It engages the content of the preceding claim at the level of the bill's text rather than merely restating opposition to the measure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we want to ensure that those people who were working for the Productivity Commission are given every opportunity to find new employment within the Government, that those people do not find themselves unfairly treated throughout this process" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: And, of course, how much is the ministry of regulation going to cost us? We don’t know.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the funding strand Seymour raised and presses it, but engages the topic rather than the specific figure: it does not take up or test the approximately $6 million a year Seymour named, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the claim as made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the new “Ministry of Regulation” that will, in part, be funded by the funding that would have gone on to the Productivity Commission—approximately $6 million each year" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Unfortunately, the work that they did didn’t transfer into actions, and actions actually matter. Having a regulations ministry gets to the pointy end, the bit that makes the difference, the little bits that actually unblock the blockages and allow people to actually get on and be more productive.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Shaw's argument — that the Commission's good work was never acted on — and turns it to the opposite conclusion (so abolish it and fund the regulations ministry instead). It engages that specific concession rather than inventing a target, but it does not touch Shaw's main contention that the two questions are distinct and must be judged separately, and the rest is prepared commendation of the bill. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Shaw: "a lot of the time that good work just fell on deaf ears"

acuity.statement: New Zealand First rises to support this New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill. Essentially, the Productivity Commission has become superfluous, replaced by the new ministry of regulation.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, but engages no part of the preceding arguments. Shaw had just insisted the new ministry is a distinct question; Patterson restates the replacement rationale without acknowledging or answering that, then moves to prepared material about reports and working groups and commendation of the Minister. The speech would read identically whatever Shaw and Smith had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Shaw argued that "the debate tonight isn’t about whether or not we should have a ministry of regulation or deregulation" and that the disestablishment must be judged on its own merits, and this statement does not take that up — it simply asserts the replacement Shaw said was beside the point.

acuity.statement: Mr Seymour described it as simple; I think it’s silly and sad. Mr Patterson, who just sat down, said that the ACT Party now believed the Productivity Commission was superfluous. Actually, that’s not what Mr Seymour said at all.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the specific claim made moments earlier by the previous speaker and does something with it — contradicts it against what the Minister himself said, to build a point about confusion on the Government benches. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged had Patterson argued differently; this is squarely engaged rebuttal, which is the top of the band regardless of how combative it is.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "the Productivity Commission has become superfluous, replaced by the new ministry of regulation"

acuity.statement: Now, was it perfect? No. I agree with Mr Shaw; I don’t think that the way it was set up helped in terms of the way recommendations were adopted. There is a lot that could be done.
acuity.explanation: Accepts a specific strand of Shaw's argument — the design flaw about responding to recommendations — and concedes it while disputing the conclusion drawn from it. The engagement is pointable and it shapes his own position (fix the statute rather than repeal it), though it is agreement rather than a worked-through rebuttal, so just short of the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Shaw: "there’s no requirement upon the Government to respond to its reports"

acuity.statement: My colleagues on this side of the House have already spoken on the irony of some of those changes, but I would just like to make the simple point that, surely, improving productivity to drive prosperity for all New Zealanders would be something everyone could agree on. And it seems like we are all in agreement that the Productivity Commission does excellent work to this end. So why is it that they are being disestablished?
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding speaker, Catherine Wedd, made a specific argument that productivity is NOT achieved by the Productivity Commission but by cutting regulation on primary industries. Verrall does not take that up at all; she instead asserts that 'we are all in agreement that the Productivity Commission does excellent work', which is precisely what Wedd had just denied. Her speech is squarely on the subject under debate and gestures at the debate ('there's clearly some confusion in the House tonight'), and the rest of it engages the Minister's earlier first-reading rationale rather than the argument she actually follows. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate, not engagement with the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "But that is not achieved by the Productivity Commission; it’s achieved by supporting our food producers and primary industries." — Verrall does not take up Wedd's claim that the Commission is not the mechanism for productivity gains.

acuity.statement: And then there was Ayesha Verrall, who I don’t think had anything particularly new to say other than a series of political attacks, but what she did manage to say is that there should be a regulatory impact statement on this bill. Well, let me be clear: one of the things I intend to do in this Government as the Minister for Regulation is make sure that regulatory impact analysis is focused on regulation that actually puts restrictions on the use and exchange of private property.
acuity.explanation: This takes the single most concrete demand in the preceding turn — that a regulatory impact statement be produced on this bill — and does something with it: it concedes the point was made, states a criterion for when regulatory impact analysis applies (restrictions on the use and exchange of private property), and draws the consequence that disestablishing a department falls outside it. The speech would have had to be different had Verrall asked for something else; he also tracks and answers the other specific contributions by name. Engagement is what is scored here, not whether the private-property criterion is a sound basis for the answer, and not the dismissive framing of her speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "I’d love to see a regulatory impact statement on this bill."

acuity.statement: Well, the difficulty is that the policy of this bill is simply to disestablish a perfectly good agency.
acuity.explanation: Seymour closed by instructing the Opposition to stop making personal attacks and to argue the policy of the bill in this reading. Webb opens by accepting that frame and immediately naming a policy objection — that the bill's policy is the disestablishment of a functioning agency — which answers the challenge on its own terms rather than restating prepared condemnation. It engages the invitation squarely but is a single assertion that does not yet take up Seymour's substantive claim that there is no contradiction in praising the Commission's work while reallocating its funding, so it sits above a topic-only glance and below full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "try being a little bit constructive, talking about the policy, talking about the bill, fewer of the personal attacks"

acuity.statement: What I would like to say is there are a couple of points that were raised by the “Minister for disestablishing the commission”, one of which was perceived politicisation of the commission itself. There is quite an easy fix for that, and it is not just to appoint people who you think agree with you. It’s actually to change the governing legislation to establish an independent nominating committee such as that we have for the guardians of the super fund, or, frankly, for the Treasury board, or for the Climate Change Commission, and so on.
acuity.explanation: Shaw takes up a specific argument made by the preceding speaker (the commission's alleged politicisation) and does something with it: he concedes the problem and supplies a remedy that would address it without disestablishment, citing comparable nominating arrangements. He also answers the Minister's invitation to put policy proposals, and anticipates and rebuts the budgetary counter-argument. The speech would be materially different had the preceding argument been a different critique of the commission. Held slightly below the top band only because the engaged turn cannot be pointed at verbatim in the window supplied, and because much of the surrounding material is prepared proposals rather than engagement. Scored only on engagement — not on whether the reasoning is sound, true, precise or polite.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon David Seymour — the argument that the Productivity Commission had become politicised, which Shaw quotes as "perceived politicisation of the commission itself" from Seymour's contribution "just now". Seymour's own turn sits immediately before this one in the debate but is outside the excerpt supplied, so the fragment is only pointable through Shaw's quoting of it.

acuity.statement: We do not lack the capacity to write reports. What we lack is the capacity to actually enact anything and get some productivity going, as Stuart Smith has just pointed out in his previous contribution.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Smith's preceding turn — that the Productivity Commission produced good work but failed to convert it into action — names it as the core issue, and does something with it rather than merely referencing it: he supplies his own figures (6,500 at MBIE, 3,500 at MPI) to argue the advisory capacity Smith credited to the Commission already exists elsewhere, which is why repeal costs nothing. Had Smith argued the Commission's reports were themselves poor, this passage would have had to change. Held below the top band because the engagement is affirmation and extension rather than a rebuttal that tests Smith's reasoning, and much of the surrounding speech (National Lamb Day, the sheep-flock statistic) is prepared material that would have been delivered whoever spoke before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But their problem is transferring those thoughts into actions and actually getting a result." — Stuart Smith

acuity.statement: And we’re not going to do it through cups of tea and what we saw at the port; we’re going to do it through good evidence. That’s what we need.
acuity.explanation: White takes Wedd's port-of-Napier anecdote — the evidentiary core of Wedd's productivity case — and directly contests its status as evidence, contrasting it with the Productivity Commission's independent 'deep dives'. The speech would have to change if Wedd had argued from something other than a site visit, so the engagement is specific rather than a mere reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "just last week I was actually at the port of Napier, and it was just incredible to see the exports going through the port"

acuity.statement: We’ve heard a lot tonight about arrogance and control. I wonder: did the Productivity Commission ask the previous Government to bloat the Public Service? Did the Productivity Commission ask the previous Government to increase the jobseeker benefit by 66,000 over the last six years? Was that arrogance or control?
acuity.explanation: Hamilton names the specific charge just put (arrogance) and glances at the substance by questioning whether the Commission actually restrained the previous Government — which bears on White's claim that losing it is a tragedy. But he mostly turns the label back on the previous Government rather than engaging her reasons (independence, evidence, no select committee), so this is partial engagement that pivots to the opponent's record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "it’s a tragedy to lose that for something that is, in fact, as many people have said tonight, a vanity project—and it’s one based on arrogance"

acuity.statement: Productivity is at the heart of this coalition agreement, and, indeed, a refocused ministry will have the tools to cut through red tape that the Productivity Commission didn’t, especially as the last Government didn’t really listen anyway.
acuity.explanation: This takes up White's concession that the Commission could have been listened to more and converts it into an argument for repeal — the body lacked the tools and was ignored regardless. It engages the specific strand of her case rather than simply asserting the Government's position, though it does not answer her independence or process objections.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Maybe we could have listened to it more. It’s a tragedy to lose that for something that"

acuity.statement: So, for me, that only points to one thing, which is this Minister wants to control the evidence that is brought to him, because he can control it if it’s a department which he controls and which he’s the Minister for. The Productivity Commission was independent. This bill is all about control.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's case was that advice is abundant, including from inside the public sector, so the Commission is redundant. Edmonds does engage that strand — her answer is that advice from a department the Minister controls is not the same good as advice from an independent body — so the engagement is pointable. But she aims almost entirely at a speech outside this window (the Minister's second reading speech), never takes up Patterson's actual pivot from advice to action or his Kāinga Ora example, and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on the Commission's statutory purpose. One strand engaged, then back to the script.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there is inordinate capacity within the public sector to give us the advice, to look at various issues as they come up" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: The irony is that this commission was set up by the ACT Party, and now it is the ACT Party that actually want to disestablish it.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — clause 11, the repeal, the ministry of regulation — but indifferent to what precedes it. Substitute any other argument on the same topic for Patterson's or Edmonds' turns and this speech is unchanged: the ACT-irony framing, the "hij-ACT Party" line and the circus/clowns quotation are all prepared. Naming Webb and Robertson is a reference, not an engagement, and repeating "vanity project" adds nothing to it. The gesture at the debate lifts it to 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Edmonds argued the Commission's value was providing independent high-level debate that the public could submit to, and Patterson argued the public sector already has capacity to supply that advice; this statement takes up neither. It gestures at the debate ("listening to the debate in the House tonight") and cites colleagues who spoke earlier outside this window (Duncan Webb, Grant Robertson), but engages no argument in it.

acuity.statement: But what happens here is the Productivity Commission is creating these reports and they’re creating some recommendations that don’t necessarily work in practice, on the ground, in the orchards, in the productive sector.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds and Leary both rested the defence of the Commission on the worth of its independent inquiries. Wedd contradicts that worth at the level of the topic — the reports don't work on the ground — but she never touches a specific inquiry, a specific recommendation, or the independence argument that was the actual load-bearing claim against the repeal. The turn is a prepared Hawke's Bay horticulture set-piece (RSE scheme, tonnes per hectare, water storage) that would have run identically whatever had been said before it; her one concession to the chamber is to justify its relevance after being pulled up. On topic, engaging no part of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Since 2011, there has been a number of inquiries into different areas: housing, frontier firms." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: As we all know, the committee of the whole House stage is probably the most important stage of the passage of a bill. If we remember our first-year law classes from Otago University, it is the stage where you get to interrogate a bill, clause by clause, line by line, comma by comma, to make sure that what comes out of this House is the most high-quality, clean, clearest, unambiguous legislation that this House can produce.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what Seymour had just said — his invitation for searching, detailed questions and his framing of what the committee stage is for — and then supplies such questions. But it engages no part of Seymour's actual substantive material (the four purposes in clause 3, the $6 million, the Crown Entities Act and Ombudsman Act consequences), moving instead to a prepared list of interpretation-clause questions. Had Seymour argued something different about clause 3, this opening would have been unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I hope that there'll be more searching questions about the details of this legislation, for Mr Robertson's benefit, exactly as the committee of the whole House stage is supposed to be used." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Well, I can inform the member that interpretation sections are normal. They are in every piece of legislation that I’ve ever seen and probably every piece of legislation that he will ever see. Why, for instance, was “employee” defined as having “the same meaning as in … the Crown Entities Act”? Well, that would be because the Productivity Commission is a Crown entity, and so, therefore, the employees are employees of a Crown entity.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific questions just put: why an interpretation clause appears in a repeal bill, and why "employee" is defined by reference to the Crown Entities Act rather than a general definition. It corrects the premise of Meager's speculation (that the cross-reference signals special treatment of commission staff) by supplying the plain reason — the commission is a Crown entity. The speech would be entirely different had Meager asked about other clauses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m very, very interested to know: what was the thinking and the process behind having this interpretation clause?" and "why this particular definition was put into this Act" — James Meager

acuity.statement: I’d really like to know some detail around how the Minister came to the decision to word that clause in such a way. Was there widespread consultation with the register of land or other entities—are they the right entity to actually be charged with this entity?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and glances at the same commission-to-Ministry renaming Seymour had just been discussing, but engages none of his answers — it is a new, self-contained question about a different clause that would read identically whatever Seymour had replied to Meager.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just explained that "Ministry" is defined as shorthand to save repeating a more complex concept, and this statement does not take that explanation up; it opens a fresh line on Schedule 1's registers clause.

acuity.statement: It takes what was originally a decent, good, well-intended idea which unfortunately has run its course. The Productivity Commission was built with all the best intentions in the world, but report after report, Government after Government—struggle to see what we could get from those reports that is going to actually make this country tick, what’s going to make the boat run faster.
acuity.explanation: Robertson's immediately preceding second-reading speech rested on the claim that the Commission does valuable big-picture work that no ministry of regulation can replace, and that the House had agreed it was a good body. Meager takes up that one strand — conceding the Commission was well-intentioned while disputing that its reports produce anything usable — and elsewhere points to the coalition agreements as what is being done "in lieu of a Productivity Commission". But he engages only the general case, not Robertson's specific arguments (the absent select committee, the urgency hypocrisy, the false-equivalence point), and most of the speech is prepared electorate and government-of-action material that would stand unchanged whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "All we've heard from around the House tonight is that the Productivity Commission is a good body that's done some good things" / "the case for the Productivity Commission is actually about big-picture thinking" — Grant Robertson

acuity.statement: Well, it’s very simple: the schedule provides that contracts will be honoured. The identity of the counterparty will change, but what they get will be delivered as if the Productivity Commission was still the counterparty.
acuity.explanation: Webb's question was specific: Schedule 1 transfers the Commission's contractual obligations to a new entity and bars counterparties from cancelling. Seymour answers that precise mechanism — novation of the counterparty with performance preserved — which is squarely the point put to him and could not have been said in response to a different question. Short of 1.0 only because he leaves the second half of Webb's question (how this sits with the ACT Party's stated view of freedom of contract) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It appears that no one's entitled to cancel their contractual arrangements on the basis that they've got a new entity, even though they don't want to contract with the ministry" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I know that the Minister in the chair will be keen to explain—in some detail, I hope—what the purposes listed in clause 3 of Part 1 are actually intended to do. Because we’ve heard during the debate on the first and second readings of this legislation a whole range of good reasons from this side of the House about the ineffectiveness of the Productivity Commission.
acuity.explanation: The preceding exchange was a concrete question and answer about whether Schedule 1 strips counterparties of the right to exit their contracts. Simpson engages no part of it, instead inviting the Minister to expound on paragraphs (a) to (d) of clause 3 — material that would read identically whatever Webb and Seymour had just said. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 because it is at least on the bill before the committee and gestures at the earlier readings of this same debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb had just raised the Schedule 1 contract-transfer problem and Seymour had answered it on novation, and this statement does not take up either; it opens a fresh line on clause 3's purposes

acuity.statement: Second of all, the final report the member’s referred to, I’m advised, will be reported back around mid-February. So that report will be added to the set of assets that New Zealand will always have from the great work that has been done by the Productivity Commission to date.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific thing Court asked about — the fate of the unfinished 'improving economic resilience' report — supplies the timing and states where it will sit. The answer would be different had Court asked about something else; only the 'which ministry' strand is left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: 'I note, with interest, that the commission is working on a report on improving economic resilience, which is due to be finalised in February 2024.'

acuity.statement: I did have a number of other questions that I thought I would ask. One of my questions perhaps is more a global question about the bill generally, and that is the budget implications, because, obviously, as has been made clear throughout the debates tonight, this is related to, and the funds will be used for, a new ministry.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the disestablishment bill — and gestures at the chamber's earlier exchanges, but engages no part of Seymour's immediately preceding answer about the wind-down date or the final report. This is a prepared list of further questions that would have been delivered unchanged whatever Seymour had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Seymour had just answered Court on the commission's 29 February wind-down and the mid-February final report, and this statement does not take either up, opening instead on budget implications.

acuity.statement: Duncan Webb asked, as a law professor, why repeal this Act. Well, actually, the law that’s being passed tonight will self-repeal, and the reason for that is that in a years’ time, when all of the transitions and savings have been done, the business has been wound up, there is no longer a need to have this Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes Webb's specific puzzle — why repeal a repeal Act, and would that revive the commission — and answers its reasoning directly, distinguishing self-repeal from undoing the earlier repeal. The reply is wholly shaped by the question it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'So if the Minister could clarify what the effect of a repeal of a repeal is, that would be really useful, because if a repeal of a repeal then restores what we had before, we’re going to be in all kinds of trouble on 30 June 2025.'

acuity.statement: The Productivity Commission—I mean, it’s not a place that has personal relationships; it’s a Crown entity. The Crown is going to honour its commitments made through the Productivity Commission through another entity—in this case, the Treasury. From the point of view of those counterparties to contract, nothing changes.
acuity.explanation: Engages Webb's specific objection about the bill overriding personal advisory contracts, disputing its premise that a Crown entity has such relationships and then answering the practical consequence for counterparties. Clearly shaped by the preceding argument rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'I am still curious as to why it is that the bill intervenes in contractual relationships even when the relationship might be a personal one.'

acuity.statement: But I’m really interested in the Minister’s responses to what are the strategic consequences of the disestablishment of the Productivity Commission, because my understanding is that, by in large, the Productivity Commission has produced a lot of great work, but not a lot has been done with that work.
acuity.explanation: Foster picks up one strand of Mooney's preceding turn — the productivity problem and what the Commission's work was for — and turns it into a question about where that work will now be carried on. He engages the topic Mooney raised rather than Mooney's specific claim about regulatory burden on small business, and then moves to his own prepared question on clause 3(c), so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "how is this going to ensure that we help address the productivity problems that have been identified for decades in this country?"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to build on this point because you can make the argument that New Zealanders continue to get sick and therefore we should disestablish the health service because we haven’t healed everybody yet, and, actually, that argument doesn’t follow that just because Governments are too self-interested or captured by vested interests to act on recommendations isn’t a good reason to get rid of the people who thought of the recommendations.
acuity.explanation: Shaw takes the exact premise Foster had just advanced — that the Commission's work was ignored — and attacks its inference directly with a reductio (we do not abolish the health service because people still get sick), then converts it into a counter-conclusion about accountability. The speech would have to be rewritten if Foster had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "the Productivity Commission has produced a lot of great work, but not a lot has been done with that work"

acuity.statement: The consequences being provided to, that are referred to in this bill, are not the wider policy consequences that both he and James Shaw have tried to refer to—for example, were there other ways to achieve a policy objective?
acuity.explanation: Seymour identifies the specific clause both members asked about and corrects their reading of the word "consequences", distinguishing legislative knock-on effects from wider policy alternatives. He engages the actual content of the two preceding questions rather than reciting prepared material; he declines to answer Shaw's substantive question, but that is responsiveness of a different kind and not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "In clause 3(c), we have, “provide for the consequences of the disestablishment;”" — and James Shaw's question "whether he considered other options"

acuity.statement: Then there is a question—well, it wasn’t really a question—from Joseph Mooney. It sort of started off autobiographical, then his speech sort of got into the pseudo-philosophical, and then he made the point that red tape and regulation are bad for business when it’s done badly and when it’s excessive. I agree with that, and we’re going to be doing a lot to ensure that that is less and less the case over this term of Government.
acuity.explanation: Seymour restates the substance of Mooney's turn and concedes the point about excessive regulation, so there is genuine engagement with its content. But he reduces a long contribution to a single proposition and declines to address the question actually put — what relief small-business owners will see — treating it as out of scope, so this is engagement with the topic rather than with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "good regulation, good law is the DNA of our society" and his question about relief for small-business owners

acuity.statement: Is it his position as Prime Minister that Ministers should be presenting to officials party policy documents and giving them those documents as instructions for further advice to be prepared?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Prime Minister's disclaimer of knowledge and converts it into the question it leaves open — not what he knows, but whether he endorses the practice. The question would be different had Luxon answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "As Prime Minister, I'm unaware of what Ministers are actually asking their officials for advice." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: So why would New Zealand First’s party policy document have been presented to officials as Government instruction?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the manifesto point and presses the distinction the answer glosses over — between officials having a manifesto and a party document being handed over as Government instruction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We campaigned on a set of policies; it's right that officials would have those manifestos." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister not find it extraordinary that the Opposition that’s raising in the House today this issue nevertheless supported the very same party writing sound policy in 2018-19 which led to the biggest drop in the whole world of cigarette smoking? That’s the fact, isn’t it?
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand about NZ First writing smoking policy, but answers it with the Opposition's past support rather than the claim about documents given to officials as instruction. One strand taken up, then a pivot to the other side's record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why would New Zealand First's party policy document have been presented to officials as Government instruction?" — Chris Hipkins

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that there is a difference between having found whether genocide has taken place or whether there is a plausible risk of genocide taking place, and that article 1 of the convention requires New Zealand to take action to prevent genocide before it occurs—i.e., when there is a plausible risk?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact ground of the answer and shows it is beside the point being put: the obligation is said to be triggered by plausible risk, not by a finding of genocide. Directly dependent on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the court did not make any findings that Israel has actually engaged in genocidal conduct" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister believe it is important to use a word as heavy as “genocide” accurately and only when fully justified by the facts, in order to respect those many victims throughout history who, tragically, have suffered from actual genocide?
acuity.explanation: Engages the preceding line of questioning only at the level of the word used, not the legal argument about article 1 and plausible risk. A gesture at the premise rather than a reply to the reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a plausible risk of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza" — James Shaw

acuity.statement: Including the Palestinians right now, who are suffering from genocide.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the "victims of actual genocide" framing in the question being asked and contradicts it on its own terms by naming a present case, rather than changing the subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the casual, lazy misuse of the word "genocide"" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: How can she say beneficiaries will be better off, when Treasury is forecasting annual wage growth to be 5.1 percent in June 2025 compared with the forecasted 2.5 percent rate of inflation in June 2025, where wage growth clearly outstrips inflation?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the assertion just made and puts specific Treasury forecasts against it. The question could not have been asked in this form if the previous answer had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Beneficiaries will be better off under our Government" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: What advice has she received on the child poverty implications for reversing the indexation of benefits from wages to inflation, and what is that advice?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and loosely glances at the "good data" answer, but opens a prepared new line on child poverty rather than taking up the dismissal of the forecasts just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Forecasts are exactly that. We'll make decisions based on good data" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Does she think snatching money away from the most vulnerable New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally acceptable?
acuity.explanation: Does not take up the claim about advice received at all; substitutes a general moral charge that would have worked after any answer on the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I've received a large amount of advice around child poverty reduction" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: What sorts of areas are firms feeling more confident in?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific finding just reported and asks for its breakdown, so it depends on the content of the preceding answer — though it is a brief, cued follow-up rather than engagement with any argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This survey showed a sharp pick-up in business confidence in the final quarter of 2023" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: But, I have to say, it started—as Minister McClay has said—with discussions in 2015 under the previous National Government. It really began to be negotiated in 2018 and, indeed, it concluded—and I too, along with the Minister, want to thank the officials.
acuity.explanation: Takes up McClay's specific origin claim (the 2015 start under National) and does something modest with it — confirms it, then supplies the next milestone, 2018, and joins the thanks to officials. It engages one strand of the preceding speech rather than its substance, and then moves into prepared acknowledgements of named individuals that would have been delivered whatever McClay said, so it sits mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: 'In 2015, under the fifth National Government, we embarked on a journey towards a free-trade agreement (FTA) with the European Union by launching the preparatory process for negotiations on an FTA.'

acuity.statement: Look, the Minister has gone through a number of the technical points of this piece of legislation in adjusting our legislation to meet the requirements of the Act. There are some critical things that we took into this negotiation that we've protected. One was Pharmac.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly inventories what the preceding speech covered — the legislative amendments needed to align domestic law with the FTA — and then supplies what it omitted: the defensive interests secured in negotiation, beginning with Pharmac. The speech is shaped by McClay's coverage, since the division of labour it announces only makes sense given what he had just set out. Not a full 1.0: it supplements rather than engages or disputes any specific claim, and the Pharmac material is prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: 'There are a number of legislative and regulatory amendments that are required to align New Zealand’s domestic law with our obligations in the FTA.'

acuity.statement: The Hon Damien O’Connor mentioned Pharmac, which has been under pressure in a number of sets of trade agreements.
acuity.explanation: Shaw's speech is substantially prepared Green Party history of FTA concerns, but he does take up a specific point the previous speaker made (Pharmac) and places it in his own argument, and he engages O'Connor's overall case for the agreement by explaining why the Greens, historically dissenters, will also support it. That is partial engagement rather than rebuttal of a specific claim — most of the speech would be unchanged whatever O'Connor had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "Again, this is a valuable agreement for New Zealand, it’s valuable for the EU, and I want to support this legislation." — Shaw picks up O'Connor's Pharmac reference and his position of support, and explains why the Greens reach the same conclusion.

acuity.statement: Finally, to those that might argue that freer trade doesn’t equally benefit all of New Zealand, all I would say is that when our rural sectors are able to get better returns for our products, the benefit flows through to all our local communities.
acuity.explanation: Hoggard follows a detailed set of specific Green objections and engages none of them; he names Damien O'Connor only in a list of thanks. The speech is on the subject under debate and gestures at an unnamed opponent of free trade, but it would read identically had Shaw said something entirely different about the FTA.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Shaw spoke about investor-State dispute settlement, intellectual property provisions, the absence of enforceable environmental clauses, and Māori rights and interests in the agreement, and this statement does not take any of those up — it answers a generic distributional objection no preceding speaker made.

acuity.statement: While we acknowledge the potentially significant gains this free-trade agreement (FTA) could bring to New Zealand exporters, it is yet another failed opportunity to re-imagine trade policy and move away from the colonial model that has been imposed on tangata whenua.
acuity.explanation: Ferris follows Unkovich, who argued the bill significantly improves New Zealand's conditions of access to its fourth-largest market. He glances at that claim by conceding the FTA could bring significant gains to exporters, but does not engage her reasoning or figures at all; everything after the concession is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on Te Tiriti, He Whakaputanga and the Māori trade chapter that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever the previous speaker had said. On topic, with a gesture at the preceding argument, so the top of the unresponsive band rather than a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "Under this bill, New Zealand's conditions of access will be significantly improved, hence this piece of legislation is incredibly valuable to our market." — Ferris concedes the gains to exporters but takes up none of the substance.

acuity.statement: I would encourage members speaking to this to get their facts correct before they stand up in this House and make accusations that are actually quite inaccurate and not particularly helpful to the debate.
acuity.explanation: Van de Molen follows Ferris's detailed critique — that the Treaty exception clause is unchanged since 2001, that the Māori trade chapter covers only commercial interests, that there is no protection for mātauranga Māori. He names those claims as inaccurate without identifying a single one or saying why, then returns to prepared material on trade volumes, select committee timing and geographic indicators. This is a mere reference to the previous speaker rather than engagement with the content of any claim, so it sits in the unresponsive band; the speech would be essentially unchanged had Ferris argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "the Treaty of Waitangi exception clause allowing more favourable treatment to Māori remains unchanged from previous free-trade agreements dating back to 2001" — van de Molen calls the accusations inaccurate but engages none of them.

acuity.statement: It’s very pleasing to see that we’ve got to this, a good solution—maybe not perfect, but good and meaningful. I do want to acknowledge those who have contributed to it, and we have heard comments reflecting the various Ministers on both sides of the House; I thank them as well.
acuity.explanation: Costley follows a substantive turn in which Parker argued that the Treaty provisions are as strong as in any agreement, that Europe's acceptance of no ISDS clauses matters, and that CPTPP wrongly closed the class of screenable investments. Costley takes up none of that. He gestures at the debate by nodding to "comments reflecting the various Ministers on both sides of the House" and later joins "the earlier comments that commended the staff", extending Parker's acknowledgment of the trade team with further MFAT names — but that is a reference, not engagement with content. The rest (horticulture savings in Ōtaki, the D-Day anniversary, service in Europe) would read word-for-word the same whatever Parker had argued. A gesture at the debate on the right subject places this at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5, since no strand of the argument is actually engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "Can I pay my accolades to the New Zealand trade team: one of the best trade teams in the world led by one of the best public servants in New Zealand: Vangelis Vitalis."

acuity.statement: I want to take a little bit of a different approach, so I just thought it would be worthwhile remembering how this would affect some of the people who work in the primary industries and in the export sectors. I listened to our colleagues talk about the Māori effort that’s gone into the free-trade agreement.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows Twyford in the same second-reading debate, so she is eligible. She gestures at the debate ("I listened to our colleagues", "a little bit of a different approach") and stays squarely on the bill's subject matter, but engages no part of Twyford's actual argument: the tension he set out between public consent for trade agreements and New Zealand's dependence on market access, Pharmac, and intellectual property rules goes unaddressed. The Māori-effort point she picks up was not made in the preceding turn, so the thing engaged cannot be pointed at in the text. The speech reads as prepared regional and sector material that would be word-for-word the same whatever Twyford had said, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 for the gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued that trade agreements have stretched public consent for free trade to breaking point while New Zealand cannot survive without open market access, and that the agreement must preserve policy space for Pharmac and against onerous intellectual property rules — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I think I can probably be a little more concise than the last speaker, James Meager. In clause 10(5), it talks about the completion of reports. Now, yesterday, the Minister for Regulation was very flattering of the work of the commission, and it’s pretty much obvious that there’s going to be a number of reports under way.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows Meager's questions on clauses 8 to 10 and names him, but only to contrast his own concision — a mere reference, not engagement. He then opens a separate point on clause 10(5) and the completion of reports, taking up neither Meager's residual-assets question nor his privacy-obligations question. The speech would read identically had Meager argued something different about the same clauses, so this sits in the unresponsive band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because it is squarely on the same part of the same bill and gestures at the preceding speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager asked the Minister about clause 10 vesting residual assets and liabilities in the Crown and about privacy obligations for transferred information, and this statement does not take either up — it refers to him only as 'the last speaker'.

acuity.statement: In response to Dr Duncan Webb, if he was listening yesterday, he would have heard me say in answer to, funnily enough, Simon Court’s question that we expect the commission to wind up on 29 February. If you may recall, I pointed out that that was an interesting point because it’s a leap year and that the report that’s outstanding would be completed by 15 February.
acuity.explanation: This takes Webb's specific question — given reports are in train, will the ministry complete the commission's work — and supplies the concrete answer: the commission winds up 29 February and the outstanding report is completed by 15 February, i.e. before disestablishment. It engages the content of the claim rather than its topic, and the speech would have to change if Webb had asked something else. Scored just short of 1.0 because the engagement is partly deflected into 'if he was listening yesterday' rather than meeting the clause 10(5) wording head-on. The jibe at Meager about filibustering and the dismissiveness toward Webb are not acuity questions and are not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is it the case that the ministry will complete the work that the commission has under way?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise and take a call in the second part of the New Zealand Productivity Commission Act Repeal Bill. I was listening from my office last night to this debate. It’s been great to hear some of the concerns that members have had and to hear that the Minister for Regulation reflects on past ACT positions and says that members should be willing to learn and grow from those past positions, and that is why we’re here today, to disestablish the Productivity Commission.
acuity.explanation: Bidois had two substantive turns immediately before him — Webb's clause 10(5) question and Seymour's answer with the wind-up and report dates — and engages neither. He attributes his own question ('who will carry out the work') to last night's debate and to 'the blog sites or in the papers', then delivers prepared material naming Motu, Phil McCann, the New Zealand Initiative, Tim Maloney, Treasury, the World Bank, the OECD and the IMF. The 'concerns that members have had' line is a gesture at the debate rather than an engagement with any argument in it, which puts this at 0.3 rather than 0.1. Whether the institutional list is a good answer is a rigor and specificity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb asked whether the ministry will complete the commission's reports in train and David Seymour answered that the outstanding report would be completed by 15 February; this statement takes up neither, and raises instead who will take up the commission's work in general.

acuity.statement: I want to just graft on to what was said there by the previous speaker, Grant Robertson, because I, years ago, worked for the Law Commission, which is an independent organisation, and those kinds of independent organisations are really rich in having a focus and a capacity for people to engage with them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Robertson's argument — the value of an independent body doing long-horizon, big-picture work — and extends it with her Law Commission experience before putting her own question to the Minister about how independence will be preserved. It engages the topic and part of the preceding argument rather than any specific claim in it, so it sits mid-band: the speech would be somewhat different had Robertson argued something else, but much of it is her own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "having an organisation whose job it is to take the big-picture view and to produce the reports that we can learn from is, presumably, a good thing" — Grant Robertson

acuity.statement: In response to Grant Robertson, clause 9 is there to give effect to the policies that were agreed on in Part 2, and, as he says, it’s a very simple clause. It says, “The Commission is disestablished.”, so he should be able to work that out. As for a number of other comments that he made, I could engage with him on that, but it doesn’t really seem worth it.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the literal first half of the question put to him — what clause 9 is for — and answers it directly, which is real engagement and would not have been said had Robertson asked something else. But he expressly declines the second half (what alternatives were considered) and the White critique, so only part of the argument put to him is engaged. Scored on engagement alone; the dismissiveness and the thinness of the answer belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why is clause 9 here, and what else did he consider that he could have done to achieve the goals he has whilst keeping in place a commission that works on the issue that virtually everyone in this House agrees we need to work on?" — Grant Robertson

acuity.statement: Now, the Hon Grant Robertson has already pointed out that it’s open to you to make your own appointments to the commission. But I would ask you to respond to the fact that what you want is a little department all of your own where you can make sure you can control the opinions that come out of it, rather than have a thoughtful and independent organisation which can give genuinely independent insight into productivity in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific alternative Robertson raised — reappointing commissioners rather than abolishing the body — and presses it into the question the Minister had just refused to engage, supplying a motive and a dated quotation to support it. The speech depends on what preceded it: remove Robertson's appointments point and Seymour's refusal and it would have to change. Not a full 1.0 because it does not rebut the reasoning of Seymour's actual answer about clause 9 giving effect to agreed policy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if that is the Minister’s concern, why did he not reappoint people that he considered would bring the commission back to where he felt it should be?" — Grant Robertson
