acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: 'he and his Government are dishing out uncertainty for local government, right at a time when they are consulting on what is often the most important conversation they have with their communities in their entire term: their long-term plans' — engaged only as a topic, not as a claim.

acuity.statement: This concept of Te Mana o te Wai, which is an anti-scientific concept that was going to be embedded in the legislation—when I’ve spoken to councils around New Zealand, what they’ve told me is that under that previous legislation, the legislation that’s going to be repealed today, even if we treated the waste water to drinking-water standards under Te Mana o te Wai, that flawed concept, we wouldn’t be allowed to discharge treated waste water into lakes or rivers.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific concept Pham built her case on — that water services must uphold Te Mana o te Wai — and disputes it directly by asserting a concrete consequence (no discharge permitted even at drinking-water standard). The speech would have to change if she had not advanced that concept. Not a full 1.0 because it attacks the concept wholesale rather than the particular use she made of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: 'in a way that upholds Te Mana o te Wai'

acuity.statement: Oh, this member here—Mr Abel—asks where the money is coming from. Well, guess what? Who pays for water? The consumers of water could pay.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies an answer to the question just put from across the chamber, naming the payer rather than deflecting. The content of the reply is determined by the interjection it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: 'Where’s the money coming from?'

acuity.statement: Mr Abel talks about privatisation. Well, what’s been very clear in the commitments made by this coalition Government is that water assets will not be privatised.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one-word charge just interjected and meets it head-on with a denial on the specific point (ownership of the assets), then distinguishes it from private contracting. Squarely engaged with what was said rather than merely naming the interjector.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: 'Privatisation.'

acuity.statement: Well, if that was the problem, then we close our roads down tomorrow, but we don’t do that either, do we.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up Swarbrick's interjection directly and immediately, answering its content with a road-deaths analogy rather than ignoring it or merely naming her. The sentence would not exist if she had said something else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only: the analogy's weakness as an inference belongs to Rigor, and the dismissive handling of deaths belongs to Civility, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "People died." — Chlöe Swarbrick, interjecting on Foster's claim that Havelock North was a massive overreaction

acuity.statement: I heard today that three waters was quoted as being a “hugely divisive” policy. I think that might be a little bit of an exaggeration. It became a hugely divisive policy after a great big race war centred around Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Māori rights, and co-governance was propagated around the country.
acuity.explanation: Ferris takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the co-governance controversy Foster presented as evidence the policy was mis-sold — and contests its causation, arguing the division was manufactured rather than inherent. Partial rather than full: he engages the topic and a characterisation attributed loosely to "today" rather than Foster's specific dissembling claim, then returns to prepared material on Te Mana o te Wai.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when the pressure came on around co-governance, there was all sorts of dissembling" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: I might just also add that at this point in time, te Iwi Māori are not contesting the ownership of water, although there are many precedents set around this country already that would lead our friends on this side of the House to consider what they say about who owns water.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the ownership question Foster raised and at members opposite, but engages no part of his actual argument, which was about council-owned assets and expropriation, not Māori rights in water. This is prepared material on the right subject with a glance at the chamber, which sits in the 0.1–0.3 band rather than being a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Those New Zealanders have built those assets up, and yet the Government wanted to expropriate them essentially without compensation." — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: The Minister of Local Government earlier today said there is a pressing need to move on these water reforms, and yet the bill that is tabled by the other side of the House is just the repeal of the previous Government’s bill, of the previous Government’s work. There has been no solution tabled today.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding government speech — Bayly's statement that the replacement proposals will come back to the House later in the year — and turns it into the charge that the bill before the House contains only repeal and no solution. It engages the government's position on the debate's central question rather than any specific figure or inference of Bayly's, and then moves into prepared material on the reform history and rates, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "I'm looking forward to doing that over this year and putting the proposals back into the House at the end of the year alongside Minister Brown."

acuity.statement: This was a divisive bill—this was mentioned earlier by my colleague Andrew Bayly. In fact, it divided up Marlborough, and Marlborough ratepayers were going to be either on one side of the border and be in one entity or the other. It was incredibly divisive. No communities of interest were considered when these boundaries were set up.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject: it restates the 'divisive' theme already raised by a colleague on the speaker's own side and adds a local Marlborough illustration, but engages no part of the immediately preceding opposition argument about funding, co-investment or balance sheet separation. The speech would read identically whatever Edmonds had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued the repeal bill contains no money and no co-investment commitment, and cited Standard & Poor's on the need for balance sheet separation so councils can borrow — this statement does not take any of that up. The only backward reference is to Andrew Bayly, a member of the speaker's own side.

acuity.statement: I wanted to make a mention, when the member talks about the visitors that we have in the gallery—our mayors—about watching their back and no longer having a job, that she should probably look up. Because the mayors are really shaking their head and disagreeing with the member’s comments.
acuity.explanation: Lu takes up one specific strand of Leary's immediately preceding speech — the claim that the mayors in the gallery will lose their jobs over rates hikes — and contests it directly by pointing to the mayors' visible reaction. She does not engage the substantive argument Leary built (the projected rates figures from Cadogan, Bell and Cadogan, the stormwater regulatory gap, the absence of a funding answer), and the rest of her contribution is prepared material about the last Labour Government's failure to deliver. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared lines: a mid-band score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I feel sorry for the mayors who are sitting in the gallery today, because I don't think they'll be around very long once they have to implement the rates hikes" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: If the member's opposite have emphasised so much on what they see locally, I wonder why nothing was delivered in the six years that they had the power and the time and the funding and, apparently, the solution to do anything.
acuity.explanation: Lu takes up one strand of Twyford's speech — his local, on-the-ground examples of polluted waterways and under-investment in Auckland — and turns it against him, asking why the previous government fixed none of it. That is a real engagement with something he actually said, so it is not merely prepared material on topic. But it engages only the local-grievance strand and leaves untouched the two arguments Twyford built his speech around: balance sheet separation and the legal framework placing stormwater duties on water entities. The rest of her turn is prepared advocacy for Local Water Done Well that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "My city—Auckland—is a case study of a city that simply hasn't invested in the water infrastructure that it has needed for several decades as it has grown"

acuity.statement: I'm just going to pick up from the comments of the previous speaker Nancy Lu around nothing being delivered, because there are examples in my own electorate of Nelson of exactly that—things being delivered. The repeal of this bill will make it so much harder for our council to deliver improvements in water infrastructure. An example in Nelson is the Saxton Creek upgrade which is about to be completed—a $30 million project that was needed because the stormwater was so deplorable.
acuity.explanation: Boyack names the specific claim just made — that nothing was delivered in six years — and rebuts it with a counterexample and figures, then goes on to address the underlying premise of the debate by distinguishing councils not wanting to pay from councils not being able to pay. If Lu had made a different argument, this opening would have to change entirely, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only: whether the Nelson example actually answers the charge is a matter for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: "I wonder why nothing was delivered in the six years that they had the power and the time and the funding"

acuity.statement: Firstly, I want to thank the member who’s just spoken, Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, for putting this bill into the perspective and context that it actually needs: seeing the challenge of this massive under-investment and our road ahead in the context of our mokopuna.
acuity.explanation: Pham takes up one strand of the preceding turn with content, not just a name-check: she restates Maipi-Clarke's intergenerational mokopuna framing accurately and adopts it as the frame for her own argument about under-investment, and she later extends Maipi-Clarke's race-rhetoric point with her own council experience. But she does nothing with the argument — no rebuttal, no consequence drawn, no figure supplied — and the bulk of the speech (councils, amend-rather-than-repeal, Future for Local Government) is prepared material that would be unchanged whatever Maipi-Clarke had said. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "we as mokopuna of Waikato will not have to wait another generation to swim in our tupuna awa or watch our river be used as a literal toilet dump"

acuity.statement: Well, I’m going to be brief on this—I made most of my points in the first reading—but I would like to say that it is quite ironic that we’re debating this bill in the city which is the worst example of good management of water infrastructure. However, the Act that was put in place to deal with it had no impact on that.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and makes a contrary assertion in the same territory — that the repealed Act did nothing for the worst-managed city's infrastructure, which cuts against the general case for keeping the Acts. But it engages no part of either preceding speaker's actual argument: it answers neither Pham's amend-not-repeal point, her funding-model point, nor Maipi-Clarke's case, and the speaker says outright he made his points at first reading. A gesture at the debate rather than a response, so the top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Lan Pham argued that "scrapping the water services Acts—is a huge missed opportunity to build on the work that has been done so far" and that there was scope to amend rather than repeal, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: The unbelievable defence of three waters reminds me of the belligerent, grumpy old man driving up the wrong side of the motorway blaming everyone else: 26 percent of people supported, at its peak, three waters, just as 26 percent supported the Labour Party. They tried to rebrand their three waters from four entities to 10 entities, but the confiscation continued.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows Boyack and takes up two specific strands of her speech: her claim that the public would not support council investment (he answers with a public-support figure) and her account of sitting on the committee that turned four entities into 10 as a better outcome (he answers that the rebrand left the asset transfer intact). He engages neither her balance-sheet-separation argument nor her Tāhunanui Hills question, and the rest of the turn is prepared election-hoarding material, so this is partial engagement rather than full. Scored on engagement only — the grumpy-old-man jibe and the merits of the 26 percent figure belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "where we elected to turn four entities into 10. Now, it wasn't going to deliver the best outcomes, but it was certainly going to deliver better outcomes than the status quo."

acuity.statement: I want to start by saying there are some elements of what’s just been spoken that I actually do agree with, but a lot I don’t. First of all, I just want to say that communities across New Zealand—there are some councils that are actually doing a particularly good job in this space, so it’s not every council that we’re trying to find a solution for.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod takes up one strand of O'Connor's argument — the blanket condemnation of councils — and disputes it directly by distinguishing the councils doing well from those needing a solution, and he concedes part of the case before contesting the rest. But he does not engage O'Connor's specific claims (the named rates-increase figures, the Auckland stormwater point, the $1.2 billion spend, the asset-sale prediction), and the remainder of the speech is prepared material restating the bill's objectives and local ownership. Partial engagement with a pointable strand, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Shame on local government leaders that campaigned against us." — Damien O'Connor, who argued that councils have failed for decades, had their heads in the sand, and face 25-50 percent rates increases because they opposed the three waters model.

acuity.statement: I’d like to ask the Minister of Local Government whether the purpose of the bill as described in clause 3 is to make small communities that belong to a body corporate pay for their own water infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding substantive turn (Scott Willis) argued that the repeal of Te Mana o te Wai requires direct, early and resourced engagement with Ngāi Tahu as a Treaty partner. Leary takes up no part of that — not the engagement obligation, not Te Mana o te Wai, not the letter of 31 January. Her question is a self-contained, clearly prepared constituency case about Waipori Falls. It is on the matter under debate (clause 3, the purpose of the bill), which keeps it out of 0.0, but substituting a different argument on the same bill for Willis's turn would not change a word of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Willis asked 'what is the Minister’s plan for correcting this oversight and ensuring meaningful engagement with Ngāi Tahu?' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I would like to ask the Minister of Local Government something from really the opposite perspective, one of a big city, because this proposal in Part 1 is to disestablish the Auckland and Northland water entity.
acuity.explanation: White orients herself against what preceded — 'from really the opposite perspective, one of a big city' — which registers that the previous questioner put a small-community case. That is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it: she takes up none of Leary's content (the body corporate, the Clutha council's refusal, the boil-water notices) and proceeds to her own prepared Mt Albert material on flooding and balance sheet separation. A different small-community argument in Leary's place would have left this speech unchanged. Scored at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band for the acknowledgement of the contrast.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: 'I’d just really like to hear from the Minister what his plans are for small communities like that' — White positions herself as the opposite (big city) case but does not engage its substance.

acuity.statement: The reason I ask that question is because the Minister himself, since making this announcement yesterday, has made a number of assurances, and one of those is that balance sheet separation could be maintained. Now, we all know—those of us that have looked into this in some detail and have followed it throughout its progression—that maintaining balance sheet separation is utterly essential in order to be able to obtain the economies of scale and, more importantly, the separation from councils’ books.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty picks up the specific strand Helen White had just pressed — whether the Minister has any assurance that the new structure delivers balance sheet separation — and does something with it: he names the Minister's assurance, asserts that separation is the load-bearing condition, and asks what advice supports it, bringing in the credit agencies and the Communities 4 Local Democracy model. So the engagement is pointable and real. It is a partial score rather than 1.0 because he does not take up White's actual reasoning (that council backing means the entity was never at arm's length, so separation 'hasn’t had that magic effect'), and much of the turn — Porirua, Tararua, the repeal-versus-amend question — is prepared material he would have delivered regardless.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'Have you had an assurance that any proposal that you have to go back to the old structure is going to give you balance sheet separation?'

acuity.statement: Building again on what was shared from Matua Adrian, I’d like to ask about hapū and iwi engagement in the development of this legislation, as there have already been questions made. Have the people of Te Awa Tupua o Whanganui been consulted?
acuity.explanation: Takes up Rurawhe's specific question about consultation of the Whanganui people over the Te Awa Tupua settlement, restates it to the Minister, and extends it to hapū and iwi engagement generally. The contribution would be different had Rurawhe not asked what he asked; she then adds her own prepared Tiriti/LGA material, which keeps it just short of the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what discussions has the Minister of Local Government had with the people of Whanganui about the impact of this bill on that settlement?" — Adrian Rurawhe

acuity.statement: There were questions in regards to the amendments in regards to Treaty settlements. I believe those are best dealt with in Part 2, but just to recognise that this legislation doesn’t actually change those; it just simply changes the references in those things, but we can get to those conversations shortly.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the Treaty-settlement strand of Rurawhe's and Lyndon's questions and makes one substantive claim about it — the bill changes only references, not the settlements — but engages the topic rather than the specific questions put (consultation with Whanganui, advice received, Tupua Te Kawa), deferring them to Part 2. A partial engagement that can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will he uphold Tupua Te Kawa as part of his responsibilities within this bill?" — Adrian Rurawhe

acuity.statement: I was curious that the Minister, in what seemed like a response to the questions about balance sheet separation, talked about discussions with Auckland Council around financial sustainability. Well, they’re two different things. You could argue that balance sheet separation is a means to financial sustainability, but there’s plenty of evidence and plenty of literature out there to show that, actually, balance sheet separation is a very powerful tool in significantly increasing the amount of borrowing against existing revenue or assets.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact thing the Minister had just said, identifies it as a substitution of financial sustainability for balance sheet separation, distinguishes the two concepts, and presses the unanswered question. The speech could not have been delivered had Brown answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we’re working closely with Auckland Council around the options they have in front of them to achieve financial sustainability for Watercare" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I have a number of questions for the Minister of Local Government. Many people have spoken about people’s health and the water, and I would like to know if in any of this process of repeal he has considered any care for the other species that depend on the clean water of our awa, or the shellfish that depend on the lack of sedimentation—sedimentation from dealing with stormwater improperly, including that famous road of national significance Transmission Gully and the subsequent degradation of the Porirua Harbour.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn in which Arena Williams set out a structured set of five questions on clause 3(b) and the Northland and Auckland entity, and takes up none of it. The gesture at 'many people have spoken about people's health and the water' is a glance at the debate's general subject, not engagement with any claim made; the speech would be identical whatever Williams had said. On topic, so not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams put five questions on clause 3 and the disestablishment of the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity, and this statement does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: In regards to the issues in terms of Auckland Council, I note that the member’s put a number of amendments on the Table in regards to the Northland and Auckland entity. The Government has stated that we will be repealing Labour’s 10-entity model, which was a co-governed, 10 entity, mandated model. And the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity, which was the only entity which was actually under way—we are repealing the model, and therefore we are repealing that entity as well. So we don’t support it continuing. So we don’t support the amendments that the member has put in place in relation to that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific thing Williams flagged — her amendments preserving the Northland and Auckland entity — and does something with it: states the reason the entity goes (it is an instance of the model being repealed) and draws the consequence that the amendments are opposed. The reply would have to be different had she raised different amendments. Short of 1.0 because the first of her questions, whether the purpose implies Aucklanders will be better off, is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I have seven amendments to this part which I seek to debate' / 'is it implied in that purpose that Aucklanders will be better off because of the disestablishment of that entity, Minister?' — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: The issue in regards to the Veolia contract is an issue for Watercare. In regards to the questions around the roads of national significance and the storm water, I understand those issues aren’t relevant to this part. And smearing local mayors, again, I don’t think is relevant to this part, either.
acuity.explanation: Identifies each of the three matters put to him and gives one of them a real, if thin, answer — the Veolia arrangement sits with Watercare, not the bill. The other two are named and set aside on relevance without any engagement with their content, which is a reference rather than a response. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'those in Papakura whose water is delivered by Veolia' — Arena Williams; and 'sedimentation from dealing with stormwater improperly, including that famous road of national significance Transmission Gully' — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: So my question, with respect to the purpose of this bill is: will this bill enable continued use of balance sheet separation for the water entities that are proposed in the future? Of course, the issue there for Wellington is that our city council is near to its debt limit. Additional debt will need to be taken on in order for the level of widespread repairs that need to be made in Wellington. It is absolutely essential that we get past some of the petty politics that were raised by other members in this Chamber earlier, and actually get on to the issue of how these reforms will support balance sheet separation and the ability for us to be able to get on and pay for the work that needs to be done.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one, including the Minister's answers on the Northland and Auckland entity and on Watercare's financial sustainability — which is the same funding problem she raises. She engages none of them. 'Petty politics that were raised by other members' characterises the preceding contributions in order to push past them, which is a reference, not engagement, and the rest is prepared Wellington material plus a new question. On the matter under debate, so not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown said officials were 'working very closely with Auckland Council and the mayor to ensure that we have a financially sustainable model for Watercare', and Celia Wade-Brown raised council water capital expenditure; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: We’re not repealing the Taumata Arowai legislation. Taumata Arowai plays an important role in terms of regulating safe drinking water in New Zealand. That’s not part of the purpose; it’s not what this legislation does. Our Local Water Done Well policy will ensure that councils are able to have financially sustainable models for water infrastructure in New Zealand, accessing long-term funding and financing so they can make the investments that they need in this important infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Verrall asked one precise question — whether the bill preserves balance sheet separation for future water entities. The reply addresses the drinking-water regulator, which she did not ask about, and then restates general policy. It stays on the subject of water funding and regulation, which keeps it out of 0.0, but no part of the question put is taken up, so it is prepared material on the right topic rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'will this bill enable continued use of balance sheet separation for the water entities that are proposed in the future?' — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The next question I will ask the Minister now is: are there no transitional and savings arrangements because the Minister’s intention is to disestablish the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity and then simply replace it with something quite similar soon?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the Minister's stated position — that the entity goes with the model while officials work with Auckland Council on a sustainable Watercare model — and presses it to a consequence he did not address: that the absence of savings provisions implies a near-identical replacement is coming. The question could not have been framed this way had he answered differently. Not 1.0 because it extends his answer rather than contesting its reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we are repealing the model, and therefore we are repealing that entity as well' and 'officials are working very closely with Auckland Council and the mayor to ensure that we have a financially sustainable model for Watercare' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I fully appreciate that it is the Minister’s prerogative to repeal that Act. However, there are a number of things there that have absolutely nothing to do with the 10 entities model.
acuity.explanation: Williams takes the Minister's stated rationale for repeal — that the Act was built for the 10-entity model — and attacks its reasoning directly, arguing the consumer-protection and Commerce Commission provisions are severable from the entity model and transferable into whatever new regime he designs. Her speech would have to be rewritten if Brown had given a different reason for repeal, and she also takes up his walk-through of the transitional provisions to press her clause 5 amendment. Engagement is scored here, not the soundness of the inference or the warmth of the delivery.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "we’re repealing that because that legislation was designed based on the 10-entity model"

acuity.statement: As I said earlier, that legislation was designed for the 10 entities, which were, of course, never set up, and so that legislation is no longer required. We’ll be developing, under Local Water Done Well, economic regulation as part of that policy.
acuity.explanation: Williams had argued at length that specific provisions — the Commerce Commission's powers, the Consumer Advocacy Council remit, independent dispute resolution — are unconnected to the 10-entity model and could be carried into any new regime. Brown restates his original premise verbatim-in-substance and asserts the conclusion again without engaging the severability argument at all. It is on the matter under debate, so not a zero, but the words would have been identical whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "there are a number of things there that have absolutely nothing to do with the 10 entities model" — the statement does not take up the severability point.

acuity.statement: I want to offer the Minister of Local Government the opportunity to answer the questions around balance sheet separation because by repealing the Acts in clause 3(a), by disestablishing the entity in clause 3(b), and, particularly, the transitional arrangements for the long-term plans, that is placing councils in a position where they will be responsible in one form or another for what happens next in terms of water service entities.
acuity.explanation: Robertson hooks onto one strand of Brown's reply — the promise of a new economic regulation model under Local Water Done Well — and presses what that model does to balance sheet separation, expressly noting "he just mentioned it in his answer just now". But the bulk of the turn is his own prepared material on Standard & Poor's and council debt ceilings rather than a reply to the severability exchange that immediately preceded him, so this is partial engagement: the topic and one strand, not the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "We’ll be developing, under Local Water Done Well, economic regulation as part of that policy."

acuity.statement: Now, what we heard from the Minister was a repetition of the information that was readily available in the policy document. In answering the questions about balance sheet separation, he didn’t actually say “balance sheet separation”, so a good opportunity there for the Minister to answer that.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty engages the actual content of what Brown said rather than merely naming him: he characterises the answer as a recitation of the policy document and identifies precisely what it omitted, then picks up Robertson's balance sheet separation line and re-poses his own unanswered question about which councils Brown worked with. The turn depends on what was just said, though much of the remainder is a restatement of his own earlier question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "We’ll be developing, under Local Water Done Well, economic regulation as part of that policy" — and Grant Robertson: "he has not answered that question"

acuity.statement: Arena Williams asked some questions and she has an amendment in relation to transitional, savings, and related provisions. This is the normal part of any piece of legislation to have this in as default, that as the water entities legislation hadn’t actually come into force, there was no actual transitional provisions or savings, hence why the schedule is there.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific puzzle Edmonds (and Williams) put — Part 1 provides for transitional, savings and related provisions while Schedule 1 states there are none — and supplies a substantive reason: the water entities legislation never came into force, so there was nothing to transition or save. The answer could not have been given in response to a different argument, which is the mark of genuine engagement. Not a full 1.0 because it addresses the empty-schedule point without touching Edmonds' further question about why employee rights sit in clause 17 rather than in the transitional provisions, which he defers rather than answers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What we see in this bill is that Part 1 provides the transitional, savings, and related provisions, and if you look into Schedule 1 it says that there is none." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: There have been a number of questions around balance sheet separation. Of course, our policy Local Water Done Well, which we’re developing, will ensure councils are able to have the revenue sufficiency and the ability to have long-term funding and financing for water services and infrastructure in their communities.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges that balance sheet separation has been raised repeatedly — McAnulty's whole complaint was that the Minister had not said the phrase — and then says nothing about balance sheet separation, substituting a general statement of the Government's own policy direction on revenue sufficiency and financing. That is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the claim: the words would serve equally well against any question about water funding, so the specific point about separating debt from council balance sheets is left exactly where McAnulty left it. Naming the topic is not taking up its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "and the Minister of Local Government has not said the words “balance sheet separation” once." — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: One of the areas I’d like to question the Minister of Local Government about is “to make transitional arrangements for local authorities’ long-term plans”. I’m wanting to get some clarity on what those transitional provisions are.
acuity.explanation: Squarely within the debate on Part 1 and the bill's purpose clause, but it takes up no part of the answer the Minister had just given. Brown had just explained why there are no transitional or savings provisions in the schedule; this opens a fresh line on transitional arrangements for long-term plans without engaging, accepting or disputing that explanation. The question would read identically whatever the preceding turn had contained, which puts it in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just answered that "there was no actual transitional provisions or savings, hence why the schedule is there" and this statement does not take up that answer.

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister of Local Government is really about the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act. That Act is not very old; it was passed last year. My question is: why is it the purpose of this bill to repeal it?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the purposes in Part 1 and what the bill repeals — but it engages nothing that was actually said before it. O'Connor had just pressed on transitional arrangements and a cost guarantee, and Brown before him on the empty savings schedule; neither is taken up, accepted or contested. This is prepared material on the right subject: delete the preceding turn, substitute any other argument about the repeal, and the question about the economic regulation Act would be delivered word for word unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor asked what the transitional arrangements assisting councils are and whether the Minister can guarantee lower costs, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister of Local Government goes back to Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles, and want to query the Minister in terms of his Government’s engagement with the 19 iwi of Tāmaki-makau-rau and the 12 iwi of Te Tai Tokerau and the many, many hapū of that region and the 219 marae of that region for the proposal to disestablish the Northland and Auckland water services entity.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific provision the Minister had just described — the disestablishment of the Northland and Auckland entity — and presses it on a strand (iwi/hapū engagement) he did not address. It engages the subject matter of the preceding turn but none of the claims he actually made in it, so this is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of his argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "There’s a number of provisions in relation, in Subpart 2, to the disestablishment of the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity"

acuity.statement: So the first one really is: what employment advice has the Minister taken around the most appropriate way of dealing with the disestablishment of the chief executive as outlined in clause 15 of this bill in Part 2? The Minister made some comments before, which I wanted also to know if he thought they were appropriate, in terms of stating publicly the salary of an easily identifiable individual and making a joke about the number of employees at that entity.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the content of the Minister's immediately preceding remarks — the single CEO, the salary, the joke — and does something with it, asking what employment advice was taken and proposing an alternative (transferring the employment to Internal Affairs). The speech would be materially different had the Minister not volunteered that anecdote, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The good news for the committee: there was only one employee, which was the CEO. The bad news was that he had a very high salary."

acuity.statement: Going back to my question that I asked and that was not addressed: was the iwi of Wanganui consulted about the impact on Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act or not? It seems a pretty simple question to ask.
acuity.explanation: Continues the Treaty-consultation strand opened in the preceding turn and presses it on a specific settlement Act, but is explicitly a repetition of his own earlier question from Part 1 rather than an engagement with anything argued in this part. He takes up the topic under debate and adds a gesture at the Minister's silence, which sits just above the prepared-material band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "My question to the Minister of Local Government goes back to Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles"

acuity.statement: In relation to the member Hūhana Lyndon’s question around engagement with mana whenua, and it relates also to the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe’s question in regard to iwi consultation, officials have been directed to consult with iwi who will have their settlement Acts amended by the bill.
acuity.explanation: Names both preceding questioners and supplies substantive content on the point they both raised — who has been directed to consult, and with which iwi. It falls short of 1.0 because it answers the general consultation question rather than the specific yes/no that was put to him about the iwi of Whanganui, which was the narrowed form Rurawhe said he was listening for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe: "was the iwi of Wanganui consulted about the impact on Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act or not?"

acuity.statement: Speaking to clause 9, the repeal of the Water Services Legislation Act, I want to ask the Minister of Local Government what advice he has had, and what thoughts he has, on what will replace the considerable body of regulation that was included in that Act to govern the way that stormwater services are managed.
acuity.explanation: Brooking had just made a detailed drafting argument about the amendment to section 14(1) of the Water Services Act and the Henry VIII problem it creates. Twyford takes up no part of it — not the drafting point, not the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy — and moves to a different clause with prepared material on stormwater. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so not 0.0, but the turn would read identically whatever Brooking had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking argued that the amendment to section 14(1) of the Water Services Act 2021 creates a Henry VIII clause by referring to any replacement of the 2020 national policy statement, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The question I’ve asked twice already, and now for a third time, is in relation to both the purpose and now the proposal to repeal. In declaring the Government’s intention to repeal the water services Acts, the Minister has said that he had worked alongside councils to develop this policy. I want to know what councils he’s worked alongside.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the repeal justification Brown had just given and presses the specific factual premise behind it (which councils were consulted), so it is anchored to the preceding turn rather than free-floating. But the engagement is mainly with what Brown did NOT say: the question is explicitly a restatement of one asked twice before, and nothing in the substance of Brown's answer on Te Mana o te Wai, stormwater or consumer regulation is addressed. Partial engagement with one strand, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the Government is repealing that legislation" / "that's why we'll be repealing it and replacing it"

acuity.statement: I thank the member for that question, and I would just like to note that our policy, Local Water Done Well, was announced about 12 months ago. It was worked on while we were in Opposition, and then we took it to a thing called the election and New Zealanders voted for it. So not only did we work with local councils but New Zealanders voted for it, and now we’re delivering it.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic McAnulty put — the claim to have worked with councils — and asserts the opposite of his proposition ("not only did we work with local councils"), so the reply would read differently had McAnulty argued something else. But it does not supply the thing actually asked for (which councils), substituting an electoral-mandate argument for the specific list, which is the 'answers the topic rather than the claim' band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "I want to know what councils he’s worked alongside" and "I propose that that’s wrong"

acuity.statement: So I want to get some clarification from the Minister of Local Government. I want to pick up on the provision for local authorities, where it says that where they have already started their long-term planning consultation under the previous policy settings before this repeal goes through, they are able to do so—put their plan through without reconsulting.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the repeal bill's transitional arrangements — but engages no part of the immediately preceding exchange. The speaker opens a fresh strand of prepared questions (flagged as continuing what she 'mentioned earlier in the previous readings'), and the speech would be word-for-word the same whichever of the preceding members had spoken, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: McAnulty and Brown had just exchanged argument over which councils were consulted on Local Water Done Well, and this statement does not take any part of that up

acuity.statement: Why would we leave aside all the things that we got to as a collaborative group, which is exactly what the New Zealand public wants from us? Why would we do that and get rid of everything, when my friend the Hon Duncan Webb has put to you a proposal which was to suspend that piece of legislation so at least you could catch the things that were useful out of it and adapt it?
acuity.explanation: Directly re-opens the specific proposition Brown had just rejected — Webb's suspend-rather-than-repeal proposal — and attacks his stated reason for rejecting it by naming salvageable content (the cross-party stormwater solution shifting responsibility for blocked urban streams to councils) that repeal would discard. The argument is built on what Brown said and would have to change had he justified the repeal differently; it stops short of 1.0 because it restates the proposal and its benefits rather than engaging Brown's 'fundamentally different approach' reasoning on its own terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the legislation is not worth putting on ice because it relates to a fundamentally different approach to how we want to deal with water infrastructure"

acuity.statement: In terms of Camilla Belich’s questions in regards to the redundancy provisions, the department did have independent legal advice, including employment law advice, in the development of provisions relating to the disestablishment of the Northland and Auckland entity. Again, I remind the committee there was only one individual actually employed, who was the CEO of the entity. Clause 17 is a general clause; it is a due diligence clause to ensure all matters are covered when disestablishing a statutory entity.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the two specific things Belich asked for in the turn immediately before: whether employment advice was received (yes, independent legal including employment law advice) and why clause 17 exists if it is redundant (it is a general due-diligence clause). The reply would read differently had she asked about a different clause, which is the test. Marked down from 1.0 only because he leaves her second, larger question — how Local Water Done Well addresses Auckland waste water — untouched, and he does not engage her distinction between the fact of redundancies and the dignity of those affected.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if what the Minister has said in relation to the disestablishment of the chief executive is correct, then doesn’t that mean that clause 17 is redundant? ... So I’d like to ask the Minister whether he’s actually received any advice on that particular clause" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: The main concern they have is that with Local Water Done Well, which was announced well over 12 months ago, there is still no plan for balance sheet separation, and that appears to be the same question that has been raised today, time upon time, without there being an adequate answer.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material introducing her own amendment to clause 8 and the Hutt City position, on the right subject but engaging no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer. The gesture at unanswered questions is a reference to the debate's shape rather than engagement with any argument in it, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band; the speech would be essentially identical whatever Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Simeon Brown's preceding turn answered on mixed-ownership rural schemes, Northland, and clause 17 as a due-diligence clause, and this statement takes up none of that content — it only gestures at the debate by asserting questions today have gone "without there being an adequate answer"

acuity.statement: A very straight to the point question: can the Minister of Local Government guarantee that this coalition Government will not breach its Treaty settlement with the Waikato-Tainui Raupatu Claims (Waikato River) Settlement Act?
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line on the bill's effect on the Waikato-Tainui settlement without engaging the preceding turn's content at all. It is squarely on the bill under committee consideration, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0, but it would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Andersen had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued there is no plan for balance sheet separation and that Hutt ratepayers face increases, and this statement does not take that up; the only member it names, Adrian Rurawhe, does not speak in this stretch of debate

acuity.statement: And then, in relation to the question from the Hon Kieran McAnulty, we asked around the Chathams. The former Minister excluded the Chathams from an entity. This did not guarantee Crown investment in the infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the preceding speech and does something with it: McAnulty asserted the bill repeals a bespoke guarantee that the Crown would pay for Chatham Islands water services, and Brown contradicts the factual premise, saying the exclusion from an entity carried no Crown investment guarantee. That part is squarely engaged and the wording would have to change if McAnulty had argued something else. But it is partial — McAnulty's central and repeated demand ('What are your numbers to justify your claims?', 'cheaper for who?') and his Tararua and West Coast cluster arguments are left untouched, so this engages the topic rather than the whole argument put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: 'What this bill is proposing to repeal is a bespoke guarantee to the people of Chatham Islands that the Government will pay for their water services moving forward.'

acuity.statement: So I was a little bit confused, because officials advised our committee that those could be happening throughout 2024, throughout 2025. The Minister seems to be saying tonight that it could wait until 2026, but that wasn’t my understanding of the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the specific factual claim in the immediately preceding turn. Brown had argued the Wellington exemption question was moot because entities would not be set up until mid-2026; Boyack identifies the mechanism he overlooked — the Orders in Council in the existing legislation — and sets her own select committee recollection of staggered 2024-25 commencement against his date. The passage could not have been written without having heard Brown's 'mid-2026', and she presses for a number rather than merely naming him as a target. Short of 1.0 only because she concedes her own recollection may be wrong rather than settling the point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: 'under the legislation we’re repealing, those entities weren’t going to be set up until mid-2026'

acuity.statement: The question was in relation to iwi consultation. I directed officials at the Department of Internal Affairs to consult with iwi who had their settlement Acts amended by the bill. That process is under way, and we’ll continue to engage with iwi as we do develop further policy.
acuity.explanation: Boyack had just put two pointed, answerable questions — whether Orders in Council under the existing Act could be made immediately and on what three- or six-month staggering, and whether Nelson, Tasman and Marlborough could be exempted so an entity with balance-sheet separation could be formed — and told him she would come back if he did not answer. He takes up neither, nor the stormwater funding request. The reply is on the matter under debate and does answer a question raised earlier in the committee stage, which keeps it off the floor, but it engages no part of the argument it follows and would read identically had Boyack said something entirely different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Boyack asked whether Orders in Council under the existing legislation 'can ... be introduced immediately, and were they scaled?' and whether Tasman, Nelson and Marlborough could be exempted, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Whilst, of course, I agree with everything that my colleague the Hon Kieran McAnulty just said, I’d also note that the title is the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill 2024. Of course, you then think, “Oh well, this bill is to repeal the Water Services Act.”, but, in fact, it’s not. It’s to repeal the Water Services Entities Act, the Water Services Legislation Act, and the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act, but it’s not to repeal the Water Services Act 2021.
acuity.explanation: She follows McAnulty's amendment on the bill's title and takes up the same strand — that the title does not describe what the bill repeals — but she does not engage his specific argument (that the thing repealed is the "affordable water reforms" and that the Government is hiding the name). Her blanket "I agree with everything" is a mere reference; the substance is her own separate point about the Acts listed in clause 3. Engagement with one strand of the preceding argument, then her prepared technical point, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "I propose that it be called what it is, the “Affordable Water Reforms Repeal Bill”, because that’s actually what this is."

acuity.statement: I’d like to raise a completely new point on behalf of people in my electorate, in Taieri, where we have a lot of rural areas and we have mixed rural and urban water supplies.
acuity.explanation: Leary follows Brown's answers but expressly opens a 'completely new point' on mixed rural-urban supplies, engaging no part of what he had just said. Her material is squarely on the bill under debate — the repeal and what it means for these schemes — so it is prepared material on the right subject rather than a speech that could have been given in any debate, which places it at the upper end of the unresponsive band but not at 0.3-plus, since there is no gesture at the preceding argument at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about the transitional flexibility councils get on their long-term plans and about establishment-board and CEO redundancy entitlements, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: But in particular, in this section of the Act, I want to know from the Minister: how is it that he is going to get Auckland to take on the Far North water provision? Because that’s the solution we had in place; it was the solution that was going to save people in the Far North $8,690. The Minister’s just walked away from it and left people in the Far North in the lurch.
acuity.explanation: Russell engages one strand of the Minister's position — that councils will have options and can negotiate their own arrangements — and tests it against a concrete case, asking what incentive Auckland would have to absorb the Far North. That is real engagement with the Minister's line, but the version she takes up is mostly from his radio interview rather than the specific transitional-provisions argument he had just made in the chamber, and much of the speech around it is prepared constituency material. Partial engagement, so mid-scale. Scored on engagement only: whether the $8,690 figure is right is veracity, and the 'walked away' jab is civility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "what we’re providing to councils is a range of options and flexibility" — Russell takes up the Minister's councils-choose-for-themselves position and presses it with the Far North/Auckland case.

acuity.statement: The three waters reform was a highly bureaucratic, divisive, and unfair policy that appropriated assets from communities which had diligently built them up for generations. ACT has been consistent in our opposition to these three waters reforms, which we are now repealing.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows a long substantive turn by Genter that disputed precisely the two claims he opens with (that the reforms were divisive, and that they expropriated community assets rather than addressing decades of under-investment). He engages none of her reasoning: no answer on consultation, on the Havelock North origin under the previous National Government, on the rates burden, or on co-governance. What follows is prepared party material — ACT's record of opposition, a 2022 quote from Simon Court, the election campaign — which would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. The word "divisive" is a bare contradiction of her claim rather than a rebuttal of it, which is a gesture at the debate and not a partial engagement; the speech is at least on the matter under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued "there was nothing divisive fundamentally about the approach of the water reforms" and that it rested on consultation "with local councils, with iwi, with hapu", and this statement does not take that up — it re-asserts the label without engaging her reasoning.

acuity.statement: As the member Mariameno Kapa-Kingi has just pointed out, it’s about clean, safe drinking water; it’s about waste water that isn’t discharged directly into our waterways; it’s about stormwater that doesn’t contaminate the places where our kids swim.
acuity.explanation: Pham explicitly picks up the preceding speaker's grounding of the issue in Te Tai Tokerau's lived water conditions and restates it as the outcomes at stake, so one strand of the previous turn is genuinely engaged and pointable. But she then moves straight into prepared material (Havelock North, the Ministry of Health report, Queenstown) that would have been delivered whatever Kapa-Kingi had said, and the one argument she rebuts directly — the "overreaction" characterisation — came from a Government member on a previous night, not from the turn she follows. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "In Whangaroa we still have to buy and boil our water—we have to buy it and boil it."

acuity.statement: One thing about democracy is it is a contest of ideas and we’ve heard that playing out in the debate this morning. This is only a few months after the election where all of the coalition parties campaigned on doing what we are doing right now.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the debate's existence ("we've heard that playing out in the debate this morning") but no engagement with any content in it: neither Pham's unanswered-questions charge, her Havelock North and Queenstown evidence, nor Kapa-Kingi's Far North infrastructure-deficit point is touched. The mandate argument that follows is word-for-word indifferent to who spoke before and what they said, though it is at least about the bill, so it sits in the low band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham argued the repeal is "a knee-jerk, misinformed overreaction" and that questions about Te Tiriti rights and councils' long-term plan consultations went unanswered, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Now, what was this all about? What was this all about? This National Government doesn’t even know. Why are they repealing the Water Services Act? Well, that’s right: because all the Māoris are going to steal the water and that’s why they’re repealing the Act.
acuity.explanation: Jackson does contest the thing Smith had just asserted — the Government's reason for repealing — by substituting an alternative account of the motive, so the speech is not indifferent to what preceded it. He engages the question of motive rather than Smith's specific mandate claim (he never addresses the election result or the campaign commitment), and most of what follows is prepared Labour history on the 49 percent asset sales and the Waitangi Tribunal. Whether the substituted motive is a fair characterisation is a rigor and civility question, not an acuity one, and does not lower this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "we’ll make promises and we will deliver on them" — Smith having just claimed the coalition campaigned on the repeal and is delivering a mandate.

acuity.statement: But he did talk about one of them, which was Tararua District, and he said that over a period of 30 years it was going to cost, I think he said, $600 million, 12,000 households. You work that out—that is $1,666.67 per household per year. Well, actually, people are paying rates right now for water. Many of them are not paying much short of that. So that’s not actually a particularly astronomical sum.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes the specific figures an opposition member put into the debate — $600 million over 30 years across 12,000 Tararua households — divides them out to a per-household annual cost, and uses that number to dispute the conclusion drawn from it. The speech would have to be different if a different figure had been quoted, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only: whether his arithmetic or his comparison to current rates is sound belongs to Rigor, and whether the $1,666.67 is right belongs to Veracity. Not a full 1.0 because McAnulty's turn is not in the window, so the engagement is auditable only through Foster's own reproduction of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty, quoted by Foster as saying Tararua District's water costs would be "$600 million, 12,000 households" over 30 years

acuity.statement: Madam Chair, I’m actually enjoying the interjections, because it actually gives me time, having just come from select committee to here, to actually look at the notes that I’ve got and get the computer working there.
acuity.explanation: Jackson put a direct, answerable question — what is the alternative — three times. This is the reply it drew, and it engages no part of the question: it acknowledges that interjections are happening and treats them as useful filler while he finds his notes. There is a gesture at the interjection but none at its content, which sits it in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5; a 'glance' that takes up no strand of the question is not partial engagement. He could genuinely have scored at the top here by naming the replacement regime, so the opportunity was real.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do you have an alternative? Do you have an alternative?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I commend the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill to the House, because we don’t agree that the only option is to take assets away from all the ratepayers. We believe that there is no one plan for all, especially not coming from the central government here at Parliament. So let the local councils do the work to service their own people. I commend this bill to the House with my full support.
acuity.explanation: A short prepared commendation on the matter under debate. It gestures at the localism side of the argument ('let the local councils do the work'), but engages no part of Jackson's specific case about the absence of a Government guarantee, bond investors, or rate rises — it would read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued at length that the repeal leaves no new funding and no Government guarantee, so 'without any Government guarantees you can't get an investment' and rates will spike, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: One thing that’s really certain about what this Government is doing is they are putting up rates for ordinary New Zealanders; they are putting up rents for people who will be at the brunt of those costs, ordinary New Zealanders; and they are setting up councils to fail. It is such a shameful day. I echo the words of my colleague Willie Jackson: this is such a shameful day.
acuity.explanation: Opens by restating her colleague's conclusion and naming him, which is a reference rather than an engagement, and passes over the intervening speaker's localism argument entirely. On the matter under debate, with a gesture at the preceding turn but no content engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "once ratepayers and renters see the spike in prices" — the rates/renters point is restated rather than developed, and Nancy Lu's immediately preceding claim that 'there is no one plan for all' is not taken up at all.

acuity.statement: What Labour did was follow up on years of planning. There was very careful stewardship, there was careful analysis, there was data gathering, there was legislation that was written up. There was a lot of thought and planning into scale and efficiency—how we could resolve this problem using scale, using efficiency, using mechanisms such as balance sheet separation that worked—so that we could get an intergenerational solution to the problem.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speaker's case — that councils should each handle their own water rather than a central plan — by defending scale, efficiency and balance-sheet separation as the reason the reform was centralised. It answers the localism premise but not Lu's specific claim about ratepayers' assets, and then runs on into prepared defence of the reform's history.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: "We believe that there is no one plan for all, especially not coming from the central government here at Parliament. So let the local councils do the work to service their own people."

acuity.statement: But this National-led coalition with ACT and New Zealand First is sweeping all that away with no credible alternative put before the people of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Twyford's speech is largely prepared material on the state of water infrastructure and Labour's reforms, but this passage does take up one strand of Brewer's turn directly — Brewer's claim that the repeal clears the way for a better, locally controlled option — and disputes it by asserting there is no credible alternative and that councils are left without tools. It engages the topic and that one claim rather than Brewer's specific evidence (the 26 percent support figure, the political casualties), so it sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "this Government is going to deliver on a much better option, with a technical advisory group"

acuity.statement: It’s an absolute shocker—and we did do something about it. We put in place the financing, the funding, and the institutions to fix this; that side of the House is repealing.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the interjection put to him immediately and answers its substance: he asserts Labour did act, names what it put in place (financing, funding, institutions), and turns the question back on the repeal. The words would be different had the interjection not been made — it is a direct, pointable engagement with the specific question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "Why didn’t you do something, then?"

acuity.statement: We are now on the way to providing a solution to our drinking water, our waste water, and our stormwater challenges. This bill, along with the two other proposed bills being introduced later on this year, will provide all the tools and legislation required to finally get our water infrastructure up to scratch and back on track.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows a detailed critique and delivers prepared commendation on the right subject. He gestures at the debate (addressing Brewer, agreeing 'gone by lunchtime') and asserts the bills will provide 'all the tools', which brushes against Twyford's 'no tools' claim without engaging the argument for it — nothing on balance sheet separation, the Crown guarantee, or rates. The speech would read identically whatever Twyford had said, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued at length that the repeal keeps the regulator while giving councils no tools, that ruling out a Crown guarantee kills balance sheet separation, and that double-digit rates rises will follow — and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: That was a very difficult speech to listen to, because the Minister for Social Development and Employment stood up and spoke as if she was doing a favour to beneficiaries by making this change. It is not a favour.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the central framing of the speech it follows — Upston's claim that CPI indexation protects beneficiaries' real incomes and purchasing power — and directly contests it as a disservice rather than a benefit. It engages the thrust of the preceding turn without yet taking apart any specific argument or figure in it, so it sits above a mere reference but below a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These changes will protect the real incomes of benefit recipients and low-income working families in the years to come" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: When we made the change, the change was an evidence-based change. We had been told by a number of key stakeholders, experts—people like the Children’s Commissioner—that this is one of the most important things that we could do to actually address child poverty and reduce child poverty in the medium to long term. And here we have a Government who are now reversing that change and putting us at risk for having increased numbers of children living in poverty moving forward.

Partial engagement, hence mid-band.

acuity.responding_to: "They’ve linked main benefits to the Consumers Price Index" — Deborah Russell, who argued the consequence is that 7,000 children will move into poverty

acuity.statement: I am not interested in talking about this Government’s actions or their 100-day plan.
acuity.explanation: The speech follows Foster's substantive turn in the same general debate and is therefore eligible. It gestures at what preceded it by naming the 100-day plan, but explicitly declines to engage it and then proceeds to wholly prepared material on Te Tiriti, the Hui-aa-motu and Waitangi mobilisation. On the deciding test, the speech would be word-for-word the same had Foster made a different argument on the same topic, so it sits in the unresponsive band; the one gesture at the debate lifts it just off the floor rather than to a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "The three coalition members have come together, and we are delivering at speed on what we promised." — nothing: Foster argued the coalition's first-100-days repeals are justified because the previous Government's rules must be cleared before new ones can be built, and this statement does not take any part of that up; it names the 100-day plan only to set it aside.
