And anyone who knows anything about infrastructure and transport in this country actually knows the investment under the previous Government: $77 billion pipeline planned for the next five years.
acuity.explanation: Halbert takes up the challenge thrown at him directly rather than ignoring it, naming congestion and supplying an infrastructure investment figure before returning to prepared Auckland material. But the substantive turn he follows — Tim van de Molen on the Waikato medical school, GP numbers and rural health — is engaged at no point; nothing in this passage would change had van de Molen argued something different on health. Partial engagement with a pointable prior utterance, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Talk about congestion." — Tom Rutherford (interjection); the substantive preceding turn was Tim van de Molen's, on the third medical school and rural GP shortages, which this does not take up

acuity.statement: So it was interesting to hear from Paulo Garcia, from the Government side, where he identified the problem right at the beginning. He almost got it right. He talked about how, actually, one of the issues that we have is that a huge proportion of those attachment orders are on people receiving income support and that those people are some of the people who are on the breadline. And yet, despite that, while also acknowledging the narrow scope of the bill and that we need to take systemic action, he didn’t speak of any intention by the Government to do anything about this.
acuity.explanation: Takes the immediately preceding speaker's own premises — the concentration of attachment orders on beneficiaries and the bill's narrow scope — accepts them, and turns them against his conclusion by pointing out he offered no alternative government action. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "in 2018, over 24,000 attachment orders for civil debt were granted against people on the benefit—beneficiaries" and "For that main reason, there is a limited scope."

acuity.statement: Our front-line service providers are at the front line of recognising that attachment orders on those who are already struggling to survive does not do anything to incentivise better money management as Paulo tried to identify. Instead, all they do is they push people into needing more hardship assistance into more debt. And the key thing here in unpacking that so broken and beaten-up argument over personal responsibility is that you can’t actually make life choices when you don’t have the choice.
acuity.explanation: Directly attacks the specific causal claim in the preceding turn — that a 5 percent cap would remove the incentive to take personal responsibility — by denying the mechanism (no discretionary income means no choice to exercise) rather than merely asserting a contrary position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "The idea of limiting to 5 percent attachment judgments will not incentivise individuals from pushing themselves to taking on that personal responsibility of being mindful of the debts that they incur."

acuity.statement: The other point I would like to make is that courts make a judgment based on individual circumstances. So it’s not like everybody who is on one type of benefit—that their circumstances, personal or family circumstances, are exactly the same, and courts can judge that.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and structured as its own prepared case against the bill, but it engages no part of the argument in the turn immediately before it — the poverty-trap and no-choice rebuttal goes unanswered, and this passage would read identically had that turn not happened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that attachment orders create "a perverse cycle of debt and hardship that creates that poverty trap" and that people "can’t actually make life choices when you don’t have the choice", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: There’s a bit of a background as to what’s going on here with these attachment orders and why it particularly applies to people with benefits, and it’s to do with the industrialisation of attachment orders.
acuity.explanation: Russell takes the specific question the previous speaker put — why is this bill needed, it is not explained — and supplies the missing rationale directly, tracing the history of attachment orders and their automated bulk processing through WINZ. Had Arbuckle argued something else about the bill, this passage would have had to be different, so it is squarely responsive rather than prepared material on the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "But my question, quickly, when I started to observe this bill was why would we want to do this? And it isn’t very well explained throughout this bill."

acuity.statement: I just want to address the issue that was raised by the member from New Zealand First, worrying about the victims of crime. Actually, he’s got a point. He’s got a good point on that one. I think there is some regard that needs to be given to the priority of debt and which debt should be repaid first. I agree that reparations to victims of crime should be perhaps further up the list, but that is exactly the sort of issue that could have been discussed through a select committee process.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the precise objection just made — that capping deductions at 5 percent short-changes victims of crime owed reparations — concedes it in part, and turns it into an argument for the bill going to select committee where debt priority could be settled. Accepting part of an opponent's argument and disputing its conclusion is the clearest form of engagement with the content of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "I think and New Zealand First thinks that’s wrong, because what about the victims?"

acuity.statement: The second reason why I’d like to highlight that we oppose this bill is that there already is a mechanism in the civil court system where 40 percent of a debtor’s net income can be deducted. So, yes, there are mechanisms that already exist, so the court could change the amount of it if it thinks the debtor won’t be able to keep up with the payments.
acuity.explanation: Andersen's central factual claim immediately before was that no protection currently exists for beneficiaries facing attachment orders; Nakhle takes that strand up directly, asserting an existing variation/suspension mechanism in the civil court system. But it engages only that one strand and is delivered as part of a prepared three-reason case: her other reasons, and the rest of the speech (personal responsibility, the Government's justice priorities, the address to Webb), would read identically whatever Andersen had said. She leaves Andersen's other arguments — the overseas outright prohibitions, the $86-a-week worked example, the indexation point — entirely untouched. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there are absolutely no prohibitions right now in New Zealand on attachment orders being made against beneficiaries despite the limited nature of their income and their ability to pay" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: While we’re talking about personal responsibility, we’ve heard from contributors today talking about, “Well, what about the responsibility for responsible lending?” Sometimes it’s just one of those things where the quickest and easiest thing is always to blame the person at the bottom of the pile.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the personal-responsibility theme Nakhle had just planted and does something with it — inverts it onto lenders and frames the Opposition's version as blaming the weakest party. That is engagement with a strand of the preceding turn rather than mere repetition, and the passage would have to change if Nakhle had not grounded her opposition in that value. It stops short of 1.0 because it answers the theme rather than the specific argument: Nakhle's actual stated reasons (District Court Act scope only, the existing 40 percent variation mechanism, the risk of creditors switching to property seizure) are not addressed here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The National Party, we unashamedly align ourselves with the value of personal responsibility" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: However, I think the previous speaker, Rima Nakhle, spoke of three reasons and tried to assume a catalogue of reasons as to why this wasn’t being supported. But the theme that I’ve noticed through the Opposition’s contributions today has been searching for excuses. None of it was particularly logical; none of it really stood out.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and her three reasons, then dismisses them wholesale as excuses that were not logical without engaging the content of any one of them — no answer to the District Court Act scope point, the existing 40 percent variation mechanism, or the property-seizure substitution risk. That is a mere reference plus a characterisation, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is at least directed at the structure of the speech it follows and stays on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ve mentioned three reasons why we don’t support it today" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: What I just heard members from the other side of the House say is that it’s OK to take 40 percent of that in attachment orders. That would leave them with $202 to live off—another punch down from that side of the House to those in poverty.
acuity.explanation: Brewer's central argument was that the existing protected earnings rate already protects beneficiaries because no more than 40 percent can be deducted. Webb takes that exact figure and does something with it: he applies the 40 percent to the $337 single jobseeker rate to show what the 'protection' actually leaves a beneficiary with ($202), turning Brewer's reassurance into the objection. The speech would have to be different if Brewer had made a different argument — the arithmetic is built directly on his number.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the PER is set at 60 percent, meaning that no more than 40 percent of a person’s net earnings can be deducted. That protection is already in place." — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: I think there’s a really important point, as was actually raised by my colleagues in the Labour Party—Ingrid Leary in particular—about the fact that there isn’t yet, I believe, enough mind paid to the far more stigmatised element of mental ill health that is, of course, substance addiction and abuse. I’m really interested here to see what progress we can make through the select committee to shine a spotlight on that, because successive Governments have commissioned advice on addiction.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick takes up the specific strand of the immediately preceding speech — Leary's point that addiction is missing from the new section 46A strategy — names it as hers, and does something with it: proposes using the select committee stage to address it and supplies the supporting evidence base (He Ara Oranga, Turuki! Turuki!) recommending addiction be moved from justice into health. She also engages Leary's observation that the strategy (Kia Manawanui Aotearoa) already exists, conceding value only in the mandating of future strategies. The speech would have had to change had Leary argued something else, so this sits near the top of the band; it is not a 1.0 only because the engagement is additive agreement rather than a test of Leary's reasoning, and much of the remainder is prepared cross-party-group material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I note that the word “addiction” is not in the heading to new section 46A, which talks about the mental health and wellbeing strategy." — Leary's complaint that addiction is absent from the bill's strategy provision.

acuity.statement: One of the things that I have noticed, actually, about some of the wording in the bill is to not only say that we are going to put something in place and speak about it but having outcomes and to have deliverable outcomes. So, yes, it is about measuring, it is about being on top of everything as well, and not just speaking to it but being specific on what these outcomes are going to be.
acuity.explanation: Unkovich follows a substantive turn by Trask on the same bill, so she is eligible. Her speech is almost entirely prepared personal and party material (her maiden speech, the I Am Hope Foundation, coalition commitment) and would read identically whatever Trask had argued. The one point of contact — wanting deliverable, measurable outcomes — lands on the same broad theme as Trask's call for monitoring, but it is sourced to the bill's wording, not to anything Trask said, and none of Trask's specific claims (youth suicide record, NGO power imbalance, Twizel, devolution with strict criteria) is engaged or disputed. That is a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement with its content, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Laura Trask: "we must also ensure that there are strict criteria for funding services and that services are monitored to ensure New Zealanders receive high-quality care" — Unkovich raises measurement of outcomes from her own reading of the bill's wording rather than taking up Trask's argument about funding criteria, devolution to community providers, or rural service gaps.

acuity.statement: He’s always acknowledged the cross-party work in mental health, and we’ve heard that from almost all the speakers today. I think that’s really admirable.
acuity.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer's immediately preceding turn praised Doocey specifically for cross-party engagement with a two-MP party and warned that current rhetoric is "creating harm", pledging support for "movements that appeal for unity". Costley takes up that strand directly — affirming Doocey's cross-party acknowledgement, noting it was echoed by nearly every speaker, and building it into his appeal that the House not make this bill political. But it is agreement that extends a theme rather than engagement with her substantive argument: he never touches her central claim that Māori mental distress is 50 percent higher and therefore requires a distinct kaupapa Māori service. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material about his electorate and quotes from submitters.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Another thing he did was he reached across cross-parties for engagement, even though one of those cross-parties only had two MPs at times." — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: I won’t be lectured to by someone who wants to talk about taking a bipartisan approach when she, as the last health Minister—like the former health Minister Andrew Little—refused to meet the cross-party mental health group as the health Minister.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Verrall's speech — her invitation to a bipartisan approach — and does something with it, contesting her standing to make it by citing her refusal as Minister to meet the cross-party mental health group. The remark would be impossible had she not called for bipartisanship, so it is squarely engaged; its low civility and the fact that it judges her record rather than the policy are separate questions and do not move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "perhaps the House could join in some reflection on what a bipartisan approach to mental health would mean" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The question was asked in the last call about “Why not have a strategy on X or Y or Z?” Yeah, I agree, but it comes down to priorities, and under this Government, mental health will be a priority—that’s why we’re legislating it as one of the strategies under the Pae Ora health reforms.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the preceding speaker's actual question, concedes its force, and then answers it with a reason (prioritisation) — accepting part and disputing the rest. The passage could not have been delivered without Verrall's question immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And why this strategy and not others? Why not a cancer strategy? Why not the elderly? Why not a child health strategy?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Yes, we have a long-term, 10-year strategy—Kia Manawanui—but the issue is that that is not about the Pae Ora entities that we are talking about today.

Engagement with the specific claim, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That strategy is called Kia Manawanui." — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Now, I acknowledge that members opposite talked about the population representation in Māori and young people—absolutely it does. But every single New Zealander is entitled—and that is the worst word we can say, but it’s the absolute truth—to mental health issues.

She concedes the point ("absolutely it does") and then disputes the inference he draws from it, arguing a mandated strategy should target those most in need without defining people by background. The passage would have to change if the previous speaker had argued something else, which is the deciding test; it is not a full 1.0 because she engages the population-representation strand rather than his specific figures or his Māori Health Authority argument, and then returns to prepared material on the strategy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "72 percent of young Māori under the age of 25 are impacted by mental health issues and addiction issues" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: They absolutely are, because they were established back in the 1800s—1867, the Māori seats were implemented to control the Māori voice in this House.
acuity.explanation: Miles Anderson interjected the flat denial "They're not Pākehā electorates." Waititi takes that exact assertion up and answers it on its own terms, giving a dated historical ground (1867, the Māori Representation Act) for why the seats are a Pākehā-made instrument. The sentence only exists because of the interjection — substitute a different objection and this reply would have to change. Scored on engagement alone; the soundness of the historical inference belongs to Rigor and is not counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Miles Anderson: "They’re not Pākehā electorates."

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge my colleague and my tuakana Mr Rawiri Waititi, because he’s right. It was used to actually push our representation and our voice down. While I heard members on the other side of the House say, “Oh, well, no, no, that’s not what it did.”, actually, one only needs to read the Hansard from the time that bill was passed—the Maori Representation Act, to up until recent times, in fact, in the 1970s and 1980s, and, some might argue, today—to see that that voice has been silenced.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding substantive turn is Waititi's, which argued the 1867 Māori seats were created to control rather than enable the Māori voice. Henare does not merely name him: he adopts that specific claim, identifies the counter-assertion made against it from the other benches, and supplies corroborating evidence for it (the Hansard record from the Maori Representation Act onward, and Māori members barred from speaking in the late 1800s). This is take-up that adds something — not a pivot to prepared material, though the remainder of his speech does return to prepared comparisons (Singapore, the Sámi, the Nash family), which keeps it short of 1.0. Agreement rather than rebuttal, but the engagement with the content is what is scored.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "1867, the Māori seats were implemented to control the Māori voice in this House"

acuity.statement: The member before me, James Meager, said “If it isn’t broke, then don’t fix it.”, and I think there’s some truth in that, in that the system is functioning exactly in the way that it was designed, which is to exclude tangata whenua.
acuity.explanation: She takes the preceding speaker's actual formulation, concedes part of it, and inverts it against him — the system is not broken because exclusion is what it was built to do. The sentence could not have been written without Meager's line, which is the deciding test. Scored just below 1.0 only because Meager's turn itself is not in the window, so the engagement is auditable through her own quotation rather than against his text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If it isn't broke, then don't fix it." — James Meager, quoted verbatim by Paul as the member who spoke immediately before her

acuity.statement: ACT has consistently opposed race-based representation and believes this kind of identity politics has no place in the 20th century where there are many Kiwis with different ethnic breakdowns making up this country. Even if we exclude the members who represent Māori electorates, Māori MPs are now overly represented in this House, proving that Māori can be democratically elected to this House. We don’t need to entrench these seats.
acuity.explanation: The middle sentence does counter one strand of Paul's case — that the general-seat system excludes Māori from representation — by pointing to Māori MPs elected outside the Māori roll. But it engages none of her specific claims (unequal entrenchment, prisoner voting, the Māori ward experience) and the passage reads as ACT's standing position, so it sits in the partial band rather than above it. The reasoning quality and the 20th/21st century slip are not acuity's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this Pākehā system was not designed for us. In fact, it was designed to actively exclude us" — Tamatha Paul, the immediately preceding speaker

acuity.statement: New Zealand First’s position on the outright entrenchment of Māori seats is clear: we do not support temporarily empowered politicians like ourselves deciding what the constitution of Parliament should be. That is a decision that the people should make, and the people should make that for a referendum.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the bill's entrenchment provision — but indifferent to what preceded it. Nothing here would change if either earlier speaker had made a different argument on the same topic; the speech is addressed to the bill's sponsor and to the 2018 precedent, not to the turns it follows. Above 0.1 because it at least states a position on the specific mechanism the bill uses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson argued the Māori electorates were a temporary measure and that Māori MPs are already over-represented, and Tamatha Paul argued the seats lack the protections general seats have; this statement takes up neither and sets out a prepared referendum position on the bill

acuity.statement: We here in the National Party are standing against this.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive first-reading speech by a different member that set out a concrete rural-access and quorum case for the bill, so there was a real opportunity to engage it. He instead states a bare position and labels the bill an overreach by Labour, engaging no strand of the argument just made; the words would be identical whatever reasons Prime had given. It is at least about the measure under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime argued remote participation is needed because, for example, four Far North members live north of the Mangamukas and it 'takes them over two hours to get to the council chambers in Kaikohe', and that meetings fail for want of a quorum in severe weather — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: So it’s all on, Mr James Meager, is it? It’s all on, Mr James Meager. The future of Māori is all on, Mr Meager. I would have backed Tama Potaka before Mr Meager.
acuity.explanation: Brewer's case rested substantially on an appeal to James Meager's authority — 'he is a man of the law', 'this is our own in-house scholar from Otago university', 'he said that he had constitutional concerns'. Jackson opens by taking that appeal up directly and contesting the standing of the cited authority, which he then develops into his own argument that a Māori MP inside a mainstream party cannot advocate kaupapa Māori. So he engages one strand of the preceding turn rather than merely naming a target: the speech would read differently had Brewer cited someone else or made the constitutional argument in his own voice. But he never touches the substance Brewer attributed to Meager — the constitutional objection, the 1993 Parliament's intention, the rarity of entrenched provisions, or the 'why didn't Labour use its majority' challenge — and from here moves into prepared material on earlier 'great brown hopes' (Peters, Tamihere, Jones). Partial engagement, hence mid-band. Scored only on engagement: the mocking register belongs to Civility and the soundness of the ad-hominem move to Rigor, neither of which is in scope here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: 'As my colleague, the chair of the Justice Committee, James Meager, said—and of course he is a man of the law... He said that he had constitutional concerns.'

acuity.statement: However, I must say, the bill seeks to entrench into the constitution matters that do not need to be entrenched. To be entrenched through a member’s bill is not the way to do it. There are 300 clauses, and only a handful are entrenched.
acuity.explanation: Garcia follows Jackson, whose turn made a specific argument: that entrenchment matters because it lets Māori members advocate in a kaupapa Māori sense without constraint from their party, and that deal-making in the name of democracy is routine when others do it. This passage takes up none of that. It restates the objection Brewer had already made two turns earlier — wrong vehicle, few clauses entrenched — in terms that would be identical whatever Jackson had said. It is at least squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it above the floor, and elsewhere in the speech there is a gesture at the chamber's mood ('I am amazed at how divisive the debate has been going'), but no part of the preceding argument is engaged here. Low on engagement only; this says nothing about whether the member's-bill objection is itself a good one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued 'This bill is incredibly important because it allows our people to be pro-Māori and to advocate kaupapa Māori all the time', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Why does the Government deem those bills to warrant missing out on the public’s participation through a select committee process?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of the business statement just delivered — the named bills to be progressed under urgency — and presses on the consequence of that urgency (loss of select committee scrutiny). The question could not have been asked without having listened to the list just read.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "Next week, the House will consider legislation under urgency to progress the Government’s 100-day plan."

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Why does the Government deem those bills to warrant missing out on the public’s participation through a select committee process?"

acuity.responding_to: James Shaw: "just to see how the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is progressing, because I notice it has been languishing at about 18 or 19 since this Government was elected"

acuity.statement: Of course, having heard Carmel Sepuloni speak, it may well be that if the Amendment Paper isn’t withdrawn, we’ll need another amendment bill a bit later on to extend it further. So I’m really just asking whether that title shouldn’t be a little more descriptive of the fact that it’s a Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill in respect of the experience pathway. Would that perhaps be a better title for the bill?
acuity.explanation: Webb's turn is substantially prepared material on a different strand — how bill titles are arrived at and whether this one is descriptive enough — but he does take up one strand of Sepuloni's argument and do something with it, drawing out the consequence that if the Amendment Paper reducing four years to two is not withdrawn, a further amendment bill will be needed later to extend the pathway again. He engages the existence and direction of her objection rather than its substance (the association's letter, the Māori and Pacific workforce effect), then returns to the title question, so this sits at partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "we very genuinely ask the Government to reconsider that amendment—in fact, just withdraw the amendment"

acuity.statement: I support the idea of withdrawing, and this is why: pathways take time. Pathways of learning take time, particularly so when systemically it prejudices particularly Māori in the process of registration. And why I know this is because I was one of those that attempted the registration process some while ago.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific proposition just put — that the Minister withdraw the amendment reducing the experience pathway from four years to two — states her position on it and supplies a reason Sepuloni had only gestured at, that the registration pathway systemically disadvantages Māori, grounded in her own attempt at that process. She then extends Sepuloni's point about the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association by asking whether the Minister has secured tangata whenua advice beyond the official body. The speech would be different had the preceding turn argued something else; it falls short of 1.0 because she does not engage the particulars Sepuloni put on record (the association's retracted submission and its email), and part of the turn digresses to section 7AA and cultural reports from an earlier debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "In fact, I would ask the Minister to withdraw that amendment."

acuity.statement: The ANZASW provided a submission to the Social Services and Community Committee recommending shortening the time frame to two years. However, we understand that, as the member says, the ANZASW have softened their view on the need for a shorter time frame.
acuity.explanation: Lee returns to the exact submission Sepuloni had just challenged, names the bodies consulted, and concedes part of the point ('as the member says') while disputing its characterisation — calling it a softening rather than a withdrawal. The turn would have been different had Sepuloni not raised the letter, so engagement is clear; it falls short of 1.0 because it does not take up the specific claim that the submission was withdrawn as a mistake, and then reverts to prepared material about the workforce shortage.
acuity.subject: speaker
