acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "Evidence—the evidence; you’re rejecting the evidence."

acuity.statement: If that previous New Zealand First member, Tanya Unkovich, would in fact have stopped reading her notes and instead read the evidence—and how about reading her own Prime Minister’s state of the nation speech right after she tried to say that we need to improve people’s self-esteem, and this very legislation that is going to deny those on the lowest incomes more income?
acuity.explanation: Lifts the specific strand Unkovich had just offered — self-esteem — and turns it against her by setting it beside the legislation and the Prime Minister's speech. The speech would have had to be written differently had Unkovich argued something else; the engagement is specific and unmistakable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "Self-esteem is a big issue here. It is about helping people to become more inclined to want to prosper"

acuity.statement: If that member who just sat down is concerned about evidence and research and work, the whole report for that member to read in her spare time, an entire report with the likes of—and I’ll repeat this again—Phil O’Reilly, previous chief executive of the Business New Zealand roundtable, who sat before people who are struggling, and who came to the conclusion that all of the research said they are not receiving enough; they are not receiving support to actually improve their lives.
acuity.explanation: Answers Unkovich's specific complaint that the other side produces no evidence by naming a body of evidence — the Welfare Expert Advisory Group report and a business-side member of it — and stating its conclusion. Squarely aimed at the claim just made rather than at the topic in general.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "in many of the words spoken on the other side, I don’t hear evidence coming; I just hear accusations"

acuity.statement: Te Pāti Māori oppose this bill. The reality is that this Government continues to push their kaupapa of poor policy on to our people—policy that will punish our whānau.
acuity.explanation: Prepared opposition to the bill, on the subject under debate but indifferent to the preceding turns: it engages neither Davidson's evidence argument nor Unkovich's welfare-dependency case, and would read identically whoever had spoken before. Sits in the low band because it is at least about the measure before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued the Welfare Expert Advisory Group found income support inadequate and that indexing to inflation rather than wages reduces incomes, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Also, the members opposite raise that the benefits will eventually have the effect of dropping by 2028, four years later, and then the picture is painted about when that happens, but we would like for others to understand, especially the ones who watch this debate, that that would mean if the main benefit is indexed on cost of living, then the cost of living would have also gone down.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the opposition's specific claim that indexing to inflation leaves beneficiaries worse off over time and supplies a counter-inference about what a falling indexed benefit would imply about the cost of living. It engages the argument rather than the speaker, though it addresses the 2028 framing generally rather than Davidson's wages-versus-inflation comparison itself, and the rest of the speech is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "this legislation, which seeks to tag income support to inflation instead of wages because that ensures that they receive less money"

acuity.statement: I heard the speech before that said lower-income people are more affected by inflation—absolutely—based on the vast amount of goods and services that they purchase. So that’s absolutely correct. We’re at a time of higher inflation, therefore those goods and services—particularly food, electricity, etc.—that people need, this inflation affects lower-income people more. So this is indexing these benefits to the CPI—to inflation. So this is going to assist, rather than what the Opposition is claiming.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific empirical claim from the immediately preceding speech, concedes it explicitly, and then turns it into an argument for the bill's CPI indexation. The speech would have had to be written differently had Russell made a different case — it is built around her premise. (Whether the inference from 'the poor feel inflation more' to 'CPI indexation therefore assists them' is sound is a Rigor question and deliberately not scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Lower-income households will be experiencing a higher rate of inflation because of the basket of goods and services that they actually purchase." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: And it’s a remarkable book. You should read it—go ahead and read it, Dan.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the interjector by name and so is visibly a reply, but engages no part of his challenge: it restates that the book is remarkable and tells him to read it rather than connecting Rawls to the bill. A gesture at the exchange without taking up its content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What does this have to do with the bill?" — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: I have some comments for Barbara Edmonds, the new Opposition spokesperson on finance, around finance. The first is that it’s not beneficiaries’ tax money; it’s actually hard-working New Zealanders’ tax money and it is being given to beneficiaries.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Edmonds directly and takes up the premise of her central charge — that the bill 'takes from' the poorest to fund tax cuts — by disputing whose money is being allocated rather than merely naming her as a target. He then goes on to engage a second strand (the fiscal cost of jobseeker numbers under the previous government) and a Green Party argument about the beneficiary/work gap. The speech would plainly have been different had Edmonds argued something else, so this is high engagement; it is short of 1.0 because the rebuttal reframes the ownership of the money instead of addressing her specific claim that recipients will receive less in the long run.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: 'taking from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible'

acuity.statement: Oh, I will be. I will be donating it to the NGOs that are closing in Nelson because there’s no funding from this Government—I will be donating it, I can assure you of that.
acuity.explanation: Boyack takes up Trask's challenge immediately and directly, accepting the specific proposition put to her and naming where the money would go. The reply would be impossible without the interjection it follows, which is the strongest evidence of engagement; it falls just short of 1.0 only because the challenge it answers is a one-line interjection rather than a developed argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Then donate your tax cut." — Laura Trask

acuity.statement: I would also like to speak to the amendment which was put through during the committee of the whole House, and I acknowledge contributions from members from the other side and that they would have liked it to be four years. The extension is for two years, but it’s important to note that we have to find a cut-off time, and that cut-off time needs to be reasonable, and at this stage, we support that amendment which was put through during the committee of the whole House.
acuity.explanation: Parmar follows Davidson's substantive third-reading speech, whose central complaint was that the lead-in should have run to 28 February 2028 rather than 2026. She takes up that one strand explicitly — naming the four-year preference of "members from the other side" and offering a reason for rejecting it (a cut-off has to exist and be reasonable) — so the passage would have to change if Davidson had argued something else. But it engages only that strand: Davidson's main supporting argument, that the structural barriers (poverty, workforce gaps for disabled, Māori, Pasifika and rainbow workers) have not been removed and so the heads-up is not sufficient, is not taken up at all, and the remainder of the speech is prepared material on the value of social workers and the 700 vacancies. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "We too would have preferred the experience pathway to be rolled back another two years—with another extra two years—to 28 February 2028."

acuity.statement: What we don’t support is the shortened time frame from four years to two years. We get it—there’s a workforce issue. There’s simply not enough registered social workers to meet the vacancy needs in our community—believe me, I know.
acuity.explanation: Kemp takes up the workforce-shortage strand that Unkovich built her whole case on, concedes it explicitly ("We get it—there's a workforce issue"), and then uses that concession to isolate the part Te Pāti Māori rejects — the four-to-two-year qualification window. That is partial engagement: the concession-and-carve-out would have to be rewritten if the previous speaker had not argued the shortage justifies lowering the bar. But the bulk of the speech that follows is prepared material on Manurewa Marae, mana ōrite and whānau ora, and does not answer Unkovich's actual argument that lived experience substitutes for qualification — indeed Kemp's demand for qualified, culturally competent practitioners sits against it without ever being joined to it. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know how short the workforce is in this area. I know how many people are on waiting lists." — Tanya Unkovich

acuity.statement: I suppose my big question about this is trying to understand what the country gains by only having a two-year period as opposed to a four-year period, and what we potentially lose. We’re probably not going to know that until two years from now in 2026, whether those 700 places have been filled and whether or not they could have been filled by people who are currently practising but who have not got the relevant qualifications to be able to be registered on any other pathway.
acuity.explanation: Fleming's turn immediately before asserted, on the authority of sector experts he had spoken to, that a two-year extension of the section 13 pathway was sufficient, and cited the 700 vacancies. Rurawhe takes up exactly that claim and contests it on its own terms — asking what is gained by two years rather than four, and pointing out that whether the 700 vacancies get filled by currently-practising unqualified practitioners is unknowable until 2026. The speech would have had to change if the previous speaker had argued something else about the duration. It then moves to prepared Maatua Whāngai material, which is why this is not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg Fleming: "Two years is sufficient for extending this piece of legislation." (and his reference to "700 vacancies at the moment")

acuity.statement: This bill addresses a concern that we have on two hands. One is that we have serious shortage of social workers, and we have heard this afternoon from many contributions to this House the huge value that the country and that this House has with our social workers, who provide a very important function in our communities, often dealing with the most vulnerable people dealing with some of the most difficult moments in their lives.
acuity.explanation: Mooney follows Rurawhe, who had put a specific question — what does the country gain from two years rather than four, and what does it lose. Mooney restates the bill's rationale and the 700-worker shortage as prepared material and never engages that question; his only acknowledgement of the debate is the generic gesture that 'we have heard this afternoon from many contributions to this House'. On-topic prepared content with a glance at the debate, so the top of the unresponsive band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe asked what the country gains from a two-year rather than a four-year period and said 'An additional two years could well have made a big difference', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The proposal to reduce it from four years down to two years was on the basis of the Social Services and Community Committee report which relied on these submissions, which the submitters said they tried to have removed, but due to some procedural errors at the select committee, that did not happen.
acuity.explanation: Garcia's immediately preceding turn defended shortening the experience-pathway extension from four years to two as appropriate because the opportunity has long been available. Prime takes up that same strand and attacks its basis — the select committee report rested on submissions the submitters tried to withdraw — so her speech is not indifferent to the proposition just advanced. But she does not engage Garcia's actual reasoning (uptake, long availability, a 'gentle push'); she addresses the Minister's third-reading remarks and then returns to prepared committee-stage material she had set out to put on the record. Topic-and-one-strand engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that's part of the reason why a shortened extension is deemed appropriate" — Paulo Garcia

acuity.statement: I know that there’s some concern from the other side of the House about the time frame going from four years to two years, and that’s why I would like to reiterate that we need to remember something that’s available, which is that applications submitted before the cut-off date will continue to be processed. That’s an important point to really make. I just feel that sometimes when we make arguments, we shouldn’t be omitting certain points.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows Luxton's turn and takes up its central complaint — the reduction of the extension from four years to two — directly, naming it as the concern from the other side of the House and answering it with a specific mitigating fact (pre-cut-off applications continuing to be processed) that she argues the opposing case omitted. The speech would have had to change had Luxton argued something else about the bill; it is shaped around the four-versus-two-year objection rather than merely referencing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "it is very disappointing that it has been reduced to two years and not four years, as was in the initial piece of legislation"

acuity.statement: I am proud to stand here as a member of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand who is the only party who have been consistent—whether it’s alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, pseudoephedrine, or otherwise—on substances. All of the arguments that we heard from the Minister just now with regard to cost-benefit analysis, with regard to people’s freedoms or otherwise, apply to the logic that we need to overhaul this Frankenstein law.
acuity.explanation: Preceded in the window by a substantive Verrall speech, so eligible. Swarbrick stays squarely on the matter under debate — the classification of pseudoephedrine under the Misuse of Drugs Act — and gestures at arguments made earlier in the debate ('the Minister just now'), but engages no part of Verrall's actual case about methamphetamine supply, pharmacy safety or registers. The speech is prepared Green drug-law-reform material on the right subject and would read identically had the preceding speech argued something different about the bill, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is a real gesture at what was said in the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall asked 'what’s changed? Meth hasn’t gone away, are we giving up on this issue?' and raised pharmacy ram-raid risk and the need for select committee evidence, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: We know that prescriptions are currently required to access products containing pseudoephedrine, but manufacturers have allowed their product approvals to lapse, so there’s currently no pseudoephedrine products available in New Zealand. These tighter controls have not affected the overall supply of methamphetamine in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive opposition turns precede this one, so it is eligible. Uffindell's speech is a prepared summary of the bill's mechanics plus a statement of support; it touches the same ground as Verrall's question about methamphetamine supply but simply asserts the Government line rather than answering her point that the safety evidence has not been produced, and it takes up nothing at all from Swarbrick's argument about the asymmetry between classifying and declassifying substances. It would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before, which puts it in the low band — 0.2 because it is at least on the bill rather than a general-debate speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I haven’t heard compelling evidence that there are reasons why that won’t be the case.' — Ayesha Verrall, on pharmacies becoming ram-raid targets and the need to test the safety evidence at select committee. This statement restates the Government's supply claim rather than engaging her demand for evidence.

acuity.statement: Unfortunately, the environment under which we currently live has changed significantly from when pseudoephedrine was re-classified. Unfortunately, there is a massive import of completed methamphetamine products into New Zealand, a rising crime trend that we need to combat. The pseudoephedrine is no longer the threat that it was at the time that it was re-classified.
acuity.explanation: Verrall framed the central opposition question as 'what's changed?', quoting John Key's 2009 case that pseudoephedrine is the precursor a first-time cook needs. Costello answers that question directly on its own terms: what has changed is that methamphetamine now arrives imported in finished form, so the precursor pathway Verrall invoked is no longer the live threat. That is a specific engagement with the specific argument just made, not a mere reference to it, and the speech would have to change if the preceding critique had been different. It falls short of 1.0 because she supplies no figures or evidence against Verrall's point about pharmacies becoming ram-raid targets and registers, and the rest of the turn returns to prepared support for the bill — but the quality of the inference and its truth belong to Rigor and Veracity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'So my question in addressing this bill, and I think what the Parliament and the Health Committee needs to turn its mind to, is: what’s changed? Meth hasn’t gone away, are we giving up on this issue?' — Ayesha Verrall.

acuity.statement: We’re also concerned that the introduction of this legislation will retrigger the crime rates at pharmacies, as we saw in the late 2000s. Officials and pharmacies have warned and warned that allowing the sale will lead to a spike in meth-related crimes. We’ve got retired pharmacists who say that prior to the ban pharmacies were regularly targeted by ram raid - style robberies.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Leary's turn — the pharmacy-crime risk Leary raised as an open question — and supplies an answer to it with retired pharmacists' and officials' warnings, and later echoes Leary's reference to Paora Stanley ("as we saw with Paora"). But the engagement is unattributed and parallel rather than responsive: most of the turn is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on meth harm in Māori communities and the bill's lack of an alternative solution, and it does not take up Leary's actual position (cautious support, send it to select committee to hear experts). A partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "Will those pharmacies that opt in then become magnets for crime? I'm not sure." — and her citation of Ngāi Te Rangi chief executive Paora Stanley

acuity.statement: I rise to support the introduction of this bill to this House. This Government is committed to ensuring New Zealanders can access quality healthcare, in this case to access some of the most effective over-the-counter cold and flu medication without the need of a prescription. This bill strikes the balance between enabling New Zealanders to swiftly recover from cold and flu, and limiting public use of pseudoephedrine for the production of methamphetamine.
acuity.explanation: Prepared government support on the right subject. It asserts the bill "strikes the balance" — the precise point the two preceding speakers contested — without engaging a single thing either of them said about pharmacy crime, Māori communities, or the absence of an alternative meth strategy. Substituting a different critique on the same topic would not change a word of it, so this sits in the unresponsive band; 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it is at least specific to this bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued the bill offers no alternative solution to the meth epidemic and will retrigger pharmacy crime, and Ingrid Leary asked what the impacts on methamphetamine production would be; this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Now, members made some comments around crime. We did have the Commissioner of Police before the Justice Committee earlier—last week—and I’ll have to check the transcription, but my recollection was that he said there’d be very little impact on the crime trade. Most of the precursor comes through the border, and so the prime issues are not actually what they may seem.
acuity.explanation: Names the crime objection the two previous speakers made and does something with it — offers contrary evidence from the Commissioner of Police at the Justice Committee and an explanation (precursor arriving via the border) for why the predicted effect would not materialise. This part of the speech would have to change if the preceding turns had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because he engages the general crime strand rather than their specific claims (the pharmacist warnings, Paora Stanley, the Māori-community impact), and he hedges his own recollection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "Officials and pharmacies have warned and warned that allowing the sale will lead to a spike in meth-related crimes" (and Ingrid Leary's "there is a risk of organised crime exploiting this law change")

acuity.statement: I’ve tabled an amendment to the motion, to delay the report back to the House by one month, to 14 April. The reason is that it is a proposal to the Government from the Opposition to meet us halfway here. Obviously, if there was an instruction to the committee to report back within a certain period of time, it’s not a debatable motion, because it’s broadly accepted in the Standing Orders that that is a reasonable amount of time at select committee. One month, as has been heard from the contributions from my colleagues, is considered, on this side of the House, to be too short.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one strand of the preceding turn — that one month at select committee is too short — and does something concrete with it by tabling an amendment extending the report-back by a month, so the speech is recognisably in the same argument rather than indifferent to it. But it engages only that strand: Ngarewa-Packer's specific point about the scale of communities affected by meth and the capacity of Māori communities to mobilise and submit is not taken up at all, and the rest of the contribution is the mover's own prepared case for the amendment (the winter timing, the official advice, Verrall's two-week estimate). Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "refer to the fact that a month is going to be way too short" — she argued the one-month select committee period was too short and that Māori communities and pharmacists needed longer to prepare submissions.

acuity.statement: But, I guess, a point of interest from the Hon Ayesha Verrall is where she talked about how it would be good to see what pharmacists think. I had the opportunity to talk to a pharmacist just today, saying, “Potentially, you’re going to have the opportunity to sell more pseudoephedrine-based products next year.”, and she said, “Finally something that works.” So that was an interesting point of phrase.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton takes up one strand of an earlier Opposition point — Verrall's call to hear from pharmacists — and does something with it, reporting what a pharmacist actually told him that day. But he engages nothing of Greg O'Connor's immediately preceding argument that pseudoephedrine is a methamphetamine precursor and a genuine community risk, and then returns to prepared material about decongestant choice and Tixylix. Partial engagement with a named prior point, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall's earlier point in this debate, which Hamilton himself renders as "it would be good to see what pharmacists think"; her turn is not inside this window, so the fragment is his quotation of it rather than verbatim Hansard. He engages nothing of Greg O'Connor's preceding turn ("be very, very wary of this product that we're dealing with").

acuity.statement: In this situation, the measure that’s being proposed is to prevent a sniffle. These are vastly different in terms of the justification for using expedited processes. You cannot compare the need for vaccine access passed under urgency to something which is a treatment for a mild symptom.
acuity.explanation: Verrall engages the specific justification put for the short reporting date — the Minister's winter-deadline argument, which she names and concedes is valid — and then rebuts it by drawing an explicit comparison of thresholds, conceding her own use of urgency for the COVID vaccine and distinguishing it on the severity of the harm being prevented. She also expressly picks up the meth-precursor concern raised in the preceding first-reading debate. The speech would have to change if a different justification had been offered. Not 1.0 because the Minister's turn itself falls outside the window, so the engagement is traceable through her own restatement of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor's preceding turn in this window — "be very, very wary of this product that we're dealing with" — which she takes up as "very valid concerns raised about the impact of pseudoephedrine as a potential source of meth on the community"; plus the Minister's winter justification, which she names as "I noted the Minister's point about winter" (that turn is not in this window).

acuity.statement: Look, I hear the Minister’s desire, being really, really keen to limit the application of logic and evidence and consistency when it comes to this bill or to the Misuse of Drugs Act or drug policy as a whole. But perhaps my proposal to the Minister would be that if his intention is to pass this through as quickly as possible, given that it’s something that the ACT Party, for example, campaigned on, there is actually an opportunity to amend the Misuse of Drugs Act as a whole.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick takes up the Minister's stated reason for the truncated timetable — the desire to pass the bill quickly — and offers an alternative route that would meet that aim, which is a real engagement with the argument rather than a mere reference to it. It is only partial: the substance is a restatement of material she says she already delivered in her first reading speech ("As I outlined intentionally in my first reading speech"), it engages nothing of Verrall's immediately preceding submission-time argument, and the opening clause about limiting logic and evidence is characterisation rather than rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: The Minister's case for the short reporting date, which Swarbrick renders as "if his intention is to pass this through as quickly as possible"; the Minister's turn precedes this one in the debate but is not inside the window, so the fragment is her restatement. She does not take up Ayesha Verrall's preceding point that "only four weeks at select committee is too short" for submitters.

acuity.statement: As if the justice system didn’t already have that bias, this legislation actually still allows those with the means and the networks and the resources to still be able to pull on more information for judges in the courts, thereby entrenching already unjust inequities, that you can have a better chance at justice if you have got the means.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows a substantive opposing-bench turn by Andersen in the same debate, so she is eligible. Her speech is on the matter under debate and converges on the same inequity theme, but nothing in it can be pointed at as engagement with Andersen's actual argument — no figure, claim or strand of it is taken up, corrected or extended, and the speech would read identically had Andersen said something different about the bill. Per the pointability rule that places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because it is squarely about the clauses under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Ginny Andersen argued the bill will increase reoffending, create more victims, and build a 'two-tiered justice system', and this speech arrives at the same inequity theme from prepared Green Party material rather than taking up any of her claims, figures or the written-parliamentary-question point

acuity.statement: Now, we’re not seeking to remove section 27 from the Act, and the Minister made that very clear. That option will still be available to all offenders, and they can call people to speak on their behalf in court and actually have personal testimonies of things that may affect their sentencing and actually explain, potentially, their offending. What we are stopping is the taxpayer funding an industry which has sprung up as an unintended consequence of paying for these reports by the taxpayer.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson takes up the central premise of both preceding opposition speeches — that the bill strips offenders of the section 27 avenue — and disputes it directly, conceding what is being removed (taxpayer funding) while denying what they claimed is removed (the provision itself), then offers his alternative account of what the funding produced. This is partial rather than full engagement: he answers the framing but leaves Andersen's reoffending and Bar Association points and Davidson's bias evidence untouched, and much of the rest of the speech is prepared campaign material. Scored on engagement alone — whether his 'industry' characterisation is accurate or well-reasoned is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "the solution that they are grabbing in wanting to remove the funding for the cultural reports ... the reports that give judges far more information"; and Ginny Andersen: "what this bill does is create a two-tiered justice system, giving those people who can pay for a section 27 report an unfair advantage"

acuity.statement: I rise somewhat astounded at the lack of faith in our judiciary and the way in which they have been discredited in their ability to understand the differential between an impassioned personal plea under a section 27 report from someone who actually has an association to the offender—whether it is whānau, iwi, hapū, friend, employer—and a pre-commissioned, rote report by someone who has absolutely no connection to the offender.
acuity.explanation: Costello picks up the specific load-bearing claim of both opposition speeches — that without funded written reports judges will lack the information to sentence well — and turns it into an argument about judicial capability, contending the bench can itself weigh a genuine personal account against a commissioned one. The speech is clearly shaped by what preceded it (she also builds on Stephenson's clarification and answers Andersen's victims argument), and would have to change had the preceding turns argued something else. Not 1.0 because she rebuts the premise by assertion without taking up the evidence Andersen and Davidson cited; the weakness of that inference belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "If a judge doesn’t know what factors contributed to an offender’s behaviour, they cannot address those factors at sentencing"; and Marama Davidson: "good information to inform decisions is what this Minister and this Government are choosing to remove"

acuity.statement: It does not cancel section 27 reports; it removes the legal aid disbursement requirement. That’s it. That’s all it does.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise characterisation Kapa-Kingi had just made — that the bill 'amends the Legal Services Act to cut legal aid funding for section 27 reports' and that the Government 'has pledged to end section 27 reports' — and corrects it by distinguishing abolition of the reports from removal of the legal aid disbursement. The speech would have to be different had the preceding turn said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: 'As part of their 100-day plan, this Government has pledged to end section 27 reports'

acuity.statement: I think that one thing members opposite should be most insulted about is that these are called cultural reports, and not for the reasons they say, but because it implies that an offenders offending is due to their culture, and that to me is one of the most insulting things that anyone in this House could ever imply.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand of Kapa-Kingi's argument about the 'cultural reports' label being used to 'make cultural/Māori wrong', accepts that the label is objectionable, and disputes the reason — turning her own objection back on the framing. He engages the content of her claim rather than merely naming her as a target.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: 'these section 27 reports are not just cultural reports'

acuity.statement: Now, today we have heard them saying that we are saying on this side that we are getting rid of section 27 reports. I’ve listened to the debate. Not a single person said that.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the specific accusation Meager had just made — that members opposite cannot read the bill and wrongly claim it cancels section 27 reports — by denying that anyone on her side said it, then restating what the Opposition's actual objection is. Squarely aimed at the content of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: 'much like many of the members who also can’t read the text of this bill'

acuity.statement: So you know this, the New Zealand Law Society, not just the Opposition, they oppose it, because it significantly limits access to justice.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Meager's position — his claim that the bill's effect is trivial and that objectors have misread it — by citing the Law Society against him and invoking his own legal training, but then moves on to a prepared sequence of sector quotations rather than answering the disbursement point itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: 'nothing in the section 27 of the Sentencing Act actually requires paid reports'

acuity.statement: We just heard from the previous speaker, the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, that this Government has just decided to introduce this bill tonight: “This Government has just decided to introduce this bill tonight” was the direct quote, if my shorthand is right. Well, no, can I get on the record that this was something that was heavily consulted with and heavily debated during a long, long election campaign.
acuity.explanation: Brewer quotes the specific claim made in the immediately preceding turn — that the bill was sprung on the House tonight — and directly contradicts it with a counter-account (campaign consultation, the coalition agreement, the 100-day plan sequence). The speech would be structured differently had the previous speaker made a different argument; its opening exists only to answer that claim. Whether the consultation account is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "This Government has just decided to introduce this bill tonight" (quoted by Brewer from her immediately preceding turn)

acuity.statement: The other side might say, “Well, we’re not taking away.” Well, what they’re doing is making it unattainable.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the precise claim Brewer made in the preceding turn — that section 27 is not being repealed, only defunded — accepts it as stated and disputes its significance, arguing that removing the funding makes the provision practically unreachable. That is engaging the content of the argument rather than referencing it, and it is the pivot of Henare's case against the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "we are not getting rid of section 27—we’re not, despite their repeated claims. All we are doing is defunding it."

acuity.statement: This is what we’re forgetting: we’re forgetting about the victims. What the other side doesn’t understand is that the victims are actually very important and should be the most important in this discussion.
acuity.explanation: Henare's preceding turn made three specific arguments — the redacted regulatory impact statement, the signal sent to whānau using the Rangatahi Court, and an offer to work collaboratively on an alternative. None is taken up. Nakhle gestures at the other side ('making it out as if we don't care') but that is a reference, not engagement, and the passage would read identically whatever Henare had argued. It stays above 0.0 only because it is on the subject under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued the redacted RIS conceals the analysis and that defunding signals a cradle-to-prison pipeline for whānau using the Rangatahi Court, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: This bill doesn’t change section 27 of the Sentencing Act in any way, nor does it place any limits on the background information that offenders can provide to the court. Offenders can continue to use section 27 to call anybody to speak on factors, either in court or in written form; the thing that is changed is the funding arrangements.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith engages the substance of the opposition case put in the preceding turns — that the bill makes the section-27 pathway unattainable and leaves courts ignorant of an offender's background — by specifying what the amendment does and does not touch and then listing the alternative channels (lawyers, pre-sentence reports, psychologists' reports, letters of support) through which that background would still reach the court. He meets the mechanism objection with a mechanism answer rather than restating the bill's purpose. Marked below 1.0 because he does not take up Henare's specific affordability point — that the alternatives are not funded either.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "The other side might say, “Well, we’re not taking away.” Well, what they’re doing is making it unattainable."

acuity.statement: So I think the first thing to clear up is that, for the record, at no point in time did any party on the Opposition benches at any stage ever say that this was going to be taken away. We’ve always focused on the defunding.
acuity.explanation: Opens by correcting the characterisation in Goldsmith's immediately preceding turn — that the Opposition's 'commentary from the other side' misrepresents what the bill does — and distinguishes removal from defunding, the precise distinction his speech relied on. The speech would have to change if he had framed the Opposition's position differently, though she does not take up his specific claim about election commitments until later.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "I’m getting plenty of commentary from the other side, and I’m sure members of the public will be able to assess that." (and "This bill delivers on a Government commitment to defund these reports")

acuity.statement: To wind up, I’d just like to point out the fact that if you’re going to have a 100-day plan, it would be great if there was some substance in it, but all of these things are simply window dressing.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the central argument of the preceding turn — that keeping an election promise is itself the justification for the bill — and turns it against him: a 100-day plan item delivered is not a solution, it is window dressing. She also uses the regulatory impact statement to show the stated 'problem' is the commitment itself, which is a direct answer to his promise-kept reasoning rather than a pivot away from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "A series of parties campaigned during an election campaign for a change, they get elected, and then, when they’re elected, they get into Government and do what they said they were going to do, and that’s what we’re doing on this side of the House."

acuity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million. This has gone unchecked and it’s time to rein it in, and that is what we are doing. The ability to put information before the court, as has been well discussed tonight, will still be available. Offenders can have people come and speak to them.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's central claim was that the ability to put material before the court survives only for those who can pay, so withdrawing funding strips access from the poor. Stephenson engages that one strand directly — the avenue remains open and whānau, employers and community members can speak at no cost — and adds the cost rationale as the reason for the change. But he explicitly addresses himself to Ginny Andersen's earlier points rather than Davidson's, and does not take up her discrimination or victims arguments at all, reverting to prepared material on the party's justice plan. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, not a rebuttal of the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they’re removing the access for people who cannot afford it" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: I can assure the House that I have held the victims after being raped, I have nursed the children who have been beaten, I have looked into the victim’s eyes, and I have retained a faith in the judiciary and the justice system to act appropriately. As was raised across the House, we have all been involved in those circumstances where we have had to advocate for people we know, for whānau, for those we are connected with, and for those who we don’t know but feel a compassion to represent. That is still available and will continue to be available.
acuity.explanation: Costello takes up Davidson's standing claim — that those who have worked with victims are on the other side of this bill — and answers it on its own ground with her own history with victims and her contrary conclusion about the judiciary, then meets the access strand by asserting advocacy without cost continues under the amendment. It engages the argument rather than merely naming the speaker, but stops short of addressing the specific contention that funded reports are what gives non-wealthy offenders access, so it is a partial engagement with a return to prepared support for the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "do not sit in this House and yell at us about who cares for victims, because removing the funding for these reports is not caring about victims" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: They’re not cultural reports; they’re section 27 reports.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise wording of the sentence being spoken as it is spoken and corrects the terminology used to describe the instrument under debate. The intervention could not have been made in any other debate, and the speaker it interrupts immediately adopts the correction mid-sentence, which is direct evidence the content was engaged rather than merely talked over. Short, but squarely aimed at the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What this bill aims to do, in terms of removing legal aid for the creation of cultural reports—" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Indeed, and we were very critical in the last Government around the failure to address issues around mass incarceration. It’s interesting that the member opposite to me, jeering about the past Government, fails to recognise their own complicity, while in Opposition, in actually just calling for more harm for the communities that actually are served by these reports.
acuity.explanation: Engages the interjection put to him directly: concedes the factual premise ("Indeed"), then disputes the inference drawn from it by distinguishing his party's position within the last Government from responsibility for its record, and turns the charge back on the interjector's own conduct in Opposition. The passage would not exist had Rutherford not interjected, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — whether the tu quoque turn is good reasoning is a Rigor question, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You were in the last Government." — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: If they were really, really concerned about the costs of these reports, why haven’t they gone out and asked Harry Tam for his template and offered to do it for free? Because that’s what they’re actually saying here. They’re saying that when you remove legal aid funding that no one will be able to access this unless they are super-rich and super-powerful.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific opposition argument that withdrawing legal aid funding puts section 27 reports out of reach, restates it in the opposition's own terms, and attacks it by asserting the reports could be produced without charge from an existing template. That is engagement with the content of the claim, not just a reference to its author. Held below the top band because it reframes the argument as being solely about affordability and does not touch the other strand put to him — that the reports supply sentencing context, not discounts — before moving to prepared material on the regulatory impact statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "taking funding away—taking funding away—lessens opportunity; it lessens the access to fair and just decisions" — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: Oh, Mr Meager—you’ve got the future of Māori in your hands.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and gestures at the stakes of the matter under debate, but engages no part of what he actually argued — neither the template/affordability point nor the redacted regulatory impact statement counterexample. Naming a target is the mere-reference case the rubric puts at 0.1-0.3; this sits at the upper end because it is at least addressed to the bill's consequences rather than to a different subject entirely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager argued that removing legal aid does not block access because a free template exists, and that redacted regulatory impact statements are not unprecedented, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The point is, of the 16 bills that have come through this House, a large proportion are affecting communities who are made up of tangata whenua, who are denied the right to come in and be part of an open, transparent select committee, an open, transparent consultation. This is affecting Māori more than anyone else in Aotearoa, which is why we have put this request for an urgent debate.
acuity.explanation: She takes up Shaw's specific count of 16 urgency bills and does something with it — breaking the 16 down by who they affect and converting his ratio argument about parliamentary democracy into a distinct argument about tangata whenua being denied select committee scrutiny. The turn would have to be rewritten had Shaw not supplied that figure, which is why it sits near the top of the scale rather than at 0.5; it stops short of 1.0 because it accepts his number without testing or correcting it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Shaw: "by my count, the Government has put 16 bills through urgency and one item of Government business not through urgency"

acuity.statement: At this stage, section 27 reports have to do with sentencing—there is no removal of the right of anyone for evidence to be presented in their favour throughout the whole process, what is being abolished is the funding for section 27 reports, because it was created to allow family and people who knew the accused to provide evidence in support of their background. Section 27 reports are not being abolished by this amendment.
acuity.explanation: Garcia takes up the specific proposition Webb built his speech on — that the bill strips the court of section 27 information and denies defendants the chance to put their background before a judge — and disputes it on the merits by distinguishing abolition of the reports from removal of their funding, and by locating them at the sentencing stage rather than the evidential stage. The speech would have had to be different had Webb argued something else, so it is clearly responsive. It is not a full 1.0 because it engages only one strand and leaves untouched Webb's central point, which was precisely about affordability — that only those who can pay privately will obtain a report — as well as the Law Society, Bar Association, regulatory impact statement and Cabinet paper evidence Webb cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Depriving the court of useful information by defunding these reports is just one of the spiteful things he’s doing." — and his claim that the measure breaches the Bill of Rights by "not providing adequate legal representation".

acuity.statement: We have heard from the Minister of Health that Te Aka Whai Ora is a bureaucracy managed out of Wellington. I argue that Te Aka Whai Ora is a really small workforce—not even 300 kaimahi.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand already live in the preceding turn — the claim that the authority is a Wellington bureaucracy — and does something with it, supplying a workforce size and saying the staff are based in the regions and hospitals rather than centrally. But the engagement is aimed chiefly at the Minister's media framing rather than at Henare's argument, and the rest of the speech is prepared material (Wai 2575, the tribunal urgency, Te Tiriti) that would be unchanged whatever the previous speaker had said. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "I challenge the Minister and members on that side of the House who talk about a Wellington bureaucracy: tell me where their office is."

acuity.statement: Dividing New Zealanders into two ethnic groups to receive public services does not help us deliver better public services, and, actually, it’s a poor analysis of the causes of poor health outcomes. It creates division and, really, isn’t the way we want to go forward.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, but engages no part of the two preceding arguments: it neither answers the tribunal/consultation point nor the claim that the authority was small and regionally based. Prepared party-position material on the right subject — it would read word-for-word the same whatever Henare and Lyndon had argued. Scored in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.0 because it addresses the bill's rationale, and there is a gesture at the debate in the reference to the Minister's speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon argued the disestablishment is a gross breach of Te Tiriti, undertaken under urgency so as to pre-empt the Waitangi Tribunal hearing scheduled for that week, and this statement does not take that up; nor does it take up Peeni Henare's claim that Te Aka Whai Ora was decentralised and based in Auckland.

acuity.statement: The option to put it forward is still there. However, offenders that are in a situation where they do not have the financial means will not be able to have this section 27 report. It is not an excuse; it is to provide a report that provides further explanation for the sentencing judge to consider those circumstances.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the fact that the bill defunds rather than abolishes the reports — the distinction implicit in Brewer's 'defunding'— and draws out the consequence he left out, that the option survives in form but not for offenders without means. She also pushes back on the framing of the reports as an excuse. But she does not engage his specific claims about cost or sentencing discounts, and returns to prepared material on the reports' purpose.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "defunding—urgently defunding—the section 27 reports"

acuity.statement: When we consider the fact that taxpayer-funded section 27 reports—the amount spent on them—has increased by at least 190-fold, when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year, I’m pretty sure that most Kiwis would agree that this money is better spent on victim services. I support its progression.
acuity.explanation: Sosene had just argued that defunding removes access for offenders without means and for groups overrepresented in the justice system. Nakhle answers neither the access point nor the overrepresentation point; she returns to the cost argument Brewer had already made before Sosene spoke. The contribution is on the right subject but would read identically had Sosene argued something else entirely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene argued that "offenders that are in a situation where they do not have the financial means will not be able to have this section 27 report", and this statement does not take up either the access point or the overrepresentation point

acuity.statement: I want to congratulate this Government! I want to congratulate you too, our Minister! From day one, you have carried on the kōrero that this is a two-tier system based on race—based on race. Your party has continued on the kōrero of this being a solution based on racial segregation. And New Zealand First, in fact, said it was about separatism. In fact, we had ACT also calling it an “act of apartheid”. Well, excuse us—excuse us for having to have a separate need to be able to have our wellbeing addressed, because we are dying earlier than everyone else.
acuity.explanation: Follows Marcroft and is squarely about the bill under debate, but engages none of her specific claims. It reaches back to things New Zealand First and ACT have said in the past rather than anything in the preceding turn, and the rest is prepared condemnation of the Government's framing. A gesture at the debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "Māori health equity should be matrixed across the entire public health system, not ring-fenced, not put into a little box on the side, with bureaucratic capture." — engaged only at the level of the separatism framing attributed to New Zealand First; Marcroft's actual arguments (Te Aka Whai Ora's limited delivery, commissioning powers for iwi-Māori partnership boards) are not taken up.

acuity.statement: We have said that we campaigned clearly that we were going to disestablish the Māori Health Authority. We were voted in by the people of New Zealand with a clear electoral mandate, and we are delivering on that mandate as part of our first 100 days in coalition agreements with coalition partners.
acuity.explanation: Prepared mandate material on the right subject. It would read word-for-word the same whatever the previous speaker had said; the mortality figures, the consultation complaint and the urgency objection all go unanswered. On topic, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued that Māori die seven years earlier, that the Iwi Chairs Forum says no alternative has been communicated, and that the bill is being taken under urgency without the Waitangi Tribunal being heard — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: What is so disappointing is that something which is the culmination of so much study and work and consultation in Aotearoa is now being removed by a Government who refuses to listen, under urgency, with no opportunity for select committee and no opportunity for the Waitangi Tribunal to be able to comment on this thing of critical importance to Māori. It is shameful, and, Dr Reti, my view is that your conduct in this is cowardly.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one live strand of the preceding debate — that the bill is being rushed under urgency with no Tribunal or select committee scrutiny — and adds the consultation history behind the Authority to it. But it leaves Uffindell's immediately preceding mandate argument untouched and otherwise runs prepared professional material, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "the wellbeing of your tangata w’enua, the indigenous people of Aotearoa, deserves to have more time and deserves, as Te Tiriti, to be heard in the tribunal" — Verrall takes up that process strand and extends it to the absence of a select committee.

acuity.statement: We’re committed to improving health outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori. We recognise that communities know best what works for them. We’ll continue to work with all population groups to improve outcomes.
acuity.explanation: A short set of prepared commitments plus a rhetorical flourish, delivered immediately after a detailed argument about localities, primary care and the missing select committee process. None of that content is engaged and the speech would be identical whoever had preceded it. It is at least about the bill, so 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued that the roll-out of localities is deferred by this bill and that the iwi-Māori partnership board / locality relationship is where primary care gains would come from, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Yes, I did say transition would be in my kind hands, in reply to a previous speech. What I would suggest is ask the staff: is there any time in this process when there has not been respect and consideration?
acuity.explanation: Reti takes up one strand of Prime's attack — the charge that he did not genuinely consult or listen — conceding his own earlier words and offering the staff's experience of the process, and later his meetings with Iwi-Māori Partnership Board chairs, as his answer. But he engages the topic rather than Prime's specific claim: he never addresses the undertaking she quotes (that he would sit with the hapū, iwi and tribunal and carefully consider their views before acting) or the Waitangi Tribunal hearing being cut off, and the remainder of the speech is prepared material on the $50m immunisation programme and the four changes the bill makes, which would have been delivered whatever Prime had said. Partial, pointable engagement, then a return to script.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It was the Minister that lied last week" — Willow-Jean Prime, charging that he had promised in the House to sit with, discuss with and listen to hapū, iwi and the tribunal, and then brought the disestablishment bill anyway.

acuity.statement: I wish to note my observations around the Director-General of Health, because it appears that powers have been delegated back to that role in the new legislation to confirm iwi-Māori partnership boards.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon speaks after Henare in the same debate and arrives at the very point he had just made — that the repeal hands approval of iwi-Māori partnership boards to the Director-General — but she raises it as a fresh observation of her own rather than taking up, extending, or building on his argument, and she never refers to the preceding speaker at all. Her speech is prepared material addressed to the Minister (Wai 2575 principles, mortality statistics, a list of questions about Te Whatu Ora's board and the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee) and would read word-for-word the same whatever Henare had said before her. Topical continuity on the right bill, but no engagement with the preceding argument, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is at least a gesture at the same strand of the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "In this repeal bill, what it’s proposing is that the iwi-Māori partnership boards can only be constructed or approved by the Director-General of Health."

acuity.statement: I just want to point to the Hon Peeni Henare’s comments relating to perhaps pretending to commit to the iwi-Māori partnership boards. Well, if I could draw his attention to Part 1, replacement section 15, inserted by clause 11, “Health New Zealand must support and engage with iwi-Māori partnership boards”.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft follows Luxton, who had asserted that iwi-Māori partnership boards will continue to work with Health New Zealand and had invited Peeni Henare to explain his objection. She takes up that same strand and does something concrete with it — names the clause and quotes the statutory duty — but the charge she answers was made by Henare in a turn outside this window, and relative to the speaker immediately before her she is extending agreement rather than engaging a claim. The rest of the speech is prepared material on the coalition's 'different way' that would read identically whatever Luxton had said, so this sits at the low end of partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "Iwi-Māori partnerships will continue to work with Health New Zealand to develop priorities to improve hauora Māori."

acuity.statement: What is your alternative model? What are you and how are you resourcing? How are the locality plans working, given that you have no data to say how they’re performing, no outcomes, and we haven’t seen any data outcomes since the DHBs were wound up?
acuity.explanation: Marcroft had just grounded the Government's case in the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora ('insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver') and in decentralisation and health targets as the alternative route. Ngarewa-Packer takes up that strand directly, demanding the alternative model, its resourcing and the performance data behind the locality plans, and asserting there is no outcome data to support the claim. That is a pointable engagement with the preceding argument, but much of her contribution is general grievance about urgency, mispronunciation and the Government's record that would stand unchanged whoever had spoken before, so it is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "overall there had been insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver" / "decentralisation is a key way we’re focusing on this"

acuity.statement: This specious and gross double-speak which suggests that putting special focus on those in need of that focus is somehow a race-based privilege, is revolting—it is revolting double-speak.
acuity.explanation: Luxton opened the window by framing targeted Māori provision as seeing citizens 'based on something as flat as race' and as division the Government is not creating. Abel takes that exact framing and attacks its reasoning — that focus directed at those with the worst outcomes is not a privilege — and he builds the surrounding passage out of the disparity figures that answer it. The speech would have to change if the preceding government speakers had argued on different ground. Scored on engagement only; the contempt in the language is a civility matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "There have been many societies in history who have seen their citizens based on something as flat as race"

acuity.statement: I ask Dr Reti: who are your people who you have consulted with? Give me two, three, one Māori professional who supports this. Does he really believe in this?
acuity.explanation: The only preceding turn in this window is Sam Uffindell's, which rested on the claim that merging the Māori Health Authority into the public system will retain the expertise needed to lift Māori health outcomes. Jackson takes up that strand — contesting whose expertise actually backs the merger and naming Māori health professionals (Jansen, Durie, Reid, Fraser, Moxon) he says were ignored — but he aims the challenge at the Minister rather than at Uffindell's specific claims about wait-lists, immunisation or retained expertise, and much of the surrounding speech is prepared material and tribute. Partial engagement of the argument, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Sam Uffindell: "we will have the expertise there that we need to deliver improved health outcomes for all New Zealanders—Māori and non-Māori alike"

acuity.statement: This Government is committed to finding more effective ways to work with all communities for better outcomes and to deliver solutions, as well as finding savings through disestablishment which may actually go to better health outcomes. You can build whatever structures you like, but till you focus on outcomes, you’re going to have increasing health inequities, and patients will suffer.
acuity.explanation: Campbell follows a substantive turn in which Willie Jackson made a specific, answerable challenge: name one Māori health professional consulted who supports the bill, and answer Dr Rawiri Jansen's Treaty submission. Campbell takes up neither. His speech is prepared government framing on the right subject — the structures-versus-outcomes line gestures at the debate about whether the Authority's structure matters, which earns a little above the floor — but it would read word-for-word the same whatever Jackson had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson demanded the Minister name the Māori health experts consulted and answer Dr Rawiri Jansen's Treaty submission, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: The Māori Health Authority seemed like such a great idea and I held out such hope, as did so many of my health colleagues but, unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
acuity.explanation: Tangaere-Manuel's preceding speech framed Te Aka Whai Ora as hope for Māori-led, kaupapa Māori health care, dashed by this bill. Weenink takes up the 'hope' strand directly — she too held out hope for the authority — and contests its underlying premise by arguing the drivers of Māori health outcomes sit outside the health system, so health-structure policy cannot fix them. That engages one strand of the argument rather than the specific claims Tangaere-Manuel made about rongoā, tohunga suppression and her mother's treatment, and the surrounding material (her anger at the previous Labour Government, the Marcia Walker anecdote) is prepared and would have been delivered whatever preceded it. Partial engagement, hence mid-band; the weakness of the inference ('nothing to do with the health system') is a Rigor matter and is deliberately not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "So I’m sad to say that this bill represents the dashing of hope, because it was something that was Māori-inspired, Māori-led, and all-inclusive."

acuity.statement: I heard the Opposition side of the House mention inequity, a failed health system, racism, discrimination, etc., but I haven't heard any members from the opposite side mention the word “self-responsibility”. As a diabetes and cardio specialist, I can tell you that with self-responsibility and discipline, some of the health issues we’re facing in New Zealand can be prevented.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows a substantive turn by Williams and takes up one strand of it — her inequity framing — naming it explicitly and countering it with self-responsibility, which he grounds in his own clinical background. But he engages none of her specific claims: not the Māori mortality figures, not the Counties Manukau waiting-list and eligibility example, not the historic hospital underfunding argument, and not the Crown Law memo on a likely Treaty breach, which was the sharpest point put to him. The rest of the speech is prepared material ("needs, not race", commending the bill) that would have been identical whatever she had said, so this sits just below the half-engagement mark.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "appreciate the deep inequities which have delivered health outcomes for Māori that would not be fixed by going back to that system"

acuity.statement: There were a number of questions that were posed to the Minister before the dinner break which, in the opinion of members on this side of the Chamber, were a light touch in the answer from the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Henare follows Prime's detailed clause 6 argument (the repeal of paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i) and (j) and their replacement by the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee). He echoes her general complaint that the Minister's answers were light, and later notes the HMAC has "already been touched upon", but he takes up no part of her actual argument — he does not develop, extend or restate the substance of what she said about clause 6, and instead moves to his own prepared material on clause 8, section 12(4) and clause 13.
