That’s important. It doesn’t talk about changing the law—the Employment Relations Act. It talks very specifically about policies that have a material effect on that employee.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific answer — that clause 43's consultation mirrors the Employment Relations Act — and does work on it: concedes the Act's merit, then argues the clause is about employment *policy* rather than law, which the Act only skeletons, and presses for an answer on what that means for Te Aka Whai Ora staff. Delete Reti's reply and substitute a different one and this speech would have to change. Scored on engagement alone; the soundness of the policy-versus-law distinction belongs to Rigor and is not counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Reti: "I’ve been advised that that terminology copies provisions of existing schedules and the consultation mirrors the Employment Relations Act."

acuity.statement: Again, the question was raised around the transfer arrangements. The transfer arrangements, as I discussed many times last night—indeed, the member who’s just taken her seat, the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, has also raised the question—are consistent with the Health Sector (Transfers) Act, which was how people were transferred from the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand into the Māori Health Authority anyway.
acuity.explanation: Reti names the question just put to him on clause 40 and supplies substantive content on it — the statutory mechanism (Health Sector (Transfers) Act) and the fact it is the same mechanism that moved staff into the Māori Health Authority — and elsewhere in the same turn takes up the clause 43(2) consultation wording she flagged. The speech would clearly be different had the preceding turns been different. It falls short of 1.0 because the specific question asked — whether he personally met the unions, delegates or kaimahi — is not engaged; he answers the transfer topic rather than the consultation claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Clause 40 is about the transfer of employees, and I want to know: did the Minister consult with the unions about this legislation that has been brought under urgency?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: We have heard, at length, the lift and shift of our kaimahi from Te Aka Whai Ora to Te Whatu Ora, but in reading the fine print of new Part 2, we can see that the chief executive officer of Te Aka Whai Ora will not become an employee of Te Whatu Ora.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's just-delivered account of the workforce transfer and points out a limit in it — that the chief executive is excluded from that transfer under clause 36(4) — which is a real, if narrow, engagement with what he said rather than a mere mention of it. The rest of the turn is prepared material on Riana Manuel and a new co-CEO proposal that engages none of Reti's reasoning, and she announces it as "a new contribution", so this sits below a half-engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The transfers Act, which I’ve just described—that describes a process by which the workforce will transfer back into Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health." — Shane Reti

acuity.statement: It also says that they may be replaced by Health New Zealand by written notice to that employee. I do want to add my support for the questions asked by the Hon Willie Jackson regarding that simple replacement by a written notice.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of Jackson's immediately preceding argument — the written-notice replacement power in replacement section 43 — names it, and explicitly endorses his question, so the turn would read differently had he not raised it. But she states up front that her point is a different one and then moves to her own prepared material on te reo Māori competency bonuses, which engages nothing in the preceding turn. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "may be replaced by Health New Zealand by written notice to that employee" — Willie Jackson, who pressed the Minister on whether Health New Zealand has a unilateral right under clause 43(1)(b)

acuity.statement: Furthermore, in replacement section 43(2), I’ve been advised that the particular words “material effect on that employee” are specific words that trigger good faith expectations. The member who has just taken her seat was also asking questions around replacement section 43, and I’ve been advised that existing terms and conditions will carry across.
acuity.explanation: He engages the specific statutory provision both preceding speakers raised, answering Jackson's unilateral-notice objection on its own terms by pointing to the good-faith trigger wording in subsection (2) — the reply would have to change if a different clause had been put to him. He does not reach the yes/no he was pressed for, and Prime's question about te reo Māori competency payments is met only with the generic assurance that existing terms and conditions carry across, so engagement is real but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "do they have their unilateral right? Yes or no?" — Willie Jackson, on clause 43(1)(b) allowing an employment policy to be replaced by written notice

acuity.statement: But in relationship to Part 2—and I hope to make more substantive contributions in the third reading—I was interested in just the line around “all information and documents held by [Te Aka Whai Ora] are held by Health New Zealand”. I wanted to pick one of the key initiatives of Te Aka Whai Ora, Te Rangatiratanga Raraunga Māori around Māori data sovereignty.
acuity.explanation: A substantive preceding turn by Ngarewa-Packer was available, and it was itself about data under Part 2, so there was ample opportunity to engage it. Instead this is a prepared new strand (Māori data sovereignty) opened with "this is the first call I'll take in this debate". It is squarely about the matter under debate — the transfer of information under Part 2 — and gestures at the chamber's exchange, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, but no part of the previous argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer asked "how the datasets are being gathered, how they can be reported on" and "what is the baseline of those?", and this statement does not take up her baseline-data argument.

acuity.statement: And it was another really good question around the baseline, actually. What will the baseline be so we can measure improvements? And what we will be needing to do is to inventory the data aggregation that has already occurred and what needs to occur to establish a baseline so we can measure outcomes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Ngarewa-Packer's specific question — the absence of a baseline against which performance could be measured — restates it accurately and supplies a substantive answer (inventory existing data aggregation, identify what else is needed to establish a baseline), then extends it to the iwi-Māori partnership boards' differing capability, which she had also raised. Delete her turn and substitute a different argument and this passage would have to change entirely. Not 1.0 only because the answer is a process commitment rather than the figure or dataset she pressed for — but that is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my question is asking how the datasets are being gathered, how they can be reported on... And what is the baseline of those?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: The data probity issues will follow exactly the same policies that all of Government is required to follow as it relates to data probity, so I do have confidence in that.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand only. It answers the general topic the member raised — protection of data on transfer — and does so knowingly ("probably the third time the question on data probity has been raised"), but it reframes a specific question about the Te Rangatiratanga Raraunga Māori initiative, its continuation and its resourcing as generic "data probity", and leaves the particular initiative untouched. Partial engagement that you can still point at, hence mid-band rather than low.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how does he intend for that data to be protected as it is transferred back to Te Whatu Ora, and whether he intends... for that piece of work to continue" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: This is actually quite a narrow bill, and the question was raised around Schedule 2, which is mostly required to adapt to places in the legislation where the Māori Health Authority appears. Clearly, if it doesn’t exist any more, that legislation needs to be changed.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Schedule 2 repeals Henare had just raised and answers their rationale — the amendments are consequential on the authority ceasing to exist — and addresses his worry about lost functions by asserting the functions transfer even though the chief executive does not. Clearly shaped by what preceded it. Held below the top band because two of the three asks put to him are set aside rather than engaged: the Māori voice in the Oranga Tamariki Acts ("I don't envisage covering that again") and rongoā Māori under the Therapeutic Products Act ("outside the scope of this bill").
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If we’re going to repeal the role of the chief executive of the Māori Health Authority in those particular pieces of legislation, in light of the Ombudsman’s report..." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: It’s already been described that the chief executive won’t be. But the role was important—the role that those staff were playing in making sure that the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and the Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Act 2022 continue to do what they’re intended to do, and that’s to continue to support our whānau.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own statement that staff transfer but the chief executive's role does not, and turns it into the premise of his question about the Oranga Tamariki Acts — so it is not indifferent to what preceded it. But that is one short reference used to launch a prepared new line on Schedule 2; the Minister's substantive answers on baselines, Pae Tū and Wakamaua go unaddressed, so the engagement is a single thread rather than a response to the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "you can have only one chief executive for an agency; and (2) it’s a board appointment not a ministerial appointment" — Shane Reti

acuity.statement: And I heed that request and that advice that you've given. I will note, though, that we have tried to engage in backwards and forwards questions with the Minister, but he didn't actually take us up on that, so you've seen us revert back to five-minute contributions.
acuity.explanation: Prime acknowledges White's request for advice and an amendment, but does nothing with it: she neither takes up the technical-redundancy argument, nor the employment-law point, nor the proposed amendment. She pivots immediately to a procedural complaint about the Minister's refusal to take questions and then to her own prepared material on Schedule 2 and the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act. The speech is on the matter under debate (the same bill, the same part-by-part committee stage) and gestures at the preceding turn, but the content would be essentially identical had White argued something else about the bill — placing it in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture, hence 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I actually just would love to get a little more information out of you on that advice, Minister." — Helen White, who asked whether the Minister had received advice that this was a technical redundancy and whether he would accept an amendment giving staff a process to crystallise a redundancy or renegotiate their role.

acuity.statement: To the last member, who asked the question—it had already been covered several times previously—the first question: existing terms and conditions transfer across. As I’ve said before, the Māori Health directorate, inside the Ministry of Health, will have input into the appropriate transfer of people, into the two respective homes. I’m very focused on continuity of services.
acuity.explanation: Reti takes up Salesa's specific questions in order — staff transfer, support for affected employees, continuity of services — and supplies substantive answers (terms and conditions carry across, the Māori Health directorate will have input, continuity is the focus). The reply would be different had she asked something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because he partly deflects by noting the ground was 'already covered several times previously' and does not reach her third question about who holds the 'by Māori, for Māori' contracts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "what are the transitions that are in place for current employees of the Māori Health Authority following its disestablishment?"

acuity.statement: Just to the Minister’s previous comments on hopes, and the “hope” of one thing and the “hope” of another thing for Māori. It’s a good title for a song, but it certainly does not give us a surety. The “hope” of how Māori will work together and do our best is not good enough to be sure, and that’s demonstrated very much in the title of this bill: the “Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority”.
acuity.explanation: She seizes on the precise word the Minister had just used three times — 'hope' — and turns it into the rebuttal: hope is not surety. This is direct engagement with the content of the immediately preceding answer, and it could not have been delivered unless Reti had framed his assurance that way. Disagreement scores high here; the remainder of her speech moves to prepared ground, which keeps it just below 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Reti: "the hopes I have that staff will “join me and guide me in the pathway forward for Māori health and Māori health outcomes”"

acuity.statement: My question, Minister, is a supplementary in a sense to my colleague Willow-Jean’s point about tāngata whaikaha. We know, as she has pointed out in the consequential amendments, the removal of the Māori Health Authority for the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act has the effect of amplifying the intersectional harm that we see to Māori.
acuity.explanation: Abel picks up the disability strand the Minister had just answered and presses it further, asking what consultation was done with disabled Māori. He engages the topic and the exchange it sits in, but does not take up Reti's actual claim — that the operational parts transfer to Health New Zealand so the expertise and consultation remain — so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Reti: "The member raised the question of legislative compliance, using the example of disability, and clearly, in her own words, said Health New Zealand will still be consulted."

acuity.statement: Now, I want to point the Minister to another piece that he’s spoken to on a number of occasions throughout this debate: the Minister says, “It’s part of the 100-day plan.” Well, if you have a look at the 100-day plan, there’s 49 actions. In those actions, the word “introduce” is mentioned eight times and the word “begin” is mentioned 10 times.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated justification for urgency — that the disestablishment is part of the 100-day plan — and works on it directly, counting the plan's own verbs to argue the plan said 'introduce', not 'pass in 24 hours'. The speech would have to change if the Minister had justified urgency on different grounds. Marked down from 1.0 only because the Minister's turn sits outside the supplied window, so the engagement is pointable through Henare's own quotation of it rather than through the preceding text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: the Minister of Health's repeated justification quoted here by Henare as "It's part of the 100-day plan" (Shane Reti); that turn precedes this one in the debate but falls outside the supplied window

acuity.statement: Just to speak to why Te Aka Whai Ora doesn’t appear in the title, it’s because it doesn’t appear in the Pae Ora legislation either and the amendment bill has to refer to the legal title in the statute.
acuity.explanation: Takes the precise question Prime put about the bill's title and supplies the drafting reason for it — the amendment bill must use the legal title that appears in the Pae Ora Act. The reply would be different had she argued something else, and it answers her specific point rather than the general topic. It leaves her urgency/commencement questions untouched, which is why it is not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "My points have been about why the Minister has not included the actual words “Te Aka Whai Ora”, which is the name—the name—of the thing we are disestablishing."

acuity.statement: And despite the commencement date being in June, we are in urgency, and we are tired, and we are pukuriri, and we are here passionately speaking to save something that our people have invested so much into.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding argument — the gap between a June commencement and passage under urgency — and reasserts it, then moves to prepared material on the Pae Ora submitters and the 100-day plan. It does not engage Reti's immediately preceding explanation about the legal title at all, so the engagement is partial rather than direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "But when we look at the commencement date, this isn’t actually going to commence until 30 June."

acuity.statement: The commencement date is months away—we’re talking about Matariki. It enables an opportunity for us to talk to the communities, the people that are important, and we’ve acknowledged the communities, we’ve acknowledged Maōri, and, particularly today, I think part of the gap in our conversation here and the opportunity to feedback is from practitioners themselves, health practitioners.
acuity.explanation: Takes the preceding speakers' commencement-date point and extends it rather than merely restating it: if the date is months away, the interval could have been used for consultation, and he names a constituency (health practitioners) the earlier turns had not. Partial rather than full engagement because much of the contribution is prepared material and he does not take up Reti's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "And despite the commencement date being in June, we are in urgency" — and Willow-Jean Prime's "That would have allowed ample time, in your rushed processes, to have a select committee process"

acuity.statement: I agree with the suggestion from the Hon Peeni Henare that the name should be changed to “Pae Mate”, and that Te Aka Whai Ora should be referenced in the title. I heard the Minister’s explanation for why it is just the Māori Health Authority, but he can choose to put whatever additional words he would like to put in there—he can hyphenate it if he likes.
acuity.explanation: Prime follows a substantive committee-stage turn by Steve Abel on exactly the question before the House — what the bill should be titled — but engages no part of his case. She resumes her own prepared material on the word “aka”, endorses a different colleague's naming proposal (Henare's “Pae Mate”), and waves away the Minister's reasoning without restating or rebutting it; the Minister's turn is not in the window, so the engagement cannot be pointed at. The contribution is squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it above the floor, but it would read identically had Abel said something else, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel argued the bill should be titled the “Tohunga Suppression Act 2.0” because it denies Māori mātauranga and tino rangatiratanga, and this statement does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: Last night, the Waitangi Tribunal, at 6 o’clock—you see, because I’m watching the tribunal all the time. They confirmed that their jurisdiction had now ended; that they could not hold the urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora. It’s now vacated.
acuity.explanation: Henare's immediately preceding turn argued the Government should have waited for the Waitangi Tribunal's urgency hearing and recommendations. Lyndon takes up that specific strand and advances it with the outcome — the Tribunal's jurisdiction ended at 6pm the previous night and the urgent inquiry is vacated — so this part of the speech would read differently had Henare not pressed the Tribunal point. It is only partial engagement, however: she picks up one thread of his contribution and then moves into her own prepared material on Wai 2575, kaimahi and Riana Manuel, which is indifferent to what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "if this Government had given the Waitangi Tribunal the opportunity for an urgency hearing, every member on that side of the House would have seen the case put forward for those statistics"

acuity.statement: We are discussing title and commencement, and I wanted to take a moment to speak to my Amendment Paper because I have a specific amendment around the commencement date.
acuity.explanation: Jackson had just argued at length that the 30 June date is an affront to the Waitangi Tribunal and asked for two more days. Boyack speaks to the same clause but takes up no part of his argument — not the Tribunal point, not the two-day request — and proceeds to her own prepared case for a year's delay. A gesture at the matter under debate, nothing engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued 'In terms of the date, 30 June, I do not get this date' and asked for two more days out of respect for the Waitangi Tribunal, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: I would like to thank all the members who have actually mentioned health outcomes, because that really was the most important thing here. Regardless of organisational form, this remains, and it needs to be addressed to make sure we have better health outcomes for Māori, and also non-Māori.
acuity.explanation: Campbell follows a long, detailed attack by Willie Jackson (urgency and lack of due process, denial of the Waitangi Tribunal's day in court, 8,000 smokefree deaths, the named Māori health experts, the charge of 'public health vandalism'). He takes up exactly one strand of it — that the Authority's organisational form was what made Māori health outcomes matter — and answers it with 'regardless of organisational form', then adds a general acknowledgement of Māori health providers continuing to serve both Māori and non-Māori, which glances at Jackson's providers-and-contracts point. Nothing else in Jackson's turn is engaged: the due-process, Tribunal, urgency and expert-advice arguments go unaddressed, and the closing material on healthcare workers, aspirin and quinine is prepared matter that would be identical whoever had spoken before. Pointable partial engagement on the topic's central strand, so mid-low rather than the 0.1-0.3 unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Māori Health Authority gave us the bureaucratic muscle to ensure Māori health outcomes mattered" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: This next layer of bureaucracy has actually failed to deliver Māori health gain. Where are the outcomes? We have not seen any from this.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft follows a substantive turn by Trask on the same bill, so she is eligible. Her speech is prepared coalition material — acknowledging the coalition commitment, thanking the Minister, restating equity-of-access principles and asserting the authority failed to deliver. It echoes Trask's bureaucracy framing but engages no claim, figure or inference she made (for instance the progress-report findings on staff transfers), and would read word-for-word the same had any other government member spoken first. On the matter under debate, but unresponsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Laura Trask argued "the Māori Health Authority provided another level of bureaucracy, another central government organisation that was failing to prove its worth", and this statement restates the same prepared theme rather than taking up any part of her argument

acuity.statement: It isn’t about race or ethnicity; it’s about rights. We have rights. We have rights and interests under Te Tiriti that were addressed here, that were addressing wrongs, and no one can deny those wrongs, because this House has acknowledged not only those Wai claims but the settlements of iwi.
acuity.explanation: She directly takes up the needs-versus-race frame that both preceding government speakers built their case on and contests its premise, relocating the question from ethnicity to Tiriti rights and settlements already acknowledged by the House. That strand is pointable and the speech would have to change had the previous speakers argued on different ground. But she engages only that one strand and then moves to prepared material — the Minister's unanswered 'when and how', Te Pāti Māori's own policy list, and demographic predictions — rather than rebutting the bureaucracy-and-delivery case itself, so this sits mid-scale. Scored on engagement alone; the insults and the tone belong to Civility, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "healthcare delivers on needs, not race" — Laura Trask (and Jenny Marcroft's "equity of access for all, based on need—based on clinical need")

acuity.statement: We will retain the iwi-Māori partnership boards, we want to empower them, we want to work with local communities, and we—as the Minister stated—believe local situations require local solutions.
acuity.explanation: Uffindell follows a substantive opposition turn and lands on the very item she pressed — the partnership boards — asserting they will be retained and empowered. But her charge was precisely that there is no 'when' and no 'how', and he supplies neither, restating the intention she had already dismissed as empty. That is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content, which puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at mid-scale. His opening thanks to members for their passion is acknowledgement, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a Minister here who admits that the iwi-Māori partnership boards need to be powered up; there was no when, there was no how" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: I want to thank the Minister of Health for nothing, actually.
acuity.explanation: The line inverts Uffindell's closing thanks, so there is a visible glance at what immediately preceded it, but it engages none of his content — not the retention of the partnership boards, not the local-solutions claim, not the overrepresentation-in-need point. The remainder of the speech is prepared material on the authority's origins and a list of the Government's first four months. Mirroring an opponent's words in order to pivot away is a reference, not responsiveness, so this stays in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to thank the Minister for his dedication to improving health outcomes across New Zealand" — Sam Uffindell

acuity.statement: Te Aka Whai Ora—the Māori Health Authority—was never really equipped to undo the health inequities for Māori. Those gaps are huge, and the responsibility lies much further outside the health system. It’s for the entire economy, and it’s for all of our Government to take note of those inequities because we can’t fix them within health alone; it has to be done across the board. So I don’t believe that this change will have any effect other than to get rid of a bureaucracy that wasn’t doing anything.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows Halbert directly and takes up the core strand of his case — that disestablishment causes harm and that the authority was delivering. She answers it by denying the body was ever capable of closing the inequity gaps and by asserting it was a bureaucracy doing nothing, which is a direct contradiction of Halbert's "that is false" and of his claim that Te Aka Whai Ora "isn't bureaucracy". But she engages none of the specific supports he offered (independence from the Crown, commissioning, the one-year measurement standard, the pending Waitangi Tribunal hauora hearing), and the rest of the speech is prepared material on symbolism that Halbert never raised. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "The disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, today returns Māori to disproportionate harm." and "I want to push back on the non-Māori across the House that take cheap shots at Te Aka Whai Ora and say it didn’t deliver anything. That is false."

acuity.statement: During the select committee stage, a member from the opposite side was talking on behalf of the first generation of immigrants.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows a substantive third-reading speech by Willow-Jean Prime, which argued that the bill disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora tramples the Treaty, that Māori die seven years earlier, that the Minister consulted no Treaty partner, and that the urgency pre-empts a Waitangi Tribunal sitting. He takes up none of those strands. Instead he reaches back to a remark by an unnamed member at an earlier stage and pivots to the ethnic composition of his own electorate — material that reads as prepared and would be unchanged whatever Prime had just said. It is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits in the low band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime spoke about the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, Māori health statistics and the cancelled Waitangi Tribunal sitting, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: My question to the members opposite is simple: what’s your excuse, because the evidence is now overwhelmingly clear—12 people a day in New Zealand die from smoking-related illness, and this Government wants to liberalise the sale of tobacco. Where is your moral compass? What is it that has happened between pre-election and post-election that has forced you to completely abandon the platform that you campaigned on?
acuity.explanation: Costello's speech rested on two planks: that none of the repealed measures are yet in force and that the existing regime is already driving smoking rates down (6.8 percent daily, 229,000 quitters, youth smokers from 119,000 to 19,000). Hipkins engages the topic and one strand of her case — the claim of continued commitment to Smokefree 2025 — by asserting the opposite characterisation (that the Government is liberalising tobacco sale) and demanding an account of the change since the election. But he takes up none of her figures, none of her "nothing currently in force is being stopped" argument, and none of her cessation-tools reasoning, pivoting instead to prepared material about tax cuts and revenue. You can point at what was engaged, so this sits above the unresponsive band, but it answers the subject rather than the specific claims just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "This Government is committed to the Smokefree 2025 goal, but we are taking a different regulatory approach to reducing smoking rates and the harm from smoking."

acuity.statement: It was the National Government who committed to this path—Smokefree 2025—and yet now we have a Government who’s huri kōaro—in te ao Māori we call it huri kōaro [you’ve flipped]. You’re a flip-flop.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Hipkins in the same debate and lands on the same subject (the repeal, the tobacco lobby, tax cuts, Māori smoking rates), but she takes up no part of his argument — she restates the pre-election-position point in her own prepared terms rather than engaging what he said, and the rest of the speech (Kawakawa outlets, prevalence statistics, Anaru Waa) would read identically whoever had spoken before her. A gesture at the same strand, not engagement with its content, so the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "although that’s not the position that they had before the election when they were supporting that"

acuity.statement: Wow! What an animated display we are seeing over this legislation. Quite quickly we’re talking about lobbying from the tobacco industry, but what about the lobbying from gangs?
acuity.explanation: Trask names the specific charge the two preceding speakers built their speeches on — tobacco-industry lobbying — and does something with it, inverting it into a counter-claim about gangs profiting from a black market and backing it with the Customs seizure figure. The opening would have to change if the previous speakers had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because she turns the charge aside rather than rebutting its reasoning, then moves to prepared ACT material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "This is a Government that is firmly in the pocket of the tobacco industry" (and Hūhana Lyndon on the same tobacco-lobby theme)

acuity.statement: New Zealand already has impressive quit rates. The latest New Zealand Health Survey results show that in 2022-2023, 6.8 percent of adults were daily smokers, down from 8.6 percent the previous year and 16.4 percent the year previous to that. What is in place has been working.
acuity.explanation: This answers one strand of what preceded it — the claim that current settings are failing and that the repeal will worsen smoking — by supplying prevalence figures to argue the existing trajectory is working. acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "This exemption was always planned to end when EVs hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet, and, right now, New Zealand has reached that target."

acuity.statement: The fact that we’re looking at moving this to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee—it’s absolutely appropriate that they do take calls of submissions from the public about the rate at which those particular vehicles pay—whether it be the $53 for the hybrids or the $73 per thousand kilometres for the electric vehicles.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows a turn whose entire thrust was that four weeks is insufficient for the select committee, and he mentions the referral and submissions without engaging the timeframe objection at all. The remainder is prepared approval of the 2 percent milestone and the fairness rationale, which would read identically whoever had spoken before. A gesture at the matter under debate puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0. Not penalised for brevity or for being a government backbencher — only for indifference to the argument it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that a 14 March report-back gives the committee too little time to test the technical definitions and weight ratings, and this statement does not take that up — it gestures at the committee referral and public submissions while saying nothing about the time available.

acuity.statement: Now, I gave a nod when perhaps I shouldn’t have, because this motion as tabled does not in fact extend the time, but I would suggest that if the House is happy with this amendment—and I hope it is.
acuity.explanation: Belich, the immediately preceding speaker, told the House that Webb's tabled amendment would 'undoubtedly increase the amount of time' the committee had, and explicitly said she had sought and received his nod of confirmation. Webb opens by retracting that nod and correcting the factual misstatement about his own amendment — the amendment restricts Saturday sittings, it does not extend the report-back period. This is a direct correction of a specific factual claim in the previous turn; had Belich characterised the amendment differently, this passage could not have been delivered at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: 'I do understand my colleague Duncan Webb has tabled an amendment to this motion which he’ll be seeking to speak to, which undoubtedly will increase the amount of time'

acuity.statement: I do agree with the honourable member that the Minister of Justice might want to consider some alternative wording, but it’s important that he responds to the premise in the proposed change, which is the fact that this bill should reflect what it does, and that is: making the work of judges more difficult when they are weighing up how to deal with someone who has offended.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of Webb's tabled amendment immediately preceding — both his concession that the Minister may prefer his own wording and the substantive premise that the bill makes sentencing harder for judges — and then develops that premise with Kim Workman's remarks about what a section 27 report tells a judge. The speech would have to change if Webb had argued something different; it is not a mere reference to him. Marked down from 1.0 because after restating the premise it moves into prepared supporting material rather than engaging Webb's particular reasoning (the regulatory impact statement, the Supreme Court remark on context).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "it makes sentencing harder for judges. So my tabled amendment, which is marked “B”, actually identifies that" — and "the Minister may want to table his own amendment, which doesn’t have quite such a pejorative suggested addition"

acuity.statement: Well, I thank the two members for their suggestions about names for this legislation. The Government has named it the “Legal Services Amendment Bill” because it amends the Legal Services Act, and we think that’s appropriate.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what was put to him — the proposed renaming — and gives an actual reason for the existing title (it amends the Legal Services Act), so this is a real answer to the naming proposal rather than prepared material. But Andersen had explicitly asked him to respond to the premise behind the amendment and to explain his rationale for narrowing the information available to judges, and that is left entirely untouched, as is Webb's point from the regulatory impact statement. Partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "I think it’s only right that we should hear from the Minister to understand his rationale for the fact that this bill narrows the scope" — and her agreement that "the Minister of Justice might want to consider some alternative wording"

acuity.statement: The fact that we have the seeming anomaly that has been released from the Minister of Transport that you could, by driving a plug-in electric vehicle—a hybrid—end up paying more than if you were driving a petrol car or a diesel car, a vehicle that ran on fossil fuels. It seems counterintuitive, and members of this House, as good legislators, need the time with officials to understand that modelling, to understand the thinking that lies behind it, and to look at whether there have to be changes made.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand Genter had just raised — the PHEV-versus-petrol cost anomaly in the Minister's own data — and converts it into a reason the committee needs officials' modelling time. She takes up the topic and the example rather than Genter's specific 'more than twice as much' figure, and then returns to her own prepared list of concerns.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "the significant discrepancy between what electric vehicle users and plug-in electric vehicle users will be paying on the same trip as a comparable car"

acuity.statement: I want to support and endorse the comments of my colleague who has spoken previously to me because, as I highlighted in my contributions in the earlier readings of this legislation, I pointed to the fact that affordability is a particular issue for many in the justice system.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific strand Webb advanced — that removing funding makes the reports available only to those who can pay — endorses it explicitly and then does something with it, supplying the Law Society's statement that the withdrawal "will significantly limit access to justice" and the regulatory impact statement's disproportionate-impact finding as support. She also engages his named amendment by offering her own alternative title. Short of 1.0 because much of what follows is her own prepared material on Maori over-representation rather than a rebuttal or extension of Webb's reasoning itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "This is about legal aid, and legal aid is for poor people, and this is removing access to funding for reports from poor people."

acuity.statement: So I believe that the Minister does need to explain why he is placing a fiscal barrier to those New Zealanders who are unable to pay for these reports, and therefore preventing them from receiving fair access to justice.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the unanswered question Prime had just put to the Minister and presses it again in her own terms, and carries forward Prime's disproportionate-impact-on-Maori strand. That is real engagement with the preceding turn, but it is partial: she is largely speaking to her own tabled amendment with prepared material, and she restates the demand rather than developing Prime's argument further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "Can the Minister please speak to the points that we have raised about how he believes that this change will not impact on those who cannot afford to pay for section 27 reports?"

acuity.statement: The title that the Government has given the bill is the “Legal Services Amendment Bill”, and that is because it is a bill that amends the Legal Services Act, and that makes perfectly good sense.
acuity.explanation: He engages the actual proposition before the committee — that the title should be renamed — by giving the reason the Government's title reads as it does, and he answers Webb's challenge to be creative by declining it on the record. That is responsive to what was put. It is not higher because he deliberately sets aside the content of the three preceding arguments (the fiscal barrier, the Law Society's view, the disproportionate impact) rather than taking any of them up, deferring them to the clause 4 debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Unless you can be a little bit more poetic in there perhaps, let’s call it what it is: stuff the poor people; they can’t have these reports."

acuity.statement: But in terms of the tabled amendment by the Hon Ginny Andersen, I do want to make it clear—and, look, it’s kind of circular: “This amends the Legal Services Act so let’s call it the Legal Services Amendment Bill.” It’s still not descriptive. We know that there’s many amendments to that Act, and they’re indistinguishable from each other.
acuity.explanation: He restates the Minister's justification for the title and attacks its structure directly, naming it as circular and then supplying the reason it fails — that many bills amend the same Act, so the name distinguishes nothing. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged had Goldsmith argued differently; it is built on the specific reasoning just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it is a bill that amends the Legal Services Act, and that makes perfectly good sense"

acuity.statement: So my suggestion to the Minister is not only to take a look at the amendment that has been tabled in the name of the Hon Duncan Webb but also to think about what additional consultation should be undertaken as a Treaty partner and also as the Government doing right by the people of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows Webb in the same committee debate on clause 2 and takes up his specific tabled amendment by name, endorsing it and extending it to a consultation argument. She engages the strand of his case (commencement is too soon) rather than its particular mechanism (deferral by Order in Council until equal access is certified), and then moves to her own prepared material on the evidence base, so this is a partial but clearly pointable engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My proposed amendment, which I think has been marked by the Clerk as “C”, says, “Let’s defer this for Order in Council…”"

acuity.statement: We’re debating the clause about when this Act would come into force, which will be 14 days after the bill is passed. That is to give people some notice and to have a process for applications or requests for approval for funding for these reports to be approved by the commissioner before the two weeks, so that people have some time to get the applications in, if they are currently under way, and they can be approved up until two weeks from when this bill is passed.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith answers the specific objection just put — that 14 days is insufficient — by explaining what the 14 days is for and how in-flight applications are handled within it. The speech would have to be different had the preceding speakers not attacked the commencement period; it supplies the rationale they demanded. Short of 1.0 because he does not engage Andersen's second strand, the absence of any research on the impact of section 27 reports.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "The point I’d like to make is the fact that 14 days is just not enough."

acuity.statement: Mr Webb suggests that we should never bring in the commencement of this legislation—and that doesn’t surprise me, in terms of a Government that was prepared just to sit on their hands while all this money was spent, and other legal aid meantime struggled.
acuity.explanation: He takes up Webb's actual amendment — deferral until equal access to justice is certified — and draws out what he says is its practical consequence, that commencement would never arrive. That is engagement with the content of the proposal, not a mere reference to the member. Whether the inference is fair is a question for Rigor, and whether the jibe about the previous Government is on-policy is a question for Focus; neither is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "So my proposal is that we don’t set a fixed commencement date."

acuity.statement: My colleague the Hon Ginny Andersen talked about the next layer, which, thankfully, the Minister actually touched on, which was the sorts of practicalities of it starting within two weeks—sorry, making sure that the Royal assent is 14 days, or two weeks after. He said for those people to get their application in in that time, before that period ends. My question to the Minister, with respect to that, is: is there flexibility, or is the Minister and the department of a mind, where there are unforeseen circumstances within those two weeks, or, where there is a known backlog in a District Court, whether or not those who are affected by that backlog have some grace here to make sure that they get their application in in respect of the time line that the Minister has just described?
acuity.explanation: Henare restates the Minister's just-given answer accurately and then presses on the gap it leaves — what happens to applicants caught by a District Court backlog or other delay inside the two weeks. The question could not exist without the preceding turn: it is built entirely out of the assurance Goldsmith had just offered, and would have to be rewritten had he said anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "so that people have some time to get the applications in, if they are currently under way, and they can be approved up until two weeks from when this bill is passed"

acuity.statement: I’m happy to tell the member that, yes, I am confident that the corrections system will be able to handle this change.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question Prime put — whether he is confident Corrections can cope with the projected extra demand — squarely and without deflection. It does not take up her specific 136/120/124-bed figures or the missing disclosure material, so it engages the question rather than its supporting detail, which keeps it short of 1.0. Its vagueness is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "is he confident that our prison system has the capacity and the resources to be able to deal with an increase"

acuity.statement: I’m glad the Minister of Justice was able to stand here and say he is confident that they are going to be able to provide these additional prison beds for those who are likely to have different sentencing outcomes in the absence of this report.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's answer, restates what he has now committed to and pins the concession to the absence of the report — so the turn would read differently had he refused or hedged. But it does not test or rebut the claim; it registers it and moves on to the next prepared question about the judiciary, which is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "yes, I am confident that the corrections system will be able to handle this change"

acuity.statement: Very happy to answer the question. I am confident that in the 14 days after this bill is passed and before the Act comes into force, the—I cannot speak on behalf of the judiciary, of course, but what I can say is that they will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders, and within 14 days. That is sufficient time for this change to be made.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific question about judicial readiness within 14 days, distinguishes what he can and cannot speak to, and supplies a counter-proposition — that other tools remain available to judges — which directly meets Prime's claim that the courts will be deprived of information. Falls short of 1.0 because retired Judge Harvey's point about the quality of rehabilitative sentencing is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "is the judiciary prepared for this change to take effect in just 14 days’ time?"

acuity.statement: Just in relation to the commencement of this bill, I note that in the very brief legislative statement that we have received, it specifies that this bill supports the Government’s priorities to restore law and order. I was just wondering if the Minister of Justice would like to say: is he relying on this bill alone to be able to restore law and order to New Zealand, or are there some other things that he’s doing?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive answer from the Minister but engages none of it — neither the 14-day adequacy claim nor the 'many tools' assertion. It is a self-contained new line of questioning drawn from the legislative statement, and would have been put in identical terms whatever Goldsmith had just said. It stays on the commencement clause under debate, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Goldsmith had just argued judges "will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders" within 14 days, and this statement does not take that up; it opens a fresh line about the legislative statement's law-and-order framing

acuity.statement: Now, one of the concerns I have is that it seems like we’re replacing a report, which is seen as expensive, with oral evidence. Oral evidence is not cheap. It is often something that is going to require costs on behalf of the witness—it may be an expert witness, which is going to really blow out the costs.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's 'other tools remain available' defence and works on it, naming what the substitute actually is — oral and expert evidence — and arguing the substitution defeats the cost rationale rather than serving it. The engagement is real but indirect: she develops the consequence of his claim rather than contesting it on its own terms, and the rest of her turn is her own proposal for a trial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "they will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders"

acuity.statement: No, I haven’t considered extending the period beyond 14 days. But what will happen is the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change. Requests up until commencement could still be approved by the commissioner. Requests approved before the date will then be paid in the date. So requests that have been approved by the commissioner within the 14 days will be paid. Requests can be considered up until the 14 days.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question Williams put — whether he has considered extending the commencement date — squarely in the negative, then explains the purpose of the 14-day window and what happens to requests already with the commissioner, which is the transitional concern she raised. Not full marks because he leaves her factual question (how many reports are in train) untouched, but the speech is plainly shaped by what she asked and would read differently had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has the Minister considered extending the commencement date specifically for those situations which are already in train now" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I do want to talk about commencement and that 14-day period because, as the Minister has just pointed out in terms of that, within that period the legal services agency will have to formulate the notice and what it means for various providers and send it out.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification for the 14 days — that it exists to notify legal aid providers — and draws out its consequence: the notification process itself consumes the window, leaving practitioners no time to adjust. This is the previous turn's premise turned into a counter-argument, and the speech could not have been given against a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: In terms of this tabled amendment, look, I just want to make sure that the Minister’s objective is achieved, because he seems to be saying, “No legal aid money for sentencing reports.” But, as I said earlier in the House, lawyers will now be completing these reports.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated policy objective and argues it will be defeated by lawyers doing the work themselves, so there is real engagement with the other bench's position — but it is with the Minister's broad narrative rather than with the specific answer he gave, and the turn is largely built around introducing Webb's own tabled amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change" — Paul Goldsmith; Webb engages the Minister's general objective rather than this specific answer

acuity.statement: I’d just like an opportunity to speak to the proposed amendment, and I’d like to commend my colleague on taking some initiative to strengthen the bill—a very short bill, really. So having a clearer description of legal services and also what’s covered in there would actually make it a lot clearer for those who are able to access these services.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the matter under debate by naming the amendment Webb has just tabled, but takes up no part of his actual argument — that the funding cut will simply shift the work to lawyers at higher hourly rates, so the amendment is needed to make the Minister's own policy coherent. Instead she recasts the amendment as being about a clearer description of legal services, which is prepared material on the right subject rather than engagement with the reasoning just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, if the Minister doesn’t want that to happen, then he’s going to need this proposed clause 3A, which says that lawyers aren’t to do that work." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: A member asked me who had we talked—well, one of the people that I talked about was the previous Minister of Justice, Kiri Allan, who accepted that there was a problem with this cottage industry developing and that we’d have to do something about it.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith picks up exactly one strand of White's questioning — who he consulted — and names a person in answer to it, which shows he listened. But the bulk of the turn is prepared material on the growth in report spending and the Government's objectives, and he leaves untouched her substantive questions about what an oral report looks like in practice, who delivers it, the equity consequences, and the comparative cost. Partial engagement, then a return to the prepared case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "So I’d like the Minister to tell me, has he talked to people about this? Who has he talked to?"

acuity.statement: Minister, I have a question, and the question is: how many reports did Harry Tam provide under this legislation?
acuity.explanation: The question takes the single concrete example the Minister had just built his case around and demands the number that would test it. The turn could not have been delivered had Goldsmith not raised Harry Tam, which is the deciding test; it engages the specific evidentiary basis of the preceding argument rather than its topic. Short, but squarely aimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "a website that is a company led by Harry Tam, a former gang-member, which is touting for business in these cultural reports"

acuity.statement: Well, I can answer the question only to say, I don’t have that figure right in front of me at the moment. There were some and there is an amount of money that’s been referred to in the past.
acuity.explanation: He addresses the question that was put rather than deflecting to other ground, and concedes he lacks the figure before offering what the website claimed instead. The engagement is direct and would be different had a different question been asked; it falls short of 1.0 only because the figure asked for is not supplied, and whether the concession is a good answer on the merits is a separate matter from responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "how many reports did Harry Tam provide under this legislation?"

acuity.statement: In respect of that, I would challenge the Minister, because either he has not got good advice on the floor of the Chamber, or his written parliamentary answers perhaps need revisiting.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes the Minister's immediately preceding concession and does something with it: he sets it against the written answer he says he already received, draws out the dilemma that one of the two accounts must be wrong, and presses for a resolution on the floor. The contribution is wholly contingent on what Goldsmith had just said moments before and would have to be rewritten had he answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "I don’t have that figure right in front of me at the moment. There were some and there is an amount of money that’s been referred to in the past."

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: did he give any real consideration to other options in the regulatory impact statement provided by officials that could have addressed some of those concerns that the Minister had without just wholesale removing—completely scrapping—the report funding for section 27 reports?
acuity.explanation: Prime accepts the Minister's stated concern about escalating cost on its own terms and then uses it against the chosen remedy, asking why the regulatory impact statement's less drastic options — a funding cap, accreditation, a seriousness threshold — were not enough to meet that very concern. The question is built out of the justification Goldsmith had just given and names the specific alternatives, so it engages his reasoning rather than merely the subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "if we didn’t do something about it, we’d be heading for 10 million and then 15 million as the industry, the cottage industry, developed"

acuity.statement: Now, previous members have said, “Well, did you consider doing other things?” Yes, we did. You could consider regulating the industry, and that would be a very Labour Government thing to do: to regulate the industry and get some regulator in to decide whether these reports were good reports or bad reports, and probably requiring an MA in history or criminology or something for the report writers, and you could set up a system to regulate it and we didn’t think that that was a very clever thing to do.
acuity.explanation: Webb's central challenge was that the Minister had been shown alternatives (including leaving the status quo) and chose a blunt tool anyway. Goldsmith does take that strand up directly, naming the two alternatives considered — regulating the report-writing industry and repealing section 27 outright — and giving a reason for rejecting each, which is a genuine engagement rather than a mere reference. He discounts it, though: roughly half the turn is prepared material on the election result, the broader law-and-order agenda and gang legislation that would have been delivered whatever Webb had said, and he does not touch Webb's specific point that the regulatory impact statement advised the status quo was as good as the change. Partial engagement that returns to prepared material, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "other options were presented to you" — Duncan Webb, who asked why the Minister did not instead address "the flaws which perhaps exist in the current system".

acuity.statement: Something else that you mentioned in one of your answers was that section 27 cultural reports are a very small part of the legal aid distribution. I wanted to understand a bit more why it’s being targeted under urgency.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's own characterisation of the bill as dealing with a small area of legal aid spending and turns it back on him as a problem: if the sum is small, why is it worth urgency? That is doing something with the specific claim just made rather than restating a prepared position, and the question would not exist had Goldsmith not said it. She also picks up his answer on regulating the industry by pressing the accreditation alternative again. Short of 1.0 because much of the surrounding turn (Harry Tam, gang numbers, vaccination outreach) responds to earlier answers outside this exchange rather than to the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is a very focused one which is dealing with a small area of the legal aid spending" — Paul Goldsmith, in the immediately preceding turn.

acuity.statement: Look, the only thing I’d say to that member is, of course, Māori are disproportionately victims of crime as well, and they have as much interest as anybody else in society of ensuring that we restore law and order and that there are consequences for serious crime, and that people are held to account for their actions, because everybody in New Zealand has an equal interest in ensuring that we are able to live in a peaceful and safe community.
acuity.explanation: He engages one strand of the four questions put to him — the claim that the bill targets minority communities already overrepresented in the justice system — by answering on the same axis, that Māori are also disproportionately victims of crime. That is a real reply to a real claim, and the fact that it reframes her point (she said Māori are overrepresented as defendants, not that they lack an interest in safety) is a reasoning defect, not a responsiveness one, so it does not pull the Acuity score down. What limits the score is coverage: he leaves untouched her explicit questions about who prepares the reports, why Harry Tam's involvement is a problem, the accreditation alternative, and why the measure is being taken under urgency, and he says so openly — "the only thing I'd say".
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "communities that are already overrepresented in our justice system: Māori, Pacific people, poor people" — Tamatha Paul.

acuity.statement: It’s not a question of ignoring the advice of officials—we’ve read the advice and we considered it—but we didn’t decide that we wanted to go down the route of regulating the report writers and having a little team of officials running around and working out who is qualified to write such things.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Andersen put to him — that the Government ignored officials' recommended option four (an accreditation system for report writers) — denies the characterisation of ignoring advice and gives his reason for rejecting that specific option, namely that accrediting report writers would require officials to adjudicate who is qualified. The sentence could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument; it is shaped by the option-four point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "they recommend option four, which is to introduce an accreditation system for section 27 report writers, to be the preferred option" — and her charge that "the advice of the officials who know quite a bit about this area is being completely ignored".

acuity.statement: The amendment is a review clause. We’ve heard from a number of eminent organisations, who are not politically motivated, that there are serious concerns around access to justice in this bill. I ask the Minister: does he take that opposition seriously?
acuity.explanation: Belich follows a long, specific turn by Webb and opens by announcing this is her first call on clause 4, then delivers her own prepared line of questioning (the 'industry' rationale, her duty-solicitor experience, her review clause). The speech is squarely on the matter under debate — clause 4 and access to justice for people who cannot pay — and her reference to 'eminent organisations' with access-to-justice concerns glances at the submitter evidence Webb had just relayed, but she engages none of his actual argument and the speech would read identically had he argued something else about clause 4. That puts it in the gesture-at-the-debate band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the Bar Association is saying to you, Minister, 'You're taking away—in some of these cases, for poor people—one of the most important tools.'" Belich gestures at eminent organisations' access-to-justice concerns, which is the same territory Webb covered at length, but does not take up his Bar Association reasoning (less informed sentencing -> higher reoffending) or his Amendment Paper H.

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is—this is my first question of many—can he tell me how this bill, this amendment, is meeting our international obligations? I have read the regulatory impact statement and the disclosure statement, and in there it says they cannot see how this bill is actually meeting our international obligations.
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn in the window is Webb's Law Society challenge to the Minister. Prime does not engage its content; she puts her own prepared line of questioning about the regulatory impact statement and international obligations. It is squarely on the matter under debate (the defunding of section 27 reports), and she gestures at the Minister's earlier framing of it as a small change, so this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at zero, but no part of the preceding argument is picked up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the Law Society's view that the bill creates unequal treatment before the law and impedes access to justice, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate line on international obligations.

acuity.statement: Now, the difficulty is, of course, that we had a period of 15 or so—maybe 13 or 14—years when the legislation was passed and people didn’t have access to legal aid for writing these reports. I don’t think people said there was no access to justice or that we were failing the Bill of Rights.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific argument put to him — the Law Society's access-to-justice and Bill of Rights claim — and answers it on its own terms, arguing from the pre-2017 period that no such breach was identified when the reports were unfunded, and then stating directly that he does not accept the Law Society's conclusions. He also names and answers Prime's documents question. This speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different preceding argument. Marked down from 1.0 only because the international-obligations strand gets a bare assurance rather than engagement. Scored on engagement alone; whether the historical analogy is sound reasoning is a Rigor question and whether the Bill of Rights characterisation holds is a Veracity question, neither of which moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this results in unequal treatment before the law, it’s a breach of human rights, and it impedes access to justice for those who cannot afford these section 27 reports. What do you say to the Law Society?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Isn’t tailored sentencing to prevent reoffending good for victims of crime because of the reduced likelihood of reoffending?
acuity.explanation: Willis follows a substantive ministerial answer but opens an unrelated line of his own on tailored sentencing and reoffending, prefacing it by saying it is his first opportunity to speak on the issue. The question is on the subject under debate and is put to the Minister, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it engages no part of the reasoning Goldsmith had just offered — the speech would read the same whatever the Minister had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith had just argued that the reports are "an additional cottage industry that had developed since 2017" and that legal aid is under fiscal pressure, and this statement does not take up either the cottage-industry characterisation or the cost argument.

acuity.statement: We also, of course, share the desire of everybody in this House to improve the chances of people rehabilitating themselves and getting back into a productive life. For example, that is one of the reasons why my colleague the Hon Mark Mitchell this week announced the fact that this Government will be ensuring that prisoners on remand will have access to rehabilitation programmes, so there are many ways in which society and Government encourages people to rehabilitate.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the premise of Willis's question — that tailored sentencing and rehabilitation reduce reoffending — concedes the shared objective, and then disputes that the bill removes it, offering the remand rehabilitation announcement as counter-evidence and arguing judges retain access to offenders' backgrounds under the Sentencing Act. The content is shaped by the specific question asked; a different preceding argument would have produced a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Isn’t tailored sentencing to prevent reoffending good for victims of crime because of the reduced likelihood of reoffending?" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: I have a follow up, in the sense, to what the honourable member Willow-Jean Prime has been saying, further to the points made on the nature of circumstance into which people come.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and claims to follow on from her, but engages none of her actual arguments (the ICERD question, the Defence Lawyers Association's alternative of report-writer standards, the Bar Association's cost-benefit request, or the cost-to-the-justice-system point). What follows is prepared material on judges' views and the value of expert report writers, which would have been delivered unchanged whatever Prime had argued. A gesture at the debate on the right subject, so 0.3 rather than 0.1, but a mere reference is not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "serious ones that disproportionately affect Māori in the criminal justice system" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: The question was raised tonight, how does it fit within our international agreements? My answer is that it fits very comfortably with our international agreements and our focus on ensuring that all New Zealanders get to live in a peaceful and safe society.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific question Prime twice put to him and answers it on its own terms, then goes on to take up the opposing side's central implication — that judges will lose access to offenders' background — and contest it. The speech would be different had the preceding turns raised something else. Scored down slightly from 1.0 because the answer asserts compliance rather than engaging the departmental disclosure statement Prime quoted, and because Abel's judges-find-the-reports-helpful question is left untouched. Vagueness of the answer and the strawman framing of the opposing case are Specificity and Rigor problems, not Acuity ones.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So what steps have been taken to determine whether this policy meets our international obligations under that convention?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: So this is one probation officer emailing you, versus the Law Society, Māori Law Society, Bar Association, Defence Lawyers Association?
acuity.explanation: Takes the piece of evidence the Minister has just read into the record and does something with it immediately — weighs its evidential standing against the professional bodies submitting the other way. Could not have been said had he produced a different argument, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just got correspondence from a former probation officer, who had retired before these section 27 reports came in" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: Yes—but the point is that there are many avenues in the legislation at the moment, through pre-sentencing reports and other reports, where people can understand the background of offenders.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the premise put to him ("Yes") and then redirects: the letter was only illustrative of a point he says stands independently. That is engagement with one strand — he accepts the factual correction — but he does not address the actual thrust, which was the weight of the professional bodies against a single retired officer, and instead returns to prepared material about alternative report types. Partial engagement, pointable, so 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So this is one probation officer emailing you, versus the Law Society, Māori Law Society, Bar Association, Defence Lawyers Association?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: In terms of why legislate for this change, it is that the commissioner, who’s responsible for the legal aid decisions, is statutorily independent. So for the Government to just send a message to him or her that we no longer want them to fund those reports would be to impinge upon that independence. So it’s appropriate for legislation to state that as the will of the Parliament.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Henare's specific objection — that section 99 already gives the commissioner wide discretion to decline claims, so the new paragraph is unnecessary — and supplies the reason the power cannot simply be exercised administratively (statutory independence), then explains the exclusions list. The answer would be different if Henare had raised a different objection. Not a 1.0 only because he does not engage Henare's reading of section 99 itself, and loses track of the second question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "I question whether or not this particular amendment was actually required, in that there is quite a lot of discretion for the commissioner to be able to make denials for those who claim for reimbursement."

acuity.statement: Winston Peters, for one, has a very strong view on these matters, and I’ve had long conversations with him and many others. So there’s a wide variety of opinions across many communities.
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand of Henare's question that asked who is putting Māori views to him, by naming one colleague and asserting a diversity of views, but does not take up the specific ask — the conversations held with his Māori Cabinet colleagues on this bill. Partial engagement with the question actually put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "can the Minister share with us the conversations that he’s had with his Māori Cabinet colleagues?"

acuity.statement: So the consultation—I come back to this consultation question because I want to ask this Minister: apart from Winston Peters, good man that he is, which iwi has this Minister consulted with?
acuity.explanation: Directly takes the content of the Minister's answer — that he had long conversations with Winston Peters and others — accepts it on its own terms and presses the gap it leaves, naming iwi and pan-tribal organisations the answer failed to cover. The question is unintelligible without the preceding turn, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Winston Peters, for one, has a very strong view on these matters, and I’ve had long conversations with him and many others."

acuity.statement: Given the urgency with which we’ve moved on this, there has not been formal consultation with different groups—with the legal community or with iwi—but it is something that we’ve flagged very carefully and clearly in our election campaign. We said we’re going to do it, and, lo and behold, we are going to do it.
acuity.explanation: Answers Jackson's repeated demand to name a single iwi or marae squarely, by conceding that no formal consultation occurred and substituting the electoral mandate as the justification. The concession is responsive to the precise question asked; the preceding jibe about Jackson's 'democracy has changed' remark is a pivot, but the substance of the turn engages the challenge.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "just name one marae or one iwi grouping who you’ve consulted with, because that would then fulfil some of the Treaty of Waitangi obligations"
