acuity.statement: Just wanted to respond to the questions around urgency. Of course, most of the legislation in the justice space that the Government’s going to be introducing will be going through the full select committee process, such as the gangs legislation coming up and the firearms changes, and that’s appropriate that they should be considered.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith follows a substantive turn in which Webb set out a specific amendment — a carve-out preserving these reports for offenders under 18, with reasons about whānau context and the nexus to offending, and an explicit invitation to the Minister to keep that tool available. Goldsmith takes up none of it: he returns to an earlier line of questioning about urgency and the process by which legal aid came to fund the reports. The speech is about the matter under debate and gestures at the debate (and at 'that member'), so it clears 0.1, but it would read identically had Webb never spoken.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb proposed a carve-out so that 'where these things are the most valuable, they’re preserved' for under-18s, and this statement does not take that proposal up.

acuity.statement: It’s in a cost of living crisis, and the Minister himself has said that the two key issues that he heard back at the election, when talking to people, was the cost of living and also law and order. So if the number one issue that came back after the election—and that same argument that, when you’re elected to do something, you need to do it.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith had just justified the urgency on two grounds: a democratic mandate ('it is the majority of the Parliament that passes the legislation') and that this is 'a straightforward change that should be made swiftly'. Andersen takes up the mandate strand and turns it back — if the mandate argument holds, the mandate was cost of living, and this bill increases costs. That is a genuine engagement with one strand of the argument just made. It is only partial: the bulk of her turn is prepared material on the regulatory impact statement, the Newsroom article and bed-count forecasts, and she does not touch his claim that the legal-aid funding change itself bypassed any democratic process.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we think it’s a straightforward change that should be made swiftly' / 'if you do it to the extent that the majority of New Zealanders aren’t happy with the direction that you’ve taken, you get thrown out' — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: To date, we’ve been discussing some of the general points. I do want to ask directly—and I’m happy to sit down if the Minister indicates he will answer this question, but it’s the question about Corrections documents which have been prepared within the corrections system being used.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Andersen's substantive turn precedes it. Webb engages none of her argument; he explicitly notes he is moving on to Amendment Papers not yet discussed and puts a fresh question to the Minister about Corrections documents. The engagement he does show is with a ministerial turn outside the supplied text, so it cannot be pointed at, which caps this in the 0.0–0.3 band. It is 0.3 rather than lower because the question is specific to this bill and continues the amendment-by-amendment discussion Andersen was part of, not material transportable to another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen spoke immediately before, supporting Webb's own victim's-voice amendment and advancing her new clause giving judges discretion to order a section 27 report, and this statement does not take up either argument.

acuity.statement: There’s a repeated pattern in the House that we find from the Government, and we heard it from the Minister this evening, which uses the argument that, because they won an election on it, therefore the legislation is good and solid. Now, I do not believe that the Minister seriously thinks that is a legitimate justice argument for this piece of legislation, because it utterly speaks to the tyranny of the majority.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it. Abel's speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Andersen or Webb had said; by the deciding test, substituting a different argument from them would require no change to it. He does attack a mandate argument attributed to the Minister and references a reply given to Willie Jackson, but neither turn is in the supplied text, so the engagement is unpointable and band-capped. 0.2 rather than 0.0 because the speech is tightly tied to this bill and this debate and could not have been delivered elsewhere.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen and Duncan Webb immediately preceded him arguing for specific Amendment Papers (the victim's-voice amendment, judicial discretion, and a $2,000 cap on legal-aid-funded reports), and this statement takes up none of those.

acuity.statement: I think in this particular area, the Minister should give consideration to a longer transitional period, because that short period of time to have that transition is insufficient for the legal profession.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows Webb's substantive argument that the transitional provision needs more flexibility, and her contribution is on that same strand — the 14-day transition is too short for the profession — proposing a longer transitional period instead. She never takes up Webb's specific suggested wording or his 'reasonable in all the circumstances' threshold, and much of the speech reads as independently prepared material on clause 5, so this is partial engagement with the topic rather than with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "it may well be that we need a little more flexibility in this new Part 3 which is inserted into Schedule 1AA" — Andersen takes up the same strand (the transition in new Part 3 is too tight) but reaches her own remedy rather than engaging Webb's proposed discretion test.

acuity.statement: So why is “defer” there? And if “defer” is there, is there some requirement for that deferral to be resolved prior to the commencement of this bill?
acuity.explanation: Belich speaks squarely on the matter under debate — the transitional provisions in new Part 3 of Schedule 1AA, and even the same clause 7 Andersen had quoted — but her contribution is a fresh set of technical drafting questions that would have been identical whatever Andersen had argued. It is on-topic prepared material with a gesture at the part of the bill just discussed, not engagement with the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "It clearly states in clause 7(1) of the Schedule" — Belich moves to subclause (2) of the same clause but engages no part of Andersen's argument about the insufficiency of the transition or the communications plan.

acuity.statement: Just in terms of the question around the use of 2024, I don’t understand the point the member is making. So perhaps—it is 2024; that is the year we’re in and so that’s the year that we’re referring to.
acuity.explanation: The reply is directly aimed at the question Belich asked and would not exist but for it, so it is genuinely responsive in form; but it engages the wrong strand — Belich asked about the bolding convention and whether delay was anticipated, and Goldsmith answers only that the year is 2024. Partial engagement: he addresses the question's surface and not its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "If the Minister could enlighten us as to why it’s bolded when it’s obviously—because of the Minister’s decision—going to be passed this year?" — Goldsmith takes up the year reference but not the drafting-convention point actually put to him.

acuity.statement: Why is it in bold? That is a mystery to which there is no clear answer.
acuity.explanation: This short turn restates and addresses the precise question Belich raised about the bolded year, conceding he has no explanation. It engages the specific point rather than pivoting away, which is responsive — though it supplies nothing of the drafting rationale asked for and does not touch her follow-on question about anticipated delay.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "That is only, as far as I’m aware, used in bills in the House; it’s not something that appears in legislation once it’s passed." — Goldsmith now takes up the bolding point itself.

acuity.statement: In terms of the second point that the member was making, the point is that there’s two steps in the process in the 14-day period: first, the commissioner gives approval to incur a disbursement. So if that happens, then after the 14 days, when the bill comes in, the commissioner can approve, defer, or decline the payment. So the payments could continue past the 14 days if, in this period, the grant for disbursement is approved, and that is the transitional period.
acuity.explanation: This takes the specific mechanism Belich asked about and does something with it: it explains the two-stage structure of clause 7 so that deferral after the 14 days is not fatal to the claim, which is the exact worry she raised. The speech would be different had she asked something else; it is not quite 1.0 only because he does not address her further question about whether a deferral must be resolved before commencement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "But what does happen when it’s deferred?" — Goldsmith sets out the two-step sequence to explain how a deferred payment can still be met after commencement.

acuity.statement: The other question was raised about the communications plan. The Ministry of Justice, of course, has a very comprehensive communications plan in place that will roll out the moment this bill is passed so that lawyers are made aware—everybody’s made aware—at the earliest possibility that it has passed and that there is a 14-day period in which they can seek to have a grant for disbursement if they’re currently in the system.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith names the question put to him by Andersen and supplies the thing she asked for — who communicates, when it starts, and what the message is — directly contradicting her premise that no communications are provided to the profession. This turn could not have been delivered in another debate and would have been different had she not asked; the quality or truth of the assurance is a separate matter from the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "what communications, whether through his own office or through the Ministry of Justice, have been undertaken in order to communicate that section 27 reports will no longer be funded?"

acuity.statement: The Minister of Justice spent two minutes talking about this significant change to our justice system, so it’s a sad day when a Minister really just doesn’t address or come back to the House after the committee of the whole House stage to give us a fair summation of what’s happened there, which is his function, and takes such a dismissive approach.
acuity.explanation: Webb's opening is plainly shaped by the turn it follows — it takes up the brevity and omissions of Goldsmith's third-reading speech, in particular its failure to report back on the committee of the whole House stage. But what it engages is the FORM of that speech, not any claim or inference in it; no part of Goldsmith's actual argument (the funding growth, the alternative free routes under section 27, the redirection of savings) is taken up here. Pointable partial engagement, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith's whole third-reading speech, which ran only a few paragraphs and closed "I would like to thank MPs for their support of this important bill. Thank you." — Webb engages its brevity and its silence on the committee stage.

acuity.statement: But the Minister did say one thing I want to latch on to and he said that the savings to be made here—we know it’s about $7 million a year—now, in the National Party’s Real Consequences for Crime election document, it said that every penny of that money would go to victims.
acuity.explanation: This takes the single specific commitment Goldsmith had just made — that the savings would go to supporting victims — names it as the thing he is latching on to, attaches the minister's own $7 million figure to it, and then does something with it by setting it against National's election document and demanding delivery. Delete Goldsmith's victims line and substitute a different justification and this passage could not stand as written; it is wholly parasitic on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Putting an end to the current funding arrangement for section 27 reports will mean that savings can be used to improve support for the victims of crime."

acuity.statement: Let me be clear—I’ve heard a lot of discussion tonight; let me be clear one more time: this makes no changes to section 27 of the Sentencing Act. Those provisions are still available for offenders to make submissions to the court.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the factual premise of the preceding Opposition speech. Tamatha Paul had argued the bill removes the mechanism for understanding offenders' backgrounds ('we're taking out that important mechanism', 'the removal of cultural reports'); Stephenson engages that specific claim by distinguishing section 27 submissions (unchanged) from the funding for reports (removed). The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had made a different argument. Not full marks because the engagement is a single assertion restated rather than an argument worked through against Paul's reasoning, and he does not take up her evidence or causal case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'those are the communities that will be most deeply impacted by the removal of cultural reports'

acuity.statement: What I’m hearing from the Opposition is that it’s as though these reports will not exist anymore. Of course they’ll exist—it is simply who is going to present the reports. Actually, I would say that it is much more valuable for the judge to get a report from people—the whānau, the friends; the people who know the offender rather than somebody who needs to be paid for it.
acuity.explanation: Names the Opposition's argument, restates it, and does something with it: denies the reports disappear and offers a counter-claim about who should write them, which answers Paul's point that the understanding of upbringing and whakapapa is being stripped out. Clear engagement with the content, not merely a reference to the previous speaker. Held below the top band because he characterises the Opposition case loosely ('as though these reports will not exist anymore') rather than taking up what Paul actually argued about funded, expert cultural reports — whether that characterisation is fair is a Rigor question, but the looseness does mean only part of her argument is actually engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'we’re not going to understand those drivers of crime, because we’re taking out that important mechanism by which we can understand that more'

acuity.statement: Indigenous incarceration is well understood right around the world. In post-settler colonial societies, the indigenous people of those nations are overrepresented in incarceration, in discrimination in justice, in police and corrections—in every possible place you can be exercising authority. This is well understood. If people in this House don’t understand that, you need to catch up quick.
acuity.explanation: On the subject under debate and aimed generally at the government benches, but it engages no part of the specific argument the two preceding speakers made — that section 27 submissions survive and only the funding for paid reports goes, and that whānau-written reports would serve the judge better. The passage would read identically whatever Stephenson and Foster had said. The gesture at 'people in this House' who 'need to catch up' is a target, not an engagement with their claim, which is why this sits in the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued the reports will still exist and only the payment for them is removed, and this statement does not take that claim up

acuity.statement: The implication from members opposite is that if they were approached by an offender who asked them for help, they’d say, “Yes, but only for a fee.” That is shameful. Reports remain; use them well; do it for free.
acuity.explanation: This short intervention exists only because of what Davidson just argued: she contended that removing legal-aid funding leaves cultural reports available only to offenders who can pay, so the system is 'only tough for some'. Meager takes that exact strand — availability conditional on money — and does something with it, turning it back on the lawyers and MPs opposite by inviting them to supply the reports without charge. The speech would have to change entirely if the preceding turn had made a different argument, which is the deciding test. It is not a full 1.0 because he recasts her funding argument as a personal willingness-to-work-for-free argument rather than engaging the legal-aid mechanism itself (a reasoning weakness that belongs to Rigor, not here), but the engagement is squarely aimed at the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "they’re still available, but just for those who can afford it" — and her conclusion that the bill is "only tough for some".

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, and thank you to that member James Meager for that wonderful contribution to the debate tonight! In fact, the quality of this debate reflects which side of the argument has the stronger case, because when I think about what is the best way of characterising what we are seeing, just this bill is a really good example of the overall theme that this Government has been carrying over the past couple of months.
acuity.explanation: Andersen names the previous speaker and sarcastically rates his contribution, but engages no part of what he actually said — that the reports remain available and lawyers could provide them free of charge. Naming an opponent in order to pivot to prepared material about the Government's overall 'theme' is a mere reference, which the rubric puts in the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.5. It sits at 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is at least a gesture at this debate and this bill, not a speech that could have been delivered on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager argued that the reports remain available and that lawyers should use them and "do it for free", and this statement does not take that up — it only characterises the quality of his contribution.

acuity.statement: Amending the Legal Services Act 2011 to exclude section 27 reports from the legal aid scheme doesn’t stop offenders from being able to get someone to speak directly to the court on their behalf. It doesn’t stop someone from being able to provide a written statement regarding their background. But it does stop the cottage industry that writing section 27 reports has become, costing the taxpayer millions—over $7.5 million last year, up from $40,000 in 2017—while doing nothing for the victims of crime.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Andersen had just made — that the bill denies poorer defendants the ability to put background material before the court — and disputes its premise directly, distinguishing what the bill removes (legal aid funding for paid report writers) from what remains available (a supporter speaking to the court, a written statement). The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been a different one; it is built around rebutting the access point rather than merely asserting the Government's rationale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "if someone can pay, if they have access to funding, they get better access to legal services"

acuity.statement: I know section 27 will still be there. We’ve heard a number of contributions that it is still in the system and is able to be put forward to the sentencing judge. But it’s only there for those who can afford it.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly concedes the point the Government speakers had just made — that section 27 survives the amendment — and then does something with it, arguing the concession is beside the point because the provision becomes available only to those who can pay for a report. She names the preceding contributions she is answering. It is not a full 1.0 because the engagement sits inside a largely prepared speech and she does not take up Redmayne's cost figures or the written-statement alternative.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "doesn’t stop offenders from being able to get someone to speak directly to the court on their behalf"

acuity.statement: We must acknowledge the challenges that face offenders and many young offenders especially. There is a lot of help needed for them long before they get to the space of being in a position to offend. But what the Legal Services Amendment Bill wishes to do is simply to bring back section 27 reports to what they were originally intended to do, which was to allow family members and friends, people who knew the offenders, to speak to the report and give them support.
acuity.explanation: Opens by granting one strand of the argument immediately preceding it — the difficulties facing young offenders that Sosene had spent her speech on — before turning to the prepared Government rationale about the original purpose of section 27 reports. That is a partial engagement: the concession is pointable and would read oddly after a different speech, but he does not answer her actual claim that the reports will now be available only to families who can pay, so most of the turn is indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "We have far too many young Pasifika people—once they enter the judicial system, they spend a lifetime trying to get out of it."

acuity.statement: Don’t allow the Government to downplay what they claim is a small change. As I spoke in the committee of the whole House yesterday, a small change, yes, but it has profound impact on the justice system.
acuity.explanation: Engages the minimising framing that Redmayne and Garcia had both just used — the bill as a simple restoration of original intent — accepting the characterisation as a small change while disputing what follows from it. The engagement is real and pointable, but it addresses the framing rather than either member's substantive claims about what the bill leaves intact or the cost of report writing, and the surrounding contribution is prepared material (Law Society quotations, the regulatory impact statement) that would have been delivered whoever spoke before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "simply to bring back section 27 reports to what they were originally intended to do"

acuity.statement: So I don't think it's such a big ask for us to say, for our lawyers, let's get back to the basics. Let's put together that list of mitigating factors for our magistrates, for our judges to make their decisions.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows Prime's third-reading speech and takes up one strand of it — the claim that removing section 27 report funding will damage sentencing outcomes — by arguing counsel can themselves assemble mitigating factors for the judge. She engages the sentencing-quality strand only, and leaves untouched Prime's actual load-bearing claims about urgency, absent consultation with iwi and the legal profession, Te Puni Kōkiri's opposition, and officials' December advice that costs will rise; the rest of her speech is a characterisation of opponents as defending criminals, which engages no content. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "all say that they have grave concerns about the impact that this Government's rushed policy to remove funding for section 27 reports will have on access to justice and on fair and appropriate sentences."

acuity.statement: They’re trying to run these businesses, and those are the people that you will hear me, in these speeches, stick up for, because this was nudge legislation which had already started to change the habits of our big companies because it shamed them.
acuity.explanation: Bayly's central argument against the Act was that the disclosed data would go unused because small businesses would never find or trust an MBIE website. White takes up that strand and offers a different mechanism for how the Act works — reputational pressure on large firms rather than search by small ones — which is a direct answer to his utility objection. She does not engage his cost figures or the Centrix alternative, and much of the surrounding speech is prepared autobiography, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "This undermines the utility of the Act as the information disclosed is highly unlikely to be used by small businesses in their decision making as to who they should do business with."

acuity.statement: This obviously had happened in Australia too, and they went after it with a law where they did something quite similar, but they had a threshold of $100 million.
acuity.explanation: Bayly put weight on the Australian precedent, citing a recent review finding it was not working and in some cases worsening outcomes. White returns to the same precedent and reads it the other way, as the model New Zealand softened — but she addresses the comparison only as background to her own account and never takes up the review finding or the five reasons he listed. Engagement with the topic he raised, not with his claim about it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "I would note that the Australian Government implemented a similar piece of legislation in 2020. There’s been a recent review of that. It’s found to be actually not working"

acuity.statement: What they’ve got is a Minister who comes from the experience of being a fund manager, and that is all about financial markets.
acuity.explanation: Bayly had just set out a six-part alternative package — Government payment within 10 working days, e-invoicing, published payment times, a Business NZ voluntary supplier code. This reply engages none of it and pivots to the Minister's professional background instead. It is at least about the matter under debate (who looks after small business), so it sits above zero, but it would read identically whatever argument he had made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly set out a six-part alternative package including "reinforce the requirement that Government agencies are to pay ordinary creditors within 10 working days" and an "industry-led voluntary code", and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This bill that we’re putting in place does repeal some unnecessary compliance costs—and in a relationship we don’t actually need to be interfering in. We’re very supportive of small business, but this is not the way to do it, and it’s also not the way to impose additional costs on other businesses.
acuity.explanation: Willis had directly anticipated and rebutted the compliance-cost argument, naming it and answering it. Stephenson simply reasserts that the Act imposes unnecessary compliance costs without taking up any part of that rebuttal, and the rest of the turn is prepared material about his party's small-business credentials. There is a gesture at the matter under debate — the same cost rationale Willis attacked — but no engagement with the argument, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "this Government is arguing that the Business Payments Practices Act imposes compliance costs on New Zealand businesses" — and his rebuttal that "This is not hurting good businesses."

acuity.statement: Now, if there is a six-month reporting period and then another four months after that, that is 10 months; whereas now there is information available. If you want to pay the fee, it is a minor fee to pay. But good business owners don’t make decisions based on 10 months of lapsed data.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of Willis's case — that repeal costs small businesses information and transparency — and answers it on its own terms, arguing the disclosure regime's data would be up to 10 months stale and that current information is already purchasable. She does not engage the power-imbalance or urgency arguments, and the turn reads as prepared rather than shaped by what Willis said, so this is partial engagement: ~0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "this is going to leave small businesses with less information, less transparency in a period of economic turmoil."

acuity.statement: Let’s take, for example, the supermarket duopoly. The Commerce Commission concluded in 2020 that major supermarkets made a profit of $430 million, but now they can delay payment to those who are providing the goods and services to those particular organisations, without them being paid over a four-month period. Nobody wants to pay another extra small fee to go and see whether those big businesses pay that money or not, because they haven’t even been paid for the goods and services that they’ve provided for those particular companies.
acuity.explanation: He takes Unkovich's specific concession — that paying a minor fee gets you the information anyway — and disputes it directly, arguing an unpaid supplier is the last party who will spend money to check whether it will be paid. That is a genuine engagement with a claim made moments earlier. It is one strand only; the bulk of the turn is prepared material on tax and wealth distribution, so this is above a topical glance but short of a full rebuttal: 0.6. The quality of the inference and the truth of the $430 million figure are not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "If you want to pay the fee, it is a minor fee to pay."

acuity.statement: If they had listened to the speech from the Minister Andrew Bayly—clearly the Green member Scott Willis had not heard that or had chosen not to listen. The Minister pointed out that there will be a bill, which I predict will be called the “Bayly Bill”, which will actually address a lot of the issues that they raised, in a much more comprehensive way, in a much more cost-effective way, and bring all of the stories of woe that were brought before us under control.
acuity.explanation: He names the preceding speaker's substantive case — the catalogue of small firms left unpaid — and answers it with a counter: that a forthcoming bill will address those same issues, and that nobody is proposing to stop enforcing timely payment. The speech would be different had Willis argued something else; it is shaped around the specific grievance raised. Not a 1.0 because he engages the thrust rather than any particular figure or clause, and part of the turn is a procedural lecture about listening. The "had chosen not to listen" jab is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one, and the accuracy of what the Minister promised is a Veracity question I am not scoring here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "The examples of small businesses carrying the big boys are so, so many." — and his case that repeal leaves small firms unprotected against late payment.

acuity.statement: I’d like to speak in support of this bill, and I’d just like to allude to the member that has just spoken, Ingrid Leary, who said that this Government has no plans that she’s seen. Well, in the first 100 days, we’ve got 49 actions, and our plans are very much focused on getting this economy back on track.
acuity.explanation: Wedd picks up one identifiable strand of Leary's immediately preceding speech — the jibe that the Government has shown no plans — and supplies a specific counter (49 actions in the first 100 days), so the opening would have to change had Leary not said it. But she engages nothing of Leary's substantive case: the Australian payment times reporting review, the $33 million cap, the select committee mitigations, or the commercial-sensitivity safeguards. The rest is prepared material on red tape and e-invoicing. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We haven’t seen a lot of plans from this new Government." — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Now, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment tells us—and other members of this House have been good enough to point this out—that there are more than half a million small businesses in New Zealand. That’s classed as a business with fewer than 20 employees—so that’s 97 percent of the businesses in New Zealand. So, in its simplest form, this is a bill that makes sure 3 percent of businesses provide information to make it easier for the other 97 percent to do business and, importantly, to stay in business. It sounds good to me.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate, and there is a gesture at the chamber ("other members of this House have been good enough to point this out"), but no part of Wedd's compliance-cost or e-invoicing argument is engaged. The 3-percent/97-percent framing sits adjacent to her red-tape claim without ever addressing it, and the rest of the speech is a prepared constituent account that would read identically whoever had spoken before. Prepared material on the right subject with a glance at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Catherine Wedd argued the Act means "strangling business with six years of red tape, regulation, compliance, and cost" and that e-invoicing is the better answer, and this statement does not take that argument up

acuity.statement: I rise to support the repeal of the Business Payment Practices Act, because businesses in New Zealand are desperate to move forward in this very challenging economy, and they’re desperate to move forward with the modern world. What they don’t need is excessive regulation in their areas that will just ask them to do additional administrative work and disclosures.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed, evidence-led speech against the repeal and engages none of it — not the cash-flow harm, not the 3-percent disclosure burden, not the constituent testimony. The speech asserts that disclosure is excessive regulation without touching the case just made that disclosure is what protects the firms being paid late. It would be word-for-word identical whoever had preceded her, though it is at least about the bill before the House, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued that late payments cripple cash flow and kill small businesses, reading a Christchurch East business owner's account of chasing three unpaid debts, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I have heard from on the other side of the House that this means that we are going to be mistreating our medium and small businesses. I think medium and small businesses need to be looking at who they’re doing business with. It is something that everyone has to take responsibility for, and it doesn’t mean that you can’t already access information from your networks and from people you interact with about the business practices of the people whom you interact with.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Willis's case — that repealing the Act abandons SMEs to late payment — and answers it with a counter-principle: that firms can already source payment-practice information through their own networks and should check who they trade with. It engages the imputation rather than the evidence Willis offered (no response to the going-to-the-wall examples, the select-committee point, or the rural-broadband obstacle to e-invoicing he had specifically asked about), and the rest of the turn is prepared material on regulatory burden that would stand whatever preceded it. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "We have so many examples of people who are going to the wall because the payments do not come in on time"

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First, and having been, well, a solopreneur for most of my working life, in a coaching and consulting small businesses, I can assure people on the other side that no one on this side wants to see small businesses fail. No one on this side wants to see late payment for small businesses or other solopreneurs out there who struggle with this.
acuity.explanation: Directly addressed to "people on the other side" and denies the specific imputation Willis had just made — that the Government bench is indifferent to small firms and serving corporates instead. But it denies the charge rather than engaging its reasoning: no answer to why repeal with nothing in its place serves SMEs, and the remainder of the turn is NZ First's own framing about compliance stress and data interpretation. Pointable but thin — an assurance about motive, not a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "The Government isn’t looking after business; the Government is looking after corporates."

acuity.statement: I wonder if this Government ever gets tired of simping for the big corporates and the 1 percent, because assuming that getting rid of a disclosure regime on late payments will actually do anything but simply benefit those who are already creaming it at the top is an illusion.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Waititi's substantive turn immediately precedes it in the text. The opening is on the matter under debate and reaches the same conclusion as Waititi, but engages no part of what he actually argued — no reference to the 120-day period, the small-business numbers, or the trickle-down claim. It is prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate's framing, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that the bill gives big businesses a four-month (120-day) window to pay small suppliers and that 546,000 small businesses are affected, and this opening does not take up that argument or its figures.

acuity.statement: But he could be presenting a bill rather than wasting our time in this place, simply simping for big businesses. If the Minister is so confident that he is doing the work on this, he could actually be introducing bills and having us do bills around this.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's interjected claim directly and does something with it: concedes the premise arguendo and turns it into a demand for legislation rather than assertion. The passage would not exist in this form if Bayly had not interjected that claim, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because it tests the claim rhetorically rather than engaging any evidence for it, and slides back into the prepared 'simping' line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have—I have." — Andrew Bayly, interjecting to claim he has already initiated work on Government departments' late payments.

acuity.statement: It’s quite incredible what we just heard. Clearly, the member Ricardo Menéndez March did not hear what the Minister said in his first reading speech, and indeed in his second reading speech. He is going to bring forward seven initiatives that will go much further than this current bill does and in a much more efficient way that doesn’t add a whole lot of costs to businesses.
acuity.explanation: Squarely rebuts the specific claim just made — that the repeal comes with no alternative — by naming the seven initiatives the Minister foreshadowed. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument. Scored on engagement only; whether the seven initiatives exist or outperform the regime is a separate question, and the opening jibe belongs to a different attribute.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is just repealing a disclosure regime that could have been improved when the Government is offering no alternative" — Ricardo Menéndez March.

acuity.statement: Some of the speeches seem to assume that the current legislation is saving all of the businesses from being not paid on time and that that is being forced by this legislation. That’s not the case. It’s a reporting Act—that’s all it is. That information is actually available from four other entities, plus Centrix—which the Minister alluded to in his first reading speech—for a cost of $35.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the premise shared by the two preceding speeches — that the Act being repealed compels or protects timely payment — and attacks it directly, characterising the Act as disclosure-only and pointing to the same Centrix source Waititi himself cited. This is engagement with the content of the arguments just made, not a mere reference to their authors.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what this Government is doing is simply making it easier for the big corporates to get away with and not be held accountable for late payments to those smaller business" — Ricardo Menéndez March (and Waititi's claim that the bill allows a four-month payment window).

acuity.statement: Coming back to the issues, we agree that businesses need to pay on time, and we’re not refuting that. But that is not done with more regulation and red tape being inflicted on business, which costs more and takes more time.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the substance of Davidson's case — that the disclosure requirement protects small businesses waiting to be paid — concedes the premise (businesses should pay on time) and disputes the mechanism, arguing the regulatory route imposes cost and time. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different, though she engages the payment-times argument generally rather than Davidson's specific 3 percent / 97 percent framing or his 'insulting to small-business owners' charge.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this repeal is of legislation that makes sure 3 percent of businesses provide information to make it easier, to make it more viable, and to make it sustainable for the 97 percent of small businesses to stay in business" — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: There are many things—there are actually seven things—that we’re going to implement. We’ve got a plan, and it’s not done through having more regulation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact strand Davidson pressed — the Minister's seven steps — and restates it with the alternative measures named (e-invoicing, agency payment requirements), so it is pointed at what was just said. But it reasserts the seven rather than answering the challenge of why the existing Act could not be kept as an eighth, so the engagement is partial and then returns to prepared material about the Government's plan.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, the Minister also spoke to there being seven other steps that are being taken to support small businesses. Well, why not take eight steps?" — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: I am glad that I’m able to stand for a second time to commend this bill to the House, because I joined this Parliament, this House, because I see so much more aspiration for New Zealand and for many, many of our small, medium, and large businesses and employers because they have the aspiration to grow New Zealand so that we have a bigger economy, so that every individual in New Zealand gets better outcomes at the end of the day. I came to this House to support faster innovations and to support creative innovations that small, medium, and large businesses can actually go out, grow their business, and bring more for everyday New Zealanders. So, therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed substantive critique of the bill (process under urgency, no select committee, an untested voluntary code, loss of the reputational-risk mechanism) and engages none of it. The speech is generalised commendation of the bill and of business aspiration; it would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had argued. It is at least nominally on the matter under debate — the bill — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that urgency removes the select committee stage so small business voices will not be heard, and that the proposed voluntary code lacks the infrastructure to be implemented, and this statement does not take up either point.

acuity.statement: The Minister also recognised, if I heard it correctly, that big businesses have routinely been late payers and so there is a problem that needs to be solved, and what I heard him argue was that he just has a different way of solving this problem. Now, Ingrid Leary, my colleague, made the point that for small businesses, security of cash flow is one of the most important things, and I think everybody can see that. When people don’t pay on time, it puts on huge stress and puts those businesses at risk. One way to think about it is that you’ve got some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the land routinely late paying small businesses because they know they can get away with it, and they’re either doing it deliberately to look after their own cash flow, using small businesses, effectively, as a bank, taking advantage of no-interest loans from struggling small-business owners.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding turn (Leary's cash-flow-certainty argument, named explicitly), accepts it, and does something further with it — restating the problem as large firms using small suppliers as an interest-free bank, and separating agreement on the problem definition from disagreement on the remedy. The speech would have to change if the preceding contribution had made a different argument on the same bill. Scored on engagement only; the strength of the inference and the accuracy of the characterisation are not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Cash flow is absolutely critical." / "this is really about paying people on time and giving them certainty, and nobody needs certainty more in the business environment than small business" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: So I would dispute that people don't know, and I wondered whether you would have information that is about whether people use the builder, for example, which is a product that MBIE has put out for small businesses.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact claim Bayly had just made — that small-business owners do not know MBIE or where to find its data — contests it directly, and asks him for the counter-evidence (usage of MBIE's employment agreement builder) that would settle it. The reply would be materially different had Bayly argued something else; she also engages his Australian comparison and his reliance on the Australian report elsewhere in the same turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "many of them do not know and wouldn't be able to quote you the full name of what we would colloquially refer to as MBIE"

acuity.statement: You made some points that it was different, organisationally different, entities involved, but, actually, largely, in the main, it's very similar.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts White's specific objection that the Australian scheme is not comparable because of MBIE's role and the different set of companies covered, and he goes on to quote the Australian Minister's finding on mandating payment times — engaging the report she invited him to rely on. Short of 1.0 because he does not take up her central question (would he accept a prohibition on payments over three months) or her request for MBIE builder usage data.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "So it's not the same as Australia, because we have MBIE; it's a little bit different."

acuity.statement: The Minister has also presented what he plans to do with the seven initiatives, the seven focus areas, subsequent to the repealing of the particular piece of legislation. This is not big businesses versus small to medium sized enterprises; this is about attacking the core issue that we’re talking about.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows Twyford and takes up two strands of his argument directly: he denies the big-business-versus-small-business framing Twyford built the speech on, and he answers Twyford's charge that there is no credible replacement plan by pointing to the Minister's seven focus areas. He does not engage Twyford's central point that a voluntary code cannot change entrenched behaviour, and much of the turn is prepared material on efficiency and the Australian evidence, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "this is an example that we see so often with the National Party, and that is a deference to powerful, vested interests" / "is this House willing to impose a cost on the largest corporations in New Zealand"

acuity.statement: Now, that seems to me to be a real admission that there is a David and Goliath situation in the market, and certainly the report that the Minister alluded to that came from Australia and the review of their legislation also acknowledged that there are market-dominant players and that it’s difficult for small business sometimes to have as many choices.
acuity.explanation: Leary takes the same Australian review that the Government side has been citing as evidence the regime does not work and turns it against them, arguing it concedes market dominance and so supports the Act being repealed. That is engagement with the specific evidence just relied on, though the bulk of her contribution is her own prepared reading of the general policy statement rather than a reply to the preceding speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "we’ve already got evidence being presented by the Minister that across the Tasman Sea, that is not the case"

acuity.statement: Thirdly, what makes him think that a voluntary code of conduct will change behaviour, when we’re talking about an entrenched pattern of behaviour that confers substantial financial benefit on the late-paying corporations, at the expense of small businesses? What are the facts on this? What is the data that the Minister has drawn on to justify his assertion that a voluntary code of conduct is a credible or serious alternative to the law that is being repealed today?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific alternative Bayly had just announced in the preceding turn — an industry-led voluntary code — and presses on its causal mechanism, asking what evidence supports it changing a behaviour pattern that financially benefits late payers. The question could not have been framed this way had Bayly not just offered the code as the replacement for the repealed law, so the speech is clearly shaped by what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Business New Zealand has also publicly acknowledged that they’ll bring in a code" — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: Look, this “reckon” thing—I’d just say to the member the Hon Phil Twyford: how can you get a qualification on a system that hasn’t actually taken place? No one could answer that question. That question cannot be answered. The only place where it has taken place is in Australia, and it’s been in place for two years, and so they’re the best people to look at what the impact is.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Twyford's specific charge that the decision rests on "reckons" rather than data and answers it on its own terms: it argues the demanded modelling is unobtainable for a regime never in force here, and points instead to the only jurisdiction with operating experience. He then quotes the Australian reviewing Minister, i.e. supplies evidence of the kind just demanded. Score the engagement, not whether the inference or the evidence holds up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is it just reckons or is there actually some information, some facts, that underpin that?" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: It is to do with one of the seven measures that the Minister talked about in his first speech and again in his second speech. I took notes from both speeches and it was talked about again now. And that is the fact that small businesses can go to some credit ratings entities and get a report on a business for the sum of $35.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's case — his package of seven measures, which he had just been running through — and takes up a particular factual claim within it to ask for the agencies to be named. It engages the Minister's material rather than the specific argument of the immediately preceding turn (the "reckons"/Australian-review exchange), so it sits mid-band: pointable engagement with the topic and with his own measures, but a question she had already prepared from notes on earlier speeches.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ve just noted previously that one of the seven initiatives is raising awareness of existing redress options under the Fair Trading Act." — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: Now, I’ve actually got no problem with e-invoicing—fill your boots. I’m thrilled to see e-invoicing promoted, and I’m also thrilled to see Government invoices paid on time. Those are good measures. But what is the problem with doing both?
acuity.explanation: White is plainly in the same committee-stage debate and is engaging arguments the Minister made (e-invoicing as a substitute, the decision not to prohibit), so this is prepared-but-on-topic material rather than wholly unresponsive. But the turn immediately before her was Russell's, and nothing in her speech takes up Russell's process/169-day argument; her speech would read identically whatever Russell had said. That puts it in the 0.1–0.3 band, at 0.3 for the clear gesture at the debate under way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell spoke about the original bill spending 169 days at select committee versus this bill being rushed through under urgency, and this statement does not take that up — it turns instead to the Minister's e-invoicing alternative, raised in an earlier turn not in this window.

acuity.statement: So I’m assuming that the Minister has done due diligence and the Minister, not wanting to take 160-plus days to get some legislation done, has gone out and has consulted widely with businesses, the small and medium enterprises, before doing such a ludicrous act as repealing something without having consulted anyone.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up one strand of Russell's preceding argument and does something with it: he borrows her select-committee duration figure ("160-plus days") and turns it against the Minister's own consultation, so this sentence would have to change if Russell had argued something else. He also reuses her "ram-roaded" framing. The rest of the turn is his own prepared questions on stakeholder consultation and the general policy statement, so the engagement is partial rather than a direct rebuttal of her claim — a mid-band 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Minister has described a process of 169 days as being ram-roading a bill through select committee" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Now, in terms of the issue around the issuing of a directive, as I made clear in my opening speech—in my initial speech—I’ll be working with the Minister of Finance, and also in her capacity as Minister for the Public Service. There are three options, actually, for how we might bring about the changes in terms of payment times. In respect of Government agencies and after consultation with Government entities, that could either be by way of a directive, it could be by way of a Cabinet decision, or it could actually be through the procurement rules, but probably most likely by way of directive, and the Minister can do that pretty easily.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Leary's directive question and supplies the mechanism (directive, Cabinet decision, or procurement rules), so the answer would be different had she asked something else. But it leaves untouched the specific things she asked about that strand — judicial review risk, what official advice he received, the "Henry VIII" concern — so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I'm really keen to know what that entails because, as has been pointed out, we are doing this under urgency." — her question about what the ministerial directive route involves

acuity.statement: In terms of the amendments to the bill—and I note there’s quite a few Amendment Papers being put up by members of the Opposition—one thing I’d say to them is that if we repeal the bill, which is the Government’s intent, then obviously you cannot attach the amendments to a bill that no longer exists. And I would suggest that some of the suggestions from the last member, who was obviously trying to be helpful, those are the type of things I would expect to be taken up in the industry code which will be developed and, hopefully, in place by the end of this year, which I would expect, because that will pick up some of those elements.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the amendment Leary had just spent most of her turn setting out, gives a reason it cannot proceed (the bill it would attach to is being repealed), and disposes of its substance by saying such elements belong in the industry code. The reply would have to change if she had not moved an amendment. Short of 1.0 because it answers the amendment's viability rather than engaging the merits of the written-notice duty and the deemed-awareness test she argued for, and it ignores her separate questions on the voluntary code's sanctions, consultation and efficacy advice.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "instead of under clause 3, repealing the Act to simply replace the purpose section 3(b) of the Business Payment Practices Act with a new subsection (b)" — the amendment she put to him immediately before

acuity.statement: Just on the issue of failure of companies, there are many reasons why nine out of 10 businesses fail over 10 years, and a lot of it is due to undercapitalised businesses simply not having enough capital. A lot of it is to do with the fact of poor management and the way they market their companies. The reasons are varied. So to attribute it always to late payment is not actually correct. But I take your point.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific causal claim just made — that company failures are caused by late payment — and disputes it directly with competing causes, while conceding the part he accepts. The reply would be different had Waititi argued something else; it is built around his attribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: “Unfortunately, 35 percent of companies, year on year, are filing for liquidation. Why? It’s because they’re not paid on time.”

acuity.statement: In terms of Māori businesses, I recently had dinner with some Pacific and Māori business leaders, and the member might be interested to know that I have reestablished the ministerial small-business advisory group.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the consultation question put to him, naming the mechanism he says he is consulting through. It engages the specific question rather than the general topic, though it names no individual Māori business as asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: “So a question is: which small Māori businesses has he consulted?”

acuity.statement: But—to the Minister, respectfully—the information that is available from those credit agencies does not seem to be the same sort of information that is available in this Business Payment Practices Bill that would have been made available by that.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's proposed alternative by testing whether credit ratings agencies actually supply payment-time data, but it resumes her own earlier line of questioning rather than taking up the argument Bayly had just made about causes of business failure and his advisory group.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: “I think what we’re proposing is actually a much more practical approach to actually getting a better outcome.”

acuity.statement: So the first point I’d like to ask the Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing is in relation to the information provided to support the repeal bill. I do understand that there is no regulatory impact statement provided with this legislation.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and asks a pointed new question, but engages no part of either preceding argument; the opening gesture at the Minister is a form of address, not engagement with what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly argued company failures are mostly due to undercapitalisation, poor management and marketing rather than late payment, and Deborah Russell argued credit agencies do not supply payment-time data — this statement takes up neither, opening a fresh line on the missing regulatory impact statement.

acuity.statement: On commencement, my question concerns clause 2, and I’m interested very much—as Helen White mentioned—to know from the Minister whether he considered a commencement date after the register had been allowed to be established. Perhaps, as has been suggested, it could be after two years in order to determine whether the regime would be useful for small businesses.
acuity.explanation: Willis explicitly picks up Helen White's two-year trial-period proposal, names her as its source, and converts it into a specific question to the Minister about the commencement clause — adding the point that at the end of a test period the Act could be replaced rather than repealed. That is genuine engagement with the preceding speaker's argument, but it is one strand alongside his own prepared questions about the title clause, which owe nothing to what preceded them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Allowing that window of opportunity of two years, which is actually the very window proposed by the Minister in the earlier Act"

acuity.statement: It’s the amendment in my name that suggests that in clause 1, we should delete the words “Act Repeal” and we should insert the words “(Asking Big Business to Play Nicely)”. So I think we should call this the “Business Payment Practices (Asking Big Business to Play Nicely) Bill”.
acuity.explanation: Her speech is on the matter under debate — clause 1, the title, which the immediately preceding speaker had also just questioned — but it engages no part of what Willis actually argued. It is prepared material introducing her own amendment, aimed at the Minister's voluntary-code proposal from earlier in the debate rather than at the turn she follows; it would read identically had Willis said something else about the title.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "what alternative titles were considered to create more clarity for the public and for small businesses" — she speaks to the same clause 1 title question but takes up no part of his argument about clarity for small businesses, nor his trial-period question

acuity.statement: Thank you. My question for the Minister is this has become a practice, it seems, in this particular period of your Government, to repeal Acts that they have just put in, and I would like the Minister to tell me why we would do that. Why would we take away the very record of the fact that we have repealed?
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn (Ginny Andersen) pressed the Minister on access to finance for small businesses and on the justification given in the legislative statement for scrapping the payment register. White takes up none of that; she opens an unrelated line on the self-repeal clause. It is squarely on the matter under debate (this repeal bill), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, but the words would be identical whatever Andersen had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued "I don’t see that as a sufficient justifying reason to scrap this bill that would help small businesses" and pressed on access to finance, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: My question does follow on from my colleague Helen White’s question, and the first time I came across one of those clauses was in another bill which was being taken through under urgency, actually. But it’s a self-repeal clause, and it would be good to get some explanation as to why we have self-repeal clauses, as Helen White asked for.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the specific question in the preceding turn — why a bill contains a clause repealing itself — restates it accurately, and then does something with it by adding the comparative point that other self-repeal clauses have run to a year rather than 28 days. The speech would have to change if White had asked something else, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because it extends and reinforces rather than rebutting or correcting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So could you just talk to me about why this wording is in this bill? It’s a new practice, as I understand it" — Helen White

acuity.statement: They were good technical questions. First of all, why do a repeal of the repeal bill? Well, some members won’t be aware of it, but this has been a practice for 10 years now. I’ve just asked for some specific notes on it. Parliamentary Counsel Office practice is that repeal bills that mainly just repeal an Act should include a clause that provides for self-repeal after a suitable time—i.e., after its work’s done—or to remove clutter on the legislation website.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question put by the two preceding speakers: names the mechanism (Parliamentary Counsel Office practice), corrects White's premise that self-repeal is a new practice of this Government, supplies precedents, and goes on to address Russell's 28-day point. Entirely contingent on what was asked of him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it would be good to get some explanation as to why we have self-repeal clauses" — Deborah Russell (and Helen White's "It’s a new practice, as I understand it")

acuity.statement: Just a couple of responses to that contribution from the Minister. It was, in fact, the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill which had a self-repeal clause on it of one year, and so the Minister has said that 28 days is the standard.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own cited example and turns it against the claim he used it to support: he offered the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill as a precedent and said 28 days is standard, and she points out that that very bill self-repealed after a year. This is engagement with the specific content of the turn immediately before it, not with its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "examples of where this has taken place recently are the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill" and "the 28 days is a standard repeal period" — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: I think we’re having a constitutional debate here which is not really relevant to the bill, but none the less you asked about the 28-day repeal. Where bills or Acts have transitional arrangements, that’s why you have a longer period of time, and that’s why the tax—I see the member; she’s probably the only one in the House that probably understands it.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the distinction the previous turn demanded — transitional arrangements explain the longer period on the taxation bill and their absence explains 28 days here — so it resolves the specific discrepancy Russell had just identified. Slightly short of 1.0 because he first disputes the relevance of the question before answering it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "just a wee explanation as to why one bill merited a year and one bill merited 28 days" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair, and thank you to the Minister for that clarification. What I’m interested to know from the Minister about the repeal process is this. I’m aware that a lot of communication was undertaken with small businesses and with industry, as well, in terms of how to get this bill right, and I would like some reassurance from the Minister. On the 28th day after the date in which it comes into force, when it is repealed, is there a sufficient plan in place so that all of those entities that may have undertaken some form of work and that may have changed their database and their pay systems and may have gone in to undertaking some sort of changes to how they make their payment so that it’s self-reporting and, potentially, undergone some expense to do that work—are there sufficient notifications and communications in place?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's stated rationale — that urgency is needed to stop businesses and MBIE incurring cost — and draws out its consequence for firms that have already built systems, which is a genuine extension of the argument just made rather than a restatement. It then returns to her prepared access-to-finance material, which engages nothing he said, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the whole purpose of doing it now, under urgency, is so that we stop people incurring lots of money" — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: So we’ve heard that e-invoicing is going to be one of the solutions. E-invoicing is not an innovation; it’s been around for 20 years. And what’s more, it’s not a solution. Why has it not been implemented? Independent research by Kordia, today, gives us some reasons as to why: more than two-thirds of people using e-invoicing experienced an impact from a cyber incident, with nearly half, 46 percent, finding it took more than a month to resolve the incident, including 9 percent saying it took more than five months. E-invoicing is not a solution.
acuity.explanation: Willis picks up one specific strand of the turn immediately before his — Helen White's argument that encouraging e-invoicing is not a substitute for the bill — and does something with it, adding independent Kordia figures against e-invoicing as a remedy. But he extends rather than engages her reasoning, and the surrounding material (the e-invoicing critique, the cyber-incident statistics, the appeal to send the bill to select committee) reads as prepared and would survive unchanged had she argued a different point on the same topic. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "E-invoices are all very well, but, obviously, the person from Xero, who is involved in e-invoicing, knows that and still thinks there is a problem." — Helen White

acuity.statement: We heard from the excellent Minister—clearly the others weren’t listening—that he is going to address all of these issues through regulation. I thought it was going to be in the “Bayly Bill”, but it’s not; it’s going to be via regulation. And what’s more, it’ll be a much more efficient and cost-effective way. He is actually doing this to save businesses who had ahead of them, if this Act wasn’t repealed, quite a significant cost to upgrade their own systems to meet the requirements of that Act, and also $2 million to $3 million at least of cost to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to develop and put in place a computer system to actually deal with it.
acuity.explanation: Smith takes up one strand of Genter's argument — her claim that repealing the Act removes a reasonable tool and that the Government's red-tape/cost justification is hollow — and answers it directly by asserting the issues will instead be handled by regulation and that the repeal avoids compliance and MBIE system costs. But he engages none of her specific points (the power imbalance between large corporates and small business, the Cabinet paper's reliance on credit agencies, the $35 versus $49-plus-GST Centrix figure), and the rest is prepared commendation of the bill. Engagement with the topic and the general thrust, not with the specific claims; roughly half marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "they’re getting rid of a perfectly reasonable tool that actually would’ve helped"

acuity.statement: Now, the reason that this is under urgency—there are a couple of reasons, but the main one is that 3,000-plus businesses would have to upgrade their technology, and then the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment would have to spend an enormous amount of money to get the system up and ready to go. So I understand that need for urgency, and we need to move quickly on this.
acuity.explanation: Willis's immediately preceding turn demanded the bill go through a select committee process rather than urgency. Trask takes that up directly, giving the reason urgency was used (3,000-plus businesses facing a technology upgrade and MBIE implementation cost). The speech would have to change if Willis had not pressed the process point, so this is close engagement with the specific argument rather than prepared praise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "if they do care, we can work together through a select committee process"

acuity.statement: There are better ways that we can encourage big business to pay than this. I 100 percent acknowledge, as a small-business owner, it’s really hard when you’re not getting paid by the bigger clients, and you need that incoming cash flow, but the previous Government’s bill would not have actually achieved that.
acuity.explanation: Willis charged the Government side with not caring about SMEs struggling to be paid. Trask concedes that strand of the argument explicitly — late payment by big clients is hard — and disputes the remedy, arguing the repealed bill would not have delivered it. Accepting part and contesting the rest is engagement with the content, not merely with the topic; it falls short of 1.0 because she then moves to prepared material on existing statutory protections.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "the desire to find a solution for our small to medium sized enterprises, for those people who are doing it hard"

acuity.statement: I stand on behalf of New Zealand First to commend this bill to the House. We are a party of common sense, and we see that supporting this bill is common sense. As the financial year comes to a close, businesses need some certainty, and these businesses who are now feeling a little bit concerned about the additional compliance costs will now have certainty that that will not happen.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, including Willis's case for referring the repeal to select committee and Waititi-side concerns about consultation. The speech engages no part of either: it is a short prepared commendation on the right subject (certainty, compliance costs, MBIE savings), and would read word-for-word the same whatever had been said before it. The repetition of 'common sense' is a mere reference, which the rubric expressly declines to reward.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Willis argued for a select committee process and for hearing from small business, and this statement does not take it up; the echo of his phrase "we haven't heard a lot of common sense from the opposite side" is a word borrowed, not an argument engaged

acuity.statement: And this is not about having e-invoices, because e-invoices have been around for a long time. A lot of people already have e-invoices. I was doing e-invoices before I came to Parliament. This is not about e-invoices; this is about tying up the ability for small businesses and taking the power away from them to ensure that they can pay their employees and the bills on time.
acuity.explanation: Trask's justification for urgency rested on the e-invoicing technology upgrade burden. Waititi takes that framing on and tries to dissolve it — e-invoicing is long established and widely used, so the real question is payment timing, not technology. He engages the specific premise of the preceding speaker rather than the topic at large, but then returns to prepared material on consultation and the supermarket duopoly, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Laura Trask: "3,000-plus businesses would have to upgrade their technology"

acuity.statement: Well, I’d just like to support the third reading of this bill, and I’d like to just pick up on a word that a member on the other side of the House used—optimism—because optimism is what we are going to be pumping back into our economy and into small business, because we believe in less regulation, less red tape, and less compliance. I think, in this debate today, we’ve all noted that we all want businesses to pay on time, but we don’t achieve it through more regulation and more red tape.
acuity.explanation: Lifts Twyford's word "optimism" and restates the shared premise that everyone wants bills paid on time, but engages none of his actual argument — that the voluntary code is implausible without public disclosure, that e-invoicing is a red herring, that Fair Trading Act redress is inaccessible to small firms, and that repeal shifts cost from big business to small. The assertion that red tape is not the answer is the very position Twyford had just challenged, reasserted rather than defended. A gesture at the debate on the right subject: the speech would be essentially identical had Twyford made a different anti-repeal argument, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band, at 0.3 for the glance at his wording and premise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "doesn’t give me any optimism that the Government has the political will to actually make changes" — and his attack on "hours of infantile rhetoric from the Government benches about red tape as if all regulation was somehow bad"

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Damien O’Connor for bringing up a part of my career, as a director of Fonterra. Indeed, he is correct that that organisation did bring in what I consider were some very challenging times for suppliers to that entity.
