acuity.explanation: MacLeod takes up the specific example O'Connor had just built his case on — Fonterra's shift to 90-day payment terms and MacLeod's own directorship — concedes the factual substance of it, and then adds first-hand detail (he was also an affected electrical contractor and part of the board drive to reverse the practice). The speech could not have been delivered unchanged had the previous speaker said something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Fonterra did a U-turn." — Damien O'Connor, who had named MacLeod as a former Fonterra director and used the 90-day payment change as his central illustration

acuity.statement: But the fact is that the problem is agreed upon. Every member of the House—I haven’t heard anybody talk cross-purposes of what the issue is; we agree with what the issue is. Dare I say it, we’ve just got a different method of actually delivering a solution for this, on this side of the House.
acuity.explanation: This engages one strand of O'Connor's attack — that repealing the Act abandons small businesses — by conceding the diagnosis and locating the disagreement in the remedy. It is a partial engagement rather than a full one: it never answers O'Connor's specific charge that removing the Act strips protection from half a million small firms, nor his point that the fair trading alternative is unaffordable for a cash-squeezed small business, and it closes on a formulaic commendation of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this coalition Government—ACT, National, and New Zealand First—is removing the protection for half a million small businesses across this country" — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: I’d like to address the member on the Opposition Reuben Davidson that we speak one language in this country, which is for the betterment of New Zealand. So if I can bring everyone in this House back to the intention of this bill, which is to improve payment times, ramping up the use of e-invoicing; incentivising small and medium enterprises to adopt e-invoicing; expanding payment targets to Crown entities—all of these will contribute to business efficiency.
acuity.explanation: She picks up Davidson's "your language" jibe only to swat it away, then pivots to prepared material restating the bill's intentions. None of Davidson's actual content is engaged — not the Minister's own rationale document he quoted back, not the Christchurch East business's late-payment complaint, not the "do eight" challenge. The speech would read identically whatever Davidson had argued about payment practices, so this is a mere reference plus on-topic prepared material: the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.3 for the gesture at the preceding speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So I’ll speak to you in your language." — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: He’s got some good ideas, it’s great that he realises that e-invoicing is around—something that has been around for 20 years. But there’s been very little process, and unsatisfactory answers to the questions that we put to him in the committee stage about that.
acuity.explanation: Lu's defence of the repeal rested on e-invoicing as the substitute remedy, delivered with "great intention" and speed. Leary takes up that one strand directly — conceding e-invoicing is a good idea while denying it is new, and denying that the process behind it exists — which is genuine partial engagement you can point at. But she then returns to her prepared line of attack on urgency and the committee stage rather than contesting the efficiency claim itself, so this sits at the mid-band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ramping up the use of e-invoicing; incentivising small and medium enterprises to adopt e-invoicing" — Nancy Lu

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, Julie Anne Genter, has mentioned, one of those projects which will be saved is the Eastern Busway, but the $341 million will also go on electric trains and stabling and road corridor improvements.
acuity.explanation: Luxton picks up the one concrete point Genter closed on — the Eastern Busway being funded from fuel tax revenue — and does something with it, extending it to the other ring-fenced projects the unspent $341 million will fund. He also glances at her concession that time-of-use pricing is not yet available by listing tolling and time-of-use charging as the coalition's alternatives. But he does not engage her central argument (that road users benefit from projects moving people without cars, and that the revenue must otherwise come from rates), and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on regressivity and congestion. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the coalition Government is happy to fund the Eastern Busway from the regional fuel tax revenue, so they do kind of understand that road users should contribute to public transport" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: We’ve also heard from the Hon Julie Anne Genter just now about all the other wonderful projects that will benefit motorists. But I think one of the issues we’re having here—and I don’t think that motorists are buying into this—is that so much of the fuel tax dollar is now going on to non-roading projects. There is a balance—public transport benefits motorists—but there is also out of balance, and I think that under the last Government, we got out of balance.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up Genter's core premise directly, concedes it in terms ("public transport benefits motorists") and then disputes its application, arguing the proportion of the fuel tax dollar going to non-roading projects went out of balance. That is accept-part-and-dispute-the-rest on the specific argument just made; the speech would have had to be different had Genter argued something else. Whether the balance claim is well-evidenced is a Rigor/Veracity question and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Road users are the greatest beneficiaries of projects that move more people with fewer cars, especially in an urban area like Auckland" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: At the last election, we campaigned on reducing the cost of living for Aucklanders, and one of the ways to do it was to remove this regional fuel tax. Guess what! They listened to us, they voted for us, and a number of the people on the other side of the House lost their seats. There’s your message. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speech — the electoral-mandate point and the "message" framing Kapa-Kingi closed on — and turns it back, with "There's your message" aimed squarely at her own words. But it engages none of her substantive claims (safety funding, cycleways, ratepayers picking up the lost revenue), so it is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "I don’t think that was what the 57.8 percent of voters in Auckland were signing up for when the Government’s current coalition was put in place" (and her repeated question "what message does this bill send to our mokopuna?")

acuity.statement: But it’s going to save—at the most, it will save a household $2.70 a week. Well, that’s a big contribution to the cost of living! Where’s the substantial change that the other side was promising?
acuity.explanation: Engages the cost-of-living rationale the previous speaker rested his whole case on, and puts a figure against it rather than merely asserting disagreement. It is still substantially prepared material — it does not take up McCallum's mandate claim at all — so this is partial engagement with one strand, not a rebuttal of the argument he actually made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "we campaigned on reducing the cost of living for Aucklanders, and one of the ways to do it was to remove this regional fuel tax"

acuity.statement: It gives me great pride to stand in support of the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill in the name of the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown. This bill legislates that the remaining unspent revenue from the Auckland regional fuel tax is ring-fenced to fund the Eastern Busway, electric trains, stabilising for the City Rail Link, and road-corridor improvements. Introducing legislation to remove this regional fuel tax was part of our 100-day action plan, and, unlike Governments previous, this is actually a Government of delivery. We’re delivering on what we campaigned on, and I’m pleased to commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Prepared praise on the right subject. The ring-fencing sentence glances at the unspent-revenue question Russell had just explained, which earns the top of the low band, but nothing here answers her argument about lost funding and the council's debt ceiling; the speech would read identically whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "the problem with removing it is not just that it removes the funding that Auckland Transport could have used but it removes the capacity to borrow more money" — and her explanation that the unspent money "was allocated but it was sitting there, waiting to be spent on the projects as set out in time"

acuity.statement: Because I love Auckland and I hear the Hamiltonian member, Tom Rutherford, who has resumed his seat asking me whether Auckland is the city of the future. He was the closest they could get to standing a speaker near to Auckland. So I have listened to his contribution.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and claims to have listened to him, but engages no part of what he said: the ring-fenced funding list and the delivery claim go untouched, and the reply is about where he is from. A mere reference plus a pivot to the speaker's own framing sits in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "unlike Governments previous, this is actually a Government of delivery. We’re delivering on what we campaigned on" — and his ring-fencing claim about the unspent revenue

acuity.statement: And the number one issue that came up time and time again—and I suspect she might be the Labour candidate for Northcote at the next election—was the cost of living, and I’m really happy to support this because this bill addresses the cost of living of those in Northcote, it addresses the cost of living of those in Pakuranga, those in Takanini, those in Mount Roskill, those in Upper Harbour, and I really support this bill.
acuity.explanation: Williams's immediately preceding turn made a specific, checkable cost-of-living argument — that the saving is tiny and more than cancelled out by other charges. Bidois asserts the opposite conclusion (the bill "addresses the cost of living") without engaging the figure, the offset, or any other strand of her case. The speech is on the right subject and would have been word-for-word identical whatever she had said; the only nod to her material is incidental suburb names, not an argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued the repeal delivers only "$1.80 a week in savings for most Auckland households" and is offset by a 22c fuel increase and $50 registration rise, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: This bill does not just—as I outlined—stop the fuel tax but it is about priorities. It is about making sure that the revenues that are collected from people who use our roads are prioritised into what is important to them. So this bill will ring-fence the remaining money, because—I mean, lo and behold, over $340 million of money was unspent.
acuity.explanation: Brown takes up one strand of Williams's case directly: she complained that Aucklanders needed a ring-fence around the remaining fuel-tax money and that the surviving projects reflect the Government's priorities rather than Auckland's; he answers that the bill does ring-fence the money and defends the priority choice, adding the unspent $340 million as his reason. That is partial engagement — he answers the ring-fencing strand but not her $1.80-a-week or offsetting-charges arguments, and much of the surrounding speech (speed bumps, red-light cameras) is prepared attack material that would have been delivered whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This is a real disappointment for the people of Auckland, who needed a ring-fence around those projects." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: So what we have got is a user-pays system which works. I would love to see more people being able to access the central city. A lot of people from the Matapihi, Pāpāmoa, Arataki area already cycle over to the Strand, and when that option’s available people can take it.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a long substantive turn by Genter immediately precedes it. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate (the regional fuel tax repeal) and supplies his own reasons for supporting it, but it is prepared material that does not take up any strand of Genter's case. Her central argument — that repeal leaves a revenue hole fillable only from rates, with named projects lost — goes entirely unanswered, as does her point that the Government itself directs fuel-tax revenue to the Eastern Busway. There is a faint gesture at her 'choice' framing (people cycle when the option is available; people choose where to live), which is pointable, so this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0 — the speech would be nearly identical whatever Genter had argued, but it is at least recognisably a reply in this debate rather than a speech transplantable to any other.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "So let’s not pretend that we’re giving people choice simply by building more roads." Luxton glances at Genter's choice-and-mode argument by asserting people already cycle where the option exists, but engages none of her substantive claims (the revenue gap, Wayne Brown's rates-rise-or-project-cuts point, or the Eastern Busway inconsistency).

acuity.statement: What we're seeing right now is a repeal that will cut the revenue-gathering tool that the Government had to be able to fund transport projects, and the Government not proposing an alternative.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Kemp and stays squarely on the bill under debate, but engages no part of her argument. The themes converge (cost of living framing, safe walking and cycling, climate) without ever taking up a claim she made, and the speech would read identically had she said something else. On-topic prepared material, so the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because it does gesture at the debate and at the Minister's introduction of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Takutai Tarsh Kemp spoke about cancelled safety projects, flashing lights for school children in Manurewa and the $24 billion Budget pothole, and this statement does not take any of it up — it is prepared Green material on the same bill.

acuity.statement: One of the other important aspects of this bill is the removal of the opportunity for other regional fuel taxes. The people of Northland certainly do not want one. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: A substantive opposing turn immediately precedes this one, and there was a real opportunity to answer it — the Greens had just asked what revenue tool replaces the one being repealed. Instead the speech introduces a separate feature of the bill and commends it. It is about the matter under debate, so not 0.0, but it engages nothing that was said and would be word-for-word the same after any preceding speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the repeal cuts a revenue tool with no alternative proposed and that the Government is not brave enough to put up progressive alternatives; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I want to start by talking about some of the things that my colleagues have talked about today, about the fear they have of the war that's being waged in this situation: I would have thought that the issue of transport and proper funding of transport was almost apolitical because it affects our entire community.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding turns — the claim that a war is being waged on safe transport infrastructure — and does something with it, reframing transport funding as something that should be apolitical, before moving to her own prepared example of a principal's email about raised crossings. Partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument's reasoning, so mid-band. Note this is scored only on engagement: whether the framing is well reasoned or precise is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a Minister of Transport that has actually waged a war on that safe infrastructure" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: As the MP for Bay of Plenty, anything we can do to support our colleagues across the country—and, in this case, in Auckland—with the cost of living, I am happy to support. Removing the Auckland regional fuel tax will provide cost of living support, saving the driver of a Toyota Hilux around $9.20 every time they fill up in Auckland, while a Toyota Corolla driver will save around $5.75. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive speech by Helen White, so it is eligible, and it is at least on the matter under debate — the removal of the Auckland regional fuel tax as cost-of-living relief — with a passing gesture to Auckland. But it engages no part of her argument: her central claim was that the per-litre cut will not be passed through at the pump, and Rutherford simply asserts per-fill savings figures that presuppose full pass-through without addressing her reasoning, her point about the replacement driver-licence charge falling on the whole country, or her safety-funding argument. The speech would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said, so it sits in the prepared-material band rather than the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued at length that the 10c a litre saving is unlikely to reach motorists ('if they expect to see the fuel come down 10c a litre every time they go to the pump, unfortunately that's very unlikely to happen') and asked what mechanism would make the cut flow through, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It’s a privilege to rise as just another fabulous Aucklander to support the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax. The people of Northcote want a Government that will truly ease cost of living pressures; the people of Northcote want a Government that will actually end wasteful spending. This bill does both of these, and therefore I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive speech by Damien O'Connor arguing that repealing the regional fuel tax will strip billions from regional and provincial road funding and from safety investment, and that fuel is already dearer outside Auckland. Bidois takes up none of it — no figure, no claim, no strand is engaged. The speech is prepared commendation that would be word-for-word identical whatever O'Connor had said, and could have been given at any stage of this bill. It is at least on the matter under debate (the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor argued that the billions of dollars of deficits left by the repeal 'will come from regional and provincial road funding, absolutely' and from safety investments, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: But while National did campaign on repealing the regional fuel tax, the truth is that under the now National-led Government, Aucklanders will be paying more, and they have had the promise of cost of living relief pulled out from under them. That is the reality.
acuity.explanation: Bidois had just asserted the bill delivers what Northcote wants because it will 'truly ease cost of living pressures'. Halbert takes that specific proposition and inverts it — concedes the campaign commitment, then denies the consequence, arguing Aucklanders will pay more on net, and goes on to itemise the offsetting costs. The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had defended the repeal on different grounds (localism, say, or waste), so this is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference. Short of 1.0 because he rebuts the claim at the level of direction rather than engaging any reasoning or figure Bidois actually offered, and then returns to prepared material on water rates and the transport programme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'The people of Northcote want a Government that will truly ease cost of living pressures ... This bill does both of these' — Dan Bidois.

acuity.statement: I commend this bill to the House.

This turn engages none of it — no part of the argument is taken up, and the sentence could be delivered in any bill debate on any day without alteration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert said 'the plan that the Minister presented this week doesn’t provide a solution to addressing Auckland’s critical problem, which is congestion' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The next one is around clause 7, and that relates to Schedule 2 of the Land Transport Management Act 2003. Now, I think it would be helpful for the Minister to outline for the committee what the rationale is in terms of maintaining three of those projects within the bill, and what is the rationale for, effectively, dispensing with all the remaining projects that are outlined in the order.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific content of the Minister's opening — that clauses 6 and 7 cut the funded project list from 14 to three after discussions with the Mayor — and presses on exactly that point, asking for the rationale both for the three retained and the eleven dropped. The question would have to change if the Minister had described the clauses differently. Not 1.0 because it asks the Minister to justify his account rather than disputing or reworking anything in it, and it sits inside a prepared run of clause-by-clause questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'reduce the list of capital projects in which revenue from the regional fuel tax scheme can be sent from 14 to three' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: So I would like to know what the process was that you went through to select projects, and you’ve said it was in consultation with the mayor, but one of those projects is obviously really important to the people that live in your area.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own stated basis for the selection — consultation with the Mayor of Auckland — and does something with it, turning it into a challenge about process and perceived conflict given one retained project sits in his own electorate. Had the Minister justified the three projects on different grounds, this line of attack would have had to change. Short of 1.0 because it then widens into her prepared local concerns rather than staying on the claim.

acuity.responding_to: 'following discussions with the Mayor of Auckland' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Look, thank you, Madam Chair, and I thank the members for their questions. Tangi Utikere, he asked about the question of whether any thinking was done about reducing the rate or keeping the framework for the future. The answer to that was: we campaigned on removing the regional fuel tax, and we were elected with a mandate to do that, and this legislation is delivering on that mandate, so we did not consider any other change other than to remove the legislation in its entirety—which is what this is doing.
acuity.explanation: Names the member, restates his actual question about a lower or zero rate and retaining the framework under section 65C, and answers it squarely — no such option was considered. He goes on to deal with the project-selection question and the clause 5(b) drafting question as well. Not 1.0 because Helen White's questions on cost-benefit analysis, the conflict of interest and road safety are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'whether or not there was any thinking around whether a lower rate, and potentially a rate of zero, could have been applied' — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I do want to begin my contribution, given that we are discussing Part 1 of the bill, which basically dismantles the structure for the Auckland regional fuel tax—I do want to focus on the fact that our largest city in New Zealand has needed for quite some time now an integrated, multimodal rapid transit network, an integrated network.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive set of questions from Wade-Brown on road safety, congestion charging sequencing and consultation, and engages none of them. The contribution is prepared material on the right subject (Part 1, the regional fuel tax), with a gesture at the part under debate but no engagement with the preceding speaker's content; it would have read identically whatever Wade-Brown had asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown asked whether red-light cameras reduce red-light running and 'how does reducing speed humps address the health and safety of New Zealanders and Aucklanders in particular?', and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: This is an important topic for Aucklanders. I stated in my speech my concern of the Minister’s decision today to ram this through in urgency.
acuity.explanation: Two members have already spoken with content to engage — Wade-Brown on safety and consultation, Radhakrishnan on the funding shortfall and replacement projects. Halbert neither builds on nor disputes either; he restates his own earlier speech and launches an independent line of questioning about Mayor Wayne Brown. On topic, but indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Priyanca Radhakrishnan argued the repeal 'will leave a shortfall in transport funding for Auckland of $1.2 billion over the next four years' and asked what would replace the cancelled projects; this statement does not take that up and opens a fresh line on Auckland Council relations.

acuity.statement: There were a number of questions from Celia Wade-Brown in relation to speed bumps, red-light cameras, and consultation. I mean, ultimately, this bill focuses on the cost of living for New Zealanders, and we are reducing the regional fuel tax to address that issue.
acuity.explanation: A mere reference, not an engagement: he correctly names the three subjects Wade-Brown raised and then pivots to the bill's cost-of-living rationale without addressing whether red-light cameras reduce red-light running or how removing speed humps bears on injury severity. Naming the questions back is not taking up their content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'does he believe that red-light cameras reduce the likelihood of drivers playing roulette through a red light?' — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: The issue in terms of what consultation was had with other organisations—I think that was Celia Wade-Brown again—ultimately, New Zealanders voted for this Government, and we are delivering on our campaign promises.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question — consultation with outside organisations — and supplies a direct, if dismissive, answer to it: the election mandate stands in place of consultation. That engages one strand of what was put to him (whether consultation was needed) without addressing the strand actually asked (whether any occurred, and with whom).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'what consultation on the projects that should be dropped was there with health, ambulance, Cycle Auckland, Living Streets Aotearoa, or any of the other knowledgeable organisations?' — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: In terms of the Hon Priyanca Radhakrishnan, she asked how we would replace the dollars. I mean, ultimately, for the rest of those projects which we are not continuing funding for, of course, Auckland Council is able to progress those. If they’re on local roading corridors, they are able to progress those. They just won’t have regional fuel tax funding to support them, and that’s a conversation that the council can have with Auckland ratepayers.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question Radhakrishnan put — what replaces the cancelled projects — and does something with it, answering that the council may still progress local-corridor projects from its own revenue. It directly engages the premise that repeal leaves nothing in its place; it stops short of 1.0 because it does not touch her figures on the $1.2 billion shortfall or the reduced borrowing capacity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'So I’d really like to know: what is the Minister going to replace a number of these projects with, whether it’s in safety measures or walking and cycling routes?' — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: Shanan Halbert asked about consultation with Auckland Council. I spoke to the mayor on a couple of occasions. These are projects that are of joint priority, and so we are ensuring that the remaining funds, of which there are over $300 million, go towards those three priority projects.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked — what consultation he had with Mayor Wayne Brown — with a specific fact, and engages Halbert's partnership framing by asserting the retained projects are of joint priority. Short of full marks because Halbert's further questions, about the relationship's current state and how he will support the council with the fallout, go unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'what consultation did he have with Mayor Wayne Brown in regards to this piece of legislation' — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: In terms of the agency’s advice, in clause 18, all the advice that the New Zealand Transport Agency is required to provide the Minister currently, continues to be provided as the scheme is wound down. That relates to collection, auditing, administrating rebates, transferring net revenue, and monitoring revenue, cost, fuel prices, and volumes. That’s, effectively, what that’s all about. Then, as I said, clause 19 is about making sure the fuel companies are paying the correct amount.
acuity.explanation: Brown takes up the specific clauses Utikere raised and describes what advice clause 18 preserves, so the reply is clearly shaped by the questions asked. But he engages only one strand: he does not address the anticipated frequency of advice, whether clause 18 is sufficient, what happens to retained records under clause 19, or the flexibility question on clause 20, and he closes with prepared framing that the provisions are 'all very sensible stuff'. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the anticipated frequency of that advice that’s being sought and whether the provision in clause 18 is sufficient" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Now that the Minister is proposing these changes, how will he make sure that the savings that the bill seeks to provide to Aucklanders are passed on to drivers who would otherwise have been paying 10c extra that would have been collected by wholesale fuel distributors?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the bill's effect on Aucklanders) but engages no part of the preceding turn; Williams announces a fresh line and the question would read identically whatever Brown had just said about the transitional clauses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the clause 18-20 provisions were 'all very sensible stuff, which I'm sure the Opposition is very happy to support', and this statement does not take that up — Williams expressly opens 'a brand-new line of questions'.

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around passing on costs, there is a range of regulatory powers that MBIE have in terms of making sure that happens, and it’s very similar to what happened when the last Government reduced the fuel excise—those expectations remain. In terms of who will receive the benefits—people who drive their cars. There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of Williams's questions in the order she put them, names the mechanism (MBIE's regulatory powers) and supplies a figure for the per-litre reduction. Short of 1.0 only because he leaves untouched the distributional point she pressed — that the $50 registration increase shifts cost onto low-mileage drivers like her father.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how will he make sure that the savings that the bill seeks to provide to Aucklanders are passed on to drivers" and "who will benefit from those savings the most?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I will ask the fourth question as well, which is in relation to his answer about this benefiting all drivers. Has he had any advice about the impact of the regulation he’s proposing, given that it would seem that it would incentivise drivers to behave in different ways?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes Brown's just-given answer that drivers benefit and presses it to its consequence, asking what advice he has on the behavioural incentive created. The question could not have been asked in this form had Brown answered differently, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In terms of who will receive the benefits—people who drive their cars." — Simeon Brown

acuity.explanation: Genter follows a substantive turn by Russell on the discontinued local projects, but opens by announcing her own prepared material ("I just want to make some general comments about the bill, and then some specific questions about this part") and asks about compliance costs of collecting the regional fuel tax — a different line entirely. The speech is on the matter under debate (the repeal bill and its project schedule), so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically had Russell said something else, or nothing. Sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because the subject matter overlaps the debate without engaging any part of the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell asked why the safety improvement at the intersection of Blockhouse Bay Road and Chalmers Street (Project 8) was discontinued and whether the Minister familiarised himself with the local projects, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede him, and his amendment concerns the very Project 8 Russell had just raised, so the material to engage was directly available. He engages none of it: he tells the Chamber he arrived late, then delivers his own prepared case on road safety costs and health-and-safety liability. Scored 0.3 rather than lower because the speech is squarely on the matter under debate and lands on the same project Russell raised — a gesture at the debate — but it would be word-for-word the same whatever the previous speakers had argued.

acuity.statement: I’m not sure if he’s had a conversation with his colleague Camilla Belich, because she has an identical tabled amendment where she doesn’t want to reinstate the road safety one but wants to reinstate active transport instead.
acuity.explanation: Brown takes up the specific amendment O'Connor had just moved and does something with it — contrasts its content with an identical amendment from a colleague seeking a different reinstatement — so this passage could not have been written without hearing O'Connor, and the engagement is pointable. But it engages the proposal rather than the argument for it: the $5 million-per-fatality costing and the health-and-safety-liability question go unanswered, as do Genter's compliance-cost and Eastern Busway questions, and he returns to prepared material on the three agreed priority projects. One strand engaged, then back to the script — a clear 0.5. Scored only on engagement; whether the inconsistency point is a fair inference is a separate question and not Acuity's.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my amendment reinstates Project 8 in the Land Transport Management (Regional Fuel Tax Scheme—Auckland) Order 2018, and it’s to do with road safety" — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: Well, as I said earlier, the Government has outlined which of these projects we’re supporting. We’ve put that forward into the bill as it stands before the committee. There’s a range of tabled amendments which seek to—through various ways—reinsert others of those projects and, as I’ve outlined, the Government will not be supporting any of those tabled amendments.
acuity.explanation: Belich put two things to him: would he support her clause 7 amendment, and if not what Aucklanders can expect for bus infrastructure. He answers the first strand squarely and in the negative — the reply is clearly shaped by the amendment having been moved — but engages no part of the bus-infrastructure case she set out (Lower Albert Street, Wynyard Quarter, Wellesley St shelters) and ignores the second question entirely. One strand taken up, the rest declined: a partial engagement, not a rebuttal. Brevity and refusal are not what holds this down — an answer that engaged the specific projects before declining them would score 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would like to know from the Minister, firstly, would he support the amendment that I have put in place? If not, what can Aucklanders expect in relation to his plans for public transportation and also for bus infrastructure" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: So, Minister, I just want to ask some quick questions with regards to my amendment because it’s important that airport access is in the suite of options—and I know the Minister has highlighted, and thank you Minister: you have highlighted what is going to be kept in terms of local road improvements. I want to really emphasise and put on record that suburbs around the Auckland International Airport, if there is not that continual funding, are going to continue to be gridlocked and you can sit on a on a busy street in Māngere trying to get into the airport.
acuity.explanation: Brown had just refused every tabled amendment outright. Sosene acknowledges that he has set out which local road improvements are retained, which is a pointable gesture at his turn, but she does nothing with the refusal — no argument against the ground he gave for it, no engagement with his claim that the retained list is sufficient. The rest is prepared material on Māngere, Te Ara Mua and airport access that would read identically had Brown said the opposite or not spoken at all. On topic, and indifferent to what it follows, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band with the glance putting it at the top of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Government has outlined which of these projects we’re supporting" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The Minister, I heard before, remarked that this is the same sort of regime as Labour’s when it introduced its fuel tax savings. The difference here, and what I’m trying to get to with these questions, is that that was only ever a temporary cost of living relief. This bill introduces a permanent change to the regime and, in fact, removes all of the Government’s taxing powers for cents per litre charge for fuel that can be used for local government transport projects that otherwise may not be fully funded.
acuity.explanation: She names the Minister's specific analogy and breaks it on a stated disanalogy: the earlier measure was temporary relief, this one is a permanent removal of the cents-per-litre taxing power, so the monitoring regime that sufficed there cannot suffice here. She then draws the consequence as a question about how a long-term regime secures pass-through to consumers, and tracks which of her numbered questions remain unanswered. Substitute a different defence of the bill and this speech would have to be rewritten, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement alone — whether the temporary/permanent contrast is accurate belongs to Veracity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is the same sort of regime as Labour’s when it introduced its fuel tax savings" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Now, this is a fuel tax that has enabled public transport, it’s enabled walkable streets, it’s given the potential for light rail—and I can’t understand why anyone would want to stomp on local initiatives, on city initiatives, to do well by their communities. Why would central government seek to destroy localism? Why would central government seek to destroy localism when it can provide for their communities, when it can provide climate safe communities? This is something that should not be thrown out.
acuity.explanation: Willis follows a detailed clause-by-clause line of questioning from Utikere and engages none of it. The speech is prepared material on Dunedin's emissions-reduction shifts and a general case for regional fuel taxes; it would be word-for-word the same whatever the previous speaker had argued. It is at least on the subject of the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere asked the Minister whether the clause 22 discretion over top-up funding sits with the agency alone and whether spending from the reserve fund under clause 23 is time-bound, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for his question, which asked, effectively, why regional fuel taxes can’t also be applied elsewhere. Our Government doesn’t support regional fuel taxes. We’re repealing the legislation, as I’ve already told the committee, and so we are repealing it through this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Brown restates Willis's question accurately and gives a direct answer to it, so there is engagement one can point at. But he answers only the topic — the Government's position on regional fuel taxes — and does not take up Willis's actual argument about local authorities' decarbonisation plans or the loss of local decision-making. Partial engagement, then a restatement of a position already given to the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can’t understand why anyone would want to stomp on local initiatives, on city initiatives, to do well by their communities. Why would central government seek to destroy localism?" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: In regards to clause 23, any incentive or disincentive to spend it, the legislation doesn’t make the spend time-bound, because obviously some of those projects are going to take two to three years, so there’s going to be no time-bounds on them. Ultimately, the council is motivated to complete them, and at the completion of it, once the funding is spent, then, of course, it’s spent.
acuity.explanation: This takes up Utikere's specific question on clause 23 and answers it on its own terms: it states that the legislation imposes no time-bound on the spend, gives the reason (project duration of two to three years) and addresses the incentive point directly. The answer would necessarily be different had Utikere asked something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my question to the Minister is: is there any incentive or disincentive for the spending of those moneys?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: This will be my second line of questioning. I haven’t received responses to my key questions at the start. The Minister of Transport acknowledged that he had met with Mayor Wayne Brown, but my question was actually framed around what the current state of the relationship is and the impact of this piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Halbert engages the content of the Minister's answer by identifying precisely what it did and did not supply: the Minister confirmed the meeting with the mayor but not the state of the relationship or the mayor's and councillors' views on the bill. That is taking up the reply and pressing the gap in it, rather than restating prepared material. Not a full 1.0 because he re-puts his question rather than doing anything further with the Minister's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There were a number of questions from Tangi Utikere in terms of the disbursement." — Simeon Brown, whose reply dealt with the Labour members' clause questions but not with Halbert's consultation question

acuity.statement: I think, again, if the Minister’s unable to substantiate his so-called cost of living impacts of this bill by backing it up with evidence and robust analysis, I just question, then, whether the cost of living argument for this bill is just based on vibes as opposed to actually robust evidence around who will benefit the most.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by Brown dealt with the prioritisation of remaining project funding and the Government policy statement. Menéndez March opens two new lines of questioning (child impact assessment, distributional assessment) that engage no part of what Brown had just said; he challenges a cost-of-living argument Brown made earlier in the debate rather than the answer just given. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the Minister's wider case, so the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Ultimately, this bill is about the Auckland regional fuel tax." — Brown's preceding answer was about which projects keep the remaining funding and the new GPS, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: There’s been a lot of talk about various projects that the Minister has decided not to exempt from the repeal of a number of these projects, and I would like, actually, a bit more of a thorough answer from the Minister. I just had a look at the Standing Orders, and the Minister is required to answer all of our questions. I’m not sure that simply saying, “I don’t want to” or “It’s not the one I picked” is a substantial enough or considered enough justification for the amount of projects which are being defunded, essentially, in Auckland.
acuity.explanation: She engages the content of the Minister's immediately preceding answer directly: she characterises it as a bare assertion of ministerial choice, says the Standing Orders require more, and then presses for the specific reasoning on clause 7 and project 9. The speech would have had to be different had Brown given a reasoned answer, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because she does not rebut a figure or argument of his so much as the sufficiency of his reply, and much of the detail that follows is her own prepared Amendment Paper material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the Government has been very clear around which of these projects will require the remaining funding to support" — she takes up that answer and disputes that it is an adequate justification.

acuity.statement: There’s a couple of questions there in relation to one from Ricardo Menéndez March from the Green Party in relation to the cost of living. This will have a cost of living impact by reducing the cost of petrol for Aucklanders, and that is something which is, of course, good news to people in Auckland and I know has significant support from the people of Auckland.
acuity.explanation: He names the strand put to him and answers the topic — the bill's cost-of-living effect — rather than the specific question, which was whether a child impact assessment and a distributional assessment were done and which groups gain. He asserts the impact Menéndez March asked him to substantiate without engaging the demand for analysis, so partial engagement at best.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "whether a child impact assessment has been done as part of the process of this bill" — Brown takes up the cost-of-living strand but not the question about assessments.

acuity.statement: In relation to the question from Camilla Belich, I have answered a range of very similar questions in relation to particular Amendment Papers which we’ve said we’re not supporting. Because ultimately we were elected to remove this tax, we’re removing it on 30 June this year. There will only be a certain amount of remaining funding and we have prioritised that remaining funding to the projects listed in the bill, and that is what we’re doing through this legislation.
acuity.explanation: A mere reference to the question put to him, followed by the same prepared mandate-and-prioritisation lines he had already given. None of the specific content Belich raised — clause 7's deletion of the schedule, project 9, the Access for Everyone programme, the painted cycle lane retrofit — is engaged, so the passage would read identically whatever projects she had named. On the matter under debate, hence 0.3 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "has he turned his mind to this particular plan?" (the City Centre Masterplan Access for Everyone under project 9) — Brown names her question and does not take up the plan, clause 7 or the cycle-lane retrofit.

acuity.statement: The number of questions there from Shanan Halbert asking me for my views, of the mayor’s views, and in relation to the views of Auckland Transport, etc., etc. I mean, ultimately, as I’ve outlined on a number of occasions, we took this policy to the election; Aucklanders voted for it—in fact, I think Auckland voted 57 percent for the coalition Government—and now we are delivering on that promise with this legislation. The bill, I think, outlines all of those various elements of how we are repealing it, what projects are remaining, and so I don’t think those questions are particularly in relation to the bill.
acuity.explanation: Names Halbert's questions and gestures at the debate by asserting they fall outside the bill, but engages the content of none of them — not the $500,000 figure, not the Auckland Transport advice, not the pedestrian-crossing examples. Catalogue plus pivot to the election mandate, so it sits in the low band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "in his second reading speech and first reading speech he continued to mention the amount of $500,000 as a cost for pedestrian crossings" — and his questions on consultation with Auckland Council and Auckland Transport

acuity.statement: I have a few questions for the Minister on the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill, Part 1, particularly on clause 4 and clause 5. My first question is: how will the Minister ensure that the abolition of the regional fuel tax does not adversely affect the funding of current and future transport projects in Auckland, especially those that are critical to reducing and improving the public transportation system?
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions squarely on the matter under debate (clauses 4 and 5 of the bill) but engaging no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer, including his claim that such questions are out of scope. On-topic prepared material, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the Opposition's questions were "not particularly in relation to the bill" because the policy was taken to the election, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: In terms of the winding up of the scheme, this legislation effectively requires, from the time of Royal assent—we’ll get to that debate later—that the funds are required to be spent on these particular projects and then on 30 June that is when the tax ends.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Salesa's five questions — the wind-up mechanism and its timing — and supplies the sequence (Royal assent, then the 30 June end date), while leaving the funding, alternative-revenue and savings-provision questions to a reference to earlier answers. Partial engagement you can point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "can the Minister detail the transitional provisions that will be put in place to manage the wind-up process of the current scheme" and "what is the time line for these changes?"

acuity.statement: Given that he was not interested in responding about either the increased personal costs of injury and death nor the cost to the Government of increased health, I will focus on the very immediate cost of living question. The median distance of travel to school in metro urban authorities is just over 2 kilometres. Is it cheaper for a family, let’s say with two children, to encourage their children to walk to school or to have to buy a second car to drive them there?
acuity.explanation: Registers the Minister's pattern of declining the wider-cost questions and deliberately re-frames onto the cost ground he says the bill is about, which is more than prepared material; but it engages no specific claim he made, re-asking her own line of questioning instead. Mid-low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "I don’t think those questions are particularly in relation to the bill" — his refusals to answer on wider costs

acuity.statement: Look, I think there’s a range of questions in relation to a range of transport policies. I mean, ultimately what we’re doing here is removing the Auckland regional fuel tax, which removes 10c a litre plus GST off the cost of fuel in Auckland. That is what this Government does. That’s what the legislation does.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown put three concrete comparative cost questions; the reply addresses none of them, classifying them as being about other transport policies and restating what the bill does. A gesture at the debate with no engagement of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "Is it cheaper to have cycle lanes and footpaths or to increase the health budget?" and her school-travel comparison

acuity.statement: One of the things that the Minister says is “We won the election.” and so on, and “Therefore, we don’t need to discuss.” Indeed, that is quite clear, but that doesn’t mean that the Government is still not responsible for discussing these matters.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's mandate argument, grants its premise outright, and then disputes the inference — that winning the election discharges the duty to answer in committee. The speech would have to change if he had argued something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "we took this policy to the election; Aucklanders voted for it... and so I don’t think those questions are particularly in relation to the bill"

acuity.statement: I mean, the first question from Arena Williams is not relevant to this bill. This bill is repealing the regional fuel tax. If the Government was to make other policy changes in regards to other types of funding and financing for infrastructure, that is something which would be done separately. So it’s not relevant to the bill which is in front of us.
acuity.explanation: He identifies the specific question put to him (whether repealing the regional fuel tax framework forecloses or eases a future time-of-use charging regime) and gives a reason it will not be answered: any such funding change would be done separately. That is a take-up of the question's topic and an implicit rejection of its premise that this bill is the relevant vehicle, but he engages none of the substance Williams offered — the proposed amendment to retain the subpart, or the assurance she asked for — and returns to a restatement of the bill's purpose. Partial engagement, pointable but shallow.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is this not the part of the law which he would seek to amend, were he to introduce time-user charging" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: In relation to the question around in-ground projects, again, that question has been asked multiple times. I would note, though, that the regional fuel tax was not proposing to spend any money on Mill Road because the last Government cancelled it.
acuity.explanation: He goes at the factual premise of the Mill Road question rather than the topic: Williams asked for assurances about cost control once the project moves from the fuel-tax pot to the national pot, and he answers that the fuel tax was funding no part of Mill Road in the first place. That is a correction aimed squarely at the claim just made, and the reply would be different if she had said something else. It falls short of 1.0 because the cost-control assurance she actually sought is left untouched and the rest is a 'asked multiple times' brush-off.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Minister is indicating that he is moving Mill Road out of this small pot of money here, which is created by the Auckland regional fuel tax, and into the big pot of money" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Now, I get that we’re not delving into specific projects that are being removed by the dismantling of this structure through this particular repeal bill—I get that—but what I really want to ask the Minister about is the gaps, because, ultimately, what we’re talking about is 11 projects that will not go ahead, which, in its entirety, means that infrastructure that would have allowed children to be able, potentially, to cycle to schools or people to be able to get to their busiest local mall is not there.
acuity.explanation: She concedes the relevance objection the Minister had just used to decline Williams' questions and reframes her own line of inquiry around it — asking about the gap left by the lost projects rather than the projects themselves. That is a real, pointable take-up of the one strand of Brown's turn, which is why this is not in the 0.1–0.3 band. But it engages only his procedural objection, not his substantive Mill Road correction, and the remainder of the contribution is prepared electorate material on Sylvia Park, road safety, accessibility and Penlink that would read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that question has been asked multiple times" and "it’s not relevant to the bill which is in front of us" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I thank the member for their question in relation to the Search and Surveillance Act. So the current legislation provides powers to issue search warrants in respect of alleged offences. Alleged offences are in relation to whether or not the people who are—in relation to the keeping of records, and this is in relation to the tax. So, obviously, it’s all about making sure that the tax is being applied and being paid appropriately. So, obviously, when the tax was in place, it’s appropriate to have penalties for non-payment. Of course, you then also need powers in order to make sure that search warrants can be done, in respect of alleged offences.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question Utikere put — why the Search and Surveillance Act reference sits in Schedule 3 and what it actively does — and supplies the rationale (search warrants for alleged offences around record-keeping and non-payment of the tax). It would read quite differently had Utikere asked about something else, so the engagement is real and pointable. Short of 1.0 because it answers one of the three strands put to him (the active provisions and, in the following passage, the consequential amendments) while leaving the GST Act definition and Legislation Act 2019 questions untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "what I’m interested in hearing from the Minister is what the active provisions are" — his question about how the Search and Surveillance Act 2012 reference in Schedule 3 operates in an active form

acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's justification for the title clause — that the title is accurate because the bill is a repeal — concedes the premise ("yes, it is") and disputes the inference, arguing a repeal need not be named in the title and that content is what governs. This speech could not have been delivered unchanged had Brown defended the title on different grounds.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "this bill is the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill 2024. That is the title, that is what it does."

I would argue that this is just window dressing.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Utikere's preceding turn made a concrete argument for a one-year delay to commencement. Radhakrishnan is on the matter under debate (clauses 1 and 2, Title and Commencement) and gestures at the Minister's framing, but engages no part of Utikere's transitional-provisions argument, instead delivering prepared material proposing alternative titles for the bill. Prepared material on the right subject sits in the 0.1–0.3 band.

She explicitly starts a fresh question rather than engaging Radhakrishnan's argument, so no part of the preceding claim is picked up — but she is squarely on the clause under debate and reaches back to what the Minister told the House in the prior debate, which is the gesture that puts this at 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Priyanca Radhakrishnan argued the bill's title is "window dressing" and proposed alternative names reflecting lost bus and airport-access projects; this statement opens a new line ("A new question for the Minister on this part") and does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Now, there are remaining funds in the Auckland Council coffers—over $340 million—and there’ll be remaining funding which will be received between now and 1 July, and as I’ve outlined publicly, 1 July was the date chosen because that aligns with the Auckland Council’s annual budget year and that’s the right time to make that change.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put — why the commencement is staggered and why the project-restriction provision bites at Royal assent rather than 1 July — and supplies a rationale (alignment with the council's budget year, and channelling funds collected in the interim to priority projects). He also disposes of Utikere's tabled amendment by name. Not 1.0 because he never answers the part about what advice he considered. Scored only on engagement, not on whether the rationale is sound or true.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "why is that earlier than 1 July?" and "what is the advice that he’s had about bringing the date forward for this particular part of the commencement clause?"

acuity.explanation: Eligible and partially responsive: he explicitly registers what has gone before ("a lot said about the effect on Auckland when this commencement occurs") and draws a consequence from the Minister's priority-projects answer, asking whether funding will be pulled from other regions to fill the gap. But he does not engage the Minister's actual reasoning about the commencement dates; he takes one strand and turns to his own prepared regional-funding theme, which is the ~0.5 band.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "We want to make sure that the remaining funds go towards those priority projects" — O'Connor draws out a consequence of that priority-funding answer for regions outside Auckland.

acuity.statement: But when we have a look at what is contained in that departmental disclosure statement, in the absence of any regulatory impact statement, it simply says that when it comes to the focus on the cost of living, removing this regional fuel tax “will result in modest savings for households and businesses, between $5-$10 per tank”—and we seem to hear that from Minister Simeon Brown frequently—but also that the actual savings, based on the average distances that are travelled in Auckland City and not collecting that RFT out to 2028, will equate to around $1.85 for a motorist, all right—$1.85.
acuity.explanation: Takes the central number from the immediately preceding speech ($5-$10 per tank), locates its source in the departmental disclosure statement, and sets against it a competing figure from the same document ($1.85 averaged out to 2028). The speech would have to be rewritten if Brown had made a different argument, which is the deciding test. Scored only on engagement — whether the $1.85 recasting is a fair reading is a veracity/rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it will save Aucklanders money as they fill up their cars from 1 July this year: $5 to $10 per tank" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: There are three projects, of course, that are going to remain in the picture, and they are projects that are going to still be eligible for regional fuel tax funding, or what is left of them, and isn’t it interesting that two of those three relate to two members in this Parliament?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one specific strand of the preceding speech — the claim that the leftover revenue goes to high-priority projects — and presses on which projects survive and who benefits. Partial rather than full engagement: it takes up the remaining-funds thread but leaves Brown's named projects (Eastern Busway, electric trains, roading corridors) untested and shifts to a conflict-of-interest point drawn from the earlier committee stage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we will ensure that the remaining funds are spent on high-priority projects" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The best thing about that contribution was when the member sat down.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding contribution without engaging any part of its content — a mere reference, which the rubric places at the bottom of the band rather than at a partial engagement. Not 0.0 only because it is anchored to the speech it follows and so could not have been delivered in another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the bill removes the 11.5c Auckland regional fuel tax, saves motorists $5-$10 a tank and redirects $340 million of unspent revenue, and this statement takes up no part of it

acuity.statement: The first one of them is that we've heard a lot from the other side of the House that the repeal of this regional fuel tax will mean the death of all these projects they are so passionate about. All it will mean is that at the moment, Auckland gets about $130 million a year from this tax. It also gets about $1.5 billion from the National Land Transport Fund (NLTF), so any good project that meets the criteria of the NLTF can get funded; it might take a little bit longer.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up the specific strand of Genter's speech that the regional fuel tax was funding worthwhile Auckland projects, and rebuts it with a funding comparison ($130m from the tax against $1.5b from the NLTF) and a mechanism by which those projects could still proceed. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different. He does not engage her other strands (central government overriding local decision-making, the Minister's cost claims), so not a full 1.0.

acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "There is an alternative to this, and that was some of the projects that were being funded by the Auckland regional fuel tax"

acuity.statement: So, to build on my kōrero from earlier this afternoon, I now stand and question the real vision of this Government. In the first 100 days, this Government has repealed Act after Act and not replaced them, and if they have been replaced, then it has been to the detriment of our people and, in actual fact, to the detriment of their so-called one New Zealand, which is the preferred rhetoric.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Foster but engages no part of it — no response on NLTF funding, the coalition agreement, or Labour's position on regional fuel taxes. It explicitly resumes her own earlier prepared kōrero and widens to the Government's general repeal programme. It stays loosely within the territory of the debate (a repeal bill, and she later lists the road-user charges amendment bill among the repeals), which keeps it above 0.1 rather than at 0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued that Auckland projects losing the regional fuel tax can still be funded from the $1.5 billion National Land Transport Fund and that the repeal meets the coalition agreement, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: There is so much to say following a lecture like that from David Parker, but what I actually want to say—as Ronan Keating sang—is that you say it best when you say nothing at all. So I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford names the preceding speaker and his speech ('a lecture like that from David Parker') but engages no part of its content: no figure, no claim, no argument is addressed. The turn is a dismissal plus a commendation of the bill, and would be word-for-word usable whatever Parker had argued. It stays just above 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate and gestures at the speech it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker argued the repeal leaves a funding hole, that the 'Roads of National Party Significance' are between $6 billion and $22 billion underfunded, and that Auckland's costs will simply shift to rates and cancelled projects — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: There is so much noise from that side, they’ve finally decided to wake up. Thank you, Mr Speaker. Labour opposes this bill.
acuity.explanation: Sosene registers that the government benches have become vocal ('so much noise from that side', later 'who have come alive in the last 20 minutes'), which is a gesture at the turns she follows, but she engages the content of nothing said before her. What follows is prepared local material on Māngere projects, Te Ara Mua and airport gridlock — on the right subject, and indifferent to Rutherford's remark or Parker's figures. A reference to the other side's behaviour is not engagement with an argument, so this sits in the 0.1–0.3 band with the gesture earning 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'you say it best when you say nothing at all' — Tom Rutherford, who declined to make a substantive case and commended the bill.

acuity.statement: The Minister’s brazen confidence in pushing a bill through without actually substantiating the cost of living impacts it will have, despite the general policy statement focusing on the cost of living relief that the repeal of the regional fuel tax will have, is, quite frankly, admirable.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive turn by another member precedes it in the same debate. The speech is plainly on the matter under debate and shares a strand with the preceding turn (who benefits from the repeal), but it takes up none of Kapa-Kingi's actual argument — it opens on the Minister's committee-stage conduct and runs as prepared material, and would read identically whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi argued the repeal lacks vision beyond three years and that 'it is largely those who cannot afford private transport who rely on transport infrastructure', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Like my colleague Lemauga Sosene, we know the results of the election, and I accept that. I’m fine with that. I accept that this Government wants to repeal the regional fuel tax for Auckland. But in this process, as with anyone who wins an election, it doesn’t mean you’re above this House. If you win an election, it doesn’t mean that you can bypass parliamentary process.
acuity.explanation: Bidois's immediately preceding turn rested its whole case on an electoral mandate ("We did win the election last year. We won it on a mandate..."). Halbert takes that exact argument, concedes its factual premise, and then disputes the inference drawn from it — that winning licenses bypassing select committee process. The speech would have had to change if Bidois had argued something other than mandate, so this is squarely responsive rather than prepared material on the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We did win the election last year. We won it on a mandate of easing cost of living pressures" — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: The number one issue for the residents of Mt Roskill is dealing with the cost of living. The Auckland regional fuel tax has disproportionally hurt those on the lowest incomes in my electorate, who often drive the oldest and most un - fuel-efficient cars. Reducing the cost of fuel will make a meaningful difference, particularly to the families who are counting every dollar at the moment.
acuity.explanation: Halbert's long preceding turn made specific arguments: no regulatory impact statement, no public submissions, no Auckland Council input, no replacement plan, and a net cost increase to Aucklanders from the $50 charge and 22c excise rise. Cheung's reply engages none of them; it is prepared electorate material on the general topic of cost of living and the fuel tax, and would read identically had Halbert said something entirely different. It stays on the subject under debate, so it is not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the repeal was rammed through without a regulatory impact statement, submissions or Auckland Council input and offers no replacement plan, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: Well, that was quite a press release, but not much else, frankly.
acuity.explanation: Opens the reply to the Minister's first-reading speech by dismissing it wholesale. It is a characterisation of her speech, not an engagement with any claim in it; the words would serve against almost any ministerial speech on any bill. A gesture at the debate but no part of the argument, so the bottom band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee set out three specific changes to the FPO regime — expanded qualifying criteria, new search powers, and a five-year review mechanism — and this statement takes up none of them.

acuity.explanation: Takes McKee's stated justification for the new search powers, concedes it explicitly ("there are really good grounds"), and then sets against it the countervailing right she did not address. Classic accept-part-dispute-the-rest; the speech would have to change if the Minister had justified the powers differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "People with FPOs are deemed to be of the highest risk to public safety. To reduce this risk, they should be subject to the highest level of monitoring." — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: The bill before the House says that this can be done without any reasonable suspicion that any offence or breach has occurred.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the content of the Minister's second change by naming the threshold she omitted — that no reasonable suspicion is required. It engages the specific provision she described rather than the topic at large. Scored on engagement only; whether the characterisation of the clause is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The bill’s second change is to give police new specialist search powers so that anyone subject to an FPO can be searched at any time." — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: But what this bill does today is it hides behind a guise of making our communities safer. Over the last few days, we’ve heard from the Government that they have a mandate to crack down on law and order and to make our communities safer. But what we know about the bills that are going through the House this week is that they’re not going to do that, because they’re targeting such a minority group in society and placing the blame squarely on that minority group in society.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the debate — McKee's community-safety rationale — and denies it, which is real engagement. But it answers the general framing rather than any specific mechanism she described, and it does not take up Webb's warrantless-search argument from the immediately preceding turn before moving to prepared material on the drivers of gang membership.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "helping to keep firearms out of their hands, ultimately making our communities safer" — Nicole McKee

I care about the safety of the people of Rangitata—safety which is threatened daily by the presence of gangs in our community. When the pad in Washdyke was demolished by the council, firearms were present. There is no doubt that this bill goes some way to making sure that no longer happens.

acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'I guarantee you that this bill before us tonight does nothing to address those drivers'
