acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Miles Anderson: "So the question remains: how much of an influence are these ratepayers actually having on voting outcomes?"

acuity.statement: Now, we’ve heard an argument put forward tonight that one person, one vote means you should only get one vote. But, really, what it means is that all votes should be equal. I’m sure the member opposite wouldn’t want to see a situation where a New Zealand citizen, who also has voting rights in another country, forfeits their voting rights in New Zealand, because that is the level of analysis being done on the other side tonight.
acuity.explanation: Luxton restates the one-person-one-vote principle that has been in contention in the preceding turns and attacks it by analogy — a dual citizen does not forfeit a New Zealand vote — which is aimed at the residency-only principle Wade-Brown had just asserted. He engages the reasoning rather than merely naming the other side, but he characterises the opposing argument loosely instead of taking up its specific terms, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "So voting should be based on residency and citizenship, not property ownership."

acuity.statement: Now, we should have a say in the use of the rates which are charged on a property which we own. I’ll address the member across the House saying that it is the renter that pays for. Well, that is not always the case. Sometimes, when your property has been left in a state of disrepair and you must go through the process of renovations, because of a leaky-home crisis or some such, you’re still paying rates. So it’s not always on the renter.
acuity.explanation: This takes the specific claim made in the immediately preceding turn — that rents effectively cover the rates, so the tenant is the real ratepayer — names it, and supplies a counterexample (an untenanted property under repair where the owner still pays rates), even conceding it is a minor case. The passage could not have been delivered without Wade-Brown's claim having been made, which is the strongest available evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "Excuse me, but we expect, generally, that the rents would cover the costs of the house, including the rates."

acuity.statement: In actual fact, what we’ve heard from this side of the House is an admission that universal suffrage actually doesn’t exist in this country, is that there is privilege in this country—there is privilege in this country where people get more than one vote. If you own one house in one city, and you own another house in another city, you get two votes.
acuity.explanation: Takes Foster's central distinction — one vote per separate election, not multiple votes — and does something with it, recasting the concession as an admission that a property owner in two cities ends up with two votes, which he then builds the rest of his argument on. The speech would have to change if Foster had argued something else; it is keyed to the specific claim he made rather than merely naming him. Short of 1.0 because it recharacterises rather than rebuts the '67 sovereign territorial authorities, separate elections' reasoning that was the load-bearing part of Foster's case. Whether that elision is sound inference is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "You don’t get extra votes; what you get is one vote in each separate election."

acuity.statement: There are holiday homes there. And you’re going to tell me that those people that own those holiday homes get a right to determine what happens with the people who were born and bred there, who live there, who contribute to the economy, who have lived there for many, many years, post- and pre-colonisation, that we’re going to allow people to determine what happens in our particular area. That is absolutely unfair.
acuity.explanation: Foster closed on the holiday-home case, arguing that someone with a bach in one place and a home in another cannot be said to have no stake in both. Waititi picks up that exact example and contests the premise directly, setting the holiday-home owner against residents of Whangaparāoa to deny that a second property confers a legitimate stake. This is squarely aimed at the argument just made, and the disagreement is evidence of having listened, not a reason to mark it down.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "They should be entitled to have that stake in both places."

acuity.statement: We are representing, Mr McAnulty, people like those that were victims of the Christchurch earthquakes, for example, that might have moved out to other suburbs beyond Christchurch and are in a fight with the Earthquake Commission (EQC) and insurance and the Christchurch City Council and they’ve been forced out of their homes. Why can’t they have a say? Why can’t they have a say on who governs and how their property taxes are spent?
acuity.explanation: McAnulty's immediately preceding speech was built on the charge that the Government benches represent only property-owning 'mates'. Brewer names McAnulty and answers that specific charge head-on with a counter-class of people he says the ratepayer roll protects — displaced quake and cyclone victims. The speech would have to change if McAnulty had argued something else, so it is squarely engaged. It stops short of 1.0 because it does not take up the strands McAnulty pressed hardest (renters, teenage workers, immigrants who pay tax but own nothing).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "They are sticking up for their mates. They are sticking up for people that own property."

acuity.statement: Referring to the last speaker, Cameron Brewer, most of those people could still vote if their primary place of residence was still where they’re not currently living. If they’re currently displaced from their house and their primary place of residence remains their old home, they can still vote there. So that’s a nonsense argument.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and dismantles the precise mechanism of his argument: Brewer's displaced ratepayers would retain a vote anyway because residence, not ownership, is the qualifying test. This is the textbook high-acuity move — it corrects the factual premise of the argument just made, and could not have been delivered against any other speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "We are representing people from all over New Zealand who can’t live in their houses for whatever reason but who need to have a say."

acuity.statement: Yeah, I know. But in the end, if it’s one person, one vote, and one extra person gets to vote in an area and sways the election because they’ve been able to vote from outside the district, that does affect the outcome.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Foster's interjected claim, concedes it ('Yeah, I know'), then disputes the inference — that other voters existed does not stop a marginal out-of-district vote determining a close result. Accept-part-and-dispute-the-rest aimed directly at the content of what was just said; marked slightly below 1.0 only because the engaged claim was an interjection rather than a full turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "There’d be a whole lot of other people who voted for them to even get to that point."

acuity.statement: I was intending to take a very, very short call to allow the member whose bill this is before the House, Greg O’Connor, to actually have the vote take place prior to the House suspending, but he’s given quite clear guidance that he’s actually not keen to have a vote on this bill at all tonight.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one real strand of the preceding turn — Parker's stated reluctance to run the clock out before a vote, and O'Connor's 'keep going' urging — and turns it back on them. But it engages only the timing of the vote, nothing of Parker's substantive case about residence and rates, before returning to the prepared position that the Government is not supporting the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "I don’t want to take this so close to the night that we’re not going to get a vote tonight, so—"

acuity.statement: I’ve watched particularly the speakers on the other side stand up, and you always know, and as you’ll know yourself, Madam Speaker, when someone’s standing up, they actually don’t believe what they’re saying. You can tell that they’re actually—they’ve read the notes, they know what they’ve been told to do by the party whips, they hunt for little examples that might be the pièce de resistance that will get them across, but, actually, they don’t really believe it.
acuity.explanation: Refers to the preceding speakers as a bloc and to their 'little examples', but engages the content of none of them — not Brewer's displaced ratepayers, not Rutherford's point about the vote. It attributes insincerity rather than answering an argument, then moves off to maiden speeches and police pay. A mere reference to the other side is not responsiveness; the passage would be near-identical whatever they had argued, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3's upper edge only for gesturing at the debate just had.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer argued displaced quake victims need a ratepayer vote and Tom Rutherford argued for taking the vote tonight, and this statement takes up neither argument.

acuity.statement: Like previous speakers, I also want to acknowledge that, yes, the dairy and the meat sector didn't get exactly what they wanted.
acuity.explanation: Parmar follows a substantive turn by James Shaw that made specific arguments: that the EU agreement's environment chapter was confirmed by officials to be 'properly, fully, legally enforceable', that investor-State dispute settlement was excluded, that Pharmac is protected, and that the Trade For All work under David Parker produced the near-unanimity in the House. Her speech takes up none of these. It is prepared ACT material on the same subject — small nation, export opportunities, market size, COVID recovery, eggs and baskets from her own 2022 NBR column — and would read identically whoever had spoken before her, apart from two nods ('Like previous speakers', 'as we have heard from the Minister') that name earlier speakers without engaging any claim they made. The quoted sentence echoes the shared concession Shaw had already voiced rather than doing anything with it, which places it in the gesture band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "No one gets everything that they fully want in any agreement" — James Shaw (Shaw's substantive claims about enforceability of the environment chapter and the exclusion of ISDS are not taken up at all)

acuity.statement: The Minister, the Hon Todd McClay, generously gave us a deadline of 4 April; we soon discovered that with efficient consideration, we could actually bring that forward 10 days, which would then enable the agreement to come into effect a month earlier than it might have, which indeed was still a month or two earlier than it could have prior to that.
acuity.explanation: Van de Molen follows Arbuckle in the same third-reading debate and covers much of the same ground (1 May entry into force, horticulture, $100 million, successive Governments), but he engages none of Arbuckle's claims — he explicitly picks up 'what the Minister said in his speech' instead, and the speech would read identically had Arbuckle said something quite different. Prepared material squarely on the matter under debate, with only a generic nod to 'all parties', so it sits at the low end of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle argued the FTA is 'the result of a longstanding bipartisan effort by successive New Zealand Governments' and cited the $100 million day-one tariff savings and the kiwifruit/onion gains, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: What I would like to do—rather than focus just on the benefits of the free-trade agreement, which has been well covered by many speakers so far—is just capture one of the key points of discussion that came up through the select committee process, and that was around enforcement provisions.
acuity.explanation: Costley follows Parker's substantive turn and explicitly notes that the benefits have been 'well covered by many speakers so far', which is a gesture at the preceding debate, but he then pivots entirely to his own prepared select committee material on enforcement provisions and article 18.38. None of Parker's specific arguments — ISDS removal, the Treaty clause, the resale royalty strategy, the misallocation of capital — is engaged, rebutted or built on. The speech would read identically had Parker argued something quite different about the agreement, so this sits in the 'prepared material on the right subject' band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the acknowledgement of earlier contributions is a real, if content-free, glance at what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker spoke immediately before about the absence of ISDS clauses, the Treaty clause, the artist resale royalty negotiating strategy and interest deductibility, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I’m pleased to be taking this call on the European Union Free Trade Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill, and I’m really pleased to see that common sense is residing throughout the House and that most members of the House will be supporting this bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Salesa's preceding turn — her point that trade is the issue on which the House agrees — and later mirrors her thanks to Todd McClay, Damien O'Connor and MFAT officials, and her acknowledgement of the previous Government's work. But it engages no specific claim she made (the Zespri tariff figures, the ILO labour and gender-equality chapters, the $1.4 billion modelling) and the bulk of the speech is prepared electorate material on wine, spirits and the food and fibre sector that would stand unchanged whatever she had argued. A partial engagement, not a rebuttal or extension.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "It is really good that on this issue—trade—we usually agree."

acuity.statement: We’ve heard reasons across the House of the need for its haste, and I agree wholeheartedly—the opportunity for our traders to be able to get into the market sooner rather later is important.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand already argued — why ratification should be brought forward — accepts it explicitly, and then does something with it by supplying the reason he says has barely been mentioned: the June EU elections and the risk of upheaval in the market before ratification. That addition only makes sense as a response to what preceded, so the speech would have to change if the earlier speakers had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because he rebuts or tests nothing; he endorses the prior case and tops it up, and the rest is committee anecdote.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "ensuring that this trade agreement is ratified earlier than originally scheduled" (the urgency argument also carried in Miles Anderson's preceding turn)

acuity.statement: This trade agreement, while not perfect, will extensively benefit many areas of our primary industries and the wider economy. From day one, the estimated tariff savings exceed $100 million and with it growing to $110 million over seven years—and I’m sure it will amount to many more, which makes for the highest immediate savings of a New Zealand free-trade agreement.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, but indifferent to what preceded it. The whole call is prepared Northland material — kiwifruit hectares, irrigation dams, mussel spat, beekeepers, Ngāpuhi settlement — and would be word-for-word identical whichever member had spoken before and whatever they had said. The clause "while not perfect" glances at Anderson's point without engaging it, which is a reference rather than a response, so this sits in the unresponsive band rather than at 0.5. Not 0.0 because it is squarely about this bill and could not have been delivered in another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Miles Anderson argued that "perfect is the enemy of good" in answer to commentary about what was left out of the agreement, and Peeni Henare argued ratification must beat the June EU elections; this statement takes up neither, beyond the passing concession "while not perfect".

acuity.statement: But what I really wanted to just give the Minister time to digest is really the question that the Hon Dr Deborah Russell had around the IMF findings and whether he had given any consideration to whether we needed to change Part 1, clause 3, of this particular bill in relation to that new IMF report.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds picks up the specific question Russell had just put — the IMF report's progressivity finding — and does something with it, pinning it to Part 1, clause 3 of the bill before the committee and allowing that the report is only a week old. The speech would be different had Russell raised something else; much of the rest of the turn is prepared exposition on why annual rates bills exist, which keeps it short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I'd like to hear from the Minister how he thinks that our income tax scale responds to that"

acuity.statement: The first question from the Hon Dr Deborah Russell in regards to the IMF report, which the Hon Barbara Edmonds also referenced in terms of her report—if I look at the IMF report, what it actually says as well is it informs and suggests to Government to ensure that it gets its spending under control.
acuity.explanation: Watts goes to the same document that was quoted at him and contests its emphasis, which is real engagement with the source rather than a mere mention. But he answers the topic (the IMF report) rather than the claim actually put (how the income tax scale answers the progressivity finding), pivoting to a passage on spending restraint instead, so this sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "that well-known left-wing organisation the IMF telling us that we need a more progressive tax scale"

acuity.statement: The practicality of considering or using this bill to actually put in place any of those personal income tax changes which will really benefit middle-income New Zealand will be an announcement that we will be doing as part of the Budget process, and it wasn’t timely or appropriate for us to put it into this bill, because it’s already a very, very comprehensive bill.
acuity.explanation: This is a direct answer to the specific question Edmonds asked — whether the bill was the right vehicle for the tax relief changes — and it supplies the reason (timing, and the bill's existing size) rather than deflecting. The reply could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "had he actually considered whether this was an appropriate vehicle in order to bring in some of that tax relief"

acuity.statement: And then I remember that this is actually a bill that was put on the Table by the Labour Party, and I didn’t see anything about capital gains in here, which is an interesting signal itself.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of what was put before the committee — the IMF's capital gains recommendation that Russell read out — and draws a consequence from it, but turns it into a point about the bill's Labour authorship rather than engaging whether the recommendation is sound, so it is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "reforms should combine comprehensive capital gains tax, land value tax, and changes to corporate income tax" (quoting the IMF)

acuity.statement: Nevertheless, Treasury has suggested that we need a capital gains tax in order to meet this ongoing gap between Crown revenue and Crown expenses. The IMF has suggested that we need a capital gains tax in order to balance what we’re doing and, in our tax system, have a sustainable tax system.
acuity.explanation: Russell takes the opening Watts created, and answers his stated opposition to a capital gains tax by marshalling two specific authorities against it, including the Treasury briefing to the incoming Minister of Finance and the forecast revenue-expenses gap. The passage exists because of what Watts said and would have to change if he had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Of course, we don’t support capital gains tax, but I thought that was also something that the IMF referred to"

acuity.statement: The point raised in regards to the sufficiency of revenue that the tax system derives—well, as of 2022, the tax system collected just over $120 billion of tax. As many people will know, there’s two ways to close a gap: one is to increase revenue through taxation; the other way is to reduce expenditure. On this side of the House, this coalition Government is absolutely committed to reducing wasteful spending, cutting expenditure, and not taxing New Zealanders more.
acuity.explanation: Watts names and takes up Russell's specific challenge — the sufficiency of tax revenue to fund services — and answers it on its own terms, by quantifying the current take and arguing the gap can be closed on the expenditure side rather than the revenue side. The speech would have been different had Russell asked something else. It falls short of 1.0 because he does not engage her specific figure (a 5 percent of GDP gap by 2061) and opens by pivoting to a quote from the Labour leader rather than the argument put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we have an ongoing worry that the income taxes we collect will not collect enough revenue, over time, to sustain the types of goods and services" — Deborah Russell, who asked how the Minister would meet the projected revenue gap

acuity.statement: In responding directly to the comments of the Minister of Revenue, I think he, right there, struck the very heart of it, which is that his Government has an ideological belief that people should pay less tax, and I think that that’s completely at odds with the outcomes that they say they want for New Zealand and that New Zealanders want.
acuity.explanation: Genter seizes on the exact proposition Watts had just advanced — that the route to prosperity is lower tax and less spending — accepts his framing of it as ideological, and turns it against him by arguing the belief is inconsistent with the outcomes his Government professes to want, then supports that with the comparator-country spending argument. Squarely built on the preceding turn rather than prepared material; disagreement here is evidence of attention, not a deduction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the ideological point around how we get ahead as a country is not through taxing more; it is through growing our economy and reducing wasteful spending" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: One is around capital gains. He has raised the issue of capital gains, and so I’m wondering how he can reconcile the fact that landlords would be able to get interest deductibility and get the interest deductibility off the interest, but then also not pay any tax on the capital gain—It would appear that it either has to be one scenario or the other—so I do hope the Minister can just tell us, when he’s been thinking about the fairness of the tax system, how he reconciles that.
acuity.explanation: Leary expressly builds her question out of the Minister's own remarks on capital gains tax and draws a consequence from them — that restoring interest deductibility while taxing no capital gain is internally inconsistent — which is engaging the content rather than merely naming the previous speaker. Not 1.0 because she poses a fresh line of inquiry rather than contesting the reasoning Watts actually offered on revenue sufficiency.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what I think was a question there around capital gains tax" and the defence of "not taxing New Zealanders more" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The Government agrees that the cost of mobility parking fines is insufficient, with the fees not having been updated since 2008, and this is part of a broader issue with outdated fees that we’re seeking to address.
acuity.explanation: O’Connor's opening turn set out the enforcement problem and ended on the inadequacy of the $150 infringement fee, flagging that later speakers would cover the committee's recommendations and the Government's response. Simmonds takes up that specific strand — conceding the fee is insufficient, dating it to 2008, and saying what the Minister of Transport has directed in response — so the reply would have to change if the preceding turn had argued the fine level was adequate. It is not a full 1.0 because the passage is also the prepared ministerial response to the committee report recommendation by recommendation, rather than engagement built around what O’Connor actually said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O’Connor: "Currently, the infringement fee is a mere $150."

acuity.statement: So I really think we should consider a public education campaign to improve the understanding around someone accessing basic needs. That’s what this is about. This is making sure that we enable the disabled community to live their best lives.
acuity.explanation: Chhour follows a substantive turn by Genter on the same petition, so she is eligible. Her speech is squarely on the matter under debate — mobility parking, enforcement, accessibility — but it engages no part of Genter's actual argument: not the removal of minimum parking requirements, not the area-based provision proposal, and not the income-proportionate fines point Genter had just put. It is prepared material on the right subject, advancing its own recommendation (a public education campaign), and would read identically had Genter said something quite different or not spoken at all. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 because it is tightly on-topic but makes no gesture at the preceding contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter spoke immediately before, arguing that minimum mobility-parking provision should be area-based rather than site-by-site and that parking fines should be set as a percentage of income, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Anā ka tautoko mātou i ngā tāngata mana hauā e whai ana i tō rātou nei mana motuhake i roto i te tūnga waka. Engari ehara i te mea e tautokotia ana tēnā kaupapa anahe, engari kia whai mana motuhake ngā tāngata mana hauā huri noa o Aotearoa, otirā te ao whānui mō ngā take pēnei i te haere ki te wharepaku, ngā mea e haere atu rā ki roto i te whare, i roto i tēnei Whare hoki, o tēnei Whare Pāremata.
acuity.explanation: Follows Foster's substantive turn on the same petition, so eligible, but engages none of his specific arguments about the fine levels, indexation or private-land enforcement. It is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on terminology ("mana hauā" rather than "whai kaha"), manifesto support and the broader accessibility of the House. There is a gesture at the matter under debate — support for the petition and a reference to car parks — so it sits at the upper end of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, but the speech would read identically whatever Foster had said about the recommendations.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued the mobility parking fine ($150) must be reset alongside the whole infringement regime (the $60 broken-yellow-line fine, the $150 red-light fine), that fines should be indexed to inflation, and that enforcement on private land would be an unwise step — and this statement does not take up any of it.

acuity.statement: I am heartened to hear quite emphatically from the member who just resumed his seat, Greg Fleming, that the Government will indeed move on all of those, because I was listening intently to the contribution by the current Minister for Disability Issues, the Hon Penny Simmonds, that was, unfortunately, incredibly lacklustre, and I thought didn’t really commit to any of those recommendations, except probably increasing fines.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of the immediately preceding turn — Fleming's enumerated six acceptances of the Petitions Committee recommendations — accepts it at face value, and then does something with it: sets it against the earlier ministerial contribution to argue the Minister had not in fact committed to those same recommendations, naming the public education campaign as the gap. The speech would have to be rewritten if Fleming had not just made that commitment, so engagement is specific rather than a mere reference. Scored on engagement only: the sharp characterisation of the Minister's speech is a civility/focus matter, and whether the Government really committed to all six is a veracity matter, neither of which moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we've listened to the recommendations on Claire's petition and we've said six clear yeses" — Greg Fleming

acuity.statement: I want to—sorry, Mr Speaker, other participants in this debate have covered off some of the detail of Claire’s petition, but I particularly just want to remind the House of what was, I think, in essence, the simplicity of her petition.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the fact that others have spoken, then proceeds to entirely prepared material on the petition's intent and the public/private property distinction. Nothing in the speech turns on Bates's inflation argument or his claim about Hipkins — substitute a different preceding speech on the same topic and this turn would be word-for-word unchanged. On-topic prepared material, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates argued that inflation since 2017 had eroded the value of a $150 fine and that the Government had committed the Ministry of Transport to a full review, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: We did not hear a commitment to that; we heard a commitment for a review by the Ministry of Transport—that is quite a different proposition.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the government speakers offered — a Ministry of Transport review — and does something with it: sets it against the actual wording of recommendation 1 (significantly increase and index fines to inflation) and argues the two are not the same undertaking. Had the preceding speeches promised the indexation itself, this passage could not have been delivered; it is wholly contingent on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Minister of Transport will direct the Ministry of Transport to undertake a full review of parking fees and fines." — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: I’m really pleased that the previous speaker, the Hon Scott Simpson, discussed the importance of private parking. But I didn’t hear the Minister herself also talk about the education campaign, because what we are seeking here is a culture change.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Simpson's private-parking strand by name and credits it, but then uses it as a hinge into her own prepared point about an education campaign rather than engaging Simpson's actual argument about public/private inconsistency. One strand engaged, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s about the consistency between public parking mobility spaces and those that occur on private property as well" — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: New Zealand has, and dare I say my colleagues in Labour and the Green Party, and, no doubt, Te Pāti Māori, seem to imagine we live in a world where a resolution or a declaration of ceasefire can be made and all of a sudden there are unicorns and rainbows. It doesn’t work like that in the real world. Someone has to get the hostages back. Someone has to keep the people of Israel safe.
acuity.explanation: Court directly takes up the core demand of the immediately preceding turn — that New Zealand use diplomatic avenues and UN Security Council Resolution 2728 to secure a ceasefire — and argues against it on its merits, that a declared ceasefire leaves the hostages unrecovered and Israel undefended. The speech would have to change if Tuiono had argued something different, which puts it above the prepared-material band. It is not a 1.0 because the engagement is with the general ceasefire strand rather than any specific element Tuiono raised (Resolution 2728's binding status, UNRWA funding, the ICJ case, the special visa category), and the bulk of the surrounding turn — the Hamas designation timeline, the 2001 'benign strategic environment' passage — is indifferent to what preceded it. Whether the characterisation of the Green and Labour position is a strawman is a Rigor question and is deliberately not scored here; the dismissive tone is a Civility question and likewise not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: 'We need to use all diplomatic avenues to achieve a ceasefire, but this is something that the Minister of Foreign Affairs should do, and that includes supporting UN Security Council Resolution 2728'

acuity.statement: We’ve been involved in a propaganda war. Some of the things we’ve heard in this House today are nothing more than propaganda from one side or from the other. Go online and look.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor follows Ngarewa-Packer, who argued at length that only one side is inflicting the disproportionate death, maiming and starvation, and that the House should impose sanctions. He gestures at what has been said in the chamber today and labels some of it propaganda 'from one side or from the other', but he does not take up her claim, dispute her figures, or engage her sanctions proposal — he dismisses the debate generically and returns to prepared material (UN resolution, casualty tallies on both sides, the ICJ ruling, Rafah). That is a reference to the preceding contributions rather than engagement with their content, so it sits in the low band with a gesture at the debate rather than at 0.5. Deleting her speech and substituting a different argument on Gaza would not have changed a word of this.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: 'what we are seeing is there is only one side experiencing the disproportionate scale of death and maiming, and the complete displacement'

acuity.statement: Fund UNRWA.
acuity.explanation: A direct answer to the specific question Peters had just put to the chamber: he asked what more could be done, and she names a concrete action squarely inside the UNRWA point he had just defended. Had he posed a different question, the interjection would necessarily have been different, which is the deciding test. Brevity is not unresponsiveness; the engagement is with the content of his challenge, not merely a reference to him.
