Engagement with the content of the argument just made, not a mere reference to the member.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "He brought the notion of wasteful spending into the debate, and I’m really interested to know, given that taxation and expenditure are kind of like two sides of a balance sheet" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Thanks very much to the member Arena Williams for those questions in regards to the amendment that has been tabled. The purpose of what we’re doing in regards to clause 8 is to return the brightline test back to its original intent of two years, and that’s the position of the Government in regards to this. We don’t support and will not be supporting the member’s amendment in relation to what has been tabled, and our position has been pretty clear in regards to our intent around returning back.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific amendment to clause 8 that Williams had just moved, gives a reason for refusing it (returning the test to a two-year 'original intent'), and so could not have been delivered whatever she had said. But it takes up only the bottom line, not her actual argument — that the change belongs in its own bill because the Amendment Paper route bypasses select committee scrutiny — so engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "So what I have done is propose to delete clause 8, which would, essentially, mean that no amendment proposed by the Minister to clause 8 would be possible" — and "I seek the Minister’s comment on that."

acuity.statement: So there’s a number of themes that are coming through in some of the contributions from members in terms of why we’re not having a separate piece of legislation and why we’re putting this as part of an Amendment Paper. Our position is clear on that: we are putting through the Amendment Paper aspects of policy that we campaigned on as part of the election, and—as I’ve given a number of examples here—many are reverting back to our prior positions that were there in the past, and that also includes around interest deductibility.
acuity.explanation: Names the precise objection Williams raised — that a major brightline change is being made by Amendment Paper rather than in a bill the House and select committee could work through — and answers it with a reason (the policy was campaigned on and reverts to a prior position). It is a direct answer to the process argument rather than a restatement, though it does not engage her point that an election mandate still leaves the policy implications unexamined by the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "what members on this side would object to is it being done in this way, when we cannot use the select committee process and use the House’s time to consider the policy implications of those changes"

acuity.statement: Firstly, then, given that the Minister will not support the sensible amendment proposed by Opposition members, can I ask him what was the original intent of the brightline test? What advice has he had that the two-year element of the brightline test will fulfil that original intent?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact ground the Minister had just stood on — the claim that clause 8 returns the test to its 'original intent of two years' — and turns it into two testable questions: what that original intent was, and what advice says two years achieves it. The questions only exist because of the answer that preceded them and would have to be rewritten if he had justified the change differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "to return the brightline test back to its original intent of two years"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m grateful to my colleague Arena Williams for pursuing some of the issues around the brightline test, but I want to pull back into some of the technical discussion as well. So here’s another issue that I would like to ask the Minister to speak to and it’s to do with the bill as has come back from select committee.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the preceding exchange and is squarely on the bill under debate, but engages no part of it: the Minister's 'original intent' justification and Williams's unanswered first-home-buyer questions are both left where they lay, and the speech turns to prepared material on clause 44 and the GloBE definitions. The reference to a colleague is a handover, not an engagement, and the turn would read identically whatever the Minister had just answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts defended the two-year brightline test and the use of an Amendment Paper rather than separate legislation, and this statement does not take either up, moving instead to clause 44 and the global anti-base erosion rules.

acuity.statement: I know that these case managers have been in place for a long time. But the difficulty here is that when the Minister first mentioned case managers, I can’t recall the exact words the Minister said, but the implication was that the case managers would be advising these MNEs—these large multinational enterprises—about where to find the law and how to apply it.
acuity.explanation: Takes Watts's specific rebuttal (the significant enterprises team is old, not new) and concedes it explicitly, then isolates the part he did not address — that his own description implied case managers give MNEs applied tax advice — and narrows the question to assessing versus advising. The speech would have to be rewritten if Watts had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Actually, that team existed under the last Government as well" / "I can assure the member that this is not a new concept" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I’m conscious of the repetition, but, again, just for context for the member, this team has existed since 1994—right? This is not a new concept—that was quite a long time ago—and the concept that IRD provides a range of taxpayers with advice and support in regards to their obligations around tax is not a new concept.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — that IRD giving advice to taxpayers is routine, which bears on the advice half of her question — but does not take up the assess-versus-advise distinction she posed, instead restating the age of the unit, a point she had already conceded, and referring her to Google. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "are they assessing the multinational enterprise’s compliance with the law, or are they advising the MNE on applying the law?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: So it is a new regime. They are a multinational enterprise, not a significant enterprise. There’s a slight difference, but if I hear the Minister of Revenue rightly, he is saying that they will be treated by that same investigations audit unit, which is the significant enterprises unit.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the premise of Watts's answer by distinguishing multinational enterprises from the significant enterprises the 1994 unit handles, states back the inference she takes him to be making so he can confirm it, and then restates Russell's unanswered question against the regime's actual entry tests. Directly contingent on what Watts just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this team has existed since 1994—right? This is not a new concept" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Just in regards to the member’s questions in regards to case management, the Inland Revenue only case manage entities that are New Zealand - headquartered entities. While there are some 800 foreign entities that operate in New Zealand, those are not within the guise, obviously, if they’re headquartered overseas in the relevant tax jurisdiction, and that relevant country will manage them in their own way.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a direct answer to the specific question just put — only NZ-headquartered entities are case managed — and adds the figure for foreign entities operating here. Leaves her follow-up about enforcement and intermediate parents untouched, so not a full engagement, but squarely addresses the central question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do they still have a case manager, even though they’re headquartered out of New Zealand?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Pillar 1 is another aspect where, again, a lot of this is through trying to get alignment across a number of countries. The reality is that hasn’t been reached in that regard.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific pillar 1 question Edmonds threw in and gives the substantive reason it is not progressing (no international alignment reached), so the answer would be different had she not asked it. Short of 1.0 because she asked specifically "when can we expect pillar 1 to have some form of agreement" and no timeframe is engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And probably, just throwing it in there, what about pillar 1?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: But then that does create a problem for New Zealand taxpayers because we are asking them, instead of being able to go to our own income tax legislation—so anyone who wants to look up tax law can go right now to www.legislation.govt.nz, and pull up the Income Tax Act and some of the associated papers and work out what the law is right now and how they have to apply it.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's efficiency rationale as a genuine solution and then disputes what it costs — the accessibility of the law to the taxpayers who must comply. The speech is built on the answer just given rather than indifferent to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s simply just driven by an efficiency mechanism and the efficiency of referencing back to the overarching rules and commentary that has been agreed" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: So I’m pleased to let the member know that the Inland Revenue Department will be providing the guidance and links to the OECD website, to the 25 entities that meet the criteria.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the exact thing asked for: who will point affected taxpayers to the law, by what means, and how many entities are involved. Directly answers the question just put rather than restating prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So where can New Zealand taxpayers find the information that they need in order to comply with these global anti-base erosion rules?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: So that’s kind of quite interesting because it’s interesting to know whether this case manager is assessing those organisations for their compliance with the law or giving advice to those organisations in terms of their compliance with the law.
acuity.explanation: Seizes on the specific detail the Minister had just volunteered — case management — and draws out a consequence he had not addressed, the assessor/adviser tension. This line of questioning exists only because of what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the 25 organisations that are headquartered in New Zealand that meet the definition of this are already case managed by Inland Revenue" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Following on from my questions to the Minister about the brightline test, which I am confident that he is working on and will soon provide me with answers to so that I can ask him about the amendments in clause 9, I would like to add one question to that, which is does the Minister intend to reintroduce, either in legislation or into Inland Revenue Department policy, the use of the intentions test?
acuity.explanation: Watts had just answered on IRD guidance, compliance burden and the hundred pages of the new rules; Williams engages none of that, instead resuming her own earlier line of questioning on the brightline test. It is squarely within the committee debate on this bill, so not a zero, but it would read identically whatever Watts had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "There's about a hundred pages of these rules, right? So it is a lot." — her turn does not take up the IRD guidance or compliance-capability argument at all, only her own prior questions.

acuity.statement: I can assure the member that we still have the intention test and, in effect, that rule is in play—that is in regards to the way in which the taxpayer and their intent in terms of what they do. Obviously, we’ve got a two-year brightline rule in place now, but that rule has not gone away as a result of the changes that we’ve proposed in regards to this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question put to him and corrects the premise it rested on: Williams asked whether he would reintroduce the intentions test, and he answers that it was never removed and remains in force alongside the two-year brightline rule. The reply is unmistakably shaped by her question and would be different had she asked something else; it is brief and imprecise about mechanism, but that is a specificity matter, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "does the Minister intend to reintroduce, either in legislation or into Inland Revenue Department policy, the use of the intentions test?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I would like to just pick up on where my colleague Arena Williams left off, to ask the Minister about, really, what are the policy objectives of the interest deductibility changes and the changes to the brightline test?
acuity.explanation: She names the preceding exchange and stays on the same clauses, but the reference is a pivot rather than an engagement: neither Williams' efficiency argument about the intentions test nor Watts' answer that the intention test remains in force is taken up, and she moves straight to her own prepared line on policy objectives, stakeholders and the Treasury RIS. A gesture at the debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "So if we were to return to an intentions test, that would represent a step backwards in terms of the efficiency of our overall tax system" — Leary cites Williams by name but does not take up this argument or the Minister's reply to it.

acuity.statement: So we’ve just heard a really interesting argument there, laboured by the Minister of Revenue at successive points throughout this debate tonight and by the Prime Minister and other members of the Government, and that is that the reason that we are currently debating this is because of the fact that it was taken to the election and, therefore, it has been widely consulted, and the Government has the mandate to just do carte blanche what it wants.
acuity.explanation: Watts had just argued that the consultation question was answered by the fact that the policy was campaigned on at the election. Swarbrick restates that exact inference, names it as the argument under examination, and then attacks it by pointing out the measure is arriving via an Amendment Paper at committee stage with no select committee scrutiny. The speech would have to change had Watts defended the process differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "the answer to the question in regards to what stakeholders were consulted in regards to this, is, in effect, the New Zealand public, because we actually campaigned on this as part of the election process"

acuity.statement: My second question on the point of the brightline test for residential land changes: has the Minister seen advice from Treasury which, and I quote, “considers it unlikely that landlords will pass on the tax change through lower rents in the short run as the stock of housing is fixed”? And could he please share that with the committee—that is, what evidence is being used to support claims that this clause will put downward pressure on rents if the stock of housing remains fixed?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific causal claim Watts had just made — that reducing cost burden will reduce upward pressure on rents — and confronts it with contrary Treasury advice, then demands the evidence base for it. This engages the content of the preceding turn rather than merely referring to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "it is our view that when we reduce cost burden out of the system, that will reduce upward pressure on rents"

acuity.statement: Goodness me, this is a large Act, and certainly makes the deliberations that we are making today complex, especially because, as others have mentioned, we are not in an urgency process but we are in a position of being in extended hours and we are in a position of having this substantial change to the taxation regime in New Zealand being brought about through an amendment that the Minister has put forward at committee stage, so there isn’t a lot of time to look at the scrutiny of this.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding turn — Swarbrick's argument that proceeding by Amendment Paper at committee stage denies proper scrutiny — and supports it from her own difficulty locating the relevant statutory definitions. It engages that process strand rather than the substance of Watts's consultation or rents claims, and the rest of the call is her own prepared questioning on the main home definition, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "we have not had the ability to have due scrutiny, as is usually applied to all legislation through that select committee process"

acuity.statement: No, the decision to keep the definition the same was the decision that we stuck by.
acuity.explanation: Belich interjects a direct question about whether the Government considered changing the "main home" definition, and Watts answers that exact question squarely — no, the definition was deliberately kept. The reply would be different had she asked anything else. (It is brief and unelaborated, but acuity scores engagement, not detail.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Yeah, did you think of changing it?"

acuity.statement: I think we’re going to have to settle in for quite a long night, because that’s just in the bill, and that’s leaving aside the Amendment Paper. And we’ve had quite a bit of discussion—already some discussion on the brightline test and on interest deductibility. Now, I want to talk on both those topics as well in due course.
acuity.explanation: Russell follows the Minister's substantive answers but engages no part of them; her turn is a stocktake of the eleven topics still to be covered in Part 2, which would read identically whatever Watts had said. The gesture at the debate — acknowledging there has been discussion on the brightline test and interest deductibility, and flagging she will return to both — keeps it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on the "main home" definition, the intention test catching speculators beyond two years, house-price uncertainty and the 1 April 2024 interest deductions, and this statement takes up none of those answers — it notes only that the topics have been discussed and defers them.

acuity.statement: I want to continue my questioning in relation to the global anti-base erosion (GloBE) rules, and, really, these are probably the last couple of questions I have in relation to that part of Part 2.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds explicitly resumes her own line of questioning rather than engaging the preceding speaker. Her questions on clause 71D binding rulings and penalty scaling are on the same part of the bill as Russell's GloBE question, so the turn is squarely on the matter under debate, but it engages no part of what Russell actually argued or asked and would be unchanged had Russell spoken on something else in Part 2.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just asked the Minister to explain the new term "fiscal year" in clause 44, new section HP 5, and how it differs from "tax year" and "income year"; this statement does not take that question up, and announces a continuation of the speaker's own prepared GloBE questioning.

acuity.statement: In regards to the member’s question around the capital gains aspect in regards to the interest deduction—I mean, in effect, what we’re doing here, in regards to allowing an interest deduction on residential property, is no different to what is allowed by someone that undertakes an interest deduction on a commercial property, which was allowed under the previous rules, or likewise for a farm, for example, that is a similar entity that may be funded proportionately by debt and equity. So, you know, what we are simply doing here is driving a degree of consistency in regards to the overall way the tax system is, so that allows that deduction to be taken. And I don’t think the point that the member’s noting, in terms of the inconsistency, is relevant.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific nexus/consistency argument about interest deductions against untaxed capital gains and answers it on its own terms, offering commercial property and farms as counter-examples of debt-funded assets that get a full deduction, and then naming and rejecting her inconsistency claim. He does not answer the narrower question of whether apportionment was considered, which keeps it short of a full 1.0, but the speech is plainly shaped by what Russell said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It goes to the consistency of the treatment of other expenses, which always have to have that nexus with income."

acuity.statement: I had some questions in regards to the proposal in here around the brightline test, and I note the Minister has touched on this a couple of times. But what is of concern is that I actually don’t think that it’s good enough for the Minister to simply say that we’re bringing it back to how things were originally.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's position — the restoration-of-prior-rules justification he has just been offering — and challenges its adequacy, then moves to his own prepared line of questioning on the brightline test and the Treasury advice rather than taking up Watts's commercial-property and farm comparison. Partial engagement: pointable, but aimed at the Minister's general rationale rather than the specific argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "So the inconsistency of that tax treatment is what this coalition Government are looking to resolve."

acuity.statement: Just responding to the member’s questions in regards to the Treasury advice, I mean, as the honourable member will know, there are circumstances where departments don’t always agree and they come from different perspectives in regards to the application and implementation of that policy. But as I’ve noted, I think on three occasions, in regards to questions on a similar matter in regards to this test, the intention rule will remain and does remain within the legislation. The point of the intention rule is to ensure that if it is the intent of the property speculator in order to develop that for the purposes of making a gain, then they will be captured, even if that period of time exceeds the two-year limit.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the question put — why Treasury's advice is being set aside — by saying departments differ in perspective, and then answers McAnulty's underlying worry about speculation by pointing to the intention rule as the mechanism that still captures speculators beyond two years. It does not engage Treasury's specific 20-year recommendation or the affordability reasoning behind it, so it falls short of a full rebuttal, but the reply would have been different had McAnulty raised something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "why on earth is he not only going in the other direction but absolutely dismissing the advice that Treasury, their own department"

acuity.statement: The simple reason—to the member’s question around, in effect, the ability for someone who is not disabled and why they can and can’t be in that—is that the rules are set up to ensure that non-disabled persons don’t, in effect, benefit from the exemption that we have provided.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific question about why the disabled beneficiary trust definition excludes non-disabled beneficiaries and gives the rationale (preventing non-disabled persons from capturing the exemption), after first restating the qualifying definition. Not full marks because the second half of her question — whether a disabled person's income from OTHER trusts could be taxed at the 33 percent rate — is left untouched. The reply would plainly have been different had she asked something else, so this sits well above the prepared-material band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "But why can we not have non-disabled people who are beneficiaries of that trust as well?"

acuity.statement: But in regards to the points raised by the member, there is no fiscal cost to the rollover relief, in the context that these aspects have already been considered as part of the broader baselines and therefore there’s no additional appropriation required.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the answer to the specific question Boyack put — the cost to the taxpayer — with a reason (already within baselines, no additional appropriation), and then goes on to give the plain-language definition of "rollover relief" she also asked for. He does not reach her questions about the extent of application to the Nelson event or the Auckland flood/Cyclone Gabrielle distinction, which keeps it short of 1.0, but the turn is shaped entirely by what she asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "I’m particularly keen just to find out more around what the cost of this will be for Government"

acuity.statement: The first is: has the Minister received advice that since the changes made in 2021 were made—being the extension of the brightline test to 10 years and interest deductibility—first-home buyers have significantly increased their share of the housing market at the expense of investors, and what was the effect of the Government’s support for rapid increase in housing supply in that period as compared to the effect of the rules change?
acuity.explanation: The Minister had just given answers on the definition of a fiscal year and on the binding rulings regime; this turn notes only that her earlier questions went unanswered and then puts a fresh set of questions, engaging no part of what he actually said. It is on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts answered 'the New Zealand Government’s fiscal year is from 1 July to 30 June' and a question on the binding rulings regime, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: But the first is actually about the tax treatment of people affected by the North Island floods. I can see that there has been a decision to extend the deadline until April of this year, and I’d like to ask the Minister whether he’s considered whether that’s actually long enough in the circumstances.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed turn by Arena Williams on brightline advice and first-home buyer market shares and takes up none of it, moving to an unrelated part of the bill with prepared questions. The speech would read identically whatever Williams had argued, though it is at least on the legislation before the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked whether the Minister 'received advice that since the changes made in 2021 were made' first-home buyers increased their market share, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much to the member Helen White for those questions. The member raises good points in regards to the implications and the uncertainty for those flood victims. The decision to extend to April was based on official advice, and we believe that that will provide the adequate amount of time for those matters to be dealt with.
acuity.explanation: Takes up her actual question — whether the April date is long enough — and answers it directly, saying the date rests on official advice and is believed adequate. He leaves her second strand (a generic rather than annual-bill solution) untouched, so this engages part rather than all of what was put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d like to ask the Minister whether he’s considered whether that’s actually long enough in the circumstances" — Helen White

acuity.statement: I think some of the aspects that the member Arena Williams noted are correct. What is challenging, though—and I think the member would also acknowledge that this is a complex system and there isn’t simply just one aspect at play here. But the other aspects at play also included, at that point, the Reserve Bank changes around to loan-to-value, there was also the implications in the changes around the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act legislation. So, while the member’s right to cite that there was some change in that, to definitively say that that’s the result of one aspect over another is hard to quantify.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific evidence just cited: concedes the figures and the direction of the shift, then contests the inference drawn from them. The reply would have to be written differently had Williams cited different data or made a different causal claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has he received advice about the Reserve Bank’s lending data showing that during the period between August 2014 and October 2017, first-home buyers’ share of total lending averaged 12 percent" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: My second question is: if it is, as he says, unclear whether the legislative changes in 2021 did not cause the number of property investors within the market to fall from the peak in 2021 down to 20 percent in 2019, then how will he continue on those factors in the legislative settings that provided for that slide in the proportion of property investors in the market?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own concession that causation is hard to quantify and presses its consequence for the policy he is proposing. The question is built on what he just said — though the sentence is garbled in delivery, which blunts how cleanly the point lands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "to definitively say that that’s the result of one aspect over another is hard to quantify" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I have some more questions on disability trusts—part of the extensive changes that were made to the trust rate rules, which we’re kind of working our way through, step by step.
acuity.explanation: Follows Edmonds' detailed brightline/rollover question and takes up no part of it, opening an unrelated strand on clause 39 and disabled beneficiaries. It is squarely on the bill under debate and gestures at the committee's step-by-step progress through the trust rate changes, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero: the contribution would have been word-for-word the same whatever Edmonds had asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "how does the rollover relief provisions which apply for a 10-year brightline, which are covered in the Amendment Paper that was introduced last year in 2023"

acuity.statement: So I can’t speak for the individual, in fact, but, as I said, the child disability allowance is the mechanism in which the Finance and Expenditure Committee assessed as the appropriate mechanism in order to deal with that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific gap Russell described — a disabled trust beneficiary who receives no Social Security allowance — and answers it on its own terms, naming the child disability allowance as the test the select committee settled on and pointing to distribution at the beneficiary's marginal rate as the alternative route. Not a full 1.0 because it does not engage her concrete counter-example of the ORS grant, which was the hinge of her point; whether the answer is adequate on the merits is a separate question from whether it engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "there must be other people with disabilities who are not receiving an allowance but who are, nevertheless, the beneficiaries of trusts set up for them"

acuity.statement: In regards to the questions around the brightline test—I think Rachel Boyack was asking in regards to the timing and the date aspects—it is technically possible that there may be individuals that are in receipt of a buy-out before 1 July 2024, which is when, in effect, the two-year rule will come in.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the commencement date Edmonds asked for and addresses her actual question — whether a pre-commencement buy-out stays caught by the 10-year test and how the rollover relief interacts with it. Engagement is clear and specific; it falls short of 1.0 because he misattributes the question to Rachel Boyack and does not step out each test's start dates as asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "at what point does the new two-year brightline test apply, and how does it apply to the North Island rollover events"

acuity.statement: Given that the Minister has not answered my first question on deceased estates, I will ask all of my questions on deceased estates now, and I hope we can deal with this swiftly.
acuity.explanation: Registers a specific omission in the Minister's immediately preceding answer and adapts her contribution to it by bundling her deceased-estates questions together. That is a real engagement with what was just said, but it engages the answer's coverage rather than any claim within it, and the three substantive questions that follow are prepared material that would have been put regardless — a partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "So just covering off that aspect." — his reply covered disability trusts and the brightline timing but not deceased estates

acuity.statement: The de minimis rule around $10,000 would, obviously, still apply as well, but it is the changes that have been noted, based on the official advice and whether it’s three or longer or less, three years is deemed to be an appropriate period of time.
acuity.explanation: Answers two of the three questions put to him in the turn immediately before: that the three-year period rests on official advice and was weighed against longer and shorter options, and that the $10,000 de minimis continues to apply to a deceased estate. The sentence could not have been delivered without her questions having been asked, which is the test; only the double-dipping characterisation is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "whether he’s had advice on that period applying in the bill as it is now" and "could it continue to get the lower rate if the trustee income was below $10,000?"

acuity.statement: I hope that the Minister of Revenue might, please, explain why the Government is prioritising these late changes to Government tax cuts for landlords and other relatively minor amendments instead of addressing more ways that tax amendments could prioritise more productive investment.
acuity.explanation: Follows a technical exchange on deceased-estate trust rates and engages none of it, pivoting to a prepared critique of the Government's overall tax priorities and property investment. It is loosely tied to the debate by referring to "these late changes" and the amendments before the committee, which lifts it off the floor, but the contribution is indifferent to what preceded it and would read identically after any other speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just explained the 33 percent rate and three-year window for deceased estates, and this statement does not take any part of that up

acuity.statement: Just quite quickly for the member, the Emergency Alliance is a group of existing charities, and, therefore, all of the individual members of that Emergency Alliance are already charities and, therefore, already have the status. So the simple fact, by virtue of that, deems them to be able to be captured and have benefits that have been analysed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question Leary put — why this charity received overseas donee status so quickly — and supplies a substantive reason (its constituent members are already registered charities holding the status), which is the crux of her puzzlement. It is squarely aimed at her question rather than prepared material, and the speech would differ had she asked about something else. Not 1.0 because it leaves untouched the other strands she explicitly listed: what advice was sought, what risk analysis was applied, and whether a precedent is set. Scored on engagement only — the brevity, vagueness and whether the answer is correct belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "why did the Government decide towards this particular donee status to the Emergency Alliance"

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell for the questions. Again, the Finance and Expenditure Committee, in its deliberations, did look at this matter as part of their considerations, and the amount of $100,000 has been set in the context of what is applicable to other penalties for other similar sized entities.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the two specific things Russell asked about clause 74: why the penalty was set at $100,000 (benchmarked against penalties for comparably sized entities, considered by the select committee) and the extent of the commissioner's discretion. He also engages her framing that $100,000 sounds large, arguing it must be big enough to register with a multinational. Short of 1.0 because her third strand — how the figure compares with penalties in other jurisdictions implementing the GLoBE rules — is not taken up at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I'd like to understand why we've gone for that amount of $100,000"

acuity.statement: Just in answer to the member’s question, the penalties regime and the discretion in terms of the time line afforded—not only in the 30-day aspect but also in the discretion around the commissioner—is also consistent with other penalties that apply to these entities. So it’s not inconsistent. That is how that works.
acuity.explanation: Watts takes up the specific strand Russell raised — the commissioner's discretion over the payment due date and the 30-day period — and answers it by locating the regime alongside comparable penalty provisions, then adds the 20-25 affected entities and IRD's significant-entities case management. It engages the question she actually asked rather than the topic at large, but stops short of the thing she pressed for: which circumstances would move the date off 30 days. Partial engagement, clearly pointable, hence mid-high rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "what would be the circumstances in which the commissioner might choose a different date?"

acuity.statement: I know this is in relation to section 139AAB of the Act, and it’s around the assessment of penalties for large multinational groups failing to meet country-by-country reporting requirements, which the Hon Dr Deborah Russell briefly touched on.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds picks up the same penalty provisions Russell had been working through and later refers back to "some commentary around the particular penalties and how much they are", so she is continuing an identified thread rather than reading unrelated prepared material. But she does not take up Watts' answer that the regime is consistent with other penalty regimes; she opens a fresh line on the disputes procedure under new section 94BB. One strand engaged, then new material — the mid band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "the amount specified by the Commissioner, which must not exceed $100,000"

acuity.statement: The other aspect to acknowledge is that, actually, these penalties, alongside any other penalties, can be disputed by a taxpayer, like any other assessment of tax. On that basis, we’re comfortable with the amendments.
acuity.explanation: This addresses the substance Edmonds put — whether and how an ultimate owner can challenge the commissioner's assessment — by asserting the ordinary disputes machinery applies. That is engagement with her actual question, not a pivot. It leaves her second question (what counts as "excessive") untouched and supplies no procedure, and the surrounding turn re-states the 30-day consistency point already made, so the engagement is partial. Note this is scored only for responsiveness: whether the answer is adequately precise is a different question and is not being graded here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "what is the procedure for them to be able to dispute that decision made by the commissioner in subsection (1)?"

acuity.statement: Now, I don’t think that’s an inherent contradiction or anything like that; there’ll be a reason for it. But what I would like the Minister to do is to give some explanation as to why, in Part 2, it’s by reference to the OECD, and, in Part 3, it is by putting the rules directly in our own legislation.
acuity.explanation: Russell does not engage any part of the Minister's answer on penalties, consistency or disputability — she abandons that line and opens a new one on why Part 2 incorporates the GloBE rules by reference to the OECD while Part 3 writes the administrative rules into domestic law. The speech is squarely on the bill under committee consideration and gestures at the state of the debate ("I admire the enthusiasm from the Government members"), so it is not indifferent to the chamber it sits in, but it would read identically whatever Watts had just said. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate: 0.3, not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts answered that the penalties can be disputed by a taxpayer like any other assessment of tax and that the regime is consistent with other penalty regimes, and this statement does not take up either point.

acuity.statement: I am looking forward to hearing the Minister of Revenue’s answers on some of these questions. We’ve raised two questions so far in which, hopefully, we’ll be getting an answer from the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Russell follows Edmonds's detailed question about interest and penalties on backdated ACC/MSD lump sums and acknowledges that questions are outstanding, but takes up no part of their content; she immediately moves to her own prepared clause 72 material on the multinational top-up tax. A gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the argument, so the bottom band applies.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "would interest and penalties apply for that new opinion or for that new assessment by the commissioner looking forward?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: The questions in regard to reassessment and the implications around penalties that could or may apply—well, obviously, in circumstances where a reassessment is undertaken, there is scope for the application of penalties if that reassessment derives a point of difference in which those penalties would be subject. So I don’t think that aspect is surprising.
acuity.explanation: This takes the precise question Edmonds put — whether interest and penalties bite if the Commissioner reopens an assessment of a backdated lump sum — and answers it directly, saying penalties are available where a reassessment produces a point of difference. The reply would be different had she asked something else. Marked below 1.0 because he does not engage her further point distinguishing the full-and-final MSD treatment from the four-year ACC averaging.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "would interest and penalties apply for that new opinion or for that new assessment by the commissioner looking forward?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: We covered penalties extensively last evening as well, but I’m happy to provide a little bit more context for the Hon Dr Deborah Russell in regard to the questions. I think it was in regard to clause 69, which is primarily around what that allows us in terms of the registration of those 20 to 25 entities. It ensures that they provide the appropriate level of reporting that allows the assessment of the tax. It also ensures that the appropriate information flows come from those entities to Inland Revenue in order to determine their taxable status. Overall, the purposes of that—again, consistent with other aspects of tax legislation—ensure that IRD can actually operationalise the implications of this legislation.
acuity.explanation: He names Russell and the general subject, but answers on clause 69 and the registration of 20 to 25 entities rather than the clause 72 question actually asked: why the multinational enterprise self-assesses when IRD case managers are involved, and how the assessment can be dated at the date the return is received. Addressing the topic while leaving the specific puzzle untouched is a mere reference, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s clause 72 that I want to have a look at... It inserts new section 92BA of the Income Tax Act" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, please bear with me because I wasn’t on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, but I did indicate last night that I was going to be asking a question about gift-exempt bodies, which is clause 66(4). And the proposed amendment would extend the definition of a gift-exempt body to include all charities registered under the Charities Act.
acuity.explanation: The contribution is squarely on the Part under debate, which keeps it out of the floor of the band, but it engages no part of the Minister's preceding answers — by her own account it is material she foreshadowed the night before and would have been delivered unchanged whatever he had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on reassessment penalties and on the registration of entities for the multinational top-up tax, and this statement does not take up either; Leary signals she is delivering a question flagged the previous night

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. To the member’s question, look, I acknowledge that the member is not sitting on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, but members within that member’s party do, and this aspect was heavily canvased as part of that select committee process. The select committee unanimously got to a position around that, and I don’t think there’s much more value for me to cover other aspects in that regard.
acuity.explanation: The reply is clearly shaped by Leary's speech — it picks up her own admission that she was not on the Finance and Expenditure Committee and answers the 'why was the whole subsection removed' strand by pointing to a unanimous select committee position. But it leaves her other questions untouched: what charities relying on the gift exemption do in the interim, the time frames for revisiting it, and whether submitters' recommendations will be followed. One strand engaged, the rest declined.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m interested to know why—it feels like, perhaps, the baby has been thrown out with the bath water—the Minister of Revenue and the select committee would throw the whole part out" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: What advice has he received in regard to the level of offshore gambling that is occurring? What is the projected revenue that he expects to receive as a result of this proposed duty?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the gambling-duty strand of Watts's opening and asks for the evidentiary basis behind the 'loophole' claim he had just made — the advice on scale and the revenue forecast. It engages one strand of the preceding turn rather than its reasoning, and reads as a prepared set of questions on a topic Watts raised, so it sits around the partial-engagement mark rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there is a loophole in which offshore gambling entities gain benefit, and we're looking to close that to level the playing field through this aspect of the legislation" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: In terms of the revenue assumptions, I’m happy to provide the exact figure: I think it was around $143 million or $153 million in regard to the overall gaming duty component, and there is an additional component in terms of what is forecasted around the introduction of the licensing regime.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific figure the preceding question asked for, and in the same turn works through McAnulty's other two questions (the limits of the advice on market size, and whether sports and racing are in scope). The turn would be entirely different had McAnulty asked something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What is the projected revenue that he expects to receive as a result of this proposed duty?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: I’m interested, in particular, in the forecast revenue that’s stated by the Minister, given that when this policy was announced prior to the election—and that is relevant to point out given that in numerous responses to Part 1, 2, and 3 during this committee stage last night, the Minister pointed to the fact that these elements were campaigned on as justification for not having a select committee process—the figures used pre-election were $180 million. So it’s interesting to note that the forecast revenue had reduced.
acuity.explanation: Takes the number the Minister had just given and does something with it: sets it against the pre-election figure to show the forecast has fallen, and ties that to the Minister's own mandate justification for skipping select committee. Directly built on the content of the answer immediately preceding it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think it was around $143 million or $153 million in regard to the overall gaming duty component" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Now, I know that the Minister will, quite clearly, say, “We took this to the election. We have the mandate to be able to do it.”, but, as members of the House quite clearly said a number of times yesterday, in order to make sure that you’ve covered all the bases, that you don’t have any unintended consequences, the public submissions process is quite important.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding exchange — the electoral-mandate justification Watts offered for the absence of scrutiny — and answers it with the unintended-consequences argument for public submissions. The rest of the turn then moves to a prepared line of questioning about the generic tax policy process and consultation that is largely indifferent to what Watts and McAnulty had just said, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "all sensible aspects of policy that were clearly articulated leading into the election process" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The Minister referred to some Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) public consultation that helped to inform these policy proposals, but my specific question was: for this particular new part, this new tax, who was consulted?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific defence — that DIA consulted in 2019 — and does something with it: accepts the consultation existed, then isolates the gap he himself conceded (the gaming duty was not formally consulted on) and presses for names and dates. The supplementary could not have been written without having heard his answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'there was consultation, and, you know, the previous Government will be aware that these are issues that were considered... so DIA did consultation in 2019.'

acuity.statement: I wish to ask some questions of the Minister of Revenue around how we’re going to ensure that this tax is actually paid—this new tax is paid. I just want to clarify a little bit as to why this question is important.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line of questioning on enforcement and detection. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the new offshore gambling duty — but engages no part of the preceding exchange on who was consulted, and would read identically whatever Edmonds or Watts had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds asked who was consulted on this particular new tax and demanded names and dates, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: What I can say is that in regards to the way in which we have come up with how this gaming duty will operate, it has been built and predicated on the GST model and the way in which that model operates for remote services and services, therefore, outside of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Answers the mechanism Russell actually asked about — how offshore operators are detected and made to pay — by naming GST registration as the proxy the duty is built on, and then supplying the $43 million GST take as evidence that the proxy works. He declines the 'unknown unknowns' strand rather than engaging it, which is why this is not a full 1.0, but the reply is clearly shaped by her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: 'how are we going to detect where these entities are operating from, and how are we going to get them to actually register?'

acuity.statement: Look, I take and hear the member’s concerns, but I go back to the point that I noted previously: the current state, the status quo, is that there is no regulation for these entities. There is a significant loophole. And the risks which the member has outlined have no ability to be mitigated by the way in which the jurisdiction deals with that currently.
acuity.explanation: Watts takes up the specific argument Tinetti made — that taxing offshore gambling without the regulatory framework risks increased harm — and answers it on its own terms: he contests her counterfactual by arguing the status quo is zero regulation, so the harms she lists are currently unmitigable, and then addresses her sequencing point directly with the phased duty-then-licensing order and the OECD comparison she challenged. The speech would be materially different had she argued something else; it is built around her strands. Marked down from 1.0 because he does not engage her strongest specific claim (that some OECD regulatory regimes increased gambling harm) nor answer the guarantee she asked for, and he closes on a generality about harm minimisation rather than the work programme she asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "In some of them, where they have put a regulatory framework in, offshore gambling has increased, and it has caused many societal problems and an increase in that." — and her demand to know when the regulatory framework with harm minimisation at its core will be in place before the duty takes effect on 1 July.

acuity.statement: The amendment that is being proposed here is to ensure that there is ability to get an exemption outside of that four year - time barred period, and this is consistent with what the member was referring to with the victims of sexual offences exemption as well. This is an amendment which is taxpayer-friendly. This drives a degree of consistency. The member is right to highlight the retrospective element of this, but, in this area and in these circumstances, we’re comfortable that the balance is in the right space in regards to providing the exemptions that are necessary for people to be able to ensure that they meet their obligations under the law.
acuity.explanation: Watts takes up two specific strands Leary raised — the retrospective element, which he names and concedes she is right to highlight, and the victims of sexual offences carve-out she called her most important question — and sets them against an explanation of what the four-year time bar currently does. The speech would clearly be different had she argued something else. But on the central strand he substitutes an assertion that the balance is right for an answer, and leaves her other specific questions (checks and balances on the commissioner, changed circumstances of the child, patchy incapacity, young fathers) untouched, so this is partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "But what really concerns me is the commissioner’s ability to cancel that exemption retrospectively."

acuity.statement: I am after a clarification from the Minister of Revenue there. He indicated that, at some point, there’s a potential for turnover to go from offshore to onshore operators. Could the Minister please clarify what he meant by that? Does he mean the proposed duty, or does he mean a possible regulatory framework that has been alluded to but not been put in place? Is it the duty or the possible framework that would lead, potentially, to onshore operators increasing turnover?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own just-stated proposition about turnover shifting onshore and presses on the precise mechanism, forcing a choice between the duty and an unenacted regulatory framework. The question could not have been asked of any other preceding speech; it is built entirely out of what Watts just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "the introduction of this gambling duty component to those offshore gambling operators will potentially look to increase the amount of gambling activity from offshore back through to those domestic providers"

acuity.statement: Yeah, the point of clarification to the member is that the introduction of the increased taxes on the offshore gambling operators will, in effect, potentially, make the New Zealand operators more competitive in regards to levelling of that playing field. As a result of that, we may expect to see some movement of gambling activity from those individuals that deal with offshore entities to domestic entities, because of that levelling up and the fact that the implication of the gaming duty on offshore operators, in effect, will, in part, allow domestic operators to be more competitive.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact disjunction put to him — it is the duty, via a levelling of the competitive playing field, not the mooted regulatory framework — and sets out the causal chain he relies on. Not quite 1.0 because he does not name or dispose of the regulatory-framework limb explicitly, but the specific question asked is what the answer is built around.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Is it the duty or the possible framework that would lead, potentially, to onshore operators increasing turnover?"

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, and thank you to the Minister of Revenue for that response. Could he please indicate to the committee how that response then correlates with the advice through the regulatory impact statement, which actually suggests that the duty being placed on some operators may actually lead to turnover being transferred from those registered operators that would be hit by the duty on to operators that are unlikely to comply?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer as given and confronts it directly with the departmental advice that points the opposite way — turnover shifting to non-compliant operators rather than onshore. This is the sharpest possible form of engagement: it uses the content of the reply just delivered as the premise of the next question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "we may expect to see some movement of gambling activity from those individuals that deal with offshore entities to domestic entities"

acuity.statement: Just as a brief break from gambling—I know that my colleagues have a lot more to ask about this new tax, but I want to direct the Minister of Revenue’s attention to something that is sitting in the original bill. But if we’re looking at the bill as reported back by the Finance and Expenditure Committee, I want to direct the Minister’s attention to clause 86—oh, it’s clause 86 on page 86, which is a happy coincidence.
acuity.explanation: The speech is about the same bill under committee consideration, so it is not wholly adrift, but it engages no part of the preceding exchange. It would have read identically whatever the Minister had answered McAnulty; the nod to "a brief break from gambling" is a reference to the topic, not engagement with any claim in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty had just put it to the Minister that the regulatory impact statement suggests the duty may push turnover towards non-compliant operators, and this statement does not take that up — it acknowledges the gambling exchange only to set it aside.

acuity.statement: The reality of this clause is primarily one around efficiency. The amendment allows Inland Revenue to communicate about deceased persons with KiwiSaver providers, and they may not otherwise have been made aware of. I don’t think anyone thinks that that isn’t a sensible thing. This was discussed by the select committee. The select committee didn’t propose any amendments in that regard.
acuity.explanation: He names the members and takes up the information-sharing strand they raised, offering a rationale (efficiency) and the select committee's silence on it — so he engages the topic and one part of the objection. But he answers none of the specific questions put: what information is reachable, whether the Privacy Commissioner advised, whether a Bill of Rights assessment was sought. Partial engagement that then falls back on "we are comfortable with where that has landed", so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has the Privacy Commissioner actually given him advice about that?" — Ingrid Leary (who also asked whether a New Zealand Bill of Rights Act assessment was done, and what information the commissioner can reach)

acuity.statement: We haven’t actually heard from the Minister around why we landed on 12 percent as the proposed rate for the duty. It was earlier referred to the Minister—to another question related but different—that we wanted to level the playing field and keep things consistent. The concern that I have around that is that this area is anything but consistent. If you look at the duty that is applied to profit on casinos, it’s 4 percent—that’s onshore, of course. If you look at the duty that’s applied to onshore pokie machines or gaming machines, that’s 20 percent. And so the proposed rate of 12 percent is inconsistent with either of the two online gambling areas that this proposed duty would cover.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the Minister's own stated justification — levelling the playing field and consistency — and turns it against the proposal with the competing domestic rates (4 percent casinos, 20 percent gaming machines, 10 percent consumption charge), which is precisely a rebuttal of the reasoning offered rather than a restatement of a prepared objection. Marked down from 1.0 because he addresses the general justification given across the Minister's answers rather than the specific move just made (the pointer to RIS sections 45 and 47).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The regulatory impact statement—sections 45 and 47, as have been highlighted by members—provides the overview and explanation in regards to the questions that have been raised." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The setting of the 12 percent rate was taken on the basis that the 12 percent in addition to the 15 percent GST takes us into the region of 25 percent and that 25 percent is assessed as the mid-point of what other like-minded countries in the OECD do in this similar area.
acuity.explanation: This supplies exactly the thing the previous turn demanded and said had not been given: the basis for the 12 percent figure, with the GST-inclusive 25 percent benchmark, the comparator countries and the RIS section that lists them. The speech could not have been delivered after a different turn. Held just below 1.0 because it answers the "why 12" question by reframing against OECD rates and leaves McAnulty's domestic-inconsistency point (4 percent versus 20 percent) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m keen to understand why they landed on 12." — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: Well, thank you very much, Madam Chair. Look, I appreciate the energy in regards to that contribution, but when the select committee reviewed the title of the bill, which actually was the title that was put on the bill by the prior Government, which we didn’t look to seek to change: the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill. I appreciate that is what it is, but we’re pretty happy with the title and the title being proposed does not align with the expectations.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one strand of Williams's contribution that is formally before the committee — her proposed retitling — and answers it with a counter-point (the existing title was set by her own former Government) plus the commencement-clause reference and the comparator countries asked for earlier. But it leaves untouched her substantive argument that the interest-deductibility amendment skews the market against first-home buyers and bypassed select committee, and expressly brushes it off as "the energy in regards to that contribution". Partial engagement, pointable at the title claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So this bill should change its name to the “Taxation (Punishment for First-home Buyers at the Expense of Landlords) Bill 2023”" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I want to develop the issue that was raised by the prior Labour Party speaker Arena Williams. Can the Minister confirm that in respect of these revisions to interest deductibility, the full nominal amount of an interest payment is going to be deductible, not just the real interest component.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker's argument and does something with it: converts her general claim about tax settings favouring investors into a specific, answerable question about nominal versus real interest deductibility, and reuses her retitling device to make the point. The speech would be different had Williams argued something else. Marked down from 1.0 because it passes over the Minister's intervening answer (that the title came from the previous Government) without engaging it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Instead, they have provided two changes in this bill that would fundamentally skew the market towards landlords and property investors, over and above first-home buyers." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Rents actually did not go up by further than inflation. That’s an interesting question from the Government member, because Nicola Willis keeps standing up in this House and saying rents went up. Well, they did, but they actually didn’t go up by more than inflation.
acuity.explanation: Answers the interjection head-on rather than ignoring or deflecting it: supplies the specific answer (rents rose, but not by more than inflation) and distinguishes it from the version he attributes to the Government. The reply exists only because of what was just put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What happened to rents?" — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: The second reason is, of course, around the information-sharing powers. Now, I raise this because I didn’t get a satisfactory answer from the Minister about this. Again, he didn’t respond to my question about whether the Privacy Commissioner had provided advice.
acuity.explanation: Disputes the Minister's claim to have dealt with the questions put to the committee by naming two he did not answer (the BORA vet on retrospectivity and the Privacy Commissioner's advice), which is a pointable engagement with his last turn. Beyond that it is her own prepared ground — the commissioner's new powers and section 220B — and it takes up nothing from Williams's or Parker's arguments on interest deductibility, so engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So that covers the questions that have been asked to date." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: While most of that was out of scope, the aspect in regards to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (BORA) vet that was noted by the member Ingrid Leary, I can assure the member—and I note that she wasn’t on the Finance and Expenditure Committee—there was a BORA vet undertaken for this bill and introduced as part of that, and there were no concerns that were raised in regards to that. The retrospective nature has been covered already, is a taxpayer-friendly aspect, and, basically, that’s as much as we need to talk about on that aspect.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific fact the previous speaker said she had not been given — that a BORA vet was done and raised no concerns — which is a direct answer to her question. Held below the top band because her second and equally specific complaint, the information-sharing powers under section 220B and the absence of Privacy Commissioner advice, is dismissed as "out of scope" rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I did ask a number of questions about whether a New Zealand Bill of Rights Act vet had been done, and what his analysis was on the retrospectivity" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: And that member on the other side likes to say we made it harder. Again, I’ll go back to the evidence that we had some of the highest consenting in the last six years.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds breaks off her prepared argument to take up Tim Costley's interjected claim directly, names it, and rebuts it with a specific counter-claim (consenting levels over the last six years) before pressing him to produce correlating data on interest deductibility. The passage only exists because of what he said, and would have to change if he had interjected differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You made it harder." — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: We’re in a really funny situation here because the bill as introduced was one which, as the previous speaker, the Hon Barbara Edmonds, has just alluded to, this side of the House actually supported at its first reading. We had a really constructive time at the Finance and Expenditure Committee as well, making changes that were roundly supported by all parties there, around particularly the de minimis changes and otherwise.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick explicitly picks up Edmonds's point that the opposition backed the bill as introduced and that the Amendment Paper changed their position, accepts it, and develops it into her own distinct argument about the select committee process being bypassed. It is genuine engagement with the preceding turn's central strand rather than a mere name-check, but it is agreement-and-extension and the bulk of the speech that follows (written questions, the costings unit, trickle-down) is prepared Green material that would have been delivered whatever Edmonds had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this side of the House will, therefore, not be supporting this bill ... When this bill was introduced, it was a good bill." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First in support of this bill. New Zealand First is committed to ensuring that our tax policies are equitable and transparent, and supportive of economic growth and social wellbeing. Our principles continue to prioritise for fairness with taxpayers, especially those who are affected by the natural disasters that we’ve previously seen.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party-position material on the right subject (the taxation bill) but engaging no part of the preceding speech. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson argued that removing interest deductibility was bad policy that put upward pressure on rents and that ACT campaigned to restore it, and this statement does not take any of it up.

Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "taxpayer school lunches" and "we have a responsibility to carefully spend that money" — Todd Stephenson, who claimed the coalition is cleaning up programmes Labour underfunded and will spend tax revenue appropriately.

acuity.statement: And there have been claims by this Government that this bill will benefit renters and that the benefits of the interest deductibility will transfer on to renters. And I can tell you that, excluding one flat that I’ve lived in for the better part of the last decade, whenever my rent has increased, it has had absolutely nothing to do with any improvements that that landlord had made to our flat.
acuity.explanation: Goes directly at the pass-through premise Stephenson used to justify the measure — that restoring deductibility reaches renters — and disputes it with her own tenancy history and, immediately after, Treasury's view. The speech would have to change if the preceding government speeches had defended the bill on different grounds. Short of 1.0 because she rebuts the claim as a general government position rather than taking up Stephenson's specific point that the 2021 removal was what drove rents up.

acuity.responding_to: "the previous Government was warned that this would lead to upward pressure on rents, and that is what occurred ... we’re delighted to be able to deliver this for landlords and renters alike" — Todd Stephenson.

acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "interest deductibility, which will put downward pressures on rents and not keep adding costs to landlords, which are then passed on to renters"

We are able to do that precisely because we build up our resources through taxation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the preceding speaker's cyclone rollover-relief example by name and turns it to a conclusion Wedd did not draw — that such relief is only possible because taxation builds up collective resources. Just short of 1.0 because it redirects into prepared material on the purpose of taxation.

acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "It’s about taking practical steps to ensuring that we are supporting the victims of the cyclone with tax relief"

acuity.statement: While the popular perception is that landlords own multiple rental properties and get big capital gains as a result, the bond data in New Zealand actually suggests this is not true, because although there are some large landlords, they were not the majority of landlords in New Zealand. But he answers the topic rather than Parker's specific claim — Parker's point was that rents rose more slowly than inflation and that rents track the marginal cost of new supply, and Brewer counters with a raw dollar figure without touching the inflation comparison or the supply argument, then returns to prepared material about mum and dad landlords. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the actual inference.

acuity.responding_to: "We heard from the other side that this would benefit tenants, because rents will go down. Every year, every quarter, since this change was made in 2021, inflation has been higher than the increase in rents." — David Parker

acuity.responding_to: "Total lending to first-home buyers averaged 12 percent between 2014 and 2017, and 29 percent went to investors. Since the law was changed, the share going to first-home buyers averaged 20 percent." — David Parker

acuity.statement: Our disability communities deserve better. She engages none of it, opening instead with prepared material on Whaikaha funding. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Seymour had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band; 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it is at least a critique of the Government whose performance is the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour spoke about Labour having 'run out of other people's money', employers and farmers being villainised, and the work of ACT ministers, and this statement does not take any of it up.

The passage would not exist, and would have to be different in content, had the interjection not been made. Scored short of 1.0 only because the engagement is with a one-line accusation rather than a developed argument, so there is less reasoning available to rebut.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I heard a member say, 'She's making it up.'" — Duncan Webb, relaying the interjection from the Government benches.

acuity.statement: I do want to acknowledge Nancy Lu, the previous speaker from the Government. It is a really hard decision to put your children into early childhood education (ECE), and I support the decision making that she had to make for her children, because, as a mother of eight, one of the most difficult things was making that decision as to whether I’d put them into ECE.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds takes up one strand of the speech she follows — Lu's account of deciding to enrol her daughter in ECE — and engages it directly with her own experience of the same decision and of 20 hours' free ECE. She does not engage Lu's policy argument (the OECD childcare-cost comparison, or the claim that FamilyBoost targets low- and middle-income families), and immediately afterwards returns to prepared material on the Budget Policy Statement. Partial, pointable engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: "That was the moment that I decided, no, my children, my child, my daughter Amber needs to go to ECE and learn how to communicate, learn how to socialise, learn how to be a good Kiwi child"

acuity.statement: The most abhorrent thing is that the Budget Policy Statement has been botched. For the first time in my public service history, there is no clear indication of what the operating allowance is for the Budget.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the Budget Policy Statement) but indifferent to what preceded it: this passage would be word-for-word identical whatever Lu had argued about FamilyBoost or childcare costs. Prepared critique on the right subject, so above the floor, but it engages no part of the preceding argument.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu argued that FamilyBoost delivers on National's mandate to reduce the cost of living and targets low- and middle-income families, and this statement does not take any part of that up
