It gets 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it is pitched at the Government's overall record, which is loosely the frame of the preceding turn's praise of that record. Scored purely on engagement: the force of her environmental critique, its accuracy and its politeness are other attributes' business.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Sam Uffindell spoke about tariff savings for kiwifruit, onion, apple and wine growers and the infrastructure needed to export them, and this statement does not take it up

The one responsive gesture in the turn — "Totally agree with Kieran McAnulty there" — points at a member whose turn is not in this window, so it cannot be scored. The speech is indifferent to what preceded it, which is the 0.1 band; his sharpness about Lee and the accuracy of the Newsroom and Herald reports he cites belong to other attributes.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham spoke about the repeal of environmental protections and the Government's fast-track legislation, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: A couple of questions have come through so far from members. The bill is in a better position, and the Government has agreed that there should be a lower plug-in hybrid rate. That is why we sent it to select committee, to test that issue, and Cabinet agreed that the rate should be $38. That issue arises by the fact that plug-in hybrids use both petrol and electricity, and the need to ensure that it is a fair approach towards how much those vehicles should pay. Ultimately, lots of other questions have been raised around fuel economy: charging infrastructure, other issues—fuel economy standards. Those aren’t relevant to the bill.
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. He takes up one strand Genter raised — the plug-in hybrid rate — and explains the $38 figure and its petrol/electricity rationale, and he expressly names the other strands she pressed (fuel economy standards, charging infrastructure) in order to rule them out of scope, which is a response rather than a non-sequitur. But he does not answer either of her actual questions: whether he consulted the joint industry group, or whether he will accept the 60 per 1,000 km EV rate. The bulk of the call is a prepared recitation of the bill's purpose that would read identically whoever had spoken before, so this sits at the middle of the band, not the top.

acuity.statement: I’d like to acknowledge that there was really good work done by the select committee over the issue of plug-in hybrids, and I’m not sure that a lot of people who are just ordinary people in the constituency would quite understand why that was important work. So I would ask the Minister to explain in his answers why there was, as I understand it, a double-whammy if we had not had that change, and how the balance has been struck in the work of the committee.
acuity.explanation: She takes the specific point Brown had just made — that plug-in hybrids pay on both petrol and electricity and the rate has to be made fair — and does something with it, naming it as the "double-whammy" and asking him to draw out how the balance was struck and why it matters to ordinary constituents. The speech would have to change had Brown not given that rationale. It stops short of 1.0 because she does not dispute or test his reasoning, and the surrounding material (whether buying an EV still makes economic sense) is her own prepared constituency question rather than engagement with his argument.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "That issue arises by the fact that plug-in hybrids use both petrol and electricity, and the need to ensure that it is a fair approach towards how much those vehicles should pay."

acuity.responding_to: "They only just opened Pūhoi to Warkworth—they announced it in 2008." — Julie Anne Genter

The claim she disputes is the one he made, not a substitute. Short of 1.0 because the engagement is one sentence inside a largely prepared case for public transport and she does not take apart his specific supports for it (the NZIER figure, the cancelled Roads of National Significance), so part of the speech would stand whatever he had argued. Scored purely on engagement: whether the 70-years-of-evidence claim is true is a veracity question and whether the inference holds is rigor, and neither moved this score.

acuity.responding_to: "If you want to create jobs, lift people out of poverty, and fix the housing challenges facing our wonderful electorate, we need to build the road." — Grant McCallum

acuity.explanation: Identifies which strand of Halbert's questioning he will take up and answers on the topic of the financial implications of the RUC, but answers the policy rationale rather than the specific thing asked — what modelling was done on the cumulative cost to Auckland families — and sets the rest aside as out of scope before returning to prepared justification.

acuity.statement: Yet I do see a little bit of hope, because, already, the Government has shown the ability to walk back bad policy by voting in select committee to reduce the road-user charge (RUC) for hybrids. So that was a great innovation; thank you, our colleagues in Labour.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "With road-user charges, it’s more complicated, and so you’ve got to have a system that is robust."

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "As the Minister has indicated, he’s expecting advice on that by the middle of the year and has made it clear to officials that he expects to be moving at pace on that issue as quickly as possible."

Short of 1.0 because it asserts the weight comparison rather than meeting Goldsmith's reasoning about why the single band was retained.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "there’s a variation, of course, between light vehicles and heavy vehicles and they pay a different rate, and that is a good system that is a good way to operate"

Maybe he did at a time that I missed, but I haven't heard the Minister reply to my original question about what consultation he undertook with the industry and whether he has considered a reduced road-user charge—RUC—rate for electric vehicles to ensure that we're not actively disincentivising purchasing new electric vehicles at a time when it's really important to meet our climate commitments.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "However, as has been outlined in my earlier replies, and also my second reading speech on this bill and my first reading speech, we sent it to select committee to test the logic and the evidence on that particular issue."

acuity.statement: The two questions are: what will the change in the rate of PHEVS save owners of PHEVS per annum on average? I appreciate that the Minister might not have an exact figure for different types of PHEVS and there is some variance in that, but I’m seeking to understand what an ordinary PHEV user can expect to save because of that. And, then, conversely, what does the change of rate from the $53 per 1,000 kilometres proposed in the original bill to the $38 per 1,000 kilometres in this current bill cost the land transport budget?
acuity.explanation: Williams takes up the specific justification Brown had just given for the reduced plug-in hybrid rate — the variance between PHEV batteries — explicitly conceding the variance point he made and then pressing the two quantities his answer left out: the per-owner saving and the fiscal cost of moving from $53 to $38 per 1,000 km. She also picks up his statement that moving all vehicles to RUC "will take more time" by noting there is no answer on when Cabinet will consider universal RUC. The questions would be different had Brown justified the rate change differently, which is the mark of genuine engagement rather than prepared material; it falls short of 1.0 because she does not contest his reasoning, only extend it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Simeon Brown: "Ultimately, that’s why we’ve reduced the plug-in hybrid rate, because there is a variance in that issue."

acuity.statement: This is a really short piece of legislation, and the Amendment Paper in my name is what I’d like to speak to today, but I’d just like to contextualise that Amendment Paper within the reason that we have this amendment bill before us.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Leary arguing for the Verrall storage amendment, but engages none of it — Swarbrick moves straight to her own prepared case for a review of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically whatever Leary had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary spoke about an Amendment Paper restoring safe-storage requirements for pseudoephedrine ("the current bill, in clause 9, removes any safe storage requirement for pseudoephedrine") and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Even though it was an incredibly short time for select committee to hear submissions and gather evidence around what the impact of this bill will have on communities, one of the points that I thought was really interesting is that there’s a proportion within New Zealand of people who have either complex drug and alcohol—a range of issues, that will take whatever’s going at the moment.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Swarbrick's preceding turn — that the select committee process was cut short — and endorses it, but does nothing further with Swarbrick's actual argument (that MODA's asymmetric classification machinery needs review). She then moves to her own prepared line of questioning to the Minister about addiction services. Partial engagement: pointable, but one strand only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the deeply truncated select committee process" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: I’m sure Customs aren’t soft on crime, but what would be soft on crime is a 6.5 percent cut to the Customs budget. That would be really soft on crime.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "The last Government was soft on crime."

acuity.statement: Let us not forget that the coordinated shoppers—the aunties that get together and who might be tools for supply of meth could come back into our community and then start cooking in their kāinga, and knowing the current social circumstances of many whānau who might be desperate in this drug space, could start cooking again in their kāinga, putting at risk both their whānau and also the wider community.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the pill-shopping and renewed-domestic-manufacture strand of the preceding Labour turn and extends it to a Tai Tokerau setting, which is a genuine partial engagement, but she then moves into prepared Green Party material on treatment and review that is indifferent to what Andersen argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "In the past, we did have instances of pill shopping, where you would see people go around and, I guess, do stand-over tactics to pharmacies in order to get the medicine."

acuity.statement: Now, I know that someone mentioned the register, so I would like the Minister, maybe, to give us a little bit more information, because I’m sure that he’s looked at these various aspects that are of concern to us. But the real-time register that we know that is used in Queensland—not a perfect system from what I understand, but it is something that could have been a starting point.
acuity.explanation: Takes the register question raised in the immediately preceding turn and does something with it — names an existing comparator scheme, concedes its limits, and converts the query into a specific demand on the Minister. Substitute a different concern for Lyndon's and this passage would have to change.

acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "I do worry about monitoring of access and if there will be a register established for the monitoring of the live sales"

acuity.statement: Ginny Andersen mentioned pharmacies and drug shopping. Again, not strictly part of this stage of considering the bill but, none the less, I think it’s pretty clear that the evidence that’s come through the Health Committee is such that people don’t believe it will be viable to manufacture methamphetamine in this way.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific concern put to him and answers its substance by denying the premise that domestic manufacture is viable, citing the select committee evidence. This is engagement with the content of the claim rather than a reference to the member who made it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "There is the potential, as outlined in the regulatory impact statement, that we could see changing domestic manufacture once this drug once again becomes more readily available."

acuity.statement: Hūhana Lyndon brought up, again, very interesting issues, but they’re not part of the legislation that we’re considering right now. The question is the drug counselling for those addicted; I think schemes like Te Ara Oranga are well worth funding, but that’s not what we’re considering as part of this legislation; that wasn’t what was agreed at the second reading of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the question asked and offers a view on the specific service she named, so he has plainly listened; but he engages only that one strand and then sets the rest aside on scope grounds rather than taking up the treatment-capacity argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "Can we increase access to services such as Te Ara Oranga and then also access across the country, referral services, and pathways for whānau affected, as well, to receive support?"

acuity.statement: I think Mr O’Connor would know that the police in their enforcement activities might well look for those kinds of things, but it would be wrong for the Parliament or the Government to tell them exactly what to do, because we just don’t direct the police in this country.
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes up O'Connor's specific ask — a monitoring regime over precursor sales such as red phosphorus — and answers it directly: police enforcement may well watch for those substances, but the Government will not direct police operationally, which is his reason for not legislating the monitoring regime O'Connor sought. He has also just restated O'Connor's homebake-heroin analogy in his own words and accepted the hypothetical, so the speech would plainly have been different had O'Connor argued something else. Marked slightly below 1.0 because he supplies the constitutional objection rather than engaging whether precursor-sales data could be monitored at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor: "Has the Minister considered the importance of ensuring that there is a monitoring regime so that by, for example, working out how much red phosphorus is being sold"

acuity.statement: Yeah, actually, that’s a good point. This Parliament is a war memorial, and we honour not just the Māori Battalion but all battalions that have fought for our safety and our freedom.
acuity.explanation: Campbell takes up Simpson's interjection directly, accepts the point and extends it, broadening the honouring of the Māori Battalion to all battalions. The words would not exist had Simpson not interjected, so the engagement is unambiguous and pointable. It falls short of 1.0 only because accepting an uncontested observation does less with the content than rebutting or developing an argument would.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Parliament is a war memorial as well." — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: Like other Opposition MPs, I’d like to welcome the National Party speakers to the right side of supporting this piece of legislation.

That is partial engagement: he answers the topic of unanimity rather than anything in the substance of Campbell's speech about modernising the regulatory systems, the scholarship fund or the Pacific Education Foundation, and then moves to prepared material about first-reading quotes. Scored on engagement only; the jibe at National's consistency is a Focus matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "All parties have indicated their support for this bill" — Hamish Campbell

acuity.statement: Also, I was not around when this bill was going through first reading nor select committee, but upon again reading the notes to, and the Hansard of, the first reading, I am glad to see that Minister Stanford is now in support of this bill. Particularly, I am delighted to hear that she said the “wonderful and amazing and talented young Māori” that she has met as part of the award ceremony. I’m hoping that this will change her mind from the stance that she took in the first reading, that this is not going to help the achievement and the root cause of some of Māori and Pasifika performance, as we have seen in the first reading.
acuity.explanation: Tinetti's one argumentative strand was that the now-government members derided this bill at first reading and should have come round to it. Xu-Nan takes that strand up and does something with it — he goes to the first-reading Hansard, names the Minister's earlier position on Māori and Pasifika achievement, and reads her current remarks as a change of mind. That is a real engagement with the preceding turn, not a mere echo (his opening 'echo what my predecessor also said' would on its own be 0.1). But it is one strand only: the rest of the speech is prepared material on the Ngarimu scholarships, the Pacific Education Foundation and uniform costs that would have been delivered whatever Tinetti had said. Half marks for partial engagement. Scored on engagement alone — whether his reading of Stanford's first-reading position is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the then Opposition members were quite scathing of this bill and didn’t seem to think that it did much at all" — Jan Tinetti

acuity.statement: I stand in support of the Regulatory Systems (Education) Amendment Bill. This is, essentially, an omnibus bill, and it’s essential that we have our education regulatory systems fit for purpose. So we definitely stand in support of this.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan's turn immediately before contained plainly engageable material — a costed claim about uniforms ranging from $80 to over $1,200, a call for the Government to legislate uniform funding for high-needs students, and an argument that funding sources for Māori and Pasifika must be determined by those communities. Trask takes up none of it, names no previous speaker, and delivers a clause-by-clause account of the bill that would read identically whoever had spoken before her. It is at least squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it off 0.0, but there is not even a gesture at the preceding contribution, so 0.1 rather than 0.3. Note this is not a quality judgement: her summary of the battalion and Pacific Education Foundation changes is accurate and on-policy — it simply is not responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that education should be a public good and free for all students and that the Government should legislate State funding for school uniforms for high-needs students, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: One of the things I’m enjoying about being a new parliamentarian is learning about all of these laws and pieces of legislation, many that I’ve never heard about. I’m very pleased to be speaking on this, because this is one that has educated me quite a lot.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one, so the statement is eligible, and the speech is explicitly constructed to be indifferent to them — she tells the House she has made notes she is going to share, and then shares them. What follows is a walk through the amended Acts and a statement of party principles; delete Xu-Nan's and Trask's turns and substitute any other argument on the bill and not a word would have to change. Still on the subject under debate, so not 0.0, and no gesture at any preceding contribution, so 0.1. The aside about heckling reacts to noise, not to the content of an argument, and so does not count as engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued for legislated State funding for school uniforms and Laura Trask spoke to the battalion board representation changes; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: I didn’t think I was going to get an opportunity, such was the passion of the chair of the Education and Workforce Committee, Katie Nimon, on matters relating, somewhat, adjunctly, tangentially to the subject matter of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Belich follows a long substantive turn by Nimon on the Ngarimu VC board position, the Pacific Education Foundation threshold and police vetting in childcare centres. She names Nimon and characterises her speech as tangential, but engages none of those claims — not the board seat argument, not the 1972 funding figure, not the vetting change. Per the rubric a mere reference to, or jibe about, the previous speaker is not engagement with its content. The speech is at least about the bill under debate, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 because there is a gesture at the preceding turn without taking up any part of its argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "On Friday, I was really privileged to join Minister Stanford in Gisborne to attend the Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarships awards." — Katie Nimon

acuity.statement: I want to come to the third part of this bill, which is around the addition of the police-vetting amendment. The amendment is to ensure that not only do all childcare workers in these part-time facilities have to be police-vetted but that they are police-vetted before being employed. I think, personally, that that’s quite a critical point.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows Belich, who argued that the police-vetting and early childhood education regulatory changes demonstrate the value of regulation and accused the coalition Government of a change of tone on it. His speech is prepared material on the same bill — maiden-speech reflections on the limits of government, board appointments, his own family's use of creche facilities, FamilyBoost, trademark protection of the Battalion name — and engages no part of her claim. The only gesture at the preceding side of the House is the glancing "As my colleague from the other side of the House referenced earlier" about clarity of ownership of the badge; the speech would read essentially identically had Belich said something else about the bill, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Of course people should go through a police check when they are looking after your children, even if it’s for a short period of time in a mall or a gym or other such location." — Bates reaches the same provision but takes up none of Belich's argument that coalition criticism of early childhood education regulation shows how important such regulations are.

acuity.statement: This bill's about ensuring legislation—some written in the mid-1900s—is still able to do the job that it was intended to do. This bill also takes an omnibus approach and makes changes not only to the Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarship Fund Act 1945 and the Pacific Education Foundation Act 1972 to ensure continued support for learning but also to the Ngarimu Act to clear up legal confusion over who can manage the use of the Māori Battalion’s names and emblems and to the Pacific Education Foundation.
acuity.explanation: Sosene's preceding turn argued the bill matters because of changing Pasifika demographics, the updated definition of an Aotearoa Pasifika person, and the $500-to-$10,000 expenditure change. Butterick engages none of that: he gives an independently prepared description of the bill's purpose and reach, followed by scholarship-recipient quotes. The speech is on the matter under debate and overlaps her topic (the omnibus approach, the Battalion legacy), but would read word-for-word the same whatever she had said, so it sits in the "prepared material on the right subject" band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "What the bill does is it’s an omnibus bill that brings together three Acts and two sets of regulations." — but this statement restates the omnibus structure as prepared material rather than taking up her argument about who benefits.

acuity.statement: It truly is an honour to be able to speak to this, and while I endorse all of the words across the House about the need for the modernisation, sadly, the modernisation wasn’t just brought about by the need to make sure that the trust can function in the modern environment, but, sadly, it was brought about because of the passing of the vast majority of the survivors of the 28th Māori Battalion.
acuity.explanation: Henare takes up the specific rationale Butterick (and Sosene before him) gave for the bill — that old legislation simply needs updating so it can still function — accepts it and then qualifies it with a different cause: the deaths of all but one of the Battalion's survivors meant the Māori Battalion trust could no longer administer itself. That is engaging the content of the preceding argument and doing something with it, not merely naming it. It falls short of 1.0 because he engages the generalised "words across the House" rather than a particular claim or figure of Butterick's, and then moves into his own prepared account of the trust's history and the Ōtara market example.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Butterick: "This bill’s about ensuring legislation—some written in the mid-1900s—is still able to do the job that it was intended to do."

acuity.statement: And as was acknowledged by the previous speaker, this Chamber recognises a lot of the battles that the Māori Battalion fought in. For example, we have El Alamein up behind us, Cassino along there. These were great battles.
acuity.explanation: McCallum follows Henare's substantive turn and takes up one strand of it — Henare's point about the battle names on the walls of the Chamber — and extends it with specific examples (El Alamein, Cassino), then later picks up Henare's Waitangi National Trust and Sir James Henare material. But he engages no argument as such; the bulk of the speech is prepared historical notes on the Māori Battalion read out, plus committee acknowledgements, which would have been delivered unchanged whatever Henare had said. Partial engagement that is pointable, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "As we look around the names on the walls of this whare, we remember the battles of the likes of Ngarimu VC, who died in the Tunisia campaign"

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Regulatory Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill, and as has been referenced by previous speakers, this is a tidy-up bill for the statutes and regulations, some of which have become redundant, and just fixing up some inaccuracies.

A short, on-subject prepared call with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson spoke about deemed value rates under the Fisheries Act and the taiapure consultation process, and this statement does not take either up.

He nods to what the House has 'already ascertained' but engages none of it, moving instead to the Government's red-tape message and the composition of the select committee. Prepared material squarely on the bill under debate, with a glance at the preceding discussion.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams described the bill as a housekeeping measure and acknowledged Rachel Brooking's contribution, and this statement does not take either up.

Engagement is real but affirming rather than doing new work on the claim, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: "Each change in the bill is small by itself, but collectively they will provide benefits across the primary sector."

acuity.statement: Yes, I mean, there’s not much more to say about this bill, except that it simply serves the purpose—as well described by the Minister, and my colleague Jo Luxton from Labour—of fixing and making minor amendments to multiple Acts, therefore lifting administrative burden and reducing the risk of legislative failure.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly adopts the characterisation the two preceding speakers gave the bill and restates its purpose in his own terms, adding the 'risk of legislative failure' rationale they had not stated. He engages their framing rather than any particular claim within it, and does not contest anything, so this sits at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd McClay: "This is a bill all about good regulatory practice and reducing regulatory burden, cutting red tape." (also Jo Luxton's "housekeeping bill" characterisation)

acuity.statement: This is a thing that we will support—that is, the Green Party, obviously—and we hope that the Minister finds it a productive process to be sending this legislation to the select committee and that that is what is done with future legislation by this Government to the relevant select committees.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific point Luxton had just made — that referring this bill to select committee is a departure from the Government's recent practice — and converts it into a hope that the practice continues for future bills. The sentence would have to change had she not raised select-committee process, which is the deciding test.

acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "actually sending it to the select committee where it will have its full process, which is something that we haven’t really seen a lot of from this current Government"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "will there be a replacement for the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill?"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Miles Anderson: "We’re all about detail over here." — and his preceding speech on the punctuation error that applied NAIT rules to wild cattle

Webb had made two engageable claims immediately before — that the Government was padding the order paper with its own uncontentious bill, and that Labour would nonetheless support it — and neither is acknowledged. The speech would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb had just argued the Government was "filibustering its own bill because they haven’t got enough work up their sleeve" while still offering Labour's support, and this statement does not take either point up

I just want to show everyone Damien O’Connor’s name on it, because, of course, it is a fine piece of work that the previous Government did to do all of this laser-focused stuff that everybody’s been talking about today, and I commend all those members for their deep interest in these pieces of legislation.

acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "As a Government, we are laser-focused on increasing productivity and growing the economy" and "Reducing regulatory burden and cutting red tape is a priority for this Government, and this bill delivers just that"

acuity.statement: Well, it is time to be aspirational for our food producers here in New Zealand. Our farmers and growers are the backbone of our economy and they drive productivity in this country. But for the past six years, there has been a war on our primary sector, with red tape, compliance, regulation—it’s been an avalanche.
acuity.explanation: The "past six years" framing glances at Brooking's claim that the previous Government authored this work, but it does not take that claim up — it neither contests the bill's provenance nor answers the point about select committee scrutiny. What follows is prepared constituency material on the right subject, so this is a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "it is a fine piece of work that the previous Government did to do all of this laser-focused stuff"

acuity.statement: He’s come to the House, he’s accepted the changes put by Opposition members in select committee, and I want to congratulate him on that and the way that he took on questions in the committee stage in a back and forth that really helped Opposition members engage with this work. Even though he cannot thank me for my contribution to his legislative programme, I can thank him.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the acknowledgement Brown had just made of Opposition support and the select committee process he described, and turns it back on him with a pointed aside about his grudging phrasing. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the last Government didn't do much, but I do acknowledge their support of this legislation thus far into the House"

And that is something that Opposition members grappled with in the committee stage and in the select committee room, and it’s something we would like to revisit with the Minister when he calls for support from across the House for the universal road-user charges regime.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific basis Brown gave for the plug-in hybrid discount — manufacturer fuel-efficiency figures, adjusted 20 to 30 to 50 percent — and disputes not the number but the rationale, arguing emissions incentives were left out of it. It then attaches a condition to the cross-House support Brown had just asked for in the same speech. Had Brown justified the discount differently, or not solicited support for the universal RUC regime, this passage would have to be rewritten.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The last Government consulted on a 20 percent rate reduction based upon what the manufacturers say the fuel efficiency of those vehicles is." — and "we look forward to receiving support from across the House as part of that reform"

acuity.statement: Now, it’s hypocritical, really, from this Government—to know that they’re lowering the class of this drug so it’s more accessible for medication during the winter wellness. This is just going to allow more things to come—increased crime. It’s another avenue for the ram raids to happen. Our pharmacists are telling us they don’t want to put it on their on their shelves. It’s not that they don’t want medication out there for our whānau to have access to, but it’s the risk that comes with the safety of their shops and of their staff by having it available.
acuity.explanation: Kemp takes up two specific strands of the speech that immediately preceded hers: Costello's claim that the winter/flu-season timing is ideal (Kemp turns the 'winter wellness' justification into the charge of hypocrisy) and Costello's claim that pharmacies that fear crime risk can simply choose not to stock the product (Kemp replies that pharmacists are telling her they do not want it on their shelves precisely because of the risk to staff and premises, i.e. that the 'option' is no answer). That is genuine engagement, and the speech would have to change if the previous turn had made different arguments. It is held to roughly the middle of the band because the remainder of the turn is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on methamphetamine harm that engages no part of Costello's reasoning about pseudoephedrine's diminished role in manufacture — and that reasoning, the core of the preceding turn, is left untouched. They are just things that people have, essentially, said are down to logical thinking or common sense or things that apparently we’ll just keep an eye on. So that doesn’t give me a huge amount of confidence.
acuity.explanation: Cheung had just claimed the bill strikes the right balance and listed safeguards — continued class 3 classification, unlawful mail importation, a face-to-face pharmacist transaction with recorded advice. McLellan takes that exact claim and does something with it: she concedes it is the theme of the reading, then rebuts it by pointing out that none of the asserted protective factors appears in the legislation itself, and that they amount to common sense and assurances to keep an eye on things. She also picks up Cheung's reliance on pharmacist feedback and submissions, holding that the pharmacy profession was 'just a small handful of people'. The speech would have had to be written differently had the preceding turn not advanced the safeguards argument.

So, when we talk about this medication, there are steps that need to be gone through for it to become methamphetamine or P. So the market drivers for people to do that, we believe, are probably not going to be a huge factor in increasing the supply of P in the community.
acuity.explanation: Most of the turn is prepared clinical material on barotrauma, nasal sprays and rhinitis medicamentosa that is indifferent to what preceded it. But the closing passage does take up one strand of McLellan's argument — the market-forces and diversion-risk question — and answers it by asserting the conversion steps make market drivers a small factor. It engages the topic of her risk claim rather than its substance: she distinguished rationality at the higher echelons of the trade from heavily addicted individual manufacturers, and Weenink's reply does not meet that distinction. A partial engagement one can point at, not a rebuttal of the specific claim.

acuity.statement: This notion of full and final Treaty settlements troubles us greatly because, like all settlements, the redress in these settlement bills will reflect only a fraction of the economic and social losses suffered by iwi because of Crown actions—perhaps 1 to 2 percent reparation; a tiny fraction and yet we stamp an obligation that that must mean the end of future claims prior to 1992. We, as te Pāti Kākāriki do not accept the principle of full and final Treaty settlement. We do, however, recognise that Ngāti Hei have determined that they wish to partake in this deed of settlement.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Henare's turn but engages no part of it — not the committee process, not the eleven submitters, not Labour's call for a speedy third reading. acuity.responding_to: "Treaty settlements are not full and final, they are just the beginning." — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

My experience is that no Treaty settlement really provides for full justice for the actions that the Crown had done in the past. These redresses and settlements are in part to acknowledge the injustice, but we know and acknowledge that it doesn’t go the full way to giving back all the land that was lost.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon's preceding turn asked repeatedly where the justice is for Ngāti Hei, given $8.5 million for 184 years of loss and whenua they must buy back. The speech would be materially different had Lyndon argued something else; not 1.0 only because he concedes rather than tests the specific redress figures she put up.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen set out Ngāti Hei's specific land losses (20,000 acres with no reserves, 93,000 acres taken 1870-1890, the 72-acre Ohinau Island taken for a lighthouse) and argued the $8.5 million redress 'is a mere drop in the bucket from what has been lost' — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The current Leader of the Opposition decided to begin his speech talking about choices, and is it any surprise when everyone behind him was sitting there thinking about choices: thinking first about a choice the New Zealand people made so definitively to boot them out, and then thinking about the choice they need to make in the coming months about who, in fact, should lead them into the future.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Hipkins' framing word "choices" but engages none of his content (landlord tax breaks, school lunches, border and health cuts); it repeats his word in order to pivot to speculation about Labour's leadership. A mere reference, not engagement — this opening would be unchanged whatever argument Hipkins had made, provided he used the word 'choices'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Fundamentally, governing is about choices, and when it comes to the choices that they are making, this Government has its priorities all wrong." — Chris Hipkins

acuity.statement: But, actually, that’s not the speech I came here to give. I came here to give a more serious speech: a requiem for the worker’s party, because, not content with delivering an intergenerational cost of living crisis to the working people of New Zealand, we now have a Labour Party whose reason for being, whose very reason for getting up in the morning, is to rail against tax relief for working people.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the topic Hipkins attacked — the Government's tax cuts — but recasts his specific claim about $2.9 billion for landlords as opposition to tax relief for workers generally, and then announces the speech she came to deliver. Topic engaged, specific claim not; prepared material resumes immediately.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They made the decision to prioritise that nearly $3 billion in tax breaks for landlords whilst considering cutting school lunches" — Chris Hipkins

acuity.statement: We will match that with targets, with accountability for the performance of our public services, with more police, and with rescuing the school lunch programme that they didn’t leave a dollar for.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the school lunches example Hipkins led with and disputes its premise with a counter-claim about the funding he left behind, rather than ignoring it. It is one clause inside an otherwise prepared speech, so the engagement is real but partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "let's start with the free and healthy school lunches, because the kids were here today, asking—" / "for the price of the tax cuts that they have given landlords, you could more than double the size of the free and healthy school lunches programme" — Chris Hipkins

acuity.statement: Over the last week and a half, New Zealanders of Myanmar descent have been asking why this Government has extended an invitation to representatives of one of the world’s most reviled regimes—the military junta that run Myanmar today—and why the Government has invited them to come to this country to take part in an intergovernmental meeting.
acuity.explanation: Twyford follows a substantive turn by Tanya Unkovich on ending vaccine mandates and the scope of a COVID-19 inquiry, which gave him arguments to engage (including her claim that the Labour-initiated royal commission is inadequate). He takes up none of it and opens a wholly prepared speech on a different subject. The only faint overlap is that both mention Winston Peters, which is a reference, not an engagement. The speech would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before, and could have been delivered on any sitting day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich spoke about ending vaccine mandates and establishing a full, wide-ranging independent inquiry into the COVID-19 response, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: One hundred days have been completed, the second hundred days are on their way, and this Government is determined to rebuild the economy, restore law and order, and actually deliver the public services in health and education that this country needs and deserves.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith follows Phil Twyford's detailed argument that the Government should refuse visas to Myanmar junta representatives — a direct criticism of his own Government with specific claims (4,800 civilians killed, 43 percent of territory held by the opposition, Helen Clark's warning) available to rebut or concede. He engages none of it and delivers prepared material on the Government's economic record and the previous Government's spending. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because a general-debate speech defending the Government's record gestures at the running contest over the Government's performance that the preceding turns also touched; there is no specific claim engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued the Government should refuse visas to representatives of the Myanmar military junta before the ASEAN dialogue meeting of 18 and 19 April, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Are you going to call them? That’s not Chlöe; it’s the independent climate commission.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific target Cameron had just named and corrects the attribution: the methane advice he is ridiculing as Green Party sermonising comes from the Climate Change Commission, and she challenges him to say whether he will dismiss that body too. The interjection would be impossible if Cameron had framed his complaint differently, which is the test. Short, but it carries a factual correction of the claim immediately preceding it rather than merely naming him as a target.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What of Megan Woods or Chlöe Swarbrick yesterday and today offering evangelical sermons of what farmers should do to farmers?" — Mark Cameron

acuity.statement: The Hon Paul Goldsmith talked about the previous Government turbocharging spending during COVID. Well, I would argue with Mr Goldsmith that that turbocharged spending saved businesses, saved lives, and saved livelihoods, and we make no apology on this side of the House for doing so by putting people first.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific characterisation made earlier in the debate ('turbocharging spending during COVID'), accepts the fact of the spending and disputes its evaluation directly. The sentence could not have been written without that prior claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the previous Government turbocharging spending during COVID' — Paul Goldsmith, as quoted by Luxton (his turn precedes this one in the same debate).

acuity.statement: I just want to begin my contribution by responding to a couple of the comments that were brought up today—in particular, the one from the New Zealand First member Tanya Unkovich, who talked quite a bit about the previous Government’s response to the COVID pandemic. Quite frankly, I found some of her comments absolutely sickening. When she questioned the efficacy of vaccination and the efficacy of other things that the Government put in place at the time to protect New Zealanders, I would ask that member: has she spoken to other members in the community?
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific strand of the earlier speech (questioning vaccine efficacy and the pandemic response) and takes it up directly, going on to answer it with first-hand accounts. Not a full 1.0 because the rebuttal shifts to anecdote rather than engaging the efficacy claim's own reasoning, and part of the reply is an expression of distaste rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich 'questioned the efficacy of vaccination' in her earlier contribution on the previous Government's COVID response, as reported by Luxton.

acuity.statement: Today I want to focus on some of the great things that are happening in West Coast - Tasman, and, as the newly elected electorate MP for West Coast – Tasman and formerly a list MP based there, I know it’s been tough.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn arguing that tax cuts are being funded by public-sector job losses, and takes up none of it. The speech is prepared electorate material on the general subject of the economy and would have been identical whoever spoke before and whatever they said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jo Luxton argued that 'Public servants are being stripped out and are losing their jobs purely to pay for tax cuts' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: So New Zealand First will not support this bill. Now, while we acknowledge the importance of environmental sustainability, the party is cautious about enshrining specific rights in legislation without considering the broader implications. New Zealand First believes that any right must be balanced with corresponding responsibilities and that the proposed amendment may not adequately address the complexities of environmental policy and decision making.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Simon Court attacking the bill in detail, but engages none of his claims: no reference to his trade-offs argument, his RMA/$1.3 billion consenting point, or his Australia comparison. It is a prepared recitation of the New Zealand First party position that would read word-for-word identically whoever had spoken before, though it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Court argued the bill revives a failed '1970s socks-and-sandal vision', that resource use lifted billions out of poverty, and that 'These are all trade-offs that James Shaw's bill would make impossible' — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The last Government did work really hard to address some of these issues with the very broken Resource Management Act. Everybody in the House agrees that the Resource Management Act was broken. It was both not doing what it needed to do for the environment and also not doing what it needed to do for an efficient economy.
acuity.explanation: Brooking follows Simmonds, whose central argument was that the existing regulatory framework is convoluted and expensive and that cutting compliance, not adding to it, is the answer. Brooking takes up that one strand — conceding the RMA was broken, then arguing the replacement with clear limits and targets was repealed by the current Government — so she engages the regulation argument rather than merely naming the other side. But it is partial: most of the speech is prepared material addressed to Shaw's speech ("it goes to what the member said in his speech, and I agree with all of that") and to a list of unrelated grievances (DOC jobs, farm plans, fast-track, genetic modification), and she does not take on Simmonds' specific claims about section 18A creating barriers to investment or the existing statutes already recognising environmental interests. Her other reference to the preceding turn — "I am disappointed about the National Party position" — is a bare mention that engages no content. Scored on engagement only; the accuracy of "everybody in the House agrees" and the quality of the inference are not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "The existing regulatory framework has grown excessively convoluted, complex, and expensive to implement, failing to deliver the outcomes that New Zealanders rightfully expect."

acuity.statement: In summary, we think that although there are great intentions and ideas behind this bill that we agree with on some level, the problems that can come from good intentions that aren’t implemented well should be something that the House is cautious of and that we guard against.
acuity.explanation: Williams's turn, immediately preceding, built its case on the tension between National's stated agreement with the bill's aims and its refusal to send it to select committee, and urged the opposing parties to change their minds. Weenink takes up one strand of that — she concedes the agreement in principle ("ideas behind this bill that we agree with on some level") and explains the implementation objection that separates the two, so the passage is not indifferent to what preceded it. But she does not engage Williams's actual argument that select committee is where those implementation risks would be tested, nor the expert-advice point Williams made about select committees; the rest of the speech is prepared party material aimed at earlier speakers (Brooking, MacLeod, Parker) rather than at Williams. Partial engagement, hence mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "This is a bill that the National Party MPs have, in speech after speech, said that they generally agree with."

acuity.statement: I wanted to acknowledge the former speaker, the Hon David Parker, with what he said about the fact that this diversity that we see across the House should be celebrated. That’s what MMP actually produces, diversity of ideas. I feel that this House is stronger because of it, because it’s the stretching of each other’s ideas and each other’s mindsets that actually provides the best possible decisions.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows Parker and explicitly takes up one strand of Parker's turn — the opening point that cross-party cooperation and civility in the House are worth celebrating — and does something with it, extending it into an argument that MMP's diversity of ideas produces better decisions and avoids groupthink. The speech would have to change if Parker had not made that remark. But it is the ceremonial strand, not Parker's substantive case (Onslow, the fast-track overrides of the Conservation and Wildlife Acts, the NPS for Freshwater Management, or the Bill of Rights Act placement question), none of which is engaged before MacLeod returns to his own prepared material. That is partial engagement: ~0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is fantastic to see our Parliament cooperating around a process step like this so that an important issue like this can be heard" — David Parker

acuity.statement: And the comment was that the environment today is worse than 10 years ago when you actually began in the House. My challenge to that is my experience of over 22 years in the Taranaki region as its chair of the regional council, which is I can point factually to some scientific evidence where we are making progress.
acuity.explanation: This is a direct challenge to the proposition that the environment has got worse, which is the topic Parker asserted in his preceding turn, and MacLeod supplies counter-evidence (regional council experience, Taranaki trend data, predator control, ring-plain farm work) rather than merely naming an opponent. Marked down from 1.0 because the specific comment he quotes back was made by a speaker whose turn is not in this window, and he does not take up Parker's actual claim about rivers and lakes or any of Parker's specific policy points — he answers the topic rather than the claim before him. Scored on engagement only; whether Taranaki trends generalise to New Zealand is a Rigor/Veracity question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We know that in New Zealand we have declining water quality in our rivers and lakes." — David Parker

acuity.statement: Our main point on this piece of legislation is that it presents itself in a member’s bill situation, where we don’t think it’s the right format or forum. We believe that this has been well canvassed and well argued over many years—one could argue 42 years, since 1982.
acuity.explanation: Brewer takes up the sponsor's actual ask — that the House refer the bill to select committee — and answers it directly with a reason for refusing (wrong vehicle, matter already exhausted over 42 years). It engages the procedural strand of Tuiono's case rather than his substantive arguments about fairness, the Privy Council ruling or the ageing elders, so it is a partial but pointable engagement, not a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So I ask for this House to send this bill to the select committee." — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: As we saw with the apology for the Dawn Raids, the Labour Government stepped up there, and also the sponsoring member, Teanau Tuiono, talked about Helen Clark’s apology in 2002. So previous Governments have had the will and done the thing.
acuity.explanation: Brewer picks up the specific historical examples Tuiono used (the Dawn Raids apology and Helen Clark's 2002 apology) and turns them against his conclusion: they show that where a Government has had the will it has acted, so the absence of action here reflects exhausted legal argument rather than neglect. The speech would have to change if Tuiono had cited different precedents.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The New Zealand administration was so appalling and so bad that Prime Minister Helen Clark had to apologise in 2002." — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: So I do find it very interesting that the member Cameron Brewer says that he doesn't want to retroactively reinstate citizenship for Samoans when it was retrospectively taken away from them.
acuity.explanation: Takes Brewer's own framing — his objection to acting retroactively — and turns it against him by pointing out the 1982 removal was itself retrospective. The sentence could not exist unless Brewer had made that specific argument; substitute a different objection and this line has to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "no, “retroactively” is the legal terminology—reinstating the citizenship of citizens affected by this Act sets a problematic precedent"

acuity.statement: There is no precedent being set when it is only being considered at select committee. That is where we get to consider the advice, the submissions from the community, and to hear from the legal experts.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the reasoning of Brewer's central objection — that referral would set a precedent — by distinguishing a select committee referral from a settled decision. Aimed squarely at the argument just made rather than at the speaker; marginally short of 1.0 because it answers the precedent point in general terms rather than engaging the four decades of precedent Brewer cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "sets a problematic precedent" / "for this to go to select committee at this stage, in a member’s bill format and forum, is not appropriate"

acuity.statement: We want to say that we do not see that that 1982 Act was about being racist, because if it was about being racist then we know that even in 1982 there were people from so many different parts of the world; the citizenships of all those people would have been revoked if it was based on race.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and substantive in its own right, but indifferent to the two speeches it follows — it rebuts a point from a letter rather than anything either preceding member put. Delete Brewer's and Sepuloni's turns and substitute different arguments and this passage would read identically, which places it in the prepared-material band; a 0.3 rather than 0.1 because it does address the historical rationale that is the live question in the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Sepuloni argued the 1982 Act was a retrospective, discriminatory removal of citizenship that the Dawn Raids apology obliges Parliament to address, and Brewer argued a precedent problem; this statement engages neither, answering instead a claim in the bill sponsor's circulated letter.

acuity.statement: I’m glad we—well, I want us to get to select committee. We should have a select committee on this—if we don’t, we are still saying we know what’s best for you. And that is simply not the truth.
acuity.explanation: Costello's turn made the select-committee stage the centre of her support for the bill, as the place for robust conversation and consideration of financial implications. Kapa-Kingi takes up that same strand and adds a condition to it — that the affected communities, not members of the House, must define the restorative action — so this part of her speech would read differently had the previous speaker not staked the case on the select committee process. But the engagement is partial: most of the speech is prepared historical material on the Dawn Raids and Pacific activism that is indifferent to what preceded it, and she does not touch Costello's specific points about fiscal implications or bipartisanship.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "that process should take place in select committee where we can hear fairly, calmly, and rationally from those who are affected"

acuity.statement: Today is a historical day because we have seen the Labour Party support the Greens, we have seen Te Pāti Māori support the Greens, we have seen the ACT Party support the Greens—never thought I’d see this day—and I’ve seen New Zealand First support the Greens, support the bill. And that is a historical day because today rights the wrongs of what happened in the 1980s.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds builds directly on the declarations of support given in the immediately preceding turns, naming New Zealand First and Te Pāti Māori specifically, and draws out a consequence from them — that the cross-party unanimity is itself what makes the day historic. The speech could not have been delivered in this form had the earlier speakers opposed the bill, which is the deciding test. It scores short of the top because she engages the fact of their positions rather than the substance of their arguments: she does not take up Costello's point about financial implications, nor Kapa-Kingi's claim that compensation remains outstanding, before moving to her own prepared material on Falema'i Lesa and the teaching of New Zealand history.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "That is why New Zealand First will be supporting this bill to select committee." (and Kapa-Kingi: "So I can stand in support of this bill")

acuity.statement: I want to call and challenge the National Government. I want to call on you because you need to reconsider your position for this bill.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford's preceding turn stated that his colleague Cameron Brewer had outlined the party's position, that the bill plainly has the support of the wider House, and that he looked forward to select committee discussion. Sosene's speech is almost entirely prepared material on the right subject — the 1929 Black Saturday shooting, the 48 years of New Zealand administration, thanks to colleagues. Her challenge to the National Government gestures at the governing party's stance rather than engaging the content of what Rutherford actually said (indeed he had just signalled support through to select committee). On-topic, unpointable engagement, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tom Rutherford said 'the bill has the support of the wider House' and spoke about which select committee it would go to, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: And I do want to acknowledge, you know, that it can be at times difficult to engage in a debate without getting too emotive and losing focus. You know, we talk about—and the member opposite mentioned—the wreath acknowledging Samoa. And on the one hand, I acknowledge that this was about opposing colonial rule and not wanting to put one country and their occupation and their rights of citizenship—but also the responsibilities that came with it—above another country. And yet, it was also done when New Zealand went in, in 1914, as was just mentioned—it was done without firing a shot; it was completely peaceful.
acuity.explanation: Costley takes the specific material from Sosene's immediately preceding turn — the memorial wreath bearing Samoa's name on the walls of the House, and her account of New Zealand's administration from 1914 — accepts part of it ('on the one hand, I acknowledge that this was about opposing colonial rule') and disputes the framing by adding that the 1914 entry was made without a shot being fired. The speech would have had to change if Sosene had argued something else about the colonial period; it is visibly built on what she said. Not a 1.0 only because the rebuttal partly pivots into a general plea against emotive debate rather than staying on her specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's the memorial wreath and ribbon of Samoa's name engraved in there." — Lemauga Lydia Sosene, who also said "The New Zealand administration was worse than the German administration of Samoa, 1900 to 1914"

acuity.statement: Now, as other speakers have said, this will not solve everything; this will not stop everybody. But man, it’s an improvement. And as others have also said, they’re surprised that these policies and procedures and requirements are not in place.
acuity.explanation: Kapa-Kingi's turn immediately before made exactly this concession-then-support argument: the amendments will not change circumstances for victims and will not prevent harm to tamariki here, but they aid prevention through increased monitoring. Brewer takes up that one strand — the bill is limited but worth doing anyway — and adds the point that it is surprising such requirements do not already exist. But he credits it only to 'other speakers' generically rather than engaging her specific claim about domestic versus international prevention, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on the bill's provisions, the select committee's unanimous amendments, and an attack on the Green Party's position, none of which Kapa-Kingi raised. One strand engaged, then back to prepared material: a partial engagement, not a rebuttal or a development of her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The amendments to this bill will not change circumstances for victims and their whānau, but it will aid" — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: As already mentioned, there is a register that already exists, which holds a record of a range of up-to-date personal information about registered child sex offenders living within the community. It is a tool to help police and corrections staff with the monitoring of people who have offended in the past, with the aim of preventing reoffending.
acuity.explanation: Unkovich follows a substantive turn by Trask in the same second-reading debate, so she is eligible. Her speech gestures at what came before ("As already mentioned") and is squarely on the matter under debate, but it engages no part of Trask's actual argument — notably Trask's specific challenge about the 48-hour threshold being a detection loophole, which Unkovich restates as a feature of the bill without addressing. The rest is prepared party material (NZ First's position, its reasons for support, a rhetorical turn on offenders' rights) that would read identically whoever had spoken before. That puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band: a glance at the debate, not an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Laura Trask argued "Some offenders may still choose to travel overseas for shorter periods to avoid detection" and urged extending the requirements to all registered sex offenders regardless of trip duration, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I echo the member Greg O’Connor’s view that, for the most part, the scary part is that offenders are often known to their victims. They are known, they exercise some authority or control or nearness—they are able to perpetuate their behaviour with people, sometimes their own family members, sometimes people that have been entrusted to their care.
acuity.explanation: Garcia picks up one strand of the immediately preceding speech — Andersen's point that offenders are usually known to the victim rather than strangers — and develops it (authority, control, nearness, family members, people entrusted to their care). He attributes it to O'Connor rather than to Andersen and then returns to prepared material describing the bill's clauses, so the engagement is partial rather than a direct taking-up of her argument, but the strand engaged is pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "many of these offenders are known to their victims. I just want to make that point." — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I acknowledge the Attorney-General’s report on the consistency, or lack thereof, of this amendment bill with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. There’s issues like the right of a person—in this case, a registered child sex offender—to benefit from the lesser penalty, and the issue of freedom from double jeopardy and retrospectivity. But these issues have been discussed in the past and were discussed recently by the current Justice Committee, and, indeed, we need to carefully balance these.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle's speech is prepared material squarely on the bill under debate — a clause-by-clause description of the reporting requirements and a moral case for them — and it does not take up any part of Williams' actual argument, which was about whether registers can be shown effective at a population level versus an individual level, and whether the Supreme Court's proportionality reasoning carries. The only pointable overlap is a gesture at the same Attorney-General report and the same lesser-penalty/retrospectivity concerns Williams had just worked through; Nakhle merely notes they exist and must be "carefully balance[d]" rather than engaging Williams' reasoning about them. Her one genuine engagement with another member (Kahurangi Carter's claim that the bill only captures convicted, known offenders) answers a turn that does not appear in this window. The speech would read essentially unchanged had Williams said something different about the same bill, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the gesture at the shared Attorney-General issues can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "there was an issue the Attorney-General identified that the stated evidence is limited as to the effectiveness of sex offender registers in improving public safety"

acuity.statement: I think, particularly, the way to work around having the provision of snacks and water goes a long way towards that, because it’s not just about how this bill can benefit businesses but how we can protect staff against intoxicated members of the public who, ultimately, would be engaging at wineries.
acuity.explanation: Takes up a specific strand of Arbuckle's preceding speech — the committee's added requirement to provide food and water, which Arbuckle justified as 'common sense' and as part of the business case — and does something with it, redirecting the rationale to protection of front-line staff rather than business benefit. It is a partial engagement: the rest of the speech is prepared material on harm minimisation, drug regulation and commending the select committee, and it does not touch Arbuckle's central argument about wineries giving away stock or the sample-size and scope points.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'The provision of having the snack food there is something, again, that is common sense. Having provisions of water, and giving people water and provisions of food, just makes sense.' — Jamie Arbuckle

acuity.statement: I think there are some worthwhile concerns that were raised around who could be caught up in this bill. I acknowledge that the Justice Committee, obviously, has made it really clear that some of the retailers that could be captured are not intended to be captured.
acuity.explanation: Engages the same definitional question Arbuckle had just addressed — whether the bill's definition adequately limits who may sell — and lands on a weaker conclusion than his, saying it will need watching and possibly further regulation rather than that it is settled. It engages the topic and the committee's treatment of it rather than Arbuckle's specific assertion that the definition gives enough ability to control who can sell, so it sits around the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'But I think that the definition gives enough ability to control who can sell and who can’t, and so that has also been well thought through, I believe, by the Justice Committee.' — Jamie Arbuckle

acuity.statement: We have a situation where—actually, as the former speaker from the Labour Party, the Hon Duncan Webb, was just outlining—there is actually a far broader point to be made. And while I wouldn’t use some of the language that he did to characterise this legislation—that being, in his own words, “snobbish”—it is the case that this House does tend to treat certain substances in far more highbrow ways than we do other substances.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of Webb's immediately preceding speech — his charge of snobbishness in singling out grape wine — names it in his own words, distances herself from his framing, and then generalises the point to other substances. The engagement is pointable and the speech would have had to change if Webb had argued something else; but she takes up only this strand, leaves his central objections (the tasting-anywhere loophole, the 35 millilitre serve) untouched, and pivots from there into prepared Green material on the Misuse of Drugs Act and medicinal cannabis. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Apart from the snobbishness of that, it’s actually—" (his argument that confining tastings to grape wine skews the market against brewers, cideries and fruit wineries)

acuity.statement: I’m looking forward to actually seeing some of those Amendment Papers from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb. I’d invite him and members of the Labour Party who have seemingly discussed this at great length to come and speak to us about some of those Amendment Papers, because we may be interested in supporting them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific thing Webb had just announced and does something with it — signals the Greens may support those amendments and invites him to bring them over. Clearly responsive to the content of the preceding turn rather than a mere reference to the speaker, so it sits above the 0.3 band; but it engages his procedural intention rather than the substance of any argument he made, so it is a partial engagement, not a rebuttal or a taking-up of his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Certainly, when we get to the committee stage, I’ll be putting in some Amendment Papers."

acuity.statement: I want to talk about the iwi for a little moment, because many people might not have heard of Uenuku, Tamakana, and Tamahaki. Actually, that’s one of the breaches of the Treaty by the Crown. The identity of this iwi is part of the grievance, in my opinion, and it’s really important that those names are heard in this Whare.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe follows Goldsmith's first-reading speech, which catalogued the Crown's breaches as land loss (public works, railway, national parks). Rurawhe takes up that strand and extends it — arguing the obscurity of the iwi's own names is itself a Treaty breach, i.e. a grievance Goldsmith's account did not include. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding argument rather than its specific claims; the rest of the speech is prepared personal and whakapapa material that would have been delivered whatever Goldsmith said. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Instead, the Crown did not uphold the promises it made, and Te Korowai o Wainuiārua have paid the price for our nation’s development."

acuity.statement: If there is not justice for Māori, there can be no legitimate place for tauiwi in these lands. We, as Te Pāti Kākāriki, stand by that principle of justice for Māori. We are not content with the idea of full and final settlements, I just want to say, but I want to salute you for your commitments, among other things, to this principle of healing that you speak of and acknowledge that it must be on the basis that the Crown does no more harm.
acuity.explanation: Adrian Rurawhe's immediately preceding turn made a specific point with content — that this settlement's cultural revitalisation redress is six times larger than the first such package, negotiated by Ngāti Apa. Abel engages no part of that: this is prepared Green Party principle (justice for Māori, opposition to full and final settlements, the Crown doing no more harm) that would read identically whatever Rurawhe had said. It is squarely about the matter under debate — this iwi, this settlement — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument to point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe spoke about the scale of the cultural revitalisation redress in this settlement ('This one is six times bigger') and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: We support full and fair and final Treaty settlements and are glad to stand absolutely in support of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Steve Abel, the immediately preceding speaker, volunteered that his party is 'not content with the idea of full and final settlements'. Cameron's closing position takes up that exact strand and states the opposite — support for full and final settlements — so the line is pointed at something actually said in the chamber. It is only a partial engagement: he asserts the contrary position without rebutting Abel's reasoning for it, and the rest of the speech is prepared historical material on the settlement that is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are not content with the idea of full and final settlements" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: It is our continued commitment to you, our whānau, our people, that Te Pāti Māori will unequivocally continue to fight for Te Tiriti o Waitangi in this House. As the only Tiriti-centric party, we will continue to hold this Government to account.
acuity.explanation: Kemp follows a substantive turn by Jones (support for the settlement, its fiscal modesty, its administrative complexity, acknowledgement of earlier Ministers), so she is eligible. Her speech is squarely about the matter under debate — the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua settlement, its history and the settlement process — which keeps her out of the 0.0/0.1 band, but it engages no part of Jones's argument: nothing here rebuts, qualifies or builds on the complexity/oversight point or the NZ First position, and the words would stand unchanged whichever member had spoken before. Prepared Te Pāti Māori material on the right subject, hence the top of the unresponsive band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones spoke about New Zealand First supporting the settlement, its complexity deriving from 'the many instruments that are in here', and the oversight burden it places on the claimant groups — and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to seek to give effect to certain matters contained in the deed of settlement signed on 29 July 2023 by the Crown and by Te Korowai o Wainuiārua.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows a substantive turn by Henare that made a pointed argument (election-time opposition to co-governance versus support for it in this bill, plus a warning against the Crown devolving its obligations to iwi).
