Bates's speech engages no part of that: it recites the bill's purpose, acknowledges the claimants and Ministers, and offers personal Whanganui connections. It is squarely on the matter under debate, and the gesture at prior speakers ('As has been already acknowledged', 'much of what has been said today') is a mere reference rather than engagement with content, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band. The speech would read identically whatever Henare had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that members of this House called co-governance between the Crown and Māori 'a bad thing' at the general election and now call the same arrangement in this bill 'a good approach', and warned the Government not to treat the settlement as passing the rugby ball to iwi — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I mihi to our Māori Affairs Committee chair, Dan Bidois, over there, and the former Ministers Andrew Little and Chris Finlayson, and Minister Goldsmith for us always being able to find a way through things, let common sense prevail, and let our people have the opportunity to develop.
acuity.explanation: Jackson follows a substantive turn by Bidois and names him, but the reference is purely a courtesy mihi — it engages none of the content of Bidois's speech (the adequacy of the financial redress, the select committee invitation). The rest of the turn is Jackson's own material on the week's mood, Shane Jones's earlier remarks and the te reo acknowledgment in the deed, and it would read word-for-word the same whatever Bidois had argued. Naming the previous speaker as a target of praise is a mere reference, which the rubric places at the bottom of the band rather than at 0.5. Not 0.0 because the speech is squarely on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Bidois spoke about the redress being 'a pittance for the amount of land that was confiscated' over 600,000 hectares, and about inviting submissions to the Māori Affairs Committee, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Treaty settlements are not just a gravy train for Māori; they honour redress for Māori, but they also provide huge economic, social, and wellbeing benefits for all, across communities, and, in this case, across the mighty Rangitīkei. They are a springboard for hope, progress, and prosperity.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, so it is eligible. Redmayne's passage rebuts an unnamed outside criticism ('gravy train') rather than anything said in the chamber before her; it does not engage Bidois's point about redress being inadequate to the confiscation, nor Jackson's point about the reo acknowledgment. The speech is entirely prepared material and would be identical whatever the two previous speakers had said. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is on the matter under debate and glances at the same future-focus theme Bidois raised, and rather than higher because no strand of either preceding argument is actually taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Bidois argued that 'no settlement can really address the actions that the Crown has made' and Willie Jackson argued the deed's te reo acknowledgment matters because such claims are 'challenged', and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: Through those meetings on our marae in Ngātiwai and then both in the tribal territories of Ngāti Paoa, agreements were made, and those agreements were based on a tikanga-led process.
acuity.explanation: Henare argued that overlapping interests in Tāmaki-makau-rau are best resolved by iwi sitting down as relatives under a tikanga-based approach rather than through the courts. Lyndon takes up that one strand directly, supplying a concrete instance of it from her own iwi's dealings with Ngāti Paoa (hui on Ngātiwai marae and in Ngāti Paoa territory, agreements reached on a tikanga-led basis, "Leave the Crown out and let us settle it as whanaunga"). She engages the strand rather than the whole argument, and the bulk of her speech is prepared material on Ngāti Paoa's historical and economic losses that would read identically whoever had spoken before — hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it isn’t the first desire of iwi to go to the court to settle it" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: When I look at some of the detail of the bill—and I won’t really go into too much because a lot of that has been traversed already—what I would like to speak to is: I’ve worked in a council in Auckland, and, during my time there, the Ngāti Paoa settlement was in select committee and the council was obviously involved with some of this land which has been returned to Ngāti Paoa.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft follows a substantive turn by Trask on the same bill, so she is eligible, but her speech engages no part of what Trask said. She gestures at the preceding debate — conceding the detail 'has been traversed already' — and then turns to wholly prepared material of her own (her Auckland Council service, Caulerpa mats, Mihingarangi Forbes's whakapapa). Substituting a different pro-settlement argument from Trask would not have required a word of this to change, which puts it in the low band; the explicit acknowledgement that others have covered the detail earns 0.3 rather than 0.1. Her later nod to Peeni Henare on overlapping Tāmaki interests is a reference to a turn outside this window and is in any case a mention rather than an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Laura Trask set out the Crown breaches acknowledged in the bill, the 1863 shelling of Pūkorokoro and the return of 12 sites plus $23.5 million of redress, and this statement does not take up any part of it.

acuity.statement: But, really, as has been spoken by others in the House, the deeper challenge to us as a nation is to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi through ongoing relationship and justice. This is not a thing that has a full stop at the end of it; this is a thing that must go on if we are to have a viable, a meaningful, and a legitimate society in this land.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Maipi-Clarke and takes up one specific strand of her argument — that a settlement is not an endpoint but the start of a continuing Tiriti obligation — restating it as "not a thing that has a full stop at the end of it" and drawing out its consequence for national legitimacy. He engages that claim rather than merely naming the speaker, but the bulk of his contribution is prepared historical material on the Hauraki Plains and kahikatea forests that would have been delivered whatever she had said, so this is partial engagement rather than a sustained reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Treaty settlements are not full and final; they are just the beginning for open doors for mokopuna like myself to come through." — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: These journeys are always tough. I was listening to Hana, and it’s really tough when one side of your family’s protesting and the other side of the family is negotiating the Treaty settlement, but that’s a reality for a lot of whānau Māori.
acuity.explanation: Jackson follows a substantive turn by Bidois that contained real argument available to engage — the select committee's grounds for transferring the Waiheke Station Trust assets, the removal of Wai 968, and the $24 million quantum. He engages none of it; his contribution is acknowledgement and personal reflection on the settlement process generally. He does gesture at the debate by naming earlier speakers (Hana, Jenny Marcroft) and picking up the theme of families split between protest and negotiation, but those turns are not in the window so the engagement cannot be pointed at, which caps the score in the 0.1–0.3 band. 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the speech is squarely on the bill before the House and does acknowledge others' contributions rather than being deliverable in any debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Bidois, the immediately preceding speaker, set out the select committee's reasons for rejecting the Ngāti Paoa Trust Board's submissions on the Waiheke Station Trust asset transfer ("we rejected their claim to do so under the grounds that") and the two Wai claim changes, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: E ai ki ngā kōrero a te mema o mua, ahakoa i te tinana āe rānei, i te wairua, i te tinana hoki nā te mea tēnei pire e pā ana ki te whai atu I te whakapūāwai o tō iwi, āe.
acuity.explanation: Fleming names the previous member and repeats her "in person or in spirit" formulation back, but that is a borrowed phrase rather than engagement with her argument — that confiscation takes the reo, the tikanga and the connection to whenua with the land, and that the Crown's errors and the mana of the water must be corrected. He then states he will not speak to the bill's details because previous members covered them, and turns to prepared personal recollection of the moana and motu. If Tangaere-Manuel had made a different argument on the same bill, this speech would read identically, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unengaged band; the explicit gesture at her words lifts it to 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Kua tae mai ā-tinana, ā, rātou kua tae mai ā-wairua" — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel

acuity.statement: But, as the previous speaker, the Hon Barbara Edmonds, spoke on the Guardians’ present use of the fund investment vehicles—and this is something that I would like to kind of point out, in particular—currently, the Guardians are able to use the FIVs, the fund investment vehicles, as a tool, as well as being able to acquire controlling interests in assets such as rural lands and real estate.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes up one specific strand of Edmonds' preceding turn — her description of the Guardians' existing use of fund investment vehicles to take controlling interests in rural land and real estate — and does something with it, arguing that this scope should have been steered toward productive rather than speculative investment and treating it as a missed select committee opportunity. But the engagement stops there: the bulk of the speech is prepared Green Party material (fossil fuel divestment, the Myanmar junta investments, keeping the superannuation age at 65, Māori and Pasifika life expectancy, the gender pay gap) that would read identically whatever Edmonds had said. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "they allowed for what are called “fund investment vehicles”, which could take a controlling interest in some entities, such as land, as I understand it, and some particular rural vehicles"

acuity.statement: I have to say, though, in response to Willie Jackson, I think we got played.
acuity.explanation: Stanford names the preceding speaker and takes up his specific characterisation of Efeso Collins as politically unsavvy, disputing it directly and then supplying her own evidence (Collins texting her about joining National, knowing how to play the game and stay connected across all parties). This strand of her speech could not have been delivered had Jackson not made that claim, which is the deciding test; the remainder is prepared tribute material, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "I didn't think he was that politically savvy, sometimes. That wasn't one of his great strengths."

acuity.statement: So I thank you here today for you coming to do what they call “restore the honour of the Crown”, though this is not a deed of settlement, in allowing us to acknowledge what happened at Ō-Rākau and that history. We cannot achieve that “E hoa”, that “haere mai”, that reciprocity, until we acknowledge what has happened in our history and what happens still today.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Henare in the same debate and picks up one strand of Henare's speech — that Māori history has been suppressed and that recording the Crown's wrongdoing matters for what is taught and acknowledged — restating it as a precondition for reciprocity. But he does not engage Henare's specific points (the warning about calls to 'balance' the history curriculum, the Ōrākau petition and its ten-year record, the call to expedite the bill to select committee), and the bulk of the speech is prepared historical narration of the Waikato invasion that would read identically after any other speaker on this bill. Partial engagement, pointable but thin.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "Our Māori history has been suppressed for a very long time." — and his delight that "the wrongdoings of the Crown will be recorded in this bill" and that this history be taught to children.

acuity.statement: We’re here today and the kaupapa of what we’re here for is to acknowledge the tūpuna and the ancestors who were lost in the great battle of Ō-Rākau—a brutal and tragic event. I’d like to tautoko what’s been said, of course, from across the House today about just how brutal that was.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows a substantive turn by Maipi-Clarke that recounted the invasion of Waikato, the odds at Ō-Rākau (300 against 1,500) and the 12,000 sq km confiscation. He gestures at it generically — endorsing that the battle was brutal — but takes up none of its content: he does not engage her figures (he gives his own, 300 versus 1,400, without reference to hers), her raupatu argument, or her account of the Crown's ultimatum. The speech is prepared commemorative and select-committee material that would read identically whatever she had said, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is at least an explicit gesture at the preceding contributions on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "Three hundred people to defend Ō-Rākau against 1,500 soldiers."

acuity.statement: I rise in support of this bill, the Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill, along with my colleagues both on this side of the House and around the House, and I’d like to just quickly encapsulate, in the short few moments I have, what the purpose of this bill is that we discuss here today.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn by Jackson that made a pointed political argument about the coalition Government's commitment to New Zealand's history and about the ACT Party. Her speech is on the matter under debate — the Ō-Rākau Remembrance Bill — but is entirely prepared material: a Mateparae quotation, a recital of the deed and the bill's purpose, then a personal anecdote. The only glance at Jackson's turn is the phrase "around the House", which gestures at the bipartisanship he mentioned without engaging his criticism. The speech would read identically had Jackson said something quite different, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band, nudged to 0.2 for that gesture.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued the coalition Government is taking "backwards steps" on this country's history and that talk of "balancing history" means not wanting to talk about Māori history, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: Kei te tautoko hoki au i ngā kōrero kua kōrerohia i tēnei ahiahi. Ki ngā kōrero, ki a ia, te koroua rawa atu o Aotearoa whānui, a Hōnore Willie Jackson, he pai ki te whakarongo i ngā kōrero a ngā pāti katoa i tēnei āhuatanga.
acuity.explanation: She names Jackson and takes up one specific strand of his turn — his point that this kind of kōrero is bipartisan and that he acknowledges all sides — endorsing it as good to hear the contributions of all parties. That is a pointable partial engagement, not merely naming him as a target. But it is endorsement rather than doing anything with the claim: she does not take up his sharper argument about the coalition Government's backwards steps or the ACT Party, and the rest of her speech is her own prepared mihi to the iwi and to Hana-Rawhiti. Partial engagement, slightly below the mid-point because the strand taken up is the least contested one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These types of kōrero that we have with regards to Treaty settlements and whatnot are very bipartisan, and I acknowledge that and I’ve always acknowledged all sides during this type of debate" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I just want to echo the sentiments of the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, the Hon Stuart Smith, and thank the Treasury and the Minister for her time in presenting to the committee. One of the things that we talked about, or we asked Treasury questions about, was their performance over the year.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds follows Smith in the same annual-review debate and refers to him by name, but the reference is courtesy only: she takes up none of his substance (the $9.4 billion deficit, structural deficits, or the Reserve Bank running the OCR alongside funding for lending). She moves straight to a separate strand — Treasury's self-reported performance and Te Tai Waiora — and her remarks would read identically had Smith argued something else about the review. On topic, prepared, engaging no part of the preceding argument, with a gesture at the debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "We started on 1 February with the Minister of Finance, the Hon Nicola Willis, who was before the Finance and Expenditure Committee with Dr Caralee McLiesh, the chief executive of Treasury, for 45 minutes."

acuity.statement: All of this leads me to this conclusion, which is: you can stamp your Budget with the word “wellbeing” as nicely as you like, and you can write as many pages of verbiage about wellbeing as you like, but if you don’t deliver low, stable inflation, fair tax, and effective spending, then none of that is worth the paper that it is written on.
acuity.explanation: Willis engages one strand of what was put to her — she attacks the premise that wellbeing reporting is the thing that matters, which is a direct answer to why she is not continuing the Te Tai Waiora approach — so the reply would have to change had Edmonds asked about something else. But she never supplies the specific thing asked for (the measures, the comparator, the statistics) and spends most of the turn on prepared material about the previous Government's spending and inflation. Partial engagement, hence ~0.5. Scored only on engagement: the quality of the inference and the attack on opponents belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "what is her plan for ensuring that there is robust quantitative evidence; what are the measures she will be using to compare to a previous measure of wellbeing"

acuity.statement: One of the questions that I have for the Minister in the chair is, given that climate change did not feature in this year’s Budget Policy Statement, I’m keen to know the extent to which climate change is going to be a focus for this Government.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Bishop on fast-track consenting, climate goals and productivity, but engages none of it: Woods turns to the Minister in the chair with a prepared line of questioning (Budget Policy Statement, the GIDI fund, megatonne figures from the emissions budgets). It is at least on the matter under debate — the Government's climate programme — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom; the speech would read identically had Bishop said something else about climate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop argued that fast-track consenting is needed to meet climate goals ("if we are serious about our climate goals—and we are a Government that is committed to that—we are going to need the fast-track consenting") and this statement does not take up any part of that argument

acuity.statement: If we were to take that member’s comments as a guide, you could measure how well someone was performing on climate change by how many times they used the phrase in a document. And that is actually how the members opposite chose to measure their performance as a Government, isn’t it?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific premise of Woods' question — that the absence of the phrase from the Budget Policy Statement shows a lack of commitment — and attacks that inference directly, then goes on to engage the second strand of her question (the axed decarbonisation fund) by defending the use of ETS revenue. The speech could not have been delivered against a different argument; it is built on the one just made. Scored on engagement only: whether the word-counting characterisation is a fair reading of Woods' point is a Rigor question, and the jibes at the former Minister are a Civility question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "given climate change did not feature once in the Budget Policy Statement" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: I’m pleased to hear the Minister in the chair talk about how committed her Government is to actually cutting emissions. So I’m keen to know, given Treasury’s reporting function on what we heard about, what will be the emissions reductions from electrifying New Zealand—in megatonnes?
acuity.explanation: Lifts the two things Willis had just asserted — commitment to 'actual emission reduction' and the electrification programme — and converts them into a single demand for the number that would test them. The question exists only because of the preceding answer; substitute a different defence and this turn would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our Government is committed to actual emission reduction achieved in an efficient way" and "to electrify New Zealand, which is about doubling the generation of renewable energy" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Has the Minister sought advice on what the emissions reductions will be and how many companies will switch from using fossil fuels as a source of fuel to electrification in the absence of there being complementary measures, which her Government has received advice on, that are necessary to achieve that?
acuity.explanation: Takes Willis's own answer — that the figure depends on who switches — and turns it back as the question: has advice been sought on how many will switch, and on the complementary measures needed to make them. This is the preceding reply being used as the premise of the follow-up, the clearest form of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that will depend on what users switch from other forms of energy generation to using electricity" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: The short answer to her question is that we have been advised that we are still on track to achieve the emission reduction for the first emission reduction plan, and we are soon to consult on our plan for the second emission-reduction period.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the question squarely — what advice has been received — but leaves the other two strands (a megatonne figure, and the gap left by cutting the decarbonisation fund) untouched, pivoting first to a complaint that the member has strayed from the financial statements. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band. That the answer is imprecise about quantities is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has the Minister sought advice on what the emissions reductions will be" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: To that effect, one of my many questions for the Minister, if we are able to engage in this back and forth—noticing that ahead of the May Budget, we have already seen that $2.9 billion tax cut for landlords or those tax deductibility changes—is: what consideration was made, if any, with reference particularly to that weight of importance on productivity, what kind of official work or otherwise was undertaken to ascertain what productivity gains may or may not be made as a result of that $2.9 billion policy decision?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the productivity strand of the Minister's stated Budget objectives and turns it into a specific question about a named policy, but is otherwise prepared material built from quoted documents rather than an engagement with the measurement list Willis had just set out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "Build a stronger, more productive economy that lifts real incomes and increases opportunities for New Zealanders."

acuity.statement: Well, the member may be of the view that it is proper for Ministers to engage in extensive policy analysis on policies that they have explicitly ruled out delivering on, in explicit contravention of the mandate they’ve been given by the New Zealand people, but on our side of the House, we don’t think that’s OK. So you should not be surprised to learn that we haven’t engaged in extensive analysis or research about the prospect of a capital gains tax. It’s long been our position that you don’t tax your way to prosperity.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand actually raised — the capital gains tax material Swarbrick quoted — and explains why no such analysis exists, but answers a question about CGT rather than the question put, which was about the $2.9 billion deductibility change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick, quoting Treasury: "We think that there would be merit in introducing one for a range of reasons"

acuity.statement: With all due respect to the Minister, I appreciate the kind of verbiage, as the case may be, on the issue of tax and productivity, but that, respectfully, was not my question. My question was about what work, if any, had been undertaken on the productivity gains that may be made as a result of the $2.9 billion package to return those tax deductibility rules to where they were prior to the decisions of the former Government.
acuity.explanation: Identifies precisely what the Minister answered instead, says so, and restates the unanswered question. The speech would be entirely different had Willis replied differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we haven’t engaged in extensive analysis or research about the prospect of a capital gains tax"

acuity.statement: I was about to say that I’d be forgiven for having missed the question because it was buried so deeply in the other stuff, but I think that I’m about to do it again, because it was similarly buried this time. I think the member’s question is: did I consider dumping a core election commitment that was also replicated in our coalition agreements? And the answer to that is, no, that wasn’t considered.
acuity.explanation: Restates the question put and gives it a direct answer, so the turn is shaped by what preceded it; the restatement reframes the question in the Minister's own terms, which is a reasoning problem rather than a failure to engage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "what work was undertaken to showcase that that $2.9 billion policy was going to result in a more productive economy?"

acuity.statement: I’m glad that we have it on the record that the Minister of Finance undertook no work whatsoever as to ascertain the productivity gains which she said is one of the core kind of things that she wants to get out of the office for our economy when it comes to delivering on an election promise solely for the sake of delivering on that election promise.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own concession from the immediately preceding turn and draws out its consequence against her stated priority, then builds the next question from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "and, again, the answer is no"

acuity.statement: I think it is a drag on productivity when New Zealand workers know that year after year, their Government is prepared to increase the tax they pay on their income by stealth, by allowing inflation to push them into ever higher tax brackets so that every hour they work, they are having to give away more of their money to the Government. There is very clear analysis that says that where marginal tax rates are too high, that is productivity-sapping.
acuity.explanation: Supplies an answer to the specific question asked — a mechanism by which the tax system bears on productivity — rather than pivoting away, though it reaches for the Government's own preferred tax argument instead of the property-tax settings under discussion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "what role does she think that the tax system has when it comes to getting more productivity out of our economy?"

acuity.statement: I get the, kind of, theatre of the House, but I am, I must say, a little bit gutted to see in some of that theatre from the Minister of Finance the personal attacks that were veiled in that contribution just then with regard to myself.
acuity.explanation: Clearly prompted by the preceding turn and points at what in it she is answering, but engages the Minister's manner rather than any part of her productivity or tax argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "the member has clearly found a new word and she’s excited by it"

acuity.statement: The Minister herself in her contributions raised the fast-track legislation, and to that I would say that we have put a number of parliamentary written questions particularly to the Minister of Climate Change in which he has said explicitly and on the record that he has not taken any specific advice whatsoever on climate change impacts of the fast-track legislation.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific example the Minister offered in an earlier turn of this exchange and turns it back with a countervailing fact about advice not sought, so the point exists only because of what Willis said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "I’d suggest that the member should be very interested in the fast-track consenting regime that this side of the House is establishing, which will significantly increase productivity."

acuity.statement: I thank the honourable member Dr Deborah Russell for her question. The Government’s goal, as we set out in the Budget Policy Statement, is to return the books to an operating balance before gains and losses surplus in the forecast period. The way that we will achieve that is through an ongoing programme of driving greater value for money for the amount of Government expenditure that already occurs.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the question's subject directly and supplies both a fiscal target (OBEGAL surplus within the forecast period) and the mechanism she says will deliver it, so the reply would read differently had Russell asked something else. But it engages only one strand: Russell's specific point was a structural mismatch between committed expenditure (superannuation and the like) and revenue, and the answer addresses the operating balance without taking up the revenue side or the committed-spending argument. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what plans the Minister has for ensuring that we have a sustainable structure to our public finance over a long term" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I do want to pursue this a little further, because the Minister seems to think that she can cut her way to sustainable public finances. But we are committed to about $30 billion of expenditure on health every year. That’s what health costs us every year. Education costs us about $20 billion a year.
acuity.explanation: Names the mechanism Willis had just offered — getting better value from existing spending — characterises it as cutting, and attacks it on its own terms by putting up the scale of expenditure that is already committed and cannot be trimmed away. The rebuttal is built from the answer just given; had Willis offered a revenue-side answer instead, this turn would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our Government is going to get better results out of the dollars that are already spent" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: It’s pretty interesting to hear the Minister of Finance there talking about some of the kind of sociological kind of surrounding issues or cultural issues when it comes to, particularly, the likes of educational achievement, for example. I’m just reflecting there on the cross-party piece of work out of the Education and Workforce Committee in, I believe, the last term of Parliament, particularly on school non-attendance. This cross-party piece of work delved through the evidence and had submissions from many members of the public, and it, basically, settled on the conclusion that the major issue that is driving school non-attendance in this country is inequality and poverty.
acuity.explanation: Willis had just argued that funding alone will not educate children and that what children need is structured literacy and to be attending school. Swarbrick takes that specific claim about attendance and does something with it — she supplies select committee evidence that attendance is driven by inequality and poverty, i.e. by the material conditions Willis's argument discounted, and adds the decile 1/decile 10 attendance gap. The speech would have to change if Willis had not made the attendance point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Actually, they need to be attending school." — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: The Minister also just said that working people pay the price. She was referring to that in the context of climate change, she was referring to that in the context of our tax system. As far as that goes, I just again want to reflect on a piece of work that has been undertaken by this Parliament particularly in the last term of Government, and that was the IRD’s high-wealth individuals report. That showed us that the top 311 families in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of average New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Willis's framing that it is hard-working people who pay for government spending and contests who actually bears the tax burden, citing the IRD high-wealth individuals report. It engages one strand of the preceding turn rather than its central contention about controlling spending, and then moves into prepared material on capital gains tax and the OECD, so it is a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "those who work hard for their money should only ever expect to pay more and more of it out the door to an ever hungrier Government" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Going back to some earlier questions to the Minister of Finance in relation to the Treasury work that they are doing in relation to measurements of productivity—in particular, in reference to the previous speaker David Seymour’s comments—Treasury did confirm under the annual review that they are going through a work stream in a project around the terms of units produced per worker.
acuity.explanation: She names the previous speaker and the shared subject of productivity, but engages none of the content of Seymour's argument — not the housing-supply claim, not the $3.2 billion figure, not the capital gains tax case. The reference is a hook into prepared questions about Treasury's units-per-worker work stream, and the question would read identically whatever Seymour had argued. A pointable gesture at the debate but no engagement with the argument, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "We're going to raise productivity, and, yes, we're also going to get more kids to school" — his speech on housing supply, the previous Government's $3.2 billion spend and a capital gains tax

acuity.statement: So the question is about productivity, and I am pleased to inform the member that the Treasury will actually very shortly be publishing a working paper on productivity and its analysis of what’s been going so badly wrong with productivity in the New Zealand economy in recent years.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what was put to her — the progress of the Treasury productivity work stream — and supplies a concrete step (a working paper to be published shortly). But Edmonds' actual question was what the measures would be, specifically units produced per worker and what else Parliament could hold the Government to account against, and none of that is addressed. Answers the topic rather than the specific claim, which is the ~0.5 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "My question to the Minister is: how is this work progressing?"

acuity.statement: It is right that the Government did cease the review that was undertaken by the prior Government, and we are currently looking at the mechanisms and opportunities in regards to ensuring that we can continue to ensure that that ETS market place is robust and credible.
acuity.explanation: Confirms the specific factual premise Woods put — that the ETS review was stopped — and then supplies the Government's position in its place, including that it does not plan significant ETS changes and will work outside the scheme instead. The answer would have to change if Woods had asked something else about climate policy. Slightly short of 1.0 because the time lines she explicitly asked for are deferred to "the months to come".
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "It's a work programme that was under way for part of the period that was under review in the annual review, but that work programme isn't continuing. I'd like to know what the Minister's plans and time lines are in terms of reform of the ETS."

acuity.statement: Emissions budget 1 is pretty much in order and on track. Emissions budget 2 has risks in regards to delivery, and that is something that we are monitoring through.
acuity.explanation: Goes budget by budget in answer to the gap Woods alleged, concedes delivery risk in emissions budget 2, and in the same passage meets her demand not to be told to wait until the end of the year by naming the emissions reduction plan two consultation in June. Engagement with the specific claim, not the topic. Not 1.0 because he does not contest or account for her 3 and 4 megatonne figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "given the hole that has been left in the emissions budgets by the mini-Budget in the year under review—3 megatonnes by the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund alone in emissions budget 2; 4 megatonnes in emissions budget 3"

acuity.statement: One of the questions was in regards to the complementary policies, and this Government has been very clear that we see that the emissions trading scheme will do the heavy lifting in regards to emissions reduction, but, in addition to the ETS, we are going to need to consider complementary policies that allow us to reduce gross domestic emissions.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Woods' specific question about replacement complementary measures, concedes the premise that the ETS alone is insufficient, and states the Government's position on mechanism; he then works through her other two questions (methane review, renewables advice from the Minister for Energy) in order. The speech would be materially different had Woods asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "the Climate Change Commission gave some very clear advice to the committee that the emissions trading scheme alone could not reach our targets, that there was a need for complementary measures"

acuity.statement: I’m not going to presuppose the outcome of that independent review, because the review hasn’t actually started.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the strand of Woods' question about the methane review and whether targets would change, supplying the status of the review rather than prepared material; it falls short of 1.0 because it does not take up her specific point that changing domestic targets would require legislative change, nor answer whether coalition discussions have occurred.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "I’m keen to get an update on that work, but also to understand if there is any plan to change either the domestic targets as a consequence of that review"

acuity.statement: I’m pleased to hear that this Government has acknowledged the climate crisis and is willing to do what is required.
acuity.explanation: A one-line nod to the preceding answer before a prepared set of asks about community energy funding, flax-roots adaptation and Warmer Kiwi Homes. On the matter under debate, but the speech would read identically whatever Watts had said in reply to Woods, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band with the gesture earning 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "we do acknowledge the need for complementary policies" — a gesture at it, but Willis takes up none of Watts' argument about mechanism, the "blank cheques" characterisation, or the claim that the repealed initiatives were "inconsequential"

acuity.statement: But the points that the member has raised in regards to empowering local communities or local groups or NGOs to take a leadership role in regards to the delivery and implementation of initiatives which make a genuine impact to achieve the outcomes that are required by that community is very much a value and principle in regards to this Government.
acuity.explanation: Engages the general strand of Willis' questions — local and community-led delivery — and accepts it as a principle, but answers none of the four specific asks (the $46 million community energy fund underspend, Te Arawa Lakes Trust's retrofits, expanding Warmer Kiwi Homes on the Otago model, fast-tracking the Community Energy Network), pivoting instead to the absence of a framework. Partial engagement that you can point at: 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "will the Minister expand that existing support—limited support—for those flax-roots resilience initiatives"

acuity.statement: In regards to the hydrogen component specifically, there is inclusion within the New Zealand First - National coalition agreement, aspects and commitments in regards to particularly progressing the hydrogen work in a broader sense, and that’s something that we are currently working our way through. I acknowledge that there is and was funding in place under the prior Government in regards to that, and we’re currently working through how that potentially flows through in regards to the commitments that we have in our coalition agreement, which is pretty clear in that space.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Woods raised — the Budget 2023 hydrogen contract-for-difference — names the funding she referred to, confirms it existed under the previous Government, and says where it now sits (the coalition agreement commitments). He goes on to address her renewables-modelling question and explicitly undertakes to come back on heavy freight, so the reply is shaped by what she asked rather than prepared material. Not 1.0 because he supplies no answer to the actual question of what advice he has received, and the key quantification request is deflected to "under review". Vagueness is a specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "whether he has had any advice from his officials in terms of the hydrogen initiative that was funded through Budget 2023, the contract for difference"

acuity.statement: I do want to reiterate my colleague’s point that we spent a lot of time on workforce, and I do recall one of the answers to questions about Health New Zealand performance raised by a committee member was that it is the workforce which is the major limit on the health system’s ability to meet its targets at present. So, in that light, I’d like to start with questions on the health workforce.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the workforce strand Uffindell reported on, accepts it, sharpens it into the proposition that workforce is the binding constraint on meeting targets, and uses that as the basis for a specific question on nursing training placements. Her line of questioning would have had to change had the chair's report emphasised something else. Short of 1.0 because she builds on his point rather than engaging any particular figure or disputed claim in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Sam Uffindell: "We have significant concerns in the workforce area." and "We have nursing shortages, and there are acute shortages there, as well as GP shortages."

acuity.statement: Just in support of my colleague, my first line of questioning to the Minister of Health is also very similar, in the vein of workforce. The committee heard, with respect to Māori health outcomes, the plan to stick to Whakamaua, its principles, its pillars in Whakamaua, and how strong it was.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — he explicitly aligns his questioning with the workforce theme Verrall had just opened — then moves to his own prepared material on Whakamaua and Māori workforce targets without taking up her specific claim about domestic nurse training placements. Topic-level engagement that is pointable, which is the middle of the band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "So, in that light, I’d like to start with questions on the health workforce."

acuity.statement: I thank the Minister of Health for that high-level answer. Of course, we are still waiting for the very important information on whether or not nursing placements have been increased so we can increase our domestic pipeline of nurses being trained here.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's just-delivered answer on the health workforce plan, names precisely what it failed to supply (whether nursing placements were increased), and then presses a further specific point (mental health nursing vacancies against the hiring freeze). The speech could not have been given unchanged after a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the health workforce plan, which is due for renewal, has been the template and is the template that I'm still currently working with" — Shane Reti

acuity.statement: In particular, Te Whatu Ora is required, through te Pae Ora legislation, to enable Māori to exercise authority over Māori health in accordance with Māori philosophies, values, and practices. So my question for the Minister is: how did Te Whatu Ora enable Māori to exercise their authority over Māori health in accordance with Māori philosophies, values, and practices?
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the right subject — Māori health in the year under review, which the Minister had just reported on — but they engage no part of either preceding turn: not Reti's claim that Whakamaua implementation is on track, nor Verrall's nursing argument. There is a gesture at the matter under debate and nothing more.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Overall, the ministry believes that the implementation of Whakamaua is on track." — Shane Reti; the topic is shared but the claim is not taken up

acuity.statement: Yes, I can confirm that mental health nurses are continuing to be recruited under international recruitment plans, and that nursing placements are determined by tertiary institutes.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the confirmation Verrall asked for on mental health nursing recruitment and answers her outstanding point about nursing placements. It does not engage the 'despite the hiring freeze' element of the question, nor Lyndon's questions, so it stops short of full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can the Minister confirm that recruitment to nursing mental health vacancies is continuing, despite the hiring freeze at Te Whatu Ora?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The issue here is that one of the benefits of having Te Whatu Ora, our largest employer in the country, being able to flex its muscle when it comes to getting what it needs out of the education sector was the opportunity to turn around to the Tertiary Education Commission and local training organisations and to say, “This is what your community, your country needs.”, and we did that work in 2023.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the specific proposition in the Minister's answer — that placements are a matter for tertiary institutes — by arguing Te Whatu Ora's scale lets it drive the Tertiary Education Commission and training providers instead. The reply exists only because of what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "nursing placements are determined by tertiary institutes" — Shane Reti

acuity.statement: First of all, I’m on record as saying that I believe that what we should be doing, and the ambition we should have for our health workforce, is to grow our own homegrown, culturally competent doctors and nurses.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually put — whether international recruitment should continue at volume or give way to domestic training — by stating his own position on homegrown training and then setting out his cautions about internationally qualified nurses' suitability and the risk of squeezing out domestic supply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is his view that that is an avenue that needs to continue at its current volume, or should we be switching to a greater focus on domestic training?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I had a couple of questions for the Minister of Health, and one was around the growing wait-list for first specialist assessments and how can he explain that.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the health year under review) but engages nothing that preceded it — it opens two fresh topics, wait-lists and immunisation, and would read identically whatever the last several turns had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Reti spoke about internationally qualified nurses, the Green List residency pathway and domestic training, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: To address that question, I will anticipate clustering a few of the themes and then I’ll pass them all in one to the appropriate delegated Associate Minister, who, to address that question, will look as to whether the period is in scope, what the Gumboot Friday initiative was, how that sat, if at all, in that period of scope, and then will answer your procurement and monitoring questions.
acuity.explanation: Follows Leary's substantive set of questions and demonstrably takes up their content — it names the procurement and monitoring strands and the question of whether Gumboot Friday falls inside the review period — but does nothing with them beyond routing them to an Associate Minister. The reply would differ if Leary had asked about something else, so it is engaged, yet no part of the argument is actually answered: partial engagement, not full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "So my questions to the Minister, really, are: what procurement process took place? What are the clinical standards assurances of the Gumboot Friday programme? What monitoring and evaluation system is in place?"

acuity.statement: I want to ask a question about hospital doctors. We noted that there had been, as the House had discussed earlier in the day, a more modest increase in filling doctor vacancies—both specialist and resident medical officers—during the year under review.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Reti's preceding turn made substantive claims about Te Aka Whai Ora's functions, Iwi-Māori Partnership Boards and the 31 inquiry recommendations. This opening engages none of it and opens a fresh, prepared line on the medical workforce. It is squarely about the matter under scrutiny (the health annual review), so it sits in the low band rather than at zero, but it would read identically whatever Reti had just said. Note this is a debate-turn judgement only: the quality and precision of her own questions are not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Reti spoke about the Te Aka Whai Ora transfer, whānau voice through IMPBs and the 31 recommendations of the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee inquiry, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: To address that member’s questions, certainly, anything coming up in Budget time is Budget sensitive, and I have no intention of discussing that. I can reassure her that, as of today, the pay equity contingency remains. It is unchanged.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the answer to the specific question just put — whether the care and support worker pay equity contingency still exists or has been returned to the centre — and states it has not. That is engagement with the content, not a mere reference. It falls short of 1.0 because Verrall's first and longer question, on whether the hiring freeze trades long-term sustainability for this year's Budget, is set aside as Budget sensitive rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "does there continue to be a contingency for settling that claim, or has that contingency been returned to the centre?"

acuity.statement: Just a couple of things, and you have been commenting—again, I’m sort of flipping from what you’re saying today, but looking at the last couple of years, for example, in hospitals and communities, where the after-hours services are being challenged and CEOs are going back to Te Whatu Ora to look at solutions.
acuity.explanation: Reti's preceding turn made specific claims about deteriorating first specialist assessments, surgical wait-lists and ED six-hour performance over the review period. This gestures at the fact that he has been speaking ("I'm sort of flipping from what you're saying today") but takes up none of those claims, moving instead to her own prepared questions on after-hours services and local iwi partnership. A gesture at the debate without engagement of its content earns the top of the low band, not a 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Reti had just reported that "the number of patients waiting longer than four months for treatment has increased" and that ED stays under six hours had decreased, and this statement does not take those figures up.

acuity.statement: I’ll come back to the member Debbie Ngarewa-Packer on regional health outcomes and the monitoring in a moment, but she’s raised the question of Kenepuru. An urgent report into after-hours care was commissioned just at the end of this period under scrutiny here tonight and I’m still waiting for that full report.
acuity.explanation: Picks out the specific matter just raised — Kenepuru and local iwi/community solutions for after-hours services — and does something with it: identifies the commissioned urgent after-hours review, places it relative to the period under scrutiny, and reports a meeting with Ora Toa three weeks earlier. The speech would be materially different had she raised something else. Not 1.0 only because her other two strands (regional health outcome data and Māori health workforce strategies) are deferred rather than answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "With Kenepuru Hospital, Porirua and Kāpiti have got solutions; we’ve got local iwi and communities that would be happy to partner and take over some of those facilities."

acuity.statement: Firstly, I’d like to invite the Minister back down to the deep South to hear in person about the infrastructure needs we have, because my question, really, is about infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Reti had just given a substantive account of the Kenepuru after-hours review and his meeting with Ora Toa. Willis engages none of that and opens a prepared question on Dunedin Hospital funding. It is on the subject under scrutiny (health capital and services), so low band rather than zero, but the turn is indifferent to what preceded it. That he quotes the Minister's past words on beds and theatres is a reference to an earlier statement elsewhere, not engagement with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Reti spoke about the urgent after-hours care report and his meeting with Ora Toa over Kenepuru, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: During the hearing process, we frequently heard about cancer. So the question to the Minister—and I appreciate the answer that we’ve already had about first specialist assessments and emergency department wait times. But do you think targets are needed for faster cancer treatment, and what can be done to address these cancer times?
acuity.explanation: Campbell picks up the targets strand that the Minister had just been defending and extends it to a new domain (cancer treatment times), and he explicitly acknowledges the answers already given on first specialist assessments and ED waits. But he does not engage the content of Reti's defence — the claim that the targets were inherited indicators — and instead puts a fresh, prepared committee question. Partial engagement with the topic rather than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can’t really accept the member’s claim around the health targets I’ve put forward" — Shane Reti, in the immediately preceding turn defending his health targets.

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Mr Chair, and to the Minister: again, I just wanted to drill a little bit deeper in terms of my questioning of Te Whatu Ora, in particular, considering they have obligations through the Pae Ora legislation to reduce Māori health inequalities.
acuity.explanation: The turn resumes her own prior questioning ("again, I just wanted to drill a little bit deeper") and runs through three self-contained prepared lines — locality funding, finance capability on the board, Māori representation. It engages no part of the preceding turn's cancer-targets argument, though it remains squarely within the same annual-review examination of the health agencies. Prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hamish Campbell asked "do you think targets are needed for faster cancer treatment" and this statement does not take that up, resuming the speaker's own earlier line of questioning on Te Whatu Ora instead.

acuity.statement: The Minister of Health has been at pains on several examples tonight to remind us that the period under review was a period that he doesn’t feel particularly responsible for. That brings to light, I think, one of the kind of caveats or one of the suppositions that we should make clear, and that is that the health reforms have afforded the Minister a very good opportunity to have a much leaner, meaner, efficient way of doing asset management and managing the capital estate.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the Minister's repeated distancing from the review period and draws out its consequence: if the reforms centralised asset management, he has the whole-of-estate view and so the infrastructure question is answerable by him. That is genuine engagement with the line he has been running, though she then moves to her own prepared infrastructure question on the 1,200 buildings and 73 live projects. Engagement with one strand rather than a rebuttal of a specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that was outside of my hands. I don’t know the answer to that, so I can’t address that." — Shane Reti, in the preceding answer on Te Whatu Ora board appointments.

acuity.statement: Thank you for that, Minister, and I acknowledge your answer. Can you be specific if any have been rescoped—any projects that are on that list are currently being rescoped or have been rescoped in the last few weeks or the last couple of months?
acuity.explanation: She hears that the answer deflected to the period-under-review boundary and presses precisely on the gap, narrowing the question to a specific, answerable form: have any named projects been rescoped, now or in recent months. The follow-up only exists because of what he just said and would have to be different had he answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do I have any plans to change the frameworks around how we deliver infrastructure? Look, that’s in a period outside under review" — Shane Reti, in the immediately preceding answer.

acuity.statement: He will know that over this period, North Shore Hospital was being expanded, with 150 new beds and eight surgical units. He has made comments about this particular piece of infrastructure, but he hasn’t provided the clarity on when that might be opened—so acknowledging that the build was in this particular review period.
acuity.explanation: The question sits in the live infrastructure exchange and gestures at the Minister's earlier remarks on this build, which is more than a cold change of subject, but it engages no part of the preceding answer about rescoping and Dunedin. It is his own prepared North Shore question, placed on the right topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the biggest scope review was to Dunedin Hospital in the period under review" — Shane Reti; Halbert stays on the infrastructure theme but does not take up the rescoping answer.

acuity.statement: The member is quite right: that’s well outside the period. But I do want to give him some sense of hope. It is my ambition for that facility to be functional in this calendar year, understanding that the opening was delayed.
acuity.explanation: He concedes the premise he disputes (the timing falls outside the review period), then supplies the very thing asked for — a date range for the beds becoming operational — and explains the construction delay that moved it. The answer could not have been given to any other question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when does he expect those beds to be operational?" — Shanan Halbert, in the immediately preceding question about the North Shore Hospital expansion.

acuity.statement: It is a good bill, and it’s a bill that has taken some time to get here. It was actually carried over from the previous Parliament, and it’s now in the name of Shane Jones—Matua Shane, we call him.
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn made a substantive case: that the bill builds on the 1992 settlement Act, empowers rangatiratanga, and that any ministerial delay should be brief given how long it has taken. Bidois gestures at the debate ("inject some lifeblood into this debate") and faintly echoes Abel's point about the time taken, but engages none of its content — he does not take up the delay point, the governance argument, or the share redistribution Abel described. The rest is prepared party material on the same bill, and would have read identically whatever Abel had argued, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band with a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "let’s remember it has taken a long time to get to this point" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: And I acknowledge the previous speaker, our chair of the Māori Affairs Committee in this term, Dan Bidois, because, speaking about rangatiratanga, the importance of governance for Māori and iwi to play in the future of Aotearoa New Zealand is very important. Co-governance, of course, is one way we can achieve that. There is not one particular way, and so it’s good to hear the National Party open to those sorts of opportunities in the future governance arrangements of this country.
acuity.explanation: Halbert takes the specific proposition Bidois had just advanced — that giving iwi more control is tino rangatiratanga — and draws out a consequence Bidois did not state, namely that this makes National open to co-governance arrangements more broadly. That is doing something with the preceding argument rather than merely naming its author: delete Bidois's rangatiratanga framing and this passage would have to change. It stops short of 1.0 because he then returns to prepared Labour support material on the bill's merits rather than pressing the point further. Whether the inference about National's openness is sound is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It gives iwi more control, and more control is mana motuhake. More control is tino rangatiratanga." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: When this bill was last before the House, it was disappointing to hear that the Minister was considering some changes. I think it will come as no surprise to the House that it’s likely that those changes will relate to clauses 37 and 25.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows a substantive 10-minute turn from Rima Nakhle that set out the bill's history, its six substantive changes, the $68.7 billion Māori economy figure and the Whakatōhea Mussels visit. His speech takes up none of that content: it is a prepared Labour spokesperson's contribution covering the same bill (the 2015 origin, the Māori Affairs Committee, an undertaking the Minister gave at an earlier stage, and clauses 37 and 25). It is squarely on the matter under debate, and it gestures at the debate's earlier stage rather than at the speaker before him, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band but not above it — the speech would read identically had Nakhle said something quite different about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rima Nakhle set out the bill's six changes, the $68.7 billion Māori economy estimate and the Whakatōhea Mussels visit, and this statement does not take any of it up.
