That is partial engagement — one strand taken up, the named particulars set aside — which is the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have a specific question around the Toloa Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Maths programme; Tupu Aotearoa; and the Pacific Work Connect service: will the Government continue to invest?" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: I just wanted to clarify: Te Aorerekura, the national strategy to eliminate family violence and sexual violence, has been a new thing for New Zealand over the last few years and has been working very well. In the action plan, it stipulates six specific changes. I'm interested to know from the Minister whether she stands by the action plan and those six shifts that need to occur.
acuity.explanation: Andersen re-puts her own earlier question rather than engaging anything in the Minister's intervening answer. It is squarely on the ministry under scrutiny and she signals she is clarifying her earlier question, which lifts it slightly, but no part of the preceding turn is engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just answered on the Independent Children's Monitor and Pacific employment initiatives, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: I'm happy to speak on the areas of my responsibility. I'm not the Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence; that is another Minister's responsibility. But, in terms of the two programmes that the member referred to, we absolutely want to see emphasis where there is a family violence prevention initiative.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the two programmes Andersen actually named and responds on them, while correcting the premise that the strategy falls within her portfolio — both are engagement with the specific question asked. Not 1.0 because the six shifts of Te Aorerekura, the core of Andersen's question, are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "those programmes in place in the community, such as E Tū Whānau and Pasefika Proud... does she stand by and support this programme" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I'll just acknowledge what the Minister was saying earlier with regards to guarantees, obviously, in funding. So I accept what she was saying with regards to projections, but it is important for us to find out if the Government is going to support specific programmes.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the part of the Minister's answer that is fair (she cannot pre-announce budget projections) and presses the part that is not, arguing that programme-specific commitments are a separate and answerable question. Accepting part and disputing the rest of the argument just made is the strongest form of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm not going to name programmes and future plans—those are for other debates" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: The member asks if we consulted the teachers. Well, no, not really, because they’re not the ones that are making decisions about when to expand or when to open or when to close a centre, so it would be unusual to consult people that aren’t really affected by a regulation on the regulation. What we have done is spoken to the people who manage and represent the people who manage centres, because we know that actually it’s them who risk their money to make things happen, who have the best insight into where centres should be built.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise consultation question put to him, answers it directly in the negative, gives his reason for not consulting teachers, and then addresses the exact group Xu-Nan sought to exclude (managers and directors) by explaining why they were consulted instead. The passage would have to be different had the question been about a different consultee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did he consult with ECE teachers on this? I’m not referring to the managers and directors of for-profit ECE companies" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: So a follow-up question from that: considering that the before-profit early childhood education (ECE) companies take a huge amount of money from taxpayer funding, how would the Minister expect to ensure that the early learning action plan is still upheld from the perspective of accountability and sustainability, and ensure that there is transparency of the taxpayer funding being delivered to for-profit companies and that taxes are being paid properly and are not being funnelled into offshore areas?
acuity.explanation: Picks up Seymour's central claim that for-profit operators build at no cost to the Crown and counters it with the taxpayer funding those operators receive, then ties that back to the accountability and sustainability objective he had cited. It engages one strand of the answer rather than the whole, and the final offshore-funnelling clause goes beyond anything Seymour said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "superb facilities that have been built by these for-profit operators at zero cost of investment capital to the Crown" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Oh no, we’ve gone from anti-business sentiment to outright xenophobia. There’s now totally unfounded accusations that early childhood education centres are actually funnelling money that they should have paid tax on into foreign corporations. Now, I’m just going to give the member an opportunity to say if he’s got any evidence to substantiate that.
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the specific insinuation in the follow-up question, names it, and challenges the member to produce evidence for it — a reply that could not have been given to any other question. The engagement is squarely aimed at what was just said, independently of how fairly it characterises it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "taxes are being paid properly and are not being funnelled into offshore areas" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Can I firstly thank the Minister for acknowledging the funding that has been given to those two schools in Palmerston North. I know those schools pretty well, and the fact that they were funded under the previous Government, I know, is a testament to the success of the focus in that space. My question for the Minister is around cultural context, in the Pasifika context.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Stanford's speech directly — the Palmerston North schools she cited and her credit to the previous Government — and turns it into a point about who funded them, before moving on to a prepared line of questioning on Pasifika learners that Stanford's speech did not raise. Partial engagement: you can point at exactly what is picked up, but the bulk of the turn is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "I recall talking to Regan Orr, the principal of Central Normal School in Palmerston North" — and her acknowledgement that the Better Start Literacy Approach "was brought in under the previous Government".

acuity.statement: Well, I’m glad the member asked, because I recently met with the Pasifika Principals Association and we had a fantastic afternoon. They are an incredibly engaged bunch of principals around the country, who do an amazing job. They had quite a lot of discussion with me and my ministerial adviser, and they impressed upon me the importance of leadership in the Pacific education space.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific thing asked — names the Pasifika body she engaged with, what they put to her, and how it fed into her priorities — so the reply would be different had Utikere asked something else. Marked down from 1.0 because it leaves untouched the other half of his question, the resource in her office for Pacific communities and the written answer withheld on privacy grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "what levels of engagement she has had with the Pasifika communities around Aotearoa New Zealand that has perhaps provided an opportunity to change some of the thinking that she’s previously had"

acuity.statement: So my question is two questions. How has the data which you mentioned before that we have on neurodivergent and disabled students been improved upon to address a way that ensures these students have what they need?
acuity.explanation: Takes up a specific strand of the Minister's immediately preceding speech — her claim that data and evidence on what learning support money buys is the first fundamental problem — and presses it on a particular cohort, asking what has actually improved. The question could not have been asked in this form if Stanford had not just made the data point ("the data which you mentioned before"), so the turn is shaped by what it follows. It stops short of 1.0 because it does not contest her reasoning or figures, and the second half returns to the member's own prepared material on the Learning Support Action Plan and ministry cuts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "The first thing is data and evidence." (and "So data and evidence is going to be absolutely crucial.")

acuity.statement: Thank you. I’ll address the last part of the question first around the shift in resources from the back end to meet front-end need.
acuity.explanation: Picks out a named part of the question just put to her — the claim that ministry cuts will remove expert roles supporting neurodivergent and disabled students — and answers it on its own terms, with the front-line/back-office distinction and an expectation that front-line learning support roles are not affected. The reply would have to change if the questioner had raised something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because she answers the resourcing strand squarely and leaves the data-improvement strand largely to prepared material restated from her earlier contribution. Scored on engagement only; whether the front-line claim is true or well-evidenced is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "when expert roles directly supporting neurodivergent and disabled students and teachers and schools will be lost in the Ministry of Education cuts"

acuity.statement: First of all, I can tell the member that, along with Minister Stanford and Cabinet colleagues, we’ve been working very quickly to get the basic ideas around policy decisions around charter schools made. And we’re doing that in order that we can pass legislation and have the first charter schools open in term 1, 2025.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question asked rather than speaking generally about the portfolio: the state of the work programme, the stage it has reached, and the timetable it is aimed at, then goes on to the two school types and the accountability rationale that answer the "why confident" limb. Substituting a different question on education would force a different speech. Not 1.0 because it is an exposition of his own policy rather than engagement with a contested argument, there being no opposing claim in the preceding turn to rebut.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Parmjeet Parmar: "how that work programme to bring in charter schools is looking, what progress has been made so far, and what makes the Minister so confident about charter schools"

acuity.statement: The reality is that we’ve come to Government at a time—and I think the annual reviews show this—where our transport infrastructure is in a poor state. It’s crucial we recognise the magnitude of the challenges that we have ahead of us and what we need to do to fix them. Kiwis are faced with worsening congestion. Our State highways have been peppered with 62,000 potholes in the last year, and the last Government was focused on trying to tell people to get out of their cars and trying to tell them to drive really, really slowly, rather than actually trying to stay focused on the basics.
acuity.explanation: Brown follows Foster's substantive report-back and picks up one strand of it — the committee's maintenance/potholes findings, explicitly invoking "the annual reviews" Foster had just summarised — and turns it into a claim about the state of the network. But he engages none of Foster's actual arguments (that the investment quantum is sufficient while quality is poor, that business cases are window-dressing, that consenting and traffic-management costs are the handbrake, that a population strategy is needed), and after that gesture reverts to prepared opening remarks on Government priorities and the previous Government's record. Thanking the chair "for your remarks" is a mere reference and earns nothing. Partial engagement with the topic rather than the specific claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "NZTA told us we’re investing about half what we should be in maintenance. So it’s no wonder we’ve got a few potholes around the place."

acuity.statement: During the hearing, we did hear about the “roads of National Party significance” and that it would come at a minimum cost estimate of between $30 and $46 billion, which leaves, as the Minister has said, a fiscal hole of $8 billion to $22 billion for him.
acuity.explanation: Brown's preceding turn built his case on reinstating the roads of national significance and on a '$200 billion hole' inherited from the last Government. Utikere takes that exact framing and turns it back on the Minister, pricing the roads programme and deriving a fiscal hole in Brown's own plan, then asking what funding and financing tools he will use. The question only makes sense as a reply to what Brown just argued, so it sits well above the prepared-material band; it is short of 1.0 because it leans partly on select committee evidence rather than purely on the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "there's a $200 billion hole between the last Government's aspirations and what was actually funded" / "reinstating the roads of national significance"

acuity.statement: The first question was in regards to public transport, and, as outlined in the draft Government policy statement on transport, there is, I think, up to $2.3 billion allocated to public transport services as part of that draft Government policy statement.
acuity.explanation: Takes Utikere's first question in order and supplies a figure plus, immediately after, a list of the concessions that survive — which engages the under-25 subsidy strand of the question directly. It falls short of 1.0 because the question's other half, how emissions reduction goals will be met, is not taken up at all; the answer substitutes aggregate funding for the specific decision he was asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "how will the Government meet goals around emissions reductions alongside continued incentivisation for public transport usage and whether or not he sees that there is a role in public transport subsidies?"

acuity.statement: Second question was in relation to the Clean Car Discount scheme, and I would note he didn’t talk about the tax side of the equation in terms of the question. The ute tax—the ute tax—of course, this was the reverse Robin Hood scheme that the last Government thought was the best thing.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked two things: does he accept the Clean Car Discount increased EV uptake, and what replaces it. Brown neither accepts nor disputes the uptake finding and names no successor initiative; he reframes the scheme as the ute tax and moves to the last Government's priorities. That is engagement with the topic but with no part of the claim or the request, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.3 for the explicit gesture at the question he was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether or not he accepts that the initiative did increase the uptake of EVs, and, if so, what other initiatives are in the pipeline"

acuity.statement: Can he confirm that State highway improvements were the No. 3 investment under the previous Government—that almost $1 billion was spent on State highway improvements just in the financial year under review, not including the New Zealand Upgrade Programme, and that the only two activity classes that exceeded that, at 20 percent and 18 percent, were State highway maintenance and local road maintenance, and that, therefore, the vast majority of the transport budget under the previous Government was being spent on highways and local roads?
acuity.explanation: Brown's preceding turns rested on the premise that the last Government starved roads in favour of other modes. Genter attacks that premise head-on with the activity-class breakdown of the fund for the very year under review and asks him to confirm the numbers. Substitute a different argument for Brown's and this passage would have to change entirely — it is built around the specific claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "their focus was spending hundreds of millions of dollars on things like Auckland light rail" / "they cancelled the roads of national significance programme"

acuity.statement: And while the Minister goes on and on about one raised pedestrian crossing in Auckland, not even 3 percent—not even 3 percent—of the transport budget was spent on walking and cycling improvements.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific example Brown had just used as evidence of misplaced spending — his '$490,000 speed bumps' line — by putting it against the share of the budget the category actually received. This is not a mere reference to the previous speaker: it takes his own illustration and uses the proportion to deny the conclusion he drew from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "other than the $490,000 speed bumps, there hasn't been a lot of delivery"

acuity.statement: I appreciate the member the Hon Julie Anne Genter outlining some of the elements of the annual review report that was from the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. I would point her to page 29 of the draft Government policy statement on transport, which invests in public transport services, public transport infrastructure, and walking and cycling improvements.
acuity.explanation: Genter asked him to confirm a set of specific figures and then asked what his plan is to give people a genuine alternative to driving. He confirms, disputes or corrects none of the figures, but the page reference does take up the last strand — where the investment in public transport and active modes sits. One strand engaged, the substance of the challenge left alone, which is the lower half of the partial band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "What is his plan to give people actual choice?"

acuity.statement: No one is questioning whether or not people in the regions need roads. The question is: what is the best investment to move people and goods now and that reduces the cost burden of transport on businesses and people in New Zealand?
acuity.explanation: Takes up McCallum's interjection directly: concedes its premise, then reframes the disagreement as one about which investment moves people and goods best. The sentences would not exist had the interjection not been made, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "People in the regions need roads." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Julie Anne Genter for her question, and I would just note that page 29 of the draft Government policy statement—and I’m happy to give her a copy—does include investment in public transport services, does include investment in public transport infrastructure, and does include investment in walking and cycling improvements. On this side of the House, we think we should be investing in a range of transport modes.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Genter raised and points to the specific page of the GPS, but answers only that the investment exists rather than the claim about its share (1 percent, down on the previous year); the turn then moves to prepared material on light rail. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the amount in the draft Government policy statement which he has just referred to is only 1 percent of the transport budget on walking and cycling improvements" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I still haven’t heard from the Minister whether or not he accepts that the Clean Car Discount’s initiative did increase the uptake of electric vehicles—that was the question that I asked and he still has neglected to address that.
acuity.explanation: Responsive in that it tracks what the Minister did and did not cover, but it engages an absence from the preceding turn rather than anything in it, and the rest of the call is a prepared list of new questions on rail, congestion charging and coastal shipping.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown's preceding answer — "On this side of the House, we think we should be investing in a range of transport modes" — contains no mention of the Clean Car Discount, and this statement engages that omission rather than any argument Brown made in it.

acuity.statement: In terms of the lower North Island—the rail improvement—that is noted on page 13 of the draft GPS as being a priority for this Government and to be funded from a combination of Crown grants, National Land Transport Fund, and local share contributions.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific thing asked for — where the lower North Island package sits in the draft GPS and what funding streams carry it. The answer is shaped by the question and would be different had Utikere asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the levels of projected funding to support the long-term future of what is the lower North Island rail package—for Manawatū, Wairarapa, and Kāpiti lines" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I’m keen to hear from the Minister of Transport around the Auckland regional fuel tax. I’m keen to know how much was collected by the previous Government on it, what it was spent on, and how much was unspent.
acuity.explanation: Prepared question on the general subject of the debate that engages no part of the preceding exchange; it would read identically whatever the Minister or Utikere had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just spoken about coastal shipping, the Port of Tauranga berth consent and the National Land Transport Fund, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Well, it raised, I think, something like $700 million or $750 million, and it spent about $450 million. There was about $300 million unspent when we came into Government.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the three figures requested, in the order requested. The content is determined by the question put, which is the strongest evidence of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m keen to know how much was collected by the previous Government on it, what it was spent on, and how much was unspent." — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: If you look at the new Government policy statement, you’ll see there are not many, if any projects in the South Island.
acuity.explanation: Opens a new line on South Island projects without engaging the preceding answer; on the subject under debate (the draft GPS) but indifferent to what came before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just given figures on the Auckland regional fuel tax and its unspent balance, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In terms of the issue in regards to Rocks Road, I mean, ultimately the New Zealand Transport Agency Board is responsible for the prioritisation of projects which are put forward.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Rocks Road strand of Boyack's two questions by name, but engages it only to the extent of assigning responsibility to the NZTA board; the specific points she raised (the road's closures in floods, its absence from the GPS and Waka Kotahi documents, and the three-year delay to the Hope bypass) are not taken up. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What is the Minister going to do about the resilience of Rocks Road, which is over 100 years old and constantly closes?" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: And if Rachel Boyack from Nelson believes there should have been a lot more roading projects on your list, why do you think they weren’t built in the last six years under her Government?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the premise of Boyack's earlier complaint about the number of projects listed and turns it into a question about the previous government's record, rather than engaging her actual claims about the Hope bypass delay or Rocks Road. A pivot off the topic she raised rather than engagement with her argument, so a weak partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we had two projects in the previous Government policy statement because our regional transport committee had identified two priority projects" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: Well, perhaps if I can clarify: have you been briefed on breaches to those obligations to notify and to consult?
acuity.explanation: Takes the minister's answer and isolates exactly what it slid past — he was asked about briefings on breaches of the obligations, not about the flight-path changes themselves — and re-puts that distinction. The question only exists because of the precise wording of the answer that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t think I’ve been briefed on those specific changes, recently, but I’ll certainly go and ask for one." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Yes, I’m aware of those obligations. I’m not 100 percent sure right now whether—I don’t think I’ve been briefed on those specific changes, recently, but I’ll certainly go and ask for one.
acuity.explanation: Answers both limbs O'Connor put — awareness of the obligations, and whether he has been briefed — directly and in order, and commits to seeking a briefing. Marked down slightly only because the second limb (briefings on where obligations were not met) is answered about the changes rather than the failures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is he aware that where there are changes to flight paths notified under what’s called a DMAP system... that there are obligations which must be met by the agencies" — Greg O’Connor

acuity.statement: I did not see any contact between the member and the member across—and I appreciate you nodding your head to that. There was no physical contact.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the load-bearing factual element of Simpson's account — that there was a physical attack — and denies it from his own observation of the footage. The contribution would be entirely different had Simpson characterised the incident differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It was a serious, intimidatory physical attack upon another member in this Chamber" — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: But I feel that no matter who it was, that was an extraordinary outburst, and it was intimidating in its nature—coming from where I was sitting.
acuity.explanation: Engages the dispute Abel opened by conceding the ground he stood on (she describes gestures and standing over, not contact) while maintaining the conduct was intimidating. It answers the characterisation question rather than Abel's specific no-contact point, and the gender comparison is her own added material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There was no physical contact." — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: I would like to add to that that from my position, it looked like a huge amount of intimidation that was going on very close to the person—standing over the person—and physically shaking a book in that person’s face. If that was me, I would have felt very intimidated, and I feel that it was really inappropriate.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Abel's benign account of the booklet and contests it — the book was shaken in the member's face, not shown — but otherwise adds her own eyewitness impression rather than engaging the rest of his account. Partial engagement, clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "she was wanting to show him the actual information in the booklet" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: If I could apologise for my actions, Mr Speaker. It was the last thing I wanted to do to intimidate anyone in this House. What has absolutely motivated me is a desire to share information that I believe would be of benefit to everyone in this House, and I’m very sorry that if in my passion to do so, I was intimidating.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the charge actually levelled across the preceding turns — that her conduct was intimidating — accepting the effect while disputing the intent, and explaining the motivation Abel had attributed to her. Responsive to the specific accusation rather than to the general subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it looked like a huge amount of intimidation that was going on very close to the person" — Karen Chhour

acuity.statement: Just going back to the Minister’s responses around the “roads of National Party significance” and the $30 billion to $46 billion cost, it really is embarrassing that only three of them relate to the South Island.
acuity.explanation: The turn is in the same estimates debate and is clearly about transport policy, so it is not wholly unresponsive, and it does quote content from the Minister's earlier replies ('roads of National Party significance', '$30 billion to $46 billion'). But the only preceding turn available here is Andy Foster's Marlborough Sounds subsidy argument, and Utikere engages no part of it — he picks up only the South Island framing and then moves to a prepared set of questions on speed, DSI statistics and licensing. The engagement cannot be pointed at within the window, so it sits in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing in-window: Andy Foster spoke immediately before, arguing that "the coastal option doesn’t get a subsidy but may be a cheaper option overall for “New Zealand Inc.”", and this statement does not take that up; it reaches back instead to the Minister's earlier answers, which are not in this text.

acuity.statement: In terms of member Andy Foster and his question around the issue in Marlborough, I acknowledge the challenges there. Ultimately, what we’re focused toward here is making sure we get the agency back to core business building and maintaining the roads. And ultimately, there’s been significant engagement between the agency and the council in Marlborough to ensure that the appropriate response is made in terms of addressing many of those challenges. But I acknowledge that with these severe weather events, they do create some difficult challenges for local communities.
acuity.explanation: Brown names the member and the locality and answers the general topic — the Marlborough Sounds roading response — so the reply would not be identical had Foster not spoken. But Foster's actual argument was a specific subsidy asymmetry distorting the council's choice between a roading and a coastal-shipping solution, and Brown engages neither the asymmetry nor coastal shipping; he restates the Government's 'core business' framing and reports that agency-council engagement is occurring. Topic engaged, specific claim not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "the coastal option doesn’t get a subsidy but may be a cheaper option overall for “New Zealand Inc.”, so the combination of ratepayer and taxpayer."

acuity.statement: In relation to the question from member Tangi Utikere around safety—and, of course, safety is one of the strategic priorities within the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on transport, and if he was to turn to page 18 of the draft GPS he would see the significant increase that has occurred in the last 10 years of deaths and crashes involving alcohol or drugs. That has gone from around 100 deaths per year involving alcohol or drugs to near 200 deaths involving alcohol and drugs.
acuity.explanation: Brown takes up one strand of the question — whether road safety is a priority — and supplies a pointable source, page 18 of the draft GPS, with a figure, so the reply is shaped by what Utikere asked. He does not engage the specific claim put to him (that the existing approach had produced the lowest road deaths in five years despite 6 percent more traffic) nor the question about advice on raising speed limits, redirecting instead to alcohol and drug deaths, breath testing and new infrastructure. Partial engagement, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "On the DSI stat—or the death and serious injury statistics—how have they informed the Minister’s decision-making approach to speed reductions in that particular space?"

acuity.statement: However, having said that, I do have some views about the ethical investing, as well. One of the former speakers was a little unsure that ethical investing was a suitable way to go, but, actually, ethical investing is starting to be well developed now in terms of what funds do and don’t invest in. There are some pretty well-established parameters, and I’m sure the Guardians of the Superannuation Fund can continue to do well in that regard.
acuity.explanation: She names the preceding speaker's position ("a little unsure that ethical investing was a suitable way to go") and takes up that one strand of his turn, asserting the opposite — that ethical investment parameters are now well established. It is a real engagement with something Smith actually said, so the speech would differ had he not said it, but she contradicts his conclusion by assertion rather than meeting his reasoning about prescription limiting choice and returns (the tractor/bank example goes untouched), then returns to prepared commendation of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That's the sort of thing that happens when you start prescribing what you can and what you can't invest in, and I think it's so short-sighted." — Stuart Smith, in the immediately preceding turn, where he worked through tobacco, whale meat, Israeli settlements and firearms and concluded prescription limits returns.

acuity.statement: I stand before you to take this to take this split call to support the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income (Controlling Interests) Amendment Bill at its second reading. This bill, in my opinion, is an essential step forward in the evolution of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund because it aims to repeal and replace the current restrictions that limit the fund’s ability to take a controlling interest in entities.
acuity.explanation: Lu follows a substantive turn by Arena Williams that made a partisan argument about public ownership and the Government's asset sales, and engages none of it. The speech is prepared material on the correct subject — the bill and the fund's controlling-interest restriction — and would read word-for-word the same whatever Williams had said. There is not even a gesture at the preceding contribution, so this sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that Labour believes in public ownership of strategic assets and that the Government "has no economic plan beyond cutting public ownership of the services that we rely on", and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Two things I would like to speak on because they’ve come up in the debate. One is around ethical investing, and, certainly, it is a growing practice in investing. acuity.statement: Nō reira kāore e kume kia roa ēnei kōrero, engari ko tā mātou e mea nei, āe, kei te kite atu he hāngaitanga ki tā mātou kaupapahere mō te mana motuhake, kia whai rangatiratanga ake te tangata whenua, kia mōhio mai te tangata whenua kei a wai ōna kōrero, nō wai ngā kōrero rānei, kia whai mana ōrite anō hoki te tangata whenua kei pā kinotia e ētahi āhuatanga i roto i ēnei tūmomo whakahaere o te ture.

acuity.responding_to: "Who owns the data? Well, this is a very good question. Who does own the data?" — Tanya Unkovich

acuity.statement: Firstly, the bill is trying to address an issue that doesn’t exist. No asylum seekers have successfully arrived in Aotearoa by boat. Well, not since 1840 anyway. And it’s highly unlikely that they would ever be able to do so, which, by the way, the Government themselves have acknowledged.
acuity.explanation: Ferris takes up the precise strand Costello built her case on — that a mass arrival is low-risk but non-zero and therefore warrants legislative preparation — and contests it directly, arguing the risk is effectively nil (no boat arrivals since 1840) and that the Government itself concedes this. He engages the premise rather than just the topic, but does not deal with her specific reasoning about preparedness or with the protective case she made for detention, and the passage reads partly as prepared material, so it sits around the middle-to-upper band rather than at 1.0.

acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "this risk is low but it is not zero" — and "The fact is that we have to be prepared, and the introduction of this bill shows that New Zealand is recognising the importance of being prepared."

acuity.statement: My second point is that, given there is no real threat, the Government are, therefore, fear mongering once again, as they have done time and time again throughout the entirety of their term in Parliament to date.
acuity.explanation: Costello accused opponents of fearmongering and emotive rhetoric; Ferris turns the same charge back on the Government. That is engagement with one strand of what preceded him — the accusation of fear-based argument — but he reverses the label rather than answering her reasoning for it, and the claim is immediately generalised into a prepared indictment of the Government's whole term, so it only partly takes up what was said.

acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "There has, in this House last night, been fearmongering about the type of venues that would be used for this detention"

acuity.statement: Those that oppose this bill—let’s imagine for a moment that this isn’t passed—are saying that we have 96 hours to ensure the legal support is provided. Well, what if that doesn’t happen? What does it look like when we don’t provide that legal support or aren’t able to, because there are only, as I understand it, approximately 40 lawyers throughout the country that have the ability to represent people who arrive in a mass arrival event, and assuming that it was late on a Friday night that this occurred, two of those days are already gone—a Saturday and a Sunday, as my learned colleague and chair of the Education and Workforce Committee has already alluded to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific point Salesa made about the shortage of refugee and immigration law practitioners and the adequacy of the 96-hour window, and turns it around as a reason the bill is needed. He cites his own figure (~40 lawyers) against her 30 and works through the weekend consequence, so the contribution would be different had the preceding speaker not raised legal-representation capacity. Not a full 1.0 because he restates rather than directly contests her number or her conclusion about safeguards.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "she found that there were only 30 refugee and immigration law practitioners across Aotearoa New Zealand" — Jenny Salesa

acuity.statement: The Opposition has spent a lot of time this evening speaking about lived experience and, at the same time, is telling us that this is a hypothetical that’s never going to happen. So let’s pick a lane, ladies and gentlemen—let’s pick a lane.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding argument — the appeal to submitters with lived experience — and alleges it sits badly beside the claim that a mass arrival is hypothetical. It is pointable engagement with what was just said rather than generic prepared material, but it works on the framing of the opposition case as a whole instead of the specific claims Salesa made, hence mid-band rather than top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We also heard concerns from people with lived experience, and they were very convincing in the reasons why they were not supporting this bill" — Jenny Salesa

acuity.statement: I just want to quickly touch on the Immigration Act itself and that it does define a “mass arrival group” at section 9A. That means more than 30 people who don’t have a visa, or are stowaways, who arrive in New Zealand on board the same craft—a craft not being something that is a scheduled international service.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by a member opposite and engages none of it: no reply to the likelihood argument, the criminalisation point, or the 28-day reading of the clause. The material is prepared statutory definition on the right subject, and the only backward reference is an endorsement of her own colleague two turns earlier, so the contribution would read identically whatever Bates had argued.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates argued that advances in boat technology make a mass arrival increasingly likely, that the bill nowhere criminalises arrivals, and that the court "must" determine within 28 days — and this statement does not take any of it up. Brooking instead endorses the earlier speaker on her own side.

acuity.statement: How will these proposed changes help farmers?
acuity.explanation: Follows Hoggard's substantive announcement about removing the low-slope map and repealing winter grazing regulations, but takes up none of it — no figure, no claim, no part of the reasoning is engaged. It is a generic prepared prompt that would read identically after almost any agriculture announcement, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because it is at least on the matter under discussion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Andrew Hoggard: "the Government will introduce legislation to remove the low-slope map from stock exclusion regulations, and repeal winter grazing regulations" — the question does not take up any part of that claim.

acuity.statement: Has the Minister read the New Zealand-EU free-trade agreement (FTA) that includes legally binding provisions to “provide for a high-level of environmental protection and continue to improve environmental protections” and “not to weaken, reduce, waive, or otherwise derogate from environmental laws to encourage trade or investment”; if so, what does he think?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific content of Hoggard's announcement — repealing environmental regulations to cut 'red tape' — and draws out a consequence by confronting it with a named binding obligation not to derogate from environmental law. The question could not have been asked in this form if Hoggard had announced something else, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 only because it supplies an external obligation rather than engaging Hoggard's own stated reasoning (that the low-slope map has 'minimal practical or environmental benefits').
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Andrew Hoggard: "the Government will introduce legislation to remove the low-slope map from stock exclusion regulations, and repeal winter grazing regulations"

acuity.responding_to: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon: "we had a bit of a mix-up in communication yesterday—we clarified it very quickly"

acuity.statement: Well, that doesn’t affect it either, because as the member well knows, and I can’t believe we’re—I feel like I’m stuck in Groundhog Day, because, you know, the entire time I’ve been an MP and Chlöe Swarbrick’s been an MP, we’ve had this ongoing back and forth about capital gains taxes. I invite the member to go to Sydney and Melbourne and London and all the other countries and places that have, in some cases, quite punitive capital gains taxes, where you will find housing markets that are utterly out of control.

acuity.responding_to: "It’s your tax settings, Bish." — Chlöe Swarbrick

We’ve already seen Kāinga Ora announce some cancellation projects. We’ve seen community housing providers, like the Salvation Army, indicate that they have cancelled projects. My question to the Minister is: how many Kāinga Ora projects and how many community housing projects have been cancelled since this Government was formed?

It stays squarely within the housing/Kāinga Ora matter under debate and continues the funding-certainty theme Bishop glanced at, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.0 — this could not have been delivered in a different debate. It is a legitimate and pointed question; it is simply not responsive to what was just said.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Bishop argued that land supply, infrastructure funding and council incentives — not rent controls or tax settings — are the only sustainable route to affordable rents, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: Well, in relation to the member’s last part of the question, you’d have to put that in writing, because I don’t know. Kāinga Ora owns 70,000 houses around the country, and it’s $45 billion company. So, at any given time, there will be any number of projects that are rephased, deferred—some may have been cancelled. The market economics of building change literally on a weekly basis.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how many Kāinga Ora projects and how many community housing projects have been cancelled since this Government was formed?" — Kieran McAnulty

Short of 1.0 because he does not resolve the timing point and defers to checking the specifics, but the reply is plainly shaped by what was just put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "I ask how he can rectify that, when considering response to written question 7084, that the advice in question was actually commissioned by the Minister of Finance later in December."

acuity.statement: Nevertheless, neither of those equate to when they came into office they were presented with the advice.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "It was either a joint memo or piece of advice to the two of us, or it was a piece of advice to the Minister forwarded to me."

acuity.statement: But what I can tell the member is that, well, firstly, in response to his first point: if his point is that late December is not “upon coming to office”, I don’t accept that. We took office on 27 November, so three or four weeks later is, I would argue, “upon coming to office”.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the precise disagreement in the preceding turn — whether late December counts as "upon coming to office" — states that he does not accept it, and supplies the date of taking office and the resulting interval as his reason. This is engagement with the specific claim, not a pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Nevertheless, neither of those equate to when they came into office they were presented with the advice."

acuity.explanation: Draws out the consequence of Bishop's assertion that his account of the funding assumptions was inaccurate, by asking whether the Minister is therefore contradicting the officials who gave that account at select committee. The question is built entirely out of the answer immediately before it.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "Some of what he says is not factually accurate around the future funding requirements."
