acuity.explanation: Answers the specific proposition put to him — whether he is calling the officials wrong — with a direct denial and a reason (that a forecast is a snapshot that is then updated), which addresses the logic of the question rather than its topic. Not 1.0 because he then turns to the previous Ministers of Housing rather than the select committee evidence itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Is the Minister therefore saying that Ministry of Housing and Urban Development officials that presented to the select committee were incorrect"

acuity.statement: I think there was a question in relation to Cyclone Gabrielle, and then it merged into whether or not the rent-to-buy homes at Toitū Tairāwhiti were progressing according to the aspirations and the intent, and I can represent to the committee that there is some significant build programme in front of Toitū Tairāwhiti.
acuity.explanation: Identifies and takes up the specific strand of Jackson's question about the Toitū Tairāwhiti rent-to-buy programme and Cyclone Gabrielle, which is real engagement, but answers the topic rather than the question asked — no progress figure against the 150 homes is given, and the turn then moves to general material about trainees and the mill workers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "what update has the Minister—and it may be Minister Potaka—have in relation to Toitu Tairawhiti and the programme delivery partnership agreement for the delivery of 150 rent-to-buy homes in the last 12 months?"

acuity.statement: The context of this, if I can, is that of the reports that Minister Potaka was referring to—I built 16 of those homes in Aupōuri, and we did a few good things ourselves as iwi—I’m very familiar with Pouahi and very familiar with the home repairs, so, yeah, that’s doing good with what we’ve got at that time, so I’m just really hoping that it gets even better.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the two specific things Potaka had just described — the Pouahi prototype and the home-repairs programme — and brings her own direct experience of them to bear on his account of how they are going. Only partial, because having done so she moves to an unconnected set of prepared questions on home-ownership rates and the Residential Tenancies Act that engage nothing he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "the question around Te Pouahi up in Te Taitokerau, which is one of the iwi housing prototypes, which has just got started"

acuity.statement: The key challenge that was sort of identified is that Police—with a $2.2 billion budget, $1.7 billion of which is in staff—is that they’re facing into a 6.5 percent budget cut, so that’s really looking at personnel. So we’re quite keen to understand what is front line and what is not front line, given that context.
acuity.explanation: Meager's speech opened the Police annual review debate, covering the committee's session and, among other things, front-line recruitment and confidence in meeting staffing targets. Andersen picks up the same session and the front-line staffing strand — her budget-cut framing cuts directly against Meager's confidence about recruitment — but she never takes up any specific claim he made, and she pivots quickly to prepared questions aimed at the Minister about statements made earlier in the day rather than at the speech she follows. Partial, topic-level engagement with one identifiable strand, so mid-low rather than mid.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We talked a little bit about recruitment of front-line staff and some of the challenges that are going to be there about making sure you get the right people into our police services" — James Meager

acuity.statement: In terms of the Hon Ginny Andersen’s question, it’s actually for the police commissioner. The police Minister does not interfere, nor does he or she have any say over how the police commissioner deploys his or her staff or how he deploys them operationally. That is for him. But the one thing that we’ve been very clear about as the incoming Government is that we want to see resources pushed to the front line. She’s right in that under the previous Government, in the 2022-23 year, there’s been a big investment in numbers but their core funding has not increased; in fact, quite the opposite.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put to him by name, gives the constitutional reason the question falls to the commissioner rather than the Minister, then expressly concedes part of her premise ("She’s right in that...") about core funding not increasing and goes on to say what the Government has decided about the competency service increment in consequence. This speech could not have been delivered had Andersen said something else. Not 1.0 only because the three concrete role-by-role questions she asked (111 responders, authorised officers, 105 call-takers) are deflected rather than engaged — a shortfall in answering, which Acuity marks down only slightly since the deflection itself is aimed squarely at her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d just like a bit of clarity from the Minister in relation to that, I’m a bit confused. Today, we established that it’s for the commissioner to determine what is front line or not" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: So, when we talk about it being dangerous for our police officers to go out there and deal with gangs, I accept that; that has never changed. They’re an organised criminal group, and they have a propensity for violence, but we have the best professional police service in the world, and they have a very strong and proud history of knowing how to deal with gangs.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Paul's question directly — the danger the patch ban places front-line officers in — and concedes it before answering it. But it leaves her central specific claim untouched: that the low number of fines under the existing ban shows it is unenforced and therefore ineffective. The Western Australian material that precedes this would have been delivered whatever she had asked, so this is partial engagement: the topic and one strand are answered, the specific evidential challenge is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "surely that’s a really dangerous and difficult position to put police officers in"

acuity.statement: As the member knows, that’s an ongoing piece of work, but the one thing that I would say to her is that we are fully committed as a Government to making our country more safe, not less safe, and the police have got a huge role to play in terms of dealing with firearms and public safety.
acuity.explanation: Andersen put a concrete operational scenario — an officer approaching a house after a firearms purchase was declined that day — and asked how that intelligence would reach the front line if Te Tari Pūreke sat in Internal Affairs. The reply is on the subject of firearms and police safety but engages no part of the mechanism she described; a general commitment to safety would have been an equally apt answer to any question about the shift. A gesture at the debate without taking up its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "how do the national intelligence agency and front-line police quickly access intelligence about who may have attempted to buy a firearm?"

acuity.statement: There have been reports that the cost of shifting Te Tari Pūreke out of Police into somewhere like the Department of Internal Affairs would cost around $100 million. What advice or reports has the Minister of Police received in relation to the cost of that shift?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the same subject Mitchell has just deflected and presses the same decision, which is more than prepared material would do — but it switches dimension rather than taking up his assertion. He claimed police would retain full access to intelligence; she does not test that, she opens a new line on cost. Engagement with the matter under examination, not with the specific claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "that’s an ongoing piece of work"

acuity.statement: Look, I can’t talk in great detail to the examples that the member has used, but I guess if I could sort of give you an overview in terms of the approach the police are taking, I have to assume that they probably involved gang members.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges that examples were given and is about the right matter, but engages none of the three specific questions put — the process authorising 60 officers at a tangi, armed checkpoints and a helicopter over the urupā, and whether police may interfere in tikanga. Instead it substitutes an assumption about the facts of her examples, which she immediately corrects. Naming what the member raised in order to set it aside is a reference, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "do police now have the authority to interfere in tikanga protocols, cultural considerations, and tangihanga?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I was reluctant to take another call because I had a good crack at the start, but given the enthusiasm of the committee on this topic, I did want to look back a little bit. I wanted to ask a question about past resourcing of police, and in particular, in the technology space, and in and around this idea that if we can get our systems to work smarter and not harder, we can actually gain a lot of efficiencies and a lot of resource out of the existing resource that we have.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn was Mark Mitchell saying retail crime is a huge focus requiring ongoing investment. Meager engages none of that; he opens a fresh line on police technology and efficiencies, explicitly framing it as looking back to a contribution he had prepared earlier. The question would read identically whatever Mitchell had just said, though it is at least within the same police annual-review debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Mitchell spoke about retail crime being 'a huge focus for this Government' requiring 'ongoing investment', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: But, look, you raise a really good point. There was a very big investment made into police back in 2013-14 in terms of technology. They got tablets and they got mobile phones. The reason for that is, obviously, we wanted a modern police force with the best technology available.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Meager's specific point about using technology to cut paperwork and free officers from the desk, and answers it with the substance asked for: the historic tablet and mobile-phone investment and its purpose. The answer would be different had Meager asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: 'if the Minister's satisfied with the work that's happened in police so far around looking at where they can gain efficiencies, where they can use technology to replace some of the paper-based systems'

acuity.statement: Well, I just think that she’s conflating the two issues. The first thing is the commissioner will decide what’s front line. He’ll decide where he deploys his staff and he’ll decide the best use of all his  resources and his staff. The member asked me as the Minister of Police what I would define as a front-line police officer and I said I consider a sworn police officer as front line.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses Andersen's request to reconcile two apparently inconsistent answers, naming the distinction he says she has collapsed — the commissioner's deployment decisions versus his own definition of a front-line officer. The reply is shaped entirely by the specific challenge put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: 'So if you could just reconcile those two different pieces of information, I'd really appreciate that.'

acuity.statement: My question’s around strategic intent, and it follows the Minister and the Prime Minister, along with the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, announcing the Local Water Done Well policy, an agreement unanimously reached by Auckland councillors that will avoid a 25.8 percent water rates increase on water users in and around Auckland this coming financial year. They were up for $348 per average household, and it will be a lot, lot less than that. So my question looking forward is to the Minister in the chair, Simeon Brown: when will the broader range of structural and financing tools be available to other councils to ensure they can finance themselves appropriately and access the long-term debt required for investment into water services?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand Boyack flagged in opening the local government review — financing of councils and investment in critical water services — and turns it into a specific question about structural and financing tools. It engages the topic she raised rather than any argument she made, and the Auckland framing is clearly prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: 'the topic of investment in critical water services and water reform was a matter of reporting to the select committee'

acuity.statement: I’d like to ask more about the Future for Local Government report, He piki tūranga, he piki kōtuku, which was issued on 16 June. I’d like to ask: does the Minister agree, first of all, that our system of local democracy and governance needs to evolve?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the first matter Boyack set out in opening the debate — the Future for Local Government review and its recommendations — and presses it further by asking the Minister to rank the report's five shifts. It engages the content she put before the committee, though it does not contest any claim and moves into her own prepared enumeration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: 'The first was around the future of local government reform.' (and that the review's 'final report was published in June 2023 and included 17 recommendations')

acuity.statement: However, I do want to clarify that, yes, one of them had gang member whānau, but two of them had absolutely no gang patches, no gang whānau. It was just a normal tangi where people were attending, and, in one instance, the police officers weren’t actually on the marae but on the actual street—the beginning road of the marae.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's specific explanatory assumption — that what she witnessed was police managing gang convoys on public roads — and directly contradicts its factual premises (no patches, no gang whānau, police on the street at the marae entrance), then presses the unanswered part of her original question. The speech would be entirely different had Mitchell offered a different explanation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "I’m only assuming that maybe what you’ve seen or what you’ve experienced is the police trying to effectively manage those convoys in a public space."

acuity.statement: I asked him about the success of the anti-gang policies and overall gang crackdown in Western Australia, and Commissioner Andrew Coster said, “They were quite successful in removing the visible presence of gangs in Western Australia.” Does the Minister expect similar success with his anti-gang policies here in New Zealand?
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the matter under review (the Police annual report and anti-gang policy), drawing on committee evidence rather than on anything said in the preceding turns. The questions would read identically whoever had just spoken, so this sits in the low band, lifted slightly off the floor because it is squarely within the item being scrutinised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Maipi-Clarke spoke about police checkpoints at tangihanga and discrimination against Māori attending tangi, and this statement does not take it up. It gestures at the debate only via "as the Minister has alluded to" earlier in the same turn.

acuity.statement: So starting with the last point first, yes. A big part of the reason why we want to remove gang patches and insignia is we don’t want the public to be exposed to that and we don’t want them being visible to the public.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put, and does something with the Commissioner's wording — picks up "visible presence" and makes removing visibility the stated object of the patch ban, then goes on to take up Brewer's Auckland constabulary numbers. Clearly shaped by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "Commissioner Andrew Coster said, “They were quite successful in removing the visible presence of gangs in Western Australia.” Does the Minister expect similar success with his anti-gang policies here in New Zealand?"

acuity.statement: One example from overseas where it was moved away from Police into another department was Canada, and it did not work so well there.
acuity.explanation: Opens a new line on the Firearms Safety Authority with prepared comparative material; it engages no part of the preceding answer. Still within the annual review, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mitchell spoke about the 500 additional officers, freeing police from mental health call-outs and foot patrols in Hamilton and Tauranga, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Well, that’s my job. I mean, I’m glad that the member highlights Canada, because, you know, I would expect and I’ll make sure that officials are looking at that so that if there’s lessons to be learnt from what Canada have done, we should be adopting and looking at those.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Canadian example Andersen offered and draws a consequence from it — officials to examine it for lessons — and addresses her request for a commitment, though the commitment he gives is reframed towards police retaining access to firearms intelligence rather than speaking out against the Associate Minister. Engagement is close; only the final strand of the question is partly turned aside.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "One example from overseas where it was moved away from Police into another department was Canada, and it did not work so well there."

acuity.statement: Is he concerned about the first two wings of the 500 new front-line police officers—that wing 376 only had 58 recruits, and then wing 377 just had 61 recruits? What does this do to the forecast date for when that 500 new police officers will be reached?
acuity.explanation: Tests a specific commitment the Minister made earlier in this debate against wing intake figures, which is real engagement with content in front of her. It does not take up the immediately preceding firearms answer at all, so this is partial rather than full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell, earlier in the same debate: "there’s a commitment to deliver an additional 500 front-line police officers in the term of this Government—the next two years."

acuity.statement: Well, our commitment hasn’t changed. We’ve committed to delivering 500 new sworn front-line police officers in two years.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the subject of the question — the 500-officer target and its timeframe — but neither disputes nor accounts for the two wing figures she put, and does not touch the forecast date, moving instead to recruitment anecdotes from Gisborne. One strand engaged, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "wing 376 only had 58 recruits, and then wing 377 just had 61 recruits? What does this do to the forecast date for when that 500 new police officers will be reached?"

acuity.statement: In relation to gangs, over the past six years, police have prevented an estimated $6.7 billion of social harm. I’m interested to know if he has done any modelling into the estimated amount of social harm that police will prevent as a result of the changes outlined in the Government’s coalition agreement.
acuity.explanation: A fresh prepared question with its own figure; it engages no part of the recruitment answer it follows, though gangs are squarely within the matter under scrutiny.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mitchell had just spoken about recruit standards and school-based recruitment in Gisborne, and this statement does not take it up; it gestures at the gang policy discussed earlier in the debate.

acuity.statement: But that question that the member just asked is projected forward, not back. I would recognise and agree with you that the police do an outstanding job of reducing social harm, and I have no doubt—and my expectations moving forward, in this term of Government—that, as we free up their resource, as we actually give them more tools, as we give them the ability to be able to dig even deeper into those issues, then we’ll continue to see very strong results.
acuity.explanation: Directly characterises the question he was asked and accepts her premise that police reduce social harm, which is engagement you can point at; but he does not say whether any modelling exists, substituting an expectation of strong results for the figure sought. Half the question is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "if he has done any modelling into the estimated amount of social harm that police will prevent as a result of the changes outlined in the Government’s coalition agreement"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and I thank you, Minister Brown, that I have the opportunity to ask a few questions, specifically around Auckland Council. You’ve made the announcement with regards to the water increase percentage. Just a couple of questions, and my first question is: can you explain the financial sustainable model for the record to ensure that these rates will remain affordable?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive answer from the Minister on the Tauranga Māori ward referendum and engages none of it, opening instead on a prepared line of questioning about Auckland water rates. It is squarely within the local government debate, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about a referendum on the Tauranga Māori ward and the commission's responsibilities, and this statement does not take any part of it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. This is a time-limited debate, and by our calculations, the National Party have roughly seven minutes remaining and there’s three full sessions to go. So it’s very disappointing to see the National Party using up their time with patsy questions that they could indeed just go and ask the Minister themselves and save the Minister’s time to be able to answer questions.
acuity.explanation: It notices that questions were asked and labels them, which is a mere reference to the preceding turn, not engagement with anything claimed in it. The complaint is about the management of debate time, and the questions he then puts are fresh material that does not build on what was said before him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the preceding questioner asked "can you explain the financial sustainable model for the record to ensure that these rates will remain affordable?" and this statement characterises the preceding questions as patsy rather than engaging their content.

acuity.statement: So if the Minister considers referendums are such a vital part of democracy, would he suggest that as well as for Māori wards, we have referendums on rates rises, cycleways—why not?—and a number of other things?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated position — that the Māori ward must go to a referendum — and draws out its consequence, asking why the same test is not applied to rates rises, cycleways, ward boundaries or councillor numbers. The question could not have been written without his answer in front of her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "there will have to be a referendum in Tauranga. The legislation we’ll be bringing to the House will mean that that referendum will have to happen between now and the next local government elections."

acuity.statement: In terms of Watercare’s credit rating: obviously, this is a review going backwards. Obviously, I’ll be very generous and answer the member’s question, but, ultimately, that will be determined as part of its separation when that separation is finalised, as the member will know.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question put to him and addresses it on its own terms, locating the answer in the timing of the separation. It engages the question squarely rather than pivoting, though it supplies no figure and leaves two of the three questions asked untouched — the vagueness is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "what is the projected credit rating of Watercare after the announcement he made on Sunday?"

acuity.statement: It’s extraordinary to hear those sorts of responses. But I do note that he didn’t answer one of my questions, so I’ll repeat it: does he agree with the Prime Minister that all local government needs to do is to stop doing “dumb stuff”, and does he agree that the rating system as it stands is currently unsustainable?
acuity.explanation: Audits the answer just given against what was asked, identifies the specific omission, and re-puts the unanswered question verbatim. This turn is wholly determined by the content of the reply it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "A number of quick answers to some questions. In regards to affordability of rates rises, in particular in the water context, in terms of—we’ll be introducing economic regulation to ensure that consumers are paying appropriate prices and to maintain investment."

acuity.statement: Well, I would agree that councils should not do dumb stuff, and also, when you think about it—and I just made the point earlier—we want councils to be focused on must-haves, not “nice-to-haves”, and that’s exactly what we’re doing as a Government.
acuity.explanation: Answers the re-put question directly with a yes and explains what he takes it to mean, so the reply turns on exactly what was asked. He then returns to prepared framing about must-haves and the inflation inheritance, and the second limb on the sustainability of the rating system still goes unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "does he agree with the Prime Minister that all local government needs to do is to stop doing “dumb stuff”"

acuity.statement: But I’d like to move from the structural to infrastructure, because there are 17 recommendations, as the member for the Greens mentioned, in that report. Many drop in the word “wellbeing” every second sentence, but none around infrastructure, none about actually delivering the quality roads and pipes and opening up opportunities for development that people need if they are indeed to have any wellbeing at all.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the same report the Green member put in play and contests what it contains, arguing its recommendations are full of wellbeing and empty of infrastructure. That is one strand of her material taken up, but her actual argument — about referendums and consultation as democracy — is left alone while he moves to prepared Kāpiti and Horowhenua material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "The Future for Local Government report—we heard much about a wider vision of democracy for local government that included citizen participation."

acuity.statement: Does the Minister of Local Government have concerns that councils do not have adequate resources to fulfil their civil defence and emergency management duties?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive answer from Simeon Brown on the three-waters approach and the future of local government review, but engages none of its content — it acknowledges that he answered and then opens an unrelated area on natural hazards. On the broad matter under debate (local government) but indifferent to what preceded it; the only echo is re-using his word 'woke', which is a reference rather than an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the future of local government review 'ended up finding all the woke answers rather than actually dealing with some of those actual challenging issues', and this question does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’m keen to sort of ask a question the Minister alluded to in his answer previously; he talked about democracy.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's preceding answer — his framing of 'democracy' and communities having their say — and presses it on a concrete case (the appointed commissioners at Tauranga City Council), before moving into prepared local material about Tauranga's prospects. Engagement is explicit and pointable, but it develops the Minister's theme rather than testing any specific claim he made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'let’s start with the word "democracy" and let’s ensure that people are able to have their say' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: It’s really important that councils do play that role, and ultimately that’s why my message to local government is to focus on the must-haves, not the “nice-to-haves”. And so that’s the focus that we expect from local government.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Wade-Brown raised — whether councils can discharge civil defence duties — and offers a relevant proposition (prioritise core spending), which is an implicit answer to a resourcing question. But it does not take up her specific claim that smaller councils employ no specialised emergency staff, nor the NEMA chief executive's evidence she cited, and gives no yes/no on whether resources are adequate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'smaller councils do not employ any specialised civil defence and emergency staff' — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around Tauranga and local democracy, we are committed as the Government to restoring democracy. We are not extending the term.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies what Rutherford asked for: a statement of the Minister's intention on the commissioners' extended appointment to July 2024 and the return to elected local government in Tauranga. The answer would have been different had Rutherford asked about a different council or a different aspect, and it resolves the specific factual question put to him rather than restating the theme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'their appointment was extended to July 2024. I’m keen to understand the Minister’s priorities in the space around the return to local democracy and the use of appointed commissioners' — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: Just a couple of questions to the Minister over this whole democracy area. Would the Minister agree that we have seen quite a diverse set of councillors over the last year or two—last couple of years?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own 'democracy' framing and turns it into a test he had not addressed — whether Māori representation is part of that democracy — which is a glance at the preceding turn rather than an engagement with its content, since Brown's answer concerned Tauranga's commissioners and did not mention Māori wards. On the matter under debate with a pointable hook, but mostly new ground of the questioner's own choosing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we are committed as the Government to restoring democracy' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: And he mentions Matua Shane Jones’ nephew, Moko. Well, Moko is not elected as the mayor of the Far North on a Māori ward; he is elected as the Mayor of the Far North District Council in an open contest against every single other person who decides to put their name forward for elected office.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific example Jackson offered as evidence for Māori wards and dismantles its relevance — the mayoralty is not a ward seat, so the example cannot support the inference drawn from it. The reply is wholly dependent on what Jackson said and would have had to be written differently had he cited any other case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'We’re seeing Shane Jones’ nephew, for instance, as the mayor up there in the North' — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: In Tauranga, we have been unable to throw the buggers out. No matter what decision they have made, there has been no opportunity for the good people of Tauranga Moana to throw the buggers out. Well, I thank you for clarifying, Minister, that there will be full democracy returning to Tauranga in the elections on 20 July.
acuity.explanation: Builds on the Minister's just-given confirmation that the commissioners' term will not be extended and that Tauranga will elect its own council, and then presses the one thing he reserved judgment on — the commissioners' conduct, specifically their handling of the Māori ward petition. Genuine engagement with the preceding answer, though the opening is a prepared riff on 'throw the buggers out' and the jibe at colleagues' questioning engages nothing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'in July this year the residents of Tauranga will be able to elect their own mayor and elect their own councillors' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: How is that sustainable for the industry, let alone the environment, and what does the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries intend to do to ensure that New Zealand fisheries remain actually ecologically sustainable and viable?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on orange roughy sustainability, delivered immediately after Williams' question about the fisheries settlement bill. It is within the same examination, so it is on the broad subject, but it engages no part of the preceding argument and would be word-identical whatever Williams had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that the first version of the fisheries settlement bill, which had cross-partisan support, was a better option than what Te Ohu Kaimoana has proposed, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: On the question of orange roughy, I’m advised by the officials, on searching for the answer in this mammoth midden heap of paper, that in 2023-24, orange roughy 3B was reduced by 40 percent.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific stock raised in the preceding question and supplies a number responsive to the depletion claim, as well as addressing the second strand on MPA instructions. The answer would be different had Abel asked about a different fishery.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Evidence showed that the fishers were having to trawl for longer yet still not catching more fish, suggesting depletion" — Jones answers the specific stock Abel named (ORH 3B) with a quota figure.

acuity.statement: We still haven’t had an answer from the Minister to industry transformation plans and the time frame for the taihoa on cameras on boats. Perhaps he’s still looking through his mammoth heap of paper there to find the answer.
acuity.explanation: Engages the preceding turn at the level of whether it answered anything, and echoes its phrasing, but does not take up the substance of what Jones said before moving to a wholly new prepared question on the Oceans Secretariat. Partial engagement only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "on searching for the answer in this mammoth midden heap of paper" — Utikere picks up the Minister's own image and notes that earlier questions remain unanswered.

Partial engagement that can be pointed at: ~0.4.

acuity.statement: So just following on from the previous comments from the member to my right—Camilla Belich—I was interested in following on the line of questioning on workers’ rights and worker safety. I think worker safety is really important to unpack more, because, ultimately, we’re talking about companies that are making profits off the back of these workers—labourers—who often actually put their own lives at risk. This has been alluded to: New Zealand does have quite a high rate of workplace mortality. So I wanted to know whether the Minister thinks that the current resourcing of the labour inspectorate is enough to ensure employers are meeting their legal obligations to workers.
acuity.explanation: He explicitly picks up Belich's immediately preceding line of questioning: he restates her fatality-rate point and carries her resourcing-of-inspectors question forward, redirecting it from WorkSafe inspectors to the labour inspectorate and adding a conditional follow-up about increased funding. Mid-band: the engagement is pointable and would have had to change had she questioned on something else, but it extends rather than engages the substance of her claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "New Zealand has twice the workplace fatality rate of Australia" and her questions "in relation to the resourcing of WorkSafe and the number of inspectors that she intends to retain in those positions"

acuity.explanation: She names the questioner and supplies precisely the statistic he asked for — the share of labour inspectorate cases involving migrant exploitation — for the year under review, which is the rubric's paradigm case of engaging the specific thing just put. Not a full 1.0 because Twyford also asked three concrete policy questions (standardised employment contracts in construction, guaranteed weekly hours, an opt-out unionisation clause for RSE workers) and none of them is taken up anywhere in the reply; the engagement is with one strand of his turn, answered well.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Has she got numbers for cases involving migrant worker exploitation?"

I noted her comments on the previous Government, but I also wanted to know: will she guarantee that the number of WorkSafe inspectors will not decrease under her watch?
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn in this debate is Twyford's, and nothing here engages its content — she re-puts her own earlier question and then moves to prepared material on modern slavery. acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.responding_to: "the 90-day trial policy is not about making it easier to hire workers; it’s about making it easier to fire them" — Takutai Tarsh Kemp. Nothing: Kemp set out Treasury-commissioned research on trial periods, the fair pay agreement repeal and the 2 percent minimum wage increase, and this turn does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I also just wanted to touch on the different type of inspectors, which is the WorkSafe investigators raised by the member Camilla Belich, asking whether or not we can guarantee that the number of inspectors will increase rather than decrease. I just wanted to alert the member to the fact that, under the previous Government, which this review is about, the number of WorkSafe inspectors dropped from 211 to 195. At the same time, the head count for WorkSafe increased exorbitantly. So that is something that the previous Government did: they cut the number of inspectors while the number of people at WorkSafe increased. I have a great lot of faith in our new chair, board, and the CEO of WorkSafe, and I understand that at April 2024, WorkSafe started training another 19 inspectors to join their investigators.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific question about WorkSafe inspector numbers by name and supplies figures to it (211 to 195, 19 in training from April 2024), so the turn would have to change if she had asked something else. Short of full marks because it redirects the question to the previous Government's record rather than confirming whether the current cuts will spare front-line inspectors, which is the part Belich actually asked about. Whether the recasting of her question is fair, and whether the numbers are right, belong to Rigor and Veracity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether the statement still stands that front-line WorkSafe inspectors will not be impacted by the cuts to WorkSafe’s budget" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: I just wanted to touch a little bit on some comments about the 90-day trials and the minimum wage. Now, for anybody who might be listening or following along on TV, it might not be very obvious from some of the comments made that, under the previous Government, 90-day trials existed. So all of these terrible, terrible comments about 90-day trials; that was the previous Government’s policy.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Kemp raised and answers one strand of it — the framing that 90-day trials are this Government's doing — but leaves untouched the question actually put, which was what evidence supports the hiring and benefit-exit rationale against the Treasury-commissioned findings Kemp cited. Pointable partial engagement that then moves to prepared ground about the previous Government.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what evidence does the Minister have that shows that reducing 90-day trials will make it easier for businesses to hire people and lead to more people off the benefit and into work?" — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: When it comes to the minimum wage and explaining a little bit about how we landed at that 2 percent increase for this year, I think that was the right measure to make because it balanced the interests of both workers in a cost of living crisis as well as business owners who are finding it really, really tough at the moment even to make sure that they can pay their employees. And so we have made that balance, but also taking into account that over the last seven years, Consumers Price Index, or inflation, went up by around 25 percent. At the same time, under the previous Government, the minimum wage went up by 50 percent. That was really, really high in comparison to what the inflation rate was going up at. So we, as a Government, have sought to rebalance that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact decision and the exact comparison Kemp put — the 2 percent increase against inflation — and argues it on its own terms with a counter-comparison over seven years, so the answer is specific to the question asked. Not 1.0 because she neither accepts nor denies the real-terms-cut proposition itself and leaves Kemp's further questions on child poverty and a commitment to annual increases alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister accept that only increasing the minimum wage by 2 percent, when inflation is at 4.7 percent, is a cut to the minimum wage in real terms?" — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: In terms of the ships the member asked about, we will be putting standards in place. Now, whether or not people build a new ship to meet those standards or renovate a ship to meet those standards, they will need to meet the standards. The standards are the standards.

acuity.responding_to: "Given that animal live exports have accounted for 0.2 percent of our primary sector revenues since 2015 and the industry is now worth over $50 billion" — Jo Luxton

acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the factual move Hoggard had just made — that the photos are offshore animals without NZ NAIT tags and so irrelevant — by naming the vessel, its prior service from New Zealand shores, and its build date, which simultaneously rebuts his 'the standards are the standards' answer on ships. acuity.responding_to: Hon Todd McClay: "We’ve heard from Minister Hoggard on biosecurity and of course on animal welfare." — O'Connor takes up the Ministers' "gold standards" assurance on animal welfare and demands the mechanism behind it.

acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it — and she could have engaged either. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hon Damien O’Connor had just asked "how will New Zealand oversee those high standards in market when the animals arrive?" and this statement does not take it up, announcing instead a move to wallabies.

The wallabies have expanded past the boundaries where we’d want them. We aim to get them back over those boundaries, and once that’s achieved, then it’s a case of squeezing them down and eradicating them.

acuity.statement: Going back to the livestock exports and the mention of the Al Kuwait boat, what I would say is that when it was in Cape Town, it was carrying 19,000 head of stock; when it last left New Zealand, it was carrying 11,000. So that is part of the problem—you know, our standards were for much fewer animals on the boat. Those were our old standards, and we will, obviously, be updating those standards.
