acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "A momentous event called an election."

acuity.statement: Obviously, my officials did engage, but at the end of the day, judgment has to be exercised. Yes, an engagement did take place with representatives from the representative Māori organisations, but I have zero interest, both as a Māori parliamentarian and as a former chair of this organisation, to see those debates, that level of discord brought from recent Māori history into this Chamber.
acuity.explanation: The question had two parts — did the promised stakeholder engagement happen, and what in it led to leaving clauses 25 and 37 alone. Both are answered: engagement is confirmed with the representative Māori organisations named, and the reason for not amending is given as an unwillingness to reimport the urban-Māori/iwi discord. Fully determined by the preceding question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether or not that engagement with stakeholders took place or whether those were words that Ministers were able to say but weren’t able to fulfil"

acuity.statement: Can I turn to the proposed new section 162, which, effectively, provides rules or criteria around mandated iwi organisations in relation to actions related to the ability to sell settlement quota, noting that that would only take place under the new section 162 if the constitutional documents expressly allowed that the sale of the settlement quota was to take place, but also that the transaction would be in line with what was outlined in the specific requirements of the organisations’ constitutional documents.
acuity.explanation: Jones had just given a substantive answer — officials engaged, judgment was exercised, and he would not revive the urban-Māori/iwi discord — which was open to being tested. This turn abandons it entirely and opens a fresh line on section 162 and settlement quota sales. It remains squarely on the bill before the committee, so it is not a 0.0, but it engages no part of the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones answered that officials and representative Māori organisations were engaged and that he had zero interest in reviving that discord, and this statement does not take it up, moving instead to new section 162

acuity.statement: My question for the Minister is on the nature of reviews moving forward. How does he see this piece of legislation as informing whether the regularity of reviews would be questioned or not, where they would fall, and whether it’s an independent nature of the review, and, if so, in what circumstances it would be independent or otherwise?
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the Minister's previous answer as helpful but engages no part of its content, moving to a new aspect of the same bill. On-topic prepared questioning rather than responsive engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones answered on alienation of quota and said 'This bill does nothing to weaken that injunction', and this statement does not take that up — it thanks him and opens a fresh line on review independence.

acuity.statement: The reference to the review—yes, it was called operational. It has led to major—well, it has led to significant restructuring. It is my hope that future reviews are infrequent, not costly, and focus on boosting economic resilience and ensuring that the legacy remains intact for the mokopuna.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the regularity strand of the question directly (origin of the 12-year review period, his hope that future reviews be infrequent), but leaves the independence strand untouched and spends much of the turn on an aside about Pete Hodgson. Partial engagement you can point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'How does he see this piece of legislation as informing whether the regularity of reviews would be questioned or not' — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: One of the most significant changes that this bill would enact, and what the committee considered very carefully in the detail of it, is how it is appropriate to change the powers to appoint Te Ohu Kai Moana directors.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new strand on director appointments. It is squarely about the bill under consideration, so not zero, but the turn would read identically whatever the Minister had just said about reviews.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones had just spoken about the 12-year operational review period and his hope that future reviews be infrequent, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Te Ohu Kai Moana, when it was created, was built around an electoral college, and there was a sense that that diminished the right of iwi to directly participate in the governance direction, the governance nomination, and the governance voting process.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific thing asked: explains the existing electoral-college mechanism and why the bill shifts to direct iwi influence. Falls short of 1.0 because the requested assurance about the independence and capability of directors is not supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I want to invite the Minister to comment on the current state of the appointment of Te Ohu Kai Moana directors and then, in his view, how this legislation will change the appointment going forward' — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I take the Minister’s response around the nature of reviews being timely and frequent, cost is a factor, and resilience and economic productivity being increased as well. There is a suggestion with this piece of legislation that when reviews are undertaken, it’s at a time that is between seven and 10 years post enactment of the legislation, as is the case in relation to special resolutions that some organisations that are iwi-mandated may have, as is the case.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's stated criteria and then tests them against the bill's seven-to-10-year window, asking whether he is comfortable with it or would prefer a default period. The question could not have been written before hearing the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'It is my hope that future reviews are infrequent, not costly, and focus on boosting economic resilience' — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: That’s an uncharacteristically shrewd observation. I think that the point is well made. This was a National settlement, and it should be subject to a collaborative approach by all parties in the House because we all have a vested interest, given the great drama, promise, and compromise that was entered into at the time that this settlement was enacted.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the premise of the question and gives the reason — a cross-party settlement warrants a collaborative process for future amendment — which is exactly what was asked. Marked down slightly because the companion question on the seven-to-10-year frame gets only a jocular 'nine to 12 years'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'does he commit to ensuring that that follows a similar process, albeit timely, rather than it appearing in an omnibus bill' — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: But my final question for the Minister is around the commencement—since we’ve taken this all as one—and there is obviously feedback that the two-year time frame post - Royal assent for commencement is ideal in order to give time for the relevant changes and amendments to be made. My final question is whether the Minister believes that that two-year time frame is sufficient, and, if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: A fresh question on commencement timing that engages no part of the answer just given. It is on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones had just agreed that future changes should follow a collaborative all-party approach, and this statement does not take that up beyond thanking him before turning to commencement.

acuity.statement: As these exchanges draw to a close, I think the member is demonstrating a growing skill in protracting debates where perhaps there’s no substance. If only the earlier speaker on immigration had showed such shrewdness as he’s got.
acuity.explanation: Comments on the questioner's conduct and reaches for an unrelated immigration debate instead of engaging the commencement question. Nothing in it is about the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere asked whether the two-year post - Royal assent commencement period is sufficient, and this statement does not take up the commencement question at all.

acuity.statement: Yes, I do, and I’ve won a lot of cases—far more than you’ll ever win, right? I’ve won $7.5 million of cases, so I might know something about it. She’s defaming someone who’s got no chance to defend himself.
acuity.explanation: This is a cross-chamber exchange rather than an answer in the oral question cycle, so it is an acuity item. Swarbrick's interjection implied Peters has personal experience of defamation; he takes that exact implication up, concedes it, turns it into a claim of expertise, and uses it to press his own point that an allegation was made against an absent person. The reply would be different if she had interjected something else, so it is squarely responsive — the quality of the inference and its combative tone are matters for other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You know a bit about that." — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: This bill is nothing short of appalling. The speech made by the Minister was nothing short of disingenuous, and the entire rationale behind this bill is racially motivated. It is a disgrace—an absolute disgrace—to stand up in this House and present this as being about democracy when the changes apply only to Māori wards and are not about any other aspect of it.
acuity.explanation: Brown built his whole case on the bill being a restoration of democracy and taunted the opposition for fearing it. McAnulty takes that specific framing and attacks its premise directly: the democratic-choice mechanism is applied to Māori wards alone and to no other ward type, so the democracy rationale cannot be the real one. The speech would have had to change if Brown had argued the bill on different grounds, which is the test. Scored on engagement only — the insult to the Minister and the quality of the inference belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what have they got to be afraid of with democracy?" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Local government finally got an opportunity to put forward the idea of Māori wards in exactly the same way that they would consider any other ward. That is all that the change did—exactly the same way—and the Government is changing this, knowing that some communities will vote these out and deprive Māori of a voice.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests Brown's characterisation of the 2021 change: not a silencing of local voices but a move to treat Māori wards by the same council process as every other ward. It engages the specific factual claim Brown made about what the previous Government did, and draws out the consequence Brown left out. Not a full 1.0 because it restates the counter-characterisation rather than rebutting Brown's petition-threshold detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In 2021, the previous Government removed the binding polls that councils had to hold if they received a valid petition to decide on whether Māori wards would be established in their constituencies. By doing so, they also silenced local voices" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: He went around the country and promised local government that if National were elected, they would help them pay for their water. What did those members do when they got elected? They broke that promise.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on a different grievance. Nothing in Brown's speech touched water funding, and this passage would read identically whatever he had said about Māori wards; it could have been delivered in a Three Waters debate on another day. Low for unresponsiveness only — whether the broken-promise charge is true or on-policy is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about restoring binding polls on Māori wards and adjusting the local electoral timetable, and this passage does not take any of that up — it moves to a water-funding promise Brown never mentioned.

acuity.statement: If you were listening, you’d actually hear that I’m not so far away from your position, because I was the Mayor of Wellington when we actually introduced a Māori ward, and, actually, I was proud to be part of doing that.
acuity.explanation: Foster breaks off his prepared line to take up Lyndon's interjection directly: he accepts part of her framing (the 'rushed' charge, which he redirects onto Labour's own fast-track legislation) and answers the 'undermining Māori representation' strand by saying he himself introduced a Māori ward as mayor. He engages one strand of what she put to him rather than the specific claim about this bill's effect on Māori self-determination, then returns to his prepared argument about the plus-or-minus 10 percent rule, so this is a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "undermines the ability for Māori to determine representation" — Hūhana Lyndon (interjecting that the bill is rushed and undermines Māori determination of representation)

acuity.statement: The argument is that Māori wards will be the demise of democracy. To remove Māori wards is an assault on Te Tiriti, the only reason a democracy inclusive of Pākehā could ever exist.
acuity.explanation: Foster's speech made a concrete argument that Māori wards escape the plus-or-minus 10 percent population requirement, so a vote in a smaller Māori ward counts for roughly twice as much, with the Rotorua bill as his worked example. Kapa-Kingi gestures at the opposing case in the abstract ('the argument is that Māori wards will be the demise of democracy') and then answers it with a Te Tiriti counter-framing, engaging no part of the vote-weight reasoning actually put to her. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate but would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Democracy has a couple of fundamental things: one person, one vote" — Andy Foster. She restates the democracy argument in generic terms but does not take up his specific proportionality claim about ward populations and vote weight.

acuity.statement: Now, the other quote that came up just now was “This shouldn’t be a surprise or a threat.” Well, why are Māori having a seat at councils a surprise and why is that a threat?
acuity.explanation: She lifts Costley's own framing device verbatim from the immediately preceding turn and turns it back on him, asking what exactly is surprising or threatening about Māori council seats. The sentence could not exist if Costley had opened differently, which is the mark of close engagement. (The inversion arguably shifts his subject from the bill to Māori representation, but that is a question about the quality of the inference, not about whether he was listened to.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill should be neither a surprise nor a threat" — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: We’ve also talked about the vote, the general vote, and absolutely there are Māori sitting in general seats around, obviously, in here, but around councils all around our country, and there will continue to be. That shouldn’t be a surprise. There are highly educated, intelligent, capable Māori in every industry in this country. However, what we also have is some Māori purely want to be the Māori voice voted for by the Māori people, and that has been supported by many councils.
acuity.explanation: This is the concede-then-dispute move on the specific claim Costley had just made: she grants that Māori do win general seats and will keep doing so, then denies the conclusion he drew from it, arguing that some Māori want to be a Māori voice elected by Māori voters. The passage is shaped around his figure-based argument rather than merely sharing its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Māori councillors fill general ward seats at a higher rate than the general population. They are already represented." — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: There was a comment that Māori voice would be deprived at the council table or in local government. Well, in my experience in local government, local government is the best example of Māori relationships, of engagement, of enactment, of enablement. So they have nothing to fear about losing voice in local government because local government, I would argue, are at best practice with local Māori relationships.
acuity.explanation: He names the claim made in the turn immediately before his — that Māori would be left without a voice at the council table — and answers that claim directly rather than pivoting away from it. The answer is an assertion from personal experience rather than evidence, which bears on the reasoning, not on responsiveness; the speech would have had to be written differently had the previous speaker not raised voice at the council table.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our level of participation is to bless chambers but not to have a seat or a voice in them" — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel

acuity.statement: This is about not just putting it through a 17-day process, as the last Government did in 2021—17-day process in 2021, rushed through without any consultation.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — her insistence that councils followed the correct process — and counters on process by pointing at how the 2021 law was passed, before returning to prepared material about submissions and middle New Zealand. It engages the process argument but not her actual point, which was about councils' own consultation rather than Parliament's timetable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the councils, the mayors, the chairs who have already written in to say, “We’ve been through that process.”" — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel

acuity.statement: Local communities should be given the opportunity to have a say on their own representation. Referendums on Māori wards allow local voters to make their own representation decisions. This bill is simply about restoring democracy to local communities.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows a long substantive speech by Arena Williams and delivers prepared material on the right subject. He asserts the bill restores local democracy, which is the opposite framing to hers, but he does not engage any part of her argument: not the 45 councils that adopted wards, not the claim that elected councils' own decisions are being overridden, not the mayors' letter, not the charge of divisiveness. His speech would read word-for-word the same whatever she had said, apart from being on the same bill, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 for the faint gesture at the local-democracy question she had raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that "These democratic decisions are being overridden by a central government who is determined not to let local governments make that decision for themselves" and that mayors warn the referendum option "will be hurtful and divisive", and this statement takes up neither claim.

acuity.statement: I also rise to question the timing. I think it’s far too short given that even with this rush, we’ve already had over 50 mayors sign a letter saying they don’t agree. I imagine that many of those councils and Local Government New Zealand, let alone iwi, hapū, and others, will want to speak.
acuity.explanation: She takes up Henare's specific strand — that the four-and-a-bit week select committee window is too short for the public to be heard — and does something with it, supplying her own evidence (over 50 mayors already signed a letter, plus councils, LGNZ, iwi and hapū who will want to be heard). That is engagement with the content of the preceding turn, not a mere reference to it. It is partial rather than full because the second half of her turn moves to a new point of her own, that the bill should be divided in two, which Henare had not raised. Agreement is scored as engagement here, in line with the rubric: the test is whether she took up the argument, not whether she disputed it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "my concerns around a truncated time frame without, seemingly, a far more clearer rationale" — and his question whether "the public" will get "the opportunity to find their voice on this very important matter".

acuity.statement: The long-term fiscal position and the long-term insights reports have been prepared. Treasury prepare those documents and they report to the Minister of Finance, and it’s quite interesting, actually, that the Auditor-General has recommended that Treasury consider whether those two reports should be put together as they are, or not. It also made some recommendations about how they could more effectively incorporate public feedback in the preparation of those documents.
acuity.explanation: Smith follows a substantive opening turn and is plainly in the same debate — he opens by calling the debate timely and works through the Treasury long-term insights report that Boyack flagged would be discussed. But this is prepared material on the right subject rather than engagement: he relays the Auditor-General's recommendations (combining the two reports, incorporating public feedback, model sensitivity, Super Fund assets in debt) without taking up, conceding or disputing any strand of the committee's criticisms that Boyack had just set out. His consultation point is sourced to the Auditor-General, not offered as a response to her consultation concern. Substituting a different argument on the same topic in the preceding turn would not have changed a word of this — a gesture at the debate, hence the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "Today, we will hear from committee chairs and members regarding three of the briefings that were prepared by Treasury, the Ministry for the Environment, and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development." — Smith takes up the Treasury briefing as the debate's subject matter but engages none of Boyack's actual arguments (that some briefings missed the big issues, that consultation was inconsistent and thin with migrant, rural and Māori communities, and that there should be more cross-agency briefings).

acuity.statement: Look, two things to say. One is, again, as I’ve said, I’ve been through rather a lot of the council’s representation reviews, and I think that what is not being recognised on the other side is that it’s not just our time frame that’s got to be considered but the councils’ collective time frames as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Edmonds' central claim — that the four-week select committee window is too short — and engages it directly by contesting which timetable is the binding one, arguing the councils' own representation-review clock also has to fit. He then expressly accepts part of her framing ("I know that the time frame is a short time frame") and even enlists her words at the close. The speech would have to change if Edmonds had argued something else about the referral; it is built around her timetable arithmetic rather than around prepared material. Not a full 1.0 because he does not rebut the specific step-by-step arithmetic (submission period, briefing, hearings, drafting) she laid out, instead supplying a competing consideration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "I really don’t believe the four-week period is justifiable on the condition that because there is an election next year; surely more than four weeks can be spent on the select committee."

acuity.statement: The second part, in speaking to Andy Foster’s point, is that the interest of allowing quality submissions actually saves time in the long run—if people have a good amount of time to be able to prepare their submission in the first place rather than having to rush it.
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance of Foster's argument rather than merely naming him: Foster said passing it quickly is what gives councils time to do the job properly, and Halbert turns that same consideration back — adequate submission time is what produces usable council submissions, and therefore saves time downstream. He names the councils Foster invoked and follows the consequence through to the committee's own questioning. Short of 1.0 because the engagement is one strand appended to a longer prepared passage about submission volumes and tikanga.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "my encouragement for you is to allow that to happen so that the councils, then, have a decent amount of time to engage with their communities and to do that twice and do it properly"

acuity.statement: I’d just take the point my friend across the House has just suggested, which is that Auckland said no. I think that’s neither here nor there in this situation, because Auckland is a huge part of New Zealand with a lot of people in it, and they don’t all say no, Cameron Brewer.
acuity.explanation: Stops her prepared Auckland material to take up an interjection and does something with its content — she disputes its relevance to the referral question and then attacks its premise, that a single Auckland position can stand for Aucklanders. The passage could not exist had Brewer not said what he said. Marked at 0.8 rather than 1.0 because the thing engaged is a one-line interjection rather than a developed argument, so there is less in it to answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer (interjection): "Auckland’s already said no."

acuity.statement: But there’s a couple of big insights and takeaways, and I absolutely agree with the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Megan Woods, about the importance of this House having a long-term approach, where we talk about long-term issues that are facing New Zealand, because I’m sure that the people who have elected us to represent them in this House of Representatives really do want us to deal with more than just the current day-to-day issues. But the long-term issues are going to affect us all, and it’s very easy to get caught up in an electoral cycle where it’s easy to kick the can down the road when it comes to dealing with long-term challenges.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Woods's argument — that the House needs a long-term, intergenerational frame — and does something small with it, supplying her own reason (electoral-cycle incentives make it easy to kick the can down the road). It engages the general proposition rather than any specific claim Woods made about the Public Service Act reports, public engagement or the combined fiscal statement, and then turns to her own prepared material on the report's pages. More than a bare reference, less than a rebuttal or development of a specific point: a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "That is the need to take an intergenerational view, and that is exactly what this work was about." — her argument that Parliament should use this debate to think beyond the petty politics of the day about the intergenerational future.

acuity.statement: Now, the previous speaker, the Hon Julie Anne Genter, might think that increasing taxes is a good thing, but if you’re printing a heck of a lot of money and you believe in modern monetary theory, I guess that is what you would think is a good thing.
acuity.explanation: Squarely aimed at the position Genter had just advanced — that New Zealand could learn from higher-taxing, higher-income OECD countries — and answers it with a counter-position that taxation suppresses the economy. The speech would have to change if Genter had argued something else, which is what responsiveness means here. It falls short of 1.0 because he never touches her actual evidence (the OECD tax-share comparison), instead restating her view in a form she did not use (money printing, modern monetary theory) before pivoting to his own side's creed. The weakness of that inference is a Rigor matter, not an Acuity one; the engagement itself is direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "most of the countries that have higher incomes per capita than New Zealand also have higher tax shares of GDP. So maybe we can learn from that" — her argument from Figure 34 that New Zealand's low tax-to-GDP share means higher tax is compatible with prosperity.

acuity.statement: I do agree with the previous speakers; I think this is a worthwhile exercise. We can be a bit tactical at times in this place. Things happen very fast, but we do need to be able to step back and look at the long-term drivers, the risks, the opportunities, things like the demographics, things like what our long-term fiscal position will be, so that we can make sound decisions as we go.
acuity.explanation: Patterson follows Luxton and gestures at the debate, endorsing the exercise in general terms and naming the same themes Luxton raised (demographics, the long-term fiscal position). But he engages no part of Luxton's actual argument — not the forecast net worth of −137 percent of GDP, not the monetary-inflation account of building costs, not the claim about the previous government's RMA and Building Act reforms. He then moves to his own prepared material on productivity, the primary sector and Fonterra's brands divestment, which would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Luxton had said. A gesture at the matter under debate rather than a partial engagement with the argument, so the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "this long-term insights briefing is a piece of the tool kit that this Government will use to make this country a better country" — and Luxton's earlier material on the long-term fiscal position and demographics.

acuity.statement: As the newly minted committee chair, it’s a pleasure to be participating in this, the first parliamentary debate on the long-term insights briefings that were part of the last Parliament’s work programme.
acuity.explanation: Simpson speaks third, after substantive turns from Luxton and Patterson, and delivers a prepared account of the Ministry for the Environment's long-term insights briefing and the previous committee's criticism of it. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the briefings themselves — which keeps it above the floor, and he acknowledges the debate as the first of its kind. But he takes up no strand of either preceding argument: nothing on Patterson's Fonterra statutory-powers point or productivity, nothing on Luxton's fiscal and housing claims. Delete Patterson's turn and substitute a different argument and this speech is unchanged, so it sits low in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson argued that Fonterra is a creature of statute created by this House in 2001 and should be called before the Finance and Expenditure Committee over its brands divestment, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: In this document—which, to me, wasn’t full of beautiful, glossy graphs; it was full of challenges that our land is under pressure.
acuity.explanation: Bennett takes Simpson's specific characterisation of the briefing — glossy, pretty pictures, warm words stating the obvious — and directly contradicts it on its own terms, saying the document was not glossy graphs but a catalogue of pressures on the land, then begins itemising those pressures (ecosystems, soil, climate change, invasive pests and diseases) as the evidence. He also challenges whether Simpson read it. Substitute a different critique of the briefing before this turn and the speech would have to change, which is the mark of real engagement; the jab about whether Simpson read the document is a civility question, not an acuity one, and disagreement of this kind is the strongest evidence of having listened. Short of 1.0 only because he rebuts the characterisation rather than the committee quotation Simpson rested it on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "it had lots of very nice warm words, lots of aspirational goals, lots of pretty pictures" and his claim that the briefing "did not actually, as the report says, go beyond stating the obvious".

acuity.statement: Our isolated island, as we’ve heard, is a biodiversity hotspot and it’s something to be celebrated, but we know that so many species—4,000—are threatened and at risk of extinction.
acuity.explanation: Pham explicitly marks the pick-up ("as we’ve heard") and takes up one strand of Bennett's preceding speech — the biodiversity-hotspot framing and his 4,000 threatened-species figure — restating and endorsing it rather than doing anything further with it, before returning to her own prepared material on this Government's decisions. Pointable partial engagement, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "we’re a hotbed for the beauty of what nature and the environment provide" and his citation of the 4,000 threatened native species

acuity.statement: We’ve heard from the Labour member that people should go out and read this report back from the Environment Committee. Well, I have to say, I’ve gone through it and it’s just a word salad.
acuity.explanation: Takes Bennett's specific exhortation to read and understand the report, reports having done exactly that, and disputes its premise by quoting the report's own language ("Futures thinking is critical to … environmental steward and system[s] leader") to argue it is unintelligible to the people Bennett addressed. The speech would have to change if Bennett had not made that call. Scored on engagement only — the derisive framing is a civility matter and the quality of the inference a rigor matter, neither of which belongs here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "all of us, on all sides of the House, need to make sure we read this, we understand it, but then of course we put this into practice"

acuity.statement: What we need to do—and what ACT and this coalition Government with National and New Zealand First are doing—is focus on replacing the Resource Management Act with a system based on property rights, because it’s only with true property rights that you can create wealth in a society, and it is only with wealth in a society that you can secure a healthy, prosperous, and sustainable environment.
acuity.explanation: Pham put a direct charge about imminent Government decisions favouring corporations and lobbyists; Luxton's closing asserts the coalition's RMA-replacement programme as prepared party material without engaging that charge, or Bennett's, at any point. But it is one strand only: the bulk of the turn is an explicit recap of his own previous speech ("I previously spoke about what this bill was really about") and it does not take up Brooking's immediately preceding point about the clause 12 detention-premises amendment, nor Bates's lawyer-capacity argument. Partial engagement, below the midpoint because the strand taken up is a passing framing claim rather than the argument of the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "I just want to acknowledge the work of the Minister of Immigration in getting this through the House, something that wasn’t able to be achieved under the previous Government."

acuity.statement: I, too, don’t disagree with the technicalities of the ruling that you have made and don’t wish to challenge you on the ruling at all. I have seen successive Speakers—I believe including yourself—have the respect and the wisdom and the discretion of understanding that the stand that was made yesterday by a rangatira of Whakatōhea was a mana-uplifting stand for this House and was a respect for this House and all of its representatives in it on the passing of a very significant bill that, after 100-plus years of raupatu and Crown breaching of their lands, asking for some minutes or seconds of a whakamana mihi to this House.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Hipkins' structure — accept the technical ruling, dispute the handling — and his mana-of-the-House strand, extending it to the rangatira's stand. But she does not take up his specific claim about past practice (that waiata from the gallery have long included karakia); she moves to her own argument about discretion and cultural understanding, so it is partial engagement rather than a reply to his point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Whilst I accept the ruling that you have made, and I don’t wish to challenge you or your ruling, I do want to make sure that in the future we don’t undermine what is an occasion where the Parliament comes together in the spirit of unanimity"

acuity.statement: This is the challenge to you, it’s about tikanga and whether the Assistant Speaker at the time would have ended up in that predicament if she had used the tools that are available to her to ensure that she was getting the cultural advice that the Speaker deserves to have.
acuity.explanation: Takes Davidson's cultural-understanding-and-discretion point and sharpens it into a specific mechanism — the advice the presiding officer could have sought — and adds the tikanga/Standing Orders distinction. Not a full 1.0 because the thrust of his contribution is aimed at the ruling itself rather than at anything Davidson claimed, and it would survive largely unchanged had she argued differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "I would have expected that there is a basic minimum cultural understanding that the discretion allows and understands the vein and the wairua of what was being offered."

acuity.statement: When the inevitable discussions take place, either this is a House of Representatives serving the primary purpose of us who are democratically elected, or circuitously it’s going to change. It cannot change and should not change unless we abide by what you have to say.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the framing Waititi had just set up — that the Standing Orders were satisfied but tikanga was breached — by asserting the primacy of the House's own rules and of mandated change over practice that drifts. It engages the strand but not the tikanga substance of the claim, and then turns to his own anecdote about the message he sent to Whakatōhea, so it is a partial rather than a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "It may not be a breach of Standing Orders, but it’s absolutely a breach of tikanga to ask somebody to sit down whilst doing a waerea or a karanga."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Mr Speaker, I heard your ruling. This is a very important kaupapa for our people. I was listening to Minister Jones. The tikanga of this House has changed considerably through the years. We never had babies being nursed in the Speaker’s Chair before—never.
acuity.explanation: Names Jones, then rebuts his premise with a counter-example: if unmandated change is the objection, the House's practice has already changed considerably, babies in the Speaker's Chair being the instance. The speech would have to be different had Jones not argued that change must be mandated, which is the test. Short of 1.0 only because he does not address Jones' point about the rules themselves.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "a creeping level of change in the House that has not been mandated within the rules of the House"

acuity.statement: My final plea is that the disorder was actually created when the Assistant Speaker failed to use her discretion to allow for the mihi to go through. The disorder and the escalation actually began as a result of many other MPs recognising the harm of her call.
acuity.explanation: Expressly a response to Jones, and it does something with his claim rather than merely referencing it: it relocates the cause of the disorder from the visitors' departure from practice to the presiding officer's refusal to exercise discretion, and recasts the escalation as members reacting to that call. Directly contests his causal account.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "I think the situation reflects both poor communication but also a creeping level of change in the House that has not been mandated within the rules of the House."

acuity.statement: That’s what you’ve got in this coalition Government: a Government that is very prepared to get into the back office to save some money; get it to the front line. That’s what we’ll find with Budget 2024. We’ve got one more sleep to go. What you’re going to see is a Budget 2024 that will prioritise investment into public services. It will deliver personal tax reduction and deliver savings to get this country’s books back on track; a Government that I’m proud to be part of, that will invest more into front-line services.
acuity.explanation: Doocey follows a substantive turn by Goldsmith on tax thresholds, bracket creep and the 80 percent spending increase, so he is eligible. His speech is prepared material about his own portfolio announcements and the coming Budget — on the matter under debate (Budget 2024, tax relief, spending discipline), which keeps it out of 0.0, but it engages no part of Goldsmith's argument: no figure of his is used, disputed or extended, and the speech would read identically had Goldsmith argued something entirely different about the Budget. The closing gesture at 'personal tax reduction' names the shared theme without taking up any claim, which is a reference rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith argued that tax thresholds have been unchanged for 14 years so that 40 percent inflation lifted the median earner's average tax rate from 15 to 21 percent, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: We have a Crown who has prioritised its coalition agreement above its obligations to te iwi Māori e tātou mā—no consultation with te iwi Māori for these widespread changes to legislation that hit us under urgency. There is a duty to act in good faith, and yet the Government fails its obligations to te iwi Māori.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows a substantive turn by Hipkins in the same take-note debate, so she is eligible, but her speech engages no part of his argument: not the Budget numbers, not the tax cut promise, not the cost-of-living drivers. It is prepared material on the Government's Treaty record and would read word-for-word the same whatever Hipkins had said, and indeed could have been delivered in a different debate on a different day. A gesture at the chamber's business keeps it just above 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins spoke about tomorrow's Budget — the $250-a-fortnight tax cut promise, the $2.9 billion in landlord tax breaks and the rents/insurance/rates drivers of inflation — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Across there, the message hasn’t changed. Even in Opposition, they’re attacking farmers. They don’t get farmers, they don’t get rural New Zealand; we do and we’re proving it.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne follows a substantive speech by Prime on Oranga Tamariki cuts and the back office/front line definition, and engages none of it: her speech is a prepared set-piece on agriculture, red tape, market access and farmer wellbeing that would be word-for-word identical whatever Prime had said. The only gesture across the House — a generic claim that the Opposition is 'attacking farmers' — names a target rather than engaging any claim actually made, which the rubric treats as a mere reference, not partial engagement. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it does address Government policy within the same debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime spoke about the Oranga Tamariki restructuring proposal, the 447 proposed job cuts and the Minister of Finance's pre-election promise to exclude the agency from savings, and this statement does not take any part of it up.

acuity.statement: What we’ve heard is the chorus of victimhood. We’ve not heard from the Māori Party; we’ve heard from a party of radical extremists—so motivated in their commitment that they couldn’t even file their own question today.
acuity.explanation: Opens by characterising the speech he has just heard, so it is not generic, but it engages no part of Ngarewa-Packer's actual argument — it labels her speech 'victimhood' and pivots to a separate jab about a missing oral question. That is a reference to the previous speaker rather than engagement with her content, which sits in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "this is a Government that has unleashed an unholy or ruthless assault on Māori" — he characterises her speech as victimhood without taking up the claim.

acuity.statement: They actively call the Government a Pākehā Government with Pākehā laws when two of the three leaders of the coalition are Māori and there are a record number of Māori in Cabinet—far more than they’ll ever have or they’ve ever had.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what she argued — that the Kāwanatanga is an alien, anti-Māori power dismantling Māori kaupapa — and answers it with a counter-fact about Māori leadership in the coalition and Cabinet. It engages the topic and the thrust rather than any specific claim she made (she did not use the phrase 'Pākehā Government' in this turn), and then returns to prepared material, so it is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "We have let the Kāwanatanga think that it has more power than it deserves, whānau mā." — he answers the characterisation of the Government as a non-Māori power.

acuity.statement: And let me tell you, some of you: we’re not listening to you. You show me one thing you’ve ever done for your people. Show me one thing you’ve ever done for your people.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific claim she had just made about who did the fighting for Māori advancement — her assertion that it was 'our own people' and people 'like myself, who were raised in the rangatiratanga and actually battled for these kaupapa'. He disputes exactly that credential and demands she name what she has done, so the speech would have to change if she had claimed something else. Scored on engagement only; the civility and reasoning quality of the challenge are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "in fact, it was our own people who did that battle" / "actually battled for these kaupapa" — he challenges her claim to that record of struggle.

acuity.statement: From the other side of the House, we hear these grand gestures of equity. One need only look at the data to show where funding needs to go in order to make sure that equity is achieved.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long substantive turn by Peters and gestures at 'the other side of the House', but engages none of his argument; it is prepared Budget material about Māori funding levels that would read identically whatever Peters had said. It stays on the matter under debate, so it is not a 0.0 — a gesture at the debate without engagement is a 0.2, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters argued the Māori Party are separatist extremists with no record of service to Māori, and this statement does not take any of that up — it moves to last year's Budget figures.

acuity.statement: Tomorrow will be a great day for Mt Roskill and a great day for New Zealand because we will deliver a Budget which will help our working class. Our Budget will rebuild the economy, restore law and order, and deliver on public services like health and education.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows Peeni Henare, who made a detailed, itemised case that Budget 2023 spending (Whai Kainga Whai Oranga, Whanau Ora, the $132m for Maori health, $225m for Maori education) delivered outcomes and that this Government is removing it, and who directly challenged the health Minister to back his Iwi-Maori Partnership Boards talk with money. Cheung takes up none of that: no figure is contested, no claim corrected, nothing conceded. The speech is prepared electorate-and-Budget material that would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had said. It is at least on the matter under debate (tomorrow's Budget and its contents), so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0 — but there is no gesture at the preceding argument at all, which is why it is 0.1 and not 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that last year's Budget investments ('in last year's Budget, $132 million was put forward for Maori health') closed equity gaps and that the National-led Government is scrapping them, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I don’t rise to say too much, to be frank, because I think this is a matter that we’re in agreement with. It is updating a will that was settled nearly 120 years ago. Maybe I’ll just give the member an opportunity to elucidate for any of those watching in the Chamber just what the intention is in terms of expanding it from its original purposes, to who it can support—those changes that this bill will allow.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific thing Webb had just described — that the century-old deed referred to 'destitute women of good character' and is being updated — and asks him to spell out the expansion of purposes. The turn would be different if Webb had introduced the bill differently; it is a direct invitation to elaborate on his own stated objective rather than prepared material. Not a 1.0 because it adds no argument or figure of its own.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'This bill is really a bill which tidies up the purposes of the McLean Institute trust deed because it’s a deed that’s over a century old, it made reference to "destitute women of good character"'

acuity.statement: The original trust deed had two classes of women who were able to be supported: one, in respect of the majority of the assets, was women of good character and high social standing who had fallen on hard times, and the other was destitute women—basically, the lower classes. Clearly, in the modern world, that’s not appropriate. The new deed, in modern language, simply says any woman who’s in need of financial support can be supported by the trust fund.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the elucidation Mooney asked for: the two original classes of beneficiary, why they are no longer fit, and the replacement wording. The content is wholly determined by the question just put; it could not have been delivered in any other debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: 'an opportunity to elucidate ... just what the intention is in terms of expanding it from its original purposes, to who it can support'

acuity.statement: I’m just confirming that the charitable purpose has been expanded to assist any women in the Canterbury area who are in need of support, regardless of social status, formal education, or other characteristics?
acuity.explanation: Restates Webb's answer back as a precise proposition to be confirmed, converting 'any woman who's in need of financial support' into a test of whether social standing and education no longer bear on eligibility. The question exists only because of the answer immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'The new deed, in modern language, simply says any woman who’s in need of financial support can be supported by the trust fund.'

acuity.statement: Yeah, that’s exactly right. The deed itself refers to the region, and you’re right: the region is the Canterbury region. The trustees are various dignitaries, including, I think, the Bishop of the Anglican Cathedral.
acuity.explanation: Confirms the proposition put to him, and specifically picks up the one element Mooney added that he had not himself mentioned — the Canterbury region — verifying it against the deed before volunteering a related detail. Squarely engaged with the content of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: 'confirming that the charitable purpose has been expanded to assist any women in the Canterbury area who are in need of support'

acuity.statement: Now, we just felt that the phrase “and is otherwise to be interpreted in its broadest possible sense” could have possibly been a bit of a concern due to its vagueness and could lead to misinterpretation and some potential bias.
acuity.explanation: On the bill under debate and on a named clause of it, but engages no part of the exchange it follows — the preceding turns settled the classes of women supported and the Canterbury region, and none of that is taken up. This is prepared amendment material that would read identically whatever Webb and Mooney had just said to each other.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb and Joseph Mooney had just established which classes of women the expanded deed covers and that the region is Canterbury, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her contribution. The trust deed has been carefully reviewed, and I don’t think there is any lack of clarity in the proposed deed, in clause 1.1.17. It is really just making sure that although you’ve got a trust which is predominantly for the protection of women in need, that any child can fall within that, regardless of whatever gender they are.
acuity.explanation: Meets Unkovich's objection on its own ground: addresses the exact clause she cited, denies the specific defect she alleged (vagueness), and explains what the contested breadth wording is there to do. The reply would have to change entirely had she raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: 'the phrase “and is otherwise to be interpreted in its broadest possible sense” could have possibly been a bit of a concern due to its vagueness'

acuity.statement: So this amendment bill, when passed—and I really would love to acknowledge our Green colleagues in the House for the change of heart that they’ve had, and I thank them for sharing the process of that thought—will mandate a number of specific requirements.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn in which Carter explained why the Greens shifted to supporting the bill (the Stanford amendments on Police-Customs information sharing, and the rehabilitation answers in committee). Nakhle notes the Greens' "change of heart" and later says information sharing was heard about "earlier", but she does nothing with the content of Carter's reasoning — no engagement with the amendments Carter cited, the rehabilitation point, or the unity argument. The rest is a prepared third-reading recap of the bill's clauses and the Bill of Rights section 7 objections, which would read identically whatever Carter had said. That is a courteous reference plus on-topic prepared material: a gesture at the debate, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "Our caucus agreed to change our position to support, and we are satisfied with these amendments and we will be supporting this bill."

acuity.statement: The protection through the prevention of further harm to tamariki that may occur at the expense of already registered offenders who travel outside of Aotearoa—this I absolutely support, and so do we as the party: the protection of tamariki and their oranga. Prevention and protection are our key drivers, especially in the context of our mokopuna.
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by Unkovich immediately precedes this one, so the statement is eligible. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the bill's regulation of registered offenders travelling overseas — and gestures at the debate by stating a position on the bill's protective purpose, which places it in the 0.3 band. But it engages no part of Unkovich's actual argument: it neither takes up the deterrence reasoning, nor the rights-of-the-offender point she raised and answered, nor any figure or claim she made. The surrounding speech is personal background and a prepared pivot to section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and would read word-for-word the same had Unkovich made a different argument on the same bill. Scored low for unresponsiveness only — not for being about the Government's record (that is Focus) nor for the quality of the 7AA comparison (that is Rigor).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich argued that the bill's extra reporting requirements could act as a deterrent during "a temporary lapse of reason" and that child safety "does outweigh the privacy or the equal protection of the sex offender", and this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: I’m wondering if the member will support that, and, if not, can he—because I understand that in his view, the cellar door must be close to the vineyard, but that’s not how I read the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up the specific account Stuart Smith has just given of what the bill does for winery cellar doors, tests it against the actual clause 4 definition, states where he thinks Smith's stated intention and the drafting diverge, and puts a direct question back to him — inviting correction if his reading is wrong. The speech could not have been delivered without Smith's preceding explanation; substitute a different rationale and it would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "This bill allows winery cellar doors to hold an on-licence and an off-licence simultaneously." / "So I’m quite happy to take questions on this matter."

acuity.statement: I have got a couple of things I want to work through, but I’ll just focus on one of them at the moment because it’s connected to the one raised by the Hon Duncan Webb, and that is my amendment on the floor which is at clause 4 and it’s the definition of cellar door from produce harvested from the land on which the retail premises is situated. So it’s a very similar problem that I’m seeing.
acuity.explanation: White does more than name Webb: she takes up the substance of his point about the geographic disconnect in the clause 4 definition and states her own variant of it, and she engages Stuart Smith's stated purpose ("I can see you're trying to support your region") in order to argue the logic should extend further. She then moves to prepared material on her second amendment about breweries, which engages nothing that preceded, so this is a substantial but partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the retail premises are located no more than 10 kilometres from where the main ingredients were grown or the wine was manufactured"

acuity.statement: With the awareness that this law change could impinge on human rights of registered sex offenders in terms of exposing them to more punishment, there have been steps proposed and accepted by the Justice Committee to ensure that all registered offenders are aware that this bill is going to happen.
acuity.explanation: Garcia's speech is overwhelmingly prepared material describing the bill's reporting requirements and the 'walking into the darkness' theme, which would have been identical whatever Webb said. But in his closing paragraph he does take up one strand of the preceding turn: Webb had argued at length that the House should pause over the Attorney-General's view that the retroactive application of the register to already-sentenced offenders is an unjustified limitation on rights. Garcia answers that strand on the merits — delayed commencement so police can inform everyone affected, and an explicit defence of the retroactive reach ('there can be no one staying in the darkness'). It is the topic rather than Webb's specific claim about the s7 report and the punitive/protective distinction, and it arrives after the prepared body of the speech, which places it at the mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I do think this House should absolutely pause when the Attorney-General says" — Duncan Webb, on the human rights report and the retroactive imposition of the register on already-sentenced offenders

acuity.statement: What I would like to do is acknowledge that those stories that have come up from people in the House who’ve had a direct and personal connection with this issue will be the tip of the iceberg.
acuity.explanation: White follows two substantive turns with content to engage — Webb's human rights argument and Garcia's account of the bill's reporting requirements — and engages neither. Her call is a generic gesture at the debate (acknowledging other members' personal stories, thanking the Greens, calling it a sober debate) plus a pivot to her own prepared ask about Budget funding for internet safety. The speech would read identically whatever the previous two speakers had argued; a mere nod to 'stories that have come up from people in the House' is a reference, not engagement with any claim. Above 0.0 only because it is squarely about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paulo Garcia set out the bill's overseas reporting requirements and defended its retroactive application, and Duncan Webb argued the Attorney-General's human rights report should not be lightly disregarded; this statement takes up neither

acuity.statement: I’m keen to talk further about the point that the member Mr Stuart Smith raised in his response there, particularly around the Amendment Paper put forward by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, around amending clause 4 and the outline that Mr Webb has put in around an amendment in the sense that the retail premises are located no more than 10 kilometres from where the main ingredients were grown or the wine was manufactured. Now, I’m interested to hear your perspective on that, Stuart, particularly because I can think of a couple of circumstances where you have the winery in a particular location and you may have the tastings done somewhere else.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Smith's own discussion of Dr Webb's Amendment Papers and carries it onto the clause 4 distance amendment, putting a concrete workability objection (winery and tasting room in different places) directly to the member. It engages the strand Smith opened rather than the specific tasting-volume point he made, so it is a strong partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "I note that one of Dr Webb’s Amendment Papers alludes to having beer available in a tasting size of 115 millilitres versus 35 millilitres for wine, but beer can have alcohol levels similar to wine."

acuity.statement: On this point of the nexus, I’m also interested in this and I think the committee would benefit from the member Stuart Smith expanding on this definition of “winery cellar door”. The member has already explained that the licensing authority in clause 7 has to have an opinion about this, and he’s explained that well, but it goes back, then, to the definition of “winery cellar door”.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly accepts the part of Smith's answer that worked — the clause 7 licensing-authority opinion — and then presses the step it leaves unresolved, the statutory definition the licensing officer must interpret. This is classic accept-part-and-push-further: the speech could not have been given without Smith's preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "So you would have to convince the licensing authorities that it was a valid cellar door."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Well, firstly, to Tom Rutherford’s question—that a very good question. We had evidence from Olivia Doonan from Tūpari Wines, and their vineyard’s in the Awatere Valley and it’s quite remote. They have a cellar door in the railway station at Seddon, which is 13 kilometres away.
acuity.explanation: Answers Rutherford's question about the proposed 10-kilometre limit with a specific counterexample from select committee evidence that falls just outside it, which is doing something concrete with the exact figure put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "is the 10-kilometre radius actually functional and workable here in New Zealand, or is it just setting an arbitrary location and distance"

acuity.statement: Well, Queenstown and Bannockburn is probably a bit far, I would have thought. But I would have thought Bannockburn and then on the road at Cromwell would be quite acceptable.
acuity.explanation: Takes Brooking's two hypotheticals on their own terms and gives a direct ruling on each, naming where in her example the line would fall. The answer is unintelligible without her question, which is the test of responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "So if you have a wine grown—say, a very fine pinot noir in Bannockburn—and you are selling that in Queenstown or somewhere on the road nearby, does the member imagine that that would count as a winery cellar door?"

acuity.statement: I’m particularly interested in whether you can expand the definition of “wine”. I think the question of location and distance—not having anything there is a bit dangerous, but I’m not certain of the 10 kilometres radius, either, at the moment. So if you could enlarge on those points.
acuity.explanation: Glances at the distance argument running through the preceding turns and takes a position on it, but the bulk of the contribution is her own prepared line of questioning about cider, perry and craft brewers rather than engagement with the radius objections Smith had just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "Often, vineyards can be owned by the same person growing for the same winery and they can be more than 10 kilometres apart."

acuity.statement: The issue is that wine is defined in the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act, so it has to be referred to in that way. We can’t expand the definition of it in this bill. So you could bring in a member’s bill for ciders and so on and have them treated similarly, but you wouldn’t be able to do it in the way this is being done in this bill. We know that because it was suggested by one of the members on the committee at a select committee, and the clerk said it would be out of scope of the bill and wouldn’t be able to be considered, so we didn’t do that.
acuity.explanation: Answers Wade-Brown's question about widening the definition of wine squarely, supplies the reason it cannot be done in this bill, and cites the clerk's scope advice from the committee she sat on. The reply is shaped entirely by what she asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "I’m particularly interested in whether you can expand the definition of “wine”."

acuity.statement: Not beer. Beer has the addition of hops, which is separately defined in the Act, but I’m just talking about Amendment Paper 32, which simply replaces “grape wine” in various places with “wine”.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact question just put to him, answers it directly in the negative, and supplies the statutory reason (hops being separately defined) before returning to his amendment. The reply would not exist if White had not asked; it is shaped entirely by her interjection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "And beer?"

acuity.statement: I appreciate the opportunity to make a call, and I thank our colleagues who have traversed and had a good kōrero about wine. I wanted to ask some questions around—I’ve been reading the commentary, but also clause 8 inserting new section 62A around snack food.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the preceding debate, but no part of Webb's argument about the wine definition or competitive disadvantage is engaged. The contribution is on the bill under consideration, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it is prepared material on a different clause and would read identically whatever Webb had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that Amendment Paper 32 removes an anti-competitive advantage for grape wine over cider and perry, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it acknowledges the "kōrero about wine" and then opens a separate question on clause 8

acuity.statement: “Snack food” is defined in regulation 10, and it includes items such as potato chips, crisps, biscuits, crackers, processed seeds, and nuts. But some wineries might choose to offer cheese and other types of food. So the whole purpose of this change is so cellar doors don’t have to become a restaurant.
acuity.explanation: Supplies precisely the thing the previous speaker said she could not find — the location of the definition and its contents — and then explains the purpose behind it. Had Sosene asked about a different clause, this answer could not have been given.

acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "because I couldn’t find it in here in terms of the definition around “snack food”"
