acuity.statement: Well, interesting you ask about the Budget, Madam Speaker—well, not you, obviously, asking, but the Opposition—because there are very key priorities in this portfolio that, again, aren’t mentioned much in this House, but are actually hugely significant for “New Zealand Inc”.
acuity.explanation: Belich's interjection asked a specific, answerable question: how much funding land information received in the Budget. Penk acknowledges that the question was asked and then pivots to the portfolio's 'key priorities' without engaging the content of the question — no figure, no appropriation line, no statement that he will not give one. This is a mere reference to the interjection rather than engagement with it, so it sits in the low band; it is above 0.1 only because the pivot stays on the portfolio's Budget treatment, which is the matter she raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How much did it get in the Budget?" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: I do want to start by saying something about health, actually—something celebratory about health, as we are celebrating a few things in the House tonight.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty's immediately preceding turn was an extended argument about health: a hiring freeze, 33 unfilled vacancies at Masterton Hospital, dropped minimum staffing levels, and the Government's silence on health in the Budget debate. Belich names health, which is a gesture at the debate she is following, but takes up none of it — she offers a celebratory aside about a youth service anniversary and then moves to prepared material on workers' rights for the remainder of the speech. Delete McAnulty's turn and substitute a different Budget argument and this speech would be essentially unchanged, which puts it in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder why, in a speech after this new Government's first Budget, they haven't mentioned health." — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: They are doing structured literacy, and they absolutely love it. Yeah, they are doing it.
acuity.explanation: Meager interjected a direct question about the school she had just mentioned, and she takes it up immediately and squarely, confirming the practice and adding how the pupils respond. The words exist only because of his question — substitute a different interjection and this line would have to change. It is brief and supplies no detail beyond the confirmation, which is why it is not a full 1.0, but it engages the specific content put to her rather than glancing off it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "Are they doing structured literacy?"

acuity.statement: I'm incredibly proud of this Budget. I'm incredibly proud of our Minister of Finance and our Prime Minister. It is a fiscally responsible Budget, the first one in seven years, I have to say.
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by a different member (Meager) immediately precedes this, so it is eligible. The opening engages no part of his argument — not the flood-funding rebuttal, not the Ashburton College figure, not the social investment pitch he explicitly asked the Opposition to support. It is prepared praise of the Budget and of the Minister of Finance that would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, with no gesture at the preceding contribution. It stays inside the band rather than at 0.0 only because it is at least about the matter under debate, the Budget. Note this is a judgement about responsiveness alone: the statement's politeness, its accuracy on 'the first one in seven years', and its vagueness are other attributes' business, not Acuity's.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager spoke at length about tax relief for working New Zealanders, the $200 million Regional Infrastructure Fund answer to Kieran McAnulty on stopbanks, Ashburton College's rebuild shortfall and the social investment approach, and this statement does not take up any of it.

acuity.statement: Like it or not, this is the three coalition parties doing exactly what we campaigned on, delivering on our promises to New Zealand. Now, you might not like it, but that is the fact of the matter.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows a substantive turn by Court and opens with prepared framing about the coalition delivering what it campaigned on. It gestures at the matter under debate (the bill as a campaign commitment), but engages no part of Court's argument about the 2021 process, the 5 percent poll threshold, or the select committee timeline. Substituting a different argument on the same topic in the preceding turn would not require a word of this to change, so it sits in the unresponsive band rather than at a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Court argued the 2021 Local Electoral (Maori Wards) amendment was rushed through with submissions closing two days after first reading, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: With over 10,000 submissions presented to the Justice Committee within a five-day period—only five days, that’s the lack of respect that this Government has to the people of New Zealand; 10,000 people and more put in submissions to the select committee so their voice could be heard, 10,000-plus.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows McAnulty's speech on the same bill, so she is eligible, but this is prepared material on the right subject rather than engagement with his argument. She opens her own evidentiary line (submission volume and the truncated committee timetable) and never takes up his central point about the referendum being applied to Māori wards and nothing else, nor his Speakers'-rulings argument. The speech would read almost identically had McAnulty argued something different about the same bill, so it sits in the low band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because her submissions material does glance at the strand McAnulty raised when he disputed the Minister's claim of a 'range of views'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Kieran McAnulty argued that the bill applies a referendum requirement to Māori wards alone and to no other ward, and that this meets the dictionary definition of racism; this statement does not take up that asymmetry argument. The nearest contact is McAnulty's "The Minister said there was a range of views. Rubbish."

acuity.statement: We sat there—come on, we sat for three days and we listened. And what? Maybe one or two opposed—those democracy groups that come on, like Hobson’s Pledge.
acuity.explanation: Meager challenged her submission claim with a direct question about how many submitters supported the measure and then told her to read the report. She takes the challenge up on its own terms rather than ignoring it, supplying her account of what the committee actually heard over three days and characterising the opposing side as 'maybe one or two' groups. That is engagement with the specific content of the challenge, and the passage would not exist if Meager had not interjected. It falls short of 1.0 because she answers from her recollection of the hearings rather than engaging the select committee report he pointed her to — that part of his challenge goes unanswered. Note this is scored purely on engagement: whether 'maybe one or two opposed' is accurate is a veracity question, and the dismissiveness toward the groups named is a civility question, neither of which belongs here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How many supported?" — James Meager (followed by his "Read the report.")

acuity.statement: So Māori wards have countered the crippling lack of understanding that exists within council and local government across the motu. By having dedicated Māori representation in councils, we can grow Māori participation in local elections and actually legitimise the actions of councils. This Government goes on about democracy, but how democratic can a system actually be if no one is paying any attention to it?
acuity.explanation: Foster's immediately preceding speech made two detailed arguments: that the plus-or-minus 10 percent vote-value rule is breached by the Schedule 1AA rounding formula (Wellington: 0.609 entitlement rounded to one councillor, 1.67 weighting, 888 first preferences vs 3,123-4,277), and that Māori wards did not lift turnout but lowered it. Kapa-Kingi opens on the same bill and the same theme of democracy and participation, and asserts the opposite of his turnout point, but she does not take up his figures, his reading of section 19V, or his claim that turnout fell — this is prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at his democracy framing rather than an engagement with his argument. Scored on engagement only; the truth of her participation claim and the quality of her reasoning are not what acuity measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "Labour's minority view said the existence of Māori wards or seats increases voter turnout, and I thought, 'Actually, I agree with that.'" — and his conclusion that "The turnout in the Māori ward was very, very low." Kapa-Kingi asserts Māori wards grow participation without taking up his evidence that it did the reverse.

acuity.statement: We heard some amazing submissions. Some were pretty emotional about it because they felt attacked. There were a few who seemed to be misled, whether it was deliberate or otherwise.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Kapa-Kingi's preceding account of the select committee hearings — the character and emotional tenor of the submissions — and adds her own reading of them (some submitters were misled). It then returns to prepared Green Party material on one person, one vote, the ratepayer roll and postal voting, which is indifferent to what Kapa-Kingi said. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There were many a submission over those three days." — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: My first thankyou goes to the white saviours on the other side of the House: Kieran McAnulty and Celia Wade-Brown. Thank you for saving us poor, helpless Māori from our own ill will!
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker but engages no content of her argument: nothing about referenda, the one-person-one-vote claim, or the Tauranga ward. It is a posture directed at who was speaking rather than at what they said, and would read identically whatever argument Wade-Brown had made for Māori wards. On the matter under debate, so above the floor, but a mere reference is not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown argued the bill forces binding referenda selectively and that a Māori ward is not an extra vote, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it names her only as a target

acuity.statement: If members care to actually read their papers and consider the departmental report, they will see that those written submissions were two-thirds opposed to the bill and one-third in favour.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the characterisation both preceding speakers built their case on — that the hearings showed overwhelming support for Māori wards — by supplying the written submission split from the departmental report. The speech would have to change if the earlier turns had not claimed the submissions ran one way. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the oral-hearing characterisation with a different population (written submissions) rather than engaging that distinction, but the engagement is specific and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Through all of the hearings, I might have heard maybe one or two, but the majority of what we heard was" — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: We heard Cameron Brewer do politics by anecdote as he ran through electors, people of Māori descent who had been elected in Auckland’s elections. But have a look at the select committee report. Between 2002 and 2019, only two councils managed to establish Māori wards.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up the same target the preceding turn raised — Brewer's case against Māori representation — and does something new with it, naming the anecdotal form of the argument and answering it with the select committee's figure that only two councils established Māori wards between 2002 and 2019. But it engages the broader topic Halbert raised rather than Halbert's own specific claims (the Ōrākau visit, the "white saviours" remark, the Minister's record), and the rest of the speech is prepared material on the bill, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal of the previous speaker's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "And there we have Cameron Brewer talking about the abolition and the unnecessary need for the Māori seats that represent Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi in this country."

acuity.statement: It’s interesting that we listened to Willie Jackson last night—he suffers from acute amnesia, because he was part of The Alliance and part of the 46th Parliament that passed the provisions for Māori seats and the community’s right to petition for a referendum back in 2002, with the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002.
acuity.explanation: Brewer takes up Jackson's immediately preceding defence of the Māori wards settings and engages it directly by confronting him with his own earlier support for the referendum provision being reinstated. The speech would have had to change if Jackson had argued something else, so engagement is high; whether the ad hominem framing reasons well is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "I'm proud that as a party, we've been going down this track." (and his argument that the referendum requirement is a racist barrier on Māori wards)

acuity.statement: Now, Willie Jackson, Mr McAnulty, and others said that there’s no way that Māori can be represented without the provision of Māori wards on council. Can I remind you of what happened in 2010 at the biggest local government elections that we saw in New Zealand, the biggest participatory rate that we saw.
acuity.explanation: This restates the specific claim Jackson had just made — that candidates with a pro-Māori agenda cannot win general council seats — and sets up counter-evidence (the 2010 Auckland results) directly against it. That is engaging the content of the preceding argument rather than merely naming its author.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "There is absolutely no chance for anyone with a pro-Māori agenda; there is no chance, there is no opportunity in getting on a council."

acuity.statement: The bill really only seeks to restore the policy settings for Māori wards, which were in place, as Mr Brewer has pointed out, for 19 years before the previous Government changed it, effectively denying the democratic voting rights of local communities to choose and to have a say about their own governance.
acuity.explanation: Garcia borrows Brewer's 2002–2021 point as a citation but does nothing with it and engages none of the opposing argument from Jackson; the rest is prepared support for the bill that would read identically whoever had spoken before. A gesture at the debate rather than an engagement with it, so the 0.3 end of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "we are reinstating what Mr Jackson passionately fought for back in 2002, and that has worked very successfully since 2002 up to 2021"

acuity.statement: Now, we support this bill because it represents critical steps towards establishing a clear and effective regulatory framework for data access and management in New Zealand. Now, this provides customers with greater control over their data and it promotes fair and transparent data practices. This bill aligns with our principles of protecting individuals’ privacy rights and fostering innovation.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn from Arena Williams that argued the bill's real value lies in driving competition against the five large banks and the financial sector's rising share of economic rents, and that the select committee will need to work out whether long-standing screen-scraping services need further regulation. Unkovich takes up none of it: no response to the competition argument, no view on the scraping question put to the committee she sits on. The statement is a prepared party position on the bill's general subject and would read identically whatever Williams had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued the bill is 'one tool' to let fintechs compete with the large banks and flagged scraping services as something 'we will need to tease out' at select committee, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: But this gives me an opportunity to speak about the more competitive space in the banking system. They made $7.2 billion last year, just in 2023. What this does is it also gives us an opportunity to look at what a Māori banking system might look like in regards to consumer data rights—and not just being served up what we have always been served up.
acuity.explanation: There is a real gesture at the live strand of the debate: Williams had argued the bill matters chiefly as a lever on banking competition and on profits flowing offshore, and Waititi picks up banking competition and offshore bank profits. But he engages no part of her actual claim — he neither accepts nor disputes her account of market concentration or the bill's power to shift it, and instead uses the topic as a doorway into prepared material on Māori data sovereignty, Te Whata and Nau Mai Rā. His one explicit reference to another member ('just to reiterate the kōrero here by ACT') is a mention, not an engagement. A gesture at the debate without taking up the argument caps this at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we need to keep that pressure up on large corporates in the New Zealand market place' / 'they’re getting up to a larger and larger proportion of their profits going offshore' — Arena Williams, on banking competition; Waititi echoes the theme but does not take up the claim.

acuity.statement: I’ll finish by saying that I will support this with caution—with caution—because the original bill was initiated to support consumers, to give consumers more power, to give consumers more information, to give people that power. There’s a risk that this bill in its current form has morphed into something that is just there to back business.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows Stuart Smith, who argued the bill is fundamentally about individual data sovereignty and about choice and competition, illustrated with electricity billing granularity and bank switching. Davidson speaks on the same bill and the same consumer-empowerment terrain, but takes up none of Smith's specific claims — he neither accepts nor disputes the individual-sovereignty framing, the competition argument, or the electricity example. His material (the Clark/Webb genesis, 'people are not products', the open-voting thought experiment, the caution that the bill backs business) would have been delivered unchanged whatever Smith had said. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate, so the upper end of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Stuart Smith spoke about how the bill gives individuals sovereignty over their own data and promotes choice and competition in banking and electricity, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: This is an excellent bill that’s well supported around the House. I’m looking forward to seeing this come through the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee and seeing if there’s anything we can do to improve or enhance the bill in any way. I’m sure it’s so well done that we will just pass it all the way through, and I’m looking forward to that process.
acuity.explanation: Weenink speaks immediately after Davidson, who had put a substantive caution: that the bill risks turning people into products and may have 'morphed into something that is just there to back business'. She engages none of it — she asserts the bill is 'well supported around the House' and that she is sure it is 'so well done that we will just pass it all the way through', which passes straight over the reservation just entered. The speech is on the right subject but indifferent to what preceded it; substituting a different critique of the bill would not change a word of it. Not 0.0 because the 'well supported around the House' line does glance at the House's handling of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued 'There’s a risk that this bill in its current form has morphed into something that is just there to back business' and this statement does not take that caution up.

acuity.statement: I agree with my colleague across the House, who is also on the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee, that those experiences that we’ve probably all had with the lack of transparency on data are serious. It builds into a few things that need to go on in a complex society.
acuity.explanation: White picks up the specific strand Weenink had just offered — her personal account of switching banks being painful and there being 'no clarity' — names her as the colleague across the House on the same select committee, and generalises it into a claim that the transparency problem is serious and systemic. That is a real engagement with the preceding turn's content, not just a reference to the speaker. It is partial rather than full: she takes one strand and then moves to her own prepared material about lobbyists and holding banks to account, and she does not address Weenink's broader competition argument. Scored on engagement only, independently of whether the claim is true or precise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "Anybody who has ever tried to change banks will feel quite grateful that we are progressing this bill. I, for one, have done it once in my life and it was a painful experience" / "It’s very difficult to get everything organised and there is no clarity."

acuity.statement: Information asymmetry creates market power and anti-competitive behaviour and it’s in that vein that this bill seeks to address these key issues in some of our biggest and most important sectors in the domestic economy in New Zealand. As my colleague Dr Vanessa Weenink said quite aptly, this is about choice and competition in those particular sectors, whether it is telecommunications, banking, or electricity providers.
acuity.explanation: Bidois names both Weenink and Helen White and repeats their formulations back ('this is about choice and competition', 'will make a significant difference'), but does nothing with either — he does not extend, test, qualify or draw a consequence from their arguments, and he does not touch White's immediately preceding point about lobbyists trying to water the bill down at select committee. Under the rubric, quoting an earlier speaker's words in order to agree and move on is a mere reference, not engagement with content. His own information-asymmetry framing is prepared material that would stand whatever had been said before, so this sits in the unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "This is about choice and competition: greater choice in the banking sector and greater choice in the electricity and communications sector." — echoed verbatim in substance but not taken any further.

acuity.statement: Look, these bills tend to be relatively uncontroversial, and we haven’t identified anything that we have issues with. I guess it is worth noting the political tensions raised by the Minister for Economic Development around this belief that sensible regulation can be really good for the wellbeing of the country, while at the same time there is a political drive to slash regulations that actually often protect, for example, the safety of workers in the workplace or allow them to stay well.
acuity.explanation: Bennett's turn immediately precedes and contains a concrete challenge (be pro-growth, but produce a plan and investment to double exports; MBIE systems are clunky). Menéndez March takes up none of it — no response on the export plan, the growth claim, or the clunky-systems point. He gestures at the debate by reaching back past Bennett to the Minister's opening speech on sensible regulation, so the speech is squarely on the matter under debate rather than generic, but it engages no part of the argument it follows. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band with a gesture at the debate: 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett challenged the Minister to 'lay out the plan, tell us how we’re going to spend money to double exports in 10 years', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: While these may not be the most exciting changes that this Government will make, cleaning up existing regulation is a necessary activity to ensure efficient regulatory systems. Collectively, the small changes in these bills will make it easier for Kiwis to understand the law and comply with Government requirements.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, both with content aimed at the Government: Bennett's demand for a plan behind the export-doubling goal, and Menéndez March's claim that the Government's deregulation drive contradicts the Minister's praise of sensible regulation — a charge that lands directly on van Velden's own workplace-relations and health-and-safety portfolios, and that she was uniquely placed to answer. She answers neither, and also does not pick up his specific invitation to discuss the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act changes at select committee. The speech is prepared ministerial material on the bills' contents, word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before; it is at least about the measure under debate rather than transposable to another day, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued there is 'a political drive to slash regulations' at odds with the Minister's first speech, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I want to particularly focus on changes to the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987 and the work that this bill is doing to ensure paid parental leave policies are inclusive, considering the diverse range of family structures that we might have these days.
acuity.explanation: Halbert's immediately preceding turn made two engageable points — that the omnibus approach across 24 Acts is a good use of the House's time, and the challenge about the Government's lack of ambition. Costley takes up neither. His speech is prepared material on his own chosen clauses of one of the two bills (pre-term babies, parents who stop work), and it would read word-for-word the same whatever Halbert had argued. It is squarely on the matter under debate and contains a passing gesture at earlier contributions ("touched on briefly before"), which keeps it above the floor, but that is a reference rather than engagement with any claim, so it sits at the low end of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert spoke about the omnibus bill amending 24 Acts and asked "is this as ambitious as we get from this Government?", and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: As my colleague Arena Williams has shared, it is disappointing that we weren’t able to complete or even address the last piece of legislation, because we all need to be ready, we all need to be here, and we all need to engage in the discussion.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Williams and explicitly picks up one strand of her turn — the complaint that the preceding bill could not proceed because the Minister was not ready — and endorses it, adding her own gloss that all members need to be present and engaged. That is a real, pointable engagement, so it is well above the prepared-material band. But it is only one strand, and the minor one: Williams's substantive argument was that the bill unlocks aquaculture assets while the Government gives Marlborough and Ōpōtiki no certainty on rail, ferries and ports, and Lyndon takes none of that up — she moves straight into prepared material on Te Ohu Kai Moana, the 32 years since the settlement, and the governance changes. Had Williams made a different infrastructure argument, the rest of this speech would read identically. Hence mid-range rather than high.

acuity.responding_to: "their last bill which they tried to introduce to this House but could not because the Minister was not ready to take the call" — Arena Williams

This is changing some of the assumptions about who is involved in heavy engineering in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Unkovich's immediately preceding turn made two substantive points (asbestos disease awareness; the significance of small definitional changes such as "notifiable incident"), so the turn was eligible to be engaged. Weenink instead delivers prepared material on a different clause of the other bill — the Heavy Engineering Research Levy Act amendment and women in STEM. Her only gesture outside her own notes is to the Minister for Economic Development's "24 different amendments", a turn not in this window and in any case a bare reference rather than engagement. The speech would read identically whatever Unkovich had said, but it is squarely about the bills under debate, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at the floor.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich spoke about asbestos-related harm raised with her during the recess and the tweaking of the definition of "notifiable incident", and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: So we're supportive of the process. We do note that, in the previous Parliament, these were intended to be bipartisan bills supported through the House. Not on every occasion was that the case under the last Parliament, so I'll just note that for the record.

That is a pointable, partial engagement with the preceding turn. It is only partial: most of her call is prepared analysis of the departmental disclosure statement and new section 169C(3), and she addresses earlier speakers only as a generic "previous speakers", so she engages the topic of cross-party support more than Weenink's specific argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "these are sensible bills that should be well and truly agreed to across the House" — Dr Vanessa Weenink

acuity.statement: It's a pleasure to rise and join the chorus of support for the Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Immigration and Workforce) Amendment Bill. This is rats and mice legislation, which has been raised in the House from the other side, that amends 24 Acts and associated regulations.

Bidois engages neither, and instead lists changes he likes (Charitable Trusts Act, Crown Research Institutes half-yearly reporting) and closes on economic growth. He does gesture at the debate: he picks up the "rats and mice" characterisation "from the other side" and jokes about Weenink's birth-year amendment. Both are mere references — repeating an opponent's phrase and borrowing a colleague's conceit — not engagement with content, so this sits in the prepared-but-on-topic band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "no formal analysis was undertaken in a number of these different bills" — Camilla Belich. Bidois does not take this up; his only pointable uptake of a prior turn is Weenink's "mainly because that was the year that I was born", which he answers with a joke rather than an argument.

acuity.statement: I’d like to just pick up on a point from the opposite side of the House around the support and the aspiration that we have for iwi in the aquaculture space. We have huge potential in the aquaculture space, which Matua Shane Jones absolutely is passionate about realising, and we support that kaupapa on this side of the House because it is through aquaculture that we can grow jobs in the regions, jobs for iwi, jobs for rangatahi, and jobs for New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Cameron's substantive third-reading speech and is on the matter under debate, but engages no part of Cameron's argument — not the 40 percent quota figure, not the claim about value to industry. He gestures at the debate by invoking an unnamed point "from the opposite side of the House" about aquaculture (and later notes the Green Party raised the funding levy), but these are references rather than engagement with content: he agrees in passing and returns to prepared material on iwi autonomy, tino rangatiratanga and the select committee's provisions. He concedes as much himself — "I'm going off-script" and "this is running down the clock". Substituting a different argument on the same bill for Cameron's turn would not require this speech to change, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 for the gesture at the debate rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Cameron argued that "some 40 percent of catch entitlement is through the Quota Management System" and that the bill will "only embolden that reality", and this statement does not take up that argument; the "point from the opposite side of the House" it gestures at was made in a turn outside this window.

acuity.statement: While this bill does advance Māori sovereignty over fisheries, for example, I think we should not conflate what is a concession from the Crown with the Government actually supporting tino rangatiratanga. I think we should be careful, or the Government should be careful, of claiming that they are honouring the Crown’s Te Tiriti obligations with just the passing of this bill, in the context of everything else that is going on that is, effectively, trampling over Te Tiriti.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding speech's framing of the bill as granting rangatiratanga and qualifies it, so the engagement is pointable; but it does not take up Waititi's specific claims (drawdown problems, hapū versus mandated iwi organisations, the onshore/offshore distribution) and quickly moves to prepared material about ocean health and the bill's components. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "this bill grants greater rangatiratanga and mana motuhake over decision making when it comes to the fishing interests of those particular iwi and Māori organisations" — Menéndez March takes up the rangatiratanga strand and draws a distinction (a Crown concession is not the same as supporting tino rangatiratanga), but aims it mainly at a National contribution not contained in this window and then returns to prepared material.

acuity.statement: I’d like to, if I may, just delve into a comment that was made earlier by one of my colleagues across the House—Arena Williams. She referenced the Ōpōtiki region and how different regions around the country, including Ōpōtiki—I think she said “including Ōpōtiki”, but she referenced Ōpōtiki and the fact that they need certainty around aquaculture.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and gestures at the debate by picking up an earlier colleague's Ōpōtiki/aquaculture point, but engages no part of the argument made by the member who spoke immediately before her; the remainder is prepared material (quoting Shane Jones' earlier speech, the Māori economy figure) that would read identically whatever preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued immediately before that the bill should not be mistaken for the Crown honouring Te Tiriti while everything else the Government does tramples it, and this statement does not take that up; the speech instead revisits an Arena Williams contribution from outside this window.

acuity.statement: What was only briefly mentioned but was actually spoken about a lot during the submissions and other engagements with respect to this piece of legislation was the environment. It’s all fair and well to talk towards the great economic benefits that might come towards Te Ohu Kai Moana, Māori, and New Zealand as a whole, but what’s very clear—and I think about a number of the projects that Māori are involved in—they also look towards the longevity, the safety, and, of course, the wellbeing of the moana.
acuity.explanation: Henare takes up the specific strand of the preceding speech — its purely economic framing of the bill — names it as what was dwelt on and the environment as what was left out, and argues the moana's wellbeing belongs alongside the economic case. That part of the speech would have to change if Nakhle had argued differently. It is only a partial engagement, though: the bulk of the turn is his own prepared material (the Ardie Savea opening, his family's High Court case, Te Ohu Kai Moana's roadshow, kina and kelp) that is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "getting our primary industries and fishing sector back on track is all part of the Government’s plan to rebuild the economy and get it working for all Kiwis" — the preceding speech framed the bill almost entirely as economic rebuild, naming the $70 billion Māori economy.

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to take a call on the third reading of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill. I do want to acknowledge the nature within which the contributions have been made by members all around the House today. It shows the level of support across party lines to get this bill over the line.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows a substantive turn by Fleming, so he is eligible. He gestures at the debate by acknowledging the tone of contributions across the House, but engages no part of Fleming's argument — not the Treaty reading, not the claim about iwi control of assets. The rest of the speech is prepared material on the committee-of-the-whole changes and the review period, and would read identically whatever Fleming had said, so long as the debate were on this bill. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band: on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate but no engagement, hence 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Greg Fleming spoke about Ned Fletcher's book 'The English Text of the Treaty of Waitangi', read out the second article of Te Tiriti on tino rangatiratanga, and argued the bill gives iwi more control over fisheries assets — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Just in response, in part, to that last member’s contribution, I’d like to thank some previous Labour Ministers as well. We’ve already heard about various different Ministers for Oceans and Fisheries—and fisheries, as it was—but of course the trade Ministers are also relevant to this, and of course our former Prime Minister the Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern and the work that she did in Europe to get both those UK and European free-trade agreements. So well done to Damien O’Connor, David Parker, as well as the Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern.
acuity.explanation: Brooking opens by explicitly taking up the preceding turn and answers one strand of it — Wedd's charge that the last government neglected exporters — by naming Labour trade Ministers and the UK/EU free-trade agreements as a counter-example. It is a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal: she does not touch Wedd's specific seafood or red-tape argument and quickly moves to her own prepared material on property rights and the settlement process. Her speech would have been different if Wedd had not attacked the previous government's export record, which puts it above the prepared-material band, but she engages the topic more than the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "For the past six years, we’ve seen an absolute neglect from that Government that was all about neglecting the provinces, neglecting our businesses and neglecting our exporters"

acuity.statement: I think, just from our Government’s perspective, we support the bill. We have done the work, alongside our colleagues across the House, to ensure that that happens. But we’re really interested in getting our primary industries and our fishing sector back on track. The Government’s plan is to rebuild the economy and get it working for all Kiwis, which includes those iwi and hapū entities that want to be able to access the fisheries as part of this.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows Brooking's argument about property rights and the differing needs of large and small iwi, and engages none of it. There is a gesture at the debate ('alongside our colleagues across the House', and elsewhere 'as has been alluded to by some of my colleagues'), which keeps it off the floor, but the passage is prepared government framing on rebuilding the economy that would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before her and whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking argued that turning fish into a property right under the quota management system is what made the Treaty settlement process necessary, and that the differing scale and needs of iwi and hapū such as Ngāi Tahu and Ngāti Manuhiri is why the governance requirements had to be reviewed — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: This situation, this manufactured crisis, goes back to the bad decisions this Government has made. They went to the election with a tax plan that didn’t add up, they made poor choices, and this underfunding of our health system is all on them.
acuity.explanation: Verrall follows Simeon Brown's general debate speech, which boasted of tax relief delivered on promise and claimed the Minister of Health 'has been fixing up the mess left behind in the health system'. She takes up both strands and inverts them — the health shortfall is not an inherited mess but a consequence of an unfunded tax plan — so the speech is not indifferent to what preceded it. But she never engages Brown's specific figures or claims directly; the bulk is prepared material about yesterday's press conference and the Health Committee, and the engagement is at the level of the topic and framing rather than any particular argument he made. That places it mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Minister of Health has been fixing up the mess left behind in the health system, and what a mess it has been" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: We see you, we feel you, and we want justice for you. That is our duty as people of this House. You deserve justice.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Willie Jackson, who closed by mihi-ing the abuse-in-care survivors in the gallery and, before that, argued at length that the Treaty principles bill is being introduced by stealth. Her opening picks up the survivors strand Jackson had just raised — acknowledging them and demanding justice — so there is a gesture at the shared occasion, but she engages none of his actual argument (the Treaty principles bill, ACT, the Cooke judgment, the departmental directives) and the remainder of the speech is prepared material on Hokianga housing that would read identically whoever had spoken before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "I want to mihi to these survivors for their courage in coming forward with their stories" — she takes up the acknowledgement of the survivors in the gallery, but not any claim or argument he made.

acuity.statement: The recent announcement that the Northland roads of national significance will proceed using a progressive public-private partnership (PPP) model should give some hope to those people living in Northland, in particular, who have to travel long distances on difficult roads that this Government is going to help solve those long-term problems.
acuity.explanation: Court follows Rima Nakhle's general-debate contribution, which made substantive claims about her electorate (Mill Road as a road of national significance, a $466 million school property package, a new 600-pupil primary school at Flat Bush). Court engages none of it: his speech is prepared material on Northland roading, PPPs and RMA replacement, and would read word-for-word the same whatever Nakhle had said. There is loose topical adjacency (roads of national significance, government infrastructure investment) but no take-up of any claim she made, so this sits at the bottom band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rima Nakhle spoke about highlights in her Takanini electorate — Mill Road's inclusion in the roads of national significance and a new primary school at 121 Murphys Road, Flat Bush — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: While we have come so far, in too many cases we have not come far enough. The stories of survivors are too often mirrored in what we hear today.
acuity.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer's turn pressed one central charge: that nothing has changed, and that the abuse described in the report is still being perpetuated today. Stanford takes up that single strand directly — conceding that the Crown has not come far enough and that survivors' accounts are mirrored in present-day Oranga Tamariki cases, with an explicit nod to the preceding turn elsewhere ("as we've heard"). But she engages only that one concession and leaves untouched the specific policy charges Ngarewa-Packer levelled (mega-prisons, the repeal of section 7AA, boot camps), returning to prepared tabling material on the report's contents. That is partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the argument made, so it sits at the mid-band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What the hell has changed—what the hell has changed?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: The hope for a better future is found within the recommendations—all 138 of them. We welcome the apology that will be offered by the Prime Minister on behalf of the State. However, an apology is hollow without change. The Green Party is unified in its cross-partisan support to accept and implement, in full, all recommendations and implores the Government to join us.
acuity.explanation: Carter follows a substantive turn by Prime that made several engageable points: that the current system is "so out of step" with the 138 recommendations, that the abuse is not historical but ongoing, and that rangatahi excluded by the 1999 cut-off have lodged a further report through VOYCE - Whakarongo Mai. Carter's speech takes up none of these specifically. It is on the matter under debate and shares Prime's reference to the 138 recommendations, and the shift from Prime's "work through" to "accept and implement, in full" plus the call for the Government to join is a faint gesture at the preceding claim that all parties are committed — but the speech is prepared party material that would read identically whoever had spoken before, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We welcome the opportunity to work through the 138 recommendations in that report." — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: The summary of the report has two very clear messages. Bad things happen to people when they are disempowered, when they are segregated away from view, and when they are silenced. Different kinds of bad things arise in people who are put in charge of vulnerable people.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft follows a substantive turn by Seymour that made pointed, contestable claims (the three specific ways the State failed; a defence of why the Government withheld an apology today; a rebuke to those who had "tried to bring politics into today"). Her contribution is prepared material on the correct subject — the royal commission report and how care should be reconceived — and would read word-for-word the same whatever Seymour had said. She sources her diagnosis of institutional abuse to the report's own summary rather than engaging his three-part account of State failure, and her later reference to a Crown apology being "to come" notes the fact without taking up his reasoning about it. That is a gesture at the matter under debate with no engagement of the argument, so it sits in the low band rather than at a partial 0.5. Note this is purely a responsiveness judgement and carries no implication about the speech's substance, sincerity or quality.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour spoke immediately before, arguing that "The State failed in three ways" and explaining that "people on this side with the Government have not apologised today" because the form of apology must be created with survivors — this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: It may be a bill of three parts, but they are detailed, and as the Minister has indicated, there is also an Amendment Paper that is thicker than the original bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what Simeon Brown had just said — the tabled Amendment Papers and the transitional/postal provisions — and uses it to argue there is too much to consider in a short committee stage, then puts a specific question to the Minister about extending the provisions to all wards. It engages the Minister's tabling rather than the substance of his Māori-ward argument, so it is partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "There's also two tabled amendments from me." — his explanation of Part 1, the Schedule and the postal time frames.

acuity.statement: No, the Government is not willing to accept that amendment. This bill is in relation to Māori wards, wards based on race, ethnicity, rather than geography.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question just put — whether he would accept an amendment covering all wards — with a direct no, and gives the reason the bill distinguishes Māori wards from other wards. The reply would be different had McAnulty asked anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Would the Minister consider an amendment to include all wards of local body areas, all wards under local councils, not just Māori wards—that they be treated the same under the proposals within this bill?"

acuity.statement: So there we have it right off the bat. The Government is treating the consideration of the establishment of Māori wards differently to all other wards—probably the most upfront thing the Minister has said in this House, and we got it right from the get-go, which I appreciate and thank him for.
acuity.explanation: Seizes on the Minister's answer immediately and draws out its consequence — that the bill by the Minister's own admission applies a different test to Māori wards than to any other ward — building the next question directly on the concession just made. Entirely contingent on what Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "No, the Government is not willing to accept that amendment. This bill is in relation to Māori wards, wards based on race, ethnicity, rather than geography."

acuity.statement: The member Kieran McAnulty’s comments in relation to my last question highlight, I think, a difference in terms of where the Opposition’s position on this is and where the Government’s position on this issue is. In relation to rural wards or urban wards, where those wards exist, everybody who lives within those wards, regardless of whether they’re on the Māori roll or the general roll, gets to vote for the person that they choose to represent them as a mayor or a councillor.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific charge just made — that Māori wards are being treated differently from urban and rural wards — and answers it with a stated basis for the distinction, that other wards do not split voters by roll. He leaves McAnulty's follow-up question about institutional racism untouched, which keeps this short of a full engagement, but the central argument of the preceding turn is taken up and contested.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "The Government is treating the consideration of the establishment of Māori wards differently to all other wards"

acuity.statement: In terms of Auckland, there wasn’t a referendum early in the year. The council did make a decision not to proceed with establishing a Māori ward. They made that decision in, I think, October or November last year.
acuity.explanation: Brown takes up Henare's specific premise — that Auckland held a Māori wards referendum at the start of the year — and corrects it as a misstatement of fact, then explains the Tauranga and 2028 dates Henare asked him to spell out. The speech would be materially different had Henare asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "he might recall the recent referendum that was done on Māori wards at the beginning of this year in Tāmaki Makaurau"

acuity.statement: The particular scenario I want to put to the Minister—and to have his response, which I think will be helpful for the committee of the whole House—is a situation where people are running in an election for a Māori ward and at the same time there is a referendum occurring on whether that Māori ward is retained or not. We have a situation where people are campaigning, outlaying money, and putting their lives on hold in order to run for an elected position, which they subsequently win, but at the same time, through that referendum, the voting public vote to disestablish that Māori ward.
acuity.explanation: Boyack takes the answer Brown has just given — that Cabinet chose to run the referendums alongside the next local election to cut costs — and draws out a consequence that answer did not address: a candidate elected to a ward the concurrent referendum abolishes. The question only exists because of the specific timing Brown described.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the decision was made by Cabinet to hold the referendums at the same time as the next local election to ensure that the costs were reduced for local councils"

acuity.statement: Why is there such inconsistency in the application of a referendum based on this idea of democracy that the Minister has put forward, which we all uphold? If you’re going to apply it, apply it to all decisions that sit under the representation review.
acuity.explanation: This engages one strand of Brown's stated rationale — that the bill is about letting local communities have their say on representation arrangements — by pointing out that Nelson's review also changed the voting system and created geographic wards, none of which get a referendum. It is a real engagement with his principle, but the Nelson material is clearly prepared and is aimed as much at his earlier contribution as at the answer just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "this is about the representation arrangements and the ability of local communities to be able to have their say in relation to those representation arrangements"

acuity.statement: The member Kieran McAnulty made a wrong assertion in terms of the comments he made earlier in relation to how the provisions passed by the previous Government treated the Māori wards the same as any other. The reality was that they took away the ability, when councils were putting forward their representation reviews, for the public to be able to go to the Local Government Commission and be able to petition or have their concerns raised around that, even through the Local Government Commission.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific factual premise of the preceding turn — that the previous Government's regime put Māori wards on the same footing as any other ward — and contests it with a concrete mechanism (loss of the public's ability to petition the Local Government Commission on representation reviews). The speech would be different had McAnulty argued something else. Not 1.0 because the explicit question McAnulty put, on the institutional-racism definition, is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “it was changed to bring it in line with the establishment of any other wards” — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: And it strikes me that at the guts of this bill is a movement away from devolution of these decisions from local government. In fact, local governments have the ability to choose, in their local body, whether or not they have Māori wards, like they have island wards or rural wards. And I was wondering if there’s been a change in the Government policies and, in fact, now the Government wants centralisation and control?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and gestures at the bill's design, but opens a fresh prepared line (localism/devolution, framed around a Luxon quote) rather than engaging the Local Government Commission point just made. The question would read identically whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the previous Government had removed the public's ability to petition the Local Government Commission (“Even that was taken away”) and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I apologise, the dinner break interrupted my ability to answer his question around localism prior to the dinner break. And, of course, as I’ve outlined in my speeches on this issue, that side of the House talks about localism, but the localism stops at the council table. We’ve actually said localism should flow through to the voters, the electors, the people who the councillors and the mayor are meant to represent.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Webb's localism charge directly and inverts the term against him — localism as flowing past the council table to electors — then goes on to the rescission/referendum question also put. Tied closely to what preceded it; short of 1.0 because the second answer restates the mechanism rather than addressing the asymmetry Webb actually asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “And I was wondering if there’s been a change in the Government policies and, in fact, now the Government wants centralisation and control?” — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I’d like to start with asking the Minister to consider—in the briefing to incoming Minister of Local Government it was pretty clear that the Minister has some responsibility for Māori-council relationships. I wonder if he could address how putting an effective veto on the introduction of Māori wards addresses that ministerial responsibility when we can see that taking us backwards, with an effective veto on Māori wards—it’s acknowledged by the Department of Internal Affairs, it’s been acknowledged by the vast majority of mayors and chairs and Māori councillors; so how he thinks he is actually taking that responsibility seriously.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the bill, and the “effective veto” characterisation sits against the Minister's “public have their say” framing, but it never engages that argument — it opens an unrelated prepared line on the briefing to the incoming Minister and on a colleague's heckling. Prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued that a council can avoid a referendum by choosing to rescind and that otherwise “the public will ultimately have their say”, and this statement does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: Now, that’s the sort of complex decision-making—whether you agree in every case or not, but it’s complex and it goes to the local people, and there were a lot of submissions from Tawa and from the rural area. There is no way that you could get that information in a binary referendum.
acuity.explanation: Brown had just argued that the public get their say through submissions, petitions and a referendum. Wade-Brown takes up that strand directly and disputes its adequacy, using the Wellington community-board example to argue a binary referendum cannot capture the information a representation review does. She engages one specific strand of his case rather than the whole of it, and the bulk of the contribution is prepared illustrative material plus a fresh question on the 6 September deadline that Brown had not raised, so this is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the public do have their say as well. They are able to submit on those processes" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I thank Her Worship for the question, and in answer to her question regarding consultation: yes, I acknowledge it’s a short period of time. But, ultimately, we’ve well signalled the change. Some councils have already started to have these conversations.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown asked specifically whether the 6 September decision date leaves councils enough time to consult. Brown takes that question up head-on, concedes the period is short, and then supplies a counter-reason with evidence from the record (Greater Wellington's select committee submission disclosing it is already consulting mana whenua). The reply would have had to be different had she argued something else, which is the mark of real engagement; it falls short of 1.0 because the fairness half of her question is answered by pivoting back to the referendum point he had already made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is 6 September really fair if local people are going to have a say on the matter that matters to them so much?" — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: I’ve submitted this because I was listening very carefully to the Minister’s response earlier, I think it was to Rachel Boyack’s contribution. Frankly, it was incredibly weak. He claims that there is a difference already, previously, before the rules were changed, because they didn’t have the option to go to the Local Government Commission, whereas all other wards would.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty restates the Minister's actual argument — the asymmetry in access to the Local Government Commission — accurately and then does something with it: he draws out the consequence that the stated grievance would be cured by equalising the commission pathway rather than by requiring referendums, and attaches an amendment implementing the alternative. The contribution would be entirely different had Brown rested his case on different grounds, which is the deciding test. Scored only on engagement here; the contemptuous framing ("incredibly weak", and later remarks about the Minister) is a Civility matter and does not reduce Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the previous Government’s legislation took away from the public the ability ... to even go and make a complaint to the Local Government Commission in relation to the distribution of the seats" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: My question around it is this: if we are to have the death star, and Māori are going to get the chop, our people vote in 2025 and say, “Na, poroa te kaki.”—chop it at the neck—the Māori goes in and they spend three years proving themselves, does that mean that we don’t get to participate in a representation review in six years’ time?
acuity.explanation: Lyndon takes up the specific timing mechanism Brown had just set out — that a referendum's effect is deferred to the next local election — and presses it to its consequence: a Māori ward councillor elected in 2025 would serve only to 2028, and she asks what Brown's scheme leaves for a representation review six years out. She also engages his framing of the referendum as the democratic instrument by contrasting it with the hui/submission/survey methods of a representation review. The engagement is real and pointable, though a substantial stretch of the speech is prepared material on Hobson's Pledge and on her own candidacies, so it falls short of a full rebuttal of his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "If there’s a referendum, the effect of that referendum does not take effect till the next local election."

acuity.statement: I just wonder if he agrees with the outcome of that decision from council—given that they didn’t move forward with establishing Māori wards—and if he agrees with their reasons why, and, if it’s good for Auckland, given it’s consistent with his position on Māori wards, why he wouldn’t offer the same confidence and trust in other councils like Gisborne, as an example?
acuity.explanation: Halbert engages the Minister's standing rationale — that the bill merely restores the prior position and leaves the choice to voters — by testing it for consistency: if Auckland's own council decision not to establish Māori wards is acceptable, why not trust Gisborne's decision to proceed. That is a genuine attempt to draw out a consequence of Brown's argument. But it bypasses the immediately preceding turn (Lyndon's question about representation reviews six years on) entirely, reaches back to McAnulty, and the rest of the contribution is prepared material plus calls for his own committee colleagues to stand up, so this sits mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "In terms of the question that was raised in regards to democratically elected members, their positions being determined to no longer exist, that is not what this legislation is doing."

acuity.statement: I’m heartened by the pātai around the why of the change, and, indeed—given the essential nature that we have Māori around the table at this time—whether the Government would actually reconsider the amendment to include other wards in this consideration.
acuity.explanation: Tana's turn is largely prepared material on two world views and mātauranga Māori, but she does pick up the 'why' strand that Halbert's interjection and Simeon Brown's answer had just established, and converts it into a specific ask of the Minister about extending the amendment to other wards. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding exchange rather than with the substance of Brown's democracy/mandate argument, so it sits at the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "In terms of why we’re doing this? Thank you for reminding me." / "ultimately it comes back to democracy"

acuity.statement: I’m just curious as to how that interfaces with what’s sometimes called the “landlord roll”, and, in particular, whether a person who is a landlord and not a resident—doesn’t actually live there but has a right to vote in a local body election by dint of being a landlord—can have a say in the poll, or whether in fact you have to live there.
acuity.explanation: A self-contained clause-7 question that engages no part of what Tana or Brown had just argued; nothing in it would change if the preceding speeches had said something different. It earns the top of the unresponsive band only because it is squarely on the mechanism under debate — who votes in the poll Brown had just been describing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown described the 5 percent petition and "then there would be a referendum of Aucklanders", and Darleen Tana spoke about mātauranga Māori and extending the amendment to other wards; this statement takes up neither and raises a fresh eligibility question instead.

acuity.statement: The second question I have, though, is based on—the Minister made a response earlier around the referendum for Māori wards, that he’s returning the legislation to what it was previously. Now, that’s actually not correct, and I’d like the Minister’s response on this because, under the previous form of the legislation, there was no automatic referendum, there was no central government imposing of a referendum on local government; it required a petition to be put forward, again by the electors of that constituency.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's own characterisation of the bill and contradicts it on the specific mechanism — petition-triggered versus automatic, centrally imposed referendum — then states what he would have to legislate for the claim to hold. She also turns his 'let the electors decide' argument against him by noting the Local Government Commission route never returns to electors. The speech could not have been delivered without having listened to what Brown said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "ultimately it comes back to democracy" and "if 5 percent of Aucklanders signed a petition, then there would be a referendum of Aucklanders"

acuity.statement: But I’m interested to know if the Minister has actually had his own consultation with mana whenua. This is on our consultation side, in terms of Part 1.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the consultation strand the Minister had just relied on — councils went out and got the views of the public — and presses it in a new direction by asking whether the Minister himself consulted mana whenua. Genuine engagement with one strand, but it then leaves the argument for prepared material about Rangi McLean and an aside at another member, so it is a partial rather than a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "They did go out for consultation. They got views from the public."

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around consultation, in terms of the policy, ultimately, we took this policy to the election at the last election and New Zealanders voted for the parties which now make up this Government and we are now implementing this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Jackson's turn put three things to the Minister: what process he followed in forming his view, where the evidence is that Māori seats cannot work given the Māori statutory board, and whether this is institutional racism. Brown takes up only the process/consultation strand, and answers it by asserting an election mandate rather than describing any process; the evidence and institutional-racism questions are not touched at all. Partial engagement with one strand, so mid-low rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "that's what Shanan Halbert asked—that the Minister went through in terms of determining his view that this was the right thing to do"

acuity.statement: In terms of the wider point that’s been made about the policy intent and how terrible it is, I would note it was the Labour Government which actually put these provisions in place back in 2001.
acuity.explanation: This squarely takes up the criticism of the policy's intent that had just been levelled at him and does something with it — pins the origin of the provisions on the critics' own party and frames the bill as a reversion to pre-2021 law. The speech would have to change if the preceding attack had been different, which is what Acuity measures; whether the tu quoque is a sound inference is a Rigor question and is deliberately not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "So where is the evidence to say that Māori seats can’t work, when you’ve got a Māori statutory board in play right now set up by the ACT Party and the National Party?"

acuity.statement: How about the Government stops doing dumb things? That’s going to help local government, because this requirement, as outlined in Part 1, is going to require councils to pay for the referenda that they don’t want.
acuity.explanation: Brown had just set out the referendum pathway as a requirement on councils; McAnulty takes that requirement and draws out a consequence of it — that councils must fund referenda they did not seek. That is genuine engagement with the mechanism just described, but it arrives inside an announced move to "a new area" and prepared material on council funding rather than a direct rebuttal of Brown's reasoning, so a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "we’ll be requiring them to either rescind or disestablish or to have a referendum"

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: when the Government was formalised and officially became the Government of New Zealand, they automatically assumed their obligation of the Treaty partner, how does removing the right of or implementing referendums of Māori wards to local government representation constitute good or appropriate Treaty partner behaviour within this bill?
acuity.explanation: The question is on the matter under debate — referendums on Māori wards — but engages no part of what preceded it. Brown had just asserted an election mandate and described the petition and referendum pathway; neither the mandate claim nor the 5 percent threshold is taken up, and the question would read identically whatever he had said. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown set out the election mandate for the policy and the petition-to-referendum pathway, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The question is in relation to the intent of the policy, and ultimately the intent of the policy is to allow councils to be able to put forward recommendations. The public then are able to petition as to whether or not there should be a referendum, and then the public get to have their say as to whether or not the constitutional makeup of the electors of that council, and that ward proposal, should go ahead or not. Ultimately, it’s about local people making decisions for their local community and those local people being the voters in those electorates.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the mechanism she asked about — the petition-and-referendum pathway in the bill — and explains what it is intended to do, so this is an answer on the matter she raised and not generic prepared material. But the specific question was whether that pathway is consistent with the Crown's obligations to its Treaty partner, and the Treaty criterion is not engaged at all; he restates the policy's intent instead of applying her test to it. Topic engaged, claim not — the ~0.5 band, placed slightly below it because the single distinguishing feature of her question is the one feature the reply omits.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how does the right of removing the Māori wards to local government representation constitute good or appropriate Treaty partner behaviour within this bill?" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: On the topic of referendum—and this is going to be the guts of my question to the Minister, and the question is pretty simple—will the Minister consider a repeals process where, after the referendum, if there is an unsatisfactory outcome or unsatisfactory process that’s been followed, will the Minister consider putting a repeals process in this bill now, while we have the opportunity?
acuity.explanation: He takes the referendum pathway the Minister had just described as the bill's safeguard and draws out its consequence: if that process miscarries, nothing in the bill lets the outcome be undone. The question only exists because of the answer immediately before it — substitute a different defence of the bill and this intervention would have to change — and he presses it with a specific remedy (a repeal/appeals clause, inserted now at committee stage). Short of 1.0 because he does not dispute the reasoning of Brown's answer so much as append a new demand to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The public then are able to petition as to whether or not there should be a referendum, and then the public get to have their say" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: We are in a democracy, like the Minister suggested, but what we are seeing here is not a democracy but an oligarchy. The more you can own, the more money you have, the more you have a say.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's own framing of the referendum mechanism as 'a thing called democracy' and turns it against him, arguing that because signing rights follow the electoral roll a multi-property owner can sign more than once, so the mechanism is property-weighted rather than democratic. He also builds directly on the Minister's earlier clarification about the 'landlord roll'. The speech would have to change if Brown had made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Ultimately what we have here is a thing called democracy where the public, if they petition and 5 percent of the population or more sign a petition, there will be a referendum"

acuity.statement: Minister, I have asked you, and other people have done follow-ups, about what evidence you took on board to help make your decision in this sense. You haven’t been clear about this yet. You haven’t spoken about the submissions that you really took on board, particularly council views.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Xu-Nan's substantive questions on the signature threshold immediately precede, and were answered by the Minister. Halbert engages none of that: he returns to his own prepared line of questioning on evidence and council costs, repeating a demand he says has been put five times. There is a gesture at the debate ('I think there was a question around cost'), which keeps it off the floor, but no part of the preceding argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that section 19ZC(2)(b) may let an owner of two properties in a region sign a demand more than once, and asked whether any provision bars it; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. This is my first opportunity to speak in this debate and I really appreciate the opportunity to take a call. This will be a technical speech, and it introduces a new point that relates to new section 19Z(2), inserted by clause 6, and again further into the amendment that the Minister has put forward at clause 7.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Glen Bennett proposing removal of the binding referendum provision, but engages no part of it; the speaker explicitly frames her contribution as a new, technical point of her own. It is squarely on the bill under debate (clauses 6 and 7, new section 19Z(2)), so it sits at the top of the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at zero — this speech would have been identical whatever Bennett had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued that the binding referendum could be removed because sections 19H and 19I of the Local Electoral Act 2001 already provide for representation reviews, and this statement does not take that up — it announces a new point of its own.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her questions. The changes in the bill don’t affect how Māori wards are implemented, such as the fair and effective representation arrangement rules.
