It is about whether or not Māori wards are established at all and, obviously, the referendum arrangements. The issues that she’s raising in relation to how those wards may be created—there is legislation and are processes already in place, and there is the Local Government Commission, which, ultimately, has the final say in terms of how those other wards may be created.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific mechanism Williams raised — councils redrawing geographic boundaries as de facto Māori wards — and answers it on its own terms: the bill touches establishment and referendums, not ward-creation rules, which sit with existing law and the Local Government Commission. He also meets her premise that councils stand to lose sitting Māori councillors by denying anyone has a right to a seat. Short of 1.0 because she asked specifically about Rotorua Lakes and Wairoa and those two are not addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Will they be in a position where they will be trying to create constituencies of their Māori voters in a geographic way, and does that create a situation where other people are not being represented in the same way?"

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I’m still waiting, actually, for answers to previous questions. One was in regard to the funding of councils, particularly those that aren’t in a position to finance easily the costs of the referenda, and that led to a subsequent question, which was which councils asked the Minister for this.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn was the Minister's substantive answer to another member, and nothing in its content is engaged. The statement notes only that the Minister answered someone else and not him, then proceeds to the speaker's own line on referendum costs. On-topic for the committee stage, but indifferent to what it follows, so it belongs in the prepared-material band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 for the gesture at the Minister's pattern of answering.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just answered Arena Williams on how Māori ward boundaries may be created and who has the final say, and this statement does not take any of that up — it returns to the speaker's own earlier, unanswered questions on referendum funding.

acuity.statement: Just to answer the member’s questions in regards to funding, ultimately, there are a range of costs. Ultimately, we as a Government decided to hold the referendums alongside the election to minimise the costs.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of what was just put to him — the cost of the referenda to councils — and supplies a real response to it, that referendums were timed with the general election to hold costs down. But McAnulty asked three things, and the two he pressed hardest, which councils requested the change and whether the 5 percent trigger in Amendment Paper 48 could be lifted, go untouched. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "One was in regard to the funding of councils, particularly those that aren’t in a position to finance easily the costs of the referenda"

acuity.statement: Well, I appreciate the member has gone from being opposed to the referendums and saying that they are just a blunt vote to now at least an openness and a willingness to explore them—so that is progress. But ultimately, this is about giving local communities the ability to decide, and that is why we are requiring these to be referendums.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the question just put to him — why binding — characterising Lyndon's shift towards accepting referendums and giving a reason (local communities deciding) for the binding requirement. The speech would be different had she argued something else; it is pitched at her specific question. Not 1.0 because he does not engage the Law Society advice or the 2020 Internal Affairs figures she grounded the question in.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And I want to explore with the Minister: why does it need to be a binding poll?" — Hūhana Lyndon

acuity.statement: The list MP based somewhere in the North Shore, Shanan Halbert, his question was around evidence. Look, I mean, I have answered these questions multiple times this afternoon in regards to the fact that on 14 October last year, the voters went to the polls. They voted for parties which said they were going to change this law, we were elected, and we’re delivering it.
acuity.explanation: Names the question put to him and answers the topic rather than the claim: asked for evidence for the policy, he offers an electoral mandate and asserts the question has already been answered. That is engagement with one strand — the demand for justification — while substituting a different kind of warrant and leaving the submissions, council costs and funding points untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "He hasn't provided any evidence." — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: I guess the other thing that I have to have, if in fact we are supporting local government’s needs for wellbeing economically, environmentally, culturally, and socially—assuming that we all agree on that—is how are you going to overcome this Government’s anti-Māori reputation—by supporting, and in fact leading, this type of legislation—with iwi, the only other investors that belong to this nation, that are going to be your biggest allies, should they be allowed to?
acuity.explanation: Follows the Minister's reply but engages no part of it — neither the local-decision rationale nor the mandate argument. The turn opens a separate line about iwi investment, PPPs and the Crown–Māori relationship. It is at least addressed to the Minister and gestures at the legislation under debate ('leading this type of legislation'), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the referendum requirement is about giving local communities the ability to decide and that the Government is delivering the mandate voters gave it on 14 October, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Evidence-wise, I just want to really reflect briefly, because it sort of keeps coming up and up, and it’s one person, one vote—all that kind of narrative.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's democratic-equality rationale and sets out to answer it with the New Plymouth representation record, which is a real engagement with one strand of what was just argued. It is only partial: he concedes this is his first call and moves into prepared reflection and his own evidence rather than addressing Brown's mandate claim or the submissions point, and he introduces an argument of the Minister's that was not made in the turns he follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is about giving local communities the ability to decide" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I have a relatively short question for the Minister, actually, which is: what advice did he receive and what thought did he give to ensure that Māori representation accords with te ao Māori rather than just simply a sort of colonised view of things?
acuity.explanation: Leary follows Simeon Brown's answer on the 5 percent threshold and the tabled amendment and takes up no part of it; she announces at the outset that she has 'a bit of a different question' and delivers prepared material on the census data and Ngāti Whātua representation. It is squarely on the bill under debate, which keeps it above 0.1, but the contribution would read identically whatever Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown explained that the 5 percent threshold restores 'what the previous legislation was, which was put in place by the Helen Clark Government' and described the tabled amendment, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The question here—and I think it’s been well put—is that we’re talking about a specified number of electors, but we’re only talking about 5 percent. That does not at all fit the descriptions of democracy that the Minister keeps talking about.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes up the specific figure the Minister had just defended — the 5 percent elector threshold — and argues it is inconsistent with the Minister's own account of democracy, rather than merely naming him as a target. He engages one strand (the threshold and the one-person-one-vote framing) and does not touch Brown's Helen Clark precedent point, and much of the rest of the turn is a general complaint about unanswered questions, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Democracy does have a cost. In terms of the 5 percent, that is, effectively, going back to what the previous legislation was' — Simeon Brown.

acuity.statement: There was an excellent contribution by someone on the Labour benches that also talked about the 5 percent requirement—I can’t quite remember who it was—but he mentioned whether the Minister of Local Government had considered setting the threshold the same as the citizens initiated referendum, which I believe is 10 percent. In my view, if it’s good enough for having the threshold set at the citizens initiated referendum, it should also be good enough to have that be the same in terms of having the specified number of electors.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez picks up the threshold strand running through the preceding turns and does something with it — endorsing the comparison with the citizens initiated referendum and arguing for consistency between local and national rules. But he opens by conceding he has only just arrived and has not followed the debate, cannot identify the contribution he is building on, and the bulk of his turn is new prepared material on the ratepayer roll, council funding and turnout, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we’re talking about a specified number of electors, but we’re only talking about 5 percent' — Willie Jackson (and the earlier Labour contribution Hernandez cannot name).

acuity.statement: My question is a repeat, because the Minister hasn’t at all answered or addressed it. It was a very simple question. It was the third time I’ve had to ask it. I asked him eight times last time we were debating a local government bill, so I’ll keep asking—what councils asked for this bill?
acuity.explanation: McAnulty is responsive to the fact that the Minister's answers left his question untouched — the turn would not exist if Brown had answered — but he engages the content of no preceding argument: not the Helen Clark precedent, not the tabled amendment, not the threshold. It is a gesture at the debate plus a restated question, which puts it at the top of the unpointable band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke to the 5 percent threshold and the tabled amendment's single change, and this statement does not take that content up — it restates a previously unanswered question.

acuity.statement: In regards to the decisions around times, the standing principle in the legislation is that significant changes to representation arrangements—e.g., establishing Māori wards, changing the electoral system—should generally be in place for two terms so there is time for the change to bed in. The poll outcomes will apply for six years, as was the case before 2021.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown's specific question was why a representation decision should bind two terms when other council planning instruments can be revisited every three years. Brown takes up exactly that point and supplies the rationale (time for the change to bed in) and the duration (six years), so the answer would have had to be different had she asked something else. Short of 1.0 because he does not engage her comparison with long-term plans and infrastructure planning at all, and he disposes of the other strands by asserting they were answered last night.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "why should one particular point in time determine the decisions about representation for two terms?"

acuity.statement: My submission to the Minister here for his consideration is whether or not he would consider pausing this to allow the important work of the select committee to continue in order to make sure that as this particular amendment, as proposed by the Government, moves forward—and we accept that they do have the numbers—whether or not we can pause it to ensure that the Electoral Commission and all the institutions that support the amendments that are being proposed here will be better executed in the future.
acuity.explanation: Henare follows Brown's answer on the two-term principle and six-year poll outcomes and takes up no part of it. He opens a fresh line — pause the bill pending the Justice Committee's election review — which is squarely on the matter under debate in Part 1 but would read identically whatever Brown had just said. On topic, not responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown explained the two-term bedding-in principle and said poll outcomes will apply for six years, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: My question for the Minister about this is whether there’s any been any consideration of group 3 local authorities, which would be the remainder of them, of the 78 that aren’t those 45.
acuity.explanation: Substantive turns by Wade-Brown, Brown and Henare precede this, and it engages none of them — it is a self-contained drafting question about the Schedule's grouping of councils, flagged by the speaker as her first call on the bill. Within the right debate, so not 0.0, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare asked the Minister to pause the bill pending the Justice Committee's election review, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Last night, I did ask a number of questions of the Minister. I don’t believe those have been answered.
acuity.explanation: This contradicts the specific move Brown had just made — disposing of questions by saying they "were answered last night" and "was explained in detail last night." Halbert denies the premise of that disposal rather than merely changing the subject, and the remark exists only because of what Brown said. Not 1.0 because he asserts the non-answer without identifying which question went unanswered before moving on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "In regards to the question around Tauranga, those questions were answered last night."

acuity.statement: The Minister has outlined repeatedly that he’s just taking it back to what the original legislation was pre - two years ago, but I don’t think that that’s true from what I’ve seen from this particular committee.
acuity.explanation: Brown had justified the timing rule as a restoration of the position "as was the case before 2021", and Halbert disputes precisely that characterisation, using the select-committee referral (Justice rather than Māori Affairs) as his counter-evidence. He engages the restoration claim rather than the two-term rationale itself, which is why this sits above the halfway mark rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The poll outcomes will apply for six years, as was the case before 2021."

acuity.statement: Another kaupapa that actually relates to the question that was asked by one of the members across from the Labour Party was one of the crucial roles that Māori wards play in our councils such as overlapping claims, mana whenua rights, Māori wards—actually, an example within my electorate is the Māori ward would work with the geographical board of Aotearoa to change names like Pūtikitiki.
acuity.explanation: A set of prepared, detailed questions to the Minister on the matter squarely under debate — consultation, by-election candidates, council capability, karakia in council meetings. There is a gesture at an earlier Labour member's question and at Willie Jackson's institutional-racism point, but neither is engaged as an argument: nothing is rebutted, conceded or carried forward. The speech would read identically had Rurawhe said something quite different about equity, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band, lifted to the top of it by the explicit gesture at the debate. Scored on engagement only; the specificity of the examples and the quality of the questions are other instruments' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Adrian Rurawhe argued that a minimum of one Māori ward per authority would solve the sizing problem and asked the Minister whether the bill 'meet[s] the standards of equity of valuing a particular group of people'; this statement does not take up that equity argument. It gestures at 'the question that was asked by one of the members across from the Labour Party' on the role of Māori wards, but that question is not the preceding turn in this window.

acuity.statement: Following on from the questions about the stakeholder groups who are asking for the change, which we haven’t had an answer about, I wanted to ask the Minister—not only to seek an answer to that question about which councils are asking for this but also to open a new line of questions about which constituents, which people, are asking for this.
acuity.explanation: Picks up a live strand of the debate rather than starting fresh: she notes that the consultation/who-wants-this line put by earlier members has gone unanswered, and extends it from councils to constituents. That is a genuine partial engagement — the question is built on the state of the debate and would be different had those questions been answered — but she takes up the thread's topic rather than engaging any specific claim or reasoning in the preceding turn, and the strand she names (stakeholder groups asking for the change) was put outside this window. Mid-band. Whether the Minister's silence was in fact unanswered is a veracity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has the Minister consulted with any Māori wards; if so, who, and what was their response?" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: Absolutely. I did vote for a Māori ward. And I did say in my speech in the second reading, Mr Willis, that I looked at that and thought, “Am I comfortable with that?”, and I hope that in the turnout in the election, people would, because they are so enthusiastic about Māori wards, vote in huge numbers and it would reduce that disparity. It was the opposite.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the charge of inconsistency squarely: concedes the vote, explains the reasoning he applied at the time, and reports that the expected turnout effect did not materialise. The reply would not exist in this form if Willis had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "And you voted for Māori wards."

acuity.statement: Well, if you read the select committee report and if you listen to the submissions, councils put forward some of those costs. Ultimately, democracy does have a cost. That is the point that I think has already been made in this debate.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific challenge — that the costs were never stated — by pointing to where the council cost figures are recorded, though it supplies no figure itself. Partial engagement with the actual objection rather than a pivot away from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "You didn’t say what they were."

acuity.statement: In regards to the question from Andy Foster, the answer to that question is that the Government’s position is that we are reverting back to what the policy was prior to 2021.
acuity.explanation: Names the member and the question but engages no part of the argument put — the plus or minus 50 percent population tolerance for a single Māori ward and the resulting disparity in vote weight. Restating the Government's general policy position is on-topic material that would read much the same whatever Foster had asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "What I’m asking the Minister is to at least give us a view on whether that is an issue."

acuity.statement: The Minister still hasn’t answered my question about institutional racism, but that’s fine. I want to come to a new question—well, that’s not fine. If he wants to answer that, I’ll be happy to hear him.
acuity.explanation: Registers a real feature of the turn just given — the Minister worked through Halbert, Henare, Brooking and Foster and omitted him — which shows he listened to it. But it takes up none of the content of any answer Brown did give before moving to prepared material on the Waitangi Tribunal report.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "I thank the members for their questions in relation to these issues. Many of these issues have actually already been discussed and debated last night." — Jackson engages the coverage of that reply, noting his own question was passed over

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Madam Chair. Yes, I have got a specific question and it’s following on from the Hon Rachel Brooking and her thoughtful questions. It’s around clause 17, amending Schedule 1 of the Local Electoral Act.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the matter under debate — the Schedule to the bill — that engages no argument made by any preceding speaker. It would have been delivered much as it stands whatever Jackson, Brown or Foster had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued the Waitangi Tribunal found the Government breached its duty to act in good faith and asked what consideration the Minister gave that report, and this statement does not take it up. The Brooking questions it says it follows are not among the preceding turns.

acuity.statement: The Schedule has a list of councils, the names are the legal names as set out in Schedule 2 of the Local Government Act. Only specific councils have macrons in their legal names, even though they might use them elsewhere.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific example raised and corrects the premise behind it — the Schedule reproduces statutory legal names, so the absent macron is not a spelling error. Directly addresses the point rather than the general topic, though it stops short of saying whether the checks Bennett asked about were carried out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "“Whakatane District Council” is missing, from what I can tell, a macron above the letter “a”."

acuity.statement: I thank the members for their commentary in relation to the title and commencement clauses, which we’re debating. The title of the Act is the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024, because it amends the Local Government Act in relation to electoral legislation and in relation to Māori wards and Māori constituencies.
acuity.explanation: Brown does take up the matter McAnulty raised — whether the existing title is the right one — and offers a reason for it (it names what the Act amends). But he engages only that one strand: he does not address the specific claim that the bill imposes processes on Māori wards that no other ward faces, nor the proposed alternative title, nor the question about which councils asked for the bill. The answer would have been near-identical whatever the critique of the title had been, so this sits just below a partial engagement rather than at a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "If we want to be honest and have the contents and intent of this bill reflected in the title, the title will need changing, because what the bill is doing is bringing in processes and barriers to the establishment or maintenance of Māori wards that don’t exist for other wards."

acuity.statement: Apologies, Madam Chair, for my enthusiasm to take a call, but I am proposing to the Minister that he consider a name change of the bill to the “Local Government (Central Government Imposition of Referenda that take New Zealand Backwards) Amendment Bill”. And my question to the Minister about that name is: is this Government’s racist policy taking New Zealand backwards? And what do whānau get from this?
acuity.explanation: Williams is squarely on the matter under debate — the bill's title — and puts a question to the Minister who has just defended it, which is a gesture at the preceding turn. But she engages no part of his justification (that the title names the Acts and subjects being amended); she substitutes a title of her own and then moves to cost of living, health and education. The contribution would read the same had Brown said nothing, or something quite different, about why the title stands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The title of the Act is the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2024, because it amends the Local Government Act in relation to electoral legislation and in relation to Māori wards and Māori constituencies."

acuity.statement: Just in relation to recent comments from members, there is a tabled amendment from Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan of the Green Party. The Government will not be supporting that tabled amendment as it doesn’t reflect what the bill does. The bill is the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill because it makes amendments on all three of those issues.
acuity.explanation: Bennett's preceding turn argued at length that the bill's title is misleading and floated alternative titles. Brown takes up exactly that contention — the accuracy of the title — and answers it with a reason (the bill amends all three named matters), while declining the tabled amendment. It is brief and does not touch Bennett's statistical material, and it frames the reply around the Green amendment rather than Bennett himself, so it is not a full 1.0; but the speech would have to change if the preceding turn had not disputed the title.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill 2024 is misleading" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: Another one of the comments that the Minister made was that this was returning the Act back to what it originally was. Now, if we were doing so, we would have allowed for a petition to lead to the referendum—so a rare misstep on behalf of the Minister, who claims that we are returning to the exact same law. But it’s not the exact same law.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Brown's substantive turn precedes her. She engages the Minister's position on what the bill actually does — the same ground Brown just asserted — and rebuts a specific claim of his with a specific mechanism (the old law required a 5 percent petition; this bill imposes the referendum). But the claim she rebuts was made earlier in the debate rather than in the turn immediately before, and the bulk of her call is a prepared amendment argument built around the 'rare misstep' refrain, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct answer to what Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government will not be supporting that tabled amendment as it doesn’t reflect what the bill does" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: When a Minister spends half his allocated speaking time talking about the Opposition, you know that what he's saying isn't actually quite the case, and that is absolutely the case for the Minister of Local Government. What he has promised New Zealand, he won't be able to deliver.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty follows a substantive second-reading speech that made specific arguments (the 25.8 percent to 7.2 percent Watercare figure, the price cap on entity A, the $1.25 billion spend). His reply gestures at the speech just delivered — remarking on how much of it was spent attacking the Opposition — but takes up none of its content: no engagement with the rate figures, the price-cap argument, the Crown facilitator provisions or the Te Mana o te Wai amendment. It is a meta-comment on the form of the speech plus a prepared assertion that the Minister cannot deliver, which would stand largely unchanged whatever specific argument preceded it. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture at the debate, so 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, members on the opposite side of the House, including the former Minister of Local Government himself, claim that their three waters plan would have delivered lower rates for Aucklanders than Local Water Done Well" — Simeon Brown; McAnulty notes that the Minister spent his time on the Opposition but does not engage the price-cap claim itself.

acuity.statement: As my colleague from New Zealand First mentioned before, having more Government oversight of what’s going on with councils is a great help, because, obviously, when we look around, some councils have made a real hash of their water infrastructure assets.
acuity.explanation: Smith takes up one identifiable strand of Foster's preceding speech — the claim that the bill's increased central oversight of councils matters — and adds a reason of his own for it (councils' mishandling of water assets, visible near the House). That is a partial engagement rather than a mere name-check, but he does not take up Foster's actual argument about the Auditor-General's failure to raise the red flag, nor any of Foster's other claims (the rates-rise counterfactual, Te Mana o te Wai, traffic-management costs), and the rest of the speech is prepared select-committee material on submissions, Standing Order 295(1)(b) and the "Henry VIII" clause that would have been identical whoever spoke before him. Agreement rather than rebuttal does not lower the score; the limited reach of the engagement does.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "Well, first of all, it creates greater oversight from Government, and actually that matters, because, actually, Government has been overseeing councils for decades through the Office of the Auditor-General (OAG)."

acuity.statement: Look, I would just like to answer to the member who’s been speaking, Megan Woods, about costs on the other side of the House and I’ll give her a figure: $1.2 billion of wasteful spending on consultants, on your controversial, divisive three waters—$1.2 billion worth of wasteful spending with nothing, absolutely nothing, to show for it.
acuity.explanation: Wedd names the cost strand of Woods' speech explicitly and offers a counter-figure, so the engagement is pointable and the opening would read differently had Woods not argued on costs. But she answers the TOPIC rather than the CLAIM: Woods argued this bill loads compliance onto councils with no funding, citing specific rates rises, and Wedd does not take up the funding gap or the rates figures — she pivots to Labour's past three-waters spending and then to prepared material. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "This bill imposes more costs on the ratepayers of New Zealand."

acuity.statement: We all know that we must do more to ensure that we have safe drinking water, but the way to do it is through localism and democratic processes.
acuity.explanation: This asserts the contrary of Woods' central charge without engaging any part of her reasoning for it — nothing on the absent guaranteed right to be consulted on water services plans, the consultation obligation extending only to the council-controlled organisations, or the Crown facilitator power. It is prepared material squarely on the matter under debate with a gesture at the localism question, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "It is a bill that does not protect local democracy; in fact, it erodes it."

acuity.statement: New Zealanders need better water quality. New Zealanders deserve to have good, clean water. Our future generations need certainty—our future generations need certainty of the sustainable water infrastructure going into the many generations. What New Zealanders don't need is the waste of time. So, with that, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Lu follows a substantive turn by Russell that makes a specific affordability argument (named rates rises, 20 percent of Far North ratepayers in arrears, poorer councils unable to fund infrastructure). Lu's close engages none of it: no reply on who pays, no figures, no rebuttal of the cost-sharing case. It is prepared peroration on the right subject — the drinking-water bill — so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read word-for-word the same whatever Russell had said. Scored on engagement only; the thinness of the content belongs to Specificity and the localism-versus-sharing merits to Rigor, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued that poorer district councils cannot fund water infrastructure from rates — 'their neighbouring district council was not in such a wealthy area, had not been able to rate in a way that enabled them to build up infrastructure' — and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I stand on behalf of the Green Party and share with this Whare that te iwi Māori are sick of the attacks of this coalition Government on our people: te reo Māori, Te Aka Whai Ora, 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, the mega-prison, boot camps, killing our people with tobacco, reviewing all Treaty clauses within legislation and ripping them out, the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—you dare attack our takutai moana, touch it, watch te iwi Māori respond.
acuity.explanation: Hipkins' preceding turn made specific arguments about this bill — that only the Māori ward decision from a representation review is made subject to a referendum, that Māori wards confer no extra votes and so are consistent with 'one person, one vote', and that 52 mayors opposed the mandated polls. Lyndon takes up none of those claims. She opens prepared Green Party material that re-lists grievances against the coalition (and echoes two items Hipkins himself had just listed, Te Aka Whai Ora and the Treaty clauses review) without doing anything with his reasoning. The speech would read identically had Hipkins made a different argument on the same subject, so this sits in the low band; it earns 0.3 rather than 0.0 because it is squarely about the matter under debate — the Government's treatment of Māori in this bill — and extends the same thread of examples rather than arriving from another debate entirely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "scrapping Te Aka Whai Ora, scrubbing te reo Māori from the names of Government departments, their divisive Treaty Principles Bill"

acuity.statement: Isn’t it a bit rich to accuse others of being poor governors when, one week after his announcement, he’s still not really clear what the management structure of Te Whatu Ora really is?
acuity.explanation: Follows Reti's defence of the published table and takes up its substance: he 'stands by' a table he collaborated on, and she presses that he still cannot state the structure. It also picks up the 'botched restructuring' charge he opened with and turns it back. The question would have to change if Reti had instead disclaimed the table, so it is genuinely shaped by what preceded it, though it pivots into a 'bit rich' framing rather than contesting the table itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Reti: "We collaborated with Health New Zealand and we produced the table that was then published in public domain, which we stand by."

acuity.statement: Does his private health insurance cover injuries sustained while being thrown under the bus by the PM?

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Reti said "We collaborated with Health New Zealand and we produced the table that was then published in public domain, which we stand by" and this statement does not take up its content, only the PM's relationship to him.

acuity.explanation: Chhour had just conceded that past boot camps were horrific and caused harm; this takes that concession and presses its consequence, demanding a guarantee that the admitted harm will not recur. The question is built on the preceding answer and would read differently had Chhour denied past harm. Short of 1.0 because it restores the 'boot camps' label she had just disputed rather than engaging her distinction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "Yes, I do agree that boot camps in the past were horrific and did cause harm to people who went on those boot camps."

acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Chhour's case — her 'military-style academy' characterisation and claim that the design drew on military programmes — by denying there is anything military about it. But it does not take up the preceding answer about risk mitigation at all, and reads as prepared material aimed at the branding rather than at the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "The Government has begun a military-style academy pilot, which got under way yesterday, as part of the Government’s response to address serious youth offending"

It engages the topic of the evidence rather than any specific figure she cited, so it is partial engagement.

acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "I’ve seen evidence that the previous approaches to youth crime saw a 291 percent increase in ram raids over the last six years."

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown said "NZTA conducted a review of temporary traffic management at 800 maintenance work sites" and this question does not take that up, moving instead to the next prepared topic.

acuity.statement: Can he confirm that one of the reasons New Zealanders are faced with a sea of orange road cones is unclear health and safety obligations, and that’s why this Government is going to make sure that our health and safety rules are clear, sensible, and proportionate to risk?
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of the answer it follows and adds a causal strand from her own portfolio, but does not take up Brown's specific claim that NZTA could not supply three years of expenditure data. acuity.statement: What will the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill do?
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific item from the answer immediately before it — Goldsmith's reference to the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill's second reading today — and asks him to expand on it. acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "today, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will have its second reading, providing police with more tools to deal with gangs"

acuity.statement: As Cameron Luxton said, what this does—and this is an area which I do think you need to think about—is you could actually support a Māori ward, and, actually, a Māori ward was introduced when I was the Mayor of Wellington.
acuity.explanation: Foster picks up the specific proposition Luxton had just advanced — that one can support a Māori ward and still support this bill — names him as its source, and carries it into his own distinct argument about the relative weighting of votes under Schedule 1A. The speech would have to change if Luxton had argued something else, which puts it well above prepared-material-on-topic; it is a partial rather than full engagement because he adopts Luxton's framing rather than testing or contesting its reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Although I do not support race-based wards, one can support Māori wards and this bill." — Cameron Luxton, immediately preceding turn

acuity.statement: Chris Hipkins said that Māori wards are one person, one vote, and that it doesn’t give Māori extra votes, and he’s correct on that. But what he has failed to see is that there is a major flaw in the Local Electoral Act.
acuity.explanation: This is the rubric's model case: he concedes the specific claim made against him, identifies precisely what it omits, and then supplies the omission — the plus-or-minus-10-percent provision that lets a Māori ward be established on half the population of a general ward. Not scored a full 1.0 only because Hipkins' turn is not in the supplied window, so the engagement is auditable through Foster's own rendering of it rather than against the original words.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is all about one person, one vote" — Chris Hipkins, earlier turn in the same debate (quoted by Foster; Hipkins' own turn falls outside this window)

acuity.statement: The incoherence of this Government that purports to believe in local democracy and speaks in terms of rights-based frameworks—we hear the term “equality” used. Well, an equality that relies on taking rights from one group—iwi Māori—to somehow make us all more equal is snake-oil equality. We are all the poorer for it. By saying that a majority can vote on the rights of a minority, or that a majority can vote on indigenous rights, betrays a profound lack of understanding of basic democratic principles.
acuity.explanation: Abel takes up the specific strand Foster closed on — that Māori wards create a democratic-structure problem — and contests it on its own ground, arguing that submitting minority and indigenous rights to a majority vote misunderstands democracy, and later pressing the one-person-one-vote point back at Foster via multiple ratepayer votes. He leaves Foster's actual evidence (population per councillor, turnout a third to a half of general wards) entirely unaddressed and spends most of the speech on prepared Te Tiriti material, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "this is a fundamental problem for the democratic structure of this bill"

acuity.statement: The strategies and actions from Government are not new nor misguided; unfortunately, they are calculated, and I listened to the calculation speech across the House earlier. All the numbers but nothing about actual tangata whenua, people.
acuity.explanation: She points at Foster's statistical case — "the calculation speech" — and characterises it as numbers without people, but engages no part of its content: not the turnout figures, not the population-per-councillor claim, not the enrolment point. The reference establishes she heard him; the speech itself is prepared material on the bill's wider significance and would read identically had Foster argued something else on the same topic. A gesture at the debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "the turnout in those wards is between a third and a half of what it is in the general wards"

acuity.statement: The bill doesn’t remove Māori wards. The bill doesn’t remove constituencies. The bill reverts the law back to where it was in 2021 under Jacinda Ardern.
acuity.explanation: This corrects a specific factual premise carried by both preceding opposition speeches — Kapa-Kingi's repeated "the removal of Māori wards" and Abel's "this law is not democracy" — by denying that the bill removes anything and locating the restored position in time. He opens by saying he set aside his prepared words because of what he had just heard, and goes on to engage Kapa-Kingi's "we Māori see you" as a claim to decide who counts as Māori. The speech is visibly shaped by the turns before it; it falls short of 1.0 only because he asserts the correction rather than taking up the democratic-principle argument Abel actually advanced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "The removal of Māori wards is merely another open invite to racists across this whenua"

acuity.statement: We’ve just heard that the only way to get this opportunity is through the provision of Māori wards. Well, can I mention a few names as to other ways that one can get elected? Can I mention the names of our two Deputy Prime Ministers: Winston Peters and David Seymour? Can I mention Shane Jones? Can I mention Casey Costello? Can I mention Shane Reti? Can I mention Tama Potaka? Can I mention Nicole McKee? And can I mention Karen Chhour? None of them were elected through Māori wards or through Māori seats. It can be done, Mr Jackson, and you too are living proof of that. There are other ways and they are proven.
acuity.explanation: Brewer opens by naming the exact proposition Jackson closed on — that Māori wards/seats are the route to Māori participation — and attacks it directly with a counter-list of Māori MPs elected by other routes, including Jackson himself. The speech would have to change entirely if Jackson had argued something else; it is built on his closing claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "the only way we’re going to get that opportunity again is if you vote for a Labour Government in 2026" (and "That’s what the Māori wards gave us, Mr Meager")

acuity.statement: It was Labour, as others have said—James Meager, our learned chair of the Justice Committee has already articulated that it was Labour who brought in local communities’ rights to petition for a referendum if they got above 5 percent, and that was through the Local Electoral Amendment Act 2002. Willie Jackson knows this very well, because Mr Jackson was in The Alliance at the time that it was fully behind their Minister leader of The Alliance—and, of course, of Māori descent—Sandra Lee. She was the champion of this, and Willie was her wingman in Parliament, arguing for this, only 22 years ago. So we are merely bringing back what Mr Jackson fought so hard for only a generation or two ago.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the democratic-legitimacy strand of Jackson's speech and turns it on him, arguing the referendum-petition mechanism being restored is one Jackson's own side legislated and he personally championed. It engages Jackson's position rather than any specific claim or figure he advanced, and relies on prepared historical material, so it is a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "There’s nothing radical going on here. No stealing of democracy. In fact, we’re strengthening democracy by allowing participation with local Māori of the community."

acuity.statement: This bill wants to put in place particular barriers that impact access to representation that is only going to be unique to tangata whenua, to Māori. This barrier is not going to be put in the way of rural-ward voters.
acuity.explanation: Follows Brewer's turn, which framed the mandatory poll as pure localism and said Māori can still get elected in general wards. Halbert takes up that claim and attacks its premise directly — the poll requirement is applied selectively, to Māori wards and to no other ward type — so the argument is aimed at the case just made rather than merely at the topic. Marked down from the top band because the second half of the speech returns to prepared material (the Minister's quote, the committee referral) and never engages Brewer's specific evidence, such as the 35 percent Cabinet figure or the Auckland councillor claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "There’s nothing more pure than a referendum. This is localism in action."

acuity.statement: I think we have heard harsh words in this debate. We have heard “extermination”, we have heard “racism”—we have heard a lot of harsh words—but what we aim for in this amendment bill is to give voice to the people that we all represent, in the places that represent.
acuity.explanation: A substantive preceding turn by Halbert was available, with a specific and answerable claim about selective application. Garcia instead notes the register of the opposition's language, restates the bill's purpose, and delivers prepared material on representation and his own community's experience. Naming the words used is a reference, not an engagement with the content behind them; the speech would read identically had Halbert argued something else about the bill. Scored 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the gesture at the debate's conduct is real and the speech is squarely on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the bill imposes a poll requirement unique to Māori wards that is applied to no other class of voter, and this statement does not take that up. It gestures at the debate only by labelling opponents' language harsh.

acuity.statement: Ko te take i tīni ai te ture kia whai tūru Māori ki runga i ngā kaunihera, koirā te take nā te mea mai i tērā ture tawhito o te tau 2002 tae noa ki te tau 2019, kotahi anake te kaunihera i eke. Kotahi anake te kaunihera i whai tūru Māori.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the record that the government case depends on: under the poll law that ran from 2002 to 2019 exactly one council ended up with Māori seats, against 50 after it was repealed. That is the empirical answer to Brewer's prediction that councils will simply win a mandate and keep their wards, and it is the figure the preceding turns left out, so the speech would have to change had the other side argued differently. Held below 1.0 because she engages the government's broad position and its "you don't understand the legislation" line rather than any one speaker's reasoning, and the surrounding passages are prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "So now we have the opportunity for those mayors and councillors to go out to the public and get a mandate to support what has been so effective for them, and I’m sure many will get across the line and retain their Māori wards."

acuity.statement: I’m just going to take it back to basics, because there has been a lot of, as my colleague prior said, unparliamentary words thrown around in this House. So I’m just going to take it back to basics, notwithstanding what’s being hurled at me from across the room.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive opposition turn in the same third-reading debate, so she is eligible. Her speech acknowledges the chamber's heat ("unparliamentary words", "what's being hurled at me") but engages no part of the preceding argument: neither the councils' opposition nor the claim that the bill attacks Māori representation is addressed. The four numbered points about the bill's provisions and the "equal citizenship" principle would have read identically whatever the previous speaker had said. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band — prepared material on the right subject — and 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is at least a gesture at the debate just had.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued "how this bill is clearly an attack on Māori" and asked "what about the 52 local and regional councils who say, 'No, this is not what we want.'" — this statement does not take up either point; it gestures only at the tone of the debate and then delivers a prepared four-point summary of the bill's clauses.

acuity.explanation: Abel follows Utikere's substantive turn in the same debate and lands on the same broad strand (councils and local input), so there is a clear gesture at the matter under debate. But he takes up none of Utikere's actual arguments — not the truncated 13-day submission window, not the rejected five-year/10-year extension compromises, not the 50 percent cap on cost recovery, not the director-general's role in initiating reviews. His own figure ("every single regional and local council") is asserted independently rather than built on or corrected against Utikere's seven-of-eight count, and the passage reads as prepared Green material on the ocean as a commons that would be word-for-word the same whatever Utikere had argued. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band: on the right subject, engaging no part of the preceding argument, with 0.3 for the topical overlap.

acuity.responding_to: "Seven of the eight were in opposition to this particular bill" — Tangi Utikere, who argued councils must be able to initiate a review of permits without the director-general's consent

acuity.statement: I want to sort of touch on a couple of notable remarks from the Opposition members—I think they’re very salient, a couple that I absolutely agree with, and that was the collegiality of the committee and how we worked, I would say, to progress the bill forward.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Abel's turn — his characterisation of the select committee process as collegial and constructive — and accepts it explicitly, before moving on to prepared material on the bill's merits. A real but partial engagement: it concedes the atmosphere point without touching any of Abel's substantive objections (finfish consenting, cost recovery, the director-general veto).

acuity.responding_to: "I thought we had some quite useful conversations across the best select committee in this House" — Steve Abel

acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the submission statistic Abel closed on, concedes the weight of opposition, then does something with the remaining share — turning the 10 percent into the body of his argument (iwi Māori in the fisheries space exercising tino rangatiratanga). The speech would have to change if Abel had not cited the submissions breakdown. Not a full 1.0 because he reframes rather than contests the figure itself.

acuity.responding_to: "we heard that 91 percent of the submissions were against this legislation" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: If we could, I’d ask the House to indulge me further and let’s delve into the sentience, the animal welfare issues, the benthic nature of sedimentation, the nutrient loading in the localised area, especially in the finfish space. I think a lot of the controversy that we heard was predicated on that concern. Industry had a different view on how they could alleviate that.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific strands of Abel's finfish case — sentience, welfare, benthic sedimentation, nutrient loading — and answers them with the industry's counter-position that investment certainty enables mitigation. Squarely aimed at the argument just made rather than at the speaker; the quality of the counter-evidence is a Rigor question and left out of this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We heard, on the impact on the fish, that they are probably risking being against our current code of welfare, in terms of animals. They are a sentient species." — Steve Abel

acuity.explanation: Redmayne built her case on what the select committee heard, quoting four supportive submitters at length. Luxton takes up that same strand and contests it on its own ground — the aggregate submission count, 1,000 of 1,100 opposed, against the handful Redmayne read out — and ties it to the 13-day window that produced them. It engages one strand of the preceding speech rather than its substantive case about investment certainty, and then returns to prepared material on process, Treaty engagement and council costs, so it sits mid-band rather than at the top.

acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "This bill removes barriers to growth and investment in the aquaculture sector, and we heard this message loud and clear from businesses and organisations during the select committee process."
