acuity.explanation: Luxton had just set out Labour's two alternative durations — the five years submitters wanted and the 10-year compromise the Opposition moved. Campbell's analogy takes both of those exact numbers in turn and argues each is too short to justify capital investment, which is precisely the ground Luxton's amendment rested on. The speech would have had to change if she had argued something else about duration. Marked down from 1.0 only because the rebuttal is an analogy rather than an answer to her specific reasoning about certainty for the sector.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "Many submitters thought that 20 years was too long and they thought that five years would be enough. As my colleague Tangi Utikere mentioned before, in the spirit of collegiality, we came up with 10 years as a medium"

acuity.statement: If we look at something like a kilogram of salmon, those greenhouse gas emissions are down to about 6 kilograms, and if we look at something like mussels, it’s probably about 600 grams.
acuity.explanation: Luxton's environmental objection singled out finfish as the high-impact case. Campbell answers on that terrain with comparative emissions figures that include salmon — a finfish — alongside mussels and beef, so he is supplying evidence against the specific distinction she drew rather than ignoring it. He engages the emissions dimension only, not her separate and more central complaint that the environmental impacts were never fully assessed, and he opened by announcing he would focus on prepared material about investment uncertainty.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "We heard quite clearly that finfishing does have quite an impact on the environment. So we thought—well, we agreed with the Green member’s proposal that perhaps the rollover shouldn’t occur for finfish farms"

acuity.statement: There were 1,100 submissions heard and 1,000 were against this bill. We continuously hear that side of the House talk about democracy and the importance and power that, in a democratic sense, they have been awarded since the election last year, but then every day since then, they’ve ignored democracy.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one strand of Wedd's case that rested on the select committee submissions and turns the submission record against her, giving the tally of opposing submissions Wedd did not mention. It engages that strand rather than the detail of her cost or export arguments, and the rest of the turn is prepared material about the Minister, so it is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "we did hear from a lot of industry players during the Primary Production Committee process" — Wedd built her case on what submitters told the Primary Production Committee.

acuity.statement: This isn’t a prospect for growth. In fact, it’s the desperation of twilight politicians whose random retorts in the House remind me of a boar that’s been captured and has just been told to get its snout out of the trough.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the growth claim just made — it is contradicted flatly — but no part of the reasoning behind it is engaged: no answer on the export figures, the reconsenting cost, or the productivity argument, only a pivot to invective about the Minister. A bare denial plus abuse sits in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "it will drive productivity and it will help our Government achieve what we want to in the next 10 years, and that is doubling the value of our exports".

acuity.statement: But, ultimately, there is a desecration of our marine spaces if we do not take the time to review resource consents.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the industry's value (she has just described whānau benefiting from oyster farms) and then disputes the inference, naming what the saved reconsenting cost buys at: unreviewed consents. It engages the trade-off Wedd asserted rather than her specific figures, so it is a solid but not complete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "So this is a cost that these industries could be putting back into innovation, into technology, into rebuilding—and building—their industries."

acuity.statement: But we’re—well, that’s fair; you do need security of tenure in order to innovate, but the idea that you would confer an additional private owner-occupier of the marine space—which is not their space; they have a licence to occupy it.
acuity.explanation: Parker is interrupted mid-argument and takes the interjection up directly: he concedes the point (innovation does require security of tenure) and then disputes what he says follows from it, distinguishing a licence to occupy from ownership of the marine space. The sentence only exists because of what was just said to him, which is the strongest form of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Hamish Campbell, interjecting: "New innovation in technology."

acuity.statement: More farming in New Zealand? Well, that might be the eventual outcome, but in terms of the question as to whether we should have more aquaculture farming or whether we should have more dairy farming, that is a proper question for New Zealand that should involve an economic question as to the cost of greenhouse gas emissions.
acuity.explanation: He repeats the interjection back, partly accepts it ("that might be the eventual outcome") and then draws out its consequence — that the choice between aquaculture and dairy is exactly the allocation question emissions pricing would settle. This is engaging the content of the heckle rather than merely naming it, though it also serves to return him to his prepared emissions-pricing material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum, interjecting: "More farming—more farming. More farming in New Zealand, then."

acuity.statement: These organisations have made a huge investment in what they’re already doing, and a lot of them need to invest in updating and improving their equipment, their plant, and the sites that they already have maintained and are managing.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one strand of Parker's argument — his point that these are renewals of consents held by operators who have already invested — and answers it by saying further investment in plant and sites is still to come, so certainty of tenure still bites. But it is reached via her colleague's framing rather than Parker's, and the rest of her speech leaves his central claims (the 26 February to 4 March consultation, the truncated select committee process, the loss of councils' ability to charge, the resource rental) entirely untouched before returning to prepared material on economic recovery.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "We’re actually not talking about new consents; we’re talking about renewals."

acuity.statement: Absolutely right—our children need jobs. There’s over 3,000 people employed by this industry, and there could be more if we could actually give it the chance.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the jobs point put to him from across the floor, accepts it explicitly and then does something with it, supplying an employment figure for the sector and extending it to the possibility of more jobs. Short of 1.0 because the interjection was brief and the figure plainly belongs to his own prepared case rather than being drawn out by what Brown said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And they need jobs—our children need jobs." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Now, there was a comment made earlier about people resisting this bill, resisting wealth. You show me one tangata whenua; one Māori; one anybody who submitted opposing this bill who doesn’t want wealth—who doesn’t want to be wealthy—for their whānau and ngā uri whakatipu, for generations to come. I will defy you to show me one.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific premise of the government speakers' case — that opposition to the bill amounts to opposition to wealth — names it, and disputes it head-on, challenging anyone to produce a submitter who does not want prosperity. Not 1.0 because she engages the framing rather than Campbell's actual figures (3,000 jobs, doubling exports), and the comment she rebuts is partly from a turn outside the stretch in front of her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We could double our exports if we could just give it a chance, and that’s why I rise to support this bill." — Hamish Campbell (and the earlier characterisation of opponents as resisting wealth)

acuity.statement: But listening to speeches in the House today, members of the public who might be watching this debate on television or listening on their wirelesses, would be thinking that, actually, this was about the difference between a Government that wants to get things done, to get things moving, to get growth in the economy, to make it easier to create jobs and business and opportunity for people in a sector like aquaculture that has become so important to not only our nation but to regions like mine in the beautiful Coromandel—then, to hear Opposition members talking about why they can’t do things.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at having listened to the preceding speeches but engages no part of their content — nothing on the 13-day timeframe, the 1,000 submissions, or the Rangitāne submission he had just heard read out. Characterising opponents as a 'can't' party is a reference to them, not engagement with their argument, and the passage would read identically whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued the select committee allowed only 13 days to consult and that her side asked only for more time ("All we ask for was more time, as are the submitters."); this statement does not take that up, and instead recasts the Opposition speeches as saying things can't be done.

acuity.statement: Actually, on this side of the House, we don’t see the environment and the economy as necessarily being binary or mutually exclusive. We think that, actually, if you have a strong and growing economy, then you can better protect the natural environment by maintaining, enhancing, and protecting it.
acuity.explanation: Does meet the environment-versus-economy strand that the previous speaker put at the centre of her case, answering the trade-off claim with the counter-proposition that growth funds protection. Only partial, because it answers the topic generically rather than the submission's specific concerns about kaitiaki responsibilities, consultation or council costs, and the material reads as a stock formulation usable in any such debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are also concerned that there is a lack of balance between commercial and environmental interests and protections. Economic growth and industry or business assurance should not be at the expense of our environment" — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel, quoting the Rangitāne submission

acuity.statement: The former speaker, the Hon Rachel Brooking, was entertaining, albeit a little bit incorrect, because whilst council-controlled organisations (CCOs) do exist and can and, in fact, are encouraged under this bill, what this does is this is only bill two out of three, so I can tell you the trilogy is not yet complete; wait for bill three. Just like the CCO in Auckland called Watercare, which now has a separate debt-to-revenue cap, which is one of the options available to us, because you asked about finance and also infrastructure funding and financing. So there's a whole raft of tools that are coming.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton opens by naming the specific claim Brooking had just made — that the bill only lets councils do what they can already do via CCOs and fixes none of the funding problem — and answers it on its own terms: he concedes CCOs already exist, then argues this is the second of three bills and points to Watercare's separate debt-to-revenue cap as the financing tool she said was missing. The speech would have had to change if she had argued something different, which is the test. Not a 1.0 because the rebuttal partly defers to unlegislated future bills rather than meeting the funding argument on the current bill's contents, and after this passage he reverts to prepared material on the previous Government's Three Waters entities. Scored only on engagement: the weakness of the 'wait for bill three' inference belongs to Rigor, and the jab at the 'entertaining' former speaker belongs to Civility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "This bill enables councils to do what they can already do, in terms of having council-controlled organisations."

acuity.statement: I rise this evening to speak in support of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill. I actually was enjoying the first few minutes of the Hon Ginny Andersen's contribution, when she outlined what a scourge gangs are in New Zealand, and the damage and harm they cause. This coalition Government has promised a crackdown on crime, and that is what we are delivering.
acuity.explanation: Paul's immediately preceding turn made four specific arguments: that the bill ignores the State-care origins of gangs, that suppression has never reduced membership, that the powers are already available under the Summary Offences Act 1981 and the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act 2013, and that non-consorting and dispersal orders fall disproportionately on indigenous people (with the New South Wales figures offered as evidence). Stephenson engages none of these. He reaches past Paul to praise an earlier speaker's framing, then delivers prepared material describing the bill's tools and the Government's law-and-order programme — a speech that would read identically whatever Paul had said. It is squarely on the matter under debate and does gesture at the course of the debate (Andersen's contribution, the Minister's accepted amendments), which lifts it above the floor, but there is no point in it where an opposing claim is taken up, so it sits in the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul argued that "all of the powers that are in the bill already exist" and that gangs originate in State-care abuse, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Let me conclude by offering some reflections of my own on the submissions that the Justice Committee received, because they’ve been referenced tonight and they got quite a shining review. I don’t think that the review should have been that shining. We pretty much received submissions from all of the national legal bodies—the Law Society, law associations, Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa, and many others—and they unequivocally, in unison, said that the bill was rubbish, that the bill should not have made it this far, that the bill should be thrown out, and that the Government should start again from a more restorative starting point.
acuity.explanation: Ferris takes up the specific claim in Arbuckle's immediately preceding turn — that the select committee process produced 'insightful' submissions that 'strengthened the effectiveness of this bill' — names it as the 'shining review' just given, and contests it with the content of those submissions. The passage would have to change if Arbuckle had characterised the submissions differently, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he answers the characterisation in aggregate rather than engaging any particular point Arbuckle drew from the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "Several points that were raised in the select committee were both insightful and strengthened the effectiveness of this bill."

acuity.statement: It was astounding that there was unanimous condemnation of the bill by the national legal community and that a Government could have brought a piece of legislation this far without taking any consultation or any advice from any of those bodies, and when cornered with the facts, the Government just reverts to saying, “Well, we campaigned on being tough on gangs and crime, we won the election, and, on that basis, we’re doing it.” Well, if that’s the quality of the argument and the rationale, then that’s just pathetic, and you should go back to the start.
acuity.explanation: This engages the mandate argument Arbuckle had just made — that New Zealand First campaigned on action against gangs, committed to it in its manifesto and is now delivering it — by restating that reasoning and then attacking it as insufficient justification against the legal advice. It is aimed at the substance of what preceded it rather than merely referring to the speaker, but it addresses the Government's position generally rather than any figure or clause Arbuckle cited, so it is a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "We are proud to deliver what we campaigned on" (and "New Zealand First had committed to this in our manifesto, and now we are delivering what was set out in our coalition agreement into legislation.")

acuity.statement: We are—unlike the views of many of the members opposite—not talking about wayward community groups who are doing their best but have a couple of bad eggs; we are talking about organisations that are systematically set up to cause misery, cause violence, and cause harm to our communities.
acuity.explanation: Meager opens by taking up the characterisation of gangs that Carter had just advanced — gangs as a community people turn to when the State fails them — and contests it directly, substituting an account of gangs as organisations constituted for harm. The opening would have to be written differently had Carter not made the community-formation argument, which is what earns a high score; it falls short of 1.0 because he restates her position in a harder form ("wayward community groups... a couple of bad eggs") rather than engaging the causal claim as she put it. Whether that restatement is fair is a reasoning question, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "we understand authoritative figures like the police and the State being so unsafe that people will find community with each other"

acuity.statement: Yes, we can talk about some of the causes of our gang culture and, yes, we can talk about some of the horrific actions of the State in decades past, and we can talk about the social investment approach which this Government believes in, which will help to go some way towards solving the challenge of gang membership in 20 years’ time.
acuity.explanation: This concedes the substance of Carter's central argument — that State abuse is causally upstream of gang formation, as set out in the royal commission report she had just cited — and then disputes what follows from it, arguing the causal remedy operates on a 20-year horizon while the bill addresses present harm. Accepting part and contesting the inference is engagement with the specific argument made, not a mere reference to it; it is not 1.0 because he does not take up her particular evidence (the 138 recommendations, or the claim that most gang members are survivors of State care) before moving to prepared committee material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "The report clearly outlines the pathway from abuse in State care to the creation of gangs."

acuity.statement: Then we heard from the previous Labour member “Let’s start the talk as to what really works.”, and something about “Let’s have a conversation.” Well, this is coming from a senior former Minister in the Labour Party, which had six years in power with an absolute majority of 65 MPs, and now they are telling us, nine months into Opposition, that we should start the conversation as to what really works.
acuity.explanation: Brewer quotes the specific strand of Webb's speech — the call to stop the bidding war and start a conversation about what works — and does something with it, answering that Labour had six years and a majority in which to have that conversation. It engages the call for a conversation rather than any of Webb's substantive claims (the Chief Science Advisor's finding, the criminologists, the unworkability of dispersal notices), and then moves to prepared material on Labour's crime record, so it is a partial engagement: the strand engaged is pointable, but the argument itself is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Let’s start talking about what we can really do, and, look, this window-dressing bill does nothing."

acuity.statement: OK, well, let’s talk about the bill then. Let’s go back to the bill because the previous speaker, Mr Webb, got into the weeds, and I’ll just remind the viewing public what the bill actually offers up as far as its provisions go. It prohibits the display of gang insignia in public places, it empowers police to issue dispersal notices that require specified gang members to leave a public place and not associate in public for seven days, it creates a new non-consorting order that prohibits association and communication between specific gang members for three years, and it amends the Sentencing Act 2002 to make gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
acuity.explanation: Leary interjected asking what is actually in the bill, and Brewer explicitly turns to answer it, supplying the four substantive provisions in order. The speech visibly changes shape because of what was put to him, which is the test. It falls short of 1.0 because what he supplies is a recitation of the bill's contents rather than engagement with the specific objection on the floor — Webb's argument that the dispersal power's trigger is too vague and its service mechanism unworkable, which Brewer dismisses as "the weeds" instead of meeting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "What’s in the bill? What’s in the legislation that you want to put forward to the House?"

acuity.statement: The provisions, as we’ve said, give police the power to disperse gang members, and we believe them to be really unworkable.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the very provision Garcia had just outlined — the police power to break up gang gatherings — and disputes it, so this engages one strand of the preceding Government turn rather than ignoring it. But it is a flat assertion of unworkability prefaced with "as we've said", i.e. prepared material that does not take on Garcia's actual reasoning about public confidence or menacing behaviour, and she immediately defers the detail to colleagues' earlier speeches. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "There is also the opportunity for police to intervene in situations where three or more are gathered, which, again, is there to seek to put some confidence in the public that the police are looking into and preventing threatening behaviour."

acuity.statement: Again, it’s relatively frustrating and really annoying that at this time of night, having heard no really substantive contributions from the Government—I mean, we’ve heard contributions that talk around the edges, that talked about the technicalities, and that talked about fairly innocuous or fairly mundane aspects of the process, but we haven’t heard anybody really come out and sell this bill tonight.
acuity.explanation: This is a gesture at the preceding Government contribution — it even characterises it ("talked about the technicalities") — but it engages none of its content. Garcia argued a specific mechanism, that criminalising patches and insignia strips gang membership of its allure and that consequences for public behaviour are the bill's object; the reply neither rebuts that mechanism nor concedes any part of it, simply dismissing the speech as not selling the bill. A dismissal of a speech is not an engagement with it, so this sits in the unresponsive band, lifted to 0.3 only because the complaint is aimed at the debate just had rather than being transplantable to any other day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "The bill seeks to reduce the behaviour engaged in by gangs and to disincentivise gang membership, because as it seeks to deal with the elements that make gang membership exciting, probably, and alluring to many, they will be dampened down." — Garcia did argue a mechanism for the bill; this statement characterises Government speeches as technical and mundane without taking up that argument.

acuity.statement: In the case of the Ngarimu Act, as the previous speaker has mentioned, the two areas—one of them is a technical amendment around the successor of the 28th Māori Battalion.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan names the previous speaker and restates the same two amendments she described, but does nothing with her argument — he does not take up her central point that the Government voted against the bill at first reading and has now come on board, nor dispute or extend anything she claimed. The reference is acknowledgement, not engagement, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on Māori and Pasifika educational attainment that would read identically whatever Tinetti had said. On topic, with a gesture at the preceding turn, so the upper end of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "The fact is that the bill amends the Ngarimu Act to create this new position for the Ngarimu Board for a person of Māori descent who has served or is currently serving in the armed forces."

acuity.statement: I rise in support of this bill. It is the third reading, and there are, obviously, some minor changes, and I think they have been well traversed in the House and we’re all in support.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns with real content precede it — but the speech engages no part of either. It gestures at the debate having happened ("well traversed in the House") without naming or answering a single thing said in it, and would be word-for-word deliverable after any pair of speeches on any uncontested third reading. Above 0.0 only because the gesture at the debate and the subject-matter are correct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued at length that Māori and Pasifika attainment is falling ("only 32.9 percent of all Māori school leavers have attained NCEA level 3") and that cuts to Ministry of Education regional offices undercut the bill's aims, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Just in response to Lawrence Xu-Nan, who called this an omnibus bill, these scholarships are really, really important scholarships. They have a proud heritage, but it is nevertheless a small omnibus, and I just think it’s curious that sometimes we have bills on issues of this scale when there are much, much larger things which don’t require legislation at all.
acuity.explanation: Takes Xu-Nan's specific characterisation of the bill as an omnibus, accepts part of it and qualifies the rest — the scholarships matter, but it is a small omnibus — and then draws out a consequence about Parliament legislating on matters of this scale. The speech would have to change if Xu-Nan had framed the bill differently, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because the qualification is a reframing rather than a rebuttal of any reasoning Xu-Nan offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "This is an omnibus bill that amends specific technical elements of a number of bills, like the previous two speakers have mentioned in terms of their contribution to this bill."

acuity.statement: I was also interested, Lawrence, in your comments about the decline in educational performance over the last couple of years. It’s good that you’ve come to that realisation and that we’ve got something to fix on this side of the House.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand of the preceding turn — the declining attainment figures Xu-Nan put on the record — and does something with it, turning the decline into a charge against the years in which it occurred and a task for the current Government. Directly keyed to what was just said and addressed to the member by name. The quality of that inference, and the needling tone, belong to Rigor and Civility; as engagement with the argument just made it is near the top of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "In 2022 we’re seeing that only 32.9 percent of all Māori school leavers have attained NCEA level 3, which is a decrease of 44 percent from 2021."

acuity.statement: I have said many times that I had the great pleasure of being up in Gisborne for the most recent Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion awards, and it was a great experience for me to see that firsthand and to see the importance of making sure that we set this up in such a sustainable way that it doesn’t require our constant intervention.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Kahurangi Carter on the Ngarimu scholarships and Māori/Pacific tertiary participation. Nimon lands on the same subject matter — the Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion awards — and gestures at the state of the debate elsewhere in the speech, but takes up no part of Carter's argument: she neither engages Carter's account of the scholarships' purpose nor her claim about Māori and Pacific access. Substituting a different argument on the same topic for Carter's turn would not change a word of this. Prepared material on the right subject, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter said "This bill provides the conditions to inspire, reward, and support Māori achievement" and argued for Māori and Pacific tertiary participation; this statement shares her subject but does not take up any part of that argument.

acuity.statement: Now, I don’t want to take away from the mana of these organisations that are involved in this piece of legislation. I think that there was some objection to that in the first reading of this, and I want to acknowledge, as my colleague Kahurangi Carter has, the words of Kelvin Davis, who was very strong at maintaining the mana of, especially, the Ngarimu VC and 28th (Māori) Battalion Memorial Scholarship Fund at the time of the first reading—which I think is really important—and the Pacific Education Foundation trust is also important.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Carter's earlier turn — her invocation of Kelvin Davis on the mana of the Ngarimu scholarships — names it as Carter's, and extends it to the first-reading objections and to the Pacific Education Foundation trust. That is a genuine partial engagement: this passage would read differently had Carter not made the Kelvin Davis argument. It is not a full 1.0 because she affirms and broadens the strand rather than rebutting, testing or drawing out a consequence of it, and the surrounding speech returns to prepared material about the bill's history.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Kelvin Davis said these scholarships and awards are a tribute to the heroes of the 28th Māori Battalion" — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: I think one particular point I would like to make in relation to this bill is the interesting context that we have with this bill coming through the House today: tomorrow we are seeing a tax relief after 14 long years, and in this bill we’re seeing the inflation adjustment of the expenditure amounts from 1972 to today of $500 to $10,000—important context if you think about the timing when we are shepherding that tax relief through the House tomorrow.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this, most immediately Camilla Belich's argument that National opposed this bill at first reading and should not discount small bills introduced by another party. Bates engages none of it — no answer on the first-reading position, no response on the bill's provisions as she described them. The substance of the contribution pivots to tomorrow's tax relief, which is indifferent to what was said before it and could have been delivered in a different debate. Only the arithmetic link to the bill's $500-to-$10,000 adjustment keeps it from 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued "those opposite who now have swapped benches with us were opposed to it" and drew a lesson about not undermining small bills from other parties; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: You told Cabinet it would cost $400 million.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure Peters had just claimed credit for setting as Minister and turns it against him — the interjection would be meaningless after any other sentence. It engages the claim rather than the topic, though it does no more than assert ownership of the number.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “we ensured a cost of no more than $400 million was set for replacement ferries—no more than $400 million for two ferries” — Winston Peters

acuity.statement: No, no, no. You’ve got it in the article, honey, don’t worry about it. Once Labour took over, they allowed the project to bloom to guess how much? To $3.2 billion.
acuity.explanation: The interjection put it to him that the $400 million figure was his own advice to Cabinet; he denies it with 'no, no, no', waves it off to the article, and immediately returns to prepared material about Labour's blowout. There is a gesture at the point put to him but no part of it is actually taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “You told Cabinet it would cost $400 million.” — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: You wouldn’t know what work is—you’ve been in here for so long.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific boast just made about having done more work and more jobs, supplying a reason (length of parliamentary service). Aimed squarely at the claim, but adds nothing beyond contradiction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “I’ve done more work than you’ve ever dreamt of doing and more jobs than you ever thought of doing” — Winston Peters

acuity.statement: Oh no—look, Mr Waititi, you wouldn’t know what work looked like, either. We all know about your background. You’re all talk, mate.
acuity.explanation: This is the opponent's words handed straight back ('you wouldn't know what work looked like, either') with no engagement with the reason Waititi gave. Mirroring a jibe is not taking up its content, so it sits in the low band despite naming the member and his claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “You wouldn’t know what work is—you’ve been in here for so long.” — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: What are specific initiatives, and what are their emissions implications, that have been introduced since the data used in this report was closed off?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact defence just offered — that the commission used older data predating the second emissions plan — and presses for the specific initiatives and emissions numbers that would have to exist for that defence to hold. The question could not have been asked in this form if the previous answer had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "We welcome the commission's advice but note it is based on older data and does not take into account the Government's draft emissions reduction plan No. 2."

acuity.statement: Will he advocate to retain the ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration, given backtracking on this policy could, according to the commission, potentially impact our ability to meet emissions budgets and the 2050 targets?
acuity.explanation: Prepared supplementary on the same subject matter (emissions budgets and the commission's report) but engaging no part of the answer immediately before it; the claim about EV chargers and being on track goes unexamined.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds had just claimed the Government is "on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets" and is "investing in electric vehicle chargers", and this question does not take that up — it moves to a prepared new strand on the oil and gas ban.

acuity.statement: How is the situation in Gaza different, as the Prime Minister keeps saying?
acuity.explanation: Isolates the single assertion the Prime Minister has repeatedly relied on and asks for the justification he has not supplied. Entirely shaped by what preceded it — it would be unintelligible after any other answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "they're different situations and we respect the ICJ rulings" / "So what we've done is we're looking at the situation in Gaza. It is different."

acuity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that every New Zealander in Gaza, contrary to what the questioner said, has been assisted out of Gaza by Foreign Affairs and other embassy work around the world in this country’s interests?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly aimed at the preceding questioner's claim and disputes it on the substance of who has been helped out of Gaza, which is genuine engagement. Marked down from full because it answers a narrower proposition than the one put — New Zealanders rather than their families — so only part of the claim is actually taken up. Whether that substitution is fair is a rigor question, not an acuity one.

Government Ministers have been very careful not to imply at all that gang membership and gang intimidation across the country is intimately linked with Māori. acuity.explanation: Takes Ferris's specific charge — that the House's framing insinuates gangs are a Māori problem — and does something with it: contests it as to Ministers' conduct, offers his own handling of the Ministry of Justice advice as counter-evidence, concedes the point that the vast majority of Māori are not in gangs, and then takes up Ferris's second strand on intergenerational causes by pointing to the Budget. The speech would have to be rewritten if Ferris had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "the subtle insinuations that this is all a conversation about Māori, and Māori being the problem of gangs in this country—it really needs a little bit of balancing out".

acuity.statement: I just wanted to respond to the earlier speech in relation to the impact of this legislation on predominantly Māori communities. I want to make the first point that the suggestion was that since this Government had come to power, a message from Wellington had a direct impact on police decision-making about where to put the helicopter or to turn up to particular events. I want to assure that member that of course the operational activities of the police are, by law, independent, and no Minister would ever seek to direct the police and how they go about those prosecutions and activities.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith isolates the specific causal claim in Maipi-Clarke's speech — that direction from Wellington since the change of government is shaping police deployment at tangihanga — restates it accurately and answers it with the operational-independence point. The reply would have had to be different had she made a different argument, which is the test. Short of 1.0 because he takes up only that one strand and then moves to general expectations, leaving her concrete questions (the definition of "reasonable grounds", what happens to tangihanga, whether attendees could be arrested) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they have been told that they’re getting clear direction and indication from Wellington, from this place here" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by another member precedes it in the same committee debate — but the engagement is a bare courtesy followed by an explicit pivot to Webb's own prepared material on the "gang insignia" definition and his Amendment Paper. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke argued the bill will licence racial profiling of Māori and police interference in tangihanga, and this statement does not take any part of that up — Webb opens by complimenting the speech and then announces he will "bring the focus a little more narrow" onto clause 4.

acuity.responding_to: "the really positive progress that has been made over the past few years" — Lan Pham

acuity.responding_to: "In terms of the non-consorting orders, well, I’ll come to that detail when we come to that." — Paul Goldsmith (and Goldsmith's earlier answer about the sticker being removed from a car)

acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "We find that, in acting in this way, Ms Genter committed a contempt of the House."

Marked down from 1.0 because he leaves Webb's second request — his view on the 'w' amendment adding a visibility test to the definition of gang insignia — entirely unaddressed.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "you’ve said that this bill is about stopping intimidation, and I’m interested in your view on whether that’s all it does"

As reflected in the research and also as laid out in the regulatory impact statement that’s been tabled, gang members are disproportionately young male Māori and live in more deprived communities in New Zealand. So the overview of that is that about three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: two substantive turns by other members precede it, including the Minister's answer on the bill's purposes. But this is prepared material on a different strand of the same bill — it engages neither Webb's visibility amendment nor Goldsmith's enumeration of purposes, and would read word-for-word the same had either said something else. Scored 0.15 rather than 0.0 because it is squarely about the bill under consideration and is addressed to the Minister in committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Goldsmith had just set out the bill's four purposes in answer to Webb's question on insignia visibility, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it opens an unrelated line on Māori impacts.

acuity.statement: So, in terms of the purpose of the bill as a whole, the Minister just spoke to those—I think it was four—overarching purposes, but how does that fit with children? Because these are quasi-criminal infringements, if you like.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given four purposes and does something with them — presses whether that purpose structure can coherently extend to a 13-year-old subject to a quasi-criminal dispersal regime. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public."

acuity.statement: Look, I just want to probe a bit at some of the underlying things I believe are missing, and it’s based, really, on the fact that, given what we know and understand around things like Māori incarceration as a country, around things like poverty that Māori endure and have endured for centuries as a country, the things that we already know—Māori are overrepresented in incarceration figures, as we know.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Andersen on the withheld implementation-challenges paragraph and police enforcement capacity, and engages none of it. The speech is prepared material on the broader subject of the bill's effect on Māori — it would read identically whatever Andersen had said — so it sits in the unresponsive band, lifted slightly off 0.0 only because it is still about the measure under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued that paragraph 118 of the regulatory impact statement was withheld under section 6(c) of the OIA and that front-line police numbers have fallen by around 124, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Now, in response to the observations by our member from the Māori party, Mr Ferris, what I would point out is that if our only response to the increase in violent crime that people have seen in our community and the rise of gang activity—if the only response from this Government was this legislation, he might have a point. But that is not the only response of this Government: we continue to invest widely in many innovations such as Te Ao Mārama, court system, and many aspects of our justice system which are designed very much to work with specific needs and requirements of Māori in relation to crime, and we work very closely with many iwi groups right up and down the country.

Not a full 1.0 because it answers the 'missing underlying things' charge at the level of programmes listed rather than engaging the historical-dispossession reasoning Ferris actually set out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "I just want to probe a bit at some of the underlying things I believe are missing ... Māori are overrepresented in incarceration figures, as we know."

acuity.statement: Just very briefly, we have many times raised the issue of the ability of the police to enforce this legislation, and we’ve been very clear that, ultimately, police always have discretion as to when it is appropriate or not to engage, and they will retain that discretion. But we have every confidence that with sufficient planning and arrangements, they will be able to enforce this law.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Andersen's case — whether police can operationally enforce the ban — and answers it with discretion plus planning. But it leaves her central and specific demand untouched: what paragraph 118 says and the grounds for withholding it under section 6(c). Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "having a law that is not operationally able to be implemented risks undermining the confidence that the New Zealand public have in the New Zealand Police"

The speech would be materially different had Webb not raised that example.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the idea that someone who has been in trouble for having gang patches, all of a sudden because they’ve got their dad’s jacket hanging in the spare wardrobe, can go to jail for a year"

Short of 1.0 because the 'why so late' and procedural strand of Webb's attack is left untouched, and the concurrence question is answered by restating the clause rather than addressing the concurrence issue.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "So here’s my questions to you: why now, why so late, and what is the harm?"

acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's answer — the court prohibition order framing — and restates it accurately before moving to a largely fresh line of questioning about firearm prohibition orders and the artistic-purpose exemption. Engagement with the specific claim just made is real but partial; most of the turn is new material on the same topic rather than a response to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "I’ll highlight that this is relating to a court prohibition order, so this isn’t a power set upon the police; it’s the court applying a prohibition order."

acuity.statement: So it is unlikely that a former gang member who is doing art will be subject to a prohibition order given that the member has just referred to them as being a former gang member who’s now doing art.

Squarely aimed at the specific scenario just put.

acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "what if it’s a former gang member who has got an FPO and a prohibition who draws some art with gang insignia on it and gets searched?"

So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose. So I think that’s a useful suggestion that the member made.

The reply could not have been given had Webb raised a different amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: “You will have seen my tabled amendment. It may be that the Minister, because he’s got the resources of the entire State behind him, has tidied up my drafting on this”

Has he spoken to the Eugene Ryders and has he spoken to the O’Reillys, who have been major commentators in this area? I’m interested to hear whether they came through.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Just in relation to that in terms of consultation, of course we’ve just had a very lengthy select committee process, where there have been more than a hundred people making submissions on the bill, and I can assure the member that the Ministry of Justice, through its many liaison committees with Māori iwi and hapū, will have had many conversations. So that’s important. In terms of the Iwi Leaders Forum, to be honest, most of the conversation that I had related to other legislation than this.
acuity.explanation: Answers both strands Jackson put: the general level of consultation (select committee, Ministry liaison committees) and, specifically, whether the bill came up at the Iwi Leaders Forum — conceding it mostly did not. acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Because of that, we don’t really wear red in Tokoroa, and that’s just the way that things are."

acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Within the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act report, it talked about how restricting what people can wear can be a contravention of freedom of expression."

But I want to dig down into why, and I want to understand from the Minister why he is setting aside the advice, which is always his prerogative, but it’s very necessary that the New Zealand public understands why that is being exercised.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "The Ministry of Justice’s preferred option is option one", which is the "status quo"

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the parties of this Government campaigned on a set of policies and won the election and included in their first 100-day plan the intention to deliver what they promised during the campaign"

acuity.explanation: Takes the specific argument just made — that self-determination covers what a person chooses to wear — and turns it against the member by citing her own earlier Tokoroa example of people not being free to wear red. acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Self-determination means that you can wake up in the morning and choose the things that you want to do—you are determining for yourself—and that includes what you choose to wear every single day."

acuity.statement: The whole idea is that if there’s, you know, a person in Tokoroa that’s wearing known gang insignia and that person is doing it to intimidate the public so that they don’t wear red, as the Minister said—well, fair enough, we don’t want that going on.

acuity.statement: Just picking up on a couple of things the Minister said—before I go into my question as well—the Minister mentioned before about greater authority for the District Court. I would like to just clarify to the Minister that it is not greater authority. The principle of comity states that it is already the rights of courts to be independent and for the judiciary and for the legislature not to impede on the independence of the judiciary.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "there is a series of consequences that flow, so as to give the judicial system greater ability to deal with recidivist offenders in this way"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to respond to one of the questions that the previous speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, raised in relation to the three-strikes legislation—and I’m sure that he’s fully aware of this: that three-strikes legislation has particular offences that are included in strike offences, which does not include the gang patch one. acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "whether they are going to be a part of the three-strike legislation later on as one of their strikes"

acuity.statement: There are two parts to this question. The first is my question about the deceased person. This is an important question because there are situations where gang insignia is displayed on a coffin.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (who is a 'person' under clause 7(1)) but indifferent to the turn it follows; the same words could have been delivered after any intervening contribution.

acuity.statement: Just in reply to the first part of the member’s questions in terms of the responsibility in terms of gang patches and funerals and so forth, the law is very clear: it is the person who displays the gang patch who is responsible, and it needs to be in a public place. Those are the matters that are relevant.
acuity.explanation: Answers the first of the two questions just put, identifying who bears liability at a tangi and on what condition, which is precisely the ambiguity Williams raised. It leaves her second question about young people untouched, so it is a partial but squarely aimed engagement.

acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "undertakers, that people who carry on the business of funeral direction, that hospitals, and that people who conduct the affairs of the marae ... are not intended to be considered as persons under his provision at Part 2, clause 7(1)"

acuity.statement: Thank you. Mr Chair, you may recall I sat down before I’d finished making a contribution, because an answer came and I was going to come back and the Minister took on that line and answered my question and was very reassuring, saying that this was only about public places. But when the discussion has gone on in this committee stage, we have talked about proposed clause 8A, which actually talks about insignia inside of the home and a prohibition occurring there.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it is the person who displays the gang patch who is responsible, and it needs to be in a public place"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb asked whether a court should have discretion under section 8A ('must' or 'may') and why there is no alternative to imprisonment in clause 8A(6), and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: As the Hon Dr Duncan Webb just said, when faced with a group of three or more people who you believe or have reasons to believe are gang members and therefore are in a group and therefore could be disorderly or cause intimidation, a constable then has to go and not just tell them that they’ve got to go away from each other but issue them in writing. As we’ve heard, you know, police don’t carry paper and they don’t have that in written form—so we’re certainly led to believe throughout this process—so it’s a matter of asking those people individually for their emails so that they can be issued that infringement notice via email, and, if they don’t give that email or don’t see the rationale behind what the question is, even asking them if they will accompany that police officer to a police station, presumably so that something can be prepared for them, printed out, and given to them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact strand Webb left with the Minister — 'how is this actually going to work' for dispersal orders — and carries it a step further, into the mechanics of serving a written notice on people who give no email and will not accompany a constable, ending in a concrete question built on that premise. The speech plainly could not have been given unchanged after a different preceding argument. Not a full 1.0 because it extends a colleague's point rather than contending with its reasoning, and some of it is prepared material on the Minister's earlier Part 1 answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the first question I have that I’d like the Minister to address—and I’ll keep my contributions short in so far as I can so that he can respond in the way he anticipated—is how it’s going to work." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: My question is around the dispersal notices aspects of Part 3 of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill. There was a little bit of commentary made by the Minister before the dinner break about pro-social activities that gangs perform within communities. So my question is around why the Minister chose to ignore advice from justice officials around enforcing this ban on gangs gathering in a public place and how it is likely to undercut “efforts to cultivate pro-social activities within gang communities, for those groups that have moved towards adopting such behaviours”.
acuity.explanation: Follows McLellan's specific question about how a dispersal notice can physically be served, and engages none of it; the question put here is a prepared line about officials' advice and pro-social activity, aimed at remarks the Minister made before the dinner break rather than at anything in the preceding turn. It is squarely on the matter under debate (Part 3 dispersal notices), which keeps it off the floor of the band, but the content is indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan asked how a dispersal notice gets issued if a person provides no email and will not accompany a constable to a station, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Is it an assumption that the police officer will see said gang members doing whatever they’re doing—they might be just chilling or walking down the street—and the police officer has to follow those individuals to issue that notice? Or how do you even know that they were the original gang members in the first place?
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Andersen and picks up one strand of her argument — the practical difficulty of establishing that the people later encountered are the same people originally served — applying it to clause 9(2)'s allowance for notices issued after the gathering, and she elsewhere nods to 'as per previous contributions' on the burden on a sole officer. But the bulk of her turn is her own prepared material on whānau, tamariki, prohibition orders and Te Tiriti consultation, which is indifferent to what Andersen said. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how will the police officer prove, how will the prosecution prove, that in fact they are the same two members" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: The member referred to three gang members watching football or rugby on the sideline and watching their kids playing rugby, and it would be surprising that that would be a case of unreasonably disrupting the activities of other members of the public. What we are thinking of, though, is if there were 50 motorcycle gang members taking over a town and meeting in the middle of town; that would be something that is potentially disrupting the activities of other members of the public.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith takes up Lyndon's specific hypothetical — three gang members on the sideline of a junior rugby game — and does something with it, saying it would be surprising for that to meet the 'unreasonably disrupting' threshold, then supplies the contrasting case the provision is aimed at. Across the turn he also answers her whānau-association concern with the immediate-family, work, education, healthcare and tangi exemptions, her sole-constable point with the discretion to issue a notice later, and her no-consultation claim with the four-month select committee process. The speech would be entirely different had she raised different objections. Marked down slightly only because her direct question on Te Tiriti obligations is left unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Gang members might be at a local rugby game for JMB, supporting their children" — Hūhana Lyndon

acuity.statement: But with respect, the member is mistaken when she’s suggesting for a moment that the so-called pro-social activities of gangs will be stopped by this process, because police need to reasonably believe that the dispersal notice is necessary to avoid the gang unreasonably disrupting the activities of other members of the public.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Paul's actual claim — that the dispersal notice power would catch gangs' pro-social activity — concedes the premise that such activity exists, and then rebuts the inference by pointing to the statutory test the notice must satisfy. The speech would have been different had she argued something else; the reply is built around her examples.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "That is providing a positive social outcome for that community, which would not be possible had these laws been in place, because these laws would be used against them."

acuity.statement: I’ve heard his answers to my colleague Tamatha Paul that there are certain examples where, in his view, dispersal notices wouldn’t be issued, and I wanted to ask him whether he had received any advice on dispersal notices in relation to activities which would fall outside of what could reasonably be expected to be covered by this clause.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's reliance on the 'unreasonably disrupting' test as a sufficient safeguard and presses exactly where that reasoning is weakest — whether anything confines the clause to gang-related activity — asking what advice he has on uses outside his examples. Directly conditioned on what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "That is the clear test for this legislation, so it won’t be capturing those things."

acuity.statement: I know that he’s said—and I appreciate—that for the purposes of protest, this is not meant to be the purpose of this section. I appreciate that and I think that’s clear, but I’m talking about other activities.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the Minister's answer she regards as settled — his clause 9(3) protest carve-out — and isolates the part it does not cover, which is the classic accept-part/dispute-the-rest engagement. Slightly short of 1.0 only because it concedes rather than works on the substance of his point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Again, I’d refer to clause 9(3), ‘Limit on issuing’"

acuity.statement: I do think the member is somewhat lacking in imagination, because it is quite possible that certain gang members might be in the habit of gathering regularly every day for a week in a manner that unreasonably disrupts the activities of the members of the public, and so the purpose of having served the dispersal notice would be to stop the re-gathering in that particular circumstance.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific objection to the words "or were gathered" and answers it on its own terms, supplying the scenario (habitual daily re-gathering) in which a post-hoc notice would still serve the bill's purpose. The reply would be different had Webb argued something else; its weakness as a rebuttal is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and the "lacking in imagination" jab does not reduce engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "to issue a dispersal notice after the dispersal is an absolute nonsense" — his argument that a notice served after a gathering has broken up is purposeless.

acuity.statement: I have a number of questions which I’ll keep really short to also make the point that the practicalities of this are really difficult.

A gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.statement: That is so dangerous, because, in my eyes and within our experiences, that is stereotyping 101, and I circle the definition of what is “reasonable grounds”, and to use the word “suspect” is very, very dangerous, because we know, and the data shows, that we are over-profiled.
acuity.explanation: Squarely about the clause under debate, so not a zero, but it engages no preceding speaker's argument — the profiling case is prepared material on the speaker's own experience and would read identically whatever Leary or Goldsmith had just said.

acuity.statement: I also note the Minister hasn’t answered my questions in relation to clause 9(1)(b). But I don’t want to talk about that any more. I want to move on to another part of the bill, which I feel also needs to be addressed.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith had just set out the 48-hour revocation process through the Commissioner of Police, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it notes an unanswered earlier question and explicitly moves on to clause 9(3).

acuity.statement: I’ve just heard the Minister in the chair, Paul Goldsmith, in his answer, talk about how he’s giving the police extra tools to be able to deal with people going about their everyday business. It is an issue for us when “on reasonable grounds”, which is very subjective for police officers, many who we have found in the past—and many reports have come out of the police, that there is racial profiling in the police department.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith's defence rested on the gang-member threshold being a real safeguard against wrongful notices; Waititi attacks that threshold directly, arguing that suspicion of gang membership on reasonable grounds is subjective and exposed to police racial profiling. Held below 1.0 because he restates Goldsmith's position loosely (as giving police tools against "people going about their everyday business") rather than meeting the test as the Minister stated it — a looseness that belongs to Rigor, while the aim at the preceding claim is genuine.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Of course, the requirement is to be a gang member, part of the three or more, and it’s necessary to avoid unreasonably disrupting."

acuity.statement: That’s the worry there: where we have the balance of probabilities that young people could be vulnerable to prosecution through this legislation just because they’ve had a photo by a policeman—you know, how long ago—because they were just sitting casually at a bus stop, and then next minute they’re deemed a gang member because they’ve got a hoodie on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause and standard Webb had just attacked — the civil "balance of probabilities" test for establishing gang membership — and draws out a consequence he had not supplied: that retained police photographs plus a low standard of proof exposes young Māori to being deemed gang members. That is engagement with the specific claim, not merely the topic, so it sits above the prepared-material band. It falls short of 1.0 because it does not take up his actual reasoning (that the provisions are punitive and therefore demand the criminal standard), and after this strand she moves to her own prepared material on penalty levels and Schedule 2. Scored on engagement only; the soundness of the inference and the truth of the photo-retention claim are other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This is the clause which says that in matters of fact arising in this proceeding, it is a civil standard of proof." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: In relation to helping out with vaccination campaigns, again, that is not captured by this legislation, because it would be very hard to describe that as unreasonably disrupting the activities of members of the public. acuity.statement: In terms of racial profiling, I think the only point I’d make there is, you know, it’s very easy to say and very damaging for the many thousands of young men and women in the police force who do their very best every day to keep the community safe. It’s a very easy allegation to throw at them, and it’s one which—we back the police to do their job, and of course recognise that over the past and in our history, and there are claims that are made that need to be dealt with carefully.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the racial-profiling strand explicitly and so is not prepared boilerplate, but engages the topic rather than the evidence advanced for it; the reply would be essentially unchanged had Waititi cited different figures.

acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "there have been already reports come out about the police already having racial profiling within the police"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued the bill's reasonable-grounds test would reach onto marae and Goldsmith replied with the clause 18 review process; this statement takes up neither and turns to the member's own Amendment Papers.

acuity.statement: I think, in this case, with clause 29, with the application of the Evidence Act, I want to seek clarification from the Minister in terms of if he had any consultation—because it’s not in the regulatory impact statement—with the District Courts in terms of the application of this particular part.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'who identifies these gangs? What do you deem as a gang' — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke. Nothing in this statement takes up her question about the gang list.

acuity.statement: So there are criteria that are already specified. When this matter was before the Justice Committee, the police did update the list of gangs by adding four, separating two, and removing several, and that list can be amended for Schedule 2 by Order in Council.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Maipi-Clarke's specific question — who identifies the gangs and by what process — and supplies the mechanism: specified criteria, police revision at select committee, amendment by Order in Council. acuity.responding_to: 'who identifies these gangs? What do you deem as a gang and how is the process of these gangs being identified?' — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke.

acuity.statement: My argument is this: that if an organisation—and this is a tabled amendment before the committee—doesn’t absolutely meet all of the criteria of being a gang, then surely the Minister must take the gang off the list. It’s not discretionary, because, again, this is a significant incursion.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand of clause 30 that McLellan opened — the Minister of Police's power over the Schedule 2 list — and carries it somewhere new, from 'how robust are the criteria' to 'removal must be mandatory, not discretionary'. acuity.responding_to: 'because it’s on the recommendation of the Minister of Police—and you alluded to the fact that there was some criteria' — Tracey McLellan.

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to take what is my first call on this bill, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill. I would like to ask the Minister a question that relates to clause 28. It’s a very discrete clause. I don’t think it has perhaps been touched on yet, so I’ll make sure that I do that.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez asked what would happen if a gang appropriated a political party's insignia under clause 29 and section 128 of the Evidence Act, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just answered Duncan Webb that a de-listing obligation 'was considered, but, actually, decided it wasn't necessary', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It is true that if being a member of a gang is an aggravating factor when you get a parking ticket, well, that’s going to be an issue for many of our people, because, ultimately, don’t we have the right to freedom of association?
