On topic but unresponsive, so the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 for being firmly inside the clause-by-clause debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere spoke immediately before, asking the Minister at what stage of 'preparation' clause 3(2)(b) bites and what 'public disclosure' in clause 3(2)(c) requires, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I want to pick up on something the Minister of Local Government said in response to one of the previous speakers. We were worrying about the difficulties, and so on—so I take your point about us going to discuss that further. He said that he’s going to assume that councils can do their job. But I do want to draw the Minister’s attention to the regulatory impact statement and to really question that comment that the Minister made, because it runs up against some of the stuff that we were told in the Finance and Expenditure Committee about how many of the councils were going to struggle with some of the requirements.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific assumption, names it, and does something with it: tests it against paragraphs 30, 31 and 40 of the Government's own regulatory impact statement and against select committee evidence, then draws the want/can distinction to show the assumption is contradicted by the Minister's own officials. The speech could not have been delivered if the Minister had said something else, which is the deciding test. Marked 0.9 rather than 1.0 only because the engaged words are reported by her rather than appearing verbatim in the window.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "he's going to assume that councils can do their job" — the Minister of Local Government (Simeon Brown), quoted by Russell from his reply to an earlier speaker in this debate; she also takes up the 'difficulties' thread from Tangi Utikere's preceding turn.

acuity.statement: What I would like to know is whether, in the Castalia report that the Hon Barbara Edmonds referred to, there is anything in there that attempts to move beyond those qualitative assessments?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific document Edmonds had just raised (the January 2024 Castalia draft report) and does something further with it — joins it to paragraph 167 of the regulatory impact statement and asks whether the report supplies the quantitative costings the department admits it did not complete. The question could not have been framed this way had Edmonds not spoken; it extends her point rather than merely naming it. Not a full 1.0 because it builds on a colleague's line rather than rebutting or testing a contested claim, and it returns to prepared overarching material about costings.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I came across, in the regulatory impact statement, a footnote in relation to a Castalia report, which was from January 2024" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: The Castalia report was commissioned by the department. I haven’t received a copy of it.
acuity.explanation: Answers precisely the question put: Edmonds asked whether the Minister or officials received the Castalia report, and this supplies the answer directly (commissioned by the department; he has not seen it). He then goes on to supply the modelling figures the two members had been probing. The reply would be entirely different had the preceding contributions raised a different document.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Did he receive that report from Castalia or is that a report that officials received from Castalia?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: So, in terms of looking at the purposes of the bill, which, essentially, seem to be structural purposes, to get a framework for delivery of water, I’m wondering why, in there, there’s nothing about the consumer.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own characterisation of the bill as a framework for local government to manage and deliver water services and presses on what that framing leaves out — the consumer's price and quality interests. That is a genuine engagement with one strand of what was just said, but the bulk of the contribution is prepared material on the previous Government's approach, airport pricing regulation and the definition of "financially sustainable", and it does not take up Brown's bottom-up/top-down modelling argument at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this bill is around establishing a framework for local government to manage and deliver water services" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: One of the questions I have for the Minister, and I’d be keen to know, is that, of course, credit ratings are something that are continually monitored by the ratings agencies, so, therefore, does the Minister foresee that this information will never be made public, that this isn’t something that we can have some transparency around? I would argue that you could put the argument that you’re continually and perpetually in a state of the credit rating agencies considering commercial sensitivities.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's stated rationale for the redactions — commercial sensitivity while a credit rating is established — accepts it, and then draws out its consequence: because ratings agencies monitor continuously, the sensitivity never lapses and the information would never be released. That is working on the specific reasoning just offered, not merely restating a prepared question. Marked down slightly because the turn then moves to a separate prepared question about the purpose clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "In regards to the question around public disclosure, this is, of course, part of the disclosure requirements that are being imposed here around economic regulation and, of course, transparency requirements."

acuity.statement: In relation to the first question, I have made it very clear that that is in relation to Watercare establishing a credit rating, and this is redacted in order to not prejudice them establishing a credit rating. Once a credit rating is in place, generally those are made publicly available, and there’s obviously processes that go on from there. In relation to the second question, this is Part 2. There’s obviously further legislation to come to the committee.
acuity.explanation: The first half squarely answers the specific point Woods pressed — whether the sensitivity is perpetual — by supplying the end condition (once the rating is in place, ratings are generally published), which is exactly the content her argument demanded. The second half dismisses her purpose-clause question about funding by location in the bill rather than engaging it at all, so the turn engages one of two strands put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "does the Minister foresee that this information will never be made public, that this isn’t something that we can have some transparency around?"

acuity.statement: Here is just a very short question from me, going back to the Minister’s previous contribution in saying that this bill was about supporting councils. I did mention, in my first contribution, that there seems to be some irony here when this Government says that they’re interested in what’s happening at the local level but there’s no funding from the centre. So can the Minister address that question?
acuity.explanation: She picks up the specific claim the Minister had just made — that the bill puts in place a regime supporting councils to deliver water services — and tests it against the absence of central funding, asking whether the effect is instead extra workload. The question could not have been written without his claim, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "We’re putting in place a regime here which supports them to do that, and it’s something which many councils campaigned for."

acuity.statement: I just have a very quick follow-up question, and I thank the Minister for his answer and for clarifying that he sees that that is about the credit rating being established and that, following that, there can be disclosure. So what I would like some clarity from the Minister on is when he sees that point being reached.
acuity.explanation: She restates the Minister's answer accurately, accepts it, and presses the one thing it left open — the point at which a credit rating counts as established — which is the precise gap in what he said. Entirely contingent on the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Once a credit rating is in place, generally those are made publicly available, and there’s obviously processes that go on from there."

acuity.statement: That is a matter for Auckland Council, which is going through the process of the financial separation for Watercare.
acuity.explanation: The reply is aimed at the question asked — it addresses who decides when the rating is established — but supplies none of the expectation or time frame Woods sought, and it leaves Brooking's immediately preceding question about central funding wholly untouched. Engagement with the topic of the question without engagement with its substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "what I would like some clarity from the Minister on is when he sees that point being reached"

acuity.statement: I will just very quickly remind the Minister that before the dinner break, he had made the comment that the bill is going to support councils, and we are yet to hear how this bill is going to support councils.
acuity.explanation: She engages the fact that her question drew no answer and re-anchors it to the clause under debate, which is responsive to the Minister's silence rather than to anything in his content. The preceding turn — about Auckland Council and Watercare's financial separation — is not taken up at all, and this contribution would read identically whatever he had said in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "That is a matter for Auckland Council, which is going through the process of the financial separation for Watercare."

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her question. The question is in relation to the definition of “financially sustainable”. It’s a definition which is a broad definition to encompass a wide range of councils in New Zealand, and this legislation requires all councils to put forward their water service delivery plans, which, of course, includes the Chatham Islands, which will be required under the legislation to also be putting forward a plan.
acuity.explanation: Brown correctly identifies the strand Genter raised (the clause 5 definition of “financially sustainable”) and applies it to her specific case, confirming the Chatham Islands will have to submit a water service delivery plan — so the reply is shaped by what she said rather than being generic prepared material. But he engages only the definitional half: he leaves untouched her central question about how a council whose rates cover 40 percent of operating costs, which cannot service debt, and which has deferred renewals for decades would ever be judged sustainable, and says nothing about her direct ask of a Crown mechanism to fund capital works. Partial engagement, then a return to the general framing of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So how will they be judged as financially sustainable?" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I want to follow my colleagues in sticking very specifically to Part 2, Subpart 1, and I want to pick up on an amendment that I’ve tabled, which is specifically related to both clause 11 and clause 13, and it’s Amendment Paper 68.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive preceding turn by a different member (Woods) is in the window and made specific claims and questions. Pham engages none of them — not the 12-month preparation window, not Buller, not affordability — and instead delivers her own tabled amendment on the plan's minimum duration and climate provisions. She does gesture at the debate by naming the same Part and subpart and by referring to following her colleagues, which lifts it off the floor, but a reference is not engagement, so this sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band. Scored on engagement only: the quality of her Taituarā and Wellington/Horowhenua evidence, and the fact that she is on-policy throughout, are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "one of the questions that we have for the Minister here is around the time frames for preparation of these plans" — and her argument about orphaned councils such as Buller and the absence of any affordability requirement. Nothing: Pham gestures at the same subpart but takes up none of Woods' claims; her turn is prepared material on her own Amendment Paper 68 and the 10-year planning horizon, which would be word-for-word the same had Woods argued something else about Subpart 1.

acuity.statement: In terms of the Hon Megan Woods’ question there, ultimately, the process is around the use of the powers which are envisaged through 3(2)(b) within Part 2 of the bill and in terms of the process, but it doesn’t change the fundamentals in terms of the water service delivery plan needing to be prepared.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the clause Woods named and asserts the delivery-plan requirement is unaffected, which is the topic she raised, but does not engage her specific point about intervening without costings that have moved beyond indicative. Partial engagement: the topic is answered, the claim is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How will it work when there aren’t any more detailed costings and these have moved beyond indicative, if that 3(2)(b) is instituted?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: The Minister suggests that that is a bottom-up approach to not put those things as overarching objectives. What it made me consider, looking at the regulatory impact statement, was: what was the background to these reviews of the way that our water is done?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's bottom-up/purpose-clause justification and turns it into the question of why safety and environmental performance are absent from the purpose, which is a real engagement with what was said. But it then runs into prepared material on the history of the three waters review and the Havelock North outbreak that would have been delivered whatever the Minister had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the purpose of this Act is to establish a framework for local government to manage and deliver water services" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The Minister talked about looking from the bottom up, rather than the top down, but this is where my confusion sits, because in the regulatory impact statement (RIS), officials have used the $120 billion tab minimum—minimum—based on the Water Industry Commission of Scotland’s (WICS) analysis.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own bottom-up/top-down distinction and presses it against the document his officials relied on, arguing the $120 billion WICS figure was itself built from information supplied by every council and so was not top-down. That is doing something with the specific framing just offered, not merely restating a prepared critique.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Rather than coming in from a top-down perspective ... we're taking a bottom-up" / "this is about a framework" — Simeon Brown's bottom-up justification

acuity.statement: The question, though—which I didn’t answer before—was in regards to public ownership. The purpose of the Act is to establish a framework for the local government to manage and deliver water services. I think it’s clear in the intent that this legislation is not about privatisation of water infrastructure. It’s very clearly about local ownership and control and management and delivery, and that’s very clear in the wording that we have determined and used in this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question he had left unanswered and addresses it squarely on the point of privatisation and local ownership. Short of 1.0 because Abel asked for guarantees in the legislation and the reply offers intent and wording rather than engaging whether the Act contains any such guarantee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d appreciate an answer as to what guarantees the Government is making that they will retain the water services in public ownership" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: In relation to the questions by Barbara Edmonds around the modelling, the key point I’d make in response is: this is about a framework. It requires water service delivery plans to be put in place that will identify, at a local level, what those costs are, what’s required to meet the infrastructure growth, and how that can be addressed. That’s the purpose of these. Rather than coming in from a top-down perspective, which is what the last Government did, we’re taking a bottom-up. These water service delivery plans will play a key role in doing that.
acuity.explanation: Names her question and stays on the subject of costings, but restates the bottom-up framing she had just challenged rather than engaging her claim that the WICS $120 billion figure was built from council-supplied data. Engages the topic, not the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder whether you still think that that $120 billion figure is still robust, given that that information came directly from councils" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: In terms of Rachel Boyack’s questions around financial support, this is requiring councils to put forward these water service delivery plans. The department will be available to support and provide advice. Ultimately, councils hold the information. We’ll be requiring them to put forward those plans.
acuity.explanation: Boyack's immediately preceding turn asked one specific question — where the central government money for preparing the plans is coming from, given councils are resource-strained. Brown names her question and answers it on its own terms: there is no new funding, the department provides advice, and existing Better Off money is to be reallocated. He engages the substance of the claim rather than referencing it and pivoting, though he does not take up her supporting point about councils losing qualified staff to the Public Service and private sector, which is why this is not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "where is the money coming from, from central government, in order to provide that support?"

acuity.statement: One of the things that the Minister responded to—and why it was that he wasn’t willing to countenance an extension from 12 months to two years for the adoption of the water services delivery plans—is that councils had their long-term plan (LTP) data that could be fed into it. One of the things that did come through in a legal commentary that has been published is the question around councils that want to defer their LTP adoption to June 2025. That presents a very difficult timing issue, given that the water service delivery plans would need to be adopted within only a few months of that date.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact reason Brown had just given for refusing a two-year window — that councils already hold LTP data — and shows it fails for councils deferring LTP adoption to June 2025, then converts that into a direct question about whether it is grounds for a ministerial extension. The contribution could not have been delivered unchanged had Brown given a different reason; it is built on the one he gave.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Councils should be able to prepare plans in 12 months, as they will use long-term plan (LTP) data."

acuity.statement: In relation to the other part of the question around the crystal balls, which she spent quite some time talking about—and she suggested that we made the anticipated future regulatory requirements relate to water services—if she just read the first part of that sentence, it says, “if any water services do not comply”. It already was referring to water services.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific request for a clarifying amendment confining "anticipated future regulatory requirements" to water services, and answers it by pointing to the opening words of the same provision to argue the limitation is already there. The reply would be different had Russell asked something else; it is directed at her exact textual proposal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it could probably be easily fixed with a little tweak that said something about anticipated future regulatory requirements with respect to water services" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around workload—and I think the Hon Deborah Russell did a very good job of reading out clause 11. I appreciate that that is now in the Hansard. But the answer there is: a lot of the answers to these questions can be found within existing long-term plan data.
acuity.explanation: Engages the content of Russell's workload argument rather than merely naming her: concedes the clause-11 enumeration and answers it with the claim that the information already exists in long-term plans. Slightly short of 1.0 because it addresses the aggregate workload claim rather than any of the specific subclauses she itemised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "clause 11 goes through and specifies the contents of these water services delivery plans—and there’s a lot in them" / "so they understand the workload that is being imposed on territorial authorities" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I think I have only a short point, but it’s in respect of joint plans, which have been touched on, and the Hon Dr Megan Woods has identified the problem of orphans. I want to identify a different problem that I’m actually just genuinely not clear what the legislation anticipates, and that is the islands problem—that is to say non-contiguous territorial authorities clubbing together for a joint plan.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the joint-arrangement strand Brown had just described and presses it on a specific gap (non-contiguous authorities, the "joint service area" definition versus clause 9), asking directly whether that is in or out. It engages a real strand of the preceding turn rather than merely sharing its topic, but it does not take on Brown's central contention that the Subpart 2 powers are only backstops, so it is a strong partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There are the powers to be able to work together with other councils: the bill includes provisions in terms of setting up joint council-controlled organisations." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Still picking up on Part 2, Subpart 1, I have another separate amendment that relates to this really important issue of time frames, and this is amendment 67, and it’s to do specifically with clause 16. I’d really be interested to hear whether the Minister would consider amending this to the bill tonight, because it’s so important to the actual delivery and success or failure of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the bill under debate, and there is a passing gesture at the Minister's position on urgency later in the turn, but the substance is prepared material on a different clause: it engages no part of Brown's backstop argument or Webb's non-contiguity question, and would read identically had either said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued the Subpart 2 powers are "backstops" and Duncan Webb raised "the islands problem—that is to say non-contiguous territorial authorities clubbing together for a joint plan"; this statement takes up neither, moving instead to the speaker's own prepared amendment on clause 16 time frames.

acuity.statement: In relation to the issue around joint plans, “Territory authorities”—as it says here; I mean the legislation is quite clear—“can prepare a joint plan in relation to delivering water services in the joint service area covered by a joint arrangement.”, and, ultimately, councils will decide and have those conversations and make those decisions.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the precise matter Webb raised and supplies the operative wording of the clause, so it is clearly shaped by the preceding turn. But it answers the general question of who decides rather than Webb's specific one — whether a non-contiguous joint arrangement with no shared network qualifies — so one strand is engaged and the sharp edge of the question is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d be really interested if you could address whether that’s in or out." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I put it to her that, if we provide two years for all councils, most councils will utilise two years, and, actually, we need to provide a level of urgency in terms of requiring councils to put forward these plans in an efficient manner so that decisions can then be made and that can then be executed so we can get from the planning stage to the delivery stage, which is critically important for New Zealand’s water infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Takes Pham's specific proposal — 12 months to two years — and does something with it: names clause 17 as the existing extension mechanism, then advances a counter-argument that a universal two-year deadline would be consumed in full. The reply would have to change if she had proposed something different, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The amendment that I’m proposing is simply to change the 12-month period to two years." — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: I do want to take it back to Genesis, in a sense, the genesis of our nationhood, because you could say that we have a Government that’s busy kind of trying to rewrite Genesis, if you like, trying to omit Genesis and burn it and remove it from various bits of legislation. I’m here to save the Minister of Local Government from this terrible omission of our founding agreement, Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows a detailed turn from Brooking on the water services delivery plan requirements in clause 8 and the central-government approval process in clause 18, and engages none of it. He announces a prepared Treaty amendment and reads it into the record; the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Brooking had argued. It is at least on the matter under debate (Part 2, clause 8 of the same bill), so it is not a 0.0, but the coincidence of both members mentioning clause 8 is placement, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking asked whether there is a hierarchy among the clause 8(1)(b) requirements and how clause 8 relates to clause 18, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and I thank the members for the questions. The questions from the Hon Rachel Brooking: there is no hierarchy in clause 8 and that is an important point. Those are all elements in terms of what must be repaired as part of those water service delivery plans.
acuity.explanation: He takes up Brooking's specific question and answers it directly on its own terms — there is no hierarchy in clause 8 — which is the precise point she pressed; the reply could not have been given in response to a different argument. Marked down from 1.0 because the second strand, Abel's Treaty amendment to clause 8, is deflected to a previously stated position rather than engaged, and Brooking's clause 18 and non-contiguous-councils questions go unanswered. Brevity and vagueness about the consequences of conflicting requirements are a specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is there a hierarchy in this? What are the Minister's expectations?" and "What happens when there is a conflict between those Roman numerals in clause 8(1)(b)?" — Hon Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: But how are they meant to deliver their water service delivery plan and specifically explain what they’re going to do to ensure that it’s financially sustainable without having the information from Government about funding that might be available to small councils like this?
acuity.explanation: Genter takes up one strand of Wade-Brown's preceding contribution — that councils cannot write a delivery plan while central government's funding contribution is unknown — and extends it with the Chatham Islands as the extreme case of Wade-Brown's 'orphan' councils. But she frames her turn as following up her own earlier contribution and the Minister's answer to her, not Wade-Brown's argument, and much of it is prepared material on the same topic. Partial engagement, pointable but not pointed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "I’m also interested in looking at how on earth a council is expected to create a water services delivery plan when we haven’t got bill three, which may look at financial support and how it’s achieved."

acuity.statement: The first one, from Her Worship Celia Wade-Brown, was in relation to small councils and amalgamations. The issue here is around shared services, so it’s not around amalgamations, and I think this legislation does put in place a framework which will enable far greater shared services between councils, which will achieve a greater level of economies of scale, but it doesn’t anticipate or require amalgamations.
acuity.explanation: Directly names the specific question put and disputes its premise — the mechanism is shared services, not amalgamation — and explains what the framework does and does not require. The answer would have been different had Wade-Brown asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "My further question there is whether it’s almost a backdoor attempt to force amalgamation with councils."

acuity.statement: In terms of the Hon Julie Anne Genter’s questions around the time frame, I’ve already addressed this question. There is an ability for councils to apply for an extension. Our expectation is that councils will comply with it.
acuity.explanation: Engages the time-frame strand Genter raised and answers it on the merits (extensions exist, DIA templates and advice will reduce the burden), but does not take up her specific proposition — an 18-month compromise — nor her point that the extension process itself consumes council resource. One strand answered, the sharpest part of the claim left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "If the Minister is unwilling to consider two years, maybe 18 months would be a reasonable compromise."

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around funding—and I’ve addressed this question already, as well—the last Government put half a billion dollars into the so-called Better Off Fund, or whatever they called it, and very, very little of it went to water infrastructure. A very small percentage went to water infrastructure. It went to all sorts of other manners of projects and cycleways and footpaths and other random things, and, actually, what we’ve asked the DIA to do is to work with councils who haven’t yet spent their Better Off funding to actually look at how it can be reallocated and utilised towards supporting them with these water service delivery plans, the advice they may need, and also then actual infrastructure, because, ultimately, that is what that fund should have been used for.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the funding topic Genter pressed and offers one concrete thing (reallocating unspent Better Off funding towards water plans and infrastructure), but pivots most of the answer to the previous government's spending and never engages her actual question — what central government's ongoing funding commitment is, or what revenue-raising tools exist for a 700-person council with no rating base or borrowing capacity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "Where is the partnership? Where is the commitment to funding?"

acuity.statement: There's a range of possible scenarios, and I don't think it's helpful for the committee to speculate, but, ultimately, this is a broad range of powers which can be applied in a broad range of circumstances, and which option is required will be used depending on what the circumstances are.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds put three specific questions to the Minister: what precedents define the subjective word "beneficial", whether subclauses (1)-(3) form a hierarchy, and what purpose subclause (2) serves given that a failure to agree means there is no joint plan at all. Brown takes up the general strand — when the intervention powers bite — and explicitly declines to be drawn further ("I don't think it's helpful for the committee to speculate"), then returns to prepared framing about expectations of councils and "backstops". So he answers the topic of the threshold rather than any of the three specific claims, and none of "beneficial", the hierarchy, or subclause (2) is addressed. That is partial engagement, not a rebuttal and not pure prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "I want to be able to test a bit more and understand what that threshold is."

acuity.statement: We’re still on Subpart 1, and this will be my only contribution for Subpart 1 of Part 2, and I want to pick up on what the Minister mentioned before in the conversation that the Minister had with my colleague Lan Pham. But I want to specifically focus on clause 17 in terms of the extension that the Minister mentioned.
acuity.explanation: The only substantive preceding turn in the window is Barbara Edmonds on clause 9's drafting and the Minister's intention behind Amendment Paper 65 to clause 15. Xu-Nan takes up none of that; he reaches back to an earlier ministerial exchange not in this window and moves to his own prepared clause 17 questions. It is squarely within the same debate (Subpart 1, Part 2) and gestures at where the committee is up to, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band, but his speech would have been identical whatever Edmonds had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds asked the Minister to clarify his intention in Amendment Paper 65 replacing clause 15 and queried the drafting of clause 9(1), and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I thank the members for their questions. In relation to clause 15 and the tabled amendment, that is responding to submissions that were raised and are clarifying that particular clause.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific clause Edmonds asked about and supplies a reason for the Amendment Paper (responding to submissions, clarifying the clause), so it engages one strand of her question. It stops short of the thing she actually pressed for — the Minister's intention on whether a separate round of consultation is required and why the Local Government Act subclauses were removed — so it answers the topic rather than the claim. Partial engagement that is still clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I haven’t quite understood what’s the Minister’s intention in relation to that clause of the Amendment Paper" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: In relation to clause 17 on when they can apply and those questions, the key, overarching point that I think is important for the committee to understand in relation to extensions is that this Government’s position is that we’re wanting councils to deliver these water service delivery plans within 12 months. An extension is not something that will be granted lightly or easily. There are clear criteria, and we have clear expectations that councils will deliver it.
acuity.explanation: He names the clause and the cluster of questions put to him and engages the extensions regime in general terms, but supplies none of the four things asked: the earliest date for applying, any guide to maximum duration, a decision timeframe, or what happens to the one-month margin if an application is declined. He restates a policy posture instead of taking up the specific gaps Xu-Nan identified in clause 17(2)(d) and (6A). Partial engagement with one strand, then prepared material.

acuity.responding_to: 'Is that the Government? Is that private owners? Is that retrospectively the Government paying for private owners' — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Also, those issues of certainty around regular changes, which we’ve already heard—as my colleague Cam Luxton has just said—it’s not just the confidence about the rating of a building, whether it’s 33 or 34 or some other number; it’s whether the standards will change over time.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up the specific strand of Luxton's immediately preceding argument — that single-digit NBS rating differences (33 vs 34) undermine confidence — restates it accurately and then does something with it, arguing the deeper uncertainty is not the rating but that the standard itself shifts over time, so a building compliant now becomes non-compliant later. The speech would have had to be written differently had Rutherford argued something else; it is built on his point rather than merely naming him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Empty buildings in our city centres and towns don’t just represent lost revenue; they represent lost jobs, lost community spaces, and lost vitality in our urban areas."

acuity.statement: We’ve got to strike a balance, and that’s what this Government is committed to with both this bill and with the review. If we don’t strike that balance, we will only see more earthquake-prone buildings rot in our rural towns and our city centres across the country, and if members want to know what that looks like, I invite them to check out the old Molly Malones building on the corner of Courtenay Place and Taranaki Street in central Wellington.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and gestures at the debate's shared framing of 'balance', but it engages no part of Webb's actual argument — neither the compel-versus-encourage distinction nor the life-risk case against deferral. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that encouragement is insufficient and the House must compel remediation because deferral means buildings falling and people dying, and this statement does not take that up — it repeats the 'balance' framing already used by the first speaker and returns to prepared material on vacant buildings.

acuity.statement: I acknowledge also the speaker before from Labour, Arena Williams. It’s interesting—I’m pleased to see that we have almost got unanimity within the House to support this bill through to select committee, with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are, to give us more time to do a better job, and yet they’re going to vote against it.

McCallum tallies the chamber's voting positions and gestures at the debate's state of play, but engages none of the content put to him; the rest of the speech is prepared material on Northland, the Minister and three supportive quotes that would have been identical whatever Maipi-Clarke had said. A gesture at the debate without engaging any claim sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke argued that extending time frames may save some marae from demolition but that 'The Government should fully fund strengthening for marae', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Whilst the member Grant McCallum, who made the contribution before me, found it somewhat perplexing that we weren’t supporting this particular bill, I likewise find it somewhat perplexing that some things that could have been helpful and could have moved us along in a bit more steady way have been cancelled.
acuity.explanation: Takes up McCallum's specific charge — that Labour's opposition to the bill is inconsistent with its supportive speeches — names him, supplies the reason (kicking the can down the road achieves nothing) and turns his own word back by pairing it with the cancellation of the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme. Had McCallum made a different argument, this passage would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Thinking about this bill, and listening to some of the contributions, always reminds me of one of those frustrating but real facts about human beings, and that is our reliability, if not always in a valid way, to favour the immediacy bias, to always be thinking about what’s right in front of us and how much it might cost, or what a hassle it might be, instead of actually putting the work into saving our own skins and doing what’s best in so far as a safety issue.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — McCallum's cost-versus-protection balance — by reframing the cost side as a cognitive bias rather than a legitimate weighting, then moves into prepared personal material on Christchurch that does not depend on what he said. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at a specific claim or figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s a delicate balance at times to get between building something that’s going to protect us in a disaster and the actual costs of strengthening the existing buildings" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: The Minister struck a lovely tone, but didn’t actually give us any reason as to why this should be truncated. He basically said two things in that speech, if I heard him rightly. One is that we’ve knocked this idea around a fair bit, so there’s been some sense of community consultation, and the other thing was that the people who, when the obligation crystallised in April—they’re in a kind of a limbo. Neither of those pressed why there should be a less than four-month report-back stage.
acuity.explanation: Webb enumerates the two specific arguments Penk had just made, names them accurately, and rebuts them on the precise ground that neither establishes why the report-back must be under four months. The speech could not have been written without having heard Penk's.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "first, there has already been considerable consultation and discussion" (and his point that those between 2 April and the bill's commencement "are in some sort of legal limbo")

acuity.statement: So that seems very strange to me, and I simply can’t accept, in terms of the limbo question, that it’s problematic. You know, we’ve all heard of the Fitzgerald v Muldoon case and we know that a Minister—and that Minister, of course, knows—can’t stand up and declare that the law will be changed in the future and change behaviour now. We get that. But, pragmatically speaking, some months ago, the Minister issued a press release and let it be known to the community that he was going to take a particular approach and that gave considerable certainty.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Penk's constitutional argument by name, concedes the legal point exactly as Penk put it, and then disputes the consequence Penk drew from it — that the sector lacks certainty — by pointing to the Minister's own press release. Concession-plus-rebuttal of the specific claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "we know from the case Fitzgerald v Muldoon and other discussions in our constitutional history that we can’t regard these changes as being effective in law until such time as that law is passed"

acuity.statement: In terms of the question of whether the Government intends that there’ll be a proportional relationship between, on the one hand, connection with gang membership and the nature of the offence, I think the Government’s position would be that that’s an appropriate question for the judge in any individual matter in the act of sentencing to consider and apply as they think appropriate.
acuity.explanation: Penk takes up Webb's specific question about whether the Government intends the aggravating factor to scale with the closeness of the offence's connection to gang membership, and gives a direct answer (it is a matter left to the sentencing judge). He goes on in the same turn to engage Webb's second point on the commencement clause and retrospectivity, and to address the lettered amendment. The speech would be quite different had Webb put different questions, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because the answer deflects rather than resolving the proportionality point, and because he loses track of which amendment he is addressing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "would it be fair to say the more of a gang crime it is, the more aggravating it is?" — Duncan Webb

Penk had just located the proportionality judgement with the sentencing judge, which is directly in tension with her charge that judicial discretion is being removed, and she does not quote, rebut, or even register it. What follows is prepared material on judicial discretion, section 27 reports, the abuse in State care report and deterrence theory — on the matter under debate, but indifferent to what preceded it. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band, at 0.3 for the gesture.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just said the proportionality of gang connection is "an appropriate question for the judge in any individual matter in the act of sentencing to consider", and this statement does not take that up — it asserts the opposite (that discretion is removed) without engaging his answer.

acuity.responding_to: "if members of the public who have committed violent acts are behind bars for the period of time that they are, society is a bit safer" — Chris Penk; Jackson contradicts the safety premise at topic level but engages none of Penk's three stated arguments.

Topical, not responsive.

acuity.statement: I wonder, in his previous answer to the question about the pecuniary penalties being $5 million for a council saying that it comes from the commerce legislation, has there been thought about the fact that this will only apply to councils or council-controlled organisations? So is that right to shift over from commerce legislation for giant companies—$5 million might be an appropriate penalty, but a council is a public entity; it's ratepayer money. How is $5 million appropriate for that?
acuity.explanation: Brooking takes the exact justification Penk had just offered — that the penalty regime is carried over from the Commerce Act — and presses on its load-bearing assumption, that a quantum designed for large commercial firms transfers to entities whose money is ratepayers'. She quotes his reasoning back and then does something with it rather than merely referencing it, and the question could not have been written without his answer. She also tracks which earlier questions remain unanswered, further evidence of engagement with the sequence of the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "As to questions around pecuniary penalties and offences, I'm advised—and I'm sure rightly—that this approach is consistent with that taken in the Commerce Act." — Hon Chris Penk

acuity.statement: I’ve got a question for the Minister in relation to new section 38A which specifically relates to commercially sensitive information. This is a particularly sensitive issue because many of our councils around New Zealand probably don’t know the full extent of some of the investment required to get water infrastructure up to the standard needed to even last over the next few years.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Arena Williams in the same committee debate on the Commerce Commission's powers, but engages no part of her two questions; it opens an independent prepared line on new section 38A. On the matter under debate, so above zero, but the speech would be identical whatever Williams had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked the Minister about 'the advice that the Minister received in granting the Commerce Commission these extra powers' and whether the Commerce Commission is the correct infrastructure regulator, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Taking the last point first from the Hon Ginny Andersen, the question around commercially sensitive information, I think the member identifies what is always a weighing exercise between the imperatives of commercially sensitive information being protected in the interests of encouraging enterprise in a way that’s appropriate while, at the same time, recognising the public interest in the disclosure of information. To argue against an exemption or to appeal against it—I imagine that usual avenues would be available for that purpose.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Andersen's specific question by name, restates it accurately as a weighing of commercial sensitivity against public interest, and addresses her revocation/appeal point directly. Not a full 1.0 because the answer on avenues of appeal is left at 'I imagine' rather than supplying the mechanism she asked for — but the engagement itself is squarely on her claim, and the vagueness belongs to specificity, not here.

acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "how will we determine what is commercially sensitive?" and "what is the cause for a local interest group or other group of people who are lobbying to then go to the commission and request for that exemption to be revoked?"

acuity.statement: In terms of whether those powers are additional to those in the Commerce Act, as Arena Williams notes, they are, and we think that’s appropriate, because we want to provide maximum ability for the mechanisms in the Act to be enforceable, and we think it’s appropriate for the provision of water services on behalf of the ratepayers and citizens of the country.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "under clause 40 of this part, the Minister is introducing new powers for the Commerce Commission" that are "extra to those that it would otherwise have under the Commerce Act".

acuity.statement: Also, whether that information might be looked at even if it is commercially sensitive, because, from what I understand under this clause, it’s being used by the commission itself for its own purpose, rather than simply to pass on to somebody in terms of disclosure. Will they be looking at information that is perhaps commercially sensitive because they’re a trusted entity to do that?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's just-given answer — the commercial-sensitivity weighing — and presses it against a case his framing did not cover, where the commission uses the information for its own purposes rather than for disclosure. Partial engagement: it extends his answer's topic rather than contesting what he actually said, and the rest of the call is a prepared question on clause 38.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "a weighing exercise between the imperatives of commercially sensitive information being protected ... while, at the same time, recognising the public interest in the disclosure of information."

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued the clause 40 powers belong with an infrastructure regulator and this statement does not take it up.

Prepared material on the right subject.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked 'whether interested parties would include the public' under clause 35(2) and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued about the $5 million penalties and the Commerce Commission's 'name and shame strategy' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: In relation to the member Arena Williams’ question around the Commerce Commission, the Commerce Commission is well practised in using these tools and the Infrastructure Commission does not have the experience in economic regulation.

The speech would have to change entirely had the preceding arguments differed; brevity is not unresponsiveness, and the quality of the reasoning is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.

acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "why isn’t that regulator the Infrastructure Commission?"

acuity.statement: The member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell may wish to look at clause 52(3), which says, “Despite subsection (2), a territorial authority may decide to undertake further consultation before making the decision.” There is no limit. We’re not putting any limits on what territorial authorities may wish to do.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight to the specific textual claim Russell made about clause 52(2) and counters it by quoting clause 52(3), which expressly preserves further consultation. The reply would be different had Russell raised a different clause. It does not supply the broader 'why' she asked for, so not a full 1.0, but the engagement with the content is direct and verifiable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I notice that in clause 52(2) a territorial authority is only required to take consultation once" — Brown takes up that exact clause and answers it with the adjacent subsection.

acuity.statement: Look, that’s a “may”—that’s a “may”—and local government entities may well take that path, and they could engage in more consultation. The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation. In fact, a local government entity could overrule what the people in the area that it administers want. They may want more than one round of consultation, but a local government entity could rely on clause 52(2) and say it’s only required to do it once and just leave it at that. It does create a capacity here for democratic participation to be reduced, and to be reduced by local government entities. Saying that another clause has a “may” doesn’t answer that question as to why reduce the capacity for democratic participation.
acuity.explanation: Takes the precise answer just given and dismantles its logic: the discretionary 'may' in clause 52(3) does not restore a participation right if clause 52(2) lets a council stop at one round. Accepts the clause exists and disputes what it proves, then restates the unanswered question. Entirely contingent on what Brown said immediately before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Despite subsection (2), a territorial authority may decide to undertake further consultation before making the decision." — Russell seizes on the permissive "may" in the subsection he quoted.

acuity.statement: In the previous part, I had a question for the Minister around the use of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 and the arrangement for the application of those funding and financing rules also apply to this part. In Part 3, the purpose, as the Minister has helpfully said, it sets up the decision-making requirements that will apply to territorial authorities when making decisions under this part, but I want to ask him whether it is this part which does not deal specifically with councils who are proposing to use the levy under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 and whether that, in fact, then means that an arrangement where they do propose to use it can be brought into this part.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — Part 3 and its decision-making requirements — and it nods to the Minister's statement of the part's purpose, so it is not indifferent to the debate it sits in. But it engages no strand of the consultation argument just made and resumes the speaker's own prepared question from the previous part, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the preceding exchange between Deborah Russell and Simeon Brown turned on whether clause 52(2) reduces consultation and whether clause 52(3)'s "may" answers that, and this statement does not take any part of it up; it opens a separate line of questioning on the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 levy.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I actually just want to draw the Minister’s attention around the consultation. We still need to get some clarification from the Minister regarding clause 52(2) around “consultation once” and its relationship with subclause (3) around “may decide to undertake further consultation”.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty's turn was mostly a sustained argument about the cost-effectiveness exemption, the $120b/$185b discrepancy and the Standard & Poor's warning, closing by noting the consultation question remained unanswered. Xu-Nan takes up that one closing strand — pressing the Minister for the consultation clarification — but engages none of the cost-effectiveness reasoning that formed the bulk of the preceding turn, and the clause-by-clause analysis that follows reads as prepared material that would have been delivered whatever McAnulty had argued. One strand picked up, the main argument left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that which remains unanswered posed by Dr Deborah Russell around consultation" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: The questions in relation to consultation can be answered, as this clarifies that consultation is only required once. Councils are currently unsure about how much consultation is required—the Local Government Act isn’t clear about this. There are no specific requirements in the Local Government Act 2002 about how many times consultation must occur. Councils have discretion about this, and so this is a clarification.
acuity.explanation: Brown does supply a rationale for the single-consultation rule — that the Local Government Act is silent on how many rounds are required and the clause is a clarification — which is a direct answer to the first of Xu-Nan's two questions and would not have been said had Xu-Nan not asked it. But he leaves untouched the specific point Xu-Nan pressed hardest: the logical ordering of subclause (4) relative to the decision whether to consult again, and the Amendment Paper 65 / clause 54(1)(e) clarification about a water services CCO transitioning into a joint local government arrangement. He then asserts "I think that answers most of the questions" rather than taking up those strands. Partial engagement: one strand answered, the rest declared answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the rationale that a territorial authority doesn’t need to consider consulting more than once?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: In relation to the Hon Kieran McAnulty’s question in regards to the exemption to the cost-effectiveness review, the elements that would be requiring the cost-effectiveness review are being already undertaken as part of the water service delivery plan.
acuity.explanation: This answers the precise question put: it gives the reason for the clause 58 exemption — that the elements a cost-effectiveness review would cover are already captured in the water service delivery plan — which is a substantive reply to McAnulty's central challenge, and it is not the reply McAnulty predicted ("they still can. They don't have to, but they still might"), so the speech is plainly shaped by what preceded it. Short of 1.0 because it engages only the exemption question and does nothing with McAnulty's supporting material: the $120b-versus-$185b discrepancy, the 10-year long-term-plan point, or the Standard & Poor's borrowing-cost warning all go unaddressed. Scored on engagement only — whether the answer is adequate or precise is not an Acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why on earth would the Minister then exempt councils from a cost-effectiveness review?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: The point’s been made a number of times around consultation. The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Utikere put two specific questions: would the Minister amend subclause (2) to read "at least once", and where does the special consultative process sit within the new consultation scheme. Brown restates his existing position on the once/may-consult-further structure and asserts it is clear, without taking up the proposed drafting change or the special consultative process at all. It engages the topic under debate and none of the content of either question, and the reply would read identically whatever drafting point had been put to him.

acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion"

acuity.statement: He has answered the questions put by my colleagues, on consultation, but he has not addressed the second leg of his own part, clause 51, which says “decision-making requirements”. The decision-making requirements that he is proposing to change are set out in section 137 of the Local Government Act 2002, and, on those decision-making requirements, which I have asked him to tell New Zealanders that he is not changing, there are three important points here.
acuity.explanation: She takes Brown's answer apart on its own terms: concedes the consultation limb he just answered on, then identifies the limb of clause 51 his answer left untouched (decision-making requirements under section 137) and spells out three specific consequences — liability for service provision, control of pricing, and retained asset ownership. The speech is shaped by what Brown actually said, since its whole structure is "that part is answered, this part is not", and it would have to be rewritten if he had addressed section 137 instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation."

acuity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.

Whether the reading of the clause is correct is a separate question; as engagement it is aimed squarely at her claim and would be different if she had attacked a different provision. Marked down slightly because the preceding passage of the same turn pivots to an "ironic... welcome them to the party" jibe rather than her argument.

acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "there is no requirement under his legislation that they would be retained in council ownership. If you join up with a buddy down the road, you can sell them off, because the provisions under section 137 will not apply to you."

The reply would be different had a different council or clause been raised. acuity.responding_to: "it would be good to hear from the Minister why there is this separate set of rules for Greater Wellington Regional Council" — Deborah Russell

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just explained that "Greater Wellington Regional Council is the only regional council which is a water supplier" and this statement does not take that up

acuity.responding_to: "it only has to be once—the mandatory is once only" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.responding_to: "I was wondering if the Minister is also thinking, then, of amending the LGA to make it clear for all consultations under that Act" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.responding_to: "This section is about supporting councils to put in place these entities quickly. It is about ensuring there’s a streamlined process." — Simeon Brown

My colleague the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has indicated some surprise from the Minister’s response around streamlining. I also heard the Minister’s response to indicate that the reason as to why clause 52 was there was to enable things to happen quickly.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: 'This part was part of the negotiation between Auckland Council and the Government in relation to the Local Water Done Well deal, announced in May, between the mayor and the Prime Minister.'

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: 'This part was part of the negotiation between Auckland Council and the Government in relation to the Local Water Done Well deal'

acuity.statement: I thank the members for their questions. What happens to Northland? Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish. How does it apply to stormwater? Auckland Council will continue to retain stormwater.
acuity.explanation: Brown answers the specific questions put to him in order: Brooking's Northland question (Part 4 is Auckland-only, but joint arrangements are not barred), her stormwater question (Auckland Council retains stormwater), the clause 59A/59B breadth question (Watercare is a monopoly provider, so the clauses clarify that status), and Williams' charter question (it was agreed the secretary would prepare it, in consultation with the council). The speech would be entirely different had the preceding members asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: 'Is there any ability for Northland to enter this arrangement or not?' — and Arena Williams on clause 62A, 'would it be appropriate for Auckland Council to develop that charter'

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: 'it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish' — Russell restates the Northland complaint without engaging this answer.

acuity.statement: There have been a number of questions in regards to consultation, many of which I have already answered. In relation to the question around special consultative procedures, the special consultative procedure is not required under provisions in the bill.

Partial engagement, pointable but narrow.

acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Can I invite the Minister of Local Government to the earlier question that I did pose around the special consultative process"

acuity.statement: Of course, it’s not actually good enough when the Minister is in the Chamber talking to the bill that’s in front of us now to say, “Oh, well, that would be a matter for the councils.” when he could address it and sort it out in this bill.
acuity.explanation: Brown's immediately preceding answer rested on it being up to councils to decide how to consult. McAnulty takes that exact move and argues against it — that leaving it to councils is not an answer when the Minister is legislating on the point and could settle it in the bill. The speech would have to change if the Minister had instead named a protection; it is aimed at the content of what he said, not merely at him. Held below 1.0 because the surrounding turn also carries prepared material on England, Scotland and Kiwibank that engages nothing just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "It is usually up to councils to decide how to consult"

acuity.statement: The answer to the member’s question around privatisation is that there are protections in place in several sections of the Local Government Act that will continue to apply unaffected. This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific question McAnulty had just pressed — what stops water assets being sold off — and answers it on its own terms by asserting that existing LGA protections survive. It engages the claim rather than pivoting, though it declines the follow-on scenario (a CCO in financial difficulty) and narrows the scope to consultation. Vagueness about which sections is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one, and does not move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "What protections are there in place here?"

acuity.statement: There are two very simple questions to answer, and that is—as the Hon Kieran McAnulty has just referred to—why is clause 59 there and why is this repeal of section 58 needed?
acuity.explanation: She picks up the clause 59 strand McAnulty had just opened — his "if it's all good in five years, why not now?" — and sharpens it into two precisely framed questions, naming him as the source. That is genuine take-up of the preceding turn rather than a mere mention. Short of the top band because the remainder of her turn returns to her own prepared question about Amendment Paper 65, and she does not engage the Minister's intervening privatisation answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Well, if it’s all good in five years, why not now?"

acuity.statement: The purpose of this part is to ensure the financial separation of Watercare and Auckland Council, to enable Watercare to be able to provide water services to Auckland in a financially sustainable way.
acuity.explanation: Brooking asked two things: the purpose of this part, and what the Amendment Paper 65 changes are for. This supplies an answer to the first, which is a real response to a question just put. It leaves the second untouched, as well as her repeated clause 59 question, so it engages one strand of the preceding turn rather than the argument as a whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "The other question was about the purpose of this part and the amendments that are made in the Minister’s Amendment Paper 65."

acuity.statement: To answer Deborah Russell’s questions about why Watercare is getting special treatment, I think that they were quite quick off the blocks, so their proposed arrangement is expected to deliver lower prices than would have otherwise been the case prior to the deal being struck. Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent, and future charges are also expected to be lower than they would have been. It is a substantial decrease in what was expected, from 25.8 percent down to 7.2 percent.
acuity.explanation: Russell's central charge was that costs and water rates under the Watercare arrangement will rise (she estimated about 8 percent), which she said contradicts the bill's stated purpose of sharing efficiency gains through lower prices. Simmonds takes that exact claim and answers it on its own terms, supplying the counterfactual baseline (25.8 percent) against which the ~7.2 percent increase is a reduction. The answer would have to change if Russell had put a different argument. It falls short of 1.0 because it leaves untouched the Standard & Poor's debt-servicing finding and the long-term infrastructure/central-interceptor question Russell also pressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent" and "I would like the Minister to speak to the costs that are going to be incurred by Watercare."

acuity.statement: The history of the regulation of monopolies in the water space is an illustration of why you actually need it. Theoretically, if you have a community-owned monopoly, you would think the incentives for excessive profit-taking are not as strong as if you have a private sector owner of a monopoly. But you can still have the problem of under-investment by the monopoly, and we’ve seen that up and down the country in the water and sewage space for a long space, which is why we have the problem in New Zealand of poor water quality delivered by some of our councils and inadequate treatment of their sewage. So I accept that history in New Zealand shows we need a regulatory model around the monopoly services that councils provide for water and sewage.
acuity.explanation: Parker picks up one strand of Simmonds's answer — her description of the Crown monitor as requiring expertise in regulating a monopoly business — concedes the premise that monopoly regulation is needed, and then presses the next question she did not cover: which pricing model that regulation embeds. That is genuine engagement with part of what was said, but the bulk of the turn is prepared material on the US-versus-New Zealand asset-base valuation debate that would have been delivered whatever the Minister had answered, so it sits mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "the Crown monitor will require, as you would expect, a range of skills, expertise, and experience in, for example, the regulation of a monopoly business"

acuity.statement: The question I have for the Minister is: we’ve heard a lot of rhetoric around this bill making sure that local services and local people are in control of local affairs, how does that work with this proposal for the Secretary of the Department of Internal Affairs to create this new charter for Watercare?
acuity.explanation: The turn is squarely on the matter under debate — the Watercare provisions of the bill — but it engages no part of what Simmonds or Parker actually said. It asserts in passing that questions have not been addressed and jabs at the Minister being from Invercargill rather than Auckland, then moves to a fresh and clearly pre-prepared line on clause 62A and the charter. Nothing in it depends on the content of the preceding answer: the 25.8-to-7.2 percent figures, the monitor criteria and the Part 10 fees framework all pass without comment. The gesture at the debate ('I don't think have been addressed yet') lifts it above a flat 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds answered on the price change from 25.8 percent to 7.2 percent, the Crown monitor's appointment criteria and the Local Government Act Part 10 fees framework, and David Parker argued about monopoly pricing models; this statement takes up none of that.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I wanted to ask the Minister in the chair, the Hon Penny Simmonds, in relation to Part 5, what is the political intent?
acuity.explanation: Follows Parker's substantive turn and takes up the same strand — a demand that the Minister explain the motivation for stripping provisions out of the NPS for Freshwater Management. But Twyford does not engage Parker's specific point about the hierarchy of obligations in clause 101 or the new section 138(3A); he reframes the question around Part 5 and the Governor-General's revocation power, then moves to prepared constituency material on Henderson Creek. Partial engagement with the topic and the general 'why' rather than with Parker's argument, so mid-low rather than 0.5 or above.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "I don't understand the driver for that."

acuity.statement: It then comes back to the question that my colleague the Hon David Parker has asked, which is: why are we doing this?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up Parker's question and carries it forward, extending the 'why is this necessary' line to a new target — whether Part 5 diminishes the role of te Taumata Arowai. That is engaging one strand and then developing it with his own prepared material (Independent Māori Statutory Board, Tāmaki-makau-rau), rather than taking up Parker's specific hierarchy-of-obligations reasoning. It is more than a mere name-check because the inherited question is actually used, but the bulk of the turn would stand unchanged whatever Parker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "I would like the Minister to explain to us why it is that this provision is necessary."

acuity.statement: The hierarchy of obligations is something that we were very clear about in our campaigning. We saw the hierarchy being an obstacle to economically viable solutions for both councils and for industries, and there needed to be a balancing of the obligations rather than the hierarchy of obligations that was there.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing Parker said he could not understand — the driver for disapplying the hierarchy of obligations — naming it as a campaign position and giving the rationale (the hierarchy as an obstacle to economically viable council and industry solutions), then backing it with the Palmerston North reconsenting figures and the Bluff treatment plant. This answer would have to be different had Parker argued something else. Marked below 1.0 only because she engages Parker's question and leaves Twyford's 'what is the intent of Part 5' and Henare's direct question about te Taumata Arowai untouched. Scored on engagement alone: whether the Palmerston North numbers are right is a veracity matter and does not move this.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "I don't understand what the need is for that revocation of that principle"

acuity.statement: I’m actually going to take the opposite angle to the previous questions about what is in clause 101 and this amendment of section 138. And then I’m also interested in talking on the “King Henry VIII” clause as well.
acuity.explanation: She follows Abel on the same clause and the same hierarchy-of-obligations amendment, and signals she is positioning against "the previous questions" — so the turn is shaped by what came before at the level of topic and framing. But she takes up none of the content of Abel's actual argument (the absence of the word "safe", the Public Health Communication Centre submission, the typhoid/cholera point); she instead pivots to her own prepared question about why clause 101 refers to an instrument the Taumata Arowai Act never mentions. One strand engaged, the specific claims untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have an amendment to propose to clause 101(3A)" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: The second question I had was around clause 102, which inserts new section 138A—which I believe people have touched on, but I have a question in relation to that. That’s in relation to the technical workings of this particular provision, and my question for the Minister is: is this a “Henry VIII” clause; if so, what is the justification for using a clause of this nature in this bill?
acuity.explanation: She explicitly picks up the strand Brooking had just finished on, acknowledges it has been "touched on", and adds something of her own to it — the Regulations Review Committee framing and the drafting-practice presumption against such clauses.
