That is real engagement, but it largely re-puts Brooking's question rather than advancing or testing her reasoning (Brooking's distinctive point, that the clause is unnecessary because the national policy statement does not apply to the Taumata Arowai Act, is not taken up). Her first question, on civil defence, is independent prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m asking the Minister what the justification is for using a “King Henry VIII” clause in this situation when it appears entirely unnecessary" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: If I can go back to Steve Abel’s questions about “safe”—and I think it’s really important that he understands that there is certainly no intent to take any provision away regarding the safety of drinking water—Taumata Arowai will continue to regulate drinking water, including its safety, and it will also continue to have powers to set waste-water standards by taking into account public health.
acuity.explanation: She names the specific argument put to her — the word-search finding and the inference that safety references are being stripped out — and answers it on its own terms: the regulator's safety functions survive, wastewater standards still take public health into account, and (immediately after) the bill does not replace the Act that sets drinking-water standards, which is the direct rebuttal to the word-count point. She also meets his hierarchy argument head-on by asserting removal gives Taumata Arowai more flexibility. The speech would be materially different had Abel argued something else. Not 1.0 only because she asserts rather than engages his cited public health submission.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just did a document search on the entire legislation for the word “safe”. And the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: I think there was a question from the Hon Rachel Brooking on the section in the Water Services Act relating to waste-water standards—why the changes are required—that don’t mention the national policy statement. The Water Services Act requires Taumata Arowai to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai as part of all its functions. The definition of Te Mana o te Wai in section 14 links directly to the national policy statement.
acuity.explanation: This is the exact question Brooking asked, and it gets a direct answer that engages the premise of her argument: she had reasoned the clause was unnecessary because the Taumata Arowai framework never refers to the national policy statement, and Simmonds supplies the specific statutory chain — the Te Mana o te Wai duty, defined in section 14, which links to the national policy statement — that would defeat that premise if correct. It identifies the provision, the mechanism and the section number. Unresponsive on the "Henry VIII" clause question, but on this strand it could not be more squarely aimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why was this inserted into this bill when Taumata Arowai, section 138, doesn’t mention the Resource Management Act or any of the instruments under the Resource Management Act?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: But I wanted to ask the Minister, in addition to that, has the Minister considered a sunset clause to this? This is one of the things that usually is a way to curb some of the power that can be granted with a “Henry VIII” clause, having a sunset clause or a particular duration. That’s my first question to the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Parker had just put a specific proposition to the Minister — that parallel RMA legislation also strips the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management hierarchy, so the effect goes wider than Taumata Arowai. Xu-Nan takes up no part of that, instead opening his own prepared line on the Henry VIII clause, a sunset clause and Schedule 2. It is squarely on the bill under committee consideration and gestures at the running exchange with the Minister, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but the speech would read identically whatever Parker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker asked the Minister "Am I correct, Minister, that in other legislation you’re also removing the effect of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management, including the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations for consents?" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I would like to ask the Minister if the words “preliminary arrangements” should be taken as meaning that there isn’t actually a fuller plan.
acuity.explanation: Belich had just put the proposition that the bill's title misdescribes what the bill does and asked the Minister whether it "truly reflect[s] the nature of this bill". Leary takes up that same proposition and supplies a different ground for it — that "preliminary" signals the absence of a full plan for small councils — rather than engaging Belich's specific central-government-control argument. Partial engagement: the strand is identifiable and the speech is shaped by the title question just raised, but it then runs to prepared material on Clutha and Mayor Cadogan.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Also my question in relation to the title: does this truly reflect the nature of this bill?" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: My question is whether or not the Minister considered, rather than amending section 138A, I think, of that Act, if it would have been much simpler to amend the section 14 to say that it applies to the functions, powers, or duty, and the hierarchy does not apply to whatever it is that the Government wants to do? So my question is: should not the bill change its name to the “Water Services Strange Te Mana o te Wai Amendment Act”, rather than the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill?
acuity.explanation: Brooking works inside the frame Belich and Leary had just set — that the title does not describe the bill — and advances it with her own alternative name drawn from the Te Mana o te Wai amendment, and she explicitly endorses Leary's point about "preliminary" needing to be in the title. But she does not take up either member's specific reasoning (Belich's central-government-control example, Leary's small-council debt argument) and the bulk of the turn is her own fresh material on section 14 of the Water Services Act. One strand engaged, then prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "should the title actually say, “Preliminary Arrangements Bill While we Wait for a Full and Final Plan”?" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: I want to propose an amendment to the title of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill. One of the substantial themes that we received in submissions from iwi Māori was a deep concern about the diminishment or removal of Te Mana o te Wai.
acuity.explanation: Abel picks up the specific device Brooking had just proposed — renaming the bill to name what it does to Te Mana o te Wai — and offers his own version of it, which he himself describes as an extension of the previous speaker. That is real engagement with the preceding turn's proposal. It stops short of the top of the scale because he does nothing with Brooking's reasoning about section 14 and section 138A, and the remainder of the turn is submission material read into the record that would have been delivered whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "should not the bill change its name to the “Water Services Strange Te Mana o te Wai Amendment Act”" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: It’s disappointing to hear the Minister’s response around the lack of support for the proposed time frames, including the one that Mr Abel has just referred to. That is disappointing.
acuity.explanation: Utikere opens by naming Abel's amendment and the Minister's refusal of it, and later in the same turn picks up the cost-recovery strand Abel argued ("there is an Amendment Paper in my name that would seek to change that"). But the engagement stays at the level of registering disappointment — he does not take up Abel's actual argument that a commercial operator, not ratepayers, should bear review costs — and he then moves to his own prepared sequence of clause-by-clause questions, which would read identically whatever Abel had said. Partial engagement: pointable, but one strand only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "I invite the Minister to support that amendment."

acuity.statement: I wondered if the Minister could enlighten us as to why those two options were not considered when the officials themselves said that these two options are likely to best deliver on the Government’s goals, with relatively similar net benefits that the Minister has spoken about.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. The turn is squarely about the bill under debate — the regulatory impact statement's options three and four — but it engages no part of the preceding turn's argument about cost implications and notification; the only thing it responds to is a ministerial reply made earlier and not in this stretch of the debate. On-topic and unresponsive, which is the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere, the preceding speaker, asked about cost implications of a live application running alongside an existing permit and how notification to the consent authority would occur, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: If I can start with the rather discursive remarks from the last speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, the focus on the date of 2050 or the 20-year duration is driven by a solid commitment to turn around the dire economic circumstances in many parts of regional New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up the specific thing Xu-Nan asked about — why the blanket 2050 date rather than a shorter extension — and gives a reason for it, then argues against a shorter term on its merits ("Five years may enable people to enjoy some short relief before they go through the thicket of unnecessary costs"). That is real engagement with the duration question. It falls short of 1.0 because he answers the topic rather than the claim: Xu-Nan's point was that the officials' own 15-year and 25-year options were assessed as delivering comparable net benefits, and Jones never addresses that comparison, substituting five years for the fifteen actually put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "option three, which is to extend all consent by 15 years, would deliver similar economic benefits that the Minister suggested"

acuity.statement: The second thing: I think the most recent speaker made reference to the fact that I am circumventing or undermining Crown obligations to iwi. A substantial settlement was entered into, in the Helen Clark Government, in terms of an aquaculture settlement.
acuity.explanation: Jones restates the specific charge Xu-Nan drew from page 17 of the regulatory impact statement and answers it directly, arguing the aquaculture settlement already exists and has been frustrated by regional councils' planning instruments rather than by this bill. The reply would have to be written differently had the preceding speaker raised something else; it engages the content of the claim, not merely its author. Scored here purely on engagement — the quality of the inference and the characterisation of councils belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "as well as upholding the Crown’s Treaty of Waitangi, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, obligations"

acuity.statement: And, yes, OK, some of my remarks may have been a bit rhetorical about the Marlborough council. I know there are some redeemable members of that council, but from time to time—from time to time—the truth must be spoken.
acuity.explanation: This answers the particular accusation Utikere pressed — and that Suze Redmayne interjected to soften — by conceding part of it (the remarks were rhetorical, some councillors are redeemable) while holding the substance. Accepting part and disputing the rest is a direct engagement with what was just put to him; it is not a 1.0 only because he does not touch Utikere's actual needle, the Arbuckle point about a government colleague sitting on that council.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "It’s actually also very disappointing to hear his disdain for Marlborough District Council."

acuity.statement: We hear about it all the time, Minister, from members of the Opposition, that we have an economic activity seen to be sitting in the doldrums. Sir, could you speak to what Part 1 looks like in terms of the extension of 20 years, given places like Auckland Council have certainly afforded a longer period of time, and what that looks like as help to our regions—especially areas like Northland?
acuity.explanation: Cameron follows a detailed clause-by-clause critique from Brooking and engages none of it. He thanks 'the other members' for the opportunity — a reference, not an engagement — and then puts an unrelated prepared question to the Minister about regional employment and the 20-year extension. The question is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive, and there is a loose gesture at Opposition framing ('economic activity seen to be sitting in the doldrums'), but the speech would read identically whatever Brooking had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking asked what the temporal scope of new section 165ZFHJ(b) is and argued that barring cost recovery leaves ratepayers paying for reviews; this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Because I can understand the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries’ appetite for growth, I’d like to ask the Minister for his reflections, please, on how this bill will serve, or relates to, our seafood sector requirements to meet our international trade obligations.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. Tana opens an entirely new line — trade and environment chapters in the UK and EU free-trade agreements, the locus of consenting power, the Director-General of MPI — without taking up any strand of the two preceding turns. Her one acknowledgement of the earlier debate is to decline it ('our colleagues on this side of the Chamber have covered those, so I won’t venture into that territory'), which names a topic rather than engaging a claim. On topic, so not 0.0, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking argued the review purpose must be consistent with Part 2 and that ratepayers will bear review costs, and Mark Cameron asked about regional employment under the 20-year extension; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: On the matter of giving evidence that a regional council has frustrated, look no further than the area I hail from. The capacity to create additional marine farming enterprises off the coast of Te Tai Tokerau hovers near zero.
acuity.explanation: This is the specific challenge Brooking put to him — that he has asserted councils are obstructive without producing evidence — named as such ('On the matter of giving evidence that a regional council has frustrated') and then answered with a concrete case: consenting capacity in Te Tai Tokerau, and the Stephenson Island mussel farm that cost millions and now holds a consent to 2050. Delete Brooking's evidence challenge and this passage has no reason to exist. Whether the example actually establishes the point is a question for Rigor, and whether the figures hold is one for Veracity; as engagement it is squarely aimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'He hasn’t provided any evidence about these “aberrant” councils reviewing consents' — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: There are a number of remarks that cannot go on in their false and ill-conceived way. There is the fiction that amenity and landscape values are of a greater level of significance than jobs and household livelihoods.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up the amenity-and-landscape strand Brooking pressed him on and states a position on it — that jobs and household livelihoods outrank it — addressing her directly as 'the former Minister for Oceans and Fisheries' and offering the salmon company's consenting costs as a counter-example. Partial rather than full engagement: he restates her position in his own adverse terms ('the fiction') rather than answering the actual question she asked about consistency with Part 2 of the RMA, and the passage then moves into prepared material about consultants and bureaucrats. The abuse of 'unhelpful scientists' and 'woke-riddled processes' is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one, and does not move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'he has mentioned, a lot, “landscape concerns” and “amenity”' and 'how can the Minister have so much disregard for the environment' — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I would like to ask the Minister whether he is satisfied, given the passage of time since he has considered this matter, that there is a view out there that, actually, a more appropriate term could be that of a 10-year period of extension that is automatic—there’s an Amendment Paper in my name that does reflect that; that’s Amendment Paper 55—or what was offered up, which was actually widely supported by the public in terms of submissions, which was a five-year period.
acuity.explanation: Parker had just put a specific question about cost recovery and the councils' charging regime for occupation of marine space. This turn takes up no part of it and opens an unrelated line on the length of the extension period. It is on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly adrift, but the words would be identical whatever Parker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "having taken away the right of a council to charge for the costs of reviewing the terms of an occupation licence for aquaculture" — David Parker

acuity.statement: My question follows on from my colleague the Hon David Parker, who raised the issue around local councils having to foot the bill if they wish to do a review of a coastal permit. In the select committee process, the majority of all councils that submitted on this piece of legislation were in opposition to this rollover of consents, regardless of environmental impacts or the ability for people to participate in the process and encourage a review.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand Parker opened — that councils cannot recover review costs — and develops it with new material (council submissions, the burden on ratepayers). It extends rather than tests the argument, and is a colleague's follow-on rather than an engagement with the strongest counter, so partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they can’t recover the costs of doing so" — David Parker

acuity.statement: Yes, it will require the council to meet the costs on the rare occasion that they may find that there is a strong need to review the conditions of farms that had existed for decades, and the next 25 years will give the confidence to the owners of these farms and their permits that they can dedicate their scarce resources to actually achieving economic outcomes, rather than playing a type of roller derby with the local councils.
acuity.explanation: Directly concedes the provision Parker identified and supplies the rationale for it, so the answer would have to change if the question put had been different. Short of full marks because the second half of Parker's question — whether the discretion to charge for occupation of marine space is also removed — is not answered here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they can’t recover the costs of doing so" — David Parker

acuity.statement: There is a situation we have here where we did receive substantial submissions from the Marlborough District Council, which the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is so disdainful of; a council, I might add, which, in its region, manages 80 percent of the entire value of aquaculture in New Zealand and has 600 of the 1,200 farms in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's dismissal of Marlborough District Council and turns it over directly, arguing that the council he dismisses is the consenting authority for most of the industry the bill is meant to help. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged if the preceding turn had not disparaged that council.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t like that council, because they actually created the seabed and foreshore debacle" — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: The other thing that we mentioned before, and one of the other speakers mentioned before, is in terms of what this does to the regions. I will also, I guess, at this stage like to point out that all regional and unitary councils oppose this bill. It would be really good to get the response from the Minister that if this is really good for regional development—and I really hope that it is; also it did state here in the regulatory impact statement that it does have certainty for industry and consent authorities; this is not my area of specialty—why then would the regional and unitary councils oppose this bill if it’s going to be good for the regions?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the claim that the extension delivers regional development and employment, which Luxton conceded as a good thing — and does something with it, pressing it against the fact that the regional and unitary councils all oppose the bill. It engages the regional-benefit argument rather than the specific 20-year/five-year time-frame case Luxton actually made, and then moves on to the speaker's own prepared questions on modelling and new section 165ZFHC(3), so this is partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "The Minister himself has said that the 20-year duration is to give certainty, to give the opportunity for growth, for regional economic development in the regions, for employment opportunities, and all those things."

acuity.statement: The member makes some very relevant points as to why the rights of an applicant to continue on with a process would be retained. In the event that this legislation does change, there may very well be applicants who are seeking, for example, to change some of the boundaries of a permit that this legislation will allocate to them into, arguably, 2050, and I would say that a lot of people have got permits well beyond 2050.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up both of the provisions Utikere named and supplies a policy rationale for preserving an applicant's appeal rights, so the answer would be different had Utikere asked about something else. But on the second limb he glides to the two-year review window and never answers the specific question put — whether the once-only review limit attaches to the permit in toto or to each condition — then moves to prepared material on councils and iwi settlements. Partial engagement, pointable but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "why is it necessary to indicate in legislation that all rights of appeal need to be exhausted?" and "must not be undertaken more than once in relation to any coastal permit;"

acuity.statement: Minister, we clearly see your bluster and certainty around the need to trample on your garden-variety Kiwis in the regions who want to have input on what happens in their commons and to make these dictates from on high from the throne of central government.
acuity.explanation: Abel picks up Jones's own framing and inverts its content rather than merely repeating it: Jones cast councils as unelected grandees obstructing ordinary people, and Abel answers that the ordinary people in question are the ones wanting a say over their commons, with central government as the body dictating. That is engagement with the substance of the claim just made. It is only partial, though — he does not touch Jones's two-year review argument or the iwi-settlement passage, and pivots to a general invitation to accept amendments.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "garden-variety Kiwis are trying to make a living" and "the depredations of unelected grandees in these councils"

acuity.statement: Now, earlier on in the evening, the Minister himself made a point around councils undertaking reviews, and he said, “which are very few”. So, if he wants the DG to be there to safeguard against councils undertaking reviews willy-nilly because of nimbyism and all that kind of stuff that he has talked about, why does he see that the director-general is such an important part of that?
acuity.explanation: Luxton takes the Minister's own stated figure — that reviews will be very few — and draws out its consequence against him: if reviews are rare, the director-general gatekeeping step is redundant. She adds a second supporting inference (councils bear the cost, so they will not review willy-nilly). This is the specific claim just made being used to build the rebuttal, and the question could not have been framed this way had Jones said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "when the review is undertaken—and they will be very, very few in number, because this is not really a troublesome industry"

acuity.statement: It is not correct to say this is exclusively an area where local representatives have the ultimate authority. They are guided by guardrails created by central government.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up the specific proposition Abel built his call on — that allocation of coastal space belongs with regional councils and that central and local allocation cannot coexist — and disputes it directly, arguing the two already interact and that councils are already bound by central guardrails via the NZ Coastal Policy Statement. He also engages Abel's specific Taranaki question about competing commercial interests, conceding friction between quota owners and minerals applicants. The speech would have to be different had Abel argued something else. Short of 1.0 because Abel's second, equally explicit question — the effect of the blanket extension on Variation 1 aquaculture management areas, which Abel expressly asked him to answer — is met only with a general remark that nothing stops future applicants, not with the impact assessment requested.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is fundamentally unsound to have both central and local government attempting to allocate the same coastal marine area" — Steve Abel, who asked how the Minister reconciles that tension and whether he is content to impose central government's will on regional councils

acuity.statement: Is this not just—for a Minister who talks about getting everything out of Wellington and out into the regions—sucking back decision making to Wellington?
acuity.explanation: Luxton engages one strand of what Jones had just said: she picks up his 'utilisation of the commons' framing and his defence of central guardrails and turns it against his own localism rhetoric, pressing the centralisation point he had just embraced. She also nods to his 'loud, shrill' remarks by setting nimbyism aside. But the bulk of the call is prepared material on a different clause — the new section 165ZFHL notification list — rather than a reply to the argument Jones actually made, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They are guided by guardrails created by central government." — Shane Jones, who argued that central government already and properly constrains local allocation of coastal space

acuity.statement: I would just like to bring to the Minister’s attention that the question I asked last night was around his wont, desire, to have an aquaculture bill. He didn’t answer my question last night when I brought up the fact that the process was quite rushed, that people didn’t have much time to submit, and I asked the question as to why he didn’t take the time, allow a longer period of consultation in order for him, perhaps, to be able to develop the aquaculture bill that he so desires to do. I look forward to the answer from the Minister with regards to that.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows a substantive turn by Jones about regional councils and aquaculture, but engages none of its content; she returns to her own prepared question from the previous sitting about consultation length. It is squarely on the bill under debate and presses the Minister for an answer, so it is not wholly indifferent to the debate, but nothing in it would change had Jones argued something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones spoke about the director-general's status and the Otago Regional Council's 'wilful disregard' of the Government's water standards, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: When we left off last night, there were still a number of questions that the Minister had not yet addressed. The three that I have on my list that I have put to him—one is just to serve as a reminder. Why is there a need to reference appeal rights within the legislation?
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn (Luxture's consultation and Te Tiriti argument) is substantive and is not engaged at all; Utikere reads out his own pre-prepared list of clause-level questions. It is on the bill and holds the Minister to questions already put, which is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the argument just made, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jo Luxton spoke about the rushed consultation period, the 1,100 submitters and iwi concerns as a Te Tiriti partner, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The reason why the ratepayers and the council will meet the costs of an intervention in the legal, rightful business of a marine farmer is because they will know that it has to be of a particularly egregious nature because they’re going to pay for it themselves. In the event that they decide that the condition problem is of such a magnitude that they need to spend the ratepayers’ money, they will also consult and seek the authority of the director-general as a further discipline.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific cost-allocation objection and supplies an affirmative rationale for it — that making councils bear the cost is itself the discipline that keeps interventions rare — rather than pivoting away. It stops short of 1.0 because it does not address the actual mechanism Amendment Paper 57 proposed (fair and reasonable, capped at 50 percent), so one strand of the argument is engaged and the proposal itself is left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is the Minister and the Government, effectively, lumping on to ratepayers of this country an additional cost, once the director-general has determined that a review can take place." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: This bill provides an opportunity for a marine farmer to enjoy the permit they already have extended till 2050, at the latest; or if they’re involved in a process to adjust elements that comprise their entitlements within that defined area, they can’t have two permits at once. Our side of the House doesn’t believe in double-dipping. The surrendering option enables the applicant to come back and enjoy the 20 to 25 years security, and it simply provides clarity that you can’t be involved with two permits at the same time.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific question put to him about surrendered permits, explaining the drafting purpose — preventing an applicant holding two permits at once — which is exactly what was asked. The speech would have to be different had the question not been asked. Marked just below 1.0 because it does not take on the follow-up point about why the word 'cancelled' is not used instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if that permit was surrendered because the applicant had decided to take up the opportunity to have the permit extended, what is the status of a surrendered permit?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Extraordinary, we’re now talking about the rights of initiation. Obviously, the authority to undertake a review of conditions depends on the concurrent authority being exercised by the director-general. Nothing is legal until such time both parties have agreed that there is a case for—within the two-year period—such an exercise to take place. It is beyond cavil in terms of the clear meaning of the law.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand Utikere had just pressed — the meaning of "initiating" a review — and offers an answer tied to the director-general's concurrence, so the opening would differ had Utikere asked something else. But it only gestures at the question: it does not say which of the dates Utikere listed counts as initiation, nor touch the companion questions on guidance for the director-general or the missing decision time frame, and closes by asserting the law is plain rather than engaging the ambiguity put to him. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "There is a clear change in the wording from “beginning” to “initiating”, and my question is: what does “initiating” mean in the context of a process for determining whether a review is successful?"

acuity.statement: Now, in respect of appeal rights, the law as contemplated here is very clear. No one is stripping away the ability of someone to take an appeal in the event statutory authority is exercised. We are putting a discipline in.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the outstanding item Utikere had just named — appeal rights in the legislation — and makes a substantive claim about it (nothing is being stripped away, a discipline is being added), so this passage exists because of what preceded it. It stops short of 1.0 because it rebuts a general worry rather than the specific gap Utikere identified, and leaves Amendment Paper 57, which he asked about twice, unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "There is still the issue of the reference to the appeal rights inclusion in the legislation, which the Minister has not addressed"

acuity.statement: The question is around: are there any provisions under the Resource Management Act Subpart 1A of Part 7A that give the permit holder the opportunity to, at their own volition, shorten a permit if they no longer deem their business to be profitable or they no longer wish to operate under that permit and not replace it with another permit?
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn in the debate (Utikere) put a specific proposition to the Minister about preserving the five- and 10-year extension options; Xu-Nan's question is on the same clause and the same Part 2/Subpart 1A material, but engages none of Utikere's argument. He gestures at engagement with an earlier ministerial answer ("the Minister answered one part of my question previously"), but that answer is not in the available turns, so the responsiveness cannot be pointed at — prepared material on the right subject, hence the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued that "the consideration of the five-year extension and the 10-year extension time frames, effectively, are still in play" and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. A number of questions for the Minister. Of course, this relates to all of the bill—the entirety of the bill—because what is happening, as my colleague Tangi Utikere described, is that this insertion is Part 1 of the bill is being acknowledged here in section 123A of the Resource Management Act (RMA).
acuity.explanation: She takes up Utikere's specific characterisation of Part 2 — that a short insertion carries implications for the whole of Subpart 1A — names him, and does something with it, extending it to the claim that the insertion reaches the entirety of the bill via section 123A. That is a real engagement with the strand immediately preceding her, but it is one strand: the bulk of the turn then moves to her own prepared line on discharge consents and the 18-year review bar, which would stand unchanged whatever Utikere had said. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Part 2, in terms of what it proposes to insert, in the sort of number of word count, is quite small, but the implications actually are quite significant because they relate to the entire part of Subpart 1A of this bill" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Now, where there is an egregious case at some ill-defined point in the future, reflective of what the honourable Green member and the former Minister of oceans have referred to through fish farming, and if it did represent a biological threat, there are other pieces of legislation that can be invoked.
acuity.explanation: He engages the specific challenge just put to him — Brooking's demand that he account for the "other legislation might apply" answer in the context of fish farming's different discharges — and restates the content of her and Xu-Nan's fish-farming point before answering it on its own terms. The speech would have had to change if the preceding turn had raised a different objection, which is what the deciding test asks. It falls short of 1.0 on engagement because he addresses the category of the question without taking up its parts (he names no statute and does not reach the advice question at all); that he gives no detail is a specificity matter and that he resolves it by assertion is a rigor matter, neither of which I have scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm wondering, then, what other legislation he's referring to, what advice he has sought on the other legislation, and specifically around environmental effects" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I would like to make a couple of suggestions to the Minister around potential title names that maybe the Minister would like to consider.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn (Utikere) pressed a specific question about Amendment Paper 58 and whether administrative charges should be capped so ratepayers do not bear up to 50 percent of cost recovery. Xu-Nan takes none of that up: he launches a prepared series of alternative bill titles. There is a gesture at the same subject matter — he later mentions the extra duties councils and ratepayers will carry, which overlaps Utikere's ratepayer-cost strand — but he engages no part of the argument itself, and the speech would be essentially identical whatever Utikere had said. That places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this will be an additional cost that is borne by the ratepayers" — Tangi Utikere. Only glanced at via a general council-burden remark; Utikere's question about Amendment Paper 58 and administrative charges is not taken up.

acuity.statement: Of course, we had a lot of discussion in the committee about how it is the council and, therefore, ratepayers that are going to have to pay for any review of these extended consent conditions. But, of course, they can only do that for the first two years.
acuity.explanation: Brooking picks up the strand running through the two preceding turns — that councils and ratepayers carry the cost of reviewing extended consents — and advances it with specifics the earlier speakers did not supply: the two-year review window, the remaining 18 years, and the Director-General of MPI's existing veto over any review. That is genuine engagement with one strand. But the bulk of the turn is her own prepared list of alternative titles, and she does not answer or rebut the particular claims of the member before her; she joins the exercise rather than taking up its reasoning. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the burden that it places on them in terms of the extra duties that local council and ratepayers will have to be responsible for" — Lawrence Xu-Nan.

acuity.statement: Look, I don’t think it uplifts the mana of this House or purpose of this bill by all sorts of extreme suggestions from the other side. This is a time for dry, focused language.
acuity.explanation: This does respond to what immediately preceded it — the renaming exercise run by Xu-Nan and Brooking — and takes a position on it, defending the existing title as sensible. So the speech would differ had the previous speakers not offered titles. But he engages the suggestions only as a category, dismissing them as colourful and fanciful, and answers none of the substantive claims embedded in them: who pays for reviews, the two-year limit leaving 18 years of unreviewable discharge conditions, or the Director-General's role. Engages the form of the preceding turns, not their content, so a little below the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is a disgrace and should be renamed." — Rachel Brooking.

acuity.statement: I appreciate it, because I actually made the error of speaking to this amendment earlier on in the wrong part, but I should clarify that it belongs in this part.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Utikere's explicit handoff on the administrative-charges amendment and takes up the one strand Utikere left to the Greens, confirming which part it belongs in. But it then proceeds to prepared material explaining the amendment and does not engage Utikere's actual question about when Subpart 1A is given effect, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "we would look to support Mr Abel's Amendment Paper because it inserts a further trigger in the sense of administrative charges being carried over, but I'll leave that to the Greens to explore a bit further"

acuity.statement: I remind the committee that we have already addressed Part 1. We have already addressed these relatively insignificant, largely marginal details reflected in the member’s amendment.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the amendment Abel had just put, and goes on to characterise Part 2's scope as covering holders whose entitlement stretches beyond 35 years — which is enough content for Brooking to take up next. But the engagement is largely a procedural dismissal (already covered in Part 1) rather than engagement with the cost-recovery argument Abel made, and it does not answer the question Utikere put about the point of engagement of Subpart 1A.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "we would like to hear the Minister's response to another very nominal and reasonable amendment"

acuity.statement: I am interested in what the Minister, the Hon Shane Jones, was just saying there about the application of new subsection (5) to section 123A of the Resource Management Act being only to do with the 35-year relationship. My understanding was that this inserts the whole of subpart 1A. If he’s saying it’s limited to the timing of only some of the extensions that may or may not apply, it would be useful for clarification on that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the Minister had just said about Part 2 being confined to the 35-year case, sets it against her own reading that the provision inserts the whole of subpart 1A, and presses for clarification of the discrepancy. The speech could not have been delivered unless Jones had said what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "Part 2 is explicitly covering those small number of rights holders, if I can use that term figuratively, that may go beyond a point where their entitlement stretches beyond 35 years"

acuity.statement: I appreciate the advice of the Minister that I’ve been speaking to the wrong section. I’d better polish up that law degree that I didn’t do.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's correction about which part he had been addressing and acts on it by re-putting the amendment against the right clause, and later in the turn takes up Brooking's capitalism strand. That is real engagement with what preceded, but he does not contest Jones's substantive claim that the cost-recovery issue was already disposed of, so this sits above a mere topical glance and short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "with the greatest of respect to the honourable member from the Green Party, that debate, that issue—not necessarily the amendment, but the issue—was covered off in Part 1"

acuity.statement: If a council officer is possessed of information requiring him or her to intervene in the legal operations of an enterprise—and these people love their enterprises; they love the environment; they’re not quietly plotting and scheming, at 11 o’clock at night, that they’re going to go tomorrow and release toxic material into the environment. It would destroy the fact that they’re growing food. This is the catastrophisation that we’ve seen for far too long from that side of politics.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific scenario Brooking had just put — a dangerous discharge that councils cannot act on — and answers it on the merits as he sees them, arguing the operators have no incentive to contaminate the food they grow, while also addressing Abel's administrative-charges point. Whether the rebuttal reasons well is a Rigor question and whether the framing is courteous is a Civility question; on engagement, the speech is plainly shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "it is saying, 'If there is a discharge that is dangerous to the environment, the regional councils can’t do anything about it, and that is fine because somebody is making money.'"

acuity.statement: Given the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries has provided a response, I want to pick up on what the Minister has just said, because he has said that there are people who are losing their jobs. That is correct—that is absolutely correct. It is the one thing, actually, that I agree with that has come from this Minister through this committee stage, is that people are losing their jobs.
acuity.explanation: Quotes back the precise premise the Minister had just advanced, concedes it, and then turns it by disputing the causation he attached to it. The turn would have had to be written differently had Jones made any other argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "Think about the New Zealanders today who have lost their jobs and who may also lose their jobs in this sector, unless we give greater certainty and greater confidence to this area of natural resource development."

acuity.statement: If that is not accepted—and I’m hoping the Minister will appreciate it—I also would like to support Tangi Utikere’s proposed titles for it: “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms”—in clause 1—“Despite Potential Degradation of the Environment)”. An obvious title, and an excellent one. I’d also like to support his other proposed amendment: “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms to Kick the Can down the Road)”. I thought that my colleague the Hon Rachel Brooking’s suggestions were similarly excellent.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows a substantive turn by Utikere and does take up one identifiable strand of it — the two specific amendment-paper titles Utikere tabled — naming them and endorsing them, so the passage would have to change if Utikere had proposed different titles. But the engagement stops at endorsement: he adds no reasoning beyond "an obvious title, and an excellent one", and ignores Utikere's substantive question about deferring commencement past Royal assent, returning instead to his own prepared case about central-government overreach, Te Tiriti and his "King Jones Ocean Giveaway Bill" title. Partial engagement with one strand, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "The first one is to call this the “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms Despite Potential Degradation of Environment)” Amendment Bill”."

acuity.statement: As the Minister has also touched on, the fact that the Minister and Cabinet made an explicit decision to remove Te Tiriti provisions and not only reference to Treaty but the principles and the other bullet points, essentially, that we will go through one at a time, from what has now come before this committee, we think is such a shame, is so atrocious.
acuity.explanation: Mitchell pre-empted the Treaty question by asserting the removal is immaterial because Corrections will keep working with Māori. McLellan takes up that specific strand and contests it directly, arguing the removed clause was the legislative foundation the rest of the bill depended on, so the whole bill must now be read through a different lens. Her speech would have to change if he had defended the removal differently, though a good deal of it is prepared context-setting about the bill's origins and her colleagues' intentions, which keeps it short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to touch on the Treaty of Waitangi provisions that were removed at the select committee stage" — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: But having the Treaty provisions in there—by the way, the Corrections Act has never had those provisions in there. They’ve never had them and yet Corrections have been extremely effective in the work that they do over successive Governments for many, many years.
acuity.explanation: He restates McLellan's argument in his own words before answering it, then supplies a counter-premise aimed squarely at it: the Corrections Act never contained Treaty provisions, so their absence cannot be what disables the department. That is doing something with the specific claim rather than referencing it and pivoting; had she argued on different grounds this passage could not stand. Scored on engagement only — whether the historical premise is accurate, and whether the inference from it holds, belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It completely guts and, quite frankly, ruins large swathes of the intentionality of this bill" — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I just want to correct one thing, and she said in her opening comments that there was nothing Corrections could do—it wasn’t their issue—around the fact that Māori were overrepresented in our corrections system. That’s not what I meant. What I meant was Corrections have got no control over who is coming into the system.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific charge Paul opened with — that he had disclaimed Corrections' responsibility for Māori overrepresentation — names it, and corrects her reading of what he said by distinguishing responsibility for people once in the system from control over who enters it. The passage would not exist had Paul not made that characterisation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "In your answer just then, Minister, you said that that was not the Department of Corrections’ problem—the overrepresentation of Māori—but it absolutely is."

acuity.statement: We know that we’re grappling as a country with Māori overrepresentation in our criminal justice system—I acknowledge that—but to say that our police and corrections officers and staff are racist: no, I completely reject that.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the central premise of Paul's argument, conceding the overrepresentation she documented while disputing the institutional-racism explanation she drew from it. Partial engagement in one respect — it answers the claim about staff rather than the structural claim backed by her statistics — but it is squarely aimed at what she had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "We know that there is racism baked in throughout our justice system because researchers have made that clear."

acuity.statement: Yes. I have lots of reports to read, and, yes, I have read the report. The member Willow-Jean Prime is right that they have made recommendations around improvements.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question Prime pressed four times, and then takes up the substance of it by conceding the point she made about the tribunal's recommendations. The reply could not have been given in response to a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So, very clearly, my question is: have you read the report? Have you read the recommendations?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: But I completely reject the premise that because the Treaty provisions have been removed at this stage with this bill—by the way, the Treaty provisions have never been a part of the Corrections Act, and it hasn’t stopped those very deep relationships being formed with Māori, hapū, and iwi.
acuity.explanation: Directly attacks the load-bearing premise of Prime's argument — that legislative Treaty provisions are necessary for the relationships and programmes to happen — and offers a counter-claim (they were never in the Act) aimed at exactly that inference. Engagement is squarely with her content, whatever one makes of the reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the recommendation is to include it in legislation to require it to happen, to give practical effects to the application of those Treaty principles" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: The Ombudsman said, more in sadness than in anger, that he had seen no real change in the corrections system despite repeated reports where the Department of Corrections said, “Yes, we agree with all of your criticisms about prisoner safety and rehabilitation and lack of resources” but ultimately did nothing.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's claim that Corrections is committed to ongoing improvement and counters it with the Ombudsman's finding that agreement with criticism produced no change — the strand of Mitchell's answer most relevant to Webb's case. He then moves to his own prepared line-by-line questions on the bill, so the engagement is partial rather than sustained.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "every agency should be focused on ongoing improvements, and that’s exactly what Corrections are doing. They are fully committed to that." — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: Now, Willow-Jean Prime has just touched on some Treaty issues, but this is not actually a Treaty issue at all.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the preceding Treaty argument only to set it aside and mark his own point as distinct; it engages no part of her claim. A gesture at the earlier turn on a debate he is otherwise on-topic about, which sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the recommendation is to include it in legislation to require it to happen, to give practical effects to the application of those Treaty principles" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: I’m assuming that, from the Minister’s perspective, the treatment of each of these three groups would be quite distinct, but I do want to know, in terms of accused prisoners and prisoners who are on remand awaiting sentence, what is the duration we’re looking at here? One of the things the Minister addressed is the length of time that we have with prisoners on remand, and that’s one of the issues of why we have such a high remand population in Aotearoa, but what are some of the thinkings around splitting those two off specifically?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own distinction between remand accused and remand convicted, accepts its premise, and presses it to the next step — why the definition splits the two and for how long each category lasts. The questions could not have been written without the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "Remand accused have to have different types of non - offence-based programmes delivered to them because, in the eyes of the law, they’re innocent until proven guilty"

acuity.statement: Remand accused have not actually been to court and had their case heard. That is the fundamental difference, and that is why, if you were to deliver offence-based programmes to someone that was remand accused, even though they may actually ask for it, that could be seen as an admission of guilt, because they’re engaging on a programme like that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — the rationale for separating remand accused from remand awaiting sentence in the definition — by supplying the reason (risk of an implied admission of guilt) rather than restating the earlier answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what are some of the thinkings around splitting those two off specifically?"

acuity.statement: I have been listening to what the Minister’s been saying in relation to this clause, and I’ve heard his assurances that rehabilitation work will continue and that the work that corrections officers are doing is good work. I don’t doubt, on an individual basis, that they do do the best job that they can, but also we’ve heard comments from members around the Chamber, and I think that we must acknowledge that the statistics in relation to Māori are not where they should be and that something needs to be done.
acuity.explanation: Concedes part of the Minister's assurance (that rehabilitation work continues and officers do good work) and disputes the rest, arguing the outcomes for Māori show the assurance is not sufficient. Engages his claim, though it then moves into her own prepared case on clause 6A.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "All the non - offence-based programmes, including cultural ones, will be made available to them."

acuity.statement: The one thing I’d say, and I’d come back to the point that I’ve been making, is that we have never had Treaty provisions inside the Corrections Act ever, and yet the system has been working very well. It’ll continue to work well. All of the obligations on the chief executive and on Corrections in terms of continuing to work on strengthening that relationship and recognising the importance of that relationship with iwi and hapū will continue, and is continuing today as programmes are rolled out and delivered.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Belich's question — whether the listed functions will still happen — and answers that they will continue, but does not engage her specific ask of which items in the removed section will no longer occur, returning instead to a point he says he has been making throughout.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "what in this section will not be going ahead as a result of the removal of this section?"

acuity.statement: Well, quite simply, it was taken out because—the member alluded to it in her opening comment—we are a coalition Government and that was a Cabinet decision.
acuity.explanation: A direct answer to the precise question just put to him about why the clause is being removed, and it explicitly picks up the member's own earlier framing. Brief and unflattering to his case, but squarely on the question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "So why take it out?"

acuity.statement: In relation to my comment around being colour-blind, if the member had been listening she would have heard that both the Police and Corrections were accused of being racist. I was very clear that I reject that accusation and that both services, in my view, are colour-blind.
acuity.explanation: Andersen devoted most of her turn to the Minister's 'colour-blind' remark, quoting the regulatory impact statement against it. Mitchell takes up that exact remark and supplies the context she omitted — that it was a rejection of an accusation of racism levelled at Police and Corrections — rather than restating prepared material. The reply would be different had she not pressed that specific point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "I'm really puzzled by the Minister's comments that the Department of Corrections should be colour-blind."

acuity.statement: In relation to the question around the removal of the Treaty provisions, again I’d say to the member that, yes, it was a Cabinet decision based on a coalition agreement.
acuity.explanation: It addresses the question that was put, so it is not unresponsive — but Andersen explicitly pre-empted the coalition-agreement answer and asked for the reasoning behind it, and this takes up only the topic, not that strand of her argument. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "You can just point to your coalition agreement, but it's your coalition agreement as well. You need to be able to explain to New Zealanders that there is more to this than just a political promise."

acuity.statement: Just because it hasn’t been done in the past, it doesn’t mean it shouldn’t be done now—now and for the future, because by locking in Te Tiriti o Waitangi into the legislation, it is for strategic purposes, it is for iwi Māori to know that there are protections in there, and it’s above and beyond obligations to a coalition agreement because the original agreement was Te Tiriti o Waitangi, signed in 1840; kia ora tātou.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's coalition-agreement justification, which he had just given, and does something with it — ranks it against an earlier agreement — rather than merely naming it. She also answers the precedent argument directly. Marked below 1.0 because the rest of her turn returns to prepared material on Waikeria that is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "yes, it was a Cabinet decision based on a coalition agreement"

acuity.statement: I want to thank the Minister for talking earlier about the importance of having the non - offence-based programmes for people on remand who are still awaiting trial. One of the things we know within the prison system, within the correction system, is the disproportionate number of people who are neurodivergent or who have dyslexia.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's case — that the bill is about delivering rehabilitation and non-offence-based programmes — and presses it on a specific group (neurodivergent and dyslexic prisoners) the Minister did not mention. But it does not engage Mitchell's actual argument in the preceding turn (that codifying the clause would risk putting Corrections in breach of the law), and the speaker then moves to prepared material on clause 5 and Schedule 1AA. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "for us to be able to deliver more rehabilitation to those that need it" — and his earlier remarks on non-offence-based programmes

acuity.statement: I think you raise a very good point around neurodivergence and people with dyslexia and whether those needs can be met. I can’t give you a very definitive answer on that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put to him, names the two conditions raised, and concedes he cannot answer definitively before describing what Corrections does. The reply would be different had the member asked about something else, so engagement is high; the concession is a limit on the answer's content, not on its responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "whether the non - offence-based programmes that have been named here have considered the neurodivergence and also the dyslexia"

acuity.statement: In terms of transitional planning, I think that you’ve highlighted one of the issues that the previous speaker was talking about, and that’s how dynamic the environment is, and a lot of that stuff is outside Corrections’ control, in terms of someone that’s going up for parole may get parole or may not get parole, how long are they going to be in the system for, and whether they are going to be there long enough to be able to complete a programme.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the member's heading — transitional planning — and so is on the matter put to him, but it redirects to operational uncertainty about parole and programme completion and engages no part of the actual claim, which was about section 26 of the Bill of Rights Act, retrospective penalty and double jeopardy. The strand engaged is pointable but thin; the substance of the question is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "around retrospective penalty and double jeopardy" and "whether that transitional plan has taken into consideration ... the risk of this bill creating a harsher punishment for these people"

acuity.statement: Coming to the Hon Willie Jackson, yes, I was definitely around in 2019; yes, I definitely support the initiative that Kelvin put in place and acknowledge him for that; yes, we’re working with iwi and hapū, as he knows; and, yes, we remain committed to making sure that we continue to develop and deliver the programmes that we think will do the best and move us towards, when people rejoin society, giving them the best possible chance of reintegration and making good decisions in their lives.
acuity.explanation: Takes Jackson's questions in the order they were put and answers them point by point — whether he was present in 2019, whether he supported Kelvin Davis's Hōkai Rangi initiative, whether contact with Māori groups continues, and whether the commitment holds going forward. The reply could not have been delivered after a different speech; it is built around the specific list of questions asked. Marked down from 1.0 because several strands of the question (the Ināia Tonu Nei justice conferences, the named ground-level workers, the level of contact with those groups, and the unmet 52-to-16 percent target) are passed over, and the final 'yes' restates a general commitment rather than the Hōkai Rangi principles he was asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is the Minister still committed to the principles of Hōkai Rangi? I’d like to know that." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: This can’t be dismissed by saying they do a great job because, I’m sorry, Minister, they don’t. We have the words of the Ombudsman on numerous reports and in person to the Justice Committee saying that’s not the case.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one specific strand of the Minister's preceding turn — his statement that he is extremely proud of what Corrections staff are doing — and disputes it directly, citing the Ombudsman's reports and evidence to the Justice Committee as the counter. That is engagement with the content of the prior claim, not merely a reference to it. Held below 1.0 because the surrounding speech is a prepared point on clause 6's three qualifiers that Webb himself flags as one 'that hasn't been touched on', so only this strand is actually responsive to what Mitchell said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m extremely proud of what they’re doing." — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: In relation to the changes around tactical options for them, the change from “non-lethal” to “less-lethal” was driven in part by the report that came out from the UN. It was just quite simply around the fact that you cannot guarantee—anything that you use, you cannot guarantee that there may not be a lethal outcome. But, of course, dependant on the tactics that you’re using, that is reduced to the bare minimum. That’s why the change was made between “non-lethal” to “less-lethal”.
acuity.explanation: Paul's central, repeated request was for the rationale behind replacing “non-lethal” with “less-lethal”. This passage takes that exact question and supplies a reason (the UN report, and the impossibility of guaranteeing a non-lethal outcome). The answer would be different had she asked something else about the clause; it is squarely shaped by her question rather than prepared material. It falls short of 1.0 only because she also asked for the two definitions themselves and whether the absence of a definition opens a risk, and that strand is not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "could the Minister define what non-lethal weapons are, and could the Minister define what less-lethal weapons are, and what the rationale was for changing that terminology?"

acuity.statement: In terms of de-escalation, I agree completely with the member. The police are outstanding in de-escalation. You referred to the power of communication, and that’s the most powerful tool that they’ve got. It’s also the most powerful tool that our corrections officers have. Yes, they do a lot of work around de-escalation.
acuity.explanation: This picks up two specific strands of Paul's turn — her account of Paremoremo officers pointing to their mouths as the first tool, and her claim that corrections officers cannot access the de-escalation training police get. It accepts the first and contests the second by asserting that corrections officers do a lot of de-escalation work. Agreement that engages the content still counts as listening; it is not 1.0 because the training-access claim is denied by assertion rather than engaged with (no training detail is given in answer to her later question about what guidance staff will receive).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "the first thing they did was point to their mouth, in terms of de-escalation and communication as the first and most important tool they have access to" / "corrections officers don’t have access to these same types of training"

acuity.statement: In terms of some of the less lethal options that corrections officers have got, obviously, there are pepper spray and batons. That is absolutely a last resort. They don’t want to be in a physical confrontation.
acuity.explanation: Paul asked repeatedly for examples of the weapons used in Corrections, so naming pepper spray and batons does engage the request directly. But she asked specifically about Cell Buster gas extractions, the Cripps case and spit hoods, and about UN guidance on chemical irritants in unventilated cells — none of which this touches, and pepper spray is offered without reference to that guidance. Partial engagement: the topic and the form of the question are answered, the specific instances put to him are not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "can the Minister, please, clearly outline some examples of weapons that are used within Corrections to restrain people in prison"

acuity.statement: Look, sadly, I wish that I could stand in the Chamber and say that we don’t have pockets of racism in New Zealand, but we do, and that applies to all ethnicities. It’s incumbent upon all of us in this Chamber to continue to lead to make sure that we become a country where we can purge that.
acuity.explanation: Mitchell takes up the specific thing Jackson pressed him on — Jackson characterised him as 'denying that there's any racism in the police' and asked him to address the history — and he concedes the point directly, allowing that pockets of racism exist and should be dealt with wherever evidenced. That strand is squarely engaged and the answer would have been different had Jackson not put it. But it is partial: he does not touch Jackson's substantive clause 19 question about deleting the cultural-activities guarantee, pivoting instead to a prepared commitment on Hōkai Rangi and rehabilitation programmes. Engaging one strand and then returning to prepared material is the mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There’s no doubt in my mind that there’s been a history in terms of racism and the police. I’d like the Minister to address that." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I think that the reason why—clearly the reason why the prisoner can’t appeal the fact that he wasn’t there is because he’s refused to actually attend. He can still appeal the actual outcome of the hearing, but he doesn’t have any appeal rights in terms of failing to appear, because he’s been given the opportunity and he’s chosen not to appear.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact provision Utikere raised (new subsection (3) removing appeal against proceeding in absence) and supplies a reason for it, distinguishing appeal against the absence decision from appeal against the outcome; then addresses Utikere's mitigating-circumstances example directly. Falls short of 1.0 only because it answers the operational question rather than the asked question of whether he would amend the clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "there is no right of appeal to a visiting justice solely against the decision of a hearing adjudicator" — and his question whether the Minister is open to changes allowing a visiting justice to consider reasons for the prisoner's absence

acuity.statement: Starting with the body image scanning technology, we are supportive of introducing this technology as a way to reduce the need for rub-down and strip searches within prison, and my question to the Minister on the body image scanning technology is: what other steps can we take to eventually remove the need for rub-down and strip searches?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the same bill but on wholly different clauses; the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Mitchell had just said about appeal rights. It is at least squarely about the bill under committee consideration, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Mitchell spoke about prisoner appeal rights for disciplinary hearings held in absence and the recording of visiting justice decisions, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: In terms of the images, the images are kept for 24 hours and then automatically deleted. The only one that sees the image is the person that’s actually operating the scanners at the time.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific fact her question asked for — the retention period and automatic deletion — and adds who can view the image. The answer could not have been given had she not asked about image disposal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "I’m also really interested in the disposal of those images too" — her question about privacy and how body-scan images are disposed of

acuity.statement: Well, first of all, I just want to reassure the member that there are no fish-hooks in the legislation at all. Yes, she is right that the legislation is designed to make our corrections officers safer and to make their operations more efficient so they actually have the time to be able to dedicate to things like case management and prisoner safety.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon's turn was an explicit set of pātai to this Minister about replacing the deleted Te Tiriti provisions and about cultural temporary release. Mitchell's reply addresses a different thread entirely (fish-hooks, staffing numbers, the "as resources allow" wording) and engages no part of her argument. It stays on the bill under debate and glances at programme delivery, which she had also mentioned, so it is not wholly unresponsive — but nothing in it would change if she had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon put three direct questions to the Minister — "could we look at amendments that would provide a provision or just one clause that can lock in improving Māori outcomes", whether "Māori" can appear in the legislation, and how to protect temporary release for cultural functions — and this reply does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Mr Chair. I’m sure I won’t take a full call here, because I only have a short point to make, but it is around a very important point and that is the use of what’s now called “less lethal” devices to restrain or suppress prisoners.
acuity.explanation: Webb is squarely on the bill under debate and goes to specific clauses (21 and 21A), which is more than generic prepared material, but he engages no strand of the resourcing argument Mitchell had just made. His call would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said about staffing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Mitchell had just spoken about corrections being "under strength", recruitment running above attrition, and what "as resources allow" means; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Look, quite simply the fact of the matter is there are many, many different situations and scenarios, inside a corrections environment, where a passive prisoner, someone that’s refusing to follow instruction, could be putting other people at risk.
acuity.explanation: Takes Webb's actual premise — that a passively resisting prisoner cannot by definition endanger anyone else — and directly contests it with counter-examples (blocking a doorway to an injured prisoner, barricading so that officers are tied up while someone else needs help). The answer would be different had Webb argued something else. Short of 1.0 only because Webb's second, narrower question — that section 88 does not contain the words "non-lethal" that clause 21A purports to replace — goes unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because passive resistance is, by definition, not threatening any other person" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: It’s a good point, because I agree with him that it is a big power—it’s at the discretion of the chief executive. Quite simply, why it refers to contractors is, of course, because we have a private prison that’s being run by Serco.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific objection — that "eligible employee" reaches employees of contractors — concedes the strength of the point about the scale of the power, and supplies the actual reason the drafting refers to contractors (the Serco-run private prison). The reply would be impossible if Webb had raised a different clause, which is the deciding test. It is brief and does not address Webb's "three steps removed" sub-point, so not a full 1.0; the concern is engagement, not whether the answer is adequate or correct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Section 111 of the principal Act says, “Eligible employee means a person who is an employee of the chief executive,”" — Duncan Webb, who argued that contractors' employees should not be able to be authorised intelligence persons

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Further to what my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has just said, when we’re talking about authorised persons and the process that’s going through—because if I go back a step, the first bullet point under the intentions of this bill is: “explicitly empowering Corrections to monitor [prisoners’] communications and information sources for intelligence purposes to improve prison and public safety”.
