There are four parts to this bill, and this is one of them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding exchange — who the authorised intelligence person is and how that authorisation works — and explicitly builds on Webb's turn, so the engagement is pointable. But it then moves to its own prepared question on new section 127K and the exempt-communications process, and it does not take up the Minister's immediately preceding answer about contractors and Serco; indeed it asserts the authorised person is "an employee appointed from the chief executive", which is the proposition Mitchell had just qualified. Partial engagement, then prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We can’t have people who are not answerable to the State being intelligence officers and surveilling prisoners." — Duncan Webb, on who may be an authorised intelligence person

acuity.statement: I heard what the Prime Minister said about our track and field gold, and I do want to acknowledge, as was mentioned to me by one of my colleagues, Dame Yvette Williams, who was one of our famed Olympians, a gold medallist in the long jump, if I recall correctly, in 1952, I think it was, in Helsinki, who did us all extremely proud.
acuity.explanation: Henare takes up the specific claim Luxon made about the track and field gold being a first, and does something with it: he supplies the missing historical counterpart, Dame Yvette Williams's 1952 long jump gold, which is precisely the earlier New Zealand field-event win that Luxon's "first male" qualifier implies. The passage could not have been delivered had Luxon not made that claim, and it engages its content rather than merely naming him, so it sits near the top of the band; it stops short of 1.0 because it adds context rather than correcting or contesting the point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "Hamish Kerr also made history by becoming the first New Zealand male to win a field event in the Olympic track and field programme."

acuity.statement: As we wrap up our celebration of the Olympics, we can look forward to the Paralympics coming up in the next few weeks. To our flag bearers, Anna and Cameron, carry our flag with pride and know that we are proud of what you have achieved and that we are excited to see you compete. My family look forward to keeping up with the Paralympics, and I wish all our Kiwi Paralympians the best of luck heading to Paris.
acuity.explanation: Willis closed by asking the House to extend the same support to the Paralympics, and Luxton's turn does gesture at that thread by moving to the Paralympics and the flag bearers. But it is prepared material on the same occasion rather than engagement: Willis's substantive points — that 14 of the 20 medals were won by women, and that the 2018 women and girls in sport initiative explains the result — are never taken up, agreed with, extended or disputed. Luxton's own emphasis on mothers returning to sport sits beside Willis's argument without touching it. Delete Willis's speech entirely and substitute a different tribute on the same topic, and this speech would read word-for-word the same, which puts it in the low band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the Paralympics passage lands where Willis pointed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "I hope our House will support the Paralympics just as thoroughly as they have supported the Olympics."

acuity.statement: With Part 2, Subpart 3 on foundational information disclosure requirements, there are actually quite a few different elements to this subpart and it’s really important for us to be able to unpack each of the elements here.

But he engages no part of Woods' argument: he opens a fresh line on clause 40A's levy and the levy/tax boundary, and reaches back instead to Rachel Brooking's remarks from a previous session, which were not the turn he followed. The speech would be word-for-word the same had Woods asked something entirely different about this subpart, which places it in the prepared-material band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because he does orient himself to the subpart actually before the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods asked the Minister what "incentives" and "innovation" mean in clause 32(2)(a)(i), what protections stop privatisation, how clause 39 interacts with the OIA/LGOIMA, and why "7 years" was chosen — and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: Dr Woods has further asked around protections against privatisation. Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions.

The reply could not have been given in response to a different argument — substitute another critique and this passage disappears. Scored on engagement only; whether the Local Government Act claim is correct is a veracity question and whether the answer is detailed enough is a specificity one, and neither moves this score.

acuity.responding_to: "we want some certainty from the Minister in the chair around what protections are in place to stop the privatisation of these assets" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Turning to some of the questions raised by the Hon Dr Megan Woods, she asked specifically about what incentives there are to innovate and to invest. Well, isn’t it wonderful that we do have this opportunity in this Chamber to rewrite this piece of legislation because we believe that transparency is a real opportunity to innovate around.
acuity.explanation: She identifies the question correctly and engages one strand of it — innovation — by offering transparency and information disclosure as the mechanism. But Woods asked two things and asked for examples of what the clause envisages; the reply answers the topic rather than the specific ask, supplies no examples, and slides into prepared framing about the opportunity to rewrite the legislation. That is partial engagement you can still point at, which is the 0.5 anchor. The weakness of the inference from "transparency" to "incentive to invest" belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d like to know from the Minister in the chair what incentives are going to be put in place for the entities in terms of the investment. I’d also like to know more what is meant in clause 32(2)(a)(i) in terms of innovation." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: The genesis of New Zealand’s change in the management of water arose from the drinking-water problems that we had at Havelock North, where under-investment by the then council for many years led to thousands of people becoming ill from contaminated water, and some of them dying.
acuity.explanation: Parker follows a substantive turn by Brooking but engages no part of it. He opens on the history of the water reforms and moves to his own prepared question on clause 37 and sewage-discharge consents. The speech would read identically had Brooking said something entirely different about the bill. It sits above 0.0 only because it is squarely within the committee-stage examination of this bill's clauses rather than transferable to any debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking questioned the clause 40A levy, the $5 million maximum penalty in clause 43, and the claim that the bill is 'bottom-up rather than top-down', and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The issue we have here is the penalty amount—for everything that is considered under clause 42(1) and (2)—can hold a maximum penalty of $500,000 in the terms of individuals, or $5 million in any other cases, per clause 43(1).
acuity.explanation: Brooking had just put the clause 43 penalty maxima to the Minister and asked why $5 million is so high for a failure to disclose. Xu-Nan takes up that same strand with the same figures and carries it somewhere new — that clause 45, which requires both mens rea and actus reus, carries a lower maximum than the party-liability route in clause 42(2). That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding argument. It is held at the midpoint rather than the top because he neither names nor answers Brooking's actual question (why the amount is high), and the passage is self-evidently prepared material he signals he intends to deliver regardless.

acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "For an individual, it’s $500,000, but for an organisation, it’s $5 million."

acuity.statement: Covering a number of different questions that have been raised by various members around the Chamber, in the committee, I start with, I think, the same member’s question around the levy and observe that different classes of providers could include distinguishing between providers by population size, but that is detail that yet could be provided in the regulation.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question Russell had just put — what the 'different classes of providers' in clause 40A(2)(d) might be — and supplies the substantive answer (population size), while locating the detail in secondary legislation. The reply would have to change if she had asked something else; marked below 1.0 only because the quoted passage answers the levy strand and leaves her clause 36/37 ordering question for elsewhere.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I’m just looking at clause 40A(2)(d) “providing different levies for different classes of providers of water services”. I’m interested in what those different classes of water services might be"

acuity.statement: I wonder, in his previous answer to the question about the pecuniary penalties being $5 million for a council saying that it comes from the commerce legislation, has there been thought about the fact that this will only apply to councils or council-controlled organisations? So is that right to shift over from commerce legislation for giant companies—$5 million might be an appropriate penalty, but a council is a public entity; it’s ratepayer money. How is $5 million appropriate for that?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification — that the penalty regime is consistent with the Commerce Act — and presses on its weak point: the Commerce Act was written for private companies, whereas this provision bites only on councils spending ratepayer money. The question could not have been asked without having listened to the specific answer just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "As for pecuniary penalties, again, this is consistent with the approach taken in the Commerce Act."

acuity.statement: I’ve got a question for the Minister in relation to new section 38A which specifically relates to commercially sensitive information. This is a particularly sensitive issue because many of our councils around New Zealand probably don’t know the full extent of some of the investment required to get water infrastructure up to the standard needed to even last over the next few years.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows a substantive turn by Arena Williams on the Commerce Commission's powers under clause 40 and engages no part of it. Her contribution is on the matter under debate (the Commerce Commission's information powers in this part) but is self-contained prepared material on a different clause; it would read identically whatever Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked the Minister about "the advice that the Minister received in granting the Commerce Commission these extra powers" under clause 40, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate question on new section 38A.

acuity.statement: Taking the last point first from the Hon Ginny Andersen, the question around commercially sensitive information, I think the member identifies what is always a weighing exercise between the imperatives of commercially sensitive information being protected in the interests of encouraging enterprise in a way that’s appropriate while, at the same time, recognising the public interest in the disclosure of information. To argue against an exemption or to appeal against it—I imagine that usual avenues would be available for that purpose.
acuity.explanation: Penk takes up both strands of the specific question Andersen had just put — how the commercially-sensitive balance is struck, and what route exists to challenge an exemption — and answers each in turn. The reply is plainly shaped by what preceded it and would have to change if she had argued something else; it is vague on the second strand, but vagueness is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "how will we determine what is commercially sensitive?" and "what is the cause for a local interest group or other group of people who are lobbying to then go to the commission and request for that exemption to be revoked?"

acuity.statement: In terms of whether those powers are additional to those in the Commerce Act, as Arena Williams notes, they are, and we think that’s appropriate, because we want to provide maximum ability for the mechanisms in the Act to be enforceable, and we think it’s appropriate for the provision of water services on behalf of the ratepayers and citizens of the country.
acuity.explanation: This directly confirms the premise of Williams's question (the powers are additional to the Commerce Act) and gives a reason for it. It is squarely aimed at the specific claim she made rather than at the topic in general, and could not have been delivered unchanged after a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "under clause 40 of this part, the Minister is introducing new powers for the Commerce Commission"—her question on whether these are extra to those the commission would otherwise have under the Commerce Act.

acuity.statement: Also, whether that information might be looked at even if it is commercially sensitive, because, from what I understand under this clause, it’s being used by the commission itself for its own purpose, rather than simply to pass on to somebody in terms of disclosure. Will they be looking at information that is perhaps commercially sensitive because they’re a trusted entity to do that?
acuity.explanation: White picks up one strand of the Minister's answer — the protection of commercially sensitive information — and presses it in a case he did not address, where the commission uses the information for its own purposes rather than for onward disclosure. That is partial engagement: the rest of the turn is a fresh, self-contained question on clause 38 that does not depend on what Penk said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "what is always a weighing exercise between the imperatives of commercially sensitive information being protected ... while, at the same time, recognising the public interest in the disclosure of information."

acuity.statement: We’re still working our way through Subpart 3 of Part 2, and I’ve just noticed, really, that we’ve done a lot of talking around the Commerce Commission’s powers and levies and so on, but we haven’t really talked about the actual information that has to be supplied.
acuity.explanation: Russell notes what the debate has so far covered, which is a gesture at the preceding turns, but she engages no part of any argument made in them and instead moves to her own prepared questions on clause 37. On topic, but indifferent to what was actually said before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Helen White had asked whether the Commerce Commission would examine commercially sensitive information for its own purposes under clause 38, and this statement does not take that up; it only gestures at the preceding turns having covered "powers and levies".

acuity.statement: The member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell may wish to look at clause 52(3), which says, “Despite subsection (2), a territorial authority may decide to undertake further consultation before making the decision.” There is no limit. We’re not putting any limits on what territorial authorities may wish to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause Russell built her argument on and answers it directly with the adjacent subsection, disputing the premise that consultation is capped. The reply could not have been given in response to a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "in clause 52(2) a territorial authority is only required to take consultation once. It means that consultation is being reduced for the setting up of the water services entities."

acuity.statement: Look, that’s a “may”—that’s a “may”—and local government entities may well take that path, and they could engage in more consultation. The fact is that by saying consultation is only done once, it does reduce local participation.
acuity.explanation: Seizes on the permissive wording the Minister had just relied on and explains why a discretion does not answer a reduction in a mandatory requirement. The rebuttal is shaped entirely by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "a territorial authority may decide to undertake further consultation before making the decision."

acuity.statement: In the previous part, I had a question for the Minister around the use of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 and the arrangement for the application of those funding and financing rules also apply to this part.

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, this is a brand new line of questions, which I was trying to get to with the Minister, because where the Government has proposed new powers, in clause 40, unlike powers which have been given to the Commerce Commission before, these are more like powers which would be appropriate with an infrastructure regulator.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell spoke about the statutory-declaration verification power in clause 37(5) and this statement does not take it up

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell spoke about the $5 million penalties and public 'name and shame' accountability, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question Williams pressed twice: why the Commerce Commission and not the Infrastructure Commission. Brown meets her comparison head-on and inverts it, asserting the Commerce Commission's practised use of these tools and the Infrastructure Commission's lack of economic-regulation experience. The sentence could not have been written without her argument, which is what high acuity is. Whether the claim is true or well-reasoned is for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'why isn’t that regulator the Infrastructure Commission?' — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: The Hon Deborah Russell has been repeating the question around penalties that’s already been addressed. Penalties represent an upper limit.

That is a genuine engagement with her premise. But it treats her turn as mere repetition and does not take up her actual question — whether disclosure and public pressure are meant to be the first rung of accountability before penalties — so this is partial engagement, not full.

acuity.responding_to: 'We’re talking up to $5 million. ... These are not rich entities at the moment.' — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I actually just want to draw the Minister’s attention around the consultation. We still need to get some clarification from the Minister regarding clause 52(2) around “consultation once” and its relationship with subclause (3) around “may decide to undertake further consultation”.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty's whole turn argued that the clause 58 exemption from cost-effectiveness review contradicts the Government's cost-effectiveness rationale, citing the $120b/$185b discrepancy and Standard & Poor's. Xu-Nan engages none of that. He does land in the same clause-52 consultation territory McAnulty flagged as unanswered, which is pointable, but his speech is a self-contained prepared reading of subclauses (2), (2A), (3), (4) and Amendment Paper 65 — it would be word-identical had McAnulty argued something different about cost-effectiveness. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate, so the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "if you link that question to that which remains unanswered posed by Dr Deborah Russell around consultation" — Xu-Nan shares the consultation topic but takes up no part of McAnulty's cost-effectiveness argument.

acuity.statement: The questions in relation to consultation can be answered, as this clarifies that consultation is only required once. Councils are currently unsure about how much consultation is required—the Local Government Act isn’t clear about this. There are no specific requirements in the Local Government Act 2002 about how many times consultation must occur. Councils have discretion about this, and so this is a clarification.
acuity.explanation: This supplies the rationale Xu-Nan asked for — the clause exists because the Local Government Act is silent on how many consultations are needed — so it engages the substance of the question and would read differently had Xu-Nan asked something else. But it answers only the general 'why once' strand and leaves both of the specific clarifications untouched: the ordering argument about considering subclause (4) before deciding sufficiency, and whether new subclause (2A) contradicts clause 54(1)(e) on joint local government arrangements. 'I think that answers most of the questions' concedes the partial coverage. Scored on engagement only, not on whether the account of the Act is correct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what is the rationale that a territorial authority doesn’t need to consider consulting more than once?"

acuity.statement: In relation to the Hon Kieran McAnulty’s question in regards to the exemption to the cost-effectiveness review, the elements that would be requiring the cost-effectiveness review are being already undertaken as part of the water service delivery plan.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact question put and answers it with a reason — the review's elements are already captured in the water service delivery plan — which is the one answer McAnulty had not pre-empted (he predicted a 'they still can if they want to' reply instead). Squarely aimed at the specific clause-58 question, so high. Short of 1.0 because it engages only the exemption question and ignores the supporting argument McAnulty built it on: the $120b/$185b discrepancy, the 10-year long-term plan limitation, and the Standard & Poor's borrowing-cost assessment. Brevity and whether the answer is adequate are not Acuity's business; being pointed at the right question is.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Why would councils be exempt from a cost-effectiveness review when that is the entire rationale behind this proposal?"

acuity.statement: I’ve answered this question in a previous part. Greater Wellington Regional Council is the only regional council which is a water supplier and so, therefore, is covered; all other regional councils are not.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question Russell had just asked — why Greater Wellington Regional Council gets its own rules — and supplies the operative distinction (it is the only regional council that supplies water). Terse, but the reply would be different had she asked something else, which is the deciding test. Not scored on whether the answer is adequate or complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "it would be good to hear from the Minister why there is this separate set of rules for Greater Wellington Regional Council"

acuity.statement: The first one relates to this consultation discussion that we’ve been having, and the Minister of Local Government has told us that the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA) is unclear as to how much balancing councils have to do with consultation, so the purpose of these changes are to make it clear that it only has to be once—the mandatory is once only. I was wondering if the Minister is also thinking, then, of amending the LGA to make it clear for all consultations under that Act.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's stated rationale (the LGA is unclear on consultation balancing) accurately and draws out its consequence: if the unclarity is the problem, does it not apply to the whole Act? That is engaging the reasoning of the preceding exchange rather than merely referring to it. Marked down from 1.0 because she then moves to her own separate prepared questions on clauses 49 and 59.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell/the Minister's preceding exchange: "that does really clarify why you only have that requirement to only do it once with the substantive reason behind it"

acuity.statement: This question is: do the provisions that currently exist in the Local Government Act, section 137, still apply to the new entity—well, the entities that would be otherwise covered by the Minister’s proposals in Part 4 of this Act?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (Part 3/Part 4 and the Local Government Act), and prompted by a prior non-answer, but it engages no part of the argument made in the preceding turn by another member. This is prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, which sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking immediately preceded with questions on the "may"/"must" change in Amendment Paper 65 and on clause 59's repeal of section 58, and this statement does not take either up — it resumes the speaker's own earlier unanswered question

acuity.statement: If the Minister wouldn’t mind, could he please identify a clause within Part 3 that will give the committee confidence that sufficient time will still need to be given for consultation, particularly as we mentioned that territorial authorities may only need to consult once.

It engages the consequence of what was established rather than the specific argument just made, and the bulk of the turn is his own prepared line on clauses 50 and 54, so a mid-band score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown / the preceding consultation exchange: "that requirement to only do it once" — the once-only consultation rule Russell and Brooking had drawn out of the Minister

acuity.statement: In reply to the Hon Rachel Brooking, she asked if the Local Government Act should be amended for all consultation—well, the scope of this bill is on water services, and councils are looking to be able to move quickly. That’s what this does.
acuity.explanation: Identifies Brooking's question correctly and answers it on its own terms — the bill's scope is water services, so no wider LGA amendment follows. He goes on in the same turn to address Williams on section 137 and McAnulty on clause 58, so the turn is shaped by what preceded it throughout. Short of 1.0 because the section 137 reply restates scope rather than engaging the subsection (4) point actually put. Whether 'scope' is a sufficient answer is a question for Rigor, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "I was wondering if the Minister is also thinking, then, of amending the LGA to make it clear for all consultations under that Act"

acuity.statement: But in the response given just now about why we had some of these consultation arrangements, the Minister said it was in order to streamline the process for local government entities. Now, that is a somewhat different answer, so I just want the Minister to clarify—streamlining enterprise: we’re sort of paring it down, we’re making it minimal, we’re making it easy to get through, versus clarifying the requirements of the Local Government Act.
acuity.explanation: Sets the Minister's just-given answer against his earlier one and asks him to reconcile them, identifying the specific tension (streamlining versus clarifying the LGA). The turn could not have been delivered had he said something else; it exists entirely because of what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "This section is about supporting councils to put in place these entities quickly. It is about ensuring there’s a streamlined process."

acuity.statement: My colleague the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has indicated some surprise from the Minister’s response around streamlining. I also heard the Minister’s response to indicate that the reason as to why clause 52 was there was to enable things to happen quickly.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the streamlining rationale that had just been contested and restates it correctly as the premise for his own questions on clauses 52 and 53, so one strand of the preceding exchange is genuinely taken up. It does not do anything further with Russell's reconciliation challenge and turns to prepared material about his own electorate, which is a mid-band engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "It is about ensuring there’s a streamlined process", and Deborah Russell's challenge to it

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. The point’s been made a number of times around consultation. The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation. That is incredibly clear. That is the clarification that councils requested, and that is what is being provided in this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Utikere put two specific questions: why not amend subclause (2) to read 'at least once', and where the special consultative process sits in the new scheme. Brown engages the consultation topic and restates the must/may structure — which is the strand Utikere was probing — but takes up neither the proposed drafting change nor the special consultative process question, and offers nothing that answers the argument that a streamlining intent will disincentivise use of subclause (3). Topic engaged, specific claims not; partial at best.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: 'why can he not just amend subclause (2) so that it’s actually just indicating that there needs to be consultation but it just needs to happen on “at least one” occasion'

acuity.statement: He has answered the questions put by my colleagues, on consultation, but he has not addressed the second leg of his own part, clause 51, which says “decision-making requirements”. The decision-making requirements that he is proposing to change are set out in section 137 of the Local Government Act 2002, and, on those decision-making requirements, which I have asked him to tell New Zealanders that he is not changing, there are three important points here.
acuity.explanation: Takes Brown's reply directly: accepts that he has answered on consultation, identifies precisely what his answer left out (the decision-making requirements limb of clause 51), and then works through three specific section 137 protections she says are lost. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged against a different preceding answer — it is built on the gap in the one actually given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: 'The legislation is very clear in relation to clarifying that the territorial authority must consult once, but they may decide to undertake further consultation.'

acuity.statement: This bill doesn’t affect what is provided in section 137 of the Local Government Act—that continues, unaffected and unaltered. This is about the consultation requirements, not in relation to the requirements in section 137.
acuity.explanation: Meets the core of Williams' argument head-on: she claimed that under clause 51 the section 137 protections (legal responsibility, pricing control, retained asset ownership) would cease to apply to councils entering joint arrangements, and he denies exactly that premise, asserting section 137 is untouched and the clause goes only to consultation. Scored on engagement alone, not on whether the denial is correct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: 'because the provisions under section 137 will not apply to you'

acuity.statement: In relation to the question around special consultative procedures, the special consultative procedure is not required under provisions in the bill. Under the Local Government Act, there are only a few occasions when the special consultative procedure must be used. It is usually up to councils to decide how to consult, using the principles of consultation in section 82 of the Local Government Act 2002.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Utikere's turn — the special consultative procedure — and supplies real content on it (not required under the bill, section 82 principles, councils decide). But it leaves untouched the substance of what Utikere spent most of his turn on: whether a council could consult on a CCO and land on a section 137 arrangement, and why section 78(1) is engaged in clause 52 but not clause 53. Partial engagement of a pointable strand, with the central argument unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Can I invite the Minister of Local Government to the earlier question that I did pose around the special consultative process and how that relates to matters."

The Minister should be able to just get up and reassure the committee and the people of New Zealand that there are protections here that would prevent them. What I hope he won’t do is stand up and say, “Well, that’s a matter for the councils.”, because quite often in many of the questions that we have posed to this Minister at various committee stages that revolved around this, that has been the response or he’s just chosen not to answer.
acuity.explanation: Directly anticipates and forecloses the move Brown had just made in the preceding turn — deferring the question to councils' own discretion — and presses instead for the protection question to be answered in the bill. The speech would have to change if Brown had not just devolved the matter to councils. It is not higher because much of the surrounding turn is prepared material on England, Scotland and Kiwibank that engages nothing Brown said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "It is usually up to councils to decide how to consult, using the principles of consultation in section 82 of the Local Government Act 2002."

This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question McAnulty had just put — what prevents sale of water assets — and answers it on its own terms, locating the protections in the Local Government Act and explaining why this part of the bill is not where they sit. The reply is squarely shaped by the preceding turn. Short of 1.0 only because it names no section, so it engages the question without closing it; that vagueness is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.

acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "If a council-controlled organisation or alternative arrangement is established and they get into financial difficulty, what is stopping them from selling them off?"

acuity.statement: There are two very simple questions to answer, and that is—as the Hon Kieran McAnulty has just referred to—why is clause 59 there and why is this repeal of section 58 needed? Is it a simple temporal issue that in five years’ time, everything will be done, or not, and what happens? Does that mean that councils can’t amend those agreements after five years? A simple question: why is clause 59 there, repealing what will be section 58?
acuity.explanation: Picks up McAnulty's clause 59 point explicitly, restates it as a precise pair of questions, and extends it with a consequence he had not drawn — whether councils are barred from amending agreements after five years. She also registers which of her own earlier questions Brown did answer, showing she tracked his reply. The turn is clearly shaped by what preceded it rather than prepared in advance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Clause 59 says that all that stuff that we’ve just talked about, “Don’t worry about it. In five years, it’s all good.” Well, if it’s all good in five years, why not now?"

acuity.statement: The purpose of this part is to ensure the financial separation of Watercare and Auckland Council, to enable Watercare to be able to provide water services to Auckland in a financially sustainable way.
acuity.explanation: Answers the second of the two questions Brooking put, supplying the purpose of the part as asked. It engages a pointable, specific request. It is not higher because the question she pressed twice and called simple — why clause 59 repeals what will be section 58 — is passed over entirely, as is the request to explain what the Amendment Paper 65 changes do.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "The other question was about the purpose of this part and the amendments that are made in the Minister’s Amendment Paper 65."

acuity.statement: My final question, for now, is: given the Minister’s statements about this as the deal for Auckland, what happens to Northland? Is there any ability for Northland to enter this arrangement or not?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own characterisation of Part 4 as an Auckland-specific negotiated deal and draws out its consequence — whether any comparable route exists for Northland. The question only makes sense as a follow-on from what he just said, so the speech would have had to change if he had framed the part differently. Not a full 1.0 because the surrounding material is prepared clause-by-clause questioning of 59A/59B rather than engagement with his argument.

acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "This part was part of the negotiation between Auckland Council and the Government in relation to the Local Water Done Well deal, announced in May, between the mayor and the Prime Minister."

acuity.statement: As he has said, this is an arrangement that has been reached by his Government and the Auckland Council. But the issue here is that the powers belong to the secretary to prepare the Watercare charter, and not to Aucklanders.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's premise that the charter arrangement was agreed with Auckland Council and turns it against him, pointing out that the clause vests the drafting power in the secretary rather than in Auckland. That is engagement with the content of his framing, not a mere reference to it; her alternative wording for clause 62A is built on what he claimed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "This part was part of the negotiation between Auckland Council and the Government" — and his reference to "putting in place a Crown monitor, a charter"

acuity.statement: What happens to Northland? Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish. How does it apply to stormwater? Auckland Council will continue to retain stormwater.
acuity.explanation: Restates each specific question put to him and supplies a direct answer to it — Part 4 is Auckland-only but does not bar joint arrangements; stormwater stays with the council. The reply is shaped entirely by the two questions asked and would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Is there any ability for Northland to enter this arrangement or not?" and "Does this limit "in its ability to extract excessive profits" apply to stormwater, and, if so, how?"

acuity.statement: In relation to the question asked by Arena Williams, this is a point that was discussed between the Government and the Crown. In relation to the preparation of the charter, it was agreed that the secretary would prepare it, but that would, obviously, be done in consultation with Auckland Council.

But it does not take up her actual proposition, that Auckland Council should prepare the charter instead; it largely restates what the clause already says, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
