acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?"

acuity.statement: I think there are some particularly important issues around what is to be done with water in Northland. Northland has been left isolated by this treatment for Watercare.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Northland point the Minister had just answered and presses it as a grievance, so the topic is squarely the one in front of the committee. But it engages only the first half of his answer and ignores the joint-arrangements qualification he offered, and the accompanying call for the Minister to explain the nature of the deal re-asks what he had just addressed (mutual benefit, independent borrowing). Partial engagement, mostly prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish."

acuity.statement: To answer Deborah Russell’s questions about why Watercare is getting special treatment, I think that they were quite quick off the blocks, so their proposed arrangement is expected to deliver lower prices than would have otherwise been the case prior to the deal being struck. Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent, and future charges are also expected to be lower than they would have been.
acuity.explanation: Russell's immediately preceding turn argued that the bill's 'lower prices' purpose is contradicted because Watercare costs and Auckland water rates will rise, citing a figure of about 8 percent, and asked the Minister to speak to those costs. Simmonds takes up that exact claim and that exact number, supplying the counter-figures (25.8 percent proposed versus 7.2 percent under the separation) and arguing the increase is smaller than the counterfactual. The reply would have to be different if Russell had raised a different objection, and it also picks up the two earlier questions on the monitor's criteria and the fees framework.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent"

acuity.statement: The history of the regulation of monopolies in the water space is an illustration of why you actually need it. Theoretically, if you have a community-owned monopoly, you would think the incentives for excessive profit-taking are not as strong as if you have a private sector owner of a monopoly.
acuity.explanation: Simmonds had just described the Crown monitor as needing expertise in 'the regulation of a monopoly business'. Parker takes up that one strand — endorsing the need for monopoly regulation and granting the point about community ownership — before moving to prepared material on US versus New Zealand asset-base pricing models that engages nothing Simmonds said. Partial engagement with a pointable strand, then a pivot to his own line of argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "a range of skills, expertise, and experience in, for example, the regulation of a monopoly business"

acuity.statement: The question I have for the Minister is: we’ve heard a lot of rhetoric around this bill making sure that local services and local people are in control of local affairs, how does that work with this proposal for the Secretary of the Department of Internal Affairs to create this new charter for Watercare?
acuity.explanation: Parker's preceding turn asked a specific question about whether the regulatory framework leaves policy space for an alternative monopoly pricing model; Simmonds before him gave figures on price increases and the monitor's criteria. Belich takes up neither, and opens an independent prepared line on clause 62A and the charter. She gestures at the debate (noting the questions have not yet been addressed and that this is the Watercare section), so it is on the matter under debate rather than wholly detached, but she engages no part of any preceding argument's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker asked whether the regulatory framework leaves policy space for a different monopoly pricing model, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister in the chair, the Hon Penny Simmonds, in relation to Part 5, what is the political intent?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Parker's turn — the demand that the Minister explain the rationale for the Part 5 / NPS-FM changes — and puts it to the same Minister. But he does not engage Parker's specific point about the hierarchy of obligations in clause 101 or his argument that the hierarchy never blocked council consents; he restates the question at a general level and then moves to prepared constituency material on Henderson Creek. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would like the Minister to explain to us why it is that this provision is necessary." — David Parker

acuity.statement: It then comes back to the question that my colleague the Hon David Parker has asked, which is: why are we doing this?
acuity.explanation: More than a mere reference: he adopts Parker's "why are we doing this?" question and applies it to a different target, arguing the provision is both unnecessary and a demotion of Taumata Arowai's role. But the bulk of the turn is his own prepared line on the Independent Māori Statutory Board and Tāmaki-makau-rau, which would have been delivered whatever Parker had said. Partial engagement, pointable, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t understand what the need is for that revocation of that principle" — David Parker

acuity.statement: The hierarchy of obligations is something that we were very clear about in our campaigning. We saw the hierarchy being an obstacle to economically viable solutions for both councils and for industries, and there needed to be a balancing of the obligations rather than the hierarchy of obligations that was there.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise thing Parker asked — why the hierarchy of obligations is being disapplied — by naming the asserted defect (an obstacle to economically viable solutions) and backing it with the discharge-to-land consenting costs at Palmerston North and Bluff. The speech could not have been given against a different preceding argument; it is shaped by Parker's question. Marked slightly below 1.0 because she leaves Twyford's question about the intent of Part 5 and Henare's about Taumata Arowai untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What is wrong in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management, particularly in relation to the hierarchy of obligations, which is referred to in clause 101 of this bill" — David Parker

acuity.statement: We’ve heard from people, and we’ve had an answer from the Minister about the hierarchy that you find in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management. I’ll make some comments about that in a minute, but my main point is: why was this inserted into this bill when Taumata Arowai, section 138, doesn’t mention the Resource Management Act or any of the instruments under the Resource Management Act?
acuity.explanation: Brooking takes up the same clause and the same hierarchy provision Abel had just argued about, and explicitly positions herself against the angle of "the previous questions" — but she does not engage Abel's public-health reasoning or his submission evidence. She acknowledges the strand, then advances her own prepared line (why is the provision in the bill at all, given section 138 never references the RMA). Partial engagement: the topic and the clause, not the specific argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the amendment proposes to remove that section" — his case that clause 101(3A) strips the hierarchy of obligations from Taumata Arowai's consideration of wastewater.

acuity.statement: The second question I had was around clause 102, which inserts new section 138A—which I believe people have touched on, but I have a question in relation to that. That’s in relation to the technical workings of this particular provision, and my question for the Minister is: is this a “Henry VIII” clause; if so, what is the justification for using a clause of this nature in this bill?
acuity.explanation: Belich picks up the one strand Brooking had just raised, acknowledges it has been "touched on", and re-puts the same justification question with her own Regulations Review Committee framing. She engages the strand without doing anything further with Brooking's reasoning, and her other question (civil defence, Schedule 2) is entirely new prepared material. Half engagement, half fresh ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "given it is in here, the justification for using the “King Henry VIII” clause needs to be strong, and it just seems to be incredibly weak" — her challenge on clause 102/new section 138A.

acuity.statement: If I can go back to Steve Abel’s questions about “safe”—and I think it’s really important that he understands that there is certainly no intent to take any provision away regarding the safety of drinking water—Taumata Arowai will continue to regulate drinking water, including its safety, and it will also continue to have powers to set waste-water standards by taking into account public health. Removing the hierarchy will actually give more flexibility to them in this area.
acuity.explanation: She answers the specific word-search point (and later says plainly that this legislation is not the one setting drinking-water standards), and she meets the hierarchy argument head-on by asserting the opposite consequence — that removal increases Taumata Arowai's flexibility on public health. The reply would have to change entirely had Abel argued something else. Marked just below 1.0 because she does not take up the Public Health Communication Centre submission he quoted at length.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero" — and his argument that removing the hierarchy of obligations deprioritises drinking-water safety.

acuity.statement: I think there was a question from the Hon Rachel Brooking on the section in the Water Services Act relating to waste-water standards—why the changes are required—that don’t mention the national policy statement. The Water Services Act requires Taumata Arowai to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai as part of all its functions. The definition of Te Mana o te Wai in section 14 links directly to the national policy statement.
acuity.explanation: She names the exact question put to her and supplies the missing link it turned on — that section 14's definition of Te Mana o te Wai ties the Water Services Act to the national policy statement — which is a direct correction of the premise that the Taumata Arowai framework has no connection to the NPS. Fully determined by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Taumata Arowai doesn’t talk about the Resource Management Act at all or its instruments. That makes no sense to me."

acuity.statement: But I wanted to ask the Minister, in addition to that, has the Minister considered a sunset clause to this? This is one of the things that usually is a way to curb some of the power that can be granted with a “Henry VIII” clause, having a sunset clause or a particular duration. That’s my first question to the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Parker's substantive turn immediately precedes. Xu-Nan's questions are squarely on the bill under debate (clause 102 Henry VIII clause, clause 103 and Schedule 2), so it is prepared material on the right subject, but it engages no part of Parker's argument about the freshwater hierarchy. The gesture at prior ministerial clarifications is a reference, not engagement with content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker argued that other legislation also removes the effect of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management for resource consents — “you’re not just stripping this requirement out from Taumata Arowai” — and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I would like to ask the Minister if the words “preliminary arrangements” should be taken as meaning that there isn’t actually a fuller plan.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Belich's substantive turn precedes. Leary is on the matter under debate — the adequacy of the bill's title — and so is in the same genre as Belich, but she takes up neither Belich's central-government-control argument nor her commencement point, instead running her own prepared case about small councils' debt ceilings. Same topic, no engagement with the specific argument: 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich asked whether the Minister “consider[ed] changing the title of this Act in clause 1 to the ‘Central Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Act’” and queried the four commencement time frames; this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: That’s one of my questions. I do think this question about preliminary—it’s a difficult word to say; too many “Rs” in it for me. It’s difficult when your name is Rachel! My colleague makes some good points about that and why it is necessary to be in the title of the bill, and when can we expect more of the changes as well?
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Leary's turn immediately precedes. Brooking takes up one strand of it — that “preliminary” signals a missing fuller plan — and carries it forward into a question about timing and whether a temporal element belongs in the title, which is more than a mere reference. But the endorsement of her colleague is largely unargued and she then returns to her own prepared material on section 14 versus section 138A, so this is partial engagement rather than a full take-up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: “Is there going to be a subsequent piece of legislation that is going to, basically, make this redundant?” — Brooking picks up the “preliminary” strand and asks “when can we expect more of the changes as well?”

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I want to propose an amendment to the title of the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill. One of the substantial themes that we received in submissions from iwi Māori was a deep concern about the diminishment or removal of Te Mana o te Wai.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Brooking's turn immediately precedes and proposed a Te Mana o te Wai-based retitling. Abel takes that specific proposal and builds on it with a sharper formulation, which is genuine engagement with the content of the preceding turn rather than a mere mention. It stays mid-band because the bulk of the speech is prepared submitter quotations that would have been delivered whatever Brooking had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: “should not the bill change its name to the ‘Water Services Strange Te Mana o te Wai Amendment Act’” — Abel proposes “(Te Mana o Te Wai Deprioritisation)” and describes it as an extension of that proposal.

acuity.statement: One of the issues that was raised by submitters—and I’d just note that even with the reduced number of days that were available for select committee submissions, actually 13, over 1,000 submissions were received. First of all, there was a consistent theme around opposition to the bill, but that to one side, if that was not going to be accepted by the Government, then there were a number of suggestions around changing the time frame within which the coastal permits would be set down. There are a couple of Amendment Papers in my name that do seek to do exactly that.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive question from David Parker on cost recovery and charging for occupation of marine space, but engages no part of it. Utikere opens a separate line on the length of the permit extension (20 years versus 10 or five) and his own Amendment Papers — prepared committee-stage material that would read identically whatever Parker had said. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker asked the Minister whether councils' discretion to run a charging regime for occupation of marine space is being removed, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: My question follows on from my colleague the Hon David Parker, who raised the issue around local councils having to foot the bill if they wish to do a review of a coastal permit. In the select committee process, the majority of all councils that submitted on this piece of legislation were in opposition to this rollover of consents, regardless of environmental impacts or the ability for people to participate in the process and encourage a review.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Parker's preceding question — the removal of cost recovery for consent reviews — and develops it with council submissions and the ratepayer-fairness argument, so the speech would be different had Parker raised something else. It does not engage his other and more technical strand (whether the RMA charging discretion for occupation of marine space is also being removed), which keeps it at partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "they can’t recover the costs of doing so" — his question on councils being unable to recover the cost of reviewing an old marine farm consent

acuity.statement: Yes, it will require the council to meet the costs on the rare occasion that they may find that there is a strong need to review the conditions of farms that had existed for decades, and the next 25 years will give the confidence to the owners of these farms and their permits that they can dedicate their scarce resources to actually achieving economic outcomes, rather than playing a type of roller derby with the local councils.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the premise put by Luxton and Parker — that councils will bear the review costs — and then supplies the reason for it, which is the specific thing asked of him. The engagement is with the content of the question, not merely a reference to the questioner, so this is high on responsiveness; the quality of the trade-off reasoning and the politeness of 'roller derby' are separate attributes and are not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "I’d like the Minister to help us understand why he feels that local ratepayers should have to foot the bill should councils wish to do a review of a coastal permit"

acuity.statement: Now, the Hon David Parker raises a very good point: what is the return to the Crown or to the public for the occupation of what you might say is the commons—i.e., private enterprises occupying either oceanic space in the future, or seabed and foreshore for the purposes of mussels and oysters? Sadly, that particular issue has been confused by the mission creep that we’re seeing in the seabed and foreshore legislation. Hopefully, we will have time to address that oversight in the near future.
acuity.explanation: Restates Parker's question about public return for private occupation of the commons accurately enough to show it was heard, and locates it against the seabed and foreshore regime — engagement with the topic of the question. But it takes up the general issue rather than the specific point put, namely whether the existing RMA charging discretion is being removed, and Parker's explicit invitation to correct him is left untouched, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "is he also taking away the discretion of councils to have a charging regime for the occupation of marine space, which is currently allowed for under the Resource Management Act?"

acuity.statement: There is a situation we have here where we did receive substantial submissions from the Marlborough District Council, which the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries is so disdainful of; a council, I might add, which, in its region, manages 80 percent of the entire value of aquaculture in New Zealand and has 600 of the 1,200 farms in New Zealand. It’s the overwhelming majority consenting authority for the wealth and value that is in marine farming, so it’s strange that we can’t pay some attention to their wisdom on it.
acuity.explanation: Fastens directly on the dismissal of the Marlborough District Council in the immediately preceding turn and turns Jones's own economic framing against it, supplying figures on that council's share of aquaculture value and farm numbers to argue its submissions deserve weight. Delete Jones's attack on that council and this passage has nothing to stand on, which is the test for high responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "I don’t like that council, because they actually created the seabed and foreshore debacle" — his dismissal of the Marlborough council and of "Marlborough bach owners"

acuity.statement: It’s disappointing to hear the Minister’s response around the lack of support for the proposed time frames, including the one that Mr Abel has just referred to. That is disappointing.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows Abel's detailed case for Amendment Paper 58 (consent-review costs falling on ratepayers rather than the commercial operator) and names Abel's point, but only as a reference — he restates that it is 'disappointing' without taking up any part of the argument's content, then moves to his own prepared questions on sections 165ZFHC and 165ZFHD. The cost-recovery theme recurs later in his turn, but tied to his own Amendment Paper rather than to Abel's reasoning. On the matter under debate, engaging none of the argument: a mere reference, which the rubric places in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: 'No one could contest that they should rightly have to pay for the costs of a review of their consent or any of their consent processes. I invite the Minister to support that amendment.'

acuity.statement: However, I wanted to ask the Minister whether he has considered some of the options that have been put forward in the regulatory impact statement, because I understand there are a lot of people—according to the Minister’s response previously—that the Minister doesn’t like or doesn’t think deserve any sort of attention or say regarding this particular aspect.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns by other members precede this one (Abel on cost recovery for reviews, Utikere on change-of-condition triggers and notification), and Xu-Nan takes up neither. His material is a prepared walk through pages 17-18 of the regulatory impact statement and options three and four, which would read identically whatever Abel or Utikere had just said. The only gesture at the debate is the glancing aside about the Minister's earlier remarks, which engages their tone rather than any argument — that places it at 0.3, not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Abel argued the consent holder rather than ratepayers should bear review costs and Utikere asked for an example of a condition change triggered by extension; this statement takes up neither, and glances only at the Minister's earlier response.

acuity.statement: If I can start with the rather discursive remarks from the last speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, the focus on the date of 2050 or the 20-year duration is driven by a solid commitment to turn around the dire economic circumstances in many parts of regional New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan asked precisely why the blanket extension to 2050 was chosen over the officials' preferred options of 15 or 25 years, given similar net benefits. Jones takes that exact question up and supplies a reason for the longer duration, then disputes the premise that a shorter term would deliver the same benefit ('Five years may enable people to enjoy some short relief'). The reply would have to change if Xu-Nan had argued something else. Short of 1.0 only because he answers on duration generally rather than engaging the option three/option four net-benefit comparison he was pointed at. Whether the reasoning is sound or the figures right belongs to Rigor and Veracity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'In this case, options three and four are extending the consent by 15 years or extending all consents by 25 years, not consents to 2050 as a blanket approach.'

acuity.statement: And, yes, OK, some of my remarks may have been a bit rhetorical about the Marlborough council. I know there are some redeemable members of that council, but from time to time—from time to time—the truth must be spoken.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's charge was specifically that the Minister showed 'disdain for Marlborough District Council' and should discuss it with Councillor Arbuckle. Jones engages that charge directly — concedes part of it (his remarks were rhetorical), disputes the rest (there are redeemable members, and the criticism was warranted). That is the accept-part/dispute-the-rest pattern the top of the band describes, and the passage could not exist without Utikere's intervention.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: 'It’s actually also very disappointing to hear his disdain for Marlborough District Council.'

acuity.statement: Thank you to the other members for giving me the opportunity to ask the Minister to illuminate further what I think is a very salient issue—I think we haven’t canvassed it at all well, and I think this is a wonderful opportunity for the Minister to do that—employment in regional New Zealand and what it actually looks like.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Brooking that posed two specific, answerable questions about the review clause and cost recovery. Cameron engages neither; he gestures at the debate ("we haven't canvassed it at all well") and at unnamed Opposition claims about economic activity "sitting in the doldrums", then puts his own prepared question about regional employment and the 20-year extension. The speech is about the matter under debate, so it is not a zero, but it would read identically whatever Brooking had argued — a mere gesture at the debate, not engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking asked what the temporal scale of new section 165ZFHJ(b) is and who pays for a consent review, and this statement does not take either up (Rachel Brooking)

acuity.statement: I do have other concerns relating to appropriateness of cost-recovery provisions, but I think our colleagues on this side of the Chamber have covered those, so I won’t venture into that territory.
acuity.explanation: Pointable partial engagement: Tana explicitly tracks that Brooking has already argued the cost-recovery point and declines to repeat it, and her second question (whether "the review provisions are strong enough") picks up the same review clause Brooking interrogated. But the bulk of the turn is new prepared material on free-trade chapters, kaitiakitanga and the locus of decision-making power that does not take up the content of Brooking's reasoning. One strand engaged, then back to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it will only be ratepayers who could possibly be paying for it, because of the avoidance of section 36 of the Resource Management Act" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: There is the fiction that amenity and landscape values are of a greater level of significance than jobs and household livelihoods. To the former Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, one need look no further than the debacle of the salmon company struggling after spending $10 million to seek a resource consent—$10 million down the gurgler of consultants, unelected bureaucrats, and unhelpful scientists, people who are driven to act in a manner inversely related to economic durability in their communities.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Brooking pressed — the weight the Act gives amenity and landscape values, and her defence of ecological assessment — addresses her directly as the former Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, and answers with a costed counter-example about consenting expense. The speech would have to change if she had argued something else. Marked down from 1.0 only because he restates her position as a priority ranking she did not assert, which is engagement with the argument as he has recast it rather than as made. Whether that recasting is fair is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and does not move this score further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "he has mentioned, a lot, “landscape concerns” and “amenity”" and "indiscriminate detritus can sometimes have important ecological effects, and those effects are ones that may need to be assessed" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: On the matter of giving evidence that a regional council has frustrated, look no further than the area I hail from. The capacity to create additional marine farming enterprises off the coast of Te Tai Tokerau hovers near zero.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the evidential demand just put to him: Brooking charged that no evidence had been offered that councils are obstructing consents, and Jones names the demand, then supplies an instance from Te Tai Tokerau including the Stephenson Island mussel farm and its consent to 2050. This is the clearest case in the window of a speech that would be different had the preceding turn been different — he supplies the thing that was asked for. Whether the example actually establishes the claim is a separate question from whether he engaged it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "He hasn’t provided any evidence about these “aberrant” councils reviewing consents" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I'm still interested to hear from the Minister around the method for notification under new Subpart 1A, new section 165ZFHD. Just further in that particular section, specifically new subsection (3), it talks about a situation where a permit holder decides to continue to operate under an extant coastal permit that would be extended under this particular subpart.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn in the window (Jo Luxton) argued for five- and 10-year rollover time frames and expressly mentioned Utikere's own amendments on duration; he takes up none of it, opening instead a fresh technical line on notification and withdrawal under new section 165ZFHD. He is squarely on the clauses under debate and gestures at an unanswered earlier question to the Minister, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jo Luxton spoke about the 20-year duration and shorter five- and 10-year rollovers ("why, aside from the reasons he's given us, he didn't seek to give a shorter time frame of the five and 10 years to the sector") and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The other thing that we mentioned before, and one of the other speakers mentioned before, is in terms of what this does to the regions. I will also, I guess, at this stage like to point out that all regional and unitary councils oppose this bill. It would be really good to get the response from the Minister that if this is really good for regional development—and I really hope that it is; also it did state here in the regulatory impact statement that it does have certainty for industry and consent authorities; this is not my area of specialty—why then would the regional and unitary councils oppose this bill if it's going to be good for the regions?
acuity.explanation: He picks up one strand of the earlier turn — the claim that the 20-year duration delivers regional development and jobs — names it as something a previous speaker raised, and puts a counter to it (that every regional and unitary council opposes the bill), which is a real engagement rather than a mere reference. It is partial: he does not touch the time-frame argument that was the substance of Luxton's turn, and the rest of his contribution is his own prepared list of questions on the regulatory impact statement and modelling.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We all want good regional employment, good regional job opportunities." — Jo Luxton, who argued the 20-year duration was justified by regional economic development and employment.

acuity.statement: When I was talking about evidence, the Minister responded with some examples of where marine farms have not been consented in the first place. But this bill is not about consenting of new marine farms; it is all about extending the consents of existing marine farms. The question was about evidence regarding reviews: have regional councils done reviews of existing consented marine farms based on these amenity values that so upset the Minister?
acuity.explanation: This is engagement of the strongest kind: she restates the answer she was given, shows why the examples in it are off-point (they concern consenting new farms, not reviews of existing ones), and re-puts the original question with the distinction made explicit. The contribution could not have been written in advance — remove the answer she is dissecting and nothing here survives. Marked slightly below the top only because the turn she dismantles is the Minister's, which falls outside this window, so the engagement is auditable through her own relaying of it rather than directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Minister responded with some examples of where marine farms have not been consented in the first place" — the Minister's reply on amenity and evidence, as relayed by Brooking; his turn falls between the turns shown in this window.

acuity.statement: The member makes some very relevant points as to why the rights of an applicant to continue on with a process would be retained. In the event that this legislation does change, there may very well be applicants who are seeking, for example, to change some of the boundaries of a permit that this legislation will allocate to them into, arguably, 2050, and I would say that a lot of people have got permits well beyond 2050.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up the clauses Utikere raised by name and gives a policy rationale for preserving an applicant's appeal rights, so one strand of the question is genuinely engaged. But the second and more specific question — whether the once-only review limit in subsection (3)(b) bites on the permit in toto or on individual conditions — is never answered; he substitutes a point about the two-year period and then moves to prepared material on councils, iwi settlements and the regulatory statement. Partial engagement, pointable but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "why is there a need to insert the reference to ensuring that all appeal rights have been exercised and exhausted?"

acuity.statement: Minister, we clearly see your bluster and certainty around the need to trample on your garden-variety Kiwis in the regions who want to have input on what happens in their commons and to make these dictates from on high from the throne of central government. But I do wonder, in considering what a reasonable piece of legislation might look like, if you have any mind to making some reasonable amendments to this.
acuity.explanation: Abel picks up Jones's own 'garden-variety Kiwis' framing and inverts its substance — on his account the ordinary locals are the ones wanting a say over their commons, and the Minister is the one overriding them, which does engage Jones's claim that councils and iwi interests are the obstacle to ordinary enterprise. It is more than a mere reference, but it stops at the inversion rather than contesting any of Jones's specifics, and then turns to a fresh ask about amendments, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "garden-variety Kiwis are trying to make a living and they fear that their enterprises are going to be hijacked or held hostage"

acuity.statement: Now, earlier on in the evening, the Minister himself made a point around councils undertaking reviews, and he said, “which are very few”. So, if he wants the DG to be there to safeguard against councils undertaking reviews willy-nilly because of nimbyism and all that kind of stuff that he has talked about, why does he see that the director-general is such an important part of that?
acuity.explanation: Luxton quotes the Minister's own claim that reviews will be very few and turns it against the bill's design: if reviews are rare and ratepayer-funded anyway, the director-general's gatekeeping step is redundant. She also pins down which earlier questions went unanswered. This is precisely the deciding test — had Jones argued something else about council reviews, this speech would have had to be different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "when the review is undertaken—and they will be very, very few in number, because this is not really a troublesome industry"

acuity.statement: I would just like to bring to the Minister’s attention that the question I asked last night was around his wont, desire, to have an aquaculture bill. He didn’t answer my question last night when I brought up the fact that the process was quite rushed, that people didn’t have much time to submit, and I asked the question as to why he didn’t take the time, allow a longer period of consultation in order for him, perhaps, to be able to develop the aquaculture bill that he so desires to do.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by Shane Jones immediately precedes it in the same committee debate. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate (consultation period, the aquaculture bill the Minister wants) and it does address the Minister, but it engages no part of the argument he had just made about regional councils and the director-general. It instead resumes a question left over from the previous sitting, and would read identically whatever Jones had said in the turn before. That places it in the prepared-material-on-topic band with a gesture towards the Minister, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shane Jones spoke about the director-general's status and the Otago Regional Council's 'wilful disregard' of the Government's water standards, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister has said that he believes that these costs should be borne by the consent authority. That means that those are costs that are to be borne by the ratepayers. It is the Minister and the Government, effectively, lumping on to ratepayers of this country an additional cost, once the director-general has determined that a review can take place.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it. The contribution is detailed and on the clause under debate, and it does characterise a position the Minister has previously taken on who bears review costs, which earns the top of the low band. But nothing in the immediately preceding turns is engaged: Luxton's consultation and Treaty argument is passed over entirely, as is Jones's regional-council argument, and the speech would be unchanged had either said something different. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the amendment's reasoning and its precision are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the preceding turns (Shane Jones on the Otago Regional Council, Jo Luxton on the consultation period and Te Tiriti obligations) are not taken up; the Minister's cost position being quoted here was stated in an earlier sitting, not in the turn before.

acuity.statement: From my perspective, the policy work behind this bill, those fears are groundless. The reason why the ratepayers and the council will meet the costs of an intervention in the legal, rightful business of a marine farmer is because they will know that it has to be of a particularly egregious nature because they’re going to pay for it themselves. In the event that they decide that the condition problem is of such a magnitude that they need to spend the ratepayers’ money, they will also consult and seek the authority of the director-general as a further discipline.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific objection just made — that the bill loads review costs onto ratepayers — and answers it on its own terms, arguing that council liability for the cost is itself the discipline that keeps interventions rare. That is genuine engagement with the strand Utikere pressed. It falls short of the top of the scale because it answers the ratepayer-cost principle rather than Amendment Paper 57 as put: neither the fair-and-reasonable test nor the 50 percent cap is addressed. Whether the 'discipline' inference actually follows is Rigor's question, not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "It is the Minister and the Government, effectively, lumping on to ratepayers of this country an additional cost, once the director-general has determined that a review can take place."

acuity.statement: This bill provides an opportunity for a marine farmer to enjoy the permit they already have extended till 2050, at the latest; or if they’re involved in a process to adjust elements that comprise their entitlements within that defined area, they can’t have two permits at once. Our side of the House doesn’t believe in double-dipping. The surrendering option enables the applicant to come back and enjoy the 20 to 25 years security, and it simply provides clarity that you can’t be involved with two permits at the same time.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the third of the three questions Utikere had just itemised, and supplies the mechanism asked for: surrender exists so an applicant cannot hold two permits over the same area while moving to the longer-duration entitlement. The speech would plainly be different had the preceding turn not raised the surrendered-permit question. Short of 1.0 because it explains the purpose of surrender without resolving the precise point put — whether the permit lies dormant and can be reactivated, or is simply cancelled.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "In the circumstance where activities operating under a replacement permit, if that permit was surrendered because the applicant had decided to take up the opportunity to have the permit extended, what is the status of a surrendered permit?"

acuity.statement: It is not correct to say this is exclusively an area where local representatives have the ultimate authority. They are guided by guardrails created by central government.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Abel's central contention — that allocation decisions in the coastal commons belong to regional councils and local people, and that central government dictates override them — and rebuts its premise by asserting that allocation is already a joint central/local matter governed by the NZ Coastal Policy Statement. The reply would have to be different had Abel argued something else; it is aimed at the specific claim, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Who is it to make the determination about how to allocate these resources if not the local people, the regional councils, those representatives of the locals?"

acuity.statement: On the question of how do you manage vexed areas such as Taranaki, I’m the first to admit that there has been a historic level of friction between quota owners and applicants wanting to extract vanadium, titanium, and a host of other very valuable rare earth minerals from the bed of the sea.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up Abel's Taranaki example and concedes the substance of one strand of it — the long-running conflict between fishing quota holders and seabed mining applicants. It engages the specific case put to him rather than the topic in general, but stops short of answering the actual question of how and by whom the competing interests are to be balanced, moving instead to a call for a national conversation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "It has been fiercely opposed—as the Minister, I’m sure, would know—by the fishing industry for 10 years because it is seen by the commercial wild fisheries industry to be a direct threat to their industry."

acuity.statement: Is this not just—for a Minister who talks about getting everything out of Wellington and out into the regions—sucking back decision making to Wellington?
acuity.explanation: Turns the Minister's own just-stated position — that central government legitimately sets the guardrails and that a further one will be passed shortly — back on him as a charge of centralisation, so the line depends on what he had just said. Partial rather than full engagement, because the bulk of her turn is a separately prepared line of questioning on the notification list in new section 165ZFHL rather than a reply to his argument about central/local allocation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "An additional guardrail with neon lights will be passed by this Parliament very shortly"

acuity.statement: My understanding was that Tai Tokerau iwi did not actually support this bill, particularly Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki, who actually had a lot of the marine farms, also did not support the extension.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan is correcting a factual claim about Tai Tokerau iwi support, which would be strong engagement — but the Minister's remark he is correcting falls before this window, so it cannot be pointed at in the text supplied. The one substantive preceding turn here is Utikere's argument for retaining the five- and 10-year extension options, and Xu-Nan does not take any part of that up; he moves to his own prepared line of questioning on voluntary shortening of permits. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate, so the top of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable in the window: Tangi Utikere argued "the five- and 10-year options which have been advanced by the community" should stay in play and this statement does not take it up; the Minister's Tai Tokerau claim that it does engage precedes the supplied text.

acuity.statement: Of course, this relates to all of the bill—the entirety of the bill—because what is happening, as my colleague Tangi Utikere described, is that this insertion is Part 1 of the bill is being acknowledged here in section 123A of the Resource Management Act (RMA).
acuity.explanation: Brooking takes up Utikere's specific structural point — that Part 2 is short but reaches the whole of Subpart 1A because it is section 123A that carries the duration — accepts it, and then does something with it: she extends it from occupation permits to discharge permits and derives the 18-year unreviewable window from it. Her speech would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument about Part 2's reach. It is not a full 1.0 because the bulk of what follows is her own prepared material on discharge and review costs rather than further engagement with what Utikere put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "the implications actually are quite significant because they relate to the entire part of Subpart 1A of this bill"

acuity.statement: Now, where there is an egregious case at some ill-defined point in the future, reflective of what the honourable Green member and the former Minister of oceans have referred to through fish farming, and if it did represent a biological threat, there are other pieces of legislation that can be invoked.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up one strand of Brooking's question — her press on what the "other legislation might apply" answer actually refers to in the fish-farming case — and engages it by restating that other statutes can be invoked where a biological threat arises. That is partial: he answers the topic rather than the specific claim, leaving untouched the 18-year review gap she built her question around, what advice he sought, and Xu-Nan's question about voluntary shortening. He then returns to prepared ground about busybodies in regional government and jobs. Vagueness about which legislation is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one; the engagement itself is real but half-made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "The Minister replied, “Well, other legislation might apply.” I’m wondering, then, what other legislation he’s referring to"

acuity.statement: Extraordinary, we’re now talking about the rights of initiation. Obviously, the authority to undertake a review of conditions depends on the concurrent authority being exercised by the director-general. Nothing is legal until such time both parties have agreed that there is a case for—within the two-year period—such an exercise to take place.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Utikere's 'initiating' question directly and offers a partial answer — that nothing takes effect until the consent authority and the director-general have both agreed — which bears on when the clock starts. But it leaves the other strands (guidance for the director-general, the missing decision deadline, which of the candidate dates counts) untouched and moves on to prepared material, so it is an engagement with one strand rather than the argument as a whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "There is a clear change in the wording from “beginning” to “initiating”, and my question is: what does “initiating” mean in the context of a process for determining whether a review is successful?"

acuity.statement: Well, it’s actually Subpart 1A. We are in Part 2, as I’ve heard from members opposite, but this relates specifically to Subpart 1A, which is referencing both the costs and the ability for decisions to be made about coastal permits, and others.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick's intervening challenge asserted the committee was on Part 2, implying his administrative-charges argument was out of scope. He takes that specific claim up, concedes the part, and corrects it by identifying Subpart 1A and saying what it covers (costs and coastal permit decisions) to show relevance. The reply would not exist if she had said something else — squarely engaged, not a mere reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dana Kirkpatrick: "We’re in Part 2, aren’t we?"

acuity.statement: We were waiting, hoping that the Minister may have something else worthy to say—yeah. I would like to make a couple of suggestions to the Minister around potential title names that maybe the Minister would like to consider.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one narrow strand of Utikere's immediately preceding turn — the complaint that the Minister has still not answered — and then moves straight into his own prepared material (title re-naming, select committee submission numbers, iwi opposition), none of which engages Utikere's actual argument about administrative charges and the 50 percent cost-recovery cap on Amendment Paper 58. A gesture at the preceding turn rather than engagement with its content, so it sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "I’m still to hear from the Minister about his view."

acuity.statement: I have been in the Chamber for most of this bill, this committee stage of this bill, and have been listening closely to the Minister. I also have some suggestions for the title, and it’s the title clause that I’d like to talk on.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes up the device Xu-Nan had just introduced — proposing alternative titles for the bill — and then develops one of his strands with added substance of her own (that councils and ratepayers bear the review cost, and that reviews are confined to the first two years of a twenty-year permit). She engages the topic and the form of the preceding turn rather than any particular claim in it, and the bulk of the speech is her own prepared list, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I would like to make a couple of suggestions to the Minister around potential title names"

acuity.statement: The name of this bill reflects the deep commitment towards giving certainty and confidence to this sector of our economy. Look, I don’t think it uplifts the mana of this House or purpose of this bill by all sorts of extreme suggestions from the other side.
acuity.explanation: He replies to exactly the thing Brooking had just proposed — that the bill is a disgrace and should be renamed — by defending the existing title and rejecting the alternatives as extreme and fanciful. So the turn is aimed at the preceding speech and would read differently had she not made those suggestions. But he engages none of the reasoning behind them: nothing on the ratepayer-funded reviews, the two-year review window leaving eighteen years, or the discharge conditions. Engagement with the demand, not with the argument for it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "This bill is a disgrace and should be renamed."

acuity.statement: I remind the committee that we have already addressed Part 1. We have already addressed these relatively insignificant, largely marginal details reflected in the member’s amendment.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the amendment that was just moved and gives a reason for not engaging it — that the issue was disposed of in Part 1 — and later names the Green member's point directly. So it is aimed at the preceding turn, but it answers the amendment's existence rather than its cost-recovery reasoning, and leaves Utikere's question about the point of engagement untouched. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the consent authority is entitled to recover the cost of review undertaken under the subpart"

acuity.statement: I am interested in what the Minister, the Hon Shane Jones, was just saying there about the application of new subsection (5) to section 123A of the Resource Management Act being only to do with the 35-year relationship. My understanding was that this inserts the whole of subpart 1A. If he’s saying it’s limited to the timing of only some of the extensions that may or may not apply, it would be useful for clarification on that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific characterisation of what Part 2 reaches, states a contrary reading of the same provision, and asks him to resolve the discrepancy. The speech could not have been delivered if the preceding turn had said something else; it is built entirely on the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "Part 2 is explicitly covering those small number of rights holders, if I can use that term figuratively, that may go beyond a point where their entitlement stretches beyond 35 years."

acuity.statement: I appreciate the advice of the Minister that I’ve been speaking to the wrong section. I’d better polish up that law degree that I didn’t do.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's correction about where the amendment belongs and then re-puts it against the right clause, so the turn is shaped by what Jones said. It concedes the placement point and the sentiment of Brooking's preceding turn rather than engaging the substance of either argument, which keeps it around the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "We have already addressed these relatively insignificant, largely marginal details reflected in the member’s amendment."

acuity.statement: All this talk about administrative charges—sadly, that was dealt with last night. If a council officer is possessed of information requiring him or her to intervene in the legal operations of an enterprise—and these people love their enterprises; they love the environment; they’re not quietly plotting and scheming, at 11 o’clock at night, that they’re going to go tomorrow and release toxic material into the environment.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of both preceding turns — administrative charges and the risk of an unchecked discharge — and offers a counter to the discharge scenario, so there is something pointable here. But the charges point is deflected as already dealt with rather than answered, and Brooking's question about the remaining 18 years is not taken up, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: “If there is a discharge that is dangerous to the environment, the regional councils can’t do anything about it, and that is fine because somebody is making money.”

acuity.statement: Given the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries has provided a response, I want to pick up on what the Minister has just said, because he has said that there are people who are losing their jobs. That is correct—that is absolutely correct. It is the one thing, actually, that I agree with that has come from this Minister through this committee stage, is that people are losing their jobs.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the specific premise the Minister had just advanced, concedes it explicitly, and then contests the causal account built on it. The turn is directly derived from the content of the preceding speech and would read differently had Jones argued otherwise; it falls just short of 1.0 only because the counter-argument is cut off mid-development.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "Think about the New Zealanders today who have lost their jobs and who may also lose their jobs in this sector, unless we give greater certainty and greater confidence to this area of natural resource development."

acuity.statement: If that is not accepted—and I’m hoping the Minister will appreciate it—I also would like to support Tangi Utikere’s proposed titles for it: “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms”—in clause 1—“Despite Potential Degradation of the Environment)”. An obvious title, and an excellent one. I’d also like to support his other proposed amendment: “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms to Kick the Can down the Road)”. I thought that my colleague the Hon Rachel Brooking’s suggestions were similarly excellent.
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn follows Utikere's substantive contribution and picks up one specific strand of it — the two amended titles Utikere had just moved — naming and quoting both and endorsing them, so the speech would have had to change had Utikere proposed something else. But the engagement stops at endorsement: Abel does nothing with Utikere's reasoning, and ignores entirely the substantive question Utikere put on clause 2 (why commencement the day after Royal assent rather than six or 12 months later). The bulk of the turn is his own prepared critique of the bill and his own proposed title. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-range.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "The other was the “(Extended Duration of Coastal Permits for Marine Farms to Kick the Can Down the Road)”, because this has become symptomatic of this particular Government in terms of their approach to, basically, anything and everything these days."

acuity.statement: As the Minister has also touched on, the fact that the Minister and Cabinet made an explicit decision to remove Te Tiriti provisions and not only reference to Treaty but the principles and the other bullet points, essentially, that we will go through one at a time, from what has now come before this committee, we think is such a shame, is so atrocious. It completely guts and, quite frankly, ruins large swathes of the intentionality of this bill, and it’s something that we intend to spend a considerable amount of time on, working our way through, because the implications are so profound.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific point Mitchell raised in the immediately preceding turn, corrects his framing of it (Cabinet's explicit decision rather than a select committee removal), and draws out the consequence he denied — that the removal changes the lens on the rest of the bill. The speech would have to change if Mitchell had not raised the Treaty provisions. Short of 1.0 because it then returns to signalling prepared lines of questioning rather than engaging his reasoning further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to touch on the Treaty of Waitangi provisions that were removed at the select committee stage" — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: She’s saying that because the Treaty provisions aren’t in the bill, that means that Corrections are not able to actually deliver the services that we all expect of our corrections service, especially in relation to Māori. I agree with you, they’re overrepresented in in our corrections system. That is not Corrections’ problem. They just have to deal with what is presented to them.
acuity.explanation: Restates McLellan's actual argument about the effect of removing the Te Tiriti clause and then disputes it directly, conceding the overrepresentation point while rejecting the inference that Corrections cannot deliver for Māori without the provisions. The reply is entirely shaped by what she just said. Whether the premise about the Corrections Act's history is sound is a Rigor/Veracity question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It completely guts and, quite frankly, ruins large swathes of the intentionality of this bill" — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I just want to correct one thing, and she said in her opening comments that there was nothing Corrections could do—it wasn’t their issue—around the fact that Māori were overrepresented in our corrections system. That’s not what I meant. What I meant was Corrections have got no control over who is coming into the system.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise charge Paul levelled at his earlier answer, names what she attributed to him, and corrects the misstatement by narrowing the claim (no control over intake, rather than no responsibility). This passage could not exist had Paul not made that specific accusation, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "In your answer just then, Minister, you said that that was not the Department of Corrections’ problem—the overrepresentation of Māori—but it absolutely is."

acuity.statement: We know that we’re grappling as a country with Māori overrepresentation in our criminal justice system—I acknowledge that—but to say that our police and corrections officers and staff are racist: no, I completely reject that.
acuity.explanation: Concedes one strand of Paul's argument (the overrepresentation she documented) and disputes the other (institutional racism) explicitly — the accept-part/dispute-the-rest pattern. Disagreement here is evidence of having listened; the quality of the counter-reasoning and its politeness belong to other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "We know that there is racism baked in throughout our justice system because researchers have made that clear."

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge too that she has put forward an Amendment Paper. I can’t support the Amendment Paper because it would be going against a decision that had already been taken by Cabinet.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a direct answer to the specific question put in the preceding turn, with a stated reason. Slightly short of 1.0 because it answers the ask without engaging the Treaty-provisions argument Paul built to support it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Can the Minister talk about whether he might consider supporting my Amendment Paper 81 to restore the Treaty provisions in the Corrections Amendment Bill"

acuity.statement: Yes. I have lots of reports to read, and, yes, I have read the report. The member Willow-Jean Prime is right that they have made recommendations around improvements.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question Prime put and repeated four times, supplies the direct answer, and concedes the specific point about the Tribunal's recommendations. The reply could not have been given after a different preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has the Minister read the report?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: But I completely reject the premise that because the Treaty provisions have been removed at this stage with this bill—by the way, the Treaty provisions have never been a part of the Corrections Act, and it hasn’t stopped those very deep relationships being formed with Māori, hapū, and iwi.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Prime's central claim — that statutory Treaty provisions are necessary to produce the relationships and outcomes — and disputes its premise directly, arguing the provisions were never in the Act yet the relationships formed anyway. Squarely engaged with the argument just made, whatever the merits of the inference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it needed legislative provisions to ensure that we are on a track to reducing those disparities" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: The Ombudsman said, more in sadness than in anger, that he had seen no real change in the corrections system despite repeated reports where the Department of Corrections said, “Yes, we agree with all of your criticisms about prisoner safety and rehabilitation and lack of resources” but ultimately did nothing.
acuity.explanation: Engages Mitchell's claim that Corrections is committed to ongoing improvement by offering the Ombudsman's contrary finding that agreement in principle has produced no change. It takes up one strand of the Minister's answer before moving on to prepared line-by-line questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "every agency should be focused on ongoing improvements, and that’s exactly what Corrections are doing" — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: Now, Willow-Jean Prime has just touched on some Treaty issues, but this is not actually a Treaty issue at all. This is just recognising that we have a diverse range of people that come into prison, who, if they are going to be treated, firstly, humanely and, secondly, put back into the community in a better place than they arrived, need to understand their own cultural context, whether that be a Sikh, a person from China, a Māori person, a person from the Pacific—whatever.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly distinguishes his point from the Treaty framing of the preceding exchange, so the passage would read differently had Prime not raised it — but the distinction is a preface to prepared material on clause definitions rather than an engagement with her argument's substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the role that Corrections do in fact have as part of the justice system to address the overrepresentation of Māori" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: In relation to my comment around being colour-blind, if the member had been listening she would have heard that both the Police and Corrections were accused of being racist. I was very clear that I reject that accusation and that both services, in my view, are colour-blind.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact claim Andersen pressed him on — his 'colour-blind' remark — and does something with it: supplies the context she omitted (the accusation of racism he was rejecting) and restates his meaning against her reading. The reply would have been different had she challenged something else, and he also goes on to address her second question about the Treaty provisions. Marked down from 1.0 because he engages her characterisation of the remark rather than her substantive evidence from the regulatory impact statement about Hōkai Rangi and whakapapa.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m really puzzled by the Minister’s comments that the Department of Corrections should be colour-blind." — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I’d like to support those who have echoed frustration in the Chamber in relation to the removal of the Treaty clauses in this legislation. Just because it hasn’t been done in the past, it doesn’t mean it shouldn’t be done now—now and for the future, because by locking in Te Tiriti o Waitangi into the legislation, it is for strategic purposes, it is for iwi Māori to know that there are protections in there, and it’s above and beyond obligations to a coalition agreement because the original agreement was Te Tiriti o Waitangi, signed in 1840; kia ora tātou.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the justification Mitchell had just given: he rested the removal on a coalition agreement, and she argues an obligation to Te Tiriti predates and outranks any coalition agreement. She then puts fresh questions to him (what hui, what official advice) on the same specific decision, so the speech is shaped by what preceded it; it is not a 1.0 because much of the turn moves into prepared reflections on Waikeria that engage nothing he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "yes, it was a Cabinet decision based on a coalition agreement" — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: I’m assuming that, from the Minister’s perspective, the treatment of each of these three groups would be quite distinct, but I do want to know, in terms of accused prisoners and prisoners who are on remand awaiting sentence, what is the duration we’re looking at here? One of the things the Minister addressed is the length of time that we have with prisoners on remand, and that’s one of the issues of why we have such a high remand population in Aotearoa, but what are some of the thinkings around splitting those two off specifically?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own distinction between remand accused and remand convicted, and his remarks on time spent on remand, and presses them against the specific drafting of clause 4(4) — asking for the rationale for the three-way split and the durations involved. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged if Mitchell had said something different; it is built on what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "Remand accused have to have different types of non - offence-based programmes delivered to them because, in the eyes of the law, they’re innocent until proven guilty"

acuity.statement: Someone who is remand convicted has been convicted—so they have been to court, they have been convicted, and they’re awaiting to be sentenced to find out what their sentence is going to be. Remand accused have not actually been to court and had their case heard. That is the fundamental difference, and that is why, if you were to deliver offence-based programmes to someone that was remand accused, even though they may actually ask for it, that could be seen as an admission of guilt, because they’re engaging on a programme like that. Fundamentally, that’s why they’ve been separated out.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — the rationale for separating the two remand categories in the definition — by giving the admission-of-guilt reasoning behind the split. Not 1.0 because the other strands of the same question (the duration of each category, and how NZBORA section 25(c) bears on the two new categories) are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what are some of the thinkings around splitting those two off specifically?"

acuity.statement: I have been listening to what the Minister’s been saying in relation to this clause, and I’ve heard his assurances that rehabilitation work will continue and that the work that corrections officers are doing is good work. I don’t doubt, on an individual basis, that they do do the best job that they can, but also we’ve heard comments from members around the Chamber, and I think that we must acknowledge that the statistics in relation to Māori are not where they should be and that something needs to be done.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes up the Minister's assurance that the rehabilitation and cultural work will carry on, concedes the part about individual corrections officers, and then disputes the inference drawn from it — that nothing further is needed. Accepting part and contesting the rest is engagement with the argument, not a pivot away from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "I do agree with you that there’s also opportunity in corrections to expand cultural-based programmes, not just te reo but to other cultures as well."

acuity.statement: The one thing I’d say, and I’d come back to the point that I’ve been making, is that we have never had Treaty provisions inside the Corrections Act ever, and yet the system has been working very well. It’ll continue to work well. All of the obligations on the chief executive and on Corrections in terms of continuing to work on strengthening that relationship and recognising the importance of that relationship with iwi and hapū will continue, and is continuing today as programmes are rolled out and delivered.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the question — whether the listed functions will still happen — by asserting that all the chief executive's obligations continue. But the question was specifically which of the enumerated paragraphs in clause 6A will cease, and that itemisation is not supplied; he returns instead to the general point he says he has been making throughout.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "in that section, specifically I’d like to know from the Minister what won’t be happening"

acuity.statement: Well, quite simply, it was taken out because—the member alluded to it in her opening comment—we are a coalition Government and that was a Cabinet decision.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question asked — why remove the clause — squarely and without deflection, and even names the point in her own speech it connects to. The reply is thin on substance, but that is a matter for specificity; as responsiveness it is aimed directly at the question put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "So why take it out?"

acuity.statement: Coming to the Hon Willie Jackson, yes, I was definitely around in 2019; yes, I definitely support the initiative that Kelvin put in place and acknowledge him for that; yes, we’re working with iwi and hapū, as he knows; and, yes, we remain committed to making sure that we continue to develop and deliver the programmes that we think will do the best and move us towards, when people rejoin society, giving them the best possible chance of reintegration and making good decisions in their lives.
acuity.explanation: Mitchell takes Jackson's specific questions in the order they were asked and answers each one: whether he was in the House in 2019, whether he supported Kelvin Davis's Hōkai Rangi initiative, and whether the Government remains committed to its principles and to working with Māori groups. The turn would be materially different had Jackson asked something else, which is the test. It falls short of 1.0 only because the commitment answer restates the aim in general terms rather than engaging Jackson's specific point about the 52 percent to 16 percent target not having been met.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "was he here in 2019 when the Hōkai Rangi strategy was launched in Parliament here by Kelvin Davis?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: This can’t be dismissed by saying they do a great job because, I’m sorry, Minister, they don’t.
acuity.explanation: Webb directly contradicts the claim Mitchell had just made about Corrections staff, and supplies a reason for doing so (the Ombudsman's repeated reports and evidence to the Justice Committee). That is engagement with the content of the preceding turn, not merely a reference to it. But it is one strand only: the bulk of Webb's contribution is prepared material on clause 6 which he himself introduces as a point "that hasn’t been touched on", so the turn is largely indifferent to what Mitchell said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m extremely proud of what they’re doing." — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: I want to thank the Minister for talking earlier about the importance of having the non - offence-based programmes for people on remand who are still awaiting trial. One of the things we know within the prison system, within the correction system, is the disproportionate number of people who are neurodivergent or who have dyslexia.
acuity.explanation: Follows Mitchell's turn on rehabilitation delivery and flexibility, and takes up the delivery-of-programmes topic by asking whether the non-offence-based programmes accommodate neurodivergent prisoners. It engages the subject matter rather than Mitchell's specific argument (that codifying the requirement would risk putting Corrections in breach of the law), and then moves to prepared questions on clause 5 and Schedule 1AA. Topic-level engagement, not claim-level.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Mitchell: "The whole focus of this legislation is to make it safer for both corrections officers and prisoners, and for us to be able to deliver more rehabilitation to those that need it"

acuity.statement: I think you raise a very good point around neurodivergence and people with dyslexia and whether those needs can be met. I can’t give you a very definitive answer on that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact question just put to him, accepts the point as valid and concedes he cannot answer it definitively before offering what he can. The reply would have to be different had Xu-Nan asked something else. The answer is thin on substance, but that is a specificity matter; the engagement with what was said is direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "whether neurodivergence and also dyslexia have been considered when we’re talking about non-offence programmes"

acuity.statement: In terms of transitional planning, I think that you’ve highlighted one of the issues that the previous speaker was talking about, and that’s how dynamic the environment is, and a lot of that stuff is outside Corrections’ control, in terms of someone that’s going up for parole may get parole or may not get parole, how long are they going to be in the system for, and whether they are going to be there long enough to be able to complete a programme.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "So I stand by my full comment, which is accurate." (defending "we’ve replicated the same law that Labour adopted")
