Bennett's opening gestures at that theme — professionalism, and the need for "the right sets of accountabilities and responsibilities" — and he notes the bill is non-controversial as others around the House have said. But it is a glance, not an engagement: he does not address the stand-down provision, the registration requirement, or Mooney's professionalisation argument, and the bulk of the speech is a prepared list of what social workers are. Nothing here would change if Mooney had argued differently about the same bill, so it belongs in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 for the gesture at the debate. Note this is scored only on engagement: the warmth of the speech and its on-policy subject matter are other attributes' business.

acuity.responding_to: "a professionalised workforce is in the best interest of everyone" — Joseph Mooney. Bennett opens on legislation that "supports the work and professionalism of social workers" and on accountabilities, but takes up no part of Mooney's specific argument about registration or stand-down.

This is engagement with the content of the preceding argument, not a mere reference to the speaker, and the sentence could not have been delivered had Smith made a different opening claim.

acuity.responding_to: "we were left with the economy in a perilous state, like the Kaitaki drifting towards the rocks" — Stuart Smith

However, it’s been almost three months since the Budget and we are having daily examples throughout the community of front-line service cuts that have been done.

Short of 1.0 because she engages the general back-office/front-line framing rather than any specific figure Willis gave, and then moves into prepared material of her own.

acuity.statement: What we’ve seen is the work from the McGuinness Institute that looks very specifically at some of those accounting standards, particularly, if we want to be specific, PBE IPSAS 19, which is an accounting standard that says that we need to take into account the likelihood an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation and the extent to which a reliable estimate can be made. This is quite different to the way Treasury has previously addressed this question of the liability and how it should be booked.
acuity.explanation: Willis had just said she was satisfied Treasury had handled the climate-change liability properly and that it should not sit on the books. Woods takes up that exact claim and contests its basis, naming the accounting standard (PBE IPSAS 19) and the new body of work that she says cuts against Treasury's prior treatment, then asks whether the Minister's thinking has evolved for Budget 2025. The speech would have had to be different had Willis given a different answer on the liability, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 only because part of the contribution is prepared material on Budget 2024 climate cuts rather than engagement with what was said.

acuity.responding_to: "I am satisfied that Treasury has considered this properly and well and that this is not something that should properly sit as a liability on the books" — Nicola Willis

This is not something that can be wholly blamed on the previous Government.
acuity.explanation: Bishop opens by taking up Willis's explicit invitation to speak to the infrastructure pipeline and then does something with the preceding argument rather than merely referencing it: he concedes the diagnosis of a productivity problem and then departs from Willis's framing, which had attributed the productivity base to "the legacy we inherit from the previous Government", by saying the problem cannot be wholly blamed on the last Government and goes back many years. The speech would be materially different had Willis not made that invitation and that attribution; it is not quite 1.0 because much of what follows (the OECD rankings, the 30-year plan, housing) is prepared material rather than engagement with a specific claim of hers.

I wonder what responsibility the Minister takes for that huge impact on our economy.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by Willis argued that the ETS, not subsidies to multinationals, is the Government's key emissions mechanism, and that the $24 billion figure is an upper range. Russell engages none of that: she turns to a remembered comment from an earlier select committee hearing and to construction-sector employment. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Willis had just said, though it is at least within the same Estimates scrutiny of the Minister of Finance, so it is not a 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis spoke about the emissions trading scheme, the emissions reduction budgets and the climate dividend, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The member has asked me whether I will take responsibility for an economy which has been ravaged for six years by the economic mismanagement of the Government she was a part of. No, I won’t take responsibility for the impact of a Government that poured fuel on the inflation fire such that interest rates rose higher than they should have otherwise.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up the specific question Russell put — what responsibility she accepts for the economic impact of her cuts — names it, answers it squarely in the negative, and then reattributes the causation to the previous Government's inflation record. She also itemises Russell's other two strands (the Wellington economy, hard hats in construction) and answers each. The reply would have to be different had Russell made a different argument, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only: whether the counter-attribution of blame is sound or true is a matter for Rigor and Veracity, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder what responsibility the Minister takes for that huge impact on our economy" — Deborah Russell

Which is it: do you want to take credit for it coming down but not responsibility for the economic activity in the outlook, or is it that you don’t want to take credit for the economic activity, which has caused the OCR to come down?
acuity.explanation: Edmonds takes the exact division Willis had just drawn — refusing responsibility for the economy but claiming credit for the interest rate cut — and presses it as an inconsistency, arguing the Reserve Bank cut early precisely because activity indicators were falling. That is engaging the content of the immediately preceding claim and drawing out its consequence, not merely referencing the speaker. Short of 1.0 because the turn then moves into prepared material on productivity, Callaghan Innovation and credit ratings that is indifferent to what Willis said.

acuity.responding_to: "What I will take responsibility for is the decisions that we have taken since coming to Government, which have seen inflation come down, the first reduction in interest rates in four years" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I think the comments that Mr Foster has already made well are worth repeating, which is that this is about those community organisations that operate class 3 gambling. This is not about any gambling that occurs offshore; it’s onshore here in New Zealand. It’s not gambling that I would say has the benefit of a profit-making exercise or for those who are interested in gambling for gambling’s sake; this is actually the type of activity that occurs in order to help fund-raise for some of our critical community organisations. I think that point has been well made by Mr Foster and I want to reiterate it. Having said that, we do know that when we take things online, it can become easier for people to access and then that can lead to harm.
acuity.explanation: Names and restates Foster's onshore/offshore distinction, which on its own would be mere repetition, but then does something with it: accepts the point and qualifies it with the access-and-harm consequence of moving fund-raising online, tying that to what the select committee should test. Partial rather than full engagement because most of the paragraph reiterates rather than advances his argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is not international organisations that are just wanting to make a profit" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: I just want to respond to my colleague on the other side of the House Tom Rutherford. We’ve heard from the Hon Barbara Edmonds. She gave a very impactful statement, and in her experience, she has been fund-raising for a very long time.
acuity.explanation: She names Rutherford and gestures at his attack on Barbara Edmonds, but engages no part of its content — the claim was that Edmonds as Minister chose the ballot over leading the work, and the reply answers with Edmonds's fund-raising experience and the quality of her speech, then returns to prepared material on the bill ("I come back to the bill"). A gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "She said when she was the Minister of Internal Affairs that it would be quicker for change to be made on this specific legislation through the member’s bill ballot biscuit tin than for her to actually lead the work herself as the Minister" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: I stand here in this House to support this bill. I would like to use this opportunity to acknowledge the 27,800 registered charities in New Zealand and all their volunteers for the amazing job they do.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. The speech is about charities' fund-raising difficulties and the Government's responsiveness; it would be word-for-word identical whatever the previous speaker had argued, and in particular never touches the gambling-harm and consultation case Sosene had just made. Not zero only because it is squarely about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene argued that the select committee must act as a filter so the public and harm-minimisation organisations can submit on making online lottery gambling permanent, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Although I have my own personal views about gambling, this is a situation where absolutely I support it because it’s going to be helping community organisations and charities. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: A short prepared endorsement that engages no preceding contribution. Her own reservation about gambling is the nearest opening to the harm argument Sosene made, yet nothing is done with it. The speech is indifferent to what it follows, though it is on the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene and Carlos Cheung had spoken on gambling-harm minimisation and charity fund-raising respectively, and this statement takes up neither argument

acuity.statement: I don’t agree with the Minister’s view that because the bill is short and only includes a couple of clauses, it’s not a big matter—that’s not the case. We can change laws where you’ve only added one clause to a piece of legislation and you can make an enormous change to a law, and we know that as parliamentarians. Even just a word inside a clause can make an enormous difference to any piece of law that we may consider from time to time.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's stated justification for the four-week report-back — brevity and simplicity — and rebuts its reasoning directly, arguing that a single clause or even a single word can change a law enormously. Had van Velden justified the date on some other ground, this passage would have had to be different, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This reflects the fact that the bill is very short—just four clauses—and very simple" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: I also rise on behalf of the Green Party to say that we are very concerned in terms of the truncated time frame that has been suggested by the Minister of Internal Affairs when it comes to the select committee process. I understand that from the Minister’s perspective this is quite a short bill and the fact that, with this particular bill, they may not need the same level of consultation as one would expect.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the same strand Boyack had just opened — the Minister's short-bill rationale for a truncated select committee period — and aligns the Greens with it, but restates the point rather than developing or testing it before moving to his own prepared material on the sitting calendar and school holidays. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "she believes that it can have a short time frame because it’s a short bill in terms of the length of it, but, actually, as I’ve already noted, that is not necessarily an indication of the impact or substance of a bill."

acuity.statement: In fact, there were no reasons given. She stated that the bill is a short bill, but that bears no rational connection whatsoever with the amount of time that it takes to deliberate on it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific contention already live in the debate — that brevity of a bill justifies a shortened report-back — and does something with it, asserting there is no rational connection between length and deliberation time and adding the norm that a fulsome explanation is owed. Not a mere reference: the speech would have to change if the argument before it had been different. Marked down slightly because the two sentences sit awkwardly together (no reasons were given, yet a reason is then quoted and rebutted), but that is an inference flaw, not a failure to engage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "that is not necessarily an indication of the impact or substance of a bill"

acuity.statement: Why is she depriving members of their right to sit in this House and debate on legislation because she wants to rush through a select committee process? That’s a very genuine point that was alluded to by the Green member Lawrence Xu-Nan, that people are elected to this House to represent their constituents in this House—not to sit in select committees and look at legislation rather than being here.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the preceding Green speaker's point about members' availability during the compressed period and carries it somewhere — into an objection to the committee sitting while the House sits. More than a name-check, but it repurposes Xu-Nan's holiday/availability point into a related but distinct objection rather than engaging it as made, so short of a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "For a lot of parents—and some of our MPs are also parents—they may actually have booked holidays for that period."

acuity.statement: I’ll take a short call just to suggest that I oppose the amendment to the motion that I have moved, based on one very important ground, that the member did not listen correctly to my original motion—that it’s my hope to provide community organisations relying on this exemption with confidence that they can continue beyond 31 October this year, which is the reason for wishing for the select committee to report back by 10 October so that we can have the law through this House in time for these charities.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise demand Webb had just made — what the real reason for the shortened report-back is — by supplying the 31 October expiry of the exemption and tying the 10 October date to it. The speech is unintelligible without the turn before it, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "The Minister gave no reasons."

acuity.statement: That’s incorrect. Under the previous Government, there were only a small specific number of class 3 lotteries that were originally allowed to have this exemption. The previous Government then changed it to all class 3 lotteries. The member is incorrect in her statement.
acuity.explanation: Takes Boyack's stated reason for opposing the motion — that a short bill can still make a large substantive change — and disputes it on its merits with the exemption's history, rather than pivoting away. Held below the top because her restatement of Boyack's reason is looser than what Boyack actually said, so part of what is rebutted is a reconstruction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "that is not necessarily an indication of the impact or substance of a bill"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to take an opportunity to take a short call on the amendment put forward by my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, and just respond to the Minister’s comment around the type of change that this is, because I disagree with the Minister. They’re actually taking something that is a temporary practice and making it permanent.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the Minister's immediately preceding characterisation of the bill as a minor extension, and then supplies the COVID rationale and its lapse as the reason permanence is a large change. Sharp disagreement squarely aimed at the claim just made, which is the strongest evidence of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "It simply extends the temporary exemption that we currently have, permanently."

acuity.statement: Now, I don’t know how often this happens, but the Chief Ombudsman himself made a submission and made an oral submission expressing his concern under freedom of expression, under freedom of access to information, on the basis that charter schools, as a publicly funded institute, will not be subjected to the Official Information Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific Ombudsman/OIA point Tinetti had just made and does something further with it, naming the Bill of Rights grounds (freedom of expression and access to information) and reporting that the Chief Ombudsman could not identify another publicly funded body with that exemption. It is a genuine extension of the preceding strand rather than mere repetition, but it sits inside an otherwise prepared run through submission themes, so it is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Ombudsman discussed his concern around the fact that the charter schools were not going to be subject to the Official Information Act." — Jan Tinetti

acuity.statement: Well, I’ve been in this House now, listening to the Opposition, and listening to them, I’m thinking “Well, they really have missed the point, haven’t they?” This is about choice, about giving parents and students choice in their education. That’s what it’s all about, right? This is where they forget that when parents go to look at where they’d like their children to go to school, they look around and at the moment, clearly with some parents, they’re struggling. Some parents are struggling to find the right school. Right?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the preceding Opposition speeches and asserts a counter-frame — that the point is parental choice and that some parents cannot find the right school — which cuts against Xu-Nan's claim that the system is already flexible enough. But it engages no part of the actual argument: no submitter evidence, no school-type list, no response to the lack-of-evidence or process points. Saying opponents "missed the point" and restating prepared material is a reference, not an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our existing education system in Aotearoa is already flexible enough and does not require yet another tier, yet another educational system" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I’d like to point out actually, yes, we received a number of submissions. Well, I notice they’ve ignored the ones that were in support of.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the immediately preceding argument — Xu-Nan's reliance on the weight of opposing submissions — by contesting its selectivity and moving to quote a supportive submitter. It does not take up the 90.3 percent figure itself or dispute how it was calculated, so it answers the topic of the submissions rather than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "90.3 percent of people said no to the repeal of the ECE network management" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: You have to! You have to! OK, well, that’s interesting—yeah, for a few people, maybe. But it’s about choice. It’s about choice.
acuity.explanation: Foster had asked rhetorically whether there is compulsion to attend a charter school; Belich answered that there is where it is the only school in the area. He repeats and concedes the point in part ("yeah, for a few people, maybe") before returning to his prepared line about choice. The concession is a real engagement with the specific counter-example, so this is more than a glance, but he does nothing with it and falls straight back to the slogan the objection was aimed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Yes, there is—if it’s the only school in your area." — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: The State looks after and aims to care for everyone. That’s the big difference here.
acuity.explanation: Court interjects that State monopoly is no better than private monopoly. Willis answers the comparison head-on, supplying the distinction he says makes the two cases different — the State's universal remit versus a private operator's. The reply is brief and asserted rather than argued, but it is squarely aimed at the specific challenge and would have to change if Court had put a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You have the State monopolise it, so what’s worse?" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: It was reassuring to hear from Andy Foster that there could be transparency and they want to see transparency, but that is not what this is doing. This is not where charter schools are heading.
acuity.explanation: Willis picks up the one concession in Foster's speech — his agreement on the need for transparency — accepts it as stated and then disputes that the bill delivers it, tying it to the Chief Ombudsman's "cloaked in secrecy" concern. This is accept-part-dispute-the-rest aimed at a specific thing the previous speaker said, and the passage could not have been written without having heard him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The one thing I do agree with them on is the need to be more transparent." — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: We’ve heard the cherry-picking of evidence, but we know, from the evidence, that there’s no support for this model.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the evidentiary strand McCallum built his speech on and characterises it as cherry-picking, so it is pointed at something that was actually said. But it engages the topic rather than the claim: the Stanford/CREDO finding on learning gains is neither quoted back, qualified nor rebutted, and Willis simply counter-asserts his own reading of the literature before returning to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "A long-running study of charter schools in the United States reached this clear verdict last year" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Well, that’s exactly my point, Mr Court—that is exactly my point. The interests of children and teachers are the same. These children and teachers are the same. There is not a teacher in this country that gets into teaching because they want to be in opposition to students; they get into teaching to help students—for the children.
acuity.explanation: She takes up Court's interjection directly and turns its content against it — the claim that caring about children means not caring about teachers is met with the specific counter that the two interests are identical. The passage could not have been delivered had Court said something else, which is the test. (Whether the inference is sound is Rigor's question, not Acuity's.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "We don’t care about them; we care about the children and their learning."

acuity.statement: Well, here we are on the second reading of a bill that would take money out of our public school system, set up an alternative school system, and for what reason? After sitting through the select committee process and hearing 90 percent of the submissions in opposition to this move, I am still not sure.
acuity.explanation: Butterick's evidence for public appetite was the count of interested schools; she answers with submission numbers pointing the other way, but does not engage his figure or his claim about it — she states her own prepared framing of the bill. On the matter under debate, with only a glance at what preceded it, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Butterick: "the appetite for participation, as evidenced by the number of schools interested, 78 so far and counting"

acuity.statement: I rise to support the second reading of the Education and Training Amendment Bill, because unlike the Opposition, they said it’s not making sense, but it’s making a whole lot of sense to me.
acuity.explanation: She repeats Belich's "doesn't make sense" formula back as an assertion that it does make sense to her, then moves to prepared personal material about parental choice. Belich's actual arguments — the MECA opt-out, the ILO and FTA advice, the select committee evidence — are left entirely untouched, so this is a mere reference rather than engagement; the speech would read identically after any opposition speech on this bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "None of it makes sense at all." — repeated back and reversed, but none of the content engaged

acuity.statement: This is a great piece of legislation. It's a great day for New Zealand. And, particularly, one of the things that I really looked at when I saw how many people had applied to have charter schools in New Zealand—and they had exceeded the demand on offer, and there were 78 applications already to open new charter schools or to convert existing State schools to charter schools.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition speech making three specific arguments (failed experiment, deregistered teachers, $150m diverted from the State sector) and engages none of them. It is prepared praise plus one application figure, delivered as though nothing had preceded it: the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Utikere had argued. It stays in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate; there is no gesture at the preceding turn at all, so 0.1. Not scored lower for brevity or for being government-bench praise — the test is engagement, and the application figure is asserted, not offered against anything Utikere said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued charter schools are 'an absolute failed experiment', that the bill means teachers 'can teach whatever they want' without registration, and that it will 'strip out more than $150 million' from the State sector — and this statement takes up none of those strands.

acuity.statement: Firstly, I just want to address the misrepresentation of members of this party from the other side. To say that we don’t truly believe in this is nothing other than rubbish.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific charge Twyford had just made — that National members privately do not believe in the bill and are supporting it only for political expediency — names it as the misrepresentation she is answering, and denies it directly. The opening would have to be different had Twyford made a different argument, so engagement is squarely demonstrable. It is a flat denial rather than a reasoned rebuttal, which is why it is not a full 1.0, but it is aimed at the content of the claim and not merely at the member.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can see from the members opposite that they don't really believe in this bill, they don't believe in this policy, but they are simply going along with it for political expediency" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: And if we gave charter schools a chance when we brought them in last time, we wouldn’t be sitting here calling them an experiment, again; we would have seen the results, and we would have seen what they have done.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Twyford's argument: his repeated 'experiment' framing and his use of the 2014-2018 period as evidence of no gain. She contests the premise by arguing the earlier model was not left running long enough for results to show, which is a response to the evidential point rather than a pivot away from it. It is partial — she does not touch the Hattie evidence, the Swedish case or the ministry report she is implicitly answering — and it returns quickly to prepared material about choice, so it sits at the mid-band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Ministry of Education's own analysis of the last time charter schools were imposed on New Zealand students and their families, between 2014 and 2018, and the ministry's own report say that there was no quantifiable increase in student achievement attributable to charter schools during that time" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: I’m really hoping that when this particular bill goes to the select committee, we will be able to hear from the public and from the health experts about some of these concerns.
acuity.explanation: Leary's immediately preceding turn was substantive (truncated committee process, the target shifted to 2061, the HTP tax cut, the $46 billion figure). Xu-Nan delivers the Green Party's prepared reading of the bill's clauses and gestures at the committee hearing the public and experts, but takes up none of her specific claims — he neither endorses nor disputes the truncation argument or the nicotine/caffeine point. On topic with a gesture at the debate, so the top of the unengaged band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "We’re deeply disappointed that we were only told about that this afternoon" — her complaint that the truncated select committee period will stop organisations being heard.

acuity.statement: The research shows that nicotine is no more harmful than caffeine, but cigarette tar is very harmful, and that’s why vaping or inhaling water vapour is a much preferable alternative to smoking cigarettes.
acuity.explanation: This takes the exact proposition Leary ridiculed and defends it on the merits, distinguishing nicotine from tar — and it also meets Xu-Nan's framing that vaping is wrongly portrayed as a route away from smoking. The speech would have to change if the earlier speakers had not raised the nicotine comparison. Not a full 1.0 because he does not name or quote them or address their supporting evidence; he restates the claim rather than engaging the researchers Leary cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "from Ministers who have talked about nicotine being as harmful as caffeine" — the proposition she held up as "smoke and mirrors".

acuity.statement: It gives me great pleasure to stand and support this bill. It has, really, some key, strong objectives, and that is to remove vaping products that are popular with young people from the market, noting that part of the appeal of these products to youth is that they’re inexpensive, brightly coloured, and easy to conceal.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one, two of them raising concrete gaps in the bill (non-disposables, retailer numbers, enforcement and prosecutions). Campbell recites the bill's objectives as prepared praise and engages no part of any of it — the words would be identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. It stays just above 0.0 because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued the bill bans disposable vapes but does not limit non-disposable vapes or the number of retailers, and Ingrid Leary argued enforcement has produced only one prosecution in two years; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: For me, I’m looking forward to seeing this bill go through the Health Committee process. I’m looking forward to hearing further suggestions, to ensure we do everything we reasonably can to reduce youth vaping.
acuity.explanation: Leary's central procedural complaint — that the committee stage has been cut short so organisations and researchers will not get to submit — sits directly on the thing Cheung says he looks forward to, and he neither contests nor concedes it. Prepared backbench material on the right subject, with a faint gesture at the committee question, so 0.2 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued the select committee period has been truncated so submitters will not be heard, and this statement looks forward to the committee process without taking that up.

acuity.statement: That smoking and vaping are no good, Mr Simon Court. It’s no good, and simply saying it’s water vapour is absolute garbage.
acuity.explanation: Court interjected to correct the speaker for talking about smoking in a vaping debate. Henare takes the correction up directly, accepts it in part by widening his claim to cover both smoking and vaping, and then presses on with the substance of the vaping point. The sentence would not exist in this form had Court not said what he said, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he absorbs the correction rather than rebutting or developing its reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s not about smoking; it’s about vaping." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: It’s really great to speak in support of this bill—it’s making some four pragmatic and reasonable changes. It’s banning the manufacture, sale, supply, and distribution of disposable vapes; increasing penalties for unlawful sales of regulated products to minors; imposing retail visibility restrictions for vaping products, including early childhood education centres; and proximity restrictions for specialist vape retailers. This is good for the safety of the New Zealand public. This is good for our next generations that are coming through. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: A government backbencher following a substantive opposition critique with wholly prepared material: a recital of the bill's four measures and a commendation. It engages no strand of Henare's "go all the way" argument, does not contest his claim about the Otago research, and does not answer the charge that the bill is too weak. Delete Henare's speech, substitute any other argument on vaping, and this turn is word-for-word identical. It sits at 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued at length that the bill does not go far enough — "why don’t we go harder?" and that the science on vaping harm is unsettled — and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: My colleague the Hon Peeni Henare has talked about experiences that I’m sure all of us have had, if not in our own families, in our own communities. I think about the invitation that some vaping products do actually share towards younger generations, things like candy floss, things like unicorn milk.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding speech — Henare's point about the flavouring of vapes — and extends it with his own examples (candy floss, unicorn milk) and the inference that the flavours are aimed at rangatahi. That is genuine partial engagement and pointable. It is not higher because he engages the flavour anecdote rather than Henare's central claim that the bill should go further, and the rest of the turn returns to prepared material on the select committee process and the bill's clauses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it smells like bubble gum or it smells like blueberry or it smells like peaches" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: We’ve heard that they are deeply disappointed that we are rushing through this anti-vaping legislation. We’ve heard about unicorn milk. We’ve heard that Labour are deeply disappointed that the bill doesn’t go far enough. Well—mind the French—what the hell did they do for six years? What did they do about vaping for six years? With 65 MPs—65 MPs!
acuity.explanation: He has plainly listened: he itemises the three things the two preceding opposition speakers actually said, including the unicorn-milk line, and his speech would have to change if they had argued something else. But what he does with them is to pivot to Labour's record rather than engage the merits of the "doesn't go far enough" claim — he never says why the bill is calibrated as it is. That is the "last person who should talk about" move, lifted above 0.2 only because he brings specific evidence bearing on the complainants' standing rather than mere abuse.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It doesn’t go far enough, in our view." and "it is disappointing to hear the possibility that this will be subjected to a truncated select committee process" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: It’s important that we ensure that these individuals, these school groups, these others are not short-changed as a result of having a shortened select committee process, so I think that making this through to the end of October will actually prevent a fulsome opportunity for folk to consider the many various things that they can engage about.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speech — that a truncated process denies affected communities a proper hearing — and develops it with his own Health Committee experience, but it does not engage any specific claim McAnulty made (the overseas-submissions point, the tax-cut comparison, the bipartisanship argument); most of the turn is prepared material on the same subject. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why not do a full select committee process and take the Hon Peeni Henare at his word and work with us to do it right?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: Well, we want to hear what’s going to work. One important thing is ensuring that the process is right and making sure that, actually, anyone that wants to have an opportunity can do that.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the interjection's content: against "we just want to stop kids vaping" he counters that the point is to hear what will actually work, and against "stop procrastinating" he defends the time as process integrity. The reply would not exist in this form had the interjection said something else. Scored on engagement only — whether the rebuttal reasons well or is precise belongs to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Stop procrastinating. We just want to stop kids vaping." — Suze Redmayne

acuity.statement: You had $153 million for charter schools, whereas the research is very questionable around the effects of charter schools for our young people. I want to know how you can reconcile that allocation with the urgent need for funds for students with existing gaps in their learning.
acuity.explanation: Stanford's opening ran through Budget '24 allocations and her priority areas without mentioning learning support or charter schools. Tinetti takes up one strand of it — the Vote Minister's allocation choices — and sets a specific allocation she says was made against the learning support shortfall, so the question is shaped by what Stanford claimed about her priorities. But it does not engage any particular figure or argument Stanford advanced; the learning support material is her own prepared line of inquiry, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "This Budget is about taking a coherent, considered, and evidence-based approach to education." — Tinetti engages the claim that the allocations were evidence-based and priority-driven, by contrasting charter school funding with learning support.

acuity.statement: I’d like to thank the member the Hon Jan Tinetti for her questions because everybody knows that learning support in education is one of the greatest challenges and, if I’m being perfectly honest, in my six priority areas is the most difficult. I’m sure that the previous Minister would agree that it is one of the most difficult problems to solve in education, which is why it’s one of my priority areas.
acuity.explanation: Stanford concedes the premise of Tinetti's question — that learning support is the sector's hardest problem — which is a real engagement with one strand of what was just put to her, and she addresses the right subject. But she takes up neither of the two specific things asked: the $5.449 million reduction in learning support, and how the charter school allocation is reconciled with it. She moves instead to her own priority framing and work programme, so this engages the topic rather than the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "the overall learning support for this Budget had reduced by $5.449 million from the previous year" and "I want to know how you can reconcile that allocation with the urgent need for funds" — Stanford takes up that learning support is difficult but not the figure or the reconciliation asked for.

acuity.statement: The Minister before was talking about informed decision-making, evidence based, and what is working. In round four of the evaluation for this that was recently received, it states that 63,730 students over four years have benefited from this, it funded 211 projects in 223 schools—and the overall evaluation being very good. That also includes lifting attendance. While I appreciate the Government’s singular—some would argue “tunnel vision”—focus in terms of a priority that advancing student achievement is important, it does not address education holistically. When we are looking at something that is informed, is evidence based, is working, then what indicators does the Minister use for evaluating programme success and the continuation of a programme? That is my first question.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated decision criterion — data-driven, evidence-based, 'what's working' — and applies it directly to a programme she cut, supplying the round-four evaluation figures that meet her own test and then demanding the indicator she used. The speech would have to change entirely if Stanford had justified the Budget on different grounds; it is built out of her preceding argument rather than merely following it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we're making sure that everything we're doing is data-driven and evidence-based" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Look, can I just start by talking about Creatives in Schools. I was initially told that it was funded as a COVID response, but have subsequently been told that it started in 2019 but had a much bigger boost as part of the COVID-19 recovery and response, in conjunction with the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific factual correction just put to her, concedes the 2019 start date she had been briefed otherwise on, and disputes the remainder by distinguishing origin from the COVID-era boost. Accepting part and contesting part is direct engagement with the preceding claim; marked down from 1.0 only because she does not reach the evaluation-indicator question that followed it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this particular programme was not introduced as a COVID measure, it was not funded as part of the COVID measures; it was introduced in 2019" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Is it a good idea to loosen up on credit regulation at a time when financial hardship cases are up 27 percent, sitting at 13,850 for July?
acuity.explanation: Bayly had just concluded from Afterpay and Centrix repayment figures that the provisions are good and will protect consumers. Williams takes up that conclusion and meets it with a counter-statistic on hardship cases, so the question is shaped by the answer it follows — though she engages his protection conclusion rather than his specific 95/92 percent figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is why these are good provisions and they will protect consumers." — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: Is it true that he tried to protect consumers, as he says, by preventing buy now, pay later providers from charging excessive fees if he was only to be overruled by David Seymour?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own consumer-protection claim back at him and presses on its premise — that the fee caps he cites were what he wanted rather than what he secured. It engages his stated rationale, not merely his topic, but stops short of taking on the repayment figures he had just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because the default fee is also capped, and if a payment is missed, then the account is suspended until the overdue payment is made" — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: Is the Minister going to stop blaming the previous Government and show some courage and make a bid for Whakaata Māori next year, or is he going to do nothing?
acuity.explanation: Potaka had just twice attributed the funding reduction to the previous Government. Jackson names that exact move as it is made and pushes past it to what the Minister will himself do next year. The question would have to be different if the preceding answer had not been a deflection to the last Government.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Ehara nā mātou i whakariterite mai i te huarahi pūtea nei, engari nā te Kāwana tawhito i whakarite mai ai kia iti iho te pūtea" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: Mehemea he whā kē ngā pou kia whakatairangatia ai te reo Māori, kua rite rānei te wā me whakawhāiti i aua poupou e whā kia kaua rawa atu te pūtea e moumoutia, otirā me waiho kia whakatōpūngia kātahi ka whiwhi pūtea a Pouaka Whakaata Māori, mā te whakahiato i aua poupou e whā?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure in the answer immediately before — more than $142 million spread across four entities — and draws a consequence from it, asking whether amalgamating those four would stop the waste and free funding for Whakaata Māori. The question is built directly out of the preceding answer's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Kua kitea hoki neke atu i te $142 miriona ka whakapaua ki ngā ohu e whā." — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: Kei a wai te hē mō te iti rawa o te pūtea mō Whakaata Māori? Kei roto i tēnei Tahua Pūtea tonu, 2024 tonu, kei te tari Kāwanatanga, kei a ia raini?
acuity.explanation: The Minister had just said he was pressing the Minister of Finance while again pointing at the previous Government's waste. Lyndon takes up precisely that attribution of blame and forces a choice between Budget 2024, the department and the Minister himself, rather than restating her earlier line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Engari me mōhio hoki ka tika, ka nui te whakamoumou i te pūtea i tērā Kāwana tawhito." — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: Kei te whakaae ia, te Minita, mō ngā whakataunga kerēme WAI11 e kīia nei, “the Māori language is an essential part of Māori culture, and must be regarded as a taonga, a valued possession”? Mehemea e whakaae ana te Minita, he aha te take kei te whakaiti i ngā pūtea mō Whakaata Māori?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — Whakaata Māori funding — but it engages no part of the answer it follows, which argued the Government was following the previous Minister's funding path and that language revival should rest with families and marae. This is a prepared next line of questioning, not a response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka said the Government is following the funding path laid down by the previous Minister and urged whānau, hapori and marae rather than Government to awaken the language, and this question does not take that up.

acuity.statement: What I suggest that we are able to reprioritise is getting artists to come into school to paint murals. I understand that it might be a “nice to have”, but I’ll tell that member that what else keeps kids at school is knowing how to read, knowing how to write, and knowing how to do maths, because when you can’t do those things, you stop turning up.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific mechanism Tinetti advanced — that Creatives in Schools lifted attendance — and contests it on its own terms, reclassifying the programme as a 'nice to have' and offering a rival account of what keeps kids at school (literacy and numeracy). The speech would have to change if Tinetti had argued something else about attendance; it is shaped by her claim rather than indifferent to it. Not a full 1.0 because it does not engage her concrete example (the Porirua school's results) or her question about teaching literacy and numeracy through the arts, instead recasting the arts as mural-painting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "Creatives in Schools was an area that was making a difference to so many kids to get them to school."

acuity.statement: Now, I’ve had a chat to my officials and, look, individual education plan data is not centrally collated, as much as I like to ask for these things. That is not available from the officials. What I can say to the member is that most of the evaluations that have been presented to me that have been done over the last few years under that member’s previous Government have been highly qualitative.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise challenge put to her — that IEP data is freely available and that the 'we don't have the data' line does not wash — by addressing the IEP channel Tinetti named and correcting the premise that it yields usable central data, then explaining what the existing evaluations do and do not contain. Directly engages the content of the preceding claim rather than referencing it in passing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "That data is also given at individual education plan meetings—IEPs—where Ministry of Education personnel are at those meetings."

acuity.statement: Firstly, given that we’ve seen a $4 million cut out of education with Te Pae Roa vanishing—Te Pae Roa’s goal was to increase Māori children’s participation in kōhanga reo kura and wharekura by 30 percent by 2040; so that’s gone. We’ve also seen a $22 million programme called Te Kawa Matakura gone. Te Kawa Matakura’s goal was to ensure that rangatahi Māori leadership was coming through education and there would be enough to lead it forward going ahead. Given that, and given education outcomes for tamariki Māori are significantly better in kura kaupapa, how does the Minister plan to not just incrementally increase but radically boost funding for Māori-medium education over the next five years?
acuity.explanation: Stanford had just argued that she could not see 'how many children and what were the outcomes' for money spent, and is building evaluative frameworks to fix that. Ferris does engage that currency in part — he answers it with outcomes evidence of his own (Māori-medium 'outperforms') and names two specific programmes that were cut, which is the exact kind of spending decision Stanford was defending. But the bulk of the turn is a prepared list of questions on a strand she had not raised, and his stated hook is her Q+A interview rather than anything said in this debate. Partial engagement, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: 'we weren’t able to see, for the most part, for everything we spend money on, how many children and what were the outcomes in terms of attendance and achievement'

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thanks for the questions from the member. I have extraordinarily high aspirations for our tamariki Māori and, as the member said, those aspirations are that our tamariki Māori are achieving at the same rate or even higher than everyone else, and there’s no reason that we can’t do that.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the specific thing Ferris closed on — his citation of her Q+A claim that Māori students can perform to the same degree of success as non-Māori — and adopts it explicitly ('as the member said'). The answer that follows engages one strand of his questions (resourcing for Māori medium: decodable texts in te reo, 12 accredited PLD providers, maths materials) and then returns to prepared structured-literacy material, leaving the STEM/STEAM, reo-Māori teacher supply and digital-inequity questions untouched. Engagement with one strand plus prepared material is the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: 'she was very clear that she has a programme that is seeing Māori students perform to the same degree of success as non-Māori students'

acuity.statement: I’d just like to point out that Māori-medium education—which is why I’m answering the question in full—includes bilingual, rumaki, kura kaupapa, everything, which is why I’m answering the question around all of the resources we are providing to all of those mediums. You’ve mentioned Māori medium education; I’m going to answer in full.
acuity.explanation: This is aimed squarely at the content of the objection just raised: Ferris complained the answer was too broad because his question was about kura kaupapa specifically, and she contests the premise by defining Māori-medium education to span bilingual, rumaki and kura kaupapa, which is why a broad answer is the responsive one. It engages the framing of his complaint rather than its crux (why Māori medium is not funded at a level signalling its results), so it falls short of the top of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: 'the response is a very broad one, and the question I asked initially, or the context, is that kura kaupapa, Māori medium education outperforms'

acuity.statement: Well, I seem to recall somewhere around 25 kids for the $4 million that we were spending. It wasn’t good use of money, and it was a pilot, a small pilot that was actually for tertiary intervention.
acuity.explanation: Ferris had characterised Te Kawa Matakura as a leadership programme for rangatahi Māori and named a dollar figure for it; she takes that exact programme, disputes his characterisation of it (a small tertiary-intervention pilot, not a leadership programme) and supplies a participation figure against the spend. The speech could not have been delivered had he raised something else, which is the deciding test. Whether the figures she gives are correct is a veracity question and does not move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: 'It was a leadership programme.'

acuity.statement: I know that the previous speaker, the Hon Jan Tinetti, who asked a question has spoken to some people who’ve decided to leave teaching. The teacher retention rate hasn’t changed—it’s 89 percent—and it’s really important that we, of course, continue to encourage people to stay in the profession and do everything we can, which is why it’s been so important to me to provide everything we possibly can when it comes to supports for implementing the new curriculum.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Tinetti had just made — that teachers are leaving the profession, evidenced by a principal who lost five staff in a week — and does something with it: it concedes the anecdote, then counters it with the aggregate retention figure and ties that back to the curriculum supports Tinetti was questioning. The answer would have to change if Tinetti had argued something else about teacher supply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "at the moment, there seems to be a number of teachers that are actually leaving the profession"

acuity.statement: We have already said publicly—maybe the member missed it—that we are reorienting all of the professional learning and development money that we have, which is about $130 million - odd a year, into structured literacy and maths and assessment to make sure that we get this right over the next few years.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages Tinetti's question about whether the professional learning and development money in the Budget goes far enough, answering with the quantum being reoriented and its multi-year framing rather than restating prepared material. It engages the funding strand of her question but not her separate request for transparency on what the supports look like, so it is strong but not complete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "the money that’s been put in from this Budget to supporting teachers with that professional learning and development is not going far enough"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to ask a few quick questions. The Minister has touched on professional learning development funding for structured literacy and I want to ask the Minister: is she confident that the funding that has been made available for Māori medium professional learning development for structured literacy is sufficient for those 12 providers to be able to deliver that professional learning development?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own line of answer on Māori-medium provision and funding and turns it into a specific question about Māori medium structured-literacy PLD. It engages the subject matter the Minister had just been expanding on rather than any particular claim she made in that turn (the advisory group, property ring-fencing, network planning), so this is partial engagement: topic-level, then her own prepared material about per-capita funding and descaling providers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "It is important that we have a really good relationship with Ngā Kura Ā Iwi and Te Rūnanga nui and I’ve been meeting with them in my office a number of times now."

acuity.statement: Just to kind of first respond to some of the things that the Minister has mentioned in terms of what is getting students to school—that what is getting ākonga into school is being able to read, write, and then do math. As someone who has stood in front of a classroom for a number of years, I can tell you that is not actually what gets ākonga to school. It is having a safe environment, it is knowing that they can wake up in the morning knowing that they love what they are doing, and, yes, although I am a believer of linguistics because that is my background, that is not necessarily what gets students there. It’s having a balanced curriculum.
acuity.explanation: He names the Minister's claim about what gets ākonga into school, denies its central proposition and offers a competing account (safe environment, engagement, a balanced curriculum). The speech would plainly be different had she not made that claim. Marked slightly below 1.0 because the claim engaged was made earlier in her answer rather than in the turn immediately preceding his, so the engagement rests on his own restatement of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford's claim, restated verbatim by Xu-Nan, that what gets ākonga into school is "being able to read, write, and then do math" — reaffirmed in her next turn as "We are prioritising reading, writing and maths."

acuity.statement: Also the other thing that the Minister has mentioned around the work that’s being done around ākonga Māori—in that case, what we’re seeing and what we’re currently being consulted on right now is also a deprioritisation of giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, which includes tikanga Māori and also te reo Māori.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's account of what the Government is doing for ākonga Māori and answers it at the level of the topic, pivoting to a separate consultation on section 127 rather than engaging her specific claims about the new Māori advisory group, ring-fenced kura kaupapa property funding or inclusion in network planning. Engagement is real but partial, and then moves to his own prepared argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "I’ve also made a commitment to them that we will include them in network planning as well—something that’s not been done before"

acuity.statement: A balanced curriculum, of course, is very important, which is why we are refreshing the entire curriculum. Every single one of the curricular areas will be refreshing. They’re all important areas; we expect all of them will be taught. Just because we’re not going to pay artists to come into school and paint murals doesn’t mean we don’t think there should be a balanced curriculum.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise point Xu-Nan ended on — that what matters is a balanced curriculum — by accepting the premise and disputing that her prioritisation denies it, with the curriculum refresh as the answer. This passage could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument; it is shaped by his.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "It’s having a balanced curriculum."

acuity.statement: The member also mentioned section 127 of the Education and Training Act, which is not a Budget question, but I want to make it clear that it does not in any way remove or reduce any Treaty obligations on school boards. It’s still there. We’re adding some other things in because, actually, achievement and assessment and attendance are also really important things. The member seems to think that just because of the order of things makes one thing more important than the other. That is completely untrue, but that clause is still very important.
acuity.explanation: Goes to the actual mechanism of Xu-Nan's argument — that demoting an objective to a secondary clause lets schools disregard it — and contests exactly that inference about the ordering of objectives, while conceding the provision is outside the Budget debate. Directly aimed at the reasoning just put, not merely at its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "By devaluing one of them, deprioritising one of them, it means that if you deprioritise them to a secondary clause, it means that if they don’t meet the objective, the primary objective, then a school does not need to consider it."

acuity.statement: Now, I’m not going to talk about future Budgets, because that’s not part of this debate, but I do want to talk about this Government’s investment into attracting people into teaching: 1,200 additional places in the on-site training programme over the next four years has been massively welcomed by the sector.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the question actually asked — what is being done to entice people into teaching in the first place — and answers it on its own terms with the on-site training expansion, rather than restating the supply measures he had already dismissed as ambulance-at-the-bottom-of-the-cliff. Marginally short of 1.0 because she declines the specific asks (paid placements, blanket bursaries) by ruling out future-Budget discussion before supplying her own list.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "What is the Minister doing to entice students going into teaching in the first place?"

acuity.statement: Now, what you’re saying is that within the 20 percent of people where we don’t know where they’re going, there might be some homeless people. That may be the case. We don’t specifically know. But what we do know is that we know a lot more about that cohort of people that are leaving emergency housing, and it’s through the hard work and diligence of the teams to find out where those people are going.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Paul's specific challenge — that the 20 percent whose destinations are unknown may be homeless — restates it accurately, concedes it may be the case, and then says what is known instead. The reply would have to be different had she not made that particular point; it is not prepared material about emergency housing generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "How do you know that that 20 percent of people who have left emergency housing are not now homeless?"

acuity.statement: There is a request—I think I understand your request is to have data that’s based on gender around women and homelessness. I think that the only credible reliable data on homelessness is actually through the census, but we are trying to be clear about and engage with people like Home Ground, Vision West, and the Salvation Army and others to get their sense of homelessness right now.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific ask put to him (gender-disaggregated homelessness data), answers it on its own terms by naming the census as the only source he regards as reliable, and describes what is being done instead. It stops short of the full engagement — he does not address the commitment she asked him to make to collect the data — so it is strong rather than complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "What is the plan to collect the data about the gender of people experiencing homelessness? And will he make a commitment to look into that?"

acuity.statement: If that Minister, the Hon Tama Potaka, will not commit to the goal—which everyone in this House should have—that Kiwis should have access to homeownership, that first-home buyers in New Zealand should be able to work hard, save up, and buy their own home, why is that Minister further weakening the rights of renters? Why are 90-day no-cause evictions back under his Government?
acuity.explanation: Picks up a real strand of the Minister's immediately preceding answer — his talk of leasehold and other models rather than ownership — and builds a challenge on it, but reads it as a refusal to commit to homeownership and then moves to her own prepared ground of tenancy law, which the Minister had not raised. One strand engaged, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "It may not be exactly the same as what our colleagues on the other side of the House are envisaging. We have to look at other models, including leasehold"

acuity.statement: Now, the question was asked: do we believe in more affordable housing and higher rates of homeownership? Many, many New Zealanders have been blocked out of homeownership and have been unable to get there. We want to see people having both the opportunity to own a home that’s affordable and also rent a home that’s affordable. That’s what we’re committed to.
acuity.explanation: Answers the homeownership-commitment half of Williams' question directly and in her terms, but leaves her actual argument — that weakening tenants' rights raises demand-side pressure on prices without adding supply, and the 90-day no-cause eviction question — entirely untouched, filling the turn instead with a prepared account of the ideological divide over Kāinga Ora. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "if he won’t commit to the New Zealand public being able to save hard and get into their own homes, isn’t it right that he would protect renters"

acuity.statement: In terms of the IRRS places, as people know, we were envisaging 1,500 new IRRS places to be contracted specifically with community housing providers over the next couple of years—500 to get going quickly to maintain some sort of momentum and 1,000 through a bit more strategic partnerships in specific areas where the needs are high.
acuity.explanation: Woods put a numbered list of specific questions: the redirect/new-build split of the 750 IRRS places, the Kāinga Ora/CHP divide, spend to date on paused developments, the island and Auckland breakdown, and progress against the 1,000-Auckland-houses undertaking. Potaka takes up the IRRS strand and supplies a contracting figure and its internal 500/1,000 split, and elsewhere in the same turn addresses the savings framing and the Kāinga Ora review, so the reply is visibly shaped by what Woods raised. But he answers the topic rather than the claims: the 750 redirect proportion, the Kāinga Ora/CHP divide, the sunk spend and the Auckland tracking question all go unengaged, and a large part of the turn is prepared material on emergency housing that Woods never raised. Partial engagement, pointable — mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "of the 750 new income-related rent subsidies places that the Government is saying it is going to fund, how many of these are redirects from pre-existing community housing provider contracts?"

acuity.statement: I’ll start by asking him whether his goal is still more affordable housing and higher rates of homeownership, given that policy changes that his Government has overseen affect the attractiveness of housing as an asset rather than a place to live, and that’s affecting the way that people are not only seeing homes for their first home but it’s also disincentivising first-home owners to save and be able to buy first homes.
acuity.explanation: Potaka had just rested his case on private development supplying most new housing, with the Government setting the conditions to encourage it. Williams takes up exactly that strand and presses it from the other side — asking whether the Government's own tax change tilts housing toward investors and adds no additionality to supply. That is one identifiable strand of the preceding turn engaged, so it clears the prepared-material band. It stops short of the top because she takes up none of his specific figures (the 5,500/2,650 net builds, the 1,500 IRRS places) and the interest-deductibility and Treasury material reads as prepared questioning that would have been asked whatever he answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "Some of that provision—actually, most of that provision—will come through private developments rather than State housing developments."

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Associate Minister of Housing about his commitment in terms of the Māori housing programmes that have been rolled out over the last few years.
acuity.explanation: Jackson's turn is on the matter under debate — housing estimates — so it is not wholly adrift, but it engages no part of what Potaka actually argued. None of the Minister's claims (the net build figures, the IRRS contracting, the emergency housing exit data, the Kāinga Ora review findings) are taken up, contested or built on. The passing "as he has acknowledged" gestures at the Minister without engaging any content he supplied in this exchange. The questions on Toitū Tairāwhiti, Ka Uruora, papakāinga and regulatory barriers would have been put in the same words whatever the Minister had just said, which places this in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka answered on IRRS places, net State home builds, the Kāinga Ora review and emergency housing, and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: Is the Minister aware of the submission of Kāinga Ora Deputy Chief Executive Central Daniel Soughtton to the Rotorua Lakes Council, where he presented that there is “no robust evidence” that Kāinga Ora activities impact house prices in surrounding areas, which refuted directly his argument that Kāinga Ora has increased the price of land, and would he like to correct his answer to the House now or later?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim Potaka had just made — that the State outbidding private developers drove land unaffordability and crowded private developers out — and confronts it with named contrary evidence from the agency's own deputy chief executive, then presses for a correction. The question could not have been asked if the preceding turn had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "private developers were crowded out because they could not afford to buy the land or to develop the land because they’re being outbid down the road—" / "—by the State."

acuity.statement: There are people who actually have lived in the property development world and there are those that have observed. Certainly, from my experience of living in the property development world, when you have low-cost debt and a very low yield expectation on the return on investment, you can outbid a private developer most days of the week, and this is what we saw in a number of instances through Auckland—and I raised it in select committee last year, at the Estimates—Kerikeri, and other places, where the feasibilities that were adopted by the State housing provider were able to be undertaken on an apples-for-oranges basis, compared to the private developers.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Williams raised and implicitly dismisses her source by contrasting those who have 'lived in the property development world' with those who have merely 'observed', then re-argues the crowding-out mechanism. But it never takes up the actual content of the Soughtton submission or the 'no robust evidence' finding, and does not answer the request to correct the record — one strand engaged, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "there is “no robust evidence” that Kāinga Ora activities impact house prices in surrounding areas ... would he like to correct his answer to the House now or later?"

acuity.statement: I’m glad that the Associate Minister of Housing in his earlier answer touched upon the plight of construction sector businesses at the moment, because the Minister will be aware that New Zealand is lurching towards a historic slump in the building and construction sector, which is relevant to all of his plans for housing in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (housing and the Minister's plans) and it gestures at an earlier ministerial answer, but it engages no strand of the preceding member's turn and the referenced answer is outside the window, so the engagement is unpointable — the 0.1-0.3 band, at its top for the gesture.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson immediately preceded this with questions on the housing pipeline, emergency housing exits and Māori access to capital ("what plans has the Minister considered to make it easier for whānau to get access to capital"), and this statement takes up none of them; the "earlier answer" it gestures at is not in the text given, so the engagement cannot be pointed at.

acuity.statement: Now, I think I mentioned earlier that the expectation of the Government is that Kāinga Ora will deliver 5,400-plus houses over the next two years, for a total of 2,650 net homes.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the figure the preceding turn asked for and continues through the other pipeline commitments (Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga, income-related rent subsidies). The answer would be different had Jackson asked something else; not 1.0 only because it is partly a restatement of material already given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "Again, in terms of homes in the pipeline, we really need to know about the targets: what are the targets, if any, in terms of building homes?"

acuity.statement: Certainly, there is an assertion that the previous Government built more houses than any other Government. I think we can all admit, especially after the events this week, it sold some public houses along the way too, and that’s no different from Governments in the past.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific claim just made, concedes it arguendo and then contests what follows from it (sales alongside builds, strain on the development system). Squarely engaged with the content of the preceding turn rather than merely referencing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "we built more houses than any other Government in the past, I think, 50 years"

acuity.statement: The Minister did not answer my question about how he will play a role in ensuring that the building and construction sector is ready to go and is building houses, so let me test with him two good ideas.
acuity.explanation: Audits what the Minister actually did and did not cover and re-presses the unanswered strand with two concrete proposals, so the turn depends on what preceded it. Short of 1.0 because it engages the omission rather than the substance of what he did say (the Kāinga Ora numbers and debt figures).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "There have been a number of questions that have been asked and they’ve been very useful questions too" — followed by an answer covering housing numbers, emergency housing and access to capital but not the construction workforce.

acuity.statement: Following on with that, will there be a coordination in terms of Māori trades training? Is that a plan from the Minister, with him knowing that background and knowing that history very well?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the preceding speaker's construction-workforce and apprenticeships strand and extends it to Māori trades training, so one strand is genuinely taken up; the rest of the turn then moves to prepared material on Te Aka Taumatua advice that engages nothing said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "the Apprenticeship Boost scheme provided certainty to employers to take on and train additional workers and to expand the construction workforce"

acuity.statement: I’d like the Minister to give examples of things that are nice to have and things that are necessary. For example, is a safer crossing outside a school a “nice-to-have” or a “necessary-to-have”? Is a local library a “nice-to-have” or a “necessary-to-have”?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific term the Minister had just used to frame his whole expectation of councils and presses on the one thing his speech left undefined, offering concrete test cases (school crossing, library) to force the distinction. The speech could not have been delivered had Brown not used that phrase.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "it is not an excuse for them to simply go and spend that money willy-nilly on “nice-to-haves” in their local communities"

acuity.statement: Who, in the Minister’s opinion, is best placed to choose or decide what a “nice-to-have” is? Is it the residents of a local area and the representatives they’ve elected, or is it the Minister?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the live question and advances it rather than repeating it: accepts Russell's framing and draws out the consequence Brown's answer implies, namely who holds the authority to classify spending. Directly contingent on what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "what is a “nice-to-have” versus what is a “necessary-to-have”?" — and Simeon Brown's "The expectation is that they pass those savings on to their ratepayers"
