acuity.statement: It’s all well and good to have another beautiful venue in Wellington for politicians to speak in, which is now losing money—the convention centre is literally losing money whilst pipes are bursting outside on the street. There’s been other examples where councils have been looking to invest and build hotels in their local communities, thinking that’s a core business. Well, it’s not.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what was asked for — named concrete instances of “nice-to-haves” — rather than restating the policy. The content is shaped by Russell's demand, though he supplies his own examples instead of ruling on the ones she put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I’d like the Minister to provide examples—concrete examples—of what are just “nice-to-haves”"

acuity.statement: Benchmarking is something that’s used in other countries. It’s used in New South Wales and Victoria to provide more clarity around performance metrics between councils so that ratepayers can understand whether or not their council is actually spending money in an appropriate way aligned with how other councils are spending that money, and also looking at a revenue cap in terms of those non-core activities—not in terms of infrastructure around water or transport, but there’s other parts of the council business and saying, “Well, actually, when inflation is running at 3 percent, why are rates running at 15 percent?” and actually putting some downwards pressure on rates so that communities are protected from decision makers who are making decisions without necessarily considering the full impact on those who have to pay.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes up Genter's question of who decides and answers it on its own terms — benchmarking and accountability to ratepayers rather than either of the two options she offered. Engagement is real and specific, though he reframes the binary rather than choosing within it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "Is it the residents of a local area and the representatives they’ve elected, or is it the Minister?"

acuity.statement: He’s raised the matter of public transport, and there are a number of councils that have raised with the Minister, with the Government, concerns about a lack of investment into public transport. The Minister talks about functionality. We’ve got a comment here from Environment Canterbury talking about the fact that they have $4.4 million less in funding that was initially provided for some of their public transport improvements. My question to the Minister is: is that a “nice-to-have”?
acuity.explanation: Turns the Minister's own functionality test back on a specific case he raised, applying his bus-stop framing to a named council and a named funding reduction. The question only exists because of what he had just said about public transport.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Ratepayers wanted a bus stop; I don’t think they needed a garden on top of the bus stop"

acuity.statement: I want to follow up this distinction between “nice-to-haves” versus “necessary-to-haves”, because the Minister’s now added another way of defining that, and that’s core versus non-core. He gave us some examples of things that were “nice-to-haves” and I presume are non-core: hotels, convention centres, and gardens on bus stops. But he still hasn’t answered whether libraries, parks, and swimming pools are “nice-to-haves” or “necessaries-to-have”—whether they are core council business or non-core.
acuity.explanation: Tracks the Minister's answer closely: accepts the examples he gave, identifies the new core/non-core vocabulary he introduced, and isolates precisely the part of her question he left unanswered. Entirely contingent on the preceding turn's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "There’s been other examples where councils have been looking to invest and build hotels in their local communities, thinking that’s a core business. Well, it’s not."

acuity.statement: Talking about “nice-to-haves”, my question to the Minister relates to: will investigating options to limit council expenditure on “nice-to-haves” put downward pressure on rates?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the debate by picking up the governing phrase, but engages no part of any argument made: it neither answers nor contests the definitional challenge running through the preceding turns, and would read identically whatever had been said before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just asked whether libraries, parks and swimming pools are “nice-to-haves” or core business, and this statement does not take that up — it borrows the phrase and invites the Minister to restate his own case

acuity.statement: This is in the context of central government spending more than ever before on transport, yet providing less and less to councils to deliver the basics. Does he think footpaths are not the basics? Are footpaths a “nice-to-have”?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own framing — back-to-basics, no-frills, gold-plating — and turns it into a concrete test: are footpaths basics, and if so why has the walking and cycling activity class been emptied of maintenance money? The question only makes sense as a reply to what Brown had just argued, and she supplies a specific council (Tararua) as the counter-case. It engages the content of his claim rather than merely naming him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they’re wanting to see a back-to-basics approach" / "we want a no-frills approach to transport infrastructure"

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister of Local Government said that the Act, when it came in in 2002, had the four wellbeings in it, and then Rodney Hide took them out and then Labour put them back in. He referred to some evidence about rates going up during that time period, and my question to him on that evidence is: is that entirely what the Minister is relying on for his decision to remove the wellbeings again?
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's specific evidential claim about the four wellbeings and the 2 percent figure, then presses on its load-bearing role — is departmental correlation the entire basis for repeal? She also audits which parts of the earlier question he answered (libraries and parks) and which he skipped (swimming pools). The speech would be different had Brown cited different evidence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The advice that I’ve received from the department is that, when those four wellbeings have been in the legislation, rates increased by an average of 2 percent more per year than when they are not in the legislation."

acuity.statement: My first one is around the concept of “nice-to-have”. In Nelson, one of the things our council is going to be investing in is new facilities for our surf life-saving club, which performs a very important function during the tourism season where we have a number of people coming to our beaches, being well supported by our Mayor Nick Smith and the rest of Nelson City Council. My question is, is that a nice-to-have?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's core-versus-nice-to-have distinction and probes it with a fresh local instance, which is engagement with one strand of his argument rather than with its reasoning. It is clearly built on his framing, but it tests the category by example instead of contesting the premise or the evidence he offered, so it sits between a partial and a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Yes, they want a library, but they want a library which is built to a more standard, modest level."

acuity.statement: The other point is that there has been a lot of discussion around what is a nice-to-have. I can remember Rodney Hide, back in the day, saying, “Stick to core services”, and immediately what happened is that councils were then asked, “How much money are you putting aside to prepare for the 2011 Rugby World Cup?”, which meant that Rodney had lost the argument right there and then about what a core service was.
acuity.explanation: Engages the core-services line of argument running through the preceding turns and draws out its practical difficulty — the last Minister to issue that instruction immediately asked councils to fund a Rugby World Cup — then proposes an alternative mechanism (a spending envelope for discretionary activity). It responds to the substance of the debate rather than restating a position, though it also carries prepared material on asset management and monitoring.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they’re wanting to see a back-to-basics approach"; and Rachel Brooking: "then Rodney Hide took them out"

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around stormwater, the Government’s made substantial announcements around the role of stormwater in our Local Water Done Well policy announcement we made about a month ago. There’s a significant amount that we are proposing there, and there’s a choice for councils whether to include stormwater as part of their water service organisations or not.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the stormwater question by name and supplies relevant policy detail, so the engagement is pointable, but it answers the topic rather than the specific question asked — whether green-space stormwater provision counts as a nice-to-have or gold-plating is left untouched, as is the list of playgrounds, museums and biodiversity. Partial engagement that returns to prepared policy material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "whether or not stormwater provision, particularly green spaces for stormwater, is a “nice-to-have” or is in some way gold-plating"

acuity.statement: In terms of the questions from Andy Foster around ensuring that there is better asset management, we’ve outlined in our systems improvements for local government about making sure there’s more use of benchmarking between councils. I think that’s particularly important in the asset management area, where, actually, there is a real need to ensure that the quality of asset management is lifted across, I’d say, central government and local government.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific mechanism Foster asked about — how the Crown would know councils had actually responded — by naming benchmarking between councils and public accountability as the monitoring route, and takes up his envelope idea by pointing to limits on rate increases for non-core expenditure. The reply is shaped by the question put, not interchangeable with any other.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "My question to you is about the monitoring process by which you can look at those councils and say they have actually responded to those great Government initiatives"

acuity.statement: In relation to stormwater, ultimately, councils have the ability to manage and fund their stormwater networks and components, including overland flow paths in parks and wetlands. It’s for council to determine this as part of their water service delivery plans.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the stormwater strand of Brooking's question and names the green-infrastructure components she had in mind (overland flow paths, parks, wetlands), but answers the topic rather than her specific request — whether he regards green infrastructure as "gold plating" — by devolving the decision to councils. Partial engagement, pointable but not a reply to the claim put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "it would be great for the Minister to give the committee of the whole House some comfort that he does not consider green infrastructure to be “gold plating”"

acuity.statement: In relation to the questions around annual plans and some of those compliance mechanisms—again, in our system improvements, we’re looking at an area around consultation decision-making to help councils adapt quickly to changing circumstances, save councils time and money while balancing democratic principles.
acuity.explanation: Names the subject of the question (annual plans, compliance) and then moves to prepared material on consultation and public-notice reform; the specific question — what analysis he has done and what concerns it surfaced — is not taken up at any point. A gesture at the question rather than an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "What analysis has he done of the annual plans and the general auditing framework of councils, and are there specific concerns from that work?"

acuity.statement: I have two questions for the Minister. The first is, again—this will be the third time I’ve asked it, and I am frustrated that we haven’t had engagement around the work that the New Zealand Transport Agency is doing to potentially change the criteria for councils to access funding for roads following a severe weather event.
acuity.explanation: Raises a new line of questioning and notes only that her earlier question went unanswered, which is a reference rather than an engagement. She does justify relevance to the portfolio under examination ("it is about the costs that are imposed on councils"), so this sits at the top of the on-topic-but-unengaged band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just spoken about council stormwater responsibilities and modernising council consultation and reporting requirements, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Ultimately, I think that the answer is quite simple, and it is that the New Zealand Transport Agency went through a consultation process. They have had submissions and the board will then make decisions based on those submissions, and, obviously, the member is more than welcome to ask further detailed questions about that tomorrow.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question asked — the status of the NZTA criteria change — and supplies the procedural answer (consultation run, submissions received, board to decide), plus acknowledges it was raised at the hearing. The reply would be different had she asked something else; marked down slightly because he partly defers the matter to another portfolio day rather than resolving her funding-burden point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "the work that the New Zealand Transport Agency is doing to potentially change the criteria for councils to access funding for roads following a severe weather event"

acuity.statement: Well, ultimately, it’s a trade-off. They could spend half a million dollars on a speed bump or they could ensure that their dog and animal welfare department in their council was actually well funded.
acuity.explanation: Restates her question accurately as one about whether central government will fund council dog control, then answers it squarely in the negative with a reason (councils must trade off their own spending). Directly shaped by the specific question put, and would read differently had she asked anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "I ask whether the Minister considers that to be a “nice-to-have” and something that could potentially get more support from central government"

acuity.statement: There’s been various programmes or partnerships between central and local government. This builds upon that and says, actually, we need to have a 10-year document which talks about those three priorities.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the comparison she asked for, names the predecessor funds including the Housing Acceleration Fund, and identifies the claimed difference (a 10-year agreed partnership and pipeline rather than a fund). Not 1.0 because he does not engage her dollar figure or whether the new mechanism carries comparable money.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Regional deals: how are they different from the $3.8 billion in the infrastructure package of the last Government?"

acuity.statement: I was pleased to announce pre-Budget that there was, I think, $60 million for Surf Life Saving New Zealand and the Royal New Zealand Coastguard to support the important work that they do.
acuity.explanation: Engages the subject matter Boyack raised (Surf Life Saving funding) and supplies a related figure, but does not take up the actual question of whether such a facility is a "nice to have". Partial engagement — one strand answered, the specific claim left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "Does he believe that the Surf Life Saving Club in Nelson" ... she asked whether it is a "nice to have"

acuity.statement: My question, then, to the Minister is: was any of that specifically going to Nelson City Council’s upgraded facilities?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the Minister just offered — the $60 million national allocation — and presses it against the particular case he was asked about. The question could not have been asked in this form had he said anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "there was, I think, $60 million for Surf Life Saving New Zealand and the Royal New Zealand Coastguard"

acuity.statement: I mentioned parks, reserves, playgrounds, libraries—I mentioned those earlier. Ultimately, though, the message to local government is around ensuring that when decisions are made, there is a focus on the core purpose and the core activity as to what that expenditure is going towards. We’ve seen far too much gold plating of infrastructure, and I’ve given some examples of that. Ultimately, ratepayers and taxpayers are wanting money being spent on the core purposes of what that is being spent on—whether it’s a park, a library, a swimming pool, a road, all of those things—they are wanting to see a no-frills approach so they keep costs down.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the category of facility the question was about and gives a position on how such spending should be judged, but declines the yes/no that was twice put to him and returns to prepared messaging about gold plating. One strand engaged, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "does the Minister believe a sports ground is a nice-to-have?"

acuity.statement: I want to go on to some of the financing issues that the Minister has raised. In particular, he has talked about how rates have increased quite a bit in recent years; we know that’s the case. He’s referenced the rate of inflation and says that when inflation is getting down to around 3 percent, then rates should be no higher than that. At the same time, we know that councils have an infrastructure deficit, that there is much delayed maintenance, particularly on hot water systems and the like. How does the Minister expect councils to keep rates down when there is this huge infrastructure deficit that needs to be repaired?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated position on rates tracking inflation and draws out the tension with the infrastructure deficit, putting the consequence back to him. Built on what he had said rather than on prepared material, though it opens a new line rather than contesting a specific figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they are wanting to see a no-frills approach so they keep costs down"

acuity.statement: Well, if the member was listening to my first speech here in terms of this debate, she would have heard about the Government’s Local Water Done Well policy, which allows councils to be able to move their water infrastructure and services into new water service organisations. Through the Local Government Funding Agency, they’ll be able to access up to 500 percent against their revenues in terms of debt to be able to make those long-term investments, spread those costs more affordably for local communities, and also release debt headroom on their own balance sheets, which means they can then put downward pressure on rates. That is an incredibly powerful financing tool for local councils, and our message to local councils is to get on with it.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a direct mechanism answering the exact question asked — how rates stay down despite the deficit — via debt headroom and the funding agency. Squarely aimed at the question put, the jibe about listening notwithstanding (that is a civility matter, not acuity).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "How does the Minister expect councils to keep rates down when there is this huge infrastructure deficit that needs to be repaired?"

acuity.statement: Carrying on with that funding issue, he has said that he anticipates lifting the debt level for local councils from 370 percent of revenue to 500 percent of revenue. That’s a substantial increase. Is he saying that the Local Government Funding Agency is going to fund all of that increase in debt for councils?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the 500 percent figure he had just given, quantifies the change it implies, and asks what follows from it. The question is entirely shaped by the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they’ll be able to access up to 500 percent against their revenues in terms of debt"

acuity.statement: Well, as I said—if the member was listening carefully to my answer—this is for water service organisations. The Local Government Funding Agency has already agreed: if a council sets up a water service organisation and guarantees that water service organisation, they will fund up to 500 percent against the revenues of that water service organisation. That financing is available now for councils to take advantage of, and my encouragement to councils is to get on with it.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the premise of the question directly — the headroom attaches to water service organisations, not to councils generally — and restates the mechanism on that basis. A precise engagement with the specific misstatement just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "lifting the debt level for local councils from 370 percent of revenue to 500 percent of revenue"

acuity.statement: So it’s not available to councils for other debt funding for other activities that they might need to carry out. That’s got me worried. I’m worried about the fact that, if we’re expecting councils somehow to keep rates down, somehow to spread the cost of infrastructure other than water across many years, and we are saying they might have to increase their debt to do that—what is that going to do to their credit ratings? What is it going to do to their interest costs? How is that going to flow on to the expenses that councils must bear?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the correction he made, then draws out its consequence for non-water debt, credit ratings and interest costs. The classic high-acuity move: take the answer given and follow where it leads.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they will fund up to 500 percent against the revenues of that water service organisation"

acuity.statement: Well, I’d just point the member again to my first speech, which was that the Local Government Funding Agency provides the lowest-cost financing to local government. They have, I think, a triple A credit rating. They are able to provide incredibly affordable financing. Under the previous Government’s reforms, those water entities would not have been able to receive financing through the Local Government Funding Agent. They would have had to go out into debt markets by themselves and would have had to be paying 1 to 2 percent higher interest rates for that debt. That would have been a huge impost to add on to ratepayers.
acuity.explanation: Engages the cost-of-borrowing strand of the question with the agency's credit rating and an interest-rate comparison, but answers about water entities and the previous Government rather than the councils' own credit ratings she asked about. Topic engaged, specific claim half-met.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "what is that going to do to their credit ratings? What is it going to do to their interest costs?"

acuity.statement: Well, the majority of councils go through the Local Government Funding Agency in order to access debt, because it is the lowest-cost financing facility available to local government, due to its joint arrangement between shareholding councils and the Crown, being a 20 percent shareholder of the liquidity facility support the council provides. That makes it the lowest-cost financing for local government.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the either/or she posed and reports what most councils in fact do, which is on the point without resolving it — she asked where such financing comes from as a matter of entitlement, and he answers with practice.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "is that coming from the Local Government Funding Agency, or are councils expected to seek that on the private market?"

acuity.statement: I understand that. What I’m asking—I’ve asked it three times now and the Minister has avoided it every time. I’m not asking about funding for water services. That’s quite clear; it’s up to 500 percent of the revenue. That’s quite straightforward. It’s the other infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the part of his answer that was sound, isolates exactly what it did not cover, and narrows the question to that remainder. Only possible as a response to what he had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the majority of councils go through the Local Government Funding Agency in order to access debt"

acuity.statement: Well, the question is, “Can they?” The answer is yes. And they will because it’s the Local Government Funding Agency. It provides the lowest-cost financing, and I’m not sure about the member, but if the Local Government Funding Agency is providing 1 to 2 percent lower interest rates than going out to the market, I’m pretty sure councils will go to the Local Government Funding Agency.
acuity.explanation: Restates her question in her own terms, separates the "can" from the "must" she had distinguished, and answers it. Directly keyed to the formulation she had just pressed on him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "can they all go and expect to get a yes all the time from the Local Government Funding Agency for any other debt they want to incur"

acuity.statement: The work programme—the systems improvements local government efficiencies work programme—has an element on bylaws and infringements, which is to ensure councils have appropriate modern tools for making and enforcing local regulations effectively. This could also include considering greater delegation for councils to set infringement fee levels.
acuity.explanation: Answers the devolution question she asked by pointing to the work programme element that bears on it and conceding it could extend to councils setting fee levels. Engages the substance, if not the "and, if not, why not".
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "would it make more sense for the Government to devolve that to local government to make that decision based on their own parking management strategy"

acuity.statement: I think when someone’s turning up to a bus stop, they want a roof over their head so they can get dry.
acuity.explanation: Stays on the bus-stop example but engages no part of the argument put — not the stormwater research, not the cost-effectiveness claim, not the yes/no she explicitly asked for. A quip on the topic rather than a response to the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "Or is he open to green infrastructure being a cost-effective solution that could actually get better outcomes for ratepayers at lower cost?"

acuity.statement: Does the Minister of Local Government understand that when you cover the ground, whether it’s with asphalt on the ground or whether it’s a building with a roof, that reduces the amount of green cover that absorbs water, and, therefore, when you have big stormwater events, less water is soaked up by plants and trees and what not, and then you have less nature in the city, less opportunities for birds and bees and all the other things we actually rely on to survive?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own roof answer and turns it into the premise of the rebuttal — a roof is impermeable cover, which is precisely the problem she raised. The question is unintelligible without his preceding reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they want a roof over their head so they can get dry"

acuity.statement: Look, I want to continue in the frame that my forebear the Hon James Shaw did in the climate space with regard to reaching out for a sense of cross-party consensus on the challenges that we face as a country and, indeed, as the world. It must be noted that friends do not let friends knowingly decimate the scientific fundamentals necessary for life on Earth, and what it is that we are grappling with, as was well canvassed at scrutiny week in front of the Environment Committee, is a draft emissions reduction plan that this Government knows will increase emissions based on what the track had been under the prior Government.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick follows a substantive turn by Megan Woods that put a series of specific, answerable questions to the Minister (which countries the climate MOUs were signed with and the cost of those offshore credits; whether the Budget 2024 climate-impacts emissions increase is additive to the mini-Budget's; the emissions consequences of dropping public-sector carbon neutrality; whether the ETS alone can shift industrial process heat after GIDI was scrapped). Swarbrick's speech takes up none of them. It opens on her own frame — continuing James Shaw's cross-party approach — and proceeds through prepared Green material on the draft emissions reduction plan, the Climate Change Commission monitoring report, 'no additional warming', and ETS auction failure. It stays squarely on the matter under debate, and her later ETS question happens to overlap the topic Woods raised, but it is an independently framed question rather than an engagement with Woods' claim; delete Woods' turn and substitute a different climate critique and this speech would not have to change a word. That puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band: 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is a genuine gesture at the debate itself (the cross-party frame, the reference to what was canvassed at scrutiny week before the Environment Committee), not merely a speech that could have been given on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods spoke immediately before, putting specific questions to the Minister including 'whether it is still his intention that the emissions trading scheme (ETS) drives most of the change that we need to see, particularly in industrial and process heat' and 'was this additional to the climate impact assessment and the obvious emissions increases that occurred through the mini-Budget', and this statement does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: In his answers, the Minister talked about being open to talking with some of our industrial and process heat users about initiatives that sit alongside or that are complementary measures to the emissions trading scheme. I’d be interested to know from the Minister what those mechanisms are. What are the things that are currently under consideration? Is he considering changes to industrial allocation and how that might be used, and is that one of the mechanisms that he is looking at here?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific offer Watts had just made — openness to complementary mechanisms alongside the ETS — and presses it for content, naming a candidate mechanism (industrial allocation) to test it. The question could not have been written without hearing the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "we are—and we signalled this in our draft emissions reduction plan (ERP)—very much open to working with emitters around putting in place mechanisms to reduce gross emissions in addition to the role which the emissions trading scheme (ETS) plays"

acuity.statement: While the Minister did address a number of questions that were put on the table, he didn’t address the largest emitter in the room—that is, of course, agriculture, which makes up more than half of our domestic emissions.

Lower agricultural emissions—there’s a huge amount of work under way in regards to innovation: 5.5 megatons in EB 3. Better public transport initiatives: 0.1 megaton in EB 2, 0.3 megaton in EB 3. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the member asking the question is on the select committee working through the process of the Fast-track Approvals Bill" — Penny Simmonds.

acuity.statement: We have committed to ensuring that there is transparency and there is a process which allows consultation and valuable input, and, particularly, consultation has started with a range of iwi in terms of specific parts of the changes to national direction—and the Associate Minister may be able to talk a little bit more there. It’s a commitment that we have made to Te Pou Taiao that we will certainly engage fulsomely in consultation there, specifically around those freshwater regulations.
acuity.explanation: Now answers the public participation strand with specifics (iwi consultation, Te Pou Taiao, freshwater regulations) rather than the select committee deflection, so it engages the question put. Partial: Brooking's further question about whether she agrees with Chris Bishop on property rights versus heritage protection is not taken up at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Where does she see public participation in the resource management system? How important is it to her that community can have a say in the planning decisions that are made around them?" — Rachel Brooking.

acuity.statement: Just adding to what the Minister has said, two pieces of work are under way in my area. There is consultation under way now with a whole range of sectors across environmental NGOs, iwi, primary production groups—across the whole sector.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the concrete consultation detail the question was pressing for in his own portfolio rather than reciting prepared material, so it is aimed at the live question; it is supplementary and does not take up the conflict between development and heritage values that was also asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How important is it to her that community can have a say in the planning decisions that are made around them?" — Rachel Brooking.

acuity.statement: Given those responses, do both the environment Ministers commit to continuing that approach with any legislation or regulations—that they provide for community input?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the two answers just given and draws out their consequence, asking the Ministers to generalise the consultation they have just described into a standing commitment. Short, but it could not have been framed this way had the preceding answers been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Feedback is being sought across everyone, so I’m fairly comfortable that we are seeking a range of views" — Andrew Hoggard, following Penny Simmonds' consultation commitment.

acuity.statement: I just wanted to dig into that a little bit because we are seeing a bit of a theme come through here where there’s a genuine desire on the other side of the Chamber to talk about regulations and red tape and compliance, but we are seeing investment and appropriations to the catchment group communities.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking had just asked both Ministers to commit to providing for community input in future legislation, and this statement does not take that up — it characterises the opposition's questions in general and opens a new line on catchment groups.

acuity.statement: I think you referred to a little bit around that; that instead of regulations and red tape and bureaucracy and things being imposed upon those that are involved with catchments, it’s actually members of those catchment groups who are coming up with the solutions—defining what the problem is, coming up with solutions, and then sharing that best practice.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Patterson's specific description of what catchment group members do and extends it into the regulation-versus-grassroots contrast, so the answer is shaped by his question. Partial because the thing he actually asked for — her forward vision for enabling the groups through the appropriation — is largely replaced by praise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they’re also talking amongst themselves, they’re analysing what they’re doing on their farm, how they can do things better and more efficiently" — Mark Patterson.

acuity.statement: On the grassroots community catchment groups, does the Minister, first of all, accept that a lot of those groups had significant Jobs for Nature funding and did some very good work with that? Does she think, though, that regulations are not needed for water if there is a catchment group and that, as she said, peer pressure is enough—does she think that peer pressure, alone, is enough, or should there be some regulations as noted by the catchment community groups that were in Parliament just last week?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own peer pressure claim back and tests it to its limit, and adds the funding premise the Minister's account of grassroots success omitted. The questions are built out of the answer that preceded them and could not have been asked without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We know that peer pressure is probably the best way of getting outcomes rather than it being forced from above" — Penny Simmonds.

acuity.statement: I’m interested to hear from the Minister for the Environment on how the prioritisation for the remediation or management of contaminated sites is happening.
acuity.explanation: Prepared questioning on the Vote under examination, so it is on the matter under debate, but it is indifferent to the exchange it follows and would read identically whatever had been said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking had just challenged whether peer pressure alone is enough without water regulations, and this statement does not take that up — it opens an unrelated line on contaminated sites appropriations.

acuity.statement: With regard to the question from the back—thank you very much for moving closer to your mike—yes, there is an assessment tool that the local authorities have to assess their vulnerable and contaminated sites, and then the applications come from the local authorities. The prioritisation is, essentially, done by the local authorities and their applications coming in, and then there are criteria to assess those.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise thing Tana asked — who sets the priority order for remediating contaminated sites — and supplies the mechanism (council assessment tool, council applications, assessment criteria). The reply would have to be different had Tana asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Darleen Tana: "I’m interested to understand how the prioritisation, if you will, for management, remediation, what have you, of those sites, is envisaged."

acuity.statement: I’ll just remind the Minister of some other questions I had. One was on the environmental reporting legislation—where that is at—and also, going back to why it is that environmental hubs are not a priority. Has she ever asked for any funding for anything for the environment?
acuity.explanation: Shaped by the answer just given: it audits what the Minister omitted and presses those strands again. Partial rather than full engagement, because the substance is her own earlier material re-put rather than a response to the content of the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "With regard to the emissions trading scheme and Māori climate, they are outside my appropriation—so outside the scope of this Estimates debate." — a reply that covered only part of what had been put to her

acuity.statement: With regard to the environmental reporting, absolutely this is an area of focus, and it is an area of work that is being undertaken in this Budget year. We are hoping to be able to have an amendment for the Environmental Reporting Act that focuses and ensures that we are monitoring and reporting the appropriate data. We’re hoping to have that in the first half of 2025.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one of the three strands Brooking re-raised and answers it directly with a timeframe, but leaves the environmental hubs question and the funding question untouched. One strand engaged out of several is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "One was on the environmental reporting legislation—where that is at"

acuity.statement: Has the Minister met with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment and had briefings on his recent reports?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the environment appropriation) but indifferent to the answer immediately preceding it — a fresh line of questioning rather than a follow-up on the reporting amendment just announced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simmonds had just described an intended amendment to the Environmental Reporting Act in the first half of 2025, and this question does not take that up

acuity.statement: Yes. Yes, we have met in person several times, and we have had phone discussions, and we have a meeting scheduled before the end of the year as well.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question squarely and adds the detail asked for — frequency, mode, and a scheduled further meeting. Entirely contingent on what was just asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Has the Minister met with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment and had briefings on his recent reports?"

acuity.statement: I can assure the member that with the fast-track consenting, as with all the work being done in the package of resource management work, there is a ministerial group, of which I am part, and our discussions are robust and fulsome. I am confident that the opportunities are there for me to have input at that level.
acuity.explanation: Engages the second half of the question — what she is doing in her ministerial capacity — by pointing to her seat on the ministerial group, but says nothing about the purpose of the bill or the environmental outcomes asked about. One strand taken up, then a return to general assurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "I did ask before about the purpose of that bill and what the Minister is doing, as the Minister for the Environment and the Minister in charge of the Resource Management Act, to ensure that there are not environmental outcomes as a result of that piece of legislation"

acuity.statement: Thank you for that response. Does the Minister accept, then, that the bill as introduced does override environmental protections with the drafting of the purpose clause?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly off the assurance just given — the "then" takes the Minister's claimed influence and tests it against the text of the bill she says she has input on. The question could not have been asked in this form before that answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "I am confident that the opportunities are there for me to have input at that level."

acuity.statement: The current forecast is that instead of 202,500 being on the jobseeker benefit in January 2025, it will peak at 214,000. That doesn’t change our target, it doesn’t change the work we’re doing, and, actually, what I would like to put on record is that our work exits in July and August this year are 1,500 up on the same time a year ago, so what we’re doing is working.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni asked specifically whether the Minister had received updated advice because the BEFU peak of 202,000 had already been exceeded. Upston takes up that exact number and supplies the updated figure (214,000), i.e. the thing asked for, and concedes it is worse than Treasury forecast. The answer would be different had Sepuloni asked something else, so it is squarely responsive. Short of 1.0 only because she then pivots to prepared material on work exits and leaves Sepuloni's food-grants strand untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the BEFU forecast of 202,000 on jobseeker support by January 2025 was meant to be the peak" — Carmel Sepuloni

acuity.statement: What I’m hearing right now is that the Minister went off vibes, in terms of just anecdotal feedback from providers, that there would have been job losses, because she hasn’t been able to answer, straight up, how many jobs would have been lost if the Government had gone ahead with a top-up—a top-up—for employers to allow disabled workers to earn at least the minimum wage.
acuity.explanation: This takes the precise concession in Upston's answer — that the disability enterprises put no number on the job losses — and does something with it, treating the absence of a figure as evidence the rationale was unsubstantiated, then re-puts the question. The speech is wholly contingent on what Upston just said; it could not have been delivered unchanged after a different answer. Scored on engagement only: the 'went off vibes' characterisation is a civility/rigor matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they didn’t put a number on the job losses, but they were very concerned that if the wage supplement was to proceed, it would mean job losses" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Going through some of the programmes that he referred to—Mana in Mahi: our target is 50 to 55 percent to be coming on to Mana in Mahi from the jobseeker benefit. If we look at the current numbers, 35 percent of participants are Māori.
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. She takes up the Mana in Mahi strand Jackson raised and restates the 50-55 percent target, but the figure she supplies (35 percent of participants Māori) answers a different question from the one put, and she leaves Jackson's other specific asks — the needs-based directive, whether Māori trade training places will be cut, and whether there is a Māori unemployment target — unaddressed, returning to general material on programmes. Engaged on topic and in part on the claim, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is the Minister on track for 50 to 55 percent of those being supported by Mana in Mahi being job seekers by June 2025? Can she tell the committee today what the current percentage is?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: Just to give an example of the employment initiatives, the member made a comment about a reduction in the employment monetary compensatory amount. The baseline amount is the same as it’s been over several years. The only difference was some time-limited funding that was related to COVID coming to an end, but the baseline has pretty much remained the same.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific numerical claim Kemp made about a funding reduction in the employment appropriation and offers a direct counter-explanation (a time-limited COVID tranche ending, baseline unchanged), then addresses her front-line-services and Māori-provider concerns with case-manager numbers and He Poutama Rangatahi participation. The answer would be different had Kemp raised different points; it is not 1.0 because she declines several of her questions as outside the delegation and does not engage the housing, superannuation or suicide strands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Takutai Tarsh Kemp: "Another concerning point is the 12.2 percent reduction in funding for the improved employment and social outcome support appropriation."

acuity.statement: I’d like to ask the Minister a couple of questions, given that she has repeatedly said that she’s committed to better outcomes for disabled people. However, we don’t really see that outlined in the Budget at all.
acuity.explanation: Same debate and a gesture at the exchange already had (she notes the Minister has been asked about the minimum wage exemption before), but the content engages none of what Upston had just said about employment baselines, case-manager numbers or He Poutama Rangatahi; it opens a prepared new line on disability support instead. The claim she does contest is one the Minister made at an earlier Estimates hearing, not in the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston spoke about the employment appropriation baseline, protected front-line services, case management and He Poutama Rangatahi, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The independent review panel made some recommendations. One of them was to maintain the level of funding to residential providers at last year’s rate while a rapid review into pricing can be undertaken to understand why, despite there being fewer people in residential care, the increase in costs is over 30 percent—right? Understanding what is driving the increase in costs is pretty fundamental in stabilising the ship, and that is exactly what we are doing.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific charge that she has frozen residential care, naming the review recommendation that produced the decision and the cost-growth figure behind it, and in the surrounding passage also takes up her other named strands — the $1.1 billion, flexible funding guidelines and the Enabling Good Lives pause. The reply is shaped by the particular list Radhakrishnan put, which is what high responsiveness looks like.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "She’s put a freeze on residential care, which means that some of the most intellectually disabled New Zealanders will not gain access to residential care."

acuity.statement: At the time of the release of the findings of the review on 15 August, a number of documents were published, so I did a full media conference, I put the press release out, the full report of the independent review panel, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet stocktake—which was released before the election, which also highlighted significant issues—and also a report called the Link report, which had dire findings in terms of the ministry’s financial capability and position. It required urgent action, and that’s exactly what’s been taken.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific transparency charge about the 15 August announcement and answers it on its own terms by itemising what was released that day, and elsewhere in the same turn supplies the review findings Radhakrishnan demanded as evidence. Not a 1.0 because the minimum wage exemption evidence question and the 'why not strengthen Whaikaha instead' question are left untouched, but the speech would plainly be different had Radhakrishnan said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "Why is there no transparency, also, between the announcement the Minister made on 15 August"

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: what changes has the Government made to reduce the number of New Zealanders who are reliant on the jobseeker benefit, given that $4.4 billion was allocated for it in the Budget?
acuity.explanation: A prepared question on a different line of the vote. It engages no part of the preceding exchange on DSS, Whaikaha or the review findings, and would read identically whatever had been said before it; it is at least about the Minister's portfolio under examination, so not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just set out the independent review's findings on Disability Support Services and her response to them, and this question does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’ve been able to traverse some of those. One of them that I wanted to just put on the record of the House, with thanks to that member for his question, is the employment investment framework.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies what the question asked for — three named changes (the employment investment framework, the focus on under-25s with the Taylor Fry figures, and the expansion of case management to 70,000 people). Short of 1.0 because the $4.4 billion appropriation figure the question hung the ask on is not engaged at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "what changes has the Government made to reduce the number of New Zealanders who are reliant on the jobseeker benefit"

acuity.statement: I just want to know why the Minister made the decision not to include any disabled people on the panel that did the review of Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People, given the motto that has been used already in this House, “Nothing about us without us”, and how can the Minister expect disabled people and disabled people’s organisations to take that review seriously, given that they weren’t even given a seat at the table to give their perspective?
acuity.explanation: Attacks the authority of the very document Upston had just read into the record, arguing its panel's composition undermines it — an engagement with the substance of the Minister's defence rather than a restatement of the original question. Held below the top band because it reaches back past the immediately preceding turn and the rest of her contribution moves to unrelated Te Pae Tawhiti material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "I’d just like to put on the record of the House the findings of the independent review of the disability support service (DDS)"

acuity.statement: The member raises an important project that is well under way at the Ministry of Social Development, and that is Te Pae Tawhiti. One of the things that was kind of strange when I came into the role was to find that a nine-year programme of work that was broken into three horizons of three years was only funded for two of the first three years, which was a bit strange.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — confirming Te Pae Tawhiti is proceeding and commenting on its funding profile — but leaves the panel-composition question, the freeze-versus-pause question and the vacant deputy chief executive question entirely unaddressed. Partial engagement: pointable, but only one of four asks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "whether or not that business transformation programme is going ahead"

acuity.statement: How, as she has claimed before, would going ahead with the wage supplement result in job losses?
acuity.explanation: Re-puts the one question in the earlier exchange the Minister passed over, narrowed to the causal mechanism rather than the evidence base. It is responsive to the live state of the debate and would not have been asked had that point been answered, but it engages a gap in the Minister's turn rather than anything she actually said in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "Where is the evidence that jobs would be lost, as the Minister has said—on record—given that Aotearoa Disability Enterprises can’t actually back that up?"

acuity.statement: Minister, one of the things that we have seen coming out of COVID and out of Cyclone Gabrielle and other adverse events where the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) sort of strode in and had to pick up the pieces was that some of these work programmes and initiatives that you’ve got behind—even though some of them have been thrown together quite hastily—have actually worked.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on rural education activities programmes. There is a faint gesture at the Minister's earlier remarks on which employment programmes are funded, but nothing in the preceding member's turn is engaged, and the question would have been asked in the same words whatever had come before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March asked how the wage supplement would cause job losses and this statement does not take it up; it glances at the Minister's own earlier employment-programme material rather than at any other member's argument.

acuity.statement: A couple of questions, but, firstly, I’d just like to pick up on the issue of the minimum wage exemption scheme, and I congratulate the Minister for recognising the value of those disability enterprises projects.
acuity.explanation: Patterson follows Upston's turn on fixing the disability system and establishing a stand-alone ministry, and takes up none of it. He gestures at the debate by praising the Minister's position on the minimum wage exemption (a matter she had traversed earlier in the committee, not in the turn he follows) and then pivots to his own prepared line on jobseeker numbers and seasonal workers. On topic, but indifferent to what immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston spoke about targeting support to those with the highest needs and making Whaikaha a stand-alone ministry, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: Just highlighting some of those quickly, because I know my time is limited, the first thing we did was actually set the expectation that there would be rights and responsibilities and that those who were receiving jobseeker support would need to fulfil their responsibilities—i.e., their work obligations.
acuity.explanation: Patterson asked her to set out the steps she had taken to address rising jobseeker numbers against low unemployment; she goes straight to those steps and enumerates them. The answer would be different had he asked about something else — it is shaped by the specific request put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know that you have taken some steps to address that and I would just like you to illuminate us on that, please" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: I want to know from the Minister why it is that she continues to say in the House that there is no funding freeze, that disabled people are getting more funding to support them and more access to services, when disabled people and disabled people’s organisations are telling the media and are telling politicians in the House that that is simply not the case, that their access to support has been frozen, and that they are no longer able to access some of the supports that they were previously accessing.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the Minister's claim that the changes deliver greater and fairer access to disabled people and sets it directly against what disability organisations are reporting, pressing the contradiction. She engages the substance of that strand, though much of the surrounding question returns to her own earlier line on the 50,000 figure rather than to what Upston had just said about jobseeker exits.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What we are committed to doing is fixing the system, getting to a place where disabled people have greater access, fairer access" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: In terms of the measure that we will focus on, it is material hardship, and we have set a target of 11 percent. It is 12.5 percent at the moment. That is 17,000 children that our Government will lift out of poverty.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni asked three specific things, one of which was which child poverty measure the Minister was using. Upston names the measure, gives its current level and the target, and in the same turn corrects her own earlier 50,000 figure to 52,000 and explains what it counted. That is supplying the figures the question asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I also want to know what the measure is that the Minister is using when she refers to child poverty—whether it’s before housing, after housing, or if it’s material hardship" — Carmel Sepuloni

acuity.statement: I’m going to once again try to ask a straight-up question that I haven’t gotten an answer to or it hasn’t been addressed, and that is how exactly would it have resulted in job losses if the Government had gone ahead with the wage supplement meant to replace the minimum wage exemption?
acuity.explanation: The turn he follows was about child poverty measures and the $1.1 billion disability investment, and he takes up none of it — he restates a question from earlier in the committee. It is squarely on the matter under debate and presses an unanswered point, but nothing in it is shaped by what was just said, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unengaged band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston's preceding turn dealt with the material hardship target and the restored budgets for needs assessors, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: That member may not be aware that one of the jobs in Opposition is that you are preparing your policies to take into an election. In the 2020 election and the 2023 election, the National Party policy was to maintain the minimum wage exemption.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one strand of what Menéndez March put to her — the charge that she never consulted providers or disabled workers — and answers it by describing her Opposition-side engagement with the sector. She leaves the actual question, how the wage supplement would have cost jobs, untouched. Partial engagement: you can point at what was taken up and at what was not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "she didn’t even consult, as a Minister, with any of these providers, let alone with disabled workers" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Why can’t the Minister tell us how going ahead with the wage supplement would have resulted in job losses? She has alluded to that before, so either she didn’t do her homework in Opposition or she hasn’t been straight up with the House about how exactly lifting the wages of disabled workers by topping up employers would have resulted in job losses.
acuity.explanation: He takes the Minister's own defence — that preparing policy and meeting the sector is the job of an Opposition spokesperson — and turns it into a fork against her: either that homework was not done, or the job-loss claim is not straight. The rebuttal is built out of the specific thing she just said and could not have been delivered against a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "one of the jobs in Opposition is that you are preparing your policies to take into an election" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Why did the Minister make claims previously that going ahead with the wage supplement would have resulted in job losses and now she is quiet when asked to substantiate those claims and explain how?
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Upston's immediately preceding answer was substantive. The question is in the same Estimates examination but engages no part of what she just said; it restates a prepared line of attack about the wage supplement and the Minister's silence. There is a gesture at the Minister's non-answering, which lifts it off the floor, but nothing in the content of her answer is taken up, so the question would read identically whatever she had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston spoke about social sector commissioning, REAP contracts and the 2,100 community job coaching places, and this question does not take any of that up — it returns to an earlier, unrelated line about the wage supplement.

acuity.statement: The first is, Minister, when will we see the first construction activity that you have promised for the key roads of National Party significance—projects like the second Mount Victoria tunnel—and what is the time line that we can expect around that?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific programme Brown had just advanced as his headline achievement and presses it on the one thing his opening left out — when anything will actually be built — naming a project within it. That is engagement with a strand of the preceding turn rather than its whole argument, and the second half of the contribution (South Island funding) moves to prepared ground, so it sits mid-scale rather than at the top. Scored on engagement only: the jibe "roads of National Party significance" is a civility/focus matter and is not allowed to move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we have issued the new Government policy statement on transport, which outlines our roads of national significance programme and puts that back on the agenda and gets it back on track" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I’m keen to know about the targets the Minister and the New Zealand Transport Authority have around the repair of potholes on our State highway networks, particularly around having them fixed within 24 hours.
acuity.explanation: Eligible, and a government backbencher is held to the same test as anyone else. The question is squarely on the subject under examination (road maintenance) and brushes the maintenance strand of the Minister's opening, but it engages no claim actually made: it supplies a new topic for the Minister to expand on rather than responding. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate — 0.3, not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Simeon Brown spoke about a "91 percent increase in funding for road maintenance on our State highways", and this question does not take that figure or claim up — it introduces 24-hour repair targets as fresh material.

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: if the goal is economic productivity and cost-effectiveness, why has he promised and committed to a series of projects for which we don’t know the true cost and we have no idea of the actual economic benefit?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact justification Brown had just given for the programme — economic growth and productivity — and turns it into the premise of the question, then confronts it with the Transport Agency chair's committee evidence that the economic evaluation does not yet exist. The question could not have been written without his claim: substitute a different defence of the programme and this contribution would have to change. Scored on engagement alone; whether the inference or the figures hold is a matter for rigor and veracity, not this attribute.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our ambitious agenda to help unlock the economic growth and productivity that these roads will do" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: My understanding is, I think, 95 percent on tier one State highways within 24 hours and 85 percent on other State highways within 24 hours—must be repaired within 24 hours.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the figure the question asked for, on the precise metric asked about, including the tier distinction. This is the clearest form of responsiveness: the answer delivers the requested quantity rather than restating the Minister's general position. Marked slightly below the top only because the figures are offered with a hedge rather than confirmed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "particularly around having them fixed within 24 hours" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: In terms of the roads of national significance, which the member likes to talk a lot about, in terms of the South Island, we’ve identified the Woodend Bypass as being a road of national significance and the Hope Bypass as being a road of national significance.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the factual premise of Utikere's charge by naming South Island projects designated as roads of national significance.
