The reply would have had to be different had McAnulty asked something else about next week's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "By my calculation, there still is one owing to the House."

acuity.statement: I think that in order to address some of the concerns the previous speaker, Rachel Boyack, has mentioned in terms of the ongoing work and policy work around harm minimisation—but I also want to draw Madam Chair’s attention and also the Minister’s attention to the fact that this particular bill has had no regulatory impact statement.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding speaker's contribution — her request for the Minister's harm-minimisation policy work on class 3 gambling — and does something with it, adding that the bill carries no regulatory impact statement and so offers no evidence base for assessing that harm. It then returns to his own prepared material on the bill's title and the permanence point, which is why this is a partial rather than full engagement; but the speech would have had to change had Boyack argued something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "what is the ongoing policy work to reflect the need for harm minimisation approaches for gambling generally, specifically related to class 3"

acuity.statement: Thank you, and I thank the committee for the range of questions on harm minimisation. I believe the concern is genuine across the committee, but I don’t believe it is accurate in proportion to the level of risk of gambling harm for class 3 lotteries. When consulted on this particular bill, officials from the Ministry of Health didn’t indicate any concern that class 3 lotteries result in harm or that any amendment would change this. When you look at some of the statistics from the Problem Gambling Foundation, a major gambling harm service provider, that they came to the Governance and Administration Committee with, they were very, very, very low statistics in terms of gambling harm. There is data that is collected, and I don’t believe any more data would change that. It would be actually very resource intensive in terms of the effective use of resources.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Davidson's specific ask — more data/insight on gambling harm so the bill's impact can be measured — and answers it on its own terms: the officials consulted raised no concern, the harm provider's own select committee statistics were very low, existing data exists, and more collection would not change the picture and would be resource intensive. The reply would have had to be different had the preceding question been about something other than harm measurement. It also picks up the Heart Foundation submission Davidson's colleagues raised. Marked down from 1.0 only because it declines to engage the review-clause mechanism as such, answering the underlying worry instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "whether the Minister had put time or thought into the idea of review clauses or further insights being made available so that the impact of this bill"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Minister, for the response to that question. I think something that the Minister mentioned in terms of how the data is currently captured also reminded me of something else that I mentioned, which I wanted to ask the Minister about, which is the way that the remote interactive method that is currently being used is done by, for example, phone calling. One of the options is that, when you’re phone calling, they’re able to take payment over the phone.
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the specific content of the Minister's answer — her point that online ticket purchases capture purchaser data and can be passed to health agencies — and draws out its consequence, turning the data-capture claim into a question about privacy and payment information under a permanent regime. It also picks up her reference to the Heart Foundation submission. Not 1.0 because it extends rather than contests the claim, and moves to a new question the Minister had not addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "If they’re buying a ticket online, that data is captured and they are able to provide any concern to the Ministry of Health"

acuity.statement: Just further in relation to the Amendment Paper, I would be interested to know whether those were changes that were generated from the Parliamentary Counsel Office—whether they were simple drafting corrections or clarifications—or whether that was, in fact, departmental advice.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: 'We also have a question around the Amendment Paper, around drafting changes. The first change clarifies that the policy intent of the bill is that the judge should look at all relevant conduct...'

acuity.statement: Although the Family Courts are part of the District Court, my question is whether these provisions will protect someone from, say, a civil claim in the District Court or a claim through the employment processes, including the employment court—say, for a family company that employs spouses—or not.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's explanation — that the court looks broadly at behaviour in and outside the proceedings — and probes its jurisdictional limit. It engages the mechanism just described rather than any specific claim made in the preceding turns, and does not take up Andersen's concern at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: 'First, they need to look broadly at the behaviour inside and out of court proceedings, focusing on the intent of the behaviour to determine whether it's litigant abuse'

acuity.statement: Given that we’re now talking about “Consequential amendments”, which also deal with proceedings of an abusive nature, including vexatious proceedings in the Family Proceedings Act and similar provisions in the Care of Children Act, I think the question still stands: what’s the scope of this, and how do we ensure that this form of family violence, which is controlling and abusive behaviour, in courts other than simply the Family Court is captured?
acuity.explanation: The speech is shaped entirely by what did and did not happen in the preceding turns: it re-puts the unanswered scope question and re-anchors it in the clause now before the committee. Had the Minister answered, this contribution would not have been given in this form. It persists with the substance rather than merely complaining of the silence, though it engages no new argument because none was offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith's reply, which answered the earlier questions on 'conduct' and litigant abuse but did not take up the jurisdictional scope point: 'Limiting the definition of "conduct" to particular types of behaviour would likely narrow it...'

acuity.statement: It won’t apply to other jurisdictions outside the scope of this bill, but protections around vexatious litigation do apply in the other areas.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the direct answer to the precise question put: the provisions do not reach beyond this bill's jurisdiction, and the gap Webb identified is covered by existing vexatious-litigation protections. The reply engages the content of the question rather than its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'Will this extend to the wider courts, only the District Court, or only the District Court in exercise of its family jurisdiction?'

acuity.statement: In terms of the procedural safeguards to protect the right of justice, to prevent it being used against victims, there is the requirement for evidence that the party’s conduct demonstrates both the intent and the effect of litigant abuse, and there is also judicial discretion about whether or not to make an order.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Andersen's specific worry — that a perpetrator could turn the new order against a victim — and answers it with the two safeguards that bear on exactly that scenario. He engages her concern rather than restating the bill's purpose, though he addresses the safeguard question more squarely than her separate request about monitoring and review.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: 'there was a concern that this provision could be used by the perpetrator against the victim when the victim was potentially seeking a protection order'

acuity.statement: The previous speaker, the Hon Ginny Andersen, has already possibly mentioned an element of this, but one of the things I would still like clarification from the Minister on is: when we are looking at this particular bill and also other aspects of the vexatious proceedings within the Family Proceedings Act, it’s still within the context of behaviours or acts that are sort of, I guess, with the knowledge of the judge or with the knowledge of the court.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker and notes she touched the same area, but does nothing with her argument: Andersen pressed on name suppression and Family Court dissatisfaction, and this turn pivots to a fresh clause 18 clarification about vexatious proceedings. A gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the content, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.

acuity.responding_to: "the issue of name suppression and the ability for victims of sexual violence to be able to have power over whether their name is suppressed or not is a very important issue that overlaps directly with litigation abuse" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb proposed that the bill be named the "Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Emily Henderson Bill" to recognise the former MP's contribution, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The Act comes into force by Order in Council or one year after Royal assent. The 12-month lead time is necessary to make changes to the court rules, such as the Family Court rules, the District Court rules, or the High Court rules, so that’s what we’re doing, and then it will take effect.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the reason the preceding question asked for — why no fixed commencement date — naming the court-rule changes that require the 12-month lead time. The answer would have been different had a different question been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to know why there are provisions around this bill that it has to come into force after an Order in Council, and, if there is no Order in Council, it will come into force one year after Royal assent." — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Whilst the Minister did pick up some of my work and require the insurer to settle a claim within a reasonable time, it simply doesn’t go far enough. Webb takes up that exact provision, accepts it as far as it goes, and disputes it on a different axis — that the list of factors lacks an enforcement remedy. The speech would have to change if Hamilton had defended a different clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "One of the things which we settled on was that insurance claims are paid within a reasonable time frame, and that was a little bit of a sticking point."

acuity.statement: However, there are definitely good elements of this bill and I think some of the speakers have highlighted that one of the key elements of this bill, among many others, is the distinction between what is considered a non-consumer insurance contract and a consumer insurance contract.
acuity.explanation: A generic nod to 'some of the speakers' that engages no claim actually made before him. The speech would have had to be different had Davidson not raised that press report.

acuity.statement: They just can’t help themselves, can they? They have to get in a dig about how much they hate tax cuts, even with inflation at all-time lows and tackling the cost of living crisis.

A gesture at what preceded it rather than an engagement with its content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'That has meant a culture of delay, denial, and deferral, and that has caused problems across the industry.' — she acknowledges the human cost in general terms but does not take up the good-faith duty argument.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'I must say, whilst this, in the Statutes Amendment Bill, looks innocuous, we do have concerns that we want to raise at select committee.' — and his specific point that the reporting time for lawyers moves 'from three days out to five days'. This statement does not take up either; it declares the bill non-controversial and universally supported.

He’s a man who prides himself on his maths, and, unfortunately, he must have read a speech that was prepared last year rather than this, because he will recall—he’s not going to sleep tonight when he realises this—that he said that the 1999 legislation that this updates was prepared just about a quarter century ago.

Not a full 1.0 because what he engages is an incidental dating slip rather than any argument about the bill's substance, so the engagement, though pointable and precise, is narrow.

acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "there are 42 Acts that are being amended as a result of this" and "I would not say necessarily minor in terms of the things that we’re updating"

acuity.explanation: Engages the modernising-language strand running through the preceding turns and supplies a counterweight to it with his own example, but engages the topic rather than any specific claim made, then returns to prepared material about public submissions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "it is a good thing that we’re modernising pieces of legislation to ensure that not only do they reflect the modern times"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that "minor, technical, and non-controversial" is subjective and that some amendments are not minor, and this statement does not take that up

Therefore, as has been said across the House, there’s not a lot to say other than to move this quickly through to select committee.
acuity.explanation: On the subject under debate but engages no part of any preceding argument, restating the housekeeping framing and urging the bill through to select committee. The gesture at "as has been said across the House" names the debate without taking up its content.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued some amendments are "not necessarily minor" and Andy Foster and Tim Costley raised specific clauses; this statement takes up none of them

acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject — his own flick-through of two amendments and a commendation — which would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said about whether the changes are truly minor.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that the wage-recovery and employment-agreement changes are not minor; this statement asserts the opposite framing without engaging it

acuity.statement: One of the things we canvassed somewhat was what does one do when a ship that is registered in New Zealand is behaving poorly in international waters. How do we manage that? Or vice versa, when there is a ship that is flagged to a different nation that is breaking international fishing rules in the jurisdiction that we have some say over. How do you manage the right to, for example, impound the vessel and take action that could be deemed as challenging in terms of the jurisdiction of our nation over that nation’s flagged vessel? One of the things we got to was the necessity to get the permission of the flagged nation to take that action.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Parker and takes up one specific strand of Parker's speech — the bill's new extraterritorial powers over foreign and unflagged vessels, which Parker described as the step that 'until recent years has been contentious' and as 'quite complex'. Abel engages that content rather than merely name-checking Parker: he sets out the two directions of the jurisdictional problem and adds the flag-state-permission requirement the committee landed on, which qualifies Parker's account of the enforcement powers. It is development of the same point rather than a rebuttal of a specific claim, and the remainder of his speech is prepared committee material on submissions, so this sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: 'There are powers now that will be conferred on New Zealand authorities to stop those vessels, particularly unflagged vessels, and to hold them up in port if they’re in a New Zealand port'

acuity.responding_to: "the Paddle Ferns, our women's canoe polo team, who were in China. They took out the finals, with a dominant performance against Italy" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: The reason for pausing this is to ensure that that work can be undertaken and that those who might otherwise be required to come up with their farm plans are not doing it against the changes—or are doing it with the current legislation rather than what’s going to be changed. It’s to avoid duplication and to enable farmers to be working with the correct information.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Pham's question directly — the reason the Amendment Papers were introduced — and supplies an actual rationale for the farm-plan pause (avoiding duplication while the system is reworked). But she leaves untouched the two sharpest things put to her: whether the timing was designed to pre-empt Otago Regional Council's notification decision, and the charge that her stated goal is workable standards rather than freshwater improvement. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to the prepared justification.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why has the Government introduced these two last-minute Amendment Papers?" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: Sticking with Amendment Paper 127, which is the one about farm plans, can the Minister explain what she means by “risk based” and what her understanding is of the regulations?
acuity.explanation: Lifts the exact term the Minister had just used to justify the pause and presses her to define it. This question could not have been written in advance of the answer it follows — had Simmonds justified the pause on different grounds, the question would have had to change. Textbook high responsiveness; the vagueness of what counts as an adequate answer is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "including ensuring that it is risk based and therefore able to react to both the risks in specific catchments and to the type of farming that is being undertaken" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: We also heard the Minister answer, too, the Hon David Parker’s question around Te Mana o te Wai not requiring everything to always be declined because something might go wrong with the health of the water, when it’s applied to consents, and the Minister responded, “Well, there are cases on this.” I would like to know what cases the Minister is referring to, and what the outcomes of those cases were. My understanding is that the cases that some submitters referred to are ones where a consent would have been declined regardless of Te Mana o te Wai.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the evidentiary basis of the Minister's earlier answer: identifies the specific claim (that there are cases where the hierarchy operated as an absolute), demands the cases be named with their outcomes, and offers a counter-reading that those consents would have failed on adverse effects regardless. Engages the content and does something with it — the strongest form of responsiveness, and disagreement does not reduce it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My understanding is that there have been varied approaches by different councils to this matter, and that in some instances the hierarchy had been considered as an absolute." — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Rachel Brooking for bringing the attention of the committee to the streamlining and simplifying of the process to prepare and amend national direction. I thank, also, the Primary Production Committee, who made considerable input into this in terms of setting the 20-working-days requirement for consultation, and other amendments which they contributed to around the transparency of the Minister making this decision and making the information public. The board of inquiry process, as the member has already noted, hadn’t been used since, I think, 2010 and therefore has been taken from the process to simplify it as one process that will be undertaken.
acuity.explanation: Answers one of Brooking's questions squarely — why the board of inquiry was removed — and even picks up her own concession that it had rarely been used, turning it into the reason for removal. She also points at the 20-working-day consultation requirement, which touches her consultation-loosening point. But she does not take up the definition of "risk based" she had just been pressed on, the environmental protections during the pause, or the named cases, so this engages some strands and not the ones most directly put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why the Government saw fit to get rid of the ability to have a board of inquiry process when developing these national policy directions" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: Has she proposed any modifications to the “manifestly unjust” provisions contained within the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill?
acuity.explanation: Eligible: McKee's preceding turn made substantive claims (submissions show overwhelming support; the proposals will strengthen the regime). Cameron's question stays inside the same matter and picks up the 'proposals' she just referred to, asking whether one specific provision is among them. But it engages none of her actual claims — not the submissions claim, not the 'go even further' claim — and reads as a prepared supplementary that would have been asked whatever she had said. Sits above the bare-topic band because the provision asked about is a live part of the thing she described, below 0.5 because no strand of her argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "these proposals to strengthen the three-strikes regime will do" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: If I may, I would just like to pick up and extrapolate on the introductory comments from my colleague the Hon Rachel Brooking, to provide those who are watching this with some context. There is indeed scheduled to be a large public meeting in Otago, which would have been at the Otago Regional Council offices normally but has moved to a public venue that is much bigger—the Hutton Theatre—so that people can watch the vote take place on this amendment that my colleague referred to, just tabled today with no input on the Primary Production Committee.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific amendment Brooking had just flagged — the one aimed at tomorrow's Otago Regional Council meeting — and does something with it: supplies the particulars Brooking left out (the venue change, the 7-5 split, the consultation spend, the OIA/LGOIMA requests) and extends her 'outrageous process' argument into a named charge of overreach. If Brooking had argued something else about Part 1, this speech would have had to change. Short of 1.0 because it amplifies rather than tests the preceding argument — it supplies evidence for a claim already made instead of rebutting, conceding or correcting any part of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "One of them seems to be specifically directed at the Otago Regional Council that is planning to meet tomorrow to notify its freshwater plan." — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: The reason why I’m asking this question is this is what, as I understand it, lies behind the logic as to why this bill amends the resource management regime by saying that the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management hierarchy is not to be used in respect of a decision as to whether someone can get a resource consent to discharge to water or to abstract water.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it in the same Part 1 debate. Squarely on the matter under debate and a gesture at the freshwater strand Brooking flagged at clause 4, but the argument is built entirely from the speaker's own Primary Production Committee exchange with officials, not from anything said in the preceding turns. It would have been delivered word-for-word had Brooking and Leary argued differently about Part 1, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the topic connection to the preceding turn is real. Note this is low Acuity with high Rigor — the inference from 'officials confirmed there is no absolute hierarchy' to 'the provision is misconceived' is tight — and the two must not be allowed to move together.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "one of those things is to do with the national policy for freshwater management. We see that straight up at clause 4" — Rachel Brooking. Engages the subject she named but no part of her or Leary's argument: Brooking argued the process was an abuse and Leary argued ministerial interference in the Otago council, and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: The reason I didn’t immediately answer the member’s question about the national direction was the manner in which the question was asked. It assumed that there was no intent by this Government to protect the environment. There absolutely is.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one named strand of Brooking's wrap-up questions — the national direction/environment point — and disputes its premise directly, then moves to prepared material on freshwater work. The two other questions put to her (what evidence exists that Te Mana o te Wai alone blocked consents, and the clause 21 identification questions) are not taken up at all, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "whether or not the Minister could give any comfort around national direction, actually, protecting the environment rather than just being a development jolly for the Government"

acuity.statement: I think what I’m really interested in hearing from the Minister is: why the stopping of the actual identification?
acuity.explanation: Pham explicitly takes up the strand Brooking opened on clause 21 and presses the same specific question about why identification must cease, adding her own reasoning about why the information itself has value. She engages a preceding member's content rather than merely naming her, but she does not take up the Minister's intervening answer, and much of the turn is her own prepared amendment case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "why is it that the identification of those areas has to stop?"

acuity.statement: Contrary to what the member said, the suspension does not undermine or otherwise change requirements set out in the RMA—I believe section 6—with respect to the maintenance or protection of indigenous biodiversity. Any area of significant biodiversity identified during the suspension period, though, will not have the SNA provisions applied to it.
acuity.explanation: This directly contradicts the specific claim Pham had just made about the clause's effect, names the statutory provision it says is untouched, and then concedes the precise respect in which Pham is right (SNA provisions will not apply during the suspension). The turn would have to be worded differently had Pham argued something else; it is shy of 1.0 only because Pham's question about the effect on councils' other NPSIB duties goes unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "this clause directly impacts the effective and consistent identification, and therefore eventually steps to protect that biodiversity"

acuity.statement: Now, I was wearing another hat at the time, but my understanding was that this was a major problem in Environment Canterbury, and there was a huge backlog of consents. There was a decision made by Environment Canterbury, or their opinion was that under Te Mana o te Wai, they were unable to grant new consents or renew consents where the river was overallocated.
acuity.explanation: Hoggard supplies exactly the thing the preceding opposition questions demanded and the Minister had not provided — a named example of the hierarchy of obligations blocking consents — and does so on his own account. The turn is unintelligible without the question it answers, which is the mark of high responsiveness; whether the Canterbury account is accurate is a veracity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "What analysis has the Minister got that Te Mana o te Wai was being used in resource consenting decisions and that aspect alone was blocking the granting of those decisions"

acuity.statement: I would like to just pick up on some of the comments made by the Hon David Parker and get your clarity on this, because I think you reference he did actually answer some of his own questions. For my clarity, the example of the Manuherikia River and the minimum flow, would that be one of the reasons why you would be bringing this measure here today?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's preceding point that the previous speaker had answered his own question, and does something with it: converts it into a concrete test case (the Manuherikia minimum flow) and asks the Minister to confirm whether that is the kind of situation the measure addresses. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had said something else. Not a 1.0 because much of the engagement is with an absent speaker's example rather than with the reasoning of the turn immediately before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The member essentially answered his question himself that the restricting of the notification of freshwater planning instruments is until either a new National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management takes effect or 31 December 2025" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. The member is absolutely correct: the Government is reviewing and replacing the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management (NPSFM), for those who perhaps haven’t picked that up, and the time frame for that is an 18- to 24-month period. The Government has previously signalled to enable councils to have sufficient time to incorporate the replacement NPSFM the extended deadline to December 2027. Although most councils have picked up on that, some have not.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the confirmation Patterson sought, accepts his characterisation and supplies the specific material it was missing — the 18-to-24-month replacement timetable, the extended December 2027 deadline, and that some councils have not acted on it. The reply is shaped by the question put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can the Minister confirm that what she is trying to do here is cut off that chain of events, to seek what she has instructed councils fairly carefully... to pause their planning process till the central government has worked through its NPSFM" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Right, as you know, I’m working through the clauses, but I would remind the Minister that there’s a number of questions I asked that have not been answered yet. A couple were on the farm plans. What does “risk based” mean, and what regulations will remain to protect our environment from pollution?
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of the Minister's preceding answer on notification and the NPSFM timetable; it is on the matter under debate (the bill's clauses) and gestures at the exchange by noting questions remain unanswered, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than below it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds had just explained the NPSFM replacement timetable and the reason for restricting notification, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it returns to the speaker's own earlier, unanswered questions on farm plans.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I don’t recall that I referred to cases. I said there was variability in how the councils had been interpreting the absoluteness or otherwise of the hierarchy. I don’t recall that, at any stage, I referred specifically to any cases. In terms of the freshwater farm plans in the short period between the pause and when the farm plan system has been improved, regional councils—many of the councils themselves—have localised regulations, and a number of the farming practices have changed considerably in that time.
acuity.explanation: Takes up both strands Brooking restated: it corrects her premise that cases had been referred to, substituting what was actually said about variability in councils' interpretation, and then addresses the interim-protection question during the farm plan pause. Short of 1.0 because the second strand is answered at the level of the topic (localised regulations, catchment groups, changed practice) rather than by naming the regulations asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Then I had a further question on Te Mana o te Wai and the cases that the Minister was referring to" and "whilst we wait for these paused farm plans, what is there to protect the environment from pollution in the meantime?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: That doesn’t answer my question, though, which was—the answer appears to be “Well, there are catchment groups now.”, and my question was: what regulation remains?
acuity.explanation: Engages the content of the answer just given by summarising what it amounted to and showing that it does not reach the question asked. It could only have been said in reply to that specific answer, which is the mark of close attention; it is vague on substance, but that is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There are catchment groups across the country, so there is considerable work that has been going on that will continue to go on" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: I actually want to bring the Minister back to an earlier line of questioning from the Hon Rachel Brooking. In the regulatory impact statement are the options for pausing the implementation of the freshwater farm plan. This is quite a specific question really. Is analysis done on the safeguards to environmental and human health?
acuity.explanation: Abel follows a substantive turn by Parker on the clause 23A amendment and engages none of it, instead reaching back past the preceding speaker to resume Brooking's earlier line on the freshwater farm plan pause. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive to the proceeding, but it would read identically whatever Parker had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker argued the clause 23A test is 'too loose' and asked the Minister to accept inserting 'meaningful' before 'reduction', and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: I have already covered that area—about the very brief pause between when the farm plans work has been done to improve that system and the fact that there are other local provisions. There is work that’s been done already with farmers, with catchment groups, so the period will be relatively short and the work that is being undertaken will continue on.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the strand of Abel's question about the pause itself, arguing it is short and mitigated by catchment work, and closes by referring to 'the sort of issues that you brought up'. But Abel asked specifically what the negative impacts on waterways and human health are, as flagged in the regulatory impact statement, and she supplies no part of that; the answer addresses the topic rather than the claim put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what are the negative impacts on the health of waterways and people that is risked by pausing the farm plans?" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: Just going back to remind the Minister of a couple of questions she hasn’t answered—then I will move on—one was about the indigenous biodiversity national policy statement (NPS) and why stopping the identification—she’s answered the implementation question that it was in the 100-day plan, and it’s had impacts that the Government feels are unreasonable on private property owners. But why stop the identification? That’s one question remaining.
acuity.explanation: The turn is firmly inside the same committee-stage debate and gestures at the exchange by noting which questions remain unanswered, but it engages no content of the Minister's immediately preceding answer. Noting that a question was not answered is a reference to the exchange rather than engagement with what was said, so this sits at the top of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds' preceding turn answered Steve Abel on the 'very brief pause' before the farm plans work, and this statement does not take that up; Brooking instead resumes her own earlier questions

acuity.statement: In terms of the restricting of the notification of freshwater plans—and, again, I’m repeating—this is to avoid inefficiencies. It’s to avoid duplication of work and costs to ratepayers, in terms of having to amend plans once the new National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management (NPSFM) is gazetted.
acuity.explanation: She comes back to the precise mechanism Brooking had just challenged — the restriction on notifying freshwater planning instruments — and offers the duplication-and-ratepayer-cost rationale plus the 18-to-24-month timeframe, so one strand of the preceding argument is engaged. But Brooking's specific challenge was her stated presumption that the replacement NPSFM will allow more pollution than Otago's plan, which she asked be answered on the record, and that goes unaddressed as the Minister returns, by her own admission, to repeating prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what she is so scared about in the Otago Regional Council’s plan—that hasn’t yet been notified" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Minister, for joining us this afternoon. I hope with your leave, Minister, we could actually talk about the slope maps and the changes to slope map rules.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed argument from David Parker about outcomes-based freshwater regulation versus input controls, and engages none of it — it is a pleasantry plus a request to change subject to slope maps. The turn would read identically whatever Parker had said, though it is at least about the bill under consideration, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker had just argued that "input controls are really simple" and that refusing to let the outcomes-based framework work will drive councils to them, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Also, thank you, Minister, before, for pointing out the new edition of new section 44(3)(a) in clause 10. Now, I do understand where the Minister is coming from in that this is something that the Primary Production Committee has discussed and, then, that (3)(a) was added as an insertion. However, the Minister hasn’t really answered my question in terms of addressing the concerns that I have around the scope of new section 43(3) of clause 10 in the first place.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific answer — that the inserted (3)(a) addresses the concern — accepts what it does establish, and then shows what it leaves untouched (the scope of new section 43(3)), going on to press the point with concrete tests: an FTA obligation under (3)(b) and removed Te Tiriti clauses under (3)(e). The speech would be substantially different had the Minister answered differently, which is the mark of high responsiveness. Scored just below the top only because the engaged turn cannot be pointed at inside the supplied window.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds' preceding answer (immediately before this window) pointing out the select committee's insertion of new section 44(3)(a) in clause 10 — Xu-Nan names it as "pointing out the new edition of new section 44(3)(a) in clause 10". The engaged turn falls just outside the text supplied, so it cannot be quoted verbatim here.

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Madam Chair. It’s been interesting over the last hour or so to listen to this debate, although it feels quite one-sided. I guess, as I come to my question—well, firstly, it’s really about the Minister feeling comfortable and explaining, herself, that she feels comfortable around allowing these two rather significant Amendment Papers to be dropped today, and if she can explain how she feels comfortable with Amendment Papers 127 and 128 being tabled by her colleague, the Hon Chris Bishop.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the Amendment Papers before the committee — but engages no part of the arguments made by the members who preceded him. The gesture at the debate ("it feels quite one-sided") is a reference, not an engagement, and the prepared questions about the Minister's comfort and Amendment Paper 128 would have been put whatever Xu-Nan or Parker had argued. That places it at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan had just argued that new section 43(3) lets the Minister bypass the section 46A process to implement an international agreement, and this statement does not take it up; the only engagement with the preceding turns is the general remark that the debate "feels quite one-sided".

acuity.statement: I’ll answer the questions from the Green Party member, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan. The bill clarifies and expands the circumstances where minor updates to national direction can be made without a consultation and submission process, but before making a decision, the Minister is required to consider the appropriateness of using the full section 46A process. After making the minor update, the Minister has to be transparent about publishing the reasons for the update. In terms of judicial review, there is always a judicial review opportunity for decisions that are made within the Resource Management Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up two identifiable strands of the question actually put — the 46A appropriateness test and the judicial-review consequence — and supplies a direct answer on the latter, so the reply is clearly shaped by what preceded it. It stops short of the top of the scale because the two sharpest strands of Xu-Nan's argument, the FTA bypass under (3)(b) and the removal of Te Tiriti considerations under (3)(e), go unaddressed, and the Regulations Review Committee limb is dropped.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "there is no guidance or clarification of how a Minister is able to make that appropriate decision on whether 46A, under clause 11, should be followed" — and his closing question about whether a misjudgement "would that trigger either a judicial review or, potentially, something before the Regulations Review Committee?"

acuity.statement: In terms of the member who has just taken his seat, Glen Bennett, I don’t think it’s of any interest to members of this committee or the wider community whether I am comfortable or not. There are amendments that have been tabled, and they are here for us to debate.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact framing Bennett used and does something with it — rejects its premise, arguing that a Minister's comfort is not a matter for the committee — so the reply is visibly addressed to what was said. But it engages only that framing and leaves the substantive questions Bennett put entirely alone, in particular why clause 40B fixes the date at 22 October 2024 and what would change if that date moved, which keeps it around the midpoint rather than above it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "it’s really about the Minister feeling comfortable and explaining, herself, that she feels comfortable around allowing these two rather significant Amendment Papers to be dropped today".

acuity.statement: I would remind the member that, while retrospective legislation is not the norm, it has been used before. In fact, the Labour Party will remember their own Sir Michael Cullen, who brought in taxation law that was retrospective. The next version of the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management (NPSFM) is going to occur over the next 18 to 24 months. There will be a considerable consultation period, and so I will not predetermine—and I think it’s unfortunate that the member is trying to predetermine—what might be in the next NPSFM.
acuity.explanation: Takes up both of Brooking's specific lines of attack and does something with each: answers the retrospectivity challenge with a precedent (Cullen's retrospective tax law), and rebuts the 'unless the new NPSFM allows more pollution' inference by naming the 18-24 month timeline and refusing to predetermine the content, calling Brooking's inference predetermination. She also addresses the exemptions-clause question Brooking asked. Would read quite differently had Brooking argued something else. Not 1.0 because she leaves Brooking's direct request to confirm the Otago Regional Council motive, and the question about incentives to split plans, untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "I also ask the Minister how she can justify the use of a retrospective clause." and "The justification of efficiency just makes no sense unless—unless—her next version of the NPSFM is going to allow more pollution."

acuity.statement: I’d like to take the Minister to clause 10(4), which inserts a new section 44(3), which describes the circumstances when a Minister, without going through a more fulsome process, can make a change to a national environment standard, is my understanding. In particular, I want to draw the attention to the one-sided nature of paragraph (d).
acuity.explanation: Eligible (a substantive turn by another member precedes, in the same committee-stage debate) but unresponsive: the speech moves to an entirely different clause and would be word-for-word identical whatever Simmonds had just said. It stays on the matter under debate — the same bill — so it sits at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0, since it could not have been delivered in a different debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds spoke about the precedent for retrospective legislation, the 18-24 month NPSFM process and the exemptions pathway, and this statement does not take any of it up — it opens a self-contained clause-by-clause analysis of clause 10(4).

acuity.statement: I would like to ask a few questions in relation to Amendment Paper 128, because I think we want to really understand what the rationale behind these changes is. What we can see here is a last-minute amendment that really looks like it’s giving the middle finger to localism and to Otago.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what precedes: he presses the same rationale question Brooking raised about Amendment Paper 128 and takes up the Otago council meeting she identified ('As has been canvassed, there will be a meeting tomorrow'), and he contests the duplication/cost rationale rather than merely naming it. But he does not engage Simmonds' actual answer — the retrospectivity precedent or the NPSFM timeline — and the rest of the turn is prepared material on the EU free-trade agreement and the Otago hospital protests that would have been delivered whatever had just been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "we know that the Otago Regional Council is meeting tomorrow on 23 October 2024 to notify their plan" — and the efficiency/duplication rationale she reported from the Minister.

acuity.statement: The member somehow is conflating this restriction as an end to localism. The restriction is in place until either a new NPSFM takes effect or 31 December next year—whichever is the sooner. It is a relatively short period of time. It is to ensure that there is not duplication of effort, time, and money so that the council can take into consideration the new NPSFM.
acuity.explanation: Names Willis' central claim and disputes its reasoning directly — that a time-limited restriction is not the end of localism — and supplies the duplication rationale he explicitly asked her to justify. Held below the top of the scale because she opens by repeating previously given information and entirely ignores his other pointed question about assessments of the impact on the EU free-trade agreement, so only part of the turn she follows is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "this amendment has made a nonsense of the idea that Otago has local decision-making independence" and "why the Minister thinks the costs will increase because of duplication".

acuity.statement: I’m sorry the member did not hear before when I made it very explicit that this Government wants to see improvements in fresh water over time and that our Resource Management Act work will be towards that. In terms of the clarifications around the consenting discharges, again, there are matters there that were creating uncertainty that some discharges in degraded catchments while providing for improvement over time might be turned down.
acuity.explanation: Takes up two strands Pham actually raised — her explicit question about whether freshwater improvement is a Government goal, and the rationale for the discharge-permit clause — and answers them on their own terms. It is partial rather than full engagement: it does not touch her clause 23 point about higher-order planning instruments, nor the Environmental Law Initiative finding that ECan has kept granting discharge consents, which was the evidentiary core of her challenge. The reply would clearly have been different had Pham argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "Is freshwater improvement an actual goal of this Government? I’m yet to hear it." — and her challenge that "the rationale for this clause change that will massively impact fresh water not only in Canterbury but across the country—the rationale is not there."

acuity.statement: The member somehow implies that this gives consent. In fact, this aligns coalmining with other extractive industries. The same gateway tests would still apply. The management of significant adverse effects on wetlands and significant natural areas (SNAs) would apply.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific premise in Abel's attack — that the bill authorises destruction of wetlands for coalmining — names it, and disputes it by asserting the clause only aligns coal with other extractive activities while the gateway tests and wetland/SNA effects management remain. That is engaging the content of the argument, not merely referencing the speaker. Short of 1.0 because it leaves Abel's second strand entirely alone: that coal is burnt and wetlands are carbon sinks, so the trade-off is doubly damaging.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "There’s an extraordinary proposal in this legislation that enables the intrusion into wetlands and removal of protection from wetlands to facilitate coalmining."

acuity.statement: Does the Minister understand that coalmining is different from other mining because coal is burnt and produces climate change emissions, and that is why there was an exclusion—or a specific “no more new coalmining”?
acuity.explanation: Aims directly at the load-bearing word in the Minister's immediately preceding answer — "aligning" coal with all other mining — and attacks the equivalence it rests on, arguing coal was treated separately precisely because it is combusted. The question could not have been asked in this form if the Minister had defended the clause on any other ground, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "So it is simply aligning coalmining with all other mining."

acuity.statement: The questions from the member the Hon Rachel Brooking regarding intensive winter grazing—and she mentioned slope land, but I don’t know that there was a question in that—yes, there have been significant improvements made, and I think that the member does an incredible disservice to farmers to suggest that this was brought about only because of the regulations that were brought in, I think, in 2022.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's central causal claim — that the improvements are an effect of the regulations — concedes the improvements and disputes the attribution, naming farmers' own long-running practice change as the cause. The speech would have been different had Brooking argued something else.
