acuity.explanation: Bennett takes up the specific causal claim Jones had just made — that the 2018 exploration ban destroyed the gas industry — and attacks it on its own ground, citing the select committee report and the Minister's own officials to date the decline to 2014. He says himself he looked the report up while the Minister was speaking; the speech could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument. Whether the rebuttal is fair or well-reasoned is a separate question from whether it engages.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Our gas fields have been in decline, driven down by the ban decision" — Shane Jones.

acuity.statement: Oh, so they’re finding them. The New Plymouth member just said this year they’ve found more. We don’t need this bill then, right? We don’t need to bother with this, because it’s already happening.
acuity.explanation: Bennett picks up MacLeod's interjection in real time and turns it into an argument against the bill: if discoveries are being made under the current regime, the legislation is unnecessary. This is engagement with the content of what was just said and drawing out its consequence, not a mere reference to the interjector. Slightly short of 1.0 only because the interjection it answers is itself a bare assertion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This year—Greymouth." — David MacLeod.

acuity.statement: As this is the second reading, before I talk about the select committee process, I would like to just say that the Green member Steve Abel, as he concluded his speech, the way he said that they are quite determined to bring the ban back if they ever come back in Government, that just shows they don’t understand how to support the economy. They don’t understand how to give that confidence to investors.
acuity.explanation: Parmar names the specific commitment Abel made moments earlier and draws out a consequence from it (loss of investor confidence), so the opening of her speech would have to change had Abel not made that pledge. It stays an assertion about the Greens' understanding rather than an engagement with Abel's reasoning, and she then moves to prepared select committee material, so this sits between a partial and a full take-up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "when there is a change of Government, insofar as it is a Green-influenced Government, we will be bringing back the ban on oil and gas exploration"

acuity.statement: I was actually quite amused to see the way members said that they actually support sun. Thank God they support sun. Thank God they didn’t oppose sun. What would have happened if they opposed sun? I would like to say to that member that oil and gas is also formed through natural geological processes. If those members support nature, oil and gas is also natural, so we need to support that.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific content of Abel's sun/nature framing and turns it against him with a counter-premise that oil and gas are also natural. Whether that inference holds is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one; the passage is unmistakably built on what Abel just said and could not have been delivered against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the Green Party, you’ll be surprised to hear across the House, supports that nuclear energy, that massive hydrogen nuclear energy super generator in the sky called the sun"

acuity.statement: One piece of information that I found very fascinating—and I had to ask again, was this really true?—was that one of the assumptions that was made when the ban happened was that the area that was under consent would stay around the same and the rate of exploration, which had been trending down, as others have mentioned, would continue at that same rate. Imagine if the graph looked kind of like that at the time. They expected that to continue down, and that was one of the assumptions: that supply and demand would keep up. However, what happened was that it went like that, and supply dropped off a cliff and we saw demand stay the same. So that gap between supply and demand went through the roof.
acuity.explanation: Weenink takes Abel's own pre-ban decline claim ('which had been trending down, as others have mentioned') and does something with it, arguing that the ban's modelling assumed that gentle decline would continue while supply in fact fell far faster than demand. The rebuttal is aimed at the specific claim, not merely at the topic, and would have to be rewritten if Abel had argued something else about supply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "gas was in significant decline, actually, before the ban came into place. Gas production peaked in 2001, and it’s been steadily falling since 2014."

acuity.statement: The International Energy Agency recommends that you switch from burning coal—as one of their recommendations for how we reduce our carbon footprint. They recommend going to gas—and they also recommend using nuclear.
acuity.explanation: This engages the exact authority Abel invoked and contests what that authority actually advises, which is a direct correction of the previous speaker's characterisation of the source rather than a pivot to prepared material. Whether her reading of the IEA is accurate is a Veracity matter and is held separate from the responsiveness scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "It even goes against the advice of the International Energy Agency that gas production needs to stop from 2021."

acuity.statement: It was interesting listening to the previous speaker, Helen White, talking about security, because if there’s one thing we actually learnt when the world supply chain was, effectively, shut down during the global COVID disruption, it was that, as a country, we were incredibly exposed and vulnerable in regard to our supply chain. What we need most is security of supply of the things that we actually need.
acuity.explanation: Butterick names the previous speaker and lifts two of her terms — "security" and "the chickens coming home to roost" ("Well, the pigeons have come home to roost") — but changes the sense of both. White's "security" was the decommissioning bond regime that stopped taxpayers paying for abandoned Tūī infrastructure; he answers on security of energy supply, which is a different proposition, and never engages her claim that the bill removes the upfront-payment liability. Her carbon-bomb argument and her brand cost-benefit point go untouched. Picking up an opponent's words in order to pivot is the rubric's example of a mere reference, so this sits in the unresponsive band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the speech is squarely on the bill under debate and his transition question ("Why on earth didn't the previous administration sit down with the energy sector...") at least glances at her concession that "we have a transition issue". Note Helen White's own turn opens the text given, with no preceding member's turn available, so she is ineligible for Acuity rather than low-scoring.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are taking away the level of security that we had, because we made people pay money upfront and we made them responsible" — Helen White

acuity.statement: I’m truly astounded by the contents of this bill tonight, and I’m astounded by the crystal clear short-sightedness of it all.
acuity.explanation: A substantive preceding turn was available, but the speech that follows this opening is prepared climate material that engages no strand of it — no mention of Taranaki, of iwi consultation, or of the transition funding point. It would read identically whatever Ngarewa-Packer had argued, though it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer spoke about Ngā Iwi o Taranaki's specific submissions, the unfunded just transition and what replaces gas in Taranaki, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: Actually, we had five days. When this ban came into place, the Government at the time actually gave only 10 days, or two weeks, and we actually heard more submissions on this bill than the previous bill had in 2018.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact figure Pham used against the bill, concedes it, and does something with it: supplies a comparator for the 2018 process and a submission count. The speech would have to change if the preceding criticism had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the five days that they had—for such a significant bill" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: It’s not a pleasure to stand to take a call on the Crown Minerals Amendment Bill, and I think there’s some irony in the fact that it says on the wall that the date is 5 November 2024 when the rest of the country is ahead of us as it is 6 November 2024.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows a substantive turn by Radhakrishnan (MFAT legal advice on the EU/UK FTAs, the $2.5 billion decommissioning figure, the 16-year exploration-to-production lag) and engages none of it. The speech is prepared material — the select committee process, read submissions, three closing reasons — and would have been delivered word-for-word whatever she had argued. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 only because it is unmistakably about this bill and this select committee, not a speech transferable to another debate. Later passages touch strands she also raised (trade agreements, trailing liability) but develop them independently rather than taking up her claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Priyanca Radhakrishnan argued the repeal is 'likely to breach New Zealand's obligations when it comes to free-trade agreements' and that 'the average time is 16 years' from exploration permit to first production, and this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: I’m reading a submission, because so many of these submissions were not heard.
acuity.explanation: Nimon's interjection makes a specific factual charge about what Davidson is doing; he takes it up directly, corrects it (a submission, not a speech), and turns it into a point about submissions the committee never heard. The reply is wholly contingent on what she said — delete the interjection and the sentence makes no sense. Short of 1.0 only because the thing engaged was itself a one-line interjection rather than an argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "He's reading a speech." — Katie Nimon

acuity.statement: The member opposite said the international advice is that we phase out. Well, the former Government did not phase out; they just stopped.
acuity.explanation: Nimon picks up the exact strand Davidson had just read from the WWF submission and does something with it: she accepts the phase-out framing and turns it against the 2018 ban by distinguishing a managed phase-out from an abrupt stop, which then carries her 'perverse outcomes' argument. Not 1.0 because the bulk of her call is prepared Government material (doubling renewables, roads, the export target) and she does not engage the IPCC evidence itself, only the word 'phase'. Scored purely on engagement — whether the distinction is sound or whether the characterisation of the former Government is fair are other questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "with both the UN Secretary-General and the IPCC calling for the world to phase out coal, oil, and gas—phase it out, not start promoting the exploration for it again" — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: I did want to talk to clause 30, which has an amendment in respect of it, and that is the clause relating to burden of proof.
acuity.explanation: Williams had just put a specific question to the Minister about the deletion of clause 11 and its downstream effect on small businesses and consumers. Webb's turn takes up none of it: he reports a UK scholar's interest in the debate and then moves straight to his own prepared Amendment Paper on clause 30's burden of proof. The speech is about the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive to the matter, but it would have been word-for-word identical whatever Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that deleting clause 11 'walks back an important provision in this bill, which was a consumer protection' and asked the Minister to explain the effect on small businesses; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Just first of all, just responding to Ms Williams’ question, she was a very active participant in our last round, but I think without trying to highlight it, she wasn’t here for the discussion around clause 11.
acuity.explanation: This is addressed to Williams' question and so engages the topic, but it engages no part of the content: it answers her request for an explanation of clause 11's deletion by observing that she was absent when the matter was earlier traversed. A mere reference to the previous speaker, with the substance left unaddressed, sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Minister needs to give the committee a better understanding of how this will impact not only on consumers but on small businesses" — Arena Williams.

acuity.statement: I note that the member has proposed in a number of his amendments that he seeks to define the role of how the courts should approach the different pieces of litigation, should it get to that. We are not proposing to do that. It’s very clear what the principles are and it’s common practice, and the approach of the bill is to leave it to the courts to decide.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's proposed new subclause (3) directly, identifies the general move it belongs to — legislating how a court should weigh the evidence — and rejects it on a stated ground: the bill deliberately leaves the civil standard to the courts. He also points back to clause 30(1) as already carrying the burden Webb is worried about. Had Webb argued something else, this reply would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My amendment suggests that an additional subclause (3) is inserted... the standard of proof is that the court must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities taking into account the seriousness of the allegation" — Duncan Webb.

acuity.statement: I really take the Minister’s comments about wanting clarity with this bill, and I would love to hear from the Minister whether he would consider the adoption of this amendment to clause 14.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's immediately preceding answer — his claim that the bill's principles are already clear and best left to the courts — and turns it against him, arguing her clause 14 amendment is what would actually deliver clarity. Beyond that hook the turn is prepared material on the 'dishonestly'/'fraudulently' distinction and the Insurance Council submission, which Bayly had not raised, so the engagement is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s very clear what the principles are and it’s common practice, and the approach of the bill is to leave it to the courts to decide" — Andrew Bayly.

acuity.statement: I’ve discussed it before, but just to reiterate what I covered previously: it is an important definition, and the member’s right to raise it, but there are different tests and they’re quite distinct, and one has a criminal implication; one has a civil implication. Fraud is used in civil compared to criminal cases, so the meaning is much less clear.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact substitution Pham asked for — 'fraudulently' in place of 'dishonestly' in clause 14(2A) — and answers it on its merits, distinguishing the criminal and civil senses of fraud, explaining why the civil frame was chosen deliberately, and citing the UK legislation's use of 'dishonestly'. The reply would be different if she had proposed a different word or a different clause. The opening complaint that the ground has already been traversed does not displace the engagement that follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Green Party proposed to replace this word with 'fraudulently'... the word 'fraudulently' sets a more appropriate, clear, and specific standard" — Lan Pham.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and it’s just good to move on. Can I say this is a very complex piece of legislation and the Minister’s done a great job in picking up my good work and coming up with many hundreds of clauses which deserve careful examination, given the importance to the commercial sector and everyday New Zealanders. I’m very glad to be here and to talk to clause 35, “What must be disclosed”.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows a detailed, specific question from Williams on the fraud/dishonesty standard in Schedule 2 and explicitly declines to engage it ("it's just good to move on"), pivoting to his own prepared amendment on clause 35. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive to the proceeding, but it would read identically whatever Williams had argued. Scored 0.2, not lower, because it stays on the same Part of the same bill and on the adjacent subject of disclosure duties.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "do we now have a situation where any dishonesty in an insurance relationship voids the entire relationship?" — nothing: Williams argued at length that replacing the "fraudulent" standard with "dishonesty" in Schedule 2 could void unrelated policies, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Look, this has had a lot of consideration about whether the use of the term “ought to know”—and there’s obviously a proposal in the amendment. Look, “ought to know” is an important term that is actually defined in clause 44, as, no doubt, the member knows. This requires policyholders to conduct a reasonable search of available information, which is a key element of fair presentation duty.
acuity.explanation: Bayly takes up the exact term Webb's amendment targets and answers it with a located rebuttal — that "ought to know" is already defined in clause 44 as a reasonable-search obligation — plus the UK-model justification. That is real engagement with the proposal and the speech would change if Webb had proposed something else. Short of 1.0 because he answers the term rather than Webb's actual argument, which was that the objective test should be made subjective to the particular policyholder; he also attributes the amendment to Reuben Davidson rather than the member who just moved it. Whether the clause 44 point defeats Webb's objection is a rigor/veracity question and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My proposed amendment is to change “or ought to know” and insert “or that a policyholder of the kind and in the position of the policyholder would reasonably be expected to know”"

acuity.statement: I just want to return to Ms Williams’ question, which, again, I’ve actually dealt with on a number of occasions. Just briefly, to deal with this, a civil law standard of fraud is wide. In civil law, fraud is knowing a statement is false or recklessly not caring whether it’s correct or not. Obviously, the “dishonest” approach is a high threshold. It would require intent and not capture consumers simply being careless or making an honest mistake.
acuity.explanation: Bayly returns to the specific question Williams put and attacks its load-bearing premise — that "fraudulent" is the stricter, more consumer-protective standard — by distinguishing the wide civil-law meaning of fraud (including recklessness) from dishonesty, which he says requires intent and so spares the careless or honestly mistaken consumer. That directly contradicts the comparison her whole argument rests on, which is the strongest form of listening. Not 1.0 because he leaves her concrete example unanswered: whether a misstatement on a car policy can reach a claim on the same insurer's home or health cover.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "We disagree with the Minister very strongly that “dishonesty” is the appropriate standard, when, in fact, “fraudulently” was used in a prior iteration of the legislation."

acuity.statement: I have a very short question, in the spirit of the committee stage, and it relates to clause 70 in “reasonable time”. What is the remedy? If there’s a breach, what’s the remedy? And will the Minister adopt my amendment, which simply states “once a breach has occurred, interest is payable on the insurance payable”?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Williams's complaint that clause 70's "reasonable time" leaves consumers waiting — and pushes it to the consequence she did not reach: what happens when the implied term is breached. But it does not engage her specific question about whether assessment time is counted within the reasonable period; it is a self-contained question about his own amendment that would read much the same after any clause 70 speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "It should give every New Zealander some confidence that their insurance claims will be dealt with in a timely manner."

acuity.statement: Just to address Ms Williams’ question specifically: yes, taking into account time to collect information is all part of that, together with the assessment of the claim itself. When a court will be assessing what is “reasonable” or have regard for both those items, it is not a separation between the two of them.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact either/or Williams put — whether the time to assess information sits inside the reasonable period or runs separately — and picks one limb of it explicitly. Had she asked a different question about clause 70, this passage could not have been delivered unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Or does this change mean that there is a reasonable time to assess the information and then there is a reasonable time to make the decisions as the insurer?"

acuity.statement: There is, under clause 70, policyholders have the right for late payment. They can apply for it. If they deem that there is an issue about delay—unnecessary, undue delay—then there is clearly provided for in clause 70 that people can apply and get interest late payment under the Interest on Money Claims Act 2016, to be specific.
acuity.explanation: Engages Webb's specific proposal by naming the mechanism he says already delivers it — interest on late payment under the Interest on Money Claims Act 2016 — which is a direct answer to why the amendment is said to be unnecessary. Marked just below the top only because it does not state outright whether he will adopt the amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Will the Minister adopt my amendment so that interest is payable on late payment of insurance?"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister, please—through the officials or if the Minister himself knows—inform the committee what the shortest time has been to pay a claim, what the longest time has been to pay a claim, and what the average time tends to be?
acuity.explanation: Responds to the Minister's defence that reasonableness varies with circumstance by asking for the actual distribution of settlement times that would let the committee judge the variation. It engages the premise of the answer just given rather than merely the topic, though it does not contest the reasoning itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "The issue we’ve tried to deal with is that what is “reasonable time” depends on the circumstance."

acuity.statement: I don’t think we actually have a view on—I’m not sure, because that’s a commercial view on it. Look, the point is that it needs to be reasonable in the context.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the request squarely — states that the Crown holds no view on claim-settlement timings because they are commercial — then returns to his prepared point about contextual reasonableness. Engagement is real and specific to what was asked, but it resolves into restating the position rather than taking the question further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "inform the committee what the shortest time has been to pay a claim"

acuity.statement: If the contract denies other rights, is that as far as we’re willing to go? I’m not sure it’s necessarily up to the courts to decide that if in fact in the contract you have expressed terms which limit the rights of the person beyond what we would consider reasonable in that circumstance.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the Minister's fallback that the courts should determine reasonableness, and supplies the reason — an express contractual term can put a remedy outside the court's reach, so leaving it to the courts does not answer the problem. The disagreement is aimed at the content of the answer just given, not at the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "It’s up to the courts to decide it."

acuity.statement: Yes, I’m very familiar with the law around implied terms and the fact that an implied term is usually an unwritten term that’s so obvious it goes without saying. We’re not actually dealing with that here. We’re dealing with something that’s deemed a term in every agreement, and so this seems inappropriate wording to me, and in fact I would ask the Minister to consider an amendment that says it is a deemed term.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's specific claim about the word "implied", accepts the doctrine he invokes, then shows it does not fit clause 70 because the term here is deemed rather than genuinely implied, and converts that into a concrete amendment request. The speech would be entirely different if Bayly had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "she of all people in the committee should know the value of the word “implied”. That means every contract—every insurance contract—has that as an express element of that contract."

acuity.statement: Just responding to the member again, I note that the use of the term “implied term” is very consistent. It is consistent with the UK approach—it’s given rise to no issue. I think it’s pretty commonly understood, as I said before, as to what that means.
acuity.explanation: Directly defends the drafting choice she challenged, citing UK practice and common understanding, so it is aimed at her objection rather than prepared material. Short of 1.0 because he does not engage her actual distinction between an implied and a deemed term — he restates that "implied" is well understood instead of answering why a deemed term is called implied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "this seems inappropriate wording to me, and in fact I would ask the Minister to consider an amendment that says it is a deemed term"

acuity.statement: I take the Minister’s point that the intention of this legislation is to set out the approach very clearly, so I’m asking him this in in good faith. Clause 71 of Part 3 is the arbitration provision that has been included in this legislation since the Labour Government first drafted it and since the formulation of what is an insurance contract that applies to consumers.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Bayly's preceding answer — his claim that the bill's approach is to set out principles clearly — and uses it as the premise of her question, but then moves to a different clause rather than engaging his argument about leaving reasonableness to the courts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "Their fundamental approach to the bill is to be clear about the principles that people need to be paid out in a reasonable time"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to move to clause 72, which has always been a tricky area of insurance law. That’s those clauses which set out a condition in the insurance policy about how a claim is to be made.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the same bill at committee stage — but engages no part of the preceding turn, announcing a move to his own topic. It would read identically whatever Williams had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams had just asked whether clause 71's arbitration provision remains the right formation given the changes to clauses 6 and 7, and this statement does not take that up, instead opening prepared material on a different clause.

acuity.statement: Just in response to Ms Williams’ question around clause 71, look, hey, this is a very longstanding provision that applies only to consumers, not to non-consumers. It maintains a status quo that arbitration clauses in them are not binding. That’s a very common approach. It’s always been that, and so we’re pretty comfortable with that approach.
acuity.explanation: Answers on the clause she named, so the engagement is pointable, but responds to the provision's history rather than her actual question about whether it still works given the redefinition in clauses 6 and 7 — the topic engaged, not the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "is he satisfied that clause 71 is the right formation for the arbitration provision ... now that he has changed clause 6, which is the meaning of a contract of insurance"

acuity.statement: Just with your clause 72, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, the first thing is this is a longstanding provision and we actually had no feedback, as I understand, during the select committee. Everyone seemed to be comfortable. Insurers are already prevented from relying on a time limit, unless it can show it’s been prejudiced or this is inequitable. An additional reasonableness test is not required.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the proposed amendment on its own terms — identifies the existing prejudice and inequity tests as already covering the ground and concludes the added reasonableness limb is redundant. It is a direct answer to the specific drafting change Webb put, not a gesture at it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My proposal is a new clause 72(3)(c) ... It would actually be a bar on unreasonably tight time frames or methods."

acuity.statement: What I’m asking is not whether clause 71 is the same as what it was before; I’m asking whether clause 71 is now both appropriate, in the Minister’s view, and good for consumers, in the Minister’s view, given his changes to clause 6 and clause 7, because those change who can use a consumer insurance contract.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer and shows precisely why it misses the question, distinguishing the provision's continuity from its continued appropriateness after the scope changes. The intervention exists only because of what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "this is a very longstanding provision that applies only to consumers, not to non-consumers ... It’s always been that, and so we’re pretty comfortable with that approach."

acuity.statement: In answer to Ms Williams’ question: yes, it is appropriate. In answer to Dr Duncan Webb’s tabled amendment around clause 73: I’m not keen to accept that and recommend we shouldn’t, because the Law Commission actually proposed the change. The member’s tabled amendment would actually reduce or narrow the scope of it, which actually would be a disadvantage to policyholders, so I think they’re actually going to end up with a perverse outcome.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific tabled amendment Webb had just argued for, gives a reason for rejecting it (its provenance in the Law Commission's wider definition) and names the consequence he says it would have for policyholders. Had Webb proposed something else, this answer would have had to be different. Scored on engagement only — whether the Law Commission characterisation is correct is a veracity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My proposal is for the tabled amendment to be adopted which adds to that clause 73 at the end of subsection (2)"

acuity.statement: One very brief point coming from Mr Menéndez March’s contribution, and my suggestion, is that regulations are required, because at the moment the legislation as drafted is permissive. There’s a real danger that a Minister might get a little busy—I know, Minister, ha, ha!—or might simply not think it’s a great idea, and therefore kind of thwart the intention of Parliament by not implementing parliamentary intent, which is to have regulations here. I’ve got a proposal there that says, “The Minister must make a recommendation under section 86B within two years of the commencement of this Act.” The time is up for grabs, but it just has to be time-bound. That’s the guts of it. That’s the first thing.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the genetic-testing regulation strand just put by Williams and Menéndez March and does something with it: identifies that the drafting is merely permissive, which is the weak point in the "opportunity to regulate" framing, and supplies a concrete time-bound amendment to close it. Not a full 1.0 because it does not engage Williams' actual question about Australia's five-year ban, and the turn then moves on to an unrelated clause 82 point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "to create an opportunity for the Minister to regulate in this area"

acuity.statement: Now, that’s a little bit curious because the set of rules around the sorts of regulations that the Minister may make seem to have the effect of ruling out genetic testing, but 86C(1)(d) seems to allow it back in again. I wonder if the Minister could explain what sort of information insurers might be able to consider?
acuity.explanation: Russell follows Bayly's defence of handling genetic testing through regulations and takes up one strand of it — the regulation-making provisions themselves — by probing clause 86C(1)(d). She does not engage his specific claims (that Australia has not legislated, that resourcing is adequate), but her question is built on the regulatory route he had just described rather than being prepared material indifferent to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "That is why we've adopted a flexible approach, which means we'll do it through Order in Council."

acuity.statement: I want to ask the Minister: when he says he will run a full consultation process when he is using the Order in Council powers, what will the consultation process look like and will those patient groups be consulted with?
acuity.explanation: She quotes back the Minister's own undertaking to consult and presses it for its operative content — who, how long, run by whom — drawing out the consequence of the very commitment just made. The question could not have been asked in this form if Bayly had not said what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "At this point, we have to consult with various groups."

acuity.statement: With clause 86C(1)(d), which the member raises, the reality is that genetic testing is happening and will continue to occur, and it’s likely it will continue to escalate. What this is referring to is that there are some conditions where, if you have the gene, it is so significant in terms of an insurance event that it would have a material bearing on whether, in fact, you could get insurance.
acuity.explanation: He takes the exact clause put to him and supplies the explanation asked for — which genetic information is material enough for an insurer to weigh — illustrating it with the Huntington's/BRCA distinction. Marked down slightly because he leaves Williams's consultation question of the preceding turns unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I wonder if the Minister could explain what sort of information insurers might be able to consider?"

acuity.statement: Can he compare the meaning of new clause 86C(3)(c) with the provision which then protects insurers that Dr Russell has asked him about?
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's just-given justification for subsection (d) and pushes it one step further, asking how it squares with the protective test in 86C(3)(c). The question is built directly out of the answer she has just heard and explicitly acknowledges it was not the answer she anticipated.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "That’s why that subsection (d) is included in this area."

acuity.statement: Huntington’s disease is, as I say, very distressing and has only one outcome. But the BRCA gene is interesting, because it is so highly associated with a pretty—what’s the word I was going to say—aggressive form of breast cancer.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the precise certainty-versus-probability distinction Bayly had just drawn between Huntington's and BRCA and tests it, pointing out the line-drawing problem and the cystic fibrosis case where treatment changes the prognosis. The speech would be unrecognisable had the Minister not given that specific answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "it’s not one like, for instance, the BRCA gene, where a person may or may not get it"

acuity.statement: In the spirit of the committee stage, my question is a straight question. Given Australia’s changing position, should New Zealand be seeking to align itself with Australia, and will the Minister exercise his powers under the new regulation-making powers in this legislation with a view to aligning New Zealand’s insurance industry up with Australia’s?
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Bayly's substantive turn on terminal conditions, new clause 86C and banding immediately precedes. The question is squarely on the matter under debate (the genetic-testing insurance regime and the Order in Council powers), but it engages no part of what Bayly had just said — it would read identically whatever he had answered. Prepared, on-topic material: 0.2 rather than 0.1 because the reference to 'the new regulation-making powers in this legislation' gestures at the clause he had been defending.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "We certainly don’t want the insurance companies saying: as a big band, we’re going to exclude you or charge a higher premium." — nothing in that answer about Australia or trans-Tasman alignment is taken up; this opens a new strand.

acuity.statement: Look, as I’ve said before, Australia is announcing an intention. It has not passed legislation, and local parliaments—and we’re the same—will go through a select committee process. It will be interesting to see where they end up. Of course we will have regard to Australia’s outcome, as we would have regard to other jurisdictions around the world.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific premise of the question — Australia's 'changing position' — and corrects its factual status (an announced intention, not passed legislation), then answers the alignment question directly ('we will have regard to Australia's outcome') and ties it back to why the Order in Council mechanism is being used. The answer would have to change entirely if Williams had asked something else. Not 1.0 only because the second half of her question, whether he will exercise the powers with alignment in view, is answered obliquely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Given Australia’s changing position, should New Zealand be seeking to align itself with Australia"

acuity.statement: Can we prevent them from requiring us to disclose information? Looking at paragraph (c) “when viewed as a group”, does that mean an ethnic group, potentially?
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's stated principle — that insurers must not treat people as a band — by testing it against the actual drafting of paragraph (c), 'when viewed as a group', and asking whether that reaches ethnic groups. That is a real take-up of his claim rather than a mere reference. Scored 0.5 and not higher because it does not engage the turn immediately preceding (his answer on Australia) and much of the surrounding material is her own prepared line of inquiry.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "We certainly don’t want the insurance companies saying: as a big band, we’re going to exclude you or charge a higher premium."

acuity.statement: Look, the examples you use are exactly what we don’t want to happen. We don’t want insurers to blankly classify people, ethnic groups, people with certain conditions—and it might be a familial relationship or whatever—we don’t want them doing that.
acuity.explanation: Picks up her actual examples — classification by ethnic group and by familial relationship — and states a position on each, so the answer is shaped by what she said. Short of 1.0 because it answers at the level of general principle and leaves her specific drafting questions (what counts as 'another source of information', the DNA heritage sites, paragraph (c)) untouched. Note this scores engagement only; whether the answer is adequately precise is a different attribute.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "At what stage does that constitute some sort of ethnic bias?" and her question about declaring relatives' diseases

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. My question is about clause 90, and it is about the insurer standing in the policyholder’s place for those claims that are made under this subpart, which is a new subpart that we have not yet debated. It’s relating to an amendment on the Table for the Minister’s consideration.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by the Minister immediately precedes and the speaker remains in the same committee-stage debate. The question is prepared material on a different clause; it would be word-for-word identical whatever Bayly had just said. Low acuity is the correct reading here and is not a criticism of the question's substance, which is specific and well-targeted on its own clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly had just set out the general principle that insurers must not classify people by ethnic group or familial relationship, and this question moves to clause 90 and an amendment on the Table without taking any of it up.

acuity.statement: I know the member is talking on behalf of a clause put forward by the Hon Dr Webb. Look, it’s already addressed—if Dr Webb looked seven clauses on, he would have seen that it’s addressed in clause 97 and also Schedule 3 of the bill. It’s already provided for in the bill that a claimant can obtain information documents relevant to the claim from the insurer.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise thing asked: whether the claimant can obtain the documents, and whether the proposed amendment is needed. He identifies where in the bill the point is already dealt with (clause 97 and Schedule 3) and states the substantive position she asked him to enunciate if he rejected the amendment. The reply is entirely contingent on her argument. The jibe at Dr Webb would tell against Civility, not Acuity, and must not pull this score down.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "whether it would be possible for the claimant to get those documents" — her proposed new subclause (3) to clause 90

acuity.statement: Look, clause 91(2) already prevents insurers from relying on certain technical defences that it would only have because the policyholder has become insolvent, so it’s already provided for. I suppose a more general principle is that it’s better to clearly identify the specific defences that insurers cannot use, to avoid uncertainty.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact mechanism she raised — insolvency-based technical defences depriving third-party claimants — explains that clause 91(2) already covers it, and then answers the drafting question she actually put (whether a new subclause (2)(d) is needed) by giving a reason for the bill's approach of enumerating specific defences. Shaped throughout by her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "whether the term saying the insurance is voided on insolvency, or anything like that, would not deprive third parties who are making a claim"

acuity.statement: I was wondering: is that quite a common phenomenon in the insurance industry? Is it a kind of common thing?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — the Minister's substantive answer immediately precedes and this is the same committee-stage debate. The speaker acknowledges jumping around and raises a wholly unconnected clause; the question engages nothing that was said before it. It is still about the bill, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly had just answered on clause 91(2) and technical defences arising from insolvency, and this question moves to Subpart 6 and clause 99 without taking any of it up.

acuity.statement: I apologise for coming back to the Subpart 4A on genetic testing, but I want to ask a specific question which I don’t believe has been answered and that there is significant public interest in—that is, how long interested groups in this, particularly patient groups, can expect consultation with them to occur for.
acuity.explanation: Returns deliberately to the Minister's earlier answers and identifies what they left out, pressing the procedural assurance he gave about clause 86C for the one thing he had not specified — the length of consultation before he must make regulations. That is engagement with a gap in a claim actually made. Held below 0.5 because it answers the topic of his earlier assurance rather than any specific proposition in it, and the turn immediately preceding (Hernandez on clause 99) is not taken up at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "That’s why adopting an Order in Council procedure, with the very clear procedural approach that has to be followed under clause 86C, gives us the flexibility to make sure we keep up to date and abreast of developments."

acuity.statement: We apologise for the earlier confusion, but I just really wanted to challenge the Minister on the inclusion of clauses 104 and 105, which provide default provisions for when—and I’ve never understood why we trouble the legislature with these clauses, which provide, essentially, a default provision.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by another member on the same Part immediately precedes. By the speaker's own account this is prepared material, and it opens a fresh critique of clauses 104 and 105 rather than engaging the definitional question just put. It is squarely on the Part under debate and adjacent in subject matter (brokers), which earns 0.2 rather than 0.1, but the speech would be identical whatever had preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams had just asked whether Part 4 is materially affected by the select committee's change to the definition of "brokers", and this contribution does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I did discuss this with the insurers and also with the brokers, so I don’t think anyone suggested to me that we should delete clause 104, which the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has proposed for both clause 104 and, consequently, clause 105.
acuity.explanation: Williams asked which submitters sought the change and whether the process was adequate. Bayly takes up the consultation strand — he names who he consulted (insurers and brokers) — but converts the question into a different one, about who asked for clause 104 to be deleted, and leaves the process complaint untouched. Partial engagement: a strand is picked up and then the turn moves to prepared defence of the clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "which submitters asked for the change which is being made here, and is he satisfied that the change in legislation, which he is overseeing and which has only been submitted on by—I think it’s one in this case—one stakeholder"

acuity.statement: There is a further point I wanted to ask. I know that the Minister holds some other portfolios which relate to small business, and this relates to clause 108, “Duties of broker in relation to payments due to policyholder”.
acuity.explanation: Bayly had just rejected Webb's own proposal to delete clauses 104 and 105, with a specific reason (the clause 101 flow-on leaving insurers unpaid). Webb neither accepts nor contests that reasoning; he opens a fresh line on clause 108. It remains squarely within the committee-stage debate on the same bill, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly argued that clause 104 "sets a statutory backstop" and that without it "the insurer could be left with no one being required to pay them" — the direct answer to Webb's own deletion amendment — and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: With regard to clause 108, there is still a requirement—and I’d just draw the member’s attention to clause 108(b). It states right at the start of it that “as soon as is reasonably practicable”, the money must be paid from the broker. That is the key tenet of it, and, obviously, there can be agreements between brokers and insurers if they want to, but that reasonableness test is a crucial test.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause Webb raised and the exact split he attacked, giving a reason for it (commercial products being more complex) and pointing to the limb Webb characterised as toothless. It stops short of 1.0 because Webb's sharpest point — that a two-day hold on a multimillion-dollar payout is "a good little earner" — is not met, but the speech would plainly be different had Webb argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Why should a broker be able to hold insurance moneys on behalf of a small business, or, indeed, any business, for longer than they can for a consumer?"

acuity.statement: Just for clarity: does the Minister expect that “reasonably practicable” to mean less than seven days or more than seven days? That’s the relevant question here.
acuity.explanation: Bayly rested his defence on the reasonableness test being well understood; Williams takes that precise claim and presses it for the one operative consequence it must have, forcing the comparison against the seven-day consumer limit. The question exists only because of what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "that reasonableness test is a crucial test. Again, we’ve talked about that and traversed that earlier in the discussions around the bill. That’s a commonly understood term."

acuity.statement: When the Minister says that the bill is drafted in a way so as to create consumer contracts for insurance and other contracts for insurance, that’s not the case. For most of this legislation’s life, the legislation was drafted in a way in which the big delineations were between contracts for insurance for policyholders who were not in a position to negotiate contract terms with an insurer because the insurer had an outsized sort of corporate interest and corporate power to negotiate, and contracts for reinsurance, which were large, commercial arrangements between two large corporate entities that had sort of relative power.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the factual premise of the answer just given, with an account of how the bill's delineation previously ran and why the new non-consumer category is not the same distinction. This is engagement with the content of the Minister's reasoning rather than a reference to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "in this bill, we’ve made a clear differentiation between consumer insurance, which is for individuals primarily, and commercial contracts, because they’re quite different types of products"

acuity.statement: Look, I beg to differ. There has been a distinction between consumer and non-consumer throughout the bill, so that’s the fundamental sort of difference in approach.
acuity.explanation: Joins issue head-on with the factual correction Williams offered, denying it and restating the drafting history as he sees it, and he goes on in the same turn to answer her seven-day question. Not 1.0 because her further specific question — whether professional indemnity cover that pays out to a consumer is caught — is left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "When the Minister says that the bill is drafted in a way so as to create consumer contracts for insurance and other contracts for insurance, that’s not the case."

acuity.statement: It seems to me that this particular scenario is one where that is almost being sanctioned by us because we’re saying that 50 days is the default and we’re saying “in a reasonable time” and it becomes the practice.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's reliance on a reasonableness standard and argues it will be set by prevailing late-payment practice rather than constraining it — a genuine engagement with the load-bearing part of his answer. Much of the surrounding turn is prepared material on Xero's payment-time research, which is why this sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "To your specific question about what is reasonable and whether it is less than seven days for a commercial contract, it is reasonable in the circumstances."

acuity.statement: Obviously, there’s ability for insurers and brokers to negotiate a different and quicker payment time, but I just want to be very clear that the 50-day test relates to money that the broker passes on to the insurer. It’s not what, I think, the member was alluding to. It does not affect payment to small business policyholder.
acuity.explanation: Identifies and corrects the specific misapprehension in the argument put to him — that the 50-day default governs payments owed to small business policyholders rather than broker-to-insurer remittance — which is the pivot the whole of her case rested on. Squarely aimed at what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "I’d like the Minister to address whether he is concerned that, by putting in a payment term like 50 days, we are almost creating a calculation of, “We will keep this money for this long."

acuity.statement: Obviously I did a poor job of explaining it. There is a requirement for insurers to pay policyholders—commercial and non-commercial—promptly. We’ve traversed that in the previous part. That is an absolute requirement. What we’re talking about here is something quite distinct from that. All we’re talking about in this clause is the arrangement between the broker and the insurer. That’s the big differentiation. There’s always been a norm, from my recollection, that brokers would have up to 50 days to pay the insurer.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise confusion in Helen White's turn — she had run together premiums held and money owed to an injured claimant, and queried the 50-day norm — and separates the two, locating the clause in the broker-to-insurer leg while conceding the prompt-payment duty to policyholders she was worried about. The speech would read quite differently had she argued something else; he even names the allegation he is answering.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "One is that we have prescribed a time of 50 days because it’s the norm. Well, actually, it sounds like a worrying norm to me."

acuity.statement: Just a brief question: how many submitters asked for this change to clauses 104 and 108, and is it a good enough legislative process that the change has been made with a minimal number of submissions and no submissions from consumers about it?
acuity.explanation: On the clauses under debate, so not unmoored, but it engages no part of the Minister's argument that the clause governs only the broker–insurer leg. It pivots to the select committee process and the number of submissions — a question that could have been put whatever Bayly had just said about the 50-day norm.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly argued the clause concerns only the arrangement between broker and insurer and carries no consequential delay to policyholders, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Then a specific question around clause 131. This is also particularly problematic given the Minister’s new powers in setting regulations. Is it his intention to formulate the regulations in some way to get around clause 131 or will he need to be back in this Chamber to amend clause 131 at the stage he’s creating the regulations? It doesn’t seem to me to be possible, unless there’s a very wide interpretation of “reasonable evidence” there, for clause 131 and new regulatory-making powers to exist if they were to limit the insurer’s ability to use genetic testing information, which is entirely the point of the regulations in the first place. Those regulations were introduced by the select committee to limit the ability of insurers to use them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Duncan Webb's clause 131 objection to insurer discretion and draws out a consequence he had not reached — that the same discretion collides with the Minister's new genetic-testing regulation-making power, leaving primary and secondary legislation pulling opposite ways. Not a rebuttal of his reasoning, but a real extension of the specific argument just made; it would not survive unchanged if the preceding turn had been about a different clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "There’s a tabled amendment there ready to go, so let’s just strike out “in its opinion”."

acuity.statement: Secondly, I’d make the point to the Hon Dr Webb that it’s a strange argument he’s putting forward, because the provision inherently turns on life insurers’ own assessments of what evidence to request. The deletion probably wouldn’t make any practical difference at all. The existing requirement for the required evidence to be reasonable already exists as a safeguard, so there is a reasonable test around that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the actual amendment proposed — strike out "in its opinion" — on its merits: the words are said to be inert because the provision necessarily rests on the insurer's own assessment, and the surviving reasonableness requirement supplies the constraint Webb says is missing. Directly aimed at the reasoning of the preceding turn rather than at its author's record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "The opinion of the insurer is not an appropriate consideration."

acuity.statement: I know the member’s been very helpful in proposing the official cash rate plus 2 percent, but that’s been plucked out of the air, I might suggest to the member, because already we’ve dealt with the issue in paragraph (a).
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific figure Webb put forward and gives a reason it is unnecessary — that paragraph (a)'s policy rate is already the backstop against the gap Webb feared. The jibe that the number was plucked out of the air is aimed at the proposal itself, so the engagement is with content, not a mere reference to the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the interest rate under that clause is deemed to be the official cash rate plus 2 percent"

acuity.statement: My concern with clause 126 is that it’s set out as exhaustive, whereas there may be other dealings in life policies, which, to use a kind of slightly arcane approach, are transfers at equity—for example, if money was to be lent and it was agreed that the life policy would be assigned as security; so if I don’t repay it, you can have my life policy.
acuity.explanation: The Minister had just rejected both of his propositions — that "in its opinion" should go, and that the OCR-plus-2-percent placeholder was needed — and this turn answers neither, moving instead to a prepared point on equitable assignments under clause 126. Still within the same Part of the bill, so not wholly adrift, but there is no gesture at the rebuttal he has just received.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly argued the deletion of "in its opinion" would make no practical difference and that paragraph (a) already supplies an interest-rate backstop, and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: I asked my question about clause 131. I asked about the Minister’s concerns. He said he wasn’t concerned. Let me ask him whether this is good for people who suffer from genetic diseases, who expect him to take powers that restrict insurers from using their genetic testing information to prohibit them from getting insurance—whether clause 131 is good for them.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn by Bayly was about equity transfers and ordinary transfers; Williams does not engage any part of it. She instead returns to her own earlier line of questioning on clause 131 and genetic testing. There is a gesture at the Minister's earlier answer ('He said he wasn't concerned') and the speech is squarely on the matter under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andrew Bayly spoke about equity transfers no longer being normal industry practice and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: It’s clause 132, “High Court may order registration”. That’s kind of a default provision, like the appointment of trustees and so on and so forth. But why the High Court? The High Court’s slow and expensive. Why not the District Court? Those District Court judges know what they’re doing.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows a substantive turn by Williams on clause 131 and genetic discrimination, and engages none of it — he opens an independent, evidently prepared line of questioning on clause 132's choice of forum. The speech would read identically whatever Williams had argued. It is at least on the bill under consideration, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that clause 131 lets insurers keep demanding genetic information before registering an instrument, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I want to address Ms Williams’ question. She’s drawing a bow between clause 131 and the discussion we had in the previous part around genetic disorders. The provisions in this bill at clause 131 relate only to Part 5, so she’s wrong to try to confuse them and conflate them and reference them back to Part 4. It deals only with issues in Part 5, around transfers, etc.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact claim just made — that clause 131 lets insurers demand genetic information — and disputes its premise by locating the clause within Part 5 rather than Part 4. The reply is specific to the argument advanced and would have had to be different had Williams argued something else. (Whether the Part 4/Part 5 answer is correct is a veracity question, and the dismissive framing a civility one; neither moves the engagement score.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether clause 131 is good for them" — Arena Williams, on clause 131 and insurers' use of genetic testing information

acuity.statement: With regard to the specifics around clause 141—this is subclause (3) that he referred to—we specifically consulted on surrender value provisions at the select committee stage. I know the member wasn’t a member of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, but the feedback the select committee heard on that was that there was no change required to this longstanding provision. In practice, insurers no longer issue these policies; they’re legacy policies only.
acuity.explanation: Engages the precise provision Webb raised — clause 141(3) — and answers it with select committee consultation feedback and the claim that the policies are legacy only. It does not adopt the suggested proviso but it addresses the concern behind it directly rather than pivoting away, so responsiveness is high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This section is subject to—(a) any rules made by the life insurer" — Duncan Webb, proposing a proviso so no rules leave a consumer policyholder worse off than the section

acuity.statement: Right. The Minister says, “I did.” It’s now on record that people who are sufferers of genetic conditions, who may be affected by the genetic provision tests, will not be subject to the provisions in Part 5 in total. I guess they can expect that the secondary legislation enacted by the Minister will exempt them from Part 5.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own answer and draws out what she says follows from it — that genetic-condition policyholders are outside Part 5 altogether — which is engagement with the content of the preceding turn rather than a restatement of her earlier question. Whether the inference is a fair reading of what Bayly said is a rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The provisions in this bill at clause 131 relate only to Part 5" — Andrew Bayly

acuity.statement: I made my point clear before. I repeat it: clause 131 is about instruments regarding the transfer of life insurance policies. “Instruments”, that is the differentiation. I would suggest to the member that she is confusing the issue in Part 4. This is about the transfer of instruments.
acuity.explanation: Aimed squarely at the conflation he says Williams has made, and names the distinction he relies on ('instruments'). It engages her point but largely restates his earlier answer rather than addressing the consequence she drew from it, so it is responsive without advancing the exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they can expect that the secondary legislation enacted by the Minister will exempt them from Part 5" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Just following on from Arena Williams, one of the questions I have and one of the suggestions I have is that these regulations are absolutely the guts of the bill, if you like, and they impose the real workings of where it hits the ground. I mean, I’m looking in particular at clause 165(4), which talks about the interest, and I’ve raised before that if the Minister doesn’t make these regulations, then there are real problems.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Williams's strand on the regulation-making powers and builds on it, but shifts from her specific question about prioritisation and timing to his own point that nothing compels the regulations to be made at all. Partial engagement: the thing engaged is pointable, but the specific claim is not answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can the Minister give some clarity on how he intends to prioritise his regulatory-making powers" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: There’s not a great requirement and not a great intent to go out and do a whole lot of regulations on it. Obviously, if we’re going to do that, we will be talking to all relevant parties, and I do meet with the consumer advocacy groups quite regularly, actually.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the consultation question Webb put, naming consumer advocacy groups, and addresses the volume-of-regulations concern. It does not take up Webb's other point about there being no requirement that the regulations be made at all, so engagement is strong but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether he will be consulting with consumers or consumer organisations" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: The final point was that he talked about the Fair Trading Act. Actually, insurers will be captured under the conduct of financial institutions regime, which comes into force on 31 March 2025—i.e., in a few months’ time. Therefore, they are subject to making sure they are operating in the best interest of their consumers, and I’ve been very explicit to all industry players that that is one of their primary objectives.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific complaint — that insurers escape the Fair Trading Act unfair contract terms regime — and does something with it, naming an alternative oversight regime and its commencement date. Across the turn Bayly also answers Webb's direct challenge about who he listened to and why the draft changed, and rebuts the premium/exclusion-clause reasoning. The speech would be materially different had Webb argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Certainly, in terms of unfair contract terms, insurers need to be brought into the regime, because as a matter of practice, insurers do rely on exclusion clauses and they need to be held to account."

acuity.statement: This is an outrageous position for us to be in, in a committee stage, where we have a Minister in the chair alleging that another member has a personal view which has coloured the way that he has engaged with this legislation, when that Minister will not answer repeated questions from me about which submitters asked for certain changes—when I know that there was only one stakeholder, in some cases, who asked for a certain change—and whether that is an appropriate legislative process for this House to conduct.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the turn she follows — Bayly's charge that Webb's drafting reflected a personal bias — and uses it to press the process question. But she leaves untouched the substantive arguments Bayly had just made (higher premiums, the all-risks versus defined-perils consequence, CoFI coverage) and returns to her prepared line about which submitters sought the changes, so the engagement is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Bayly: "I think that the previous drafting reflected his personal view about insurance companies, which was, basically, a very negative view about that industry."

acuity.statement: Look, the member may feign enragement about the whole thing, but these changes were included in the draft bill that went before the Finance and Expenditure Committee.
