acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson argued that the select committee's genetic-testing provision has 'futureproofed New Zealand's law' and puts New Zealand ahead of Australia, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Under Labour, we saw the largest public-housing build programme that this country has seen since the 1960s. I stand by that record. I stand by that record, because, on their record, not only did they not build houses, they sold off New Zealand State housing stock.
acuity.explanation: Van de Molen's turn challenged the Opposition to concede its housing and tenancy record had failed, citing a quadrupled social housing wait-list. Halbert takes up that challenge directly and refuses it, defending Labour's build record and counter-posing National's state-house sales. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding argument, but he takes up none of the specific claims put to him (the $170 weekly rent rise, the 7,000-to-27,000 wait-list figure, the healthy homes legislation), returning instead to his own prepared record-comparison.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "it would be, I think, a measure of the Opposition if someone was to stand up over there and say, “Look, we didn’t quite get it right.”"

acuity.statement: They are shameless, and today they stand here wanting to be empathetic to renters. They want to be empathetic to renters. The truth is that all the National Party and this Government cares about is giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax break, looking after their mates, and looking after Philip Morris.
acuity.explanation: This picks up the posture of the preceding turn — van de Molen's claim that the bill is good for tenants as well as landlords — but engages no part of its content. It asserts bad motive and pivots to the tax package and tobacco policy, neither of which van de Molen raised. Naming the opponent as a target and echoing their framing is not engagement with the claim, so this sits in the low band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "I think it is a great day for tenants and landlords in New Zealand."

acuity.statement: Now, I want to ask the House: what’s wrong with having a balance—what’s wrong with finding the balance between rights of the tenant and rights of the landlord? Do you know what? Absolutely, we need to make sure that we get the power balance right, because there can be an imbalance—I agree 100 percent.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle identifies the Opposition's stated ground of opposition (the 90-day no-cause notice) and meets Halbert's charge that the bill simply serves landlords by arguing the measure balances the two parties' rights, conceding that the imbalance he alleges can exist. She engages the specific objection rather than the topic generally, which lifts her above a glancing reply, but she leaves his other claims untouched (the stalled Auckland builds, the 1,727 units, the homelessness consequence), so this is not a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "The reality is, under this Government, they’re just looking after landlords. They actually don’t care about tenants—they don’t care about tenants."

acuity.statement: There’s something that the Opposition members have failed to delve deeply into, and this is the sadness of it all: what about what we’re doing with respect to family violence? We’re removing the barriers to leaving unsafe situations by confirming that a tenant can leave a tenancy if their child or their dependant is in danger of domestic violence.
acuity.explanation: This is prepared material on a provision of the bill under debate, so it is on the right subject, and the gesture at what the Opposition omitted keeps it at the top of the low band. But engaging an absence is not engaging an argument: the passage would read identically whatever Halbert had said, and nothing in the preceding turn is taken up, rebutted or corrected.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the bill will boot tenants out the door without explanation and increase homelessness in Auckland, and this statement does not take that up — it observes only that the Opposition did not discuss family violence.

acuity.statement: They may think that it’s not relevant, but, actually, this bill did see changes as we’ve changed Governments, and we think that some of the changes tilt the balance beyond just modernising our insurance laws and protecting consumers, to actually undermining consumer rights.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the relevance objection thrown at him mid-speech and answers its substance — why the comparison to a bill reworked across a change of government bears on this bill — rather than simply ignoring or deriding the interjector. It is a real, if brief, engagement with the specific objection made; it falls short of 1.0 because the substantive preceding speech (Kapa-Kingi's on plain language and te reo Māori, and on insurance being unaffordable for whānau Māori) is not taken up at all, and the remainder of his contribution is prepared material on dishonesty language and genetic testing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Not relevant" — Ryan Hamilton, interjecting on his reference to the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill.

acuity.statement: This bill is really going to help with creating more fairness, more transparency, which has been touched on a lot within this debate today.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive opposition turns immediately precede her — Menéndez March on the narrowed 'dishonesty'/'fraudulency' wording shifting risk onto distressed claimants and on the genetic testing provisions, and Kapa-Kingi on insurance being inaccessible for whānau Māori — and her speech engages neither. It is prepared support for the bill (committee thanks, Cyclone Gabrielle, named Tukituki communities) and would read identically whoever had spoken before her. It is not 0.1 only because she gestures at the debate having 'touched on' fairness and transparency, which is a nod rather than an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the changed language on dishonesty and the regulatory rather than prohibitionist approach to genetic testing "actually undermining consumer rights", and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: This bill—and putting it, you know, long story short—is a bill that is about facilitating the well-functioning insurance markets for both the insurers and the policyholders. This had been commented through the debate before me.
acuity.explanation: Lu follows Russell's substantive case that the Minister stripped out consumer protections, that insurance is becoming a privilege for vulnerable households, and that climate risk will price people out. Her speech is on the same bill and gestures at the prior debate, and her disclosure-duty example sits in the same consumer-protection territory, but it engages none of Russell's specific arguments: no answer on the walked-back clauses, no engagement with affordability or climate. The speech would read identically whatever Russell had said, so it is prepared material on the right subject with a passing nod to the debate — the 0.3 end of the unpointable band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued that "the bit where we cannot support it is where he has walked back the provisions that would have supported ordinary consumers", and this statement does not take that claim up — it only gestures at the debate with "This had been commented through the debate before me."

acuity.statement: The importance of the insurance market can’t be underestimated. It provides an ability for peace of mind, as my colleague from the opposite side mentioned before; the ability for businesses, consumers, and households to share risk; but, also, it provides opportunities, economic opportunities, for those in this sector.
acuity.explanation: Bidois closes the debate after Webb and echoes Webb's 'peace of mind' point with an explicit nod to him, but engages none of Webb's four substantive criticisms (no brightline 12-month settlement period, trivial damages, the exclusion-clause carve-out from the Fair Trading Act unfair-contract provisions, no help for small businesses). The passage is a prepared summary of why insurance matters and would read identically had Webb argued something else about the bill, so it is a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "insurance isn’t just about restoring property; it’s about peace of mind" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: One of those, in fact—let’s talk about them, OK?—is around the right that insurers must present policies in a very clear and plain language way.
acuity.explanation: Menéndez March interjected demanding that Bidois actually name the improved policyholder rights he had just asserted the bill provides, and Bidois audibly breaks off his prepared line ('let’s talk about them, OK?') to supply a specific one — the plain-language presentation duty — before going on to the misrepresentation and fair-presentation duties. The content of the demand changed what he said next, which is genuine responsiveness; it falls short of 1.0 because he supplies the example and then resumes prepared material rather than taking the challenge further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Tell us about them." — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Some of the members opposite talked about the Hon Duncan Webb’s bill being better. Unfortunately, in their three years, they didn’t advance that case, despite his 15 amendments at each part. I can say with confidence that he certainly did contribute to the iteration of the committee and by and large, I think, in his heart will actually support much of what we’re doing today. One of the things in the old bill, for example, was that consumers had to disclose any information that might influence a prudent insurer—but who understands that? The left talk about looking after the little people. These bills actually look after the little people and put the onus on the insurance companies to ask the hard questions, and put the onus on them, where it should be.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Helen White had just made — that Labour will not support the bill because Duncan Webb's original member's bill was better — names it, and does something with it: disputes Labour's record of advancing it, claims Webb's own support for the current version, and then contests the comparison on substance by naming a provision of the old bill (the 'prudent insurer' disclosure duty) that he argues was worse for consumers. The speech would have had to be different had the preceding speaker not argued the original bill was superior. Part of the reply pivots to a record-and-tu-quoque attack rather than the merits, which is a Rigor/Focus matter and not scored here; the engagement itself is close to the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "The only reason that the Labour Party isn’t going to support it today is because it could be better. The original bill was better."

acuity.statement: We actually got to look at the regulation-making power that came through from the Finance and Expenditure Committee with regard to the genetic testing and regulation-making powers and such things as “Henry VIII” clauses and whether there was an inappropriate delegation of power. Actually, with the appropriate mitigations that the Finance and Expenditure Committee accepted, we felt we got the balance right, where, with genetic testing, rather than make a rule, when it’s such a dynamic environment, we’ve actually enabled the Minister to have some discretion and some nuance through these regulation-making powers.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Helen White's immediately preceding argument — her stated unease at the House leaving the genetic testing question unsaid and delegating it to regulation — by reporting that the Regulations Review Committee examined precisely that delegation question and giving a reason for the choice (a dynamic field favours ministerial discretion over a fixed rule). It answers her concern in kind rather than engaging her specific 'veil of ignorance' reasoning, and the surrounding material reads as prepared committee narrative, so this sits mid-band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "it is such a big move to leave something unsaid by the House and leave it to regulation"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does the Government intend to have any other contentious legislation lined up for when the Prime Minister isn't here?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the business just announced and presses on what is missing from the list — whether further contentious items are being scheduled around the Prime Minister's absence. The question only makes sense following that specific statement of next week's programme, though it engages the schedule in general rather than any particular bill named.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Next week, the House will consider the committee stages of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2) and the Residential Tenancies Amendment Bill."

acuity.statement: Well, we've got a very busy agenda, as that member knows.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the subject of the question — the Government's legislative agenda — but engages neither strand of what was asked: not whether further contentious bills are coming, nor the timing against the Prime Minister's absence. A reply that would have served for almost any question about the programme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Does the Government intend to have any other contentious legislation lined up for when the Prime Minister isn't here?"

acuity.statement: What analysis has she reviewed on the social investment implications of repealing section 7AA, disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora, cutting front-line Oranga Tamariki social workers, and the social division caused by rewriting the Treaty of Waitangi?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated test — measuring impact on the most vulnerable — and turns it onto decisions she did not mention, which is real engagement with her framing. But it is a prepared list of four items rather than a response to any particular claim she made, so it answers the topic more than the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "Social investment is about funding, delivering, and measuring the impact of social services in a way that ensures better results for the most vulnerable New Zealanders."

acuity.statement: Does he agree with 42 King's Counsel that the Treaty principles bill and the intended referendum on the implementation of the bill is "wholly inappropriate" as a way of addressing such an "important and complex constitutional issue"; if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under discussion but engages no part of the answer just given — the claim about equal citizenship, and the concession that National does not think the bill achieves it, both pass untouched. The next item in a prepared sequence, which would read identically whatever had been answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "Well, we believe in equal citizenship and equal opportunity for all New Zealanders, but we do not believe that this bill is the way to achieve that."

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister there saying that members of the National Party are free to vote with their conscience this afternoon on the Treaty principles bill?
acuity.explanation: Takes the denial just offered and converts it into a concrete test that would settle it, so the dismissal either becomes a commitment or collapses. The question could not have been asked in this form had the previous answer been anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "The member is confecting things that haven't occurred."

acuity.statement: Are we to take from that that the Prime Minister is blocking his MPs from exercising their conscience on one of the most significant constitutional votes that has come before this House in living memory?
acuity.explanation: Draws the consequence directly out of the four words just answered: if the vote is a party vote, the conscience question is settled against the member being told she confected it. Entirely built on the preceding reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "The vote this afternoon will be a party vote."

acuity.statement: This bill seeks to give Māori rights and indigenous rights to everyone, and there’s no doubt that Mr Seymour wants to totally change the Treaty as we know it. That’s the view of the best legal minds in the country: the King’s Counsel who have said to abandon this bill; the Waitangi Tribunal, who have said that by engaging with this process, the Crown was sanctioning a process that will take away indigenous rights; and, in fact, there’s a view of Crown Law, the Government’s own lawyers—the Government’s own lawyers—who have said that this bill will undermine Māori rights.
acuity.explanation: Takes Seymour's central claim — that the bill extinguishes no right and merely universalises Treaty rights — and contradicts it head-on, arguing that universalising indigenous rights is itself the change, then marshalling the KCs, the Waitangi Tribunal and Crown Law as authorities for the opposite conclusion. The speech would have to be different if Seymour had not made the 'takes from no one' argument. Scored only on engagement: the abuse elsewhere in the turn and the soundness of the authority-based inference are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "thus the bill does not extinguish any right; it does not take from anyone. It reinforces the rights of the Treaty as universal human rights" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: By introducing the bill, though, National are allowing David Seymour to launch a six-month hate tour. He’s using that six-month hate tour to launch a citizens initiated referendum to fight the National Party in 1996. The Minister’s “Vanity Treaty Principles Bill” will cost us $4 million—$4 million—at a time when we’ve got the cost of living going through the roof.
acuity.explanation: Seymour pre-emptively answered the 'other priorities' objection; Jackson restates that objection in cost-of-living terms without taking up the rebuttal at all — no engagement with 'walk and chew gum', no answer on whether the bill has displaced other work. It is on the matter under debate and gestures at a point Seymour raised, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than lower, but there is no part of Seymour's argument you can point at being engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There are those who may agree with the sentiment of the bill but believe that there are other priorities. The simple answer is that this Government has not been stopped by this bill ... You can walk and chew gum at the same time." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Our concern comes, however, with the process under this bill, whereby Parliament would simply set down its interpretation of the Treaty and then seek a majority of the public to confirm it in a referendum. This is a crude way to handle a very delicate subject. With a wave of the wand, as it were, we would unwind more than 30 years of jurisprudence—winner takes all.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the premise Seymour and Jackson fought over — that the principles were never defined and the courts filled the vacuum, so the interpretations 'are not gospel' — and then disputes the remedy, locating the objection in the bill's mechanism rather than its sentiment. That is engagement with one strand (the legitimacy of Parliament defining the principles by majority) before returning to National's prepared position on the coalition agreement, so a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill fills a silence this Parliament has left for five decades. In so doing, it affirms the basis of our country." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Of course there will be a wide variety of views amongst Māori, just as there is amongst any group, but those opposed to the changes will likely conclude that fundamental change is being imposed on them by a majority if it were to pass. That would risk stoking an already keen sense of grievance. It would risk increasing divisions in our country rather than reducing them.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests Seymour's claim that the bill reveals rather than creates division, accepting his premise that Māori opinion is not monolithic and then turning it against him: a majority-imposed settlement would deepen grievance. The speech would have to change had Seymour not argued the bill is uniting, which is what makes this responsive rather than prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The division that you are seeing was not caused by this bill; it has been built up over decades" and "It is not division. Treaties are supposed to unite people, not divide them." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: New Zealand First has a very long and consistent history on our position regarding the Treaty principles. As a party, we have brought legislation to this House in order to deliver clarity and certainty to this nation regarding the Treaty and its influence on who we are. We have, and continue to, reject that there are principles.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party-history material on the matter under debate (whether the Treaty has principles), but it engages no part of Goldsmith's preceding argument about the tension between Treaty commitments and democratic equality, nor the list of government actions he gave. Substituting a different argument on the same topic for Goldsmith's turn would not change a word of this passage; it sits in the low band because it is at least squarely about the bill's subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith argued "There is a tension between those two things, between honouring commitments to Māori flowing from the Treaty and the basic expectations of equality in a modern democracy" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Everybody, every single one of the members sitting on that side of the House have enabled this bill to be introduced to the House. You are complicit in the harm and the division that this presents and are complicit in the euthanising of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Costello's turn — her defence that supporting the bill only to first reading is a democratic duty — and answers it directly: whoever enabled the bill's introduction owns its consequences. It engages the enabling claim rather than her substantive argument that there are no Treaty principles or that open debate should not be feared, and then moves to prepared material, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal. Scored on engagement only; the accusation of complicity is a civility and focus matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "New Zealand First will, as we’ve committed to, support this bill to the first reading; it is our commitment to this Government and to this democracy." — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: ACT are seen to be pulling the strings and running the country, like the KKK with a swipe card to the Beehive, and Luxon doesn’t even care. There’s a ghost in his chair.
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of either preceding turn: it is an attack on ACT's influence over the Government and on the Prime Minister's passivity, and would read identically whatever Goldsmith or Costello had said. It could have been delivered in almost any debate of this Parliament, which puts it at the bottom of the band; it gets 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because the coalition's handling of this bill is the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Casey Costello spoke about the free and open exchange of ideas in the House and New Zealand First's position that the Treaty has no principles, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: And now we go to a futile select committee process—one where the National Party said they’re not going to vote for it; we’re not going to vote for it. It’s wasteful, it’s divisive. That Government should be ashamed.
acuity.explanation: Webb's speech is largely prepared condemnation of the bill (historical statutes, the King's Counsel letter, Luxon), but this passage does take up one specific strand of Upston's preceding turn — National's announced plan to send the bill to select committee while opposing it at second reading — and draws out a consequence from it, that the committee process is therefore futile, while turning her own word "divisive" back on her. Partial engagement with an identifiable claim, not the main constitutional argument, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "National will uphold the coalition agreement with ACT and support their Treaty principles bill at first reading, allowing it to go to select committee. However, we will vote against it at the second reading"

acuity.statement: In doing so, I want to echo the words of my National Party colleagues who have already spoken. It’s National’s long-held position that a referendum on the Treaty would be divisive. We therefore do not support this bill becoming law.
acuity.explanation: Simpson follows a forceful, specific critique and explicitly announces he is repeating his own colleagues' prepared lines, reproducing Upston's framing almost phrase for phrase (referendum divisive, simplistic approach, case by case, MMP compromise). Nothing in the speech engages the content of Webb's argument; it would read identically whatever Webb had said. It is at least on the matter under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that this is the most racist legislation in a hundred years, that 40 King's Counsel say the bill rewrites the Treaty and erases the article 2 guarantee of tino rangatiratanga, and that the select committee process is futile — and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: Yes, the Treaty is a topic of debate in this country, and it has been for the almost 200 years since its signing, and different people will have different views about what it means. But the things that people stop me in the street about, in my electorate, are the same things that National is squarely focused on addressing.
acuity.explanation: Tangaere-Manuel's immediately preceding speech attacked the bill's stated objective of promoting a national conversation, arguing that conversation has been under way since 1840 and that the Government's belated arrival should not usurp it. Meager takes up that one strand — conceding the Treaty has been debated for almost 200 years and later that the bill could not end that debate — which is a real engagement with her point and not merely a reference to her. But he does not contest her central claims (that the bill is divisive, wasteful, or an attack on Māori), and the sentence immediately turns back to prepared material on National's cost-of-living focus that would have been delivered whatever she had said. Partial engagement, then prepared text: the mid-band score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Māori have held national conversations about all aspects of Te Tiriti since 5 February 1840 at Taurangatira. It's been debated on every marae, the length and breadth of Aotearoa since." — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel

acuity.statement: Mr Speaker, thank you for the opportunity just to respond very briefly to the amendment that is on the Table, which I think deserves consideration to the extent that I feel the need to point out that the Government regards it as prudent to provide a notice that will be long enough, at least until such time as the industrial action takes place, and a bit longer.
acuity.explanation: Belich's central argument was that she "cannot see any logical reason" for the authorisation to run two weeks past the strike notice. Penk takes up that exact gap and supplies the reasons for it — possible prolongation of the action, roster lead time, and the fact the notice can be cancelled at any time. The speech would be materially different had she moved a different amendment or raised a different objection, so it is squarely responsive; it stops short of 1.0 only because her other specific questions (the Employment Relations Act s97 alternative, the delay in reporting the 5 November notice) go unengaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would like to move, That the words “14 February 2025” be replaced with the words “31 January 2025”." — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: I am simply making a suggestion to amend and noting the circumstances, and I’m sure that member has as much respect as I do for the civilians in the defence force who are on strike at the moment, and additionally for the members of the defence force who have been, as a result of this motion, asked to perform the work of the civilian defence force; showing, I think, proving, the essential nature of the work that the civilian staff do and the importance of the work not only to their day-to-day jobs but, in fact, as we’ve seen in many of these authorisations that have been made, to the workings of the defence force.
acuity.explanation: Costley's interjection put a specific charge to her: that she is indifferent to uniformed personnel. She takes up that strand directly — asserting respect for the uniformed members now being tasked with the civilians' work — and turns it into her own point about the essential nature of that work. That is a real engagement with the content of the challenge, not merely a reference to it; it is partial rather than full because she first deflects to an invitation to take a call, and then returns to her prepared case about the authorisations.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What about people in uniform? Do you care about them?" — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: Well, I just welcome the member who has so much to say about this to come over here and run a response to a national emergency, and then can lecture me about what to do in that situation. When you’ve saved 20,000 lives in a health emergency, come and tell me how to run a Government.
acuity.explanation: Costley's interjection puts a specific counter-example to her claim that this Government is uniquely pulling uniformed front-line staff into non-uniformed jobs: that the previous Labour government did the same at isolation hotels. She replies squarely at the member who said it, so she plainly heard it, but engages no part of its content — she neither disputes that defence personnel staffed isolation hotels nor distinguishes that deployment from this one. Instead she pivots to her own credentials and record, which is the 'the member opposite is the last person who should talk about this' move: engaging the target rather than the claim. Mid-band rather than 0.1 because the reply is visibly shaped by the interjection (an emergency-response defence) and would not exist without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Like isolation hotels, for example?" — Tim Costley

acuity.statement: What we are being asked to do is to support an extension motion for the exact same reasons that were given yesterday by the Minister, but all the way out to 14 February. Nothing given today is any different to the reasons given yesterday. Those reasons were to justify 14 days; we would have expected something more compelling to justify all the way up to 14 February.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn in the window is Verrall's, and nothing here engages her Budget-and-funding-envelope argument: his speech would be word-for-word identical had she never spoken. It sits above the floor because it is not merely prepared material on the right subject — it is pointed at the specific justification offered in the debate (that the same 14-day reasons are being used to buy three months, with 'wriggle room' for logistics) and rebuts it on the Defence Act's fortnight limit. But that engagement is with a contribution I cannot point at in the text given, so by the rubric's own rule the score is capped in the 0.0-0.3 band; 0.3 for a real gesture at the debate rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued that the zero percent pay offer and the resulting strike are consequences of this Government's Budget 2024-25 cuts to Vote Defence ($4.949 billion, a $308 million reduction), and this statement does not take that up. It engages the Associate Minister of Defence's justification for the extension, which is not a turn in this window.

acuity.statement: Following that contribution from my colleague the Hon Kieran McAnulty, which differs slightly from the amendment that I had put up, I think it is incumbent on me to make some comments about his amendment that he has made, which does make a lot of sense to me.
acuity.explanation: She opens by taking up the specific amendment McAnulty has just moved, notes how it differs from her own intended amendment, and then reshapes her contribution around his — going on to supply the statutory grounding (Defence Act 1990, section 9 and its 14-day review) for why a shorter extension is warranted. Had McAnulty moved a different amendment, or none, this speech would necessarily have been different. Not a full 1.0 because she largely endorses rather than works through the detail of his 17 December date.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "what I’m proposing is, That we amend this extension motion to replace “14 February 2025” with “17 December 2024”"

acuity.statement: In terms of Mr McAnulty’s contribution and amendment, though, I do think that we haven’t been provided with—as he’s said—the additional reasons as to why such a significant extension would be given without the requirement on the Minister of Defence to come back and report to the House.
acuity.explanation: This picks up the precise strand of McAnulty's argument — that the Minister should have to come back and justify any further extension — attributes it to him explicitly, and then develops it by setting out what the Minister did and did not explain to the House, before proposing a complementary two-weekly reporting requirement. The content of the previous turn is engaged, not merely referenced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "I’d be very interested to hear why the Government wouldn’t support that." and "I think the Minister deserves to justify any extension."

acuity.statement: I concur with the comments that have been made around this being a very unusual step to take. acuity.explanation: Takes up Abel's specific claim that the bill excludes public participation, names the project Abel raised, contests the claim with a mechanism in the bill (councils must be invited to comment), and then concedes the part that is true (fewer participation rights) while disputing that this is a defect. The reply would have to be different if Abel had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "The public will not be allowed to make submissions, but there must be a taking into account of that."

acuity.statement: My question to that point is: does he consider that that whole point would be fixed—any distinctions wouldn’t have to be made—if, of course, there was no Schedule 2 and no listed projects, as suggested by the Hon David Parker in the debate at the outset about whether or not the amendment bill should be set aside or not?
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's preceding defence — that the listed projects were panel-recommended and so go into the schedule — by asking whether removing the schedule dissolves the problem. But it returns to her own earlier amendment and Parker's earlier proposition rather than taking up the process argument Bishop had just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The Trans-Tasman Resources project, like all of them that were listed in the schedule, were recommended by the panel and therefore it will go into the bill."

acuity.statement: Well, of course that is true, but the Government wants there to be a schedule. That’s why we’ve moved the schedule and that’s why we’ve listed the projects. Of course, that point is true, but it doesn’t take you very far, because we don’t agree with that proposition.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the hypothetical put to him, concedes its logic outright, and then locates the disagreement in the premise rather than the inference. The answer is unintelligible without the question that precedes it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "does he consider that that whole point would be fixed … if, of course, there was no Schedule 2 and no listed projects"

acuity.statement: Thank you. Still on the purpose clause, has the Minister considered the submissions of Straterra and the advice of officials that there should be in a clause, a subclause, referring to the environment—in my amendment, I’ve called it “sustainable management”; it could be something else—and the submission that without such a reference and because of the mechanisms of the Act that I’ve already talked about, that this will enable cowboys?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the purpose clause — but engages no part of the answer just given. The Minister had conceded her schedule point while rejecting the proposition; she does not take that up, and instead opens a prepared new line on Straterra's submission and her own amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just said the schedule point "doesn’t take you very far, because we don’t agree with that proposition", and this question does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Of course, what the Minister just talked about I will want to ask questions on when we get to Part 2 and, particularly, the schedules, where I very strongly disagree with the Minister when he says that there are environmental protections there when this purpose is given the greatest weight.
acuity.explanation: Picks out the precise proposition in the answer just given — that environmental considerations are provided for elsewhere in the bill — and joins issue with it, identifying why she thinks it fails (the purpose clause carries the greatest weight). Not 1.0 because she defers the actual argument to a later part of the debate rather than making it here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "there’s a variety of mechanisms that are scattered throughout the bill in order to give effect to environmental considerations"

acuity.statement: No. The projects listed in the schedule are renewable projects. There’s a whole mixture of solar; from memory, there’s some wind; and there’s a whole variety of different projects which are really, really important.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific request squarely — he will not add a renewable-electricity reference to the purpose clause — and engages the premise by describing the renewable projects already scheduled. Partial because he addresses the subject of renewables rather than her actual reason for asking, which was the mixed ownership models that make project-by-project naming awkward.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "would he consider putting in a specific reference just to fast tracking renewable electricity generation, rather than specifically naming them project by project"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chairman. A question for the Minister in the chair: he said one of the problems that New Zealand’s energy sector faces that this bill is seeking to rectify is the fact that it takes so long to get a consent for a renewable energy project. Could the Minister, please, tell the committee how many megawatts of consented but unbuilt renewable energy projects there are in New Zealand?
acuity.explanation: Quotes back the exact claim the Minister had just made — that consenting delay is what holds renewables up — and tests it with the one figure that would falsify it, the consented-but-unbuilt capacity. The question could not have been asked had he argued anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "one of the reasons why it’s so difficult to fill that gap, or that shortage, is resource consenting. It takes for ever to get consents."

acuity.statement: Well, it’s nothing to do with the bill, but I’m happy to answer it.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the question put to him and proceeds to answer it on its own terms rather than deflecting, acknowledging the specific challenge even while disputing its relevance to the bill. Short of 1.0 because the first move is to contest the question's admissibility rather than its substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "how many megawatts of consented but unbuilt renewable energy projects there are in New Zealand?"

acuity.statement: The more substantive contribution was made by Lan Pham. I won’t relitigate what I’ve said; the Government is not going to change the purpose clause, for the reasons that I’ve already given. I was intrigued by her remarks that the Resource Management Act (RMA) is an enabling piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Bishop names Pham's specific characterisation of the RMA as enabling legislation and spends the bulk of his turn contesting it (1991 intent vs outcome, house price growth, consenting costs, quarries), so the speech would be different had she argued something else. He also answers Duncan Webb's two earlier points directly. Short of 1.0 because he declines outright to engage the actual amendment — the purpose-clause insertion she asked him about — and pivots to a prepared case against the RMA generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "given the RMA has still been enabling development and, essentially, the decline of the environment?" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: Can I for a start say that I agree with much of what he said in the last speech, but not everything, and I agree that one of the reasons house prices went so high was having too strict rules around land markets.
acuity.explanation: Parker takes up Bishop's land-supply argument explicitly, concedes the premise, cites the specific measures his own Government used to address it, and then isolates the point of disagreement — that excluding environmental concerns goes a step too far. He also goes back to Bishop's earlier geothermal consenting point and rebuts it with the renewals detail. Accepting part and disputing the rest is textbook engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the RMA has been one of the biggest public policy failures in New Zealand history, because the RMA is almost directly responsible for the fact that over the last 20 years we have had the fastest house price growth in the OECD" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Oh, OK. Well, there is the ability for people affected by projects like that to be part of the expert panel process.
acuity.explanation: Bishop answers the specific question Parker put — whether a non-adjacent affected party can participate — and accepts the correction when his first reading of the letter (that the writer was an adjoining landowner) is put right. Not higher because the reply engages only the participation limb and leaves the substance of the example, the scale of the mine and the claimed loss, untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how can it be justified that that application for something that vast could proceed without public input from the likes of that person there, who says he’s already suffered an $800,000 loss?" — David Parker

acuity.statement: One of the couple of questions we have for the Minister is: what is New Zealand’s experience in seabed mining? What is the cost that the new expert panel will be bearing and what will taxpayers expect to bear, given they already have three or four court cases, three DMCs, two Environmental Protection Authority meetings?
acuity.explanation: Williams' immediately preceding turn put a specific, four-part line of questioning to the Minister about Amendment Paper 130, new clause 3A and the constitutional guidance (Cabinet Manual 2017, the 2017 Cabinet Office circular, the LDAC guidelines, the Public Service Act 2020). Ngarewa-Packer does not engage any strand of that: she puts her own prepared questions about Trans-Tasman Resources, seabed mining costs and officials' experience. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate — the same bill, and later the same clause 3 and Te Tiriti theme — so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically whatever Williams had argued, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band with a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked the Minister "what considerations have the Minister and other Ministers responsible for this legislation given to the Cabinet Manual 2017 guidelines on how our Cabinet Ministers should give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi" and new clause 3A, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Well, the member needs to actually get familiar with the bill. I’d also encourage her to read clauses 18B, 19A, and 24WA, which impose a variety of obligations on decision makers and panels when it comes to the effect of Treaty settlements.
acuity.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer's interjection made a pointed content claim — the clause he told her to read (4A) is the very clause her amendment targets. He does not take that up at all; he restates that she should get familiar with the bill and extends the list of clauses to read. It is a gesture at the exchange on the same subject rather than engagement with what she said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "That’s what my amendment is: 4A."

acuity.statement: It’s disappointing to hear the focus on settled iwi and post-settlement governance entities (PSGEs), knowing that Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations are beyond an entity and beyond a settlement.
acuity.explanation: Bishop's defence was that the bill's Treaty protections are carried by clauses covering existing Treaty settlements and customary rights. She takes exactly that defence and identifies its limit — the obligation is not bounded by a settlement or a settlement entity. The speech would have to change if Bishop had defended the bill on different grounds, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "the obligations arising under existing Treaty settlements; … customary rights"

acuity.statement: There are many Māori that need protection from fast track, and that’s well beyond having a settled iwi framework.
acuity.explanation: Draws out the consequence of the clause-by-clause defence Bishop had just given: if the protections run through settlements, Mana Whakahono ā Rohe and MACA, then hapū and whenua Māori outside those pathways are unprotected. Engages the structure of his claim rather than merely naming him, though it broadens into prepared material on her own amendment paper.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I think we’ve done a really good job balancing the right interests."

acuity.statement: I want to ask a number of questions about that discussion on the Resource Management Act (RMA), and one is: does he acknowledge that this bill doesn’t fix the fundamental timing and cost problem with the RMA, which is that when you compare the consenting time frames and cost to developers, which are far too high, the problem when you compare it internationally is with those smaller and medium sized projects, which, of course, are not covered by this bill because this is for large projects?
acuity.explanation: Bishop's argument was that the RMA is the binding constraint and that this bill addresses it. She accepts the premise that consenting time and cost are too high and turns it against him — the international gap is in small and medium projects, which this bill does not cover. A direct rebuttal of the reasoning just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it’s just that the Resource Management Act makes it very difficult to get access to that cheap energy"

acuity.statement: The Minister made the point that we are the same land size or bigger than Great Britain, we only have 5 million people, but we still have a housing problem. I do not disagree with that, but one of the main problems for putting more houses anywhere, even in increasing density, is the infrastructure funding, and I cannot see anything in this bill that addresses that problem.
acuity.explanation: The textbook form of engagement: concedes the part of the Minister's case she accepts, then disputes the inference that planning law is the binding constraint, nominating infrastructure funding instead and noting the bill is silent on it. Responsive to the content of his case, not to his presence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "Actually, we’ve got plenty of cheap energy in this country; it’s just that the Resource Management Act makes it very difficult to get access to that cheap energy."

acuity.statement: The answer in relation to all of the three areas that the member, the Hon Rachel Brooking, raises—prohibited activities, water conservation orders, and previously declined projects—is the same in all of them, which is that the bill is designed to facilitate projects with significant regional or national benefits.
acuity.explanation: Takes up each of the three specific exclusions Brooking asked the Minister to add and gives a single reasoned answer to all three (deliberately wide scope; the matters are to be weighed in the panel process rather than excluded up front). The speech would have been different had she raised different categories, since he enumerates hers. Short of 1.0 because he does not supply the analysis or evidence on prohibited activities she specifically asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Will the Minister consider including prohibited activities as ineligible activities? — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: Specifically, when it comes to previously declined projects, I take a different view to the member Rachel Brooking, which is the Government’s view that there have been projects under the RMA that have been declined that we would like to see progressed.
acuity.explanation: Engages the premise of her strongest argument rather than deflecting: she treats re-approving declined applications as a contradiction, and he accepts the description and disputes that it is a flaw, saying it is an explicit policy decision because the current law is too restrictive. Disagreement aimed squarely at the argument just made is the strongest evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: applications that have previously been declined because of their adverse effects on the environment can be approved under this bill — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: My question is about the Cabinet sector in 2017 and the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee’s (LDAC) advice around clauses like the one I’ve proposed at 3A is simply that: is the provisions that he has relied on in his answer to me at clause 6 and clause 7—those are about existing settlements and about ineligible Māori land—is that enough, in his view, to satisfy what are essentially constitutional conventions here?
acuity.explanation: She is continuing her own prepared series of questions ('the last three of my four questions') on LDAC advice and the Māori land definition. It is squarely on the matter under debate and glances at the Minister's earlier answers, but engages no part of the argument in the turn immediately preceding — hence the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop's preceding turn was about the RMA reform bills, infrastructure funding, medium-density zones and clause 4 on competing applications, and this statement does not take any of that up; it gestures back at an earlier answer of his on clauses 6 and 7 that is not the turn she follows.

acuity.statement: The member’s suggestion that we should just create a carte blanche “The bill must give effect to the Treaty” would be a licence, with respect, for utter legal chaos. The Government is not willing to do that.
acuity.explanation: He takes the specific alternative Williams had just put — a general duty on decision makers to give effect to Te Tiriti instead of the clause 4 definition — characterises it, gives a reason for rejecting it and states the Government's position. The speech would be different had she proposed something else. Scored on engagement only: the 'utter legal chaos' inference is unsupported, but that is a question for Rigor, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "should give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi" — Arena Williams, who proposed removing the Crown-land limb of the Māori land definition and instead requiring decision makers to give effect to Te Tiriti.

acuity.statement: Listening to what the Minister responsible for RMA Reform has just been saying in his last two contributions, I guess my caution is that several learned lawyers during the select committee space—one challenged this Government about this bill having the potential to be this Government’s KiwiBuild disaster, and you just spoke about that.
acuity.explanation: He picks up one strand of what Bishop had just said — the KiwiBuild comparison — and turns it back, reporting select committee lawyers who warned this bill could be the Government's own KiwiBuild, before moving on to prepared material about litigation risk, process and the purpose clause. A pointable partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the Minister's actual argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "he was saddled with the disaster that was KiwiBuild" — Chris Bishop, who used KiwiBuild as the example of Labour's housing failure.

acuity.statement: Well, the member, the Hon Rachel Brooking, makes some reasonable points, but all I would say is this: she seems to be drawing a distinction between various different rationales for the bill and trying to claim that they are different; they’re not. There are multiple rationales for the bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise structure of Brooking's challenge — that the stated rationales (process, speed, one-stop shop) are inconsistent with the claim that the bill protects the environment — names it, and rebuts it by asserting the rationales are plural rather than conflicting. He then concedes her substantive point that the bill changes the decision-making framework to allow more projects, and answers her question about where environmental protection sits (expert panel stage, parent statutes layered through). The speech would be materially different had she argued something else; he does not supply the project-by-project justification she asked for, which keeps it below full marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "does he agree that that is then inconsistent with the Prime Minister’s remarks in question time yesterday that this bill will protect the environment?"

acuity.statement: When you were asked specifically, “Where do environmental outcomes fit in this bill?”, you’ve just said that this bill will still maintain core environmental protections. The question is: by what means will it do that? In its drafting, it clearly, specifically, and explicitly rules out multiple pieces of environmental legislation. That is what the legislation does.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the exact assurance Bishop had just given seconds earlier and presses on its mechanism, arguing the drafting excludes the very environmental statutes that would deliver it. He also corrects Bishop's characterisation of the prior exchange — that the Green argument was not only that the RMA failed development but that it facilitated environmental decline — and concedes common ground that the RMA is failing. Entirely contingent on what Bishop said; substitute a different argument and this speech must change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "while still maintaining core environmental protections"

acuity.statement: It depends on what your definition of a public benefit is. The debate last night, as I demonstrated, was about this proposition—nuts proposition, frankly—that a privately owned electricity generator didn’t deliver private benefits. The member Lan Pham’s argument seems now to be that renewable energy is a public benefit. I agree—I agree with her—there are public benefits from renewable energy, but much of New Zealand’s renewable electricity infrastructure is privately owned.
acuity.explanation: Bishop takes up the exact proposition in Lan Pham's amendment — that fast track should be narrowed to projects conferring public benefit, with renewable energy as the exemplar — names her, restates her position, concedes part of it, and then disputes the inference by distinguishing ownership structure from benefit. He goes on to work through her own listed categories (housing, quarries, mining) to argue each carries a public benefit, which is a direct answer to her request for a narrowing definition. The speech would be materially different had she argued something else; scoring is on engagement only, not on whether his characterisation of her argument as having 'changed' is fair (that is a rigor question).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if this is the thing that, publicly, the Government wants to point to about fast track, then let’s actually make the fast-track bill about these public projects" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: I’m really appreciating the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform’s responses, in basically saying that the sky is blue, but I don’t accept the quite disingenuous assumption, or assertion, that my argument is changing. It’s not changing. What I’m saying, and what we’ve been saying all along, is: make it really clear within the fast-track bill that companies that apply for fast track need to prove that they are conferring these public benefits. I disagree that every project in the list confers a public benefit, and if you narrow it, again, like many submitters suggested, including the Infrastructure Commission, you would actually avoid a lot of the controversy about these much more damaging projects which are included in the bill.
acuity.explanation: She engages two specific strands of the reply immediately preceding: she rejects his claim that her argument has shifted, and she denies his core contention that every listed project confers a public benefit, restating her position as a proof requirement on applicants. That is genuine take-up of the content, not a mere reference. It falls short of the top band because she does not engage his actual counter-argument about mixed ownership structures and private delivery of housing, and the remainder of the turn moves on to prepared material on Amendment Paper 151.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The argument seems to have changed." and "all of the projects and all of the activities listed in the fast track deliver public benefits" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: The member says, “Is the Government’s position development at all costs?” No, it isn’t, and I point him to clause 24WD, which is “When panel must or may decline approvals”, which is the panel must decline an approval if the panel forms the view that there are one or more adverse impacts in relation to the approval sought.
acuity.explanation: Bishop takes Abel's own framing question, answers it directly in the negative, and grounds the answer in a specific clause of the bill said to supply the decline test Abel claimed was missing. The reply would have had to be different had Abel asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Is the Minister suggesting development at all costs?" and "where do environmental outcomes fit in this bill?"

acuity.statement: In relation to Trans-Tasman Resources and the offshore wind, I mean, it is a true statement of fact that there is no regulatory regime for offshore wind, but there is for the activities that Trans-Tasman Resources wish to undertake.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the specific factual premise Abel put to him — that there is no regulatory regime for seabed mining — and names the statutes he says supply it. Squarely engaged with the claim just made, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "What is the regulatory regime for deep-sea mining, Minister? There is no regulatory regime for that."

acuity.statement: In relation to projects that we would like to see advance that have been previously declined, I’m going to decline the member’s invitation to get into the specifics about that.
acuity.explanation: He identifies the precise request Abel made and addresses it explicitly, but engages it only by refusing to supply the examples, so the engagement is acknowledgement rather than substantive take-up. Partial on Acuity's own terms; the refusal itself is a Forthrightness matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "I wonder if the Minister can outline some examples of projects that were turned down in the previous regime that the Minister would like to progress"

acuity.statement: Well, contemporary—I mean, it depends what your definition of a contemporary breach is. The Waitangi Tribunal’s currently seems to be that literally anything the Crown does is a contemporary breach; the Government has a different view, unsurprisingly. That’s a conversation for another day.
acuity.explanation: He picks up the exact term Lyndon used — contemporary breaches — and disputes how it is being defined, which is engagement with the content of her interjection; but he then defers the substance rather than answering whether the bill's Treaty-settlement references cover anything beyond historic agreements.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "Those are only historic agreements. That does not recognise contemporary breaches that you’re doing."

acuity.statement: Firstly, Glen Bennett asks whether I am comfortable with so many statutes being included in fast track? Yes, we are. That’s why it’s in the bill. Secondly, he asks “What is a substantive application?” Well, it is literally an application under the fast track; that is what it means. It’s a standard application to go to the expert panel.
acuity.explanation: Takes Bennett's questions in the order they were put and answers two of them directly — confirming comfort with the number of statutes and defining "substantive application". The reply could not have been written without Bennett's turn, though the third question (the complex freshwater fisheries activity) goes unaddressed, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "I just want to get clarity from the Minister about what a “substantive application” is, just so we can understand as a committee."

acuity.statement: Rachel Brooking made a number of points. In relation to small and medium projects versus large projects, yes, she’s right that we need to make it easier for small and medium projects. We agree. That is why we have a comprehensive programme of Resource Management Act (RMA) reform, in particular quite a large suite of national direction coming next year, which respectfully builds on some of the work developed by the last Government.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific comparative claim Brooking made about small and medium projects, concedes it, and then does something with it by pointing to the national direction programme as the answer. The passage would have to be rewritten if she had made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "compared with international comparisons, it is the smaller and medium projects that take too long and cost too much"

acuity.statement: In relation to non-settled iwi, there are a range of protections—not just for settled iwi—throughout the bill as well. In particular, I would point her to the make-up of the panels where there has to be a person on the panel with the knowledge of te ao Māori and Māori development.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact gap Brooking identified — unsettled iwi and hapū — and disputes it by naming specific provisions (panel composition, ineligible Māori land). Short of 1.0 because it answers the narrower "not mentioned" charge rather than her point about the absence of a general Treaty clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "iwi or hapū that do not have settlements or do not have Mana Whakahono a Rohe agreements, which are very rare, are not really mentioned in this bill"

acuity.statement: Mr Meager asks, “What’s No. 3?” Of course, if he looks at Schedule 2, he will see that they are not numbered.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the interjection immediately and corrects the premise of the question rather than ignoring it or merely naming the interjector — the schedule's projects are not numbered, so the question cannot be put as asked. Entirely contingent on what Meager said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "What’s No. 3?"

acuity.statement: That’s because it’s required; it’s not in this bill. We’ll get to that in Part 2.
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just argued that energy projects involve 'a huge amount of community consultation, engagement'. Brooking takes that exact claim and does something with it: the consultation happens because existing law requires it, so it is not a feature this bill supplies. Short, but it engages the content of the claim rather than referencing or deflecting it, and the speech would be different had Bishop said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "there’s a huge amount of community consultation, engagement—"

acuity.statement: This is a public Government entity which is now going to pay out tens of millions of dollars in taxpayers’ money for land which was not valuable before and is now. It is not only a private benefit; that is public money going into the hands of Winton Land Co. for a residential development that they have lobbied successive Governments for, and it has been turned down over and over again.
acuity.explanation: Bishop's preceding turn rested on the proposition that private development can carry public benefits in a mixed economy. Williams takes that proposition up and inverts it on a named Schedule 2 project: the flow she identifies runs the other way, from the public purse (NZTA land purchase, ratepayer-funded infrastructure) into private hands. She also presses precisely the project-specific questioning Bishop had declined to entertain. Not a full 1.0 because much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on the Winton project rather than engagement with his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "private development can have public benefits because we live in a mixed economy"

acuity.statement: The first thing is to publicly acknowledge that, in relation to the particular project the member’s talking about, as that went through the Cabinet process I declared a conflict, out of an abundance of caution, on advice from the Cabinet Office in relation to a press release I issued in relation to that particular project back in 2022, from memory.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what was put to him — the propriety/transparency implication around the Winton project and the donation — by volunteering his own declared conflict. But it leaves untouched the substance of Williams's case (the valuation uplift, NZTA paying tens of millions for rezoned land, the infrastructure cost shifted to Auckland ratepayers), and the rest of the turn pivots to characterising her allegations as facile. Partial engagement, pointable but narrow.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Winton Land Co. donated $100,000 to the National Party in its campaign year."

acuity.statement: Firstly, councils are able to charge development contributions for housing developments. The bill does not change that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific mechanism in Williams's argument — that the bill stops Auckland Council requiring the developer to fund roads, pipes and facilities, pushing the cost on to ratepayers — and rebuts it directly by naming the development contributions regime and asserting the bill leaves it intact. The reply would have to change if the preceding critique had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Auckland Council cannot require the developer to put in the kind of infrastructure that will cost the developer many millions more"

acuity.statement: Now, my question for the Minister is: given his recent statements about non-inclusion of Te Tiriti considerations, what is the say and rights of iwi impacted by that project if they do not have customary marine title, if they are not settled, and if they do not have mana whakahono?
acuity.explanation: Bishop's preceding turn asserted that objections to any listed project are answered by the expert panel process and that the answer is identical for every project. Abel takes that general claim and tests it against a case it cannot absorb: iwi who are unsettled, hold no customary marine title and have no mana whakahono, and who therefore fall outside the clause 4A ineligibility protection, so the panel route leaves them no standing. He also takes up Bishop's stated position on Te Tiriti considerations directly. Not a full 1.0 because he does not engage the panel mechanism's own wording and partly delivers a prepared project brief, but the question would have to change if Bishop had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "all of those issues will be dealt with through the expert panel process. The answer is the same for all of them."

acuity.statement: I asked the Minister how he can justify doing that without rights of public input, as opposed to discretions for public input.
