acuity.statement: Just very, very quickly on the question of the six months to one year, the residential tenancy laws are amended quite frequently, and it’s just an opportunity to improve the situation—so, more fair, as the member, I think, acknowledges. Our view was that it was a better situation, so we’ve taken the opportunity.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific clause and question raised, and even picks up Hernandez's concession that the change is an improvement, but engages only the 'why change' half and leaves the 'was a longer period considered' half unanswered. Pointable partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "I just want to explore with the Minister why the change from six months to one year—was a longer period considered?"

acuity.statement: I thank him for his commitment to consider this later, but just to address his concerns around the pet bond thing not being up and running for a while, that’s all good because greyhound racing isn’t set to be banned until 2026 and the proposal in the first part of this is for a period of four calendar years to account for that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific practical objection — that the pet bond regime will not be operational until late 2025/early 2026 — and answers it directly on its own terms, pointing out that the ban does not take effect until 2026 and that the amendment's four-year window is designed to cover exactly that gap. The speech would have to be different had Bishop raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The pet-bond system won’t be operational until probably late 2025, early 2026."

acuity.statement: The other thing is that the Minister has said that the pet bonds won’t be up and running for quite some time. I would ask the Minister whether he would consider going away and having a discussion with the Minister for Social Development and Employment to see whether or not that recoverable assistance—they do pay it back—can be included.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's timing point and turns it into a concrete ask — use the lead time to negotiate recoverable assistance with MSD — but the bulk of the contribution is prepared material (the regulatory impact statement, the Citizens Advice Bureau submission) that is indifferent to what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "There’s a bunch of back-end stuff that the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment is in the middle of"

acuity.statement: Now, one of the other things that I think the Hon Carmel Sepuloni put very nicely from the Citizens Advice Bureau is: what is the workability of some of these reasonable grounds? But, from my perspective, just going a little bit deeper, what was concerning, and what we’re hoping to address with Amendment Paper 225, is the fact that the list is non-exhaustive.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly names and adopts the preceding speaker's workability argument about section 42F and then extends it to a distinct defect she had not raised — that the list of reasonable grounds is non-exhaustive — tying it to a specific Amendment Paper. The contribution is built on the content of the previous turn, not merely cross-referenced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "the broad categories of “(a) the premises are not suitable for the pet or pets … (d) the pet or pets are not suitable for the premises” invites subjective assessment by the landlord"

acuity.statement: It’s 21 days, not working days—to answer that. As to “Why 21?”—I mean, is there an argument for 28? Sure. Is there an argument for 14? Sure. You’ve got to put a number at some point. There’s no science to it, and it’s not rational in that sense; it’s just what we think is reasonable.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of the specific questions put to him in the immediately preceding turn — first the calendar-vs-working-days point directly, then the choice of 21 days, including the shorter period Hernandez asked about. The reply would be different if a different number or question had been raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My first question was: is that working days or just calendar days?" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: I want to ask a question about the evidential basis behind this bill, because, from following this bill through the select committee process, it became apparent to me that it seems like there was a decision that you arrived at, Minister, that you decided—no-cause evictions coming back to New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive exchange on the 21-day pet-consent provision and takes up no part of it — she concedes she missed the earlier discussion and opens a prepared line on the bill's evidential basis and no-cause evictions. A thanks to the Minister for "your answers" is a reference, not engagement, so this sits in the unresponsive-but-on-the-bill band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just explained that "There’s no science to it" in settling on 21 days for a landlord's reply on pets, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The evidence for pet bonds, which is Part 1, is really clear. I think the member would probably agree with me that there are a lot of tenants who wish to have a pet who can’t have a pet. I think most reasonable people realise that’s been a bit of a gap in the law. The law’s been unclear. Probably most people would agree it’s been too hard to have a pet, so the evidence underlying it is that we want to make it easier, and I think most people broadly accept that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific demand just made — "what is the evidence?" — and supplies an answer for the part actually before the committee, naming the gap in the law it is said to address. Short of 1.0 because it answers only the Part 1 strand and leaves the regulatory impact statement and submission figures she cited untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What I want to understand is: what is the evidence?" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: In responding to your concerns that the original proposal might have a perverse outcome, primarily focused on the disincentive that this may prove with landlords who would be less inclined to take on a pet if the bond wasn’t there—I get that; there’s some logic there.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's objection on its merits, states it back accurately, concedes its logic, and redrafts the amendment to meet it — the pet-bond quid pro quo the Minister had just described is exactly the mechanism being reworked. Not 1.0 because the objection being answered was voiced in an earlier turn than the one immediately preceding, which was about Part 1 evidence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the quid pro quo of that being the ability to charge up to two weeks for a pet bond" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I suppose my point would be that, if you exempt greyhounds from the pet bond rules and you’re not allowed to charge an upfront bond—so that tenants don’t have to pay an upfront bond, so it’s more likely that a landlord will take on a tenant with a greyhound or it’s more likely that tenants will go and get greyhounds as they’re more likely to be able to have a home with a pet in it—but then you say at the back end of it that you can charge up to two weeks for damage, why not just have a two-week bond, because that two-week bond is meant to cover the damage?
acuity.explanation: Works through the mechanics of the amendment just described and draws out what he takes to be its consequence — that extended back-end liability of two weeks collapses into the two-week bond it replaces. The objection is specific to the wording McAnulty had just read out and could not have been made about a different proposal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Tenant liability for pet damage caused by a greyhound as defined above" … "could be extended by up to two weeks’ rent to account for the lack of a pet bond" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: Now, I actually agree with your argument that, in general, if this was a proposal across the board, it’s counterproductive and sort of misses the point—I get it—but this is specific for former racing greyhounds and greyhounds bred for racing. We know there are people that would take them but can’t afford the bond. We know that there are landlords that will allow them if the tenant pays a bond.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's "why not just charge a pet bond" point as a general proposition and disputes its application to this narrow case, supplying the distinguishing reason — that the barrier is the upfront cash, not the liability. Textbook concede-part-dispute-the-rest engagement with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why not just have a two-week bond, because that two-week bond is meant to cover the damage?" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I want to dig into the evidential basis behind no-cause evictions, because, Minister, you’re making a really big call in bringing these back, given that this is going to impact more than 1 million renters in our country and make them vulnerable to being evicted and kicked out of their home for no good reason.
acuity.explanation: Paul follows a substantive turn by Williams on the same clause, so she is eligible, but she engages no part of Williams' argument — she opens a fresh line of her own ("what I was trying to get at previously") about the evidence base and submitter numbers, addressed to the Minister rather than to anything just said. The speech is clearly on the matter under debate (no-cause evictions in this part of the bill), which earns the top of the unresponsive band rather than 0.0, but it would have read identically whatever Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked the Associate Minister whether clause 22's reintroduction of 90-day no-cause evictions would drive rents up and whether he accepted Treasury's rent forecasts, and this statement does not take up either the rent mechanism or the Treasury prediction.

acuity.statement: I need to question the Minister on how he would allow this to go through, why he will not consider any changes, given the fact that the submissions were overwhelmingly opposed to this and even the officials’ advice states or reiterates the same concerns that were raised by—I do believe, as Tamatha said—97 percent of submitters.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni takes up the specific strand Paul had just pressed — the missing evidential basis — adopts Paul's 97 percent submitter figure by name, and does something with it: she supplies the regulatory impact statement's own wording on no-cause terminations discouraging tenants from exercising rights, which is precisely the evidence Paul said did not exist. She then extends beyond the preceding turn with her own select committee question about how long it takes to secure another rental, so this is a substantial engagement that returns to fresh material rather than a full point-by-point rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Where are the facts to back up bringing them back" — and her "97 percent of submitters were opposed to no-cause evictions being brought back".

acuity.statement: It’s pretty disappointing, to say the least, that the Associate Minister of Housing hasn’t taken the opportunity to stand up and respond to what are genuine and, frankly, straightforward questions. If we are actually to be able to dive into this part—the substance of the bill, essentially—we need to understand the Government’s rationale.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty picks up one strand of the preceding turns — that the questions Williams, Paul and Sepuloni put have gone unanswered — and carries the regulatory impact statement forward as the fallback source in the Minister's absence of reply, which is the document Sepuloni had just quoted. He then pivots to his own prepared line about the housing crisis, interest deductibility and the 7 percent rent rise, which engages the Government rather than anything Sepuloni argued, so this is partial engagement: pointable, but topic-level more than claim-level.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "I want to know from the Associate Minister of Housing why he has decided to ignore the advice in the regulatory impact statement" — and her and Paul's unanswered questions to the Minister.

acuity.statement: It’s lovely that that Minister cares so much about pet bonds and that those are close to his heart, but this part of the bill is about the termination clause that he’s bringing back in so that there will be no cause for termination and people can be booted out of their homes with no reason whatsoever. His own advice is telling that Minister that Māori are going to be disproportionately impacted.
acuity.explanation: Takes Potaka's own opening framing (what is 'close to his heart') and turns it against the substance of the part under debate, then confronts his claim that the changes are 'sensible and much needed' with the regulatory impact statement he is working from. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different turn — its structure depends on what Potaka actually said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It was really unfortunate I was unable to sit in the chair in relation to the pet bonds, because that’s quite an issue dear to my heart" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: We heard the spin from the Minister: that this will result in more properties being tenanted and a “broader suite” of tenants getting access to rental properties. I don’t know what “broader suite of tenants” means, but I do want to assume that he means Māori getting access to rental properties as well. However, if he is inferring that, then it’s interesting to see that the evidence he was giving contradicts what he said when he took his feet.
acuity.explanation: Quotes Potaka's specific phrase and does something with it: interrogates what the claim would have to mean, supplies the group it would have to cover, and argues the departmental evidence cuts against it. This is engagement with the content of the preceding claim, not a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are able to see a lot more landlords be interested in broadening the suite of tenants and people who may rent homes" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: The benefit to landlords is clear, but what does the Minister think is the benefit to tenants? Does he think that tenants will really be empowered to raise the retaliatory power?
acuity.explanation: Concedes one half of Potaka's argument (the landlord-side benefit he asserted) and presses the other half — the claimed tenant benefit — which is a real strand of the preceding turn. But the engagement stops there and the rest of the contribution is prepared material: personal anecdote, healthy-homes inspection, and international comparisons that are indifferent to what Potaka said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the changes that are being proposed ... will increase supply at the margins by giving landlords greater flexibility to rent to tenants" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: Noting that the previous Chair, Greg O’Connor, had talked about broadening the scope of the debate as a result of the Associate Minister of Housing, and noting how Part 2, particularly, touches on the impacts of no-cause evictions on people, I wanted to take it first of all to the Growing Up in New Zealand study, which identified that young people who had to move from their homes for reasons outside of their control, such as tenancy terminations, were more likely to experience homelessness and live in greater levels of hardship.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Ginny Andersen on the same clauses, and is clearly about the matter under debate (Part 2, no-cause evictions and their effects on tenants), but engages no part of her RIS/causation argument. There is a gesture at the debate's scope (the Chair's ruling, the Associate Minister's framing) rather than engagement with the preceding speaker's content, so this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued from the regulatory impact statement that there is 'no clear evidence that the changes in 2020 caused an increase in rental supply or caused rent prices to go up', and this statement does not take that argument up — it opens a separate line on the Growing Up in New Zealand study and on the Minister's earlier remarks.

acuity.statement: In terms of supply, though—which I think is important to mention, given that the Associate Minister of Housing said earlier that this will lead to better supply of rental property—it’s zero; this policy will not necessarily lead to more houses or more rental supply on the market.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding thread — the regulatory impact statement's treatment of rental supply, which Andersen raised — and supplies the RIS's own effectiveness rating on supply as 'zero', then returns to her own prepared line on efficiency and churn. It engages the topic and one element of the prior argument rather than Andersen's specific causation point, which puts it mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the regulatory impact statement does say that there is no clear evidence that the changes in 2020 caused an increase in rental supply" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Actually, a lot of the questions that I asked previously were responded to, except for one, and so I am going to re-ask it. Given that the Minister of Housing has said that there will be a longer lead-in time for introducing the pet provisions, is he going to go away and talk to the Ministry of Social Development about extending the housing product that will support lower-income New Zealanders and beneficiaries to get access to additional bond to cover the expense for the pet bond, given that his own regulatory impact statement does state very clearly that it is low-income New Zealanders and beneficiaries that will be disproportionately and negatively impacted by a pet bond being introduced?
acuity.explanation: She has clearly listened: she audits the Minister's reply, accepts that most of her questions were answered, and isolates the single one his answer left untouched. But she does not engage the substance of what he argued (reasonableness, the tribunal as the test); she re-puts her own earlier question, so this is partial engagement rather than taking up his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: 'I mean, there will be—I think this deals with the Hon Carmel Sepuloni's point as well—tribunal cases as a result of the pet provisions'

acuity.statement: I know the Minister is trying to find a balance here, but we’ve established through various exchanges that for some people the level of pet bond may well be a barrier to them being able to have a pet, even if the landlord is willing to do so.
acuity.explanation: Detailed, well-prepared material squarely on the matter under debate (pet bonds), and it nods at the Minister's general stance, but it engages no part of the argument that immediately preceded it. The speech would read identically had Bishop said something else about the pet provisions, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band, with 0.3 for the gesture at the Minister's position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing in this window: Bishop argued that 'reasonable' is used in the Residential Tenancies Act over 140 times and that tribunal cases on the pet provisions are appropriate and iterative; McAnulty opens a declared 'new question' on clause 8's bond-increase provision and does not take that argument up. He gestures at the Minister's balance-seeking but points at no claim Bishop made here.

acuity.statement: Firstly, in relation to the Hon Carmel Sepuloni’s point, we’ve made a decision not to do that. She’s asked me to go away and talk to the Ministry of Social Development. I’ve done that. We’re not doing that at this time.
acuity.explanation: Takes the one question she re-asked and answers precisely that: he restates what was asked of him, reports that he did it, and gives the decision. The reply could not have been given in response to any other question, which is the mark of full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: 'is he going to go away and talk to the Ministry of Social Development about extending the housing product that will support lower-income New Zealanders and beneficiaries'

acuity.statement: In relation to the Hon Kieran McAnulty’s point, basically, this replicates what is the existing law for general bonds. If you are a landlord and you increase the rent lawfully, say $20 a week, technically you can require a bond payment—the bond that has already been lodged—because you’d be increasing it.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the specific provision McAnulty raised and supplies the rationale asked for: the clause mirrors the existing general-bond rule, worked through with a concrete rent-and-bond example. The content is wholly determined by the question that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: 'If the landlord lawfully increases the amount of the rent, the landlord may require payment of a further sum of pet bond not exceeding the amount by which the rent payable for 2 weeks has been increased.' — his question on the rationale for the annual pet-bond increase in new section 18AA(3)

acuity.statement: That’s a good point from the Minister that we don’t want to accidentally cause a situation in the law where it’s cheaper and therefore easier for a landlord to limit their risk to pet damage by making sure that if there is going to be a dog in the property, it’s not going to be a greyhound.
acuity.explanation: She accepts the Minister's objection to the earlier amendment and builds a different mechanism that avoids it, which is genuine engagement with an argument rather than restatement of prepared material. Capped at the mid-band because the argument she takes up is not in the turns supplied here, and she does not engage the bond-increase exchange that immediately precedes her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop — the Minister's objection that compensating landlords for greyhound damage would make it cheaper for them to refuse greyhounds altogether. She concedes that objection and redesigns around it, but his words were spoken in a turn earlier than this window, so no verbatim fragment of the immediately preceding turn can be pointed at.

acuity.statement: I thank the Associate Minister of Housing for engaging on this point about the effect of this change, specifically to 90-day no-cause evictions, to the availability of rental properties, and to the price of rents. It’s helpful to have the Minister’s analysis on the record, although I don’t think we’ve gotten to the bottom of whether this helps or hinders.
acuity.explanation: Williams picks up the exact strand McAnulty left the committee with — whether the Government has evidence for the 90-day change and whether it helps — and carries it forward by testing the Minister's stated evidence against Treasury's forecast and the Stats NZ rent series rather than restating McAnulty's complaint. The engagement is partial in that much of her call is directed at the Minister's intervening answer and returns to her own prepared line about speculative investment and new versus existing stock, but the continuity with the preceding turn is clearly pointable: she concedes the Minister did engage, then says the help-or-hinder question remains open.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Two very simple questions which the committee deserves a direct answer to. What evidence is this based on and how will this help?"

acuity.statement: The Government’s proposals are intended to support supply and continue to keep downward pressure on rents.
acuity.explanation: Paul's turn repeatedly demanded the policy basis of the bill and the evidence behind no-cause evictions. Potaka supplies a statement of intended purpose, which takes up the topic of the question directly, but leaves untouched the specific strands she pressed — the evidential basis, the RIS findings, and whether alternatives were explored. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "what is the policy basis and what is the problem that we’re trying to solve for this bill?"

acuity.statement: There was also a number of comments around Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Guess what, people? Māori are disproportionately renters in this country, but also Māori are landlords, and those Māori landlords would welcome the flexibility to offer tenancies and houses to renters, whether they are Māori or not Māori.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Treaty/Māori strand Paul raised from paragraph 106 of the RIS and offers a counter-consideration (Māori as landlords as well as renters). It engages the topic she raised and reframes it, but does not take up her actual point — that the RIS says the proposals may push more households into emergency and social housing. One strand engaged, then a pivot to prepared contrast material, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "it just so happens to be the Treaty of Waitangi analysis of the termination proposals"

acuity.statement: Again, there’s a whole range of comments that have been made by members opposites about risks, but as the previous Minister for social development knows, and knows very well, the actual social-allocation system is based on risk and need. So, again, those members opposite who have commented around risk should take some time to undertake the relevant research required to better understand the housing system.
acuity.explanation: Names the opposing speakers' use of 'risk' and offers one relevant fact about the social-allocation system, but that fact is about housing allocation rather than the tenancy risk Paul was questioning, and the remainder tells members to go and research. It is more a reference to the argument than an engagement with it, sitting just below a genuine partial rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "because we’re talking about these riskier tenants—and I’m sorry, but it’s hard to not jump to the conclusion of who you’re talking about when you’re talking about these “riskier tenants”"

acuity.statement: Well, it’s been quite interesting hearing the comments from the Associate Minister of Housing, accusing us of having a bunch of opinions when actually he’s responded with zero substance on the matter. I think that does a disservice to the process here, which is to actually scrutinise the Government and the Minister’s own understanding of his own legislation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Potaka's framing of the opposition as offering only opinions and rejects it, but only by asserting the reverse. None of the content Potaka advanced — supply, rental inflation, Māori landlords, risk and need — is taken up here. A characterisation of the previous turn rather than an engagement with its claims, so it sits in the band for a mere reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "you are entitled to your own opinions but perhaps not your own facts"

acuity.statement: It was noted in the regulatory impact statement—which I’m surprised that the Minister’s dismissing as just kind of opinions and ways to fill the Hansard—as potentially increasing the need for emergency housing.
acuity.explanation: Takes Potaka's specific dismissal of opposing comments as Hansard-filling and turns it against him by pointing out that the emergency-housing concern comes from the Government's own regulatory impact statement, not from opinion. It engages the substance of his characterisation, though it is an aside within a question on a different clause rather than a sustained rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I think that that myopic nature of that particular comment is merely to fill out the Hansard"

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, I appreciate the time just to stand and make a couple of comments. I just want to address the observation that perhaps my name is on the door of xenophobia and the innuendo that’s been introduced in some of the observations in the Hansard today. Just to reject that innuendo, the comment that I made was that rents and supply can be affected by a number of factors: wage growth, cost to build, immigration—a whole range of things can influence supply and can influence rents. That’s the context in which it was made, and we got a little bit of a run-on of what the implications or consequences or interpretations of that might mean.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez explicitly invited the Minister to explain, in his own words, why immigration was raised in a housing-supply answer. Potaka takes up exactly that invitation, names the inference he is rejecting and restates the context of the original remark, so the speech would be different had Hernandez not pressed that point. Not 1.0 because the second half of Hernandez's turn — the demand for quantification of the mental-health effects of weakened security of tenure — is left untouched in this passage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just want to invite you, in your own words, to explain why you even mentioned it in the first place in response to some of the earlier questioning" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: I would also like to know from the Minister why he has chosen to actively reinstate the disparity, given that it was only a few years ago that we took this away and ensured that landlords couldn’t enforce no-cause terminations. Now he is reinstating the disparity that, clearly, disproportionately impacts Māori.
acuity.explanation: This is prepared material on the matter under debate — the termination provisions — but it engages no part of the argument Potaka had just made. It neither tests his build-incentive rationale nor his retaliatory-notice assurances; it opens a fresh Treaty-of-Waitangi line as if the preceding turn had not occurred. The gesture at the debate (the reference to the departmental disclosure statement and to what has already been traversed) puts it at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka had just argued that removing no-cause termination flexibility "is a disincentive to actually build those houses or those apartments" and set out the retaliatory-notice and 21-day changes, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: Therefore, I think the onus needs to go back to the Minister—because he claimed to care a lot about facts—to actually tell us what robust analysis has been done in terms of ensuring that, actually, this provision doesn’t create financial hardship, stress, as has been identified by tenants and The People’s Review of Renting, compared to, for example, the additional capital gains that a landlord or a property investor will be able to make by having a property being vacant when trying to sell.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of the Minister's position — the Government's cost-benefit framing of landlord flexibility — and turns it back, demanding the vacant-possession premium be weighed against tenant harm, and he holds the Minister to his own professed standard of relying on facts. But he moves to a new provision, subsection (2)(b), and much of the turn is prepared material on The People's Review of Renting rather than engagement with the build-disincentive claim just made, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the specific argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if I am the landlord—around no-cause terminations, that, in the view of the Government, is a disincentive to actually build those houses or those apartments" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: Thank you, again, for the opportunity to have a kōrero on this matter in relation to the questions that were just asked regarding the retaliatory provisions. We do believe that there is a strengthening of the notice provisions in the Residential Tenancies Act, giving tenants a high level of assurance.
acuity.explanation: Potaka takes up the strand Bennett actually put to him — whether the retaliatory-notice settings are tight enough — and asserts that the provisions are strengthened, and later in the turn supplies the 90-day family-occupancy requirement and tribunal recourse as the answer to the 'landlords lying' concern. But on the specific question (are the checks and balances adequate, is section 54 tight enough) he answers the topic with a statement of belief rather than engaging the mechanism Bennett pointed at, and then moves to notice periods, which was not what was asked. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does the Minister believe that he has got this right; that it's tight enough and that it has good checks and balances to ensure that the tenant is protected" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: I’m really pleased to take a call on this. I realise that there are some areas that may have been traversed, but I need to, particularly with this Minister in the chair, the Hon Tama Potaka, traverse some of the impacts for Māori on this.
acuity.explanation: Jackson follows Potaka's answer and acknowledges that ground has been covered, but engages none of its content: he does not dispute the claimed strengthening of the retaliatory provisions, the 63-to-42-day reduction, or the 90-day family-occupancy safeguard Potaka offered. Instead he names the Minister as his target and moves to prepared material on clause 22(1) and Māori consultation. Naming the previous speaker is a reference, not engagement. The speech is at least about the bill under debate, so it sits above the floor of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka had just answered on the retaliatory-notice provisions and the reduction of the periodic-tenancy notice period "from 63 to 42", and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I think this is quite concerning, because it’s like we have this whole narrative that the Government’s created around the purpose, of how people are going to enable pet bonds to then allow pets to more easily cohabitate with tenants in their property, but the way that this is written, in my view, prevents the ring-fencing.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Arena Williams's substantive turns on the same Part 3 / clause 31 debate precede it. But the speech engages no strand of her argument (jurisdiction limits, cost awards against vexatious parties); it is prepared material on a different question, double-dipping between the pet bond and the general bond. It gestures at the debate by anchoring to the same clause (31(1) and (2)) and the same bill, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0. The speech would read identically had Williams said something else about clause 31.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams spoke about the $100,000 Tenancy Tribunal jurisdiction limit and about allowing referees to award filing-fee costs, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Just to note one of the comments by the member for Manurewa around awards through the tribunal process: if a party is successful, their filing fees can actually be awarded against the unsuccessful party. That’s one pathway for an award that offsets things. The other item that was raised, around the $100,000 threshold, or current level for Residential Tenancies Act disputes, it has been in place for nearly 15 years.
acuity.explanation: Takes up both specific points Williams put and does something with each: corrects the premise of her filing-fee question by stating the award pathway already exists, and answers the $100,000 question with the limit's history. The speech would have to change entirely had she asked something else — the engagement is pointable sentence by sentence. Scored on engagement only; whether the filing-fee answer is accurate or sufficiently detailed belongs to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Why didn’t the Government consider that change, or changes like it, which essentially allow a referee more tools in the toolkit to award costs" — and her question "why isn’t the $100,000 limit higher?"

acuity.statement: A landlord would only be able to access those funds that are set aside on the basis of pet bonds for non-pet-related damage or costs with the agreement of the tenants or by a Tenancy Tribunal order.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the mechanism Menéndez March described, disputing it by naming the gates on a landlord accessing pet bond funds — tenant agreement or a Tribunal order. Not a full 1.0 because it rebuts the premise of unconstrained access rather than addressing his specific ask about the ring-fencing amendment and the analysis of the effect on tenants, but what is engaged is unambiguous and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "it allows landlords to dip into either bond, the general bond or the pet bond, to try and literally maximise profit when somebody’s exiting a tenancy"

acuity.statement: In dealing with Part 3 of the bill here, to follow on from my colleague Arena Williams, clause 35 does address the issue of email address and facsimile number and moves us forward into the new world of electronic addresses. It assumes, of course—and it’s an issue for rural New Zealand; I know you will understand this, Madam Chair—that everyone has access to electronic communication instantaneously, every day, and every minute of every day.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact strand Williams ended on — whether service to an "electronic address" can be relied on as actual receipt — and does something with it: adds the rural-connectivity case, quotes the specific sub-clause (new section 136(10), "properly transmitted"), and proposes a confirmation obligation as the fix. The speech would read differently had Williams not raised clause 35 service, which he expressly says he is following on from.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "how can we be sure that we’re not setting the bar so low that people can honestly not reasonably be expected to have read the documents that they are meant to have?"

acuity.statement: I think it’s really important that we make sure that, in allowing the Tenancy Tribunal to hold decisions on papers rather than doing the full thing, we’re not creating barriers for justice, and we’re not exacerbating any existing inequities.
acuity.explanation: Eligible (two substantive turns by other members precede it in the same committee debate) but engages no part of either argument. It is on the matter under debate — the same Part of the same bill, clause by clause — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom, but the speech would have been identical whatever Williams and O'Connor had said about service of documents.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams and Damien O'Connor both argued that clause 35's electronic-service test sets the bar for proof of receipt too low, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a fresh line on clause 33 and decisions on the papers.

acuity.statement: Certainly, the view of the Government, in relation to the qualifying evidence in the family violence issue, is ultimately that the Tenancy Tribunal is not the right body to assess whether or not family violence has occurred.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question Williams pressed — who is to determine whether violence in a household amounts to family violence — by naming the body that is not to do it. It engages the content of her question rather than the general topic, though it stops short of supplying the alternative definition or Act she also asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Should that be up to the referee in each given case to determine?"

acuity.statement: Certainly, I respect the observations as being very genuine, but it is up to the tenant to advise whether or not the fax machine is a method by which the tenant is happy to be contacted. There are other options, of course, open to that tenant, whether or not that be email or, of course, the well-known snail mail.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic both members raised — the channel by which a tenant is served — and offers the tenant's choice of channel as the safeguard, but it answers a different question from the one asked. Neither Williams's "bar set too low" point nor O'Connor's request for a confirmation obligation on proof of transmission is taken up. Partial engagement: you can point at what it addresses, but it returns to general reassurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "In proving service of a document transmitted to an electronic address, it is sufficient to prove that the document was properly transmitted to that address."

acuity.statement: I have confidence in the expertise of the tribunals and the Tenancy Tribunal, but if a tenant can’t represent himself or herself adequately, this would, I expect, be considered by any tribunal. Parties can also share their views on the hearing format.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Hernandez's power-differential strand and his specific suggestion that tenants should have a say, answering that parties can share views on the hearing format and that a tenant's capacity to represent themselves would be weighed. It engages one strand squarely while ignoring the two concrete asks beside it — the statistics on outcomes by ethnicity and the rationale for the change — so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "Maybe there should be some sort of component on making sure that the tenants are OK with that, because there is a kind of power differential in this situation."

acuity.statement: Turning my attention to clause 39, around section 91A and, well, the parts that changed in section 91A—particularly inserting subsections (e) and (f)—I’m really interested in, well, two parts around this.
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn (Brooking) put a specific drafting question about "all or any" in Regulation 9. Menéndez March engages no part of it, moving straight to his own prepared questions on clause 39 and email service. The speech would read identically whatever Brooking had said, but it is squarely within the same Part 3 committee debate and directed at the Minister on the bill in front of the House, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking spoke about the phrase "all or any" in Regulation 9 of Schedule 2 and the qualifying evidence for withdrawal following family violence, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Just in relation to the matter raised around “all or any”, as you’d expect to interpret it, it does not need to be all. No concerns have been raised along the way in relation to this particular provision; no concerns have been raised by officials.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact interpretive question Brooking asked and answers it: the provision does not require all of paragraphs (a) to (d). That is the specific thing she asked for, and the reply would be different had she asked about something else. Short of 1.0 because it addresses only the interpretation and not her second request — that the drafting be tightened by deleting "all or" — and the appeal to officials is offered in place of engaging the drafting point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s that phrase “all or any” that I’m interested in—why it’s needed to be “all or any”" — Rachel Brooking.

acuity.statement: In relation to the email issue that member Menéndez March has raised, certainly there’s flexibility for tenants to provide multiple contact arrangements. I too have had the experience of having a series of emails where I’ve completely forgotten the passwords and am unable to access those, especially that tama_potaka@yahoo.com—gone, never to be forgotten.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — that tenants abandon old email addresses — and concedes the premise from personal experience before answering it with the availability of multiple contact arrangements. But it leaves untouched the two questions Menéndez March pressed hardest: how the Tenancy Tribunal would establish that a former tenant actually received a communication, and what evidential basis supports extending landlord applications beyond two years. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it assumes that people operate like, frankly, older generations, who tend to hold an email for decades, and that is not the case for young people" — Ricardo Menéndez March.

acuity.statement: I thank the Leader of the House for that. Between now and then, given the number of relatively late—shall we say—amendments in the Minister’s name to that piece of legislation, the fast-track legislation, will the Government recommit the bill if it’s found that there are drafting errors in it?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific item just announced in the business statement and draws out a consequence of it, asking what happens to the third reading if the late amendments have introduced drafting errors. The question could not have been asked had Bishop announced a different programme, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 only because it extends the announcement rather than contesting any reasoning in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Next week, the House will consider the third reading of the Fast-track Approvals Bill" — Chris Bishop.

acuity.statement: Well, I don’t want to get ahead of finding those errors. At the moment, there are no errors, and so our provisional view is no.
acuity.explanation: Answers the conditional that was put to him and answers it squarely in the negative, with the reason attached — no errors are presently known, so no recommittal is contemplated. The reply is wholly determined by the question asked. It is brief and gives no detail, but brevity is a Specificity matter; on engagement it is near the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will the Government recommit the bill if it’s found that there are drafting errors in it?" — Kieran McAnulty.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I am interested in clause 33, which inserts new section 91AB, and that gives the tribunal the power to make decisions on the papers. In terms of speed and efficiency, I’m all for it, and it’s obviously a discretion to decide a matter on the papers, but I’m interested, really, for the Minister of Housing to put on the record the basis upon which that discretion should be exercised.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows McAnulty in the same committee-stage debate on the same bill, but his contribution is self-contained prepared material on a different clause (33) and engages no part of McAnulty's jurisdiction/qualifying-evidence argument. It would read word-for-word the same whatever McAnulty had said, though it is at least squarely on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued that clause 31(3) leaves a family violence victim with no forum if the landlord disputes their qualifying evidence, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Thank you, and thank you to the members for explaining what was apparently being discussed before the break when I wasn’t here. Let me deal with Duncan Webb’s question first. The change we’re making is to allow Tenancy Tribunal issues to be dealt with on the papers, but there is the ability to do oral hearings—I’m advised that that is essentially standard practice for a range of tribunals which have that discretion, and, clearly, in complicated cases you would want the tribunal to do hearings. I envisage the papers-only hearings to be relatively simple matters. I’m also advised that any termination has to have a hearing rather than be dealt with on the papers, and I think that is wise.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific question about how the on-the-papers discretion in clause 33 is to be exercised and supplies content in answer: oral hearings remain available, that is standard tribunal practice, complex cases would be heard, papers-only is envisaged for simple matters, and terminations must be heard. The speech could not have been given if Webb had raised something else; it falls just short of 1.0 because it does not address Webb's specific ask for a stated presumption in favour of an oral hearing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will the tribunal officer, the referee, have regard to what they see, and, in particular, will they call an oral hearing when they see that there may be a problem of literacy or expression or capability?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: In relation to points around evidence, that’s dealt with in Schedule 2—types of qualifying evidence: protection orders, police safety orders, and charging documents. There’s no intention for the tribunal to get involved. The tribunal is not going to replicate the role of the police or the courts or safety orders or anything like that.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages McAnulty's strand about qualifying evidence and the tribunal's exclusion from family violence disputes, pointing to Schedule 2 and confirming the policy intent. Partial rather than full engagement: it restates that the tribunal has no role without naming the alternative forum McAnulty specifically asked for, which was the whole of his question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in the absence of the tribunal, what avenues does the tenant have available to them?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: However, I wanted to ask the Minister whether there was consideration by him and by his officials for extending it beyond family violence. Of course we take family violence seriously, and we are very relieved that this provision is in the bill, actually, but people live in different circumstances, and there are a lot of people who aren’t necessarily family that are living in the same houses and could be vulnerable due to violence that is committed against them as well.
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by Henare precedes this one, and Sepuloni engages no part of it; she explicitly flags that her point is a different one and proceeds to prepared material on another clause. It is squarely about the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but the speech would read identically whatever Henare had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare spoke about clauses 34 and 35, email service and the 5 p.m. deadline, and this statement does not take any of that up — it opens a separate point on clause 31 and family violence.

acuity.statement: We didn’t consider that. I’m happy to go away and have a look at it. As the member knows, these changes were made by the previous Government—I think, with broad support—as I indicated just a few moments ago, adding the dependants in there.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question just put to him and answers it directly — concedes the extension was not considered, commits to looking at it, and places the existing provision in its legislative history. Had Sepuloni asked a different question, this passage could not have been delivered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "I wanted to ask the Minister whether there was consideration by him and by his officials for extending it beyond family violence"

acuity.statement: In relation to this email address point, I’m advised that section 91A of the Act, which clause 34 amends, prescribes how documents can be served on tenants following an application to the Tenancy Tribunal after the tenancy has terminated. The bill enables the use of an email address, where the tenancy was ended more than two months ago, if one has been appropriately provided by the tenant. The reason is, obviously, that email is likely to be a much more reliable method for service than a physical address for contacting a tenant who no longer lives at that rental property.
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance of Henare's objection to email as the service standard by supplying the clause's rationale and the safeguards on address currency. It does not take up Henare's separate points about spam folders or the 5 p.m. / Monday-to-Friday ambiguity, so it engages most but not all of the argument put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "whether or not an email is really the only standard that we’re setting here"

acuity.statement: It’s actually quite an important point, because I can see the quite appropriate shift towards electronic means of communication. It’s a point of detail, but it’s something that cuts across a whole lot of Acts.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand of Bishop's answer — the move to electronic service — and accepts it, but then develops a new drafting point about the word "transmitted" rather than engaging Bishop's claim to have struck the right balance. Partial engagement with what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "email is likely to be a much more reliable method for service than a physical address"

acuity.statement: Well, I mean, the member makes a good point, and I think, respectfully, it’s probably beyond the scope of this bill because the word “transmitted” probably appears in lots of statutes and over time Parliament has updated its language around things. He makes a good point about the Electronic Transactions Act 2002—goodness me, I remember when that passed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific drafting objection and the Electronic Transactions Act reference he raised, concedes the ambiguity could be litigated at the tribunal, and argues it belongs outside this bill rather than ignoring it. This is engagement with the content of the argument, not a mere mention of the previous speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Does “transmitted” mean it enters the system of the person to whom it is addressed?"

acuity.statement: I think what the member is saying is that you reverse the onus so that it’s about the landlord proving that, rather than the tenant proving that. That’s something we could potentially pick up as part of potential amendments in the future, if indeed it’s proven that it is a problem, but we don’t have any evidence of that, because it’s new law.
acuity.explanation: Bishop takes up McAnulty's specific objection to new section 48, restates it accurately in its own terms (reversal of the onus of proof), quotes the same provision back, gives a reason for keeping it as drafted (a date must apply to tenancies in train), and commits to considering an amendment if the problem materialises. The speech would be materially different had McAnulty raised a different clause, so this is engagement with the content rather than a mere reference to the member.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Then it’s on the tenant to prove otherwise." — his objection that new section 48 lets a landlord simply assert the date they became aware of damage, leaving the tenant to disprove it

acuity.statement: I acknowledge the contribution of the Minister of Housing there. It is quite extraordinary, though: we’re in urgency rushing through a bill that you are now proposing doesn’t come into effect for a while, and, in part, because something isn’t ready.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty engages one strand of Bishop's commencement speech — the deferred start dates and the admission that the pet bond system is not yet built — and draws out a consequence (the inconsistency with taking the bill under urgency). But he then explicitly declines to contest the amendment and moves to prepared material on the bill's title, which engages nothing Bishop had just said. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, then a return to his own argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "the commencement will be by Order in Council to allow flexibility and time for the pet bond functionality to be developed" — his explanation of Amendment Paper 213's fixed commencement dates and the delay for the Bond 2000 pet bond work

acuity.statement: Thank you to the member for the reasonable questions. In relation to family violence, I am advised that it is 20 March. In relation to the pet bonds, the member makes a good point that that’s the most popular part of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni's committee-stage turn put a list of specific questions: the family violence commencement date, the pet bond timeframe, and why tenancy terminations were prioritised. Bishop takes them up directly — supplying the date asked for (20 March) and conceding the substance of her point that the pet bond is the most popular part of the bill. The speech would be different, and the date would be absent, had she asked something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when do the family violence provisions come into effect here?" — Carmel Sepuloni

acuity.statement: In relation to the residential tenancies changes around no-cause terminations, reasonable people can disagree around this. Clearly, the Opposition has a different view to the Government. I appreciate that point of view. We want to bring them in. It just reverts the law back to actually what was the law until 2021, from memory—it might have been 2020—so it’s not a radical change in that sense, and rather than just have the six weeks, as I’ve said before, we’ve gone for 30 January so that there’s maximum clarity for everybody.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question Sepuloni pressed — why the tenancy termination provisions were brought on fast and set at 30 January — and gives a reason for the date (maximum clarity) plus a characterisation of the change as a reversion to the pre-2020 law. It does not answer her sharper sub-question about cost savings or who stands to gain, and opens with a concessive framing rather than the substance, so it engages most but not all of the argument put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why can that be moved forward so quickly ahead of all the other provisions?" — Carmel Sepuloni

acuity.statement: The premise behind this, the Government argues—not that you’d know from the Minister’s third reading speech—is that if you make it easier for landlords, there will be more landlords and, therefore, more rentals. It is a flawed logic in the context of the current housing situation in this country.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact causal claim Bishop closed his third reading speech with — that the bill gives landlords extra incentive to enter the rental market — names it as the Government's premise, and then argues against it on the specific ground that the other settings (Kāinga Ora builds, community housing funding, interest deductibility) break the chain. The speech would have to change if Bishop had argued for the bill on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it will provide a bit of extra incentive for landlords to enter the rental market"

acuity.statement: But none of that outweighs the destructive changes that this bill does, and the gall of the Minister to stand up and say that this Government is a pro-tenant Government—rubbish.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the specific characterisation Bishop had just made of the retaliatory-termination clause as "a pro-tenant move", disputing it rather than merely mentioning him. Low civility and high responsiveness sit together here; scored only on the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "that’s a pro-tenant move"

acuity.statement: The pet bonds stuff makes sense, and I wish that it was actually in a different bill, so that we could vote for it.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the specific provision Bishop spent most of his speech on — the pet bond — and explains why conceding it does not produce a vote for the bill. Accepting part and disputing the rest is engagement with the argument actually made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "These pet provisions are a win-win."

acuity.statement: There are five bullet points, and every single one of them talks about the reduction of tenant rights proposed in this bill, the reduction of notice periods, and the reintroduction of no-cause terminations, but if you listened to that third reading speech, people would be forgiven that it was actually about something different altogether.
acuity.explanation: Engages what Bishop's speech covered and points at the notice-period and no-cause-termination provisions he omitted, so it is tied to the speech just delivered rather than prepared regardless of it. But it contests the Minister's choice of emphasis rather than taking up any argument he made, so it falls short of rebutting the reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The major change is that we are, essentially, reversing what we have at the moment, which is making it easier for tenants to have a pet"

acuity.statement: I hear them saying “90 days”, but again, they forget that, actually, this bill has provisions that allow for landlords to have people leave in less than 90 days. In fact, if a landlord says that they have a family member coming over, they can use 42 days.
acuity.explanation: Takes the interjected figure and does something with it: concedes it was said, then rebuts it by pointing to provisions in the same bill permitting shorter notice, naming 42 days for a landlord's family member. Had the interjection been different, this passage would not exist in this form.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "90 days—three months."

acuity.statement: Much has been said about this legislation being used by landlords to kick people out, their tenants out, without reason, when reasonableness dictates that the landlord-tenant relationship is one of accountability and respect, and that this, in general, would not really be happening.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the preceding charge that landlords will use the bill to evict tenants without reason and disputes it, but only in the generalised form "much has been said" and by bare assertion about landlord-tenant reasonableness; it leaves untouched the specific arguments just made about the evidence base, urgency, and the 42-day provision. Partial engagement, then back to prepared commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "to literally gift to landlords across the country the ability to make more people homeless"

acuity.statement: Let’s start where she left off with those targets: 70 percent of people moved out emergency accommodation in the last year, 1,600 kids out of emergency accommodation—making it easier to build more homes.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni closed by challenging the Government's emergency-housing and social outcome targets; Costley explicitly picks up that closing point and answers it with figures on emergency accommodation exits. He engages the specific claim rather than merely naming her, though he supplies only the target side and does not take up her evidence about 90-day terminations or the submissions. Not a full 1.0 because the engagement is brief and he then pivots to a prepared commendation; the quality or truth of the figures is not an acuity matter.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "how does that stack up with the Government's target to reduce emergency accommodation?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. There’s a term that’s come up in recent years—certainly in the time that I’ve been in Parliament—and that term is “Generation Rent”. Our ancestors wouldn’t believe that this country has now turned to call its present generation “Generation Rent”.
acuity.explanation: Henare follows Costley's defence of the Government's emergency-housing figures but opens with prepared framing about 'Generation Rent' that engages no part of it. It is at least on the matter under debate (housing security), so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0; 0.2 because the speech would read identically whatever Costley had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley claimed "70 percent of people moved out emergency accommodation in the last year" and was proud of the Government's housing record, and this opening does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In fact, it’s just dipped below 30 percent—28 percent. There you go: Māori homeownership. I can tell that member, in the time of my parents, that homeownership rate was just above 80 percent—just above 80 percent. If that member doesn’t believe it, then he might want to have a look.
acuity.explanation: Campbell interjected asking for the numbers, and Henare supplies exactly the figure demanded, names what it measures, and adds a comparison point for the earlier generation. This is the rubric's 'supplies the figure it asked for' case: the reply would be different had Campbell asked something else. Whether the 28 percent figure is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one, and the jibe at the end does not reduce responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "What are they?" — asked after Henare said homeownership numbers have plummeted.

acuity.statement: As we’ve heard, the other side of the House did so much for renters—$175 a week increase in rent under the previous Government. Is that doing things for tenants? No, it is not. This bill helps balance the approach between tenants and landlords, because it is a relationship.
acuity.explanation: Campbell follows Twyford's substantive speech and takes up one strand of it directly — Twyford's claim that Labour's package made renters more secure and brought down rental costs — countering it with a rent-increase figure under the previous Government and an assertion that the bill rebalances the landlord/tenant relationship. He engages that strand and the topic, but leaves Twyford's central argument (security of tenure and the removal of no-cause termination protections) entirely untouched before moving to prepared listing-volume figures. Partial engagement that can be pointed at: ~0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We did all that to make housing warm and dry and healthy, to make renters more secure, and to bring down the cost of rental housing." — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: Prove to me, ACT Party, that you didn't do that. Can the ACT Party prove to this House that the Government did not take away that support for first-home buyers? No, they can't. Crickets. Silence.
acuity.explanation: Henare turns immediately to the interjector's party and demands an answer, so there is a visible gesture at what has just been said, but he engages no part of Court's actual claim (that he himself rented and then bought, as 'everyone did'). Instead he restates his own prepared point about first-home buyer support and treats silence as proof. A gesture at the interjection rather than engagement with its content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "Mate, I rented for a decade and then I bought a house—everyone did."

acuity.statement: I rise to speak in favour of this bill. I think there's been a number of provisions laid out—sensible, pro-tenant changes to the Residential Tenancies Act, which, along with the introduction of interest deductibility, will increase the supply of rental housing and make landlords more willing to enter into arrangements. This is going to be a good bill for tenants and for the rental supply in New Zealand, and I support this bill.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. Uffindell asserts the bill will increase rental supply, which happens to sit near Henare's supply complaint, but he does not take up Henare's argument, numbers, the no-cause termination point, or the bipartisan-overhaul invitation; the speech would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said about this bill. Not 0.0 because it is squarely about the bill under debate and could not have been delivered in another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that "What we're not hearing from this Government is how they are going to build more houses", that no-cause terminations leave tenants precarious, and that the Minister conceded tenancy law needs a serious overhaul — this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: I think this is a positive bill to address the harm that youth vaping is causing. There are number of parts to that, including banning disposables, visibility limits, and increasing the fines. I do want to thank the members of the Health Committee for their work on this bill.
acuity.explanation: Luxton's turn immediately before raised a specific point: under-resourcing of smoke-free enforcement officers, as reported to the Health Committee by Hūhana Lyndon. Uffindell does not take that up. His speech is prepared support for the bill — listing its parts and thanking the committee — on exactly the right subject but engaging none of the argument put. The nearest glance is the later generic "There is more work to do", which does not pick up the enforcement-resourcing claim.
