acuity.statement: What I will say in relation to what the speaker had asked—there is one point that I would really like to make, and that’s in regard to the comments that were made about the policy makers and the drafters, of whom I have the utmost respect for the work that they do and the hours and time that they put in to make sure that we have right legislation that is fit for purpose and that looks after and addresses the community’s concerns on public safety.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Webb's speech — his remark that policy makers and drafters take pride in over-complicated solutions — and answers it directly with a defence of the drafters. But it leaves untouched the substance he put: the section 86KA 'second first warning' problem and his proposed replacement wording. A partial engagement rather than a reply to the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "It troubles me that sometimes our policy makers and drafters pride themselves on these really complicated so-called solutions, but we don’t put ourselves in the shoes of the people who are affected by it."

acuity.statement: Just in closing last night, I did recall the Minister standing and speaking to—or reading, which is not quite the same as speaking and thinking one’s thoughts through oneself. Just reading off a paper and landing with the same old “I won’t be dealing with this” or “I won’t be voting for it” is, I think, more than a disrespect; it is a neglect on the Minister’s part.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's immediately preceding refusal to speak again to the tabled amendment and characterises that pattern of declining to engage as neglect, so it is not indifferent to what it follows. But the rest of the turn moves to prepared material on rehabilitation and hohou te rongo that addresses earlier speeches rather than the turn just given, so engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "That’s all right, because I’ve already actually spoken to that, so I’m not prepared to speak to it again."

acuity.statement: In regard to the debate that that member keeps bringing up, saying that the party or the Government is racist, I think what the member needs to do is have a look at the bill and realise that the bill is not based on race; the bill is based on bad behaviour. The bill is based on those that create the most serious violent and sexual crimes, not on race.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the charge Kapa-Kingi had just levelled — that the party's rejection of her Tiriti-related amendments reflects racist rhetoric — by contesting the premise that the bill's trigger is race rather than offending. The turn also takes up her reading-from-paper jibe and her rehabilitation point in sequence, so it is clearly shaped by what preceded it; short of 1.0 only because it sidesteps her specific question about whether she can explain hohou te rongo.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "I know that her party think that way because, sadly, it shows up in their majority of racist rhetoric."

acuity.statement: I remind Dr Webb that, last night, we indicated that we also didn’t support the amendments, and I’ve checked with my colleagues in the ACT Party and New Zealand First, and they won’t be supporting the amendments either—just to give Dr Webb some assurance that this side of the Chamber won’t be supporting the amendments the Minister has already well and truly covered off.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific objection Webb opened with — that an Associate Minister with one vote cannot announce how the House will vote — by supplying the missing information: the other government parties have been checked and will also oppose. It then asks the Minister to state a view on Webb's amendment tabled that morning. The speech would plainly be different had Webb not raised the point, though it moves on to prepared material on clauses 11 and 12.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "She has one vote; she is a member of the executive. She doesn’t speak for the House of Representatives in which we sit today."

acuity.statement: When the Minister says, for instance, “the strikees will have received and therefore understood a warning”, there’s a huge assumption—and the word “understood” is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's immediately preceding assurance that offenders will be made to understand the warning and attacks the specific assumption buried in the word 'understood'. The speech would have to change if McKee had instead described a tested comprehension process.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "The warnings will be communicated to the offender, and the court can use whatever words they wish to use to be able to help that individual understand what’s happening."

acuity.statement: It’s not OK for a Minister to sit in the chair and just say that the court staff, after a brief period of six months of preparation—in which time, all of the IT, all of the training; there’s an awful lot going on in a six-month period, to have logistical preparation for an efficient and effective system to be carried out.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific remedy McKee had just offered — six months of judicial education and court-staff training — by disputing that the period can carry the IT and training load placed on it. Squarely engaged with the preceding claim rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "judicial education and the six-month preparation for the implementation of this law will help with that because that’s where the training of court staff and the judiciary will be undertaken"

acuity.statement: In respect of my proposed new section 86KA, this goes to the deterrence effect, because the Associate Minister of Justice is retrospectively reviving former strikes and yet, I mean, the offenders who had those strikes, and will again have those strikes, won’t know about them.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's statement that revived strikes will not be re-notified and draws out its consequence for the bill's own deterrence premise, which is exactly the point his amendment turns on. Responsive to the content of the answer just given, not merely a reference to the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "In regard to re-warning people after they have left prison, the intention is not to do that"

acuity.statement: Throughout the bill, it talks about recalling an offender to the court if the sentence was imposed at a time they were not in court. Now, I find that very unusual, because, by definition, it’s a sentence of imprisonment that is being imposed.
acuity.explanation: Engages the same provision and recall mechanism McKee had just explained, but does not take up her actual explanation (a reserved Court of Appeal judgment), instead advancing his own AVL hypothesis before returning to prepared amendment material. Partial engagement with the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "Therefore, the offender is not always in court at that time. This means that the offender will have to go back to the original court in order to receive the sentence or the warning"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just would like to address the questions from Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, the member from the Greens, about new section 86V(2A), inserted by clause 7. Section 86V(2A) allows the Court of Appeal to take the necessary actions if they feel that that is appropriate, and subsection (2B) is also reflecting that, in some cases, the District Court may have taken the actions relating to the earlier warning ceasing, while the later qualifying sentence may relate to an offence that the District Court does not have jurisdiction to deal with.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise drafting question Xu-Nan had just put — why subsections (2), (2A) and (2B) are split — and supplies the specific reason (Court of Appeal powers, and District Court jurisdiction limits over category 3 and 4 offences), with a worked example. The answer would have had to be different had a different question been asked. Marked down slightly only because the other strand before her, Duncan Webb's amendments, is waved away by reference to a previous evening rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "why separate out the High Court from “not the High Court” and from “District Court”?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I think we’re almost a quarter of the way through my tabled amendments. The next tabled amendment I’d like to talk about is the amendment to clause 7 to insert paragraph (d) into new section 86M(2), filed at 12.46 p.m.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive question on clause 7 and engages no part of it, moving straight to his own prepared sequence of tabled amendments. The remarks are on the matter under debate — the same clause of the same bill — and he gestures at the debate by invoking an earlier point about court systems struggling, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero; the speech would have been word-for-word the same whatever Xu-Nan had asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked the Minister why new section 86V separates the High Court from "not the High Court" and from the District Court, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: In relation to the last member Camilla Belich’s comments, there were 749 submissions, of which 188 submitters were opposed to the bill, and the member listed off quite a number of them. However, there were 515 submitters who either supported the bill or they didn’t support the bill because they wanted the bill to be harsher and, therefore, wanted it gone so that they could have an even stronger bill, including reinstating three strikes as it was in its old regime.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise argument just made — that the weight of submitter opinion runs against the bill — and does something with it, supplying the submission breakdown to contest the characterisation, and then addressing the specific clause Belich raised (new section 86T). The reply would be different had Belich argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "There is a significant amount of opposition to this bill" (preceded by her list of opposing organisations and her question on what the Minister relies on)

acuity.statement: The one I want to start with is about the centrepiece of this legislation, which is the warning itself. I was about to say, before I was sat down before, that I’m concerned that judges aren’t given guidance as to what the warning should be because the understanding on the part of the offender is the critical point of this piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate (clause 7 and the warning regime) and he puts a genuine question to the Minister, but he engages no part of the preceding turn — he explicitly picks up his own earlier thread rather than McKee's figures or her 86T answer. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate in progress.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee spoke about the 749/188/515 submission split and said she had already addressed new section 86T, and this statement does not take any of that up — Webb resumes his own prepared run through his tabled amendments

acuity.statement: I’ll just take a quick call here, looking at the amendments proposed by my colleague Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan in Part 2: one’s relating to clause 14; one’s relating to clause 16. I’m keen to understand from the Associate Minister of Justice whether or not she’ll be supporting those amendments and the rationale as to whether she will be or not, and then I’m keen to move to the more substantive parts of the legislation that we’ll be progressing.
acuity.explanation: Relevant to the committee stage and to amendments before the House, so not wholly unanchored, but it engages no part of Webb's argument about warning wording or his question on whether a defective warning is of no effect. Asking the Minister her position on different amendments is a new line, not a response to the preceding one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb spoke about his tabled amendments to clause 7 on the wording and effect of warnings under new section 86M, and this statement does not take that up — it moves to separate Part 2 amendments and asks the Minister a procedural question about them

acuity.statement: I guess the clarification I need from the Minister is whether replacement section 180(4)(b) requires both or are they mutually exclusive? If indeed they are mutually exclusive, will the Minister consider my amendment?
acuity.explanation: McKee had just dismissed his clause 14 amendment as duplicative. Xu-Nan takes that up in part: rather than restating his amendment he explains what it actually turns on (whether 'and' in replacement s 180(4)(b) requires both warnings), contrasts it with the 'or' used in clause 18, and puts the resulting question back to her with a conditional ask. He engages the Minister's dismissal on substance, but much of the surrounding turn is his own prepared clause-by-clause walk-through rather than a rebuttal of her reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "This is adding items to the list that have already been covered. Therefore, I will not be supporting that either."

acuity.statement: Thank you to that member. I did just speak to the member’s tabled amendment to clause 14, replacing paragraph (b) and inserting a new subclause (4)(c), which I thought was unnecessary.
acuity.explanation: She returns to the right clause and explains what the replacement definition of 'sentence' is meant to cover, so she engages the topic Xu-Nan raised. But she does not take up his specific point — the 'and' versus 'or' construction and whether both warnings are required — and instead repeats her earlier conclusion that the amendment is unnecessary. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "does the Minister consider that a sentence will only be considered or is only defined when you have both a first warning and subsequent warning?"

acuity.statement: A lot of this part is in some ways administrative, but I do have two things I want to ask and, to be fair, it’s simply around the complexity of this legislation and how it interacts, and that’s in respect of the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act and also a bit later on, if I get to it, the Parole Act.
acuity.explanation: The turn is squarely on the Part under debate and on clause 16, which the previous two speakers had both addressed, so it is not unresponsive to the matter. But it engages no part of what either of them actually argued: McKee's claim that the court retains sufficient discretion goes unanswered, and the speech would read identically had she said something else about clause 16. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee had just said of clause 16 that "The court already has the discretion in being able to decide about what is a qualifying sentence, and we’re happy with that provision", and Webb does not take that assertion up — he opens his own line of questions on the same clause.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for his question. The changes that are being made to the availability of orders, under the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act 2003—I can see why the member has asked some questions on this. The bill, as introduced, actually restricted the availability of post-conviction orders for treatment instead of a sentence, when the court would have otherwise imposed a qualifying sentence at all three stages.
acuity.explanation: She answers the exact worry Webb put: she confirms the restriction on post-conviction treatment orders exists, explains that as introduced it applied at all three stages, and supplies the fact he was missing — the Justice Committee narrowed it so stage-1 is unrestricted because no mandatory penalties bite there. The answer would be different had he asked about a different clause; she takes the specific provision he quoted and does something with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "I'm just a little concerned that the proposed insertion provides that 'No order may be made under subsection (1)(b) in respect of an offender who is convicted of a stage-2 offence, or a stage-3 offence'"

acuity.statement: I must say, just in response to that, that it is extremely disappointing that people who are mentally ill and in the corrections system by dint of this legislation—that orders can’t be made to put them in a facility where they receive the treatment that they actually need. I’m quite sure that that’s in breach of our international obligations under the United Nations convention known as the Mandela Rules. That’s actually quite disturbing.
acuity.explanation: He treats the Minister's answer as having resolved his factual uncertainty, accepts her account of what the provision does, and draws out its consequence — that mentally ill prisoners cannot be diverted to treatment facilities — then raises an international-obligations objection to it. The response is entirely conditioned on the answer he just received; had she said the restriction did not apply, this passage could not have been delivered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "because there are mandatory penalties at stage-2 and stage-3, we are happy with where we’ve landed with this"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Minister, for your response to my question on clause 14. The Associate Minister of Justice was saying that it is not required, but that didn’t answer my question, which was whether they are mutually exclusive. But I’m going to take that answer from the Minister as saying that they are mutually exclusive and they don’t need to be considered together.
acuity.explanation: He takes the Minister's reply apart on exactly the point at issue: identifies that she said the amendment was 'not required' rather than addressing mutual exclusivity, notes the gap, and then draws a working inference from the non-answer for the record. He also corrects her characterisation of which clauses his amendments concerned. The turn is wholly shaped by what was just said and could not survive substitution of a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "It’s amended to include records of first warning and subsequent warnings, including the giving and the recording of those warnings"

acuity.statement: Look, I agree with Dr Webb. Dr Webb mentioned that this is, essentially, an administrative part. It makes a number of consequential amendments to other pieces of legislation. My first question to the Minister in the chair is, essentially: does she agree with that assessment, that it is an administrative part and it makes the amendments to other pieces of legislation that will operationalise the three-strikes regime?
acuity.explanation: McKee had just characterised clauses 14, 16 and 22 as technical tidy-ups. Meager takes up that framing and puts it back to her as a direct question to confirm, which is real engagement with the preceding turn's central proposition. But he engages only that one strand — none of her specific claims about section 34(1)(b) orders or the Parole Act repeal error — and the rest of the turn addresses members (Webb, Xu-Nan) who did not speak immediately before. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is a technical tidy-up" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: Yes, that member is correct. This is just about technical tidy-ups and ensuring that the legislation fits within different areas of law and that they will all speak with each other.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question put to her in the immediately preceding turn, confirms the characterisation, and then does something with it — explaining what the alignment between the Criminal Procedure (Mentally Impaired Persons) Act and the Sentencing Act is for. The reply would be different had Meager asked something else. Not a full 1.0 only because she does not take up his second strand, the clause count he explicitly asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does she agree with that assessment, that it is an administrative part" — James Meager

acuity.statement: It’s a sad day for justice when we’ve got a bill which cuts across constitutional principle, intentionally imposes disproportionate sentences, doesn’t have the effect of reducing the number of victims, and, in fact, if anything, it will have the likely effect of increasing crime in our communities in the long term, and, as I was saying, the regulatory impact statement says it won’t have any good effect but it will detrimentally affect many families, including families of Māori.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes the central justificatory claim of the minister's third-reading speech — that the regime will reduce victims of violent crime — and contradicts it directly, citing the regulatory impact statement as counter-evidence and drawing out the opposite consequence. The engagement is specific and pointable, though it attaches to one claim in her speech rather than working through the mechanism she set out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "supports the Government’s commitment to 20,000 fewer victims of violent crime by 2029" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: For the Minister in charge of this bill, the Hon Nicole McKee, to suggest it is not retrospective is some kind of gymnastics. There are people today who are on no strikes and, once this bill is assented to, will be on two strikes.
acuity.explanation: This engages the minister's own description of the bill head-on: she presented the reactivation of previous-regime warnings as a feature supporting workability, and Webb takes that exact mechanism and shows what it entails — people currently on no strikes waking up on two. He names the claim, supplies the mechanism, and draws the consequence. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged against a different argument. Scored on engagement only; the sharpness of the "gymnastics" jab and the soundness of the inference belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "reactivated warnings from the previous regime that meet the strike thresholds" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: Do you know what Māori are victims of? Māori are victims of a deeply long-lasting racist justice system dispensed by the police, dispensed by the Department of Corrections.
acuity.explanation: Costello's preceding turn built its case for the bill entirely on victims — looking a rape victim in the eye, reducing 'the number of victims that we have to look in the eye'. Ferris explicitly abandons his prepared speech to take up that victim frame and invert it: the relevant victimisation, he argues, is of Māori by the justice system itself. He engages the specific premise rather than merely naming the topic, so the speech would have had to change had the previous turn argued something else. Short of 1.0 because part of the 'over-represented as victims' line he answers was said by members earlier in the debate rather than in Costello's turn, and he pivots to a historical account rather than contesting Costello's own claim about repeat serious offenders.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we look forward to the impact on reducing the number of victims that we have to look in the eye in New Zealand" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: What another great day for law and order in this country, and what another great day for democracy, something that this Government campaigned hard on since 2022: the reinstatement of three strikes.
acuity.explanation: Ferris had just named Brewer directly and argued that every legal association in the country calls the bill rubbish, that the Justice Committee heard the evidence and ignored it, and that Māori incarceration rates reflect systemic racism. Brewer takes up none of it — no legal opinion, no committee evidence, no response on over-representation — and delivers prepared material on campaign commitments and crime statistics. The speech is on the subject under debate, which keeps it off 0.0, but it would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tākuta Ferris argued the bill is "utter rubbish, but those members don't like evidence, they don't like legal opinion" and named Brewer personally, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: There are a couple of problems with his contribution. First of all, Dr Xu-Nan says this will lead to more prison beds. Well, if it’s a choice between more prison beds and fewer deathbeds, then we’ll take fewer deathbeds any day of the week.
acuity.explanation: Meager clearly listened to a specific prior contribution: he names its claims and does something with each — accepting the prison-beds point and trading it off against harm, and conceding the rehabilitation gap as deliberate design. But the argument he engages belongs to a speaker outside this window, and he is wholly indifferent to Webb, the turn he actually follows, so the engagement is only partial as measured against the preceding turn. Held mid-band because the thing engaged cannot be pointed at in the text provided.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan's earlier turn is not contained in this window; the immediately preceding speaker is Hon Dr Duncan Webb ("A mountain of evidence tells us that this bill will have worse criminal justice outcomes"), whose argument Meager does not take up at all. He instead takes up named claims from an earlier Green turn (more prison beds; nothing on restorative justice or rehabilitation).

acuity.statement: And we’re speaking on the bill because the purpose of the punitive justice system is to actually prevent them making more victims. That is the purpose of legislation that looks at this specific aspect of how we deal with serious recidivous offenders who continue to make more carnage and more victims.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Xu-Nan's objection on its own terms and rebuts its reasoning directly: he claimed victims were outside the bill's scope, and she argues that preventing further victims is precisely the bill's purpose, so speaking to victims is speaking to the bill. The sentence would not exist, and could not read as it does, had the interjection been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Because it’s not part of the bill. We speak on the bill." — Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Yes, and we can talk about Māori, because I love that narrative. I love the amount of victims that are being created over and over again—60 percent of them are Māori, and we need to stand up and say that we will stop them being made victims.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the subject Ferris put to her and offers a counter-figure on it rather than ignoring the interjection, so the engagement is visible and the passage is keyed to what was just said. But she answers the topic (Māori and this bill) and not the claim (Māori overincarceration and the Ministry's own target), reframing incarceration as victimisation instead of addressing the measure he named. Partial engagement, mid-band. Scored on engagement only — the tone of "I love that narrative" is a civility question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How about you achieve the Ministry of Justice’s outcomes of lowering Māori overincarceration? How about you focus on that one?" — Tākuta Ferris

acuity.statement: The evidence I’m interested in is the evidence of the store owner in Takanini that has had to build a cage inside his store for him and his family to serve customers from because of repeat serious offenders. The evidence I’m interested in is Uday in Wattle Downs, who was bashed all over his body when he was trying to open his store in the morning, by repeat serious offenders. That’s the evidence I’m interested in, not elitist academics.
acuity.explanation: Andersen's speech was built on the claim that the Government ignores the evidence (the Ministry of Justice RIS, the 2018 evidence brief, international research on deterrence). Nakhle takes up that strand directly — she picks up the word 'evidence' as Andersen used it and contests what should count as evidence, offering constituent accounts of repeat serious offending in place of research. That is engagement with one strand of the argument rather than with its content: she does not dispute the RIS findings, the 1996-2014 crime-rate trend, or the deterrence research Andersen cited, and the anecdotes are prepared material she would plausibly have delivered regardless. Pointable partial engagement, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They're not interested in the regulatory impact statement developed by the Ministry of Justice, they're not interested in international research" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Well, that means, Mr McCallum, that victims are dragged into a court system which does not serve them.
acuity.explanation: Williams takes up McCallum's interjection directly, naming him and answering its implication: she accepts the frame of offenders' conduct and draws out what she says follows from it — that refusing to plead guilty drags victims back through the courts. The reply would not exist, and would read differently, had McCallum interjected something else, so there is real engagement rather than a mere reference. It is short of 1.0 because she does not rebut the content of his point (that avoiding offending is the answer); she pivots to restate her own prepared line about victims and the court process rather than contesting his claim on its own terms. Scored on engagement only: whether the inference from 'offenders avoid pleading guilty' to 'victims are dragged through court' is sound belongs to Rigor, and the sharpness of the retort belongs to Civility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Maybe they should avoid the crime." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: We've heard several people conflate and confuse and try and turn things into correlations and causations that simply don't make sense today and, actually, over the whole process of this bill.
acuity.explanation: McLellan follows Garcia's claim that law and order has deteriorated and that this bill is part of turning it around, and she takes up the causal logic of that claim directly, challenging the inference from crime trends to the effectiveness of three strikes. But she addresses it to 'several people' in general rather than to Garcia's specific assertion, and then returns to prepared evidence material (California, the regulatory impact statement). Engagement with one strand of what preceded, not with the specific claim — a middling score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This situation is turning, but more needs to be done—this legislation being one" — Paulo Garcia

acuity.statement: There are elements of Dr Tracey McLellan’s speech that I did actually agree with, and that was primarily around the fact that this here is about serious crime that has been committed on a repeated basis, and keeping people safe.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod names and accepts the one concession in McLellan's speech — that recidivist serious offenders must be dealt with — and builds on it by pointing to the 42 qualifying serious violent and sexual offences, which is a real use of what she said rather than a bare mention. He leaves her central arguments (the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement, the courts' record-keeping capacity, the section 34 treatment-order point) entirely untouched and returns to prepared commendation, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "People who are recidivist, serious offenders do need to be dealt with so that society can feel safe" — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I just want to clear up a couple of things. With the repeal of the TPA, we won’t be unregulated. Medical devices and medicines will still continue to be regulated; it will just be under the old regime.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Verrall's central claim that repeal leaves New Zealand without a regulatory framework and contests it on the specific point — regulation continues under the prior regime. The speech would have to change if she had argued something else; he also engages her timing point by noting the Act was not due to commence until 1 September 2026. Not a full 1.0 because he does not engage her concrete examples (COVID-19 vaccine approval, monkeypox advertising restrictions, surgical mesh).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "It seems to me that this repeal leaves us without a framework, parts of a framework that we would agree on in many areas" — and "there is just nothing in place except the old dunger of the Medicines Act 1981."

acuity.statement: I also just want to reflect that taking 20 years to update the regulations and the laws in this area is part of the problem. It shouldn’t take that long.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact fact Verrall offered as evidence of wasted effort and turns it against her conclusion — the 20 years is itself the failure, not a sunk investment worth preserving. Clear evidence of having listened to the specific argument rather than delivering prepared praise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "We have known we’ve needed to replace the Medicines Act for 20 years, and we’re just undoing all of the work that’s been done".

acuity.statement: The Therapeutic Products Act Repeal Bill is a simple bill. It’s a repeal bill. The Therapeutic Products Act hasn’t even commenced yet. The vast majority of the submissions were in favour of the repeal bill, and the Government is working to build an enduring piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, and it gestures at the chamber's dispute by asserting the Act has not commenced, but it engages no part of the argument put against the bill — no response on medical devices, emergency approvals or the lost prescribing provisions. The speech would read identically whatever the Opposition had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued the repeal returns medicines regulation to the 1981 Medicines Act, leaving no framework for medical devices or for expediting vaccine approvals in a public health emergency, and this statement does not take any of that up. This is prepared material squarely on the matter under debate with a gesture at the other side's framing, so it sits at the top of the unengaged band rather than being a partial engagement with the preceding argument.

So, therefore, I commend this bill to the House.

acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "but it is a challenge to Te Tiriti itself" (and his closing "To me, it’s just despicable and terrible")

acuity.responding_to: "Most reasonable people are in favour of that, and that is the Government’s goal as well." — Chris Bishop

Direct engagement with the content of the preceding turn, not a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "an enabling framework that also protects and upholds environmental protections and also sets environmental bottom lines" — Chris Bishop

So, no, we won’t support this bill, because it’s poorly done and there are a number of provisions that just aren’t consistent with Green Party policy.

His opening covers the same ground (repeal by urgency, the once-bipartisan MDRS) but never takes up any specific strand of her argument to extend, qualify or dispute it — it reads as prepared Green Party material that happens to converge on the same subject, and would have been delivered unchanged whatever she had said. On-topic but not responsive, so the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 for the gesture at the repeal point she had just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "this is a set of different pieces of legislation to replace what we had done and what that Government has repealed"

acuity.statement: Just finally, this is all about providing certainty to farmers that it’s going to be good operating going forward, that they’ve got certainty to invest—they know where the rules lie and they can invest well. That’s so critical with section 70. That, combined with the section 107 rules, placed a huge degree of uncertainty, particularly for many farmers in the South Island, as to whether or not they could go ahead with their farming businesses.
acuity.explanation: Brooking raised the section 70 / section 107 linkage as a process complaint — that the 107 change was out of scope, unconsulted, and should have been debated here. Hoggard picks up exactly that linkage and supplies the substantive rationale for it (uncertainty for South Island farmers over consents and investment), which is engagement with the strand rather than with her specific objection: he answers why 70 and 107 matter, not whether the process was proper. One strand taken up, then a return to prepared primary-industries material — mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Then, there is a change to section 70, and the Minister noted that that links in with that out-of-scope, in my opinion, change to section 107 that came through the last RMA amendment bill a month or so ago"

acuity.statement: That is really, really important—and, yes, it might challenge that in some ways. Look, the other thing to say there is that if we had allowed councils more power, we probably would not have had the Christchurch red zone, and that has cost this country enormously.

acuity.responding_to: "Fast-track bill." — Glen Bennett, interjecting while Foster praised the bill's expansion of council powers to manage natural hazards

acuity.statement: So, here we are, the Government are using renewable energy and housing projects as an excuse to continue to remove Māori rights and voices from the consenting process and to diminish Māori rights and interests in our whenua, our moana, our fresh water, our geothermal areas, everything.
acuity.explanation: Ferris follows Foster's substantive case that the RMA is a process-heavy barrier to development and that the bill devolves decisions to councils. His speech is on the bill under debate and glances at the same energy/housing rationale Foster invoked, but it engages none of Foster's claims — not the Infrastructure Commission advice, not the MDRS devolution argument, not the natural-hazard point. The speech would read identically had any other government member spoken first, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band.

acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable: Andy Foster argued the RMA is 'a barrier to development' and that the bill hands medium-density decisions back to councils, and this statement does not take either claim up

acuity.statement: I want to just make the point in the House this afternoon that this bill is a part of the fix-it plan that we campaigned on as a Government, a coalition Government, just over 12 months ago. This time 12 months ago, we were busy repealing the previous administration’s natural and built environment and spatial planning legislation because we knew that that would just further stymie and act as a further roadblock to getting the country growing and thriving, particularly in economic terms.
acuity.explanation: Simpson speaks immediately after Ferris's detailed argument that the bill strips Māori rights from the consenting process and that the Ministry for the Environment itself identified Treaty breaches and inadequate engagement. He answers none of it — no mention of Te Tiriti, consultation, or the ministry's advice — and instead delivers a prepared endorsement listing the bill's five themes. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Ministry for the Environment admitted that the short time frame afforded to the bill prevented full engagement with te iwi Māori" — Tākuta Ferris; this statement does not take it up

Butterick takes up none of it: no reference to any previous speaker, no engagement with Parker's productivity argument or his specific reservations. The speech is prepared affirmation that would read identically whatever Parker had said, and could have been delivered in any RMA debate this term. It is at least about the bill under debate, so not a 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker argued that "it's a little bit overstated that it's planning constraints that lie behind New Zealand's lack of productivity growth" and raised Maori article 2 consenting rights, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does it need fixing? Yes, it does. Can we fix it? Yes, we will." — Mike Butterick

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued "this legislation is more about tinkering than fixing anything" and that the medium-density standards agreed in 2021 are being watered down, and this statement does not take either up.

Luxton had just argued the consultation was inadequate, the trade risks unexamined and the Māori advisory committee tokenistic; none of that is engaged. This bill puts in place the regulatory enablement to allow the exciting advancements in potential in health research and biotech, in the plant and food sector, and especially in our Crown research institutes, like Scion.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed, document-quoting critique and engages none of it. The speech would read identically whatever O'Connor had argued; the only reference to the preceding turns is "as many have said", which repeats a slogan rather than engaging any claim. It stays on the bill, so it is not a 0.0.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor argued the regulatory impact statement shows the policy work was rushed, benefits unquantified, and risks to trade and market access excluded from consideration; this statement does not take any of it up.

This bill may not be about a treaty between two people, but it is a treaty between humankind and all living things, the environment, animals, and food.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson spoke about the GE-free competitive advantage, taking guidance from major food exporters like Fonterra, and consumer pushback against Bovaer, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the adequacy of the regulatory checks and balances — and answers it with the regulator the bill establishes, then returns to prepared material on climate change, pre-election commitments and coalition agreements. acuity.responding_to: "we must ensure that these checks and balances in our regulatory system framework are in a place that is robust enough to counter the potential risk factors" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.responding_to: "We know that Local Water Done Well works." — Simeon Brown

It makes clear that councils need to provide an assets condition register and also a plan to show how they envision investing for long-term upgrades and maintenance and capital upgrades. The water services providers are natural monopolies and so having a strong and credible regulatory framework is vital.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: McAnulty argued the Government's figures understate councils' $185 billion need and Pham argued the bill narrows drinking-water compliance and ignores te mana o te wai; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.responding_to: "From councils’ own numbers, over the next 30 years they need to spend $185 billion." — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "this Government put $16 billion into healthcare over the next three years. That’s not a myth, that’s not a dream, that’s not some hairy idea; that is fact"

acuity.statement: I also want to just acknowledge some of the points that were raised around funding and resourcing. Of course, funding is very important and, as the Hon Louise Upston spoke about—72 hours and this being ring-fenced and ensuring that we have that set aside for those first three days for mums after they have had their babies.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Russell pressed — funding and the midwifery shortage — and gestures at ring-fencing, so it is more than prepared material on the right subject. But it does not take up the actual question put (whether the Government will commit funding) and returns to thanks and select-committee process, so it is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It is time for the Government to put their money where their mouth is on this one. Will they actually fund this fine promise?"

acuity.statement: I do like what these rules achieve, but I do think there are questions that we need to answer—for example, the tension between the public holiday being on the Monday and the no-trading day being on the Sunday. What this means is even if workers—yes, it is true, they have their rights protected and under this member’s bill that would also apply to Good Friday, but they don’t have the backup of it being a public holiday. If they do work, they get time and a half or they get a day in lieu—they have those other provisions in place. It does feel a little bit messy to me to have a public holiday Monday but the trading days on other days. I do hear the call from the other side that they want to ensure people have the freedom not to work. I know it’s never quite that simple that everyone feels they’re in a position to say no, but I do think this is an issue worth teasing out.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of Belich's case — that removing the trading restriction would pressure workers who are not really free to decline a shift — concedes part of it ("it's never quite that simple that everyone feels they're in a position to say no") and answers it with the Monday-public-holiday/Sunday-trading-day mismatch and the time-and-a-half provisions. It engages the worker-protection argument rather than the religious one, which is exactly the ground Belich chose, so the passage would have to change had she argued the religious case instead. Not a 1.0: he leaves her wider claims (the Holidays Act review, the minimum wage, the rollback of worker rights) untouched and returns to his own prepared Christmas/Anzac consistency argument. Scored only on engagement — not on whether the reasoning or the entitlement facts are sound.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "protecting the rights of workers to be able to enjoy that time off and to not put additional pressure on them to work" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: As a House, we often talk about mental health and the declining mental health in New Zealand. One of the big contributors to that is loneliness, alcohol.
acuity.explanation: Maipi-Clarke's immediately preceding turn made a specific alcohol-harm argument with figures (37 percent of Māori men hazardous drinkers; Māori women rising from 21 to 29 percent) and a demand that the Government restrict alcohol advertising before she could support the bill. Unkovich arrives at the same topic — alcohol as a harm reason to oppose the bill — but takes up none of that argument: no engagement with the harm statistics, the disproportionate-harm claim, or the religious-privilege point. She gestures at the debate ('many have already been mentioned') and then delivers prepared material on family togetherness, loneliness and NGOs. The speech would read identically had Maipi-Clarke argued something else about the bill, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "Allowing the sale of alcohol on Good Friday and Easter Sunday will encourage drinking and worsen alcohol-related harm." — engaged only as a shared topic, not as a claim taken up.

acuity.statement: Now, I’ve heard the arguments in favour around supporting choice and supporting businesses to be able to make choices and also individuals being able to make choices, and I appreciate those arguments, but I also would like to point out that there are many businesses, particularly small businesses in New Zealand, who ultimately have very limited choices.
acuity.explanation: Brown names the choice-and-business strand of the pro-bill case, concedes it, and then inverts it with a worked example — the family-run fruit and vegetable shop that competes whenever the supermarket opens, going from 3½ closed days to 1½. That is a genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding argument, including Maipi-Clarke's small-business fairness point, which he turns on its head: she argued restricted trading disadvantages small businesses that cannot absorb the $1,000 fine, he argues repeal is what strips them of their only closed days. But he does not take up her specific claims — the fine, the harm statistics, the one-religion-privilege argument — and the rest of the call (heritage, council discretion, the consistency challenge about Christmas Day and Anzac Day) is prepared material aimed at speakers earlier in the debate. Partial engagement, pointable, then back to the script.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "This means that some large businesses are able to pay the fine and sell alcohol anyway. This is unfair to small businesses."

acuity.statement: Absolutely you can write into the law that there are workers’ protections. You can write that on a piece of paper, but how does it work in practice?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the strand Tuiono had just put to the House — that a statutory right to refuse is defeated by a power imbalance at work — and does something with it, supplying six years of retail-organising experience (the Blenheim supermarket's failure to issue written notices, her having to build the opt-out form herself) as the practical test of the paper right. It is not a mere reference to the previous speaker: the argument would read differently had Tuiono not raised the boss/worker pressure point. Marked down from 1.0 because she frames the reply as answering the member in charge rather than Tuiono's specific formulation, and the bulk of the speech is her own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "There is a power imbalance which is not addressed in this bill, so I have concerns about that."

acuity.statement: There is no justification for restricting another person’s freedom to transact with someone else that wants to be there, that wants to do it. They still get time and a half, because it doesn’t change the Holidays Act. They still don’t have to work, because of the Shop Trading Hours Act, but they can work—they can choose to if they want to.
acuity.explanation: Aims squarely at the specific objection Boyack had just made — that Easter Sunday is not a public holiday and that many workers trading that day get neither time and a half nor a day in lieu — and answers it on its own terms by naming the two statutes he says preserve the penal rate and the right to refuse. Whether the answer is correct is a Veracity question, not an Acuity one; the engagement is with the content of the preceding claim, so it scores high. Short of 1.0 because he asserts the counter-position rather than addressing her evidence that the protections were not followed in practice.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "Easter Sunday isn’t a public holiday, and so workers are required to work on Easter Sunday" — and that many workers "don’t receive time and a half and don’t receive a day in lieu".

acuity.statement: The second critique is a version of the one I long held—i.e., it’s healthy to have a few days each year where the shops are closed and alcohol is less available. Others also add that it’s important to honour Easter. As I tested my opinion, I reminded myself that law restricts human freedoms. This is a serious matter and thus must be well justified.
acuity.explanation: Fleming follows Helen White and takes up the substance of her case — that closing shops and restricting alcohol for a few 'sacred' days protects everybody — naming it as the second of two critiques and answering it with a freedom-restriction test the justification must pass. He engages the strand of her argument rather than her specific claims (he does not touch her evidence on alcohol availability or her bargaining-power point), and then returns to prepared reasoning, so this is a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "In a way, having these days that are a little bit sacred and where we close down our materialism actually protects everybody"

acuity.statement: I acknowledge this bill could address the fact that employees are required to work on Easter Friday. This bill would mean that they could choose not to work on Easter Friday and Easter Sunday. However, the cost of that is removing the significance of these two days. I feel that this is then, simply, a slippery slope to Christmas and Easter. I remain very sceptical that employee protections provide real-world protection. They are good in theory, but, in this case, questionable in practice.
acuity.explanation: Bates concedes the employee-choice point Fleming had just made the centre of his case and then disputes exactly the premise Fleming rested it on — that the statutory protection can be trusted in practice because we must trust enforcement of our laws. That is engagement with the specific claim just advanced, not merely the topic. It sits short of the top because it is one item in a pre-listed set of points and the scepticism is asserted rather than argued against Fleming's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg Fleming: "We need to trust the enforcement of our laws."

acuity.statement: I think that the idea that restricting the sale of alcohol, as the member from the Labour Party Helen White said, increases the harm works if you think about it as in just a quick grab off the shelf, but if you’re thinking about it in a way that someone who has got alcohol-dependency issues may feel rather nervous that they’re not going to have access to that and stock up, maybe by three dozen instead of two dozen for the weekend, the worst thing we can be doing is locking people in their homes with the alcohol which is causing them so much harm.
acuity.explanation: This takes White's specific counter-argument — that restricting sale hours reduces an alcoholic's consumption rather than prompting stockpiling — and answers it on its own terms, conceding the 'quick grab off the shelf' case and arguing the dependency case runs the other way, with a concrete mechanism (buying three dozen instead of two). The reply would have to be written differently had White argued anything else. Whether the characterisation of her claim is fair or the reasoning sound is a matter for other attributes, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "By closing alcohol sales off in time, you actually do affect the ability of people to drink"

acuity.statement: There were a couple of members who raised the slippery-slope argument that this is going to lead to the removal of Christmas and Anzac Day. The reason for bringing this bill isn’t because of an attack of we just want to get rid of religious—as I gave in my speech, I deeply hold respect for the founding religion of our country. This hasn’t been a debate to try and extend the slippery slope out to include Anzac and Christmas; what it is doing is addressing the concerns that address the confusion throughout the country that New Zealanders experience every year.
acuity.explanation: Luxton names the slippery-slope objection Bates had just pressed and answers it, distinguishing Easter from Christmas and Anzac Day on the ground that no one is confused about the latter two. He engages the objection rather than ignoring it, but much of the answer is about his own motives rather than the mechanism Bates alleged — that removing the two days' significance is what sets the slide going — so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "I feel that this is then, simply, a slippery slope to Christmas and Easter."

acuity.statement: Because it’s all about people. Every single number in the HYEFU is about decisions that impact people, that impact communities, that impact organisations, and that impact businesses in our country.
acuity.explanation: Bishop's intervention charged that one minute into her speech she had not addressed the HYEFU at all. Her reply takes up that exact charge and answers its premise rather than deflecting: the opening about children is about the HYEFU, because every number in it is a decision about people. She then proceeds into the fiscal figures, which is the charge being met head-on. Not a 1.0 because she rebuts the premise of the objection without conceding or engaging the narrower point that a general-debate speech had displaced the granted subject; it is a substantive engagement of the specific claim just made rather than a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we've had a lot of talk about children, or one particular child, but the HYEFU has yet to be mentioned" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: So who is correct, then: the Prime Minister, who says that his whole Government is relentlessly focused on his quarterly action plan, or his Deputy Prime Minister, who says—and I quote—“I don’t have this sort of dashboard crap that I see other people perform on and a 50-point plan, or a 100-point plan, or a quarter-year plan”, and if Winston Peters thinks that his plans are crap, why should Kiwis think otherwise?
acuity.explanation: Luxon had just made the quarterly action plan the centrepiece of his answer, claiming 42 completed actions. Hipkins takes that exact claim and puts a specific contradiction to it — the Deputy Prime Minister's own recorded dismissal of multi-point plans — forcing the PM to reconcile the two. Delete Luxon's preceding turn and substitute a different argument and this question could not stand as asked, which is the deciding test. Not a mere reference or a pivot: the content of the prior claim is what the question operates on. Scored on engagement only; whether Peters really said it is a veracity matter and the sharpness of the jibe a civility one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "Yes, and especially our work to complete our latest quarterly action plan."

acuity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that New Zealand’s minimum wage at around 70 percent of the median wage is one of the highest in the developed world, and does he find it surprising that the Labour Party would like directors of public Government-owned companies to be paid a fraction of what private sector companies are paid?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the premise Hipkins had been pressing across several supplementaries — that minimum wage earners are going backwards while directors are paid too much — and inverts it, offering a comparative figure against the first half and a private-sector comparison against the second. That is real engagement with the argument in the room rather than prepared praise. It stops short of 1.0 because it answers the topic rather than any specific claim just made (it does not touch the KiwiRail or Transpower figures), and the second clause turns into framing aimed at the Opposition rather than at the argument. Focus and civility would read that second clause differently; this score is for engagement alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "why has he agreed to giving its directors a 90 percent pay increase while minimum wage workers go backwards?"

acuity.statement: You cannot cut your way to prosperity, and here I just want to point out a few things from the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update (HYEFU). The fiscal decisions of this Government and of this Minister of Finance have exacerbated the recession. The Reserve Bank initially indicated that we were facing just a light downturn, but now the growth numbers keep on getting worse. This time last year, HYEFU was projecting a 1.5 percent growth this year; now, the actual rate is minus 0.2 percent.
acuity.explanation: Willis's preceding turn rested on two linked claims: that her Government's fiscal discipline and savings are the responsible course, and that the HYEFU books show a turning point allowing confident forecasts of sustained growth. Swarbrick takes up exactly those, naming the same document, attributing the recession's depth to the Minister's own fiscal decisions, and setting the deteriorating forecast track (1.5 percent projected vs minus 0.2 percent actual) against the turning-point claim. The speech would have to change if Willis had argued something else about HYEFU, and she goes on to use the Government's own spending-reduction path (34 to 30 percent) as the mechanism. Not a full 1.0 because she does not engage Willis's specific debt and deficit figures, and part of the passage is prepared Green framing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are now able to forecast confidently a sustained period of economic growth" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: She said that this is an austerity Government that’s spending so little money so that it can make businesses go broke and then point to the failure. Now, I just want to bring some facts into the debate. In the back of this document we’re debating today, it says very clearly that in 2018, 2019, when Chlöe Swarbrick was on the Government benches, voting for every Budget, the Government spent 27 percent, 28 percent at max; today, in this statement, the Government is spending 33 percent of GDP.
acuity.explanation: Seymour restates Swarbrick's immediately preceding austerity argument in her own terms and then attacks it directly with a spending-as-share-of-GDP comparison drawn from the document under debate. The speech would have had to be different had she argued something else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the inference (whether total spend/GDP answers her claim about public-service defunding) belongs to Rigor, and the tone of the surrounding remarks to Civility, neither of which is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "This is the austerity playbook. It is to defund public services to failure, to watch them fail, point that out to the public"

acuity.statement: The value of today is that the New Zealand public has been given access to data which reflects that Treasury itself realises it needs to do better. This is a revision of forecasts where Treasury itself says that it’s had to go back and rework its own modelling, and this document says that those forecasts reflect nothing in terms of what this Government is doing to remedy and turn around the situation that the Government has inherited.
acuity.explanation: Jones takes up one strand of Swarbrick's case — her reliance on Treasury's deteriorating forecasts — and disputes its standing, arguing the forecasts were reworked and do not capture the Government's remedial changes. But he engages neither her specific figures nor Seymour's spending comparison, and the rest of the turn is prepared growth-strategy material, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the claim itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "Treasury’s forecasts have only massively deteriorated since the Government took power."

acuity.statement: This debate started, within the first minute or so, with the Leader of the House calling a point of order and asking why our finance spokesperson in Labour was talking about people. I think there could be no greater moment in this debate that shows what this Government is about—and it certainly is not about people.
acuity.explanation: Prepared Labour material squarely on the matter under debate (the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update), and it gestures at the debate by recalling an earlier procedural moment and naming earlier contributors. But it engages no part of the argument of the member who actually spoke before her: delete Waititi's speech and substitute any other attack on the HYEFU and this speech is word-for-word the same. Because the content it does reach for sits outside the window, the engagement cannot be pointed at, which caps this in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 for the live reference to how the debate has run.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi immediately precedes her and argued that "unemployment is up" and that the Government is "facilitating the biggest transfer of wealth in a generation from hard-working whānau to property developers and landlords", and this statement does not take any of it up; the turns she does reach back for (the Leader of the House's point of order, the Minister of Finance's speech, Barbara Edmonds, Minister Jones) are not in the text supplied, so nothing engaged can be pointed at here.

acuity.statement: It is interesting listening to members opposite, because, as various colleagues on this side of the House have pointed out, it is an extraordinary fiscal fantasyland that the Opposition live in.
acuity.explanation: This names the previous speakers and labels their position, but engages none of the content Russell actually advanced — the Health New Zealand deficit being listed as a fiscal risk, flat tertiary and science funding, or the substitution of OBEGALx for OBEGAL. It is a mere reference followed by a pivot to the speaker's own prepared debt comparison, which the rubric puts in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is at least about the fiscal matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued the Government created a new measure, OBEGALx, because the standard OBEGAL did not show what it wanted, and that science and tertiary education funding are flat — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We also want to be able to build stuff, and after the nincompoops on the other side created an obstruction economy, it’s getting ever-harder to do that. We spend, according to the Infrastructure Commission, over $1.3 billion a year on consenting. That is a sunk cost that we cannot afford in a housing crisis, in a massive infrastructure deficit, and in a country where we are signing up to ambitious climate change targets.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows a long, specific critique of the bill by Lan Pham — submission numbers, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, two named projects, the status of prohibited activities — and engages none of it. The only acknowledgement of the preceding turn is the label 'nincompoops on the other side', which is a reference and not an engagement with any claim. The remainder is prepared ACT material on productivity and consenting cost: it would read identically whatever Pham had said, though it is at least about the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham argued the bill subordinates environmental outcomes and Te Tiriti to development, citing that only 0.6 percent of submitters supported it and naming the Waimate incinerator and Bendigo-Ophir mine, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This is a great bill, and this will get our infrastructure and our economy back on track. I’m thrilled to commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: A substantive opposing turn by Lan Pham and a supporting turn by Cameron Luxton both precede this, so the statement is eligible. It engages no part of either: no claim is rebutted, conceded, corrected or extended. It is generic commendation that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before; the gesture at 'infrastructure and our economy' keeps it nominally on the subject of the bill, which is why it is 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham argued environmental protections are 'relegated to mere considerations' and that councils and mayors oppose the named projects, and Cameron Luxton argued consenting costs $1.3 billion a year; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: From Trans-Tasman Resources in Taranaki, where the extraordinarily destructive seabed mining is scheduled to occur—the people have resisted for over a decade. The local community, the local iwi, and the fishing industry themselves have resisted, and non-Government organisations. It has been kicked back by the Supreme Court. It has been kicked back by every consideration body in the country.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Ngarewa-Packer and picks up two of her strands — Trans-Tasman Resources in Taranaki and the courts' refusal of it — rather than opening new ground, so the engagement is pointable. But he does nothing with her specific claims (he neither extends the four-courts point nor adds to the community-funded litigation argument); he restates the same frame and then moves into his own prepared catalogue of projects. The speech would read almost identically had she argued the same case differently, which keeps it below a partial-engagement 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "the communities in Taranaki that, through their own hard efforts, funded numerous courts, right up until the Supreme Court, who ruled against Trans-Tasman Resources' ability to be able to safely mine"

acuity.statement: I stand in support of the Fast-track Approvals Bill, a bill which says yes to jobs, yes to opportunities, yes to energy security, yes to building the roads that are needed to unlock economic growth and opportunity, yes to houses, and yes to making sure that this country can actually deliver the opportunities which keep our children here in New Zealand. On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things, and the people of New Zealand will say no to them at the 2026 election.
acuity.explanation: Brown follows a detailed, project-by-project critique and engages none of it — no answer on the court refusals, the Glenavy incinerator approval, or the local-consent objection. The 'other side says no, no, no' line names opponents as a target rather than engaging a claim, which the rubric treats as unresponsive. It is at least on the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0; it is prepared material that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel argued that the bill revives projects already refused by the Supreme Court and other consenting bodies (Trans-Tasman Resources, Ruataniwha, Waitaha) and overrides local communities, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The Opposition parties, including the Labour Party, have long acknowledged that there is a problem with excessive costs for consenting mid-size infrastructure, particularly—not so much the larger infrastructure, but the mid-size and smaller infrastructure projects in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Parker takes up one strand of the immediately preceding speech — Brown's charge that the Opposition opposes consenting reform outright — by conceding the premise that consenting costs are a real problem and narrowing it to mid-size and smaller projects. That is a pointable engagement with the specific caricature just made, but it is a single strand and he then returns to his prepared account of the differences between the three versions of fast track, so it sits at the partial-engagement mark rather than the top of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "On the other side of the House, we see the people who say “No, no, no” to all of those things"

acuity.statement: Mrs Ngarewa-Packer is ranting away, as she always does, but just not listening to the facts, which is that so many issues that she purports to care about could be solved through economic growth.
acuity.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer's interjection made a specific claim — that the Government could have spent its first 100 days on renewable energy regulation. Bishop names her and characterises her as not listening, then returns to his prepared line about economic growth; he engages no part of the renewable-energy-regulation point. This is a mere reference to the interjector rather than engagement with the content, so it sits in the low band, with a gesture at the debate rather than none.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Regulations for renewable energy. You could have spent 100 days on that." — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: The Ministers who have alleged that those comments are defamatory owe the House an explanation about what is untrue; about the value of private benefit that is going to this company because of this legislation, not only from the value of uplifts of the options that they own on the land but also from the public purse, going straight into the hands of developers who only owned an option on this land and don’t in fact own the land at all.
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just, in the immediately preceding turn, called her committee-stage remarks defamatory and argued that the public/private ownership distinction was facile because ownership is irrelevant to the public benefit test. Williams takes up that exact charge, demands the Ministers specify what in her remarks was untrue, and answers the public-benefit argument on its own ground by identifying the mechanism — option uplift plus NZTA land purchase. The speech would have had to be different had Bishop not made the defamation allegation. Not a full 1.0 because she restates the private-benefit claim rather than rebutting his mixed-economy reasoning directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I was really disappointed to hear the defamatory remarks of Arena Williams during the debate on the committee stage" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Mr Mooney, I have read the bill. I’ve been on the committee for the past six months, so I know it very well and know the fact that you can—sorry, you do not need to in terms of there’s some responsibilities, but there’s some “mays”: they may have to do this; they may have to do that.
acuity.explanation: Mooney interjects with a direct challenge to whether Bennett has read the bill; Bennett answers it head-on, states his six months on the committee, and immediately points to the specific textual feature he relies on (the discretionary "mays" rather than mandatory duties). The reply would be different had the interjection been different, and it supplies substance rather than merely naming the interjector.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Have you read the bill?" — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: Do you know what is truly despicable? It’s that members opposite talked about respecting Te Tiriti, but guess what! Last week, there was an Amendment Paper put forward to remove Mana Ahuriri from this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding speech — that the bill breaches Te Tiriti obligations and that aspects of it are "despicable" — and turns it back with a concrete counter-instance (the Amendment Paper removing Mana Ahuriri, a post-settlement group). This is more than a reference: it engages the content of Bennett's Te Tiriti claim and offers a rebutting fact. Not a full 1.0 because it answers only that one strand and leaves the statutory-override and natural-hazard arguments untouched before closing with prepared commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is a challenge to Te Tiriti itself" / "To me, it’s just despicable and terrible" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: Hopefully I’m a reasonable person, and the list that the Minister, the Hon Chris Bishop, just gave out, many of the things—I cannot recite it verbatim, but they are things that I certainly agree with. We should move this system and the resource management system to the national instruments and away from a bespoke consent-by-consent issue.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Bishop's immediately preceding appeal to what 'most reasonable people' favour, answers it by placing herself in that category, and concedes the specific strand of his list she agrees with (moving to national instruments and away from consent-by-consent). The speech would read differently had Bishop not closed on that consensus claim, so it is a direct take-up rather than prepared material — short of 1.0 only because she concedes the list rather than doing anything further with a particular item.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Most reasonable people are in favour of that, and that is the Government’s goal as well" / "I think most people are in favour of greater standardisation" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I heard, in that list, that we do need to protect the environment, and that is not what the fast track does.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim in Bishop's speech — that the reform programme maintains environmental protections — and disputes it by pointing at the fast-track legislation he himself cited as part of that programme. This is engagement with the content of the preceding argument, turning his own stated commitment against another limb of his record; substitute a different argument from Bishop and this sentence could not stand as written.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "making improvements to the existing RMA, to cut red tape and green tape for primary industries and development in infrastructure, whilst maintaining environmental protections" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: This bill makes a wide suite of changes to the Resource Management Act (RMA) and, ironically, it wouldn’t even have been needed, and actually isn’t needed in this form if the Government hadn’t embarked on a wholesale destruction of legislation through urgency; legislation like the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act.
acuity.explanation: Brooking's turn argued the bill is no substitute for the repealed Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act and was rushed to meet a checklist. Willis picks up that same strand — the repealed Acts and the urgency used to repeal them — and pushes it one step further, arguing the bill would be unnecessary had those Acts survived. It engages the topic and one strand of her case rather than any specific claim or figure she made, and then moves into prepared Green Party material on density and transport, so this is a partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "It is not a replacement for the RMA at all. It’s not a Natural and Built Environment Act or a Spatial Planning Act"
