acuity.statement: There’s an old farming saying: “Every dog has its day”. The Resource Management Act, as we know it, is well past its use-by date. Is it past its use-by date? Yes, it is. Does it need fixing? Yes, it does. Can we fix it? Yes, we will. Yes, we can, and, yes, we will, thank you.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive Parker turn that made several specific, contestable claims — that planning constraints are an exaggerated explanation for weak productivity, that geothermal and papakāinga consenting could be delegated to Māori owners, and that infrastructure costs must be internalised. This speech engages none of them. It restates the general case that the RMA is past its use-by date in rhetorical-question form and commends the bill. It is on the subject under debate, so not a zero, but it would be word-for-word identical whatever Parker had said.

acuity.statement: I have said this before and I will say this again: we cannot continue to feel proud standing up and saying that we are GE-free, because that means we are still stuck in that trial-and-error method of selective breeding.
acuity.explanation: Parmar follows a substantive turn in which Abel built a detailed economic case against the bill: an NZIER estimate of a $10-20 billion cost to value-added primary production, a quoted regulatory impact statement passage putting GMO-free certification costs (A$14.00 per tonne in the Australian canola example) on existing producers, the claim that only 27 of 195 countries commercially grow GE crops, and a specific claim about a 95 percent premium on GMO-free New Zealand apples. acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "This legislation, effectively, forfeits New Zealand's current non-GMO producer status at a cost of potentially tens of billions of dollars to the economy." Parmar engages the general GE-free framing but not the cost or certification-burden claims.

acuity.explanation: Brown takes up one live strand of the debate — the choice/small-business argument — and does something with it, inverting the small-business fairness point Maipi-Clarke made: she said the $1,000 fine lets large businesses undercut small ones, he answers that small businesses have no real choice but to open and will lose family days. That is genuine partial engagement, and he names the concession ("I appreciate those arguments") before disputing it. It is not a 1.0 because the argument he addresses is the bill sponsor's general case rather than the specific claims in the two turns immediately before him — he never touches Maipi-Clarke's alcohol-harm case or Unkovich's loneliness argument — and he then returns to prepared material on councils' discretion and consistency.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "This means that some large businesses are able to pay the fine and sell alcohol anyway. This is unfair to small businesses."

acuity.statement: Can I thank the Deputy Prime Minister for those comments. Mr Deputy Prime Minister, I read in the paper this morning that the reason that the airport was closed in Vanuatu was that there were problems with contaminated fuel. Is that the reason why New Zealand relief aircraft have not been able to land in Vanuatu until now?
acuity.explanation: Peters' motion statement said a second aircraft would go 'once the airport is open'. Parker takes exactly that conditional and probes it, supplying a reported reason (contaminated fuel) for the airport closure and asking whether it is what has prevented NZ relief aircraft landing. The question could not have been asked in this form had Peters not made that specific statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: 'another one, once the airport is open, to transport a search and rescue team and deliver relief supplies'

acuity.statement: Right. Well, in that case, sir, I would endorse the Deputy Prime Minister’s statements. I’m sure that the House would be interested to know when it is that New Zealand aircraft are likely to be able to actually land and take assistance to the people in Vanuatu. I wish the members of the New Zealand Defence Force and supporting agencies who will likely be working through the Christmas period—I thank them for their service on behalf of New Zealand and the assistance that they are giving to the people of Vanuatu.
acuity.explanation: Endorses the motion and picks up one strand of Peters' statement — the timing of aircraft being able to land — but does not engage the detail of the deployment schedule beyond restating the open question, then moves to a prepared tribute to the Defence Force that would read the same whatever Peters had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: 'the deployment of New Zealand military planes today; the first this morning to undertake surveillance and assess the damage'

acuity.statement: The second critique is a version of the one I long held—i.e., it’s healthy to have a few days each year where the shops are closed and alcohol is less available. Others also add that it’s important to honour Easter. As I tested my opinion, I reminded myself that law restricts human freedoms. This is a serious matter and thus must be well justified. To my understanding, those two justifications are: to protect people and our world from exploitation or harm, and to, secondly, maximise participation or access. I do not consider the Easter restrictions on trading and liquor meet either of those tests, particularly given the clear protection of employees as discussed. Enforcing rest time does not meet those tests.
acuity.explanation: Fleming names the two critiques raised in the debate and takes up the second one, which is precisely Helen White's case that closing these days protects everyone and that rest time is scarce. He engages it by proposing a test (harm prevention or maximising access) and finding the restriction fails both, and he also glances at her bargaining-power point via the 'protected choice of those workers' reply. But the engagement is with the general shape of her argument rather than her specific claims (he never touches her alcohol-availability research or her section 44 point), and the speech is substantially prepared material on his own change of mind, which he says he could not finish. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'In a way, having these days that are a little bit sacred and where we close down our materialism actually protects everybody, and everybody gets a day off consumerism, which doesn’t do them a scrap of harm.'

acuity.statement: I remain very sceptical that employee protections provide real-world protection. They are good in theory, but, in this case, questionable in practice.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific claim Fleming had just made — that the statutory protection of workers' choice is guaranteed and that doubting it is really doubting law enforcement itself — and disputes it on the ground that the protection is theoretical rather than real. It engages the substance of the preceding argument rather than merely referencing the speaker, but it asserts the scepticism without meeting Fleming's 'then we have a deeper issue about trusting our laws' rejoinder, so it is a partial rather than complete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg Fleming: 'For those people who say that we can’t trust the law, then, as lawmakers, we have a deeper issue than the one before us.'

acuity.statement: I think that the idea that restricting the sale of alcohol, as the member from the Labour Party Helen White said, increases the harm works if you think about it as in just a quick grab off the shelf, but if you’re thinking about it in a way that someone who has got alcohol-dependency issues may feel rather nervous that they’re not going to have access to that and stock up, maybe by three dozen instead of two dozen for the weekend, the worst thing we can be doing is locking people in their homes with the alcohol which is causing them so much harm.
acuity.explanation: Luxton takes White's specific counter-claim — that the research shows dependent drinkers buy opportunistically when hours are extended rather than stockpiling ahead of a closure — concedes the mechanism she describes holds for impulse purchasing, and then disputes its scope by arguing the anticipated closure drives bulk buying and leaves families shut in with more alcohol. The reply is squarely aimed at the content of her claim and would be different had she argued otherwise. Scored on engagement only; whether the stockpiling claim is empirically right is a veracity question and whether the concession-then-rebuttal reasons soundly is a rigor question, and neither moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'The research suggests that that’s not actually the case, sir. What happens, when there is an issue with alcohol, is that an alcoholic will buy more alcohol if there is availability.'

acuity.statement: Is she concerned that MSD themselves have decreased some of their own targets for getting people into jobs because of the worsening economic conditions, and how can she then assert that her 50,000 jobseeker reduction target is still achievable?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific assertion just made — that 'our plan is working' on the basis of 30,000 jobseeker exits into work — and puts a counter-fact to it (MSD lowering its own employment targets), then presses the consequence for the 50,000 target. The question would have to be different had Upston not claimed the plan was on track. Not a 1.0 only because it attaches the MSD point to the primary question's target rather than to the 30,000 figure Upston actually cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our plan is working" — Louise Upston (who went on to cite "over 30,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit exit into work")

acuity.statement: What does she say to the New Zealanders who will be accessing welfare support this Christmas, Christmas 2026, Christmas 2027, Christmas 2028, and Christmas 2029, given the economic outlook is so bleak that the unemployment rate will not even be back to 2023 levels by 2029?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand Upston had just conceded — that conditions will be 'worse, deeper, for longer' — and extends it across the forecast period to test the 'we're on track' claim. That is real engagement with what was said, but it is carried on a prepared rhetorical frame (the roll-call of Christmases) rather than contesting the specific 'on track' reasoning, so it sits mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because the economic conditions are going to be worse, deeper, for longer—because of the record we have inherited—the jobseeker numbers will be higher than we anticipated" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Is maintaining the rail freight connection between the North and South Islands by ensuring we have at least one rail-enabled ferry important for the economic prosperity of the regions, particularly in the South Island?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under discussion — regional economic prosperity — but engages no part of what Jones actually argued (geothermal funding, summits, aquaculture consenting, mining, OMV). It is a prepared pivot to the questioner's own issue that would read identically whatever Jones had said about the regions, so it earns the 'gesture at the debate' end of the low band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Certainty, confidence, and growth is about to hit regional New Zealand in the aquaculture sector" — Shane Jones; the question takes up his general prosperity frame but none of his claims

acuity.statement: Will he speak to the Ministers for rail, finance, and transport to ensure they understand the regional development and prosperity implications of not having a rail freight connection between the North and South Islands before decisions are made on ferry procurement?
acuity.explanation: Directly reworks the deflection just delivered: Jones said the Minister beside him was the right person to answer, so she asks instead whether he will take the regional-development case to those Ministers. The question could not have been framed this way had he answered on the merits, which is the clearest evidence of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the man to my right is the appropriate person to respond to it" — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: How can New Zealanders take her financial management seriously when she cancelled the ferries, costing the taxpayer hundreds of millions of dollars, undertook creative accounting to make her books look better, and has delivered the highest debt in decades?
acuity.explanation: The 'creative accounting to make her books look better' charge is aimed squarely at the OBEGALx change Willis had explained earlier in the window — stripping ACC revenue and expenses out of the headline indicator — so one strand genuinely engages a preceding turn. But it does not take up Willis's actual rationale (that a self-funding, levy-based scheme should not drive short-term fiscal policy, or the BNZ comment she quoted in support), and the surrounding ferry and debt lines are prepared attack material that would stand unchanged whatever she had said. Scored as engaging the topic and one strand, not the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The simplest way to look through them is to take ACC revenue and expenses out of the OBEGAL. That is what we've done by creating a new measure called OBEGALx" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement that “We’ve set ambitious goals for ourselves.”, and, if so, can he please outline for the House what exactly is ambitious about his Government’s goals to decrease emissions and persistent child poverty by just 1 percent?
acuity.explanation: Luxon had just taunted Green MPs over climate credibility; Swarbrick's question is on the same subject (emissions targets) but takes up no part of what he actually argued about fast track or renewable projects. It is prepared material pointed at a prior, unrelated quote of the PM's, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unengaged band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “I call on all those Green MPs who actually care about climate change to back the projects, back the economy, and back renewable energy and housing”

acuity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that his Government has cut services for vulnerable children and whānau, increased benefit sanctions by 133 percent, and cut 9,000 jobs from the public sector, with 1,500 more to go at Health New Zealand, while setting aside $2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords, in just this year alone?
acuity.explanation: The question glances at the PM's closing claim to be supporting low and middle income New Zealanders by listing cuts that cut against it, but it engages nothing of his emissions-reduction-plan answer and would read identically whatever he had just said. Prepared material, broadly on the matter under question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “we want to support low and middle income, working New Zealanders”

acuity.statement: Is there a job for every New Zealander who is currently unemployed and on the jobseeker benefit?
acuity.explanation: This takes the premise of the answer just given — that obligations on jobseekers are the route off the benefit — and tests it directly by asking whether the jobs those obligations point at exist. The question is unimprovised and would have made no sense had Luxon answered differently; it is short and vague on detail, but responsiveness, not precision, is what is being scored.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “meet with your case manager, put a resumé together, and show up for the job interviews”

acuity.statement: Did the Government cut taxes for landlords or simply restore the very consistent and sensible tax policy that was the case for the first four years of the Labour-Green Government?
acuity.explanation: Seymour picks up the specific characterisation Swarbrick put into the debate — tax cuts for landlords — and contests it as a restoration rather than a cut, offering an alternative description of the same measure. It is a friendly question designed to let the PM re-answer, and it does not engage the immediately preceding answer, but it does take up a named claim from the exchange and do something with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: “$2.9 billion in tax cuts for landlords”

acuity.statement: Does he agree that it would be unfair to judge his Government for the poor forecast of the half-yearly fiscal update because one year is not long enough to influence any significant change?
acuity.explanation: Waititi takes the exact defence just offered — that a government needs time and inherits its predecessor's conditions — and invites the PM to accept it as a general principle, setting a trap he can only escape by abandoning his own answer. The question could not have been asked in this form had Luxon answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “It is a consequence of economic mismanagement and vandalism over the previous six years, but this a Government cleaning it up”

acuity.statement: So why did his Government decide to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, because the authority was unable to unwind 182 years of oppression and unequal treatment in only nine months?
acuity.explanation: The question applies the PM's own inherited-conditions-need-time reasoning to a body his Government abolished after nine months, which is a real use of what he had just said. It is partial rather than full engagement because it also pivots to an entirely new policy area and does not touch the fiscal substance of the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: “our Government is taking responsibility for the challenging economic conditions we’ve inherited”

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister’s message to Te Pāti Māori and some of its supporters something that’s totally alien: that shortly, they’ll have to get off their backside and do some work?
acuity.explanation: The question engages no part of the preceding answer on interest deductibility and rents; it reaches back to gesture at the earlier Te Pāti Māori exchange and could have been put on any day of the question cycle. The gesture at the wider matter under debate keeps it above zero, but naming an opponent as a target is not engaging their content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Luxon had just rejected the characterisation of interest deductibility as a tax and defended rental stability, and this question does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: How can her target to reduce jobseeker beneficiary numbers by 50,000 be on track when the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts there will still be 204,000 people on jobseeker benefit in 2029, and her target for 2030 is 140,000 jobseeker beneficiaries?
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni takes the “yes, absolutely” on-track assertion just made and puts the specific forecast figures against it, forcing the arithmetic of the claim into the open. It does not take up Upston's peak-in-January or global-financial-crisis comparison, so it engages one strand of the answer rather than all of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: “Yes, absolutely. Our Government is committed to having 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030 and achieving this target is a priority for our Government.”

acuity.statement: Has she spoken to her finance Minister about the record numbers of people on benefit, and her beneficiary reduction target being at risk, given it is the economic conditions and job losses en masse that are putting her target at risk, or will she solely rely on sanctioning beneficiaries to get her numbers down?
acuity.explanation: The question adopts the Minister's own concession about a longer and deeper downturn and turns it into the reason her target cannot be met, while contesting the case-management answer she had just given by asking whether sanctions are the real mechanism. It engages the reasoning of the preceding turn rather than merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: “Treasury now forecasts this economic downturn to be longer and deeper compared to the Budget update.”

acuity.statement: It doesn’t take a lot of parliamentary time, it doesn’t take a lot of select committee time, but it is an important check on the ability of the executive to increase the costs on society, the most important of which, probably most years, is adjusting the excise and excise duties, the equivalent duties, on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products.
acuity.explanation: Bishop introduced the bill by calling it pro forma, grumbling that the House must do this every Christmas and suggesting the law be changed so it need not. Parker takes that specific proposition up and answers it directly: the annual confirmation costs little House or committee time and exists as a constitutional check on the executive imposing tax-like levies. The speech would have had to change had Bishop not argued the exercise was a pointless annual ritual.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "maybe one day in the future, we’ll change the law so we don’t have to do it" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: In this case, we are not supporting this bill and made our concerns noted in the first reading. We do take the point that traditionally these bills have been relatively technical and non-controversial; we don’t think that this is the case, actually.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the characterisation both preceding speakers relied on — Bishop's "relatively pro forma piece of legislation" and Parker's framing of the instruments as routine confirmations — by conceding the general pattern and then disputing that it holds for this bill, going on to name the heated-tobacco excise reduction and the CPI indexation of benefits as the substantive content he says makes it political rather than technical. Squarely engaged with the argument just made rather than prepared condemnation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is, as they say, a relatively pro forma piece of legislation" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: The Minister has also highlighted the pathway that has been trod by Operation Burnham and the significant hard work of a working group led by Lyn Provost to make sure that we can come to this point and make this appointment. I thank the Minister for explaining the process moving forward after having set the date for Mr Horsley’s appointment. We look forward to working with the Government on that particular appointment when that time comes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of Penk's speech — the interim nature of the appointment and the process for confirming a longer-term one — and responds to it by signalling Labour's intention to work with the Government on that later appointment. It also picks up Penk's reference to Operation Burnham and supplies the detail of the Provost working group. Partial rather than full engagement: it accepts the Minister's case rather than doing anything with its substance, and most of the turn is prepared support and seasonal good wishes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "he will provide experienced and expert oversight of the role until I am in a position—or perhaps a ministerial colleague is in a position—to confirm a longer-term appointment. I anticipate that that will take place in late 2025." — Chris Penk

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Greens to also support this motion appointing Mr Brendan John Horsley as the Inspector-General of Defence, noting, as others have noted—the two speakers before me, the Hon Chris Penk and the Hon Peeni Henare—that he has significant experience—for example, in his role within intelligence and security and other statutory bodies as well.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speakers and takes up their shared proposition that Horsley has the relevant experience, then adds further specifics of his career that neither had listed, and later restates the office's two statutory functions for listeners. So it engages the content rather than merely gesturing at it, but it adopts and elaborates the case instead of doing anything with the reasoning, and the bulk of the turn would read the same whoever had spoken first.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Mr Horsley has held the office of Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security since June 2020." — Chris Penk (and "Mr Horsley brings significant experience to the role." — Peeni Henare)

acuity.statement: I heard, through another committee today, that it’s not just about revenue but about the ability to contract for other services that were previously limited because of this advertising restriction—for example, with the Cricket World Cup for TVNZ.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of Marcroft's central objection — that the repeal is only worth a small, probably displaced advertising revenue figure — by arguing the restriction also blocks broadcasters from contracting for content such as the Cricket World Cup, a benefit her revenue arithmetic does not capture. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different. Short of 1.0 because the rebuttal is implicit and sourced only to "another committee today" rather than engaging her $6 million figure head-on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Whilst the case may be able to be made that a little bit of revenue—it’s predicted about $6 million, inside this bill—might go and be generated for some of these media entities in a deregulated situation, a counter case can also be made that the same amount could be spent on either side of the days that are currently restricted." — Jenny Marcroft

acuity.statement: Firstly, my colleague Minister Goldsmith is working very, very hard and diligently in this portfolio. He does have COVID, which is why he wasn’t able to be at the select committee, but let’s come back to the facts of the industry.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific factual charge just made — that the Minister was absent from the select committee and "missing in action" — and supplies the reason (COVID) rather than talking past it. The speech would have to change if Davidson had not raised the absence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "He wasn’t at select committee this morning to hear from NZ On Air, to hear from RNZ, and to hear from TVNZ"

acuity.statement: That member was part of a Government, and Labour had six years in which they were actually able to enact changes, and what did they do? They didn’t make any changes at all.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding argument — the charge of inaction — by turning it on the previous speaker's own government, but it does not take up any of Davidson's specific evidence (the timeline of closures, the 73-word repeal, the $6 million figure) before moving to prepared material on the changing media landscape.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "The inaction to do anything about that is, ultimately, a threat to our democracy"

acuity.statement: We have got stuck because we now have a Government that is very committed to this idea for everything, “We’re just going to get rid of regulation. We’re going to get rid of rules.” Well, there’s a place for these things. It’s all about balance. I want to fix things too.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the deregulatory premise the previous speaker had just stated as his reason for supporting the bill, and disputes it on its own terms while conceding part of it. The passage is clearly shaped by what Bidois said rather than being indifferent to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "I certainly want, and most of my colleagues I hope would agree, a country with fewer regulations, not more"

acuity.statement: What evidence, if any, does she have that a strategy of cuts would lead to growth?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the growth claim Willis had just made and demands the evidence connecting it to her spending restraint, but recasts "careful about New Zealanders' tax and how we spend it" as "a strategy of cuts" rather than engaging the words actually used, so it answers the topic more than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we are a Government that is going to drive growth"

acuity.statement: Is her Christmas present for Kiwis higher debt, more borrowing, no ferries, fewer jobs, more Kiwis moving overseas, and no growth?
acuity.explanation: A prepared, seasonally themed list that is on the matter under debate but takes up no part of the debt figures or the attribution argument Willis had just advanced; it would read identically whatever answer preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "net core Crown debt went from $57 billion to $175 billion during the six years of the Labour Government"

acuity.statement: Why was a matched-funding approach chosen for this fund?
acuity.explanation: On the subject just announced, and gestures at the fund's design, but engages no claim in the preceding answer — matched funding had not been raised in it. Prepared material on the right topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey announced the first three recipients of the Innovation Fund and described each programme, and this question does not take up any part of that.

acuity.statement: How will this announcement support the Minister’s priorities for mental health?
acuity.explanation: A scripted pivot to the Minister's priorities that engages nothing in the answer it follows; it would be word-for-word the same whatever Doocey had just said about NGOs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey argued that the solutions are already in the sector and that "Wellington doesn't always know best", and this question does not take that up.

acuity.statement: What does the Minister think the value of takatāpui and rainbow-specific mental health and suicide prevention organisations is, like OutLine Aotearoa?
acuity.explanation: Opens a new line about rainbow-specific providers rather than engaging the priorities just set out; it stays within the matter under debate (who the fund reaches), which keeps it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey listed his four priorities as mental health Minister, and this question does not take them up.

acuity.statement: Does he think there are some instances where criteria for funding should be based on the unique and significant needs of marginalised communities, like takatāpui and rainbow; if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: Reframes after the previous answer sidestepped the question, pressing instead on the eligibility criteria that decide who the remaining money can reach — a genuine follow-on from the answer given, though it does not take up the $3 million availability point itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "out of the $5 million for the mental health and addiction innovation fund, we’ve only announced $2 million of that"

acuity.statement: Is she seriously saying that cutting Stand Tū Māia’s contract in April next year—an organisation that provides specialised trauma treatment and intensive wraparound family support for thousands of highly vulnerable children and their families, with a waiting list of over 450 children—is the right thing to do?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's aggregate-spending defence and tests it against a named provider whose contract ends, which is exactly the move the preceding answer invited; the question would have to change if Chhour had defended the decision differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "there has not been a cut to the overall amount Oranga Tamariki is spending on contracted providers"

acuity.statement: Why didn’t she go back to the Minister of Finance to ask for extra money when Stand Tū Māia has been told the reason their contract for last resort services to thousands of children has been cut is that there is no more funding left this year?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the specific provider the answer addressed and presses the funding rationale, but engages neither the contract figures Chhour recited nor the resolution she offered as her answer — one strand taken up, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "Oranga Tamariki has reached a resolution with Stand Tū Māia and legal proceedings were withdrawn"

acuity.statement: Will there be more cuts to community providers delivering front-line services in the next financial year?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and a reasonable next question, but it leaves the Minister's outcomes-not-inputs argument entirely untouched and simply moves the same question forward a year.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Karen Chhour argued that "spending more money seems to have been the solution to all the problems" and that outcomes got worse, and this question does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: Is it true that despite all the word games, in fact, she has broken a promise to the people of New Zealand that front-line services would not be impacted, when across the country we have seen cuts to vital services for our most vulnerable children and whānau?
acuity.explanation: "Despite all the word games" directly engages the renewal-versus-cut distinction the Minister had been drawing across her answers and puts the promise test to it, though it supplies no instance beyond the general assertion of cuts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "It’s normal process to go over contracts when they’re being renewed."

acuity.statement: Now, Steve Abel made the very good point that the Environment Committee reported back to this House unanimously in support of this legislation. Subsequent to that, there has been indication that Cabinet want to make a change to just two of the high protection areas to allow a small number of individually named fisherfolk—I think five or six.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Abel's two central factual claims by name — the unanimous select committee report and the late change to two high protection areas — accepts both and supplies additional detail (Cabinet's intention, a named handful of fishers). The speech would read differently had Abel not made those claims. Marked down from 1.0 because, having engaged the claim, he declines to contest or defend it ("Today is not the day for that debate") and moves to prepared material on the bill's history.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "it was an unanimously supported bill at the Environment Committee" and "the Government will be making last-minute changes to allow a type of fishing known as ring netting to take place in two of the new high protection areas"

acuity.statement: Is this piece of legislation perfect? No. Is this piece of legislation going to achieve everything for everyone? No. Is this piece of legislation going to keep commercial fishers happy? No. Is this piece of legislation going to keep recreational fishers happy? No. Is this piece of legislation better than nothing? Absolutely yes.
acuity.explanation: Answers the strand of Abel's case that says the bill must be got right or it fails, with a pragmatic better-than-nothing counter-frame. It engages the thrust of the objection rather than the specific claim about ring netting in two high protection areas, and the passage would survive largely intact against any critique of the bill's adequacy — partial engagement, not close rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Can this Government not be bold enough to commit to the bare minimum of not allowing commercial fishing in areas explicitly designated for protection?"

acuity.statement: The chair of the select committee has said, “Well, we can have that debate during the committee of the whole House”. Of course he is correct: there can be a debate during the committee of the whole House, but whether or not questions are answered is a very different matter.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the preceding speaker's exact proposition, concedes it is formally correct, then draws out the consequence he omitted — that the opportunity to debate is not an assurance of answers. This is the precise argumentative move the rubric's top band describes: accept part, dispute the rest, and it is unintelligible without Simpson's prior turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "Now, we’ll have an opportunity during the committee of the whole House to discuss that potential change that may be introduced by the Minister."

acuity.statement: The member just said that there’s going to be individually named fisherfolk, and that these are going to be commercial fishers. We’ve heard from Ministers some ideas about how they’re going to be feeding people who can’t otherwise afford kaimoana, but nothing in the press releases that I’ve seen demonstrates how that will be done.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific detail Simpson had just volunteered — individually named commercial fishers — and tests it against the stated public-benefit rationale, pressing that nothing on the record shows how it would work.
