acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O’Connor argued that "this coalition Government has driven our economy into recession" and that health is being deliberately underfunded, understaffed and undermined ahead of privatisation, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: It is a great honour to rise and speak in support of the Prime Minister’s statement, and I’m privileged to follow on from my fellow Christchurch MP, Dr Vanessa Weenink. It is a great privilege. We are on the verge of great growth and potential, and of course this is going to be across many sectors of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Weenink's preceding turn was substantive (school lunches, social investment, incomes and health), so the turn is eligible. Campbell names her but engages no part of what she said — a mere reference, which the rubric explicitly says not to reward. The speech that follows is prepared material on growth, mortgage rates and Christchurch tech that would read word-for-word the same whatever Weenink had argued. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 because it is at least addressed to the matter under debate (the Prime Minister's statement) and gestures at 'a lot of my colleagues'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanessa Weenink spoke about the school lunch programme, social investment and raising incomes to improve health outcomes, and this statement does not take up any of her claims.

acuity.statement: We’ve heard time and again the other side saying, “Oh, we’re in trouble. It’s tough for New Zealanders.”, and that that’s because they inherited bad inflation and they’ve got inflation down. Inflation in the quarter ended December 2023 was 0.5 percent. Multiply that by four quarters, and it was already at 2 percent. Inflation was already tamed by the time the Government changed.
acuity.explanation: Parker takes up the exact claim Campbell had just made — that times are tough but the Government's economic management is now delivering — and attacks its premise directly, with a quarterly inflation figure offered to show inflation was already under control before the change of government. The engagement is with the content of the argument, not just its author, and the speech would have to change if the preceding turn had defended the Government's record on different grounds. Short of 1.0 because he rebuts the Government's general economic-management case rather than Campbell's specific mortgage-rate numbers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We appreciate it is tough times, but just in The Press earlier this week, independent economists indicated that, since our economic management has come into play, lower mortgage rates mean that households will have, combined, another $45 million a week to spend." — Hamish Campbell

acuity.statement: The cost of living issue was also something that this National-led Government campaigned on. Has it been addressed? Well, we’re experiencing the steepest economic downturn, as our former Minister for Trade spoke about before, since 1991. Yet, despite this, the cost of living relief has vanished from the Government’s agenda.
acuity.explanation: Salesa follows a substantive turn by David Parker on the same debate (the Prime Minister's statement) and is on the same subject — cost of living and the state of the economy. But she engages no part of his actual argument: she does not take up his claim that inflation was already under control when Labour left office, the 32,000 fewer people in employment, the ferry and Project Onslow cancellations, or the Budget surplus/deficit tally. Her reference to "our former Minister for Trade" is a nod to his having spoken, used to launch prepared material of her own rather than to develop or contest anything he said. The speech would read the same had Parker made a different argument about the economy, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 for the gesture at the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "The cost of living—well, inflation is under control, but it was by the time we left Government."

acuity.statement: Mr Speaker, I hesitate to do this, but I have to point out that the leader of the Labour Party stood up and misrepresented a television broadcast. He specifically misrepresented the words in it.
acuity.explanation: Hipkins' preceding turn rested its privilege argument on what the TV news broadcast showed — that Seymour was twice told the Speaker had forbidden driving up the steps. Seymour takes up precisely that evidentiary claim and disputes the content of the broadcast and its captions, rather than pivoting to prepared material. The statement would be different had Hipkins cited different evidence. Short of 1.0 because he asserts misrepresentation without supplying what the captions actually said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Subsequently, it has now become apparent on the TV news last night that before taking that course of action, David Seymour was twice told that you had specifically said that the Land Rover was not allowed to be driven up the steps of Parliament."

acuity.statement: See, I told you that they were the de-growth party. The Greens don’t believe in growth. Well, here’s the rub: they’re the first people to complain about underfunding in hospitals and schools, and all of the living standards and the public goods that the New Zealand Government should and does provide.
acuity.explanation: Bishop breaks off his prepared riff to take up Abel's interjection directly, and builds from it: he treats the interjection as evidence for his de-growth characterisation and then argues the underlying question (that the public services the Greens want funded depend on growth), later inviting 'the member' to travel through the developing world. But he never engages the actual content of the interjection — that neo-liberalism, rather than saying no to growth, explains the 30-year record. He answers the topic and the opponent's general position rather than the specific causal claim put to him, then resumes prepared material, which is the ~0.5 band. Scored on engagement only: the strength of the inference belongs to Rigor, the pivot onto the Greens' character belongs to Focus, and neither moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s called neo-liberalism." — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: We heard it from the last person to speak, Kieran McAnulty, talking about the fact that as a country we have no money to pay for things. No kidding. Look at what happened for the last six years under their Government. That’s why we need growth.
acuity.explanation: Costley names the preceding speaker and picks up one specific strand of his argument — that the country has no money to pay for things — and does something with it, turning it into the premise of his own case for growth. But that is the only part of McAnulty's speech he engages; he then dismisses the rest as containing 'not one idea' and delivers a prepared list of five growth measures that would be unchanged whatever McAnulty had argued. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty, 'as a country we have no money to pay for things' (Costley's rendering of the preceding turn's point about the fiscal position)

acuity.statement: I love Waitangi week—love it. Love being in Northland, love what it is that we’re celebrating up there, love the vision.
acuity.explanation: Fleming follows a substantive turn by Costley setting out five specific growth measures — skills, regulation, innovation, international connections, infrastructure — and takes up none of them. The speech is prepared material on the same broad subject (economic growth and the Government's plan), moving straight to Northland business visits, Invest New Zealand and two Maungakiekie businesses; it would read word-for-word the same whatever Costley had said. On topic, so not 0.0, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley set out five specific measures to deliver growth (skilled workforce, regulation, innovation, international connections, infrastructure) and this statement does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: It’s always interesting, in these things, that what’s not said is often more important than the things that are. The Prime Minister didn’t mention the southern hospital even once in his statement, and no wonder why: we find out why, a few days later, when his newly minted Minister of Health confirmed that the hospital rebuild would proceed but it would proceed with less beds than the current Dunedin Hospital.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez follows a substantive turn by Julie Anne Genter, who argued at length that GDP growth is a false measure of wealth, that the Rongotai fast-track road tunnel worsens traffic by the Government's own documents, and that productivity comes from investing in people and leaving fossil fuels. Hernandez takes up none of that: no part of his speech would change if Genter had made a different argument on the same motion. He is, however, squarely on the matter under debate — he works through what the Prime Minister's statement did and did not contain (the southern hospital, the coalition partners, the Government targets) — so this is prepared material addressed to the debate's subject rather than to the preceding speaker, which sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter spoke about real wealth not being measured in GDP and about the Rongotai road tunnel not saving travel time, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Firstly, I think it would be rude of me to not address the speech made by the previous Green member, Francisco Hernandez. I think the Deputy Prime Minister in waiting has achieved an awful lot in this Government, as have quite a few of the Ministers from the ACT team and across the House. What I would say is we have a Ministry for Regulation set up to cut that red tape, the likes of what Nicole McKee has been talking about—a hotline where Kiwis can actually tip off this bad regulation; something that people have been screaming about for years.
acuity.explanation: McClure picks up one strand of the preceding turn — McKee's deregulation/red-tape argument — and does something with it, naming the Ministry for Regulation and its tip-off hotline as the machinery delivering the relief McKee described. That part of the speech would be different had the previous speaker argued something else. But the engagement stops there: the nod to Hernandez names him without taking up any content of his speech, and the rest of the turn is prepared material on charter schools that is indifferent to what preceded it. Partial engagement, then a return to the prepared text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Government is about removing the red tape and all of the regulations that are binding people up and stopping them from going about living their lives." — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: The latent potential that we’ve been sitting on within New Zealand, particularly over the last six years, we’re about to unshackle. We’re about to unlock the potential of this great country, and within the regions, and it’s going to be awesome.
acuity.explanation: Garcia's immediately preceding turn made concrete claims (98.5 percent of duties reduced under the UAE FTA, wages outpacing inflation, $17 billion in health). Hamilton engages none of them — no figure is picked up, confirmed, extended or disputed. The speech is prepared material on the right subject: it is a Prime Minister's statement debate contribution that gestures at the debate item ('It's great to rise and speak on the Prime Minister's statement') and covers the same government themes, so it sits in the lower band rather than at zero. Substituting a different pro-government argument from Garcia would not require a single word of this speech to change, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paulo Garcia spoke about the Government's focus on economic growth, trade agreements such as the United Arab Emirates free-trade agreement, and wages growing faster than inflation, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’d like to begin by acknowledging the Prime Minister’s address and his focus on economic growth. It is under his stewardship that we have seen a focused drive not only towards economic growth but also towards enhancement of the services that a modern-day society demands, from healthcare—and, yes, this will include delivering Dunedin Hospital, which services not only Dunedin but a much wider area including the Waitaki electorate—to education, infrastructure, and digital connectivity.
acuity.explanation: Anderson follows a substantive Opposition speech that made specific, checkable attacks on the Government's recession framing, housing numbers and school lunch programme. He engages none of them: he pivots straight to prepared praise of the Prime Minister's stewardship, Dunedin Hospital and his own electorate's primary industries. The speech would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before him, though it is at least on the subject of the Prime Minister's statement and economic growth, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0. His only acknowledgement of the other side is a brush-off of an interjection ("Hold your horses"), which engages no content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued that the Prime Minister's claim of a three-year recession is contradicted by Treasury (recession only for nine months in 2024), that the 2,000 extra homes were Labour-funded, and that emergency housing criteria, school lunches and rural bus subsidies have been cut — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s my pleasure to take a call in support of the Prime Minister’s statement. It’s going to be a great year. We are excited. We have turned the dial from no to go; from woe to let’s go.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows a substantive turn by Miles Anderson on regional primary industries, mining and renewable energy in Waitaki, but engages no part of it. Her speech is prepared material — a list of the Government's achievements and plans, then East Coast examples — that would read word-for-word the same whatever Anderson had said. It stays within the matter under debate (she expressly supports the Prime Minister's statement and speaks to economic growth), which keeps it out of the 0.0 band, but the only gesture outward is at 'the Opposition going on and on', not at the argument it follows. Scored on engagement alone; the content and quality of her claims are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Miles Anderson spoke about mining at Macraes, the Oamaru stone quarries and the Waitaki Hydro Scheme, and about Minister Patterson's attendance, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Well, Philip Polkinghorne was charged with murder, if I recall correctly. Perhaps he’s talking about someone else who was charged with sexual assault, who David Seymour sent the victim’s wife to an ACT Party lawyer instead of to the police.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up the precise factual objection just put to him — that the person was not charged — and answers it directly by naming Polkinghorne and the murder charge, then offers an alternative case McClure may have been thinking of. The reply would have been entirely different had McClure objected on other grounds, so it is squarely responsive; the quality and truth of the claims are matters for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I believe that that was a misleading comment because the person in question wasn’t actually charged under that investigation" — Laura McClure

acuity.statement: This is my first opportunity to address the House this year and I should be excited, but so underwhelming was the Prime Minister’s statement it almost isn’t worth rebutting.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — substantive turns by other members precede it in the same debate — but it engages no part of their arguments. It is prepared material on the right subject: it dismisses the Prime Minister's statement as not worth rebutting and then proceeds to its own themed address, which would have read identically whatever the previous speakers had said. A gesture at the matter under debate puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston said she was "delighted to speak in favour of the Prime Minister's statement because actually I'm proud to be part of a Government", and Duncan Webb argued David Seymour rather than Christopher Luxon is running the country; this statement takes up neither, gesturing only at the Prime Minister's statement under debate before moving to prepared material on growth in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.

acuity.statement: Growth, growth, growth. That’s what this Government is about. I’ll say it again: growth, growth, growth. Something that’s unusual to the other side of the House, but that’s OK.
acuity.explanation: McCallum follows Nakhle in the same debate and picks up her theme words — "growth" and the "No"/"yes" framing (he later calls Hipkins the "Minister of No", echoing her "Doctors of No"). But he engages no claim she actually made: not the FamilyBoost/tax-bracket/fuel-tax examples, not the Takanini door-knocking evidence. The speech then goes to prepared Northland material (roads, dams, Fonterra) that would read identically whatever she had said. Echoing a slogan is a reference, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’re saying yes—yes to FamilyBoost, which we have said" / "We’re going for growth." — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: I’d like to welcome the former member for Northland—who I wish had actually done her job last time and stood up for that road. It would have been great if she had, but never mind.
acuity.explanation: Prime put a specific, answerable question: which section of the Whangārei four-laning is actually under construction. McCallum names and addresses her but supplies nothing of what was asked — no section, no timeline — and pivots to her record as the former local member. The content of the question is left entirely untouched, which is the textbook mere-reference case rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Which bit’s under way?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Well, I found it extraordinary that that member stood up and spoke about growth under this Government. This Government has had no growth. There is more growth on my face than this Government has had, and that’s a fact!
acuity.explanation: Webb takes McCallum's central proposition head-on, names it as the thing he is answering, and denies it, then immediately supplies counter-material on the same measure (the 2.4 percent he says was handed over, successive negative quarters, 30,000 more unemployed). Had McCallum argued something else on the same topic, this opening would have had to change. Not a 1.0 because he rebuts the headline claim rather than the specific Northland evidence McCallum offered (the roads, the dams, the Fonterra payout), and then moves to prepared material on asset sales.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Growth, growth, growth. That’s what this Government is about." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker, for this opportunity to talk on the Prime Minister’s statement and all this growth that we’ve been hearing about this afternoon. Now, I want to talk about some growth: the growth in pollution, the growth of broken promises, the growth of cynical political moves, the growth of undermining our conventional safeguards, the growth of economic policy via text message, and the growth of a radical departure from previous conservative National Governments that we are seeing from this Government.
acuity.explanation: She takes the organising term of the two preceding Government speeches — growth — and does something with it, inverting it into an itemised list of what she says is actually growing under this Government, then spends the speech substantiating those heads (fast track and the 149 listed projects, defunded conservation, the Dunedin Hospital bed and theatre counts, the ferries and the Kāinga Ora review). The structure of the speech is built out of what she has just heard and would have to be rewritten if the preceding speakers had made a different case. Not a full 1.0 because she engages the governing theme and the general safeguards claim rather than rebutting a specific figure or inference Bidois or Cheung advanced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because 2025 is the year of economic growth for this Government, because we want growth, growth, and growth" — Carlos Cheung (and Dan Bidois's "It is all about growth" / "we're going for growth").

acuity.statement: The Prime Minister stood in this House and delivered his Prime Minister’s statement, which outlined his Government’s vision: economic growth, personal responsibility, and getting New Zealand back on track. What I heard was a vision steeped in ableism, a broken vision, one that actively leaves behind disabled people.
acuity.explanation: Carter follows Sosene, who argued at length about cuts to community services, lost jobs and the school lunch programme in Māngere. Carter takes up none of that; she delivers prepared material on ableism and disability support. It is squarely on the matter under debate (the Prime Minister's statement, whose themes she names and contests), which earns the top of the unresponsive band, but the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Sosene had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene spoke about cut budgeting services in Māngere and the school lunch programme ("your programme of school lunches, a reduced lunch programme, is not working in my local community") and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Now, we have heard a lot from the other side about “growth”, which is a bit new from them. Last year, we were hearing about the cost of living, and I was wondering why we’re suddenly hearing about growth when cost of living is currently still the main concern for most New Zealanders and hasn’t really been fixed.
acuity.explanation: Belich follows Carter's argument that the Government's vision is ableist and has harmed disabled communities, and engages no part of it — nor Sosene's local-services case, though she re-uses the same 33,000 unemployment figure without doing anything with it. She does engage the subject of the debate, the Government's growth framing, which places her at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero; but nothing in the speech depends on what the previous speaker said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter spoke about ableism and the restriction of disability support funding ("this Government has made decisions that have profoundly harmed our disabled communities") and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I would begin by acknowledging the Prime Minister’s inspirational address to the House. The statement was about economic growth and becoming a nation that says yes. For too long, we’ve made a habit of saying no.
acuity.explanation: Butterick follows a substantive turn by Nancy Lu on economic growth and migrant communities, but engages none of its content. He opens by acknowledging the Prime Minister's statement — the matter under debate — and then delivers prepared material on saying yes, trade deals and the primary sector. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Lu had said, though it is squarely within the debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu spoke about economic growth being urgent for New Zealanders including ethnic and migrant communities ('we need growth, we need to see our country back in shape'), and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Well, simply because this Government is failing on the economy. That has become extremely clear—that this is a Government that is failing on the economy. Nicola Willis seems to talk up her credentials all the time. She talks up a big game, but she is simply not delivering.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows Butterick's case that the Government is delivering growth — $1.3 billion UAE deal, GCC deal, $56.9 billion from the food and fibre sector — and takes up none of it. He asserts the contrary conclusion (failure on the economy) without touching any figure or argument just offered, then moves to prepared constituency material on Palmerston North health services and housing. It is a topical counter-assertion rather than engagement, so it stays in the unresponsive band; the grounds for the low score are responsiveness only, not the force or legitimacy of the criticism.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Butterick argued the Government is delivering growth, citing 'The United Arab Emirates deal—$1.3 billion' and the primary sector's '$56.9 billion from the sector', and this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: We just look back over what this Government inherited when we came to office in late 2023: inflation—inflation out of control, left behind by those people on the other side who, as the Prime Minister describes, are like arsonists who’ve just lit the house on fire and there they are criticising the people, the firefighters, trying to put the fire out.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the economic strand Williams had just pressed and contests it on its own ground — he accepts that the economy is the test and argues the inherited inflation is the cause and that it is now being brought back under control, following with interest-rate relief figures. But he engages the framing rather than her specific claims: the 1991 downturn comparison and the quarterly GDP decline go unanswered, and the arsonist line is prepared material the Prime Minister had already used. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the actual numbers put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they’re failing on the economy" — Arena Williams, who argued the Government has imposed pain without economic results, citing "the steepest downturn in the economy since 1991" and GDP declining every quarter.

acuity.statement: I think it’s an absolute shame what that last Government did to our healthcare system. It is one of the crying shames that they have left behind after their six years in office—what they left behind for New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: He is the new Minister of Health and Williams had just attacked that portfolio directly, including the sacking of his predecessor, so the subject matter is squarely the one under debate — but he engages none of her claims. The nurses, the doctor shortage and the health plan all go untouched; instead he pivots to the previous government's emergency-department and elective-surgery record. This is the "the member opposite is the last person who should talk about waiting lists" move: on topic, indifferent to the argument actually made, and the passage would read identically had she attacked something else in health.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These Ministers are saying no to the health system; they’re grinding it into the ground until it is worth nothing" — Arena Williams, who cited 2,200 nurses seeking jobs and an 8.5 percent doctor shortage.

acuity.statement: Just by way of a brief synopsis, the main objective of this bill—as has been perused so far throughout the speeches with respect to the Māori Purposes Bill—is that, essentially, we’re proposing some minor technical and, if I may be so straightforward to say, non-controversial amendments to a suite of Māori affairs legislation.
acuity.explanation: Peeni Henare's immediately preceding turn argued the opposite of this characterisation — that 'the devil is in the detail', that the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act provisions are substantive rather than merely technical, and that Labour will interrogate them at select committee. Nakhle gestures at the debate ('as has been perused so far throughout the speeches') and is squarely on the subject of the bill, but she simply asserts the amendments are non-controversial and moves to prepared material (the list of Acts repealed, the Maori Community Development Act 1962, acknowledgements to the Māori Council and wardens). She never points at Henare's claim or answers it, so this sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that 'the devil is in the detail' and that the substantive Te Ture Whenua Maori Act changes need close inspection and consultation with Māori communities, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’m especially intrigued too, as Peeni Henare did discuss, about the opportunities for our reo and enhancing its understanding and respect throughout Aotearoa. Obviously, Te Ture Whenua Maori Act will be scrutinised, as will every other part of this bill, though Labour support it, but whenua is something that is still controversial in Aotearoa today.
acuity.explanation: This takes up two identifiable strands of Peeni Henare's earlier turn in the same debate — the te reo/Te Mātāwai provisions and the warning that the Te Ture Whenua Maori Act changes will be interrogated — and does something with the second, supplying the reason (whenua remains contested) and localising it to Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and Te Tairāwhiti. It is agreement rather than rebuttal and it engages only part of what preceded (nothing of Rima Nakhle's 'non-controversial' characterisation), and much of the rest of the speech is her own prepared material about marae committees and Putaanga Marae, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ve already spoken about Te Ture Whenua Maori Act and why it’s important that we get that right" — Peeni Henare.

acuity.statement: Like the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, has mentioned, while we are seeing potentially a $150 million blowout in the projected cost of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, for us to so prudishly restrict the number of judges, and having that in the primary legislation, seems to defeat the purpose, and, in fact, may also impede on the judicial independence and the principle of comity that we do have within our constitutional arrangement.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes a specific element of Webb's preceding speech — the $150 million cost of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill — and does something new with it, setting it against the statutory cap to argue the one-FTE restriction is disproportionate and may cut against judicial independence. That is genuine uptake, not a mere name-check: the argument would have to change if Webb had not supplied the figure and the point about the two bills being introduced together. It sits below the top of the band because the bulk of his contribution is prepared select-committee material on submitters, and he engages one strand of Webb's speech rather than its reasoning as a whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "that reform, the Sentencing Act reform, is estimated to cost $150 million" (and Webb's point that this bill was "originally intended to be associated with the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill")

acuity.statement: Nō reira ko tā mātou he tautoko i te pire, engari tērā anō ētahi kupu whakatūpato, kei puta he āhuatanga kāore pea i āta kitea, kāore pea i āta whakaaro iho.
acuity.explanation: Ferris follows a substantive turn by Arbuckle and speaks to the matter under debate — support for the bill, with cautions about te reo Māori, tikanga and Māori participation in the courts — but engages no part of Arbuckle's argument about the adequacy of one additional judge or the Sentencing Reform driver. The speech would read identically had Arbuckle said something else on the same subject, so it sits in the 'prepared material on the right topic' band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle argued that raising the bench from 182 to 183 is 'a sensible and pragmatic response to the challenges that the District Court is facing' because of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill workload, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The truth is that, when we look at the explanatory note in and of itself—of the other bill that has been referenced: the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill—it does raise concerns as to why this bill is considering increasing the number of District Court judges by only one. I think that that is a genuine conversation to be held.
acuity.explanation: He takes the preceding speaker's own premise — that the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill is what creates the need for the extra judge — and turns it against the conclusion, arguing that the same reform's explanatory note makes a single additional judge look inadequate. He also picks up the earlier point that previous years saw larger increases. The argument depends on what was just said and would have to change if the preceding turn had justified the bill differently; marked below 1.0 because he does not quote or contest a specific figure from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "We've also heard from the Minister in charge, Paul Goldsmith, that the reforms in the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill will place additional demands on the District Court, and that that's the major need for this additional judge."

acuity.statement: Look, we are a Government which takes a whole-of-system approach to the justice sector from start to finish—a cluster-based approach, a pipeline of justice approach. Whether that is addressing the causes of crime through our Social Investment Agency and the investment that Nicola Willis is making into our most vulnerable or whether that is through the support of victims through the criminal justice process, rehabilitation in the corrections system, and, of course, post-release support for our incarcerated, we are taking a whole-of-system approach.
acuity.explanation: Meager opens by answering the specific charge just levelled — that the Government is not addressing the root causes of crime — with a claim about addressing causes of crime through the Social Investment Agency and spending on the most vulnerable, then invites the critics to back the companion bill. The engagement is squarely on the point raised, though it meets a costed, specific critique with a general framing rather than contesting its substance, so it falls short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "a Government that is not investing in addressing the root causes of criminalisation—namely, things like poverty, exclusion from people's culture, etc."

acuity.statement: Yes, it’s one District Court judge that this bill, when it passes, will increase the total number of District Court judges, but one effective District Court judge can help a lot of victims get through the pain and the suffering and the grief that they’re going through as they’re waiting for their case to be heard.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows Andersen, whose central argument through her whole speech was that one additional judge cannot meet the Government's stated expectations on backlog and victims. Nakhle takes up that one strand directly — she concedes the bill delivers a single judge and argues that one judge can still materially help victims waiting for a hearing — and she also acknowledges the backlog point "as has been mentioned a number of times tonight". But she engages none of Andersen's specific claims (the freezing of Te Ao Mārama, the absence of funding for victim advocacy or courtroom modernisation, AVL) and the remainder of the turn is prepared material: an anecdote about visiting Manukau District Court with the Minister and praise for him. Partial engagement with a pointable strand, then a return to prepared content, so mid-band rather than high. Scored on engagement only; the weakness of the "one effective judge can help a lot of victims" inference is a Rigor matter and the praise of the Minister a Focus matter, neither of which is counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I still don’t think that one judge is going to meet those expectations" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Increasing the District Court judge by one is a very small measure—and I emphasise the “very small” part of that—toward making that a reality, but yet this is the bill before us, so we are happy to support it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Meager's immediately preceding turn — his characterisation of the bill as a very simple change, and the submissions he reported asking for many more judges — and turns it into a point about the measure's smallness relative to the backlog, before returning to prepared material on the cap and the Government's tough-on-crime stance. Partial, pointable engagement rather than a direct rebuttal of a specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "It’s a very, very simple bill. It makes a very, very simple change." — and his report that submitters "thought that the number of judges should be increased by a significant amount more"

acuity.statement: This bill is focused on ensuring that we support the fact that judges have had an increased workload and complexity in their workload, and so this bill, combined with the implementation of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, will go a long way to ensuring that we practically implement the changes that will enable us to deliver on that election promise of restoring law and order in this country.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and gestures at the cross-party support McLellan had just voiced, but engages no part of her argument: she put a mismatch between the sentencing agenda and a single extra judge, and called the Sentencing bill the problematic partner, and he simply asserts the two bills together will deliver the law-and-order promise. The speech would read the same whatever she had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "on one hand, the Government seems very confident about their tough on crime stance and the impact that will have on the criminal justice system; on the other hand, they’ve decided to increase the number of judges by one" — and her description of the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill as "a much more problematic partner"

acuity.statement: This bill is just going to increase the number of District Court judges by one, and while that is a really good thing, we do have a real problem in the country with delay in the District Court.
acuity.explanation: Mildly contrasts with the preceding claim that the bill delivers on law and order by noting the delay problem, but takes up no part of Bates's argument — the $100 million precinct, the workload claim, or the sentencing package. What follows is prepared material on judges, drug courts and boot camps that would be unchanged whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "This bill supports their work and supports our campaign promise to restore law and order to this country."

acuity.statement: This relatively simple bill could have been brought in alongside the other pieces of legislation at the same time, around what the Justice Committee did on capping discounts for offenders—the Sentencing reforms they’ve had there. There was the opportunity for this to be done at the same time as that piece of legislation, so let’s just set the record straight: there was an opportunity for that to be done at the same time. It could have saved the House the opportunity to have to debate this bill in the first place, but the members opposite said no.
acuity.explanation: Answers the earlier complaint about the cost of running this as a separate parliamentary process by claiming the opposition itself refused to have the two bills progress together — a real uptake of that strand. But it engages nothing from the immediately preceding turn on delays and court capacity, and quickly becomes a prepared riff on the "no" team, so engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "we find ourselves going through what is a relatively expensive process, as all processes in Parliament are, to have to do it again"

acuity.statement: Kei te tāpiri atu āku nei whakaaro, aku nei kōrero, ki tā tōku tuahine o te Nōta e mea atu, whakanuia ana ōna whakaaro i a Whina Cooper. Kei te mihi tonu ana mātou ki tērā o ngā tauira o te mana motuhake, o te tino rangatiratanga.
acuity.explanation: Tuiono explicitly picks up the Whina Cooper strand of Kapa-Kingi's immediately preceding speech, names her as the member from the North, endorses and extends her acknowledgement (adding Dame Iritana Tāwhiwhirangi), and later takes up her point about Ngāpuhi turning their backs at Waitangi. That is a pointable, partial engagement: he adopts one strand of her case and builds on it rather than taking up her specific arguments about section 7AA, cultural components or the abuse-in-care report, and the bulk of the speech is prepared Green Party material on whakapapa, whanaungatanga and Te Tiriti that would stand unchanged had another member spoken before him. Scored for engagement only — not for how well it reasons, how polite it is, or whether it is about the Government rather than the policy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "When Dame Whina Cooper said, “Not one more acre.” back in 1975, we saw our people rise to the occasion." — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: It does not encompass or ensure the full breadth of what was enabled through section 7AA, and that member knows it really well. It is limited.
acuity.explanation: Sepuloni takes up Mooney's repeated interjection that strategic partnerships/relationships were retained in the bill and engages its substance directly — conceding the provision exists but arguing it does not cover the full breadth of what section 7AA enabled. The passage would not exist had Mooney not pressed that specific point, which is the mark of genuine responsiveness; the engagement is squarely on the claim rather than a mere mention of the interjector.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney, interjecting: "You’re ashamed of not voting for strategic partnerships. You voted against it." / "Who voted against retaining strategic partnerships?"

acuity.statement: While this bill repeals references to cultural considerations in section 7AA, it does not remove existing provisions in other parts of the Act that require decision makers to consider cultural factors in care decisions.
acuity.explanation: Butterick follows Sepuloni and takes up one strand of her case — that repealing 7AA strips cultural considerations out of the Act — by asserting that other parts of the Act still require decision makers to weigh cultural factors. That is a real engagement with the point just made, but it is only partial: he answers the topic rather than her central claim about the overwhelming weight of submissions and the evidence base, and the rest of the speech is prepared material (thanks to submitters, his own family, the safety of children) that would read identically whoever had spoken before him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "There was an opportunity to actually take some of the “more”, take the components of 7AA and actually put them throughout the legislation in a different way, to ensure that all of that was still included in the legislation."

acuity.statement: You're changing it, all right, because all our groups are saying that now these kids will get lost in the system.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes Mooney's denial head-on, contradicts it directly, and immediately supplies a reason (what the providers and groups are telling them). The sentence only exists because of what Mooney just said, and would have to change if Mooney had denied something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "It's not changing, Willie."

acuity.statement: As my colleague Joseph Mooney clearly articulated, this bill does not eliminate cultural considerations, as Opposition members would have you believe. This bill does not remove existing provisions in other parts of the Act which require decision makers to consider cultural factors in care decisions.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one strand of the Opposition case just put by Jackson — that the repeal strips cultural/whakapapa placement out of the Act — and answers it by pointing to the surviving provisions. But it engages the Opposition generically rather than Jackson's specific claim about children losing whakapapa links, credits a colleague's earlier speech for the rebuttal, and then returns to prepared commendation. Partial engagement only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "The dangers are that these kids won't go to the whakapapa, won't go to the whānau who they should be with, and they will have a whole loss of identity."

acuity.statement: The problem with this—and I heard the chair speak and talk about how this doesn't eliminate the current arrangements that are in place. The problem is it doesn't enable them—it doesn't enable them. That's exactly the reason why this bill was introduced.
acuity.explanation: This is the sharpest engagement in the window: he accepts the government's premise that the bill does not 'eliminate' cultural arrangements and then disputes its force, drawing the eliminate/enable distinction and turning it into the reason the bill exists. The passage is unintelligible without the claim it answers, which is exactly what high acuity looks like.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "this bill does not eliminate cultural considerations, as Opposition members would have you believe" (the same claim she attributes to Joseph Mooney)

acuity.statement: If we look at the regulatory impact statement, it says there's a lack of robust evidence to support the view that section 7AA causes harmful changes to long-term care arrangements.
acuity.explanation: Directly meets the government's central justification — that section 7AA has produced unintended consequences harming children in care — by citing the departmental evidence base on that exact question. It answers the specific claim rather than the general topic, though it is cited material he would likely have deployed regardless of the precise wording used against him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "Section 7AA as it stands has led to unintended consequences which compromise the welfare of children that it is aimed at protecting."

acuity.statement: While this bill repeals the references to cultural considerations contained in section 7AA, it does not remove existing provisions in other parts of the Act that require decision makers to consider cultural factors in care decisions.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows Halbert in the same second-reading debate and takes up one strand of Halbert's argument — the loss of cultural provision for Māori and takatāpui children — by asserting that repealing section 7AA leaves other cultural-consideration duties intact, and by reading the new strategic-partnership clause. He engages the cultural-considerations theme rather than Halbert's specific points about Oranga Tamariki's practices or takatāpui needs, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on the select committee process, so this sits at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We know that Oranga Tamariki doesn’t have the right cultural practices in place; they need to continuously be strengthened" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: So I rise, as a member of the Privileges Committee, in support of the address just given by the deputy chair of the committee, and I want to reiterate some of the significant points that the deputy chair has just made.
acuity.explanation: Simpson follows Webb's presentation of the same report and takes up the same strand — the deliberateness of the denial — adding material Webb did not detail (the 4 November letter, the "average, normal person" argument, the invitation Ferris declined and why the committee extended it). But it is substantially a parallel recital of the committee's findings rather than engagement with anything specific in Webb's reasoning: the speech would read almost identically had Webb spoken first or not at all, so long as the report was before the House. Partial engagement, mostly prepared material, hence mid-low rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we found that Mr Ferris had deliberately misled the House" — Duncan Webb, presenting the committee report immediately before.

acuity.statement: I take note of the comments by the previous two speakers. I also take note of the report that I myself participated in the committee, and endorse the recommendations.
acuity.explanation: A bare acknowledgement of the two preceding turns followed by a general reflection on the consequences of alleging dishonesty. It is squarely on the matter under debate, but it engages no content: neither the plain-meaning argument, the question of intent, nor the significance of Ferris declining to appear. Naming the previous speakers is a reference, not a response, so this sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 because there is a genuine gesture at the debate's subject rather than none.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb and Scott Simpson both argued that Ferris's letter could not be reconciled with the plain meaning of his words in the House, and this statement does not take that reasoning up — it names the previous speakers and endorses the recommendation without engaging any part of their argument.

acuity.statement: Yes, the committee did invite Mr Ferris to front up and explain himself. He refused. He instead wrote a letter that the committee found contradictory and confusing.
acuity.explanation: Jones ended his contribution asserting, against an interjection, that an invitation to appear before the Privileges Committee had been issued and not taken up. Parmar's 'Yes' picks that disputed factual point straight up, confirms it from her position on the committee, and adds the new detail that Ferris instead sent a letter the committee found contradictory and confusing. The passage would read differently had Jones not just litigated the invitation, so it is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference; it falls short of 1.0 because it corroborates rather than reasons with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: 'No, it's in here—I can quote that the invitation was given. The invitation was not taken up by the very member who says that a number of us are too afraid in our political life to stand up and be counted.'

acuity.statement: Just like maraes, temples, or churches have their own tikanga, so too does this Parliament, which must be respected.
acuity.explanation: Jones's central argument was that tikanga and Māori culture were being weaponised to claim exemption from the rules that bind every member. Parmar takes up the tikanga strand — asserting Parliament has a tikanga of its own, on a par with a marae — but she engages the topic rather than his specific claim about ethnic exemption, and the line reads as prepared material that happens to sit on the same ground. Partial engagement, pointable but thin.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: 'this is a small element of seeking to deploy and weaponise tikanga and Māori culture to pretend that if you have Māori blood and you're in this Parliament, you don't answer to the same rules and regulations'

acuity.statement: As an example, a future change that MPs may wish to consider is how apologies are delivered to the House. It may be desirable that the apologies are delivered in the same language in which the original breach was made, and perhaps at the time when most MPs are in the House—for example, before question time.
acuity.explanation: Jones devoted a passage to the apology having been given only in te reo Māori and not also in English, which he said showed contempt for the public. Parmar takes exactly that grievance and does something with it — converts it from an accusation into a proposed standing-orders change about the language and timing of apologies. The speech would not contain this paragraph had Jones not raised the language point, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0: she neither endorses nor contests his reasoning about contempt, she simply reframes the complaint procedurally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: 'An attempt not to offer the apology in both languages, and I'm saddened by that.'

acuity.statement: I think it’s fantastic that we have cross-party Parliament support for the Victims of Family Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill in its third reading. I think it’s a testament to the work that we can all collectively do as parliamentarians.
acuity.explanation: Carter's turn immediately precedes this one and made several engageable claims — the submitters' concern that the new section could block victims bringing proceedings, the committee's response on new section 12, and a direct plea to the Government to honour Te Aorerekura. Cameron takes up none of them: he acknowledges the former and current Ministers and then canvasses the bill's provisions as prepared material. The speech would read identically whatever Carter had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band; it earns slightly above the floor only because it gestures at the shared cross-party character of the debate rather than being deliverable in any debate at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter spoke about honouring Te Aorerekura, the Community Law and Backbone Collective submissions on victims needing multiple Family Court applications, and the need for monitoring and reporting, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This bill is about reducing abuse of litigation, and, as many speakers before me have much more eloquently put it, abuse of litigation, in simple terms, is people who use the court as a weapon and use it to further harm and further victimise the people before it. It made me think about other places within our justice system where abuse of litigation can happen, and it happens so often particularly for women who are victims of sexual violence.
acuity.explanation: Paul follows Costello's turn and takes up one strand of it — the abuse of the court system as a means of further victimising vulnerable people — restating it as 'abuse of litigation' and extending it to a domain Costello did not raise (sexual violence defences, the Grace Millane case, the UK ban). That is a real engagement with the preceding argument's content, and she signals she has been listening to the debate. But she engages nothing specific Costello actually asserted: not the claim that law and order is no longer the most prevalent issue, not the claim that this side of the House does have a plan on the drivers of crime, not the economic-growth argument. After the shared framing she moves to prepared material, so the speech would have needed little alteration had a different member made a different argument on the same bill. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "the saddest thing we can see in the abuse of the court system"

acuity.statement: We heard from the previous contributor that there was some dismay at this side of the House suggesting that the Government doesn’t appear to have much of a plan in so far as tackling crime and tackling the drivers of crime, and I stand by that and I reiterate that today. I don’t see much of a plan. It’s one thing to talk tough about crime and it’s one thing to rattle off a list of things that are happening in the Justice Committee, but whether they are efficacious or not, whether they’re grounded in decent policy formation or not, or whether they’re just a signal to people to emphasise the fact that the Government thinks they’re tough on crime is a whole other conversation.
acuity.explanation: Meager's turn complained that Labour keeps claiming the Government is not addressing the causes of crime, and answered it by listing the Justice Committee's and the Government's legislative programme. McLellan takes up that exact move: she restates his objection, holds her position, and attacks the specific form of his rebuttal — that a list of bills and committee work is not evidence of efficacy or sound policy formation. The speech would have to change if Meager had not offered that list, so it is squarely responsive rather than prepared material. Not a 1.0 because she engages the general shape of his list rather than any of the particular bills he named (e.g. the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill), and the surrounding speech is otherwise prepared bill material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "it is frustrating to hear again and again across the House about how the Government’s not focusing on addressing the causes of crime" — and his answer, "I can only point to bills like the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill".

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. There have been many speeches given this afternoon on the importance of this legislation, and I commend members from across the House for their delivery on this.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows Russell's substantive argument that the bill is not enough — that judicial education on litigation abuse and on the discredited parental alienation syndrome is still required, and funding must be allocated for it. He engages none of it. His speech is a generic commendation of "many speeches given this afternoon" plus prepared praise for the bill's purpose; it would read word-for-word the same whatever the previous speaker had argued. There is a gesture at the debate (he acknowledges the other speeches and names the bill), which keeps it out of the 0.0 floor, but a reference to prior speeches that engages no part of their content is not partial engagement. He had a real opportunity here — as the final speaker he could have answered Russell's challenge about judicial training — so the low score is earned rather than structural.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "there's education that needs to be done now around this litigation abuse" — her argument that funding must be allocated so judges can get up to speed, and that some judges appear to believe in the discredited "parental alienation syndrome". Nothing: this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I think the previous two speakers have already mentioned a number of instances, such as trusts, such as smaller businesses, that potentially have had the same level of scrutiny and the same level of administrative and compliance burden being placed on them. I think it is important to have that level of risk-based approach.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding Labour speech — the compliance burden falling equally on trusts and smaller businesses — and endorses the risk-based remedy, naming the specific instances raised rather than merely noting that others spoke. But it is agreement that adds nothing to the argument before returning to wholly prepared material (international students, sanctions obligations), so it sits at partial engagement rather than genuine take-up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the AML countering financing of terrorism (CFT) compliance has been onerous to some, and that time frames can be prohibitive" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Members who have spoken previously, the Minister who was introducing the legislation, and then Labour and the Greens both have thrown their support behind the bill—it’s really positive to see.
acuity.explanation: Counts the votes rather than engaging the content: it notes that Labour and the Greens support the bill, which is a reference and not a response. The specific gaps both preceding speakers identified — omitted statutory review recommendations, sanctions obligations, the burden on individuals opening bank accounts, the vulnerability of laundering meth profits — go unanswered, and the speech would read identically whatever they had argued. It stays on the matter under debate and gestures at the preceding turns, which keeps it off the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that recommendations of the 2022 statutory review were left out of the bill, that it is "still very much focused from the perspective of businesses", and that sanctions obligations were omitted — and this statement does not take any of that up. It registers only the fact of their support.

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge Ginny Andersen, who was the Minister who introduced this bill into the House in August 2023. I will put on record my concern that it’s taken until now for this bill to actually work its way through.
acuity.explanation: Bates had just claimed the bill as proof of this Government's effectiveness against a do-nothing Opposition, and had interjected that it came 'in the dying days of the Labour Government'. She takes up the provenance strand directly — naming the Labour minister who introduced it and the date — and turns the delay back on the Government. It engages the credit claim but not his wider drivers-of-crime argument, and the rest of the speech is her own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: 'It must be difficult for those who have left these benches because they weren’t effective at doing anything, to see effectiveness on this side of the House.' (and his interjection 'In the dying days of the Labour Government.')

acuity.statement: Many speakers have mentioned the abuse, and the nature of that abuse, that’s perpetuated by people in family situations and in other forums, but it all comes down to intimidation and control.
acuity.explanation: A generic nod to 'many speakers' followed by her own framing. Boyack had just set out a specific mechanism — vexatious litigation as a cost-asymmetry weapon, and a named constituent sued over a Facebook post — and none of it is taken up, rebutted or built on. The speech would read identically had Boyack argued something else about family violence, so it sits in the gesture-at-the-debate band rather than partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Rachel Boyack set out how self-represented litigants impose legal costs on respondents ('they are not racking up a bill, but the people who are having to respond are racking up a massive legal bill') and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: New Zealanders are sick of the anti-money laundering requirements that just go too far. Everyone appreciates the need for ensuring that New Zealand meets the requirements of our international standards, and this bill will ensure that we continue to do that, but it also recognises that we just need to wind the clock back a little bit, make it more practical for Kiwis, for businesses, for small businesses, to get on and do the things that actually create wealth in this country, that drive productivity, and make this country tick.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Arbuckle on border loopholes, stored-value instruments and enforcement, and engages none of it. Bates delivers prepared material on the opposite theme — that compliance has gone too far — with only a passing gesture at the shared premise about international standards that Arbuckle had also raised. The speech would read identically whatever Arbuckle had said, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle argued the bill 'closes those loopholes' around stored-value instruments such as casino chips and pre-paid vouchers at the border, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: This week, New Zealand lost its coveted first place, not in a sporting event but actually in the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index, and we dropped from first to fourth. There were some really surprising remarks, actually, from the Acting Prime Minister, Winston Peters, saying he thought we didn’t actually deserve the first place in the first place, which I found quite astounding. We’re really keen to get back up to first place, and this legislation will go a little way towards doing that.
acuity.explanation: Leary follows Bates's argument that the AML regime is excessive and should be loosened, and engages no part of it; her case runs the other way (we need more transparency, not less) but she never meets his claim. The contribution is squarely on the matter under debate and substantive about the bill's purpose, so it earns the top of the unresponsive band, not a partial-engagement score — nothing in it would change if Bates had argued the reverse.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates argued that the requirements 'just go too far' and that we 'need to wind the clock back a little bit', and this statement does not take that claim up.

acuity.statement: Try being a director of a company. Try being someone who has tried to buy a property through a trust. Any of these things are absolutely tedious. Changing this and making it simpler for business is one more thing we’re doing to make it simpler for business, one more way we’re getting rid of red tape, and I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Weenink speaks immediately after a detailed turn from Leary setting out Anne Tolley's three-part transparency framework and the beneficial-ownership register, and engages none of it, returning instead to the red-tape theme already run by Bates. There is a gesture at common ground ('we all agree') but no uptake of the preceding argument; the speech would be unchanged whatever Leary had said, which places it in the on-topic unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that a public register of beneficial ownership, financial transparency of political parties and lobbying transparency are needed alongside this bill, and this statement does not take any of those up.

acuity.statement: This is a very important principle that we in the Labour Party share, and it’s heartening to hear the Minister talk about boosting access to justice, because at the moment we are seeing a number of other policies in different areas actually impeding that.
acuity.explanation: Belich follows McKee's first-reading speech and takes up the specific justification McKee gave for the Courts bill — that it boosts access to justice — accepting the principle and then turning it against the Government's wider policy programme. The speech would have had to change if McKee had framed the bills differently, so this is real engagement rather than prepared praise or condemnation; it is partial rather than full because she contests the Government's consistency generally rather than any particular claim or figure in McKee's argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "It supports this Government’s priority of improving court timeliness and boosting the access to justice."

acuity.statement: We support this bill. The intention behind the Act, when it was first introduced a few years ago, was of course to prevent money-laundering. It has worked relatively well, but probably too well in some instances, and has caused some issues which have gummed up the system. Our job now is to un-gum it. The select committee will do its best to make sure that the bill gets thoroughly scrutinised and that the Act that comes out is well and truly un-gummed.
acuity.explanation: Bennett's turn immediately precedes this and had content to engage: a thorough-review-process case for the bill, the 26 proposals drawn from the statutory review, and a specific demand for a six-month select committee that hears sole traders. Meager lands on the same general theme (the Act over-complying and needing to be loosened, and the select committee doing its job), but he takes up none of Bennett's specific claims — he does not address the six-month request, the sole-trader burden, the 26 proposals, or the review timeline, and never refers to the preceding speaker. The speech would read identically had Bennett argued something different about the same bill, so this is prepared-feeling material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s just too much red tape in this piece of legislation" — Glen Bennett, who argued sole-trader lawyers and real estate agents in the provinces are over-burdened and asked for a fulsome six-month select committee

acuity.statement: First of all, I want to echo the previous speakers: when we’re looking at a regulatory systems bill, this is not a new concept that only this Government has introduced; this is, in fact, something that has always sort of happened on a regular basis in order to make the improvements in effectiveness and efficiency of a regulatory system, in general.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Belich's framing of these bills as routine, consensus, efficiency-focused housekeeping and affirms it, adding that the practice is not particular to this Government. It engages the topic and one strand of the preceding argument rather than any specific claim within it, and then moves to prepared material on the three bills, so it sits at the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "This is an example of that: three bills that look to make pragmatic changes to ensure efficiency of things that are already happening in New Zealand"

acuity.statement: As was mentioned by the previous speaker, something like a regulatory systems bill—the idea that we have this restrictive scope is the intent to ensure cross-party support and is meant to be improving efficiency and effectiveness of the regulatory system; it is not meant to be a politically charged mandate through these systems. However, we believe that this removal of the sanctions for not completing a compulsory professional development course is politically motived as a result of certain real estate agents refusing to take mandated and compulsory courses around Te Tiriti o Waitangi and who are subject to section 15 and also the sanction and the deregistration under section 54 of the Real Estate Agents Act 2008.
acuity.explanation: Takes Belich's stated test — that a regulatory systems bill should not carry anything beyond efficiency changes, and that going further is a concern — and does something with it: names the specific provision in the Occupational Regulation Bill that in his view fails that test, with the sections of the Real Estate Agents Act and the reason he thinks it is political. The speech would have to change if the preceding speaker had argued differently about the bills' proper scope.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Anything that goes further than that, that is more of a policy change, would be of concern to us."
