acuity.statement: I’d like to start with that, just to get that out of the way, and then welcome Ngā Ahi e Toru—Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato—representatives to this room to receive this or to hear what is being given out and receive what we’re trying to say in this House, which I think is that we are, as a Crown, recognising the blood on our hands—perhaps, as the previous speaker, Steve Abel, would say; I am going to quibble and say I don’t want to hear someone say there’s blood on my children’s hands. I don’t think that’s going to help, so I repudiate that, but I do think the Crown has got a debt to pay and this is a very small part of paying it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific image Abel built his argument on — collective British-descended guilt and the blood on our hands — names it, accepts one half (the Crown owes a debt, and this bill is part payment) and disputes the other (inherited personal guilt extending to his children). The speech would read differently had the preceding speaker framed the redress some other way. Not a full 1.0 because the engagement is confined to this passage and the remainder is prepared personal material about visiting battle sites.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we must, for the good of our descendants, seek to dull the blood on our hands" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: I agree with pretty much what everyone has said, but I wanted to, in particular, point out what Steve Abel said around the—well, these are my characterisations of what he said, that something that happened 161 years ago was not an honourable act and today we do an honourable thing so that in the future we might remember not to do this again. Every member in this House should remember that, in 161 years, they’re going to judge what we’re doing today.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe is plainly contributing to the same debate and has listened to it: he notes he is the eighth speaker, declines to repeat what has been said, and takes up the remembrance-and-learning strand Bidois had just advanced, carrying it further by turning the honourable/dishonourable framing into a standard the House will itself be judged against. But the argument he singles out and develops is Steve Abel's, delivered earlier and outside this window; he engages no specific claim of the immediately preceding turn, and the surrounding material (Rātana, Tupu Taingākawa) is prepared content on the right subject. Partial engagement, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "I agree with my whanaunga across the way that it is important that we learn and continue to remember the significance of the Battle of Ō-Rākau, to name just one." Rurawhe takes up this remembrance/learning strand ("So that our future generations will know the truth about our own history. Growing up in Aotearoa New Zealand, I did not learn that at school") but aims his specific engagement at Steve Abel's earlier argument, which lies outside this window.

acuity.statement: Today is one of those wonderous days for us in Parliament—for us as Māori, a Māori Affairs Committee, for all members who serve in this House—because we get to do something that’s right, to correct some of the challenges of our past, to apologise for the things that the Crown has done wrong, and most of all to make it right.
acuity.explanation: Halbert follows a substantive turn by Kirkpatrick that described the bill's vesting and ownership arrangements, the deed between the Crown and the three iwi, and the committee's site visit. His contribution is prepared tribute material on the same kaupapa — acknowledgements, the rangatahi petition and the curriculum, his recollection of Pārāwera and Anzac Pīkia — and engages none of her specific claims. He independently recounts a site demonstration (Matua Kaawhia laying out the geography) which touches the same strand she described, but as parallel recollection rather than engagement with what she said; the speech would read identically had she said something quite different about the bill. On-topic prepared material, so a gesture at the debate rather than nothing at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dana Kirkpatrick set out what the bill does ("This bill enables the record of title for the Ō-Rākau site to be held in the names of the ancestors who fought at the Battle of Ō-Rākau") and recounted the select committee's visit to the site, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: And I of course want to acknowledge the occasion and acknowledge the Ministers for their mahi, but there’s always a sense of frustration when you come to this point and all the good kōrero beforehand sort of ignores some of the kōrero that’s in front of us.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes up the celebratory framing of the preceding commendation speech and responds to it directly — naming the 'good kōrero beforehand' and arguing it omits present grievances. You can point at what is engaged (the preceding speakers' uniformly celebratory treatment of the settlement), but he engages its tone rather than any specific claim in it, then moves to his own prepared material on funding and the Treaty. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I rise and add my commendation to this bill" / "I pray that the history of this last battle is enshrined in all of our memories for many years to come" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: It’s wonderful to talk about the 300 against 1,500, but right now we’ve got Māori who are feeling under threat and we’ve got 400,000 people who’ve been making submissions to a select committee.
acuity.explanation: He takes the specific historical framing Nakhle had just set out — the 300 defenders against 1,500 troops — and does something with it, conceding it and turning it into a contrast with a present-day threat and the select committee submissions. The sentence would have to change if the previous speaker had framed the battle differently or not recounted it, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because he repurposes the image rather than engaging a claim or figure in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "300 iwi defenders protecting this piece of land and all that dwelt on it, against all odds, against about 1,500 British troops" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: I would have to take a couple of points about what was said across the House. This idea that we are punching down on our rangatahi, we are punching down on our youth—no. We are protecting them.
acuity.explanation: Costello follows a substantive turn by Cameron Luxton, so she is eligible. Her speech is on the matter under debate and gestures at the debate generally ("a couple of points about what was said across the House", rebutting a "punching down on our rangatahi" charge), but that charge was made by members whose turns are not before her here; she engages no part of Luxton's actual argument and the speech would be identical had he said something else. That is a gesture at the debate on the right subject, so 0.3 rather than 0.5 — I cannot point at a fragment of the preceding turn she takes up. Scored only on engagement: the force of her victims-and-accountability case, its reasoning and its tone are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Luxton, the preceding speaker, argued about ram raids, the 40 percent sentence discount cap, 500 more police and gang numbers, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I heard the member opposite earlier, Dr Tracey McLellan, say that this would make sentencing more complex. Well, let me make it simple for that member and for everyone watching this this evening, wanting to see the Government deliver on its promise of restoring law and order in this country.
acuity.explanation: Bates immediately follows Andersen, who made two pointed arguments: that the bill strips judicial discretion against the weight of submitter and expert evidence, and that the Ministry of Justice's own regulatory impact statement says the bill harms victims. He engages neither. He names a claim made by a different member in an earlier turn (McLellan on complexity) and uses it as a springboard into a prepared six-point enumeration of the bill's contents. That is a reference-and-pivot, not engagement: the enumerated list would have been delivered word for word whatever Andersen had said. It sits in the 0.0-0.3 band because nothing in the preceding turn can be pointed at as engaged, and 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the speech is squarely on the matter under debate and does gesture at an opposition argument about the bill rather than at the party generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued that 'the legislation reduces the range of sentences that a judge may impose on an offender' and that the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement warns the bill 'will have detrimental impacts on victims and outcomes for victims', and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: This is a bill that’s really hard to hear the Government talk about, because they are extremely pompous in the way they’re talking about it and they’re extremely out of touch. Everybody in this House cares about victims, and a melodramatic appeal to them by somebody who barely understands what it is to be one is actually really offensive.
acuity.explanation: White opens by taking up the exact move Bates had just made — a direct televised address to victims asserting that only this Government has their back. She concedes part of it ("Everybody in this House cares about victims") and disputes the rest, contesting both the sincerity of the appeal and the standing of the member making it. Delete Bates's appeal and substitute a different argument on the bill and these opening sentences would have to change, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because what she engages is the rhetorical posture rather than any substantive claim about the bill's effects, and she turns to the speaker's standing rather than his reasoning. Scored on engagement alone: the personal edge to it belongs to Civility, not here, and the fact that it is about the other side's conduct rather than the policy belongs to Focus.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to speak to victims out there this evening. If they’re watching and listening to this this evening, I want them to know that we have their back" — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: Why would we have an issue like youth taken into account? We have youth taken into account—and I’m sure there were submissions on this—because, actually, children’s brains are plastic. They are changing. Men don’t actually have a fully set brain until their mid-20s. They are still developing their brain. If they are actually coming on a second offence and they are remorseful, it may well actually make more sense as they reach maturity.
acuity.explanation: This is the fifth item on Bates's own list, picked up and answered on its merits. He presented ending repeat youth and remorse discounts as self-evidently sensible ("you just can’t keep saying sorry"); White supplies the reason the discounts exist — adolescent neurological development continuing into the mid-20s — and draws the consequence for precisely the case he raised, a remorseful second offence. She rebuts the specific proposition rather than the topic, and names both strands he bundled together. The speech would be different had he not made that point, which is the top of the scale. Whether the neuroscience premise is sound is a Veracity question and whether the inference carries is Rigor; neither is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Number five: it prevents the repeat use of sentence reductions for youth and remorse. My colleague Tom Rutherford made that very clear earlier and explained that point. You know, you just can’t keep saying sorry." — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: That is why Parliament doesn’t set compulsory sentences for every type of crime and every type of offending. There is a reason why this House is not the court that decides every sentence for every person in every case, and especially in those circumstances like the member who has just resumed his seat, Greg Fleming, has described. There is a need for harsh punishments for people who reoffend on parole or when they are in home detention, but those circumstances are always some of the most complex. These are people who have been engaged in rehabilitative systems and, as the member acknowledged, in a system that is trying to get them on a better path.
acuity.explanation: Takes Fleming's own case — offenders who reoffended while on monitoring bracelets — and works with it rather than around it: accepts that reoffending on parole or home detention warrants harsh punishment, then turns the same facts into an argument for judicial discretion and complexity, and explicitly cites what Fleming acknowledged about rehabilitation. The speech would have had to change if Fleming had made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "When the police did finally apprehend them, they discovered both of them were wearing monitoring bracelets." — Greg Fleming, who argued the offenders' release showed a "well-meaning but misguided sentencing system"

acuity.statement: One of these world views is that this bill, what it does is it’s not about victims, as one of our Green members said—“This bill is not about victims”—he said—“it is about punishing people further.” Really? Does the speaker think that’s what it’s about? Absolutely we want to punish people further.
acuity.explanation: Engages the live strand of the debate — whether the bill serves victims — and quotes an opposition formulation in order to answer it head-on by owning the aim of harsher punishment. But she picks up a Green member's phrase rather than the preceding speaker's specific claims about the Minister of Justice's advice and the research on victim outcomes, and then returns to prepared material (her Takanini neighbours, the select committee exchange). Partial engagement with the topic rather than with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is certainly not looking after the victims when the Minister of Justice’s own advice says that this is not something that will help victims" — Arena Williams; Nakhle takes up the victims strand but answers a Green member's earlier line rather than Williams's claim about the Minister's advice and the research

acuity.statement: Nō reira, ki roto i te kotahi tau kua kite atu i ngā ture e haere mai ana i te Kāwanatanga, ā, tērā tōna āhuatanga ko te patu i ngā kēngi tētahi, tērā anō ahakoa kua turaki ināianei ko te ram raids bill tētahi, anei tētahi ko te strengthening sentencing, arā tētahi, arā noa atu ngā ture kua taetae ki mua ki te komiti whiriwhiri o justice.

It is on the matter under debate, which keeps it off 0.0, but it would read identically whatever Costello had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Casey Costello spoke about offenders being 'held accountable' and wanting 'our victims have faith in the justice system that’s supposed to protect them', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The difference between the Government and the Opposition on this piece of legislation, the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, could not be starker. It could not be starker. On this side, we are relentlessly focused on restoring law and order and putting victims at the heart of our justice system; on that side, they are soft on crime and they do not support this legislation. The only thing they want to do is reduce the prison population.
acuity.explanation: Ferris had just argued, citing legal experts and the agencies' own research, that these laws will increase Māori incarceration. Rutherford touches the prison-population theme only to recast it as the Opposition's motive, and engages neither the disproportionality argument nor the expert opposition. The glance at the topic keeps it above 0.1, but no part of the argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: 'the number of Māori incarcerated within the justice system will increase' — this turn mentions reducing the prison population only as an Opposition motive, not as the claim Ferris made.

acuity.statement: It would be helpful if the Minister was prepared to perhaps make that available, rather than have us rely on the Official Information Act for it, given that it was raised by members opposite—the Hon Kieran McAnulty, in particular. I invite the Minister to maybe think about proactively releasing that information.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise mechanism Bishop had just offered — release of the advice via an OIA request — and does something with it, pressing instead for proactive release and giving a reason (the advice was sought in response to an opposition member's point in the second reading). The remark would have to be different had Bishop simply agreed to release it or refused outright.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "If someone sends me an Official Information Act (OIA) request, I’m sure we can—"

acuity.statement: Whilst the 20 units might be an appropriate threshold, as such, or trigger point for urban areas or cities or larger towns, just some understanding of how this might be approached in those regional—I take the Minister’s point that these numbers might not be at a huge level of scale, but having a bill that makes some fundamental change to thresholds is, obviously, important, and making sure that it’s like for like is not always necessarily the right thing in terms of it turning out in that particular way.
acuity.explanation: Engages Bishop's substantive answer on the regions: it concedes the scale point he made (build-to-rent being less viable and smaller developments finding domestic finance) and then disputes the inference that a single national threshold is therefore right. Not a full rebuttal of the complexity argument he rested the refusal on, and it trails into a general plea rather than a counter-case, so a partial engagement rather than a complete one.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I’m also advised that build-to-rent is less likely to be viable in smaller regions, given the market conditions, to make it profitable and that smaller developments are also more likely to find finance in the domestic market."

acuity.statement: Well, OK, if you send me an email, it’s technically an OIA request anyway. I can make it available to you.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Utikere's interjected demand for proactivity, concedes it, and supplies a concrete route (an email, which he notes functions as an OIA request). The words exist only because of what was called across at him. Marked below the top of the band because it accepts the demand without addressing the proactive-release principle behind it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Come on—be proactive."

acuity.statement: I guess I want some clarifications from the Minister on what the rationale is behind limiting the scope of the bill in the first place to consider some of these, and particularly when we’re looking at the first-principles review.

Xu-Nan thanks him for the earlier explanation but takes up none of that reasoning; he opens a fresh line on the regulatory impact statement's constrained scope. On the matter under debate, with a gesture at the previous turn, but no engagement with its content — the 0.1–0.3 band, at the top of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop argued the 20-dwelling threshold 'reflects the Income Tax Act, which reflects policy decisions made by successive Governments' and that build-to-rent economics only work in 'the major metros', and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Two points there from the member. In relation to the first, I think the question was: why did the Government not do a first-principles review of the Overseas Investment Act in relation to housing? There’s a couple of answers. The first is that we do have an intention to reform the Overseas Investment Act, which is being advanced by the Hon David Seymour, who’s the Associate Minister of Finance in charge of that.
acuity.explanation: Restates the member's specific question about why no first-principles review of the Overseas Investment Act was undertaken and answers it directly — reform is in train under another Minister. The reply would be different had Xu-Nan asked something else; it is shaped entirely by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I guess I want some clarifications from the Minister on what the rationale is behind limiting the scope of the bill' — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Let’s say, hypothetically speaking, we have residential land—let’s say it’s a single site—and it consists of 20 dwellings suitable for use or conversion to residential dwellings, that’s 20, which means it meets the test under subclause (1)(a), but then, because there are only 20, it wouldn’t meet the test for subclause (1)(b), but both tests must be met.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own answer — that this is a conjunctive test and both limbs must be met — and builds a worked hypothetical to show the two limbs may not be satisfiable at 20 dwellings. It uses the exact concession just made and presses it; nothing of this turn survives if the preceding answer had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Both limbs of the legal test must be met' — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Well, maybe I’m missing something. I mean, I did pretty well at School C English, so I don’t quite understand what the member’s saying. It’s “20 or more”, which is the same as “at least 20”. So, yeah, I think that deals with that, right?
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the specific semantic claim — that 'at least 20' implies 21 — and contradicts it by asserting the two phrases are equivalent. That is engagement with the content of the question, not a pivot, even though it is dismissive in tone and offers no drafting authority for the reading.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'you need at least 20, which means that you need a minimum of 21—so it’s “21 or more” is how you would read “at least”' — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Here it is in a nutshell: meeting the 20-unit minimum in the cities is probably not going to be an option—in fact, in places like Auckland, 20 units will probably be a proportion of the total number of units, so that just won’t be a problem—but where I live, any developer that comes along and proposes 12 units is a big developer, but they don’t meet this. If the logic behind this change is that—through feedback from the sector—they will struggle to on-sell their development unless overseas investment is utilised, and therefore without doing so, they would be less keen to put money and invest in the development or indeed build these units in the first place, surely that logic would apply in the cities as much as elsewhere. Is this Government really telling Parliament that it wants build-to-rents to become a significant part of our housing portfolio in this country, but only in Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, and Christchurch?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's claim that build-to-rent only makes economic sense in the major metros and turns its own logic against it: if overseas capital is needed to make these developments viable, the need is greater outside the big centres, where a 12-unit project is a large one and the 20-unit threshold bites. Directly aimed at the specific reasoning of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'We’re talking about the major metros here' — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Frankly, I thought the response from the Minister—although good on him for addressing it—was a little bit dismissive: “We don’t get into details. We should understand this.” Like, I get it—this is consistent with what previous Governments have done. But the reason we’ve got an amendment bill is because what previous Governments have done in trying to establish build-to-rent as a separately recognised asset class—it wasn’t there before; it was brought in. Now we’re amending it because it didn’t quite touch the mark. Why are we saying that, because it’s done previously, therefore we’re content? I just struggle to understand the logic.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the Minister's precedent argument — that the threshold reflects decisions of successive Governments — and rebuts it on its own terms: the existence of an amendment bill concedes the earlier settings were imperfect, so precedent cannot justify leaving this one alone. Engagement with the specific justification offered, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the 20-dwelling threshold reflects the Income Tax Act, which reflects policy decisions made by successive Governments' — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: At no point have we advocated for the threshold to be one, and at no point have we advocated for the rules to be loosened. What we have advocated for is a recognition that the minimum threshold that’s outlined in this bill would be hard to meet for many areas of the country.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects Bishop's characterisation of his position, then restates the actual proposal (a two-tier threshold with a high build-to-rent percentage outside cities) and presses the specific consequence Bishop's position has for 10-12 unit developments. The speech would be different had Bishop argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "if you have a lower threshold in the regions—which is, as I understand it, what the member is arguing for—the closer you get to kind of one"

acuity.statement: I could have just turned up here and ignored your second reading speech, not sought any advice, not turned up here willing to engage on the issue. I’ve done that in good faith. Most Ministers don’t actually go away and listen to the Opposition and seek further advice on something, by the way.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of McAnulty's complaint — the charge that the undertaking to look into it was not honoured — and answers it directly, but engages none of the substantive threshold argument. Partial engagement that is clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "you did say you would look into it. I’m not convinced that it actually has been"

acuity.statement: The member makes a not unreasonable point, but the advice I’ve had, which I agree with, is that the additional complexity that the member’s proposed amendment would introduce into the Act would outweigh the benefits gained from it. People are entitled to disagree with advice. Reasonable people can disagree. The Government’s not proposing to make the change.
acuity.explanation: Engages McAnulty's specific proposed amendment and gives a reason for rejecting it (complexity outweighing benefit), conceding it is a reasonable point; it does not take up the particular 100-percent mechanism or the regional-affordability evidence, so engagement is strong but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "keep the threshold as it is for the cities and look at the requirement that if, say, 100 percent of the development"

acuity.statement: I wondered if he could tell us how many applications there have been under the “benefit to New Zealand test” for the sale of large-scale rental developments to overseas investors, and how many of those, if any, were declined.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, but engages no part of the argument immediately preceding it — a fresh prepared question rather than a response to what was said.

acuity.statement: I heard the member who spoke previously saying, “Well, pistols, you know, they’re way more dangerous.” Now, true, they can be concealed, and TV tells us that they’re the weapon of choice for gangsters. Well, it’s not actually true. The weapon of choice for most criminals in New Zealand is an ordinary rifle that you can buy with a standard licence at any firearms store.
acuity.explanation: Webb names the preceding speaker's specific proposition — that pistols warrant stricter rules because they are the more dangerous class of firearm — and does something with it: he concedes concealability, then contests the premise with a counter-claim about which weapon criminals in New Zealand actually use, and goes on to argue rifles are 'differently dangerous'. If Bates had instead defended the pistol/non-pistol distinction on some other ground, this passage would have had to change. Engagement only is scored here; whether the counter-claim is true belongs to veracity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "It makes sense to have stricter rules for pistols because they’re a smaller type of gun."

acuity.statement: Sure, we had a number of operators of gun ranges and so on and sporting gun enthusiasts who vehemently promoted and supported the bill, and good on them—I can understand; most people want less rules rather than more—but critical submitters were deeply concerned with the bill, and I’m deeply concerned when the Police Association comes along and says they do not support the bill and there’s, essentially, a ministerial shrug of the shoulders.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bates's characterisation of the select committee evidence and disputes its composition rather than changing the subject: he accepts that range operators and shooters supported the bill, then sets against it the critical submitters and the Police Association's opposition. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the breadth of the submitter pool rather than Bates's actual point that the submitters were safety-focused, but the thing engaged is clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "The Justice Committee heard from a range of submitters, who were all focused on safety"

acuity.statement: It concerns me that there’s a sense of polarisation here: that if you think that these reforms are bad, you in some way vilify gun owners, and I want to make it absolutely clear that I don’t. In fact, until recently, I was a gun owner myself and have been hunting on a number of occasions.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — Bates's framing of opposition criticism as hyperbole implying that legislation cannot be improved without abandoning safety — by rejecting the dichotomy and establishing his own standing as a former firearms owner. It answers the framing rather than any specific claim about ranges, and then moves to prepared material on process, so it sits mid-band rather than high.

acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "We hear a lot of hyperbole about this piece of legislation from the Opposition through the discussion"

That’s all very well and good, but apply that to almost everything. There are some things that warrant suitable and risk-appropriate regulation, and we think that this leaves room for negligence and misuse.
acuity.explanation: She names and takes up one strand of the preceding government case — that licensed owners' own ingrained safety culture and personal responsibility are sufficient — and answers it with a reason (some risks warrant risk-appropriate regulation) before returning to her prepared three-point critique of the bill. The engagement is pointable but partial: the bulk of the speech is structured prepared material that would have been delivered whatever Anderson had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Miles Anderson: "for many in our rural community shooting is an integral part of the rural way of life, and the first thing we learn—and, might I say, have drummed into us—is safety"

acuity.statement: One of the things that really caught my eye was, as my colleague Miles Anderson said in his contribution before, there is a small amount of people in New Zealand who are registered gun and firearm owners. Many who supported the bill were from that community—those that actually are directly impacted by this legislation and the impact it has on them.
acuity.explanation: The speech immediately follows McLellan's detailed critique and engages no part of it — not the inspection frequency, the self-regulation point, the ammunition records, nor the regulatory impact statement. It is prepared material on the right subject (select committee submission counts, commending the bill), and its only backward reference is to his own colleague's earlier contribution rather than to the argument just made. The gesture at the submitter balance keeps it off the floor of the band, but it would read identically had McLellan said something else entirely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "Consultation on the bill was heavily biased towards firearms users, ignoring broader public safety concerns and the recommendations from various other experts" — and her wider case that the bill weakens police oversight and creates loopholes for criminals and extremists. This statement takes up none of it; it reaches back past her to quote a same-side colleague.

acuity.statement: Other members have referenced and spoken to the term “self-regulation”, which seems pretty strange. It’s a very difficult concept to give communities safety and assurance and, at the same time, to talk about this notion of self-regulation for shooting clubs and shooting ranges in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at what earlier members have said, but takes up none of the content of the turn immediately preceding — Nakhle's point about the five-yearly inspection provision and its change-of-circumstances override. The speech is on the subject under debate and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued, so it sits in the unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rima Nakhle argued that new section 38XJ provides inspections "once every five years unless there is a change of circumstances that may affect its safety" and that members had not read the bill, and this statement does not take that up.

It sits at the midpoint and not higher because Anderson made no argument to rebut or qualify, so she takes up his topic and then runs through prepared material on each bill in turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’re looking to streamline the process for these bills, remove redundant clauses" — Miles Anderson

I think that the strong theme—and it has been mentioned—is about the strengthening of the quality of our regulation, improving court timeliness, and enhancing our access to the judicial system.
acuity.explanation: Twice signals awareness of what came before ("as has been stated in this House", "it has been mentioned") and is squarely on the matter under debate, but the content is a prepared summary of the three bills' themes. Nothing in it would change if Nakhle had made a different argument on the same bills, so it sits in the gesture-at-the-debate band rather than partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "Essentially, we’re going to be improving the effectiveness and the efficiency of a number of areas when it comes to regulation" — Costello nods that the theme "has been mentioned" but takes up no part of Nakhle's argument about regulation burdening businesses.

acuity.statement: While the Government frames this as a technical and procedural package of so-called non-contentious bills, we know that hiding within this legislation is a calculated political decision, one that directly undermines Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the education required to uphold its principles.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the framing the two preceding government speakers used — that the package is a technical efficiency tidy-up — and contests it, then grounds the objection in the occupational regulation strand Costello had just itemised (real estate). Not a full 1.0: it engages the characterisation of the bills rather than any specific claim or figure, and then proceeds to prepared material on Te Tiriti and mana motuhake.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "Collectively, we are talking in this legislation about improving efficiencies and about creating some better outcomes for the public" — and her reference to "the real estate regimes" in the occupational regulation bill.

These bills, as my colleague Rima Nakhle said earlier, will improve the effectiveness and efficiency of the courts and tribunals, occupational regulation, and criminal law, particularly focusing on anti - money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition attack on a specific provision and answers none of it, offering instead a prepared bill-by-bill description. The reference to a colleague on his own side is a mere citation, not engagement. It stays on the subject under debate, which keeps it off 0.0, but the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Kemp had said.
acuity.subject: speaker

They were all subject matter experts and it was quite technical, and I’m sure that we all learnt a lot.
acuity.explanation: McLellan picks up the one substantive strand of Nakhle's short preceding turn — the 16 submissions and their value — and does something with it, agreeing they were expert and technical and later building on their select committee amendments. But the engagement stops there: the bulk of the speech is prepared material explaining the bill's purpose and the exceptions, which would have been delivered whatever Nakhle had said. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "I’d like to acknowledge the 16 submissions that were made with respect to this bill" — and that although a small number, "it was quite impactful"

acuity.statement: The Privacy Amendment Bill, as we’ve heard from contributions tonight and on previous nights, is making a minor tweak but a really important one for the privacy of New Zealanders and the collection of their information. I support the legislation and I commend it to the House, and I’m looking forward to hearing the contribution coming up from my colleague the Hon Andrew Bayly.
acuity.explanation: A generic closing speech. It waves at the preceding contributions without engaging any part of McLellan's account of new section 22(2), the exceptions, or her point about back-office administration, and would read identically whatever she had argued. The gesture at the debate and the characterisation of the bill as a minor but important tweak keeps it just above the floor rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: McLellan set out the bill's indirect-collection notification requirement and the select committee's archiving-in-the-public-interest and national security exceptions, and this statement takes up none of it — it only gestures at "contributions tonight and on previous nights"

acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific substantive strand of the preceding speech — Williams' objection to derived data and her argument that the Australian regime's handling of it was a mistake to be learned from — and adopts and extends it, agreeing that the Minister's privacy changes are supported while the derived-data position remains a concern and that the lesson should be drawn from Australia and the UK. It engages one strand rather than the whole argument (he does not take up her delegation/governance or electricity points at this moment and then returns to prepared Green material on implementation and equity), so it sits below the top of the scale, but the engagement is pointable and the sentence would have to change had the previous speaker argued differently.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Hipkins had been pressing — whether Lester Levy is succeeding in the role he was appointed to — and does something with it, conceding the struggle while relocating the cause in the inherited health structure. acuity.responding_to: Hipkins: "given that, only six months later, a task force has reportedly been established to rewrite the turn-around plan that the commissioner himself was appointed to come up with?"

(The recasting is a rigor problem, not an acuity one, and is not scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "does the Prime Minister think that it is the job of Government to reduce inequality?"

acuity.statement: There you have it, what happens in the first year of Opposition when a former Prime Minister loses an election: you end up living in a twilight world where “New Zealand was perfect, but we lost the election because New Zealanders didn’t realise”.
acuity.explanation: Opens by characterising the speech just given, but engages none of its content — not the cost-of-living claims, the power-price argument, the cancelled State house build, nor the ministerial-standards charge. It is a caricature of Hipkins' position ('everything Labour did was perfect') that Hipkins did not advance; a mere reference to the previous speaker, which the rubric puts in the 0.1–0.3 band. Scored slightly above the floor because it is at least aimed at the preceding speech rather than being generic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "what they have proven since they became the Government is that stringing together a bunch of slogans will not make up for the fact that they simply don’t have a plan" — McClay gestures at the speech as a whole but takes up no part of this argument.

acuity.explanation: The textbook high-acuity move: concedes the specific premise the previous speaker argued at length (that life is getting harder for New Zealand families) and then disputes the causal attribution, assigning it to the previous government rather than this one. The sentence could not have been delivered if Hipkins had argued something else; substitute a different critique and this reply has to change. Whether the causal claim is sound is a Rigor question and whether it is true a Veracity one — neither is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Things are getting harder for New Zealand families" — McClay accepts this and contests the cause.

acuity.statement: The reason our farmers are happy: not what Chris Hipkins said, not because the Government is patting ourselves on the back, but because we are recognising farmers work hard, we are recognising they’re important, and we are helping and working with them to fix the rules that were holding them back, that were costing them, and that were putting them out of business and sending jobs and production overseas.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the preceding speech — the repeated charge that the Government is merely congratulating itself while conditions worsen — and answers it with a counter-example (the Federated Farmers confidence result) plus a competing explanation. It engages a real claim rather than just naming the opponent, but it answers only the sentiment strand and then returns to prepared farming material, leaving the substantive charges (power prices, emergency accommodation, cancelled builds) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "this Government are patting themselves on the back saying how wonderful everything suddenly is" — McClay denies this is the source of farmer confidence.

acuity.statement: We’ve done a couple of trade deals in the Middle East where they will want this lamb because it’s high quality, it tastes good, and as I said last week, if you want to feel good, eat lamb.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material that engages no part of the preceding speech and is only loosely connected to the matter under debate. McClay himself flags it as a repeat of remarks given the previous week, which is the clearest possible evidence it would have been delivered word for word whatever Hipkins had said. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it still sits inside an economy-and-exports debate rather than being transplantable to any debate at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins argued the Government has no plan on power prices, supermarkets, banks and housing, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "an explanation of the $100 million is that that is over a long period of time"

It is prepared material on the right subject: it would read identically whatever the Minister had just said about that school.

Topic engaged, argument untouched — the 0.1-0.3 band, at the top of it because the slogan jibe at least latches onto the framing of the preceding speech.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.statement: It also puts some management and Government disciplines around it and says that this fund would manage, essentially, independently. It keeps it away from the politicians, as you’ve already heard in this debate, and I think that that is a very good move as well.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows Court and picks up one strand of Court's case — that the fund's value is in insulating the assets from politicians — explicitly acknowledging it ("as you’ve already heard in this debate") and endorsing it. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "The other good thing is that these assets won’t be a political plaything for politicians in the future."

acuity.statement: New Zealand First, of course, has always taken a very strong approach on asset sales, because we believe if you’re going to, as Simon Court said, recycle assets to pay for something else—another asset—you want to make sure that that new asset actually earns you a return, which is pretty much commensurate with what you were selling before. To sell an asset to then buy another asset which earns you nothing, and is probably a liability, is not a very smart move.
acuity.explanation: Foster names Court's proposition — recycling existing assets to fund new ones — and does something with it rather than merely referencing it: he accepts the mechanism but attaches a condition Court did not, that the replacement asset must earn a return commensurate with what was sold, and spells out the failure case where it earns nothing. The turn would have had to change if Court had made a different argument about council balance sheets.
