acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "It has affected our small businesses." and "I say to the National Party and to ACT, who have spoken tonight: it is not a time for defeatism."

acuity.statement: We’ve heard about scooters and lithium ion batteries. I wouldn’t be encouraging anybody to have a wee tinker with a lithium ion battery. We’ve all seen the sorts of fires that can occur by doing that.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact example the previous speaker built her case around — the scooter battery — and turns it against her by supplying a consideration she omitted (lithium-ion fire risk). The passage would not exist had White not told that story, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "When I replaced that scooter with what I thought was an identical one, it turned out that I couldn’t get the battery in any more."

acuity.statement: All of the valid reasons—there were some very invalid reasons, but the so-called valid reasons that I have heard in the House tonight from politicians who are not going to support this bill are reasons to get it to select committee right now rather than delay the bill.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes the objections just raised by the opposing speaker — scope, practicality, safety — and does something with them: concedes some are genuine and argues they are themselves grounds for sending the bill to select committee rather than voting it down. That is engaging the reasoning, not restating a prepared position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "While I do actually support the objectives of this bill and I think they’re sound, I think the current scope is far too expansive."

acuity.statement: Around the world, we have several countries and places where repair legislation has been in place for a number of years. I mentioned the US, the EU, the UK, Canada, Australia, France—and that’s several states across the US. After several years, there is absolutely zero evidence of price increase to consumer, and I know why: when you think about right to repair, actually, at the moment, manufacturers will often replace the whole entire thing for a little thing that is wrong with it—a whole product replacement.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the specific cost claim made in the immediately preceding turn, names it, and attacks it with comparative evidence from jurisdictions that already have the legislation plus a mechanism for why costs do not rise. The rebuttal is aimed squarely at the inference just offered and would have to change had he argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "In the end, we’d actually end up making things far more expensive"

acuity.statement: We used to make better-quality goods. It’s no good in this House to pretend like going back to better-quality goods will hurt the world. It is actually planned obsolescence that has been hurting us and Papatūānuku for many, many years.
acuity.explanation: Takes the 'bygone era was less environmentally friendly' line from the preceding turn and contests precisely that premise, asserting the opposite causal story (planned obsolescence, not older goods, is the environmental harm). It engages the content of his point rather than glancing at it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "I appreciate that there are certain members of this House who want to go back to the bygone era when things were very simple, not very environmentally friendly."

acuity.statement: I think we all agree that there is a housing shortage. What we seem to disagree on—certainly in the speech from the Green Party member—is what the solution to that might be. It is always a pleasure to follow after, particularly on housing issues, Cameron Luxton, who I think is probably the only person who has actually built houses with his own hands. He is our resident builder.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows a substantive turn by Luxton that made several arguable claims — that price rises incentivise building, that restrictive planning law is the real constraint, and that overseas capital for build-to-rent is a missing piece. He takes up none of them. He restates the one point of agreement (there is a shortage), gestures vaguely at disagreement with an earlier Green speaker without naming the disagreement, and then pays Luxton a personal compliment about being a builder. The reference to Luxton is courtesy, not engagement: the passage would read identically whatever Luxton had argued, so it sits in the mere-reference band rather than at partial engagement. A gesture at the debate's subject keeps it at 0.3-ish ceiling; nothing in the content is engaged, so 0.2.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "no one in this House is denying that New Zealand has got a massive housing problem" — Cameron Luxton (who also argued that rising prices are themselves an incentive to build and that the binding constraint is "designed-to-say-no legislation" plus a shortage of capital)

acuity.statement: From our perspective, in the essence of this bill, yes, it does remove barriers for overseas investors to build-to-rent, but what it does then is replace the barrier and put it smack in front of hapū and whānau and tribal—iwi—investors.
acuity.explanation: Foster's immediately preceding turn argued in detail that the bill is a small but useful supply-side contribution, that New Zealand First has ensured foreign investment benefits New Zealand (defending the $5m threshold over $2m), and attacked the Greens' public-housing alternative. Kapa-Kingi's speech is squarely on the matter under debate and asserts the opposite characterisation of the bill, but it takes up no part of Foster's actual argument: it does not address the supply/demand reasoning, the thresholds, the Property Council's 0.1 percent figure, or the New Zealand First benefit test. It is prepared material on community-centred development with a passing gesture at the builder-credentials theme Foster had been joking about ('Unlike Cameron Luxton, who is actually a builder'). The speech would read identically had Foster made a different argument on the same bill, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is at least a glance at the preceding exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: 'This bill is just a small part of the answer to a very big, complicated problem.' — and his earlier remark 'Sometimes we flush hidden talents out of the House when we make statements like that, which need to be corrected.' Neither claim is taken up; she restates her own framing of the bill instead.

acuity.statement: However, the basis of this bill is that we want to see more rental properties or more housing that is affordable for the people of Aotearoa. Does this bill serve that purpose? The bill itself is simply to buy existing, large rental developments, not in terms of creating or increasing the stock of the rental market but the existing ones.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speech — Kapa-Kingi's claim that the rental-shortage justification is a smokescreen — and supplies his own reason for it (the bill lets investors buy existing developments rather than add stock). It engages the topic and that strand rather than her specific argument about whenua and overseas competitors crowding out whānau buyers, and the rest of the speech is prepared Green material on the housing crisis, so it sits at partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The smokescreen here is that this will assist with the rental shortage here at home." — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: What another great day for a Government that can now proudly claim and own the fact that we are the party for mum and dad landlords, we are the party for homeowners, and now this is just another step to confirm that we are the party for renters. It gives me great pleasure to rise and support this third reading of the Overseas Investment (Build-to-rent and Similar Rental Developments) Amendment Bill.
acuity.explanation: Opens with prepared praise of the Government's housing record and a recap of unrelated measures (brightline, interest deductibility, consenting reform). It is on the subject under debate, but it engages no part of the immediately preceding argument — neither the claim that the bill only transfers ownership of existing developments nor the claim that revenue will leave Aotearoa — and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that the bill will not increase housing stock and that rental revenue will be sent overseas, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: No, no. If you’d let me finish, you might learn something, the Hon Megan Woods. Through the Kāinga Ora wasteful-spending situation, we’ve pulled some of that money back, and we’re creating competition with community housing providers to build more housing. We’re actually going to get a more diverse typology of housing, including affordable rentals, for you, Megan.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Woods' specific charge that the Government scrapped the community-provider affordable-rental fund and answers it on its own terms: concedes money was pulled back, attributes it to Kāinga Ora spending, and argues the money now funds CHPs to build a more diverse typology including affordable rentals. The reply would have to change had Woods made a different criticism, so engagement is real; it falls short of 1.0 because he does not engage her actual point (the gap between market and public housing) and slides straight back into prepared supply material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this Government has removed that piece of the puzzle by scrapping the fund that would have allowed our community providers to do that" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: I’m going to explain something else back to that member Ryan Hamilton, and that’s to do with rent and what drives rents. It was something that he might have missed in the Monetary Policy Statement around what was happening with rents. Existing rents are staying high; new rents are going down. We know that a large part of what drives rents is demand. Now, if it was the case that rents dropped in response to interest drops, those existing rents should have dropped too, but they have not.
acuity.explanation: Directly attacks the causal inference in Hamilton's immediately preceding turn — that Government action and the OCR cut are pushing rents down — by splitting existing from new rents and pointing out that an interest-rate mechanism would have moved both. It names him, cites the document he relied on, and supplies a rival explanation (demand, net migration). Delete Hamilton's turn and this passage has nothing to do; it is maximally responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it was great news, only yesterday, to have the official cash rate drop by 50 basis points. The flow-on effect is just another example of the compound effect that we’re doing towards housing" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: As members of the Labour Party have set out, this is a very narrow set of circumstances in the Overseas Investment Act. It does streamline the test in order to make things slightly quicker for those who have the volume of build-to-rent units. It has not removed some of those protections from the Overseas Investment Act, which is why this side of the House is supporting it—it makes it slightly easier because of the type of test it is with the volume and the 20 units that it’s put in, but also because some of the other protections which are still within the Act apply.
acuity.explanation: Nancy Lu's immediately preceding turn argued the bill's merit through job creation — apprentices, tradies, suppliers, flow-on spending in local businesses. Edmonds' speech is on the same bill and the same subject matter, but engages no part of that argument: it sets out Labour's own reasons for support (the narrowness of the test, the retained Overseas Investment Act protections) and acknowledges earlier Labour speakers not present in this window. Delete Lu's turn and substitute any other pro-bill speech and this passage would be word-for-word identical, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu spoke about the jobs and local-business benefits of build-to-rent ("more apprentices will get into the projects with construction, more work for tradies") and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I think all that has been said in this House is relevant. I don’t have much more to contribute other than to say I agree with the statements made from many sides of this part of the House. It is part of the solution. It is good news for Auckland. It is good news for renters.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Edmonds, who had made two pointed contributions: that the bill preserves the Overseas Investment Act's other protections, and that Labour failed to persuade the Government to allow proportionality for regional developments where 20 units is hard to reach. He engages neither. Blanket endorsement of "all that has been said" gestures at the debate without taking up any content from it — a reference to the other speakers is not an engagement with their claims. The speech would be unchanged whatever Edmonds had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued the bill retains the Act's protections and that the Government refused proportionality for the regions, where "20 units actually could be quite difficult to build"; this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Now hearing from the Minister, in terms of some of the broader work that is being done in terms of the judiciary and around capacity, etc., I want to check with the Minister: why, then, did this bill get introduced at this particular moment when other works are already being done?
acuity.explanation: This takes a specific element of McKee's immediately preceding speech — her volunteered point that a much wider court-timeliness programme is already under way, with duty lawyer, bail scheduling and Te Au Reka reforms being rolled out and monitored — and turns it back on her as an objection: if that work is in train and not yet assessed, why legislate the cap increase now rather than wait for the results. The question is constructed out of her own material and could not have been asked had she not made that point, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Government also has a much wider timeliness programme under way" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: I thank the Green member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan for his question. I understand why it’s being asked. If I can just relate to the last increase that occurred in 2019, where we actually increased the number of judges from 165 through to 182. That was for a number of reasons at the time, and we quickly went up to, I believe it was, about 172 judges within that appointment. The officials have gone away, looked at what the reforms are that this Government is putting through will require in terms of how many judges will be needed.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan asked specifically why this bill now, given other work already under way. The reply addresses that question directly rather than restating the bill's case: it supplies the 2019 precedent (165 to 182, with appointments reaching only about 172), and says officials have assessed what the Government's own reforms will require. Whether the answer is adequate belongs to other attributes; on responsiveness it is squarely aimed at the "why now" put to her and would be different had he asked something else. Marked slightly below the top because it answers the timing question partly by restating history rather than addressing the sequencing objection head-on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why, then, did this bill get introduced at this particular moment when other works are already being done?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I want to pick up on, with the Minister, what you mentioned before. Can I just check in your expert opinion, also in terms of the information you have from the officials—what you are saying is that the addition of one at this stage is anticipatory in case the capacity increases, but the actual capacity we have now in terms of the court system is actually sufficient, based on the 2019 increase. Would that be a correct assumption?
acuity.explanation: This is the strongest form of engagement available in a committee stage: it takes the Minister's answer, restates its logical content back as a proposition — that the extra judge is anticipatory and that present capacity is already sufficient on the back of the 2019 lift — and asks her to confirm or deny it. It draws out the consequence of what she said rather than repeating her words, and is entirely dependent on her having said it; a different answer would have produced a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we do think that just one additional judge will be required, should we actually need it" and "This really is a bit of a backfill just in case it’s needed" — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: I thank the member for his question, but I don’t see anywhere in the title where it talks about the number of judges. The District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill is about initiating one more judge—from 182 and to 183.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the subject of Webb's question and supplies the bill's actual figure (182 to 183), but engages the admissibility of the question rather than its substance — whether one extra judge is enough given the sentencing, three-strikes, gang-patch and young-serious-offender reforms. Partial engagement: pointable, but it answers the topic rather than the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Well, it’s the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill, and the question is around the number of judges."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I will have another go, because I didn’t get a very satisfactory answer last time. I’ll reframe it to be a question about the number of judges rather than a general policy question.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's relevance objection — that the title clause says nothing about the number of judges — and reshapes the question to meet it, then splits it in two. This turn could not have been delivered had the previous answer been different; it is built entirely out of what McKee said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "I don’t see anywhere in the title where it talks about the number of judges"

acuity.statement: Thank you to the member Duncan Webb for his questions. The advice that we have received is that one judge, at this stage, should be enough.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — whether the advice supports one judge being sufficient — and goes on to give a reason for not repeating the earlier large increase. It does not supply the substantive evidence on backlog reduction that was asked for, which keeps it short of a full engagement, but the central claim is taken up squarely.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "whether she is confident that, in respect of the Sentencing Act, just one judge is enough"

acuity.statement: That is fine, but I want to check with the Minister if she has received advice in terms of the number of judges specifically, and if she or her officials have taken into consideration the 2022 report Improving Access to Civil Justice, and particularly when it comes to the fact that in that report it does specify that despite the fact that there is an increase in the number of District Court judges, like the Minister has said, from 160 to 182, we are still seeing a decline of District Court’s civil jurisdiction and that we’re still catching up to it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own reliance on the earlier 165-to-182 increase and turns it against her conclusion, citing a named 2022 report that found civil jurisdiction declining despite that increase. The question is constructed out of the specific justification just offered, and would be different had she justified the single judge another way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "we are not looking to do a massive increase like we did previously, from 165 to 182"

acuity.statement: Just very quickly, I totally understand where the Minister in the chair is coming from, but by locking us into one additional judge, surely the Minister is anticipating this, because this was the advice the Minister has given.
acuity.explanation: Engages the reasoning of the answer just given — that nothing further is being anticipated and placement cannot be known because the legislation has not passed — by pressing the point that settling on exactly one judge is itself an act of anticipation. It works on the inference in the Minister's reply rather than restating the earlier question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee (untagged ministerial reply): "I did not make mention of any further legislation coming."

acuity.statement: The proposals contained within this bill will, effectively, limit police inspections of clubs and ranges to once in every five years—at the first application for enrolment or certification, and then at a five-yearly application for renewal. The reduced ability for police to carry out inspections, we consider, undermines the ability to enforce safety.
acuity.explanation: McKee's opening speech set out the new inspection timing (on enrolment, then every five years) as a reduction of undue compliance burden. Andersen takes that exact provision and turns it against the bill's stated purpose, arguing the same five-yearly schedule strips Police of enforcement capacity, and she attaches a concrete amendment to it. The speech would have to change if McKee had described a different inspection regime.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "For non-pistol clubs and ranges, inspections can take place upon application for enrolment and then every five years."

acuity.statement: I’m going to, first of all, move to the enrolment system that we have introduced. The member has made the allegation that we are going to be returning to what it was before; we are not. Before, we did not have any enrolment system whatsoever, except for the pistol clubs, where police would go along and check on the ranges.
acuity.explanation: Directly identifies Andersen's central premise — that the bill returns New Zealand to the pre-2019 settings — and contests it on the facts, stating that no enrolment system existed before for non-pistol clubs. It is a point-for-point correction of the specific claim just made, not a pivot to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "The bill provides to return, really, to a system which was here in New Zealand before 2019"

acuity.statement: I’m going to, just now, speak to the petition that the member spoke to about a range volunteer’s ability to monitor extremists. That is not a volunteer’s job, and the moment we start putting that on to volunteers in New Zealand, then I have to have grave concerns about what the role of New Zealand Police would be, because that’s for them.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific Petitions Committee point Andersen raised about operators screening criminals and extremists, and answers it with a counter-argument about where that duty properly sits, rather than restating the bill's merits. It does not say whether she has read the petition, which Andersen also asked, so the engagement is close but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "Parliament’s Petitions Committee questioned the ability of operators of shooting clubs and ranges to be able to monitor or screen for criminals and extremists who use the facilities"

acuity.statement: I say this as a firearms owner: I was astonished to hear—I’ve had my firearms licence since I was 16—that I’m now observed by the police day and night for my behaviour because I have a firearms licence. I can tell the Minister, that is not true. It is certainly not true.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific factual claim from the immediately preceding turn — that police receive a nightly list on licensed firearm owners — and directly contradicts it from his own position as a long-standing licence holder. The speech would have to change entirely if McKee had not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "they get, every night, every 24 hours, a list of licensed firearm owners who have come to the attention of New Zealand Police"

acuity.statement: The Minister is correct that the police should be notifying or keeping tabs on those who are in the criminal underworld, but, of course, our volunteers who run the ranges should be able to notify the police and should be keeping tabs on that as well.
acuity.explanation: Concedes one strand of the Minister's argument about police monitoring and disputes the rest by arguing the obligation must run in the other direction too — an explicit accept-part/dispute-the-rest engagement with what she had just said about range officials' relationship with police.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "those that were in charge of firearms activities had a relationship with New Zealand Police and were able to go knock on their door and tell them when they had concerns about an individual’s behaviour"

acuity.statement: In relation to the tabled amendment—it’s amendment 12.30.02, and it’s about removing section 38XJ, deleting subsection (2)—I’m again quite shocked that the member actually wants to remove the ability for Police to be able to go and check on a range every five years, because that’s what it says.
acuity.explanation: Willis asked her directly to address the specific amendment; she identifies it by number, states what the subsection does, gives her reading of the amendment's effect and declares how she will vote. Squarely takes up the thing just put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "I’d like the Minister to respond to whether she will at least do that" — his request that she say whether she will accept the amendment to clause 5 deleting section 38XJ(2)

acuity.statement: The Green member referred to the regulatory impact statement, which said, in his view, that there is no evidence for change of the status quo. I’m going to ask the member to reflect on the statements that were made when the legislation came in that said there was no evidence there was a problem that needed to be fixed.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific evidentiary point Willis made about the regulatory impact statement and takes it up, but answers it by turning the same complaint back on the original legislation rather than addressing what the RIS says — partial engagement with the strand he raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "there is "little evidence of any positive and negative impacts of the requirements.""

acuity.statement: The member had made mention about the New Zealand Police, like we’re leaving them out of the equation—we are not. What we are removing from New Zealand Police is the administration and regulation of the Arms Act. New Zealand Police will still be there for the enforcement.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Woods' specific argument — that the amendment is needed because the Government is removing police from the firearms regime — names it, and distinguishes administration/regulation from enforcement to rebut it. The reply would have had to be different had Woods argued something else about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "What my colleague Ginny Andersen is doing is inserting the police right back into the equation around our gun laws"

acuity.statement: What we are doing is ensuring what Labour should have done in the last Government when they created the Firearms Safety Authority, which was make it the truly independent authority that the royal commission of inquiry—which I have read—outlines that it should be.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers Woods' suggestion that she may not have read the royal commission report, and turns the report's own recommendation on independence back against the previous Government's implementation. Engages the content of the challenge rather than merely referring to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "I do encourage the Minister, if she has not read the report of the royal commission"

acuity.statement: Then, when further information was asked for, there was actually no evidence that any clubs had closed at all as a result of those additional administrative requirements that were put on clubs post-2019. The whole purpose of this piece of legislation is that it’s going to improve safety by stopping clubs shutting down, and if they shut down, then people would be practising with firearms in an unregulated or an unsupervised manner.
acuity.explanation: McKee's preceding turn rested on the claim that the 2020 administrative changes had a damaging flow-on effect for clubs and volunteers. Andersen takes up that one strand directly, disputing its evidential basis (no evidence any club closed) and the bill's stated rationale, but the rest of her turn is prepared material about her own commencement amendment and the Regulatory Standards Bill, and she does not engage McKee's specific arguments about the Shooting Range Manual or new section 38XJ(2). Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "Those changes that were made in 2020 have had this flow-on effect, and the lack of support is expected from them."

acuity.statement: There is a benefit to society—and this is speaking to the other member’s point as well—if we have these clubs and ranges operating. Two clubs have actually shut down, and there were a series of individuals who had approached me before the legislation came in to tell me they were shutting their clubs down as well.
acuity.explanation: Andersen's turn made two specific demands: show the problem being solved (she asserted no clubs had closed) and show the benefits outweighing the costs. McKee takes both up in order — she supplies a factual counter to the central empirical claim (two clubs have in fact shut down, plus others signalling closure) and then sets out the benefit side she was asked for. The speech would have to change if Andersen had argued something else; it is answering her claim rather than merely naming her. Not a full 1.0 only because the counter-claim is asserted without the evidence Andersen asked to see.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "there was actually no evidence that any clubs had closed at all"

acuity.statement: I have listened carefully to Associate Minister of Justice McKee and been astonished sometimes to hear that this side of the House considers all firearm owners as criminals or terrorists—or something like that—when I am a firearm owner and I respect other firearm owners, certainly those who are correct in their practice and who are safe. This is not about condemning firearm owners, but I do take issue with the Minister who made the statement that all firearm owners are good people. Clearly that is false.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific characterisation McKee had just made of licensed firearms owners, rejects the imputation that his side calls them criminals or terrorists, and disputes the generalisation directly. The speech would have to change if McKee had not made that claim, so engagement is close and specific — though the counter-argument itself is thin, which is a rigor matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These are good people. These are really good people in our society, those that have been judged to be fit and proper by New Zealand Police. They are not criminals. They are not potential terrorists." — Nicole McKee

acuity.statement: In answer to the Green member Scott Willis’ first question, the effect of new section 38XJ(2) is to provide certainty to clubs and ranges on when their inspections are going to occur while still allowing the police to actually carry out those inspections. That could be in response to safety concerns that they may have or, as I mentioned in my opening speech, also in regard to a change in circumstances. The reason why I said that this could create a safety issue if it’s removed is because removing the clause creates uncertainty for those volunteers who run the clubs and ranges, and it places a regulatory burden on them.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — why not accept the removal of subsection (2) — by stating what that subsection does and why its deletion would, on her account, reduce rather than increase safety. It engages the clause Willis read out rather than pivoting to general praise of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s my question to the Minister: why not accept an amendment that increases safety" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: Outside of the four walls of this building, people loathe the piety of politicians—“You said it.”, “He said it.”, one side of the House pointing fingers at the other. It happens all the time, the left and the right. No one really resolved anything other than the chap—he’s quit.
acuity.explanation: Cameron follows Simeon Brown's long comparative litany (Wood, Nash, Allan, Halbert, Andersen) and takes up one strand of it directly: he accepts Brown's framing that Bayly took personal responsibility and resigned, but rejects the trading of records as the thing worth debating — the "one side of the House pointing fingers at the other" is a recognisable description of the speech he has just heard. He then returns to prepared ACT material on the cost of living, so the engagement is partial rather than a rebuttal of any specific claim Brown made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "On this side of the House, we take personal responsibility. On that side of the House, they drag these issues out."

acuity.statement: I don’t have much more to add to what my good friend and colleague the Hon Simeon Brown said in his contribution. This is really a waste of Parliament’s time. A Minister made a mistake, he owned up and took accountability for it, and he resigned. I mean, the matter is literally as simple as that.
acuity.explanation: Bishop names the preceding government speaker only to say he has nothing to add, then delivers prepared material on the comparative record of the last government (Whaitiri, Wood). Per the mere-reference rule, naming a previous speaker and endorsing them wholesale is not engagement; the gesture at Cameron's "this is not the salient issue" theme keeps it in the 0.3 band rather than 0.1, but the speech would read the same whatever Cameron and Brown had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Cameron: "Let’s talk about the salient issues, not this." — Bishop gestures at the same "not worth the House's time" point but engages no argument Cameron or Brown actually made.

acuity.statement: To sit there and justify this by saying “So and so did it in 2000”, “Such and such did it but he’s now my friend” is actually poor form. It’s poor form for those who have to survive and work amongst us in this environment.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific move Bishop had just made — citing Michael Wood, Kiri Allan and Stuart Nash as precedents, and calling Nash "a friend to this side of the House" — and rebuts it as an illegitimate justification rather than disputing the facts. The passage would have to change if the preceding speech had not relied on past-minister comparisons, which is what makes it responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would point him to the Michael Wood saga of 2022, 2023, and so on." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Now, we have heard from that side of the House that the resignation has been given; he is no longer a Minister. I think Minister Bishop said, “That’s the end of the matter.” Well, actually, it’s not the end of the matter because in this country we expect transparency. We expect accountability.
acuity.explanation: Quotes Bishop's actual conclusion that the resignation ends the matter and directly contests that conclusion, giving a reason (transparency and accountability are still owed). This is engagement with the content of the preceding claim, not merely naming the previous speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Did he take accountability and resign? Yes, he did. And that is really the end of the matter." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Then, what we hear from that side is a constant desire to reflect back on other examples where Ministers were had up for a level of misconduct. OK, I get that. However, at some point in time that Government has to take responsibility, that Prime Minister needs to take responsibility.

Concedes-and-rebuts is genuine engagement with the specific argument made, though it answers the pattern of examples rather than any one of them.

acuity.responding_to: "I would also point him to the Kiri Allan disaster" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: There is mention of the victim, and the victim is an important part of this process; we’ve acknowledged that throughout.

The sentence would not exist had McLellan not interjected, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because he rebuts by flat denial and then returns to prepared material about the Government's priorities rather than substantiating the point.

acuity.responding_to: "Not one mention of the victim." — Dr Tracey McLellan

acuity.explanation: Names Rutherford's actual argument — that the debate is a farce and the House should be on cost of living instead — and then does something with it rather than merely citing it: she turns the premise around, since Bayly was the Minister holding the cost-of-living portfolios, so his departure is itself a cost-of-living matter. Her speech would have to change if Rutherford had made a different argument. Not 1.0 because she does not engage his specific accountability claim (resignation offered and accepted) and moves on to prepared material on the supermarket plan.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This debate is, effectively, a farce, because actually the Minister has taken accountability for what’s happened" / "They’re worried about putting food on the table" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: The vain hunt by the Opposition for a conspiracy in this whole case is ridiculous. There is no conspiracy—it’s been dealt with and we have now put it to bed.
acuity.explanation: Williams put specific, answerable constitutional questions — who knew what, and when, and whether that timeline has been compiled. Kirkpatrick labels the inquiry a conspiracy hunt and declares the matter closed without engaging any part of it: no timeline, no account of what the Prime Minister or Cabinet knew. It is a gesture at the debate under way rather than prepared material on an unrelated subject, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band, but repeating the recap of the resignation would have read identically whatever Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is not clear whether the Prime Minister himself knew about the situation of how the worker was treated, and it is not clear whether Cabinet knew" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I think that the last Minister of Transport spent a whole year editing this legislation that was probably ready to go under the last Labour Government, making it far more centralised, giving far more control to central government. I think that's going to be problematic. I think it'll be less likely that the local councils will take it up unless we have some practical changes there.
acuity.explanation: Genter follows Utikere, who argued that Labour did the groundwork, that the former Minister failed to progress it, and that his main worry is the Minister's power to foist a scheme on communities rather than letting local councils lead. This passage takes up both strands — it accepts the bill was effectively ready under Labour, attributes the delay to the previous Minister, and converges on the centralisation complaint, drawing out the consequence that councils will not take it up. But she never addresses Utikere's specific claims (the equity/revenue-hypothecation argument, the $6 billion figure) and most of her speech is prepared Green Party material on density, parking pricing and low-emission zones that would have been delivered whoever spoke before. Partial engagement with one strand, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "it's unfortunate that the former Minister of Transport didn't take the steps that the current Minister is taking to get this under way" and "the stark ability of the Minister of Transport to just basically foist on to communities a charging scheme"

acuity.statement: It’s interesting also to reflect that the Infrastructure Commission—who, I think, gives us really, really good advice—has also suggested that pricing across the board, and where there’s peak demand, not just for roading services or transport services but peak demand, we should put a price on that peak demand. We’ve already had that reference to milk, but it might apply to other resources as well—for example, power. We do that at the moment for a lot of our power use.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up the specific pricing-signal analogy Luxton had just developed at length (winter milk premiums as a model for peak road pricing), names it, and does something with it: he generalises it beyond transport to peak demand for other resources, citing the Infrastructure Commission's advice and the existing example of power pricing. The passage would have to change if Luxton had argued the point differently or not raised the analogy at all. Not 1.0 because he extends rather than tests the analogy, and the surrounding speech returns to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "similar to winter milk, it’s sending a signal" — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: I am a member of the hard-working Transport and Infrastructure Committee, ably chaired by Andy Foster here. I’m looking forward to receiving this bill and to interrogating the details further, and, to what the member from the Māori Party, Takutai Tarsh Kemp, said, to understanding the risks for working class members in our cities across the country and to making sure that it is workable, that it minimises risk not just for workers but also for small businesses, who are doing it tough out there at the moment.
acuity.explanation: Bidois names Kemp and takes up one strand of her argument — the burden on working-class people — and commits the select committee to examining it, so the speech would differ had she argued something else. But he engages none of her specific claims (the scrapped half-price fares, the Covec MRCagney finding on trip suppression, cut West Auckland train services); he converts the objection into a matter to be interrogated later and returns to prepared material on the bill's merits. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is our cleaners, our caregivers, our construction workers, many of whom are Māori and Pacific whānau, who will feel this the most." — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: This is a tool that, like congestion being a tax on time, can be an option that will make people rethink about travel arrangements. They’ve got an option of whether they can afford to pay the little bit extra because it’s worth it and built into a business model, or they’ll look at car pooling or public transport, or maybe starting earlier and finishing earlier. There’s a myriad of options.
acuity.explanation: Williams, immediately before, argued specifically that carpooling, off-peak travel and public transport are unavailable to rostered shift workers in South Auckland. Hamilton lists those same three options as "a myriad" without taking up the objection at all. His speech is on the matter under debate and contains a gesture at the other bench ("great to see the support from the other side of the House"), but engages no part of the argument just made — it would read identically whatever Williams had said. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "fair for shift workers like people who cannot choose when they travel, and how they travel, and are needing to get to work at times when there are no other colleagues that they can go with" — and her Wiri manufacturing-worker example.

acuity.statement: The Government members are talking about a tax on time, but we do need to recognise, actually, that this is a tax on Aucklanders. It’s a tax on Aucklanders because it costs them money to get from A to B.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact framing Hamilton had just used and does something with it: concedes the phrase, then inverts it to a tax on Aucklanders and supplies the reason. If Hamilton had framed the bill differently, this sentence would have to change, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — whether the reframing is a fair or well-reasoned move belongs to Rigor, and whether it is precise belongs to Specificity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "As the Minister mentioned, congestion is really a tax on time"

acuity.statement: Alone, I agree with Government members that this isn’t just one tool to fix congestion. What I’m looking for is what are the other tools alongside that that they are putting in place to ensure that Aucklanders have meaningful alternatives to take, at a lower cost, to get them from A to B in the speed that they want to.
acuity.explanation: Accepts Hamilton's "tool in the tool box" premise explicitly and then draws out its consequence — if the bill is only one tool, name the others — turning the concession into the question the Government must answer. This is the classic accept-part-and-press-the-rest move and is the strongest available evidence of having listened to the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "This is just another tool in the tool box" / "It’s not a silver bullet, but it’s another option"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to appreciate the contribution made by the Hon Dr Deborah Russell just then, walking us through the changes that were made at the Finance and Expenditure Committee. It is, of course, in those moments that we see that cordial working across the aisle to try and improve pieces of legislation, even if indeed we are opposed to those laws. Herein I just want to speak to firstly some of the parts of the legislation that the Greens do support but make the point that we cannot support the bill in its entirety because it entrenches the Government’s trickle-down tax cuts.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the preceding turn — she praises Russell's contribution and mirrors her structure (support some parts, oppose the bill over Part 1) — but does nothing with any argument Russell made, immediately pivoting to prepared Green material on trickle-down tax cuts. The speech is on the matter under debate and would read identically whatever Russell had argued, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Sitting in the Finance and Expenditure Committee, we did some work on that and to improve the particular set of measures that could be rolled out." — Swarbrick names Russell's walk-through of the select committee changes but takes up none of its content (the generic emergency-event measures, the QROPS/KiwiSaver change, the minor beneficiaries rule, or Russell's argument that the annual rates fail the country's fiscal needs).

acuity.statement: Well, that’s right, because under the last lot, we didn’t measure how public services were actually being delivered and what they were getting, and so we’re taking a different approach.
acuity.explanation: He takes up Swarbrick's interjection on the spot rather than talking past it: he concedes the point that services were not being delivered and turns it into an argument about the previous government's failure to measure delivery. The sentence only exists because of what she said — delete her interjection and the words "Well, that's right" have nothing to attach to. Not full marks because the interjection carried little content and he moves straight back to prepared ground about the Government's "different approach" rather than engaging a developed argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They’re not." — Chlöe Swarbrick, interjecting on the claim that New Zealanders are getting the public services they deserve

acuity.statement: But, again, the people who have specialised knowledge—and I do acknowledge the Hon Dr Deborah Russell and her contributions during the committee stage, because this stuff in here can put the ordinary New Zealander to sleep.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the turn immediately before — he echoes Stephenson's acknowledgement of Deborah Russell's technical contribution — but it engages a courtesy, not a claim or an argument. The rest of the speech (support for the thresholds, the Order in Council mechanism, pension transfers, submitter numbers) is prepared material on the bill that would read word-for-word the same whatever Stephenson had argued, so this sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is good to actually have some tax experts like the Hon Dr Deborah Russell on our committee." — Todd Stephenson

acuity.statement: Yes, there were parts that have been mentioned that were a technical change, but let us be clear: this bill is a technical solution. It is a gentle edit to the potential hopes and dreams that people of Aotearoa New Zealand could achieve, and this bill does nothing for most of the people of Aotearoa, in this case.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what preceded — the concession that parts of the bill are merely technical changes — and reframes it as the bill's central weakness, but then moves into prepared Green Party material (RIS figures, superannuation calculator, child poverty, Ka Ora Ka Ako) that engages none of Waititi's specific arguments about landlord tax cuts or wealth concentration. The speech would be largely identical had the preceding turn argued something different on the same topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "Yes, there are some good things in there, but there are a hell of a lot of other things we should be doing with our tax system."

acuity.statement: This is a tax cut that only benefits those that are earning those dollars—the dollars treated beneath $78,100. It’s a tax cut from low to middle income workers; it’s not skewed towards the wealthy. It’s effectively capped: the tax-cut benefit stops at every dollar earned after $78,100.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the central claim of both preceding Opposition turns — that the package favours the rich — and does something with it, supplying the threshold figures and the mechanism (the benefit caps out at $78,100) as a rebuttal of the distributional charge. Falls short of 1.0 because he does not take up the specific numbers put to him (the $1.6 billion to the top 40 percent, the 130,000 households getting nothing, the $750 million for landlords) and instead answers the general charge with his own prepared figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "the top 40 percent get a break of $1.6 billion or 55 percent of the break"

acuity.statement: It’s very telling what the last speaker Camilla Belich just said—things like “We take a holistic approach.” and “Tax reduction is all about timing.” We actually felt that, after 14 years and a cost of living crisis, it was actually pretty good timing.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton takes up the specific strand of Belich's argument — that the timing of the tax cuts was wrong — quotes it back and contests it directly with a counter-reason (14 years of the previous government and a cost of living crisis made the timing good). The engagement is real and pointable: this opening would have to change had Belich argued something else about the tax changes. It falls short of 1.0 because he disputes the conclusion without engaging her supporting evidence (health system pressure, the school lunch funding reduction) and then moves into prepared material on FamilyBoost, KiwiSaver and special purpose vehicles that is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "unfortunately the thing with tax cuts is timing is really important"

acuity.statement: Well, look, the irony, with a couple of minutes to go, of hearing from the spokesperson for economic development that he would oppose this bill. The best way to achieve economic development is actually to make sure hard-working people get to keep more of their hard-working dollars. Wellington does not know best, but people do.
acuity.explanation: Bidois picks up the specific strand Bennett built his speech on — that he speaks for economic development and that tax contribution underwrites wellbeing — and turns it directly against him, asserting that economic development is best served by people keeping their own earnings. That is a real engagement with the preceding turn and the speech would read differently had Bennett not framed himself that way. But it engages only the framing, not the substance Bennett actually argued (where hospital, school and public transport funding comes from after tax cuts, and the Kāinga Ora build cuts in New Plymouth), and then closes with prepared Friedman material that is indifferent to what preceded it. Partial engagement, so mid-band.

acuity.responding_to: "As the spokesperson for economic development, it is really interesting to look into the taxation and what it means" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: I’m very proud to be standing, as the last speaker, to support the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2024–25, Emergency Response, and Remedial Measures) Bill at the second reading. I think it’s time to make it clear now, after the 11 speakers before me, who spoke about the different parts in this bill: yes, it is a giant bill, in the way that it includes so many hundreds of changes.
acuity.explanation: Lu speaks immediately after Henare's opposing speech and gestures at the debate — she notes the 11 speakers before her and offers to "summarise all of the speakers above me" — but engages none of his actual claims. There is no answer on the Privacy Commissioner's submission, the overseas-superannuation problem, the family tax credit, or the $250-a-week figure; the speech is prepared summary plus a Deloitte quotation praising the bill, and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued. A gesture at the debate without engaging any strand of it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued the bill's information-sharing provisions drew concern from the Privacy Commissioner, that last year's tax cuts did not deliver the promised "up to $250 a week", and that the family tax credit is being mismanaged — "We can’t support this bill despite there being some parts in there that were started under our Government." — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: As others have noted, we’ve seen a change of Ministers who are shepherding this legislation, and I want to acknowledge the work of the select committees in charge of this legislation, particularly because, as the previous speaker, Glen Bennett, noted, it is technical legislation. It actually touches on a broad range of issues, so that requires some technical advice as well on behalf of the different public servants who were guiding us through these bills.
acuity.explanation: Takes up two identifiable strands of Bennett's turn — the change of Minister and the bill's technicality — and does something modest with the second, turning it into the premise of his own argument that MPs depend on well-resourced public servants for technical advice. It does not rebut or test anything Bennett said, and the bulk of the speech that follows is prepared material on immigration advisers that would have been delivered whatever Bennett argued, so this sits at partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "This bill, as I said, is technical." (and his observation that the bill arrived under Melissa Lee and returns under Nicola Willis)

For example, he mentioned the stand-down period for those who come from backgrounds like working in Immigration New Zealand, the Ministry for Primary Industries, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), or if somebody is a Minister of Immigration—the stand-down period for them to become a licensed immigration adviser. Those kinds of things came through, but they were not in the scope of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific submitter material the previous speaker spent most of his turn on — the immigration adviser stand-down periods — names it, and disposes of it by ruling it outside the bill's scope. The speech would have to change if he had raised something else, which is the deciding test. It falls short of 1.0 because it answers only the scope half and leaves untouched his actual argument, that the Government should pursue those contributions anyway rather than let them 'enter into a void'; whether she characterises his point accurately is a veracity/rigor question and is deliberately not scored here.

acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "I can accept that perhaps it would have sat outside of the scope of what we were looking at in the bill, but I think when we were asked to look at this—and particularly the changes to the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act—this is something that was encouraged to us to pay attention to"

acuity.statement: Ko te tino pūtake o tēnei, o ngēnei pire e rua, ko te whakawhanake ake i ngēnei o ngā ture, ka nui ngā ture ka whai pēhitanga ngēnei o ngā pire e rua.

Her speech is on the same matter — the purpose of the two bills is to modernise old statutes — but engages no part of what Unkovich actually argued; it is prepared material on the right subject and would read identically whoever had spoken before. Above 0.1 only because it is squarely about the bills under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich spoke about the 18 submitters to the Economic Development bill, the charities-law submission, the large-company audit fees of up to $100,000 and electronic signatures, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan picks up the characterisation the earlier speakers made — that these are technical, maintenance-style fixes needed to keep pace with technology — and restates it as his own premise before moving to his prepared material on offshore immigration advisers and the Regulations Review Committee. That is more than naming the previous speakers, but it is a glance at their framing rather than engagement with any specific claim they made, so it sits at the top of the low band rather than at 0.5.

acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "It’s a bit like repairs and maintenance, you may say, of a whole group of legislation." — and her account of the submitter who explained the need for electronic signatures.

acuity.statement: One of the more hotly contested bills we’ve had to consider! I serve on the Education and Workforce Committee. It’s my privilege to review bills like this very exciting omnibus legislation that the member who spoke before, Cameron Brewer, described. I wanted to just make, in my contribution, a couple of brief comments about the part of the bill that deals with amendments to the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act.
acuity.explanation: Brewer's turn described the bill as an omnibus measure amending 24 Acts, recommended unanimously by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee. Twyford names Brewer and borrows his 'exciting omnibus legislation' framing, but engages none of its content — he immediately pivots to prepared material on the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act clauses from his own committee's perspective. That is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the argument: his speech would read identically had Brewer said something else about the bill. On topic, so not 0.0; a mere reference, so not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is an omnibus bill that amends 24 Acts" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: I’d like to pick up the last comments of the previous member there, the Hon Phil Twyford, that this is about fine-tuning. When you’re trying to tune a radio and you’re a just a few clicks out, when you hear it, it’s that sweet sound, and if you’re in Hamilton or the mighty Waikato, you go to 97.8 or The Rock 93FM, or maybe ZB 97FM.
acuity.explanation: Twyford had made a substantive case about licensed immigration advisers, rogue unlicensed advisers, and the removal of the 12-month stand-down period. Hamilton quotes a single word from him — 'fine-tuning' — and turns it into a joke about Hamilton radio frequencies, engaging no part of the argument. Repeating an opponent's words in order to pivot away is explicitly not responsiveness; the speech would be unchanged whatever Twyford had argued. It remains nominally about the bill under debate, so above 0.0.

acuity.responding_to: "they allow a number of different regulatory Acts to be fine-tuned so that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment ... has an easier job of administering and carrying out its task" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: I am a part of the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee, but I want to talk, first of all, about the impact of the work done by my colleague on the Education and Workforce Committee, because I was listening very carefully to what the Hon Phil Twyford just said, and it resonated in my own electorate.
acuity.explanation: White takes up the specific strands of Twyford's contribution rather than the topic in general: she adopts his point that licensed advisers with knowledge of the system should become trusted advisers, and she corroborates his claim about unlicensed advisers with a case of her own ($5,000 charged for an unnecessary and misdirected application). Her speech would have to change had Twyford argued something different about the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act clauses, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because she accepts his case and extends it without rebutting or testing any part of it, and the back half of her speech returns to prepared material on employment agreements and the Financial Markets Authority. Agreement is scored on engagement, not on consensus.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Hardly a week would go by without someone coming to my office, seeking assistance and seeking immigration advice, who hasn’t fallen foul of an unlicensed immigration adviser" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: The second area that I wanted to cover was the amendments to the Health and Safety at Work Act. These are, as other members have stated, pragmatic changes that will make the Health and Safety at Work Act work more effectively.
acuity.explanation: Belich follows a substantive turn by Nancy Lu on the same two bills, so she is eligible. Her contribution is prepared material organised around her own three chosen areas; she gestures at the chamber's work ("as other members have stated", the select committee process) but engages no part of Lu's efficiency-and-growth argument, and would read identically whatever Lu had said. On topic but unresponsive to the specific claim, which sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu argued that the bills reduce red tape and that "efficient regulation is good for economic growth, which is exactly what we do as the National-led Government", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: As we know, not all change is, you know, sexy retail change that we go out and campaign on. A lot of it is around marginal tweaks to regulations that help improve people’s daily lives, and that is what these bills seek to do: to make very small tweaks to regulations so that people can go about their lives in a daily manner more efficiently, more effectively, without cumbersome regulations.
acuity.explanation: Bidois speaks immediately after Belich, who put a specific, addressable proposition to his party about bipartisanship on health and safety law. He engages none of it; his closing remarks characterise the bills in general terms and merely relay a colleague's earlier point that the legislation is omnibus. A bare reference to another member's words plus on-topic prepared material scores low, and the speech would be unchanged whatever Belich had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich made a direct plea to National members — "let us not lose the benefits of a bipartisan approach to health and safety" — and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I just want to say that the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has raised a lot of really, really important points. Because, again, let’s not forget that, from a criminal law perspective, the interaction between the Crimes Act 1961 and the Sentencing Act 2002 forms the very foundation of our criminal law system. In terms of getting these sorts of clarifications from the Minister, it’s absolutely crucial in guiding the way that we do look at criminal law cases going forward.
acuity.explanation: Webb's preceding turn made a detailed, specific argument: that the bill's new definition of a 'personal mitigating factor' in section 4 leaves it unclear whether things like provocation or self-defence fall inside the capped category. Xu-Nan names Webb and endorses his points as important, but engages no part of the content — he does not take up the personal/circumstantial distinction, the section 4 definition, or the provocation example, and instead moves to his own prepared questions on Amendment Paper timing, section 27 reports and consultation. That is a mere reference plus a gesture at the debate, which the rubric places at 0.3 rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a distinction between a mitigating factor of the circumstances of the offence and a personal mitigating factor" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Well, obviously there’s a wide range of opinions across society around sentencing law. For example, when we went to see members of the Sandringham Business Association in Auckland and people operating in the retail space, on many, many occasions it has been expressed to me the deep frustration of people who are just trying to make a living running a business or a dairy or any kind of retail business and find that they’re being attacked physically, and then, if someone is finally actually held to account and convicted in a court, reading the very long list of discounts offered so that the sentence ends up—and it’s always a question of judgment, but they feel it is—very far removed certainly from the maximum sentence, and maybe a home detention or some such outcome for a violent assault. There have been many, many people who have been concerned about the message that society is sending in terms of the seriousness of the consequences for convictions.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan closed by demanding to know who had expressed the concern that discounts are too high, having argued from the departmental report and regulatory impact statement that legal experts do not share it. Goldsmith answers that specific question directly and with named particulars — the Sandringham Business Association, retailers and dairy operators, and public reaction to open-justice court reporting — so the answer would have been different had the preceding question been different. Short of 1.0 because he does not take up the evidentiary core of Xu-Nan's challenge (that the departmental report and supplementary analysis show officials and the legal profession did not share the concern, and could not assess the new aggravating factors), nor the section 27 and consultation questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to check with the Minister: who are these people who expressed concerns about the fact that the current discount is too high?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I guess the second part, in terms of the delay in terms of this Amendment Paper as well, is whether the Minister has sought advice from the office of the Attorney-General, as all Amendment Papers should. One of the things I am interested in, and also have observed repeatedly, is that, particularly within the justice portfolio, there has been a reoccurring habit of Ministers introducing Amendment Papers during or just before the committee stage without going through the select committee process.
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by Helen White immediately precedes this, putting a specific question to the Minister about whether the guilty plea and youth discounts retain enough judicial flexibility. Xu-Nan takes up no part of that argument; he gestures at the debate by picking up an earlier contribution from Duncan Webb and noting the Minister is seeking advice on his own earlier question, then delivers three prepared questions on Amendment Paper 224. On topic (the same bill, same committee stage) but indifferent to what it follows, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band with the gesture earning 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White asked 'Are those factors sufficiently flexible in this situation?' about the guilty plea and youth discounts, and this statement does not take that up at all.

If you plead guilty at the first opportunity, yes, you get a significant discount; if it’s later in the time, you get a less significant one.

Goldsmith takes up one strand — the guilty plea discount she named — and explains the sliding scale, which bears directly on the timing of a plea she raised; but he answers the design of the discount rather than her question about preserved judicial discretion for genuine later remorse, and otherwise delivers prepared material on the 40 percent cap. acuity.statement: Now, just quickly addressing some of the issues raised by our friend from the Greens in terms of Amendment Papers being delivered late in the process: yes, this is an extremely busy Government. We’ve got a lot on our legislative agenda—a lot going on—and the blockage in the pipeline to getting even more done is working our way through all the pieces of legislation and the policy advice. Sometimes, in an imperfect world, we have an opportunity with a piece of legislation before the House on a particular topic to add a couple of things to it, and we take that opportunity rather than starting a whole new process with a separate piece of legislation.

acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "my understanding is that we are not punishing anybody who's involved in any white-collar crime whatsoever"

Marked down slightly only because Xu-Nan's immediately preceding party-liability questions are left untouched.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the 40 percent, where does it start?" — and "The courts and lawyers and defendants and prosecutors need to know where this discount starts."

The speech would have to change if he had itemised different factors, so it is squarely engaged with the content of what he just said rather than with the topic in general. acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "whether the offender has taken steps during proceedings to shorten the proceedings or reduce their cost"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan pressed the Minister on the rationale for the personal mitigating factors in section 4(a)(v), and this statement does not take that up — it sets it aside and opens new questions on clauses 5 and 6.

This reply takes up that strand directly — accepting both the restorative and rehabilitative purposes he named, then setting against them a third statutory purpose, denunciation, as the thing the amendment is aimed at. That is engaging the argument and doing something with it. Held at ~0.6 because only one of the several points raised is picked up: the statutory-interpretation question about the cross-heading and the request for a definition of 'adult' go unaddressed, and the remainder of the answer is general material on lenient sentences.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "it should be one that is restorative in nature and not punitive in nature"

Webb takes up that exact mechanism and does something with it — objecting that using legislation to dictate the House's own Standing Orders is unusual and, in effect, binds future Parliaments. The speech would have had to change if Goldsmith had proposed a different safeguard, so this is engagement with the content of the argument, not a gesture at the topic.

acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "The bill as introduced addresses that concern by strengthening the checks and balances on the Government through the select committee requirement to help balance the effect of a longer term."

This is a rebuttal aimed at the specific construction just explained.

acuity.statement: It’s not just three years to four, because, as Paul Goldsmith mentioned, with election campaigns and the bedding in an establishment of new Governments, three years is really two of effective debates and policy making and thinking. If we go to four years in total, we’re really going from an effective two years to an effective three years. It’s not a 33 percent increase; it’s a 50 percent increase in the effective length of a Government.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown's central objection was that three versus four years is a trivial difference against the horizon that real planning needs. Seymour takes up that one strand and does something with it — recasting the change as a shift from two to three effective years, a 50 percent rather than 33 percent increase — and elsewhere picks up her infrastructure-stability point by name ("parties as diverse as the National Party and the Greens"). But he credits the framing to Goldsmith rather than engaging her directly, and leaves her other arguments (the conditional, uncertain-in-advance term, the mismatch with local government terms, Matike Mai and broader constitutional reform) entirely untouched while delivering otherwise prepared ACT material. Partial engagement, pointable, then back to script.

acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "whether it’s three years or four years makes very little difference when you ought to be thinking several generations in advance"

acuity.explanation: Nakhle picks up one specific strand of the immediately preceding speech — Belich's call to study the Queensland transition to a four-year term — and supplies the detail of who the visiting member was and that he favoured the change, and echoes her due-diligence point. acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I would also like to encourage those on the Justice Committee to look to the examples of our near neighbours in Australia who we’ve been recently discussing the experience that they’ve had in Queensland"

acuity.statement: I also want to reflect on the fact that we have had referenda on this exact issue. In fact, if you’re six months older than me, you would have at least had your say on a referendum. That is because in 1990—when I was 17½—they had a referendum, and the results were this: 69.3 percent of Kiwis supported three years, and 30.6 percent of Kiwis supported four years a term. That was 35 years ago. More than two to one supported a three-year term, but 35 years is another generational shift, and perhaps we need to test them.
acuity.explanation: Henare complained that the debate lacks any analysis of why New Zealand rejected this question in past referenda. Brewer takes up exactly that strand, supplies the missing figures (1990: 69.3 to 30.6 percent; the earlier referendum at 68.1 percent), concedes the margin was more than two to one, and turns it into an argument that a generational shift warrants re-testing public opinion. He does not engage Henare's broader claim that the evidence does not show four years improves lawmaking, and some of the material (the LGNZ poll) is clearly prepared, so this is strong engagement with one strand rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "an analysis of why New Zealand rejected this same question or very similar question in previous times in the past" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: I guess my question is seeking the Minister’s clarification, because what we’re seeing as part of the regulatory impact statement for this is that, with the changes to the income tax bracket as set out in Schedule 1, we are seeing the fact that 130,000 New Zealanders will get no tax break, 8,000 New Zealanders would be worse off with the tax break, and the top 40 percent will, in effect, get 55 percent of the tax break, equating to $1.6 billion.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Megan Woods on the same Part 1 debate, so eligible. The statement is squarely on the matter under debate (the rates in Schedule 1) and gestures at the same general theme of whether alternatives were considered, but it engages no part of Woods' actual argument — not the school lunch funding claim, not the blame-shifting point about the previous Government, not her specific question about alternative revenue measures. It is prepared material on the right subject: it would read identically had Woods said something else about tax rates.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued Part 1 fails to 'generate sufficient revenue to adequately fund a school lunch programme' and asked the Minister whether 'they considering any alternative revenue measures', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: We don’t have that debate at any other time; the Part 1 debate of the annual tax bill is the time we do have this debate, so I would invite the members on the other side of the Chamber to consider participating in it.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by a different member (Xu-Nan, with specific regulatory impact statement figures and a tax-free-threshold question) immediately precedes it. The statement engages none of it: no response to the distributional figures, no comment on the tax-free bracket, no reference to his question to the Minister. It is a procedural-tradition framing of the Part 1 debate plus an invitation to Government and ACT members to speak, which would be word-for-word deliverable in any year's annual rates debate whoever had spoken before.
