It stays just above 0.0 only because it is about the subject actually under debate (tax rates in Part 1).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked whether there had been 'consideration around a tax-free bracket, for example, which we have seen working in Australia', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: These regulatory systems bills, for those who are watching the committee, are unanimously agreed and are non-contentious. I thank the member for her question around education, and I’ll take that back and ask the Minister in charge to consider that.
acuity.explanation: Belich put three things to the Minister: why the Education and Workforce Committee changes were absent from the legislative statement, how the new employer-retention duty interacts with electronic sharing of agreements and employee copies, and whether employees/employers will be educated and monitored. Upston takes up exactly one strand — the education question — and does something with it (undertakes to refer it to the Minister in charge). The legislative-statement question, which Belich flagged twice as her "first question", is left untouched, and the rest is a general characterisation of regulatory systems bills that would have fitted any question at all. One strand engaged, the rest prepared framing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if any information will be going out to employees about this additional obligation as well" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: Additionally, a question in general is these regulatory systems bills make sensible changes to Acts that help them to work more effectively, and I, in fact, wondered if the review that the Minister is undertaking in this area could perhaps, in many ways, be dealt with through a regulatory systems bill because of the fact that, in my view—and I’d be interested if the Minister shares this view, which I expressed yesterday—the health and safety in New Zealand should be ideally approached in a bipartisan manner. These are bipartisan bills that obtain support from parties, ideally, across the House and make sensible, pragmatic changes.
acuity.explanation: Belich picks up the Minister's own characterisation of these bills as unanimous and non-contentious and turns it into an argument: if that is what this vehicle is, then the health and safety review could be progressed the same way and keep its cross-party support. That is a real use of the preceding turn rather than a mention of it. But she concedes the point is prepared ("which I expressed yesterday") and the bulk of the turn moves on to fresh questions about Part 4 and the mining clauses that owe nothing to what Upston said, so this is partial engagement, not a reply built around the previous turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These regulatory systems bills, for those who are watching the committee, are unanimously agreed and are non-contentious" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I’m sure every member in this committee shares the member Camilla Belich’s interest in health and safety, but the review is out of scope of this regulatory systems bill, so I won’t be commenting on that.
acuity.explanation: This is aimed squarely at the thing Belich asked — the health and safety review and whether the Minister could say anything about it — and gives a stated reason for not answering it (scope), which is engagement with the question rather than a pivot elsewhere. It falls short of the top of the band because it meets the question on admissibility and not substance: Belich's specific proposition, that review-type changes could be carried in a regulatory systems bill and so preserve bipartisan support, is not taken up at all, and her Part 4 questions about the tourist-mining clarifications go unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm interested if she has any views that she can share, maybe she can't because of the fact that it hasn't been released yet, on how these will interact with that review" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: The other matter which I would be interested to find out some additional thoughts from the Minister on is in relation to Part 7, which is the section that talks about pre-term baby payments. Now, the Minister—and I thank the Minister for this—answered favourably in relation to the idea of education following this bill, but I think that perhaps this section is even more important.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's one substantive concession — that the education point would be referred on — and extends it to a different Part, arguing the case for publicity is stronger for pre-term baby payments than for the employment-agreement duty where the undertaking was given. The turn is therefore shaped by what the Minister actually conceded. It is only partial: the immediately preceding turn was the scope refusal on health and safety, which she does not contest or test, and most of what follows is prepared description of Part 7 that would have been delivered whatever the Minister had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I thank the member for her question around education, and I'll take that back and ask the Minister in charge to consider that" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Now, one of the things I highlighted in the second reading is the fact that we do see this loophole in our immigration system where unlicensed immigration advisers offshore are able to provide advice to potential international students when they are coming onshore to study. This has been also highlighted in media a number of times, where we do see international students being exploited as a result of having unlicensed immigration advisers offshore.
acuity.explanation: Eligible because substantive turns by two other members precede it, and it is about the bill under committee consideration, so it is not a zero. But it engages no part of anything said before it — not Belich's questions, and not the Minister's scope answer, which went to the very point he is about to run into. He expressly tells the committee this is material from his own second reading speech. It would read identically if the preceding turns had been on different Parts or had never been given, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich questioned the Minister on the legislative statement, the employment-agreement retention duty, Part 4 health and safety, and Part 7 pre-term baby payments, and Louise Upston answered that the health and safety review was out of scope — this statement takes up none of it

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and I thank the member for his question. This was a matter that was raised in the select committee consideration of the bill, but it was considered to be outside of the scope of this regulatory systems bill. They’re very tight in scope in nature and are non-controversial, so it wasn’t able to be considered as part of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan asked two linked things: whether amending section 11(h) of the Immigration Advisers Licensing Act had been considered, and if not, what advice the Minister had received on why it was left alone. The reply answers the first directly and informatively — the matter was raised at select committee and ruled outside scope — and supplies the reason, which is the content of his second question. The speech could not have been given in response to a different question. Short of 1.0 only because it does not address the advice limb or the substantive loophole he described.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "was there any consideration being given when we are looking at potentially amending section 11?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, just talked about, the particular context in relation to this bill is that there is a number of—actually, probably what’s more missing is revenue measures to help the Government balance their books, and I do understand the Government is taking a sort of cut across the board in order to bring in that type of revenue—or “savings”, as they would say—very similar to the fiscal savings programme that our Government ran of 1 to 2 percent just before the election.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds takes up the specific strand Russell closed on — that the Government has notified no new revenue measures and is relying on cuts instead — restates it as 'what's more missing is revenue measures', and develops it into her own questions to the Minister about corporate tax cuts and the digital services tax. She engages the substance rather than merely name-checking the previous speaker, but after that one strand she moves to her own prepared lines of questioning, and she does not contest or extend Russell's specific examples (health, education, school lunches, defence spending). Partial but pointable engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "and that Minister of Revenue has not notified any new measures that he is going to take in order to increase revenue"

acuity.statement: Of course, at the election, we had National coming out and talking about the number of people that would be eligible for $250 a fortnight in the tax cuts that were laid out in their plan. How is that translated into the legislation, and how many New Zealanders or New Zealand families have received $252 or more from the tax measures laid out in this piece of legislation?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive ministerial turn immediately precedes it. The question is squarely on the bill under debate (Schedule 1), so it is not unmoored, but it opens an entirely new strand and engages no part of what Watts had just said about growth, company tax or the digital services tax. The question would read identically whatever the Minister had answered, which places it in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on economic growth, corporate tax and the digital services tax, and this statement does not take any of those up

acuity.statement: It does raise the question—because the Minister said that the strategy is to go for economic growth; there’s a good question around that, Minister—and that is: which measures in this bill are going to generate the economic growth that you say will look after the revenue system? Now, there’s not any in particular that I can see that actually go towards economic growth, per se.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated answer to her earlier question, restates it accurately, and then does something with it: presses it for the specific bill provisions that would deliver the growth it relies on, and asserts there are none. The speech could not have been delivered had Watts answered differently — it is built entirely on the answer he gave. Disagreement scored high, per the rubric; the quality of the inference and the tone are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the thing that the Minister of Revenue is doing, and what all Ministers in this Government are doing, is focusing on increasing economic growth" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Because I know that there was a change in the Minister in the chair, just to remind the Minister that I did ask a question earlier on, around clause 3, which is with regard to the fact that we have seen in the report that the way that the tax adjustment has worked in Schedule 1 of this Act meant that 130,000 households are going to get no tax relief, and 8,000 households are going to be worse off as part of this.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: substantive turns by Watts, Woods and Russell precede it. The statement is on the matter under debate (Schedule 1 and clause 3), earning it above the floor, but it explicitly re-puts a question the speaker had asked before this exchange rather than engaging anything said in it — including Woods' closely related question about how the Schedule 1 cuts are distributed. Prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just pressed the Minister on which measures in the bill generate economic growth, and this statement does not take that up — it re-puts the speaker's own earlier question

acuity.statement: This question earlier on around one of the policies in here that does support economic growth—we’ve got the approved issuer levy as one example of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the thing the preceding turn demanded — a named growth-supporting measure in the bill — which is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference, and the reply would be different had Russell pressed a different point. Short of 1.0 because it offers a single example and does nothing with her stronger claim that no such measures exist, and it leaves Xu-Nan's two questions untouched. Whether one levy actually answers the challenge is a Rigor question, not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which measures in this bill are going to generate the economic growth that you say will look after the revenue system?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Thank you, Minister, for your response. I just want to have a very quick follow-up question regarding this having unintended consequences. I want to just check again with the Minister of Revenue that, when we are looking at those personal tax rates, the Minister has received any advice around the fact that, in Australia, they do have a A$15,000 tax-free bracket, and whether that has been taken into consideration on the rate of emigration out of Aotearoa New Zealand as a result of the fact we have unfavourable tax conditions for people who are at the start of their career or earning lower salaries.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated reason for rejecting a tax-free band — 'unintended consequences' — names it back and presses on it, asking what advice sits behind it and offering the Australian A$15,000 band as the comparator the Minister's claim has to survive. The question could not have been asked in this form if Watts had given a different answer, which is the mark of real engagement; it stops short of 1.0 only because it adds a fresh strand (emigration) rather than contesting the consequences argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our policy position was that the counterfactual on those type of tax-free bands has unintended consequences on certain taxpayer groups" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Just to the member Lawrence Xu-Nan’s question in regards to the comparatives between Australia and New Zealand, I think it’s a fair question. What we do know is that, when you compare a like-for-like example in terms of salary between New Zealand and Australia, while there are some points of differential in the thresholds as you proceed through different income levels, actually in the main, there is a degree of where the New Zealand taxpayer actually starts to move ahead of the Australian taxpayer, particularly at the upper ends of the income threshold.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific comparison that was just put to him: he accepts the question as fair, meets the Australia/New Zealand threshold comparison head-on, and gives a substantive counter — that across income levels the New Zealand taxpayer comes out ahead, particularly higher up. This reply only exists because of the question asked immediately before it. Not 1.0 because it addresses the threshold comparison rather than the emigration consequence Xu-Nan hung the question on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in Australia, they do have a A$15,000 tax-free bracket" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I just wonder if the Minister could tell us whether or not the Government—he as Minister; or the Government more broadly—received advice on raising tax revenue from sources other than taxing income and salaries, what other measures was the Government given advice on in terms of that, particularly advice from Treasury, and whether or not the Government has given any active consideration to that.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the setting of tax rates and the advice behind them — and it borrows the 'has the Minister received advice' framing from the exchange it follows, but it engages no part of the argument Watts had just made about jurisdictional comparability. It is a prepared question on the right subject that would read identically whatever the Minister had just said, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just argued that a like-for-like Australia/New Zealand comparison fails because of New Zealand's abatements and Working for Families, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: We charge on every dollar that a cleaner earns, that a security guard earns, that a teacher earns, that a nurse earns, but we do not have what the Minister described as a “broad based - low rate system”—his words just before the dinner break. I think the Minister needs to defend that, because we do not tax all the income that is earned from buying and selling houses in this country. We do not tax capital gains in this country. In fact, we have very few taxes on capital income at all. To describe us as having a “broad based - low rate system” is just not correct.
acuity.explanation: Takes a specific phrase the Minister used earlier in the debate, quotes it back with attribution, concedes the half of it she accepts (the rates are low enough) and then attacks the other half with reasons — that income from house sales and capital gains goes untaxed, so the base is not broad. The speech is wholly shaped by what Watts said; substitute a different ministerial answer and it would have to be rewritten. Demolishing an argument is the strongest evidence of having listened to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The broad based - low rate model that we have in terms of the bandings is an area in which, as a Government, we felt was the most appropriate manner." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I’m also interested in the Minister’s thoughts about whether the revenue stream generated is enough for the costs which the Government is facing, because it’s pretty clear the Government has made some decisions which have reduced revenue over time, including brightline and interest deductibility—that obviously has shrunk the revenue pool.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one live strand of the preceding turn — that the revenue system is not raising enough for what the State must fund — and advances it with specific causes Russell had not named, brightline and interest deductibility. But it takes up neither her central challenge on the 'broad based - low rate' description nor Watts's comparability argument, and much of the surrounding call is a prepared curiosity about the annual rate-setting cycle, so this sits at partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are concerned about the extent to which it is not generating sufficient revenue to pay for everything that Government needs to do." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I guess one context that has been raised is: have we got a tax system that is able to deliver upon the revenue required in order to fund our public services? The reality is, for those who are watching at home, there’s a correlation between the size of the economy and the tax on that economy and how much tax we collect. Surprisingly, when the economy is in recession and is smaller, the tax take is smaller, and I appreciate that that might be enlightening for many, but, actually, that’s the reality.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the shared question the previous two speakers put — is the revenue adequate to fund public services — restates it and answers it on its own terms, arguing the tax take tracks the size of the economy and that growing the base beats raising rates. That is genuine engagement with one strand. It is only half marks because the specific challenges left on the table go unanswered: Russell expressly demanded he defend the 'broad based - low rate' description and named untaxed capital gains, and Webb named brightline and interest deductibility, and this reply takes up neither.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether the revenue stream generated is enough for the costs which the Government is facing" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Actually, what’s on the Government books is showing no matter what this Government’s mandate is around growth, the actual accounts for growth are affected more by what’s happening overseas, and it hasn’t really been taken into account in the fiscal policy by this Government.
acuity.explanation: Watts closed his turn by resting the Government's fiscal case on growing the economy. Edmonds takes that exact claim and tests it against the Government's own forecasts, quoting the Treasury chief economist's downward revision, and then puts two consequential questions back to the Minister about where the growth policies in this bill are. Her speech would have to change entirely if Watts had argued something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are focused on growing the economy, and I think that that’s the most sustainable place that we can take our country, going forward" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The approved issuer levy (AIL) scheme allows them to use a rate in the region of 2 percent versus the non-resident withholding tax rate of 10 to 15 percent. Quite simply, two is less than 10 to 15.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds asked specifically why the approved issuer levy counts as a growth measure given it already exists and differs only from non-resident withholding tax. Watts takes up that precise point and supplies the mechanism and the rate comparison she asked about. Marked down from 1.0 because he engages only the AIL strand and leaves her questions about the forecast growth figures and the $9 billion revenue loss untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m a little bit perplexed as to why the approved issuer levy (AIL) would be a growth policy for this bill." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: He’s been talking a lot about this Government and their obsession with economic growth—growth, growth!—and my question is around that because I don’t feel like he’s actually addressed the question.
acuity.explanation: Bennett picks up the growth theme of the Minister's turns and asks for something more tangible, so he is engaging the topic under debate, but he does not take up the AIL mechanism Watts had just explained or the rate comparison he offered. After the opening gesture he moves to prepared material about touring economic development agencies and the previous Government's industry transformation plans, which would read the same whatever the Minister had just said about the levy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are focused on growing the economy, and I think that that’s the most sustainable place that we can take our country, going forward" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I want to take a slightly different line of questioning to the Minister and ask him about the relationship between the annual rates of income tax and the predictors and drivers of that in terms of how much tax is collected and then the impact of some of the changes that were made under the previous Government in some big areas of spending, particularly related to multi-year funding.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Parker's substantive turn precedes it. Boyack announces outright that she is taking 'a slightly different line of questioning' and then delivers prepared material on multi-year health funding and revenue adequacy. It engages the matter under debate (Part 1, annual rates of income tax) but no part of the preceding argument; the speech would read identically whatever Parker had said. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is squarely on the clause before the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Parker spoke immediately before, arguing that the Inland Revenue high-wealth study and Treasury analysis were not politicised and asking what evidence the Minister had to the contrary, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I want to go back to this issue of economic growth that the Minister of Revenue raised. In particular, I want to talk about the economic growth measures that he asserted were in this bill.
acuity.explanation: She explicitly reaches back past the two preceding members to an earlier ministerial answer, so her engagement cannot be anchored in any preceding turn in this stretch. That puts it in the 0.0-0.3 band; 0.3 because it is closely tied to the debate in progress and to a specific claim made in it, not generic prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing in the preceding turns: Rachel Boyack immediately before asked 'how can we be sure that the annual setting of tax is sufficient to provide for the multi-year funding?' and David Parker before her argued the IRD study was not politicised; Russell takes up neither, instead returning to the Minister's earlier call ('he said that the change to the approved issuer levy (AIL) was an economic growth measure'), which is not among the turns preceding her here.

acuity.statement: The Minister made the proper point that the Government wants to have a tax system that promotes growth, and I think we all want that. My question of the Minister is: what advice has he received as to whether the current tax settings promote investment that is in new plant and investment and jobs, compared with investments that are in speculative asset classes, the income from which is not taxed?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the growth strand Russell had just pressed, concedes the premise ('I think we all want that'), and then turns it into a sharper version of her question — whether the settings actually direct capital to productive investment rather than untaxed speculative asset classes. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had been on a different strand, which is what earns an above-0.5 score; it is not 1.0 because he does not engage Russell's specific AIL point or her figures, and reverts to his own prepared OECD/IMF/Treasury line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell, immediately before: 'given that the Minister had said that the way we grow our tax base is by growing the economy, I want to know what other growth measures are there in this tax bill?'

acuity.statement: I mean, it would be fair to say that I receive a wide range of advice in regards to the broader tax settings. In the context of the priority for this Government, around economic growth, we are very much looking at what opportunities in terms of tax settings changes would enable us to fuel that economic growth that is required within our economy.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand and not the claim. He answers the 'what advice' frame and expressly agrees with Parker on lifting investment in value-deriving assets, which is pointable engagement; but he never takes up the specific contention that OECD, IMF and Treasury advice identifies a distortion toward residential rentals, and finishes on general government-priority material. Half-engagement, so 0.5. Scored on engagement only — the vagueness of the answer belongs to Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker, immediately before: 'Has the Minister received any recent advice from Inland Revenue prior to setting these rates that would justify him ignoring the advice of the OECD, the IMF, and the Treasury?'

acuity.statement: I want to pick up a point that the Minister of Revenue discussed in relation to debt. He spoke about the Government’s compliance focus and around an $8 billion debt—basically to try and attack that $8 billion debt. I want to ask the Minister if he can provide a breakdown of what that $8 billion debt is—like, the different tax types there are.
acuity.explanation: She picks up a ministerial point, but not the one in the turn she follows, so her responsiveness cannot be anchored to a preceding turn in this stretch and sits in the 0.0-0.3 band. 0.3 rather than lower because she names a specific figure the Minister had put into the debate and asks a pointed question about it, so it is clearly a contribution to this debate and not portable prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing in the preceding turn: Simon Watts immediately before said 'we are very much looking at what opportunities in terms of tax settings changes would enable us to fuel that economic growth', and Edmonds does not take that up, reaching instead to an earlier ministerial remark about an $8 billion tax debt.

acuity.statement: This part of the bill confirms income tax rates at the same rate as last year on the same narrow definition of income. I want to ask the Minister of Revenue: what is the most up-to-date information that he has as to the distribution of income at the top end, and how much of the income of high-income and wealth holders in New Zealand is taxed?
acuity.explanation: Bennett has just spent a full turn arguing the Government's growth commitment is rhetoric and that mining and oil and gas are 'short-term sugar hits'. Parker takes up none of that — not the growth argument, not the sugar-hit framing, not the Kāinga Ora point. He opens an entirely new line on the effective tax rates of the wealthy. It is squarely on the part of the bill under debate, which keeps it out of the 0.0 band, but the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Bennett had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued the Government's growth agenda is 'platitudes' and that coal and gold are 'short-term sugar hits', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The high-wealth work that the member the Hon David Parker is referring to was a piece of work undertaken by the last Government in 2023. This has not been further investigated since that point, and the reason, for a little bit more history on why—you’ll recall that the calls by the Finance and Expenditure Committee of the time to call in IRD to be able to discuss the integrity and the substantiation in that report were blocked by the Government members of that time.
acuity.explanation: Parker asked three specific questions, the first being what the most up-to-date information on the taxation of high-income and wealth holders is. Watts identifies the exact study Parker was quoting and answers that first question directly — 2023, nothing since — and then supplies a reason. That is genuine engagement with the substance, and the speech would have to change if Parker had cited different evidence. It falls short of 1.0 because the two remaining questions (compounding inequality, the OECD comparison) go untouched and he does not engage any of Parker's figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the most up-to-date information that he has as to the distribution of income at the top end" — David Parker

acuity.statement: The other thing that Inland Revenue—and the member over there interjects and says that was, like, four years ago, but it’s important to understand that that’s the basis of the return on investment, and it goes directly to the Minister’s comments about $8 billion of debt being left around.
acuity.explanation: She takes up MacLeod's interjection by its actual content — that the COVID period is too long ago to matter — and answers that specific objection by explaining why the 2020-22 diversion of IRD staff is the baseline for the return-on-investment claim. The sentence would not exist if MacLeod had said something else, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because the thing engaged was a one-clause interjection rather than a developed argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Three, four years ago." — David MacLeod

acuity.statement: Thanks to the member the Hon Barbara Edmonds for the question. The breakdown in terms of the $8 billion—this is as at 30 June 2024—and these are rounded numbers just for the context of the discussion, but $2 billion of that relates to individuals; $1 billion of that relates to companies; $3 billion relates to GST; $1.5 billion to employers, so PAYE; and then half a billion of others, such as Working for Families.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing the preceding turn asked for: a component-by-component decomposition of the $8 billion, with the as-at date. This is the textbook high-acuity case — the reply is wholly determined by the specific request that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If the Minister can provide a breakdown, I’d be really appreciative of that." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I mean, no one’s arguing with the member in the context of the challenges that New Zealand went through at that time; I’m simply recognising the fact that, as a Government, that’s the situation in which we’ve inherited, and for every dollar that we don’t collect in tax debt, that’s a dollar that needs to be borrowed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up her COVID-context argument, concedes the factual part of it, and then disputes what she drew from it — that the pandemic explanation changes the case for resourcing compliance now. Accepting part and contesting the rest is engagement with the argument as made, not merely with its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we were coming from a very different period in time because of the pandemic" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I’ve got a question about the income tax rate for companies. There’s been a bit of discussion in the media and from the Minister in the chair, I think, as well as contributions from other members, with some people speculating that it might be a good idea for New Zealand to drop the company tax rate, and I’m not expressing an opinion for or against that.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the bill's rates — and it gestures at earlier contributions in general terms, but it engages no part of the preceding answer and would read identically had Watts said something entirely different. Prepared material on the right subject, so the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 for the gesture at what others have said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just broken the $8 billion of tax debt into its components and argued uncollected debt must be borrowed, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Thanks to the member the Hon David Parker for the question. There are no elements within the current bill that we’re discussing that relate to any changes of the corporate tax rate. In that context, there’s nothing further to add.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the question put rather than pivoting elsewhere, and answers it by contesting its premise — that the bill touches the company rate. But it takes up none of the substance Parker actually asked about (advice on imputation credits versus a lower final tax), so it is engagement with the topic and not the claim. Whether the deflection was evasive is a Forthrightness question, not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether he’s had any analysis done by the ministry as to what would be the distributional effects and the fiscal effects of moving from a dividend imputation credit regime" — David Parker

acuity.statement: It’s an interesting question because, of course, the Minister made the point that collecting a dollar of money owed was perhaps one less dollar that needed to be borrowed. I’m not quite sure it’s quite such a simplistic relationship but, I take the point. But it won’t have any impact on Government revenue, because that has presumably already been booked in previous years.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own proposition back and then does something with it: draws out its accounting consequence, that debt already booked as revenue in prior years cannot add to this year's operating balance. The argument is built on the preceding turn and could not stand without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "for every dollar that we don’t collect in tax debt, that’s a dollar that needs to be borrowed" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Just to provide the Minister of Revenue with some time, as he considers a response in relation to that previous question by the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, is to actually jog the committee’s memory back to when the brightline test actually came in.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific clause 5 question and does something with it: supplies the legislative history of the brightline test (the subjective intention test under section CB 6, the 2015 bright-line, the extension to 10 years and the return to two), then extends the same question to clause 16 and offers a hypothesis — that the provision corrects a drafting error — asking which change introduced it. The speech would be materially different had Russell raised a different point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m just curious as to why, if an executor or beneficiary disposes of it, that doesn’t count within the brightline test." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: This actually is a remedial matter to correct a drafting error. The context of this is that obviously when someone inherits land, that’s not planned in that context, and hence why we’ve used the opportunity to ensure that there is an exclusion for transfers of inherited land. That means, in effect, that land that is inherited will not be subject to the brightline test.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — why the executor/beneficiary disposal sits outside the brightline test — and confirms Edmonds's hypothesis that it is a drafting-error correction. Marked down from the top because it leaves Edmonds's second question (which legislative change introduced the error) untouched, and opens with content-free banter.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "an explanation as to why that disposal by an executor, administrator, or beneficiary of an estate to a third party is actually exempt from the brightline test" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The drafting error getting fixed—that makes good sense, obviously. It does beg the question of what happened to the people who were affected by it while the drafting error was in place.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's answer and draws out its consequence: if the drafting was wrong, what of taxpayers caught by the defective wording before the fix. The follow-up exists only because of what Watts just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This actually is a remedial matter to correct a drafting error." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: It’s a retrospective change going back to 1 July 2024, which was when the two-year brightline test comes into effect, for those individuals that are watching this evening, because we did think about that and that’s why we’re doing a retrospective change.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the precise answer to the consequence Russell had just drawn out — the amendment applies retrospectively from the date the two-year test took effect, so those caught in the interval are covered. Directly keyed to the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what happened to the people who were affected by it while the drafting error was in place" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The question I have, therefore, is that the Minister has said that only a small amount of people will be affected by this. How much revenue does the Minister expect to collect from this particular new income tax—because it’s a new tax, or it actually just clarifies that royalties from artists’ resale rights are, basically, taxable. The question is: if it’s a small amount, do those taxpayers that now will have an assessment which is backdated—what is the impact of interest and penalties on those taxpayers?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim Watts had just made — that only a very small number of people are involved and so retrospectivity has no significant implication — and does something with it: asks what revenue that small number yields, and presses the consequence he left out, namely interest and penalties on backdated assessments. The speech would be different had Watts not rested his answer on smallness of scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "a very small number of people are involved as art market professionals in regards to the implications around GST, so our assessment is that that won’t have a significant implication"

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Barbara Edmonds for the question. I think, in the context of Estimates, it’s within a quantum of $150,000. It’s not a material amount of money. It impacts, I think, of latest stats, probably less than 100 individuals, or 100 sales of qualifying artwork have occurred since the scheme came into play, from 1 December 2024.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the figure asked for — the expected revenue and the number of affected taxpayers — which is squarely responsive to one strand of Edmonds' question. But the second strand she pressed hardest, the interest and penalties consequences of a statutory backdating, is left untouched, so the engagement is partial rather than complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "How much revenue does the Minister expect to collect from this particular new income tax"

acuity.statement: There’s plenty of stuff we could carry on and talk about, and I do want to get through it. There’s just one little bit that’s a little bit interesting in clause 11B, which amends section CE 5—it’s expenditure on account of an employee, is the particular.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive answer by Watts on the resale royalty revenue immediately precedes — but this turn engages no part of it, neither accepting nor contesting the $150,000 figure or the penalties point her colleague raised. It opens a fresh line on a different clause. The material is on the right subject (the bill in committee), which keeps it above zero, but it is indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts gave a revenue quantum of $150,000 and fewer than 100 affected sales, and this statement does not take that up, moving instead to clause 11B.

acuity.statement: There was a question earlier around clause 11B, and I actually think this is quite a—well, it’s an innovative and a positive change in the tax legislation; this is in regards to employer-funded flu vaccinations. The amendment that’s being proposed here is to ensure that employers are no worse off if they reimburse an employee for the benefit relating to a specific workplace health and safety risk.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Russell's request to explain how the new CW 17D exemption fits with section CE 5's definition of expenditure on account of an employee, and answers it with the actual mechanism (a fringe benefit tax exemption for employer-funded flu vaccinations). It falls short of 1.0 because her other specific question — how much of the emergency-response package was inherited from the previous Government's work versus novel to his own — is answered with a description of the Order in Council mechanism rather than the continuity question she put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Could the Minister of Revenue explain how that fits into the definition of that particular section—how it works?"

acuity.statement: The amendment ensures that the brightline period does not restart where land is acquired as co-owners and is subsequently subdivided. I think you would get that it would make sense that the fact that the land is being subdivided subsequently shouldn’t automatically trigger the brightline test coming into play. It was never intended from the brightline test period that it should, in effect, restart in periods such as a subdivision, for example.
acuity.explanation: Russell asked specifically what the amendment to section CB 15E achieves and what common-sense purpose the convoluted wording serves. Watts supplies exactly that: the effect (the brightline period does not restart) and the policy intent behind it. The answer would be different had she asked about a different clause, so it is squarely shaped by the preceding turn. Short of 1.0 only because he explains the effect rather than unpacking the (b) wording she quoted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I wonder if the Minister could just sort of unpack that clause a little to explain what the effect of the amendment to section CB 15E is and how it actually achieves a common-sense purpose."

acuity.statement: Can the Minister just clarify from his response: will this new extension of the scope—which, basically, as I understand it, is to assure that the rules applied when the land was acquired on a subdivision between co-owners and then subsequently disposed of are operating as intended—actually apply to actual property developers? I would have thought that that would be covered under a different set of rules. Could the Minister clarify that or get some advice on it?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given answer, restates its content accurately, and draws out the consequence he left open — whether the co-owner subdivision carve-out also reaches people in the business of developing and subdividing land. The question could not have been asked without having listened to the specific answer, and would have to be rewritten if he had described the amendment differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "The amendment ensures that the brightline period does not restart where land is acquired as co-owners and is subsequently subdivided."

acuity.statement: The example that we’re referring to here is land that is co-owned. If the three of us at the top table here own a section of land and we’ve purchased it, what we are saying is that, if we subsequently then subdivide that land for our own purpose, the mere point of subdivision isn’t a trigger point for the brightline test having to reset again, OK? That’s the context which this specific point of tax detail is relevant to, and it’s not anything broader than that.
acuity.explanation: Engages the scope strand of Edmonds' question — the closing "it's not anything broader than that" answers whether the provision reaches beyond co-owners — and illustrates it with a worked example. But it does not take up her distinct point about how the land rules treat those in the business of developing and subdividing, nor does he undertake to get the advice she asked for, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "does this apply to property developers and to those where there has been a substantial change in ownership"

acuity.statement: This ordinarily would be counted as income. We don’t even need a special rule for this. This is just income according to ordinary accounting concepts and so on. Why the need to put sections into the Income Tax Act to say something is income, which according to ordinary accounting concepts—which I know the Minister is familiar with himself—would actually be counted as income anyway?
acuity.explanation: A prepared question on the next clause of the same bill. It is plainly on the matter under debate, but engages no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer on co-ownership and the brightline test — the question would read identically whatever he had just said about subdivision. On-topic prepared material rather than responsive debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just explained that subdivision by co-owners does not reset the brightline test, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: I still don’t know the answer to this, as to why an amount of income derived by a trustee of the Auckland Future Fund is exempt income. I wonder if the confusion is arising because—it is a long time since I looked at the trust. If it’s derived by a trustee, is that—it’s actually the trust’s income rather than the trustee’s personal income?
acuity.explanation: Takes Watts' answer about new section CW 39B and says precisely what it failed to resolve, then narrows the question to a specific legal distinction (trust income versus the trustee's personal income). The speech would be different if Watts had explained the exemption rather than the GST framing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "You’re right that that is in the context of the income exemption only."

acuity.statement: No problem; that’s why we’re here, so let’s engage in a little bit more dialogue on what is a very important clause in this very important bill. The income of the trustee is the trust’s income, not the income of the person doing the role. The purpose of this legislative change is just simply recognising that point of detail and ensuring that the overarching trust is taxed appropriately.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact distinction just put to him, in the same terms it was put, and connects it to the purpose of the clause. Could not have been delivered against any other preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "is that—it’s actually the trust’s income rather than the trustee’s personal income?"

acuity.statement: It took me a while to figure that out. I’m glad I was getting to the explanation myself, because I knew there was something weird going on which I wasn’t quite getting. We’ve got that clarified now.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly accepts the clarification just given and registers that it resolved her question, but then moves on to a separate prepared line of argument about the New Zealand Superannuation Fund rather than doing anything further with the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "The income of the trustee is the trust’s income, not the income of the person doing the role."

acuity.statement: The question that I have in relation to clause 16 is that I just need to understand whether—because I understand when this came in or when the application date—I think the application for that will be effective for disposals of land as part of partitions or subdivision transactions on or after 27 March 2021. That’s the application date for this clause 16, which we just spent a bit of time fixing up the drafting of it because it was a little bit unclear and some of the submissions were coming through to say just to clarify it a little bit.
acuity.explanation: On the right matter — the same bill, in committee — and gestures at the running exchange with the Minister, but engages no part of the preceding argument. It is her own clause-by-clause tour of the bill and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said about the Future Fund.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued that the Auckland Future Fund's exempt income is special treatment relative to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much. Just going back to the member Deborah Russell’s point around the Auckland Future Fund and the question of whether they’re receiving special treatment in the context of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. Well, as the member will be aware, councils are exempt from most income tax. In the context, Auckland Council is exempt from income tax, and the Auckland Future Fund will also receive the same treatment as other councils.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific charge put to him and supplies a reason directed at it — the fund takes the council's own exempt status, so the comparison class is other councils rather than the Super Fund. Reaches back past the immediately preceding speaker to answer an argument actually made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Why is the Auckland Future Fund getting this, frankly, rather special treatment?"

acuity.statement: I want to go back to this Auckland Future Fund, and I take the Minister of Revenue’s point that local bodies, councils are not by and large subject to taxation. That’s a very good point.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the Minister's answer on its own terms and then reasserts the narrower part of her claim that it did not meet — special treatment relative to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund rather than relative to councils. Accepting part and disputing the rest is direct engagement with the reasoning just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "councils are exempt from most income tax"

acuity.statement: Going back to clause 16B, which is referencing section CW 3C, the question was in regard to the date and the timing of that. In effect, what this remedial is doing is it’s applying from the date that the section was originally applied for—i.e., that the change came into effect on that date—and we’re making sure that the legislation is aligned and refers to the date on which it came into effect.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the application-date question and gives a reason for it, so one strand of the question asked is genuinely answered; but it leaves untouched her second strand about the treatment of disposals made before 2021 under earlier bright-line periods.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "why is it to 27 March 2021?"

acuity.statement: The second question, in regard to the points around royalties, is the section which I provided a context for earlier this evening, in the context of the number of individuals that are impacted and the quantum of impact. We’ve covered that.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the question that was asked and locates it, but engages it only by declaring it already dealt with earlier in the evening; the policy intent she asked about is not taken up. Pointable engagement with the question, little done with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "could the Minister please explain the policy intent behind this deemed payments for services relating to resale royalties"

acuity.statement: Thank you very much to the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell for those two questions. First one, in regards to the question regarding clause 7B on the emissions unit: in effect, this is, I guess, what you’d define as the legislative clean-up clause; it simply covers the surrender of emissions units because of being no longer involved in forestry under the emissions trading scheme—i.e., the forestry exit—the ETS. That’s the purpose of that clause 7B.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific outstanding question about clause 7B that had been pressed from the other side and supplies the policy intent asked for — that it is a clean-up clause covering surrender of units on exiting forestry in the ETS. The answer could not have been given in response to a different question, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "understanding the policy intent behind that, because I couldn’t find the commentary in relation to that" — Barbara Edmonds, on clause 7B and the disposal of emissions units

acuity.statement: I’m sorry, I have found that explanation quite confusing because new section CW 39B is a section that will fit within Part C of the Income Tax Act. I’m not sure then how it relates to the GST, which is the Goods and Services Tax Act. That was just a little bit confusing.
acuity.explanation: Engages the content of the answer just given rather than the topic: identifies precisely that the Minister's GST-based explanation cannot account for a provision sitting in Part C of the Income Tax Act. Had he answered differently, this reply could not have been made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the proposed amendments would provide that the Auckland Future Fund is deemed to have a taxable activity for GST purposes" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: My question is: if a trustee is sitting on the Auckland Future Fund—so they’ve been appointed as a trustee. They may have received distributions from the trust—for example, for their time, for payment for them, as some trustees do; professional trustees get paid for the time that they sit on a trust and for the work that they do. I just don’t understand why this is being treated differently from normal income basis, because it would appear to be regular, it would appear to be that it’s a payment from the same source, which is the Auckland Future Fund.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand left unresolved in the preceding exchange — whether a trustee's own remuneration falls inside the exemption — and advances it with a concrete case (professional trustees paid for their time) rather than restating the earlier question. Partly, though, it returns to her own prepared line on the Amendment Paper rather than taking up the GST/Income Tax Act mismatch just raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "just being a trustee of the Auckland Future Fund shouldn’t excuse them from being taxed on those amounts of incomes" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The member’s right: new section CW 19B refers to the provision of funding relating to an emergency situation to an employee to the extent that it relates to both accommodation, which I think would be pretty reasonable and sensible. Also, in the context of non-accommodation funding, which is under a threshold set of $5,000, that means that, obviously, those individuals under those circumstances can do what they need to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause and both limbs Russell asked about (accommodation and the $5,000 non-accommodation amount) and says what they are for, so the reply is clearly shaped by her question. But it does not resolve the specific distinction she pressed — business-continuity support versus gratis assistance to the employee — and settles into a general statement that the exemption is sensible. Partial engagement, mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "exactly what is the policy intent here? Is it to ensure that a business could provide accommodation for an employee in order that that would help the business get back going? Or is it just gratis assistance to the employee?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I now go back to clause 16B, which, as I previously noted, the Finance and Expenditure Committee had done some substantial changes. I just want to acknowledge the Minister of Revenue for answering my earlier question around the application date, which advised us of the date that change was originally made, which was on the 27 March 2021.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive turn by Watts on CW 19B immediately precedes it, in the same committee-stage debate. The speech engages none of that content; it is prepared material on a different clause of the same bill. The courteous acknowledgement of an earlier answer on the application date is a glance at the exchange rather than engagement with the argument just made, which places it at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just explained the purpose of new section CW 19B and its $5,000 emergency-funding threshold, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it returns to clause 16B and a prepared walk-through of the redrafted section CW 3C.

acuity.statement: The general point I want to make is that this bill—like many tax bills that have come before it—includes a large number of remedial matters which are designed to ensure that the law aligns with the policy intent. Importantly, in the context of what the member is referring to, I am comfortable that the drafting is appropriate to ensure that taxpayers can interpret and apply the law as easily as possible.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually put — he states he is comfortable the drafting is appropriate and workable for taxpayers, which is the reassurance Edmonds asked for, and he addresses her complaint about complexity as a balance that has been struck. He leaves untouched her other specific question, whether officials advised on simplifying the clause, and does not engage the 95 percent test or formula she detailed. Engages one strand squarely; not the whole of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does he feel confident with the revised draft of this bill that it still meets the original intent to ensure that the brightline period does not restart when land is reallocated to the co-owners" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Does the employer get a tax deduction? If the employer pays for accommodation for the employee to the tune of whatever it is or pays an amount of up to $5,000, is that tax deductible for the employer?
acuity.explanation: Takes the two limbs Watts had just set out — accommodation and the $5,000 amount — and draws out a consequence he did not address: that exempt income normally carries no deduction for the payer, so the treatment of the employer side is unresolved. The question only exists because of the answer that preceded it, and would have to change if that answer had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in the context of non-accommodation funding, which is under a threshold set of $5,000... the amounts in question are exempt from tax" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Landlessness is a key theme of the people of Korowai o Wainuiārua, and I pay tribute to them for the tolerance that they have had as a people—tolerance and patience for the Crown to finally honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi in some small way. This settlement goes a small way in righting the wrongs of the past.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows a substantive turn by Andersen on the same bill, so she is eligible. Her speech is squarely about the matter under debate — the Te Korowai o Wainuiārua settlement, landlessness, the DOC estate, the commercial redress — and it overlaps Andersen's themes because both are describing the same bill, not because Lyndon takes up anything Andersen argued. She names no point of Andersen's, rebuts nothing, corrects nothing, and builds on no figure Andersen gave; her material is drawn from the morning's pōwhiri and her own reflections. Substituting a different speech on the same bill before her would require no change to a word of it, which puts this in the prepared-but-on-topic band rather than at 0.5. 0.2 rather than 0.1 because the speech is tightly tied to this specific bill and iwi rather than being deliverable in any debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen set out the bill's provisions in detail — the formal apology, the 22 statutory acknowledgements, the 19 cultural redress properties and the $21.7 million financial redress she called "a drop in the bucket" — and this statement does not take up any of it.

acuity.statement: Yes, it has been a long and difficult journey, as Ginny Andersen has mentioned, and Hūhana Lyndon noted also the tolerance of the iwi of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua throughout this settlement journey.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft follows a substantive turn by Mark Cameron, so she is eligible. Her speech is prepared New Zealand First material on the right subject — the settlement, its breaches and its redress — and engages no part of Cameron's contribution: she neither takes up his point that the Crown's failure to protect te reo breached Te Tiriti, nor his remark that $21 million seems small, and she states the figure as $21.7 million without noting any difference. There is a gesture at the wider debate (naming earlier speakers and 'we've mentioned that here today'), which lifts it off the floor, but nothing of the preceding argument's content is taken up, so this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Cameron spoke about the settlement, saying 'The Crown’s failure to actively protect te reo o Whanganui is a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi' and that the $21 million 'seems like a small amount', and this statement does not take either up — it acknowledges earlier speeches by Ginny Andersen and Hūhana Lyndon that are not in the preceding turn.

acuity.statement: We in this House have the immense honour and indeed duty to stand on behalf of the Crown to bear witness and give support to this piece of legislation. As this bill is set down for all remaining phases in the House today, I wish to give a brief call for the second reading and will follow with a more substantive address during the third reading. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Doyle follows a substantive turn by Kemp that made claims about the Crown's acquisitions, the settlement's redress and the Government's conduct over the past 16 months. He engages none of it: the speech is a formal commendation that expressly defers substance to the third reading. It is at least on the matter under debate (this bill, this iwi), so it is not a 0.0 — but it would read identically whatever Kemp had argued, so there is no engagement to point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Takutai Tarsh Kemp spoke about the Crown's acquisition of land for public works, the loss of kaitiakitanga, and the Pōkākā Eco-sanctuary, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: When it comes to the second reading, we reflect on that select committee process and on how we opened up for submissions and what took place before and during the submissions and, indeed, after. As has been traversed very briefly, when it came to the submissions, we received 16 submissions, with 14 public submissions. I think it’s very important to acknowledge today in the House that eight of these 14 submissions were opposed to the bill, and the opposition was around a few concerns.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows two substantive-to-formal turns and brings new material — the committee's submission count and the split for and against — but it is prepared select-committee reportage rather than engagement with anything Kemp or Doyle said. The nod 'as has been traversed very briefly' is a gesture at the debate without taking up its content, and her own later line that 'nothing, actually, will suffice to repay for the deep loss' is flagged as something she has 'mentioned many times in the House', not a pickup of Kemp's parallel point. On topic, unresponsive, with a glance at the debate: 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Takutai Tarsh Kemp argued the settlement 'returns the tools which were wrongly taken' and reaffirms kaitiakitanga in the national parks, and Benjamin Doyle gave a brief call of support; this statement takes up neither argument, only gesturing at the debate with 'As has been traversed very briefly'.

acuity.statement: Through the great strength that has allowed those who were landless—landlessness is a term we’ve heard in the speeches so far. To maintain that strength and cohesion and your whanaungatanga between everybody during a time when you’re not—well, you always had a place that was your land, whether the title said it or not.
acuity.explanation: Luxton explicitly picks up the term of art from the preceding speech ("landlessness is a term we've heard in the speeches so far") and does something with Doyle's landlessness claim — reframing it from dispossession-by-Crown into enduring customary connection to land regardless of title, and he similarly takes up Doyle's Pōkākā naming by asking after its etymology. But that is one strand only: the bulk of the turn is prepared personal material (building in Ohakune and Raetihi, the acreage figure, encouragement to New Zealanders about place names) that would be unchanged whatever Doyle had argued, and he engages neither Doyle's central argument about whose historical record is treated as official nor the claim that a treaty must be honoured rather than settled. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "At the hands of the Crown, ngā iwi o Te Korowai o Wainuiārua have been left virtually landless." — Benjamin Doyle

acuity.statement: So, yes, I'm an angry Ngāpuhi, like my tungāne, but I'm also really honoured to be here to address you, because when we had the first reading, it was a rushed process, too—remember?
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Peeni Henare and picks up one identifiable strand of his speech — his Ngāpuhi vantage point and his stated grievance about how the House has handled this bill's readings — aligning herself with it ("like my tungāne") and extending it from the proceedings he complained of to the rushed first reading. That is genuine engagement with the previous turn, so it sits above the prepared-material band. But it is a single strand: she does not take up his substantive points (his endorsement of the Minister's account of the settlement path, the pōkākā naming argument, the Defence land) and immediately returns to her own prepared address to the iwi, so it is a partial engagement rather than a reply that works on his argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Taku amuamu ki ngā nekehanga kua kitea e au, i taku tāima ki roto i te Whare Pāremata" — Peeni Henare, whose preceding third-reading speech spoke as a Ngāpuhi member and complained about the way these proceedings have been handled

acuity.statement: Like with most iwi and hapū around Aotearoa, it was your resources and it was your lands that forged a pathway for my people to build our towns and our cities. It was your forests that were cut down to build our schools and our houses and our main streets.
acuity.explanation: Bennett picks up one strand of Redmayne's preceding speech — the iwi's landlessness and the Crown's use of their whenua for infrastructure ('developments and activities the Crown proceeded with on your land') — and develops it by naming who benefited: his own Pākehā communities, their towns, schools and houses. That is a real engagement with the substance just put, and the passage would read differently had the previous speaker framed the history another way. But it is only partial: the bulk of the turn is prepared ceremonial acknowledgement (greetings, tribute to the departed, hopes for tamariki) that could have followed any speech in this third reading, and he takes up none of Redmayne's specific material — the Hauhau label, the Pīpīriki division, the named negotiators, the trust board, the mill closure. Engages the topic and one strand of the argument, then returns to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "Despite the strength of your people, by the 20th century you were virtually landless and were forced to face the social and economic challenges which followed."

acuity.statement: I’d take it with a little bit of a grain of salt when someone says to move on, probably because I’m a whanaunga of yours, and when I’m hearing that, I’m not hearing it as a member across the other side of the House.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe takes up one specific strand of the turn immediately before him — Fleming's endorsement of reframing the settlement away from grievance and towards hope, and his report that the iwi were not asking for more time but inviting the House to them. Rurawhe qualifies that framing rather than restating it: he accepts moving on for future generations but insists the breaches and the apology in the bill cannot be set aside, and notes other business before the House that will affect the same three iwi. The speech would read differently had the previous speaker not pressed the hope-and-promise framing, which is what lifts this above prepared material. It is only a partial engagement, though — he does not take up Fleming's substantive points about the select committee process or the cancelled hearing, and after this passage he returns to prepared material addressed to the next generations, so this sits around the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg Fleming: "I loved the way that he moved away from the language of settlement and towards one of hope and of promise."

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in support of the District Court (District Court Judges) Amendment Bill. However, there are a number of things that I would like to address.
acuity.explanation: Webb's immediately preceding turn made specific, contestable claims — that the bill is a trivial fig-leaf for a jail-first policy, that the Government has made "zero progress" on court backlogs, and a prediction that remand populations will increase. Xu-Nan's speech engages none of them. It is detailed and squarely on the bill under debate (judge numbers, the 2019 increase, the civil-jurisdiction report, the higher-court bottleneck), and it does respond to things said by the Minister at the earlier committee stage — but the committee stage is not the preceding turn, and nothing in this speech would have to change had Webb argued something different. Prepared material on the right subject with a clear gesture at the debate puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero. Note the low score reflects responsiveness only: the substantive quality, precision and courtesy of the speech are not being judged here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that "the only reason this bill is needed is because this Government wants to put more people in jail" and predicted remand populations would rise, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: We acknowledge that there are long delays in our justice system that need to be addressed, and this Government is also addressing that issue and those concerns in various other reforms, and those reforms are through court technology and modern case management systems.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Chhour's preceding point about timeliness — conceding the delays and adding the other reforms aimed at them — but the rest of the turn is prepared party-position material (restating the 182-to-183 change and commending the bill) that would read identically whatever she had argued. Partial engagement on the topic rather than on a specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "justice must be delivered in a timely manner" — Karen Chhour

acuity.statement: It may seem insignificant in nature, increasing the amount of District Court judges from 182 to 183. It doesn’t seem like much, but when you consider it in an ecosystem of bills, in an ecosystem of ministries of the House, it maintains the settings, the societal settings that have been produced out of the behaviour that the Crown just apologised for.
acuity.explanation: Directly attacks the framing both preceding speakers used — that this is a simple, self-contained one-judge change — by granting the premise and then disputing the inference drawn from it. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged if the earlier speakers had not characterised the bill as trivially simple, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s quite that simple." — Jamie Arbuckle (and Karen Chhour's "This is a relatively simple bill")

acuity.statement: I think, to me, what was really telling is that the bill was described by members of the Government as a common-sense bill, but, as my colleague Lawrence already explained at the committee of the whole House, actually there was little common sense explained by the Minister when it came to justifying the increase of District Court judges by just one.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the specific characterisation Arbuckle had just used and does something with it — turns it back as a demand for the justification of the number one, which is the content of the Government's claim rather than merely a reference to it. Would have to be rewritten had the preceding speaker not called the bill common sense.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is common-sense action again from this Government." — Jamie Arbuckle

acuity.statement: Actually, if they followed the evidence on what some of the best ways to support victims are, yes, sure, supporting and resourcing the judiciary is one way, but when you already have people who work at the front lines telling this Government that some of the other reforms that relate to this will actually lead to victims being potentially worse off—for example, when it comes to issues around retail crime—I think it reeks of a disconnection with the evidence, in relation to what else they are proposing.
acuity.explanation: Engages the victims-focus justification Chhour put at the centre of her speech, concedes the judiciary-resourcing part of it, and contests the rest on the evidence about front-line effects. Short of 1.0 because it answers the general justification rather than a specific figure or argument she advanced, and then moves into prepared Green material on legal aid and income support.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "focus on victims in our communities" — Karen Chhour

acuity.statement: Give them the ability to join things up, because otherwise, yes, I heard the previous speaker say, “Isn’t it wonderful. We’re going to fill more jails up.” Well, they cost money.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor follows Carl Bates and does take up one strand of what Bates argued: Bates's claim that rising prison numbers show accountability working is answered with two counters — that prisons cost money, and (developed over the rest of the speech) that the fact of imprisonment deters more than its length, so longer sentences are counter-productive. That is real engagement with Bates's premise rather than a bare reference. But it is partial: the bulk of the speech is prepared material on judicial discretion, the 'ecosystem' of the courts, Ben Scully, Sir David Carruthers and his own undercover police career, and it is aimed at a different bill still to come ('another piece of legislation which has been oft referred to') rather than at Bates's argument. Much of it would have been delivered word-for-word whoever had spoken before. Mid-band: the topic and one claim are engaged, then he returns to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "because they have us on when the prison numbers go up because we actually hold people accountable" — O'Connor quotes this back as "Isn't it wonderful. We're going to fill more jails up" and answers it on cost and on deterrence.

acuity.statement: This is a job where we really are encouraged to think deeply about things, so while I take the member Tom Rutherford’s point, I think it is very important we join the dots in this situation.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford's whole argument was that the debate had strayed and the bill is narrowly about one extra judge, so the House should 'just talk about the legislation'. White names him, concedes the point in part, and then disputes exactly that narrowing — arguing the single-judge change cannot be understood without the delays, the backlog and the support the courts need.
