The speech is visibly shaped by the turn before it: had Rutherford argued something else about the bill, the framing would have had to change. It is not a full 1.0 because after the opening rebuttal she moves into prepared material on the Chief District Court Judge rather than continuing to contest his claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "we’re just increasing the District Court judges from 182 to 183, and we’re enabling it. That’s all we’re doing."

acuity.statement: I don’t want to get too judgmental about this; 183 sounds like a fantastic idea. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: White had just made a substantive argument with figures and a named critique of government policy. Hamilton's turn engages no part of it — no number, no claim, no counter-argument. It is at least on the matter under debate (the bill's judge number) and offers a pun on it, which keeps it above 0.0, but it would have been word-for-word identical whatever the previous speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued that adding a judge obliges the House to ask whether judges are adequately supported, and cited that 83 percent of 18- to 20-year-old prisoners had been in State care; this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m just wondering if the legislative programme will be better organised than the Deputy Leader of the House.
acuity.explanation: Upston had just set out a detailed order of business (two third readings, extended Government hours, a members' day, the Budget Policy Statement debate replacing the general debate, and a special debate on climate adaptation). Webb takes up none of it — no item, no timing, no omission is engaged. The jibe at the Deputy Leader of the House would have worked word-for-word whatever programme had been read out, which places it in the bottom band; it is 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because 'the legislative programme' at least names the matter before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston said 'Next week, the House will consider the third readings of the Regulatory Systems (Immigration and Workforce) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill' and set out the week's business, and this statement does not take up any part of it.

acuity.statement: If 103 years ago, a brilliant scholar in law, who got a law degree in two years flat—Sir Apirana Ngata—said that the Māori ceded sovereignty, then who in this House is so historically illiterate now?
acuity.explanation: This goes straight at the specific charge just levelled — that Prebble is 'historically illiterate' for holding that Māori ceded sovereignty — and does something with it: it names a Māori legal authority said to have held the same view, so that the illiteracy label would have to extend to him too. The intervention would have to be rewritten if Lyndon had made any other criticism of the appointment, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the characterisation by counter-authority rather than engaging the substance of the two-texts point Lyndon actually raised. Scored on engagement only — whether the Ngata claim is accurate, and whether the retort is courteous, are other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: 'he appointed someone to our Waitangi Tribunal who has proven themselves historically illiterate'

acuity.statement: Well, what I’ve got to say, Mr Goldsmith, is that this is another job that David Seymour has given Paul Goldsmith, because, yet again, the Government, which should be focused on things that are important to hard-working New Zealanders, has, in fact, been distracted by things like the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill and a four-year term with bizarre select committee rules by the ACT Party.
acuity.explanation: Follows the Minister's first-reading speech and is on the matter under debate — it gestures at the coalition-agreement origin Goldsmith himself flagged — but engages none of his actual argument about why a generic framework is needed or the Electoral Commission's lead-in time. Prepared material on the right subject with a jab at provenance, so the bottom of the band's upper end.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "In line with coalition agreements, a separate bill is being progressed that would enable the extension of the maximum term of Parliament, subject to a binding referendum."

acuity.statement: Look, if you’re going to run a referendum, we accept you’ve got to get your rules right, and in some ways, I’m curious as to why we’re doing a kind of patch-up, rather than having a long-term look at how we run referenda. If you’re going to do it, you may as well do it right, and this bill is really only aimed at a referendum that’ll happen in one of the next two elections.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific scope limitation in the Minister's case — that the framework covers a referendum at the first or second election — and turns it against him as a reason the bill is a patch-up rather than durable reform. The speech would have to change if Goldsmith had argued for a permanent framework instead, so it is squarely engaged, though it then moves to its own prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the Referendums Framework Bill provides the necessary legislative framework to govern the conduct of a referendum if required at the first or second election after commencement"

acuity.statement: It’s funny that the Minister was talking about the Electoral Commission and the work that it does, including in referenda, because, at the moment, it’s under siege. It’s had a walkout from its IT department, and there are deep problems with it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the precise premise of the Minister's timing argument — that the Commission needs lead-in time to plan — and disputes the Commission's current capacity to do so. This is a direct rebuttal of a named strand of the preceding speech, not a reference to it; it could not have been delivered unchanged against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Our Electoral Commission needs to be able to plan appropriately."

acuity.statement: This bill only applies to referendums at the next two elections, but why? If you’re not very sure about the legislation, perhaps a five-year review period would be more sensible. Why are referendums good for two rounds and not for longer?
acuity.explanation: Interrogates the specific two-election limit the Minister set out and proposes an alternative mechanism (a five-year review) in its place. It engages the content of the preceding case rather than its topic, and would read differently had Goldsmith presented an open-ended framework.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the Referendums Framework Bill provides the necessary legislative framework to govern the conduct of a referendum if required at the first or second election after commencement"

acuity.statement: As the Minister said, the bill does allow for advertising for referenda, but, again, this Government has not listened to the Independent Electoral Review. Is the balance between free speech and undue influence correct?
acuity.explanation: Names the Minister's own balance claim and contests it on its own terms, going on to test the spending thresholds he announced against the Independent Electoral Review's recommendations. This is the specific argument just made being taken up and disputed, which is the top of the scale regardless of whether the inference or the figures are right.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "To achieve an appropriate balance between freedom of expression and transparency, the bill regulates referendum advertising in much the same way as the Electoral Act regulates election advertising."

acuity.statement: The idea that we would have a discussion about framing up a four-year reality, whatever it looks like, in a piece of legislation; having a referendum, or a referenda—whichever way you want to frame it—and inviting New Zealand to have its say, and they’re “rednecks”—gracious me! Unbelievable.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the preceding speaker's actual words and draws out what he says follows from them — that inviting the public to vote is being cast as pandering to rednecks — so one strand of her speech is genuinely engaged and pointable. But it engages only that phrase, not her substantive case about when a referendum is an appropriate instrument or about advertising controls, and the rest is indignation rather than rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "They are a simplistic lever for rednecks deciding on rural wards"

acuity.statement: That’s not particularly exciting in itself, but what we’ve heard in the debate from the Opposition—or at least from one part of the Opposition—does get a little bit exciting, it does open up a debate, because what they have said is that they, essentially, do not believe that there’s much value in the public as a whole engaging in a referendum question. I find that quite remarkable.
acuity.explanation: Foster names the claim he is answering (that public-wide referendum participation has little value), restates it, and then does something with it — the Swiss comparison, the long lead-in debates, MMP. The speech would have to change if the earlier Opposition speeches had argued something else, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because the claim he engages is his own summary of 'one part of the Opposition' rather than a specific argument or figure he takes up on its own terms, and because much of the surrounding material (the Swiss, the list of past referenda) reads as prepared. Whether the restatement is a fair rendering of what the Greens said is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one, and I have deliberately not let it move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Cameron: "How many referendums would New Zealand and New Zealanders want to be engaged with?" — and the Opposition contributions Cameron and Foster both answer, which Foster restates as denying "much value in the public as a whole engaging in a referendum question".

acuity.statement: Te Pāti Māori supports the essence of this bill, because we support giving power to the people to decide on our laws in some situations. What we do not support is allowing the majority to decide the rights of minorities and dismissing the constitutional rights of te iwi Māori through Te Tiriti o Waitangi along the way.
acuity.explanation: Ferris takes up one strand of what immediately preceded him — Foster's claim that everyone getting a say is the high end of participatory democracy — and answers it directly with the limiting case of a majority voting on minority rights, then engages Cameron's own raising of a Treaty principles referendum. That is real engagement with the preceding turns, so it sits above the prepared-material band. It is not 1.0 because he does not take up Foster's specific supports (the Swiss record, the MMP referendum, the extensive lead-in debate Foster insisted always happens) and instead returns to Te Pāti Māori's prepared position on the Treaty and Māori wards.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "I think that is very much the high end of it because that means that we all—we all—get to have a say about something." Also Mark Cameron: "Incidentally, the Treaty principles bill—that’s come up in the House, so I’ll reference it."

acuity.statement: Well, you obviously haven’t been following the whole speech, bro. These are the dangers of referendums, and this is our position.
acuity.explanation: A direct contradiction was put to him and he had a clear opportunity to resolve it — he had in fact drawn exactly that distinction (supporting the mechanism, opposing majoritarian use of it), so answering was available. Instead he dismisses the questioner's attentiveness and restates his conclusion without engaging the apparent inconsistency. That is a reference to the interjection rather than engagement with its content, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because it is at least about the matter in hand. The 'bro' is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one, and has not moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: An unnamed member (recorded as "Hon Member"): "So you don’t support referendums, but you support this bill?"

acuity.statement: All members of this House, I’m sure, got votes from Māori voters across New Zealand, so I’m looking forward to the day that they recognise that there are other views than their own.
acuity.explanation: Bates does engage the turn that immediately preceded his — he answers Ferris's objection to majority decision-making with the point that Māori voters are spread across every party, which is a response to the topic Ferris raised. But he engages a recast version ('will only agree with New Zealanders that vote for them') rather than Ferris's actual claim about constitutional rights under Te Tiriti, and leaves the tyranny-of-the-majority argument and the Māori wards example untouched. That is the ~0.5 pattern: one strand taken up, the specific claim not met, then back to commending the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "What we do not support is allowing the majority to decide the rights of minorities and dismissing the constitutional rights of te iwi Māori through Te Tiriti o Waitangi along the way."

acuity.statement: Someone made the comment on the other side of the House that we on the Justice Committee, which I’m so proud and privileged to be part of, should be focusing on things that matter—I’m paraphrasing here. Look, the fact is, to us here on this side of the House, the Gangs Act is a law that really mattered, and we focused on that and we got that done, much to the happiness of people in South Auckland that are feeling a lot safer.
acuity.explanation: She identifies the preceding criticism about priorities and the use of House/committee time and answers one strand of it — that the Government can do this alongside other work — but then moves into prepared material on the Gangs Act, three strikes and the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill rather than engaging the claim that this bill is on the order paper only as ACT's companion piece. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Increasingly, this House and the legislative agenda in this Parliament is dominated by ACT's political programme."

acuity.statement: The member who has just resumed her seat, Rima Nakhle, managed to talk mostly about something that was completely irrelevant. I congratulate her for sneaking that one in. Unfortunately, what we’re here to do, in a proper sense, however, is talk about this particular bill, the Referendums Framework Bill.
acuity.explanation: This names the previous speaker and characterises her speech as irrelevant, but engages none of its content — not the multitasking claim, not the Gangs Act or sentencing examples offered as evidence of it. A gesture at the preceding turn followed by a pivot to the speaker's own prepared framing of the debate, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "This is multitasking, and this is what people that are used to multitasking can do."

acuity.statement: Again, my colleague the Hon Phil Twyford talked about some of the examples of how the three- versus four-year term—which, on the surface, when I heard it in the media, I kind of thought, “Well, that’s relatively novel.” Then, as more details came out about the Government being able to opt in or opt out, we looked at the fiasco and the debacle in terms of this Government being able to form a Government after the last election and the sheer amount of time that that took—and you add another level of complexity about taking that coalition and then being able to choose whether they would have a three- or a four-year term and the ramifications of how the select committees would work post that decision—and all together that’s quite a substantial amount of time.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific objection raised in the preceding turn — that the four-year term bill makes each incoming Government choose the term length and adjust select committees — and does something with it, drawing out a consequence Twyford did not state: that the choice would be bolted onto an already lengthy coalition-formation process and so erode certainty. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "the idea that you would give future Governments the responsibility to have to choose between the three-year or a four-year term and some consequent adjustments to the select committee process every time the Government changes, every time there’s a new parliamentary term, is gaga in my view"

acuity.statement: It seems that the debate has been taken offtrack, and I’m keen to bring it back on track. Members have talked about a variety of different subjects, but this is a really generic bill. There have been complaints made from the other side about priorities and bringing legislation to the House, and things like that, yet they’re supporting the legislation, so you can see the hypocrisy there.
acuity.explanation: He engages the specific argument just made — that the House's time is being wasted on an ACT project — and turns it against the opposition by pointing to their support for the bill, then disputes the premise by characterising the bill as minimal and purely enabling. Pointable and squarely aimed at the preceding claim; the inference (that supporting a bill is inconsistent with criticising its priority) is weak, but that is a rigor matter, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "it is, as I said, frustrating that Parliament’s time is being consumed by yet another ACT Party pet project when some more pressing things should be done"

acuity.statement: Too often our data is locked away in corporate silos, used to predict our behaviour to sell us things that we may not need, but how many times can we actually use the data for our benefit? We’ve heard from the other side about how we need to open it up so we can actually stop some anti-competitive behaviour.
acuity.explanation: Campbell explicitly picks up the strand of Helen White's speech about big entities hoarding data for anti-competitive purposes and builds his own case (the electricity-switching example) on it, and later acknowledges her committee points on privacy and derived data. But he does not engage the specific claim she pressed — that the bill under-weights consumer rights and that penalties may be too low — and most of the speech is prepared material on the same topic. A partial engagement: one strand taken up, then back to his own script.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "There has been a tendency of our big entities to hold information like this for anti-competitive purpose."

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party also in support of the Customer and Product Data Bill. Like many have mentioned already, I think the bill does strengthen the laws that protect against anti-competitive behaviour, it does allow greater customer control over the data, and also potentially allows for innovation of new products.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Unkovich's substantive second-reading speech immediately precedes it. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and acknowledges that others have spoken, but engages no part of what Unkovich actually argued; the privacy and clause 126 material would have been delivered word-for-word whatever she had said. A gesture at the debate without engagement sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich spoke about the bill's technicality, the 40 submitters and the committee's privacy checks, and this statement does not take up any of her claims — it gestures at the debate with "Like many have mentioned already" and then proceeds to prepared Green Party material (clause 126, Te Kāhui Raraunga consultation).

acuity.statement: We heard some of the experiences that happened in Australia, where there’s been less valuable uptake of a similar kind of approach in their jurisdiction. Part of that was because of a lack of confidence in the system around trust and privacy, and because we have a Privacy Commissioner and we have quite robust privacy law in New Zealand, we were able to make ourselves very comfortable that privacy would not be breached and that all of the elements of privacy law would actually apply and protect people within this framework as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the privacy strand both preceding speakers raised and supplies the committee's reasoning for being satisfied (Australian uptake, the Privacy Commissioner, existing privacy law) — so it answers the topic rather than any specific claim, and leaves Xu-Nan's actual asks (clause 126(1)(f) and (g), and the Te Tiriti consultation concern) entirely untouched before returning to prepared committee material. Partial engagement, below the mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "One of the key elements of this bill is the privacy provisions that have been given." — Lawrence Xu-Nan, who asked for the privacy provisions and the regulation/standards split to be teased out and raised the omission of iwi, hapū and whānau Māori consultation on data sovereignty.

acuity.statement: I’m very supportive of this bill. Great to see it moving through. Great to see some progress, and we just heard about the importance of things like open banking and open electricity markets. We want to see more competition in the market. That’s one of those underlying values that is driving a lot of the policy of this Government, and it’s been great to see colleagues like Cameron Brewer, like Ryan Hamilton, really holding the feet to the fire of those big four Australian banks, to see a better result for Kiwis who deserve it.
acuity.explanation: Costley follows Twyford's second-reading speech and nods at it ("we just heard about the importance of things like open banking"), but that is a bare reference to the topic rather than engagement with anything Twyford argued. Twyford made three specific criticisms — the purpose clause is not tough enough on consumer benefit, the derived-data restrictions modelled on the Australian regime should have been cleared out further, and the penalties and dispute-resolution provisions should have favoured consumers more. Costley takes up none of them; he does discuss the select committee's changes and new clauses 96A to 96H, but as prepared material on standards-setting, and he characterises the removed provisions as compliance-cost reductions without addressing Twyford's claim that the bill was left too weak. Delete Twyford's turn and substitute any other speech supportive of open banking and this speech would be word-for-word identical, so it sits in the unresponsive band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because of the explicit gesture at what was just said and because it is squarely on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the other really powerful idea in this space is open banking" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: Credit to the previous speaker, Reuben Davidson: he has an artform of being able to turn really interesting and fascinating legislation into the most bland, boring 10 minutes of monotone drivel—absolute drivel.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford names the preceding speaker and comments on his delivery, which is a mere reference rather than engagement with content. He then says he was not on the select committee, relays a colleague's impression that submissions were interesting, and restates the $524 switching saving that Davidson had already given — repeating the opponent's figure rather than doing anything with it, and adding a 10 percent uptake figure as prepared support for the bill. acuity.statement: I don’t know how many other ways to say it: the Firearms Safety Authority is being removed from the New Zealand Police. They’re being put into a different agency. Usually when you do that you make sure that the Minister in charge of that agency has some say over what’s going to happen. The changes are happening now because the Ministry of Justice—who may not be the end home carer for the Arms Act—needs to make policy changes, administrative changes, be able to have the ability to do that as we work through the other phases. It is logical that we put that in there now.
acuity.explanation: Andersen's question was specifically why the ministerial transfer in amended section 74A(1) sits in this gun-ranges bill rather than in the wider Arms Act reform. McKee answers that exact question — the agency move is happening now, so the receiving Minister needs the policy-making power now. The speech would be different had Andersen asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question to the Minister is in relation to amended section 74A(1), inserted by clause 13, as to why it’s in this tranche of legislation" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: The reality is, if we’re going to do it and do it well, we need to make sure that there is good information-sharing arrangements between New Zealand Police and the new home agency for the Firearms Safety Authority. I make no apology for putting that into this bill, because that allows the Ministry of Justice to get on with their work, and while they do that they can ensure the safety of our front-liners while they work through the process of the exchange.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the second strand of Andersen's argument — that front-line officers need real-time intelligence and that the Police Association is worried about front-line safety — and answers it on its own terms by pointing to the information-sharing arrangements being settled before the transfer. Engages the specific concern rather than the topic generally.

acuity.responding_to: "need to have real-time intelligence and real-time information" — Ginny Andersen

Phase four is the Arms Act rewrite, and this will be about a whole regime of modernisation.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "are these changes that you’re putting through now because of 15 March, the first tranche of Arms Act reforms; or was it the second tranche?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I’ve also been thinking, because a lot of the comments have been around 15 March and what happened there, and we know, thanks to the royal commission of inquiry, where the loopholes were and what went wrong—I’m wondering why we would separate out these kinds of regulations and operations from the police when they also hold lots of important intelligence around the actions and maybe offences or patterns that they’ve observed of people within their community that they might consider when they’re granting somebody a firearms licence. I’m keen to dig into that around why we would separate out this regulation from the New Zealand Police.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests McKee's claim that moving the Firearms Safety Authority out of Police is simply logical, by naming the specific thing she says is lost — the local intelligence police hold when vetting licence applicants. It engages the preceding answer's reasoning rather than merely restating the topic, though it partly re-asks Andersen's question rather than advancing past McKee's reply about information-sharing.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: 'This is not to be overthought and overanalysed and create scaremongering amongst the public.'

acuity.statement: Hanga tūmeke ahau i tēnei āhuatanga, me te kawe tere nei i tēnei whakatikahanga, me te kī atu kua pai ināianei, me haere tonu ahakoa te kauparetanga o te reo o te iwi Māori, ahakoa te kore whai whakaaro ki te tokomaha o te iwi Māori e noho nei i roto i ngā tikanga whakahaere a Te Tāhuhu o te Ture.
acuity.explanation: Costello justified the use of urgency as needed 'to ensure there is the clarity that members across the House are seeking'. Ferris takes up the urgency justification specifically and disputes it — that a decade-old defect is now rushed through and declared fixed, without consideration of those affected. He engages the urgency strand of her argument rather than the clarity claim itself, so this is a strong partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal of the reasoning she offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: 'That is why we are doing it under urgency—to ensure there is the clarity that members across the House are seeking'

acuity.statement: I’m happy to take a five-minute call to support this bill, which is going through, and it’s fitting because I actually visited Whanganui Prison yesterday.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one, and the speech engages neither. Ferris had just argued at length that Māori voices and Ministry of Justice warnings are being ignored and that urgency is inappropriate; Paul does not take up the urgency objection, the select committee point, or the scaremongering exchange. What follows is self-contained prepared material — a prison visit, a quote about muster, an anecdote about a 14-year-old in Dunedin — on the correct subject (electronic bail and the remand population) but indifferent to what was said before it. She even notes 'I’ve pulled out all the stories I have', confirming prepared content. It sits in the 0.1–0.3 band: on the matter under debate, with no gesture at the preceding arguments.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tākuta Ferris argued the bill is being rushed under urgency while Māori concerns and Ministry of Justice warnings are set aside, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It's not a simple thing. There's been several contributions from the other side of the House that have almost been flippant to the fact that questions have been raised on this side of the House.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the preceding speaker's framing of the bill as a simple, pragmatic change done quickly, and disputes exactly that — arguing the change is not simple, that the brevity of Government contributions has left the impetus and urgency unexplained, and that unintended consequences will need to be teased out in committee. It engages one strand (the 'simple/pragmatic, no questions needed' claim) squarely, but much of the speech is prepared material on the bill's background and the remand population that would have been delivered whatever preceded it, so it sits between a partial and a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "This is a pragmatic change—really good legislation. We're doing it quickly so we can ensure nothing falls through the cracks"

acuity.statement: There is no need to wander and waffle. This is a required change, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: The jibe about wandering and waffling glances at the previous speaker's manner, and 'This is a required change' bare-asserts the necessity she had just questioned, but no part of her argument is engaged — not the missing rationale, not the urgency, not the flagged clauses. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever she had said, so it scores in the gesture-at-the-debate band rather than as partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued the Government had not explained what judicial decision or advice triggered the bill, how long the problem had been known, and that clauses may need tightening in committee — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Look, I rise to support the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill because this is a common-sense approach, it rectifies a process. It’s all about ensuring that we have safe electronic monitoring in our community, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Belich's immediately preceding turn made three pointed, engageable claims: that retrospectivity is normally to be avoided and is only justified here because it benefits those monitored, that the reason for urgency is unclear given the practice is over a decade old, and that the NZBORA vet had not been able to be read before the reading. Wedd's turn answers none of these. It asserts the bill is 'common-sense', 'rectifies a process' and supports safe monitoring, then commends it to the House. The speech is word-for-word indifferent to what preceded it — substituting a different critique of the bill would require no change to it — so it sits in the unresponsive band. It earns 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate. Note this is an acuity judgement only: the turn is civil and on-policy, and those are separate questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich spoke about whether the bill's retrospectivity is justified, why urgency was necessary for a practice 'in place for over a decade', and the unread Bill of Rights Act vet — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I know that our Government absolutely has a plan to crack down on crime. That’s why we want to get through this bill very quickly and get back to those other bills, like the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill, which I’m very, very excited about passing very soon in this House.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle's very short contribution takes up the specific charge Andersen had just closed on — that the Government has no plan on crime — and contradicts it directly, naming another bill as the evidence. It is genuinely aimed at the claim just made, so it is not prepared material indifferent to its predecessor; but it is a bare counter-assertion that engages none of Andersen's reasoning (the remand rate, the cut to support services, the cycle of reoffending) and quietly shifts 'a plan to break the cycle of crime' into 'a plan to crack down on crime'. One strand engaged, then straight to her own prepared enthusiasm — mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "we do not have a plan to break the cycle of crime"

acuity.statement: A number of people have made the point that there’s a lot of people on there. And, yes, that is a symptom of delays for justice and that is why one of the primary focuses of our broader justice policy is to speed up the processes of the courts: so less people are waiting for so long to get their things sorted out.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith explicitly picks up the point Andersen had pressed at length — that the volume of people held or monitored pre-trial reflects court delay, and that the House should look at why — concedes it outright ('yes, that is a symptom of delays for justice'), and then does something with it by tying it to the Government's stated court-speed priority. Accepting part of an opponent's argument and answering it is high responsiveness. Short of 1.0 because he engages the general proposition about delay rather than the specific comparative figures Andersen put up (43 percent here against 18.3 percent in the UK), and he does not take up her claim about funding cuts to support services.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "43 percent of people in prison in New Zealand are not sentenced and are awaiting court processes"

acuity.statement: Since late 2024, some judicial decisions have also raised questions as to whether this common practice was clearly enabled under the Bail Act, and in some cases, the courts imposed conditions that required the defendant to seek specific authorisation from the court for each absence, instead of using the practice in place since 2013 of defendants asking Corrections to approve absences. I’m not going to name the specific cases, because a Minister shouldn’t comment on matters before the courts, because there may be appeals.
acuity.explanation: Webb asked specifically whether a court case gave rise to the bill and in what forum the courts' concerns were raised. Goldsmith takes up that exact question, identifies judicial decisions since late 2024 as the trigger, describes what the courts actually did, and explains why he will not name the cases. The answer would be different had Webb asked something else; he leaves Webb's third question (victims) unaddressed, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I really want to know in what forum that happened. Was that a court decision?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I think, from what I’m hearing, in terms of from the Minister, there was an operational review by the Ministry of Justice and they suggested simplifying the language and standardising the practice. Then the Minister mentioned some judicial reviews in 2024. I think my first question for him, from that, in terms of the judicial review—which does raise a concern—is: despite that, and despite the fact that there might be some recommendations from the judicial review, why does the Minister or the officials feel the need to do this under urgency, with the same level of speed that we’re doing now?
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's just-given account of the two triggers accurately, then draws a consequence from it: if the cause is only a tidy-up review and some 2024 decisions, that does not explain urgency. The question is built out of the preceding answer and could not have been asked before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there was an operational review by the Ministry of Justice conducted to simplify the language used in bail notices" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: I’m a little alarmed at the idea that cases which are actually likely to be public cases wouldn’t be discussed in this context, because, as people have pointed out, we absolutely need to understand the practical implications of this situation.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the reason the Minister gave moments earlier for withholding the cases, arguing that public cases carry no such bar and that the House needs them to assess the bill. The sentence engages the specific ground of his refusal rather than merely noting it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m not going to name the specific cases, because a Minister shouldn’t comment on matters before the courts" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I just had a couple of questions for the Minister of Justice. I know there’s been some discussion about how we can’t talk about what’s before the courts, but it would just be really interesting to understand what brought this particular issue to the Minister’s attention, if we’re able to know. Was it a smart person in the Crown Law Office doing some extra hours work who just happened to stumble across it in a bill somewhere, or was it by something going a bit wrong that was picked up later on? It would just be interesting to know. We’re all voting for it, we’re all pretty much happy here, but you always do things better if you understand kind of where things weren’t picked up initially. Is there any information that the Minister might want to share or be able to share on what triggered the haste of this passage of legislation under urgency today, and how it kind of came to light?
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith had just justified urgency on the basis that 'questions have arisen over the last few months' about whether the legislation sustains the practice. Andersen takes that exact claim and presses on its unstated part — what the questions were and what raised them — rather than delivering prepared material. The questions would have to change if Goldsmith had offered a different rationale, and he in fact answers them with a timeline in his next turn. Not 1.0 because she engages the origin of the issue rather than contesting any of his reasoning about the urgency itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: 'As I’ve said, questions have arisen over the last few months as to whether the legislation actually sustains that. The question is: why are we doing this with urgency?'

acuity.statement: I am concerned that the Minister says that if it is something that’s already working, is not broken, we will just introduce a bill and then get it all through. I guess, you know, that is something that if the Minister wouldn’t mind considering as part of future bills when we are looking at something like this.
acuity.explanation: Takes Goldsmith's own justification — that this is a longstanding practice which 'has worked well for more than a decade' — and draws out its consequence as a precedent: that 'it already works' would licence passing any validating bill under urgency without select committee. He also corrects himself to '10' after Goldsmith's interjection and explicitly builds on Andersen's relationship point, both signs of listening. This is a rebuttal built out of the previous speaker's premise and could not have been delivered against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: 'The system’s been in place since 2013. It has worked well for more than a decade and ensures timeliness for defendants and the courts, and it’s pragmatic.'

acuity.statement: Just in terms of the timeline, Ministers were made aware of the issue in late 2024. We were formally briefed on 20 February this year, and agreed to drafting a Cabinet paper, which was completed before introducing this bill. We moved swiftly when the issue was raised.
acuity.explanation: Supplies precisely the thing Andersen asked for — the chronology of how the issue surfaced and what triggered the urgency — with dates, and in the following paragraph takes up her devolution-of-power concern by pointing to the court's retained role. The reply is shaped by the questions put to him and would be different had they not been asked. Short of 1.0 because he leaves Xu-Nan's specific new section 30MB(2)(b)(i) inconsistency questions untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: 'Is there any information that the Minister might want to share or be able to share on what triggered the haste of this passage of legislation under urgency today, and how it kind of came to light?'

acuity.statement: I want to thank the Hon Dr Duncan Webb for raising that issue. I have given it full and fair consideration, but it is a separate policy issue, because this bill is amending only section 30M—it doesn’t amend section 30L, which is a separate policy issue. To the point he himself has made, it is already possible to undertake a vote from home, but that is an issue that’s not been covered by this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific amendment Webb had just moved and does something with it: identifies the clause it would alter (30L) against the clause the bill actually amends (30M) to ground a scope objection, and turns Webb's own concession about telephone/special voting back on him. The reply would be different if Webb had proposed a different amendment, so it is squarely engaged. Not 1.0 because it rests on the scope point rather than meeting Webb's substantive argument about accessibility for people who do not know telephone voting exists.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "It suggests an amendment to section 30L(1)(b), which actually lists things that you’re automatically allowed out for"

acuity.statement: I just had a question in relation to new section 30MA in clause 5. In that section, the court must specify the authorisation’s purpose or purposes, and, in particular, the defendant is able to be absent from an address, so it does kind of relate to the point made by my learned colleague Duncan Webb.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it. She names Webb's point and the clause under discussion, but the Minister's scope argument — the thing just said — is not taken up at all, and the turn proceeds to a self-contained prepared set of questions on Corrections operational instructions and training that would read identically whatever Goldsmith had replied. On the right subject, engaging no part of the argument, with a nod to the debate: 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it is a separate policy issue, because this bill is amending only section 30M—it doesn’t amend section 30L"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Minister, for your response in terms of some of the clarifications around new section 30MA, particularly on the fact that courts do specify the purpose and purposes. I think that is very helpful, but I think the Minister of Justice hasn’t really responded to my question around what is the current process and procedure for when the court and the electronic monitoring (EM) assessor—the details that are provided are inconsistent. Who then prevails in those kind of circumstances?
acuity.explanation: Audits the Minister's answer against what was asked: accepts the part that was addressed, names precisely the part that was not, and re-puts the unanswered question with the clause reference (30MB(2)(b)(i)) attached. This is responsiveness in its strongest form — tracking which strand of an answer landed and which did not — and it could not have been delivered if the Minister had answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith's reply on new section 30MA, which Xu-Nan quotes as "the fact that courts do specify the purpose and purposes"

acuity.statement: I do actually think that this is something that the Greens will be supporting, but I also think that if this is something that the Minister considers that is not actually, for example, within the scope of this bill, we are looking at the Minister introducing something like this.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's scope objection on its own terms and draws out its consequence: if the amendment is out of scope for this bill, the remedy is a separate Government measure, which he commits Green support to. That is doing something with the argument just made rather than restating a position, and the sentence only exists because Goldsmith framed the refusal as scope rather than merit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it is a separate policy issue, because this bill is amending only section 30M"

acuity.statement: Just quickly, in relation to the first question about who prevails when there’s inconsistency, the court prevails.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing the preceding turn asked for, identified by reference to the question itself. Terse, but responsiveness is about whether the specific question put was engaged, and this answers it and nothing else. (That it leaves Xu-Nan's second question on new section 30MC(c) unanswered bears on forthrightness, not on whether this sentence engaged what preceded it.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "how does the EM assessor and the court resolve inconsistency?"

acuity.statement: My friend was just talking about that problem—about understanding who is making these decisions. I take my friend the Hon Ginny Andersen’s point here—that she was talking about that close connection. It really is a very different thing giving a court, which is off at a distance—there is an element of impartiality about that system.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one strand of Webb's immediately preceding argument — the indeterminacy of who the decision-maker actually is — and extends it into a point about the loss of a once-removed judicial decision-maker. But she does not take up Webb's specific statutory point about the definition of 'electronic monitoring assessor' in section 30E, and the bulk of her contribution then moves to her own prepared demand for the names of the cases. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "you haven’t identified an electronic monitoring assessor" — Webb's argument that the bill fails to specify which person or group of Corrections officers holds the power.

acuity.statement: Now, we’ve talked about the cases, but the advice that I’ve had was that bail decisions had been made orally in list courts, so they didn’t provide the full reasoning of the court. There were three instances, and then there were two in Christchurch which are not finally concluded. That is, they’re under appeal, and that is why I do not want to be referring to them.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question just put to him rather than the topic generally: it gives the number of instances (three, plus two in Christchurch), says what was defective about them (oral decisions in list courts with no full reasoning), and supplies the reason for non-disclosure she asked for (they are under appeal). The reply would have to be different had White asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "What is that case? I would like a further understanding of why the Minister won’t share those cases with this place" — her demand to be told the cases and the reason for withholding them.

acuity.statement: I can understand, then, if that is the case, that that is the Minister’s desire not to have to go back to the court for all of the extant electronic bail conditions that have previously been imposed, which now perhaps need that clarity of condition going forward, or is an addition to that retrospectivity a retrospective validation of the decisions that have already been made without that power?
acuity.explanation: He takes the Minister's own stated rationale and presses it to a distinction the Minister had not drawn: whether the retrospectivity merely confers a forward-looking discretion on existing bail conditions, or additionally validates past decisions made without power. That is drawing out the consequence of the preceding argument, and the question could not have been framed this way without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the concern is that all those decisions, individually, will have to go back to the courts, which would gunge up the system" — his stated rationale for the bill.

acuity.statement: The bill will validate existing and historic conditions that authorised electronic monitoring on bail (EM bail) assessors to approve absence of defendants from their bail addresses. It will validate those existing and historic conditions that were imposed by the assessors. This will prevent the need for those conditions of approximately 2,000 current defendants on EM bail to have to go back to the courts to have to be remade once the bill passes into law.
acuity.explanation: He picks the second limb of the alternative Parker offered and confirms it directly — the bill validates existing and historic conditions — and supplies the scale figure (approximately 2,000 current defendants) that the question implied. Entirely shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Parker: "is an addition to that retrospectivity a retrospective validation of the decisions that have already been made without that power?" — the either/or he put to the Minister.

acuity.statement: Maybe others will have more specific questions, but my broader question is: if this is a genuine concern for both the Minister and also for the current judiciary system, particularly in light of the judicial review that the Minister mentioned before, what are some of the repercussions that we’ll see if this bill isn’t being done in the way that we’re doing it now, essentially?
acuity.explanation: He explicitly builds on the information the Minister had just supplied, treating the validation rationale as a premise and asking for its counterfactual — what happens if the bill is not passed this way. That is engaging the content rather than referencing it, though the question remains broad rather than fixing on a particular element of the Minister's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "This will prevent the need for those conditions of approximately 2,000 current defendants on EM bail to have to go back to the courts" — the validation rationale he had just given.

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister stems from the fact that I don’t feel as if I’ve heard a sufficient answer to a question that was posed earlier about the procedural training aspects. I understand it’s operational, but it is important to this process because it potentially has an impact on the successful implementation, so to speak, post this process.
acuity.explanation: McLellan follows David Parker, whose two questions were (a) whether the bill removes any existing right to seek a court exception and (b) whether an EM assessor might apply stricter reasoning than a court. She stays squarely on the matter under debate — the EM assessors and their decision-making — and gestures at the chamber's running exchange, but she takes up neither of Parker's strands; she pivots to her own prepared line on training, change management and industrial relations. The speech would read the same whatever Parker had argued about rights, so it sits in the 'on topic, engages no part of the argument' band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Gesture only, not engagement: David Parker asked "whether it is possible that the EM assessor may apply their reasoning in a way that might have been more strict than a court would have done before the passage of this legislation?" — McLellan continues the EM-assessor thread but on training and change management, not on Parker's strictness or rights-removal questions.

acuity.statement: Just in terms of training, it’s been the practice for more than 10 years. Updated material will be provided to corrections staff as soon as the bill is passed, but my advice is there is not a need for updated training.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith opens by taking up McLellan's training question directly and answering it on its own terms — that the practice is over a decade old, that updated material will follow passage, and that his advice is no new training is required — and then turns to Parker's rights question, denying that any right of access to the court is removed and supplying the approval/decline figures bearing on Parker's assessor-strictness point. Delete the two preceding turns and this answer could not stand as written; it is shaped by the specific questions put. Not a full 1.0 because Parker's second question, about whether an assessor might reason more strictly than a court, is answered only obliquely via the volume figures rather than head-on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t feel as if I’ve heard a sufficient answer to a question that was posed earlier about the procedural training aspects" — Tracey McLellan (and, on rights, David Parker's "whether there is any instance where rights are being taken away compared with the status quo?").

acuity.statement: In relation to the requirement for a review, the defendant can return to the court to obtain authorisation for their absence if they don’t like the decision of the authorised assessor. And if they go to the court and obtain an authorisation and they don’t like that, then they’ve got the right of repeal, and we think that is sufficient.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Webb's specific request for a right of review of the electronic monitoring assessor's decision and answers it on the merits — naming the existing mechanism (return to court, then appeal) and asserting it is sufficient, which rebuts Webb's premise that there is no way to revisit the decision. It is not a full 1.0 because it engages only one of Webb's three asks and does not address his actual reasoning that a court route is the wrong-sized remedy, nor the immunity and post-legislative scrutiny points.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "We do need some sort of ability to revisit that decision, because just making the same application again and again isn’t actually going to do that."

acuity.statement: Just picking up the points made by my colleague the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, in relation to people who may have unwittingly broken the law and have not known that they have broken the law. My question to the Minister of Justice is: what steps has he taken to communicate to those people directly that they did not break the law, so that there is an element of certainty?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly takes up Webb's immunity-from-prosecution argument about people who breached bail believing they were authorised, and draws out a consequence he had not covered — that a deeming provision is worthless unless those affected are told. The speech would have to change if Webb had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because it extends rather than tests his argument, and does not engage the Minister's just-delivered answer on review at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "There are people out there who’ve acted in good faith and honestly, but they’re actually now in real strife."

acuity.statement: I think we are now getting to the crux of this particular bill, which is whether the restriction that is being granted by Corrections is more strict than the restriction that would be granted by the court, as some of the previous speakers have been asking.
acuity.explanation: Webb's preceding turn made two specific arguments: that the bill provides no right of review or appeal against a corrections officer's decision, and that new section 30MB uses no power-conferring words. Xu-Nan gestures at the debate by crediting 'previous speakers' with having raised the Corrections-versus-court question, but takes up neither of Webb's arguments; he then proceeds to his own prepared material on the Bill of Rights consistency report (sections 18 and 26) and two questions of his own. The speech would read almost identically had Webb argued something different about the same bill, so it sits in the low band with a gesture rather than an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "If they make the wrong decision, what right of review or appeal do they have?" — Xu-Nan acknowledges 'previous speakers' asking about Corrections versus court restrictions but does not take up Webb's review/appeal or drafting points.

acuity.statement: The question was raised around the ability to appeal the decisions that were made, and the advice is that the defendant could bring a judicial review or can simply go to the court to request an absence if they’re not happy.
acuity.explanation: This supplies the answer Webb explicitly asked for — what review or appeal exists against a corrections officer's refusal — and names two routes (judicial review, or a fresh application to the court). That is responsiveness to the specific question rather than a reference to it, and it is the strongest form of engagement available to a minister in committee: the content is determined by what was put to him. It is not 1.0 because he then meets Webb's second, more technical argument that section 30MB contains no power-conferring words with an assertion that the drafting 'is sufficient for the task', which engages the conclusion but not the reasoning, and he leaves Parker's standard-conditions question and Xu-Nan's two Bill of Rights questions untouched. Note this is scored on engagement only: whether the judicial review answer is correct is a veracity question, and the bare 'the advice is' is a specificity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "what right does the person have?" — Goldsmith answers the review/appeal question directly with judicial review and a fresh court application.

acuity.statement: A question was asked about the approvals by Corrections “and others”, and who might that be. My advice is that they’re small numbers, but, for example, it could have been the staff at a residential treatment facility in the past, but going forward, only “EM assessors” from Corrections will be able to approve absences. They’re validated for 60 days, and the conditions will be replaced in that time.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact question put to him — who the "others" are — and supplies the answer (residential treatment facility staff), then adds the forward position (only Corrections EM assessors) and the 60-day validation that Webb asked about. The reply would be unrecognisable had Webb asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "he refers to “social workers and others” who have made these decisions" and "I’m very keen to know who the others are"

acuity.statement: The second one I touched on in the debate on Part 1, but this is where it really comes up. The Act itself talks about electronic monitoring (EM) assessors, whereas in new section 11(2) of Schedule 1AA, you refer to the “Department of Corrections EM bail team”.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's answer — the reliance on "EM assessors" from Corrections — and presses on the mismatch between that term in the principal Act and the "EM bail team" wording in the bill. But the surrounding call is largely his own prepared drafting points (Police vs Corrections) rather than engagement with what Goldsmith said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "going forward, only “EM assessors” from Corrections will be able to approve absences"

acuity.statement: Currently, there is a small number of employees from residential treatment centres who are granting some of these bail leaves in the capacity of some of these electronic monitoring (EM) assessors, but I’m just checking: is a residential treatment centre employee an employee of either the Department of Corrections or the New Zealand Police?
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's specific answer back to him, checks he has heard it correctly, and then draws out its consequence against the bill's employee test — exactly the kind of follow-up that could only exist because of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it could have been the staff at a residential treatment facility in the past"

acuity.statement: So one of the questions that’s come up is whether the use of discretion will be equitable—i.e., that Māori will not be discriminated against by the electronic monitoring assessor. Is there a breach of Te Tiriti rights? Corrections or Police, or there have also been known as private companies or private security groups, are in these assessor roles; we must remember that private security are not Crown and therefore it’s a breach of Te Tiriti.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — who may act as an EM assessor — and the observation that non-Crown bodies sit in assessor roles glances at the Minister's disclosure about treatment-facility staff. But it engages no part of the argument made before it; the member says the questions come from her external rōpū, and the call would read the same whatever had just been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it could have been the staff at a residential treatment facility in the past" — the non-Crown-assessor point is a gesture at this, but the questions are externally sourced and not aimed at any claim made in the preceding turns

acuity.statement: I know that my colleague Dr Duncan Webb has already referred to the quite unusual definition of “old law”, which is defined in the interpretation section here. I think readers of this bill will note immediately that there isn’t a definition of electronic monitoring (EM) assessor in this bill. We’ve had a couple of questions around who an EM assessor can be, and I think those are valid questions which I understand remain unanswered.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the definitional thread from the earlier turns, identifies the gap those questions exposed (no definition of EM assessor in the bill), says she checked the point against the principal Act, and converts it into a concrete request for an amendment. The call is built on what preceded it rather than beside it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "it seems to me that there’s no really good definition of an authorisation that occurred under the old law"; and Lawrence Xu-Nan's questions on who an EM assessor can be

acuity.statement: Then, if it’s not covered under 11(1)(a), therefore, any decisions that are currently made or have been previously made by residential treatment centres would not be validated by this amendment and by this particular schedule—which just ties into some of the discussions we had before in terms of judicial review; whether that would then still create the same potential legal challenge that the Minister is trying to avoid in the first place by bringing all of this under urgency.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given answer — that residential treatment facility staff are not Corrections or Police employees — and draws out its consequence for the validation scheme, arguing it leaves exactly the judicial-review exposure the bill is meant to close. The speech would be different had Doocey answered otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "residential treatment facilities are not employees of Corrections or Police" — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: Just responding to the Hon Dr Duncan Webb and his question about commencement the day after the Royal assent, I’ve been advised by officials that that’s a standard approach.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies an answer to the specific question Webb put about why commencement is the day after Royal assent rather than on assent. It engages the actual question rather than pivoting, though it leaves Webb's second point (the title amendment) untouched and offers only the bare 'standard approach' reason.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why not just have it come into force at the moment of Royal assent, which is what you see in other legislation?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: For example, I think the Minister for Mental Health previously mentioned, quite accurately, that there is a definition of “EM assessor” under section 3 of the principal Act, the Bail Act 2000, but all it says is that the EM assessor’s definition is the same definition as in section 30E, and section 30E was precisely what we discussed before around what is the definition of “EM assessor”. What we’re seeing is sort of this ouroboros circle; we are not really getting the clarification, because all of them just say, “Please refer to this one section.” and neither of those sections actually refer to it very clearly and succinctly.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific answer — that 'EM assessor' is defined in clause 3 of the Bail Act and that this is standard practice — follows the citation through, and rebuts it by showing the definition only refers on to section 30E. This is engagement with the content of the answer, not a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "“EM assessor” is defined in clause 3 of the Bail Act." — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: I think, most importantly, like the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, has mentioned, electronic monitoring isn’t really what the issue is here; it is the authorisation of the electronic monitoring that is creating the issue that we have here. I wanted to check with the Minister if the Minister would consider amending the title clause to “This Act is the Bail (Electronic Monitoring Authorisation) Amendment Act 2025”, or even, alternatively, “Electronic Monitoring Authorisation Reform” or “Authorisation Improvements” or “Retrospective Authorisation Amendment Bill”?
acuity.explanation: Picks up Webb's argument that the title misdescribes the bill, accepts its premise, and does something with it — converting the point into concrete alternative titles put to the Minister. Had Webb argued something else about the title, this passage would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this isn’t really creating electronic monitoring, so the title we’ve got is actually a little misleading" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister for Mental Health: is the commencement clause appropriate, given the inherent retrospectivity of this bill?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the commencement strand Webb opened and the Minister answered, but engages the topic rather than the specific exchange — it neither tests Doocey's 'standard approach' reply nor Webb's one-day-gap point, substituting a separate retrospectivity argument. A partial engagement on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s just a little odd to say the Act comes into force the day after Royal assent" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Again, we hear that this is to make sure that it is legal and what we do is legal—which would be very much appreciated, because like the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, mentioned, it is nice when we do things legally in Aotearoa. But in this case, one of the things that we weren’t able to clarify, for example, is the fact that the whole point of this is to ensure that the EM assessor is able to have a level of certainty that they’re able to issue some of these absences, but there’s no ability to challenge any of the decisions that are made, because there are no provisions in place in terms of an independent review—which is normally what we see in other bills of a similar nature, when you have a member of the executive, which includes our departments, that can make decisions that affect others—and how they are able to be held accountable by matter of specific provisions within the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes up one identifiable strand of Webb's preceding speech — the absence of a workable right of review over EM-assessor decisions, and Webb's point that the legislation is being passed to make an illegal practice legal — names Webb explicitly, and extends it with his own argument about the lack of an independent-review provision. But the engagement is partial: the nod to Webb is largely rhetorical and the substance is his own prepared committee-stage material (drafting consistency, section cross-references, the BORA report), most of it aimed at the Minister rather than at Webb's argument. It would read much the same had Webb argued something else on the same bill, so this sits at the mid-band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My suggestion that there be a quick-fire right of review, rather than having to go back and make an application to the courts for variation of bail, was, in fact, focused on the efficiency of the bail system" — and Webb's related point that the bill does not confer power on EM assessors.

acuity.statement: It is important to clarify that what we are dealing with is that the Bail Act did not adequately provide for the approach that was in place. The Minister of Justice, who is focused on effective and efficient justice, identified this anomaly and acted as he should to ensure that we rectify this and continue on a pathway of effective and efficient justice.
acuity.explanation: Follows Stephenson and names him, but only restates the same government framing (an anomaly was spotted by officials/the Minister; courts should not be overburdened) without taking up, extending or testing any part of his argument. The speech would read identically whatever Stephenson had said in support of the bill, so this is prepared party position on the right subject rather than engagement — a mere reference, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "This is a very sensible piece of law, clarifying the fact that Corrections can make these changes and codifying what is usual practice."

acuity.statement: We’re in urgency and Te Pāti Māori do not support any bills when they’re going through urgency. Why? Because we need to have the time to actually meet and discuss these amendments and bills with our communities.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what preceded — Costello's defence of handling the bill under urgency as the proper, proactive course — and contests the urgency directly, so the speech is not indifferent to what it follows. But it engages only the process strand and not the substantive justification both earlier speakers gave (that the Bail Act does not cover existing practice and defendants would otherwise be pushed back to court), and then moves to a standing party rule and a list of unrelated grievances. Partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "Therefore, it is being done as it should be, as a priority in this House"

acuity.statement: I do acknowledge the concerns that have been articulated by the previous speaker, Takutai Tarsh Kemp. Obviously, urgency is never an ideal way to do business, and I think that all of us in the House would much rather prefer it if we avoided the use of urgency, but I think that, in this instance, our not using urgency could create the risk that some people who, through no fault of their own, would be unfairly illegalised for a mistake that was made almost over a decade ago, and so that’s not ideal.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the immediately preceding speaker's central objection, concedes the part he accepts (urgency is undesirable and should generally be avoided) and disputes the rest with a specific counter-cost — that delay would leave people unlawfully affected by a decade-old drafting error through no fault of their own. Had Kemp argued something else about the bill, this passage would have had to change, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because he does not engage her specific consultation/select-committee remedy or her figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Takutai Tarsh Kemp: "We’re in urgency and Te Pāti Māori do not support any bills when they’re going through urgency."

acuity.statement: I rise to speak in this third reading in support of the Bail (Electronic Monitoring) Amendment Bill. It’s an urgent legislative change that was required to ensure the longstanding and efficient practice of management for defendants on electronically monitored bail. Most of the parties in this House support it. Therefore, any more debate would just be a waste of time, so therefore I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn (Camilla Belich) made two specific, content-rich points: that the BORA vet, signed off the day before, addresses the limit on freedom of movement but not the bill's retrospectivity, and that the reason for the urgency remains unexplained compared with other recent urgent bills. Campbell's speech takes up neither. He asserts the change was 'required' and that debate is a waste of time, which is on the subject of the bill but engages no part of the argument just made — it would read identically whatever Belich had said. There is a faint gesture at the debate itself ('any more debate would just be a waste of time'), but that is a comment on the debate's length, not an engagement with its content, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued that the BORA vet 'doesn’t really address the retrospectivity aspect of it' and that she 'still really don’t know exactly the reasons as to why this bill has suddenly come about in such an urgent fashion', and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Labour, as we have said, obviously will be supporting this at third reading, as we have done at first reading and at second reading, but, certainly, the committee of the whole House stage highlighted the fact that there are several holes, a few gaps, and so our support is somewhat begrudging in so far as this doesn’t feel like it’s a well-planned-out piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Rutherford whose single argument was about Te Pāti Māori's blanket opposition to urgency. McLellan's speech is on the matter under debate (the bill, urgency and the missed select committee stage) but engages no part of Rutherford's claim; the preceding turn is waved away rather than answered, and the speech would read identically had he said something else about the bill. Prepared material on the right subject with only a gesture at what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tom Rutherford argued that Te Pāti Māori "do not ever support the use of urgency—ever, full stop" and would be unable to pass a Budget, and this statement does not take that point up — it dismisses the preceding turn and moves to Labour's prepared position on the bill.

acuity.statement: E te Māngai o te Whare, e tautoko ana au i te pire ki te Whare.
acuity.explanation: Fleming follows a detailed critique of the bill's gaps, the urgency process and the unexplained advice behind it, and responds with a bare commendation of the bill. It engages none of the preceding argument and would have been word-for-word the same whatever McLellan had said; it is at least directed at the bill under debate, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued the bill was rushed under urgency, left the retrospective immunity and civil liability questions unresolved, and that the impetus for it was never disclosed; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: What I would like to say is I really appreciate the expressions of concern from across the House about urgency, but what I will say is this: when we have the best justice Minister in over seven years at the helm of the justice ship, I know that this urgency for this bill is a sound move.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn by Helen White that made two concrete criticisms: that urgency was being misused, and that the Minister never answered who makes these decisions or what checks and balances protect the person on bail and the victim. Nakhle gestures at the first of these ("expressions of concern from across the House about urgency") but takes up no part of the argument: she answers the urgency objection by asserting the Minister's quality rather than addressing the rushed process, and ignores the checks-and-balances question entirely. The speech would read identically whatever argument had preceded it, so long as someone had voiced some concern about urgency — a gesture at the debate, not an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "that does not mean that you haven't heard quite a vigorous Opposition tonight to a flippant use of urgency" — and her repeated question about who makes electronic-bail decisions and what checks and balances exist.

acuity.statement: Amendment Paper 256, in the name of Chris Bishop, is something new, since we were able to traverse the many rights implications. It’s also new since the Attorney-General gave her opinion on the way that rights were being limited in this case.
