I’d like the Minister to step the committee through the provisions in the Amendment Paper that apply to Part 1, please.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Utikere's preceding turn — the Attorney-General's report on rights limitations as the matter not yet dealt with — and advances it by noting the Amendment Paper postdates that opinion. But it engages none of his specific questions (the "family of qualifying drugs" examples, the Minister of Police definition, the December timeline) and otherwise delivers her own targeted request. A partial engagement, pointable but thin.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "there are a number of concerns that have been addressed by the Attorney-General in her report to the House"

acuity.statement: I rise to take a first call on this first part, seeing as how the Associate Minister of Transport isn’t standing to respond to questions that have been put forward thus far. I want to broadly start with raising the concerns that were raised by many submitters, and then a series of questions to the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Observes the procedural fact that prior questions went unanswered, which is a reference to the existence of those questions rather than to their content, and then proceeds to prepared select-committee material on evidence of impairment. On the matter under debate, so not 0.0, but the speech would read identically whatever Utikere or Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere questioned the interpretation section and implementation timeline and Arena Williams asked the Minister to step through Amendment Paper 256, and this statement takes up neither — it notes only that the Minister has not risen to answer.

acuity.statement: I’ll start with Tangi Utikere. I liked the question where he asked, “Who will approve screening devices?” Asked and answered: Minister of Police. He meant to ask whether I’m comfortable that the Minister of Police’s definition in the Act is the right one. Yes, I’m very comfortable with that. The Minister of Police is also defined and already in the Land Transport Act as well.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question put, and goes further by restating what the member actually meant to ask before answering it, then supplies the reason — that the term is already defined in the Land Transport Act. The reply could not have been given in response to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "my question for the Minister is whether the definition of the ‘Minister of Police’ in the interpretation section is appropriate"

acuity.statement: Arena Williams asked if we could step the committee through the amendments in Part 1. Absolutely; there are only two. The first is to insert a definition of “elective oral fluid sample”, which means “a sample of oral fluid taken from a person under section 71DC(2)”. The second change is a change in the “oral fluid sample” definition, from section 71DA(1A).
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what the preceding turn requested, clause by clause, naming both Part 1 amendments and the sections they insert and replace. Entirely contingent on what Williams asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "I’d like the Minister to step the committee through the provisions in the Amendment Paper that apply to Part 1, please"

acuity.statement: We think it is a justified limit on the right to be free from unreasonable search and seizure, because the policy purpose of the bill is to prevent road incidents and road deaths in New Zealand. We think this is not an unreasonable step to take in order to prevent that kind of behaviour.
acuity.explanation: Meager names both of the points Williams actually put to him and takes up the first one directly, giving the government's reasoning on why the section 7 limit on freedom from unreasonable search and seizure is justified. The reply would be different if Williams had raised something else; he does not fully engage the specific compounding-invasiveness/detention-time strand, and defers the second-oral-test question to officials, which holds it just below the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "They’re about what the Attorney-General set out for the Transport and Infrastructure Committee when she was giving her view on whether this was an unreasonable search and seizure."

acuity.statement: Minister, there is an attempt here to introduce a new scheme of oral fluid screening tests that will come along with other impositions, as we heard, on civil liberties for New Zealanders who are going about their lawful business. I would just like to understand from you, Minister: what do you think should be going into these calculations on approving an oral fluid screening test based on time frames? I’ve had a look through the bill and I couldn’t see anything regarding time limits for these new devices, so I’d be interested to hear your thoughts on that, Minister.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and in the same committee stage, with a glancing "as we heard" at the civil-liberties concern Williams developed, but the substance is his own prepared question on time limits for device approval and engages no part of either Williams' search-and-seizure argument or Meager's justified-limit answer. The speech would read the same whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "That amount is, for some people, quite hard to produce in the time frame, and so we will have people who are then either required to have another oral fluid sample or are then required to take what is a pretty invasive search, and the invasive search, here, is the blood test, and that is also something that might not be administered on the roadside; that might be administered elsewhere." — a gesture only; Luxton's "as we heard" nods at the civil-liberties strand but does not take up the argument.

acuity.statement: This is my first opportunity to take a call on this question, and I can say with confidence that we do support safer roads and we support an evidence-based way of getting there. The Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Bill seeks to amend the Land Transport Act 1998 by changing the testing threshold from an oral fluid containing evidence of use to an oral fluid that indicates use of qualifying drugs.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Arena Williams's substantive turn immediately precedes. Willis is squarely on the bill under debate and even touches the same Attorney-General NZBORA report, but he engages none of her argument: he opens fresh with his own prepared questions on the evidence base, prescription medicines and discriminatory screening. The speech would read identically whatever Williams had said, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band; the shared NZBORA subject matter earns a little above the floor, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that the Amendment Paper's new step allowing a person to elect a laboratory test of an oral fluid sample at their own cost was not weighed in the Attorney-General's rights analysis, and asked the Minister to walk the committee through the likely time a driver would be detained; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In the first reading debate, it was the Hon Matt Doocey who said, during his speech, that part of the legislative intent was to keep New Zealanders safe on the roads. He alluded to the 65 lives that are being lost. During the second reading speech, the Hon Chris Bishop alluded to drug deterrence as one of the legislative intents of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it. Hernandez engages the debate's earlier record (Doocey's and Bishop's statements of legislative intent, and the Minister's introduction) rather than anything the preceding speakers argued, so there is a real gesture at the debate without engagement of the turns he follows. That places it at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band, not at 0.5: nothing in Williams's or Willis's calls had to be said for this speech to run as it does.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Willis asked how the regime will 'avoid penalisation of those who have ingested prescription medicines' and how screening will avoid being discriminatory; this statement does not take either strand up. Hernandez instead works from speeches given at earlier readings, which are outside this window.

acuity.statement: I have a question for the Associate Minister of Transport, and it’s starting with clause 4(2) around the “family of qualifying drugs”. I would like to come back to the conversation around the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (BORA), because, again, I’m sure that the Minister is very conscious as well that this is one of the few bills which has a specific section 7 report, in which case that has incredibly high thresholds, so I think it does warrant for us to come back in terms of some of the potential BORA violations that we do see here and some of the concerns around that, which I’ll discuss in a bit.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn by Meager answered Arena Williams' question about a second step in the sampling process; Xu-Nan engages no part of that answer, instead launching prepared questions on the qualifying-drug definition and the section 7 report. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but the speech would read identically whatever Meager had just said about Amendment Paper 257.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just explained that "Amendment Paper 257 before the committee of the whole House provides for an opt-in regime where a person can elect to provide a further sample", and this statement does not take that up — it opens a fresh line on clause 4(2) and BORA.

acuity.statement: I understand there’s probably not enough time left in the night to answer all the questions from members—I’m sure there’ll be some time in the morning when we get up after having some beauty sleep—but I want to address Mr Xu-Nan’s points around the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (BORA). I’m not here to provide legal advice, but if I was to provide some guidance as to why we think it is a justified limit, there are a number of limbs to any BORA test.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put — whether the limitation on rights is justified under section 5 — and answers it on its own terms by working through the limbs of the justified-limitation test (important purpose, rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality). The reply would have had to be different had Xu-Nan raised a different objection. Not a full 1.0 only because the companion question about benzodiazepines not listed in Schedule 5, Part 1 is explicitly deferred rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Does the Minister then have the confidence that the test is reliable enough that it meets the threshold for limitation under section 5 of BORA?"

acuity.statement: What came as somewhat of a surprise from the Minister’s response last night was that the police Minister can consider relevant operational matters. Now, on a day-to-day basis—yeah, OK, you can consider those, but we’re talking about relying on a piece of legislation that is seeking to deliver change in the reduction of fatalities and serious injuries due to drug driving.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the precise element of the Minister's previous answer — that operational considerations bear on the approval of screening devices — and disputes it on the ground that the legislation should not be driven by procurement or day-to-day operational constraints, adding that the select committee did not accept it as the driving factor. The contribution is contingent on what Meager actually said; had he justified the device-approval timeframes differently, this passage could not stand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "the Minister must take into account that it will be a relevant operational consideration for police"

acuity.statement: This is not a good thing having people driving around under the influence of drugs. We’re intending to do something about this. I think it’s something the previous Government looked at doing. We’re intending to deliver on that, and there are some technicalities around that. We are working through that today. Of course, I’m sure successive Governments will look upon making this as effective as they can, but these are the measures that we are putting in place at this time. We intend to deliver on them.
acuity.explanation: Patterson explicitly takes up Hernandez's final question and engages one strand of it — whether the legislation would be revisited — by saying successive Governments will look at making it as effective as they can. But he does not supply the thing actually asked for, a criterion of success, and instead restates the Government's intent to deliver. Partial engagement with a pointable target, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "Again, the question is: what is the criteria for success for this Government, in terms of introducing this legislation?"

acuity.statement: The main issue I want to bring up and question in this part is under Subpart 2 of Part 1, clause 5(1). This is really the crux of the issue because, prior to this, the rules have been around responsibilities of drivers not to drive while impaired. And that is the key issue: not being impaired.
acuity.explanation: Genter follows Patterson's answers but engages none of their content — she opens by reiterating questions left unanswered the previous night and then moves to her own prepared line on clause 5(1) and impairment. The speech is squarely about the matter under debate and gestures at the exchange (the complaint that answers are outstanding), but it would read identically whatever Patterson had just said, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson had just answered the criteria-for-success question and explained that the police Minister must consider accuracy and device thresholds when approving a screening device, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: And their prescription says, “Don’t drive within eight hours.”—then they don’t drive within eight hours; it’s really simple. If it’s prescribed medication you’re worried about, then prescriptions are clear.
acuity.explanation: An interjection, but one that carries a claim and aims directly at the specific question Genter had just posed — how a person lawfully taking prescription medication is supposed to know whether they may drive. Weenink answers it on its own terms: the prescription label states the stand-down period. The remark would be meaningless if Genter had argued anything else, which is the mark of genuine engagement; whether the answer is adequate is a matter for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "how are people meant to know?"

acuity.statement: If oral fluid testing is not accompanied by reliable impairment assessment—like when it comes to pain management and cannabis use, if they are not impaired, they’re not at risk at driving in a way that’s going to be dangerous but they’re still going to fail the oral fluid test and the blood test because they have to take the medication to be able to go on with their lives.
acuity.explanation: This takes up Weenink's interjection and disputes its premise: the prescription stand-down answer assumes dosing can be timed around driving, and Genter's reply is that chronic-pain patients must take the medication continuously to function, so they will test positive while unimpaired. It engages the specific objection rather than restating her earlier material, though it stops short of addressing the labelling point head-on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "If it’s prescribed medication you’re worried about, then prescriptions are clear."

acuity.statement: As has been pointed out by some of the commentary coming from my right, on the boxes, on the prescriptions, you get advice. It’s no different to the alcohol situation where there is some discretion that you have to use. You can still have a beer or a glass of wine and drive and still be within the limit, and it’s the same scenario we’re talking about here. There is the defence of the prescription, which I am sure will be utilised for those people who may be inadvertently caught out by these rules.
acuity.explanation: Patterson engages the specific scenario Genter raised — a lawfully medicated, unimpaired driver failing an oral fluid test — and answers it with the statutory prescription defence, conceding the grey area she identified before drawing an analogy to the alcohol limit. He does not take on her core evidential claim that oral fluid presence does not track impairment, so it is a substantial but incomplete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "There’s a very good chance that people who are legally taking a prescribed medication can fail two oral fluid tests, then be banned from driving for 12 hours"

acuity.statement: What today’s Minister, Minister Patterson, has very helpfully clarified is that that is not the case, that the operational matters will be considered by the Police in terms of what they propose as suitable or not to the Minister of Police. I think it is important that that has been clarified, because members certainly on this side of the House were very surprised to hear that from the Minister last night, that suddenly there would be this change that is not reflected in the transport Minister’s Amendment Paper 256 that has been tabled.
acuity.explanation: Utikere takes the precise content of Patterson's answer on screening-device approval, restates what it establishes, and uses it to show that the position differs from the one put by a different Minister the previous night and is unsupported by the tabled Amendment Paper. The contribution is wholly dependent on what Patterson had just said and would not exist in this form otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "Other issues, such as the time it takes for a device to return a result, are operational matters that Police will consider before making a recommendation to the police Minister to approve a particular screening device."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. It does surprise me that Government members are taking closure motions in a bill which is supported around the House but is intended to be the best piece of legislation it can possibly be, and we still have a Minister who hasn’t answered questions about what this amendment does.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact strand Utikere left open — that the new sections 71D/71DE introduced by Amendment Paper 256 have not been explained — and presses it, naming the same provisions. It takes up one strand (the unanswered explanation) rather than engaging the detail of Utikere's definitional point, and then moves to the closure-motion complaint, so it sits above the prepared-material band without being a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "I would be interested to hear from the Minister, please: what is the explanation of those particular changes?"

acuity.statement: I’m very grateful that the Minister did want to engage on the question of police bias previously, because I would particularly like the Minister to think about the August 2024 independent report Understanding Police Delivery, where it was reported that being Māori increased the likelihood of prosecution by 11 percent compared to New Zealand Europeans.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (police powers under this bill) and gestures at an earlier exchange, but engages no part of the argument actually made in the preceding turns, which concerned detention time and the rights analysis. Prepared material on the right subject, with a glance at the debate, so the top of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked whether the changes to the definition of "second oral fluid testing" "change the inputs into the Attorney-General’s analysis of rights", and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate line on police bias, gesturing at an exchange that does not appear in the preceding turns.

acuity.statement: I will address that last point first from Mr Willis. I’ve probably brought this upon myself by responding to his earlier allegation, because I thought it was very unfair on the New Zealand Police to make that allegation. I will point the member to the fact that this is an empirical test. You either pass or you don’t. It’s not something where bias can occur.
acuity.explanation: Answers the bias claim head-on and attacks its mechanism — that an empirical pass/fail test leaves no room for bias — which is a direct rebuttal of the inference Willis drew from the report. Not a 1.0 only because it does not engage the specific 11 percent prosecution finding or the screening-coverage question Willis actually asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "I certainly would like a response to the suggestion that there isn’t bias"

acuity.statement: This is inserted to support the proposed changes in the Amendment Paper which provide for a person to provide an elective sample, if needed, for possible future independent testing. That is, of course, discussed further in Part 2.
acuity.explanation: Supplies precisely the explanation Utikere twice said was missing, giving the purpose of the new definition. Squarely responsive to the specific question asked; slightly short of 1.0 because it defers the substance to Part 2 rather than drawing out the consequence for Part 1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "we are yet to hear an answer to why the Minister has sought to introduce a new term called “elective oral fluid sample”"

acuity.statement: To Arena Williams’ point on whether the Amendment Paper proposes a more invasive search, again, this is a Part 2 matter, but to get ahead of the play now, no. The Amendment Paper provides for an elective sample, if needed, to enable a person to seek independent analysis. It mitigates concerns in the bill reported back that it could require prolonged detention to attain a sample of oral fluids sufficient for both laboratory and independent analysis.
acuity.explanation: Takes Williams' two-part question — more time, more invasive search — answers it directly in the negative, and then explains why the amendment runs the other way by addressing the prolonged-detention concern she raised. The answer would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Has he introduced a stricter sense of detention with these new amendments?"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister tell us if the amendments made at the Transport and Infrastructure Committee or the Amendment Paper that has been put forward for this committee stage addresses in any way—have we had any further feedback from the Attorney-General on whether it would provide a safeguard?
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of Patterson's mitigation claim and tests it against the Attorney-General's section 7 threshold, but does not take up his answer on its own terms or dispute its reasoning; most of the surrounding contribution is prepared material on deterrence, cost and the section 7 report.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "It mitigates concerns in the bill reported back that it could require prolonged detention"

acuity.statement: Devices are not 100 percent accurate. They can produce both false negative and false positive results. In recognition of this, there must be two positive roadside screening tests before a driver is prohibited from driving for 12 hours, which may address any road safety issue. There must be a positive laboratory test before an infringement notice is issued.
acuity.explanation: Genter's immediately preceding turn argued that non-impaired drivers on legally prescribed medicines could fail an oral fluid test, be detained and lose their licence, and that there is no evidence the regime improves road safety. Patterson's speech is mainly a prepared clause-by-clause outline of the Government's position on Part 2, but this passage does take up one strand of her objection — device fallibility and wrongly caught drivers — by pointing to the two-screen-plus-laboratory safeguard, and elsewhere he concedes the regime uses recent use only as a proxy for impairment. He never engages her central demand for evidence that harm will be prevented, nor the prescription-medicine threshold point, so this is partial engagement with the topic rather than a rebuttal of the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they can still fail this oral fluid test, they can still be detained, they can still lose the ability to drive" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: What recourse will the people of New Zealand have if oral fluid testing devices are approved that are found to have very high rates of inaccuracy or take such a long time that people are detained—assuming that the Government’s not going to support my colleague Mr Utikere’s Amendment Paper, which I think is a good idea, and we will certainly be supporting that Amendment Paper.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of Utikere's preceding argument — his 20-minute detention-limit Amendment Paper and the Attorney-General's arbitrary-detention concern — states a position on it and folds it into her own question. But she engages none of his reasoning (the 15-minute identity-check precedent, the absence of safeguards); the bulk of the turn is prepared material on a different clause and the accuracy of approved devices. Partial engagement that is pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "the tabled amendment in my name is one that will provide, actually, not 15 minutes but 20 minutes"

acuity.statement: The reason we don’t support a 20-minute cut-off, as proposed in the Amendment Paper, is because it does take some time for these devices to return a result.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question put — the Government's position on the 20-minute amendment — and then supplies reasons engaging the proposal's own mechanics (device turnaround time, uncooperative drivers, the cut-off as a 'stop clock' that could be gamed). The speech would have to be different had the preceding turn proposed something else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only; the strength of the gaming inference and the Auditor-General/Attorney-General slip belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether the Government is prepared to support an amendment that will basically ensure that there are protections for people in this country who are going about their lawful business so that they won’t expect to be arbitrarily detained for a period in excess of 20 minutes"

acuity.statement: I actually have a similar point to the previous speaker, Cameron Luxton, around a particular point, and this is clause 10(5). Basically, it says, after section 59(2), insert new subsection (3)—and I’m looking at paragraph (b)—which is when a person committing an infringement offence “fails or refuses to accompany without delay an enforcement officer”.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan picks up the exact provision Luxton had just raised (the duty to accompany an enforcement officer under clause 10 / amended section 59) and carries it forward, adding the self-incrimination and Bill of Rights dimension and noting which sections were absent from the section 7 report. That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding turn — the speech would have had to change had Luxton raised a different clause — but he does not take up Luxton's main argument about a time limit and automatic progression, and much of what follows (the Taylor v New Zealand Poultry Board material, the plan to work through Subparts 1 to 6) is prepared material rather than a response. Mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "amended section 59, inserted by clause 10, and that is failure or refusal to remain in a specified place or to accompany an enforcement officer" — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: Yes, it is true that under the primary legislation, or including this amendment bill, enforcement officers would have the power to do that, but, again, it comes down to the lack of specificity or unless there is specific secondary legislation that will be specifying the powers that are granted to an enforcement officer. The reason I mention about the level of specificity is when it comes to something as important as our New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, often when it does get challenged in a court of law, it favours the side that did not draft the bill, and it doesn’t favour the side that doesn’t have any level of specificity.
acuity.explanation: Patterson had just answered the Taylor v NZ Poultry Board civil-liberties point by saying existing alcohol-enforcement powers cover it and police will behave the same way. Xu-Nan concedes that premise explicitly ('Yes, it is true that under the primary legislation... enforcement officers would have the power to do that') and then disputes its sufficiency, arguing the absence of specified powers is what loses Bill of Rights challenges. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged against a different answer, and it accepts part while rejecting the rest.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: 'There are existing powers that the police have within the alcohol enforcement laws, and we expect that the police will conduct themselves in exactly the same way with the drug testing as they do with the alcohol provisions on those matters.'

acuity.statement: For drink-driving, we’re looking at possibly—correct me if I’m wrong—one specific compound, which is ethanol, whereas with drug-driving, we’re looking at a whole myriad of different potential comedowns, different levels, and, again, it comes down to the idea that, yes, there is the level of accuracy, but different people have different pharmacological effects as a part of that, and the first-pass effect, in terms of how your liver functions, all factors into that.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's accuracy figures and argues they are the wrong measure: a device accuracy rate transfers from alcohol to drugs only if the analyte behaves the same way, and he contests that by contrasting a single compound with multiple drugs and variable pharmacokinetics. That is doing something with the specific claim just made rather than restating a general objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: 'We know that the screening tests now are about 95 percent accurate and the laboratory tests are almost 100 percent accurate, so there is a high degree of accuracy.'

acuity.statement: As we know and if we follow the data, Māori are four times more likely to receive a conviction for drug possession. How far does the testing go in terms of the powers of an enforcement officer? Are we just testing for what appears to be somebody who is under the influence, or does it allow, then, for the fishing expedition of that particular person who has been pulled over? I don’t see anything in the legislation that isolates this as just an isolated case.
acuity.explanation: Waititi picks up one strand of the exchange immediately before him — how far an enforcement officer's powers extend once a driver is stopped — which Xu-Nan had pressed on the Minister, and his only other reference to the previous speaker is a joke about eggs. He then moves to prepared material on structural racism and the Understanding Policing Delivery report that engages neither Xu-Nan's specificity/Bill of Rights argument nor Patterson's answer. Engages the topic rather than the specific claim, which is the middle band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'I understand that both the primary legislation, as well as this bill, may confer certain powers, but what those powers extend to—does it extend to, for example, we’ve seen the enforcement officer being able to detain'

acuity.statement: We have been, in this section, in this Part 2, talking about the issues around the length of time that drivers might need to be detained, so I guess the question that flows from the answers that the Minister just gave is: if drivers know that certain substances will be tested for, it’s also the case that a whole lot of other—dozens of other—substances won’t be tested for. What is to stop people from switching the substance so that maybe they’re using less of the substance that’s being tested for but still using other impairing substances that won’t be tested for? How can we have the policy objective of deterring people from driving impaired if we’re only testing for two or three substances and drivers know what those are—when we know there’s many, many more substances that can impair driving?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's immediately preceding answer — that drivers will be told which drugs the devices test for — and draws out its consequence as a new objection (substance substitution defeating the deterrence objective), then ties it back to the detention-time strand under debate and to the crash statistics he had just cited. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged had Meager answered differently; it is built on his specific answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "The bill does require the police Minister to approve the oral fluid screening devices by notice, and that notice must specify the qualifying drugs or families of drugs that the devices will be used to detect"

acuity.statement: Just finally, there’s the amendment from Tangi Utikere amending new sections 71G(3) and 71GA(2), inserted by clause 22. We don’t support these amendments. The sections require the police Minister to consult the Minister of Transport and the science Minister. If the police Minister considers it appropriate to do that, they can do it; there’s no need for the bill to provide mandatory consultation for this discretionary action.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn was almost entirely an argument for a 20-minute cap on roadside detention, ending in a direct question to the Minister in the chair. This reply answers questions carried over from the previous sitting and then disposes of a separate Utikere amendment on consultation, giving a reason for that rejection but engaging no part of the 20-minute argument just made. On-topic and within the same committee stage, so not 0.0, but the engagement cannot be pointed at in the argument it followed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "I ask the Minister in the chair why he thinks that it is appropriate to have limitations to that extent." — the direct question put to him, which this reply does not take up; it instead rejects a different Utikere amendment about mandatory consultation.

acuity.statement: The first question to the Minister, kind of in response to what the Minister has said—I think that fundamentally, based on the independent police report from August last year, it signals that the police themselves, as well as the independent report, suggests that there is a level of bias when we’re looking at basically stopping people to administer that drug test.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific assurance Meager had just given (that faith in police integrity answers the bias concern) and meets it with contrary evidence — an independent police report — rather than restating a prepared objection. The speech would have had to change if Meager had defended the regime on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we've got utmost faith that our police operate with integrity and we have high confidence in our police" — James Meager

acuity.statement: Oh, the independent report from August 2024. If you haven’t seen it, have a look. It’s really enlightening.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the thing demanded of him: challenged for his evidence, he names the source and its date on the spot. Entirely shaped by the challenge it answers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Where's your evidence of that, Lawrence?" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Just want to quickly address one of the points the member who just took his seat, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, raised around bias. I think we’ve well and truly covered this topic. We have the utmost faith in the New Zealand Police that they will treat everyone fairly and equally, and I think to continue to labour the point might border on repetitive.
acuity.explanation: Names the member and the topic but engages no part of the content: the independent report just cited is not addressed, confirmed or disputed, and the reply simply restates the assurance that prompted the objection. A mere reference plus a complaint about repetition sits in the low band, not the middle.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "based on the independent police report from August last year, it signals that the police themselves, as well as the independent report, suggests that there is a level of bias" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: My point becomes: if those two tests, which have tested positive through the saliva test, then come back not confirmed through a lab test, is it fair that the driver of the vehicle is then required to pay for the towing or taxi or Uber fares for themselves when the lab test has proven that there’s no conclusive evidence that a prohibited substance was detected in that final test?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the operation of Part 2's testing regime — but indifferent to what preceded it: the questions on rural distance, towing costs and refusal would read identically whatever argument the Associate Minister had just made. The passing "I apologise if this has been covered" is a gesture at the debate, not engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just defended the bias safeguards and explained the compulsory impairment test available to suspecting officers, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: I know the Associate Minister of Transport is a new Minister but he has yet to address the second point that the Attorney-General has raised as a concern. Now, there has been some conversation about the arbitrary detention point, but the unreasonable search and seizure point that the Attorney-General has raised in her report is something that the Government really do need to respond to.
acuity.explanation: Utikere takes up what Meager's preceding answer did and did not cover — granting that the arbitrary-detention limb has been canvassed and pressing the unanswered search-and-seizure limb — and his later questions about private analysis fees pick up Meager's false-positive/negative-lab-result scenario. But the bulk of the turn is a prepared list of clause-by-clause questions (blood test fee, 'may' vs 'will', clause 17) that would have been put whatever Meager had just said. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "On the case where there are two false positives and a laboratory test comes back with a negative, that may well cause some inconvenience or some issues with those individuals that are picked up" — Meager's reply on rural impact and false positives, which did not reach the Attorney-General's second BORA concern.

acuity.statement: We think that, in terms of the requirement to test for those substances, we’re in a pretty reasonable space and we think it is a justified limit on people’s rights to be free from unreasonable search and seizure. Hopefully, that gives us a pretty good round-up on NZ BORA.
acuity.explanation: This is squarely aimed at the specific gap Utikere had just identified: he demanded a response on unreasonable search and seizure rather than arbitrary detention, and Meager walks the justified-limitation limbs (important purpose, rational connection, minimal impairment, proportionality) and lands on that exact right. Short of 1.0 only because he frames it as a repetition of an answer given on previous days rather than engaging anything new in Utikere's formulation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "the unreasonable search and seizure point that the Attorney-General has raised in her report is something that the Government really do need to respond to"

acuity.statement: Just finally, we will come back to some of the other questions around—the one thing in there that I can, I think, address now from Mr Utikere was: will people be forced to undertake blood samples? No, I understand in no legislation in this country are people required to undertake medical treatment or be provided to give blood tests.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked twice, directly, whether a person unable to give two oral fluid samples is effectively forced into a blood test. Meager names the question, answers it with a flat no, and gives the ground for the no. The answer could not have been given in response to anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "When someone is unable to provide two samples, oral fluid samples, is it correct that the only option for them then would be to go and have their blood taken?"

acuity.statement: I’ll address the questions from Tangi Utikere around why does replacement section 71A(8)(b)(ii), inserted by clause 16, provide that an officer may issue an infringement notice if a laboratory test comes back positive. The answer to that is that police have a discretion to issue infringements in all contexts, and that aligns with the standard practice of police across the board.
acuity.explanation: Restates Utikere's 'may' versus 'will' question on the exact provision he cited and supplies the reason — standing police discretion over infringements. The specific point put to him is taken up and disposed of.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Can the Minister provide a response as to why it is “may” and why it is not “will”?"

acuity.statement: New section 71D sets out the process for obtaining oral fluid samples that are required to be provided. You would never set a maximum limit as to the number of times you want to try to administer a test, because, for example, what happens if in the process of administering the test, the particular device or implement is dropped on the ground?
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific clause 18 question about a cap on the number of screening tests, names the relevant provision and gives a reason (contamination from a dropped device) for not fixing a maximum. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the question about attempts rather than the one actually asked about the statutory cap of three, but the speech is plainly shaped by the question just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Can the Minister confirm that, in those circumstances, the maximum number of oral fluid screening tests that any individual who is stopped at the roadside would undertake is a maximum of three"

acuity.statement: How confident am I that changes to the roll-out will work to bring down impairment? I’m incredibly confident that these changes will work. We have a high level of confidence in our police service. They are a tremendous group of men and women who serve our country fantastically well.
acuity.explanation: Repeats Utikere's question back and answers the topic (confidence in the roll-out) but engages no part of the actual argument about CIT certification numbers and rural coverage, pivoting instead to general praise of police. A partial engagement: the question is picked up verbatim, the substance of it is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "there is specified, specific training and certification that is required for these CITs" — asking whether the number of trained officers, particularly in rural communities, will increase

acuity.statement: There was some consternation on the other side of the Chamber around some of the answers to whether or not there would be maximums put in place for the number of tests you can take. I was referring to the fact that you would never put a specific maximum in terms of attempts at tests or anything like that. Of course, under new section 71C(4), in clause 18, a person may be required to undergo only one further oral fluid test under this section, only if the first or second screening test fails to produce a result.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the earlier exchange to correct his own answer and supply exactly the provision Utikere asked him to confirm, distinguishing failed attempts from further tests under clause 18. The speech would be different had the question not been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "If there is a malfunction with the first or the second screening test, as this bill indicates, and as I understand it, there would be a requirement for one further test to be given."

acuity.statement: Secondly, I will just briefly touch on Ms Genter’s questions. Again, we raised the issue of the Attorney-General’s report and the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and I would hope that we wouldn’t need to traverse our position on why we think the limits placed on people’s freedoms are justifiably limited by the particular importance of the purpose of the bill. I can rehash them again for the committee if they’d like to hear them again.
acuity.explanation: Genter put three specific questions: whether the Attorney-General's seizure concern is answered when the 12-hour ban needs no laboratory confirmation, what remedy a wrongly-banned driver has, and why the specified review matters in Part 9 were deleted. Meager names only the first strand and asserts the Government's conclusion on it (the limits are justified) while expressly declining to traverse the reasoning, and leaves the remedy question and the Part 9 question untouched. He engages the topic she raised rather than the content of her claims, so this sits between a pointed reply and prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That was one of the issues that the Attorney-General raised, and said that they didn’t think it was deemed justified for the seizure." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: It’s unfortunate that we can’t kind of delve into that as that may have had an impact as to how other parties may have voted on the previous part, but I do sort of cite that there is a little bit of a disconnect in the Minister’s response under the existing regime when it comes to blood-alcohol testing, which relies on a conviction for cost recovery or non - cost recovery. This is not about criminal convictions; this is about infringements and it’s about demerit points. They are two different things.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given assurance about the blood-sample fee and does something with it: identifies that the assurance rests on conviction-based cost recovery while this regime operates through infringements and demerit points, so the reassurance does not reach the people affected, and turns that into a further question about whether criminal convictions are now in play. The speech would have to change entirely had Meager answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In practice, police only apply this to recover the fee if the driver is convicted of a criminal offence as part of court-ordered costs on sentencing." — James Meager

acuity.statement: I want to pick up on the new Part 9 that is to be inserted in Schedule 1, because, I have to say, I agree with the Hon Julie Anne Genter, and I was surprised to learn that what had been proposed is a bit of a change. I know that that’s what has come through in the select committee process, but there were a number of concerns that were raised by submitters. I look at one that’s proposed to be deleted under what was the old clause 29(3)(e), and that’s “whether the amendments have had a disproportionate impact on Māori and Pasifika people:”.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Genter's specific argument that new Part 9 strips the review of its specified matters and extends it rather than merely endorsing it, naming a particular deleted paragraph (old clause 29(3)(e) on disproportionate impact on Māori and Pasifika people) and tying the deletion to submitters' concerns. Not a full 1.0 because it adds to her case rather than testing it, but the engagement with her content is specific and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What new Part 9 seems to be doing is removing a bunch of that detail." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: First of all, I just want to remind the Minister that, despite the fact that we do sometimes go back to specific reports, we asked you to contextualise it in situ to the particular subsection that we are referring to.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the Minister's complaint about members back-tracking to previously considered parts and answers it on its own terms — that returning to earlier evidence is legitimate when contextualised to the subsection under debate. Engagement is squarely with what was just said, though the speaker then moves on to prepared questions on clause 27(2), so it is a strong but partial engagement with the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "Well, let that be a lesson to me to try in good faith to answer questions, that have previously gone by, for fear of back-tracking on previous parts already considered."

acuity.statement: Then Mr Xu-Nan’s questions right now—raising points about arrest without warrant. I don’t think that’s particularly unusual. Police officers arrest people all the time without warrants, so I’m not quite sure where that one’s heading to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific point just put — arrest without warrant under section 94A(3) — and answers it, denying that warrantless arrest is anomalous. Clearly shaped by what Xu-Nan said and would read differently had he argued something else; marked down from the top because it addresses the general practice rather than the specific concern about non-compliance with a sample request.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "For someone to be non-compliant with wanting to provide a sample, is the Minister saying that they are able to be arrested without warrant?"

acuity.statement: Also, Mr Xu-Nan raises a point about why we would extend this control over people who fail or refuse to provide oral fluid screening tests or refuse to accompany an officer. Well, that aligns with the current regime around drink-driving. It is to ensure that, in the absence of those positive tests, the assumption is that there could be some impairment.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific argument just made — the added fail/refuse criteria for a 12-hour forbiddance — and supplies the rationale asked for, grounding it in the existing drink-driving regime and the impairment assumption. The answer could not have been delivered without the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I wanted to check with the Minister what the intent is behind expanding the scope of power to the enforcement officer by allowing them to also ban driving under another six additional purposes."

acuity.statement: I think the real risk with the simplified requirements around the review is that a future Government could have a review that doesn’t consider any of these relevant factors. Then they’re complying with the law, but they’re not actually addressing the issue of ensuring that the data is there, that we’re addressing all of the different concerns that were raised by submitters and that are legitimate concerns.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification for the simplified review provision — that future Governments should not be constrained by statute — and inverts it, arguing the absence of constraint is precisely the defect because a future Government could run a compliant but empty review. The rebuttal is built on the specific reasoning offered in the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I think that’s a sensible approach so that future Governments aren’t restrained by statute in terms of what they can actually review in the Act"

acuity.statement: I just want to check with the Minister, in regards to these three additional sections that are introduced: are they in line with other parts of that particular schedule in terms of demerit points? Seventy-five demerit points is reasonably significant, so for that to be simply due to non-compliance seems to be a very high penalty for, comparatively speaking, a lower offence, in comparison to some others that I’m seeing in terms of Schedule 2.
acuity.explanation: Penk introduced Part 4 as consequential regulation changes flowing from the new refusal offence and said he would not spell them out; Xu-Nan takes up exactly that — one of the unspelled-out regulation amendments (clause 36(5)) and the penalty attached to the refusal offence — and asks for the benchmarking rationale. Engagement with the strand Penk left open, though the question is substantially prepared clause-by-clause material rather than a rebuttal of an argument Penk made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "Part 4 is really related and consequential amendments" and "the new infringement offence of failing or refusing to undergo an oral fluid screening test"

acuity.statement: In lieu of any, or perhaps pending any, detailed advice that I might receive in terms of the extent to which these penalties of 75 demerit points would be considered to be in line with other demerit point levels or penalties more generally, I think, if I may say, that the point is really more that the Government views the seriousness of those offences—for example, failing or refusing to remain at a specified place or to accompany an enforcement officer without delay—as being sufficiently serious to merit that degree of penalty with those 75 demerit points.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific figure and the specific test Xu-Nan proposed (consistency with the rest of Schedule 2), concedes he lacks the comparative advice to answer it on those terms, and substitutes an explicit alternative justification — seriousness of the named offences. Not a full answer on benchmarking, but the reply is shaped by the question and would read differently had Xu-Nan asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "are they in line with other parts of that particular schedule in terms of demerit points?"

acuity.statement: As the member has rightly noted, there is, in fact, a slight difference between the original intention being the first anniversary of Royal assent having been given on the one hand and—as now being proposed—1 April 2026. We think—it seems to me—that in these cases, almost always it’s the fact that with a particular calendar date, you provide certainty and clarity in a way that doesn’t require the presupposition that a person would know when Royal assent has been given and then needing to add 12 months to that.
acuity.explanation: Confirms Utikere's reading of Amendment Paper 256, then supplies the reason for the switch from an anniversary-of-assent trigger to a fixed calendar date — the certainty-versus-flexibility trade-off and the backstop structure of clause 2(2). Directly built on the distinction Utikere drew; it would have to change had he asked about something else. It does not take up his insinuation that the change signals a procurement problem, which caps it short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "What was originally proposed was that it would be by the first anniversary of Royal assent. That is suggested to be changed to 1 April 2026"

acuity.statement: Following up from the questions around procurement, I guess the first part, I think, going back to the procurement issue in general: is there a requirement for this bill to be passed before procurement is able to be procured? That’s the first question.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the sequencing premise in Penk's commencement answer — that commencement waits on devices being purchased — and presses the prior question of whether procurement itself is gated on the bill passing. Explicitly follows on from the preceding exchange, then moves to its own prepared material on clause 22's labelling requirements.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "an Order in Council could bring forward, or introduce, as soon as reasonably possible, such measures—pending that technology being purchased"

acuity.statement: I think, while I would be unwise to speculate on the extent to which discussions around procurement are advanced sufficiently to know exactly how that will play out, I do observe that sometimes there’s a chicken and egg proposition whereby if procurement only should take place in accordance with the requirements of the law, as determined by legislation, the earliest one needs to pass the legislation in order to set those wheels in motion—but one is doing that, I guess, somewhat blind, to the extent that we don’t know exactly what will be available in terms of that equipment.
acuity.explanation: Answers the first of the two questions put — the legislation must pass first to set the procurement requirements, hence the 'chicken and egg' — and openly declines the second about whether suppliers have been approached. The reply is organised around Xu-Nan's two questions rather than prepared material, though half of it is a refusal to speculate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "is there a requirement for this bill to be passed before procurement is able to be procured?"

acuity.statement: I’d just like to thank the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs for that summary of some of the issues that are in Part 2. I do just want to traverse a little bit of where we were at in the debate, and what we were working through is we’re making a quite methodical process through Part 2, going clause by clause—of course, not particularly concentrating on clauses which just involved, say, substituting a heading or putting a new heading to a section, because that would be a little ridiculous, but we were working through the substantive issues that are contained within this tax bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Simpson's summary directly — accepts his framing that Part 2 holds substantive issues, agrees on the emergency provisions still to come, and then selects one item from his own enumeration (the exempt employee share scheme thresholds, clause 21) to interrogate. That is real engagement with the content just put. But the bulk of the turn is prepared material directed at a different Minister about last week's exchange on the approved issuer levy, which Simpson did not raise; the speech would largely survive unchanged had he summarised differently. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Part 2 of the bill contains amendments to the Income Tax Act of 2007" — Scott Simpson's summary of the substantive measures in Part 2, including "the increases to the thresholds for exempt employee share schemes"

acuity.statement: Again, I acknowledge the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs’ earlier comments around some of the more significant policy issues in the bill, but also I want to affirm where we got up to with the debate a week ago. At the time, I was currently debating with the Minister and had a number of questions around clause 16B of the bill.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at what preceded — she confirms Russell's account of where the debate stopped and acknowledges Simpson's summary — but that is procedural continuity and a mere reference, not engagement with content. Russell's actual argument (is this a growth measure, and what revenue assessment backs the approved issuer levy claim) is not taken up at all, and the detailed clause 16B / section FC 9(4) material is prepared and would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Russell had argued. On-topic prepared material with a glance at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my colleague the Hon Barbara Edmonds discussing clause 16B" — Deborah Russell, recapping where the debate had reached; Russell's substantive argument was that the share scheme threshold change should be tested as a growth measure

acuity.statement: On the answer to the question that my colleague the Hon Barbara Edmonds put about whether or not the Minister had sought advice, it’s useful for us to understand, now, that the Minister hasn’t sought advice on the Law Society submission, but we would like to know: will the Minister be, in the future, seeking advice around that advice?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister in the chair's specific answer, restates what it concedes (no advice sought on the Law Society submission), and converts it into a sharper follow-up about future intent. The sentence could not exist in this form if Simpson had answered differently, which is the deciding test. Not a mere reference: the content of his answer is what the question is built on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "I’m advised that the Minister has not received any further advice on the drafting of clause 16B, notwithstanding the submission from the Law Society."

acuity.statement: If we’re taking the fundamental element of the exemption from fringe tax being “on the employer’s premises”, how does it relate to new subclause CW 17D(1) where it says it “pays an amount to, or on behalf of, an employee” when that amount may be off premises?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it in the same committee-stage debate on the same bill. The question is close, technical and well-formed, but it is self-contained prepared material on a different clause that engages no part of what either preceding speaker argued, and it would read identically whatever they had said. On-topic (the bill under debate) but unresponsive, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is addressed into the live clause-by-clause exchange. Note this scores only responsiveness — the precision of the drafting point belongs to Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods spoke immediately before about clause 20, the emergency-event accommodation provisions and whether the $5,000 figure is a cap, and this statement does not take any of it up; nor does it engage Scott Simpson's answer on clause 16B.

acuity.statement: I’d like to, again, thank members for their useful and probing questions, particularly the Hon Megan Woods, who knows well from her personal experience of being in Government that Ministers receive information, advice, and supportive submissions from a variety of sources and organisations—not least of which is the Law Society—on a very regular basis.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Woods raised — advice from the Law Society — and is clearly shaped by her question, so it is not indifferent to what preceded it. But it takes up only the general strand (Ministers hear from the Law Society anyway) and leaves the specific question, whether the Minister will seek advice on the alleged drafting errors, untouched. Partial engagement, below the 0.5 midpoint because the specific claim put to him is answered with a general observation about how advice reaches Ministers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "will the Minister be, in the future, seeking advice around that advice?"

acuity.statement: She asked some questions specifically around emergency events. The whole purpose of the clause 20 changes are to actually provide certainty. I think any legislation that assists in providing certainty, depending on the nature of the event—which can sometimes be uncertain—is helpful. The drafting is intended to provide in that subsequent recovery phase some certainty for people who are involved.
acuity.explanation: Names the matter Woods raised and so gestures at the debate, but engages none of her three concrete questions: the function of the colon, whether $5,000 is a cap, and what exceptions exist for long-duration events. It restates the clause's general policy intent, which could have been said in answer to almost any question about clause 20. A gesture at the debate without engaging the argument puts it at 0.3, not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "it would be useful for us to know what purpose that colon is serving in this clause and whether or not this is indeed a cap that has been introduced"

acuity.statement: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked some questions around clause 19, particularly in relation to fringe benefit tax. There were some good questions in that, particularly relating to the fringe benefit tax liability if a benefit occurs on an employer’s premises. I can remember from my own days of being in business situations where, for instance, providing a barbecue and sausage sizzle at the end of the working week—was that considered a fringe benefit - type contribution to the employee? I think some of this is a matter of degree and some of it is actually a matter of just good judgment.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the strand Xu-Nan pressed — the on-premises condition in the fringe benefit tax exemption — so it demonstrably listened and would differ had he asked about something else. It then substitutes a personal anecdote and a general appeal to judgment for the interaction between section CX 24(c) and new subclause CW 17D(1) that was actually asked about. Partial engagement at 0.4; whether the anecdote is a sound answer is a Rigor question and is deliberately excluded here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "how does it relate to new subclause CW 17D(1) where it says it “pays an amount to, or on behalf of, an employee” when that amount may be off premises?"

acuity.statement: Look, I know that we are in the realm of post-truth politics, but I don’t think that I have seen a clearer indication of the gap between rhetoric and reality than what we have contained within the Budget Policy Statement—the rhetoric and the promises that this Government came in on with regards to the cost of living, and the reality that is biting everyday New Zealanders as a result of the decisions that this Government had made to knowingly in its Going For Growth strategy grow inequality, grow child poverty, grow climate changing emissions, and actually de-grow the wellbeing of New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive preceding turn by Megan Woods on the same Budget Policy Statement debate. Swarbrick stays on the matter under debate — the Budget Policy Statement — but engages no part of Woods' actual argument: not the $700 million residual allowance, not the forecast jobseeker numbers, not the Treasury advice on OBEGALx. Her own frame (rhetoric vs reality, Going For Growth, inequality and emissions) would read identically had Woods said something quite different, and the only backward reference is to the committee chair's earlier remarks rather than to the immediately preceding speaker. There is a gesture at the debate's subject, so 0.3 band rather than 0.0, but nothing pointable in Woods' turn is taken up, so it sits at the low end.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued that after pre-commitments the $2.4 billion operating allowance leaves only $700 million, and that Treasury advised against the new OBEGALx measure, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Why has the Minister allowed the overhaul of Whānau Ora, given that there is unclarity on how many audits Whānau Ora has passed, 19 audits in 10 years, two including an Auditor-General audit and a ministerial review?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the answer just given: Upston said audits do not issue passes or fails, and the supplementary turns that into 'there is unclarity on how many audits Whānau Ora has passed', supplying its own count of 19 audits in 10 years. It engages the pass/fail framing rather than the substance of the re-letting argument, and the 'overhaul' premise is prepared material, so this is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Audits and reviews do not issue passes or fails." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: What does Minister Potaka have to say to the 1,800 kaimahi who will lose their jobs as a result of his decision?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the commissioning change) but engages no part of the preceding answer about the tender process and selection criteria. The question would have been asked in these words whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just argued that Te Puni Kōkiri went to market as MBIE recommends and that providers were selected against criteria, and this question does not take that up — it opens a new line on job losses.

acuity.statement: How will the Minister ensure that the 540,000 whānau who currently access Whānau Ora services will not be negatively impacted by the sudden change in commissioning agencies?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the continuity-of-service assurance just offered and presses for the mechanism behind it, which is a real engagement with one strand of the answer. It stops short of contesting the answer's reasoning or its 'too early to tell' claim, so it sits mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have every confidence that they will do their best to ensure continuity of service for those who need it the most." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: If the Minister agrees with this statement, how can he justify cutting $500,000 from Whānau Ora through last year’s Budget?
acuity.explanation: Built entirely on the concession just extracted: the Minister answered 'yes' to the Auditor-General quote, and this question draws out the consequence of that agreement against the Budget cut. Had the answer been 'no', this question could not have been asked in these terms, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "yes, and that is why the key shifts in commissioning the next round of Whānau Ora commissioning agencies are based on a greater service reach" — Louise Upston (answering on behalf of the Minister)

acuity.statement: Given that Whānau Ora is a proven success and that the Auditor-General has recommended that its whānau-centred approach should be expanded, why did the Minister decide to gut and replace the current commissioning agencies instead of increasing Whānau Ora funding to incorporate new commissioning agencies alongside the already established ones?
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the debate — it proposes an alternative course (fund alongside rather than replace) which brushes against the spending argument — but it does not engage the effectiveness-of-spend reasoning just put, and reads as prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just answered that every Minister is focused on spending taxpayers' money effectively so it reaches those with the highest needs, and this question does not take up that value-for-money argument.

acuity.statement: Does a provider that has banked over $100 million in profit not suggest that the taxpayers’ money has not gone for the purpose in which it was given in the first place—right?
acuity.explanation: About the matter under debate but indifferent to what preceded it; the question engages neither the 'normal process' argument nor the support-for-Whānau-Ora claim, and would have been put in the same form after any answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just said the Government supports Whānau Ora and that going to market is a very normal process run by Te Puni Kōkiri, and this question does not take up either claim — it opens a separate line about a provider's accumulated profit.

acuity.statement: Your debt levels—yes, I have read your debt levels. We have set a very high bar for any new spending, so we will get the public sector; we will get the Government books back under control.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Shanan Halbert's interjected question directly enough to answer it ("yes, I have read your debt levels") but supplies no debt figure or engagement with the implied point about this Government's own debt track, pivoting straight back to prepared material on spending discipline. A partial, surface-level engagement rather than a rebuttal of the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "Did you read your debt levels?"

acuity.statement: It is an overwhelming feeling to hear all the speeches in this House and not once mention wellbeing. The last speaker talked about inheriting a wrecked economy. Well, I wonder how he feels when we’ve inherited or been subjected to a stolen one.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up Arbuckle's "inherited a wrecked economy" framing and inverts it into a claim about a stolen economy, so the opening would read differently had the previous speaker argued something else. But it engages the frame rhetorically rather than contesting any of Arbuckle's substance (debt track, inflation, operating allowance) before moving to prepared material on wellbeing and equity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "This Government, however, has inherited a wrecked economy"

acuity.statement: It’s not about productivity, because productivity will be achieved once we have closed the gaps between those who have and those who have not. And the Budget doesn’t look at any of that.
acuity.explanation: Takes Mark Cameron's interjected question head-on and does something with it: rejects the premise that productivity is the relevant measure and subordinates it to his own equity argument, then ties it back to the Budget under debate. The reply could not have been given in response to a different interjection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Cameron: "What about productivity?"

acuity.statement: The former member talked about public-private partnerships. That’s just one tool, and we’re looking at special purpose vehicles. We’re looking at infrastructure funding and financing tools. We’re looking at tolling. There are multiple ways that we can fund infrastructure, but we can’t keep doing it the way we’ve done it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Genter's attack — her claim that PPPs are being treated as free money and will load repayments onto future New Zealanders — and answers it by placing PPPs as one of several funding tools alongside special purpose vehicles, IFF tools and tolling, with a reason (councils and the Crown are at debt ceilings). It engages the topic and reframes it rather than meeting her specific argument that the PPP repayments still have to be accounted for, so this is partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I believe the Prime Minister actually believes public-private partnerships (PPPs) are free money, that all this foreign capital is just going to come here and build infrastructure in New Zealand for free."

acuity.statement: The previous Green member, again, left the House and didn’t get to hear my contribution but she mentioned that this reminds them of the 1990s.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker's 1990s comparison but engages none of its content — her argument was that early-1990s National policies drove a measured increase in inequality and left infrastructure and public housing under-invested. The reference is used to pivot to a joke about Spice Girls and Pearl Jam and then to prepared RMA material, which is a mere reference rather than engagement; the speech would read the same had she made any other historical comparison.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "In the 1990s, inequality dramatically increased in Aotearoa New Zealand because of policies from a National Government in the early 1990s."

acuity.statement: Now, some members spoke before me in the Opposition, including members from the Labour Party and the Green Party, and referred to some of the diagrams in the BPS. I find it very funny that the Green member kind of stopped talking about the net Crown debt that went all the way up under the Labour Government.
acuity.explanation: Lu follows Russell directly and names the preceding Opposition speakers, but the reference is a pivot rather than an engagement: she does not answer Russell's charge that the new OBEGAL-excluding-ACC measure is an accounting fudge (her own OBEGAL passage is about deficits since 2019 under Labour, a different claim), nor the living-wage, science-redundancy or infrastructure points. Her complaint is aimed at an unnamed Green member's turn, not at the argument immediately before her, and the speech would read identically whatever Russell had said — prepared BPS explainer material on the right subject. A gesture at the debate without taking up its content sits at 0.3 at best; 0.2 because the gesture is a jibe about what a speaker omitted rather than any part of what was actually argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "They couldn't get the books to say what they wanted, so they fudged them instead." — nothing: Russell argued the Government invented an OBEGAL measure excluding ACC to hide a missed surplus target, cut 500 scientists, removed the living-wage procurement requirement and mishandled the ferries and Dunedin Hospital, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: To claim, as they have, to have contained inflation with their austerity Budget is a nonsense and a falsehood. As we all know, inflation skyrocketed because COVID shut down global supply chains. For National to take credit for inflation falling because those global supply chains reopened is such a load of nonsense it’s not funny.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Lu had just made — that inflation is back under control and that this vindicates the Government's fiscal approach — and contests the causal attribution behind it, offering an alternative mechanism (global supply chains reopening). The passage would have to change if the preceding speaker had argued something else, which is the deciding test.
