Not a full 1.0 because he rebuts the causation without engaging her actual figures (the 7.3 percent peak, the OCR cuts) and moves on to prepared material; scored on engagement only, independent of whether the supply-chain explanation is correct or how politely it is put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: "Inflation now has finally returned to the Reserve Bank’s target range between 1 and 3 percent."

acuity.statement: I acknowledge the member for North Shore, Simon Watts. He made many acknowledgments; I want to acknowledge that I have two colleagues that live on the North Shore too: Camilla Belich and Shanan Halbert. As I said, this is non-controversial. All of the detail has been traversed adequately by the previous speaker and the person who brought the local bill to the House, the Hon Simon Watts.
acuity.explanation: Follows Watts' substantive second-reading speech and gestures at it — names him, mirrors his acknowledgments, and expressly defers to his traversal of the detail — but engages no part of his argument (the 1923 restrictions, the revenue question, the committee's definition of community purposes). It is a reference plus a move to get on to the next bill, which sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'd also like to thank, once again, all of those that have made this bill possible" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I want to note a couple of quick fun facts, acknowledging that the club has already spent $600,000 to restore the roof and the foundations, but they need about 10 times that to do the full restoration.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Watts' case — that the site cannot raise the revenue it needs to maintain itself — and supplies the scale of the shortfall ($600,000 spent, roughly ten times that still required), which bears directly on why the commercial-use restriction matters. It then returns to prepared colour about the building's history, so it engages the topic and a strand of the argument rather than the argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Takapuna Boating Club Bayswater clubhouse has been in a sorry state for a long time" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: One of the things that this bill has thrown up is how many anachronistic pieces of legislation we have on the book that stop New Zealanders from transforming their lives, from becoming more productive, and from actually doing the things that their communities want them to do.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Watts' claim that this case is not unique and that other local treasures sit under similarly restrictive statutes, and draws out its consequence — a general stock of anachronistic legislation obstructing productive use — rather than merely naming him or restating support. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had argued the opposite, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm sure many are subject to similarly restrictive legislation that inhibits their full potential" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: We too had discussion around the whenua around if there was any consultation. We also questioned who owned the land before 1923.
acuity.explanation: Foster's turn immediately before gave a detailed history of the building and the club, explained the removal of the 1923 prohibition, and reported the committee's discussion of where commercial revenue would go and how broadly "community purposes" should be drawn. Kemp's speech is on the bill and glances at the same select committee process and the same 1923 date, but it takes up none of Foster's actual argument — it restates Te Pāti Māori's prepared position on mana whenua consultation, quoting her own colleague's first-reading speech rather than engaging anything Foster claimed. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "it started life in about the 1880s as a tannery on the shores of the Tāmaki River in Panmure"

acuity.statement: If you just head a little bit down from Bayswater, the chief Patuone—who you may have seen his picture in one of the Lindauer paintings—is buried just down the road in Devonport, and I wanted to honour him in response to my colleague Takutai Kemp’s kōrero about the importance of honouring the mana whenua and making sure that we are living in true partnership with the mana whenua o tēnei takiwā, of the North Shore, and honouring Patuone, a great chief who was buried there and came from a long line of navigators.
acuity.explanation: Carter explicitly picks up one strand of the turn before hers — Kemp's insistence on the land's history and the standing of mana whenua — and does something with it, supplying Patuone and the Bayswater/Devonport connection and tying it back to the club's young navigators. But she engages the topic rather than Kemp's specific claim: Kemp's substantive point was that Auckland Council has not disclosed who it consulted, and that Te Pāti Māori will oppose at third reading absent assurance. Carter neither addresses that transparency charge nor the conditional threat, and the rest of the speech is prepared North Shore and Green material. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Takutai Tarsh Kemp: "the importance of understanding the land’s history and ensuring that mana whenua are actively consulted"

acuity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to allow commercial activities to be used in order to help raise the funds that are necessary to restore the building to its former glory. We’ve heard the rough sums of money that will be required to do that.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows a turn by Carter and, two turns back, a direct conditional threat from Kemp to withdraw support at third reading over consultation with mana whenua — a challenge a government committee member was well placed to answer. His speech instead delivers prepared material: North Shore praise, acknowledgements, the bill's purpose, and a recital of the two select committee amendments. The "We've heard the rough sums" clause is a bare gesture at the debate rather than engagement with any preceding argument, and the speech would be unchanged whoever had spoken before him in this debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Takutai Tarsh Kemp warned that "if Te Pāti Māori is not assured that comprehensive and genuine consultation with mana whenua has not taken place, we will oppose this bill at its third reading", and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The issue is that currently the club can only charge minimal rental to tenants who use the building currently and, as we’ve heard, it’s in a bit of a state of disrepair. The money that they’re getting from their tenants does not cover the upkeep for the building, hence the desire from them to have some more commercial activities conducted so that they can raise more monies for the restoration.
acuity.explanation: Halbert's turn immediately before rested on one substantive claim — that the existing Act's restrictions stop the local organisation generating revenue to reinvest in the facility. Costley takes up exactly that strand ("as we’ve heard") and does something modest with it: he supplies the concrete mechanism Halbert only gestured at — minimal permitted rental, tenant income short of upkeep, hence the request for commercial activity. That is a pointable partial engagement rather than a rebuttal or a figure supplied, and the rest of the speech is prepared material (acknowledgements, submitter quotes, the select committee's "community purposes" discussion) that would have been delivered whatever Halbert had said. Mid-band, not high: his sharper responsive moments — correcting "some of the dates that were stated earlier" and answering "the hypothetical situation which Mr Foster covered before" — reply to turns outside this window, so they cannot be audited against the preceding turn here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "the restrictions that it actually places on enabling the local organisation to generate revenue in order to reinvest in the facilities and make them available for our local community"

acuity.statement: As previous members have said, this is a bill of common sense. It’s a bill that fixes a situation where, dare I say, there must be many buildings around New Zealand that have similar situations.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod gestures at the debate twice ("from what I've heard from around the House", "As previous members have said") but engages no content from Belich's preceding turn; his speech would read identically whatever she had said. It is on the matter under debate and he names the committee that reported the bill, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero — a mere reference to previous members is not engagement. Notably he attributes the committee's chairship to Rachel Boyack immediately after Belich said she herself now chairs it, which is further evidence the preceding turn was not absorbed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I was lucky enough to speak at the first reading on this bill and I set out at length the reasons why I continue to support this bill." — nothing specific from that turn is taken up; Belich acknowledged councillors Chris Darby and Richard Hills and her committee chairship, and this statement does not engage either.

acuity.statement: I just found out that my friend in the Green Party had a relative who was the Mayor of Takapuna. In fact, my great grandfather was the Mayor of Takapuna too.
acuity.explanation: White picks up the one strand MacLeod opened — the local history and the former mayors attached to these local bills — and adds to it from her own family connection, tying it back to why the bill matters ("This bill will make sure that that history continues"). It is a genuine partial engagement that can be pointed at, but it takes up a colour passage rather than any argument about the bill, and the remainder is her own prepared material, so it does not reach the top band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "Maybe I can also acknowledge Fred Thomas, our member across the way there, the former mayor of this place here. It’s great to hear some of the history that comes from some of these places where these local bills come from itself."

acuity.statement: There’s a lot of talk about orange chocolate chip ice cream, but this is beyond our realm, because this would be more to do with the district licensing authority and the local boards’ policies on alcohol.
acuity.explanation: Brewer takes up the ice-cream-parlour strand running through the earlier turns and does something with it: he corrects the implied scope of the House's decision, pointing out that what may be sold on the site is a matter for the district licensing authority and local board policy rather than this bill. That is engagement with the content of what preceded, not just a restatement of it. It is only partial — the surrounding speech is largely prepared acknowledgements and digression that would be unchanged whoever had spoken before — so it sits mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "I can’t quite see how an ice cream parlour can fill the whole building, but maybe it is actually part of the building."

acuity.statement: One of those, of course, is the impact that it makes on the criminal justice system. Of course, to acknowledge the points that we’ve already made and continue to make, there is already an Employment Relations Act that covers any dispute between an employee and an employer. The process exists, the civil court action exists, and making it a criminal offence—obviously, adding penalties, adding criminal repercussions to employers—not only clogs up the justice system, as we have made clear, but also takes down a different path something that has otherwise had a path for resolution between the employer and the employee.
acuity.explanation: Nimon follows Belich's third-reading speech, which argued the bill is needed because existing avenues leave underpaid workers (especially migrants) without redress and that it 'imposes serious criminal sanctions in order to stop this practice'. Nimon takes up that one strand directly — contesting the criminalisation by asserting a civil path already exists under the Employment Relations Act — so she engages the mechanism Belich defended. But she does not take up Belich's actual grounds for it (the MBIE finding, the specific underpayment cases, the point that good employers face no new burden), and she frames the contribution explicitly as restating the position already given at second reading, so much of it is prepared material that would be unchanged whatever Belich had said. Partial engagement: ~0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "This bill imposes serious criminal sanctions in order to stop this practice."

acuity.statement: Members opposite said, “Tough on crime.”—absolutely. Do you know what I’d rather our police be dealing with? I’d rather our police be dealing with people crashing cars into a dairy, people robbing someone’s house, and people wearing gang patches in public and intimidating members of the community.
acuity.explanation: Nimon breaks off her prepared line ("actually, Jo, I'm going to come back to that point") to take up Boyack's interjection and does something with its content: she accepts the label ("absolutely") and turns the charge of inconsistency into an argument about police prioritisation, listing the offences she would rather police time go to instead of employer-employee disputes. The engagement is pointable and the passage would not exist in this form had Boyack not interjected, which is why it scores well above the prepared-material band. It falls short of 1.0 because the interjection is a thin two-word jibe rather than a developed argument, and after the list she returns to her prepared case about the civil-court pathway.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Tough on crime." — Rachel Boyack (interjection during Nimon's speech)

acuity.statement: I love doing some speeches after the Green Party. Firstly, what I would like to say is ACT is not anti-worker; in fact, we are extremely pro-worker.
acuity.explanation: Tuiono's turn charged ACT with being 'the big business on hyper-capitalism' who 'will do anything to burn down workers' rights'. McClure opens by naming the Green Party and directly denying that characterisation of her party's stance on workers. The opening would have to change if the preceding speaker had attacked something other than ACT's attitude to workers, so it is squarely aimed at the claim just made. It is a flat contradiction rather than an argument with evidence, which keeps it short of 1.0, but the engagement is specific and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they will do anything to burn down workers' rights" — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: The system is actually working. Why would this House want to create another layer of bureaucracy on top of what we have, under the premise of keeping our workers safe?
acuity.explanation: Tuiono's central argument was that the existing civil-action pathway is inaccessible and unaffordable for migrant workers whose families do not speak good English. McClure takes up the strand about the existing mechanisms and asserts, with enforcement and penalty figures, that they work — so she engages the topic of the existing pathway, which is the thing he attacked. But she answers the question of whether the system produces enforcement, not his question of whether a low-paid migrant worker can reach it, and then returns to prepared material about bureaucracy and police priorities. Partial engagement: one strand taken up, the specific objection left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how are they supposed to at least not only access that pathway but afford that pathway?" — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: When you make something a criminal offence, does it really deter people? That’s the real question. This is creating a new pathway into criminal law when there is already a pathway for resolution through the civil courts.
acuity.explanation: Weenink takes up one strand of Webb's central argument — his claim that the criminal law should apply where an employer intentionally withholds wages — and contests it on the ground that a civil pathway already exists and that criminalisation would not deter. She does not engage his equivalence argument (employee theft vs employer theft), his point that 84 percent of submitters supported the reform, or his explicit rebuttal that an employer without the money faces liquidation, not jail; after this strand she returns to prepared material on select committee submissions. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the criminal law should kick in" — he argued that wage theft by an employer is theft like any other and that the criminal law, not the Employment Court, should apply

acuity.statement: Look, I’m not going to take side comments from the Greens this evening, who want us to hug the middle, right?
acuity.explanation: Bates follows Menéndez March's interjection by naming it as a Green side comment and explicitly refusing to take it up, then pivots to tax cuts and to questioning whether the Greens are entitled to an opinion. Nothing in the interjection's content — that his recital of statutes does not match what workers experience — is engaged. A mere reference to the interjector is not responsiveness, so this sits in the bottom band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March interjected 'Talk to some workers.' and this statement does not take it up — it dismisses the source rather than the point.

acuity.statement: How do you know that if you say you have no data?
acuity.explanation: This takes two things Bates had just said in consecutive breaths — that the committee asked for data on wage theft and was given nothing that 'couldn't accurately provide a number', and that '99.9 percent of all employers are good employers' — and puts them against each other. It is squarely aimed at the specific claim just made and would make no sense after any other argument, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 only because it is a one-line challenge that poses the contradiction rather than developing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I take the point from our New Zealand First colleagues that 99.9 percent of all employers are good employers." — Carl Bates, immediately preceding, following his statement that no accurate figure for wage theft could be provided.

acuity.statement: Well, I’m simply quoting a member who has shared that perspective earlier this evening, and a perspective that I value significantly more than anything that comes from that corner of the House.
acuity.explanation: This does engage the content of the challenge: asked how he can know the 99.9 percent figure having just said no data exists, Bates answers on the provenance of the figure — he is not asserting it himself but quoting another member. That is a real, pointable response to the specific objection, and the speech would have been different had the interjection been different. It stops short of 1.0 because it resolves the inconsistency only by disowning the figure's basis, never defending the number, and then closes with a dismissal of the questioner rather than the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How do you know that if you say you have no data?" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I'd like to start with this: the previous speaker, the Hon Phil Twyford, was—let's see—focused on what it would be like in the National caucus. Well, I've got a question: I wonder what it was like in the Labour caucus when they were in power.
acuity.explanation: McCallum picks up the specific device Twyford had just used — imagining the National caucus discussion — and inverts it into a question about Labour's own caucus and why Labour never put the bill on its Order Paper. That is a pointable engagement with one strand of the preceding turn, and the opening would have to change had Twyford framed his speech differently. But it takes up the framing rather than Twyford's actual argument (that National systematically protects employers' economic interests), and the speech then moves to prepared material — acknowledgements, the risks of being an employer, the Northland Expressway — so it sits at partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "I'm trying to imagine the National Party caucus meeting when they discussed this bill"

acuity.statement: The member opposite says that we don’t know that. It’s already been pointed out that neither do they, because there is no good data on that, and maybe that is because there hasn’t been the ability for people to bring this before the law.
acuity.explanation: She halts her prepared line to take up the exact objection just interjected — that she has no data for claiming only a tiny number of employees are affected — concedes the premise (there is no good data), turns it symmetrically back on the interjector, and offers an explanation for the data gap. The passage could not exist unless that specific interjection had been made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "You don’t know that. You just said there is no data."

acuity.statement: I’ve heard that theft from an employee is equivalent to a layer of bureaucracy. We’ve also heard that not stealing is too much compliance—we don’t want to do that—and also that making it a criminal offence doesn’t deter people.
acuity.explanation: She does take up strands of the opposing case just put — the clogging/compliance objection and the deterrence objection — and names them, which is pointable engagement. But she restates them as caricature and moves to ridicule ("having a good laugh") rather than rebutting the reasoning, before returning to prepared material on workers' rights. Partial engagement, not a rebuttal of the argument's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "However, everything that happens that is added through this process will slow down the justice system."

acuity.statement: I think that this bill is heavy-handed. There are already a lot of ways in which employees can go about exercising their rights under the Employment Relations Act, the Minimum Wage Act, and the Holidays Act.
acuity.explanation: He contradicts the core premise of the preceding speech — that existing law gives workers no adequate remedy — by naming the statutes he says already supply one, so one strand of what was just argued is clearly engaged. He does not take up the civil-versus-criminal distinction Andersen rested that premise on, and then moves into prepared material (ideology, litter laws, Northcote crime) that is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "The law as it stands does not address this; it’s currently carried out in a civil jurisdiction."

acuity.statement: The Crown continues to steal the land through its legislation that they’re still moving today. This is not 2012; it’s 2025. Fast track will allow the same thing. The Regulatory Standards Bill allows the same thing.
acuity.explanation: Foster's central argument was that the Public Works Act poses no live threat to Māori land because none has been taken since 2012. Waititi takes that specific claim up and disputes its relevance rather than ignoring it — conceding the date and arguing the mechanism continues through current legislation (fast track, the Regulatory Standards Bill). The speech would have to change if Foster had argued something else, which puts it above the prepared-material band; it is only partial engagement because he does not contest the 2012 figure itself and the surrounding material is historical narrative he would plainly have delivered regardless. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the inference and the hostility of the framing belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "No Māori land has been taken since 2012, but dozens of pieces of land have been taken which are not Māori land, OK?" (and his interjection "Nothing since 2012.")

acuity.statement: Now, I cannot for the life of me reconcile what happened as being good—what happened in Māori history was terrible—but if we live in this grievance-a-side reality, we always look backwards.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Jackson's speech — his grounding of the bill in the historical record of confiscation (the 1974 land march, Taranaki, the bowling-club example) — and concedes it before disputing the conclusion drawn from it. It engages the backward-looking frame rather than any of Jackson's specific claims about Public Works Act acquisitions, and then moves into prepared material about Northland infrastructure, so it is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is always worth putting up, if only as a reminder to the House and people listening; a reminder to them of the type of injustices that our people have endured for decades and decades and decades" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: If we’re going to move forward as a country, we have to stop looking through a myopic lens, Willie Jackson, in our past, move forward—we have a settlement process—look after the people that were aggrieved and actually start building stuff.
acuity.explanation: Addresses Jackson by name and offers a counter-remedy to his demand that the law be changed: the existing settlement process is said to deal with those aggrieved, so the answer is building infrastructure rather than prohibiting acquisition. That engages the conclusion Jackson argued for, but not his reasoning for it (the 5 percent land figure, the Public Works Act cases he cited), and it reads as the prepared thesis of the speech rather than something shaped by what Jackson said — mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What I’m saying tonight is we should never give up because of all the technicalities." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I stand here with no comfort in this House. I stand here offended on behalf of te iwi Māori at what has been shared in this House by members who are historically illiterate—historically illiterate—to the loss of te iwi Māori. It’s not historic; it’s today.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Nakhle's own framing twice over and inverts it: her repeated claim to be "comforted" is answered with "no comfort in this House", and her placing of the harm in "the horrendous history" / "the pain that took place" is directly contradicted — "It's not historic; it's today" — then evidenced with Patricia Grace and the quarries. Delete Nakhle's turn and substitute a different argument and this speech would have to change, which is the deciding test. Disagreement scored high, as the rubric requires; the insult ("historically illiterate") is a civility matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "I'd like to say that I'm comforted that I feel that the reforms that we're making with the Public Works Act are taking a balanced approach with the backdrop of the horrendous history when it comes to Māori land."

acuity.statement: We can all give examples of some of the wrongdoings and, if you look particularly at Māori Land, we can talk about the unfair nature of compensation, like the member Adrian Rurawhe—whether that’s in a monetary sense. I think there is some sense in the fact of looking at other means of recompensating with regards to whenua or something like that as well.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows Rurawhe and takes up one strand of his argument — that land taken from Māori cannot be made good in money — and does something with it, endorsing non-monetary (whenua-for-whenua) recompense as a live option. But he engages only that strand: Rurawhe's central challenge (no Māori land has been taken since 2012, so why not make that prohibition permanent, and let the bill go to select committee to find a workable solution) is not taken up at all, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on shareholding fragmentation at Parininihi ki Waitotara and Te Tumu Paeroa before he declines to support the bill. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe: "it doesn’t have a monetary value when I say that. It’s not about the money."

acuity.statement: This bill has some problems with it, but these are things that we can resolve at select committee. This is an opportunity to get around the table in a cross-partisan way and have a discussion about what are the bottom lines here, because anyone who is in charge of this will have some bottom lines.
acuity.explanation: Williams follows MacLeod, who conceded the Public Works Act is flawed but concluded it must be reformed as a whole rather than piecemeal and so would not commend the bill. She answers the topic of that objection — conceding the bill has problems and arguing select committee is where they get fixed — which is a glance at his reasoning, but she never engages his actual claim that piecemeal amendment is the wrong vehicle, nor his evidence about Māori land decision-making. Most of the speech is aimed at the ACT and NZ First contributions rather than the turn immediately before her, and she expressly exempts National from her attack rather than answering what National's speaker said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "I think it needs to be looked at as a whole and not in piecemeal here."

acuity.statement: I know the member is excited about a three-week sitting of the House when we return on 25 March; he will have to wait and see.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked a two-part question about extended sittings/urgency in the coming three-week block and jabbed at the Government's legislative schedule. Upston's reply picks up the specific item asked about (the three-week sitting block returning 25 March) and squarely declines to disclose plans, so the reply would have had to change had a different question been put — but it engages no part of the content, neither confirming nor denying urgency plans nor taking up the schedule charge, and returns to deflection. Partial engagement with the topic rather than the substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Government have any plans for any extended sittings or urgency over the next three-week sitting block" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: But clause 21 has a question, so I’ll answer that. This Government is focused on economic growth. No surprise there. Employee share schemes support people that are doing business start-ups in the tech sector—that’s good for New Zealand; that’s good for that sector. We’re making it a little bit easier for them to do that. We’re increasing the threshold in which they get tax-free income. We’ve applied a process to get to that number and we have come up with the numbers which we’ve got, and which industry are heavily supportive of and anyone working in the tech sector are very supportive of.
acuity.explanation: Russell put two specific questions on clause 21: what the two monetary items are, and how a flat 50 percent uplift relates to inflation. Watts explicitly takes up clause 21 and answers the topic — why the thresholds are being raised, who benefits, that a process produced the figures — so the engagement is pointable and the speech would differ if Russell had raised a different clause. But he engages no part of the actual argument, which was that 'inflation doesn't come out in nice round numbers'; 'we've applied a process to get to that number' restates that a method exists without touching the reasoning. Topic engaged, specific claim untouched: mid-band, slightly below 0.5 because the remainder is generic prepared material about growth and industry support.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I’d like to understand just how that 50 percent increase was arrived at and its relationship to inflation."

acuity.statement: Now, in the last session when we were debating this bill, my colleague the Hon Dr Megan Woods was asking some questions on emergency events. I’m going to jump forward to clause 30, which inserts new cross-heading “Emergency events” and new section DB 69, “Deduction for interruption expenditure due to emergency event”.
acuity.explanation: Watts had just answered on clause 21 thresholds and employee share schemes. Brooking notes that he is answering 'clause by clause' — a reference to the previous turn that engages none of its content — and then moves to her own prepared question on a different clause. That is prepared material squarely on the matter under debate (the same bill, in committee), with a gesture at the preceding turn but no take-up of it, which puts it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5. Raising a fresh clause is a legitimate committee-stage act; this is a measure of responsiveness only, not of worth.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts answered on clause 21's employee share scheme thresholds and the process behind the figures, and this statement does not take any of that up; it refers only to his going clause by clause.

acuity.statement: Well, I’m not going to get into circular egg conversations, but what I can say in regards to this is that there’s a range of expenditures that individuals will incur as a result of dealing with emergency events. What we’ve been very simplistic about around this provision is to say that there’s a threshold in regards to the $5,000 that will be applying to those individuals. They’ll have the discretion to think about that.
acuity.explanation: Brooking asked a precise question — if the emergency stops the income-earning activity, what expenditure is left that bears a nexus to that income — and framed it as possibly circular. Watts takes up her framing by name and answers the substance of it: he asserts there is a real range of such expenditure, and explains that rather than specify it the provision sets a $5,000 threshold and leaves the judgement to the individual. That is a direct response to the question put, and the speech could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument. Short of 1.0 because he supplies no instance of the expenditure she asked about, so the nexus point itself is answered by design rather than by evidence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "If the person can’t earn an income because of the emergency, what expenditures will they be incurring linked to that income that they are now going to be allowed a deduction for?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chairman, and I thank the Minister of Revenue for that contribution. I believe my colleague Dr Deborah Russell will come back to that—that that wasn’t addressing the questions around the clause that the Hon Rachel Brooking had put.
acuity.explanation: Woods takes up the answer Watts has just given and makes a claim about it — that it did not address Brooking's clause 30 question — and then reminds him of her own outstanding drafting question about whether the $5,000 in clause 20 is a cap. That is pointable engagement with the preceding turn, and the opening would have to change had Watts answered differently. But the engagement stays at the level of 'you did not answer' rather than contesting anything he actually said, and the turn then moves to prepared questions on clauses 14 and 23. One strand taken up, then prepared material: 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Well, I’m not going to get into circular egg conversations" — Woods characterises that answer as not addressing Brooking's question.

acuity.statement: Clause 20 was a question as well, raised by a member previously around whether it was a cap or not. Yes, it is a cap. I said that when I raised it. I actually said that twice when I got asked the same question in prior sessions on the same point. But, again, it is a cap of $5,000, and that is that.
acuity.explanation: Woods had just complained that questions were going unanswered. Watts works through the outstanding items clause by clause and here supplies the direct answer asked for (yes, a cap, of $5,000), which is squarely responsive. It falls short of the top band because he partly meets the complaint by asserting he has already answered it rather than engaging the substance of why the answer was thought inadequate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "there is a large and growing number of questions that are still outstanding that the Minister has not either addressed or answered"

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister replied, and he replied talking about the new emergency provisions in general, and why we were having them in place. He said, “That’s why we have this clause 30.” But, actually, that’s kind of a very big, broad, and general answer to what was a very specific question. The very specific question was this: it was to do with the nexus with income.
acuity.explanation: She quotes the Minister's own answer, identifies precisely what it did and did not address, and reformulates the specific point (the section DA 1 nexus with income) that the general answer missed. The speech is entirely contingent on what the Minister said and could not have been delivered against a different reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "That’s why we have this clause 30" — quoted back by Russell from the Minister's earlier reply on clause 30

acuity.statement: It is important to note that this new section DB 69 inserted by clause 30, in regards to deduction, supplements the general provision which the member has noted. The purpose of this new section is to prove that there is a nexus between the income and expenditure, acknowledging that that would have been disrupted by the event.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the exact strand Russell isolated — the nexus requirement in the general permission — names the provision that modifies it, and in the following passage answers her second question about what bounds the claimable expenses. The answer is shaped by her specific objection rather than by prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "The very specific question was this: it was to do with the nexus with income."

acuity.statement: We had the real question, through the Canterbury earthquake sequence, of whether or not interruption insurance would apply under these circumstances. So have we fixed that in terms of the tax situation and in terms of the new definitions?
acuity.explanation: She presses the boundary question the Minister had just claimed was settled, testing it against a concrete case (an undamaged building cut off by a neighbouring demolition). It engages the subject of his answer and probes its limits, but does not take up his actual reasoning about section DB 69 supplementing the general permission, so it sits in the middle band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "the deduction has to be relevant to the income-earning activity of the specific example, and so within that, that provides the bounds of what is reasonable or not"

acuity.statement: As the member has highlighted, this is a remedial matter. The definition as it stands excludes livestock held for any other income-generating purpose. As a Government that is listening to taxpayers, particularly those in the primary sector, they’ve said to us that the inaccurate wording can cause confusion and potentially could result in some businesses valuing their livestock incorrectly or simply not valuing them at all.
acuity.explanation: Russell's whole line of questioning was whether any actual harm flowed from the old wording of section EC 1 and what therefore justified the committee's time. Watts takes that specific question up and supplies an answer to it — the current definition excludes livestock held for other income-generating purposes, primary-sector taxpayers reported confusion, and the risk is incorrect or absent valuation. The reply would have had to be different if Russell had asked something else about the clause. Not a 1.0 because he never addresses the narrower part of her question (whether there were any actual tax cases or disputes).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "was there actually any harm being caused by the previous standing of the words?"

acuity.statement: In regards to the option that we selected, we went for option 3, which is a step-down approach. There’s a table in the back that outlines the five different options that were considered.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez asked which of the five regulatory impact statement options was implemented, flagging option three as officials' preference. Watts names option three and points to where the options are set out — the precise item requested, directly from the preceding turn. Only short of 1.0 because one of the three questions put (a layperson's definition of 'uneconomic to repair' in new section FP 14) is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "which of these options was the one that was implemented in this legislation—noting that the preferred option of the officials was option three"

acuity.statement: It’s good to be able to take a call on this and to ask some questions specifically around—not clause 30, you’ll be pleased to know—clauses 14, 23, and 29. Now, this really comes from a question both around speed and also around the ability for tax law and tax legislation to keep pace with the speed at which the tech sector and platforms move, because we know that platform developments, platform shifts and changes, often happen at incredible speeds.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive answer by the Minister immediately precedes. Davidson is squarely on the bill under debate and even returns to clause 29, which Boyack had raised, but he engages no part of either preceding contribution's content — not Boyack's reading of the flat-rate credit deduction, nor Watts' answer on the breadth of the emergency-event definition or the limited-partnership remedial. The jocular "not clause 30" is a reference to the prior exchange rather than an engagement with it, which the rubric places in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because the gesture at the preceding debate is there and the questions are on the matter in front of the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered "the Hon Dr Megan Woods’ point around clause 30 inserting new section DB 69" and the partnership questions on clauses 31 and 32, and this statement takes up none of that content — it names clause 30 only to set it aside before delivering prepared material.

acuity.statement: The question relates to clauses 14, 23, and 29, consistent with a question answered more, but I’ll provide a little bit more context for the member’s purpose. First and foremost, this is an optional area for a taxpayer. It is primarily looking at hosts, drivers, and deliverers, and this is a result of the platform economy GST rules that came into force on 1 April 2024.
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. Watts picks up exactly the clauses Davidson raised and explains the mechanism they create — the option to treat the flat-rate credit as assessable income so GST can be deducted — so the answer is pointed at the member's subject matter and would differ if Davidson had asked about different clauses. But he does not take up the actual thrust of the question: whether tax law can keep pace with platform change over a five- to ten-year horizon, who identifies the underlying suppliers, and how often that is reassessed. He answers the topic rather than the specific claim and then closes on the select committee's view, which is the ~0.5 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So the questions, really, are: what steps are in place to ensure that the tax and tax capture keeps up and it’s not left behind but also that it doesn’t get ahead of the movement and actions of those platforms?" — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: I think it’s important to recognise that this is not new tax law. It’s actually a combination of measures used in past events, and those past events include the Canterbury earthquake, the Kaikōura earthquake, and the North Island flooding events.
acuity.explanation: Takes the central characterisation in Russell's immediately preceding turn — that Subpart FP is a large block of brand-new tax law — and contradicts it directly, giving the provenance of the measures. The reply would have to be different had Russell framed the subpart any other way; he also expressly takes up her question about how often the rules have been used and concedes he cannot answer it. Not a full 1.0 because the rebuttal asserts the provenance rather than engaging her point that 27 sections over 20 pages are nonetheless new statutory text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "This new Subpart FP is very, very new tax law."

acuity.statement: So my question is: why has that threshold been chosen—the $5,000 threshold? Is that the one that’s already in the parent legislation, or is that the one that the Minister of Revenue has had advice on that that’s the appropriate measure?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the clauses of this bill — but it engages no part of what Watts had just said. Watts had asserted the subpart is not new law and described the 700-item remedial list used to select the measures; Hernandez neither tests that account nor builds on it, and instead works through a prepared list of clause-by-clause queries. The question would read identically had Watts answered differently or not spoken at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just argued "this is not new tax law" and described the Inland Revenue remedial list of "about 700 or so items" used to pick the rules, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The $5,000 threshold was the amount that the Finance and Expenditure Committee and also officials thought was the appropriate number for that circumstance. The eight-week question is in regards to new section FP 20, and, obviously, my response there was for FP 21(2). Eight weeks is a cap. It can go beyond that, but the eight weeks is a period of exempt income.

Held below 1.0 because the third question put to him, on the 75 percent livestock threshold, is left unengaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "why was $5,000 the one that was chosen?" and "what are the implications of going over the eight-week period?"

acuity.statement: Just for the member’s interest—and, of course, all those watching at home—about where the definition sits, it’s actually defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I just want to know whether that definition does or will actually sit within the Income Tax Act."

acuity.statement: I wanted to check with the Minister if it’s the standard definition of a person in this case.

The questions are squarely on the matter under debate (clause 53B of the same bill) and there is a gesture at the exchange — thanks to the Minister for answering the eight-weeks question — but no part of the preceding answer's content is engaged. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just stated the definition of an emergency event sits in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002, and this statement does not take that up — it opens two prepared questions on 'person' and beneficiary relief.

Delete Watts's answer and substitute a different one and this speech could not stand as written. Disagreement scored high, per the rubric.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "it’s actually defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002"

acuity.statement: What I would like to know is whether there are other provisions within these emergency measures where there’s been policy advice or policy discussions that the Minister has had around where we may need to retain some of those backstop ways of putting in support in case the emergency event isn’t declared in accordance within the definition that the Minister has spoken about when he has addressed other aspects of it.
acuity.explanation: Takes one strand of the preceding answer — the declaration-based definition the Minister had just given — and draws out a consequence of it, asking whether Order in Council backstops survive elsewhere for events that fall outside that definition. That engagement is pointable. The bulk of the turn is nonetheless prepared material on use-of-money interest and section 183ABA that stands independently of what Watts said, so this is partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "It’s a Government-wide definition, and that is where the definition of an emergency event resides."

acuity.statement: I think it was in regards to Rachel Boyack’s point in the context of a specific example in her electorate. The clause states that it is a declared event. That can include national and local events. It will depend on the specific circumstances, but one would expect if it is of significant scale that triggers what is considered a local emergency, then, on that basis, it would be captured.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question Boyack put rather than the topic around it: whether a locally declared emergency is captured. He states that the clause turns on a declaration, that this can include local events, and gives the qualifying condition (significant scale, case by case). The content of the reply is determined by her specific claim, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "the difference between a national emergency and a local emergency" — she asked whether the bill would cover the Nelson local declarations.

acuity.statement: The question asked by the Hon Dr Megan Woods in the context of use of money interest around section 183 under the Tax Administration Act, the late payments portion—I think the question was: did officials consider more broadly the application of that or whether that is included in the broader bill. The purpose of this bill fundamentally is to deal with emergency response and the related implications of that event, and that is what the officials have targeted in this case, and that’s what the Finance and Expenditure Committee supported.
acuity.explanation: He restates her question and engages its general shape — what officials turned their minds to — so there is real, pointable engagement. But he answers at the level of the bill's purpose and does not address the specific thing asked: whether Order in Council backstops are retained for Inland Revenue supports other than use-of-money interest. Engages the topic and one strand, then returns to general framing, which is the 0.5 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "whether those backstop provisions for using Orders in Council are retained in regard to other Inland Revenue supports"

acuity.statement: In the context of the registrations: to date, it’s sitting at around 70,000 of that. So that’s a good way there—it’s more than a majority in that context. The IRD are working actively through their operational matters to increase that number, and it’s something we’re monitoring very closely.
acuity.explanation: Takes Genter's specific claim that the majority of eligible families have not claimed FamilyBoost and corrects it with the registration figure, and also supplies the eligibility data she asked whether IRD held. The answer would have to be different had she made a different claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government’s FamilyBoost tax credit, as I understand it, has actually not been claimed by the majority of people who are eligible for it." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: The second part sort of in relation to what my colleague the Hon Julie Anne Genter mentioned, in terms of the FamilyBoost tax credit in clause 91C—I’m looking at 91C, the newly introduced new section MH 3, subsection (7), which is to do with “Separated persons”. Again, it’s the same thing that I’m looking at in terms of the use of the phrase “at the end of that quarter”.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding FamilyBoost exchange — whether the clause helps or hinders access — and extends it to a specific drafting consequence in subsection (7). acuity.responding_to: "So what I’m interested in is whether these changes are estimated to make it easier for people to claim that credit." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: So the purpose here is that the current way that the legislation is drafted is that it doesn’t deal with the case of a large cull of livestock—I appreciate that is what it is—but the existing scheme isn’t adequate for that scenario. Obviously, in the context of biosecurity and Mycoplasma bovis, a scenario or an event such as that, then the mechanism needs to be in place to deal with that scenario, and hence why we’ve made the change.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put — why the pre-existing income-spreading provisions were insufficient — by naming the gap (a large cull) and the triggering case. Marked slightly below the top because the Green member's two questions asked immediately before are left unaddressed in this turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why weren’t the existing provisions good enough? Why did we have to add in these extra provisions to cope with that situation for farmers?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I want to start off with the crypto-asset reporting framework, and if you thought tax law was cryptic, well, then you try crypto-assets, because they’re pretty tricky. There’s some really interesting policy questions sitting around the crypto-asset reporting framework and it’s around the automatic exchange of information, all right. So part of what these rules do is try to set up common reporting across jurisdictions about crypto-assets.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one substantive item the Minister had just singled out in his introduction to Part 3 and draws out a consequence of it — the onward flow of New Zealand taxpayer information through automatic exchange. Not a rebuttal of an argument, which is why it sits short of the top, but squarely on the content just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The main policy item that was not already covered in Part 2 is in regards to the crypto-asset reporting framework." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell for the question. The member’s right: the area of crypto-assets and the financial flows that relate to that are significant. There was in the region around US$1.4 billion of potential fraud and hacking of this currency at a global level, so there’s a lot of money flowing through there. IRD do see this as an area of risk and hence have applied what they believe is proportionate penalties to deal with the scale of potential risk that they deal with, and they do that across all tax types.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the proportionality strand of Russell's question and gives a rationale (scale of the risk, IRD's assessment), so the reply would differ had she asked something else. But it leaves the specific comparison she asked for — how these penalties sit against other penalties in the Tax Administration Act — untouched, offering only a general "across all tax types". Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I want to know how proportionate those penalties are, especially in relation to other penalties within the Tax Administration Act."

acuity.statement: Madam Chair, I want to touch on a matter that’s associated with the new emergency provisions, the emergency response provisions, but it’s a matter that’s canvassed in the Tax Administration Act, not in the Income Tax Act. So it’s very properly within Part 3 and we haven’t touched on this previously.
acuity.explanation: She lets the Minister's answer pass without testing it and opens an unrelated line on clause 151B. The turn is squarely within the same committee-stage debate on the bill, which keeps it above the floor, but it engages no part of what was just said and would read identically whatever answer Watts had given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on the proportionality of the crypto-asset penalties ("IRD do see this as an area of risk and hence have applied what they believe is proportionate penalties") and this statement does not take that answer up.

acuity.statement: One would appreciate that emergency events are fast moving, they are complex, and they are not always the same. What we are simply acknowledging in this case is that sometimes the circumstances do mean that the Commissioner of IRD, who is highly competent and experienced in dealing with this, has the ability to be able to make a call in regards to a scenario to allow decisions to be made quickly.
acuity.explanation: Goes directly to the clause and subsection Russell named and supplies the rationale for the discretion — fast-moving, variable emergencies needing a quick call by the Commissioner. Short of 1.0 because he explains why the discretion exists rather than giving the insight asked for into what would actually count as exceptional, which was the point of her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I wonder if the Minister could just give us a little bit of an insight into what he would regard as being exceptional circumstances" (on new section 226H(5))

acuity.statement: I want to continue on with talking around the crypto-asset reporting framework, and so I thank the Minister of Revenue for that answer. I too have a very high regard for our officials in Inland Revenue and their standards of integrity and probity.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of the Minister's answer — his appeal to IRD's diligence and competence — and explicitly concedes it, which shows she listened to the reply to her own earlier question. But she engages only that concessionary point before turning to wholly new prepared material on clause 117(3); she neither tests nor disputes the substance of what he said about international benchmarking. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I'm very confident as Minister in the IRD ensuring that they've done due diligence and due process."

acuity.statement: Look, as the member knows, there’s a lot of information sharing that goes on between jurisdictions. This is a very routine piece of legislation around the format in which that information is shared. There is a lot of robust consideration around releasing any of that information, of course, but these things get updated regularly, as do a lot of these clauses, and this is simply reflecting those changes.
acuity.explanation: He identifies the exact clause she raised and takes up her premise that the CARF document is amended from time to time, conceding "these things get updated regularly". That is real engagement with one strand of her point, so this is not merely on-topic prepared material. But he answers the topic rather than her specific claim — the notification mechanism for affected taxpayers — recasting it as a routine information-sharing matter instead. Mid-band: engagement is pointable but partial. (Whether the reply was evasive is a Forthrightness question and does not move this score.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "the CARF document is amended from time to time, so how is Inland Revenue going to be advising people who are affected by this that in fact the OECD document has been amended?"

acuity.statement: Thank you so much, Madam Chair. I was excited when I thought that Mr Carl Bates was actually going to take a call on Part 3. I have a question for the Minister of Revenue—I have, actually, a number of questions for the Minister on the Minister’s Amendment Paper 247, specifically the new clause 118BA, “New section 7AAAA inserted”, on the final-year fees-free scheme.
acuity.explanation: There was substantive content immediately before him — Russell's question on advising taxpayers of OECD amendments and Watts's reply that such updates are routine — and he engages none of it. The only backward glance is a jibe about Carl Bates's closure motion, which is a reference to procedure, not to anyone's argument. The speech is at least on the bill before the committee and gestures at the debate it sits in, so it is not a 0.0; but it would read identically whatever the previous speakers had said. Scored low for unresponsiveness only — raising fresh questions on a new Amendment Paper is proper committee-stage work, and the detail of the questions is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts and Deborah Russell had been exchanging on the CARF definition in clause 117(3), and this statement does not take any part of that up — it opens a new line on Amendment Paper 247 and the fees-free scheme.

acuity.statement: The other question was around the submissions and whether there were any submissions from those within the tertiary sector or students. Well, as the member will know, there were 28 written submissions. I think the Finance and Expenditure Committee saw 16 of those in person.
acuity.explanation: He names the consultation question put to him and supplies figures to meet it, which is the strongest form of engagement available here — the speech would be different had Xu-Nan asked something else. He engages that strand squarely but not the specific thing asked: Xu-Nan asked which student bodies, naming Māori and Pasifika organisations, and the answer gives aggregate submission counts instead. He also sets aside the Tiriti analysis, participation-incentive and TEC-eligibility questions as outside the taxation bill rather than taking them up. Above the midpoint for pointable, figure-bearing engagement with one of several strands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what student bodies—and particularly when we're looking at student bodies from disadvantaged communities like Māori and Pasifika student organisations—has the Minister or officials consulted with this particular policy?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’ve got some more questions on the crypto-asset reporting framework. I want to go to clause 150 of the bill; it’s on page 146—as we’re trying to keep track of where we’re all going on this!
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn by another member was the Minister's fees-free answer, and she engages no part of it, resuming her own prepared line on crypto-asset reporting instead. The speech is plainly about the bill under committee consideration, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band rather than at 0.0. Low here reflects responsiveness alone; continuing a distinct line of questioning across calls is normal committee practice and the quality of the question itself is not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered Lawrence Xu-Nan on fees-free consultation and the 28 written submissions, and this statement does not take that up — it resumes her own separate thread on clause 150.

acuity.statement: Yeah, well, the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell will be aware that IRD have a big and significant focus on compliance and integrity matters. They received additional funding by this Government to increase the amount of work—that obviously includes the components around the crypto-assets framework. It’d be fair to say that many taxpayers—actually over 95 percent—generally will comply without any problem, and that’s because that is the appropriate mechanism.
acuity.explanation: This takes the actual structure of her question — will self-assessment work for assets that are by nature hard to track, or will IRD have to chase holders down — and answers both halves in order: most will comply voluntarily, a few need support, and evaders face the full weight of IRD's powers. He also supplies a figure where she asked about the extent of voluntary compliance. The speech could not have been delivered in response to a different question; it is shaped by hers throughout. Not a full 1.0 only because he does not engage her specific premise that crypto-assets are harder to trace than salary and wage income, which was the point of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "whether he anticipates that, in fact, people will come forward and report on their own crypto-assets, or that Inland Revenue will have to employ various measures to try and track them down"

acuity.statement: I agree, actually, with the previous speaker, Jamie Arbuckle, that everyone is looking—and I can’t believe this is Thursday afternoon—for certainty and clarity at our worst time. I agree with the Greens that we’re at a period where we are normalising adaptation speak and mitigation isn’t a deal. It worries me that we’re giving up the mitigation speak, because there are fossil fuel implications on climate, and I just want to put that there.
acuity.explanation: She names and takes up the specific strand Arbuckle closed on — the demand for certainty about what happens when a disaster hits — so the engagement is pointable. But she only endorses it rather than developing or contesting it, then pivots to her own concern that adaptation talk is displacing mitigation, which engages nothing Arbuckle said (he argued New Zealand cannot change the climate profile). Partial engagement, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "We want certainty and we want to know what actually happens when a disaster hits."

acuity.statement: I want to talk about the Provincial Growth Fund. Actually, I was on the board that that initially came from, He Kai Kei Aku Ringa. It was a Regional Development Fund economic. What would be really great is to also seek consideration for those who cannot futureproof for insurance—the businesses, the communities—and be able to look at how regional development can be done in a way that looks at adaptation, not just from a business economic sense but a social economic sense.
acuity.explanation: Arbuckle had just offered the Provincial Growth Fund and Regional Infrastructure Fund as his party's proof of practical adaptation spending, citing over a hundred projects. She takes that exact instrument, supplies her own history with its origin, and then does something with it — arguing its regional-development logic should be extended to those who cannot insure, on social as well as business grounds. This passage would have to change if the preceding speech had not raised the PGF; it falls short of 1.0 because she neither disputes his figures nor his wider claim, but redirects the instrument he named.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "Through the Provincial Growth Fund and the Regional Infrastructure Fund, we have put money into practical projects like river protection."

acuity.statement: A model where the exacerbator pays is more appropriate with a course of adaptation, as is managed retreat rather than trying to move to a beneficiary-pays model, which doesn’t actually account for historical inequities and—as the previous speaker articulated—class inequities that might have occurred.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez takes up one strand of Russell's speech — her argument that a climate adaptation response must reckon with class, because poorer people hold property on flood plains that cannot be sold — and does something with it, using it as grounds for an exacerbator-pays rather than beneficiary-pays funding model. He also picks up her South Dunedin example by acknowledging the South Dunedin Future work. But the bulk of the speech is prepared Green material (Zero Carbon Act as template, Treaty partnership, resourcing local government) that would have been delivered whatever Russell had said, and his other reference to her is a bare name-check of the Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle. Partial engagement, pointable: mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "in the Government’s response, we need to see more of an analysis based on a word that is hardly ever used in New Zealand: class"

acuity.statement: Madam Speaker, as you’d acknowledge, I’m not a member of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, but periodically, as the previous speaker, Francisco Hernandez, just mentioned, I sit in on the process and I’m cognisant of the very many issues that the member Cameron Brewer opened up on in his 10-minute speech in terms of climate adaptation.
acuity.explanation: The only thing Cameron takes from Hernandez is the procedural fact of occasionally subbing in on the committee — a parallel about himself, not an engagement with any claim. None of Hernandez's arguments are taken up: not exacerbator-pays, not centring Māori as Treaty partners, not resourcing local government for land-use planning, not the claim that a purely market individualised-risk approach would exacerbate inequities — even though Cameron goes on to argue for property rights, private-public partnerships and seawall investment, which cut directly against that last point. His speech is on the matter under debate (coastline length, erosion, how to pay, Simon Court's points) and gestures at the previous speaker, so it is not a zero, but substituting a different argument on climate adaptation would not have changed a line of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing beyond a procedural parallel: Francisco Hernandez said "I was not the permanent representative on the committee—my co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick was—but I was occasionally subbed in", and argued for exacerbator-pays funding and community-led rather than market-individualised risk; this statement takes up only the subbing-in, not the argument.

acuity.statement: In Labour, we very much want to discuss and talk about the fact around how do we work across the floor. How do we reach out across the aisle? How do we have cross-party collaboration? Because we are too small, as a nation, to fight over this.
acuity.explanation: Bennett follows Nancy Lu, who closed on the cross-party character of the inquiry (the Minister moving it to the Finance and Expenditure Committee so all parties were included) and on doing this well "across the parties across this House". Bennett picks up that one strand and makes it his theme, so the engagement is pointable. But he takes up none of her specific content — not the six findings, not the 30-year adaptation plan, lead agency, RMA reform or retreat strategy she listed — and the rest of the speech is prepared material that would read the same after any pro-cooperation speech on this report. One strand engaged, then back to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if we do this well, across the parties across this House, we will minimise future costs and hardship" — Nancy Lu

acuity.statement: There’s another one in Westport that needs to be carried forward—the relocation of the town—and I think we have to experiment by doing now. Rather than writing more plans as to what we might do, we actually need to crack on and do it.
acuity.explanation: Parker takes up one strand of the immediately preceding speech — Bidois's closing claim that the inquiry is only a tool and that reports must give way to action — and does something with it, supplying concrete worked examples (Dunedin City Council's movable-building rules, the sports-ground land swap, Forbury Park, the Westport relocation) as the practical action Bidois called for, and he also picks up Bidois's point that councils once consented homes where they should not have, converting it into a specific proposal on strict rules for new risk and on PIMs being amendable without litigation risk. But most of the turn is clearly prepared material on South Dunedin that would have been delivered whatever Bidois said, and it does not engage Bidois's specific contentions (the 2035 targets, insurance premiums reaching uninsurability, the four recommendation areas) as claims to accept or dispute, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We don’t need more reports; we actually need action." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: Why did the Government ignore official advice that Compass had failed to meet the nutritional standards required in more than half of the assessments of its meals under the previous programme and had prolonged issues with undersized meals and inconsistent portioning, while Libelle had been the subject of 163 complaints about food quality, food safety, and food suitability?

It engages the substance of the answer rather than merely moving to the next prepared item, but it is plainly the next link in a pre-written chain and does not address the deflection to the Minister, so it sits in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "There was a standard procurement process. But if the member wants to direct more specific questions, feel free to direct it to the Minister."

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to whether he was aware that those three supplementary questions were all written before the primary question from Chris Hipkins, which meant that, no matter what the Prime Minister said, he wasn’t paying attention?
acuity.explanation: Contingent on the exchange that just happened, but engages no part of its content: it is a remark about the form of the questioning rather than about procurement, providers or the lunch programme. There is nothing in the preceding argument that this takes up, so it sits at the bottom of the band despite being prompted by the moment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Why did the Government ignore official advice that Compass had failed to meet the nutritional standards required in more than half of the assessments of its meals"

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that last week the healthy school lunch programme delivered 99.8 percent on-time delivery, and surplus meals of 5.7 percent compared with 9 percent surplus last year, and is he then surprised to hear feedback from a teacher just last night: “The meals are varied, wholesome, and, in my opinion and that of the majority of my class, far more filling than last year. They are a meal!”?
acuity.explanation: Answers the topic Hipkins has been pressing — the quality of the new lunch programme — with counter-data on on-time delivery and surplus meals and a quoted teacher, and the surplus figure speaks fairly directly to the earlier "uneaten lunches and food waste" charge. But it does not take up the specific claim just made about nutritional value being lower; it substitutes a different metric, which is engagement of one strand rather than of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "why is the nutritional value of school lunches now being provided consistently lower than under the previous school lunches programme that his Government scrapped?"

acuity.statement: When our country has to pay for the profit of shareholders on top of the cost of building public infrastructure like our schools and hospitals, does that equation ultimately cost New Zealanders more or less?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim just made — that investor-built public infrastructure brings profound benefits — and tests it by putting the shareholder return on the cost side of the same ledger. The question would have to be rewritten had the Prime Minister argued something else, though it presses a prepared thesis rather than engaging his "pull forward infrastructure" reasoning about timing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "there is massive interest from investors who want to build public infrastructure in New Zealand, and the benefits to New Zealanders economically, socially, and environmentally are profound"

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister accept that his plans for public-private partnerships will ultimately, then, cost New Zealanders more and send that profit offshore?
acuity.explanation: Restates her own two earlier questions as a conclusion rather than engaging what was just said. The preceding answer asserted that attracting investment raises living standards and that she misunderstands the economics; none of that is taken up or rebutted. It stays squarely on the matter under debate and can be read as pressing an unanswered point, which keeps it above the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "The member seems to be confused about how economics works."

acuity.statement: Has the Prime Minister seen any reports that profit is not a cost that you just add on and charge the customer but a surplus that remains if you do a very good job of using your resources more efficiently, and could failing to understand that be a reason why someone’s one-time business of a little hole-in-the-wall cafe on Mount Eden Road only lasted a few weeks?
acuity.explanation: Goes directly at the premise of Swarbrick's line of questioning — that profit is an extra charge stacked on top of the build cost — and contests it with a competing account of profit as a residual from efficient resource use. The question is unintelligible without her preceding claim, which is the strongest evidence of engagement; that it also carries a personal jibe about her cafe bears on civility, not on whether she was listened to.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "When our country has to pay for the profit of shareholders on top of the cost of building public infrastructure"

acuity.statement: The member may recall, from select committee proceedings, that the New Zealand Law Society identified a scenario on this exact point.
