He also returns to her second question on clause 157 and emissions units. The speech would be entirely different had Russell asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "what I want to know from the Minister of Revenue was whether there was any actual mischief going on or whether it is just a possible mischief that could have gone on"

acuity.statement: I just want to continue the debate in relation to Part 4, specifically in relation to the Minister of Revenue’s Amendment Paper 247, which he has tabled. I think it’s always important that if an Amendment Paper has been tabled by the Minister, we do have the ability to scrutinise it a bit more, because it hasn’t gone through the select committee process.
acuity.explanation: On the same bill and the same committee-stage debate, so not wholly adrift, but it engages no part of the answer the Minister had just given — it opens a fresh line of questioning on a different instrument that she would plainly have put whatever Watts had said. A gesture at the debate (the Minister's Amendment Paper) without engaging its content places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.

Partial engagement that is clearly pointable: mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what they are not considering is how we tax capital, and that is the gap in this bill" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I stand up here today, proud and sad, in some respects. I’m proud to support this, being the third reading of a bill which has had much deliberation, but sad because the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee’s father passed away in the early hours of this morning.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a substantive turn by Foster in the same third-reading debate, so he is eligible, but his speech engages no part of Foster's argument — it is a condolence for the committee chair's bereavement plus a commendation of the bill, and would read word-for-word the same whatever Foster had said. It sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0 because it does gesture at the matter under debate (the third reading of a bill 'which has had much deliberation') rather than being deliverable in any debate on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what I’ve heard from the Opposition—it’s really quite interesting, they’ve basically said, 'We like what’s in there; we don’t like what isn’t in there.'" — Andy Foster. Nothing: Foster argued at length that the Opposition's reason for opposing the bill is incoherent and that higher tax brackets gain more in dollar terms, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We’re presenting a comprehensive policy that will actually enable the critical public services that we rely on, that doesn’t rely on imaginary market-based mechanisms, that actually relies on making sure that everyone has what they need to thrive, unlike this Government with its record unemployment rate, with an economy that’s still actually—well, one member there was saying “degrowth”, but the economy is actually more than it was this time last quarter, so they’ve done the degrowth and we will green grow New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez breaks off his prepared peroration mid-sentence to take up Bidois's one-word interjection and turn it against him, asserting that the economy is larger than the same quarter last year and so the degrowth is the Government's own. The engagement is specific and pointable: the clause would not exist had Bidois not interjected, and the rebuttal addresses the content of the jibe rather than merely naming it. Short of 1.0 only because the interjection carried a single word of content to engage, so the reply does the work of a riposte rather than of dismantling an argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Degrowth." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: I think I can agree with one thing that the Opposition has said today: it has been through a thorough committee of the whole House. I think we spent a good amount of time getting into every little bit and asking multiple questions, sometimes on the same topic.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows Hernandez but engages no part of his case — not the regressivity arithmetic, not the final-year fees-free analysis, not the unanswered question on extending emergency tax relief to beneficiaries. What he does take up is the committee process and, later, a quote from Deborah Russell, who spoke outside this window; and that quote is repeated back as a springboard for a cargo-cult jibe rather than answered. This is prepared material on the matter under debate with a gesture at the Opposition's committee questioning, which keeps it at 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez argued the bill's tax changes are "deeply regressive", citing $20.50 a week for a deputy chief executive on $348,000 against about $2 a week for a single parent on a benefit, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: And that member, who’s quite new to the select committee, says, “You didn’t mention this in select committee.”—Dan Bidois. You don’t mention this in select committee, because the purpose of select committee is to try and make a bill workable. That is the purpose of a select committee, and you’ll have your chance here in the House to defend your decisions to confirm the annual tax rates, to take more money out of Kiwis, and to take more money out of the healthcare system.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific objection just put to her and answers its substance directly, explaining why select committee is not the forum for the argument (its purpose is to make a bill workable) and where the Government's defence of the bill properly belongs. The passage could not have been delivered had Bidois said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You didn't mention this in select committee." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: I’m still the MP for Mana until 2026. At least I know where Mana is, unlike Tim Costley from Ōtaki.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the information the interjection asked for — her electorate and her term — before adding a jibe. The engagement with what was just said is direct and pointable, even though the follow-on clause is personal rather than substantive (that is a civility question, not an acuity one).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Which electorate are you in?" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: A little bit of myth busting, because our Opposition members seem to think that 3.4 percent of New Zealand taxpayers get most of the tax cuts and pay less of the tax income, but that is not the truth—they pay 30 percent of New Zealand’s tax income.
acuity.explanation: She follows a substantive turn and is plainly on the matter under debate (this tax bill), and she gestures at the Opposition's position, so this is not a 0.0. But the strand she rebuts — that 3.4 percent of taxpayers get most of the cuts — is not the argument Edmonds advanced; the revenue hole, service cuts and borrowing claims go unaddressed, and the rest is prepared commendation of the bill that would read identically after any Opposition speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued immediately before that the bill's tax cuts create a revenue hole that forces cuts to health and GP funding and required borrowing, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it rebuts a distributional claim about who gets the cuts that Edmonds did not make.

acuity.statement: The matters involved in this bill have been traversed extensively through this House. In fact, we spent more time at the committee stage in this House than we did in the select committee process, and all we heard from the committee stage is “More tax” from the opposite side.
acuity.explanation: Henare's turn immediately before made specific arguments — that every emergency is unique so the streamlined emergency tax response must allow for different circumstances, and that tinkering at the edges leaves taxpayers more confused. Bidois takes up neither. He gestures at the debate by referring to the committee stage Henare had also described and by characterising the opposition's contributions as 'More tax', then delivers a general statement of the Government's tax philosophy and commends the bill. Substituting a different Labour speech on the same bill would not require a word of this to change, so it sits in the prepared-material band; the gesture at the debate earns 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'if you tinker around the edges, there is also the fear that many of our taxpayers or all of our taxpayers out in New Zealand continue to be far more confused by what's happening as a whole' — Bidois does not take up the confusion argument or the emergency-uniqueness caveat, only the fact that a committee stage happened.

acuity.statement: We’ve heard members of the Government stand up and say that this is a bill that is about going for growth, despite the fact that, when the Minister was in the chair for 7½ hours in the committee stage, when we examined this bill, he could not point us to where the growth was coming in this bill; how we were going to create wealth in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Bidois had just asserted that the Government believes in an efficient and minimal tax system 'and that is what this bill tries to do', and had cited the length of the committee stage as evidence the bill was properly traversed. Woods engages both strands: she turns the committee-stage length back on the Government (7½ hours in which the Minister could not identify the growth) and disputes the claim that the bill delivers growth. That is one strand of the preceding argument taken up and used, but she then pivots to prepared material on homelessness and Kāinga Ora that is indifferent to what Bidois said, which places this at a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: 'We are a Government that believes in an efficient tax system but, ultimately, a minimal tax system, and that is what this bill tries to do.'

acuity.statement: It’s been great spending time with the minutiae of legislative maintenance, which I think was first recommended by the Productivity Commission in 2014. They ran the ruler over this House’s legislation-making performance and concluded that there was a need, actually, to set aside a bit of time to review and tune up laws so that they could be properly and efficiently implemented. That’s what we’re doing here.
acuity.explanation: Twyford follows Doocey's third-reading speech and takes up one strand of it — Doocey's rationale that the House must give priority to maintaining its stock of legislation — supplying the Productivity Commission's 2014 recommendation as the origin of that practice and endorsing it. He engages the rationale rather than any specific claim or figure in it, and the remainder of the turn moves to prepared material on unemployment, housing and health that is indifferent to what Doocey said. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "It can be a challenge to get priority to make relatively small changes to legislation, but these changes are important if we are to keep our stock of legislation up to date and fit for purpose."

acuity.statement: Now, they are small changes, across these two bills. However, collectively it does make very important, big change. It creates more clarity, cuts red tape, and streamlines processes that are identified over time.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Twyford that attacked the Government's wider employment relations record while still supporting the bill. Unkovich's contribution is prepared commendation of the two bills plus thanks to select committee staff; it engages no part of Twyford's argument and would be word-for-word identical whatever he had said. It is at least squarely about the bills under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford spoke about the destruction of fair pay agreements and members voting against a bill criminalising wage theft, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Koinei tōku wā tuatoru kua kōrerotia ki tēnei o ngā pire. Hākoa te moroiti o tēnei pire, kua panoni i ētahi wāhanga i roto i tēnei kāwana, waihoki i ngā pire tae atu ki ngā rautau tahi mano iwa rau. Nō reira e tautoko ana mātou Te Pāti Māori i tēnei pire.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns (Twyford, Unkovich) precede this one. The speech states Te Pāti Māori's support, describes the bill as minor, and notes its relevance to Māori tourism businesses — prepared material on the right subject that engages no claim made by either preceding speaker. The speech would be unchanged had they argued something else about these bills, so it is low on responsiveness while remaining on-topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tanya Unkovich spoke about the bills creating clarity and cutting red tape, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: But it’s interesting that this is sort of the bill that gets introduced in the House with reasonable frequency, but people kind of talk about it from the perspective of, like, “Oh, look, we need to cut red tape. We need to cut green tape. We need to cut all of the tapes.” But, at the same time, you can say all of that that you want, but these sorts of bills and the quality of life it provides are still really important.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding framing — Unkovich's commendation of the bills as cutting red tape — and pushes back on it, arguing that the value lies in robust regulation rather than in deregulation, before returning at length to prepared material on offshore immigration advisers. A partial engagement one can point at, not a full rebuttal of a specific claim or figure, so mid-band. Scored only on engagement: whether the counter-framing reasons well or is accurate is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It creates more clarity, cuts red tape, and streamlines processes that are identified over time" — Tanya Unkovich

acuity.statement: I rise in support of the Regulatory Systems (Immigration and Workforce) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Economic Development) Amendment Bill and associated bills. These are sensible pieces of legislation that tidy up a lot of small changes, in many cases, to many different bills.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows a detailed, specific critique of the scope of the immigration and workforce bill. The reply is generic commendation plus thanks to officials and submitters, and engages none of it — substituting a different argument on the same topic into the preceding turn would not change a word of this speech. It names the bills under debate, so it is prepared on-topic material rather than wholly off-subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that offshore education agents should be required to register with the Immigration Advisers Authority because international students are being exploited, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It’s an honour to be the final speaker in this third reading of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2024-25, Emergency Response, and Remedial Measures) Bill. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, detailed critique from Megan Woods covering housing funding, health revenue, construction job losses and the Christchurch transport money. The turn engages none of it — no figure disputed, no claim corrected, no argument answered. It is tied to this debate only by naming the bill, which keeps it off 0.0; it would otherwise be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued that $78 million Labour had allocated to Christchurch public transport had been taken to pay for a reinstated roading project, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I want to focus my comments on the key areas of jobs, health, and homes, because what this bill basically does is reinforce the movement from New Zealand to Australia of many of our most qualified people—including the 13,000 mentioned by my colleague the Hon Dr Megan Woods—who have gone to Australia or elsewhere from the construction sector because there is not enough money to be able to support the pipeline of construction projects.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the preceding turn — Woods' 13,000 departing construction workers — names it, and builds her own structure (jobs, health, homes) on the same three areas Woods raised, so the speech is not indifferent to what it follows. But it extends rather than engages: she does not test, extend the reasoning of, or add to the claim beyond citing it, and the remainder (Dunedin Hospital, pathology, school lunches, the Octagon) is prepared material that would be unchanged had Woods argued something different on the same topic. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0. Her opening riff on Weenink's "final speaker" line is a glance at the previous turn's form, not its content, and does not lift the score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "13,000 construction workers" — Hon Dr Megan Woods

acuity.statement: A lot of these two bills has been traversed already this evening. Of course, we have a whole range of legislation here in New Zealand, and often some of these pieces of legislation need to be brought up to date. These bills make changes to 31 different Acts, including the oldest, from 1908, and I think the latest one is from 2002. They’re all really sensible changes, therefore I’m happy to commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Henare that raised specific concerns (mining safety definitions, charities and Incorporated Societies reform, the pronoun amendment, PSGE implications). Campbell gestures at the debate having happened (“traversed already this evening”) but engages no part of its content: he offers a generic count of amended Acts and a blanket “all really sensible changes” commendation. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had argued, though it is at least on the bills under debate — hence the 0.3 band with a mere reference, scored 0.2 because the reference is purely procedural acknowledgement rather than any attempt to answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued the bill must not blur the line between “tourism mines” and full commercial mining given the Government's mining agenda, and asked what the removal of gender-specific pronouns from the Heavy Engineering Research Levy Act signals — “I’m wondering if this Government’s signalling to the House and indeed the New Zealand public whether or not they’ll be taking a ruler, line by line, across Acts old and new” — and this statement does not take up either point.

acuity.statement: I see harmony has broken out across the House and everybody is in agreement that these are very good changes. So, with that, I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Anderson follows a substantive Labour speech and notes only that the House is in agreement. That registers the fact of cross-party support but engages no part of the preceding argument — nothing about migrant worker conditions, employer clarity, or progressive procurement. The speech would be word-for-word identical had Tangaere-Manuel made any other supportive argument, so it is a mere gesture at the state of the debate rather than engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "I am here on behalf of Labour to support this bill." — and her argument about migrant workers' experiences and the lost opportunity of progressive procurement

acuity.statement: Part of that beautiful journey is because there is consensus in the House, and there was at our Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee. But that consensus and that shared support isn’t always black and white.
acuity.explanation: Davidson takes up the one strand the previous speaker offered — the claim of unanimous agreement — and qualifies it, arguing that shared support does not mean the bill delivers the certainty it promises. That is a real engagement with the preceding point, and it would have had to be framed differently had Anderson not rested his contribution on harmony. But it is one strand only: the bulk of the speech then runs to prepared material (the omnibus summary, the RNZ parent-visa ballot article, school lunches, the Prime Minister's India trip) that is indifferent to what came before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Miles Anderson: "I see harmony has broken out across the House and everybody is in agreement that these are very good changes."

acuity.statement: That was a long 10 minutes—for a bill that is unanimous in the House. On this side of the House, we are really keen to drive productivity and growth and efficiency. With that, I commend these bills to the House.
acuity.explanation: The only reference to the preceding turn is to its length, which engages no content. Davidson's specific claims — the parent-category ballot, the uncertainty in immigration casework, Winston Peters' remarks on immigration settings in the India talks — go entirely unaddressed, and the pivot to generic government priorities would read the same whatever had been said. It is at least on the subject of the bill, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued the bill fails to deliver the certainty immigrants are seeking and that pre-election immigration promises were not kept, citing the parent-visa ballot; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: However, there is a lack of evidence that this bill or the drug-driving regime will address the root cause of dangerous or impaired driving, or of drug harm. I just want to unpack some of that, and what we observed in the committee stage.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan speaks immediately after Utikere, who made several pointed, specific arguments (no statutory limit on roadside detention, the 15-minute identity-check precedent, procurement driving the legislation, the Minister's amendment removing the Māori and Pacific impact review). None of these are taken up. The speech is prepared Green Party material — pharmacology of benzodiazepines and amphetamines, Schedule 5 thresholds, Taylor v NZ Poultry Board, Lawrence v NZ Police — and would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Utikere had argued, so it fails the substitution test. It is, however, firmly about the matter under debate and shares ground with Utikere on the Attorney-General's section 7 report (arguing it did not go far enough), which is a gesture at the debate rather than silence on it, placing it at 0.3 rather than 0.1. No specific engagement can be pointed at, so per the rubric it cannot reach 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued that the bill has 'no limitations on how long someone could be detained' and that the Government should have acted on the Attorney-General's concern, and this statement does not take that up; it gestures at the same committee-stage debate and later returns to the section 7 report on its own prepared terms.

acuity.statement: To me, the previous speaker, Andy Foster, gave us a lot of good reasons as to why we should be cautious about this bill, and there’s actually a lot of really good, valid reasons that would lead us to believe and argue that this is not the solution to the problem. One of the issues that was identified by the previous speaker was the sort of technology that was emerging in relation to having accuracy in those roadside tests, including in the laboratory.
acuity.explanation: Takes the immediately preceding speaker's own concession about the immaturity of roadside testing technology and turns it into an argument against the bill he supports — accepting Foster's premise and disputing his conclusion that monitoring can manage the risk. The speech would have to change if Foster had not raised the technology problem. Only partial because it then returns to prepared Green material on community-level interventions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "the technology just simply doesn’t exist to be able to do the testing at roadside and be able to determine someone effectively guilty at roadside, because the technology is not there."

acuity.statement: The previous speaker spoke about the randomness, I guess, of how this may be administered. But what we do know, and the evidence can point at this, is that, actually, Māori and Pacific communities are already disproportionately targeted by our authorities.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Foster's specific admission that the nominally random testing regime will in practice be operationally targeted, and draws out a consequence Foster did not — who the targeting will fall on. Engages one strand of the preceding turn rather than its whole argument, then moves to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "The bill is based, in theory, on random, but random, as you’ve heard my colleague Cam Luxton say, actually is a bit targeted."

acuity.statement: I do want to highlight both to the House and to the general public that in 2023, there were 64 fatalities where the presence of drugs was detected in the driver, and a further 32 drivers were found to have both drugs and alcohol in their system whilst operating on the road. So this legislation is simply about ensuring that for New Zealanders and international visitors and anyone who drives on our roads, they can feel comfortable and safe knowing that drug drivers will not be operating vehicles and that the New Zealand Police have the enforcement and the tools they need to ensure our roads are safe for everyone and that we can reduce fatalities in this country.
acuity.explanation: Halbert's turn immediately before made two specific, engageable arguments — the refused 20-minute detention limit recommended by the Attorney-General, and unfair targeting of Māori, Pasifika and young drivers. Rutherford answers neither, and does not touch detention limits or safeguards at all. He offers prepared material on the right subject (drug-driving fatality statistics and a general case for police enforcement powers), and the speech would read identically whatever Halbert had said, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; there is no gesture at the preceding argument, placing it at 0.1 rather than 0.3. His only backward reference, 'As my colleague said', is to a government colleague's committee service, not to the content of any claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the Government had not supported a 20-minute time limit on roadside detention and raised the disproportionate impact of such testing on Māori, Pasifika and young people, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: It’s good to see also that there’s a five-year review period, because we know that one of the holdups, really, to getting this under way quicker is the fact that we want good, reliable technology that gives results that can stand up and be verified in the lab.
acuity.explanation: Bidois's turn leaned on the five-year review as the answer to concerns raised in the debate; Andersen takes up that same strand and supplies her own reason for valuing it (evolving testing technology), rather than engaging his claim that the review answers the objections. One strand picked up, then a return to prepared material on the bill's operation, so mid-low rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But I think that is why there is a five-year review of this bill." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: The reality is that this bill is about getting people off the roads who are driving while impaired, whether that be with legal or illegal drugs, or alcohol. Indeed, it doesn’t matter to the victim whether the drugs are legal or illegal; they just don’t want to be caught up in an accident on the road.
acuity.explanation: Andersen spent much of the preceding turn on the prescribed-versus-illicit distinction and how courts and devices would handle it; Smith takes up that strand and pushes back on its relevance, arguing the legal/illegal line does not matter to a crash victim. He engages the topic of the distinction rather than her specific claims about concentration thresholds or court challenges, and his framing is aimed at an earlier Green speaker not in this window, so partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "one being potentially legally prescribed; one being an illicit substance purchased on the black market" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: For far too long, drugged drivers have put other road users at risk. Well, guess what! Those days are over, and anyone driving while impaired can expect to get caught and face the consequences. Finally, police will have the tools they need to help keep Kiwis safe from drugged drivers.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, substantive turn by Arena Williams raising specific problems — that the roadside tests measure the presence of a substance rather than impairment, that the Act sets no limit on how long a driver may be held at the roadside, and that arbitrary rules erode public consent. Butterick's speech engages none of it: it is a generic endorsement of the bill that would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. It stays within the subject under debate (drug-driving enforcement), so it is not a 0.0, but there is nothing in it that answers Williams.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued the tests measure 'the substance in people's systems ... rather than the way it has affected their driving' and that she would have preferred a stated limit on roadside detention time; this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: I rise to present Te Pāti Māori’s views on the bill. Let me just be clear that we do not support driving under any impairment—drugs, alcohol, or any other thing; we’re 100 percent pro safer roads. But what we cannot not address in this House is the Government’s continuation of dismissing the negative impacts on Māori, and in this bill I’m going to speak to the negative impacts on rangatahi Māori.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one. Ferris gestures at them — he frames his contribution as adding to what members have already said, and his opening concession that Te Pāti Māori opposes impaired driving accepts the shared premise Williams and Butterick both asserted. But he then opens a new strand (the effect of police interactions on rangatahi Māori) without taking up any specific claim either member made: not Williams's impairment-versus-presence problem or her worry about roadside detention time, and not Butterick's assertion that police will now have the tools they need. This is prepared party material delivered on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, which places it at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than in partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: ngā kōrero kua hori nei e ngā mema o te Whare / 'what has already been said by the members of this House' — a general acknowledgement of the preceding turns by Arena Williams and Mike Butterick, but no specific argument of theirs is engaged.

acuity.statement: I just want to pick up on what Dr Duncan talked about not so long ago: the mitigating factors as to why our youth are in that particular predicament in the first place. I look at the complex, interrelated challenges that many of our rangatahi face.
acuity.explanation: Waititi names the previous speaker and gestures at 'mitigating factors', but the Webb turn he follows was about prosecutorial failure and late pleas under section 9G, not youth mitigating factors; nothing in Webb's actual argument is engaged. The material on cultural reports, Māori incarceration rates and youth neurodisability is prepared content on the matter under debate (Part 1 mitigating factors) and would read identically whatever Webb had just said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.3 for the explicit gesture at the preceding contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb's preceding turn argued for a tabled amendment adding a subsection (5) to section 9G so that a late plea "can be attributed in whole, or part to failures or misconduct" of the prosecutor, and this statement does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: In response to the previous speaker, Rawiri Waititi, it is my hope that this bill will ease the pain, particularly for Māori victims of crime. Yes, Māori are overrepresented in the prison population. They are also overrepresented amongst the victims of crime and have a real interest in seeing that justice is done and that part of the justice response is real consequences for crime.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith takes the exact question put to him, concedes the premise about Māori overrepresentation in prison, and turns it by adding overrepresentation among victims — accepting part and disputing the framing. He also picks up the specific driver Waititi listed, answering 'those drivers of crime that the member referred to, like not being in school'. The reply would have to be different had Waititi asked something else, which is the deciding test. Not a 1.0 only because the central question about what the bill does for Māori incarceration rates is answered as a statement of hope rather than with a mechanism.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does this bill ease the pain for Māori in those percentages" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: In terms of the cultural reports, what this Government did was stop the cottage industry that developed around the writing of those reports but the Sentencing Act still, obviously, provides the opportunity for the background of the offender to be taken into account.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question Waititi asked — why cultural reports were ended — and corrects the implication that offender background can no longer be considered by pointing at the surviving Sentencing Act provision. It is pointable, squarely aimed at the claim made, and could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument. Whether the 'cottage industry' characterisation is fair or whether the Act really preserves the same latitude is a question for Veracity and Rigor, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just want to take into consideration as to why the cultural reports were declined by this particular Government" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: Finally, in relation to Mr Duncan Webb’s references around prosecutorial misconduct, that is excluded from the 40 percent cap as it’s not a personal factor.
acuity.explanation: Webb built a detailed case for a section 9G amendment to handle late pleas caused by prosecutorial failure and ended by asking directly whether the amendment would be adopted. Goldsmith engages the precise mechanism at issue, answering that prosecutorial misconduct falls outside the cap altogether because it is not a personal factor — which, if right, dissolves the problem Webb posed rather than sidestepping it. Highest band: the specific point is taken up and something is done with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And will you adopt that tabled amendment which would make sure that prosecutorial misconduct can be taken into account to get a just outcome?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: You’re not saving anyone’s lives—the road toll hasn’t come down.
acuity.explanation: Costello interjected that the drug-driving regime exists to save lives; Ferris takes that exact claim and contradicts it on its own terms, offering the road toll as the test of whether lives are being saved. The reply would have had to be different if Costello had interjected something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "To save their lives." — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: I see the ex-mayor of Wellington is talking over there. He might want to think about this—he didn’t do such a great job in Wellington when he was the mayor.
acuity.explanation: Foster made a specific factual rebuttal of Ferris's road-toll point with a per-capita comparison. Ferris engages no part of it — he does not dispute the statistic, the measure or the comparison — and instead pivots to Foster's record as Wellington mayor, which is irrelevant to the claim made. A mere reference to the interjector is not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The lowest per capita since the 1920s—a hundred years." — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: Yes, we have returned to this particular bill. Just so I can kind of keep my thought process and work through this bill systematically as well, the last time we left this bill I was talking about clause 6, which is section 9 amended, around aggravating factors.
acuity.explanation: Eligible, since Webb's substantive turn in the same committee debate immediately precedes it, but the speech engages none of its content. It is on the right bill and openly picks up where the speaker's own earlier contribution stopped, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0 — it could not have been delivered in a different debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that the once-only youth discount risks sweeping aside a judge's ability to weigh cognitive development, and this statement does not take it up — Xu-Nan resumes his own prepared sequence on clause 6 aggravating factors instead.

acuity.statement: In terms of the youth discount, the member referred to fetal alcohol syndrome and so forth, and those matters can be dealt with separately from youth. The youth discount applies to offenders aged 18 and over, and so our point of view is that they should have the potential for a discount for that youth once, not multiple times.
acuity.explanation: Takes Webb's specific example and answers the specific question put — that cognitive impairment is handled separately from the youth discount, which is the pivot Webb's tabled amendment turned on. Marked below 1.0 because he then returns to prepared victims framing without addressing Webb's follow-up about how judges will be enabled to weigh cognitive development.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is he satisfied that a judge can look at a person who is young and say that person has cognitive impairment, perhaps fetal alcohol syndrome" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: In terms of party liability, my advice is that party liability is determined at the conviction stage, not in sentencing.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the answer Xu-Nan said was outstanding and gives a reason that bears directly on it — party liability is settled at conviction, so a sentencing bill does not reach it. Partial rather than full engagement: neither of Xu-Nan's two specific strands, the Ahsin v Queen withdrawal point and the removed marital-compulsion presumption for victims of long-term abuse, is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I still haven’t received a response from the Minister of Justice regarding my previous question, which is around subclause (1)(cb), including section 66(1)(b), (c), or (d), or (2) of the Crimes Act 1961 around party liability" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I get what the Minister is saying—that he doesn’t mean that the victim needs to make a separate application for protection order. But I wondered if what we’re doing here is very much the last resort, bottom-of-the-cliff kind of approach, whereas what we’re not seeing here is what is actually beneficial for the victims and what are the tools that allow an offender, in those circumstances, to be aware and to be able to change their actions or change their perspective because of the fact that there is a guidance, a kind of an education, following on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Goldsmith's specific claim — that the clause spares victims a separate protection-order application — restates it accurately, accepts it, and then presses the consequence he did not address: that a section 106 discharge amounts to an acquittal, so a protection order without accompanying guidance may be a bottom-of-the-cliff measure. The speech would have to change entirely if Goldsmith had said something else about clause 18.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "That prevents victims having to make a separate application for a protection order and saves court time, which is better for the victims of crime."

acuity.statement: So I’m interested to note why there’s this carve out here for section 106, “Discharge without conviction”, when the entire kind of ambit, the purpose, of the bill is to strip away the discretion of judges.
acuity.explanation: Anchored to the judge-centred justification Goldsmith had just given for clause 18 ("if a judge considers the conduct warrants a protection order, that they can grant one") and draws out its consequence: that the clause preserves the very judicial discretion the rest of the bill removes. It engages the specific point rather than the general topic, though much of the surrounding turn returns to prepared material on judicial discretion across the whole bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it is important that if a judge considers the conduct warrants a protection order, that they can grant one"

acuity.statement: This legislation doesn’t change the threshold for the granting of protection orders, and so we’re not dealing with that. All it does is it stops the need for a separate hearing on matters. So that prevents victims having to have a separate application, which saves court time, which I think the member just said she was concerned about—and that is the purpose of this whole bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Andersen's turn — her point about court delays — and turns it back on her, and makes a narrowing claim (the threshold is unchanged) that bears on the discretion argument. But it leaves her central question (why discretion is preserved here and curtailed elsewhere) and Xu-Nan's question about the evidential basis untouched, returning instead to the same two sentences he had already given. Partial engagement, pointable but thin.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "A prescriptive approach can drive significant court delays"

acuity.statement: But going on to the title of this bill, I wholeheartedly agree with the previous speaker the Hon Dr Duncan Webb in his analysis that this is not a reform. There are many other words that start with the prefix “re” that we should be using. I think that “retrograde” is a good one. “Retrospective” is another good one.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific argument about the word "Reform" in the title and does something with it — accepts his "retrograde" coinage and extends the list with "retrospective" and "repugnant", tying the latter to his own retrospective-penalty point on clause 2. But this engagement sits at the end of a turn that is otherwise prepared material on commencement dates and the 40 percent cap, which would have been delivered whatever Webb had said, so it is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Duncan Webb: "I'm not sure what the opposite of "Reform" is. Perhaps "Retrograde" or some such word would be appropriate, but this, certainly, is not a reform bill."

acuity.statement: Just briefly in response to the member Lawrence Xu-Nan’s question about if I considered changing the commencement from three months to six months: yes, I have considered it, and I’m not going to do it. In response to the changes of the names, I think they’re all just cheap, political shots and I won’t be responding.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question that was put — whether he would accept the three-months-to-six-months amendment — and gives the direct answer, so the turn could not have been delivered after a different preceding speech. Not 1.0 because he engages only the question's existence and not its reasoning (the retrospective youth-penalty rationale), and explicitly declines to take up the title arguments at all. Note the bluntness of the refusal is a specificity/forthrightness matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I want to check first with the Minister of Justice whether the Minister would consider my amendment that would change "3 months" to "6 months""

acuity.statement: I note that the Minister of Justice has just responded by stating he did give consideration to extending the commencement date of this particular piece of legislation but he did not furnish it with any further information as to what he weighed up and how he arrived at his decision not to extend that period.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's reply seconds after it was given, identifies exactly what it did and did not contain, and builds the rest of her contribution on that gap — pressing for the reasoning, the judicial training programme and the engagement with the judiciary. If Goldsmith had given reasons, or had accepted the amendment, this speech would have had to be different, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Paul Goldsmith: "yes, I have considered it, and I'm not going to do it"

acuity.statement: We will see more young people who will be harmed as a result. We will see that lawyers and judges will find different ways, like the previous speaker the Hon Dr Duncan Webb has mentioned, of being able to balance what they see in front of them.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan follows Webb, whose central argument was that the 40 percent discount cap will be worked around by judges lowering the starting point and by increased discharges without conviction. Xu-Nan picks up that one strand and endorses it by name, so the fragment can be pointed at — but he does nothing with its content (no reasoning about starting points, no extension or qualification) before returning to prepared Green material on youth justice, Te Tiriti, white-collar crime and Plato. That is a gesture at the preceding argument rather than engagement with it, so it sits above the pure-prepared band but below a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "They're simply going to lower the starting point. There's no rule against lowering the starting point." — Webb's argument that the discount cap will simply be worked around by judges.

acuity.statement: And what did Ginny Andersen in the Labour Party just say? “This is a sad bill.” Do you know what’s sad? For the victims in New Zealand who see the people who commit those crimes being tagged and released under that Labour administration and not serving the time for the crimes they’ve committed.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows a long speech whose substance was that the bill cannot be 'tough on crime' while methamphetamine use rose 96 percent, gangs profit, gun laws are being weakened, and the 40 percent cap removes judicial discretion in complex cases. He takes up none of that. He lifts the phrase 'a sad bill' and uses it only as a springboard to a prepared contrast about victims and 'tagged and released' sentencing — quoting the opponent in order to pivot away, which the rubric treats as unresponsive rather than partial engagement. It stays on the matter under debate (the bill and sentencing), so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0; nothing in it would have to change had Andersen argued a different case about this bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is a sad bill" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill. I was a member of the Justice Committee that heard from a number of submitters, and, I must say, we’ve heard one view from the other side of the House, but there was also a view that this bill is going in the right direction. It restores real consequences for crime.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Stephenson's substantive third-reading speech immediately precedes it. Arbuckle's contribution is prepared material on the right subject — a restatement of the Minister's three themes and an attack on Labour's prison-population record. Nothing in it is shaped by what Stephenson actually argued; the gesture at "one view from the other side of the House" points at speeches outside this window, not at the preceding turn. On-topic but unresponsive, so the bottom band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson spoke about ACT's campaigned-for aggravating factors for public transport and sole-charge workers and the limit on the 40 percent sentence discount, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This sentencing reform bill is going to result in more people being funnelled into our prisons and it does not make our communities any safer. I don’t know what la-la land you might be living in on that side of the House, but if you’d actually set foot in a prison there’s no rehabilitation going on in there. I’ve been to 10 prisons in the last year; there’s no rehabilitation going on at all in there.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the central claim of both preceding speeches — that the bill makes communities safer — denies it directly and gives a reason (no rehabilitation capacity in the prisons the bill will fill), citing her own prison visits. That is engagement with the content, not a mere reference. Short of 1.0 because she does not touch the specific mechanisms the previous speakers advanced (the aggravating factors, the 40 percent discount cap, or Arbuckle's prison-population figures); the rebuttal is aimed at their conclusion rather than their reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "actually making our community safer, which is what ACT is here for" — Todd Stephenson; and "It restores real consequences for crime" — Jamie Arbuckle.

acuity.statement: But it’s easy for that side of the House to sit there and hand wring and talk about personal responsibility because they’ve had more options in their lives than all of the young people that are in prison.
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up the principle Arbuckle named a turn earlier and contests it on its own terms, arguing that personal responsibility is cheap to invoke for those with options and tying it to the bill's removal of youth as a mitigating factor. The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had framed the bill differently. Not 1.0 because the counter is an argument about the principle's proponents rather than an engagement with Arbuckle's stated evidence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "restoring the principles of personal responsibility" — Jamie Arbuckle, listing the bill's three key areas.

acuity.statement: Because if they were listening to that contribution that’s just been made, they would think that their contribution to rehabilitation is not appreciated, and I want all of those corrections officers to know that it is, by this Government.
acuity.explanation: Eligible and visibly shaped by the preceding turn: he takes Paul's claim that no rehabilitation happens in prisons and responds to one strand of it, the implication for corrections staff, offering his electorate's reform and rehabilitation work as a counterweight. But he engages the claim's audience rather than its substance — nothing here addresses whether rehabilitation programmes work, her 7 to 15 percent figure, or prison capacity — so it sits at partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s no rehabilitation going on at all in there" — Tamatha Paul.

acuity.statement: The Government members, the people opposite us in this House, have said several times today that this is about putting victims first, and that’s just vacuous. That’s just an utterly rubbish, vacuous comment that doesn’t make any actual sense. It’s as if you say it out loud and that makes it true. Rima Nakhle can sit there and shake her head but just because she stands up and says this is about making victims’ lives better doesn’t actually make it true. There is nothing in this bill that does that.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific claim Nakhle had just built her whole speech around — that the bill puts victims first — names her directly, and disputes it on the ground that no provision of the bill delivers anything for victims. The speech would have had to be different had the preceding turn argued something else. Not a full 1.0 because she counters the claim by assertion and labelling rather than engaging Nakhle's concrete example (the Timaru sentencing discount), and then moves to prepared material on clause detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "on this side of the House, we actually put victims first" / "It’s actually a very good day for victims" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: Very many statements have been made in this debate, but they’re simply out of scope of this debate. The Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill is very specific in its purpose to amend the Sentencing Act of 2002. We in this National Party and this Government strongly support the strengthening of accountability for crimes.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the debate — he acknowledges that statements have been made and rules them out of scope — but no part of the preceding argument is engaged, rebutted or even named. The remainder is general prepared support for accountability and consequences that would read identically whatever had just been said about the bill, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued the 40 percent cap and the removal of the youth and remorse discounts rest on no robust analysis and will undermine judicial discretion; this statement declares such arguments out of scope without taking up any part of them.

acuity.statement: The reframing of this bill as a customer product right from what Labour was developing as a consumer data right is a pretty large change in terms of what the scope of it is and what people can expect the Government to be creating here as a sort of framework going forward.
acuity.explanation: Williams follows the Minister's overview and takes up one strand of it: he described the bill as introducing a "consumer data right regime", and she engages that characterisation directly, pointing out the scope has been reframed from individuals and organisations to customers and asking the Minister what that narrowing means for personal data rights. That is a real engagement with the content of the preceding turn rather than a mere reference to it. But it is partial — most of the call is prepared clause-by-clause questioning plus thanks to officials and predecessors, and would have been delivered largely unchanged whatever the Minister had said in his introduction, so this sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the bill introduces a very long overdue consumer data right regime to New Zealand, to make customer and product data accessible for the benefit of New Zealanders" — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: And the Minister is completely right when he says, “It’s not the bank’s data; it’s my data. I should have the ability to say how that data is used.” He is completely right. That is exactly the regime that we have.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's own framing of customer ownership of bank-held data, accepts it explicitly, and then does something with it — pressing that the regime cannot reach the second layer of data (risk assessments about 'someone like you') now that derived data has been removed, and asking what protections replace it. The speech would be different had the Minister argued something else; she also returns to his claim that he had already covered her non-customer question by re-stating why she asked it via clause 4(4). Engagement, not mere reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "It’s actually not the bank’s data; it’s my data."

acuity.statement: What are the specific outcomes the Minister is seeking as a result of greater competition and innovation, and, if he thinks that there are some specific outcomes that should be part of the purpose of this bill, were these explored in terms of incorporating them in clause 3 and, subsequently, I guess, then being further defined in the interpretations in clause 5.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — clause 3's purpose and clause 5's interpretation — and it glances at the preceding turn ('other members have touched a bit on the language of competition', 'I totally acknowledge the Minister's words and others that this bill will touch on a range of sectors'). But it engages no part of the framework-versus-regulation argument the Minister had just made, and would read identically had that answer been different. A gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson had just argued that "it’s the broad framework of the legislation that we want to be stable and secure" with sector-specific regulation tweaked as technology changes; this statement does not take that reasoning up.

acuity.statement: Thank you to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs for that helpful answer. It leads me to my next question, which is: what is the impact on non-customers of the change to clause 3(1)(a), and then no subsequent change to clause 3(2)(a)?
acuity.explanation: She takes up the thread the Minister had just opened — the altered wording of the purpose clause and who the bill's benefit accrues to — and presses it onto a specific pair of subclauses, probing the asymmetry between a changed 3(1)(a) and an unchanged 3(2)(a) and what that means for non-customers. But it engages the topic rather than the Minister's specific claim: she does not dispute or test his assertion that the changed wording still secures customer benefit, and the question reads as the next item in a prepared sequence ("my next question"). Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "So the wording has been changed, but the purpose of the bill is to establish a framework to realise the value of that data for the benefit of customers, whether they be individuals and/or businesses."

acuity.statement: I wonder, then, if that’s the case, with respect to in clause 3(2)(c), where it says there, “requiring certain safeguards, controls, standards, and functionality in connection with those data services.” if it is (1) the intention of the Minister to continually come back and update that regulatory framework through omnibus bills, through further legislation, or whether it’s just simple regulatory change that can be done at another level; or (2) as my colleague’s already mentioned, when we look towards what the penalties will be eventually, whether or not that will continue to need to be updated, reiterated, and of course debated in the House, given the scope of what the Minister’s answer was with respect to opening up to other parts, other sectors, other businesses.
acuity.explanation: This takes the Minister's own answer — that sector detail arrives in regulations which vary by sector, with banking first, then electricity, then others — and draws out its consequence: if the framework must be extended sector by sector, what is the mechanism, omnibus legislation or regulation made at another level, and will penalties have to return to the House each time. The conditional construction ("if that's the case") and the explicit anchor "given the scope of what the Minister's answer was" make the question dependent on what was just said; substitute a different answer about scope and the question would have to change. Not full marks only because it does not test the answer's reasoning, it extends it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "those specifics will come in secondary legislation provided by regulations. Now, those will vary depending on the sector."

acuity.statement: I’d also just like to pick up on my friend’s question about clause 3(2)(c) and the issues there around the safeguards in place here. That was touched upon a little bit, but what sort of safeguards are there in this legislation, and why is it necessary to have them? What’s the balancing act that’s been brought to bear in this legislation?
acuity.explanation: She names the strand the immediately preceding speaker raised, notes that it has only been "touched upon a little bit", and re-puts it in a sharper form — not just what the safeguards are but why they are necessary and what trade-off they represent. That is engagement with the content of the previous turn and an attempt to stop it being passed over, which is more than a reference. It falls short of 1.0 because she restates and reinforces the question rather than contesting any claim in it, and it sits alongside her own separately prepared material on the purpose clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "where it says there, “requiring certain safeguards, controls, standards, and functionality in connection with those data services.”"

acuity.statement: The broader picture that Helen White has just sort of painted for us is really at the nub of what this legislation is all about. It’s the potential opportunities for unexplored, as yet sometimes unimagined, benefits to New Zealand consumers. Because we haven’t had a regime where data is open and available, there are many opportunities that can be explored that most New Zealanders will not even yet have contemplated.
acuity.explanation: He identifies the specific question put to him — what long-term benefit the public is currently missing out on — and answers that strand directly, with the counterfactual that no open-data regime has existed and so the benefits are as yet uncontemplated. He goes on to supply the concrete real-time personal-budgeting example her question asked for. Scored at 0.6 rather than higher because the other half of her question, which sectors are the next targets and what the low-hanging fruit in something like healthcare would be, is met with "a whole range of other areas" rather than taken up; whether the answer is vague is a Specificity matter, but declining to engage that half of the question is an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "I just wondered if you could explain for the benefit of the public what that long-term benefit that they’re missing out on at the moment is and why it would be that something like this would free up innovation and competition."

acuity.statement: I have a different line of questions for the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs regarding clause 3 of Part 1 of the bill, which is under “Purpose”. I wanted to start with clause 3(1)(b) around “competition and innovation”. Now, going through the regulatory impact statement, we have seen a number of instances where the consultation was done with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), which is understandable. However, what I couldn’t see—and this is a concern—is any consultation that was undertaken with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT).
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Arena Williams on derived data and the Amendment Paper, but expressly sets it aside to open a prepared line on clause 3, MFAT consultation and trade agreements. No strand of Williams's argument is engaged — not her cross-partisanship point, not the Xero submission, not the privacy-framework claim. It is at least about the bill under committee consideration, so it sits at the upper-middle of the unresponsive band rather than the floor: this speech would have been delivered essentially word-for-word whatever Williams had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams spoke about whether Amendment Paper 254's designated customer data provisions honour the select committee's cross-partisan removal of derived data, and this statement does not take it up — it announces "a different line of questions".

acuity.statement: I just want to go back to the derived data question that Arena Williams raised, because it is interesting. I want to make it very clear that my Amendment Paper actually doesn’t reintroduce derived data into the legislation. The Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee made it very clear that for a variety of reasons it needed not to be included. But what the Amendment Paper does do is it clarifies the designated customer data as the specific types of data designated through the regulations.
acuity.explanation: Takes Williams's specific worry — that the new designated customer data provisions smuggle derived data back in against the committee's cross-partisan agreement — and answers it on its own terms: denies the premise that the Amendment Paper reintroduces derived data, affirms the committee's conclusion, and explains what the clause does instead (pushing detail into regulations). He then supplies the timetable and points her to paragraphs 73 to 77 of the departmental report. The speech could not have been given had Williams raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "can the Minister assure everyone that that commitment to cross-partisanship here is being honoured and that there won’t be an unnecessary slowing down of creating the useful products that derived data would have otherwise brought in?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked some questions around the role of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade—had they been consulted. What I can confirm is that the officials working on this bill have consulted very widely indeed and that no issues of the sort that he has questioned have arisen. So I take that to mean that, from an officials’ point of view, no matters have been brought to their attention.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Xu-Nan's first question by name and addresses that exact question, reporting what officials have told him about the consultation and the absence of trade-agreement issues. It is engagement with the specific claim, not a pivot — scored just short of the top only because it answers the adjacent question (no issues were raised) rather than the one asked (whether MFAT itself was consulted). Whether that answer is satisfying or precise is a matter for other attributes; the attention to what was said is clear.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my first question is around whether the Minister has any clarity or clarification on whether MFAT has been consulted, in the context of this particular bill, specifically under the digital economy chapters" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: But in making that point—because I think he raises an interesting question about trade agreements and the international scene and so forth—data doesn’t have geographic barriers. Data is data. What the barriers are are technical barriers. They are system barriers rather than lines on a map around the planet.
acuity.explanation: Engages the onshore-data and data-sovereignty strand of Xu-Nan's questions, but by reframing rather than answering: it disputes the framing that data has a geographic location at all, and defers the substance to the sector-by-sector regulations. That is a real engagement with the premise of the question, so it is well above prepared material, but it leaves the specific trade-agreement constraint he cited untouched, so it does not reach the top band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in certain trade deals, we are not, under those trade deals, allowed to have that data being held onshore" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: How were the four needy groups outlined by Mr Hipkins in his last question assisted by trying to find housing, accommodation, emergency housing, hospitals, schools, and infrastructure for the 133,000 net that the previous Government brought in that we inherited?
acuity.explanation: Counter-argues the preceding claim that housing outcomes were enabled by the previous Government's building record, by reframing that Government as the source of the demand pressure. It engages the housing-record strand but not the specific state-house-building claim, then runs to its own prepared theme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "every single one of the families moved out of emergency accommodation into State housing was only possible because we built record numbers of new State houses"

acuity.statement: I agree with the member. We inherited an infrastructure crisis—we’re working our way through it. But my frustration is this is not an issue to politicise—this is not an issue to politicise. We are getting families out of motels into proper houses—that is the reality of it. Eighty percent of those families in households are now in proper homes and houses. You can politicise it, but you shouldn’t be doing that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the infrastructure-inheritance premise of the preceding question and endorses it, but does nothing with the migration figure or the question actually asked before moving to prepared material on emergency housing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "trying to find housing, accommodation, emergency housing, hospitals, schools, and infrastructure for the 133,000 net"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I want to go to clause 4 and ask about the overview. What I noticed was, first of all, it’s a very unusual way of laying out a clause, and it seems a very effective way, actually.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Henare on clause 5(2) and third-party liability and engages no part of it, opening an entirely new line on clause 4 and the overview provision. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had said. It stays in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.0 because it is squarely about the bill under committee consideration and continues the committee's clause-by-clause questioning of the Minister.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare spoke immediately before, on clause 5(2)'s "involved in a contravention" definition and whether deceit captures third parties, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Look, I just sense that we’re getting a little bit repetitive. So I just want to make it very clear that there is a provision at clause 5(2) which defines a terminology, and that says “involved in a contravention”, and I draw members’ attention to that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause Henare raised and answers one strand of his question — that the "involved in a contravention" wording is a broad catch-all that already reaches third parties — and expressly acknowledges the member may pursue it later. It does not engage the specific deceit/Crimes Act limb Henare asked about, and opens by characterising the questioning as repetitive rather than answering it, so this is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker

It is the duty of this House to take time to look at laws that were passed and see if they are still relevant. To quote members who supported a piece of legislation when they responded to a horrific incident that brought the whole country to its knees, where we all stopped and responded to the fact that this was something we needed to deal with quickly, and, therefore, that legislation was passed exactly as was criticised across the House—in rush, without consultation, without thinking about what the implications were going to be.

acuity.responding_to: "This bill is, essentially, a rushed bit of legislation." — Scott Willis (also his "it has not gone out to the wider public")

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I would like to thank the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries for being very open in terms of his response, but also in terms of his broader experience in this area."

acuity.statement: But it’s also appropriate to support it because if we maintained the status quo, New Zealand would become an outlier in terms of this space, in terms of ensuring that we strengthen our ability to manage the fisheries and to enforce the rules to prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paulo Garcia spoke about the Government's commitment to a strong domestic framework against illegal fishing in the Southern and Pacific Oceans, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Similar to the last presenter from the other side of the House, Glen Bennett, this bill brings New Zealand up to the international expectations to meet our obligations.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod explicitly picks up Bennett's turn and takes up one strand of it — that without the bill New Zealand falls short of international expectations — restating it as common ground before moving to his own prepared points about trading partners and fish stocks. More than a bare name-check, but he does nothing further with Bennett's reasoning, so it sits between a glance and genuine engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "New Zealand would become an outlier in terms of this space" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: There are some heckles coming from the other side of the House that I have to even congratulate the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries for shepherding this through the House.

It is live engagement with what was said a moment earlier and is pointable, but what she engages is a goad rather than an argument, so it is partial rather than full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Go on, say it!" — David MacLeod (and "You know you want to!" — Jenny Marcroft)

acuity.statement: Essentially, this bill, as we’ve heard traversed around the House today, is amending the principal Act, the Fisheries Act 1996, so that Aotearoa New Zealand can better meet its international fishing management obligations in a more efficient way. With that, since we’re so good here on this side of the House with efficiency, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle immediately follows Brooking and lifts her word 'efficiency' back at her, which shows she heard the jibe, but she addresses no part of Brooking's actual argument about urgency compressing the committee stage and unanswered questions. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can say it is a lot more efficient, if this Government is interested in efficiency, to have a little bit of time to make sure that questions raised do not identify problems" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Next week, the House will consider further stages of the Building (Overseas Building Products, Standards, and Certification Schemes) Amendment Bill, the Victims of Sexual Violence (Strengthening Legal Protections) Legislation Bill, and the Privacy Amendment Bill." — Louise Upston

One strand engaged, pointable, nothing done with it: a mid-band score. Scored independently of its evasiveness, which is a Forthrightness matter, and of its vagueness, which is Specificity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm wondering if there's a backlog and the Government will be calling urgency again." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I think I want to ask similar questions to the Minister for Hunting and Fishing, first and foremost, around the interaction between our domestic privacy legislations and how it intersects with some of the broader international best practices, but also the broader international commitment around this. I think, previously, we’ve heard from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb around the fact that this largely is following in line with what the EU is doing in terms of privacy, which, by the way, is one of the golden standards when it comes to privacy protection, as opposed to, for example, the US.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan picks up one strand of Webb's preceding turn — the claim that the new privacy principle is imported from the EU for cross-border reasons — names Webb as its source, and does something modest with it by characterising the EU as the gold standard against the US, then moves to his own prepared line of questioning on the section 4 definition of "agency" and the regulatory impact statement diagram. He does not take up Webb's actual argument (the subjectivity of the first exception and the threshold for "prejudice"), so this is partial engagement on the shared topic rather than a rebuttal or extension of the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "It has, essentially, been imported from the EU for good reason, because we need to have an international framework for privacy so that organisations can work in a cross-border way."

acuity.statement: I don’t have a huge amount to add to that comprehensive description of the proceedings of the Privileges Committee. I note, as I recall, the committee was unanimous in its resolution on this matter, which is always a good thing.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows Collins' presentation of the interim report and explicitly takes it up — he accepts her account as comprehensive, declines to repeat it, and supplements it with two things she did not say: that the committee was unanimous and that Henare's written and oral candour helped it dispose of the matter promptly. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "However, we find that Mr Henare’s actions do not amount to a contempt." — and her account of Henare's written explanation and committee appearance.

acuity.statement: The Green Party acknowledges the report that we’re debating today and the existing rules that therefore guided us to come to the conclusion in this report. I want to acknowledge the Hon Peeni Henare for his contributions to the oral hearings and particularly acknowledging his comments that helped us understand that he was carrying the many, many, many constituents behind him when he chose to make the actions that led to this report.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and glancing at the preceding turn — it picks up Webb's point about Henare's contributions to the committee and extends it with a reason of its own (the constituents he was carrying).
