acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "he was fulsome in his comments—and frank and sincere—and that assisted the committee in its deliberations considerably"

acuity.statement: Firstly, I would like to acknowledge the chair of the Privileges Committee for producing a record of the disruption that occurred in the House before the first reading vote on the Treaty principles bill. I will not repeat all that, and I will also not repeat the details that are covered in the committee report, other than to reiterate the conclusion that Peeni Henare’s conduct, including participating in a haka, was disorderly and did obstruct or impede the business of the House as the vote was not able to continue. Peeni Henare has apologised for his conduct, and ACT accepts his apology.
acuity.explanation: Parmar takes up Collins' specific finding — that stepping onto the floor obstructed or impeded the business of the House because the vote could not continue — reproduces it as the operative conclusion, and states her party's position on the apology Collins reported had been given. acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "Mr Henare’s conduct in stepping on to the floor of the Chamber to participate in the haka while a vote was being taken did obstruct or impede the business of the House, as the vote was not able to continue."

acuity.statement: I understand where the Minister’s coming from, that let’s say we’re filling out a Google form or a Microsoft form, that the agency itself is the person who drafted the form, but the medium or the mode that is being used to process the data may not be the agency that is collecting it. However, we also know that, for example, Microsoft or Google—I’m going to use those two examples because they are universally understood—are also the ones who keep that information.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's just-given distinction between the collecting agency and the software 'mechanism' accurately, accepts it provisionally, then presses on the specific weak point in it — that the provider also retains and stores the data, so it is not merely a conduit. The speech would be materially different had Meager answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "my assumption would be that the “collecting agency” would be yourself and that a piece of software that you’re using to do that—say, a Google doc or a Google survey form—is just a mechanism by which to collect the information"

acuity.statement: I’m advised that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade were closely involved in the development of the policy, including discussions with the EU during their adequacy status review, and they’re comfortable with where the law is sitting. Just for the avoidance of doubt, the Act does apply to social media companies.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the information the preceding question asked for — whether MFAT was consulted and on what — and also resolves the second strand of that question, whether large tech/social media companies fall under the Act. Directly shaped by the question just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "has the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) been consulted in terms of our current trade agreements"

acuity.statement: I know that this was a hot issue during the Justice Committee, and we had various submitters who were concerned that this might curtail their ability to do archival work, particularly studying things like whakapapa and family heritage and having the ability to go in and look over those past records that may contain issues or details around personal privacy. I’m just interested to know from the Minister for Hunting and Fishing if he believes that the concerns that he was present for and saw at the committee are adequately addressed by the provision here.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the same clause 4 of the same bill, and addressed to the Minister in the chair — but it engages no part of the exchange it follows, opening an unrelated strand on the archival carve-out in section 22(5)(a). It would read identically whatever Xu-Nan or the Minister had just argued, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than being scored as partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan and the Minister had been debating whether big tech firms are collecting agencies under IPP 3A and whether MFAT was consulted on trade-agreement consistency, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: Another question I have for the Minister is in section 22(4) inserted by clause 4, and this is to do with when an agency doesn’t need to comply with the requirement under paragraph (a).
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the Minister's preceding answer — the section 22(4) protections he invoked for submitters who missed out on the express exception — and presses him to explain the 'reasonable grounds' test inside it. It is a genuine pick-up of the previous turn rather than prepared material, but the bulk of the speech is a separate question Xu-Nan brought with him, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there are other protections in place under section 22(4)" — James Meager

acuity.statement: I’ll try and address the first one because it seeks, in essence, a legal opinion on where liability will lie, and it’ll depend on a case-by-case basis. Issues arise when you talk about negligence under contract compared to the actions of the agency making the collection itself, so I’m wary of providing a legal opinion on where liability will arise, apart from the fact to say that the legal obligations sit on the agency doing the collecting, whether that is directly or indirectly, and other contractual relationships that sit underneath that may well have vicarious liability or not.
acuity.explanation: Takes the precise hypothetical just put to him (a hacked third-party software provider versus the collecting agency), says why he will not give a case-specific legal opinion, and then does answer the question the Act can answer — obligations sit with the collecting agency, direct or indirect, with contractual liability sitting underneath. The speech would be different had the question been different, so engagement is near-total; it stops short of 1.0 only because it declines the sharpest part of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Would the liability lie on the agency itself or would the liability lie on the software provider?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: So a person who has consented to share their information to a commercial provider, why it is, as I understand it, that, under this piece of legislation, they will still have to be told that their information has been passed to a third party, even though it’s within the bounds of the arrangement that they have agreed to.
acuity.explanation: Picks up exactly the group the Minister had just waved off — submitters who sought but did not get an express exception — and asks why the consented-sharing case was not carved out, which is a direct test of the Minister's claim that the existing protections suffice. Engagement is real and pointable, but much of the turn is his own prepared case about commercial data brokers rather than a reply to the specific reasoning just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when we’re talking about meeting the concerns of similar submitters who didn’t quite get the express exception, there are other protections in place under section 22(4)" — James Meager

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I do have the advice and I’ll just read it out. During the select committee process, those additional exceptions were sought and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner provided some additional thoughts. They thought that the existing exceptions, combined with guidance from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner, is sufficient.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked — why the commercial providers' submission for a further exception was declined — by naming the Privacy Commissioner's advice that the existing exceptions plus guidance were sufficient, and then walks Webb through the IPP 3A(3) example and section 22(4)(d) that cover his scenario. This turn could not have been delivered after a different speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why, in your view, or the Minister’s view, it was not appropriate to accept that submission" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I have a question for the Minister for Hunting and Fishing regarding section 13 of Part 2, which is “Section 49 amended (Protection, etc., of individual as reason for refusing access to personal information)”, and it specifies, interestingly, replacing section 49(1)(c), which is around disclosure of information for those under the age of 16.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the part Meager has just commended to the committee and tests his characterisation of it as merely technical, but engages a different clause (13) from the one Meager actually explained (12), so it answers the topic rather than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "It makes other amendments to the principal Act which are technical in nature and address minor issues that have arisen since the Act came into force."

acuity.statement: I’m advised that this is actually an expansion of protection for people under 16. It changes protections to the individual involved, who the information might be collected from, to any individual under the age of 16.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the misreading put to him — the questioner read clause 13 as removing protection from under-16s, and the reply engages that exact reading and reverses it, supplying the mechanism. The answer would be different had a different interpretation been advanced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Would the Minister mind clarifying if I have interpreted that correctly, where there is no protection for the collection in the first place?"

acuity.statement: I have just a very short question. I understand what the Minister for Hunting and Fishing is saying, but section 49 says that an agency may refuse access to any personal information requested. I understood it as: if an under-16-year-old requested information, they may be refused access. That’s not the correct interpretation?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly accepts what the Minister has just said as the thing to be tested, then puts the statutory wording of section 49 against it and asks whether his reading survives. Entirely shaped by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I’m advised that this is actually an expansion of protection for people under 16."

acuity.statement: No, my understanding is that it’s a protection provided to both the individual and any other individual who is under 16 who might be prejudiced or affected by the collection of information, because to request information, it must be relevant or related to you in the first instance anyway.
acuity.explanation: Answers the alternative interpretation squarely with a 'No' and gives the reason it fails — that a request must relate to the requestor — which is a direct response to the specific construction just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I understood it as: if an under-16-year-old requested information, they may be refused access. That’s not the correct interpretation?"

acuity.statement: However, I do want to check, considering that we’ve seen a number of bills being introduced in the House very recently where we have been given confidence by the Minister that the transition and changes can be done within a three-month period, we’re still technically within a three-month period to 1 June 2025. So what is holding, for example—if the Minister wouldn’t mind providing clarity—the agency or the Government or even the Privacy Commissioner back from actually imposing this on the day that we have here in the bill, as opposed to pushing it out to 14 months from now?
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the precise change the Minister had just announced in his clause 2 explanation and contests the stated rationale, pointing out that the original date is still three months away and asking what specifically prevents commencement as drafted. The question could not exist without the explanation it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "This is subject to changes in the Amendment Paper to replace 1 June 2025 with 1 May 2026. That just gives agencies more time to prepare for those changes and get their systems in place."

acuity.statement: Of course, our friend the Privacy Commissioner and their office—they need some time to develop guidance on how this might be interpreted or implemented. So giving the Privacy Commissioner a significant amount of time to pull together some really good, robust, strong guidance on this would be a good thing, so why rush them over the next three months, when we could give them slightly more time to consider that?
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question asked — why not keep 1 June 2025 — by naming the Privacy Commissioner's need to prepare guidance, one of the very actors the questioner said should not need the extra time. The reply is built on the objection it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "So, yes, the main question is: why didn’t the Minister—or via, you know, advice from officials—decide to stick to the existing time line?"

acuity.statement: I think, as part of this bill, the Government should be looking at other pieces of legislation and frameworks to change, including, for example, addressing the fact that while I accept that this bill is coming in, accepting the reality that we import most of our building products, but there could be some work that the Government and the State could be doing to process things like our timber onshore so that we, as Mariameno Kapa-Kingi talked about, don’t face these additional costs that come from the fact that, actually, we haven’t unlocked the potential in our own people and in our own materials to build good quality buildings.
acuity.explanation: He takes up a specific strand of the immediately preceding turn — Kapa-Kingi's account of building 16 homes in Te Kao from their own forest product to avoid funding being swallowed by transport — and draws a policy consequence from it: that the State should process timber onshore. That is genuine engagement with the content of her argument, not a mere name-check, and the passage would have to change if she had argued something else. It is only partial, however: the rest of the speech is prepared party material on secondary legislation, workforce certainty and Kāinga Ora that is indifferent to what preceded it, so this sits mid-scale rather than at 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "All the bulk of the funding would have been lost in transport. We decided to do it ourselves, in collaboration with the builders just down the road"

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise and join the chorus of support in this House today for this bill. It is a good bill. It’s a good bill that will speed up the productivity of building and there’s a lot of merit in this bill. I’ve actually heard a lot of the debate and I think the Minister for Building and Construction actually stole most of my speech, but it’s a very good Minister in Chris Penk.

Menéndez March's specific request for a guiding-principles framework in the regulations and Kapa-Kingi's local-materials and don't-cut-too-much-red-tape warnings go unanswered; the speech would read identically whoever had spoken before. A gesture at the debate on the right subject, with no uptake of its content, places it just above the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the Government should set a framework of guiding principles to govern the secondary legislation, and should own up to other decisions leaving people in mouldy, cold, damp homes — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: That all gets brought together by that third part, which is requiring building consent authorities to accept these new ones. So you put the three together: more products gets us cheaper homes; consenting pathways gets us faster homes; and the third part, around consenting authorities, ensures this will be done.
acuity.explanation: Costley follows a substantive turn by another member on the same bill, so he is eligible, but his speech is prepared material organised around his own three-part framing of the bill. None of Utikere's specific points are engaged: not the advisory-panel amendment, not the Regulations Review Committee's primary-versus-secondary-legislation objection, not the 7 percent GDP figure. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere spoke about the select committee's recommended change formalising the Minister's access to the building advisory panel, the Regulations Review Committee's concern about leaving decision-making to secondary legislation, and the sector being around 7 percent of GDP, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: One of the points that hasn't quite been canvassed yet, though, is around the 2022 market study, done by the Commerce Commission, on residential building supplies, where they said they found that competition for the supply of key building products was not working as well as it could be.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows Twyford, who had just discussed the 2022 Commerce Commission market study at length and raised two specific concerns: that plasterboard is used structurally in New Zealand and so overseas standards may not transfer, and that point-of-sale practices may stop new products reaching builders. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: 'It was the market study in 2022 under our Government'

acuity.statement: But Labour is cautious about the product substitutions for plasterboard being approved in groups. They are used in a structurally different way in other countries. It may be that the rules in other countries for plasterboard should not apply here because of the way it is used by New Zealand house builders.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one identifiable strand of Twyford's preceding turn — that plasterboard is tacked to framing as a structural material here but not overseas, so grouped approvals of overseas standards need care — and converts it into a stated party position on the grouping mechanism in the bill. That is real engagement with a specific claim rather than a mere reference. It stops short of the top band because it restates the concern rather than developing, quantifying or rebutting anything, does not engage Rutherford's intervening argument about a small trading nation and removing barriers, and the rest of the speech is prepared material (Northcote developments, the Project Auckland luncheon, apprenticeships and Te Pūkenga) that would have been delivered whoever spoke before.

acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: 'we have this quite unusual practice in New Zealand of using plasterboard as a structural material when it gets tacked up on the framing'

acuity.statement: I’m honestly very confused by that previous speech. I was quite heartened by the beginning of the speech, thinking we may have a cross-Parliament work where we are actually in agreement that the most important thing in this world is keeping our most vulnerable safe, especially from sexual violence and from people who are sexual offenders out in our communities. I’m still confused by that speech to be perfectly honest, because I’m not even sure if the Greens are supporting or not supporting this bill by that speech.
acuity.explanation: Chhour engages a real feature of the speech she has just heard — that Carter canvassed arguments on both sides of the retrospectivity question and never declared a position — and the opening would have to be rewritten had Carter stated one. But it takes up the speech's posture rather than any of its specific claims (the NZBORA section 26(2) conflict, the 48-hour reporting change, the PhD recidivism findings), so this is partial engagement: she points at what she is answering, then moves to prepared material on victims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "As policy makers, we must carefully consider that balance, ensuring that legislative measures are both effective and consistent with our legal and human rights obligations." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: The whole point of the Te Aorerekura action plan—which was absolutely amazing because it had cross-Government support—was that we, as a Parliament, work together towards a better future for our children and do everything we possibly can to put in place a system that allows our agencies to work better together for the betterment of our children, which is part of what this bill is aiming to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific authority Carter had just invoked — Te Aorerekura and its cross-party basis — and turns it to the opposite conclusion, that its cross-party purpose is precisely inter-agency co-operation of the kind this bill provides. Had Carter grounded her hesitation in something other than Te Aorerekura, this passage could not stand as written, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because it redeploys the reference rather than rebutting Carter's reasoning about it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That means honouring our cross-party agreement to honour Te Aorerekura, that action plan and that work plan, working with communities for prevention so that we can eliminate family and sexual violence in Aotearoa." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: How can you even contemplate putting the perpetrators’ rights ahead of a young person not being sexually violated? Sometimes we have to put the most common-sense thing at the forefront of our decision making.
acuity.explanation: Aimed squarely at the substance of what preceded it: Carter's framing of the decision as a balance between registered offenders' rights under the NZBORA and child safety. Chhour engages that balance directly and resolves it one way. Scored on engagement only — that she restates Carter's reported arguments as an actual preference for perpetrators' rights is a question for Rigor, not Acuity, and the heat of the rhetorical question is a question for Civility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "At the same time, the concerns raised about retrospective application and potential inconsistencies with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act warrant our close consideration." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: I think, for this particular scenario and for this particular bill, I really want to echo the previous speaker on the fact that we are having conversations around child protection, which is incredibly important, on the same day as we, as a Government, are looking to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act.
acuity.explanation: Kapa-Kingi's immediately preceding turn made the specific point that the House is passing a child-protection bill on the same day it debates repealing section 7AA, and called that ironic. Xu-Nan takes up that exact argument by name, adopts it, and draws out its consequence — that child protection may not be at the heart of the Government's decision making. The speech would have to change if she had argued something else on the same topic. Not a 1.0 because he adopts and extends her point rather than testing it, and the bulk of his contribution is prepared material on the section 7 report and the Law Society submission.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "How ironic it is that we're prepared to care and protect the most vulnerable—and this bill does that—but it's what we're prepared to remove in terms of the care, protection, and understanding of what it means for mokopuna Māori."

acuity.statement: I rise to speak in support of the Child Protection (Child Sex Offender Government Agency Registration) Amendment Bill. This bill enables Government agencies to better manage the risk posed by child sex offenders in our community. It enhances the options and the effectiveness in the operation of the Child Sex Offender Register.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn raised substantive objections — the Attorney-General's section 7 report, the Law Society's opposition to the bill's retrospective element, a double-jeopardy inconsistency, and foreshadowed Amendment Papers the Government was asked to consider seriously. Bates engages none of it, not even to acknowledge that amendments had been signalled; he delivers a prepared enumeration of the eight substantive changes and closes by commending the Government's law-and-order focus. acuity.responding_to: "if the financial jurisdiction is doubled, therefore the application fee is doubled" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: I hear the comments from the other side, I understand that perspective about the filing fee, but remember it only applies to the portion above $30,000. There is no barrier that isn’t already there. There is nothing new for the $0 to $30,000.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific objection made in the preceding turn and does something with it: concedes the perspective, then rebuts it on its own terms with the fee's actual scope (only the portion above $30,000, nothing new below it). He also picks up O'Connor's dine-and-dash example and turns it to his own conclusion. The speech would have had to be different had the previous speaker raised something other than the filing fee, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — whether the 'no barrier that isn't already there' inference holds is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The court filing fee: that will be a barrier for many people." — Greg O'Connor

acuity.statement: We need to—as the Minister said—improve court timeliness and access to justice so that Kiwis can get on with their lives. The change in the level at which you will be able to apply to the disputes tribunal will mean that a Master’s degree student who was paid just $9,000 for a full year’s worth of work, who had to cut her losses and abandon the claim for the $41,000 she was owed, would be able to actually take that claim under this new law. On that note, I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows a detailed critique of the bill's lack of appeal rights and of court delay, and engages none of it. He cites the Minister rather than the preceding speaker and delivers a self-contained illustrative example plus a commendation — the speech would read identically whatever White had said. On-topic prepared material, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued at length that the $60,000 cap without a right of appeal leaves too few checks and balances, and proposed recording hearings or a limited appeal on fact and law; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Look, the Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill makes sense. The New Zealand courts’ Rules Committee recommended that the cap be upped. Why wouldn’t we listen to them? They know what they’re talking about. The fact is that most members in this House have provided examples where, because the cap was at $30,000, people who would have claimed and won and would have got more were restricted by the cap. That doesn’t make sense.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty picks up the examples just given — Bates's student abandoning a $41,000 claim under the old $30,000 cap — and generalises them into the argument for raising the cap, then goes on to take up White's concern that the bill contains no right of appeal. The speech is shaped by what preceded it: remove the members' examples and the "most members in this House have provided examples" move has nothing to stand on. Not 1.0 because he accumulates the prior points rather than contesting or correcting any specific claim in them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "who had to cut her losses and abandon the claim for the $41,000 she was owed, would be able to actually take that claim under this new law"

acuity.statement: How can New Zealand exporters trust her “stay the course” plan in relation to US tariffs when the Government’s position is that it “could have been worse”, and that they have not corrected the assumption that New Zealand imposes a 20 percent tariff on US goods based on our GST rate?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exporter strand of the Minister's immediately preceding answer, but does not engage the substance of what she said about it — instead it pivots to prepared material on the GST/tariff assumption and the "could have been worse" framing, neither of which appeared in the answer. Partial engagement with one strand, then own ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "There will be direct and indirect impacts on our economy, such as exporters being affected by tariffs that make it harder for them to sell into the US market."

acuity.statement: Does she regret cancelling and delaying housing, hospital, and school builds, which has caused the collapse of the construction sector and the deepest recession seen in 30 years?
acuity.explanation: The preceding answer disputed the accuracy of the member's paraphrasing; this question neither defends the paraphrase nor engages the challenge, and switches to an unrelated prepared line on builds and the construction sector. It is at least within the broad economic subject of the question, so not a zero, but nothing in the previous turn shaped it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis said "I would have to check that paraphrasing of my comment in the context in which it was made" and this question does not take that up at all, moving instead to infrastructure cancellations.

acuity.statement: As a matter of education, if the economy is growing at 0.7 percent or annualised at 2.8, how could you possibly describe that as being a recession?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific word used in the question immediately before and attacks it directly with counter-figures, challenging whether the growth numbers can be reconciled with the label 'recession'. The intervention would be impossible had the previous speaker not made that claim, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the inference and the accuracy of the figures are not Acuity's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "the deepest recession seen in 30 years"

acuity.statement: Would the Minister of Finance characterise the significant and dramatic and sudden changes in US tariffs as an “excuse”, or the biggest thing to hit the world economy in a long time that is creating turmoil in every market in the world?
acuity.explanation: Lifts the operative word 'excuse' from the question put seconds earlier and builds the whole intervention around contesting it, offering an alternative characterisation of the same event. It is a planted supplementary and is framed to help the Minister, but it is unambiguously built on the content of the preceding turn rather than indifferent to it. Marked down slightly because it restates the opposing framing rather than engaging the 'economic mismanagement' substance behind it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "Is the Government going to use US tariffs and worsening global economic conditions as an excuse to hide their economic mismanagement"

acuity.statement: In the interests of the nation’s understanding, could you please describe who’s the informational genius behind this brilliant policy?
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed turn on implementation mechanics and engages none of it, asking instead who authored the policy. It is at least on the subject under discussion, which keeps it above zero, but it would have read identically whatever the Minister had just said about the policy's design.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just described the Building Act amendment, the consent exemption criteria and the planned national environmental standard, and this question does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Given the Minister of Finance’s earlier comments around that the Treasury had the pre-election fiscal update wrong, I would just like to ask the Minister: given the checks and balances that Treasury have done previously and which they’ve set out in the annual review, what further checks and balances has she asked Treasury to put in for future forecasts?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opening turn by another member and is on the matter under debate (the Treasury annual review), but engages none of Brewer's claims or figures — it would read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer presented the five annual reviews, including the claim that the savings exercise 'will deliver—given the environment that she inherited—$23 billion worth of savings over a four-year period', and this question does not take any of that up; it opens a prepared line on Treasury's forecasting models.

acuity.statement: Well, as is very apparent in the world right now, forecasters must always work with the best information they have at the time, and their forecasts are always subject to revision in hindsight, which demonstrates that assumptions that they have made have turned out to be incorrect. In the case of the pre-election fiscal update, there were a number of factors which Treasury now acknowledge they were over-optimistic about, including trends around revenue collection, including the way that they accounted for future labour productivity, and, overall, this had the effect of flattering the outlook at the pre-election update in such a way that what it forecast was in fact wrong, as I have previously said.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific premise Edmonds built her question on (that the PREFU was wrong) and itemises what Treasury got wrong, but addresses the topic rather than the question actually asked — what she has required of Treasury going forward.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what further checks and balances has she asked Treasury to put in for future forecasts?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: So given that the Minister advised that fiscal risks is one area that she has asked Treasury to relook at, what are the other areas and checks and balances that she’s required of Treasury to ensure that their forecasts—yes, their forecasts—are more accurate, given her belief that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update was incorrect?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on what the Minister had just said, accepts the one area she covered and presses for the rest; the question could not have been asked in this form before her answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there were a number of factors which Treasury now acknowledge they were over-optimistic about" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, as you’d expect, I have regular engagement with the Treasury in which I test their forecast assumptions, query how they are learning lessons from mistakes made in the past, and how they are projecting those forward. In addition, I’ve previously shared with the House that I will be proposing a series of amendments to the Public Finance Act.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific thing pressed for — the other mechanisms she has required — naming her own engagement with Treasury and the planned Public Finance Act amendments.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what are the other areas and checks and balances that she’s required of Treasury" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: The Minister has referred to the Public Finance Act amendments, which I note the annual report does refer to. When can the House expect the amendment bill on the Public Finance Act?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the single new element in the preceding answer and draws out its consequence by asking for a timetable; wholly dependent on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I will be proposing a series of amendments to the Public Finance Act" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: The Minister has referenced the fact that she does her own quality assurance. What is that quality assurance?
acuity.explanation: Aimed squarely at the Minister's own account of testing Treasury's assumptions and presses her to specify it; the characterisation is contested, but the engagement with what was said is direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have regular engagement with the Treasury in which I test their forecast assumptions" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I think the member mischaracterises what I said. What in fact I said was that I engage with Treasury officials to understand the assumptions that are feeding into their forecasts, to compare their forecasts with those of other bank economists, and to understand how they are making judgments and what goes into those judgments, and I think that that process of engagement is constructive both for me and my advisers.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the characterisation in the question put to her and restates what she had actually claimed; the reply is entirely shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Minister has referenced the fact that she does her own quality assurance" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Treasury, in the annual report, said that they have begun work to collect more detailed information about the changes in their forecast during the production in order to better assess the accuracy of Budget forecasts. Can the Minister elucidate what extra or more detailed information she has asked Treasury to do, or what are Treasury looking for?
acuity.explanation: Carries forward one strand of the Minister's answer — what she has asked of Treasury — but introduces a fresh passage from the annual report rather than engaging her correction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I engage with Treasury officials to understand the assumptions that are feeding into their forecasts" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Look, I think what that reference refers to—but the member would have to put it to the writer of the annual report themself—is a situation that occurred in the lead-up to the last Budget, where, as members of this committee may be aware, the Treasury needs to conclude a series of different forecasts in the lead-up to the Budget being agreed and published.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific passage of the annual report quoted at her and offers an account of what it refers to, while disclaiming authorship of the wording.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they have begun work to collect more detailed information about changes in their forecast" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I would note that while the member is always happy to impose new taxes on New Zealanders to steal from them today, she is not ever advocating that that be done in order to improve our fiscal position. In fact, the arguments we hear from the other side of the House are always about how that money could be spent. I would be clear with the member that the way to actually get ourselves into a stronger position for the future is to get disciplined about the spending.
acuity.explanation: Russell asked a specific question about uneven capital income taxation as a response to the structural deficit. Willis takes up one strand of it — the revenue proposition — and argues that new taxation would not improve the fiscal position because the proceeds would be spent, which is a genuine engagement with the premise of the question. But the bulk of the turn is prepared material on the last Government's debt and the Budget Policy Statement's three spending disciplines, and the specific question (capital income taxation) is never addressed. Partial engagement: you can point at what was taken up, but the speech would have been largely the same had Russell asked about any revenue measure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "In terms of addressing the structural deficit, is the Minister considering addressing that issue of uneven capital income taxation?"

acuity.statement: I just want to follow up on what the Minister of Finance believes is prudent or not. From the way that the Minister was speaking, she referenced being a prudent Government and that turned out to be cutting services and cutting costs all around the place. Of course, that is one definition of prudent. But Minister, I put it to you that it’s also prudent to consider future revenue streams to address the structural deficit that has been identified by the IMF, by Treasury, by a number of agencies. Can the Minister consider what might be prudent on the revenue side?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact term Willis built her answer around, characterises the content she gave it (spending and service cuts), concedes it as one definition, and then turns it against her by asking whether prudence also runs to the revenue side. The follow-up is wholly shaped by what Willis just said — substitute a different answer and this question could not have been asked in this form. High responsiveness; the weakness of the characterisation of "cutting services" is a separate question from whether she engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "it is so important that we have economic and fiscal management that is prudent in the here and now" — and her account of prudence as spending discipline

acuity.statement: To the member, I again make the point, and I urge her to engage with it: it is not enough to simply say, “We’ll tax them more”, because if all you’re intending to do is to spend that tax on new things today, then you’re no better prepared for the challenges that you will face tomorrow and, at the same time, you are sapping the blood of an economy that relies on investment, that relies on business, that relies on New Zealanders facing good incentives to employ people, to pay them, and to grow.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Russell's revenue challenge and answers it with a reason — that raising revenue only improves the fiscal position if the proceeds are not spent, and that new taxes carry an economic cost. The whole turn is organised around Russell's chosen word ("Prudent: let me count the ways"), so it is visibly shaped by the preceding turn. Short of 1.0 because she restates the point she had already made rather than meeting the specific question of whether revenue measures are under consideration; that the rebuttal mischaracterises Russell's position is a matter for Rigor, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Can the Minister consider what might be prudent on the revenue side?"

acuity.statement: Well, the Minister didn’t answer my question, which is: what’s prudent in terms of revenue? However, I wish to shift to another aspect of prudence, then, and I want the Minister to consider our debt levels.
acuity.explanation: Engages the preceding turn to the extent of identifying what it did not do — correctly noting that the list of spending-side examples left the revenue question unanswered — which is a real response to the content of Willis's answer. But it does not take up any of the examples Willis gave, and immediately pivots to a new prepared line on debt servicing and defence spending that would have been put whatever Willis had said. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "Prudent: let me count the ways." — her list of spending-side examples offered in place of a revenue answer

acuity.statement: Well, that was a string of poorly evidenced assertions in lieu of a question. I found many assertions that were wrong in there. First of all, the member has already been corrected in this House on her use of data when it relates to construction jobs, where she uses a selective measure that Stats NZ themselves say is novel, and she ignores the stat which shows there has actually been increases in construction jobs.
acuity.explanation: Takes Andersen's specific list of statistics and works through them item by item — disputes the construction-jobs measure as selective, attributes the unemployment forecasts to the pre-election fiscal update, and answers the homelessness point with the motels and social housing wait-list. The answer would be entirely different had Andersen listed different claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "the construction sector has lost thousands of jobs, building consents are down 7.2 percent"

acuity.statement: In particular, the interest deductibility—the reinstatement of it—had a price tag of $2.9 billion, and yet the Minister is talking about incentivising productive assets and the investment into productive assets.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under examination and gestures at the Minister's stated position on productive investment, but takes up no part of the argument actually just made to her. It is a prepared new line of questioning rather than an engagement with the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing in the preceding turn: Nicola Willis's immediately preceding answer was about construction-jobs data, unemployment forecasts and the social housing wait-list; Edmonds instead picks up the Minister's earlier answers to Chlöe Swarbrick on productivity, which do not appear in this exchange

acuity.statement: Well, two things: first, I reject the way that that member perpetually characterises interest deductibility. Interest deductibility has been a rule in our tax system for many decades, under successive Governments, and the principle has always been that it should be equally applied to different asset classes, lest we create significant distortions in the economy—so all we have done is restore things to a tax principle that had long been the case.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of Edmonds's question — that reinstating interest deductibility is a distortionary subsidy to housing — by arguing the opposite distortion case, and then takes on her implicit claim that houses are not a productive investment. Squarely aimed at the argument just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "it's quite clear it's giving residential housing investment a bigger lift because now they're able to deduct the interest deductibility from it"

acuity.statement: So the rule in the Income Tax Act is quite straightforward. A person may claim a tax deduction to the extent to which they earn income. Of course, a large amount of the income on residential rental properties is capital gains, which are currently untaxed. Therefore, there is no good reason to have the interest deductibility.
acuity.explanation: Meets Willis's stated tax principle head-on with a competing statement of the rule — deductions match taxable income, and untaxed capital gains break the symmetry — and corrects her account of what the previous Government did by noting deductibility was retained for new builds. The speech is shaped entirely by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "the principle has always been that it should be equally applied to different asset classes"

acuity.statement: The second thing that I would say is that in terms of driving housing supply, as I articulated in a previous answer, our focus has been getting at the underlying constraints which have prevented houses being built at scale and pace in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Supplies an answer to the question actually asked, listing land markets, RMA zoning, infrastructure funding and consenting. But it engages only that strand: Russell's substantive argument about deductions matching taxable income and about new-build deductibility is brushed aside with a jibe about tax lecturers rather than taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Could the Minister please clarify what her Government has done to increase housing supply?"

acuity.statement: Well, what I can confirm is that we will continue to do the Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment process, which is the examination, at the Budget, of the impact that Budget policies have on our climate objectives.
acuity.explanation: Engages the subject of the question and speaks to the assessment process, but shifts from the specific thing asked — whether Treasury will be commissioned to produce another standalone assessment — to the Budget process generally. Partial engagement, which Russell's immediate follow-up confirms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "is she prepared to commission Treasury to give us another Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment?"

acuity.statement: Just to be clear, then, for the Minister, there will not be a specific Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment from Treasury?
acuity.explanation: Hears the substitution in the answer just given and pins it precisely, restating the Minister's words as the concession they amount to. Short, but it could only have been said in response to that particular answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we will continue to do the Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment process, which is the examination, at the Budget"

acuity.statement: I want to pursue a little further in terms of the climate change commitments because they were quite an issue in our discussion of the Government’s financial statements. I want to see if I can clarify from the Minister—we know that the costs of meeting our international obligations are going to range from somewhere between $3.3 billion and $23.7 billion.
acuity.explanation: Stays within the climate thread under examination, so it is at least on the matter in hand, but opens a fresh line with a prepared figure rather than engaging anything in the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis's preceding answer confirmed the Budget-time Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment process would continue, and this question does not take that up, moving instead to the cost of international obligations

acuity.statement: Well, the member is suffering from a grave misunderstanding. The numbers that she is presenting are a dated estimation of what it would hypothetically cost the Government to purchase emissions credits, hypothetically, if it didn’t meet its targets by a hypothetical amount and if, hypothetically, there was a legal obligation to meet those costs.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figures put to her and does something with them — disputes their currency and the conditional chain behind them — before setting out what she says the better spending is. Directly shaped by the number Russell quoted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "the costs of meeting our international obligations are going to range from somewhere between $3.3 billion and $23.7 billion"

acuity.statement: I think we need a serious clarification here. The Minister described the agreements under the Paris accord as being hypothetical. She also talked about not actually doing anything around climate change ourselves. She said, “Why should we put on a hair shirt? Why should we make any effort here?” Is the Minister committed to meeting our Paris obligations?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the answer just given back and draws out what she says follows from it, pressing for the commitment the answer avoided. Whether the characterisation is fair is a question for Rigor, not here; as engagement it is tightly bound to what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "we are not a Government that is going to send more than $20 billion overseas into a carbon market to wear a hair shirt for New Zealanders"

acuity.statement: Well, the member, yet again, mischaracterises me. This Government has published an emphatic emission reduction plan for the second emission reduction period, which demonstrates very clearly our ability to meet our domestic emission requirements, and, sensibly, we’ve aligned our international commitments for the future with our domestic efforts, because we don’t subscribe to the school that James Shaw and your merry band of mates subscribe to, which is, to say, a big dramatic thing offshore that goes well beyond what is required by our domestic law in order to make us feel good at a climate change conference.
acuity.explanation: Rejects the specific characterisation just put to her, answers the commitment question by pointing to the emission reduction plan, and explains the alignment of international with domestic commitments. The reply exists only because of the question it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Is the Minister committed to meeting our Paris obligations?"

acuity.statement: Well, there are two separate parts to the question. First, in terms of its productivity assumptions, Treasury has looked at historical trends of where labour productivity has been and, long story short, it’s a bad and sad story, which is that labour productivity in New Zealand has been falling for many years and has been below par for where we would need it to be to be the productive, growing country that we want to see. So Treasury looks back on those assumptions, and then they feed forward, test that against other assumptions about the economy, and then provide their best estimate of future labour productivity.
acuity.explanation: She splits Swarbrick's two-part question explicitly and takes up the first part on its own terms, describing the backward-looking trend method Treasury actually uses rather than changing the subject. The answer could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what specific assumptions is Treasury presently making when it comes to forecasting productivity" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: The Minister answered the first part of the question—which I really did appreciate—which was that there are massive issues with regard to the way that Treasury currently projects and forecasts productivity and potential productivity growth in this country, which she herself has explicitly said is reflected in the work that we’ve done whereby Treasury’s fiscal strategy model assumes a relatively constant rate of productivity growth, or extrapolates, as the Minister was saying, from past trends.
acuity.explanation: She takes the specific content of the Minister's answer (extrapolation from past productivity trends), accepts it, and builds the next question on it. Whether her gloss of that answer is fair is a rigor/veracity matter, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Treasury has looked at historical trends of where labour productivity has been" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, that’s a very confused argument from the member Chlöe Swarbrick, because it makes two wrongful assumptions. The first is that all Government spending is good spending, and I would invite the member to consider that the trade-off for a single dollar that the Government spends is always this: that dollar could have been spent by mum or dad or the residents of Auckland Central in their own household.
acuity.explanation: She addresses the question put to her head-on, naming the premises she says it rests on and arguing against them; the reply is shaped entirely by what Swarbrick asked. That the premises may be a recasting of Swarbrick's actual argument bears on rigor, not on whether she engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how then does she seek to get a sense of an understanding of the efficacy of the spending or the cuts that she is making" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: I entirely reject the claim that I’m not interested in evidence, because, actually, in six years of a Labour-led Government, which her party supported, we have very clear empirical evidence of what happens when you have a “spend, borrow, hope, and tax” policy.
acuity.explanation: She identifies the charge against her — that spending decisions are not being tested against data and evidence — and answers it directly, though she then pivots to the previous government's record rather than to how her own spending is evaluated.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the promise that was made in the coalition agreement that decisions would be made based on data and evidence" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: Well, thank you for the question. What we conducted was an exercise that was very successful and instructive. We set public agencies with clear targets for the savings we expected them to deliver. They put forward a range of propositions and then, as Ministers, we evaluated those proposals before finalising them in our Budget.
acuity.explanation: She engages the subject Hamilton raised — how the savings exercise ran and what it yielded — but answers the process rather than the specific thing asked, which was which sectors or departments produced above-average savings. No department or sector is named.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether there were some sectors or departments which actually yielded greater savings, what areas they were" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: That will be a matter for Treasury and that will be a matter that we update at the Budget when it’s published on 22 May.
acuity.explanation: The reply is aimed squarely at the question asked and would make no sense after any other question, but it engages the question only by deferring it to Treasury and to Budget day rather than taking up whether the tariffs change the forecast.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does she expect Treasury to revise its unemployment forecasts, given the recent US tariffs?" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: The chair of the committee pointed to one of the core issues here—well, two key areas. One is the funding on maintenance versus the funding on new projects. In fact, it was pointed out that an insufficient amount has been spent in terms of repairs and maintenance. The second critical area that we have to keep coming back to is that, actually, there’s a $6 billion shortfall in what is needed in the land transport plan—at least $6 billion. How is the Minister going to fund that?
acuity.explanation: O'Connor takes up the two substantive strands Foster had just put — the maintenance-versus-new-build split and the NZTA/Ministry funding gap — names them as the chair's points, quantifies the gap Foster left general ($6 billion in the land transport plan), and turns both into a direct question to the Minister in the chair. The speech would have had to be different had Foster raised different issues. Not a full 1.0 because he then moves to prepared material on the Government policy statement and the North Island/South Island split of the "roads of National Party significance", which Foster did not raise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "the Infrastructure Commission said that we should be spending more of the infrastructure budget on maintaining assets, as opposed to building new ones" and "we heard from both of those agencies that there is a very, very large funding gap"

acuity.statement: To come back to the Minister having set the scene for ever-increasing pressure on repairs and maintenance on our roading network and the Minister acknowledging the $6 billion - plus shortfall, he referred to tolling, and so there are a couple of questions around tolling. The principle in the past was that you would only toll where there was an adequate alternative so that people didn’t have to pay the toll, and that was the principle.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bishop's specific position that tolls will be the starting point for new roads and that revenues are not keeping pace with expenditure, accepts the premise, and presses it to a concrete consequence — whether the alternative-route principle survives, and what happens if toll revenue falls short. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different argument; it is built on the Minister's own framing. Not a full 1.0 because the historical 'sweat the assets' passage is prepared material rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "we have said, for example, that the starting point for all of the new roads we build around the country will be to use tolls"

acuity.statement: The short answer in relation to tolling is, yes, there needs to be an alternative. In relation to tolling revenue, I’d just repeat what I said before, which was that it’s not the answer to everything, but it can make a contribution.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put — whether the adequate-alternative principle still applies — with a direct yes, and then addresses the second limb about the revenue shortfall and future RUC/excise settings. This is a committee-stage debate turn rather than an oral question, so responsiveness is the relevant measure, and the reply is wholly shaped by what O'Connor asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "will that still be the principle applied, so that those who either can’t afford it or who choose to go off the toll road can do so in a reasonably efficient manner?"

acuity.statement: Look, it is in reference to a provocation from the Minister—or perhaps he might see it as an answer—regarding the “roads of National Party significance”. The fact that there are only two, and one of them, yes, is the Hope Bypass—there’s no four-laning to Ashburton, which was something, I think, the National Party campaigned on, actually, in the lead-up to the election.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the exchange — Bishop's rebuttal about the Hope Bypass and the 'roads of National Party significance' jibe — and does something with it by naming an omitted South Island project. But it reaches back past the immediately preceding tolling answer and then returns to prepared material on South Island maintenance funding, so the engagement is partial rather than squarely on the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "his own colleague Rachel Boyack, member of Parliament for Nelson, spent most of the committee stage of the Fast-track Approvals Bill desperately trying to make sure the Hope Bypass... was included in the fast-track bill"

acuity.statement: My reference to the Minister of Climate Change is that he is internationally responsible for and chairing negotiations with other countries to facilitate what it looks like to purchase offshore credits. We’re hearing from the Minister that there is not an intention to purchase those offshore credits, yet we simultaneously are getting press releases from the Minister of Climate Change about memoranda of understanding that are being signed internationally that will count towards our nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise objection just made — that the Minister's reference to the Climate Change Minister made no sense — and answers it directly by specifying the role she meant (chairing offshore-credit negotiations), then turns it back into a contradiction with the Minister's own stated position. The speech would be different had Willis not raised Watts' whereabouts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Minister Watts was sitting opposite me at a Cabinet committee this morning, so I’m not quite sure what her reference to the Minister of Climate Change was" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: But then the next question, which members on this side of the House have asked her about, which is around the estimations of those nationally determined contributions; those have come from an actual report, the Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment 2023, and that’s where those numbers are coming from. This side of the House is not just picking them out of thin air for the Minister of Finance to stand there and say, “Well, that report is wrong. That member’s wrong. Actually, Treasury is wrong.”, because it seems like everybody is wrong except for the Minister of Finance.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the Minister's dismissal of the NDC cost figures by naming the source document they came from (the Climate Economic and Fiscal Assessment 2023), i.e. engages the specific rejection just made rather than the topic in general. Does not take up the five caveats Willis listed, so short of a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is, I think, a significant assumption to then equate that that will require $20 billion worth of purchases of credit by New Zealand. That is the assumption that I have rejected." — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, I actually find that mischaracterisation of my statements characteristic of the member, but it also demonstrates she hasn’t been listening because I have said that I do think that Treasury has used its best professional judgments in assessing forecasts, that I do think they use the best data available to them in delivering their forecasts, and that I do have confidence in the methodology they use to create them.
acuity.explanation: Meets the charge head on: denies the characterisation and states her actual position on Treasury's professional judgment, data and methodology, then distinguishes trusting the method from forecasts turning out wrong. Squarely engaged with the claim just made, even though the engagement is wrapped in a jibe.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "her continual debunking of forecasts, reports, and pre-election fiscal updates, which are all prepared by either independent organisations or are forecasts that are done by Treasury" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I noticed that the Minister hasn’t actually answered the question: which reports can we, as the Opposition and members of the public, in her opinion, actually rely on? She’s trashed the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update. Are we going to be allowed to rely on the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update in that case?
acuity.explanation: Identifies the part of Edmonds' question the answer left untouched and presses it with a concrete follow-up that turns the Minister's own point about the pre-election forecasts into a test case for the Budget update. Depends entirely on what Willis just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is also true to characterise that Treasury, along with others, got their forecasts prior to the election wrong." — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, again, I reject the characterisation of the member’s question. There are a range of reports available to members, which they should read thoroughly, noting the many caveats that those reports often contain.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of the question — what the Opposition can rely on — but answers at a level of generality that takes up neither the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update nor the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update that were specifically put to her. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which reports can we, as the Opposition and members of the public, in her opinion, actually rely on?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: But speaking to the Minister’s point, if it’s mischaracterisation of the dependency by the Opposition and the New Zealand Government on the forecasts by Treasury, why, then, did she say earlier, in her response to one of my earlier questions around forecasting, that Treasury is beholden to the Minister given the Minister is also supposed to be independent of the Reserve Bank—and the Reserve Bank, post the Governor resigning, all of a sudden has a capital requirement rule change.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own defence — that she is being mischaracterised — and tests it against a specific thing the Minister said in the same debate about Treasury being beholden to the Minister. The question only exists because of the answer that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I reject the characterisation of the member’s question" / "I actually find that mischaracterisation of my statements characteristic of the member" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I wish to state very plainly and clearly for the record that I reject the perpetual attempt by members opposite to mischaracterise my statements. I continue to have confidence in the independent forecasting of the Treasury. It is also true that Ministers of Finance always face choices about the fiscal treatment of their initiatives. It is not questioning the independence of Treasury to point that out, and to simplify it in those terms I think is misleading and I would urge the member to reconsider that approach. I respect the independence of the Reserve Bank—have done, will do, always will do.
acuity.explanation: Answers the trust-the-Minister-over-Treasury framing and separately addresses the Reserve Bank independence strand of the question, drawing the distinction between ministerial fiscal choices and Treasury's independence. Leaves the specific capital requirement rule change allegation untouched, so not a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is she saying that, basically, the New Zealand public should trust her as the Minister of Finance ... rather than the forecasts of any other professional agency" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I just would like the Minister of Finance to clarify the words—because I wrote them down because I was so astounded by them—right at the start of the debate. Can she clarify exactly what she meant when she said, “Treasury is always beholden to the Minister of the day.”?
acuity.explanation: Isolates the exact wording the Minister had just glossed over and demands she account for it, quoting it back as the point in dispute. Precisely aimed at what was said immediately before rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is not questioning the independence of Treasury to point that out" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: What I meant by that was while Treasury—and particularly in New Zealand, actually, and to our credit—has an independent forecasting function, which I think is respected by Ministers, it is always also the case that the Treasury has the Minister of Finance as its responsible Minister and, therefore, is beholden to that Minister when it comes to decisions, for example, like how big the operating allowance should be.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what was asked for: an explanation of the disputed phrase, distinguishing the independent forecasting function from the responsible-Minister relationship and giving the operating allowance as the concrete sense in which Treasury is beholden.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can she clarify exactly what she meant when she said, “Treasury is always beholden to the Minister of the day.”?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Is that, then, the explanation for why we have the sudden appearance of a new fiscal measure, operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses?
acuity.explanation: Draws out the consequence of the concession just made — that the Minister shapes what appears in the Budget — and applies it to a specific new fiscal measure. The question is built directly out of the previous answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "you can have an independent forecasting function and also have a Minister of Finance who, lo and behold, actually has some impact on what ends up in the Budget" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: That matter is traversed extensively in the Budget Policy Statement, and I invite the member to read it.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the subject of the question by pointing at a document, but engages no part of its content — neither confirming nor denying the suggested explanation for the new measure. A referral is a gesture at the question, not an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is that, then, the explanation for why we have the sudden appearance of a new fiscal measure, operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I have limited time, so I would like to just focus on two areas that were considered by the committee. I have a series of questions for the Minister, so I’m hoping we can get a back-and-forth flow.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive ministerial turn on road maintenance funding and targets but engages none of it, instead announcing her own two prepared areas. It is squarely within the same transport estimates debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just given figures on road maintenance funding ("It is $4 billion over the three years that we’re in, from 2024 to 2027") and pothole targets, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I would point out that it does require safer speeds around schools. Most submitters supported the reversal of the speed limit reductions under the previous Government, so that is the position, as it stands, and Road Controlling Authorities are now getting on with implementing the rule.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific rule Genter named and answers the safety strand of it (safer speeds around schools, the balanced-approach requirement), but leaves her second question — the NZTA advice on deaths and serious injuries — untouched, citing the judicial review. Partial engagement with the actual question put, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I wanted to ask the Minister if he believes that speed limit reversals will only happen where it is safe to do so, and whether the Minister has received any advice from the New Zealand Transport Agency—or Waka Kotahi—on what the impacts of the setting of speed limits rule of 2024 will be on deaths and serious injuries"

acuity.statement: Thank you very much for that. Can the Minister tell us how many of the Road Controlling Authorities and local councils who submitted on the rule opposed some part of the rule?
acuity.explanation: Lifts the Minister's own characterisation of the submissions and immediately tests it, asking for the count on the other side of it. The question could not have been asked had he said something else — it is built entirely out of the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "Most submitters supported the reversal of the speed limit reductions under the previous Government"

acuity.statement: Well, I thank the member for her spirited advocacy on behalf of her constituency. As the Government, we’re always interested and open to receiving our feedback, particularly that expressed passionately.
acuity.explanation: A reference to the member and her manner of speaking, with no engagement of the content — neither the exemption proposal, the Berhampore example, nor the claimed absence of time savings. A mere acknowledgement of the previous speaker is not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter asked whether he would "allow there to be an exemption where communities have demonstrated strong support" and set out the Adelaide Road case, and this statement does not take up the exemption question or any of the evidence offered.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Can I acknowledge the Minister. In this debate today, I’m interested in the shift in position from the previous Minister, particularly their style of politics.
acuity.explanation: Begins a wholly prepared line on Auckland funding and the Minister's self-description as an urbanist, engaging no part of the speed-limits exchange that immediately preceded it. It remains within the transport estimates debate and gestures at the Minister, so it is not wholly adrift.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just responded to Julie Anne Genter on the setting of speed limits rule and the judicial review, and this statement does not take that up, opening instead on the previous Minister's style and Auckland funding.

acuity.statement: Look, I don’t have anything hugely more to say to what’s already been said publicly about the Auckland regional fuel tax. The member still holds a candle for it, obviously. We took two successive elections repealing it. There is more money going to Auckland Transport notwithstanding the Auckland regional fuel tax’s abolition as of 1 July last year.
acuity.explanation: Goes directly to the regional fuel tax question Halbert put, disputes the premise that abolition left Auckland worse funded, and separately takes up the "debt challenge" framing to reclassify it as a funding challenge and list the options under consideration. The answer would be different had Halbert asked about something else; it falls short of 1.0 because the specific shortfall figure asked for is not supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "What was the shortfall in revenue that came as a cancellation by this Government to the regional fuel tax in Auckland, and how has that impacted the programme of work that he needs to achieve?"

acuity.statement: The Minister hasn’t answered my question. The question, and I’ll reframe it for him because I am interested in the revenue side of how we are going to achieve the transport infrastructure that we desperately need in Auckland. The figure that I have—and the Minister didn’t mention the shortfall to investment in Auckland—is $564 million. Maybe the Minister would like to clarify that, given that he is saying that more money is going into Tāmaki-makau-rau Auckland.
acuity.explanation: Identifies precisely what the answer omitted, puts a counter-figure against the Minister's claim that Auckland is better funded, and invites him to reconcile the two. The turn is built on the content of the reply it follows, not merely on the subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "There is more money going to Auckland Transport notwithstanding the Auckland regional fuel tax’s abolition as of 1 July last year"

acuity.statement: I know the Minister is very interested in value for money. So if a whole lot of really high-value public transport projects could be funded for a small percentage of the funding that has been committed to some of the urban roads of national significance—and, in fact, they’re higher value for money, the public transport projects, and they deliver more for housing than the highway projects do—will the Minister consider prioritising the higher-value projects that do more to help people get around the area and do more for housing?
