acuity.explanation: Takes Bishop's own value-for-money / 'best bang for buck' frame from the preceding answer and turns it into a test he has to meet on roads of national significance, and also notes he left the road-controlling-authorities question unanswered. But the bulk of the turn is a fresh line of questioning about the NLTP that would have been put whatever he had just said, so this is partial engagement rather than a take-up of his specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "We want to optimise and get the best bang for buck and we want to do it in a sequenced way"

acuity.statement: There are always proposals for things that councils want to fund that don’t always get funded. That was true under the last Government and the Government before that, and it’s true under this Government.
acuity.explanation: Engages Genter's specific factual claim head-on: he accepts that proposed projects went unfunded and explains it as chronic oversubscription rather than a choice against public transport. The answer would be different had she made a different claim, though he does not rebut her comparative value-for-money point, instead widening to 'every government' — so engaged but not fully.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "the new National Land Transport Programme for three years did not approve funding for the majority of the public transport infrastructure projects that were proposed by public transport authorities"

acuity.statement: So can I take it then that the Minister will not be enabling funding of the public transport infrastructure projects that were applied for by the Greater Wellington Regional Council, even if they are high-value and important projects, because of the constraints on the funding due to the promises around the roads of national significance?
acuity.explanation: Draws out the consequence of the answer just given: he has said he is comfortable with the balance and defers change to 2027, so she puts to him the implication that the Wellington projects will not be funded. The question is built entirely out of what he had just said and could not have been asked in that form otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "We’re pretty comfortable with where we’re at, but there’ll be another opportunity to do a new national land transport programme in 2026 moving into 2027"

acuity.statement: Well, as the member knows from her time as associate transport Minister, I don’t make funding decisions around those things; they’re made by the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) board. We set the activity classes, we set the overall funding envelope, but the individual project decisions are made by the NZTA board. So I don’t have responsibility for that.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the premise of the question just put, rejecting the assumption that he decides individual projects and drawing the line between activity classes and board decisions. It is squarely aimed at what she asked, even though it declines the substance — a deflection on the merits can still be high responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "can I take it then that the Minister will not be enabling funding of the public transport infrastructure projects that were applied for by the Greater Wellington Regional Council"

acuity.statement: But the Minister does clearly set a direction through the Government policy statement on transport funding, and it is within the Minister’s ability to amend the Government policy statement so that it would be possible to fund these projects. If they are projects that are high value and leading towards the outcomes that we want when it comes to housing and public transport, why would the Minister not take that action?
acuity.explanation: Rebuts the exact escape route he had just used: he conceded he sets the activity classes and envelope, and she points at the Government policy statement as the lever that concession implies he holds. The question exists only because of the answer immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "We set the activity classes, we set the overall funding envelope, but the individual project decisions are made by the NZTA board."

acuity.statement: The specific questions with this project—and I’ve stood in the House and asked these questions of the previous Minister of Transport, and he was able to tell me at that time that $13 million had been committed towards that project. Now, the only issue there is that it is in fact only $6.5 million that’s so far been committed to the project. It’s an $80 million project.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the general subject under scrutiny (transport funding) that engages no part of the preceding argument. Picking up Bishop's 'bun fight' wording is a rhetorical pivot, not engagement with his content, and the questions about the bridge's funding, strength rating and tolling would have been identical whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just argued that individual project funding decisions are the NZTA board's and that he wants 10-year funding pipelines, and this statement does not take either up — it borrows his 'bun fight about niche funding' phrase only to set up an unrelated line of questioning about the Pages Road Bridge.

acuity.statement: Yeah, look, thank you. It was good to hear that, because before you came into the room, I started off talking about what the Transport and Infrastructure Committee have been doing in terms of the reviews, and the consistent message which we had from the Infrastructure Commission is the need for long-term pipelines of investment.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Bishop's complaint about three-year funding cycles and funding discontinuity and corroborates it with the select committee's own evidence from the Infrastructure Commission on long-term investment pipelines — a real engagement with the strand just put. It then moves on to its own prepared line on maintenance versus new build rather than pressing Bishop's point further, so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "We go through this merry-go-round of three-year funding cycles and it gets worse once you've changed the National Land Transport Plans after elections, which always tends to happen."

acuity.statement: Well, as I said before, there is a substantial increase in maintenance funding in this year’s National Land Transport Programme, from $2.8 billion to $4 billion, so that is very important. The member makes an interesting point, and he might’ve been talking to the Southland mayors, who made this point to me a week before when I was in Invercargill speaking to the planning conference. They made this point strongly to me. I mean, to state the obvious, it would be a radical change to divvy up transport funding regionally on the basis of GDP—that’s, as I understand, how the member is suggesting—or even done on distance or kilometres travelled.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the maintenance figure the question asked for, then restates Foster's Southland revenue argument as a proposal to allocate transport funding regionally by GDP and draws out its consequence — that it would be a radical change the Government is not contemplating. The speech would be different had Foster argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "given that the Infrastructure Commission has said we need to spend more on maintenance, have we got the structure right?" and "there are more road-user charges and fuel excise duties generated in Southland than is spent in Southland"

acuity.statement: The question is very simple: what’s the calculation on the impact of the roading network at that time—the one that is still being used now—and has it been reviewed, given the reality of places like Southland, where those roads are going backwards very quickly because of those heavy trucks?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding exchange — the deterioration of the Southland roading network — and pushes it to a new causal question about truck weight limits. It engages the topic and one specific claim rather than the structural-funding argument Bishop and Foster had been contesting, and then runs into its own separate prepared question on the ferries.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "very, very long roading network, but it’s a roading network which is going backwards"

acuity.statement: In relation to the issue around the heavy trucks, just to correct the member the Hon Damien O’Connor, I’ve never worked for the Minister of Transport as a staffer before entering Parliament. So you can’t blame me for that—you can’t blame me for that. It’s factually inaccurate.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a specific factual premise embedded in the question just asked — the claim that he advised the Minister who lifted truck weights — before dealing with the substance. This could only have been said in response to that particular question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "can I ask the Minister of Transport who was an adviser to the Minister of the day when they lifted the weight of trucks"

acuity.statement: In relation to the ferries, I’m not sure he’s accurate about the numbers of $1 billion spent already on the ferries.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure put in the preceding question and disputes it directly, rather than answering around it. Aimed squarely at the claim made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "The question is about a billion dollars that was spent by KiwiRail through that process"

acuity.statement: I could, but I would be breaching commercial-in-confidence negotiations. So I won’t.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the exact request made and gives the reason it will not be met; it is unmistakably shaped by the question asked. Withholding the figure is a separate matter from whether the reply engages what was put — on engagement it is near the top, falling short of 1.0 only because it supplies nothing of the substance sought.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "Can the Minister of Transport give us an update on the estimate that KiwiRail or the Government will have to pay for the cancelled contract, and what that compensation might be?"

acuity.statement: The Minister hasn’t spoken to the Mayor of Auckland City. He is focused on roads, just like the last Minister. He isn’t so concerned about the increase in public transport fees to users.
acuity.explanation: Opens a wholly new line on Auckland public transport and congestion charging without engaging any part of the preceding exchange; the characterisation of the Minister as road-focused is prepared framing rather than a response. It stays inside the transport estimates under examination, which keeps it off the floor, but it would read identically whatever Bishop had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just been answering Damien O'Connor on the ferry replacement, the cancelled iReX contract and KiwiRail consultant costs, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: To that point, the Minister said, “Let’s get the legislation in place.” Does that mean he’ll consider the impact on low-income workers after the legislation is through?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own closing formulation — pass the law first, debate the detail later — quotes it back and draws out its consequence as a direct question about sequencing and distributional impact. The question could not have been asked in this form if Bishop had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “Let’s get the legislation in place and then have those debates.” — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Mr Chairman, thank you. Look, I want to go to the Government policy statement and a couple of laudable targets there that the Government’s put in place. First, emissions reduction plan: 41 percent reduction in transport emissions by 2035 and decarbonising, enabling the shift to zero-emission vehicles. How’s it going, Minister, given that the transition and the uptake of low-emissions vehicles—electric vehicles—has slumped since the change in policy of the incoming Government? Are we going to get to these targets; if so, how?
acuity.explanation: Opens a fresh line of questioning on emissions targets without taking up any part of the congestion-pricing exchange immediately preceding it, including the low-income impact question just put. It is on the matter under examination (the Government policy statement on transport) but engages nothing that was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert asked whether the Minister would consider the impact on low-income workers after the legislation passed, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Well, it’s a long-term game—it’s a long-term game—as the member knows, when it comes to climate change. I’m an electric vehicle (EV) evangelist—we are a two-EV family—and I know many, many members of the Government are as well. It’s a long-term game.
acuity.explanation: Engages the premise of the question — that a slump in EV uptake imperils the target — by reframing the timeframe as long-term rather than near-term, and later in the same turn defends the specific policy change the member pointed at. It does not take up the 41 percent figure or the 2035 date, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “the uptake of low-emissions vehicles—electric vehicles—has slumped since the change in policy of the incoming Government” — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Speaking of bridges, this afternoon, I guess it would be important for me to ask as the only representative in the Chamber asking a question around the Waitematā Harbour crossing to the Minister: what is your investment, in this particular period, in the Waitematā Harbour crossing, how does it differ to the plan that Labour had in place, and what costings has he done as opposed to what Labour did in their time?
acuity.explanation: Pivots to a new project with only a linking phrase (“Speaking of bridges”) and does not engage anything in the Minister's answer on EVs and the Clean Car Discount that it directly follows. On-topic for the transport debate, but prepared material rather than a response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just defended scrapping the Clean Car Discount as a regressive wealth transfer, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: There’s money in the National Land Transport Plan for investigations as part of that. The barge and the harbour will be funded through some of that. We can get the member the exact numbers, but there’s no funding for delivery in this National Land Transport Plan.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — what investment is in this period — by distinguishing investigation funding from delivery funding, conceding he does not have the exact figure to hand and undertaking to supply it. Squarely addressed to the question's terms rather than to the topic generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “what is your investment, in this particular period, in the Waitematā Harbour crossing” — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: I’m surprised that the Minister of Health’s or the Health Committee chair’s remarks did not canvass what was absolutely remarkable about the Health Committee’s annual review of Health New Zealand. That included that the financial reports were public for Health New Zealand, were published only a day before the committee’s hearing, and when they arrived, oh boy, $300 million attributed to the wrong financial year.
acuity.explanation: She keys her speech off what the two preceding speakers said — naming the omission in their remarks and then supplying the annual-review material she says they left out — so the opening would have to change if Brown had framed his remarks differently. But she engages none of his specific claims (wait-list growth, the restored targets, the $16.68 billion over three Budgets) and moves into prepared material on governance and redundancies. Partial engagement: pointable, but it answers the topic rather than the claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "I’m just going to make a few opening remarks, and then I look forward to engaging with members from across the House in regards to the annual review of the health portfolio."

acuity.statement: Now, I’m not sure if the member’s actually read the Deloitte report into Health New Zealand’s financial management review. I suggest the member takes a read of the issues behind the financial challenges at Health New Zealand, which can all be sheeted back to the former Government and the decisions that they made.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the substance of the charge just levelled — that Health New Zealand's finances were mismanaged and misreported — and answers it with a named source and a quoted key finding, offering a competing causal account (loss of district governance levers under the restructure). The speech is directly shaped by her argument and would read differently had she attacked something else. Marked slightly below 1.0 because he answers her financial-mismanagement theme at the level of causes rather than addressing the specific $300 million restatement she raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "$300 million attributed to the wrong financial year" / "If that isn’t cooking the books, I don’t know what is."

acuity.statement: In that sentiment, Mr Chair, why did the Minister of Health just express so much concern about the restructuring of the health system when in private—while he’s planning to hock off our hospitals to foreign investors—he’s happy to sing the praises of a centralised health system?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific attack Brown had just made — that the previous government centralised the health system — and turns it directly against him, alleging he privately praises centralisation. The question only makes sense as a reply to what immediately preceded it, and would have to change if Brown had attacked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They centralised the health system. They put a new logo on the top and said “job done” and walked away." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I note in the annual review—and also in the Minister’s opening salvo around focusing on targets—that there was talk around the immunisation targets. We also note a 7 percent increase in vaccine hesitancy rates.
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the matter under examination, with only a glance at the Minister's earlier framing about targets. The immediately preceding exchange about centralisation and hospital ownership is not engaged at all; these questions would have been asked unchanged whatever Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So, yes, we are making sure we are fixing Health New Zealand. We are focusing it back on the basics." — Simeon Brown. Henare gestures at the Minister's framing on targets but does not take up the centralisation argument Brown and Verrall had just been exchanging.

acuity.statement: I’ve got another question about immunisation which it may help to put up at this point. So the committee heard a lot about the restructuring of data and digital, and part of that, we have subsequently learnt, is the work on the Aotearoa Immunisation Register—or AIR—which was an important piece of digital technology to help health providers see who was and wasn’t vaccinated, to enable initiatives to target those people better, including outreach initiatives; some of which the Minister, we’ve already heard today from the Government, they have funded.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the immunisation strand Henare had just opened and extends it into the data and digital restructure and the immunisation register, and acknowledges outreach funding the Government had already described today. It builds on the preceding turn's topic rather than engaging its specific claim, so it is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did the targeted funding that was spent on increasing Māori immunisation rates achieve the target that it was set out to do?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: I have questions to the Minister—and I’d just like to run them in quick succession—relating to the restructures of the National Public Health Service and the impact of the destabilisation of a workforce, whether it’s Māori health, Pacific health, and even, still, for data and digital.
acuity.explanation: A list of prepared questions on the right subject, with a passing overlap with the data and digital restructure Verrall had just raised. Nothing in the content of the preceding turns is taken up or used, so the speech would be essentially identical whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the committee heard a lot about the restructuring of data and digital" — Ayesha Verrall. Lyndon touches the same restructuring subject but does not take up Verrall's immunisation register question or Henare's immunisation figures.

acuity.statement: I thank the members for their questions. One of the themes there is around vaccination rates, and, of course, this is one of the priorities for the Government. Under the previous Government, vaccination rates for two-year-olds dropped from 92.4 percent to 77.1 percent, and I think all members across the House would agree that we need to be increasing immunisation rates rapidly to ensure that our children are protected from a range of diseases.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the common theme in the three preceding questioners' turns and supplies substance on it — figures, the $50 million initiative, Plunket — and goes on to address the data and digital restructure, the National Public Health Service and Iwi Māori Partnership Boards that Lyndon and Henare raised. Marked down because the specific items put to him (the 7 percent hesitancy figure, the immunisation register's status and funding) are not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did the targeted funding that was spent on increasing Māori immunisation rates achieve the target that it was set out to do?" — Peeni Henare; and "what is the status of work to improve the Aotearoa Immunisation Register?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Look, I acknowledge the Minister of Health’s response with respect to the immunisation rates and—agreed—we must get them lifted. I did ask a very specific question about how they came to the 7 percent increase in the vaccine hesitancy numbers over the past year as reported in the annual review.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the Minister's answer that is common ground and identifies precisely what in his own question the answer left out. This is the model case of engagement: it could only have been said after that particular reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "One of the themes there is around vaccination rates, and, of course, this is one of the priorities for the Government." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I thank the member for his questions. The first question around vaccine hesitancy is a question I am happy to come back to the member in regards to, if you put it in writing, as well as the question around how much has been spent on Iwi Māori Partnership Boards (IMPBs). If you can put those in writing, I can provide an answer to the member on that.
acuity.explanation: Names the two specific questions Henare had just pressed, says how each will be dealt with, and then does something with the term itself — arguing the sector should move on from 'vaccine hesitancy' and not use it as an excuse. Engagement is squarely with the preceding turn, even though the figures asked for are deferred to writing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I did ask a very specific question about how they came to the 7 percent increase in the vaccine hesitancy numbers over the past year as reported in the annual review." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: I have a set of questions about patient safety, and we discussed some of these at the annual review hearing, as well.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line on patient safety with prepared material referring back to the committee hearing rather than to anything just said. It is on the matter under examination, but would be word-for-word identical whatever the Minister had answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just answered on vaccine hesitancy terminology and on Iwi Māori Partnership Boards, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: In relation to the member the Hon Peeni Henare’s question around Iwi Māori Partnership Boards (IMPBs), what I said was that the position around commissioning—my position is the same as the previous Minister of Health, which is that IMPBs should not be commissioning services.
acuity.explanation: Henare explicitly asked for clarification of the Minister's earlier remark about supporting the previous Minister's stance on commissioning. Brown takes up exactly that strand and states the substantive position (IMPBs should not commission services), so the answer would be different had Henare asked something else. Not a full 1.0 because he restates rather than engages any reasoning, and leaves Henare's iwi-settlement funding question for later.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question is specifically about the commissioning role, and so I’ll leave that for the Minister to reflect on" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: In regards to the member the Hon Peeni Henare’s last question about the Ngāti Hine land, the advice I’ve received is that the subdivision is progressing, that work is progressing. So that’s just an answer to your prior question.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the specific question asked about progress on the Ngāti Hine land matter and supplies the state of play he has been advised of. Squarely engaged with the particular question, which is what Acuity measures; the vagueness of 'progressing' is a Specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how has the conversation with Ngāti Hine gone around the land matter that’s been raised with them—how far progressed is that?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: In relation to the issue around health equity for Māori, of course this is an issue which is of importance to the Government, and that is why we’ve put in place the health targets: to make sure that we are ensuring New Zealanders are being seen faster through emergency departments, that we are seeing faster cancer treatment, that we are making sure we have targets around immunisations, and that we’re focused on our wait-lists.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the topic Kemp raised — Māori health equity — and so is not unresponsive, but engages none of her specific claims (the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora, workforce shortages in rural and Māori communities, the life-expectancy gap) before returning to prepared material on the health targets. Topic rather than claim, which is the mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Māori life expectancy continues to lag behind Pākehā, and, despite repeated promises, there has been little progress." — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: The Government claims to be investing in Māori health, yet the dissolution of Te Aka Whai Ora has centralised decision making back under Crown control.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn put a directly relevant proposition on the table — that IMPBs should not commission services — which this line of questioning could have engaged head-on. Instead a prepared set of party questions is fired out. It is on the matter under examination, which earns the top of the unresponsive band, but it engages no part of what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just stated his position that Iwi Māori Partnership Boards should not be commissioning services, and this statement does not take that up despite being on the same question of Māori control of health decisions.

acuity.statement: In response to the question about mental health, I suppose—how do we protect the budget? This year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding. That was an uplift of $200 million, from Budget 2024.
acuity.explanation: Answers the funding question put to him with the ring-fence total and the uplift, which is the figure the question called for. Short of the top because he reframes 'what additional resources are being allocated to meet increasing pressures' into the narrower question of how the existing budget is protected, leaving the growing-demand premise untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "with growing demand for mental health services, how does the Government justify the current level of funding, and what additional resources are being allocated to meet increasing pressures?" — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: The first one is regarding the ring-fence. The Minister has given us some numbers. Could he please confirm whether those amounts do equate to 11 percent of the ring-fence being for addiction, and 33 percent being for mental health, or have they gone down in terms of the total Budget allocation?
acuity.explanation: Takes the figures the Minister had just given and does something with them, asking what share of the ring-fence they represent and whether the proportions have fallen. The question is unintelligible without the answer it follows, which is the strongest evidence of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding. That was an uplift of $200 million, from Budget 2024." — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: The second one is in relation to the targets that he spoke about. Why are Māori and Pacific users not monitored to the same extent as other population groups and why did the under-25-year-old cohort not reach any targets in any regions within the last 12 months in terms of that three-week segue into specialist care?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific three-week specialist-access target the Minister had just listed as his accountability mechanism and presses it on breakdown by population group and on the under-25 cohort's performance. Directly contingent on what was said, though it moves on to a second strand (monitoring of Māori and Pacific users) that the preceding turn did not raise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "80 percent of Kiwis to access specialist mental health and addiction services within three weeks" — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: Minister, you’ve talked a lot about reducing the wait time for GPs. We also heard, during the annual review, about the wait-list for elective surgery. What plans does the Minister have to actually address that issue that we’ve heard so much about during the annual review process?
acuity.explanation: The turn immediately before him was the Minister's answer on Iwi Māori Partnership Boards and Health NZ commissioning, which Campbell engages not at all; he opens a fresh topic (elective surgery wait-lists) with a loose backward gesture at the Minister's earlier GP remarks. It is on the matter under scrutiny — the health annual review — so it sits in the low band rather than at zero, but the question would have been identical whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just said of Iwi Māori Partnership Boards "They are not to be commissioning agencies themselves; they are to work through and support the work that is being delivered by Health NZ", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Well, absolutely, in terms of the issue around wait times for GPs—and we’ve been very clear about what we need to do there, which is to ensure we are providing more funding for general primary practice and general practice to make sure that they are getting the funding that they need, but we also need to make sure we are training more doctors and more nurses and making those opportunities available to work in primary practice.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of Campbell's question — the GP wait-time framing in its preamble — and builds a detailed primary-care answer on it, so the engagement is pointable and the reply is not generic. But the question actually put was about the elective surgery wait-list, and the answer never reaches it, running instead through prepared primary-care material on doctor and nurse training. Partial engagement with the preamble rather than the claim: mid-low, not high. Scored on responsiveness only — the accuracy of the training figures and the quality of the reasoning are other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "you’ve talked a lot about reducing the wait time for GPs. We also heard, during the annual review, about the wait-list for elective surgery" — Hamish Campbell

acuity.statement: Is the reason for the delay due to official advice that there were concerns about resource constraints for the Suicide Prevention Action Plan? And a subsequent question: does he have any plans to review or cut back on the Access and Choice programme?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim Doocey had just made about the Suicide Prevention Action Plan being on track and presses on the cause of the delay, naming official advice about resource constraints as the suspected reason. The question would be different had Doocey said something else; the added Access and Choice question is new material, which keeps it short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "it is on track and it will be delivered in the time frame that it needs to be delivered"

acuity.statement: Look, I’m excited to announce to the committee, there will actually be increased resources into the Suicide Prevention Action Plan, because that’s an issue we, quite frankly, need to do a lot better in New Zealand responding to.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what was put to him — the resourcing question — by asserting resources will increase, but leaves untouched the question about official advice and the delay, and ignores the Access and Choice question entirely. Partial engagement that can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "concerns about resource constraints for the Suicide Prevention Action Plan"

acuity.statement: We’ve heard in the annual reviews that Health New Zealand’s financial situation was significantly worse than expected, doubling from a $500 million deficit to a billion-dollar deficit in 2022-2023, and then it was a $722 million reported deficit in 2023-2024. This raises really serious concerns about the financial sustainability of the healthcare system following the previous Government’s reforms, so, given these substantial financial shortfalls, does the Minister believe it reflects the previous Government’s failure to grasp the true costs of these health reforms?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material delivered in the same debate but engaging no part of the preceding turn; the speaker explicitly announces he is returning to his own earlier topic rather than taking up what was just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey spoke about suicide prevention resourcing and the associate psychology role, and this question does not take any of it up — it opens a prepared line on Health New Zealand's deficits, as the speaker himself signals with "sorry to drag you back on to this topic".

acuity.statement: I thank the member for his question. The reality is, as outlined at the Health Committee, there have been some significant financial challenges which this Government has inherited. As I outlined earlier, the Deloitte report into the Health New Zealand Financial Management Review is, I think, a report that all members should read and see what the result of the previous Government’s reforms has left this Government and the challenges that we are now having to address around the financial performance of Health New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question asked — whether the deficits reflect the previous Government's reforms — and supplies the evidence he rests it on (the Deloitte financial management review), then goes on to the mechanism he says caused the breakdown. Squarely engaged with the question put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "does the Minister believe it reflects the previous Government’s failure to grasp the true costs of these health reforms?"

acuity.statement: What efforts, for the Minister, have been made to improve access to primary care? We’ve heard a lot about the delays in getting an appointment to see your local GP, and, therefore, what role can multidisciplinary teams play to help alleviate that pressure on a practice, and will this have a positive impact on wait times?
acuity.explanation: A prepared question on a different strand of the review; it is on the matter under debate but engages no part of the argument immediately preceding it, and would read identically whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about Health New Zealand's financial controls, the Oracle system and the previous Government's "letterhead", and this question does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Even today, the Associate Minister of Health David Seymour and myself just announced changes to the Medicines Act, which will allow nurse practitioners to be able to prescribe more medicines, which, as the member said, will play a critical role as part of the health workforce working in general practice to support patients so they can have more access to timely, quality access to healthcare.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand of the question about multidisciplinary teams and answers it with a named, dated measure on nurse practitioner prescribing, explicitly tying it back to what the member asked. Responsive to the content, not merely to the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "what role can multidisciplinary teams play to help alleviate that pressure on a practice"

acuity.statement: You’ve said previously, Minister, that Iwi Māori Partnership Boards are not for commissioning, and yet there is a requirement for Health NZ to work with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards on the commissioning of investment into kaupapa Māori services.
acuity.explanation: Substantive and pointed, but aimed at an earlier remark outside this exchange rather than at the argument just made; within the debate's subject matter while engaging no part of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about primary care access, overseas-trained doctors and nurse prescribing, and this question does not take that up — it engages a statement the Minister made on another occasion, not the turn it follows.

acuity.statement: In particular, I want to ask the question about—the language you used was “mirrored in te reo Māori” and “consistent across the country”. What does she mean by “mirror” when talking about te reo Māori resources? What feedback has she received from Māori-medium education on those mirrored resources that they have received?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own two phrases from the speech just delivered and presses on what they actually mean in practice, plus asks for the sector feedback she had claimed. The question could not have been written without having listened to the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "everything we did was mirrored in te reo Māori as well" / "te reo decodables that are consistent across the country"

acuity.statement: But the way that the Opposition are describing this as a “cut” is not right. All of that money has been reprioritised into front line—every single dollar.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages and rebuts the characterisation of the funding change as a cut, which was the premise of the question put to her. Partial rather than full: it leaves the "mirrored" definition and the Māori-medium feedback question untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "these resources were funded through cuts to Te Ahu o te Reo Māori"

acuity.statement: Now, I have said that we will re-contract Te Ahu o te Reo Māori, and we are working on that and will look to do so, but the member is going to need to wait until after or around the Budget for that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific "where is that at?" question by confirming the undertaking and giving a timeframe tied to the Budget. It engages the actual question asked rather than reverting to prepared material, though it stops short of detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "the Minister said, “We will look to re-contract this.” Where is that at?"

acuity.statement: I want to check: out of the $30 million that were reprioritised, let’s say from Te Ahu o te Reo Māori into math resources, only $24.8 million has been spent on resources. Potentially, $2 million has been spent on restocking. What was the remainder of the $3 million being spent on?
acuity.explanation: Takes the $30 million figure the Minister had just volunteered and does something with it — decomposes it and asks where the unexplained residual went. The question is built entirely out of the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "we reprioritised $30 million into making sure every single child, including all those tamariki in the mainstream, have access to high-quality, world-leading, curriculum-aligned maths resources"

acuity.statement: The other question was around where the rest of that is, because you mentioned $24.8 million was into resourcing. The rest of it has gone into professional learning and development.
acuity.explanation: Restates the questioner's own breakdown and supplies the missing destination for the residual, which is precisely what was asked. The reply would be different had a different figure been put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "What was the remainder of the $3 million being spent on?"

acuity.statement: I just note that the Minister of Education didn’t answer my question about what she means by “mirrored in te reo Māori”. Are these Māori resources or Pākehā resources translated into Māori?
acuity.explanation: Tracks what the Minister's answer did and did not cover, and sharpens the unanswered point into a concrete either/or. This is engagement with the content of the reply, not a mere reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "the mirroring of those math books, workbooks, textbooks, and teacher guides in te reo Māori as well"

acuity.statement: Just for the Minister of Education, I’m interested to know—one of the important factors we focused on was student achievement—what was it that led to you bringing such a big focus to the numeracy aspect and the structured numeracy aspect? What were the results that you found that led to that?
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line on numeracy that engages no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer about how the Māori-medium resources were developed. It is at least on the portfolio under examination (student achievement/curriculum), so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at zero. The question would have been identical whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just explained that the te reo Māori resources were created by Māori academics and specialists rather than translated from English, and this question does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: It’s fair to say that mid - last year we had a bit of a shock when we saw the School Improvement Plan (SIP) results. The SIP results are an assessment that we do with a randomised number of students, about 2,000 or 3,000, in different subject areas, and the maths one was particularly bad. I look at the year 8 results: those year 8 results had about 22 percent of kids at curriculum for mathematics before they went into high school.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what the preceding question asked for: names the assessment, describes it, and gives the year 8 figure that she says drove the numeracy focus. Delete McCallum's question and substitute a different one and this answer would have to change, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What were the results that you found that led to that?" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Just a question about those maths books provided to Māori-medium schools: how many of them were printed upside down, and how much did that cost? Further to that, what feedback has she got from principals and teachers about those maths resources, from Māori-medium education?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the Minister had just boasted about — the half-million printed and delivered maths books — and tests it, asking about misprints, cost and sector feedback. It engages the content of the preceding claim rather than merely referring to it; short of 1.0 because it probes the claim with a new allegation instead of engaging the Minister's reasoning about why the books were produced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "half a million maths books that went out to market ... they were printed, they were delivered" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Just in response to the member Willow-Jean Prime’s question about the Māori maths resources, the feedback that we’ve had has been excellent. The resources—I’ve got some of them here—are, as I say, developed by experts, and I know that the Opposition are looking to find issues everywhere. I’m not aware of anything that’s been printed upside down; it’s not been brought to my attention.
acuity.explanation: Addresses both strands actually put to her — reports the feedback received and answers the misprint allegation directly, if only to deny awareness of it. Held below the top band because the cost element goes unanswered and the remainder of the turn pivots to characterising the Opposition rather than the substance; the pivot is a Focus/Civility matter and is not what is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how many of them were printed upside down, and how much did that cost?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Since we are on the curriculum, let’s actually talk about the curriculum. I want to ask questions to the Minister around the ministerial advisory group for the curriculum. Let’s start with, say, literacy. The Minister says “world-leading experts”, but let’s face it, in the beginning it was, essentially, just one or two people—there might be a whole team of them, but it was mainly led by one or two people—and I think we all know who they are.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own invitation to ask about curriculum content and her "world-leading experts" characterisation and disputes the latter on its own terms, arguing the work was led by one or two people. This turn could not have been delivered unchanged after a different preceding speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "developed by world-leading experts in Pāngarau" / "a good, smart question might be "Hey, Minister, on page 29..."" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: I put together a ministerial advisory group when I first became the Minister. They were only in place for a very short period of time and did one report for me on the state of the curriculum and where they saw it going—their work was then finished. It is up to the ministry to contract writers on different curricula areas.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the central question — whether the advisory group wrote the curriculum — by setting out the group's remit and duration and stating that writer contracting sits with the ministry. Short of 1.0 because the conflict-of-interest process and the contracted-company allegation, both specifically put to her, are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether the ministerial advisory group did also take part in the writing of the curriculum—which is a big no-no—and what the conflict of interest process is" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Just a quick follow-up, since the Minister of Education mentioned the senior English curriculum: can the Minister enlighten the committee on why the New Zealand Association of Teachers of English pulled out, citing that there is a lack of transparency, there’s a lack of ability to consult, and there’s a lot of secrecy behind that consultation?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact evidence the Minister had just offered — testimonials from individual principals and a claim of many voices — and sets the withdrawal of the national subject association against it, treating her own example as anecdotal. This is engagement with the content of the preceding argument, not a reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I had the principal of the largest school in the country text me to say how good it was" / "we had so many voices in the process" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Look, it’s up to them, and the questions need to be put to them around why they wanted to be involved or not. But I would note that their feedback so far on the English curriculum has been pretty muted, because, frankly, I don’t think there’s much in the English curriculum to be upset about; because, as I say, it is world-leading, knowledge-rich, year by year.
acuity.explanation: Engages the association's withdrawal squarely, characterising their subsequent feedback as muted and disputing that there is anything to be upset about. Not top of the band because the specific charge in the question — lack of transparency and secrecy in the consultation — is redirected to the association rather than answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why the New Zealand Association of Teachers of English pulled out, citing that there is a lack of transparency" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: What can the Minister of Education report back, in the progress reports that the Education Review Office (ERO) provides, on its curriculum development work with iwi arising from pou reo evaluations, and, in particular, the teaching of New Zealand war histories—Te Pūtake o te Riri—within Hauraki-Waikato and in these schools nationwide? That’s the first question.
acuity.explanation: A prepared new line on ERO's iwi curriculum work that engages no part of the preceding turn. It is squarely within the annual review under examination, so it belongs in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at zero; the question reads identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan had just asked about the remainder of the $3 million being spent on professional learning and development, and this question does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’m just really interested to understand what definition the Minister of Education uses for the “science of learning” when she often refers to it. Can she, please, explain, step by step, how implementing the science of learning will meaningfully change how students are being taught, particularly in terms of the curriculum we’ve been talking about?
acuity.explanation: A fresh prepared line on the "science of learning" that takes up nothing the Minister had just argued. It earns the top of the unresponsive band only for the gesture at the curriculum discussion and at the Minister's habitual use of the phrase; a reference is not an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it is world-leading, knowledge-rich, year by year" — Erica Stanford; the question gestures at "the curriculum we’ve been talking about" but engages none of the Minister's argument about the English curriculum or the teachers' association.

acuity.statement: While we are on the curriculum pātai that has been brought up, I just kind of want to ask some pātai around NCEA.
acuity.explanation: Stanford had just made a substantive argument about the science of learning, explicit teaching and whole-class instruction, including a direct invitation ("I know the member will be interested in the shift away from grouping to whole-class teaching"). Maipi-Clarke gestures at the fact that curriculum has been raised, but then puts her own prepared set of questions — kawenata, the ERO Māori strategy report, and Te Ao Haka credits — none of which take up any strand of Stanford's argument. A gesture at the debate without engaging its content sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
