We did hear, during that time, some terrible, terrible stories around what was happening in that triangular relationship. We heard about people who were entering into workforces where they were alongside people who were on collective agreements, doing exactly the same work—exactly the same work—and earning less money but being treated, as the member rightly pointed out, with terrible conditions and much worse conditions.
acuity.explanation: Patterson had used the 2019 Act and his own time on the Education and Workforce Committee as the ground for opposing this bill: that committee identified a problem and the 2019 Act fixed it, so the further step is unneeded complexity. Tinetti, who was on the same committee, accepts that premise explicitly ('I think you're right about 2019'), confirms the evidence they both heard, and then turns it against his conclusion — the pay gap is the part 2019 left unfixed. That is the classic partial concession plus dispute: the speech would have to be written differently had Patterson not invoked the committee, and she points at the specific strand she is taking over. Not a full 1.0 because she engages his 2019/committee argument rather than his central evidentiary claim that the bill would not raise wages.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I was actually on the Education and Workforce Committee when that bill came through and it was clear that we did have to tidy up these triangular employment relationships' — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: We were told that it was complicated and it was red tape. Well, I’m sorry, how silly are people? That’s not red tape. We have employment in this country, and it’s pretty simple: you calculate the amount that you pay the hire company based on the terms and conditions you pay your own workforce. That isn’t that hard. Our employers are pretty much smart enough to do that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise objection Bates had just made — that the bill imposes unquantified compliance burden on small labour-hire businesses — names it back ("it was complicated and it was red tape"), denies it, and then supplies the mechanism she says makes it simple: calculating the hire-company payment off the controlling employer's own terms and conditions. The passage could not have been delivered unchanged after a different argument; it is shaped by the red-tape claim it rebuts. Held short of 1.0 only because part of the rebuttal is assertion ("That isn't that hard") rather than engagement with Bates's specific example of an employer having to ask about another firm's employment relationships.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "This bill adds red tape. You hear the Labour Party want to say, ‘Hey, we don’t know what that red tape is.’"

acuity.statement: The last thing is that there’s been a lot of comment about this hurting small businesses, and that it’s going to add all this red tape. The member’s been very clear: this only applies when a collective agreement is in place, and the majority of collective agreements are at large employers. It doesn’t add any other, extra party to this.
acuity.explanation: Takes up McCallum's specific objection — that the bill lands on small business as extra paperwork and red tape — and does something with it: argues the bill's trigger (an existing collective agreement) confines it to large employers and adds no new party to the arrangement. The passage would have to change if the preceding speaker had attacked the bill on different grounds. Short of 1.0 only because it answers the scope objection without engaging the compliance-burden mechanics McCallum gestured at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "it’ll be small business, because it’s small business that struggle, that have to deal with more paperwork, more red tape"

acuity.statement: The funny thing is, I’ve talked to so many of them and actually done this as a job for years. They don’t. They actually don’t. This law needs to change.
acuity.explanation: A direct contradiction of the interjected claim immediately before it — McClure's assertion that good employers usually do take labour-hire workers on permanently — answered on its own terms with the speaker's own experience of those workers. The reply is unintelligible without the interjection, which is the strongest evidence of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Laura McClure: "They usually do, when they’re good."

acuity.statement: It’s because Labour voted, as a bloc, down a bill that would have fixed it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the rhetorical 'why' McAnulty had just repeatedly posed about why the restrictions persist and supplies a direct causal answer — that Labour bloc-voted down the bill that would have removed them. The interjection is shaped by the specific question just asked rather than being a generic heckle, though it answers why the law was not fixed rather than why the rule originally exists.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Why is it that hospitality workers have to concern themselves with monitoring what people eat in order to do their job"

acuity.statement: Now, I expected this. I expected the ACT Party to heckle this, because I understand they’re disappointed that Cameron Luxton’s bill got voted down. I get it.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the interjection and names its source, but engages the content of the claim only by ascribing a motive (disappointment) to the interjector rather than addressing whether Labour's bloc vote is the reason the restrictions remain. A gesture at what was said, then a return to prepared material, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "It’s because Labour voted, as a bloc, down a bill that would have fixed it."

acuity.statement: The previous speaker spoke about the rights of workers, and workers ultimately have the right to say no. I remember back when I was an apprentice butcher on $6 an hour and I could choose to work stat days, I could choose to work extra days if I wanted to, to get ahead. And if I didn’t want to, then I could say no and that business would go to another worker.
acuity.explanation: Bidois takes up the precise claim Tuiono had just made — that low-paid workers cannot realistically refuse a roster — names it as the previous speaker's argument, and contests it directly with his own low-wage experience of declining shifts. Had Tuiono argued something else about the bill, this passage would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "It’s very, very hard to turn the boss down when they come and have a chat to you saying that they want you to come in on a shift."

acuity.statement: I’ve heard the arguments for the bill and I want to acknowledge my colleague because he does have a point, and I’ve heard from across the House that we’re evolutionary and we’re changing in New Zealand. However, in some communities, alcohol is a really major problem, and in my community, over 60 percent of our population are under—they are the youngest population in Aotearoa.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one strand of Bidois's argument — that the bill reflects New Zealand's evolution — and qualifies it rather than ignoring it, conceding the general point while arguing it does not hold for communities like hers. She then returns to prepared material about Māngere, so the engagement is partial rather than a full rebuttal of his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "A lot has changed since the 1980s, and New Zealand will continue to change. I believe that this is an evolution"

acuity.statement: Now, there’s a number of reasons, but one thing I do want to put on the record is that New Zealand First have exercised their conscience vote, as we did in the last bill, and it just so happened that eight members individually said no. So I just wanted to put that on the record for my colleague.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford's preceding turn named New Zealand First among the parties he said had block-voted and denied their members a conscience vote. Unkovich takes up that specific allegation about her own party and corrects it on the facts — the vote was a conscience vote and eight members independently landed in the same place — and explicitly addresses it to "my colleague". The passage would not exist if Rutherford had not made that claim, which is the deciding test. It is not a full 1.0 because she rebuts only the NZ First strand and then moves to her prepared case against the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "members of the Labour Party, the Green Party, and New Zealand First all voted collectively as a block in one way and did not allow their members to use their right and use their conscience" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: I want to address some of the claims that have been made in the House, just briefly, about block voting. Hopefully, the House will be noting that Labour is treating this as a conscience issue. Labour did actually treat the previous vote as a conscience issue; it just so happened that we all shared the same conscience—a bit like New Zealand First!
acuity.explanation: Boyack names the claim she is answering (block voting), disputes Rutherford's characterisation of Labour's previous vote directly, and then turns Unkovich's own defence of New Zealand First back on the charge — if unanimity among NZ First members is consistent with a conscience vote, it is equally so for Labour. The speech would have to change entirely if the preceding turns had argued something else, which is the top of the scale. Scored on engagement only: whether the reasoning holds or whether the jab at other parties is on-policy belongs to Rigor and Focus, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I remember the Labour Party voting 34 votes No as a block. That was really disappointing" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: Rachel Boyack, actually, we’re concerned about supermarkets too, because some supermarkets don’t have the choice to open on some of these trading days and there are inconsistent rules, as you pointed out. But my concern is not whether they should be able to sell alcohol or not.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson takes up by name the one reservation the immediately preceding speaker raised — supermarkets and inconsistent trading rules — concedes part of it and then distinguishes his own concern from hers. That is real engagement with a specific strand of her turn, but it occupies one paragraph before he returns to prepared ACT material on freedom and choice and Queenstown tourism, none of which would change had Boyack said something different. Mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "I would want to see the rules around supermarkets looked at really closely, because I’m not as convinced around that"

acuity.statement: Oh, I mean, I am conflicted, and I think it is good to be conflicted in this world. And this is why I hugely value the principle of the conscience vote. The conscience vote is a great thing; I wish we did it more often.
acuity.explanation: Abel takes the interjection put to him, accepts its characterisation rather than deflecting it, and turns it into an argument for the conscience vote — he does something with the point rather than merely acknowledging it. The passage is unmistakably shaped by what was just said to him and could not stand if Butterick had said something else. Short of 1.0 only because what he engages is a one-line interjection rather than a developed argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Butterick: "Oh, you’re conflicted, Steve?"

acuity.statement: The Treaty doesn’t mention anything by race.
acuity.explanation: Seymour had just asserted that the partnership principle ranks Kiwis by ancestry and that 'the idea that your race matters' is the problem. Waititi's interjection goes straight at the premise of that claim — that the Treaty itself is racially framed — rather than at Seymour personally or at a different topic. It engages the specific content, which is what Acuity rewards, though it is brief and supplies no detail (a Specificity question, not an Acuity one).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: 'The idea that your race matters is a version of a bigger problem.' (and earlier, 'Kiwis should be ranked by the arrival of their ancestors')

acuity.statement: He named his party after a race. Of course you have a problem with race in this country under our current policies.
acuity.explanation: Seymour does take up Waititi's interjection rather than ignoring it, and the reply would not exist had Waititi not spoken — so it is not prepared material. But he engages only the 'it's not about race' strand, and answers it with a point about the party's name rather than with the textual claim Waititi actually made about what the Treaty does and does not mention. Partial engagement that then returns to his prepared line of argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: 'The Treaty doesn’t mention anything by race.'

acuity.statement: Normally when I rise in this House to speak on a bill, I say it’s a great privilege to speak on the bill. That is not the case today. This is a grubby little bill, born of a grubby little deal.
acuity.explanation: Seymour had just read out the bill's three proposed principles and explicitly challenged opponents to say which words they object to, and had argued that select committee submissions are not a referendum. Hipkins's opening engages none of that: it characterises the bill and the coalition deal behind it. It is at least about the measure under debate, so it sits above the floor, but it would read identically whatever Seymour had argued. (That it is dismissive is a Civility matter; here it scores low purely for non-engagement.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour read out the bill's three principles and challenged opponents to 'explain specifically why they oppose the words in the bill', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The people are not fooled by the ACT Party trying to ignore the injustice and inequity that has seen, for example, that Māori are three times more likely to be arrested and convicted of a cannabis-related crime than non-Māori are—but let us be clear—for doing the same thing.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows a substantive turn by Hipkins, who argued at length that the bill rests on 'the myth of Māori special privilege' and marshalled disparity statistics (life expectancy, cancer mortality, deprivation) against it. Her speech reuses the same 'myth of Māori privilege' framing and adds a disparity statistic of her own, so it gestures at the matter under debate, but it takes up no part of his actual argument: it neither builds on, disputes nor extends his reasoning, and is aimed at ACT rather than at anything just said. She states explicitly that she will use her slot 'mostly to amplify the voices of the submitters', and the speech would read identically whatever the preceding speaker had argued on this bill — prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "this is a bill based on a mythology, a mythology that is far too easily turned into outright lies: the myth of Māori special privilege" — engaged only as shared framing, not as an argument taken up.

acuity.statement: Clearly, it shows that many people feel passionately about the topic, and I want to acknowledge the effort that so many people put in to expressing their views. Some of the submissions were truly remarkable. It’s equally true that the bill has provided a convenient vehicle for political campaigns on all sides, and that is politics.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith follows Marama Davidson, who characterised the 300,000 submissions, the marches and the petitions as a sincere generational grassroots uprising against the bill. He takes up that one strand — conceding the scale and sincerity of the public effort, then disputing its character by recasting it as a vehicle for political campaigning 'on all sides'. That is a partial engagement: the concession-and-reframe would read differently had Davidson not just built her speech on the movement. But he does not touch her specific points (the ACT MP's questioning of Anjum Rahman, her 'they could sniff the division a mile away' claim), and the rest of the speech is prepared material setting out National's position, its Treaty-settlements record and its programme, which would have been delivered whoever spoke before. He also deflects the division charge Davidson made onto Labour rather than answering it, which is a pivot rather than an engagement. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "they came to the select committee, they marched the streets, they signed petitions, they wrote postcards" — her framing of the submissions and marches as a genuine popular movement against the bill.

acuity.statement: This treaty principles bill has been an emotional rollercoaster. I know that for many of the people who made their voices heard, they didn’t have the time or the money or the energy to give, and yet they showed up in droves.
acuity.explanation: Paul follows a substantive turn by Maipi-Clarke, who argued that the real question of privilege is the House recognising only one culture and language, and who credited the mass of submitters and the hikoi with killing the bill. Paul gestures at the same debate and the same submitters, but takes up none of Maipi-Clarke's specific argument — nothing about the rules of the House, tikanga, or the submission statistics is engaged, rebutted, or built on. What follows is prepared material on the right subject: her own select committee experience, her acknowledgements of colleagues and campaigners, and her list of what the party collected. The speech would read essentially unchanged had Maipi-Clarke made a different argument on the same bill, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the opening does glance at the shared theme of the submitters' voices that the previous speaker had just raised. (Her later line answering a New Zealand First member engages a turn that is not in this window, so it cannot be pointed at and does not lift the score.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it was their voices—their powerful voices—that engaged to drown out this bill" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: As we’ve heard earlier and throughout this whole conversation, the National Party strongly asserts that a referendum on the Treaty would be a simplistic approach to a very extremely complex and challenging issue, and so today, we are voting to ensure it will go no further. I say this respectfully to our coalition partners, but this is our strong view.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a long, argument-dense speech from Willie Jackson (referendums produce wrong answers — Australia's Voice, homosexual law reform, the te reo petition; Treaty rights pre-date the Treaty; Luxon failed to stand up to Seymour) and takes up none of it. Her speech is prepared National Party material — party values, committee thanks, the National position on a referendum — and would read word-for-word the same had any other member spoken before her. The phrase "As we’ve heard earlier and throughout this whole conversation" is a gesture at the debate, and she lands on the same conclusion as Jackson on referendums, but she engages no part of his reasoning: hence the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "Finally on referendums, Mr Seymour, they’re not always the solution that you make out they are." Nakhle reaches the same destination — a referendum is the wrong instrument — but asserts the National Party's position rather than taking up Jackson's examples or argument.

acuity.statement: My colleagues have already said that this law is a simplistic tool that does not address the underlying issues. They have highlighted the steps that the National-led Government has been taking to address the genuine concerns that Kiwis have, so now let me turn to the vision that National has for our country. We want a thriving, united New Zealand where every Kiwi enjoys equal opportunity and equal citizenship and takes pride in our shared future.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows Webb's substantive attack on the bill's equality premise and his specific RMA challenge, but engages none of it: he cites what his own colleagues have said and pivots immediately to National's prepared vision statement. The speech is on the matter under debate (the bill, the Treaty, equal citizenship), so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read word-for-word the same had Webb argued something entirely different on the same subject — hence the low band rather than 0.5. A gesture at the debate ("this law is a simplistic tool") keeps it above 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan McBeth Webb — Duncan Webb — argued that "the lie in that and the falsehood underlying that statement is that difference is inequality", pressed the question "What is the special advantage that Māori have under the Resource Management Act?" and said the bill rests "on premises which are fundamentally racist"; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: While we don’t necessarily always agree, successive National Governments have always worked well with Māori on Treaty issues, and we’ve always ensured that there are equal citizenship rights and equal opportunity for all New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Tangaere-Manuel's immediately preceding turn charged the National-led Government with letting the bill into the House and with causing divisive conversations. Simpson takes up the topic — National's record with Māori and the risk of division — and offers a defence, but he engages the general subject rather than her specific accusation, and he signals the material is a reiteration of his first-reading speech. A partial engagement you can point at, not a rebuttal of the claim made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "it has been this National-led Government that has allowed this ugly monster to rear its head in the light of day"

acuity.statement: Now, unlike James Meager, I’m not going to spend 10 minutes whining about process, but I will say two things. Firstly, there are 105,000 submissions that aren’t on the parliamentary record today, and to suggest that that’s all OK is false.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by a different member was Simpson's, and Webb engages no part of it: not the case-by-case claim, not the co-governance reversals, not Simpson's own rejection of the bill. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it above the floor, but it is prepared material aimed elsewhere and would read identically had Simpson said something quite different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson argued that National works through Treaty issues case by case and that this bill achieves none of the Government's goals, and this statement does not take any of that up — it reaches past Simpson to James Meager's earlier turn and to the select committee process.

acuity.statement: This agreement is also unlikely to have immediate commercial or economic benefit to exporters in Aotearoa, and there’s no evidence that the enforceable Investment Facilitation chapter and the enforceable bilateral investment agreement will increase investment from UAE to Aotearoa as well.
acuity.explanation: Follows O'Connor's substantive speech endorsing the deal. This sentence directly contradicts O'Connor's exporter-benefit claim, and later in the turn the member also takes up the worker/women's-rights strand O'Connor raised by saying MFAT gave no confidence that partners can be held to account on human rights and labour law. But the bulk of the turn is the prepared Green party case (tariff value, Digital Trade chapter, Sudan, Te Tiriti) and it engages none of O'Connor's specifics — the negotiating history, the UK/EU standards, the procurement access — so it is partial engagement of a strand rather than a rebuttal of the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "It does provide opportunities for our exporters and for the service sector, where they will be able to bid into a procurement for Government services in the UAE—a big, large, dynamic economy."

acuity.statement: We know, as opposed to the de-growth Greens, that free trade benefits us. It is huge. We have seen, with the multiple free-trade agreements that this country has entered into, that results have come back to this country.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding Green speech — the claim that New Zealand's FTAs and CEPAs have not delivered proportionate returns — and contradicts it directly, so the turn would read differently had Xu-Nan not made that argument. But the engagement is a flat counter-assertion plus a label ("de-growth Greens"), with no figure, chapter or mechanism answered: the $42.6 million tariff estimate, the duty-exemption point, articles 10.13/10.14, the Sudan concern and the Te Tiriti non-paper all go untouched, and the member expressly declines to reiterate the case for the deal. Naming the opponent is not engaging them, so this sits at partial, not full, responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "the FTAs and CEPAs that we have signed up to have not yielded the kind of return that we are hoping to see."

acuity.statement: This Government is committed to delivering timely and quality healthcare for all New Zealanders. This bill will increase access to medicines for New Zealanders by introducing a streamlined verification pathway for medicines. Faster access to medicines leads to better patient outcomes. For that, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition speech arguing the bill is a token gesture without funding and that overseas standards must be scrutinised before being adopted here. This contribution takes up none of it — it is prepared praise that would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had said. It is at least about the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued the bill “means nothing unless the funding is there to purchase those particular medicines” and that international standards must be tested against an independent judgement, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It’s possible that this might work, but it’s also possible that it might not. It’s valid to pose the question: is it possible to use the assessment processes of other countries and apply it here to streamline the approval of medication? Fair enough. But are the assessment criteria in other countries suitable for here? Are they as good as our processes here?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the mechanism the previous Government speaker commended — the streamlined overseas-verification pathway — and presses on the premise it rests on, namely that foreign assessment criteria are equivalent to Medsafe's. It engages one strand of the preceding claim rather than rebutting a specific figure or assertion, and then returns to prepared material on health funding, so it sits mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “This bill will increase access to medicines for New Zealanders by introducing a streamlined verification pathway for medicines” — Carlos Cheung

acuity.statement: I rise to support the Medicines Amendment Bill. This is about faster and more efficient access to medicines, and it will support better outcomes for families across Aotearoa New Zealand. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed challenge to the bill's central premise — whether overseas approval criteria are as rigorous as Medsafe's — and engages none of it. Prepared commendation that would read identically whatever had preceded it, though it is at least on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty asked “are the assessment criteria in other countries suitable for here?” and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Look, I’d like to reinforce the comments that the previous speaker, the Hon Mark Patterson, had. They are absolutely correct, and I agree with him that the Green Party are just out in the cold on this particular bill, and with trade in general.
acuity.explanation: Anderson names the previous speaker and endorses one strand of his speech (the attack on the Greens' position) but does nothing with it — no argument is taken up, extended, or tested. This is a mere reference plus agreement, which the rubric places in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5; 0.3 because there is at least a gesture at a specific point Patterson made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "I can’t believe what I’m hearing from the Greens over there not supporting this bill."

acuity.statement: The reason why the Labour Party is supporting this bill is because it’s one of those rare times where we do agree with the Government, and then when Governments change over, we usually see this continuation of agreements, particularly when it comes to free trade.
acuity.explanation: Patterson explicitly appealed for Labour's support and framed the bill as urgent in a tumultuous trade environment; Edmonds answers that appeal directly, stating Labour's position and the continuity principle behind it, and elsewhere develops the timeliness strand with the US tariff shocks. But the bulk of the speech is prepared material on productivity, the forced-labour and women's-empowerment clauses, so this is partial engagement — one strand taken up, then a return to her own text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "with that we as a responsible Government—and, hopefully, with support from the Labour Party, at the very least—have an opportunity in front of us here"

acuity.statement: This bill cements our brand new free-trade agreement with the UAE, removing 98.5 percent of export tariffs for Kiwi exporters, making it easy for our businesses to sell products overseas and grow jobs here in New Zealand. So, without hesitation, I commend this to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Edmonds' substantive contribution on productivity, labour standards and the tariff environment and engages none of it. The contribution is on the subject under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but it would have been word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds spoke about New Zealand's low productivity, the US tariff shocks and the agreement's forced-labour and women's-empowerment commitments, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I think it’s really important just to set out for the record that it isn’t just lower tariffs across various goods; it’s also making sure that there aren’t inappropriate non-tariff barriers, which can be things like working conditions and environmental conditions, to make sure that both economies are trading on an even footing.
acuity.explanation: Brewer had just reduced the agreement to the removal of 98.5 percent of export tariffs, and Webb corrects that framing on the record by identifying non-tariff barriers as the other half of what the agreement does — a partial but pointable engagement with the immediately preceding characterisation. The rest of the speech (the Treaty clause, trade delegations, no need for protection) is his own prepared material, so it sits at the midpoint rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "removing 98.5 percent of export tariffs for Kiwi exporters"

acuity.statement: Trade is good, and therefore I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Webb's detailed contribution on non-tariff barriers, the Treaty of Waitangi clause and cross-party trade delegations, and engages no part of it. It commends the bill under debate, which keeps it just off 0.0, but the words would be identical in any trade debate on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb spoke about non-tariff barriers and the agreement's Treaty of Waitangi clause, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I do want to respond to the previous speaker, Willow-Jean Prime, because I think it’s important to note that the previous Government received the royal commission redress interim report in December 2021. They had two years to implement a redress entity if they thought that it was important, but they didn’t.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Prime's central charge — that putting more money into the existing claims system rather than building an independent entity is the wrong call — and answers it directly with a counter-record claim about Labour's own two years with the interim report. The speech would have to change if Prime had attacked something else; it is squarely aimed at the argument just made, even though the reply is a tu quoque rather than a defence of the policy on its merits (that is a Rigor matter, not an Acuity one).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "Funnelling more money into systems that have harmed them in the past is, without question, the wrong call."

acuity.statement: The advice that I had received around creating something new and complex—it would have taken an extraordinarily long period of time and would have been very expensive on the one hand.
acuity.explanation: Prime put a list of direct questions about the advice the Minister received on an independent redress system and how she could call it too difficult and time-consuming. This engages that strand — it supplies the substance of the advice and the reasoning behind the call — but answers only part of it, leaving the 'when did she receive it' and 'will she release the high-level design group's proposal' questions untouched before returning to prepared defence of the announcement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I want to know what advice the Minister received about establishing an independent redress system."

acuity.statement: Now, we looked at what the royal commission had said in their recommendations, and it was clear that we needed to have something that felt and looked like one system.
acuity.explanation: Contests Prime's reading of the royal commission — she said the commission was clear that survivors wanted an independent system; Stanford reads the same recommendations as calling for a single-feeling system, which is what she claims to be delivering. That is engaging the specific authority Prime leaned on rather than merely asserting a different view, though it restates the announcement rather than quoting the recommendation back against her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "The final report from the royal commission was clear: survivors wanted an independent redress system."

acuity.statement: Now, that is not a separate system in itself, but quite frankly, I would rather that all of that $774 million be invested into the survivors than building up a new system that may take years when these survivors have waited long enough to have their claims addressed.
acuity.explanation: Carter's central charge was that the Government's response abandons the promised independent, survivor-led redress system. Chhour takes that specific demand up and answers it on its merits — conceding the seamless service is not a separate system, and giving a reason (time cost versus money reaching survivors) for not building one. The speech would have had to change if Carter had argued something else about the package. She does not engage Carter's other strands (the faith-based exclusion, the 12-of-105 figure, the international comparison), so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There is no independent survivor-led redress system, as promised." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: But this end point, this new redress system—as we’ve said repeatedly in this House, there is no perfect system. We could have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to develop this new redress system, but what we do have is something that we can hear what have been the issues and what have been the frustrations.
acuity.explanation: Costello takes up one strand of Carter's case — the absent new redress system — and offers a counter (the time it would have consumed), then returns to prepared material about there being no perfect solution and not letting the perfect be the enemy of the good. The specific claims Carter made (the $774m being below other jurisdictions, the exclusion of faith-based institutions, only 12 of 105 recommendations accepted, the quoted survivors) go unaddressed, and her 'political football' framing names the opposing speech as a target rather than engaging its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There is no independent survivor-led redress system, as promised." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: I note the concern that is being addressed and has been raised in response to this urgent debate, which is the concern that there isn’t an independent organisation that’s responsible for that redress system and the redress payments, but the Government was faced with a difficult choice. Does the Government spend more time and money on setting up a new scheme, or does it provide more to survivors now through the current redress process? The decision of the Government was to ensure that as much of that $774 million that is going to go towards redress would go directly towards those affected rather than spending that additional money and time on setting up an independent process.
acuity.explanation: Mooney follows Bennett in the same urgent debate and takes up Bennett's central demand — that redress be run by a separate, independent system rather than by the institutions that caused the harm. He names that concern precisely, concedes its basis (the royal commission's finding on low trust), frames the Government's choice as a trade-off between setting up a new scheme and maximising money to survivors now, and offers an independent review of claims as the answer to it. The speech would have had to be different had Bennett argued something else, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because the trade-off framing partly sidesteps Bennett's specific point that an appeal route inside the oppressor's system is not independence, and the latter half of the speech is prepared package detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "We need to look forward, we need a separate system, and we need the Government to do what they said they were going to do and create a new system."

acuity.statement: We had a royal commission that did incredibly good work and it came out with a finding. It said that what had to replace the system was a survivor-led, survivor-designed redress system. Now, I have heard the Minister talk about how—today, she said: “we were trying to create one single entity system and that was too difficult in the time frame.” I’ve heard another Minister say, “We can’t wait for the perfect system.” I don’t think many survivors in this country expect the perfect system. I think they expect a half-decent system, a system that doesn’t re-traumatise them, and it’s our job—because we lead this country—to do a better job of giving them what they need.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the preceding speaker's rejection-of-the-commission's-findings strand and develops it into the specific finding (survivor-led, survivor-designed redress), then rebuts the time-frame and 'can't wait for perfect' justifications by reframing what survivors actually expect. The engagement is real and pointable, but the claim she rebuts most directly was made by the Minister in a turn outside this window rather than by Kapa-Kingi, so it is partial rather than full engagement with what immediately preceded.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "To reject the findings—let me just say that again: to reject the findings of the commission—is to reject the truth."

acuity.statement: I want to put very carefully on the record the enormous time and energy that the Minister in charge of the Government response, the Hon Erica Stanford, has put into this. For the comments from the other side to suggest that she hasn’t wholeheartedly listened to survivors, met with them, and heard their views, and, although many of those views differed, to then try to find a way through—it will never satisfy everybody’s concerns, but it satisfied enough for us to at least make a start in righting the wrongs.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific charge made by the two preceding speakers — that the Minister failed to listen to survivors and should be ashamed — and contests it on its own terms by asserting the listening happened and that differing survivor views had to be reconciled. The speech would have to change if the preceding turns had made a different criticism; it falls short of 1.0 because it asserts the contrary rather than engaging the evidence they offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "the Minister should be ashamed—deeply ashamed"; also Helen White: "when a Government this new has forgotten how to listen"

acuity.statement: But, actually, members on the opposite side of the Chamber can’t just sit there and say that this is about the Government’s intentions. We’ve actually announced a significant way forward, which is a start, and no amount of money—no amount of money—will ever take away what has happened to a group of New Zealanders that it should never ever have happened to.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific 'intentions are not enough' line from the earlier turn and answers it by pointing to an announced measure as the counter to a charge of mere intention. Pointable and squarely aimed at the preceding argument, though it answers with an assertion of action rather than engaging the adequacy case (the $30,000-per-survivor arithmetic) that the same speaker built.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "Good intentions—and I heard that phrase earlier, too—are simply not enough."

acuity.statement: That’s all well and fine providing there is a job for every single person on the jobseeker benefit or unemployed person all together. Can I ask whether the Minister is aware as to whether there is a job available for every single person on the benefit, and, if not, what is the Minister doing to ensure that there is a job for every single person on the benefit?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific premise Upston had just stated — that the default is that if you can work you should — quotes it back and immediately tests it against a condition it depends on (whether jobs exist for every beneficiary), then draws out the consequence for sanctions. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different opening; it is built on the Minister's actual words.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "we believe the default that if you can work, you should" — the speaker quotes this as "everyone who can work, should work" and interrogates its precondition.

acuity.statement: I would also like to know about the employment issue a little bit raised by my colleague Ricardo Menéndez March in the Green Party there, but it’s really around this expectation of employment when you’ve got a rising amount of unemployment. Now, we had record low levels of unemployment under Labour. My alarm is raised by the fact we’re now up to our highest level in many years and my understanding is that clusters around certain groups.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding Green turn — the mismatch between work expectations and job availability — and develops it in a new direction (youth unemployment and Reserve Bank mandate settings), but does not engage Menéndez March's specific challenge about whether a job exists for every beneficiary, and much of the surrounding call is prepared material on emergency housing and MSD capacity drawn from the annual report.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "is there a job available for every single person on the benefit" — she explicitly names his employment question and extends it to rising and youth unemployment.

acuity.statement: I also want to ask about whether her directive asking to apply sanctions more often has directly contributed to the recent statistics that came out that show that food insecurity is increasing in Aotearoa. This matters because people are often deprived of the means to survive when they’re being sanctioned—which also ties in with a subsequent question, which is whether she believes that the increase in the rate of food grants being declined has contributed to a higher rate of food insecurity experienced by children in this country under her watch.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated sanctions position directly, pressing it toward a consequence she did not address (food insecurity and declined food grants). It takes up the content of her claim rather than merely naming her, but it engages one declared position rather than rebutting her reasoning, and the surrounding call largely restates his own earlier unanswered question and opens unrelated emergency-housing material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "Our Government believes benefit sanctions should be fully applied to incentivise job seekers to fulfil their work obligations."

acuity.statement: The Treasury forecast under the previous Government was for unemployment to reach 5.3 percent. That is the continued forecast despite there being more challenging economic times than were originally anticipated. That is the good news. For the year in review, compared to the year previous, the youth unemployment rate went up 25 percent.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Helen White's specific claim that unemployment has risen to its highest level in years and that youth unemployment in particular is through the roof, and supplies figures against it — the Treasury peak forecast and the year-in-review youth rate movement. The content is shaped by what White said; a different preceding argument would have required a different answer. It falls short of 1.0 because it reframes the comparison onto the previous Government rather than fully answering the forward-looking question about what is being done.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "My alarm is raised by the fact we’re now up to our highest level in many years" and "youth unemployment is through the roof in Auckland".

acuity.statement: Which brings me back to the previous Labour member Helen White’s question around the Public Service and the front line. She will remember that a big part of the savings exercise for Budget ‘24 was protecting the front line, and one of the really important things, which is about ensuring the balance of rights and responsibilities for those on the jobseeker benefit, actually means that the responsibility sits more fairly with the job seeker, and that is an example where, instead of a Ministry of Social Development (MSD) front-line worker having to chase a job seeker, now the responsibility equally sits with the job seeker.
acuity.explanation: Names and takes up White's front-line capacity question and offers a substantive response to one part of it — that the front line was protected in the savings exercise and that shifting obligations onto job seekers frees up staff time. But it engages only the framing, not the specific things she asked: how much MSD was affected by job cuts and what ground-level feedback says about capacity. Partial engagement that then returns to the Government's rights-and-responsibilities theme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "How much were they affected by job cuts?" and "I'm worried about the front-line capacity of MSD, full stop".

acuity.statement: I have a few questions around what Minister Potaka has said, because we still have questions that the Minister might be able to inform us on, in terms of where do some of these people go, and the impact of homelessness. That’s been one of the big questions that, Minister Potaka will know, has come from this side of the House. Is there any research, is there any data that can tell us about the impact on homelessness, and is there data in terms of the sanctioned regime, how it affects Māori in particular?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Potaka's answer — that applicants are moved into other accommodation instead of emergency housing — and presses it by asking where those people actually end up and for the evidence base, including the Māori breakdown. It engages one strand rather than the whole answer (the gateway settings, responsibilities framework and non-entitlement period go untouched) and then moves on to a prepared list of questions for the Minister in the chair, so it sits above a topic-only glance but short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "the team will try and figure out how we can move that person into private or other forms of accommodation rather than reverting to emergency housing"

acuity.statement: In terms of the Māori Trades and Training Fund, it was not rated but needs to be. In terms of the participation, 93 percent are Māori, and we’ve seen 75 percent had gained an employment outcome for the year 30 June 2024.
acuity.explanation: Supplies precisely the figures the preceding question asked for — Māori participation share, employment outcome rate, and the evaluation status of the fund — against the year under review. The answer would have to be different had Jackson asked something else, which is the deciding test. Not a 1.0 only because it gives the numbers and leaves the 'is the programme delivering' judgement implicit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "what feedback has he seen during the past year regarding Māori trade training, how many people have gone through the programme, how many Māori have progressed into work, and generally, if the programme is delivering?"

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around the number of children in poverty, well, actually the cost of living and the state of the economy is the significant contribution to that. That’s why our Government is focused on the cost of living.
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance put to her by offering a counter-causal account — cost of living and the state of the economy rather than her sanctions settings — which is a real if partial take-up of the claim. But it reframes the question from sanction-driven food insecurity to child poverty generally and then returns to the prepared cost-of-living line, so the specific causal link alleged is never addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "whether her request to increase the use of benefit sanctions has contributed to an increase in children facing food insecurity across Aotearoa"

acuity.statement: We too have been hearing out on the ground that there are pressures in front-line services. So we want to know: how are these pressures in front-line services impacting Māori communities, knowing that it’s our people that are those that are impacted the most?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the front-line capacity claim made in the preceding turn, corroborates it from her own sources and extends it along a new dimension by asking about the effect on Māori communities. That is engagement with one strand of the argument rather than the whole of it — the rest of her contribution (Te Pae Tata, iwi provider resourcing, Tiriti-based approaches) is prepared material she announces she is moving to, so a partial score is right.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "we have heard from MSD themselves that admits that the front line is 'oversubscribed'"

acuity.statement: I’d like to know, from the Minister, what are the initiatives that her Government has introduced to assist people? Not sanction—the opposite: to support and assist people to develop skills, to have training, to have financial support in order to be able to develop the independence and the requisite skills to be able to enable them to take up meaningful employment, and also to continue in those jobs and to hold down those jobs once they have already received them, and, as well as that, well-paying jobs—jobs that pay enough for people to live off.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and acknowledging that the sanctions changes have already been raised, which is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it. The question put — what positive employment support exists — is prepared material that would read identically whatever Upston or Kemp had just said, and it does not touch Upston's specific answer that the graduated sanctions system was unchanged as at 30 June.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Upston had just said "as of 30 June last year, there were no legislative changes, and the graduated sanctions system remains" and Kemp had asked about Te Pae Tata and iwi provider resourcing; this statement takes up neither, though it gestures at the debate with "Part of that has already been mentioned".

acuity.statement: In terms of the employment programmes and their effectiveness, Flexi-wage, effective; Mana in Mahi, effective; He Poutama Rangatahi, which was introduced by the previous National Government, effective.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked by naming the support-side programmes one by one with their effectiveness ratings, which is the content Andersen demanded rather than a restatement of the sanctions position. Slightly short of full marks because several of the programmes named predate this Government, so the specific challenge — what this Government has developed — is only partly met.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "What are the measures or the programmes that this Government has developed in order to assist people into employment, not just penalise them?"

acuity.statement: Just following on that Māori stuff, I appreciate that the Minister doesn’t want to repeat herself, but I just need to know—we did have a specific Māori employment programme that she’ll be aware of, so I just wanted to know from the Minister: we thought that we were on target with it—the Minister’s absolutely correct in terms of the number of Māori organisations out there, but we did have a specific Māori employment programme, as we had a women’s programme. Why was that discarded in the end? That’s the question.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the part of the Minister's answer that holds — that many providers are Māori organisations — and then isolates what it does not answer: the existence of a dedicated Māori employment programme and why it was dropped. Accepting part and disputing the remainder is the strongest form of engagement, and the question could not have been framed this way had Upston answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "so those employment programmes, many of them are delivered by Māori providers. I don’t have a list on me"

acuity.statement: So, to get the facts straight: the Minister may have been right when she said no legislative reforms have been passed under the year of review, but she did write to Ministry of Social Development (MSD) to ask them to implement sanctions more often, and she has introduced a traffic light system, which is why I asked, once again—which hasn’t been answered properly—whether her directive to increase benefit sanctions contributed to more children facing food insecurity.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the Minister's own answers directly — conceding one part of her claim ('may have been right when she said no legislative reforms have been passed') and disputing the rest by naming the non-legislative directives she did issue. The speech would have to change if she had answered differently. Marked down from 1.0 because the ministerial answer he engages is quoted by him rather than visible as a preceding turn in this window, so part of the engagement cannot be audited from the text supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston's answer that 'no legislative reforms have been passed under the year of review', quoted inside this statement; the only preceding in-window turn by her is 'There was no funding reduced for Māori employment programmes in Budget ‘24.'

acuity.statement: I’ve got two questions about targets—not at the back end, which is what the Hon Willie Jackson’s talking about, but at the front end. The first is regarding emergency housing. What do we know, what statistics have we got, about how long it’s taking for people to be placed in emergency housing when they first come and ask for it, in comparison to previous years?
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the right subject — the department under review — but they engage no part of the argument just made. There is a gesture at the surrounding debate ('not at the back end, which is what the Hon Willie Jackson's talking about'), which lifts it off the floor, but she does not take up the sanctions/food-insecurity line the previous speaker pressed, and the questions would read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that the Minister's own sanction directives contributed to children facing food insecurity, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I also wanted to ask the question once again on the relationship to emergency housing. Has everyone who has been rejected for emergency housing been deemed as not having a genuine need?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand the previous speaker opened — people being declined or turned away from emergency housing — and sharpens it into a testable question about whether every rejection reflected a genuine-need assessment. Partial rather than full engagement: he takes one strand of her questions and otherwise returns to recapping his own prepared lines.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'how many people are being turned away?'

acuity.statement: So in terms of the target, actually, the target in terms of the total number on the jobseeker benefit is more ambitious than just exits into work. In terms of the graduated sanctions regime, that remains the same and has remained the same in the year in review.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific claim put to her — that officials had recommended the target be about exits into work rather than a headcount reduction — by contesting the comparison directly ('more ambitious than just exits into work'), and then addresses the preceding speaker's traffic-light/sanctions point by stating the graduated regime is unchanged. The reply is clearly shaped by what was said before it. Short of 1.0 because it engages the characterisation rather than the officials' advice itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'the ministry initially recommended that the Government jobseeker target be about people leaving the benefit and going to work, rather than just a reduction in the numbers'

acuity.statement: Just further to the whole question around sanctions, it’s a tough area, this, because the Minister for Social Development and Employment feels that she’s repeating herself. But it’s incredibly important, given that so many of our communities are affected by sanctions, and so we need to get some feedback from the Minister in terms of the effect of sanctions and how the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) are treating many of our people at the coalface. So I’m asking the question, and I think it’s a different question: what is MSD doing to measure how the sanctions regime is working?
acuity.explanation: Builds on the exchange he has just heard: he registers the Minister's position that the sanctions regime is unchanged and that she is repeating herself, then deliberately shifts the ground to measurement of effect rather than design. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding answer rather than a rebuttal of its substance, so it sits mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: 'In terms of the graduated sanctions regime, that remains the same and has remained the same in the year in review.'

acuity.statement: We are very concerned about Māori beneficiaries, and we want to make sure that we are continuing to share their voices and concerns. Given 41 percent of the Ministry of Social Development’s clients were not receiving their correct income support, what measures are being implemented to improve accuracy, and how many Māori beneficiaries are being affected by these inaccuracies?
acuity.explanation: New prepared questions on payment accuracy, delivered on the right subject but engaging nothing in the turn before it, which pressed the Minister on whether she accepted her officials' advice about frontline capacity. Later in the same turn she signals the running theme ('I want to go back to food insecurities'), which is a reference to the debate rather than engagement with an argument in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March pressed whether the Minister agrees with MSD officials that frontline capacity is oversubscribed, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I’d like to ask about food security and family violence, in the last minutes of this debate. The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) do some incredible work actually giving funding for very important services in the food security area.
acuity.explanation: Opens two fresh lines — food security funding and the family violence strategy — in the closing minutes without taking up the frontline-capacity question put immediately before. On the matter under review, but indifferent to what it follows; the only lift is that food security is a theme other members have raised, not an argument she answers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March asked whether the Minister agrees with her officials that MSD's frontline capacity is oversubscribed, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. If I can just add to the questions about the cuts to community services, because I think it’s important. We are just a week away from the next Budget and we still do not have answers from the Minister for Children and from the ministry, from Oranga Tamariki, about last year’s Budget cuts to community service providers.
acuity.explanation: Prime explicitly picks up Carter's strand on cuts to community services and sharpens it into a specific unanswered demand about which contracts were cut or changed, so this part of her turn would read differently had Carter not raised provider capacity. But she engages the topic rather than any specific claim or figure of Carter's, and the remainder of the turn moves to her own prepared material on military-style academies — partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "in 2023-24, community providers consistently raised concerns about loss of capacity"

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask, first of all, a philosophical question. I’d like to know what the Minister for Children actually believes about the community organisations that we rely upon in this sector.
acuity.explanation: White is on the matter under debate — the community sector Oranga Tamariki relies on, which both preceding speakers raised — so this is not wholly unresponsive. But she signals new ground ("first of all, a philosophical question") and engages no claim, figure or argument from Carter or Prime; the pay-equity and workforce material that follows is prepared and indifferent to what preceded it. Gesture at the debate, hence 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime asked why the committee still has no information about which community-provider contracts were cut or changed, and this statement does not take that up; White opens new ground on the Minister's beliefs and on pay equity.

acuity.statement: In regards to the Pay Equity Amendment Bill: once it receives Royal assent, any future pay equity claims across the public sector will need to meet the new requirements of the Act, but any pay equity funding received by Oranga Tamariki this year or on previous years for social workers in the community, and iwi organisations, has been allocated. So in this financial period we’re talking about right now, the pay equity bill has not made any changes.
acuity.explanation: Chhour takes up the precise claim White made about last week's pay equity legislation and disputes its application, distinguishing future claims under the new Act from funding already allocated in this financial period. The answer would have to be different had White raised a different objection; she is engaging the content of the claim, not merely naming it. Not 1.0 because she addresses the bill's effect and leaves White's workforce-pipeline question untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "last week, we saw legislation in the House which cut away any settlements that those groups had made for pay equity"

acuity.statement: On the funding information that Willow-Jean was asking for, I understand that Oranga Tamariki is planning to publish the information on its spend on contractor services, broken down by service, in the coming months, once all the final contract adjustments have been completed for this financial year.
acuity.explanation: This directly supplies an answer to the specific request Prime pressed — the contract-by-contract spend information — naming her question and giving a timing and a reason for the delay. Squarely engaged with what was asked. Short of 1.0 because it answers the "when" and not Prime's further question about where reinvestment was made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "why do we still not have that information available to us about those contracts that were cut or changed in the last round?"

acuity.statement: So I’m weighing that up against the investment that also has been made in this financial year towards the military-style academies, and I wanted to ask: what has been the sacrifice to early prevention, such as those fast-track programmes, in the trade-off towards giving more resources towards things like military-style academies, which have been shown to have no evidence—to not work and to have failed in the past?
acuity.explanation: Paul extends Prime's military-style academy line by setting the same $30 million against prevention spending, so she is taking up a strand already in the room. But she opens by announcing a new line of questioning on youth offending, engages nothing in Chhour's immediately preceding answer, and the fast-track material is clearly prepared — one strand engaged, then prepared content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I also want to ask the Minister questions about the investment into the military-style academies, which is $30 million over four years"

acuity.statement: I just want to clarify that $30 million worth of funding has not gone into the military-style academies.
acuity.explanation: The entire turn exists to correct a factual premise in the question just put to her, taking the specific figure Paul used and denying it. Had Paul framed her question differently this reply could not have been given at all — the strongest form of engagement, a direct correction of a misstatement in the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "particularly around that $30 million that has gone into the military-style academy"

acuity.statement: Tēnā koe. I want to move to disabilities. With the transition of the disability support services to the Ministry of Social Development and the restructuring of Whaikaha into a stand-alone policy department, how will the ministry address concerns from the disability community about potential service-delivery issues, particularly for Māori with disabilities?
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by Upston immediately precedes, with checkable figures open to challenge, but the speaker announces a move to a different topic and engages none of it. The question is on a matter properly within the annual review, so it is prepared material on the right subject rather than wholly unresponsive; it would read identically whatever Upston had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston spoke about Māori unemployment, the 78 percent entitlement-accuracy figure and the family and sexual violence action plan, and this question does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: Since stopping the work on the wage subsidy, which would have enabled people earning under the minimum wage under the minimum wage exemption, has she started any work to look at alternatives that would’ve lifted the incomes of those disabled people to the equivalent of the minimum wage?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the disability-support thread Kemp has just opened and extends it to the minimum wage exemption, so there is a real gesture at the line of questioning in progress. But it engages no part of Kemp's actual question about service delivery under the Whaikaha restructure — it is a separate prepared question in the same subject area, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how will the ministry address concerns from the disability community about potential service-delivery issues" — Takutai Tarsh Kemp

acuity.statement: I’m going to ask a rangatahi homelessness question, and this actually came from our community in South Auckland, from Mā Te Huruhuru, who look after and focus on rangatahi homelessness. Their questions are: what is the Government doing to prevent rangatahi Māori from becoming homeless after they leave Oranga Tamariki care at the age of 18?
acuity.explanation: Openly reads in a pre-supplied set of questions from a community organisation on a new topic. Nothing in the preceding turns — Menéndez March's minimum-wage question or the dispute about unanswered questions — shapes a word of it; substitute a different preceding argument and this turn is unchanged. It is at least within the scope of the review, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March asked whether work had begun on alternatives to the minimum wage exemption for disabled people, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Is the Minister concerned that, under the period we’re reviewing, Māori have been disproportionately targeted by benefit sanctions?
acuity.explanation: A fresh prepared question that engages no part of the immediately preceding turn, nor the Minister's earlier answer on Māori unemployment and entitlement accuracy, which it could easily have pressed on. acuity.statement: The Minister of Police gave a rollicking speech earlier on, including a story about Ōpōtiki around gangs and how good they’re doing on it. acuity.responding_to: "Is it not correct that your policies have made water quality worse in this country?" — Steve Abel

acuity.responding_to: "the Minister has paused the ban and the work on the third tranche of the hard-to-recycle plastics. I’d like a comment on that, please." — Glen Bennett

acuity.explanation: Takes the answer just given and disputes its premise — that the work could not proceed — by asserting it was already on track, then presses the 'why allow it' question the answer left open. acuity.responding_to: "we have paused some of those plastics that industry did not yet have replacements for" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.responding_to: "46 percent of lakes larger than one hectare have Trophic Level Index scores indicating poor or very poor health" — Steve Abel

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "under her watch, we had to rush through some legislation around Otago Regional Council" — Glen Bennett

acuity.responding_to: "how many farms will no longer be required to have a freshwater farm plan under the Government’s proposed changes?" — Glen Bennett

acuity.responding_to: "did the Associate Minister for the Environment receive any analysis to support the decision that was made to reduce the number of farms subject to the freshwater farm plans" — Glen Bennett

acuity.explanation: Addresses each of the three specific items raised in the immediately preceding turn — Wai 262, section 4 and the ariki's recent comments — and routes the last of them to the Tongariro National Park negotiations, which is a substantive answer to a specific question. Held below the top band because she asked for his views on their importance to conservation and settlement, and he supplies awareness and process rather than engaging that question.

acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "I’d like to know his views on the statement that, recently, Ariki Sir Tumu Te Heuheu has made around Ruapehu and how important that is in terms of Treaty settlement."

acuity.statement: The “30 by 30” target is not a domestic legal obligation: it is global target. As I’ve said before, it’s aspirational for the globe to get to the 30 by 30. Now, there are biodiversity challenges—no one’s disagreeing with that, and I’ve outlined a number of projects that we have reinvested International Visitor Conservation and Tourism Levy and other funds into to ensure that we actually attack some of the key contributors to biodiversity loss; for example, getting rid of feral pigs and cats down at Maukahuka—the subantarctic islands.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the two specific things Radhakrishnan put to him in the immediately preceding turn: whether his 'aspirational, not a legal obligation' characterisation of 30 by 30 still holds (he restates and defends it directly), and whether he accepts there is a biodiversity problem and what he has done about it (he concedes 'biodiversity challenges' and names funded actions). acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "I would also like to ask him whether his comment that he made at Estimates around the “30 by 30” initiative being aspirational and not a legal obligation still holds"

acuity.statement: In 1846, when conflict broke out in the Wellington region, Ngāti Hāua tūpuna were targeted and punished not for wrongdoing but just for their presence, for their resistance, and for their identity. Te Rangiātea was sentenced to life imprisonment and died behind bars. Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu was hanged. Five others were exiled to Australia. These were the actions of a Government not seeking peace; they were acts of domination, they were acts of fear, and they were acts of injustice.
