But the substantive preceding turn was Helen White's, and nothing in his speech engages her case: the bus-drivers' contracting model, the lockout over toilet breaks, or the claim that the bill lets an employer deduct 10 percent for such action. He does not take up her explicit challenge ("Prove me wrong"), and closes with prepared commendation of the bill that would read identically whoever had spoken before. One strand engaged, the main argument left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What about badges? What about work to rule?" — Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: As the member said, this is about driving productivity. Partial strikes usually involve someone turning up to work and refusing to take part in key parts of the job, and, of course, that’s really disruptive. Under these changes, employers have the ability to respond to partial strikes proportionately.
acuity.explanation: Wedd follows Andersen's substantive second-reading speech and takes up one strand of it — productivity — explicitly naming it as the member's framing, and later counters Andersen's health/education examples by asserting that partial strikes themselves disrupt healthcare and education, and that the bill returns the law 'to how it was, which worked', which cuts against Andersen's 2018 restoration-of-balance argument. But she engages the topic rather than the specific claim: Andersen's central point was that the regulatory impact statement contains no evidence of a productivity effect and that banning partial strikes will drive escalation to full strikes, and Wedd neither addresses the RIS, the independent review panel's criticism, nor the badge/T-shirt freedom-of-expression contradiction, returning instead to prepared balance-and-fairness material. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There is no evidence, right throughout the regulatory impact statement, that this bill will have one iota of difference on productivity or on working." — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: We would like to see student representation in these newly independent polytechnics. This legislation doesn’t actually create any specific provisions for it. I echo the words of the previous speaker, Shanan Halbert, that it dilutes Māori representation. Not only does it dilute that but it also doesn’t ensure student representation. So we would like to see that on the table.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez takes up Halbert's specific claim about diluted Māori representation by name, adopts it, and extends it to a second governance gap (no student representation provisions). Much of the surrounding speech is prepared Green material on funding and asset sales, so the engagement is one strand rather than a sustained rebuttal — but the strand is pointable and the speech would read differently had Halbert not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "she’s diluted the representation of Māori within those polytechnics, despite the good work that the sector and iwi do together"

acuity.statement: It is also important to note that there has been talk from the other members about financial viability. We fully understand that financial viability is an important factor. Along with financial viability, academic rigour is needed as well as community engagement.
acuity.explanation: She names the financial-viability objection raised by the two preceding speakers, concedes it is a real factor, and then widens the test to academic rigour and community engagement — an engagement with the strand rather than a rebuttal of the specific claim that the bill contains no funding answer. Pointable partial engagement, not a glance, but she does not meet the figures-and-costings point head on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "no solutions as to how the sector can become financially viable long term" (and Francisco Hernandez on institutions entering the reform with debt)

acuity.statement: What this bill does is reform New Zealand’s vocational education system by making an amendment to the Education and Training Act. It disestablishes Te Pūkenga, and it re-establishes a network in the regions. New Zealand First is very in favour of doing this, because we feel that, in the regions, they will be able to more effectively address the needs and do it more efficiently and effectively.
acuity.explanation: Prepared support on the right subject. The speech describes what the bill does and endorses decentralisation; it would be word-for-word identical whatever the three preceding speakers had argued, and the only reference to another member is thanks to the Minister for her overview, which engages no content. On topic, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Halbert argued the bill provides no costings or funding certainty and Hernandez asked whether institutional debts would be written off; this statement takes up neither, and only thanks the Minister for her overview.

acuity.explanation: Andersen takes up the one strand Bates conceded — the uncertainty caused by disestablishing Te Pūkenga — and turns it into the charge that the Government cancels without a replacement plan. She does not engage his specific claims that the Opposition created the mess or that money was wasted on centralisation, and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on other cancellations (construction projects, Kāinga Ora, Callaghan). Topic engaged, specific claim not, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know and I appreciate that there are people around New Zealand who are challenged at the moment because of some uncertainty created by the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga" / "They created this mess, and we said we would fix it" — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: As a member of the Education and Workforce Committee, I look forward to looking at the details of this bill and doing what we can to make sure that it is a judicious process, that it is taken through all the required rigour, and that we see a decent plan as it’s coming forward, because vocational education is vital for our economy.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows a detailed critique (no provision for workforce development councils, ministerial power to establish polytechs with limited consultation, Māori representation only "as far as is reasonably practicable") and engages none of it. The phrase "that we see a decent plan as it's coming forward" is a glance at Andersen's no-plan charge rather than an answer to it, and the rest is prepared support for the bill that would be identical whoever had spoken before. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And now we have this bill which disestablishes Te Pūkenga with no plan as to what’s going to happen" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.explanation: Goldsmith takes the specific factual premise Helen White advanced in the immediately preceding turn — that sexual offenders often have multiple victims, which she used to argue for retaining judicial discretion — accepts it, and turns it into a reason for the opposite conclusion: that permanent name suppression prevents those very victims from warning others. The speech would have had to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument. It is not a full 1.0 because he does not engage the amendment actually on the Table or the Law Society's listed exceptional circumstances, and the remainder of the turn is prepared material on the policy rationale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "The reality is that sexual offenders often have more than one victim, and they are often intergenerational victims in a family, they are often sisters, for example."

acuity.statement: I do—I do have the detail. Would you like me to talk to it? I’ll talk to the detail. The job losses are happening, Mr Bates, in the following programmes: engineering, beauty therapy, construction, applied science, social services, music, entertainment and events technology, photography, early childhood education, and some business programmes as well.
acuity.explanation: Bates interjected to challenge whether she knew the detail of the UCOL job losses; she takes that exact challenge up and supplies the programme-by-programme list asked for. The passage would not exist, and could not have been written in advance, had Bates not put that question — the strongest form of engagement with what was just said. (Scored on engagement only; the precision of the list belongs to Specificity and its accuracy to Veracity, neither of which is scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But where are the jobs? Do you know the detail?" — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: Te Pūkenga has been a failed experiment—a $300 million failed experiment. That’s what it’s cost the New Zealand taxpayer. But more importantly, it’s cost the students of New Zealand the opportunity in the regions of New Zealand to get a good vocational education.
acuity.explanation: He follows immediately on Boyack and speaks to the same subject, Te Pūkenga, but only counter-asserts the contrary verdict rather than engaging any part of her case — he does not touch her account of the ITO/polytechnic competitive model, the apprenticeship employers who told her not to change it, or the programme closures she listed. The speech would read identically whatever she had argued, so it sits in the prepared-material band with a gesture at the debate (0.3), not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What we did with Te Pūkenga was actually smooth that across and get these two sectors to work together finally." — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: Those are my two questions. The first one is whether clause 5 of the bill, increasing the penalty from 14 to 20 years, is to be consistent with the Crimes Act 128B.
acuity.explanation: White had just put a specific question to the Minister about whether the bill closes the under-12/over-12 charging gap. Xu-Nan is squarely on the same part of the same bill, and even touches the under-12 threshold, but he takes up none of her argument about the incentive to charge a lesser offence — he puts his own prepared clarifications instead, noting he was not on the Justice Committee. On-subject prepared material with a gesture at the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d ask the Minister of Justice if he can explain what the purpose of this part is in his view" — Helen White

acuity.statement: In terms of aligning the penalties: sexual violation has a maximum penalty of 20 years’ imprisonment, whereas sexual connection with a child has a maximum penalty of 14 years. We didn’t think that that distinction was appropriate, so one of the things that the bill does is increase the maximum penalty to 20 years of imprisonment to align with sexual violation.
acuity.explanation: This is a committee-stage reply, not an oral question, so Acuity applies. He takes the member's specific proposition — that the 14-to-20-year increase is there to align with the sexual violation penalty — confirms it, and gives the reasoning behind it. The answer is fully determined by the question asked and would have been different had Xu-Nan asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether clause 5 of the bill, increasing the penalty from 14 to 20 years, is to be consistent with the Crimes Act 128B" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: In terms of what happens when there are multiple victims, the court will treat each victim individually. Each victim will be asked to provide their decision on name suppression. If the victims’ decisions are the same, then the decision applies; if the victims’ decisions are not the same, the court must consider the victims and the individual charges separately. The offender may be named in relation to some convictions, but not in relation to other convictions.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Helen White's specific practical question about multiple victims in one family and supplies the mechanism the bill uses — per-victim decisions, and divergent decisions handled charge by charge. The answer would have to be different had she asked something else. Not full marks because her second question (the open-justice/non-disclosure-agreement parallel) is left unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "What happens when you’ve got two people in a family—or, actually, multiple victims, historic victims, etc.—and actually, there’s only one complainant"

acuity.statement: The Minister of Justice made the comment that it is at the discretion of the Attorney-General to conduct that vet. That was the case on the introduction of the bill. What is unique in this case is that we have an amendment to the initial bill which is quite significant.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's just-stated justification and does something with it: concedes it held at introduction, then shows it does not cover the later amendments, and converts that into two specific questions (did he request advice; did he conduct a section 5 analysis). The speech would be materially different had Goldsmith answered otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the Crown Law Office obviously vets Ministry of Justice bills for the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, and they do that at their discretion"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Well, I can give the member the answer that we thought four months was the appropriate length of time.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn put two specific, answerable questions; the reply engages no part of either, offering instead a one-line statement about a timeframe. It is at least within the bill under debate, so not a 0.0, but nothing in it depends on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters asked whether he requested New Zealand Bill of Rights Act advice and whether he turned his mind to a section 5 analysis, and this reply takes up neither — it states a view on a four-month period she did not raise.

acuity.statement: Yes, I can assure the committee and the member that I have considered those risks, and I acknowledge that they are risks and no system can be designed that is perfect, and the current arrangements, of course, bring an enormous number of risks as well that people who have been convicted of a sexual offence and can’t be named—that of course brings enormous emotional consequence and pressure on the victim, who can’t tell their story and can’t warn others and has their story supressed by the courts.
acuity.explanation: Andersen's turn was a list of unintended consequences, asking whether the Minister had turned his mind to them. Goldsmith answers that question directly, concedes the risks are real rather than denying them, and sets against them the countervailing risk in the status quo — the suppressed victim who cannot tell her story. The speech would be different had Andersen argued something else: he accepts her framing of 'risk' and then disputes the balance. Not 1.0 because several of her specific strands (removal of appeal rights, discharge without conviction, the layperson without access to counsel's submissions) are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "I think it’s only right that we can be reassured that he has turned his mind to all of those potential consequential risks that could actually make life more difficult for victims of crime."

acuity.statement: I’m just looking here at new section 200(8)(b), inserted by clause 6A. I think it’s a great day when we can come together and really look at how we protect children, how we protect victims of sexual violence. I’m just really interested to know if the Minister of Justice could talk us through the process of when the court is satisfied that a complainant has been contacted to find out whether they actually want this name suppression lifted or not.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith had just argued that no young victim has to engage, and that on balance the change serves the greater number of victims. Carter takes up no part of that: she opens a fresh line on the contact process in new section 200(8)(b). There is a gesture at the shared business of the committee ('a great day when we can come together'), and the question is squarely on the clause under debate, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero — her speech would have been identical whatever Goldsmith had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith argued that nobody has to make a decision in this space and that on balance the change serves the greater number of victims, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Just in answer to that, my advice is that “reasonable efforts” is established in case law. There is not a precise date—you know, you’ve got 15 days or 20 days. Each case can be dealt with on a case by case basis by the courts, but there is sort of a broad precedent around what that refers to.
acuity.explanation: Carter asked exactly one thing — what 'reasonable efforts' means and how much time counts — and offered candidate periods. Goldsmith answers that precise question, and answers it in her own terms: he addresses the duration point directly ('there is not a precise date'), echoes the kind of figure she was reaching for, and locates the standard in case law applied case by case. Delete her question and this reply makes no sense; substitute a different question on the same clause and it would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "how much time is considered reasonable? Is it three months? Six months? A year? Three years? What is considered reasonable effort?"

acuity.statement: I do want to talk, also, about this name suppression issue. It is a difficult issue and I do want to recognise the intent of empowering victims and giving them agency over this question. I’m interested in what New Zealand Bill of Rights Act analysis was done around this amendment, because it was a late amendment.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up one strand of the Minister's case — the empowering-victims rationale Goldsmith advanced as the justification for the change — names it accurately and concedes it, before turning to his own prepared line on the Bill of Rights Act and disproportionate punishment. He does not engage the answer immediately preceding his (the case-law meaning of 'reasonable efforts'), and the BORA question would have been asked regardless of what was said before it. Partial engagement: pointable, but one strand only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "it provides the best way for the greater number of victims of sexual offending be able to tell their story and to warn others"

acuity.statement: I have two questions for the Minister of Justice, on clause 6A, new section 200(9)(b)(ii). I think a lot of that does touch on it, and I want to, first, acknowledge Labour’s concern, particularly around the fact that there is no lower or bottom age limit on the victim being consulted and, potentially, we’re placed in a position where children are able to make these sorts of decisions.
acuity.explanation: He points precisely at Andersen's no-minimum-age objection and endorses it, which shows he was listening, but he does nothing with it — no development, no new evidence, no response to Goldsmith's answer that young victims need not engage at all. The acknowledgement is a bridge into two questions of his own on subsection (9)(b)(ii) that would have been asked whatever had preceded them. Engagement is real and pointable but shallow, so below the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "it’s important to point out that there’s no bottom age limit on when victims would be consulted"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I thank the Minister for Racing for the response around that. I think that is important because it is something that did come through the process around allowing the chief executive to basically pursue some of that information.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's answer and identifies the specific strand it bore on (the chief executive's ability to pursue information), accepting it before moving to his own prepared material on clause 8. Partial engagement — he names what was answered but does nothing with the Minister's reasoning about lacking evidence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "All we are saying is we don’t have the evidence for that yet. There may come a time yet when we’ll have to, but I don’t think that time is now."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’ll just take the opportunity to ask the Minister for Racing a very quick question relating to sporting codes. One of the things that did come up during select committee was submissions from sporting bodies around how they are able to access funding and that there was, they felt, some discrepancy there.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (Part 1 of the bill and the select committee's submissions) but engages no part of the preceding argument; the question would read identically whoever had spoken before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere had just argued that the bet-refusal criteria in clause 8 should sit in primary legislation rather than regulations, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: Can I say, experience is a funny thing. I can recall when the sporting organisations wanted to get off the board because they were in a full-scale fight amongst each other, and in the end they decided maybe they’d be better served with none of them on it. That’s the truth.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the submitters' request for mandated sporting representation on the board and answers it with the history of why those bodies left the board. Not the full question (the distribution formula goes unanswered), but the reply is unmistakably shaped by what Boyack asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "They also wanted it actually to be written into regulations about requiring representatives of Sport and Recreation New Zealand or sporting organisations to be represented on the board."

acuity.statement: The other thing is—if I could answer the first inquiry—yes, you’re right about clause 8, but we have moved the concerns that the Governance and Administration Committee had into the regulation powers and left them open for consideration at the time we acquired the evidence to sustain such a statement as was being made by the select committee at the time.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — confirms the Amendment Paper's effect and gives the reason the criteria sit in regulation powers rather than primary legislation (insufficient evidence as yet to lock in the select committee's position). The response could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "our perspective is that that criteria needs to be in legislation. Ideally, we would like to see it in the primary legislation, but if it’s going to be in the regulations, well, we can certainly live with that."

acuity.statement: One would be looking at clause 8 and when bets may be refused. We had a number of submissions that actually talked about the assumption—but it’s only an assumption because they weren’t given the reasons—that some bettors were just too successful. I want to be assured that by amending the refusal to accept all or any part of a bet from an individual, any other grounds would not include just being the winning bettor.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the clause 8 amendment the Minister had just described and presses it on a different strand — whether the widened refusal grounds could capture winning bettors. Engages the subject of the preceding answer rather than the Minister's specific claim about regulation powers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "yes, you’re right about clause 8, but we have moved the concerns that the Governance and Administration Committee had into the regulation powers"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, for the opportunity to be able to ask some questions. Whilst I am a member of the Governance and Administration Committee, I only listened to some of the contributions from different submitters—certainly with the racing. I want to draw the attention of the Minister for Racing to clause 9, in terms of the department who will monitor the compliance.
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the right bill but indifferent to the preceding turns; the contribution would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before her, though it stays within the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown had just asked about clause 8 refusal grounds and the confidentiality of the codes' agreements with the TAB, and this statement moves to clause 9 monitoring without taking any of it up.

acuity.statement: As for Labour talking about some certainty around a haste to effect Governance and Administration Committee intent, yes, there is a lot of haste to do that. The TAB was asked, “Do you not foresee that they might go to select committee and then”—what’s the word?—“go rogue and go down their own pathway?” They said no; they thought they would see the common sense of a very balanced, cross-party, bipartisan-generated paper, and if they had an intent they might ask them to come along and make a further submission.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise request Utikere made — the Minister's expectations about the speed of the policy/regulation work giving effect to the committee's intent — names it as the question being answered, affirms it, and then supplies the underlying account of why the TAB did not anticipate the committee's change. The passage would be different had Utikere asked something else; it is built around his specific ask rather than around prepared material. Not 1.0 because the answer concedes 'a lot of haste' without supplying any timeframe, which is the part of the question with content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "I do think it would be helpful if he was able to give some certainty around what his expectations would be, as racing Minister, around the haste within which the TAB would be expected to undertake"

acuity.statement: As for the disbursement of profits, well, you see, the sporting codes originally asked for confidentiality. I find it very confusing, because over the years there’s been such a disparity. First of all, they wanted to all be on the distribution group, then they found they were at loggerheads so often that it wasn’t worth it. They wanted to get off it and leave it to the then established committee, and, as a consequence, aspects of the confidentiality remained.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what was put to him — why the funding of national sporting organisations is opaque — by explaining that the codes themselves sought the confidentiality, which is a genuine answer to the 'shrouded in mystery' charge. But the specific question Utikere asked him to respond to was the codes' call for a guaranteed seat on the TAB board and the ministerial appointment power, and that is not taken up here; the passage then moves into the history of tobacco sponsorship. Topic engaged, specific question not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "those national sporting organisations who do receive an element of funding, and, as Celia Wade-Brown has said, that’s somewhat shrouded in some mystery"

acuity.statement: I’ve got a quite specific one about what recourse is there for a bettor who feels they’ve been unjustly refused or restricted? It’s pretty clear, the grounds that TAB will exercise that refusal. But where a bettor thinks they have been unjustly refused, what are their options?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the thread the Minister had just been discussing — bettors who are 'so much better than others' and the circumstances in which the TAB refuses or restricts them — and presses it one step further to the bettor's remedy, noting what the Minister had made clear ('It’s pretty clear, the grounds that TAB will exercise that refusal') before identifying the gap left unanswered. It extends the exchange rather than rebutting the Minister's reasoning, and the recourse question would have been asked much as it is whatever Peters had said about lucky punters, so it sits short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "some being better than others, well, there’re some who are so much better than others"

acuity.statement: Even the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs in the past has acknowledged that it is unusual to intervene in a case before the courts—that the banks potentially broke the law and consumers should have the right to challenge them for it. Yet, the Government is taking this away from consumers by applying this bill retrospectively. I think this talks a lot about the Government’s priorities. As the member to my right, Arena Williams, said in her speech, this is coming off the back of a really, really busy media cycle just before the Budget—key distraction politics and poor lack of engagement on the ground with affected parties as well.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding speech — Williams' claim that the bill was timed to be buried in the pre-Budget news cycle — naming her and endorsing it, and adds the "poor lack of engagement" point to it. But he does nothing further with her argument: he does not develop, test or extend her retrospectivity reasoning, and the rest of the turn is parallel prepared material on the same bill (the Commerce Commission settlements, the late addition of retrospectivity) that would read identically whatever she had said. Partial engagement that is pointable, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "we will change things behind closed doors and hope that nobody notices when we introduce it a couple of days before the Budget"

acuity.statement: I mean, people never stop trying to avoid the system, and the truth of the matter is that the products could be—because of improper or negligently established betting systems—the whole thing could be unprofitable, just like that.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked a precise question about where the onus sits in clause 16A and whether a deterrent is needed for individuals. Peters takes up one strand of it — that individuals will keep trying to evade the system — and generalises it into risk to the betting products, then moves into anecdote (the 1994 paper, the wine box, match-fixing, COVID sport) and finally concedes he has no answer. The strand engaged is pointable, but the specific onus/deterrent question is not addressed, so this sits at partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "whether he is satisfied that is the case, and that there is not a need for any deterrent for an individual who may be seeking to rort the system and try and place a bet through an online provider offshore"

acuity.explanation: This takes the specific example the Minister had just offered — a match-fixing allegation in India — and does something with it, putting to him that betting on cricket there is already illegal, which bears directly on what his example was meant to show. The question could not have been asked if the preceding turn had been different, which is the deciding test. acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "And you’ve seen, sadly, a recent allegation—dare I say it—in India, of it happening."

That is a real engagement with the claim rather than a pivot. It stops short of 1.0 because the actual thing asked for, whether specific advice was received from TAB or the department, is left unanswered, which is why Utikere immediately had to repeat it.

acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "has the Minister received any specific advice from either the TAB or, indeed, the department around the plausibility of that early implementation?"

acuity.statement: We have heard two members from that side, the Labour Party and the Green Party. I would say that, to that comment that there hasn’t been enough consultation on this bill, this bill is going to the select committee, as the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has said, the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That will be the opportunity for people to submit and have their say during the select committee process.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific objection made in the immediately preceding turn (inadequate scrutiny and consultation) and answers it directly with the select committee submission process. The passage would not exist, or would have to be rewritten, had the Green speaker not made that complaint.

acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "We look forward to engaging with officials on a piece of legislation that we can tell they didn’t receive adequate scrutiny and consultation on"

acuity.statement: There has been a lot of talk from those members about this bill being applied to any errors in documents between 2015 to 2019, and, yes, there is that retrospective element in here, but it is very important to note that it doesn’t take away the responsibility of banks.
acuity.explanation: Concedes part of the opposition case (the retrospective element is real) and disputes the consequence drawn from it, which is genuine engagement. acuity.statement: This isn’t just some minor tweak. This isn’t just some clarification. This is stripping the rights away from consumers. Under section 99 of the Act, as the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs admitted, it says that a bank cannot charge interest where they don’t accurately disclose the terms of the loan. We need clauses like that to keep banks in line.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes the immediately preceding characterisation of the bill as a proportionate tidy-up and denies it head-on, naming the specific provision (section 99, non-disclosure barring interest) that Hamilton had reduced to an envelope error, and giving the reason the clause exists. Substitute a different argument on the same topic and this passage would have to change, which is the test. Not a full 1.0 only because he rebuts the framing rather than engaging the proportionality mechanism Hamilton described.

acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: “This bill is a tidy-up, it’s appropriate, it’s proportionate, and therefore I commend it to the House.” (and his “return address on an envelope” example of disproportionate liability)

acuity.statement: Now, some members have raised questions over the retrospective element of this bill. So let me be clear: there is a method to what we are doing. As New Zealand Herald business editor Jenée Tibshraeny reported, the previous law forced banks to cancel and repay interest and fees for minor administrative errors that caused no harm—underlined.
acuity.explanation: Lu explicitly picks up the retrospectivity objection just raised and offers a justification for it, which is real engagement with one strand of the preceding turn. But she answers the topic rather than the specific claim: nothing here addresses accrued rights, litigation already on foot, the named case being halted, or Webb's point that the banks themselves deny insolvency risk, and she then returns to prepared material on the Government's reform programme.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: “The Legislation Design and Advisory Committee has an entire chapter devoted to non-retrospectivity and it makes it very clear that the most vile kind of retrospectivity is where rights have accrued and when litigation is on foot.”

acuity.statement: I think these changes do feel unnecessary, particularly in relation to making sure that the workforce in some of these places are well equipped and trained, but, at the same time, we also do think there is scope to unpack at the select committee the issue around communicating the price of services or products, and this needs to be worked in such a way that there is genuine accountability, as well, and that some of the reforms in this bill do not become a tick-box exercise, as the previous member mentioned.

acuity.responding_to: "These three bills should be debated separately and scrutinised separately at the select committee stage, but at the same time I think they all are, one way or another, interconnected" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: As Ryan Hamilton so eloquently said earlier, this is part of a “Holy Trinity” of financial reform, with this being the second bill that we have had the first reading on. It will go to the Finance and Expenditure Committee for scrutinisation over the next five or so months before it gets reported back, so the work has only just begun.

He names an earlier colleague's phrase ("Holy Trinity"), restates procedural facts about the select committee, digresses to constituents watching, and then recites the bill's own purpose clauses. The contribution would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said, though it is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle spoke immediately before about the FMA's new on-site inspection powers and about reducing compliance costs, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: What’s pretty apparent, having heard the speeches from the other side of the House, is they don’t actually know what the conduct of financial institutions (CoFI) legislation does. They just know that it’s something to do with the consumer and finance and insurance sector. What CoFI does is it puts the consumer at the centre of the regulatory framework of financial institutions, and, in fact, in the election campaign, Andrew Bayly said that he was going to do away with it.
acuity.explanation: Webb's speech is shaped by the two government speeches he follows: he characterises what they said, supplies the content about CoFI he says they omitted, and then directly contests their central proposition about compliance costs and a single regulator. Substitute a different government argument and this speech would have to change. The engagement is adversarial, which is high acuity, not low; whether the characterisation of his opponents is fair or the inference sound is a matter for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "In summary, by reducing compliance costs, streamlining regulation, and enhancing the FMA’s oversight, this legislation will foster a robust and efficient financial sector." — Webb takes up exactly that claim about what the regime does and what lowering compliance costs means.

acuity.statement: I just wish to come back to what my colleagues said, which was that the Financial Markets Authority does have good people in there, but this is actually about making sure they’ve got the right processes and that we’ve got the right processes in the financial sector, so that it runs efficiently for the benefit of consumers and for the businesses, as well.
acuity.explanation: One strand of the preceding speech is genuinely taken up: Bidois concedes the point about the FMA's people and redirects it to processes rather than personnel, which is a real, if brief, engagement. He does not touch Webb's actual objection — that a single regulator and single licence are wrong for a diverse industry — and the rest reverts to the prepared "Holy Trinity" line and a commendation, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Now, the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) does do a good job. It has got good expertise in there, but we’re not sure that moving to things like having a single regulator or a single licence is the appropriate thing in a very diverse industry" — Bidois picks up the FMA-expertise concession (misattributing it to his own colleagues) and answers it.

acuity.statement: We also had reference in some people’s speeches to simplifying the requirements, and we’re getting used to this simplification. It’s simply cuts, and we’ve had a lot of them from this team. One of the things I think is really dangerous in this bill is the removal of training and monitoring—so removing the requirements around legal obligations and removing the requirements about regular reviews of fair conduct, which, ultimately, really places consumers at risk.
acuity.explanation: Davidson quotes back the government speakers' own framing and does something with it: he names the specific provisions he says that simplification amounts to and argues the inverse of their conclusion. That is real engagement with the preceding claims. It is only partial, because the bulk of the contribution — the Saturday-sport analogy and the loan-shark material he says he used in an earlier debate — is prepared and indifferent to what was actually said before him.

acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "In summary, by reducing compliance costs, streamlining regulation, and enhancing the FMA’s oversight, this legislation will foster a robust and efficient financial sector." — Davidson takes the government's "simplifying the requirements" and "administrative burden" framing and recasts it as removal of training and monitoring obligations.

The speech asserts the opposite case as prepared text and would be word-for-word the same whoever had preceded her. It stays on the bill, so it is not a 0.0.

acuity.statement: So this is something that is incredibly important. However—and I think this is something that the previous speaker, Arena Williams, alluded to as well—what we’re fundamentally looking at in this bill is allowing more executive power and regulatory-making power for the Minister. I think this is something that is going to be really important to flesh out during the select committee stage when we’re looking at this—the scope of such executive power and how it can be used.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding Labour speech — the new regulation-making power and where it should sit — and develops it rather than merely naming it, extending to who should scrutinise it (the Regulations Review Committee), what criteria bind the Minister, and the risk of politicising board disqualification. He also picks up her class-action point. Not a full 1.0 because he does not dispute or test her reasoning and much of the surrounding speech is prepared description of the bill, but the speech would plainly have been different had she argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "it will be very useful for the committee to turn its mind to where that appropriate power would sit, whether that would be with the Minister or with the chief executive"

acuity.statement: It seems like of the three bills we’ve now got some support across the House for this bill, which—I think this has already been outlined—is looking to improve the financial dispute resolution aspects of our financial services sector. I think we should get this off to the select committee as quickly as possible so it can meet up with the other two bills and get the work under way of hearing submissions.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns with concrete arguments preceded it. The speech is on the matter under debate and gestures at the preceding turns by noting cross-House support and that the bill's purpose "has already been outlined", but engages no part of either argument: the questions put about executive power and consumer rights go unanswered. Noting that others support a bill is not engaging their content, so this sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams and Lawrence Xu-Nan both questioned the scope of the Minister's new regulation-making power and Williams raised the extinguishing of the ASB/ANZ class action, and this statement takes up neither; it registers only that support exists across the House

acuity.statement: This bill gives improved oversight of the scheme’s providers, which is going to be very important, and it’s effective in partial governance of those scheme boards that this bill was set up so that it’s efficient. So, on that note, New Zealand First will support this. We look forward to the submissions with the other two bills that make this a tranche of three, actually seeing how they all interconnect and hearing from submitters.
acuity.explanation: Eligible and on-topic — it describes the bill's oversight and board-governance provisions, which is exactly the subject matter in dispute — but it is indifferent to what preceded it. The immediately prior speaker had just questioned whether Ministerial power over board membership and disqualification could be politicised; this speech commends that oversight as "very important" without acknowledging the objection. The reference to seeing how the three bills interconnect is close to Williams' scrutiny point but reads as prepared, so there is a glance at the debate and no engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued the bill's core effect is to hand the Minister executive and regulation-making power over scheme boards, and this statement praises that same oversight provision without taking up the objection

acuity.statement: As has been canvassed with the previous two bills, this is the third leg in the trinity of reforms that we are putting through the House and sending off to select committee for extra scrutinisation over the coming months for the House to report back. acuity.explanation: Eligible — four substantive turns, two of them raising specific objections, precede it. The speech would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said; the backward reference is to the earlier bills' debates, not to any argument in this one. It is a commendation that could be delivered on any of the three bills, so it belongs at the bottom of the unresponsive band; not 0.0 only because it does identify this bill's place in the package and the select committee stage ahead.

acuity.statement: Simplify, remove undue compliance costs, and improve outcomes for consumers—that’s really the purpose of this bill. It’s very simple: an improved oversight of the approved dispute resolution scheme performance, which is fantastic. As my good colleague said, robust scrutinisation is what we’re all about.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition turn that raised specific, answerable objections (ministerial appointment of reviewers, timing of reviews, the bounds of delegated rulemaking). Hamilton engages none of them: he restates the bill's purpose in prepared terms and picks up only the word "scrutinisation" from the previous speaker's joke, which is a reference rather than engagement with content. The speech would read identically whatever Webb had argued, so it sits in the low band, lifted off the floor only because it is squarely about the bill under debate and glances at the exchange that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that ministerial appointment of reviewers, ministerial dictation of review timing and delegated rulemaking threaten the independence of the dispute resolution schemes, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: You know it’s getting close to 10 o’clock when people start reading dictionary definitions and doing accents. We are now getting into the third bill of the “Holy Trinity”, and it has been a little bit like Groundhog Day. It has been a little bit like Groundhog Day—it has been a little bit like Groundhog Day, because the same people have stood and made more or less the same speeches along the same points from the same part of the House, looking after the same part of financial transacting and transactions and financial services. They’ve been looking after the big guys. They haven’t been looking after everyday consumers and the people who rely on these financial services, sometimes not when everything’s going well and you’ve got, you know, a calm state of mind and the ability to assess the kinds of contracts that you’re signing.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the immediately preceding turn and contradicts it: Hamilton's stated purpose was improved outcomes for consumers, and Davidson answers that the government speakers have been looking after "the big guys" and not everyday consumers who rely on these services. But he disputes the characterisation rather than the substance — no engagement with the oversight provisions themselves — and then moves to his own prepared material about correspondence from a law lecturer, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "Simplify, remove undue compliance costs, and improve outcomes for consumers—that’s really the purpose of this bill."

acuity.statement: I am in full, strong support of the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Amendment Bill, because this bill is about one thing: protecting Kiwi consumers by making our financial dispute resolution schemes more effective, more independent, and more accountable.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one, two of them critical and both pointing at the same issue — the independence of the schemes and how much say the Minister gets. Lu's contribution is an unmodified summary of the bill's three provisions and a commendation; it contains no acknowledgement of, or answer to, anything said before her, and would have been word-for-word the same whoever had spoken. It is at least on the bill under debate, so it is not a zero, but there is no gesture at the debate to point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued the bill's backers have been looking after "the big guys" rather than everyday consumers and that the bill requires a lot of scrutiny, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: One day to go; one day to go until this Government’s second Budget. They’ve got a chance to talk about all the things that they’ve supposedly done and what do they talk about? Us. They don’t talk about them. They talk about Barbara Edmonds. A confident finance Minister doesn’t talk about her opposite; she talks about herself and what they’ve achieved and they didn’t mention that once and New Zealanders know exactly why: because they have done bugger all, because they’ve buggered up the Budget.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty takes up something real about the turn he follows — that Willis, on the eve of her own Budget, spent her whole speech on Barbara Edmonds and the Opposition rather than on the Government's record — and turns that choice into his argument. This could not have been written before hearing her. But he engages the fact of her subject matter, not the substance of any claim in it: he does not dispute that Hipkins walked back Edmonds' comments, does not defend the 50 percent debt cap position, and does not touch the surplus-by-2029 point, instead pivoting after the opening into prepared material on tax cuts and emergency housing. That is partial engagement — one strand taken up, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Members, spare a thought for Barbara Edmonds. She got thrown under the bus this week by no one less than her party leader." — Nicola Willis, whose entire take-note speech was an attack on Barbara Edmonds, Chris Hipkins and the Greens' fiscal plan.

Brewer takes up none of it. He names the Opposition only to dismiss them and then delivers prepared Budget-eve material on inflation, the OCR, mortgage repricing, Crown debt and tax policy. The speech would be word-for-word identical had Leary argued something entirely different, so the mention of the Opposition is a mere reference, not engagement. It scores above 0.0 only because it is at least about the Budget debate under way.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary spoke about pay equity cuts to mental health community workers, service closures and the Minister's handling of the psychiatry/psychology targets, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Try and defend that in your local electorate."

The passage would read identically whatever argument the Opposition had actually made, provided it was not about GDP growth, so it sits in the prepared-material band with a gesture at the debate.

They might learn a thing or two. I’m proud to be part of this Government that will deliver a pragmatic and sensible fiscal plan for the next year.

acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise shared by both preceding speakers — that the disallowance is the Government's act — by drawing the distinction between the Government and the committee and defending majority decision-making as the committee's normal practice. She engages no strand of Parmar's dilution-and-integrity argument, and nothing in this passage would have to change had Parmar argued something different about tikanga. That places it in the prepared-material-on-the-right-subject band rather than at 0.5, since there is no fragment of the preceding turn I can point at as engaged.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Parmjeet Parmar argued 'By mixing it, you’re diluting the significance of tikanga Māori and also compromising the integrity of the legal system' and this statement does not take that argument up.

acuity.statement: If we accept the facts, if we know that Māori disproportionately pass through the judicial system, then it becomes essential that those trained to operate within that system—our lawyers—are equipped with an understanding of tikanga Māori. Without such training, our systems will continue to oppress our people and exacerbate the reality that Māori are one of the most incarcerated peoples in the world.
acuity.explanation: Webb's immediately preceding turn argued that criminal law and sentencing cannot be taught without tikanga because half the prison population is Māori. Kapa-Kingi takes up exactly that strand and develops it, supplying the figures behind it (20 percent of the population, 37 percent proceeded against, 45 percent convicted, 52 percent of the prison population) and drawing the consequence for who must be trained. That is partial engagement, not full: she leaves untouched Webb's central argument — that the Regulations Review Committee has overstepped because Parliament delegated the rule-making power to the Council of Legal Education — and the bulk of her speech is prepared material aimed at earlier speakers not present in this window ('tikanga isn't really a thing', 'cultural indoctrination'). Scored on engagement only; the stridency of her language is a Civility question and the inference quality a Rigor question, and neither moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "If you’re going to teach criminal law and sentencing law, where half of our imprisoned population are Māori, and what the appropriate approach to a rehabilitative sentence might be, I don’t think you can do that without some appreciation of tikanga."

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to be speaking on what I’ve dubbed the “Takapuna Ice Cream Bill”, because that’s a fundamental change that takes place here. I would like to ask the member for North Shore some questions.

acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "these types of bills are very important for acknowledging local issues" and "Labour will be supporting this bill"

acuity.explanation: Van de Molen gestures at Watts' preceding answer — naming "the Minister's comments" and "the robustness of the consultation that happened" — but takes up no part of its content: he neither accepts, disputes nor builds on Watts' account of the Auckland Council consultation or of clause 5(2). He then pivots to an entirely new point of his own about the word "or" in clause 4. The contribution would read almost identically whatever Watts had said about consultation, so it sits in the band for prepared material on the right subject, with 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the reference to the preceding turn is explicit and the question is squarely about the bill under debate. Scored on engagement only — the clause-4 drafting point is a genuine and reasonably careful one, but that is rigor, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It was a very thorough consultation process undertaken by Auckland Council." — Simon Watts, whose turn immediately precedes this one and answered members' questions on consultation, the mayor, and unintended consequences under clause 5(2).

acuity.explanation: Watts had just explained that clause 5(2) removes the restriction preventing the building generating income, and that the envisaged use is a cafe. The question would have to be different had Watts described a different intended use, so it is genuinely shaped by the preceding turn, though it is a probe rather than a rebuttal of the reasoning.

acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "the changes in the building is governed by very restrictive legislation, which means it can’t generate income to, in effect, maintain and wash its own face" / "primarily, a cafe—that’s going to be the original purpose, and that’s what’s going to be done under clause 5(2)"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts spoke about the restrictive legislation governing the Takapuna Boating Club building and the cafe use envisaged under clause 5(2), and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Look, local bill, and I’m really proud to be able to shepherd this through the House." (also his "While this bill is tiny—it’s got one part and one associated schedule; all in, about 2½ pages")

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "The purpose is primarily going to be the cafe format."

acuity.statement: The Enabling Crown Entities to Adopt Māori Names Bill—and I do just want to start by going through, in case it wasn’t crystal clear, because there are some technical differences between different Crown agencies and departments, the intent of this bill, which, as I understand it, is to allow Crown entities to adopt a Māori name, as Mr Halbert just specified, on the recommendation of their Minister. acuity.explanation: Takes up the mechanism Halbert had just described and restates it, adding the technical distinction between listed Crown entities and Public Service departments that Halbert had only gestured at (section 23 of the Public Service Act). acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "The bill enables, on the recommendation of the relevant Minister, for Crown entities to adopt Māori names in addition to, or instead of, the names given them to them by the Acts that established them."

acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "But while a number of Crown entities already use a Māori name, these aren’t their legal names and are not currently recognised in New Zealand legislation."

Hernandez's contribution is prepared Greens caucus material on the right subject (support for the bill, the voluntariness of name adoption, colonisation) but engages no part of Costley's claim that the bill is redundant; the speech would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued. Scored on responsiveness only — the thanks to colleagues and the quality of the underlying case are not acuity.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley argued that Crown entities such as Sport NZ and the Walking Access Commission have already adopted te reo Māori names and changed their English names without any legislation, and this statement does not take that up

As we’ve actually heard from Mr Costley, this bill covers around 21 Crown entities.

Not a mere name-check — the speech would have to change if the preceding turn had argued something else. Marked down from 1.0 because it extends rather than tests the argument, and does not engage Hernandez's intervening point that adoption is voluntary and iwi-consulted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These Crown entities have already adopted Māori names; they’ve changed English names. To do that, nothing had to change in the law." — Tim Costley

Mid-band. The virtue-signalling jibe and the Peters quotation are not acuity questions.

acuity.responding_to: "almost without exception, they actually already all have a name in te reo Māori" — Tim Costley
