acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "We are enabling a system which will repeal the entire RMA system, which we plan to have introduced to Parliament later this year"

acuity.statement: Well, give them a bottle of water! I mean, that’s the whole point.
acuity.explanation: The interjection keys off the specific claim Brooking had just relayed about an aquifer drying up, answering it with a dismissive suggestion about bottled water. It engages the topic of the claim and nothing of the reasoning behind it, so it sits mid-scale: pointable engagement with one strand, no attempt on the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "there is a real worry that an aquifer is drying up and that things need to change"

acuity.statement: Oh, we’re hearing, “We don’t like that hierarchy. We don’t think that the health of the water is the most important thing.”, from the other side of the House. If that water is not healthy, then how can humans drink that water?
acuity.explanation: Grant McCallum interjected that the real issue is the order of priority — 'It's a hierarchy.' Brooking immediately takes up the hierarchy point and argues the substance of it: that the health of the water must rank first because drinkable water depends on it. The speech would read differently had he interjected something else, so engagement is high; that she restates his point in a more extreme form is a reasoning question, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s the order of priority. You know it. It’s a hierarchy." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: I’m hearing why didn’t we pass it? Those Acts were passed, and you, this Government, repealed those Acts, just as they repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers McCallum's interjected question by correcting the factual premise inside it — the legislation was passed, and it was this Government that repealed it. This is the clearest form of engagement: taking the specific challenge and disposing of it on its own terms rather than pivoting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why didn’t you pass it?" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Fresh water is life. Apparently we all agree on that, yet we take it for granted every day and we’re continuing to do that, it sounds like, in the House tonight.
acuity.explanation: Pham follows Brooking, who argued specific points — the removal of te mana o te wai from the freshwater national policy statement, the repeal of the three waters Acts and of the Natural and Built Environment Act. Pham gestures at the debate ('it sounds like, in the House tonight') but takes up none of those claims, moving instead to prepared material on plastic bottles and water-bottling consents. Her one responsive passage engages the Environment Committee chair's priorities argument, which is not a turn in this window, so it cannot be pointed at here; a gesture at the debate without engaging any part of the preceding argument sits in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking spoke about the removal of te mana o te wai and the repeal of the three waters and Natural and Built Environment Acts, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: We know things are pretty dire when the emergency departments at hospitals become the place of last resort for people with mental illness. That is exactly what is happening, thanks to this Government and a lousy Budget that put virtually no new money into mental health.
acuity.explanation: Leary follows a substantive turn by Verrall on the health Budget, so she is eligible. Her speech is on the matter under debate and glances at the same territory (emergency departments, Budget underfunding), which earns the top of the unresponsive band, but it engages no part of Verrall's actual argument — not the $1.3 billion/deficit arithmetic, not the pay equity and superannuation calls on Health NZ's baseline, not the capital expenditure case about Nelson, Dunedin and Wellington. The whole speech is prepared mental-health material that would read identically whatever Verrall had said, or had Verrall not spoken at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued that the extra $1.3 billion for health is 'almost entirely swallowed up by the health system's deficit, which stands at $1.1 billion', and this statement does not take that up; it only shares her general subject of emergency departments and Budget underfunding.

acuity.statement: When will he release MFAT advice on the impact of the $200 million gas subsidies on New Zealand’s free-trade deals?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the gas and petroleum investment policy Jones was defending and presses one specific angle (trade-deal exposure of the $200m fund), but engages none of his actual reasoning about investor confidence — it is a prepared line on the same subject with a glance at it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Government is rebuilding investor confidence, which, in the gas and petroleum sector, suffered a decline" — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: Can the Minister give the House any reason why a country would prefer inferior coal from another country rather than superior coal from its own?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the imported-coal strand of the answer immediately preceding and draws out a consequence from it, so the question would differ had Jones not raised imported coal; it is a friendly set-up rather than a rebuttal, but it is pointed at something actually just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "energy in relation to access to imported coal" — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: Does he think empowered clinicians in Middlemore emergency department would choose for patients to suffer harm on 43 separate occasions, as reported, or is it a sign of under-resourcing and indifference from the Government?
acuity.explanation: Re-runs her previous question with a new fact and engages no part of Doocey's answer about regional decision-making or the previous Government; it is on the matter under debate but indifferent to what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that’s why we wouldn’t have taken a wrecking ball to the health system in the middle of a pandemic" — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: If the Minister’s claim of record investment is correct, why were clinicians’ requests for merely $3 million in one of our largest emergency departments to ensure it was properly staffed turned down by the Government?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim just made — record investment — and turns it directly against the answer by setting it beside a $3 million request, so the question could not have been asked in this form had Doocey not just made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Government has put a record amount of funding into health: $16.68 billion over three years." — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: Is the Minister saying that a request for $3.6 million to address staffing in Middlemore Hospital’s emergency department was not made?
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the precise denial just given and asks him to own its implication, pinning the factual dispute; the question is wholly derived from the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Nothing was declined. What she is referring to is a quality report that went to a quality committee." — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: Well, why won’t he accept responsibility for under-resourcing in the department instead of passing the blame on to clinicians and management, when he’s the Minister of Health?
acuity.explanation: Does not contest the no-request denial that immediately preceded it and instead pivots to a general charge about ministerial responsibility; on the topic of the exchange, but it engages no part of the answer's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I have been advised that there was no request. It was a quality report sent to a quality committee" — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: How does the expansion of the early intervention scheme deliver for learners with additional needs?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one named strand of the answer just given (the Early Intervention Service expansion) and asks for its effect, so it is anchored to the preceding turn, but it engages no argument or claim in it beyond inviting elaboration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "extending it to the end of year 1, with hundreds of additional specialist teachers" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Is he concerned, then, that Treasury forecasts found the two primary policy changes noted in his Budget’s Child Poverty Report—which is lifting the Working for Families threshold and changes to the accommodation supplement—will not have a statistically significant impact on child poverty measures?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the matter Luxon answered and narrows it to the Budget's own named measures, which implicitly tests his claim that the Government is acting on child poverty; but it does not take up his growth-and-macroeconomics argument at all and reads as the next question in a prepared sequence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the way we do that is that we run a really good economy, and that means cutting the wasteful spending, lowering inflation, lowering interest rates" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Does he agree with Dr Bonnie Robinson, director of the Salvation Army’s Social Policy and Parliamentary Unit, who said, “This Budget shows a government content with maintaining the status quo in terms of child poverty. But when the status quo means children living in cars and families relying on foodbanks, that is simply not good enough.”, and, if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: Puts an external authority's verdict directly against the pride in the Budget he had just expressed, which is a partial engagement with the stance just taken; it still substitutes someone else's judgement for a rebuttal of his growth argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Well, I’m actually proud of this Budget, because what we’re doing is growing our economy so that we can lift wages for all." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Budgets are a choice. You can choose to build for the future or to cut. Make no mistake: in Budget 2025, National and the Government are cutting back plans for the rebuild of Nelson Hospital.
acuity.explanation: Boyack follows Peeni Henare in the same Budget debate and picks up two strands of his turn: his opening framing that budgets are about choices, which she restates as a choice between building and cutting, and the Nelson healthcare claim he explicitly handed to her ('my colleague will speak to that'). She then supplies the specifics his general claim lacked — bed numbers, theatres, the $500 million single building. This is genuine but partial engagement: she extends and evidences a colleague's strand rather than taking up and doing something with a specific argument or figure, and the bulk of what follows is prepared Nelson material that would have been delivered whatever Henare had said about Nelson.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'What we know in places like Nelson—and my colleague will speak to that—and other places that have an expectation of healthcare and delivery in their communities is that it is not being met, and nothing in this Budget has said to them that that promise will be delivered upon.'

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of Te Rōpū Kākāriki to speak about the health system—and a cup of tea that I shared with a rural GP in Northland.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive preceding turn by a different member (Davidson's conservation critique of the same Budget) was available. Lyndon opens a prepared speech on an entirely different portfolio and engages no part of Davidson's argument — no strand of it is picked up, disputed or extended. The speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Davidson had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band; it stays above 0.0 only because it is still about the Budget under debate. Scored on engagement alone: the health material itself is detailed and sourced, but that bears on specificity, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson spoke about Budget 2025's cuts to conservation — the Department of Conservation, Predator Free, the Nature Heritage Fund and species extinction — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Oh no, no, I’m really well aware of what’s going on in primary care and they feel ignored despite the little bit of funding that you’ve provided. I look forward to seeing what this Government’s going to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Foster's specific claim that the Government is already doing what she demands and that she has missed it, and answers that claim directly: she denies the imputation of ignorance and counters that primary care providers feel ignored notwithstanding the funding provided. That is a real engagement with the content of the interjection, not merely a reference to it, so it belongs above the unresponsive band. Held short of 1.0 because the rebuttal asserts rather than dismantles — no figure, programme or mechanism is set against Foster's claim — which is partial engagement with the strand he raised. The thinness of the counter is a specificity matter and is not double-counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s what we’re doing; you’ve missed it" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: That goes to the landlords, the renters, and everyone in New Zealand. That is real relief, driven by responsible and disciplined fiscal management.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan interjected twice to press that the mortgage-rate relief she was describing accrues to homeowners and landlords rather than renters. She does take up that strand directly — she inserts "and that also goes to renting" and then asserts the saving reaches landlords, renters and everyone — so the speech is visibly altered by the interjection. But she only names the category rather than engaging the substance of the objection (no account of why a landlord's lower costs would reach a tenant), then returns immediately to prepared Budget material. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Are they homeowners or are they landlords?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan (following his earlier "What about renters?")

acuity.statement: Possums, the thing that this Government loves: this Budget got rid of what the National Government established when it was last in Government. The John Key Government set up Predator Free 2050 Ltd. Then the Minister of Conservation was just the week or so before setting out objectives for Predator Free 2050, so maybe nobody had told him what was in the Budget.
acuity.explanation: Brooking follows Radhakrishnan, who raised the disestablishment of Predator Free 2050 Ltd mid-consultation as a conservation failing. Brooking takes up that specific item and does something with it: she points out it was a National (John Key) Government creation and that the Minister of Conservation had been setting out Predator Free objectives weeks earlier, drawing out the consequence that the Minister was not told. The passage would have to change if the preceding speaker had not raised Predator Free. It is not a full 1.0 because she extends an allied speaker's point rather than engaging a contested claim or figure, and then returns to prepared material on utes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the disestablishment of Predator Free 2050 Ltd in the middle of a consultation that this Government is running about Predator Free" — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: So what happens the next week when the Budget rolls around? Well, anyone listening closely to the House when the Budget dropped at 2 p.m. on the Thursday will have heard me give an audible gasp when I read a Newsroom story on Twitter—because that got to me faster than the Budget being delivered out—that $12 billion was looking to be saved from pay equity. Yet the Prime Minister had the gall to say to us just the week before, “No, no, no. This has nothing to do with pay equity.” It is astounding.
acuity.explanation: Radhakrishnan's immediately preceding turn opened on the claim that Budget 2025 was funded by cancelling 33 pay equity claims. Brooking takes up that same strand and supplies corroborating material (the $12 billion pay-equity saving reported on Budget day, against the Prime Minister's denial a week earlier). It engages the strand rather than any specific claim or number Radhakrishnan made, and most of the surrounding material is clearly prepared, so this sits at a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal or correction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Budget—Budget 2025—was funded by the choice that this Government made to cancel 33 active pay equity claims." — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: Now, we did hear the previous Green speaker, Kahurangi Carter, talk passionately about energy, and I do want to talk about energy. Basically, the comments were: well, where does gas fit in this? Of course, it’s in the negative mind-set from the Green Party and my mind-set is absolutely to the positive.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod names the immediately preceding speaker and claims to be answering her, but the argument he ascribes to her ('where does gas fit in this?') is not one she made: Carter's speech was entirely about child welfare, Oranga Tamariki funding, oversight cuts and child poverty targets. None of her specific claims — the 37 percent advocacy cut, the $182 million back-office saving, the prevention share, the 2028 targets — are engaged anywhere in his turn. Naming the previous speaker as a springboard to prepared Taranaki energy material is a mere reference, not engagement. It sits above 0.0 only because the speech is at least about the Budget under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter spoke about Vote Oranga Tamariki ('the Minister has cut funding to independent advocacy services by 37 percent from $6.37 million to $4 million') and child poverty, and this statement does not take it up — it attributes to her a speech about energy and gas that she did not give.

acuity.statement: I note that many of the Government members that have stood up and made contributions in the Chamber today, including senior Ministers and including the Prime Minister when he stood up and made his contribution a week or so ago, all they could talk about was Labour. I say that’s because they know that this is one of the most unpopular Budgets this country has seen in decades.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows Webb's substantive turn and is plainly in the same Budget debate, but she engages no part of what he actually argued — no figure, no clause, no claim of his is picked up or carried further. What she offers is prepared material on the right subject, with a general gesture at the debate (characterising other members' contributions as being only about Labour), which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at a partial engagement; 0.3 because the gesture at the day's debate is there. Her speech would read identically whatever Webb had said, so the deciding substitution test fails.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that the Budget funds a $200 million gas subsidy by halving the KiwiSaver contribution, cutting Best Start and taking $12 billion from working women, and that the Ministry for Regulation gets 5 percent a year while Te Ao Mārama is cut — this statement takes up none of those arguments.

acuity.statement: Madam Speaker, this is a “BS Budget”. It is a “BS Budget” because it takes $12.8 billion out of the back pockets of women workers: our mums, our sisters, our aunties, our nieces, all of the women that matter in our lives.
acuity.explanation: Halbert follows Prime in the same Budget debate and picks up her framing that this Budget is paid for out of cancelled pay equity claims, but he engages none of her actual arguments — not the $614 million learning support reprioritisation, not the Kāhui Ako role losses, not boot camps or charter schools. What follows is prepared material on his own portfolio (tertiary education, Te Pūkenga, student fees) that would read identically whatever Prime had said about education and children. The shared pay-equity theme is a gesture at the debate rather than a response to a claim, which puts it at the top of the unengaged band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "it is being funded by “gutting pay equity”"

acuity.statement: Just further to what my colleague Helen White was saying: it’s the stigmatising, in terms of our people at the coalface, that is really, really making us angry on this side, and the punitive nature of this whole bill. That’s why we’re trying to help you, Mr Smith, with our different amendments that we’re putting up.
acuity.explanation: Jackson follows a substantive turn by Helen White, names her, and gestures at the shared theme (stigma, punitive effect) before moving straight to his own prepared amendment deleting new clause 105 and the 52-week review. He takes up none of the content she actually put: the open-ended designation power in new section 438A, the unprincipled list of prescribed circumstances, whether MSD could weigh individual distress, or what happens when a benefit is renamed. The speech would read identically had she argued something else about the bill, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the reference is more than ornamental — it is on the same clause-by-clause committee debate and adjacent in theme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "I’d like to ask about new section 438A and I’d like to ask about subsection (1)(a) of that where you’ve described the right to make regulations" — the regulation-making scope question is what precedes this turn and is not taken up.

acuity.statement: Well, this is the job of the Minister to answer the question for the public, who haven’t got that information.
acuity.explanation: Stuart Smith's interjection is a substantive counter to her own line of attack — that broad regulation-making powers are precisely what you want when a benefit's name changes, which is the case for the clause she is criticising. She could have engaged it directly (conceding the convenience while arguing the breadth is the problem). Instead she deflects to whose job it is to answer, engaging the fact of the interjection rather than its content. Low acuity for pivoting away from the point put to her; this is not a civility or specificity judgement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Stuart Smith: "You think the regulation powers might be handy if the name changes."

acuity.statement: I did want to ask if the Minister would name the set of circumstances that MSD will check in this new clause 105 to see as part of the Schedule, and if relationship is part of that, what else would she see MSD touching.
acuity.explanation: Follows Upston's insistence that the debate is only about regulation-making powers and that other matters are irrelevant. He does not take up her 52-week/transitional point or rebut the relevance claim directly, but he does answer the relevance challenge in part by anchoring each question to a named provision of the Schedule (new clause 105, new Part 11) and repeatedly explaining how it relates. On-topic questioning with a gesture at what the Minister just said, rather than engagement with her actual argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know members have talked about a whole range of other things that are completely irrelevant to this bill." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I did go through this in Part 1—the circumstances—it’s all about eligibility and about rate. And just a reminder to the committee that when somebody signs on to a benefit, they commit to identifying and notifying the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) when there is a change of circumstance.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific question just put to her about what 'circumstances' means in new clause 105 and supplies an answer — eligibility and rate — plus the existing notification obligation that frames it. Partial rather than full: she leaves untouched the other strands he raised (whether relationship status is included, the distributional breakdown of the $238 million, and whether overpayment debt would be established), declining them as Part 1 material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does MSD already have a set of circumstances that they will check up against? If so, what are those?" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I’m wondering what happens in the transitional arrangements, if there is something where the regulations would speak to that, or are the transitional arrangements all included in the subsequent section? Which could be problematic because we’ve got 52 weeks specified, and in transitional arrangements there may not be 52 weeks.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own assurance that the regulation-making power covers transitional arrangements with a 52-week review clock and draws out the difficulty in it: a transitional case may not have 52 weeks to run, so the specified period and the transitional arrangements may not fit together. The speech would have to change if Upston had not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in the regulation-making power, this part also includes the transitional arrangements, so clients will have their first review 52 weeks after their specified benefit commenced" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I want to ask about, first of all, the commencement date, and I’ll go back and ask about the title. My amendment on the commencement date is one that asks for a four-year extension.
acuity.explanation: Upston had just opened the title-and-commencement question, asserting the 2 March date allows sufficient time. White takes up exactly that strand — the commencement date — and puts a rival date (a four-year extension) against it, so the speech is not indifferent to what preceded it. But she does not engage Upston's actual reasoning that 2 March allows sufficient lead time for the IT systems and client notification; she argues instead from cost-of-living conditions and from her own prepared amendment, and the rest of the turn (the explanatory-note legal question, the two-class title point) would read identically whatever Upston had said. One strand engaged, then prepared material: mid-low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "It comes in on 2 March, which allows sufficient time for—"

acuity.statement: In terms of the way the benefit system works is that anyone who is receiving assistance has to already provide a change in circumstances. It’s fascinating what the Opposition are trying to do in terms of filibustering a very, very straightforward bill that most New Zealanders would actually think there’s already a mandatory review.
acuity.explanation: The opening clause glances at White's boarder comparison by noting that beneficiaries must already declare a change in circumstances, but it does not take up her actual contrast (that a non-beneficiary may take boarder income undeclared while an accommodation supplement recipient cannot) or draw any consequence from it. The three questions White expressly asked the Minister to answer — the four-year commencement amendment, the legal status of the explanatory note's non-exclusive benefit list, and whether the title should reflect a two-class effect — are not engaged at all; the turn pivots to characterising the Opposition as filibustering and then restates the 2 March date she had already given. Characterising the opponent and restating prepared material is not engagement with the content, so this sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "People who get an accommodation supplement must not have a boarder, because they are poorer than I am." — and White's explicit legal question, "what is the legal status of that when you’ve got a regulation and you’ve got no list in the actual bill?"

acuity.statement: It’s to amend clause 1 from the Social Security (Mandatory Reviews) Amendment Act, to “This Act is the Social Security (Make Life Harder for Beneficiaries for No Reason) Amendment Act.” That’s just following in line with Ingrid Leary over here. I would have thought the Minister would be very interested in that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the device Leary had just been running — offering the Minister alternative short titles — and extends it with his own, explicitly placing himself in line with her. But he engages the mechanism rather than any of her specific arguments (discretion being nullified, automation, seniors), so this is partial engagement: one strand of the preceding turn, then his own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether she would consider some of my alternative titles which I offer very genuinely" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: No, it’s not a general debate; this is totally in relation to this amendment bill that’s been put up, because the vulnerable, Mr Mooney, are suffering. So we want to know how the Minister would explain how she is going to ensure that the vulnerable are being looked after. We haven’t had adequate explanations on that.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Mooney's challenge that he is making a general debate speech, denies it, and supplies the connection to the amendment under discussion to justify the denial. The words would be different had Mooney interjected anything else; the engagement is specific and immediate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is this a general debate speech?" — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: It’s already been said that sanctions are not the way to go. It’s already been proven.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the sanctions strand Mooney had just introduced and contests it, so the reply is clearly shaped by the interjection. But it answers the topic rather than Mooney's actual claim about what the bill assesses — a general assertion that sanctions do not work, which leaves the specific point untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s actually an assessment of sanctions, under this bill." — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: It is an appropriate title, Mr Mooney, given what’s happening with beneficiaries, given the response of our communities who are saying they have not had enough consultation on this, who are saying this is too punitive, who are saying that they want opportunities, who are saying they want a strategy with regards to employment, with regards to Māori, with regards to housing.
acuity.explanation: Answers Mooney's objection head-on in form — the title is appropriate — but shifts ground, defending it on substantive grounds (consultation, punitiveness) rather than addressing the procedural claim that it is out of order. Engagement with one part of what was put to him, then a return to prepared themes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Completely out of order. As an experienced member, he knows that." — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: As I said before, in answer to the question around IT systems: yes, they will be well in place by 2 March in terms of commencement. The date is also clear in terms of changes to the accommodation supplement legislation that was passed last week that was signalled in Budget ’24, so there’s been plenty of time and plenty of warning. There is already a requirement that people provide a change of their circumstances to the Ministry of Social Development, and this just makes a mandatory review every 52 weeks.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the substantive answer on one of the strands actually put to her — the commencement date and IT readiness — and counters the opposition's framing of the bill as a wholesale change by characterising it as an extension of an existing obligation. It leaves the consultation and Māori-impact questions untouched, so this is engagement in part rather than in full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "with regards to the title, with regards to the change of date, with regards to the Schedule" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I’m not going to cover things and answer questions that are outside the title and commencement. I’m sure the members can come up with all sorts of names about things that have got nothing to do with this bill, but it is very straightforward.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the preceding turns — she acknowledges that alternative names have been offered and that questions have been asked — but engages the content of none of them, declaring them out of scope instead. Naming the opponents' material in order to set it aside is a reference, not a response, so this sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "One of the constant questions that has been asked throughout this debate is the effect on Māori particularly—that the Minister has not responded to, really, at all." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: This, as my colleagues have said, is a piece of legislation brought in under urgency, and the Government has failed to push it through as quickly as they would have liked. There are many questions around, firstly, the reason for rushing this through. Then, of course, now that we have a little bit more time, we can ask the why of what this bill achieves.
acuity.explanation: Follows Russell's substantive turn and picks up one strand of it — that the bill was taken under urgency and the committee stage is the only chance to examine the policy — and does something with it (the Government has not got it through as fast as it wanted, so there is now time to ask 'why'). But it takes up none of Russell's actual argument, the absence of any analysis of the earlier Investment New Zealand entity, and moves instead to his own prepared line on land values and net benefit. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this bill was introduced under urgency in the Budget, went immediately through its first and second readings" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Of course, it will differ from the existing New Zealand Trade and Enterprise (NZTE), of which I, very proudly, am a former employee. NZTE, as members will know, has a dual mandate, and that means that it is playing multiple roles, and indeed I saw it myself in my years there.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question both preceding speakers put — what does this entity do that NZTE does not — and answers it on its own terms with a concrete distinction (NZTE's dual mandate versus a single inward-investment mandate), drawing on her own time at the agency. The speech would have to change if the Opposition had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because it leaves Russell's central point, the missing analysis of the defunct Investment New Zealand, entirely untouched.

The reply would have been different had Russell asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "I want to know if that's a standard arrangement with the chief executives of Crown entities" — and her premise that the special adviser "will be the chief executive of Invest New Zealand".

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. This is my first call on this bill, and I want to, hopefully, have a backward and forward with the Minister in the chair, Nicola Grigg, regarding, first of all, the objective of Invest New Zealand and the question around strategic risk. Then, perhaps on the same call or on a later call, I’d really like to drill down into some of the transitional arrangements to understand what happens with staffing, intellectual property, liabilities, and unfinished projects.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive ministerial answer immediately precedes it and the speaker is in the same committee debate — but the call engages no part of it, instead announcing a fresh agenda of the speaker's own (objectives, strategic risk, transitional arrangements). It is on the right bill, so above the floor, but it would read identically whatever Grigg had just answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Grigg had just confirmed that appointing a head of department as special adviser to a Crown entity board "is indeed common" and that the MBIE Secretary would fill the role, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: And also based on what the previous speaker, Ingrid Leary, has mentioned as well, the Minister hasn’t yet elucidated the committee on what the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s advice was.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes up one specific strand of Leary's immediately preceding contribution — her point that MFAT's consultation advice is missing from the regulatory impact statement and that the Minister should say whether she has now received it — and presses it as still unanswered, which shows he was following her argument rather than reading prepared material. He then returns to his own prepared questions on clause 13 and AML/CFT vetting, so the engagement is partial rather than a full rebuttal or development of her point; the speech would be somewhat, but not wholly, different had she argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade was asked for consultation, but the Minister had not received it"

acuity.statement: The one around investment, I’ve referred to it briefly earlier on in principle, but in clause 15 “Invest New Zealand may charge fees and recover costs”. This is a $54 million commitment by taxpayers to an agency that’s going to be selling New Zealand, and the question is: why not, like every other real estate agency, doesn’t it fully recover—in fact, they’re making good, healthy profits—from any of the actions and the functions of it?
acuity.explanation: He picks up the same clause 15 fee-charging provision Walters had just raised, so the turn is not indifferent to what preceded it, and he expressly welcomes her questions. But he engages only the topic, not her argument: she asked what safeguards prevent the brokering function being abused, and he converts the clause into a different, prepared point about the level of taxpayer cost recovery and then into his own "does ownership matter" theme. One strand taken up, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "Clause 15 allows “Invest New Zealand [may] charge any fees and recover any costs in respect of the provision of services, information, or advice requested from Invest New Zealand in relation to its functions under this Act.""

acuity.statement: Speaking to questions from the member Vanushi Walters that are specific to this bill, she asked about Invest New Zealand and whether or not it may be able to charge fees and recover costs. I think the keyword there is “may”. Invest New Zealand “may” charge any fees, recover any costs. It is simply being put in here to futureproof the legislation. It will be an option in the future. It is not unusual. I think of Immigration New Zealand, indeed the Overseas Investment Office. There are multiple cost recovery and fee charging agencies within the public sector.
acuity.explanation: She identifies the specific question put to her and does something with it — fixes on the permissive "may", explains it as futureproofing, and supplies comparator agencies (Immigration New Zealand, the Overseas Investment Office) to show the drafting is standard. The speech would be different had the question been different, which is the deciding test. Held below 1.0 because she takes up only the fee-charging strand and leaves untouched Walters' chief-executive definition and safeguards questions and O'Connor's cost-recovery percentage challenge, explicitly narrowing to questions "specific to this bill".
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "Clause 15 allows “Invest New Zealand [may] charge any fees and recover any costs in respect of the provision of services, information, or advice requested from Invest New Zealand in relation to its functions under this Act.""

acuity.statement: As my colleague Deborah Russell has said, it could be named in different ways. There are two questions I have of the Minister in the chair, really: why not call it “Buy New Zealand 2025” because, clearly, the fairly blunt and crude way that this bill is being constructed with few, if any, qualifications on what kind of investment we will be getting into New Zealand, then why not just call it the “Buy New Zealand Bill”?
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's immediately preceding argument — that the bill's title misdescribes it and should be renamed the "Sell New Zealand Bill" — accepts its premise and does something with it, proposing his own variant ("Buy New Zealand 2025") and giving a reason tied to her point about the absence of qualifications on incoming investment. The speech would have had to change had she argued something else about the title, though a substantial part of what follows is his own prepared material on the $575 billion stock and the $54 million cost.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "So I’m going to suggest that instead of calling this the Invest New Zealand Bill, we should be calling this the “Sell New Zealand Bill”."

acuity.statement: The member’s going on about trade. As a former trade Minister, I know what we have done is negotiated increasing the thresholds to allow more investment into New Zealand, all with qualifications.
acuity.explanation: Breaks off his prepared line to answer the specific challenge just thrown at him — that as a former trade Minister his record contradicts his argument — and meets it on its own ground by stating what he negotiated and that it carried qualifications, which is the exact distinction his critique of this bill rests on. Directly shaped by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "What happened to trade?" (and "This gentleman was the Minister for Trade, what happened?")

acuity.statement: For clarification, if the applicants apply before they have a SuperGold card, they will be assessed under the lower income abatement threshold. If they apply later in the year, they will be assessed under the higher income abatement threshold and receive the top-up available.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's question had two strands: (a) what happens to someone who becomes eligible late in the rating year and does not yet physically hold the card, and (b) whether the drafting should say 'eligible to hold' rather than 'card holder'. Costello takes up strand (a) directly and supplies the operative mechanism — applying before the card is in hand is assessed at the lower abatement threshold, applying later at the higher one with the top-up — so the answer would be different had Utikere asked about something else. She leaves the drafting-definition proposal untouched and the follow-on sentences drift into the income-threshold point she was not asked about, so this is a substantial but partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "how someone who is eligible to hold a SuperGold card but who may not physically be in possession of a SuperGold card, or be determined as a card holder under the regulations, would still be able to access the rates rebate"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I want to start with clause 4 of this bill in terms of the section 2 amendment, particularly around definitions. I think my first question is around the type of card holders that meant that they were eligible for this scheme in the first place.
acuity.explanation: Leary's immediately preceding turn made a substantive argument about the Regulatory Impact Statement's evaluation design and the broad-brush eligibility settings. Xu-Nan engages no part of it: he opens prepared questions on clause 4 definitions, SuperGold card eligibility for migrants, and alternative card holder types. His only gestures at the surrounding debate are to a different, earlier speaker (Tangi Utikere) and to the second reading, not to the argument he follows. The speech would read identically had Leary argued something else entirely about this bill, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because it is squarely on the clauses under debate and does nod to what has been said in the chamber.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that the RIS measures success by 'higher uptake of this scheme', an outputs rather than outcomes measure, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’ll first just run through a few questions. With regard to the measure of success that the member Ingrid Leary was talking about, I think it’s important to remember that this rates rebate is an existing system that’s in place that we are enhancing; it’s not a new system.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the specific measure-of-success objection Leary raised about page 2 of the RIS and does something with it: she concedes the point in part ('I take on board the need to ensure that we have good measures in place', 'I don’t think it’s an end position') while disputing its framing, on the ground that the scheme is an enhancement of an existing system and that uptake data is needed first because the SuperGold card trigger is new. Delete Leary's turn and substitute a different critique and this answer would have to change, which is the deciding test. Scored independently of whether the reasoning holds or the claim is true.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: 'the success of this policy will be demonstrated by the higher uptake of this scheme. I wonder if that is the right indicator'

acuity.statement: In terms of the members’ questions about exploring eligibility for the SuperGold card, there is no work under way at this point to change the eligibility of the SuperGold card. The other card holder types, I think you’ve got to be cognisant of the fact that for the Rates Rebate Scheme, it’s about an income threshold. Those that don’t hold a SuperGold card can still be eligible for the rates rebate under the other income thresholds.
acuity.explanation: This takes both of the preceding speaker's SuperGold questions in turn and supplies the substance each asked for: a flat statement that no work is under way on SuperGold eligibility, and a direct answer to the community services card point — that the Rates Rebate Scheme turns on an income threshold, so non-SuperGold holders remain eligible by that route. It engages the content of the questions rather than merely naming them, and would have to be different had Xu-Nan asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'whether other card holder types were considered who are also in similar vulnerable situations' and 'whether we are looking at some sort of intention from the Minister on expanding the scope and eligibility criteria of the SuperGold card holders'

acuity.statement: We understand what the purpose is, because we had a discussion about this last night. But just following on from the previous speaker, the Hon Damien O’Connor, who was the previous trade Minister—and he captured it quite nicely—we already have a number of one-stop shop agencies for this. What is unique about this particular one?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's just-delivered purpose statement and pushes back on it directly (we already know the purpose; we already have one-stop shop agencies; what is unique here?). That is genuine engagement with the content of the preceding turn. But it is a single strand — he immediately pivots to prepared questions on the commencement date, the MFAT advice and the title, which would have been delivered whatever the Minister had just said. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The purpose of the bill is to establish Invest New Zealand to promote increased overseas investment into New Zealand" — Tama Potaka

acuity.statement: It’s great to be able to continue this morning the debate around the Invest New Zealand Bill, because last evening when we were discussing through the committee stage aspects of the bill, it was good to see the commitment from the Government parties to sticking around for as long as was required to go through, one by one, the various amendments that we had suggested to try and make this bill better, because there’s a lot of concern around the House that there isn’t the correct governance certainty and structure provided in the bill to give New Zealanders the certainty they deserve. So my suggestion when it comes to the title is that we really ought to be calling this bill what it is.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the title of the Invest New Zealand Bill — but it engages no part of the preceding argument. Xu-Nan's commencement-date question and his specific title proposals are left untouched; Davidson launches his own independently prepared list of names. A gesture at the debate (the title, last night's committee stage) without taking up the content, so the 0.3 end of the unresponsive band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked whether the 1 July 2025 commencement date is feasible given transition measures and collective agreements, and proposed "Divest New Zealand" as an alternative title; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: Again, the inventiveness and foxiness in the vernacular that’s being promoted by the Opposition commentariat will not change the intentions and the commitment of this Government to get the economy back on track and to ensure that we enable and expedite and accelerate co-investment, not only with public and local providers but also with Māori and iwi developers.
acuity.explanation: A direct question was put to him — which of the proposed titles best fits the bill — and the reply names the exercise ("inventiveness and foxiness in the vernacular") only to dismiss it, then restates the Government's prepared commitment to co-investment. That is a mere reference to the previous speaker, not engagement with the content: the words would stand unchanged whichever titles Davidson had proposed. Scored above 0.0 because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question is really which of these the Minister thinks best fits the bill." — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: I think I can allay concerns. In 2008, Cabinet agreed that the maximum rebate and income abatement threshold should be adjusted annually in line with movements to reflect inflation from the previous calendar year. Cabinet adjusts that rate by Order in Council. The extension in section 3(1) will ensure that the additional threshold for SuperGold card holders will also be able to be adjusted annually in line with inflation through an Order in Council, similar to that process.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Walters' question — what the Order in Council power in section 3(1) is for — and answers it by pointing to the 2008 Cabinet inflation-indexation decision, so the reply would be different had Walters raised something else about the clause. But it leaves untouched the specific things asked: whether a section 7 NZBORA vet or advice exists, what that advice said, and what the reasonable limitation is on a power that could set the non-SuperGold thresholds lower. Partial engagement, then a return to the mechanics of the scheme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The questions are really around whether the Minister received any advice in terms of the engagement with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: I just have some questions to the Minister around the transparency and understanding. It says here, Minister, that the department doesn’t hold any demographic information. Why is that, regarding rates rebates recipients?
acuity.explanation: The contribution is squarely on the bill under debate and raises a real gap in the regulatory impact statement, but it engages no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer on the Order in Council indexation power. The opening courtesy to the Minister's comments is a reference, not an engagement, and the material that follows would read identically whatever Costello had just said about section 3(1).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Casey Costello had just explained that section 3(1) extends the existing annual inflation adjustment by Order in Council to the SuperGold threshold, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate line about the RIS and demographic data

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her impassioned presentations on advocacy for our seniors. I would, first of all, highlight the fact that, again, this is an existing scheme that we’re adding to, and the challenges that the collection of data—because age was not a component of eligibility under the previous Rates Rebate Scheme, it was only income threshold, so it would have been inappropriate for the department to be gathering data about age, when it wasn’t relevant to the eligibility component of the rates rebate scheme, as it was before. We will be collecting that data, moving forward.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put: the department holds no age data because age was never an eligibility criterion under the existing income-tested scheme, and adds that it will be collected from now on. It also picks up Sosene's uptake and accessibility concern in the following remarks about council and Office for Seniors communications. The reply is wholly shaped by what preceded it and could not have been delivered against a different contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It says here, Minister, that the department doesn’t hold any demographic information. Why is that, regarding rates rebates recipients?" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: I also looked at the question of timing and the Minister just referred a moment ago to the coalition agreement. The coalition agreement of November 2023—you must have been doing a lot of work on this beforehand, but this comes to us with the regulatory impact statement saying that in the time available and given the decisions taken by Cabinet, only one option has been assessed. So I just wonder what the Minister was doing about this proposal, this amendment bill, in the time between November 2023 and the announcement in this Budget that they were only able to look at one item.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the constrained-analysis thread the Minister had just defended and presses it from a different angle — if the policy dates from the November 2023 coalition agreement, the "time available" excuse for assessing only one option does not hold. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding answer, and it is pointable. But much of it sits alongside prepared material on rates postponement and Local Government New Zealand's tool list, and it does not take on Costello's actual reason (eligibility criteria) for the data gap.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the ability to analyse has been restricted because it wasn’t a criteria for the rates rebate eligibility as it sat previously" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: In terms of the discussion points broadly about the decisions being made around this Rates Rebate Scheme and how we came to these conclusions, I will highlight yet again that this is an existing system that we knew was successful—we knew it was favourably received by seniors, that they valued the system. Therefore, what we have introduced here is an opportunity to provide some immediate relief, and deferring things and all of that seems counter to the discussion around wanting to give relief as soon as we can to those that are desperately in need.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of Leary's challenge — the option of deferring implementation to 1 July — and answers it on its merits (deferral is counter to delivering immediate relief). But it engages only that strand: Leary's central point, that the RIS says no cost-benefit analysis was done and that it cannot say whether benefits outweigh costs, is not addressed at all, and the answer otherwise restates prepared material about the scheme being existing and well-received. Partial engagement that you can point at, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "including delaying the implementation until 1 July, which I think would be eminently sensible, given some of the issues that have been raised" — and her repeated "why could she not wait at least until 1 July?"

acuity.statement: In terms of the commitment, this is a broad commitment to cost of living relief, not just purely a coalition commitment around the rates rebate. It was an opportunity to improve cost of living pressures.
acuity.explanation: Does take up the coalition-agreement strand Leary put directly to her, and reframes it — the commitment is to cost-of-living relief broadly, not merely a coalition line item. That is a recognisable engagement with the question asked. But it sidesteps the actual proposition Leary wanted on the record (whether a coalition agreement displaces the need for policy development and a cost-benefit analysis), so it answers the topic rather than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "there is a different philosophy from that side of the House, certainly from New Zealand First, that says that something that’s in a coalition agreement supersedes all else; there is no need for policy development or a rigorous process. I’d like to hear a little bit more about whether the Minister agrees with that."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I do have a question that I don’t believe has been traversed at all, and that is in relation to clause 4, which has a definition of “cardholder” in it. Now, I was interested in looking at this particular definition, and I see that it refers back to the Social Security Regulations 2018, which I also have.
acuity.explanation: Squarely within the same committee-stage debate on the same bill, and a substantive question of her own, but it engages no part of the argument the Minister had just made — by the speaker's own framing it is new ground. The acknowledgement that prior ground has been covered is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content, which places it at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band. Scored low for responsiveness only; the quality and relevance of the question itself are not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Casey Costello had just answered on why deferral was rejected, on consultation with local government, and on the coalition commitment, and this statement takes up none of it — the speaker states outright that her point has not been traversed and opens a new line on clause 4.

acuity.statement: I’d sort of first calculate, in terms of the levels being set and how much discretionary income you would allow in that system—unfortunately, the allocation of limited Government resources in the context of social policy is complex and requires brightline tests to be set. Like, there have to be some limitations on what we’ve done. So this has been based upon the foundation of a couple who are solely reliant on superannuation as their only source of income.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific question about allowing for discretionary income and supplies the actual basis for the $45,000 figure — a couple solely reliant on superannuation — rather than restating the bill's merits. The speech would have to change if Utikere had asked something else. Short of 1.0 because the twinned question he put in the same turn (whether the appropriation is $154 million or $155 million, and how it was derived) is left unanswered in this passage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "But my first question for the Minister is: was there any consideration around increasing the level so that it took into account discretionary income?"

acuity.statement: I know the Minister mentioned before the variation in terms of the threshold between one setting for SuperGold card holders and one setting for other ratepayers. That has been clarified, but I want to check with the Minister: in the regulatory impact statement, it does state that the rate for SuperGold card holders was $47,000 for a couple.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the Minister's answer that settled the two-tier threshold, then presses the remaining gap by setting her couple-based rationale against the $47,000 couple figure in the regulatory impact statement and the Act's household basis. It builds directly on the answer just given instead of restarting from prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "So this has been based upon the foundation of a couple who are solely reliant on superannuation as their only source of income."

acuity.statement: In answer to the first part, regarding the combined household income, if they weren’t a couple or they were on their own, they would be well below the threshold and therefore fully apply for the full rebate.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question asked — whether the $45,000 is a household or individual figure — and draws out its consequence for a single ratepayer, who would fall well below the threshold. Directly indexed to the preceding turn; it could not have been delivered against any other question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "The $45,000, in terms of what we see in clause 5, which inserts new section 3(1AA)(a), is not for an individual amount?"

acuity.statement: In terms of the suggestion that we gather more data, I think we’ve already discussed the fact that we want this process to be as accessible and as encouraging as possible. I think it would be both administratively more difficult, but I think it would also be obstructive to the application process if we were asking such personal information about an applicant.
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand about collecting personal information and gives a reason for declining, so it is plainly shaped by Xu-Nan's turn. But it answers a related question rather than the one put: his amendments concerned matters the chief executive would NOT be required to verify, and treating them as a request to gather more data leaves the actual proposal, and his Te Tiriti analysis question, untouched. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "but I really want to check with the Minister whether the Minister would consider some of my amendments to include additional matters as a part of that list."

acuity.statement: Now, if we all reflect on what $200,000 would mean in our local communities for councils to do, some would say that, in the bigger scheme of things, it’s a little drop in the pot, but that is a significant amount of money. Is there confidence that the transition provisions are able to and are actually going to be delivered to avoid the geographical inequities that Ms Leary has referred to?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Leary left open — council capacity producing geographical inequity under the transitional provisions — and does something with it, supplying the RIS cost figure for councils and turning her equity worry into a costed question to the Minister. The contribution would read differently had the preceding turn argued something else, which is what the deciding test asks. Not a full 1.0 because it extends a colleague's handed-over point rather than engaging a contested argument, and part of the material was pre-arranged between them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to know that the seniors in my electorate are not going to be unfairly disadvantaged due to the capacity constraints that have been clearly listed in the RIS as a risk for this policy" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: In terms of the engagement, in the regulatory impact statement, as you can see from the councils, it was the larger councils where there was some concern about the technical systems that they operate and whether they would be able to adopt it. That consultation has been ongoing and continues. Those councils have all, along with many others that have been consulted, confirmed that they are happy.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the selection question that was put — the five were the larger councils with technical-system concerns — and addresses Leary's capacity risk by reporting that consultation has continued and councils confirm they can deliver. That is real engagement with the specific claim, not a mere reference. Held at the middle of the scale because two other strands squarely put to her go untaken: the nature and content of the engagement, and the administrative costs and absence of funding, after which she returns to prepared material about MPs helping constituents fill in forms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question to the Minister is: why those five? Why were those five selected for some form of consultation?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: The second question, then, that I have for the Minister is—the Minister also just mentioned that this is, again, something that you apply for. Let’s say a person applies for it after this bill comes into effect, will they then get retrospectivity given the fact that they may apply it in September?
acuity.explanation: Lifts a specific premise out of the answer just given — that the rebate is applied for, and that the scheme is an existing system already in place — and draws out a consequence the Minister did not address: whether a September applicant gets the higher threshold backdated. The question could not have been written in advance of her reply, which is the strongest evidence of listening. Just short of 1.0 as it opens a new consequence rather than rebutting or correcting the reasoning offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the ability for constituent MPs to offer support to their constituents in terms of assisting and filling out the forms" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: I would say it again, and I’m not sure how many times I can repeat this: we have not just engaged with five councils. All 67 territorial authorities have received information through their ratings officers. Webinars with councils have engaged with 57 of those councils.
acuity.explanation: Sosene's turn rested on the premise that only five territorial authorities had been engaged, and built her question about fairness of the rates rebate roll-out on it. Costello takes that exact premise up and corrects it with the specific counts (67 authorities contacted via ratings officers, 57 via webinars), then goes on to address the engagement question itself. The reply would be materially different had the preceding speaker made a different argument, so this is engagement with the content, not a mere reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "particularly if only five territorial local authorities have had engagement that they have raised" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: In response to the member from Labour’s questions about the processing, I think there’s a misunderstanding about what I was talking about. I wasn’t suggesting that members assist with SuperGold card applications. What I referred to earlier on was that I know of MPs who have assisted members in filling out their rates rebate applications. I’m not suggesting that is compulsory and I’m not suggesting that that needs to be done.
acuity.explanation: Leary built several minutes of her contribution on the premise that the Minister expects MPs to help constituents apply for SuperGold cards as a matter of course. Costello takes that specific premise up and corrects it on the facts — the reference was to rates rebate applications, not SuperGold cards, and it was descriptive rather than an expectation. The reply would have been different had Leary asked something else, and it also disposes of her retrospectivity and cost questions in the surrounding paragraphs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is the Minister seeing that as a matter of course, or is this something just more as a backstop?" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and I thank the Minister for Seniors for that clarification. I think what I’m hearing from her is that it is the application day, but is there any discretion that relates to any other time frames, particularly around when councils would be expected to have to undertake particular tasks?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given answer — that the application date fixes eligibility regardless of processing delay — restates it to check he has it right, then presses on its unresolved consequence for council time frames and the Schedule 1 transitional provisions. This could not have been written before hearing Costello's reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can assure you that the application date will determine the eligibility." — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: I think, perhaps, I’m not making myself particularly clear, but, as I’ve said repeatedly, there has been ongoing communication with the councils. I think 57 of the 67 have been engaged with webinars, and they’ve been in Local Government New Zealand and sent out communications that they’re supportive of it. Of the five councils that were mentioned in the regulatory impact statement, they have, again, come through this process and supported it. They are just five of the many councils that have been engaged with; they will continue to be supported through this process.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's central challenge was whether consultation extended beyond the five councils named in the regulatory impact statement. Costello answers that specific question with a figure for the breadth of engagement and addresses the five named councils directly, and later in the turn addresses his question about issues raised. She engages the cost question only weakly ("How they quantify that cost I'm not quite sure"), which keeps this short of full marks, but the engagement is squarely with what was put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has there actually been a wider level of engagement with a wider level or range of councils outside of those five" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: On to the title, I take note of what the previous speaker, Tangi Utikere, mentioned in terms of his amendment, and I think his rationale is a really important one where through this bill, we’re not looking at a complete system change of rates rebate, but instead we’re looking at some minor adjustments. We are in support of Tangi Utikere’s amendment as well, but we also propose something else here which is that it is best to look at it maybe from a SuperGold card holder perspective or even simply a threshold adjustment, which is what we have here.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific reasoning of Utikere's Amendment Paper — that a title should signal the narrow content of the change — accepts it, states support for that amendment, and then extends it with a rival formulation ("(Threshold Adjustment)"). The passage could not have been delivered if the preceding turn had argued something else about the title.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "I have an Amendment Paper which would seek to change the name of this bill to, I think, actually, call it exactly what it is, and that is the “Rates Rebate (SuperGold Card Eligibility) Amendment Bill”."

acuity.statement: Just to confirm: the 1 July date is the start of the new rates year. As you know, the rates year is up to 30 June, so this is to come into effect from the start of a new rates year—immediately upon the start of a new rates year.
acuity.explanation: Engages the commencement strand that was put to her and supplies the rationale for 1 July (the rates-year boundary), but does not take up the actual question asked — whether commencement could be pushed slightly beyond 1 July to let over-burdened council systems catch up — nor Xu-Nan's query about what "immediately after" means, beyond echoing the word. Partial engagement with a pointable strand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "So is the 1 July date still appropriate, or would she be open to amending that so that it is somewhat—just slightly—further out?"

acuity.statement: In reference to the title, I think it is a very small piece of legislation. It is amending the current Rates Rebate Scheme. I think the title accurately reflects that.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the title question that both previous speakers raised and gives a direction (the existing title is adequate), but engages none of their reasoning — neither Utikere's point about a future reader needing the annotations to work out what changed, nor Xu-Nan's point that the measure is a threshold adjustment reaching only rate-paying homeowners. Answers the topic rather than the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "So I wondered if the Minister would consider other title amendments that actually, again, more accurately capture the fact that while this is something that is going to benefit, it’s only going to benefit seniors who—to be honest—are eligible to a rates rebate in the first place"

acuity.statement: I think, to me, this is a really important consideration, because if we take away all the discourse that the Minister just presented around the notion of fairness, the real-life impacts of this bill is that some people could actually be placed in hardship as a result of this.
acuity.explanation: Van Velden's immediately preceding turn built its whole case on a "rebalance of fairness", illustrated with the MRI technologists and teachers' partial strikes. Menéndez March names that fairness framing and counterposes hardship to it, so the sentence is not indifferent to what preceded it — but he sets the argument aside ("take away all the discourse") rather than engaging its reasoning or its examples, and the bulk of his contribution is prepared questioning on clause 5, the Social Security Act definition of "strike", MSD consultation and KiwiSaver, none of which she had raised. One strand engaged, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is at the heart of why this Government is passing this legislation—it’s about a rebalance of fairness across industrial action" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: Now, can I just check: if the employment agreement doesn’t specify anything about items of clothing, is it a break of the employment agreement and what would be the determining factor on that?
acuity.explanation: Twyford's preceding turn argued that the 'partial strike' definition in new section 82AA catches conduct that sits outside the written employment agreement. Xu-Nan takes up that same strand — what happens when the agreement is silent — and presses it on a concrete case (clothing) with a question about who gets to interpret the agreement. But he attributes the thread to Camilla Belich's earlier question rather than to the argument immediately before him, and the rest of the turn runs through four prepared questions for the Minister, so this is partial engagement on the right strand rather than a direct taking-up of the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "It’s not in the employment contract, but it’s just one of those things that you’d do to make sure that the team works effectively and that a workplace is efficiently run."

acuity.statement: We talk about working to rule, and my colleague talked about teachers and their ability to be able to take sports outside of their normal time. I really would like to know whether the Minister thinks that that is the same as a partial strike.
acuity.explanation: Tinetti picks up the specific example from Twyford's earlier turn — teachers coaching sports outside their agreement — and does something with it rather than merely restating it: she converts it into a direct question to the Minister and ties it to a tabled amendment defining 'normal performance' in new section 82AA, the very provision Twyford said contained the contradiction. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument about the same clause. Marked down from 1.0 because the engagement is with a colleague's supporting example and she then returns to her own prepared material on FENZ and her amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "The example that we talked about a lot in select committee was teachers who coach sports teams, and that’s a very common example."

acuity.statement: The other thing I wanted to ask while we are still on clause 5—and it is related to my other questions—is whether she considered that we do have a definitional section in clause 5, which is what we’re talking about at the moment. We have got a definition of “partial strike” and we do have a lot of discussion around normal duties. Did she consider putting in a definition of “normal duties”?
acuity.explanation: Follows van Velden's answers and takes up the strand she leaned on hardest — that whether something is a partial strike is "very case-specific" and turns on "normal" duties/output — by proposing the definitional fix that would remove that indeterminacy from clause 5. It engages one strand of the Minister's reply rather than rebutting her reasoning, and the rest of the turn is prepared material drawn from the RIS and disclosure statement, so it sits mid-band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: once again, that’s very case-specific — Brooke van Velden, answering whether a deduction can be made where the employment agreement does not require a uniform, and relying throughout on what reduces an employee's "normal output"

acuity.statement: Look, I have seen private sector partial strikes. This was apparent with the train operators in Wellington. It is also important to note that this is not actually a very radical bill. This is going back to the 2017 era, before Labour changed the law in 2018. Public sector productivity is important and private sector productivity is important, but there are other jurisdictions around the world that have regimes for partial strikes, including Australia and the UK, which are countries that we quite often compare ourselves to—and so I see that as a response also to Camilla Belich.
