acuity.explanation: Names Belich and lands on the private-sector topic she raised, but answers a different question from the one asked: Belich asked whether the private sector was consulted for the RIS, and the reply offers examples that private sector partial strikes exist plus a comparable-jurisdictions point Belich had expressly deferred to clause 6. Her substantive asks — the Ministry of Justice advice, the redacted international relations section, the UK/EU FTA and ILO obligations, the health-and-safety carve-out she offered to write into her amendment, and the "normal duties" definition — go untouched. Topic engaged, claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Was there any consultation with the private sector? — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich was also asking about the ability to make a fixed deduction of 10 percent in relation to her tabled amendment. I’m not supporting her tabled amendment, because removing the ability to make a fixed deduction of 10 percent would impact employers’ ability to make a deduction in situations where it’s difficult to calculate a proportionate pay deduction.
acuity.explanation: Belich's immediately preceding turn argued for deleting new section 95C(3) so that only proportionate deductions could be made. Van Velden identifies that exact amendment, states her position on it, and gives a reason specific to its content — that removing the fixed 10 percent option would leave employers unable to deduct where a proportionate calculation is difficult. The reply would have to be different had Belich moved a different amendment. It falls short of 1.0 only because it does not take up Belich's supporting strands (the MBIE option in the regulatory impact statement, or the UK and Australian comparison) or her 2 percent / 10 percent worked example.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "So my amendment is to change that by deleting new section 95C(3) and to actually implement a proportionate system similar to that of Australia and the UK in New Zealand."

acuity.statement: “Unprecedented punishment” was the headline, but the punishment is not without precedent. Only weeks ago, the Privileges Committee passed another judgment on the fourth participant in this “haka party incident”, who also left their seat, who also actively aided the interruption of the voting process, who also stepped out onto the hallowed grounds of the debating chamber, who also failed to return to their seat when the Speaker was on his feet.
acuity.explanation: Webb's preceding turn rested substantially on the claim that the sanctions are 'unprecedented' and 'wildly out of step with previous decisions of the committee', backing it with the Muldoon, Hunt, van de Molen and Genter cases. Ferris takes up that same precedent strand and does something with it — he disputes the 'unprecedented' characterisation and supplies a different, more recent comparator (the fourth participant in the same incident, who was not suspended). The engagement is pointable and specific, but it is one strand of a speech that otherwise sets the procedural argument aside for prepared material on colonisation, which is why this sits above a partial engagement rather than at the top of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "The proposed sanctions of seven days and 21 days are disproportionate, unprecedented, and vindictive."

acuity.statement: Now, can I just say very clearly, Standing Order 417 was about a haka occurring as the votes were being counted—that’s the chronology. As the Green representative said, she’s entirely wrong. Go and look at the Hansard—it’s all there.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the single specific factual claim Davidson built her first criticism of the committee on — that the vote had already been completed when the haka occurred — names her as its source, asserts the opposite chronology, and points to the record. The passage would have to be rewritten if the preceding speech had not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "an assertion by the chair of the committee that the conduct had prevented the vote being taken, which was simply incorrect as all parties had completed their vote" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: It’s not in there. It’s not in the Hansard. Haka is not on the Hansard.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact evidentiary move just made against him — the invitation to check Hansard — by disputing that Hansard records haka at all. Vague in content but squarely aimed at the claim it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Go and look at the Hansard—it’s all there" — Winston Peters

acuity.statement: Now, haka have been done countless times in this Parliament, but after first consulting the Speaker so that the House and its timing is not disrupted. That’s what happened here—there was no attempt whatsoever. They told the media they were going to do it, and they didn’t tell the Speaker, did they?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the strand of Davidson's argument that haka has an established place in the House, then disputes the inference by drawing a distinction she did not address — prior notice to the Speaker. That is engaging the argument rather than restating prepared material, though it answers her cultural-expression case only in part.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the haka is used in many different ways for many different reasons and has long been a respected cultural expression" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: The second thing I want to say is that if you’ve just heard two speeches—one from Te Pāti Māori and one from the Green Party—you can see that there is no sincerity in what they’re saying, because their speech had to be written for them.
acuity.explanation: Refers to the preceding speeches but engages no part of their content — it comments on how they were delivered rather than on the proportionality, precedent or clerks'-advice arguments made in them. A mere reference, which the rubric places at the bottom of the band rather than mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued the recommended suspensions were severe, unprecedented, partisan and contrary to the clerks' advice, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: No stumbling through it. They have no licence, and they’ll find very shortly that they’re going to be out of this place.
acuity.explanation: Peters had asked "where did they get their licence from?"; Maipi-Clarke answered "Māori voters", and he takes that answer up directly and contradicts it — the licence claim is denied outright. The words would be different had she not supplied that answer, so engagement is high. That the rebuttal is bare assertion with no supporting reasoning is a Rigor matter, not an Acuity one, and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "Māori voters." — her answer to Peters' question about where the party got its licence from

acuity.statement: He can’t help himself—see? On the marae, they hear you out. Their so-called epitome of Māori behaviour—he can’t even keep his mouth shut for five minutes.
acuity.explanation: Peters reacts to Waititi's interjection in the moment and makes something of it — he treats the act of interrupting as evidence for his prepared theme about marae protocol. But he engages no part of the content put to him (the charge that he is playing for laughs goes unanswered), so this is a partial engagement that turns straight back to prepared material rather than a rebuttal of what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "Grow up. And you’re trying to garner some laughs over there?"

acuity.statement: If we’re being fair, Mr Waititi—if we’re being fair—over the last 20 years, various Speakers have had a shot at it. Trevor Mallard had a shot at it, Jonathan Hunt had a shot at it, Lockwood Smith had a shot at it, Gerry Brownlee is trying to do it, and the best of them has been Adrian Rurawhe. The reality is, if you want to kōrero Māori you can speak Māori all day and night. You want to sing, if you want to do the haka, you can do all of that. Is it enough? No, it’s not enough. But in terms of tikanga Pākehā, I think we have to accept that that’s the reality of this place.
acuity.explanation: Waititi interjects to deny Jackson's claim that a partnership exists or is being built. Jackson takes that denial up directly: he concedes the core of it ("Is it enough? No, it's not enough"), but disputes the absolutism by naming successive Speakers who have attempted it and the specific accommodations that do exist (te reo, waiata, haka), then frames the limit as the tikanga Pākehā character of the House. Had Waititi interjected something else, this passage would have had to be different — it is built around the word "partnership" he threw in. Scored for engagement only; whether the inference or the history is sound is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There's no partnership here, Willie." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: I think we need to take the right strategy here, Mr Ferris—my whanaunga. You know, there’s got to be a bit of concession, a bit of compromise, because there are good people all around the House who want to embrace some of our values.
acuity.explanation: Ferris interjects a correction about Jackson's reference to Ku Klux Klan members. Jackson answers the strand Ferris raises — how Māori members should characterise the other side — and reasserts that there are "good people all around the House", which is responsive to the underlying point. But he does not address the correction itself (that it was his own mouth that aired the phrase, even as a quotation of others), and instead returns to his prepared theme of concession and compromise. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Stop calling them KKKs, Willie." — Tākuta Ferris

acuity.statement: Just to bring all of us back to the actual substance of the debate that we are having today, which I think that we lost with the co-Deputy Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, and his contribution earlier: what we are talking about and what we are debating as a House right now, is a completely unprecedented punishment, handed down by a committee that is operated in such an explicitly partisan way, departing substantially from the convention that this House is currently saying that it intends to try and uphold—so riddle me how we try and make sense of that logic.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick is squarely on the matter under debate and does engage earlier turns in it (Peters, and later James Meager's heckling), so this is not a speech that could have been given on another day — but it engages no part of the argument of the member who spoke immediately before her. Jackson's substantive offers, the Labour amendment and his claim that the House is not racist, go unanswered; the speech would read identically had he never spoken. Per the rubric, an unpointable engagement with the preceding turn sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is a clear gesture at the debate rather than wholly free-standing prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke immediately before, arguing that the House is not in fact racist, that Te Pāti Māori should offer an apology and a measure of compromise, and that Labour's amendment (a day's suspension each) should be adopted — and this statement takes up none of it, reaching instead past Jackson to Winston Peters' earlier contribution.

acuity.statement: This is not about the haka—it’s not about the haka at all. It’s about the rudeness and the disrespect that was given to this House, to the Speaker who sat in that Chair, to all the elected colleagues around this House, and it’s about the invasion on a process that we call democracy. That’s what the privileges complaint was about.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the preceding speaker's framing — that the sanction is about haka, culture and silencing Māori voices — and contests it by relocating the complaint in process and conduct. It engages that one strand squarely, so the speech would have had to change had the previous turn argued something else, but it leaves untouched the more specific claims just made (double punishment eight months later, 210,000 voters, the absence of a Tiriti provision in the Constitution Act), after which it returns to prepared material about democracy and the chamber.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I mean, this is ridiculous. We can’t even do a haka and celebrate our culture at the Aotearoa Music Awards in peace." — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who framed the suspensions as punishment of Māori culture and voice

acuity.statement: And if we listen to the members of Te Pāti Māori, they’ve just told us in their speeches that this is the beginning. They have no intention of complying to the rules of the House.
acuity.explanation: Quotes back the substance of what the immediately preceding speaker committed to — refusal to apologise, a continuing stance — and does something with it: uses it as the premise for why the committee's recommendation is not disproportionate. The argument depends on what was actually just said and would collapse if the previous speaker had instead accepted the sanction, which is the mark of real engagement. Short of 1.0 because it characterises the prior speeches in aggregate rather than rebutting any single stated reason.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But I will not apologise for my actions." — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke (also "We will never be silenced, and we will never be lost.")

acuity.statement: What I would like to see from Te Pāti Māori is where we look to unify as a country. Where we look to come together to find solutions. But we don’t hear that from Te Pāti Māori. All we hear is aggression. All we hear is bullying. All we hear is yelling.
acuity.explanation: She repeats the interjector's words back and then pivots away from the Treaty entirely to a general characterisation of the other party's conduct. Per the rubric, echoing an opponent's words in order to change the subject is a mere reference, not engagement: nothing in the Treaty challenge is taken up, though the remarks remain inside the matter under debate, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Oh, go back to the Treaty part. Tell us more about that." — Tākuta Ferris

acuity.statement: It's demonstrably clear to me that it is the Government that is punishing the members today, not the Parliament, because if it was the Parliament, we would have the support of every party in this House, like we have had many other times when members have been referred to the Privileges Committee.
acuity.explanation: McKee's turn immediately before was a defence of the Privileges Committee recommendation as proportionate and as a response to Te Pāti Māori's conduct. Rurawhe engages that position in part — he contests the standing of the recommendation by arguing the absence of cross-party support makes it a Government punishment rather than a Parliament one — but he does not take up her specific claims (proportionality, the six-month process, the refusal to participate), and most of the surrounding speech is prepared material addressed to earlier speakers from his own side. Engagement with the topic and the general position rather than with the specific argument just made: a mid-band score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "I fully support what the Privileges Committee are recommending to this House and request—"

acuity.statement: I'll answer that interjection. You're here; you're in this House. You have the opportunity to change it—absolutely change it. You can't change it by not turning up for a vote in the House. That ain't going to change anything.
acuity.explanation: Ferris interjects with a direct question challenging Rurawhe's point that Te Pāti Māori should use the Standing Orders Committee to change the rules. Rurawhe stops, names the interjection, and answers it on its own terms — the opportunity exists now, and boycotting votes forfeits it. The passage could not exist unchanged if Ferris had said something else, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 only because he reframes the 'how long' question as a 'whether you turn up' question rather than addressing the timeframe asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "How long do we have to wait?"

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Greens as the Green Party member on the Privileges Committee, and I am astounded by the last three ACT Party speakers, who seemed far more offended about alleged finger guns than actual gun violence, children living in poverty, or workers being exploited.
acuity.explanation: Chhour's immediately preceding turn argued the House should be dealing with real community harms rather than this debate. Menéndez March names the ACT speakers and asserts the mirror-image charge — that they care more about finger guns than real harm — without taking up anything Chhour actually said. It names a target and pivots to prepared framing, which the rubric treats as a mere reference rather than engagement, though it is at least on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "We have issues in our communities where families are losing their babies, where our people are becoming victims of crime, where our people are suffering, and we're debating this."

acuity.statement: I just heard the previous ACT Party speaker talking about cruelty when, actually, we have had members of the Government using terms like “sick idiots” to refer to other members in the House—idiots, actually, just up until recently—and constant slurs and languages and literal anti-migrant rhetoric in this Chamber. They should look in the mirror.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific strand Chhour had just developed — her redefinition of what counts as cruelty in the House — and contests it directly by offering counter-instances of Government members' own conduct. The speech would plainly have been different had the preceding speaker not raised cruelty; he quotes the move and answers it rather than just naming her as a target. Not 1.0 because the reply redirects to the other side's record instead of addressing Chhour's actual example, but the engagement is specific and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "Now, we talk about cruelty. We talk about accusations of cruelty." — and her claim that the cruelty lies in mocking the video on Facebook

acuity.statement: I found it staggering that when the ACT Party member justified the decision, she didn’t explain why; she just said it was justified. But that’s seven times as much as we’ve had before. I don’t think it’s justified, and I challenge members of the Government to actually give us an actual justification as to (a) why they find the haka intimidatory, because I think most New Zealanders wouldn’t agree with that; (b) to explain to us why they thought setting a punishment seven times higher than it’s been set before is justified, because so far they haven’t.
acuity.explanation: Chhour closed by commending the recommendations on the ground of absent contrition; this passage goes straight at that conclusion, says it was asserted rather than reasoned, and sets out the two specific questions it leaves unanswered (why the haka is intimidatory, why a penalty seven times the precedent). Deleting Chhour's turn and substituting a different argument would force this passage to change. Whether his characterisation of her reasoning is fair is a rigor/veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "But because there’s been no sign of remorse and no sign of contrition, I will actually commend the recommendations."

acuity.statement: Let’s not make this debate about something it isn’t. This debate is about the rules of this House, and if we need to change the rules in this House, then we do so within this House. We do it within the process that we have.
acuity.explanation: Waititi's central argument was that the sanction is not a Standing Orders matter but a colonial suppression of indigenous expression. Costello takes that framing up directly and disputes it, asserting the debate is precisely about the rules and that the remedy for bad rules is the House's own process. It is a counter-assertion rather than an engagement with his supporting reasoning (she leaves the 21 days, the Privileges Committee's reasons and the Regulatory Standards Bill untouched), and she then returns to prepared material about rules in pigeonholes — so partial engagement rather than full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This punishment is not about noise control or Standing Orders." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: Let’s make it very clear why we are here. We had to suspend the sitting of this House in order to bring it to order. We have accommodated karakia, waiata, and haka.
acuity.explanation: Waititi repeatedly pressed the claim that nobody has explained why Te Pāti Māori are being punished and that the objection must really be to haka. Costello answers that specific question — the sitting had to be suspended to restore order, and haka as such is accommodated — which is the claim he put, taken up and contradicted on its own terms. Not a 1.0 because she supplies no detail on the part he pressed hardest (where 21 days came from), and the answer is brief before she moves on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Because it’s still unclear why we are being punished, sanctioned. Why? Was it the haka?" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: There is much in the statement by our Minister of Foreign Affairs that I completely agree with. We also welcome the possibility of a ceasefire. We also endorse the non-expulsion of ambassadors from countries who have taken actions that we disagree with.
acuity.explanation: Hipkins picks out two specific positions from the ministerial statement he has just heard — the welcome for ceasefire signals and the decision not to expel ambassadors — and states where he accepts them before departing to his own material on the legality of the US strikes, which Peters did not address. The passage could not have been delivered without having listened to the particular content of Peters' statement, which places it well above prepared material on the right topic; it is not a 1.0 because it accepts rather than works on the reasoning, and the bulk of the speech that follows is self-contained.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "we have resisted the pressure from some to expel from New Zealand the ambassadors of some Middle Eastern countries" and "We note and welcome positive signals in the last few hours about a potential ceasefire."

acuity.statement: In the context in which the Leader of the Opposition asked that question, we note the United States’ decision to undertake targeted attacks aimed at degrading Iran’s nuclear capabilities was based on the US statement to the UN Security Council that it was acting in collective self-defence consistent with the UN Charter. That was a statement they made, and, of course, in time, that will depend on the emerging evidence.
acuity.explanation: Peters takes up the exact legal test Hipkins raised, naming collective self-defence under the UN Charter, so one strand of the question is genuinely engaged rather than ignored. But he engages it by relaying the United States' own characterisation and deferring to emerging evidence rather than taking up whether that characterisation satisfies article 51 — partial engagement, which is why Hipkins immediately rose to say the question had not been taken up. (Whether a minister answered the question put to him belongs to Forthrightness; scored here only on how far the reply engages the content.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "does the New Zealand Government believe that the US’s pre-emptive strike on Iran meets that criteria?" — the article 51 collective self-defence test he had just quoted.

acuity.statement: I heard in the ministerial statement that the Minister of Foreign Affairs prides themselves on wanting to prioritise diplomacy, wanting to push for de-escalation, and wanting to push for enduring peace, and yet we did not see a statement that recognised and acknowledged the dangerous escalation of the US strikes on Iran. So, in response to the statements from the ministerial statement, we are looking for that condemnation of Israel and the United States’ illegal strikes on Iran.
acuity.explanation: Takes a specific strand of the Minister's statement — his stated commitment to diplomacy and de-escalation — and turns it against him, drawing out the inconsistency with his silence on the US escalation. The speech would have to change if the Minister had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "we have made the wise decision—in my view—to hold our counsel until we know all the facts before we rush to judgment" (and his ministerial statement on diplomacy/de-escalation)

acuity.statement: The Minister also spoke in his statement about the ceasefire and having a look into it to check out whether it’s worth anything. I too want to speak to that part of the Minister’s speech, where if it is then true, of course we would all welcome that; it’s what we all want. But we know from the continued genocide in Gaza that a ceasefire with Israel isn’t worth the paper it’s written on; they have continued to breach and breach and breach ongoing calls and so-called settlements of a ceasefire.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's specific 'trust but verify' point about the ceasefire, concedes the part she agrees with, and then disputes the rest with a reason — the model of accepting part and contesting the remainder.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "We’re going to trust but verify." — on whether a ceasefire has held

acuity.statement: I made it very clear, in the ministerial statement, the Government’s position, but I have to say when it comes to the proxies for Iran that have committed so much terrorism and the loss of thousands of lives—Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis, with respect to Iran—the Greens have been not a syllable, not a sound, not a mutter, not a murmur, no condemnation whatsoever.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the demand for condemnation in one clause — the position is already clear — but then leaves the substance of her argument (that the strikes breached international law) untouched and pivots to the Greens' own record on Hamas and Hezbollah. One strand engaged, then prepared counter-attack.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "Will the Minister condemn Israel and the United States’ illegal strikes on Iran?"

acuity.statement: How is New Zealand contributing to de-escalation and to diplomacy if we continue to only selectively condemn breaches of international law from those countries we think we agree with?
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the claim just made — that the Government has condemned all parties and is even-handed — by putting the charge of selectivity to him. The question is built on what he had just asserted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "We’ve condemned all parties"

acuity.statement: Because the premise of that member’s question is demonstrably false. As I’ve pointed out in my speech and countless speeches, there are no rightful parties in this dispute or in this disaster.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the load-bearing assumption of the question — that condemnation has been selective — and denies it with a reason, that the Government treats no party as in the right. Squarely aimed at the claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "if we continue to only selectively condemn breaches of international law"

acuity.statement: As my colleague said, agriculture is the backbone of this country, and protecting it in the biosecurity space is what protects that backbone.
acuity.explanation: Hoggard follows Mark Cameron in the same imprest supply debate and takes up one strand of it — Cameron's framing of the primary sector as the country's backbone — and does something with it, drawing out the consequence for his own biosecurity portfolio. Beyond that single thread the speech is prepared material: a general defence of fiscal restraint, 'best bang for buck', energy security and food-safety red tape, aimed at unnamed critics ('I hear a lot about "Oh, you're not throwing enough money at this"') rather than at anything Cameron actually argued. If Cameron had made a different argument on the same topic, almost all of this speech would be unchanged, so it sits below a full partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the primary sector, which, by the way, is the backbone of the very country that you speak to and should be supportive of" — Mark Cameron

acuity.statement: Te Pāti Māori will not be supporting either of these bills, and this is why: because what we recognise is that it will legitimise a Budget and a policy agenda that protects power and not people.
acuity.explanation: She follows Arbuckle's substantive turn on the same two bills and takes the opposite side of the question before the House, and she gestures at having listened ("I was listening to the Minister and the range of debate"), so the speech is squarely on the matter under debate. But it engages no part of the preceding argument: nothing in it responds to the Budget-variance figure, the reprioritisation case, the Regional Infrastructure Fund or the horticulture passage. Substitute a different pro-bill argument for Arbuckle's and this speech would be word-for-word unchanged, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because of the gesture at the range of debate. Scored on engagement only — the force of her Treaty and Vote Māori Development case belongs to other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle argued that the 2024-25 outturn was only "a 5.4 percent difference" from Budget and that New Zealand First supports the bills "because it upholds the integrity of the financial system while enabling the necessary amendments", and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Probably about now, I’d be depressed if it wasn’t for such a great Budget and a great imprest bill, after the Chiefs’ narrow four-point loss on Saturday night.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a substantive speech by Woods that made specific, checkable claims about housing appropriations and energy spending. His opening engages none of them: it asserts the Budget and imprest bill are great and pivots to a rugby result. The remark is at least nominally about the measure under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but it would be word-for-word identical whatever Woods had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued the Supplementary Estimates show emergency housing cuts, 3,500 cancelled State house builds and a $200 million fossil-fuel allocation, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: You won’t have heard the Opposition criticise us about our investment—our significant investment—into the disability support services this Budget. Has anyone heard that?
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive Green turn full of specific, engageable claims and takes up none of them. He pivots to a Vote the Opposition had not raised and scores a point off their silence, which is a gesture at the Opposition rather than engagement with Genter's argument. The speech is at least on the bill under debate (imprest supply / Budget votes), so it sits in the prepared-material band rather than at zero; it would have read identically whatever Genter had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued the Budget removed a fair-pay pathway for over 300,000 workers, that billions are going to landlords, and that the Government's transport plan is unfunded, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I have to first address and actually correct what was spoken before me, particularly about the economy shrinking, because I believe the member who just spoke before me, Peeni Henare, clearly didn’t watch the news last week and clearly didn’t watch the news another quarter ago. Stats New Zealand last week reported that the economy of New Zealand grew 0.8 percent—grew—in the first three months of the year, twice the rate forecasted by Treasury and the Reserve Bank a short time ago.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific factual premise of the immediately preceding speech — that the Government has shrunk the economy — and contradicts it with a named source and figure (Stats NZ, 0.8 percent quarterly growth, against Treasury/Reserve Bank forecasts). The speech would have had to be written differently had Henare argued something else; this is direct engagement with the content of his claim rather than a mere reference to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this Government, through their decisions in this Budget, have shrunk the economy" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: I do want to go back to some comments from the other side—in particular one from Megan Woods—and say to her, look, we don’t measure our success as a Government based on how much we appropriate; we measure it based on the outcomes that we are actually able to achieve.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Russell's substantive turn, which argued the Government had chosen not to fund health, welfare, education and had cut emergency housing. He does take up one strand of that — housing and homelessness — and answers it on its merits by reframing the test as outcomes rather than appropriation and citing families moved out of motels, so this is more than a bare reference to the other side. But the engagement is aimed at Megan Woods's appropriation point rather than at the case Russell had just put, and the whole of Russell's substance (the annual GDP contraction, the stalled second quarter, food and electricity price rises, the $14 a fortnight against Best Start, partial expensing, the forecast tax debt write-offs) goes untouched. The speech would read almost identically had Russell argued something different about housing, so this sits at a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We know that this Government has cut emergency housing." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Well, in my 46 years—but probably only 30-odd of paying attention to these things—it seems that exports haven’t managed to save us yet. Neither has foreign investment. All it’s done is managed to entrench the people who live in the lower end of society—all of the New Zealanders out there—into their category.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's immediately preceding turn made specific arguments — that the bill triages genuinely sensitive transactions, that NZ First has carved out farmland, fishing quota and family homes, and that the complaint about feudalism was overblown. Ferris engages none of those. His speech is prepared material addressed to the Government's general 'open ourselves to the world' theme and to the Associate Minister's introductory speech; the only glance toward the preceding speaker is a passing reference to Te Tiriti removal 'as promoted by New Zealand First', which names a target rather than engaging a claim. It is squarely on the matter under debate, hence 0.3 rather than 0.1, but the speech would read identically whatever Patterson had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson spoke about NZ First having 'drawn a line around farmland, around fishing quota, and, essentially, the stock of family homes' and about the bill's streamlining and trusted-investor provisions, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: As you start to look at these things in context, it’s starting to say New Zealand is open for business. We can’t survive by selling things to ourselves; we need to open ourselves up to more investment to get things done.
acuity.explanation: Ferris had just put two specific propositions: that decades of exports and foreign investment have entrenched rather than relieved hardship, and that no iwi Māori were consulted despite two years since the coalition agreement. Hamilton answers neither. He restates the case for openness as a bare assertion, cites Federated Farmers in support, and commends the bill — a speech that would be word-for-word the same whoever had preceded him, though it does stay on the bill under debate. Scored on engagement only; whether the openness claim is true or well-reasoned is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tākuta Ferris argued that 'exports haven’t managed to save us yet. Neither has foreign investment' and that the bill proceeds 'with no regard for Te Tiriti o Waitangi' without iwi consultation, and this statement takes up neither point.

acuity.statement: I hear Dan Bidois, the MP for Northcote, say it’s because they don’t need the money. If that is the problem you’re trying to solve, how is cutting Government KiwiSaver contributions going to help deepen our capital pools? On that point, it doesn’t incentivise greater savings and investment, which is why Australia has greater pools of investment, of superannuation savings.
acuity.explanation: She takes Bidois's interjected explanation of why Australia and Canada can afford a restrictive regime and turns it into a counter-argument on its own terms: if capital depth is the problem, cutting Government KiwiSaver contributions works against it, and Australia's superannuation pools are the example. The reply would be different had he interjected something else. Not a full 1.0 because what she engages is a one-line interjection rather than a developed argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They don’t need the money." — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: Aotearoa New Zealand is a country that could be very, very prosperous if we looked after all of our people.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the matter under debate — foreign ownership and whether it benefits New Zealanders — with a gesture at the bill and at the case made for it, but no engagement with any strand of the argument actually just made by the preceding speaker. Sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because it is squarely about the bill rather than a generic speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued immediately before that the bill strips the seven factors from the benefit test and that the Minister omitted the four OECD countries with more restrictive regimes, and this speech takes up neither. Genter addresses "the Minister who spoke to this bill" and general ideology instead.

acuity.statement: Don’t try to pretend that allowing foreign hedge funds to come in here and own our retirement villages—which is already the case, by the way—and to own more and more of New Zealand is something that is going to benefit New Zealand, and that those who question the benefits are somehow against people from other countries. That’s not the case.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Mooney's charge directly and does something with it: separates opposition to foreign capital ownership from hostility to foreign people, denies the imputation, and then supplies the Green Party's immigration and refugee-quota record as the test of it. The passage only exists because of what Mooney said. Short of 1.0 only because the thing engaged is an interjection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Proudly against foreigners, against foreign accents?" — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: As the Minister had articulated before, the importance of having overseas investment into New Zealand and making sure that we have the right settings is not without dispute; what is indisputable is that we do have one of the most restrictive foreign investment regimes in the OECD. That is what has been ascertained from a number of studies by a number of organisations over a number of years, and this bill will help open the door to that new investment.
acuity.explanation: Re-asserts as "indisputable" the very proposition Edmonds had just disputed with named countries and a citation to the regulatory impact statement, without acknowledging or answering that rebuttal; the appeal to unnamed "studies" does not engage her source. Also leaves Edmonds's benefit-test argument and Genter's wage argument untouched. On the matter under debate, so above 0.1, but the speech would read identically whatever the two previous speakers had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there are four other countries that are more restrictive than New Zealand: Australia, Canada, Iceland, Mexico" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Other, more prosperous, countries around the world understand this, and that is why they welcome foreign direct investment. They also make it super easy to get foreign investment into their countries. I welcome this bill. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Megan Woods' substantive case that the bill strips the benefit-to-New-Zealand test, but engages no part of it. The turn is a prepared frame (Solow's three capitals, other countries welcome FDI) plus a commendation, and it refers back only to his own side's Minister. It would read word-for-word the same whatever Woods had said, though it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued the bill 'removes the benefit to New Zealand test' and that guard rails are needed, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: We’re actually better than a couple of countries now, in terms of openness to foreign direct investment. Do you know who those two countries are listed in here? They’re Canada and Australia. Our rules at the moment are pretty much the same as Canada’s, but they are way less restrictive than Australia’s. I don’t know what problem this bill is trying to solve. We’re actually sitting alongside our OECD and our Commonwealth peers.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Bidois's comparative claim that more prosperous countries make foreign investment easy — and pushes back on it with the OECD restrictiveness ranking, naming Canada and Australia as the comparators. She does not address him by name or engage his capital-formation argument, and the bulk of the turn is prepared regulatory-impact-statement analysis, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Other, more prosperous, countries around the world understand this, and that is why they welcome foreign direct investment" — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: Like the previous speaker, the Hon Phil Twyford, said, they expanded the special direction of power. There are certain areas in here—some of the aspects around stronger restrictions on out-of-hours immigration rates; these are good things to see, because we have seen our migrant community being harmed as a result of over-the-top treatment towards them in the form of the Dawn Raids and others.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Twyford's preceding speech — the out-of-hours compliance provisions and the Dawn Raids history — names him, and endorses that part of the bill for the same reason he gave. But it is agreement that adds nothing to his argument and does not take up anything else he raised (the Casey review and detention of asylum seekers, the right to seek asylum, the employment-premium offence); the bulk of the speech is prepared Green Party material on the levy that would read identically had Twyford said something else. A partial engagement, not a rebuttal or a development.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Given the scars that the Dawn Raids of the 1970s left on this country, clearly that compliance activity needed guard rails put around it."

acuity.statement: The previous speaker, I think, when he read that statement on the first page of the bill, completely forgot that the statement also says that it is to take into consideration the interest of people—those who are already here in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact text the previous speaker quoted from the bill's first page and corrects his reading of it, arguing he dropped the half about those already in New Zealand and so missed that the clause is about balance. The speech is directly shaped by what Xu-Nan said and would have had to change had he opened differently; the following sentences build the balance point out of that correction. Whether the correction is fair is a question for rigor, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "to manage immigration in a way that balances the national interest … and the rights of individuals" — he quoted the purpose clause on the bill's first page and argued the rights half is not honoured in practice

acuity.statement: This is to expand the immigration levy - payer base, and it is very, very clear in the bill, that it will have to be justified which groups this expansion can be done to.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the subject Xu-Nan made his central objection — the expanded levy-payer power — and answers one aspect of it, that the expansion is constrained and must be justified by a benefit linkage, with worked examples of employers and education providers. But it answers the topic rather than his actual claim, which was that the levy is being repurposed as a tax to fund health and education; that charge is left untouched. Partial engagement from largely prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "That then is no longer a levy. We are adding an additional immigration tax."

acuity.statement: On one hand, we have the “golden visa” scheme fast-tracking residency and citizenship for the wealthy. On the other hand, the bill introduces harsher deportation powers for refugees—people who arrive with nothing but hope for a better life—by allowing the Government to cancel resident visas of refugees even if deportation would result in them being tortured in their homeland. This is not an immigration policy; this is class warfare disguised as legislation. Let’s be clear: in the past 10 years, no one has been certified as being a national security risk under section 163 of the Immigration Act 2009.
acuity.explanation: Costello's speech defended the visa-cancellation power as being about managing genuine security risks and protecting the system's credibility, and separately praised the bill's exploitation protections. Kemp takes both strands up directly: she concedes the exploitation and warrant provisions as positive, then attacks the very power Costello justified, supplying a specific counter-fact (no section 163 security certification in ten years) that goes to whether the risk Costello invoked actually exists. Had Costello argued something different about the bill, this passage would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "also provides the ability to cancel resident visas for security risks. Again, this is about the credibility of our immigration system"

acuity.statement: A couple of things that have already been highlighted and that I think are really important are creating an offence for charging for jobs in New Zealand and, also, requiring a warrant for out-of-hours enforcement actions.
acuity.explanation: Kemp had just argued the bill is a two-tiered, class-based system that sends refugees towards torture, while conceding the exploitation and warrant provisions. Weenink's reply nods at provisions "already been highlighted" — the very two Kemp conceded — but engages none of the content of Kemp's objection; it is prepared endorsement on the right subject with a gesture at prior speakers, and would read identically whatever Kemp had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Takutai Tarsh Kemp argued the bill "reinforces a two-tiered immigration system—one rule for the rich, another for the poor" and introduces harsher deportation powers for refugees, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It just gives us—and it’s been previously mentioned—a few more powers in the immigration space, once again to kind of balance our national security with the rights of individuals. It addresses the recommendations from a number of independent reviews.
acuity.explanation: Follows Henare's substantive turn, which pressed specifically on whether the new ministerial powers are adequately checked. Campbell's speech is a prepared summary of the bill's purposes and would read identically whatever Henare had said. The phrase 'it's been previously mentioned' is a bare gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that the select committee must interrogate the checks and balances on the powers Ministers hold in immigration cases, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: This bill also grants the Minister of Immigration really broad new powers to be able to set the levies to determine who actually pays and how much they pay. This is only with periodic consultation and a five-year review. We should be careful when we look at centralisation of power in the Minister’s office that it should not go unchecked.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn: Campbell characterised the bill's new powers as a benign balancing of national interest against individual rights, and Salesa engages that same claim about the powers, disputing that the balance is adequately checked and naming the specific mechanism (levy-setting with only periodic consultation and a five-year review). She then returns to prepared material on costs and values, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It just gives us—and it’s been previously mentioned—a few more powers in the immigration space, once again to kind of balance our national security with the rights of individuals" — Hamish Campbell

acuity.statement: The other one that actually hasn’t really been touched on much is the concept that people who are facing deportation will actually be monitored on electronic bail as opposed to being in a jail. I think that was highlighted through the KCs’ reports.
acuity.explanation: Prepared praise on the matter under debate. He gestures at the state of the debate by claiming electronic monitoring 'hasn't really been touched on much' — which is why this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than lower — but he engages no part of the preceding argument; Salesa had in fact already named electronic monitoring as a useful aspect, and he neither builds on nor corrects her. The speech would be unchanged whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jenny Salesa argued the levy expansion comes with no analysis of how costs flow through the economy and that centralised ministerial power should not go unchecked, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: The Labour Party will offer very cautious support for this bill through to the select committee. It is cautious because of the very short report-back date, because we think some of the issues that need to be worked through are quite significant, and it is cautious because, in some ways, this bill just doesn’t go far enough; in some ways, it maybe goes too far.
acuity.explanation: Follows McClay's first-reading speech and takes up specific things he had just moved and claimed: the report-back date he nominated (13 August 2025) and the bill's scope, stating a position that is calibrated to those particulars. The speech would read differently had he moved a longer report-back or a wider bill, so it is responsive rather than prepared boilerplate; it engages the frame rather than rebutting a specific figure, so not top of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I intend to move that the bill be reported to the House by 13 August 2025" — Todd McClay

acuity.statement: Under this bill, as it’s come to the House, land categories 1 through 6 will only be able to have 25 percent of the land planted up in forestry. But category 6 land—there’s a special category in there to say that more than that can go for forestry: you can do whole-farm conversions or significant amounts of forestry conversion, up to 15,000 hectares per annum. Whose 15,000 hectares? Well, it turns out that’s going to be decided by a ballot. Everyone who wants to convert some of their farmland over and above that 25 percent will need to go into a ballot. That, of course, means that their land, by virtue of a ballot, may become more valuable for the purposes of sale.
acuity.explanation: Takes the two specific mechanisms McClay had just listed — the 15,000-hectare annual ballot on class 6 land and the 25 percent cap — and does something with them, drawing out a consequence he did not mention (that ballot success capitalises into land value, raising whether the entitlement attaches to the land or the farmer and whether it is transferable). Substitute a different design for the ballot in the preceding speech and this passage could not stand unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "an annual ballot allowing 15,000 hectares of exotic forest on class 6 land" — Todd McClay

acuity.statement: The Minister introducing the bill spoke of the need to balance and complement our productive farming, our food production systems. I agree. We need to do that, but we also need to balance what we are doing with respect to climate change as well.
acuity.explanation: Directly quotes back the balance framing McClay built his speech on, concedes it, then disputes what he left out of the balance — the climate side. This is engagement with the content of the preceding argument (accepting part, contesting the rest), not a mere reference to the previous speaker; the score falls short of 1.0 only because the counter is asserted at the level of principle rather than against a specific claim or figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it must be integrated in a way that complements, not replaces, our food-production systems" — Todd McClay

acuity.statement: There has been a whole lot of consideration of the costs of the preferred option on ETS forestry participants—good people to consider—on farmers, obviously; on foresters; on Māori land owners; of the effect on the regulator; of the effect on others. What we haven’t got is an assessment of the cost or the impact on the emissions trading scheme.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of McClay's case — his assurance that the bill does not undermine the climate settings — by pointing to a gap in the regulatory impact statement behind it, namely that the costed options stop at affected groups and never cost the effect on the ETS itself. It answers the topic McClay raised and identifies a specific omission, but it does not take on a particular claim or number he advanced, so it sits mid-band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It does not undermine our climate commitments." — Todd McClay

acuity.statement: Now, you may argue it doesn’t go far enough, it goes too far, or whatever, but let’s get started with something, because if we do nothing, like what happened with the previous Government, then more land will keep going out of farming.
acuity.explanation: Abel's central criticism was that the bill is only a step in the right direction and fails to remove forestry from the ETS. Hoggard takes that strand up directly — he names the 'doesn't go far enough' objection and answers it with a do-something-rather-than-nothing argument, and earlier in the turn says the preceding speeches 'sort of missed' what the problem is before substituting his own diagnosis (rural community decline rather than gross emissions). That is partial engagement: he answers the shape of Abel's objection without touching its substance (the ETS distortion, the ballot system, land-class inversion), then returns to prepared material about his neighbour and the elegance of the solution. Scored on engagement only — not on whether the 'get started with something' reasoning is sound or whether the previous-Government jab is fair.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "I think, however, this bill isn’t biting the bullet."

acuity.statement: It does create opportunities to integrate forestry in with sheep and beef farming primarily, in a mosaic-type approach, and it can help cash-flow farm succession.
acuity.explanation: Abel's closing argument was that agroforestry, silvopasture and mixed 'mosaic' landscapes go unrecognised and that the bill does not address them. Patterson picks up that exact strand and the same vocabulary, arguing the opposite — that the bill creates opportunities for integrated forestry/sheep-and-beef mosaics — and elsewhere concedes openness to 'sensible changes around some of the settings' at select committee. Partial rather than full: he asserts the counter-position without engaging Abel's specific mechanisms (the ballot lottery, the land class 6/7 value inversion, removing forestry from the ETS), and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on rural decline and carbon pricing. The mere nod to 'some of the Opposition speeches' on its own would not have scored above 0.3; the mosaic rebuttal is what lifts it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "These things are not recognised for their valuable use of combinations of diverse mosaic landscapes where you’re planting trees and you’re raising livestock and you’re producing crops and food."

acuity.statement: Noting how the last speaker, Catherine Wedd, said that enough is enough and that this bill will fix everything, I think that’s slightly ambitious, but we’re all agreeing there is a problem that needs some fixing. We think that some more fixing will be needed in addition to this bill.
acuity.explanation: Opens by taking up the specific claim the immediately preceding speaker made — that this bill ends the problem — names her, concedes the shared premise that a problem exists, and disputes the sufficiency claim. The speech would read differently had Wedd made a narrower claim, so it is genuinely shaped by what it follows. Not a full 1.0 because she characterises rather than quarrels with Wedd's reasoning, and then moves on to her prepared material on offsets, mapping and select-committee timing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Enough is enough. This bill is a practical approach" — Catherine Wedd

acuity.statement: Look, I rise to support this bill tonight. It’s great to see some cross-party support on this, and I am looking forward to it coming to our Environment Committee, where we can navigate it further.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the debate — she notes cross-party support — but she engages no part of the preceding argument: nothing on the Māori land exemptions, the rangatiratanga point, or the claim that removing methane weakens the ETS. The rest of the speech is prepared constituency material on Hawke's Bay pine conversion that would have been identical whatever Maipi-Clarke had said, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 for the glance at the chamber.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Te Pāti Māori considers the bill to also undermine the integrity of the ETS and weakens it further by removing methane" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: One of the saddest things I’ve had to experience driving around the electorate of Northland and the rural parts of it is seeing all the beautiful rolling hill country that has been converted into carbon forestry. I want to make a quite distinct difference here. There’s production forestry, which we fully support—it’s an important part of the Northland and New Zealand economy. It’s the carbon forestry that’s been causing the problems.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive critique and engages none of it — not the offsets-versus-decarbonisation framing, not the transitional provisions, not the select-committee timetable. The speech is prepared Northland material followed by an attack on the previous Labour government's inaction, and would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before. It stays above 0.0 only because it is about the matter under debate, carbon forestry on productive land.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking argued that the ETS's focus on offsets rather than decarbonisation is the underlying problem and that the bill's transitional provisions and the 30 August report-back date are inadequate, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: I just want to say that it’s ironic that the Opposition has finally realised that the rural economy is the backbone of this country and that they have finally realised that it was their policies that ruined rural communities in the East Coast and ruined the schools. I am so pleased that they’re now supporting it and they’ve figured that out.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows Boyack's substantive turn in the same first-reading debate, so she is eligible. She notes the fact of Labour's support — a bare reference to the position Boyack had just stated — but engages no part of Boyack's actual argument: nothing on the short report-back time frame, the risk of unintended consequences, the ETS-distortion point, or the charge of an anomaly in ACT's property-rights stance. The speech would read identically whatever Boyack had argued, provided Labour was supporting the bill, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we will be supporting this bill to select committee but there are some concerns around aspects of the bill" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: No, you haven’t. Read the regulatory impact statement. To the member who says, “We have”, here’s a wee heads-up: the purpose of a regulatory impact statement is to give an independent view of the pre-introduction work that has been done, and it says that there has not been adequate public consultation—a C- is what you get.
acuity.explanation: Webb was in the middle of arguing the Government needed to engage rural and remote communities when Kirkpatrick interjected that it had. He takes that specific assertion up directly rather than brushing past it: he denies it, then supplies the counter-evidence — the regulatory impact statement's own quality-assurance finding of inadequate public consultation — and explains why that source is probative (it is an independent view of pre-introduction work). The passage would not exist, and the rest of the speech would run differently, had the interjection not been made, which is the deciding test. Marked down slightly from 1.0 only because the "C-" grade is his own gloss rather than something in the document he is quoting; the engagement itself is squarely on the claim. Scored on engagement alone — not on whether the rebuttal is true, polite or well-evidenced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We have." — Dana Kirkpatrick, interjecting to assert the Government had engaged with rural and remote communities

acuity.statement: If that particular member thinks that everybody knows that, then why do we need a truncated seven-week stage and to add additional pressure to the select committee? It is, frankly, insulting and idiotic.
acuity.explanation: He takes the content of the interjection directly and turns it into a counter-question: if the matter is already universally understood, the Government's own premise undercuts the need for a seven-week report-back. The sentence could not have been delivered without the preceding remark and would have to change if Peters had said something else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — the closing insult belongs to Civility, not here, and the fact that he is attacking the Government's conduct rather than the clause belongs to Focus.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Everybody knows that." — Winston Peters (interjecting on the report-back period debate)

acuity.statement: What’s more, and colleagues have spoken about this, but this Government had the time to allow the public to digest this information. They had the regulatory impact statement in October last year. These have been issues that have been around for years, but people are being given six weeks to engage. There was an option to, and they’ve chosen not to.
acuity.explanation: Walters follows Utikere's substantive speech on the shortened report-back date and takes up his specific evidentiary point — that the regulatory impact statement was completed in October of last year and the policy has been in the pipeline since — and draws out its consequence: the Government had time to let the public engage and chose six weeks instead. The speech would have had to change had the preceding turn not made the RIS-timeline argument, so this is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference; it falls short of 1.0 because it extends the previous speaker's point rather than contesting or refining it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "this is something that was completed—the initial regulatory impact statement—in October of last year"

acuity.statement: As my colleague Vanushi Walters pointed out, this issue has been an issue for a long time, and on 4 December, the Minister made announcements at a Federated Farmers event in Gore about this legislation being on the way. Why is it now being rushed at the last hour, when it should be thoroughly prosecuted through a select committee process?
acuity.explanation: Abel takes up Walters's strand that the issue is long-standing and that the compressed timetable is therefore unjustified, and extends it with the 4 December announcement; he also builds directly on the four-month amendment she urged support for by proposing five months instead. But much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on the bill's substance rather than engagement with her specific claims, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct taking-up of her reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "they would be taking the time to hear from New Zealanders" — her argument that the Government has not allowed New Zealanders adequate time to be heard on this bill

acuity.statement: Of course, we’ve had my colleague Tangi Utikere put up a four-month time frame. We’ve had Steve Abel put up a five-month time frame, pointing out that the six-month time frame, which is the standard time frame for bills in the Standing Orders, would result in a Christmas report-back date, which is obviously problematic.
acuity.explanation: Brooking restates the competing amendments accurately, accepts Abel's Christmas-date reasoning as settling that six months is not needed, and then uses that concession to narrow the question to whether seven weeks is too short. The speech would have to be rewritten if Abel had moved a different time frame or given a different reason for it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "This is recognition that if it were to be six months, the closure of the submission process would be Christmas day—that is too long, but the current proposal would mean as little as 10 days"

acuity.statement: The Government has said a number of times, “Look, people have been aware of this issue; we put out a press release on 4 December 2024.” That is true, there was a press release put out on 4 December 2024 in the names of the Hon Todd McClay and the Hon Simon Watts, being both agriculture and climate change and, I believe, Todd McClay is also forestry.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the 4 December announcement that Abel had just raised, concedes it was made, then does something with it — showing the press release omits the ballot that makes up much of the bill, so prior notice does not cover the part submitters most need time on. This is engagement with the specific content of the preceding turn and of the Government's answer to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "on 4 December, the Minister made announcements at a Federated Farmers event in Gore about this legislation being on the way"

acuity.statement: Oh, do you think so, Joseph Mooney? Oh, it’s a surprise to hear that from you!
acuity.explanation: Jackson turns directly to Mooney's interjection, so he is plainly reacting to what was just said, but he engages none of its content — there is no account of what the Opposition does know, only a sarcastic acknowledgement of the heckler before he returns to his prepared attack on the bill. Per the rubric, naming the previous speaker as a target is a mere reference, not engagement, which puts this in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 because the gesture at the exchange is explicit and immediate. The main body of his speech is ineligible for acuity, since no other member's turn precedes it in this window.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Opposition doesn’t know what it’s talking about" — Joseph Mooney

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand to strongly oppose this bill, because this is a bill that is continuing this Government’s agenda to punch down on the poor, to create more blue tape for the people of Aotearoa New Zealand, and, to be perfectly honest, to a Government that loves cars so much they want more people to live in them.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan follows a substantive turn by Willie Jackson but engages none of its content; his speech is prepared Green opposition to the bill that would read identically whatever Jackson had said. It stays squarely on the matter under debate and gestures at the debate's course (the Minister's short third reading speech, the committee stage), which puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but the engagement is with the Minister and with his own colleague Ricardo Menéndez March, not with the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We can see no value in harassing job seekers any more than they currently are." — Willie Jackson. Nothing: Jackson argued the bill denies welfare and harasses job seekers, and this statement does not take up any part of that argument.

acuity.statement: That member believes that this bill is going to punish those who are on a benefit, and the member who just spoke before, Lawrence Xu-Nan, believes that this is about reducing or cutting benefits. Actually, this bill doesn’t do that. What this bill does is ensure that the information of clients that is held by the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) is up to date.
acuity.explanation: She names both preceding speakers' central claims — punishment of beneficiaries, cutting benefits — denies them directly, and then supplies an alternative account of what the bill does (placing an information-updating duty on MSD so the correct level of assistance is set). The speech would have to change if the previous speakers had made a different argument about the bill, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because she restates their positions in her own summary form rather than taking up a specific figure or provision they relied on, and some of her reply is prepared ACT material on the welfare system.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a Government whose agenda is to reduce or cut $200 million of cost into the people, into beneficiaries" — Lawrence Xu-Nan (and Willie Jackson's claim that the bill is a way "to deny people welfare").

acuity.statement: Much has been said about the Social Security (Mandatory Reviews) Amendment Bill and what it is not. But what it is is a structured approach, an annual check-up, an opportunity for beneficiaries to be able to check and confirm their circumstances, and to update their entitlements. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Walters had just made two specific arguments — that inserted sections 310C/310D place no statutory limit on the information a beneficiary can be compelled to provide (a s 14/s 5 BORA problem the Ministry of Justice advice resolves only by "expectation"), and that automated decision-making with a human late in the chain compounds bias. Garcia engages neither the legal argument, the advice, nor the automation point. He acknowledges that "much has been said ... about what it is not" and then asserts a prepared characterisation of the bill as a "structured approach, an annual check-up" before commending it. The speech would read identically had any other critic preceded him, so this sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the opening clause does at least nod at the criticisms made in the debate, and the content is squarely on the bill under consideration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is clearly a prima facie breach, yes, but potentially a complete breach of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act" — Vanushi Walters; also her point on automated decision-making. Garcia takes up no part of either: "Much has been said ... about what it is not" is a bare gesture at the preceding debate.

acuity.statement: Although I didn’t get to speak much on this bill previously, I do commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposing turn by Belich that set out specific objections (the review power already exists, disability is permanent, automated decision-makers will wrongly remove entitlement, the Salvation Army's opposition). The reply engages none of it — it simply commends the bill. It would be word-for-word identical whatever Belich had argued, so it sits in the bottom band; 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it at least names the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued the bill's mandatory 52-week reviews of the disability allowance are cruel and that automated decision-making will strip entitlements from people with permanent disabilities, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Sanctions do not help people find jobs—despite the kōrero; you know, “Get off the couch.” Of course get off the couch, but who will be there to help make that happen? The majority of people that I know, having worked in the sector, are not lying on the couch because they’re hopeless; they’re lying on the couch because they are disconnected and they do not belong.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding NZ First speech — the personal-responsibility / "teach them to fish" framing — and answers it directly by contesting the premise that people on benefits are idle and that sanctions produce work. She then returns to prepared material about her sector experience and the Minister's earlier speech, so the engagement is partial rather than a full rebuttal of the argument just put. Scored on engagement only, not on whether the reasoning or the claim holds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tanya Unkovich: "So New Zealand First, we really do believe in personal responsibility, and whilst we really agree in ensuring that everyone gets a leg up and a hand up"

acuity.statement: I rise with a heavy heart to speak at this third reading. At this final stage, I want to speak directly to the truth of this bill, in that it completely ignores the advice of experts, including that of the Welfare Expert Advisory Group.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it — but the speech is prepared material on the correct subject. The opening whakataukī about manaakitanga faintly glances at Unkovich's "big hearts" claim without engaging it, and nothing in the speech would need to change had the two previous speakers argued something else about the bill. On-topic but unresponsive, hence the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kapa-Kingi argued that sanctions increase poverty and homelessness and that policies that read reasonably on paper are harmful when applied, and Unkovich argued for personal responsibility and a "hand up"; this statement takes up neither, opening instead on prepared material about the Welfare Expert Advisory Group's advice.

acuity.statement: This bill is very simple. It amends the Social Security Act to enable an efficient and proactive welfare system where clients receive the correct entitlement and ensures that every year—every 52 weeks—there is a requirement that the Ministry of Social Development must review a client’s eligibility and the rate of a specified benefit to ensure they’re getting the right amount.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific 52-week point Doyle had just made, recasting it as a duty on the Ministry to check entitlement rather than a burden on the claimant to reapply — so the speech is not indifferent to what preceded it. But it leaves the substance of the preceding arguments untouched (the expert advice, the effect on people with permanent disabilities, Kapa-Kingi's harm claim), and the surrounding "nonsense that the Opposition's been on about" is a mere reference that engages nothing. Partial engagement, below the 0.5 mark. Scored for engagement alone — the dismissive framing belongs to Civility and the quality of the characterisation to Rigor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Benjamin Doyle: "It told us clearly in recommendation 11 to remove the requirements to reapply for a benefit every 52 weeks."

acuity.statement: The question I pose to the Government, of course, is: is an extra 58c, which is the increased amount over the last 12 months for this rebate, per fortnight, the sort of alleviation of cost pressure that seniors who’ve worked so hard actually deserve?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own framing — that hard-working seniors deserve relief — and tests it against a specific quantity (58c a fortnight), turning his premise into a question about the adequacy of the measure he just commended. The passage would have to change if Watts had argued the bill's merits differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Now, seniors have worked hard throughout their years and deserve to enjoy their retirement without added financial stress."

acuity.statement: We’ve heard the Minister acknowledge the New Zealand First Party because it is accepted that, yes, this is part of the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, but that’s been the case for quite some time. The question that needs to be posed is why has it taken the Government so long since they have addressed that as part of their negotiations—to actually deliver on that commitment.
