acuity.explanation: Picks up the precise item Watts had just offered as a credit — the coalition commitment — and draws out its consequence against him: if the commitment is that old, the delivery is late. Directly keyed to the preceding turn rather than a mere mention of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "The National Party and New Zealand First in their coalition agreement included a commitment to enhance local government rates rebate schemes for SuperGold card holders"

acuity.statement: I reference the fact that this bill has been progressed under urgency with a tinge of sadness, because what would have been really helpful, I would have thought, would be to hear about the impact that this would have on households out in the community—but perhaps, actually, the impact that it would have if the threshold had changed, the impact that it may have had if some of the other components to the criteria that’s been proposed in this bill would change as well.
acuity.explanation: Engages the urgency Watts had just thanked the House for and disputes it on a specific ground — the select committee evidence on thresholds and criteria that urgency forecloses. Partly prepared opening material, so it engages the strand rather than a particular figure or inference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I want to thank the House again for considering this bill under urgency" / "That’s why it is important we consider this bill under urgency."

acuity.statement: But the message I send to this Government—the question I ask to members opposite and to the Ministry of Education—is: what is the Government doing to ensure that communities like Rongotea and Ashhurst are able to utilise bus services and routes?
acuity.explanation: Prepared constituency material that engages no part of the preceding turn and is not even on the matter under debate; it would read identically whoever had spoken before and could have been delivered in a different debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts spoke about the rates rebate abatement threshold and the SuperGold card, and this statement does not take any of it up — it raises Ministry of Education rural bus funding in the speaker's own electorate, which another member then challenged as irrelevant to the bill.

acuity.statement: Just for context, again this is one of the bills that was introduced under urgency, which meant that it had very little public consultation. We do have a regulatory impact statement, which is at least the minimum that the Government could be doing when we are introducing a bill under urgency, but what we did hear from the Minister during the committee stage was that there were no other policies that were considered as a part of this.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the turn immediately before it — Utikere's complaint that the bill was rammed through under urgency without hearing from the community — and extends it with the regulatory impact statement point, then moves to prepared material drawn from the committee stage rather than engaging Utikere's other arguments. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is unfortunate that the Government has decided to ram this through under urgency when they've known that this was coming. They have not wanted to hear from the community" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: So we will not support it, because there is so much more that we could be doing, this Government could be doing, and they chose to do nothing.
acuity.explanation: Lands on the contrary position to the speaker immediately before him without engaging his stated reason for voting the other way; it is prepared caucus positioning on the right subject, with only a gesture at the live disagreement in the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You know, it would be irresponsible, actually, if we did not support this, because at a time when households are doing it tough" — Tangi Utikere. The conclusion is the opposite of Utikere's, but the reasoning he gave for supporting the bill — that any small help to households is worth taking — is not taken up or answered.

acuity.statement: Finally, just to echo what my colleague Cam Luxton has just said, this will help some ratepayers, but the other thing that needs to be done across the board is councils have the monopoly ability and statutory ability to rate; that comes with responsibility and that means the responsibility to use the money that they get from ratepayers wisely, carefully, and to deliver good value for money.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the immediately preceding ACT speech — that real rates relief comes from councils restraining their own spending — and extends it by naming the statutory monopoly to rate as the source of that responsibility. It engages the topic and direction of Luxton's argument rather than any specific claim or figure in it, and arrives at the end of otherwise prepared NZ First material, so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster responds to Cameron Luxton: "Councils need to focus on services and infrastructure that can only be delivered locally, not duplicating roles that are the purview of central government."

acuity.statement: Te Pāti Māori considers this to be one of the only areas of the Budget it can support, but questions why the income abatement threshold was not raised across the board.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party material squarely on the bill under debate, delivered after two substantive turns it does not take up. Foster had just set out the specific abatement-threshold change (32,000 to 45,000, about $600 a year) and Luxton had argued relief must come from council spending restraint; this speech raises the abatement threshold as its own point without engaging either account of it. On topic, but indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued the threshold moves from 32,000 to 45,000 and is worth about $600 a year, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: New Zealand First talks about “homes”. It only means owner-occupied homes. Some people call their rentals “homes”.
acuity.explanation: Seizes the exact rhetorical move Foster had just made — his distinction between "houses" and "homes" when describing superannuitants priced out — and turns it against his conclusion, arguing the word covers renters too and that the bill therefore privileges owners. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged if the previous speaker had framed the bill differently; this is engagement with the specific content, and disagreement is the strongest evidence of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown responds to Andy Foster: "they are really concerned that they might be priced out of their own homes—not their houses; their homes"

acuity.statement: Madam Speaker, did you hear that? Every superannuitant should be listening to that. The Green Party is opposing this bill, as is the Labour Party.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the conclusion of the preceding speech — that the Greens will oppose the bill — but engages none of the reasoning that produced it: nothing on renters paying rates through rent, nothing on single and widowed women over 65, nothing on under-investment driving rates. Repeating an opponent's position back in order to pivot to commending the bill is a reference, not a response, so this sits in the low band despite being aimed at the previous turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer responds to Celia Wade-Brown: "So we will be opposing this bill."

acuity.statement: Well, Mr Bates, the reason that I would suggest that you would know the correct position of our party is because it has been said numerous times in the House, and that is the role of people in the House; to be part of the debate and listen to those who are taking part in it.
acuity.explanation: Bates had just asked, as an interjection, why National should not have assumed Labour would oppose the bill. Belich takes that exact question and answers it on its own terms: the reason he should know Labour's position is that it has been stated repeatedly in the House, and listening is part of a member's job. She names him, addresses the question put, and supplies a direct answer rather than pivoting. If Bates had interjected something else on the same topic, this sentence would have had to change, which is the deciding test. Not a 1.0 only because the answer restates her prior point rather than doing anything further with his claim that Labour is 'the party of no'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "Why would we not think that you were going to say no?"

acuity.statement: You’re the party of no. Why would we not think that you were going to say no?
acuity.explanation: Belich had just complained that the other side had not been listening and so did not know Labour supports the bill. Bates engages that specific complaint head-on and offers a reason why the assumption was reasonable — a characterisation of Labour's general posture. It is responsive to the actual point she made, not merely to the topic, which is why it scores above the prepared-material band. Held below 0.9 because he engages her complaint with an assertion about Labour rather than with her evidence that the position had been stated repeatedly in earlier readings. Scored on engagement only; the jibe's tone and its argumentative weakness belong to other attributes and are deliberately not reflected here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "a number of speakers, not only in this debate but in the committee of the whole House stage and in the second reading and the first reading said that, indeed, Labour supports this bill"

acuity.statement: I’m so pleased to stand. Sixty-six thousand seniors will be better off. I’m going to repeat that: 66,000 seniors will be better off with this bill—one of many cost of living relief payments we’re doing. I commend this bill.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a long, specific critique: that the bill was taken under urgency with no select committee, that consultation in the departmental disclosure statement covered councils but not affected ratepayers, that questions in committee went unanswered, and that the measure does not go far enough against rising costs. He takes up none of it — not the process objection, not the consultation gap, not the adequacy argument. The speech is prepared praise plus a headline figure and would be word-for-word identical whatever Belich had said. It stays in the 0.0-0.3 band rather than at 0.0 because it is at least about the bill under debate and gestures at the cost-of-living frame she raised; a government backbencher following a minister's bill with unaltered commendation is exactly the case this rubric scores low, and the same test would apply to an opposition member doing the reverse.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued the bill was rushed through under urgency without a select committee process and does not go far enough on the cost of living, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: As the last contributor in this debate, I just want to say that I’m the last person that is standing in the way of 66,000 senior gold card holders getting rates relief. So, without further ado, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Bidois had a full speaking slot immediately after a substantive critique and used it only to waive his time and commend the bill. He echoes the 66,000 figure Sosene had just used, but a repeated number is a reference, not an engagement: none of her actual arguments (no select committee process, councils left to communicate the scheme, superannuitants without English or internet access, the limitations flagged in the regulatory impact statement) is taken up, conceded or rebutted. The words would have been identical whatever the preceding speaker had said, so this sits in the unresponsive band; it earns 0.2 rather than 0.0 only because it is squarely about the bill under debate and acknowledges its place as the last contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene argued the bill 'only goes part way' because there was 'nil discussion that has been had with the community' and no select committee process, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I appreciate that the speaker before me, the Hon Jenny Salesa, addressed the need of particularly the 66,000 seniors in New Zealand, who would appreciate the support from this Government—and relatively soon, actually. But I do also want to emphasise that the Green Party oppose this bill because they believe it’s either everything for everyone, all at the same time, from money falling out of the tree—or nothing, for everyone. And that is absolutely impractical and, basically, just living in la-la land. But, anyway, this Government, the National Government, is about targeting the relief and delivering for people who need it, so I commend this bill.
acuity.explanation: Lu names the preceding speaker and acknowledges the seniors she spoke for, and her closing claim that the Government is "about targeting the relief and delivering for people who need it" is a real, if brief, counter to Salesa's central charge that the bill is too narrowly drawn. But she never takes up the specific gap Salesa identified (non-homeowners, multigenerational households, the under-65 working poor) and instead spends most of the turn attacking the Green Party, who had not spoken in this debate stretch. That is partial engagement — one strand answered, the rest prepared material — hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill gives some help to some people, but, unfortunately, it gives no assistance to many thousands more." — Jenny Salesa

acuity.statement: In our community in South Auckland, there is a real problem with the gambling on those pokie machines. They’re just too prevalent in our local community, and it does not reduce in terms of gambling harm behaviour. That is part of this legislation, and I did want to raise it.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Brewer's substantive turn precedes it. Sosene speaks to the bill under debate (class 4 gambling is within its scope), so this is prepared material on the right subject, but she engages no part of Brewer's content about the TAB's extended online wagering monopoly. Her only cross-reference is to Peeni Henare, who does not speak in this stretch. Scored 0.2 on engagement alone; the merit of her harm argument belongs to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer commended the third reading and wished TAB New Zealand well as it 'extends its monopoly on race wagering to include online betting', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I rise to support this bill on behalf of the National Party. TAB New Zealand is the financial backbone of New Zealand’s racing industry.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Sosene's turn immediately precedes and makes a concrete claim about gambling harm. Wedd's speech is wholly prepared commendation (board acknowledgements, economic contribution figures) and would read word-for-word the same whatever Sosene had said. It stays on the bill, so not 0.0, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lemauga Lydia Sosene argued that pokie machines are 'just too prevalent in our local community' and that the bill was a missed opportunity on class 4 gambling harm; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I think that some of my colleagues, like Peeni Henare and Lemauga Lydia Sosene, have made some very good representations around the concerns that we have as a Labour Party about the impact of gambling products like pokies. Gambling products like betting on horse racing are far more regulated, are far safer, and cause significantly lower levels of harm for people. There would have been an opportunity here to take some steps and take some action around reducing the harm that comes from the use of class 4 pokies, which I’ve certainly seen in my community—some examples of significant harm that it causes to people in communities.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Sosene's class 4 strand explicitly by name and does something with it — draws the contrast with race betting as a more regulated product and names the specific consequence, that work which 'would have removed TAB's class 4 licence' did not proceed. Not 1.0 because the engagement is with an ally's point rather than a rebuttal, and the bulk of her speech is prepared select-committee material that would stand unchanged whoever spoke before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "In our community in South Auckland, there is a real problem with the gambling on those pokie machines."

acuity.statement: It gives me great pleasure to stand in support of this bill, a bill which goes a long way to supporting the racing industry in New Zealand, which is a big part of our DNA. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a detailed preceding turn by Boyack offered plenty to engage. This is generic commendation of the racing industry that would be identical whatever had just been argued. It names the right bill, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Boyack argued at length that the bill was a missed opportunity on class 4 pokies and canvassed the sporting codes' asks on sections 82 and 56; this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I rise just to say well done to all of those involved. This is a great bill. I did my time on the board of Hawke’s Bay Racing, and I know all of that team will be very pleased. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — substantive preceding turns by Boyack and Anderson. A short personal commendation that engages no claim made in the debate; indifferent to what it follows. Scored 0.1 because it is at least about the bill in front of the House.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.statement: I just wanted to pick up on the question that my colleague asked around the appointment of a judge as a board member. I think the concern that we have, and we just want to raise that in the committee, is because they would be able to potentially continue—so they bring over skills, relevant skills and expertise, like we saw with Judge Becroft when he was the Children’s Commissioner. But the concern, I suppose, I want to raise here is: given it is the Independent Children’s Monitor of the children’s system, and courts play a role in that entire system, it doesn’t create some kind of potential conflict there that could threaten the true independence of the monitor and the board.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific point — that the bill preserves judicial tenure so a judge is not precluded from the board — accepts the skills rationale she gave (and the Becroft precedent she herself cited), then draws out a consequence she did not address: that courts sit inside the system being monitored. The speech would have to change if Upston had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "if a judge was appointed on to the Independent Children’s Monitor board, the same provisions would allow, because what we wouldn’t want it to do is preclude a judge for considering being on that board"

acuity.statement: I thank the member, and I think what is useful—and it’s a good issue to raise—but just thinking about the three entities of the Independent Children’s Monitor, is they provide advice; they do the monitoring. It’s not advocacy, and I think that’s where—obviously, when the appointments are being made to the board, that would be something to consider, but I don’t see it would be an issue.
acuity.explanation: Meets the conflict-of-interest objection on its own ground by distinguishing the monitor's advisory/monitoring function from advocacy, and concedes it is a consideration at appointment. It engages the specific claim rather than the topic, though it does not take up the 'courts are part of the system' element directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "it doesn’t create some kind of potential conflict there that could threaten the true independence of the monitor and the board"

acuity.statement: Given that answer, I do think we need to note on the record that when we look at the experiences shared in the royal commission and the complaints made, a lot of distrust exists amongst the community of the oversight in the past, and still of the current systems between courts, agencies, and so on.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly builds on the answer just given and presses the unanswered part of it: that even if the board's role is advice rather than advocacy, survivor distrust of courts and agencies is the live problem. Directly contingent on what Upston said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "It’s not advocacy... but I don’t see it would be an issue"

acuity.statement: I thank the member the Hon Willow-Jean Prime for raising that, and my feedback to that would be: this is a board, and I think, at an operational level—so when it is the staff themselves who go in to monitor a facility or go in to monitor and engage with providers—I could absolutely see that survivors would be concerned if they were confronted with a member of the judiciary who is doing that work. But this is at a governance level, and their role doesn’t include any oversight of the judicial system; that would, clearly, be inappropriate.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the survivor-distrust point where it would bite — operational monitoring — and disputes it where the bill actually applies, at governance level. Accepting part and distinguishing the rest is the strongest form of engagement with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "a lot of distrust exists amongst the community of the oversight in the past, and still of the current systems between courts, agencies"

acuity.statement: I suppose what I would note here is that it does have a five-year review clause, and maybe if that turns out to be an issue once this is enacted, then that is something that could be looked at through the review process—that it didn’t have any unintended consequences.
acuity.explanation: Responds to the governance/operational distinction by accepting the answer provisionally and proposing the review clause as the remedy if it proves wrong. Engages one strand — whether the risk can be revisited — rather than the substance of the distinction itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "But this is at a governance level, and their role doesn’t include any oversight of the judicial system"

acuity.statement: So I just wanted to know: what specific legislative provisions, either in this bill or in other Acts, override or limit the monitor’s independence? And can the Minister please provide some of those expectations?

acuity.statement: Also, the ability to appoint a Deputy Children’s Commissioner, I think, is an important addition in terms of continuity and in terms of having support for the Children’s Commissioner. I’m aware of the importance of administrative support for a Children’s Commissioner, and you might appoint a Children’s Commissioner that is an amazing advocate who isn’t necessarily the best person at managing an organisation, and so I’m clear that the legislation that we are presenting today has the flexibility to ensure the Children’s Commissioner is able to be supported with an organisation, to cover off those skill sets, because the Children’s Commissioner should be first and foremost focused on advocacy rather than administration.

acuity.statement: So having this independence and having this independent oversight, and also having the extra accountability of the additional reporting—for agencies having to respond to that reporting and having to keep coming back and showing their progress in those recommendations—adds that extra bit of accountability to make sure that it’s not just another report that sits on a shelf and grows cobwebs while people forget all about it.

Chhour engages that same point in her own terms — agencies must respond and come back showing progress so it is not 'another report that sits on a shelf'. She also implicitly corrects Carter's framing by insisting the bill concerns the whole cross-agency system, not Oranga Tamariki alone. Beyond that, however, the speech is prepared material walking through the bill's three features and her own history of opposing the split model, and it would mostly have been delivered unchanged whatever Carter had said — in particular she does not touch Carter's central claims about colonial structures, Māori overrepresentation or breaches of the National Care Standards. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Hopefully, this will mean that the monitor will no longer issue report after report with little to no action being taken." — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, the Hon Karen Chhour, said, we’ve traversed quite a lot over this bill over the past little while, so there isn’t a lot to add.

acuity.statement: This is a very good bill that is going to strengthen the independent monitoring of the Oranga Tamariki system. It literally creates more independence for the independent monitor, and as the Oranga Tamariki system, that includes, without limitation, the delivery of health, education, disability, and other services by those agencies or contracted partners within the Oranga Tamariki system.

acuity.statement: On this third reading of the Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Legislation Amendment Bill, we confirm that the object of the bill is for the improvement of the outcomes of young children and youth in the care of Oranga Tamariki. I commend this bill to the House.

But it never takes up Bennett's actual claim about diversity, inclusion or seeing oneself represented, and the rest ('agreement across the House', 'I commend this bill') is prepared third-reading material that would read the same whoever had spoken before. Partial engagement with one strand, then back to prepared text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: we had more voices around the table — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: I stand to take, I think, the last call on this bill, the Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Legislation Amendment Bill. acuity.statement: But I have a question that’s in relation to clause 11, amended section 6(2), and it refers to the specified pay deduction and having that meaning. acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "In this particular clause, as it’s currently written, the employer is given 10 working days to do that, which is actually quite a long time" — Andersen takes up the same clause 11 but not this argument about the recovery period.

acuity.statement: In terms of clause 14, I guess this is a little bit more on the line of semantics. I hear from the previous speakers regarding some of the elements of collective agreements. Now, the current wording of section 587(2) of the Education and Training Act states that “the powers referred to in that subsection include the power to lock out [employees] or suspend [the] employees.” It creates an either/or situation and it is in some way exclusive to those two particular options.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan picks up the exact provision Belich had just queried — new section 587(2) in clause 14 — and does something further with it, drawing out a drafting consequence she did not raise: that the restated list, lacking a conjunction and introduced by "include", may no longer be exclusive and could expand the powers beyond the three named. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had not put 587(2) in play, which is high responsiveness; it stops short of 1.0 because he then proceeds to his own prepared pair of questions rather than resolving or disputing Belich's "why restate existing law" point itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "So in this particular section, it specifically states that employers are allowed to lock out, suspend, and make pay deductions. That already exists in law. Why is it outlined again, as in this bill?"

So that’s 10 days.

acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "So I’ve suggested that that is changed to “5 working days”, and that is simply so there is a more immediate onus on the employer to discover when the alleged overpayment has been made"

My questions are about the relationship between this and various other Acts, one being the Wages Protection Act and the other being the new wage theft legislation. They need to meet the requirements in the Employment Relations Act, and so that’s the answer to your question.

Scored only on engagement; whether the answer is adequate in substance is not an acuity question.

acuity.responding_to: "would you think that would come under the issue in the Wages Protection Act of an unreasonable deduction" — Helen White

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued the bill removes the courts' ability to assess 'the real nature of the job' and lets anyone earning over $180,000 'be fired at will', and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: If this Government is going for growth, they’re doing it the wrong way. This is holding people back. This is paying people less. This is paying it to their mates and looking after their own group of friends while watching the rest of New Zealand suffer and not even be able to put food on the table.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding speaker, Weenink, grounded the bill in growth — 'It's about going for growth. Economic growth will lead to greater opportunities for workers.' Andersen takes that strand up directly and inverts it: if growth is the goal, this is the wrong route, because it holds people back and pays them less. That is a real engagement with one strand of the argument just made, and it is pointable. But she does not engage Weenink's actual mechanism — the claim that the personal grievance 'industry' is a handbrake on productivity — and the rest of the turn is prepared material on the 30-day rule and the $180,000 threshold. Partial engagement, so mid-band rather than 1.0. Disagreement does not lower this score; the limit is how much of Weenink's reasoning is actually taken on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's about going for growth. Economic growth will lead to greater opportunities for workers." — Vanessa Weenink

acuity.statement: This bill does actually help support the Government’s going for growth agenda, and isn’t that what we all want? Growth provides opportunities, and that’s what everyone in this House should actually aspire to.
acuity.explanation: Andersen had just said 'If this Government is going for growth, they're doing it the wrong way', and Butterick's 'does actually help support' contradicts that flatly — but contradiction is not engagement. He supplies no answer to why the growth route is the right one, and takes up none of the specific claims Andersen had just made: the removal of the 30-day rule undercutting collective coverage, the $180,000 personal grievance bar, or the sexual harassment consequence she raised. What follows is generic prepared material on flexibility, compliance costs and 'red tape that we all love to hate'. The gesture at the growth frame earns 0.3; there is nothing of Andersen's reasoning actually taken on, so it does not reach the 0.5 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If this Government is going for growth, they're doing it the wrong way. This is holding people back." — Ginny Andersen (asserted against, but its reasoning is not engaged)

acuity.statement: The Legal Services (Distribution of Special Fund) Amendment Bill recognises the valuable service that community law centres provide to the public. They give information, give support to the public, and enable the normal person on the street the opportunity to understand the legal circumstances they may find themselves in. The bill enables and facilitates this support and the work of community law centres.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Andersen that made specific points about what is and is not explicit in the current Act, the overheads example in the legislative statement, and funding adequacy. Garcia's speech engages none of it — it is general praise for community law centres and a commendation of the bill, and would read identically whatever Andersen had said. It is at least on the subject of the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued that the current legislation is not explicit about the special fund covering overheads and that Crown funding is presently required for support functions, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Government members have made the point that making this change will reduce the pressure on the Government Vote—so Vote Justice. I think we need to be a bit cautious about proceeding down that line of argument. In truth, the special fund, at times, in the past, has not been sufficient to meet the needs of Community Law funding. If you look back to 2012, for example, the interest received on the fund was actually just under $5 million, which wasn’t anywhere close to the $10.97 million that was needed to fund Community Law at the time.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what preceded — whether the special fund can carry the funding that Crown money currently carries — and supplies a historical figure to argue it cannot, then moves on to her own prepared points about the scope of the contracting provision and the banks' 40 percent. It engages the line of argument being run in the debate rather than a specific claim in the immediately preceding turn (Garcia's), so this is partial engagement, not a direct rebuttal of the previous speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "Currently, Crown funding is required to fund functions that facilitate or otherwise support the delivery of those community legal services. It’s important that they are funded properly." Walters takes up the adequacy-of-funding strand and pushes back on the argument that the change relieves Vote Justice.

acuity.statement: I’d just like to, in the first instance, acknowledge and thank our community law centres for the services that they provide in our communities and, often, for those who are our most vulnerable. I’ve met with them a number of times in the Wairarapa electorate, and they’re very passionate and compassionate, and I would like to thank them for what they do.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows a detailed critique that invited a government response on the Vote Justice argument and the scope of the contracting power. Butterick's contribution is thanks to local community law centres and a commendation of the bill; it would be word-for-word the same whatever Walters had argued. It remains on the subject of the bill, so the floor of the on-topic band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters had just raised two specific select-committee cautions — that the special fund has historically fallen short of Community Law's needs and that the contracting scope should not be widened beyond Community Law — and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I put it to the Minister that if we could see those Amendment Papers before we're in the committee stage of the bill, that would be a useful thing to do.
acuity.explanation: Bishop twice flagged, in the speech immediately preceding, that Amendment Papers on the Auckland City Rail Link upzoning and on the Gordon Wilson Flats would only appear at the committee of the whole House stage. Brooking takes that specific disclosure and does something with it — asks that the papers be released before the committee stage so the House can consider them. The request could not exist without what Bishop had just said; substitute a different speech and this sentence would have to change. Not 1.0 only because she engages the timing of the papers rather than the substance of the changes he described.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there will be Amendment Papers that will become available for the House during the committee of the whole House stage" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I want to start by saying this bill touches on many different resource management issues, and we've heard a few of them covered by the Minister for Infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: This acknowledges that the Minister spoke and that he covered some of the bill's issues, but engages no part of what he actually argued — not the Auckland PC 78 withdrawal, not the decision to abandon the MDRS opt-out the Government campaigned on, not the heritage delisting. It is a gesture at the preceding turn rather than an engagement with it, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop argued the bill's Auckland housing-capacity, MDRS and heritage changes were justified, and this statement does not take any of that up — it only notes that he covered some issues.

acuity.statement: Over 90 percent of the land in Southland is covered by catchment groups doing good work on fresh water.
acuity.explanation: Simmonds' interjection lands directly on the specific premise Pham had just asserted — that there has been two decades of inaction on nutrient run-off in Southland waterways — countering it with a claim about catchment-group coverage of Southland land. It engages the content of the claim, not merely the topic, and would have had to be different had Pham argued something else. Scored just below 1.0 because, as a single-line interjection, it asserts the counter-fact without drawing out the consequence for Pham's argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There’s largely been complete inaction over those two decades" — Lan Pham, on Southland nutrient pollution and estuaries

acuity.statement: I really appreciate the comment that I’m hearing across the House about catchment groups; there is amazing work going on from the catchment groups, which we actually heard about on these trips down there. But what I really want to stress, and what I’m absolutely sick and tired of with this Government, is this constant conflation with any form of environmental protection being “anti-farming”.
acuity.explanation: Pham takes up the interjection explicitly, concedes its substance (catchment groups are doing good work, confirmed on her own Southland visits), and then engages what she reads as its implication — that her criticism is an attack on farming. That is a genuine partial engagement: she accepts the strand offered rather than disputing the 90 percent figure or the inaction point it was aimed at, and uses it as a bridge back to her prepared theme about this Government and farmers. Responsive enough to be clearly shaped by what preceded it, short of the top band because the specific counter-claim about catchment coverage is never actually contested.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Over 90 percent of the land in Southland is covered by catchment groups doing good work on fresh water." — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: The changes to section 70 take a pragmatic position so farmers don’t, effectively, get shut down in some parts of the country.
acuity.explanation: Radhakrishnan's immediately preceding turn made clause 15 / section 70 the centre of her objection, arguing the amendment permits the further pollution of already-polluted waterways. McCallum takes up that same provision and offers a competing rationale for it — that without it farmers in some catchments would be shut down — rather than ignoring her case. He engages the clause and its justification but does not address her specific point about already-degraded waterways or the Environmental Defence Society/High Court argument she raised, so it is a squarely aimed but partial rebuttal rather than a full one. Would clearly have been different had she argued something else about freshwater.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "what this amendment allows for is the further pollution of waterways. For that reason, we don’t agree with this part of the change."

acuity.statement: Then, with respect to farm plans, it’s really important now that, actually, the Minister can approve the industry organisations that can approve farm plans, not each individual council, so, therefore, it makes it more efficient.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the second strand of the preceding speech — her objection that the bill strips regional councils of their role as certifiers and auditors of freshwater farm plans — by defending exactly that shift on efficiency grounds. The engagement is pointable and specific to her complaint, but he counters only with an efficiency assertion and leaves untouched her actual argument (that the primary regulator of the waterway should retain certification), and ignores her 50-hectare threshold criticism entirely. Partial but real engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "This bill removes regional councils from being the approved certifiers and auditors, and that’s problematic because, as the primary regulator of the waterway, they should have a role"

acuity.statement: We also have concerns about fresh water, and I was interested to hear earlier Rachel Brooking talking about farm plans. Yes, some of us are involved in our local catchment communities—the Wairarapa Catchment Collective is quite all-encompassing.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown follows Ngarewa-Packer, whose turn was a sustained argument that the bill breaches Te Tiriti, marginalises tangata whenua and undermines Treaty settlements, backed by a roll-call of iwi submissions. Wade-Brown takes up none of that: no mention of Tiriti, settlements or Maori submitters, and no response to the claim that the bill's efficiency gains come at tangata whenua's cost. Her speech is prepared material on the right subject (RMA history, fresh water, greenfields vs density) and would read identically whatever Ngarewa-Packer had said. She does gesture at the debate — naming Andy Foster and Rachel Brooking from earlier turns — which lifts her off the floor of the band, but those turns are not in the window and the engagement with the preceding speaker is nil.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued 'every time this Government talks about making things effective and efficient, it always seems to have an impact on us as tangata whenua' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I rise to support the Resource Management (Consenting and Other System Changes) Amendment Bill. This is a much-needed piece of legislation which makes targeted amendments to the Resource Management Act (RMA).
acuity.explanation: Two substantive opposition turns precede this one — Ngarewa-Packer on Tiriti breach and iwi opposition, Wade-Brown on fossil gas consents, farm environment plans under 50 hectares and greenfields growth. Wedd engages the content of neither. Her nearest approach is a bare reference, noting that consultation 'has already been pointed out by a member of the House', which borrows Ngarewa-Packer's acknowledgement of the Minister and pivots straight to praise rather than answering her objection; she then asserts that 'many supported a lot of this bill' among 300 submissions without touching the iwi submissions Ngarewa-Packer itemised, or Wade-Brown's specific point about the under-50-hectare exemption. The speech would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before. Low on Acuity for unresponsiveness alone — it is on-topic and courteous, which other attributes would score separately.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said 'There were concerns about the marginalisation of tangata whenua, specifically a lot of our iwi who are settled' and this statement does not take it up; the only nod to a prior turn is a reference to consultation having been pointed out.

acuity.statement: It’s great to hear such consensus across the House. I’ll be very brief—three things, really. Firstly, to our select committee chair, Catherine Wedd, happy birthday. I just acknowledge her on this special day. The definition of “long-lived infrastructure”, I think, has been a great addition to this amendment bill: something that’s 35 years consentable, 50 years durable—fantastic.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a substantive opposition turn that made three specific criticisms of the bill, and engages none of them. The opening line characterises the preceding speech as consensus — a bare reference that actually smooths over Luxton's stated reservations rather than answering them — and he then moves to prepared praise of the long-lived infrastructure definition, a birthday acknowledgement, and the proportionality clause. The speech would read identically had any other member spoken before him, but it is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits in the low band with a gesture rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jo Luxton argued that new section 70(3) in clause 15 would let councils permit discharges that "could result in adverse effects to aquatic life", and raised the 50-hectare farm plan threshold and the independence of industry-body certification; this statement does not take any of that up. Her words "it is with some reservations, but I do commend this bill to the House" are glanced at by "such consensus across the House" and then dropped.

acuity.statement: Part of the select committee process was hearing from submitters, and, like the previous speakers have said, there were some concerns about labour issues. I do hear those concerns. I think the United Arab Emirates UAE is making rapid improvements, it’s becoming quite a modern society, and it’s one that we do really want to trade with. But we also need to think about some of our other trade agreements that we have with other partners, and I think it is a bit contradictory to bring up labour rights issues when we know that those are things that, actually, some of our other trading partners have as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific labour-rights strand of the preceding speech, concedes part of it (improvements in the UAE), and disputes the rest by arguing the objection is inconsistent with New Zealand's existing trading partners. The speech would read differently had Xu-Nan not made that argument, so it is clearly responsive; it does not, however, engage his other main strand about the lack of public scrutiny in treaty-making, which keeps it short of full marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the trade and sustainability development chapter is not enforceable" — Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, who argued the agreement risks feeding into UAE labour-rights violations, particularly for migrant workers

acuity.statement: Yep, this is, potentially, of small economic benefit right now, which I think the previous speaker, Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, talked about, but it’s actually the opportunities that this presents for our markets here and what it could actually bring in.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker's central economic claim, accepts its premise that the immediate gains are small, and does something with it by reframing the benefit as future market access and investment optionality rather than present tariff savings. This is direct engagement with the content of the claim, not a mere reference to it; it falls just short of 1.0 because it does not contest the figure or supply a counter-figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the most tangible benefit of this trade agreement is a reduction of tariffs worth less than $42.6 million per annum" — Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: As chair of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, it’s been a privilege to help guide this through its process in that committee, and I particularly want to thank the members of the committee for their efficient and effective consideration of this bill, and Opposition members in the Labour Party in particular, acknowledging that no deal is quite perfect but, actually, this is a very good deal—I will take Mr O’Connor’s concession on that regard—and it will be a fantastic benefit for the country.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Patterson that made several arguments (diversification, the Greens' spending demands, the investment-threshold trade-off) and engages none of them. It is committee-chair thank-yous and prepared praise for the bill, and would read identically whatever Patterson had said. It stays squarely on the matter under debate, and the glance at 'Mr O'Connor's concession' refers to a speaker whose turn is not in this stretch, so it cannot be pointed at as engagement here — hence the low end of the on-topic band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson spoke about diversifying trade, the Greens' position on taxation and the lift of the Overseas Investment Act threshold from $100 million to $200 million, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The other part that my colleague, I think, summarised quite well around lifting the investment threshold is that it is important that we get good investment into this country. It’s just as important that we make sure that there is strong accountability mechanisms when we look at how money comes into this country, what’s being invested in, where that money comes from, and in what way that money comes into this country is a really important question that not only this House should be asking but I know people across the country are asking, as foreign investors look to invest in this country.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding argument — Patterson's claim that lifting the screening threshold from $100 million to $200 million is sensible because scrutiny of large strategic purchases is retained — and puts the counter-weight on it, insisting accountability mechanisms over the source and destination of foreign money must be in place and will continue to be interrogated. That is genuine partial engagement, but it is framed as agreeing with his own colleague rather than answering Patterson's reasoning, and the rest of the speech (the Treaty of Waitangi submissions) is prepared material on the subject, so it sits at the mid-point rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "It still gives us the ability to scrutinise large strategic purchases, and we haven’t traded that away."

acuity.statement: Look, just in lieu of the time and to keep things moving, I just want to cover one aspect which was touched on briefly by the Minister for Trade and Investment, which is around the investment screening threshold lifting from $100 to $200 million. It was an area that I interrogated and it didn’t seem to have been something people had looked at particularly much previously through select committee processes around how this works, as it was explained to us. I think that it’s important that we get this right. It applies where the purpose of the business coming to New Zealand in that investment is specifically to facilitate trade in relation to this economic partnership, and I think that is important.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact strand the immediately preceding speaker pressed on — whether the lifted screening threshold leaves adequate oversight of incoming foreign money — and supplies content on it: the threshold applies only where the investment's purpose is to facilitate trade under this agreement, and a named LINZ team monitors it. That is a partial answer to the accountability concern rather than a direct engagement with Henare's reasoning (he credits the Minister for raising the topic, not Henare), so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "It’s just as important that we make sure that there is strong accountability mechanisms when we look at how money comes into this country"

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise in support of the United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill. This is progressing the process so that we can ratify the agreement that has been made, and I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Walters that raised specific, contestable points about rules of origin, self-certification and the investment threshold. The speech engages none of them — it is a formulaic statement of support that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. It is at least about the bill under debate, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued that the rules of origin are 'the real anchor of a trade agreement' and that the self-certification rule and the $200 million LINZ investment threshold need watching, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I want to devote my remarks in the debate to the issue of human rights in this trade agreement. I want to respond to some of the comments made by submitters at select committee and by colleagues in the House tonight who have questioned whether we should be making a trade agreement with the United Arab Emirates when the UAE falls well short of the human rights standards that we hold ourselves to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one strand of the preceding turn that had content to engage — Walters's glancing treatment of the Council of Trade Unions submissions and whether our trade partners must share our worldview — and does something with it, building out the pragmatism argument she only gestured at (we cannot trade only with countries that share our human rights standards; China; ASEAN). Partial rather than full engagement because the strand is developed into largely prepared material on human rights and foreign policy, and it addresses submitters and unnamed colleagues at least as much as the specific claim in front of him. Scored on engagement only: whether the pragmatism inference is sound belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think it is tempting to want all of our trade agreements to evolve on the same plane, with the same requirements in terms of our worldview. However, that’s not always going to be possible" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Look, it’s essential to the Government’s vision for doubling the value of exports from New Zealand—the fastest trade deal done to date. We’re not here to muck around and I’m not here to muck around. There’s no point belabouring the point. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows a detailed argument about whether human rights concerns should bar this agreement, and engages no part of it — not the premise, not the conclusion, not the UAE's record. The speech is prepared praise of the Government's export target and would be unchanged whatever the previous speaker had said. It stays on the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0. Brevity is not the fault being scored here; indifference to what preceded is.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued at length that the UAE's human rights record falls well short in labour rights, migrant workers' rights, freedom of expression and assembly, but that 'we cannot only trade with countries who share our views of human rights and democracy', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The other thing I can confirm is that councils are well advanced in their plans because this has been well signalled. So there will be no problem in this being implemented.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson follows Lan Pham's central charge that the bill is a rushed process councils could not keep up with, and takes that specific claim up directly, flatly contradicting it: councils are 'well advanced' because the change was 'well signalled'. He also glances at her objection on waste-water and stormwater standards and at her claim about councils' options ('I've heard a lot of talk across the House tonight, but this actually does provide flexible options for councils'). The engagement is real and pointable, but it answers assertion with counter-assertion rather than with the submissions she cited, and the rest of the turn is prepared ACT material on the three-waters rejection, so this sits at a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they didn't even have the time to consult with their communities" — Lan Pham, citing the submissions of Ōpōtiki, Thames-Coromandel District Council and Palmerston North City Council on the rushed process

acuity.statement: Well, this is what you get when you get the billboards all across the country, the knee-jerk, division-stoking “Stop three waters and co-governance” billboards across the country, and, in the words of the Prime Minister, you make policy based on bumper stickers.
acuity.explanation: Abel opens by seizing the exact point Foster had just made — the anti-three-waters billboards — and turning it against him: where Foster offered the billboards as evidence of public rejection of Labour's scheme, Abel makes them the cause of policy made 'based on bumper stickers'. The specific claim, not just the topic, is taken up and inverted, and the speech would have had to open differently had Foster not raised the billboards. It then moves on to prepared material on the infrastructure deficit, which keeps it just short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "Did we see hundreds and hundreds, if not thousands, of billboards all over the country saying no to three waters? No, we did not."

acuity.statement: That’s straight out of Otago University, Suze Redmayne. I can give you the paper if you’d like. It’s published international academic literature.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne's interjection challenges the evidentiary basis of the nitrate/bowel-cancer figure, and Abel answers that exact challenge by naming the source and offering the paper, rather than restating the claim or abusing the interjector. Squarely responsive to the content of the objection; marked slightly below the top because the thing engaged is a brief interjection and the answer cites provenance rather than engaging any reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: "Oh, that’s a long bow."

acuity.statement: The so-called bumper sticker of “Stop three waters” was not a bumper sticker by this Government. That was a bumper sticker that was being held up—have a look on the internet—by New Zealanders, that was being held up by community groups, that was being held up by the mayors of this country.
acuity.explanation: Brewer's first words correct the specific factual premise of Abel's charge — he disputes whose bumper sticker it was, attributing it to the public, community groups and mayors rather than to the Government, and then contrasts it with what he says National's own slogan was. The speech is directly shaped by the preceding turn and would have had to open differently had Abel argued something else; this is engagement with the content of the claim, not a mere reference to the previous speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "in the words of the Prime Minister, you make policy based on bumper stickers"

acuity.statement: I don’t know how we get accused of adding more costs on. We go back to the Nanaia Mahuta model where there were four entities and co-governance, and today we’ve heard most of these entities have all chosen their own pathway: 65 percent have grouped together. That’s democracy.
acuity.explanation: Opens by taking up the specific accusation Woods had just built her whole speech around — that these reforms raise costs on ratepayers — and answers it on the merits: councils have voluntarily grouped (against Woods's claim that the bill forces small councils to go it alone), the Auckland fix cost $300k against a billion, and CCO borrowing headroom has been lifted to 500 percent of revenue, which is a direct response to the funding-mechanism gap she raised. He also picks up her closing taunt about having no vision ("You want a vision—here's a good one for you"). It is partial rather than full engagement: he never touches the Department of Internal Affairs advice to the select committee or the $185 billion figure, which were her two load-bearing pieces of evidence, and much of the turn is prepared contrast with the previous Government's model.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "imposing more costs on New Zealanders during a cost of living crisis" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: In the Hamilton City Council—this is for you, Mr Hamilton—rates are going up 15.5 percent.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton had just denied that the reforms add costs; Russell answers that denial with a figure from his own city and names him while doing it, then runs the same move on Stephenson's electorate councils (Clutha, Queenstown Lakes). The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had been a different argument — the council-by-council list is aimed squarely at the member who said he did not know how his side got accused of adding costs. Not a 1.0 because she does not engage Hamilton's actual counter-mechanism (the lift in CCO borrowing capacity to 500 percent of revenue), which is his answer to who pays; she rebuts the denial rather than the reasoning behind it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t know how we get accused of adding more costs on" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: On this side of the House, we were busy during the most recent recess restoring law and order and restoring real consequences for crime. We’ve been concerned that New Zealanders should feel safe in their communities so we’ve built on the work that we’ve done ending the culture of excuses that we inherited from the previous administration by restoring three strikes, tougher sentencing laws, tightening up the sentencing laws to restrict the ability of judges to massively reduce sentences, and giving the police the extra powers that they need to take on the gangs.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith follows a substantive turn by Davidson in the same take-note debate, so he is eligible on responsiveness. His speech engages no part of her argument: it takes up neither the advisory group's disestablishment, nor Te Tiriti, nor family and sexual violence prevention, and instead delivers a prepared recitation of the Government's law-and-order programme followed by an attack on Labour's absence of justice policy. If Davidson's turn were deleted and replaced with any other argument, this speech would be word-for-word identical. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it is at least delivered within the debate slot she had just spoken in, but there is no gesture at what she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued that the Minister's discontinuation of Te Pūkotahitanga, the Tangata Whenua Ministerial Advisory Group — "This current Minister has decided to discontinue that tangata whenua advisory group" — undermines Te Tiriti and the Te Aorerekura violence prevention strategy, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: There is something that I know absolutely about vocational education and training, and that is that locals know best; local industries know best, local communities know best. And guess what! That member who just finished his speech didn't understand that when he set up that failed institution Te Pūkenga, he didn't understand it, and he disrespected those local communities.
acuity.explanation: Simmonds follows a substantive Hipkins speech and so is eligible, but she engages no part of its content. She names the previous speaker as a target ("that member who just finished his speech") and pivots to prepared material on vocational education and Te Pūkenga's deficits — the rubric's explicit case of an unresponsive pivot rather than a partial engagement. The speech would be essentially unchanged had Hipkins argued something else, so long as it was Hipkins speaking; it is at least within the broad matter before the House (government spending and young people's prospects), which keeps it above 0.1 rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins spoke about rates, power and insurance bills rising, 15,000 to 17,000 construction jobs going, and cuts to State house builds, hospital rebuilds and school upgrades — this statement takes up none of it, naming him as the architect of Te Pūkenga instead.

acuity.statement: We then saw homeowners—like the example the member just gave, and it is terrible for anyone in that situation—that, under that Government, could get cheap interest rates initially, and then the inflation took hold. Notably he claims the bill is 'too broad' while Halbert had just argued it was too narrow and inconsistent, and he never joins that disagreement. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the bill is inconsistent because it prohibits only bottled-water extraction while larger export water users (grapes, dairy, kiwifruit) are untouched, and this statement does not take that up — it asserts the opposite problem (too broad) without engaging Halbert's claim.

acuity.statement: It was interesting to note that Ryan Hamilton, the member who has just resumed his seat, talked about the fact that the Government acknowledges the need to protect fresh water to some degree, he said, and I find that particularly interesting in light of the changes that the Government has made which don’t protect fresh water to any degree.
acuity.explanation: She takes the specific formulation Hamilton had just used — protecting fresh water 'to some degree' — and does something with it, turning it into the premise of a rebuttal that the Government's own actions protect fresh water to no degree, which she then supports with the NBA repeal, the weakening of section 107 of the RMA, the blocking of Otago Regional Council's land and water plan, and the Te Mana o te Wai provision in the Act coalition agreement. Had Hamilton made a different argument, her opening would have had to change. Short of 1.0 only because after that engagement she moves into prepared material she concedes other speakers on her side have already made, rather than continuing to work on his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We acknowledge the intent of this bill, and there is a need to protect to some degree our fresh water" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: Just in—well, in Takanini, I went door-knocking the other day, unlike others, and they were telling me on the doorsteps to “Please keep going”, as they continuously tell me on the doorsteps. So to the list MP across the House—I don’t know if he goes door-knocking much, because he’s a list MP, but I go door-knocking very often and I hear what they’re saying on the doorsteps in Takanini, and they’re really, really looking forward to the continuous growth of our country to help them improve their lives and the lives of their children.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific place named in the interjection and answers it directly — Takanini residents on the doorstep telling her to keep going — so the speech would have been different had Halbert named a different electorate or said nothing. But the engagement is anecdotal rather than with the substance of the claim (whether living standards are in fact lifting there), and it slides quickly into a jibe about his being a list MP, which engages nothing. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Not in Takanini." — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: I know that this legislation is an attempt to rebalance the law. While there is capacity to make an application to have evidence heard in a different way, what I understand from my interactions with people like that woman is how incredibly devastating those kinds of violent situations are to people’s confidence and their trust in any system whatsoever.
acuity.explanation: White takes up one strand of the preceding turn directly: Nakhle had relayed the Law Society's doubt about the bill's necessity because applications for alternative ways of giving evidence can already be made. White concedes that capacity exists and answers it on the ground that an existing right of application is worthless to someone whose trust in the system has been destroyed. That concession-and-rebuttal is pointable engagement, but it is one clause, and the rest of the speech is prepared personal material (the Ōtāhuhu client, the lawyer attacked in the lift) that would have been delivered whatever Nakhle had said — hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "questioning the necessity of this bill, especially given the existing provisions" — Rima Nakhle, reporting the New Zealand Law Society's submission that applications for alternative evidence are already available and routinely granted

acuity.statement: I’ve repeatedly heard how many people submitted and supported this bill. Yes, there was support for this bill, but there were people who didn’t support this bill and there were some substantial reasons made why people didn’t support this bill.
acuity.explanation: Parmar takes up the specific submission-count claim Tuiono had just made and disputes the weight placed on it, then goes on to quote the dissenting submitters' reasons at length. The passage would have to change if the preceding speaker had not leaned on the submitter numbers, so it is genuinely shaped by what it follows. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "Nearly 90 percent of the submitters supported this bill. There were a small number that didn’t support the bill"

acuity.statement: Second thing: it’s a voluntary disclosure, so it’s up to that employee if they want to disclose how much they are earning, what their remuneration is. So, again, what’s the point?
acuity.explanation: Tuiono had addressed the voluntary-disclosure clause directly at ACT, inviting the party to reconsider on the ground that nobody is compelled to share their pay. Parmar engages that exact feature of the bill and turns it the other way: if disclosure is voluntary anyway, the bill achieves nothing. That is engagement with the strand aimed at her party, though she answers the clause rather than Tuiono's specific argument that voluntariness removes ACT's objection.

acuity.statement: Having said that, I also do feel that the select committee managed this bill really well in terms of not unfairly tilting the fine balance that colleagues have mentioned between both access and procedural fairness to the accused but also in terms of retaining the powers of the judge to be able to make decisions and refer back to what was the ordinary process.
acuity.explanation: Follows Garcia's speech and is squarely about the same bill, but takes up none of his content — not his point that the bill makes alternative evidence automatic, nor his claim that it aligns the Family Court with criminal-process protections. It gestures at 'the fine balance that colleagues have mentioned' and then proceeds with prepared material; the speech would read identically whatever Garcia had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paulo Garcia argued the bill removes the forced face-to-face giving of evidence and makes the alternative mode automatic ('So the bill will make this opportunity automatic'), and this statement does not take that up — it only gestures at colleagues having 'mentioned' a balance.

acuity.statement: I’ve got four kids, and two of those are girls that work in predominantly male-dominated industries. As a father, I think it’s important for the girls as well, when one of our girls is at tradies night—local night at the pub—that she should actually be able to talk to fellow tradies and say, “Well, what are you getting paid?”, because she needs to understand that she’s being paid fairly based on her skill level.
acuity.explanation: Butterick follows Patterson's substantive case against the bill (contract-law principle plus a defence of pay secrecy as merit-based and traditionally normal) and engages none of it. He gestures at the preceding turns ("as a number of other speakers have") and at the select committee, then delivers prepared personal material about his daughters in male-dominated trades. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the value of being able to discuss pay — and so sits above the floor, but it neither rebuts the sanctity-of-contract objection nor answers the claim that pay differentials are usually merit-based. The speech would be essentially identical whatever Patterson had argued, so it belongs in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 for the glance at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson argued that "this bill runs smack into the brick wall of New Zealand First's belief in the sanctity of contract law" and that "There's a reason why pay secrecy or, you know, some discretion around pay rates has traditionally been the norm in workplaces" — this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: It was interesting listening to the ACT Party contribution earlier, because the member made some assertions that this bill wasn’t required, and so I thought I might just bring an example to the House of when I’ve seen this exact issue play out in reality for women workers at a large retail store in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Boyack is squarely on the matter under debate and signals that she is answering an earlier assertion that the bill is unnecessary, but the turn immediately preceding her — Wedd's supportive speech on transparency, the gender pay gap and National's record — is engaged nowhere: her speech would read identically whatever Wedd had said. The assertion she does engage is not in the window, so no verbatim fragment can be cited for it, which places this in the 0.0-0.3 band rather than at a partial 0.5; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because there is a real gesture at the debate (an example offered specifically to meet a prior claim) rather than wholly prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable in the window: the preceding turn is Catherine Wedd ("this bill really does create more transparency in the workplace and it will make it safe for people to talk about their pay"), and Boyack does not take up any part of Wedd's argument — her rebuttal is aimed at an ACT Party contribution that falls outside the text provided, so the claim she engages cannot be pointed at here.

acuity.statement: It still puzzles me why the National Party chooses to define itself as the party of low pay.

It engages the substance of the preceding turn's self-characterisation rather than its specific figures, and the surrounding material is clearly prepared, so it sits short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "We in the National Party have a strong track record on reducing gender pay gaps."

acuity.statement: Wouldn’t it be great if the National Party actually was serious and reflected some concern that they evinced in the House tonight for fairness, for equity, being in opposition to discrimination, and actually stood up for New Zealanders getting decent pay and conditions in the workplace?
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up the professed commitment to fairness and transparency made in the immediately preceding speech and in other National contributions that evening, and challenges whether it is genuine. It engages the sentiment of the previous turn rather than any of its arguments or evidence, so it is a partial engagement that then returns to prepared themes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "We in the National Party support it because we believe it promotes fairness and transparency in the workplace"

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to take the last call in this debate and to restore some decorum in this debate, after the drivel that we heard from that previous speaker, the Hon Phil Twyford. In that time—in that five minutes—he didn’t even talk about the bill; didn’t even talk about the bill.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker and characterises his speech as off-topic drivel, but engages none of its content — not the three exhibits on fair pay agreements, the minimum wage or pay equity, nor the challenge about empathy for low-paid workers. This is naming an opponent as a target and pivoting to prepared praise of the bill, which the rubric treats as unresponsive rather than partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "They have cut the minimum wage in real terms since they’ve been in office." — Bidois does not take up this or any other of Twyford's claims, only asserts that Twyford never mentioned the bill.

acuity.statement: The National Party could have looked at it and said, “Oh, it’s a Labour Party bill.” It’s something that we don’t really normally—you know, we would normally say, “Oh no, we won’t do that.” But when you think about the context and the actual principle of it, it made sense for us to support this bill. So I’m proud that we’re supporting it.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows Bidois in the same second-reading debate and is on the matter under debate — she supports the same bill and explains National's reasoning — but engages no part of his argument. She does not take up the free-market/efficient-pricing case, the challenge to ACT's dissenting view, or the freedom-of-contract rebuttal; she even gives the gender pay gap as 8.2 percent without noting that the previous speaker had just said 8.6 percent. The material (her cadet-reporter anecdote, the Speaker's Directions, the closing employer/employee framing) would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before, though it is clearly prepared for this bill rather than any debate. The glance at 'one of my colleagues spoke of his children' points at a speaker outside this window, not at Bidois's content, so it is a mere reference, not engagement.
