acuity.statement: I think it’s rather rich of the National Party to claim that they’re not supporting something because of tinkering around the edges. If that was the case, I don’t think they would be supporting most of their own members’ bills, because that’s basically what they do most of the time.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific objection Rutherford had just made — that the bill is a 'narrow regulatory tweak' / 'tinkering around the edges' — and turns it against the government's own members' bills. It engages the content of the objection rather than merely naming the previous speaker, though the engagement is a tu quoque rather than a defence of the bill's substance, so not a full rebuttal of the reasoning.

acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "While Labour and their members focus on narrow regulatory tweaks that might help a handful of cases, we’re tackling the fundamentals of the housing crisis we inherited from them."

acuity.statement: While I don’t disagree that there are other areas in the housing space that will lead to greater affordability, what this bill does do is protect consumers. It adds a level of protection, and it prevents greedy property developers and multiple-home owners, that are basically raking over the housing market, from benefiting at the expense of everyday people.
acuity.explanation: Accepts one strand of Rutherford's argument (that supply and planning reform matter for affordability) and disputes the inference he drew from it (that the bill is therefore the wrong approach). The speech would have to be different had the preceding turn not framed the choice as supply versus contract law.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "This is fundamentally a planning and supply problem, not a contract law problem."

acuity.statement: If the Government side of the House was so concerned about addressing the fundamentals, they would stop treating housing as a commodity to make a profit from. And if they were so concerned about supply, they would not be cancelling so many Kāinga Ora projects.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the claim made in the immediately preceding turn that the Government is addressing the 'fundamentals' of housing supply, by pointing at Kāinga Ora cancellations as counter-evidence. Aimed at the specific claim rather than the general topic, though it attacks the claimant's record rather than the bill-specific reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "we’re tackling the fundamentals of the housing crisis we inherited from them" and "The economic reality is that housing supply is our critical challenge."

acuity.statement: I guess what we’re hearing, particularly from this side of the House, is that the greater the risks are, what you start doing is you’re putting more barriers in the way of creating new housing. That, I think, fundamentally, is our concern as well, because the more risks you put in place, what it means is you’ve either got to price those risks in, upfront, or you might actually say, “Well, actually we’re not going to do that off-the-plan development at all.” That, of course, reduces the supply of housing.
acuity.explanation: Foster explicitly picks up the strand Luxton had just argued — that unmitigable risk gets priced upfront and off-the-plan builds fall away — names it as what has been heard from his side of the House, endorses it, and then carries it one step further in his own terms (developers would have to be further advanced before contracting, making finance harder and more expensive). So the speech is visibly shaped by what preceded it on one specific chain of reasoning. It is not a 1.0 because he extends and restates rather than testing or adding evidence to the claim, and the bulk of the surrounding turn is prepared material on sunset clauses and new section 41B that would have run unchanged whatever Luxton had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "a developer would then have to look at that and then say, “OK, I’m going to have to price that up front because it’s a cost that I can’t mitigate.” That’s what would happen. We’d end up with higher costs. We would end up with fewer off-the-plan builds"

The speech would have to change if Watts had introduced the bill on different grounds.

acuity.statement: I’m going to give you an example here: Auckland, Whangārei, and Tauranga, and also councils in the Wairarapa and Wellington regions have adopted their own climate action plan. acuity.statement: Under this bill, local councils shall be gutted. They will be gutted; gutted of their power to tailor decisions to their local needs, effectively turning councils into administrative arms of central government, as if to imply that out-of-touch politicians know better than the communities themselves. The claim by the Government that these moves will reduce rates pressures and improve efficiencies is an outcome that’s hardly likely to materialise, as they then set out to deal with all the backlash that’s going to come to them. The claim from this coalition Government, it’s just out the gate; it won’t be there.

acuity.explanation: Answers the "why only travel restrictions and not asset freezes" question squarely with a reason, rather than pivoting. Vague as to what justification would be required, but that is a specificity matter, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "Why did New Zealand only implement travel restrictions on two Israeli Ministers and not also asset freezes like those announced by the UK and Canada?"

acuity.statement: We do not accept this Government’s pathetic lip-service calling for a ceasefire. It’s your fifth time in two years.
acuity.explanation: Prepared condemnation on the matter under debate that leaves the Minister's actual argument — that sanctions and a genocide finding must await the international court — entirely untouched; it would read identically whatever the Minister had just answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters argued "it’s wrong to prejudge the court’s decisions" and that purely symbolic actions would be avoided, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Do we recognise a Palestine State? We have made it clear that, for us, it’s a question of not if but when. But we need to ensure we do not lower the standards of what statehood comprises.
acuity.explanation: Restates the yes-or-no question put to him and gives a direct, qualified answer with the condition attached, so the reply is keyed to the question asked rather than to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "Does the Minister, and this Government, recognise Palestine as a sovereign State—yes or no?"

acuity.statement: Well, perhaps, because one of the conditions has yet to be met, like giving back the hostages.
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the word "unconditional" in the question and answers by naming a condition he says is unmet; the reply only makes sense as an answer to that precise question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "Why does this ministerial statement not call for an immediate and unconditional ceasefire by Israel?"

acuity.statement: That last claim is false; it has not been declared by the international courts to be that, so we are not going to add our support to something that is not based on facts but is based on what someone would hope to be the case regardless of legal precedent.
acuity.explanation: Identifies and contests the specific factual premise embedded in the question — that the International Court of Justice has identified the conduct as genocide — and derives the Government's position from that correction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "as identified by United Nations experts and the International Court of Justice"

acuity.statement: The same answer for that question is given in the previous two answers I gave that member. Perhaps he should pay attention to the fact that the international courts are yet to make a judgment on that matter—or does he think he knows more about the law than they do?
acuity.explanation: Applies his stated reasoning to the question asked and explains why it is the same answer, which is engagement, but it does not take up the specific point about obligations under the genocide convention and spends part of the turn on the questioner instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rawiri Waititi: "Why does the ministerial statement fail to acknowledge New Zealand’s obligations under the genocide convention?"

acuity.statement: What tangible actions, beyond words, is the Government taking to stop arms sales, diplomatic ties, or trade with Israel?
acuity.explanation: Moves to the next prepared question without engaging the Minister's just-stated reason for declining such measures; it is on the subject under debate but indifferent to the answer immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters answered that "the international courts are yet to make a judgment on that matter", and this question does not take that reasoning up.

acuity.statement: So is he saying that the reason that the 21,000 families he promised were going to be getting the full benefit of his FamilyBoost childcare tax rebate haven’t been getting it is because it’s their fault?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact defence Luxon had just offered — that 'everyone who has applied has received their full entitlement' because entitlement varies with income and costs — and draws out its consequence, that the shortfall must therefore be the families' own doing. The question could not have been asked in this form if Luxon had answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: 'everyone who has applied has received their full entitlement. Their full entitlement is subject to their income level and it’s also subject to their costs.'

acuity.statement: Could the Prime Minister answer this question very slowly: given that this is a sliding scale payment, are those entitled to their full amount on the sliding scale getting their full benefit?
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism at issue in the preceding exchange — the sliding scale and what 'full entitlement' means on it — rather than changing subject. It is a friendly question rather than a rebuttal, but it is built on the content of the answers just given and would make no sense after a different exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: 'everyone receives their full entitlement. So the full entitlement that each family gets is subject to their income and also their costs.'

acuity.statement: Why did he cancel 20 hours a week of free early childhood education that all families with young kids could’ve benefited from, given only 153 families have received the full benefit of his complicated tax rebate replacement?
acuity.explanation: Partly engages: it contests the preceding answer's '62,000 families' framing with a competing figure of 153 receiving the full benefit, which bears directly on the entitlement claim Luxon had made, but it also opens a fresh line about the cancelled 20 hours that was prepared independently of the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: 'we have 62,000 families that have received payments to support them on their early childcare education costs.'

acuity.statement: Does she accept that her Government’s decisions are making it worse for people living in poverty, considering the report found that things actually improved between 2018 and 2024, but this Government has reversed this trend, and by 2026, according to the report, more families are expected to be unable to afford the basics such as housing, utilities, and food?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and sourced to the report named in the primary question, but it does not take up anything in the answer immediately before it — the 80,000 benefit exits and the 20,000 infrastructure jobs go unaddressed. This supplementary would have been put in the same words whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just claimed 'over 80,000 people exit the jobseeker benefit into jobs' and 'in excess of 20,000 jobs' from infrastructure projects, and this question does not take either figure up.

acuity.statement: Now, let’s look at the way that these amendments have been rushed through with no evidence, based on vibes. There was no issue in the first place that this legislation is meant to be fixing. There has been no engagement with any of the public on this.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon follows Verrall, who had argued the bill is ideological, does nothing to fix the health system, and strips iwi-Māori partnership boards of decision-making power. Lyndon delivers a prepared Green Party speech on the same bill, covering some of the same ground (partnership boards reduced to advisory) in parallel rather than taking up anything Verrall said — she neither builds on, qualifies, nor disputes any of Verrall's claims, and makes no reference to the preceding turn. The speech is squarely about the matter under debate, which keeps it above 0.0, but it would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued 'I would say this bill is both ideological and utterly political, and not actually directed at changing anything meaningful in the health system' and that the bill 'has removed much of the power from and decision-making role of iwi-Māori partnership boards', and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Repealing some of the provisions in here that require Health New Zealand to do specific report-backs to Māori, and maintaining some cultural frameworks, is actually about streamlining the processes our health system works under and ensuring that universal standards apply. We are certainly not saying that Māori health outcomes don’t matter, but what we’re saying is that the focus for the system needs to be designed for everyone equally, and we need to make sure everyone gets access to healthcare when they need it.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson speaks third, after two speeches arguing the bill strips Māori voice and equity provisions from the health system. He gestures at that line of attack — the disclaimer that ACT is 'certainly not saying that Māori health outcomes don’t matter' is aimed at the general objection in the air — but he engages none of the specific claims put: not the removal of iwi-Māori partnership boards' evaluation and accountability roles, not Wai 2575, not the repeal of the Te Mauri o Rongo charter, not the loss of the population health strategies. The content is ACT's pre-existing campaign position ('ACT supported and campaigned on some of these changes'), and it would be delivered unchanged whatever the previous two speakers had argued. A gesture at the debate, not an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: 'It’s forgetting about inclusion and equity for all of us who face challenges within our communities.' — Stephenson glances at the equity objection with his 'designed for everyone equally' reply but takes up none of her specific claims.

acuity.statement: New Zealand First were in bed with Labour in 2017, so let’s stop having that argument.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft's turn immediately before rested on blaming 'the former Government' for pulling the health system apart under cover of COVID. Ngarewa-Packer takes that specific argument up and turns it back on its author, pointing out New Zealand First sat in the government she is disowning — the riposte only makes sense as a reply to what Marcroft had just said, and would have to change if the preceding speaker had argued on different ground. It is a partial rather than full engagement: it attacks the standing of the argument's source rather than rebutting the substantive claim about the timing of the reforms, and the rest of her speech is prepared material on Te Tiriti and the iwi-Māori partnership boards.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "the former Government, under the cloak of COVID, decided to basically pull apart the health system"

acuity.statement: That previous speech was one of the worst I’ve ever heard in the House. The Minister’s one, which was the first one, was spot on. I’m looking forward to looking at this in the Health Committee. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Uffindell follows a detailed argument from Ngarewa-Packer about the repeal of Te Tiriti provisions, the removal of Māori equity targets and the demotion of iwi-Māori partnership boards to advisory status. He names that speech only to dismiss it as 'one of the worst I've ever heard' and engages none of its content — not the Tiriti clause, not the targets, not the partnership boards. This is a bare reference plus prepared praise of the bill, which the rubric puts at 0.1; the speech would read identically whatever she had argued, though it does at least stay on the bill under debate rather than wandering elsewhere.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued the bill repeals Te Tiriti, removes Māori equity targets and relegates iwi-Māori partnership boards to advisory only, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Crucially, health targets are now going to be enshrined in law. This provides clarity and certainty and ensures a laser focus on getting real results for patients. This is things like cancer care, it is immunisation, it’s emergency department times—it is about accountability.
acuity.explanation: Prepared first-reading support on the right subject. It lands on the same topic Leary had just attacked — the Government's health targets — but engages none of her reasoning: it neither defends the choice of measures nor answers the absence of a screening target, and the speech would read identically whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary, immediately before, argued "When we look at the targets that the Government is so wedded to, are they measuring the right things? I don't think so" and that there are no cancer screening targets; this statement praises targets being enshrined in law and lists cancer care without taking up the screening-versus-treatment point.

acuity.statement: I find it quite ironic that the Minister would say, and the contributors would say, in one breath that this bill seeks to improve the health system and then systematically go through and do so many things that do just the opposite.
acuity.explanation: Directly names the preceding contributors' central claim — that the bill strengthens the health system — and disputes it, conceding the shared goal of affordable universal access before arguing the bill's provisions contradict its own purpose statement. Partial rather than full: having taken up that one strand, the speech moves to prepared material on workforce neutrality and privatisation that Campbell did not raise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "This legislation is a critical step in strengthening and making our healthcare system more effective."

acuity.statement: The previous Government’s changes to the health system were a complete omni-shambles, or to put it another way from the military, we would call it FUBAR—and I won’t spell out what that stands for. But the overall effect of the previous administration’s changes have been to disorientate the decision making and communication. No one has had either the authority or, frankly, the temerity to make any decisions, and the responsibility for the consequences of that have been opaque as well.
acuity.explanation: A short prepared speech condemning the previous administration's restructure. It is about the health system under debate, so not wholly off-topic, but it engages no part of the argument just made — neither the chilling-effect claim nor the privatisation claim — and would be word-for-word identical whoever had preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued immediately before that the bill misuses Public Service neutrality to silence clinicians and opens the door to privatisation by stealth, and this statement takes up neither point.

acuity.statement: Again, one of the things we’ve heard is around the fact that, yes, there is this idea that we want to make it easier for people to open bank accounts—absolutely. But at the same time, we have seen in the past where bank accounts, and particularly bank accounts of children, have been used for AML/CFT purposes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific example Webb had just raised — children's bank accounts as a money-laundering vector — accepts the easing-of-access objective and then presses the same risk, before widening it to a new strand Webb did not raise (financial inclusion in rural communities). Clearly pointable engagement with the preceding claim, but it sits alongside prepared Green material rather than doing the full work of rebutting or developing Webb's reasoning, so short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "or that we should just open the gates and kids can open bank accounts. Well, kids’ bank accounts can be used for money laundering and for the financing of terrorism."

acuity.statement: I think the last thing that I want to also mention in terms of this particular point is the extent the bill extends the delegation of secondary legislation under this Act to better enable risk-based regulations. I also think this is an interesting perspective—that we are moving things from primary to a secondary legislation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the same delegation-of-rule-making concern Webb had just set out and asks what it means for regulation-making power and Ministers' Orders in Council. It engages the strand squarely but mainly restates the worry as a question for select committee rather than advancing or contesting Webb's accountability argument, which puts it between the partial and full bands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "One of the key things that this bill does is it moves the place where the rules are made down substantially—essentially, into Government, into the Department of Internal Affairs."

acuity.statement: We believe that the move to a single supervisor will create regulatory efficiencies and reduce some of the complexity that is currently facing the system. We support the introduction of an industry levy to balance the cost, and, most importantly, that we are delivering a risk-based legislation that is proportional to the risks we’re dealing with and allows us to streamline some of the approaches.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party position on the right subject. It asserts the levy and the single supervisor are good without engaging Webb's specific objection that enforcement should come from general appropriation, or his and Xu-Nan's concern about what loosening exposes the financial system to. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever the two previous speakers had said, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that AML/CFT rules are not red tape, that lowering the bar across the board risks aiding organised crime, and that enforcement is a core function of the State that should be funded from general appropriation rather than an industry levy — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise in support on behalf of the National Party on the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Supervisor, Levy, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill. I look forward to discussing this at select committee.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one, two of them setting out specific concerns a supporter of the bill could have answered. The contribution names the bill and the committee and nothing more, so it engages no part of any argument made — on topic, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb and Lawrence Xu-Nan both raised the risk of loosening customer due diligence on family trusts and children's accounts, and Webb objected to funding enforcement by levy; this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m looking forward to seeing it go to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee for a change, rather than the Justice Committee, which, I know—as Vanessa Weenink outlined—will make some very positive contributions to the bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one pointable thing from the preceding turn — Weenink's committee reference, which also sets against Casey Costello's reference to the Justice Committee — but it is agreement about which committee will consider the bill, not engagement with any argument advanced in the debate. A gesture at what came before rather than a partial engagement with its content, so the top of the unresponsive band rather than 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "The Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee is very collegial, and I’m sure that we’ll have lots of discussion."

acuity.statement: I can understand why we have a focus on this side in cutting red tape, because we want to see the average mum and dad with a little family be able to purchase a little home, their first home, without having to go through the burdens that gang members that get $2.7 million from former Labour Governments didn't go through.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Andersen's immediately preceding objection — that cutting red tape is the wrong move given organised crime — and offers a reason for the red-tape focus (first-home buyers' compliance burden), with a gang jibe attached. It engages the topic of her complaint rather than its substance (she argued the risk is laundering by criminal networks, which this does not address), so it is partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It does seem really strange that we're seeing the cutting of red tape at a time in New Zealand when we should be really looking closely at what additional loopholes we can be closing" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: While I do rise in support of the bill, I would like to echo some of the comments made by my colleague Dr Duncan Webb, firstly, in terms of whether it’s appropriate for some of the regulation or some of the rules to be pushed down into regulation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the secondary-legislation strand raised in the preceding turn and develops it (the shift to "framework legislation" and Regulations Review Committee comment on substantive matters sitting in regulation), before moving to her own prepared Bill of Rights analysis. One strand engaged and extended, the bulk of the speech independent of what came before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’re concerned that these kinds of important decisions are potentially going to be made by secondary legislation" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Regulated entities will benefit from the simplified compliance requirements. We support this bill, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: A restatement of the bill's purpose and a commendation. It is on the matter under debate, but would read word-for-word the same whatever the three preceding speakers had argued — no engagement with the regulations point, the Bill of Rights issues, or the money-laundering warning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters set out search-and-seizure and detention concerns from the section 7 Bill of Rights vet, and Ginny Andersen warned about secondary legislation and organised crime, and this statement takes up none of it

acuity.statement: The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act, which this bill will amend, was developed without input from tangata whenua, and it shows. This Act has prevented tangata whenua from accessing financial services and capital for two decades, because many of our people do not have proper documentation.
acuity.explanation: Substantive and squarely about the bill, but self-contained prepared argument: it addresses no claim made in the preceding turns, including Andersen's directly opposed position that verification requirements should be tightened rather than loosened. The asides to members in the chamber are references, not engagement with content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued the deregulation risks opening loopholes for organised crime and Vanushi Walters raised search and detention issues in the section 7 vet; this statement takes up neither, arguing instead from Māori land-trust verification burdens

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise on behalf of the Green Party, and we will not be supporting this particular bill. Again, the reason for that is we didn’t support the agreement, so I don’t know why the House is so surprised that we wouldn’t be supporting this particular bill.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan follows a substantive Labour turn and delivers the prepared Green position. He touches the same topics Twyford raised (ISDS, the $100m to $200m threshold) but engages none of Twyford's actual claims — he does not dispute that ISDS is now settled policy nor answer Twyford's case that the Treaty provisions and sustainable-trade chapters make the agreement worth supporting. There is a gesture at the chamber ('I don't know why the House is so surprised'), which lifts it off the floor, but the speech would read identically whatever Twyford had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford spoke about the absence of an investor-State dispute settlement mechanism and the rise in the screening threshold from $100 million to $200 million, and this statement does not take up either argument.

acuity.statement: I’m not surprised to see the Green Party is not supporting this bill, because the Green Party only knows how to spend money. They don’t know how to bring the revenue into our country. It’s very clear from that speech that, yes, on one side they’re saying that trade is good, but they don’t know how trade works—they don’t know how trade agreements work.
acuity.explanation: Parmar names the preceding speech and quotes its 'trade is good' strand, but does nothing with the content: Xu-Nan's argument was about the treaty examination process under Standing Orders 405 to 408, the national interest analysis being drafted by MFAT itself, and the kafala system, and none of that is taken up. Repeating the opponent's position in order to assert they don't understand trade is a reference and a pivot to ACT's own prepared material, not engagement with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "to say that the Green Party does support trade; we do care about trade" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: This has been through our Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, and I think we’ve done a lot of scrutiny on it, trying to work through all of the issues, which have been well aired. I want to commend the Minister for his work, and the previous Minister, Damien O’Connor, for his initiation of some of the conversations. I feel like it’s a great day for New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows a substantive turn by Walters that listed four specific drafting and oversight questions still awaiting ministerial answers. Her reply engages none of them: it asserts generally that the committee did "a lot of scrutiny" and the issues "have been well aired" (which cuts against, but does not address, Walters' point that answers are still outstanding), then delivers prepared commendations of the current and former Ministers. The speech would read identically whatever Walters had said. It earns above 0.1 only because "all of the issues, which have been well aired" is at least a gesture at the debate that has just occurred, and the speech is squarely on the bill under consideration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters immediately preceded her and set out specific unresolved questions — "I do then just wonder why we wouldn’t put that provision in primary legislation as opposed to putting it in secondary legislation", the Land Information New Zealand threshold/parcelling issue, the missing definition of "business activity" and the policing of self-certification — and this statement does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: We are just so focused, on this side of the House, on reducing the cost of living, and our strategy, in part, is all about going for growth. We want to double the value of our exports over this 10-year period, and we've seen great progress with the EU free-trade agreement, and now here we are with this record-breaking trade agreement that has been delivered in only around four months.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive speech by Cushla Tangaere-Manuel on the Māori economy's growth, the need for cross-House work on utilising whenua Māori, and the risk to Māori intellectual property under the agreement. Costley takes up none of these strands: no reference to the Māori economy figures, no answer on land development, no response on intellectual-property protection. The speech is prepared material about the Government's growth and export strategy — on the right subject (this trade agreement) but indifferent to what preceded it. Substituting any other speech on the bill would require no change to a word of it, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band; there is not even a gesture at the previous speaker, so 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel spoke about the Māori economy's 83 percent asset-base growth, making it easier to utilise whenua Māori, and protecting Māori intellectual property, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I just want to pick up on some of the points that have been made by other speakers. We are a country that depends on exports. We are a country where most of its agricultural production is for the purpose of export and we rely on a principle that that surplus of production that we manufacture—in the case of the dairy industry, 95 percent of what is produced is a surplus to what is needed domestically—is produced for the purpose of exporting and earning money.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's turn argued that farmers, exporters and foresters want market access and a fair return, and mocked the Green position as ivory-tower. Abel explicitly turns to that strand, accepts the premise that the country depends on exports, and redirects it to the unpriced domestic costs of the export surplus. That engages the topic and one strand of the argument rather than Patterson's specific claims about this deal's market access or tariff removal, and it sits alongside prepared Green material on Te Tiriti and Sudan. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do you think that the farmers, the exporters, the foresters give a rat’s arse about Greek philosophy?" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: Those exporters do pay tax, but that is not their sole purpose.
acuity.explanation: A direct reply to McCallum's interjected claim that exporters pay the tax that funds public services: Abel concedes the factual half and disputes the inference drawn from it. The sentence could not exist if the interjection had been different, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — whether the retort is well reasoned or precise is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "To pay tax to support the services you need." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: After that brief diversion to another planet, I’m happy to bring the debate back to reality here in the third reading on the United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill. Now, economic growth is critical for the success of New Zealand. This Government is firmly focused on growing prosperity for our country, because without that we can’t deliver better public services: health, education, law and order—all those things that the other side purport to advocate for.
acuity.explanation: Abel had just made three specific arguments — that the Crown's "non-paper" misrepresented Te Tiriti, that chapters 13 and 15 use permissive language like "endeavour" and "may", and that the environmental costs of the export surplus are not borne by the industries causing them. Van de Molen names the preceding speech only to dismiss it as "another planet" and then delivers prepared material on growth and tariff removal. A mere reference, not engagement: the speech would read identically whatever argument the Greens had advanced, though it is at least on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the costs of that surplus on our domestic wellbeing and our domestic natural resources, in particular, is not borne by the industries that impact them" — Steve Abel; the statement gestures at his speech but takes up none of its content.

acuity.statement: I rise to support the United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Legislation Amendment Bill, because the United Arab Emirates trade deal is so important for strengthening our economy, creating jobs and opportunity across New Zealand—and especially in my region, Hawke’s Bay, the fruit bowl of New Zealand, where we produce the best fruit in the world. We need markets to send that fruit to, markets where they will pay a premium for our fruit and help us grow our businesses here in New Zealand, and put more confidence back into our horticulture sector, our dairy sector, and our red meat sector. This is good for exporters, it’s good for trade, it’s good for New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Reuben Davidson's immediately preceding turn made several engageable points — the select committee concerns about the investment-screening threshold moving from $100 million to $200 million, the Treaty of Waitangi provisions in the CEPA, the digital trade chapter, and a jab about Minister Goldsmith. Wedd's speech takes up none of them. It is prepared, on-topic support for the bill that would read word-for-word the same whatever Davidson had argued; the only faint contact is a shared mention of the horticulture, dairy and red meat sectors, which is the debate's general subject rather than any claim he made. On topic, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson spoke about the select committee's investment-screening concerns, the Treaty of Waitangi chapter and digital trade, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It is a pleasure to rise and support this Legislation Amendment Bill in the first reading. I think what’s important is that this actually goes back to 2014, based on two inquiries: one is the Regulations Review Committee’s inquiry into the oversight of disallowable instruments that are not legislative instruments, and the Productivity Commission’s report on regulatory institutions and practices.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive critique by Duncan Webb of the Part 4 repeal and the Regulatory Standards Bill, and engages no part of it. The speech is prepared material on the correct subject (the bill's origin and the single register) and would read identically whatever Webb had said; there is not even a gesture at the preceding argument, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that the bill repeals Part 4 of the Legislation Act to clear the way for the Regulatory Standards Bill, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I do echo the concerns that my colleague Duncan Webb made around repealing Part 4 of the Legislation Act and around the almost preparation that the Government is doing for the Regulatory Standards Bill. That is of course legislation that we don’t support and, in fact, purports to do a somewhat similar job to this bill but, actually, as we’ve seen with a lot of those debates, goes a lot further than that. I think, to also agree with what Dr Duncan Webb has said, this particular bill took a long period of time because sometimes legislation does take a long period of time, and especially legislation which is genuinely bipartisan and genuinely seeks to solve a real problem that members across the House can agree exists and that we know that we can do better around moving forward.

But it never acknowledges the previous speaker, leaves her Māori data sovereignty and Tūhoe-raids argument untouched, and otherwise reads as the Green Party's prepared clause-by-clause position, so it engages the topic and part of the concern rather than her specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The convention means that we could be compelled to hand over private data to foreign Governments for offences that are not crimes in Aotearoa New Zealand." — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: Essentially, what this bill does, as we’ve heard—if we’re going to put it down in a nutshell—is align our domestic laws with the obligations that we signed to on an international level, in international law, under the Budapest Convention, essentially, to fight cyber-crime.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi argued the bill permits preservation directions without judicial oversight and endangers Māori data sovereignty, and Lawrence Xu-Nan asked what safeguards protect people against foreign authorities; this statement takes up neither, offering instead a summary of what the bill does.

acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed, clause-by-clause set of reservations from Webb and engages none of them. The speech is prepared material on the general subject of the bill — cyber-crime risk to seniors and Budapest Convention compliance — and would read word-for-word the same whatever the previous speaker had argued. It is at least about the matter under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that the right of review for preservation orders in new section 79J is purely administrative and conducted at the same level, and that new section 49B lets notice of handing evidence to a foreign State be given in secret, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Now, one of the important things about cyber-crime—and most speakers have touched on this, but it would be remiss of me not to—is that cyber-crime is borderless. It happens, and can happen, with an actor in one country, a victim or a target in another country, and crucial content regarding that cyber-crime sitting in a third country.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges that earlier speakers have made the borderlessness point and repeats it, which is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with it: Webb's actual argument was that borderlessness does not lower the threshold for surveillance and that two specific clauses lack judicial supervision, and Davidson takes up neither. The remainder is prepared material on Maori data and copyright. Repeating a previous speaker's words back does not count as taking up the content, so this sits in the 0.1-0.3 band at its top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "cyber-crime is, essentially, borderless, but we still do need to be really cautious" — Duncan Webb

So I commend the bill to the House. Let’s get on with it. Thank you.

Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.explanation: Boyack takes up one strand of Pugh's subject — the Tasman flooding and its human toll — and adds content Pugh did not have (the death of Peter Lines, the rain forecast for the coming Thursday and preparedness work), so this opening would have been different had Pugh spoken on something else. Partial engagement with the topic rather than with the argument.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Parmjeet Parmar spoke about Watercare and Auckland water-supply constraints stopping construction companies building houses ('They are stuck because there are water-supply constraints there'), and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Around 110,000 enrolled or updated their enrolment details on election day last year only because they were told they could, so some people did."

acuity.statement: It is that all of the advice that the Minister has got has said that this is a bad idea.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith leaned on official advice to justify the earlier enrolment deadline; Webb directly contests that specific prop, asserting the advice ran the other way and then pointing to the regulatory impact statement and the Attorney-General's report. This engages the content of the Minister's justification rather than merely naming him, so it sits near the top of the band; it is marginally short of 1.0 because the characterisation of 'all of the advice' is asserted before the supporting citations rather than engaging Goldsmith's own stated advice about count timeliness on its own terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "The advice I received is that if we leave things as they are, it could well take even longer in future elections."

acuity.statement: There has been a lot said already about enrolment on voting day. As has been outlined, one of the changes the Minister spoke about is just ensuring that people have to be enrolled 13 days before the election. Voting in a democracy such as ours does come with some responsibilities, and it’s one of those responsibilities to actually be on the electoral roll—that’s a legal requirement. If you can’t be bothered doing that within a short period before an election, you’ve really got to question whether you have a commitment to being a participant in our democracy.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's immediately preceding turn argued that removing same-day enrolment puts barriers back in place for young people, renters, Māori, Pasifika, Asian communities and disabled people, citing Auditor-General and independent election reports. Stephenson takes up the same strand — the 13-day enrolment deadline — and offers a counter-principle (enrolment is a personal and legal responsibility, and the window is modest), so the speech is engaged with the topic she had just put. But he answers the topic rather than her specific claim: he does not touch who the evidence says misses out, nor the reports she relied on, and the framing is otherwise the prepared ACT position he announced at the outset. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "by it removing the ability to enrol and vote on the same day" — her argument that this reinstates barriers for identified communities.

acuity.statement: The other one, which we are very pleased to support, is actually stopping prisoners in prison from voting. Labour made this change, and we think it was unprincipled. As people in New Zealand understand, if you’ve committed a crime, you’ve violated someone else’s rights, and there are consequences for that, and so for prisoners in jail, not voting is one of those consequences.
acuity.explanation: Davidson had just made a specific argument on prisoner voting: that the justice system contains inbuilt systemic discrimination, that Māori, Pasifika and low-income people are imprisoned disproportionately, and that disenfranchisement is therefore an extra penalty on top of the sentence which the Auditor-General called a denial of basic rights. Stephenson's passage is on exactly that matter under debate but engages no part of that argument — no response on disproportionality, no response on double punishment, no response to the Auditor-General. It restates ACT's prior position and attributes the earlier change to Labour, which would read identically whatever Davidson had said about it. A gesture at the debate without engagement, so the low band rather than the middle.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "it’s no wonder that the Auditor-General really called that out as actually denying basic, fundamental human rights" — her case that disenfranchisement is an extra penalty on a discriminatory system.

acuity.statement: The other two things I wanted to say: first of all is this issue that we’ve heard raised by the Opposition about 110,000 people now somehow being disenfranchised because they chose, in the last election, to enrol on the day. Well, the reality is that if you say to people, “Look, you’ve got to enrol a number of days in advance of the election to make sure that the electoral rolls are ready and the system is ready to go and is able to deliver the electoral result more efficiently, effectively, and earlier”, then there is a different deadline. Instead of being on the day, it’s some days before that, and that, as we’ve heard before, is about some degree of personal responsibility to be able to get yourself organised in time to enrol.
acuity.explanation: Foster names the Opposition claim he is answering — the large number of election-day enrolees said to be disenfranchised, which Davidson had put as hundreds of thousands turning up to vote on the day — and does something with it: he disputes that a changed deadline amounts to disenfranchisement, tying it to the count-speed rationale he had already been developing. The speech would have to change if the preceding Opposition turn had made a different argument, so this is well above prepared material. Short of the top because he reframes the claim rather than contesting the figure or the evidence about who is affected, and the characterisation "somehow being disenfranchised" glosses the argument it answers. Reasoning quality and politeness are not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "The fact that we had hundreds of thousands of people turning up to vote on election day speaks to the fact that people want to have a say" — the Opposition claim that ending same-day enrolment disenfranchises those voters.

acuity.statement: This is a great piece of legislation. It’s time for people around New Zealand to take some personal responsibility. The law already requires you to be enrolled to vote, so get on and get enrolled in advance of next year’s election. Don’t wait for election day to do it; do it now. Get enrolled today. Get in there and do it. This improves timeliness and efficiency of electoral administration. It’s great to see Te Pāti Māori turn up to the debating chamber today.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition speech that argued the 13-day enrolment ban could disenfranchise over 100,000 people, disproportionately Māori, Pasifika and Asian, citing the Attorney-General and 2023 enrolment figures. The speech would read identically whatever the preceding argument had been, so it sits in the low band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "could disenfranchise over 100,000 people disproportionately: Māori, Pasifika, Asian" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer. The statement does not take up that claim.

acuity.explanation: Directly inverts the preceding speaker's framing that late enrolment is a failure of personal responsibility, locating the fault in the system rather than the voters, and pairs it with the 'dropkicks' characterisation to say what that framing amounts to. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s time for people around New Zealand to take some personal responsibility." — Tom Rutherford

acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.subject: speaker

Directly shaped by the reply she follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Jones: "It is probably superfluous at this stage to go into answers on both of those points when we will get to the necessary detail as we plough through the remainder of the bill."

The contribution would not exist in this form had Russell and Woods not narrowed their request to clause references.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "All we’ve asked for is which clauses."

This is engaging the content of the previous argument and extending it, not restating it.

acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "I just would like the Minister for Resources to explain to the committee, first of all, why that is being deleted, what the impact would be, and what the policy rationale is for the removal of that clause."

acuity.statement: To simply remove a chunk of an amended piece of legislation that’s gone to the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee, that hearings have been held on, that submitters have had the chance to submit on—I can understand sometimes that we need to have clauses of bills that need to be tweaked and fixed, and there might need to be the odd word changed, but to simply just remove quite a large portion of this clause of the bill is quite unusual.
