acuity.statement: The other question, I believe, in regards to clause 4, the interpretations, which is the definitions section, I think the key element there to highlight is that the definition element within that, for example, deals with the Watercare entity and ensuring that the definition of “water service provider” and “water organisation” clearly incorporates that Auckland water organisation, which is the primary purpose of that clause 4.
acuity.explanation: He reaches the right clause but not the question. Utikere asked specifically whether the expanded "water services infrastructure" definition is drafted to cover everything the bill needs, given the struck-out "infrastructure" definition excluded conveyance of water; the answer is about a different element of clause 4 entirely — the Watercare and "water service provider" definitions. That is engagement with the topic rather than the claim, which the rubric places around the middle of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether he is comfortable, on the advice that he has received, that that definition of infrastructure for water services ... has been drafted in a way that, basically, covers all aspects" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I know the Minister has touched on Treaty settlements, but we do see a conflation between Te Tiriti obligations and Treaty settlements, because not all hapū and iwi would have those kinds of Treaty settlements. Treaty settlements are very separate and have been well covered in the definition and certain parts of this bill. What I’m more interested in is the broader Te Tiriti obligations, understanding that there aren’t any specific Te Tiriti clauses within Part 1 of this bill, neither under clause 3 nor, as far as I can see, under clause 4.
acuity.explanation: This is a direct attack on the reasoning the Minister had just offered: it identifies the move Watts made (answering a Te Tiriti question with settlement obligations) and names it as a conflation, then specifies what the answer left unaddressed — the absence of any Te Tiriti clause in clauses 3 and 4. The passage is unintelligible without Watts's answer immediately before it, which is the strongest evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Treaty settlement obligations apply when the settlement is made; therefore, as and when those iwi enter into agreements, that will be covered off through that" — Hon Simon Watts

acuity.statement: My second question is around the removed definition of “infrastructure”. It is also kind of peculiar that there was no indication that such a definition should be removed, especially since that the recommendation by the department was to amend the definition to include other aspects. I want to check with the Minister on what the rationale is to remove the definition for “infrastructure” here.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the removed "infrastructure" definition that Utikere raised and that the Minister's reply passed over, and adds something to it — the departmental recommendation was to amend rather than delete. Partial rather than full engagement: it is labelled as his own second prepared question and does not take up the specific drafting concern (the exclusion of conveyance of water) that Utikere had built the point on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "removing a definition of “infrastructure”. What was originally in the bill was a very broad—well, it was infrastructure." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: In regards to the other question, I have answered the point around clause 4, subclause (3). The other element that was raised in regards to the exclusions around stormwater as well is relevant to the points I raised around the overland flow paths before.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Wade-Brown's stormwater questions — the exclusions — but only by cross-referencing an earlier answer about overland flow paths, and leaves the small-settlement, intermittent-stream and permeable-surface strands untouched. Topic engaged, specific arguments mostly not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "My third question for the moment about stormwater is about why you're excluding the transport corridors."

acuity.statement: I was hoping to hear from the Minister a response to the issue around the “infrastructure” definition.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the answer just given by identifying what it omitted, so the turn would be different had the Minister covered the infrastructure definition. It engages the completeness of the reply rather than any of its reasoning, so not full marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Thanks. I'll just answer the last remaining questions."

acuity.statement: I guess the related point to that question—and Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan talked about the removal of “infrastructure”. I didn’t pick up on the concerns around whether it was adequately removed or not. But the follow-up question was the issue around water conveyance, which was not in the original definition of “infrastructure” but now is in the “water services infrastructure” piece.
acuity.explanation: Builds on a specific point made earlier in the debate by Xu-Nan about the removal of 'infrastructure' and presses the unaddressed water-conveyance strand of it, then moves into its own prepared material on the district plan definition. Clear partial engagement, pointable to a particular prior claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan's earlier point on the removal of "infrastructure", referenced as: "Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan talked about the removal of “infrastructure”."

acuity.statement: I asked a question before about development contributions, which I don’t think the Minister answered. We have at, I think, clause 6: “section 109 partially exempts the Crown from making development contributions”, and you go to that section, and it says there’s an exemption for Kāinga Ora. What analysis and thought has gone into the sorts of development contributions that the Crown might be not paying by this exemption?
acuity.explanation: Responds to the Minister's claim to have dealt with the remaining questions by naming the one left out and re-putting it with the clause and the Kāinga Ora exemption attached. Engagement is with the gap in the answer rather than with its substance, which keeps it short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Thanks. I'll just answer the last remaining questions."

acuity.statement: Just in regards to that question by the Hon Rachel Brooking, the provisions within the Local Government Act 2002—this basically preserves the status quo in regards to those aspects. The development contribution will obviously be replaced by development levies, which is the work under way at the moment, but the Local Government Act clause, as I’ve noted, deals with the aspect that’s been raised. So that covers that point.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the questioner and the clause she raised and supplies a substantive position on it — status quo preserved, contributions to be superseded by levies — so the reply is shaped by what she asked. It answers the topic rather than her actual question about what analysis was done, so it sits around the middle-to-upper band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "What analysis and thought has gone into the sorts of development contributions that the Crown might be not paying by this exemption?"

acuity.statement: Now, the interesting thing around that is there is this reference that where the offer for employment is for, substantially, the same position as the position the employee held at the previous provider prior to the transfer, that, basically, there would be no entitlement to any additional benefit. OK, I understand that. But my question for the Minister is: what specifically guides the criteria outlined in clause 1(3)(a), (b), and (c) of Schedule 1?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the clause Xu-Nan had just opened — affected employees transferring between providers under Schedule 1, Part 1, clause 1 — and extends it to the cessation and offer-of-employment criteria, but does not take up his specific question about collective agreements. Same ground, different strand, developed independently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Part 1 of Schedule 1, clause 1, “Identification of affected employees” and a transfer of any from one service provider to another water service provider"

acuity.statement: So the provisions within the Local Government Act deal with the rights protections in regards to collective contracts, and those apply irrespective of where these individuals will transfer to. It’s obviously acknowledged that a large number of local government employees are under these type of arrangements and the mechanisms I’ve outlined. To the question that the member’s asking—what over-pins that—well, the provisions from the Local Government Act over-pin it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up both live strands — Xu-Nan's collective-agreement protections and Utikere's question about what underpins the clause 1(3) criteria — and names the latter explicitly before answering it. The answer is thin and somewhat circular, but that is a reasoning problem, not a failure to engage what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what sorts of precautions, if any, have been put in place around collective agreements?"

acuity.statement: I’m happy to take this session offline, on exactly the point and page, but I can clarify the Schedule 1, clause 7 aspect, which is primarily around the transitional arrangements for—where you’ve got an example of an existing council-controlled organisation that is going to become a water organisation upon commencement, basically, those aspects of detail, in terms of the board adopting a document and within the time period, is what that clause of that Schedule is outlining primarily.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact clause Xu-Nan had just named (Schedule 1, clause 7, the alternative form of funding impact statement) and supplies substantive content about what that clause does — transitional arrangements for an existing CCO becoming a water organisation, and the board adoption timing. The answer would be different had a different clause been raised, so it is genuinely shaped by the preceding turn; it falls short of 1.0 because Xu-Nan's question was cut off before its specific point and Watts also offers to deal with it offline rather than fully on the record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So I have a question for the Minister of Local Government regarding clause 7 of Schedule 1. This is on page 338. This is about the “Alternative form of funding impact statement”." — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I want to just reiterate, perhaps for the Minister of Local Government’s benefit and other colleagues, the position that we were heading down when we were considering this late last night. We had some issues with the flexibility component that the Minister has started to address, not necessarily the sustainability part, and how that might be undermined by that sense of bitsy-ism or fragmentation of the possible service delivery opportunities.
acuity.explanation: Follows Watts's clause 7 answer and Brooking's definitional question but takes up neither. Instead it restates Labour's prepared position from the previous sitting and opens fresh lines of questioning (purpose clause, binding the Crown, clause 8(4) timing). There is a gesture at the debate — he notes the Minister 'has started to address' flexibility and later refers back to Xu-Nan's contribution — but no part of the argument just made in the chamber is engaged, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band at the upper end.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just explained that Schedule 1, clause 7 covers transitional arrangements for an existing CCO becoming a water organisation, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: Thanks, members, for the questions. In regards to the points raised by both aspects of the Opposition around environmental standards, I don’t want to go into other parts of the bill, but for those that have read the bill, they will see that in the next part they cover off quite clearly the objectives of water services providers. I’m just simply noting that for navigation for those that are working their way through the bill, but they are covered there and deal with the questions that have been asked.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific strand just put to him — the Opposition's complaint that environmental objectives sit too lightly in the purpose clause — and answers at the level of the topic by directing members to where objectives of water services providers appear later in the bill. But it does not engage Utikere's actual question, which was why the purpose clause itself was not strengthened, nor his points about the interpretation clause or binding the Crown. Partial engagement, one strand only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why has he not sought to beef up the environmental protectional standards as part of the purpose clause in Part 1 of this bill?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I was reflecting on the questions I asked last night, and I’ve also been contacted. There were people watching our questions about water services last night, as well, and I don’t feel that I got any answer to whether small settlements like Pōrangahau were considered urban or not in the context. I don’t consider that I really received answers about the permeability and design issues and why the transport corridor was unilaterally ruled out, given that the corridor is often bigger than the road. I appreciate that the Minister is aiming to answer people’s questions—he’s not brushing us off; he’s not treating them as unimportant—but, on reflection, what I asked and what got answered last night, I wonder if he could be a little fuller in his response.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the assertion Watts had just made — that the matters raised 'are covered there and deal with the questions that have been asked' — by naming three specific questions she says went unanswered (whether Pōrangahau counts as urban, permeability and design, the ruling out of the transport corridor). That is engagement with his claim rather than a pivot. It sits below the top band because the questions she lists are from the previous sitting rather than the particular answer just given, so part of the turn is a restatement of her own earlier material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but they are covered there and deal with the questions that have been asked" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m still interested in this difference between “water organisation” and “water service provider”. I note that the Minister of Local Government just said there’s more to come on water service providers, but there must be a reason why there are these two quite separate definitions.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer — that the objectives of water services providers are covered in a later part — and presses on precisely why it does not dispose of her question: a signpost to a later part does not explain why the bill carries two separate and overlapping defined terms. She then builds on Utikere's clause 8 point to ask why a deeming provision is needed when the definition in clause 4 already captures both existing and new CCOs. The turn is visibly shaped by what was said immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "for those that have read the bill, they will see that in the next part they cover off quite clearly the objectives of water services providers" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Just in response to the questions in regards to the urban-rural portion and also the points around rural connections, rural connections is covered in future parts of the bill, not the part we’re currently discussing, and I’m happy to answer it when we get to that point. The context around what is the definition of urban and rural—primarily, that is a determination made by and through the district plans of the relevant councils, and so that’s where that aspect is dealt with.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the substantive answer Wade-Brown had just said she was missing — that urban versus rural is determined through the district plans of the relevant councils — which is responsive to her specific complaint about small settlements like Pōrangahau. It is held below the top band because it leaves Brooking's immediately preceding and twice-asked question about the 'water organisation'/'water service provider' distinction untouched, and defers rural connections to a later part.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t feel that I got any answer to whether small settlements like Pōrangahau were considered urban or not in the context" — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: The evidence, as we stand five weeks away from when the deadline for the plan is, is that the majority of councils will form together in regional groupings. That is the reality of where we’re at, and those numbers are increasing and changing as we work.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific evidentiary claim — that the evidence before the House shows regional collaboration is not happening — and contradicts it with a counter-claim about the majority of councils forming regional groupings before the 3 September deadline, then answers the 'where are the incentives' question on its own terms by asserting collaboration occurred without any fiscal incentive. The turn would have to be different had Utikere made a different argument. Not docked for the mocking 'magic money tree' reframing, which belongs to civility, nor for whether the council numbers are accurate, which belongs to veracity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the evidence that is currently before this House strongly signifies that that is far from the case" — Tangi Utikere, who argued the decentralised model produces no regional collaboration and asked where the incentivisation sits

acuity.statement: The one thing that I’m unsure about with all of these sections, and I’d really appreciate the Minister providing some answers for councils—because we’re talking about these lack of incentives for them to actually work with their neighbours.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the same clauses 7 to 11 and the same incentives thread — and there is a gesture back at the preceding exchange. But it engages no part of Watts' actual answer: he had just denied the premise of absent incentives, and she proceeds past that into a new question about council exit rights rather than contesting or conceding it. Prepared material on the right subject with a glance at what came before, which puts it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is without blank cheques being written by this Government in order to incentivise councils to get it" — Simon Watts. Pham restates the lack-of-incentives premise as settled but does not take up Watts' answer that financial sustainability is itself the incentive.

acuity.statement: The question is: do councils have options in terms of whether they stay in or out? Well, the short answer is: those are local decisions made by local councils, and, in short, the answer is yes.
acuity.explanation: Restates Pham's specific question and supplies a direct answer to it, then points her to the clause she asked to be shown (clause 15) and adds the converse case of councils whose announced structures admit others later. The turn is unintelligible without her question, which is the test. Whether the clause reference genuinely answers the shareholder-permission half of her question is a rigor and specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can councils actually exit multi-entity water service providers or do they need the permission of all the shareholders—i.e., all the other councils—who are actually part of that?" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: Yes, there are issues, but what I want the Minister to address is how councils can possibly square limiting rate rises and fixing—whether it is past investment, whether it is issues like floods, or whether it is issues like earthquakes—with his view that we should not be increasing rates at all.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Deborah Russell's immediately preceding argument — the contradiction between demanding rates restraint and requiring councils to fund water infrastructure — and puts it to the Minister as a direct question, adding her own Wellington CAPEX and earthquake material. It engages the topic and that specific contradiction, but much of the turn is prepared material (graphs, roading FAR, the waste levy) rather than a rebuttal or development of Russell's reasoning, so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "This Government is pushing that cost on to local bodies, at the same time as advocating for a rates cap. The cognitive dissonance is extraordinary."

acuity.statement: The point was raised in regard to more generic terms around how we’re funding it. I would simply point the member to the fact that a number of councils have already submitted their plans for water services entities, and they have been approved.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the question just put to him and answers the general topic — how the arrangements are funded and delivered — rather than the specific claims made: he does not engage the 18 credit-rating downgrades, the roading financial-assistance-rate parallel, the waste-levy precedent, or the central charge about squaring a rates cap with infrastructure costs. Pointing to approved council plans is on the subject and responsive in part, but it answers a different question from the one asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "18 councils have had their credit ratings downgraded, which doesn’t just mean that new debt is going to be more expensive but existing debt is going to be more expensive"

acuity.statement: Perhaps I can rephrase the question for the Minister, which is still related to clause 7, and that is perhaps not what incentive but what support is the Government going to be giving to councils to deliver on the water reform needs that this council is expecting them to do—not an incentive, but what is the support? I’ll leave that with the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the Minister's stated obstacle — that he cannot respond without a specific clause — by anchoring the question to clause 7, and then reworks the substance of his own question from 'incentive' to 'support' because the Minister's earlier answer treated incentives as a demand for a blank cheque. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged had the Minister said something else; it is shaped turn-by-turn by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I am finding it difficult to be able to answer specific members’ questions without a specific clause and general statement"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. There is so much in this part that has serious implications for the bill, so it would be fantastic to be able to step through it. I would like to speak directly to—as the Minister for Local Government pointed out—the objectives of the water service providers.
acuity.explanation: Pham follows Utikere's orphan-councils question and engages no part of it, moving instead to prepared material on clause 15 objectives. The turn is squarely within the same committee-stage debate on the bill, and she gestures at where the Minister had earlier directed the committee, but her speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Utikere had said. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 for the gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere spoke about orphan councils and Queenstown's water debt ("I'll get back to my question for the Minister, and that's about the orphan councils.") and this statement does not take it up; the reference to what "the Minister for Local Government pointed out" is a signpost to a turn outside this window.

acuity.statement: In terms of the questions from Lan Pham, in regard to clause 15(1)(a)(vi) and the challenge in regard to water environmental quality, it is very clear there that clause 15 that I’ve referred to says, “meet all regulatory requirements”. It is fair to say that because of the importance of water quality for health and safety and the importance of the environmental, we have, and prior Governments also have, been supporters of the establishment of a water quality regulator that has powers of enforcement, powers to set consistent standards.
acuity.explanation: Watts takes up the specific clause Pham raised, quotes its operative words back, and answers her anticipated objection about the regulator doing the environmental work by arguing the regulator's existence amplifies rather than diminishes those factors. The speech would have to change if she had argued something else. Not a full 1.0: he does not address her central ask — reinserting the safe-drinking-water and adverse-effects objectives — nor Water New Zealand's proposal to recast them as obligations.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "The other aspect that I’m suggesting is reinstating “do not have adverse effects on the environment;”." — and her "I know the rationale about there being a regulator and that they can do the environmental regulation and the pick-up of this".

acuity.statement: I want to raise an issue—we’re still working on Subpart 1 of this really substantive part. I want to go to Subpart 1, clause 8. We’ve had a little bit of discussion of clause 8, but not the particular subclause that I’m interested in here, and I want to understand its interaction with clause 15.
acuity.explanation: Russell follows the Minister's reply but engages none of its content, opening a fresh line on clause 8(3) instead. She is plainly in the same debate and explicitly notes the prior discussion of clause 8, which is a gesture at what preceded rather than engagement with it, so this sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band. Raising a new and legitimate question is not responsiveness, and the low score reflects only that.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts explained clause 8(2)'s permissive wording as "flexibility within the bill" and said clause 15 "says, ‘meet all regulatory requirements’", and this statement does not take either answer up — it acknowledges that clause 8 has been discussed and then moves to a subclause not yet raised.

acuity.statement: Yeah, so the clause that the member’s referring to does articulate the points that I’ve noted already in my prior response in regards to the ability to allocate operational and management responsibilities in regards to that. The questions raised by the member in regards to arrangements for transport corridors—just for the purpose of helping the member—that is part of the next part, Part 3, clause 176, so I won’t answer it here and I will in the next part.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bennett's specific question about clause 10 and separates it into two strands: the allocation of operational and management responsibility (which he says the clause already covers, referring back to his earlier answer) and the transport-corridor arrangements, which he locates precisely at Part 3, clause 176. The reply is clearly shaped by what Bennett asked — it would read differently had Bennett asked about something else — but half of it defers rather than engages, so this sits above a partial engagement without reaching a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "can the Minister assure this committee that what the Minister is doing in this piece of legislation will clarify, will be clear, will be directive around ownership, around operation, and around maintenance of the stormwater networks?"

acuity.statement: What is being done by this point in the legislation, which is the point the member raised around the distortion effect—if you look at clause 16(3)(b), it actually provides a clear mechanism: “The organisation must not pay a dividend”, etc., etc., and it refers back to clause 16(1)(b), which ensures that the revenue is being spent on providing the core purpose of the entity. So that aspect there deals as a protection mechanism to counteract, you know, potentially, a scenario that the member is saying.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages Abel's central argument — that referring to dividends distorts a water provider's primary purpose — and answers it on its own terms by pointing to clause 16(3)(b) and its link back to 16(1)(b) as the counteracting mechanism. The reply names the specific objection ('the distortion effect') and supplies clause text against it, so it could not have been delivered against a different argument. Short of 1.0 because Abel's first question (what 'growth' means in clause 16(1)(a)) and his Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009 point go unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "I’d appreciate also, as a second question, that the Minister clarify why there was a decision to include dividends"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister just confirm that councils aren’t forced to consider different options, but they have different options, and in that case the Queenstown Lakes District Council has assessed a range of available options and settled on the one they wanted to look at, which was the water services council-control organisation, which they consulted on with their community?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by Watts precedes it in the same committee debate. The question is on the matter under debate and nods to earlier contributions, but engages no part of the argument actually just made; it opens a fresh line about council choice. A gesture at the debate without engagement sits at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts spoke about the clause 58F(3) safeguards (Medical Officer of Health input, due process, public disclosure) around a closure decision, and this question does not take any of that up; it gestures instead at unspecified 'misinformed comments that we heard earlier' about Queenstown Lakes District Council.

acuity.statement: Based on the Minister’s earlier comments about there not being a magic money tree, how exactly can Tasman District Council in particular have some certainty and some opportunities to actually fund significant infrastructure going forward?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's position and puts a consequence to him, so the question would have to change if he had said something different. But the surrounding speech is prepared Nelson/Tasman material that engages neither Watts' clause 58F answer nor Mooney's question, so this is partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts' earlier remark in this debate that there is no 'magic money tree' — Boyack quotes it back and presses it against Tasman's funding position.

acuity.statement: In particular, it says here that a council should not transfer the ownership or control of any transport corridor stormwater infrastructure. So my first question to the Minister is: how is this going to work with any kind of integrated catchment planning?
acuity.explanation: Eligible: substantive turns by Watts, Mooney and Boyack precede it in the same committee debate. The speech is squarely on the bill, but it is self-contained prepared material built from a submission; it would read identically whatever Boyack had just argued. On-topic with no engagement puts it in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Boyack spoke immediately before about the Nelson and Tasman councils, the Waimea Dam and the rating burden on Tasman, and this statement does not take any of that up — it moves to clause 10 and a Water New Zealand submission.

acuity.statement: However, obviously, having duplicate control and ownership is not an optimal state, so what the bill allows is that councils can allocate management and operational responsibilities of those transport corridors to the water services entity but not the ownership aspect of that, and I think that is reasonable.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — management and operational responsibility can be allocated, ownership cannot — and gives the reason (avoiding duplicate ownership). The answer would be different had Wade-Brown asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "If you can’t transfer ownership or control, can you choose to contract with a water organisation—a water organisation could be a trust or it could be a council-controlled organisation—to manage the transport corridor stormwater network?"

acuity.statement: The point around why they are not forming a regional entity—well, our mechanism is deliberately structured so that that is a decision for local communities between the Nelson community and the Tasman community, potentially.
acuity.explanation: Directly identifies and takes up the core of Boyack's complaint — why no regional entity across Nelson and Tasman — and answers it by locating the choice with the communities, conceding her efficiency case is reasonable while disputing who should decide. Slightly short of 1.0 because it does not engage her specific Waimea Dam and rating-base figures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "Yet under this legislation, in terms of setting up the provision of water services, they’re staying separated." — her argument that Nelson and Tasman should have been required to join up.

acuity.statement: I did mention to the Chair and to the Minister before that I have some questions around transfer agreements. A specific provision I want to focus on is clause 13, “When new transfer agreement required”.

The gesture at the shared topic (transfer agreements) earns the top of the unresponsive band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere asked how the Minister would ensure transparency in clause 11 transfer agreements and sought his view on Amendment Paper 337, and this statement does not take either up (the only engagement is with the Minister's reply to Xu-Nan's own earlier question, which is not in this window).

acuity.statement: I want to follow on from my colleague Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan’s questions around transfer arrangements and pick up on an aspect that he hasn’t spoken about. If we look at clause 12(1)(b), it’s talking about the purpose and effect of a transfer arrangement.
acuity.explanation: Russell takes the preceding speaker's line of questioning on transfer agreements, names precisely which strand of it he left untouched, and extends it to a specific adjacent provision — clause 12(1)(b)'s "can be readily ascertained by the public" — then carries it into clause 13, the very clause he had just raised, to ask whether a new transfer agreement inherits that requirement. The speech would have had to be different had Xu-Nan raised different clauses; it is built on top of his questions rather than beside them. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "A specific provision I want to focus on is clause 13, ‘When new transfer agreement required’" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I refer the member to clause 14, which stipulates clearly that the requirement there is for transfer agreements to be published, and that obviously provides a context in terms of the transparency that’s required that the member is alluding to.
acuity.explanation: Watts answers the specific question just put to him — how "readily ascertained by the public" is meant to work — by pointing at the provision he says supplies it, clause 14's publication requirement. That is engaging the content of Russell's claim, not merely acknowledging her; the reply would be different had she asked about a different clause. Held below the top because she asked two questions and the second, whether a new transfer agreement under clause 13 also falls within the clause 12 transparency requirement, goes unanswered, as does her question about who bears the cost. (Precision and adequacy are Specificity's business, not Acuity's; only the partial coverage is scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Two questions there. How does that ‘readily ascertainable’ work, and how does it apply to new transfer agreements?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: My question is: why the wording “take into account”, which is sort of a lower bar—i.e., it’s not a strong articulation? We have a tabled amendment from my colleague Lan Pham, which proposes that it could be changed to “seek to protect and provide for” that list.
acuity.explanation: Abel follows Utikere's detailed case for Amendment Paper 339 and engages no part of it, opening instead on a different clause (26(3)) and a different amendment. The speech is at least within the same committee-stage debate on the same bill, and he gestures at the Chair's concern about progress, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0 — substitute any other argument about clause 17 for Utikere's and this turn would read identically.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued for the five paragraphs Amendment Paper 339 would insert into clause 17 (freshwater quality, drinking-water compliance, public health, a referendum, an annual public meeting) and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I have reflected on the Opposition members’ Amendment Papers, and have made a decision that I do not support them because I don’t believe that they are going to be adding more than the amendments that have been made—over 300 or so—through the select committee process which the members were part of.
acuity.explanation: Watts supplies the one thing Utikere explicitly asked for — a stated position on the circulated Amendment Papers — so this is not prepared material indifferent to what preceded it. But it engages none of the four or five specific proposals put to him (no declination in freshwater quality, drinking-water compliance, public health obligations, a referendum, an annual public meeting); the volume-based reply would be word-identical whatever those paragraphs contained. Answers the topic, not the claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Minister has had at least a couple of days to consider his position on this. In light of that, I would welcome a response from him." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: In regards to the answer to clause 26(3) by the member, the wording in subclause (3), as I outlined last night in response to a similar question, is taken from the Local Government Act, and that has the precedent in terms of the way in which the interaction and responsibilities by councils and the Treaty are required, and those set precedents in the context of this bill that’s on the Table.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact clause and the exact phrase Abel questioned and does something with it: accounts for the wording's provenance in the Local Government Act and the precedent it carries. Short of 1.0 because he answers where the words came from without engaging Abel's actual proposition — that the bar is too low and should be replaced with "protect and provide for" — and leaves the unsettled-iwi and Te Tiriti strand untouched. Whether the precedent argument is a good inference is a Rigor question and is deliberately not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why the wording “take into account”, which is sort of a lower bar" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: I just have one last question I wish to raise in respect of the clauses in Subpart 1 of Part 2, and it’s just to do with the interaction of a couple of clauses: the financial principles, clause 16, but also then the clause around obligations before entering into contracts, clause 22.
acuity.explanation: Russell opens a fresh line on the clause 16 / clause 22 interaction rather than engaging the answer immediately before her, so this falls in the 0.1-0.3 band. It earns 0.3 rather than 0.1 because it is squarely within the same clause-by-clause debate and does pick up the Minister's own earlier explanation of clause 16 ("as the Minister has explained to us") — a gesture at the exchange, though not at the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just declined the Opposition Amendment Papers and traced clause 26(3)'s wording to the Local Government Act, and this statement does not take either up; it builds instead on his earlier account of clause 16.

acuity.statement: What this clause reflects is, in effect, belts and braces to the aspects that the member has referenced in regards to how these entities may interact with the water service entities. In regards to clause 22(4), it outlines there that a public-private partnership means a long-term contract for the delivery of water services, and it goes on to outline the specifics around that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the clauses Russell actually raised, points to the 22(4) definition she said she had not had time to trace, and supplies a concrete instance (Veolia's long-term Watercare contract in Papakura) — the turn would have to change if she had asked about something else. It stops short of 1.0 because her core argument, that an investor's expected return accelerates the profit motive and pulls against the clause 16 financial principles, is met with assurance that controls exist rather than engaged on its merits.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder if the Minister could just give us a bit of his thinking around the use of public-private partnerships in the context of water supply" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: how will he ensure—if he intends to ensure at all—that those water organisations that will be established will not be used to privatise or, effectively, corporatise what are essential services?
acuity.explanation: Follows Lan Pham's substantive turn on contracting out water services. It shares her underlying worry — privatisation — but does not take up any part of her actual argument (the 50-year maximum, the proposed 20-year replacement, or the day-to-day-operations subclause). Instead it announces a move to Subpart 3 and puts prepared questions on clauses 36 and 37. On the matter under debate with a thematic gesture at what preceded it, but the speech would read identically had Pham argued something else about the same bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "we're really concerned about that acting as de facto privatisation" — this statement raises privatisation in relation to a different clause but engages none of her reasoning about contract length.

acuity.statement: I just want to query that a little bit in respect of the chief executive officer of a water organisation. It’s fairly common for CEOs to be on the board of an organisation. It’s not an unheard of arrangement.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's immediately preceding turn put a developed case about public accountability and protections against the dilution of public ownership, and asked the Minister to respond to it. This turn moves to clause 40 and director eligibility without touching any strand of that — no agreement, no extension, no dispute. It is prepared material on the right subject (governance of water organisations under the same bill), which keeps it out of the 0.0 band, but there is no gesture at what was just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere asked "what protections exist to ensure that the future ownership of these organisations remain in public ownership" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: In regard to the questions from members around accountability, the public accountability of water organisations is, obviously, through the councils or consumer trusts that are shareholders of these organisations. Councils and trustees are, obviously, elected by the public, and there are various requirements through the legislation and other mechanisms in regard to shareholders’ responsibilities, including through Part 4 of the bill, which I’m eagerly looking forward to progressing to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific question — where does public accountability sit, and what stops privatisation — and does something with it: locates the accountability chain in council and consumer-trust shareholding, then names clauses 17, 18 and 37 as the ownership restriction answering the privatisation point. The answer would have to be different had Utikere asked something else. Marked down from 1.0 only because Lan Pham's explicit request for the Minister's view on the 50-year contract limit, also preceding, goes unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "what protections exist to ensure that the future ownership of these organisations remain in public ownership"

acuity.statement: The question around can a CEO of an organisation sit on the board—I mean, I’m not going to do an Institute of Directors 101 course on corporate governance, but I would go as far to say it’s probably not good practice to have a chief executive be a member of your governance board, because, last time I looked, governance boards set the strategy and actually employ the CEO, so a bit of conflict there.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the specific premise Russell advanced — that a CEO on the board is a common and unremarkable arrangement — and supplies a reason for the contradiction (the board sets strategy and employs the CEO, so the seat is conflicted). It then answers the live part of her question by saying the CEO would attend in an executive capacity. Squarely engaged with the content of the preceding claim; the dismissive framing is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one, and does not reduce the score here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It’s fairly common for CEOs to be on the board of an organisation."

acuity.statement: In regards to the question on clause 45 around consumer trusts and how they deal with consumer engagement, clause 45 requires that a trustee sets out how trustees will engage with consumers, and the ultimate accountability that is in place for consumer trust is consumer trust elections, and that ensures that the accountability mechanism is in place.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific clause 45 question about public engagement and answers it on its own terms — pointing to the deed requirement that trustees set out how they will engage with consumers, and adding trust elections as the accountability mechanism. The reply would be different had Utikere asked about a different clause. Not a full 1.0 because it leaves two of Utikere's three questions (community diversity in the deed, provenance of the $200,000 penalty in clause 51) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "why has the Government not mandated for a stronger level of public engagement requirements in the trust deed?"

acuity.statement: Exemptions from clause 38 are provided for in clause 55(3). That’s the reason why clause 55 is in place—there was a prior question in regards to clause 38.
acuity.explanation: Engages the clause Pham moved to delete and explains why it exists, so it is clearly a reply to her amendment rather than prepared material. But it answers the general purpose of clause 55 rather than the specific claim she made — that clause 55(5) opens an avenue to privatisation via a cooperative company, a reading backed by the Wellington councils, Tauranga City Council and the Institute of Directors. One strand engaged, the substance of the objection not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "My suggested amendment—which I’ll get straight to—is to delete clause 55."

acuity.statement: My suggested amendment to further ensure that these water entities are protected from possible avenues of privatisation is to delete clause 55, and I’d like to hear that being considered.
acuity.explanation: On the same subpart and the same bill, and framed as building one step further on something said earlier in the debate, so it is not wholly indifferent to its surroundings. But it engages no part of the preceding substantive turn by Utikere; it is a prepared amendment with prepared submitter support, delivered as it would have been whatever Utikere had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere had just questioned clause 45's public engagement requirements and the source of the clause 51 penalty, and this statement does not take either up. Pham gestures at an earlier assurance by the Minister of Local Government about an avoidance-of-doubt clause, but that turn is not in this window, so the engagement cannot be pointed at here.

acuity.statement: The member’s points are out of the scope of this bill because they relate to the fact that water service providers’ obligations are to comply with the water quality regulations. So all of that lovely stuff and conversation is very nice but it’s not relevant to this provision because the regulations in terms of water quality are outlined under the requirements for the water services regulator.
acuity.explanation: Abel's central question was whether a water supplier has any obligation to advise its community about health risks from nitrate, or whether it need only meet the maximum acceptable value. Watts takes that exact question and gives it a direct answer — obligations run only to compliance with the water quality regulations, which sit with the regulator, not with this provision. The reply is squarely aimed at the question asked and would have had to be different had Abel asked something else; it loses a little for not addressing the second half (whether a council could call the water 'perfectly safe'). Dismissive tone is a separate matter from responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "or does it simply have to meet the maximum acceptable value" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: Some colleagues have touched on the proceeding clauses around what information is to be made available for the assessment of services and the like. This clause is very specific, and it relates to the possible transfer or the closure of small water services.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by Watts immediately precedes, containing a contestable claim about the scope of the bill. Utikere does not engage it at all; he opens a fresh line on clause 58F with prepared questions that would have been identical whatever Watts had just said. There is a gesture at the debate ('Some colleagues have touched on the proceeding clauses'), which lifts it off the floor, but it is a reference rather than an engagement, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just ruled Steve Abel's nitrate and public-health questions out of scope because providers' obligations run to the water quality regulations, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Clause 58F(3)(a) refers to a number of 200 persons to provide an indication of 200 or fewer, which is the point that the member’s potentially getting to, into the context around what is seen as small. There is no subsequent definition of what is small, but the context around 200 provides some guidance.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's first question was that 'small water service' is nowhere defined in the interpretation clause or in Subpart 4, and he speculated that 'fewer than 200' might be the trigger. Watts takes up that specific point, confirms the absence of a definition, and supplies the figure and the clause it sits in — doing something with the member's own guess. He then engages the referendum point, but leaves the asked question about why 75 percent for closure and 50 percent for transfer unanswered, and declines points (b)–(d) as already covered, so the engagement is strong but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there is no definition that I can see for a “small water service”" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Why 200? Why not 150? Why not 300? Did officials do some survey work to have a look at what might be called small water services and do some work and find out that, actually, 200 was a kind of reasonably good demarcation between small and not so small, or was it just a number dragged out of the air?
acuity.explanation: Watts had just answered that there is no definition of 'small' but that the number 200 in clause 58F(3)(a) provides the guidance. Russell takes that answer and presses on precisely the weakness in it — if 200 is doing the defining work, what evidence picked 200 rather than 150 or 300, and was any survey of small water services done. She also notes it counts persons rather than connections. The question only exists because of the answer that preceded it; it drops to 0.8 rather than 1.0 because she then moves on to a separate prepared line about voter eligibility in the referendum.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the context around 200 provides some guidance" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: In regards to the questions around defined terms, again, this was discussed at length through the select committee process.
acuity.explanation: Brooking's preceding turn asked a specific drafting question: why Part 3 uses the defined term "water organisations" rather than "water services provider", and how the two interact. Watts names that strand and then defers it to the select committee process without engaging any part of the distinction she put. That is a mere reference to the question, not engagement with its content, so it sits in the low band rather than the 0.5 partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Rachel Brooking: "why is it that this subpart is just about water organisations and not water service providers?"

acuity.statement: If you’re relying on direct user-charges but we’re excluding the ability of transport corridor managers to be charged, where is the incentive going to come from for the corridor manager to minimise the impact on the stormwater system?
acuity.explanation: Watts had just argued that economic regulation assures fair prices and that hardship mechanisms exist. Genter does not take up that claim at all; she opens a new line on clause 61(3) and the stormwater incentive problem. The material is squarely on the subpart under debate — charging for water services — so it is not a 0.0, but the speech would read identically had Watts said something else about pricing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts spoke about economic regulation assuring that water prices are fair and about hardship mechanisms, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for the question and agree in principle, because the points that the member’s making in regards to whether stormwater is, in effect, in or out are absolutely areas that I’m having flashbacks now of discussing in prior lives. That is the point of why we have given, under this structure, the choice around how that works.
acuity.explanation: He takes up Genter's stormwater strand directly, concedes the difficulty she identified, and supplies a reason from the bill's design — the deliberate flexibility over where stormwater sits — illustrated with the Watercare/Healthy Waters split. That is real engagement, but with the adjacent question: Genter asked where the incentive on corridor managers comes from if they cannot be charged, and the answer addresses where stormwater sits rather than the clause 61(3) exclusion. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Julie Anne Genter: "why transport corridor managers have been excluded" / "whether stormwater is, in effect, in or out"

acuity.statement: Presumably—and I apologise; I haven’t looked up what that section says—a transport corridor manager could be the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA); it could be a council. My question is: could it be anybody else?
acuity.explanation: She picks up the clause 61(3) exclusion Genter had just raised and advances it onto specific ground the previous turns had left open — who in law can be a "transport corridor manager", given the term is not in the definitions section. The question only exists because of what Genter asked and what Watts answered, so the turn would have to change if the preceding contribution had been different. Marked down from 1.0 because she extends the line rather than engaging the reasoning of Watts's reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Julie Anne Genter: "A water organisation must not collect a charge for stormwater services from a corridor manager." and "why transport corridor managers have been excluded"

acuity.statement: I want to also make the point that the Minister, in his answer to my other question, was a non-answer. He said the select committee have traversed the issue of the phrases around water organisations and what it means, and the different phrasing in the bill. This opportunity that we have in the House, in the committee stage, is to get things into Hansard and to have things explained in a way that they are not in the select committee report.
acuity.explanation: She quotes back the exact content of the Minister's reply — that the defined terms were traversed at select committee — and does something with it: she identifies why that answer does not discharge the question at the committee stage, namely that the purpose of this stage is to get an explanation into Hansard that the select committee report does not contain. The engagement is with the substance of his answer, not merely with him as a target.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Simon Watts: "In regards to the questions around defined terms, again, this was discussed at length through the select committee process."

acuity.statement: There’s a very specific instance of this. I know, in Gore, they’ve, literally, just spent money to drill a bore so they can pump water from the Mataura River into the water supply to dilute it so that the nitrate is below the maximum allowable value. They’re spending public money to fix a contamination problem. Can they seek compensation from the entity that is causing the contamination?
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn follows a substantive ministerial answer and is framed as continuing it, but the content is an entirely new line of inquiry — recourse to compensation for contamination under clause 16 — illustrated with the Gore bore. Nothing in Watts's answer about the 200 threshold or the select committee process is engaged, rebutted or built on; the question would read identically had the preceding answer been about something else. It stays squarely on the bill under debate, so it sits at the upper end of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "The number of 200 is actually used in other aspects of legislation, including health legislation, in the context of quantification around that size." — Abel opens with "it's on the same question" but takes up neither the derivation of the 200 figure nor Watts's claim that the select committee already covered such detail.

acuity.statement: In the absence of confirmation from the Minister that this is a simple transfer from elsewhere in the bill, I want to turn to what is proposed to be clause 58L, “Water services delivery plans: adoption and consultation”, and this is set out on Amendment Paper 346 in the name of the Minister.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one real strand of the immediately preceding turn — Russell's unanswered question about whether Subpart 5 was transferred — and makes the absence of an answer the hinge for proceeding. But he does nothing further with it, pivoting straight to a prepared examination of clause 58L and the referendum thresholds. Partial engagement that you can point at, which is the ~0.5 band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "was this transferred from another part of the bill?" — Utikere expressly picks up that the Minister has not confirmed the transfer, then moves to his own prepared material on clause 58L.

acuity.statement: Yeah, in regards to the clause reference—so, as the member will see on page 81, in the little small font under Subpart 4, there’s a little number there which refers to the Local Government Act reference. I know the member’s read the bill, but just helping him again to identify clause 131 as referring to the aspect in regards to the 200 number that I answered before.
acuity.explanation: The reply is on the bill and does hand over a precise locator (page 81, clause 131), but it answers a clause-reference point already dealt with earlier rather than the question just put to him about a higher voting threshold for adopting a water services delivery plan — nor does it address Russell's question about where Subpart 5 came from. There is a gesture at the debate, so 0.3, but no part of the preceding argument is engaged. Scored on engagement only: the precision of the reference is a specificity matter, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "was there any thought about having a different threshold around the adoption of a water services delivery plan, even if it was at 75 percent?" — Watts supplies a page and clause reference for the earlier 200 figure instead, and does not take up the threshold question at all.

acuity.statement: And it has—the Minister’s right; it has. Actually, we had to go through and extend it a little bit further because of the complexities in the regulatory approaches of this bill. That was the opportunity for the community and others to have their say. Just because something’s gone through a full select committee process doesn’t mean that we need to short-tail this particular opportunity for all members of the House who may not have been part of that select committee process to have their say.
acuity.explanation: This is the sharpest engagement in the window: he grants the Minister's factual premise outright ("the Minister's right; it has"), adds that the committee stage had to be extended because of the bill's regulatory complexity, and then disputes the conclusion Watts drew from it — that prior select committee scrutiny licenses curtailing committee-stage questioning by members who were not on that committee. Delete Watts's select-committee point and this passage could not stand as written, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I am looking forward to some good questions but concise, taking account that this bill has been through a full select committee process." — Utikere concedes the premise and attacks the inference drawn from it.

acuity.statement: In regard to clause 109 around the exemption portion noted there, this is basically a continuation of the status quo. Development contributions are being replaced by a new development levy mechanism—again, that I noted last evening—under the Going for Housing Growth policy.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the exact clause Wade-Brown asked about and supplies a reason (status quo continuation, superseding levy regime), so the answer is clearly shaped by her question. But he engages only the topic, not her specific argument — the Kāinga Ora versus other-Crown asymmetry, the submitters who wanted clause 109 deleted, and the partnership question all go unaddressed. Partial engagement, then back to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "in clause 109 it suggests that the Crown should be exempt from development contributions"

acuity.statement: You touched on, last night—and you just touched on it then again—the changes to the development contributions from the primary legislation, being the Local Government Act (LGA), changing at some point in the future to development levies. A question, then, is: how does he foresee those changes impacting on all these provisions in this bill relating to development contributions?
acuity.explanation: She picks up the specific thing Watts had just said — that development contributions are to be replaced by a levy mechanism — and draws out its consequence, asking what that does to the development contribution provisions in the bill in front of them. The question could not exist had he answered differently; it is built directly on his answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Development contributions are being replaced by a new development levy mechanism"

acuity.statement: My point is: there you have some criteria in a statute that seem sensible and also give enough room for the local water organisation to work out how they’re going to do the development contribution under those criteria. So why not have criteria for the waiver policy and—and—include in those criteria the issues of equity that seem to be missing from everywhere in this bill?
acuity.explanation: Watts defended the waiver policy as leaving the matter to local choice; she accepts that framing and turns it against him, showing via section 101(3) of the LGA that statutory criteria can coexist with local discretion, so 'local choice' is no reason to leave the waiver policy criterion-free. A rebuttal aimed squarely at the reasoning of the answer she just received.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "Basically, this is providing for local choice. It’s really up to the local water organisation and the shareholding council to determine the appropriate mechanisms"

acuity.statement: My question for the Government progressing this bill is really around how the Government intends that there will be a guarantee or an assurance that this information will be shared and made in a timely manner. What we’re hearing a lot from the Minister of Local Government is that there are provisions already contained in other legislation to guide this, whether it’s a carrot or a stick sort of approach.
acuity.explanation: He characterises the Minister's repeated answer — that the governing provisions sit in other legislation — and presses on whether that actually guarantees timely information sharing, which is a real engagement with the pattern of the replies. But the bulk of the turn is prepared material opening a new clause (81/83) rather than taking up any specific claim just made, so this is partial rather than direct responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "the provisions for monitoring and ministerial intervention are included within the Local Government Act and not this Act"

acuity.statement: In regards to clauses 81 and 83, the question is primarily seeking guidance around additional powers to ensure that the information disclosure components outlined in the bill actually do occur, and, if they don’t, what mechanisms are in place to ensure that they do. I’ve outlined already the ministerial intervention powers. In addition to that, as part of this, these entities will be subject to economic regulation by the Commerce Commission.
acuity.explanation: He restates Utikere's question accurately in his own terms — what enforces the information disclosure obligations if they are not met — and answers it with named mechanisms (ministerial intervention, Commerce Commission economic regulation). The reply is specific to the question asked; it falls short of 1.0 because the timeliness and council-support strands of the question, and Brooking's earlier questions, are not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "how the Government intends to ensure that the data sharing or information sharing that’s provided is transparent but also that there is some accountability around that"

acuity.statement: So the question was around—and maybe the Minister of Local Government answered it—could there be private roads that are considered? Also, where does the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) fit with it, and if NZTA is a transport corridor manager, should there not be some ability to charge for the stormwater service so the farmers don’t get blamed?
acuity.explanation: Watts had just disposed of her transport-corridor question by referring her to clause 176 and asserting that each participant carries its own costs. She takes that answer up directly, notes it may have been given by the other Minister, and presses the parts it left unresolved — private roads, and whether NZTA as a corridor manager can charge for stormwater. The speech would be different had he answered differently, but it largely re-puts the original question rather than contesting the clause 176 reasoning, so it is strong engagement rather than full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I refer the member Rachel Brooking to clause 176, which provides for the integrated management of that aspect. Each participant carries their own costs in regards to the way in which those components operate."

acuity.statement: I note that the Minister of Local Government has talked about the amount of time that this seems to be taking, so my first question to the Minister: is he expecting that this will be done before 1 o’clock, or is he actually prepared to work through some of the issues that have been raised to identify the fact that households in this country would rather he focus on ensuring that they can actually meet these costs rather than what he’s going to have for lunch? That’s the first question.
acuity.explanation: This seizes on the specific thing Watts had just said — that five hours in he was hungry and thinking about lamb chops instead of answering — and turns it into a question about whether he intends to work through the issues raised. It could not have been delivered in any other debate or after any other remark. It falls short of 1.0 because what it engages is an aside rather than an argument, and it does not take up any reasoning about the clauses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I was just thinking, coming up to lunchtime and five hours into this bill, how hungry I am and I was thinking of lamb chops, but I can’t make any other further comment in regards to that question."

acuity.statement: In regards to questions on clause 62 and the member’s question to me asking am I comfortable with that, I am comfortable. The due process in regards to that, again, has been well considered by officials and input from the Finance and Expenditure Committee to enhance it. In regards to clause 62(3) and the percentage, I refer the member to that clause where it stipulates the Local Government (Rating) Act reference in regards to the proxy for that number, and that’s the basis for it.
acuity.explanation: He takes up two of the specific things Utikere put to him: the direct question of whether he is comfortable with the serviceability-charge variation, and the question of why 50 percent is the threshold in clause 62(3), for which he supplies the source of the number (the Local Government (Rating) Act proxy). That is real engagement with the content. It is partial rather than full: the modelling question, the clause 61 transparency question, and the legacy-infrastructure question all go untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Why is it 50 percent is the particular threshold there, whereas land might actually be non-rateable at a higher threshold?"

acuity.statement: We heard in an earlier contribution from my colleague Tangi Utikere about whether or not there have been any equity considerations.
