But he attributes the argument to an unnamed member rather than engaging Walters' actual reasoning about evolving customary norms, and the bulk of the speech is prepared material on the benefits of recognition that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "If you look at when a nation State can and should be recognised, historically we are leaning on treaties that come out of the 1930s, including the Montevideo Convention"

acuity.statement: If you look at yesterday’s Order Paper for this House’s business and today’s Order Paper for this House’s business, there is no primary question on the question of Palestine from the Opposition—not one.
acuity.explanation: Follows Henare's substantive take-note speech in the same debate. It does take up one strand of what Henare said — his claim that Labour has repeatedly pressed this matter through questions in the House — and counters it with the Order Paper. But it engages the sincerity of Labour's pressure rather than Henare's central argument (that waiting until September costs lives), and immediately moves to prepared material. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'This has been a matter that has been put as questions in the House since it began.'

acuity.statement: As we outlined in our press release yesterday—and here it is—this is not straightforward or a clear-cut issue. Some of our partners are in favour of recognition; others are not.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific premise of Henare's speech — that New Zealand's close partners and allies are uniformly 'leading the charge' and that NZ is being left behind — by asserting the partners are divided. The speech would have to change if Henare had argued something else about allied positions; this is a rebuttal of the claim rather than a pivot away from it. Short of 1.0 because it asserts the counter-position rather than engaging the evidence Henare offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'Many people we call close partners, the people we call close allies, and others are leading the charge of the recognition of Palestine as a State.'

acuity.statement: For the Labour Party’s benefit, they had 15 years to recognise Palestine statehood. I heard Helen Clark this morning. Well, she was the Prime Minister from 1999 to 2008. Did she do that then? No.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific boast Henare made — that Labour in office acted quickly on urgent international matters and stands proudly by that record — and answers it with Labour's own terms in government on this very question. Squarely aimed at the claim just made; the engagement is high even though the inference is a tu quoque that does not address whether recognition should happen now (that is a Rigor matter, not Acuity).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'when Labour was in power—for the urgent matters that faced not only this country but the world—we came together quickly, with urgency' / 'We stand proudly by that record.'

acuity.statement: Relatively straightforward rats and mice bill, for the most part, amending 23 Acts—small changes, from the age that you can buy a Lotto ticket through to creating more opportunity for people to stand for local authorities, modernising rules that date back some almost 45 years. Yep, I acknowledge there's always an opportunity to improve things at select committee, and happy to look at that.
acuity.explanation: Belich's preceding turn argued the bill is not merely operational — it makes 'substantive changes' to passports, Births, Deaths and Marriages and FENZ — and said Labour would take a microscope to it at select committee. Costley takes up one strand of that: he characterises the contents the opposite way ('rats and mice bill ... small changes', with examples), and concedes the select committee point ('Yep, I acknowledge there's always an opportunity to improve things at select committee'). But he engages no part of her specific argument about the regulatory-systems instrument being used for substantive matters, and the rest is a bare commendation that would read the same whoever preceded him. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "it does cover a number of matters that appear, on the face of it, to be substantive"

acuity.statement: Oh, it shouldn’t be criminal law? OK, well, you’re entitled to that view, and I look forward to you explaining that view. I think members of the public will be intrigued to learn that the Greens don’t think that excessive noise in a public place should be subject to the criminal law.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan put a specific legal-classification claim — that excessive vehicle noise belongs in public law rather than criminal law, 'for a reason'. Bishop registers the claim and repeats it back, but engages none of its content: he does not say why the criminal law is the right instrument, nor address the public-law alternative. He restates the position in order to pivot to characterising the Greens as politically exposed and then returns to his prepared material on sleepless neighbours. Repeating an opponent's words to pivot away sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because he does at least name the proposition accurately and promises to debate it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'It’s public law for a reason.' — Lawrence Xu-Nan (interjecting that excessive vehicle noise should not be dealt with by criminal law)

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to rise and take a call on this bill. This is a law and order Government, and our goal is to make our streets and our communities safer. That is why we have this law, the “boy racer legislation”, looking at cracking down on boy racers.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Andy Foster that made specific arguments — the new 'frightening or intimidating convoy' offence, the onus on vehicle owners to identify the driver, the Greens' objection to temporary area closures, and the Levin King's Birthday event with 22 arrests. Bidois takes up none of it: he restates the Government's law-and-order framing, offers a personal recollection of boy racers in East Auckland, and quotes a colleague's earlier line. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Foster had argued, though it is at least on the bill under debate and gestures at the wider debate by citing Dana Kirkpatrick, so it sits at the upper edge of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued the bill creates a new offence of 'taking part in a frightening or intimidating convoy', shifts the onus onto car owners to identify drivers, and answered Green objections to temporary area closures with the Levin event — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: But there was actually something that the Minister said in his speech introducing this bill, which was, “the problem is our current suite of offences and penalties are clearly not enough to deter those people.” We oppose this bill on the basis that we don’t believe that this bill will increase people’s knowledge or adherence to these new laws, because it relies on the assumption that people understand that these things are against the law or what penalties they carry. It’s the myth of deterrence; it’s existed for a long time, and we think that it’s not the basis of good lawmaking.
acuity.explanation: Takes a specific sentence from the Minister's introduction and turns it into the ground of opposition: if the existing offences already fail to deter, adding more offences cannot work. The speech would have to change if the Minister had justified the bill differently. Not a full 1.0 because the engagement is with the bill's mover rather than the immediately preceding speaker, whose points (committee choice, registered-owner defence) she does not take up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the problem is our current suite of offences and penalties are clearly not enough to deter those people" — the Minister, in his speech introducing the bill earlier in this debate (quoted by Paul)

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party to speak in support of the Antisocial Road Use Legislation Amendment Bill. I’d first like to make the observation that it’s quite interesting to see the Green Party voting against a bill that’ll crush more internal combustion cars. It’s quite a bit of a surprise there.
acuity.explanation: A reference to the preceding speaker's vote, not to any part of her argument. It names a target and pivots to an unrelated incongruity about internal combustion cars; the words would be unchanged whatever reasons she had given. Scored just above 0.1 because it at least registers that the Greens opposed the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul opposed the bill on deterrence, Bill of Rights and fatal-pursuit grounds, and this passage takes up none of that — it notes only that her party is voting against

acuity.statement: I have heard too many times from people talking about police chases from one side of an opinion, saying they should happen more and some saying they should happen less. Really, they should not be needing to happen. There should be a consequence for fleeing drivers. There should be a state of affairs in New Zealand where police can follow those drivers and bring it to an end, and not abandon pursuit to later find a car on its roof with a 14-year-old inside. That is not what we need to be doing in New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the very harm Paul put at the centre of her case — teenagers dying in pursuits — and contests the conclusion drawn from it, arguing that abandoned pursuits rather than enforcement produce the dead 14-year-old. That is engagement with her evidence, not avoidance of it, though it reframes rather than disputing her figures, so it is a partial-to-strong engagement rather than a direct rebuttal of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "teenagers make up half of all victims of fatal police pursuits in New Zealand" and "we have all seen the stories of 12-year-olds, 13-year-olds, 15-year-olds who are killed in pursuit by police" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: Yes, people who are being pulled over should know the rules, in reply to the previous speaker Tamatha Paul’s speech. If you’re going to be on the road, you must have a licence; you must demonstrate you know what the rules are. This is not about education; this is about punishing antisocial behaviour, just going about and disturbing the communities. These are sensible steps.
acuity.explanation: Answers Paul's central premise directly: licensing means drivers are required to know the rules, so her assumption objection fails, and the bill's purpose is punishment rather than education. He names the strand he is answering and the passage would be different had she argued on other grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it relies on the assumption that people understand that these things are against the law or what penalties they carry" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: This bill gives police the power to shut down the illegal convoys, close roads, issue fines, and introduce a presumptive court order sentence of vehicle forfeiture and destruction.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows a substantive Labour speech that made two checkable arguments — that the previous crushing regime failed on drafting details, and that without front-line numbers the new tools cannot be enforced. His speech engages neither. It opens on Liam Lawson, moves to Mt Roskill dirt bikes, then recites what the bill does and commends it. It is on the subject under debate, so not a 0.0, but it would have been word-for-word identical whatever Andersen had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued the 2009/2010 crushing legislation crushed only about two cars because of ownership and hardship clauses, and that the binding constraint is front-line police resource rather than new powers; this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Right now, there is a proposal to cut police officers in Lyttelton, leaving just one single point of contact for that whole area. This isn’t an abstract policy change. From August last year to August this year, there were 125 victimisation incidents in Lyttelton alone: break-ins, graffiti, vehicle thefts—dozens more across both Diamond Harbour and Governors Bay.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one specific strand of a preceding turn — that enforcement capacity, not penalties, is the binding constraint — and does something with it, grounding it in a named local proposal to cut Lyttelton officers and an incident count for that area. The speech would have to change if that resourcing argument had not been made. It is only partial engagement, though: she does not touch the immediately preceding speaker's contribution at all, and the remainder is prepared Banks Peninsula material, so this sits above the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "if you do not have the workforce in place to be able to implement the law and be able to enforce the law, then you’re wasting your time" — McLellan names her ("as my colleague Hon Ginny Andersen has just said") and supplies local evidence for the same proposition.

acuity.statement: For many years, with my doorknocking around South Auckland, East Auckland, and Takanini, so many people and so many of our gentlemen have said, “So what are you going to do about these boy racers?”, and to them, I say that the National-led Government is cracking down on this reckless, dangerous, antisocial behaviour.
acuity.explanation: The turn immediately follows a speech that conceded support for the bill but put a specific, answerable challenge about enforcement resourcing. Nakhle offers doorknocking anecdote and a line of government advocacy, engaging no part of that challenge. It is at least about boy racers and this bill, which keeps it off 0.0, but a mere restatement of the Government's position is prepared material, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan had just argued that the bill's powers will fail without local police to enforce them, citing a proposal to cut Lyttelton officers and 125 victimisation incidents; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her questions. She is right that the Amendment Paper that the Government has tabled has not gone through select committee process; however, in mitigation, most of the changes in the Amendment Paper have been publicly announced—in some cases, a couple of months, if not earlier, than today, so members have had a good opportunity to kick those issues around.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific process complaint, concedes the factual core of it (the Amendment Paper bypassed select committee) and then disputes the inference by arguing the changes were pre-announced. The reply would be different had she complained about something else, and it accepts part while contesting the rest — the hallmark of engagement rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These changes have not been through any public process" — Hon Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: In relation to the issue that the member raises around clause 4 and around specified energy generation, the Government’s taken the view that it’s an inclusive regime in the sense that we want renewables to be quicker, but we also want all forms of electricity generation to be quicker—and so, ultimately, the market will build what the market builds.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put to him — why thermal generation was added to 'specified energy activity' in clause 4 when the bill was sold as a renewables measure — by naming the clause and supplying the Government's rationale, and he goes on to engage her alternative of limiting it to firming and peaking. Scored on engagement only; whether the 'market will build what the market builds' reasoning is sound is a Rigor question, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how does he justify that, given everything that was said about the bill being to promote renewable energy?" — Hon Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I want to share my colleague’s absolute frustration and disappointment about these last-minute amendments, particularly as a member of the Environment Committee. A great many of the changes that are in these amendments were discussed at select committee, and I’d really love to hear from the Minister about what role he sees select committees actually playing—just broadly—in the development of legislation, and particularly quite substantial legislation like this.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what preceded: she picks up the process objection and her claim that the changes were already canvassed at select committee cuts against the Minister's mitigation that members had ample opportunity to consider them. But she does not take up his actual defence — that the changes were publicly announced months ago — and moves instead into her own prepared line of questioning about the role of select committees. On topic, partially aimed, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "most of the changes in the Amendment Paper have been publicly announced" — Hon Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Thank you to the member Lan Pham for her question. I mean, the obvious point is I’ve got a deep respect for the select committee process, as a person who sat on the select committee for nine years in Opposition and in Government. Select committees play an important role, and I thank the Environment Committee for their consideration of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the question asked — what role he sees select committees playing — rather than restating the case for the bill, and the remainder of the turn goes on to answer her second question about why the changes came at short notice. The speech is plainly shaped by her question and would not survive a different one unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what role he sees select committees actually playing—just broadly—in the development of legislation" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: Yes, thank you to my colleague Rachel Brooking. I certainly would like to look at clause 4, the new definition of “long-lived infrastructure”, and I also want to reflect on the Minister responsible for RMA Reform’s statement earlier that we will have a National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up the exact strand Brooking flagged and handed to him — the deletion of gas pipelines/"natural or" from the new definition of "long-lived infrastructure" in clause 4 — and develops it into a specific amendment request to the Minister. He also engages the Minister's earlier NPS-REG claim with dated delivery failures. The speech would be different had Brooking raised something else; it is not 1.0 only because much of what follows is prepared material on the Government's undelivered energy documents rather than further engagement with her particular questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "there is an amendment to delete—and it’s in the name of Scott Willis; he might want to speak to this as well—in “long-lived infrastructure” the “(a) pipelines that distribute or transmit natural or manufactured gas:”"

acuity.statement: The member asked about the National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation. That is under consultation right now.
acuity.explanation: Bishop identifies the specific factual complaint in Willis's turn — that the renewables NPS promised for June last year has not been delivered — and answers it with the current status, the May draft, and a date by which he intends it promulgated. That is engaging the content of the claim, not merely naming the member who made it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "the National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation was to be delivered in June last year; it still hasn’t been delivered"

acuity.statement: I understand where the member is coming from, but we’re not proposing to adopt his amendments to delete thermal generation from the definition of “long-lived infrastructure”. We are advancing the renewables policy statement.
acuity.explanation: Willis explicitly asked the Minister to respond to his amendment and to delete "natural or" from clause 4; Bishop gives a squarely responsive refusal rather than ignoring the request. Marked below 1.0 for Acuity only because he restates the amendment as deleting "thermal generation" rather than the words Willis actually moved on, so the engagement is with the gist rather than the text — the accuracy of that restatement is a separate question from responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "The simple thing this Government can do—and I hope the Minister will take this on board; I would like the Minister to respond, please—is delete “natural or” from clause 4"

acuity.statement: Just picking up on that same vein in the definition of “long-lived infrastructure”. It was one of the more entertaining parts of the select committee process, where literally every business or company thought they should all be considered long-lived infrastructure and their infrastructure should be long-lived infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Pham stays on the live clause Bishop had just refused to amend and acknowledges the contest over what belongs in that definition, but she engages none of his actual reasoning (the 80-87 percent renewable figure, the energy shortage, the inclusive consenting regime) and moves straight to her own prepared water-infrastructure amendment. Partial engagement with the matter under debate rather than with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "we’re not proposing to adopt his amendments to delete thermal generation from the definition of “long-lived infrastructure”"

acuity.statement: The member makes a really good point. I’m advised that it was—the definition of “long-lived infrastructure”, including waste water and stormwater, which I think the member is rightly saying should probably be included, was excluded from the scope of this bill as it potentially conflicts with the Local Government (Water Services) Bill, which has been subject to a separate process as we go through.
acuity.explanation: Pham asked the Minister to consider inserting water, stormwater and wastewater infrastructure into the definition; Bishop addresses that precise proposal, concedes its merit, supplies the specific reason it was left out (conflict with the Local Government (Water Services) Bill), and names where it could be revisited. The reply could not have been given had she proposed something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "inserting a new line, a new paragraph (db), about “infrastructure providing water supply, stormwater and wastewater distribution”"

acuity.statement: We did look at the issue that the member raises, so the bill makes some amendments to coastal permits—it extends their duration, as the member knows. The issue of dredging is more complicated—technically, and environmentally as well—and so the decision was made to leave that until RM3, as we’ve been calling it, which is phase 3 of resource management reform, which is the new legislation which is coming before the House later in the year.
acuity.explanation: Foster asked specifically for surety that the Government would deal with the right to dredge, noting it was absent from the bill. Bishop takes up that exact point: he confirms the issue was considered, distinguishes what the bill does do (extend coastal permit duration) from what it does not (dredging), gives the reason for the omission (technical and environmental complexity), and names where and when it will be handled (RM phase 3, later this year). The speech would be materially different had Foster raised something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "I understand it’s not in this bill, but I’m really seeking some surety—not just for me but also for the ports, because I know they’re very interested in this—that the Government is on to this and will deal with this in due course"

acuity.statement: I want to speak to an Amendment Paper (AP) that I’ve put forward. This is still related to the issue of long-lived infrastructure, but it’s specifically about clause 69, where there’s a new regulation power being given to the Minister to be able to prescribe infrastructure as “long-lived infrastructure”.
acuity.explanation: Genter follows a substantive answer from Bishop about why dredging was deferred and how reform has been split into manageable chunks, but engages no part of it. She thanks the Minister — a mere reference, not engagement — and turns to prepared material on her own Amendment Paper to a different clause. The passage is on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically whatever Bishop had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop argued that resource management reform has been divided into manageable chunks and that dredging was deliberately deferred to phase 3 because it is technically and environmentally complicated, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In relation to Ms Paul’s point, I think she was talking about clause 6 on Amendment Paper 347 in the Government’s name, which amends section 25A. One of the things that I think people sometimes misunderstand about the Resource Management Act (RMA) is that it actually gives the Government quite extensive intervention powers in local authorities already. This amended section strengthens that up and makes it clear that if a national policy statement requires a local authority to prepare a document and the authority hasn’t done that, the Minister can direct the authority to do that or amend the document to meet the requirements of a national policy statement.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Paul's clause 6 / section 25A question directly, identifies the Amendment Paper she means, and answers the substance by explaining what the amended section does and what the statutory fetters on the power are. He also picks up her own Wellington housing example and turns it back on her argument, so the speech would plainly differ had she asked something else. Short of 1.0 because he answers the general justification for intervention powers rather than her narrower question about why the scope was broadened beyond the NPSUD — which is why she had to re-put it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "what is the policy justification for extending those ministerial powers to apply across national direction?"

acuity.statement: I’m still on clause 4, and, noting that the Minister has spoken at some length about the importance of renewable energy and planning for infrastructure and getting rid of planning red tape so we can do better with our housing, I of course want to note that that is why Labour did its legislation to repeal the Resource Management Act and do the Spatial Planning Act and the Natural and Built Environment Act, and work on an infrastructure chapter as part of that. So when the Minister says nothing has happened, it was happening.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Bishop's preceding argument — his account of a failed planning system and of nothing having been done — by contesting it with her own party's repeal legislation, and expressly concedes his point on ports and dredging. She then moves to a prepared and quite separate question on the clause 4 definition, so the engagement is partial rather than sustained.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "a sclerotic and labyrinthine planning system that has made it too hard to build houses in this country"

acuity.statement: I understand all the answers that the Minister responsible for RMA Reform gave in relation to national direction and pulling local authorities into line, and I just kind of wanted to make my question a bit more clear. In the first reading of this bill, the national policy statement (NPS) references in the bill only referred to the urban development NPS. What has happened since then is that that has been amended to include all the national policy directions, including freshwater management, indigenous biodiversity, etc. My question is: why are we expanding into those areas as well?
acuity.explanation: Classic accept-part-and-press-the-rest: she grants the Minister's answer on step-in powers and on housing, identifies precisely the part of her question his reply did not reach (the widening of scope from the urban development NPS to all national policy statements), and re-frames it more narrowly. The contribution exists only because of what he just said and could not have been delivered in any other debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it actually gives the Government quite extensive intervention powers in local authorities already"

acuity.statement: Just in relation to Rachel Brooking’s point, I’m advised that waste to energy is included as a specified energy activity only if it’s biomass to waste, if that makes sense—so “maybe” is the short answer.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question put — whether waste to energy falls within paragraph (a) of the new "specified energy activity" definition — including the qualification and a direct bottom line. Maximum responsiveness; the brevity and hedging are matters for other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "does it include waste to energy? Is he expecting that waste to energy would be included in paragraph (a) or not?"

acuity.statement: In relation to Ms Paul’s point around why we’ve expanded it, well, it’s because the Government came to the view that if it was good enough for the National Policy Statement on Urban Development (NPSUD), it should be good enough for the other suite of national directions that there are—for example, the national policy statement on renewables, which may require councils to do particular things, or it may not.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the rationale for the specific thing Paul narrowed her question to on her second attempt — the extension of the power from the NPSUD to the other national policy statements — and gives an example of another NPS it would reach. Not quite 1.0 because he does not take up the second half of her question about how local objectives in the freshwater and biodiversity space would be weighed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "why, then, are we expanding into the other areas, and what support does that give you in achieving the Government’s national objectives around resource management?"

acuity.statement: I want to continue on my colleague’s topic of fisheries, particularly when it comes to clause 8 of the bill. This is page 11 around “Section 32 amended (Requirements for preparing and publishing evaluation reports)”.
acuity.explanation: Pham follows a substantive turn by Boyack and gestures at it only by topic ("my colleague's topic of fisheries") before moving to her own prepared case for deleting clause 8. She neither supplies, disputes nor builds on Boyack's aquaculture-comparability question, so the contribution would be identical whatever Boyack had asked about fisheries. A topical hand-off is a mere reference, not engagement, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 because the gesture at the debate is explicit and she is squarely on the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Boyack asked the Minister whether RMA aquaculture regulation is comparable to the new wild-capture fishing rules, and whether the Amendment Paper differs from the select committee report, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: Further to the Minister’s insistence earlier that the reason why we are lagging in energy security and renewables—the Minister mentioned the oil and gas ban, and was quick to blame previous Governments, when this Government has failed to deliver a national policy statement for renewable electricity generation; it has failed to deliver a national energy strategy; it did throw out the Spatial Planning Act; it did throw out the Natural and Built Environment Act; and, clearly, this Government carries the blame for high electricity prices, and for the failure—the failure—to build the renewable electricity generation we need.
acuity.explanation: Willis is answering an attribution of blame for the energy shortfall by counter-listing this Government's own omissions, which is content engagement in form — but the turn he is answering is outside the supplied window, so the engagement cannot be audited against a preceding turn here, which caps the score at 0.3. Against the turns actually before him (Boyack, Pham) he takes up nothing, though he is squarely on the bill and on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: not pointable in this window: Willis reports a Minister's earlier remark on "the oil and gas ban" and blaming previous Governments, but that turn is not in the text given; the turns that do precede him here are Rachel Boyack's and Lan Pham's fisheries questions, which he does not take up

acuity.statement: Just answering some of the questions in the order they’ve come in from the member Rachel Boyack. Just confirming that the rules that control fishing—your question was is there any difference in clause 5, new section 2B versions tabled today? No, there is no difference.
acuity.explanation: She restates the specific question put to her and supplies the answer asked for: whether the new section 2B in the Amendment Paper differs from the committee's report back. This is the narrow factual confirmation the member sought, and the statement could not exist in this form if Boyack had asked something else, which is the deciding test. Scored only on engagement — the brevity and lack of detail are a specificity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there isn’t anything different between what is in the report back from the committee and what the Minister has tabled today" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: With regard to Lan Pham’s wanting to delete clause 8, no, we do not support that. The purpose of this clause is, as we have stated, to clarify and to support balanced section 32 assessments that cover both benefits and risks. This clause doesn’t enable councils to make fisheries management decisions. That is done under the Fisheries Act and therefore it doesn’t stray into the Fisheries Act purposes.
acuity.explanation: She takes up Pham's actual proposition — that the clause 8 change to section 32 assessments strays into the Fisheries Act's purpose — and contests exactly that, on the ground that the clause confers no fisheries-management power on councils. She also states a position on the amendment Pham moved. Whether the reasoning is sound or the premise true belongs to Rigor and Veracity; here the engagement is direct and pointable.

acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "what we’re really asking the regulator to do—the task here of the regulator—is an infrastructure regulation like, say, regulated airports, regulated ports"

acuity.statement: Thank you so much to the Minister for that fulsome answer; that’s really helpful. The question, then, I think remains: who is a consumer under this legislation, and how should local authorities give effect to those people who would not usually be defined as a consumer in the consumer legislation that we have? They’re not people and they’re not households; they’re industrial-sized users.
acuity.explanation: Accepts part of the Minister's answer and identifies precisely the part of her question it left unanswered, then narrows it to the specific provision. The speech would be different had Watts answered differently — it is built on what he did and did not say about who counts as a consumer. Close engagement with the content of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "that consumer in the context of water services needs to be adequately protected and treated fairly by, in effect, what will be a water services entity"

acuity.statement: The other question that was asked was in regards to “What is a consumer?”, and this was actually covered in prior parts. I acknowledge the member may have missed that earlier on, but in this context, it’s around the account holder. The account holder is, in effect, in this model, the one that is liable for water charges and is, in that context, the entity in which it’s seen as the consumer.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the definition the previous turn pressed for — the consumer is the account holder liable for water charges — which is exactly the thing asked. That directly resolves the question put, and the answer could not have been given to a different preceding turn. The barb about the member having missed it is a civility matter, not an acuity one, and does not reduce the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "who is a consumer under this legislation, and how should local authorities give effect to those people who would not usually be defined as a consumer"

acuity.statement: I hear what the Minister is saying in terms of they’ll provide financial separation between local authorities and water organisations—I think that’s really important—which will also, hopefully, encourage and support consumer trusts owned by water organisations. I guess my question here is: with that separation, one of the challenges would be that the current threshold application is not appropriate in the context of financial independence.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated ground — financial separation — accepts it, and draws out a consequence he did not address: that the existing method of calculating the civil defence reimbursement threshold may no longer be fit once the entities are financially independent of councils. That is engaging the content of the preceding answer and extending it, not merely referencing it. Short of 1.0 because it builds on rather than tests the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "there is financial separation between the new water services entities and the local authorities that previously would have had these services activities within them"

acuity.statement: The question asked was: is that going to lead to increases in pollution or other aspects? Well, the water quality standards, including the discharge standards, are set by the independent water quality regulator, so that has no consequential difference.
acuity.explanation: Watts names and takes up the specific question Brooking put — whether the new performance standards will allow more pollution — and gives a direct answer with a reason (discharge standards remain with the independent water quality regulator). The speech would clearly be different had she asked something else. It falls short of 1.0 because two other strands of her question (how Water Services Act instruments align with the RMA purpose of sustainable management, and how the two bills amending the RMA in parallel interact) are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Rachel Brooking: "Does the use of these performance standards mean that there will be more pollution?"

acuity.statement: I wanted to pick up on the Minister’s comments just then about those single set standards that sit outside of this regulation but are given effect to in Part 5, Subpart 7, and he was basically saying they’re inconsequential. Now, what we’re hearing and what we’ve heard very clearly from submissions was really quite the opposite, and I wanted to touch specifically on Selwyn District Council’s submission.
acuity.explanation: Pham restates the Minister's immediately preceding claim that the standards have "no consequential difference", contradicts precisely that proposition, and then supplies submitter evidence (Selwyn District Council, Environment Canterbury, the Christchurch plant limits) directed at it. Had Watts argued something else, this contribution would have had to change. Not 1.0 only because her characterisation of him as saying they are "inconsequential" stretches his narrower claim about discharge standards.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Simon Watts: "the water quality standards, including the discharge standards, are set by the independent water quality regulator, so that has no consequential difference"

acuity.statement: As at 9.55 p.m. yesterday evening, the Minister of Local Government dropped another amendment on the table. We thought at the time, “Well, that’s pretty unusual, having a tabled amendment dropped”—not exactly at the 11th hour; it was the 10th hour by then I suppose; we might call it that, who knows?
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one — Watts on how the design standards relate to the RMA and Pham on the leniency of the single wastewater standards — and neither is engaged in any part. Russell opens a fresh line about the timing of a tabled Amendment Paper; the words would be identical whatever had just been argued, though they are at least about the bill before the committee, so this sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham argued the proposed single wastewater performance standards are far more lenient than Environment Canterbury's current consent limits, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Well, far be it from me, Mr Chair, to cast doubt upon the role of the Minister to put the amendment in at that hour, but clarity and certainty is important and that’s what this amendment seeks to achieve, and I’m sure the member will understand the necessity for those matters.
acuity.explanation: Simpson answers the question actually put to him — he acknowledges "that hour" and offers a purpose for the amendment — so this is a genuine reply rather than prepared material. But he engages the topic more than the claim: Russell asked why the amendment had to be tabled at 9.55 p.m. mid-debate, and the reply explains what the amendment is for without addressing the timing she called extraordinary.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Deborah Russell: "could explain why we needed to have this particular tabled amendment dropped on the table at 9.55 p.m."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and I thank the Minister for his brief clarity in that regard. What I find really interesting is, at a moment when the only contributions Government members were seeking as part of committee stage were closures, they were seeking closures at the same time as this Amendment Paper was basically landing on the Table.
acuity.explanation: Utikere picks up the exchange he follows — Simpson's answer and the timing of the 9.55 p.m. Amendment Paper — and develops one strand of it by setting the tabling against the Government's closure motions. That is real engagement with the preceding turn, but he does not take on Simpson's actual justification ("clarity and certainty") and then moves to prepared material about his own Amendment Paper 342, which puts this in the partial band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Scott Simpson: "clarity and certainty is important and that’s what this amendment seeks to achieve"

acuity.statement: The proposed new standards in clause 269 will help fix that problem by prioritising clear requirements. That’s pivotal and fundamental to this new proposed legislation. So, yes, standards do vary from region to region in terms of the receiving environments. The consenting authority cannot impose requirements more or less stringent than the standards, but the consent authorities will still have to consider the impact on the receiving environment as part of the usual resource consent decision making.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Pham's questioning — whether the performance standards are set with regard to the state of the receiving environment — and gives a direct answer to it (standards vary by receiving environment; consent authorities still assess receiving-environment impact), and picks up her own 20 percent expired-consents figure. But the rest of her specific asks are left untouched: no examples of the international best practice the standards are said to rest on, no justification for new section 58JA(3) letting the standards prevail over NPSs, the coastal policy statement and regional/district plans, and no response to her proposed substitution of wording. Engages the topic and one claim, then returns to prepared material about RMA failure, so a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether they are respective or irrespective on the current state of the receiving environment" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: The Minister’s talked about an inconsistent approach to water standards, and I’m in no disagreement there. But what I’m interested in is that these standards are imported from different legislation into the RMA—into the Resource Management Act. That is what this part of Part 5 is doing: it’s importing something from waste-water legislation into the Resource Management Act.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the premise Simpson had just relied on (regional inconsistency is real) and then disputes that it answers anything, re-framing the issue as the importation of standards made under other legislation into the RMA. The contribution would have to be written differently had Simpson argued something else; it is built directly on the words he used.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The member makes cogent observations about the historic inconsistency of environmental water standards across regions" — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: We heard in the last contribution some concern that some of these standards are being created at an international level. How do we know that these international standards will be appropriate for New Zealand - specific ecology? That has not been answered—when the Minister talks about an inconsistent approach of the RMA, that’s across regions but not across different countries.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific unanswered question from the preceding exchange — the international basis of the standards — and draws out the limit of Simpson's own answer, that consistency across regions is not consistency across countries. It identifies precisely which part of the prior argument fails to reach the question, which is engagement with content rather than a mere reference to the previous speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we heard from officials during the select committee process that they were based on international best practice" — Lan Pham (which Scott Simpson's reply did not address)

acuity.statement: Just hearing the Minister’s response in terms of clarity and transparency, it is important, I think, on the basis of transparency, that the Minister consider what my colleague Lan Pham has proposed in her amendment in terms of the ability for the public to be notified of such changes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Lan Pham's immediately preceding argument — her amendment on public/limited notification — and supplies a reason (transparency) for adopting it, but does nothing with the substance of her case about regional plans or local input, and then moves straight into his own prepared questions on clauses 218/225 and new section 57AB. Partial engagement: the opening would have to change if she had argued something else, but the bulk of the speech would not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "surely it would warrant public notification so that local people actually get to input and have their say"

acuity.statement: Responding to the member’s question relating to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, I can tell the member he can be assured of the diligence and proactive attention of the Minister in relation to that. I can give that personal assurance.
acuity.explanation: Names the question put to him moments earlier but engages no part of its content: Xu-Nan asked whether the power to declare what is and is not a water service sits with the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and the Commerce Commission rather than under local government. The reply offers an assurance about the Minister's diligence, which would read identically whatever the question had been about that portfolio. A mere reference, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "is what we’re seeing here that the secondary legislation of determining or declaring a water service is not done under the local government but done by the commerce Minister and the Commerce Commission?"

acuity.statement: Lan Pham asked some questions that relate to different receiving environments, and the point I would make in response to her line of questioning is that there are seven kinds of receiving environmental processes provided for in discharge to water standards, and different regions will, as I mentioned earlier, differ from one to another.
acuity.explanation: Goes to the specific thing Lan Pham asked — how regional variation can sit inside a national standard — and supplies substance in answer: seven kinds of receiving environment are provided for, and regions differ. It does not reach her sharper sub-question about whether there is a formula and how it maps to distinct ecosystems, so the engagement is direct but incomplete rather than complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "Is there literally a regional formula? How would that actually apply versus the actual different ecosystems and different environments that these discharges are actually going into?"

acuity.statement: Now, the improvement of water services is quite different from the improvement of water quality from the receiving environment.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-delivered justification — that the provisions serve this bill's purpose of progressively improving the quality of water services — and drives a distinction through it, arguing that improving water services is not the same as improving water quality in the receiving environment, and so asks whether the controls on a discharge to a river or the coast rest on the RMA's Part 2 sustainable management purpose instead. The speech is unrecognisable if the Minister had grounded the provisions in anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "the relevant purpose in providing for this piece of legislation is for the progressive improvement of quality of water services, and that is the nub of it"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I think that while the Minister in the chair, the Hon Scott Simpson, is getting some advice, I just want to touch on a few additional points here. The first one is clause 269 inserting new sections 58JA to 58JC. One of the things that I’m interested in—and again, just for the Minister’s sake and also clarity, the things that I’m looking for and have questions for the Minister on by and large refer to the new amendment that has been released post - select committee, which is an Amendment Paper from the Minister of Local Government, Amendment Paper 346.
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn was Utikere's set of questions on clauses 307A and 308C. Xu-Nan engages no part of them, explicitly framing his contribution as 'a few additional points' and moving to his own prepared list of clauses under Amendment Paper 346. It stays squarely on the matter under debate (the same committee-stage bill), which keeps it above the floor, but the speech would read identically whatever Utikere had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere asked the Minister about clause 307A's list of drinking-water suppliers and about public notification of contamination under clause 308C, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Tangi Utikere asks a question about, “Why list some drinking water suppliers?” I think that was in particular reference to clause 307A. I’m advised that the provision limits application of information and related powers to limited categories of drinking-water suppliers to ensure any burden is proportionate to the risks and the costs. Again, it’s a balancing proportional test, which I think, under the circumstances, is appropriate.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question put by the preceding speaker — why clause 307A enumerates categories of drinking-water supplier rather than referring to suppliers generally — identifies the clause correctly, and supplies the rationale (proportionality of burden to risk and cost). The answer would be different had Utikere asked something else. Marked slightly below 1.0 only because the reason given is asserted rather than tied back to subsection (3), which was the pivot of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "is there actually a requirement to list those; and why not just leave it as, actually, a drinking-water supplier?"

acuity.statement: But that doesn’t answer my question to the Minister, which is: is there anything, then, in the Water Services Act around what the quality of a water service is defined as, or in the provisions of the Act, which I don’t have in front of me, that relates to improving the environment, so improving the environmental quality—so the quality of the receiving environment, be it the river, the coastal environment, whatever it is? Is there any requirement to improve that quality, rather than the quality of the water service? Can the Minister understand the distinction that I’m making here between a water service and the receiving environment?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer, restates its content accurately, and shows precisely where it falls short — that 'quality of water services' is not the same thing as quality of the receiving environment. The whole statement is built out of the preceding turn and could not have been delivered had he answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "a relevant purpose is providing for progressive improvement of quality of water services, and then usual Resource Management Act considerations will apply through the consent process"

acuity.statement: The member Rachel Brooking has asked the question three times now. I’ve given two answers and I’m not intending to give it a third time, but I think that the previous answers that I’ve given make it clear that there is a requirement for environmental improvement. That’s the whole purpose of not only this piece of legislation but a variety of other pieces of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — it asserts an answer to her actual question, that a requirement for environmental improvement exists — but declines to take up the distinction she drew between the quality of a water service and the quality of the receiving environment, which was the entire point of the question. A partial engagement that then falls back on the fact of having answered before rather than on the substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Is there any requirement to improve that quality, rather than the quality of the water service?"

acuity.statement: I want to turn to the question specifically that the member Lawrence Xu-Nan asked, which was in relation to when a water service is and is not a water service—clause 57(2)(a) and (b). I’d simply respond by saying that it allows flexibility, given the developing nature of New Zealand’s water services. So, again, it’s part of the ongoing development of the water services regime.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific point Xu-Nan pressed for a response on and gives a reason for the drafting — that the dual characterisation is deliberate, to allow flexibility in a developing regime. The engagement is squarely aimed; the thinness of the reason is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "around this interesting case of a Schrödinger declaration, where water service is both a water service and not a water service, potentially at the same time"

The reply would not exist, and could not stand, if the preceding question had been about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Rachel Brooking: "Was it proactively raised by the Minister?"

acuity.statement: I just want to make it clear to the member, and also to members of this committee, that clause 347(3) is being deleted because it refers to section 148 of the Local Government Act 2002, which is actually being repealed by Schedule 12. Now, the role of the Minister of Health is transferred to the Water Services Authority as the drinking-water quality regulator, and section 148, which requires by-laws to be sent to the Minister of Health, is therefore not required.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked why the Minister was deleting the consultation timeframe in clause 347(3), and whether the requirement sat somewhere else. Simpson answers that exact question at the clause level: the subclause goes because the section of the Local Government Act it cross-refers to is repealed and the Minister of Health's role passes to the Water Services Authority. Substitute a different objection and this answer would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "And so my question for the Minister is: why is he seeking to remove that time?"

acuity.statement: It’s good to have that explanation from the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs. Of course, it would be a much simpler process if when Ministers put little amendments on the Table at 9.55 p.m. at night that they tell the committee about what they're doing and even why they're doing it—imagine that!
acuity.explanation: Takes up Simpson's explanation directly — accepts it as an explanation, then disputes the part it does not answer, namely that the committee had to extract it rather than be told. She then turns to her own prepared material on clause 347(1)(d), which keeps this short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Scott Simpson: "That’s an explanation of the Amendment Paper that was produced last night."

acuity.statement: That's nice to say that in the House, we are still in Wednesday. That does not detract from the fact that it was at 9.55 p.m. on Wednesday night that a very small Amendment Paper was put on the Table and nothing was said about it until the next session, which we are in now, when we had to raise it as a topic, which seems a very bad way to make laws.
acuity.explanation: Luxton's interjection corrected her 'last night' with the extended-sitting convention that the House is still on Wednesday. That is engaging the content of the interjection rather than brushing past it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "In the House we are."

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson said of clause 347(1)(d) that "it provides that they can impose requirements on private landowners" and this statement does not take it up

The speech would be entirely different had Xu-Nan asked something else; it is wholly shaped by the preceding turn. (Whether the answer is correct is a veracity matter and whether 'clarity' is detailed enough is specificity — neither moves this score.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "would that then apply to other areas whereby the enforcement of such collection of fines can only be limited to that particular by-law jurisdiction, or can it be expanded more broadly nationally?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just want to remind the committee that the Minister in charge of this bill put an Amendment Paper on the Table at the start of committee stage.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn was the Minister's answer on the jurisdictional reach of clause 357 infringement offences. Russell engages no part of it, instead opening prepared material on clause 374 and the Māori land definitions in the Amendment Paper. It is on the bill before the committee, so it is not entirely unresponsive to the debate, but there is nothing in it that would have had to change had the Minister's clause 357 answer been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson explained that "clause 357 is limited to those water by-laws; it doesn’t extend beyond the water by-laws" and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: The short answer to the member’s question is that it’s simply to provide clarity and certainty.
acuity.explanation: Russell asked specifically what the policy thinking was behind the additional paragraphs inserted into clause 374(6) of the Amendment Paper. This answers that exact question — the purpose was clarity and certainty — rather than pivoting to prepared material or to Labour's record. It is a thin answer, but thinness is a specificity failing, not a responsiveness one; the reply is unmistakably shaped by the question just put and would be different had Russell asked something else. Held just below 1.0 because it does not engage her further challenge about whether the added text actually does any legal work.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Just if the Minister could clarify what the policy thinking was behind that."

acuity.explanation: Brooking's preceding turn put a specific question about the link between the enforcement provisions and the power to shut off water. Xu-Nan engages no part of it and proceeds to his own prepared thematic questions on mens rea in clauses 394, 396 and 403. The speech sits in the band for prepared material that is at least on the matter under debate — it is squarely about the Part 6 offence provisions — so 0.3 rather than lower, but nothing in it would change had Brooking said something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking asked whether a breach of a by-law lets a water services provider turn off a property's water supply, and this statement does not take that up

There is a provision, at clause 178A, that a water service provider must provide necessary water in “a sufficient quantity” to, for instance, provide for sanitation.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific question and supplies the provision she asked for, naming clause 178A and the "sufficient quantity" obligation, then draws out the consequence that flow can be dialled back but not cut below sanitation needs. The content of the answer is wholly determined by what she asked; had she raised a different point the passage could not stand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "I was wondering if there is any link into this part of the bill about that ability to turn off the water source for a breach of a by-law"

Is that ability fettered by the clause that you just mentioned, in that there must always be this provision for the good sanitary provision?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of Simpson's answer that holds, then does something with the specific clause he had just cited — asks whether that sufficiency duty fetters the separate by-law shut-off power. The question is built directly on the provision he named and could not have been framed without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "There is a provision, at clause 178A, that a water service provider must provide necessary water in "a sufficient quantity""

acuity.explanation: A bare affirmative, but it answers precisely the question put — whether the shut-off power is constrained by the sufficiency clause — rather than pivoting away. Marginally short of 1.0 only because it engages the question without engaging its reasoning; brevity and vagueness of this kind belong to Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Is that ability fettered by the clause that you just mentioned"

acuity.statement: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan asked about existing protections against incrimination—whether they continue to apply—and the answer to that question is yes. Without getting into a protracted discussion of the fundamentals of mens rea and legal principles involved, I think he can rest assured that those principles apply.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of the question — mens rea principles — and gives an assurance that they continue to apply, but recasts what was asked as a question about protections against self-incrimination, which is not what Xu-Nan put, and leaves the second question (an example of strict or limited liability for an individual under clauses 395(2)(a), 397(2)(a) and 404(2)(a)) untouched. That is partial engagement on the subject rather than on the specific claims, so mid-band and below 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "subclause (b) conflates three very different areas of mens rea—intention, knowledge, and recklessness"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Minister, for that clarification. That was very helpful. I want to focus on the next section, which is clause 421, and this is serious, but it’s also really interesting that there is a section in here on that in terms of assault.
acuity.explanation: Polite acceptance of the Minister's assurance followed by a move to prepared material on the next clause. He does not test, dispute or build on what Simpson actually said, despite the answer having sidestepped one of his two questions. On the matter under debate and so in the 0.1–0.3 band at its top, not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "I think he can rest assured that those principles apply" — acknowledged but not taken up

acuity.statement: I just want to confirm for the member that provisions of this sort that provide protections for enforcement officers and agencies are pretty standard in legislation that is widely used by the New Zealand Parliament. So this is not an unusual provision from that regard; to have those specific offences when undertaking compliance roles is common—not unusual, not weird, strange, or odd in any way. And it is separate from general assault offences.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put: the clause 421 offence is separate from general assault offences under the Crimes Act, such provisions are standard, and the choice of charge is a prosecutorial matter rather than one the legislature settles. Short of 1.0 because the related strand — why the maximum here is a $50,000 fine against three years' imprisonment for assault with intent to injure — is addressed only by implication.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Are those two going to be separate charges that are going to be placed on the individual, and if not, what then prevails?"

acuity.statement: Then we go to Lan Pham’s suggestion, which was—I didn’t catch it all—“Again Deprioritising the Community and Ecosystem Health”. This is a very good point because what this bill does—and it’s not in the title at all, we can’t see it; we just see “water services” and “local government”; there is nothing about the Resource Management Act (RMA) and the further degradation of the environment that this Government seems intent on doing with every bill that seems to come in front of this House.
acuity.explanation: Brooking takes up the specific amendment Lan Pham had just proposed in the immediately preceding turn — that the title should record the deprioritising of community and ecosystem health — restates it, endorses the reasoning, and extends it with her own material on standards being imported into the RMA without assurance they meet sustainable management. The speech would have had to be different had Pham argued something else about the title; it is built on her amendment rather than merely name-checking it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "My proposal to adequately capture what this bill is doing is in my tabled amendment to change clause 1, where we would call this bill the “Local Government (Perpetually Deprioritising Community and Ecosystem Health Water Services) Bill”."

acuity.statement: So in speaking to the title of this bill and speaking to the failure of this bill to address the fundamental challenges we have in terms of local communities’ access to safe and uncontaminated drinking water, I want to acknowledge that the Minister refused the option for an amendment that ensured an equality of access to water. That has fundamentally disadvantaged our rural people more than any, because most New Zealanders, 80 percent of New Zealanders, have access to drinking water that is about 1 or lower milligrams per litre of nitrate—and that’s a safe level of nitrate to be in water. But 800,000 New Zealanders are exposed to potentially hazardous levels of nitrate in their drinking water, and they are mostly in rural New Zealand.

When we’re developing infrastructure, we need the certainty that there will be some cross-bipartisan agreement at least. None of this committee has done this with any sort of light-heartedness. Her reply that the committee took its work seriously and did an excellent job would be word-for-word unchanged whichever critique had preceded it, so this is a mere reference plus prepared commendation — the 0.1–0.3 band — rather than partial engagement. 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the one gesture (acknowledging the cross-House support Bennett had just offered) is pointable.

acuity.responding_to: "that’s why it is important for us to cautiously support this legislation—so that things can continue to move forward" — Glen Bennett

As the member Hūhana Lyndon said, it’s a Government that actually has as one of its centrepieces the protection of private property, and yet here this bill—which we support—is in fact undermining private property rights for the benefit of the State.
acuity.explanation: Webb picks up the same earlier critique Bidois had just been answering, but a different strand of it — the tension between the Government's stated defence of private property and a bill that overrides property rights — and develops it rather than restating it. He does not, however, take up Bidois's own claims (the Māori-land exemption, the "country of no" framing), and the strand he engages was put by a speaker before the window, so engagement is partial rather than direct take-up of the preceding turn.

acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "To address the previous speaker Hūhana Lyndon’s concerns, protected Māori land is actually exempted from this process."

A gesture at the debate on the right subject, so the upper end of the 0.1–0.3 band.

acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "But, anyway, it’s a bill that does more good than harm, and in that case, if it makes New Zealand better for most New Zealanders, we’ll be supporting it on that basis."

I look forward to conversing about the pros, and maybe there might be some cons, in the Justice Committee, one that I’m very privileged and honoured to be part of—a very hard-working committee.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown asked the Minister to respond to whether removing same-day enrolment contradicts this bill, and Todd Stephenson and Andy Foster disputed her on it, and this statement does not take any of it up.

The many points that many members from across this House have made—I’m looking forward to fleshing those out through the select committee process and receiving the submissions to the Justice Committee as well.

acuity.statement: It may be small, it may seem like just a practical piece of work that we’re doing that makes sense, but the challenge I want to put to the Government and to the Minister is that that democracy is under threat around the world and also in New Zealand, and there is a need to protect democracy and people’s faith in democracy.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — substantive turns by Walters and Rutherford precede it. Bennett expressly declines to engage the bill's content ('I won't really go into it, actually, because it has been traversed'), and his argument for a six-month committee period is aimed at the Minister's reporting motion rather than at anything the two preceding members said. That is prepared material on the right subject with a real gesture at the debate in progress, which sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific in the preceding turns: Tom Rutherford said he was 'looking forward to fleshing those out through the select committee process', and Bennett does not take up his point or Walters' caretaker-provisions argument. He instead contests the Minister's four-months-and-one-day reporting motion, whose turn is not among the preceding turns given.

I actually think that these changes have been thought about for many terms prior to now.

Naming that the bill 'has already been traversed by numerous speakers' is a reference to the debate, not engagement with any claim in it. On-topic prepared closing remarks, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued a four-month reporting period sends the wrong signal and that the select committee process must be visibly open so 'faith in democracy is protected', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.explanation: Goes directly at the content of Hipkins' earlier supplementary, taking the $300 million figure and disputing the causal story behind it — that a fall in excise revenue from reduced tobacco sales is not a tax cut handed to tobacco companies. acuity.responding_to: But it also would seek to clarify the role that pedestrians, or those who might be classified as pedestrians, are able to utilise in some of the spaces on the roading network. — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: And what we’ve just heard from that Government Minister, the Hon Casey Costello, is a very clear indication and message to households all around the country that it is coming your way; it is coming your way: the increase in costs that households can expect to receive.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker and gestures at her speech, but engages no part of her actual argument — Costello argued costs must be met fairly, that growth should pay for growth, that borrowing spreads cost equitably, and that Auckland water charges were curbed. None of that is taken up; the reply simply asserts the opposite conclusion. A mere reference to the previous speaker, which the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band.

acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "Growth should pay for growth, and appropriate levels of borrowing will allow costs to be spread equitably between current and future ratepayers."

There is no adequate financial support for the changes that this Government is seeking to implement to support households through what is a difficult time now and what will be a difficult time in the future under these reforms initiated by this Government.
acuity.explanation: Lands on the same proposition Costello devoted a paragraph to — whether councils get the financial support to fund this investment — and denies it, so the speech is at least pointed at a claim she made. Instead, actually, what we’re seeing are councils all around this country opt out of a regional opportunity; or the other side of that is that they are left as orphan councils, because they have no other opportunity.

What is also really interesting is that I find it interesting when the member on the left decides to use Māori words like takiwā—no other side of that does he use Māori words in any other way, but suddenly, when he wants to damn an idea, he uses our reo, te reo Māori.

Scored on engagement alone — the hostility and the racism charge belong to Civility, not here.

acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "Isn't it great to get rid of co-governance from this piece of legislation? Get rid of it!" and "We do not want takiwā boundaries, like we had in Marlborough, which was absolutely nonsense."

But it leaves the specific objections untouched: the removal of the adverse-effects objective, the single national standards overriding stricter local rules, and the prohibition on notification. Partial engagement with the topic rather than with the claims.

acuity.responding_to: "the Government constantly reiterates this misguided, ill-informed myth that the Government is somehow better placed to make decisions that should stay with local government" — Lan Pham
