Cameron names the charge Genter actually made and disputes it directly, and earlier in the same turn he attempts a counter (Indonesian coal imports feeding the grid, so electrification also has an end-user pollution problem) aimed at that characterisation. That is genuine engagement with something said, and it is pointable. But it takes up only the climate-denier epithet — one strand, and the rhetorical one — leaving untouched Genter's substantive arguments that the standard and the feebate were designed to work together, that EVs are more efficient regardless of generation source, and that the bill makes the targets harder to hit. Partial engagement that answers the characterisation rather than the policy claim, so ~0.5. Scored on engagement alone: the quality of the coal counter-argument belongs to Rigor and the politeness of the disagreement to Civility, and neither moved this score.

acuity.responding_to: "But this is a Government of absolute climate deniers who can’t even understand how the economy works." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "Statistics New Zealand figures just out show that emissions in New Zealand decreased to December last year by 1 percent—total greenhouse emissions... something is working in the coalition Government with respect to emissions."

acuity.responding_to: Carlos Cheung: "For communities like Mt Roskill, home to many hard-working families, this bill matters." — and his interjection "You are here to advocate for people in South Auckland."

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "all families who meet those criteria have indeed got a rebate of $250"

acuity.statement: Well, when you go back and check the Hansard, you'll see that the word “maximum” wasn't used in her earlier questions; she's inserted that later. I can confirm that more than 60,000 families have received their full entitlement for the FamilyBoost payment.
acuity.explanation: Disputes a specific factual claim about what was asked and offers a checkable figure in reply; it engages the exchange closely, though the figure answers a different question from the one pressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "153 was the number that the Minister of Finance reported at select committee"

acuity.statement: I would refer members of the public who may be watching along at home to the official information and advice that was given to the Government about the impacts of the decisions that they were intending to make, because, in fact, the information is objective and it is clear.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Willis's specific move of reducing the criticism to a partisan 'characterisation' and answers it directly: the source is official advice to the Government, which is objective rather than a Green framing. The reply would have to be different if Willis had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'd just simply call that the Green Party's characterisations of the Government's policies" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I reject the member’s characterisation, because, actually, I believe that this Government is pursuing policies that will deliver better housing affordability and less homelessness, in particular because we have the courage to address the underlying driver of unaffordable house prices in this country, which is restrictive green and red tape primarily through the Resource Management Act, which we are replacing—also because we are advancing the fast track regime, which will see subdivisions that that member would say no to go ahead, meaning more housing supply for the country.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific harms Swarbrick's advice-based critique alleged (housing affordability, homelessness) and contests them with named mechanisms — RMA replacement and fast track. Engagement is squarely with the content of the preceding claim, whatever one thinks of the inference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the decisions it intends to make will do all of those negative things for our country and for our society" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: To the member’s question about cuts, I’d just remind her that we are running a deficit this year of $12 billion, which is one of the largest deficits of countries in the OECD and reflects the fact that the Government is taking a gradual path to fiscal consolidation, in which we are continuing to increase spending in health, in education, in law and order, and in critical public services because we think it’s the right thing to do for Kiwi households, businesses, and the economy as a whole.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the topic of cuts and names it explicitly, but answers with the fiscal position rather than the question actually put — what long-term cost analysis was undertaken. One strand engaged, then prepared fiscal material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what analysis, if any, did she decide to undertake ... on the costs in the long term of all of these cuts to social service provision?" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: The Minister herself—and I’m sure this House and members of the public will be aware that the Government is currently being sued over its Emissions Reduction Plan because it’s not actually worth the paper that it is written on.
acuity.explanation: Targets the exact claim Willis had just made about the Emissions Reduction Plan and attacks its standing with a specific counter — that the plan is the subject of litigation. The speech is wholly shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we've presented a thoughtful Emissions Reduction Plan which shows us achieving our zero carbon targets" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: In terms of the specific question that she has asked, look, the Estimates clearly show that we are not forecasting spending billions of dollars offshore to meet the Nationally Determined Contributions, which James Shaw signed us up to.
acuity.explanation: Supplies an answer to the precise thing asked — whether offshore mitigation for the NDC is budgeted — by pointing at what the Estimates show. Falls short of 1.0 because it does not engage the second limb about reduced onshore investment raising that cost.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is the Minister going to be budgeting for ... meeting our Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement, particularly ... for offshore mitigation" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: Just one question to the Minister of Finance based on her last comment: what is the average time in New Zealand for a new oil and gas field to come into production?
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the premise of the answer just given and probes the one fact that tests it — field lead times. The question could not exist without the preceding turn, and it is explicitly built on it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'd love to wind back time and not ban oil and gas, as Jacinda Ardern and the Greens did—that would be a better position" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Off the top of my head, it can take up to six years, which imagine if they hadn’t banned it—we’d have some new ones on score by now.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the figure asked for and immediately turns it back on the questioner's implied point. Direct engagement with the specific question rather than a pivot away from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the average time in New Zealand for a new oil and gas field to come into production?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Could it also be the case that, if you knock the stuffing out of an industry, the skilled people leave and the ability to keep production up is reduced in the short term?
acuity.explanation: Takes the lead-time exchange just had and draws out a further consequence — loss of skilled labour compressing short-run production. It builds on the specific strand under discussion rather than restating a position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the average time in New Zealand for a new oil and gas field to come into production?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Well, the member makes a good point, but the broader point here is that we have these tears on the other side of the Chamber about how long it’s going to take to find gas, which has half the emissions of coal, when they’re the ones that banned the gas exploration in the first place.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges Seymour's point but does nothing with it, pivoting instead to the opposition's record on the ban. It stays on the strand under debate, which keeps it above the bottom band, but the substance of the point raised is not developed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if you knock the stuffing out of an industry, the skilled people leave" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: But what I would like to ask the Minister is how much money was invested in existing New Zealand oil and gas fields between 2018 and 2023, since the Minister is talking about there being capital flight in her comments.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the capital-flight premise just advanced and asks for the investment figures that would test it over the exact period in question. The question is built on the preceding claim and would change if that claim changed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if you knock the stuffing out of an industry, the skilled people leave and the ability to keep production up is reduced" — David Seymour, taken up by Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, I didn't take advice on this matter because, due to the management of conflicts of interest and in alignment with the Cabinet Manual, I was not involved in Cabinet discussions relating to this matter.
acuity.explanation: Answers the 'did you take advice' limb squarely and gives the reason. The comparative-investment limb of the question goes unaddressed, so the engagement is real but partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did she take advice on the level of investment that happened between 2018 and 2023" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: It felt appropriate to respond, given that the Minister, in attempting to answer my questions, threw back some quite nasty stuff. So I just want to make it crystal clear that genocide is a biodiversity and climate disaster—in fact, more military intervention and more war results in all the more climate-changing emissions, which result in an all the more unlivable planet for everybody, including New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific jibe Willis made about her priorities and answers its substance by linking military conflict to emissions, rather than merely objecting to the tone. The content of the preceding remark determines what is said here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Normally, Palestine is what gets her more passionate" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: To the point that is being heckled at me right now, I have put multiple Official Information Act requests, parliamentary written questions and oral questions—both to Minister Todd McClay and to the Prime Minister—asking for any clear and explicit evidence that it is not a subsidy.
acuity.explanation: Picks up an interjection made seconds earlier and meets it on its own ground, describing the attempts made to obtain evidence for exactly that proposition and demanding it be produced. Maximally shaped by what immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's not a subsidy—co-investment" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: Can I just sincerely say to the member that when it comes to the situation in Gaza, I think we can both agree that we are both equally appalled by the loss of life and the devastating events that are occurring there. For me, it's more about children dying than biodiversity, but I think we can both agree that we're both concerned by that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Swarbrick's specific framing of genocide as a biodiversity matter, accepts the shared concern and disputes the framing by relocating the harm to children. Direct engagement with the content of the previous turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "genocide is a biodiversity and climate disaster" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: No, it doesn’t say that, and I congratulate the member on catching up with a report that was first released around, I think, a month ago. What that report does is look 15 years ahead.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question put directly, denies the reading of the quoted Treasury passage, and contests it with a specific property of the document — its 15-year horizon. Squarely engaged with the particular claim rather than the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does this not explicitly say that she plans to degrade services in health and education?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Because the World Trade Organization defines a “subsidy”, effectively, as a form of investment, whether that be co-investment or just taxpayer money being used and put into something that the private sector would not do by itself. By that definition, this is a subsidy.
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just asserted flatly that a Crown commercial stake cannot be a subsidy. Swarbrick takes that exact assertion, asks for the evidential basis behind it, and supplies a competing definition under which it is a subsidy. The speech would be different had he said something else — it is built on his claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is not a subsidy, and it cannot be a subsidy if the Government has a commercial stake in a field." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Sure, I’m happy to address that. It’s a good question from the member. As I think the member well knows, the Government doesn’t release privileged legal advice as a matter of course, so we won’t be doing that.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the question put — whether he has seen or will engage with the commissioned KC advice — by stating the Government will not release privileged advice, then reasons the subsidy point out by analogy (Meridian, Genesis, Kānoa). Not full marks because he engages the general concept of subsidy rather than the ACCTS definition she asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether he’s engaged in or looked at the independent King’s Counsel advice that we commissioned, in order to get some clarity around this definition of subsidy?" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: Just further to that point, if I may, Madam Chair, I just want to be crystal clear with the Minister that this is not a matter of my personal opinion. This is about the definition of what is considered a fossil fuel subsidy under the Agreement on Climate Change, Trade, and Sustainability (ACCTS).
acuity.explanation: Corrects the precise move Bishop had just made — recasting her argument as a personal dislike of gas — and re-anchors the exchange on the treaty text, then quotes the specific article and applies its two limbs to his policy. Entirely shaped by what he had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know the member doesn’t like gas, but she needs to divorce her views on gas from the basic—" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: The Government remains really confident in its view that it is not. I know the member has legal advice to the contrary, but, respectfully, we disagree.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges her legal advice and takes up one strand — distinguishing a payment to induce activity from a commercial co-investment — but does not engage the article 4.3(2)(b)(i) test she had just set out limb by limb, instead restating his earlier position and noting disagreement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is a subsidy per article 4.3(2)(b)(i)" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: So the answer to the member’s questions is yes, this Budget is absolutely about delivering better outcomes for Māori, alongside all New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Answers the strand asking what the Government's settings are, listing education, health, Investment Boost and KiwiSaver initiatives, but engages none of the specific figures Waititi put — the widened mortality gap, the $110 million cut, 0.2 percent of the Budget, or 10 percent Māori unemployment. Topic engaged, claims not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just want to ask the Government: have you got specific, targeted funding to improve these statistics?" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: Specifically, what is her plan for the 19,842 more 15- to 24-year-olds who no longer are in work?
acuity.explanation: Willis had just made a specific comparative claim — that PREFU forecast higher unemployment than has actually occurred. Andersen does not take up the forecast comparison at all, but she stays squarely on the unemployment numbers and narrows to a demographic within them, so she engages the topic rather than the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "those numbers are higher than what has occurred under this Government" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: It’s of concern to this Government to see any young person unemployed and on a benefit, because it’s our view that every young person who cannot find a job should take up the State’s generous provision of taxpayer-funded education that is available to them in the tertiary education system. When it comes to those aged 15, 16, and 17, they should be at school.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact demographic put to her and works through it age band by age band (15-17 at school, older into tertiary, 18-19 benefit testing). The answer would be different if a different cohort had been raised; it stops short of 1.0 only because no 'plan' for the 19,842 already out of work is supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my question is specific to the 19,842 more young people who no longer have work" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I’m just interested in her views on workers falling behind in terms of the cost of living.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line on wages and administered costs without touching any part of the youth-unemployment and tertiary-education answer just given. It is on the broad matter before the committee, which keeps it out of 0.0, but it engages nothing that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willis set out her policy for 18- and 19-year-olds' Jobseeker eligibility and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: My response to those families is that this Government is working hard every day to get on top of the cost of living for you. That is why we are so focused on strengthening the fundamentals of this economy, because we understand that, when inflation is allowed to get out of control, that drives price increases across the economy that affect every family.
acuity.explanation: Answers the topic — cost of living for working families — and later picks up the wage-growth strand via Investment Boost, but leaves untouched the specific figures put to her (1.5 percent wage growth against 2.7 percent inflation, 10 percent administered inflation) and reverts to general inflation-targeting material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we have approximately a 10 percent increase in administrative inflation" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Does she accept that administered inflation last month hitting 10.8 percent has been done under her watch?
acuity.explanation: Presses the one strand Willis's answer avoided: Willis answered on the headline inflation target, and Andersen re-puts administered inflation specifically and attaches responsibility to it. Partial engagement — it largely re-asks her own prior question rather than rebutting the inflation-target reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s why we target an inflation rate of 2 percent" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: As I traversed in question time today, the biggest rise in administered costs is rates rises, and, actually, the decisions that individual councils make to increase their rates are their decisions. So, no, I don’t take responsibility, for example, for Wellington City Council’s rates increase, because, if I were leading that council, it would be a lot more careful with its money, which is why the Government is looking into our ability to, through legislation and policy, have a little bit more influence on the rates that councils levy.
acuity.explanation: Engages the administered-cost claim directly, decomposes it to identify rates as the largest component, and answers the responsibility question put to her with an explicit 'no' plus a reason. The answer is specific to the claim made rather than reusable prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does she accept that all of those increased fees and levies have gone up under her watch" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Does she stand by her pre-election promise that National will co-invest in water infrastructure?
acuity.explanation: Willis had just pushed rates rises onto councils; the water co-investment question bears on that defence because withdrawal of co-funding feeds rates, but Andersen does not make the connection explicit and instead returns to a point from her own earlier question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the decisions that individual councils make to increase their rates are their decisions" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, we already are. The Regional Infrastructure Fund, under Shane Jones’ watch, is investing in stopbanks and all sorts of protections for flooding and the like.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question squarely in its own terms — asserts the co-investment is already happening and names the vehicle — though the instances given (stopbanks, flood protection) sit beside rather than inside the water-infrastructure commitment asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does she stand by her pre-election promise that National will co-invest in water infrastructure?" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Well, we fully expect and expected that there will be claims made under the new pay equity regime, and such was the completeness of that expectation that I, in this Budget, have put aside funds in contingency needed to address future claims.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand — whether the low number of claims was intended — by asserting claims were expected and provisioned for. It leaves untouched the officials' warnings about unintended consequences and the Seymour quotation that framed the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "was that an unintended consequence or an intended consequence" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: I’ve heard some other supportive commentary around that during the week and taking that even further, but could you give us your thinking behind why it’s important that we grow our savings pool in this country?
acuity.explanation: A friendly invitation to expand on KiwiSaver that engages no part of the pay equity exchange immediately before it; its reference point is an answer given earlier in the day, not anything in the turns it follows. On the matter before the committee, so not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willis's preceding answer was about pay equity claims and Budget contingency funding, and this question does not take it up

acuity.statement: It is the case that, when people contribute more to their KiwiSaver fund, that accumulates massively over time and can afford them a high living standard in retirement. It’s also the case that countries that have private pension schemes of that sort have more capital available to be deployed in those economies.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what was asked for — the reasoning behind growing the savings pool — in two distinct limbs (retirement incomes and domestic capital availability), and goes on to the New Zealand investment share. Responsive to the specific question rather than to the topic generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "could you give us your thinking behind why it’s important that we grow our savings pool in this country" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: That doesn’t relate to the Estimates debate, so I haven’t come with the appropriate material to respond to that question.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the question put to her and gives a reason specific to it — scope and lack of material — so she is not ignoring it, but she engages none of its content (the 24 February advice, the select committee report).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does she stand by those statements?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Well, it is simply the case that when the Government negotiates contracts with service providers, all sorts of factors go into the final price that the Government pays.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the subject of the question — why funded-sector prices might differ — but supplies no answer to the 'if so, how' that was pressed twice, offering a general proposition about contracting instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how does she justify that there could be a difference in those cost pressures" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Would she then expect that there would be modelling to be able to show—and evidence—what the difference in the cost pressures would be to justify the difference in uplifts?
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the answer just given: if 'all sorts of factors' set the price, she asks what modelling demonstrates them. The question could not have been framed this way had Willis answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "all sorts of factors go into the final price that the Government pays" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, look, I think that these questions relate more specifically to Vote health, which the member in this Estimates debate will have the opportunity to address with the appropriate Minister. But what I’d say is that it’s been the practice of successive Governments that we don’t reveal information that would prejudice the Crown’s commercial position.
acuity.explanation: Partly engaged: she deflects the line to another vote, but then gives a reason addressed to the actual request — that such information would prejudice the Crown's commercial position — rather than simply declining.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Would she then expect that there would be modelling" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Would it be her expectation that the Minister in charge would have access to that modelling?
acuity.explanation: Reframes around the deflection just made: if the health Minister is the right person, she asks whether that Minister would hold the modelling. The question is shaped by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "these questions relate more specifically to Vote health" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, I don’t know what modelling the member is referring to; what I can say is that the overall funding uplift we provided for health was based on Treasury modelling about demographics and inflation.
acuity.explanation: Engages the modelling question head-on — disputes that the referenced modelling is identified, then names the modelling that did inform the uplift. It then pivots to a comparison with Labour's fiscal plan, which is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s important to understand what level of evidence and modelling the Minister would find acceptable" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Just going back to the Minister of Finance’s response in relation to my question of whether she stands by her statement that she was advised on 24 February by the Secretary to the Treasury that employment discussions had commenced between Adrian Orr and the Reserve Bank board, I just want to confirm from the Minister: is it that she’s not prepared to answer that question or she has not prepared to answer that question, given that this is on page 5 of the select committee report?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the precise wording of Willis's refusal and turns it into an either/or she must choose between, while contesting the scope objection by pointing at the page of the select committee report. Tightly shaped by the answer it responds to.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I haven’t come with the appropriate material to respond to that question" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Look, it’s simply that I want to give an accurate answer. The member’s put the question on notice, and I’m happy to address it when I can do so accurately.
acuity.explanation: Answers the either/or put to her by choosing a third characterisation and explaining it, and addresses the status of the question. Responsive to the specific challenge rather than restating the earlier refusal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is it that she’s not prepared to answer that question or she has not prepared to answer that question" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Does the Minister have any plans to address the pay for care and support workers, given that she cancelled their claim and made it so they are unable to raise another claim until 2026, given that many of them are on the minimum wage now during a cost of living crisis?
acuity.explanation: Counters Willis's earlier assertion that claims are expected under the new regime by naming a workforce that is barred from claiming until 2026. It engages a turn from earlier in the debate rather than the Reserve Bank exchange it immediately follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we fully expect and expected that there will be claims made under the new pay equity regime" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Well, care and support workers, as with any workforce group, if they meet the criteria of the pay equity regime—which is a legal judgment and not a judgment for me to make—would be able to put forward a pay equity claim.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the named workforce and the question of whether they can claim, and adds who makes that determination — but does not engage the specific obstacle put to her, that their claim was cancelled and none can be raised until 2026.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "she cancelled their claim and made it so they are unable to raise another claim until 2026" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: No, but I would observe that, across the economy, Australia is a wealthier economy that has grown faster than New Zealand for some years, which means it is in a position to pay its people more across many professions. That’s why I have an aspiration to grow this economy faster, to have a more productive economy that can afford to pay its workers more. It’s simply the case that wealthier countries pay their workers more. That’s exactly why I want this to be a wealthier country.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question put squarely ("No") and then takes up the specific premise of the question — the New Zealand/Australia wage differential Leary itemised — and offers a causal account of it. The answer would have to change if the comparison had been drawn with a different country or on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has the Minister done any modelling on how many care and support workers from New Zealand, out of the 60,000 that have had their pay equity claim cut, have gone to Australia" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: So, therefore, in relation to that response and in relation to her response during question time where she said that New Zealand’s growth will outstrip Australia, will she therefore revisit her decision and ensure that if care and support workers—because the Government does the funding; an element of that funding—will she ensure that it’s above the Australian growth?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-stated explanation (Australia has grown faster, so it can pay more) and turns it into a demand, pairing it with her separate claim that New Zealand's growth will outstrip Australia's. The question is built entirely out of the preceding answer and could not have been asked of a different one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Australia is a wealthier economy that has grown faster than New Zealand for some years" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I’d hope that that member would understand that it’s going to take more than a year or two of faster growth than Australia for us to make up for the around 30 percent gap between Australia and New Zealand. We’re going to need successive years of that. The best way to achieve that would be for Labour to never get elected ever again.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific inference Edmonds drew — that faster-than-Australia growth should translate into funding above Australian growth — by disputing the timescale and quantifying the gap it would have to close. It declines the commitment rather than supplying it, and the final sentence is a pivot to partisanship, which keeps it short of full marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will she ensure that it’s above the Australian growth?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: In light of the Minister’s comments about Australia being a richer economy, would she attribute that to the fact that, in Australia, they have a strongly unionised workforce and fair pay agreements?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own causal claim and tests it by proposing a specific alternative mechanism for it. The question exists only because of what was said immediately before and names the claim it is probing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Australia is a wealthier economy that has grown faster than New Zealand" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: No. They dig a lot of wealth out of the ground, and that party doesn’t seem to like mining very much. I would say it’s also about a succession of policies. I wouldn’t put it down to the ones the member chose to mention.
acuity.explanation: Rejects the proposed causal explanation outright, offers a competing one, and explicitly disposes of the two factors Russell named. Maximally keyed to the specific question asked; disagreement of this kind is the strongest evidence of having engaged it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "would she attribute that to the fact that, in Australia, they have a strongly unionised workforce and fair pay agreements?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Given the Minister’s answer in relation to pay equity claims, has she done any analysis about the value that giving low-paid workers pay equity claims would give back to the economy in terms of increased spending and how that may impact New Zealand’s economic position?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the matter under debate and gestures at the Minister's answers, but it does not take up the mining-and-policies explanation just given; it opens a fresh line about the economic return from pay equity. Engagement with the topic rather than with the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They dig a lot of wealth out of the ground" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: You can do whatever model you like, but if a country can’t afford something and borrows for ever to deliver it, then, ultimately, that country goes bankrupt.
acuity.explanation: Engages the modelling Belich asked about by dismissing what any model could show and countering with affordability, which is a direct answer to the frame of her question. It never says whether the analysis was done, so one strand of the question goes untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has she done any analysis about the value that giving low-paid workers pay equity claims would give back to the economy" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: How does the Minister intend to fill the sector gaps in care and support work for an aging population when we already have a burnt-out workforce, we have workers going to Australia for higher pay, and we do not have immigration policies that will meet the demand and, in fact, are competing with Australia, which is why Australia have given a 30 percent uplift to their workers? How does the Minister plan to address that gap? Can she tell us how that is at all value for money and cost effective? And what immigration policies and other levers is she using given that we are not going to be able to get the workforce in our own country?
acuity.explanation: The "value for money and cost effective" strand does pick up the Minister's affordability answer and turn it back on her, but the bulk of the question is a prepared enumeration of workforce and immigration pressures that does not take up the bankruptcy argument. Partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if a country can’t afford something and borrows for ever to deliver it, then, ultimately, that country goes bankrupt" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Similar to this member’s previous questions, she is asking what I think are important questions about the aged care sector and its workforce. Those are questions that are more appropriately put to the relevant health Ministers in their Estimates debate.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the subject of the question and so is not indifferent to what preceded it, but engages no part of its content — it redirects the question to other Ministers instead. A gesture at the matter under debate rather than an engagement with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what immigration policies and other levers is she using" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: The Government is not slow and it is living up to its promises. This is a Government that is absolutely, completely focused on getting the economy growing, making New Zealanders richer, and repairing the damage of six years of a laissez-faire, borrow, hope, and spend approach. Now, that’s going to take a little bit of time.
acuity.explanation: Answers the two things actually asked — slowness and promises — in the terms they were put, and so is clearly keyed to the question. But the substance Williams built the question on, the defunded regulators and rising market concentration, is not taken up at all, so the engagement is with her conclusion rather than her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why is this Government slow to act on the cost of living and why is it not a priority that has lived up to the promises that National made in the election?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I have seven areas I wish to concentrate on with the Minister in this debate. They are banking, groceries, electricity and power, ports and airports, airlines, and labour market competition. I’d also ask him to comment on his Commerce Act review of which much has been made in the media by this Government, and there are a number of stakeholders who would be interested in that.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. The Minister had just denied her central premise outright, and this turn neither defends it nor acknowledges it, simply setting out her own agenda for the debate. It would read identically whatever he had answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson rejected the premise that the Government is slow to act on the cost of living and said he rejects how she characterised the state of play, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Well, issues relating to mergers and takeovers, or what have you, are the purview of a couple of organisations that have distance and independence from Government, and rightly so. So the Takeovers Panel and also the Commerce Commission are responsible for good judgment and guidance on those matters, and, as Minister, I’m not about to instruct the Commerce Commission on how to do their job.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the merger question that was put and gives a reason for not answering it in the form asked — that these are decisions for independent bodies. That engages the ask, but the specific request for an update on decisions he has taken is deflected rather than met.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can he give us an update about what we can expect to make sure that mergers which concentrate market power will not proceed under this Government’s watch?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: The issue of Manawa Energy, the issue of the supermarkets is one which the Minister could surely be accountable to the public to, instead of brushing this off to regulators who he is defunding. This is in the context of regulators that have had their funding cut in two successive years.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's appeal to regulator independence and attacks it on its own terms, pointing out that the bodies he defers to are the ones whose funding has been cut. The rebuttal is constructed from the answer immediately preceding it and could not stand without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "as Minister, I’m not about to instruct the Commerce Commission on how to do their job" — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: Well, again, the member, I think, misinterprets what I said, but I do have some good news for the member, and I’m sure that she’ll be delighted to know that the changes to the Commerce Act re merger settings are going to be announced very shortly and that Cabinet has made some decisions, and they’ll be announced in due course.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the merger-settings update she had twice pressed for, which is a direct response to her ask. The accusation she actually made in this turn — that he is deferring to regulators he is defunding — is dismissed as a misinterpretation without being engaged, which caps it mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "instead of brushing this off to regulators who he is defunding" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Just a couple of brief points, if I may. First of all, I’d be interested to know whether the Minister will be reinstituting the Consumer Advocacy Council that has been disbanded under this Government, which is a watchdog for consumers in the electricity market, given that electricity prices are skyrocketing and this Government isn’t doing anything about it.
acuity.explanation: On the portfolio under examination, but it engages no part of the preceding answer — it opens prepared questions on the Consumer Advocacy Council instead. The turn would be unchanged whatever the Minister had just said about mergers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson had just announced that Commerce Act merger-settings changes would be announced shortly, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, I’m not 100 percent sure which bill the member is referring to. Maybe she could be a bit more specific.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the actual question put to him and identifies precisely what is unclear about it (which bill), so the reply is shaped by what was just asked. But it supplies no part of the answer and hands the work back to the questioner, which is partial engagement rather than doing something with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Firstly, there’s a bill coming in November that will allegedly speed up the consenting and the land use arrangements for supermarkets. Will he be in charge of it?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: It has been reported that the Government’s groceries announcement includes a bill to be progressed by this House and for its first reading to be in November. The question is which Minister will be in charge of it: will it be the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs or will it be the Minister for resource management?
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the specificity the Minister asked for — the source of the report, the timing of the first reading, and the two named Ministers between whom the answer must choose. The turn would be unrecognisable had the preceding reply been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m not 100 percent sure which bill the member is referring to. Maybe she could be a bit more specific." — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: The member well knows that in matters related to grocery issues, I have a personal conflict, and so I’m not at all comfortable about answering that question. But maybe the Acting Minister responsible for the groceries delegation would make a comment.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question of ministerial responsibility rather than the general topic, explains why he cannot take it, and routes it to the member of the executive who can. That is shaped by the question, though it stops short of answering the substance put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The question is which Minister will be in charge of it" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I welcome the member’s new-found support for the Fast-track Approvals Act, which is the Act that enables this—and I agree with you—important amendment to fast track more supermarket competition.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the questioner's own framing of the measure as a sensible market intervention, names the statute it amends, and goes on to set out the scope that was asked for. One strand of the question — the supplier/farm-gate power imbalance — is left untouched, so this is strong rather than complete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m hoping to understand a little bit the scope of that bill" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Look, there are a couple of points there, which is simply to say that we do watch food price inflation across the economy carefully, and while it’s no longer in the double-digit percentage increases that it was under the member’s party in Government, we have noted that it has tracked a little higher.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific inflation figure put to her, concedes the direction of travel ("tracked a little higher"), and contests its comparative significance. She also expressly accepts the 'price gouging' part as a fair question before redirecting to misleading pricing, so the reply is built on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Radio New Zealand reports that New Zealand grocery prices are higher than the OECD average and are still rising at 4.4 percent this year." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Well, I’m sure that the member will join me in congratulating the spokespeople from Pic’s Peanut Butter for having the courage to say out loud things that many suppliers have only felt comfortable saying to me in quiet corridors, because it is the case that many suppliers in New Zealand do feel that they are not treated fairly by the supermarkets and that in some cases they are exerting market power in ways which potentially breach a range of Acts.
acuity.explanation: Takes the particular example offered, endorses it, generalises from it to the supplier complaints she has received, and then sets out the enforcement machinery as her answer to the monopsony question asked. This reply could not have been given in response to a different example.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "recently there was reporting on Pic Picot, of Pic’s Peanut Butter from Nelson, who was saying that the supermarkets were so bad to deal with" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Look, unlike the previous member Arena Williams’ Government, this Government does have both the willpower, the intelligence, and the commitment to address this issue of mergers in the Commerce Act, which your party and your Government left unaddressed.
acuity.explanation: It is on the specific statute the question named and implicitly rejects the premise of inaction, but the engagement is mostly a pivot to the questioner's own government's record plus "await future announcements". It takes up the topic of the question more than the content of the claim about Australia and the merger regime.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why, Minister, have you not progressed the changes to the mergers and acquisitions regime in New Zealand" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Let’s move to questions about the banking sector, which the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs is clearly responsible for and has the delegation for, even though he was not able to answer those simple questions on his mergers announcement and the speech that he gave in August which parked those mergers decisions that he has taken.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the exchange just had — a complaint that the mergers questions went unanswered — but it engages no part of the Minister's actual claim about progress before moving to an entirely new line on bank debt. A reference used to pivot away is not engagement with the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has made an awful lot of progress in this area, and she should await future announcements" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: In light of that “Kumbaya” happy answer for all members of this House getting to have a say on that important legislation, can I ask him: the inquiry into banking competition outlined a number of things which have broad cross-partisan support in this House, and I want him to give us an indication of what he would prioritise as areas for reform that are those things which are broadly agreed on to increase competition from the banking inquiry.
acuity.explanation: She characterises Simpson's process answer back at him ("Kumbaya happy answer") but engages none of its content — the select committee referral, the retrospectivity rationale, the discretion argument. She then asks a prepared question about the banking inquiry's agreed reform areas, which would read identically whatever he had just said about the CCCFA. A mere reference plus a pivot sits in the low band, with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "we’ll make decisions based on the select committee report-back"

acuity.statement: So the banking inquiry that was presented from the Finance and Expenditure Committee has just recently received back a number of recommendations. We have yet to make final decisions on those recommendations, but what I can tell the member is that back in December of 2024, this Government accepted all of the Commerce Commission’s recommendations made in terms of competition and their market study into personal banking and banking services.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the banking inquiry she asked about and explains where it sits, but declines the specific thing requested — a prioritisation among the cross-party-agreed reforms — and substitutes the Commerce Commission market study instead. One strand engaged, the specific ask not supplied: partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "what he would prioritise as areas for reform that are those things which are broadly agreed on to increase competition from the banking inquiry"

acuity.statement: Well, the member’s referring to what is commonly known, colloquially known, as open banking, and we passed the framework legislation, customer data legislation, in March of this year. The legislation itself provides a framework, a platform from which to create bespoke regulatory regimes for certain sectors of the economy. We’ve made it very clear that the first sector will be banking. That’s partly why it’s called open banking. Those regulations are due to be promulgated very soon, and the intention is that open banking, in terms of what is commonly known as open banking, should be available from early December this year.
acuity.explanation: He supplies the thing asked for — a date, early December — and sets out the regulatory sequence that produces it, so the answer would be different had she asked something else. He leaves untouched the second strand she invited comment on, the Payments New Zealand governance characterisation, which keeps it short of full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "When can New Zealanders expect to see a sort of proliferation of services, of apps, that allow New Zealanders to switch easily"

acuity.statement: When will he be concerned, if there aren’t new fintechs open to offering these services, that it is in fact Payments New Zealand’s governance arrangements which are holding things back? I ask that because you would expect a number of fintechs to be out in the market already—some overseas, some homegrown.
acuity.explanation: She fastens on the precise soft spot in the answer just given — his admission that he does not know how many fintechs will be operating by his December date — and converts it into a test: at what point does the absence of entrants indict Payments New Zealand's governance. The question is built out of his words and could not have been asked of a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "I’m not sure exactly how many new fintech entities will be up and running by that period of time"

acuity.statement: No, I think the member is being overly pessimistic. I think that the indications we’ve had so far have been very positive and that there are a number of fintechs that are already operating, and a number have made it very clear that they are just dying to get into the space and create some opportunities.
acuity.explanation: He contradicts the specific factual premise of her question, that fintechs are not in the market, by asserting that a number already operate and more are waiting, and he later addresses the Payments New Zealand confidence point she raised. He does not take up her claim that fintechs face rules the banks do not, which is the one strand left hanging.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "you would expect a number of fintechs to be out in the market already—some overseas, some homegrown"

acuity.statement: With the greatest respect, the member just resuming his seat is a new member. He has entirely the wrong portfolio. These are questions to be put to the Minister of Revenue.
acuity.explanation: A jurisdictional deflection: it registers that a question was asked and says who should answer it, but engages no part of the substance — not the discharge of the bill, not the Treasury estimate, not the profit-shifting claim. That is a gesture at the matter raised rather than engagement with it, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "Why, during a cost of living crisis and in the face of ongoing cuts to public services, is the Minister happy to write off $500 million in tax revenue?"

acuity.statement: Well, again, the member is being a little bit pessimistic and should just wait a little while. I take the point that is sometimes raised about exiting from subscriptions—it can be challenging, it can be difficult, but we already have a significant range of options available to people who feel that they are being shortchanged in that regard.
acuity.explanation: He picks up one strand of a multi-part question — the difficulty of exiting subscriptions — and concedes it before disputing that nothing exists. The rest of what she put, the unbundled service charges and card fees and the Australian and European comparison, goes unaddressed, so this is partial engagement on a question with several named limbs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "make it easier to leave subscriptions for digital services that plague consumers online"

acuity.statement: Well, again, this is probably a matter that is better put to the appropriate Minister. Look, I'm interested, as Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, in ensuring that New Zealanders have access to a range of options.
acuity.explanation: A yes/no question about price gouging receives neither, and no part of the proposition is engaged — only a statement that someone else should field it, plus a general gesture at his own interest in electricity competition. On the subject under discussion, but engaging none of the claim put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "is there price gouging in the New Zealand electricity sector?"

acuity.statement: I would guess that that answer might be, “Well, perhaps there is, but it's nothing to do with me.” Can I ask him: why is Powerswitch being defunded when it is one of the few tools that consumers can compare, contrast, and make sure we have a competitive market for those services?
acuity.explanation: She draws out the consequence of the deflection he just made, paraphrasing it as an evasion, and then narrows to something squarely inside the portfolio he claimed as his own — consumer comparison tools. The first half engages the answer just given; the second half is a fresh question, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "this is probably a matter that is better put to the appropriate Minister"

acuity.statement: Governments need to be careful and prudent with the allocation of taxpayers’ money, and when entities and organisations that are funded with taxpayers’ money are not producing the impacts and the positive outcomes that were expected, then that's a good reason not to continue throwing good money after bad.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a general rationale for defunding the bodies Williams asked about, so it answers the 'why' at the level of principle, but it never takes up the specific tool she named (the power price dashboard) or her claim that manufacturers and large employers used it to compare prices. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Why, if Powerswitch is out of the system, has the Electricity Authority also dropped the power price dashboard?"

acuity.statement: I'm happy to know that the Minister considers that money badly spent when those were the two things that the Government had on its books to increase competitiveness in the electricity market.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's 'good money after bad' formulation and draws out its consequence — that he is calling the Government's own two competition measures badly spent money. The sentence could not have been said if Simpson had justified the cuts differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "that's a good reason not to continue throwing good money after bad"

acuity.statement: Well, unlike the member's colleague who was a new member, this member's been around a bit longer and would certainly, I would think, know that, actually, this is a matter that needs to be referred to the appropriate Minister, the Hon James Meager.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the subject matter of the question just put and names who it should go to, which is a targeted reply to the question as asked; but it engages no part of the aviation-competition argument itself, so engagement sits well below a genuine half.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Will this Government use its power, as Air New Zealand's largest shareholder, to ensure that regional connectivity and that route competitiveness is a priority?"

acuity.statement: The Minister is responsible for the $73 million appropriation to the Commerce Commission, which is the regulator. Is he saying that he is considering stripping the Commerce Commission of that responsibility, or is it just him that's not responsible for the rising cost of living?
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the ground of the deflection just offered, pointing to the appropriation he does hold and forcing the dilemma that follows from his disclaimer. The reply is shaped entirely by what Simpson said immediately before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "this is a matter that needs to be referred to the appropriate Minister, the Hon James Meager"

acuity.statement: Again, for the benefit of the member, the appropriate Minister is the Hon James Meager, and she should, at the appropriate time, address those questions to that Minister.
acuity.explanation: Repeats the same referral without taking up either the airport-regulation argument or the appropriation point Williams had just raised to rebut the referral. A gesture at the matter under debate and nothing more.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Wouldn't it be sensible for him to have a joined-up competition strategy on the regulation of airports so that they could accept as many international travellers as possible" — and her point that he holds the $73 million Commerce Commission appropriation

acuity.statement: Is the Minister getting used to his delegation for groceries not being his responsibility, and so would he like all the other Ministers to take responsibility for commerce in these sectors?
acuity.explanation: Seizes on the delegation defence he has now used three times and pushes it to its limit, asking whether every commerce matter is someone else's. It engages the content of his answer rather than merely naming him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "There is a Minister with delegated responsibility for those matters, and that is the Hon James Meager."

acuity.statement: This is a debate on the Estimates of the commerce and consumer affairs portfolio. The member has asked a series of questions that relate to other portfolios, not the least of which is her last one; the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety is the Hon Brooke van Velden.
acuity.explanation: Identifies specifically which question is out of scope and who owns it, which is a gesture at the exchange, but engages no part of the non-compete and labour-market-restraint argument — including its competition dimension, which is his own portfolio.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Is the Minister going to seek any advice on essentially the monopsony situation that's created by this reducing dynamism and innovation in the New Zealand economy?"

acuity.statement: I am out of time, but I would like to ask the Minister the first question that I asked him: why have his responses been that there is something always coming in the pipeline? Why did it take 18 months for this Government to even request information about what they should do about rising grocery prices? Why is this Government slow to act on the cost of living when they said it was a priority at the election?
acuity.explanation: Turns the pattern of the Minister's own answers across the exchange into the question, quoting the 'in the pipeline' formulation back and demanding it be defended. Partly prepared cost-of-living material, but visibly built on what he had been saying.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson's repeated referrals to other Ministers, and his earlier answer that matters are in train — "the appropriate Minister is the Hon James Meager"

acuity.statement: That question was answered the first time the member asked it. There are three bills before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment designed exactly to help achieve those matters, and more legislation in the pipeline.
acuity.explanation: Meets the specific charge of empty 'pipeline' talk by naming what is actually before the select committee. The answer is directly keyed to the challenge just made, though it leaves the 18-month grocery delay untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "why have his responses been that there is something always coming in the pipeline?"

acuity.statement: Well, speaking briefly to that, it’s difficult for me to comment on conversations involving phone calls that I wasn’t privy to. There is a substantial investment in Christchurch through the National Land Transport Fund, which is part of the Budget, obviously, through the Estimates. Most recently, of course, we announced the Brougham Street upgrade, and construction has started on that. It’s a welcome project for Christchurch. There is a range of other improvements that are being undertaken, all of which are publicly available, and the member can see that. But I can’t comment on a conversation that I wasn’t privy to. Actually, many of these decisions are not made by Ministers or mayors; they are made by the Transport Agency board independently of Ministers.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific allegation just made — the Mauger/Brown phone call — and does two things with it: declines on the ground that he was not party to it, and rebuts the premise by asserting that these allocations are made by the NZTA board, not by Ministers or mayors. He also offers Christchurch investment as a counter to the 'short-changed' charge. Short of 1.0 because the second half of McLellan's question (will he restore the funding) is not taken up, but the speech would plainly be different had she argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Mayor Phil Mauger admitted on stage at The Pressa press debate the other night that he simply phoned then Minister Simeon Brown and told him that Christchurch didn’t, in fact, need the money" — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I don’t know what happened in the phone call, because I wasn’t on the other end of it. It’s sort of difficult for me to comment on that. All I would say is that there’s a really thorough process that many members will be familiar with because they lobby the New Zealand Transport Agency for particular projects in their local patch or, indeed, they lobby the council or both, which is we go through this convoluted process of setting up the National Land Transport Fund and then the plan for three years. Councils go through an equivalent process at their end to look at what their priority projects are. That feeds into a funding process. At the end of the day, projects get funded. Is the process of that cumbersome? Yes. Could it be more streamlined? Absolutely. Should it be more long term? Absolutely. I agree with all of those things and, actually, the Government’s got a series of reforms under way.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of what was put to him: the question of whether the process is an acceptable way to decide funding, which he answers by describing the lobbying/NLTF process and conceding it is cumbersome and should be more long term. He does not take up the specific contention that Christchurch's needs were traded away, repeating the can't-comment line instead, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "do you think this is an acceptable way for business to be conducted—that Christchurch long-term transport needs were simply traded away in a political phone call?" — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: Well, there’s a range of funding pressures on the National Land Transport Fund. Fuel tax has not been adjusted since 2019, from memory. So iIn real terms, the fund has decreased at the same time as construction cost inflation has increased at pace. So there’s a range of pressures around rail, around public transport, both infrastructure and operating, and also roads and road maintenance.
acuity.explanation: Answers the topic — the gap between spending intentions and revenue — but not the question actually asked. Genter asked about a specific driver on the spending side (the roads of national and regional significance); the reply addresses the revenue side (static fuel tax, construction cost inflation) and then lists pressures generally, never confirming or denying that the RoNS list is the major driver. Engagement with the subject, not with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is the major driver of that spending intentions the list of roads of national and regional significance that are included in the most recent Government policy statement (GPS)?" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: Is there more money allocated to new capital, especially new State highways, or to road maintenance?
acuity.explanation: A follow-up built directly on the answer just given: Bishop claimed the GPS prioritises looking after existing assets, and this question puts that claim to the test by asking for the comparison that would verify it. The question is unintelligible without the preceding turn, which is the strongest evidence of listening. Vague on figures, but that is Specificity, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the GPS signals a very strong focus on looking after what we’ve got" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Well, there’s an increase across the National Land Transport Plan (NLTP) period compared to 2021 to 2024. The activity classes are all publicly available in terms of the operating ranges that the member will be familiar with. We have placed a real priority on road maintenance and the member can see all the rest of it for herself.
acuity.explanation: Addressed to the right question but supplies neither side of the comparison asked for, referring the member to publicly available activity classes instead. Points at where the answer could be found, which is a glance at the question rather than an engagement with it; a 1.0 here was easily available — the two numbers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is there more money allocated to new capital, especially new State highways, or to road maintenance?" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: But if the Government’s serious about prioritising taking care of what we have, why is there so much money being allocated to new projects relative to preserving what we already have?
acuity.explanation: Takes the assertion just made — that maintenance is a real priority — and presses the tension between it and the capital programme, i.e. accepts the stated intention and disputes that the allocation matches it. Directly contingent on the previous turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We have placed a real priority on road maintenance and the member can see all the rest of it for herself." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Well, the Government came to office with a mandate to build a range of projects around the country, a long-term pipeline of major roading upgrades, and also a range of major public transport projects. I’d point the member to the Northwest Busway, which we’re making good progress on, which will be a transformational project for north-west Auckland and, indeed, the wider Auckland region.
acuity.explanation: Offers a genuine answer to the 'why' — an electoral mandate to build a pipeline of new projects — which engages the question rather than deflecting it, then moves to an unrelated project example. Partial: it explains the choice without addressing the balance between new build and preservation that she asked about, and the remainder of the turn departs from the question altogether.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why is there so much money being allocated to new projects relative to preserving what we already have?" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: Well, I’m very keen to ask the Minister about level crossings in Auckland. If I could just come back to my original question, which was around the intentions in the Government policy statementGPS laid out for roads of national and regional significance and the tens of billions of dollars that they are likely to cost and the gap between those spending intentions and revenue. I do want to know: does the Minister think that the process set up by the Infrastructure Commission—the Infrastructure Priorities Programme—is a useful way to ensure there is a long-term pipeline that has agreement broadly across the House?
acuity.explanation: Picks up a thread the Minister had just raised (Auckland level crossings), identifies that the long answer did not reach her question, and converts his own framing — a long-term pipeline of projects — into a new question about whether the Infrastructure Priorities Programme is the right way to build one with cross-House agreement. Clearly shaped by what preceded it; short of 1.0 because it restates her earlier question rather than rebutting the reasoning in his reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are getting on with the job of the level crossing removal project in Auckland." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: So the highest priority is the Southern Line stuff. There's a programme business case being done—PBC—for the Western Line, and I just want to reassure the member, yep, we're upzoning around these stations, many of which are in her electorate, but zoning capacity doesn't equal immediate housing growth, particularly with the way the construction market is at the moment. You know, we need an economic recovery under way before you're going to see some of that action.
acuity.explanation: Takes up White's specific premise — that fixing the level crossings now would unlock the housing being zoned in her area — and disputes it directly, arguing zoning capacity does not convert into near-term building given the construction market, while conceding the Western Line work is being business-cased.
