acuity.explanation: Halbert registers that the Minister's intervening turn did not answer him, which is a gesture at the state of the debate, but he engages no part of the content of the preceding turns — he goes straight into his own prepared questions on Kick Back and Auckland youth homelessness. On the deciding test, this speech would read much the same whatever Potaka had said in his turn, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band: on-topic prepared material with a nod to the exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I don't think Shane is from the West Coast in Poutini, but thank you" — Halbert points only at the fact that this turn left his question unanswered, not at anything said in it.

acuity.statement: In the event that we have young people hitting the streets, that is very unfortunate, and I have met some of these young people, as you have mentioned, and they have told me that they have serious disconnect from their whānau.
acuity.explanation: Potaka picks up one strand of Halbert's questions — the meetings with rangatahi from Kick Back — and reports what those young people told him, which is a real engagement with what was just put. But it answers neither of the two things actually asked (how many places have been offered for the estimated 11,000 young people, and what the group's recommendations were), returning instead to the announcement he intended to talk about. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "he’s met with the rangatahi from that group who have experienced housing—is: what were their recommendations?"

acuity.statement: Given that the chair of the committee has just been speaking about the waste levy, I’d like to ask some questions about that. Of course, this was a levy that has always been hypothecated to waste, and it’s split 50 percent between the Crown and local government. At the Budget—not this year, but last year—the Government’s part was split, so it could be spent on anything to do with the environment. As a result of those decisions, the amount and the waste minimisation fund will reduce by about 49 percent.
acuity.explanation: Brooking takes the specific element of Wedd's account of Vote Environment — the increased waste disposal levy funding presented as a 38.7 percent uplift in waste minimisation — and does something with it: she traces where the Crown half of the hypothecated levy now goes and puts the opposite figure, a roughly 49 percent fall in the waste minimisation fund, before building her questions on that. The questions could not have been framed this way had the preceding speech not made the levy a centrepiece.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "The waste minimisation work includes increased funding from the waste disposal levy" (and her "38.7 percent increase in waste minimisation").

acuity.statement: Yes, we are utilising the levy across other departments—the Department of Conservation, across the Ministry for Primary Industries—for things such as the Community Conservation Fund and predator and erosion control, and I don’t think anyone would argue against those being beneficial to the environment.
acuity.explanation: This concedes the factual core of Brooking's question — that levy money is being spent outside waste — and then contests its significance by naming the recipient programmes and arguing they are environmental goods. That is accepting part and disputing the rest, which is squarely responsive. Short of 1.0 because it does not reach the scrutiny half of what was asked (what oversight is applied to the environmental outcomes of that diverted spending).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "With the money from the levy being diverted to other environmental things—and we can talk about those other environmental things soon—what will it do for her action that she’s going to undertake on waste?"

acuity.statement: In terms of the waste minimisation legislation, one of the matters that was consulted on was changing slightly the 50 percent that goes to the local authorities and enabling some of that to go as base grant, not all by population. That’s important because there are smaller local authorities that don’t have the scale, and also there are smaller local authorities that get big numbers of tourists and so it impacts upon them. We think that’s going to be a better balance and, on the whole, the submissions supported us being able to do that. At this stage, we are anticipating the waste minimisation amendment legislation going into the House in the first quarter of next year.
acuity.explanation: Brooking asked where the promised waste minimisation legislation had got to; Simmonds supplies the content consulted on, the reasoning behind the base-grant change, and the timing — the specific thing requested. The passage exists because the question was asked and would not survive a different question. It leaves the circular-economy strand untouched, which is why it is not a full 1.0, but on the legislation question it is directly engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "The Minister has said that she’s going to do some waste minimisation legislation. Where is that at?"

acuity.statement: I would really like to pick up on the Budget cuts generally, and particularly in light of this question. I’d like to hear from the Minister as to whether she actually does expect, as a result of the Budget decisions, that environmental outcomes will actually improve.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Brooking's preceding question — the 'improving' versus 'maintaining' the environment framing — and redirects it at the Budget, then continues into her own prepared material on the $650 million of forecast cuts. Partial engagement that is clearly pointable, not a full rebuttal of Brooking's specific point about the analysis of environmental benefit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "There is talk of “maintaining” the environment, but not “improving” the environment."

acuity.statement: Look, I just thought I’d grab the opportunity to ask the Minister whether she has, in her Budget, provided for money to assist small communities where the changing environment has caused them to spend a lot of money.
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of the preceding arguments by Brooking or Pham; it is self-declaredly an opportunistic new question about nitrate-affected water supplies. It stays on the matter under debate (whether the Minister's Budget provides for a given cost), which is the only reason it is above the floor, but the words would be identical whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham argued that more than $650 million has been cut across Budgets 2024 and 2025 and asked whether environmental outcomes will improve, and this statement does not take any of it up — the speaker says explicitly that he is grabbing the opportunity to raise a separate matter.

acuity.statement: I will start with the funding for small communities to source lower nitrates water. I will just note for the member that, actually, the reporting of too-high nitrates levels is very few and far between. You will, perhaps, recall that Gore District Council recorded one instance of being above the level, and Waimate District Council was the other; that was twice, in 2022 and 2024. There is no specific budget, but that is because the number of times that drinking water has exceeded the allowable nitrates level has been very, very minimal.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — no, there is no specific budget — and supplies the premise she is disputing with named councils and years, i.e. that the problem O'Connor describes is rare. The answer would have to be different had O'Connor asked something else; it is built entirely around his claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "has she provided for funding that will assist those ratepayers to find water that is drinkable, because of the changing environmental circumstances?"

acuity.statement: I think it’s the entirety of the forecast periods and the $400 million from last Budget which is very significant, hence why it looks like an increase in this Budget but, overall, it’s a ginormous decrease.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the Minister's challenge to her figure by explaining its derivation — the whole forecast period plus $400 million from the prior Budget — and reconciles it with the Minister's point that this Budget shows an increase. The engagement is exact even though the arithmetic is left loose; vagueness is a specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "I am not sure where the member gets the $650 million reduction from"

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister whether she sees her role, as the environment Minister, as one that would be advocating for the protection of the environment, given her comments. If so, how does she then expect Te Papa Atawhai, the Department of Conservation, to do the role that it is meant to do in terms of promoting biodiversity and promoting predator control when it has had, under her Government’s watch, 200 jobs cut and also a significant reduction in its Budget appropriation over successive years under her Government?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the advocacy question Pham had just left unanswered and develops it with new material — DOC job cuts and appropriation reductions set against the Minister's own earlier remarks on biodiversity and predator control. It builds on a preceding turn rather than merely restating it, but much of the content is prepared and anchored to the Minister's earlier contribution rather than to the argument immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "I’m wanting to hear directly from the Minister whether she sees her role in this process as actually advocating for the environment."

acuity.statement: Again, repeating what I have now heard two colleagues say, does the Minister believe she has a role in advocating for the environment? And, going back to my question, is wanting to improve the environment or talking about a circular economy ideological?
acuity.explanation: Tracks the debate well enough to notice that a question put twice by preceding speakers has gone unanswered and to press it, which is responsiveness to the state of the exchange. But it restates rather than engages the content of what was said, and the rest of the turn is her own prepared EPA material, so this sits at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "whether she sees her role, as the environment Minister, as one that would be advocating for the protection of the environment"

acuity.statement: The $10 million loan that the member mentioned indeed occurred for the EPA. It was a loan agreement with the Crown to support the implementation of the fast-track regime, and they made their first six-monthly interest repayment of $208,000 to Treasury. The EPA had raised sufficient levies from applicants to be able to make that repayment.
acuity.explanation: Confirms the specific fact the member raised and supplies the figure her question asked for — the first repayment and how it was funded — then addresses whether repayment is on track. Squarely built on Brooking's question; marked just below the top because the accompanying advocacy-for-the-environment question in the same turn is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Is that on track? Are they going to be able to pay back their loan?"

acuity.statement: The Minister has referred, I suppose, in response to us a couple of times, to the term “circular economy”. She has said, variously, that it’s not a term she uses or a term she likes or a term she’s picked up on. Obviously, that implies a fair degree of knowledge about what a circular economy is. Could the Minister, please, explain what she understands by a circular economy and tell us why she doesn’t like to use that term?
acuity.explanation: Built entirely out of the answer just given: it quotes the Minister's own disavowal of the term, draws out what that disavowal presupposes, and turns it into a new question testing that presupposition. Substitute a different answer from the Minister and this contribution could not exist in this form.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "The term “circular economy” is one that the previous Government enjoyed using. It is not a term that I have picked up on."

acuity.statement: Certainly, there is no dilution of the Environmental Protection Authority’s requirement to be protecting the environment, none whatsoever. That does not mean that they should not seek to be more efficient, to be more effective, to be able to process faster, because that, in fact, enables better protection of the environment by being able to get more environmentally difficult chemicals out of the system and bring in, more quickly, softer chemicals that are better for the environment.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific premise — that an efficiency focus at the EPA comes at the cost of environmental protection — and disputes the link directly, arguing faster processing itself serves protection. Her following paragraph also answers the second question, on what "not aligned to Government priorities" meant for the defunded entities. The reply would be different had Brooking asked something else; it falls short of 1.0 only because the Environmental Reporting Act question and the missing word "improvement" are left unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m wondering if any of the reprioritisation or any emphasis on the EPA is about protecting the environment." — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: My question, again, is: does the Minister commit to, in some way, upholding existing water conservation orders in the resource management (RM) reforms that are directly in her expenditure environment? My other question is: what is her commitment in the freshwater space to environmental bottom lines within the RM reform?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the Minister's environmental expenditure — and gestures at her earlier remarks on conservation, but engages no part of the argument just made about EPA efficiency or the defunding decision. These are fresh questions that would read identically whatever Simmonds had just said, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds argued the EPA's efficiency drive enables rather than dilutes environmental protection, and defended discontinuing funding to the Environmental Defence Society and Forest & Bird; this statement takes up neither strand.

acuity.statement: There are a couple of questions there about the Resource Management Act reform. Let me deal with the first two in particular; I think the third one was better directed to the Minister for the Environment. As I think the member knows, we are working through water conservation orders and also fresh water in the context of a pretty comprehensive replacement regime for the Resource Management Act, so no decisions have been made.
acuity.explanation: Addresses Pham's two RM reform questions squarely and in the order she put them, placing water conservation orders and freshwater inside the replacement regime, and explicitly triages the third to the responsible Minister. Scored on engagement only: the substance is a 'wait and see', which is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister commit to, in some way, upholding existing water conservation orders in the resource management (RM) reforms" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: I’d just like to dispute the statement the member made around the fact that there is a proven link and the direct assertion that somehow the dairy industry is responsible for 40 deaths.
acuity.explanation: Names the exact claim Abel had just made, contests it with a counter-source, and then goes on to answer his separate question about the synthetic nitrogen cap with a worked example. The speech is unintelligible without Abel's turn preceding it, which is the strongest evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a hundred new cases of bowel cancer and 40 deaths per year attributable to nitrate in drinking water in New Zealand" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: To my mind, given the Minister for the Environment’s contribution previously and the fact that she has said that improving biodiversity is part of her environmental priorities, how does she justify the continued decline in biodiversity and native species, given all of what I’ve outlined, and how does that fit within her environmental priorities and how does she justify it?
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's funding-priorities defence by pressing the environmental consequence of the cuts, and narrows her own earlier question after accepting a portfolio objection. But the specific thing she quotes back — that the Minister said improving biodiversity was a priority — is not what Simmonds had just argued (Simmonds immediately denies saying it), so much of this is prepared material on the adjacent subject rather than engagement with the argument actually made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this Government did not carry on with funding a number of entities that the previous Government felt they should fund" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: I think if the member looks back, I haven’t mentioned biodiversity—she has. However, I will again note that, for the funding that has gone into predator control in the Department of Conservation, she will need to discuss or ask those questions of that Minister.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a misstatement of fact in the question put to her, then takes up the two specific programmes named — predator control and Jobs for Nature — and gives a reason for the latter not continuing. Directly shaped by what preceded it. Scored on engagement alone; the closing remark about the member showing herself to be irresponsible is a civility question, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "she has said that improving biodiversity is part of her environmental priorities" — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: I would like to hear the Minister for the Environment address her role in the fast-track process, which, again, is a very clear expenditure item. Does the Minister see her role as advocating for the environment in this process?
acuity.explanation: Opens a new line of questioning on fast-track consenting without touching the Jobs for Nature or affordability argument just made. It remains within the expenditure under scrutiny, so it is not wholly unmoored, but it would have been delivered word-for-word whatever the Minister had just answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds argued Jobs for Nature was always short-term COVID funding that could not be sustained, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I did go to Otago as well. That was the first one I went to; the member will be very pleased. As I said, I had visits to eight of the 10 that are going to stand up and, I would have to say, it was enormously encouraging the amount of work that has been done and the enthusiasm of each of the entities. In general, I met with the senior management team, the establishment advisory groups, the community liaison person, and the mayor of the city. They were all very enthusiastic about having their polytechnics back. They had done an incredible amount of work and were well down the path with their sustainability ability. Thank you.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question asked — the 10 stand-alone polytechnics and their pathway to sustainability — reports on visits to eight of them and ends on their progress on sustainability, while also picking up Halbert's interjection about Otago by name. The answer would be different had a different question been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "my question for the Minister is about how each of the 10 stand-alone polytechnics are going on their pathway to sustainability because of Budget 2025" (and Shanan Halbert's interjection "What about Otago?")

acuity.statement: It’s wonderful to be able to have this debate with the Minister tonight, because her leadership—she said that Te Pūkenga is getting rid of wasteful spending and getting the sector back on track. I wonder if we could just have a little bit of a quick to and fro with the Minister, of quick-fire answers. Does she still stand by her statements in that regard?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand the Minister had just advanced — that the sector is progressing well — and tests it by asking whether she stands by her earlier claim that the sector is back on track. But the thing engaged is a prior public statement rather than the content of the turn just delivered, so it is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "it was enormously encouraging the amount of work that has been done and the enthusiasm of each of the entities"

acuity.statement: I definitely do. There were some polytechnics that needed to undertake significant work and they have undertaken that work and, I believe, have put their organisations in a much better position to be sustainable in the long term.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question squarely with a direct affirmation and then gives the reason — the work undertaken and the resulting position of the institutions. The reply is shaped entirely by what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "Does she still stand by her statements in that regard?"

acuity.statement: There has been additional spending. There has been new investment of $398.3 million. That is going to be across the tertiary sector. There has been additional funding put in for 175 additional Youth Guarantee (YG) places a year, and, of course, additional volume put in targeted subsidy increases. So considerable additional funding to support the sector right across the private training establishments (PTEs), polytechnics, and universities.
acuity.explanation: Engages the question and supplies figures for the Budget's tertiary investment, which is what was asked for. One strand is left alone — the question was about real terms and the answer is given in nominal new spending — so it engages most, not all, of the claim put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "In this Budget, is it more or less, in real terms, of an investment in tertiary education?"

acuity.statement: There is no doubt that there was work that needed to be done, when there were institutions that had, for approximately eight out of 10 years, run deficits. On the other hand, there were institutions in the vocational sector that had never run a deficit until they were forced into Te Pūkenga. There were extremes within the sector.
acuity.explanation: The reply is on the matter under debate — the financial state of the vocational sector under this Budget — but engages no part of the question actually asked: no advice is reported, and job cuts, campus closures and course reductions go unmentioned. It is material about the sector's deficit history that would have served whatever question had been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "What advice has she received about job cuts, campus closures, and course reductions in relation to this Budget?" — this answer does not take up job cuts, closures or course reductions, turning instead to the deficit history of the institutions.

acuity.statement: My question now turns to the job cuts issue, which my colleague Shanan Halbert has touched on. There are around 620 jobs that are forecast to be cut by the end of this year according to advice that the Minister has received. According to information that she has released, there were 855 staff that were lost from 2023 to 2024. Is this the total amount of jobs that will be lost as a result of this reform, or has the Minister had advice that there will be further cuts made next year, and what advice, if any, has the Minister received around what the impacts of those job cuts will be around the wider communities?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly returns to the strand the Minister had just left unanswered, names the earlier exchange, and presses it with the specific figures she has released, so the question cannot be met with the deficit history again. The turn is shaped by what the Minister did and did not say.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "There is no doubt that there was work that needed to be done, when there were institutions that had, for approximately eight out of 10 years, run deficits" — given in answer to Halbert's job-cuts question

acuity.statement: There‘s quite a bit there. I’m not quite sure where that reference to a text message came from, but there was quite a bit of considerable correspondence from a variety of councils and other stakeholders in relation to section 107. There almost certainly were texts as well—a bit like the last Government, Ministers in this Government do use cellphones.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific insinuation about text messages to Ministers preceding the section 107 change, locates the correspondence she is pointing at and disputes the implication. The reply would be different had she not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "recently we’ve seen a lot of text messages and the like to Ministers and then suddenly the law will change" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: In relation to the plan stop, the Minister for RMA Reform—that’s me; I’m responsible for dealing with that. We’ve had some applications to continue, which will be analysed and dealt with as per the law. I think it’s a pragmatic step to make sure that the system stops, unless there’s good reason, while we prepare for the oncoming regime.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question of which Minister holds the plan-exemption decision, names himself, and explains how applications will be handled. Directly keyed to the question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is she involved in those exemptions as the Minister for the Environment, or is it just the Minister for fast track?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I don’t believe we’ve had answers to questions around the Environmental Reporting Act or the Minister’s definition of circular economy.
acuity.explanation: Engages the preceding answer by auditing its completeness and naming the two strands left unanswered, but does not take up the content of what Bishop actually argued on green spaces or the plan stop.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ll take the member’s comments under advisement around that as part of the policy process" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: There are two lots of funding available. The first amount, the $20 million per annum, is for the contaminated sites and vulnerable landfills—those with local authorities, so assisting local authorities there. Then there’s the additional $40 million over the budget period for remediation of Crown contaminated sites. They aren’t just Department of Conservation sites; there are also Defence sites and Land Information New Zealand sites.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the clarification sought, distinguishing the local-authority fund from the Crown land stream and confirming conservation land sits in the latter alongside Defence and LINZ sites.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just want clarification whether that includes public conservation land as well or whether it doesn’t." — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: The Hon Rachel Brooking noted that I hadn’t answered a question on the reporting Act. I’m sorry, I don’t have the question down here, but I can advise that, yes, we are intending to amend the Environmental Reporting Act (ERA).
acuity.explanation: Returns explicitly to the gap Brooking had just identified and supplies the missing answer on the Environmental Reporting Act. Plainly shaped by what the previous speaker said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t believe we’ve had answers to questions around the Environmental Reporting Act or the Minister’s definition of circular economy." — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I do not equate more spending with more efficient and more effective environmental protection. In fact, it would be very foolish of members to think that just continually throwing money at entities somehow gives better performance.
acuity.explanation: Engages and rejects the premise embedded in Pham's question — that lower investment is itself an environmental risk — rather than merely speaking to the topic, though it does not take up the request to name risks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what does she see as some of the risks—or maybe, say, the top three risks—when it comes to the environmental space and her Government’s decisions on investment or lack of investment in that space?" — Lan Pham

acuity.statement: This is actually a question for the Minister for the Environment, because the Minister for the Environment undertakes the environmental reporting. The question was whether these changes are going to lead to more pollution—and I suspect that they would lead to more pollution, like most of the changes that this Government has made to freshwater—and if she disagrees with that, what advice is she asking for and what monitoring will she undertake?
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the attempted hand-off and rebuts it with a reason tied to the portfolio's reporting function, then restates the specific strand left open. Entirely contingent on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m looking at the Resource Management Act (RMA) Minister to see if he wants to answer that." — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: My understanding is that the receiving waters have to be degraded before a consent can be approved and that there must be long-term provision for improvement.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — the statutory test governing consents under the changed provision — but leaves untouched the questions about analysis undertaken and monitoring to follow.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The question was whether these changes are going to lead to more pollution" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: The member can keep using the term as much as she wants to. It is not an intention that I have of using it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up only the parenthetical jibe about not wanting to use the phrase and engages no part of the actual request for a definition; a gesture at the exchange rather than engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does the Minister for the Environment have a definition of “circular economy”—the phrase she doesn’t want to use?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: The equity funding, in terms of the disability funding and the funding for those that have not had prior achievement in their compulsory education is still there. We consider that the equity funding based on disabilities and low prior achievement ensures that the focus on those that need it regardless of ethnicity.
acuity.explanation: Halbert put a specific charge — that she cut equity funding for Māori and Pacific learners in polytechs. She takes up the subject of equity funding and answers one strand of it (the disability and low-prior-achievement lines survive), but does not engage the claim actually made, which was about the ethnicity-based line. Topic engaged, specific claim not; that is the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "Under your watch, you’ve reduced equity funding for Māori and Pacific, particularly in polytechs."

acuity.statement: Why did you cut only the Māori and Pacific equity funding line in vocational education?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer that equity funding "is still there" and isolates exactly the gap in it — the one funding line she did not mention — turning her own framing into the follow-up. The question could not have been asked in this form had she answered differently, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "The equity funding, in terms of the disability funding and the funding for those that have not had prior achievement in their compulsory education is still there."

acuity.statement: Because vocational education is my responsibility and the Minister for Universities will have whatever his intention is there.
acuity.explanation: Engages the "only" in the question put to her — explaining the scope of her own portfolio against the universities portfolio — so it is aimed at the question's premise rather than at prepared material. It does not take up the substantive half of the question (why the line was cut at all), so it is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "Why did you cut only the Māori and Pacific equity funding line in vocational education?"

acuity.statement: Yes, which we cut, but have retained the equity funding for disabled students and students with low prior achievement. That is the focus, on those with most need, regardless of ethnicity.
acuity.explanation: Halbert interrupts to redirect her to the Māori and Pacific line specifically, and she takes that up head-on: concedes the precise point ("which we cut") and then disputes the implication by setting out what was retained. Accepting part and contesting the rest of the thing just said is the strongest form of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "Sorry, I’m talking about Māori and Pacific equity funding."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. The Minister for Vocational Education hasn’t answered my core questions around how many job cuts she is expecting as a result of this Budget, and campus closures and course reductions. I invite her to respond to those.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the answer just given and identifies precisely which of the questions it left unaddressed — job cuts, campus closures, course reductions — then puts them again. The turn would be different had Simmonds covered them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ve had no update information across the whole sector" — actually responding to Hon Penny Simmonds' preceding answer, which addressed staff disruption, the $20 million fund and meetings with Otago but not job-cut numbers

acuity.statement: Thank you. My apologies. I didn’t refer to the job cuts. I’ve had no update information across the whole sector in terms of the final number of job cuts because some institutions are still working through that. Also, the strategically important fund will take some of the pressure away from areas where they may have been considering cuts.

acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing the previous turn said did not exist, and names it. It leaves the sawmill-closure and MSD-demand strands of the question untouched, so it engages the main claim rather than the whole turn.
