acuity.responding_to: "where is the employment strategy in terms of this Government? We don’t see one." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I’m going to have a third go at asking the Minister. She’s promised that her Government will create 240,000 new jobs. Could she please confirm how that number was calculated?
acuity.explanation: On the subject of the debate but indifferent to the answer just given — by her own account it is the same question put a third time, so it would read identically whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just set out the Employment Investment Strategy, case managers and Mana in Mahi, and this question does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: Well, from Budget 2025, it was Treasury’s forecast at that time that there would be job growth of 2.7 percent, 240,000 jobs.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question asked by naming the source and the derivation of the figure. It does not reach the second half of the question about population growth, which is why it is not a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Could she please confirm how that number was calculated?" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Can she confirm that that calculation that she’s referred to by Treasury is actually job growth based on population growth, not any specific action that her Government has taken?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer just given and draws out its consequence — that a Treasury forecast is not a government achievement. The question is built entirely on the preceding reply and could not exist without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it was Treasury’s forecast at that time that there would be job growth of 2.7 percent, 240,000 jobs" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I’ll correct the member, because I’ve already said it in this House. The Government is very different from the previous one in terms of who they believe creates the jobs: businesses create jobs.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — the premise that government action should be visible in the number — by arguing that businesses, not governments, create jobs, then moves to prepared material on Qantas seats and infrastructure projects. It never addresses how the 240,000 figure was calculated, which is what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is actually job growth based on population growth, not any specific action that her Government has taken" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: It is really a question that I have asked and I have not had an answer for. I think it’s a central one. Twenty-six thousand more people are unemployed than there were under our Government. While the Minister for Social Development and Employment gave me figures for what it cost the country this year, she did not give me the answer to the question, which is: what is the difference in cost between what it cost under a Labour Government, when we had less unemployment, and the cost that it is now because we have 76,000 people that are unemployed and having to receive that money?
acuity.explanation: Works directly off the figure the Minister supplied, identifies precisely which part of the question it left unanswered, and restates the comparison sought. It engages the answers given rather than the immediately preceding turn on job creation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The member asked specifically: what is the taxpayer bill for those on the jobseeker benefit for 2025-2026? It’s $4.6 billion." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: As I said, we now are forecasting in the 2025-26 appropriation documents $4.6 billion on the jobseeker benefit. That member wants to ask a question about comparing a cost to 2023. I’ve gone through the figures, I’ve explained how we get to this point in terms of the economic cycle, and she seems to have missed the point that we have come in at a time where high spending, high interest rates, high inflation led to economic recession and the harshest economic times since the 1990s.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the comparison being asked for and explains why she declines to make it, which is engagement with the question; but it then returns to the prepared economic-cycle account rather than supplying or refusing the number on its merits.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the difference in cost between what it cost under a Labour Government, when we had less unemployment, and the cost that it is now" — Helen White

acuity.statement: No, it’s not continuous, it’s someone who goes on and off, but hopefully your maths will tell you that 12.2 is a lot less than 18.2, which just happens to line up with the six years that Labour was in office.
acuity.explanation: Takes the interjector's specific objection, concedes it outright, then argues why it does not disturb the comparison she drew. The reply would be different had the interjection been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Not continuous—they're not continuous years." — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I was asking the Minister specifically around the 19,000 fewer jobs for those young people and what the Government’s solution was to finding a place for them if there was no job there. The Minister’s answer was that her Government was going to create 240,000 new jobs. Well, I would just like to understand, from the Minister, how did she get that figure?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and pursuing a ministerial claim, but it engages nothing in the turn it follows; it resumes the member's own earlier line of questioning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston's preceding turn was about lifetime years on jobseeker support and CPI indexation of benefit rates, and this statement does not take any of it up — it returns to an earlier answer not in this exchange.

acuity.statement: I’m not going to list the infrastructure projects that have been already quoted in this House around the creation of new jobs. One thing that’s very different about the Government we have today as opposed to the one that was outgoing in 2023 is we’re clear that it’s not the Government creating the jobs.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand — the request for the initiatives behind the figure — by expressly declining to list them, then pivots to a general contrast with the previous Government. The central question, how the 240,000 was derived, is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If she's able to, what specific initiatives will produce those 240,000 jobs?" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: Does she think it is fair for a greater proportion of people to be declined assistance at a time of high cost of living pressures and front-line organisations talking about increasing homelessness?
acuity.explanation: Squarely within the estimates debate and directed at the Minister, but it engages no part of the preceding turn; it opens a separate line on declined advances.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston had just argued that the Government creates the conditions for jobs rather than creating jobs itself, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Minister, is it factually correct that disabled people will be disproportionately pushed into deeper hardship as a result of the changes that she has made when it comes to eligibility for accommodation supplements for people who have boarders?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on a different aspect of the same portfolio; nothing in it depends on what was said immediately before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen had just pressed the Minister on how the figure of 240,000 jobs was calculated, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I just want to come into the sanctions area now. In terms of the culture, what communities are saying to us is that the culture, sadly, has changed tremendously given where we were a couple of years ago.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the previous speaker's 'changing culture' strand and corroborates it from community feedback, then moves to his own prepared questions on sanctions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it could instead be because of a changing culture at Work and Income due to increased anti-beneficiary rhetoric" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: The other great news, of course, is that we introduced non-financial sanctions for the very reason that there was a concern for a blunt financial sanction where there are children in the household. There will be a review after 12 months, and the next two non-financial sanctions don’t come in until 1 October. That was very deliberate and about giving Ministry of Social Development case managers more options to have a sanction that was more suitable and appropriate to that family.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the children-in-household strand of the questions put to her and explains the policy response, though the specific asks — the size of the increase in sanctions and the correlation with jobseeker numbers — go unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How many of those families are ones with children who have been punished by the sanctions strategy?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: Just going back to those 240,000 new jobs, I am aware that the Minister has said that’s going to come from a range of infrastructure projects and she doesn’t want to list them out, but I would still like to know how she arrived at the figure of 240,000 additional jobs. I would also like to know: is she using job growth based on population growth?
acuity.explanation: Quotes back the Minister's refusal, accepts it, isolates the part of the question it left unanswered, and sharpens it into a testable hypothesis about population-based job growth. Could not have been delivered against a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm not going to list the infrastructure projects that have been already quoted in this House around the creation of new jobs." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Does the Minister accept that there’s a real possibility that the increase in sanctions may have led to an increase in previous beneficiaries not having enough food and seeking help from food banks, and this also may have led to an increase in beneficiaries becoming homeless?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the sanctions exchange and implicitly contests the Minister's minimising framing by asking about downstream effects, but it does not engage her traffic-light figures or any specific claim she made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The number of people who are actually under a sanction is incredibly small, which I think is great news." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I’m not sure if the Minister for Social Development and Employment has answered my question, which is: has an increase in sanctions correlated with a reduction in job seekers?
acuity.explanation: Audits the answer he received, identifies precisely which of his questions it left out, and re-puts it. That is engagement with the content of the reply, though he adds nothing new to the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The number of people who are actually under a sanction is incredibly small, which I think is great news." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I will say again in this Chamber—because it tends to be misrepresented on frequent occasion—no one is sanctioned for not getting a job; they are sanctioned because they are not fulfilling their work obligations, which are things like going to an interview, having a CV, fulfilling their appointments with the Ministry of Social Development, and taking the necessary steps to look for, prepare for, and find a job.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the premise she takes the questions to rest on — what sanctions are actually imposed for — which engages the framing of the questions, but leaves the correlation, food bank and homelessness questions entirely unaddressed and returns to the review point she had already made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has an increase in sanctions correlated with a reduction in job seekers?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: Has she made an inquiry? I’ve asked about specific payments, not Consumers Price Index, which we know is a flawed system and it doesn’t quite manage to do that. Has she looked to make sure that those families can pay their bills?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's CPI-indexation answer by name and rejects it as non-responsive to what was asked, redirecting to actual payment adequacy. Engages a specific earlier claim rather than merely restating the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is why we index to CPI the jobseeker benefit." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: In relation to her first question—what sort of money was freed up from potential early childhood pay equity claims—the answer to that is none, because it was held in contingency. As to what amount was held in contingency on behalf of early childhood education (ECE), I don’t have that figure. I’d be happy to ask the Minister responsible, which is the Minister of Finance, for that information, if indeed it exists.
acuity.explanation: Takes Tinetti's first question in its own terms, gives a direct answer to it (none), explains why (held in contingency), and then addresses the obvious follow-on about the contingency amount by saying he does not hold the figure and naming who does. The reply is structured around her question and could not have been delivered had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how much funding, if any, for Budget 2025 was freed up specifically pausing or stopping ECE sector pay equity claims?" — Jan Tinetti

acuity.statement: Well, first of all, the great thing about our democracy is that the people can vote for whoever they like. Maybe one day you’ll be able to vote for the Treasury, but the Treasury wasn’t on the ballot at the last election. These people over here were elected to make decisions, so the fact that we’re not doing everything the Treasury tells us to—that’s called democracy.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the load-bearing premise of the question just put — that departing from Treasury's advice requires justification — and disputes it, arguing that elected ministers rather than officials make the decision. Whether the argument is sound is a separate question; as engagement it is squarely aimed at the claim it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why did the Associate Minister of Education go ahead with setting up a ministerial advisory group (MAG) for an ECE funding review when that was against Treasury’s advice" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: One very short question, again following on from the Hon Jan Tinetti on early childhood education (ECE): why did the Associate Minister of Education go ahead with setting up a ministerial advisory group (MAG) for an ECE funding review when that was against Treasury’s advice, especially now we see there are already members of that MAG who have left the MAG?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under examination and explicitly placed in the running ECE line of questioning, which is the gesture at the debate, but it engages no part of the answer immediately preceding it — Seymour's case for devolving remuneration judgment goes untouched. Prepared material on the right subject sits in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just argued that "those people should have more say about how they apply their funding to remunerate the teachers" and that the pay parity changes "will really enhance the value of teachers and skills, experience, and qualifications"; this question does not take up either point, raising the MAG and Treasury's advice instead.

acuity.statement: I think it is peculiar that the four-year period that the Budget is in—I’m assuming that means that the Minister of Education has decided that NCEA changes will not happen until 2029, so we will see how that goes.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific point Prime had just made about the Budget's forecast period and draws a consequence from it (that NCEA changes are therefore not planned before 2029), before moving on to his own prepared line on curriculum. Partial but pointable engagement with the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Budget actually covers a forecast period" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: As the Opposition are failing to ask any questions, I thought I would help out with the whole procedure and start by just talking a little bit about the communities of learning, which I understand are being disestablished.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn contained a specific question about curriculum funding; this engages no part of it. The reference to the Opposition is a dismissal, not engagement with content. Still within the same Estimates debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan had just asked "What is in the Budget on the implementation of new curricula and new subject lists?" and this statement does not take it up — it dismisses the Opposition as asking nothing and opens an unrelated topic.

acuity.statement: That’s OK. It’s a nice to get a question about this Budget rather than imaginary future Budgets. But it was something that the sector had called for very loudly. They wanted an extra learning support budget; they wanted additional funds put into the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme and teacher-aides and learning support coordinators, and they overwhelmingly lobbied me to disestablish the communities of learning or kāhui ako. We listened to their feedback. We have done that. We’re winding it down over a number of years while we power up the learning support budget, and it has been very, very well received by the sector.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific matter put to her — why the communities of learning are being disestablished and where the freed-up money goes — and supplies the sector-demand rationale and the learning support destination. Loses something because the money question is answered only in general terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a lot of money that has been freed up that can be used for other purposes" and the invitation to "talk to the committee about the disestablishment" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I don’t know why the Minister did not answer the questions about curriculum and subjects. Regardless of the NCEA change programme, or entire scrapping of it that the Minister is proposing, curriculum is supposed to start next year.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the exchange by observing a non-answer, but takes up no part of the substance Stanford actually gave; it returns to the questioner's own prior line. On-topic prepared pressing, so the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just explained the disestablishment of kāhui ako and the learning support budget, and this statement engages none of that content — it notes the earlier curriculum question went unanswered and re-presses it.

acuity.statement: In terms of this year’s Budget, there was plenty put aside for additional curriculum advisers, specialty secondary curriculum advisers, and the member will be able to find that in the information sheets that are printed on the ministry website.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the curriculum-funding question just put, naming what the Budget contains and where the member can find it. The reply would have been different had Prime asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "curriculum is supposed to start next year... Can the Minister please talk to the Budget for that" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m so glad that the Associate Minister and the Minister of Education mentioned about kāhui ako, because can I check with the Minister that when in this Budget, kāhui ako has been removed, has the Minister consulted with unions, which was advised as a priority?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own claim of having listened to sector feedback and tests it against a specific omission — whether unions were consulted. The question exists only because of what was said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they overwhelmingly lobbied me to disestablish the communities of learning or kāhui ako. We listened to their feedback." — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Look, I thank the Minister of Education for referring this very good question to me. I want to talk a little bit about how the Healthy School Lunches Programme is performing. In short, it is performing exceedingly well.
acuity.explanation: The speech engages no part of any preceding member's argument and would read identically whatever had been said before it. It remains within the Estimates debate on education, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan had asked whether unions were consulted before kāhui ako was removed, and this speech does not take that up; it answers a question the speaker put to the Minister himself.

acuity.statement: Historically, Māori education has been underfunded across the board, only getting, at most, 1 percent of the full Budget, no matter who’s in Government. I’d just really like to know from the Minister what in Budget 2025 is going to eradicate these waiting lists so that there are more resources and there’s some more capacity for Māori education for tamariki Māori across the board in Māori education.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on a different strand of the same Estimates debate. It is squarely about Budget 2025, which is the matter under debate, but it engages no part of the preceding speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just spoken about the Healthy School Lunches Programme's on-time delivery and savings, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her question; I thank all members for questions on early childhood. In relation to kōhanga reo, and te puna reo for that matter, in this Budget we have carried on with business as usual.
acuity.explanation: Answers the Budget-2025 strand of the question put to him, stating plainly that nothing changed this Budget and pointing to the previous one. He engages the funding question but not the waiting-list claim that was the core of it, so partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what in Budget 2025 is going to eradicate these waiting lists" — Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: is she comfortable being the Minister of Education who oversaw the daylight robbery of teachers’ rights to pay equity? Will the Minister commit, like the Associate Minister of Education did earlier, to asking the Minister of Finance what the figure was that was saved from the cancellation of those pay equity claims? I want that commitment.
acuity.explanation: New prepared material that engages nothing of the preceding answer, though it is on the Budget under debate and glances back at an undertaking the Associate Minister gave earlier in the session. Top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just spoken about kōhanga reo and te puna reo funding being unchanged in this Budget, and this statement does not take it up; it opens the separate subject of pay equity.

acuity.statement: Just this week, we announced that our Elective Boost at the beginning of this year performed over 16,000 additional outsourced elective procedures to ensure more Kiwis get access to the treatments they need, and puts us on track to meet the 2024-25 milestone of 63 percent of patients receiving treatment within four months.
acuity.explanation: Uffindell put a specific list to the Minister (Elective Boost, wait-lists, primary care, cancer medicines). Brown takes up Elective Boost by name and supplies the figure and target asked for, and elsewhere in the same turn works through the cancer medicines and primary care items. The turn would read differently had Uffindell asked about something else, though much of it is prepared ministerial framing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My questions for the Minister would be if he could give us a little bit of thought around Elective Boost, the wait-list progress around the primary care action plan" — Sam Uffindell

acuity.statement: This Government campaigned on making cuts to back-office services in order to be able to, in their logic, free up more funds to support clinical services. I’d like the Minister to describe how the programme of cuts for the current financial year will go ahead, what level of cuts have been identified, and whether that quantum of money to be released by cuts matches the difference between the deficit at the end of the last financial year of $900 million and the projected deficit of $200 million at the end of the current financial year.
acuity.explanation: She engages the subject of Brown's opening — Health New Zealand's funding position — and presses its other side (the savings programme and the deficit path), but she does not take up any of his specific claims about staff numbers, Elective Boost or cancer medicines. Topic engaged, claims not; a partial engagement that then runs on prepared lines.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government is delivering record investment in our health system in Budget 2025" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I have a pātai to the Minister in relation to the hauora Māori appropriations and am wanting to examine where the spend has gone. What gains have been made in terms of reaching the proposed targets for closing the life-expectancy gap between Māori and nonMāori, and what are the specific initiatives that are funded through new money in the hauora Māori appropriation?
acuity.explanation: A prepared line of questioning on the Vote under examination, so it is at least on the matter before the committee, but it engages no part of the Minister's opening or of Verrall's question. It would have been put word-for-word whatever had been said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about record health investment, additional nurses and doctors, cancer medicines and Elective Boost, and this statement does not take any of it up — it opens an unrelated line on hauora Māori appropriations.

acuity.statement: I would point her to page 38 of Health New Zealand’s statement of performance expectations, which outlines Health New Zealand’s revenue and expenditure for the financial year that has to do with this Budget.
acuity.explanation: He names the member, takes up her subject (Health New Zealand's budget) and answers it with a document reference and revenue/expenditure figures, so one strand is engaged. But the specific question — the scale of the identified cuts and whether they close the $900m-to-$200m deficit gap — is not taken up; he answers with the expenditure side instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether that quantum of money to be released by cuts matches the difference between the deficit at the end of the last financial year of $900 million and the projected deficit of $200 million" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The question, however, related to the scale of the cuts or the, you might prefer to call it, “savings programme” or “efficiencies”.
acuity.explanation: She works directly on the answer just given: identifies the mismatch between what she asked and what he supplied, and pre-empts the terminological dodge by naming the alternative labels he might prefer. This sentence could not have been spoken before his reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would point her to page 38 of Health New Zealand’s statement of performance expectations" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Well, as I said, we’re focused on the delivery of services, and as pointed out on page 38 of the statement of performance expectations, we are investing more into Health New Zealand than ever before.
acuity.explanation: Verrall had just said the document did not answer her question; he restates the same document and the same investment framing without engaging the savings question at all. There is a faint gesture later in the turn ("when it comes to the organisation and how it operates"), which keeps it off the floor, but the substance of her correction is untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The question, however, related to the scale of the cuts" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The Minister can direct me to a document that does not answer my question as much as he likes, and I will take this opportunity to be clear that the question wasn’t answered.
acuity.explanation: Aimed squarely at what he had just done: it names the device (pointing to a document), states what it failed to do, and draws out the consequence for the committee's scrutiny of the Vote. Wholly dependent on the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I point the member to the statement of performance expectations, which clearly demonstrates that this Government is investing more" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: There have been change processes done, but those change processes have been completed. There are no major change programmes under way at Health New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Pressed a third time, he finally takes up the actual question and gives it a substantive answer — that the change processes are finished and none are under way. That is engagement with the specific claim, not just the topic; the rest of the turn reverts to prepared delivery-for-patients material, which holds it short of the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Would he reconsider answering what programme of cuts is under way at Health New Zealand?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The Minister didn’t answer my first question, which was: how much money is budgeted for recolonising the curriculum? In fact, I’ll point out that in the Minister’s answer, she talked about most Māori being in English-medium schools, and so that question is particularly relevant because it is the recolonising of that particular curriculum.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific point Stanford had just made (most Māori children are in English-medium/mainstream schooling) and turns it back as the reason her unanswered question matters. The turn would have to be different had Stanford not made that claim, so this is genuine engagement rather than a restated question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You’ve got to remember that most Māori children are in the mainstream." — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: The member will be well aware that there wasn’t anything in this Budget for curriculum design.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question just put — the budget line asked about — with a flat denial that it exists. Blunt and unelaborated, but squarely aimed at the thing asked; vagueness would be a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how much money is budgeted for recolonising the curriculum?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Why does the Minister listen to people like Elizabeth Rata, with an established history of anti-Māori views?
acuity.explanation: Still within the matter under debate (curriculum and its authorship), but engages no part of the answer it follows; it neither disputes the claim that no money was appropriated nor draws a consequence from it. A gesture at the subject rather than the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just said there wasn’t anything in this Budget for curriculum design, and this statement does not take that answer up — it opens a fresh line about who is writing the curriculum

acuity.statement: In answer to that, I didn’t hear that particular interview, so I can’t comment, but I would say that there is a huge amount of resource going into this Budget to raise Māori achievement.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand — she addresses the premise about the source by saying she did not hear it — and then returns to prepared material on Budget resourcing for Māori achievement. Partial engagement that can still be pointed at, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why does the Minister listen to people like Elizabeth Rata" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Our follow-up question is: we have seen the statistics around the fact that ākonga Māori and kaupapa Māori-medium education do better at NCEA, so is what the Minister’s saying that the only way for ākonga Māori to achieve is through a Eurocentric pedological framework?
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated framing directly, supplying counter-evidence (Māori-medium NCEA results) and pressing her to own the implication. Whether the implication is a fair reading of what she said is a Rigor question; the engagement itself is close and specific.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think about making sure that outcomes for tamariki Māori are equal to, if not better than, everybody else in the system" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: The member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan is exactly right, which is why there is so much investment going into kura kaupapa Māori.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the premise just put to her and uses it as the pivot into her own answer about kura kaupapa Māori investment, which answers the topic rather than the sharper charge about a Eurocentric framework. Real engagement with one strand, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ākonga Māori and kaupapa Māori-medium education do better at NCEA" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Minister: has she consulted with Ngā Tapuwae college with regards to NCEA, where they’ve had some of the most successful results in terms of Māori students over the last few years, led by Arihia Stirling?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — NCEA and consultation — but it is a fresh, self-contained question about one school rather than any engagement with the budgeting question or the principals' letter just raised. Prepared ground on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan had asked how much has been budgeted for the scrapping of NCEA and whether the Minister would respond to the open letter from 121 principals, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: I see that the Minister of Education didn’t answer the first questions around the Budget for the replacement of NCEA. We find it interesting, through others, not herself directly, that apparently there is no budget for it, when it is supposed to come into effect next year.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the unanswered budgeting question from the preceding exchange and pushes it a step further by setting the apparent absence of funding against the stated start date. Engagement with the strand rather than with a specific claim, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how much has she budgeted or is she intending to budget in supplementary budgets for the scrapping of NCEA?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: On that question, I think we are a little bit concerned by the fact that this is something that is happening within the financial year of Budget 2025, yet the Minister could not respond to the fact that something as major as replacing the qualification of Aotearoa New Zealand has been considered.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the preceding turn's point about the timing mismatch and draws out its consequence, naming the financial year. It builds on rather than restates, though it adds no new evidence to the strand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "apparently there is no budget for it, when it is supposed to come into effect next year" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: We are in a consultation phase. No decisions have been made. I was very clear in this year’s Budget when I talked about the massive investment, predominantly in primary schools, and I said that next year’s Budget would be a secondary Budget. We haven’t made decisions. Nothing has been budgeted for at this point because we’re only just at the very start of consultation, which is going to take some time. In terms of speaking with Ngā Kura ā Iwi o Aotearoa on te reo Māori, we have been doing, and I spoke with Arihia this morning.
acuity.explanation: Answers two different members' questions in one turn: it supplies a direct answer on the NCEA budget (nothing appropriated, with the reason) and answers Jackson's consultation question by naming the person he named and when she spoke to her. The turn would be unrecognisable had those questions not been asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has she worked with this school, which is one of te ao Māori’s most successful schools" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: We see, in terms of the Budget document—particularly the Cabinet paper and the Budget paper that was released last week—that anything to do with the Budget is a long-term process, so what conversations has the Minister had with the Minister of Finance around something like this in anticipation to any changes to NCEA?
acuity.explanation: Attacks the reasoning in the answer just given: if Budget processes are long-term, being early in consultation does not explain the absence of any provision. It cites the documents that support the premise and converts the answer into a new, narrower question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Nothing has been budgeted for at this point because we’re only just at the very start of consultation" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: I mean, this is very difficult, because it is something that we’re talking about right now, and for it to be able to be effectively implemented, if it is to be approved, we need to know how much consideration the Minister has given to the funding that is going to be required for the effective implementation of this—for example, what budget is there for additional teaching and staffing and professional learning and development? What budget is there for industry skills boards, who are going to have the role of developing the curriculum and assessment under this proposal? Surely the Minister and the ministry have done some thinking about this, because if they haven’t and it starts next year, then we have a problem.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer that nothing is budgeted and works out what it would mean, itemising the cost lines (staffing, PLD, industry skills boards) that the answer implies have no provision. The closing clause states the consequence of the answer rather than ignoring it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Nothing has been budgeted for at this point" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Well, as I stated earlier, if the member looks at page 38 of the statement of performance expectations, the organisation has a projected deficit of $200 million. That means that their expenditure will be $200 million more than their revenue. The Government is supporting Health New Zealand to deliver services and for the organisation to spend more than what it has been provided in its revenues so that we can maintain and deliver the services that it needs.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Verrall's specific $200 million figure and confirms it is still the projected deficit, pointing to the page of the document it comes from — genuine engagement with the number put to him. But two of her three strands (whether a capital injection is coming, and the revised expected deficit) are left untouched, and the answer slides into revenue appropriations instead, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: “is it the Government’s position that that $200 million deficit target no longer applies at the end of this financial year?”

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. We heard from the Minister of Health about the revenue and expenditure in Health New Zealand; we would really like to hear about the deficit for Health New Zealand and how the deficit from the 2024-25 financial year will be addressed. Is it by revenue from the Vote or by a different capital injection?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly isolates what the Minister did supply (revenue and expenditure) from what he did not (how the deficit is to be funded), and narrows the question to a binary — Vote revenue or capital injection. The question would be worded differently had the Minister answered differently, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: “Overall, there is increased revenue for Health New Zealand and increased expenditure being provided for.”

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. In terms of hauora Māori services, there’s been an increase in the appropriation. Again, the statement of performance expectations highlights total revenue increasing from $484 million to $555 million. The expenditure is projected to be $555 million in the Budget 2025-26 year. One of the key initiatives—and the member touched on it—was in relation to the immunisation target that we have set.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the appropriation movement Lyndon asked for and then takes up her immunisation-targets strand by name with Māori two-year-old immunisation rates. Two of her four strands (maternity access and kaupapa Māori youth mental health funding) are not engaged here, which holds this below the top of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: “seeking answers from the Minister of Health in relation to what new money has eventuated in terms of spend for hauora Māori services”

acuity.statement: In fact, this Government set the first targets for this country ever in mental health—five mental health targets. Three of them are around faster access. One specifically the member referenced for our young people: accessing specialist services. The target we set is 80 percent to access specialist services in three weeks. The latest data for quarter three of the financial year 2024-25 is a national average of 82.4 percent. There was a question more specifically for the access rate for Māori, and I’m happy to report Māori are accessing our services faster than the national average, at 84.9 percent.
acuity.explanation: Identifies which of Lyndon's strands he is answering, gives the youth specialist-access target and figure she asked about, and volunteers the Māori-specific access rate because she asked for the Māori cut. Falls short of 1.0 because the funding half of her question goes unanswered and the target framing is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: “for kaupapa Māori mental health youth services, how are we treading in terms of both the funding that has gone into those services and what targets may have been set for our young people”

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, if I can please then ask the Minister for Mental Health, just following on from those questions about under-19-year-olds—the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission has got data showing that there are worsening trends in youth access to specialist mental health services—I’m sure he’s aware of it—to March 2025, where, for GP referrals for under-19s, nearly 30 percent were declined. That was up from nearly one in four last year. Is the mental health Minister now saying that that has improved—and I’m speaking here about specialist mental health services, not about accessing services for more complex needs.
acuity.explanation: Confronts the Minister's just-stated improvement claim with countervailing Commission data on the same cohort and the same service tier, and pre-empts the obvious deflection by stipulating which services she means. This question cannot exist without the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: “we know people are accessing specialist services by well over the target of 80 percent in three weeks”

acuity.statement: I can report that the access has increased. If you look back at specialist services for under-25s, in quarter one of the financial year 2024-25, the access rate was 72.8 percent were being seen within three weeks. In the following quarter, quarter two, that went up to 77.1 percent—so from 72.8 percent to 77.1 percent—and in the latest data we have for quarter three, it even goes up again, to 77.5 percent.
acuity.explanation: Answers her direct question with a yes and a quarterly series, so one strand is squarely taken up. But the metric he answers on (share seen within three weeks) is not the metric she raised (share of GP referrals declined), so the specific claim of worsening decline rates is engaged only at topic level.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: “Is the mental health Minister now saying that that has improved”

acuity.statement: I’m wondering then if the Minister can explain in Official Information Act response 00092305, released on 11 July 2025, why the numbers are showing that the number of young people being declined and not being referred from general practice services has risen under his watch rather than declined? Is this because he is measuring different things, and is he prepared to provide a response to that question, which is from his own officials?
acuity.explanation: Diagnoses exactly how the Minister's answer missed hers — that he may be measuring a different thing — and pins the counter-evidence to a numbered OIA release from his own officials. This is the mismatch between his figures and hers taken up and pressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: “in the latest data we have for quarter three, it even goes up again, to 77.5 percent”

acuity.statement: Well, I think you’ll agree that when you look at the reasons for people being declined, more often than not it is because there is a more appropriate service than the service that the individual has been referred to. I’d only look to investments into programmes like Gumboot Friday: an extra 10,000 young people seen, an extra 30,000 sessions.
acuity.explanation: Finally engages the decline figures themselves by offering an account of why a referral is declined — redirection to a more appropriate service — which is a direct answer to the thing she asked him to explain. It then leaves the OIA numbers unexplained and moves to investment figures, so engagement is real but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: “the number of young people being declined and not being referred from general practice services has risen under his watch”

acuity.statement: A significant part of this Budget is aligned with supporting general practice in a number of ways: increased capitation funding, increased funding to support practices to make them more accessible, performance-based funding to improve immunisation outcomes, and $26 million in additional funding to help GPs keep fees capped for community services card holders and those on low incomes, and to ensure those under 14 continue to receive free GP access.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a list of named Budget measures in direct answer to the question asked, several of which (fee caps, free under-14s) bear on cost specifically. It engages the question put rather than reciting unrelated material, but drifts toward access and does not take up the survey finding that one in six miss a GP visit because of cost, so it is a strong but incomplete engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "what initiatives does the Government have under way to reduce the cost of general practice visits?"

acuity.statement: Will any of the initiatives that the Minister listed bring down the cost of seeing a GP during this cost of living crisis?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer just given and tests it against the measure originally asked about, pressing the point that the listed measures went to access rather than price. The question could not have been asked in this form if the Minister had answered differently, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "There’s a number of things the Government’s doing to improve access to general practice."

acuity.statement: As I outlined in my answer, there’s a number of initiatives that we do to provide lower-cost access for New Zealanders: those community services card holders, to make sure they can access GPs at much lower cost than non - community services card holders; the Very Low Cost Access scheme, which has been in place for many years, that continues to support access for many New Zealanders living in low socioeconomic neighbourhoods and communities to be able to access lower-cost general practice.
acuity.explanation: Refers back to the same list rather than answering the new question of whether the cost of a visit will fall, but it does engage one strand — that some patients already pay less — rather than ignoring the question. Partial engagement, largely recycled material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "Will any of the initiatives that the Minister listed bring down the cost of seeing a GP"

acuity.statement: Is it acceptable, in a cost of living crisis, to pay $94 for a standard GP appointment?
acuity.explanation: Follows the strand of the previous answer by setting a concrete price against the Minister's claim that patients can access lower-cost care, which is a sharpening of the exchange rather than prepared material. It engages the topic of his answer more than any particular proposition in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "a number of initiatives that we do to provide lower-cost access for New Zealanders"

acuity.statement: Well, the vast, vast majority of New Zealanders don’t pay that much money to see a GP—and the misinformation being put out by the Labour Party, when the vast majority of patients pay far less than that to see a GP.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the specific figure just put to him and disputes its typicality, which is exactly the content of the question. The reply would be impossible if the previous turn had not cited a price — strong engagement, scored independently of its courtesy or accuracy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "to pay $94 for a standard GP appointment?"

acuity.statement: My first question is: is the risk structure of the capitation funding going to include addressing health inequities along ethnicities, and, if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the capitation funding the Minister named earlier and asks how it will be weighted, so it is anchored to something said in the debate, but it opens a prepared set of three questions rather than engaging the cost-of-visits argument that immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "increased capitation funding"

acuity.statement: In terms of the re-weighting of capitation, the factors that will be considered will be age, gender, deprivation, multi-morbidity, and rurality.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific list of weighting factors the question asked for, which is a direct answer to the first half of it. It leaves the "if not, why not" half untouched, so the engagement is real but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "is the risk structure of the capitation funding going to include addressing health inequities along ethnicities, and, if not, why not?"

acuity.statement: Just following on from that, does the Minister of Health accept that cultural safety is clinically relevant for patient outcomes?
acuity.explanation: Takes up precisely the thing the previous answer left out — ethnicity and cultural factors — and converts it into the next question. The question is shaped by the omission in the answer it follows, which is the mark of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the factors that will be considered will be age, gender, deprivation, multi-morbidity, and rurality"

acuity.statement: Well, this is getting into very much a sort of—it’s gone from the Budget to more of a philosophical debate here in terms of policy.
acuity.explanation: Addresses whether the question belongs in an Estimates debate rather than any part of its content; it recognises a question was asked but engages none of it. A gesture at the exchange, not an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "does the Minister of Health accept that cultural safety is clinically relevant for patient outcomes?"

acuity.statement: Well, ultimately, the role of our health workforces is to ensure that they are providing services which meet the needs of a variety of cultures who live in New Zealand, and a variety of ethnicities.
acuity.explanation: After the point of order he does take up the substance, affirming that workforces must meet the needs of different cultures, which is one strand of the question. He does not address the clinical-relevance proposition directly and moves on to the status of a consultation, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "does the Minister of Health accept that cultural safety is clinically relevant for patient outcomes?"

acuity.statement: The Health Infrastructure Plan, I note, doesn’t specifically talk about what is going to happen regarding the reduced dementia and psychogeriatric beds which were taken out of the Dunedin Hospital. You are on record, Minister, saying that that’s because the beds are better in the community, and I don’t actually disagree with the philosophy.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Health Infrastructure Plan that Brown had just held up as his Government's achievement and does something with it — names a specific gap in it (dementia and psychogeriatric beds at Dunedin), concedes part of his position on community care, and presses on the consequence. The question would have had to be written differently had Brown not just rested his answer on that plan.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "That is what we are doing with the Health Infrastructure Plan."

acuity.statement: There’s a range of work under way. Ultimately, the priority is to get the new hospital built. That’s my priority as Minister of Health: getting the new hospital built.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic Leary raised — Dunedin, models of care, where the beds sit — and later in the same answer gestures at care 'in the community', so there is something pointable. But the specific thing asked, what steps have been taken to create community beds, is set aside in favour of the hospital build and expectations of Health New Zealand. Partial engagement, not rebuttal or supply of the asked-for detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "what work has been done under your Government to create those beds in Dunedin"

acuity.statement: Can I just confirm, then, Minister, that when you said to the Otago Daily Times that work was under way to provide those beds in the community, in fact, nothing had been done by your Government?
acuity.explanation: Built directly out of the answer just given: it takes Brown's non-specific 'range of work under way' and converts it into a sharp inference against his earlier public statement, forcing him either to supply the steps or to concede. This follow-up could not exist without the content of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "There’s a range of work under way."

acuity.statement: Work is under way, and that work will continue to be done by Health New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Squarely refuses the proposition put to him — Leary asked him to confirm nothing had been done, and he denies it in the first clause — which is engagement with the specific claim. But he then returns to the hospital-construction material rather than the community work the confirmation was about, so the engagement is real yet shallow.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "in fact, nothing had been done by your Government?"

acuity.statement: Since the Associate Minister of Justice is in the chair, I actually want to start by asking a question to the Minister around court timeliness, particularly around some of the latest data coming out of the High Court regarding the time for scheduled trials.
acuity.explanation: Arbuckle's overview listed timeliness among the Courts Estimates themes and then put a legal aid question to the Minister; Xu-Nan picks up the timeliness heading but engages no claim or argument from that turn, delivering his own prepared line of questioning on High Court wait times. On the matter under debate, with a gesture at it, but not responsive to its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "In the Courts Estimates, we talked around timeliness and, again, infrastructure projects."

acuity.statement: Legal aid is at $328 million in there, and why is it important? It’s really important that people are given access to justice. It also means that they have the ability to get representation and also advice, especially when they go through a court or a justice system.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked, in its own terms: Arbuckle asked why legal aid matters and why funding rose, and she restates the figure he gave, explains the access-to-justice rationale, and then attributes the increase to rising volume. Directly shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "why is legal aid so important, and why is the Government funding increased levels?"

acuity.statement: To the member from the Green Party, when we’re talking about timeliness in the High Court, yes, I think what is important to note is that for the first time our timeliness measures are actually being put in place around the courts. For example, in the District Court, District Court Chief Judge Taumaunu has for the first time implemented some timeliness in the District Court. Now, I know that you’ve asked about the High Court, but we are making some improvements.
acuity.explanation: Addresses Xu-Nan's High Court timeliness question, openly acknowledges that she is first answering with District Court material rather than what he asked, and then does return with High Court case-volume and disposal figures. Clearly engaged with the specific question; marked down slightly because the initial substance is diverted to a different court from the one asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Auckland’s average wait time is 486 days" / his question on High Court trial timeliness

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Seeing as we have the Associate Minister of Justice in the chair, I thought I’d follow on, on the theme around stresses on the court system.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly continues the court-pressure thread McKee had just been answering on, and his material about judicial numbers and dilapidated courthouses is on exactly that question. But he engages none of her actual claims — not the timeliness categories, not the case-volume figures, not her assertion that improvements are demonstrable — and instead sets out two prepared documents. Topic engaged, specific argument untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "the timeliness improvements are slow but demonstrable. We’re getting there."

acuity.statement: I have a two-part question to two different Ministers to go back to primary care to discuss with the Minister around the revision of capitation funding and how those decisions were made to focus on the multimorbidities, on the gender, on the rurality, all of that. That came from, I believe, an analysis across 18 primary health organisations.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Leary in the same Estimates debate but engages none of it, opening a separate line on capitation funding. On-subject (health) prepared questioning rather than responsive debate; her second part touches mental health wait-lists but not Leary's claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary spoke about community-sector capacity, Waikato bed-locking and the mental health innovation fund's cofunding requirement, and this statement does not take any of it up (fragment of her turn: "what does he say to community providers who were promised to be able to access funding through the mental health innovation fund")

acuity.statement: In terms of the re-weighting of capitation, effectively, the work the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand are doing, yes, has analysed—and there’s been a piece of work done which does analyse—practices in a range of primary health organisations to look at need. Decisions have been made in relation to what the factors are, which will go into that re-weighting, as I outlined earlier in relation to the question from your colleague.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific premise of Lyndon's question — the PHO analysis and the weighting factors she listed (multimorbidity, rurality) — and explains what the re-weighting will do for those practices. Not a full 1.0 because he confirms rather than explains the methodology she asked about, and the equity/high-need strand is answered only by restating the factors before he moves to rural anecdote.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "That came from, I believe, an analysis across 18 primary health organisations. Are you able to give us more of a fulsome explanation as to how you landed in that space"

acuity.statement: I’d like to turn to investment in the health system infrastructure. The Minister received a briefing that was directed at identifying if the health system had the capacity to particularly meet demand for surgeries and planned care.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows Brown's capitation answer and is indifferent to it — she announces a turn to infrastructure instead. The question is substantive and on the health vote, but it would be word-for-word identical whatever Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about the re-weighting of capitation funding for general practice ("those practices which have patients who have a higher degree of deprivation or multimorbidity or rurality") and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: The member did, quite rightly, ask the question around an important issue where we have people on our mental health inpatient facilities that might be clinically ready to be discharged but there, potentially, is not the support services there. That is another task I’ve given the regional directors to look at—the occupancy rates of their inpatient facilities within their respective regions, and to ensure that we build out the system, that there is step-down care that we can discharge people into the community.
acuity.explanation: Restates Leary's specific mechanism (patients clinically ready for discharge with no step-down support, blocking beds), accepts it as a real problem, and says what he has tasked regional directors to do about it. The reply could not have been given against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "they are unable to be discharged because there are no community services available for them to be able to access, so they’re taking up beds"

acuity.statement: I thank the previous speaker for the question in relation to infrastructure and I acknowledge the infrastructure deficit, which is a challenge that we’ve inherited, but is also something which—if you look at the average age of health infrastructure, I believe the average age of health buildings owned by Health New Zealand is 47 years.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — he concedes the infrastructure deficit Verrall put to him — then answers the general topic (the plan, modular wards, named redevelopments) rather than her specific question about the regional bed shortfalls she enumerated. Partial engagement, pointable but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "what progress is being made now to address that bed deficit so that we can meet today’s demands, much less the future’s?"

acuity.statement: Why is it that the Health Infrastructure Plan did not set out those initiatives to have the modular hospital beds created and the number—why didn’t it state the bed deficit? Why didn’t the infrastructure plan name the number of beds to be added this year or in the next five years or in the next 10 years? In fact, there was more specificity in the Health Infrastructure Plan around the building of car parks than there was around the building of hospital beds.
acuity.explanation: Takes the document and the modular wards Brown had just offered as his answer and turns both against the answer, pressing on what the plan omits. Entirely dependent on what he had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "That’s why, as Minister of Health, we have released the Health Infrastructure Plan, which outlines the need to invest" and "in this year’s Budget we allocated funding for modular wards"

acuity.statement: Well, as much as I can answer that, because corrections isn’t the justice portfolio; it’s under the corrections portfolio—well, no, it actually has its own portfolio and its own budget as well. But what I can say is that this Government makes no apologies for holding people to account for bad behaviour.
acuity.explanation: Paul asked how the Government justifies the prison pipeline given recidivism rates. McKee flags the portfolio boundary but then does supply a justification — accountability changes attitudes, and incapacitating recidivists is itself a good outcome — so she takes up the 'how do you justify it' strand squarely. She does not engage the specific capital-spending comparison with hospitals and schools, nor the recidivism evidence, asserting the contrary instead. Engagement with part of the argument, not the whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "how does the Minister and her Government justify continuing an endless pipeline of people into prisons when recidivism rates show that sending people to prisons does not result in safer communities?"

acuity.statement: I actually just want to pick up from the question my colleague Tamatha Paul asked, and I’m interested in the Minister’s answer, because in Aotearoa New Zealand alone, data from the Department of Corrections as well as the ministry itself says that about 44 to 49 percent of released prisoners are reincarcerated within three to four years, with high rates among young male Māori and repeat offenders. It also says that there’s very little evidence that suggests longer sentences—they fail to deter repeat offending and may even increase risk of creating a criminal learning environment.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer as its starting point and attacks its load-bearing premise — that holding recidivists in prison changes attitudes and produces a positive outcome — by putting the department's own reincarceration figures and the deterrence evidence against it, then turning that into a funding question. The speech would be different had the Minister justified the policy on other grounds; it is built on what she actually said rather than merely referring to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "showing accountability actually can change attitudes" and "perhaps getting rehabilitated, then that is also a positive outcome"

acuity.statement: It’s quite simple, really. If you lock up violent criminals who repeatedly victimise people in the community, then they’re not in the community re-victimising people. It’s as simple as that.
acuity.explanation: Meets the deterrence-and-rehabilitation evidence with an incapacitation counter-argument, which engages one strand of what was put to her — repeat offenders and community safety. But it leaves the reincarceration figures untouched and never reaches Xu-Nan's actual question about the reduction in community-based rehabilitation funding, pivoting instead to an attack on the member. Partial engagement, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "there’s very little evidence that suggests longer sentences—they fail to deter repeat offending"

acuity.statement: Just in terms of meeting that objective of having the votes counted more quickly, has the Minister of Justice received advice that, actually, it may not be the case that the votes are counted more quickly? There would still be a substantial number of special votes.
acuity.explanation: Takes the rationale the Minister had just offered — that the count time forced an extended caretaker period, so enrolment must close earlier — and tests whether the change delivers it, pointing to special votes that would still have to be processed. The follow-up is shaped entirely by the answer given; a different justification would have required a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "what we found after the election was that the time taken to count those votes meant that we had to also ensure that the caretaker Government was extended as a result of that"

acuity.statement: The Government’s view is that it’s reasonable to require people to enrol before voting begins. Enrolment is compulsory in New Zealand, and the Government considers there’s plenty of advance notice ahead of an election for people to organise their enrolment.
acuity.explanation: Answers on the subject Walters raised — the enrolment deadline change — and defends it, so there is something pointable being engaged. But neither of the two questions actually put is taken up: the logic of letting serious offenders vote from a mental health facility while banning prisoners, and whether funding the Electoral Commission to count within 14 days was considered instead. Topic engaged, specific questions not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "This is a really substantial proposal to change to our electoral law" — though her questions on the mental health facility anomaly and on simply funding the Electoral Commission go unanswered

acuity.statement: The first question is in terms of some of the other jurisdictions the Minister mentioned before. Could I ask the Minister how many of those jurisdictions have automatic enrolment at the age they’re entitled to enrol? Something like automatic enrolment would make a simple and reasonably low-cost and effective way of ensuring that people are enrolled to vote. Yes, what the Minister quoted undoubtedly is what those jurisdictions are doing, but I do want to know from the perspective of automatic enrolment.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own international comparison and does something with it: concedes the deadlines she quoted are accurate, then presses the specific omission — whether those same jurisdictions pair short deadlines with automatic enrolment. The speech could not have been delivered had she not run the comparative argument, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicole McKee: "When looking at the enrolment deadline in other countries, in Australia, the enrolment closes seven days after the issue of the writ for federal elections" / "In the United Kingdom, enrolment closes 12 working days before election day."

Over time, this should result in fewer hours for issuing and processing special votes, with associated cost and time savings.
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic he raised — automatic enrolment — and can be pointed at, but answers a different question from the one asked: it describes the Government's own automatic enrolment update policy rather than how many comparator jurisdictions enrol automatically, and leaves his second question on overseas New Zealanders untouched. Partial engagement, then prepared material.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Could I ask the Minister how many of those jurisdictions have automatic enrolment at the age they’re entitled to enrol?"

Engages the substance rather than restating prepared material.

acuity.statement: I just want to pick up on, particularly, the points that both the Minister and the Labour spokesperson Ingrid Leary just alluded to with regards to the Expert Advisory Committee on Drugs. The expert advisory committee was an amendment made to the Misuse of Drugs Act to allow for the classification to be recommended by the expert advisory committee in, I believe, the early 2000s. The really important thing to understand about the way that the expert advisory committee operates—and their mandate—is that they can only recommend where a substance should be classified in relation to where other substances are currently classified within the Misuse of Drugs Act. In layman’s terms, that basically means that all the expert advisory committee can look at is the harm of substances that are currently classified and recommend the classification relative to those other classified substances. That is, the expert advisory committee is not empowered to make recommendations with regard to other health-based, evidence-based interventions to actually reduce drug harm. It is therefore self-referential.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick names the preceding Labour speaker's specific reassurance — that the expert advisory committee is genuinely expert and so a sufficient safeguard — and does something with it, explaining the committee's statutory mandate to argue that its expertise is confined to relative classification and therefore cannot bear the weight Leary puts on it. The speech would have to change if Leary had rested her support on something other than the committee; it is not merely a reference or a pivot. Marked just below 1.0 because the surrounding material (Vienna 2019, the Law Commission, He Ara Oranga, Turuki! Turuki!) is prepared and would have been delivered regardless.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "it’s great to see we have an expert advisory committee truly made up of the experts"
