The speech would have to be written differently had Watts not just run through ERP2 and its market-led approach.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'Our second emissions reduction plan is a blueprint for reducing emissions in the second half of this decade. The plan includes a market-led approach'

acuity.statement: Notably, we’re coming today off the back of yet another failure of an ETS auction under this Minister and under this Government, to which I cheekily asked him in scrutiny week, I believe last year, about whether the most effective climate policy that we are seeing from this Government is their inability to provide that certainty for the market so that those units ultimately end up getting cancelled and those permissions to pollute end up being cancelled.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the claim Watts had just made that the updated ETS settings are 'providing confidence and certainty to that market', by pointing at a failed auction as evidence the certainty is absent. It engages the specific assertion rather than the general topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'these settings would better support the scheme to meet emissions reduction targets, providing confidence and certainty to that market'

acuity.statement: Just on agricultural emissions reduction, I found it quite galling for the Minister to get up and talk about the investment that this Government is making in agricultural emissions reduction. Well, it turns out that the Minister announced a fund of approximately $400 million to “accelerate commercialisation of tools and technology to reduce on-farm emissions.” Well, guess what, guys! He reannounced the fund that already existed under the last Government and simultaneously managed to cut $48 million from it while reannouncing it.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the agricultural strand of Watts's ERP2 overview and disputes the substance of it with a specific counter-account of the fund's provenance and quantum. It is aimed at what he said rather than at him, and would change if he had not raised agricultural emissions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'ensure that we have an efficient and competitive agricultural sector to boost sustainable investment'

acuity.statement: Because out of the one side of your mouth, Minister, with your climate change hat on, you are going offshore and you are telling people that we are still holding to the same international negotiating positions that we did under the former Government; that is, the phase out of fossil fuels and fossil fuel subsidies. Yet out the other side of your mouth, here at home with your energy hat on, you are signing out $200 million in fossil fuel subsidies.
acuity.explanation: Engages the framing Watts opened with — that cutting emissions and growing the economy go hand in hand — by alleging the two portfolios pull in opposite directions, but the fossil fuel subsidy material is prepared ground he did not raise, so it answers the theme rather than any specific claim he made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'this Government is committed to meeting our climate change targets while driving economic growth'

acuity.statement: Unfortunately, it appears as though exactly what our concern was, which was that the Minister of Climate Change would open by reading off two sheets of paper, soaking up about 10 minutes of time, so that he could then sit himself down and not engage meaningfully whatsoever with the detail that we are asking him to share for the New Zealand public—because he has a responsibility to, because we have started to unpack the very nature of the document that he is saying is going to solve all of our problems.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand running through Russell's preceding turn — that the Minister is refusing to answer a straightforward question — and presses it as a complaint about non-engagement. But it does not take up the substance Russell put (the Paris Agreement commitment, the NZ First/ACT scepticism); it generalises to the Minister's conduct. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It's a very straightforward question that shouldn't take any thinking on the part of the Minister of Climate Change."

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair, for the opportunity to answer some of those questions. For those who are watching at home, the limitations on the ability and the time that we have to speak is constrained. I have about 10 minutes of total time to respond to questions during this 90-minute period, so it is not for the sake of not answering; it is simply to acknowledge that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific accusation just made — that he is deliberately declining to engage — and meets it head-on with a competing explanation (a 10-minute speaking allocation across a 90-minute session). It engages the charge rather than ignoring or merely naming it; it stops short of 1.0 only because it answers the accusation about his conduct and not yet any of the substantive questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "he's not willing to get up or defend or engage meaningfully whatsoever"

acuity.statement: In the context of the questions asked, on the opening statement of the climate change strategy that was produced, it notes very clearly that the coalition Government is committed to meeting its climate change targets. This is our climate strategy. That is the coalition Government’s strategy, and in order to respond to the question asked, again that remains the Government’s position.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the topic Russell raised and explicitly frames itself as responding to the question, but answers a different proposition from the one put: she asked specifically about the Paris Agreement after citing NZ First and ACT scepticism about it, and the reply restates commitment to 'climate change targets' without naming Paris. Topic engaged, specific claim sidestepped.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Can the Minister, please, confirm that this Government is committed to meeting the Paris Agreement?"

acuity.statement: Getting rid of the Māori Health Authority has impacted on all marae in the country. Downgrading the value of te reo Māori has done the same. My question to the Minister is: if he wants to engage with Māori, how is he going to do that given that Māori don’t trust this Government at all and the Government is going to be on the back foot in being able to do that work?
acuity.explanation: Clearly in the same debate and gestures at the Minister's remarks, but no part of the preceding turn's content (gas supply, ETS clearing, waste methane) is engaged, and the material it does respond to cannot be pointed at in the text available. Prepared ground on the right subject, so the top of the unpointable band rather than zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts' preceding turn addressed CCUS, the ETS auction and waste management, and this statement does not take any of that up; it engages the marae stocktake from the Minister's opening speech, which is not in this window.

acuity.statement: Yeah, I do want to respond to those comments because I think they are without substance in the context of the allegations that were made. To make a comment and a gross generalisation that Māori do not trust this Government is simply not one which is based in any evidential fact or substance.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the precise premise of the question just asked and disputes it directly, then supplies the engagement mechanism Rurawhe asked about (the Iwi Chairs Forum relationship, the marae stocktake, 145 risk assessments). The speech would be entirely different had Rurawhe argued something else. Combativeness here is evidence of listening, not a deduction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe: "given that Māori don’t trust this Government at all"

acuity.statement: I find it very interesting that the Minister of Climate Change has not answered the question put by my colleague the Hon Deborah Russell with respect to committing to the Paris Agreement and affirming for this House and the general public that this Government continues to be committed to the Paris Agreement. I want to know from the Minister: what would be the international implications for us withdrawing our support for the Paris Agreement?
acuity.explanation: Identifies the exact gap in the Minister's reply — that 'climate change targets' was offered where 'the Paris Agreement' was asked — and builds on it rather than restating the original question, adding the international and trade consequences of withdrawal. Tracks what was actually said; short of 1.0 because much of the turn then runs to prepared material about the Prime Minister at the Pacific Islands Forum.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "it notes very clearly that the coalition Government is committed to meeting its climate change targets"

acuity.statement: I want to be very clear and categoric that this Government is committed to its climate change targets and New Zealand’s climate change targets—that is, both our domestic targets and our international targets. Our international targets are in the context of the Paris Agreement, and they are clearly, as I’ve noted, coalition commitments in regard to this Government.
acuity.explanation: Closes the precise gap Sepuloni had just identified, naming the Paris Agreement rather than the generic 'targets' formula, and then answers her 'why does this matter' and Pacific points with the multilateral argument and the China and Australia NDC timelines. Directly shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "whether or not that Minister and this Government are committed to the Paris Agreement"

acuity.statement: I hear the points that you’ve noted around councils and the way in which we absolutely believe that they should be using evidence-based data to make those decisions. We know there are inconsistencies there, and we want to work through that. That’s why the climate adaptation framework—the major part of it—is making sure that the data that’s being used is appropriate, evidence based, accurate, and consistent. Therefore, we should ensure we get that balance right around managing the risk.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Foster's question — council decision-making and the "right balance" Foster explicitly asked about — and names the adaptation framework's data workstream as the answer. But it engages none of the specifics put to him (the RMA's inflexibility, the Christchurch red-zone precedent, Kāpiti's district-wide inundation mapping, the Canterbury lake-raising case), and then moves to prepared material on insurance premiums and cost of living. Partial engagement: the topic is answered, the particular claims are not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "what are we doing to assist those councils to be more nimble, to make sure that we’re not building the wrong things in the wrong place?"

acuity.statement: The Minister’s response: “We’ll just deal with the regulatory environment.” No specification about what that actually means. He did not say that the Government will be investing in making this a reality. If we are to create the regulatory environment, well, the Minister must know that that means the price of emissions must go so, so much higher.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own words back and does something with them: identifies what they leave unspecified, then draws out the consequence she says must follow (a much higher emissions price) and builds her next question on that consequence. The passage could not have been written without having heard his answer; substitute a different answer on carbon capture and this changes. Scored on engagement only — whether the inferred consequence is sound is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts, in his earlier answer in this same committee debate, which Swarbrick quotes verbatim: "We'll just deal with the regulatory environment" (said in reply to her question on carbon capture).

acuity.statement: The Minister was talking about how, apparently, the reason that we have a gas shortage in this country is because of the offshore oil and gas ban, which came into effect in 2018. The Minister knows these facts. He knows that gas production peaked in this country 20 years ago. He must know that it started steadily declining year on year from 10 years ago. That is multiple years before the oil and gas ban came into effect.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's causal claim and attacks its mechanism directly on chronology: production peaked and had been declining for years before the ban, so the ban cannot be the cause. This is engagement with the content of what was said, not a reference to the speaker. Low Civility in the same passage ("gaslighting", "do you even believe what you're saying") is a separate judgement and is deliberately not allowed to pull this score down.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts, earlier in this debate, attributing the gas shortage to the 2018 offshore oil and gas ban — restated here by Swarbrick before she contests it.

acuity.statement: Minister Simmonds will be administering the waste management programme; she has prioritised organic waste solutions and will be continuing to make decisions around specific projects in this area. This Government—and please put this on your TikTok—is 100 percent committed to the Climate Change Commission, and the work this Government has done around appointing Dame Pasty Reddy to the leadership of that function conveys the important role that that entity plays and the independent advice that it provides to all Governments.
acuity.explanation: Answers the third question squarely enough to be pointed at — a commitment to the Commission, with the Reddy appointment offered as evidence — though it does not address "with all of the powers that it currently has". On waste he names who administers the programme but does not take up the specific double-counting allegation about the $30 million, and he leaves the emissions-pricing question and the no-additional-warming question untouched. One of three questions engaged, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "is the Minister committing to keeping the Climate Change Commission with all of the powers that it currently has into the future?"

acuity.statement: Given all of those, my question to the Minister is: what within his adaptation plan deals with the protection and the improvement of ecosystems and biodiversity, in this case with a particular focus on the marine environment?
acuity.explanation: Hooks onto the Minister's adaptation work by name, which is a gesture at the debate, but engages no claim anyone has made: it opens a fresh line on marine biodiversity, warming seas and acidification that would read identically had the preceding turns argued something else about adaptation. On-subject prepared material rather than responsiveness, so the upper end of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "That’s why the climate adaptation framework—the major part of it—is making sure that the data that’s being used is appropriate, evidence based, accurate, and consistent." — she hangs her question on his adaptation plan but takes up no part of what he said about it.

acuity.statement: The Government remains committed to making decisions in regard to setting the methane target this year. Cabinet has not made a decision on that at this point. However, while the member and I disagree on many things in this context, I would agree that the importance of having certainty in this conversation is an area that is an imperative, and we’ll be doing everything we can to ensure we get that outcome.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact question put — the timing of the methane decision — states the decision point has not yet been made, and then engages the second strand of Russell's case (that the sector wants certainty) by conceding the importance of certainty. The reply would read differently had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "First of all, when will we have a decision on methane? A decision that, the Minister said, would be made this year."

acuity.statement: Is the Minister committed to maintaining New Zealand’s international competitive edge as world leaders in low-emissions food and fibre production? Does he see any risks if his Government weakens the methane target and moves it away from the target range that was agreed to by virtually all of this House—bar one party—in the Climate Change Response Act? Is the Minister committed to that 24 percent to 47 percent methane reduction range in the Climate Change Response Act?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under examination (the methane target) and it follows her own stated plan of "a series of questions", but it engages no part of the Minister's answer — neither the Cabinet-timing point nor his concession on certainty. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate via the Climate Change Response Act range.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts said "Cabinet has not made a decision on that at this point" and conceded the importance of certainty, and this statement does not take either up — it moves to the next prepared question in her series.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I will just reiterate the question that I asked the Minister of Climate Change earlier, with regard to the impact of climate change on biodiversity more broadly, but specifically on the impacts to our oceans and, therefore, our fish stock.
acuity.explanation: Eligible (substantive turns by other members precede it) but engages none of them; by its own words it reiterates a question she had already asked. It remains within the climate change examination, so it is not wholly detached from the debate, but nothing in it depends on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued that failing to set a realistic methane target carries economic and trade risks, and this statement does not take it up — it restates the speaker's own earlier question on a different strand.

acuity.statement: Without doubt there are significant impacts on aquaculture as a result of the impacts of climate change. In the Pacific particularly, you see the migration of fish species because of the warming temperatures moving from some countries to others, which has an implication in regard to food security. This is a real issue that is in play within our region.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the warming-oceans-and-fish strand and accepts its premise, then supplies a related case (Pacific fish migration and food security). But it answers the topic rather than the specific question asked — what in the adaptation plan protects biodiversity, and the hoki and salmon examples go unaddressed — so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "increasing ocean temperatures is likely to cause a decline in the population of this particular fish species"

acuity.statement: We know the Government has a strategy of substantial offsetting to pine forestry; many have asked already and canvassed what the strategy is around the methane, but when you simply look across our emissions profile as a country, you can start doing the maths on where we are going to achieve the direct cuts in emissions.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the prior methane exchanges exists but engages none of their content, and nothing of the Minister's immediately preceding answer on oceans and biodiversity. It opens a new prepared line on gross emissions cuts — on the subject under examination, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Simon Watts had just described biodiversity as "one of our five key pillars", and this statement does not take that up; it acknowledges only in general terms that "many have asked already" about methane.

acuity.statement: Two key areas: Electrify NZ, which will double the amount of renewable energy in this country, is a key area of focus. The second is co-investment with the private sector on solutions to reduce biogenic methane, such as animal genetics, which will reduce methane from cows by 10 to 20 percent and is already pretty much ready to roll out in the Waikato in the coming years.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies what was demanded — named programmes for gross cuts, in the energy and agricultural sectors Abel had itemised, with a figure attached. It leaves the transport strand of the question untouched, which is the only reason this is not a full 1.0; the answer plainly could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Where is your plan, Minister? Give us the numbers. How will we achieve gross emissions cuts?"

acuity.statement: However, the Environmental Defence Society and other key environmental NGOs have said that the concept of “no additional warming” would undermine commitments under the Paris Agreement. How does the Minister make these two things stack up? When are we going to get a clear and explicit target around methane? Is the Minister going to reject this concept of “no additional warming”, given our commitments under the Paris Agreement?
acuity.explanation: On the subject under examination and it gestures at the Minister's earlier assurance on the Paris Agreement from elsewhere in the session, but it engages no part of the turn it actually follows, including his claim that animal genetics will cut methane by 10 to 20 percent — which bears directly on whether a methane target is achievable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just named Electrify NZ and animal-genetics co-investment as the route to emissions cuts, and this statement does not take either up — it returns to her own prepared methane sequence.

acuity.statement: In the context of any target, there is the amount of emissions that the economy produces. Projections and an update of those projections in regard to how much emissions the New Zealand economy is producing will be released later this year. That is an important consideration in the context of what the interrelationship is with the pathways for emissions reduction, and that will provide us with an updated position in terms of what the gap is across those targets. But we do remain on track in regard to both emissions budget one and emissions budget two at this point.
acuity.explanation: Russell put a specific reconciliation question built on three strands of the Climate Change Commission's July monitoring report: EB1 only met partly through accounting-method changes, EB2 at significant risk from unrealised carbon capture and storage, and EB3 requiring urgent further action. Watts takes up one strand — the status of budgets one and two — and restates that the Government remains on track, and he partly concedes the premise by pointing to forthcoming projections that will update "what the gap is across those targets". That is engagement with the topic and with the on-track claim she challenged, so the answer would have been different had she asked something else. But he leaves the accounting-methods point, the CCS risk and budget three untouched, and the bulk of the reply is a general statement about projections rather than the reconciliation asked for. Partial engagement sits at the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "how the Minister reconciles his claims that we are going to meet our emissions reductions plans, our emissions reductions budgets, given that the Climate Change Commission, in its monitoring report, has said that the first emissions budget is likely to be met due a combination of emissions reductions and changes to accounting methods"

acuity.statement: As I noted in my opening comments, we are progressing work around a carbon removals framework, and this includes components of wetlands and other aspects, including the blue carbon components within forestry.
acuity.explanation: Radhakrishnan put three strands: marine protection, knowledge gaps on ocean warming/acidification, and wetland and peatland restoration. The reply takes up only the wetlands strand, and does so by folding it into an existing carbon removals workstream rather than engaging her specific case about peatland rewetting or the 0.9 percent figure. The marine and knowledge-gap questions are not touched at all. Partial engagement with one strand, then prepared material on afforestation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what are the steps this Minister is taking to restore wetlands to contribute to our climate targets?" — Priyanca Radhakrishnan

acuity.statement: Now that the Minister of Climate Change has some more time available to him, I’d like to redirect his attention to the issue of international risks.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly a redirection rather than a response: the speech announces a move to international risks and then quotes the Minister's words from an earlier hearing. Nothing in the preceding turn on nature-based solutions is engaged, accepted or disputed — the statement would read identically whatever Watts had just said. It is on the matter under debate (the Minister's climate portfolio), so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just spoken about "nature-based solutions that address climate change", the carbon removals framework and native afforestation on Crown land, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Within the coalition agreements that the National Party have with ACT, we have committed to undertaking a scientific review in regard to methane—which we have undertaken—and we will be considering that alongside the Climate Change Commission’s advice in regard to the methane targets that will be considered later this year.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the methane-target topic Russell raised and describes the process by which the target will be set, which is a real engagement with part of her question. But the two specific things she asked for — a view on the "no additional warming" concept, and the political and economic risk of not setting a realistic target — are both left unaddressed in this passage, which recites the process instead. Engagement with one strand of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I invite the Minister to express what he thinks of the concept of no additional warming and whether that is going to affect the methane target" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The Government is progressing at pace in the context of designing the building blocks for a national adaptation framework. We remain committed to be able to say more about that later this year, and it remains our intent to continue to work with all political parties.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the timing question in general terms ("later this year"), so it is pointed at what was asked. But Russell's substantive challenge — how the short independent review is to be reconciled with the select committee report and the expert working group's findings, given she argued they reached the same answers — gets no engagement whatever. The reply would be unchanged had that argument not been made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Could the Minister please give an indication of when we might see the legislative framework for adaptation?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The Minister has made quite a large play around the use of carbon-capture technology. It underpins a large amount of the second emissions budget, and it is a key plank of the Government’s strategy around reducing carbon.
acuity.explanation: Moves to a fresh topic rather than engaging the adaptation answer just given, which had notably failed to address her reconciliation question — an obvious opening she does not take. There is a gesture at the Minister's own stated position on carbon capture, which lifts it off the floor of the band, but the preceding turn's content is not engaged at any point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just said the Government is "progressing at pace in the context of designing the building blocks for a national adaptation framework", and this statement moves to carbon capture instead of taking that up.

acuity.statement: Any CCUS-related risks—noting the comments that that member has noted that have been raised in the media—will be considered by Cabinet as part of the annual process that we undertake around adaptive management approaches, which is set out in the emissions reduction plan.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the specific material Russell raised — the reported collapse of the Kapuni proposal — and locates it in a Cabinet process, so the reply is shaped by what she said. It does not, however, take up the claim itself (that the unit is too expensive to work) or answer the yes/no funding question put, which keeps this below a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has the Government decided whether or not to put extra funding into that carbon capture technology that was supposed to take place at Kapuni?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: We have a greater disparity between the haves and the have-nots, and this Government, instead of addressing those very same issues, is pushing forward a bill that will make it harder for Governments to have the information that they need to address how, for example, the rich hide their wealth in things like trusts.
acuity.explanation: Russell's preceding turn made a detailed case that repealing section 17GB and dropping trust-settlor information removes the state's ability to track wealth, against officials' advice. This passage lands on the same theme — trusts, hidden wealth, lost information — but does not take up any part of her argument: it cites no element of it, does not build on the officials' recommendation point, and does not name or qualify her position. If Russell had argued something different about the same bill, this would read identically, which is the deciding test. Scored in the 0.1-0.3 band as prepared material on the matter under debate with a gesture toward it, not as a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "both those measures enabled us to track wealth in this country" — but only thematically; nothing of her argument is taken up

acuity.statement: We’ve just heard from the Green speaker Ricardo Menéndez March—and, to be fair, the Greens are at least honest: they want a wealth tax; they want a capital gains tax. What I think I heard, though, from Dr Deborah Russell was that she’s setting the groundwork for Labour to announce their wealth tax and capital gains tax policy.
acuity.explanation: This names both preceding speakers and so is clearly eligible, but it is a mere reference rather than an engagement. Neither Menéndez March's claim about asymmetric scrutiny of beneficiaries versus the wealthy nor Russell's case on section 17GB and trust information is addressed; the passage instead imputes an unannounced tax policy to Labour and pivots. Repeating or naming an opponent in order to turn away from what they said is the textbook 0.1-0.3 case, and the imputation of a hidden motive is not a rebuttal of anything either member argued. Scored 0.2 rather than lower because it is at least anchored to the two turns it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "it absolutely sends a message that the poor deserve a huge amount of scrutiny, whereas the rich can get a free pass" — named, but its content is not engaged

acuity.statement: Obviously, we have a totally different position from the Greens on digital nomads. We actually want to encourage people to come to New Zealand and to spend and invest their money, so it will be good to look at those changes, and the residential solar—I was really pleased when the Minister announced that.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one identifiable strand of the immediately preceding turn — the digital nomad provisions — and states a directly opposed position on it, so the speech would have been different had Menéndez March not raised it. But it answers the topic rather than the specific claim: the gentrification argument, the Airbnb point and the overseas unrest cited are all left untouched, and the sentence moves on to prepared approval of the solar measure. That is the ~0.5 pattern: a pointable partial engagement followed by a return to prepared material. Disagreement itself is not penalised here; the limit is how little of the argument is actually met.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "Those very same people—often on high incomes—end up contributing to gentrification in communities."

acuity.statement: I just wanted to focus on one aspect of this omnibus taxation bill, and that is the fact that it’s going to encourage digital nomads. It’s going to make New Zealand a more attractive place for what they call a “workcation”. That’s important, given the global workforce is more digitalised and more mobile.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive Labour turn in the same first-reading debate, but engages no part of it. Bennett's case was about ministerial access to agency information and trust transparency; Brewer announces he will focus on one aspect of his own choosing — digital nomads and the 275-day non-residence rule — and commends the bill. He does not rebut the overreach argument, concede any of it, or even correct Bennett's one point of agreement (the solar feed-in exemption, which Bennett praised and which Brewer ignores). The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Bennett had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band; it earns 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it is squarely about the bill actually under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued the bill is an overreach because it lets Ministers step in and access information held by Kāinga Ora, ACC, Police and NZTA beyond the existing approved information-sharing agreements, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: New Zealand First has always stood for pragmatic, common-sense reform in the national interest, and we do also commend the bill addressing solar on rooftops. The bill proposes to introduce an income tax exemption, which is seldom heard from the other side of the House because we do know that they do quite like tax in any way that they can possibly inform it and in any way they can support it, so they have more room to spend on the policies that they like.
acuity.explanation: Mooney's immediately preceding turn made a substantive case about digital nomads and about growth rather than taxation. Wilson's speech is a prepared party-position statement on the bill as a whole and engages no part of it; the only engagement is with members and exchanges outside this window (section 17GB, and 'the member who said that I told him that he was wrong'). It gestures at the debate around it, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but the speech would read identically whatever Mooney had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Joseph Mooney argued that digital nomads should be welcomed and that 'just adding more taxation' is not the solution, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: We want to transform the tax system in Aotearoa for the 99 percent instead of the 1 percent. We want to remove income tax from earners making less than $30,000 per year. We want to start taxing wealth instead of incomes. We want to ease the cost of living crisis by removing GST from kai.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns (Mooney, Wilson) precede this one, and Wilson in particular invited debate on section 17GB and praised the solar exemption. The speech is prepared Te Paati Maaori tax platform: it lists the party's own tax proposals and later notes 17GB and the solar exemption as features of the bill itself, not as answers to Wilson. There is no gesture at any preceding speaker, so this is prepared material that happens to be on the right subject.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued that the new Auckland Regional Transport Committee's voting membership of ministerial appointees extends central control, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: This is where the rubber hits the road. This is where we have serious concerns about how this has been done, because the Labour Party did deal with this in 2022 when we reformed the payment systems legislation and gave the Commerce Commission extra powers to be able to set what would be reasonable surcharges. In fact, when the Commerce Commission did come up with its reasonable surcharges, they were lower than what this Government has in fact opted for in the end.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's specific account of the 2022 Act and the Commission's unused capping powers and turns it around: she accepts the 2022 reform as her own party's, then contests his premise that cost-reflective caps were unworkable by asserting the Commission's own figures were lower than the Government's chosen settlement. She also engages his "we listened to feedback" claim by naming Visa and MasterCard's second-round submissions. The speech would read differently had Doocey made a different case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "Back in 2022, the Retail Payment System Act gave the Commerce Commission powers to regulate New Zealand's retail payment system... The commission is yet to utilise its powers to limit surcharges, and overseas evidence has shown that it would face difficulties if it tried to do so."

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Retail Payment System (Ban on Merchant Surcharges) Amendment Bill. When you go to purchase something—you see something on the shelf, you take that to the checkout—that’s what you should pay, and it’s as simple as that. We’re talking $150 million worth of savings here for consumers. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: On the subject under debate but indifferent to what preceded it — a statement of support that would be word-for-word identical whichever argument Williams had made, and which does not touch her claim about the Commission's lower caps or the cost shifted onto small retailers. Prepared material on the right topic, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued that the Commerce Commission's own cost-reflective surcharges were lower than the Government's settlement and that small businesses will absorb merchant fees of around $500 a month, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s still a bunch of paperwork. No one is actually accessing this. The people who need it most can’t get it.
acuity.explanation: Willis had just argued FamilyBoost is easy to apply for and is already putting cash into tens of thousands of bank accounts; this directly contradicts both strands — administrative burden and actual take-up, especially among those most in need. It engages the specific claim rather than pivoting to another topic, though it supplies no figure or evidence (which is a Specificity matter, not Acuity).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "The feedback that Ministers and MPs have had directly from parents, and through Inland Revenue, is that, actually, FamilyBoost is pretty easy to apply for once you’ve got that clear invoice from your ECE service."

acuity.statement: That’s from the general policy statement, but what does it actually do? What it actually does is it makes sure that everybody pays. It spreads that $150 million across the price of everything for everyone because banks will still charge the small businesses those fees, and those small businesses will need to recoup those costs so they will pass those costs on to consumers.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact figure the preceding speaker used to praise the bill ($150 million in surcharges) and turns it against the conclusion drawn from it, arguing the sum does not disappear but is redistributed into shelf prices because the bank fees on small businesses remain. The speech would have to change if Brewer had made a different case for the bill, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because it answers the framing rather than any specific mechanism Brewer put forward (Brewer offered little beyond the figure and the cost-of-living claim).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "consumers, at present, pay around $150 million annually in surcharges. Banning merchant surcharges is another great cost of living initiative by this Government."

acuity.statement: I’m so pleased that those interchange fees are coming down and we’re going to tidy up PayWave and surcharge bills across the country. It’s a good thing. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed argument that the ban merely relocates the $150 million into retail prices, and engages no part of it — no answer on whether small businesses absorb or pass on the fees. The contribution is on the right subject but would be word-for-word identical whatever the previous speaker had said, and contains no gesture at the debate it follows, which puts it at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued the bill "spreads that $150 million across the price of everything for everyone because banks will still charge the small businesses those fees", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: This could be a good idea but what a dog’s breakfast this Government’s made of it. Let’s have a look at it. We could actually support this bill to the select committee but, by crikey, if this is what you do with a good idea, goodness gracious—it’s how to make a good idea into an absolute mess.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the preceding commendation by conceding the premise — the idea is a good one — and disputing the execution, which is a real engagement rather than a mere reference. But it engages only the 'it's a good thing' framing and not any specific content (there was little), and the speech then moves to prepared material about feedback the Minister received in question time, which responds to a turn outside this debate. Partial engagement that you can point at, so 0.5 rather than higher.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "It’s a good thing. I commend the bill to the House."

acuity.statement: Unfortunately, when I look at this bill—acknowledging it is a bill that has come through here with urgency—we were expecting it to address some of the fundamental flaws that we saw when this scheme was first introduced into the House, but we see that those have not been addressed.
acuity.explanation: Follows Russell's substantive critique and is squarely on the matter under debate, but engages no part of her argument — it is prepared Green material on the bill's flaws, and lands on a near-identical uptake figure (249 families) without acknowledging or building on her 244-family claim. The speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Russell had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued the bill is a catch-up for a botched FamilyBoost ('it's because they mucked it up the first time around and, now, they are coming back to try and fix it') and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: You know what? This bill—and I’m pretty astonished, actually, that the Opposition is actually supporting it, given all the hype that they’ve been rousing around this isn’t enough, there’s not enough families getting enough money out there.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of what was actually just said — Labour's declared support sitting alongside its 'huge mess' criticism — and points at the tension in it. But it engages only the stance, not the substance (the bureaucratic claim-back, the 244 families, the unmet $250 promise), and then turns to prepared material about squeezed middle incomes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Labour will be supporting this bill" and "We are supporting this bill because it gives money to families, but all it is is a huge mess" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: It’s a shame that the member did a little hit and run from across the aisle with the attack on the economy, but I would just like to show that, sometimes, good ideas can come from wherever you think they least come from.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the preceding critique rather than engagement with it: the economic attack is labelled and dismissed, not rebutted, and the speech then moves to an unrelated anecdote about a productivity debate at the Institute of Public Policy. The reference identifies a target without touching the content of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are in a cost of living crisis precisely because of this Government." — Deborah Russell. Named as an 'attack on the economy' but not engaged.

acuity.statement: The National Party’s very, very happy with this bill. It increases the percentage of early childhood education expenses claimable from 25 percent to 40 percent, raising the maximum quarterly tax credit from $975 to $1,560.
acuity.explanation: Four substantive turns precede this one, two of them arguing the credit is unclaimable in practice for low-income families. The statement recites the bill's headline parameters and engages none of that — no answer on uptake, on the receipt-based claim-back, or on the retrospective-refund objection. It is on the right subject and indifferent to everything said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Teanau Tuiono argued the credit remains 'administratively burdensome to claim' and 'a retrospective refund, so many families will struggle to be able to get that', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It’s funny when they talk about poor policy but then say, “Oh, but we’ll support it.” Sixteen-thousand families will be better off with up to $1,560 a quarter. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: He engages the specific structure of the immediately preceding speech: Edmonds spent her turn calling the policy a failure and then announced Labour would vote for it, and Hamilton seizes on exactly that juxtaposition, then offers a counter-figure on the bill's reach. He does not touch the substance of her numbers (27,000 of a promised 100,000 families, 244 receiving the full amount), so the engagement is partial rather than a rebuttal — but the remark would have to change if she had argued something else, which keeps it above the prepared-material band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is a really poor policy, a super poor policy, which is why Labour will support this bill" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Sorry, Mr Speaker. I’m still collecting my thoughts after listening to the Minister of Finance laughing over there at the contribution of my colleague the Hon Barbara Edmonds; the Minister gleefully laughing and welcoming Labour’s support for this legislation this morning, not listening to the reason why Labour is supporting this. Labour are supporting this to fix up your mistake—sorry, Mr Speaker; not you, sorry, Mr Speaker—the Minister of Finance’s, the Government’s mistake.
acuity.explanation: She answers the charge the government side had just made — that Labour calls the policy poor yet backs it — by supplying the missing reason: the support is to repair a mistake, not an endorsement. The engagement is real and pointable, but she addresses it to the Minister of Finance's laughter rather than to Hamilton's argument, and then moves into prepared material on election promises, so this sits at a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s funny when they talk about poor policy but then say, “Oh, but we’ll support it.”" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: Labour’s spokespeople who talked earlier on pointed out that 20 percent of the fees will go to admin. What percentage will go to corporate profit from centres that are soon going to have far more unqualified teachers looking after our most precious tamariki?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific figure Edmonds had just put to the House — 20 percent of the FamilyBoost money going on administration — and does something with it rather than merely repeating it: she accepts the number and presses the accounting one step further, asking what further share is lost to corporate profit in private centres. The closing would have had to change if the preceding speaker had argued something else about where the money goes, which is the deciding test. Not a 1.0 because the engagement comes only in the final two sentences; the bulk of her turn (the Masterton visit, buildings funding, the first $10,000 tax-free) is prepared material that would have been delivered whoever spoke before her. Scored on engagement alone — the rhetorical loading of "most precious tamariki" and the unevidenced claim about unqualified teachers belong to other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "that’s 20 percent of the money that the Government has set aside for this policy spent on administering this policy"

acuity.statement: As—Mr Brewer—I failed to mention the other day, I don’t think the National Party actually has the support of the people of Rongotai, because the Green Party got 50 percent more party votes than the National Party did.
acuity.explanation: Brewer interjected a specific charge of inconsistency — that Genter herself supports a tunnel in Seatoun while condemning spending on Wellington road projects. Genter names him and replies, but engages no part of that charge: she neither denies the Seatoun position nor explains how it is consistent with her motorway argument, pivoting instead to party-vote shares in Rongotai and the Government's mandate. The reply is aimed at the heckler rather than the claim, so it sits in the low band: there is a clear gesture at the exchange (0.3 territory) but the substance is a different argument altogether.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You're pro-tunnel in Seatoun—you're pro-tunnel" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: I heard a couple of quotes in there that might be considered relevant. We heard “not accessible to families” and “certainly not all families will benefit”. Well, I can only assume, based on that, that the Green Party is not supporting because, to surmise, that’s because their average voter base earn above the cap, but, other than that, I couldn’t see why the House wouldn’t support this unanimously.
acuity.explanation: Luxton quotes back the two specific strands of Genter's case — that FamilyBoost is not accessible and does not reach all families — and does something with them, offering an account of why the Greens oppose the bill. But what he does is impute a motive (that Green voters earn above the income cap) rather than take up the accessibility claim itself: he does not contest the 249-families figure, the quarterly claim-back mechanism, or the two-year-old 20-hours alternative. That is one strand engaged and the specific claim left untouched, which is the middle of the band. It would be a different speech if Genter had argued something else, but only in which phrases it harvests.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this policy was not going to be accessible; it was not going to reach the families that needed it most" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I find, with some irony, that members across the aisle are casting aspersions on the management of the economy when one particular party was fully in charge of the economy and it was like looking at a train wreck in slow motion.
acuity.explanation: Wilson picks up that Genter attacked the Government's economic competence, so there is a real gesture at what preceded him, and the follow-on about a 'Marxist manifesto' where 'we'll all be equally poor' glances at her free-universal-ECE proposal. But he engages none of its content: not the Iceland comparison she offered as proof of affordability, not the return-on-investment comparison with the Wellington road spend, not the claim that for-profit centres absorb the funding. The move is to redirect to a previous government's record — the 'last person who should talk about waiting lists' pattern — which is topic-level engagement at best, and the aspersions sentence would read almost identically after any Green or Labour economic critique.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They think if they go out there and brand themselves as good managers of the economy" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: How embarrassing—how embarrassing—for the Government to get their policy settings so wrong and to get their systems so wrong that they have to return to the House.
acuity.explanation: Brewer had just cited the regulatory impact statement ($50 million to 60,000 families) as proof the policy was already successful. Walters opens against the general framing of success by asserting failure, but takes up no part of his evidence — not the figures, not the RIS he quoted. The rest of her contribution is prepared material on consultation and Order in Council powers that would read identically whatever Brewer had said, so this sits in the on-topic-but-unengaged band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "Just looking at the regulatory impact statement as to how successful this policy already has been: $50 million has been paid out to 60,000 families."

acuity.statement: There has been a bit of discussion in the last few contributions—one of the members on the other side of the House was boasting about the almost $70 million that has been paid out so far, but what that member failed to acknowledge is that, actually, they were expecting to pay out up to $174 million.
acuity.explanation: She takes the payout figure a government member had just cited as evidence of success and does something with it: sets it against the forecast spend of $174 million to turn the same number into evidence of under-delivery. The speech would have had to change if the preceding government speakers had not run the payout-total argument. Marked slightly below 1.0 only because she engages the figure in the aggregate rather than the specific number and source quoted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "$50 million has been paid out to 60,000 families. This is about improving FamilyBoost, making it more rewarding and more accessible to more Kiwi families."

acuity.statement: I support more tax credits for the 22,000 additional families who can be supported by the FamilyBoost. Therefore, I support the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Two detailed critiques immediately precede this — on consultation with parents, uptake, administrative cost and declined claims — and none of it is touched. The contribution is a bare statement of support that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, and could have been delivered at any stage of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime argued that only 27,000 households consistently received a payment, that $13.9 million had gone on administration and that 41,482 claims were declined, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Here we are, cleaning up Nicola Willis’ mess because she couldn’t get it right: she couldn’t design an effective, simple, and straightforward system.
acuity.explanation: Lu had just offered a reason to support the bill (22,000 additional families); Webb engages none of it, and nothing in his opening depends on what preceded him. It is prepared condemnation aimed at the Minister, on the right subject — the bill repairs a scheme — but it would be unchanged whatever the previous speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu said she supported more tax credits for the 22,000 additional families, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I, too, want to speak to the appropriateness of this name. In particular, I want to talk about it because, although on the face of it what this bill does is just increase the amount of FamilyBoost available to families—and this is a good thing which we’ve said we support because of the cost of living—in actual fact, it disguises what really has gone on with this bill.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the immediately preceding speaker's line of argument — that the bill's title does not capture what it does — and extends it with her own reason (the delivery mechanism and data were never there), before moving to her prepared alternative title. That is engagement with one strand of the previous turn rather than with any specific claim or figure in it, so it sits mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "I do think that the title doesn’t really capture what this bill does" — Russell takes up the same strand (the title misdescribes the bill) and supplies her own version of it.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. For those watching this debate at home, you can tell by the quality of the contributions from members of the party on my left that they are not taking what is a significant benefit for New Zealand families seriously at all. The fact that we are increasing the income threshold for people to be eligible for FamilyBoost from $180,000 to $230,000 is a significant increase in scope, and the fact that we’re increasing the credit from 25c to 40c is significant.
acuity.explanation: He answers the characterisation of the bill as a trivial patch by naming the two parameters it changes, which is a real if shallow engagement with the preceding speeches' framing. But he takes up none of their actual claims — not Webb's point about abatement running up to high incomes, not Russell's point that the $250 was never deliverable — and the bulk of the turn is a complaint about tone rather than a rebuttal, which keeps it below the halfway mark.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Here we have a derisory patch on a policy that, in fact, favours the well-off" (and Russell's renaming) — Watts answers the "derisory" characterisation with the threshold and credit changes.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. It is with the utmost seriousness that I begin my contribution, because, of course, Labour is supporting this bill. We recognise the Government has owned up to its mistake, today, and has finally—after months of pressure in this House from my colleague Barbara Edmonds and from my colleague Dr Deborah Russell—seen the light.
acuity.explanation: The opening is shaped by the turn it follows: Watts accused the Opposition of not taking the measure seriously, and she answers that charge on its own terms (utmost seriousness, Labour is supporting the bill) rather than ignoring it. She then returns to prepared renaming material, so the engagement is real but partial; this would read differently had Watts not made the seriousness complaint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "I think, in all fairness, let’s take this issue seriously" — Verrall opens by taking up the charge of unseriousness directly and answering it.

acuity.statement: So there are many alternative titles, but it’s like “Income Tax (FamilyBoost) Amendment Bill” is not a title that actually captures the impact of the policy. I very much agree with the Hon Barbara Edmonds, the previous speaker, who has said that this should be called the “Income Tax (Trying to Save FamilyBoost from Failing) Amendment Bill”.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific proposal in the immediately preceding turn — Edmonds' alternative bill title, grounded in her claim that the policy failed — names the member, adopts and restates the proposed title, and supplies her own supporting figures on uptake. The speech would read differently had Edmonds proposed something else. Not a full 1.0 because she substantially restates rather than develops or contests the reasoning, and returns to prepared Green material on ECE.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my suggestion to the Minister, in relation to this bill, is maybe calling it the “Income Tax (Save FamilyBoost from Further Failure) Amendment Bill”" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Look, a better solution would be not to do this legislation at all, but to go back to what the Green Party have supported, or at least the halfway house of what Labour has suggested, of extending 20 hours’ free early childhood education to two-year-olds. What if we just said that all tamariki are eligible for free, universal public and community early childhood education—why not?
acuity.explanation: Engages the counterfactual Edmonds put up — that extending ECE to two-year-olds was the better course — and does something with it, distinguishing the Green position from Labour's as only a "halfway house" and pushing to universal free ECE. Partial rather than full: it accepts and extends one strand of the preceding argument before moving into prepared party material, and does not take up Edmonds' administration-cost or FTE points.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "When both the Green Party and the Labour Party, in earlier speeches, said, “You should have just extended early childhood education to two-year-olds”" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I do want to speak to my amendment which addresses a similar query, and I guess we’re looking to the Minister in the chair for some response on that. My amendment also states the commencement date should go back to 1 July 2024 when FamilyBoost was first introduced, because noting that the date 1 July 2025 is already retrospective, there’s no reason for us to go back even further.
acuity.explanation: Russell's preceding turn argued the commencement date should be moved from 1 July 2025 to 1 July 2024 and flagged a tabled amendment to that effect. Xu-Nan explicitly links to that query, adopts the same proposal, and extends its reasoning (if 2025 is already retrospective, retrospectivity is no objection to 2024), then adds that the regulatory impact statement does not explain the chosen date. He does not take up Russell's specific point about receipts already being in IRD's hands, and much of his turn is his own prepared questions, so this is strong but partial engagement rather than a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "why not make the commencement date for this bill 1 July 2024?"

acuity.statement: Thanks, members, for those questions. In regard to the question on the ability for people to reapply, people will not need to reapply for claims open on 1 October 2025 for early childhood education fees from the 1 July 2025 to 30 September 2025.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan asked whether the Minister would streamline the process so families who had already applied would not have to reapply, with IRD paying the difference proactively. Watts supplies the specific answer with dates attached — no reapplication is needed for claims open on 1 October 2025 covering the 1 July to 30 September quarter. The speech would be different had the question not been put; it is marked slightly below 1.0 because it addresses the reapplication half of the question and not the proactive top-up mechanism asked about.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "would the Minister, then, consider streamlining the process of rather than having people reapply for that period if they have already made application"

acuity.statement: In regard to the question around retrospectivity in the amendments, we will not be accepting those amendments. We’ve had 240,000 applications. To have to go back and reopen every one of those 240,000 applications, re-evaluate, and make that is simply not a practical reality—hence the practical pathway that’s been outlined.
acuity.explanation: Both preceding speakers moved amendments to shift the commencement date back to 1 July 2024, and Russell specifically argued it would be "quite straightforward for Inland Revenue to go back and pay out the additional subsidy". Watts takes that exact proposition and answers it on its own terms — rejecting the amendments and giving the reason, the administrative cost of reopening 240,000 existing applications, which directly contradicts the claim that the rework would be straightforward. Whether the practicality argument is sound is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It would be quite straightforward for Inland Revenue to go back and pay out the additional subsidy to those families who had already been there." (and Lawrence Xu-Nan's amendment to the same effect)

acuity.statement: I think the questions that my colleagues have raised are incredibly valid because I think the current commencement date does not seem to meet the intent of the bill as publicly stated by the Government, which is to have more families access this payment. So I’m curious to know as to whether the Minister even bothered exploring this option.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding turn — that a 1 July 2025 commencement defeats the bill's stated purpose of widening eligibility, and the tabled amendment to move it to 1 July 2024 — and does something with it, turning it into a new line of questioning about whether advice and costings were sought for that earlier date. Not a 1.0 because much of the turn is prepared material on urgency and the absence of a select committee process rather than engagement with Edmonds' reasoning, and it endorses her point rather than testing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why can’t this go back, then, the full four years in which the FamilyBoost payment came into force, which is 1 July 2024? It meets all the purposes of this bill" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: As part of the policy development process, the Government received a wide range of advice. The four specific options that were considered in the context of this bill are, as the member noted, outlined in the regulatory impact statement, and I refer the member to look at those bullet points which outline the key considerations that were given to this policy.
acuity.explanation: Engages the question in part: it answers the topic of what advice was taken and points at the four RIS options the member himself raised. But the member's specific point was that the RIS does NOT show whether the 1 July 2024 date was explored, so referring him back to those same bullet points answers the subject rather than the claim, and supplies neither a yes/no on the earlier date nor any costings. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether, if at all, the Minister of Finance sought advice on an earlier commencement date; if not, why not? If she did ask for the advice, did she get given any costings as to the implications of moving this to 1 July 2024" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: In the circumstance where a family has not made any claims to date in regards to any periods, they will still be able to make a claim; however, their claim, again, will be relative to the period from the start on 1 July 2024 through to 30 June 2025 at 25 percent, and then beyond that at the new rate. That is the way in which it will be calculated. It is a clear-cut point in time of which the rate has changed. From a practical implementation point of view, that allows the department to do what it will do. There is no intent for the department to increase resourcing as a result of these changes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact scenario Russell constructed — a family with receipts straddling the 1 July 2025 threshold — and supplies the mechanism (25 percent for 1 July 2024–30 June 2025, the new rate after), then answers her resourcing question directly with a flat 'no intent to increase resourcing'. The reply would have had to be different had she raised a different problem; it is only short of 1.0 because her question about what analysis was done on the processing/compliance work, and whether it drove the start date, is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to know if Inland Revenue is anticipating having to hire any more people because of this change in the rebate." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: One of the questions that I’m still seeking adequate engagement on, because the answer that I got is “I sought a range of advice”—but I specifically asked the Minister of Revenue as to whether he sought advice on the commencement date being made on 1 July 2024, and, if so, whether he sought any costings? Because we didn’t have a select committee process, I don’t think it’s good enough to just say “I sought a range of advice.” I think the Minister should honour the fact that this is a process that has been led by urgency.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own formula back and argues why it is an inadequate answer in the absence of a select committee stage — a pointable engagement with one strand of what the Minister has said. But it takes up nothing from the immediately preceding answer on how the two rates will be calculated or on departmental resourcing, and the rest of the turn moves to prepared material (child impact assessment, child poverty targets) that would have been delivered whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I sought a range of advice" — Simon Watts' answer, quoted back by the member as insufficient

acuity.statement: In regards to the questions on a child impact assessment, all the analysis that the member is referring to is in the regulatory impact statement, and while no specific child impact assessment was undertaken, the reason, the rationale, why this is is because this is dealing with tax legislation around impacted family—family—income, and in that context it is not deemed appropriate. However, the broader considerations are outlined in the regulatory impact statement. If the member had read that, he would know.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — was a child impact assessment done — with a direct 'no', gives the rationale, and redirects the member to where the analysis he asked for actually sits. The reply is wholly shaped by the preceding turn and would not exist in that form had the member asked something else. Short of 1.0 because the parallel questions about child poverty reduction targets and the Children's Commissioner are not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether a child impact assessment has been done in relation to the bill in front of us" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. In terms of the principal Act, I actually want to talk about the overall amendment we’re looking at in terms of the Income Tax Act, because one of the things we’re looking at in terms of FamilyBoost is subpart MH.
acuity.explanation: Follows Edmonds' question to the Minister on the same clause and cites the same regulatory impact statement, so it is squarely on the matter under debate, but it engages no part of her argument about withheld information — it opens a separate line of inquiry on the purpose provision in MH 1 and declined claims. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds asked the Minister why elements of the regulatory impact statement had been withheld under section 9(2)(f)(iv) of the Official Information Act and whether they could now be released, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: In response to the question in regards to the elements that have been withheld, those elements are being withheld because they remain under active consideration.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put to him and supplies the actual ground for the withholding, so the reply would be different had Edmonds asked something else — clear engagement with the content, not a mere reference. Short of 1.0 because it answers only the first half of her question (why withheld) and leaves the release question and Xu-Nan's MH 1 question untouched. Scored on engagement alone; the thinness of the answer is a specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why have they been withheld, and given the date of this particular regulatory impact statement, can they actually be released?" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, thank you. I will keep this short, but I didn’t actually get an answer from the Minister in the chair in terms of the administrative load around this changed commencement date.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Edmonds' substantive turn precedes this one. Russell continues the same complaint-of-non-response thread and stays squarely on the matter under debate (the commencement date), but she takes up no part of Edmonds' actual argument — the 1 October 2024 amendment, the fiscal envelope, the 52 percent uptake figure. Her speech would be essentially identical had Edmonds argued something else on this bill, because it is aimed at the Minister's earlier reply rather than at the member who just spoke. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is a genuine gesture at the live debate rather than generic prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I didn’t hear a response from the Minister to the Green Party member’s question" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: There isn’t a significant increase in workload on the IRD team as a result of this policy change; it is simply a process change.
acuity.explanation: Russell drew an explicit distinction between the rebate calculation (which she conceded the Minister had already answered correctly) and the processing workload created by splitting receipts either side of 1 July 2025, and asked specifically about that workload given the 95 FTE cap. Watts answers that exact distinction: workload, not calculation; process change rather than volume change; and he closes the loop on the staffing point by saying there is no material impact on staffing. The reply would have to be different had Russell asked a different question, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 only because he asserts the conclusion without supplying the analysis she asked whether anyone had done — but that is a specificity shortfall, not an engagement shortfall.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So if the Minister could speak to the actual workload, not the calculation." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Can the Minister point out exactly where in the regulatory impact statement there are comments relating to a child impact assessment? There doesn’t seem to be any.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Watts' substantive answer on IRD workload immediately precedes. Menéndez March engages none of it — no mention of workload, process, or staffing — and instead opens a separate line about the child impact assessment. He is plainly in the same committee debate and is pressing content the Minister asserted, so this is not a 0.0, but the preceding turn is interchangeable: had Watts said something else about workload this speech would read identically. The engagement he does display is with an out-of-window turn, which cannot be pointed at in the text, capping this at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just told Deborah Russell that "There isn’t a significant increase in workload on the IRD team as a result of this policy change", and this statement does not take that up — it reopens the child impact assessment claim from an earlier Watts turn that falls outside this window

acuity.statement: I’d encourage the member to look at the Hansard of my response to his question, and if he had listened to my response, the answer would be within that.
acuity.explanation: This is the mere-reference case the rubric warns about. Watts names the question and points at his own earlier answer, but engages no part of the content of the challenge actually put: the specific claim that the regulatory impact statement contains no reference to a child impact assessment, the request to identify where in the RIS it appears, and the offer to let him correct himself. Referring a member back to the record is a pivot away from the argument rather than a reply to it. 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is addressed to the question just asked and could not have been delivered in another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is the Minister confident that a child impact assessment was done" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Thanks, Madam Chair; thanks to the member for the question. The inherent nature of any forecast is that it will change. The latest estimated uptake rate is at 64 percent based on 10 September. That is an increase, obviously, from the numbers that are included—that the member has been quoting—and that is because a new quarter's worth of data is now included within that.
acuity.explanation: Russell's turn rested on two RIS figures — a 52.8 percent current uptake rate and a 71 percent assumed future rate — and asked for clarification of how the 52.8 percent was constructed across quarters. Watts goes straight to that number, supplies a more recent figure (64 percent as at 10 September) and explains the difference as an additional quarter of data, which is exactly the quarters-of-data point Russell was querying. The reply would be different had she quoted something else, so engagement is specific rather than generic. It is not a full 1.0 because he leaves untouched her other two strands: whether erring on the low side was a deliberate choice, and whether the Order in Council power in the annual rates bill exists because of this uncertainty.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the current FamilyBoost uptake rate to date is 52.8 percent. Now, it does say this reflects three or four quarterly payments" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Yes, forecasts are forecasts, but I actually want to ask some questions in relation to the actual data set that his officials used, on page 8 of the regulatory impact statement (RIS). Table 2 talks about the claims that have been denied. The total year to date, as of 11 June, was around 28,540. Does the Minister have any updated numbers on this?
