acuity.explanation: She concedes the one proposition Watts advanced — that forecasts change — and then uses it as a hinge to move off forecasts onto realised data in the RIS, asking for an updated version of a different table on the same ground (how many families are actually reached). That is engaging one strand and converting it into her own prepared line of questioning, rather than testing his 64 percent figure or disputing his reasoning. The concession is pointable and on the specific claim, so it is above the prepared-material band, but the bulk of the turn would read the same had he said something else about the data.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The inherent nature of any forecast is that it will change." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Is it true, then, that the Minister is making an abatement rate from 9.75 percent down to 7 percent on the premise of the 71 percent assumption in order to lock in the 71 percent accessibility as a target and it shall not go more than that?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figures the Minister had just set out and presses on the reasoning behind them, tying the abatement change to the 71 percent uptake assumption and to paragraph 54 of the RIS. The question could not have been written without the preceding turn, though it also carries forward his own earlier unanswered questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "clause 5 of the bill proposes reducing the abatement rate from 9.75 percent to 7 percent"

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister has said that the idea here is really wanting to extend the reach of FamilyBoost to ensure it got to more families, but there was a choice to be made here, because another way to ensure it got to more families would have been to work with families to make sure they’re claiming the rebate in the first place.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's stated rationale for widening eligibility and contests it by offering the alternative means to the same end (outreach to non-claiming families), using the uptake figures in play in the debate. It engages the Minister's argument rather than the Green member's amendment that immediately preceded her, and much of the surrounding material is prepared, so this sits above the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "both within the original Budget 2024 funding allocation for FamilyBoost, so that is the rationale of why 7 percent" — and his earlier stated aim of extending reach

acuity.statement: To the questions noted by the member in regards to why “9.75” to “7” percent, the abatement rate decreased to 7 percent and the relevant changes that we had made in regards to, or are proposing to make in regards to the rebate rate increase to 40 percent are both within the original Budget 2024 funding allocation for FamilyBoost, so that is the rationale of why 7 percent.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question put — supplying the fiscal-envelope rationale for the 7 percent figure — and then corrects the confusion over what the 71 percent refers to. The reply would be different had the member asked something else. Not 1.0 because he leaves the Bill of Rights Act question and the case for a 5 percent rate untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "why 9.75 percent to 7 percent, in terms of lowering the abatement rate?"

acuity.statement: Again, to the third point, which is where my question to the Minister is: could this fit within the fiscal envelope or the appropriations that he referred to before, given the significant underspend on this policy, to date?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own fiscal-envelope justification for choosing 7 percent and turns it into a test of the tabled amendment, asking whether the underspend leaves room for 5 percent. The question is built directly on what he had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "both within the original Budget 2024 funding allocation for FamilyBoost"

acuity.statement: Since the member has clearly not read the regulatory impact statement, I can take him through the policy problem—the policy failure—that this bill is intending to address.
acuity.explanation: Engages the interjection head-on and discharges it with the document itself, reading the RIS's own account of the policy problem back at the interjector. The engagement is squarely with the content of the challenge; the scorn in the framing is a separate matter from responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "That’s your opinion."

acuity.statement: So where does 71 percent come from, and is that a target or is that a measure? That’s my first series of questions.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive ministerial answer giving a specific household figure, and engages none of it; instead launches a prepared set of questions off the regulatory impact statement. Squarely on the clause and bill under debate, and he does engage the Minister's earlier stated position on the child impact statement later in the turn, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom — but the preceding turn's content is untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts said "there will be 15,636 unique households with declined claims due to their income being over the threshold" and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Just a quick response to those questions. With regards to the 71 percent rate, that’s based on the FamilyBoost uptake rates to date, as well as observed uptake for other Government assistance programmes. In regards to the consultation, the member asked around public kindergartens and other aspects: they are part of the Early Childhood Advisory Committee, which was consulted with.
acuity.explanation: Takes the two specific questions just put and supplies answers to them — the provenance of the 71 percent figure, and why the kindergarten sector counts as consulted. The speech would be entirely different had Xu-Nan asked something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because the third question (the BORA report and section 19) and the target-versus-measure half of the first are left unengaged. Whether the answers are adequate or correct is a matter for other attributes, not this one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "So where does 71 percent come from, and is that a target or is that a measure?" and "why has there been a cherry-picking of ECE service providers who have been consulted?"

acuity.statement: I guess I’m worried that by making the choice to increase the amount of the rebate that’s available rather than trying to get to some of the families who aren’t receiving FamilyBoost and should be getting it—here, I’m particularly thinking of some of our low-income families, our Māori and Pasifika families, who are not claiming it—was that a really deliberate choice to go after that $250 a fortnight, rather than thinking about where the need is?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right clause: it neither takes up the Minister's uptake-rate answer nor his consultation answer, both delivered immediately before. It does gesture at the surrounding debate by picking up colleagues' earlier contributions, which keeps it off the floor of the band, but nothing in it would have to change had the preceding turn said something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered that the 71 percent rate is "based on the FamilyBoost uptake rates to date" and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Deborah Russell alluded to, as far as we know, there is no family out there that has received the amount per week that the National Party had campaigned on and claimed that they were going to deliver in the election campaign.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific claim in the immediately preceding turn — that no family was found receiving the promised combined amount — and puts it to work as the premise for the Green amendment she is advancing. That is genuine engagement with content rather than a bare name-check. Not higher because the strand is adopted rather than examined, and the rest of the call is prepared argument for the tabled amendment that would stand whatever Russell had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "we couldn’t find a single family who had received both FamilyBoost and sufficient tax cuts to get to $250 a fortnight"

acuity.statement: I just want to ask the Minister why he needed that specific subclause (3) to that clause when we already know that the Act comes into force from 1 July 2025.
acuity.explanation: A self-contained drafting question on clause 4(3) that engages no part of any preceding turn — not Genter's distributional-analysis question, not Russell's argument about who the policy reaches, not the Minister's answers. It is tightly tied to the text of the clause under debate, so it is not wholly unmoored, but it would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter had just asked whether a distributional analysis of the policy had been done, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge that when this Government recognises a problem with laws that have been made, we act very quickly to fix them. We don't stand here in the House and pretend we don't know what the problem is. We are here to fix things that matter.
acuity.explanation: Genter spent her speech reading the regulatory impact statement's admission that FamilyBoost reached far fewer families than intended. Court takes up that one strand — he concedes a problem with the law exists and frames the bill as the quick fix for it, which is a direct answer to the 'a change is required' point — but he engages none of her specific evidence (the 249 families on the full subsidy, the $50m of $174m paid out, the distributional figure) and then returns to prepared ACT framing about fixing things that matter. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, not a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "The policy problem is that FamilyBoost is reaching far fewer families and providing less financial assistance than originally intended. A change is required."

acuity.statement: We have established across the House today that early childhood education is not just an investment in our kids; it's an investment in our long-term human capital, productivity, and prosperity. We congratulate the Minister for her work on this bill. It's the right policy in the right place at the right time. We commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Wilson repeats Genter's 'investment' formulation back as supposed common ground across the House and then delivers prepared praise of the Minister and the bill. Echoing an opponent's words and asserting the policy is right 'in the right place at the right time' engages no part of her claim that two-thirds of the appropriation went unpaid and that the scheme misses the families who need it most. The speech would read identically whatever the preceding critique had been — barely saved from 0.0 by gesturing at the day's debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "Early childhood education is an investment in our country. It's an investment in our future." — echoed, but her actual argument (that FamilyBoost is failing on the Government's own RIS) is not taken up

acuity.statement: We’ve just heard from the Opposition that some of their amendments have said, basically, “Let’s do more and more—even than what we’re doing now.” Yet they voted the first one down. They say, “Shame”, but they’re going to support today’s amendment. They’re trying to have their cake and eat it too.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows Edmonds and does take up one strand of her case — her claim that Labour came to the House to be constructive with tabled amendments — and turns it into a charge of inconsistency (they voted one down, yet will support this amendment). So the speech is not indifferent to what preceded it: you can point at what is being engaged, and it would read differently had Edmonds not built her turn around constructive amendments. But it engages none of the specific substance she put up: the commencement-date amendment, the move from a 7 percent to a 5 percent abatement threshold, or the regulatory impact statement's 52 percent uptake figure and the fiscal headroom she drew from it. It restates the amendments at the level of 'more and more' and then returns to prepared material ($6,240, eligibility increased, I commend this bill). That is topic-plus-one-strand engagement rather than rebuttal of the argument, which sits at the middle of the band. Scored only on engagement: whether the 'cake and eat it too' characterisation is a fair reading of Labour's position is a rigor question, and whether the $6,240 figure holds is a veracity question — neither moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "We came to this House today to be constructive, to offer constructive tabled amendments, to help the Government"

acuity.statement: I was surprised by Arena Williams’ remarks that there were some children who would not be eligible for the policy. That is the case. Children in very high-income households who already receive subsidies through the early childhood education system, through the education system, will not qualify for this rebate.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes up the specific claim Williams had just made — that identifiable families are missing out on claiming FamilyBoost — concedes that some children are indeed ineligible, and then supplies her own account of which households those are and why. The passage would have to change if Williams had argued something else about the scheme, which is the mark of genuine engagement. It is not a full 1.0 because she restates the objection in narrower terms (very high-income households) than Williams put it (Māori and Pacific families identified in the Government's own documents), engaging one strand rather than the whole of it; whether that recasting is fair is a question of reasoning, not of responsiveness, and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "own policy documents show are missing out on being able to claim this policy"

acuity.statement: New Zealand, don’t believe them, don’t believe anything they say. They don’t support this. They don’t support more money for working New Zealanders. Check the Hansard: they voted against it in committee stage every single clause; they don’t support it.
acuity.explanation: Prime's turn rested on the claim that Labour supports the bill, and Meager takes that exact claim up and contests it directly, offering the committee-stage voting record as counter-evidence and naming Labour members' stated opposition to extending the scheme. The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had not asserted Labour's support. It does not engage Prime's other strand (the 244 families / administrative burden figures), so not a full 1.0. Whether the voting-record inference is sound is a Rigor question and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "Labour is supporting this because these families were promised this money, and they have not received it because the Government overpromised and under-delivered."

acuity.statement: I look forward to a 10-minute contribution on this bill, which will be somewhat more fulsome than the Minister’s earlier contribution. Labour supports this bill, the Income Tax (FamilyBoost) Amendment Bill, because it puts money where it’s desperately needed, and families under immense pressure need that support, as the Hon Willow-Jean Prime has said.
acuity.explanation: Williams takes up one strand of Meager's immediately preceding charge — that Labour does not support the bill — by stating the support plainly and giving a reason for it, and later picks up his attack on Deborah Russell's universality position. But she leaves his central proof point (the committee-stage votes against every clause) untouched and moves into prepared material on construction job losses, the minimum wage and food prices. Partial engagement, pointable but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "They don’t support this. They don’t support more money for working New Zealanders."

acuity.statement: I rise in support of the Customs (Levies and Other Matters) Amendment Bill. This legislation modernises our border cost recovery by introducing targeted levies that reflect the actual services provided by the Customs Service. It ensures fairness, and that those who benefit or create risk at the border will contribute appropriately. The bill amends three Acts, introduces safeguards, and prevents double-charging. In our view, it’s a practical, future-focused reform that strengthens our border systems while supporting trade and economic resilience. We commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition turn that made specific, answerable criticisms (Order in Council delegation, whether levy revenue covers administration cost, double-charging on returned goods) and engages none of them. The speech is prepared endorsement of the bill, and would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had said; it sits in the low band but not at 0.0 because it is at least squarely about the bill under debate and glances at fairness and double-charging.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued at length that setting levies by Order in Council erodes the democratic powers of the House and asked what the level and purpose of the charge are, and this statement does not take any of it up — its reference to safeguards and double-charging is a general description of the bill, not an answer to his argument.

acuity.statement: Ultimately, this is about efficiency—making the system better—and that is one of the core aspects of this Government: improving efficiency. That, ultimately drives productivity gains, and that drives economic activity. That’s what we want to see on this side of the House, so I commend this bill.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Nicole McKee that praised Part 3's GST refund provisions and asked the Minister to ensure goods-management levies account for importers of prohibited goods who already face a second set of agency fees. Van de Molen takes up none of it — no mention of levies, double fees, or GST refunds. The speech is on the right bill, and about the committee process, but would read word-for-word the same whatever McKee had argued; it is prepared government framing about efficiency and productivity rather than any engagement with the point just put. Not a gesture at the debate's content, so the bottom of the on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee asked the Minister to be 'fulsome' and ensure that 'when the levies are set for businesses who may end up having two sets of fees to pay, that is considered at the time that the levies are set', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: As has been noted in the first reading of this bill, it is largely technical in nature. It seeks to improve the way Government agencies, particularly Customs, recover costs and manage imported goods, while also progressing product stewardship schemes and providing greater clarity for consumers on GST refunds. There are incremental but important changes and, on balance, the Green Party continues to support this bill.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede this one — McKee on the levy-setting risk of double fees, van de Molen on efficiency and productivity gains. Carter engages neither. Her speech is detailed, on the bill, and accurate about which Acts it amends, but it is self-contained prepared Green material on product stewardship and the waste hierarchy; its only backward reference is to the first reading and her own colleague Francisco Hernandez, not to anyone who spoke before her in this debate. Delete van de Molen's turn and substitute a different argument and this speech changes not at all. Scored in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band, slightly above the floor because it does at least characterise the bill under debate rather than speaking past it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim van de Molen argued 'this is about efficiency—making the system better' and that this 'drives productivity gains', and this statement does not take that up; nor does it take up Nicole McKee's request about how levies are set.

acuity.statement: Look, waste minimisation was one area discussed in select committee; another big one was around GST refunds and whether this was opening a loophole for those that might claim it back on damaged goods but also might import more goods duty-free. I’m satisfied that, from the work in the House, that doesn’t apply, so this bill becomes one more part of our plan for economic growth to deliver better quality of life and more affordable living for every Kiwi. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Carter's substantive case for product stewardship and waste minimisation. Costley names waste minimisation — the preceding speaker's whole theme — which is a genuine gesture at the debate, but he does nothing with her argument: he neither disputes the repair-over-replacement claim, nor confirms the stewardship-fee mechanism she described, nor answers her point about shifting responsibility upstream. He notes only that the topic came up in committee, then pivots to the separate GST loophole question and to prepared economic-growth framing. A naming of the previous speaker's subject without engaging its content sits at the top of the unresponsive band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: 'Waste minimisation is about moving to the top of the waste hierarchy.' — Costley names waste minimisation but engages no part of Carter's argument about it.

acuity.statement: It sounds like all the parties are all for this moving to the next stage. This Customs (Levies and Other Matters) Amendment Bill obviously has powers that the Opposition has identified. I look forward to the committee of the whole House questioning, and answers from the Minister passing judgment on why it's been drafted the way it has.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows Belich and takes up one strand of what she actually argued: that the bill's levy-setting powers are the Opposition's concern and that the committee stage is where they should be tested. His speech would read differently had Belich not raised the powers and flagged the committee stage, so it is not wholly prepared material. But he engages no part of the substance — not clause 6's 'without limitations' wording, not the prohibited-goods paragraph, not the tabled amendments, and not the claim that the bill erodes the House's oversight. He acknowledges the concern exists and defers it rather than rebutting, conceding or answering it, which is partial engagement, not a reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "we have clear concerns around Part 1" and "I'm looking forward to the committee stage where we will be looking to see if the Minister is minded to make some improvements."

acuity.statement: This is quite clear: it introduces new rules to help Customs recover costs and improve certain fees and levies and how they’re managed. I haven’t heard any dissent across the House during this reading. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive critique of the bill and engages no part of it. The only gesture at the preceding turn — "I haven't heard any dissent across the House" — does not take up any content of O'Connor's argument, and in fact asserts that no dissent was voiced. The speech would be identical whatever the previous speaker had said; it stays at 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor argued at length that clause 6's "without limitation" levy power hands charge-setting to the Minister without parliamentary oversight, asked Government members to explain how prohibited goods could be levied, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The bill makes three key changes, which have been outlined: introducing a levy regime into customs legislation and providing an assurance that it is a levy regime and that the establishment of any levies would work through a process, which would require Cabinet approval and would definitely require consultation, so that it isn’t at the discretion of a Minister individually.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise objection just made — that the levy power rests with the Minister alone, without consultation or wider oversight — and answers it directly by asserting Cabinet approval and mandatory consultation, closing on the exact words "isn't at the discretion of a Minister individually". The speech would have to change if the preceding critique had been about something else; it is marked 0.9 rather than 1.0 because it asserts the safeguard rather than pointing to where in the bill it sits, which is what O'Connor said was missing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but it is on the basis of the Minister, not a process of consulting with stakeholders, consulting with affected parties" — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: As the Hon Jenny Salesa is a former Minister of Customs, I had assumed there was some sort of level of understanding, but if you read the legislation as it’s written, the “without limitation” is referring to the list of functions, not to the levy itself.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact textual claim Salesa built her whole contribution and her amendment on — that "(without limitation)" removes any cap on the levy — and corrects the reading, locating the phrase as qualifying the list of functions. The turn would be unrecognisable had Salesa argued something else; she then reads the clause into the record to show the grammar. Squarely engaged (the jibe about her having been Minister is a civility matter, not an acuity one).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "it does not give any minimum or maximum limitations on the costs to our small businesses"

acuity.statement: I think it’s important to differentiate that a levy is not a tax, as you’ll be aware from the border-processing levy. It is a levy that is established on a cost recovery basis.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts Salesa's second premise — that the charge is a tax under another name — by drawing the cost-recovery distinction and citing a precedent Salesa herself administered. Engages the content of the claim rather than merely naming the member; marked slightly below 1.0 because it asserts the distinction more than it tests her reasoning for it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "It’s called a levy, but it is actually a tax"

acuity.statement: I just want to make a quick contribution to ask a question around a point that the Hon Damien O’Connor raised in a speech in a previous section of the debate. It was the question around how a levy order would be applied to prohibited or prescribed goods.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and gestures at the debate's earlier course, but engages no part of the immediately preceding argument — it even reverts to "taxed" framing Costello had just disputed. Prepared material on the right subject rather than a partial engagement, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Casey Costello had just argued that "without limitation" governs the list of functions and that a levy is not a tax, and this statement does not take either point up — it revives a question Damien O'Connor asked in an earlier part of the debate.

acuity.statement: Again, this is not about a tax; it’s about a levy. If we’re talking about prohibited goods and if there’s a cost incurred to respond to those prohibited goods, to deal with those prohibited goods, those that have generated the risk should be paying the levy or the cost for dealing with that prohibited good.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific nexus Hernandez asked about — the charge attaches to the Customs cost of handling the prohibited good, not to the illegal good as a taxable item — and corrects the "taxed" premise in the question. Short of 1.0 only because his subsidiary question about legislative precedent is left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "Definitionally, if something is illegal, how could that be taxed?"

acuity.statement: To reassure you, the “without limitation” refers to the functions—“performing a function under this Act, or any other legislation, relating to goods management, including, (without limitation)” the list below. What we’re saying is the “without limitation” relates to the functions. I’m not sure if I’ve got that clear still. As the member will be aware, I do not have the authority to create anything. This is a Cabinet process that requires Cabinet approval. I do not have the authority, and no Customs Minister would have the authority, to set a levy.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise textual point Salesa built her whole argument on — the placement of "without limitation" in new section 414A(2) — and disputes its grammatical referent, arguing it qualifies the functions rather than the recoverable costs. It then engages her second strand, the "just trust this Minister" charge, by denying the Minister holds unilateral levy-setting authority. The speech would be entirely different had Salesa not read the clause out; it is built around her reading of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "the use of “without limitation” to define the scope of the costs recoverable means that the executive and the Minister gains wide discretion to decide what Customs costs to recover from small businesses"

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister made a comment on this in terms of there being a process in place; the process is that the Minister recommends. There is a lot of power in that recommendation. As the Minister will know, the Governor-General doesn’t often not grant—or I struggle to recall a time when the Governor-General has not granted—that Order in Council on the basis of a ministerial discretion.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the reassurance just offered, conceding the process exists but attacking its force: if the step is a ministerial recommendation that the Governor-General does not in practice decline, the process is not the constraint the Minister claimed. Not full marks only because the rest of the call runs to prepared material on framework legislation generally, but this passage engages the specific defence just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "This is a Cabinet process that requires Cabinet approval. I do not have the authority, and no Customs Minister would have the authority, to set a levy."

acuity.statement: The scope of the costs that are recoverable are limited to those that are incurred by Customs in performing a legislative function relating to goods management. This is a limit that is built into the levy-making power. This isn’t just “We can apply a cost to anything.”; this is about costs that are generated by Customs and are performing a legislative function.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — the claim that the power is unusually broad — by pointing to the goods-management limit and to the existing fees-by-secondary-legislation precedent. But Walters asked a specific question twice: why the deliberate choice to make the Order in Council non-confirmable rather than subject to the House's agreement. That question is not taken up, and the reply returns to the Cabinet-process material already given, so this is partial engagement rather than a full response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "the Minister has selected the option that gives the Minister the most scope and the least oversight of this House in relation to this bill"

acuity.statement: I thank the member. Yes, it is a memorandum accounting model. Again, this is the mechanism stuff. We’re talking about the mechanism to create the levy.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor's closing question asked directly whether clause 7 amounted to a memorandum account and whether that process would be used. Costello opens by confirming exactly that and then explains the activity-based costing and three-year reset mechanism that makes it work. The answer supplies the specific assurance that was asked for and would have been different had a different question been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "can she give us an absolute assurance that it’s only cost recovery, and will that memorandum account process be the one that is used?" — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: The “without limitation” isn’t referring to the cost without limitation; it’s referring to the list of functions below. We’re not limiting the list of those functions as there may be other ones for which there may be a cost, for good management, that could come under this.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor asked her to repeat and clarify whether "(without limitation)" attaches to the costs or to the activities, saying a non-lawyer reading it would see a danger. Costello goes to the placement of the brackets in the clause and corrects the reading directly, distinguishing "including (without limitation) costs incurred" from "costs without limitation". This engages the precise textual point rather than the general topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but I do need to check with the Minister about that “(without limitation)”." — Damien O'Connor

acuity.statement: To the Minister of Custom’s point, might the Minister be clear to the Chamber, then, about what some of those other ones might be, to help us understand where she’s going with this?
acuity.explanation: Henare takes the specific load-bearing element of Costello's answer — the unenumerated "other ones" that "without limitation" is said to preserve — and presses her to name them, which is the natural consequence of her own explanation. He then returns to prepared material on the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee and secondary legislation, so the engagement is close but not sustained throughout; scored just below the top for that reason.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there may be other things for which there’s a legislative requirement for us to recover costs" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: The Minister of Customs is in a really difficult situation; she has to front the charges or the costs, but if, as she suggested, this allows the flexibility for other costs incurred through other agencies to then come through customs and be imposed on someone who’s importing or exporting, then that’s quite a huge impost.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification for removing the exhaustive list — that Customs may collect levies arising from other legislation — and draws out its consequence: an open cheque-book in which other agencies' costs land on importers and exporters. The speech could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument; it is built directly on what she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "there may be levies that Customs would be asked to collect on behalf of other agencies and this is the part where we’re trying to ensure that we have the ability to collect levies as they arrive from other legislation"

acuity.statement: If we are acting on another agent, all we are talking about is the costs that Customs incur; the levy is about Customs recovering its costs.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of O'Connor's open-cheque-book scenario by narrowing the scope of the levy power to Customs' own incurred costs, and in the same turn answers his memorandum-account question (they are audited, with performance-band reporting). Both strands of the preceding turn are taken up; it stops short of 1.0 because the checks-and-balances mechanism he asked about is asserted rather than engaged in detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "We don’t want to leave an open cheque-book here."

acuity.statement: The question is: does the other legislation refer to other parts of the importation process or does it just come back to Customs?
acuity.explanation: Accepts part of the Minister's answer and disputes the rest — he concedes her explanation of "(without limitation)" and then tests her scope claim against the actual words of new section 414A(2), isolating the residual ambiguity in "or any other legislation". Classic engaged committee-stage responsiveness: the reply is shaped entirely by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "The only thing this applies to is the costs that Customs incurs."

acuity.statement: I suppose the logical one is the Misuse of Drugs Act. We stop drugs on behalf of the misuse-of-drugs legislation, which incurs a cost to Customs because we do that on behalf of another agency.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing the preceding question asked for — a worked example of what "any other legislation" means in practice — and nothing else. The whole turn exists because of the question put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "does the other legislation refer to other parts of the importation process or does it just come back to Customs?"

acuity.statement: A further question about the levy, to the Minister: is she going to consider ring-fencing this levy so that, following up on a question that the Hon Damien O’Connor had before, it actually just stays within Customs because this levy is being collected for Customs?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the exchange she follows — O'Connor's worry that the levy becomes a conduit for other agencies' costs — and converts it into a concrete ask about ring-fencing. But she announces at the outset that she is moving to a different clause, and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on clause 4 and the delegation of lawmaking power that would read identically whatever the Minister had just said. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "this allows the flexibility for other costs incurred through other agencies to then come through customs and be imposed on someone who’s importing or exporting"

acuity.statement: The Minister just then referred to border processing, and so I wonder whether there are examples of language that the Minister has contemplated which could draw down those powers in the way in which the Minister does intend, but also not without that unintended effect of limiting the ability of those complaints to be very validly brought to fora such as the Regulations Review Committee, and then instruments to be disallowed should they be outside the scope of the Minister’s and the Government’s intent.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-made distinction between goods management and border processing and presses it: if the intent is narrower than the drafted power, what drafting language would narrow it, and does the breadth of the power foreclose an ultra vires complaint to the Regulations Review Committee. The question could not have been asked in this form had Costello not drawn that distinction, so the speech is shaped by what it follows; it is marked below 1.0 because the second half returns to her own prepared ground on the OAG advice rather than resolving Costello's claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "This bill relates to goods management, not border processing, so we're talking about the cost incurred with border processing."

acuity.statement: My question is around whether there are any safeguards that would prevent the fees that are enabled to be collected by this legislation from being spent outside of product stewardship?
acuity.explanation: Prepared Green material on the Waste Minimisation Act and dehypothecation, delivered on the right bill but engaging no part of the preceding exchange on the goods management levy drafting. He announces it as such — "I just want to take a quick call on this topic" — and the speech would read identically whatever Walters or Costello had said. Above 0.0 only because it is squarely about a part of the bill before the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued the exemption and liability powers in new sections 414A and 414B are too broadly drafted and asked about conflicts of interest, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: My last question is: will all the fees collected by Customs under this part of the bill be transferred to the appropriate environmental fund in full—in other words, can the public be assured that the levies she is collecting are ring-fenced for environmental purposes, and not mingled with other general revenue?
acuity.explanation: A prepared set of three questions on Part 2 that lands on the same ring-fencing worry Hernandez raised moments earlier, but gives no sign of having heard him — it neither builds on the dehypothecation example nor asks the Minister to reconcile her earlier ring-fencing answer with it. On topic, so a gesture at the debate, but not engagement with the argument in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez had just asked whether anything prevents fees collected under this legislation being spent outside product stewardship, and this statement restates the same concern without taking up his point about the Waste Minimisation Act already having been dehypothecated.

acuity.statement: The one issue raised by my colleague Hon Jenny Salesa is the one around tyres, of course. We know that is a nightmare, and there has been a fee put on. The proposal, of course, is to make it more efficient and bring it under Customs.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one specific strand of the preceding turn — the tyre fee — and does something with it, extending it to plastic containers and lithium batteries and to whether Customs' own collection costs are covered. That is real engagement with what was just said rather than a mere name-check, but it is a continuation of a colleague's question rather than a response to an argument, and the rest of the turn is his own prepared ground on the principles of product stewardship.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "is she considering, say, having the tyre-recycling fee under the Tyrewise ready to be collected at the border by Customs"

acuity.statement: Just first, the assurance that the fees collected have to be used for the purpose that was collected—so this is a product stewardship fee; it has to be used for that function.
acuity.explanation: Opens by supplying precisely the assurance the previous speaker asked for, in the terms she asked for it — hypothecation of the fee to the purpose for which it was collected. The answer is ordered by the questions put to her rather than by prepared notes, and she goes on to deal with Salesa's request for dollar estimates as well; short of 1.0 because she asserts the ring-fencing rather than pointing to the provision that secures it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "can the public be assured that the levies she is collecting are ring-fenced for environmental purposes, and not mingled with other general revenue?"

acuity.statement: Yes: absolutely committed to future product stewardship. That’s why we think it should be in this legislation without defining—it’s just about setting up the mechanism, because, logically, it is an opportunity for Customs because we see the goods coming in and out.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific assurance O'Connor sought, and then takes up the implicit premise of his question — that the absence of named future schemes signals a lack of commitment — by explaining the clause as a collection mechanism rather than a list of products. The reply would be different had he asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "can she give us an assurance that, actually, the Government is committed to product stewardship fees?"

acuity.statement: Thank God we were in charge. There are tens of thousands of New Zealanders who are alive now because we were in charge.
acuity.explanation: A direct riposte to the interjection just thrown at him: he takes the pandemic claim and turns it into a counter-claim about lives saved under the previous Government. Clearly shaped by what immediately preceded it, so responsive; it is not higher because what it engages is a one-line barb rather than an argument about the bill, and he answers the jibe instead of the substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "You even caused the pandemic"

acuity.statement: Look, I find it kind of ironic that the Labour Party, despite supporting this bill entirely, decided to pull the pin last minute, raising, actually, some fairly good points, but it leads me to the question of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee. We’re a great select committee—and I’ve got some of my colleagues over here—and these points could have been discussed and they weren’t raised with us.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows a substantive turn by Hernandez that argued the bill's Part 2 enables priority product stewardship (refrigerants at the border), and that the Minister's assurance about fees not becoming general revenue should be treated sceptically given the de-hypothecation of the Climate Change Response Fund and the Waste Minimisation Fund. McClure takes up none of that content. She gestures at the same matter under debate — the late-raised Labour concerns Hernandez also discussed — and pivots to a process complaint about the select committee, then to her own prepared praise of the GST change. That is on-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez argued that Part 2's product stewardship provisions justify Green support but that the Minister's assurance on fees deserves scepticism ("we do have to treat the Minister’s claim with a little bit of scepticism"), and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Actually, we saw them concerned for the first time about the potential of increased tax. It’s a very un - Labour Party thing. I was surprised to hear that coming from the member. Rest assured that that, indeed, is not a risk under this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Van de Molen does take up one strand of what preceded him: the concern that the fee-setting powers could become a revenue-raising measure, which Hernandez voiced as scepticism about the Minister's assurance. He identifies the concern (increased tax), and gives a direct denial that it is a risk under the legislation. But he engages it only by assertion and by a jibe about it being un-Labour, does not touch Hernandez's specific evidence (the Climate Change Response Fund and Waste Minimisation Fund de-hypothecations), and otherwise returns to prepared closing praise. Partial engagement — the strand is pointable, the reasoning is not supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we do have to treat the Minister’s claim with a little bit of scepticism" — Francisco Hernandez, on the fee-setting powers in Part 2 being broadened to general revenue.

acuity.statement: The information I’ve received in terms of schemes that are in the pipeline includes tyres, electronics, and farm plastics. Those are some of the indications of the things in the pipeline.
acuity.explanation: Takes up O'Connor's specific request for an indication of which further product stewardship schemes are coming and names three, and also addresses his point about an efficient existing collection system reducing cost. Partial because she does not engage the 'five other products' framing or whether they will be fast tracked, so one strand of the question is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "Maybe, the Minister could give us an indication of whether the other five products are still in the process and whether, because of the new, efficient system that will be now put in place under Customs, whether that will be fast tracked into this new scheme"

acuity.statement: The Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee looked at this and basically saw it as a logical step forward, but I think the questions that the Hon Jenny Salesa asked are ones that the Minister of Customs, hopefully, will answer.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Salesa's line of questioning on the GST refund window and adds substance to it — the select committee's view, the rise in online purchasing, and the concrete case of a low-value item on which GST would be paid twice. This speech would be different had she asked something else, though it largely endorses and amplifies rather than contesting or resolving her questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "why was the original GST refund window only two months, and does she or her Customs Service officials have evidence that drove the decision to extend it to 12 months?"

acuity.statement: Just in answer to the two months only previously, so as most trade was within New Zealand, this was not a bigger issue previously. Now, there is a lot more purchasing from overseas directly by individuals as well as that process. I think the 12 months is more aligning to that warranty period, so that equates to that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question put — why the old window was two months and what the 12 months is calibrated to — and in the same turn takes up her communications question about how consumers and traders will learn of the entitlement. The content is determined by what Salesa asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "why was the original GST refund window only two months, and does she or her Customs Service officials have evidence that drove the decision to extend it to 12 months?"

acuity.statement: The member on the other side of the House is most welcome to get up and contribute and ask his questions in the normal way, because this is why we are having this committee stage.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Costley's interjection and answers it on its own terms — if the questions are frivolous, he is free to take a call and ask better ones in the committee stage. Partial rather than full engagement because she rebuts his right to heckle rather than defending the substance of the questions he called frivolous.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "These are frivolous questions—frivolous!"

acuity.statement: Just in answer to the last part, which is what I alluded to, this was discussed in the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee. It was addressed in my answer previously about Customs providing assurance around the process, the review, and the provision of documentation at the export stage.
acuity.explanation: Engages the fraud question squarely by pointing to the export-stage documentation requirement, and in the same turn disposes of her other two questions by locating them outside the bill's scope — domestic shop returns and consignments under $1,000. Every part of the turn is shaped by what was just asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Salesa: "are there any protections against abuse of this refund system—for instance, what is to stop someone from importing and then exporting to claim GST back in a fraudulent way?"

acuity.statement: My question on that part is whether there was a consideration of applying any timing restrictions in terms of the original importation and the time between the original importation and the current importation.
acuity.explanation: Probes the time-limit question that Costello had just answered by reference to the warranty period, extending it to the gap between the original and current importation and to changes in the value of refurbished goods. Half credit: the connection to the preceding answer is real but she is largely working through prepared material on clause 17(1AB) rather than taking up Costello's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "I think the 12 months is more aligning to that warranty period, so that equates to that."

acuity.statement: That time frame relates to where there’s a written guarantee, so it’s the period of the written guarantee.
acuity.explanation: Answers the first of the two parts Walters put, identifying what bounds the period between importations. It is squarely on the question asked but leaves her second part — refurbishment or replacement that substantially changes the value of the goods — entirely untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "One was the consideration of limiting the period between the two for that section."

acuity.statement: I have just a couple of questions here, and I think there was a question about people perhaps fraudulently using this provision and saying that goods are faulty and then getting a replacement, and then, in fact, some importer is getting two for the price of one and getting an exemption on GST.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's stated safeguard — proof of export — and tests it against a case it may not cover, where the overseas seller tells the buyer to dump the goods and ships a replacement because return freight costs more than the item. That is doing something with the answer just given, not merely restating the concern; the later tariff question is new material and keeps it short of full marks.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "It normally requires submission of supporting information such as showing a record of the export to ensure that the refund is appropriate."

acuity.statement: I do find it extraordinary that many of the questions raised were not asked in the select committee process by the other side. I think that is the place where they should have been asked, and if they weren’t, then that is something that could be addressed by them in the future.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick follows Henare and takes up one strand he had directly addressed — where the questions about the levy regime should have been raised — so her opening is not indifferent to what preceded it. But she restates the select-committee objection rather than engaging Henare's actual counter-argument (that the committee of the whole House exists precisely to revisit matters after submissions, and that urgency removed that opportunity). The remainder of the speech is prepared commendation of the bill that would read identically whatever Henare had said. Partial engagement with the topic rather than the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I've heard members from the other side of the House say that it should have been raised in the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: It’s a great bill. It’s about a Government getting on with the business of running a country, going for growth so that we can make life more affordable and deliver more opportunities for Kiwi families. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Carter's immediately preceding third-reading speech made a substantive argument — that the bill closes a gap by shifting end-of-life product costs from households and councils onto producers and importers, with the EU/Apple USB-C example and a claim that New Zealand is behind Europe on circular systems. Costley's turn engages none of it: it is generic commendation plus growth framing that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. It is at least about the bill under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but there is no gesture at the content of the preceding argument, which places it at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter spoke about product stewardship shifting end-of-life waste costs upstream to producers and importers, and this statement does not take any part of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to take a call on the Customs (Levies and Other Matters) Amendment Bill. It’s a useful piece of legislation, and I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Duncan Webb's detailed critique of the bill (inadequate regulatory impact statement, no consultation, fee-versus-levy distinction, Salesa's confirmable-instrument amendment) and engages none of it. The two sentences would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had argued; the only tether to the debate is naming the bill. Not 0.0 because it is at least a stated position on the measure actually before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued "this is one of the worst regulatory impact statements I’ve ever seen" and that the levy power is unconstitutional, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s designed to, I guess, update and modernise the legislation, but what it does do is shift from a process in Parliament of oversight to a process with the Minister, where there are obligations to consult but they are not that robust, and we say they are at risk of being abused by a Minister who just decides to cover costs and a bit more, as my colleague previously said.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one specific strand of Webb's preceding argument — that the levy power lets the Crown recover more than cost with no return to the House — names it as his colleague's point, and extends it with the consultation-obligation and oversight-shift angle. He then moves into prepared material on Parts 2 and 3 that is indifferent to what preceded it, and he does not engage Webb's central regulatory-impact-statement or fee-versus-levy reasoning, which is why this sits at partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It doesn’t have to be cost-neutral." — Duncan Webb (relaying Peeni Henare), arguing the levy lets the Government take an uplift above cost

acuity.statement: Of course, a lot has been said about this bill in the previous readings. We’ve had some of the Green Party members say that they’re just filibustering, even though they support it. I don’t think there’s much more to say on this bill. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows O'Connor's substantive case (oversight shifting from Parliament to the Minister, submitters' evidence that compliance cost will land on SMEs, the unfulfilled product stewardship schemes) and takes up none of it. It gestures at the debate having happened and at another party's conduct in it, then asserts there is nothing left to say — a reference to the debate rather than engagement with any claim in it, which the rubric places in the low band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor argued "this will likely shift more cost on to small and medium enterprises" and that the bill moves oversight from Parliament to the Minister; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Yes, it’s quite exciting to get all these new Amendment Papers with no notice. It’s a pity, because this is a bill that we had some substantive conversations on at the committee, and certainly the Green Party deliberated at length in determining whether we would support or oppose the bill because it addresses a very serious problem, a very real problem of conversion of arable land to forestry, and it attempts to make a step in the correct direction on that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Russell's preceding complaint — that the Amendment Paper arrived without notice to non-government parties — and extends it with his own party's committee experience, before moving on to entirely prepared material on clause 6 and the LUC classes. The opening would have to change if Russell had not raised the no-notice grievance, but the bulk of the speech would not, which is the ~0.5 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "dropped with no notice to the Opposition" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: To answer the member’s question, the bill very clearly does not distinguish between production and carbon forestry. It does not restrict emissions trading scheme registration on Land Use Capability classes 7 and 8, because of the very principle that it is aiming to protect our most productive land for that food production that I’ve explained, but also allowing for sustainable growth in the forestry sector.
acuity.explanation: Takes Abel's specific question about LUC classes 7 and 8 and answers it on its own terms: it corrects the premise that the bill treats carbon forestry separately, confirms that classes 7 and 8 are not restricted, and gives the rationale. The content is determined by what Abel asked; a different question on the same bill would have required a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why would it be a good idea to have any percentage of carbon forestry permitted on Land Use Capability (LUC) 8?" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: To respond, also, to the Labour Party member’s questions—and I can sense her outrage about the consultation—but, you know, this bill has been widely canvassed. It has been through the proper parliamentary process. It has had a thorough hearing at the select committee process. In fact, the amendments made in the Amendment Paper that we’ve put forward today—there’s been plenty of hours since it was put forward—are as a direct result of industry feedback that the select committee heard. I can confirm that all parties have been consulted on the changes in the bill during that parliamentary process, and I would have thought that those parties who are making grand statements of outrage at the moment would have had something to say about that during the select committee process.
acuity.explanation: Engages Russell's actual contention — that the Opposition got no notice and no consultation on a substantive Amendment Paper — by disputing it directly (all parties consulted, the amendments follow select committee evidence). It does not supply the specific explanation she demanded of why no phone call was made, and part of the reply pivots to characterising her outrage rather than the process, so it falls short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "dropped with no notice to the Opposition... There was no attempt to consult with us over the nature of the changes" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I would just point out that two of my questions are still outstanding. One is on whether or not New Zealand First and ACT were aware of adding the regulations around changing the annual hectare limit to the requirement for consultation with iwi. For the first one, on why we weren’t informed about the introduction of this Amendment Paper, the Minister in the chair, the Hon Nicola Grigg, tried to say that it was because there was a select committee process. acuity.statement: First and foremost, the question asked was: why didn’t the Government do a full review of forestry of the emissions trading scheme (ETS)? Well, if we go back to the cold, old, dark days of 658 days ago when we came into Government, we inherited a scenario where the ETS market was in a state of massive volatility. Why? Because the prior Government had initiated a review of forestry in the ETS and it completely shocked the market. The first thing we did was stop that review.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific question put to him by the preceding speaker and answers it with a reason — that a previous forestry-in-ETS review destabilised the market, so the Government deliberately stopped it and will not restart it. acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "I do want to ask the Minister why that wasn’t done, why the Government made the choice not to go the whole hog and to review the role of forestry within the emissions trading scheme (ETS) but instead to come up with this option."

One of them is in the context of the generic definition; the other is specifically for the context around the 25 percent.

acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel said "I have an amendment which proposes to remove the ballot system entirely" and this statement does not take up that proposal or his 15,000 question.

Scored purely on engagement, not on precision or completeness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "So I’m little bit confused as to why the regulations come into force ahead of the whole Act coming into force, and I would be grateful if the Minister could clarify that."

If we were actually trying to solve this problem, which we know is a problem, we would be addressing it directly; we wouldn’t just be tinkering around the edges. We would, for example, be taking forestry out of the emissions trading scheme because of the way it has influenced it and is, essentially, ineffective.

Engagement is pointable but partial, which is the 0.5 band.

acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "The obvious solution is to take forestry—carbon forestry—out of the emissions trading scheme."

We had the second-oldest and most mature ETS marketplace in the country, which does the heavy lifting in terms of carbon reduction. The policy positions of simply saying, “Well, let’s just remove it” when it’s a long-dated sector and industry is just simply market-destructive - type language.
acuity.explanation: This goes straight at the specific proposal Pham had just made — take forestry out of the ETS — and argues a consequence of it: market shock and volatility in a long-dated sector that needs certainty. He also meets her 'tinkering around the edges' charge by naming the cap as the thing that addresses the underlying issue. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "We would, for example, be taking forestry out of the emissions trading scheme because of the way it has influenced it and is, essentially, ineffective."

It’s going to support food and fibre. It’s going to support sheep and beef.” Which is it? Is it going to do both or is it going to do nothing?

He then returns to prepared material (the Green Budget, the Tomorrow Together event), so the engagement is partial rather than sustained, but it is pointable and the speech would read differently had Foster not made that distinction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "they are seeing the problem that they think we are trying to solve as being the climate problem, but that’s not really what this bill is about; this bill is about the afforestation and the impact on our rural communities"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "Well, work with people rather than accuse them of—"
