acuity.explanation: Mooney follows a substantive turn by Seymour in the same third-reading debate, so he is eligible. His speech is on the matter under debate — farm-to-forestry conversion and restoring the farming/forestry balance — but engages no part of Seymour's actual argument: it neither takes up the 15,000-hectare cap, the property-rights tension Seymour said the Government resolved, nor any claim Seymour made. It reads as prepared valedictory material that would be word-identical whatever Seymour had argued, with only a thematic overlap ('carbon forestry had skewed the balance') rather than engagement, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour spoke about reducing the ETS incentive to "only 15,000 new hectares per year" and about property rights, and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: It’s obvious that the Opposition haven’t visited a rural school in the past two decades, because when you visit rural schools, usually they are full of diverse, rich cultural backgrounds from our wonderful migrant communities who make an enormously great and valuable contribution to our dairy sector, to our sheep and beef sector, to our farming sector, and we should acknowledge the contribution that they make to help get food on the table for New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor's immediately preceding turn argued that farmers employing migrant workers who 'come without families' is why rural schools are seeing fewer pupils. Meager takes up exactly that strand — rural schools and migrant workers — and contests it directly, asserting rural schools are full of migrant-background children who contribute to farming. The speech would have been different had O'Connor argued something else, so engagement is high. (That he recasts O'Connor's labour-market claim as a slight on migrants is a reasoning/fairness问题 for Rigor, not Acuity; it is not scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "There’s been a massive shift in the people working in rural New Zealand because farmers are employing migrant workers over New Zealanders. Most of them come without families. That’s why the schools are seeing less people."

acuity.statement: This is a really good bill, and it was really disheartening to hear about the lack of plans from the other side, of course. For the two years that we’ve seen them so far, they’ve planned to do absolutely zip, zilch, nothing apart from wait for Scott Willis to lend them a copy of his budget.
acuity.explanation: O'Connor had made a specific claim — that the coalition Government has no emissions plan beyond planting trees, and is caught between saying it doesn't want to and that it has to. Meager mirrors the word 'plans' straight back at the Opposition without engaging any part of that claim: no answer on the emissions plan, no rebuttal of the petard point, just a reversal and a jibe. Mentioning the previous speaker's theme while engaging none of its content sits in the 0.1–0.3 band; the gesture at the debate puts it at 0.2.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Damien O'Connor: "The fact is that this coalition Government has no plans to reduce emissions other than to plant more trees."

acuity.statement: We know that that wholesale shift to forestry has led to a loss of employment, a loss of jobs, and that has then had flow-on impacts on rural communities when it comes to the closure of schools and the closure of services. We don’t agree with that, and, for that reason, we are cautiously supporting this bill.
acuity.explanation: Meager's preceding turn asserted rural schools are thriving and full of migrant-community children. Radhakrishnan takes up the rural-schools strand — attributing closures to the forestry shift rather than accepting his picture — and ties it to her party's voting position, so part of the exchange is engaged. But she answers the topic rather than his specific claim (she does not dispute that rural schools are culturally diverse or that migrants contribute), and the passage is otherwise prepared material explaining Labour's cautious support. Partial engagement that can be pointed at: 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "when you visit rural schools, usually they are full of diverse, rich cultural backgrounds from our wonderful migrant communities"

acuity.statement: The member who resumed his seat claims that we did nothing in this space. We actually initiated a more comprehensive review into the ETS. The Climate Commission has also agreed that that is actually what the direction of travel should be, but, of course, this is not a Government that actually wants to do anything of substance.
acuity.explanation: Mooney's interjection made a definite claim — that the previous Government did literally nothing on this. Radhakrishnan names the claim, contradicts it with a specific counter-fact (an initiated ETS review) and cites the Climate Commission as supporting that direction of travel, then turns it into her own argument. The reply is directly contingent on what was just said and would read differently had the interjection been anything else, which is the top of the band. Whether the review claim is accurate is a Veracity matter and not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "Your Government did nothing—literally nothing."

acuity.statement: I think in considering clause 1, and speaking to the title of the bill, it would be worth us getting a solid understanding in the committee of the environment our local media sector is operating in. This is relevant to both the advertising revenue available to our broadcasting, television, and radio sector, but also to the wider sector and the extreme challenges that they have faced over the last two years.
acuity.explanation: Penk opened the committee stage by defending the repeal of section 81 on the grounds that modern media is consumed across many platforms and should be aligned. Davidson follows on the same bill and gestures at the debate (clause 1, the broadcasting sector's revenue environment), but takes up none of Penk's actual reasoning — he neither disputes the platform-alignment argument nor the claim about less-commercial programming, instead moving straight into prepared material on Newshub and TVNZ job cuts. On topic, but the speech would read identically whatever Penk had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there are many different ways and many different avenues—channels, so to speak—in which we consume media" — Chris Penk

acuity.statement: The title’s an appropriate title for the bill because it describes what the bill does.
acuity.explanation: Davidson put a two-part question. Penk answers the second part squarely and gives a reason for it, so the reply is clearly shaped by what was asked, but he engages nothing of the revenue question or of Davidson's argument that the bill's small financial return makes the title overstated. One strand taken up, the rest left alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "how much revenue does the Minister believe this will bring for the sector; and does the Minister think, given the very small revenue bought, that the title is an appropriate title for the bill?"

acuity.statement: I wonder if the Minister would put it in the Hansard and on the record: what percentage of the revenue that this bill will bring by repealing advertising restrictions, as per the title, will make up a percentage of the amount of total revenue?
acuity.explanation: He picks up the title thread Penk had just closed off and presses the revenue half Penk left unanswered, sharpening it into a specific quantitative ask. That is engagement with the exchange rather than prepared material. But he does not take on Penk's actual reasoning — that a title describing the bill's content is by that fact appropriate — he restates the question in a new form.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "The title’s an appropriate title for the bill because it describes what the bill does."

acuity.statement: The content of this very short bill is to repeal advertising restrictions. It’s appropriate, therefore, that its title is “Repeal of Advertising Restrictions”. Anything more or less than that would be remiss on the part of the Minister, and I’m pleased that he has gone for a very descriptive, straightforward title.
acuity.explanation: A restatement of the answer he had already given, expanded slightly. The question asked for a proportion of total revenue; nothing in the reply engages that, and the reply would read identically had Menéndez March asked any other question about the title. It stays on the matter under debate, which keeps it above the floor, but re-asserting a prior answer is not engaging new content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "what percentage of the revenue that this bill will bring by repealing advertising restrictions, as per the title, will make up a percentage of the amount of total revenue?" — the figure asked for is neither supplied nor addressed.

acuity.statement: Given that this bill is called a repeal of advertising restrictions bill—but it does, in fact, take away only the advertising restrictions that were on those Christian holidays and Anzac Day and does not repeal any other advertising restrictions that are still in law—it’s quite useful for us to understand not only what we are doing here but the historical context that we are, effectively, erasing here by taking away those two particular dates.
acuity.explanation: This sentence contradicts the premise Penk had twice rested on — that the title describes what the bill does — by pointing out the bill repeals only the holiday restrictions and leaves other advertising restrictions in law. That is a real engagement with the specific claim just made. It sits inside a long, plainly prepared passage on her 25 commencement-date amendments, however, so the engagement is one strand rather than the shape of the speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "The content of this very short bill is to repeal advertising restrictions. It’s appropriate, therefore, that its title is “Repeal of Advertising Restrictions”."

acuity.statement: It’s clear, however, that—from the Government point of view, and as members Opposite have actually pointed out—this is a well-signalled move. It’s important to bring it in as soon as reasonably possible. We’re not talking about doing this on Christmas Eve or on Maundy Thursday or on 24 April; there is sufficient time for arrangements to be made such that advertising will be restricted in the way that the bill sets out.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Williams's proposed alternative commencement dates and answers the substance of why they are unnecessary: the move is well signalled, and the day-after-assent date does not fall on any of the restricted days her amendments were built around. He also meets her point about other days of significance by noting advertising is already permitted on them. The speech could not have been delivered had she argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "I don’t think the day after Royal assent is the most appropriate date. I think it would be appropriate to choose one of the important days also in the range of Christian holidays to assent to this bill and for it to commence".

acuity.statement: I’d just like to highlight a point from our broadcasters who this bill will affect—is that as soon as possible for this bill to be put through the House, giving them time so that, if possible, they are able to get advertising booked in time for this Christmas? That is what they are hoping for.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Davidson's preceding argument — that commencement timing relative to the Christmas/Easter quarter determines the revenue the industry recovers — and supplies the broadcasters' own position on it. She does not engage the specific question he put (the $6 million estimate, the per-day revenue value), and her remark otherwise passes on a prepared message, so this is partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "So if the assent was to miss the ability to be implemented prior to that quarter, in the next 12 months from now, then the net benefit of the projected, very optimistic, $6 million that this change claims to return to the industry would in fact be significantly eroded"

acuity.statement: I ask the Minister to consider the fact that maybe Maundy Thursday would be the day of Royal assent because it is mysterious and the darkness of the future of broadcasting is upon us.
acuity.explanation: The contribution is squarely on the matter under debate — clause 2 and the date of commencement — and opens with a gesture at the committee's exchange ("It’s interesting to listen to the different arguments coming from the committee"), but it engages no part of the arguments actually put by the preceding speakers. The Easter riff would read identically whatever Davidson or Marcroft had said, so it sits at the top of the unpointable band rather than above it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the two preceding turns in this window (Reuben Davidson on whether assent will fall before the holiday quarter, Jenny Marcroft on broadcasters wanting it done in time for Christmas advertising) argue for the earliest possible commencement, and this statement does not take either up — the Maundy Thursday remark it builds on was made by the Minister in a turn outside this window.

acuity.statement: He’s contradicting his own colleague around the fact that his colleague is talking about bringing in this as soon as possible to ensure that we include the weight of Christmas in those first quarter occasions.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific proposal just made — set Royal assent at Maundy Thursday — and does something with it: shows it is inconsistent with the position Bennett's own colleagues argued moments earlier (commence before the Christmas quarter to capture the advertising revenue), and draws the consequence that any delay defeats the bill's purpose. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "I ask the Minister to consider the fact that maybe Maundy Thursday would be the day of Royal assent"

acuity.statement: One of those is the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, which is a great piece of legislation that was sitting there ready to go and was, for a time, worked on by the Minister and by a select committee, but, unfortunately, progress has slowed significantly or, potentially, entirely on the important work happening there, which means that we are relying on this Act—the Broadcasting Act 1989—which is the Act referred to in this third part.
acuity.explanation: The turn is on the matter before the committee (clause 3 and the age of the principal Act), so it is not wholly unresponsive, but it engages no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answer on commencement timing. The catalogue of alternative bills reads as prepared material that would be identical whatever Penk had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk argued "the day after Royal assent is literally the fastest that we can do that", and this statement does not take that up — it moves to a list of other legislative options the Minister could pursue.

acuity.statement: But, of course, it’s the case that unless we were to regard as sacred, from the point of view of restricting advertising, every single day that is important to some New Zealander or other, we will simply not have any advertising at all.
acuity.explanation: Takes Abel's actual argument — that Christmas, Easter and Anzac morning are days whose freedom from commercial intrusion should be preserved — and pushes it to its consequence, that a sacredness test cannot be confined to those days without arbitrariness, so the choice is consistency or no advertising at all. The speech would be different if Abel had argued something else; it is built on the premise Abel supplied and names him. Not a full 1.0 only because it answers the principle rather than any specific claim about the 6 a.m.-to-midday Anzac window Abel raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "These are days when the absence of commercial intrusion is something that we should think it is appropriate to preserve."

acuity.statement: It’s helpful that the Minister has, in this debate, recognised, I guess, the principles at play here, and though Labour is supporting this, we have a number of questions around those days which are important to New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the strand of Penk's reply that conceded the principle of sacredness, and builds on his framing of 'principles at play' before moving to her own prepared material on clause 3 and the word 'amends'. She does not take up his fairness-and-consistency reasoning or his point about advertising continuing on unrestricted platforms, so this is engagement with one strand and the topic rather than with his argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "I’m sympathetic to the point that Mr Abel makes, in general terms, about whether we preserve something as sacred"

acuity.statement: It’s not appropriate for that type of provision to go into the explanations the member is seeking. If she wants a statement on the general policy, there is a general policy statement. If she wants a note as to explanation, there’s an explanatory note.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific request just made — Williams's proposed amendments replacing 'amends' in clause 3 with an explanatory phrase — and rebuts it on its own ground by naming where such material belongs instead (the general policy statement and the explanatory note). The reply is unintelligible without her preceding turn and would have had to change entirely had she argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "To clause 3, and I have a number of amendments that the Minister might consider."

acuity.statement: Just to address briefly the points helpfully raised by the member, starting with the final one: the Minister for Broadcasting interacted with a wide range of stakeholders, and I can answer the question on my own behalf, wearing a different hat, so to speak, as Minister for Veterans. I was and remain interested in the views of ex - service personnel in terms of the restrictions being lifted from Anzac Day. However, there’s a diversity of views among the veteran population—I see my colleague and friend Dr Vanessa Weenink nodding, and she’s one herself, of course.
acuity.explanation: Takes Tangaere-Manuel's questions in order and answers the specific one about consultation with the RSA and serving/ex-service personnel, speaking to it in his own capacity as Minister for Veterans rather than deflecting to general praise of the bill. The speech would be different had she asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "i kōrero koutou ki te hunga e kīia nei ko te RSA—Returned Services Association—i kōrero rānei koutou ki ngā hōia?"

acuity.statement: I am hoping for a number of calls on this clause because I do have a large number of questions. Many of them are on the basis of things that the Minister for Building and Construction has said or answers that the Minister has given or points that he’s referenced throughout his very generous answers, for which we’re very grateful as we’ve stepped through some of the meatier issues across clause 1, clause 2, and clause 3 of the bill as we’ve gone through it this afternoon.
acuity.explanation: On the right subject and gestures at the Minister's earlier answers in general terms, but engages no part of the content Penk had just given on consultation with veterans, Māori broadcasters or the churches; it moves to prepared material on clause 4 and the section 81 penalty. A generic nod to 'answers the Minister has given' is a reference, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "there was consultation with Whakaata Māori, Te Māngai Pāho, and Te Puni Kōkiri" — Davidson does not take up this or any other strand of Penk's answer, only nods generally to the Minister having answered.

acuity.statement: Do you know what happens? It gets absorbed in the cost of administering the system at significant and net detriments to the country.
acuity.explanation: Interjected directly into Davidson's argument that repeal risks losing fine revenue to the Crown, and supplies a counter on that exact point — that the revenue is consumed by administration costs. Short, but squarely aimed at the claim being made rather than at the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "are we at a risk here of losing a source of revenue for Government, because all money that comes into Government can be spent on other things?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I thank the member for his question. I think any foregone revenue in the form of penalties that won’t be able to be applied would be outweighed by the taxable activity being the payment for the advertising.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question Davidson put — the revenue forgone by repealing the penalty provision — and answers it on its own terms, arguing the lost penalty income is outweighed by tax on the newly permitted advertising. The reply would be different had Davidson asked something else. Its vagueness (no figure supplied) is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "can the Minister clarify the level of revenue that has come in, and, therefore, if this part of the Act is repealed and that revenue can no longer be gathered?"

acuity.statement: As I’ve said, we’re going from a situation where there was no advertising allowed on Christmas, Easter, Anzac Day, and Sunday mornings, and there will now be unrestricted advertising at those times. What’s unusual about that is that those are still important days, as the Minister has said, but for linear media to now have no restrictions at those times is something that some people would consider unusual. The first question I want to ask the Minister is: is it the case that after this repeal is through, it will be acceptable, and does the Minister think it is acceptable, to advertise gambling, alcohol, and tobacco products on a Sunday morning?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the effect of the section 81 repeal) and there is a gesture at the Minister's earlier remarks about important days, but it engages no part of the revenue argument Penk had just made. Prepared material on the right subject, re-launching her own question rather than testing his answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk argued that forgone penalty revenue "would be outweighed by the taxable activity being the payment for the advertising", and this statement does not take that up — it restates the speaker's own earlier framing and opens a new line of questioning.

acuity.statement: One of the things that was interesting is that in that detailing, the bill doesn’t include Waitangi Day and it doesn’t include Matariki. So there are two other public holidays that the bill could have considered that would have been repealed.
acuity.explanation: Squarely about the clause under debate — which days the repeal of section 81 covers — and nods at earlier exchanges ("we did speak through this at some length at an earlier point"), so not wholly unresponsive. But it engages neither Williams' question immediately before it nor Penk's revenue answer; it works through a prepared list of further questions that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams asked whether it would be acceptable "to advertise gambling, alcohol, and tobacco products on a Sunday morning", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: They already advertise on a Sunday morning, but it’s television advertising that will be freed up here on the Sunday morning as well as on Anzac morning, and both TV and radio broadcasting advertising on Christmas Day, Good Friday, and Easter Sunday. There is some advertising from radio on a couple of those days already.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the factual premise of Williams' characterisation of the status quo — radio already advertises on Sunday mornings and on some of the affected days, so it is television that the repeal frees up. That is engagement with a specific claim just made, but she takes up only that one strand before returning to prepared material on revenue assumptions and the sacred-days theme, so a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "we’re going from a situation where there was no advertising allowed on Christmas, Easter, Anzac Day, and Sunday mornings"

acuity.statement: He pai te whakaaro o tēnei pire, kia whai pūtea ngā kamupene nui, engari kei te haere te pūtea ki ngā kamupene nui, ehara ki ngā kamupene hanga hōtaka. Nā reira, me pēhea kei a koe he oranga mō rātou?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's preceding answer — the extra advertising revenue the bill is said to generate — and presses on who actually receives it, arguing it reaches large broadcasters rather than production companies. It does not engage his reasoning about enforcement or advertising standards, and the bulk of the turn is her own prepared material on Māori media, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "The figure of $6 million per year is considered a conservative estimate, but, of course, we'll see that in due course."

acuity.statement: My question to you, Minister, is: has there been any consideration to how having advertising for online gambling is going to go down in many New Zealand households, if they are faced with that on those deeply significant, spiritual days of Anzac Day, Christmas, Good Friday, and Easter?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. The question is squarely about the bill under debate and the significance of the four days, so it is not wholly adrift, but it engages no part of any preceding argument — neither Tangaere-Manuel's funding-flow point nor the Minister's reasoning about existing advertising-standards regimes. The speech would read identically whatever had been said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel had just asked how Māori programming would be protected if the bill's revenue flows to large companies, and this statement does not take that up; it opens a fresh line on the Online Casino Gambling Bill.

acuity.statement: The proposed legislation that the member references is not legislation. I don’t think it’s appropriate for me to comment on what the ultimate shape of that might be as it relates to this.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific premise of Foster's question — the Online Casino Gambling Bill — and does something with it, namely points out it is still before select committee and so has no settled shape to comment on. The reply is shaped entirely by what Foster asked and would not exist if he had asked something else. Not a full 1.0 because it disposes of the question on status grounds rather than engaging the substance of the household-reaction point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "has there been any consideration to how having advertising for online gambling is going to go down in many New Zealand households"

acuity.statement: In relation to the thoughtful questions posed by Cushla Tangaere-Manuel—thank you for sharing your experience with us—in terms of the flow of revenue internally or as between content creators and the platforms themselves, I think that’s an internal matter for those media companies. I would only comment that in terms of this bill, by lifting the restrictions, it will enable for more revenue to be generated and, therefore, a larger pie that can then be sliced and distributed as they see fit and as legally required, as the case may be.
acuity.explanation: Identifies her exact concern — the distribution of revenue between broadcasters and the production companies that make the programmes — and answers it directly with the 'larger pie' argument plus a jurisdictional point that allocation is internal to the companies. The answer is specific to her claim and would have to change if she had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "engari kei te haere te pūtea ki ngā kamupene nui, ehara ki ngā kamupene hanga hōtaka" (the funding goes to the big companies, not the programme-making companies)

acuity.statement: My understanding is that some YouTube users choose not to monetise their content on certain days, including—that must be the experience the member’s had, so I respect that and understand that. I certainly respect and understand that that’s a choice that those content creators and uploaders may wish to take.
acuity.explanation: Takes the member's specific factual claim and recharacterises it — not a platform-level prohibition but individual creators choosing not to monetise — which, if accepted, removes the counter-example's force against the bill. This is the sharpest possible form of engagement: accepting the observation while disputing what it shows. The reply is unintelligible without the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "is the Minister aware that YouTube doesn’t have advertisements on certain days, similar to linear platforms?"

acuity.statement: Just really briefly, if I can respond to those important points, the Advertising Standards Authority will continue to have a mandate to uphold standards of decency and social responsibility, and to consider questions of offensiveness. I think that they would do that in the context of all the circumstances, including—as they currently do—the time of day but also the particular day of the year and its special significance. I think these are serious matters, but I also think that we must be able to trust our institutions to be able to make reasonable judgment calls in the fullness of the context in which they occur. For that reason, we think it’s best not to be too prescriptive or to try to over-engineer the solution.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact proposition Williams put — that the Advertising Standards Authority lacks and needs explicit powers for Sunday, Anzac Day and Christmas — and answers it on its own terms: the ASA's existing mandate already extends to the particular day and its significance, so prescribing it in primary legislation would over-engineer the solution. Delete Williams' argument and substitute another and this reply would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will he not at least accept one of my amendments—there are only two—that would make it clear that the Advertising Standards Authority needs some extra powers here to consider those specific days" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: That might seem tempting, devoid of context, to particular members of the House with particular perspectives, bearing in mind the broad range of views of New Zealanders on various different matters, and in the case of Anzac Day, it seems to me that the legal precedent is actually strongly in favour of freedom of expression, under section 14 of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. There was the Morse case, which the member Arena Williams may have studied at law school—as did I—where burning the flag on Anzac Day was not legally prohibited precisely because we value that freedom of expression, notwithstanding the fact that that might be and, in fact, it deliberately was, designed to calculate the offence and the outrage of some.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific premise of Williams' Anzac Day example by naming the authority that cuts the other way (Morse, and s 14 of the Bill of Rights Act), arguing the precedent protects offensive expression rather than restricting it. This is engagement with the content of her claim, not a reference to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We have very well-developed case law, for instance, on what is acceptable speech on Anzac Day and what is acceptable to do at an Anzac Day celebration, remembrance day, or parade." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on this, the third reading of the Privacy Amendment Bill. It is an important piece of legislation to exercise privacy rights. It is important to have knowledge about the collection of the information when it is not from the source—that is, the individuals themselves.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party-position material on the right subject. It restates the bill's purpose without engaging any part of the preceding contribution — notably not the select committee change Stephenson singled out — and would have read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson spoke about the select committee's added exception so that use of information for public good by galleries, libraries, archives and museums would not be inhibited, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The Privacy Amendment Bill was one of the first few bills that came through the Justice Committee at the beginning of this term and it was great to be contacted by different librarians and archivists who have a real interest in making sure that people’s rights and privacy and information are both protected but also treated with sensitivity, and also that when information is within the public interest, it is able to be accessed.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand the previous speaker highlighted — the librarians-and-archivists exception and public-interest access — and adds the select committee's engagement with those groups, but does not do anything with his claim beyond converging on it, and her nod to "the two speeches before me" is only about brevity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ensuring that information, when it’s being used for public good—so galleries, libraries, archives, and museums—wouldn’t be inhibited by these new principles" — Todd Stephenson

acuity.statement: What I’d like to just comment on is that in this fast-changing digital world, it’s great to progress a bill like this that further protects the personal information of all my neighbours in Takanini.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate but engages no part of any preceding contribution; it is a general commendation that would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul spoke about the librarians and archivists who made submissions and about balancing privacy against public-interest access, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Now, in this modern day and age, as the world moves and shifts and changes, there are so many places and spaces, as my colleague has said, where information is gathered. We need to make sure that we know, that I myself as a consumer and I myself as a citizen understand and know, what happens with information about myself—where it goes; who has it—to make sure that my privacy is protected but also that the privacy of my family is protected and the privacy of my community.
acuity.explanation: Bennett follows Webb in the same third reading debate and gestures at him twice ("as my colleague has said", "As has been talked about"), reusing his examples of indirect collection (cards, cameras, registrations). But he takes up no part of Webb's actual argument — that the bill is non-trivial, that private surveillance feeds supplied to police raise search-and-seizure as well as privacy rights issues, or that collectors such as museums and archives will be caught by clause 4. The speech is prepared material on the right subject, and would read almost identically had Webb argued something else about privacy; the reference to him is a courtesy, not an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is about the collection of information and the provision of it to third parties." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: For people in Mount Roskill, this bill is a critical step towards protecting our privacy and ensuring fairness for all New Zealanders. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed, substantive critique of the bill's exemptions, the entity-discretion test for notifying the Privacy Commissioner, and the loss of four Human Rights Review Tribunal deputy chairs. The statement engages none of it: no acknowledgement of the exceptions point, no answer on the tribunal capacity claim, no defence of the serious-harm threshold. It is prepared commendation that would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, and could be delivered at any reading of any bill the member supports. It is at least on the subject under debate (this bill, privacy), which keeps it off the floor, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument, so 0.1 rather than 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters spoke about the breadth of the new IPP 3A(4) exceptions and about access to justice — "you take decision makers down from six decision makers to two decision makers" — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The fact that this unrest does create an elevated level of risk from foreign interference is something we cannot ignore. It is important that we continue to evolve and respond and develop the powers and authorities and the abilities for us to keep New Zealand citizens safe; and the protection from foreign interference is exactly one more step in that direction.
acuity.explanation: Costello follows a substantive turn by Stephenson in the same second-reading debate, so she is eligible. Her speech is prepared material on the correct subject — the general threat of foreign interference and the need for enforcement powers — but it engages none of Stephenson's specific content: not his claim that the bill codifies existing law, not the unanimous select committee recommendation, not his Victorian university example. The speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Stephenson had said about the bill, though it does at least address the matter under debate, which keeps it above 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson argued that the bill largely codifies existing law while making it clearer, and creates new offences to address gaps in criminal liability, and this statement does not take up any part of that argument.

acuity.statement: Israel’s treatment of humanitarian flotillas has been heavy-handed and unlawful. The Government must stand up for its people and demand their safety without hesitation.
acuity.explanation: Peters had devoted a passage of the ministerial statement immediately preceding this to the three New Zealanders detained from the flotilla, framing them as people who 'freely chose to place themselves in a dangerous situation but now expect their Government to bail them out'. Henare takes up that exact strand and inverts the framing — the fault lies with Israel's unlawful interception, and the Government's duty is unconditional rather than grudging. That is a pointable engagement with one specific element of the preceding turn, but it does not rebut Peters' reasoning (the consular assistance already offered, the irony he drew), and it sits inside otherwise prepared material about the Prime Minister's lack of courage, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: 'Another irony is that three private individuals freely chose to place themselves in a dangerous situation but now expect their Government to bail them out.'

acuity.statement: New Zealand deserves a leader who will stand with humanity and most of the international community and not one who will wobble indecisively. New Zealand’s reputation and moral authority has already suffered thanks to this Government, and that must stop.
acuity.explanation: Peters had pre-empted precisely this charge in the turn before, saying others 'have expressed the concern that by not recognising Palestinian Statehood, New Zealand’s international reputation will suffer' and reporting that 'we have not received criticism from partners'. Henare asserts the contrary — that the reputational damage has already occurred — which is a direct contradiction of a specific claim just made and so is clearly pointable. But he supplies nothing against Peters' stated evidence (the absence of partner criticism) and does not engage the ceasefire-first argument that is the core of the Minister's case, so this reads as prepared condemnation that happens to collide with the claim rather than a rebuttal of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: 'we can report that we have not received criticism from partners or from other countries near to, or far from, the Middle East'

acuity.statement: Now, what’s fascinating about that question is that there was a poll where 60 percent of New Zealanders did not express support for recognition. It was almost as though that majority is of no moment; 60 percent did not express it. And it was followed up by a Stuff poll that said 55:45 percent against recognition until it was distorted by people voting countless times. So to make the statement that New Zealanders in the majority are for recognition is demonstrably numerically wrong.
acuity.explanation: This answers a question put directly to him, and it fastens onto one identifiable component of that question — the appeal to 'hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens' as representative of public opinion — and attacks it with polling figures. The reply would have had to be different had Henare framed the question without the public-support premise, which is the deciding test and puts it above the prepared-material band. It is only a partial engagement, though: the question asked whether the Government should impose sanctions, and the substance of sanctions is never taken up at all; he contests the premise and leaves the request itself unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: 'does he agree with the hundreds of thousands of peaceful citizens in this country that the Government of New Zealand needs to take more action, like sanctions'

acuity.statement: The reality is, again, that is a misstatement of the actual facts here. But here’s the point, really. Helen Clark had nine years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Jacinda Ardern had five years to recognise Palestine; she didn’t. Mr Hipkins had a year to recognise Palestine and he didn’t. We are sick of people who are lions in Opposition and lambs in Government.
acuity.explanation: Asserts the question misstates the facts but engages no part of the ICJ/genocide-obligation claim and never reaches the "what actions has the Government taken" element; pivots instead to the recognition records of three former Labour leaders. Engages the broad topic (recognition of Palestine) rather than the claim put, and the pivot material would have been identical whatever the question was.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister agree that New Zealand was put on notice in 2024 by the International Court of Justice that it had a legal obligation to prevent genocide in Gaza" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: The reality is, there has been no International Court of Justice ruling to that effect. Or does he think that we should just ignore the International Court of Justice and just come to our own interpretation, legally qualified or otherwise?
acuity.explanation: Takes the legal premise underlying the question head-on, denying that any ICJ ruling establishes the duty asserted, and turns it into a counter-question about who is entitled to interpret the convention. The reply would have to change if the question had rested on a different legal source, which is the test; the inference's soundness and the terseness of the answer are matters for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what does the Minister believe constitutes the New Zealand Government’s duty to prevent genocide under the genocide convention" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: The Minister, in his speech, spoke about not recognising Palestine in fear of rewarding the actions of Hamas, and yet straight after he did not recognise Palestine, the Israel officials were celebrating, as if it was a reward for their genocide. So that does not hold, Mr Peters.
acuity.explanation: Names the Minister's own stated rationale (withholding recognition so as not to reward Hamas) and attempts to turn it against him with a consequence he did not address, and her later passage on conditions engages his criteria-based defence of non-recognition. Not a full 1.0 because much of the surrounding speech is prepared Green Party material that sits beside rather than inside the exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the primary answer to the question began with the criteria from the Montevideo convention about recognition. That has not been satisfied." — Winston Peters

acuity.statement: The Green Party co-leader just said that they had a motion in 2021. What you didn’t tell the House is what happened to it. My question now is: what did Labour do with your motion? Why didn’t you tell the country? Why didn’t you tell the people listening around New Zealand, instead of thinking that we will just ignore the facts? The silence is deafening on that one question.
acuity.explanation: Fastens on one specific detail Davidson supplied — the 2021 motion — and supplies missing context about its fate, so it is not merely prepared material; but it answers none of her actual question about how deferring recognition advances a two-State solution, using her detail as a springboard to a question about Labour instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "recognising Palestinian Statehood, the likes of which the Green Party put forward a motion to propose to do exactly that in 2021, was opposed by National and ACT MPs" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: New Zealand’s decision not to recognise a Palestinian State at this time is the right one, and ACT supports it. Recognition should be based on clear, democratic principles, not just political pressure or symbolism. A State must have a legitimate, accountable Government; respect for the rule of law; and a commitment to peace.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate, and sets out criteria that bear on the question, but engages no part of the preceding argument — not the claim that Israeli officials treated non-recognition as a reward, nor the objection to outside powers imposing conditions. The speech reads as prepared party position and the long Freedom House passage could have been delivered in a different debate entirely, so it sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued that withholding recognition rewards Israel and that Palestinians must set their own conditions, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: There was a statement made there about genocide that is not authorised, supported, or precedented by any international court whatsoever, but they make the statement anyway, and, sadly, that’s been far too often the case on this very, very sad issue.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand squarely — the factual standing of the word 'genocide', which is the load-bearing premise of the question — and disputes it. But he leaves the actual question (how the Government can know its influence is small when it has taken no action) entirely untouched and moves to Myanmar and Sudan. Partial engagement: you can point at what was engaged, but the question itself survives unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the genocide that they are committing in Palestine" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, asking how the Minister would know how little influence New Zealand has

acuity.statement: Well, here’s the reality: there are clear guidelines out in the 1990s Montevideo Convention on recognition, which is not met. We’ve had decades and decades of political parties supporting this criteria when all of a sudden, despite Clark having the 90s to do that, despite Jacinda Ardern having five years to do that, and despite Mr Hipkins having one year to do that, they all of a sudden want to change the criteria. Now that doesn’t bespeak, surely, to the ethics and morality of their argument.
acuity.explanation: The question asked for a causal mechanism: how does recognition complicate a ceasefire. He answers an adjacent question instead — why recognition is not warranted on Montevideo criteria — and then pivots to the records of Clark, Ardern and Hipkins. On the topic put to him, and engaging one strand of it (recognition), but the specific link he was asked to explain is never addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in what way would recognising Palestinian Statehood complicate achieving a ceasefire?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: Isn’t it amazing: you’ve got countries like Saudi Arabia setting out criteria—which they’ve never accepted—that Hamas must go; they must lay down their arms and leave the country. You’ve got the Arab people next door to them—strictest rules possible because they know there’s no possible peace with Hamas still there. And here you’ve got sympathisers trying to make a defence today in this House.
acuity.explanation: The question put a specific contradiction to him — negligible influence on one hand, decisive interference on the other. Neither horn is taken up. The Hamas material is at most a gesture at why peace is hard, and the turn ends by labelling the questioner's side sympathisers rather than engaging the inconsistency alleged. On the matter under debate, but engaging no part of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how can it be true that we have little to no influence over the genocide in Gaza, yet our recognition of Palestine as a State could also distract from and complicate a ceasefire?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: Well, I’m pleased to say that when we dealt with the United Nations food programme and this marvellous lady, Senator McCain’s widow, on their food programme—and many others as well—they were aware of a country called New Zealand, not one that’s just been made-up over here. And might I say, on the so-called aid programme, the flotilla was offered—by the Italian Government—a military ship to take all of their so-called aid on those boats and to make sure they got to the destination. Guess what? They refused it. They refused it because they’re virtue signallers—they are performative; they aren’t real.
acuity.explanation: He engages the aid half of the question with something concrete — New Zealand's dealings with the UN food programme — and then takes up the flotilla, which the questioner had raised earlier in the exchange, with the Italian ship offer. Genuine partial engagement, but the ceasefire half of the question is dropped and the second half of the answer turns to characterising the flotilla's participants.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what actions is Aotearoa taking to ensure that aid reaches Gaza, and to ensure a ceasefire is achieved" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: Well, the flotilla, as a member of the Green Party found out a number of years ago, was never going to make it. They were told that. They were told that by the New Zealand Government, but they left anyway so that some people could perform and carry on and say things like this, “We are being starved.”, and the next announcement was “We’re on a hunger strike.” I mean, I expect the people over there to have the maturity to see through people like that.
acuity.explanation: This is aimed at the thing he was asked about: he effectively answers no and gives a reason — the flotilla was futile and was told so before departing. That is doing something with the question. What he does not take up is the tension the question was built on, between declining to commend the flotilla and his own calls for unimpeded aid, so it stops short of a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does he commend the flotilla for trying to deliver aid to Gaza when he has consistently called for the unimpeded flow of vital aids to Gaza?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: Well, look, you can’t argue with success and we’re hoping there is success with the American-led plan. It’s backed by farsighted people, people I’d recommend. If you’ve got a chance to listen to the President of Indonesia in his speech, it was something to listen to. There are countries—massive populations of Islamic or Muslim people—with a different view to what I’m hearing in this House. That’s the sad part about it. We might be a long way away, but there’s no reason for us to be blind to the facts.
acuity.explanation: He engages one side of the question — defending alignment with the American-led plan on the grounds that it may succeed and has wide Muslim-world backing. The other side, what New Zealanders want from their foreign policy, is the actual point of comparison in the question and is never addressed; he substitutes the views of other countries for the views of New Zealanders.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is what the USA and Israel want more important than what New Zealanders want to see in their foreign policy?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: The amendment bill that was dropped at the eleventh hour, as Priyanca Radhakrishnan puts it so aptly to this Chamber, these were carve-outs for ring-net fishers, which Ministers justified as supposedly allowing for cheaper or more affordable fish for whānau in South Auckland. We interrogated this abject ridiculousness at the committee of the whole House stage, and the Minister could not provide us with any evidence whatsoever for those fundamentally baseless assertions, nor was the Minister willing to engage in the many amendments that we put forward as members of the Opposition to try and actually work with—if we were to take in good faith—the rationale from the Minister to protect high-protected areas: to do what it says on the tin.
acuity.explanation: Radhakrishnan's immediately preceding turn argued that eleventh-hour amendments allowing commercial ring-net fishing weakened the bill and that the Minister 'could provide no clear rationale for it'. Swarbrick explicitly picks that strand up, names the rationale Ministers actually offered (cheaper fish for South Auckland whānau), and rebuts it with what happened at the committee of the whole House — so the speech would read differently had the previous speaker made a different argument. It is not a full 1.0 because the engagement is one strand of a largely prepared speech (acknowledgments, Caulerpa, the 6 percent versus 30 percent target) that she returns to on either side of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "It was clear the Minister could provide no clear rationale for it."

acuity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to contribute to the restoration of the health and mauri of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana. The bill intends to do this by introducing high protection areas and seafloor protection areas.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft's immediately preceding turn made two substantive claims — the protected-area expansion figures, and an extended case that Watercare's consented discharges (200 per annum, 4 million litres, 158 days of oyster-farm closures) are degrading the gulf — and closed by calling on every MP around the gulf to take the issue up with Watercare. Maipi-Clarke's contribution engages none of that: it restates the bill's purpose and then runs through Te Pāti Māori's own prepared material on the Hauraki Gulf Forum, Te Ohu Kaimoana, customary rights and the party's committee-stage amendments. The speech would be word-for-word identical had Marcroft argued something entirely different about the bill, so there is no engagement to point at — but it is squarely on the matter under debate (the third reading of this bill), so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0. Scored only on responsiveness: the substance about criminalising whānau gathering kai rather than commercial fishers is a real argument, and its merits belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jenny Marcroft spoke about Watercare's waste-water overflows into the Mahurangi River and the expansion of the protected area from 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s a good day in the House. It’s a small step for Parliament but a big step for Tīkapa Moana. I’d also like to acknowledge the Minister, the dark knight of Hamilton West, Minister Potaka, for bringing this bill to fruition. It sat still for too long, and, finally, we are advancing it.
acuity.explanation: Boyack's immediately preceding turn made a specific criticism: that the Minister's own Cabinet paper said ring-net fishers could have fished elsewhere with minimal impact, that the eleventh-hour amendments weaken the bill, and that the Government promised to accelerate it but left it on the Order Paper for two years. Hamilton's turn is on the same bill and glances at the delay point ('It sat still for too long'), but inverts it into credit for the Government without taking up any part of her argument — no mention of the amendments, the high protection areas, the Cabinet paper, or the ring-net carve-out. It is prepared commendation plus acknowledgements that would read identically whatever she had said, so it sits in the unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: 'They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.' — engaged only as a topic (the delay), not as a claim; her substantive criticism of the amendments is not taken up.

acuity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf. This bill is a win for our environment and the Hauraki Gulf.
acuity.explanation: Pham's immediately preceding turn made a specific argument: that protecting only 6 percent of a 99-percent-exploited sea, while still permitting commercial fishing inside the high-protection areas, is not a compromise. Wedd speaks to the same bill and offers her own protection figures (tripling the protected area, 800 square kilometres), which touches the same dimension, but she does not engage the claim at all: she neither disputes the 6 percent figure, nor addresses commercial fishing in high-protection areas, nor defends the late changes Pham called reckless. Opening with "As we all agree across this House" talks past a disagreement voiced seconds earlier. The only trace of the preceding turns is the acknowledgement of people "who haven't been acknowledged here today" — a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its substance. This is prepared commendation on the right subject, and it would read almost identically whatever Pham had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "Barely protecting 6 percent, and allowing commercial fishing and exploitation, is not compromise"

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge all their advocacy and their many reports that have got us here. This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf. I commend the bill.
acuity.explanation: Brewer speaks immediately after Brooking, who made a specific, pointed challenge to the Government benches: that the fisheries plan excluding 74-89 percent of the gulf from bottom trawling was shelved in May, that Gazette notices for the South-East Marine Protection areas remain outstanding, and that protecting only parts of the gulf is insufficient. Brewer engages none of these claims — no rebuttal of the shelving, no figure, no defence of the fisheries plan decision. His turn is prepared commendation that is at least on the matter under debate (the Hauraki Gulf bill and the history of its protection), so it is not fully unresponsive boilerplate, but it would read word-for-word identically whatever argument had preceded it. The assertion that the Government is "delivering the highest ever level of protection" sits beside, rather than against, Brooking's point that protection of parts of the gulf is not enough; it is a pivot to the speaker's own side's record, not an engagement with her content. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band, and at 0.1 because there is no gesture at anything she actually said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking spoke about the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelving the bottom-trawling exclusion plans ("In May of this year, the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelved those plans, and I want the other side of the House to really think about that") and argued that "more needs to be done" on sedimentation and trawling, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Firstly, I’d just like to acknowledge and thank all those that farm pigs and produce pork in New Zealand. I’d thank them for the contributions they make to our food supply and to our economy. This bill reflects a commitment to high standards of animal welfare and also respect to those men and women who produce our food, so I look forward to this bill coming in front of our select committee.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed critique from Damien O'Connor arguing the bill is a backward step that denies the international direction of travel on farrowing crates and mating stalls, and that half the industry has already moved. Butterick takes up none of it — no engagement with the 40-50 percent figure, the trade/alternative-protein argument, or the claim that the industry lobbied for this. The speech asserts the opposite conclusion ('reflects a commitment to high standards') without touching the reasoning just offered, and would read identically whatever O'Connor had said. It is at least on the matter under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Damien O'Connor argued 'you’ve done the pork industry a disservice' and that the bill 'is denying the reality of the direction of travel internationally', and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Ten years is a long time, and what this bill does is say, “Oops, we haven’t done enough on animal welfare for pigs, so we’re just going to delay everything by a decade.” It’s outrageous, totally outrageous.
acuity.explanation: Brooking contradicts the proposition just put by Mike Butterick — that the bill 'reflects a commitment to high standards of animal welfare' — by characterising it as a decade-long delay, and she picks up the ten-year frame that O'Connor had also used. But she does not engage the content of either preceding argument: she does not answer Butterick's claim about standards on its terms, and her substantive material (regulations amended by primary legislation, loss of judicial review, the SPCA not being consulted) is prepared argument addressed to the Minister's earlier speech rather than to the turns immediately before her. On topic, with a gesture at what preceded, so the top of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Butterick: 'This bill reflects a commitment to high standards of animal welfare' — contradicted in general terms but not engaged on its own reasoning.

acuity.statement: Look, I’d just like to take this opportunity to acknowledge our hard-working farmers and the contribution that they make to our New Zealand economy and the very, very high standards of animal welfare that we have here in New Zealand. This bill is going to raise those animal welfare standards. In fact, these new requirements in the bill will be among the highest animal welfare standards in the world. In New Zealand, we have extremely high animal welfare standards. This will continue our reputation on the global stage and in New Zealand, so I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Immediately precedes the vote and follows Rachel Brooking's specific procedural argument — that amending regulations by primary legislation removes any recourse to judicial review, and that the SPCA was never consulted. Wedd answers none of it: no mention of judicial review, consultation, or the ten-year delay, only prepared praise asserting that standards are high and will be raised. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Brooking had argued; it stays on the subject of the bill, hence 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Brooking argued 'there is no recourse to the courts for judicial review for those regulations' and that 'the SPCA ... has not been consulted by this Minister', and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Like my colleague who just spoke, Rachel Boyack, we understand there needs to be some transition period, but that must be a transition to free farrowing.
acuity.explanation: Abel's speech is overwhelmingly prepared Green material on the bill, but here he explicitly takes up one strand of Boyack's immediately preceding offer — that she would work with the Minister to extend the current law by a year or two — accepts the premise that a transition is needed, and qualifies it by specifying what the transition must be towards. That is genuine partial engagement with a specific proposal just made, not merely a reference to the previous speaker, but the rest of the speech would read identically whatever Boyack had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "Here's my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right"

acuity.statement: This bill seeks to establish clear, robust standards, setting minimum space requirements, improving the living environment, minimising the use of systems such as farrowing crates and gestation stalls, but over a period of time, because we’ve already lost a large number of our pork producers and the last thing we want to do is lose a large number more.
acuity.explanation: Anderson follows two speeches whose central charge was that the bill delays the end of farrowing crates by a decade and delivers only a 13.3 percent space increase matched to NZ Pork's own ask. He gestures at the timing question by defending phasing 'over a period of time' on producer-viability grounds, so the speech is at least about the matter under debate, but it engages neither the ten-year claim, the welfare evidence, nor the consultation allegation. Substitute a different argument on the same topic and this speech would be word-for-word the same.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "this bill means 10 more years of misery for mother pigs and piglets—10 more years" — engaged only as a general defence of phasing, not taken up as a claim

acuity.statement: As we’ve seen, across the floor, around the farrowing crates, yes, that is an issue, but it’s also an issue if they’re not used and young piglets are squashed.
acuity.explanation: Arbuckle names the argument made across the floor, concedes the crate welfare problem that Boyack and Abel had both pressed, and then disputes its completeness by supplying a countervailing piglet-mortality consideration that neither opposition speaker addressed. That is conceding part and contesting the rest of the specific claim, which requires having listened; it falls short of 1.0 because he does not engage the particular evidence either member cited and moves straight back to prepared select-committee material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years" (and Rachel Boyack's "Farrowing crates are terrible for pigs and their piglets")

acuity.statement: Well, no—not according to any of the advice that the Government has received, and not according to what’s actually happened so far, Mr Bates.
acuity.explanation: Direct, immediate rebuttal of the specific claim just interjected: Bates asserts the bill is a win for communities, and Hernandez takes exactly that proposition and denies it on two grounds — the Government's own advice and events to date. The reply would be impossible if Bates had said something else, which is the test. Vagueness about which advice is a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "This bill is a win for the communities—that's right."

acuity.statement: The member from the Labour Party did speak about it, and what I want to highlight here is that when you are appointing members to a polytech’s council, what would you take into consideration? I would take into consideration merit. I would take into consideration their ability, their proficiency. But those members want to focus on gender. Those members want to focus on those people’s ethnicity.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding criticism — the removal of representation provisions from the council-appointment clause — and defends it as a positive change, so part of the speech is shaped by what came before. But it engages only that strand (and credits it to a Labour member rather than the speaker who just sat down), and ignores the substance of Hernandez's main case: the Treasury viability finding, the job-loss numbers, and the free TAFE comparison. The rest is prepared ACT material on the mega-merger and the amendments ACT secured.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "what were already weak provisions for Māori representation in the bill were stripped even further during the select committee stage"

acuity.statement: These are the things, Shanan Halbert, that I actually heard from people in the comments. I didn’t get to sit in the select committee, but I certainly hear these kind of things around the country as I meet with people.
