acuity.statement: I just have to say to Mr Costley, not to be pedantic, as he was not being pedantic either—I just want to draw his attention in section 360E(2), inserted by clause 5, to that little word “if” at the start of that, so if the alternative address is at a set of offices. The implication is that offices can be elsewhere. It could be your mum's address, it could be your neighbour’s, or whatever.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight to the clause Costley queried, identifies the conditional "if" he had overlooked as the answer to his reading, and resolves his exact hypothetical in his own terms — he asked whether a non-office address could be used and specifically whether someone could use their mum's house. The speech could not have been delivered without having heard his question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "Could someone use their mum’s house?"

acuity.statement: I’m disappointed that the member hasn’t addressed the questions that I raised earlier, because we were directed to move from clause 4 to clause 5, and we did so, and then we also have not opposed closure motions nor did we take any debate on new clause 4A, so with that good faith of moving through to clause 5—then the Chair will look at his worksheet and see that there are a number of questions without any ticks beside them that haven’t been addressed by the member.
acuity.explanation: Responds to the scope of the answer just given — Russell dealt with Costley's two points and left his own earlier questions untouched — so the remark is contingent on what preceded it and would be withdrawn had she answered him. But it engages the fact of her reply rather than any content in it, and he then proceeds to his own prepared drafting-error argument on new section 360D(2).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "so that does cover the sorts of concerns Mr Costley had"

acuity.statement: My first question is going to be about multiple company applications. As we know, many directors across New Zealand serve on multiple company boards, and the bill makes some attempts, in my view, to address this, but there’s still some outlying questions. If we look at new section 360D(4), “An application under this section may relate to more than 1 company.” How will the new section 360D(4) provision for applications relating to multiple companies actually work in practice?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the clause under debate, but engages nothing anyone before him said: he neither takes up Meager's reasonableness-drafting argument on new section 360D(2) (which he later quotes for an unrelated purpose) nor Russell's answers to Costley. This is prepared clause-by-clause questioning that would read identically whatever the previous two speakers had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager argued that "reasonableness applies to (a) and not to (b)" in new section 360D(2) and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: But, further, there’s a wider point on this and it goes to the matter that the Hon James Meager was just raising around the slightly different wording in parts of these. These were all actually drafting suggestions. So our officials and, particularly, the drafters from the Parliamentary Counsel Office said, actually, if we really want to capture the intent of this bill, if we want to capture the nuances, then this is the way to draft it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Meager's specific complaint — that the varying wording across sections 360D, 360F and 360G is confused drafting — and answers it on its own terms, explaining the variation as deliberate Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting designed to capture different situations. The reply would be different had Meager raised a different objection. Slightly short of 1.0 because she answers the general charge of confused drafting rather than the particular contrast he drew between 'as soon as practicable' and the unqualified wording.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "the drafting here is confused and may be incorrect and may need rectification before we potentially vote on this clause"

acuity.statement: So there’s nothing really in new section 360E that actually talks about the serviceability of the alternative address.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the alternative-address provisions of the same bill at committee stage — but engages no part of Russell's immediately preceding answer that the drafting follows Parliamentary Counsel Office recommendations and captures the policy intent. It opens a fresh line of inquiry about section 360E that would have been delivered unchanged whatever she had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell said the varied wording came from Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting recommendations and that she is satisfied it captures the policy intent, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Clause 6 is around “Section 387A amended (Service of documents on directors in legal proceedings)”. How will clause 6 affect legal practitioners serving documents on directors and how will legal practitioners know whether to use the residential address or the alternative address to use for service?
acuity.explanation: Stays squarely on the clause before the committee, and the service-of-documents theme overlaps with Campbell's earlier worry about serviceability, but it takes up no claim from any preceding turn — it restates his own prepared question about clause 6 rather than engaging what another member argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hamish Campbell asked whether service at an alternative address would be legally effective, and this statement poses a separate question about hierarchy of service methods rather than taking up his point.

acuity.statement: Am I serious? I am serious. This is the intention of the committee of the whole House stage: to stand in this House and go line by line through legislation.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Abel's challenge — the implied claim that line-by-line questioning of clause 6 is not a serious use of the committee's time — and answers it with a justification of the committee of the whole House stage. The passage only exists because of what Abel said and would be dropped if he had said nothing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Are you serious?"

acuity.statement: There are already a number of methods for delivering documents for service. All this clause does is enable an alternative address to be used as one of the many methods, and lawyers are quite accomplished at delivering those documents already, despite the plethora of methods that are already available to them.
acuity.explanation: Answers Rutherford's exact question by reading the existing list of service methods in section 387A and drawing the consequence: because section 387A already offers six alternatives with no hierarchy, the clause adds one more and raises no new problem of choosing between addresses. The answer is shaped entirely by the question put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "how will legal practitioners know whether to use the residential address or the alternative address to use for service?"

acuity.statement: There’s a whole variety of methods someone may use—whichever one is most convenient. They are not in any hierarchy. Frankly, I do rather trust our legal practitioners to be able to work it out as to which one is easiest to use.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford's whole turn turned on one question — whether the service methods in section 388A are ranked, and how a legal practitioner would know which address to use. Russell takes that exact question, reads the paragraphs of 388A back against it, and answers it directly: the methods are not hierarchical and practitioners can choose the most convenient. The reply would have been different had Rutherford asked something else, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Will there be any hierarchy of service methods, or will alternative addresses, under these provisions, have equal status with residential addresses?"

acuity.statement: Surely, the second clause here actually supersedes the first clause, really, because, otherwise, we’re not really adding anything more under (ba). I think it’s maybe a bit of a drafting error here, and we have ended up adding a bit of complexity.
acuity.explanation: Campbell is squarely on the clause under debate and glances at the preceding discussion ("I’ve already heard about the risk of confusion in the other uses of some of the addresses"), but he engages no part of Russell's answer about hierarchy. He opens a separate drafting argument that would read identically had Russell said nothing, so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just argued that the methods in section 388A "are not in any hierarchy" and that practitioners can pick whichever is most convenient; this statement does not take that up, raising instead a fresh drafting point about subclauses (1) and (2)

acuity.statement: To the member’s question—did I think about taking the opportunity to eliminate facsimile machines?—alas, it would have been beyond the scope of this particular bill. But I invite the member to mention to his colleague, the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs, that now would be a good time to remove facsimile machines—although I understand some medical doctors and pharmacists still use them quite a lot.
acuity.explanation: She restates Meager's specific question, gives a direct reason for not doing it (outside the bill's scope), and then draws out its consequence by pointing him to the Minister who could do it and noting who still uses fax machines. Entirely contingent on what the previous speaker asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I just wonder whether the member thought for a second about taking the opportunity to once and for all eradicate facsimiles from the record and make our lives just a little bit easier."

acuity.statement: I just can’t believe the misreading of the law that’s going on there. I’m just going back to clause 6, amending section 387A. It gives a number of different places where documents may be served. If we go back to new section 360E, inserted by clause 5: the alternative address must not be the company’s registered office, but the company’s registered office can still be used for service. It doesn’t stop it being used for service; you just have an alternative address instead of the residential address. It doesn’t say you cannot use the company’s office for serving documents, it just simply says that the alternative address cannot be the company’s registered office. It needs to be an alternative address.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Meager's specific textual argument — that new section 360E(3) bars the alternative address from being the address for service and so contradicts clause 6 — and rebuts its reasoning by distinguishing what may be used for service from what may be nominated as the alternative address, citing both provisions he cited. The speech would be entirely different had he raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "that alternative address cannot be the company that they work for, which is the legal address of service. So there’s a contradiction in terms there."

acuity.statement: I’m going back just to make this point about section 360E: “(1) The alternative address of a director or shareholder … must not be—(a) the company’s registered office or address for service;”, and then it’s got “; or [the other thing]”. It must not be the address for service. In this section, it says: “The alternative address”—blah, blah, blah—“must not be … the company’s registered office or address for service;”, which does contradict, as my learned colleague pointed out, the clause that we are now looking at, clause 6, which is section 387A amended, which is “Service of documents on directors in legal proceedings”.
acuity.explanation: Engages the same provision in dispute and re-asserts, against Russell's immediately preceding denial, that a contradiction exists — so it is on the specific claim, not just the topic. But it does not take up the distinction Russell actually drew between an address for service and an alternative address, which was the substance of her rebuttal; it restates Meager's reading rather than answering hers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "It doesn’t say you cannot use the company’s office for serving documents, it just simply says that the alternative address cannot be the company’s registered office."

acuity.statement: Members will recall the extended discussion we had earlier this evening about why we needed to use “alternative address” rather than “address for service”. An address for service is a place where documents may be served to someone. They can be served in a variety of places, including the company’s address for service. However, a director’s alternative address, which is not the same as an address for service, cannot be the company’s address for service. Straightforward, right? So it really, really cannot be. But the alternative address can be used for service, as can the company’s address for service. That’s fine; no worries about that. It’s just that the director cannot use the company’s address for service as their alternative address. So there is no confusion here; there’s a very careful delineation of terms.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers Weenink's re-assertion that section 360E contradicts clause 6, by spelling out the two-term distinction her reading collapses and showing both addresses remain available for service. The reply is shaped by the specific claim just made and would have to change had a different objection been raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "which does contradict, as my learned colleague pointed out, the clause that we are now looking at, clause 6"

acuity.statement: There is confusion in the law because section 387A(1) of the Companies Act is in regard to a director in their capacity as a director. Now, you can serve legal proceedings on someone in their capacity as a director or you can serve legal proceedings on someone because they've defamed you and called you an untrustworthy accountant, having nothing to do with their directorship. So the issue is in an ordinary course of action, the member is right, you can get served at your address for service, which is ordinarily your solicitor or your company's office, or you can get served at your residential address.
acuity.explanation: Opens by contradicting Russell's closing proposition that there is no confusion, concedes part of her account explicitly ("the member is right") and then disputes the rest by locating the problem in the capacity in which a person is served — a new strand built directly on the distinction she had just drawn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "There is no confusion in the law; the point’s been addressed."

acuity.statement: That’s right. So if you were then to say, “Oh, why don't you include an initial for your middle name,” for example, where you've got John B Smith and then the options open far and wide, hypothetically—then it’s unlimited. Just the list goes on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific example Weenink has just supplied — that two John Smiths may really be John Brent and John Bob Smith — and does something with it, arguing that adding a middle initial as a disambiguator generates an unbounded set of variants rather than solving the identification problem. The passage would have to change if Weenink had raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "they might be John B Smith for John Brent Smith or John Bob Smith"

acuity.statement: The DIN, which is promised in the Minister's legislation. As I said earlier this evening, this is a band-aid; it's not a solution itself. I have given the Minister the commitment that if his bill is through the first reading before the end of the year, I will withdraw my member’s bill—I will hold off on the third reading.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put to her — whether the bill should wait for director identification numbers — by conceding the point (her bill is a band-aid, not a solution) and then setting out the sequencing arrangement that addresses the gap Rutherford identified between her bill and the Minister's. Substituting a different objection on the same topic would require a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "was there any consideration around whether potentially this should wait for direct identification numbers to solve the identification problem properly?"

acuity.statement: Our question, to start off, in terms of Part 1, is similar to Helen White’s questions to start off. And it’s really to understand how survivors have been involved in this process and how, since the first reading of this bill, has the Government listened to that feedback from survivors.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the preceding turn — White's question about insufficient survivor consultation — and expressly aligns her own question with it, adding the first-reading feedback dimension. But it endorses and restates the topic rather than advancing or testing White's argument, and the rest of the turn is prepared material on the history of abuse in State care, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "why has there not been the consultation and what plans are there to consult?"

acuity.statement: First thing: we had a royal commission for six years, and they were very clear in their recommendations. This bill responds to that. Secondly, it’s been a year that we’ve had a select committee process. People have been able to have their views heard. We’ve taken those into account.
acuity.explanation: Paul asked specifically how survivors had been meaningfully incorporated into producing the bill. Stanford answers that question directly, naming the two consultation channels (the six-year royal commission and the year-long select committee process) and what was done with the views heard. The reply would be different had Paul asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "firstly, I’m keen to start off with how have survivors been incorporated meaningfully into leading us to the bill we have in front of us today."

acuity.statement: My simple question to the Minister this morning—following what you've just said is: yet there has been a six-year process and survivors have been a part of it all the way through. We understand there's a ministerial advisory group that survivors are part of, but I guess my question to the Minister is just around trust.
acuity.explanation: Bennett restates the specific content of Stanford's answer — the six-year process and the ministerial advisory group of survivors — accepts it, and then presses the next step from it: whether that process is enough for survivors to trust the result. The question is built out of what was just said rather than merely following it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "I have set up a ministerial advisory group of representative survivors to help guide the Government in its work over the next few years."

acuity.statement: Thank you. I have quite a specific question, which is about the responsiveness of Part 1 to new offences. I know that we're moving hopefully to a law where we change the rules around trafficking and they're quite a significant change, and I really welcome the work done in that area where we move away from consent.
acuity.explanation: A prepared question opening a fresh line on specified offences and trafficking law. It is squarely on the matter under debate (Part 1), but it takes up no part of Bennett's trust argument or Stanford's consultation answer that preceded it — it would have been delivered in the same words whatever they had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett asked the Minister whether survivors can trust that she has "leaned in, that you've listened", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: We think it’s already clear, in this bill, that we are adding specified offences, as I mentioned in my opening speech. It’s very clear that, as things come up, we will consider adding them to the specified offences list, as we’ve done in this bill today.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of White's question — whether the specified-offences list can be extended as new offences emerge — and answers it. It leaves untouched the other strand she pressed, about overseas offences and whether the mechanism is a regulation, so the engagement is partial rather than complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Is it that there's a regulation where, in fact, specified offences can be added to"

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Minister, thanks for your answers before, as well. I really appreciate you illuminating some of these issues for us. I’m keen to ask another, more of an overarching, question just because I understand that Minister Stanford is here with us for Part 1, and then we’re moving to a different Minister for Part 2.
acuity.explanation: Thanks the Minister for the previous answers and then moves to an unrelated overarching question about which Whanaketia recommendations were implemented. A courteous reference to the earlier replies is not engagement with their content; the question is prepared material on the right subject, timed to the Minister's availability rather than to anything just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just said "as things come up, we will consider adding them to the specified offences list", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: As I already said in my opening speech, this was a bill that we introduced a year ago—it was the very first piece of legislation. There is an enormous amount of work to do. There are hundreds of recommendations that need to be looked at, considered, and enacted, potentially, and we’re going through that work.
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance of Paul's question about how recommendations were selected, offering the triage rationale — the known gaps that could be closed quickly, with the rest still in train. It does not address the specific recommendation she named, the independent survivor-led redress system, so it answers the general question but not the pointed one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "what was your decision-making process when you were going through those recommendations, and how did you choose which ones you would implement through this bill"

acuity.statement: I think to do due diligence is to actually spend a bit more time, because people are listening and wanting to make sure that we are held accountable.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests White's reasoning that time should not be spent on matters of agreement, countering with the accountability value of continued scrutiny. He engages that one strand squarely and then turns to a fresh clause-5 question, so the engagement is real but brief.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "I don’t want to waste time on things that we actually agree with"

acuity.statement: Just to be clear, this part already exists in the legislation for core workers who have a conviction in New Zealand. We’re just aligning the law so that people who have an overseas conviction and now fall under this piece of legislation also have an appeal right. So this is not about survivors having appeal rights. This is about the core worker having an appeal right against not being able to work.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the factual premise of Bennett's question outright: he assumed the new section 28D(2) appeal right belonged to survivors facing High Court costs, and she identifies that the appellant is the core worker, not the survivor. The answer is wholly determined by what he asked and dissolves the concern rather than deflecting it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "the State then requiring them to potentially pay to have their appeal heard by the High Court"

acuity.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime. So we’re following the recommendation of the royal commission.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific substitution Paul proposed — "at-risk" for "vulnerable" — and supplies a reason against it (the term's existing reach across the Crimes Act), then grounds the drafting choice in the royal commission's recommendation. The speech would have to change if Paul had argued something else about the definition. Short of 1.0 because the second half of her question — the FASD example and whether a defined list of disabilities exists — is never engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "I’m really keen to understand that choice to use “vulnerable adult” over “at-risk adult”, but also the choice to connect disabilities to that definition of being a vulnerable adult."

acuity.statement: I wanted just to start with this in a methodical way and focus on clause 16. What has happened in the amendment of the law, or will happen, is that we’ll move from a continuous period of 72 hours of detention, and we’ll be moving to a situation where there is clarity over the period that there hasn’t been before, including the actual period “commencing on the day on which the child or young person is first placed in secure care”.
acuity.explanation: Picks one item out of the list of changes Chhour had just enumerated — the secure-care duration — and presses on its mechanics, specifically the new commencement point. It is engagement with a strand of the preceding turn rather than the whole of it, and it puts a question rather than disputing a claim, so it sits above a topic-only response but below a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: "It clarifies the duration in secure care, which will be three days before court authority is required"

acuity.statement: In response to that member’s question, “core worker’ is an existing term defined in the Act. Specified offences only apply to core workers for restriction. The key is that when people are working with children and have unsupervised access to children, they are teachers, learning support people, teacher-aides and those types of people who generally have unrestricted access to children that we need to protect children from. That’s why we had this known gap and that’s why it’s being closed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question just put — what 'core worker' means and why the restriction stops there — and does something with it: locates the term in the existing Act, states the restriction's scope, and gives the unsupervised-access rationale for the boundary. Had the member asked about a different clause this answer would have had to be different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to understand what “core worker” means and why we’ve only focused in on core workers" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: I just want to clarify, because it’s been repeated a couple of times that we landed on a 72-hour time frame: actually, this legislation will be deleting the 72-hour time frame to make sure that we are very clear that it clarifies that three days in secure care before court authority is needed is what was landed upon; not 72 hours.
acuity.explanation: Paul's central question, repeated several times and again in her summary, was 'how did we land on 72 hours'. Chhour takes that exact premise and corrects it as a misstatement of fact — the bill deletes the 72-hour figure rather than adopting it — and then explains the day-counting gap that motivated the change. Had Paul asked about a different clause, this passage could not have been delivered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'how did we land on 72 hours; is that aligned with other international standards'

acuity.statement: So this picture of sitting in a cell, with the door locked, dark and dank, and not being able to leave their room, and have no contact with people for three days, is absolutely untrue and overexaggerated.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Paul's characterisation of secure care — her 'let's just call it what it is: it's a cell' and her account of a young person without human or social contact — and disputes it on the substance, describing a unit the young person can move around in with staff and social worker access. The engagement is with the content of Paul's depiction, not merely a reference to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'Let’s just call it what it is: it’s a cell.'

acuity.statement: Why do we need secure care at all? Secure care is only used as allowed in law and where necessary.
acuity.explanation: Picks up by name Paul's question 'Why would a young person need to be put into secure care in the first place?' and answers it, going on to name absconding and the safety of other young people as the statutory grounds. The opening sentence restates the question before answering, so it is squarely responsive, though the answer itself leans on a general assurance before the specifics arrive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'Why would a young person need to be put into secure care in the first place?'

acuity.statement: So I have some follow-on questions around the use of force, so maybe this will mean that the Minister could address both of our questions around the use of force and a consideration of our amendments that seek to put some more safeguards in place where force is used.
acuity.explanation: Walters had just put a series of use-of-force questions to the Minister, including what advice was sought about consistency with the royal commission's findings and whether she would accept amendments requiring de-escalation training. Paul takes up that strand explicitly — she identifies her questions as 'follow-on' on the same subject and asks the Minister to answer both members' use-of-force questions and consider the amendments together. That is a real engagement with the topic and with the procedural thrust of Walters' request, and the opening would have been worded differently had Walters spoken on searches alone. But she does not take up the content of any specific argument Walters made (the breadth of the search discretion, the Prime amendments' wording, the pat-down definition in Amendment Paper 354); she bundles and then moves to her own prepared material about access to youth justice residences. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "I do also want to speak to some of the amendments that the Hon Willow-Jean Prime has proposed. A first question here would be what advice did the Minister seek regarding how the use of force is consistent with the royal commission's findings"

acuity.statement: I want to take us to the question about training, and I think that there’s something really important in that. I’ve heard words like “de-escalation” from my colleagues on the right as a being a smart and good idea, but that takes real, solid, enduring training and monitoring and assessment as to whether people are up for that. So I’m keen to know if you can tell us what the model of care is, because if we’re talking about moments of securing—putting young people into security, for whatever reasons—it’s the moments before and after they’re secured.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive ministerial turn on harmful items and safeguards and engages none of its content. It stays squarely on the bill and gestures at the morning's exchanges ("From what I'm hearing this morning, I can hear intention, but I don't hear deep conviction"), so it is on-topic prepared material rather than unresponsive to the debate altogether, but nothing in it would change had the Minister's preceding answer been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Karen Chhour argued that items such as vapes can be used as shanks, that the harmful-items list mirrors the Corrections Act, and that the select committee added consultation safeguards — this statement does not take any of that up, and instead opens a new line on training and the model of care.

acuity.statement: Standard operating procedure is that physical intervention can only be used when verbal de-escalation techniques have failed. I do agree that in the past that hasn’t really been followed very well because there wasn’t a very good training programme in place when people came to work within youth justice.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the training strand of the preceding turn directly: supplies the standard operating procedure on de-escalation before force, concedes the point that it was poorly followed in the past, and goes on to the post-event review and escalation process. The answer would read differently had the previous speaker pressed a different concern; it falls short of 1.0 only because the specific request for the model of care, and for mokopuna Māori in particular, is left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "but that takes real, solid, enduring training and monitoring and assessment as to whether people are up for that" — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi

acuity.statement: My questions are on a few other parts of the bill. Can I, first, just thank the Minister for her extremely thorough responses and addressing the Amendment Papers individually. That was very helpful and actually addressed a number of questions I would have otherwise asked. So thank you for pre-empting that.
acuity.explanation: A courteous acknowledgement that earlier answers pre-empted some of her questions is a reference, not an engagement — no part of the Minister's account of training or use-of-force review is taken up. The turn remains closely on the bill under consideration, which keeps it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Karen Chhour had just set out the de-escalation standard operating procedure and the post-use-of-force review and escalation process, and this statement does not engage that; it thanks her in general terms and moves to clauses 23 and 28.

acuity.statement: I just want to come back to questions from Helen White and Tamatha Paul around the period of time in secure care and repeated use of secure care, because that’s been raised a couple of times.
acuity.explanation: Sets aside both of the questions put in the turn immediately before and returns to a different strand raised earlier in the debate. It is plainly on the matter under consideration and picks up a concern voiced in the committee, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band, but responsiveness to the preceding turn cannot be pointed at.

Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.

acuity.subject: speaker

We’re setting it in a place where we can seek some clarity around the intention of the legislation so that we can make it crystal clear. Therefore, I commend it to the House.

They must have been held in a substantially uninterrupted way, and that is the test that was presented to the courts. The Court of Appeal took one view, but the Attorney-General appealed and the Supreme Court actually took it back—took it back. Yet, the Government presses on with this bill, stripping property rights from Māori.
acuity.explanation: Takes the precise rationale just offered — that the Court of Appeal decision left the intention unclear and needs restating — and attacks its premise: the original test was already explicit and demanding, and the Court of Appeal view was appealed and taken back by the Supreme Court, so there is nothing left to clarify. It is, actually, cynical. When we’re talking about cynical—someone from the other side of the House spoke about cynicism—it’s cynicism to work people up into a frenzy when they’re not saying what the actual truth is. We’re restoring what Parliament’s intent was when we were fixing up the brokenness of Māori, thanks to the 2004 bill that was passed under that Labour Government back then. I commend this bill to the House.
