acuity.statement: As the Hon Scott Simpson has said, it was a privilege and pleasure to listen to the well-thought-out contributions of all of those who had made submissions on a bill like the Parliament Bill. It's not the kind of bill that many people would take an interest in and write down their thoughts about, this particular bill, and so I believe the quality of submissions that we got was excellent and was helpful for the committee.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe names Simpson's point about the quality of the submissions and does something modest with it: he endorses it and supplies a reason it is notable (the bill is one few members of the public would bother writing in about, so the quality received was better than expected). That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding turn rather than a bare reference, but it is agreement that adds a gloss and then returns to his own prepared account of the committee's work, so it sits at the midpoint rather than the top. Scored on engagement only — the warmth of the agreement is a civility matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The special select committee received 62 submissions from some notable New Zealanders who had given some of the constitutional, weighty matters great thought and great consideration. It was actually a real privilege to sit and listen to those contributions." — Scott Simpson

acuity.statement: Just a really short call from me this afternoon, to say this is a really collaborative and proactive approach to the legislation around how this place actually operates and how it works, bringing together four different Acts to enable a modern framework for Parliament to work as best as it possibly can, and the agencies that support this incredible place.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows a detailed turn containing several concrete and arguable propositions (transparency of the proposed funding committee, the unresolved Government veto, the reporting thresholds for security powers) and engages none of them. The speech is a generic commendation on the right subject — accurate as far as it goes about the four Acts being consolidated — and would be identical whatever the preceding speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe had just set out specific contested points — that Parliament should set its own budget, that he rejects the claim the new funding process would be less transparent than the current system, that the Government's veto question is unresolved, and the new three-day/annual reporting requirements on security officers' powers — and this statement takes up none of them.

acuity.statement: I want to highlight the fact that this bill empowers Parliament’s security team, and I’d like to take this opportunity to thank and acknowledge the security officers in Parliament, especially Manoj Thattipron, who’s here this afternoon, and also Geno Wharakura, who, I think, has just left.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne picks up the security-powers strand that Rurawhe had raised earlier in the debate, which is more than an arbitrary pivot. But she engages no part of his actual argument — he addressed the concerns about whether reporting and monitoring of the new powers would be sufficient and described the three-day and annual reporting requirements added in response; she simply affirms that the bill gives the officers the tools to do their job. A gesture at the debate rather than an engagement with a claim in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In terms of security, I encourage MPs to actually go and speak to some of our security officers around Parliament, and especially some of the ones that have been around for a little while, and they'll happily tell you why these changes are necessary." — Adrian Rurawhe

acuity.statement: I wanted to touch on the fact that the bill makes the Parliamentary Library a standard business unit in the Parliamentary Service, and just acknowledge the role that the parliamentary librarians play in supporting us as MPs, particularly with our constituency work—the ability to engage and contact and get feedback that helps us answer constituents’ queries on a daily basis, for those of us who are hard-working constituent MPs like my colleagues on this side of the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed substantive speech on the bill's security powers, complaint avenues and accessibility, and engages none of it; the turn is prepared acknowledgement of a different part of the bill (the Parliamentary Library) and would be word-for-word identical whatever Walters had said. It stays in the low band rather than at 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued at length that 'Part 7 of the bill is modelled on the Courts Security Act', that the search powers are drafted restrainedly, and challenged the House on disability accessibility — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I fully support what my friend Vanushi Walters just said about disability. I think that's a really key issue where we could show some leadership with a change in the rules.
acuity.explanation: Takes up a specific, identifiable strand of the preceding speech — Walters' challenge that Parliament review its accessibility for disabled people — and does something modest with it by endorsing it and framing it as a rule change the House could lead on. It is only partial engagement: the rest of the turn is prepared material on whānau provisions and a buddy system, and it adds no counter-argument or new evidence to the strand it picks up, so it sits mid-scale rather than at the top. Agreement is not penalised as such; what caps it is that most of the speech is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s certainly a need for Parliament to consider whether it’s time for us to have that kind of review in place" — Vanushi Walters, on making Parliament accessible for people with disabilities.

acuity.statement: This amendment bill restores clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, ensuring Parliament’s original intention. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe's immediately preceding speech was built entirely on the claim that Parliament's intent must not be confused with the outcome, and that the 2011 Act's intent was the opposite of what this amendment does. Cheung simply re-asserts 'Parliament's original intention' as settled and commends the bill. It is prepared, formulaic material on the right subject that engages no part of the argument just made — the two sentences would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before. On topic, so not 0.0, but a bare assertion of the contested point is a reference, not an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe argued 'I don't think we should confuse intent with outcome because they're two different things' and that the original intent was not what this amendment delivers, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Such a simple bill, after more than a year, from a Minister who promised immediate action.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith had just characterised his own bill as 'short and simple, but ... an important change'. Davidson takes that exact characterisation and turns it back on him: the simplicity is itself the indictment, because a 73-word bill is all the 'immediate action' the Minister has produced in over a year. That is doing something with the specific concession the previous speaker volunteered, so the line would have to change if Goldsmith had framed the bill differently. It is only a partial engagement, though — it takes up one strand (the bill's smallness) and then moves to prepared material on media job losses rather than engaging Goldsmith's substantive claim about the $6 million and the competitive disadvantage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is short and simple, but it’s an important change for the media sector" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: I think that member ought to check the growth in the digital audience of RNZ, because I think you’ll see astronomical growth in the digital audiences and platforms of RNZ.
acuity.explanation: Court's interjection makes a specific factual claim — RNZ is losing its audience — and Davidson takes that exact claim up and contradicts it on its own terms, pointing to growth in RNZ's digital audience. The sentence would not exist, and could not be the same, had Court said something else; it is a direct rebuttal of the premise rather than a pivot. Short of 1.0 only because he supplies no figure or source for the counter-claim, offering the correction in general terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "They're losing their audience. Why would you fund losers?"

acuity.statement: To be fair, when we hear about the potential income that could be generated from allowing advertising on Sundays and public holidays, it’s just approximately $6 million. That’s not going to fundamentally fix the shortfalls that we have.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon picks up the one strand of the preceding speech that is a concrete figure — the $6 million the bill is said to be worth — and makes the same inadequacy argument in her own terms, later also echoing Davidson's "biscuit tin" framing. But she engages only that strand and then returns to prepared Green material on the sanctity of Anzac Day, Easter and Christmas, which is indifferent to what Davidson actually argued. Partial engagement: pointable, but not a reply to his case.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "no one believes it's worth $6 million; it's more broken promises from a Government that keeps making things worse"

acuity.statement: It’s important that they do increase their revenue. This is one tool. Apparently, $6 million could be generated in this way. But I also point out that another really good way for linear television broadcasters to increase their revenue is to produce products that people actually want to watch, and so if people watch it and then the advertisers get revenue, maybe that’s another way to fill the gap.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding speech argued that $6 million cannot fix the sector's funding shortfall and objected to advertising on days of remembrance; Court answers neither. He repeats the $6 million figure with a hedging "apparently" and then delivers prepared ACT material about broadcasters making programmes people want to watch. The gesture at the debate's shared number earns the top of the unresponsive band, but the speech would read identically whatever Lyndon had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "this little $6 million that might be generated out of advertising ... is not going to fix the fundamentals" — but Court does not take up her argument, only the figure

acuity.statement: I guess I want to echo the points that people have made: that this change will bring in $6 million of revenue into these broadcasters. However, that is really a drop in the bucket compared to the type of funding that these organisations need.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific $6 million figure Marcroft put on the table and does something with it — recasts it as negligible against broadcasters' funding need — but then leaves Marcroft's actual argument (the cultural value of commercial-free days) and returns to prepared material on Government broadcasting cuts. One strand engaged, pointable, then a pivot: mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "This broadcasting amendment bill will only increase advertising revenue by $6 million."

acuity.statement: I’m sure that, along with myself and Mr Costley, other veterans have far better things to be doing on Anzac Day than watching television. It’s probably one of the busiest days of the year for us. Therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: A very short turn, but it picks up the premise Paul had just volunteered — that people are not watching television on Anzac Day anyway — and turns it into a reason to support the bill rather than to protect the restriction. The speech would have been different had Paul not said it. It engages that one strand only and does not touch the protection-of-special-days argument itself, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "I would hope that, on days like Anzac Day and other special days, people wouldn’t be watching TV"

acuity.statement: But the reality of this one is, as with most of the New Zealand calendar, which was imported from England, it is the Christian tradition that we always commemorate. I don't see any broadcasting advertising being taken away for Eid or taken away for Ramadan or those kinds of things.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the religious-observance case Marcroft built the New Zealand First position on, and attacks its reasoning rather than the member: if the restriction protects faith, why only the imported Christian calendar and not Eid or Ramadan. Substituting a different argument on the same topic would require this passage to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "to reflect the views, if they hold Christian beliefs and believe that those days when advertising will now be available if the bill is to pass"

acuity.statement: Now, a comment was made by a previous contributor about the fact that if TVNZ just produced better material, then people might watch it. Well, that's not the point. It's not the point, because you look at what was just said by Tamatha Paul, and, obviously, we're very generationally the same because I have a YouTube account; in fact, the only paid subscription I have in my life is YouTube—it's amazing—so I get to watch Q+A and I get to watch all of those TVNZ shows without ads.
acuity.explanation: Names a prior claim, rejects it, and then recruits Paul's own account of her viewing habits as the evidence for why it fails — the audience has moved to ad-free platforms regardless of content quality. Engagement with the content of two preceding turns, not a mere reference to them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "because I’m subscribed to YouTube, I don’t get any ads" — and an earlier contributor's claim that better TVNZ material would draw viewers

acuity.statement: So we really do need some action in broadcasting from this Minister, because this small change allowing advertising on otherwise prohibited days might go some small way, but it's not really stopping the rot, the decline in broadcasting.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bennett's specific claim that the bill is trivial 'small change' and does something with it — concedes the scale, then converts it into a demand for action from the Minister. The wording of the reply is shaped by the preceding turn (it reuses and answers the 'small change' framing rather than merely naming Bennett), so it would read differently had Bennett argued something else. Not a full 1.0 because much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on linear-vs-streaming regulation that Bennett never raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "This is $6 million; this is small change. It's significant change, but it's small change."

acuity.statement: As technology changes, so does culture, and so does legislation. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: On the subject under debate, but engages no part of the argument immediately before it. The two sentences would be word-for-word identical whatever Webb had said; nothing in them is contingent on the preceding turn. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because the generality about technology and legislation is at least about this bill's rationale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued broadcasting is in a parlous state, that the Government has an obligation to fund non-commercial New Zealand stories, and that Te Karere funding is at risk — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Yes, we are seeing broadcasting change across the world, globally and here in Aotearoa New Zealand. With that, we do need to shift and change some of the legislation and restrictions to enable the broadcasting industry to be at its best.
acuity.explanation: Echoes the topic of Costley's preceding proposition — change in the sector requiring legislative change — but does not engage it as a claim: it neither disputes, qualifies nor draws a consequence from it, and immediately returns to prepared material about the Government letting New Zealanders down. A gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "As technology changes, so does culture, and so does legislation."

acuity.statement: The New Zealand media sector has long called for these changes and this Government is responding. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Prepared praise following an opposition attack, with no contact with the content of that attack: the charge that the Government over-promises and under-delivers goes unanswered. The sentences are indifferent to who spoke before and what they said, so this sits at the bottom of the unresponsive band while still being about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the Government sets big expectations and continues to let New Zealanders down, and that Jenny Marcroft would do a better job as Minister — this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Does he think that paragraph 2.68 of the Cabinet Manual has been upheld, where “Public perception is a very important factor. If a conflict arises in relation to the interests of family, whānau, or close associates, Ministers should take appropriate action”; and if so, what appropriate action did the Minister take to avoid public perception of a conflict of interest?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Prime Minister's expressed comfort and immediately tests it against the specific standard that governs it, quoting the Cabinet Manual clause on public perception and asking what action was taken under it. The question would have had to be framed differently had he instead denied any engagement occurred, so it is shaped by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "I’ve been completely comfortable with the engagement between the Minister for the Environment and the MP involved."

acuity.statement: Which thing is he most proud of: a shrinking economy, rising unemployment, more kids living in poverty, more homelessness, or record numbers of New Zealanders giving up and leaving the country?
acuity.explanation: Engages the subject matter — it answers the Prime Minister's list of claimed gains with a counter-list — but takes up no part of the actual argument he made about the previous Government's spending, inflation and interest rates. It is prepared material on the right topic, with only a gesture at what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "We’ve got spending under control. We’ve got inflation down. We’ve got interest rates down. Growth is coming; jobs are coming."

acuity.statement: So why did he cut $3 billion of public investment in infrastructure in his first year as Prime Minister?
acuity.explanation: Shows that the preceding answer was listened to by identifying that it did not reach the figure put to it and re-putting the question stripped to its core. It engages the answer's omission rather than its reasoning about interest rates, so it is a partial engagement, not a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "in construction, interest rates are the critical piece that enables developers to actually borrow money to go off and get things built" — an answer that never addressed the $3 billion

acuity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “We’re determined to get the building and construction sector firing on all cylinders.”; if so, is 20,000 job losses in the construction sector the type of firing he was referring to?
acuity.explanation: A pre-written quote-and-pun in the same mould as the preceding supplementaries; it is on the subject of construction but would read identically whatever the Prime Minister had just answered, including his specific $7 billion and 2.7 percent claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Christopher Luxon had just claimed "we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas" and brought inflation "to 2.7 percent", and this question takes up neither the $7 billion nor the inflation figure.

acuity.statement: Is it possible to “Spend money on tax cuts”, or is a tax cut when people just keep more of the money that belongs to them in the first place? How does it work?
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the premise buried in the preceding question's wording — that a tax cut is an item of spending — and disputes it. The question only exists because of the phrasing Hipkins used, which is the test of responsiveness; that it is also a friendly question to the Prime Minister does not change what it engages.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "why does he think billions of dollars of public money is better spent on tax cuts for landlords and tobacco companies"

acuity.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the cost of utilities are up 19.3 percent from a year earlier, including rates, water charges, and energy bills?
acuity.explanation: Offers a rival cause for the departures in place of the pull-factor explanation just given, which is an engagement of sorts, but it does not take up the specific claim about Australian wages or the point that many return. One strand engaged, then a move to the speaker's own prepared cost-of-living figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: the Minister of Finance's answer (speaker untagged in the transcript): "Often their decision is based on opportunities available overseas. It is a reality that Australia is a wealthier country than New Zealand and can pay higher wages"

acuity.statement: To the specific point of his assertion that the intention of Parliament has been departed from, the Minister of the day, Christopher Finlayson, who the Minister also mentioned in his opening remarks, said, “These amendments”—meaning the amendments that the Minister has before us—“do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them. Let there be no doubt about that at all.” So I invite the Minister to actually express the basis for his primary proposition, which is that Parliament's intention has not been met.
acuity.explanation: Takes Goldsmith's central proposition — that the amendment restores Parliament's 2011 intention — and attacks it directly, using the words of the 2011 Minister whom Goldsmith himself had invoked, then puts the demand for his evidential basis back to him. The speech would have had to be different had Goldsmith argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "That's not what the Parliament passed in 2011, and so there have been different interpretations of what that threshold should be, and that's what we're seeking to establish clearly with this amendment bill."

acuity.statement: So I think it is for the Minister to establish clearly his case about why, in 2011, what was passed was his version of how this law should be interpreted, and not in fact what the Minister at the time, or the official documentation of the day, said it was.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's specific "how it was always explained" claim about the 2011 two-limb test and contests it with the 2010 statement of policy intent, including the clause that customary marine title is not exclusionary. She engages the content of his claim rather than merely naming him, and presses him for the case law he says informed it; slightly short of 1.0 because much of the surrounding material (the Canadian authorities) is prepared argument she would likely have delivered regardless.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "That was the goal and that's how it was always explained: that you had to achieve two legs, the first being to recognise it through tikanga, and the second requiring applicants to have held a specified area and "exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption"."

acuity.statement: A number of us have sat here, and given that this is—as my colleague described—the first time I’ve seen a preamble used in a way such as it has been in this particular bill, my questions follow on from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb with respect to the difference that the Minister recognises in the court decision, and what he is, effectively, trying to change here. It’s easy to say that it wasn’t the intention, but words matter in this, and the preamble is the start of what we would consider, in the Māori world, the wairua to the rest of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Henare explicitly picks up Webb's two strands — the unusualness of a preamble outside a Treaty settlement bill, and the preamble's claim about Parliament's original intention — and does something with the second ('It's easy to say that it wasn't the intention, but words matter'), rather than merely name-checking the previous speaker. He then moves to additional questions of his own (previous customary title recognitions), so the engagement is real but partial: the speech would have been different had Webb raised different objections, but a good deal of it would survive unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "it’s quite unusual for bills that are not themselves Treaty settlement bills to have preambles" and "To say, as I think it does, that the decision departed from the original intention of Parliament—it was probably untrue at the start, but it’s certainly untrue now."

acuity.statement: The bill has a preamble to explain the background. It’s not that common that Parliament brings in legislation to overturn Court of Appeal rulings, as was the case in the original bill, and also Supreme Court rulings, as is the case with this bill.
acuity.explanation: This is a direct answer to the specific question put — why a preamble exists in a non-Treaty-settlement bill — and supplies the reason (the unusual step of legislating over appellate court rulings). Not a full 1.0 only because it reframes rather than addresses Webb's particular premise that preambles belong to Treaty settlement bills; but the answer is squarely aimed at the question asked and could not have been delivered unchanged after a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "firstly, why do we have a preamble in this bill, because it’s not a Treaty settlement bill"

acuity.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise claim Webb made — that the Supreme Court cured the Court of Appeal problem, so further legislation is unnecessary — and contests it with the specific ground offered for continuing: post-Supreme Court decisions awarding title over large stretches of the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coasts. Delete Webb's argument and substitute a different objection and this sentence has to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the concerns in the Court of Appeal were entirely ameliorated by the Supreme Court case. Now what we have is a further tightening, which is entirely not necessary."

acuity.statement: There was just one point there that the Minister raised—I think, seeing as we’re talking about the kind of genealogy of this bill, because the Minister talked about resource consents and he suggested that, and I may be putting words in his mouth, the ability of hapū and iwi to intervene and to say that resource consent shouldn’t be granted because it interfered with their customary rights was not something which New Zealanders would expect in an equal society.
acuity.explanation: Isolates one specific proposition from the answer just given — the equal-say objection to customary consent rights — restates it with an explicit caveat about not misrepresenting the Minister, and then presses its consequence by recasting customary rights as property rights and asking why they rank below other property rights. Wholly dependent on what Goldsmith had just said; a different ministerial answer would have produced a different intervention.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "enabling one group of New Zealanders who had received customary marine title to grant resource consents is a very significant deviation from normal expectations of New Zealanders living in this country in a democratic, modern democracy to have an equal say in decisions affecting their lives"

acuity.statement: I’ll just reply to a few questions. One member asked which applicants we’ve met with in the development of this amendment and legislation. I have met with a number, including Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Te Whānau-a-Apanui, Ngāti Kauwhata, and Ngāti Porou.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Andersen's substantive question immediately precedes it. The reply is squarely within the committee-stage debate and supplies a concrete answer, but to a consultation question rather than to the cost-pressure argument just put to him; the specific claim about court-cost blowouts and claimant funding is left entirely untouched. Prepared-style material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate's question stream, so the 0.3 end of the unpointable band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen asked whether 'the cost pressures of claimant funding proceeding through the court process' were a factor behind legislating over the courts' findings, and this reply does not take that up — it answers a different member's question about which applicant groups he had met.

acuity.statement: We’re talking about the Māori customary right, and then as the Minister’s talking about balance, we’re talking about the public’s right. I do have a question for the Minister about the extinguishment of that Māori right to the takutai moana that was vested to them in Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's immediately preceding answer — the two competing sets of rights and the 'balance' framing — and turns it into a direct question about whether any extinguishing statute exists. But most of the turn is his own prepared constitutional argument about 1854–2004 and the Queen's Chain, which would have been delivered whatever the Minister had said. Partial engagement that can be pointed at: 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: 'In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example' — Ferris picks up the Minister's framing of whose rights are in play and his talk of balance.

acuity.statement: I’m concerned in terms of the resources. We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — three substantive turns by other members precede it. The speech is clearly on the matter under debate (the Amendment Paper's preamble and the physical use and occupation test) and addressed to the Minister, but it engages no part of the arguments just made; it reads as prepared material on the right subject that would be identical whatever Goldsmith or Ferris had said. Low end of the 0.1–0.3 band, with 0.2 for the standing orientation to the Minister's amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith's preceding reply named the applicant groups he had met and gave examples of consent holders whose rights could be affected, and Tākuta Ferris argued no statute between 1854 and 2004 extinguished the customary right; this statement takes up neither, opening instead on recitals (6) and (7) and the cost of implementation.

acuity.statement: I’ve been wanting to really unpack the perspectives of Minister Finlayson because, last week, he was at the Waitangi Tribunal conference speaking to these very issues, along with Geoffrey Palmer, and the importance of the Waitangi Tribunal providing safeguards for us as te iwi Māori and the way in which legislation impacts upon Te Tiriti and tangata whenua. So it would be good to know what is the current status of the whakaaro of Minister Finlayson instead of quoting kōrero from the past.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the move Goldsmith had just made — duelling 2010 Finlayson quotations — and turns it over, pointing to Finlayson's remarks at the Tribunal conference the previous week and asking for his present view rather than selectively quoted historical ones. The intervention only makes sense as a response to the exchange it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we can debate this all day bringing up different quotes from the Hon Chris Finlayson and we'll all be able to find one that suits our argument" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: Under 11(b), it does say, “require inferences by a decision maker (including the Court) to be based on evidence of physical use and occupation:”. My question to the Minister is: does that include all courts? Could that extend itself to other judiciary arms such as the Waitangi Tribunal, who are well-acknowledged in the House as storekeepers of a heck of a lot of evidence with respect to these matters that we’re debating here in the Chamber.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the clauses of the bill before the committee — but engages no part of the preceding argument. The questions on whether "decision maker" reaches the Waitangi Tribunal would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said; the only gesture at the exchange is "It is complex indeed" earlier in the turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon had just pressed the Minister on which iwi — Whakatōhea, the Wairarapa tribes, Aotea Harbour — he consulted, and this statement does not take any part of that up; it opens a prepared clause-by-clause line of questioning on clause 4(11)(b)

acuity.statement: But who is interfering with whose rights? Whose specific rights are there mischief being caused to by the current, most recent interpretation of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, i.e., that of the Supreme Court? Who is the Minister talking about when you refer to “interfering with rights”? It’s a very specific question, and a specific answer to whose specific rights are being interfered with would be appreciated.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's stated justification — that the Supreme Court's interpretation of the Act causes a problem by interfering with other users' rights — and presses on its load-bearing premise, demanding the identity of the rights-holders being harmed. Also picks up Lyndon's preceding point about non-Māori rights being preferenced. The speech is wholly shaped by what preceded it and would have to change if the Minister had argued differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT. So that is why we believe this legislation is required" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. To the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations’s last point, one of the key questions around this is: on whom is the burden of proof that exclusivity is maintained or is not maintained or has been broken? Is it the Minister’s opinion that the original intent of the legislation was to place the burden of proof not on iwi Māori but on those who wished to disprove that iwi Māori had exclusive use and therefore a right of customary title?
acuity.explanation: Abel names the Minister's final point and engages its substance directly: Goldsmith's third 'point of difference' was that the bill shifts proof of every section 58 element onto applicants, and Abel puts precisely that allocation of onus back to him, then supplies contrary authority (the Supreme Court's reading of Ngāti Apa, and Keith and Anderson JJ on the Crown bearing the onus of extinguishment). The speech would have to change if Goldsmith had ended on the inference or tikanga point instead of burden of proof. Not 1.0 because he does not take up Goldsmith's specific claim about what the current Supreme Court test requires, arguing instead from the original intent of the legislation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "The approach of the bill is to say that applicants must prove all the elements of the section 58 test now."

acuity.statement: I'll take the Minister to page 3 of the amendment bill. I'm asking him about his clause 5 that amends section 9 of the Act. I want to ask him whether there should be a definition of “physical use” in this section, because that is a concept which he has been talking about as an important part of this bill, and yet I have some questions around how that meaning should be interpreted.
acuity.explanation: Williams fastens onto the exact term Goldsmith had just used to describe his second point of difference — that the test must rest on evidence of physical use and not only spiritual or cultural association — and presses him on what it means, anchoring the question to the clause that carries it. She draws out a consequence he did not address: that 'physical use' is a concept of older British land law rather than tikanga, and that it is a narrow right. Scored below the top because much of the turn is a prepared excursus on feudal law and the Tītī Islands that engages the topic rather than Goldsmith's specific claim about the Supreme Court's reliance on inferences.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the legislation focuses on influences on the extent and continuity and exclusivity of use and occupation must be based on the evidence of physical use and not only spiritual or cultural association"

acuity.statement: I’ll actually be quite short, because I just want to pick up on a point that Steve Abel raised, and I want to just take it a step further. The point was around onus, and I’m loath to say that the member as elegant as Steve Abel didn’t quite capture, I think, what he perhaps intended, because there are two concepts: one is establishing marine title, and then another is to say that it’s been extinguished.
acuity.explanation: Webb engages the content of a preceding member's argument and does something with it: he accepts the thrust of Abel's question on onus, identifies a conflation in it between establishing marine title and establishing extinguishment, and separates the two so the question can be put properly to the Minister. The turn is unintelligible without Abel's preceding contribution and would be different had Abel framed the onus question differently, which is the strongest evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the Crown bore the onus of proving extinguishment" — and his question on "on whom is the burden of proof that exclusivity is maintained"

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
acuity.explanation: Andersen picks up one strand of the turn immediately before her — Williams's attack on the "physical use" wording — naming "physical" and the occupation test as the serious concerns, and extends it with the regulatory impact statement to ask whether the drafting was predetermined by ministerial direction. But she does not take up Williams's actual argument (that the clause gives no indication of evidential weight and so is unworkable for a decision maker); she moves to her own allocated paragraph (7)(c) and her own prepared RIS material. Partial engagement on the same thread, not a reply to the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "This makes gobbledygook of an already confusing and complex law" — her critique of the "evidence of physical use" wording in the proposed preamble.

acuity.statement: I just wanted to respond to the member Tākuta Ferris’s—I thought—quite interesting speech, where we’re really just sort of grappling with conflicting, or balancing, two separate rights. One is the customary marine rights, and the other is the expectations of all New Zealanders to have a say in what goes on in their neighbourhoods and in their coastal areas.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns by other members precede this one, both putting questions squarely to him as the responsible Minister, and he answers neither. What he does engage — Ferris's speech — is not in the window, so the engagement cannot be pointed at and the score is capped in the 0.0-0.3 band. It sits at 0.3 rather than lower because the content is genuinely about the matter under debate: the threshold the Act set and why Parliament is now asserting one through the Amendment Paper.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable: Goldsmith addresses a speech by Tākuta Ferris that falls outside this window, and does not take up either of the two turns that immediately precede him — Williams on the absent weighting for "evidence of physical use", or Andersen's direct questions to him on whether colonisation counts as interruption and whether the wording was predetermined by his direction to officials.

acuity.statement: Look, it’s a relatively simple point but I’m a bit perplexed as to why there’s a sense that we’ve got to have this massive, long preamble in respect of all of the Court of Appeal’s decisions on it.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows the Minister's defence of the Amendment Paper and engages none of it — not the balance-of-rights framing, not the claim that three courts read the threshold three ways, which is the closest point of contact with his own argument about the Court of Appeal being overruled. He opens a new clause (clause 4, the main Act's preamble) with his own drafting objection and his own question to the Minister. Clearly on the matter under debate, so not 0.0, but indifferent to what immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Goldsmith argued that the Act was passed to strike a balance between customary marine rights and all New Zealanders' expectations, and that three courts reached three different readings of the threshold; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: So the proposal in this amendment is to delete this section, because it’s unfair. It is unfair on tangata whenua to have to show that somehow we’ve got a physical manifestation of connection to that space, when we may not own by Western law the whenua abutting that part of the takutai moana.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by Andersen precedes it in the same committee-stage debate. Lyndon delivers her own prepared case for deleting clause 8(1); the only backward glance is a generic 'my colleagues in the Opposition have spoken', not engagement with Andersen's specific preamble-omission argument. Her speech would be word-for-word the same whatever Andersen had said, but it is squarely on the Part under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen asked the Minister why the Cabinet decision of 28 November 2023 endorsing the coalition agreement is omitted from the Part 1 preamble, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The only thing I'd say in relation to that member's speech, of course, is that nothing in this legislation impacts on the ability of Māori or non-Māori to go and collect shellfish and have a connection with a piece of coastline that continues, and there's all sorts of arrangements in place in relation to customary fishing rights and shellfish-gathering rights and tītī gathering rights.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the substance of the preceding turn: Lyndon argued the physical-use test is unfair because connection is disrupted and often not land-based, and Goldsmith answers that continuing practice and gathering rights are untouched, then supplies the rationale for the high threshold (the valuable consenting rights attached to customary marine title). Not a 1.0 because he leaves her direct question — when and how customary rights were extinguished — entirely unanswered and returns to the 2011 balance argument. Scored purely on engagement; whether the rebuttal is sound or complete is not an acuity matter.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the expectation that somehow we have to reach this new threshold of demonstrating the physical manifestation of activity or use of natural resources" — Hūhana Lyndon

acuity.statement: So my question is—and I desperately hope it’s a no—does the overriding effect clause here mean that this Act overrides the Crown’s obligation under Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Goldsmith's substantive answer immediately precedes it. Webb opens with 'Again, my point is a relatively short one' and proceeds to a self-contained reading of new section 9B(3)(b); nothing in it turns on what Goldsmith just said, even where the Treaty's 'lands, forests, and fisheries' touches Goldsmith's fisheries claim. Prepared material on the clause under debate, so the low band, not zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith argued that the high threshold is the balancing act for the valuable rights conferred by customary marine title and that existing gathering rights are unaffected, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Well, the last part of that member’s comments were irrelevant to this discussion. I just wanted to clarify because the previous member was suggesting that through this legislation we were going to override the Treaty of Waitangi. As he well knows, what the section refers to is that it prevails over section 7 of the legislation, which has the title “Treaty of Waitangi”; it’s not the Treaty of Waitangi itself. It is simply overriding section 7.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim just made — that the bill would give itself overriding effect over Te Tiriti — and corrects it by identifying what the provision actually prevails over (section 7 of the 2011 Act, not the Treaty). The reply would be different had the preceding argument been different. Marked down from 1.0 because the other strand actually put to him, the clause 9B(2) interpretive duty and the preamble, is dismissed as irrelevant rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "the Crown's obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi are not a creature of statute. So to purport to have an overriding effect over them gets us into some trouble."

acuity.statement: But to the point that Arena Williams was making about the gathering of shellfish in her own family history, it is a problem for this complex history we have here for the courts to have clarity as to the character of customary use in customary marine title. Narrowing the things that the court can consider is particularly unhelpful for that court, because that very particular story that a member of this House was able to tell, that showed the relationship of her father’s iwi to the marine coastal environment would be exceedingly useful and informative for a court. But under this Amendment Paper from the Minister, that sort of articulation would not be able to be considered.
acuity.explanation: Picks up a colleague's argument about pre-existing customary rights and the courts' task, and extends it into a concrete objection to new section 58(1A)(b) excluding spiritual and cultural association as evidence. Partial rather than full engagement: it builds on one strand of the preceding contributions and does not take up the specific interpretive-duty argument Williams had just made, and most of the turn is his own prepared amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "These are rights which existed before that, so to suggest that a decision maker then needs to interpret those rights—which are part of the common law of New Zealand—in a way which is, in effect, promoting their purposes and application, which are set out in what is a political narrative plonked on the top of something which purports to be legislation is a bizarre way to make law."

acuity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that. So the question of extinguishment is not covered by what we're talking about when it's in relation to the burden of proof.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact outstanding question just restated — where the onus of proving extinguishment falls — by citing the statutory provision that carries the presumption and stating that the bill leaves it untouched, then distinguishing it from the section 58 elements the applicant must prove. The reply exists only because of what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "The onus of proving extinguishment—we still haven’t had an answer on that, but you out-eloquented me on that, Mr Webb, so I appreciate it."

acuity.statement: My friend and colleague Arena Williams just went through a particular claim that has been decided but will have to be relitigated, which raises the transitional provisions. I must say, I’ve seen some transitional provisions in my time—this is in new Schedule 1AA, inserted by clause 11—but these ones take the cake. They probably take the cake because they’re trying to do something extremely complicated.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up the specific case Williams raised (a High Court decision that will have to be relitigated), identifies the exact provision that produces that result — clause 4 of new Schedule 1AA inserted by clause 11 — and draws out its consequence as a breach of the rule against retrospectivity. The speech would be materially different had Williams not raised the Ruapuke decision; it generalises her particular grievance into a drafting objection rather than restating it. Not a full 1.0 because much of what follows is his own prepared line of questioning about interim steps and interlocutory decisions rather than further engagement with her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why must they go back—using taxpayers’ money, the $15 million, or a portion of that—to be reheard?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: In terms of having to go back to the start, no, it's not our expectation that the cases that have been heard have to go right back to day one and start the whole process again, merely that they would presumably need to reconsider or hear any extra evidence that's required in relation to the amended test or the clarified test. So it's not going right back to the start.
acuity.explanation: This answers the precise disjunction Webb put: it picks the second limb, states that completed hearings do not restart, and specifies what would be needed instead (reconsideration or extra evidence against the amended test). The reply is unintelligible without Webb's question, which is the test. Short of 1.0 only because it engages one of the three questions and leaves the status of interim and interlocutory steps untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Do those people have to go all the way back to square one and, essentially, file a new claim under the new regime, or can they use all of the work that’s been done to date?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: There are a number of questions there, but in terms of where the date of taking effect came from—and this is in relation to the date that we had in June last year—I mean, in essence, the goal was to ensure that we had as much consistency with the rest of the vast majority of cases that haven't yet come forward, to have a consistent test, but to recognise that those that had been concluded and granted before the date, we didn't want to unscramble. So that was the logic there.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith engages the topic Webb pressed — why the cut-off falls where it does and why pre-date grants are left alone — and supplies the policy rationale of a consistent test. But Webb asked for a principled justification for legislating retrospectively over decisions already crystallised in the interim period, and this answers the adjacent question of where the date came from instead, without taking up the rule-of-law objection itself. That is engagement with one strand, not with the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So can he please explain, in a principled way, why he can’t adhere to the principle that we don’t legislative retrospectively?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: The second point itself has two legs, and that is about the work that has been put into these claims. It’s not cheap. Much of the work is done, as Arena Williams has sort of alluded to, by oral history and voluntary work.
acuity.explanation: Webb picks up one strand of Williams's turn — that the evidentiary work in these claims is oral history done largely unpaid — and repurposes it as a premise for his own new argument about compensation under the Schedule's clause 6. That is genuine partial engagement rather than mere reference, but the bulk of his contribution is prepared material on a different clause, and his only other nod to her (the sandflies joke) engages no part of her argument about section 58(1A)(b).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "He compiled much of the evidence in Tauranga Moana, for example, by interviewing orally and then writing down the evidence that was presented around physical use of those lands" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I think the member knows the answer to that question, which is, no, it doesn’t. It’s in relation to claims about property rights and compensation, and our view, of course, is that this bill is reasserting what Parliament intended in the original bill.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific legal question Webb put — whether new clause 6 fetters the court's costs discretion — with a direct no, and states the clause's actual scope (property rights and compensation) as the reason. He then goes on to engage Webb's second leg about money already sunk into claims. The reply would be different had Webb asked something else, which is the test. Scored for engagement only: the dismissive "the member knows the answer" framing and the vagueness of "I don't have the exact figure" belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does new clause 6 mean that courts cannot award costs against the Government in marine and coastal area claims?" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: My final point, to clarify the question, is that you just gave us an oral testimony of your own family history here in Aotearoa New Zealand, and we accepted that testimony.
acuity.explanation: Abel takes Williams's account of her father's Waitangi Tribunal work and turns it into an argument against the Minister: the House credited her unevidenced oral account, so why should a pātere be barred from supporting inference. That is doing something with a preceding turn's content rather than restating it. It is not a 1.0 because he does not engage the turn immediately before him — Goldsmith's answer on compensation and costs goes untouched — and he returns to a prepared question on clause 8.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My father was a historian for the Waitangi Tribunal in the 1990s." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: In response to that, all evidence has been and will continue to be relevant to the decision maker. The change is that cultural or spiritual evidence needs supporting evidence of physical use, but tikanga and oral evidence remain important.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the two-part question Abel asked — whether a chant counts as evidence, and whether paragraph (b) excludes it — by stating that all evidence stays relevant and that the change is a requirement for supporting physical-use evidence. The answer is squarely aimed at the question and would read differently had Abel asked something else. Marked below 1.0 only because it does not take up the sharper form of the challenge (that paragraph (b) prohibits drawing inferences from such evidence at all); its brevity and lack of detail are matters for Specificity, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister regard the likes of a chant articulating that as evidence?" — Steve Abel

acuity.statement: In this instance, my question to the Minister, because I haven’t heard it yet, is whether or not the Minister has made it clear to the House, at this point in time, whether or not he intends on supporting a number of the amendments that have been made?
acuity.explanation: Henare follows a substantive turn by Andersen on the same Part 1 provisions, but engages no part of her argument about the adequacy and timing of the policy analysis. He opens his own prepared line of questioning (support for Arena Williams' Amendment Paper, the "occupation" threshold for urupā and sites of significance, toheroa spat). It is squarely on the matter under debate — clause 10 and the "and occupation" threshold — so it is not wholly unresponsive, but the speech would read identically whatever Andersen had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued that the regulatory impact statement shows Cabinet decided the meaning of "exclusive use and occupation" without adequate analysis, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Just in relation to the question, I'm not of a mind to support the Amendment Paper that the member refers to. I do thank the member for his advice on the matter of toheroa spat which was indeed new to me.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question just put to him and answers it directly — he will not support the Amendment Paper deleting "and occupation" — and acknowledges the toheroa spat point Henare raised, so the reply is visibly shaped by the preceding turn and could not have been delivered in another debate. Short of 1.0 because he engages only the first of Henare's three questions, leaving the tikanga/urupā "occupation" threshold and the aquaculture point untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The first question is whether or not the Minister will support the Amendment Paper tabled by my colleague, which I think is a reasonable one." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: So this is the question of the interruption of the exclusive use and occupation. I’m particularly interested in the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations’ explanation where the customary right is, perhaps, a seasonal or even an occasional customary right.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows substantive turns by Henare and Goldsmith and opens a fresh, evidently prepared line on new section 57B(c) and the meaning of "substantial interruption". He gestures at the Minister's earlier explanation of seasonal customary rights, but engages no claim made in the turns immediately before him, including Goldsmith's refusal to support the "and occupation" amendment. Clearly on the clause under debate, hence the top of the low band rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith had just declined to support the Amendment Paper deleting "and occupation" and this statement does not take that up; Webb instead gestures at an earlier ministerial explanation not contained in the preceding turns.

acuity.statement: Supporting my colleague, I think he makes some very good points. My contribution to this particular part is quite clear. It asks a very specific question about the announcement that the Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations made with respect to the moves that he’s making to amend this particular legislation through this bill, which is that at the end of the Schedule, inserting New Schedule 1AA, it does say in there at new clause 6, “No entitlement to compensation”, “A person is not entitled to compensation of any kind on account of the operation of the CMT amendments.”, which begs the question, once again: does that only apply to the ones that are listed here? Those are the questions that Dr Webb has made quite clear to the Minister. Who else does that or does that not apply to?
acuity.explanation: Webb's argument was that Part 2's named cases are a non-exhaustive list of judgments overridden, so readers will wrongly infer an unlisted case still stands. Henare takes exactly that strand and carries it onto a different clause: if the list is non-exhaustive, does the Schedule 1AA bar on compensation reach only the cases named? He names the argument he is extending and poses the consequence as a question to the Minister, and later restates it ("as to Mr Webb's point... Part 2 actually seems moot"). Not a full 1.0 because he does not test Webb's reasoning itself, and part of the turn is his own prepared question about the $15 million announcement; but the engagement is specific and pointable, and the speech would have to change had Webb argued something else about Part 2.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If you’re going to list them in a non-exhaustive way, it’s actually quite misleading." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Just briefly, in relation to Mr Steve Abel’s amendment, which says that interruptions caused by the establishment of ports and other infrastructure without the group’s consent, however that would be gained, wouldn’t be into stopping customary marine title being granted. I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith takes the specific limb of Abel's tabled amendment No. 8 — the exclusion of port and infrastructure establishment from 'substantial interruption' — and draws out its practical consequence (CMT over a port site plus resource-consent powers), then states his position on it. The speech could not have been delivered had Abel's amendment listed something else; it is squarely aimed at the content of the proposal just put. Marked slightly below 1.0 because he engages only one item of Abel's list and does not rebut the colonisation premise underlying it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "it does not mean interruptions caused by the establishment of ports, harbours, or other infrastructure without the group's consent" — and his direct invitation, "I wonder if the Minister could respond to that proposed amendment".

acuity.statement: The Minister spoke to the use and the ability to have ports, etc. I wonder if I can take the Minister to another place with respect to that, and that is around the substantial interruption. I want to take him to the Far North and there is a place up there called Waimahana, which is private land all the way down to the beach.
acuity.explanation: Henare notes that the Minister spoke about ports, but does nothing with the argument — he neither contests the consenting difficulty Goldsmith raised nor accepts it; the reference is a springboard to his own prepared material (the 'stewardship' amendment in Arena Williams' name and the Waimahana example). That is a mere reference used to pivot, which the rubric places in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5, though the gesture at the preceding turn and the fact that his question is on the same clause under debate put him at the top of that band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country" — acknowledged in passing but not engaged; Henare moves to a different scenario.

acuity.statement: I want to ask him first in respect of his change to the interim period, which at new clause 4 in new Schedule 1AA says, “Certain CMT [customary marine title] decisions made in interim period,”—so say, Ruapuke—“and related agreements and orders made, have no legal effect and never have had legal effect”; what does that mean for the cases where other decisions have been made in reliance upon them, and has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?
acuity.explanation: The question is closely worked and plainly about the matter under debate, but it engages no part of what the preceding members said in this stretch — not Goldsmith's port/consenting objection and not Henare's Waimahana question. It opens a fresh line on Amendment Paper 380 and the transitional provisions that would have been put in identical terms whatever had just been argued, anchored instead to a pre-dinner exchange outside this window. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate's subject matter: 0.3, not 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare asked the Minister to consider the word "stewardship" and raised the Waimahana boat-launching case, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Just in relation to that question, when this policy to overturn the Court of Appeal decision was announced originally in July 2024, the Government signalled, of course, right at that point that we would seek to have the legislation take effect from that point. So any arrangements that have been entered into would have been done in the knowledge that there was a risk that this legislation would pass and that the legislation would require those examples to be heard again under the new test, so I think everybody would have gone into it with eyes wide open.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith takes up one strand of Williams' question — the status of arrangements entered into in reliance on interim CMT decisions — and answers it with a reason (parties were on notice from the July 2024 announcement). But he leaves the specific questions she asked untouched: whether councils can rely on completed consultations, the effect on taonga tūturu and koiwi arrangements, and how far 'never have had legal effect' reaches. Engagement with the topic and one strand of the argument, then no further: the middle of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "has the Minister had advice about what decisions may have been made in reliance upon them?"

acuity.statement: I’d like to thank the member for his suggestions for titles, but I think we’ll stick with the current one which is the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill. That is because that is what it does. It does not break any deals; it is set out in its goal to find that balance between enabling Māori to establish customary marine rights and title, while also recognising the wide interests that all New Zealanders have in the marine and coastal space.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's turn directly on its own terms: declines the proposed titles, then contradicts the specific charge that the bill breaks the 2011 deal and the charge that it strips rights, offering the balance rationale as the counter-account. Had Webb argued something different about the bill's name, this reply would have had to change. Short of 1.0 because it does not engage the sharpest strand — litigants who already hold a favourable judgment — answering instead at the level of the general public's access ('nobody will wake up tomorrow with less ability'). Scored on engagement only; whether the balance claim is true or well-reasoned is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "That was the deal struck some years ago in 2011, and it’s a deal that this Government is breaking. Maybe we should call it the 'Broken Promises (Takutai Moana) Act' as well."

acuity.statement: Further to that, I have an additional name and suggestion, which I think is, actually, something that is practical. It reflects, actually, what’s going to happen on the ground. While some in New Zealand will be entitled to quiet enjoyment of the takutai moana and protection of their private property rights, Māori don’t get the same. I propose a name amendment of the “No Entitlement to Compensation for Māori Act”, because, ultimately, our people will not be eligible for compensation for the lost time, for the opportunity cost, for the years of preparation and going through the hearings.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Goldsmith's reply — his 'wide interests that all New Zealanders have' balance and his claim that no rights are taken away — by asserting the entitlement runs one way and that Māori groups bear an uncompensated loss. But the bulk of the turn is her own prepared amendments and the roll of seven affected groups, which would have been delivered whatever Goldsmith had said, so this sits at partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of his argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "It seeks not to take away rights—nobody will wake up tomorrow with less ability to enjoy the coastal area or have a connection with it."

acuity.statement: Well, I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific device of Henare's turn — commemorative dates — and answers it with a counter-date, then explains the 2011 Act's origin and the threshold the amendment bill restores.
