acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years"

acuity.statement: Look, it is described as “may”, but it is, effectively, mandatory because the chair will be appointed. It’s not about bringing someone in from outside.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise drafting question asked, and goes on to address the two other things put to her in that turn — the Amendment Paper ('I have read the member's Amendment Paper. I don't think that it's necessary') and the request for the funding document. Nothing here is transferable to another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "in section 319(1), instead of using the word “must”, why does it use the word “may”?"

acuity.statement: I'll be very brief because I think that, as the member has pointed out, new section 315(2)(b), added by clause 22, covers that very open “consult other persons or bodies that the Minister thinks fit;”. It opens the door to consult with all of those entities that the member brought forward.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact provision Twyford interrogated — paragraph (b) — and answers his specific list of regional bodies by arguing the open wording already admits them. The reply would be different had he asked about a different paragraph. Short of 1.0 because it leaves his other strand (why the region's characteristics are not a mandatory consideration under subsection (2)) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Why is there not, for example in paragraph (b), the requirement to consult, for example, local institutions, regional industry groups, local community organisations, iwi and hapū?"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to follow up. I’ve got a new point that I want to ask the Minister for Vocational Education about and it’s about clause 20 in relation to Crown observers and also the operative clause, which is new section 341J, which will be the new section of the of the bill once it becomes an Act.
acuity.explanation: On the same bill and in the same committee dialogue with the Minister, so it is not wholly detached from the debate, but it engages no part of the answer immediately preceding it — the adequacy of "persons or bodies that the Minister thinks fit" goes uncontested. Prepared material on the right subject, hence the 0.3 band rather than 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds had just answered that new section 315(2)(b) "opens the door" to consulting regional bodies, and this contribution does not take that answer up — it opens a separate line on clause 20 and Crown observers. It gestures back at an academic-freedom exchange that preceded this window rather than at what was just said.

acuity.statement: It’s very good to be discussing this, because, of course, this mirrors the legislation for Te Pūkenga. I’m a great believer in nothing is all good or all bad, and so I’ve been prepared to look at what was put in place for Te Pūkenga by that member’s party when it was in Government. I’ve seen this and thought that it’s wonderful to have early intervention, to have different stages of intervention, because the worst thing possible is to allow a polytechnic to keep going and getting itself more and more in trouble and racking up huge amounts of debt.
acuity.explanation: Answers one strand of Belich's question — the provenance and purpose of the polytechnic-specific intervention clause, said to be lifted from the Te Pūkenga regime — so the engagement is pointable. But it leaves her two sharper questions alone: the drafting asymmetry with the academic freedom section, and whether "consulted" in new section 341J(3) is the right word if a council refuses. Partial engagement, then a return to general advocacy for staged intervention.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "why has a specific polytechnic clause been put into this new bill, and what is the purpose of that?"

acuity.statement: I appreciate, Minister, that you are being very responsive to the questions, that’s really helpful in this committee stage so thank you. But you are talking about some of the costs of Te Pūkenga, you’re talking about costs, as an example of funding via the strategic fund, to particular polytechnics. What I would like to hear from you is what advice you have received around the sheer costs.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own cost-and-debt framing and turns it into a demand for the underlying advice on establishment costs, so the question is shaped by what she said. But it is also the continuation of his own prepared line on insufficient financial information, and it moves to a different subsection rather than contesting her intervention argument, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "racking up huge amounts of debt" — her defence of staged intervention as the way to stop polytechnics getting into financial strife.

acuity.statement: Treasury’s advice was interesting over the period of time. We got that advice at different periods of time, and over the last 18 months, things have changed as the institutions have got stronger and more viable.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the specific evidence Halbert raised — the Treasury advice and his own concession that it was dated — and answers it on his terms by arguing the advice is a series of dated snapshots overtaken by events. Not 1.0 because it supplies no figure in response to his repeated request for the advice on actual establishment costs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "I acknowledge that Treasury has advised you against this, they’ve highlighted the risks financially for this particular structure. That was some time ago, so I’d be really keen to hear the centre of that."

acuity.statement: When I looked at what examples there might be, I could think of, for example, that if there were polytechnics that wanted the anchor polytechnic to develop a particular course but it was going to cost the anchor polytechnic a lot of money and divert them from other development, this might come into play.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez asked two things about new section 328(1)(b): who judges whether an action is detrimental, and what "detrimental" means. Simmonds takes up the second strand directly and supplies a worked example of a detrimental action (a course the federation wants that would divert the anchor polytechnic's resources), which is a concrete answer to the definitional question. She leaves the "who judges" half unanswered, so this is a partial but clearly pointable engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "And is there a specific definition around what “detrimental” might mean in this context?" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: In terms of the consent rather than just consulting, can I just say, it’s really, really difficult when a polytechnic gets into that downward spiral either academically or financially. Sometimes they don’t see the wood for the trees, and I think that the whole nature of the federation is not punitive—it’s not to punish polytechnics, it’s to support them.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez tabled an Amendment Paper to replace consultation with consent under clause 339 and asked the Minister directly to consider it. Simmonds names that exact substitution ("consent rather than just consulting") and gives her reason for refusing it — that a failing polytechnic may not recognise its own position, so a consent requirement would block support. She engages the reasoning of his proposal rather than merely acknowledging it, and the answer would have to be different had he proposed something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Will the Minister consider upgrading the requirement from consultation to requiring the consent of the communities?" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: Speaking of regions served by the anchor polytech, how will the Minister ensure local autonomy in multi-region providers like UCOL Wairarapa? What protections will be in place to prevent populous areas or those perhaps better off economically from dominating, and what will the funding structures be, and how are they different from Te Pūkenga?
acuity.explanation: Simmonds had just asserted that the federation is a collective with equity of decision making between small regional polytechnics and the large Open Polytechnic. Tangaere-Manuel takes up that specific claim and tests it against a concrete case, asking what prevents populous or wealthier areas dominating and how the funding differs from Te Pūkenga. She engages one strand of the answer rather than its whole, and pivots to her own regional example, so this is a solid partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ensuring that the federation polytechnics and the services that are provided to them are not cost-plus but are only cost-recovery" and "there is equity of decision making" — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: In the cluster that you’ve established is the anchor polytechnic of the Open Polytechnic, who are the educational delivery partner—that is their core business. They are not the financial partner, as I understand it. So who, therefore, in that live example, is offering the fiscal advice to assist Otago Polytechnic to get to a place of sustainability as required by this legislation?
acuity.explanation: Simmonds had just grounded her case on the federation existing to support polytechnics in academic or financial deficit. Halbert takes that claim and draws out its consequence against the live Otago Polytechnic arrangement: if the problem is debt and the anchor is an online delivery provider rather than a financial one, the support the Minister describes has no identifiable source. He also picks up and extends his colleague's preceding example. The speech would have to change if the Minister had defended the federation on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The federation is not punitive; it is there to support." — Penny Simmonds

acuity.statement: In terms of the financial situation, for example, for Otago Polytechnic, their council of course will be responsible for their financial improvement plan. They have an improvement plan there and they are working towards that; we are looking at what we can do with their debt. So I’m very confident that we can assist them there.
acuity.explanation: Halbert's question was specifically who provides the fiscal advice to Otago Polytechnic given the anchor is a delivery partner. Simmonds answers the question as put — the council carries the improvement plan, the Government is working on the debt, and the federation's financial contribution is avoided development cost via the Open Polytechnic's existing programmes. That rebuts his premise that the model leaves the financial side unowned, rather than restating prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So who, therefore, in that live example, is offering the fiscal advice to assist Otago Polytechnic to get to a place of sustainability as required by this legislation?" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: Once again, just in relationship to Schedule 6, Part 1—and I particularly wanted to pick up this area just because I understand there has been a bit of debate on the nature of the industry skills boards and workforce development councils, which is specifically noted in the replacing of section 157, and so this is specifically between lines 10 and 25.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Halbert's substantive turns on ISBs and workforce development councils immediately precede this, and Menéndez March continues the same committee-stage debate. He gestures at that debate ("there has been a bit of debate on the nature of the industry skills boards and workforce development councils") but takes up none of its content — not the funding halving, not the board count, not the timeline. His questions on Schedule 6, the Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers Act and student/worker voice are prepared material on the right subject that would read identically had Halbert argued something else. Gesture at the debate without engagement puts it at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "In that is the proposal to disestablish workforce development councils." — Halbert had just put a series of specific questions to the Minister about ISB funding being halved, the two extra boards, and the 1 January 2026 timeline.

acuity.statement: It’s really important that our ISBs set up the vehicle and the structure that enables the voices of those industries so that it isn’t a domination of the biggest industries within the ISBs but that they hear from all of those industries that are encompassed by an ISB. I thank the member for his question and, yes, certainly the ISBs are being asked to ensure that they have structures in place that enable them to hear the voices of all the trades and all the industries within their ISB.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: follows a substantive question turn by a different member in the same debate. She takes up the specific provision he raised (the Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers Act 2006 and section 157's ISB relationship) and answers his voice question directly, explaining the specialist-trades naming of the construction ISB and committing to structures that prevent domination by the biggest industries. The speech would plainly be different had he asked about something else. Short of 1.0 because she converts "voices within the workforce rather than just industry" into voices of all industries and trades, and leaves his questions about student voice and engagement with the Minister for social development untouched. Scored only on engagement — not on whether the answer is adequate or true.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "would she see the need for voices within the workforce rather than just industry as part of that board and those respective areas noted in Schedule 6?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m coming back to new section CW 55BAA, inserted by clause 41, and the discussion around workforce development councils (WDCs) and industry skills boards (ISBs).
acuity.explanation: Eligible: the Minister's substantive answer immediately precedes it and the debate is continuing. Halbert engages no part of what she said — not the specialist-trades point, not the claim about structures enabling all industries to be heard — and returns to prepared questions about WDC redundancies, mandate and transition timing. The turn is on the matter under debate, which keeps it off 0.0, but nothing in it would change if the Minister had said something entirely different, and there is no gesture at her answer at all. Scored purely on responsiveness; the substance of his transition questions is not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Penny Simmonds spoke about the construction ISB covering specialist trades and about structures to let ISBs hear from all industries, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I also want to give an assurance to the member about my commitment to Māori, Pasifika, and regional communities. They are at the heart of what I am doing here, and I would extend an invitation to the member, once we are now through this, to come and meet with me and I will talk through some of the financial viability matters, particularly once we get the recapitalisation landed. That is going to make a huge difference to those polytechnics and industry skills boards.
acuity.explanation: She picks up two of the specific strands Halbert raised by name — access for Māori, Pasifika and regional communities, and the financial viability argument — and adds a concrete new fact (the recapitalisation) to the second. But she converts both into an offer to discuss them offline rather than meeting the argument in the Chamber, and leaves untouched the one direct question he put to her, on the practicality of the 1 January commencement date and the gap between disestablishment of the workforce development councils and the stand-up of industry skills boards. Engaged in part, pointable, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "I’m still not convinced that this setup offers better access to learning, particularly for Māori, for Pasifika, and for ethnic communities" — and his claim that he is "yet to see any evidence of whether the Minister is able to demonstrate that what she has put up is better than what was there before" on financial viability.

acuity.statement: I note the Minister’s comments that a couple of Amendment Papers were sorely tempting. I suspect it’s not the one that I’m about to speak to, but I do want to speak to Shanan Halbert’s amendment to replace “vocational education and training system” with “undoing reform and taking vocational education backwards”. It is probably a little bit strong, but the point that I want to make is just to pick up on a point that Shanan Halbert made—I think the Minister’s responded partially to it, but there’s another part to it that I would like to traverse in my short contribution—and that’s around both the characteristics of polytechnics and also new section 318, inserted by clause 23, which is “Matters to be considered when appointing members of polytechnic’s council”.
acuity.explanation: She locates herself precisely in what has just been said — names the Minister's "sorely tempting" remark, identifies which strand of Halbert's argument the Minister answered and which she did not, and then carries that unanswered strand forward into a clause-level argument about the removal of ethnic, gender and socio-economic diversity from new section 318. That is a genuine extension of the preceding turns rather than prepared material dropped in, so it sits above the glance band. It falls short of 1.0 because the bulk of the contribution is her own new ground on clause 23 and she does not test or rebut the assurance the Minister actually gave.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "I’m still not convinced that this setup offers better access to learning, particularly for Māori, for Pasifika, and for ethnic communities"; and Penny Simmonds: "One or two were sorely tempting for me to accept, around the change of title".

acuity.statement: I ask the Minister: you have assured and thanked the staff around the country for what they do in vocational education and training, but how do we assure that, going forward, there is stability; that the sector can feel confident; that it’s not going to be just another set of people rolling in from Wellington or from Auckland to places like Taranaki or Southland or the West Coast and again creating instability and creating fear in terms of that job uncertainty?
acuity.explanation: He takes the Minister's thanks to staff — delivered two turns earlier — and turns it directly into the question it leaves open: thanks are not assurance, so what guarantees stability for those same staff going forward? The speech is built on what Simmonds actually said and would have to be rewritten had she not acknowledged staff at all. Short of 1.0 only because he presses the consequence of her remark rather than engaging any reasoning in it, and the surrounding material on WITT is his own prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "I also acknowledge the impact on staff over the years of change, and I want to take this opportunity to thank all the staff for their professionalism."

acuity.statement: I’m just struggling a little bit with the member’s questions. He quoted new section CW 55BAA, inserted by clause 41, which is about the Income Tax Act 2007 and amendments there. I’m just trying to see what his question was regarding the Income Tax Act?
acuity.explanation: She picks up a real, specific feature of the preceding turn — the clause Halbert cited — and would not have said this had he cited a different provision, so it is not prepared material. But she engages no part of the three questions actually put (transfer of WDC roles, the 1 January 2026 runway, ISB recruitment), confining herself to the relevance of the clause reference. Partial engagement with one strand, which is the middle band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: 'how will ISBs be enabled to deliver on their statutory functions from day one when, in some instances, only two or three roles from the workforce development councils to their corresponding ISBs have been identified for transfer via an expression of interest process?'

acuity.statement: Just to check: the three questions that I asked, which were in relation to that particular point, new section CW 55BAA of the Income Tax Act 2007, inserted by clause 41 of the bill, industry skills boards (ISBs). Is she unwilling to answer the three questions about transition from workforce development councils to industry skills boards?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific objection — that his questions were pinned to an Income Tax Act clause — confirms the clause reference she named, and converts her objection into a direct challenge about whether she will answer. The statement is entirely contingent on what she just said; a different objection would have required a different reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: 'He quoted new section CW 55BAA, inserted by clause 41, which is about the Income Tax Act 2007 and amendments there.'

acuity.statement: Well, the relationship, Mr Chair, is that we’re talking about a transition of a structure which has fiscal implications no matter which way that you look at it.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the connection the Minister said she could not see — that a transition of structures carries fiscal implications and therefore bears on a tax clause. It answers the specific point of difficulty raised rather than the general topic, though it asserts the link rather than demonstrating it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: 'I’m just trying to see what his question was regarding the Income Tax Act?'

acuity.statement: Then show us what your sustainability plan is. I accept from Suze Redmayne, who says there is no magic money tree. I’m not proposing that there is a magic money tree, but what I am proposing is that any educational legislation that comes through this House should offer equity of access to learning opportunities no matter where you live.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the interjection's content explicitly, concedes its premise, denies that his argument depends on it, and restates what he is actually claiming. That is accept-part-and-reframe, which is genuine engagement rather than a mere mention — though the interjection was brief and he returns promptly to his own line about regional access.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Suze Redmayne: 'The magic money tree wasn’t real money.'

acuity.statement: Look, the wānanga are not involved in this legislation and this legislative change, but I do want to take a quick moment to celebrate our three wonderful wānanga: Te Wānanga o Aotearoa (TWOA), Te Whare Wānanga o Awanuiārangi, and Te Wānanga o Raukawa.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn pressed her on ISB funding, transition timing and regional provision, and asked directly whether she would answer those questions. This reply raises wānanga, a subject the preceding turn never mentions, and engages no strand of it. It remains within the general subject of the vocational education bill, which keeps it off zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert asked 'are you willing to answer the questions relative to industry skills boards that you have proposed under this legislation?' and this statement does not take that up, addressing wānanga instead.

acuity.statement: Following that contribution—and we just tabled some amendments from my colleague Francisco Hernandez which I’d like to speak to—I did want to ask the Minister for Vocational Education whether she believes that the title accurately represents the scope and intent of the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific move the previous speaker made — proposing an alternative short title by amendment paper — and carries it forward into a question to the Minister about whether the existing title matches the bill's intent, later asking her to consider Halbert's amendment alongside his colleague's. The contribution is shaped by what preceded it, though it does not engage Twyford's underlying Treaty-references reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: 'I would want to invite the committee to support Shanan Halbert’s Amendment Paper that would replace “Vocational Education and Training System” with “Dilute Māori Representation”.'

acuity.statement: Yes, I think it’s a very appropriate title. I acknowledge that “vocational education and training” perhaps isn’t explicitly known by everyone, but it is a good explanation of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question put squarely, and concedes the specific sub-point that was offered in support of it — that the phrase may not be widely understood by the public — before disputing the conclusion drawn from it. The reply tracks the structure of the question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: 'when we’re engaging with the public, if I go out into the community and I say, “Have you heard of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill?”, people may not know that behind it there was a broader intent of undermining our vocational education institutions.'

acuity.statement: I note from the member Phil Twyford his suggestion of the alternate naming, which I think is entirely inappropriate because, as I answered five or maybe six times, the references here around the expectations and engagement and representation of Māori in new sections 314(d), 318(1), 321(c), 370(e), inserted by clause 23, and the overarching general duty in the main Act to acknowledge the Treaty.
acuity.explanation: Meets the factual premise of the earlier speech head-on: he claimed the bill systematically strips Treaty and Māori-engagement references, naming particular provisions, and she answers by naming provisions where she says those expectations remain. Engagement with the specific claim, not merely the topic; whether the sections bear her reading is a rigor and veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: 'a systematic stripping out of references to Te Tiriti and also a weakening, a removal, and a dilution of commitments for the various institutions in the vocational education sector to engage with, consult with Māori organisations'

acuity.statement: Does he think New Zealanders are feeling better off or worse off after two years of his leadership compared to before he became Prime Minister?
acuity.explanation: Luxon had just made a series of specific claims (29,000 fewer victims, a 16 percent reduction in serious youth offending, spending up 84 percent under the last government). This supplementary engages none of them and puts a general sentiment question on the same broad subject — prepared material on the right topic rather than a reply to the argument. There is a gesture at the debate (the 'better off' framing picks up the 'make things better' theme), so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than lower.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I'm proud to say there are 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime' — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Does he stand by his statement that the economy is now growing; if so, will he resign if the figures for the September quarter that has just ended show that the economy has actually been in recession?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim Luxon had just made — that a two-speed recovery is already under way and the year ahead looks good — and tests it against the one piece of evidence that would contradict it, the September quarter outturn. The question would have had to be written differently had Luxon not asserted current growth, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because it challenges the growth claim rather than engaging the explanation Luxon gave for it (the April tariff shock).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'we've actually got a two-speed recovery under way already' — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: So why is he willing to accept a pay rise in line with inflation, claim a $50,000 housing allowance, and spend $44,000 on a helicopter ride so he could take a photograph for his Facebook, while his Government makes pay offers to workers like firefighters, nurses, and teachers that amount to pay cuts in real terms?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the answer just given — Luxon's assertion that the Government has bargained in good faith — and puts a contrast to it, but does not engage his actual argument, which was that the unions are prioritising their interests over pupils and patients. Partial engagement with prepared material attached: you can point at what is taken up, but the substance of the preceding claim goes unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I think the Government has been acting in good faith in negotiation with the unions' — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: If his Government is so supportive of pay equity, how many of the 33 active pay equity claims that were in the process when he became Prime Minister have been settled during his two years as Prime Minister?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact proposition Luxon had just advanced — 'this is a Government that supports pay equity legislation' and that the regime is 'still available for people today' — and converts it into a checkable test with a number attached. The question is built directly out of the words of the preceding answer and could not have been asked in that form had Luxon said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'this is a Government that supports pay equity legislation' — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: How can she stand by her statement in April this year that “We’ve been seeing green shoots across the economy.”, when at that time the economy was shrinking by almost 1 percent?
acuity.explanation: Jones had just closed his answer with 'Green shoots are emerging'; this question seizes that phrase, traces it back to an earlier use of it, and sets it against the contemporaneous contraction. The engagement is with the content of the answer immediately preceding, not merely a reference to it, and the question is unmistakably shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Green shoots are emerging.' — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: How will this extension improve early detection and survival rates for women with breast cancer?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under discussion and glances at the Minister's point that early detection is when treatment is most effective, but it engages no claim he made and invites more of the same prepared material. A supplementary of this kind would have been asked in identical words whatever the answer before it had contained.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'detect breast cancer early, when treatment is most effective' — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: How is the Government ensuring that women across the country, including the Kāpiti Coast, can access these breast screening services?
acuity.explanation: Introduces an electorate-specific access question that takes up nothing from the preceding answer, which was about eligibility numbers, staffing and equipment. It is about the matter under debate, which keeps it off zero, but it is prepared material indifferent to what came before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown set out the age extension and the investment behind it, and this question does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: Two parts per million methane—biogenic methane. That side of the House eviscerated rural New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Cameron follows a substantive turn by Simeon Brown, so he is eligible, but his contribution engages no part of what Brown argued. Brown's turn was about Opposition disunity, a prospective Labour/Green/Te Pāti Māori tax programme, and a list of Government health and crime results; Cameron opens on biogenic methane concentration and the previous Government's treatment of farmers, and the whole speech runs on prepared rural-advocacy material (Damien O'Connor, David Parker, the zero carbon Act, the methane target revision). The deciding test fails: substitute any other argument of Brown's and this speech would be word-for-word unchanged. It sits at 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it shares the debate's broad Government-delivery-versus-Opposition-record frame; the specific things it does answer (Arena Williams on the world burning, Marama Davidson on lobbyists 'yesterday') were said outside this window, so they cannot lift the score here. Scored purely on engagement — not on the truth of the two-parts-per-million claim, the quality of the inference, or the sharpness of the attack.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown spoke about Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori as an 'unholy coalition of chaos' united on 'increased taxes for New Zealanders', and about the Government's delivery on inflation, ram raids and health wait-lists — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I would say to Chris Hipkins that, well, if you’re going to do all these things, mate, then how come you didn’t do it in the six years that you were there?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Hipkins' speech — his prospectus of better decisions Labour would make — and puts a direct question to it, asking why none of it was done in Labour's six years. It engages the alternative-prospectus claim rather than the particular figures Hipkins cited (construction at a seven-year low, $3 billion less building spend, unemployment), so it is a partial engagement that then moves to Collins' own prepared account of Labour's record. The reasoning is a tu quoque, but that is a Rigor matter and does not reduce the responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "There are better decision that we can make. We can invest in our own future; we can back New Zealanders in a way that this Government is failing to do."

acuity.statement: When they keep talking about New Zealanders going to Australia, they’re going to work in the mines. They’re not going to work as baristas; they’re going to work in the mines. That’s why they’re going because New Zealand, in the last six years of the Labour Government, decided to cut the mines.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Hipkins' central exodus argument and does something with it: it accepts the departures as fact and supplies a competing causal account (mining jobs closed off by the previous government) that would, if accepted, defeat his inference that the current Government is to blame. This speech would have to change if the preceding turn had not run the emigration argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "We cannot sustain the exodus of talent that we are seeing under this Government."

acuity.statement: The economy is turning. It’s turning the right way. We see interest rates dropping. We see New Zealand businesses getting a bit more confidence, and that will help them to employ more people.
acuity.explanation: Contradicts the specific claims just made — a shrinking economy and rising unemployment — on the same ground, with interest rates and business confidence offered against them. It is a flat counter-assertion rather than a rebuttal of the reasoning or the figures, so it engages the claim without doing much with it; its vagueness is a Specificity matter, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Increasing unemployment; an economy that’s shrinking"

acuity.statement: Instead, what we’re doing on this side is we’re growing the economy. Even the Defence Force is now a great source of growth in the economy. We’ve released the defence industry strategy.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the matter under debate — the Government's economic record — but it takes up no part of the preceding argument. Hipkins argued specifically for backing businesses to grow and investing in future assets; this pivots to the defence industry strategy without engaging that, and would read identically whatever he had said about the economy. The gesture at the debate ('Instead, what we're doing on this side') keeps it off the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hipkins argued the Government should be investing in assets and backing businesses to grow rather than selling off what is left, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: I think it’s also practically a miracle this week—you think it’s the Middle East? No, no, the miracle is that the Green Party has actually asked some questions on conservation of the environment.
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of the preceding speech and is not about the matter under debate either; it is a prepared aside about another party's question choices that could have been delivered in any debate on any day. Nothing in it would change had the previous speaker made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hipkins spoke about the Government's economic and health record and the emigration of New Zealanders, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: I want to celebrate progress on the science reforms—the biggest reforms in 30 years—but I want to start with a shout-out, first of all, to the gaming sector. Exports in one year are up from $500 million to around $750 million.
acuity.explanation: Verrall's immediately preceding turn was a sustained argument that government underfunding of general practice has pushed GP fees towards $100, that fee caps without funding increases have simply produced new charges, and that one in six New Zealanders cannot afford to see a doctor. Reti's speech takes up none of it: he turns to gaming exports, then to CRI mergers and science funding, and the only contact with the Opposition is a set of jibes mapping game titles onto Opposition parties and KiwiBuild — naming a target rather than engaging a claim, which the rubric treats as unresponsive. Delete Verrall's turn and substitute any other argument and this speech would be word-for-word identical; it could have been given in a different debate on a different day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued that 'because of that Government's underfunding, GP services have had to put their prices up' and that 'one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It’s been two years since the election, when Christopher Luxon stood in front of voters in 2023 as an economic genius who declared that he would fix the cost of living and the economy, and he has failed to do so.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's preceding turn made a specific argument — that the Government's growth strategy is environmentally self-defeating and that the Greens' jobs plan is the alternative. Boyack's speech is prepared material on Nelson-Tasman job losses and National's economic record: it never references Davidson, her environmental premise, her 36,000-jobs claim, or the Greens' plan. It is on the broad subject under debate (the economy) but engages no part of the argument just made, and would read identically whoever had spoken before. Scored low for unresponsiveness only — the quality, accuracy and politeness of the speech are not at issue here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson spoke immediately before, arguing that "there is no economy when our environment is destroyed" and that fast-track mining and conservation-land projects serve overseas corporates, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Today, I want to talk about international rural women’s day. It’s a day celebrated globally on 15 October to recognise the vital contributions of rural women to agriculture, to food security, and to rural development; a day to celebrate the extraordinary women who are the backbone of our rural communities.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns with contestable claims precede this one, including Boyack's detailed account of Nelson job losses and Davidson's attack on the Government's environmental and economic strategy. Redmayne opens a wholly new subject and the speech is indifferent to what it follows — it could have been delivered word-for-word in a different debate on a different day. That is the 0.0 band. No other attribute is scored: this is a courteous, on-its-own-terms tribute speech with no real opportunity to score across a 0–1 range elsewhere.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rachel Boyack spoke immediately before about job losses at Carter Holt Harvey, Sealord and Pic's in Nelson and National's economic mismanagement, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I think that member, over the last two years, must have been taking a thing or two in, sitting and watching this National-led Government start to get this economy under control. All of a sudden, there’s a revelation that debt has a cost. She wants to talk about the impact of debt and the cost of debt—well, $66 billion later, New Zealanders are paying the price of that Government’s disastrous run trying to lead this country.
acuity.explanation: Bates takes up one strand of Williams' speech — her argument that government decisions are loading debt on to households — and does something with it, turning the cost-of-debt point back on the previous Labour government's borrowing. But he swaps her subject (household and consumer debt) for Crown debt without engaging her actual causal claim, and the remainder of the turn is prepared material (the merger jibes, the delivery list) that would have been delivered whatever she had said. Partial engagement that is pointable, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that’s pushing more and more personal debt on to people and household debt and consumer debt" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: When we talk about the attendance management plan, one of the points that the Green Party member made was about the plan should include how the school will respond to underlying causes of student absences. Yes, that is important because we do want to know why students are not attending school.
acuity.explanation: She names the specific provision Menéndez March attacked — the requirement that attendance plans address underlying causes of absence — and does something with it: she accepts the clause he objected to and defends it on different grounds (diagnosis rather than schools fixing poverty), citing the select committee clarification. The passage would have to change if the preceding speaker had raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "we’re asking schools to then show how they will respond to these underlying causes, and not actually take any responsibility"

acuity.statement: The member, the Green Party member who spoke before me, instead of supporting that, he was actually providing excuses for students to not attend school.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of his argument — that material hardship drives non-attendance — and recasts it as excuse-making before returning to prepared material about attitudes and attendance being "a must". You can point at what is engaged, but she characterises the argument rather than engaging its reasoning, so this sits in the partial band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "child poverty plays a huge role in attendance"

acuity.statement: They want stronger schools, clearer pathways, and real opportunity for their children. That’s what the schools should be focusing on to ensure that every child learns, progresses, and succeeds, and this bill is about lifting student achievement, improving attendance, and making sure that every young New Zealander gets the best possible start in life.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed critique of the bill's university free-speech provisions with entirely prepared electorate material on schools and student achievement. It engages no part of the preceding argument, and would have been word-for-word identical whatever Hernandez had said; it stays above 0.0 only because it is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is trying to fix a problem that’s not even a problem in the first place" — Francisco Hernandez. Nothing: Hernandez argued the bill's free-speech provisions are evidence-free overreach into university autonomy, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: As colleagues have already pointed out, the only example—the only example—that the Minister could come up with, when asked at select committee, was of the notorious incident of Don Brash, I think, being denied the opportunity to give a Hobson’s Pledge speech at Massey University.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the preceding Green speech — the Minister's select committee answer on how many speakers were actually restricted — and does something with it, qualifying the "zero" by naming the single Don Brash/Massey instance and adding the regulatory impact statement's own admission of limited evidence. It is partial rather than full engagement: the rest of the speech is prepared material on academic freedom versus free speech that is indifferent to what preceded it, and it does not engage the immediately preceding National turn at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In the select committee stage, I asked questions of the Minister about how many universities in 2024 had actually restricted speakers from their campuses. The Minister’s answer was zero." — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: It must be difficult being on the Opposition benches today, as we put this piece of legislation through the House this afternoon. I have 72 schools across the mighty Whanganui electorate, and to teachers and principals and parents and students it's pretty simple: they go to school to learn.
acuity.explanation: Names the Opposition but engages no content of Twyford's argument about academic freedom, the regulatory impact statement or university autonomy; a mere reference plus prepared praise for the bill's school provisions sits at the bottom of the band, lifted off 0.0 only because it concerns the bill being debated.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Using the law, as this bill will, to force our universities to bend the knee to the State through these provisions sets, I think, a very unfortunate precedent." — Phil Twyford. Nothing: Twyford argued the bill's free-speech provisions are an unevidenced State intrusion on university autonomy, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Speech is not harm. This is where you’re flawed.
acuity.explanation: Williams had just explained that a university denied Don Brash a platform because it judged the speech would harm the institution's role as a forum. Court's interjection goes straight at the load-bearing premise of that account — that speech can constitute harm — and denies it. It is thin, and it does not develop the point, so it falls short of 1.0, but the engagement is squarely with the content just uttered rather than with the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "that was a call that the university made because they thought it would harm the overall ability of that university to be able to be that kind of forum that New Zealanders expect"

acuity.statement: The thing that should be fine, Simon Court, is for academics to take a stand. When, earlier in the debate, you said “The academics should just get elected then if they want to take public positions”, that betrays any of the arguments that you have made around promoting fair speech and free speech.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Court's intervention and his earlier stated position, quotes it, and draws out its consequence — that on his logic only elected members may hold public positions, which contradicts his own free-speech case. The speech would have had to be different had Court said something else, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because it asserts the contradiction rather than working through the reasoning behind it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "Speech is not harm. This is where you’re flawed."

acuity.statement: This is another piece of legislation that proves and shows why National is more trusted in education compared to that lot these days, and so I commend this bill.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed speech arguing the bill limits institutional academic freedom, imports a culture war, and cross-subsidises international students with domestic fees. None of that is taken up — not the Don Brash example, not the fee change, not the union notice provisions. The remark is about the matter under debate (the bill, education), which keeps it off 0.0, but it would have been word-for-word identical whatever the preceding speaker had argued. The gesture at "that lot" names a target without engaging any claim, which the rubric treats as unresponsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued the bill prevents universities themselves from taking institutional positions and lets the Minister cross-subsidise international students with domestic fees, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: Just to acknowledge, at the top of my contribution, that the member Cameron Brewer took only 25 seconds to claim to be more trusted in education but was unable to make an argument longer than 30 seconds to convince, which would suggest to me it’s not an argument he’s confident in and neither is it an argument he’s prepared to make on the record in the House. Just a spurious claim.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the single claim Brewer actually made — that National is more trusted in education — and does something with it: observes that it arrived unsupported and infers a lack of confidence in it. That is engagement with what was just said, and the remark could not have been made had Brewer spoken differently. It sits short of 1.0 because it attacks the absence of argument rather than the proposition's merits, and because the speaker then turns to prepared material on school boards; in fairness, Brewer supplied little content to rebut.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "why National is more trusted in education compared to that lot these days"

acuity.statement: So that was the opinion of the Free Speech Union, who claim authorship for large parts of the bill and who received a resounding “Hear, hear” from ACT Party member Simon Court in the House, so you can give that submission the kudos that those clues might deserve.
acuity.explanation: Court put a direct challenge — explain why the Free Speech Union's submission is wrong. The reply does not address the submission's substance at all; it repeats Court's own words back and uses his endorsement as a discrediting marker. That is the "mere reference" pattern the rubric puts in the 0.1-0.3 band: the previous turn is quoted in order to pivot away from it. It stays above 0.1 because it is at least on the free-speech provisions under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "Hear, hear. Tell us why that’s wrong."

acuity.statement: I have sat here and listened to about seven speeches from the other sides, and do you know what? I have not heard—I have not heard—about lifting the educational achievements of our children, and that is absolutely shameful.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Reuben Davidson, who argued the free-expression provisions are unnecessary because academic freedom is already protected in the Education Act and the Bill of Rights, citing Paul Rishworth KC and the Tertiary Education Union. Campbell gestures at the preceding speeches only to say what they did not mention, then delivers prepared material on achievement, attendance and the Government's focus. He engages no part of Davidson's argument — the speech would be identical whatever the opposition speakers had said — but it is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued "It addresses issues that do not need a new Act; they are already covered in existing regulation or law" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The committee reported back that, actually, diverse opinions should be expressed in a respectful manner, consistent with any statutes made by a university. What we heard from Labour and the Greens is their contention that hearing different opinions is akin to some kind of violence.
acuity.explanation: Court announces he is rebutting the opposition's free-expression objections and does take up that strand, citing the select committee's report-back on respectful expression. But he answers a characterisation of the Labour/Green position (that hearing different opinions is dangerous) rather than the specific claim made in the preceding turn — that the experts told the committee there was no evidence universities are limiting free speech and existing law already covers it. He then moves to prepared material about Don Brash and ACT's role. Partial engagement with one strand: you can point at what is engaged, but not at the preceding claim itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "there was a lack of evidence that universities were limiting free speech" — Court engages the free-expression objection generally but not this evidential claim.

acuity.statement: I know why that is: it’s because the promise that the National Government sold last election—to reintroduce regional autonomy for polytechnics—this bill does not achieve that. It may give people the right to think that suddenly they have regional decision-making again, but what does that mean if you only have half of what you had?
acuity.explanation: Takes the central claim of the immediately preceding speech — that the bill restores local decision-making to polytechnics and their communities — and disputes it directly, arguing the restored autonomy is nominal because only half the institution remains. He also engages the form of Simmonds' speech (the long list of thanks) and turns it against her. Delete Simmonds' turn and substitute a different argument and this speech would have to change. Scored on engagement only; the accuracy of the 'half' characterisation is a veracity question and the combativeness is not an acuity penalty.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "restore local decision-making to polytechnics and their communities which support regional development"

acuity.statement: This bill is not going to fix it. Where have you been?
acuity.explanation: Halbert breaks off his prepared argument to take up Simon Court's interjection directly, and the words would be different had Court said something else — so this is genuine engagement, not prepared material. But it engages only by flat contradiction: he negates the assertion and then turns to the interjector rather than giving any reason why the bill will not fix the problem, or tying the denial back to the financial-viability case he was making. One strand taken up, nothing done with it, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill's going to fix it, Shanan." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: The decision of merging polytechnics was a disastrous decision, and just listening to the Labour member and the Green member there, it felt like they have finally woken up. They have realised that there were issues with the vocational education and training system, but when they were in Government they didn’t realise that they didn’t ask those kind of questions.
acuity.explanation: She names the preceding speakers and gestures at the fact they raised problems with the VET system, but engages none of the content of Hernandez's argument — no response on consent, Treasury's viability advice, the exit mechanism or representation. The passage pivots immediately to the previous Government's record and would read identically whatever Hernandez had said. A reference is not engagement, so this sits in the low band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez argued that the federation is forced on polytechs without community or institutional consent and that Treasury advised viability would be the same or worse, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The second change that I want to highlight here is about industry skills boards’ functions and duties. The original legislation said that they must act in a manner that contributes to an education system that honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relations. Now, we need to look at the core function of industry skills boards and we need to ensure that industry skills boards are able to deliver on those core functions—that is, to plan for workforce needs, set and maintain skill standards and qualifications, and other things. So when we see these kind of things in the legislation we think they are quite irrelevant. They are actually unnecessary and are distractions and that’s why that has been changed as well, to say that it has regard to the needs of Māori and other population groups as identified in the tertiary education strategy.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one strand of the preceding speech — the dilution of the Te Tiriti and Māori-representation provisions, which Hernandez named as a loss — and supplies a reason for it, identifying the exact wording removed and what replaced it. But it is framed as prepared highlighting of select committee changes rather than a rebuttal: it does not dispute his characterisation or answer his wider case on consent, exit clauses and viability. Partial engagement with a pointable strand, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the stripping down and watering down of the Te Tiriti clauses and the requirements for Māori representation, which is another loss in the bill" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: The independence that we’re hearing in terms of regionalisation and giving the rangatiratanga back to the communities—well, there’s a good number of staff that have their jobs on the line right now in NorthTec. They are support services; they are the admin staff; they are the marketing staff; the pastoral support people that, apparently, some of members in the House reckon we need more of—their jobs are on the line; even student voice—the coordinators of student advocacy events and tautoko for students—their jobs on the line too.
acuity.explanation: Takes Foster's two specific claims — that regional polytechs like NorthTec are getting extra support, and that they need extra pastoral care — and turns both against him with the concrete counter that it is precisely the pastoral support, admin and student-voice roles at NorthTec that are being cut. The speech would have to change if Foster had argued something else; it also answers his jibe that the Greens had not been listening. Scored on engagement only, not on whether the claim is true or well-evidenced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "so there is an extra need not only for extra resource or maybe hybrid models but also for extra pastoral care" (and his claim that NorthTec's far-flung areas "need extra support and that is being acknowledged there as well")

acuity.statement: I appreciate the opportunity to tautoko the work that the Minister has done in bringing regional polytechnics back to the regions. Our own of the Universal College of Learning (UCOL) in Whanganui is a really positive step for our region.
acuity.explanation: Prepared praise on the right subject: it is about regional governance of polytechnics, so not wholly off-debate, but it engages no part of the preceding critique about consultation or job cuts. The words would be identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon argued immediately before that NorthTec staff face job losses before Christmas and that iwi in Te Tai Tokerau were never consulted on the changes, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: Now, the steps taken in this bill, the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, do not do anything for the growth of jobs in our creative economy. This bill does not even see that our creative economy exists.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the merits of the bill — but entirely indifferent to what preceded it. The regional-governance and industry-skills-board arguments made by the two previous speakers are left untouched, and this material (Haeata, the game developers conference, the WeCreate submission) reads as prepared for delivery in any slot in the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates had just argued that regional influence on UCOL's governance is "a really positive step for our region", and Andy Foster that the bill strengthens regional responsiveness and industry alignment; this statement engages neither and opens a separate line about the creative economy

acuity.statement: Carl Bates, you’ll find they are no longer required to consider emerging technologies. I don’t know if you’ve been keeping up. I don’t know if you’ve been keeping up, but artificial intelligence is moving at great speed—at great speed—and ISBs are no longer required to consider emerging technologies. That seems beyond bizarre.
acuity.explanation: Takes Bates' interjected challenge head-on and supplies a reason why the removed requirement matters (the pace of AI and emerging technology), naming the interjector and answering his question rather than ignoring it. Not a full 1.0 because he answers about ISBs rather than the polytechnics Bates asked about, and partly repeats his own prepared line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why did polytechnics need to worry about any of this?" — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: I rise to give a short call on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill. I say one thing: look north. Look north over the Brynderwyns; look up to the NorthTec and you will see that we are going to have great vocational education available to the people of Northland. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: On the subject under debate — vocational education — but engages no part of the preceding speech. The call would be word-for-word identical whatever Davidson had argued; it is a prepared regional endorsement ending in a commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Reuben Davidson argued at length that the bill removes requirements for industry skills boards to consider Māori and underserved groups, emerging technologies and the changing nature of work, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: There remain a number of questions—as my colleague Shanan Halbert has pointed out earlier in this debate—that remain; that create a large amount of uncertainty for those in the industry as well as students, many students who are already engaged in studies at these institutions.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the debate as a whole — the committee of the whole House stage, and a colleague's earlier questions — but engages nothing in the immediately preceding turn, which asserted the bill will deliver good vocational education in Northland. The material is prepared submission-based criticism on the right subject, so it sits at the top of the unengaged band rather than being a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "look up to the NorthTec and you will see that we are going to have great vocational education available to the people of Northland" — Grant McCallum. She does not take up McCallum's claim; she gestures only at the debate's prior course and a colleague's earlier points.

acuity.statement: It’s a great honour to rise and speak about this wonderful bill. Here we are correcting another failure of the former Labour Government, the centralisation of polytechnics—what a disaster.
acuity.explanation: Prepared praise for the bill immediately after a detailed, submission-based critique, engaging none of it — not the costs question, not the equity-funding point, not the claim that only 11 percent of submitters fully supported the changes. It is at least about the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters set out submitters' concerns about transition costs, funding clarity for industry skills boards and impacts on disabled students, and this statement does not take any of them up.

acuity.statement: I mean, he said, “no cost benefit analysis” and it was a financial disaster. Well, that’s exactly what we had with Te Pūkenga.
acuity.explanation: Smith picks up the specific charge Twyford had just made — that no cost-benefit analysis supports the new model — and does something with it, redirecting it at Te Pūkenga and supplying a concrete counter-example (Marlborough/Nelson: $23m in, $11.7m out). That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding turn, and the speech would have had to change had Twyford argued something else. But it is partial: he never addresses whether a cost-benefit analysis exists for this bill, which was the actual claim, and after the counter-example he drops into prepared peroration ("This is a great day for New Zealand") that engages nothing. Scored on engagement alone — the opening "projection" jibe and the tu-quoque structure of the inference are matters for other attributes and are not allowed to move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We still haven’t seen a cost-benefit analysis that would justify the policy design and the architecture of the system that the Minister has chosen." — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: It seems to me that Ms Williams brings up a couple of major areas of focus. One is in terms of the intended or expected outcome of 13,000 new units over a 10-year period, as she has quite rightly outlined. That was the advice. It’s not a number that I can particularly vouch for.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific 13,000-unit figure Williams asked about and does something with it — identifies it as official advice, declines to vouch for it, and then addresses her follow-on concern about council capacity via development contributions and the rating base. The answer would be different had she asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Can the Minister give the committee a sense of how that number is predicted?"

acuity.statement: Yes, it’s slightly larger, but, in fact, the relatively risky areas are those wet areas, so-called—kitchenettes and bathrooms—and particular provision’s been made to mitigate the risk associated with those. We don’t think there’ll be much additional risk of latent defects as a result of that change which we made along the way to increase the footprint.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the officials' latent-defects point Williams raised, locating the risk in wet areas and explaining why the extra 10 square metres is not where defect risk sits. He does not answer the monitoring half of her question, which keeps it short of a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "officials raised with the committee the part of their advice around the number of latent or undetected building defects that might increase because of the increasing size from 60 square meters to 70 square meters"

acuity.statement: Just a quick question, based on the remark that the Minister made: what do you see as the other trade-offs between increasing the housing supply and potential trade-offs to safety?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the trade-off framing the Minister had just used and presses it into a new area — safety — rather than restating prepared material. The question only makes sense as a follow-on from Penk's immediately preceding remark.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "we thought it was a reasonable trade-off to have the extra housing capacity as compared with all the strain and cost associated with, for example, greenfield developments"

acuity.statement: I should say that the building code standards still remain applicable, but the relevant qualified trade professionals—for example, licensed building practitioners, registered plumbers, drain layers, electricians, and so on—will be conducting the work and certifying it. That’s the main sort of trade-off, and we think it’s a reasonable one in terms of a relatively low restructure, in conjunction with those persons who should be able to vouch that there work complies with the code.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific safety trade-off Hernandez asked about — consent oversight replaced by trade-professional certification — and justifies it, so the reply is squarely shaped by the question. Marked down because Hernandez also asked whether 'non-consented small stand-alone dwelling' differs from the Building Act definition, and that strand is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "what do you see as the other trade-offs between increasing the housing supply and potential trade-offs to safety?"

acuity.statement: Just really briefly, the passionate advocacy on behalf of Uncle Kelly, I think it’s really sensible, compelling. These matters can and will be addressed through resource management changes that essentially sit alongside the bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific proposition Williams advanced — that the marae amendment is in scope and should be adopted today — accepts the merit of her example, and answers it on substance by locating the fix in resource management changes alongside the bill rather than in this bill. acuity.statement: I thank the member Cameron Luxton for his comments. I don’t disagree that we need to be more enabling, and of course that’s the whole animating spirit of this legislation. I hope that that is interpreted and applied as such, but, of course, as always, there’s a balance.

The reply is shaped by Luxton's framing of a council 'culture of saying no' and would read differently against a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "What I really want to hear is that this is an enabling piece of legislation that will get housing built" and his question on whether councils are expected to be enabling under section 71.

acuity.statement: I know the intent of the bill is to make this a seamless process, but in the new requirement of the memorandum to accompany the project information memorandum, if a council identifies that where the proposed granny flat is going to be built is an area where when there is severe weather it does flood and that there are flow issues, and the person is informed of that and they do it anyway, it makes the issue worse for those around them. Now, surely that is something that we do want to prevent, even though we want to see in the majority of cases that these things are seamless.
acuity.explanation: Draws out the consequence of the answer just given: if the safeguard is merely information to an informed decision-maker, what happens when the builder proceeds anyway and worsens flooding for neighbours. He takes the Minister's own mechanism and tests it, having also expressly picked up Luxton's clause 11 line of questioning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "the provision of natural hazard information is a good way to ensure that those who are responsible will not inadvertently make a mistake" — his account of where the bill strikes the balance.

acuity.statement: Of course, we’re not in the business as a Government of directing either lenders or insurers of a private nature on what they must or can or should ensure. They’ll make those decisions themselves. Obviously, case by case, it may vary according to their appetite for risk. However, I would say there are tens of thousands—probably hundreds of thousands—of dwellings in this country that do not have consents at the moment. They were built before the current regime. Typically, that’s not a reason for them not to be insured.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question put — whether insurers and banks will lend on unconsented granny flats — and answers it on its own terms: the Government does not direct private lenders, and the existing stock of unconsented dwellings is nonetheless insured. The reply would be different had Williams asked something else. Short of 1.0 because the narrower sub-question (whether lending is available against the new asset itself rather than against existing equity) is not reached.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "can people get lending for these granny flats, or do they have to borrow against their existing dwelling, if they have equity available?"

acuity.statement: First of all, the question about a small stand-alone dwelling being a definition in the Building Act, could the Minister point us to that section in the Building Act? How do we have that as a definition?
acuity.explanation: Squarely within the same committee debate on the same bill and addressed to the same Minister, which is the gesture at the debate that lifts it off the floor, but it engages no part of the preceding exchange on insurance and lending. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk spoke about whether insurers and banks would lend on dwellings built under the new regime, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it opens a separate line on the statutory definition.

acuity.statement: The reason that we have the regime include only existing properties—residential, zoned, yes, but also with an existing dwelling is that by saying that there must already be a dwelling there, we’re confident and comfortable. We know the characteristics of the land and also we’re not requiring extra infrastructure such as pipeline infrastructure and water services and so on to be added new as though we’re a Greenfield development or a site that had not those connections already. So it will be literally possible to tap into those existing pipelines and infrastructure provision for all the services you’d expect for a residential property, precisely because there’s already a dwelling on site.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question asked, giving the rationale for the existing-dwelling requirement (known land characteristics, no new infrastructure provision needed), and goes on to concede that Luxton's alternative — bare residential-zoned land — is a reasonable argument but outside the bill's scope. Entirely determined by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "why would a small stand-alone dwelling necessarily need to be on a site with an existing—what would you call it?—major dwelling?"

Did they need to have the information that it even existed? They did not. So, to some extent, would you agree that this legislation has, by replacing the 30-square-metre rule, in a limited number of cases, without extra plumbing and things like that, actually made it more difficult?

That is engaging the content just supplied, not merely the topic; it falls short of 1.0 because the surrounding material on her own cabin and the Wairarapa electorate is prepared and independent of what Penk said.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "“less than 70 square metres” in terms of floor area, and “has a single storey only.”" — the Schedule 1A characteristics he had just read out

Even though it’s similar in philosophy, as the member has quite rightly pointed out, nevertheless it’s different because this will be able to be used in a proper residential sense, not only for a so-called sleep out, but also with shower or bathroom facilities and also a kitchen area; it could be more independent.

It later concedes her off-grid point as "a fair point" and that he was "overly simplistic". The speech is wholly shaped by the question it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "would you agree that this legislation has, by replacing the 30-square-metre rule, in a limited number of cases, without extra plumbing and things like that, actually made it more difficult?"

acuity.statement: To the first point that Mr McAnulty makes, it’s fair question about consistency of application by building consent authorities, or BCAs. acuity.explanation: Takes up McAnulty's specific question about inconsistent council decision-making by name, concedes it is a fair point, and answers it with a named mechanism (council function consolidation for regional consistency) before going on to address his second strand on insurance. The speech would be materially different had McAnulty asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "if you can explain what considerations were done to avoid inconsistent application of this across the country from councils, that would be useful"

acuity.statement: That is where a council says, “Yep, look, the level that floods are expected to get to is X and therefore you can build there, but you must build at a level where the floor levels or the areas which you don’t want to get flooded are higher than the expected flood areas”. So I’d be interested in your comment on that because that might alleviate some of the concerns which are being raised.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "district plans shouldn’t consent or allow the provision of housing in areas that are flood prone and otherwise unsuitable for residential development"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "district plans shouldn’t consent or allow the provision of housing in areas that are flood prone"

acuity.explanation: Explicitly sets aside prepared questions to go back to the answer just given, restates the Minister's council-discretion mechanism accurately, and asks for the trigger and the landowner's options after it — while also locating Luxton's concern about it.
