acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the bill's Schedule 1A requirements) and plainly attentive to the committee, but it engages no part of the hazard/height argument immediately preceding; the gesture at the debate is a reference to an earlier member's marae question rather than to the arguments just made. acuity.subject: speaker

That gives the council a chance for involvement without being required to give a consent in most cases.

The answer would be different had she raised a different scenario.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "it would certainly put pressure on that infrastructure. Is there any wriggle room or was there any thinking around that?"

acuity.statement: As for the suggestion—and I think I understand the point that “non-consented works” might sound as though there’s some sort of value judgment being created, but, nevertheless, it’s just a straightforward statement of fact. It is possible for works not to be consented but not to be illegal, given that they didn’t require a consent, and I think that we’ve covered that well enough.
acuity.explanation: Engages the second strand McLellan put to him — the proposed insertion of "but otherwise legal" and whether "non-consented" reads as a judgment — restates her concern accurately and rejects it on the ground that the term is descriptive and the legality point already covered. Squarely on her claim rather than a pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "any thoughts about the harshness of just the term “non-consent” and any potential ramifications of that"

acuity.statement: He didn’t say it was fine, but he said that would be within permissive, as Todd Stephenson says. He also said, for the Hansard, that it is permissive. But what we are intending to do here is not that. That is not the expectation of Parliament here.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just explained why a development contribution would be returned where a development does not proceed ("if the development doesn't take place, then the development contribution which is used to support funding infrastructure isn't needed anymore for that purpose"), and this statement does not take that up — it opens a fresh line of questioning on clauses 52-54.

acuity.statement: In terms of question that Arena Williams asks regarding the failure of a trusted professional to provide what they are required to do under the Act, I would say—and as a lawyer who’s self-sure, hopefully—I recognise that there are a number of different categories of obligation. One is statutory, in terms of what’s required under the Act; another would be contractual, as between the building professional, which is some other tradie or a builder in the sense of a Licensed Building Practitioner; and also occupational.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific claim just put to him — that the bill leaves no recourse when compliance certificates are not handed over — and answers it on its own terms by naming the three categories of obligation (statutory, contractual, occupational) through which a defaulting professional can be pursued, which is a direct rebuttal of the 'no obvious end point' premise. The reply would have had to be different had Williams raised a different objection. Marked short of 1.0 only because it addresses the recourse question while leaving her second question, about whether 'policy' is broad enough in clause 59(2), untouched in this passage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "there is no obvious recourse, there is no sort of obvious end point if these certificates of compliance or certificates of safety are not handed over in that period... Are they enforceable? What recourse do the homeowners have here?"

acuity.statement: Whilst I’m not going to argue with her about the previous suggestion where she said about it being “House Sized”, I particularly like the one that says “Extra House in the Backyard”. I like that one in particular because, from my perspective, it lends itself a little bit more closely to the type of scenario that I’m envisioning, insofar as it is an extra house in the backyard and, by definition, therefore is one that’s drawing on the utility that’s already existing, it’s drawing on the infrastructure that’s already there.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "my amendment changing it to the “Building and Construction (Big Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill” is better"

acuity.statement: Much has been covered of his career, but I would point out that his first election as Leader of the Opposition, in 1987, was a catastrophic loss, and yet he carried on.

acuity.statement: These people who suffered in State care ended up in prison because of what they suffered, and yet now have legislation that is ignoring the call for creating a new, independent survivor-centred system as per the recommendations of the royal commission and, instead, uses a thing called “presumption” because the Government is worried about disrepute on its system that it has established, and that all we’re doing is entrenching the existing Crown-based system that protected itself.
acuity.explanation: Follows Prime's turn and takes up its two central strands — that the royal commission recommended redress for survivors with criminal records, and that it recommended a single independent scheme rather than a continuation of the Crown's own. Lyndon develops the prison-to-care link with named survivor testimony and names the 'presumption' mechanism Prime had attacked, and later explicitly nods to the preceding argument ('it should be independent, as we've already heard'). Not a rebuttal and much of it is clearly prepared, so it sits short of 1.0, but the engagement is pointable and specific.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "The royal commission explicitly recommended that all survivors be able to access redress, including those in prison or with a criminal record."

acuity.statement: Listening to the Opposition’s comments about the point around the bill about those that have committed serious violent offences, sexual violence offences, and done more than five years—look, I unreservedly accept the fact that those that suffered that kind of abuse may have gone on to commit crimes; 100 percent agree. But it does not do the victims of those crimes any justice to know that, potentially, their abuser may now be getting financial compensation.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific argument made by the two preceding speakers — that abuse in care leads to offending and so survivors with convictions should not be presumptively excluded — concedes its factual premise outright, then disputes the conclusion by introducing the interests of the victims of those later offences. The speech would be materially different had Prime and Lyndon not made the care-to-prison causation argument, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only; the merits of the inference and the delicacy of the exchange belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "These people who suffered in State care ended up in prison because of what they suffered" (and Willow-Jean Prime's claim that presumptively excluding survivors with criminal records is discriminatory)

acuity.statement: The system broke them long before any laws were broken. Many of those convictions were born out of the trauma inflicted by the very institutions this bill now seeks to protect. To deny redress on that basis is to deny responsibility for the harm that the Crown and the Church caused in the first place.
acuity.explanation: Costello's preceding turn rested on the premise that some claimants are themselves serious offenders and so warrant a different framework. Ferris takes that exact premise up and inverts its causal direction — the convictions are products of the State's own abuse, so using them as a filter is the Crown evading responsibility. He engages the strand that carries Costello's case rather than merely naming her, and the passage would have to change if the preceding argument had been different. It falls short of 1.0 because he does not engage the mechanism Costello described (the 'slightly different framework' with its own process) and moves on to prepared Te Pāti Māori material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We cannot ignore the fact that, in amongst those victims, there are those who have caused victimhood." — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: Instead, these survivors can apply to have their financial redress considered by an independent decision maker. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The abuser has no grounds to criminalise the survivors for their abuse—the State's abuse—and deny them redress." — Tākuta Ferris

The bill implements the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State and Faith-Based Care to, firstly, recognise the experience as a person of abuse in care, and, secondly, to offer an alternative to litigation to be able to provide that redress. I commend this bill to the House.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson argued 'the royal commission recommended that survivors who are in prison or have a criminal record should not be unduly penalised' and that this bill does penalise them; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: 'The bill implements the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State and Faith-Based Care'

acuity.statement: It has been quite annoying, actually, to sit over here on this side and listen to some of the claims that have been coming from across the House, because I think that there will be abuse survivors who are listening at home and some of them may actually be upset to hear the claims from the other side—which are untrue—that this is going to mean that some people aren’t going to be able to get access to redress. Actually, this doesn’t apply to most people. Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
acuity.explanation: Directly identifies the specific claim made in the preceding turn — that the bill presumes the excluded group has no right to redress — labels it untrue, and does something with it: supplies a scope figure (5 to 6 percent of claimants) and asserts an alternative independent process remains available. If White had made a different argument on the same topic this speech would have to change, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only; whether the figure is right is a veracity question and the 'clowns' remark is a civility one, and neither is allowed to move this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: 'a presumption that people in this situation have no right to redress'

acuity.statement: I’m not quite sure how to take that previous speech where we have all been categorised into a box and it was saying that this side of the House doesn’t care about the harm that was caused to victims of abuse in State care. I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
acuity.explanation: Chhour follows Davidson's third-reading speech and takes up one specific strand of it — Davidson's charge that the Government benches dismissed survivors' harm and told the House not to be emotive — disputing that characterisation of her side. The engagement is real and pointable, so this is not merely prepared material on the topic. But she does not rebut the substance (the use-of-force clause, the 28-of-138 recommendations figure, the redress hierarchy) and instead dismisses the speech as "rubbish", which engages the framing rather than the argument. That puts it in the middle band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "What is that bench saying about the level of recognition that violence deserves?"

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker, Karen Chhour, outlined, this is not only a legislative response. There is a lot of work and policy that is being driven.
acuity.explanation: Costello follows Chhour in the same third-reading debate and explicitly picks up one strand of her argument — that the response to the royal commission is not confined to legislation and that much is happening operationally — and endorses and extends it, adding why the legislative part took as long as it did ("It is a difficult process to pass legislation"). But that is a single strand of a long speech by Chhour, and the rest of Costello's contribution is prepared New Zealand First material on the bill being a starting point that would have read much the same whoever preceded her, so this is partial engagement rather than a reply shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Not everything requires legislation, but what it does require is level-headed conversations around what is best for those who have been through the system" — Karen Chhour

acuity.statement: Then with the report with the 138 recommendations, how we can see the recommendations coming into full effect? This is incremental change, and we believe it is not moving fast enough to bring about some reconciliation for those who have been harmed at the hands of the Crown by those who were meant to look after them.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the immediately preceding speech — that the bill falls short of the Whanaketia report's 138 recommendations and is not transformational — and restates it as 'incremental change' that is too slow. But it engages the topic rather than any specific claim Ngarewa-Packer made (she listed particular missed recommendations: disestablishing Oranga Tamariki, a survivor-led authority, banning strip-searches), and the rest of the turn is prepared material: the prison correlation statistic and Mr NK's story. The speech would largely survive a different opposition argument on the same subject, so a partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "that was to adopt the 138 recommendations of the Whanaketia report—138 recommendations"

acuity.statement: As the Government made it very clear from the very outset, it is to implement urgent reforms or broader responses to the commission’s 138 recommendations—they’re still in development. There’s a lot more work to come.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the central charge of both preceding speeches — that the bill omits the 138 recommendations — by asserting the bill was only ever scoped as urgent reform with the broader response still being developed. That is engaging the content of the claim rather than merely referencing it. It stops short of 1.0 because it rebuts the framing in general terms and does not take up any of the specific omissions either member itemised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "What the bill misses is what the survivors asked for." (also Hūhana Lyndon: "how we can see the recommendations coming into full effect?")

acuity.statement: I'm just going to give one example of things I think the Opposition has been irresponsible about: that is making some changes around the Oranga Tamariki Act, around de-escalation and the use of reasonable force for young people in that environment. Unfortunately, I have heard endless critique against that.
acuity.explanation: Picks out a specific provision the preceding opposition speech attacked — the use-of-force and de-escalation changes to the Oranga Tamariki Act — names it, and argues against the critique, which is evidence of having listened to what was actually said. Not 1.0 because he answers it with a personal anecdote about being assaulted in Invercargill Prison by an adult prisoner rather than engaging the reasoning about children in State care; the weakness of that inference belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "They wanted to ban strip-searches of children, stop the treating of trauma with trauma."

acuity.statement: Alongside the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill, this bill, the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, is a further step—another step forward in the Crown’s response to the royal commission’s findings, making an important start to changes to improve the safety and wellbeing of children, young people, and adults in care. The bill aims to protect people in State care today and into the future.
acuity.explanation: Garcia follows a substantive turn by Willie Jackson that argued the bill is a missed opportunity, that experts and survivors were ignored, that the use of force contradicts trauma-informed practice, and that the Treaty should have been built into the legislation. Garcia takes up none of it — no rebuttal, no concession, no figure, no correction. The speech is prepared framing of the bill plus a commendation, and would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. It is at least on the matter under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson said "But the bill does not go far enough and, in many ways, is a missed opportunity." and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: As my colleague the Hon Willie Jackson said, we will support this bill not because it’s enough, but because we want it to be enough.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe picks up a specific strand of Jackson's preceding contribution — the reasoning behind Labour's qualified support — restates it accurately and then extends it with his own point that "redress" will mean something for some survivors and nothing for others. That is a pointable engagement with the content of a prior turn, not a mere name-check. But it is agreement-extension rather than engagement with the argument of the immediately preceding speaker (Garcia's "step forward" framing), and the rest of the turn is prepared material on the topic, so it sits at partial engagement rather than the top of the scale. Scored on engagement only: whether his reluctant-support position is well reasoned or well evidenced is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We also don’t resile from supporting this bill today—obviously, with reservations, because we want so much more to be done." — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: In this third reading of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, we are not doing everything in one hit. As other speakers have talked about, we are doing many things in the background. We cannot do it all at once.
acuity.explanation: Weenink answers the central objection the two preceding opposition speakers made — that the bill does not go far enough — by meeting it directly with the claim that the work is staged and cannot all be done at once. The speech would have to change if the prior turns had not pressed the sufficiency point, which puts it above prepared-material-on-topic. It is only partial, though: she engages the general "not enough" theme rather than the specific claims put (survivors who will qualify for no redress at all, the exclusion of survivors from the process, the Treaty consultation point), and the remainder of the turn is generic reflection. Whether "we are doing many things in the background" is true or substantiated is a veracity and specificity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we will support this bill not because it’s enough, but because we want it to be enough" — Adrian Rurawhe

acuity.statement: I think that that really reflects the intent, knowing that it is a bit of fast-track medicine legislation and we don’t know what the amendments will be, and that’s a pity, because we could have had that interrogation by submitters if it had been received earlier.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific grievance Leary had just raised — that a substantive amendment is arriving after the select committee stage so submitters cannot be heard on it — and endorses it from the Greens' side with reference to the submitters her committee did hear. It is a genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding turn rather than the whole of it, and the rest of her speech is prepared material on Northland primary care that would have been delivered whatever Leary had said, so it sits around the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "there will be an amendment dropped at the committee of the whole House—without the ability for submitters to submit"

acuity.statement: It's with great pleasure I rise to support the Medicines Amendment Bill, and it's great to hear the other parties in the House so far are supporting this bill as well.
acuity.explanation: Notes that other parties are supporting the bill but engages none of the content of the two preceding turns: Leary's objection to the unforeshadowed advertising amendment, her concern about the Medicines Classification Committee becoming a ministerial appointment, and Lyndon's workforce-capacity questions all go unanswered. This is a bare reference to the fact of support rather than engagement with what was argued, and the remainder of the speech is generic prepared advocacy for the bill that would read identically had either member said something else. Scored in the band for prepared material that is at least on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I don't understand why this was not foreshadowed. I don't understand why it has to be introduced now as a fast-track rather than earlier in the piece so that submitters could express their opinions."

acuity.statement: A couple of things that really excite me about this: firstly, the expansion of nurse practitioners to be able to prescribe unapproved medicines where that’s appropriate to their scope of practice. That was very painful, I’d have to say, as a GP, to have to prescribe medicines just because they were unavailable—that made it a section 29.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows a substantive critique of the bill's scope and engages none of it. Her speech is prepared praise on the correct subject (the same bill), offering a GP's account of section 29 prescribing and nurse practitioners — material Walters never mentioned. Deleting Walters' turn and substituting any other argument on the bill would not change a word of it, so it sits in the unresponsive band; 0.1 rather than 0.3 because there is not even a gesture at the preceding argument, only commendation of the Minister and the committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued that "while this certainly does address one of the issues, it doesn't address the second leg of the issues" — Pharmac funding, prescription charges and the ministerial appointments process — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The key limitations remain. It still requires a sponsor application. Companies need to see a commercial reason to apply in the first place, and the biggest barrier to that is going to be and will remain Pharmac funding, not necessarily Medsafe approval times.
acuity.explanation: Takes the preceding speaker's central claim — that the rule of two will reduce approval times and so improve access — and does something with it: concedes the mechanism while locating the binding constraint elsewhere (sponsor incentive and Pharmac funding rather than Medsafe timelines). The argument would have to be rewritten if Marcroft had made a different case for the bill, so engagement is specific rather than merely topical.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "This will reduce the time it takes to get the medicines approved."

acuity.statement: It's unfortunate that on something that has wide support of the House, the member who just resumed her seat, Tracey McLellan, couldn't but help herself to take the opportunity to spread misinformation about what this Government is doing in the health sector. I find it is my obligation to remind the House that this Government is putting more money into health than ever before—ever before.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — the claim that patients are worse off under this Government — but answers it with a funding-input counterclaim rather than taking up the access claim actually made, then moves to prepared material listing the recognised jurisdictions. Partial engagement: pointable, but aimed at the topic rather than the specific assertion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "we know that, certainly under this Government's watch, it's become harder than ever to see a doctor or a nurse or a specialist"

acuity.statement: I want to start my call by talking about the things that are really good about this bill and that we very much support. I think the swift approval process makes a lot of sense, and it looks like the Health Committee did some very good work making sure that there are a great deal of standards around that situation, and I like the amendment with regard to nurse practitioners and prescribers.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the prescriber-scope strand raised earlier in the debate and supplies supporting detail on training hours, which is a real if partial engagement. It does not take up anything in the immediately preceding turn (the funding/misinformation exchange), and the bulk of the speech is prepared material on select committee process, so it sits at partial rather than full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "whether they're nurse practitioners, or, as we included, pharmacist prescribers, will be able to work at top of scope. Because they have really good clinical skill levels"

acuity.statement: The purpose of this bill—the Medicines Amendment Bill, in its second reading—is to speed up the approval of, and access to, medicines for patients in need in New Zealand. Therefore, it is good for patients in need; it is good for the families of the patients. We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Restates the bill's purpose and commends it. The words would be identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said; no part of any preceding argument — the Pharmac funding limitation, the committee-appointment objection, or the unseen amendment — is engaged. It is at least about the bill under debate, which keeps it off the floor of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued that a substantial new amendment about medical conferences should have been available for select committee scrutiny, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: As he said, in 2011 there was an exacting test to establish customary marine title, and we all accept that there is such a thing. That has, unfortunately, been undermined by a number of court decisions, including, obviously, the Edwards decision. So we will be supporting this because it does restore what Parliament intended, it does restore an exacting test, and I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn immediately before was a detailed argument that new section 106 reverses the burden of proof and therefore does NOT restore the original Act's intent. Stephenson asserts the opposite conclusion ('it does restore what Parliament intended') but engages none of the reasoning offered against it — no mention of section 106, the presumption of non-extinguishment, or 'substantial interruption'. He attributes the case to the Minister rather than taking up the critique just delivered, and the speech would read identically whatever Abel had argued. On-topic prepared party position with a gesture at the matter under debate, so the bottom band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "it is founded on a tissue of myths that, somehow, the Minister's bill restores the intent of the original Act. I've just outlined that, in new section 106, it clearly does not"

acuity.statement: It revoked the foreshore and seabed legislation and bought in an opportunity where the Māori Party at the time recognised there would be discrete, limited numbers of claims. The Prime Minister of the time, John Key, made it very clear that there would be very limited numbers of successful claims because of the need to prove uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one strand of Abel's central argument — what the 2011 Act originally intended about proof — and answers it directly, claiming the original scheme always required applicants to prove uninterrupted title since 1840, which if true undercuts his reversal-of-burden claim. It engages the intent question rather than the specific statutory mechanism (s 106(3)'s presumption of non-extinguishment) that Abel actually relied on, and then returns to prepared New Zealand First material about equal citizenship and claims over the whole coastline. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the burden of proof, as per the original Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (MACA Act), should fall on those trying to prove extinguishment. This reverses the burden of proof."

acuity.statement: Right now, people are burning the bill on the coastline, affirming that they are there now and they will be there tomorrow because we are not going anywhere. And Tākuta is right, for it just raises another generation of Māori with issues. Māori got issues.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon explicitly takes up Ferris's central argument from the immediately preceding turn — that the legislation condemns future generations of Māori to continued fighting — and endorses and restates it in her own terms. But she does little more with it than affirm it before returning to her own prepared material on extinguishment and the courts, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal or development of the reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tākuta Ferris: "condemning our children, our tamariki, to needless, endless, perpetual fighting"

acuity.statement: It is Parliament, not the courts, that makes the laws of this land, and this bill makes clearer what “exclusive use and occupation” means, and it strengthens the requirement for physical evidence of exclusive use. It delivers on a coalition agreement commitment with New Zealand First, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: The opening clause answers one strand of the preceding Opposition turns — Lyndon's complaint that the Government is changing the rules because the courts had begun recognising customary rights — by asserting Parliament's primacy over the courts. Beyond that single glance, the remainder is a generic commendation of the bill that would read identically whatever had been argued before it, so the engagement is real but shallow.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "you change the goal posts because the courts start endorsing us"

acuity.statement: This bill is not, as the Government insists, a tidy clarification of an old law; it is an incredibly blunt instrument that tears at the very foundation of justice, up-ends our court processes, and undermines a hard-fought relationship between te iwi Māori and the Crown. We are told that it will restore Parliament’s original intention, but in truth, it rewrites that intention, it narrows it, and it applies new rules retrospectively, overturning the work of the courts and reopening wounds.
acuity.explanation: Andersen takes the framing offered by the immediately preceding speaker — that the bill merely 'makes clearer' an existing test and restores Parliament's role against the courts — and contests it directly: not a clarification but a rewriting, not a restoration of intention but a narrowing of it applied retrospectively. The speech would have to be rephrased had the previous speaker defended the bill on different grounds, which is what responsiveness looks like; it falls short of 1.0 because it rebuts the characterisation rather than the specific statutory wording Bates cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "this bill makes clearer what “exclusive use and occupation” means"

acuity.statement: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill restores to clarify to the Act that ensures Parliament’s original intent is followed. The amendments align the recognition of the customary marine titles more closely with tikanga and address concerns addressed by the courts.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, detailed critique from Ginny Andersen covering the rewritten evidential test, the retrospective application to 24 July 2024, the ignored official advice and the Waitangi Tribunal finding. This speech takes up none of it — it asserts the bill's purpose in general terms and commends it. It is on the subject of the bill, so not a 0.0, but it would have been word-for-word identical whatever Andersen had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued the bill 'raises the bar to make it absolutely impossible for iwi and hapū to meet the requirements' and that 'It applies the new test back to 24 July 2024', and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: Now, after 20-plus years—and here we thought we had an agreement binding by the laws of this land—here we are. The self-proclaimed party of property rights, trampling all over the rights guaranteed to us, even though they were our rights before the courts were even established in this land.
acuity.explanation: Partly engages the preceding claim. Nancy Lu asserted the bill merely restores Parliament's original intent and aligns title with tikanga; this reply contests that framing directly — the rights were settled by binding agreement, and predate the courts, so the bill is not a restoration but an override. But most of the turn is prepared iwi narrative and a challenge aimed at the Minister rather than at Lu's argument, so it engages one strand and returns to its own material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: 'restores to clarify to the Act that ensures Parliament’s original intent is followed'

acuity.statement: The bill seeks to restore the clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, it seeks to protect property rights that foster legal clarity, and it seeks to reduce legal disputes and ambiguity.
acuity.explanation: Follows Cushla Tangaere-Manuel's speech, which disputed precisely these grounds — that there is no evidence of the public being denied access, that a binding settlement is being overridden, and that the bill will destroy rather than build trust. This turn restates the bill's stated aims and commends it without touching any of that. On topic, but indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued 'this Government have no evidence that public have been denied access' and that a 20-year negotiated agreement is being trampled, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: As the last speaker on this third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, I don’t want to drag it out, but I do want to just put on record that Ngāti Porou has got a carve-out from this Act and their takutai moana is not going to be affected by this bill.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows a long, substantive speech by Jackson built on the Waitangi Tribunal's findings, Finlayson's criticism and the Law Society's opposition, and engages none of it. She offers one narrow, prepared point of her own — the Ngāti Porou carve-out — which is at least about the bill under debate, so it is not wholly off-topic, but the speech would be word-for-word identical had Jackson made a different argument. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band: 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the carve-out point does gesture at the debate's subject (which iwi this bill affects) rather than being generic commendation alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "The Crown has breached the principle of tino rangatiratanga by exercising kāwanatanga over Māori rights and interests in te takutai moana" — and his quotation of Chris Finlayson that "These amendments do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them." This statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The people in Mt Roskill actually face daily congestion and long travelling times. It impacts families and businesses alike. This actually drags down our productivity. So this bill encourages travel outside the peak hours, which can ease congestion and improve travel reliability.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows a substantive turn by Twyford in the same debate, so he is eligible. His speech is squarely on the matter under debate — time of use charging and congestion — and it even lands on the same productivity point Twyford made, but it engages no part of Twyford's reasoning: nothing about induced demand, Spaghetti Junction, the declining petrol excise base, the zoning-reform pairing, or the claimed 10-15 percent traffic shift, and no reference to the previous speaker at all. The speech would read word-for-word the same had any other member spoken before him on this bill, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is tightly tied to the specific mechanism of this bill (charging outside peak hours) rather than being generic transport material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued that 'cities of scale that are growing cannot build their way out of congestion' and that congestion 'is dragging down our productivity in the city', and this statement does not take up either argument — it restates the congestion/productivity theme as prepared electorate material.

acuity.statement: It’s been a pleasure to be part of the select committee process. In summary, we’ve made four broad changes that, I think, address the key issues that came from the select committee submissions.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows a substantive turn by Wade-Brown that both supported the bill and made three specific criticisms (no low-emission zones, air-pollution costs ignored, unbalanced board governance). His speech is squarely on the matter under debate — the same bill — and gestures at the chamber by crediting Andy Foster for the New York example, but it engages none of her claims: it is a prepared select-committee summary of the four changes plus overseas statistics. The one point of contact, that revenue must be ploughed back into public transport, is framed as answering submitters rather than her, and the speech would read identically had she said something quite different. That puts it at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown argued the bill ignores the evidence on low-emission zones and the ~$10 billion in social costs from vehicle air pollution, and that Waka Kotahi and the three Wairarapa mayors give the board a lopsided governance weighting — this statement takes up neither, and instead reports the committee's four changes as prepared material.

acuity.statement: Look, in the interest of brevity, I was really pleased to see in the introduction, mechanisms for a scheme board to adjust to charges, manage scheme operations, etc., because I remember going to the Mount and paying the gold coin at the little toll booth with the people in the booth. They eventually did rid of that, and I knew that was probably a bit of an antiquated system. Then, they moved to digital, but I’d never pay my bills on time, and I’d always get a snail mail $8 bill with a $5 admin fee, and I was just like, “If I knew about the bill, I wouldn’t have the admin fee.” So there’s definitely room to improve, I think, but I’m all for this process, so I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a substantive turn by Leary that made specific arguments about fare safeguards, equity, council partnership and ministerial control under clause 4. His contribution engages none of those strands: it is a personal anecdote about toll-booth and digital tolling admin fees, offered in support of the scheme board provisions, and would read word-for-word the same whatever Leary had said. It stays on the matter under debate (the bill's charging mechanisms), so it sits in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at zero, but there is no engagement with the preceding argument to point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued the congestion charge needs public transport safeguards (restoring half-price fares, buses and trains) and that new section 65C(2) allows too much ministerial control, and this statement does not take up either point

acuity.statement: We are supporting this bill, as has been traversed well. There are a number of reasons why congestion charging is a great idea: the environmental benefits, the revenue generation beyond what we already have, the sustainable infrastructure, improved cities, and, of course, economic efficiency, which is what we’re all about on this side of the House: economic growth and efficiency. London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Russell on the same bill, which made a specific argument (congestion charging only works where viable public transport alternatives exist, and the hypothecation of revenue should favour public transport). Kirkpatrick engages none of it: she recites a prepared list of generic benefits and two overseas examples. The speech would read identically whatever Russell had said, though it is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell argued 'we need to have those good public transport networks to make congestion charging really work', that revenue should be directed to public transport, and rejected the claim that money collected in Mount Roskill should be spent in Mount Roskill — and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Eleven pages; no detail. I think there was one figure. Oh, and there was a photo of Chris Hipkins—that’s meant to fill in the blanks of the detail of this future fund. They don’t even understand how Temasek works: when you buy assets, you then sell assets for ones that have better returns.
acuity.explanation: Upston follows Hipkins and takes up the specific policy he had just advanced — the future fund built on the existing asset base — rather than only his topic: she attacks the document's length and absence of costings and disputes the Temasek model the fund rests on, arguing that an asset-based sovereign fund buys and sells assets, which cuts directly against Hipkins's contrast between Labour investing in assets and the Government selling them. The speech would have had to change if he had announced something else. Not 1.0 because a large part of the engagement is characterisation ('stupid, illiterate nonsense', 'flop') rather than argument, and the second half (roads of national significance, crime targets, welfare sanctions, inflation) is prepared material that engages nothing he said. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the Temasek inference belongs to Rigor and the personal 'illiterate' jibe to Civility, neither of which moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins, immediately preceding turn: "A future fund that uses our existing asset base to grow opportunities and grow jobs for New Zealand—a Government that backs innovation here in New Zealand is what the Labour Party stands for."

acuity.statement: To the member’s point: you can say that Labour copied you—however, the problem is, I couldn’t find any detail on your particular policy to be able to copy.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Patterson's specific charge that Labour's Future Fund is a rip-off of New Zealand First's own announced sovereign wealth fund and turns it directly back on him: she concedes the framing ('you can say that Labour copied you') and then rebuts it on the ground that no detail of the NZ First policy exists to copy, before pivoting to welcoming his stated support. The speech could not have been delivered without Patterson's preceding claim; substitute a different argument and this passage would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a pale, cheap rip-off of our $100 billion sovereign wealth fund, announced some 14 months ago" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: I wanted to reflect on the birth of Te Pāti Māori. Recently, having seen the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill and what it was, to crossing the floor.

acuity.statement: Easier doesn't necessarily mean accessible. One of the barriers—which I accept that this bill removes a lot of barriers and that's why we support it—when building on whenua Māori, especially, there are enough barriers you have to go through.

The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument. Short of 1.0 because much of the surrounding material is prepared constituency narrative rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "currently, it’s far too hard to build a home in New Zealand. Even the simplest dwellings are tied up in red tape" — Hamish Campbell

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued the sub-$250,000 price tag is still out of reach for many whānau and warned of health and safety risks from makeshift papa kāinga without infrastructure, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Let’s just be really clear about what the legislation is intending to do here: it’s about strengthening the criminal law, and providing a means to better hold people accountable for undertaking foreign interference.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Phil Twyford that argued the bill must balance protection against the McCarthyite risk of suppressing dissent, and named Chinese Government operatives, the United Front Work Department and transnational repression as the test case. Rutherford takes up none of it: no response on the balance question, no engagement with the China examples, no comment on the Green Party concerns Twyford acknowledged. The 'let's just be really clear' framing is a faint gesture at the debate he follows — an implicit refocus on the bill's mechanics — but it engages no part of the preceding argument, and the speech would read identically whatever Twyford had said. Prepared committee material on the right subject, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford spoke about the balance between countering covert foreign interference and avoiding a McCarthyite crackdown on dissent, and about Chinese Government operatives and transnational repression in the Chinese New Zealand community, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Mr Twyford spoke to some of the well-documented and publicly known instances where there have been cases where it has been proven that there has been foreign interference, but also cases where it has been proven that it doesn’t quite meet that threshold, or in fact that we might have had a rogue or a person acting on their own.
acuity.explanation: Takes up a specific strand of Twyford's preceding speech — the publicised activities he said 'would qualify as foreign interference' — and does something with it, adding the qualification that other instances have been shown not to meet the threshold or to involve a lone actor. That is engagement with the content of the claim, not a mere name-check, and it bears on the definitional threshold question the bill turns on. It falls short of 1.0 because the qualification is asserted rather than developed against Twyford's actual examples, and the rest of the turn returns to prepared material on the threat assessment, cyber attacks and the day's strike action.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: 'the quite well publicised activities of operatives from the Chinese Government who have been engaging in, I think, foreign interference, in the way that it is defined in this bill—their activities would qualify as foreign interference.'

acuity.statement: Labour’s position is that while the bill is a necessary step, it must be accompanied by strong safeguards, resourcing, and oversight to ensure that it protects our democracy not only from foreign interference but also from overreach at home.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows a substantive (if brief) turn by Kirkpatrick commending the bill as making the criminal law fit for purpose and better equipping agencies. Her speech is prepared party-position material on the same bill: it sets out Labour's support-with-safeguards line and would read word-for-word the same whatever Kirkpatrick had said. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the bill's scope, the foreign interference offence, allegiance and espionage liability — so it is not a 0.0, but no strand of the preceding argument is engaged, rebutted or built on, which puts it in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dana Kirkpatrick said "this legislation will help to ensure that our criminal law is fit for purpose to address what we see as a harmful activity and will better equip the relevant agencies to hold people to account", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’m appreciative of the of the 49 oral submitters and 705 submitters, in general, that expressed their concerns. Some of those concerns were listened to—well, they were all listened to—but there were some amendments that were made as a result.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle immediately follows Andersen's extended case that the bill needs stronger safeguards against overreach, framed around what came out of select committee. Saying submitters' concerns were all listened to and produced amendments is a gesture at that strand, but it is only a gesture: it supplies no amendment, answers none of Andersen's specific worries (prosecution thresholds, judicial oversight, dual citizens, chilling effects on diaspora communities), and the substance of the remark would be unchanged had a different member spoken before. A thematic glance rather than engagement with the content, so 0.3 is the top of that band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "But we will continue to push for stronger safeguards, resourcing, and oversight to ensure the defence of democracy never comes at the cost of democracy itself."

acuity.statement: We also do have some concerns around the $468 - filing fee. We consider that this may well be a barrier to some people bringing legitimate claims before the tribunal. There are legitimate reasons for a filing fee to cover the costs associated with a dispute resolution process; however, $468 is high to many New Zealanders right now—significantly higher than the $260 filing fees for the District Court and there is no associated fees waiver on the basis of hardship; there is such a waiver for the District Court.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith pre-empted the barrier-to-justice objection in his third reading speech, arguing the new $468 tier only looks like a barrier and is small relative to claim value, and that the tribunal remains cheaper than the District Court. Andersen takes up exactly that defence and contests it on its own ground: she compares the $468 against the $260 District Court filing fee (reversing his cheaper-than-the-District-Court comparison) and points to the hardship waiver that exists in the District Court but not here. The speech would have to change if Goldsmith had not made that defence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Whilst the new fee tier might seem a barrier to justice, it's a very small portion of the potential value of the claim. Disputes Tribunal proceedings remain significantly cheaper than bringing proceedings to the District Courts"

acuity.statement: Labour also notes the recommendation of the Rules Committee last year, which suggested an even higher cap to $70,000 or even $100,000 by consent, along with clearer appeal rights. We support the Government taking steps in that direction and we will continue to encourage a broader look at just how our civil justice system serves ordinary New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith justified $60,000 as the sensible new boundary given accumulated inflation. Andersen engages that choice of figure in part — accepting the direction but setting it against the Rules Committee's higher recommendation — without directly contesting his inflation reasoning, and then moves on to prepared material about the wider civil justice system. A pointable partial engagement with the specific number he defended.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "There has been a lot of inflation and we think it makes sense to extend that boundary further to $60,000"

acuity.statement: In essence, what this bill does is it amends the Disputes Tribunal Act by increasing the jurisdiction of the disputes tribunal from $30,000 to $60,000. This will mean that people who cannot afford to take a claim to the District Court or who choose not to because the associated fee exceeds the value of the claim would indeed be able to access the disputes tribunal for those claims. The bill also introduces a filing fee of $468 for those claims over $30,000.
acuity.explanation: This restates, almost in the minister's own terms, the description of the bill he had just given — the jurisdiction change, the people who cannot afford the District Court, the new fee tier. Repeating a previous speaker's content back is not engaging it: nothing is disputed, qualified or developed, and the passage would read identically whatever argument Goldsmith had made for the bill. On the right subject, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "The bill enhances access to justice for people who either cannot afford to take a claim to the District Court or choose not to because the associated fees would exceed the value of the claim they're pursuing."

acuity.statement: While people can now make a claim up to $60,000, there is no sort of, I guess, empirical evidence other than the assumption that we have seen throughout the committee stage that suggests there's any rationale behind the idea that people making claims above $30,000 naturally have nearly $500 that they're able to pay for this in the first place, which is one of the reasons why the Greens supported the Labour Party's amendment from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb in terms of having an opportunity to look at the hardship situations where the filing fee could be waived.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Andersen had just pressed — that the doubled filing fee is prohibitive and that Labour's suggested change was not adopted — and does something with it: names the Webb amendment the Greens backed, and identifies the unevidenced assumption (that a $30,000-plus claimant can front $468) that the fee setting rests on. Not a full 1.0 because much of the surrounding material is prepared committee-stage recapitulation rather than a reply to Andersen's reasoning as such.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "We still believe that that filing fee is too high and it will be prohibitive to those who want to pursue justice through the courts."

acuity.statement: ACT in Government is about actually fixing what matters, and this is an important bill that adds to everything that the Government and ACT is doing to support our court system and ensure people actually have access to justice.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed critique of the filing fee and the absence of a waiver mechanism and engages none of it; the speech would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before. It is at least on the bill under debate, which keeps it above 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued at length that doubling the filing fee to $468 with no hardship waiver blocks access to justice for claimants above $30,000, and this statement does not take it up — it asserts the bill ensures access to justice without engaging the fee objection at all.

acuity.statement: There are mechanisms under which the fees can be addressed through existing processes within the justice system. Therefore, the bill is very effective and will deliver exactly what it’s aiming to do, which is access to justice.
acuity.explanation: Directly meets the one load-bearing objection of the preceding speech — that the disputes tribunal lacks the hardship-waiver mechanism the District Court has — by asserting that existing processes already address fees. Engagement is real and pointable, but it is a bare assertion that names no mechanism and does not touch the phase-in or reimbursement-timing points, so partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "we are disappointed that the Government hasn't decided to consider that particular option of a waiver"

acuity.statement: As it did at the first reading and as it did during the select committee process, the Labour Party supports this bill at the second reading. This is a timely bill and, actually, it’s a very collaborative one. It builds on work that was under way under the previous Government that was picked up and carried on with by the current Government, and it is much-needed legislation.
acuity.explanation: Russell takes up one strand of Doocey's opening speech — his claim about cross-party collaboration and his framing of the bill as a delivery of the Government's own Electrify NZ mandate — by confirming Labour's support through all stages and correcting the provenance of the bill as work begun under the previous Government. That engagement is real and pointable, but it addresses the collaboration/origin framing rather than any of the bill's substantive provisions Doocey set out, and the turn then moves to prepared material on wind conditions and Taranaki.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "we’re criticised quite a bit that we’re not as collaborative or cross-party, working on bills like this" (and his prediction that "what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space")

acuity.statement: It is my pleasure to talk to the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill, and, as you might expect, the Green Party does support renewables. However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand Russell had just developed — BlueFloat abandoning its New Zealand wind plans because of the Taranaki seabed mining proposal — and does something with it, attributing the loss to fast-track and the writing-in of Trans-Tasman Resources. It engages one strand rather than Russell's wider competing-uses/Amendment Paper argument, and then moves to prepared Green Party framing, so it sits in the partial-engagement band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: You can’t build wind turbines without minerals.
acuity.explanation: The interjection fastens directly onto the claim Willis had made one clause earlier — that the focus should be the renewables transition rather than extracting more minerals — and presses the dependency of turbines on mined material against it. Short, but squarely aimed at the content of the argument it follows rather than at the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: Oh, that’s an interesting comment—you can’t build wind turbines without minerals. Actually, there is so much potential. We see in Scandinavia wooden wind turbine towers.
acuity.explanation: Repeats Court's claim and then answers its substance with a counter-example — wooden turbine towers in Scandinavia — plus circularity in the wind sector. The reply would be different had the interjection been different, which is the strongest evidence of engagement; the quibble that keeps it off a flat 1.0 is that the counter-example addresses substitution in towers rather than the mineral content of turbines as a whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You can’t build wind turbines without minerals" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Look, that’s why we’ve called on them to not reverse the oil and gas ban, because one of the things we need to do is give confidence to people who want to invest in New Zealand. I do believe we are giving them confidence in the House today, because the House is sending a very strong signal that you should invest in offshore renewables and that you should invest in renewable energy policy, because that is something that every single political party in this House does agree on.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez names Arbuckle's argument — that energy security and a stable transition require investor confidence — accepts the premise, and turns it to the opposite conclusion: that confidence means not reversing the oil and gas ban. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument, since it is built on inverting Arbuckle's own investor-confidence reasoning rather than merely rebutting the bill's topic. Not a full 1.0 because he engages the principle rather than any specific claim or figure, and then returns to prepared material on this Government's wider energy record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "But importantly, we need investor confidence, and I think the previous speaker again touched on that with the oil and gas ban."

acuity.statement: We’ve heard it today: these foreign investors need certainty and they need to make sure that the economics can work, because this is a tough sector to actually make viable for commercial businesses, in terms of setting up the infrastructure, setting up the pipeline that’s required to connect to the grid, and then making sure that the commercials actually work. So we did make a number of changes to the bill around the feasibility permits, changing the permitting regime, making sure that the decommissioning obligations were clarified, including being clear about what infrastructure is excluded as part of the feasibility and commission regime, and also dealing with the competing offshore renewable energy applications and how that was to be addressed.
acuity.explanation: Bidois takes up two of the strands Bennett actually raised — investor certainty (Bennett's BlueFloat withdrawal point) and the decommissioning obligations Bennett said he would probe at committee stage — and answers them by reporting what the select committee changed. It is partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal: he does not take up Bennett's specific concerns about permit-hoarding or the Tūī field precedent, and the passage largely returns to prepared select-committee material. His opening characterisation of Bennett as raising "so many 'if', 'but', and 'what' questions" is a mere reference and does not lift the score; the engagement with certainty and decommissioning does.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Glen Bennett: "we’ve had BlueFloat who were there, who were in the mix and have pulled out, have moved on, because of the challenges of getting the regime and getting the settings right" and his questions on "the obligations regarding decommissioning and financial security"

acuity.statement: I wanted to let some of the members opposite, whose characterisation of our position on this side of the House is not entirely accurate, know that we were early starters on this issue and it’s taken a long while for this current Government to get to this date. It was already in train when we were in Government.
acuity.explanation: This directly engages the claim Bidois had just made — that Bennett's speech made you doubt Labour supported the bill — and disputes it on the substance by asserting Labour began the work in government and that the delay is the current Government's. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had not characterised the Opposition's position that way; the rebuttal is squarely aimed at that characterisation rather than at the topic in general. Short of 1.0 because he contests the characterisation without engaging Bidois's specific content on permitting or decommissioning changes, and part of the turn addresses a member (Mr Court) whose contribution is not in this stretch of debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "this is a good bill, but you wouldn’t get that, necessarily, from listening to the speech of the previous member, Glen Bennett"

acuity.statement: I’m really pleased that the House had the opportunity to hear from my colleague the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe to correct the record, really, that this is a piece of work that Labour started because of our commitment to unlocking the potential for renewables, and it has been picked up by this Government, which we are really happy about.
acuity.explanation: Brewer's immediately preceding turn claimed the regime as National's own delivery ("the National Party are committed to this as part of our Electrify New Zealand... we are now delivering"). Leary takes up that credit claim and contests the provenance of the bill, so she is engaging one strand of what was just said rather than ignoring it. But she routes the correction through an earlier Labour speaker rather than engaging Brewer's reasoning, and the rest of the turn moves on to prepared caveats about the regime — partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are now delivering" — Cameron Brewer, claiming the bill as part of National's Electrify New Zealand programme

acuity.statement: The actual size of this, as the member has just spoken—it’s talked up to maybe even up to two gigawatts of generation capability here. Now, if we think about the current stored generating capacity of all the wind turbines in New Zealand at the moment just being north of one gigawatt, this one farm can be actually immense—huge, in fact.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure Leary had just supplied (up to 1 GW) and does something with it: revises the ceiling upward to two gigawatts and then sets it against total existing NZ wind capacity to draw out the consequence for the generation mix. The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had given a different number or a different comparison, which is the deciding test. Not a 1.0 only because it extends rather than contests her claim and does not resolve the discrepancy between 1 GW and 2 GW.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "generate up to 1 gigawatt of electricity, and that’s equal to 1 billion watts" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: It’s recently been established that you can easily have gigawatts of wind generation and the potential of the Trans-Tasman Resources proposal existing together.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific caveat Leary had just entered — that the regime must clarify how offshore wind will be reconciled with mining in the same maritime space — by naming the seabed mining proposal at issue and asserting the Bight has room for both. This is engagement with the content of the preceding claim, not a mere reference to the speaker. Scored below 1.0 because the rebuttal asserts the coexistence finding without pointing at the work establishing it, so it only partly discharges the point put to him (that is an Acuity-neutral weakness of support, scored here only insofar as it leaves her compliance-and-conflict strand half-answered).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "clarifying how maritime space conflicts will be managed in terms of mining and aquaculture" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: The reason I’d be interested in the Minister making a contribution is just for the public to understand what this is about, because I very much think this bill is about this place and about the people in this place and how it’s funded, and the goings-on.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe had just made two specific points — that the four Acts are rightly consolidated, and that the Official Information Act was ruled out of scope despite submissions asking for it. Bennett takes up neither; he returns to clause 3 and asks the Minister to explain the bill's purpose from scratch. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate (Part 1, the purpose clause) and gestures at the committee stage having begun, which earns the top of the unresponsive band, but it would read identically had Rurawhe said something else about Part 1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe spoke about bringing the four Acts into one statute and about the Official Information Act being deemed out of scope, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: This is an important piece of legislation and probably one that’s a little bit overdue and one that past Governments and past parliaments have looked at. It brings together the Clerk of the House of Representatives Act 1988, the Parliamentary Service Act 2000, the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Act 2013, and the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014.
acuity.explanation: Bennett asked for exactly this: a contribution from the Minister so the public could understand what the bill is about. Bishop supplies it directly — naming the four Acts, then explaining why a single statute matters to the rule of law, which Acts are out of date, and what changes to the funding model follow. The speech is shaped by the request that preceded it; had Bennett instead pressed on the Official Information Act exclusion, this answer would have had to be different. Marked down slightly from 1.0 because it addresses the broad request rather than engaging any contested claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The reason I’d be interested in the Minister making a contribution is just for the public to understand what this is about" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: As the Minister has pointed out, the Parliamentary Privilege Act 2014—some submitters thought that it should stand alone. The committee decided that it could be included in there and that it stood on its own mana, basically, in my words. So I just wanted to make that comment at the committee of the whole House.
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just explained that the Parliamentary Privilege Act was enacted in response to court judgments and would now be folded into the Parliament Act. Rurawhe picks up that specific strand and adds what Bishop could not — that submitters argued the Act should remain standalone and that the select committee he chaired concluded otherwise. It supplies the committee's reasoning on the very provision just described, so the contribution is contingent on what preceded it; it extends rather than contests, which keeps it just below the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So the Parliamentary Privilege Act was a response to court judgments and now it’s going to be a part of the Parliament Act." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: For the record, I thought it was Part 7 as well. I just want to recognise that in Part 3, the Speaker of the House will have the ability to delegate certain functions to the Deputy Speaker, which I think is wholly appropriate, in the same way that a Minister who also has responsibilities under the Public Finance Act, say, might delegate something to an Associate Minister or an under-secretary.
acuity.explanation: The opening sentence does take up something pointable from the preceding turn — Bishop's admission that he had misread the Hipkins amendment as relating to Part 7 — and corroborates it. But that was an aside, not an argument, and Bishop's substantive content (that the House cannot imprison for contempt, and the 1865 House of Commons powers in section 8) is not engaged at all; the rest of the turn moves to prepared material on Part 3 delegation. Partial engagement with a minor strand, so mid-low rather than bottom of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I mistakenly looked at the amendment and thought it was in relation to Part 7, so I thought we might have a bit of time, but it’s actually in relation to Part 2." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I just want to draw the Minister’s attention to clause 55. It talks about the Speaker controlling and administering the parliamentary precincts. It talks specifically about the powers that are vested in the Speaker, and then it kind of self-refers, in subclause (2), to subclause (1), but it’s pretty unclear about what the precincts mean.
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just asserted that the bill makes the meaning of 'parliamentary precincts' clear, with an indicative map in Schedule 2. Leary takes up that one strand — the clarity of 'precincts' — and disputes it for clause 55, but then moves to her own prepared line of questioning about staff, security and the press gallery rather than engaging his argument about flexibility to expand the grounds by resolution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it makes it clear that the “parliamentary precincts” in clause 53 are Parliament buildings"

acuity.statement: Hopefully I can be helpful on that particular question. It’s actually a question I asked at select committee. What we need to remember is that under the new set of rules and under this new legislation, which we’ll talk about in Part 7, there’s a clear monitoring role and reporting role and the direct reporting is with the CEO of Parliamentary Service. The Speaker of the House has overall authority but doesn’t actually carry it out himself or herself.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific question Leary had just put — whether the Speaker can direct security guards and staff — by supplying the mechanism: overall authority sits with the Speaker but operational direction runs through the Parliamentary Service CEO, at arm's length. The turn would be unrecognisable had Leary asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "is it the Minister’s view that the Speaker has authority and powers under this legislation to direct and control members of various workforces, such as security guards"

acuity.statement: Then the other thing I would say is that the Speaker has to act reasonably. Why do I say that? Well, there’s quite a long line of case law around this, most notably the Beggs case which has to do with protest and assembly on the forecourt.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Leary's specific worry that clause 55 confers power without clear boundaries and answers it on its own terms, naming the constraints — control of the House, a reasonableness duty grounded in case law about the forecourt, and section 3 of the Bill of Rights Act. Marked below 1.0 because he does not address her concrete example of an order to remove the press gallery.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "which really does confer an awful lot of power on the Speaker"

acuity.statement: I wonder if the Minister can indicate whether he is open-minded about looking at the devil in the detail about how that should happen, so that the reasonableness test—which, we know, is incredibly broad—is not the litmus test, but there is something a little bit more substantial, so that those delegations happen appropriately and everybody is clear about what the rules are and what they do and don’t need to do.
acuity.explanation: Seizes on the precise safeguard Bishop had just offered — that the Speaker must act reasonably — concedes it exists and then presses that its breadth makes it an inadequate litmus test, folding in Rurawhe's point about clear lines of delegation. The question only makes sense as a reply to what those two had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "the Speaker has to act reasonably"

acuity.statement: Well, I’m happy to have a look at it. The ship has sailed, somewhat, to be honest, because the committee has reported the bill back unanimously, and, as I understand it, there’s no Amendment Paper from the member in relation to that—but I’m happy to look at it in the future.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked — whether he is open-minded about tightening the delegation detail — gives a direct answer, and supplies his reasons for not acting now: a unanimous select committee report and no Amendment Paper from Leary.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "whether he is open-minded about looking at the devil in the detail about how that should happen"

acuity.statement: I’m advised it does not include contractors; it applies to people employed by Parliament. The member Glen Bennett makes a good point that this is a change, and it is largely to clarify the law and make sure we have a modern approach to parliamentary security.
acuity.explanation: Bennett asked two things: whether "security officer" is confined to Parliamentary Service employees or extends to contracted Armourguard-type services, and for an explanation of what the change does. Bishop answers the contractor question directly in his first clause, concedes Bennett's framing that this is a major change, and then supplies the explanation asked for (the Courts Security Act model, the enumerated powers, where they apply). The answer could not have been given to a different question; only the direct resolution of the contractor point rather than engagement with a competing argument keeps it off a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Or does that go beyond it to contracted Armourguard-type of services?" — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: I just have another question for the Leader of the House regarding this section. I’m looking at the bold part of clause 172A to about 175, and I think that’s to do with a definition of a “detected item”.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn was a substantive explanation of the new security powers, including seizure of items, so there was content to take up. Xu-Nan instead opens a fresh clause-reading question about "detected item" that is adjacent in subject matter but engages no part of what Bishop said — he does not test, accept or dispute any element of the answer.
