On-topic prepared questioning with a gesture at the same section: the 0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The bill gives parliamentary security officers statutory powers of consent, search, denial of entry, temporary seizure of specified items, and temporary detention." — Chris Bishop. The question is framed against the bill text rather than against anything in that answer.

acuity.statement: We know, as the Minister has pointed out, that the New Zealand Parliament provides more physical access to the public than many, many overseas parliaments, and we do not want to lose that. But its security arrangements are, really, way out of step with our international counterparts.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one specific strand of Bishop's answer — his comparison of New Zealand's unusually open Parliament with harder-to-enter overseas legislatures — expressly attributes it to him, accepts it, and then turns it against him by noting the security arrangements are also out of step internationally. That is genuine engagement with a named part of the preceding argument. It is partial rather than full: the bulk of her contribution is prepared material on training and post-incident support for security officers, which Bishop had not raised and which would have been delivered whatever he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We also need to make sure that Parliament is as accessible as possible." and the comparison with the House of Commons — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I’m thinking here about both the ability of the members of the public to protest in a strong way, but also security officers having clarity about what is reasonable grounds, because the Minister’s mentioned the safeguards in a retrospective element, which is annual reporting, and so on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific safeguard Bishop had just offered — the annual reporting duty under clause 190B — and argues it is retrospective and therefore no help to an officer making a split-second judgement, then presses the reasonableness test against the Speaker's powers. The question would have to be rewritten if Bishop had offered a different safeguard.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "clause 190B, the “Chief executive must report annually on the exercise of specified powers”" / "there are also checks and balances in place as well"

acuity.statement: The member makes good points, but if I could summarise what is reasonable, the answer is: it depends. That’s the beauty of the word “reasonable”, and it’s why it appears multiple times in the statute books and throughout the common law, because what is reasonable in the circumstances is fact specific, and it’s impossible, by definition almost, to give a definition.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the reasonableness-test strand of the question just put and answers it on its own terms — that the standard is fact-specific and cannot be defined in advance. Falls short of 1.0 because the second half of her question, the interplay with a Speaker's direction given outside a settled process, is not engaged here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I’d just like to get an understanding from the Minister about that reasonableness test. Should it be considered alone, or how does it interplay with the Speaker’s powers?"

acuity.statement: In relation to the other point the member makes, parliamentary service officers can exercise powers only in the parliamentary precinct, a place where select committees are meeting, electorate offices where the chief executive has authorised it. Beyond that place, police have jurisdiction and the necessary power.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the answer the preceding turn asked for: the geographic limits of a parliamentary security officer's powers, including the electorate-office case she raised, and who holds jurisdiction once a protest spills beyond the precinct. The reply is shaped by her question and would read differently had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "what is a test for adjacency—that is going to have practical implications when it comes to electorate offices?"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to add, on this section, that the committee considered a number of things. There was, as the bill was originally drafted, a procedure in there that required that when an object was removed from someone, they had to be detained. The committee decided that we wanted to give the security officers as many options as possible.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's answer on detected items and adds the select committee's reason for decoupling removal of an object from detention — real engagement with that part of the exchange, but it is supplementary committee background rather than a response to the argument in the turn immediately preceding, and the nod to the Minister's "reasonable" point does nothing with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "any item found by a parliamentary security officer during a search, the security officer can ask to examine it and determine such matters such as whether it may have been used for an offence"

acuity.statement: We seem to get nothing but excuses like the nonsense that the oil and gas ban has resulted in an energy crisis, or that burning fossil fuels is better than clean energy from wind and solar.
acuity.explanation: Willis follows a substantive turn by a different member on the same energy debate, so he is eligible. His contribution is squarely on the matter under debate (fossil gas versus renewables, electricity prices), but it engages no part of Russell's actual argument — not her LNG-depot objection, not her inflation/price figures, not her utility-versus-commodity framing. The speech would read identically had Russell made a different argument on the same topic; there is a gesture at the debate's subject but no engagement with its content, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "This is where I really disagree with part of what the Government is proposing to do in its energy strategy." — she argued specifically against a permanent LNG import facility and for treating power as a utility rather than a commodity; this statement does not take up either argument, and instead answers the Government's 'oil and gas ban' framing with prepared Green Party material on the same broad subject.

acuity.statement: There are three things that we need out of energy: we need cost—for it to be affordable—we need reliability, and we need sustainability; and sometimes, those things are in conflict, especially at the margin.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up one strand of the immediately preceding speech: Court's triad of what New Zealanders want from energy (reliability, affordability, certainty). Foster restates the criteria and does something modest with them — he adds that the objectives can conflict at the margin, which Court's framing had elided — before returning to prepared material attacking Labour's oil and gas ban. The engagement is pointable but partial: it answers the topic and the framing rather than any specific claim or figure of Court's, and most of the rest of the speech would have been delivered whatever Court had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what they want is reliability, they want affordability, and they want certainty" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Oh, there is some good news, Labour! I can say well done on the electric arc furnace, because that’s really good stuff.
acuity.explanation: Bennett interjects to claim Labour's GIDI Fund deserves the credit for the Glenbrook work Foster was praising. Foster takes that specific credit claim up directly, concedes the electric arc furnace to Labour, and then disputes the rest by turning to the gas-dependent rolling mill now at risk. The concession only exists because of what Bennett said, so the speech would have been different had the interjection been different — accept-part-dispute-the-rest engagement, short of 1.0 only because he concedes rather than contests the substance of the GIDI point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Thanks, Labour, for the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry (GIDI) Fund." — Glen Bennett

acuity.statement: Natural gas currently provides about 20 percent of our electricity generation, particularly during peak demand and dry years. It is the firming fuel that steps in when the wind doesn’t blow, the sun doesn’t shine, and the lakes are low.
acuity.explanation: A prepared set-piece ("I rise to speak on a matter of national significance") that is squarely on the matter under debate and shares Foster's firming theme, but engages no part of his actual argument: it neither accepts nor contests his capacity-factor figures, his consenting claim, or his call for deep geothermal, and instead substitutes gas as the firming fuel without reference to the geothermal case just made. Delete Foster's turn and substitute a different pro-gas or anti-gas argument and this speech is word-for-word identical. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is at least on the debate's subject, and 0.2 rather than 0.3 because there is no gesture at the preceding contribution at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued immediately before that geothermal runs at about 98 percent of capacity against solar's 16 percent and that short consents under Labour's water reform would have stopped geothermal plants being built — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I would like to hear, in this debate, some solutions, because what we heard from the last speaker, David MacLeod, who did largely read his speech, is that natural gas is our insurance policy. That was the key line we took out of that. That’s their plan: hoping to find natural gas.
acuity.explanation: She isolates MacLeod's own formulation, names him, and does something with it rather than merely referencing him: she treats the insurance-policy line as the sum of the Government's plan and draws out its consequence (a plan that depends on finding gas that has not been found), then puts a direct question back about how renewables investment will be incentivised if gentailer profits are baked into fossil fuels. The speech would have to change if MacLeod had argued differently. Not 1.0 because she characterises his claim and challenges it rather than engaging its reasoning or figures, and the jab about reading his speech engages nothing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Until we have more renewable generation and large-scale storage, natural gas is our insurance policy, a stabilising force in an increasingly complex energy system." — David MacLeod

acuity.statement: I stand by the work that Labour in Government did. In fact, I stand by the work that the Labour and New Zealand First Government did, when they stood up on the podium and announced the fact that there will be no more offshore permits issued.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick's turn immediately before attacked the previous Government's decision on coal and gas as "lazy thinking" and "energy thuggery" done with "no solution in hand". Bennett takes up exactly that decision — naming the offshore permits announcement, owning it, and arguing the onshore/offshore split got the balance about right because both oil-and-gas and environmental critics were angry. That is a direct defence of the specific measure just attacked, so the passage would read differently had Kirkpatrick criticised something else. It is only partial engagement, however: he does not answer the substantive charge that there was no replacement supply, and the surrounding speech (tourism, "100% Pure", Megan Woods' portfolio work) is prepared material that would stand unchanged whatever preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dana Kirkpatrick: "when the previous Government landed on this notion that we shouldn’t have coal and gas in this country and that we should wage a war on energy infrastructure like Marsden Point, they did it with no solution in hand"

acuity.statement: David Seymour has just made it clear to the House that he provided incorrect information, but he hasn’t done the second part of that, which is to discharge his responsibility for correcting incorrect information; it is to provide what the correct information actually is. So he has indicated that the Fire Service were disrupted more than once by having faulty equipment in responding to calls, but he hasn’t told us how many times.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of Seymour's withdrawal and identifies precisely what it implies and what it omits — that the number of breakdowns is now known to be more than one but has not been stated. The speech would be impossible if Seymour had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "I said I’d been advised that only one breakdown had delayed a fire truck arriving at a job... I’d like to withdraw that statement."

acuity.statement: Well, I’m sorry, but the Leader of the Opposition’s assertion is incorrect. You do have an obligation to address questions, which I did at the time, and to correct any incorrect information, which I have. There’s no further obligation.
acuity.explanation: Directly disputes the exact proposition just advanced — that the duty to correct carries a further duty to supply the correct figure — by naming the two obligations he accepts and denying a third. Squarely engaged rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "there is also an onus on them to provide the correct information"

acuity.statement: David Seymour sought leave to correct an answer, and on that basis, the House unanimously gave him leave to do so. He didn’t seek leave to withdraw information; he sought leave to correct information. He has not done that.
acuity.explanation: Engages Seymour's claim to have discharged his duty by drawing the distinction his reply rests on — withdrawing versus correcting — and applying it to the leave actually granted. Responsive to the specific reasoning just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "to correct any incorrect information, which I have. There’s no further obligation."

acuity.statement: I’ve been advised that a number is not currently available, so therefore it’s not possible to answer the question—which is what I’ve been trying to get through to the simple man over there this whole time.
acuity.explanation: Answers the conditional Hipkins put — whether he has been advised of the number and withheld it — by stating that no number is available, which is the fact the question turned on. Engagement is high even though the reply is wrapped in a personal jibe.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "If it, therefore, becomes clear that David Seymour has been advised what the number is and he has chosen not to give that information to the House"

acuity.statement: How is it fair that hard-working New Zealanders pay tax on every dollar they earn through income while the super wealthy passively accumulate more and more untaxed wealth without lifting a finger?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer's defence — that the income tax system is progressive — and turns it against itself, drawing the distinction between tax on earned income and untaxed accumulated wealth. The question is built on the reply just given rather than read off a list.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We have a progressive income tax system in New Zealand, and the more money you earn, the more tax you pay." — the Prime Minister's (Christopher Luxon's) immediately preceding answer

acuity.statement: So when does he expect his tax cuts and Public Service cuts to trickle down?
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand of the preceding answer that claims the Government's programme is repairing conditions for working New Zealanders, pressing it on timing. It does not take up any of the specific figures offered (84 percent, 7.3 percent, 12 rate rises), so it is a partial engagement with the topic rather than the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The consequence of all of that is that working and middle-income New Zealanders got incredibly hurt and damaged." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: What is more important to the Prime Minister: allowing the wealthiest to amass hundreds of millions in untaxed wealth or properly funding our hospitals, our schools, our emergency services, and our infrastructure?
acuity.explanation: Returns to prepared material on wealth taxation and public funding without engaging the list of indicators just offered as an answer to her own previous question. On the subject under debate, but indifferent to what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Christopher Luxon had just listed positive economic indicators ("We have job ads up. We have building consents up. We have exports up.") and this question does not take any of them up

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree with the assertion from his Minister, just then, that climate emissions are “mythical”?
acuity.explanation: Abandons prepared ground to seize a single word used seconds earlier by another member and put it to the Prime Minister. This question could not exist if the preceding turn had been worded differently — the clearest possible evidence of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the onerous obligation of reporting mythical climate emissions" — Shane Jones, in the supplementary immediately before

acuity.statement: On the matter of Government actions, can the Prime Minister confirm that, by exempting a substantial number of companies from the onerous obligation of reporting mythical climate emissions, our economy will be better off for it?
acuity.explanation: The opening phrase "On the matter of Government actions" is a hook rather than an engagement; the substance moves to climate reporting exemptions, a topic nobody in the preceding exchange had raised. Prepared material, loosely pinned to the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Christopher Luxon had just answered on redeploying "about $40 billion of inefficiency" into health funding, and this question does not take that up

acuity.statement: How many families have received the full $250 tax cut that was promised by this Government?
acuity.explanation: Moves to the next prepared supplementary on the same topic without touching the 1.9 million figure just put in front of her. On the matter under examination, but not responsive to the answer given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just said "But 1.9 million households were better off", and this question does not take that figure up

acuity.statement: If the cost of living relief is on its way, why are KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals the highest they have been, more than double what it was this time two years ago?
acuity.explanation: The conditional clause picks up the relief claim just made and sets evidence against it, but she does not engage the sliding-scale defence that was the actual substance of the answer. Half engagement, half prepared line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is able to reduce taxes rather than putting new taxes in front of them" — David Seymour's preceding answer about the sliding scale of relief

acuity.statement: Are families getting more, when 5,530 people made KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals in the month of September?
acuity.explanation: Echoes the claim just made — that New Zealanders have more money left over — and puts a counter-figure directly against it. It engages the conclusion of the answer rather than its reasoning about overseas factors and historic policy, so it falls short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "so that New Zealanders have more money in their pocket left at the end of the week" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Who else is there to blame for her economic mismanagement, given her Government has blamed Labour, power companies, Fonterra, insurance companies, supermarkets, US tariffs, “merchants of misery”, teenagers, John Key, teachers, firefighters, doctors, nurses, local councils, and unions?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer's central move — attributing conditions to external and inherited causes — and makes it the target, cataloguing the parties previously blamed. The question is shaped by the explanation just offered and would not land the same way against a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "caused by a combination of factors overseas, historic policies by the New Zealand Government" — David Seymour's preceding answer

acuity.statement: How could an invasive species or a disease that impacts animals have such a big impact on our economy?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the economic-advantage strand of the statement just delivered and asks it to be drawn out, which is a real link to the preceding turn. It engages the topic rather than testing any claim in it, which is the ceiling for an invitation to elaborate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "our relative freedom from pests and diseases is a big part of our competitive advantage and underpins our primary sector" — Andrew Hoggard

acuity.statement: No—the ACT Party doesn’t want to debate human rights. The ACT Party is not interested in human rights. The ACT Party is interested in property rights.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up Cameron Luxton's interjected claim immediately and does something with it — he converts the objection that human rights are out of scope into evidence about ACT's ordering of priorities (property over rights), which is the argument he is already making about the bill's principles hierarchy. It is squarely pointed at what was just said rather than a pivot away, though it reframes the interjection instead of addressing the scope point on its merits, so it is short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We're not debating human rights." — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: Firstly, the creation of the Regulatory Standards Board, which we've just heard will cost in excess of approximately $3 million of taxpayers’ dollars per year.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick explicitly picks up the specific costing Webb had just given for the Regulatory Standards Board and puts it to work as the first item in her own tally of the 'yellow tape' the bill creates, adding the per-year framing and then stacking the compliance-statement and $60 million review costs on top. That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding speech — the expense argument, which she also credits to Webb by name earlier — but the surrounding speech is otherwise prepared Green material on Te Tiriti, the Waitangi Tribunal and inequality that would have been delivered whatever Webb had argued, so this is partial rather than full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Not only will he have to set up its Regulatory Standards Board as a little pet board at a cost of probably $2 or $3 million" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: But I wish to clear up some mistruths about this bill that have been fed from the other side. The first is that this takes away the sovereignty of Parliament. It does not take away the sovereignty of Parliament. There’s nothing in this bill that prevents us from passing legislation, and, with that, I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Brooking's speech and takes up one strand of it — the parliamentary-sovereignty theme — denying that the bill removes sovereignty and giving a reason (nothing in it prevents Parliament passing legislation). But he engages the loosest version of her point: her actual argument was that the bill does not shift power from executive to Parliament, that the criteria are Seymour's rather than neutral, that Part 4 of the Legislation Act 2019 and the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee already serve the stated purpose, and that all-stages urgency is the real problem. None of that is taken up; the rest of the turn is prepared material restating the bill's purpose and thanking submitters. Partial engagement, then back to the script.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "this Parliament of all of us, the executive members and the non-executive members, is sovereign"

acuity.statement: Look, red tape and regulation has been holding this country back for far too long—much of it introduced under that previous Government. We need to get rid of the unnecessary red tape holding our farmers and our growers, our primary sector, our horticulture sector back. We need to get the wheels moving. We need transparent regulation, smarter regulation, and less regulation so that we can strengthen this economy and lift wages for everyone. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Wedd follows a substantive speech by a different member on the same bill, so she is eligible. Her speech is general prepared material on the bill's subject matter (red tape, regulation, the primary sector) and engages no part of Henare's argument: not the submission figure, not the MACA clarification, not the claim about truncated select committee processes. It would read word-for-word the same whatever Henare had said, and the only reference to the opposition is a generic jibe at the previous Government rather than engagement with the preceding claim. It is at least on the matter under debate, which keeps it above 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that over 98 percent of submitters opposed the bill, that the legislative statement rubs salt in the wound over customary marine title under MACA, and that select committee processes have been truncated — and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This bill is very clear: it aims to bring the same discipline to regulation that some argue we already accept and expect in our fiscal management. It aims to set clear principles for good regulation, and then requires Ministers and agencies to disclose and explain any inconsistencies. The board’s advice to Parliament is non-binding, contrary to what we’ve heard. It cannot strike down laws.
acuity.explanation: Campbell follows Woods' substantive attack on the bill and takes up one strand of it — the character and power of the board she described as Seymour-appointed and Seymour-directed — by asserting its advice is non-binding and that it cannot strike down laws, explicitly flagged as 'contrary to what we've heard'. That is a pointable engagement with a claim from the preceding turn. But the rest is prepared framing of the bill's purpose: it does not touch Woods' specific points on the regulatory impact statements, the Transpower submission on clause 8(c), the 98.7 percent of submitters, the taking-of-property principle, or the Treaty submissions. The opening 'a lot of hyperbole and a lot of rubbish' is a mere reference and earns nothing. Partial engagement, so mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It sets up a board that is appointed by David Seymour, and can be directed by David Seymour, to look into legislation." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: New Zealand First supports this bill because it promotes open and accountable government that legislates with key principles in mind: the rule of law, efficiency and regulation, property rights, an independent judiciary, and a belief that every New Zealander is created equal before the law.
acuity.explanation: Prepared party position delivered immediately after Brewer's substantive account of the select committee process and the amendments made to the bill. It engages no part of that — no reference to the submissions, the consultation, or the independence changes — and would read identically whatever Brewer had said. It is at least on the matter under debate (this bill, at second reading), so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer spoke about the select committee hearing 30 hours of oral evidence and about amendments tightening the board and chair's independence, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: This bill and the sham select committee process to ram it through the House is proof that true democracy doesn’t exist in this country.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the immediately preceding case for the bill — Brewer's claim that the committee ran extensive, collegial, liberally-admitted consultation — and flatly contests it as a sham used to ram the bill through. It engages the process claim rather than the substance of Brewer's specific evidence (the hours, the submission counts), and then moves to prepared material, so a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "As chair of the relatively collegial Finance and Expenditure Committee, we also undertook extensive consultation on these matters." — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: Our people know this and this is why 98.7 percent of New Zealanders oppose the Regulatory Standards Bill, and yet not a single recommendation provided by the people was adopted.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the factual claim Brewer had just made, that submitters' feedback produced key amendments, by asserting that no recommendation from submitters was adopted at all. It is squarely aimed at the preceding claim and would have to change if Brewer had argued something else; it stops short of 1.0 because it does not take up the specific amendment Brewer named (board and chair independence).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Following many submitters’ feedback, key amendments to this bill have seen a best-practice tightening of the board and chair’s independence and separation from the Minister and Government of the day" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: We’ve had Mr Seymour not even give the full speech—eight minutes—we’ve had a one-minute speech from Mr Brewer over there, and we’ve had a one-minute speech from Ms Costello over here, because, fundamentally, they know that this bill is actually indefensible.
acuity.explanation: This notices the preceding turns and draws an inference from them, but only from their length — it engages none of the content Brewer or Costello actually advanced (the consultation record, the amendments, equality before the law, compensation for property). A reference to the previous speakers used as a springboard is not engagement with their argument, so it sits in the gesture band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: the one-minute contributions of Cameron Brewer ("The Regulatory Standards Bill gives effect to National’s coalition agreement with ACT") and Casey Costello ("For these reasons, New Zealand First commends the bill to the House")

acuity.statement: We’ve heard claims that this bill will cut red tape and actually introduce a new era of prosperity where there’ll be fun for all and a new level of economic activity. But if you actually listen to what the Government’s own advisers have to say about this, they’ve said the opposite.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the productivity-and-growth strand of the case the two preceding government-side speakers made for the bill and answers it with the Government's own advisers and a cost figure, rather than restating opposition in general terms. It engages the economic claim as a class of claim rather than Costello's precise formulation, so a strong partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "cost-benefit analysis of legislation ensures that economic policies that will impede productivity and growth are adequately scrutinised" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: The object of the Regulatory Standards Bill is to increase transparency in regulation and the resulting accountability with the New Zealand public. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed, hostile critique of the bill's cost, its effect on the Public Service and the quality of its legislative process, and answers none of it. It restates the bill's stated object and commends it — word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, and deliverable in any reading of any bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez had just argued the bill creates "a tsunami of yellow tape" costing a minimum of $60 million and contradicting the Government's own advisers, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Interestingly, while submitters on this issue to the bill disagreed with the proposal to remove them, the School Boards Association did their own survey of school board members—so this is more like the public; you could imagine parents and people who are serving on school boards. The survey received 55 percent agreeing with the removal of the NELP. So there is a diversity of views out there.
acuity.explanation: Prime's immediately preceding turn rested on the claim that the majority of select committee submitters opposed the proposal and that the sector supports the NELPs. Stanford takes that exact claim up, concedes it ('submitters on this issue to the bill disagreed'), and counters it with a different evidence base and a specific figure. The speech would have to change if Prime had argued something else about consultation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the majority of those that submitted opposed what is being proposed here' — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Does she think that it’s a zero-sum game that schools cannot chew gum and walk at the same time; that is, they cannot strive and improve educational achievement and do it while operating in a way that is consistent with Te Tiriti? And, if she does think it’s a zero-sum game, and that any energy that a school puts into operating in a way that’s consistent with Te Tiriti is energy that cannot be put into educational achievement, what evidence does she have to support that?
acuity.explanation: Stanford's preceding turn justified removing the Treaty duty by pointing to school boards' heavy workload and to urgent, plummeting achievement. Twyford isolates the implicit trade-off in that argument, names it as a zero-sum assumption, and demands the evidence for it. He engages the structure of the argument just made rather than the topic at large, though he presses by question rather than rebutting the 'core Crown' reasoning directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'The explicit duty for school boards to give effect to the Treaty is being removed in recognition that schools are not part of the core Crown' — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: The member will be very aware that the Cabinet Manual sees the Treaty as a constitutional document, of course. Since 1989, we have had school boards, and we have not had a clause in any part of the Education Act which has conferred or deferred a Treaty obligation away from the Crown to a group of parents who are volunteers on school boards.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question Twyford had just put — whether she accepts Te Tiriti has constitutional status — squarely and in the affirmative, then draws the consequence she disputes by distinguishing the Crown's obligation from a school board's. Directly shaped by the question asked; it would read differently had Twyford asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Does she accept that Te Tiriti has constitutional status in New Zealand?' — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: So on section 127, this is clause 8 we’re looking at and this is something that we sort of never got clarity on despite the select committee stage, and I understand the Minister’s position is that we want to have a single paramount objective, but then the Minister was also like, “Nothing is going to change.” So the question then is why make that change if nothing is going to change?
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan follows Willow-Jean Prime and takes up one strand of her contribution — her point that the ministry claims nothing changes under the new drafting while the drafting plainly has interpretive consequences — and sharpens it into an operational question for the Minister. He also adopts her proposed thematic ordering. But the bulk of the turn is his own prepared material on clause 8 and Amendment Paper 428, and he does not engage her specific submissions figure or her coalition-agreement argument, so this is a partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "While the Ministry of Education and the Minister of Education portrayed a view that nothing will change under the new drafting, there is a reason why statutory interpretation actually exists"

acuity.statement: In relation to the first question that was questioning the consultation, there has been consultation on section 127. There was public consultation on the proposal to amend section 127 and to remove the National Education and Learning Priorities provisions from the Act between 2 September and 14 October 2024.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question both preceding members put to her — where is the evidence of consultation on these changes — and supplies the dated consultation window rather than deflecting. It would read differently had the question been something else. Marked just short of 1.0 because she answers consultation on section 127 generally and leaves untouched the narrower strands actually asked (consultation with the New Zealand School Boards Association, and the 80.5 percent of submissions opposed).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "So my question to the Minister is: where is the evidence of her engagement and collaboration with the sector on these proposed changes?"

acuity.statement: Just making some comments in relation to the second question about the process, I’d just like to point out that the process is that the Amendment Paper should go up I think 24 hours beforehand—which it did, yesterday afternoon—and from all my time on the Opposition benches, the job of the Opposition was to keep an eye on the website to make sure that any Amendment Papers were brought to their attention. That’s certainly how it’s been working since 2017, and so that’s what the member should do.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts Xu-Nan's specific procedural complaint that the Amendment Paper appeared without notification: she states the 24-hour rule, asserts it was met yesterday afternoon, and contests his premise that notifying the House is the Minister's obligation rather than the Opposition's to monitor. The response is wholly contingent on the claim he made — delete his complaint and this passage has nothing to say.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "the Minister has released a very substantial Amendment Paper yesterday, without public consultation, without notifying anyone"

acuity.statement: In addressing the point around evidence, the evidence is that there have been decades of decline in student achievement, and I know that it hurts the Opposition—especially Willow-Jean Prime—to know that they had six years in Government and didn’t manage to raise achievement for tamariki Māori, or any students, at all.
acuity.explanation: She names and takes up Prime's claim that the changes are not evidence-based, and offers an answer to it (decades of declining achievement), so there is real engagement with the argument put. But the answer occupies one clause before the turn pivots to the previous Government's record, which is not what was asked; Prime asked for the evidence of collaboration and of the change's basis, not for a comparison of terms. Partial engagement, then a move to the opponent's record.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I would also make the point that these changes are not based on evidence; they are based on the Government having a coalition agreement between the National Party and the ACT Party."

acuity.statement: It is not the job of well-meaning parents who run schools who are effectively volunteers to be deferred a Treaty duty.
acuity.explanation: This supplies the rationale Xu-Nan asked for — why the duty to give effect to Te Tiriti has been lifted out of new section 127(2)(e) — by arguing the obligation sits with the Crown rather than with volunteer boards. It engages the substance of his objection rather than merely restating that other criteria remain. Short of 1.0 because it answers the 'why' and not his further question about what advice she received or what consultation was undertaken with the School Boards Association.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "that’s very different to giving effect to Te Tiriti, because giving effect to Te Tiriti is far more holistic than that"

acuity.statement: We’ve just had the Minister, once again, standing up and talking so proudly about her record of te reo Māori. My question to the Minister is: what gave the Minister the right to determine that Te Tiriti o Waitangi means providing resources in te reo Māori? Who gave the Minister and the Crown the sole right to determine that giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi is to simply provide resources in te reo Māori? Who did she talk to?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific move Stanford had just made — equating support for te reo with making resources available — and presses on its premise, asking by what authority and with whose agreement resource provision was made the measure of giving effect to Te Tiriti. The questions only make sense as a reply to the answer just given; had Stanford defended the clause on other grounds the questioning would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "we are supporting te reo Māori in schools, not only making sure that school boards have an obligation to make sure that they're offering te reo Māori but also making sure that everything is available in te reo Māori"

acuity.statement: Going back to the start of that contribution where the member was asking around the provision of te reo resources—and this may go to part of my questions as to why the previous Government didn’t do this; I’m now starting to understand it. But under the Waitangi Tribunal’s decision, Wai 11—and the member would be advised to go and look at that decision, which says that treating te reo Māori as a taonga is important and that te reo Māori is, in fact, a taonga under the Treaty of Waitangi and it deserves active protection.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific challenge put to her by naming the authority she relies on (Wai 11 and the active-protection duty over te reo as a taonga), and later in the same contribution takes up Prime's second question about what honouring the Treaty means. The reply is shaped by the questions asked rather than being prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "what gave the Minister the right to determine that Te Tiriti o Waitangi means providing resources in te reo Māori?"

acuity.statement: Beyond te reo and beyond resources, can the Minister of Education accept that giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi looks different according to iwi, hapū, community, and the tikanga and kawa processes of that iwi, hapū, and community? If so, how can the Minister monitor effectiveness and, of course, ensure consistency?
acuity.explanation: Opens by conceding and then stepping past the exact ground Stanford had just claimed — resources and te reo — and puts the consequence to her: if the duty varies by iwi and hapū, how is effectiveness monitored. The question is built on the answer just given and would read differently had Stanford argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "The way that we do that in education is to make sure that we are providing resources"

acuity.statement: One of the easiest ways to ensure that you are raising achievement—which is, again, the core tenet of a Treaty duty: to make sure that tamariki Māori are succeeding to their full potential, which we have not done in this country for some time—is to make sure that we're assessing our young people. That's why we created Hihira Weteoro, which is a phonics check that is designed specifically—a world first, as far as we can tell—for Māori children learning in bilingual units.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the question — the monitoring mechanism — and answers it with assessment tools, but leaves untouched the premise it was attached to, that giving effect to Te Tiriti looks different in each iwi, hapū and school community, and says nothing about consistency across them. Partial engagement, then prepared material on assessment policy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "how will the Minister monitor the effectiveness of this?"

acuity.statement: If I can paraphrase what I've heard from the Minister today, she's more interested in educational achievement than she is in, somehow, the kind of symbolism of having Te Tiriti in our education legislation.
acuity.explanation: Twyford picks up the same strand Halbert had just opened — the Minister's separation of Māori educational achievement from Te Tiriti's place in the legislation — and does something with it, granting the distinction at face value and then pressing the 'why not do both' consequence. But he aims the engagement at the Minister's earlier (unquoted) answers rather than at Halbert's specific claim, and much of the intervention is his own prepared line of questioning, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct take-up of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "The Minister has talked a lot about equity but we haven't unpacked the role that Te Tiriti plays in achieving equitable outcomes for tamariki in our education system."

acuity.statement: I've already said this a number of times and I’m in danger of repeating myself, but if the member looks at the Amendment Paper, firstly, it does say, “takes [all] reasonable steps to ensure the policies and practices [at] the school reflect New Zealand's cultural diversity:”, and I expect that schools, as self-managing entities, will continue to do exactly that.
acuity.explanation: Leary asked directly whether removing the give-effect duty would strip away culture-and-identity protections such as uniform and grooming protocols. Stanford answers by pointing at the operative wording of her own Amendment Paper on cultural diversity and at the retained section 127 rights, which is a substantive engagement with the premise of the question rather than prepared material. It falls short of 1.0 because she answers the general protection question and never takes up the specific item Leary pressed on — the Human Rights Commission uniform guidelines — so the reply would have been much the same against any version of the cultural-protections question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "does that mean that those school uniform protocols that have been adopted by many schools and welcomed with open arms by many boards of trustees and by many students and that no doubt have led to higher achievement are to be thrown out"

acuity.statement: While I appreciate what the Minister of Education’s saying in terms of the dates, the Minister will certainly be aware that anything you put on the table—we can actually ask that. Considering that we are looking at amendments—and we have seen multiple instances, including the fact that, under clause 3, we’re able to discuss maybe more broadly some of the purpose and principles around the Education and Training Act 2020—it is not beyond the scope of a committee stage for us to also ask questions around the Education (School Planning and Reporting) Regulations in general.
acuity.explanation: Stanford had just fenced the debate to the date extension alone; Xu-Nan takes that specific scope claim and contests it on its own terms, citing the clause 3 precedent for broader questioning, and later takes the very date she named and proposes moving it a further year to 2028. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged if she had framed Part 2 differently. Not 1.0 because the middle of the turn then runs through prepared material on TALIS and teacher autonomy that engages nothing she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "Part 2, the consequential amendment, is very narrow. It is around extending the date—January 1, 2026 to January 1, 2027—for school boards to prepare and deliver their strategic plan. So I’ll answer questions around that."

acuity.statement: Almost everything that the member mentioned is completely out of scope, and I’m not going to address it for that reason. In answer to his second part, which is in scope, his amendment to change the time, I would note that this change from 1 January 2026 to 1 January 2027 was something that the select committee themselves had put forward and was accepted by the select committee.
acuity.explanation: She separates Xu-Nan's turn into the part she rules out of scope and the part she will answer, then addresses his actual amendment with a specific reason for refusing it — the 2027 date originated with the select committee and was accepted there. That is taking up the precise proposal just put and doing something with it, so the reply would read differently had he proposed a different date or no amendment at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I do ask, in combination with the questions I asked before, that the Minister consider my amendment that moves the date from 1 January 2027 to 1 January 2028."

acuity.statement: I don’t deny the fact that the Minister has put resources into it. However, 97 percent of ākonga Māori are in English medium; they’re not in Māori medium. So while we’re celebrating Māori-medium success, what are we doing, signalling to those 97 percent of ākonga Māori in the English medium, saying “We are now removing the school boards’ need to give effect to Te Tiriti.”? What, then, would the Minister say to these 97 percent?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific defence Stanford had just offered — that resourcing te reo teaching, literacy materials for kura kaupapa and whare kura discharges the Treaty duty — concedes it, then turns it by pointing out where the overwhelming majority of Māori students actually sit. The speech would have to change if Stanford had defended the clause on different grounds, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "all the literacy resources we're providing to schools, secondary schools, kura kaupapa, whare kura—is important"

acuity.statement: I really want to pick up the question from my colleague Cushla Tangaere-Manuel, because, I think, that question is really important, because what we are hearing from the Minister is that, yes, parents, caregivers, students can request it, but what that translates to is: if you want to do anything that is culturally yours, you’ve got to bat for it—you’ve got to ask for it; it is not naturally given to you as your birthright.
acuity.explanation: Engages the precise mechanism Stanford had just read out — provision of te reo teaching "to students whose parents or caregivers request it" — and draws out its consequence rather than merely restating it. Directly aimed at the content of the preceding claim, not at the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "to take all reasonable steps to provide for teaching and learning in te reo Māori to students whose parents or caregivers request it"

acuity.statement: I’ll just run through those questions. Firstly, there's no requirement for a child impact statement. Secondly, the question around consultation—there was full ministerial consultation, as there always is in a Cabinet process, and Minister Potaka was also on Minister Goldsmith's ministerial advisory group around the Treaty principles work that was done, so he was consulted, of course.
acuity.explanation: Answers the two questions put to her in order and supplies a specific name on the consultation point, so the reply is clearly shaped by what preceded it. Short of 1.0 because several of the strands he itemised — Te Arawhiti specifically, Waitangi Tribunal exposure, Mana Mokopuna — are not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "why was there no child impact statement being made? What consultation has she done specifically with things like Mana Mokopuna"

acuity.statement: With the National Education and Learning Priorities (NELP), I appreciate the member’s position, but this Government has come in with six very clear priorities. The NELP are overly burdensome. They are just one of many documents that school boards have to look at.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific amendment he asked her to consider and gives a reason for declining it, so it is a real engagement with one strand. It answers the topic rather than his actual proposition, though — he argued for reinstating NELP at the stronger "give effect" standard, and the burden objection addresses retention, not the strengthening, before returning to prepared material about the six priorities.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I would ask the Minister to consider my amendment, Amendment Paper 403, which is to reinstate NELP but actually make it stronger by saying “to give effect”"

acuity.statement: Unlike the section on universities, I haven’t seen within this bill, anyway, and the Minister may like to speak to that, that allows school boards to be compliant with the new requirement—or at least shift towards the new requirement—once it has been enacted, if it’s only the day after Royal assent. I think a six-month transition period is sensible for the schools to be able to do something like that, unless the Minister is suggesting that while the commencement date comes into force the day after Royal assent, school boards may not need to immediately be compliant or need to make the relevant changes that we see in this bill.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the six-month commencement thread Hernandez was probing and extends the universities/schools distinction to school boards, but much of the call is prepared material advancing his own Amendment Paper 402 rather than engaging Hernandez's specific retrospectivity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "it is particularly important on what does apply with that six-month period commencement"

acuity.statement: I think this is relevant to clause 2—“Commencement”—because of the late nature of the two Amendment Papers, and the primary ones that I’m looking at are 364 and 428, which I’m not looking to debate at this stage. But I think that because they raise such significant changes to the bill that perhaps the Minister of Education could consider later commencement dates for the changes contained within those Amendment Papers.
acuity.explanation: Lands on the same strand as the immediately preceding speaker — a delayed commencement for the late Amendment Papers, including AP 364 on the Teaching Council — but arrives at it independently, opening with her own framing ('this is my first opportunity to make a contribution') and never taking up Xu-Nan's specific proposal or reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I think a six-month transition period is sensible for the schools" — and his concern about Amendment Paper 364 on the Teaching Council

acuity.statement: I'm not sure if the member Camilla Belich was here earlier when we were discussing the fact that we are giving schools a whole additional year to do their next strategic plan. The last bit we've just finished voting on moves that from 1 January next year to 1 January 2027, and so there is plenty of time for schools to look at the new section 127 and the new regulations, and then put them into their strategic plans.
acuity.explanation: Answers Belich's specific request for later commencement by supplying the dates already moved (1 January 2027) and the mechanism, and then goes on to address her Teaching Council and title suggestions in turn; the reply would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "perhaps the Minister of Education could consider later commencement dates for the changes contained within those Amendment Papers"

acuity.statement: Just for absolute clarity for all of our schools and kura out there, are you saying that their current strategic plans which give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, which outline the things that I said earlier about the legislation, which have now been replaced with the strategies in your Amendment Paper—so for all of next year, their current strategic plans are the ones that they will be governing their schools in accordance with?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-made claim about the extra year and draws out its consequence, pressing for confirmation of exactly what it means for schools' existing Treaty-based strategic plans through 2026.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "we are giving schools a whole additional year to do their next strategic plan"

acuity.statement: To be helpful to that member, that particular part in Schedule 2 that she is talking about has been replaced, so all of the things she was talking about have been replaced by Schedule 2 in my Amendment Paper that we already voted on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the exact provision Prime built her questions on (the replacement regulation in Schedule 2) and does something with it — asserts it has already been superseded by the Amendment Paper and voted on. The reply would be different had Prime raised a different clause; it is aimed squarely at her specific textual claim. Whether the scope ruling is correct, and whether she thereby avoided the substantive question, are other attributes' concerns, not Acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "My questions for the Minister are around these consequential amendments that are being made to the Education (School Planning and Reporting) Regulations"

acuity.statement: Given that you did not say that these are out of scope, I would like the Minister to answer my questions that I asked in terms of the consequential amendments to Schedule 2, which is the “Education (School Planning and Reporting) Regulations 2023” and, in particular, my questions around the “local curriculum”.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Stanford's reply — the out-of-scope assertion — and disposes of it by reference to the Chair not having ruled that way, but does not take up the substance of the claim (that the Amendment Paper replaced the very provision quoted). It then returns to the prepared list of questions essentially unchanged, which is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "We've already voted on it, so that is out of scope."

acuity.statement: Once again, for the member, the bit that she is talking about is being replaced. So she keeps mentioning the words “local curriculum”; I just draw to her attention that that part in Schedule 2 has been replaced by my Amendment Paper 428, so she should look at the Amendment Paper for the correct part.
acuity.explanation: Points at the specific phrase Prime pressed on — "local curriculum" — and answers it by naming Amendment Paper 428 as the superseding text, so the reply is shaped by what she asked. It engages the status of her question rather than its content (the effect of dropping "local curriculum"), and adds little beyond the earlier answer, which keeps it mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "my questions around the “local curriculum”. What does that actually mean in terms of these regulations?"

acuity.statement: I think one of the things that we were querying earlier was the fact that the Minister of Education mentioned that we have already voted on that. I think in terms of the voting part, this part on Schedule 2 will not be voted on until we conclude Schedule 2.
acuity.explanation: Isolates the precise premise of the Minister's scope objection — that the House has already voted on the Schedule 2 provision — and corrects it on the procedural fact that Schedule 2 is not voted on until the committee concludes it. He goes on to concede part of her point (that the Amendment Paper substantially changes Schedule 2) and turn it into a counter-argument about the absence of select committee scrutiny. The speech could not have been delivered without having heard hers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "which we have already voted on. It is no longer in scope."

acuity.statement: I could help the member. If he looks at the relevant schedule, it’s six months after the Act comes into force that the university must have a plan.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific figure the preceding question asked for — the period before universities must have a plan — which is the strongest form of engagement with a question put in debate. It answers only the commencement strand and sets the rest aside as already debated, which is why it is not a full 1.0, but the response is plainly shaped by Hernandez's particular query.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "does the Minister anticipate that there’s like a transition period for the university councils to adopt these statements on freedom of expression?"

acuity.statement: My colleague has picked up on clause 6, so another question in relation to clause 6, which lists the contents of an application under the verification pathway. I’d like the Associate Minister of Health David Seymour to explain how these requirements interact with the common documentation system used by some of the regulators we are likely to recognise.
acuity.explanation: Follows Peeni Henare, whose substantive point about clause 6 was that paragraph (m) matters because medicines are repackaged and renamed overseas and origin must be traceable. Verrall names the clause he raised but engages none of that reasoning, instead putting an unrelated question about standardised documentation. The clause reference is a hand-off, not an engagement: her question would read identically had Henare argued something else about clause 6, so this sits in the 'gesture at the debate, on the right subject' band rather than partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "The other matter I wanted to raise is, in clause 6, the following particulars are required"

acuity.statement: I’d just like to support the vote of confidence in this bill from my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall, who really gave it some good scrutiny at the Health Committee. I think it’s important to note that, in the broader constitutional policy space, there is quite a shift of power from legal, prescriptive sorts of requirements through to empowering Ministers to act through notices and rules, and I do think that raises a number of legal questions.
acuity.explanation: Praises Verrall by name and endorses her scrutiny, then moves entirely onto her own prepared material on delegation, secondary legislation and sections 22/22A. Verrall's actual question — whether the paragraph (a)-(m) requirements mesh with the common technical dossier — is never taken up in any part. A commendation plus a pivot is a mere reference, which the rubric puts at 0.1-0.3; 0.2 because the contribution is at least squarely about the bill under debate and the committee scrutiny of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "we’ve been told repeatedly at the Health Committee that there’s the potential for great efficiency through the use of standardised documentation"

acuity.statement: Finally, Ingrid Leary asked about what she says is a shift of power towards Ministers. It’s certainly true that it talks about a Minister granting consent. That, at a constitutional, technical level, may be true, but, ultimately, this decision making is not done by a Minister; it’s done in their name.
acuity.explanation: Takes Leary's specific constitutional claim — that the bill shifts power from prescriptive statutory requirements to ministerial notices and rules — concedes the technical point, and then disputes its practical force by distinguishing a decision made by a Minister from one made in a Minister's name by qualified pharmacologists. That is accepting part and contesting the rest; the passage could not have been delivered against a different argument, and would have had to change had Leary objected on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "there is quite a shift of power from legal, prescriptive sorts of requirements through to empowering Ministers to act through notices and rules"

acuity.statement: In terms of the question about accountability and stability—and I was pleased to hear about, you know: how do we make sure that there’s certainty for people who are applicants? I just make the point that any rules, made under this law, that will set out how it operates do need to be presented to the House and are subject to disallowance by Parliament.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the concern Leary raised about operational detail living only in rules not yet drafted and the resulting loss of parliamentary scrutiny, by naming the specific mechanism — presentation to the House and disallowance — that she said was in doubt. It supplies the answer her argument demanded rather than restating a position, and is indifferent to nothing that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "there are questions around parliamentary scrutiny, and there are questions about the transparency of Gazette notices"

acuity.statement: The first question I have—and this is partly because one of my degrees is actually in pharmacology—is on subsection (2)(h), “reports of toxicological, pharmacological, and clinical studies that support the application:”. I want to check with the Minister whether there is a requirement for that particular study to be conducted or to be peer reviewed as well.
acuity.explanation: Verrall's preceding turn made a substantive point (welcoming the criteria-based approach in new section 22AA) and asked specifically about revocation of recognition. Xu-Nan's turn is on the same bill and the adjacent clause, but it engages no part of her argument or question — it introduces his own prepared questions on clause 6. On-topic prepared material, so the bottom band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall said "I would like the Minister to expand on what type of circumstances he imagines an authority’s recognition might be revoked" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: So my question was in relationship to new section 22AA(1)(e), inserted by clause 7. This is in relationship to the recognised regulatory authorities. One of the requirements that's been set out in the legislation is for those to conduct their business and release reports in English. I wanted to ask whether the Minister for Regulation thinks that that may potentially hinder the ability for us to access medicines where the business may be conducted in another language.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns precede him. He lands on the same provision Verrall opened on (new section 22AA) and sets it against clause 6, which Xu-Nan had just been questioning, so there is a gesture at the shape of the debate — but he takes up neither Verrall's revocation question nor Xu-Nan's peer-review point. Prepared material on the right clauses.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "also potentially recognises the regulatory authority that has been touched on previously in clause 7, which inserts new section 22AA" — Menéndez March arrives at the same provision but engages no part of Xu-Nan's or Verrall's actual questions.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I’d just like to ask a further supplementary question based on the question raised by the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall regarding the revocation or designation of a recognised authority. Normally, ministerial decisions are not subject to explicit procedural safeguards. If it’s in the Gazette and a decision has been made, normally there are notice and comment requirements beyond publication. So my first question to the Minister on that natural justice and transparency issue is: are there other forms of contesting decisions either with designation or revocation, except via judicial review, which we know is incredibly expensive and again could have a chilling effect on the market?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question Verrall put — the circumstances and mechanics of revoking recognition — and does something with it, extending it to the natural-justice consequence: if the only route of challenge is judicial review, the safeguard is nominal. The speech would have to change if Verrall had asked about something else. Later in the same turn she also picks up the Green member's localised-safety point, which is further evidence of listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "I want to draw the Minister’s attention to the revocation of recognition of an authority."

acuity.statement: Then she asked a question about revocation. The test is whether the regulator continues to meet the criteria set out in paragraphs (a) to (e) of new section 22AA(1) in clause 7. If it starts failing to meet those, then it would be revoked, and so those are the criteria set out in the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing the preceding question asked for — the test governing revocation — and points to the provision that contains it. Directly keyed to Verrall's question; it could not have been delivered in response to a different one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "I would like the Minister to expand on what type of circumstances he imagines an authority’s recognition might be revoked".

acuity.statement: Ricardo Menéndez March raised an interesting question about: does limiting ourselves to English-speaking jurisdictions restrict the possible range of overseas agencies that we could rely on for verification? Potentially, but I think that members might be surprised. For example, I asked about Japan. I’ve been informed that the Japanese consenting authority actually conducts its business in English, and so that’s a significant country with its own language that none the less uses English to work with the rest of the world.
acuity.explanation: Restates the questioner's point accurately, concedes part of it ("Potentially"), then answers it with a specific counter-example aimed at the premise that a non-English-speaking country's regulator would be excluded. Engagement with the content, not a mere reference to the member.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "whether the Minister for Regulation thinks that that may potentially hinder the ability for us to access medicines where the business may be conducted in another language".

acuity.statement: I’m going to speak to clause 7, 22B(4) and just ask for a bit of clarification, so this won’t take very long: “The Director-General may issue the applicant with 1 or more invoices for any fee payable under regulations in respect of the application.” Is that only those that are successful? Does that include those that are declined?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (a clause of the bill before the committee) but engages no part of the preceding argument; it is a self-contained clarification question that would read identically whatever Verrall had said. No gesture at the prior turn, so the bottom of the on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued the bill departs from the coalition agreement's automatic-approval commitment and asked how that changes its efficiency benefits, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: My colleagues have talked about the drivers, if you like, of efficiency with the system and how that will look compared to the original coalition agreement. I think, extrapolating on that, there is a real potential for a streamlined process to reduce scrutiny of pharmaceutical submissions if the decision making becomes overly reliant on the second stream.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the coalition-agreement/efficiency strand from the preceding turn and draws out a consequence Verrall had not reached (reliance on the second stream reducing scrutiny). Not a full 1.0 because it extends rather than contests the argument, and then moves into her own prepared concern about lobbying.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the purpose of the bill is to speed up the approvals of new medicines in New Zealand" / "the change between what’s envisaged in the coalition agreement and the bill that we have now" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Ayesha Verrall asked about the perceived difference between the ACT - National confidence and supply agreement and the workings of this legislation. As a Minister, I’m not actually responsible for political agreements. All I would say is that I’m a very thoughtful and receptive Minister who’s always prepared to make the legislation work in the best interests of all New Zealand. I’ll also just make the point that having an applicant, as the member asked, demonstrates that there is a company that will take responsibility for the supply chain within New Zealand. So that is a worthwhile benefit in my view.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the named question and engages one strand of it with a reason — why requiring an applicant is a benefit (supply-chain responsibility) — which directly answers her point that the bill is not automatic approval. Sets aside the 'why did the thinking change' half as outside his responsibility, so partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why has the thinking, with respect to how this bill will operate, changed from what was envisaged in the coalition agreement and what’s in the bill now?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Peeni Henare asked about what fees these foreign pharmaceutical companies might be charged. I have to say that I’m heartened by the Labour member’s concern for foreign pharmaceutical companies; it’s a new development, but not an unwelcome one. The fees will be published, they’ll be set by regulation, and they will be transparent. But they’re not currently set, so that will come as a consequence of the law of passing, if the Parliament decides to pass it.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific information the previous turn asked for — the fees will be set by regulation, published and transparent, but are not yet set. Short of 1.0 because it leaves Henare's other specific question (whether declined applications are invoiced) untouched, and spends a sentence on a jibe instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is there transparency around those particular invoices we can expect to be made public to allow us the confidence that there’s consistency in their fees framework?" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: Ingrid Leary repeated the question by Ayesha Verrall and then also asked about the lobbying and political influence on overseas consenting agencies. All I would say is that if you imagine a place like, say, Switzerland, which was in the original bill, or if you imagine a place like the EU or the United Kingdom, your mind doesn’t immediately think, I’m sure, that their consenting authorities consent dangerous medicines because of undue influence. I think that would be a surprising thing to most people; there’s no evidence to believe that is the case. All of those jurisdictions do have much greater access to medicines than New Zealand and that is one of the things that we are trying to fix here.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific premise of the preceding turn — that comparator regulators are captured by commercial lobbying — names the jurisdictions at issue and denies that premise, then turns it round by arguing those same jurisdictions deliver better access. The speech would have to change if Leary had raised a different concern.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There are jurisdictions that we compare ourselves to that have far more lobbying and political influence in their system." — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Going back to Ayesha Verrall, she also asked if it might be that because companies are unlikely to—well, she posits that companies are unlikely to apply for consent if they don’t believe they’ll ultimately get Pharmac funding. That may be a calculation for some companies, but at the margin what we’re doing here is making the consenting process easier and quicker. So you would expect the net effect of that to increase medicines’ availability.
acuity.explanation: Restates the preceding argument accurately, concedes part of it ('that may be a calculation for some companies') and disputes the conclusion with a marginal-incentives counter-argument. Classic accept-part-dispute-the-rest engagement with the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They’ll think, “Well, is it really worth our while to put something through a process when”—perhaps, they would say—“unlikely to get it funded.”" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Finally, Lawrence Xu-Nan asked if there would be a review clause. Much secondary legislation—I expect all secondary legislation—will be made in best practice.
acuity.explanation: Names the question asked but engages none of its content: it does not say whether a review clause was considered, rejected, or might be added, and the assurance about 'best practice' addresses a different thing. A gesture at the point under debate rather than an engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did the Minister, as always, consider some sort of review clause in terms of how the Minister may make rules setting out some of that requirement" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: The amendment simply allows a promoter of a medical conference—you can imagine a place where the primary audience is people who are registered as clinicians under the health practitioners assurance legislation. If you’re holding such a conference, then you can get consent to advertise medicines that are not currently consented by Medsafe. The reason that you would want to do that is that clinicians go to these sorts of conferences, in part, precisely because they would like to find out about medicines that are new.
acuity.explanation: Supplies what the preceding turn asked for — an explanation of the content and purpose of the Amendment Paper — so the turn is shaped by the request that prompted it. Not higher because it ignores her specific point that the amendment was never considered by the select committee.
