acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d like to take the opportunity to ask the Minister to engage in some back and forth, if we may, on the content of this amendment." — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The member is correct that there might be people coming from overseas inbound to learn about medicines at conferences in New Zealand, but I would interpret this as those people are people who come under the same professions and, indeed, would be regulated under that Act if they were in New Zealand. Of course, in this instance they wouldn’t be, but they’re equivalents. They just happen to be from overseas.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise point Verrall had just put — that overseas conference attendees are registered abroad and so fall outside the HPCA Act — concedes it is correct and supplies an interpretation (equivalence of profession) that answers it. The answer would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "in an international conference many visitors from overseas won’t be regulated by that Act, because they will be registered overseas" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: This concern about medical conferences was raised in the course of the last Parliament’s debate on the Therapeutic Products Bill, so can the Minister explain why this amendment has appeared in the bill now?
acuity.explanation: Stays squarely on the amendment under debate but opens a fresh line (timing and select committee process) without taking up any part of the answer Seymour had just given on the HPCA Act definition or the overseas-equivalence point. On topic, not responsive to the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Seymour had just argued the HPCA Act is "a tidy way to do it" and that overseas attendees are professional "equivalents", and this statement does not take either up

acuity.statement: So why would we not put this in the bill initially? Because we were preparing a bill primarily for the purpose for the rule of two. Once it was brought to my attention that it would be useful for New Zealand clinicians to be able to have medical conferences with advertised medicines in New Zealand, I made a judgment that it was well worth enabling that at the earlier opportunity, which is this bill.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the specific question just put — why the amendment was absent from the bill as drafted — by giving the bill's original purpose and the point at which his view changed. Only the speculation about a medicinal products bill is deflected.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why wasn’t it in the original bill that was drafted and considered and went to select committee?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I noted that the Minister mentioned that such conferences—if I heard correctly—were to bring $90 million to the country. Can I just test where that figure came from, and who produced the analysis on that amount of money?
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific figure the Minister had used in the same debate and interrogates its provenance, and explicitly builds on Verrall's select committee point. The question could not exist without what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: the Minister's claim that conferences "were to bring $90 million to the country", and "Why wasn’t it in the original bill ... went to select committee?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: As far as the distributional analysis is concerned, I also don’t have that. I only have the headline figure. In terms of consultation, I haven’t directly consulted people with this.
acuity.explanation: Answers the itemised questions just asked in the order they were asked — provenance of the figure, distributional analysis, consultation, dates — conceding each rather than pivoting. Wholly shaped by the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the distributional analysis for benefits; additionally, the list of stakeholders or entities that were consulted" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I’m a little bit concerned to hear that the $90 million was kind of made up on the spot. I guess the question I had in relationship to that—or from the top of his head—is whether he asked any Government body to do some analysis on that figure?
acuity.explanation: Takes the concession just made (the figure was off the top of his head) and does something with it — narrows the question from where the figure came from to whether officials were ever asked to produce one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the $90 million was a figure off the top of my head" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: The justification for this does not rely on any specific figure. If it was $9 million, $90 million, or $900 million, it costs next to nothing to do, and it increases people’s freedom to do as they please within New Zealand so long as there are no risks to others, and, therefore, we should do it.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the question — the evidential weight carried by the revenue figure — but leaves the actual question asked (did he commission advice from officials) unanswered, falling back on a general argument from freedom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if he did not commission such advice, then what basis is he using to get to a point where he feels confident about the amount of money" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Whilst the Minister noted that this doesn’t change immigration law—I accept that—there is an interface between immigration status and who owes allegiance to the Crown.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's stated point and then disputes its sufficiency, drawing out the consequence for resident and worker visa holders under new section 2A(3)(c). Classic accept-part-and-press-the-rest engagement with the turn immediately before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This legislation is not changing our citizenship laws or making amendments in any of those areas." — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: Then, in the new section 2A(2), inserted by clause 4, it says, “this section is not an exhaustive code of the law relating to the circumstances in which a person owes allegiance to the Sovereign … of New Zealand;”, so it’s just opened the gate. The thing about criminal law is that you want to be pretty clear about when you’re liable, when you could be charged with a crime, right?
acuity.explanation: Walters raised several strands (Ross Dependency, Niue, embassy staff, and the reliance on unspecified common law). Webb takes up the common-law/open-endedness strand specifically, locates it in the actual text of new section 2A(2), and develops it into an argument about certainty of criminal liability. He does not engage her Ross Dependency, Niue or embassy questions and instead returns to his own prepared line of attack, so this is a developed engagement with one strand rather than with her contribution as a whole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "the statement that the common law would continue to apply rather than specify what the common law is in terms of who owes allegiance and who doesn’t"

acuity.statement: Everybody who’s here in the country is somebody who owes allegiance to the Sovereign if they’re in the country, unless they’re a diplomat or a person who is an enemy alien. It’s reasonably clearly outlined in the legislation, and I think we’re getting slightly distracted, trying to draw what this legislation here is, which is focused on dealing with foreign interference, which is a real threat that we face, and I don’t think it’s helpful to try and draw into a debate around citizen rights of children of actors in relation to this topic.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith engages the general "who's in and who's out" question by reading the operative exceptions in new section 2A(3) back to the members, which is a direct answer to the category-by-category framing Webb and Walters used. But the specific claims put to him — that the statutes may not reach the Ross Dependency, the Niue Constitution Act point, embassy staff abroad, and above all Webb's challenge to the "not an exhaustive code" wording — are not taken up; he asserts the scheme is clear and characterises the questioning as a distraction. Partial engagement with the topic rather than with the arguments made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "A lot of the bill kind of steps through—my previous contribution talked about, well, what about if you’re a resident? What about if you’re a tourist?"

acuity.statement: I note the comments made by Vanushi Walters around Niue and the Ross Dependency, and also, as a Cook Islander, I’m interested as well, because Cook Islanders hold New Zealand passports. The Cook Islands and Niue are part of the New Zealand Realm—so, technically, in New Zealand. So it would be good for the Minister to draw out exactly what that would mean for Cook Islanders in this instance, because I know that people will be listening with interest as to whether they owe allegiance, and exactly what that means.
acuity.explanation: Tuiono picks up Walters' realm-territories strand by name and extends it to a case she did not raise — Cook Islanders holding New Zealand passports — drawing out a consequence for how Pacific peoples in the realm may hold differing views on relationships with foreign states. He also explicitly endorses and extends Webb's non-exhaustive-code point to Pacific Islanders. The speech would plainly be different had those two turns not occurred. It is marked down because it does not engage the Minister's immediately preceding reply that the exceptions in section 2A(3) make the position "reasonably clearly outlined"; it restates the question as if the answer had not been given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "Similarly, they spoke about how the law would apply to Niue."

acuity.statement: In relation to the last question about whether we considered views, I’m not sure the extent to which detailed consideration of temporary allegiance was given, but we have certainly not decided to go down that route.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific concept Walters pressed him on by name and states where the Government landed on it — the sentence could not have been spoken after a different question. It engages only one strand, though: Walters also asked squarely about an officially induced error defence and about those on temporary class visas, and neither is taken up, so this is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "whether temporary allegiance was considered as a concept; if not, why not?"

acuity.statement: I do understand where the Minister’s coming from, and I think that foreign interference is incredibly serious. Even if you’re looking at something that we’ll touch on later, in terms of clause 7—if you’re looking at section 69 of the Crimes Act, particularly new subsection (1B), inserted by clause 7(1), it is punishable by up to 14 years of imprisonment. So we understand the severity of it, which is why this new definition that has been introduced, of the meaning of a person who owes allegiance, is particularly important because this is the crux of a lot of what is going to be coming in terms of the rest of the bill, in terms of the actual offence itself.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's point that the conduct targeted is serious rather than mere expression, and then turns that concession into the premise of his own argument — because the penalty is severe, the allegiance definition must be tight. That is genuine engagement with one strand of the preceding turn, but he immediately moves to prepared material on 'family', 'property' and 'enduring connection' that does not depend on anything Goldsmith said, so it sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "this is not a question of free speech or expressing views. It’s about people who engage in covert, deceptive, coercive, or corruptive conduct"

acuity.statement: So if you could explain to me why inciting mutiny is 14 years in prison, but being mutinous is 10 years in prison, that would be a really handy elucidation.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the bill under consideration, but indifferent to what precedes it: Webb announces he is 'moving on to clause 7' and puts a self-contained prepared point about penalty proportionality between section 69(1A) and section 77. The passage would read identically had Xu-Nan argued anything else, or nothing at all. The brush with Xu-Nan's mention of the 14-year term is coincidence of subject, not engagement with his argument, so this belongs in the low band rather than mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked for the definitions of 'family', 'property' and 'enduring connection' in new section 2A and for who determines an enduring connection, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: This bill records the acknowledgments and also the apology made to Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu by the Crown when the deed of settlement was signed. It gives effect to the redress in that deed that requires this legislation today.
acuity.explanation: Andersen follows a substantive first-reading speech by Goldsmith that set out the claim history, the negotiation timeline and the specific contents of the redress package. Her contribution is prepared material on the same bill: it describes the deed, the apology and the redress in parallel to him rather than engaging anything he said — it neither builds on, corrects nor disputes his account (she gives a different signing date and a different negotiation length without acknowledging his). Beyond a courtesy gesture at the occasion, the speech would read identically had any other member spoken before her, so it sits in the low band, lifted to 0.3 only because it is squarely on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith opened the first reading by setting out the claims history and the contents of the settlement package — "The settlement includes $5.5 million of financial and commercial redress." — and this statement does not take up any part of it.

acuity.statement: The history of the town being built is a sad one for Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu, with so much promise but, actually, so much let down, as we see in this bill here today, which gives effect to the Deed of Settlement, signed many years ago but, as my colleague who has just spoken mentioned, initiated many, many, many decades ago.
acuity.explanation: Luxton explicitly takes up the preceding speaker's point that the claim long predates the Deed of Settlement and does something with it — he folds Tuiono's 1877 history into his own framing of generational loss, and elsewhere notes "We've heard contributions today about the alienation that's happened on both sides of the Kaimai." But the engagement is one strand only; the bulk of the speech (Te Aroha's tourism history, the Waikato Wars, the redress provisions) is prepared material that would stand unchanged whatever Tuiono had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "this issue had come to Parliament in 1877 under the Native Affairs Act"

acuity.statement: This bill is a result of many long years—I was going to say 15, but we’ve heard, actually, it goes back to the 1800s.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft audibly revises her own prepared figure against what an earlier speaker established — she had a timeline of 15 years and corrects it to the 1800s on the strength of Tuiono's 1877 petition evidence. That is visible engagement with the content of a preceding turn rather than a mere reference to it, and the sentence could not have been delivered had Tuiono said something else. It is a single correction, though, after which she returns to prepared material on whakapapa, rohe and the broadcast tower, so this is partial rather than sustained responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "this issue had come to Parliament in 1877 under the Native Affairs Act"

acuity.statement: Look, this is, I think, an important step, and it is great to see, now, having this first reading. I would like to, of course, thank the negotiators on both sides, bringing to an end 15 years of negotiations on this process, which I think will be a welcome relief and provide that certainty, that confidence, that this legislation going forward will bring finality to those historic claims, putting a line under some of the deeds that happened in the past, the unfortunate situations that we saw that impacted significantly on Tumutumu.
acuity.explanation: Kaipara's preceding speech set out a specific account of the Crown's wrongs — confiscation after the Waikato war, individualised title breaking collective ownership, unhonoured reserve promises, the taking of the Te Aroha waiariki — and what the redress acknowledges. Van de Molen's speech takes up none of that. It is about his own connection to the region, local tourism, the negotiators and the Meads Cup, and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said about the history. It stays in the 0.1-0.3 band because it is at least prepared material squarely on the bill under debate, with a gesture at 'the unfortunate situations that we saw that impacted significantly on Tumutumu'; there is no strand of Kaipara's argument that can be pointed at as engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Oriini Kaipara spoke about the Crown's confiscations of Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu land ('That is the legacy that this redress acknowledges—a legacy of confiscation and broken promises') and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Welcome to the House, and the speeches this morning have already spelt out much of the historical facts that are known to Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu, as well as the Crown. They don’t capture the fullness, though, of much of the story and the history that I know Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu and many of the other hapū and iwi of that rohe continue to carry.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the content of the preceding turns — Kaipara's historical account of the confiscations and Van de Molen's remarks — accepts that they state the agreed historical facts, and then qualifies them: they do not capture the fullness of the history the iwi and neighbouring hapū carry, which is a limitation he attributes to what could be negotiated with the Crown. That is a real engagement with one strand of what was just said, and he glances again at 'the many places that members have already mentioned in the House this morning'. It is not higher because he does not contest any particular claim and the bulk of the speech is his own prepared story about the naming of Neve Te Aroha, which would have been delivered whatever preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is the legacy that this redress acknowledges—a legacy of confiscation and broken promises" — Oriini Kaipara's account of the historical grievance, which Henare says is accurate as far as it goes but does not capture the fullness of the history.

acuity.statement: I do not want to get too political on this, but while it’s lovely to hear the acknowledgments of the Government, please take heed. Please take heed and consider some of the legislation we are considering now that could land us back in this situation.
acuity.explanation: She takes up one strand of what the Government speakers before her said — their acknowledgments of historical alienation — and does something with it, turning the acknowledgment into a warning that current legislation risks repeating it. She does not engage the specific content of Rima Nakhle's immediately preceding speech (mandate timeline, Papakura Marae), and the rest of her turn is prepared material on the settlement, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith (quoted by her in this debate): the Minister's "acknowledgment of alienation and 'the undermining of cultural structures over the years'", echoed by Rima Nakhle's acknowledgments of grave loss

acuity.statement: I want to acknowledge too, though, that this isn’t the end, and there isn’t anything in the world—as my colleague Cushla Tangaere-Manuel said—there is nothing that will make right what happened.
acuity.explanation: She names the preceding speaker's specific claim that the redress can never pay for what was taken, adopts it across the benches, and draws a consequence from it (that this is only the next step in a chapter). The engagement is pointable and would read differently had Tangaere-Manuel argued something else; it is agreement rather than development, and the remainder of the speech is prepared material on the rohe and the Crown acknowledgments, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "this redress we are offering here today—$5.5 million, 18 sites—will never, ever pay for what has been taken"

acuity.statement: It is 15 long years that it has taken for Ngāti Rāhiri Tumutumu to reach this point, but, as others have said, it’s been a lot longer than that; this is just the Treaty settlement part.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the timeline Nakhle put on the record — mandate in 2011 to deed in 2025 — restates it as 15 years and accepts Nakhle's qualification that the grievance long predates it. It engages one strand of the earlier turn and then returns to her own prepared recital of the deed's contents, so a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "mandate was recognised in 2011, but as we said, the deed was signed this year" and "that in no way undermines the decades of struggle in order to get to this point"

acuity.statement: The challenge for many of us tangata whenua and tangata Tiriti is that with every Treaty settlement read in this Whare, we find ourselves standing between sorrow and hope, between what was taken and what is being restored.
acuity.explanation: Kaipara follows a substantive turn by Marcroft, so she is eligible. Her speech is on the matter under debate — the third reading of the Ngāti Paoa Claims Settlement Bill — and she explicitly notes it is a reflection that applies to 'every Treaty settlement read in this Whare', which is the mark of prepared material rather than engagement. She engages no part of Marcroft's content: nothing on Caulerpa, the Mahurangi contamination, the kōura survey, or the mayoral-vote comparison. Where she does respond to someone, it is to Herearoha Skipper's words at the morning whakatau, not to a preceding turn in the debate. The speech would read identically had Marcroft said something entirely different about this bill, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because it is squarely on the item before the House and acknowledges those who spoke to the journey, but gestures at no argument made in the chamber.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jenny Marcroft spoke about the Caulerpa infestation in the Hauraki Gulf, Watercare's sewage spills into the Mahurangi River, and the Waiheke Marine Project's crayfish counts, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Much like my colleague, I also have on the hotline Herearoha Skipper, and I want to acknowledge her today, because so frequently whenever anything is happening in particularly our moana space, we want to know immediately what it is that Ngāti Paoa has to say about that and the positions that we should be taking and considering in our mahi as parliamentarians.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick's speech is largely prepared Green Party material on the settlement, but it demonstrably takes up strands of the turn immediately before it: she picks up Peeni Henare's acknowledgement of Herearoha Skipper and builds her own account of working with her on the moana onto it, and later explicitly extends his 'give it to Māori woman' observation to the post-settlement entity board. That is partial engagement — she takes up one thread of the preceding turn and then returns to her own prepared argument about Te Tiriti and the inadequacy of settlements. She does not engage any claim or argument of Henare's, because his turn was largely acknowledgement rather than argument, so this sits at the middle of the band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I also want to acknowledge Herearoha and my tuahine Mihingarangi." — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: This bill confirms the finality of these claims. That’s important not just for the Crown but for you too. You deserve closure and certainty for generations of effort to get to this point.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows a substantive turn in which Swarbrick argued at length that the settlement 'does not and cannot represent justice', that the redress is 'nowhere near adequate', that Te Tiriti is 'not a thing to be settled', and that the settlement process itself 'fans the flames of conflict'. Her speech engages none of that. It is prepared ACT material correctly on the subject of the bill — the deed, the redress, the historical record — and its emphasis on 'finality', 'closure and certainty' passes directly over the opposing case just made without acknowledging or rebutting it. The speech would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before her and whatever they had said, though it is at least squarely about the matter under debate, so it sits in the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chlöe Swarbrick argued that "This does not and cannot represent justice, because it is a mere drop in the bucket of what was stolen" and that Te Tiriti and He Whakaputanga "are not things to be settled; they are things to be honoured", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It is no doubt difficult in one of the most tumultuous Governments that we have seen as Māori. Some have talked about attacks, but those of you who know me will know that, prior to politics, my time was spent in education, and this has been one of the most difficult weeks, as this Government, a National Government, has removed Te Tiriti o Waitangi from our governing bodies in ngā kura o Aotearoa.
acuity.explanation: Bidois closed by claiming a proud and continuing National record on Treaty matters. Halbert takes up that strand directly, contesting it with a contrary action by the same Government in the same week (removing a Te Tiriti requirement from school boards), and he accepts Bidois's framing that today is a good day while disputing the wider record — 'one step forward and two backwards'. That is partial engagement: the rest of the speech is prepared material about his own whakapapa, Mōkai Pātea and Northcote that would have been delivered whatever Bidois had said, and he does not engage Bidois's substantive points about the deed, the $23.5 million, or the 'peanuts into plantations' argument. Pointable engagement with one strand, then a return to prepared material, so mid-scale rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "National does have a very proud track record of Treaty settlements, and they will continue" — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: Chlöe Swarbrick talked about it too, and I want to acknowledge what she was saying: there’s such a sacrifice from our people. We subsidise this country in terms of the Treaty settlements. You’re talking about iwi taking 2 or 3 percent of what the settlement was worth.
acuity.explanation: Jackson takes up the quantum of redress that the preceding speaker presented as a good outcome and argues it represents only 2-3 percent of the loss, explicitly naming the argument of a previous speaker and carrying it forward rather than restating it. That is genuine engagement with a strand of the debate, but it is one strand among a largely prepared, ceremonial speech, and he never engages van de Molen's own "strong track record" claim directly — a partial engagement, not a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "cultural redress with the return of 12 culturally significant sites, 23 and a half million dollars" — and, as Jackson names it himself, Chlöe Swarbrick's earlier argument about the sacrifice borne by iwi (her turn falls outside the supplied window).

acuity.statement: I want to want to want to wrap up by doing a mihi to Kerrin Leoni too, because I thought that, Jenny Marcroft, was a bit uncalled for there. Kerrin Leoni actually got 76,000 votes—77,000 votes—and she was the co-chair for Mr Hon Peeni Henare’s Tāmaki Makaurau electorate, so thank you, Kerrin, for your commitment to the kaupapa.
acuity.explanation: This is directly contingent on what another member said: he names the member, identifies the remark he objects to, and supplies a specific vote figure to answer it, then does the same for Swarbrick's mayoral run. The speech would have to change if that remark had not been made. Marked down from 1.0 only because the engaged turn cannot be quoted from the window, so the exact claim being corrected is inferred from Jackson's own account of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft's dismissive remark about Kerrin Leoni, which Jackson identifies and rebuts ("I thought that, Jenny Marcroft, was a bit uncalled for there"); Marcroft's own turn is not contained in the supplied window, so no verbatim fragment of it can be given.

acuity.statement: I rise to speak on the second reading of the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill, and, like other speakers so far in this second reading, where the usual custom is to talk about what happened at select committee, I also was not on the select committee. However, I have read this bill a couple of times and gone through it. The history is, as my colleague Teanau Tuiono has described, important to learn.
acuity.explanation: Luxton follows Tuiono and picks up one strand of what Tuiono actually said — that this is a heavy, painful history that we should all learn — naming him and then extending it with his own reading of the raupatu record and of the same two tūpuna, Te Rangiātea and Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu, that Tuiono singled out. He also takes up Tuiono's framing about not having sat on the committee. But it is agreement and parallel narration rather than engagement with Tuiono's arguments: nothing takes up the claim that the Treaty is about ongoing relationships rather than an end point, the call for Government MPs to reconsider the education-sector changes, or the point that $19 million is a minuscule sum against what was lost. Much of the speech would stand unchanged whoever had preceded him, so this sits between a glance and a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "This history is incredibly painful and I want to acknowledge your resilience in that."

acuity.statement: I also stand in acknowledgment for the tupuna Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu and te Rangiātea. I am related to Tini Te Whareaitu and the Tamaka whānau, who my kuia was, and I hope this goes some way towards lifting the trauma of what the whānau and the hapū and the iwi have had to endure.
acuity.explanation: Marcroft's preceding turn was built almost entirely around the statutory pardons for these two tūpuna and what the pardons recognise. Ngarewa-Packer takes up that same strand and adds to it — her own whakapapa connection and what she hopes the pardon achieves for the whānau — so the engagement is pointable. But it is one strand of a largely prepared contribution (Parihaka day, settlements as capped, mana motuhake) that does not otherwise take up Marcroft's claims, and would read much the same whoever had spoken before. Partial engagement, not rebuttal or development of her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "it’s those pardons that I would like to speak to, particularly, today: the pardon for the two Ngāti Hāua ancestors, Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu and Te Rangiātea."

acuity.statement: We also recognise that this deed is what Ngāti Hāua iwi members have themselves agreed to: over 96 percent of valid votes. That matters because our job in this place is not to impose what we think justice looks like for tangata whenua but to follow the directions and decisions of iwi themselves.
acuity.explanation: Carter picks up the ratification-vote figure Marcroft cited and does something with it — turns the mandate into an argument about the House's duty to follow iwi decisions rather than substitute its own view of justice — which also meets Ngarewa-Packer's complaint that iwi are 'told and dictated what to do' in settlement processes. That is genuine engagement with one strand of what preceded her. It stops short of 1.0 because she does not contest or correct either preceding claim (she restates the figure slightly differently without addressing the discrepancy) and the rest of the speech is prepared Green Party material on the historical account and Te Tiriti.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jenny Marcroft: "their people voted 97 percent in favour of Te Pua o Te Riri Kore and the establishment of the post-settlement governance entity"

acuity.statement: It was really important that the Māori Affairs Committee heard from those—particularly those who were against the bill and the settlement—but, afterwards, I’d have to say that we were satisfied that what we heard from the negotiators from the trust addressed all of those issues.
acuity.explanation: Rurawhe follows a substantive turn by Bates in the same second-reading debate, so he is eligible. His contribution is squarely on the matter under debate — the select committee's handling of submissions, Whakapapa Island, and the agreement with Ngāti Tūwharetoa — but it engages no part of what Bates actually said. The passage would read identically whatever Bates had argued; it responds to select committee submitters, not to the preceding speaker. Prepared material on the right subject, with a clear gesture at the debate: low band, not zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates spoke about the statutory pardons for tūpuna Te Rangiātea and Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu and about the book Fragile Foundations, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Financial redress is important, but it’s not everything. There is so much more. Through this process, injustices are acknowledged, like the people of Ngāti Hāua being pushed out of Heretaunga, like the execution of your tupuna Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu in 1846—“when the ink was barely dry”, as Tinka says, on the Treaty of Waitangi—and the incarceration and subsequent death in custody of Te Rangiātea.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne speaks third, after substantive turns by Bates and Rurawhe, so she is eligible. The speech is clearly about the bill before the House and even nods at the select committee members' work, but it engages no claim or argument made by either preceding speaker — it is prepared acknowledgement and narrative that would be word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before her. That places it in the low band on responsiveness, independent of the fact that the content is on-topic and the debate is a consensual one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe had just described the Māori Affairs Committee hearing submitters opposed to the settlement and the trust's agreement with Ngāti Tūwharetoa over Whakapapa Island, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise as the final kōrero that's going to be given in the second reading of this settlement bill that we're considering today, the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn by Peeni Henare, who set out a personal and historical account tied to the bill — his grandfather's Anzac Day commemorations at Taumarunui, the wrongful conviction of Te Rangiātea named in the bill, Mātene Ruta Te Whareaitu, and Pōmare's care for unjustly imprisoned leaders. There was content available to take up. Her speech instead delivers prepared material of her own: the select committee's site visit, the tenor of the submissions, a reference to an earlier remark by Minister Goldsmith, and a closing quote from a submitter. It would read word-for-word the same had Henare said something different about this bill, so it engages no part of his contribution. It is not a 0.0, because it is squarely about the matter under debate and gestures at the debate itself — she positions herself as the final speaker in this reading and refers to the submission process and to another member's earlier contribution — which puts it at the top of the unengaged band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare spoke about his grandfather Sir James Hēnare's Anzac commemorations at Taumarunui, about Te Rangiātea's wrongful conviction as mentioned in the bill, and about Pōmare taking food to Māori imprisoned unjustly by the Crown, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: How does he reconcile his statement that the Government is still committed to the Paris agreement with the Government’s announcement late last night that it will remove reference to “contributing to the global effort under the Paris agreement” from our climate change laws?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact commitment Seymour had just asserted one turn earlier and puts a specific, dated fact against it, demanding he reconcile the two. The question could not have been asked in this form had Seymour answered differently; it is wholly shaped by his preceding reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Yes, the Government is committed to the Paris climate agreement as it signed up nine years ago." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Does she think forecasts from the Ministry of Social Development and the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet are wrong, that show she is failing to meet her own target and that she will be 40,000 people over by June 2029?
acuity.explanation: Upston defended her target by leaning on a forecast; this question turns the same instrument back on her, naming the agencies whose forecasts contradict the target. It engages the specific move just made rather than the general topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The pre-election fiscal update had unemployment at 5.3 percent. Today, it was announced at 5.3 percent." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Why is she cherry-picking the best number that suits her, when she has said “Forecasts aren’t reality”, and the reality is things are worse?
acuity.explanation: Characterises and challenges the selection of figures Willis had just recited in place of answering, and pairs it with Willis's own prior line about forecasts. It engages the manner of the preceding answer rather than the substance of the fast-track claims, so it is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Auckland port expansion permitted with 140,000 being supported over the coming decades. It has seen the Milldale housing development fast tracked, supporting 3,500 jobs" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: How can she stand by her target when figures released today show unemployment at a nine-year high, job seekers have increased every quarter, and she is nowhere near meeting her own target?
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the standing-by claim Upston had just made and supplies counter-figures against it, though it leaves her 83,000-off-benefit number untouched. Engaged on the central claim, not on the whole answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Yes, I absolutely stand by our target of 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker support by 2030." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: If she’s happy to use pre-election forecasts, will she compare her recessionary minus 1.1 percent growth rate to that in pre-election forecasts, which was 2 percent?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the asserted recovery and tests it against a growth figure, which is engagement with one strand of the answer; but the premise it opens with (that she is happy to use pre-election forecasts) was not something Willis had said in the preceding turn, so part of it is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I particularly stand by my statement that with a hard-won economic recovery now under way" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: Is the 160,000 unemployed people—the highest in 30 years—a sign that her economic plan is working?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. Willis had just made a detailed migration argument and this question neither accepts, disputes nor acknowledges it, moving instead to a fresh unemployment statistic. It would have read identically whatever Willis had answered, so it sits in the low band, lifted off the floor only because it remains on the economy under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued that net migration of New Zealand citizens rose by 38,000 in the 21 months before the Government took office against 5,800 in the 21 months since, and this question does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: No genuine opposition parties will be allowed on the ballot and it’s clear that people will be forced at gunpoint to vote. The regime has in recent weeks passed three repressive laws criminalising the criticism of the elections, and there are currently teenagers in jail because they dared to criticise the elections on Facebook.
acuity.explanation: Twyford speaks immediately after Peters moved the motion, and takes up the motion's two stated grounds directly — the absence of genuine Opposition parties on the ballot and the repressive laws criminalising criticism of the elections — supplying the specific detail the motion asserted in general terms (three laws, passed in recent weeks, teenagers jailed for Facebook posts). The speech would have had to change had the motion rested on different grounds, so engagement is close rather than merely topical; it falls short of 1.0 because it extends and corroborates the motion rather than doing anything with it in dispute, and the surrounding passages read as prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "repressive laws have been passed criminalising public criticism of the elections" — Winston Peters, moving the motion

acuity.statement: What everybody said was that this is a sham election. It is not a general election; it’s a generals’ election, and they highlighted that for a number of reasons. One of them is the fact that the military junta itself controls less than a third of the country.
acuity.explanation: Tuiono follows Twyford and picks up Twyford's exact formulation — 'not a general election; it is a generals' election' — but does more than echo it: he supplies grounds Twyford did not give (the junta controls less than a third of the country, it is guaranteed 25 percent of the ballot and chooses who else appears on it, and the phasing can be moved around). That is engaging the content of the preceding claim and building on it. Not 1.0, because the engagement is agreement-plus-addition and much of the rest of his turn is mission recollection and acknowledgements that would have stood whatever Twyford had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is not a general election; it is a generals’ election" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: Well, ACT is fixing what matters in this Government, and, for our children, nothing matters more than a good education.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows a substantive turn by Chris Bishop, who argued at length that Labour's newly released capital gains tax is not 'narrow', that it will hit almost every business with commercial property, and that Labour has not learnt the lessons of its last term. McClure takes up none of that: no engagement with the CGT, with the 'narrow' claim, with the commercial-property examples, or with Bishop's closing question. Her speech is prepared ACT material on the education curriculum, and it would be word-for-word identical whatever Bishop had said. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 only because it keeps up the broad theme of criticising Labour's record in government ('For the past six years, under the Labour Government, our education was in a steady decline'), which is a gesture at the matter the previous speaker was pressing. There was a real opportunity to score across the range here — a general debate speaker can and often does pick up the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop argued 'Almost every business in the country will be affected, but he says "Don't worry, don't worry—it's all under control."' about Labour's capital gains tax, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Let’s talk about banks—and I think I’ll make it exciting for you. The recent banking inquiry has concentrated on increasing competition, but there is more work to be done.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn (Andersen) made a detailed argument about unemployment, youth joblessness, jobseeker means-testing and cuts to trade training, and invited the next speakers to answer it directly ("maybe some of the other debaters this afternoon can enlighten us"). Wilson's turn opens a wholly separate topic — bank profits, mortgage margins, Kiwibank and scams — and engages no strand of her argument. The one backward reference, "scams, which were mentioned earlier", points at some earlier speaker, not at Andersen's claims. Substituting any other argument on unemployment for her turn would leave this speech word-for-word unchanged; it sits in the 0.0-0.3 band. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it is a general-debate contribution that does gesture at the earlier debate, and 0.1 rather than 0.3 because there is no gesture at the matter the preceding speaker actually put. Nothing here is scored for the quality of his banking argument or its civility — those are other instruments.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen spoke about the unemployment figures, youth joblessness and the removal of jobseeker eligibility for 18- and 19-year-olds, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Here’s the first credibility fail for the Labour Party. The $700 million raised on average per year will not be enough to fund free doctors visits for all 5.3 million New Zealanders three times a year, plus all the other health initiatives they’re promising with their CGT grab.
acuity.explanation: Henare's immediately preceding turn made two linked claims: a capital gains tax on property profits after 1 July 2027, and three free GP visits for every New Zealander funded from it. Brewer takes up exactly that pairing and does arithmetic against it, putting the CGT's annual revenue at $700 million and arguing it cannot cover three visits for 5.3 million people plus the other health promises. That is engaging the content of the specific claim just made, not merely naming the opponent or the topic — had Henare promised something else, or not costed the GP policy against the CGT, this passage would have to change. Marked down from 1.0 because the funding rebuttal sits inside an otherwise largely prepared speech (the fire-engine song, the Chambers column, the 2023 Hipkins quote) that engages Labour's announcement in general rather than Henare's own argument. Scored on engagement only: whether the $700m figure is right is veracity, whether 'Trojan horse' is fair is rigor, and the mockery is civility's business, not acuity's.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we will give our families—every person in this country—three free GP visits" — Peeni Henare (who also said "part of our plan is a capital gains tax")

acuity.statement: Let’s talk about Labour’s capital gains tax (CGT). It is the wrong tax, at the wrong time, for the wrong reasons. It will not build a single extra home for New Zealand, it will not lift productivity, and it will make it harder for New Zealanders to save, to invest, and to grow.
acuity.explanation: Paul's preceding turn was a sustained argument about why the State rather than the market should own and manage public housing, including the claim that the Crown can borrow more cheaply to build. Lu opens a prepared case against the capital gains tax and engages no part of that argument; the only glancing overlap is that a CGT 'will not build a single extra home', which does not take up anything Paul said. The speech would read identically whoever had spoken before, so it sits in the unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul argued 'why should the State own and manage public housing?' and that the market 'doesn’t have social or environmental obligations', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Don’t you like it when Labour tries to rewrite its own history? Labour’s like an arsonist who then complains about the fire brigade’s efforts to extinguish the fire. Let’s run through Labour’s track record and what they left this Government.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn (Lu) ran the same prepared themes Bidois now runs — $66 billion of COVID spending, no detail until after the election, cannot trust Labour on tax — and Bidois restates them in parallel rather than engaging them, adding his own figures without taking up or developing anything Lu argued. He engages nothing of Paul's housing argument either, and names Labour as a target rather than addressing a claim. Re-stating a colleague's figure is a reference, not engagement, so this stays in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nancy Lu: 'During the COVID period, the Labour Government spent $66 billion.' Bidois repeats the same $66 billion framing as prepared material rather than engaging what Lu did with it.

acuity.statement: It is a targeted tax on investment property and on commercial property, and what have we heard in response from the Government? Mistruth, disinformation, and, frankly, hysteria about what it might entail. So what I want to do today is set the record straight.
acuity.explanation: Russell follows Bidois, who characterised the Opposition's alternative as 'tax more, borrow more, and spend more'. She takes up the tax strand of that attack and frames her speech as a reply to the Government's characterisation of the capital gains tax, then delivers what is plainly prepared material — a list of what the tax will not apply to — rather than engaging Bidois's specific claim about borrowing and spending or his growth figures. She answers the topic rather than the claim, which is the middle band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: 'Tax more, borrow more, and spend more—tax more, borrow more, spend more.'

acuity.statement: The vexed issue of the application of the Official Information Act (OIA) to Parliament is one that members with long memories will know has been around for a while, and the proposal in the Parliament Bill is not to make any changes there. There is a case that Parliament should be subject to the Official Information Act; it applies to everything else, basically, including school boards of trustees, for example.
acuity.explanation: Takes up precisely the point Webb asked him to address: confirms the bill makes no OIA change, concedes there is a case for coverage, then explains the disentanglement problem that has blocked it. The answer would be different had Webb raised a different submission.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the usual grounds for transparency under the Official Information Act still don’t apply to these agencies" — Webb explicitly invited the Minister to speak to the OIA exclusion.

acuity.statement: I think this is, for me, my final contribution on this part. It's actually about clause 211, which replaces section 80 of the Public Finance Act.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the same part of the bill) but engages no part of the answer just given — it is a new line of questioning that would read identically whatever Bishop had said about the OIA.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just explained why no one has been able to formulate an OIA carve-out for Parliament and that the OIA is therefore excluded from the bill; this turn does not take that up, acknowledge it, or test it, and opens a fresh question on clause 211 instead.

acuity.statement: The member asked earlier about an Address—how that works. An Address is prepared by the Speaker to reflect the House's resolution about its contents. In practice, it's prepared beforehand to reflect the recommendations of the select committee.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific procedural answer Webb said he was curious about, including a worked example (the Ombudsman's appropriation). Directly keyed to the question asked rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "I’m a little curious—I probably should know—what an address to the Governor-General would look like in this House"

acuity.statement: The Leader of the House commented on the new section 26EB, inserted by clause 203, and particularly in terms of the consultation that happens before a determination is made on the specific appropriation. I did note that the Council for Civil Liberties, in their submission, asked the question of what participation the public would have in terms of inputting into the appropriate amount of appropriations, if you like.
acuity.explanation: Clearly on the matter under debate and framed as a question to the Minister, but no part of the argument in the immediately preceding turn is engaged, and the remark it does reach for is not locatable in the window, which caps this in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing pointable in the preceding turn: Chris Bishop had just dealt with the form of an Address and the reporting requirements reproduced in new section 45FA, and this statement does not take either up. It reaches back to an earlier remark of his on section 26EB that falls outside this stretch of the debate, so the thing engaged cannot be pointed at here.

acuity.statement: I wasn’t familiar with Treasury instructions either, Dr Webb, but I now know slightly more than I did five minutes ago. The advice I’ve received is that Treasury instructions largely follow accounting standards, so it just really relates to the accounting treatment of the way in which things are done.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific constitutional worry Webb raised, narrows the scope of Treasury's power to accounting treatment, and names the one provision under which instructions may issue. Entirely shaped by the question just asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "is it appropriate for Treasury to be able to tell Parliamentary Service and the Office of the Clerk how to do their job?"

acuity.statement: In relation to Vanushi Walters’ point, it will ultimately be over to the select committee that considers the appropriations of the Officers of Parliament Committee or whatever select committee the House determines to reflect public input. My own view is that there probably is a bit of a role around public input in a way that there hasn’t been in the past.
acuity.explanation: Answers both halves of her question — where public input can enter, and that the special committee did not adopt the Council for Civil Liberties' mandatory-consultation proposal — and volunteers his own position on it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "the question is really to the Leader of the House about whether that was considered and, if not, what sort of influence the public can have in this process"

acuity.statement: Clause 219 seems perfectly sensible: that we move to internet instead of newspapers. I am unsure about clause 218 replacing section 6, section 6(2)(c), where it talks about “the contact details of the person or their representative”, and why it has an address rather than just email and phone number contacts.
acuity.explanation: Within the same committee debate and squarely on the bill, but indifferent to what preceded it — the questions would have been put in identical terms whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just answered Webb on Treasury instructions and Walters on public input into appropriations, and this statement takes up neither; it opens an unrelated set of questions on the citizens initiated referendum clauses.

acuity.statement: That old chestnut—that’s right. There hasn’t been that many of them, and those that we have had have not often times been—well, I was about to say they’ve been ignored, but I think that’s probably a bit unfair actually.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand about whether citizens initiated referenda still do any work, conceding how few there have been and half-withdrawing the claim that they are ignored, but then drifts into recollection of 1999 rather than addressing the clause-level questions or whether the mechanism should continue.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "what is the role of a citizens initiated referendum when we have petitions? Is it something that we think will continue?"

acuity.statement: So, what we have is that the Electoral Commission must return it within two months, which means five months if there’s an election on—it’s one of those fantastic drafting things where two months means five months—but that’s quite a long time. I just wonder if, Minister, you’ve considered whether that’s appropriate.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific justification for shifting the count to the Electoral Commission and does something with it: accepts the premise (the Commission is the right counter) and then traces a consequence the Minister did not mention, pinning it to the exact provisions (new section 18(4), clause 226, subsection (5)) and converting the two-month deadline into five months in an election year. The speech would be different had Bishop defended a different clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "the responsibility for counting of the votes and working out the number of electors and the registered number of voters and all that stuff"—that’s the Commission’s core job; that’s literally why they exist"

acuity.statement: In relation to Dr Duncan Webb’s point around the two-month versus five-month glitch in the system, it was probably true. But I suppose the lesson, the take-home point out of that, is don’t organise a citizens initiated referendum for election year; organise it for the off-years.
acuity.explanation: Engages the precise point just put to him, concedes it is probably correct, and offers a reason the consequence is tolerable. The answer is flippant rather than substantive — but acuity scores engagement, not the quality of the reply, and this reply exists only because of what Webb said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the Electoral Commission must return it within two months, which means five months if there’s an election on"

acuity.statement: But the status quo is that they use a sample so that we don’t have to go through the laborious process. Again, let’s put the people who are expert at that in charge of it; in relation to New Zealand, that’s the Chief Statistician. So that’s what we do.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Webb's objection — defending sampling as the status quo administered by the expert agency — but answers the policy topic rather than the specific worry about projecting a defect rate across 400,000 signatures, and the surrounding passage drifts to the 10 percent threshold, which Webb had not questioned. Partial engagement you can still point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "I’m wondering whether it’s appropriate for the Electoral Commission to not verify each signature but to simply verify a few and project that across all"

acuity.statement: I’m advised that this clause 231 replacing section 8(b)(vi), in relation to section 8(b)(vi)(B), “personal information obtained by a parliamentary security officer”—I’m advised that’s intended to be included, after consultation with the Privacy Commissioner. It’s to make it clear that any information obtained by a security officer through a search or security action on the precinct—which we dealt with a couple of weeks ago—is subject to the Privacy Act, essentially.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the clause Webb raised and explains the security-officer limb he identified, so the engagement is real and specific. But Webb asked two different questions — the Office of the Clerk and the Parliamentary Corporation — and neither is taken up here, which is why Webb has to ask again. Engagement with part of the argument, not the claim actually put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "That amended section 8(b)(vi)(B) is the new bit." — and his two questions, on whether the Office of the Clerk and the Parliamentary Corporation fall within the Privacy Act

acuity.statement: Is the Minister confident that the Office of the Clerk is not subject to the Privacy Act?
acuity.explanation: Hears that the reply dealt with a different limb of the clause and re-puts the unanswered question in one sentence, narrowed to the single point left hanging. Brief, but it exists wholly as a response to what the Minister just failed to cover; vagueness is not in issue and precision is not what is being scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I’m advised that’s intended to be included, after consultation with the Privacy Commissioner" — an answer about the security-officer limb only

acuity.statement: Perhaps we could take that one on notice, Dr Webb? I mean, I don’t want to particularly hold the debate up. The officials are checking. We think the answer is no, but perhaps we can take it on notice and get back to you.
acuity.explanation: Meets the question head on rather than deflecting past it: states the working answer, flags that it is provisional and that officials are checking, and undertakes to return. The content is directly shaped by the question asked a moment earlier.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Is the Minister confident that the Office of the Clerk is not subject to the Privacy Act?"

acuity.statement: Anyway, I now have the answer to the question on the last part, and I hope the committee will indulge me so I can answer it. The Office of the Clerk is subject to the Privacy Act 1993.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the specific answer the earlier turn asked for, interrupting his own prepared material on the Legislative Council Abolition Act to do it — and in doing so corrects his own provisional "we think the answer is no". The strongest form of responsiveness: the chamber is told the thing it asked to be told.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Is the Minister confident that the Office of the Clerk is not subject to the Privacy Act?"

acuity.statement: Well, the member the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, I think, knows that bills have dates in them as they go through the process, but they get updated to the Royal assent. So when it gets eventually to the Governor-General, it will say “Parliament Bill 2025”, and it will eventually become the Parliament Act 2025.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's first specific point — the year in the short title — and answers it directly by explaining the drafting convention that dates are updated at Royal assent, which is exactly why no Amendment Paper was needed. The reply would not exist if Webb had raised something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Firstly, the Act when it’s an Act will be the Parliament Act 2025, not 2024. Just wondering why he didn’t tidy that up with the Amendment Papers"

acuity.statement: Part 9, as the member rightly notes—he’s quick on the uptake—is in relation to the citizens initiated referenda, and it will be because of the variety of things that need to happen between the Clerk and the Electoral Commission. And the Electoral Commission is obviously getting ready for an election next year, so there will be a range of other things going on as well, and I think a huge amount turns on that. That’ll be the reason.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the reason Webb asked for on clause 2(2)(c) — Electoral Commission readiness and Clerk coordination ahead of next year's election — engaging the specific question rather than the general topic. Slightly short of 1.0 because it does not address Webb's suggested alternative hard dates of 30 June 2026 or 1 January 2027.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "But is there any reason why you thought an Order in Council was needed there rather than just setting a hard date?"

acuity.statement: The short answer to the member the Hon Julie Anne Genter’s question is no. As the member herself acknowledges, exemptions, by definition, start to chip away at the integrity of why you have congestion pricing—it works, the more people pay, because that affects behaviour. And the moment you chip away and say, “Well, you are exempt and you don’t have to pay, and you don’t have to pay, and you don’t have to pay.”, by definition, you diminish the utility of the scheme.
acuity.explanation: Answers Genter's Amendment Paper 376 squarely with a no, and does something with the concession she herself made about a narrow approach — turning it into the reason why the further exemption is refused. He goes on to engage her disability case and the line-drawing problem directly, so the speech is shaped by what she argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "We absolutely agree with the bill taking a narrow approach to exemptions. However, the bill, we think, could make exemptions for mobility parking permit holders."

acuity.statement: I just reflect on something that the member who resumed her seat over there said, that she wouldn’t expect ACT to support an amendment to support people of the disability community. Well, actually, our starting point is, we certainly would, because at least two ACT MPs have people living with disability in their family. Our empathy and compassion for the disability community is long and strong.
acuity.explanation: Points precisely at a claim in the immediately preceding turn and contradicts it with a reason. It engages an aside about ACT's likely position rather than Genter's substantive case for a mobility permit exemption, so it is a partial but clearly pointable engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I wouldn’t expect members from ACT to support it"

acuity.statement: As Tangi Utikere pointed out, this is all about getting the ability for there to be public buy-in and political support at a local level, because a congestion charge will not be brought in unless local authorities are able to get it over the line.
acuity.explanation: She names the strand of Utikere's speech about building multipartisan/local support and extends it into her own argument that scheme boards need more flexibility over exemptions to make the charge politically deliverable. The speech would have to change if Utikere had argued something else — she adopts and builds on his specific reasoning about the disability exemption rather than merely citing him. Not a 1.0 because she does not rebut or qualify any part of it; she absorbs it into prepared material about Auckland Council's submission.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "given that this is something that we’re looking to try and get some multipartisan support around this bill" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Well, the member the Hon Julie Anne Genter, I think, makes the right point, which is that we've been waiting 20 years for this.
acuity.explanation: He takes Genter's specific '20 years' point and does something with it — inverts it into an argument against her conclusion, reasoning that a 20-year wait is precisely why the scheme should not be compromised with exemptions. That is engagement with the content, not a mere reference, and the turn could not have been given if she had not made that point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’ve been waiting 20 years for this, Minister—20 years" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: Now, London clearly had to make political compromises along the way, but just because London did it and other countries did it, does not mean that New Zealand has to.
acuity.explanation: This is a direct rebuttal of Genter's central claim that every jurisdiction with a congestion charge has a disability exemption and they have all worked: he concedes the comparative fact, supplies a counter-figure on London's non-payment rate, and denies that the overseas precedent is binding. The argument is built entirely around the claim just made and would be unrecognisable if she had argued otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "virtually every jurisdiction that has brought in a congestion charge has some form of exemption for people with disabilities, and they have all worked" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I’d just like to acknowledge Julie Anne Genter’s clarification. I withdraw my comments that she was nasty towards the ACT Party, and I’d like to just record her acknowledgment of the ACT Party’s microeconomic chops.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the precise thing Genter had just said — her disavowal of any intended insult and her remark about ACT's staunchness on exemptions — and acts on it by withdrawing his earlier characterisation. Clearly contingent on her turn. Held below 1.0 because what he engages is the personal strand of her speech rather than her substantive argument about disability exemptions and scheme-board flexibility, which he leaves untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wasn’t intending any insults in my comments" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: The member makes a good point around rebate schemes, which, potentially, are a way of reallocating distribution—you know, people who are affected by it. Actually, I'm advised that new section 65Z(2)(d) inserted by clause 4 requires an analysis of the distributional impacts as part of the scheme.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Hernandez's specific question about distributional impact analysis and his rebate-scheme suggestion, and does something with both: accepts the rebate point as a mechanism for reallocating distribution and supplies the clause of the bill (new section 65Z(2)(d)) that already requires distributional analysis. The reply would be different had Hernandez asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has there been a distributional impact analysis done on the impact of congestion charging" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: I'm interested in the Minister's analysis of the percentage of vehicles that would be likely to have mobility stickers. I think you were talking about the fact that surely we don't want 50 percent of vehicles going through these schemes to be let off, but surely if the proportion of people is somewhere between a quarter and a fifth, depending on whose figures you take, the likelihood of them travelling at congested times is not as high.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's mobility-exemption reasoning directly, disputing the quantitative premise behind it (the share of vehicles with mobility permits, and their likelihood of travelling at peak) rather than restating a position. Not a full 1.0 because she then adds several new prepared questions about capital expenditure and scheme duration that are indifferent to what Bishop said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The other point I'd point out is the Total Mobility scheme, which provides very generous subsidies to people who have disabilities, for example." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I do not believe that schemes will fall over at a council level because people with disabilities will be subject to a congestion price. I just do not believe that will be the case.
acuity.explanation: Answers precisely the question Wade-Brown put — whether refusing mobility exemptions would deter councils from adopting a scheme — and gives his direct judgement on it, conceding he could be wrong and could revisit. The answer could not have been delivered without her specific question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder if the Minister would address the question of whether not allowing mobility exemptions could actually make a council less likely to proceed with the scheme." — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: I am disappointed in the Minister’s answer, but I accept it. The issue we haven’t talked about, of course, are the buses, the rural school buses. There might not be many of them to be exempted because the current Government seem to be cancelling all the rural school buses anyhow, so the narrow approach to the exemptions will be very narrow indeed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Bishop's just-stated refusal to allow exemptions and extends it to a category he had not addressed (rural school buses), but does not engage the Minister's actual reasoning about diminished scheme utility, and the rest of the turn moves to prepared questions on new sections 65C(4) and 65D that are indifferent to what preceded.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the moment you start exempting groups or people, you could find any reason to" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: I wanted to thank the Minister again for responding to the issues. We had some quite good discussion around a number of issues that were raised by the select committee. That was one. Another one was the governance arrangements, and the third one was the way in which any revenue was going to be spent. The committee was quite strong on those, and the Minister responded to those, and I thank him for that.
acuity.explanation: Follows Bishop's turn in the same committee-stage debate and takes up one strand of it — how scheme revenue is to be spent, plus the exemptions point — acknowledging the Minister's response rather than engaging its reasoning, before moving on to a separately prepared privacy question from a colleague. Partial, pointable engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The bill, essentially, envisages revenue generated from the time of use being funnelled back into mechanisms in order to provide transport choices for people" — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Obviously, the Privacy Act applies to other information that is collected, which has been amended many times, and I think that it works quite well.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific question Foster had just put, addressing the residual gap it raised — information collected beyond the charging purpose — by pointing to the Privacy Act. The reply would have to change had Foster asked something else; short of 1.0 only because the assurance is general rather than evidenced.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'd just like to ask the Minister if he can give the public some assurance that there are going to be no issues with privacy around this scheme" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: The Minister has rightly noted the cost of congestion being in the order of a billion a year, maybe, for Auckland. The Minister might realise that the cost of harmful air pollution in Aotearoa is upwards of $10 billion a year.
acuity.explanation: Same debate, and there is a gesture at the Minister — borrowing his congestion-cost figure as a comparator for air pollution — but no part of the preceding turn is engaged; the material is her prepared case for Amendment Paper 374 and would read identically whatever Bishop had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop's preceding turn answered Andy Foster's privacy question under new section 65ZF, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: The Minister’s talked about the support across the House, and that that is certainly my perspective here, which is why I’m working my way through different aspects that haven’t been touched on.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows a substantive Bishop turn that argued congestion pricing must not be loaded with emissions-based charges and that disability exemptions are unnecessary for social licence. He picks up only Bishop's passing remark about cross-House support, uses it as a transition, and then moves to prepared questions on new section 65E consultation — engaging no part of Bishop's actual argument. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the preceding turn, which is the 0.3 band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s why I’m really pleased that I think I’m right in saying we have unanimous support for it across Parliament." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: The member Tangi Utikere makes good points. In relation to public consultation, look, this is local government’s bread and butter. This is what they do, I would argue, probably far too much. I think it's relatively straightforward; the scheme board, before they submit something to the responsible Minister, have to do public consultation. My expectation would be that they'd be relatively comprehensive.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked two specific questions: what minimum level of public consultation a scheme board must undertake under new section 65E(1)(a), and by what process the Minister would signal a need for further information under 65F(2)(c). Bishop takes the first question directly and answers it — he states his expectation (comprehensive) and explicitly declines to prescribe a number of months, which is the answer to the question asked — and then goes on to address 65F(2)(c) as a catch-all read in light of (2)(a) and (2)(b). The speech would be entirely different had Utikere raised a different clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question for the Minister is around expectations for the level of public consultation that a scheme board must undertake before they even submit that to the Minister." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I do want to pick up on what the previous member Tangi Utikere has mentioned in terms of clause 6A of this bill. I think it is important for the Minister to respond to the fact of what that implies in this particular instance, but I also want to check that this particular section is to do with when a car is travelling and potentially has an unpaid toll or unpaid time of use charge, using vehicle surveillance equipment.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's clause 6A point by name, presses the Minister to answer it, and then extends it with a related question about whether the surveillance-equipment provision treats tolls and time-of-use charges alike. It engages the specific clause rather than the general topic, but the engagement is a hand-off plus an extension rather than a rebuttal or resolution of Utikere's drafting point, and the rest of the turn is his own prepared questions on clauses 8 and 10.
