acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "what is proposed to be inserted here is “the fact that”. Now we don’t have that for the toll."

acuity.statement: I’ll have a crack at the last one first because Schedule 4 of the Legislation Act lists those pieces of legislation that need to be confirmed by a deadline, which, I think, from memory, is clause 4 in that legislation confirmation. So it’s the idea that a regulation that is made must be confirmed by a deadline, otherwise it automatically expires.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight to the question just asked and explains what the Schedule 4 listing actually does — the confirmation-by-deadline mechanism — which is directly responsive to the executive-overreach concern. Short of 1.0 only because it explains the mechanism without taking up the review-provisions strand of Xu-Nan's question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I’ll be really interested to know from the Minister about what that particular regulatory-making power would look like, so that we don’t see an executive overreach."

acuity.statement: The question around the use of the terminology “the fact that”, if Mr Utikere goes to the original provision in the Land Transport Act, section 145(1)—ironically, before the phrase “a toll has not been paid” is the phrase “the fact that”. So it’s a consistency between the two.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the precise factual premise of Utikere's drafting objection by pointing to where the disputed phrase already sits in section 145(1), turning the inconsistency complaint into a consistency argument. The answer would be unrecognisable if the preceding speech had said anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "It doesn’t say, you know, after “the fact that a toll has not been paid”, but for some reason we have “the fact that a time of use charge has not been paid”."

acuity.statement: So this inclusion will include other entities that enforce time-of-use charging schemes in accordance with an order. They may well be local authorities or road-controlling authorities, but it does capture those entities that may fall outside of that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question of why the new 'entity' wording is needed when existing bodies already hold enforcement-authority status: it is there to capture entities that fall outside the existing definitions. Squarely on the claim put to him, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "is it actually required that they be identified or is there, effectively, a transfer or transference of that status if the entity themselves has that elsewhere in legislation?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I thank the Minister for those responses and the clarification. I just have one further point on this section, and it’s in relation to clause 7.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's answers in a blanket thank-you and immediately pivots to new prepared material on a different clause. The acknowledgement is a gesture at the exchange rather than engagement with the substance of the correction he had just received on 'the fact that', so it sits at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "So it’s a consistency between the two." — acknowledged as a clarification but no part of its content is taken up before moving to clause 7.

acuity.statement: I do have a similar question to the previous speaker Tangi Utikere, but, I think, from a different perspective. In Part 1 of this bill, people have talked a lot in terms of the consultation mechanism, and so there is a pertinent question of whether 12 months is sufficient when we’re looking at the ability to bring this bill into effect.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise proposition Utikere put — whether the 12-month commencement is appropriate — names him, and turns it the other way: Utikere argued the period may be unnecessarily long because the preparatory steps could begin at Royal assent, while Xu-Nan argues it may be too short for consultation to finish. The speech would have had to change if Utikere had raised a different point, so this is real engagement rather than a reference; it stops short of 1.0 because he does not rebut Utikere's reasoning about which steps need lead time, he simply opens a second front on the same clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does he believe that the 12-month provision, or the first anniversary of Royal assent, is appropriate?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: My understanding is that the particular phrasing used in the commencement date is the preferred phrasing provided by the drafters of the legislation to indicate a 12 month or a one year or a first anniversary after the Royal assent.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the answer to the specific drafting question Xu-Nan asked — why the clause says 'first anniversary' rather than '12 months' — rather than dismissing it as the interjectors did. It engages the exact content of the question asked and would not exist had Xu-Nan not asked it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What is the difference between 12 months, or one year, and the first anniversary?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Now, the reason for that length of time, to Mr Utikere’s question, is to allow for sufficient time both for, I guess, local authorities to prepare for what this might look like in their area but also to allow for a series of regulations to be developed and put into place prior to the commencement date.
acuity.explanation: Answers Utikere's actual contention head-on: Utikere said the preparatory steps could begin at Royal assent so the delay may be unneeded, and Meager identifies the step that cannot — the regulations that must be made before commencement — which is the substantive rebuttal the question invited. Short of 1.0 only because he does not reach Xu-Nan's follow-on question of what happens if a year proves insufficient.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "A lot of the steps that are being outlined in the bill are steps that could be done as soon as Royal assent is actually given" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I’m sure the Minister wouldn’t be so arrogant as to say he wouldn’t answer questions on any given section, because every section, of course, is part of the legislation and properly appropriate for debate in this House and scrutiny in this committee of the whole House stage.
acuity.explanation: Seymour had just announced he would take questions on Parts 2 and 3 but not debate those clauses during Part 1. Webb's opening takes up exactly that declared intention and disputes its legitimacy, arguing every section is properly open to scrutiny at committee stage. Had Seymour instead said he would answer anything, this sentence could not have been delivered — the speech is shaped by the turn it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t intend to engage in any debate on those clauses through this part" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: To say that this is about the exercise of stewardship over regulatory systems is duplicitous. In fact, it’s the opposite. This is a way to clog up the system to make it harder to pass laws that we like and you don’t.
acuity.explanation: Seymour read the purpose clause aloud and rested on it as the bill's stated aim. Webb takes that exact phrase and inverts it, asserting the real effect is to obstruct legislating rather than to steward regulation. This engages the content of the quoted clause, not merely the topic, and would have to change if Seymour had defended the purpose differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "(ii) the exercise of stewardship over regulatory systems;" — David Seymour, reading clause 3(1) as the bill's purpose

acuity.statement: Thank you. Just following up on questions in relationship to clause 3(2), I’ve noticed that there are some definitions in there, but it seems to me like “high-quality” wasn’t defined in the bill, and so I’m just wanting to get an explanation as to what definition the Minister would be using when it comes to high quality.
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up the strand Xu-Nan opened — the undefined term "high quality" in clause 3 — and presses it on the same clause, later naming Xu-Nan and his "responsible regulation" point. Engagement is real but largely reinforcement of the same question rather than doing something new with it, so mid-high rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what does the Minister actually mean when we're talking about high quality legislation?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Just a short contribution from me in relation to the clause 3, “Purposes”, section, clause 3(1)(c). I just have a question for the Minister in relation to the intersection between this clause and the reference to Part 5 of the Legislation Act 2019, within that clause.
acuity.explanation: On the clause under debate, and so not wholly unresponsive, but it engages no part of the two preceding definitional arguments; it is prepared material on the same provision. Sits in the 0.1–0.3 band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that "high-quality" and "responsible regulation" lack definitions in clause 3, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate line on clause 3(1)(c) and Part 5 of the Legislation Act.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chairman. My contribution and questions for the Minister for Regulation are also focused on clause 3, and they are building on an earlier contribution that we’ve had from a Green Member of Parliament. It is around this development of high-quality legislation.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly builds on the Green member's definitional argument and then does something with it — supplies the Law Society submission's point that "quality" is undefined and appears nowhere outside clause 3, and cross-references Belich's Legislation Act 2019 line. Short of 1.0 because much of the turn is prepared material rather than engagement with the specific reasoning offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "it seems to me like “high-quality” wasn’t defined in the bill"

acuity.statement: So to address “high quality” first: it, indeed, is defined in the Act. If you read a little bit further on, it goes on to say that “The purposes of this Act are given effect to only by—(a) setting out principles of responsible regulation;”.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact claim put by three members — that "high quality" is undefined — and contests it on its own terms by pointing to the subsequent subclause as the definition. The answer would be different had the preceding speakers argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "the word “quality” is not defined in the bill, and this term is not used outside of clause 3"

acuity.statement: There's also a question about how this law will interact with Part 5 of the Legislation Act—what the relationship will be—and that was Camilla Belich who asked that question. Clause 5 deals with how Parliament can scrutinise secondary legislation. This bill—and, again, this comes in a later part—provides for consistency assessment statements; those, you could think of as being similar to regulatory impact statements but guided more strongly by the principles set out in statute by this bill.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific question Belich put about the relationship between the purpose clause and Part 5 of the Legislation Act, and supplies the mechanism (consistency assessment statements) by which that relationship is said to operate. Squarely engaged with the content of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "is he intending for the entire of Part 5 to be upheld through the overseeing and control powers in other parts of this legislation"

acuity.statement: My question is: did the Minister look at alternative models for how the board could have been appointed, and alternative models for how different functions and how different set-ups could have accommodated the function of this Act and the function of the Regulatory Standards Bill to support the task of Parliament in scrutinising legislation?
acuity.explanation: Hernandez follows a substantive turn by Webb on the same clause 3 purpose section, but engages no part of Webb's circularity or verbosity argument. His questions on alternative appointment models (Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, Climate Change Commission) are prepared material that would read identically whatever Webb had just said. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 because it is squarely about the clause under debate and he ties his questions back to the Minister's stated purpose.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that the Minister's quality test in clause 3(2) is circular and that the purpose section is verbose, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a separate line on board appointment models.

acuity.statement: I’d just like to reiterate what my colleague the Hon Duncan Webb said in terms of the circular nature of the definition of “high quality” that the Minister has given us that hasn’t really provided the House with that clarity.
acuity.explanation: Woods picks up the specific strand of the preceding debate — Webb's circularity point about the definition of "high quality" — and adds something to it, citing the Law Society's substantive submission on clause 3 and the fact that clause 3 is the only place the term appears, so the House has no later chance to scrutinise it. It is partial rather than full engagement: she restates and buttresses the point rather than developing it against a counter-argument, and then moves to prepared questions on clause 4 that are indifferent to what preceded her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "he essentially said, quality will be achieved if you do what is set out in clause 3(2). That just seems entirely circular, because there is no actual quality test in there."

acuity.statement: Vanushi Walters spent a lot of time debating the principles—as I’ve indicated, I’m very happy to do that in the appropriate part, which is Part 2—for our current purposes, in the preliminary provisions there is a reference to the principles, but their content or definition is in another part, where I’ll be really happy to debate it.
acuity.explanation: Seymour correctly identifies what Walters' contribution was about (the content and genesis of the clause 3 principles) and gives a located reason for not engaging it now — that the principles' content sits in Part 2 — which is a real engagement with the strand of her argument rather than a mere mention of her name. But he takes up none of her specific points: the omitted definite article, whether the list is exclusive, or the comparison with the Bill of Rights Act's derivation from the ICCPR. Partial engagement that then returns to his prepared framing, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question is also in regards to clause 3. This is setting out principles of responsible regulation." — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: I accept the Minister will no doubt explain in further detail, either now or later, that there is a small chunk of the Act which is about the work of the Regulatory Standards Board, essentially, asking for information and undertaking inquiries, for which they do have legal powers, but the important part of the Act is that you must provide these consistency and accountability statements, that you must consult, and that you must comply with these principles.
acuity.explanation: Webb follows Seymour, who had just answered the circularity charge Webb himself was named as making, and does not engage that answer at all; he opens a fresh line on clause 4(1)(h). The speech is squarely about the bill under debate and gestures at the Minister's anticipated reply, which lifts it off the floor, but it would read identically whatever Seymour had just said. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour argued that the charge his definition of "high-quality legislation" is circular "is a mistake" because high-quality legislation is "adherent to the principles, which can be found in Part 2", and this statement does not take that up — Webb opens a new point on clause 4(1)(h) instead.

acuity.statement: They are sensible amendments, ones in which we’d like to understand whether, on these two particular amendments, the Minister will entertain them, and, if not, what his reasoning is for not—for not wanting to clarify and make it crystal clear that it is the Ministry for Regulation that is the responsible ministry here and whether or not we can clarify that interface.
acuity.explanation: Woods takes up Seymour's blanket refusal to make changes and presses it down onto two named Amendment Papers, demanding his reasoning on each rather than accepting the general answer — a pointable engagement with what he just said. Against that, the bulk of the contribution is prepared description of the two amendment papers and their lodgement times, and she does not rebut Seymour's actual stated ground (that the bill comports with the principles agreed at second reading). Engages one strand, then returns to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t intend to make changes to that at this time." — David Seymour

acuity.statement: OK. Well, I mean, I think probably people can interpret the word “see”. It’s only three letters; two of them are the same. It’s been around for a long time. I think we’ll just keep it simple. But thank you.

The reply would be different had she raised a different drafting point, so it is squarely responsive. Not 1.0 because he does not engage her underlying concern that the clause's intention would be better articulated as "as provided for or consistent with", resting instead on the word's familiarity. Dismissiveness and brevity belong to other attributes; here only the engagement is scored.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I wondered if he or his officials would consider a clearer word, as opposed to “see”"

acuity.statement: We haven’t really nutted out the definition section, which is the real nuts and bolts in this part. The other section that I’m going to talk about in this contribution is actually really important, and it’s what is excluded.

He engages none of that — no concession, no rebuttal that clause 5 is inadequate — and opens instead on prepared material about Schedule 7 exclusions. It stays within the Part 1 debate and the first sentence is a gesture at the state of that debate, which places it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Seymour addressed Webb's own amendment, pointing him to clause 5's definition of "regulatory standards Ministry" and saying "You just had to turn two pages to see the answer to your question, then you could have saved time drafting that amendment", and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: No, no, you newbies haven’t actually engaged in these treaty validation bills. It’s a quite different exercise of this House’s authority. One of the fundamental principles in it is that you can’t rewrite the treaty obligations that the Crown has entered into; it’s a yes/no question. That’s why it shouldn’t be subject to this framework.
acuity.explanation: Luxton's interjection carries a real challenge — that excluding treaty validation bills reduces the House to rubber-stamping the executive. Webb takes that content up directly and answers it: the House's role in such bills is a different exercise of authority because the Crown's treaty obligations cannot be rewritten, making it a yes/no decision, which is precisely why the regulatory filter does not fit. The reply would have to change had Luxton put a different objection. The "newbies" jab is a Civility matter and does not reduce the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "If the executive says it, we just have to approve it?"

acuity.statement: Finally, the Hon Dr Duncan Webb raised a few very important points in terms of what is included in the excluded legislation in Schedule 1A, but, while the Minister is considering it, I want to check two other things that the Hon Dr Duncan Webb didn't mention.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's immediately preceding argument about which legislation should sit in the Schedule 1A exclusions and does something with it — accepts the frame, then extends it to two categories (members' bills, local bills/local Acts) Webb left out, naming the specific clause and Parts. The speech would be materially different had Webb raised different exclusions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Duncan Webb: "they are the observations about the exclusions that I think the Minister should carefully consider in terms of how this Act operates"

acuity.statement: He then asked if treaty validation legislation should be exempt, and his argument seemed to be that it might undermine representatives of a New Zealand Government going overseas, negotiating treaties with foreigners, if they felt they might face scrutiny by the people’s Parliament when they got home. I can see why he would be concerned about that from the point of view of a Government representative negotiating overseas, but as a New Zealander back home, I kind of see it from the opposite perspective: that, actually, it is important that if people are going to go overseas and sign up for things on behalf of all of us in our home in New Zealand, then they should be accountable to a set of principles that are designed to protect New Zealanders’ rights.
acuity.explanation: Restates the specific argument put to him, concedes the premise from the negotiator's standpoint, and then inverts it to reach the opposite conclusion. This is engagement with the content of the reasoning, not a reference to the speaker; it could not have been delivered against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Duncan Webb's argument for exempting classes of legislation from the bill — "they are the observations about the exclusions that I think the Minister should carefully consider" (Webb, on treaty validation and other exclusions)

acuity.statement: Finally, there was a proposed amendment by Lawrence Xu-Nan suggesting that the bill cannot override the Treaty of Waitangi or tino rangatiratanga. We have no intention of adopting an amendment like that. It is unclear what that would achieve.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the specific amendment just moved and answers it squarely with a refusal, so one strand is engaged. But it leaves untouched the reasoning Xu-Nan actually offered — that the Bill of Rights Act and Human Rights Act reference international obligations including UNDRIP, and that those Acts likewise do not mention taxes, levies and fees — and moves to prepared material on the Treaty principles work programme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: "no regulation should override, diminish, or reinterpret the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and all regulatory decisions must demonstrate active protection of Māori rights and tino rangatiratanga"

acuity.statement: I, too, want to focus on clause 8, which is stated as the rule-of-law principle in this bill. I was listening carefully to the Minister last night when he was talking about the reason that he decided to implement this bill.

Her material is a prepared audit of clause 8(a)(i)-(v) against the Government's own legislative record, addressed to the Minister's remarks from the previous sitting rather than to the speaker before her; it would read identically whatever Webb had argued. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band, at 0.3 because there is a genuine gesture at the debate and the same clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued that clause 8 is "100 percent silent on how good lawmakers adhere with the most fundamental principles of our country: the very founding document" and moved an amendment on the Treaty of Waitangi, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: Judges have not come out publicly to criticise Governments, to criticise Ministers, or to criticise the legislature, nor do they criticise the executive. They interpret the law through legislation. However, we have seen the executive and the legislature come out and openly criticise the judiciary, which violates the principle of comity.
acuity.explanation: He takes up the same two sub-paragraphs Belich had just raised, 8(a)(iii) and 8(a)(iv), and this passage extends her strand that the executive is the party undermining judicial impartiality, generalising it into a comity argument rather than her specific van Velden example. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding turn rather than with its claims: he neither adopts, disputes nor builds on her evidence, and the rest is prepared questions put to the Minister. Partial, pointable engagement on the same ground, so just below the half mark.

acuity.responding_to: "there should be an independent, impartial judiciary:"; we have heard comments from the Minister’s own deputy leader, Brooke van Velden—the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety—questioning the impartiality of existing Employment Relations Authority members" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: The Government tells us that it is a Government that wants to advance the build out of New Zealand’s infrastructure, but we are in danger, in this bill in clause 8(c), of actually imposing more cost, making it more difficult, and, indeed, imposing uncertainty in a number of those build projects.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Webb's substantive turn on clause 8 precedes hers. She is squarely within the same debate and the same clause, and addresses questions to the Minister, so this is not wholly unresponsive prepared material. But she engages no part of Webb's rule-of-law argument — the speech would read identically had Webb said something else about clause 8 — which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band with a clear gesture at the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "my proposal is simply saying that if you’re going to have a principle of the rule of law, say, ‘the importance of maintaining consistency with the rule of law’" — Duncan Webb. Nothing of this argument is taken up: Webb argued clause 8(a)'s bullet list is a thin, limiting articulation of the rule of law, and Woods moves to clause 8(c) and property/infrastructure without engaging it.

acuity.statement: In terms of Duncan Webb’s question about the definition of the rule of law—and there was quite lengthy philosophical treatise that, I’m sure, must have impressed first year law students back in the day—but here it’s very simple: we have set out a series of criteria that define the rule of law and then said, in clause 8A, that other criteria can also be considered. This is not an exhaustive list; that’s what the law says if you read it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific claim that clause 8(a)'s listed aspects operate as limiters and answers it with a point of statutory construction — clause 8A admits other criteria. The reply would have to change entirely had Webb argued something else, so engagement is high. Short of 1.0 only because Webb expressly pre-empted this answer (the board may test legislation against these principles alone) and that pre-emption is not addressed. The disparaging aside about first-year law students does not lower Acuity — it is aimed at the very argument being engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now I can hear the Minister’s likely going to say it’s OK, we all know that this is a non-exhaustive list of principles." — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: What’s really interesting is to draw out what Megan Woods is actually saying. She says that, if people want stuff to be cheaper, it might be OK to make it cheaper by taking other people’s property and not compensating them for it. This is quite an extraordinary proposition.
acuity.explanation: Engages the content of Woods's Transpower point directly, drawing out what he takes to be its consequence — that cheaper electricity would be bought by uncompensated impairment of property. That is responsiveness, and the recasting of her position as something more extreme than she put it is a question for Rigor, not Acuity. Below 1.0 because her two express questions — whether he considered Transpower's amendments and whether officials advised him on infrastructure interplay — are left unanswered; he engages the premise rather than the request.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Their submission was that they be explicitly excluded from this legislation, that there does have to be some national interest and the national grid needs to be given some protection in that space." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. I also have questions in regards to clause 8 of the bill. I indicated to the Minister earlier during this committee stage that I had questions around the genesis of the principles chosen as compared to the rights that we have expressed in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA).

Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate sits at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul spoke about the meaning of 'equal before the law', Maori prosecution rates and the omission of tikanga Maori from clause 8, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: He went on to say that he has an Amendment Paper to insert a Treaty of Waitangi clause. The Government has no intention of doing that. The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, the Constitution Act, and a number of important Acts do not have Treaty clauses.
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes up one strand of what preceded him — the proposal to write Treaty/tikanga recognition into clause 8 by amendment — and does something with it, giving a reason for refusal (comparable constitutional Acts carry no Treaty clause, and such a clause would reopen a definitional debate). But he frames it as answering Duncan Webb rather than the members in front of him, and leaves untouched Paul's substantive challenges (the equality-of-access and Maori prosecution-rate questions she expressly asked him to answer) and Walters' question about whether these principles or NZBORA take precedence. Partial engagement with a return to prepared ground: 0.5.

acuity.responding_to: 'which is why I've drafted an Amendment Paper to amend this part to include the importance of maintaining consistency with the following aspects of the rule of law, noting that nothing below precludes tikanga Maori being recognised as the original law of this land' — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: Obviously, clause 8 is the absolute work horse of this bill, and discussion as to how it might be improved is not really talking about what isn't in the bill; it’s actually talking about very bricks and mortar of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Webb opens by directly rebutting Seymour's immediately preceding relevance objection — that members were debating matters outside the bill — answering it with the claim that clause 8 is the bill's core and amendments to it are squarely in scope. But after that single rebuttal he moves into prepared material on his two lodged amendments (democratic-society values, delegation of legislative power) that engages nothing Seymour actually argued — the bill-of-rights precedence point, the clause 25 point, or the international-law point all go untouched. One strand taken up, then a return to prepared ground: a mid-band score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "but it’s not actually relevant to this part" — Seymour had just ruled several members' critiques out of scope as being about things not in the bill

acuity.statement: Just before I start on the liberties, I want to check with the Chair, just a point of clarification, that the Minister before did say they were happy to have a debate on access to justice. I wondered if the Chair is allowing that to be a green light for a broader discussion on access to justice in relation to everyone is equal before the law.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes the Minister's specific concession — his stated willingness to debate access to justice — and does something with it, trying to convert it into licence for the very debate Seymour had just declared out of order. That is engagement with the content of the preceding turn, not a mere reference to it, and it is precisely pointable. It falls short of the top band because he explicitly declines to take up Webb's argument ("I want to move on from the rule of law") and because he engages Seymour's procedural ruling rather than the substantive reasoning behind it — Seymour's claim that equality before the law concerns only like treatment in adjudication goes unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "I’m very happy to have a debate about access to law and legal aid and so on in another in another format, but it’s not actually relevant to this part."

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister a question about his drafting choice in terms of looking at what I would call, simple incompatibility with his principles, versus a potential drafting choice he could have made for justified incompatibility. I referenced this in my previous question, but I don't believe that the Minister has responded.
acuity.explanation: Walters engages Seymour's reply closely enough to identify what it omitted: he answered the precedence question but not the sections 4/5/6 engagement question she had put, and she says so and re-puts it, narrowing it to the specific drafting distinction between simple and justified incompatibility and supplying Dean Knight's concrete alternative wording for clause 8 to make the question answerable. The speech is entirely contingent on what Seymour said and would have to change had he addressed the point. Not a 1.0 only because she restates her own prior question rather than rebutting the reasoning he did offer on non-competition.

acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "As I’ve already stated in Part 1, I don’t believe that would lead to a conflict. I don’t believe that these laws are in competition." — his reply to Walters on the Bill of Rights Act

acuity.statement: I’d like to move to the “Taxes, fees, and levies” section, clause 8 paragraphs (d) and (e). It talks about authorising imposition of a fee for a good or service “only … [as it] bears … proper relation to the cost”. How would that function, do you think, Minister for Regulation?
acuity.explanation: Seymour had just worked through paragraph 8(g) (the courts' role), 8(b) (liberty and reciprocal obligations, with the noise-restriction example) and 11(b) (ministerial statements of inconsistency). Luxton takes up none of it: he opens a fresh line of questioning on the fees and levies paragraphs. The call is on the clause under debate, so it is not wholly off-topic, but it would read identically whatever Seymour had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour spoke about paragraphs 8(g), 8(b) and 11(b) — the courts' interpretive role, reciprocal limits on liberty, and ministerial statements of inconsistency — and this statement does not take any of that up, moving instead to the taxes, fees and levies paragraphs.

acuity.statement: That does what the ACT Party does, which is break everything down into individuals. The fact of the matter is that there might be values about the wider society, generally, which isn’t so much about that person’s liberty to go about their business but about building a strong and good society, for which is reasonable to place limits on someone else’s liberty.
acuity.explanation: Seymour had just defended paragraph 8(b) on exactly this reasoning — liberty may be curtailed only to protect another person's liberty, with the obligations 'reciprocal' and the benefits 'mutual'. Webb engages that premise head-on, names it as Mill's harm principle, and argues it wrongly reduces the test to individuals, proposing the 'demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society' formulation instead. Partial rather than full engagement: he answers the framing Seymour articulated but not Seymour's specific noise-restriction illustration, and the rest of the call is prepared material on his tabled amendments to the takings clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "the obligations are reciprocal and the benefits are mutual, and that argument could be extended to free speech or any other law that curtails liberty for reciprocal obligations and mutual benefits."

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask about what the threshold was that the Minister considers for “severely” impaired versus merely impaired. Are there any case law examples he can give on what the difference of those two might be?

Hernandez picks up that exact distinction and presses the Minister on where the threshold sits and whether case law illustrates it, and separately endorses Webb's suggestion by asking why the takings and the taxes/fees clauses are not merged. Not a full 1.0 — he converts Webb's argument into questions rather than doing anything with Webb's reasoning — but the call clearly would differ had Webb spoken differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "they took it from being just any impairment to a severe impairment to make sure we didn’t have just trivial matters clogging up the wheels of lawmaking."

acuity.statement: In the spirit of the speaker who’s just sat down, Francisco Hernandez, I’d also like to move to the good law-making clause; specifically, the importance of carefully evaluating the issue concerned and how that interacts with the effectiveness of any relevant existing legislation in common law—as in, if there is an issue concerned, that there are already laws with it, is that going to the review?

Luxton names him and borrows his short-call manner, then moves straight to a different paragraph (8(j)) on evaluating the issue and the responsible agency. A courteous reference to the previous speaker that engages no part of his argument — scored above 0.1 only because the gesture at the preceding call is explicit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez asked about the threshold for "severely" impaired versus merely impaired and whether good justification and fair compensation are defined, and this statement does not take those questions up, turning instead to the good law-making paragraphs.

acuity.statement: Vanushi Walters raised a question about that, where she said, “Isn’t that undermining Parliament where everyone has a right to submit to Parliament?” I agree with her about that. But if you go back to the purpose statement of the law, which we traversed in Part 1 yesterday, this is designed to improve the quality of lawmaking by furnishing consistency accountability statements. It’s for the purpose of those consistency accountability statements, not all of Parliament’s lawmaking, that we are doing this.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Walters' specific objection — that a "directly and materially affected" consultation test would cut across the universal right to submit to a select committee — restates it accurately, concedes the point, and then supplies the limiting answer: the clause bites only on consistency accountability statements, not on Parliament's own lawmaking. The reply could not have been given against a different preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "everyone—everyone—in New Zealand has the ability and the right to submit their views to Parliament whether they’re materially directly affected or not" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Then Vanushi Walters asked about limits on parliamentary process. She also asked, “Is it early or late in the process?” Again, go back to the purpose. This is to furnish consistency accountability statements. It’s not necessarily putting any restrictions on people early in the process.

Her companion questions, the "reasonably practicable" threshold and whether the pay equity legislation would have fallen foul of it, and her query about the omission of sunset clauses and post-legislative scrutiny, are not taken up at all, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Are we talking about consultation in the early stages of the development of law, or are we also talking about the parliamentary process?" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: If a Minister could not reasonably practicably produce a CAS as part of a Government amendment—because, again, I think that one of the things that we have heard from a previous speaker was that there was a clear difference between what is a Government amendment, which is covered by this bill, and members’ amendments. He neither adopts, extends nor disputes Webb's clause 15 stewardship argument, and his questions would stand word for word whatever Webb had said. Naming a member as having covered something is not engaging the content, so this sits in the unresponsive band rather than at 0.5; 0.3 because the reference is at least a real glance at the turn before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "in my tabled amendment 10.45.05 a.m., I’ve suggested why not just say “a responsible agency”, whether it’s a public service agency or not" — Xu-Nan names Webb's amendments as having settled a point, but does nothing with their content.

acuity.statement: I’m just going to take the advice from the Chair earlier in this committee to move this debate along a bit, because we have rehashed a few topics, and the Minister has been incredibly responsive to those rehashings. I specifically would like to know about Subpart 5 and how the Minister sees clause 24 operating: the Act does not confer or impose legal rights or obligations.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — three substantive member turns precede him, two of them putting detailed questions to the Minister. But his speech engages no part of any of them. Dismissing what came before as rehashed and praising the Minister's responsiveness is a comment on the debate's management, not on anyone's argument, and the clauses he raises were untouched by the previous speakers. The speech would be identical whoever had spoken before him and whatever they had said, though it is at least tethered to this bill's committee stage rather than deliverable in any debate at all, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked the Minister what "reasonably practicable" means in clause 12, what safeguards prevent it being stretched, and when a briefing might be required before the four years are up — Luxton takes up none of it, characterising the preceding turns collectively as "rehashings" and opening fresh questions on clauses 24 and 26 and Subpart 6.

acuity.statement: Similarly, the procedures of the Regs Review Committee; that’s not something this legislation can change. So, no, they would not be required to consider a consistency accountability statement, unless, of course, the Standing Orders Committee decided to make that a requirement for them under Standing Orders, which could happen, but not under this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes Walters' exact either/or — required or merely a relevant consideration — and resolves it directly ('no, they would not be required'), adding the only route by which it could become a requirement. The answer could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "I’m interested to know whether the Minister’s view is that that is required or that it’s purely a relevant consideration and the committee has complete discretion as to whether they consider it or not."

acuity.statement: I want to talk about clause 16, which hasn’t been talked about yet, and I want to talk about the cycle of briefings, and a number of other things.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just answered Webb's own question about why the review duty applies only to Public Service agencies ('That’s because they are the stewards of the vast amount of the legislation') and this statement does not take it up; it announces new ground instead.

acuity.statement: We have a requirement to have an election within three years and three months of the last one, but sometimes in our history we’ve actually broken that cycle and we may well do again, or we may move to a four-year cycle, although that’s not currently the law. The reason it’s four years is precisely so that there is flexibility within the four-year cycle not to have the reporting or the briefing coincide with the election if that’s what the Government of the day wants. His amendment might actually defeat the very purpose that he is trying to achieve, so we certainly won’t be adopting that.
acuity.explanation: Attacks the premise of the amendment just moved — that there is a three-year electoral cycle to align with — and then turns Webb's own stated purpose against the fix he proposed. The reply would have to be rewritten if Webb had argued anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "this be a three-yearly cycle. The reason for that is you’re out of kilter with the electoral cycle"

acuity.statement: I have a short question, and as I indicated to the Chair before, I am moving on in Part 2—I’m now talking about Subpart 4, clause 23. This is around “a chief executive must act independently”.
acuity.explanation: On the bill under debate but indifferent to the turn it follows; the Minister's answer to his own question goes unexamined. Could have been delivered identically whatever Seymour had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just answered Xu-Nan's earlier question ('this bill does not interfere in the workings of the House') and this statement does not take that answer up, moving instead to a fresh clause.

acuity.statement: Of course, you would assume that the Public Service Act prevails in all other purposes.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "This section applies despite section 52 of the Public Service Act"

acuity.statement: When it comes to carry out inquiries, we’ve heard, from one perspective, they can be complaints or members of the public raising it. Can I just check with the Minister for Regulation for clarification: can then a Minister direct the board to carry out an inquiry?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the account of inquiry triggers that Seymour gave and Webb elaborated (complaints, or members of the public) and presses the gap in it — whether a Minister can also direct an inquiry, given the new clause 30A independence requirement. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they can be complaints or members of the public raising it" follows Seymour's "it is to, first of all, carry out inquiries" and Duncan Webb's "it's really unusual to have a complaints-driven inquiry system"

acuity.statement: That turns me back to the amendments suggesting that declarations of inconsistency be outlawed. I don't think that that is necessary, and I was thinking about something that Vanushi Walters said: that the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act was campaigned on through two elections, it finally became law in 1990, and it was another 25 years or so before the courts made declarations of the type that Dr Duncan Webb has referred to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise thing Webb put to him — the proposed new subclause (1A) barring declarations of inconsistency — states a position on it, and supplies a reason drawn from the BORA analogy Webb himself used, arguing the declaration remedy took 25 years to emerge. The speech would be materially different had Webb moved a different amendment or raised a different concern; he also engages Webb's textual reading of clause 24 by pointing to the qualifier 'that is enforceable in a court of law'. Engagement scored here, not the soundness of the inference or the civility of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "my amendment of 11 minutes and 7 seconds a.m., inserts new subclause (1A) in clause 24 and simply says that “no declarations of inconsistency with this Act may be made by any court”"

acuity.statement: We know that, from a secondary legislation perspective, we have the Regulatory Standards Board, and the Minister has already mentioned that, and that is something that is bipartisan. I think there is also another possibility, which was raised by my colleague Francisco Hernandez, when it comes to the Regulatory Standards Board.
acuity.explanation: Follows Seymour's answer on clause 24 and declarations of inconsistency but engages no part of it, announcing instead a move to Subpart 7 and the board's independence. It is squarely on the matter under debate and makes a gesture at the debate by noting what the Minister has already said about the board being bipartisan and a possibility raised by a colleague, which puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom. The gesture is to earlier remarks I cannot point at verbatim in this window, so it caps at 0.3 and is not a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour argued that clause 24 and sections 25-26 are designed to stop the courts' role being expanded, and that an amendment barring declarations of inconsistency is unnecessary; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The Minister mentioned the Standing Orders earlier, and I’m just wondering whether it’s the Minister’s intention to take proposals to the Standing Orders Committee—of course, they’re sitting at the moment—in terms of ensuring there’s clarity about the interaction between this process and the role of Regs Review.
acuity.explanation: A set of clause-by-clause clarification questions on clauses 19, 20 and 22 that engages nothing in the immediately preceding turns by Xu-Nan or Seymour. It is firmly on the bill, and it picks up a Standing Orders remark the Minister made earlier in the debate to ask a follow-up, which is a gesture rather than engagement with an argument put to her. Because the remark being picked up is not pointable in this window, the score is capped at 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked whether the Regulatory Standards Board could sit as an Office of Parliament to preserve its independence, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Earlier during the debate, I asked the Minister whether the secondary legislation included council bylaws, for example, and I believe that the Minister replied in the affirmative.
acuity.explanation: Builds on an answer the Minister gave earlier in the debate and draws out a consequence from it (who the responsible Minister is under clause 35(1)(d) for a council bylaw), which is real engagement with the debate's content, but it engages nothing in the preceding turn by Walters and the ministerial answer relied on is not in the window, so it cannot be pointed at and is capped at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band. On topic throughout; the precision of the Crown fee-schedule question is a specificity matter, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters asked about clauses 19, 20 and 22 and the Regulations Review Committee interaction, and this statement does not take that up; it returns to an earlier answer by David Seymour on whether council bylaws are covered.

acuity.statement: He also raised the question of whether the reports of the Regulatory Standards Board given to the complainant should be redacted in the same way as the ones that are public. That is an interesting point; however, I think sometimes we just have to trust that most people, most of the time, know what they’re doing and are sensible. If you are the Regulatory Standards Board and you expect that a person is going to leak or publish a report, as the Minister has suggested, then you needn’t include private information in that report. Sometimes we don’t need to legislate everything; we can just use common sense.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific amendment to clause 35 by name and content, concedes it is an interesting point, and then supplies a counter-argument aimed squarely at Webb's leak scenario — that the board can simply omit private information rather than have redaction legislated. The speech would have to change entirely if Webb had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "my amendment proposes that in clause 35 you insert a subclause (4), which basically is a mirror of clause 36(2), saying that you can redact on Official Information Act grounds the copy of the report that goes to the complainant"

acuity.statement: I’d reply in the same manner to his suggestion that we should legislate the qualifications of a person on the Regulatory Standards Board. I was pleased to see that he values the knowledge and expertise of economists. A lot of socialists prefer to shoot them, as David Lange once quipped, so that’s progress. However, I also say that the member is actually living proof that we should not take august qualifications as proof of competence. We would rather appoint people who are capable of doing the job as the legislation sets out than specify what those qualifications should be.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the question Webb put about prescribing board qualifications, picks up Webb's own remark about economists, and states the opposing principle — appoint for capability rather than specified qualification. Marked down from 1.0 because a share of the reply is a personal jibe rather than engagement with the Human Rights Act precedent Webb cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "Why have we not taken that approach here to say we need people who have expertise in legislative quality, expertise in the law, and a range of other expertise which we could then debate in this House?"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that all of her excellent education reforms have been signed off by a Cabinet with no less than seven Māori members and that perhaps the views put about in the House today are not the way all Māori think?
acuity.explanation: Seymour is not answering a question put to him, so this is a debate-style intervention rather than an oral answer. It takes up one strand of Ngarewa-Packer's preceding line — her premise that the Cabinet decision signals Māori language and identity are unwelcome — and counters it, but by pointing at the composition of Cabinet rather than engaging the claim about what the decision signals to students. The question would have to change if the preceding questioning had been on different grounds, so it is partially responsive; it is not a close engagement with the specific claim, and the counter is an appeal to who made the decision rather than to its effect.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer: "their language, their culture, and identity no longer belong in the system meant to uplift them"

acuity.statement: However, most of this bill is not about that issue. Most of this bill is not about the groceries. It's not about the supermarkets. This bill is a Trojan horse for watering down—even more—this Government’s version of the fast track.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Bishop's own framing of the bill — that it is about promoting supermarket competition — and directly contests the proportion claim, arguing the grocery content is a small part of a bill whose main effect is elsewhere. The speech would have to be written differently had Bishop not led on groceries; it is aimed at the structure of his introduction rather than at the topic generally.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "It’s very pleasing to introduce this amendment bill for the Fast-track Approvals Act, to promote supermarket competition and to improve the application process so it’s more efficient for all fast-track projects."

acuity.statement: So now what this bill is doing is removing that ability, the one little check in the system for those expert panels to ask for additional evidence and for different groups to come and give them information. That discretion is goneburger with this amendment.
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance of Bishop's "technical and machinery" characterisation by naming the specific amendment she says it conceals — the removal of expert panels' discretion to seek further evidence — and draws out its consequence. This is a rebuttal of the content of his claim about what the amendments do, not a reference to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "It’s a range of technical and machinery amendments that are also aimed at speeding up the application process by up to six weeks, or potentially more in some cases."

acuity.statement: This is not just a simple little bill that's doing a little bit of fixing up and we don't need to worry about it because really it's about good supermarket changes; it is not that. If it was only about supermarket changes, we would be in support of it.
acuity.explanation: Quotes back Bishop's closing characterisation of the bill as simple and straightforward in order to deny it, and then concedes the part she accepts (the grocery provisions) while disputing the rest. Accepting part and rejecting the remainder of the argument just made is the strongest form of engagement with it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "This is a relatively straightforward, simple amendment bill that we want to get through the House so that we can make those machinery and technical improvements"

acuity.statement: Now, anyone listening to the speeches in this House would be forgiven for thinking that according to Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, and Shane Jones, this bill is just about creating a consenting express-lane for new supermarkets to improve grocery competition. Sadly, that’s not what it’s about; that’s not all that it’s about.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific framing Willis had just advanced — that the bill is an express lane for supermarkets to boost grocery competition — names it, and disputes it directly by arguing the bill's stated purpose is not its whole content, then goes on to itemise the roughly hundred other changes she says Government speakers left out. The speech would have had to be written differently had Willis argued something else; she concedes she would support a bill that was only what Willis described. Scored on engagement alone, not on whether the Trojan-horse characterisation is fair or correct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill helps to create an express lane for new supermarkets, to boost competition in the grocery sector." — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: I rise to support the Fast-track Approvals Amendment Bill because we need to get things built in this country. We need things consented faster. That includes supermarkets, where we need to see more competition, where we need to see more choice for New Zealand shoppers so that we can reduce the cost of living.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed critique — that the amendment concentrates ministerial power over consenting, squeezes the expert panel's time and information, and limits appeal rights — and engages none of it. The speech restates the Government's supermarket-competition framing and adds a local roading example; it would read word-for-word the same whatever Radhakrishnan had said. It is at least about the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0. Prepared material on the right subject is not partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Priyanca Radhakrishnan argued the amendment "will introduce a hundred changes that will give Ministers much more power over the consenting process" and limits the right of appeal, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I’m proud to stand here on behalf of the ACT Party to support the Fast-track Approvals Amendment Bill. This bill is about fixing what matters, making sure the one-stop shop for complex consenting actually functions as Cabinet intended, because it turns out that some of the things Kiwis need, like more supermarkets, actually need a bit of a nudge.
acuity.explanation: Genter's immediately preceding turn made two specific, answerable arguments — that a national policy statement on supermarket developments was an available and simpler alternative, and that fast track grants excessive discretion without transparent decision making. Court's opening takes up neither; it restates ACT's prepared case for the bill. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it out of the 0.0 band, but it would read word-for-word the same whatever Genter had said, and there is no gesture at her argument at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued that 'Having a national policy statement was a simple fix that could have addressed any issues' and that fast track is an 'undemocratic' process, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: On that side of the House, all we hear is no. We've heard no to infrastructure, no to airports, no to roads. We've heard no to housing, no to energy projects, no to the supermarkets, because they're not going to vote for it. They said they would, but they won't.
acuity.explanation: This does point at something Genter actually said — her declaration that the Greens will not support the bill — so it is not pure prepared material. But it engages only the fact of her opposition, not any part of her case: nothing on the national policy statement alternative she proposed, nothing on her claim that fast track confers too much discretion, nothing on the ombudsman. Naming the opposition as a target and listing what they vote against is a characterisation, not an engagement with content, which the rubric puts at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at partial engagement. Note this is an Acuity judgement only — the jibe's content is a matter for Focus, not for this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'The Green Party will not be supporting this bill' — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: The last speaker seems to have forgotten about the 7.2 percent inflation that we inherited from them, and we have done a lot of great work to change that.
acuity.explanation: Williams's turn had two strands: a cost-of-living indictment, and a specific procedural ask — split the bill so the supermarket provisions can be debated apart from the fast-track machinery changes, plus the claim that grocery participants can already use the fast-track process so the bill changes nothing. McCallum takes up only the first strand, and by pivoting to the inherited inflation figure rather than disputing her price numbers. He engages the topic she raised and supplies a counter-figure, which is more than a bare reference, but the central argument of her speech (the split, and the redundancy of the new track) is left entirely untouched; his speech would read the same whatever she had said about the bill itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Prices are rising at the grocery store. They're rising in electricity by 11 percent, the highest jump in 30 years." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: On the surface, this bill sounds reasonable. After all, we all want lower food prices and better access to groceries for New Zealanders, but if the Government is serious about improving the lives of all New Zealanders, they should ensure that Māori have equal opportunity.
acuity.explanation: This concedes the rationale McCallum had just given for the bill — competition to lower food prices — and then disputes that the bill delivers it equitably, so it does take up one strand of the preceding turn rather than ignoring it. It is a partial engagement, not a full one: the bulk of the speech is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on section 7, Te Puni Kōkiri's advice and the notification-versus-consultation point, which answers the Government's position generally rather than anything McCallum argued, and his speed/"getting things done" framing is met with a general aphorism rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What we're looking to do here is to allow for more competition in the supermarket sector so that people can lower their cost of living—that's what it's about." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: I invite members across the House to work collaboratively and put aside party politics as we move forward, to ensure that these two bodies are adequately resourced because it benefits us all. No Government lasts forever. Each party will find themselves on the other side eventually, and they will be using those very same resources that the Parliamentary Service and the Office of the Clerk often provide for us.
acuity.explanation: Webb's turn conceded that the funding reform is imperfect because the Government dominates Parliament, so it rests on a convention of cross-party cooperation he hoped would be strengthened. This passage takes up that one strand and supplies a reason the convention should hold — every party will eventually be on the other side and dependent on the same services — rather than merely restating that the bill is good. It engages a single strand and not Webb's wider case (the constitutional significance of the determinative funding say, the absence of iron bars and perspex shields), and the surrounding speech is prepared Green Party material on resourcing and family provisions that would have been delivered whatever Webb said, so this sits mid-band rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "The Government of the day could abuse its position, but we do have a long and strong tradition in this House of those particular committees, those committees that deal with things like Officers of Parliament and the way Parliament operates acting in a cross-party manner and cooperatively."

acuity.statement: It’s great that we’ve got to this point of completing this bill after its gestation across three terms of Parliament. It’s got cross-party support. I think this is about making our Parliament more accessible and more open.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows a substantive turn from Cameron Luxton, who argued for splitting the bill into a repeals bill and a fresh statute and listed the principles it codifies. Foster takes up none of that: he announces a short call, says he made his points at second reading, and offers a general endorsement of accessibility and openness. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Luxton had argued, though it is at least about the bill under debate, so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Luxton spoke about splitting the bill into a repeals bill and a clean-start statute, and praised the Clerk's team and Duncan Webb's committee input, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Duncan Webb made a similar phrase: “It's everybody's House.” So if that is true, then safety in this House cannot be defined only by institutional comfort. It must reflect the realities and the values and the tikanga of all who enter.
acuity.explanation: Kapa-Kingi picks up the openness/"everybody's House" strand that Foster had just put ("more accessible and more open") and does something with it — treats it as a premise and draws out a consequence about what safety in the precinct must therefore mean, before moving to her own prepared Treaty-clause argument. That is partial engagement: it takes up one strand of the preceding framing rather than any specific claim, and the figure she quotes directly (Webb) spoke outside this window. Mid-band, not high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think this is about making our Parliament more accessible and more open" — Andy Foster. She adopts the openness premise and pushes it toward tikanga and safety, then returns to prepared material.

acuity.statement: I think also, in terms of that, what we are seeing as well is the kind of ability for Parliament to make certain decisions—as many people have mentioned—in order to modernise.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan gestures at the debate — "as many people have mentioned" acknowledges the modernisation theme Kapa-Kingi had just developed — but engages no part of her actual argument, which was that the bill lacks explicit recognition of Te Tiriti and that Treaty-based design is needed for the security powers it confers. He proceeds to his own prepared material on budget independence, parliamentary diversity and the Welsh Senedd, and closes by echoing thanks everyone else had already given. A mere reference, not engagement; top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I guess the word “modernisation”, when it shows up, it gives a little bit of hope" — Mariameno Kapa-Kingi. He names the shared modernisation theme but takes up neither her Treaty-clause point nor her argument about the security powers.

acuity.statement: I don't want to go on any further because others have spoken very eloquently about the provisions of this bill, but I would simply remind those listening and colleagues from around the House that although we are individual members of Parliament and we come to this place as members of Parliament, ultimately, we are all parliamentarians and we have a role to play as parliamentarians.
acuity.explanation: Simpson expressly declines to engage the provisions others have canvassed, and his speech bears no trace of the two arguments immediately preceding it — Xu-Nan on one branch of government controlling the budget of the other two, and Kapa-Kingi on the absence of a Treaty clause. What he offers instead is prepared material on New Zealand's 150-year democratic record, a visit to Australia and a reminder that members are parliamentarians. It is about the bill's subject matter, so not a 0.0, but it is indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued that Parliament's ability to bid for its own budget matters because the executive currently controls the other branches' funding, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Look, everything has been said. I concur with all the main points, so to quote Shakespeare, “Brevity is the soul of wit.” I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Rurawhe covering committee amendments, staff tools, the new funding model and the financial veto question — none of which is taken up. A blanket concurrence engages no part of the content; the words would be identical whatever Rurawhe had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe argued for Parliament's funding independence from Government and questioned whether the financial veto should survive, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: There are many Parliaments who don't give security staff on precinct the powers that we have decided to. A point I made in the second reading was it is something I do think we should monitor, not only for the public in terms of their access, but also for the safety of the staff who are in these buildings as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Rurawhe's turn — the new powers and tools given to security officers, and the committee's strengthened monitoring requirements — and adds a qualification that the powers should be monitored for both public access and staff safety. It engages the topic rather than rebutting any specific claim, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on the OIA and accessibility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m happy, for example, that our security officers will have the tools that they need to be effective" — Adrian Rurawhe

acuity.statement: Look, I don’t think there’s very much more to add. I agree with everything that the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe said, and my colleague Scott Simpson. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker but engages no part of his argument — a bare reference plus agreement. Under the rubric a mere reference is not responsiveness; the statement is at least about the bill under debate, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Adrian Rurawhe spoke about the committee's strengthened monitoring and training requirements and the new funding arrangements, and this statement does not take any of it up beyond naming him.

acuity.statement: One of the main provisions of this bill that I want to quickly talk about is that it gives our security officers the powers to do their job more efficiently and more effectively. I want to acknowledge and thank them all, especially today, for what they do. A special shout-out to Tuakana, who I met today, who is a new recruit to the parliamentary security team. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Her turn follows a substantive speech by another member on the same bill, so she is eligible. She lands on one topic McAnulty dwelt on — the statutory powers given to parliamentary security — but engages no part of his argument: nothing about the threat environment he described, the adjustment of the original security provisions after other parties' concerns, or the Standing Orders point he pressed. The remarks are self-contained thanks and a commendation that would read identically after any preceding speech on this bill, which places them in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the subject she picks is squarely the matter under debate and overlaps the strand just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued that the bill's funding provisions remove a theoretical financial veto over Parliament, that Standing Orders consideration should follow the same cross-party approach, and that the security provisions were adjusted after concerns raised by other parties — this statement takes up none of that, though it lands on the same security-powers subject matter.

acuity.statement: The reason is clear: a small number of large banks dominate the market, supporting the kōrero of Dr David Wilson just to my left.
acuity.explanation: Kapa-Kingi takes up the core claim of the immediately preceding speech — that the sector is structurally dominated by a handful of banks — names the member who made it, and adopts it as the premise for her own argument about Māori land trusts. That is genuine engagement with one strand of Wilson's case rather than a bare mention of him. acuity.statement: The Education and Training Amendment Bill is focused on one thing: lifting achievement—lifting achievement so that every Kiwi kid can reach their full potential in school, which will equip them with the knowledge and skills they need to take on life and thrive. Thank you to our Minister of Education for being bold, for being courageous and being game-changing, and for believing in the power of achievement and the power of education to lift our kids from poverty of aspiration.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive critique with prepared commendation that engages none of it — no mention of the Te Tiriti clause, the Teaching Council composition, or the committee-stage process. The speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Tinetti had said; a faint gesture at the bill's purpose keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jan Tinetti argued that the committee-stage amendments removed the requirement for boards of trustees to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi and altered the composition of the Teaching Council, and this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: I just note the last two contributions by Dr Duncan Webb. In the first one, he said that really none of these powers is necessary because it can be sorted out amongst Cabinet Ministers. I made the point that Cabinet has a general view and hopes the Parliament will pass a law reflecting the general view that this central agency should have power to request information. Now, Duncan Webb is saying that the Ministry for Regulation will abuse this power and run unfettered, as though he's forgotten that only a few minutes ago he was saying that of course departments are responsible to Ministers who can sort out matters amongst themselves back in Cabinet.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the substance of Webb's claim that clause 42 confers an unconstrained power and does something with it — sets it against Webb's own earlier position that Ministers in Cabinet can resolve such matters, and answers that collegial moderation is the intended constraint. The speech would be different had Webb argued differently. Not full marks because the specific requests Webb put (a prescribed time frame, a reasonableness test, a dispute-resolution tiebreaker) are left untouched, with the amendments refused as a class rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "So that's a pretty expansive power and I'm very surprised that it isn't limited in some way."

acuity.statement: My second question is specifically around clause 42(1), but it’s also a bolder question because I know that the bill uses similar language in this clause, which is the phrase “necessary or desirable”. Why has the scope been expanded to such a wide extent? I mean, I understand “necessary”, but “desirable” seems to widen that up quite substantially.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the breadth of the clause 42 information-gathering power, which is what the preceding turns were about — but it engages no part of either preceding argument. Seymour's claim that ministerial collegiality is the safeguard goes unaddressed, as does Webb's proposed reasonableness constraint; these are self-contained prepared questions put to the Minister, and they would read identically whatever the previous two speakers had said about the clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Seymour argued that Cabinet and Parliament can give a general direction while responsible Ministers moderate the use of the power, and so no Opposition amendments would be adopted; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I point the member to clause 6A(1), which says “Nothing in this Act”, so clearly, from reading that, the answer to his question is actually in the paper in front of him.
