Then the question of whether privacy applies—well, of course, if the Ministry for Regulation was to acquire information, it would still be governed by the Privacy Act regardless of whether it got it from this mechanism or any other, so I don't see why that would change.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of the questions just put, each on its own terms: the first by quoting the opening words of the clause Hernandez named to show it overrides clause 41(1), the second by locating privacy protection in the Privacy Act rather than in new drafting. Wholly contingent on what the previous speaker asked. Scored for engagement only — whether the reading of clause 6A(1) is correct is a veracity question, and the dismissiveness of "in the paper in front of him" belongs to civility.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "The first is around whether clause 41(1) trumps the earlier clause 6A(1), or whether clause 6A(1) still stands."

acuity.statement: The second point I was going to make is that the difference between why we are discussing the Regulations Review Committee now as opposed to what was discussed last week is that, last week, the report on the briefing on regulatory reform was not publicly available, and it is now publicly available. As a major stakeholder in a lot of these, I thought it was important to address the report that just came out of the Regulations Review Committee.
acuity.explanation: Walters's immediately preceding turn raised the overlap between the new board and the Regulations Review Committee and argued it should be specified in the legislation, and Xu-Nan takes up that same strand, advancing it with the committee's now-public report and its constitutional-overlap concern. But he does not engage her specific proposal (spelling the interaction out in section 41) or her clause 43 cost-of-contractors argument, and the rest of the turn is his own prepared set of three clause questions, so this is partial engagement with one strand rather than a response to what she actually argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “Other members have raised questions about the interaction with Parliament’s Regulations Review Committee” — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: It is interesting: the Minister seemed to suggest that there weren’t going to be many private agencies that administer regulations. As I thought about that, I thought of Serco, that administers a prison, which is just a raft of regulations. If the ministry were to inquire into how the regulations around prisons worked, and asked Serco to provide reports on all of its investigations, inquiries, complaints, and what have you, at no cost, that would, essentially, be rewriting the contract with Serco, which is an unusual thing for the ACT Party to advocate.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Seymour's immediately preceding answer on contracted parties under clause 43(2)(b) — that the power bites only on those performing a statutory regulatory function and is therefore narrow — and tests it with a concrete counter-example (Serco running a prison), then draws out the consequence Seymour did not address: that compelling free provision rewrites the contract. The speech would have to change if Seymour had defended the clause differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Seymour: "it’s only if they are performing a function that is imposed under legislation. What we have in mind is a regulatory function there."

acuity.statement: The particular exclusion question goes to two other classes of people. One is members of Parliament. Now, as members of Parliament, we may not be an agency, but nevertheless we are part of this institution which has regulatory powers. If we’re excluding the House of Representatives, which I struggle to see how it’s an agency as well, actually, shouldn’t we be excluding members of Parliament?
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific rationale Seymour had just given for the clause 44 exemptions — that they exist only to protect parliamentary sovereignty and so the Clerk is covered but the Ministry's powers go no further — and presses its logical extension to members of Parliament. It takes up one strand of the preceding answer rather than the whole of it, and then moves on to the Governor-General as fresh material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Seymour: "the purpose of this exemption for Parliament and its various Officers is simply to ensure that the sovereignty of Parliament is not in any way affected by this law."

acuity.statement: The Minister’s comment was that because it would be a across the public service, the information wouldn’t be shared outside of public entities. However, my understanding of the changes to the Privacy Act is that a notification would still be required. I was just making the point that there’s obviously a cost associated with that as well. So I’m just asking whether that is intended that this would be an additional burden and cost that’s put on those entities as well.
acuity.explanation: Restates the precise reasoning Seymour had just offered — that no third-party notification is needed because the information stays inside the public sector and the Privacy Act obligations travel with it — and disputes exactly that step, asserting the amended Privacy Act still requires notification, then draws out the cost consequence and puts it back as a question. Entirely shaped by what immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Seymour: "I wouldn’t view there as being a need for a notification in that sense, because the Ministry for Regulation is part of the public sector."

acuity.statement: I noted Dr Duncan Webb asking whether an organisation like Serco would face punitive or undeliverable demands for information. I thought that was interesting—the Labour Party’s new-found concern for Serco—but my answer was actually given earlier: just because this power exists for a ministry, to use it under legislation, a ministry still has a Minister.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Webb's specific concern that a contractor such as Serco would face unreasonable information demands, names it, and supplies a substantive counter-mechanism (the contractor's department has a Minister who can intervene, and informing the other chief executive is what enables that). He also rules on Webb's tabled clause 43 time-limit amendment in the same breath. The jibe about Labour's "new-found concern for Serco" is a civility matter, not an acuity one, and does not displace the engagement; the answer would have been different had Webb raised a different objection. Short of 1.0 only because part of the reply is deferred to an answer "given earlier" rather than argued afresh.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "your citizen contractor, who, in the contract, isn’t expected to and isn’t paid to provide all this addition information" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: I want to talk about a clause that nobody has talked about tonight, and that is clause 47, which talks about the powers of the High Court. One of the difficulties is it kind of falls short.
acuity.explanation: Seymour's immediately preceding turn addressed clause 47 directly, including a claim that court adjudication would be a rarely-used backstop because Ministers would avoid the spectacle of departments suing each other. Webb opens by asserting nobody has discussed the clause and proceeds through his own two Amendment Papers without engaging that claim at all. The material is squarely on the matter under debate — the bill's clause 47 — so this is not a 0.0, but the speech would read identically whatever Seymour had just said about the clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Seymour had just said of clause 47 that "we don’t" have advice on the likelihood of adjudication and that "it would seem extremely unlikely" to be used, and this statement does not take that up — it opens prepared material on the same clause as though it were untouched.

acuity.statement: I’ve had members of the Government benches suggesting that Dr Duncan Webb is actually trying to audition for a role on the Regulatory Standards Board, which I find an interesting proposition, but, at this point, I’m not very persuaded, because he asked whether the court should be told in legislation that it can set aside an application. The court can already do that.
acuity.explanation: Takes Webb's first amendment on its own terms and rebuts its premise: the power Webb wants spelled out already follows from "may make the order", so the drafting is redundant. He then takes up Webb's second limb — new clause 47A letting a notice recipient initiate proceedings — characterises it as a "Mexican stand-off" and rejects it. Both strands of the preceding turn are engaged, and the reply could not have been delivered against a different argument. Whether the inference about what "may" implies is sound belongs to Rigor, and the audition jibe to Civility; neither affects the responsiveness being scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it says the court can set aside the notice, so it makes it clear that the court has the power to make one of two orders" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: It may come as a surprise, but I have some amendments on this, and one of them actually suggests that we title this Act—and this isn't a joke title; it's actually quite a serious title—the “Regulatory Constitution Act 2025”. There are two reasons for that: one is that it actually reflects what this piece of legislation will do, which is to change the very structure of our constitution in New Zealand, and it will change the way in which the organs of Government work with and speak to each other.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up the exact strand Seymour had just closed off — the proposed alternative titles — and answers the implied dismissal (that the alternatives are frivolous) by insisting his is a serious title and giving a substantive reason for it. The speech would have to change if Seymour had not refused to entertain renaming. It is only partial engagement, though: Seymour's other and more substantive point, the staged commencement of Parts 1-3 and the up-to-six-month delay for Part 2, is left entirely untouched, and the rest of Webb's contribution is prepared material on the bill's intellectual provenance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government has no intention of entertaining any of the alternative names that members have proposed" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: I stand on behalf of the Green Party to offer our tautoko towards this legislation also. I echo the sentiments of my colleague within the Labour Party around the small changes that are being made that look at patient care and the health and wellbeing of all New Zealanders. But of course, reformation of the entire system is required. I thank the former Minister of Health for reminding the House about the challenges of access to medications, to immunisations, vaccinations across the board, but particularly with COVID-19.
acuity.explanation: Lyndon's opening takes up two identifiable strands of Verrall's immediately preceding speech: the point that the bill's changes are small but welcome, and the pandemic-era failure of the Medicines Act to permit expedited vaccine approval, which she names and credits to Verrall. The engagement is agreement-plus-extension rather than rebuttal, and she moves fairly quickly into her own prepared material on workforce and rural access, so it is partial rather than full responsiveness — but the opening would have had to be written differently had Verrall argued something else, which puts it above the prepared-material band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We saw that in the pandemic, when we had to debate, as a Parliament, retrospective changes to the Medicines Act to get an emergency approval for vaccines" and "our entire regulatory system is out of date" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: We do have concerns, of course, around the Amendment Paper that was tabled without notice really. It's a missed opportunity that the Minister brought it into the committee of the whole, because we could have interrogated and provided community and the health sector the opportunity to have a voice on the amendment that the Minister put forward at a very, very late stage.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific procedural complaint Verrall had just made about the medical-conference advertising amendment appearing at the committee of the whole House stage, and does something with it: it names the consequence Verrall left implicit — that the select committee process, and therefore the sector and community submitters, were bypassed — and adds the unresolved definitional question of what counts as a conference. It is a direct continuation of the preceding argument rather than a mere reference to it, though it extends rather than contests, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "officially, the first I heard about this change was when the amendment got tabled" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Yet, while we support this bill, it was concerning to see a last-minute amendment being added which would add—this is the new addition of clause 12A—the exemption for advertising medicines at medical conferences. I think good process would have meant that this change would have been introduced at the select committee stage so that it would have been adequately canvassed.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Marcroft's substantive supporting speech immediately precedes. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate, but it is prepared material about the committee of the whole House stage and the Minister's amendment, not an engagement with anything Marcroft argued — her Rule of Two case, her prescribing-rights point and her coalition-agreement quote all go untouched. It would read identically had she said something else, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it does orient itself to the stage of the debate it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jenny Marcroft spoke in support of the bill as a 'smart track' resting on the Rule of Two and expanded prescribing rights, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: This Government has been focused on increasing our access to pharmaceutical interventions. When we look at the money we’ve added to Pharmac, we can see we’ve added an extra $604 million for those really important cancer medications and other life-saving medications.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive Green turn precedes it. This is prepared praise for the Government's record that engages no part of the critique just made — not the process objection, not the English-language-jurisdiction point, not the pharmacy-resourcing ask. Substituting a different argument on the same topic would require no change to a word of it. 0.1 rather than 0.0 because it is at least about the bill's subject matter (access to medicines and prescribing), not a wholly transplantable speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that the clause 12A advertising amendment was sprung at the committee stage with no analysis, and that pharmacies need resourcing to make the bill work — this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: That was a very big claim from a very short contribution, which is probably summing up this bill quite nicely—it claims a lot, and doesn’t necessarily do everything that’s written on the till.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim Campbell had just made — that the bill will speed up access to life-extending medicines — and disputes it directly, that the bill claims more than it delivers, which is then the organising thesis of the rest of her speech. The opening would have had to be written differently had Campbell made a different claim, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because part of the engagement is with the brevity of the contribution rather than its reasoning, and she does not yet touch his $604 million Pharmac figure. Scored on engagement only: the sharpness of the jibe is a Civility question and the strength of the inference a Rigor one, and neither moves this.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This is a step that makes very good sense so that we can speed up access to cutting-edge medicines that actually will extend people’s lives and make people’s lives better" — Hamish Campbell.

acuity.statement: This bill is another critical step by this Government to ensure New Zealanders have access to timely and quality healthcare. This Medicines Amendment Bill increases patient access to medicine by introducing a streamlined ratification pathway for medicine approval, the rule of two, allowing safe and effective treatment to reach patients more quickly.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a long, detailed opposing turn immediately precedes. The speech is a prepared restatement of the bill's contents and the Government's intentions; it answers none of the three distinct challenges just laid out, and does not even contest the characterisation of Government contributions as thin. Word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before. 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it describes the bill actually under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued at length that the bill is a largely symbolic technical fix, that ministerial appointments to the Medicines Classification Committee risk politicisation, and that scrapping free prescriptions is the real access issue — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Because of the way our supply chains are often interrupted, some medicines have to be sought that are alternative sources. That means that they are, effectively, unapproved medications and come under what’s called section 29. Previously to this, only a registered medical professional could sign a prescription for those, even if another prescribing authority could prescribe the same medication, because it comes from a different factory, it’s, essentially, not allowed to be prescribed any more.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows a substantive turn by Utikere, so she is eligible, but her speech engages none of his claims. He made two pointed arguments available to her: that the bill's access gains are undercut by the removal of free prescriptions and free GP visits, and that the safeguards and the ministerial appointments to the committee could be compromised or politicised. She answers neither — not even to say the safeguards concern is misplaced. Instead she delivers prepared clinical material on section 29 unapproved medicines and prescribing authority, and closes by commending the bill. Applying the deciding test: substitute a different argument on the same bill for Utikere's and this speech would not have to change a word. It sits in the 0.0-0.3 band, and within that band it is 0.1 rather than 0.3 because there is no gesture at the debate at all — no reference to the previous speaker, no acknowledgment that an objection was raised. It is not 0.0 only because the content is specific to this bill's section 29 changes and so could not have been delivered in a different debate. Note that this low score is about responsiveness alone: the speech is on-policy, technically precise and courteous, and nothing here counts against it on those other questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued that the Government has 'stripped away free prescriptions', that three free GP visits would do more for access, and that the ministerial appointments to the recommending committee must not become 'jobs for the boys' — and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: When we’re looking at multiple authorities around the world that do approve these sorts of medicines already, we should be reassured that those kinds of data can be extrapolated or used here in the Aotearoa New Zealand. I think, in particular, part of the concern with that is, in terms of the pharmacological properties, that we’re still not entirely sure if sufficient work has been done on local disease epidemiology and how that relates to, particularly, Māori populations and Pasifika populations, as other regulatory authorities overseas may not have access to some of those data, bar a few particular regions.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan takes up the same mechanism Stephenson had just endorsed — reliance on two overseas regulators' approvals — and presses on whether overseas evidence transfers to local disease epidemiology, so the engagement is pointable and on the specific device of the bill rather than merely its subject. But it stops short of a rebuttal: he does not address Stephenson's actual claim that this is "a great step forward", nor Stephenson's funding/Pharmac point, and the material is explicitly recycled committee-stage argument addressed to the Minister's answers, not to the preceding speaker. The speech would read much the same had Stephenson said something different about the bill, which caps it in the partial band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This pathway of allowing us to recognise two other highly competent international regulators who have approved a treatment and then expedite it into the New Zealand market is a great step forward" — Todd Stephenson

acuity.statement: I just want to also do a very small recap because again, my previous question to the Minister hasn't had a response or acknowledgment yet, and that is around new section 2A(4), inserted by clause 4, regarding persons outside of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Follows Walters' substantive turn on new section 2A(3) and picks up only her framing complaint of unanswered questions from the last sitting, before turning to an entirely separate clause (2A(4)). None of her Ross Dependency or Niue argument is taken up, rebutted, built on or even mentioned; this is prepared committee-stage material on the same bill, so it sits in the low band with a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there were a few questions I had last time we were considering this bill that I didn’t get a response to" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Regarding the Ross Dependency, Niue, and, also, include there the Cook Islands, persons owing allegiance who are outside of New Zealand are clearly defined. These explicitly include persons who hold New Zealand’s citizenship. Beyond this, it is intended that the status of people in New Zealand’s realm jurisdictions be determined by the common law. Maybe going a bit more tightly defined, in response to the question, a New Zealander in the Ross Dependency will be covered. The status of a foreigner in the Ross Dependency or Niue will be determined by common law.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the two specific questions Walters put — the Ross Dependency and Niue — and does something with them, distinguishing a New Zealander in the Ross Dependency (covered) from a foreigner there or in Niue (left to common law), and extending the answer to the Cook Islands. The speech would be materially different had Walters raised different jurisdictions. Marked down from 1.0 only because it answers the first of Xu-Nan's two questions and leaves the party-liability question on new section 69(1)(1A) untouched. Scored purely on engagement, not on whether the common-law answer is adequate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The question is whether the Ross Dependency counts as being part of New Zealand or not—so whether the lean is on section 3 of the economic zone Act or section 2 of the Crimes Act." — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: I wonder if the Minister could give us some clarity, because there will be those of us from the Cook Islands and Niue who have used our own passports wondering how this would impact us. I heard the Minister saying that it will be left to the common law, but what does that mean?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's answer back and presses on the precise weak point in it — what 'left to the common law' actually means for Cook Islanders and Niueans holding their own passports — and supplies his own case and his child's as the test. This is engagement with the content of the reply just given, not a mere reference to it. Not 1.0 because the follow-up is brief and the bulk of the turn then moves to his own prepared Amendment Paper 431.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The status of a foreigner in the Ross Dependency or Niue will be determined by common law." — Matt Doocey

acuity.statement: Just responding to, I think, probably the latter questions of Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan, I’ve been advised that the usual rules which apply to party liability generally will be applied to section 69, amended by clause 7. There is nothing unusual about the terms, which are regularly considered and interpreted by the courts.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the party-liability strand that the immediately preceding turn put to him and gives a substantive answer on it, so the reply is not interchangeable — but it answers the mechanism (ordinary party-liability rules, familiar terms) rather than the specific point actually pressed, which was why a secondary party faces the same 14-year maximum as the principal. Engagement with one strand, not with the claim; that is the middle of the band, not the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "why is it such a serious penalty for an offence that is not being the main perpetrator but being a party to the offence?"

acuity.statement: I’m just noting that in the Crimes Act, there’s a definition of enemy in section 73, “Treason”, where the definition of treason includes “an enemy at war with New Zealand, or any armed forces against which New Zealand forces are engaged in hostilities, whether or not a state of war exists between New Zealand and any other country;”. I’m just checking whether it’s the Minister’s intent that the scope of liability under section 73 wouldn’t apply in this case, and that that is an active policy decision in terms of the shift from “enemy alien” to “that is at war with New Zealand;”.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the bill under debate and technically detailed, but indifferent to what preceded it: had the Minister answered differently on advocacy or party liability, this passage would be word-for-word the same. There is a gesture at the preceding turn elsewhere in her contribution (thanking the Minister for "the substance of the last answers"), which lifts it off the floor of the band, but acknowledging that answers were given is not engaging their content. Scored on responsiveness only — the precision of the question belongs to Specificity, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey had just answered that party-liability rules apply unchanged to section 69 and that "there is no need to include “advocacy” in new section 78AAA(4A)(a)", and this statement does not take either answer up — it opens a fresh line on the clause 4 "enemy alien" change.

acuity.statement: I'm interested to know whether there are some additional things that are not captured within this legislation that the Government is looking at or aware of that we can remain vigilant of and consider how we can make sure our laws are always kept up to date, because this is essentially the first piece of legislation in some time that we've updated those previous offences.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. She notes the committee process "has been good" but engages no argument or answer made by any earlier speaker in the debate, and the question about an ongoing review programme would read identically whatever had just been said. Not zero, because it is anchored to this bill's coverage gaps rather than being deliverable in any debate on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters had just raised the "enemy alien" definition and the vagueness of the common law reference in new section 2A(2)(b), and Matt Doocey had answered on party liability and advocacy; this statement takes up none of it, asking instead about the Government's forward programme of work.

acuity.statement: It sounds like there may be some agreement in terms of the status of the common law. I think the problem we have is that the current provisions make it feel like the common law position of retaining your obligations of loyalty may endure even if you have renounced, which I think is problematic in the legislation but—yeah, unfortunate that it won't be fixed at this stage.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own concession on the common law — that he agrees clarity is desirable but the bill specifies nothing — and does something with it: names the agreement, then draws out the consequence that the pre-renunciation duty of loyalty may survive renunciation and will go unfixed. She then builds a remedy (an officially induced error defence) on that same thread. This speech could not have been delivered had Penk answered differently, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "there isn't anything, to my understanding, in the legislation that specifies that. I don't wish to go out on a limb and suggest that that's the case definitively."

acuity.statement: But if you are reading it in the context of the Crimes Act, section 76, in terms of treason—as in an individual actively conducted treason, etc.—the penalty’s “not exceeding 7 years”. And if you’re looking at section 77 of the Crimes Act, for mutiny it is no more than 10 years. So I guess the first question to the Minister is: why then is party liability a doubling of the penalty, as opposed to a person performing it themselves?
acuity.explanation: Directly tests the Minister's answer on penalty relativity by putting the specific comparator figures against it — 7 years for treason under s 76 and 10 for mutiny under s 77 versus 14 for party liability — which contradicts the claim that the penalty merely carries across a treason-equivalent seriousness. Not a full 1.0 because the turn also opens new prepared ground on clauses 8 and 10, and the nod to Walters is a mere reference that engages no content of hers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "my understanding is that the penalty referred to has been carried across from the existing law, and it's considered as serious as espionage and treason"

acuity.statement: So I just want to be clear—and I think, to be perfectly honest, the answer is yes. But the question is this: if, on behalf of a foreign power, I organise or participate in a protest which is intended to be disruptive outside a person’s residence—an ambassador would be the most obvious one, but anyone—am I liable for foreign interference and, therefore, liable to 14 years in prison for engaging in a disruptive protest?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate and a sharp question about the interaction of the foreign interference offence with the new residential-protest offence, but it engages no part of the answer just given to him; the speaker flags that he is jumping to a fresh point. Prepared material on the right subject, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk answered Webb's own earlier point on penalty relativity by saying the penalty "has been carried across from the existing law, and it's considered as serious as espionage and treason", and this statement does not take that up — Webb states he is "leaping ahead" to the substantive offence instead.

acuity.statement: That aside, for the average New Zealander who is a citizen of New Zealand who may have come from somewhere like South Africa, in the case of my wife—not yet a citizen—but would she owe allegiance? And, say, in my example where I've got a British passport but also a New Zealand passport, would I have that allegiance to New Zealand? I just want some clarity on those sorts of typical examples for the average New Zealander.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the allegiance strand the Minister had just addressed and presses it further, asking him to apply it to concrete cases (a non-citizen spouse, a dual passport holder). It engages the topic Penk answered rather than the specific limiting claim he made — Penk's point was that allegiance only bites once espionage or treason acts are made out, and Bates does not take that up or test it. Partial engagement, then a prepared constituency-flavoured framing, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "As for the question about the owing of allegiance and whether this would come into play: only if a person has otherwise done the acts constituting espionage or treason."

acuity.statement: As to recklessness, it would require in the usual way that the person would recognise a real possibility—or, in other words, foresee the risk—that their actions would likely compromise a protected New Zealand interest, and then, having regard to that risk, that those actions would be unreasonable. I think, going back to that point about travelling with phones without all the necessary protections as recommended—it seems to me that that would be unlikely in any given case to result in a prosecution against said member.
acuity.explanation: Penk takes up the specific worry Tuiono had just voiced — that members glancing round for their laptops and iPhones could be caught by the recklessness limb — sets out the actual mens rea test, and applies it to that example to conclude it would not support a prosecution. The answer could not have been given had the preceding turn raised a different illustration.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "I did note that when Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan mentioned people missing their laptops and iPhones and so on and so forth, I saw a number of people looking around the room wondering if they knew where their laptops and iPhones were, including myself as well."

acuity.statement: Finally, in terms of Amendment Paper 433 in the name of Teanau Tuiono, the proposed penalty reduction we don’t think is appropriate. Our starting point, and the position of the Government, is that the current penalty is appropriate and consistent. I wouldn’t wish to suggest that having the foreign interference element merely topping up the other offence would be appropriately punishable by only an additional three months, as opposed to the seven years that’s put forward.
acuity.explanation: Directly engages the named amendment paper just put to him and the three-months-versus-seven-years proportionality argument behind it, rejecting the substitution on its merits rather than deflecting; it does not, however, give the Sentencing Act rationale Tuiono twice pressed for, so engagement is strong but not complete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "I’ve got another Amendment Paper—Amendment Paper 433—which is about that proportionality aspect."

acuity.statement: Just to add to the checks we’re doing in terms of the other Acts referred to in the Schedule, my question is in relation to the Bail Act changes.
acuity.explanation: Her contribution is squarely on the bill under committee examination and gestures at the running scrutiny of the consequential Schedule, but it takes up no part of the Minister's immediately preceding answers on strict liability, recklessness or Amendment Paper 433 — it opens a fresh line of inquiry that would read identically whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just answered on strict liability, the recklessness test and Amendment Paper 433, and this statement does not take any of that up; it moves to the Bail Act amendments in the Schedule.

acuity.statement: The member mentioned or asked whether the search provisions are warranted. I think he meant in that general sense of justified, as opposed to warrants that are put forward in terms of search powers. On that note, then, I can provide some assurance either way, actually, that the bill introduces no new search powers, instead it simply relies on existing powers in the Search and Surveillance Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Tuiono's specific question about warrantless search powers, first disambiguating the sense of 'warranted' the member used, then answering it on the substance — that the bill creates no new search powers and leans on the existing Search and Surveillance Act, followed by the urgency/reasonable-grounds test and the warrant preference rule. The reply would have been materially different had Tuiono asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "my question to the Minister is around the justifications for allowing warrantless searches for such broad offences under new sections 78AAA and 78BBB and without additional safeguards"

acuity.statement: But nevertheless, I think it's entirely possible to separate good investigative journalism on the one hand, for example, and conducting certain activities is defined on behalf of or for a foreign power.
acuity.explanation: Engages the journalists strand of Tuiono's question directly, offering a distinction between investigative journalism and acting for a foreign power rather than ignoring it. It is one strand answered at a level of principle rather than addressing the specific warrantless-search exposure Tuiono raised for journalists, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "Could the Minister also clarify how the current proposal might impact journalists, activists, and advocacy groups"

acuity.statement: The second question is also coming to the Search and Surveillance Act. Thank you to the Minister for that response but my question is: what we saw in terms of the power granted under the Search and Surveillance Act as part of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, and the subsequent amendment of that is that when a person's being searched and if they found something that was incidental that wasn't part of the original intention of that search, that that material can still be used for them to be charged with additional offences.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's answer that the bill relies on existing Search and Surveillance Act powers and presses on precisely that point — drawing on how those powers have operated under the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill to ask whether incidentally found material could support charges under the new offences. The question only makes sense as a reply to what Penk just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "the bill introduces no new search powers, instead it simply relies on existing powers in the Search and Surveillance Act"

acuity.statement: If I was on that side of the House this morning, I would be embarrassed by the scaremongering they are creating in this House.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows a detailed critique by Tinetti (the narrowed purpose clause, 78 of 107 opposing submissions, the omission of Te Tiriti). He gestures at it by labelling it 'scaremongering' and asserting the opposite conclusion ('it's not the truth', 'this bill will support the development of early childhood education'), but engages no part of her reasoning — not the purpose wording she read out, not the submission count, not the Treaty point. The speech would be essentially identical whatever specific argument had preceded it, so it sits in the unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "I would hate to think that, as a Parliament, we were setting our young people up to be in a really unsafe situation." — Bates takes up her alarm only to name it scaremongering, not to engage its basis.

acuity.statement: I heard the words “gold standard” uttered by Jan Tinetti, and, look, I can well recall a number of early childhood education centres which were looking to upgrade what they were.
acuity.explanation: This quotes Tinetti's phrase back and then pivots to a different sense of it. She used 'gold standard' to describe how overseas ministers regard kōhanga reo and puna reo; Foster repurposes it as a regulatory compliance tier that centres could not afford to reach. Repeating an opponent's words in order to move to his own prepared material is a mere reference, not engagement with the content of her claim, so it stays in the low band despite naming her directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "You have the gold standard of what you’re doing with kōhanga reo and puna reo. Teach us how to do it."

acuity.statement: I also heard, as Carl Bates has said, a lot of scaremongering from the Opposition parties about things like health and safety. Those are all in the bill. There is the primary purpose and a whole bunch of objectives, and that includes health and safety.
acuity.explanation: Here Foster does take up a specific strand of Tinetti's argument — her reading of the current Act's purpose clause, which includes 'supporting the health, safety, and well-being of children', against the bill's replacement clause — and answers it on the merits by pointing to where health and safety sit in the bill's structure (primary purpose plus objectives). That is a direct correction of what he says is a misstatement about the bill's contents, and the speech would have to change if she had made a different criticism. It falls short of 1.0 because he engages this one strand and leaves her other specific points (the labour-market purpose, the submission numbers, Te Tiriti) untouched, and he supplies no clause reference.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "(b) supporting the health, safety, and well-being of children" — her reading of the current Act's purpose, contrasted with the bill's narrowed purpose clause.

acuity.statement: Now, we have specific objections to this bill that were articulated already quite nicely by the previous Green speaker, but I'll go through them again. One of the concerns that we have is the speed at which this legislation and all the wider Government reforms are actually taking place.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez follows a substantive turn by Waititi built entirely on Te Tiriti, kōhanga reo and rangatiratanga, and engages none of it; he instead flags that he is re-running objections already made by an earlier speaker from his own party. The speech is squarely on the bill under debate and gestures at the debate as it has gone (noting the brevity of the Government speakers' calls), which lifts it to the top of the unresponsive band, but it would read identically whatever Waititi had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued the bill strips away Te Tiriti protections and the community/hapū foundation of kōhanga reo, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The bill that has come through is a sensible one that focuses on safety, and it makes sure that it clarifies regulations for the education providers so that they can be there for the children and have a better opportunity to be able to start up businesses and therefore improve competition and reduce costs across the board. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Weenink speaks immediately after a detailed critique naming a specific regulation (HS5), the shift to risk-based monitoring, the missing child impact statement and the unreleased consultation data. She asserts the opposite conclusion — that the bill 'focuses on safety' — without engaging any part of the argument just made, and her reference to hearing from submitters is thanks rather than a reply to the consultation objection. Prepared commendation on the right subject: it would be word-for-word the same whatever Hernandez had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez argued the removal of HS5 safe assembly areas and the shift to risk-based monitoring would compromise children's safety, and that the consultation data was not proactively released; this statement does not take up either claim.

acuity.statement: I respectfully disagree with Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan in terms of a lack of clarity within the legislation. As to courts having the ability to consider how these scenarios might play out, the scenarios that they will see are cases that will be brought before them in due course, and, on that basis, they will have the opportunity to consider how the law should be applied. It’s no grace period; otherwise, we provide a window of opportunity—a mixed message in terms of the kind of behaviour that we consider to be appropriate in this country.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually put: Walters asked whether a period of education before commencement was a consideration, and he rules it out explicitly ('It's no grace period') and gives his reason. He also takes up the clarity objection by name. The speech would be different had the preceding turn argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "So I ask whether that is a consideration for the Minister." — her request for a period of education before the bill becomes law

acuity.statement: I agree with the comments made by my wonderful colleagues as they have traversed this bill, and we do not agree with many of the comments from the other side. We support the bill, and I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Kirkpatrick takes the final call immediately after a substantive opposition speech that made three pointed, engageable claims: that the whole cost section of the regulatory impact statement is redacted, that the RIS itself records limited analysis and no consultation with service providers, parents and Māori, and that the bill abandons a child-centred approach. She engages none of them. The blanket "we do not agree with many of the comments from the other side" is a bare reference, not engagement with any content, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at a partial 0.5. It earns the upper part of that band only because it names the bill and gestures at the debate just had; the words would be identical whatever the preceding speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett argued the RIS's cost section is "completely redacted" and that the bill shifts away from a child-centred approach, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Listening to the Opposition, anyone would think that the world was going to end. Actually, we’re very focused on providing an early childhood education (ECE) sector that is both safe and provides high-quality education for young children. But what we do have to remember is parents.
acuity.explanation: Twyford's core charge was that the bill frames the director's mandate around getting parents into work instead of around quality, safety and wellbeing. McCallum takes up that exact trade-off — asserting the sector will be both safe and high-quality, and then defending the parent-side framing as a legitimate objective (availability and affordability). That is engagement with one strand of the argument rather than its substance: the opening "listening to the Opposition, anyone would think that the world was going to end" is a mere reference, and he offers no answer to the claim about how the mandate is actually worded. On topic and partly aimed at the claim, then straight to prepared commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "why isn't the important framing for this new measure the quality of early childhood education—learning, the safety and wellbeing of the children who are in that system?"

acuity.statement: I also want to quickly touch on these changes to the purpose of Part 2 of the Act, and that is where the focus becomes on the parents participating in the labour market rather than on all children being able to participate and receive a strong foundation for learning and positive wellbeing. That is a terrible change, and we’ll have more to say about that in the committee of the whole House stage.
acuity.explanation: McCallum had just defended the parent-centred framing as the point of the bill; Brooking names the specific statutory change that effects that shift (the purpose of Part 2 moving from children's participation and wellbeing to parents' labour-market participation) and rejects it. You can point at the strand engaged — the parents-versus-children framing — but it is also her side's prepared case restated after Twyford made it, and she defers the detail to the committee stage rather than meeting McCallum's affordability and availability point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "the parents actually need the ability to find an ECE facility to use, and to also have the ability to afford it"

acuity.statement: I agree with the previous speaker: this is about education. If we tie up our educators with a high compliance burden, that’s less time for genuine educational engagement and children interaction.
acuity.explanation: He takes Brooking's own premise — that this is education, not babysitting — grants it explicitly, and turns it to the opposite conclusion: if it is education, then compliance time is time taken from teaching. That is accepting part of an argument and drawing out a consequence, so the speech would have had to change had she framed it differently. Short of 1.0 because he leaves untouched her central contention that the regulated industry will become the regulator, which was the substance of her opposition.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "We are not talking about daycares or childcares; this is childhood education. It is not babysitting"

acuity.statement: Kia ora, Madam Speaker. As I rise to reflect on this piece of legislation and, I guess, echo the words of my colleague the Hon Rachel Brooking, who was talking about the Dunedin Study, I say that I was about two years old and I was too young.
acuity.explanation: He picks up Brooking's Dunedin Study material, which is a gesture at the preceding turn, but does nothing with the argument she built on it — that the first thousand days make this legislation important. What follows is biographical (his birth year, his age when the study began) and would read the same whatever conclusion she had drawn from the study. A reference to the topic rather than engagement with the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "one of those has demonstrated the importance of the first 1,000 days of life"

acuity.statement: The new Police inspector-general adds another layer of oversight, but I want to add some of the things that we are pushing for to add further accountability to the police.
acuity.explanation: Paul's speech is overwhelmingly prepared Green material (survivor acknowledgement, IPCA resourcing, body cameras, search and seizure limits) that would read identically whoever spoke before her. The one point of contact is the Inspector-General: Andersen presented the appointment as the safeguard Labour supports, and Paul takes that strand up to concede it adds a layer of oversight while arguing it is insufficient. One strand engaged, then back to the prepared list.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "including the appointment of an Inspector-General of Police" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I’ve noted the issues that the member has brought forward, in terms of the changes they wish to see. In relation to the Independent Police Conduct Authority of New Zealand (IPCA) recommendations, both the Police and the Government have been clear that we accept all of those recommendations.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question just put — which recommendations will be implemented — and answers it directly (all of them), then goes on to address her separate question about legislation amending the Policing Act. This answer could not have been given in response to a different preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We want to know which of the IPCA’s recommendations the Government will be implementing, and by when." — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: In terms of public confidence: absolutely; it would be naïve to think that there hasn’t been an impact on public confidence.
acuity.explanation: Answers the third question squarely and concedes the premise rather than deflecting, before qualifying it with the 'small group' point. Scored for engagement only; whether the qualification is a fair characterisation is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I also want to ask the Minister whether he’s concerned about the impact this cover-up will have on public trust in the police" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: I wanted to know whether there was a timeline on that significant piece of work that the Minister talked about and when we can be expecting to see introduction of anything, or when that work might occur.
acuity.explanation: Builds directly on the answer just given: Mitchell flagged probable new legislation without a date, and Paul presses on exactly that gap. The follow-up only exists because of the content of his reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there will probably have to be new legislation that will deal with the formation of an inspector general" — Mark Mitchell

acuity.statement: To the second part of the question: absolutely. There should be cross-party work on this, and I’m very happy to chair that myself to make sure that work is done.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific proposal put to him, accepts it, and goes further by volunteering to chair the work. Entirely contingent on what was just asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether there would be any space or room for cross-party collaboration on increasing the accountability and oversight of the Police" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: Last night I had the privilege of the Governor-General’s company as we acknowledged this year's Royal Society of New Zealand recipients. But before I revisit that, I want a place this in the context of what is the biggest reform of the science sector in 30 years. What we're trying to do here is we're trying to solve how we can improve the impact of our science spend so that more New Zealanders feel tangible benefit from science and technology.
acuity.explanation: Reti follows McKee in the same take-note debate on miscellaneous business, so a substantive preceding turn with plenty of contestable content was available to him. His speech engages none of it: it is prepared material on the science sector reform, the five completed science items and the Royal Society awards, and would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before him and whatever they had said. It earns 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because a take-note debate on miscellaneous business admits any subject, so he is nominally within the matter under debate, and his opening acknowledgement of the Day of Reflection ties it to the day's proceedings rather than to McKee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee opened the take-note debate arguing that "For too long, politics in this country has been driven by grievance and guilt" and set out ACT's record on the history curriculum, section 127, firearms and the zero carbon Act, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m really sad that members opposite, particularly from the Greens, are disparaging our fantastic hospitality sector.
acuity.explanation: Upston breaks off her prepared answer to take up Swarbrick's interjections directly, characterising the Greens' position on the Michelin announcement and contesting it, before returning to prepared material on employment and the Tourism New Zealand figure. She engages what was actually just said rather than merely naming an opponent, but engages its thrust rather than any specific claim — a partial engagement, so mid-band. (Whether 'disparaging' fairly represents 'they think this is a waste of money' is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They do not think this is a good idea." — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: Far from it. We’re standing for them.
acuity.explanation: A direct rebuttal of the specific charge Upston had just levelled one line earlier: it denies the characterisation ('far from it') and substitutes the opposite ('standing for them'). The remark would be unintelligible had Upston said anything else, which is the deciding test. Marked down from 1.0 only because it rebuts by flat denial without doing anything further with the charge — that is a Specificity shortfall as well, but it is the engagement being scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "members opposite, particularly from the Greens, are disparaging our fantastic hospitality sector" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Look, we've had some fantastic news coming out recently and it's about our wonderful kiwifruit sector: they are thriving. It's a good thing because it means that our economy is getting back. We are growing and there is good news—those green shoots, those blue shoots coming back into New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Hipkins had just mocked the Government's "green shoots" framing by name and set against it a specific counter-case: record unemployment since 1994, 200 emigrants a day, 78 percent more unemployed in Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, 20,000 construction jobs lost, and liquidators saying business failures will worsen. Uffindell picks the phrase "green shoots" back up and asserts growth, which is a gesture at the argument he follows, but he engages none of its content — no unemployment figure, no emigration, no liquidators, no regional claim is taken up or corrected. The remainder is prepared constituency material on Zespri's season that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Hipkins had said, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "Despite what Nicola Willis and Christopher Luxon are speaking about "green shoots" and how "the economy's turned the corner, and we're in recovery", the liquidators are saying, "We've never been busier""

acuity.statement: Even in Northland, Grant. We care about Northland too. Our targeted capital gains tax will boost health, with every dollar ring-fenced for your hauora, paying for three free doctors visits for everyone in Aotearoa, because health is wealth.
acuity.explanation: She takes up McCallum's interjection directly — names him, answers the Northland jibe, and then does something with the substance of his claim by specifying what the capital gains tax is for (ring-fenced for health, three free doctor's visits). The passage would not exist, or would read differently, had he interjected something else, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because she reframes rather than contesting the characterisation of the tax itself, and pivots quickly back to prepared campaign material. Scored on engagement only: the truth of the tax claims is veracity's business, the slogan-like delivery charisma's, neither moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s a tax plan. Tax, tax, tax." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: I just want, firstly, to articulate for those who may be following along at home what this bill actually does, because I think it’s important to note that this bill does not action the selling of assets. That has already been done. What this bill does do is set up a framework for the fund that is to be established with the revenue that is generated from the sale of those assets, with requisite guardrails around it—namely, to ensure that there is a protection of the real value of Auckland Council’s intergenerational assets, so that they can continue to benefit future generations.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick follows a substantive turn in which Sepuloni framed the fund as built on airport share sales and drew a contrast with 'asset sales proposed by the other side of the House'. Swarbrick takes up that asset-sale strand and does something with it — clarifying that the sales are already done and that the bill only creates the fund's guardrails — so the engagement is pointable. But it answers the topic rather than any specific claim or figure Sepuloni advanced (the $1.31 billion, the South Auckland councillors' sense of loss), and the remainder of the speech is prepared material on local government revenue, the Shand inquiry and rates caps that would read identically whatever had preceded it. Partial engagement, hence mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "That doesn't mean that asset sales proposed by the other side of the House would necessarily be done in the same way."

acuity.statement: It gets you nothing, Helen White. That is why we need to use what we have to build what we need.
acuity.explanation: Helen White interjected a specific counter-claim to Court's assertion that the $66 billion of COVID borrowing produced 'not a hospital, not a school, not a road, not a port' — namely that things were in fact built. Court names her and flatly reasserts his own line ('It gets you nothing') without taking up any part of her claim: no example contested, no distinction drawn between borrowing and delivery, no figure supplied. It is on the matter under debate and aimed at her, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but a bare repetition of the proposition she disputed engages none of its content. Note that Chlöe Swarbrick's preceding speech, which Court does engage substantively elsewhere, is not contained in this window, so that passage is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But we did do it; we built a whole lot of shit." — Helen White

acuity.statement: This bill is putting the proceeds from asset sales into a long-term fund. It is trusting the council to manage its own assets, and, in a way, that’s almost quite patronising. But given the attacks on local government from the Government benches, I think it is still worth noting your support for this bill.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown follows Patterson, who justified New Zealand First's support by respect for the democratically elected council and argued Dunedin balked at a similar sale because of 'an underlying lack of trust' that a council would squander the proceeds. She takes up that one strand — the question of whether Parliament should be trusting or distrusting councils with their own assets — inverting it (trusting the council is 'almost quite patronising') and acknowledging the support voiced from the Government benches. She then leaves the specific argument behind for prepared material on local-government funding shares, the 2019 Productivity Commission report and international GDP comparisons, none of which responds to anything Patterson said. Partial engagement, pointable, then a return to prepared material — the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: “I think one of the reasons why Dunedin didn't go down this path was because there was an underlying lack of trust—that a big lump sum of money like this going back to a council would just be squandered over time.”

acuity.statement: I want to reinforce that this is the Government for Auckland—this is the Government for Auckland. How do we know that? Well, we know that when you look at the SkyCity convention centre—the keys have been handed over, and the opening will be next year.
acuity.explanation: Helen White's preceding turn argued the fund is "not a get out of jail free card for the Government" and that the Government must step up on Auckland's infrastructure — rail, public transport, stormwater. Brewer takes up that strand directly, asserting "this is the Government for Auckland" and offering a list of delivered Auckland projects (convention centre, City Rail Link, congestion charging, Hauraki Gulf protection) as his answer. But he engages the topic rather than her specific claims: he does not address stormwater, the intensification she raised, or her point about respecting and resourcing councils, and the roll-call of achievements reads as prepared material he would have delivered whatever she had said. Partial engagement, pointable — ~0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "So it is really important that this Government support the infrastructure needs of a growing Auckland, because the taxpayers' dollars come from Auckland, and it needs to be adequately supported."

acuity.statement: The future we need to talk about is the level of debt that this country has endured and has accumulated, largely due to the $66 billion that that Opposition spent in the last six years.
acuity.explanation: Halbert supported the bill but charged that transport and infrastructure investment in Auckland has been cut under this Government. Bidois speaks to the same broad matter — how Auckland's future is to be funded — but takes up no part of that charge: he does not dispute the cut, defend the Government's Auckland spend, or test Halbert's figures. Instead he pivots to the Opposition's own spending record and the interest bill, which is prepared material that would read identically whatever Halbert had argued. That is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the claim, so it sits in the low band; the pivot-to-your-opponent's-record shape puts it at 0.2 rather than 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "back in infrastructure that has been cut under this Government" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: Being the last speaker in the Chamber, it just feels like I’m repeating everything that everyone else is actually saying. I just want to quote you something from the website of the Auckland Future Fund—their vision.
acuity.explanation: Lee follows a substantive turn by Williams that made a specific fairness claim about South Auckland's contribution to the airport asset, a $70 million playground investment gap, and a question about the privatised energy trust. Lee engages none of that content: she acknowledges Christine Fletcher (as Williams did), concedes she is repeating others, then reads the fund's own website vision and its capitalisation figure, and glances at a colleague's remark about Kuala Lumpur. That is prepared, on-topic material with a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the argument just made, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Arena Williams argued "this has to be fair, and it has to be fair for South Auckland" and asked whether the Auckland energy trust privatised in 1993 should be brought back under council accountability, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I think, ultimately, this is pragmatic, it's forward thinking, and it's fiscally responsible legislation, and that's what we like to see as a National-led Government. That's what we like to see in 2025 and that's why I think this is a fantastic piece of legislation and therefore I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford speaks after Lee and, earlier, Williams, both of whom put content on the table (the fund's capitalisation and investment design; the South Auckland fairness claim and the energy-trust question). His speech credits Cheung's stewardship and labels the bill pragmatic and fiscally responsible, and would read identically whatever either previous speaker had said. It names the specific bill and MP, so it is not fully generic, but it engages no part of any preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Melissa Lee quoted the Auckland Future Fund's vision—"an investment for all Aucklanders and future generations"—and explained it was capitalised from the $1.31 billion airport divestment, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I heard my colleague from the Green Party talk about some of the bad behaviours that are involved in being a director. I just want to give you a different view of that from being in that perspective.
acuity.explanation: Wilson names the Green strand of the debate (bad director behaviour) and sets out to answer it with a counterweight — the many burdens directors already carry, so "to add harassment to that is actually not really fair". That is genuine partial engagement: he takes up one strand and offers a rebuttal direction. But he never engages the specific content of the claim (phoenixing, the named misconduct), and when it is put to him directly by interjection he deflects with a jibe about his colleague being aggrieved and returns to his own prepared anecdotes about directorships, Italy and Parliamentary Service. Half-marks: pointable engagement with the topic of the opposing argument, not with its substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Phoenixing is objectively bad." — Ricardo Menéndez March, whose Green critique of director behaviour Wilson explicitly picks up

acuity.statement: I appreciate that there is work going on, a more comprehensive review of the Companies Act, but this, of course, is a bit of a stop-gap measure that will actually fill a real gap that we have at the moment.
acuity.explanation: Foster made the pending Companies Act review the whole basis of NZ First's position, and Wilson echoed it as "the never-ending wait". Campbell takes that strand up directly: he concedes the larger review is coming and supplies the answer to it — this bill is a stop-gap filling a real gap now. That is one argument from the preceding turns engaged and used, so the speech would read differently had Foster not raised the review. It is only half-marks because the rest of the contribution is prepared material on the Act, the harms and the committee's recommendations, and it leaves Xu-Nan's immediately preceding challenge about committee-stage closure motions and the hour-per-page standard entirely untouched despite his having expressly invited the Government members' reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s a review of the Companies Act. That’s a really substantive piece of work—clearly, it is not going to turn up in the time frame that we anticipated" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: Other speakers before me have spoken about this. The Government is working on a comprehensive Companies Act amendment bill, which will go beyond what is proposed in this bill and deliver more comprehensive protections for directors, but that doesn’t take away from this being great step forward in providing a solution to a longstanding issue.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand Williams pressed — the relationship between this bill and the wider Companies Act review — and states a position on it, agreeing the review goes further while insisting that does not diminish the bill. But it engages the topic rather than her specific argument: she cautioned explicitly against waiting for a 'fully gold-plated version' and against over-doing the wider review, and he neither endorses nor contests that, and the passage would read much the same after any speech on this bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "There’s more work to be done by the Government." and "That piece of work shouldn’t hold us up in doing this."

acuity.statement: For the second night in a row, I have the great pleasure of rising to speak in this House on a bill that we all agree on. That is why I love members’ days—love, love, love members’ days. We have heard a full rendering of the bill in hand, and we’ve heard many congratulations to Deborah Russell.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Walters that made specific claims (the 2023 protection-order case, Kirsten Patterson and the Institute of Directors, the 1998 statutory-declaration change). Fleming gestures at the debate — he notes 'we have heard a full rendering of the bill' and adds his own congratulations to Deborah Russell — but engages no part of anyone's argument, and the speech then turns to members' days generally, the upcoming Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill and Carl Bates waiting for the chair. It would read identically whatever Walters had argued, so it sits in the unresponsive band; 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is at least about the bill under debate and acknowledges the preceding contributions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters spoke about the bill's genesis, the Institute of Directors' support for it, and the 1998 removal of post-shop managers' power to take statutory declarations, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I wanted to note that one of the things the bill does is, as we’ve heard, that if you make a statutory declaration, it has a threshold that it is likely to result physical or mental harm. So that is a higher threshold than I expected upon looking at the bill but there it is. So you have to do that to get this alternative address.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the statutory-declaration strand that Walters had just been addressing and does something modest with it: it supplies the actual statutory threshold (likely to result in physical or mental harm) and observes it is higher than expected, which bears on whether requiring a declaration is a real hurdle. That is one strand taken up and developed, not a rebuttal of Walters's specific point about who may take declarations, and the turn then moves to her own prepared material about her directorships, Googling addresses and thanks to Sarah Pallett and Deborah Russell. Partial engagement, pointable — mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My very last point was just in response to Todd Stephenson’s lament at the fact that statutory declarations are still needed" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: It’s interesting that the Companies Act 1993 indicates a time when things were very different, when there weren’t as many small businesses in this country, where the examples that have been shared in the Parliament this evening were not the examples that those who are in public service or in office were able to experience at the time.
acuity.explanation: Utikere follows Rutherford's substantive third-reading speech, which argued at length that the register was built for an era of walking into an office to inspect a paper file and that the threat landscape has changed (councillors threatened at home, directors installing cameras). Utikere gestures at that debate — 'the examples that have been shared in the Parliament this evening' and the 1993 Act reflecting a different time — but does not take up any specific strand of Rutherford's argument (service of legal documents, accountability being refined not reduced, the proportionality point). The rest of the call is prepared material: acknowledgements of Deborah Russell and Sarah Pallett, and his own point about submissions showing directors already withhold addresses. The speech would read identically whatever Rutherford had argued, so this sits in the gesture band rather than partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: 'the Companies Register was built in a time when transparency, as Rachel Brooking just quite rightly said in her contribution, was walking into an office, requesting a paper file, and then physically inspecting it' — engaged only as a generic nod to the era point and to 'examples shared in the Parliament this evening', not to the argument itself.

acuity.statement: I have a few clauses I’d like to ask the member in charge about, but I’d also like to start with the title. I do want to focus on the word “Excusal”, but I come from maybe a slightly different angle.
acuity.explanation: Costley picks up the exact strand Rutherford opened — the appropriateness of the word "excusal" in the title — and explicitly positions himself as coming at it from a different angle, so the opening is shaped by what preceded it. But he does not take up Rutherford's specific proposal (dropping "excusal" and inserting "72"); he moves instead into his own prepared material on service clubs, volunteering and community breakdown, and ends with a differently-framed suggestion of his own. One strand engaged, then prepared material: a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "had the member considered whether, actually, looking to include the age specifically in the legislation?" — Rutherford's question to the member in charge about the title and the word "excusal".

acuity.statement: But I understand the intention or the question of adding a specific age into the bill. I think the challenge with adding a specific age, 72 or 70, if there was to be amendment to the actual age during the committee of the whole House—the challenge with adding a specific age to the title could be that in times in the future, we're here in this House again, having to go through this process again and not only update the age—because life expectancy is intended on continuing to grow—but we'd have to change the title, as well.
acuity.explanation: This takes Rutherford's specific proposal — putting the number 72 into the bill's short title — and does something with it: it supplies a reason the proposal would be unwise (the title would have to be re-amended each time the age moved with life expectancy), and goes on to note it would confuse the title's intention. The speech would have to be different had Rutherford proposed something else; it is aimed squarely at the content of the suggestion rather than merely referencing that a question was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "but whether he'd considered actually including the word “72”, which, I think, is vitally important."

acuity.statement: I think one of the things that's intended by this amendment, as I said in both my first reading and second reading speech, is the need for a reminder to our community that this is a civic duty, and that civic duty doesn't end at 65. We'll get to this, no doubt, when questions are asked on the age a little bit later this evening. But for now, when we're talking about the context of the title, I think keeping the idea of excusal in there reflects the intent of the underlying legislation, which is that you have to go and be excused.
acuity.explanation: Bates answers the substance of Costley's objection rather than just acknowledging it: he accepts the premise that civic duty and service matter, then gives a reason for declining the proposed re-framing — that "excusal" tracks the mechanism of the underlying Act, under which a person must apply to be excused. He defers part of the exchange to the later clause on age, which stops this being a complete engagement, but what is engaged is the specific claim put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "would he consider one if we were to flip it on its head?" — Costley's argument that "Age of Excusal" sets a tone of avoidance rather than service.
