acuity.statement: But to focus on your specific question at this stage as to why there should be any age at all, it’s interesting that this was something—and you’ll recall it was raised as part of the select committee process as one of the questions by, for example, the Christian Council of Social Services.
acuity.explanation: Bates takes up Stephenson's specific proposition — abolish the age threshold entirely rather than move it from 65 to 72 — names it as the question he is answering, locates it in the select committee record, quotes the submission that put the same argument, concedes it is valid, and then gives his reason for declining (he does not want to lose committee support) while inviting Stephenson to lodge an amendment. The reply would be materially different had Stephenson argued something else about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "would the member just actually consider getting rid of age? It does seem quite a discriminatory attribute."

acuity.statement: In turn, I reflect on the commencement date of the Juries (Age of Excusal) Amendment Bill and how it says it's “the day after Royal assent”, and I was just wondering if there’s any whakaaro around whether that could be or you would want to change that to a longer period of time, given what may be involved for the court system to implement this change?
acuity.explanation: The turn is on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly adrift, but it engages no part of the exchange it follows: the age-discrimination argument from Stephenson and Bates's practical-politics answer are left untouched. What is offered instead is prepared material — praise for the member in charge, a recounting of her own member's bill, and a new question about commencement timing — which would read identically whatever the preceding speakers had argued. The gesture at the debate (the bill, the Justice Committee) keeps it just above the floor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates spoke about whether any age threshold should be in the bill at all and why he will not remove it tonight, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a fresh question about the commencement date.

acuity.statement: Will courts be ready to support older jurors, such as with more regular breaks, and actually provide more flexibility so that older jurors can participate in what are very long, very emotionally and physically stressful days, hearing what is often very disturbing testimony from victims and witnesses and family members?
acuity.explanation: Bates had just closed the implementation question by asserting the Ministry of Justice had confirmed its readiness to update summons material and systems, so the commencement date would not be an issue. Court takes up that readiness strand and presses it in a different place — not ministry paperwork but whether the courtroom itself will be ready to support older jurors — which is a genuine extension of the claim just made rather than a rebuttal of it. The rest of his turn is prepared personal-experience material on jury service that would have been delivered whatever Bates had said, and he leaves the specific Ministry assurance untested. Partial engagement: one strand picked up, the specific claim not contested.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "I had the assurance of the Ministry of Justice that they have confirmed their readiness and that they are able to update their summons material and systems in order to implement this change quickly, effectively."

acuity.statement: So when we have that understanding that we already have jurors who are over the age of 65, our courts are already managing some of those challenges that the member raises about potential fatigue, about ensuring appropriate breaks, and about the make-up of people in the jury itself—which I suppose is part of the answer to the question about slang.
acuity.explanation: This takes both of Court's specific questions — how older jurors will cope with unfamiliar language, and the physical and emotional toll of long sitting days — and does something with them: it corrects the factual premise underneath them (that over-65s are not currently on juries, when in fact many serve and automatic excusal is merely available on request), and then draws the consequence that the courts are already managing fatigue and breaks today. It names the strands it is answering and routes the slang question to the jury's cross-section of peers. The speech could not have been delivered if Court had asked something else. Scored on engagement only: whether the 'courts already manage it' inference actually answers the concern is a Rigor question, and the accuracy of the excusal description a Veracity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "how do we expect older jurors to understand lingo, street jive, and slang" and "what about the tiring—emotionally and physically tiring—effort that jurors put in?"

acuity.statement: The second question that I had was in your explorations, Mr Bates, and mastery of this issue from issues around the world, you've mentioned Scotland and a few other countries—you said there was an upper limit on age. I want to just understand, because is that an upper limit on jury duty service and did that influence your thinking, or was that an upper limit on the age of excusal?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific comparative figures Bates offered moments earlier and does something with them: presses whether those overseas limits are caps on jury service or on the age of automatic excusal, a distinction that would undercut the comparison if conflated. The question could not have been asked without having listened to Bates' Scotland/England example, so the speech would change if the preceding turn had cited different material. Not a full 1.0 because the contribution's other strands (incremental age increases, academic reports on demographics) are self-declared new ground rather than engagement with what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In England and Wales, they have an upper limit of 76 in jury duty; Scotland has the age of 71." — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: So if we were to take your suggestion and have an automatic increase now, as is proposed by the bill to 72, that would provide an opportunity maybe for you to come in with a member's bill that introduced the idea of beginning that incremental increase now so that when we hit 2050, we are at that 75½ point.
acuity.explanation: Takes Luxton's specific proposal — three months a year reaching 72 by the mid-2050s — accepts the premise, runs it against the 2000-2025 increase in average age, and draws out the consequence that the target would need to be 75½ rather than 72, then tells him where the mechanism could be introduced. The answer is wholly shaped by the arithmetic Luxton put, and would have to be different if a different escalation had been proposed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did the member explore or did the committee explore having incremental age increases for the age of excusal? I mean, if you would have increased the age by, say, three months a year, how would that work?" — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: Yes. I’d like to thank the member for getting this bill so far—congratulations. I’ve just got one basic question: what happens to a juror who at the start of the jury proceedings is 71 but turns 72 during the trial?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and courteous about the member in charge, but it engages no part of the argument that immediately preceded it — the congratulation is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content, and the question would read identically whatever Bates or Luxton had just said. That places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 for the acknowledgement of the preceding speaker's progress with the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carl Bates had just argued that incremental age escalation would need to reach 75½ by 2050 and that it is not Parliament's place to judge how juries reach determinations; this statement does not take either strand up, raising instead a fresh transitional-age point.

acuity.statement: It’s actually a really important question, and it was considered as part of the select committee process around the transitional arrangements. I want to acknowledge the select committee for actually improving the bill through the select committee process by addressing this point. The age you are at the point the summons is issued is the age that is relevant here.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the operative rule the question asked for — age is fixed at the date of summons — and answers the second half about whether the committee considered it. The reply is specific to the 71-turning-72 scenario put to him and would have to be a different answer to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what happens to a juror who at the start of the jury proceedings is 71 but turns 72 during the trial? Has the committee considered what that means and what that means in this bill?" — Miles Anderson

acuity.statement: The supplementary question that the member asked was around whether or not those other reasons for excusal—health, personal circumstances, disability—can lead to permanent excusal. Now, the answer to that question is yes.
acuity.explanation: Bates takes Rutherford's specific question about whether an excusal granted on non-age grounds is permanent or applies only to a single summons, names it as the question asked, and answers it directly with a yes plus an illustrative case. The contribution would have been materially different had Rutherford asked something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Is the excusal that the member of the public uses permanent? Does it last?"

acuity.statement: Now, all of those things limit the jury-of-your-peers concept because, all of a sudden, you have a range of people with a range of characteristics that are more commonly excused or not part of juries to the point where you have to question whether or not juries truly remain a group of your peers.
acuity.explanation: Meager takes up the list of excusal grounds Bates had just enumerated in answer to Rutherford and draws out a consequence from it — that the breadth of excusal categories erodes the jury-of-peers principle — before moving to his own suggestion of a semi-professional jury pool. He engages the content rather than merely referencing it, though he neither disputes Bates's answer nor engages the permanence or frequency figures, so this is a consequence drawn from one strand rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "There are a variety of reasons for why someone can be excused from a jury duty."

acuity.statement: I thank the Acting Leader of the House for that update. Everyone seems to be talking about urgency next week. Could you just confirm to the House whether that’s happening?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the content of the business statement just delivered and presses on the specific thing it left out (whether urgency will be taken next week). It is a direct engagement with what was said, though the thing engaged is an omission rather than an argument, so it sits short of a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The House will consider the Retail Payment System (Ban on Merchant Surcharges) Amendment Bill, the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill, and the Education and Training (Early Childhood Education Reform) Amendment Bill" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I have gone through what the business of the House will be next week.
acuity.explanation: Gestures back at her own prior statement but takes up no part of the specific point put to her about urgency; the reply would have been identical whatever had been asked about the week's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Could you just confirm to the House whether that’s happening?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: This bill is a bit like a cockroach: we keep stamping it out, but it just won't die. They tried this three times before, as Duncan Webb just said. They've tried this in the past, and every single time it failed.
acuity.explanation: Paul follows a long, detailed speech from Webb that made several specific arguments — the sub-1% submitter support, the $60 million MBIE compliance cost, the unconstitutionality of an unelected board second-guessing the House, and the Minister's own sub-standard regulatory impact statement. She names Webb and gestures at one strand of his case (that this has been attempted repeatedly before), but takes up none of the content: no engagement with the cost figure, the constitutional argument, or the procedural-flaw argument. Her material (the cockroach metaphor, the complaint that the bill is deliberately boring and technical, the list of intentions) would have been delivered word-for-word had Webb argued something else about the same bill. That is a gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.5. Note this is scored only on responsiveness — the thematic echo of Webb's "cover/camouflage" point is not an engagement with his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "a piece of legislation—and let's face it, which has been waiting in the ACT Party wings for this moment for 20 years"

acuity.statement: We heard and we consulted widely—we heard approximately 30 hours of oral evidence, and received over 159,000 written submissions. Of course, that was on top of over 23,000 submissions last year, after considerable departmental consultation.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows Paul's attack on the bill and takes up one strand of it — her claim that there was no consultation — by supplying submission and hearing figures, and later touches her point about Seymour controlling the new ministry by citing amendments separating the board and chair from the Minister. But the bulk of the turn is prepared congratulation of the ACT Party that would have been delivered whatever Paul had said, and he engages none of her substantive arguments about Te Tiriti, tikanga or collective rights. Partial engagement, pointable, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There was no consultation with Māori, which actively breaches principles of good faith and partnership." — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to speak on the third reading of the Regulatory Standards Bill and to bring some context back into the very emotional debate that has occurred and bring it back to some semblance of fact. Again, the trouble with the principles of socialism, as we've heard so many times before, is that, eventually, you run out of other people's money.
acuity.explanation: Costello gestures at the preceding speech — characterising it as emotional and picking up its invocation of socialism — but what follows is a stock aphorism rather than engagement with any part of Paul's case (the Treaty breach, the absence of consultation, the regulatory impact statements, the collective-rights argument). The rest of her turn is a prepared list of the bill's principles. This is a reference to the previous speaker plus prepared material on the right subject, which the rubric places in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because the gesture at the debate is explicit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we're going to burn capitalism to the ground, because socialism is about honouring and upholding the dignity of all people" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: This bill, essentially, embeds a neoliberal cuckoo egg in every legislation. It is a parasite that is going to be wiggling its way throughout everything that this Government and any other Government does.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan follows Rawiri Waititi, who made a substantive argument in the same third-reading debate: that the bill is 'the cold, calculated arson of a Government' aimed at constitutional protections, and that Te Tiriti is 'the first and highest regulatory standard of this land'. Xu-Nan takes up no part of that — not the Tiriti-as-standard claim, not the constitutional-protection claim, not the timing point about the Treaty principles bill anniversary. His speech is prepared material on the right subject (the Regulatory Standards Bill: the 'cuckoo egg' framing, the near-100 percent select committee opposition, urgency, pay equity, school lunches) and would read identically whatever Waititi had said. It is squarely on the matter under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, but there is not even a gesture at the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued the bill is 'the cold, calculated arson of a Government that wants to burn down the constitutional protections that stand between our people and exploitation' and that 'Te Tiriti o Waitangi is the first and highest regulatory standard of this land', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I don't have time to talk about the fires burning and the ahi mentioned by Te Pāti Māori, even as they engage in their own acts of self-immolation. In a brief contribution, I just want to focus on the comments made by the Hon Duncan Webb alleging some form of democratic deficit.
acuity.explanation: Penk expressly declines to engage the two turns that precede him here. Waititi's ahi/arson argument is named only to be set aside — a mere reference, which the rubric scores as unresponsive — and Xu-Nan's specific charge that the bill's sponsors do not in fact empower the legislature (urgency, extended sittings, the pay equity amendment without consultation) goes untouched, even though Penk's own case rests on the bill being an accountability mechanism that leaves Parliament free to legislate. He does aim at one identified argument, Duncan Webb's alleged democratic deficit, and answers it with reasoning (the courts' existing power to declare legislation Bill of Rights inconsistent is 'much more muscular' than this), which is real debating — but Webb's turn is not in the window, so there is no preceding fragment here to point the engagement at, which caps this in the 0.0-0.3 band. Scored at the top of that band because the contribution is unmistakably in and about this debate and is directed at a named argument from it, not at a different day's speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I remember the ahi, a righteous, raging inferno in the puku of everybody that walked the hīkoi' — Rawiri Waititi. Penk refers to 'the fires burning and the ahi mentioned by Te Pāti Māori' only to say he will not address it, and engages no part of it; the argument he does engage (Duncan Webb's 'democratic deficit') was made in a turn outside this window.

acuity.statement: I stand to speak in support for the third reading of the Regulatory Standards Bill. The Finance and Expenditure Committee (FEC) that I'm part of have worked really, really hard to improve the bill from its original state until now to pass in the third reading. We have tightened the board and the roles and responsibilities for the Minister of the day. The FEC have put in the hours of the work to improve the bill. This bill also gives effect to the National-ACT coalition agreement that New Zealanders actually voted for. Therefore, congratulations to the ACT Party, and I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Prepared commendation delivered immediately after a sustained attack on the bill's cost, its necessity and the advice against it. It answers none of those points: no figure, no rebuttal, no concession. The claim that the select committee 'worked really, really hard to improve the bill' sits beside McAnulty's claim that 98.7 percent of submitters opposed it without engaging it, and the reference to tightening 'the roles and responsibilities for the Minister of the day' is generic rather than a reply to the kowtowing charge. The speech would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before, which puts it in the bottom band; it is at least about the bill under debate rather than an unrelated matter, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty argued the bill is unnecessary (the Ministry for Regulation advised against it), costs up to $60 million a year, drew 98.7 percent opposition at select committee and will make every Minister kowtow to David Seymour, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Look, I've listened to some of the contributions, and I think they were debating an entirely different bill in an entirely different time. The Regulatory Standards Bill is very easy to pick up and read. If we actually look at its purpose, it does some of the things that it's being criticised for, like supporting Parliament's ability to scrutinise bills, ensuring we're developing high-quality legislation, and exercising stewardship over regulatory systems—that's just in clause 3 of the bill.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson follows Russell's substantive speech and does acknowledge the criticisms as a class, answering them at the level of the bill's stated purpose (clause 3) and later re-reading clause 8 and naming Russell on the rule of law. But he does not take up her actual argument — that rights exist in tension and that the bill elevates property rights above group, environmental and other rights. The 'entirely different bill' line dismisses rather than engages, and the remainder is a prepared walk-through of the bill that would read the same after any critical speech. Topic engaged, specific claim untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What this bill does is it reifies property rights above other rights." — Hon Dr Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: We've witnessed this through the debate. The National Party don't want to talk about this. They've taken very short calls, and they've even given one of their calls to the ACT Party. They do not want to be associated to this bill.
acuity.explanation: McAnulty speaks immediately after Stephenson's defence of the bill and engages none of it — not the clause 3 purpose claim, not 'it doesn't stop Parliament doing anything', not the Treaty-property-rights point aimed at the Opposition. He pivots to the coalition's internal politics and the allocation of speaking calls. There is a gesture at the debate itself ('we've witnessed this through the debate'), which keeps it out of the 0.0-0.1 floor, but the speech would be identical whatever Stephenson had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson argued that clause 3's purpose and clause 8's principles do not restrict Parliament and merely give the public more information to judge a Minister, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’ve listened intently to the debate in the House today and there’s nothing new that has come from this debate that I haven’t heard already in the Finance and Expenditure Committee. This bill is all about accountability of the executive. On balance, I think this is a positive step forward. I certainly look forward to the day when we see more cost-benefit analysis. I’ve seen far too many bills across this House with very poor drafting, very poor cost-benefit analysis, and I want to congratulate the ACT Party and I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows a long, specific speech by Arena Williams arguing the bill shifts power from accountable MPs to the executive, that fewer than 1 percent of submitters supported it, and that it sidelines the Regulations Review Committee's cross-partisan scrutiny. He opens with a gesture at the debate — saying he has listened and heard nothing new — and then counter-asserts that the bill is about executive accountability, but he takes up none of her reasoning, none of the submitter evidence, and nothing about the committee. The remainder is prepared commendation that would read identically after any other speaker, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band on the strength of the glance alone.
acuity.subject: speaker
