Delete the preceding speech and substitute any other argument on the bill and this contribution would be word-for-word identical. It is at least on the subject under debate (the overseas investment regime), which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued that only 0.6 percent of submitters supported the bill, that calling these "less-sensitive assets" disregards the meaning of whenua, and that the bill is inconsistent with Te Tiriti o Waitangi — this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: It was only two days ago that I was speaking to a lady who has got property on the edge of our city, and it’s ripe for development. She wants to offload it, but no local buyers will take it. She’s been dealing with the Overseas Investment Office. It’s too hard and she’s been pulling her hair out. She said that lawyers want tens of thousands of dollars. This bill is all about streamlining and making it easy, and instead of that going on and on for up to 70 days, in some cases, it limits it to 15 working days. It’s a no-brainer, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Patterson that set out which safeguards were retained and why, and engages no part of it. It is prepared material on the right subject — an anecdote plus the processing-time figure — and would read identically whatever Patterson had said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than the 0.5 band; 0.1 because there is not even a gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mark Patterson spoke about New Zealand First's caution on overseas investment and the retention of the national interest test and protections for farmland, fishing quota and residential property, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I picked up this piece of legislation, and it’s actually been one of those moments when I look at a piece of legislation and really worry. I worry partly because of the kinds of comments that I heard from the Minister presenting it but also from Ryan Hamilton, who has just stood up. Now, he said very little in that speech, but he did heckle one of the other members when they suggested that some formidable economists had been concerned about this legislation. He said in his statement across the House “Did those people run a business?”, and I thought, well, did David Seymour run a business?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the immediately preceding turn directly, characterising its brevity and then engaging the content of Hamilton's premise — that business experience is what licenses a view on this bill — by offering a counterexample. It engages one strand (the qualification-to-comment point) rather than the bill argument Hamilton actually made about processing times, so it is a partial engagement, not a full rebuttal. Pointable and above the reference-only band, below 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s a no-brainer, and I commend it to the House." — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: We are living in unprecedented times. What we are doing in this piece of legislation is easing up the scrutiny that we have on foreign investment, and that’s a very dangerous thing to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the previous speaker commended the bill for — streamlining and shortening the screening process — and recharacterises it as easing scrutiny, then draws out the consequence. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had argued something else about the bill. Scored on engagement only; whether the inference is sound or the claim true belongs to Rigor and Veracity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill is all about streamlining and making it easy, and instead of that going on and on for up to 70 days, in some cases, it limits it to 15 working days." — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: This bill is all part of the Government’s plan to go for growth. This is all about growth, and how do we get growth? We get it by investment, and either it’s domestic investment or, in this case, foreign investment. You can’t just say you’re all about growth and then not be prepared to actually welcome foreign investment.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, detailed critique and engages none of its claims — not the regulatory impact statement, not the removal of the character test, not the concentration of ministerial power. The "you can’t just say you’re all about growth" line gestures at an unnamed opponent without engaging anything White said; she had in fact said foreign investment is "a really good thing". Prepared material on the matter under debate, so 0.2 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued at length that the bill eases scrutiny, removes the character test and concentrates decision-making in a Minister's hands, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: New Zealand has had one of the most restrictive regimes for investment in the OECD countries. This legislation is balanced, pro-growth reform. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, substantive speech arguing that lowered thresholds and ministerial discretion will hand strategic assets (forests, conservation land, Treaty-protected assets) to offshore owners. The reply asserts the opposite general characterisation of the regime and commends the bill, engaging no part of that argument: no answer on thresholds, on the Minister of Finance's discretion, on the submitters, or on the forestry example. It is on the right subject, so not 0.0, but it would be word-for-word identical whatever Henare had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Peeni Henare argued that lowering investment thresholds hands strategic assets offshore — "it continues to—in a concern for all of us—lower thresholds to allow more people to come in and to invest and to buy up assets in this country" — and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It was the New Zealand Māori Council that took the Crown to court over forestry, and it went all the way to the Privy Council. They won, and those lands were put aside for the purpose of Treaty settlements. Imagine today, with this bill, an act that, if this bill was in place then, probably wouldn’t have happened—so a shortcut doesn’t always give the best outcomes for all New Zealanders, because what that did was give an opportunity to grow the Māori economy that my colleague Cushla Tangaere-Manuel spoke about and that my colleague the Hon Peeni Henare spoke about.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speech — Treaty protection of forestry assets and the growth of the Māori economy — and does something with it, supplying a concrete case (the Māori Council forestry litigation to the Privy Council) and drawing out the counterfactual that the bill would have foreclosed it. He names the argument he is extending. It is partial rather than full engagement: he does not take up Nancy Lu's immediately preceding claim that the regime is among the OECD's most restrictive or that the reform is balanced, and the 'weak leadership / shortcut' framing is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m always concerned when we look towards the erosion of Treaty rights" — Peeni Henare, who argued the bill erodes Treaty protection over forests and strategic assets and that holding and developing assets builds the Māori economy.

acuity.statement: In terms of this, we have heard from the fact that the Teaching Council is going to have their power removed. We have seen already in the previous bill that the balance of scale is tipped towards ministerial appointees, but, now, we’re seeing that has been further reduced from 13 members to between seven to nine members, with only three being from the sector. Most of them are going to be appointed by the Minister, and that is going to politicise the teaching profession.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speech — Tinetti's claim that moving the Teaching Council's functions politicises the profession — and extends it with council-composition detail, but it does not engage her specific claims about standards, registration criteria or the code of conduct, and otherwise reads as prepared material. Partial engagement that can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "That means that teaching standards become political instruments."

acuity.statement: I actually think that having spent years teaching in a secondary school in an international school and also in a university would be sufficient, Mr Carl Bates, because, frankly, that is sufficient.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question just put to him squarely and on its own terms, naming the interjector and supplying the teaching experience asked for. The remark would be unrecognisable had Bates not asked what it asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "And what are your qualifications?"

acuity.statement: I was just listening to that speech, and there’s a lot I could say, but the member Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan seemed to think it was a problem that the Minister is influenced by other parties in coalition. Now, think about this for a moment: the whole premise of the member’s political party is that one party can influence another in coalition. This shows how a person can be very smart and very stupid all at the same time.
acuity.explanation: Picks out a position from the speech immediately preceding and turns it against the previous speaker's own party, so the passage would have to change if Xu-Nan had argued something else. Whether the attributed position is a fair reading of what Xu-Nan actually said is a rigor question, and whether the "very stupid" line is acceptable is a civility question; neither is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Most of them are going to be appointed by the Minister, and that is going to politicise the teaching profession."

acuity.statement: Then there’s—oh, Shanan Halbert says “you just cut it.”; actually, we just increased educational attendance funding by $140 million.
acuity.explanation: Breaks off prepared material to take up the interjected claim directly and answers it with the specific counter-figure it calls for — an immediate, pointable engagement with what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "You just cut our service—you just cut it."

acuity.statement: Supported by research, tamariki attend and succeed in education when they feel safe, recognised, and valued. Attendance is a symptom, never the cause. But instead of supporting whānau, this bill leans further into punishment.
acuity.explanation: Foster's case for the bill rested in part on poor attendance and the claim that the status quo is indefensible. Kaipara takes up that one strand and inverts its causal logic — attendance is a symptom, not the cause, so tightening expectations is punishment rather than support. That is a real engagement with a specific plank of the preceding turn, but the bulk of her speech is prepared material on the bill's clauses that would read identically whoever had spoken before, so it sits at a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Attendance levels are poor." — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: Watch this, this evening, Madam Speaker, and you can understand why we can’t, because we have an Opposition that, regardless of the quality that we put forward, stand up to oppose. Māori education this year got $60 million for property development from a National-led Government.
acuity.explanation: The first sentence is a mere characterisation of the Opposition and engages nothing. The second, however, is aimed squarely at the central claim of the turn immediately before it: Kaipara argued that property access is the biggest barrier for Māori education and that the bill adds a Crown gatekeeper rather than resources, and Bates answers with a specific property-funding figure for Māori education. If Kaipara had argued a different point on the same bill, that line would have to change. Scored on engagement only — whether the $60 million figure actually answers her objection about control of land, and whether the dismissal of the Opposition is fair, are questions for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Property access is already the single biggest barrier for Māori early learning." — Oriini Kaipara

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to speak on the Education and Training (System Reform) Amendment Bill. There are many elements to this bill that have been well traversed. The thing that I am so excited to see is the property changes because, in my own electorate, I’ve seen how long it can take to advocate for the right kind of property that’s needed.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Twyford attacking the bill as centralising and politicising education, and engages none of it. The speech is on the right subject (the bill) and notes elements have been 'well traversed', but it pivots immediately to prepared local praise about classrooms at Cashmere High; it would be word-for-word identical whatever Twyford had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford argued the bill shifts education from local control to centralised and politicised decision-making, with politicians designing the curriculum, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: It’s disappointing, tonight, to have to speak again on another education and training bill that doesn’t achieve better outcomes for learners. In the politicisation of Minister Stanford’s approach to mātauranga education, at every step along the way, tamariki ākonga learners have not been at the centre of the debate in this House.
acuity.explanation: Immediately preceded by Weenink's argument for the bill's property provisions, which this speech ignores entirely. It is squarely on the matter under debate and gestures at the chamber ('tonight', 'the debate in this House'), but it engages no claim made by the preceding speaker — prepared condemnation that would read the same whatever Weenink had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanessa Weenink spoke in favour of the bill's property changes and the 14 extra classrooms coming to Cashmere High, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I think that we just need to remember who the education system is actually there for. It’s not there for the teacher unions, it’s not there for teachers, and it’s not there for parents. It’s there for the students.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speeches — the claim that the bill wrongs the teaching profession and that the profession should lead the system — and denies its premise by asserting the system exists for students, not teachers or unions. The engagement is real and the speech would differ had Halbert not run the profession argument, but it is a single-strand counter-assertion rather than an answer to any specific claim (the RIS evidence point, the cancelled attendance contract), so it sits mid-band. Quality of the inference is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is an absolute attack on the profession, an absolute attack on the teaching profession." — Shanan Halbert (and Phil Twyford's claim that the system should be "led by the experts, the people who do the work")

acuity.statement: In no way, shape or form does this actually stop the ability for industrial action. Anyone at home might think that may be the case, but that is not the case. Any type of industrial action is actually highly disruptive to the Defence Force; there’s a lot of planning and time that goes into that. So that alone is still there, and there is still an ability for people to take that action. It’s a really small change; it’s just extending the time frames for the Chief of Defence Force and the Minister to make sure that we cover periods when this House isn’t sitting.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows Tuiono's central contention that the bill weakens the right to strike and that it removes the parliamentary guardrail on extended use of uniformed personnel, and she takes both up directly: she denies the bill stops industrial action, and she recharacterises the change as merely extending time frames to cover non-sitting periods — which is precisely the parliamentary-approval point Tuiono objected to. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different. It is not a 1.0 because the rebuttal is bare assertion that leaves untouched the specific strands Tuiono pressed (the undefined scope of "core defence outputs", the ILO conventions 87 and 98, the 2024 section 9 authorisation), and it then returns to prepared commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "At the heart, this bill weakens the right to strike by allowing striking civilian staff to be replaced with uniformed personnel" — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: I think what was really telling, as well, throughout the debate, is that members could not identify the problem with the status quo; they just talked about how this is a common-sense bill. But, for example, the member prior to me was not able to articulate what the problem is with having an adequate parliamentary check for when the Minister chooses to extend the time in which those roles are going to be filled with military personnel.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the immediately preceding speaker's actual framing — that the bill is 'practical common sense' — and turns it against her, naming the specific thing she did not address (the parliamentary check on extending the period military personnel fill civilian roles). The speech would read differently had Costello identified a concrete defect in the status quo, so it is genuinely shaped by what preceded it. Not a 1.0 because it does not engage her central assertion that the bill leaves the right to strike intact; it moves to a different objection rather than rebutting her reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Casey Costello: "It is a practical common-sense piece of legislation." (and her repeated "it does not remove the ability to take industrial action")

acuity.statement: Well, according to the National member, they don’t seem to help at all, so I’m looking forward to the member talking about the contributions of the civilian Defence Force and how important they are.
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up Costley's interjected question and the implication behind it, characterising it as a claim that civilian staff do not help and inviting him to say otherwise. That is engagement with the content of what was just put to him, not prepared material. Only partial, though: he restates the interjection's implication and defers the substance to a future speech rather than answering why non-deploying civilians matter to Defence capability.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "How are they going to help if they’re not deploying?"

acuity.statement: I think anyone watching this will realise that was a typical Green Party contribution where the wokeness comes through. They dislike the military being able to do military functions and would rather have them disbanded until it comes to the point where they actually need some support and then they’ll be crying foul and wanting help.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker and his party, but engages no part of what he argued: the parliamentary accountability point, the select committee's bargaining concern, and the urgency argument all go unanswered. This is a mere reference plus a characterisation of the opposing party, which the rubric places in the 0.1–0.3 band; the remark would be word-for-word serviceable after any Green speech on any bill, so it sits at the bottom of that band. Scored on engagement only — the quality or politeness of the remark is another attribute's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "this bill does is that it allows the Minister to have one less level of accountability in Parliament" — this statement does not take up the accountability-check argument, nor the challenge to explain how the bill does not undermine civilian bargaining

acuity.statement: It didn’t get any better with Jan Tinetti, as she stands up and says, “Oh well, you know, the military had to help in managed isolation and quarantine.” That’s right, uniformed personnel had to do it. That’s not the job that they wanted to do; this is people doing the job they would normally do, and military security force personnel filling a civilian role. They don’t understand it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific MIQ argument Tinetti had just made (that the Minister herself said such deployments were not what personnel signed up for) and does something with it: concedes the MIQ case involved uniformed personnel in unwanted duties, then draws a distinction between that and what he says the bill does — security force personnel doing the job they normally do while filling a civilian role. The speech would have to change if Tinetti had argued something else about the bill. Scored on engagement only; the abuse around it and the soundness of the distinction belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "being deployed into civilian roles such as providing security to managed isolation and quarantine (MIQ) facilities is not what they signed up for" — Jan Tinetti

acuity.statement: It wasn’t that long ago that a National Government got the troops out and deployed them to keep the ports operating during a major industrial dispute in New Zealand. Army, Navy, and Air Force personnel were used to load and unload cargo on the wharves to keep essential goods moving. Troops, effectively, were used to replace striking watersiders on the docks to guard strategic infrastructure and goods, and the ports were, basically, militarised during that dispute.
acuity.explanation: Prepared historical material on the matter under debate (defence personnel used to backfill striking workers), but it engages no part of Costley's immediately preceding argument. Substituting a different argument on the same topic for Costley's turn would not require this passage to change at all, so it sits in the unresponsive-but-on-topic band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley argued that the unions and the Opposition do not understand that military personnel normally guard main gates and bases, and that the MIQ case is different from this bill — and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: So I did take the point from the Hon Peeni Henare in his suggestion that the title be the “Denigrating Workforce Bill”—a bit harsh, but if he does put it down as an amendment, it’s probably something that we could probably support as well. But I think it could be more accurate to describe it as the “Impacting Civilian Personnel (Workforce) Bill”. That might be, I don’t know, a nicer way to put it instead.
acuity.explanation: Tuiono takes up the specific proposal in the immediately preceding turn — Henare's suggested renaming of the bill — and does something with it: he accepts the underlying point, registers a partial disagreement ("a bit harsh"), undertakes to support it if moved as an amendment, and counters with his own alternative title grounded in the civilian/military distinction he has just developed. The speech would have had to be different had Henare proposed something else, so engagement is close rather than incidental; it is short of 1.0 only because he does not contest Henare's reasoning about the bill's intent.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I suggest then, perhaps, that there could be a better title for this particular bill—something along the lines of 'Denigrating Workers' Rights Bill'" — Peeni Henare

acuity.statement: This bill does not mean that no one can strike in the Defence Force—in the civilian workers in the Defence Force. They’re still entitled to strike. This bill continues the ability for the Defence Force to carry out its vital activity in the security of our nation, and anything to the counter is just absolute rubbish.
acuity.explanation: She takes up Twyford's central characterisation of the bill and denies it directly, asserting that civilian Defence Force workers retain the right to strike — the speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different. But she engages only a loosened version of the claim (Twyford argued the bill removes parliamentary oversight of using troops to break strikes, not that striking becomes illegal) and dismisses the rest as rubbish rather than answering the oversight point, so this is partial engagement, not full. The strawman quality is a rigor matter and is deliberately not counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "This bill is about strike-breaking; there's no two ways about it. It is about breaking industrial action, and defence members of the defence forces will be asked to cross the picket lines of striking workers."

acuity.statement: How do I respond to that speech? That was outstanding. I think the summary of that in its entirety was: “That was gobbledegook, and this is a good bill.” I think you could say that about anything, really—but, never mind, we’re here to discuss this piece of legislation, which is a direct consequence of the cuts that this Government has driven right across the public sector and right across New Zealand’s front-line services.
acuity.explanation: She quotes the previous speech back and ridicules its brevity, but engages none of its content: Weenink's substantive claim that civilian defence workers retain the right to strike and that the bill preserves the Defence Force's operational capability goes entirely unaddressed, and the speech pivots immediately to prepared material on public-sector cuts. Mocking and summarising an opponent in order to turn away from them is a mere reference, which the rubric places in the 0.1–0.3 band; it earns 0.2 rather than 0.1 because the pivot stays on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanessa Weenink: "They’re still entitled to strike. This bill continues the ability for the Defence Force to carry out its vital activity in the security of our nation"

acuity.statement: My son is a 19-year-old in the Defence Force. He was one of the youngest to graduate, as an 18-year-old, last year. He would be ashamed of hearing the ramble, the Labour lies from the left-hand side right now.
acuity.explanation: The speech characterises the preceding contribution as a ramble and lies without engaging a single one of its claims — not the backfilling of cut civilian roles, not the zero pay offer, not the removal of the parliamentary resolution requirement. It is a generalised dismissal of the other bench plus a commendation of the bill, which would read identically whatever Labour had just argued; it scores 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because it gestures at the preceding speech and at this bill's status quo.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen argued the bill is a direct consequence of public-sector cuts, that the Government is backfilling cut civilian roles with uniformed personnel, and that PSA members in the Defence Force only won a better offer than a zero pay increase by striking — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I appreciate that the Minister comes from a very different point of view from the Labour Party on this, but even the Minister must accept that the Defence (Workforce) Amendment Bill tells the public nothing. It doesn't inform them.
acuity.explanation: Collins had just asserted the title is accurate, clear and unambiguous; White takes that exact claim and contests it, naming the title and arguing it conveys nothing to the public, then puts a direct question back to the Minister on it. The speech would have to change if Collins had defended the title differently. Not 1.0 because after engaging the title claim she returns to prepared material on forced labour and her volunteers rather than testing Collins's reasoning further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So the title is exactly as it as should be. It is clear, it’s unambiguous" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: I’m happy to be told by the Minister that my listening to the debate is wrong somehow, but I really think that something along those lines would be a much more accurate description of what this bill does.
acuity.explanation: Brooking engages the specific proposition Collins advanced — that the title is accurate — by reporting what she took from Collins's own account of the bill, offering an alternative title that would describe it, and inviting the Minister to correct her if her reading of the debate is wrong. She also takes up Collins's 'emotional rubbish' jab by disavowing emotion. Short of 1.0 because she engages Collins's conclusion about the title rather than the substantive argument about the Chief of Defence Force's deployment powers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s nothing wrong with this title to the bill. It’s accurate and it doesn’t have all that emotional rubbish that I’ve just been listening to" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Just so that we are all clear as we start this discussion as to what the problem statement is, it doesn't feel to me like there's an absence of power. There is a power there for those authorisations to continue over a summer period.
acuity.explanation: Collins grounded the bill in the claim that the Chief of Defence Force was powerless over the summer recess because Parliament could not be recalled to vote. Walters goes to the statute, reads section 9(8)(b) of the Defence Act 1990 into the debate, and uses it to deny the premise — the Governor-General can extend an authority by Proclamation when Parliament is not sitting — then asks the Minister why that existing power was insufficient. The contribution is explicitly triggered by what the Minister said ('it did spark a question that I didn't have in my head before') and would be different if Collins had framed the problem another way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "for the Chief of Defence Force to be powerless to actually put in uniformed staff over that Christmas period when Parliament had risen, and we couldn’t actually come back to get Parliament to vote again, was outrageously unacceptable" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: From what I could see, and what I understand, is that actually didn’t eventuate, and this is one of those stopgap precautionary measures, if you will, to make sure that, during that time, there’s still an ability for the Chief of Defence Force and even the Minister to play their role to backfill a number of those positions should there be industrial action. My question to the Minister is, put simply: is that correct?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the topic the Minister had just set out — what gap the bill fills and whether it is a precautionary stopgap — and puts a direct confirmatory question on it. But he engages the Minister's remarks from the previous night rather than the specific adjournment-provision claim just made, and the rest is his own prepared line of questioning about timing, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the argument in front of him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "There’s no current provision for when the House is adjourned, and the bill addresses that."

acuity.statement: In terms of the commencement, just following on from the Hon Peeni Henare around the commencement date, there are things—as we heard from the second reading and select committee stage—that are concerns. Particularly, I think we’ll explore this a little bit more and it’s more appropriately under clause 4, but I just want to flag that there are also interactions with other parts of the principal Act, section 9 as well, that I think deserve a little more teasing out in terms of the implementation.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up Henare's commencement-date strand and carries it forward, adding a concrete alternative (an Order in Council date rather than the day after Royal assent) that only makes sense as a continuation of that thread. It extends rather than tests the preceding argument, and much of the turn is a pitch for his own amendment, so it sits above a mere topical gesture without reaching full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "here we are, in urgency, going through three stages of this bill" — his questioning of the commencement timing

acuity.statement: I had another question related to the identification of the problem, which is that current sections 9(2) and 9(4) give the Minister powers to make these authorisations. I can’t spot whether there is a restriction on how many authorisations a Minister is able to make or the duration between authorisations.
acuity.explanation: Goes directly at the premise of the Minister's case — that existing provisions leave a gap — by naming the specific sections that may already supply the power, and asking whether anything stops the Minister simply issuing a fresh 14-day authorisation. The speech would have to change if the Minister had justified the bill on different grounds, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "The existing provisions only cover a situation where the House of Parliament was dissolved or expired."

acuity.statement: The Hon Peeni Henare has asked whether last year’s action prompted the need for the bill. Well, yes, it certainly showed that existing provisions were insufficient and not practical. One of the provisions addresses the risks that an extension is required when the House is adjourned, and that’s one of the issues that we dealt with last night, after a question from Vanushi Walters. The risk didn’t eventuate, but it may well in future.
acuity.explanation: Names the question put to her, answers it squarely (yes, last year's action showed the provisions were insufficient), and then qualifies Henare's own framing by conceding the risk did not eventuate while arguing it may recur. This is the specific claim engaged and reworked, not a pivot to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "if it was indeed that instance this time last year that has, one, caused this bill"

acuity.statement: There is no restriction on the number of authorisations that the Minister can make, or the period before them, but, of course, we have the opportunity in the House for members to ask the Minister of Defence—in this case, me—questions or to have urgent debates and to bring the matter to the attention of the House.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the piece of information the preceding speaker said she could not locate, confirms the premise of her challenge, and then answers the consequence she drew from it by pointing to the House's scrutiny mechanisms. Maximum responsiveness; the quality of that answer belongs to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "I can’t spot whether there is a restriction on how many authorisations a Minister is able to make or the duration between authorisations."

acuity.statement: I do take a point from the Minister that we did have a select committee process and there were a number of submissions we heard, and that’s helped to shape the bill as it is, but we are moving through the last remaining stages through urgency, which, if we weren’t moving through urgency, would give us time to pause and reflect given the gravity of the issues at stake here.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the Minister's answer that holds — the select committee process and submissions — and disputes the inference she drew from it, that the urgency complaint is therefore baseless. Concession-plus-rebuttal aimed at the argument just made; it could not have been delivered in this form against a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "When I hear all these cries about urgency, we’re talking about a second reading, committee of the whole House stages, and a third reading. It’s already gone through a full process."

acuity.statement: One more time, I go back to whether there’s a gap in the legislation, and I think the point of real clarity was when the Minister spoke to the fact that there is no limit on her ability to make those announcements, make a new power—a second power if you like—on the expiration of the first. I’m, again, just curious about the benefit of changing legislation to extend when that power is already there to make a second—forget the language around it—authorisation. In my mind, while there might be administrative ease rolled into a decision to do this, it removes some oversight.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated rationale — that the Chief of Defence Force must be able to act over the adjournment — concedes the readiness point, and turns the Minister's acknowledgement that a second authorisation can already be issued into an argument that the amendment is unnecessary. The speech would have to change if Collins had argued differently; it uses what she said rather than merely referring to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "it is very important that the Chief of Defence Force has the confidence to go into this break knowing that he’s got the ability to pull in the right people at the right time"

acuity.statement: I imagine that the Minister, if a circumstance like this arose, would have a fair warning that there might be an expiry in the period, as we do now, in fact, heading into the Christmas period. So an assessment could be made before the actual expiration of the first authorisation in time for the Minister to, with due diligence, consider the circumstances and whether the second authorisation was needed over a period, and also take some advice about how far that second authorisation would get us and whether the House was likely to be sitting again or to resume at that period in time.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's specific Christmas-adjournment scenario and answers it on its own terms — foreseeable expiry, advance assessment, a second authorisation — but sits inside a largely prepared reading of section 9, so it takes up one strand rather than the whole argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "As for the proximity of Christmas, of course that’s an issue—to make sure that the House isn’t adjourned and we have a problem"

acuity.statement: But also, I think my second question is that the purpose of the bill and the intention of the bill, as the Minister stated in some of the earlier debates, is to address the instances where the House is not sitting during the holiday period, and, therefore, if the Minister isn’t able to do what is needed in the event of a strike, for example, then the House needs to be recalled to be able to make that decision, but I don’t see how that relates to the 30 days, because the scenario that the Minister has referred to is covered under subsection (2).
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's stated purpose accurately and then draws out its consequence — that the scenario she described is already covered, so the 30-day extension does not follow from her own justification — and ties the point to a named amendment. Squarely aimed at the preceding argument's reasoning rather than at the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "whenever Parliament is adjourned during the Christmas break, not only is it difficult to do anything through Parliament"

acuity.statement: The proposals here and much of the context and the speeches that have been given to date have talked about the threat to national security, the need to uphold national security, and matters around health and safety, and those are all things that I think everybody in this House will agree to. That's the reason for the amendment tabled in my name that looks towards proposing tightening up this area. This is where I believe the greatest grey area section is.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding substantive turn was Vanushi Walters, who put two specific questions to the Minister: how the 30-day figure was arrived at and whether a middle-ground ministerial re-affirmation of a first authorisation could be written into the Defence Act, plus a question about caretaker-government powers under section 9(8)(b). Henare's speech takes up none of that. It is prepared material on the clause actually under debate — his own tabled amendment narrowing the permitted NZDF functions — and gestures at the debate generally ('the speeches that have been given to date', 'I appreciate the enthusiasm of my colleagues') and at Teanau Tuiono's earlier point, but it engages no part of Walters' argument or proposal. Deleting her turn and substituting a different argument on the same bill would not change a word of this speech, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band: on-topic, unresponsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters asked 'what is the background in terms of understanding how that number was arrived at and what's the logic of getting from 14 to 30?' and proposed writing into the Defence Act a ministerial power to approve continuation of a first authorisation; this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: As for bringing in the Governor-General to make rulings on all this, I think it’s always best to actually try not to politicise the Governor-General or her role. I think that it’s incredibly important that Governors-General are able to undertake their constitutional role without us trying to put them in a difficult position and politicise them.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific mechanism Henare built his whole case on and supplies a reason to reject it (constitutional propriety / not politicising the office) rather than ignoring it. The passage would not exist had Henare not argued the Governor-General fallback, so it is squarely responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "the commander in chief, in this case the Gover-General, can in her power extend these powers anyway until at least the House comes back" — his central argument that clause 4 is unnecessary because the Governor-General provides a plan B.

acuity.statement: There has been some suggestion that the Government is pushing this through. This bill is not something that we—it’s not on our mandate and it’s not something that we campaigned on. The reason is that the issue has arisen at the request of the Chief of Defence Force.
acuity.explanation: Engages Henare's "not needed" claim head-on by locating the need outside her own discretion — in a request from the Chief of Defence Force. It answers the asserted absence of need with a claimed source of need, which is engagement with the content, not a pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "actually what’s being proposed here by the Minister in this particular bill in clause 4 are just simply not needed. They’re just simply not needed."

acuity.statement: Why are we changing the expiry of an authorisation in relation Public Service employees outside the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) from 14 days to 30 days—that was the question that was pretty much asked. Well, it’s a practical and pragmatic change. The 14-day expiry is no longer fit for purpose in the context of present-day industrial action.
acuity.explanation: Engages the 14-versus-30-day strand Henare raised and gives a reason for the extension, but does not take up the specific 21-day compromise he put to her; she restates and justifies 30 days instead of answering the middle-ground proposition. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Peeni Henare: "Of course, the Minister wants to do 30 days. I say, why don’t we meet in the middle? Why don’t we just call it three weeks and call it 21 days?"

acuity.statement: But I think there’s a good argument here, and I find myself agreeing with the Minister in terms of the ability to have a partial strike to allow people to express themselves and have that point as well, because, as the Minister was saying earlier, the reason why we’re turning towards the 30 days or 14 days and so forth is because of the likelihood of stronger industrial action, because that is the only pathway forward.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own premise about partial strikes and longer industrial action, accepts it, and draws out a consequence she did not — that partial strikes should therefore be permitted in the defence sector — turning her justification into the basis for an amendment request. The speech would have to change entirely had Collins reasoned differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "Modern industrial action—including practices of work to rule, or partial strike—mean that industrial action is now more likely to last longer than 14 days"

acuity.statement: I think this is important because—even though I see the language in the clause in relation to the work needing to be done to not prejudice national security or “the ability or readiness (or both) of the Armed Forces to perform specific operational activities”, or when it is necessary for reasons of health and safety—there doesn’t seem to be a provision around also having those relevant skills, qualifications, and experience for those roles.
acuity.explanation: Collins had just defended the bill's design on the ground that it keys on the effects of industrial action rather than on which roles are in or out. Menéndez March takes up that same effects-based test and identifies what he says it omits — any requirement that the backfilling personnel hold the relevant skills — and he also picks up her remark about having to come to Parliament by noting the earlier-triggered parliamentary debate has been diminished as a safeguard. So he engages a real strand of the preceding argument rather than merely naming it. But he does not rebut her claim that a role-based test would be unworkable, and the bulk of the turn is a prepared four-part question about advice sought and skills gaps that would have read the same whatever Collins had said in defence of the clause. Partial engagement: mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "That’s why the bill’s requirements are around the impact of the industrial action, not the specific roles that are in or out."

acuity.statement: They would only conduct the work of civil staff if they had the suitable skills for the roles, and the fact is, you’ll see in many parts of the Defence Force; there are both civilian and uniformed staff there.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific gap Menéndez March had just alleged: he said the clause contains no skills requirement, and she supplies the substantive counter — that backfilling would only happen where the suitable skills exist, and that uniformed staff already hold the trades and professions (engineers, lawyers, doctors, electricians, technicians) and already sit alongside civilians across the Defence Force, including in health and safety. The speech would be materially different had the preceding question been about something else. Short of the top of the band because she never addresses the narrower question actually put — whether she sought advice on the ratio of personnel with the relevant qualifications, and what the advice said — and closes by pivoting into a recruitment pitch. Scored on engagement only: the opening suggestion that the member is "probably not very familiar" with Defence Force personnel is a civility matter, not an acuity one, and I have let it move neither way here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "there doesn’t seem to be a provision around also having those relevant skills, qualifications, and experience for those roles"

acuity.statement: What I'm interested to understand from the Minister is how this change under new section 9A addresses some of those systemic workforce issues and, in particular, the ability to not only attract but to retain those specialist roles that we want to make sure that we have in place, and to fix some of those basics, such as making sure that those specialist roles are paid fairly, that they're not overworked, and they're given the resources to do jobs safely and professionally, because it's some of those pressures within the workforce that effectively make it really difficult for those people who continue to work in those roles.
acuity.explanation: The turn is squarely on the clause under debate — new section 9A — and so is not unresponsive to the debate itself, which keeps it off the floor of the band. But it engages no part of what Collins had just said. Her answer on skills and cross-over between uniformed and civilian roles goes unacknowledged, and the training question is simply re-put rather than tested against her reply. The material here is a prepared workforce case drawn from the member's police experience — attraction and retention, pay, overwork, workforce cohesion — and it would have been delivered word-for-word had Collins given an entirely different answer, or had the previous speaker been someone else. A gesture at the debate without engagement sits at 0.3, not at the mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Judith Collins had just answered that military personnel "would only conduct the work of civil staff if they had the suitable skills for the roles" and set out the trades and professions held by uniformed staff; this statement does not take that answer up, and later in the turn re-asks "are they trained for them?" as though the answer had not been given.

acuity.statement: This is to deal with what the Minister said before, and I think this is really timely, because the Minister just said that “Look, I'm not the Minister responsible. That is on the advice of the Chief of Defence Force.” This is an amendment that is replicating what we're currently seeing in section 9(4) of the Defence Act, which states that the Minister, on information supplied by the Chief of Defence Force or a Vice Chief of the Defence Force, may grant the authority.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own stated position — that these are the Chief of Defence Force's decisions, not hers — and turns it into an argument for his amendment, which would require the authority to rest on information supplied by the Chief or a Vice Chief. The speech could not have been delivered as written if Collins had not just disclaimed that role; it is built directly on what she said moments earlier.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "it is not my role as the Minister of Defence to decide where staff are shifted, what roles they do, or anything like that; that's the Chief of Defence Force."

acuity.statement: Now, this is an interesting one, because the Minister and various members during the committee stage have consistently used the term “health and safety”, but in the legislation it is not “health and safety” or “safety and health”; it's “safety or health”, as two mutually exclusive elements.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact wording the Minister had just used repeatedly ("health and safety") and uses the mismatch between her language and the bill's disjunctive "safety or health" as the ground for an amendment. This is engagement with the content of the preceding turn at the level of the words actually spoken, not a mere reference to the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "Should there be an amendment to require the health and safety risk to be imminent?"

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is in relation to some of the risks that have been highlighted in the regulatory impact statement. There’s a direct risk that has been highlighted that this will impact on the bargaining power of civilian staff to some extent.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's central assurance that the right to strike is untouched by putting the regulatory impact statement's bargaining-power risk against it, and elsewhere picks up the "core defence outputs" strand raised earlier. But it is largely a fresh set of prepared questions on the right subject rather than a rebuttal of the specific reasoning Collins gave, so engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "The bill very clearly maintains the right to strike."

acuity.statement: So what is the process in order to identify when there are gaps because of an industrial dispute to move people from one particular spot to another? How is that identified? Also, what happens if you don't have qualified staff at that particular skill level available at that time?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (how clause 5 would work in practice when civilian staff strike) and genuinely reactive in form, but it takes up no part of the preceding speaker's argument. The questions would be put in identical terms whatever Walters had said about her amendments, because he is pursuing an exchange with the Minister rather than engaging the turn he follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters spoke about her tabled amendments on the right to strike and on what the Minister must turn her mind to when exercising discretion, and this statement does not take any of it up; the answers he engages (to Ricardo Menéndez March) are not in the text.

acuity.statement: But just to remind those at home, in no shape or form does this reduce the ability for industrial action. I think I said it in my second reading speech, that it’s awfully disruptive to any industry when there is industrial action.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows Tuiono's substantive third-reading speech, whose central claim was that the bill limits and weakens the right to strike by permitting uniformed personnel to replace striking civilian staff. Her opening sentence does take up that specific strand and contradict it head-on, which is real engagement rather than a mere reference. But it is a bare denial — she supplies no reasoning, figure or clause to meet the argument — and she immediately signals the material is prepared ("I think I said it in my second reading speech") before returning to general praise of the bill and commending it to the House. None of Tuiono's other points (partial strikes, union consultation, the zero pay offer, the use of urgency, Waiōuru housing) are touched. Engages one strand, then prepared material: mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this bill weakens the right to strike by allowing striking civilian staff to be replaced with uniformed personnel" — Teanau Tuiono

acuity.statement: What used to require a resolution of this House will now require only the stroke of a Minister’s pen.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's immediately preceding turn defended the bill on the ground that parliamentary oversight and checks and balances remain. Kaipara takes up that one strand directly, contrasting the former requirement for a House resolution with ministerial sign-off, and elsewhere notes the House is only notified after the fact. But the engagement is confined to that strand; the rest of the speech is prepared Te Pāti Māori material (kaupapa framing, incomes policy) that would read identically whatever Patterson had argued, so this sits at a partial engagement rather than a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there are checks and balances; there is still parliamentary oversight" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: It’s hard to believe their speeches are thanking those very same workers they’re about to undermine, when we have a bill in front of us that follows, literally, a 2024 zero pay increase for the Defence Force civilian staffers, which would have seen them take effective pay cuts due to inflationary pressures.
acuity.explanation: Patterson opened with thanks to Defence Force personnel and praise for what they do. Menéndez March takes that specific move — the tribute — and turns it against the preceding speaker, setting it beside the 2024 zero pay offer to the civilian staff the bill concerns. The speech would have to change if the prior turn had not contained the acknowledgement it attacks. Short of 1.0 because it engages the rhetorical gesture rather than Patterson's substantive argument about the bill's mechanism.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would also like to acknowledge the incredible work that our Defence Force does, being prepared to put themselves into harm’s way on our behalf" — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: I do not buy, nor believe in, any of the Government’s arguments that this is not about undermining the ability to strike, because even though the Minister says that striking is part of a democracy, well, clearly this Government doesn’t really believe in the right for workers to take part in strikes without those very same actions undermining their ability to make ends meet, because, otherwise, they would have not introduced legislation this term to actually add pay deductions to striking workers.
acuity.explanation: Patterson's central defence two turns earlier was that the bill does not undermine the right to strike. Menéndez March names that exact claim and argues against it, offering a reason (this Government's separate legislation deducting pay from striking workers) for disbelieving it. This is the specific proposition just put to the House, taken up and contested — near the top of the band; scored on engagement only, not on whether the inference about intent holds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This does not undermine the right to strike. There is absolutely the right for those civilian personnel to strike." — Mark Patterson

acuity.statement: Of course, since then, it’s grown rather substantially, and quite rightly, the Minister and others have pointed to the fact that the defence force plays an integral role in terms of national security, but also in terms of peacekeeping and our aid contribution, and also in terms of emergencies. Certainly, on this side of the House, we respect that role and we are grateful for that role.
acuity.explanation: Van de Molen's immediately preceding turn claimed Opposition speeches contained 'not a single mention about upholding national security' and that the bill is needed to maintain national security on bases. Walters takes up that strand directly — affirming the defence force's national security role and her side's respect for it — and later disputes the premise that a gap exists by pointing to the Minister's power to make a second authorisation. But most of her contribution is prepared committee-stage material on the problem statement, urgency and select committee timeframes that would have been delivered whatever van de Molen said, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of his specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "It’s, frankly, embarrassing that neither of those two previous speeches, and indeed some of those before, from the Opposition benches had not a single mention about upholding national security."

acuity.statement: It is telling to see the Labour Party and the Green Party come out firmly opposing that support—not only that they won’t debate the issue that exists, but they spread these mistruths.
acuity.explanation: The turn immediately before him was Walters' detailed argument that there is no legislative gap because the Minister can issue a second authorisation, plus a proposed alternative of a ministerial extension power. Costley asserts the Opposition 'won’t debate the issue that exists' and pivots to rebutting claims about the 1951 wharf strike and forestry workers, which came from earlier speeches not from Walters. He names her side as opponents and characterises their position, but engages no part of the no-gap argument he had just heard, so this is a mere reference, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued "There is no gap. The Minister can make a second authorisation." and proposed a ministerial extension power, and this statement does not take either up — it only characterises Labour and the Greens as refusing to debate.

acuity.statement: It really fills me with sadness hearing some of the comments from the other side of the House. I haven’t had the pleasure of being on the select committee that dealt with this bill, but, from the basic reading, I can see and hear that what’s being said on the other side does not reflect what we’re doing here. As the Hon Judith Collins just said, the arguments against are showing actually how much the other side cares about our defence force—or, rather, doesn’t care for our defence force. This law, essentially, keeps New Zealand safe around the clock while still respecting the right of civilian staff to strike.
acuity.explanation: Follows Helen White's detailed argument that ordering military personnel into struck civilian roles undermines both the power of a strike and the military's own industrial rights, and that removing the requirement to return to the legislature erodes checks and balances. Nakhle gestures at "comments from the other side" and flatly asserts the opposite conclusion (the law "still respect[s] the right of civilian staff to strike") without taking up any strand of the reasoning — no engagement with the strike-breaking mechanism, the extension period, or the checks-and-balances point. A bare contradiction plus a reference to the previous speakers is a gesture at the debate, not a partial engagement, so it sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "having an impact on striking and being a strike-breaking tool"

acuity.statement: The member Rima Nakhle, who has just resumed her seat, talked about the fact that they care about the Defence Force. My question would be why then did this Government offer them a zero percent increase in pay? Then when they took industrial action, they’ve introduced this legislation as a direct response to prevent those civilians from being able to take collective action such as strikes in the future.
acuity.explanation: Names the immediately preceding speaker's central claim — that the Government side is the one that cares about the Defence Force — and does something with it, confronting it with the zero percent pay offer and the sequence from industrial action to this bill. The speech would have had to change if Nakhle had made a different argument, so engagement is high and pointable. Scored on engagement only: whether the zero percent characterisation is accurate is a veracity question, and the argumentative leap from the pay offer to the Government's motives is a rigor question, neither of which moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "the arguments against are showing actually how much the other side cares about our defence force"

acuity.statement: No, they don’t. There are limited life-preserving facilities.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the specific factual assertion Kirkpatrick had just made about hospital strikes, and supplies the reason — that only limited life-preserving services are maintained. The intervention would be meaningless if the preceding sentence had said anything else, which is the hallmark of real engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dana Kirkpatrick: "nurses and doctors leave the hospital when they strike and nothing is put in place to help people in that hospital"

acuity.statement: Yes, they do, because I know some that do it.
acuity.explanation: Takes up McLellan's denial head-on and disputes it, so the reply is squarely aimed at what was just said. It engages only the bare "no, they don't" and leaves the substantive qualification — that strike cover is limited to life-preserving facilities — untouched, so it is engagement of one strand rather than of the whole point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tracey McLellan: "There are limited life-preserving facilities."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you to the Minister for walking us through what this bill purports to do, in his view. Labour strenuously opposes this bill, because it doesn't do what it says on the tin.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's just-delivered account of the bill's purpose and contests its framing — that what he described is what the bill "purports" to do rather than what it does. That is engagement with his characterisation, but at the level of the topic and his overall claim rather than with any particular clause, objective or quotation he set out.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "The purpose of this legislation, as has been said, is to establish a Director of Regulation with a set of statutory objectives and some powers and some obligations."

acuity.statement: The member Ingrid Leary has just taken 8 minutes to ask two very simple questions. First of all, a playgroup is defined in the wider Education and Training Act as a group that meets on a regular basis but where children don’t attend for more than four hours at a time. There are other definitions, but the point is that the definition is already in the wider Act.
acuity.explanation: Leary's clause 4 questions asked directly for the Minister's definition of a "playgroup". Seymour supplies that definition and locates it in the wider Education and Training Act, i.e. he answers the specific question put rather than delivering prepared material. The reply would be different had Leary asked something else. The opening jibe about taking 8 minutes bears on civility, not on responsiveness, and is not counted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can he please define a playgroup for us?" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: On the absence of a definition of the Treaty in the “Interpretation” section of this bill: I’m an ambitious politician, and I thought about perhaps getting some of my ideas about defining the Treaty into this education amendment bill, but I actually just don’t think defining the Treaty of Waitangi should be done here in this interpretation section of the Education and Training Act.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Leary's specific question about why Te Tiriti is absent from the key definitional clause and gives a reason — that the interpretation section of this Act is the wrong vehicle for defining the Treaty. Squarely aimed at the claim raised, though it engages only the definitional strand and not her related question about Crown obligations, hence just short of full marks. Whether the answer is adequate or well-reasoned is a matter for other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we want to understand why Te Tiriti is not mentioned in clause 4" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: But what the Minister said was interesting to me because new section 14(b), inserted by clause 5, to “support the choice of parents and caregivers to participate in the labour market.” is not in the existing legislation. That is new.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's specific claim — that these purposes are long-standing and merely being restated in statute — and tests it against the text of the clause, pointing out that the labour-market limb has no counterpart in the existing Act. The speech would have to change if Seymour had argued something else; it is built directly on what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "I think it’s clear to most people that early childhood education policy has those objectives now, it has for a very long time."

acuity.statement: He then asked, “Why do we not include teachers?” Well, very simply, this is about children. This is about getting outcomes for children. I know that there will be people who want the service provider to be put at the centre of the policy, but it’s not—we’re doing this for children, and we have no intention of supporting the member’s amendment.
acuity.explanation: Restates the question just put to him, answers it with a reason (the provision is child-centred, not provider-centred) and states a decision on the specific amendment moved. This is engagement with the content of the preceding turn, not a reference to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "why in the purpose and objectives, are teachers not mentioned at all?"

acuity.statement: So my question to the Minister, with regards to section 14(b), is: if everybody knows that that’s what was happening and occurring in ECE, then why feel the need to make a specific purpose of this piece of legislation?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification — that this is simply obvious reality — and turns it into the difficulty for his case: if it is already universally understood, the statutory purpose is unexplained. The question only makes sense as a reply to what Seymour just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "it reflects the simple reality that many New Zealanders actually do send their child to early childhood education so they can go to work"

acuity.statement: Then the question is, has there been enough consultation? Well, actually this is a process that began in June 2024, 18 months ago. The Ministry for Regulation began consulting literally thousands of teachers, centre owners, parents about their desires for regulation of early childhood education.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the challenge just made and supplies the dates, body and scale of the consultation it asked about. The content of the answer is wholly determined by the question that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jo Luxton: "throughout the regulatory impact statement, there has been constant referral to the lack of consultation"

acuity.statement: My first question, then, in this part is on the difference around the provision wording in the original section in the Education and Training Act, and then the words “to provide for”, which the Minister has chosen.
acuity.explanation: On the clause under debate and gestures at the Minister's drafting choice, but engages no part of the argument just made about consultation or the purpose of putting the regulator's duties in statute. Prepared material on the right subject rather than a reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour had just answered on the June 2024 consultation process and the statutory rights and responsibilities of the regulator, and this statement does not take either up — it opens a separate line on the drafting of "to provide for".

acuity.statement: Grandparents can be caregivers for the purposes of this Act. There is not any type of new service envisaged that we are putting in place.
