acuity.statement: That was quite a balanced and reasonable contribution from Peeni Henare, and I commend him for it. But the gap between his contribution and the others that we’ve heard, particularly from Te Pāti Māori, is extremely stark. The tinfoil-hat wearers over on that side better have a listen to actually what their potential coalition partner just said in his contribution, because the gap is incredibly large.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows a substantive turn and gestures at it, but only to commend it in general terms and use the contrast as a springboard against Te Pāti Māori. He takes up none of the content Henare actually put: that fines do not deter foreign interference because the payoff exceeds any penalty, that the bill must be tested for fitness given how fast interference evolves, or that the rhetoric risks putting question marks over migrant communities. The rest of the speech asserts the legislation is common sense and attacks conspiracy theories — it would read almost identically had Henare said something quite different, or nothing. That is a named reference plus a pivot, which the rubric places in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5; 0.3 because there is at least a real gesture at the preceding contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it does seem rather inflammatory" — Peeni Henare, on Rawiri Waititi's contribution

acuity.statement: The Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill strengthens New Zealand criminal law. It ensures New Zealand criminal law sufficiently addresses the harm of foreign interference, and it will better equip relevant agencies to hold people to account. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn in which Ingrid Leary supported the bill but raised specific caveats — unintended consequences for Chinese New Zealanders driving them underground, the weakening of overseas investment rules, the difficulty of drawing lines in application, and the need for more resourcing. Garcia takes up none of it. His speech is a three-sentence prepared commendation that would be word-for-word identical whatever the previous speaker had said; it is at least on the bill under debate, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued 'I had concerns in my IPAC role about potential unintended consequences of this bill for Chinese New Zealanders' and that 'This is not a silver bullet', and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Well, I’ve heard a lot this evening, and what we have here is a Government that continues to use scaremongering tactics with our people here in Aotearoa, without any true evidence. We’ve had a few bills passed through this House this year. One was about regulating space because there was an imminent threat—we weren’t told what that imminent threat was.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Costello's case — her premise that a real foreign-interference risk makes this legislation necessary and uncontroversial — and disputes it by denying any evidenced threat, drawing an analogy to the unnamed 'imminent threat' cited for the space bill. It does not engage her specific legal argument about mens rea, actus reus and the 'and, and, and' structure of the offence, and it moves quickly into Te Pāti Māori's prepared foreign-policy material, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "with that comes the risks of foreign interference" / "This is a very clear piece of legislation, which is raising questions as to why it’s causing so much consternation" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: That’s not a matter of opinion. Read Te Tiriti o Waitangi. This is your problem, sir. This is your problem. That member hasn’t read Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It never ever said that Māori ceded sovereignty.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the specific proposition just put to him — that whether Māori ceded sovereignty is a matter of opinion — and supplies the ground for the contradiction, the text of Te Tiriti. The reply would be impossible if Foster had said anything else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only; the jab at Foster for not having read the Treaty is a separate question from whether the interjection was answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s a matter of opinion." — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: This is an important question and this is an important point, and I love the fact that people are saying, “Well, what is the fact?” To be honest, we are already seeing that. We have seen that this very week and also last week, in terms of some of the bills that get passed in this House.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the fact-versus-story challenge thrown across the chamber and turns it into his own question — what counts as foreign interference, and whose conduct the Government has in mind — before returning to prepared material on migrant communities and Te Tiriti. He engages the frame of the challenge rather than offering the facts demanded, which places it mid-band: you can point at what is being taken up, but no specific claim is rebutted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Don’t let facts get in the way of a good story." — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: The deeper that we get into this evening, the more we see drama, theatre, performance, and fiction, and over here, we see fact and a Government that is looking to get things done to get this country back on track. Let me give you some facts this evening.
acuity.explanation: Characterises the preceding speeches as drama and fiction and then recites a prepared list of the bill's clauses. Labelling opponents' arguments as fiction is a reference, not an engagement: nothing is said about Waititi's claim that criminalising allegiance to the Sovereign presumes a cession of sovereignty Māori never made, nor about Xu-Nan's question of what counts as foreign interference, nor about the absent consultation with hapū and iwi. The gesture at the evening's debate and the on-topic clause list keep it above the floor, but the speech would read identically whatever had been argued before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Waititi argued the allegiance clauses presume Māori ceded sovereignty and that consultation with tangata whenua was inadequate, and Xu-Nan asked what is to count as foreign interference; this statement takes up neither, dismissing both as fiction.

acuity.statement: I feel really privileged to be in this position, where, as the last speaker, I am ushering the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill from a bill stage to an Act of Parliament stage. As our excellent Minister of Justice said earlier, foreign interference is not acceptable. As someone of a Lebanese background, I know first-hand what foreign interference does to countries like my beautiful parents’ homeland of Lebanon.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by a different member was substantive and specific — Walters put several arguments on the table: the breadth of the "ought to know" mens rea in new section 78AAA, the inadequacy of the section 7 Bill of Rights analysis on freedom of expression, the Law Society's proposed foreign-jurisdiction defence, and the Canadian foreign interference commissioner as a model. She also complained directly that "We haven’t seen the Government members engaging with some of the rights issues that were raised in select committee". Nakhle engages none of it: she asserts that foreign interference is unacceptable, cites her own background, and commends the bill. This speech would be word-for-word identical whatever Walters had said, so it fails the deciding test; it sits in the low band because it is at least about the bill under debate. It is not 0.0 only because the subject matter (foreign interference and this bill) is the matter before the House. No gesture at the argument is present, so 0.1 rather than 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued immediately before that "the section 7 report didn’t conduct an adequate analysis of whether the limitation of the right to freedom of expression was reasonable or not" and called for a public review of foreign interference, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I think, lastly, just to my colleague Tamatha Paul’s point in terms of her amendment. This is something that we’re hoping that we have adjusted this particular amendment from “constable must consult” to “inform” but considering this is something that we’ve seen in overseas jurisdictions and it’s hugely beneficial, we do seek the Minister’s support on this particular amendment.
acuity.explanation: Most of the turn is his own prepared Amendment Papers, but this passage takes up the specific amendment Paul had just asked the Minister to consider, supplies the detail that its wording was changed from 'consult' to 'inform', and adds an overseas-practice reason for it. The passage would not exist had Paul not raised it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "we really would like the Minister to consider our amendment around the constable having to inform person B before serving the notice to person A."

acuity.statement: If you took that away and just said “ought to know”, or lowered that threshold, there is a real risk—you know, there is potential maximum five-year prison sentence. If there was a lower standard, there is a risk, given the wide net of specified acts, that we would subject people who are annoying but innocuous to being liable to a lengthy prison sentence.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact wording Paul proposed inserting — 'ought to know' — and gives a reason against it: with a wide list of specified acts and a five-year maximum, a lower mental threshold would expose merely annoying conduct to prison. The answer would be different had a different amendment been put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "I wanted to ask whether the Minister would consider inserting provisions around “ought to know”"

acuity.statement: I just want to mention briefly that the National Party has decided to agree to Tamatha Paul’s Amendment Paper 439, that a constable must inform person B before providing a notice under the subsection of the Act, so that police can inform victims. Now, that was something that was raised by committee members and submitters. The advice I’ve had is that Police operational guidelines already require staff to consult with victims when decisions are made to issue warnings or other notices. We don’t think it’s strictly necessary, but we’re prepared to accept that one.
acuity.explanation: Responds to the police-notification amendment put by Paul and backed by Xu-Nan: identifies it by number, states the position on it, and gives the advice he received about existing operational guidelines — accepting it while disputing that it is necessary.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "we do seek the Minister’s support on this particular amendment" (and Tamatha Paul's amendment on the constable informing person B)

acuity.statement: Just a question for the Minister of Justice, just in relation to the Amendment Paper by Tamatha Paul, it does seem sensible, but I do want to just understand in more detail what the actual term “consult” does mean. You referred to police operations already consulting, but what does actually consulting mean in this case with “person B”, and would that actually—yeah, I mean, we just want to understand a bit more about what that means, just to make sure that this isn't going to inhibit people actually being charged under this regime.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the particular element of the Minister's answer — the claim that police guidelines already require consultation with victims — and presses on what consultation would mean in practice and whether it could impede charges. Marked down because he attaches the question to the wrong word, the amendment using 'inform' rather than 'consult'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "Police operational guidelines already require staff to consult with victims when decisions are made to issue warnings or other notices"

acuity.statement: Well, my reading of Amendment Paper 439 is that the constable must inform—the word “consult” is not used; it’s “inform”, 439.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the factual premise of the question just asked: the amendment under discussion says 'inform', not 'consult', so the question about the meaning of consultation does not arise on its text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "I do want to just understand in more detail what the actual term “consult” does mean"

acuity.statement: OK, thank you, well, that’s helpful clarification, but maybe if the Minister of Justice can just make sure he has the right amendment and we are clear about what we're agreeing to.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the correction as clarification, so it engages what was just said, but does nothing with the substance of it — instead of taking up the 'inform' wording he questions whether the Minister has the right paper in front of him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "the word “consult” is not used; it’s “inform”, 439"

acuity.statement: There is no number because it's a tabled amendment, so I guess the tabled amendment that is 9.15.04 on 19 November 2025 is the most accurate code I can provide.
acuity.explanation: Answers the Minister's question squarely: explains why no Amendment Paper number exists for a tabled amendment and supplies the identifying code and date instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "With the same number?"

acuity.statement: To the Minister of Justice: I want to get, if I could, some sense of your confidence in the application of when—like, in this instance, if we’re talking about “inform” or “consult” or whatever it is, probably the key word is “before”—that sentiment or that expectation is. When patterns are as they are in stalking, or patterns in family harm, or patterns in domestic violence—patterns when they’re set are hard to break.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the exchange she follows — the inform/consult wording — and isolates 'before' as the operative word, but then moves to her own concern about implementation on the ground rather than engaging the Minister's claim about existing police guidelines.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith / Todd Stephenson exchange: "the word “consult” is not used; it’s “inform”, 439" (Paul Goldsmith)

acuity.statement: There has been much said in this House already around the importance of this legislation. One of the things that I know and appreciate strongly about victims and the reality that they face is that the ability to be heard and seen and understood is a big part of a healing process.
acuity.explanation: Follows Chhour's detailed account of the lived effects of stalking and of victims being told their experience did not meet the offence threshold. Costello gestures at the debate ('much said in this House already') and speaks to the same subject — victims being heard — but takes up no specific claim Chhour made; the speech is prepared NZ First material on the bill's merits and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued. Sits in the 0.1-0.3 band because nothing specific can be pointed at as engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Karen Chhour described how victims were told that 'the creepy, obsessive behaviour that they face didn't meet the threshold of the offence' and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: I reflect particularly on our Minister Chhour’s kōrero tonight because, as wahine, you can affiliate with what has been shared, particularly the intergenerational ripples of the impact of stalking and harassment, not just on the mother but also on the children and mokopuna. I agree that there is a change—a change in the family, a change in the way in which they behave—and there are the constant stress levels that ripple through a home and through the lives of loved ones.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific substance of Chhour's speech — that the harm extends past the victim to family and children, and that it 'changes a person' and the way the household behaves — names it, accepts it, and extends it into an intergenerational frame reaching mokopuna. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had argued something else. Not 1.0 because after this engagement she moves to her own prepared material on rehabilitation and the amendment rather than contesting or developing Chhour's argument further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: 'It changes how everybody behaves in their everyday lives.' (and her account of the effect on 'their family, their children, and their wider network')

acuity.statement: Mr Speaker, thank you for the privilege of being able to speak in the third reading on this bill as we pass it this evening in this House. During the process of guiding the legislation through the Justice Committee and through the House I had the opportunity to meet with a group of women in my electorate who advocated for a change to the number of specified acts and the period of which those acts covered.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede him, including Lyndon's argument that the bill may leave no room for rehabilitation and offender support and her account of what the amendment agreed tonight does. Bates engages none of it: he gives his own process narrative and thanks his coalition partners. The speech is on the right subject but would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before him, so it sits at the bottom of the unpointable band rather than at 0.0 only because it is about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon argued the legislation may not provide room for treatment, rehabilitation and support for the offender, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: To say we’re doing something about it—it’s not about a particular political party taking a win, but it’s actually about this Parliament saying that we’ve listened to the victims across New Zealand who came and spoke to the legislation, who've numerously shared their stories with many, many members of Parliament, and finally, Parliament has come together and said we’re going to do something about it.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford follows Webb's detailed speech on the offence's mental element, the specified-acts list, the two-incidents-in-a-limited-period threshold and the operational burden on police, and takes up none of it. His remarks are on the right subject — the same bill, the same point about victims being predominantly women — and gesture at the debate's cross-party tone, but they would be word-for-word the same had Webb made any other argument about this bill. That places it in the unpointable band rather than at partial engagement; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the material is squarely about the bill under debate and glances at the chamber's shared position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the new offence turns on a mental element — that the perpetrator must 'know that their behaviour is likely to cause this effect' — and that 'the police will need some time to work through exactly how it can assist them'; this statement does not take up any of that. It echoes the general theme of cross-party credit ('the credit does go largely to the women who have advocated for this change') without engaging the argument.

acuity.statement: I recognise the number of stories that have been shared tonight. I think, sometimes, we might get a bit like, “It’s another story, and people say certain names often.”, but what is critical about it is telling the story, lest we forget. I want to acknowledge all the women that have stood in the House tonight to say the names, to repeat those stories, and to keep the reality of these things front of mind.
acuity.explanation: Kapa-Kingi follows Nakhle's turn and takes up one real strand of it — the naming of victims and the retelling of their stories — defending that practice against the thought that it becomes rote repetition. That is a pointable engagement with what preceded her, not merely a mention. But she engages the practice rather than any specific claim Nakhle made, and the rest of the speech is her own prepared material on the bill, acknowledgements and her sector background, which would stand unchanged whoever had spoken before. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whenever I look at a picture of Farzana Yaqubi, my heart weeps" — Rima Nakhle, who named Farzana Yaqubi and recounted David White's submission about his lost daughter

acuity.statement: Stalking can be randomly triggered, escalate quickly to dangerous levels. This bill seeks to clearly define the elements of stalking and harassment. By doing so, it also recognises the vulnerability of victims and the real harm and risk they face.
acuity.explanation: Prepared third-reading remarks on the correct subject that engage no part of the preceding speech. The words would be word-for-word identical whatever Helen White had argued — her specific claims about spyware, refuge statistics and shifting social norms about surveillance are left untouched, and nothing here rebuts, accepts, qualifies or extends them. It stays within the debate's subject matter (the bill's definitions and victim harm), so it is not wholly unresponsive, which places it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White spoke immediately before about stalking as a precursor to lethal violence, the use of spyware, and a "wave of misogyny" reaching New Zealand, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: So, yes, it is important that we change the law, but it’s also important that we change the way we listen when complaints are made, and that is in many ways a bigger problem.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the proposition running through the preceding turns — that this bill is the significant response to stalking — concedes it, and then contests its sufficiency, arguing the handling of complaints is the bigger failure and supporting that with the Yaqubi reporting timeline. The speech would have had to change if the earlier speakers had framed the problem as one of police response rather than of law; it is engagement with one strand of what preceded rather than with a specific contested claim or figure, and much of the surrounding material (select committee submissions, the RIS tables) is prepared content, so it sits around the middle of the scale rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "So it is an important time for a piece of legislation like this" — Walters grants the legislation's importance and then disputes that it is the main thing needed.

acuity.statement: The emissions trading scheme (ETS) doesn’t work on fuel, and that’s why—fuel is not in the European ETS. And there’s a really simple reason for this. It’s because people don’t make their decisions about which vehicle they’re going to buy based on what the fuel economy is, what the price of petrol is.
acuity.explanation: Court interjects proposing the ETS as the alternative instrument; Genter takes that specific suggestion up and answers it on its merits — the ETS does not bite on fuel, and vehicle purchase decisions are not driven by the small ETS component of the petrol price. The passage would not exist had Court not raised the ETS, which is the deciding test. (Her later pivot to who funds the ACT Party is a separate matter and belongs to Focus/Civility, not here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What about the ETS?" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: It’s going to cost them more money because they’re going to be spending more money to run their vehicles.
acuity.explanation: McCallum's interjection concedes a cost but confines it to purchase price. Genter engages that exact distinction rather than the general topic, relocating the cost to the running of the vehicle. Brief, but it is a direct answer to the point just put, and the sentence changes entirely if the interjection had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "To buy their vehicles, yes." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Grant McCallum, I know I’m never ever going to be successful in explaining basic economics to you, my friend.
acuity.explanation: This answers McCallum's repeated interjection by naming him and disparaging his grasp of economics, but engages no part of the purchase-cost-versus-running-cost point he was making. A reference to the interjector plus a put-down is an unresponsive reply on the right subject, so it sits in the low band rather than at a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "To buy them." — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: What we heard quite clearly from submitters is that submitters don’t want to buy the vehicles that are being imported to try and meet the clean vehicle standard. So importers, manufacturers are bringing in a certain collection of vehicles and the public of New Zealand—so it’s not the Government choosing, it’s not anybody being paid, you know, or say the fuel industry paying us to persuade people to buy particular cars. It is New Zealanders who are choosing to buy a particular set of cars.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows Court in the same debate and takes up one strand of what Court had just put: the allegation that government members are influenced by the fuel industry, which Foster rebuts by locating the choice of vehicles with consumers rather than with government or industry payment. He also engages Court's point about the deficit building up in importers' trading accounts by explaining the credits/debits mechanism that fails to 'marry'. But the bulk of the turn is prepared select committee report-back material (thanks to submitters, officials and committee, the timing of the report) that would have been delivered whatever Court had said, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal built on the specific argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "being somehow beholden to or under the influence of what she called the “fossil-fuel industry”" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: Well, there’s something that the people on the other side of the House haven’t worked out. It’s that the people of this country love their utes, and we need to be able to have our utes so that we can drive up to Northland—the electorate that’s miles above the rest—over the Brynderwyn Hills, and do it in an affordable manner. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Halbert had just argued the bill weakens the clean vehicle standard, extends carbon credit lifespans from three to four years, and responds to industry pressure rather than evidence. McCallum takes up none of that reasoning; he gestures at the debate only by asserting a competing claim about what New Zealanders want (utes, affordably) against Halbert's claim about what they want (to protect the planet). It is a counter-assertion plus a reference to 'the other side of the House', not engagement with any part of the argument, and could have been delivered whatever Halbert had said about the standard.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "New Zealanders don’t want to go backwards. They want to protect our planet."

acuity.statement: The children in that area will die at a greater rate because of the emissions from those utes that Grant McCallum just talked about.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific thing the previous speaker defended — utes driven for affordability and pleasure — and draws out a consequence he did not account for, locating it in her own electorate's exposure to motorway emissions. The sentence would not exist in this form if McCallum had defended something else; she names his example and turns it against him rather than merely citing him before pivoting. Short of 1.0 because it answers his affordability case with a health consequence rather than contesting the affordability reasoning itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "the people of this country love their utes, and we need to be able to have our utes"

acuity.statement: But he’s in the dark ages. He’s saying he’s got the right to go across the Brynderwnys in his ute. Well, that is an important right for Grant McCallum, but it is not as important as the right of the children in my area to have a clean environment. That’s a more important right.
acuity.explanation: Restates McCallum's claim accurately as a claim of right, concedes it has weight ('that is an important right'), and then does something with it — ranks it against a competing right and accepts the trade-off has to be made. This is the structure of engaging an argument rather than referencing it: accept part, dispute the rest, state the ground of the disagreement. Substitute a different pro-ute argument on the same topic and this passage would have to be rewritten.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "we need to be able to have our utes so that we can drive up to Northland"

acuity.statement: Choice is often the realm of the privileged. It is not something that is extended to all, generally, particularly where I come from, in Te Tai Tokerau, and that’s not because we don’t want it.
acuity.explanation: She takes the single concept Wedd built her whole case on — choice — and disputes its premise directly, arguing choice is not universally available. The speech would have to be rewritten if the preceding turn had defended the bill on, say, industry compliance costs instead; it is shaped around the word Wedd used. Not a mere reference: she engages the content of the claim rather than naming the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "That is what this bill is all about, because, like she has said, people want choice."

acuity.statement: The weakening of the clean vehicle standard, a policy designed to reduce emissions and prevent Aotearoa from becoming a dumping ground for inefficient vehicles rejected in countries with stricter environmental rules—that purpose is worth remembering, even if you do own a ute and drive up the Brynderwyns.
acuity.explanation: She picks up Wedd's exact illustration — the ute over the Brynderwyns — and does something with it, conceding the driver's position while asserting the standard's purpose survives it. The engagement is with the substance of Wedd's example, not just a repetition of her words, which is why it sits above the 0.5 band; it stops short of 1.0 because she restates the policy's purpose rather than rebutting Wedd's reasoning about consumer cost.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "If they want to drive their ute across the Brynderwyns, they should be able to have that choice."

acuity.statement: Furthermore, it is fixing the wrong problem. The problem, as has been discussed, was the removal of the Clean Car Discount, not the standard itself. Instead of reinstating an effective policy, the bill compensates.
acuity.explanation: Foster, the immediately preceding speaker, argued the scheme's founding assumptions were wrong and so the standard itself must be reset. Willis takes up that specific diagnosis and contests it directly, locating the cause instead in the cancellation of the Clean Car Discount and characterising the bill as compensation for that absence. That is a pointable engagement with the strand of Foster's case that mattered, and the passage would have to change if Foster had blamed something else. It is only a partial engagement, however: Willis does not touch Foster's evidence (the regulatory impact statement, the industry's credit deficit and stockpiling) and otherwise returns to prepared climate material, so it sits above the midpoint rather than at the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "What the regulatory impact statement quite clearly says is that the assumptions behind the scheme when it was set up, basically, are wrong."

acuity.statement: It's time we get back to Earth on this bill and, in particular, the select committee process. We heard very clearly from submitters two bits of feedback. The first is around the supply and demand mismatch for electric vehicles, and the second, and equally important, is that most importers are not going to meet the target and that will basically impose a hell of a lot of charges on the sector.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows Willis's substantive case that the bill weakens climate action and treats the wrong cause. "Get back to Earth" dismisses the tone of that case without engaging any part of it: he does not dispute that the Clean Car Discount's removal caused the compliance slump, nor that extra flexibility delays emissions cuts. What follows is prepared select-committee material on the right subject — submitter feedback and the Minister's review. A reference or a brush-off is not responsiveness, so this belongs in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 because the gesture at the preceding speech is real and the content is squarely on the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "it is fixing the wrong problem. The problem, as has been discussed, was the removal of the Clean Car Discount, not the standard itself." — but Bidois does not take this up; "get back to Earth" is only a gesture at Willis's climate framing.

acuity.statement: The member is right—the proposed rates that are being proposed by the Government are different. They are lower rates; they have different impacts.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Williams' interjected claim that the rates differ and does something with it — specifies that the new rates are lower and draws out the consequence that different rates mean different impacts, which feeds directly back into his argument that the old regulatory impact statement cannot cover this bill. Not merely agreement: he develops the point. Held short of 1.0 because the preceding turn was a brief supportive interjection rather than an argument requiring engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Exactly. The rates are all different." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: If the member wants to give me more than 3½ seconds to answer his question, I’ll give it a really good crack for him. I’m advised that the correct versions are currently being printed on paper with ink and are on their way down for the member to read with interest.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific complaint put to him — that the only RIS on the Table relates to bill (No 1) — by asserting an updated version exists and that printed copies are on their way. That is a direct answer to the availability strand of the question, so the speech would be different had Utikere asked something else. It leaves untouched the substantive strand (step us through the rationale for the RIS and how it relates to this bill), which caps it around the middle of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why is not here?" — Tangi Utikere (on the regulatory impact statement available from the Table)

acuity.statement: I think the Minister is referring to a two-page document called the short-form supplementary departmental disclosure document, which the simple contributions from officials here are, “No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no”—end. I’m not sure whether that seeks to address the points my colleague has raised, but we hope that the Minister will engage with this in good faith or else it will be a very long day from here.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's immediately preceding answer by identifying the document he pointed to and contesting that it answers anything, which is engagement with the content of his reply rather than a mere reference to it. Partial rather than full: having disputed the document she moves to a prepared block of questions about the $264 million that does not depend on what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m advised that the updated regulatory impact statement is on the ministry’s website" — James Meager

acuity.statement: How many young people could benefit from public transport? Well, in mid-Canterbury and South Canterbury, in parts of the world where rural people live, not many, because we live in far-flung destinations where we rely on, predominantly, a lot of second-hand vehicles.
acuity.explanation: Restates Williams' specific question and answers it on its own terms, then turns it against her premise by arguing that in rural electorates public transport benefits few and cheap second-hand vehicles benefit many. The reply is structured around her list of alternative uses for the money and would be unrecognisable had she asked something else. Scored on engagement only — whether the rural-benefit inference is sound, or whether any figure was supplied, belongs to Rigor and Specificity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How many young people would have benefited from a $264 million contribution to, say, subsidised public transport" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: A couple of questions in that one. So: who in the industry was consulted with? I think as Minister Bishop outlined in his second reading speech, yes, the Motor Industry Association (MIA) and the Imported Motor Vehicle Industry Association were both consulted. Of course, MIA represent BYD and Toyota. Every industry player also had the opportunity to submit during the select committee process and have their views heard and incorporated into the departmental report. I’m advised that no individual car companies were consulted, as that could be seen to confer specific market advantage during consultation so it wouldn’t have been appropriate.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Genter's specific question about whether individual car companies were consulted separately from the industry bodies, names the two companies she named (BYD, Toyota) in relation to MIA's membership, and supplies a direct answer with a reason (no individual companies, to avoid conferring market advantage). The speech would have been different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I’m wondering if the Ministry officials and the Government consulted some of the car companies, independently, that are bringing in zero-emissions vehicles, like BYD, Tesla, and I also was wondering if there was any specific consultation with Toyota."

acuity.statement: I’m advised, in terms of the question around penalties, the equivalent Australian penalty is AUD$50. Ours will be NZD$15. Apparently, it’s $50 imposed by the regulatory and $100 imposed by the courts for Australia.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the exact comparative figure Genter asked for — the Australian penalty against the New Zealand fee in Amendment Paper 444 — having sought advice mid-debate in order to answer it. This is the textbook case of engaging the specific claim rather than the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I’m wondering if the Minister can tell us what the equivalent penalties are or would be in Australia, and how that compares to the fees that are laid out on Amendment Paper 444 in new clause 5A"

acuity.statement: The Minister talks about this regulatory impact statement (RIS), but where is it? The only—oh, he holds it up. Well, is that the RIS that’s dated finalised 25 June 2024? That’s the first question for the Minister, because if it is, then that is the RIS that is being used for bill No. 2.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Meager's correction that the Opposition had been reading the departmental disclosure statement rather than the RIS, and turns it into a specific challenge about which RIS the Minister is relying on and whether it is even before the committee. He later departs into prepared material on school bus routes, which is why this is not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I think the issue is that she was reading the departmental disclosure statement and not the regulatory impact statement."

acuity.statement: Well, I think the member needs to go back and do his history, because when the Labour Party introduced this policy—whenever it was, back in the last Government—they were quite clear that it was not intended to raise revenue, and it’s not designed to raise revenue. I don’t know where Mr Utikere’s magicking up his $264 million from, but it’s not from this policy, because that’s not how the policy works. If he wants to go and campaign on borrowing another $264 million, he’s welcome to do that.
acuity.explanation: Engages the precise figure Utikere built his contribution on and disputes its premise — that the scheme generates revenue available for reallocation — rather than merely naming him as a target. The reply could not have been given against a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "this is about prioritisation: the revenue that’s been generated, the $264 million, could be spent in other areas"

acuity.statement: This goes to the member’s point around what the options were and what the top charge could be. Well, if you double the top charge, you’re just doubling what the importers have to pay and pass on to their customers.
acuity.explanation: Meager takes up the specific question Williams had just put — why $15 rather than $30 or zero — and answers it on its own terms: he states the consequence of doubling the top charge (cost passed to consumers), gives the rationale for the chosen rate, names the Motor Industry Association's $15 proposal, and directs the committee to the pages of the regulatory impact statement that contain the analysis she said was unavailable. The speech would have had to be different had she asked something else, which is the deciding test. It is not a full 1.0 because he leaves two strands of her question untouched: the zero-rate option and the relative market-share effect on smaller versus larger importers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "what I’m asking here is about the trade-offs between those options" (the $30, $15 and zero top-charge options)

acuity.statement: I couldn’t quite discern many questions from that, but I’ll address the one at the top around clause 4. I think the member misunderstands how the clause works. It actually allows the Minister to set a weight-adjusted rate or a uniform rate. Currently, if you just set a strict uniform weight, that would be harder for heavy vehicles to meet, and I think that was the intention of the previous Government’s policy. Clause 4 actually gives the Minister the flexibility to do one or the other, and so I think that’s what he actually wants and that’s what the clause achieves.
acuity.explanation: Meager takes up the specific premise of Utikere's clause 4 question and corrects it on the merits — arguing the clause permits either a weight-adjusted or a uniform rate rather than ruling weight-adjustment out — and then engages the tabled reporting amendment item by item against existing NZTA and Ministry of Transport publications. The speech would have to be different if Utikere had argued something else. Not a full 1.0 because several strands put to him (modelling and advice sought, retail affordability metrics, Māori and Pacific impact) are left unaddressed, and part of his reply dismisses the remaining amendments as inconsistent with Government policy rather than engaging them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why is it that there hasn’t been, really, any thought around a gradual approach to weight adjustment" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I just wondered if the Minister had done any distributional analysis of who these changes were most likely to affect, because by my calculations, the changes in the new clause 5A in Amendment Paper 444, new subsection 2(b)(i) and (ii), what they show is that with the change in the fees, the benefit to the new vehicle industry who are bringing in polluting vehicles above the target is twice that of the used vehicle sector imports. So that means that, actually, there's a disproportionate benefit to new vehicle importers.
acuity.explanation: Genter takes up the affordability justification Meager had just restated and tests it against the fee schedule in his own Amendment Paper, arguing the benefit to new-vehicle importers is double that to the used-import sector and therefore misses low- and middle-income buyers. That is engaging the content of his claim, not merely naming it. Held below the top band because much of the turn is prepared material on the Greens' own tabled amendments and on when Amendment Paper 444 was tabled, and she does not take up Meager's specific rebuttal that the information sought is already published by NZTA and the Ministry of Transport.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what we’ll do is we’ll change the legislation to make it easier for working New Zealanders to buy a car, get to work, do the job, live their life, and have a happy future" — James Meager

acuity.statement: This is an all-stages change. It hasn’t been to a select committee. No need to be so rude.
acuity.explanation: Meager had just argued that members could find the RIS via the URL on the Amendment Paper and that no Standing Order requires tabling a RIS, inviting Labour to make a submission to the Standing Orders Committee. Brooking takes up the substance of that defence by disputing the premise that normal scrutiny applies — she asserts the change is being made at all stages without select committee consideration, which is the reason a tabled RIS matters. She engages the procedural claim rather than just objecting to tone, though the engagement is brief and a third of it is about his manner.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "there is no requirement under the Standing Orders to table a RIS, and I look forward to that suggestion being made to the Standing Orders Committee by the Labour Party"

acuity.statement: It’s actually not. We’ve just come from a select committee and had the second reading.
acuity.explanation: Direct, specific correction of the factual claim in the interjection he had just taken: Brooking said the change was an all-stages one that had not been to select committee, and he denies exactly that and gives the countervailing fact (the bill has been through select committee and second reading). The reply would be different had she said anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "This is an all-stages change. It hasn’t been to a select committee."

acuity.statement: My second question is: in terms of our balance of payments and the cost to New Zealanders, if the Minister and the Government are concerned about the cost of vehicular transport to New Zealanders, to what extent did the Minister evaluate the impact of our dependency as a nation on the whole on petroleum imports?
acuity.explanation: Meager had just stated that the policy intent is "to reduce the costs of vehicles imposed by the previous Government on everyday working Kiwis". Abel takes that stated intent as his premise and presses it on its own terms — if cost to New Zealanders is the objective, what analysis was done of the cost of petroleum import dependency? He engages the Minister's stated rationale rather than restating prepared Green policy, though the question is framed so that it would have worked against most versions of the Minister's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "the intent of the policy is to reduce the costs of vehicles imposed by the previous Government on everyday working Kiwis"

acuity.statement: If we then go to the issue around what was looked at in terms of the impact on the balance of payments: I’m advised that it was looked at generally in terms of the impact of lost fuel savings, and as I outlined at the start, this is approximately $115 million, but that is more than offset by the $264 million in charges that will not be passed on to hard-working everyday New Zealanders who get up every morning, get into their vehicle, clean our offices, stack our supermarket shelves, work in our pack-houses, and generally just want to get on with life in their second-hand, low-cost vehicle—because if you come from a part of the world where, like some of us, we didn't have a car until we were seven or eight, you're very grateful just to have any vehicle.
acuity.explanation: Takes the balance-of-payments question Abel had just put and supplies the figure asked for — $115 million in lost fuel savings set against $264 million in avoided charges — stating what the analysis did and did not cover. It answers the question actually asked rather than the topic, then runs into prepared material about working New Zealanders, which is why it is not a clean 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "to what extent did the Minister evaluate the impact of our dependency as a nation on the whole on petroleum imports?"

acuity.statement: What is the impact on the targets? Well, we all know, and we've had this traversed many, many times in this House: vehicle emissions are contained within the emissions trading scheme (ETS). The ETS is a closed-cap system; it has a sinking lid on emissions over time.
acuity.explanation: Restates Abel's specific question about the effect on carbon dioxide reduction targets and answers it with a mechanism — that transport emissions sit inside a capped ETS, so a sectoral increase is offset elsewhere. Whether or not the inference holds, this is squarely aimed at the claim just made and would have to change if Abel had asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "how did the Government evaluate the impact that this policy would have on targets for reducing carbon dioxide emissions"

acuity.statement: Now, Mr Abel talked about reliance on fuel and gas. Well, then I look forward to him supporting our efforts to maintain our domestic fuel and energy security in terms of repealing the oil and gas ban: investing in liquified natural gas; making sure that we have greater fuel security and storage requirements at our airports and in our fuel facilities; making sure that we have good import controls for our fuel import terminals, including the one down in PrimePort Timaru, which is a great source of opportunity and employment for the people of South Canterbury.
acuity.explanation: Names the strand Abel raised — dependence on imported petroleum — and then uses it only as a springboard to a list of unrelated Government energy initiatives and a demand for Green support. Abel's point was that the policy locks motorists into imported fuel; nothing here takes up that argument or the import figures he cited. A reference plus a pivot, on the right subject but engaging no part of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Did he consider the extent to which he is locking New Zealanders into an ongoing dependence on that expensive imported petroleum"

acuity.statement: So I just want to point out, first of all, although the Minister says that clause 12 is technical, given some of the issues, the impact of it is not technical and is worthy of scrutiny, because what it does is it amends regulation 17 of the Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Standard) Regulations 2022, which is around credit expiry and use.
acuity.explanation: Meager's immediately preceding turn walked through clauses 10-12 and characterised them as three very straightforward, consequential amendments. Leary takes up that exact characterisation of clause 12 and disputes it directly, naming the regulation it amends and the substantive effects (credit expiry, hierarchy of use, transferability, retrospectivity) she says make it more than technical. The speech would have had to be different had the Minister described the clause differently or not reached clause 12 at all, so it clearly engages the content rather than merely referencing the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "These are three very straightforward clauses that give effect to the change made in the previous part." — James Meager

acuity.statement: Now, in terms of how you reduce emissions in the vehicle fleet, well, you ensure that it’s part of the comprehensive and capped emissions trading scheme (ETS) system whereby emissions budgets are set for five-year periods where there is a sinking lid for emissions over time.
acuity.explanation: Meager takes up Genter's central question — how emissions from the fleet will fall if charges are cut and credits extended — and supplies a substantive mechanism (the capped ETS with a sinking lid) as the answer, then draws out its consequence for other sectors' NZUs. He also directly addresses her clause 11/12 framing by locating the substance in Part 1 clause 6. Not a full 1.0 because he leaves her specific questions on stockpiling, modelling and whether the Climate Commission was consulted untouched, and partly rules them out of scope rather than engaging them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "It would be helpful to understand, from the Government’s point of view, how we’re going to achieve the goal of reducing emissions from the vehicle fleet when the combination of these two changes is to make it easier for the industry"

acuity.statement: What I find interesting is that the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, in its report, didn’t really make changes to any of the aspects in relation to Part 2. A lot of the changes from the select committee were in Part 1—all of them were. In Part 2, it’s as it was reported back. So the select committee, after hearing from the community, determined that no changes were required for Part 2.
acuity.explanation: Utikere engages one strand of what Meager had just said — the claim that Part 2 is merely consequential alignment — by pointing out that the select committee itself sought no changes to Part 2, so the Minister's Amendment Paper 444 changes to clauses 11 and 12 are a late Government initiative rather than mere tidying. He also revives the industry-consultation question Meager had left unanswered. But he does not take up Meager's ETS argument at all, and the bulk of the call is his own prepared set of questions on Part 2.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "Part 2 provides consequential amendments to the regulations, so, therefore, I’m happy to take questions on whether or not amending regulations is the right thing to do"

acuity.statement: Further to the member’s point—I don’t know what the point really is that he’s trying to make—simply because a select committee agrees or doesn’t agree or recommends or doesn’t recommend something doesn’t mean that the committee or the Minister can’t put amendments forward.
acuity.explanation: Squarely aimed at the specific inference Utikere had just drawn — that a select committee's silence on Part 2 is a reason the Minister should not amend it — and rebuts it, then presses the point by noting it would equally invalidate Genter's own amendments. Clearly shaped by what preceded it. Held below the top band because Utikere's three explicit questions (extent of industry influence, whether the year is calendar or financial, and the rationale for the clause 12 transfer provision) go unanswered apart from a general restatement that clauses 11 and 12 merely align the regulations with clause 6.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "So the select committee, after hearing from the community, determined that no changes were required for Part 2."

acuity.statement: Just in response to the member’s 10-minute contribution, she raised a number of questions. I'll get some advice on some of the specific ones, but a couple that were mentioned in there were around: is this inconsistent with the Act? I'll point the member to—and I should have done this at the top, actually—Amendment Paper 444, which actually does make some amendments to Part 2 as well. That Amendment Paper does directly cross-reference to the Act to ensure that consistency, so that should resolve that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Leary's specific question about consistency with the Act and answers it with a named instrument (Amendment Paper 444) that he says cross-references the Act. Not a full 1.0 because he explicitly parks most of her other listed questions for later advice rather than engaging them, but the engagement he does make is pointable and content-specific — the reply would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "is it consistent with the zero carbon Act budgeting framework?"

acuity.statement: To go to the impact on clauses 10, 11 and 12, and to look at that, I think that very relevant in the RIS are the paragraphs at 48, which are about credit deficits and credit surpluses and that that will result in additional fuel costs and emissions in 2050. That's an incredibly important point, and it relates to this part of the Act in that way. That's the part that I was quoting in terms of the change in value of those credits.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand already in the debate — the clauses 10/11 point and the incomplete modelling — and extends it, but then moves into reading prepared RIS passages aloud rather than engaging the Minister's intervening answer that the RIS risks attach to the Amendment Paper and not clause 12. Partial engagement: pointable, but it leaves the live counter-argument untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "but also just to pinpoint on clauses 10 and 11, as well, which may sound quite technical but have only come to our attention"

acuity.statement: Look, just with regard to the question around retrospectivity, the bill doesn’t apply retrospectively. For something to apply retrospectively, it would say that it would reach back into the credits or charges incurred by an individual prior to the commencement date and say, “We’re going to retrospectively hit you with a penalty or provide you with a refund for those credits.” It applies from the day going forward. So if you cash in your credits today, it will be at the price before the bill passes, and if you cash the credits in on the day after its commencement, it will be at the new price.
acuity.explanation: Squarely addresses the retrospectivity challenge White had just pressed, defining what retrospectivity would require and applying it to the commencement date. Held below 1.0 because he answers the legal characterisation rather than her evidentiary point about the 2023-issued credits expiring into a reduced-value window — one strand of her claim is engaged, the figure she cited is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Am I right, Minister Meager: as I understand it, the price for the credits currently, if people hold a lot of those credits, they will plummet in their value in the time period"

acuity.statement: Finally, again, the member brings up for, I think, the third time in this debate the fuel savings, or the opposite of fuel savings. As she pointed out, the officials estimate that the temporary charges will reduce projected fuel savings by $115 million, and, as mentioned twice before, that is offset by avoiding about $264 million in net charges being passed on to consumers in higher vehicle prices. By my very quick firth form maths, that makes a net benefit of $149 million to consumers in the system.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact figure the previous speaker quoted from the RIS and does something with it — accepts it, nets it against a $264 million offset and derives a $149 million balance. This is the textbook high-acuity move: the specific number raised is engaged and transformed, so the reply is wholly contingent on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "would spend an extra $115 million on fuel between 2026 and 2050 with this proposal"

acuity.statement: I do have a technical question for the Minister. Let me preface this by saying that we’re in the same situation we were in yesterday where we have an amendment that is purporting to amend a principal Act; that when we look at the purpose of the principal Act it is quite different. So my question is different from my colleagues, because this is not really about whether there is confusion over the title.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the strand of the preceding contribution about whether the bill's short title describes the bill, and explicitly positions her own question against it — not confusion over the title, but whether the title can carry the principal Act's purpose for statutory interpretation. That is a genuine engagement with one strand of what was just argued, and her speech would read differently had the earlier speaker not pressed the naming point; but it then proceeds into her own prepared line of legal questions rather than contesting the earlier reasoning itself, so it sits around the middle of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It would be good to actually have the name of a bill that really did indicate what it was" — the preceding contribution on the bill's title (Tangi Utikere)

acuity.statement: The Interpretation Act was repealed in 2021, and maybe the member can ask a colleague who was in Parliament at that time. The title does what it says: it calls this Act the “Land Transport (Clean Vehicle Standard) Amendment Act”; that’s what it does. In terms of its relation to the principal Act, it amends the Land Transport Act.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific question put: it corrects the statutory basis Leary relied on (asserting the Interpretation Act was repealed in 2021), then addresses her second point about the fit between the amendment and the principal Act by explaining why the Clean Vehicle Standard can only be amended through the Land Transport Act. The reply is unusable against any other preceding argument — it is built on the content of hers — which is the top of the band. The jibe about asking a colleague who was in Parliament at the time is an incivility, not an acuity deduction, and the correctness of the repeal claim is not an acuity question either.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Madam Chair, that is a legal question under section 5 of the Interpretation Act" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: The idea that amending the term “four years” to “94,608,600 seconds” would provide individuals with clarity and certainty is an interesting one. It’s not one we support.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific strand of Williams' argument — that the four-year expiry period is insufficiently clear and predictable — and answers it by naming the amendment she filed to that effect and rejecting it on the ground that the proposed substitute would not in fact deliver clarity. The reply could not have been given had Williams argued something else; he also flags a procedural objection specific to that amendment. Marked slightly below 1.0 because the rebuttal is made by ridicule of the drafting rather than by addressing why four years is predictable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that four years doesn’t seem to me to be very clear when you have a number of these transactions happening on any given day" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Look, though, the points the member raises are all very interesting in terms of the substance of the policy and the regulatory impact statement, etc., but unfortunately the committee has already determined the question of what the substantive policy is or should be when it considered Part 1.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the two strands Williams actually pressed (the financial impact on importers' credit accounts, and page 3 of the regulatory impact statement) and gives a reason for not answering them — that Part 1 settled the substantive policy and Part 2 only gives effect to it. That is engagement with the admissibility of her questions rather than with their content, which is a partial response: he can point at what she asked but supplies none of the impact analysis she sought. Scored on engagement only; whether the scope argument is sound is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I would like to know, from the Minister, whether this has a material impact that is financially positive for those importers who receive a detrimental impact by the reduction in price." — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: First, we have the title. The Minister has said that he’s not prepared to entertain any of the proposed changes there. We all know that what’s really important, when bills progress through this Parliament, is that they are named so that those that can follow them, if they choose to, might be able to actually ascertain what the bill is about.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's stated refusal of the title amendments and offers a counter-principle — that a bill's title should let a follower work out what the bill does. One strand of the preceding turn is genuinely taken up and the speech would read differently had Meager not ruled the amendments out. It stops short of rebutting Meager's actual reasoning (that the three clauses are concise and correct) and moves instead to a point about the bill being a (No 2), so engagement is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But, just in general, we don’t support those amendments. We think that we’ve got it pretty bang on with those three very short, concise amendments" — James Meager

acuity.statement: The amount of times I’ve heard the “clean vehicle discount” used as a phrase, and I know that’s the official phrase, but in working New Zealand we called it a ute tax for a reason. It was a clean vehicle discount for the wealthy, and it was a ute tax on the workers, the farmers, and the producers.
acuity.explanation: Genter's turn immediately before built its case on the Clean Car Discount being an objectively successful feebate, and Luxton takes up that exact policy and the phrase she used repeatedly, contesting it on distributional grounds (wealthy buyers vs workers/farmers). That is engagement with one strand of her argument — the merit of the feebate — rather than with any of the evidence she offered for it (the import graph, the RIS Figure 5, the Simon Lucas quote). He then returns to prepared ACT material on scrapping the standard and the ETS, including restating the ETS-is-enough line that Genter had explicitly pre-rebutted. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "That policy is objectively incredibly successful at supporting the uptake of zero emissions vehicles."

acuity.statement: The Opposition said that the Government has bowed to industry pressure. Well, that’s nonsense. Actually, what the Government has done is it has listened to evidence.
acuity.explanation: Genter's central charge in the preceding turn was that the Government is legislating for vested corporate interests rather than on the merits. Foster names that charge, denies it, and substitutes a competing account with a reason attached — that select committee evidence showed the scheme's underlying assumptions were not working, hence amendment rather than repeal. The speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different, which is the test. It falls short of 1.0 because he rebuts the framing by assertion and does not touch any of the specific evidence put up against him; the weakness of the inference is a Rigor matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "they are only listening to vested interests and they are ignoring the objective benefits that New Zealand can get from good public policy"

acuity.statement: I do welcome the review of the scheme. I think there are some really fundamental flaws with the scheme, and I welcome the Minister’s six-month review of it.
acuity.explanation: Bidois follows a substantive turn by Willis that made specific claims — that the bill leaves New Zealand with laxer standards than China, the UK, the USA, Canada and South Korea, that clean-car demand plunged when the standard was weakened, and that supply problems are self-inflicted. None of this is taken up, contested or conceded. The speech is prepared endorsement that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, though it is at least on the subject of the bill under debate, so it sits at 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Willis argued the bill "gives us laxer standards than China, the UK, the USA, Canada, and South Korea" and that supply has collapsed because of Government signals, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: This bill is practical and it's affordable. The importers are currently having to pay more, and that, ultimately, lands on the consumers, who are the tradies and the farmers. This bill takes the pressure off Kiwis still dealing with the fiscal spoon of medicine that the last Government dealt up to them. If the members of the Opposition want more Kiwis using electric vehicles or hybrids, then guess what? They need cheap, abundant power. They should have voted for the fast-track bill, because there's a shortage of renewable energy, and that’s in large part due to the rash decision to ban oil and gas and a complete failure to plan.
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. He answers the topic White was on — who bears the cost of the scheme (tradies) and whether more EVs on the road is achievable — and he addresses her stated wish for greater EV uptake by asserting cheap power is the precondition. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That's right—do more about modern slavery." — Arena Williams

The reasons for this have been very well traversed, and I couldn’t say it more eloquently than the previous speaker, and, therefore, I commend the bill to the House.

acuity.statement: I think my colleague the Hon Jenny Salesa was right to refer to the Dawn Raids as being one of the terrible examples where we came close to what we see over in Australia, for example, with detention centres where people have lived for years or on Christmas Island and in other places. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we do not want to see, in our present and into the future, a repeat of the Dawn Raids" — Jenny Salesa

acuity.statement: This bill improves the integrity of the immigration system as well as the fiscal sustainability of it. The changes are sensible and serve New Zealand’s national interests while still respecting individual rights. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said; it asserts the bill respects individual rights without engaging the specific rights concerns just raised. It does concern the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that the large electronic-monitoring Amendment Paper tabled that night, plus the arrest and search-and-seizure powers, need scrutiny so the net is not cast too widely over trafficked people, and this statement does not take it up.

It gestures at the debate — crediting select committee work, noting points 'highlighted by my colleague Phil Twyford' and that the measure 'isn't being unanimously supported throughout the House' — but engages no claim actually made in the preceding turns, so it tops out at the 'gesture at the debate' end of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Butterick commended the bill as sensible and as serving the national interest while respecting individual rights, and Ingrid Leary raised the electronic-monitoring Amendment Paper; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: We, too, want to spend a little time on the committee of the whole House stage for this bill because this is quite a technical bill and there are a lot of different parts to it. I want to start with clause 4. I want to first start with the definition of “first available craft”.
