If Twyford had asked about something else entirely in the same bill, this opening would have been identical, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "it's our intention to work through sequentially each of those nine initiatives and have a good debate and a good exchange on all of them" — and his specific question on the clause 5 definition of "a group of aircraft"

acuity.statement: Now, because “craft” captures such a broad range of vehicles, I did want to ask the Minister as to why she didn't choose to use the language “aircraft”; and that is because we've heard a lot of the terms of preparation under this bill.
acuity.explanation: Menéndez March follows a substantive ministerial answer on the flight-group definition and the identity threshold, but takes up none of it — he says himself the point "hasn't been addressed yet" and reads in his own prepared line of questioning on clause 4. There is a gesture at the debate's shared framing ("we've heard a lot of the terms of preparation under this bill", and a later nod to the clause 5 mass-arrivals definition the Minister had just discussed), which keeps it above the floor, but the speech would read identically had the Minister said something different about the 24-hour window.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just answered on the 24-hour flight definition ("Have they arrived in the last 24 hours?" is the definition in the bill) and the identity threshold, and this statement opens an unrelated line on clause 4's "first available craft" instead

acuity.statement: There’s a long-held definition in the Immigration Act of “craft”. Of course, we usually put people on the most direct, humane, fastest, and first available craft, which is usually an aircraft. But you could imagine that if somebody lived on a Pacific Island who needed an airline and then a boat, we would want to do that, and so it allows those options.
acuity.explanation: This takes the precise question asked — why "craft" rather than "aircraft" — and supplies the reason, with a worked example (an island route requiring a flight then a boat) that explains why the broader word is needed. Had the member asked about something else, this answer could not have been given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I did want to ask the Minister as to why she didn't choose to use the language “aircraft”" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I’ll note that when the powers were available under COVID, it was used about 50 times, and since then, we’ve had situations arise like when Vanuatu airlines got into trouble. We had recognised seasonal employer workers who were stranded here, and we had to individually go and either grant or change conditions on people’s visas.
acuity.explanation: The member asked specifically for scenarios in which the clause 8 power to impose further visa conditions would be used; this supplies concrete ones (COVID-era use, the Vanuatu airline collapse stranding RSE workers) and goes on to separate the two provisions she believes he had conflated. It is aimed squarely at the content of the question put, not merely at its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don't think we've received clarity as to the scenarios in which you would need to impose additional conditions on a group of people" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I do want to ask some questions about Subpart 2, but before I do, I just wanted to go back to clause 5, amended section 9A on the definition of mass arrivals. I want to just be absolutely clear or try to get absolutely clear that a group of aircraft—group, in this context, if I heard the Minister right—means only that this is more than one aircraft to arrive within the 24-hour period.
acuity.explanation: Twyford defers his own prepared subject in order to test the exact proposition the Minister had just advanced, restating her definition back as a yes/no proposition and probing whether any further connection between the flights is required. The intervention exists only because of what she said and would have to be rewritten had she defined the term differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it's pretty clear in the bill that it's just flights arriving within a 24-hour period—there's really no other definition that you need" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Now, the department is very powerful and controls many things, but to say “any circumstance that is outside the Department’s control:” pretty much means any circumstance that the universe might offer up. So the effect of that is that there is no limit on this circumstances under which these powers could be used.
acuity.explanation: The Minister had defended the new special-direction powers on the ground that the bill constrains her; Twyford engages that claim on its own terms, accepts the benefit-only guardrail she described and then attacks the one guardrail she did not mention — the triggering circumstances — arguing the drafting leaves them unbounded. He rebuts the limitation argument rather than restating his own position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It limits the powers of the Minister. It has to be in the favour, or not to the detriment of the group of people" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Right, those questions are all very similar around the types of situations that we expect to happen. Let me run through some examples that were given to me in the advice that I was given: situations where New Zealanders overseas wish to repatriate their families quickly in response to a conflict, like in Ukraine; the collapse of Air Vanuatu, which we’ve already talked about, which stranded Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme workers here; education institutes folding; a large labour-hire firm going into receivership with serious implications for migrant workers; and, of course, the volcanic eruption in Tonga.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing asked for — the examples contained in the officials' advice — and picks up the member's own Tongan eruption and RSE worker scenarios, then goes on to answer her safeguards question. The answer would be different if she had asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "I really wanted to understand, firstly, the advice that you have received from officials with regards to your flexible powers"

acuity.statement: My colleague and I worked on an amendment that we’ve just tabled, too, and this is why I wanted to just go back to it, because we just wanted to put an amendment to make sure that the first available craft—so if people need to be put in a boat or a vehicle afterwards, kei te pai—isn’t anything other than an aircraft. Because, I think, to me, that is really important to clarify in legislation so that if the Minister genuinely intends to say the most humane craft available, that it is an aircraft and not, say, a boat that may not adequately protect the wellbeing of people or may not contain humane conditions.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the claim that a benefit-of-the-migrant test is sufficient safeguard — and presses that it would not guarantee humane conditions on a non-aircraft craft. The bulk of the contribution, however, returns to his own earlier line of questioning on "craft" rather than to what was just said in this turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "the use of powers would be subject to many safeguards including the overarching safeguard that they can only be used to their benefit, or at least not to their disadvantage"

acuity.statement: Going back to the issue of a craft—again, very minor point. We’ve not been able to think of any time—that’s not to say there isn’t, but my officials can’t ever remember a time—that the first available craft was not a plane.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific factual question put to her, concedes the point as far as officials' recollection goes, and then gives the reason for not narrowing the definition. Directly shaped by the question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "have there been cases in which the first available craft has been anything else other than an aircraft"

acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's safeguards claim and disputes its sufficiency, arguing the scale of the regulatory power warrants a notice period on top — engagement of one strand of the preceding turn, though most of the contribution is a prepared walk-through of his own tabled amendments.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "I’ve been very clear that there are a number of checks and balances."

Had Boyack raised different objections the answer would have had to be different; it does leave her best-interests-of-the-child question untouched, which is why this is not a full mark.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether it might be wiser to have a judicial warrant, as opposed to a decision by the Minister" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: Now, the previous Minister also talked about the Ahmed Zaoui case. I just want to make very clear, that was very, very separate. It was dealt with at the time. There were a raft of changes that were made to the Immigration Act at the time around that case to put guardrails in place—special provisions around the use of classified information. That is out of the scope of this bill, but that was dealt with then, so those things are not relevant to this case.
acuity.explanation: Twyford's central argument for a judicial process rested on the Ahmed Zaoui precedent — untested security advice, no chance to respond to the evidence. Stanford takes that precedent up by name and does something with it: she distinguishes it, asserts the Act was amended at the time to add guardrails around classified information, and concludes the precedent does not bear on this bill. The speech would have to change if Twyford had argued from a different example or a different ground. It falls short of 1.0 only because she asserts the distinction rather than engaging the specific gap Twyford identified (the absence of a tested, contestable process under the new power), and leaves his livelihood/visitor-visa question untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "I think that the Ahmed Zaoui case is a pretty powerful story of why we should think very carefully about enshrining this sweeping power for the Minister of the day to simply certify—through secondary legislation—that a person is deemed to be a risk to our national security."

acuity.statement: It places us in a very difficult position when people are protected and we can't return them home. But what we can do, and I think what the Opposition agrees with, is that we can revoke their residency status. The point of that is so that if things change and their situation changes in their home country and at some point they can be returned, we can then deport them.
acuity.explanation: Twyford asked squarely whether the provision is intended as punishment/deterrent, or as leverage, or whether a facilitated community-engagement approach is contemplated. This passage answers one strand of that — the purpose is to preserve future deportability if conditions in the home country change, which is the alternative Twyford himself floated — so it is a genuine engagement with his question rather than prepared material. But it addresses only the deportability limb, ignores the facilitated-rehabilitation option he set out at length from his own time as Associate Minister, and does not take up his punitive/deterrent framing directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Does the Minister see this as essentially punitive, and has the Minister considered whether or not this is a way of the Government of the day having some leverage to sit down with the person in question and work out some sort of deal?"

acuity.statement: There is already a review period, as I’ve already mentioned, built into this. There will be a report back to Cabinet no more than three years after the powers come into effect, to identify whether there have been any unintended consequences, and, if so, whether we need to make further legislative adjustments.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific amendment just moved and answers it on its own terms and on its own timeframe: the three-year review Xu-Nan asked to legislate already exists as a report-back to Cabinet. The reply would have to be different had he proposed a different mechanism or period, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I understand there’s a sunset clause, which is fantastic, but I’m seeking the Minister’s support on new subsections for each of these" — his proposed review clause requiring review no later than three years after commencement.

acuity.statement: We have a process in Immigration, whereby if you do something that makes you liable for deportation, there is a process that you go through. It goes to a delegated decision-maker, it may end up with the Immigration and Protection Tribunal, but there is a process. Circumnavigating that process is what’s happening at the moment, where judges will discharge without conviction to avoid people having to potentially be deported—not actually deported.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of the amendment just moved — that the court is the right place for this judgement — by arguing the statutory process sits in Immigration and that discharge without conviction routes around it. She engages the reasoning rather than merely naming the member or the topic; scored just short of 1.0 because she restates the Government's framing more than she rebuts his specific point about the section 206 safeguard.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "The court already has the ability to consider" whether deportation liability should be an appropriate consequence of the offending — his argument for keeping clause 18 at "convicted".

acuity.statement: I just wanted to say that there are nine discreet and substantive parts to this bill. So far we’ve covered off the cancellation of residence class visas, we’ve covered off the new flexible powers of the Minister to benefit classes of persons, and we’ve dealt with the definition of mass arrivals.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the bill in committee) but engages no part of the argument immediately preceding it; the words would be unchanged whatever the Minister had just said about deportation. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is specific to this bill's progress on this day and so could not have been delivered in another debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just argued that judges are circumnavigating the Immigration Act's deportation process by discharging without conviction, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it inventories which parts of the bill remain unexamined.

acuity.statement: There is still the discretion of the judge to discharge without conviction if he so wishes. But, essentially, the process that is being eroded is the process that already exists under Immigration New Zealand—the established process where delegated decision makers and the Immigration and Protection Tribunal have absolute full information about a case of a person who is liable for deportation. That is not the same when you have that situation with a judge and it is circumnavigating another process at Immigration New Zealand where all of the relevant information around someone’s deportation liability is considered.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Twyford's case squarely — the claim that judicial oversight is eroded — answering that the judge's discharge discretion survives and reframing which process is actually being bypassed. But it engages none of his three evidence questions (post-RIS data, evidence for the public-confidence framing, whether Ministry of Justice advice was sought) and none of the early-guilty-plea/defended-trials argument, returning instead to the Minister's own rationale. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Phil Twyford: "Concerns that the change undermines legal certainty and fairness, and it erodes judicial oversight and due process protections."

acuity.statement: You asked in your amendment, amendment 8.40.31, around why we need the part around—you want to remove the bit about failing to comply with the Act. For an example, failing to comply with the Act might be failing to comply with the terms of the RRRA—the residence and reporting requirements agreement. That is very important and that is one of the things that would be failing to comply with the Act, which is why we won’t be accepting that amendment either.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific amendment and the specific words Xu-Nan sought to delete, and meets his argument on its own ground by supplying a worked instance — breach of a residence and reporting requirements agreement — of conduct that the deleted wording would capture. The reply would have to be different had he moved a different amendment or given a different reason, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Absconding, I agree, is an important part, but failing to comply with the Act isn’t."

acuity.statement: OK, going through those one by one, the first thing the member was asking about was the process and the safeguards in doing an-out-of-hours compliance visit. As the member knows, in this bill the warrant has to be signed off by a judge. The judge needs to make sure that the actions are proportionate, that all other avenues or possibilities have been exhausted, and they do need to take into effect whether or not there are vulnerable people or children or situations in the household. So there are plenty of protections in the issuing of that warrant.
acuity.explanation: Answers the last-resort question directly, pointing to the warrant test — proportionality, exhaustion of other avenues, presence of vulnerable people — which is precisely the content Twyford said the bill lacked, and in the same order he raised it. Entirely contingent on what the preceding turn argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Phil Twyford: "I wanted to ask some questions of the Minister about whether or not specific provisions were considered to ensure that out-of-hours visits are a measure of last resort."

acuity.statement: So can I ask the Minister, why not just follow that recommendation, and rather than leaving it at the discretion of basically a judge, just make it extremely clear that we’re narrowing it down to two specific criteria as to then prevent loading the judiciary with additional work to be able to determine as to when out-of-hours visits are appropriate or otherwise?
acuity.explanation: Stanford's immediately preceding turn rested the defence of out-of-hours visits on judicial sign-off: a judge weighs last resort, vulnerable people and proportionality, and 'those safeguards are baked in'. Menéndez March takes that exact mechanism and presses on it — if the safeguard is real, why leave it to judicial discretion rather than write the Heron KC report's two criteria (public safety, national security) into the clause? The speech would have to be different had she defended the clause on other grounds; it is built around the discretion argument she just made. Scored only on engagement, not on whether the inference or the policy is sound.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: 'any out-of-hours activity needs to be signed off with a judicial warrant, and the judge will have to take into account many factors' / 'And those safeguards are baked in.'

acuity.statement: Dealing with those two in reverse order, the definition of “national security” is not in scope of this bill; it is a previously determined definition and we won’t be entertaining any changes, as it’s not in scope.
acuity.explanation: She identifies and takes up the two questions Menéndez March had just put, and answers the second one directly — but by ruling the definition out of scope rather than engaging his substantive claim that the principal Act's security definition is broad enough to reach 'reputation'. That is a real, pointable response to the specific question asked, so well above prepared material, but it addresses the admissibility of the question rather than the content of the claim, which caps it mid-scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: 'can she please clarify how she would apply the provisions in the principal Act on security when it comes to reputation for the purposes of stripping someone’s residency away'

acuity.statement: Now, neither the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees guidelines nor the Casey report identify failing to comply with the Immigration Act as a factor which justifies detention. Both of them say—both the guidelines and the Casey report—that short-term detention may be justified where there are threats to national security or public safety or genuine and real risks of absconding. I agree with the Law Society on this case that detention outside of those limited circumstances is not justified.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn was Stanford on clause 26, out-of-hours visits and the Menéndez March amendments. Twyford moves to his own prepared case on clause 32 and the wording of new section 317AA, engaging no part of what she had just said; he gestures at the debate only with 'We’ve dealt with a similar issue in principle, but not in relation to clause 32.' It is squarely on the bill under debate, which keeps it off the floor, but it would read identically whatever Stanford had just argued. acuity.statement: The select committee that examined this bill heard submitters talking about worry about this early redress in vesting Kororipo Pā in Ngāti Rēhia forming some kind of obligation on behalf of Ngāpuhi to settle. I think we all want to see Ngāpuhi settle, but it was clear from the select committee’s process that that won’t be an encumbrance; an obligation that’s being increased because of the settlement.
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn immediately before raised the submitters' concern that the vesting might be read as a precursor to a wider Ngāpuhi settlement, and the question of the retained encumbrances. Luxton takes up that same specific strand, naming the concern and supplying the select committee's resolution of it, so this part of the speech would read differently had Abel raised something else. It affirms rather than tests or extends the point, and the rest of the turn (the airport anecdote, the call for Kiwis to learn their history) is prepared material that merely references Abel rather than engaging him — hence a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "it was very clear to us that this vesting is not to be seen as a certain precursor to a broader Ngāpuhi settlement"

acuity.statement: So as mana e te whenua, hapū have had to endure the footprint of the Crown to whakahaere this whenua, to finally getting a bit of a co-management agreement and getting a few trustees on there and finally we get the land back. But it’s full of encumbrances. It’s full of fishhooks.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Kapa-Kingi's insistence that this is not a gift but something Ngāti Rēhia had to endure and fight for — and carries it further into a specific objection that the vesting is encumbered and falls short of full mana whakahaere. Partial rather than full: she leaves Kapa-Kingi's central point (that 'return' is the wrong word because Ngāti Rēhia never left) untouched, and the bulk of the speech is prepared whakapapa and history that would read identically after any preceding speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mariameno Kapa-Kingi: "What Ngāti Rēhia have had to do really is to tolerate this process, is to endure this process, and to hold the line to this point."

acuity.statement: This bill gives effect to the deed signed between the Crown and Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rēhia Trust on the 1 August 2025, as was mentioned this morning by the Minister. It vests Kororipo Pā Historic Reserve, which is 1.8 hectares—not a lot in size, but huge in consequence and importance. It was managed by the Department of Conservation, but it re-vests it now in the Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Rēhia Trust as kaitiaki on behalf of all Ngāpuhi. Public access will remain unchanged, and the site will retain its historic reserve status to protect its heritage and conservation values.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the matter under debate, hence not 0.0, but indifferent to what it follows. The immediately preceding speaker's substantive criticism was that the Crown keeps effective control through the reserve's encumbrances; McCallum lists those same features approvingly and never acknowledges the objection. Substituting a different critique on the same topic would not change a word of this speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon argued immediately before that the vesting is "full of encumbrances" and does not deliver "full mana whakahaere", and this statement does not take that up — it recites the retained reserve status and unchanged public access, the very constraints she objected to, as merits, without engaging her claim.

acuity.statement: When we reported back to the House, as Adrian Rurawhe has said, there were two amendments, with one being the change to the definition of “vesting date”. Usually, it is 20 working days after the Act enters into force, but that did have some risk for Ngāti Rēhia and we wanted to make sure that this did indeed come into law and was concluded in all matters, and so we have put the particular date of 23 January 2026 as the vesting date.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific committee amendment Rurawhe had just described in general terms and does something with it — names the actual vesting date (23 January 2026) and gives the reason the 20-working-day default was replaced, i.e. supplies the figure and rationale the preceding turn left out. Marked down from 1.0 because it co-reports a shared committee account rather than engaging Rurawhe's central argument about the missing apology, to which this speech is indifferent.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe: "One of them was to change the commencement date so that we had an actual date rather than 20 days after being signed by the Governor-General."

acuity.statement: I know that a lot has been said, both this morning and in the process, around the fact that this is a stand-alone event, but can I, just for a moment, acknowledge the incredible significance of what this is and what this might, potentially, signal.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turns — the point that this is not a full settlement but a stand-alone vesting — and pushes back on its deflationary reading by arguing the bill signals wider momentum. But it concedes the point in a single clause and then moves to prepared material (the submitter quote, Dharamshala, Āpirana Ngata) that would have stood unchanged whatever had been said before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Adrian Rurawhe: "Of course, if it was an actual Treaty settlement, there’d be a lot more in it." (and David MacLeod: "Although it’s not a settlement bill itself")

acuity.statement: As much as I’d like to respond to some of the comments made just before me, I won’t because I want to focus on this important, colossal kaupapa that is such an important and beautiful day in our history, that I’m privileged to be standing up and adding some thoughts amongst the thoughts that were conveyed today.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle immediately follows Jackson's substantive turn, which argued at length that the bill passes under a Government that is continually attacking Māori rights (Treaty principles bill, Regulatory Standards Bill, fast track, the UN finding). She names that she could respond to it and expressly declines, then delivers prepared material on the bill itself. That is a gesture at the preceding turn with no engagement of any part of its content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band: the rest of the speech would have been word-for-word the same whatever Jackson had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "we move these bills and we move these initiatives off the back of a Government that is continually attacking Māori rights, and that's a problem."

acuity.statement: There was a lot of conversation, back and forth, about what this vesting bill means in terms of a settlement for Ngāpuhi. All I’d like to say is this: I hope that this bill is a seed for a tree that grows into that long-awaited settlement for Ngāpuhi.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding turn — whether this vesting bill amounts to, or leads to, a Ngāpuhi settlement, which Jackson raised sceptically — and offers a position on it (a seed, not the settlement itself). It engages the topic and the question rather than Jackson's specific claim that settlement is impossible while the Government keeps attacking, and it is framed as answering 'a lot of conversation, back and forth' generally rather than his argument in particular, then returns to prepared imagery. Pointable partial engagement, hence the middle of the scale rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "We’re talking about the Ngāpuhi settlement today. That’s the hope. I don't even know when Ngāpuhi is going—well, Willow-Jean Prime might know, but we'll never know when Ngāpuhi is going to settle."

acuity.statement: When we talk about the quality of life of older people in New Zealand, we are talking about respect—respect for people who built this country, who paid their taxes, who raised families, and who have contributed to their community over decades. What we are seeing from Christopher Luxon's Government is not respect; it is neglect.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Ingrid Leary's substantive turn precedes it in the same debate, and Sam Uffindell's point of order disputed a factual claim. Verrall's speech is prepared Labour material on the matter under debate — seniors, health access, the medicare card policy — and echoes Leary's framing of people who 'paid their taxes' and 'raised families', but it engages no specific claim, figure or argument Leary made, does not build on or qualify any of them, and does not touch the Uffindell dispute. It would read word-for-word the same had Leary made a different argument about seniors. The gesture at the debate's subject matter puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0. Scored only on engagement: the vigour of the attack on the Government is a Focus/Civility matter, and whether the 'neglect' characterisation is fair is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary spoke about the Otago Daily Times survey finding two-thirds of Otago seniors reporting declining quality of life and one in three delaying medical care, and about the retirement villages changes raised by Sam Uffindell, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: The issue of seniors is a serious one, and I tautoko with what all previous speakers have said. This is something that we should look at carefully and seriously and with a long-term goal that is non-partisan—this is what we heard this morning from the Retirement Commissioner.
acuity.explanation: A blanket endorsement of "all previous speakers" is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with anything in it. Verrall's specific claim — that price and fixed incomes bar older people from healthcare — is never taken up, confirmed, extended or qualified; what follows is prepared material (Retirement Commissioner statistics, the Green Budget) that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Verrall had argued. The gesture at the preceding contributions and the shared topic put it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ayesha Verrall: "They face greater barriers when accessing healthcare because of the price and their fixed incomes."

acuity.statement: I believe it is one of the best times ever to be an ageing New Zealander. It is better than in so many years of the past, because we have people who are living longer than ever.
acuity.explanation: This is the antithesis of the picture Xu-Nan had just painted, but it is an opposed mood rather than an opposed argument: none of his figures (poverty above the OECD average, a third of older people at risk of malnutrition, the rejection rate for hardship food grants) is disputed, corrected or accounted for, and his direct request that the Government revert the public transport subsidy cut from 75 to 65 percent goes unanswered. Characterising the other bench as "all doom and gloom" names a target without engaging its content. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and is otherwise prepared material, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "16.8 percent over the age of 65 are in poverty, which is higher than the OECD average of 14.2 percent"

acuity.statement: If we want people to age well, the evidence is clear. Three things matter most. First, connection—and research and work of organisations like Age Concern consistently show that social isolation and loneliness are amongst the strongest predictors of poor health and poor outcomes.
acuity.explanation: Campbell follows Ngarewa-Packer and takes up one strand of her speech — loneliness/social connection as a health determinant — and develops it with evidence (Age Concern research, isolation as a predictor of hospitalisation and cognitive decline), which is a real partial engagement rather than a bare mention. But it is only one strand: her central claims that the decline in seniors' quality of life is "a policy failure", that 41 percent say the system is not culturally fit, that whānau carers should be paid, and that "public capacity, not privatisation, should be a priority" are all left untouched, and the speech then returns to prepared material on the electorate, housing and food prices. His opening acknowledgement of "the thoughtfulness" of the preceding speech is courtesy, not engagement, and does not lift the score. Scored on engagement only: the accuracy of the life-expectancy and inflation figures elsewhere in the speech, and its pivot to his own Government's record, belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think tackling loneliness as an infrastructure is something that was really hard to read, and I have seen that in my own community" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, in the turn immediately preceding this one

acuity.statement: Today, I just want to focus on two key issues: the financial burden and loneliness.
acuity.explanation: Cheung follows a substantive turn by Cushla Tangaere-Manuel, who argued specifically that there is no aged care in Te Wairoa, that rural whānau are forced into hospital care, that moving a kuia into urban aged care strips the marae and whānau of knowledge, and that voluntary whānau carers go unremunerated. Cheung's speech takes up none of that: it is a prepared contribution on seniors in general (KiwiSaver, loneliness, culturally appropriate services for ethnic communities) that would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before him. It is at least squarely on the subject under debate, so it sits at the bottom rather than the floor of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel spoke about the absence of aged care in Te Wairoa and the cost to rural communities and marae of sending pakeke into urban facilities ("In Te Wairoa Hōpūpū Hōnengenenge Mātangi Rau, there is no aged care available"), and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Some speakers from the other side of the House have raised the issue of social isolation and exclusion. A very real concern for our older New Zealanders is that either they do not have access to those services, or, if they do have access to those services, that’s at the expense of their engagement and their inclusion in community activities and in community conversations, which are so important to address those issues of social isolation and exclusion.
acuity.explanation: Davidson picks up one identifiable strand of the preceding turn — Cheung's nominated "second major issue", loneliness and social isolation — and does something with it rather than merely naming it: he argues the cost of devices and connectivity means access to digital services can come at the expense of the very community engagement that would relieve isolation. That is genuine partial engagement, but it is one strand used as a hinge back into his own prepared material on digital inclusion, AI, the Medicard and named digital-equity organisations, and he does not touch Cheung's specific claims about KiwiSaver contribution rates or culturally appropriate services for ethnic seniors. Mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The second major issue, repeatedly raised by seniors, is loneliness." — Carlos Cheung

acuity.statement: Difficult choices like the Government choosing to freeze hiring for the health sector at the front line, which they still continue to say is not happening.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick follows a substantive turn by a different member in the same local debate, so she is eligible. Her speech is self-contained prepared material about Auckland Central and the Government's record; it makes no gesture at McAnulty or at any part of his argument. The health hiring freeze is the one point of thematic overlap with his claim that Wairarapa is 14 nurses short and 'not allowed to hire', but she raises it independently as one item in her own list rather than engaging, extending or disputing his claim — nothing here would change had he spoken about something else, though the subject matter is at least adjacent to the debate just conducted, so it is not a full 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty spoke about the Wairarapa Hospital settlement money ('We wanted to know how much of that settlement, which was for the sole purpose of fixing our hospital, would be ring-fenced for Masterton Hospital, and the answer is none of it') and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Last night, this House had the first readings of three pieces of legislation that will have transformational effects in my electorate of Banks Peninsula. The planning, natural environment, and the earthquake-prone building bills will have profound impacts in not only Christchurch in the South Island but also the whole of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn made specific, contestable claims (112,000 without shelter, 426 to 940 in Auckland, a $79m cut, a legal duty to assist modelled on Wales and Canada) and an explicit appeal to everyone in the House to hold rangatahi homelessness in mind. Weenink engages no strand of it — not the figures, not the bill, not the appeal. Applying the deciding test: if Kaipara's speech were replaced with a different argument on any subject, this speech would be word-for-word identical, since it is prepared material about last night's first readings and her own electorate. It sits in the bottom band rather than at 0.0 only because it is tethered to business actually before the House this week (the planning, natural environment and earthquake-prone building bills) rather than being deliverable in any debate on any day. Scored on engagement alone: the speech is coherent, on-topic for her electorate and civil, and none of that bears on responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Oriini Kaipara spoke about rangatahi homelessness in Tāmaki-makau-rau, the Salvation Army's doubled homelessness figures, the $79 million cut from housing support programmes, and her Youth Homelessness Prevention Bill going into the members' ballot, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We've heard the Opposition rant and rave about challenges that existed when they left office and, unfortunately, for New Zealand, they did not fix.
acuity.explanation: Bates follows a substantive turn by a different member, so he is eligible, and he does gesture at it — he characterises the preceding speech as the Opposition ranting and later refers to "the prior member who ranted and raved earlier in this debate". But that is a label, not engagement: he takes up none of Andersen's content (MSD's garage criterion, the eviction-notice threshold, the cancelled Hutt social housing build, the claim that funding followed media coverage), and instead delivers prepared Whanganui material on earthquake-prone buildings, an events fund and a Pātea cell tower. Deleting Andersen's turn and substituting any other Opposition speech would leave this speech word-for-word the same, apart from the dismissal. It stays in the 0.1–0.3 band because it is at least within the same end-of-year debate; 0.2 for the gesture at the previous speaker without engaging the argument. Scored only on responsiveness — the merits of his earthquake-strengthening savings figures, and the civility of "rant and rave", belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "Mark is one of many examples right across New Zealand where that is not true and people cannot access the help and the support they need." — Andersen's turn argued that homelessness support in the Hutt Valley is inaccessible (garage criteria, eviction-notice requirement, a cancelled social housing build).

acuity.statement: Well, that’s true. I wasn't complaining, I was merely making a prefatory remark about we are at in the system.
acuity.explanation: Bishop takes up Williams' interjection directly: he concedes her specific point (that the scheduling of the bill was his own choice) and then disputes her characterisation that he was complaining about it. The reply would be different had she said something else — it is shaped entirely by her claim. Not a mere reference or a pivot; it accepts part and rejects part.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: “It’s up to you; you could’ve made it the other day.”

acuity.statement: But I do think that one of the ones the previous speaker has noted is the one that is of most concern to the Greens, and it is important for us to spend a little bit of time unpacking this particular secondary legislation, or the regulation, and this is to do with the Excise and Excise-equivalent Duties Table (Tobacco Products Indexation and Reduction) Amendment Order 2024, which, I believe, was ratified on 1 January 2025.
acuity.explanation: Williams devoted most of her speech to arguing the heated tobacco excise reduction was an unusual use of the regulation-making power. Xu-Nan takes up that specific instrument by name, names the order and its dates, and then develops the same argument with the Standing Order 327(2)(c) 'unusual or unexpected use' test and the Customs advice. The speech would have had to be substantially different had Williams raised a different instrument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "That power is to be found in the excise setting for heated tobacco products. Heated tobacco products will see an excise reduction under this bill of 50 percent."

acuity.statement: It is a call to the permanent members of the Regulations Review Committee to actually put forward a disallowance motion under Standing Order 329 for next year on this particular part.
acuity.explanation: Williams floated a possible disallowance motion as still under discussion; Xu-Nan takes that strand up, notes he is not a permanent member and so cannot lodge one himself, cites the specific Standing Order that lets permanent members do it, and converts her tentative flag into an explicit call on them. Directly builds on the content of the preceding turn rather than merely referencing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "this is something that members of the committee are interested in potentially bringing a disallowance motion to the House about. It's still under discussion"

acuity.statement: As members have rightly said, our Government’s supporting the courts to be more efficient and to minimise delays. We’ve actually seen that by the end of 31 March this year, cases disposed of within expected time frames had actually gone up to 81 percent after almost a decade of declining timeliness. That’s progress.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition turn in the same debate and is on the right subject (court timeliness and the bill's efficiency aims), but engages no part of what Webb actually argued: nothing about the judicial review losses, the Corrections case, or the O'Connor amendment and the Minister's reversal of his own whip's vote. "As members have rightly said" is a gesture at the debate rather than engagement with its content, and the disposal-timeliness statistic is prepared material that would read identically whatever the preceding speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the Government is repeatedly losing judicial reviews and breaking the law ("You’re a bit busy is not an excuse for breaking the law") and that the Government should have adopted Greg O’Connor’s amendment to set a floor on judge numbers — this statement takes up neither point.

acuity.statement: The Judicature (Timeliness) Legislation Amendment Bill presents practical changes aimed at improving the timeliness, the much-needed timeliness, of judicial processes, increasing the number of High Court judges and District Court judges so that they’re enabled to consolidate pre-trial processes and coronial inquiries that may be closed when deemed appropriate. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Belich that made two concrete arguments — that the Government reversed a better amendment raising the cap to 65, and that the new abusive-process powers should be used sparingly — and engages neither. The speech is a prepared one-paragraph recital of the bill's purpose and a commendation; it would read word for word the same whatever Belich had said. It is at least on the matter under debate (the same bill, including the judge-number increase she discussed), so it sits at the bottom of the on-topic band rather than at 0.0, but there is no gesture at the preceding argument to lift it to 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich argued that Greg O'Connor's amendment to lift the judge cap to 65 was a missed opportunity after the bill was recommitted and the increase reversed, and she asked that the new vexatious-litigant powers be used sparingly; this statement does not take up either point.

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of New Zealand First to support the Judicature (Timeliness) Legislation Amendment Bill. In 2023, when New Zealand First went to election, we wanted to speed up the justice system and get our victims justice quicker. That’s something, on this side of the House, this Government is achieving within this bill.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by McKee but engages none of her claims or figures. It is prepared party material on the correct subject — it walks through the bill's clauses (judge numbers, striking out abusive proceedings, coroners) and would read identically whatever McKee had said. There is a faint gesture at the debate ("on this side of the House, this Government is achieving"), which keeps it off the floor of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicole McKee argued the bill builds on measured timeliness gains (a "20 percent reduction in the District Court criminal case backlog since April 2023") and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I guess the one thing I did want to talk about though is there are other contributing factors to the court backlogs. When this Government was passing three-strikes legislation and when they were passing the sentencing law reforms, the regulatory impact statements were really clear on the impact that would have on the judiciary in terms of those backlogs, because it meant opening up more space for re-litigation and more space for judicially reviewing some of those decisions that were being made.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding case: McKee presented the Government as a net reducer of backlogs, and Paul contests the causal account by pointing to the Government's own three-strikes and sentencing legislation as backlog-creating, citing the regulatory impact statements. That is a pointable engagement with the argument, but it sits alongside a good deal of prepared Green material (parole board meeting, victims of violence, the word "plainly") and does not address McKee's specific figures, so it is partial rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The bill builds on the significant improvements in court timeliness under this Government" — Nicole McKee.

acuity.statement: I can’t believe I’m standing up in this House speaking on a bill that the Greens have just said they are going to support, just before me. So it definitely must be that time of year, and I’m excited to end the year on such a positive note as we do good work to improve the justice system in this country and continue to reduce the number of victims in the system.
acuity.explanation: A bare reference to the previous speaker's position, used as a pivot rather than an engagement: Paul's substantive criticism goes unanswered. What follows is a single prepared point about consolidating pre-trial processes in one District Court office — a point Arbuckle had already made — delivered as though nothing had been said before it. On topic, so not 0.0, but a mention is not a response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul argued that the Government's three-strikes and sentencing reforms themselves add to court backlogs, and this statement does not take it up — it notes only that "the Greens have just said they are going to support" the bill.

acuity.statement: I thought Tamatha Paul’s contribution on how to reduce or improve timeliness in court—that is to say, don’t get caught drink driving and stay out of court—is a very good idea, so thank you for that piece of wisdom, Tamatha Paul.
acuity.explanation: Demonstrably built on what immediately preceded it: Webb picks up a specific line from Paul's closing and recasts it as advice on court timeliness, so the opening could not have been delivered after a different speech. But what he engages is an aside rather than her argument about the Government's own legislation adding to backlogs, which he only begins to reach as he is interrupted. Pointable engagement with a non-argument, so below the midpoint.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "don’t drink-drive, have a great Christmas" — Tamatha Paul.

acuity.statement: Essentially, this bill increases the number of High Court judges, improves the operation of senior and District Courts and grants coroners more power to close inquiries, aims to better judicial time on critical matters like serious criminal cases, because, on this side of the House, victims come first.
acuity.explanation: Vanushi Walters had just made a detailed set of arguments immediately before — the three-year strike-out period being disproportionate, the risk that coroners closing inquiries will leave families without answers on cause of death, the comparative judges-per-100,000 figures, and tribunal-level delay. Nakhle takes up none of it. Her contribution restates the bill's own summary description plus a slogan and seasonal greetings; it would be word-for-word identical whatever Walters had argued. It is at least on the matter under debate (it describes what the bill does), so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued the three-year strike-out rule is 'quite an extraordinary step', that coroner closures need monitoring because 'for other families, there are true questions about cause of death', and that tribunal-level delays remain unaddressed — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: When you increase the number of High Court judges, when you fast track processes, when you tighten rules around so-called abusive civil proceedings, you are not addressing the root causes.
acuity.explanation: This takes the three mechanisms the preceding speaker had just listed as the bill's merits — more High Court judges, improved court operation, faster disposal — and turns each one into the objection that capacity is not causation. That is a genuine engagement with one strand of what was said, and it also overlaps the strike-out provision Walters had flagged. But it engages the framing rather than any specific claim: it does not touch Nakhle's 'victims come first' rationale or Walters' concrete points (the three-year bar, the comparative judge ratios), and the bulk of the speech is prepared material on systemic bias, section 27 reports and legal aid that would have been delivered whatever preceded it. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this bill increases the number of High Court judges, improves the operation of senior and District Courts and grants coroners more power to close inquiries" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: Interestingly enough, Leon Smith, under the current rules, is not eligible to be celebrated on Anzac Day. This bill—and this is the reason why we do support this bill—means that people, like Leon Smith, who died an absolute hero and received the New Zealand Gallantry Declaration and the Charles Upham Bravery Awards for an operation—not the operation, unfortunately, in which he died, but one just a month before in Kabul.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific defect Penk identified — that the Act's six listed conflicts exclude later service — and supplies a concrete excluded case (an Afghanistan death in 2011) as the reason for supporting the broadening. It engages that strand of the preceding speech rather than Penk's account of the select committee's amendments, and the rest of the turn moves into prepared personal reflection, so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it currently restricts commemoration to those who served in six specified conflicts, the last being the war in Vietnam" — Chris Penk

acuity.statement: We will turn these current polls into confetti. We are on a trajectory to make a major shift in the political landscape, and we aim to do even more than that. We have the team, we have the candidates, we have the party machine, and we have the support of Kiwis.
acuity.explanation: Seymour's preceding turn addressed Peters directly, both by name and through the claim that the coalition is united and unusually productive legislatively. Peters engages no part of it: no response to the coalition-unity point, no reference to the legislative-record claim, no acknowledgement of Seymour at all. The passage is prepared party-positioning about New Zealand First's polling and election prospects and would be word-for-word identical had Seymour argued something entirely different, or had another member spoken instead. It stays within the matter of the adjournment debate (reflecting on the year and looking to the next), which keeps it off 0.0, but there is not even a gesture at the preceding speech, so it sits at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour said "For those who say that we fight like cats in a sack, hear this one simple fact: this Government has passed more legislation in the first two years of its three than any MMP Parliament has passed in its whole three years" and acknowledged Peters by name as a Government partner, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I dare because I knew them, but you don’t, because you didn’t.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick's interjection challenged his standing to invoke Rod Donald and Jeanette Fitzsimons; Peters takes up precisely that challenge and answers it on its own ground (personal acquaintance), rather than continuing his prepared text. The line would not exist had she not interjected, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because the engagement is with her standing-challenge only and adds no substance beyond the assertion of acquaintance. Scored independently of civility, which this line would score low on.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Christopher Luxon spoke about backing Resource Management Act reform and fast track to build renewable projects, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: What is his plan to build resilience in Ikaroa-Rāwhiti so they’re not having to continuously rebuild and respond to these extreme weather events?
acuity.explanation: Follows an answer about iwi being seated in coordinating executive groups and Peters' jibe about 'pretenders', and engages neither; asks a prepared forward-looking resilience question. Same topic, no take-up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Christopher Luxon spoke about iwi being included in coordinating executive group teams for response and recovery, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware of the marae in north Whananaki called Whakapaumahara, where the Ngāti Wai people live, because they were able, at the critical time, to assist the people who were in desperate need because we had fixed the marae up in the first place?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Davidson's attack — that the Government has cut proactive Māori climate resilience — by offering a counter-instance of marae prepared in advance that then served their community. It engages the general premise rather than the specific $20 million cut, and is clearly prepared material, so a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "given his decision to cut $20 million from Māori climate resilience" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to whether the Government is assiduously listening to the word of the Māori MP for Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, who has been reporting to this Government, to which we’re responding, and we don’t want to hear from pretenders?
acuity.explanation: Registers that Waititi has been pressing on Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and answers by disputing his standing to speak for it rather than anything he claimed about material support. A gesture at the exchange, not engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I asked what material support, not what he thinks they think he is doing." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to why he’s given any credulity to the $6 billion fund, which was an announcement made in a press release with no money set aside in the first place?
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the specific figure Waititi built his question around and attacks its premise — that there was a $6 billion fund to scrap at all. The question would have to be rewritten entirely had Waititi raised a different criticism, which is the mark of engagement; marked down only because it largely restates the interjection he had already made and rides on the answer just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How does he justify his Government’s decision to scrap the $6 billion national resilience plan" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: What activities in the health cyber-security roadmap were cancelled after the cuts in Budget 2024?
acuity.explanation: Brown had just countered her premise with specific figures ($9m in Budget 2024, $10m in Budget 2025). She stays on the same subject and presses for the operational consequence, but does not take up or contest the figures he offered, restating her own framing instead. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “It is correct that we invested more into cyber-security under this Government, with an additional $9 million in Budget 2024” — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: When Health New Zealand answered at annual review that “planned future work on the next stage of cyber-security capability uplift has been cut”, did that reflect the defunding of cyber-security initiatives in Budget 2024?
acuity.explanation: Directly meets the Minister's repeated claim of continued investment by producing Health New Zealand's own annual-review wording that work was cut, and asks him to reconcile the two. The question would have to be different if he had not just asserted continued investment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “Well, we have continued to invest into cyber-security.” — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Why has his response been to deflect and blame at every opportunity but not answer a straight question about his cuts to cyber-security projects?
acuity.explanation: Takes up what the Minister has actually been doing across the preceding answers — pivoting to her 2023 Budget rather than addressing the cancellation — so it is aimed at the turn just given. It engages the conduct of the answer rather than the substance of any claim in it, so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “I would point to Budget 2023 and the reduction in Health data and digital foundations and innovation” — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Talking about patient health data, would informed observers that have noticed that the massive drop in cigarette smoking has led to a fall of $200 million in taxation going to the Government understand that to be serious progress by way of steps forward, rather than describe it as a $200 million benefit to the tax industry, which only a four-flushing moron would say in the first place?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the question under examination with its opening clause and then engages nothing in the exchange about cyber-security or the Manage My Health incident, moving instead to tobacco excise revenue and an insult. A mere reference to the topic, not engagement with any claim made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown and Ayesha Verrall were exchanging over whether Budget 2024 defunded Health New Zealand cyber-security projects, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: What further information can he provide regarding the status of the Waiōeka Gorge?
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific item the Minister had just raised — the continuing work and 40 slips on State Highway 2 through the Waiōeka Gorge — and asks him to draw it out. It takes up one strand of the preceding answer rather than engaging a contested claim, which is a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: “In the Bay of Plenty, work continues on State Highway 2 through the Waiōeka Gorge.” — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Here we are at the start of the third year of this Government, and one of the focuses of this Government has been to restore law and order in this country. The good news is that we have made great progress as a country over the last two years. We now have 38,000 fewer victims of crime in this era.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds' immediately preceding turn was a sustained economic argument built on specific Treasury forecast figures, the Minister of Finance's 'overly optimistic' answer, and a list of employment law changes. Goldsmith's speech engages none of it: it pivots to prepared law-and-order material (victims of crime, three strikes, sentencing discounts, gang patches) and then to Te Pati Maori and Green prison policy. It would read identically had Edmonds made a completely different argument, or none. It is not a 0.0 because it is still a contribution to the same wide-ranging debate on the Government's record at the start of the parliamentary year, so there is a gesture at the matter under debate, but no engagement with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued from Treasury's Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update that forecast real GDP for 2026 has fallen from $304 billion to $289 billion and that 50,000 more people are forecast to be unemployed than in 2023, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I hear the Government talking about some of the response that they have in regard to those who have been affected by the weather events: campervans, cabins, and all those types of things. It’d been nice to hear a definitive answer to many of the questions asked at question time about what is the long-term goal here?
acuity.explanation: Patterson's turn immediately before made a specific, contestable case that the Government has been proactive, with figures ($200m in the Regional Infrastructure Fund, 74 flood protection schemes, Taradale, Motueka). Waititi is plainly in the same debate and glances at the Government's response package, but he engages none of Patterson's reasoning or numbers; the long-term-objective question is directed at question time answers, not at the preceding speech, and the rest of the turn is prepared oranga material that would read identically whoever had spoken before. That is a gesture at the debate without engagement of the argument, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mark Patterson: "I have heard some criticism on the other side of the House and a lot of the questions coming forward about us not being proactive enough around managing these severe weather events. Nothing could be further from the truth" — Waititi gestures at the Government's response but does not take up that claim or the flood-protection funding Patterson cited.

acuity.statement: But it is important to acknowledge that we do need a clear adaptation framework to make sure that we are best placed and prepared to respond: simple things like providing clear guidance to councils for how they prepare to adapt, and also the introduction of a national flood map so that New Zealanders can understand the risks they face. This is all work that is under way. This isn’t political.
acuity.explanation: Waititi had just put two concrete things to the Government: that families from Bola and Gabrielle are still unable to navigate insurance and capital to replace homes, and that slash removal needs stricter criteria. Watts's reply is on the matter under debate — adaptation to severe weather — but it answers neither point, and the adaptation-framework, energy, rates-capping and City and Regional Deals material would be word-for-word the same had any other member spoken, or none. The claim that "this isn't political" asserts consensus rather than engaging the disagreement actually voiced. Note this is low Acuity only; the speech is on-policy and reasonably specific, which are separate questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that long-term support is missing — "It’d been nice to hear a definitive answer to many of the questions asked at question time about what is the long-term goal here?" — and called for stricter criteria on forestry slash in Te Tairāwhiti; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: It’s been an interesting time, being able to sit in the House and observe over the last 48 hours speeches from both the Government and the Opposition benches in relation to the Prime Minister’s statement. It’s been really interesting to see and observe the reaction of other members in the House when speakers are standing up and delivering their response.
acuity.explanation: Watts's turn immediately before offered several checkable claims — renewables commissioned, the Forsyth Barr energy security finding, rates capping — any of which an Opposition finance spokesperson was well placed to contest. Edmonds instead comments on the conduct of the benches during the debate. That is a reference to the preceding speeches rather than engagement with their content, which the rubric puts in the 0.1–0.3 band; she gestures at the debate itself, so 0.2 rather than 0.1. The earlier parts of her turn (condolences, the Paekākāriki Hill crash, the valedictory acknowledgements) are ceremonial and not scored.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts argued "we do need a clear adaptation framework" and claimed New Zealand's energy security is "the strongest that it has been in more than 15 years"; this statement turns to how Government MPs behaved while listening rather than to any of that.

acuity.statement: I would just like to remind that member that methamphetamine use has doubled under his Government. I’d like to remind that member of that, because that is an actual objective measure of the state of law and order in our community. Not performative bills passed in this House, but an actual thing that is oppressing communities up and down the country—meth use—doubling under that Government.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith's case was that the Government's sentencing and gang legislation has improved public safety. Verrall takes that claim on directly and disputes its measure, offering a counter-indicator (meth use doubling) and explicitly rejecting legislation passed as the test ("Not performative bills passed in this House"). The speech would have to change if Goldsmith had made a different argument. Not a full 1.0 because she engages the metric rather than the specific 38,000-victims figure before moving to prepared health material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "They voted against everything that we have done over the past two years which has brought about the improvement in public safety and has brought about 38,000 fewer victims of crime than what we inherited."

acuity.statement: This debate is about the Prime Minister’s statement. Of course, we heard the speech yesterday, and then we had the statement here presented in Parliament. Of course, I took the time, rather than racing through a floridly psychotic contribution like the last member, to actually read the statement and will offer some commentary on that.
acuity.explanation: The previous speaker is referred to only as a target for a jibe about his delivery, and the passage then pivots to prepared commentary on the Prime Minister's statement. Per the rubric a mere reference is not engagement; it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, and 0.2 rather than 0.1 because it is squarely within the same debate and acknowledges what the last contribution was.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing beyond a reference: Paul Goldsmith argued Labour and the Greens have voted against every law-and-order measure and have announced no justice policy, and this passage names him as a target without taking up any part of that

acuity.statement: As we enter our third year in Government, I believe we can say this plainly: the foundations are being restored, momentum is strong, and the future is opening up. Economic growth is strengthening. Confidence is lifting.
acuity.explanation: Potaka follows a detailed health and affordability critique but engages no part of it; the passage is prepared government framing that would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before. It stays in the low band rather than 0.0 because it is addressed to the matter under debate — the direction set out in the Prime Minister's statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued that inflation-adjusted per capita health funding has fallen for the first time since the 1990s, that graduate nurses cannot get jobs and that GP visits now approach $100, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: I do recognise your argument, and what I am saying is that this is a difficult question. If you were listening, you’d know that we support this bill, rather than walking in and out and heckling with half of a thought.
acuity.explanation: Webb takes up Nakhle's specific accusation head-on, acknowledges the argument she is making, and corrects the misstatement of his position by stating that his party supports the bill. The reply would have to change if she had said something different, which is the mark of genuine engagement. It is not a 1.0 because a substantial part of the passage is a complaint about her conduct in the chamber (walking in and out, heckling) rather than the substance of the child sex offender question itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You’re defending child sex offenders" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: I’d like to acknowledge the Minister of Police and the Justice Committee for the work they’ve done on this bill, which is, as Casey Costello pointed out, a very delicate topic. This bill is about giving protection to children and to communities, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Webb on the protective/punitive tension and the administrative justification for retrospectivity, and engages none of it. It is on the right subject and gestures at the debate by crediting the committee and citing Casey Costello's characterisation of the topic, but the words would be identical whatever Webb had argued. On-topic prepared commendation, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the bill 'sits awkwardly between being both protective and punitive' and that the retrospectivity's motive 'is not particularly protective; it is administrative', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: As we heard in the quite animated debate just prior to me taking this call, the retrospectivity part applies to the first part that I was talking about, which is the changes to the notification, and not to the second part. I won’t relitigate that; there’s nobody here to spar with on that one in particular, so with that, I will end my contribution by saying that we do support this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding argument — the scope of the retrospectivity — and does something with it, locating it in the reporting-requirement half of the bill rather than the seven new offences. That is a substantive clarification of the point just contested, so the passage would read differently had the earlier turns argued something else. Short of 1.0 because she explicitly declines to engage the disagreement itself and closes on prepared party position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "even in the Attorney-General’s report it notes that the retrospective nature, the motive of it, is not particularly protective; it is administrative"

acuity.statement: I have spoken before on this; I’ll just acknowledge Willow-Jean Prime—we don’t always agree on everything—and the point that she made before about us having an epidemic of offending against children in this country, and we need to do a lot more at every level of our society to address that. This is one really important step, and I say that, having worked for about 10 years in criminal courts and prisons across New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific claim made in the immediately preceding turn — that offending against children is at epidemic levels and that much more is needed beyond this bill — accepts it across party lines and extends it with his own courts-and-prisons experience. The engagement is pointable and the speech is shaped by what Prime said, but it adopts one strand rather than testing the argument, and the remainder is his own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "we have a serious problem in our community, in our country, and there is so much more that we need to do to prevent this harm happening to our tamariki"

acuity.statement: After the Hon Willie Jackson, I feel like we need to just calm it down a little bit, come back to me. I rise as the final speaker in the third reading of the Ngāti Hāua Claims Settlement Bill.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn by Jackson that contained real content — the Tāme Iti pardon request put to the Minister of Justice, the tribute to Archie Taiaroa, the charge that National has 'gone off the track' on the Treaty, the point that $20 million does not reflect the loss, and a set of questions about rangatahi, urban Māori and the iwi's future. She engages none of it. She names Jackson only to set her own tone against his ('calm it down a little bit') and later picks up his 'Tinkerbell' joke about Graham Bell, which is a reference rather than an engagement with any claim. The rest of her speech responds to what Graham Bell said at the morning mihi whakatau, not to the preceding turn in the debate. The speech is clearly about the matter under debate and makes a passing gesture at Jackson, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0; it would have read almost identically whatever Jackson had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Most of them are called “Ding-Dong” and you’re called “Tinka” Bell.' — Willie Jackson (a joke picked up, not an argument engaged; Jackson's substantive points on the pardon, the $20 million quantum and National's Treaty record are not taken up)

acuity.statement: Also, I support what has also been said about the Uber drivers as well. The thing about the Uber drivers is this: they won every single time in the courts. They won in the Court of Appeal, they won in the Supreme Court, and now we have amendments in this bill which will make it harder for them to get their workers’ rights.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of Twyford's speech about the Uber drivers' litigation and the contractor provisions, and extends it by adding the Supreme Court outcome and tying it to the bill's amendments. It engages a real part of the preceding argument rather than merely naming it, but much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on the Government's wider record, so this is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "what it had said in the Uber drivers’ case was that those Uber drivers were, under New Zealand law, found to be employees"

acuity.statement: Anyone would think that the world is about to end. Well, actually, I think we, on this side of the House, understand that the world is changing: we’re going into a gig economy, and taking Uber rides has become something that we’re all using all the time, even those on the other side of the House, as it happens.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the gig-economy/Uber theme that dominated the two preceding Opposition speeches and contests its premise — that gig work is simply precarity to be litigated away — by framing it as an inevitable and welcome change.
