But it answers the topic rather than the specific claims put (that the gateway test blocks court access, that the courts already found the drivers to be employees), and the rest of the turn is generic framing about the 1970s and unions that would stand whatever had been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "what this does is it makes gig economy workers even more vulnerable"

acuity.statement: We do support some of the tweaks to the gateway test, but we have also taken note of the Court of Appeal decision. We support the lift to $200,000 for the personal grievance provisions. We certainly heard some feedback that the previous threshold, which was $180k, was capturing the likes of health professionals and, actually, making us unappealing in terms of the international market.
acuity.explanation: Engages the two specific objections just made — Twyford on the gateway test and the Court of Appeal ruling, and Tuiono on the $180,000-to-$200,000 personal grievance threshold — and does something with each: concedes the Court of Appeal point as something taken into account, and supplies a substantive reason for the threshold change the previous speaker had attacked. The speech would read differently had those arguments not been made; it falls short of 1.0 because it does not rebut the reasoning so much as register agreement and supply a counter-rationale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "the work of the select committee, who raised it, I think, from $180,000 to $200,000 as well"

acuity.statement: The Prime Minister’s statement in an election year sets the vibe of the year. It tells the House where the energy’s at. It’s a way to think about how the year’s going to show up, and nothing’s said it more than Christopher Luxon, day one of the Parliament sitting.
acuity.explanation: Woods follows Meager, who closed with a substantive claim that fixing the basics now is the only route to prosperity, plus a jibe about the Opposition not joining the "shared path". Her speech engages none of that: it is prepared material addressed to the Prime Minister's statement debate generally — the length of Luxon's speech, the tax-cut promise, the LNG levy — and would read identically whatever Meager had said. It earns the top of the unresponsive band only because it is squarely about the matter under debate (the Prime Minister's statement itself), not a different subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager said "there is only one way we can guarantee prosperity in New Zealand, and for us on this side, it’s to fix the basics now so that we can build for a future tomorrow" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The long-term insights briefings are being reduced down to just one prepared by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. Those long-term insights briefings are incredibly important; they provide a considered piece of advice, they go to select committees so that all of Parliament benefits from them, and they’re published for the public.
acuity.explanation: Foster's preceding turn defended the consolidation of the long-term insights briefings into a single briefing by DPMC, expressing confidence in DPMC's capability and citing the select committee's monitoring commitment. Verrall takes up that same specific provision and argues the opposite case, so this strand of her speech would have to change if Foster had defended a different clause. But she engages only the topic of the consolidation, not his actual reasoning — she does not address DPMC's claimed capability or the committee's monitoring undertaking — and the passage otherwise reads as prepared material restating her first-reading position. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, who are going to be charged with doing that—very, very confident about their ability to be able to deliver a very good, high-quality long-term insights briefing" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: Look, that member’s attempt to put that joke across earlier, I think just sums up the last Labour Government: great promise, lots of noise, but totally failed to deliver, and everyone is left wondering just what the heck had happened.
acuity.explanation: Woods had just made a specific argument that LNG firming is an expensive and avoidable choice because cheaper storage and firming options were taken off the agenda. Van de Molen names her and her 'joke' but engages no part of that argument — no answer on LNG, firming costs, or energy options — before moving to prepared Waikato material. A mere reference to the previous speaker, not engagement with the content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does it have to be LNG? No, it doesn’t. There are cheaper options, and this Government took them off the agenda" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: The Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament for 2026 was delivered on 27 January, and I still encourage New Zealanders to have a read of or listen to some of the speeches that were delivered in this House since then.
acuity.explanation: Substantive opposition and government turns precede this one, but the speech opens and proceeds as entirely prepared material on the Prime Minister's statement — a school opening in Flat Bush and classroom costs. It would have been word-for-word identical whoever spoke before. It is at least about the item under debate, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods argued the Government chose an expensive LNG 'band-aid' over cheaper firming options, and Tim van de Molen spoke about Waikato roads and health; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: It was quite interesting listening to the speeches from the other side today, and I was kind of a little bit perplexed as to exactly what I should be taking away from that. We saw that James Meager could adequately read a speech; that’s what I took away from his particular contribution. We heard that Tim van de Molen’s favourite electorate is the one that he represents. And we heard a great description from Nancy Lu of actually what constitutes a classroom and the fact that it needs walls and a roof.
acuity.explanation: Belich demonstrably listened — she characterises three preceding contributions, including Lu's classroom passage — but she repeats them back only to dismiss them and then pivots to her own prepared material on jobs and the public service. Lu's actual claim (that classrooms are now built for less than half the former cost) goes unaddressed, so this is a reference rather than engagement with content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It needs four walls and a roof, warm and dry so students can focus on learning" — Nancy Lu

acuity.statement: Like I said, what this absolutely presents is an opportunity for the Government to come true, particularly on their promise for fixing the basics and building the future: upgrading roads, schools, hospitals, and infrastructure. Let’s see it. They’ve got a very concrete opportunity to deliver and reconnect Wharekahika, Te Araroa, and Pōtaka to the rest of Aotearoa.
acuity.explanation: She takes the 'fixing the basics and building the future' formulation the preceding government speakers used and turns it into a concrete test — roads, schools and hospitals in the flood-hit north of her electorate. That engages one strand of what was put, rather than the specific claims made about Waikato roads or classroom costs, and the rest of the speech is her own prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Thank goodness for them, on this side there is a Government that is fixing the basics and building the future" — Tim van de Molen

acuity.statement: Two years ago, this Government was elected on an ambitious agenda to get New Zealand back on track and, since then, has been relentlessly focused on fixing the basics and building the future.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn was a direct, answerable challenge about reconnecting flood-isolated communities, and the turn before that gave job and underutilisation figures. Mooney engages neither and proceeds through prepared Southland material. On the matter under debate, so not a zero, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel asked the Government for concrete guarantees that Wharekahika, Te Araroa and Pōtaka would be reconnected, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I rise in strong support of the Prime Minister’s statement. Over the past two years, this Government has been working tirelessly to bring New Zealand back on track.
acuity.explanation: Belich's jobs and public-service figures were squarely available to be rebutted, and Cheung's own section on the economy asserts recovery without touching them. The speech would read identically had any other member spoken before; it is prepared praise on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich claimed 32,000 fewer jobs and 165,000 people out of work, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: As I listened to the Prime Minister address the nation following the catastrophic floods from the East Coast to the Far North, his praise for our marae, our hapū, and our iwi communities could only be received as hollow words and shallow praise, particularly when we take into account the actions of his Government over the past two years.
acuity.explanation: Ferris is responding to the Prime Minister's statement and to the flood response, which is the item under debate and overlaps the theme Tangaere-Manuel raised, but he engages no claim made in any preceding turn in this debate — not Cheung's figures immediately before him, nor the Labour contributions on the same floods. Prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Carlos Cheung spoke about record satisfaction with Government services, education reform and crime, and this statement engages none of it.

acuity.statement: I don’t know where those members on the other side actually come from, because this bill actually talks about clarity of role for the Public Service. One of the changes that this bill actually makes is that it is mandatory for the Public Service Commissioner to set minimum standards of integrity and conduct, rather than leaving it optional—optional; having no standards is what that side wants.
acuity.explanation: Verrall had made four specific charges against the bill (removal of pay equity provisions, removal of the requirement to reflect the population, loss of long-term insights advice, risk to political neutrality). Lee gestures at the other side and then recites prepared material about what the bill does — mandatory minimum standards, core values, CE tenure. She asserts the opposite of Verrall's neutrality claim without engaging any part of her reasoning, and the speech would read identically whatever Verrall had argued. A gesture at the debate on the right subject, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall: "It removes a long-term consideration of the public interest from the purpose of the bill that governs the Public Service. It introduces a risk to our political neutrality."

acuity.statement: I also heard members before talking about how good it’s going to be when the chief executives (CEs) are on this limited time frame—well, they already are, by the way. They have terms. The terms come to the end, but there is political neutrality in those appointments. The Minister does not make those appointments currently, because they need to be politically neutral.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific point Lee had just praised in the bill — fixed-term chief executives — and does something with it: asserts that CEs already serve fixed terms, so the change is not the innovation claimed, and identifies what the change actually does (shifts the appointment to the Minister). If Lee had praised a different clause this passage would have had to change, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Melissa Lee: "just because you happen to be the chief executive of a Government department does not mean that it continues for ever; the best person gets the job"

acuity.statement: I want to start by addressing the diversity, equity, and inclusion. We hear from the other side: “Oh, it should be about merit.” When you give effect to diversity, equity, and inclusion, the two are not mutually exclusive of each other—with merit.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the merit argument advanced from the government benches and attacks its premise directly — that merit and diversity are alternatives — rather than restating her own position. It engages the strand rather than a specific figure or clause, so it sits just below a full rebuttal of a particular claim, but what is being engaged is plainly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Melissa Lee: "the best person gets the job"

acuity.statement: I agree with the last sentiment from the previous speaker, the Hon Jan Tinetti, that the Public Service should support all New Zealanders. That’s something we agree on. When I was at school and we’d play sports in primary school, you’d pick two captains organically amongst yourselves, and then you’d choose who you wanted on your team. You wouldn’t pick the Māori boy or the Chinese boy or the girl out of diversity; you’d pick the ones that would help you win the game. That was all about merit.
acuity.explanation: Opens by quoting Tinetti's closing sentiment in order to agree with it and then pivot, which the rubric treats as unresponsive. The schoolyard analogy does take up the merit-versus-diversity topic she had just argued about, but it simply reasserts that the two are alternatives rather than engaging her claim that they are compatible. Topic engaged, specific claim not — the low end of the partial band. (The weakness of the analogy is a Rigor matter and is deliberately not scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Jan Tinetti: "the two are not mutually exclusive of each other—with merit"

acuity.statement: Actually, that last comment from the last speaker was totally offensive. There is no “cooking” of the books. We are continuing to deliver, in fact, enhanced transparency and accountability. In fact, I’ll just have a look at the select committee report. That speech would have been great; probably, they should have just put it in as a differing view. I noticed the Greens didn’t even bother to do a differing view, so I’m not really sure where that content came from.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson takes up the specific charge Hernandez had just made — that the Government is "cooking the books" to avoid accountability — names it, denies it directly, and counter-asserts that the bill enhances transparency and accountability. He also engages the provenance of Hernandez's argument, noting the Greens filed no differing view in the select committee report. The speech would clearly have been different had the preceding turn said something else, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 because he engages the headline accusation rather than the substance beneath it (the new OBEGAL-excluding-ACC metric, emigration, youth unemployment) and then moves to prepared material; the rebuttal is flat denial rather than argument, but that is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which is why they’re cooking the books—so that they don’t have to be accountable" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: So, in terms of wellbeing reporting, the whole objective of that is to try to be accountable to New Zealanders for making lives better and for setting it up and reporting on it in ways that New Zealanders actually understand. That’s the point of wellbeing Budgets.
acuity.explanation: Willis's preceding turn mocked wellbeing reporting as a fiction of glossy documents that uses the word "wellbeing" enough times. Russell takes up that specific strand and answers it directly — arguing that narrative reporting is what readers actually consume and that wellbeing reporting exists to be accountable in terms the public understands, so the defence is aimed at the charge just made. But it engages only one strand of Willis's speech: nothing in it addresses the bill's fiscal-risk disclosure argument, the Treasury review of 25 years of statements, or the debt/household analogy, and the bulk of the turn (the 2018 select committee witnesses, the Bobby Kennedy passage, the list of Budget Policy Statement objectives) is prepared material that would have been delivered whatever Willis had said about wellbeing. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-range rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "this absolute fiction introduced by the last finance Minister that if you want to enhance the prosperity of your people through the Budget process, what you do is you do a wellbeing report"

acuity.statement: The Government is amending the Public Finance Act to prevent future Governments from exceeding the extent of fiscal risk in Government accounts. These changes are intended to improve the transparency and accountability of future Governments for New Zealanders. The National-led Government are in support because we have nothing to hide. Now, the Opposition members are voting in opposition. They are voting down this bill and New Zealanders should be very, very concerned. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Edmonds that made specific claims about the PREFU, the Votes and the tax-cut promise. Lu's speech engages none of it: it restates the bill's purpose, asserts the Government has nothing to hide, and notes that the Opposition is voting against. The reference to the Opposition's vote is a mere mention, not engagement with Edmonds' content, and the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever she had said — though it is at least on the matter under debate, which keeps it above 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued the Government promised tax cuts it could not afford because it had not read the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, and that the fiscal risks were already set out in the Votes — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: And we know, like we just heard from Barbara Edmonds, that there are votes in a Budget and there are different years associated with those votes and people can choose to read those Budget documents if they want to. That is transparency and it already exists. More transparency is a great thing and nobody on this side of the House has opposed more transparency, but when that side of the Government says, “Oh, there was a fiscal cliff that we didn’t know about Pharmac.”, when they then chose to not put it in their Budget, it is deeply ironic.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific inference in the immediately preceding turn — that voting against the bill means opposing transparency and having something to hide — and rebuts its reasoning directly: transparency over Votes and out-years already exists, and nobody on her side has opposed more transparency. She then turns Lu's transparency claim against the Government over the Pharmac 'fiscal cliff'. The speech would have to change if Lu had argued something else, so this is high responsiveness; the quality of the irony argument belongs to Rigor, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, the Opposition members are voting in opposition. They are voting down this bill and New Zealanders should be very, very concerned." — Nancy Lu (and Lu's framing of the bill as improving transparency)

acuity.statement: Now, I’ve heard from the Opposition around reducing and getting rid of the wellbeing out of this Act. Well, I can come back to that a little bit, because I’ve spent a lot of time and I understand where they’re coming from with wellbeing economics. In fact, I’ve read the same Bobby Kennedy quote myself on a number of occasions.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the wellbeing-economics strand that the preceding ACT speech dismissed and engages it on its own terms (the Kennedy quote, the Living Standards Framework capitals), rather than ignoring it — but the engagement is with the Opposition case in general and the speech then returns to prepared historical material on the 1989 Act.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We don’t need wellbeing measures, because what we’ve introduced is Government targets." — Todd Stephenson

acuity.statement: Let’s start by addressing the mythic elephant in this House, which is the fact that we have seen a pandemic that was unprecedented globally, and those kinds of debt that have been taken on from the shock event is something that the Treasury has factored in. From a global perspective, Aotearoa New Zealand has actually done better than most other countries, yet we have seen this Government not having any pandemic yet still managing to tank our economy, because this is this Government’s legacy.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the preceding speaker's central claim that Labour left a hole of debt and supplies a competing causal account (a global pandemic shock, already factored in by Treasury) plus a comparison that turns the claim back on the Government. The speech would have to change if the previous turn had not argued about inherited debt.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Well, he was right—it was a deep, dark hole of debt that we had to climb out of." — David Wilson

acuity.statement: We talked about GDP. Now, the submitters for this particular bill have mentioned that there is a risk for GDP and national debt and argue this will be a step backwards for Aotearoa New Zealand, because GDP, while it can be measured, cannot be used to measure equity and equitable distribution in our community.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific inference just made — that countable GDP and financials are superior to wellbeing metrics — by conceding measurability and disputing what it captures, then listing what GDP omits. Squarely aimed at the preceding argument's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s a funny thing: in the end, GDP—you can count it." — David Wilson

acuity.statement: If there was ever a time to bring in a Public Finance Amendment Bill and strengthen the transparency and accountability and responsibility around our fiscal management, it was after the last Government.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and gestures at the other bench, but engages no part of the preceding argument; the contribution is a prepared frame around a list of headlines and would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued the pandemic debt was an unprecedented global shock already factored in by Treasury and that GDP fails to capture unemployment and hardship, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Now, what we have is some remarkable rewriting of history in the House tonight. We’ve had a New Zealand First speaker stand up and rail against decisions that were made by the 2017-20 Government, which New Zealand First were part of. New Zealand First was sitting around the Cabinet table making those decisions—a remarkable retelling of history.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific attack made two turns earlier and does something with it: identifies the speaker's own party as a member of the Cabinet that made those decisions, which is a direct rebuttal of the standing he claimed to criticise them from. The passage could not have been written without having heard that turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Well, the net effect of that is an extra $50 billion that Labour and the finance Minister could spend on behalf of us all to inject money into the economy, called quantitative easing." — David Wilson

acuity.statement: I don’t think any of us anticipated just how nasty this debate on a piece of public finance reporting legislation would get. The chair of the select committee could muster one minute on the bill, and even in that one minute, he managed to fill it with vitriol.
acuity.explanation: Refers to the immediately preceding contribution but engages only its brevity and tone, not its content — the Treasury long-term insights findings on COVID spending go unaddressed. A characterisation of the previous speaker is not engagement with his claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That side of the House has given us every reason why we need this Public Finance Amendment Bill." — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: They went back and they filled in the précis form with two lines under “Cultural” and two lines under “Social” and two lines under “Environmental”. It changed nothing. It was well-meaning but, unfortunately, meaningless as well.
acuity.explanation: Answers the preceding argument's core proposition — that a wellbeing lens is good discipline — with a counter-instance in which the lens produced only form-filling. It engages that strand rather than her specific claims about the five fiscal variables or OBEGALx, so the engagement is partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The purpose of a Government needing to stop and examine what it is funding in its Budgets through its wider policy lens of wellbeing is a good practice for any Government." — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: We have seen bigger numbers of visitors than we have seen for a really long time, and my colleague Stuart Smith just talked about that.
acuity.explanation: Nimon's turn follows a substantive turn by a different member (Smith, on the wine industry's oversupply problem and the return of tourists to Kaikoura). She picks up one strand of it — Smith's observation that visitor numbers are at post-earthquake highs — and does something with it, folding it into her claim that the Government's tourism package caused the rise. But she takes up only that strand: Smith's substantive point about wine production outpacing sales goes untouched, and the rest of the speech is prepared material on the events and tourism portfolio that would read the same whoever had preceded her. Partial engagement, so mid-band rather than a mere name-check.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the numbers in the summer are back to the numbers not seen since before the earthquake in 2016" — Stuart Smith

acuity.statement: I’m so glad that the speeches before me were from this side of the House. If they were from that side of the House, I know that they would have been full of negativity, because that is how they are.
acuity.explanation: Parmar follows a substantive turn by Nimon on the Government's tourism and events growth plan. She refers to the preceding speeches only to note which bench they came from and to speculate about what the other bench would have said, engaging none of Nimon's content. That is a gesture at the debate rather than an engagement, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; the rest of the speech is prepared material that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Katie Nimon: "All of these are part of our growth plan in events and tourism, and it is all there to help grow the economy and put money into the back pockets of everyday Kiwis."

acuity.statement: Yes, those kind of comments—it’s important that New Zealanders hear those kind of comments because, on this side, we believe that tertiary education institutions should not be used to indoctrinate young people with one-sided political views.
acuity.explanation: She picks up Halbert's interjection immediately and visibly — the sentence exists only because he said it — but she does not take up the claim that she lacks cultural competency. She holds the comment up as an exhibit and pivots straight back to her prepared line on indoctrination in universities. Pointable engagement with the fact of the interjection, no engagement with its content, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "You have no cultural competency whatsoever."

acuity.statement: In this unlikely cartoon coalition, I think Mr Willie Jackson should be very worried that Donald Duck may just pip him to the post for a Cabinet position after that appalling rant of a speech.
acuity.explanation: Stanford follows a substantive Jackson turn on housing, homelessness, subsidies, emigration and Māori-Crown relations. She names him and characterises his speech, then pivots entirely to prepared education material that engages none of his claims — no housing figure, no response on Māori relations, no answer on the subsidies he alleged. The speech would read identically whatever Jackson had argued, so this is a mere reference plus a gesture at the debate, not engagement with content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "this Government's policies are just driving people into homelessness" and "Māori-Crown relations are at an all-time low"

acuity.statement: The previous speaker, Erica Stanford, just finished her speech talking about people getting across the ditch, and aren’t we seeing exactly that under this Government? “Everyone Must Go”—everyone must go across to Australia, because that’s what’s happening under this Government and under Christopher Luxon’s leadership.
acuity.explanation: Boyack picks up Stanford's exact closing phrase and inverts it, which is a real glance at the preceding turn — but she takes the words, not the argument. Stanford's claim was that structured-literacy and maths reforms are producing measurable gains and that there is international consensus behind them; Boyack engages none of that and uses the phrase as a springboard to emigration. Quoting an opponent in order to pivot away sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "I suggest that the Labour Party get across the ditch and get with the programme"

acuity.statement: When New Zealanders were looking for hope, they were looking for aspiration, and they were looking for some sort of vision, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon delivered that speech. It was short, it was boring, and it was limited.
acuity.explanation: Boyack's preceding turn characterised the Prime Minister's statement as empty and truncated, and attacked the electricity levy as a tax; Halbert picks up both strands (the speech being short and limited; "now they want to add an additional tax on to people's power bills") but largely restates rather than develops them before moving to his own prepared material on NEET rates and vocational education. You can point at what was engaged, which puts it in the partial band, but the engagement is echo rather than argument, so it sits below 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we heard a speech that was kind of full of nothing" — Rachel Boyack

acuity.statement: Look, all I have heard from that side of the House this afternoon is negative, negative, negative, no, no, no, and literally no plan, no solutions, and no action.
acuity.explanation: Wedd names the preceding Opposition speeches as a target but engages none of their content: Halbert's NEET figure, the claimed rise of more than 6,000 in a year, the polytechnic job losses and the apprenticeship decline all go unanswered, as does Boyack's Nelson Hospital and Alpine Fault argument. She then pivots to prepared material on school phonics, maths textbooks and NCEA reform — tertiary and vocational education, which was Halbert's subject, is not touched. There is a gesture at the debate, so 0.2 rather than 0.1, but the speech would be essentially unchanged whatever the previous speakers had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There are 93,000 young people not engaged in education, training, and employment" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: This morning, I attended the launch of the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation Report and I thought they offered a really useful way forward for all of us in this beautiful country of ours.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows a substantive turn by MacLeod in the same debate on the Prime Minister's statement, so she is eligible. Her speech engages no part of his argument — not the RMA reform claim, not the economy-first framing, not the energy announcement — and instead delivers prepared material built around the Salvation Army report. It is on the matter under debate (the state of the nation as framed by the Prime Minister's statement) and she gestures at the debate itself in general terms ('the system sets us up to just keep firing shots across the aisle at each other'), which lifts it just above the floor, but the speech would be word-for-word the same whatever MacLeod had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David MacLeod spoke about Resource Management Act reform reducing consents by 46 percent, the economy building 'the coffers', and the LNG announcement for New Plymouth, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I wanted to take this opportunity to focus on the Auckland part of the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament and the progress that is being made with our largest city and the country’s commercial capital.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive turn with a specific, checkable claim and an explicit cross-party invitation — material squarely available to answer, accept in part, or rebut. He engages none of it: no reference to hardship grants, to the material-hardship figures, or to the collaboration proposal. The speech is a prepared recitation of Auckland projects, on the right subject (the Prime Minister's statement) but indifferent to what preceded it, with not even a gesture at the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued that food hardship grants have been left at the same nominal level since 2008 and invited the House to agree one simple non-legislative change to alleviate child material hardship; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I recall very vividly campaigning in 2023 and the excellent, awesome tagline of the National Party was “Back on Track”.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows a substantive turn by another member in the same debate, so she is eligible. Nothing in her speech depends on what Brewer said — she opens with her own campaign recollection and proceeds through prepared 'fixing the basics' material on crime, inflation, exports and a new school. The test fails cleanly: substitute a different argument on the same topic into Brewer's slot and this speech would not change a word. Scored low for unresponsiveness only; the quality and accuracy of her claims are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer argued the East West Link was cancelled by Labour in 2017 but National will deliver it, and set out Auckland transport and water progress; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: They’re screaming and they’re laughing on the other side, but instead of holding themselves accountable for how bad the situation became, they’re just screaming things out. I don’t even know what they’re saying, because it doesn’t make sense.
acuity.explanation: Two specific counters were put to her crime-is-falling claim — meth use and assaults on children — and she takes up neither, instead characterising the interjectors as screaming and expressly declining to make sense of them. She notices that she was interrupted but engages no part of the content, which is the band below a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "How about assaults on children?" (and Reuben Davidson: "How about meth use?")

acuity.statement: That was an interesting revision of reality, wasn’t it? Today, we had a report come out from the Salvation Army, and they’re a pretty trustworthy bunch, the Salvation Army.
acuity.explanation: A dismissive label for the preceding speech ("revision of reality") followed by an immediate pivot to her own prepared material on the Salvation Army report. None of Nakhle's figures on violent crime, youth offending or ram raids is taken up or contested, so this is a mere reference rather than engagement — on the subject of the debate, indifferent to what it followed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "By banning gang patches, violent crime has gone down by 38,000; youth offending down by 16 percent."

acuity.statement: He was there, but the flight schedules allow you to be in more places than one. He didn’t disassemble Air New Zealand to that extent.
acuity.explanation: Meager's interjection made a factual claim about where the Prime Minister was in 2025, and the reply engages that claim directly — conceding the location while arguing it is compatible with his point, since one can fly between places. The words would be meaningless had Meager said anything else, which is the test for high responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "He was in Akaroa; he was in Christchurch. He was in your electorate."

acuity.statement: But it’s time for some good numbers, and I’m pleased that the member from the other side asked what our answers are, what our solutions are. The best number for New Zealanders today is 269, because it’s the number of days until 7 November when we’ll have an election and when New Zealanders can vote this awful, awful Government out. They can vote for a future that’s made in New Zealand. They can vote for a political party and a Government that will bring in the future fund so that we can invest in some of our best and brightest New Zealand innovation.
acuity.explanation: He takes the interjected question up explicitly and then supplies content against it — the future fund, a tax shift and free GP visits. Marked below the top because the answer first detours into the days-to-the-election line before naming any policy, so engagement is real but partly spent on a rhetorical pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Sam Uffindell: "What are your solutions?"

acuity.statement: We have heard a lot of rubbish from the other side. When we took office two years ago, we inherited a country that felt like it was in a terminal downward spiral.
acuity.explanation: A one-line dismissal of the preceding two speeches followed by prepared inherited-mess material. Neither White's claim that inflation has hit beneficiaries harder than the wealthy nor Davidson's unemployment percentages is addressed; the passage would read identically whatever the opposition had argued, with the gesture at the debate placing it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "we have record—record—levels of unemployment in this country" (and Reuben Davidson's unemployment figures)

acuity.statement: January’s severe weather event has been spoken about by a number of members across the course of this debate, but I would like to add my voice too, in acknowledging the passing of Tekanimaeu Arobati, who was swept away in the Mahurangi River in Warkworth, and the community has rallied around his whānau.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: a substantive turn by Greg Fleming immediately precedes. She acknowledges only that the weather event 'has been spoken about by a number of members' — a generic gesture at the debate rather than engagement with any claim or argument made in it. Nothing in the speech that follows (community radio, the Regional Infrastructure Fund, flood walls and wharfs) would change by a word if Fleming had said something entirely different, so this sits in the unresponsive band, lifted slightly above the floor by the explicit nod to the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Greg Fleming spoke about mental health funding in Maungakiekie, the drop in Onehunga property crime, school attendance and the Nelson Tenths settlement, and this statement does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: The Opposition today were talking about the future fund. Well, we already announced that about six months before they did.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: substantive turns by Fleming and Marcroft precede. The speech is prepared material squarely on the subject under debate — the Prime Minister's statement, fast track, the RMA replacement, primary industries — and it gestures at the debate twice ('We’re now hearing the Opposition already shouting at me', and this future-fund line). But the gesture engages no argument: it reports that the Opposition mentioned a policy and claims priority of announcement rather than taking up any reasoning. Substituting a different Opposition argument on the same topic would leave this speech word-for-word unchanged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the future fund' — attributed by Arbuckle to unnamed Opposition speakers earlier in the debate; no preceding turn in this window (Greg Fleming, Jenny Marcroft) raised it

acuity.statement: It’s not the wool sector, Mark Patterson, but it is, indeed, New Zealand’s horticulture (hort) sector.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Arbuckle's turn immediately precedes and makes claims about the primary sectors. Grigg takes up one strand of it — Arbuckle's wool and horticulture list — and does something with it, picking horticulture over wool as the fastest-growing sector and then supplying the SOPI export figures ($8.8 billion, 25 percent above forecast) that Arbuckle asserted only loosely as a 'boom'. That is partial engagement and pointable, but the strand is taken up in an aside before she returns to a prepared ministerial speech on horticulture and trade, so it sits at the middle of the scale rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'We’ve got wool—for once, wool’s coming back. We’ve got dairy doing really well. We’ve got horticulture, kiwifruit—they are on a boom.' — Jamie Arbuckle

acuity.statement: And they are deeply, deeply unhappy with this National-led coalition because at every turn, food, electricity, housing, rates, insurance, almost every item in the household budget has become more expensive under National, even though they promised to fix it.
acuity.explanation: Grigg's turn was a defence of the new RMA/planning system and the economic benefits it would deliver. Twyford takes up none of that argument — no reply on the RMA, the select committee process, or the investment-to-jobs chain. What he does is gesture at the broad claim Grigg ended on, that the Government is delivering benefits for New Zealanders, by asserting the opposite on household costs, then moves into prepared material on health staffing. The speech would be essentially unchanged had Grigg argued something else on the same topic, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than in the partial-engagement band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Grigg: "we're doing the job because we see the benefits to New Zealand and New Zealanders" — and her argument that surety "drives investment, which is what drives business growth and therefore job growth".

acuity.statement: It’s pretty simple: having the LNG facility—listen up, listen up—means lower energy costs for New Zealanders.
acuity.explanation: The substantive turn immediately preceding Bates was Twyford's, built on named evidence — the Troy Stewart case, the 70 percent below-safe-staffing figure, the Farley-Naiker email, the 65,000 NZ Health Survey number. Bates engages none of it: no reply on staffing, nursing graduates or the health system at all. His opening answers a 'scaremongering' charge that does not appear in the turns he follows, and the rest is prepared material on LNG, a hypothetical capital gains tax and the Whanganui events fund. Energy prices brush the cost-of-living theme Twyford listed in passing, but that is a shared topic, not an engagement with his claim, so this stays at the bottom of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Phil Twyford spoke about unsafe staffing levels at Waitākere Hospital, unemployed nursing graduates and the cost of living, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We’re seeing a concerning shift in our foreign policy, but if you read the Prime Minister’s statement, you wouldn’t know it, and that’s a concern in itself.
acuity.explanation: Walters follows a substantive turn by Costley on cost of living, education and crime, and engages none of it — she opens a prepared case on foreign policy instead. The speech is anchored to the document under debate (she quotes the foreign affairs section of the Prime Minister's statement), so it is on the matter before the House rather than wholly unresponsive, but it would be word-for-word identical whatever Costley had said. That places it in the prepared-material-on-the-right-subject band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley spoke about mortgage savings, Investment Boost, literacy results, school property funding and crime reduction in the Kāpiti/Ōtaki area, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: When it comes to the example that Helen White has asked for, in terms of there being anything within this section 6 change that would help people who might be vulnerable as contractors, I can absolutely assure you that there is. There was one area in particular that I was quite keen on making as an addition, which is that in order to meet the gateway test, the contract has to be written down.
acuity.explanation: Takes up White's specific question about protection for vulnerable workers under the section 6 change and supplies a concrete feature of the bill (the written-contract requirement) as the answer, then goes on to address what happens to the existing test if the gateway criteria are not met. Not full marks because the three specific tests White named — independence, integration, and the chance to make a profit — are only answered obliquely via the section 6 fallback.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "I want to know: how is it that this law will protect such people?"

acuity.statement: I did hear the Minister talk about the gateway test, and she did say, “Well, if it’s not written down, then they can’t use the gateway test.” I guess it’s a start of a number of questions that I have as well. Not just having it written down, what are the other criteria?
acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's just-given answer, accepts it as a partial point ("it's a start"), and presses the obvious next step by asking what the remaining criteria and safeguards are. The passage could not have been delivered unchanged had the Minister answered differently, which is the mark of genuine engagement; it sits short of 1.0 because it extends the question rather than contesting the reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "in order to meet the gateway test, the contract has to be written down"

acuity.statement: I’m asked further about what other parts of the gateway test uphold rights for workers, and I’m very happy to oblige because there are a number of them within here which I think are of benefit to a worker in that arrangement—especially the fact that there is the availability criterion, which essentially says that if a person is in this arrangement with this business, they cannot meet the gateway test if they’re being told as a worker they cannot work for any other person.
acuity.explanation: Directly supplies the information Tuiono asked for, naming the availability criterion and then the termination criterion and explaining how each bears on worker rights. The answer is shaped entirely by the question put to it. Held below 1.0 only because the turn leaves Tuiono's second question — whether she would accept his tabled amendment — untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Teanau Tuiono: "Not just having it written down, what are the other criteria?"

acuity.statement: Those of us who’ve worked in this industry know, and I actually think probably most New Zealanders would know this, that very few people ever actually go through and read that document, especially young people going into their first jobs. It’s really unusual for people to take the time to read the document. One of the concerns I have is that while there is a gateway test and we’re changing the rules in the law to say that it needs to be agreed between the two parties, there will be many people, especially young people, who will sign a document and not know what they are signing.
acuity.explanation: Attacks the load-bearing part of the Minister's answer — that putting the arrangement in writing protects a vulnerable worker — by arguing that signing is not the same as reading or understanding, and then proposes remedies (cooling-off period, independent advice) aimed at that gap. The argument depends on what the Minister had just claimed, rather than merely sharing its topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "in order to meet the gateway test, the contract has to be written down"

acuity.statement: The bill clarifies that the authority and the court can make 100 percent reductions because case law has put an effective 50 percent cap on remedy reductions. As a result, the average reductions were around 40 percent in 2013 and they decreased to around 22 percent in 2023, and I don’t believe that that is a great trend for levels of contributory employee behaviour.
acuity.explanation: She names the strand Belich (and Xu-Nan) raised and does something with it: explains why the clarification is needed — case law has imposed an effective 50 percent cap — and supplies the trend figures (40 percent in 2013 to 22 percent in 2023) as the reason for acting. The passage would have to change if the preceding turn had made a different argument, so this is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference. It falls short of 1.0 because it answers only one of Belich's strands: her two tabled amendments ('significant and blameworthy', and employer-initiated conduct) and her direct question on discrimination grievances are not taken up in this answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "and so because of that, the reduction was made down to 100 percent" — Belich argued the 100 percent reduction point is already covered by existing case law and asked the Minister to clarify it.

acuity.statement: She raises the idea of giving some time before the document is signed, and I just wanted to point out to the member and other members, and members of the public listening, that one of the parts of the gateway test allows for that very idea. The criteria already requires the employer to provide a reasonable opportunity for this person to seek advice. That’s already been something that we’ve thought about. I thank her for the amendment, but I won’t be accepting it because that’s already part of the thinking of the gateway test.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific amendment Boyack had just foreshadowed, restates its content accurately, points to the gateway-test criterion she says already covers it, and states and justifies a refusal. The reply would have had to be entirely different had Boyack foreshadowed a different amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "particularly around having a cooling-off period and actually ensuring that people have sought independent advice and have been offered that by their employer before such time as they actually sign an agreement"

acuity.statement: But each arrangement will be assessed on a case by case basis, and so it will really depend on what the parties have agreed and whether they can meet the gateway test criteria or not—or the section 6 test. But there are actually many examples currently where workers do similar things but have different arrangements—for example, having an in-house IT worker versus having a contractor that provides extra IT support.
acuity.explanation: Engages Boyack's consistency objection on its own terms — concedes that status will vary arrangement by arrangement, names the tests that decide it, and offers a current-law parallel (in-house versus contracted IT) to argue such variation is not new. Not quite 1.0 because it answers the general objection rather than the specific fast-food scenarios posed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "We’re going to end up with inconsistent employment relationship applications within the same job and industry depending on which employer is in operation"

acuity.statement: I wanted to know whether the Minister has considered collective bargaining for this group of what I consider are particularly vulnerable workers, and whether you would consider it if I were to put an amendment on the Table.
acuity.explanation: Resumes her own prepared anecdote and puts a fresh question about collective bargaining without engaging the Minister's just-delivered answer. It is squarely on the matter under debate and is addressed to the Minister, which lifts it off the floor of the band, but the content of the preceding reply leaves no mark on it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just said "the goal here is to give businesses flexibility to choose the business model that does work for them" and had answered on retirement savings and tax advice, and this statement does not take any of that up

acuity.statement: I just wanted to move to clauses 6 and 7, under Subpart 2. I’m sure that there are going to be plenty of questions on clause 6 from other people, but I particularly wanted to home in on the language in new section 123B in clause 6, around the prevention of the courts, effectively, when it comes to remedies—which are reinstatement or compensation, basically—to determine whether an employee contributed to the situation that gave rise to the personal grievance and whether those actions amount to serious misconduct.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on a different subpart of the same bill. He gestures at the debate around him ("plenty of questions on clause 6 from other people") but nothing in the Minister's preceding answer is engaged, and the contribution would read identically whatever she had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden had just answered on redacted international-obligations analysis in the RIS and on what happens when the relationship changes under the gateway test, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: For example, Mr Menéndez March talked about health and safety, but there are many others—and I could come back to this in a future contribution, if necessary. One of which, as was pointed out in the Harris v The Warehouse case—which was a case of public interest—is serious defections in the procedure.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the strand of his argument — that factors beyond the employee's conduct bear on whether contributing behaviour amounts to serious misconduct — accepts it and extends it with a further factor, procedural defects, drawn from a decided case. Partial rather than full engagement: she characterises his point loosely as "health and safety" and the bulk of the speech is her own prepared account of Harris v The Warehouse.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "I wondered whether the Minister has considered the factor of psychosocial harm in the workplace when she was putting this bit in the bill"

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich was also asking if can there be contributory behaviour for discrimination and harassment personal grievances. I do, in good faith, believe this is a genuine concern. Look, I’m advised that there have been no cases of contributory behaviour being established in sexual harassment, racial harassment, or discrimination personal grievance cases in the last 10 years, which is as far back as my officials were to look through all the cases.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific concern about discrimination and harassment grievances by name, concedes it is a genuine concern, and supplies the case-law evidence it asked for (no contributory-behaviour findings in those grounds over 10 years). The reply would have been different had Belich raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they’re suddenly going to have sexual harassment, sexual discrimination, and race discrimination claims brought against them" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: Did you get any advice about the chilling effect that this might have economically, because this does not seem like flexibility? What we want with modern, productive employment relationships is something called portability, where people move and they are actually able to do so.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's just-made rationale — that removing these rights improves fit and mobility — by contesting it with a chilling-effect/portability counter-argument, but then moves on to a prepared sequence of separate questions (restraints of trade, good faith, precedent value) that do not take up anything van Velden said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it also helps for people who are coming up through the career ladder to have a go at a higher income role within that company" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: What I would like to ask the Minister is: what evidence supports the claim that underpins Subpart 4, that removing the 30-day rule improves genuine freedom of association rather than just undermining one of the two core principles of the Employment Relations Act, and that is to promote collective bargaining?
acuity.explanation: Twyford follows a substantive ministerial answer on the remuneration threshold but opens a new subpart with prepared explanatory material on the 30-day rule. He gestures at the preceding discussion ("the demolition of the personal grievance system", "the contractor changes that we've been discussing") in his cumulative-impact question, but engages none of the Minister's actual claims — nothing she said would have changed this speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Look, this threshold doesn’t remove access to all personal grievances." — Brooke van Velden, whose immediately preceding turn answered questions on the high-income remuneration threshold and personal grievances.

acuity.statement: I don’t believe that this change will impact on collective bargaining or disincentivise employees from joining a union. Ultimately, the decision made and taken by Cabinet on this provision is to uphold Cabinet’s original intention of reintroducing the 90-day trials.
acuity.explanation: She names Twyford and takes up one strand of his question — whether the repeal undermines collective bargaining — and supplies the actual rationale (the 90-day trial omission). But she supplies no evidence as asked, and leaves his second question, on MBIE advice about cumulative impact, untouched. Partial engagement that is clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what evidence supports the claim that underpins Subpart 4, that removing the 30-day rule improves genuine freedom of association rather than just undermining one of the two core principles of the Employment Relations Act" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister: is that genuinely the main reason for this change? If so, why is there not a change to allow 90-day trials to be agreed as part of the 30-day rule, as opposed to just getting rid of that rule entirely?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific reason the Minister had just given seconds earlier, tests whether it is the real reason, and draws out its consequence by proposing the narrower remedy it would imply. This speech could not have been written before hearing van Velden's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the decision made and taken by Cabinet on this provision is to uphold Cabinet’s original intention of reintroducing the 90-day trials" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: I can answer this one quite straightforward. Ultimately, this is not an attack on trade unions; this is about allowing the flexibility for businesses up and down New Zealand to be able to use the 90-day trial provision.
acuity.explanation: Answers Belich's question squarely in the negative, and the explanation that follows addresses her proposed alternative directly — that under the 30-day rule an individual agreement must mirror the collective terms, so a 90-day trial cannot simply be agreed within it. Engages both the question and the alternative put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is a genuine question to the Minister: is this an attack on trade unions in New Zealand?" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: To come back to the Amendment Paper 504, the question is: is the Government cancelling debts owed by a few large corporates to IRD?
acuity.explanation: Williams follows a substantive turn by Camilla Belich on the transitional provisions, the $200,000 remuneration threshold and the commencement-date drafting error. She takes up none of it, opening instead her own separate line of questioning on IRD debts. The speech would be identical whatever Belich had said, but it is squarely within the same committee-stage debate on the same Amendment Paper, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than the bottom.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich asked the Minister about the transitional provisions, the $200,000 personal-grievance threshold and the wrong commencement year, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: She hasn’t answered it—and if you know the answer, tell me the answer, because I haven’t heard it.
acuity.explanation: Suze Redmayne interjected that the question had already been answered. Belich takes that specific claim head-on, denies it, and puts the burden back on the interjector to supply the answer if it exists. The remark exists only because of what was just said and would be meaningless after any other preceding line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's been answered" — Suze Redmayne

acuity.statement: Firstly, to Arena Williams: will the gateway test affect employment rights pre-commencement—and she gave an example about debts owed by an employer to IRD. Look, it’s starting to become ad nauseam, but the bill does not impact tests applied pre-commencement.
acuity.explanation: The Minister names Williams's question, restates it accurately including the IRD example, and gives a direct answer on the pre-commencement point. But Williams's question was narrower than the one answered — she asked specifically about debts that have already crystallised under the Supreme Court decision and whether companies' booked liabilities are released, which the reply does not reach. Engages the strand, not the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm asking about the debts that are owed now, have been tested in the court, and have been found to exist" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich has also asked how employees will be made aware of the threshold changes. Officials will develop and publish guidance to support both employers and employees in understanding their legislative changes and obligations. They do that on a range of different laws when they change. Camilla Belich has also asked for the references to the 2025 amendment Act to be updated to 2026. That’s a yes.
acuity.explanation: Takes up two specific things Belich asked in her preceding turns and does something with each: supplies the communication mechanism she asked about for employees caught by the new threshold, and accepts outright her correction of the wrong commencement year. The reply could not have been delivered after any other speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So what is the communication going to be for people in that position" and "I think that is a normal drafting thing that will be changed to 2026" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: In terms of these initial parts—and I’m speaking overall but this is in relation to Part 1 as well—the definitions around what the Public Service is to do in the objectives have changed and there’s been a little bit of moving around of the spirit of service to the community. It’s been deleted from some parts and added into other parts. The main thing, though, that came up in submissions around the purpose of the Act was the move away from active citizenship. I think that’s an interesting clause to get rid of, at this point in time. I wouldn’t mind a response from the Minister on the process to make those changes.
acuity.explanation: Belich takes up one strand of the Minister's opening — the changes he described to the Act's objects and purpose — and presses him on a specific deletion (active citizenship) and on the process behind it, which is a genuine engagement rather than prepared praise or condemnation. But she leaves untouched the bulk of what he actually argued (the defence of removing the reappointment provisions and of designating key positions), and the centre of her speech is her own prepared complaint about lack of bipartisan consultation, a subject he did not raise. Partial engagement, pointable, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The changes also, in our view, generated excessive prescription, which in some places duplicates other legislation and ends up distracting our agencies from their core mission." — James Meager, opening the Part 1 debate on the objects/purpose amendments

acuity.statement: In terms of consultation, I mean, Government has a legislative agenda and has to implement changes that it sees fit. Of course, that’s why we have the select committee process, so that every member of the Parliament, regardless of the party that they’re in, has the ability to sit on those select committees to input into the questions or the testing or the rigor of the legislation that’s put before them.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific complaint Belich made — that the Opposition was not consulted on the objects change and that such legislation should be attempted on a bipartisan basis — by naming the select committee as the mechanism through which members of any party had input. It would have to be written differently had she not made the consultation point, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because it answers the bipartisanship request with a general defence of process rather than engaging her claim that consultation here was 'constrained', a point she drew from the regulatory impact statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s a certain amount of disappointment from the Opposition on the fact that we weren’t consulted around specifically the objects change within the Public Service Act" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: Given this, we don’t think having a broad reference in the purpose statement acknowledges that choices of when and how to engage the public will depend on the context of what’s happening and what the Government—or the Parliament, in fact—needs to do on a particular occasion. We consider it’s a better approach to take a principles-based approach, and that your active citizenship principles are already provided by the principle of open government in section 12 and the value of responsiveness in section 16.
acuity.explanation: This takes the exact objection Belich raised — the removal of active citizenship from the purpose provision — concedes the part of it he accepts (that public participation is fundamental to democracy), and then disputes the rest by locating the substance she wants in two named surviving provisions, sections 12 and 16. Had she objected to a different clause, this passage could not have been delivered at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The main thing, though, that came up in submissions around the purpose of the Act was the move away from active citizenship." — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around mentioning active citizenship and receiving thousands of submissions. No, I was using that as an example of a way that you can be an active citizen, whether that is by voting in a general election or by making a submission to Parliament or by filling out a petition or by running for Parliament itself.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific insinuation — that 'active citizenship' was removed from the purpose section because of the submission volume on the treaty principles bill — denies it, and corrects her reading of why he had cited the submissions at all. The answer would be different if she had asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "is this change to the purpose of the Public Service Act that removes the phrase “active citizenship” because of the number of submissions that were made on the treaty principles bill?"

acuity.statement: Finally, is the rewording of long-termism a diminishment? No, it’s not. As I think I explained to Helen White before, there are many parts of the bill and, in fact, the Act, which refers to long-term views needing to be taken by chief executives in stewardship roles and, of course, the lengthy diatribe I went on about the benefits of long-termism, including in this House as well.
acuity.explanation: Brooking posed an explicit disjunction — diminishment, or merely replicated elsewhere in the amendment bill — and he picks the second branch and names where the long-term duty survives. Directly shaped by the question just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "is that removal of the long term in the purpose section a diminishment of the need to consider the long term, or is his argument that it’s simply been replicated through other provisions in the amendment bill?"

acuity.statement: I do have a slight rebuttal to the spirit of service point that the Minister was making, because it has been—the Minister, I’m sure, will agree—reworded in a way that is not as expansive as in the current Act. Although it does still include the spirit of service, it does not include it in such fulsome way as in the primary piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Meager's immediately preceding answer — his claim that spirit of service is preserved and heightened in the purpose section — and contests it on the ground of how expansively it is worded, before moving to her own prepared questions on the deputy commissioner and new section 11A.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "Spirit of service is included in the purpose of the Public Service"

acuity.statement: Just before I do touch on 11A, I was going to raise Camilla Belich’s question around the reduction of deputy public service commissioners from two to one. There’s a question about whether or not it limits the capability of the commission to deliver on functions and oversight—and it doesn’t. The purpose of a deputy commissioner is essentially to act in the place of the commissioner when they are unable to, and to carry out any delegated functions. It’s our view that you only need one deputy commissioner to do that, so that’s the reason behind that change.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question Belich asked — how he sees the deputy commissioner's role and why the reduction is necessary — by stating the role's function and drawing the inference that one post suffices for it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "to have some explanation as to how the Minister sees the role of the deputy commissioner and why this change is necessary within this particular bill"

acuity.statement: I think our view would be that when it comes to the operation of Cabinet and Ministers, that’s probably something that’s more appropriate, under our constitutional make up, to be governed by the Cabinet Manual and in internal political processes. Section 11A is not actually an entirely new section, much of it’s been shifted from existing sections, but it actually applies to the obligations on chief executives supporting Ministers and discharging their stewardship obligations.
acuity.explanation: Addresses Belich's question about how new section 11A interacts with ministerial responsibility, explains why ministerial duties are left to the Cabinet Manual rather than statute, and corrects her premise that 11A is a wholly new section.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "why are we putting this in, and how does this interact with ministerial responsibility?"

acuity.statement: I wondered about the issue about United Nations missions, multi-force groupings and organisations—for example, the UN peacekeepers—and to what extent that was a scope that had some discretion in it.
acuity.explanation: Meager had just answered her earlier peacekeeping question by pointing to clause 4's new definition of warlike conflict. She re-raises peacekeeping and UN missions without taking up the clause-4 answer he gave — on the matter under debate, but engaging no part of his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I think that quite fairly and squarely would capture those in a peacekeeping role."

acuity.statement: In terms of the inclusion of those who have served—and I use that term deliberately very broadly and openly—it’s quite explicitly our aim with this legislation to take it from the relatively narrow, confined, even constrained circumstances that are currently reflected in the wording of the bill, to a place that actually can be much more inclusive, as we stand here in this war memorial that doubles as a debating chamber for our House of Representatives.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of White's question — the breadth and flexibility of who is covered — and answers it at the level of intent, but does not engage her specific questions about multi-force groupings or the certainty of the 'warlike conflicts' definition before moving to prepared material on Anzac Day and the amendment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "to what extent that was a scope that had some discretion in it"

acuity.statement: So a quick question: I’m just quite interested in whether the Minister has some more examples that he could use to further advance what the select committee has put in their commentary.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specificity-versus-breadth strand Penk had just raised by pressing for concrete examples of warlike conflict, but frames the question off the select committee commentary rather than off anything Penk actually argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "There’s a bit of a tension between wanting to be as specific as possible and, of course, not losing the intent"

acuity.statement: Deliberately, again, to be as broad as possible, I see in front of me the New Zealand Wars, I see Afghanistan, I see Timor-Leste, I see Vietnam.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing just asked for — a list of further examples of warlike conflicts — and confirms the peacekeeping case she raised. The answer would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "whether the Minister has some more examples that he could use to further advance what the select committee has put in their commentary"

acuity.statement: Now, I think of people you mentioned: Keith Park. Now, of course, he would be—if you just said it was purely New Zealand and it wasn’t in the colours of any other nation, and my amendment simply says, “including through service with other nations”. So Keith Park served in the Second World War with the Royal Air Force (RAF), not with the Royal New Zealand Air Force (RNZAF)—in fact, we barely had an RNZAF at that particular point in time—but he served with the RAF.
acuity.explanation: Takes the very example Penk used to argue the amendment is unnecessary and turns it back as the reason the amendment is needed, disputing the Minister's reading of the drafting. Directly built on the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "I would respectfully say I don’t consider that amendment to be necessary" (and his Sir Keith Park example)

acuity.statement: Again, I acknowledge the intent of the member’s amendment. I’m very happy to clarify, in the clearest terms that I can manage, that it is every intent of the legislation, and I think tolerably clear in its construction as well—that is to say, its specific wording—that in serving New Zealand we include the likes of Sir Keith Park.
acuity.explanation: Gives precisely the on-the-record assurance Foster asked for, on Foster's own Keith Park example, and addresses his claim that the wording is interpretable two ways.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "At the very least, Mr Minister, I would really like to hear from you that those people are explicitly included."

acuity.statement: I think it’s important that we are remembering those that served—and there is a difference between those that served in the Royal New Zealand Air Force who were posted overseas through the Commonwealth training scheme and served in Royal Air Force units, but serving New Zealand, compared to those that maybe had moved to the UK some years earlier and were actually fighting for their new country, just as people now move to New Zealand and serve New Zealand even though they were born in another country.
acuity.explanation: Rebuts the amendment's premise directly, drawing the distinction Foster's wording would blur and answering his First World War navy example with the 1941 Royal New Zealand Navy case. Disagreement built on the specific argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "my amendment simply says, “including through service with other nations”"

acuity.statement: In previous debates in the House on this bill, there’s been unanimous support, and we have really spoken in quite broad terms. It’s quite interesting, with this amendment, that it has, probably, raised some issues that, perhaps, we hadn’t thought of.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the amendment debate he has just heard but engages none of Costley's argument, instead opening a fresh line about what practical difference the bill will make.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tim Costley argued the amendment should be rejected because service under RAF units through the Commonwealth training scheme is already service to New Zealand, and this statement does not take up any part of that reasoning.

acuity.statement: In terms of those who have served—for example, as recognised in what sounds like a wonderful gesture and tribute by the Tawa RSA, and I know that others engage in similar remembrance—it seems to me that there will be nothing tangible that is different on any given ceremony on 25 April this year or any other.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question squarely in the negative, uses O'Connor's own Tawa RSA example, and takes up his point that the bill carries no entitlements.
