acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor: "Will it make any difference to this Anzac Day or subsequent Anzac Days?"

acuity.statement: My question for you, Minister, is: while you’ve alluded to the scope of who will be acknowledged in terms of non-military service, will this recognition be retrospective, and, if so, how far back will it go?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's symbolism answer and his statement of scope and pushes them further, but the retrospectivity and execution questions are new ground rather than engagement with the substance of what he argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "The importance is really, I suppose, symbolic."

acuity.statement: Actually, for the member, it will be up to every community to continue to celebrate Anzac Day in a way that is appropriate for them—of course, celebrating that broader sense of marking or commemorating, not celebrating in a jingoistic way of suggesting there’s anything to glorify or honour the fact of war, except of course that it’s an unfortunate reality of human existence so far.
acuity.explanation: Answers the delivery/ceremony strand of her question directly, but leaves the retrospectivity question she put first untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel: "How will the execution, the delivery, of these acknowledgements be practically managed, and how will, for example, RSAs be a part of that process?"

acuity.statement: The Minister has previously articulated the ability for communities to commemorate Anzac Day in a way that is fit for the community, and also, this bill doesn’t really preclude that. I guess my first question for the Minister is: if it doesn’t preclude that and communities are still able to do it in a way that is most appropriate to them, what is the purpose that, then, the updated legislation would serve?
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's immediately preceding position accurately and draws out its consequence as a challenge — if communities are already free to commemorate as they wish, what does the amendment do? The question could not exist without the previous turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "it will be up to every community to continue to celebrate Anzac Day in a way that is appropriate for them"

acuity.statement: However, there is another area that opens up, and that is where people immigrate to New Zealand who may have served in overseas forces. I’m just giving an example of Afghanistan, of people who have come here, who were translators, who very much worked with the New Zealand forces, and, under this, will be entitled to be recognised on Anzac Day.
acuity.explanation: Extends the earlier Foster/Costley exchange about service under another nation's colours to its mirror case — foreign nationals who served alongside New Zealand forces — but takes up nothing of Xu-Nan's immediately preceding questions about purpose and entitlements.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "including through service with other nations" — and Tim Costley's reply on who New Zealanders serve alongside

acuity.statement: I’ll have a crack, as the member suggests. I think if you were reading what will hopefully soon be the new Act and you see that it says, “In commemoration of the contribution of all those who have served New Zealand in time of war and in warlike conflicts”—I think the purpose behind this provision is just to enable us to recognise the wide and varied and many different types of service that people have given over many years to New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the invitation and the specific interpretive problem O'Connor posed about New Zealanders born elsewhere, walking through the operative wording to answer it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor: "it would be useful to have some sort of clarity as to how those matters may be treated"

acuity.statement: That “served New Zealand” piece was critical to the importance of this Act but actually was specifically left more broad than might otherwise be the case with legislation to allow for that sort of flexibility that Mr O’Connor raised, where people may indeed have been born in another country and have been supporting New Zealand’s efforts whilst citizens still of that other country but have now ended up here in New Zealand. In that instance, interpreters, for example, absolutely would be covered under that service to New Zealand in times of war and warlike conflicts.
acuity.explanation: Answers O'Connor's translator example by name and explains the select committee's drafting choice as the reason it is covered, also picking up the earlier 'what tangible difference' question. Slightly reduced because it is framed as reiterating select committee points.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor: "of people who have come here, who were translators, who very much worked with the New Zealand forces"

acuity.statement: A question for the Minister, and he may like to consult his officials: where did Police sit on this, given that the police have served in all the modern conflict zones?
acuity.explanation: Tests the breadth claim just made with a concrete case — deployed police — which is a live probe of the preceding assertion, though it does not engage van de Molen's reasoning about the drafting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim van de Molen: "those in uniform or outside uniform but who have supported our military efforts are indeed acknowledged through this"

acuity.statement: Yes, that’s why it doesn’t say New Zealand Defence Force.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question just asked and gives the textual reason in one line; the reply is unintelligible except as a response to that specific question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg O'Connor: "where did Police sit on this, given that the police have served in all the modern conflict zones?"

acuity.statement: How can he claim that he is supporting the front line when the Police Association reported in February that almost 60 percent of police officers had considered leaving due to insufficient pay and staffing shortages?
acuity.explanation: Takes the precise claim Goldsmith had just made — that his Government backs and supports the front line — and puts contrary evidence directly against it (a Police Association figure on officers considering resignation over pay and staffing). The question would have to be reworded if the preceding answer had asserted something else, which is the test for high responsiveness. Scored on engagement only: whether the 60 percent figure is accurate is a veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: "those police are supported by a Government that backs the police to do their job and to restore law and order in this country"

acuity.statement: Does he agree with Karpowership, a company that participated in the Government’s own LNG process, that it would place upward pressure on gas prices, thereby making prices more expensive for Kiwi families and businesses, and, if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the answer just given — the conclusion that LNG is the right option — by producing a participant in the Government's own LNG process who says it would push gas prices up. It does not take up the feasibility or firming-capacity reasoning Watts actually offered, and the price argument is a prepared line she has run through the set, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal of the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "none of those, with the exception of LNG, were deemed to be feasible nor to provide the sufficient firming capacity and scale required to meet dry-year needs. LNG is the right option."

acuity.statement: What, if any, mechanisms will be put in place to protect against large increases in the levy, given his Cabinet paper says the levy can be annually adjusted?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate (the LNG project and its cost to consumers) but indifferent to the answer it follows: Watts had just talked about Electricity Authority powers and penalties, and nothing in this question engages that. Substituting a different answer on the same topic would not change a word of it, which places it in the prepared-material band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts answered on beefing up the powers of the Electricity Authority and penalties for rule-breaking, and this question does not take that up — it opens a new strand on the levy

acuity.statement: Can I ask the Minister: is there a time that he might take some advice from the very person who shut down the critical energy infrastructure at Marsden Point?
acuity.explanation: Engages the topic of the exchange (whose advice the Minister should take on energy infrastructure) but no part of the argument just put. It is the pattern of answering a claim by attacking the standing of the person who made it, which is responsiveness to the speaker rather than to the content. Acuity is scored on engagement alone here; the jibe's tone and its accuracy about Marsden Point belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods asked whether the Minister had received advice or modelling on investing the $2.7 billion in alternatives such as solar and storage, and this question does not take up any part of that — it pivots to the questioner's own record

acuity.statement: Will the Minister be taking advice as to whether overseas investors who may participate in this LNG project could be fearful that their rights would be terminated, as was the case with the cancellation of the oil and gas industry?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the LNG item, so it is not wholly off-debate, but it opens an unrelated sovereign-risk line that is plainly prepared and would read identically whatever the Minister had just said. No part of the preceding answer is engaged, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band; a government-side member is held to the same test as an opposition one here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just declined to comment on a supposition about parties in the commercial negotiation, and this question does not take that refusal or its reasoning up

acuity.statement: Does he agree with the Police Association President, Steve Watt, who says, “You don’t solve this by spending millions trying to attract new people while the ones you already have are burning out and questioning whether they can stay.”; if not, why not?
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith had just rested his whole answer on money — $480 million and $226 million — as 'the most important thing we do'. Andersen takes that exact claim and puts an authority against it on precisely that point: spending to recruit while incumbents burn out. The question would have had to be different if he had argued something else, and it is pointable at his own words.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: “The most important thing we do is give them the support through extra budget: we’ve had more than $480 million over four years to support the front line in Budget 2025”

acuity.statement: Does the Minister envisage a time when the police front line will be used in moving out the mōnaroas, the criminals, the gangs, the layabouts, and the vagrants blighting Queen Street?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Goldsmith's preceding answer — the extra powers given to police to pursue gangs — and extends it to street disorder in Queen Street. It engages the topic and one thread rather than any specific claim, and the rest is the member's own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paul Goldsmith: “I also support the additional powers in legislation we’ve given the police to go after the gangs, who create misery in this country.”

acuity.statement: How does she justify allowing 15 multinational gambling companies to operate and advertise in Aotearoa when New Zealanders lost $2.79 billion to gambling in the last year alone, according to the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation report released yesterday?
acuity.explanation: Builds on the answer she had just been given — that the Minister cannot say which licensees will be local — by treating the 15 licensees as multinational and asking for a justification. That is a partial engagement: it carries one implication of the previous answer forward, but the harm figure and the Salvation Army citation are prepared material the answer did not prompt.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: “I can’t know that for sure, because the licence and the auction has not occurred.”

acuity.statement: Does the Minister intend to take a race-based approach to online casino gambling, as the original question suggests?
acuity.explanation: Aims directly at the premise of the preceding member's questions — the distinction between companies based in Aotearoa and multinational operators — and names it as the thing being responded to. Whether that is a fair reading of Kaipara's question is a matter of reasoning, not responsiveness; the engagement itself is specific and pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: “How many of the proposed 15 online casino licences will be issued to companies based here in Aotearoa?”

acuity.statement: Was the Government warned, when it chose to scrap the three waters programme, that further delaying investment in water infrastructure would likely lead to disasters like the one in Moa Point in Wellington?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own diagnosis — systemic under-investment in water assets — and turns it back on the decision to scrap three waters, asking whether he was warned that delay would produce exactly this. It accepts the premise and disputes where responsibility lands, which is engagement with the content rather than a pivot.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: “It is fair to say that what we are seeing reflects systemic under-investment in water assets by local government.”

acuity.statement: What advice has the Minister received on the effect of successive Green-Labour councils prioritising spending on cycleways, arthouse public toilets, and utopian urban development designs instead of basic water infrastructure?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the Minister's earlier cycleway remark but does nothing with it — it restates the same claim as a question and invites the answer already given. Nothing in the preceding answer about council contracting arrangements is taken up, and the question would be identical whatever had just been said on this subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: “I have, however, read some commentary that certain councillors championed increases in cycleway spending, all while the council continued to under-invest in water.”

acuity.statement: Does the Minister plan on holding Veolia to account for their environmental destruction, and, if not, is it his view that Veolia are not responsible for the ecological disaster happening on the south coast?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's unnamed 'those responsible' and presses him to say whether the contractor is among them. That engages one strand of the preceding answer and forces a consequence from it, but it does not take up the substance of his point about prioritising essential services.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: “No, but what it is an example of is a failure by those responsible and those that have power to ensure that they prioritise spending on essential services”

acuity.statement: Does he accept that his own officials’ modelling shows that there are only two viable ways to fund this programme: either significantly higher transport taxes, or around $40 billion in additional debt; if so, which of those will he choose?
acuity.explanation: Bishop had argued in the abstract that roads must be paid for and that work on the funding blend continues. Utikere converts that into the concrete fork his own officials put to him and demands he pick one, supplying the figures the previous answer withheld. The question is shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: “We are doing further work at the moment around the right blend of funding options in order to deliver roads of national significance.”

acuity.statement: Has the Minister spoken to the Minister of Finance about adding $40 billion of net core Crown debt; if so, what was her response?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the $40 billion the Minister had just addressed, but does not engage his answer that the figure is a strawman and will not be pursued — it repeats the number in a new frame instead. Topic engaged, specific rebuttal not taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: “Likewise, borrowing $40 billion in order to fund the roads of national significance programme is also not realistic or economically responsible.”

acuity.statement: What announcements has the Minister made today about roads of national significance, like Transmission Gully?
acuity.explanation: A prepared invitation to announce, on the general subject under discussion but engaging no part of what preceded it. It would be word-for-word the same whatever the Minister had just said about debt, tolls or the Minister of Finance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just answered on his conversations with the Minister of Finance about transport funding, and this question does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Our Government was elected with an ambitious goal: to get New Zealand back on track. We’re seeing evidence of economic recovery, infrastructure investment, and better health and education outcomes. We’re on a roll, ladies and gentlemen.
acuity.explanation: A substantive turn by Ryan Hamilton immediately precedes this one, making concrete claims (the medical school, visitor numbers, the new BNZ Theatre) that were available to engage. Redmayne's speech is prepared constituency material that opens afresh on the Government's goals and then moves to Rangitīkei; it would be word-for-word identical whatever Hamilton had said. The only overlap is the recycled party slogan 'fixing the basics and building the future', which repeats his words rather than engaging their content. Not 0.0 because it is at least continuing the same general debate on the Government's record, i.e. the matter under discussion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ryan Hamilton spoke about Homegrown and Balloons Over Waikato coming to Hamilton, the Waikato medical school training 120 GPs a year from 2028, and the Chiefs, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: We’ve heard the Prime Minister say he’s serious about building the future. We’ve heard this over and over again, and it’s clear that the future he is building is for the privileged few and his big-dog corporate mates, who keep lining their greedy pockets with hard-working Kiwis’ money.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Simeon Brown arguing that the Opposition is a "Coalition of Taxation" and that the Government is "fixing the basics and building the future". Carter takes up only the slogan — inverting "serious about building the future" — and engages none of the content: not the capital gains tax charge, not the claim Labour voted against tax reductions, not the claimed improvements in safety or health. Everything after the opening is prepared material on Christchurch that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Brown had said. A gesture at the debate's framing, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’re focused on fixing the basics and building the future" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I rise in support of the Prime Minister’s statement to begin this, the election year of 2026, a year of fixing the basics and building the future. Indeed, it’s been a term of that, and I look forward to explaining to the House just how well we’re going in the various parts of the economy that we are restoring, along with law and order, and providing those health and education services so well for this country.
acuity.explanation: Penk follows a detailed, specific critique from Kahurangi Carter: almost a billion dollars of Christchurch transport funding cancelled, school lunch cuts, child safety organisations defunded with a claimed 44 percent rise in violence against children. He takes up none of it — not one figure contested, not one claim conceded or rebutted. The speech is on the right subject (the Prime Minister's statement) but is wholly prepared: a construction-sector progress report that would read identically had the preceding speaker argued the opposite, or said nothing at all. No gesture at the preceding turn at all, so the bottom of the on-topic band rather than 0.3.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kahurangi Carter argued that "His Government cut almost a billion dollars in planned transport funding for Christchurch" and that funding cuts to child safety care organisations preceded a 44 percent rise in violence against children, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: It’s also important to note in this bill, particularly in clause 4, another aspect that has been added to it, which includes the death outside of war or warlike conflict. In addition to commemorating the people who have served and died in a war and warlike conflict, it is important that the bill includes those who have died in or are connected with the New Zealand military service—for example, during military training as well. Of course, like the previous speaker, Rachel Boyack, has mentioned, it is important for us to make a special reference to Australian troops at Gallipoli as a part of this.
acuity.explanation: Boyack's turn immediately precedes and made two substantive points: that the bill extends commemoration to deaths connected with military service such as training, and that the Gallipoli clause should specifically name Australian and other Allied troops. Xu-Nan takes up both strands explicitly, naming her and endorsing the Gallipoli point, and locates the training provision in clause 4. But he does no more than restate and agree — he neither disputes, extends nor adds a figure or consequence to her argument, and the bulk of the turn is prepared material on the bill and the committee stage that would read identically whatever she had said. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-scale rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "it’s important that we specifically acknowledge the role of our Australian brothers and sisters who are very much part of the Anzac Day community for us" (and her quotation of the select committee on deaths "during military training")

acuity.statement: It’s good to see the National Party MPs choosing to conclude all of their contributions to the Prime Minister’s statement in a very similar way that the Prime Minister started it, isn’t it, this afternoon: a bit lacklustre, a bit boring, and a bit short.
acuity.explanation: McLellan follows Glen Bennett in the same Prime Minister's statement debate, so the turn is eligible. She gestures at the debate by characterising the other side's contributions as lacklustre and short, but that is a mere reference to the fact of their speeches rather than engagement with any claim in them, and nothing in what follows turns on what Bennett (or the preceding National speakers) actually argued. The speech is on the matter under debate but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Glen Bennett spoke about LNG economics 20 years ago, the seabed mining ruling and a 200 percent rise in homelessness in Taranaki, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I don’t hear that side at all, and I commend the Prime Minister’s statement in the House today.
acuity.explanation: Bidois speaks immediately after McLellan's detailed critique of the Government's economic record and explicitly dismisses the other side without engaging a single claim — no response on unemployment, emigration or the absence of a plan. The remark would be word-for-word identical whatever McLellan had said, and the surrounding material (praising colleagues present, looking forward to the campaign) is prepared content on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued that unemployment is rising, that businesses are going under and that there is no credible long-term plan or strategy to ease the cost of living; this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I think it’s very important that we lay out clearly the key focus of this bill, which is around the small- and low-risk small businesses in New Zealand that are not quite sure of the risks they should focus on and balance with the high cost associated with identifying the risks that they’re confused about, and trying to do something so they can satisfy the very rigorous and overrated red-tape legislation.
acuity.explanation: Lu follows Helen White in the first reading of the same bill, so the turn is eligible. She restates the bill's rationale about small, low-risk businesses and red tape without touching White's concrete argument that deaths followed from employer practice and that worker involvement fixed it — she neither disputes the Ports of Auckland or Salters examples nor explains how the bill handles them. On the matter under debate, but engaging no part of the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued that worker participation at the Ports of Auckland ended fatalities, that people died under the previous shift system, and that the man who died at Salters was 24 and a victim of a 'she'll be right' attitude; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The ACT Party supports this bill, and I just want to reflect very briefly on why it’s important. I have close friends and family members who’ve served in conflicts that are not currently recognised under the current Anzac Day legislation, such as Timor, Bosnia, Bougainville, where they knew they were risking their lives to go into these places on so-called peacekeeping missions, and there were bullets and bombs going off all around them in some places, and they lived with the constant threat of army conflict breaking out between different parties.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive Green speech precedes it. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate (which conflicts the Act recognises) but engages no part of Xu-Nan's argument; it is prepared material that would read identically whoever had spoken before. Low Acuity only — this is not a judgement on its quality, which is high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan spoke about Anzac commemoration, Egypt and the need for post-service financial and mental-health support for veterans, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: What I think this bill is doing is, in a way—I think we’ve already heard that when we go down to the Anzac services, as so many of us do, and it is great to see, the numbers had dropped off for a while, but it’s great to see those numbers growing again. As we’ve heard so many of the speeches already say, younger people are coming, because people want to recognise those who have been and served and sacrificed for our community.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding speeches — the observed growth in young attendance — and builds his "legislation catching up with where New Zealanders are already at" point on it, then returns to extensive prepared material on Keith Park, Alfred Shout and his own family. Partial, pointable engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I see younger and younger people joining the march and joining the Anzac Day service, along with their family" — and Simon Court on servicepeople who "put themselves in harm's way", which Foster also takes up.

acuity.statement: I take the points from the previous speaker, Andy Foster, around the sort of symbolic nature of this bill, but there is power in language, right? I acknowledge the changes in the select committee that were made to focus on the language of commemoration as opposed to recognition.
acuity.explanation: Names Foster's symbolism argument, accepts it, and then does something with it — pushes it further into a claim about the force of the specific statutory wording (commemoration vs recognition). He also takes up Foster's withdrawn broadening amendment by name. The speech would plainly differ had Foster argued otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "because while it’s symbolic in many ways, it’s symbolism is very, very important"

acuity.statement: It’s a good way to end this parliamentary week with the finalising, hopefully, of the Anzac Day Amendment Bill. I just want to thank those members from the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee who spent a great deal of time on this bill, and agonising over the wording in it, so it’s fitting that we have got to this point.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — several substantive turns precede. Thanks the committee generically and moves to prepared personal recollection; nothing in the contribution turns on what Menéndez March, Foster or Court had just argued. On topic, unresponsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued the select committee's shift from "recognition" to "commemoration" and the acknowledgement of the living as well as the dead were substantive, not merely symbolic, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I take the point of my New Zealand First colleague, who talked about how we have some of those people who are our bravest people, they are our most famous and bravest soldiers, and they have no recognition until now of this kind. So I think that that virtue in our society is something that we also need to concentrate on at this moment, because we have a world that seems to think that one way to go is really just bullying; it’s really just “might is right”.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Foster's specific Apiata example and draws a further consequence from it about which virtues the country rewards. Engagement is real and pointable, but it is one strand inside an otherwise prepared contribution on peacekeeping and Colonel Mel Childs.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "Now, at the moment, in law, Anzac Day doesn’t recognise him. That’s an absurdity" — on Willie Apiata.

acuity.statement: But finally, the legislation is catching up to mention, to encompass, people—as Helen White just shared—like Colonel Mel Childs, who was in antenatal class with me, actually, so a little shout-out to Mel and Chucky and their family; well done. But that’s the point, these are real people that just chose to serve their country instead of doing something else, whether it was 1915 in Gallipoli or 2015 in Iraq.
acuity.explanation: Takes White's chosen example, supplies first-hand knowledge of the same person, and uses it to make a general point the preceding speech had only implied. It also engages Kirkpatrick by name on her image of the march. Had White told a different story, this passage would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "It’s a story of a woman who is Colonel Mel Childs." He also takes up Dana Kirkpatrick's "boots marching down the road".

acuity.statement: I don’t have the same connections or stories that the member for Ōtaki has. But I thank you for your contribution and reflecting on friends, on colleagues, on family members, and the ripple effect that situations—whether it be in combat or whether it be in peacekeeping—may have on the lives of our communities.
acuity.explanation: A courteous reference to the previous speaker's contribution that summarises its theme without engaging any claim in it, then pivots to prepared material on the Merchant Navy and the Waitara RSA. A gesture at the debate rather than an engagement with it, which puts it at the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "Every Anzac Day since that terrible day in 2011, I’ve remembered him. The law didn’t capture him."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Helen. Thank you for acknowledging Mel. Mel Ryder and I served in Afghanistan together.
acuity.explanation: Responds directly to the example White chose and supplies something only she could: personal service alongside that officer. Pointable and specific engagement, though the bulk of the speech is her own prepared reflection on her identity as a veteran and her Afghanistan deployment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Now, I want to just take one story that I have never shared before in this situation." — her account of Colonel Mel Childs in South Sudan.

acuity.statement: If fast track has driven an uptake in renewable energy, can he name one single renewable energy generation project that has been completed and brought to market under fast track?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact causal claim just made — that fast-track legislation drove the renewables increase — and tests it by demanding a completed project under that regime. The question could not have been asked in this form if the preceding answer had made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What drove renewable energy? Fast-track legislation, which he failed to support." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Can he name one single new electricity generation project that has been approved under fast track and is now producing electricity?
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific slippage in the previous answer — projects 'listed' in the programme rather than generating — by narrowing the test to approved projects now producing electricity. Directly shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We have about 40 percent extra generation of projects listed in our fast-track programme." — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Is the Turkish company who expressed interest in supplying New Zealand with an LNG import option wrong when they said that the Government’s plan to build an LNG import facility will put upwards pressure on New Zealand gas prices?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the price claim made in the preceding answer and confronts it with a contrary source, but introduces fresh material (the Turkish supplier) rather than engaging the $50 figure's basis, so it is a partial engagement with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this is going to deliver about $50 off Kiwis’ power bills—that’s about $1.2 billion worth to the economy" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: When Ministers in his Government say, “We can’t do anything about the impacts of weather”, is he suggesting that he is powerless to reduce emissions, strengthen resilience, and better prepare communities from climate-charged storms and floods?
acuity.explanation: Presses the point the previous answer sidestepped — whether the Minister's 'nothing we can do about the weather' line is being endorsed — rather than taking up the Greens-pitch characterisation itself, so it engages one strand of the exchange and otherwise continues a prepared line of questioning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if the Greens’ pitch is “Give them another chance and global weather will improve”, that’s just not true" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: The people who hold our economy together are not the shareholders, not the CEOs, certainly not the tobacco and fossil fuel CEOs that this Government cosies up to; it is the everyday people, who currently, under this Government, are struggling to make ends meet due to decisions made by the other lot that have resulted in an increased cost of living and diminishing rights for workers.
acuity.explanation: Menéndez March follows Ngarewa-Packer in the same debate on the same employment bill, but opens with prepared framing about shareholders, CEOs and the cost of living rather than engaging any strand of her argument. He neither names her, adopts her points, nor builds on her specific claims about personal grievance rights or the 30-day rule — the passage would read identically whatever she had said. It is not a 0.0 because it is at least about the matter under debate (workers' rights and conditions under this bill), earning the low end of the 'prepared material on the right subject' band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued the bill 'removes and narrows personal grievance rights', removes 'collective protections like the 30-day rule' and 'makes it easier to misclassify workers', and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister completely unaware that his Cabinet made a decision in September of last year to delay all work on climate adaptation cost-sharing until after the election?
acuity.explanation: Luxon's immediately preceding answer was the bare assertion that the work 'hasn't stopped'. Swarbrick takes that exact claim and confronts it with a dated, specific Cabinet decision to delay the work — the question would have to be written differently if he had said anything else. Engagement scored only; whether the claim is true or well-mannered is not acuity's business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "as I explained to the member last week, it hasn’t stopped" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that spending hundreds of millions of dollars on stopbank resilience work is actually a practical demonstration of how we cope with volatile weather, and also that it’s work carried out by the local communities, who look for confidence in the face of adverse weather events?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Swarbrick's critique — that the Government will not fund community-led resilience and acts only ad hoc — and offers stopbank spending delivered by local communities as the counter. It engages the topic and the 'community-led' framing rather than her specific claims about cost-sharing or the named programmes, and is plainly a prepared invitation to the Prime Minister.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "does he want to continue with his current plan, where Government makes ad hoc decisions" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: If the Māori seats were worth defending, why is it that the people who preside in the Māori seats have spent less time in Parliament than somebody who has been overseas for 206 days and yet spent more time in Parliament than the Māori Party seats altogether?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the representation strand that Luxon had just asserted and that Ngarewa-Packer's line of questioning rested on, but answers the topic rather than any specific claim put — it leaves the constitutional-recognition point and the enrolment figure untouched and substitutes an attendance comparison. Partial engagement, pointable but loose.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "they have representation with the biggest Māori contingent in Cabinet of any Government in recent times" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that the number of Māori enrolled on the Māori roll has increased by over 13,000 since the 2023 election?
acuity.explanation: Luxon had deflected to what Māori voters supposedly want and to service delivery; this follow-up does not take that up at all, and instead advances the next step of a prepared line about the Māori roll. It is squarely on the matter under discussion, which keeps it above the floor, but there is no engagement with the content of the answer given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what Māori voters want and what the Māori public want is a Government that’s on their side" — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: If it is her responsibility to create the conditions for jobs, why are there so many New Zealanders who are still losing their jobs?

acuity.responding_to: "As the member should know, employment is a lagging indicator" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: We have heard things about these big multinational companies. acuity.responding_to: Hon Jan Tinetti: "they are letting down those good employers who really care about their workplaces"

acuity.responding_to: Dr Hamish Campbell: "We need labour laws where people can have flexibility and we can get what we need out of both sides."

The speech would have to change if the previous speaker had argued something else; this opening is built directly on what Mooney said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: "The other side of the House talks doom and gloom" and "they care deeply about the employees"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr Hamish Campbell: "Most people realise it is a tight relationship between employer and employee."

acuity.statement: It’s been quite contrasting listening to one side of the debate and then listening to the other side of the contributions. We just need to cheer up a little bit, I think; we just need to have an actual look at some of the great changes we’re making in this space.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich set out the five limbs of the gateway test and argued they can be satisfied by almost any employer, and this statement does not take up any limb of it.

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I again reject the assertion that political neutrality is being tampered with in this bill. If you look at a range of strengthening aspects in this bill, including the stewardship requirements, the requirement in section 12 for the Public Service to maintain their ability to serve successive Government’s by being politically neutral, and the expectation that agencies build long-term thinking into their advice, there are a number of ways where political neutrality is strengthened throughout this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise claim just made — the cumulative-effect argument about political neutrality — names it, denies it, and answers it with specific countervailing provisions (stewardship, section 12's successive-governments duty, long-term thinking expectations). The reply would read differently had she argued something else, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "the accumulation of these different changes in different parts of the amendment do exactly that because it removes the tools that allow for politically neutral planning and analysis"

acuity.statement: This is a technical amendment to those existing provisions, which provide immunity for public servants who are carrying out their functions and duties in good faith. It provides an immunity from civil proceedings. The intention of this change is to clarify that the immunity applies both to the Public Service Commissioner as well as other Public Service chief executives; and also that it applies to chief executives when they are exercising both their general administrative functions but also specific functions under the Act.
acuity.explanation: Belich asked specifically whether the immunity in new section 104(1A) was cut and pasted from existing provisions or a new and unusually broad immunity covering chief executives 'acting in any capacity'. Meager answers that precise question: it is a technical amendment to pre-existing immunity provisions, limited to good-faith performance of functions and to civil proceedings, and the breadth she queried exists to clarify that it covers both the Commissioner and other chief executives across general and Act-specific functions. The reply would have to be different had she asked something else, so it sits at the top of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "whether that's one of the things that has been kind of cut and pasted from existing provisions, or if that, in fact, is a new provision that gives chief executives what seems quite a large amount of immunity"

acuity.statement: I think the member might have made a comment around getting rid of advisers who provide advice that you don’t particularly like. I think, if that was the case, there wouldn’t be a Government filled with any advisers in the history of the country, because the whole point of the public sector is to provide advice, often advice which Ministers don’t like.

The speech would be different had she asked different questions. Scored slightly below 1.0 only because the detail of her questions sits just outside the window, so the engagement is pointable through his own restatement rather than a direct quotation of her words.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "Those are a few questions that I would like to ask from the perspective of somebody who has not been so closely involved with this bill." — Meager answers those questions, including her point about removing advisers who give unwelcome advice.

acuity.statement: Additionally, the Minister made some comments around events-based employment. I’m sure the Minister’s aware that the collective agreement now states that employment for any employees employed by Parliamentary Service who are not affected to the extent that their job no longer exists after an event is continuous, and so there has, actually, been a change to make that more consistent with general employment law, and so that’s perhaps not the best example to use.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's own illustrative example — events-based employment — and does something with it, supplying the current collective agreement's wording to argue the example no longer holds. That is engagement with the content of his argument rather than a reference to it. Marked below 1.0 because the Minister's events-based remark was made in an earlier turn of the committee stage that is not reproduced in this window, so the thing engaged cannot be quoted directly from the preceding text.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager, in an earlier turn of this committee stage not reproduced in this window: his comments on events-based employment as an example justifying fixed-term contracts, which Belich cites as "the Minister made some comments around events-based employment".

acuity.statement: I didn’t want to interrupt the member’s flow state, but I will just clarify that what this clause is doing is it’s lifting and shifting existing provisions from Schedule 8 into what is going to be Part 3. Nothing in the law is changing; it’s just shifting it from that schedule into here.
acuity.explanation: This answers the precise question Belich had just put — whether new section 89A takes away rights employees held before the bill — by contradicting its premise and pointing to clause 47(3) and clause 37 to show the provisions are relocated rather than altered. Substituting a different question on the same clause would have required a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "The other thing is: to what extent is this taking away rights that people would otherwise have prior to the introduction of this bill?"

acuity.statement: Now, just from Helen White’s contribution, I think there were three threads I picked up there. Below 1.0 because Helen White's turn is not reproduced in this window, so the engagement is auditable only through his own restatement of it.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.statement: Here, she’s shouting now, right? I know her type. She took a very profitable group called Ngātiwai, a committee that we set up all those years ago, where the total cost used to be $22,000 a year, and it’s now broke. That’s her record.

That is a reference to the speaker rather than engagement with the claim, which the rubric places in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because the reply is at least prompted by, and aimed at, the member who spoke.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Huri te ao—huri te ao." — Hūhana Lyndon, interjecting that the world has turned/changed, i.e. contesting Peters' appeal to the 1986 Royal Commission and to Sir Apirana Ngata's century-old reasoning

The question could not have been written without hearing Bishop's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "They're a small agency and they would not have the capacity or financial resource to do every project"

acuity.statement: Does he therefore disagree with the NZTA-commissioned Kanofski review, which states, “NZTA does not have a rigorous independent investor assurance process.”, and, if so, why wouldn’t he therefore take up the Infrastructure Commission’s offer to do that work?

The 'therefore' is doing real work: the question is built on the answer immediately preceding it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "When it comes to the transport agency, as a Crown entity with its own balance sheet and with its own funding stream through fuel taxes and road-user charges, historically the arrangement has been that they make their own investment decisions"

acuity.statement: Does he therefore agree with the National Infrastructure Plan’s recommendation to “align investment expectations with available revenue”?

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "we are in the bottom in the OECD for efficiency of spend and we all need to do better"

acuity.statement: Does he at least, therefore, accept that having NZTA projects independently assessed by the Infrastructure Commission could help give the sector the certainty and assurance that they’ve been asking for and help prevent the situation where promises were made to the tune of $56 billion, and yet there is no clear plan on how to pay for it?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the $56 billion figure Bishop had just thrown across the Chamber as a jibe and turns it into the evidence for his own case about unfunded promises, while returning to the independent-assurance ask Bishop had deflected. The question is shaped entirely by what immediately preceded it.

acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it was true under the previous Government in which Crown loans, borrowing, and capital injections have been put into the National Land Transport Fund"

acuity.explanation: Within the infrastructure debate and loosely adjacent to the maintenance-and-renewals theme, but it engages no part of the answer immediately before it; it introduces a prepared set of rail figures that would read identically whatever Bishop had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop said "the commission's plan is a wake-up call for many people across the Parliament" and committed to responding to the plan in June, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It’s a real privilege to speak in this general debate. There’s been a lot of yelling this afternoon, gosh, and I guess it gives me cause to just reflect. I’ve been here—I’m a relatively new politician—only a little over two years and can only but see the cracks falling through the Opposition. We had Chris Hipkins, today, yelling in his general debate and his question time, asking about deflation and throwing tones of racism on us.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows a substantive turn by Waititi on Māori seats and a referendum, and engages none of its content. He acknowledges the preceding exchange only as atmosphere ('a lot of yelling this afternoon') and names the previous speaker in passing ('I like Rawiri, but he's going'), which is a mere reference rather than engagement; he then pivots to prepared general-debate material about the Opposition, Chris Hipkins, the Prime Minister's maiden statement and Kieran McNulty. Substituting a different argument on Māori seats would not have changed a word of this speech, though the gesture at the afternoon's tone keeps it off the floor of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that the push to remove Māori seats exists only because those seats have become more powerful, and called on National and Labour to 'rule it out' — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: We’ve had a number of motivating and inspiring speeches today, but I’m here to talk about the economy and to focus on values and fundamentals—values like sustainable developments, equal opportunity, reward for achievements in limited government; fundamentals like fixing infrastructure; sorting out productivity of land and sea; jobs in the regions, Matua; certainty for businesses; and responsible management of our natural assets.
acuity.explanation: Potaka acknowledges that speeches have been made and then explicitly turns to his own prepared material on the economy and his portfolios. The reference to earlier speeches is a mere nod, not engagement: the speech would read word-for-word the same whatever Peters had said before him, so it sits in the unresponsive band with only a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "They are not from the Māori people. They are not for the people of this country; they are for separatism and division" — nothing: Peters attacked Te Pāti Māori as separatists and communists and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: It’s been a really interesting general debate because, for once, in the last two years, you finally have Government Ministers talking about stuff that they’re doing.
acuity.explanation: She notices the preceding minister's speech and characterises it (Ministers talking about their own achievements), but engages no part of its content — none of the conservation concessions, Māori horticulture figures or housing claims are taken up. The remainder of her speech is prepared counterfactual material aimed at the Minister of Finance's question-time answers rather than at Potaka's argument, so this is a reference to the previous turn, not a response to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "That’s exactly what we’re doing as this Government."

acuity.statement: Since then—let’s just fast-forward to today—the Māori seats are in one of the most powerful positions they have ever been—they have ever been—and that frightens people like Winston Peters and New Zealand First.
acuity.explanation: Waititi takes up Peters' attack on Māori-seat MPs directly, supplies the 1867 origin of the seats and roll-enrolment figures, and reframes the attack as evidence that New Zealand First fears the seats' electoral leverage. The speech is plainly shaped by what Peters said — remove that turn and it would have to change — though it answers the broader attack and the Māori-seats topic rather than rebutting the specific separatism and communism charges clause by clause, which holds it below 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "They are not from the Māori people. They are not for the people of this country; they are for separatism and division"

acuity.statement: Well, that was a dud. I mean, that speech was an absolute dud. The one opportunity that members of the Government get as a backbencher to contribute in the general debate, and they spend most of the time talking about us and not talking about the real issues.
acuity.explanation: Utikere plainly listened to the speech he follows: he characterises what Hamilton actually did with his slot (spent it on Labour and Te Pati Maori rather than policy), which is an accurate and pointable reading of the preceding turn, and he makes that omission the hinge into his own material — Hamilton indeed never mentioned the cost of living. But he engages none of Hamilton's actual claims (the 1972-2023 deficit history, the inherited 'mess', the RMA reform), and after the opening characterisation the speech is prepared transport and cost-of-living material that would have run unchanged after any National backbencher. Partial engagement, with the engaged thing clearly identifiable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "Barbara Edmonds said we always talk about them; we've got plenty to talk about, but it's about context."

acuity.statement: Next week, the Labour Party will deliver its state of the nation address. That is part of democracy, but New Zealanders—especially those trying to rebuild homes, businesses, and lives—will judge all of us on results, not rhetoric.
acuity.explanation: Utikere had just put specific, answerable propositions: a $56 billion shortfall, Chris Bishop's earlier cost-overrun figure, the Infrastructure Commission's verdict, and the changed benefit-cost ratio assumptions. Rutherford, immediately following, takes up none of them — the pivot here is to a pre-scheduled Labour event and a prepared list of National's record. The speech brushes the same subject area (inflation, interest rates, roads) but engages no claim made, and would read word-for-word the same had Utikere spoken about anything else. A gesture at the debate rather than a response to it. The disaster material that opens his speech is not scored here: it opens a new subject rather than answering one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere argued the Government is prioritising roads of national significance at a $56 billion shortfall against the Infrastructure Commission's advice while households carry cost-of-living pressure, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Submissions on the Arms Bill have now closed, and I would like to take this opportunity to give a huge thankyou to everybody that was a part of the process and gave their Arms Bill submissions to the Justice Committee.
acuity.explanation: Three substantive turns precede this one and McKee engages no part of any of them. The speech is a self-contained portfolio update on the Arms Bill select committee process, delivered identically whoever had spoken before and transplantable to any sitting day. Scored low for responsiveness only; nothing here is a defect of reasoning, subject matter or manner, and a general-debate convention that permits members to raise their own topic is the reason, not an excuse the instrument recognises.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tangi Utikere spoke on cost of living and transport funding and Tom Rutherford on the Bay of Plenty landslides and the Government's record, and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: This is no longer just storms; this is climate change. It’s not just weather; it is climate change. It is climate change that is exacting a toll on our country, that is driving costs in our country that will have long-term costs for all of us.
acuity.explanation: Russell takes the specific material of the preceding speech — Rutherford's account of the Mount Maunganui landslides, which she names him and his community for — and does something with it: she recasts the event as a climate-change cost rather than a weather event, then answers his framing that recovery needs 'a Government focused on doing the basics well' with the counter-claim that the country is good at recovery and bad at resilience, citing the Sapere and Ministry for the Environment work and the folded-in $3 billion. The speech would have had to change substantially had Rutherford spoken about something else. Short of 1.0 because she leaves his economic and law-and-order claims untouched and the back half runs on prepared climate material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "On 22 January, severe weather triggered catastrophic landslides in Mount Maunganui on Mauao, Welcome Bay, Pāpāmoa, and surrounding communities."

On the right subject, engaging no argument.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the politicisation of social housing was a bad idea and that councils coming and going harmed maintenance and rents, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.statement: I think the question that we had raised in the last speaker’s contribution about “Are there other ways to do this?” is a fair question. acuity.explanation: Woods identifies the specific question Costley put — whether a trust-deed variation really needs the House's time — concedes it is fair, and then supplies the missing fact that answers it: the trust took legal advice and was told the High Court and other routes were not available. The speech would have to change if Costley had raised something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'do we need to keep using up the House’s time to go over these bills and these variations that maybe could have been handled in another way' (Tim Costley)

acuity.statement: The purpose of that clause in the bill is that, for example, if social housing is built in Ashburton or Timaru or in Rangiora, and then the trust winds up, those assets wouldn’t then revert to the ownership of Christchurch City Council; they instead would revert to ownership in the communities in which those assets rest.

Directly keyed to the specific point just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'shouldn’t the majority of assets, if they were at one point in time funded by ratepayers, be going back to that area?' (Tim Costley)

acuity.statement: I do have to point out that, against any claims that this bill is evidence that we don’t need central government in terms of the provision of social housing, in our time in Government, more community housing provider houses were built than in any point in history.
