acuity.responding_to: 'It demonstrates that the Government doesn’t have to hold the answer to every problem that we face.' (Tim Costley)

acuity.statement: Now, Ricardo Menéndez March says to talk about the bill. Well, this is literally what the legislation is about. It’s about serving on juries in New Zealand and the experience for people, because it’s really important that when New Zealanders get their summons in the post, they actually take that responsibility seriously.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford takes up the specific charge just put to him across the floor — that his jury-service anecdote is off the bill — and answers it directly by arguing the bill is precisely about jury service and the experience of serving. The passage would not exist had the interjection not been made, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because what he engages is a one-line interjection rather than a developed argument, and he returns to prepared material immediately after.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Tell us about the bill." — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: There was discussion around the age of 70 and, as I say, those other ages that it could have been, but 72 did tie in to the retirement age for the appointment of the previous Ombudsman, and that has survived that contest of discussion through the select committee and the committee of the whole House.
acuity.explanation: Arbuckle picks up the one strand of the preceding speech he can be shown to engage — Rutherford's rationale that 72 was chosen to match the Ombudsman's retirement age — and adds that it survived both the select committee and the committee of the whole House. He also names Rutherford's contest over 66, 67 and 68. But he endorses the point rather than doing anything with it, and the rest of the speech (submission counts, commencement date, his son's summons) is prepared material on the topic that would be identical whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "you are correct that 72 was decided on because it’s the Ombudsman’s age of retirement" — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: Look, I support this bill. Listening to all the contributions, I’ve thought about my parents. My mum’s 65, and dad’s 72. I think about the time that they have—other than taking care of my kids—and what kind of contribution they could make to being on a jury. They’re at that time in their life when they do have a little bit more time and their contribution is really valuable.
acuity.explanation: McClure follows Arbuckle, who argued that juries benefit from having older, more life-experienced people on the panel alongside the young. She takes up that one strand — the valuable contribution available from people in their sixties and seventies — and illustrates it with her own parents, but she engages none of the specific material Arbuckle actually worked through (the interaction of amended s 15(2)(aa) and s 15A(2), the particular-occasion versus permanent excusal distinction he said had been clarified at select committee). The rest is prepared personal reflection plus a procedural aside about filibustering, which would have been delivered whoever spoke before her. Partial engagement, pointable, then back to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "There is, I believe, good sense in having people from all age groups on a jury service"

acuity.statement: It’s quite different to be hearing the members from the Government side do anything other than just saying, “I commend this bill to the House.” It’s interesting to have just heard the ACT Party member admit that, perhaps, they were doing a bit of filibustering, which is interesting, because we just heard the National Party MP talk about how important this member’s bill is. You would think, therefore, they would want, in their interests—if they thought this bill was really important—to make it an expedient process, so that it can actually become law.
acuity.explanation: This takes the admission McClure had just volunteered — that Government members were filibustering a member's day — and does something with it, setting it against the Government side's professed view that the bill matters and drawing out the contradiction. The speech could not have been given in this form if McClure had not made that concession moments earlier; it is built on her words rather than merely citing them. Not a full 1.0 because after that opening he moves to prepared Green Party material (the biscuit tin, same-sex marriage, be more ambitious) that engages nothing specific from the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Laura McClure: "Some of them are probably wondering why Government members are filibustering 10 minutes out of a member’s bill speech."

acuity.statement: I just want to pick up on a quick point that was made—quite a serious point, actually—by the Hon Duncan Webb. When I think about the number of hours that we have spent as parliamentarians, and the taxpayer money, for something that really could have been tidied up in an omnibus bill, it is great to see the level of process that has occurred with this bill and I wish that would happen with all bills.
acuity.explanation: Leary picks up the proportionality argument that the immediately preceding speaker, Menéndez March, had just endorsed and restated — that a Government MP with the numbers behind them could have handled this trivially and should have used the ballot slot for something more substantive. She carries it a step further by costing it in parliamentary hours and taxpayer money and contrasting it with bills passed under urgency. She engages the argument rather than the detail of any particular claim in it, and part of her contribution is congratulation and anticipation of the maiden statement, so this sits above a partial engagement but short of a direct rebuttal or extension of a specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "perhaps you would think of something a bit more substantive"

acuity.statement: But if there's anyone out there who's over 72—73, 74, 75—get out your pen and paper, type up an email to carl.bates@parliament.govt.nz and write him a letter and ask him why he's being age discriminatory against those 73-, 74-, 75-, 76-year-olds—80-year-olds.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the life-expectancy rationale Nakhle spent much of her speech on (men to ~80, women to ~83) and draws out its consequence — if longevity is the reason, why does the bill stop at 72? That is engagement with the argument's logic rather than prepared material, though it is aimed at the bill's sponsor rather than rebutting Nakhle's specific reasoning, and it pivots quickly into a rhetorical device, so it is a partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "life expectancy is changing, and so we should change with it"

acuity.statement: The second point is—Rima Nakhle said: what changes can we make to improve lives? Well, I think they could do better—I think they could do better.
acuity.explanation: Quotes the preceding speaker's framing by name, but uses it only as a springboard into prepared cost-of-living material (doctors, food, insurance) that engages no part of Nakhle's case about jury excusal ages. Repeating an opponent's words in order to pivot away is a gesture at the debate rather than a response to its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "they answered questions along the lines of what changes we could implement as a Government to make things work more smoothly"

acuity.statement: But in truth, this bill doesn’t create a new right—there was always the ability of people to serve beyond 65. What it does do is impose a new duty on our older New Zealanders, and so I do think we need to recognise that that is indeed what this bill does—for all those older New Zealanders who might want to write to Mr Bates.
acuity.explanation: Takes the immediately preceding speaker's characterisation of the bill — that it recognises seniors' value and opens an opportunity without compelling anyone — and directly contests it, arguing the ability to serve past 65 already existed so what the bill actually does is impose a duty, then draws out the consequence (an extra administrative step for 65-72 year olds seeking excusal). The speech would have to be different if Garcia had framed the bill another way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "it recognises the value of our seniors in that it shows the belief in seniors that they can continue to perform jury duty" and "It does not mandate that they must excuse themselves"

acuity.statement: The changes that this bill makes accomplish a few good things. One of them is that it recognises the value of our seniors in that it shows the belief in seniors that they can continue to perform jury duty and contribute to the civic duty of being engaged and involved in the process.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject: a clause-by-clause description of what the bill does, delivered as if nothing had preceded it. It engages no part of Andersen's sarcastic charge that jury service is irrelevant to the financial pressures seniors face, and would read identically whatever she had said. On topic, so not 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen had just mocked the bill's priorities for seniors — "if they're worrying about that, they can sign up to a jury and it'll be good as gold!" — and this statement does not take up the point about seniors on fixed incomes at all

acuity.statement: Some of the members on the other side actually made fun of it. Well, for those of us who are boomers, this is a serious matter.
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the other side having 'made fun of it' but engages no content from the preceding turn — and the preceding Labour speaker in fact supported the bill and made a substantive duty-versus-right argument, which goes unanswered. The surrounding speech is a prepared riff on famous baby boomers that would be unchanged whoever spoke before and whatever they said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued the bill imposes a new duty and an additional administrative burden on New Zealanders aged 65 to 72 who must now establish a health ground for excusal, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: I would like to say to the member—interestingly enough, one of the strongest points I got from the member’s kōrero just now is that apparently the lack of access to alcohol on these days appears to be determined by religion.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle follows McAnulty's substantive speech in the same debate and explicitly takes up one strand of it — the religious character of the restricted days — before returning to prepared personal material about alcohol harm in South Auckland. She does not engage his actual load-bearing arguments (that the select committee advice was that the changes will not increase alcohol harm, that only already-operating premises are affected, or the RSA duty-manager trade-off), and the strand she attributes to him is a loose reading of his appeal to those who regard the days as important. Partial engagement, pointable but not aimed at the specific claims.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "I respect those that feel that these days are extremely important and I respect those that feel that we shouldn’t make any changes, but I would just ask them to consider the pragmatic approach that we have taken as a committee"

acuity.statement: My reading on this has been a little bit different from what some of the other members have spoken to. My feeling through the select committee process was that we actually heard the majority of people oppose this legislative change. We heard, yes, from hospitality in particular, and their support for the bill. But through agencies, such as the Salvation Army, it was very clear how they opposed this extension to these 3½ days.
acuity.explanation: Arbuckle, a fellow Justice Committee member, takes up the precise evidentiary claim Rutherford had just made about what the committee heard, concedes the hospitality strand of it, and disputes the overall balance by naming the opposing submitters. The speech would have to change if Rutherford had characterised the submissions differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "On the Justice Committee, we heard from hospitality groups, business sectors, restaurants, cafes, and bars, who got in touch and said, 'We'd love for you to bring about this change.'"

acuity.statement: If we go to something like Anzac Day: on Anzac Day, their members already have the ability to consume alcohol, and there is the ability for RSAs to have that special licence. We heard, through RSAs, actually, quite a concern—even though the member was trying to do the adjustments—that RSAs got into a routine of already doing that special licence and managing that situation.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the specific Anzac Day/RSA argument Rutherford had just built his support on, using the same fact (existing special licences) and drawing the opposite conclusion — that RSAs are accustomed to the current process rather than burdened by it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "Many of them either already have special licences or they have to apply for exemptions, and it's a bureaucratic and onerous task that they have to undertake."

acuity.statement: While we are a country built on Christian values, we still are a Christian country, and I really respect and celebrate those values. But, over time, things change and it’s not as strictly observed by people as it has been in the past—some other Christian countries have quite liberal alcohol laws, so I don’t think the two are mutually exclusive.
acuity.explanation: Engages the tradition-and-values ground on which the previous speaker rested his opposition, accepts the premise that those values matter, and contests the inference by pointing to other Christian countries with liberal alcohol laws.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jamie Arbuckle: "I think where I stand is you draw the line in our tradition and in our values."

acuity.statement: I just want to give you one small example, which I know that Miles Anderson, my colleague from Waitaki, touched on in terms of the major event that’s coming up at Easter in Wānaka. In Marlborough, the classic fighters at Easter—it’s very frustrating for international tourists who’ve come around the world to celebrate these classic fighters in a wine region, our biggest wine region in New Zealand, and they’re not able to go to a cellar door or a winery to have a glass of wine on Easter Sunday.
acuity.explanation: Prepared constituency material on the right subject — cellar doors at Easter — delivered immediately after a direct criticism of exactly that cellar-door widening, which it does not engage. The passage would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jamie Arbuckle argued that the bill has widened rather than narrowed, specifically that "even around the cellar door exemptions, we've now gone from restricted days being on Easter Sunday to actually opening that up to every day", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The health concerns about people having access to supply—the member in his speech didn’t quite say what I want to say right now, which is if you restrict people on days from buying alcohol, they stock up. There is no drop in the amount of alcohol consumed. People stock up beforehand.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle's immediately preceding turn opposed the bill on the ground that it means more access to alcohol. Luxton takes up that availability-harm strand directly, arguing restriction does not reduce consumption because people stockpile — a genuine counter to the claim just made. But he frames it against the bill's sponsor's speech rather than her argument, and after this strand he returns to prepared material (his own earlier member's bill, red tape, freedom, Easter trading), none of which would change whoever had spoken before. Partial engagement, hence mid-band rather than 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t want extra access to alcohol." — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: The Greens have long fought for workers’ rights. This bill would increase trading days, meaning workers have fewer public holidays, which means less time off with whānau, especially for low-wage workers in our hospitality and retail sectors.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Luxton and Nakhle both made substantive arguments before her. This is prepared caucus material on the right subject: it opens a workers'-rights line nobody had raised and later recites the Alcohol Healthwatch submission's three points. She asserts the bill "would increase access to alcohol" without addressing Luxton's claim that restricted days do not change total consumption, and the speech would read word-for-word the same had he argued anything else. Low for unresponsiveness, not for disagreeing — a sharp rebuttal of his stockpiling point would have scored high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Luxton argued immediately before that "if you restrict people on days from buying alcohol, they stock up. There is no drop in the amount of alcohol consumed" and that the rules burden small operators, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: For example, I guess, there are some differences in my electorate—compared to one of the previous speakers talking about hers—where a big portion of those that would be seeking hospitality during these days are tourists and are generally used to, in other countries, receiving a full suite of what’s available from the hospitality providers, in the countries they come from or a lot of the countries that they travel through.
acuity.explanation: He explicitly sets his own electorate against the community-based case an earlier speaker made from hers, and does something with it: where she argued the restricted days protect family time, he argues his constituents are largely tourists expecting a normal hospitality offering. That is a pointable engagement with a preceding turn, but it answers the topic (whose community the rules affect) rather than her specific claim about parental engagement, and the rest of the speech is his own prepared constituency account.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "so I do not support this bill, because I want the kids to have full access to their parents on these little few days" — Rima Nakhle

acuity.statement: For example, I guess, there are some differences in my electorate—compared to one of the previous speakers talking about hers—where a big portion of those that would be seeking hospitality during these days are tourists and are generally used to, in other countries, receiving a full suite of what’s available from the hospitality providers, in the countries they come from or a lot of the countries that they travel through.
acuity.explanation: This is the exact point in dispute: Luxton had just said the select committee's removal of the off-licence changes was unnecessary and that ACT would amend to restore the original intent. Anderson lands on the opposite side of that same amendment, and he does so knowingly. But he only registers a contrary position — he does not engage Luxton's reasoning about stockpiling or about why the narrowing was wrong — so this is a partial engagement rather than a rebuttal. Note: this is a second, separate passage of the same speech, scored on its own engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think that that narrowing was unnecessary and quite disappointing, actually." — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: The point of difference I would make is I was less concerned about the supermarkets and more concerned about your other off-licences—the Bottle-O down at the shops that was open. I would argue that potentially there's harmful drinking that can come out of there, but if harmful drinking is the reason not to do it, I get that that's a good thing; we don't want to see harm that comes from alcohol.
acuity.explanation: Costley takes up the specific off-licence argument Boyack had just made, accepts the harm concern as the right frame, and then disputes where it bites — supermarkets versus standalone bottle stores. He addresses her named carve-out directly and marks his divergence from it, so the speech would have to change had she argued something else; he also picks up Stuart Smith's Marlborough tourism point in the same turn. Not a full 1.0 only because he narrates his own anecdote and prepared position at length around the engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "The ability for people to buy large amounts at a supermarket is a big part of that problem, and I do not support extending to supermarkets when they currently can't sell alcohol."

acuity.statement: When it comes to choices around alcohol, for people who are adults, even though they may make decisions that we don’t agree with or approve of, and even if we think that they should be making different choices, the key thing is that it is their choice to make.
acuity.explanation: Weenink follows Todd Stephenson, who argued that holding your own views about drinking on special days does not entitle you to impose them on others. She takes up that same strand — the adult's choice being theirs to make even where others disapprove — and adds her own counterweight from medical practice before resolving it the same way. But she does nothing with Stephenson's specific points (the off-licence/on-licence problem, the claim that no one will be made to work more), names an earlier speaker rather than the one she follows, and the bulk of the speech is prepared personal reflection that would read the same whatever Stephenson had said. Partial engagement with one strand, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "But having your own views doesn’t mean you should actually impose those views on others, and that’s where we obviously have issues with these restrictions."

acuity.statement: As my colleague the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has pointed out, this Government has given us no rationale for shortening the report-back period of this bill. This is a bill that will come to the Environment Committee, of which I am a permanent member. We sat the whole morning this morning. We went back and forth trying to figure out how we were going to fit in 45.5 hours of submissions to the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's two specific strands — the absence of any stated rationale, and the Environment Committee's constrained timetable — and advances them with first-hand detail as a permanent member of that committee (the 45.5 hours of submissions already scheduled on the Planning and Natural Environment Bills). The content would have to change if Russell had argued something different; it is not a mere name-check, though it then moves on to prepared material of her own.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "given that the Minister introducing the bill didn’t give a reason as to why there should be a shortened report-back period" (and her account of the Environment Committee's meeting that morning and the pressure on its chair)

acuity.statement: The report-back date of 24 April is needed because the environment amendment bill needs to pass and receive Royal assent before 30 June 2026 to transfer the functions of the Ministry for the Environment (MFE) to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) on 1 July 2026. This is a short bill, and no material changes are being proposed to MFE’s existing functions.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick had just demanded that a Minister get up and give the rationale for truncating the select committee process, noting that so far only the Opposition had been left to guess at reasons. Simpson rises and supplies exactly that: the statutory deadline driving the 24 April report-back. The speech would not exist in this form had the preceding turn not asked for it; Webb and McAnulty both treat it as the answer to that demand. Not a full 1.0 only because he answers the demand for a rationale without engaging Swarbrick's further charge that the rationales available are disdainful of democracy.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "I implore, actually, the co - Deputy Prime Minister to get up and to argue for the rationale for truncating the select committee process."

acuity.statement: Minor and technical. To collapse the watchdog for the environment, the single voice in Government for the environment, into another ministry is not minor and technical.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own characterisation of the bill, repeats it as the thing in dispute, and denies it with a reason — that the change abolishes the single environmental voice in Government. The whole opening is built on the specific words Simpson had just used and would have to be rewritten if he had justified the timetable some other way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "This is a minor and technical bill to transfer functions from the Ministry for the Environment to the Secretary for the Environment"

acuity.statement: Now, that might be administratively convenient, but it’s not a reason to circumvent the entire procedures of this House. In fact, there have been plenty of instances of major, structural changes within Government happening. The re-establishment of the Social Investment Agency didn’t happen on 1 July—in fact, I think that happened on 1 January. The creation of the Ministry for Regulation happened on 1 May.
acuity.explanation: Engages the second limb of the Minister's rationale — the 1 July commencement — and attacks it with counter-examples of machinery-of-government changes that started on other dates, i.e. it concedes the date is convenient and denies it is a reason. This is a direct answer to the specific justification just offered, not prepared material on the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Simpson: "needs to pass and receive Royal assent before 30 June 2026 to transfer the functions of the Ministry for the Environment (MFE) to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) on 1 July 2026"

acuity.statement: I challenge the backbench MPs in Government. Those members talk about it all the time, and we need to make sure that we get it right. For us to shorten this process is not good lawmaking, it doesn’t engage key stakeholders, and it’s just not holding our executive to account.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the shortened referral period — but engages no part of the argument that preceded it. The Minister had given a specific statutory reason for the 24 April report-back and Webb had contested it in detail; Bennett takes up neither, naming Mr Peters only in passing and delivering a general appeal about holding the executive to account that would read identically whatever reason the Minister had given. A mere reference is not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Scott Simpson gave the 30 June 2026 Royal assent deadline as the reason for the report-back date and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: It’s a big building full of books, with big signs to it, but because it doesn’t say “Library”, they don’t know that it’s the library if they’re New Zealand First voters.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the one strand of Peters' case that matters most — that te reo primary naming of services leaves people unable to identify what a facility is — and answers it by reductio, arguing the physical and visual context makes the referent obvious. It engages the confusion claim rather than its reasoning or evidence, and does so as ridicule rather than rebuttal, so it is a partial engagement: the content of Peters' chart and signage examples is never addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "We have some very real situations now where communications and names of important services are using te reo as primary names and language, and the room for confusion and miscommunication is huge."

acuity.statement: You don’t want to freeze it. A language is a moving thing. If you listen to a conversation in New Zealand today, you don’t actually hear English English; you hear New Zealand English.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and aimed at the bill Peters commended, but it answers the topic rather than Peters' actual argument: Peters argued for statutory English status on clarity-and-safety grounds, and Webb raises a different objection — ossification — that would read identically had Peters argued for the bill on any other ground. One strand is engaged (the bill's effect on the English language), then the speech proceeds on its own line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "This bill is an important clarification of the official status of the English language in New Zealand in legislation."

acuity.statement: All across the world, official language status is provided to protect languages under threat, in order to put a spotlight on the need to protect and resource their survival and revival. Here, in Aotearoa, that status has been granted to te reo Māori as the indigenous language of this country, which was once physically, violently beaten out of the mouths of Māori by those who imposed English as the only language.
acuity.explanation: This engages the inferential core of Peters' opening case — that because Canada, Ireland and Wales legislated official status for English, doing so here shows the importance of statutory recognition — by supplying the condition those precedents share (a language needing protection) and arguing English in New Zealand does not meet it. That is doing something with the argument put, not merely restating a position. Short of 1.0 because she engages the general rationale for the bill rather than Peters' specific evidential claims about health services, road signs and navigational charts, which go unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "Other jurisdictions have taken similar measures to recognise English as an official language, including Canada, Ireland, and Wales."

acuity.statement: This week, parts of Aotearoa will once again plunge underwater in the most recent climate emergency. These one-in-100-year weather events that we consistently see are occurring week after week after week. Sewage is spilling into the waters in our capital.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material that engages no part of either preceding contribution. Two members had just argued about te reo naming, confusion and the ossification of English; this opening is about flooding, sewage and drinking water and would be word-for-word identical whatever had been said before it — it could have been delivered in a different debate on a different day. Scored 0.1 rather than 0.0 only because the passage is the run-up to a claim about the Government's choice of business, which is at least adjacent to the matter before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Winston Peters spoke about te reo place names on electronic navigational charts and the risk he says they create at sea, and Duncan Webb about ossifying the English language; this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: He aha te aha ka pahawa i tēnei pire? I ahu mai tēnei pire i hea? He aha ngā hua ka puta ki a Ngāi Pākeha nō rātou tonu tēnei reo.
acuity.explanation: Opens by putting the question Court's claim invites — what will the bill actually achieve, and who gains from it — which takes up one strand of the "simply practical, common sense" case made immediately before her. Beyond that opening the speech is largely prepared material on the history and status of te reo Māori, and its only named interlocutor (Chlöe) spoke outside this stretch, so the engagement is partial rather than a rebuttal of the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "It doesn’t have to be a culture war issue, Chlöe Swarbrick and the Greens or Labour; it’s simply practical, constructive, common sense."

acuity.statement: English has long been a de facto language in this country. This bill simply recognises that and makes no other changes.
acuity.explanation: "Makes no other changes" gestures at the harm Kaipara had just alleged, but it asserts the opposite rather than engaging any part of her case — nothing in it answers the extinction-risk argument, the Treaty argument or the Te Aho Matua point. This is prepared material on the right subject; it would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "He whakatamariki i te reo rangatira, he tāmi i te mana Māori" ("To trivialise the Māori language, suppress Māori autonomy")

acuity.statement: It is remarkable, at a time when New Zealanders are struggling with the cost of living, when food prices are going up, where people are struggling to pay the rent, where unemployment is at record highs, that this is the Government’s priority.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and glancingly adjacent to Bates's claim that the bill changes nothing — she treats it as empty symbolism — but she does not take up his de facto-language premise, and the argument she joins is Duncan Webb's, from outside this stretch. The remainder of the speech is a prepared passage on her mother and the English language that would have been delivered whatever preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carl Bates: "This bill simply recognises that and makes no other changes."

acuity.statement: Yep, they’re going to do more of the theatrics, walking out, and we’re all upset, but how about we just calm down a little and stop the theatrics and talk about what this is. It’s OK. We’re only making English official. It’s not the end of the world.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at the subject under debate ("talk about what this is", "we're only making English official"), but no part of the preceding argument is engaged: the reply is aimed at a swear word and at the Opposition's theatrics rather than at anything Verrall claimed. Scored low for unresponsiveness only — the incivility of the passage is a separate question and is not what moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall argued the bill is misplaced symbolism at a time of cost-of-living pressure and that political language about race licenses harm outside the House, and this statement does not take any of it up — it responds to an off-text interjection and to Opposition conduct generally.

acuity.statement: The US and Israel bombing of Iran is a clear breach of international law. There is no UN mandate for it. There is no evidence that these attacks were a necessary act of self-defence.
acuity.explanation: Luxon raised the legitimacy of the US/Israel strikes and deliberately left it open while framing them as justified prevention. Hipkins takes that exact question up and closes it the other way, naming the specific grounds (no UN mandate, no self-defence necessity) that Luxon's framing relied on. acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "I want to acknowledge that there are different views on the legitimacy of the actions taken by the US and Israel." — and his framing that they are "actions that are designed to prevent Iran from continuing to gravely threaten international peace and security"

The speech would read word-for-word the same had Waititi said something different on this topic, so it sits in the unresponsive band; it earns above 0.1 only because it is squarely on the matter under debate rather than a speech transplantable to another day. acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "I just need to check it’s not a drafting error."

The answer is shaped by the interpretation just put to her.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Is that how I’m supposed to interpret clause 8, inserting new paragraph (c)?"

acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "this is essentially removing a requirement for the Minister of Finance to approve the establishment of an MCA; rather, it just allows Cabinet to do it"

acuity.explanation: Confirms the part of Edmonds' summary that is right and corrects the part that is not — approval was never the Minister of Finance alone, it was Cabinet or joint Ministers, and what changes is the removal of the separate Finance Minister step. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "The Minister referenced that it’s no longer the Minister of Finance; that now it goes straight through to Cabinet."

As I have made very clear, the bill removes the requirement for the Minister of Finance to approve the establishment of multi-category appropriations, leaving the approval with Cabinet or joint Ministers. In terms of administration and use of appropriations, it is for departments to use the appropriations of another department.

One strand engaged, the cross-reference question and the administrator example left untouched, so a partial engagement rather than an answer.

acuity.responding_to: "any other department may incur departmental expenses of the same type as the category or categories of departmental expenses in the multi-category appropriation" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: One was in relation to just an example of what the appropriation administrator is, and the second one was actually in relation to section 5 under the current Public Finance Act and the reference to 7C(2)(c) in clause 8.

The reply would be different had Willis said something else; it exists only to correct her characterisation.

acuity.responding_to: "The member’s now repeating the same question, just using more words" — Nicola Willis

This has been done by convention. This brings it into statute.

acuity.responding_to: "in the case of an appropriation for expenses and capital expenditure to be incurred by an intelligence and security department,” which I think the Minister of Finance had said there is no more requirement for that to be reported" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: The question really highlighted something that I hope my colleagues agree with, which is that I’m glad it is the people of New Zealand who democratically elect their Government and not a report writer at the United Nations, because if that member wishes to press the case that, by simply inserting wellbeing objectives into his Budget Policy Statements, Grant Robertson was about to deliver more wellbeing, I would suggest to her that 33 months of out-of-control inflation reaching an intergenerational high, the accumulation of tens and tens of billions of dollars of debt, a cost of living crisis, a crash in the economy, which led to his Government being voted out, would suggest that most New Zealanders judged that the insertion of wellbeing objectives did not, in fact, enhance wellbeing. I’d also address the member’s questions by saying that we have retained the child poverty Act, so in relation to her questions around that, those reporting measures remain. I’d also point out that the inclusion of wellbeing measures did not prevent people sleeping in cars, which was a common occurrence under her Government in which the social housing wait list was much, much longer than it is under ours.
acuity.explanation: Takes up each of the specific strands Edmonds advanced and does something with them: contests the authority of the UN committee's endorsement, answers the child-poverty measurement point by noting the child poverty Act is retained, and turns her 'people sleeping in cars' illustration back against the wellbeing provisions. The answer could not have been delivered against a different question; disagreement here is evidence of close engagement, and the scoring of the inference and the tone belongs to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "given the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child recognised the introduction of the wellbeing objectives into the Public Finance Act as crucial for safeguarding children’s rights" — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I made very clear at the start, when I was talking about repayments, that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) does have a statutory duty to take all reasonably practical steps to recover debt. It is not discretion around debt; it is discretion around the repayments and taking into consideration the situation of the client. MSD already has that discretion.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise point Menéndez March put to her — that the bill gives MSD no discretion and that she should engage with Amendment Paper 522 — and draws the distinction her answer turns on (discretion over repayments, not over whether debt is recovered), identifying what the existing statutory position is. The speech would have had to change had he argued something else about discretion, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t believe she has engaged with the substance of the amendment, because the bill itself does not give MSD that level of discretion" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: We’ve had a slight exchange here. It did appear that she was saying there was discretion already. I wonder if she was talking about the social security regulations and if she was referring to that at all, because I have had a relatively close look at some of the regulations, specifically No. 208, but my understanding is that only occurs when there’s been an error by the Ministry of Social Development (MSD), which would not be the situation in most of these particular situations.
acuity.explanation: Directly tests the claim Simmonds had just made, naming the instrument she thinks the Minister must be relying on and the limit on it (it bites only where MSD has made an error), and asks her to confirm that is the only existing discretion. acuity.responding_to: "MSD already has that discretion." — Penny Simmonds

While the Minister made a case that there should be no discretion because that could lead to inequity, in fact it’s based on a similar provision, as I understand it, that works well in the ACC setting.

She later also takes up Belich's High Court point by name ("I take Camilla Belich's point: the law as it is now doesn't do this because the High Court has said it won't"). Not 1.0 because the bulk of the turn then moves to her own new material on accredited employers, moral hazard and the ACC briefing, which would have been delivered whatever Belich had said; the opening, though, would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, the Minister notes that sometimes discretion can be applied in a way which is unjust and that that’s a risk." — Camilla Belich

In relation to clause 20, this is simply a transparency measure, and I note that it was actually welcomed by Opposition members on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, which is to put in a requirement where there is this tax expenditure, that there is some reporting on the outcomes of it.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "why are outcomes not required to be included in the tax expenditure statement in the legislation, compared to the RIS?" (and Barbara Edmonds' question on the UN convention on the rights of the child)

That is precisely the reason to ensure fairness between those two types of ACC payment.

But she engages only the framing, not the specific mechanism put to her — that supplementary assistance spent on treatment and rehabilitation is then recovered out of weekly compensation, leaving the recipient worse off. The claim of harm goes unanswered, and the rest of the turn is about the Green and Labour discretion amendments rather than the question just asked.

acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "they are paying for their own treatment and their own rehabilitation costs, and so they are worse off?"

But my understanding is, and the High Court agrees, that a lot of this supplementary assistance is not necessarily comparable and it is just because people needed it while they waited for their claims to come through.
acuity.explanation: This takes the Minister's stated justification — that the bill exists to ensure fairness between claimants paid promptly and those paid late — and attacks its load-bearing premise, that the two forms of support are equivalent. He names the comparison she made, disputes the framing explicitly, and offers a reason it fails (the assistance met needs arising from the wait, not the injury). The speech would have to change if the Minister had defended the bill on different grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "That is precisely the reason to ensure fairness between those two types of ACC payment."

acuity.statement: Thank you for the question from the Green Party member about the savings provision, and, of course, the amendment came about because of the very issues that the member talked about, that was heard from submitters at the select committee. And so the inclusion now has been made to those who have made application for a review by the benefits review committee, and they include those who have filed. So just absolutely clarifying that for the member.

Not a full 1.0 only because the deferral leaves half the turn unengaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "whether the change that she is making through her amendment would also include people who have filed reviews of decisions"

acuity.statement: And so MSD—we were told that the reason we were doing this was it was just going to be a nightmare, administratively, to actually change things for people away from long-standing practice. There’ve been a whole lot of people who had money clawed back and there would be a lot of work involved in doing it, because it’s so uncertain what was going on. Isn’t this an example of it being a nightmare the other way where there’s got to be calculations and then there’s uncertainty?
acuity.explanation: She takes up the administrative-clarity rationale the Minister advanced for the bill and turns it back on the drafting, arguing the new Schedule 3 calculation creates exactly the uncertainty the Government said it was avoiding. That is genuine engagement with the Government's stated intent. But it reaches past the turn immediately before her to select committee evidence, and most of her contribution is prepared clause-by-clause questioning (winter energy payment, subclauses (1A) and (2)) that would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "which is to provide clarity and consistency in how ACC payments are treated in the welfare system"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to note that we have had a few generalised questions around specific amendments that are in relation to this part, but there are a number of clauses that we haven’t touched on at all, so my intention is to ask specific questions on those clauses.

So the turn is visibly shaped by what came before. It does not, however, engage the substance of any argument made: it is about the conduct of the debate rather than the merits of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "I know that she may choose to address her amendment in another part of the bill, but I would none the less like some engagement on it at any point in this debate."

Not 1.0 because it engages only the determinability strand and leaves Kaipara's actual proposal (an operational guidance developed in partnership with Māori) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "in clause 7(2), replacement clause (1A)(2): “If MSD cannot determine the period”"

acuity.statement: The second one is in relation to—the Minister’s amendment touches a little bit on it, but she hasn’t addressed that, and I think clause 7 is the best place for us to potentially address it—the interactions between the mandatory reviews that are coming into place in March and how this works.

acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "I had given an example earlier of where it can be difficult to determine a period" (and her amendment on mandatory reviews)

acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "it goes back to a question that she hasn’t engaged with from earlier—before the current Chair was in the Chamber, I believe—about whether she believed the existing practice was right"

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "As we know, retrospective legislation is not the norm in this House."

acuity.statement: One of the things that I am also particularly interested in, and I haven’t had engagement with the Minister on, is on the range of debts imposed by Part 2. There hasn’t been engagement on the upper end of debts that are imposed and who is particularly affected.
