acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White proposed ring-fencing large clawbacks over $5,000 or $10,000 and offering a six-month window for reviews, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: In terms of the interaction between MSD and ACC, MSD worked with ACC throughout the select committee process and they engaged on all the relevant questions that have been asked. Just noting with regard to the question from the Green Party member about rehabilitation requirements, that responsibility sits with ACC. This bill is about clarifying how income from ACC is treated in the welfare system.
acuity.explanation: Answers two specific questions put by two different members in the turns immediately before: White's question about MSD-ACC liaison, and March's question about whether the entitlement covers rehabilitation as well as weekly compensation. The reply names the Green member's question and resolves it on the merits (rehabilitation sits with ACC; the bill only addresses how ACC income is treated in the welfare system), which is engagement with content rather than a mere reference. Not 1.0 because several of the questions actually asked — White's ring-fencing and claim-window alternatives, March's question about MSD communications after the High Court decision — are left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "whether the provisions in there include an entitlement to “treatment or rehabilitation” or simply “weekly compensation”" — and Helen White: "whether there was any liaison with ACC over these issues".

acuity.statement: I do thank the Minister for engaging in some of that discussion around retrospectivity, because it is very, very important and significant in this bill. A slightly different matter that hasn’t been specifically addressed by the Minister is in relation to the changeover date, which is in Part 11.
acuity.explanation: Audits the Minister's answer against what was asked: credits the part that was addressed, then identifies precisely what the answer left out and presses on it, drawing out that the changeover date is an unusual form of retrospectivity because it attaches to publication rather than commencement or Royal assent. It also takes up the Minister's own savings provision for the review cohort and turns it into a new question about claimants whose benefits review cases were declined. The speech is unmistakably shaped by the reply it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "The reason for the retrospectivity of it is that it’s important to ensure that the fairness occurs outside of that very small cohort that are currently before review."

acuity.statement: I think we’ve made it very clear: yes, the changeover is 2 p.m. on the date of the bill being introduced. That isn’t the standard approach but there is a very clear reason why there is the need for retrospectivity on this bill, because we need to ensure that current policy and current practice is upheld for as many people as possible.
acuity.explanation: Confirms the specific fact Belich asked about — the changeover is 2 p.m. on the day of introduction — and concedes it is not the standard approach, which is genuine engagement with the question just put. But the justification offered is a restatement of the general retrospectivity rationale already given rather than a reason for that particular date, and Belich's direct ask about whether the Minister would consider amending it is not taken up; the declined-BRC question is handed to officials. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I would like to hear the Minister specifically on that changeover date and why in fact it was necessary".

acuity.statement: Oh OK, well here are the facts: between 2018 and 2023, people living in severe housing deprivation increased, at a time that tens of billions of dollars were spent by the Government on housing support. If it was a money problem, the previous people in charge of the Government books would have fixed it.
acuity.explanation: This is not an answer to a question put to him in the question cycle but a reply to an interjection by another member, so it is a genuine debate turn. McLellan's interjection argues that the Government's housing delivery is insufficient because homelessness is worsening. Bishop takes up that reasoning directly: he accepts the premise that severe housing deprivation rose, places it in 2018-2023, and attacks the inference that the problem is one of funding. The reply would have to be different had she argued something else, and he engages the content rather than merely naming her. Not 1.0 because he shifts the period to the previous Government's term rather than meeting the claim about the present trend.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It's not enough, otherwise homelessness wouldn't be getting worse." — Dr Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I’m really excited about the future ahead with the changes that we’re going to be making under this bill, the Data and Statistics (Census) Amendment Bill. I thank the Minister of Statistics, Dr Shane Reti, for driving this forward. When quality data is collected more regularly, essentially what it means is that we can provide better outcomes with more knowledge.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive Labour speech that raised a specific worry about data quality under the new method, and engages none of it — prepared praise for the bill and the Minister. The words would be identical whatever the previous speaker had said, though it is at least on the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich spoke immediately before, supporting the bill but "wanting some assurances that the statistical data in New Zealand will not be left in a worse place", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It has been identified that we are concerned—there are two things that I would say are main concerns. One is: will this new method capture everyone?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand his colleague left open and gives it content (coverage of people who do not touch State agencies), and it cuts against the preceding government speaker's claim that more frequent collection simply yields better knowledge. Partial rather than full engagement: it develops a concern already on the table and then runs through prepared material on the reference date and small-language communities rather than rebutting a specific argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "wanting some assurances that the statistical data in New Zealand will not be left in a worse place" — and Rima Nakhle: "When quality data is collected more regularly, essentially what it means is that we can provide better outcomes with more knowledge."

acuity.statement: Of course, we have relied on the traditional method of census—a traditional, paper-based method—so it’s great that we’re going to be moving to this new method, because despite escalating costs, we have been getting data that is getting poorer and poorer.
acuity.explanation: Follows a detailed critique of the new method's coverage bias and the data lag, and answers neither; asserts the opposite trend about data quality as prepared material rather than engaging Webb's reasoning. On the right subject and gestures at the method change under debate, hence 0.2 rather than 0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued immediately before that "an admin data - first approach has a bias towards people who are administered" and that the reference date pushing out to 2030 means "every year that passes, data becomes less reliable", and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: On a lighter note, I’d like to take the opportunity to welcome the 5,200-odd voters that will be joining the wonderful Whanganui electorate at this year’s election. When we think about new people moving boundaries, moving electorates, needing to understand what electorate they are part of, and connecting with it, having two terms in an electorate before there’s another boundary change and anything there happens makes sense.
acuity.explanation: Follows Waititi's claim that the boundary changes and the census changes form an agenda to suppress Māori voters. Bates gestures at the preceding turn only in tone ("On a lighter note") and engages none of its content, offering prepared material on the two-term cycle. It is on the matter under debate, which keeps it above zero, but the speech would be identical whatever Waititi had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That is to make sure you suppress Māori voters" — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: We heard from the previous speaker, Rawiri Waititi, that there are some boundary changes happening this election, and we know it’s really important that New Zealanders are clear about what’s happening there.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker and takes up one strand of his point — that boundaries are changing and voters need clarity — then pivots to her own electorate and prepared material on the bill's mechanics. She does not engage his actual contention (that the change suppresses Māori voters), so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "these boundary changes—" ... I will not splice; the engaged claim is Rawiri Waititi's "it’s tied to the statistics stuff and the data stuff that you just talked about in the last bill."

acuity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to align the policy setting in the Electoral Act with the Government’s work to modernise the census—the census, of course, being every five years. We’re changing that every year. The electoral boundary changes are tied to the census. We don’t want to end up doing it every year, so this tidies up that part.
acuity.explanation: Entirely prepared material restating the bill's purpose. Andersen had just raised a specific, answerable concern about whether the modernised census will capture hard-to-reach populations; Campbell reaches the same subject matter (the census link) without touching that concern, and the speech would read identically had she said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ginny Andersen raised concerns about "the efficacy of the new census approach, and its ability to capture all New Zealanders" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: In October 2025, there was a paper produced that, essentially, looked at how well the administrative data does against the census data. It was a bit of an experimental test to see how well it compares, and the results were not too bad. However, they did point to second-layer data as being a potential issue. When people respond to the higher-level categories, that was fairly accurate, but those second-level categories are quite difficult to get right.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the data-quality concern raised earlier in the debate and does something with it: supplies the specific October 2025 comparison of administrative against census data, accepts that the headline results held up, and locates the problem precisely at the second-level categories. Had the preceding argument been different, this passage would have had to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we do have some concerns about the way that the census will be changed, the efficacy of the new census approach, and its ability to capture all New Zealanders" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: It’s a pleasure to support this bill and to take the opportunity, as my colleague Carl Bates did, to welcome the 4,100 constituents that are moving from the Upper Harbour electorate to the great electorate of Northcote: welcome. I have doorknocked every street in that new part, and I can confirm it’s very diverse and very supportive of the current coalition Government.
acuity.explanation: Echoes an earlier member's welcome-your-new-voters device, which is a reference to form rather than engagement with any argument. Walters had immediately before raised the constitutional significance of reserved provisions, the risk if the term moves to four years, and the voting age; none of that is taken up. On topic, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued "should we ever move to a four-year term, we may want to revisit whether the two-term cycle is the best way for us to invoke boundary changes" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we’ve just heard and the scaremongering that’s going on. This bill is putting patients first, contrary to what the previous Government did. This Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill is about shifting the focus from bureaucracy to delivery, ensuring every New Zealander has timely access to quality healthcare. We’re mandating health targets that ensure focus remains on what matters: reducing emergency wait times, improving cancer management, increasing childhood immunisations—that all went backwards under their Government.
acuity.explanation: Campbell directly contradicts the strand of McLellan's turn that the Government is not funding health ("contrary to what we've just heard") and defends the specific targets she called useless by naming them. But he engages only that one strand by flat assertion, offering no figures against hers, and ignores her substantive points on prevention and the cost of GP access before returning to prepared bill-commendation material. Partial engagement that is pointable, hence mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why aren’t they investing in the infrastructure that the health system needs?" / "These ones are useless health targets." — Tracey McLellan

acuity.statement: I don’t put the blame on officials for ruling these out of scope; I simply don’t buy it: if the Minister genuinely believed that sexual violence survivors and abuse in care survivors or victims of crime should be excluded from this bill, she could have sought out-of-scope amendments through the Business Committee.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand of the preceding Labour speech that absolved the Government by blaming officials, rejects that explanation, and supplies a counter-mechanism (out-of-scope amendments via the Business Committee). The rest of the speech is prepared material aimed at the Minister, so not a full 1.0, but this passage would have to change if the previous speaker had not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "it was let down by officials who were unable to come up with a discretion clause" — Jackson blamed officials for being unable to draft a discretion/exclusion clause.

acuity.statement: The second point the member makes is that somehow some people should be excluded from the intention of the policy. The member thinks that it’s OK if the policy doesn’t deliver on its intent.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly numbers and takes up the preceding speaker's arguments (the rushed process, and the exclusion amendments) and answers the second one directly. Whether the characterisation is a fair reading is a rigor question, not an acuity one; the speech is plainly shaped by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "we indeed also tried to put forward amendments to minimise the harm that this bill was causing, to exclude sexual violence survivors and abuse in care survivors"

acuity.statement: I also heard that the Ministry of Social Development had discretion to look at these cases, and we support that.
acuity.explanation: Touches the discretion question that dominated the preceding speeches, but only as something reported from colleagues and taken "at their word", without engaging Jackson's claim that no discretion clause could be written or Menéndez March's claim about out-of-scope amendments. One strand glanced at, then back to a prepared party position.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "MSD found it impossible to write in a discretion clause" — Jackson's central complaint was the absence of a discretion to write off debt.

acuity.statement: That is why many of us argued that if legislative change was required, it should have been clearly prospective in effect, not retrospective, providing certainty for the future, rather than revisiting the past.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material squarely on the matter under debate (retrospectivity, Te Tiriti obligations, who is affected) but indifferent to the arguments immediately preceding it. The speech would read the same whichever of the earlier members had spoken.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Parmjeet Parmar had just argued it is "our responsibility to fix" a policy the courts interpreted differently, and David Wilson that MSD has discretion; this statement takes up neither and restates Te Pāti Māori's prepared position.

acuity.statement: All we hear is “Oh, we’ve got to stop the double-dipping. We’ve got to fix the inequities.” All you are doing is entrenching inequities by hurting the most vulnerable—people who were waiting sometimes years and years and years for the ACC claim to be accepted and, while they were waiting, they were having to live on a benefit and they were having to get supplementary allowances just to survive.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Government benches' framing rather than any one member's specific claim: it answers the topic (double-dipping, equity) and inverts it, but paraphrases a generic "all we hear" position instead of taking up the argument just made and doing something with its reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Parmjeet Parmar: "we have seen that the policy has been interpreted differently, so it is our responsibility to fix it" — the Government side's fairness/fixing framing.

acuity.statement: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you’re outraged about everything, you’re really outraged about nothing. Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won’t get it twice.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker's party and pivots to an assertion about entitlements that engages no part of the evidence just put. A mere reference plus a restated slogan sits in the low band; it is about the right subject, which keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Davidson had just given the select committee figures — 65 percent sensitive claims, 70 percent women, close to 900 submissions with only two in support — and read a submitter's account, and this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: If you have somebody who breaks their arm—if Tim Costley breaks his arm, then the accident compensation scheme kicks in without fault, and Tim Costley will receive 80 percent of his earnings; he will also receive household help because that will be helpful for him in his recovery; he will receive physio; he will receive taxis to and fro, as he needs them; there will be rehabilitation that he gets.
acuity.explanation: Takes the previous speaker's exact claim and tests it by working his own case against a sexual assault claimant's, step by step, to show the two are not treated alike. The speech could not have been given against a different preceding argument; it is built directly on the one just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tim Costley: "Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won’t get it twice."

acuity.statement: The current situation, as interpreted by the courts, is those who receive lump-sum payments are treated more generously than the former, which are those on ACC and welfare. So the Government has a duty to fix this.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right bill delivered immediately after a detailed contrary account of who is treated more generously, with no acknowledgement of it. Identical whatever the previous speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White had just walked through why the sexual assault claimant is treated less generously than a claimant with a broken arm, and this statement asserts the opposite generosity comparison without engaging her account.

acuity.statement: The member opposite just talked about fairness, and we all know fairness is too subjective of a term. This is not about fairness; this is about justice.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the preceding speaker's organising term and contests it, substituting justice for fairness, before moving to a prepared walk-through of the ACC/MSD sequence. Genuine engagement with one strand of what was just said rather than with its substantive reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Bidois: "Well, this bill is about fairness."

acuity.statement: And for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn’t be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what’s lawful or not.
acuity.explanation: Aimed at a point actually made earlier in the debate about lawfulness and rightness, and answers it in the chamber rather than reciting prepared lines — but it converts the point into a party jibe instead of engaging its reasoning, which caps it mid-band. Whether the characterisation is a strawman is a rigor matter, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "Just because they had been implementing it doesn’t mean it was right; it doesn’t mean it was just."

acuity.statement: I want to also acknowledge Minister Louise Upston and her leadership in the Ministry of Social Development space. I also want to acknowledge our ACC Minister and his leadership in the ACC portfolio.
acuity.explanation: Closing remarks of thanks and portfolio praise, including a rehabilitation statistic from question time, delivered after a specific legal argument that goes unmentioned. The words would be unchanged whoever had spoken before; only the ACC subject matter keeps it above 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich had just argued the bill may amount to indirect discrimination against women with sensitive claims under human rights law, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Speaking to the point of order, the royal commission finds that, on 22 December 2021, the briefing was made available to the Minister for COVID-19 Response, the Hon Chris Hipkins, of those concerns.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact claim Hipkins had just made — that the commission found Ministers were never given the advice — and meets it with a date and a named recipient for the briefing. The reply would be different had Hipkins objected on any other ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "The royal commission specifically found that Ministers were not presented with the advice that the Minister has just claimed they were presented with."

acuity.statement: I’ll quote directly from paragraph 495 of the royal commission’s report: “We consider the failure to ensure that this specific advice reached Ministers and the public was significant.” That is the finding of the royal commission.
acuity.explanation: Answers Brown's specific assertion that the briefing reached him by citing the paragraph of the same report that, on Hipkins' reading, says the advice failed to reach Ministers. It engages the source Brown relied on rather than changing the subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the briefing was made available to the Minister for COVID-19 Response, the Hon Chris Hipkins, of those concerns"

acuity.statement: The Vaccine Technical Advisory Group advice against two doses for 12- to 17-year-olds never went to Ministers, and the royal commission finds that.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the Minister's account of the under-18 two-dose advice, locating the disagreement on the precise factual point in dispute (whether the advice reached Ministers) rather than restating prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The two-dose mandate remained in place regardless of both workplace environments and extracurricular activities such as sport."

acuity.statement: This is the guy, when he was Minister of Police, crime went up. When he was Minister of Education, school attendance went down.
acuity.explanation: Engages no part of the argument just made and leaves the subject matter of the debate entirely, running through unrelated portfolios. The remark would be word-for-word usable in any debate in which Hipkins had spoken.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins quoted the royal commission's finding that "Evidence shows New Zealand had among one of the best pandemic responses in the world" and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: The reality is that that advice was provided to the Ministers, and the mandates that it related to continued to stay in effect for some time after that. Concerns were clearly made, and the reality is that the questions around why those decisions were made are questions that would need to be put to the former Ministers.
acuity.explanation: Meets Hipkins' denial head-on by reading the paragraph he says establishes the opposite and drawing the consequence that the mandates continued afterwards. The engagement is with the specific claim, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "The Vaccine Technical Advisory Group advice against two doses for 12- to 17-year-olds never went to Ministers, and the royal commission finds that."

acuity.statement: Could I ask the Minister: how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected as a result of the Government of that time ignoring the advice of people who knew what they were talking about?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand just established — advice on under-18 mandates that was not acted on — and asks for the scale of its effect, so the question depends on what preceded it. It takes the premise as settled rather than testing the dispute about it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The reality is that that advice was provided to the Ministers, and the mandates that it related to continued to stay in effect for some time after that."

acuity.statement: Well, the reality is that there would be tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of young people in that age group, and the reality was—as is outlined in paragraphs 413 and 414 of the report—that a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the magnitude the question asked for and cites the paragraphs said to support the premise. The answer is shaped by the question rather than being a return to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected"

acuity.statement: Does the report mention any officials who were sacked for failing to advise the Government Ministers of the time, or is it a case where they did advise the Government Ministers of the time and the Ministers who are claiming today to be innocent are denying all knowledge? Is there anybody in the report who was fired for failing to advise Ministers?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the live disagreement about whether officials failed to pass the advice on and puts the two branches of it as alternatives, but asks about a matter the preceding answer did not address, so it engages the strand rather than the specific claim made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins"

acuity.statement: Speaking to the point of order, sir, I never said that the Labour Government gave its permission; I said that the Labour Government approved of it in the context of an agreement—i.e., they expressed their agreement. If you have any doubt, I shall table the Cabinet paper where they say that. And why don’t we ask the Clerk to consult the dictionary as to whether “approval” can be an expression of agreement, as opposed to offering a consent or permission?
acuity.explanation: Takes up Hipkins's specific objection — that Labour did not approve the closure because it was a private business — and answers it directly by distinguishing two senses of 'approval', offering a Cabinet paper as evidence and inviting an adjudication on the word. The reply would be entirely different had Hipkins objected on other grounds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'The Labour Government did not approve the winding down of Marsden Point; it was a private business' — Chris Hipkins

acuity.statement: Mr Speaker, based on Shane Jones’ logic, then every closure of a factory that’s happened over the last couple of years has been approved by this Government. The fact that it happened to happen whilst we were in Government does not mean that the previous Government approved it.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact inference Jones had just offered — that a government in office at the time of a closure thereby 'approved' it — and runs it out to its consequence for this Government's own record. The statement is wholly contingent on the reasoning in the turn immediately before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I said that the Labour Government approved of it in the context of an agreement—i.e., they expressed their agreement' — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: Roughly 20 percent of the global oil supply, not exclusively feedstock, does pass through the Strait of Hormuz. But more importantly, two-thirds of the crude used by the refineries in Asia which deliver our fuel does come from the Middle East.
acuity.explanation: Supplies precisely the Middle East material McAnulty had just complained was absent, with figures for the Strait of Hormuz and Asian refinery feedstock, rather than continuing on Marsden Point. Not a full 1.0 because it addresses the subject McAnulty pointed to rather than disputing anything he argued, and the surrounding answer returns to the prepared Marsden Point line.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the question was about the Middle East; the answer has nothing to do with it' — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: A far-sighted nationalist party, New Zealand First, put it in the coalition agreement. However, it’s important that our wee nation does develop and implement a fuel security plan, and I’ll be the first to acknowledge that all sides of the House have an interest in fuel security—with the exception of the Greens, who do not believe in fossil fuels.
acuity.explanation: Hipkins had just made a specific point — that the Minister conceded all of Marsden Point's feedstock was imported, which undercuts the vulnerability claim — and none of it is taken up. The statement is on the subject of fuel security but would read identically whatever had preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins argued that Jones had just admitted 100 percent of the fuel refined at Marsden Point was itself imported, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: At new section 76, I just wanted to make one more quick plug for my amendments, which speak specifically to this. Again, I have no issue with commencement beginning on publication date. The issue I pointed to the Minister who was in the chair was that should that secondary piece of legislation fall off a website, it would still be law, regardless of people not being able to access it. So my amendment—and I’ve proposed a couple of alternatives—could go some way to addressing that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's specific answer — that clause 20's commence-on-publication rule 'kind of takes care of' the publication concern — concedes the commencement point, and identifies the residual case it does not cover (legislation falling off the website while remaining law). The speech would be different had Meager answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "the fact that the secondary legislation doesn’t come into force until it’s published kind of takes care of that"

acuity.statement: I think the question from the member is: “Should there be a requirement to publish an exempted piece of secondary legislation on the official website at some stage or within a certain time frame?” I’ll grab some advice from the officials on that, but the reassurance from new section 76(a) and (b) is that a similar effect will take place, and it would be good practice, in my view, if we are trying to get all secondary legislation in one place, to have that on the official record at some point.
acuity.explanation: Restates the member's question in her own terms and answers it on the substance by pointing to the combined effect of new section 76(a) and (b), while being explicit about what he must take advice on. Directly shaped by what Walters asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "what about the possibility of having subsequent publication requirements where there is an emergency initially"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Yes, just to acknowledge the fact that the nod before was from the officials around the consolidation.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the preceding exchange — confirming whose nod it was — rather than engagement with the content of the Minister's answer on publication exemptions or official versions. On the matter under debate, but a mere reference, not a response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "I’ll take the member’s word that the nods are from officials" — acknowledged, but the substance of his answer is not taken up

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and thank you to the Minister for that response, although it does sound like there may well be cases where there are more permanent exemptions in place. Potentially, the argument still stands, and just to support the question from my colleague Lawrence Xu-Nan, that was a question raised by the Law Commission, as well, in terms of why it was that we had the unusual situation where we have one department that is drafting primary legislation while the rest is done through the Parliamentary Counsel Office.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific load-bearing element of the Minister's answer — that exemptions would be temporary and so published by process — by noting his own caveat (Schedule 3 exempt Acts) implies permanent exemptions, so her concern survives. Also picks up Xu-Nan's IRD point and adds support to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "because they’re temporary, they would also be required to be presented to the House"

acuity.statement: I think the issue would be that the new section says that “A report may include—(a) recommendations for the repeal of redundant or spent legislation or provisions of legislation;”. If it was “must include”, then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn’t have to do it, or otherwise you’d be requiring it to report on something that it might not be recommending. That’s the reason why it’s a “may” rather than a “must”.
acuity.explanation: Answers precisely the question put — whether the annual report's repeal recommendations were considered as a mandatory item — by quoting the provision the member cited and giving the drafting reason for 'may'. The answer is wholly determined by her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "My question to the Minister is whether there was consideration given to making that mandatory."

acuity.statement: Then there was the question from Dr Xu-Nan about the IRD, and whether we could go back to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for consistency. As he reflected, they have been doing this since 1995. There are benefits in having separate policy and drafting responsibilities.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Xu-Nan's actual argument — that the 1990s capacity rationale no longer holds, so the select committee's recommendation to return drafting to PCO should be accepted — and answers it with a competing rationale (separate policy and drafting responsibilities, specialist expertise, enhanced collaboration). Engages the reasoning rather than just the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker

Not 1.0 because it then moves to fresh, prepared question areas rather than pressing the engagement further.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins' preceding answer locating the repealed duties — Belich: "in clause 51, we’re repealing section 58; where are those new duties? I believe that she said they’re in 45"

acuity.statement: So questions around the Data and Statistics Act: clauses 54, 55, 56 amend sections 6 and 12 of the Data and Statistics Act 2022 to provide the Government Statistician to be appointed under this Act while retaining some of the process elements of the Public Service Act. So, basically, they must advertise and run a contestable process, but does not require the forwarding of recommendation by the Minister or the approval of the Governor-General; so a slightly different process.
acuity.explanation: Answers the exact question put: names the amending clauses, and supplies the substance Belich asked for — what process will now apply to appointing the Government Statistician, including which existing requirements (ministerial recommendation, Governor-General approval) fall away. The reply could not have been given to a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "what process will now occur in relation to the appointment of the Government Statistician, under that?"

acuity.statement: Thanks for your answers around the Government Statistician. It appears that that’s not as substantial a change as it might have appeared, and I think the Crown pastoral land stewardship duties remaining unchanged. That’s helpful to know as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up both specific answers just given (the Government Statistician appointment process and the carried-over Crown pastoral land stewardship obligation), accepts them on the record as resolving her earlier concern, and then moves on to fresh clauses. Clearly shaped by what Collins said rather than prepared material, though the engagement is acceptance rather than argument, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Government Statistician is deemed to be the Chief Executive of Stats NZ. So that is not affected." — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: There is a question about judicial review that is still able to be undertaken and that’s to maintain the rights of people to do that. So that’s from Schedule 8 to Part 3 of the Public Service Act.
acuity.explanation: Directly addresses the deletion Belich asked about and supplies the provision that preserves the right, which is the confirmation she requested. It engages the specific question rather than the general topic, but answers only part of it (it does not address whether the change is substantive, or her Legislation Act point), so mid-high rather than top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether that was a substantive change to the judicial review rights in the Employment Relations Act because it was, in fact, a deletion and not a replacement" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: In relation to policing, well, the police, they’re not—the Chair will know this—strictly public servants in terms of taking instruction. In fact, quite the opposite. Policing independence and independence of actions are absolutely inherent in our Policing Act, so the issue, really, is independence versus oversight.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact tension Belich identified in the select committee insertion — independence of policing versus Public Service Commissioner oversight — names it as the issue, confirms her reading ("The member's correct"), and draws out the limit that constabulary functions must not be interfered with. The speech would have been different had she raised a different concern.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there will be some Public Service agencies or organisations, like the Police, who do have to carry out independent duty but still require some oversight" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: I just wanted to come back to ask a question under the new section 11A, inserted by clause 11, item (f).
acuity.explanation: Eligible — a substantive turn by another member precedes it — but it engages no part of that turn. It is on the matter under debate (the same bill at committee stage), which keeps it out of 0.0, but it is self-contained prepared material on a different clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Judith Collins had just explained policing independence versus Public Service oversight and the appointment of commissioners, and this question takes up none of it, opening instead on financial stewardship under clause 11.

acuity.statement: So the financial stewardship, which says that they’ve got to have that, “including building and maintaining a financially literate workforce”, is actually critically important to getting the best value, but also really ensuring that the staff working in these agencies add skills—get skills for themselves—because pretty much anybody’s work is going to be improved if they understand the numbers behind those decisions and also what these decisions mean in terms of the budgets.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise phrase Sosene asked about, quoting it back and then supplying the rationale she requested — both the value-for-money purpose and the staff-skills purpose. The reply is unmistakably built on her question rather than on prepared notes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m just really interested in that “financially literate workforce”" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: Just in terms of unpacking that, Minister, I appreciate that chief executives of various Public Service agencies are required to have those financial skills, but I just wanted to understand what the level would be.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the answer that was given (chief executives' obligations) and presses on exactly what it left open — how far down the organisation the expectation runs. A follow-up that could only have been framed this way because of the answer immediately preceding it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "not only for the chief executives to have to be financially literate, but for them to help their staff to gain skills that they may not have" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, I think quite a few of these questions are actually relitigating over Part 1, but I’m happy to say that I’d expect that Part 2 is just consequentials; changing cross-references to the Part 1 provisions have already been dealt with. But I would say that I expect chief executives to use their common sense and their knowledge in understanding their staff, if that would be helpful.
acuity.explanation: Engages the question in part: it characterises where the question sits relative to the bill's parts and offers a gesture at an answer (chief executives' discretion over their own staff), but declines to supply the thing actually asked for — how far the financial-literacy expectation extends through an agency. One strand taken up, the specific claim left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just wanted to understand what the level would be" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: This amendment would allow for loot boxes to be incorporated into what we considered online casino gambling technology, and I have provided in that amendment specific definitions of what a loot box would be considered to be, as well as the definition of a video game, with the intent of genuinely engaging constructively with the Minister to see whether she’s received feedback or heard about the damage that loot boxes can create in families and young people as a relatively new form of online gambling.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Leary's substantive turn precedes this one in the same committee-stage debate. But the speech is self-contained prepared advocacy for his own Amendment Paper 542: it addresses the Minister directly and would read word-for-word the same whatever Leary had just said. It sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.5 because no strand of her argument is engaged — there is only a thematic gesture at the debate (both concern the narrowness of the clause 5 definitions), which earns 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that "The definitions are narrow and operator focused" and pressed the Minister on enforcement of the territorial provisions, and this statement does not take up either argument.

acuity.statement: Firstly, the bill does enable both offshore and domestic operators to apply for a licence because it’s reflecting the reality of the status quo, which is that most online casino gambling in New Zealand is currently provided by offshore operators who operate outside of New Zealand law.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding critique — why operators need no New Zealand presence — and does something with it, supplying a rationale (status quo of offshore provision, free-trade obligations, competitive pressure). Not 1.0 because it answers the adjacent question rather than the specific one put: Leary asked what the enforcement mechanisms are and challenged Seymour's blocking claim, and neither is addressed; the loot-box question from the immediately preceding speaker is also left untouched. Scored on engagement only — the persuasiveness and truth of the free-trade and consumer-choice reasoning belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the territorial part, which allows operators to operate in New Zealand from offshore" and "how does she expect this regime to be enforced when operators will have no legal presence in New Zealand?" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: I thank the member for her questions. The member asks whether or not this bill is going to be an improvement of the status quo, and absolutely it is because it’s not a shock to anyone that this Government cares about regulating the online casino market and we are acting on it more so than the previous Government did, who recognised that there was an issue but never actually passed any legislation to deal with this issue.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's central question — whether New Zealand is better off under the regime than under the status quo — states a direct answer to it, and in the same turn addresses her specific request to see the regulations by pointing to the proactively released Cabinet decisions and the May Cabinet timetable. The reply would be materially different had Belich asked something else; the pivot to the previous Government's record is a Focus matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is the Minister satisfied that New Zealanders will actually be in a better position and there won’t be a huge influx" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: It’s a strong word, “prevent”; to stop. I guess what you just said earlier was how do we limit harm? The Minister said, “How do you limit harm?” So, immediately, we go into that, basically, we can’t prevent it.
acuity.explanation: Engages the Minister's own framing — that the bill restricts and limits gambling harm — and sets it against the stronger word "prevent" in clause 3(c), drawing out the inconsistency and asking her to resolve it. Partial rather than full: the specific phrase he quotes back comes from an earlier exchange outside this window, and the second half of the call moves to his own prepared Amendment Paper 539.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This bill will actually restrict advertising and it will restrict quite a lot of what is happening with online gambling at the moment" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: Minister, you’ve talked about advertising and minimising harm, etc., and it’s really helpful that you also remind members where the information is online to help us further understand.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the Minister's answer that the regulatory material is already published and builds on it by pressing for the underlying official advice and the specific advertising controls. That is engagement with one strand — the topic the Minister raised — rather than with her claim that advertising requirements will be "very strict"; the bulk of the call is her own prepared questions on offshore advertising and licence numbers.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ve proactively released the Cabinet decisions about regulations and I think those went up, potentially, last year" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: In reference to Mike Davidson’s comment about whether or not we should have a new provision within the bill about limiting or reducing the growth of online casino gambling, I don’t believe that is necessary because ultimately the online casino gambling market, at the moment, is completely unregulated.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific amendment just moved, states a position on it, and gives a reason tied to its content — that the bill's purpose is ring-fencing an unregulated market rather than growing it, so a growth-reduction purpose is redundant. The speech could not have been delivered without Davidson's amendment having been put. Whether that reasoning actually answers his "prevent harm" point is a Rigor question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that was just to seek to control the growth of gambling. So that Amendment Paper 539 was to add another clause to limit or reduce the growth of online casino gambling" — Mike Davidson

acuity.statement: Look, I think we’re already starting to get off track in terms of the parts of the bill that we are talking about. You’ll note that Part 5 deals with the regulations and the minimum standards, with specific mention and reference to regulations relating to harm prevention and minimisation, and regulations relating to advertising and marketing.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies what Sosene asked about — advertising controls and harm-minimisation regulation — and locates it in Part 5, but declines to engage the content of the question on relevance grounds. That is a partial, procedural engagement rather than a reply to the claim or question itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how will there be specific wording, specific tools, specific regulations on advertising? ... What controls are in place?" — Lemauga Lydia Sosene

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Speaking to all of those questions, I’m also interested in futureproofing for new technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) is one of those areas. The regulations do actually allow for the regulatory framework to respond quickly to changes in technology, which is why we haven’t been so explicit within the law but we are becoming more explicit within the regulations so that we can adapt to new technology over time. AI is one of those areas where the regulations can give the member some comfort.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific concern that clause 5(a) omits artificial intelligence and that the bill will date quickly, and supplies a direct answer to it: the omission is deliberate because the futureproofing is done in regulations, which can be changed faster than primary legislation. The reply is shaped by the precise question asked — it names the clause-level worry (AI not listed) and explains the drafting choice behind it — and would have had to be different had Belich raised a different objection. She goes on in the same turn to answer the clause 5(b)(iv) administrative-purposes question and the Schedule 1 timing question she was asked, which confirms engagement rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Artificial intelligence isn’t specifically listed here, and I wondered whether that would be something that may mean that the definition of “advertisement” is too narrow to cover some of the new technologies that might be emerging."

acuity.statement: But just to, I guess, provide another angle to what the previous speaker, Camilla Belich, mentioned in terms of verification process, I would just like to ask, further, how the Secretary for Internal Affairs would verify “source and amount of capital available” as a part of that criteria process.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up one strand of Belich's preceding question — how DIA verifies applicant information — and extends it to a specific further criterion (source and amount of capital). The rest of the turn is his own prepared material on clause 15, so the engagement is partial rather than a full taking-up of her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "to what extent will the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) be checking the validity of the information provided?"

acuity.statement: I’d like to turn to Subpart 3, which I note we’ve only had about half a question on, I think, some time ago, and it’s quite a big section. I really want to frame these in terms of the risk of regulatory capture, because what we can see from this licensing regime is that there are a number of purposes, including competition in a commercial market, but also revenue gathering for the Government.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate — the same bill and the same licensing regime — but engages no part of the two preceding arguments. The only acknowledgement of what came before is a procedural observation that Subpart 3 has had 'about half a question'. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich and Lawrence Xu-Nan had just put detailed verification and clause 14/15 questions, and this turn does not take any of them up; it only gestures at how little of Subpart 3 has been covered.

acuity.statement: Ingrid Leary then also asked about the flexibility of regulations and whether or not we needed to have more, I guess, detail in the bill because the regulations might be too flexible. I disagree because, as we’ve been referring to earlier today with some of the concerns from her colleague Camilla Belich about the use of artificial intelligence, having flexible law that allows for modernisation and technological changes, as well as some of the regulations to be updated with the changing dynamics that might happen on social media and the online environment, does require the bill itself to be flexible in nature so that we can adjust to technological developments without needing to go through an entire new Act and law of Parliament.
acuity.explanation: States Leary's argument back in its own terms, says plainly that she disagrees, and gives a reason aimed at that argument — that regulatory flexibility is the point, because the technology moves faster than primary legislation. The answer would have had to be different had Leary argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "a lot of the devil in the detail will be in the regulations" and "does she accept that it will be really difficult to change the regulations in that environment?"

acuity.statement: Ingrid Leary also asked about the threshold not to renew a licence. Licence holders must meet the requirements of a licence to be able to get a renewal. If they no longer hold a licence, it will be known that they no longer hold one, as they won’t be on the register.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question by name and supplies an answer of sorts — the licence requirements are the threshold, and non-renewal is visible via the register — which also folds in her transparency point. But it restates the requirement rather than naming the statutory threshold Leary said was absent, so it engages the question without fully meeting its substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "the Secretary for Internal Affairs can decide not to renew a licence, but what is the threshold that’s to be applied there? There seems to be silence on that matter."

acuity.statement: You have stated that there will be very limited information in the public arena because it’s commercially sensitive, so even though the bill will be passed, probably, this year—in terms of the timeline of that, when will the public know what decisions are being made, and will there be further processes where the public can question the Secretary for Internal Affairs in their role?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer the Minister had just given on commercial sensitivity and draws out its consequence — if the information is withheld, when does the public ever learn what was decided, and by what route can they scrutinise the secretary. The earlier part of the turn (why 15 licences) is prepared material, so the engagement is real but confined to the closing question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "No, that’s unlikely as a lot of the information that’ll be sent to the Secretary for Internal Affairs should be commercially sensitive and we want to ensure they are having a fair, standard process."

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich did ask a question about the self-exclusion register. The self-exclusion register regulations need to be implemented by December 2027, because officials are currently working on this as it was a later edition, and so it won’t necessarily be ready when the bill passes; however, I would just suggest that, under the current status quo, there is no exclusion register.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question just put to her — the timing of the self-exclusion register relative to the bill's commencement — supplies the actual date (December 2027), concedes the gap, and argues the comparison should be with the unregulated status quo. The answer would be different had Belich asked something else; across the turn she also names and answers the questions from Sosene, Davidson and Leary individually.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Will the self-exclusion register be available at the time that the main bill comes into effect?"

acuity.statement: Just to point out that my question around clause 37 was not about the 90 days; it was about the minimum mandatory duties, and I’d really welcome a response to that.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects a misstatement of her own question in the answer she has just heard, identifying precisely which part of clause 37 was mischaracterised and what remains unanswered. This sentence could not exist without the Minister's preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Ingrid Leary also asked about platforms and why they must operate within 90 days."

acuity.statement: Mike Davidson had a question in relation to his Amendment Paper 549 about credit. Look, the clause that’s in the bill is modelled off the Gambling Act, and it’s very clear that no credit must be offered by operators, regardless of the type of credit. Credit sourced by consumers, such as credit cards, will actually be restricted through the regulations, so his amendment is not necessary.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the amendment just proposed on its merits — accepts the subject matter, explains why the existing drafting already covers every type of credit, and locates consumer-sourced credit in the regulations instead — reaching a reasoned conclusion that the amendment is unnecessary. She also takes up Leary's pronunciation point and minimum-duties question and Sosene's amendment in the same turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "I’m just wondering whether the Minister would consider supporting that amendment."

acuity.statement: It was actually in relation to a matter that was raised earlier, around clause 42. I guess it’s very clear that it’s quite a vague clause, because it doesn’t quite lay out what they’re talking about when they mention “credit”.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand of the preceding exchange — the ambiguity of "credit" in clause 42 — and offers a specific remedy for it, so the contribution is shaped by what came before. But it does not engage the Minister's actual answer about what does and does not count as credit; it restates the vagueness claim and moves to his prepared amendment paper.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Camilla also asked, “Will free credit be available if the money is not to be paid back?” That is not credit."

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and to the Minister. I do have some questions with clause 46, and I do have an Amendment Paper 536.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the bill under debate, so not wholly unresponsive, but the turn engages no part of any preceding argument — including the Minister's answer to her own earlier question. It is prepared material on her own amendment paper and a different clause, and would read identically whoever had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Davidson spoke about the vagueness of "credit" in clause 42 and his Amendment Paper 549, and this statement does not take it up; nor does it take up the Minister's earlier answer that protections for Sosene's question are "fleshed out in more detail in the regulations"

acuity.statement: I know that my colleague Camilla Belich does have further questions; I just haven’t heard an answer from the Minister in relation to how monitoring and compliance will occur for operators, to ensure people don’t spend hours gambling across multiple platforms—or is she comfortable with the fact that the bill is silent on that?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — monitoring and compliance of online gambling operators — and it registers that the Minister has not answered, but it engages no part of the content of the preceding turn. Leary introduces her own distinct question (multi-platform play) rather than carrying forward Belich's points about continuation of operation or a secretary-held complaints register. A gesture at the debate without engaging the argument, so the 0.3 end of the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I think these are prudent provisions to have in a bill, but I just wonder whether they go far enough" — Leary notes her colleague has further questions but does not take up any part of the clause 43-49 argument (significant influence, key officers, complaints registers).

acuity.statement: Well, it’s a difficult situation to be in because we have had important questions that haven’t been answered in this part. I’d like to give the Minister the opportunity to answer those questions, or some assurance that these may be able to be addressed in a latter part of the debate.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — the complaint that the Minister has left questions unanswered — and does something with it, pressing for either an answer now or an assurance of one later. It does not engage Leary's specific substantive point about gambling across multiple platforms, and returns to her own earlier framing that the clauses 'seem quite prudent'. Partial engagement that can be pointed at: 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I just haven’t heard an answer from the Minister" — Belich picks up that strand and converts it into a direct invitation to the Minister to answer before the part closes.

acuity.statement: Speaking to some of the questions from Camilla Belich: firstly, she asked whether or not there would be a separate requirement for complaints to the Secretary for Internal Affairs. Section 68 sets out the process for complaints to the secretary.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question put to her and supplies the thing it asked for: the clause of the bill that creates a complaints process to the secretary. The speech would be different if Belich had asked something else — it is built around her questions. Not a full 1.0 only because the second half of Belich's question (whether an operator may keep trading while due diligence on new key officers is outstanding) is answered with the three-licence rule rather than on the pause point, and Leary's question is not taken up at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "was there any thought given or will there be a separate requirement for the secretary to have its own complaints register" — van Velden names that exact question and supplies the provision that answers it.

acuity.statement: The reality is that that advice was provided to the Ministers, and the mandates that it related to continued to stay in effect for some time after that. Concerns were clearly made, and the reality is that the questions around why those decisions were made are questions that would need to be put to the former Ministers.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise factual claim Hipkins had just made — that the CV TAG advice never reached Ministers — and contradicts it by citing the report paragraph he says records the advice being provided, then draws the consequence that the former Ministers must answer for the mandates staying in force. The turn would be different had Hipkins not made that claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "The Vaccine Technical Advisory Group advice against two doses for 12- to 17-year-olds never went to Ministers, and the royal commission finds that."

acuity.statement: Could I ask the Minister: how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected as a result of the Government of that time ignoring the advice of people who knew what they were talking about?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand just established by the Minister — the CV TAG advice on under-18 vaccine mandates and the mandates remaining in force — and presses it one step further by asking for the scale of the affected cohort. Not a full engagement with the reasoning, but clearly built on the content of the preceding turn rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "that advice was provided to the Ministers, and the mandates that it related to continued to stay in effect for some time after that"

acuity.statement: Well, the reality is that there would be tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of young people in that age group, and the reality was—as is outlined in paragraphs 413 and 414 of the report—that a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the quantity asked for directly and immediately, then grounds it in the report paragraphs. Marked below 1.0 because he then falls back into re-reading the same paragraph 414 passage he had already quoted in his previous turn rather than developing the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Winston Peters: "how many tens of thousands of 12- to 17-year-olds could have been adversely affected"

acuity.statement: Does the report mention any officials who were sacked for failing to advise the Government Ministers of the time, or is it a case where they did advise the Government Ministers of the time and the Ministers who are claiming today to be innocent are denying all knowledge?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's answer — that the advice did reach Ministers — and turns it into a dilemma about where responsibility sits. But it ignores the figure the Minister had just supplied and opens a fresh line about officials being dismissed, so it engages the topic and one implication rather than the answer given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "a briefing was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins"

acuity.statement: But the truth is that there are more. This is the guy, when he was Minister of Police, crime went up. When he was Minister of Education, school attendance went down.
acuity.explanation: A list of unrelated portfolio grievances against the previous speaker that engages no part of the argument he had just made. It would read word-for-word the same whatever Hipkins had said, and is not even directed at the royal commission report under debate — only a gesture at the fact that Hipkins was the target keeps it off 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins had just defended the COVID-19 response, disputed the claim that the Auckland boundary was in place over Christmas, and asserted the level 4 extension was not against health advice — this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: At new section 76, I just wanted to make one more quick plug for my amendments, which speak specifically to this. Again, I have no issue with commencement beginning on publication date. The issue I pointed to the Minister who was in the chair was that should that secondary piece of legislation fall off a website, it would still be law, regardless of people not being able to access it. So my amendment—and I’ve proposed a couple of alternatives—could go some way to addressing that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's clause 20 answer directly and disputes its sufficiency: she concedes commencement-on-publication is fine but identifies the gap it does not cover (legislation disappearing from the website after commencement), and ties that to her own amendments. The speech would be different had Meager pointed elsewhere.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the fact that the secondary legislation doesn’t come into force until it’s published kind of takes care of that" — James Meager

acuity.statement: I’ll stand to be corrected, but my instinct would be that the legal status of any secondary legislation or, in fact, legislation, would be that the Order in Council or the regulation which is signed off by the Minister or the Governor-General is the one that is the final version and has legal force, in the same way that the statute which is given the Royal assent is the final version, but I’ll take some advice if that’s to the contrary.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific question just put — the legal status of official versions — with a substantive answer by analogy to Royal assent, while flagging that he will check it. Squarely engaged with the content of the preceding turn rather than the topic in general.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder if the Minister could speak to the effect of having official versions of legislation and what their legal status is" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Yes, just to acknowledge the fact that the nod before was from the officials around the consolidation. I think a really important aspect maybe for people who don’t spend as much time on the legislation website—particularly, I think, when we’re looking at it from a judiciary sense—it’s really important for agency drafting and published secondary legislation to be able to track some of those version histories.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the preceding exchange (confirming whose nod it was) and then prepared praise of version-history tracking. It engages no part of the argument Meager had just made about new section 76 or official versions, so it sits in the low band with a visible glance at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ll take the member’s word that the nods are from officials" — James Meager; but nothing of Meager's substantive answers on exemptions or the legal status of official versions is taken up

acuity.statement: I’ll address the question from Vanushi Walters around that exemption. Essentially, the publication exemptions in new section 76, inserted by clause 19, would, in most circumstances, if not all, I think, be temporary. So, because they’re temporary, they would also be required to be presented to the House.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the member's specific question, having taken advice, and answers it with the mechanism that bears on it — exemptions being temporary and therefore published by process once they end. Entirely shaped by the claim it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what about the possibility of having subsequent publication requirements where there is an emergency initially, so you do want the secondary legislation to commence, but in due course you also want it to be published" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and thank you to the Minister for that response, although it does sound like there may well be cases where there are more permanent exemptions in place. Potentially, the argument still stands, and just to support the question from my colleague Lawrence Xu-Nan, that was a question raised by the Law Commission, as well, in terms of why it was that we had the unusual situation where we have one department that is drafting primary legislation while the rest is done through the Parliamentary Counsel Office.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the answer in part and presses the exception to it — that permanent exemptions would escape the temporariness argument — and then reinforces a colleague's unanswered question with an external source. Direct work on the reasoning just offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because they’re temporary, they would also be required to be presented to the House" — James Meager

acuity.statement: If it was “must include”, then, therefore, the report would be legally required to include recommendations on something that it might not have a recommendation on. A report has the option of including a recommendation, but it doesn’t have to do it, or otherwise you’d be requiring it to report on something that it might not be recommending. That’s the reason why it’s a “may” rather than a “must”.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise drafting question asked about new section 83A(2) and gives the reason for the drafting choice. The response could not have been given to any other question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My question to the Minister is whether there was consideration given to making that mandatory" — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: Then there was the question from Dr Xu-Nan about the IRD, and whether we could go back to the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO) for consistency. As he reflected, they have been doing this since 1995. There are benefits in having separate policy and drafting responsibilities. The IRD, or Inland Revenue (IR)—although I think it’s been the IRD for a while—has the ability to require particular expertise and dedicated resource.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the member's own framing, including the date he cited, and supplies a reason for retaining the arrangement rather than restating the clause. Engagement with the specific objection raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why was there the intention to continue this anomaly of IRD drafting its own bills" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Just moving along, we do have a few more parts to Part 1, and I want to move to a new clause, which is clause 31. Actually, let’s take clauses 30 and 31 together, in terms of editorial changes.
acuity.explanation: Proceeds to the next clause without engaging the answer just given to his own question. The material is on the bill under debate, so it is not wholly unresponsive, but nothing of the preceding turn's content is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just answered this member's IRD question by citing the benefits of separating policy and drafting responsibilities, and this statement does not take that answer up before moving on to clauses 30 and 31

acuity.statement: I’ll have to think about the interaction between the powerful Regulations Review Committee and the Parliamentary Counsel Office’s editorial change ability. Somewhere in the back of my mind is the thought that the threshold for Regulations Review Committee complaints or inquiries into the validity of regulations is relatively high under the Standing Orders.
acuity.explanation: Names the exact interaction the member asked about and offers the beginning of an answer — the Standing Orders threshold — before conceding he must take advice. Clearly shaped by the question, though it stops short of resolving it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which department trumps which in those kinds of situations, where you have the possibility of multiple people seeking to make editorial changes" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I know that in his inimitable way, Mr Xu-Nan is going very methodically through the legislation, but there is a point that I would like to raise, and it is skipping ahead a bit. It’s about revision bills, which is clause 37, and one of the cornerstones of this piece of legislation is broadening what a revision bill is, because it was the view of the Attorney-General and the Justice Committee that revision bills weren’t being used to full effect.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the previous speaker's manner but engages no part of the argument he or the Minister had just made, announcing instead a jump to a different clause. Prepared material on the right bill, which puts it in the low band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan and James Meager were debating editorial changes under clause 31 and the Regulations Review Committee's powers, and this statement expressly skips ahead to revision bills in clause 37 without taking that up

acuity.statement: I’ll address Dr Webb’s question in a second, after I’ve had time to recover from a piece of work I did on a revision bill when I was a practising lawyer, and spent many hours trying to go back and forth about what the definition of “minor” could be with a client and whether or not they could have recommended this particular change because it was minor or not.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Webb's point — the difficulty of defining "minor" in revision bills — with a relevant anecdote, but defers the substance of the question about how broadly new subsection (3)(b) should be read until advice arrives. Partial engagement that can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it says that a revision bill may also make minor amendments, and in this draft the word “minor” has disappeared" — Duncan Webb

acuity.statement: Just to pick up on the revision bill, I think the revision bill aspect is probably the most substantial and—well, all of this bill is substantial, but it’s probably the part that we don’t have certainty from the Minister on in terms of how it’s going to function.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding turn by Meager answered a question about the interplay and hierarchy between the Regulations Review Committee and agencies for editorial changes. This turn does not take that answer up at all — it opens a fresh line on revision bills and the word 'minor', with prepared material and three tabled amendments.
