It is squarely on the matter under debate (the same committee stage of the same bill) and gestures at the Minister's general position, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager said 'But in terms of the interplay, there is no real hierarchy' regarding the Regulations Review Committee and agencies, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In this instance, I would encourage those who have concerns about the removal of the word “minor” to look at both section 92 of the Act, which sets out the purpose, and look at new section 98, which is around the certification of revision bills, which requires that the certifiers are satisfied that the powers in section 96, which is what Dr Webb pointed to, have been exercised appropriately, having had regard to the purpose of section 92.
acuity.explanation: This takes the exact request just put to him — reassurance that the intention of 'minor' survives its removal from the text — and answers it on its own terms: it explains why the word was dropped (to avoid litigating 'minor' over century-old language), points to the specific statutory safeguards that do the work instead (ss 92, 98, 99 and the qualifiers in clause 37(5)), engages Webb's 'nefarious Parliament' worry, and states plainly that the amendments will not be supported. The speech would be unrecognisable had Xu-Nan raised a different point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'I ask the Minister: is there a way for us to have the reassurance that, though it is not specified, the intention of “minor” remains?' — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: If the mechanism already exists using a statutes bill, as an example, or even other forms of omnibus bills, like a regulatory systems bill that we have seen a number of times in this House, why then do we need to expand the scope?
acuity.explanation: He picks up the Minister's own worked example (the Valuers Bill) and the Minister's stated rationale — that the back-and-forth over 'minor' should be avoided — and presses it: if Statutes Amendment Bills and regulatory systems bills already achieve the tidying-up the Minister wants, the expansion of scope is unnecessary. He also concedes the select committee safeguards in clauses 38 and 39 while maintaining the core objection, which is the mark of having listened rather than recited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Essentially, the intention is to avoid those long back and forth debates on whether or not a change is minor or not.' — James Meager (who also raised the Valuers Bill as his example)

acuity.statement: To have two bills go through in 14 years since the system’s been available is probably not a great reflection of its accessibility and usability. Part of the reason for these changes is to provide a bit more flexibility and scope for revision bills to meet the threshold for certification.
acuity.explanation: He takes the specific count Xu-Nan had just supplied — only a couple of revision bills have ever met the threshold — and turns it into the answer to Xu-Nan's 'why expand the scope' question, then goes further and accepts the member's broader premise that statutes amendment and regulatory systems bills will make the mechanism progressively redundant. This is engagement with the content of the preceding argument, including the part that tells against him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'there’s only been, I think, two other instances of revision bills that have actually met the threshold' — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Thank you for that, Minister. I’m now moving on to, I think, probably the last few clauses of Part 1.
acuity.explanation: The Minister had just conceded a good deal — that two bills in 14 years is a poor reflection on the mechanism, and that it may eventually be worth repealing the revision-bill machinery altogether. That concession is left entirely unexamined; the member acknowledges it and proceeds to prepared questions on clauses 45 and 49. On the same bill and the same debate, so not 0.0, but no part of the preceding argument is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager argued 'It could be the case that there would be an argument in the future to amend the Standing Orders to remove the need or requirement for revision bills', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: On the second of those two points that he’s raised: I see that it’s proposed to amend the principal Act, such that in the interpretation section—being section 5 but clause 6 of the bill—the definition of “minimum legislative information” would have inserted after it “ ‘or MLI’ ”, effectively defining that term, albeit that it’s an acronym that is, at least as yet, not as well known as, for example, “PCO”. I take his point around that.
acuity.explanation: Takes Webb's specific drafting complaint and corrects the premise by pointing to the exact place in clause 6 where the acronym is in fact defined, while conceding the point about relative familiarity. The answer could not have been given to any other question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "my concern is that MLI is never defined"

acuity.statement: My first one is really about an aspect of the bill that we probably generally agree with—this single point of access for primary and secondary legislation. The Greens think anything that makes legislation more accessible to the ordinary person is a good thing.
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on the right subject — the bill's single point of access — but engaging no part of the exchange that preceded it. The contribution would have been identical whatever the Minister had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just answered Duncan Webb on the definition of "MLI" and on "instrument of the Crown", and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: My new understanding, the new knowledge on which I’m relying, is that an “instrument of the Crown” is not a department but might otherwise describe—I’m trying not to use the word “entity”, because a Crown entity is different again. An example of the instrument of the Crown, I’m told, is PCO, the Parliamentary Counsel Office—there’s an acronym, and for our Speaker, who loves acronyms so much, I might just add “L-O-L”, which, of course, means “lots of love”.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the precise question Webb asked earlier, supplies the definition and a worked example, and distinguishes it from the adjacent category Webb had raised. Squarely responsive to the content of the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "how, outside of Crown entities, local authorities, and departments, exactly what this ‘instrument of the Crown’ is"

acuity.statement: I wonder if I can connect that back to a point that was made by Celia Wade-Brown, which I think I understand to be around having a single point of failure in terms of where all the information might be, which could have an implication for, you know, vulnerability in the case of a cyber-attack or other outage, even of non-suspicious origin. I think, if I understand correctly, the mechanism by which the websites would operate, it includes that the sites in question sometimes has an aggregator function and it can sort of point to other Government agency or, indeed, Crown instrument sites.
acuity.explanation: Restates Wade-Brown's single-point-of-failure argument accurately, then does something with it — explains that the site's aggregator architecture means the data is not in fact all in one place. Also ties Webb's sovereignty question into the same answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Celia Wade-Brown: "whether the single point of access also creates a certain vulnerability"

acuity.statement: Ms Walters would surely know that the Regulations Review Committee doesn’t need 100 working days to do anything. But, you know, I understand the point she’s making in her amendment to the amendment to the Legislation Amendment Bill.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific number in her proposed amendment to his amendment and answers it, albeit with a jibe first. The reply depends entirely on what she had just proposed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "I have proposed a number of different days, including 100 working days after the time required to do so under the House’s rules and practice"

acuity.statement: That’s understandable, but can I just check with the Minister in terms of the operationalisation of secondary legislation: for example, when they haven’t been published—now on the single-source website—or have not been presented to the House and then they’re still considered effective, what would happen if someone is non-compliant with that regulation but doesn’t actually know that regulation has happened or taken place?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own concession of a "glitch in the matrix" and draws out its consequence — what happens to a citizen bound by a rule they could not have read. Builds directly on the preceding answer rather than reciting prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Penk: "she rightly notes, I suppose, a potential glitch in the matrix"

acuity.statement: On his first question, which I found really interesting, I think he’s highlighting a scenario in which there could be non-compliance with a rule of which a person is unaware, or potentially, compliance with a rule that no longer exists in a brief moment of time by reason of not having been presented, I suppose, in the first instance, or having perhaps lapsed in a way that Ms Walters has identified. I think he’s asking whether the law or the rule would be said to be effective or not, in that situation.
acuity.explanation: Reconstructs Xu-Nan's hypothetical in his own words, links it to Walters' separate lapse scenario, and then answers it. The response is shaped wholly by the question put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "what would happen if someone is non-compliant with that regulation but doesn’t actually know that regulation has happened or taken place?"

acuity.statement: The words I want to focus on are the words “as far as practicable” because that’s a balancing word. The question then becomes: is that the right threshold? I would have thought “as far as possible” would be a better framing because there’s a price quality trade-off.
acuity.explanation: A substantive and well-aimed point about the bill, but it opens a fresh line of its own; nothing in it turns on what the Minister or any other member had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just answered Lawrence Xu-Nan on the consequences of non-compliance, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: It’s a very fine distinction that Dr Webb highlights, not entirely without meaning, if I may say, in my view, but I sense that if we were to say that it must be available as far as or as much as possible, then that would inevitably be read in a way as to mean something along the lines of “reasonably possible” or “possible in the circumstances”. If the circumstances were that the first and second server were down and there was not a third, then that would be a matter of impossibility as well as impracticability.
acuity.explanation: Rebuts the precise wording argument on its own terms, accepts part of it, and uses Webb's own server-failure example to show why the substitution would not bite. Disagreement that demonstrates close listening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "I would have thought ‘as far as possible’ would be a better framing"

acuity.statement: The question for the Minister is: this feels like we have a moment to potentially make a change that New Zealanders may like, and I looked up why we have the Sovereign’s birthday in June. It turns out the origin of the Queen’s second birthday, or the June birthday, can be tracked back to the dilemma of planning a party around fickle British weather.
acuity.explanation: Entirely prepared material on a clause not yet under discussion; it would read the same whatever had preceded it, though it remains within the bill under examination.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just debated the "as far as practicable" threshold with Duncan Webb, and this statement moves to the Sovereign's birthday without engaging it.

acuity.statement: In terms of the point that Vanushi Walters made about the Sovereign’s birthday, the Associate Minister for Emergency Management Recovery has told me there’s no good time in New Zealand at which we can avoid inclement weather for the purpose of celebrating the Sovereign’s birthday—God save the King—so it’s not something that had occurred to me in terms of changing, but it seems to me that any change is as good a time as any, and one’s likelihood is no worse than any other time to have some kind of celebration, accordingly.
acuity.explanation: Answers the weather premise of her suggestion directly and on its own ground, sought advice on it, and gives a view on whether a change is warranted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "the origin of the Queen’s second birthday, or the June birthday, can be tracked back to the dilemma of planning a party around fickle British weather"

acuity.statement: The next two questions are in relation to clause 19. Lawrence Xu-Nan has asked one of the questions that I had on disability and access. My view, if the Minister was wanting to make an amendment, is that replacement section 74(3) may present an opportune place to add some language about accessibility for disabled people.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Xu-Nan's accessibility strand and advances it by naming the specific provision where it could be drafted in, rather than merely repeating the concern. Partial, in that the rest of the call returns to her own prepared list.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "will there be ways for us to be accessible from a disability lens"

acuity.statement: Just in response to Dr Xu-Nan’s last point: there’s no intention in this bill to look at mandatory drafting in te reo Māori, or, I guess, the equivalent in New Zealand Sign Language. There are, probably, very good reasons for that. I think our country has had quite an interesting history of drafting legal texts in two languages, and trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question squarely with a direct no and gives the reason against it, engaging the comparative-jurisdictions framing Xu-Nan had used.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "whether there is any consideration as part of this bill to also be able to draft—other than settlement bills—bills in te reo Māori"

acuity.statement: Just to address one of the questions around access, from Vanushi Walters, I’ve just got some advice here that the bill does support disabled communities’ access to legislation both in-house, published on agency websites, and the features of the new website. Regulations made under the bill will set out what forms and formats legislation must be published in.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the substantive answer to the accessibility questions put by Walters and Xu-Nan, including the specific standard the new site will aim at. Responsive to the content, not merely to the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "replacement section 74(3) may present an opportune place to add some language about accessibility for disabled people"

acuity.statement: Thank you for that response, Minister, but I guess this is a broader conversation for the House to consider when it comes to publishing in dual languages. Again, other countries—I mentioned Canada, but also other regions, I guess: Canada and also Wales are already doing things like that and they have no issues in terms of publishing in two languages.
acuity.explanation: Disputes the Minister's stated reason head-on by pointing to jurisdictions where the reconciliation problem has not materialised. The rebuttal is aimed at the specific objection just raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "trying to reconcile, perhaps, different interpretations of specific words in different languages can cause issues"

acuity.statement: I’d invite Dr Xu-Nan to maybe just reframe that question in the next call, because I was nodding in understanding of his position, not necessarily in response.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a misreading in the immediately preceding turn — the member had treated a nod as confirmation — and tells him what to do about it. Brief, but wholly determined by what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I’m seeing nods, which is great, so I’m guessing that has been clarified"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair—and thank you, Minister, because it does clarify it because I think the key definition here, when it comes to clause 52(8) and replacement clause 15(5) of page 37, is “on a date specified in the regulations”. I assume that the date specified in the regulation is to do with the commencement date in itself and not a specified date of a built-in revocation clause. So I think that clarification is an important one because what that means is if a piece of secondary legislation hasn’t met the requirement of subclause (2A), it is not just automatically revoked carte blanche as part of that. It has to have that built-in revocation clause which then limits the number of pieces of secondary legislation that you will have.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's immediately preceding explanation — that the sunset/revocation effect only operates where the revocation clause and date are contained in the instrument itself — restates it as a precise consequence for clause 52(8) and replacement clause 15(5), draws out what it means for subclause (2A), and offers his own reading of 'on a date specified in the regulations' for confirmation. The speech could not have been delivered without the Minister's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "the sunset clause sort of description I gave it only applies if it's actually contained within the regulation or the secondary legislation itself"

acuity.statement: Now, in terms of the Civil Aviation Act, I will get some more advice on this, but my instinct is, having had some experience with the orders that are drafted, that it is possibly to do with a similar situation that the IRD falls under, in that there is particular expertise within civil aviation, in terms of the regulation, it being a regulator there, that would encourage or require those to be drafted by those certifiers or those officials. But I’ll get back to the member.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question just put — why Schedule 4's Civil Aviation Act amendment expressly carves the PCO out of drafting — by offering a substantive hypothesis (in-house regulator expertise, by analogy with IRD) rather than a generic answer, while undertaking to return with advice. Not a full 1.0 because the figure/answer asked for is deferred rather than supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "is there a reason why it is specified explicitly that it cannot be drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office?"

acuity.statement: I acknowledge what the Minister said in terms of civil aviation having specific expertise, but that’s also the intention of secondary legislation, which is that, often, people who do draft secondary legislation—particularly when we’re looking at agency-administered, agency-drafted, or -published legislation—do use specific expertise within that agency or within that broader sector, but none of them specify that this clause is not to be drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office (PCO). So I’m still curious as to that level of specificity.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's premise and then rebuts the inference drawn from it: if agency expertise explained the carve-out, every agency-drafted instrument would carry one, and none do. The rebuttal is aimed squarely at the reasoning offered seconds earlier and would be impossible if the Minister had argued anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "there is particular expertise within civil aviation, in terms of the regulation, it being a regulator there, that would encourage or require those to be drafted by those certifiers or those officials"

acuity.statement: I’ll answer the question around the transitional provisions. The transitional provisions require all existing agencies’ secondary legislation to be republished. So everything needs to be republished. If an agency fails to republish, regulations can be made under the Legislation Act, which can provide the possibility that the legislation is revoked. However, those regulations haven’t been made at this stage, and, in all reality, it would likely only be made after the transitional period is finished.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the question the previous speaker had just pressed — what exactly is revoked if an agency misses the republication deadline — by explaining that revocation depends on regulations under the Legislation Act that have not been made, which resolves the specific uncertainty raised rather than restating prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "if it doesn’t get updated by the end of next year, is it just a consolidation—i.e., the previous version that’s revoked, or the entirety of the secondary legislation that’s revoked"

acuity.statement: I’ve got two questions on commencement. Picking up from where the Minister left off, I want to specifically focus on clause 2(4), which is the five-year aspect.
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact provision the Minister had just explained (the subclause (4) five-year fallback for clauses 9, 20 and 52) and presses on the part the Minister passed over, asking specifically why clause 20 needs five years. The questions could not have been written without hearing the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "And then for subclause (4), that just takes care of clauses 9, 20, and 52—same situation, but that gives a five-year anniversary from Royal assent rather than six months."

acuity.statement: Just for the first question, I’ll rack my brain, but I have done a bit of work in the past on the Incorporated Societies Act when that came into force. From memory, that’s the Incorporated Societies Act 2020, and I think there was sort of a fallback provision of being five years or six years after Royal assent for some of those provisions.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Xu-Nan's claim that he has never seen a five-year anniversary provision, offering a precedent and then explaining the transition rationale. Marked down slightly because he supplies a comparable statute rather than the specific agency example asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "were there any particular agencies or particular aspects of that in mind when this was drafted where the five years is required as kind of a prudent measure?"

acuity.statement: I think, if I can just deal with these notes, clauses 48 and 49 amending the Child Poverty Reduction Act is to provide an accurate cross-reference to the new section 11A, which is the principal responsibilities of chief executives. This maintains the existing provision under this Act for the Government Statistician and the Secretary for the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to act independently when publishing reports on child poverty.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put — whether the substitution of section 11A for section 52 preserves independence — naming the officeholders whose independence is retained. Not a full 1.0 because she then loses track of one of the questions asked and has to be prompted on clause 5C.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "will this particular clause and the change of section 52 to new section 11A maintain the same independence that is currently in section 52?"

acuity.statement: Well, that was suggested by the Public Service CEs themselves, and the point of that was to help them to know—they want to be clearer about the need to collaborate and to ensure, basically, interoperability as much as possible.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez's question was specifically why the broad principle "improving ways of working across public service agencies" became new section 11A(1)(g)'s interoperability/co-ordination wording. This answers that precise point — the change was requested by Public Service chief executives, to make the collaboration expectation clearer — so the reply would be different had a different clause been raised. Short of 1.0 because she had to be prompted from the floor to recall which clause was asked about, and she never addressed the second half of the question (whether any other transliterations were missed).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "why was that change made, and have I missed any other transliterations in the change from section 52 to new section 11A, and what were the reasons for these changes?"

acuity.statement: This is change which is not the same as the change which we’ve already discussed in relation to 11A, but it’s a specific change in relation to including section 11A(1)(j) in the primary piece of legislation.
acuity.explanation: Belich takes up the new section 11A the Minister had just been explaining and distinguishes her own question from it — the cross-reference to 11A(1)(j) in the Crown Pastoral Land Act rather than the drafting change just discussed — which shows she followed the preceding answer. But the engagement is one strand only: she then moves into prepared new areas (Crown Pastoral Land Act, Data and Statistics Act) that are indifferent to what Collins said, so this sits at partial responsiveness rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "which inserts new section 11A, "Principal responsibilities of chief executives of departments and departmental agencies""

acuity.statement: Questions about the Crown Pastoral Land Act; clauses 52 and 53 amend 22A(1)(a) of the Crown Pastoral Land Act 1998 to provide an accurate cross reference to new section 11A.
acuity.explanation: This answers the specific clause-level question Belich put — identifying the amending clauses and stating the amendment's effect as a cross-reference correction rather than a substantive change to the chief executive's stewardship duty. The reply is wholly dependent on what she was asked and would have to change entirely for a different question. Not 1.0 only because she worked through the questions out of order and openly lost one of them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I wanted to ask the Minister if there was a substantive change in repealing section 52(1)(d) of the primary Act"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. That is helpful. Probably one thing I’m not just 100 percent sure on is just a civil defence one, but I’m happy to come back to that later. Thanks for your answers around the Government Statistician. It appears that that’s not as substantial a change as it might have appeared, and I think the Crown pastoral land stewardship duties remaining unchanged. That’s helpful to know as well.
acuity.explanation: Belich takes up the substance of both answers Collins had just given — the Government Statistician appointment process and the carried-over Crown pastoral land stewardship obligation — accepts them, states what she now concludes from them, and then builds her next questions on that footing. The turn would read differently had Collins answered differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "The Government Statistician is deemed to be the Chief Executive of Stats NZ. So that is not affected."

acuity.statement: There is a question about judicial review that is still able to be undertaken and that’s to maintain the rights of people to do that. So that’s from Schedule 8 to Part 3 of the Public Service Act.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific question Belich had just asked — whether the deletion in the Employment Relations Act amendment removes judicial review rights — and answers the point by locating where the right is preserved. It engages the claim, not merely the topic, though it leaves her Legislation Act question untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "whether that was a substantive change to the judicial review rights in the Employment Relations Act because it was, in fact, a deletion and not a replacement"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to come back to ask a question under the new section 11A, inserted by clause 11, item (f). I’m interested, Minister, if you could explain, just in terms of the “financial stewardship of their agency, including building and maintaining a financially literate workforce“. I’m just really interested in that “financially literate workforce”.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new line of questioning on financial stewardship without taking up any part of Collins' immediately preceding answer on policing independence and commissioner appointments. It is squarely on the bill under committee consideration, so it is not unmoored from the debate, but it is indifferent to what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Judith Collins had just explained that the Public Service Commission assists but does not decide commissioner appointments, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: So the financial stewardship, which says that they’ve got to have that, “including building and maintaining a financially literate workforce”, is actually critically important to getting the best value, but also really ensuring that the staff working in these agencies add skills—get skills for themselves—because pretty much anybody’s work is going to be improved if they understand the numbers behind those decisions and also what these decisions mean in terms of the budgets.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact phrase Sosene asked about and explains what it is for and why the workforce limb was included, drawing out the purpose she was asking to have unpacked. The answer is wholly shaped by the question put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "I’m just really interested in that “financially literate workforce”."

acuity.statement: Just in terms of unpacking that, Minister, I appreciate that chief executives of various Public Service agencies are required to have those financial skills, but I just wanted to understand what the level would be. Would it just be the chief executive and those who are in senior public roles in terms of the staffing, or will that go to a certain point all the way down to different levels?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of Collins' answer about chief executives' obligations and presses the gap it left — how far down an agency the financial-literacy expectation reaches. A follow-up built directly on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Judith Collins: "not only for the chief executives to have to be financially literate, but for them to help their staff to gain skills that they may not have"

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, I think quite a few of these questions are actually relitigating over Part 1, but I’m happy to say that I’d expect that Part 2 is just consequentials; changing cross-references to the Part 1 provisions have already been dealt with. But I would say that I expect chief executives to use their common sense and their knowledge in understanding their staff, if that would be helpful.
acuity.explanation: Engages the follow-up in part: it characterises the question as already covered under Part 1, then does supply a position on the point asked — that the reach down an organisation is left to chief executives' judgement rather than prescribed. Less squarely engaged than her previous answer, since much of the turn is about why the question should not be asked here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "Would it just be the chief executive and those who are in senior public roles in terms of the staffing, or will that go to a certain point all the way down to different levels?"

acuity.statement: Thank you so much, Madam Chair. I want to speak to my Amendment Paper 542, which is in relation to clause 5.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Ingrid Leary attacking the bill's narrow, operator-focused definitions and the enforceability of clause 4, so the turn is eligible. Menendez March is plainly in the same debate and on the adjacent question of whether clause 5's definitions capture modern online harms, which is a gesture at the matter under debate, but he takes up no part of Leary's argument: he neither adopts her consumer-protection-versus-harm-minimisation framing nor engages her claim about the advertisement definition. The speech is a prepared case for Amendment Paper 542 and would be word-for-word the same had Leary made any other argument on the bill, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band at 0.3 rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued "The definitions are narrow and operator focused, and so, again, that speaks to the creation of a regulated sector more than the harm minimisation" and asked how clause 4 would be enforced; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Firstly, the bill does enable both offshore and domestic operators to apply for a licence because it’s reflecting the reality of the status quo, which is that most online casino gambling in New Zealand is currently provided by offshore operators who operate outside of New Zealand law.
acuity.explanation: Two substantive turns by other members precede this, so it is eligible. She engages one strand of Leary's territorial challenge - why the regime licenses operators with no New Zealand presence - and supplies a reason (the status quo is offshore provision outside New Zealand law, plus free-trade obligations), which is pointable engagement rather than mere reference. But she does not answer the specific question put, namely what the enforcement mechanisms are for operators with no legal presence, nor does she address the claim that David Seymour misdescribed the bill as containing technical blocking mechanisms, and she says nothing about Menendez March's loot-box amendment. Engaging the topic and one strand while returning to prepared justification is the ~0.5 case. Scored independently of whether the free-trade and competition reasoning is sound, which is a Rigor question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "how does she expect this regime to be enforced when operators will have no legal presence in New Zealand?" and "The other questions I have are just in terms of the territorial part, which allows operators to operate in New Zealand from offshore".

acuity.statement: The member asks whether or not this bill is going to be an improvement of the status quo, and absolutely it is because it’s not a shock to anyone that this Government cares about regulating the online casino market and we are acting on it more so than the previous Government did, who recognised that there was an issue but never actually passed any legislation to deal with this issue.
acuity.explanation: She restates Belich's central question — whether New Zealand ends up better off than under the current unregulated market — and answers it directly, then in the same turn takes up Belich's specific request for the Cabinet-approved regulations by saying they have been proactively released and that final approvals are intended for May. The turn would read quite differently had Belich asked something else, so it is squarely shaped by the preceding contribution. (Whether the rebuttal reasons well or is accurate is not scored here.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is the Minister satisfied that New Zealanders will actually be in a better position" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: So I’m just wondering, when I read through this, I can’t see how we actually prevent harm. So I’d love to know the Minister’s thoughts on actually how we prevent harm based on clause 3(c), especially when the Minister just said how do we “limit” harm.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one strand of the Minister's preceding contribution — her framing of the bill as restricting and minimising harm rather than preventing it — and turns it into a question about the gap between that framing and the word "prevent" in clause 3(c). He then moves to prepared material advocating his own Amendment Paper 539, which engages nothing the Minister said. Partial engagement, and the specific words he attributes to her ("limit harm") are not in the turn immediately before him, so the pointer is weaker than a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it will restrict quite a lot of what is happening with online gambling at the moment" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: Minister, I want to focus my questions on advertising. Because I appreciate that you’ve pointed us to the information in terms of advertising, but I want to question, firstly, how the officials provided the advice around advertising, because advertising is one word but can mean a lot of things.
acuity.explanation: The acknowledgement that the Minister pointed members to the released information is a courteous reference rather than engagement with it. She does press on the one assertion the Minister made — that licensed operators will face "very strict advertising requirements" — by asking what those controls actually are, which keeps her on the claim rather than merely the topic. But she does not take up the Minister's actual argument that controlled advertising is needed as an incentive to draw gamblers into the licensed market, and the bulk of the call is prepared questioning about officials' advice and offshore saturation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "for those who are licensed, there will be very strict advertising requirements" — Brooke van Velden

acuity.statement: Speaking to all of those questions, I’m also interested in futureproofing for new technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) is one of those areas. The regulations do actually allow for the regulatory framework to respond quickly to changes in technology, which is why we haven’t been so explicit within the law but we are becoming more explicit within the regulations so that we can adapt to new technology over time. AI is one of those areas where the regulations can give the member some comfort.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Belich's specific concern that clause 5's definition of 'advertisement' omits AI and is therefore not futureproofed, and supplies the government's reasoning for leaving it out of the statute — that the regulations can be amended faster than primary legislation. The answer would have been different had Belich raised a different drafting concern, and it names the strand she raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Artificial intelligence isn’t specifically listed here, and I wondered whether that would be something that may mean that the definition of “advertisement” is too narrow to cover some of the new technologies that might be emerging." — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: There was a question about a change for communications for administrative purposes. The answer to this is yes; it is only for administrative purposes, so the member is correct. She had a concern about the definition of “communication device” being quite broad and referring to any other communication or things, and that, once again, just goes back to the overall issue of AI. It’s intentionally broad to deliberately futureproof for new technologies.
acuity.explanation: Directly gives the on-the-record confirmation Belich asked for on clause 5(b)(iv), affirming her narrow reading, and then takes up her second point about 'communication device' being defined as merely 'a thing', accepting the breadth but explaining it as deliberate. Slightly short of 1.0 because it recasts the breadth concern as the AI point rather than engaging her worry that over-breadth is itself a defect.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "My understanding is that it’s narrow and it is purely for transactional communication, but it would be good to get the Minister’s view on that." — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: In terms of the question regarding the timing of this bill coming into force, I do consider that the time frames are reasonable because the regulations will be in place before people can advertise.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific request to extend the Schedule 1 commencement dates and gives the reason for declining it — that regulations precede the advertising start — which is the premise Belich's question rested on. Not a full 1.0 because it asserts the sequencing rather than engaging her point about the dates having already slipped from July to December 2026.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "would the Minister not consider extending those time lines out to make sure that we have all of the regulatory harm minimisations in place" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: But just to, I guess, provide another angle to what the previous speaker, Camilla Belich, mentioned in terms of verification process, I would just like to ask, further, how the Secretary for Internal Affairs would verify “source and amount of capital available” as a part of that criteria process.
acuity.explanation: He takes up one identifiable strand of Belich's turn — how DIA will verify information supplied by applicants, especially overseas ones — and extends it to a criterion she did not raise (source and amount of capital). That is real engagement rather than a mere reference, but it is a single strand bolted onto an otherwise prepared set of discrete questions on clause 15, so the bulk of the speech would have been identical whoever preceded him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "to what extent will the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) be checking the validity of the information provided?"

acuity.statement: I’d like to turn to Subpart 3, which I note we’ve only had about half a question on, I think, some time ago, and it’s quite a big section. I really want to frame these in terms of the risk of regulatory capture, because what we can see from this licensing regime is that there are a number of purposes, including competition in a commercial market, but also revenue gathering for the Government.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate (the Part 2 licensing regime) and it glances at the state of the debate by noting how little Subpart 3 has been covered, echoing Belich's same observation. But it engages no part of the content of either preceding argument — not the verification questions, not the capital-source question — and the regulatory-capture frame and the clause 27/30 questions would have been delivered word for word whatever Belich and Xu-Nan had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "We also haven’t talked about Subpart 3 at all" — the coverage point is picked up, but no argument of hers or Xu-Nan's is taken up

acuity.statement: The second question was: will there be a fee? That was to do with clause 13(2)(c). Yes, there will be a fee, but that fee will be a part of the regulations. Ultimately, we’ve put in a fee there because if we didn’t have a fee, there is the possibility that people who don’t actually have true ability to be part of the competitive process might vexatiously attempt to apply, and the poor secretariat and staff would be spending a lot of time going through applications that were not actually as valid as you would hope. A fee is there to dissuade those who are not legitimate from being part of the auction.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question that was put — is there a prescribed fee under clause 13(2)(c) — confirms it, locates it in regulations, and supplies the rationale for it. The content is wholly determined by what Belich asked; substitute a different question about clause 13 and this passage could not stand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I wanted to ask the Minister if there will be a prescribed fee under clause 13(2)(c) and what that prescribed fee will be"

acuity.statement: Ingrid Leary then also asked about the flexibility of regulations and whether or not we needed to have more, I guess, detail in the bill because the regulations might be too flexible. I disagree because, as we’ve been referring to earlier today with some of the concerns from her colleague Camilla Belich about the use of artificial intelligence, having flexible law that allows for modernisation and technological changes, as well as some of the regulations to be updated with the changing dynamics that might happen on social media and the online environment, does require the bill itself to be flexible in nature so that we can adjust to technological developments without needing to go through an entire new Act and law of Parliament.
acuity.explanation: Restates Leary's argument that detail should be in statute rather than left to regulation, disputes it directly, and gives a counter-reason drawn from another opposition member's own earlier concern about AI. It does narrow Leary's point — her worry was regulatory capture making tightening impossible, not flexibility as such — so the engagement is slightly off-centre, but the passage plainly could not exist without the argument it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "does she accept that it will be really difficult to change the regulations in that environment?"

acuity.statement: You have stated that there will be very limited information in the public arena because it’s commercially sensitive, so even though the bill will be passed, probably, this year—in terms of the timeline of that, when will the public know what decisions are being made, and will there be further processes where the public can question the Secretary for Internal Affairs in their role?
acuity.explanation: Takes the answer the Minister had just given Belich — that application information will not be public because it is commercially sensitive — accepts it as given and draws out its consequence, pressing on when the public will ever learn what was decided. The question is built out of the preceding reply and would not exist without it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "No, that’s unlikely as a lot of the information that’ll be sent to the Secretary for Internal Affairs should be commercially sensitive"

acuity.statement: I know that my colleague Camilla Belich does have further questions; I just haven’t heard an answer from the Minister in relation to how monitoring and compliance will occur for operators, to ensure people don’t spend hours gambling across multiple platforms—or is she comfortable with the fact that the bill is silent on that?
acuity.explanation: Leary speaks into the same committee-stage debate and notes that questions put to the Minister remain unanswered, but she engages none of the content of Belich's preceding argument (the continuation-of-operation and complaints-register points). Her own question about monitoring across multiple platforms is fresh material on the right subject rather than an engagement with what was just said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "I think these are prudent provisions to have in a bill, but I just wonder whether they go far enough" — Leary acknowledges that her colleague "does have further questions" but does not take up any part of that argument.

acuity.statement: Well, it’s a difficult situation to be in because we have had important questions that haven’t been answered in this part. I’d like to give the Minister the opportunity to answer those questions, or some assurance that these may be able to be addressed in a latter part of the debate.
acuity.explanation: Belich takes up one strand of Leary's immediately preceding turn — that no answer has come from the Minister — and does something with it, yielding the floor so the Minister can respond. She does not engage Leary's specific substantive point about monitoring gambling across multiple platforms, instead returning to her own general characterisation of the clauses as prudent. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "I just haven’t heard an answer from the Minister in relation to how monitoring and compliance will occur for operators"

acuity.statement: Speaking to some of the questions from Camilla Belich: firstly, she asked whether or not there would be a separate requirement for complaints to the Secretary for Internal Affairs. Section 68 sets out the process for complaints to the secretary. There was also a question about significant influence, and the bill also suggests that there must be all reasonable steps taken to ensure that an operator or a person doesn’t have significant influence over more than three licences.
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific questions just put and supplies the answer to them — naming the clause that handles complaints to the secretary, and addressing the significant-influence point. The speech would be entirely different had Belich raised different clauses, which is the deciding test. Short of 1.0 only because it answers two of the questions asked and leaves the pause-in-operation question, and Leary's monitoring question, untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "was there any thought given or will there be a separate requirement for the secretary to have its own complaints register"

acuity.statement: Camilla Belich did ask a question about the self-exclusion register. The self-exclusion register regulations need to be implemented by December 2027, because officials are currently working on this as it was a later edition, and so it won’t necessarily be ready when the bill passes; however, I would just suggest that, under the current status quo, there is no exclusion register.
acuity.explanation: Belich's immediately preceding turn asked specifically whether the self-exclusion register would be available when the main bill comes into effect, and stressed the timing. Van Velden takes up that exact question, supplies the date (December 2027), concedes it will not coincide with the bill's commencement, and argues the delay is still better than the status quo. The answer would be different had Belich asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "Will the self-exclusion register be available at the time that the main bill comes into effect?"

acuity.statement: There is also a question from Camilla Belich about the registration audio mark. The secretary is developing guidance on the registration icon. Whether this will be linked to a website is yet to be determined, but the icon itself will be published by public notice, so people will know what it is, and that, in some ways, just allows people to know that what they’re hearing is actually a licensed provider.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Belich's question about what a registration audio mark is and whether it links to Internal Affairs, and answers the linkage point (undetermined) and the publication mechanism. It leaves untouched the second half of her question — the 24-hour takedown requirement under clause 41(3) and her suggested date-stamp fix — so engagement is close but partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "What is the registration audio mark?" and "will it be that every advertising piece that is put forward by online casino gamblers is then linked to the Department of Internal Affairs?"

acuity.statement: Just to point out that my question around clause 37 was not about the 90 days; it was about the minimum mandatory duties, and I’d really welcome a response to that.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a specific misstatement in the turn immediately before it: van Velden had attributed to Leary a question about the 90-day operating requirement, and Leary identifies what she actually asked and presses for an answer. This could not have been said without having listened to the preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "Ingrid Leary also asked about platforms and why they must operate within 90 days."

acuity.statement: It was actually in relation to a matter that was raised earlier, around clause 42. I guess it’s very clear that it’s quite a vague clause, because it doesn’t quite lay out what they’re talking about when they mention “credit”. I have Amendment Paper 549 that just, I guess, removes a little bit of that doubt that actually expands on what they’re talking about.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the clause 42 credit strand that Belich raised and the Minister answered, and builds on the ambiguity that exchange exposed by offering a definition. But it does not engage the Minister's actual answer — that free money is 'not credit' and no credit may be offered — so it takes up the topic and one strand rather than the specific claim made in reply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "That is not credit. Otherwise, no credit is allowed to be offered under the law."

acuity.statement: My Amendment Paper talks about specific explicit information with regards to publishing the information online and recognising that, with a new system, it will take time to bed in. Specifically, when there will be complaints, where do the public go to view the information?
acuity.explanation: On the bill under debate, but prepared material on her own Amendment Paper that takes up no part of the preceding turns. The Minister had answered her earlier question by saying protections are 'fleshed out in more detail in the regulations', and she neither accepts nor disputes that; nothing here would change if Davidson or van Velden had said something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden answered that specific protections are "fleshed out in more detail in the regulations around harm and consumer protections" and Mike Davidson spoke on clause 42 credit, and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: To the question that Ingrid Leary actually did have about minimum mandatory duties, there is a requirement for operators to minimise harm and that is provided for throughout the regulations. Harm minimisation strategies will show how operators will minimise harm to consumers and that must be provided as part of the application process. Consumers can also block transactions with gambling operators via their own banks, and that liability should lie with operators, so that is why it is included like that in the definition and not through other industry organisations or the tech companies themselves.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question Leary had just said was missed (minimum mandatory duties) and then addresses her substantive proposal to extend 'operators' to payment providers, affiliate marketers and software providers, giving a reason for not doing so — liability should sit with operators. Squarely shaped by the two preceding turns by Leary.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "it was about the minimum mandatory duties, and I’d really welcome a response to that" and her proposal to extend the definition beyond "operators"

acuity.statement: Mike Davidson had a question in relation to his Amendment Paper 549 about credit. Look, the clause that’s in the bill is modelled off the Gambling Act, and it’s very clear that no credit must be offered by operators, regardless of the type of credit. Credit sourced by consumers, such as credit cards, will actually be restricted through the regulations, so his amendment is not necessary.
acuity.explanation: Takes Davidson's specific amendment — naming buy now pay later, credit cards and other deferred payment methods — and disposes of it on its own terms: the clause already covers credit offered by operators regardless of type, and consumer-sourced credit is handled in regulations, so the amendment is redundant. A direct rebuttal of the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "I’m just wondering whether the Minister would consider supporting that amendment."

acuity.statement: Does he believe that the Government withdrawing funding from local government for things like roading and water infrastructure has had any impact on the rates increases that councils are imposing across the country?
acuity.explanation: Luxon deflected the cost-of-living question onto rates rises as the driver. This supplementary takes that exact move and turns it back on him, asking whether his own government's funding withdrawal caused the rates rises he is blaming. The question could not have been asked in this form if Luxon had answered differently, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "a lot of increases in fees and charges across New Zealand are linked to increases in rates"

acuity.statement: Did cutting $2 billion from school-building funding, $1.5 billion from State house building, and funding from hospital rebuilds contribute to the $5 billion collapse in construction activity between when he became Prime Minister and last year?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the construction-sector strand Luxon had just claimed credit for and puts a contrary figure against it. It engages one strand of the preceding answer rather than its central claim about the infrastructure pipeline, and the specific numbers look prepared, so this sits between a partial and a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "It’s also a Government that’s lowered the cost of building and construction by opening up the market to overseas building products"

acuity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that a Government shouldn’t measure its success by how much it spends and, in fact, wasteful spending is itself inflationary?
acuity.explanation: On the matter under debate and loosely continuous with the preceding exchange about wasteful council spending, but it engages none of the content of either Hipkins' question or Luxon's answer. It invites a fresh proposition the Minister can run with, and would read identically whatever had just been said about rates.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "councils need to get back to basics" — a gesture at the same theme of wasteful local spending, but this question takes up no part of the argument about council funding and rates

acuity.statement: What reports has she seen on the Employment Leave Bill?
acuity.explanation: A generic prepared supplementary that would be word-for-word identical whatever the preceding answer had contained. It is at least on the subject under question, so not a zero, but it engages no claim, figure or argument from the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: van Velden had just given detailed consultation findings — "70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change" — and this question takes up no part of it

acuity.statement: Did two-dose vaccine mandates remain in place for 12- to 17-year-olds, despite former Ministers Chris Hipkins and Ayesha Verrall having been advised of concerns about mandating the COVID-19 double-dose vaccine for this age group?
acuity.explanation: Takes the fact the Minister has just conceded — that the Ministers received and considered the advisory group's safety concerns — and presses it to its consequence, asking whether the mandates nonetheless stayed in force. The question depends on the content of the answer immediately before it; had Brown denied the briefing was received, this supplementary would have had to be different. Not a full 1.0 because it extends rather than contests the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "The royal commission found the briefing received by Ministers on 22 December 2021, which raised concerns from the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group, was considered by the Hon Ayesha Verrall on 7 January 2022."

acuity.statement: What does he see as the difference between the people displaced by a war of aggression in Lebanon, whom he will not commit to providing aid to, and the people displaced by Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine, which he did provide aid to?
acuity.explanation: Picks up both what Luxon said (displacement is real and his response acknowledged it) and what he declined to say (no commitment to aid), and turns the omission into a consistency challenge against the Ukraine precedent. It engages the answer rather than restating the original question, though it answers the evasion more than the self-defence reasoning Luxon actually offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "Well, Israel obviously has a right to self-defence against Hezbollah." — and his accompanying failure to answer the aid question

acuity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that this stabilisation in rents is particularly remarkable given quite recent history in which rents went up $170 a week?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific rent series the Minister has just read out and asks him to set it against a prior rent increase, which is a use of the preceding answer rather than a new line. Capped below the top band because it adds context to a friendly answer rather than engaging a contested claim — it is a prompt for elaboration, not an argument taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s tenancy bond data, Prime Minister, shows median rents down 1.6 percent in the year to January 2026"

acuity.statement: Can he confirm that front-line providers such as the Auckland City Mission, the Wellington City Mission, and the Christchurch Methodist Mission have told him to his face that homelessness has reached unprecedented heights and they point to his policies as to the reason why?
acuity.explanation: Confronts the overall picture the Minister has just painted with counter-evidence on the same subject, which is genuine engagement with the topic and with the 'delivering for all Kiwis' claim. It is only half-engaged with the content, however: it contests none of the rent or affordability figures actually cited and shifts the ground to homelessness, which is prepared material aimed at the right target.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "We are delivering on housing affordability, and we are delivering for all Kiwis and the people of New Zealand."

acuity.statement: Is the Minister expecting people so committed to evidence and data, not ideology, to congratulate him on these results, or have they been a bit quiet lately?
acuity.explanation: Gestures at the figures just given — 'these results' — but engages none of them; the question is a jibe at absent opponents rather than anything that uses the content of the answer. Would have worked identically after any favourable answer the Minister might have given, which places it in the low band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I’m advised that the credible measures of rent price changes show that rents are flat."

acuity.statement: What other evidence has he seen on improved housing affordability in New Zealand?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the premise of the answer and asks for more of the same, which is the barest possible glance at what preceded it; it takes up none of the Cotality figures, the deposit-years number or the mortgage-payment series. The word 'other' is the only trace of the previous turn, and the question would read identically after any positive housing answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "Cotality says that in quarter four 2025, the house price to income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021."

acuity.statement: We had it in the COVID report released yesterday, which obviously many have now used as an opportunity to insert into this debate, so I think it's important to respond. The basic question that this Government has to answer is whether we now, two years into their stewardship, are in a better or worse place to respond to the next pandemic.
acuity.explanation: Russell's preceding turn was largely a defence of COVID-19 spending ('to say that the COVID spending was irresponsible is simply wrong'). It’s incredibly important that we see the wood for the trees in this House, but we also allow people access to the branches of that tree, to the little things, because that’s power in the hands of the people.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding turn — Twyford's access-to-justice framing and his claim that technology is what makes the mass of secondary law reachable — and develops it into the argument that not knowing the law is disempowering and that publishing at the level of the detail puts power in people's hands. It is a partial engagement rather than a full one: she does not test or add to Twyford's specific claim about the 120 publishing agencies or the decentralised model, and the bulk of the speech is her own prepared material on the Regulations Review Committee and regulatory impact statements. Points to a strand that can be named, so 0.5 rather than the unresponsive band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Phil Twyford: "Access to the law is an important part of the broader access to justice issue." — and his point that the internet is "so perfectly suited to giving people instant and efficient access to large amounts of data like our laws".

acuity.statement: This is a good bill. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Entirely unresponsive. Follows a detailed speech raising a specific unanswered question about regulatory impact statements for substantive revision changes, and engages nothing in it. The words would be identical whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said, and could have been delivered in any third reading on any day.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White had just argued at length that the bill's requirement that unpresented secondary legislation be invalid is a real check and balance, and raised the open question of when revision changes should attract a regulatory impact statement; this statement does not take up any of it.

acuity.statement: Is he aware that his Government cancelled plans to build a 70 million litre diesel strategic reserve in 2024?
acuity.explanation: Luxon's answer listed the lifting of minimum stock holdings and the National Fuel Plan without addressing the cancelled reserve. Hipkins takes up that gap directly, re-putting the cancellation as a question of the Prime Minister's awareness rather than moving on to new material. It engages the evasion rather than the reasoning in it, so it is strong but not a full rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "Our Government is doing everything we can to increase storage across the fuel network across New Zealand."

acuity.statement: Was Shane Jones correct when he advised Cabinet in 2024 that cancelling the strategic diesel reserve would “prolong our vulnerability to a diesel supply disruption until potentially 2028”?
acuity.explanation: Sustains the same thread but does not take up what Luxon had just said about Channel Infrastructure and ongoing dialogue; instead it introduces fresh evidence from Cabinet advice. On-topic and advancing the line of questioning, but indifferent to the content of the immediately preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "I'm well aware of the plans of Channel Infrastructure to expand diesel infrastructure and storage."

acuity.statement: How will the Government ensure diesel supply security for critical sectors such as emergency services, food distribution, and public transport, in the event of a major and prolonged supply disruption, given that it cancelled plans to have a strategic reserve capacity in place by this year to do just that?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the substance of Luxon's defence — that expanded minimum stock holdings were the action taken — and tests it against the scenario the cancelled reserve was designed for. Engages one strand (whether stock holdings substitute for a reserve) while largely restating the prepared premise about cancellation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "he did take action, and the Cabinet did take action, to expand the minimum stock holdings across all three fuel types"

acuity.statement: What would trigger a move from response level 1 to response level 2 on the Government’s fuel emergency response framework?
acuity.explanation: Luxon had just deferred discussion of the National Fuel Plan to 'should a bunch of other scenarios eventuate'. Hipkins seizes precisely on that deferral and asks for the escalation trigger it presupposes. The question would be different had the previous answer not invoked the plan, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "We'll talk about a National Fuel Plan, should a bunch of other scenarios eventuate, in due course."

acuity.statement: Why should New Zealanders have confidence in the Government’s response, when, weeks into the crisis, he can’t even say what would trigger a move from level 1 to level 2 and doesn’t seem to be aware that the Government cancelled plans to build a 70 million litre strategic diesel reserve?
acuity.explanation: Built entirely out of the two answers immediately preceding it: the refusal to name an escalation trigger and the earlier denial of awareness of the cancellation. It draws out their consequence rather than referring to them in passing, and could not have been delivered if those answers had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "We've said that we'll talk more about the National Fuel Plan escalation, and what triggers would enable us to move from different steps, later on."

acuity.statement: The Prime Minister has now asserted that the previous Government made that decision; it was a private business.
acuity.explanation: Corrects a specific factual claim in the answer delivered seconds earlier — that Marsden Point's closure was a previous Government's decision — by identifying the decision-maker as a private company. This is the clearest form of engagement: a direct contradiction of the content just asserted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "It was a critical piece of national infrastructure and that was a decision of a previous Government."

acuity.statement: Would all of this anxiety about supplementary reserves be relevant if they hadn’t shut down Marsden Point?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the topic of the preceding exchange — the adequacy of reserve capacity — and offers a counterfactual that relocates the cause. It engages the subject rather than any particular claim Hipkins made, and pivots to blame, so it is partial engagement at best.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "given that it cancelled plans to have a strategic reserve capacity in place by this year"

acuity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that rather than going ahead with the previously agreed plan, in April 2025—last year—Cabinet agreed that large diesel importers must hold an additional seven days’ supply onshore, thereby achieving the same resilience outcomes that were argued for?
acuity.explanation: Addresses the premise running through the whole preceding line of questioning — that cancelling the reserve left resilience unaddressed — by naming the substitute decision and asserting it reached the same outcome. A government supplementary that engages the opposition's actual argument rather than ignoring it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "it cancelled plans to have a strategic reserve capacity in place by this year to do just that"

acuity.statement: Did the Minister note in the Fitch Ratings report that fiscal consolidation could occur either by saving money and spending less or increasing taxes, and, if she did read that, which one did she think of at the time?

acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "I saw a report from Fitch Ratings placing New Zealand's AA+ long-term credit rating on a negative outlook"

acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "this Government is taking a temporary, targeted, and timely approach to the current crisis"

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Vanushi Walters argued the Government's joint statement 'puts New Zealand at risk in expressing New Zealand's readiness to assist in opening the Strait of Hormuz', and this statement does not take it up — it addresses only the length of her speech.

Had she made a different argument, this sentence could not have been delivered. Whether the contradiction is real (she distinguished the statement's wording from the policy behind it) is a question of reasoning quality, not of responsiveness, so it does not lower the Acuity score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'because the words of the statement are clear' / 'the unprincipled, irresponsible, and unclear foreign policy' — Vanushi Walters

He names the claim ('rushing to contribute military forces'), attributes it to her, and rebuts it with a flat statement of intent. That is engagement with the content, not merely a reference to the speaker; the crudeness of the wording is a civility matter and is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'the associated costs and risks of committing Defence personnel and Defence resources' — Vanushi Walters

She argued the Government acted without advice on international law and risks complicity in breaches of the UN Charter; he answers a different claim, that the Government should issue a public legal ruling. The strand engaged is pointable, so this is partial engagement rather than prepared material, but it does not meet the specific argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'In terms of the failure to consider international law, the war began with the US and Israel breaching the UN Charter.' — Vanushi Walters

acuity.statement: As the previous speaker has already said, this is a very long and very complex bill.

He engages the complexity claim but not McClure's actual conclusion (that a simpler, flatter tax system is the answer and the bill deserves support), and the remainder of the speech on digital nomads, IRD data collection and the fuel crisis package would have been delivered unchanged whoever spoke before him. Partial engagement, pointable, then prepared material.
