acuity.statement: One thing I wanted to focus on—and the previous Green member actually just threw some accolades at it, so I want to highlight that—was a provision within this bill that encourages residential solar uptake, ensuring residents up and down this country who export excess power back to the grid—i.e., selling any excess to their electricity retailer—won’t face income tax, recognising that the compliance burden would outweigh any benefit and it will encourage solar and battery uptake.
acuity.explanation: Brewer builds his contribution around the one concession Hernandez made — that the exemption for income from selling electricity to the grid is a good measure — and draws out its consequence, that it will encourage residential solar and battery uptake. He then answers Hernandez's specific charge that the Government cut incentives for electric vehicle uptake by citing the announcement of 2,500 further EV chargers. The speech would have had to change if Hernandez had conceded something else or made a different climate criticism, which is the deciding test. It falls short of 1.0 because the bulk of Hernandez's argument — the distributional claim about handouts to the top, and the deletion of the IRD's tax-information power — is left untouched rather than rebutted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "One good measure that this bill does that we do support is the change to exempt income from selling electricity to the grid."

acuity.statement: We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough, whether some of the measures were actually too narrow, which is why you’re getting this sort of very scattered debate about some bits that we support and some bits that we don’t.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds follows substantive turns from Hernandez and Brewer but engages the content of neither. She offers a meta-observation on why the debate is scattered — a gesture at the debate she is in, which keeps her above the floor — and then moves to acknowledging the select committee's work and the parliamentary volleyball team. Nothing here takes up Brewer's solar provision or EV-charger defence, or Hernandez's distributional critique; the passage would read identically after any other speaker on this bill, so it sits in the unpointable 0.0-0.3 band rather than at a partial 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer argued the bill's grid-export exemption will encourage residential solar and battery uptake, alongside EV chargers and the New Plymouth LNG facility, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m just sitting in here listening to insults and snaps and barbs being traded and personal insults being made; it always leaves out the actual human people’s realities who are at the centre of the violence of an illegal war, and those real lives and the harm on them is quickly forgotten in a tit-for-tat political debate. I abhor that.
acuity.explanation: Davidson opens by taking up the character of the exchange she has just heard — Peters' jibe at Twyford — and turns it into her point that the human cost is lost in tit-for-tat. She engages the preceding turn's conduct rather than any substantive claim in it (Peters made none here), then moves to prepared material on the Government's statement, so this is a partial engagement: pointable, but one strand only.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if you're the architect of a plan to build 100,000 homes and you build less than 1,000, then you'd talk that sort of trash, wouldn't you?" — Winston Peters

acuity.statement: What is their answer? To leave them alone, to wait until they have nuclear weapons, to wait until they’ve oppressed more of their own people, and to wait until they achieve their stated aim of a second Holocaust in Israel. Is that their answer, as they stand in Geneva and O’Rourke, and talk so nicely about international law and the protections that apparently it offers even to the most evil dictators on the planet?
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes the specific strand of the immediately preceding speech — the appeal to international law and to the illegality of the US/Israel attack — and attacks it directly, asking what the alternative policy would be. The speech would have to change if Davidson had argued on different grounds. It caricatures her position, but that is a reasoning fault, not an unresponsiveness one; marked slightly below 1.0 because it rebuts the general posture rather than any particular claim or figure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That has been clearly put by independent scholars in foreign and international and human rights law across the world" — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: We hear the message, “Let’s commit to international law.” Well, I give you, then, international law on the law of the sea and the rights for this country and other countries to be able to have commercial shipping, and we call on Iran to comply with the United Nations Security Council Resolution 2817.
acuity.explanation: Collins picks up the opposition's international-law argument and does something with it: she turns the same body of law to the law of the sea and freedom of navigation, naming the Security Council resolution. That is engagement with the content of the claim rather than a mere reference to it, though much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on the joint statement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Greens absolutely will continue to be consistent in wanting us to at least be honest about whose lives are being honoured here" and the appeal to international law — Marama Davidson

acuity.statement: We had one of the speakers today talk about the most evil regime in Iran. Those of you that would have read The Lancet scientific journal would know that it reported that USA sanctions on other countries between 1971 and 2021 have murdered over 38 million people.
acuity.explanation: Waititi names the specific claim made earlier in the debate and answers it on its own terms, offering a counter-measure of harm to contest the ranking of evil. He also takes up Collins' immediately preceding point about what New Zealand could deploy by noting the frigate on the sea floor. Clearly pointable, specific engagement with what was said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Irani regime is the most evil around in the world today" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Now, in the course of this debate, the Foreign Minister and the defence Minister have made a great joke out of the idea that New Zealand might deploy our New Zealand Defence Force personnel or defence assets, aircraft, or naval vessels to the Strait of Hormuz, as if that was the most ridiculous thing. I say to this House that, in light of the words that this Government has signed up to in the joint statement, it is a fair question to ask.
acuity.explanation: Twyford takes Collins' mockery of the deployment question and rebuts it by reading paragraph 6 of the very statement the Government signed, then puts the question back as a direct challenge. The speech is built around what the preceding speaker said and would have to be rewritten if she had argued differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Would you like me to find some stealth bombers? I don't have any of those. How about an aircraft carrier?" — Judith Collins

acuity.statement: Mr Twyford also mentioned, or seemed to suggest, that we were imminently deploying troops to the region, and of course that is not the case. The statement does mention that we express our readiness to contribute to appropriate efforts to ensure safe passage.
acuity.explanation: He names the immediately preceding speaker's argument and answers it, quoting the same paragraph of the statement and explaining how the Government reads it; elsewhere in the turn he also takes up Twyford's international-law charge and reads the statement's first sentence against it. Scored just below 1.0 because he restates Twyford's question as a stronger claim ('imminently deploying') than was made — but that is a reasoning fault, not a failure to engage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Will you rule out sending New Zealand personnel and New Zealand defence assets to the Strait of Hormuz?" — Phil Twyford

acuity.statement: Now, I agree with much of what has been said on the other side: the Iranian regime is a despicable regime that has an atrocious human rights record. We rightly recognise the people of Iran, both resident in Iran and the communities in New Zealand and around the world, and the suffering that they and their families have as they come to their annual celebration of Nowruz.
acuity.explanation: Webb explicitly concedes the part of the Government speakers' case he accepts and then disputes the rest — the classic accept-part/dispute-the-rest move, which only works if you have listened. The rest of the turn also engages van de Molen's claim that the statement upholds international law by arguing it is internally inconsistent, though that strand overlaps with his colleague's earlier prepared argument, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the brutal regime that they have had to survive under for some decades is terrible as well" — Tim van de Molen

acuity.statement: As the chair of our select committee has already mentioned, the residential solar power tweaks that we did was a sensible addition among many in this bill, which make practical changes to make this system more effective. They remove barriers that hold back investment and growth. With this bill, we’re backing businesses, attracting investment, and creating the conditions for a stronger economy. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton follows Edmonds' detailed critique — the narrowness of the new revenue account method, John Cantin's scope advice, and the Law Society and Privacy Commissioner concerns about ministerial information-sharing — and engages none of it. He gestures at the debate by acknowledging the previous speaker and the select committee chair, but the substantive content is prepared praise that would read identically whatever Edmonds had argued, so it sits in the low band rather than at 0.0.

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Barbara Edmonds argued "The changes that are within this particular bill, however, don’t go far enough" on the foreign investment fund rules, and that the ministerial information-sharing clauses have "insufficient safeguards", and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker, and I acknowledge the member Rawiri Waititi for his impassioned contribution on the bill. I’m also welcoming—finally—a member of Te Pāti Māori turning up to the Justice Committee, because that hasn’t happened for 2½ years of this term of Parliament, so I would look forward to that finally taking place.
acuity.explanation: Rutherford names the previous speaker and his contribution, then pivots immediately to an attendance jibe about Te Pāti Māori at the Justice Committee, and the remainder of his turn is prepared commendation of the bill ('We on this side of the House put victims first'). None of Waititi's substance — the IPCA and Privacy Commissioner inquiries, photographs of children, storage of images on police phones — is engaged. A mere reference plus a target is unresponsive under the rubric, so this sits in the low band; it earns a little above the floor only because the speech is at least about the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued the bill would legalise the previously illegal practice of police photographing rangatahi who 'look out of place or suspicious', and asked how the resulting data on police phones would be managed — this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The member who’s just resumed his seat, Tom Rutherford, talked about victims. I think with this particular bill, I don’t think anyone would disagree with the fact that the police have to have some ability to take photos and videos. Of course, that will form part of their evidence. But what we need to make sure that we’re not doing with a bill like this is creating more victims by making wide powers that encourage the incorrect collection or unfair collection of information that will impinge on people’s privacy.
acuity.explanation: Belich takes Rutherford's own organising concept — victims — concedes the part of his case that stands (police must be able to take photos as evidence), and then turns the concept against the bill by arguing broad collection powers will create a further class of victims. The speech would have to be written differently had Rutherford framed his case any other way, which is the deciding test. Scored purely on engagement: whether the inference holds or the claims are accurate is not an acuity question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We on this side of the House put victims first." — Tom Rutherford

acuity.statement: Absolutely, Wellington would make better decisions. What Government members are pointing out is that they are not actually supportive of localism when it comes down to it. They campaign on it, but they don't do it—they don't do it. They're all about consolidating money and power in central government hands when they hold it and then forcing their will on communities. acuity.explanation: Takes up Sam Uffindell's interjection head-on: answers its implied claim directly ('Absolutely, Wellington would make better decisions') and then draws out a consequence from it — that Government members who exempt Wellington from devolution do not really hold the localism position they campaign on.
