acuity.statement: That’s not for you to determine. That’s for Māori to determine.
acuity.explanation: Foster had just posed the problem of how the new committee would work out who speaks for Māori given that a fifth of the population has Māori whakapapa. Waititi's interjection goes straight at the premise of that question — that the decision about who speaks for Māori is the Crown's or the committee's to make — rather than at the topic generally. It would not read the same way after a different preceding argument, which is the test. Not a 1.0 because it contests the premise without taking up the specific identification difficulty Foster raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how do you identify who on earth it is you are trying to engage and do that authentically" — Andy Foster

acuity.statement: We thought that was very difficult to do that—well, it might be for Māori to determine that, but when you’ve got to ask 350,000 people, probably, of that order, it’s going to be a heck of a consultation to try and work out who is going to speak for Māori on that and put those particular issues right up front.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Waititi's interjection directly: concedes the principle ("it might be for Māori to determine that") and then disputes it on practicality, putting a figure to the scale of the consultation it would require. The sentence is unintelligible without the interjection it answers, which is the strongest evidence of engagement. Short of 1.0 because it answers the determination point with a logistics objection rather than engaging whose decision it properly is.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s for Māori to determine." — Rawiri Waititi

acuity.statement: The problem was that Auckland Transport, effectively, was insulated from that. They didn’t have, as Simon Court has said, the cold wind, if you like, of the ballot box sitting there that gets councillors very interested in making sure that they are responding.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up Court's electoral-accountability point explicitly and does something with it: he applies the ballot-box discipline Court invoked for councillors to explain why Auckland Transport, not being subject to it, was unresponsive and unpopular. That is drawing out the consequence of the preceding argument rather than merely naming the previous speaker. Not 1.0 because the strand is then folded into prepared material on localism and democratic accountability that would largely have survived a different preceding speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If Auckland councillors continue to support this crap, we can vote them out." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: The decisions were unanimous but, as you’ve heard from Simon Court, there were a couple of areas where we had a bit of backwards and forwards and we didn’t entirely agree. We’ve reflected that in our report and I’ll come back to that shortly.
acuity.explanation: This acknowledges that Court raised points of disagreement on the committee and is plainly about the matter under debate, but it engages no part of their content — not the exclusive role for unspecified Māori groups, not the exclusion of freight and emergency services from the design phase. It names the previous speaker and defers the substance to later, which the rubric treats as a mere reference rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ACT does have some residual concerns. We do need some improvements." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: This is a bill that responds to concerns of Aucklanders that have been building for many years, since the introduction of the Auckland Transport governance legislation in 2009. Those frustrations have been building and building, and it’s, I think, to the credit of many that this bill is here today.
acuity.explanation: Wade-Brown's preceding turn put a specific point — that the bill undersings the value of consistent transport vision across mayoralties, with Paris as the example — and signalled Green support. Bidois's speech engages none of that strand: it opens with prepared framing on the 2009 governance legislation and runs through acknowledgements, the accountability rationale and the select committee changes. It is squarely about the matter under debate, which keeps it off the floor, but it would read word-for-word the same had Wade-Brown said something entirely different about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Celia Wade-Brown argued that 'the consistency of vision of mayors and cities is something that is undersung in this piece of legislation' and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: We go back to 2009, when the then National-ACT Government put in place the Auckland super-city. At that time, they chose to establish a council-controlled organisation that was Auckland Transport. Some of that structure, indeed, has worked for our city.
acuity.explanation: Halbert picks up the exact starting point Bidois used — the 2009 Auckland Transport governance settlement — and does two things with it: names whose Government built it, and partly disputes Bidois's verdict that Auckland Transport 'has not delivered' by conceding that 'some of that structure, indeed, has worked'. That is a genuine but partial engagement; he takes up one strand and then moves into prepared material on congestion, the transfer of functions and the new regional transport committee that is indifferent to what Bidois said. Scored on engagement only — whether the concession is well-reasoned or accurate is not this attribute's question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'since the introduction of the Auckland Transport governance legislation in 2009' and 'it has not delivered in terms of a satisfactory nature for our community' — Dan Bidois

acuity.statement: They’re removing the cycle lanes in Takanini because nobody was using them.
acuity.explanation: Halbert was in the middle of claiming credit for the last Labour Government shifting investment from roads towards walking and cycling; the interjection lands directly on that specific claim, offering a counter-instance of cycling infrastructure being taken out for lack of use. It engages the content of the claim just made rather than merely naming the speaker or the topic, which is what this attribute rewards. Not full marks because it answers an investment-shift claim with a single local example rather than taking up the funding argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'shifting some of that funding through increased funding to public transport and to active transport—that being walking and cycling' — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: Not cut; redirected—not wasting it on walkways to nowhere, light rail to nowhere.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim just made — that money was cut — and disputes its characterisation directly, substituting 'redirected' and naming the projects she says it was moved off. The interjection would read differently had Halbert said something else, which is the test; whether 'to nowhere' is a sound characterisation is a rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "$564 million cut from Auckland's transport budget; $213 million cut from public transport alone."

acuity.statement: This is from a member across the way, heckling at me on my commentary tonight, who says that congestion is an issue, but it’s her Government that has cut over $120 million out of the transport budget in Auckland.
acuity.explanation: Names the interjector and the fact of her heckling, then re-asserts the cut figure without engaging her actual point, which was that the money was redirected rather than removed. That is a reference to the previous turn rather than engagement with its content, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "Not cut; redirected—not wasting it on walkways to nowhere, light rail to nowhere."

acuity.statement: This bill is another perfect example of this Government fixing the basics and building the future. We heard the words of Aucklanders, and we responded. This Government is committed to improving transport in Auckland and putting decision making back in the hands of Aucklanders. For motorists, this is a positive step.
acuity.explanation: Prepared government praise for the bill delivered immediately after a sustained critique of transport funding cuts and fare rises. It engages no part of that critique — not the figures, not the 'roads only' charge — and would have been word-for-word identical whatever Halbert had said, though it is at least on the subject under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert argued the Government has taken a 'roads only' approach and cut $564 million from Auckland's transport budget, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: I question the claim that there’s a lot of local democracy in this Government. I have been concerned that that’s been said a lot but it’s not happened a lot. I take, for example, the issue around Plan Change 120 and the recent announcement that those plans will be taken to Cabinet for approval.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand of the preceding speech that carried a claim — that this Government is handing decisions back to Aucklanders — and contests it with a counter-example in Plan Change 120 going to Cabinet. Partial rather than full engagement, since the remainder of her turn returns to prepared local Eden Park material, but what is engaged can be pointed at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Carlos Cheung: "putting decision making back in the hands of Aucklanders"

acuity.statement: It really is a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, even though I didn’t have the pleasure of being on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee. Since being voted in, I approached a couple of the Ministers about a by-law with respect to semi-trailers parking in residential streets in my electorate of Takanini, specifically in areas like Goodwood Heights and around Manukau Heights.
acuity.explanation: Entirely prepared constituency material on semi-trailer parking, following a speech that put two specific challenges to the bill. Neither is acknowledged, and the speech would be unchanged whoever had preceded her; it stays above 0.0 only because it is about the bill before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White questioned whether this Government delivers local democracy and asked for detail on which roads fall inside the Eden Park precinct, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I can assure the House I have presented no Cabinet paper agreeing with the closure of Wattie’s or the closure of McCain Foods, but I can table a Cabinet paper where they agreed to close the refinery.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Hipkins's specific counter-analogy (other factory closures) and does something with it: draws the distinction he says matters — the existence of a Cabinet paper in the refinery case and its absence in the others — and offers to table it. The remark would be unintelligible, and would have to be different, had Hipkins named anything else. Scored on engagement only; whether the Cabinet paper actually shows agreement to close is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "the McCain Foods factory, the Wattie’s factory, the Kinleith factory, the Winstone factory have all been closed—"

acuity.statement: I took the good liberty of consulting that great paragon of knowledge, the dictionary, before I came here.
acuity.explanation: Engages the actual crux of Hipkins's objection — what "approved"/"agreed" means — rather than restating the original assertion, so it is aimed at the content of the preceding challenge. Marked below the top band because it engages the definitional strand only and does so by gesture at the dictionary rather than by meeting the substantive claim that considering a report is not approval.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "The Labour Government did not approve the closure of Marsden Point; it was a private business."

acuity.statement: We had the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee say that the Minister of Finance came and said that this is not a Government that is going to operate on borrow and hope. Well, this is a finance Minister who has borrowed more we did when we were in Government, and the only strategy that she seems to have is hope, and that has been no more evident than what we’ve seen over the last three or four weeks as New Zealand has navigated a cost of living crisis.
acuity.explanation: Takes Brewer's own framing phrase from the preceding turn and does something with it rather than merely quoting it: she names him as the source, disputes the premise on its own terms (that this Government does not borrow and hope) by asserting it has borrowed more than Labour did, and then inverts the 'hope' half against the Minister. The speech would have to change if Brewer had argued the Budget's discipline on different grounds. Scored for engagement only — whether the borrowing comparison is true, and whether the jibe is fair, are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now is not the time to borrow and hope." — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: If we have a look at the context in which this Government is going to deliver this year’s Budget, we had the Minister of Finance say that it would be a responsible Budget. Well, let’s have a look at any marker that we would look at for that. We have GDP that is lower than it was two years ago. That will be a context for the delivery of this year’s Budget. We have unemployment that is higher now than it was two years ago. We have business liquidations higher now than they were two years ago. We have the number of children in poverty higher now than it was two years ago. And our economic outlook from our credit agency, Fitch, has been downgraded under this Government.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — Brewer's claim that the country is in its strongest position for years and that the fiscal approach is working — and sets a counter-list of markers against it. It is a partial engagement rather than a full one: she answers the general proposition about economic condition rather than any specific figure or argument Brewer put (the $11 billion of savings, Investment Boost, the 50 percent debt ceiling), and the list reads as prepared material on the right subject. Pointable, so above the 0.3 band; not aimed at a specific claim, so short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we as a country are in the strongest position we have been for several years for New Zealand to weather these events" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: I rise to oppose the Budget Policy Statement. This Budget Policy Statement was hopelessly out of date and out of touch even just four months ago, when it was issued. It’s painfully obvious now, in today’s context, that it reflects a fundamentally out-of-touch Government that is completely all at sea on how to build a modern, productive, resilient economy, despite the words in the Budget Policy Statement aiming to that effect.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez follows a substantive turn by Woods in the same Budget Policy Statement debate, so the statement is eligible. The speech is squarely on the matter under debate — the Budget Policy Statement — but engages no part of Woods' argument: it opens with prepared condemnation of the document that would read identically whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. Unemployment is mentioned much later in his own prepared frame rather than as a response to her claim. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.2 because it is at least on the debated item, but there is no point in the preceding turn one can point at being engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods spoke about unemployment, the absence of a Government plan to fix it, and the need for long-term investment so young people stay, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I also commend our chair for the excellent speech he gave. And thank you to the leader of the ACT Party for a number of measures in there and a number of indicators that have pointed us in the right direction. This lays the ground for me.
acuity.explanation: Follows Seymour's substantive speech on spending restraint, ACT's claimed savings and the fiscal outlook, but only names him and thanks him in the abstract for "a number of measures" and "a number of indicators" — no part of the content is taken up. Polite acknowledgement that engages nothing, then straight into prepared material about the December 2025 Budget Policy Statement and the previous Labour Government. The passage would read identically whatever Seymour had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "I commend the committee for its report. I commend our Minister of Finance for the Budget Policy Statement."

acuity.statement: Immediate effects: energy crisis, longer-term challenges. The Strait of Hormuz carries a multiplicity of trade categories, not just oil. We need to be prepared.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the energy situation and Middle East conflict that Seymour closed on and develops it — naming the Strait of Hormuz and widening it from oil to trade categories generally, then on to supply chains and alternative fuels. That is engagement with the topic Seymour raised rather than with any specific claim he made, and it sits inside a largely prepared survey of the fiscal position, so a partial engagement you can still point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "We’ve got a lot more work to do, rolling up our sleeves as we go through some tough times with this energy situation and conflict in the Middle East."

acuity.statement: Statistics New Zealand actually showed GDP, and the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific figure the preceding speaker used (0.2 percent GDP growth), names it as hers, supplies the quarter she omitted and re-states the total. The passage could not have been written without having heard Russell's claim, and it does something with it rather than merely referring to her. Score sits just below 1.0 because the engagement is confined to one number in a wide-ranging critique, with the rest of the speech prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it was, I think, a 0.2 percent growth in GDP over the entire last year" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The opening remarks referenced the Minister of Finance stating that Budget 2026 will be a “responsible Budget”. Let’s reflect upon what responsible budgeting has looked like for Māori under this National-led Government so far: Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, gone; cuts to Māori housing; cuts to Māori trade training budgets; cuts to Māori education programmes; cuts to Māori economic development programmes; removal of references to Te Tiriti o Waitangi; Progressive Procurement, which contributed $900 million to Māori business and the Māori economy, and therefore New Zealand, gone.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate and gestures at the debate by picking up the "responsible Budget" framing, but it engages no part of the preceding speech — the $66 billion COVID cost, the Fitch negative outlook and the discipline-is-not-cruelty argument all go unanswered. The speech would read identically had the previous turn argued something else about the Budget Policy Statement, so it is prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nancy Lu argued that $66 billion of COVID-era spending caused the inflation outbreak and that fiscal discipline protects headroom for the next shock, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: In short, her speech was about saying that the Government’s role is, essentially, to hand money out to different groups. Ironically, that’s not the case, and it was almost as though the Government has money that it gives out, but the Government doesn’t have money. It raises money from taxes or it borrows, or it does a combination of both, and one of the things that I think is quite important to understand is the size of the debt that we currently owe as a country.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly names the preceding speaker's contribution, restates its thrust and then rebuts it on principle — that funding programmes presupposes revenue or borrowing — before turning to the debt and interest cost. The speech would have had to change had the previous turn made a different argument. Held below 1.0 because he answers the general shape of her case rather than any specific claim in it (the $1 billion of targeted funding, the $900 million procurement figure) and misidentifies her party, and because the restatement is a loose version of what she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "cutting $1 billion of targeted funding has deprived Māori of the opportunity to provide services in our way" — Cushla Tangaere-Manuel

acuity.statement: Can I ask, please, Minister, how does this temporary brief oversight for a few minutes compare with the over $52 million bribe through the Public Interest Journalism Fund?
acuity.explanation: Takes the incident Stanford had just characterised and immediately pivots to an unrelated comparison with the Public Interest Journalism Fund. It glances at the subject under question but engages no part of the content of the answer just given — a reference and a pivot rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The real question around this email was what was it about." — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Who removed the video from the National Party YouTube channel at around 10 p.m. last night?
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the answer just given — the timeline Stanford established with "after 9 p.m." — and pushes it an hour forward, but does not take up the substance of what she said about rectifying the error. Partial engagement with the preceding answer rather than with its claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "When I was made aware of the issue last night after 9 p.m., I of course called the Prime Minister's office" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: In the middle of a global fuel crisis, is it her habit to bother the Prime Minister with matters like the subject of this question?
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific fact the Minister had just volunteered — that she rang the Prime Minister's office — and does something with it, drawing out a consequence about the triviality of the matter. The question would not exist had the previous answer said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I of course called the Prime Minister's office to explain what had happened" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Has the Minister considered engaging a private detective to get to the bottom of this weighty matter—who did it, who took it off the YouTube channel, and how do we make sure it never happens again?
acuity.explanation: Built directly on the answer immediately preceding it: Stanford had just said she did not know who took the video down, and this question takes that exact gap and works it. Mockery rather than argument, but it is squarely aimed at what was just said, which is what Acuity measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don't know the identity of the exact person that did it." — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Is she concerned that there is a pattern of behaviour with her and her office regarding email distribution, that she herself has previously described as untidy and not best practice?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's concession that an error occurred and generalises it into a question about a pattern, anchoring it in her own earlier characterisation. It engages the admission just made, though it moves to the broader frame rather than testing any specific part of the answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when we were made aware of it we realised there was an error, we took it down" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Who is better at managing emails: her or the former education spokesperson for the Labour Party?
acuity.explanation: Echoes the words "education spokesperson" from the answer just given and otherwise engages nothing in it, pivoting to the other party's record. On the matter under question, but a repetition of the previous turn's words is not engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I know that the member is very excited about her very first question as education spokesperson" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: Are families in poverty also squeezed, and, if so, why is she not really seeing any relief for them?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact framing the Minister had just read into the record — the "squeezed middle" — and turns it against the policy by asking who else is squeezed. The question is shaped by the words immediately preceding it and would have to change if she had quoted something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The policy is carefully targeted to families in the squeezed middle" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Is she aware that the legally and annually required $12 increase to jobseeker support, indexed to last year's inflation, is much less than $50 a week?
acuity.explanation: Directly tests the claim just made: the Minister asserted beneficiaries get a rise in line with the cost of living, and this supplementary supplies the figure for that rise and sets it against the relief on offer. Engagement with the specific assertion, not merely the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "on 1 April beneficiaries do get a rise directly in line with the cost of living" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: Is $12 extra enough to meet the additional costs of fuel and other living expenses, or does she expect people living in poverty to get further into debt simply to survive?
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding answer corrected his figure, and this question restates $12 without acknowledging or disputing the correction. On the matter under debate, but it proceeds as prepared material despite the specific factual point just put to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Yes, it is $20, not $50." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: How will the closures of Wattie's and McCain contribute to the growth of unemployment, which is already at a 10-year high of 5.4 percent?
acuity.explanation: Answers the Minister's aggregate-employment defence with the counter-statistic on the other side of the ledger, so it engages the strand of her answer that put individual firm closures in a wider macro context. It does not take on the 15,000 figure or the manufacturing index specifically.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "2.9 million New Zealanders are working in jobs across the country, and that this rose by 15,000 in the last quarter" — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: What improvements has he seen against the other health targets?
acuity.explanation: Follows on from the two targets the Minister had just reported by asking for the remainder, so it is keyed to the structure of the preceding answer, but it tests no part of it and invites prepared material rather than engaging a claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are seeing encouraging improvements across elective surgeries and first specialist assessments" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: This is the Government that’s making Auckland Transport more accountable to Auckland ratepayers. It’s transferring most of Auckland Transport’s functions back to Auckland Council. This is the Government that’s establishing an Auckland Regional Transport Committee—council and Crown working collectively, members appointed from each side—on a 30-year integrated transport plan for the region.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive opposition turn on the same bill at the same reading, so he is eligible, but his speech is prepared material that would be word-for-word identical whatever McLellan had said. He does not answer her point that Auckland Transport was created by a previous National-ACT Government, does not engage the fragmentation concern she flagged, and does not take up her "watching brief" caveat about how little detail the public transport delivery mandate carries. He does touch the same furniture she did — the 30-year plan, the transfer of functions back to council — but only as a list of Government achievements, which is a shared topic rather than engagement with her claims. On the right subject with no engagement puts this in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.2 because the overlap of subject matter is real but no strand of her argument is picked up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan spoke immediately before on the same second reading, arguing "it’s actually trying to fix some structural problems that actually do impact on final outcomes", that "These were changes that were made by a previous National - ACT Government in establishing Auckland Transport", and that submitters warned decision making "could become fragmented across, I think there’s 21, local boards" — this statement takes up none of it.

acuity.statement: What we're seeing is that this is very focused on income tax rates, this part. As my colleague the Hon Dr Deborah Russell pointed out, every cleaner that goes off and does their work, they have to pay their income tax, and every other worker in New Zealand has to pay their tax. What consideration, in terms of thinking about the revenue inside of the equation, did the Minister give to broadening that base and to thinking about taxing things other than income?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of Russell's preceding turn — that wage and salary earners are taxed on every penny while capital gains are not — and does something with it, converting it into a direct question to the Minister about broadening the tax base. The speech would have to change if Russell had argued something else about the tax system, so this is more than a mere reference; it is not a 1.0 because much of the surrounding material (World Bank, IMF, structural deficit) is prepared content on the same theme rather than engagement with Russell's argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Every single penny that the cleaners who clean our offices earn is taxed on their wages." — Deborah Russell, arguing the gap in the system is untaxed capital gains

acuity.statement: Yeah, a lot of consideration in regards to revenue methods. The primary method that we're focused on is growing our economy so that we can grow the revenue of every business and every household in this country. That's been a major focus of this Government, and one of the ways we achieve that is through a broad based - low rate tax system. I receive a wide range of advice from Treasury as part of my role.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the question put to him in the committee debate: Woods asked what consideration was given to revenue-raising measures and whether Treasury advice on broadening the base had been seen, and he answers that there was consideration, names growth as the primary method, and confirms he receives a wide range of Treasury advice. He does not take up the specific claim at the centre of the question — that the base should be broadened beyond income via a capital gains or land value tax — so it is a partial engagement rather than a reply to the argument, and the 'broad based - low rate' line gestures at the base question without addressing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What consideration, in terms of thinking about the revenue inside of the equation, did the Minister give to broadening that base and to thinking about taxing things other than income?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: So I would like to understand from the Minister to what extent he has considered where else he could raise revenue from. It's interesting that he's not the Minister of taxation, right? Taxation is very, very important, but it's not the only source of Government revenue. There are other ways to raise income for Government.
acuity.explanation: Follows the Minister's answer and presses the part of it that was left unaddressed — he spoke of growth and of receiving Treasury advice but not of other revenue sources, and she re-puts that question and widens it to royalties and investment. That is engagement with the topic of his reply rather than with its specific claim: she does not rebut the proposition that growing the economy is the primary revenue method, and the IMF quotation is prepared material she had written down in advance. Partial engagement, pointable, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The primary method that we're focused on is growing our economy so that we can grow the revenue of every business and every household in this country." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: If anyone wants to see the points of difference between the sides of the House, in regards to tax policy, one only needs to play back: has the Government considered a land value tax? No. Has the Government considered a capital gains tax? No. Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No.
acuity.explanation: He takes up Russell's actual questions (land value tax, capital gains tax) and answers each with a flat 'no', so the reply is shaped by what she asked. But he engages none of her reasoning — the mishmash of existing quasi-CGT rules, the creaky FIF rules — and pads the list with a 'death tax' and 'taxes made up off the cuff' that she never raised, turning a specific set of questions into a prepared points-of-difference set piece. Partial engagement: the topic and the question list, not the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has he considered a land value tax?" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: In regard to the corporate tax rate, yes, we did consider, as part of the assessment when we put in place Investment Boost, whether we would be better to reduce the corporate tax rate or do another alternative. We selected to do Investment Boost, because Investment Boost is a targeted mechanism in order to ensure that the benefit goes to those who most need it.
acuity.explanation: This directly answers the question put: was changing the company tax rate considered, and what was chosen instead and why. The reply would be different had she asked about something else, and it supplies the substantive alternative (Investment Boost) rather than deflecting. Short of 1.0 only because he does not take up the specific thing she pointed at — the 2022 Inland Revenue long-term insights briefing and whether any of its ideas were used.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "has he given any attention to that long-term insights briefing that Inland Revenue prepared in 2022, and has he picked up any of the ideas from it as ways to think about the corporate income tax rate" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I’m also interested to learn, from the Minister sitting in the chair—when he ruled out the taxes that the Government had ruled out, he, of course, didn’t list a gas tax, which the Government has gone on to implement—whether or not that levy was considered on the revenue side of the equation.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's just-delivered list of taxes ruled out and works on it directly, pointing at an omission from that very list and turning it into a new question. The intervention could not have been written in advance: it depends on exactly which taxes he enumerated moments earlier.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has the Government considered a death tax? No. Has the Government considered a whole lot of taxes that one wants to make up off the cuff? No." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister asserted that we have a broad based – low rate tax, but I do not see how that can be consistent with his assertion that we should not have capital gains. If we’re not taxing capital gains, it is not a broad-base system, so I’m just going to invite the Minister to walk that one back.
acuity.explanation: She lifts the Minister's own self-description and sets it against the other thing he said in the same answer — that capital should not be taxed — to draw out a contradiction between them. The whole passage exists because of what he said; substitute a different defence of the tax system and this speech would have to be rewritten. Textbook engagement of the specific claim just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We are a broad base – low rate party. We are not looking to increase tax." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The problem is, I’d like to know how he knows that. There’s no data—there is no data as yet—so it’s a very real question to the Minister: how can he make that claim?
acuity.explanation: She takes up the Minister's defence of Investment Boost — which he introduced into the debate in his reply — and presses on its evidentiary basis, asking what he is relying on to assert success. It is squarely aimed at the claim just made rather than at the topic generally. Marked slightly below the top because the words she attributes to him ('real success') are not in the turn immediately preceding, so part of the engagement reaches outside this exchange.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We selected to do Investment Boost, because Investment Boost is a targeted mechanism in order to ensure that the benefit goes to those who most need it." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: The answer in regards to asset sales is no. The Government has not considered that and is not considering that at this point. The context in the question around Investment Boost—again, it provides a targeted intervention which, in effect, has an overarching effect to reduce the broader rate of tax that businesses pay, which is important.
acuity.explanation: Russell's question was narrow and pointed: what evidence supports the claim that Investment Boost is a success, given IRD data does not yet exist. Watts names Investment Boost and restates its policy rationale (a targeted intervention reducing effective business tax), but supplies no evidence and does not address the absence of IRD data at all. He engages the topic, not the claim — prepared policy framing on the right subject, with a gesture at the question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'd like to invite the Minister to just give us some evidence as to why he thinks that Investment Boost has been a success." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: My question is around the imposition of the income tax rate. We know in the statements that the Minister of Revenue has made in the introduction that the Minister wants to realise a broad-based system with fiscal responsibility. We know that there will be an Amendment Paper that gives tax discounts. Has there been any consideration done to, essentially, raising the tax rate of the top income bracket, to make sure that the changes the Government is making don’t lead to any kind of changes in the operating allow?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the Minister's position — the broad-base, fiscal-responsibility framing just asserted — and turns it into a specific question about whether raising the top bracket was considered to protect the operating allowance. That is a real engagement with the preceding claim, but it then moves into prepared Green material (tax-free threshold, the Green Budget) that would have been delivered whatever Watts had said. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The context of our focus is on making sure that we are broad based – low rate, to encourage economic growth." — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: No. Quite simply, the Government is not considering increasing taxes for hard-working Kiwis; quite the opposite. We’re wanting to create a broad based - low rate tax system to encourage economic growth.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — whether raising the top rate has been considered — squarely and immediately in the negative, so the reply would have been different had Hernandez proposed something else. It stops short of 1.0 because it engages none of the reasoning (the $373m cost against the operating allowance) and leaves two of the three named suggestions, including the tax-free threshold and new brackets, untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Has there been any consideration done to, essentially, raising the tax rate of the top income bracket" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: Also, for the Minister, given we’ve just caught that one, when I flip over to the bill commentary on clause 9, which my colleague the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has just been discussing, which is the equalisation of fringe benefit tax (FBT) and PAYE in clause 9, that is taking effect from 1 April 2026. I would like to know from the Minister whether there are any other clauses in the bill that have retrospective application?
acuity.explanation: Opens a fresh line of questioning on retrospective application rather than engaging anything in the answer she follows. It is squarely on the matter under debate — the same clauses and the same FBT/PAYE provisions Penk was discussing — and "given we’ve just caught that one" gestures at the exchange, but no part of his reasoning is taken up, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive-but-on-topic band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just explained that treating open-loop gift cards under PAYE is more complex because it requires a gross up for student loans and KiwiSaver, and that employer-provided accommodation rules predate FBT; this statement does not take either point up.

acuity.statement: In terms of the reason for that excess electricity provision and feeding back into grid, I think it’s worth noting there are good public policy reasons that we want to encourage that kind of provision. And, of course, excess electricity is the very definition of a good problem to have. I don’t think one needs to land on the side either of fairness or the deduction in simplicity type argument. There can be different ways and different routes at which we arrive at the same point, and it seems that that is what has taken place with the select committee making this recommendation and it being accepted.
acuity.explanation: Russell posed a precise either/or: does the Minister see the 'occupied as a residence' requirement as a fairness measure (the select committee's reasoning) or as the officials' deduction/simplification rationale. Penk names that exact dichotomy and does something with it — he argues the two routes converge on the same point, so no choice is required. The speech would be different had she asked something else, which puts it well above the prepared-material band. It is not 1.0 because he declines to supply the answer she sought (which side he falls on) and does not engage her account of what submitters argued at select committee.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Deborah Russell: "So does the Minister regard this just as a fairness measure; that it has to be occupied as a residence by the person?"

acuity.statement: And then to her prior point about whether commissioner discretion could have been used in lieu of amending the Act: of course, the commissioner, powerful an individual as he or she inevitably is, nevertheless, they cannot act in an ultra vires manner—that is to say in a way that’s outside the law of the land—and nor should we have in tax legislation, so far as possible, “Henry VIII” provisions where we’d simply allow, in effect, the primary legislations provisions to be changed in a way that doesn’t reflect the will of Parliament, as evidenced, for example, through the committee of the whole House process.
acuity.explanation: Andersen asked specifically why legislative amendment was required rather than relying on the Commissioner's discretion to reach the same outcome. Penk takes that exact question and supplies a reasoned answer: the Commissioner cannot act ultra vires, and delegating changes to primary provisions would amount to a Henry VIII clause that bypasses Parliament. He is clearly answering the argument put, not reciting prepared material; had she asked a different question this passage could not stand.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Ginny Andersen: "could have the same outcomes, such as fairness for taxpayers, come through, potentially, some of the Commissioner’s discretion—like, why is legislation required for these changes?"

acuity.statement: “Public entertainer” is a defined term within the Income Tax Act, so the member can look at that when he reads the legislation.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's turn set out a three-part problem: who decides between 'public entertainer' and 'digital nomad', what happens to someone who is both, and what advice was received on how often the overlap arises. Watts takes up one strand — the definitional question — by pointing to the statutory definition, which is a real engagement with what was asked. But he leaves the substance of Davidson's argument (the overlap case, the commentary/news boundary, the administrative cost of a split system) entirely untouched, so this is partial engagement rather than a reply to the argument made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: REUBEN DAVIDSON: "who decides whether someone is a public entertainment or, for want of a better term, a digital nomad; what happens when someone is both"

acuity.statement: I wish I could provide more guidance on the lost liquidity date issue that the Hon Ginny Andersen mentions.
acuity.explanation: Names the exact question Andersen put to him and then supplies no answer to it, turning instead to a pun about honorary PhDs and fringes. Elsewhere in the turn he answers points attributed to other members (retrospectivity, lost receipts, meals), but Andersen's two questions — what problem clause 9 is fixing, and what counts as a liquidity event — are referred to and left untouched. A mere reference to the question, on the right subject, with no engagement of its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we still don’t know what the liquidity event would be" — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: I just want to go to clause 11. Clause 11 includes trustees in a list of people who don’t get taxed when they get a gratuitous payment. I was puzzled by this.
acuity.explanation: Opens a fresh line of questioning on a different clause without touching anything in the Minister's immediately preceding answer — not the retrospectivity rationale, not the clause 9 meals point. The passage would read identically whatever the Minister had just said. It is squarely on the bill under debate, which keeps it off the floor, but there is no engagement to point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just answered points on retrospectivity, the commissioner's open-loop-card guidance date, lost receipts and the clause 9 treatment of meals, and this statement takes up none of them

acuity.statement: The question I had also is: why does there seem to be this bespoke definition that is out of kilter in terms of the time that needs to be here? It doesn’t line up with other tax law.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Russell had just left open — why the digital-nomad day threshold uses a bespoke 18-month window — and extends it with a second objection, that the period does not line up with the rest of the tax law, and a further one about 'resident' versus 'tax resident'. Partial rather than full engagement, because the bulk of the turn then moves to prepared material on the influencer examples (Josh and Ben) that Russell had not raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "But why 18 months? ... why 18 months is my first question around the digital nomads" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I think—in the case of Ben, now of Milan; and Josh, whose art deco expertise is apparently in such hot international demand—it’s worth observing that while the nature of their digitally nomadic activity might be that they end up being treated differently in different nations—OECD or other—the Minister of Revenue received good advice about different jurisdictions’ treatment of these kinds of policy areas.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight to the specific question just asked — whether the regime aligns with other OECD jurisdictions and what advice was taken on it — using Woods' own two worked examples, and answers in the negative on identical regimes while asserting that comparative advice was received. The reply would have to change if Woods had asked something else. Marked down only because it stops short of the treatment of Ben's overseas income, which she also asked about; vagueness about what the advice said is a Specificity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is there alignment with other OECD countries? ... How is it that his income in those countries is treated?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: Continuing with the discussion of digital nomads, which was one of the major policy pieces of this bill, one of the things that happens here is that a person is living in New Zealand, residing in New Zealand—they’re here for up to 18 months; it’s quite a long period of time—and, in that time, they are earning an income from overseas, and they are paying taxes overseas.
acuity.explanation: Stays on the digital-nomad topic and gestures at the running discussion, but engages no part of the Minister's answer about international alignment or the advice he says was received. Instead it opens a distinct argument of her own about the tax base and the services nomads consume. On the matter under debate, indifferent to what immediately preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Penk had just said the Minister of Revenue received good advice on other jurisdictions' treatment and declined to claim OECD regimes are identical, and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: Of course, she’s right that we are giving up, in a sense, the income tax that these people might otherwise be paying to New Zealand. Then again, there’s also benefit to New Zealand in the way that digital nomads oftentimes will promote New Zealand, including in the influencer example that we’ve had brought forward tonight.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the precise point Russell made — forgone income tax — then disputes the balance of it with the promotional benefit and an additionality argument, and takes up her own GST qualification rather than ignoring it. Later in the same turn he returns to her earlier unanswered question and supplies the missing figure's rationale: the 18-month period tracks the general visitor visa period. Accepting part, contesting the rest, and answering what was asked is the strongest form of engagement available.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "because of these rules, they won’t be making a contribution to our tax base" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: The member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell may be aware that Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), at the moment—which is the lead agency in regards to providing advice around fuel security—has mechanisms to capture, in effect, the average price of fuel across the different liquid fuels available in New Zealand, in this case 91 octane. MBIE will be calculating that information and providing that information through for consideration. It will take, in effect, an average based on all of the fuel outlets across the country in the context of determining that price.
acuity.explanation: Russell's immediately preceding turn put a precise question: is the sub-$3 test one station at one place, or a national average, and how will it be judged? Watts takes exactly that question and supplies the answer — MBIE as lead agency, an average across all outlets, on 91 octane — and then also addresses her second question about the four-week period. The speech would be entirely different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Deborah Russell: "So that below $3 a litre: is that just one station in one place at one four-week period, or is it an average across the country?"

acuity.statement: Following on from the initial questions by the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, I think this is a good time for us to sort of examine this part at length, noting that this particular amendment, Amendment Paper 560, has no departmental disclosure statement. It also doesn’t have a regulatory impact statement, and it does affect people quite significantly.
acuity.explanation: Watts had just explained the MBIE averaging mechanism and the rationale for the four-week window; Xu-Nan names Russell's earlier questions but engages no part of the answer that had just been given, instead opening a separate line on the missing disclosure and regulatory impact statements and the adequacy of the $50 amount. The reference to a previous speaker is a gesture, not an engagement, and the material is squarely on the amendment under debate — so 0.3 rather than lower.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just set out how MBIE would calculate an average 91-octane price and why four weeks was chosen, and this statement does not take any of that up; it only gestures at "the initial questions by the Hon Dr Deborah Russell".

acuity.statement: I’m going to keep this very brief: I’m wanting to know from the Minister how many people out of the 143,000 who are set to gain from the $50 a week—or the supposed $50 a week—are actually going to have their accommodation supplement deducted as a result of the increase to the in-work tax credit?
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan had just argued, with clause references, that the unindexed baseline makes the increase worth less than $50 — effectively $38. Sepuloni's "or the supposed $50 a week" sits in the same territory of doubting the headline figure, but she does not take up his CPI argument or any other preceding claim; this is a fresh, prepared question on accommodation supplement abatement. On-topic prepared material with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan argued "it is not $50 a week; it’s less than that" because the baseline is unindexed, and this statement does not take that argument up, opening a separate line on accommodation supplement deductions.

acuity.statement: My questions are: what happens within that 12-month period if we experience flows in and out, over and above that $3 threshold? I note that the Minister has also said that the four-week period is probably enough for us to say there’s been a structural shift in the price of petrol, but what happens if, over those 12 months—it’s conceivable—we see three or four cycles of this that go over the four-week period? Is it the intent of the Government that every time we go over that threshold this will start again, or is it a one-time measure, and the first time that we come out of the period of more than four weeks below $3 a litre, the measure will be taken off the table?
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's own stated reasoning — that four weeks below $3 signals a structural reset — and draws out its consequence, asking what happens if that cycle repeats several times inside the 12 months. The question is built from his answer and could not have been asked in this form had he said something different; it falls just short of 1.0 only because she does not dispute the four-week premise itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Simon Watts: "a four-week period of stability under that threshold would indicate a structural reset of the price point, which, on that basis, means that the temporary intervention is no longer required."

acuity.statement: Just in regards to the question from the member in regards to the criteria that will be put in place in regards to the payment, the legislation and the amendment that is putting through this tax bill is only in effect a one-way trigger. What that means is that, in a scenario where we go from where we are to a period where the fuel price is sustained at a rate below $3 a litre for a period of four weeks, at that point, that will crystallise a decision point around a stop date.
acuity.explanation: Woods asked precisely whether the mechanism re-triggers each time the threshold is crossed or is a one-time measure. He answers that exact binary — it is a one-way trigger — and then explains what happens on a subsequent price rise. The answer is wholly shaped by the question just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Megan Woods: "Is it the intent of the Government that every time we go over that threshold this will start again, or is it a one-time measure"

acuity.statement: My follow-up question from that is: what additional measures are being put in place, other than what’s already there, in terms of the Commerce Commission and the fuel price monitoring of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, to ensure that there isn’t a perverse incentive for fuel companies to, say, keep the price of fuel at $3.01, which will mean that this additional income flows to families, with the idea that they may, in their calculations, decide that there will be more money available for people to fill up their cars, and that they will sell more of their product if that money is kept flowing?
acuity.explanation: She accepts the one-way-trigger answer just given, states that it is new information, and builds the next question directly on it — if the subsidy switches off only below $3, fuel companies have an incentive to hold the price just above it. This is drawing out the consequence of the Minister's answer rather than returning to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Simon Watts: "the legislation and the amendment that is putting through this tax bill is only in effect a one-way trigger"

acuity.statement: The Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and the Minister for Energy—being myself—have already clearly indicated to the broader fuel market that the regulator, which is the Commerce Commission, is monitoring pricing and ensuring that it is appropriate, in accordance with the costs that fuel companies incur. That mechanism is already in place, and as part of that process, we expect that the regulator will be monitoring this situation to deal with the scenario which the member has set out at this point.
acuity.explanation: Woods asked what additional monitoring would guard against fuel companies parking the price at $3.01. He addresses that specific scenario by name, naming the regulator responsible and saying the existing mechanism is expected to cover it. Whether the answer is adequate is a separate question; as engagement with the claim just made it is direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Dr Megan Woods: "to ensure that there isn’t a perverse incentive for fuel companies to, say, keep the price of fuel at $3.01"

acuity.statement: To the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, there were questions around what were the gaps that needed to be filled. The advice I’ve received is that there is no significant change from the original legislation. It covers other types of asset classes other than depreciable property where it was always intended to include improvements, but the definition wasn’t included in relation to the relevant sections. The proposed change introduces the definition to those sections.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific question about clauses 33 to 35 by name and supplies the substantive reason for the amendment — a definition that was intended to apply but was omitted from the relevant sections — and in the same turn answers her double-deduction and complexity questions about new section DI 6(2). The reply would be different had she asked something else; it falls short of 1.0 only because it explains what the change does rather than what feedback triggered it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "what feedback the Minister and Inland Revenue were getting that made these amendments necessary"

acuity.statement: Those are my questions for the Minister: what’s the process; where is the discretion, if there is any; would there be specific instances of variation of that 20-day limitation, or is there a facility for a blanket ruling that would shift that 20-day discretion for the commissioner?
acuity.explanation: Eligible because a substantive ministerial answer immediately precedes it, and Davidson could have pressed on the double-deduction or complexity answers. Instead the turn opens new prepared ground on clause 40 and the employee share scheme rules. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so it is not a 0.0, but it engages no part of the answer just given — the acknowledgement of the answers is a reference, not engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Matt Doocey had just answered on the Investment Boost definition, double deductions and the complexity of new section DI 6(2), and this statement does not take any of that up — it thanks him for the answers and moves to a different clause.

acuity.statement: In response to the Hon Deborah Russell, who asked her question, as to why include petroleum and mining expenditure, I’ve been advised that the decision to include petroleum and mining expenditure—these were included in Investment Boost so that all expenditure and capital investment is treated equally. It is a good policy that aims at driving productivity for all sectors.
acuity.explanation: Directly answers the specific question Russell put about why petroleum and mining expenditure is inside Investment Boost, and gives a reason (equal treatment of all capital expenditure) rather than a deflection. Held below the top of the band because it reaches back to Russell's earlier question and leaves the question Davidson had just asked, about the 20-day notification and the Commissioner's discretion, untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "behind the policy decision for allowing petroleum mining and allowing coal mining to be supported in this way"

acuity.statement: I thank the Minister for his answer to that question. I think that we debated it substantially at the time on Budget night, and if you’re going to do that, I don’t agree with doing it, but if you’re going to do that, then a consistency reason applies.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact rationale just offered: she concedes that the equal-treatment argument holds internally ("a consistency reason applies") while maintaining her objection to the underlying policy. Accepting part and disputing the rest is the pattern the top of the band describes, and the sentence could not have been written without hearing Doocey's answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Matt Doocey: "these were included in Investment Boost so that all expenditure and capital investment is treated equally"

acuity.statement: In terms of this Amendment Paper I have a completely new question to ask. I’m hoping that we’ll get through the Amendment Paper tonight and we can return to the rest of Part 2 tomorrow morning. In terms of this extra $50 a week, I want to bring the Minister’s attention to a possible interaction within his own department that is going to matter here.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Woods's substantive turn precedes it and had plenty of content to engage. Russell engages none of it and says so explicitly, opening a fresh line on Working for Families debt. It is squarely on the matter under debate (the $50-a-week Amendment Paper) and thematically adjacent to Woods's intersection-of-systems theme, so it is a gesture at the debate rather than a speech transplantable to another day — 0.3, not lower. The merits of her inadvertent-debt argument are a Rigor question and do not lift the Acuity score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Megan Woods asked about the abatement of the accommodation supplement, a breakdown of the 143,000 recipients, volunteer drivers and Treasury advice on net costs, and this statement does not take any of it up — it announces 'a completely new question'

acuity.statement: The Government did increase investment in regards to compliance activities for IRD earlier in the term. The assessment by IRD in regards to this policy adjustment is that they will be able to manage the impact and the implications of this new policy within their baseline.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's specific resourcing question and supplies an answer to it: IRD assesses it can absorb the policy within baseline. The speech would be different had she asked something else. Not 1.0 because he engages only the resourcing strand and leaves the second strand — the inadvertent-debt mechanics and the call-centre staffing — untouched. Whether 'within their baseline' is true is Veracity, and whether the inference holds is Rigor; neither moves this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I do want to know from the Minister of Revenue what extra resources he is considering within his own department in order to help people deal with this likelihood of inadvertent debt" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I actually just have one question for the Minister of Revenue, and this is specifically to do with the formula itself.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — Watts's answer immediately precedes and had content to engage. Xu-Nan engages no part of it, but the question is tightly tied to the instrument actually before the committee (Amendment Paper 560), so it is prepared material on the right subject rather than a speech deliverable in any debate at all. The precision of the question is Specificity, not Acuity, and must not be allowed to inflate this.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on the $10–13 billion tax debt figure and IRD managing within baseline, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a new question on the amount B formula in new section MF 4L(3)(b)

acuity.statement: Madam Chair, I just wanted to come back to the question around the accommodation supplement because it is an important point of clarification. I’ve just got a little bit more advice from the Ministry of Social Development coming through, which has taken a bit more. It is important to clarify that Working for Families is not classified as income in the assessment of the accommodation supplement. I retract the word “rare” and say that it won’t have any impact at all.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the specific interaction Woods pressed him on and corrects his own earlier characterisation of it, retracting the word 'rare'. That is engagement with the content of a preceding member's claim, and the strongest form of it — conceding and amending on the point raised. Short of 1.0 only because it does not take up the rest of Woods's turn and bypasses Xu-Nan's immediately preceding question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the intersection of the tax system with the Ministry for Social Development in terms of the abatement of the of the accommodation supplement" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: I don’t believe the Minister of Revenue answered my questions that I asked about what is the number of families with children who are working part time and are also receiving part benefit—the Minister is giving me a signal but I need the answer for the Hansard . What advice did you receive around those people, and what other support did you consider?
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. She tracks what the Minister did and did not cover across his answers and presses the gap, which is responsive to the exchange rather than prepared material. But what she engages is chiefly her own earlier question, not the substance of the clarification Watts had just given, so it sits mid-band. The quoted remark she calls inaccurate is a Veracity matter about a relayed claim, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just wanted to come back to the question around the accommodation supplement because it is an important point of clarification" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: As the member the Hon Willow-Jean Prime will be aware, people’s circumstances change on a daily and ongoing basis. It’s not reality that I’m going to be able to give you a definitive number, because the reality is that because those circumstances do change, and whether they’re in work tomorrow or they’re out of work is different.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the precise demand just made — the number — and does something with it: explains why he contends no definitive figure can be given. The reply is unintelligible without her turn, which is the test. Whether declining to supply a figure is an adequate answer is Forthrightness, and whether the churn argument actually defeats the request for a point-in-time count is Rigor; Acuity scores only the engagement, which is direct.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to know the number and what consideration was given for them" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: If you’re saying, “in the following income year”, that’s very specific; that’s next year. If you’re saying in “a later income year”, that’s very broad. That’s potentially any year following the one you are in, which implies, or could imply, a period of deferral—well, an infinite period of deferral, because you’re saying, “a later income year”, not “the following income year”.
acuity.explanation: Davidson follows a substantive turn by another member in the same committee-stage debate, but engages none of its content. He opens a fresh line of probing on a different clause (share-lending arrangements and the 'a later income year' wording) with prepared textual analysis. There is a gesture at the debate — he frames it as 'further probe into one of these clauses', continuing the pattern of putting clarification questions to the Minister — so it is not wholly indifferent to what it follows, but his speech would be word-for-word the same whatever Russell had argued. That places it in the 0.1–0.3 band, at 0.3 for the gesture.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just asked the Minister to clarify what restrictions on disposal of employee shares are envisaged under new subsection (4B) and whether they engage the associated-person rules; Davidson does not take that up, moving instead to clause 41(2B).

acuity.statement: What is revenue account method (RAM) interest? It is not a liquid foreign share, which means not easily able to be sold or converted, such as not on the stock exchange. That might be adequate to protect something, but it might not be reasonable to do so.

acuity.statement: I think it’s an interesting discussion because there are obviously trade-offs when you incorporate something into statute versus secondary legislation. One of those is that the benefit of having something in statute provides rigidity and a little bit of untouchability, to a certain extent. The downside is that if that particular provision or condition of storage of biometric data is in primary legislation, there is no challenge to the rights-limiting factor of that beyond a declaration, say.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of the question just put — that statute is necessarily the higher protection — by naming what primary legislation forecloses (judicial challenge beyond a declaration) for the very category Walters raised, biometric data.
