acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "I maybe neglected to mention the changes around domestic solar. Of course we support that—of course."

acuity.statement: It’s quite ironic listening to the other side of the House talking about sensible spending. I have to laugh, because over on this side of the House, I support this bill, and I support this bill because we are giving targeted relief to families, to the middle class, the mums, the dads, that get up every day, drive to work to put food on the table, drop their kids off at school, and they, over the other side, are complaining because we are not borrowing any money to do this.
acuity.explanation: McClure gestures at the preceding contribution ("listening to the other side of the House") but engages no part of its content: Genter's case was about wealth concentration, the repeal of section 17GB and trust disclosure, and said nothing about borrowing. McClure instead attributes a borrowing position to the other side and restates prepared support for the bill. It is on the matter under debate, which keeps it out of the floor, but the speech would read identically whatever the previous speaker had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "We continue to see an irresponsible Government who has taken irresponsible policy actions from the very beginning of taking power" — glanced at, inverted, but not engaged

acuity.statement: These changes strengthen the Commerce Commission’s ability to promote competition and hold dominant players to account. That matters because competition drives lower prices, better choice, and, of course, innovation and the type of services that are available to Kiwis.
acuity.explanation: Genter had just argued that oligopoly and light-handed, under-resourced regulation benefit big players, that the Commerce Commission lacks the investigative powers its Scottish counterpart has, and that the loss of the named grocery and telecommunications commissioners is unfortunate. Court's speech is prepared ACT framing on the same subject — competition lowers prices, remove red tape — and takes up none of those claims: not the powers comparison, not the named commissioners, not the public-sector role. It would read word-for-word the same whatever Genter had said. On topic, hence not 0.0, but there is no strand of her argument one can point at being engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Julie Anne Genter: "It’s this light-handed regulation, we never resource proper enforcement, and who does that benefit?" — and her argument that a bigger public-sector role is needed

acuity.statement: The member from the member ACT Party was talking about how markets will take care of this; sometimes markets are not enough. Sometimes there is market failure, which is why we absolutely need a strong Commerce Commission and we absolutely need good governance in that respect as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes the core premise of the immediately preceding speech — that functioning free markets deliver the outcome — names it, and rebuts it with the market-failure case, drawing the consequence that a strong Commerce Commission is therefore necessary. He also engages Arena Williams' earlier point about the agency's potency and concedes it while holding his own line on governance. The speech would have to change if Court had argued something else; short of 1.0 only because the rebuttal engages Court's general stance rather than any specific claim or figure in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "It backs free markets, clear rules, and personal responsibility because when markets work properly, Kiwis get a fair deal."

acuity.statement: The Finance and Expenditure Committee is looking forward to handling this bill and is grateful that it’s been directed towards us. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Commission, led by its chair, Dr John Small, and it’s very good that he is going to be a big part of this transition, as the Minister said.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Wilson (and before it Court and Genter) and engages none of it — not the market-failure argument, not Genter's complaint about losing the named commissioners. It restates the bill's provenance in the Rebstock review and the select committee's willingness to take it, which would be identical whoever had spoken before. It is at least about the bill under debate, so 0.1 rather than 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Wilson argued that market failure means markets alone are not enough and that the Commission needs both potency and board-led governance, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Now, they’ve also talked big about supermarket competition, but this bill—this very bill—removes one of the key institutional reforms that was designed to and was successfully keeping pressure on the sector. The Grocery Commissioner was created because the supermarket duopoly was failing consumers, suppliers, and competitors.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the pro-competition case made from the government benches — groceries specifically — and turns it against the bill, arguing it removes the one institution that was holding the duopoly to account. That is genuine engagement with a strand of what preceded him, and he can point at the mechanism. But it is one strand of a largely prepared condemnation that also detours into the Aranui bus route and Robbie Williams, and he does not touch Wilson's market-failure argument or Brewer's point about the Rebstock review's provenance, so it sits at partial engagement rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "We’ve seen it in groceries, in building materials, and in banking—where barriers are high, prices stay high."

acuity.statement: The other side of the House had six years to do something about competition, so that they could bring grocery prices down. It didn’t happen in six years; at least on this side of the House, we’re moving.
acuity.explanation: Rosewarne's immediately preceding speech argued the bill weakens competition oversight in a concentrated grocery market and credited Labour with creating the Grocery Commission to drive prices down. Nakhle takes up one strand of that — Labour's record on grocery competition — and counters it directly, so the remark would not read the same had Rosewarne not claimed Labour acted. But she engages only the record claim and leaves the substantive argument (that removing the Grocery Commissioner role and watering down enforcement raises prices in an 80 percent concentrated market) entirely untouched, pivoting instead to a six-years jibe and prepared commendation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Rosewarne: "That’s exactly why Labour acted and that is why we created the Grocery Commission"

acuity.statement: The Freudian slip from Megan Woods, when she said, “Oh, but we put out lots of press releases.”, that’s the problem. Putting out a press release saying something’s happening, but not allocating money, doesn’t deliver anything.
acuity.explanation: Costley picks up one strand of Woods's immediately preceding speech — her reference to press releases and time-limited funding — and does something with it, turning it into an argument that announcements without appropriations deliver nothing. He engages no part of her central claim (that excluding ACC from the fiscal indicators makes surplus look closer and destroys comparability), and the rest of the turn is prepared material about unfunded classrooms and the fiscal cliff. One strand taken up, then back to prepared ground: a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "because she can’t pick up a press release and see what time-limited funding looks like"

acuity.statement: Well, that is a choice that maybe the Government would choose to make, but we would be none the less liable for it.
acuity.explanation: Takes Court's interjection head-on and distinguishes the two things it conflates — whether the money is paid versus whether the liability exists — rather than talking past it. The sentence only makes sense as a reply to that specific claim and would have to change if Court had said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "No one's paying the money."

acuity.statement: I think one of the challenges that we have, and the previous speaker talked about it, is the GDP per capita measurements that we have. They are a blunt instrument for measuring the state and the wellbeing of a society and an economy. We can have GDP go up, and sometimes even GDP per capita goes up, at the same time as the country is experiencing growing household debt, increased material hardship for children, and longer delays for people to access things like basic healthcare.
acuity.explanation: Explicitly picks up the preceding speaker's defence of GDP as the consistent measure and concedes the consistency point while disputing its sufficiency, giving concrete counter-cases (household debt, child hardship, health waits). It engages the strand about measurement rather than the specific internal-inconsistency claim about proxies, so it is strong engagement rather than a direct rebuttal of the exact assertion.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr David Wilson: "I would remind those people that think that GDP is not consistent that, actually, the public sector has a multiplicity of agencies who are quite adept and will be able to address those wellbeing measures"

acuity.statement: We're also repealing the wellbeing statements, the necessity for Budget Policy Statements, and the Treasury to deliver on wellbeing reports and wellbeing statements. We remember those Wellbeing Budgets and their huge operating allowances.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right bill — fiscal cliffs, Pharmac, school lunches, repeal of wellbeing statements — delivered as though the preceding speech had not happened. It would read identically whatever the Green member had argued, and it answers none of the measurement or liability claims put a moment earlier. On topic, so not a 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ricardo Menéndez March argued that GDP per capita is a blunt instrument that can rise while household debt and child material hardship worsen, and that unpriced climate liabilities should be disclosed; this statement does not take up either point.

acuity.statement: One of the fundamental things that has come up in this debate is the removal of the wellbeing objectives. This is a Government that came in with the intent to remove them because they were something that Labour had put in place—or so they told us. But what this belied was that, actually, the wellbeing approach to budgeting, for us looking at something broader than just the simple traditional economic measures, was work that had begun when Bill English was the Minister of Finance.
acuity.explanation: Directly attacks the premise both preceding government speakers relied on — that the wellbeing framework was a Labour ideological invention — by dating its origin to Treasury work under a National finance Minister in 2011. The rebuttal is aimed at the specific characterisation just made, not merely at the bill in general, though it then moves into prepared material on Budget Policy Statements.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dr David Wilson: "For too long, the previous Government cluttered our public finance reports as wellbeing measures that often served more as an ideological exercise in a practical, economic tool" — and Cameron Brewer: "We remember those Wellbeing Budgets and their huge operating allowances."

acuity.statement: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it’s got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
acuity.explanation: Davidson had just argued at length that the bill's real effect is removing the five wellbeings, and that the last Government's commitments were plainly readable in budgets and press releases. MacLeod takes up none of that: no mention of the wellbeings, and no engagement with the claim that the funding was legible to anyone who read the Budget properly. He asserts the contrary position (fiscal cliffs, unfunded promises) as prepared material and moves to commending the bill and praising the select committee. There is a gesture at the matter under debate — transparency of funding commitments — which keeps it above 0.1, but the speech would read identically whatever Davidson had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "As other members have pointed out there were a large number of media releases and there was a large number of budgets available to be read." — MacLeod does not take this up; he restates the fiscal-cliffs claim without addressing it.

acuity.statement: The members on the other side who talk about fiscal cliffs, it really just shows their own ignorance, because anyone who reads the actual Budget—not just some press release on it but that Budget—will see that it tells you year by year how much is allocated. If it doesn’t say out-years, then those further years aren’t funded.
acuity.explanation: Webb opens by taking the specific claim MacLeod had just made — that opening the books revealed fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding — and rebutting its reasoning directly: a Budget states allocations year by year, so an absence of out-year figures is itself the disclosure that the funding ends. He supplies the mechanism that, on his account, makes the surprise impossible, and names the alternative explanation (innumeracy rather than concealment). Had MacLeod made a different argument, this opening would have had to change. The rebuttal is insulting, which is a civility matter, not an acuity one; engaging an argument in order to demolish it is the strongest evidence of having listened.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding" — Webb takes up the fiscal-cliffs claim and argues the Budget's year-by-year allocations already disclose them.

acuity.statement: Well, Dave, the bill will pass its first reading, but be assured that our position is crystal clear; we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits.
acuity.explanation: Redmayne follows Tangaere-Manuel in the same first-reading debate, so she is eligible. Her speech is prepared constituent correspondence read into the record; it never engages Tangaere-Manuel's argument about kaitiakitanga, customary consultation, or the unsuitability of blanket legislation to particular rohe. The only overlap is the size-limit topic, which Tangaere-Manuel also mentioned, but Redmayne restates National's position rather than taking up anything the previous speaker claimed. Her one back-reference, to Cameron Luxton's earlier speech, is a passing mention, not engagement with content. The speech would read identically whatever Tangaere-Manuel had said, but it is at least squarely on the bill under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued that 'The amendments proposed in this bill threaten that. They threaten kaitiakitanga, they threaten the value of consulting with kaitiaki' and this speech does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Like many others in this House today, I can also claim to be a recreational fisher. We love getting out on our boat.
acuity.explanation: Tinetti speaks after Redmayne in the same debate, so she is eligible. Redmayne had just made a specific and testable commitment on behalf of National — that the size-limit provisions would be removed and that National would withhold support at second reading otherwise — and Tinetti engages none of it: no acceptance, no challenge, no demand that it be honoured. What she offers is general prepared material about the sea, Tauranga, and her own fishing, plus a passing nod to Cameron Luxton that mirrors Redmayne's own reference rather than responding to her. It stays on the subject of the bill, which keeps it above the floor, but the deciding test fails: substituting a different argument on fisheries before it would require no change to these words.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Suze Redmayne said 'we will take out the sections of the bill that remove the minimum size limits' and this speech does not take that commitment up.

acuity.statement: I have spoken—this being Part 1—on that interjection I had with Steve Abel there, he was referring to one of my later Amendment Papers, but the Amendment Paper that I have right in front of us, on Part 1, Amendment Paper 566, relates to a rebuilding of trust. I hope that the Minister takes this opportunity to take a call, in Part 1, and that pregnant pauses, as directed by the chair, do not lead to moving on before such parts are addressed.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Abel's preceding turn — correcting which Amendment Paper Abel was actually addressing (a later one, not the Part 1 paper now before the committee) — but does not engage Abel's substantive point about the transitional agency's treatment of industry participants, instead turning to prepared material urging the Minister to address Amendment Paper 566. A partial, largely procedural engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "Sure, I can speak to your amendment later if you'd prefer." / "Perhaps the Minister can respond in terms of the intention that he expects of the transitional agency and how those who are part of the industry are treated."

acuity.statement: I’m speaking to Amendment Paper 567 specifically, from Mr Luxton. The concern we have with that amendment—what I think the Minister has expressed—is just how broad it is. It does set a problematic precedent if there’s an expectation that, when an industry has fallen out of favour with the public and has moved beyond being acceptable, in terms of social licence, they will be compensated if the Government does what is appropriate and brings an end to that industry. That would be a problematic precedent for us to set in the House.
acuity.explanation: Engages Luxton's amendment directly and on its merits: names it, identifies the specific defect (breadth), states the consequence he objects to (a precedent that industries losing social licence get compensated), and then offers a narrowed counter-amendment confined to retraining support. The speech would be materially different had Luxton proposed something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "relates to a rebuilding of trust" / "an historic and culturally important industry in New Zealand, a legally abiding and complying industry" — Luxton's call for his Amendment Papers on transition and compensation to be addressed

acuity.statement: Well, maybe you’d be surprised that we’re not—how much, Minister, above the Ministry of Social Development jobseeker and retraining schemes we already have in New Zealand does he think it would cost to implement Mr Steve Abel’s amendment? Why would we need that? I suppose I couldn’t really ask the Minister that, but how much does he think it would cost to retrain, how much to compensate for earnings, and how much to compensate for capital?
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific content of Abel's just-proposed retraining amendment and draws out a consequence of it — what it would cost over and above existing MSD jobseeker and retraining schemes — rather than merely naming Abel as a target. It engages the amendment's substance, though it does so by putting questions to the Minister rather than rebutting Abel's precedent argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "recommend the establishment of a scheme that seeks to support retraining for those affected persons" — his proposed narrowing of AP 567 to retraining support

acuity.statement: The member asked that question seven times. It didn’t improve.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges that a question was repeatedly put but engages no part of its content — supplies no figure, no range, and no account of the cost question itself. It is about the matter under debate and aimed at the preceding speaker, which keeps it above the floor, but it is a dismissal of the asking rather than an engagement with what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "how much does he think it would cost to retrain, how much to compensate for earnings, and how much to compensate for capital?"

acuity.statement: We’ve heard those concerns and we’ve responded. Last week, the Prime Minister, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, stepped in to ask that amendments removing commercial minimum legal sizes for nine fish species be dropped.
acuity.explanation: Butterick follows Tinetti, who called the dropping of the size-limit clause an embarrassing 'back-down' and evidence of a shambolic process. He takes up that same episode and reframes it as the Government listening and responding, and elsewhere in the turn takes up two further strands she raised (that select committee cannot make broad-ranging changes, and that governing parties are conditioning further support). But he does not engage her central claim that the work should have been done before introduction, and most of the speech is prepared material about fishing as a way of life that would read identically whoever had spoken before. Partial engagement: one strand taken up, then back to the set speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "It is a very embarrassing situation when a bill just gets tabled and then already we’re starting to see a back-down, and that was on the size limit clause."

acuity.statement: Well, I’m sorry, if your proposition is that central government should dictate on a street-by-street level what happens in Auckland, good luck explaining that to your constituents in Wellington Central.
acuity.explanation: Bishop replies directly to Paul's interjection that community objections to upzoning are 'nimbyism', drawing out what he takes to be its consequence (that central government would have to dictate street-by-street) and turning it back on her own electorate. The reply is plainly shaped by what she said and would be different had she interjected something else, so engagement is high; it does not, however, take up her actual claim that the objections are nimbyism, instead substituting a proposition she did not advance — which keeps it short of a full 1.0 on engagement with the specific content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "No, that’s nimbyism, Bish’, you know it."

acuity.statement: Well, no, I just put that proposition, and she told me I was wrong. We are not going to do that.
acuity.explanation: This takes up Swarbrick's interjection on the spot: he acknowledges her denial that anyone is proposing central direction, accepts it as settling the point, and uses it to state his own position that the Government will not do that. The sentences only make sense as a response to her words and would have to change entirely if she had said something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "No one is proposing that."

acuity.statement: There’s people that say, “Oh, well, we want to talk about the market.” Let me tell you a little bit about the market, is that there are such things as natural monopolies. In case you wonder if I know what I’m talking about, a natural monopoly is a service that has constantly increasing returns to scale, so one provider is the most efficient way to provide.
acuity.explanation: Seymour takes up the specific charge put in the preceding turn — that ACT, the supposed party of markets, is behaving anti-market by restricting intensification — and answers it on its own terms, arguing that the network infrastructure cities depend on is a natural monopoly and therefore that zoning is the market-consistent position. The passage would read differently had the preceding speaker not pressed the market point; it is aimed at the content of the claim rather than merely naming it. Not a full 1.0 because he answers the general market framing rather than the particular evidence Swarbrick offered, and then moves into prepared ground.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "ACT is meant to be about the marketplace, but they are the most anti-marketplace outside of Russia" — Chlöe Swarbrick, reading Mayor Wayne Brown's charge that ACT is anti-market in opposing intensification

acuity.statement: And so today, I’m proud to stand here in this House and support legislation that says that the required number of homes will only be 1.4 million. We’re not going to force on Aucklanders something that they did not want.
acuity.explanation: This engages both strands of the preceding turn: it supplies the figure behind Swarbrick's 600,000-unit reduction (2.078 million down to 1.4 million), owning rather than denying the cut, and it answers her localism challenge by casting the reduction as returning the decision to Aucklanders and the Auckland Unitary Plan. Scored below the top because the engagement is with her framing rather than with her specific counter-evidence (the Plan Change 120 consultation and the mayor's own stated position), which he does not take up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "If this Government believes what it says about localism, then let’s be honest and hand back the local decision-making powers to Auckland Council" and the claim the bill is "cutting 600,000 units from that potential supplier" — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: I’m going to start with some personal reflections, because one of the things that central government has done, whether it’s a red-led Government or a blue-led Government, is continuously interfere in the way in which cities are designed.
acuity.explanation: Foster picks up one strand of the preceding turn — central government dictating city form to councils, and the MDRS specifically — and adds a first-hand Wellington district plan anecdote that corroborates it, so the contribution is not indifferent to what came before. But it engages none of Seymour's distinctive reasoning (natural monopolies, the 1.4 million figure, localism as the justification for this bill) and is explicitly announced as prepared personal reflection, so it answers the topic rather than the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "When Wellington decides and says it’s three by three-storey houses everywhere, they missed the most critical and important facts on each streets and in each suburb of our city" — David Seymour

acuity.statement: Let’s be clear about what this bill is, for the Hon Phil Twyford and for others who’ve weighed in. This is a clean-up job. Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons. So the member Tamatha Paul makes a good point: the Resource Management Act is broken.
acuity.explanation: Court takes up the specific strand of Paul's speech about heritage and character being used to stop development, concedes it by name ("makes a good point"), supplies his own concrete instance of it (the K Road seven-storey refusal on heritage grounds), and then draws a consequence from the concession — that the Greens should therefore support the Planning Bill. The speech would have to change if Paul had argued something else on the same topic, so this is genuine engagement rather than a mere reference; it falls short of 1.0 because he reframes her point into his own prepared pitch rather than engaging her actual claim that the bill has been gutted.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "they weaponise this concept of character, protecting the special character of an area" — her argument that heritage/character provisions are used to block housing in wealthy suburbs

acuity.statement: This bill, of course, locks in the Government’s decision this week to reduce the minimum housing capacity required by Plan Change 120 from 2 million to 1.4 million. This comes from the earlier 2 million number and is up from the 2016 unitary plan capacity targets. It’s a very good place to land.
acuity.explanation: Follows Andy Foster, who argued that growth pays only 30-50 percent of its own infrastructure costs and that MDRS failed because it was a non-targeted 'three by three'. Brewer's speech takes up neither strand: it recites the capacity change, recaps what MDRS was, and quotes a former mayor's approval. It is prepared material squarely on the matter under debate and would read identically whatever Foster had said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band with a gesture at the subject but no engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued that 'Growth is not paying for growth' and that MDRS was 'a completely non-targeted approach', and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Here we are again today, and this National Government have pandered to the ACT Party to reduce the number of houses that will be built in Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland to address the housing crisis to make it more affordable for young Aucklanders to get into the property market and buy their own first home.
acuity.explanation: Brewer had just presented the cut from 2 million to 1.4 million as listening to Aucklanders and 'a very good place to land'. Halbert contests that exact decision, attributing it to pressure from a coalition partner rather than to public consultation — so one strand of the preceding turn is taken up and can be pointed at. But he does not engage Brewer's reasoning (the opt-out, the consultation, the CRL-node targeting) and moves straight back to prepared material on urgency and Northcote, which places this between the partial-engagement and on-topic bands.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: 'We’ve listened to Aucklanders and we’ve dropped that capacity requirement from, again, 2 million to 1.4 million'

acuity.statement: Some members of the House that had six years to do something about it didn’t do something about it. We are embarking on doing something maybe swiftly, but we need the swiftness after we’ve listened to our neighbours all around Auckland.
acuity.explanation: Halbert had just argued that using urgency is bad process because it denies the Opposition and Aucklanders scrutiny. Nakhle concedes the speed and offers a justification for it — that listening came first — which is a real, pointable take-up of his central procedural objection, though a one-clause one. The rest of the turn pivots to the previous government's six years, which engages nothing. Partial engagement, not a rebuttal of his reasoning about scrutiny.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: 'Bringing this through urgency is bad process.'

acuity.statement: They don’t get to participate, in the way they should have, in the process, and I do not accept that there is any reason why this has to happen so urgently. They need to be involved in those processes.
acuity.explanation: Nakhle, immediately before, defended the speed on the ground that the Government had already listened to Aucklanders. White asserts the opposite — that constituents do not get to participate and that no reason for urgency exists — which lands on the same question but does not take up Nakhle's justification or test it; she proceeds to her own prepared material on stormwater, Mt Albert and the regulatory impact statement. On-topic with a gesture at the dispute rather than engagement with the argument, so the top of the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: 'we need the swiftness after we’ve listened to our neighbours all around Auckland'

acuity.statement: The Labour Party is completely out of touch. Aucklanders have been clear that they support growth, but as long as it happens in the right place and is backed up by the right infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Helen White had just charged that intensification is being steered away from certain MPs' electorates in an election year, and that the regulatory impact statement concedes almost no stakeholder engagement. Cheung opens by naming her party as out of touch and then delivers prepared material on Mt Roskill, the Balmoral Residents Association and the 1.4 million figure. Naming an opponent as a target is not engaging their content, and nothing here answers the exempted-suburbs charge or the RIS — indeed he welcomes intensification not being forced into his own area without noticing that is her point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued that 'the interests of some MPs in election year are being looked after rather well' and that the RIS records very little engagement with stakeholders, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: What we’re arguing about, it seems to me, is that there is a certain number of houses, and I do note that it is a minimum number. Now, if Auckland Council say, “We actually don’t want that minimum; we want to go further than that.”, isn’t that up to Auckland Council to decide that?
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the immediately preceding turn — Court's claim that the decision now rests with Auckland Council — and does something with it, pointing out the target is a minimum and that the council could therefore choose to go higher. Partial rather than full engagement: it engages the council-decides point but not Court's zoning/property-rights argument, and the speech then moves into prepared material on migration and infrastructure funding.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The ball’s now in Auckland Council’s court. They can choose to live out a SimCity planner’s unicorn world ... or they can choose to listen to Aucklanders." — Simon Court

acuity.statement: As I said in the first reading and as I’ve stood up in this House many times before and said, we actually don’t have a long-term strategy of any sort around migration.
acuity.explanation: Self-described repeat material ("as I said in the first reading ... many times before") that engages no part of the preceding turn. It is at least on the matter under debate — growth driving the Auckland housing numbers — so not wholly unresponsive, but it would read identically whatever Court had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Court spoke about property rights, zoning setbacks and the Planning Bill handing the decision to Auckland Council, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Today, what we are doing is we are making sure that David Seymour’s area does not have the kinds of houses that are going to be going into my area. You have heard the passionate response of Phil Twyford today about his area, which already has those.
acuity.explanation: White follows Kaipara's turn and engages no part of it — the Treaty clause, the mana whenua role and papa kāinga all go unmentioned. Her speech is on the matter under debate (the Auckland housing bill, Epsom, council planning, Wesley) and gestures at the debate by naming Twyford's earlier speech and saying 'I take the point that some people have made tonight', but it would read identically whatever Kaipara had argued, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Oriini Kaipara argued the bill has no Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause, no role for the 19 mana whenua of Tāmaki and no commitment to papa kāinga as the Māori housing solution, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Well, I must say, I feel like I’m debating different bills in this House. We are here talking about the Resource Management (Auckland Housing) Amendment Bill, which seeks to provide Auckland Council with greater flexibility in how housing capacity is allocated across the city. That is what this bill is about.
acuity.explanation: Bidois takes up the two specific claims in the turn immediately before his: that the bill's 'flexibility' is a weasel word, and that it centralises decisions away from Auckland Council. He asserts the opposite on both — that the bill's purpose is to give the council greater flexibility over housing capacity, and that 'the next step is that council will decide how this is going to be applied to the city' — and then turns White's own appeal to trusting elected local representatives back on her. The speech would have to change if White had argued something else, which is what the deciding test asks. Whether the characterisation of the bill is accurate or fair is a veracity/rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They are weasel words. It is not about flexibility" and "We are deciding, in our centralised system—not the council—that, no, we know best" — Helen White

acuity.statement: I want to commend this bill to the House because, unlike the other side of the House, which talks about what officials were saying and about consultation between bureaucrats in Wellington and bureaucrats in Auckland, on this side of the House we actually listen to Aucklanders.
acuity.explanation: Brown's opening directly picks up the strand of Walters's speech that rested on the regulatory impact statement and departmental disclosure statement — her claim that officials were engaged but no wider consultation occurred — and answers it by reframing consultation as listening to Aucklanders rather than to bureaucrats. It is pointable engagement with one strand of her argument, so above the prepared-material band, but he does not take up the specific documentary claims she made (that the options were modelled on 1.6 million, and that councillors learnt of 1.4 million overnight), nor her Glen Eden infrastructure example; the rest of the speech is prepared contrast with the previous Government. Partial engagement, hence ~0.5. Scored only on responsiveness: the merit of the 'bureaucrats versus Aucklanders' inference belongs to Rigor and the dismissiveness to Civility, and neither moved this score.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Vanushi Walters: "the documents say that while officials were engaged, no other consultation was undertaken on the proposals"

acuity.statement: If it is for the avoidance of doubt, can the Minister comment on why there is this building consent trigger and whether he’s got analysis that the 400 that he was just referring to will all be picked up by the mechanism that is the building consent.
acuity.explanation: She takes Bishop's own two claims — that the fix is merely 'for the avoidance of doubt' and that 400 people were caught — and presses both: if it is only for doubt, why a building consent trigger, and does the trigger actually capture all 400. The question could not have been asked without hearing his answer, and she goes on to test his 'no advice' assertion against the timing of the Amendment Paper.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The MDRS lacuna—the 400 or so people affected by the lacuna in the law—was not a foreseen consequence" and "We’re now legislating for the avoidance of doubt."

acuity.statement: The building consent point links to this, because what happened is that people went and got building consents and were about to build or, in some cases, were building already, not needing a resource consent because of the medium-density residential standards (MDRS), and then the Government let the council withdraw Plan Change 78, which took away the underlying MDRS zoning.
acuity.explanation: He answers the specific question about why the building consent is the trigger by explaining the mechanism that stranded consent-holders, and in the next paragraph takes up her second question about whether the primary legislation or the Amendment Paper caused it, conceding he does not recall advice and that it is probably both. Directly shaped by what she asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "can the Minister comment on why there is this building consent trigger"

acuity.statement: My last point on this one, then, is in terms of what the Minister responsible for RMA Reform just said about the building consents and because there was this problem. What about the people who might have been relying on a certificate of compliance and were not yet at the building consent phase?
acuity.explanation: She accepts his account of the building-consent trigger and immediately probes the gap it leaves — owners not yet at consent stage who were relying on a certificate of compliance. The question exists only as a consequence of the answer just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "They were stuck in this limbo land of having a building consent but having to go off and get a resource consent... That’s the trigger there."

acuity.statement: No, I’m advised that Auckland Council dealt with that through their processes, which they thought they had the power to do.
acuity.explanation: A direct answer to the certificate-of-compliance question, naming who handled it and on what basis. Brief, and it leaves the limits of the council's power vague, but it squarely addresses the case she raised rather than returning to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Are they able to get a certificate of compliance to say that it was permitted as of “X” date and they can still continue with it?"

acuity.statement: The fact that the process the Minister responsible for RMA Reform has explained for dealing with developers who had begun a process under the medium-density residential standards rules really puts the spotlight on what has been a pretty torturous process, where the target for the number of enabled dwellings for Auckland started out at 2 million; it went to 1.6 million; Auckland Council have been consulting on the 1.6 million figure in the associated plan; this bill reduces the target to 1.4 million; the mayor is sort of apoplectic about it.
acuity.explanation: He uses the Minister's just-given explanation as the premise for his own point, drawing out a consequence (that the process has been chaotic) rather than simply ignoring it. But he then moves onto the sequence of dwelling targets, which is prepared material that would have survived whatever Bishop said, so the engagement is real but partial.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "They were stuck in this limbo land of having a building consent but having to go off and get a resource consent" — his explanation of how affected developers were handled

acuity.statement: Let’s start with clause 63 in new Part 10 of Schedule 12, inserted by clause 4. So this says, “Nothing in the amendment Act affects the validity or status of any submission made or struck out”, blah-blah-blah-blah.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the bill under consideration and gestures at the debate by invoking what the Minister said at first reading about interested parties, but it takes up no part of the arguments in the preceding turns — the building-consent trigger, certificates of compliance, or Twyford's question about public confidence. It is on-topic prepared material beginning a new line of questioning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Twyford had just asked what the process has done to Aucklanders' confidence in the planning process, and Bishop had explained the building-consent and certificate-of-compliance mechanics; this statement opens an unrelated strand on the validity of submissions under clause 63.

acuity.statement: The short point, legally, is there are about 10,500 submissions that are all valid and will be taken into account through the independent hearings panel process and then, subsequently, by the councils. That is, literally, the purpose of clause 63 of new Part 10 of Schedule 12, which is inserted by clause 4 of the substantive bill.
acuity.explanation: He answers the exact question with the number of submissions and the clause that preserves them, then takes up her second and harder argument about future generations having no voice, concedes sympathy for it, and explains why the planning system privileges present residents. The whole reply is built around the strands she raised.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "What is to come of the validity or the status of their submissions that they’ve made for 2 million—if not 1.6 million—homes to be enabled in Auckland?"

acuity.statement: When I talked to Auckland councillors, their argument is that Plan Change 120, or the Auckland Unitary Plan in its original form, took that into account. What it was a reflection of is where the infrastructure best exists in terms of where the transport exists, where the waste water is, where the libraries, the hospitals, all of the things that make up infrastructure, that was a key element of Plan Change 120 as they had already looked at the infrastructure capacity and enabled it.
acuity.explanation: Paul first pins the Minister's premise down ('Fair characterisation?') and then disputes exactly that premise — that the new plan change is the one calibrated to existing infrastructure — by reporting that councillors say the original Plan Change 120 already did that work. The contribution would have to be rewritten if Bishop had rested his case on something other than existing infrastructure.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "Getting zoning in the right place where infrastructure has been invested in and already exists close to where people live, work, and play, and close to where the jobs are, is one of the most significant things we can do to aid Auckland productivity."

acuity.statement: The other thing is the Minister talks about flood zones—I’m sorry that my numbers weren’t completely correct; we just found out about this two days ago—and natural hazard zones; the Minister also talks about the importance of a plan around where flooding might happen, in the context of Gabrielle and the Auckland anniversary floods, but my understanding is another key element of Plan Change 120 is to allow flexibility so that housing isn’t only built in places that are flood-prone. But by, you know, hamstringing these rich suburbs from doing their part, that means housing will be built in areas that are more prone to natural disasters.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's own flood-zone justification and turns it against him — accepting that flood-prone land should not be built on, then arguing that limiting upzoning in well-served suburbs pushes housing toward hazard-prone areas. She also volunteers a correction to her own earlier figures. Not the full 1.0 only because the counter-argument is asserted rather than drawn from anything specific in his reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "It’s really important that this plan change proceeds because there are whole swathes of Auckland that should be downzoned because they’re in flood areas."

acuity.statement: In relation to how many submissions were from mana whenua into Plan Change 120: I don’t know; you’ll have to go and ask the council that. They ran the submission process on that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put to him, squarely and without evasion of the question itself (he says he does not know and names who would). Short of 1.0 because he engages only the submissions-count strand and leaves untouched the second half of her question — whether any further consultation with mana whenua would be directed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "Do you know how many of those 10,000 submissions were from people who belong to mana whenua or local iwi within Auckland?"

acuity.statement: I think people broadly understand the point, which is that you can have development capacity, but whether or not something actually gets turned into houses depends on market economics, it turns on development economics, it turns on demand, it turns on bank finance, a whole range of other things, and the point that we’re trying to create is a surplus of development opportunity so that we have competitive land markets and competitive development opportunities.
acuity.explanation: Engages the exact distinction Paul challenged the Government to demonstrate it understood — zoning capacity versus houses actually built — and supplies the mechanism (demand, development economics, finance) plus the policy rationale of a capacity surplus. The answer is specific to her claim and would not survive unchanged if she had pressed a different point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "some of those speeches were acting like zoning means that the housing happens tomorrow"

acuity.statement: The latest version of Plan Change 120, which will go through some iterations over the next few months as it gets landed next year, is better calibrated to the existing infrastructure, not only because of the City Rail Link, but also in relation to the Auckland waste-water and stormwater networks as well.
acuity.explanation: Meets her challenge on its own ground, distinguishing Plan Change 78 from the latest Plan Change 120 and naming the networks (City Rail Link, waste-water, stormwater) the calibration rests on. Below 1.0 because he does not take up the councillors' and mayor's contrary assessment that she cited, gesturing instead at unnamed 'analysis floating around'.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "So really going to challenge you on the infrastructure capacity assumption you’re making, because that’s not what Auckland councillors and the mayor say about the infrastructure assumptions that underline the original Plan Change 120."

acuity.statement: Well, I’ve dealt with this issue a couple of times now, maybe even three times: the submissions that have been made are valid; that is one of the provisions in the legislation and they will be listened to. There will be an opportunity for people who’ve made a submission to update or amend their submissions in light of the revised maps.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Williams' question — the standing and future handling of the submissions — and supplies a substantive answer about validity and the chance to amend after revised maps. But it leaves her specific points untouched: the 10,500 figure and the counter-submission stage she asked him to locate, why the independent hearings panel gets up to a year if the aim is to save consultation time, and the Prime Minister's January statement. Engagement with the topic and part of the claim, not with the specific questions put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "What is the status of those submissions in the first place" / "I want the Minister to clarify where we’re up to in that submission process."

acuity.statement: The member raises an interesting point, which is a bugbear of mine, which is this ridiculous notion that councillors and local board members are not allowed to have views about things that they are elected to local councils to do.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the precise strand of Williams' argument — that elected members met on 10 March and took a position before submissions closed — and contests its premise head on, arguing that elected members having views is legitimate and that the constraint itself is the problem. The speech would plainly be different had she not made that point. Short of 1.0 because he converts her specific objection (a statutory prohibition in this bill) into a general grievance about unelected officials rather than addressing the clause she cited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "it’s very unusual for local body members, and actually in the bill they are prohibited from taking a position before they have been able to consider submissions"

acuity.statement: I’m going to go specifically to this, but just on that answer around councils, there were some valid points you were just saying. I agree councils shouldn’t be the handbrake to housing and they shouldn’t be able to control every little element and aspect of development. But there are some important precedents or rules that councils can set; things like minimum room sizes.
acuity.explanation: Classic concede-and-divide: accepts Bishop's general claim that councils should not police every detail of a development, then separates out the one item on his list she disputes — minimum room sizes — and gives a reason for the carve-out. She also adopts his own example (the colour of the door) to mark where she agrees. The passage could not have been written without his immediately preceding argument. Not a full 1.0 only because she then returns to prepared questions on clause 6(8).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "The way your living room faces, where your TV faces, the size of your bedrooms, all that sort of stuff—those are not legitimate roles of the planning system."

acuity.statement: This is a relatively simple issue. The short point is that the National Policy Statement on Urban Development (NPS-UD) requires the council to start doing a Future Development Strategy and a variety of different things soon, and we don’t want them to do that, because we’re in the process of doing this existing plan change and also the new planning system is on the horizon, and so—this has actually come from the council—the council does not want to start a process that will be defunct soon at some point. It’s just an attempt to try and save some time and money, which I think we’re all in favour of.
acuity.explanation: Brooking asked precisely why the NPS-UD exemption was needed and whether the demand/capacity and future development strategy work had already been done. Bishop takes up that exact question and supplies a reason (the council itself does not want to begin a Future Development Strategy that the new planning system will make defunct). The answer would have to be different had she asked something else, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he does not address her linked question about the backstop long-term plan date in the same breath.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "The questions are very simple ones in terms of: why is this exemption needed?"

acuity.statement: Now, I want to actually start with clause 3 in terms of the principal Act, in Part 1, because I know we haven’t quite touched on that particular bit.
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by Bishop explained the NPS-UD exemption and the recommencement trigger in clause 66(2)(a). Xu-Nan engages none of that; he explicitly opens an untouched clause and proceeds with his own prepared questions on clauses 3, 4 and 65(6). He is squarely on the bill under debate and gestures at the debate so far ('we haven’t quite touched on that particular bit'), which places him at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0, but the speech would read identically whatever Bishop had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just explained why the NPS-UD exemption is needed and what clause 66(2)(a) does, and this statement does not take either up — it moves to a clause the member notes has not been touched.

acuity.statement: Look, the member shouldn’t overthink it. In Part 1, clause 3 says the Act amends the Resource Management Act 1991. There’s not a lot of debate to be had about that. That is what it does, so don’t overthink it. The bill amends the primary Act. That’s pretty straightforward.
acuity.explanation: This is aimed at the right target — Xu-Nan's first question, flagged as 'specifically on clause 3' — so there is real engagement with the topic put to him. But the substance of that question was whether a reduction in enabled capacity from 2.07 million dwellings could still meet the sustainable-management purpose in section 5(2) of the RMA, and Bishop answers only the literal mechanics of clause 3 as an amending provision. He takes up one strand and declines the argument, which is the partial-engagement band rather than the top.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "would a reduction meet the threshold of the purpose of the RMA? That is my first question specifically on clause 3."

acuity.statement: Given his comments around saving time and money on this, and the sort of laughs that he must have when the Greens and the Labour Party are standing up and saying, “We’d love more consultation”—a staple of every right-wing politician and local government on any planning bill who knows that the best way to do this sort of thing for the villa-loving constituents is to ask for more consultation. But that’s what you’ve got on the left tonight, so enjoy it for a bit.
acuity.explanation: Williams picks up the Minister's own stated rationale — that the exemption is 'an attempt to try and save some time and money' — and turns it into the frame for her question about whether time could be saved on the submissions process instead. That is genuine engagement with the specific justification just offered, and she concedes the awkwardness of the left arguing for more consultation rather than ignoring it. It sits below the top band because a good part of the passage is a general characterisation of right-wing planning politics rather than work on Bishop's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "It’s just an attempt to try and save some time and money, which I think we’re all in favour of."

acuity.statement: Let me start with that last point. I mean, the key point here is we’re not master planning Auckland in this bill, OK? Auckland Council is planning Auckland and that is a really important thing to just remember. There are no underlying assumptions in the bill around where the infrastructure is in Auckland. That exists now and the council has that information and they are the appropriate body to work that through with local communities. It is true to say—and officials have done some analysis on this—that the new Plan Change 120 that is now under way is better calibrated to where the existing infrastructure is than Plan Change 78, for example.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Paul's specific question about the bill's underlying infrastructure-capacity assumptions and answers it squarely: there are none in the bill, because the council holds that information and is the planning body; then supplies the officials' comparative analysis (Plan Change 120 better calibrated to existing infrastructure than Plan Change 78) and goes on to address her second question about what happens as growth eventuates. The reply would have had to be materially different had Paul asked something else on the same topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what are the underlying assumptions around infrastructure capacity now?" — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: Since my last contribution, the Minister has raised many issues, and I would like to note that I agree strongly with some of what the Minister was saying about infrastructure and the importance of the upzoning and the intensification. I am interested in how he can say that this legislation, though, is the next step in making progress, because my reading of this is that this is a backwards step. Was the Minister referring to a forward step or a backwards step? That is my first question.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's immediately preceding turn directly: concedes the part about infrastructure and intensification, then disputes his characterisation of the bill as progress and puts the forward/backward question to him. She goes on in the same turn to quote back his own answer on clause 6(3) and the 1.6 million figure and press on what that means for Auckland Council's past six weeks of work. The speech would be substantially different had Bishop argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I deny the member's point—I just reject absolutely the idea—that zoning doesn't matter. It does. It will lead to more affordable housing over time."

acuity.statement: The member asks around is this a forward or backward step? Well, like, objectively, it is a forward step. The Auckland Unitary Plan allows for 1.2 million. With this, we’ll end up at about 1.6. It’s obviously not as high as 2 million, but it is undoubtedly a step forward.
acuity.explanation: Names the specific question just put to him and answers it with the numbers it turned on (1.2 million baseline, 1.6 million outcome, conceding it is short of 2 million). The same turn also answers her technical question about the 'and'/'or' change to Schedule 3C and her social housing point, so the reply is shaped throughout by what Brooking said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Was the Minister referring to a forward step or a backwards step? That is my first question."

acuity.statement: Thank you so much, Mr Chair. I just want to pick up on some of the Minister’s earlier comments in response to Tamatha Paul’s questions. These are the kind of questions we would have been able to ask at the select committee, should this have not been brought in urgency. Particularly with the stuff in clause 6(3) around the reduction on the minimum housing capacity, basically, I wanted to ask if any work had been done on the modelling and changes around job creation as a result of this change.
acuity.explanation: On the clause under debate and gestures at the Minister's remarks, but engages no part of the argument in the turn it follows — Bishop's answers on the forward/backward step, social housing and the Schedule 3C qualifying matters are left untouched. It instead reaches back to an exchange outside this stretch of debate and opens prepared questions on job-creation modelling and demographics, which would read identically whatever Bishop had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop had just argued "The member asks around social housing. The key point is that social housing is just another form of housing." and explained the "and"/"or" change to Schedule 3C, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Very briefly: no, in relation to the modelling around job creation, we haven’t done that, and, no, in relation to—I think the member’s second question was around demographic trends. I think the key point is that there is now going to be more theoretical development capacity in Auckland as a result of Plan Change 120, and, also, that capacity is better calibrated to the existing infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of the questions just asked, in the order asked, and concedes directly that the job-creation modelling was not done before supplying what officials' analysis does say about capacity and infrastructure. The content of the reply is wholly determined by Menéndez March's two questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "So just to recap, any modelling on job creation, and, if not, does he accept that the downgrading of the minimum housing capacity will likely result in less jobs available for people?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. First of all, I just wanted to reflect on a comment that the Minister made. I still don’t actually know how many real houses would be built, but I am really pleased to think that there is some work going on in that area of coordination of central planning in cities. That seems very sensible, and, obviously, has already been done in Wesley, but I won’t labour that.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's answer — his appeal to 'theoretical development capacity' — by pointing out it still does not tell her how many real houses get built, then explicitly sets that aside and moves to her own prepared material on submissions and the regulatory impact statement. A partial engagement you can point at, not a rebuttal of the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "there is now going to be more theoretical development capacity in Auckland as a result of Plan Change 120"

acuity.statement: The regulatory impact statement—I mean, the member herself says there wasn’t enough time; it is what it is, so to speak. We are making quick changes, but this issue has been extensively debated backwards and forwards and I generally think what everyone needs now is just some clarity and some certainty. It’s not an ideal parliamentary process; the member knows I don’t like urgency and I don’t like not sending bills to a select committee.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific criticism just made, quotes her own characterisation of the RIS back and accepts it rather than disputing it, and concedes the process point about urgency and select committee referral. It stops short of the precise thing she asked — whether any further consultation was attempted after the February RIS — which keeps it below a full engagement, but the reply is clearly built on her question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "Was there any attempt to just mitigate the damage by letting there be a further process of consultation; if so, what was it?"

acuity.statement: OK, cool. The problem with that, though, is—has the Minister considered this bill and those provisions that I just read out in relation to future changes to local government?
acuity.explanation: Bishop had just asserted that there is 'good reason' for the provision in question. Paul acknowledges it ('the problem with that, though') but never engages what the reason was or why it fails; she immediately moves to her own prepared line on the rates cap, Auckland Council's borrowing limits and land value capture. The gesture at his answer is real but no part of it is taken up, so this sits in the glance band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: 'there are always good reasons for it and this is one of those examples where there is good reason for it'

acuity.statement: In relation to the member’s second point around value capture, the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act (IFFA) is a form of that. I would prefer to use the term cost recovery because it doesn’t so much capture value but it does allow for cost recovery on the basis of infrastructure investment already made.
acuity.explanation: Takes Paul's specific question about land value capture and does something with it: identifies the existing instrument that performs that function, disputes her framing of it as value capture rather than cost recovery, and explains what the amendment bill before select committee changes about its scope. The answer would be entirely different had she asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: 'Have you considered land value capture, and how does a rates cap interact with—'

acuity.statement: We heard contributions on this Eastern Busway and we’ve heard contributions about other transport issues, and I’ve already said that I agree with the Minister on his point around infrastructure and, where there is that good infrastructure, to make best use of it for intensification.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Bishop's immediately preceding answer — his list of Auckland infrastructure investment including the Eastern Busway — and concedes the principle that intensification should follow good infrastructure, before returning to her own prepared clause-by-clause questions about the named stations and the council's work plan. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, not a reply to the substance of his infrastructure-funding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: 'whether it’s in Drury or in the North West or in the central areas, through things like the Eastern Busway'

acuity.statement: As I think the member knows, special character is not listed in the resource management Act as a qualifying matter. Heritage is a qualifying matter, and there’s a long debate about exactly what heritage is and how it’s determined.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Brooking's specific legal point, concedes it directly — special character is not a qualifying matter, heritage is — and then draws out the consequence by explaining that special character sits under the 'any other matter' catch-all and that the Government is not changing it in this bill. Marked below 1.0 only because her two other questions, on whether other stations were considered and on the council's work plan, are left unanswered in this turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: 'my recollection is that special character is not a qualifying matter; that qualifying matters are Part 2 matters'

acuity.statement: Not only were the houses built but new schools, new water infrastructure, new recreational centres, new shopping centre, and that, in fact, enables what we call the “upzoning”, the discussion point today where we are able to intensify key areas on main arterial transport links for people to live, for people to build their families there, and for communities to thrive.
acuity.explanation: Halbert picks up one strand of Bishop's immediately preceding argument — upzoning around transit routes — and turns it toward the condition Bishop left out, that infrastructure (schools, water, centres) is what makes intensification on arterial links work. But he engages none of Bishop's specific claims (the 1.4/1.6/2 million capacity figures, the delegation of the decision to Auckland Council) and moves quickly into prepared constituency material on Northcote and Chatswood that would read much the same whatever Bishop had argued on the same topic. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I think it’s really important that we zone around the route, you know, in advance of it actually being built."

acuity.statement: My first question to the Minister is: why is there a difference between the height of those two buildings when we’re bringing that into subclause(4) here, in terms of Mt Albert stations? I think that deserves a little bit of attention.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Halbert on the North Shore, Chatswood submissions and the 10km radius, and engages none of it — Xu-Nan proceeds straight into his own prepared clause-by-clause questions (clause 6(4) storey heights, Watercare, 'city centre', PC 120 resourcing). The speech would read identically whatever Halbert had said. It sits in the low band rather than at 0.0 because it is squarely about the bill actually under committee consideration and gestures at the running debate by noting a colleague has already raised the same clause.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Shanan Halbert spoke about the 10 kilometre radius capturing the Chatswood coastal area and about no voices discussing upzoning along the Northern Busway, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I also want to ask about something that my colleagues from the Greens just touched on there about what is the city centre, and this is in clause 6(9), which says: “For the purposes of clause 4, housing capacity does not include the housing capacity in the city centre as at 6 June 2025 when the Plan Change 78 changes to the city centre became operative.” There is talk in the documents that go with the bill about the fact that the city centre has already undergone some rezoning in Plan Change 78. There is also discussion generally about how important that CBD area is, yet Plan Change 120 doesn’t hit on that CBD area, and I take my colleagues’ point about definitions around that, and I’m interested in the Minister’s answers.
