acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Well, as the member will be aware, this Government is focused on security of electricity supply and we're taking a number of actions in order to achieve that, including making sure that we have the back-up generation needed."

acuity.statement: Does he agree with Simon Watts, who said, “If we don’t have an LNG terminal, we haven’t got a plan B for a dry year.”?
acuity.explanation: Engages the substance of the Minister's repeated position that the Government has a range of actions beyond LNG, by confronting him with a government colleague's statement that no alternative plan exists. Aimed squarely at the claim just made rather than at the topic generally, though it introduces fresh material rather than working on his reasoning directly.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown (answering Simon Court): "I can tell the member: hope is not a strategy."

acuity.statement: As I have answered in this House—probably as many times as the Hansard quotes that she’s referring to—definitions of front-line services tend to vary, with that member seeming to count absolutely everything the Government funds as a front-line service. It is the case that this Government has delivered $43 billion in savings in public expenditure across two Budgets. That has been a necessary step to help repair books left in tatters by the last Government.
acuity.explanation: Edmonds put a specific question: does the Minister stand by 'no cuts to front-line services', and were there cuts since Budget 2024. Willis takes up that exact claim, contests the definition of 'front-line services' on which the charge rests, concedes the savings were made and defends them, and later in the same turn returns to 'We have stood by the words I've used in this House.' The speech would be materially different had Edmonds asked about something else. Not 1.0 because she does not engage the asserted 'actual proof' of cuts, pivoting instead to a prepared list of spending priorities.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Barbara Edmonds: "does the Minister stand by her statement that there will be no cuts to front-line services?"

acuity.statement: We did, in fact, end up seeing that the private sector didn’t fill that gap. In fact, the Government ended up, through its fiscal strategy, kneecapping the very growth and productivity that it so frequently likes to crow about. I’d just like to put that question to the Minister again: whether, looking back, she believes that the Government’s decision to suck billions of dollars of investment out of the economy was ultimately filled by the private sector.
acuity.explanation: Willis had just defended the $43 billion of savings as a 'necessary step'; Swarbrick engages that one strand by arguing the spending reduction suppressed growth rather than repairing anything. But she frames it as re-putting a question she asked months earlier in select committee and then runs prepared material on unemployment, construction jobs, flood protection and Fitch, taking up none of Willis's actual points (the definitional argument, the health/education/police spending claims). Partial engagement with the fiscal strand, otherwise prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "this Government has delivered $43 billion in savings in public expenditure across two Budgets. That has been a necessary step"

acuity.statement: She described the Government’s spending less as “sucking money out of the economy”. Now, I want to be clear with the member about where the money that Government spends comes from: it comes from the tax that working New Zealanders pay. What the member is actually saying is that, in her book, the way to grow an economy is to suck more money out of the pockets of working people.
acuity.explanation: Willis takes Swarbrick's own formulation, quotes it back and then does something with it — she attacks the premise by tracing the money to taxpayers and draws out what she says follows from it. She also answers the second half of Swarbrick's question on resilience by naming fast-track consenting of solar and wind projects, which Swarbrick opposes. The turn could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument. Scored on engagement only; whether the inference is a fair reading of Swarbrick's position is a Rigor question, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "the Government’s decision to suck billions of dollars of investment out of the economy"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I thank the Minister for answering some of the questions put forward by colleagues. Given the Minsiter’s proclaimed concern for working families and their pockets, we’d like the answer that we’re still waiting for, to the question “How many families have received the full $250 a fortnight that was promised to them?”, in terms of that relief that the Hon Barbara Edmonds asked about.
acuity.explanation: Woods hooks directly onto Willis's immediately preceding claim about caring for working people's pockets and uses it to press an outstanding specific figure, and at the end of the turn she again picks up Willis's fast-track electrification point to note it began under Labour. Between those, however, the bulk of the contribution is prepared questions on Treasury's climate-liability accounting and PREFU timing that engage nothing Willis said. Half engaged, half prepared.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "members on the other side of the House, while claiming they care about the cost of living faced by New Zealanders"

acuity.statement: In answer to the latter question, one of the bits of advice I’ve had is that if the member hadn’t banned oil and gas exploration for New Zealand, we would most likely have more sufficient gas supply and not the acute electricity price increases that we were left with.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question put to her — what further advice she has received about helping families heat their homes — and supplies an answer to it, naming gas supply and electricity prices. The reply would have to change if Woods had asked something else, so it is squarely responsive; it is not a 1.0 because she answers with a counter-charge about the ban rather than engaging the EECA funding claim that framed the question. Scored on engagement only, not on whether the causal claim is sound or fair.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "Has the Minister since received any other advice from Ministers across the Government about what we might have to do to help families afford to heat their homes?"

acuity.statement: Here’s the reason why they should believe the Minister. You see, there are people who say that a ban in 2018 can’t possibly have led to a restriction in oil and gas availability today, because it takes 15 years for a new well—and that is true—but sometimes you meet people who grab on to one fact and hold it so tightly they squeeze out any relevance it had.
acuity.explanation: Directly picks up the exchange immediately before him: the challenge to the Minister's credibility, and then the specific counterargument that a 2018 ban cannot restrict supply today because a new well takes 15 years. He concedes that premise explicitly ("and that is true") and disputes its relevance, which is accept-part-dispute-the-rest engagement. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different preceding argument. Whether the inference about confidence and old wells holds up is a rigor question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Willis: "She just said that no one believes me when I say that" — and the opposition's 15-year-well objection to her claim about the oil and gas exploration ban

acuity.statement: My question to the Minister is: did she get her priorities right in the Budget, given the record levels of job losses that New Zealanders have sustained right across the regions?
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on a matter genuinely under debate — regional employment and the Budget — delivered immediately after Seymour's argument that the 2018 ban drove Taranaki workers to Australia. She lists regional job losses including Taranaki but engages no part of his reasoning, and the question she puts would read identically had he spoken on any other subject. There is a gesture at the debate's territory, which puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Seymour: "I was in New Plymouth last week, and there’s a lot of people there who still commute to Australia, where they’re welcome to work." — Andersen cites Taranaki job figures but does not take up his argument that the exploration ban destroyed that employment

acuity.statement: The points that I am making—the point that the Green Party is making—is that you do not grow when you starve. That is the approach that this Government has taken to our economy.
acuity.explanation: She opens by announcing she is responding to the Minister of Finance, but the scored sentences are the Green Party's prepared thesis about starving the economy; naming an opponent and then pivoting to one's own line is a reference, not an engagement. It is clearly about the fiscal strategy under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band. Her objection to being called a socialist does engage the heckles from Willis and Seymour, but that passage is not a complete sentence and so is not quoted here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued that the Government's spending comes from New Zealand taxpayers and defended its fiscal position, and these sentences restate the Green Party's own framing rather than taking that argument up

acuity.statement: No, I didn’t say it was a mistake. I said it was a mistake to roll it out the way you useless guys rolled it out. What we are now doing is fixing it.
acuity.explanation: Takes the interjector's exact characterisation and corrects it, distinguishing what he said was a mistake (the rollout) from what the interjector attributed to him (the programme itself). The reply would be different had the interjection been different, so engagement is direct. Scored for responsiveness only — the insult in the second sentence is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You said it was a mistake." — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I thank the Minister for his contribution. I did want to ask a couple of questions of clarification about the numbers he just gave us. I believe he said $1.8 billion—was that annual or over the three-year period? Is that for public transport services and infrastructure or just services?
acuity.explanation: She picks up a specific number from the Minister's preceding speech and presses on what it covers (annual vs triennium, services vs infrastructure, real vs nominal), which is only possible by having listened to it. Marked down from 1.0 because the figure she engages is not visible in the supplied window, so the engagement is pointable only by her own quotation of it, and she then moves on to prepared material about declined funding.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: The figures in Chris Bishop's immediately preceding contribution, which she quotes back as "$1.8 billion"; the nearest in-window fragment of that turn is "there is an enormous amount of resilience being built into the system" (Chris Bishop). The specific figure she takes up sits in a part of his contribution not reproduced in this window.

acuity.statement: In relation to the member’s last point, those are operational decisions for the Transport Agency in conjunction with the public transport authorities. I think it would be fair to say, from the central government point of view, our focus at the moment is on looking at any additional support that’s required from the Crown to enable existing services to run.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific proposition just put — that the Queenstown fares-and-frequency model be extended to smaller centres — by locating the decision with the Transport Agency and PT authorities, then gives a direct "the answer is no, not from a central government point of view" to her funding question. The speech would have to change entirely had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "That’s something that could happen in Dunedin and New Plymouth and Nelson and other places." — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: As that Minister of Cabinet yells out that this is fiction, we also have a Prime Minister who says that we are committed to meeting our obligations under the Paris Agreement.
acuity.explanation: Takes the interjection made moments earlier and does something with it — sets the Minister's 'fiction' against the Prime Minister's stated commitment to build her contradiction argument. The sentence could not exist if the interjection had not been made, which is the deciding test. Not 1.0 because the interjection carried minimal content to engage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Fiction! Fiction!' — Shane Jones

acuity.statement: To argue that we should be borrowing more in the same set of remarks in which Chlöe Swarbrick notes the Fitch report, which puts New Zealand on watch, saying that, actually, fiscal sustainability matters, is obviously inherently contradictory.
acuity.explanation: Names the preceding speaker and attributes a tax-and-borrow position to her, but does not take up the argument she actually made or answer the direct question she put. A reference plus a pivot to a prepared critique of capital gains and wealth taxes; it does gesture at the fiscal matter under debate, so 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chlöe Swarbrick asked 'is this Government going to meet our entire nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement domestically or not?' and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: It is also wrong for the member to claim that I promised a certain number of people would get $250. I did not. What I said was that that was the maximum amount a family could receive as a result of our tax package. That remains true, because guess what we did? We delivered on every single one of those commitments that supported that $250 figure, which I am proud of and which I think that member should hang her head in shame about because she opposed every single one of those measures to ensure working families could have more cash in their bank accounts to meet the needs of them and their kids.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the specific claim just put — that she promised a number of families the full $250 — and corrects it to a maximum entitlement. The passage would be different had the preceding speaker framed the promise differently. The closing insult is a Civility matter, not an Acuity one; engagement with the content is what is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Then, at Budget 2024, the Minister of Finance said that 21,000 families would get the full $250.' — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: What indicators were there prior to the war in Iran that the economy was in recovery mode?
acuity.explanation: A prepared question on the right subject that engages no part of the preceding turn's argument about tax packages and FamilyBoost payments. It would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said, but it is at least about the economy under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued about tax thresholds and the $250 FamilyBoost figure and this question does not take any of it up

acuity.statement: What they were able to share with me at that time was that the signs of an economic recovery had taken such hold—in terms of business confidence, consumer confidence, investment intentions, and employment intentions—that they were forecasting 3 percent growth for the coming year, which is an extremely healthy level of growth. They were forecasting lower unemployment. They were forecasting a return to balanced books. They were forecasting a lower debt track.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what the preceding question asked for — the indicators of recovery present before the conflict — itemised. The answer is shaped by the question and would change if a different one had been asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'What indicators were there prior to the war in Iran that the economy was in recovery mode?' — David Wilson

acuity.statement: It’s really about the changes that she made to the Department of Internal Affairs Digital Safety programme funding. Were those cuts or were those savings?
acuity.explanation: Opens an unrelated line of questioning on digital safety funding and engages nothing in the preceding turn on Treasury's growth forecasts. On-portfolio and so within the debate, but indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis spoke about Treasury's pre-conflict forecasts and this question does not take them up

acuity.statement: Just while the Minister’s getting some advice around the Department of Internal Affairs—was it cuts or reprioritisations, or some other terminology, to the Digital Safety programme—I actually want to ask about the State-owned enterprises.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the previous member's cuts-versus-savings framing and presses it a step further ('or some other terminology') before turning to her own prepared topic. One strand of the preceding turn is genuinely taken up, but the bulk of the contribution moves on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Were those cuts or were those savings?' — Reuben Davidson

acuity.statement: I can confirm that the State-owned enterprises (SOEs) work that public officials are working on is for a Government purpose.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the specific assurance sought about whether the SOE work would run on a party track, answering it in the terms in which it was asked. Short of 1.0 because it substitutes 'for a Government purpose' for the party-track assurance rather than confirming the latter outright.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'that that work in relation to State-owned enterprises will not go along a party track' — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: Well, I put it to her that there are 32,000 fewer jobs under her Government, and I still haven’t heard a response as to the 9,400 people in Hawke’s Bay who no longer have a job; the 6,300 in Taranaki who don’t have work; and in Tasman and Marlborough, the 2,600 there.
acuity.explanation: Re-states prepared regional job figures and engages no part of the preceding turn on SOE dividends and the Budget hole. It continues her own earlier line rather than the argument just made, so the speech is indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis spoke about SOE dividends funding health and education and this statement does not take that up

acuity.statement: Today, the seventh major housing project was announced through the fast-track process: Ashbourne in the Waikato. The member mentioned Nelson Tasman. Well, there, we’ve got another housing development under way, which is seeing people in jobs constructing those houses and will in future see families living in those homes.
acuity.explanation: Takes one specific item from the preceding turn — the Nelson Tasman job losses — and answers it with a named development in that region. It never engages the headline 32,000 figure, so this is partial engagement followed by prepared material on fast track and Investment Boost.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'in Tasman and Marlborough, the 2,600 there' — Ginny Andersen

acuity.statement: What do you think, looking back now, has had the biggest impact in terms of providing the buffer zone that we now are experiencing through the fuel crisis?
acuity.explanation: A prepared invitation to the Minister that engages nothing in the preceding turn on jobs, fast track and education standards. It is about the Budget under debate, which keeps it above 0.1, but it would be identical whatever had just been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Nicola Willis argued that job creation requires investment and education standards, and this question does not take that up

acuity.statement: Well, it’s a very good question because, across that $43 billion worth of savings, there are a number of items which have been very significant. One of those is the ongoing drive from the Government to be more efficient with our own shop, which is to say those who serve the Government and its own policy development and analysis. In the Public Service, we’ve asked them to do that more efficiently, and we’ve had significant reductions in the back-office bureaucracy, which has allowed us to invest more in front-line services.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question actually asked — which of the 2024 Budget changes mattered most — by naming specific savings items and ranking their significance. The content is determined by the question put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'What do you think, looking back now, has had the biggest impact' — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: Talking about a hole in a Budget, given the supposed savings—and I note some of Treasury’s comments in the actual annual review around fiscal consolidation; we’ll let the Minister have a look at the transcripts there, around holes.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the 'hole in your Budget' charge aimed at her directly and gestures at Treasury's fiscal consolidation comments as a counter, but does nothing with the $12 billion pay equity figure that the charge rested on before moving to a prepared question on the natural hazards levy. More than a bare reference, less than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'There’s a hole in your Budget, the Hon Barbara Edmonds.' — Nicola Willis

acuity.statement: As the member knows, we were faced as a Government with a choice to hike the levies on insurance policies for New Zealand homeowners by around $200 a year. I was reluctant to progress that at a time when I knew New Zealanders were facing significant cost of living pressures, but also where I was not able to access clear data about the uptake of insurance products and whether or not increasing prices for insurance was impacting on uptake.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific question about whether the natural hazards levy will rise and the state of the advice, giving the decision taken, the figure involved and the reasoning. Short of 1.0 because the second limb — what support the Commission gets if no increase is made — is not addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'how is that advice progressing, and will we see an increase to the natural hazards insurance levy?' — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: We’ve heard a lot in this debate about the ideology of socialism and the idea that spending money is a kind of aroha, or love; that the more money that is spent, the more the Government loves the people. Perhaps we’ve even heard about the warmth of collectivism. But what we may have missed is some basic facts about the year in question.
acuity.explanation: Characterises the debate in general terms and announces a pivot to prepared spending figures without taking up any particular claim made in the turns before it. The gesture at what has been said keeps it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: the preceding turns concerned the natural hazards insurance levy and the Budget savings, and this statement does not engage either

acuity.statement: I’m advised that the key is to get out and do a bit of a once-over, and if you can fix them the first time, you can, but do some work, and then come back and do a proper job. Of course, there will be cases in which people go back and repair them. In 2018, there were 39,000 potholes repaired on the State highway network.
acuity.explanation: Utikere's specific complaint was that the pothole patrol returns to the same holes two to five times. Bishop takes up exactly that point: he explains the repair method as a deliberate two-pass approach, concedes outright that crews do go back, and offers a historical comparison figure to argue repeat repair is not new. The answer would be different had Utikere raised a different criticism. Not 1.0 because the second limb of the question (the NZTA integrated delivery model) is set aside as operational and the reply detours into a jibe about the Labour Party funding hole.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "many of these potholes have been fixed not just once but two, three, four, and sometimes five times" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Well, I was going to make that point, because I think the member’s embarrassed himself. I have no ministerial responsibility for school buses.
acuity.explanation: Engages the question by correcting the premise built into it — that the Minister of Transport can act on school bus provision — which is a direct hit on what was just put to him rather than prepared material. But it engages only the premise and not the substance Utikere raised about Manawatū, Rangitīkei and Tararua communities, so it is a partial engagement that then redirects him to another Minister.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Does the Minister of Transport see this as an issue for those existing communities, and what does he intend to do about it?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: So I suppose that’s kind of a long way of saying the member raises an interesting issue. We don’t have any active policy work under way on it, but it is definitely true that we need to make some improvements over time and I’m very aware of the problems the member raises.
acuity.explanation: Genter asked what he would do to allow rational comparison between new State highway spending and alternatives rather than having the allocation dictated by the GPS. Bishop answers the 'what will you do' limb honestly — no active policy work, though the Infrastructure Commission's suggestions will be looked at — and volunteers the 10-year funding window as his own reform. He does not take up her specific claim about how the GPS ring-fences new-infrastructure funding to State highways while public transport money only maintains existing services, so he engages the topic and one strand of the question rather than the argument itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So I’m interested in what the Minister is going to do to enable us to have an approach that enables a more rational assessment of the use of money" — Julie Anne Genter

acuity.statement: I acknowledge and sympathise with the wider points, which is that the regional connectivity funding which has been available through Minister Jones’ Regional Infrastructure Fund is to stabilise what was already a vulnerable regional airline sector prior to the current fuel crisis. We continue with that funding allocation, but we’re under no illusions as to the fact that it was to provide stability and we need to look further at what we can do to continue to provide confidence in the airline sector.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Utikere's specific claim that the concessionary loans package is no longer satisfactory for the demand, and concedes the substance of it — the funding was stabilisation for a sector already vulnerable before the fuel crisis, and more will be needed. He also disposes of the Air New Zealand limb by correctly locating it with the shareholding Minister and then answers the routes limb with the assurances he has received. The reply tracks the question put to him point by point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether there has been any briefing provided around the possibility of that airline requiring any further Crown support" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: On the first question, I’m advised that it’s too early to say in relation to the speed limit changes. The New Zealand Transport Agency is monitoring it, obviously, but too early to draw any conclusions.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the exact question asked — whether crash-rate measurements exist for roads where speed limits were reinstated — and answers it squarely, if unhelpfully for the questioner, before moving to the second question on the graduated driver licensing changes. The reply is wholly determined by what was asked; it could not have been delivered after a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whether he’s aware as to whether there have been measurements taken in terms of the change in crash rates on roads where speed limits were reinstated at a different level" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: In relation to Arlington, nothing has changed since I last talked to the member about this. We are working away on it. Just to remind the committee of the brief background here, this is a piece of land that Kāinga Ora has leased from the council, and the plan back in the day was to put 300 social homes or apartments on there at around $296 million, which is $1 million per apartment. That was expensive back then, but then the plan blew out to $420 million, so $1.3 million or $1.4 million per apartment. Even the last Government blanched at that extravagant price, and the project was paused and delayed. If the member has complaints about Arlington, she should direct them to the Hon Megan Woods, who was the relevant Minister at the time—and, indeed, the Cabinet, because it requires Cabinet sign-off. The land is being looked at by Kāinga Ora for future use. It is a challenging site, which is partly why it’s so expensive to build on, but they are looking at exactly what they can do there. I hope to have more to say in due course.
acuity.explanation: Paul asked him to turn to her local Wellington items and he does: he itemises Arlington specifically, gives the project history and costings, and explains where it now sits. The reply is shaped by what was asked rather than prepared material — it would be different had she steered him elsewhere. Marked down from the top band because the specific Arlington complaint he is answering was put outside this window, so the in-window turn he engages is a topic request rather than an argument, and part of his answer deflects to a former Minister instead of engaging the substance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Yeah, so—local Wellington questions, please, Minister." — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: It’s not the process; it’s the price.
acuity.explanation: A precise correction of the premise of the answer just given: Bishop defended the Dixon Street Flats transaction by naming the RFR process, and she identifies that as answering a question she did not ask, relocating the objection to the price paid. It engages the specific content of his claim and could not have been said in response to anything else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The Dixon Street Flats are an example of the right of first refusal (RFR) process which Kāinga Ora went to." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Well, this is the RFR. Like, this is what happens. This is the way it works. Yes, the iwi have profited from that, but I thought the member was for rangatiratanga and economic development.
acuity.explanation: He glances at the price strand — "Yes, the iwi have profited from that" concedes the thing she raised — but then re-asserts the process she had just excluded from the argument and pivots to a jibe about her own stated principles rather than addressing the price. Partial engagement: one strand taken up, the specific claim left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s not the process; it’s the price." — Tamatha Paul

acuity.statement: The Minister has made a claim, yet again, that those in need can access emergency housing. Everybody knows that’s not true.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the housing debate and attacks the Minister's position, but it engages no part of the argument actually just made about consenting delays and the RMA; the material would read identically whatever Bishop had just said on housing. Prepared criticism on the right subject rather than engagement, so it sits in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Bishop's preceding turn argued that council consenting delays are holding up Kāinga Ora's social housing builds ("one of the reasons why they’re struggling in a few regions to deliver on their build targets that we set for them is council consenting problems"), and this statement does not take that up — it returns to an earlier claim of the Minister's about emergency housing access.

acuity.statement: Given the real shortage in terms of Māori home ownership at the moment, looking on page 31, Māori home ownership is still lagging very much behind the general population. Where in the report is there a single policy that points to an uplift in terms of Māori home ownership?
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns by other members precede it — but it engages neither of them, opening fresh questions off the annual report instead ('I just want to chuck a couple more questions'). The questions are on the matter under debate and anchored to report pages, which keeps it above zero, but nothing in the preceding turns is taken up, so it cannot be pointed at and stays in the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Kieran McAnulty had just argued the Government is "saving money by keeping people on the street" and asked how many Housing First places had been filled; this statement does not take up that argument or figure, and opens a separate line on Māori home ownership.

acuity.statement: We have seen around 600—I think it was 592 not two days ago—people come out of rough sleeping and go into the Housing First 300 places, and an additional around 110 places that were already existing before we made that announcement.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the precise figure the preceding turn asked for, and contests McAnulty's premise that the places 'haven’t been fully allocated' by giving a count and a date. The speech would have to change if McAnulty had asked something else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — whether the numbers are correct is a veracity question, not an acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How many of the Housing First places that were announced six months ago have been filled, and how many of the subsequent 300 have been filled?" — Kieran McAnulty

acuity.statement: Going on to Mr Jackson’s observations and questions, yes, we would like to see more home ownership. We think a property-owning democracy is the way New Zealand should be. We absolutely agree to that.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Jackson's question explicitly and answers the topic — home ownership — then moves to prepared material on rezoning, fast-track, the flexi fund and affordable rentals rather than naming a policy directed at the Māori home-ownership gap, and leaves the baseline-cut and damp-and-mould questions untouched. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, which is the middle of the scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Where in the report is there a single policy that points to an uplift in terms of Māori home ownership?" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: This is more in the Māori housing space for Minister Potaka, I would say: on page 39 of the annual report, it records a $40 million baseline saving from new supply and capability of Māori housing. I ask the Minister: how can he claim to be improving outcomes for Māori when his Government’s first move was to rip funding out of the Māori housing supply and provider capability?
acuity.explanation: Jackson opens with a glance at Bishop's use of mana motuhake, then moves straight to his own prepared questions from the annual report. Nothing in Bishop's Dixon Street answer is taken up; the questions would be word-identical whatever Bishop had just said, though they are on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "it was an operational decision made by Kāinga Ora and the board" — Bishop's answer was about the Dixon Street Flats and his own involvement in that decision.

acuity.statement: Just in response to the various noble questions of the member opposite, the $40 million savings are related back to a savings effort in 2024, and many, many portfolios had to, essentially, offer savings up across nearly all the ministries, actually—nearly all the Crown agencies.
acuity.explanation: Takes Jackson's specific figure and does something with it — explains its origin as a 2024 cross-government savings exercise and where the money was reinvested, then answers the second question with delivery numbers. The reply is shaped by what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "on page 39 of the annual report, it records a $40 million baseline saving from new supply and capability of Māori housing"

acuity.statement: One of the initiatives that I understand was funded through this Budget is the youth outreach service run by Māhera Maihi in Tāmaki. I just wanted to ask the Minister what he’s seen from that programme, whether he thinks it’s been successful, whether it’s something that they might be looking into rolling out across the country, and what he is hearing from youth transitional housing providers across the country in terms of their need and what they would like to see in upcoming Budgets.
acuity.explanation: Prepared questions on a different strand of the same portfolio. She notes who should answer, which is a procedural glance rather than engagement, and the questions would be identical whatever Potaka had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka had just given figures on the $40 million Māori housing saving and on how many of the 1,000 approved homes have reached code compliance, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: The view that rough sleeping has increased is, I think, one that cannot be generalised across the country. I think in some places, actually, there have been some serious improvements, and in some places there have been some challenges.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of Paul's question with counts he attributes to Auckland Council, then supplies the allocation criteria and the regional split she asked for (Tāmaki 207, Hamilton 31, Wellington 35, Christchurch 26) and addresses the Māhera Maihi funding. Engagement is with the specific claims, not just the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "as someone based down here in Wellington who understands that rough sleeping has increased 24 percent"

acuity.statement: We know that some of the fast-track projects are retirement villages, which have occupational rights agreements. There are 55,000 residents currently in retirement villages, so there’s going to be a burgeoning retirement village market for those occupational rights agreements.
acuity.explanation: Opens an entirely new strand of prepared questioning. There is no gesture at the preceding exchange at all, though it remains within the housing portfolio under scrutiny.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka had just spoken about rough sleeping counts in central Auckland and the 300 Housing First places, and this statement moves to retirement village repayment law without taking any of it up.

acuity.statement: The proposal around time frames for repayments have been set and proposed at 12 months for mandatory repayment. In fact, some retirement villages do repay earlier no matter what the status of the occupational rights agreement happens to be.
acuity.explanation: Engages the 12-month figure Leary attacked, adds the needs-based assessment and a proposed six-month interest trigger, and argues the retrospectivity point she raised. He leaves her 'what would ordinary New Zealanders think' strand untouched, which is why this is not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "would he consider reducing the repayment time, given that he seems to have arbitrarily chosen one year, which is what the operators want"

acuity.statement: I want to ask the Minister: based on this kind of rationale, since this annual review, has the Minister or his officials or Cabinet considered any reviews of accommodation supplement amounts or the income-related rent subsidy rate as an attempt to save costs?
acuity.explanation: A prepared question to a different Minister on a different subject. It follows a substantive turn but is wholly indifferent to it; only the shared housing subject area keeps it off zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka had just argued that retrospective mandatory repayments would have liquidity impacts on retirement village operators, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In relation to Kāinga Ora, we are proud of the work that has happened there. There’s a variety of views across the House around that agency, but certainly the view of the Government was that it was underperforming and not delivering good value for money, and also not delivering for its tenants either, frankly.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the cost-savings framing of Paul's preamble and defends it with the debt track and tenancy satisfaction, but never reaches the actual question about Accommodation Supplement or IRRS reviews before returning to prepared material on the investment plan and the New Plymouth case. Partial engagement: one strand, not the specific question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "all of the different efforts that have been directed by the Minister in order for Kāinga Ora to save costs"

acuity.statement: I found it extraordinary that Tama Potaka is trying to convince us that there’s only 24 homeless people in Auckland. Yet the front-line providers are telling him to his face that those numbers are inaccurate, that they are wrong, and then they’re going and telling us what they’ve said to the Minister, and he doesn’t care because that number suits his narrative.
acuity.explanation: Seizes the specific figure Potaka had just given, disputes its provenance, and draws out what he says is its inconsistency with the Government's case for move-on orders. The speech could not have been delivered without having heard Potaka's number.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "It came down to 200, and now it’s down to about 25 to 30."

acuity.statement: I didn’t get a straight answer to my question: is the Government, is the Minister, or is his officials considering adjusting the amount of the Accommodation Supplement or the Income Related Rent Subsidy?
acuity.explanation: Engages the preceding answer by identifying precisely what it omitted and re-putting the question. That is responsiveness to the answer's shape rather than to its content, so it sits above a topical glance but below a rebuttal that takes the substance on.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chris Bishop: "I think it would be fair to say that one of the things we are doing some thinking about is how the new investment plan—in fact, we’ve published the first one—framework fits in with Kāinga Ora."

acuity.statement: Yes, Mr Chair, just further to Kieran McAnulty’s call with regards to what’s happening with rough sleepers. I want to ask Minister Potaka: what’s the response he’s had from iwi leaders?
acuity.explanation: Picks up McAnulty's strand on rough sleeping and extends it by adding iwi leaders to the list of those contradicting the Minister, which is real engagement with the live dispute. He then returns to his own prepared page-39 question on Māori housing baselines.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "the front-line providers are telling him to his face that those numbers are inaccurate"

acuity.statement: Just keen to get some more fulsome answers from Minister Potaka regarding a couple of things he said in the exchange that we had. First he said that there is a difference in applying the proposed laws regarding capital repayments versus repairs and maintenance, that it was significantly different.
acuity.explanation: Quotes back the distinction Potaka drew and presses for the legal basis and the advice behind it, then identifies the question he left unanswered. Whether she has characterised him accurately is a veracity matter; the engagement itself is squarely with what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "Some things are a little bit easier to apply retrospectively—let’s say, stopping weekly fees when people actually move out of the villas"

acuity.statement: I did not say anything connecting the R and M issue—repairs and maintenance—with capital repayments, and the member might want to check the record on what I did say.
acuity.explanation: Corrects what he says is a misstatement of his own earlier words, and in the same turn answers McAnulty on the Auckland numbers and Jackson on iwi leaders by naming specific leaders. Each strand of the preceding turns is taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "First he said that there is a difference in applying the proposed laws regarding capital repayments versus repairs and maintenance"

acuity.statement: Based on that exchange, is he saying that none of his proposed laws will apply to existing contracts? And secondly, does he believe that more people are concerned about what he calls sanctity of contract than they are about the fairness of the retirement village repayment laws?
acuity.explanation: Both questions are built directly out of the answer just given — testing the scope of his retrospectivity position and putting his 'sanctity of contract' claim against fairness. The turn is unintelligible without the preceding one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "most ordinary New Zealanders believe in the sanctity of contract, particularly when it comes to material provisions"

acuity.statement: In relation to the second question, I actually attend retirement villages and other places of importance in this particular issue and many, many residents are absolutely certain that the sanctity of contracts should prevail and retrospectively applying a mandated repayment timetable in the nature that the member has suggested in her own proposals is completely inappropriate.
acuity.explanation: Answers the question he names, offering residents' views as his evidence on exactly the point she raised. He ignores her first question about whether any of the proposals will apply to existing contracts, so engagement is squarely aimed but only half the turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "does he believe that more people are concerned about what he calls sanctity of contract than they are about the fairness of the retirement village repayment laws?"

acuity.statement: I just wanted to address Tamatha Paul’s question. We are always interested in looking at funding settings in relation to social housing, as what I was trying to indicate to the member through my answers in relation to Kainga Ora and the wider housing picture through the investment plan is that over the last two or three years—two and a bit years since we came into Government—we have conducted quite a thorough scale review of almost every aspect of housing policy, particularly our funding settings.
acuity.explanation: Returns to the question Paul had put three times and engages it on its own terms, confirming interest in funding settings and supplying the detail that the Accommodation Supplement was last changed in 2018 on 2016 relative rents. The content is determined by what she asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tamatha Paul: "is the Minister, the Government, Cabinet, or his officials considering adjusting the Income Related Rent Subsidy amount or the Accommodation Supplement amount?"

acuity.statement: That is a statistical fact that the Minister should be able to respond to and show what is happening. Immunisation is really important, but so is the life expectancy gap, and we need to think beyond just one thing.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the exact ground Brown chose to stand on — immunisation percentages — concedes its importance, and then argues it is a partial metric by setting it against the life expectancy gap, which his answer omitted. The speech would have to be different had Brown led with a different statistic, and she goes on to engage his 'needs-based' framing directly. Squarely responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The latest advice that I have received is that it is now up to 71.5 percent" — Simeon Brown, citing improved Māori child immunisation rates

acuity.statement: On 12 March 2025, the Minister told the House that outcomes for all New Zealanders means that Māori and non-Māori have the same life expectancy. One year on, in his own annual report, he still has Māori life expectancy stuck at 76.8 years. It’s unchanged and the gap is still sitting at almost six years.
acuity.explanation: He picks up the preceding speaker's life expectancy point and does something with it: pins it to a dated statement the Minister made in the House and to the figure in the annual report, then draws the consequence that nothing has moved. He names the engagement explicitly ('reiterates what the previous speaker Debbie Ngarewa-Packer has said') and builds on it rather than restating it. Not a 1.0 only because much of what follows is a prepared list of separate questions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "this Government and this Minister continue to allow a persistent six-year life expectancy gap between Māori and non-Māori" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: When you look at some of the key stats, Māori life expectancy has increased to 75.8 years, reducing the gap with non-Māori from seven years to six years. While this signals progress, there is more work to do.
acuity.explanation: He engages one strand of the critique squarely, supplying a life expectancy figure and a claimed narrowing of the gap in direct answer to Jackson's charge that it is unchanged. But the remainder returns to prepared material on doctor numbers and provider funding and leaves untouched the specific questions put to him about iwi Māori partnership boards, the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee and the Te Tiriti framework. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "he still has Māori life expectancy stuck at 76.8 years. It’s unchanged and the gap is still sitting at almost six years" — Willie Jackson

acuity.statement: I’d like the Minister of Health to account for the milestones that were met in the year under review, and then the milestones that are on track to be met in the current financial year.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's own invocation of targets and outcomes as the measure of success and turns it into a demand for the milestone record, which is a real if narrow pick-up. She does not engage any of the figures he had just cited, and the question itself reads as a prepared new line of examination on the same subject, so this sits at the low end of partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "everything we do has to be measured by the outcomes that it meets and the targets that we are seeking to achieve" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The target results for the last financial year have been published, and the target results for this financial year are yet to be published, because the year has not yet been completed.
acuity.explanation: He addresses the structure of the question asked, distinguishing the completed year from the current one and giving a reason why the second half cannot be answered. That is engagement with the content, not a pivot. It falls short of full responsiveness because the first half of her question — which milestones were met in the year under review — is answered only by pointing at publication rather than by taking it up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Which targets have the milestone for the year under review been met and which have or will be met in the current financial year?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: The Minister could do what he just did—which is avoid my question and not speak to whether the target was met in the year under review—and, if he does so, I would, then, have a follow-up question for him, which would be: how does he expect to hold the health system to account for meeting the target if he will not be met to account in this House for meeting the target?
acuity.explanation: She identifies precisely what the immediately preceding answer did and did not contain, names the omission, and draws out its consequence by turning the Minister's own accountability framework back on him. The statement is impossible to write without having heard the exact answer that preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The target results for the last financial year have been published, and the target results for this financial year are yet to be published" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: Look, I apologise to people who are watching at home. There’s a bit of a meltdown occurring on the Labour benches.
acuity.explanation: Follows Verrall's complaint that the Minister named the health targets without saying whether they were met. Seymour dismisses the Labour benches as having a "meltdown" and then delivers prepared praise of Pharmac and Medsafe officials — a mere reference to the interruption, engaging none of its content. The passage is on the broad subject (medicines) so it is not a 0.0, but it would read identically whatever Verrall had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ayesha Verrall said "I can’t believe he won’t even speak about the targets" and this statement does not take up whether the targets were met

acuity.statement: Fortunately, I took notes of the Minister of Health’s dodging of my last question. He made a quip about social media, and I understand he’s jealous of my follower numbers! He named the targets. He said they were published. He did not answer whether or not they were met. He talked about other programmes that the Government has under way.
acuity.explanation: Itemises exactly what the preceding answer did and did not contain — the social-media quip, the naming of targets, the claim of publication — and identifies the specific gap (whether the targets were met in the year under review). The speech is wholly shaped by what Brown just said and could not have been delivered after a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we’ve been publishing them in the newspapers; we’ve been putting the information out there" and "In the financial year that has been referenced, we made significant progress against the health targets" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: We also know—milestones, Dr Weenink—that since the year under review—I’ll explain for the good doctor over there: each year, the milestone increases because the idea that this Government promoted is that they would continue to make improvement, and so the milestones are set higher for this year. I can tell the committee that, currently, only one milestone has been achieved, and that is the cancer treatment times milestone.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Weenink's interjection directly, corrects her terminology, and explains why the milestones rise annually before supplying the count of how many are currently met. It engages the interjection rather than merely naming its author, though the material it leads into is largely her own prepared line of questioning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We didn’t expect them to be." — Vanessa Weenink, interjecting on the milestones not being met

acuity.statement: It’s ironic that the member is asking questions about health targets—the very health targets that her Government chose to remove, and which left many thousands and thousands of people sitting on wait-lists which simply ballooned under her watch.
acuity.explanation: Verrall asked what responsibility he takes for four targets deteriorating under his ministry. This opening engages the topic of health targets and the questioner's standing to raise them, but takes up no part of the question about his own responsibility — it redirects to her record instead. A gesture at the debate rather than engagement with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "for the other four, what responsibility do you take for some of them, for the performance getting worse against some of these targets since you came to office?" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: We have seen significant improvements against our targets. Improved immunisation rates—77.1 percent of children aged two years of age were immunised when Labour left office in 2023; that has increased to 82.9 percent against the most recent quarterly update.
acuity.explanation: Answers the topic she raised — performance against the targets — with figures on one of them, rather than the specific claim that only the cancer milestone is currently being met or the specific question about first specialist appointments. One strand engaged, then a return to prepared target-by-target material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "currently, only one milestone has been achieved, and that is the cancer treatment times milestone" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I would point out that the number of people waiting less than four months was 62.1 percent for an elective treatment when she left office; it’s now back up to 64.5 percent. That is an increase. Is that good enough? No, there’s more work to do—there is significantly more work to do.
acuity.explanation: Takes the interjected claim that performance has worsened and meets it head-on with a before-and-after figure on elective waiting, states what it shows, and concedes the standard is still inadequate. The reply is directly shaped by the interjection and would differ had she asserted something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Minister, your performance is getting worse. It’s worse under you. It’s worse under your Government." — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I’m thrilled to know that this Minister of Health is running political lines, which the people of Dunedin know with their own eyes because they’ve been watching that hospital being built, that that is utterly false.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise claim Brown had just made (that he signed the construction contract and the hospital is now being built) and contests it directly, invoking what Dunedin residents have seen. The sentence would make no sense following a different argument, so it is squarely responsive — the muddled phrasing and the lack of a counter-figure are matters for other attributes, not responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the good Dunedin Hospital is now getting built" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: This Minister manages to speak in total sound bites, and never once manages to deviate from talking points that he’s picked up from the National Party research unit, probably polled on in focus groups by David Farrar.
acuity.explanation: Characterises the manner of the Minister's delivery rather than engaging the content of anything he said. It would read identically whatever Brown had argued, though it is at least directed at his contribution tonight rather than an unrelated matter, so it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown argued that a signed construction contract is what delivers a hospital bed and that Dunedin Hospital is now under construction, and this statement does not take up any part of that argument

acuity.statement: That is from a former Minister of Health who absolutely failed our health system, left more and more thousands and thousands more patients waiting on wait-lists, and now she’s here complaining about the very people trying to clean up her mess. She was more focused on restructuring a health system during a pandemic, rather than actually getting patients seen, and getting patients off the waiting lists. That’s what this Government is doing. That’s what we’re achieving, and I’m the first to acknowledge there’s more work to do, but we are getting it done. I would just say, one of the additional talking points I might add to my repertoire is the good people of Dunedin are seeing the Dunedin Hospital getting built, and that’s good.
acuity.explanation: Partial engagement. It picks up Verrall's talking-points taunt and turns it back on her Dunedin claim, which is a real response to one strand of what she said; but her substantive charges (nurses unable to get jobs, no improvement in service quality, an hour of unanswered questions) are left untouched in favour of prepared material about her own record as Minister. Whether the pivot to her record is fair reasoning, or polite, is not scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "maybe he should get some new talking points" and "They know that you stuffed around on the Dunedin Hospital for 18 months" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: This is the Treaty section, which is something that happened during this particular annual review year.
acuity.explanation: A direct answer to the question just interjected: it identifies the part of the review being examined and asserts that the matter falls within the review year, which is exactly what Meager challenged. Brief and unelaborated, but it supplies the thing asked for rather than deflecting.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What annual review was that in?" — James Meager

acuity.statement: I find it quite ironic that that member would say that these targets don’t measure the right thing, because, ultimately, when I meet patients who talk to me about getting a cataract operation done, that is life-changing for them and the opportunities that they have.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Verrall's specific outputs/outcomes distinction and disputes it directly, arguing that the things the targets count (cataracts, hips, knees) are themselves outcomes for patients. The speech would be different had she argued something else; whether the rebuttal fairly represents her claim is a rigor question, not acuity.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "All of these targets reflect outputs; they don’t reflect outcomes." — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I know you’re debating between the left and the right on whether there should be targets or not. You have stated there are targets. What is the substantive measure that we can say tonight to our communities that is on the cards be done?
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the targets argument that has just been running between Brown and Verrall and declines to re-litigate it, then moves to her own prepared lines of questioning on elective treatment and Māori health funding. Engages the topic and the posture of the exchange rather than any specific claim in it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are going to continue to fight for the patients of New Zealand so they can be seen sooner" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: The latest data in regards to the health targets shows that there has been an improvement since health targets were reintroduced for shorter wait times for elective treatments, and so it is progress in the right direction and, ultimately, there is significantly more work to be done.
acuity.explanation: Takes up her elective-treatment target figure and counters it with a direction-of-travel claim, and separately supplies Māori provider funding numbers. Partial rather than full: the specific 60-to-59 percent drop is not addressed on its own terms, and her question about the $105 million unspent Māori health funding is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the target, I understand, is 95 percent. It’s dropped from 60 percent down to 59 percent" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: Minister, there were considerable changes in staffing at Health New Zealand during the year under review. I wonder if the Minister can account for the decrease in nurses employed by Health New Zealand on a per capita basis during the period under review.
acuity.explanation: On the matter under scrutiny (Health New Zealand in the year under review) but engages no part of the answer that preceded it. Prepared material on the right subject; it would read identically whatever Brown had just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simeon Brown had just given Māori health provider funding percentages and dollar figures, and this statement does not take any of it up — it opens a fresh line on nursing staffing.

acuity.statement: One of the great things about being a New Zealander, as every New Zealander understands, is per capita, because, you know, we’re always thinking about our medal tallies at the Olympics on a per capita basis. So could the Minister please account for the reduction in nurses per capita employed in the public health system in New Zealand, please?
acuity.explanation: Spots that Brown answered with an absolute headcount when the question was per capita, and presses exactly that gap. The intervention exists only because of the specific form of his answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think there are around 2,000 additional nurses working at Health New Zealand today than when we came into Government" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I’ve answered the question. We’ve continued to increase investment in our nursing workforce, and we will continue to do so.
acuity.explanation: Asserts the question has been answered and restates the investment line; engages no part of the per capita point that was put to him. A reference to the question is not engagement with its content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "could the Minister please account for the reduction in nurses per capita employed in the public health system" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: What hope can the Minister offer to graduate nurses, who are bearing the brunt of the restrictive hiring policies at Health New Zealand when it comes to nursing jobs?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the nursing-workforce claim he has just made and tests it against graduate recruitment, which is one strand of it, rather than pursuing the per capita dispute she had been running. Engages the topic he raised without taking on the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’ve continued to increase investment in our nursing workforce, and we will continue to do so" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: I’m advised that Health New Zealand is targeting to employ 80 percent of graduate nurses from last year’s mid-year graduation and end-of-year graduation. I’m advised over 1,400 of those graduate nurses have already been employed in Health New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the recruitment figures the question asked for and directly contests the premise that graduate hiring has been cut back. The answer is shaped by the specific claim put to him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "multiple rounds of graduate nurses having reduced levels of recruitment and many leaving for Australia" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: I would agree that—and I’ve made my expectations clear—Health New Zealand does need to be focused on the permanent employment of doctors. At the same time, where there are vacancies, locums do play an important role to ensure that those services continue to be provided in those communities, and that balance must always continue to be struck so that patients get the care that they need.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the part about preferring permanent employment and disputes the part about locums, which is the classic shape of genuine engagement. Accepting some of an opponent's case and resisting the rest cannot be done without having followed it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "make sure that regular employment in the health system is preferred ... and that we also stop paying a premium for locums" — Ayesha Verrall

acuity.statement: Yes, I would highlight to the member that to make progress in health decisions and work doesn’t always require Cabinet papers. A measure of success isn’t the number of Cabinet papers that is delivered.
acuity.explanation: Goes straight at the inference underlying the question — that the absence of Cabinet papers shows an absence of action — rather than restating the plan. The answer is built around the specific test Leary proposed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there doesn’t appear to be any Cabinet papers to endorse that. I’m asking the Minister if there is a Cabinet-backed response to the refreshed plan" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: Thanks for those responses, Minister. What specifically has changed, then, since she cut the ribbon at the action plan, and what specific plans are in place, particularly for young-onset dementia, given that that cohort faces a particular set of challenges which are quite different from the older set, including respite support and employment support for their families?
acuity.explanation: Takes Costello's answer that work is continuing and presses for what concretely changed, which is the follow-up that answer invites. The question only makes sense as a response to the one just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We continue to work in this space. Health New Zealand has acknowledged the action plan, and the recommendations are being worked through" — Casey Costello

acuity.statement: In terms of the areas of those with younger-onset dementia, that doesn’t sit specifically under my delegation, so, therefore, I would be unable to respond to those questions. To suggest that we attended to cut the ribbon—as the member will be aware, I gave a detailed speech around the commitments this Government has to responding to this important issue, and it will continue to be a programme of work.
acuity.explanation: Addresses both strands actually put to her: declines the young-onset question on a stated delegation ground rather than ignoring it, and answers the ribbon-cutting jibe on its substance. Not full marks because the young-onset strand is deflected rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "did she just turn up to cut the ribbon?" and "particularly for young-onset dementia" — Ingrid Leary

acuity.statement: I have a number of questions about the curriculum in particular. I would like to understand from the Minister: is she confident in her previous assertions that the curriculum was, in fact, written by Kiwis, for Kiwis? I would like to know if she would categorically state that not one line of the curriculum was written by anyone based outside of New Zealand.
acuity.explanation: Same debate and same portfolio, so it is squarely on the matter under discussion, but it engages no part of the Minister's preceding argument about consultation, section 127 or the Crown's Treaty duty. It is prepared material plus new questions, and would read identically had the Minister said something else about the curriculum.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just said "the key responsibility for the Treaty of Waitangi sits with the Crown. It is not to be delegated out to a school board" and defended the unconsulted section 127 decision; this statement does not take either up, it opens a fresh line of questions about who wrote the curriculum.

acuity.statement: I want to respond to the member’s claims about facts. I hear this a lot from people in her party and from her persuasion that kids don’t need to know facts; that, in fact, you can just use the internet, use AI, use Google, and they’re all at the touch of a finger. I would suggest that that member go and read some of the research that’s been undertaken by people like Dan Willingham, Nathaniel Swain, and Natalie Wexler, who talk in depth about the importance of knowledge.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim just made — that a facts-based curriculum is not modern learning and that analysis matters more — names it, and argues the opposite case from cognitive-science research. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different argument; it is built on the one just offered. (That it recasts Andersen's position as 'kids don't need to know facts' is a rigor question, not an acuity one.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "a curriculum built on memorising facts and being tested on them is not modern learning. Young people need to analyse, problem solve, and think for themselves."

acuity.statement: Now, I think the other thing that the member wanted to know about was the vocational subjects or the industry-led subjects. We’ve said many times that we want them to be seen on an equal footing with the ministry-led subjects. Our intention is that they will be ready at the same time as the ministry-led subjects when they come to implementation in 2028-2029.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific question put in the preceding turn and supplies the timing asked for, including a date. Directly keyed to what was just asked rather than prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "would she be able to clarify whether vocational pathways will be ready in time in that curriculum?"

acuity.statement: I also note that I asked five questions of the Minister and she answered two. In the standard assessment, that would be considered not achieved.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the exchange just had, but it takes up none of the Minister's reasoning about prior knowledge or her answer on vocational subjects; it then moves to an unrelated set of new questions on NCEA consultation. On-topic prepared questioning with a scoring remark attached rather than engagement with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford's preceding answers on knowledge, facts and vocational subjects — engaged only as a tally of how many questions were answered, not on any of their content.

acuity.statement: Around the question about NCEA and the curriculum, as I think that member knows, or should know, the NCEA reforms have gone out for full public consultation. We put some ideas out for consultation. They went out and we have had full feedback on that. We’ve had over 10,000 pieces of feedback come in.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific consultation questions just asked and answers with a figure and a process account, including the phase 1-4 six-month period and phase 5. Not a complete answer to all six questions — it leaves the curriculum-versus-syllabus and 'cart before the horse' points alone — but what it does engage is the content of the questions just put, not prepared material.

acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "how many people were consulted on the scrapping of NCEA?" and "Was the scrapping of NCEA ever explicitly consulted on?"

The statement depends entirely on what the Minister said and would have to change if she had claimed something else.

acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "we’ve been open and honest about the fact that we didn’t undertake any consultation, but it is a decision that we made."

acuity.responding_to: "I think that parents watching this at home would like to know if AI was used to generate any of the curriculum." — Ginny Andersen

acuity.responding_to: "Just in answer to those ones, I can tell the member Ginny Andersen that the Ministry of Education officials wrote the curriculum" — Erica Stanford

acuity.explanation: Concedes the specific premise of the question just put and then gives the reason for it, which is exactly what was asked. The answer is shaped entirely by the preceding question.

acuity.responding_to: "I also wanted to ask about why the consultation time for Te Marautanga is half that of the curriculum’s time." — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: In answer to Lawrence Xu-Nan’s questions around who we consulted with prior to putting these proposals forward, I got together a group, a professional advisory group of principals from around New Zealand representing a range of different schools—area schools, rural schools, kura kaupapa, different deciles or equity indexes; a range of different people—chaired by Patrick Gale. They helped in framing some of that.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise distinction Xu-Nan drew — who was consulted before the decision was taken — naming the advisory group and its chair. It engages the specific question rather than the general topic, though it does not give the numbers asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "whose report and how many people were consulted when that initial consideration was made?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: The member is quite right that Not in Education, Employment or Training (NEET) numbers have increased over this time. Obviously, when unemployment goes up, NEET numbers go up and it’s an area that I am very concerned about, as are a number of my colleagues.

The answer would be different had he asked about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What action did she take over this period, and why did this number increase over that period?" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.statement: Yes, the member is quite right that there have been unfunded places in the universities and also in a number of private training establishments (PTEs) and polytechnics as well. It’s not an uncommon thing to have unfunded places.

It does not supply the number of universities asked for, which keeps it short of a full engagement.

acuity.responding_to: "how many universities have had to carry unfunded domestic students as a result of her Government’s choices?" — Shanan Halbert

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Penny Simmonds: "It's not an uncommon thing for the universities, polytechnics, and PTEs to run unfunded places."

acuity.statement: No, the member Shanan Halbert isn’t quite right on that. It is common to carry unfunded places at different times. Most institutions do that, particularly if they are looking for growth. So I would disagree with the member when he says it is uncommon.

acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "it is uncommon that the Government does not fund the additional places through overs and unders"

acuity.statement: Around the letter I wrote to the Teaching Council, it wasn’t specifically about the Fisher case; it was in relation to the report that Debbie Francis had undertaken and the serious claims that were raised in that report around the fact that the Teaching Council were not acting in a way that was properly protecting children.

acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "the letter she wrote to the Teaching Council in which she’s asked them to bring in a King’s Counsel to look at the Fisher case"
