acuity.explanation: Concedes part of the Minister's deflection and reframes the question onto ministerial judgement, which the 'operational' answer cannot cover. The reframing exists only because of what Stanford just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "That is completely operational; I can’t answer any of her questions."

acuity.statement: On the Debbie Francis report, I hear what the Minister of Education is saying. Can I check with the Minister: what is the Criminal Records (Clean Slate) Act? Does the Minister understand the Criminal Records (Clean Slate) Act?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Francis report strand the Minister had just set out and probes a legal constraint bearing on it, but then moves into his own prepared sequence of questions rather than engaging her reasoning about the Teaching Council's failures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "it was in relation to the report that Debbie Francis had undertaken and the serious claims that were raised in that report"

acuity.statement: In relation to the Teaching Council, the first thing was that the chair, Mr David Ferguson, was appointed to the Teaching Council mid-2025, by which time the Teachers’ Institute was already delivering on-site teacher training. I understand that a full conflict of interest process was undertaken in line with the Public Service Commission guidance.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the sequencing fact that Andersen's conflict-of-interest question turned on — the date of the appointment relative to the funding — having earlier declined it as operational. Squarely aimed at the claim put to her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "was his appointment active at the time when those two bodies then clearly approved his $750,000 worth of funding"

acuity.statement: It is the case that we have paused the bus route reviews in order to undertake a proper review of the entire school transport system. There always has to be a point at which you pause. I recognise that that’s difficult, but if we had made it earlier, term 4 would have then had the same argument, and if we’d made it term 4, then term 3 last year would have, as well.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the precise grievance — that one region got a pause and his did not — by defending where the cut-off line falls, before drifting into the previous Government's record. Engagement is specific but partly trades into prepared comparison material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "why is she prepared to penalise Palmerston North schools and families in my community by refusing to pause the rural bus changes"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I just wonder if the Minister of Education will answer my question from half an hour ago.
acuity.explanation: Stanford had just made a substantive claim about school transport policy and the member opposite's advocacy; this turn takes up none of it, and instead reverts to the speaker's own unanswered question from earlier. It gestures at the debate (chasing an outstanding answer in the same committee stage) rather than engaging the argument just made, so it sits in the low band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "School transport policy has not changed in 100 years" — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: The simple answer is that at the time I made the changes to section 127, a separate process was being undertaken by Minister Paul Goldsmith. At that particular time, the Treaty Reference Advisers Group had provided a report that recommended changing Treaty standards to be consistent, but what they didn’t say was what they would be changing to and that there would be full consultation, and the like. At that point, it was very, very high level. When I made those decisions last year, Cabinet had not made any call—in fact, those calls were only made recently—about changes.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific question put — why the House was not told about the other clauses being changed — and answers it with the sequence of events: a separate Goldsmith process, a high-level advisers' report, and no Cabinet decision at the time of her section 127 changes. The speech would be entirely different had Prime asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why you didn’t tell us about that" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: The member can cast aspersions, but the fact is, at the time, all that had been talked about was the fact that they needed to be consistent. I still, as I said earlier, take those obligations extraordinarily seriously, as is evident in all the work that I’ve done, which I can honestly say is far more work than the previous Government undertook.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of Prime's insinuation of concealment — what was actually known at the time (only that the clauses needed to be consistent) — then turns to prepared material about her own record and a comparison with the previous Government, which engages nothing Prime said. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "talk about all the other clauses you are intending to change, and why you didn’t tell us about that" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I have a few quick questions for the Minister of Education. Number one, I’m still waiting on a response from the Minister regarding my questions on Student Monitoring, Assessment and Reporting Tools (SMART).
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive ministerial answer on the Treaty clauses and engages no part of it, moving instead to the speaker's own outstanding question on a different subject. Prepared material that would read identically whatever the Minister had just said, though still within the same committee-stage scrutiny of the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford had just explained the timing of the section 127 Treaty changes relative to Cabinet decisions, and this statement does not take any of it up — it opens a separate line on SMART tools.

acuity.statement: We now have 203 inspectors, with a target of 240 by June this year, which will be the highest number of front-line inspectors ever, I understand, in WorkSafe’s history, whereas the previous Government oversaw quite a large bloat in the back office.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez asked for a dated breakdown of WorkSafe inspectorate staffing following a written question. Van Velden takes up the inspectorate-numbers strand and supplies a current figure and a target, and addresses the front-line/back-office split, but does not give the breakdown at the dates asked for and instead folds the answer into a prepared contrast with the previous Government. Partial engagement: one strand taken up, then prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "What is the breakdown of WorkSafe New Zealand inspectorate staff enrolled as at 30 January 2025 and as at 1 January 2026"

acuity.statement: Just following on from the question that the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety has just addressed then, can the Minister then explain why many in the sector feel that work safety is being deprioritised in favour of reducing compliance costs for businesses?
acuity.explanation: Tinetti explicitly picks up the answer just given and presses the premise behind it — that the reforms are driven by compliance-cost reduction — against what the sector told the select committee. She engages the topic and the thrust of the Minister's resourcing claim rather than its specific figures ($138m, the front-line/back-office ratio), so this is a substantial but not pinpoint engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "WorkSafe is not being asked to do more; it’s being asked to do better with the resources that it has."

acuity.statement: Now, I would argue that that side of the House has been catastrophising and, in some ways, been a bit misleading about what it is that these reforms are actually supposed to do. I’m not surprised there are many members of our community out there a little bit worried about what has happened, because of course I’d be worried too if I believed what I’ve been hearing.
acuity.explanation: Tinetti asked precisely why the Minister thinks the sector feels safety is being deprioritised. This supplies a direct causal answer to that question — the feeling exists because of how the Opposition has described the reforms — which is squarely the thing asked. The speech could not have been delivered unchanged after a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "I would really like to know why the Minister thinks that that is a feeling that’s within the sector."

acuity.statement: Minister, I’d really like to know the evidence that you’ve got that shows that these reforms are going to make a difference. We’ve asked that question before, and I haven’t been able to get an answer, so I’d like to know the evidence that sits behind that.
acuity.explanation: Tinetti takes the Minister's just-made assertion that the reforms deliver cost-effective health and safety and demands its evidential basis — a direct challenge to the claim rather than a new topic. She engages the claim's warrant without taking up its specifics (the consultants, the files on bookcases), and then moves on to ACC and psychological harm, so this is partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "the reforms make it really clear that one of the ideas that we’re going behind here is that you can actually have cost-effective health and safety"

acuity.statement: In terms of the questions regarding the road cones and how many were removed and at what cost, I’m afraid to say I don’t actually have the figures in front of me, at hand, about the number of road cones that were removed, but in the first week of the hotline being made available, there were 375 valid notifications made to that website. My officials advised that, in one specific example, over 30 road cones were removed from one site.
acuity.explanation: She returns to the specific question put earlier by Hernandez, states plainly which part she cannot answer, supplies the figures she does hold on notifications and one site's removals, and undertakes to supply the cost in writing. The content is wholly determined by the question asked; had Hernandez asked something else this passage would be different. Marked down from 1.0 only because the quantity actually asked for — total cones removed and total spend — is not supplied.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Francisco Hernandez: "how many road cones were removed from the roads as a result of that, and what was the total spend on that unit?"

acuity.statement: I just want to go back to that question that I asked about the evidence. I just thought about something else, and tying in with that, I’d like to know what the evidence is in this particular area that the Minister’s got, but also how that relates to countries, similar or not similar, like the UK and Australia, who have way better statistics than we do.
acuity.explanation: This is on the matter under debate and gestures at the sequence of exchanges, but it engages no part of the content of the turn it follows; it reiterates the speaker's own prior question and extends it. On-topic material that is indifferent to what preceded it sits at the top of the 0.1–0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Brooke van Velden's immediately preceding turn gave road-cone hotline notification figures and offered a written reply, and this statement does not take any of that up — it re-puts the speaker's own earlier question with an added comparison to the UK and Australia.

acuity.statement: To the question of what evidence do we as the Government have that there is a need for change, that became really, really clear to me when I went out on the ground to hear from workers and businesses directly. I know this might be different to some of the ways that Governments have done evidence in the past, but I like to actually get out across New Zealand and hear from people. We had over 1,000 people show up and give us their stories about health and safety and how they interact with the current law and what they were hoping to see from change, in my 2024 roadshow.
acuity.explanation: She names the question asked and answers it on its own terms, setting out what she treats as the evidence base — the 2024 roadshow and what she heard there — and even concedes it is a different kind of evidence from what past Governments relied on. She does not take up the second strand Tinetti pressed, the comparison with UK and Australian statistics, so this is strong engagement with one strand rather than the whole question.

acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "I’d like to know what the evidence is in this particular area that the Minister’s got, but also how that relates to countries, similar or not similar, like the UK and Australia"

acuity.statement: It might surprise the Prime Minister I wasn't asking him about the pandemic. I was asking him about how critical customers are going to be identified by fuel companies.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific move Luxon just made — the pivot to the pandemic and his record — identifies it as a non-answer, and restates the precise thing left unaddressed (how fuel companies identify critical customers). The turn is wholly determined by what immediately preceded it and could not have been delivered in any other context.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "I appreciate the member has had experience running a crisis in the past, but we have taken the mistakes of his management and we are doing it differently."

acuity.statement: How is he saying that fuel companies will be expected to ensure that critical customers are prioritised if the fuel companies aren't expected to know who the critical customers are and aren't expected to check?
acuity.explanation: Takes Luxon's bare "No" and draws out its consequence, putting the two halves of his own position against each other: companies must prioritise critical customers yet are not expected to know or check who they are. Had Luxon answered "yes", this question would necessarily have been a different one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Christopher Luxon: "No, and as I said to the member, we are working closely with industry so that, should we ever get to phases 3 and 4—which we hope never to do—we will work together on how we allocate and prioritise the rationing of fuel in that situation."

acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "his decision to spend at least $1 billion of taxpayer money on a liquefied natural gas (LNG) import facility?" — and her interjection "Tell the truth!"

acuity.responding_to: Chris Hipkins: "How will the Government prioritise fuel supplies to critical customers, as indicated under level 2?"

acuity.statement: Is the Minister saying that his counterpart, trade Minister Goyal, was misleading when he said that “If they do not invest, there will be a clawback of benefits”; in other words, if New Zealand does not invest $34 billion over 15 years, then India will claw back the benefits it has given New Zealand in the FTA?

acuity.statement: Surprise, surprise, we had a rise in crime and we had very poor educational outcomes, including in maths, which we’ve just had a beautiful example of with the previous speaker talking about 511 days of this Government. I think you’ll find that we’ve been in more than 511 days. I think it’s 877, according to Copilot. We’re nearly up to three years in Government. I’d just encourage the member to think about that a bit more carefully.

But it engages only the day count, not the substance she advanced ($1 billion of cuts to Māori housing, reo, education, media), and the rest of the speech is prepared campaign material. Partial engagement, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "One billion dollars in 511 days" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.responding_to: "What have we done in two years, under the great leadership of Christopher Luxon" — Paul Goldsmith

That is primarily through fuel and prices. We’ve announced some targeted, timely, and temporary support for 143,000 middle working class New Zealanders out there.

acuity.responding_to: "we have a renewables boom currently under way in this country, which is doing a fantastic job" — Simeon Brown

acuity.responding_to: "does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

Short of 1.0 because it answers the quip rather than her harder questions on offshore ownership and dry-year supply.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Enjoy the conversation of indigenous oil—do we have indigenous solar?" — Debbie Ngarewa-Packer

acuity.statement: On top of that, my understanding and perhaps the Minister could illuminate, the impact that fast track has had on drawing that investment—that we’re actually competing with Victoria in Australia. If the Minister could answer those questions, please.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s what happens when you have fast track" — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: But given that the solar plant would only operate less than 20 percent of the time, in effect because it’s not sunny all the time, it certainly doesn’t operate at night, by the time you set what level of energy it generated, the geothermal plant was actually the cheapest by the amount of energy that it generated, and, of course, it’s operating close to 100 percent of the time.
acuity.explanation: Qualifies the capacity-based solar boast made two turns earlier by distinguishing installed megawatts from energy actually delivered, which is a real engagement with the substance of that claim. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the total forward pipeline of indigenous solar is 1,867 megawatts" — Simeon Brown

Case management is the most effective programme that the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) funds and delivers, and it is the significant increase in the number of people in case management that is a strong correlation to what we are seeing in terms of work exits.

The answer would have to be different had Prime raised a different alternative explanation. Not a full 1.0 because the second half of the question — why the review itself excluded exits into work — is handled by ruling the evaluation out of period rather than engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "How does she know that it’s not the case management system or job coaching that is actually achieving work exits and that it is nothing to do with the sanctions?" — Willow-Jean Prime

acuity.statement: I appreciate the Minister saying that the review isn’t in this period that we’re covering, but it is to review something that is in the period that we are covering, so I believe that the Minister can actually talk to what is from that review.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the specific procedural objection just raised — accepts that the evaluation post-dates the review period, then distinguishes the timing of the review from the timing of what it reviews, and draws the consequence that the Minister can still be asked about it. The sentence could not exist without Upston's immediately preceding out-of-period claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The evaluation of the traffic light system that the member referred to isn’t within this annual review period." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: I wanted to raise an issue that relates to people having their benefits cut or prevented from accessing a benefit because they’re deemed to be in a relationship in the nature of marriage. We know that disabled people are particularly hard hit by this policy.
acuity.explanation: Same debate (the MSD annual review) and squarely on the matter under examination, but it engages no part of the exchange it follows — neither Upston's 84.7 percent sanctions figure nor her case-management causal claim is taken up. The question is prepared material that would read identically whatever Upston had just said; the only backward reference is to earlier annual review debates, not to this turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Louise Upston argued that sanctions resolve 84.7 percent of cases and that case management drives work exits, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: The reason why I raised the relationship rules is because historically we know that most investigations, or the largest reason for investigations, is to do with someone’s relationship status. I accept that there may be other reasons, but that has been the largest reason historically.
acuity.explanation: Answers the clarification put to him squarely: it supplies the link the Minister asked about, explaining that the relationship rules are raised because they are historically the largest ground for investigation, and it concedes the Minister's implied point that other grounds exist. Wholly determined by what was just asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Are you asking specifically in question two in relationship to the relationship rules, or is it a much broader question?" — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: In terms of the relationship rules, they are longstanding rules, and they are in place because an underpinning principle of the welfare system is that it’s based on a household rather than an individual. I know that there are some people who disagree with it and believe that support should be based on each individual. There is no view to changing a longstanding principle of the Social Security Act.
acuity.explanation: Menéndez March asked whether she supports the relationship-status policy itself rather than merely noting it is longstanding. She answers the question as put — gives the rationale (household rather than individual basis), names the disagreement he represents, and states there is no intention to change it. Short of 1.0 only because she restates the longstanding-policy framing he had pre-empted rather than defending the policy's effects on disabled claimants.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’m interested in knowing whether the Minister supports the policy altogether that has been used in the period we’re reviewing" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: I’ve got the figures in front of me.
acuity.explanation: Answers the Minister's stated reason for not addressing the ethnic disparity — that she lacks the detail — by offering the figures himself and starting to read the early intervention comparison. The turn exists purely as a reply to the preceding sentence and would not be said otherwise.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I don’t have that detail in front of me in terms of the disproportionate number that he is suggesting are being investigated." — Louise Upston

acuity.statement: In terms of the question around the use of financial sanctions versus non-financial sanctions, in the year in review, the non-financial sanctions hadn’t been implemented.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one specific strand of the multi-part question put to her — the financial versus non-financial sanctions comparison — and answers it with a reason, while declining the homelessness strands on scope grounds. Partial but pointable engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "how has the Minister’s decision to impose financial sanctions instead of non-financial sanctions improved rangatahi homelessness or homelessness in general?"

acuity.statement: Going to non-financial sanctions, what does she make of the fact that out of the total sanctions that have been applied, non-financial sanctions, to my understanding, make less than 0.5 percent of total sanctions?
acuity.explanation: Picks up precisely the point the Minister had just made about non-financial sanctions and presses it with a counter-figure, then draws out the consequence (policy failure, unworkable design). The question could not have been asked had the preceding answer been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "the non-financial sanctions hadn’t been implemented"

acuity.statement: The policy for non-financial sanctions had only just commenced with two of the sections, and there are conditions around when they can be applied, for clients who are either in case management or who have dependent children and it’s their first obligation failure.
acuity.explanation: Engages the central strand of the challenge — why so few non-financial sanctions have been used — with an explanation about commencement and eligibility conditions, but leaves the specific sub-questions about money management design and front-line uptake untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "how does she explain the fact that basically no one is able to be placed in community work experience or money management?"

acuity.statement: The example that the member gave in Tokoroa, project phoenix, was stood up as a combination of work across Government agencies, council, and Toi Ohomai to work really closely with affected workers, and I’m really proud of what MSD have done on the ground.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific locality and institution the questioner raised and supplies what was done there, rather than offering generic material; the answer would have been different had a different region been named. It narrows the question to portfolio scope rather than answering the 'conditions for jobs' framing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "She’ll be aware that Toi Ohomai in Tokoroa had 60 job losses in and around the same time that we’ve seen three closures of wood manufacturing."

acuity.statement: Does she think it was the right use of Government money to be giving a significant amount, undisclosed, for, for example, Robbie Williams to come to Auckland when people in her own electorate aren’t being given adequate support by the Ministry of Social Development to be able to retrain and to get the support, and those on the ground unemployed are not receiving adequate support?
acuity.explanation: Disputes the Minister's claim that MSD support on the ground has been adequate, which is the substance of the answer just given, but pivots to unrelated discretionary spending rather than engaging the redeployment examples offered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "MSD have been on the ground early, supporting those workers"

acuity.statement: As I said in my answer to the previous question, it is incredibly challenging when a business makes the decision to close. I’ve given two examples of the support that the Ministry of Social Development has provided in the year in review, and I’m not going to speak outside that time frame.
acuity.explanation: Refers back to her own earlier answer and restates it without taking up any part of the question — neither the named regions nor the asserted absence of a regional plan. A reference to the exchange is not engagement with its content, though the reply is at least on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "What is the plan for regional New Zealand to be creating the conditions for jobs and going for growth when we have seen record levels of people laid off?"

acuity.statement: No.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question asked, squarely and without deflection; the reply is wholly determined by the question it follows. It engages the content rather than the topic, which is what responsiveness measures, even though it supplies no detail.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "Did the ministry receive any direction in 2024-25 to shift away from equity-focused or Tiriti-based approaches?"

acuity.statement: I’m not going to comment on things that are outside the year in review, and as the whips have warned me, I’ve got to keep my comments short.
acuity.explanation: The questioner had just stated the evaluation was carried out last year, which is the review period; the reply asserts the opposite scope without taking up that correction or addressing the release date asked for.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "It was undertaken last year."

acuity.statement: The review was undertaken last year, which is the year in review. When will it be publicly released?
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the factual premise of the refusal just given — that the material falls outside the review period — and repeats the unanswered question. The turn is entirely shaped by the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "I’m not going to comment on things that are outside the year in review"

acuity.statement: In terms of the non-financial sanctions, what I’m concerned about is if they had not come into effect and the policy wasn’t being implemented, does that mean that there have been people who should have been eligible for the non-financial sanctions who have actually received a financial penalty instead?
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's stated position that non-financial sanctions were not in use during the review period and draws out its consequence — that eligible people may have been financially penalised instead. Engagement by following the admission to where it leads.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "the non-financial sanctions hadn’t been implemented"

acuity.statement: During the year in review, there were 69 non-financial sanctions that were applied, and it was not throughout the entire year of the financial review.
acuity.explanation: Supplies a specific figure bearing directly on the premise of the question just put, qualifying her own earlier statement; it does not reach the question of whether eligible clients were financially penalised instead.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "if they had not come into effect and the policy wasn’t being implemented, does that mean that there have been people who should have been eligible for the non-financial sanctions who have actually received a financial penalty instead?"

acuity.statement: I will say again that this is the annual review for the financial review from the 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025, and so that is the year which we are considering. I’ve given specific examples of how the MSD redeployment team works, and if the member wanted to ask questions of the Minister for Economic Growth around our growth plan and “Going for Growth”, then that would be the appropriate place to ask those questions.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question Andersen put, but engages its admissibility rather than its content — rules it outside the review year, redirects it to another Minister, and returns to her own theme. One strand engaged, then prepared material, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "What is the Minister's plan for the Hawke's Bay for creating the conditions for jobs in that area, which has had increasing unemployment over the past year?"

acuity.statement: I’m interested to pick up on an issue that we covered over the last year—and at the last select committee, as well—in the Hutt Valley in terms of youth employment. There has been a recent termination of a contract.
acuity.explanation: Opens a fresh line of questioning rather than engaging Upston's answer, but visibly accommodates the one strand of it she could — anchoring the issue in the review year and the last select committee rather than in the recent closures just ruled out of scope.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "this is the annual review for the financial review from the 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025"

acuity.statement: In addition to those questions, I’m quite interested in how many young people who received job coaching have found employment—what percentage—and how long they have stayed in employment.

acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "What steps is she taking to make sure that there are opportunities available for young people who need to get the additional support?"

acuity.explanation: Supplies the exact figure the previous turn asked for and addresses the Youth Inspire procurement query Andersen raised. The content is wholly determined by the questions it follows; a different question would have produced a different answer. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "how many young people who received job coaching have found employment—what percentage"

acuity.explanation: Does not take up or contest the scope objection just made to her; proceeds to separate prepared questions. They are squarely within the ministry under review, which keeps it at the top of the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at the floor.

acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "The questions you asked around Dame Karen Poutasi and Oranga Tamariki are outside the scope of the Ministry of Social Development."

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Oriini Kaipara asked how the ministry measures the effectiveness of Te Pae Tata and how it would address whaikaha service-delivery concerns, and this statement does not take either up — it announces a change of subject.

acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I’d like to ask the Minister what this funding was actually spent on and if it is having an impact."

acuity.explanation: Accepts the limit the Minister set on the procurement answer, names it, and reworks her question into a general one the Minister can answer. acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "In terms of the questions around Youth Inspire, a fair and partial procurement process was undertaken by the ministry."

acuity.explanation: Corrects the commencement date Prime offered and confirms the policy falls in the review period, which is a small factual engagement with her framing. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I understand that this is just coming into effect now in 2026, but my questions are around the advice that the Minister received"

So the question around what advice did the Minister receive about it impacting on accommodation support and demands for other income support, therefore, potentially cancelling any savings that is being planned by this budget initiative? The Minister didn’t speak to that. Could she please answer that question?
acuity.explanation: Identifies precisely what the preceding answer did and did not cover and presses the omitted element. The turn could not exist in this form if Upston had answered differently — it is shaped entirely by the gap in the reply it follows.

acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "It was based on the principle of fairness where every contribution from a boarder should be taken into consideration"

acuity.statement: Yes, we are disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment, but for very good reason. We’re establishing what is commonly referred to as MCERT—the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport. We are, of course, merging all of those ministries together.
acuity.explanation: Meets the charge head-on, conceding the disestablishment and then contesting what Brooking draws from it. Engagement is with the general accusation rather than any specific figure or reasoning she put, and much of what follows is prepared defence of the merger, so this is strong but not complete responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "this Government does not seem to be one that cares about the environment at all, and New Zealand deserves better"

acuity.statement: Actually, the reality is: how do you do proper transport planning in a spatial sense in a region and how do you do land-use planning in a city or a district, without thinking about the environment?
acuity.explanation: Brooking put three things to him: how splitting the RMA into a Planning Bill and a Natural Environment Bill enables integrated management, how the merger handles rural as well as urban environments, and whether environmental functions will take precedence and keep an independent voice. He takes up one strand — the integration rationale — and argues that isolating the environment in its own ministry is what gets its advice ignored, which is a direct engagement with her integration premise. But he leaves the two-bills point, the rural/urban point and the Parliamentary Commissioner's independent-voice concern untouched and returns to prepared material on officials and housing levers. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I'm interested in whether the Minister for resource management reform might want to comment on how that is enabling an integrated approach" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I just have a few comments in response to Minister responsible for RMA Reform’s speech, and one is: if, as he is so adamant, this Government is going to suddenly change course and do better for the environment, will he agree here, today, that every single part of that new ministry will do better for the environment?
acuity.explanation: She takes the specific claim Bishop had just made — that the merger amplifies rather than diminishes the environment — and draws out its consequence, pressing him to commit to it on the record for every part of the new ministry. The question could not have been asked in this form if he had argued something else; it is built entirely out of what he just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment is not about reducing the importance of the environment to New Zealand; in fact, it is the opposite. It is about amplifying the environment." — Chris Bishop

acuity.statement: Yes. In the round, the new ministry, I believe, will lead to improvements of our natural environment over time. That’s the reason we’re setting it up.
acuity.explanation: He answers the question actually put to him, in its own terms, and then supplies supporting detail — the national flood map, waste, and stormwater and waste water — as worked examples of why the merged functions should improve environmental outcomes. The reply is wholly determined by what Brooking asked; a different challenge would have produced a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "will he agree here, today, that every single part of that new ministry will do better for the environment?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: I just want to point out to the committee that there’s still an “E” in MCERT, for “Environment”. Environmental capability is very much going to remain a core capability of this new agency.
acuity.explanation: Grigg announces she is answering Lan Pham, whose turn is not in this window, but the preceding turn in the debate is Brooking's, which asked where green infrastructure and environmental work will sit in the new ministry. This takes up that topic — environmental capability inside MCERT — without engaging the specific claims Brooking made about the repealed Spatial Planning Act or the dismantled three waters entities. Topic engaged, specific argument not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "where is it going to fit with the new ministry?"

acuity.statement: She just referred to “We now know that Canterbury has leaky soils and there have been problems with nitrate.”—I’m sorry; I’m paraphrasing there. Why is she now going to make sure that the regulations that have lapsed that relate to that, which stopped intensification there—will she reinvigorate those to stop further conversions of dairy farms on those soils? That’s one question.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own concession about Canterbury's leaky soils and nitrate and draws out its consequence as a direct question: if you now know, will you restore the lapsed intensification restrictions? The question could not have been written without Grigg's preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Grigg: "Quite extraordinary that the Canterbury Plains—alluvial flood plains, very leaky soils, piling on nitrogen over decades, starting about 30 years ago. Nobody knew the consequences. We do know those consequences now"

acuity.statement: I’ll just touch on a couple of those points. In regard to reinstituting land use change restrictions, no, we have no intention of doing that. The reality is that farmers have got new science, new knowledge, new systems to enable them to do things better now than they ever have before.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question just put — the land use change restrictions — squarely and in the negative, then gives the reason he thinks they are unnecessary. Slightly short of 1.0 only because he leaves the second and third questions in Brooking's turn untouched at this point.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "will she reinvigorate those to stop further conversions of dairy farms on those soils?"

acuity.statement: I did ask the Minister—any Minister is welcome to answer this—whether we should have swimmable rivers and what steps are being taken to improve freshwater quality. That answer Minister Hoggard just gave there was that everything’s fine, don’t worry about it, but then at the end there, he decided to say that something was happening, so I’m interested in what that something is that might be happening.
acuity.explanation: Characterises the answer just given, identifies the strand at the end of it where Hoggard conceded something would change, and presses on exactly that. It engages the shape of his reply rather than any one factual claim within it, which keeps it just below the top band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Hoggard: "we’re going to be asking for better management than there has been in the past, and we expect to see that"

acuity.statement: Of course I believe there should be swimmable rivers. My daughters love swimming in the river beside our farm every summer.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the direct answer to the question asked twice, and the rest of the turn then answers her follow-up about what that "something happening" is with named examples. The turn is wholly shaped by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "does he think that there should be swimmable rivers?"

acuity.statement: Look, I do want to commend the attitude change. I think humans changing behaviours and mindsets is an absolutely crucial part of the way that we’re actually going to turn this table, particularly when it comes to fresh water. Unfortunately, we’ve been doing a lot of talking and a lot of attitude work for years, and, unfortunately, when we look at the actual statistics, the actual environmental statistics that our Minister for the Environment has within her own ministry, they’re going backwards, and very concerningly so.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the premise Hoggard built his answer on — the change in farmer attitude — and then disputes that it is doing the work he claims, by pointing at the ministry's own trend statistics. Accepting part and contesting the rest is engagement of the argument itself, not of the topic.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andrew Hoggard: "The attitude I see amongst farmers around trying to do the right thing, understanding where the problems are coming from and then thinking about what are some of the solutions to those problems, is impressive."

acuity.statement: Let’s just get a few things straight: number one, farmers are not the enemy in this country. Number two: you can improve the environment and grow the primary sector at the same time. Number three: our farmers are world leading and world class, and they deserve this House’s support, not condemnation.
acuity.explanation: Prepared framing on the subject under debate that answers none of the question just put. It rebuts a position — that farmers are the enemy and cannot grow while improving the environment — that the preceding turn did not advance; it would read identically after almost any opposition contribution on the environment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lan Pham asked what specific measures are proposed for rural communities whose drinking water is contaminated, and about the removal of the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy, and this passage does not take either up.

acuity.statement: Number one, from Rachel Brooking: will the new local government system, which we haven’t landed yet—should it be based on a catchment-based approach? Yes, is the short answer, and we’re doing quite a bit of thinking about that.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the questioner and her specific question about catchment-based planning for regional councils and answers it directly, including the state of decision-making on unitary authorities. The content is determined by what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "I’m asking about regional councils and the idea of catchment-based planning."

acuity.statement: There’s so much to respond to in that, but I really want to move on to climate adaptation because that is such a key part of the work.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive ministerial answer full of specific statistics and explicitly sets it aside ("so much to respond to in that, but I really want to move on"), then delivers prepared material on climate adaptation. There is a genuine gesture at what was just said and the speech stays within the same annual-review debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0 — but no figure, claim or argument of Grigg's is engaged, and the speech would read identically had Grigg said something else about the report.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Nicola Grigg: "Yes, worsening sites are reduced from 41 percent to 32 percent." — nothing taken up: Grigg set out the freshwater report's groundwater and nitrogen-trend figures and this statement explicitly declines to engage any of them.

acuity.statement: The member refers, of course, to our freshwater report that was released just a matter of weeks ago, I think, on the day that I got told that I had this ministerial warrant, so I’ve had to think fast. Look, I think it’s really important to acknowledge that this report is neither a win nor a loss; it’s quite a balance report.
acuity.explanation: Pham's intervention asked that the committee return to the Ministry for the Environment's freshwater report rather than three waters, and Grigg does exactly that — she names the report and then supplies figures from it (998 groundwater sites, 45 percent E. coli exceedances, worsening nitrogen sites down from 41 to 32 percent). That is engagement with the topic that was pressed for, and with the report's own framing, rather than with a specific argument or number put by an earlier speaker; much of the answer is prepared ministerial material. Scored on engagement only: whether the characterisation of the report as "neither a win nor a loss" is accurate belongs to veracity, and the selective use of the 20-year trend belongs to rigor.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "I’m really interested in hearing from the Minister for the Environment on a number of questions about the Ministry for the Environment report."

acuity.statement: Just quickly, in response to the Hon Rachel Brooking’s question, in terms of farm plans—“Will we still need consents?”—I would think there would still be a need for a consent when you are having a water take, so trying to manage those allocation-type regimes. Where it comes to things like, in some regions, there having to be a consent for winter grazing, I believe a farm plan would be a much more useful tool to replace those consents.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific question put to him, quotes it, and does something with it: splits it into the case where consent remains necessary (water takes, allocation regimes) and the case where a farm plan should displace consent (winter grazing), then gives a concrete instance. He also answers the second question squarely in the negative with a reason. The speech could not have been given against a different question — it is shaped by the one asked. Not quite 1.0 because the answer is to a question from earlier in the debate rather than to the immediately preceding speaker's argument on climate adaptation, which he does not take up. Scored on engagement only; whether a farm plan is in fact a better instrument than a consent is a separate question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: "Will we still need consents?" — quoted verbatim by Hoggard from her earlier questions in this same committee debate.

acuity.statement: In regard to the points around the clean car or EV subsidy, this Government has focused and is focusing on a least cost approach versus what was, in effect, a ute tax by the prior Government.
acuity.explanation: Radhakrishnan asked three specific things: why the Minister overrode his officials' advice that scrapping the scheme costs double its benefits, whether he had received other advice, and what he is doing to capture the cheaper-EV-battery opportunity the Climate Change Commission identified. This reply is on the subject of the EV subsidy but takes up none of the three; it substitutes a prepared 'least cost approach versus ute tax' framing. A gesture at the matter under debate, not engagement with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Priyanca Radhakrishnan said "the costs of scrapping this particular scheme are double the benefits of the scheme" and asked why he overrode his officials' advice; this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In regard to the flood map, the work is under way. We have commissioned a party to prepare those maps. It will be ready, in terms of the first part of that, by the end of this year, the beginning of next year.
acuity.explanation: Brooking asked a direct question — where is the promised national flood map — and this supplies exactly the information asked for: it is commissioned, under way, with a date for the first part. The answer would be different had she not asked it. Marked slightly below 1.0 because it addresses only the mapping question and leaves her Sunfield fast-track question untouched, but on the strand it takes up it is squarely responsive.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "where is the promised national flood map?" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: In regard to energy, well, the reality is, when you don’t look for something, you don’t find it and that’s the reality with what happened with the last Government around stopping oil and gas exploration. We now have less and not sufficient molecules to run industry and also make electricity in a dry year.
acuity.explanation: Brooking put three things to him: whether he has advice that the exploration ban caused reliance on foreign fossil fuels, whether he grasps the difference between exploring and actually finding and extracting, and whether electrification would be quicker. He engages one strand — the claim that the ban is the cause of the shortage — and restates it with a supply figure, but he answers none of the three questions and does not address the exploration/extraction distinction beyond asserting the premise. Partial engagement, then prepared material on LNG and dry-year risk.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if he understands that there is a difference between exploration and actually finding and then taking that fossil fuel" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: Is the Minister aware that in the United States of America—which is one of the biggest oil drillers and oil explorers in the world; they’re one of the people that produce the most fossil fuels—that the gas prices have increased by 35 percent since the beginning of the Iran war and in New Zealand, which is not, at all, a big producer of fossil fuels, that gas prices have only increased by 20 percent?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-stated premise — that not looking for gas is why New Zealand lacks secure, affordable supply — and attacks its logic with a counter-case: the largest driller in the world saw a bigger price rise than New Zealand, so domestic production does not insulate a country from an internationally priced good. This speech could not have been delivered if the preceding turn had argued something else; it is built on it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the reality is, when you don’t look for something, you don’t find it and that’s the reality with what happened with the last Government around stopping oil and gas exploration" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: Minister, I’m interested in your views on how we might ensure that New Zealand’s major industries that are emissions intensive and trade exposed are supported through this difficult time where energy prices have risen significantly, whether it’s natural gas, that many of them depend on, or electricity, which many of them depend on.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez had just argued that fossil fuel prices are set internationally so domestic drilling does not deliver cheaper or more resilient energy, and Brooking had asked whether Court believed rising CO2 was positive because it makes plants grow. This turn takes up neither, and opens a self-contained prepared line on emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries. It is at least on the matter under debate — energy costs and the carbon price — so it is not a 0.0, but it is indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez argued "fossil fuels are actually an international good so the price of it is still set internationally", and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I want to be really clear that this is not a price issue; this is a lack of molecules issue. We do not have the gas—sufficient gas—to run the industrials that Under-Secretary Court was referring to; that’s the problem.
acuity.explanation: Hernandez's case rested entirely on comparative gas prices. Rather than mention it and pivot, this reply names the premise and disputes its relevance — the constraint is physical volume, not price — which is a direct answer to the specific argument just made, and it also picks up Court's industrials. Whether the rebuttal is sound is a Rigor question; as engagement it is squarely aimed at the claim it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the gas prices have increased by 35 percent since the beginning of the Iran war and in New Zealand... gas prices have only increased by 20 percent" — Francisco Hernandez

acuity.statement: And so the mechanisms to support those industries, first and foremost, need security of supply of the fuel they need to make the product, which is gas, which we are moving our way through, and we also need medium- and long-term solutions, as well.
acuity.explanation: Court asked specifically how the Government and the regulatory system should support emissions-intensive trade-exposed manufacturers facing a carbon price their overseas competitors do not. This answers the question asked, naming security of gas supply as the first mechanism and conceding that medium- and long-term solutions are still needed, and it engages Court's carbon-leakage point by comparing the emissions profile of imported cement. Short of 1.0 because the regulatory and carbon-cost half of the question — the part Court pressed hardest — is left unanswered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "how do you think New Zealand, the Government, and the regulatory system should support these vital industrials now and into the future?" — Simon Court

acuity.statement: I wonder, Minister, if you can respond to the glib and trivialising comments of Simon Court, who thinks that the existential challenge of humanity is merely a good way to help make plants grow.
acuity.explanation: Court's preceding turn made a substantive argument about carbon costs falling on trade-exposed manufacturers, and the Minister then answered it on gas supply. This statement engages neither; it reaches back past both to an earlier heckle and asks the Minister to disavow it. Naming the previous speaker as a target is not engaging the content of what he said, so this sits in the low band, above 0.0 only because it stays within the climate debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Court's preceding speech argued that cement, steel, aluminium and fertiliser makers face "additional costs, not faced by competitors overseas", and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: We haven’t spent it and it’s a current investment. You’re welcome.
acuity.explanation: A short interjection, but it takes up the precise factual premise of Abel's question — that $200 million has been spent subsidising gas exploration — and contradicts it directly. The interjection would be meaningless if Abel had said anything else, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "So why would you be spending $200 million on subsidising gas exploration, when you could be spending that money on decarbonising?"

acuity.statement: Here’s the Hon Megan Woods chirping in from the sidelines as if she doesn’t have the black ash of the arsonist all over her hands. Minister, I’m interested: was there any alternative, or is this the only solution that can possibly solve the dry-year risk and help us secure New Zealand’s energy future right now?
acuity.explanation: The preceding turn by Abel put four specific questions to the Minister (gas reticulation in new builds, the exploration subsidy, the history of exploration since 2007, ETS leakage on cement). Court takes up none of them; he attacks a member for an interjection and asks his own prepared invitation to the Minister. It is at least on the subject under debate — energy and dry-year risk — so not a zero, but no part of the argument just made is engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel asked about new-build gas reticulation, the $200 million exploration subsidy and ETS-exempt imported cement, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: Now, we’re working through a procurement process with LNG, and we will be making decisions once that procurement process has been through. Ultimately, the answers to the members’ questions will of course be dealt with as part of that process.
acuity.explanation: He identifies the LNG questions put to him and addresses that strand, but engages the specific question — was there an alternative, or is this the only solution — only by deferring it to a procurement process. The topic is taken up; the claim is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "was there any alternative, or is this the only solution that can possibly solve the dry-year risk"

acuity.statement: I also would like to know whether the Minister is still saying that there will be a signed contract by July; whether that is the intention of the Government and whether that is the timeline he is working to. I’m also interested whether or not the Minister will guarantee that, if a liquefied natural gas terminal goes ahead, it will solely be for the purposes of dry-year risk—that it won’t be used more broadly than that, and that it won’t become a de facto way of supplying gas more fully in the New Zealand economy, because that is what the Cabinet paper, on the surface, purports to claim.
acuity.explanation: She takes the Minister's immediately preceding answer — that decisions follow the procurement process — and presses it on the two points it left open: the July contract timeline and whether the terminal is confined to dry-year risk, citing the Cabinet paper against his framing. The questions could not have been written before his answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "we will be making decisions once that procurement process has been through"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair, and I would make the point—and I think the Minister also has made this point—that hope is not a strategy and yet we have heard from the Electricity Retailers’ and Generators’ Association (ERGANZ) this morning, we’ve heard from downstream, we’ve heard from all the leaders in the energy sector, that we need a national energy strategy.
acuity.explanation: He picks up the Minister's own "hope it will rain" line, grants it, and turns it into the premise of the opposite conclusion — that a national energy strategy is required. The sentence is built out of what was just said and would have to be rewritten had the Minister argued differently.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "the way I’ve described their plan is “Hope it will rain, hope it will rain.”"

acuity.statement: I’ve also heard that the Minister is very keen to see that we need a competitive market, and on that we agree. To that point, there is a bill sitting in the biscuit tin that the Minister can adopt at any moment, and it is called the Electricity Industry (Separation of Generation and Retail Businesses) Amendment Bill.
acuity.explanation: Accepts one specific claim from the preceding answer — that what is needed is a competitive market — and draws out its consequence by naming a particular bill the Minister could adopt to get one. This is engagement with the content, not a reference to the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "what we need to see is a competitive market which provides affordable energy for all New Zealanders"

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, I love it when members on the Opposition talk about wanting bipartisanship. Well, what they have failed to do is back the reversal of oil and gas—the ban on oil and gas exploration—which they put in place. They didn’t consult on it, they didn’t come and talk to the National Party, they didn’t try and seek a bipartisan approach to that; they simply went and announced it on the steps of Parliament, for the Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern to be able to then go to Paris and get a headline and be on the front page of a magazine.
acuity.explanation: He seizes the specific offer just made — bipartisanship on an energy strategy — and contests the Opposition's standing to make it, with a claim about how the exploration ban was itself announced. Whether the inference is sound is a Rigor question; as engagement it is squarely aimed at the thing just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "the Government opening the doors and bipartisanship"

acuity.statement: Mr Chair, the question was: do we want a strategy? Well, we want to make sure we have lower prices and affordable energy and abundant energy for New Zealanders, and simply, on that side of the House, they want paperwork but won’t actually back the solutions which actually deliver value to people, value to households, value to consumers, and value to businesses and jobs.
acuity.explanation: He restates the question put to him and engages it by rejecting its premise — that a published strategy is what matters — in favour of outcomes. He does not supply the date asked for, but he does take up the substance of the demand rather than ignoring it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "when are we going to see the Government’s release of a national energy strategy"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. Certainly, it sounds as though the Government has no strategy, has no plan, just hopes the market will deliver. Given that there is only one remaining offshore wind developer still floating around, when will the Government finally deliver the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill?
acuity.explanation: He draws a conclusion from the answer just given — that the reply amounted to relying on the market rather than a plan — which is a real engagement with it, but then moves to fresh prepared questions on offshore wind rather than contesting the Minister's reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "they want paperwork but won’t actually back the solutions"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Mr Chair. That bill, as the member will know, is making its way through Parliament as we speak.
acuity.explanation: A direct, if brief, answer to the specific question about the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill's progress — it supplies the status asked for. Short of the top of the scale because the second half of what was put to him, on risk-sharing with Taranaki Offshore Partnership, goes unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Scott Willis: "when will the Government finally deliver the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill?"

acuity.statement: Now, in relation to the baseline funding, the baseline funding has been secured. There’s a suggestion that we should be inflation-proofing any baseline funding in the future, but decisions are made, and the decisions will be made in this Budget as well, and that will be up to the Minister of Finance to announce in sure course.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific ask Abel had just put — a commitment to inflation-indexed baseline funding for Te Māngai Pāho — names it as such and answers it directly (baseline secured; indexation is a Budget decision for the Minister of Finance, on which he will not pre-empt). The reply would read differently had Abel asked something else, so engagement is genuine. Short of 1.0 because he restates Abel's request in his own looser terms rather than engaging the committee-review evidence Abel offered for it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "will you commit to baseline funding that, at least, is adjusted to inflation so that there is not this uncertainty every three years"

acuity.statement: I’m just waiting on a response to my Whānau Ora questions, but I’ll continue on because I do want to understand, effectively, where the buck stops with the Minister in his responsibilities to Whānau Ora, given the significant cuts to this particular area and the structural changes.
acuity.explanation: Registers that the Minister's intervening speech did not reach his questions, which is a gesture at what just happened, but engages no part of what Potaka actually argued about baseline funding or housing completions. He then proceeds with his own prepared line on Whānau Ora, which would have been identical whatever the Minister had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tama Potaka spoke about Te Māngai Pāho baseline funding and Māori housing providers, and this statement does not take up any of that content — it notes only that his own earlier questions went unanswered.

acuity.statement: Just following up on that. I think those are relevant questions. The minister still hasn’t answered previous questions in terms of where the Māori strategy is, and also this question, I think, would be good to get from the Minister answered tonight: has he actually increased the Māori development budget by one cent since he’s been the Minister for Māori Development?
acuity.explanation: Does more than name the previous turn: he adopts Halbert's line of questioning, identifies what remains unanswered, and sharpens it into a single checkable question about budget growth. But he engages only the fact of the non-answer rather than the substance Potaka put up (the secured baseline, the housing figures), then moves to his own prepared material on Te Puni Kōkiri staffing — one strand engaged, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "where the buck stops with the Minister in his responsibilities to Whānau Ora" — Jackson explicitly picks up Halbert's unanswered questioning and presses the same gap.

acuity.statement: Just in relation to a couple of the issues that have been raised and questions that have been raised, I’m advised by the officials that there was no material change in the level of funding for Whānau Ora in the relevant periods announced; that it is around $170 million to $180 million that is dedicated to the Whānau Ora initiatives.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the thing asked for: a direct answer on the year-on-year funding difference for Whānau Ora, with a figure attached, and then turns to Halbert's second question about his own role in the recommissioning process. The speech is shaped by the questions put to him. Held below 1.0 because Jackson's specific question — whether the Māori development budget rose at all — is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shanan Halbert: "what was the difference in funding in this financial year, 2024-2025, to the prior year"

acuity.statement: What modelling has the Minister for Māori Development seen on the cumulative impact of $9.5 million in expiring funding on Māori broadcasting capability? Further to that, what planning has the Minister undertaken to address the further $4 million in funding that expires for Whakaata Māori in the following financial year?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive question by another member to the same Minister on the same subject, but engages no part of it. It is a prepared set of funding questions that would read identically whatever Abel had said; on-topic prepared material sits in the 0.1-0.3 band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel asked how the loss of the national Māori news service reflects on the Minister's record and how it squares with Te Tiriti, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Further to the question from Steve Abel with regards to national Māori news: does the Minister think that te ao Māori should have national Māori news on radio?
acuity.explanation: Expressly takes up Abel's point about the lost national Māori news service and develops it into a sharper question to the Minister about radio news. The contribution would have to change if the preceding question had been about something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "the nation has lost its national Māori news service—and what is he going to do about it"

acuity.statement: Just to recalibrate some of the confusion that members opposite have laced our Parliament with this evening: there have not been cuts to the baseline budget for the four Māori language entities. Yes, there was time-limited funding, instigated by the former Minister for Māori Development.
acuity.explanation: Directly contests the premise of the expiring-funding questions put to him, distinguishing baseline funding from time-limited funding and attributing the latter to his predecessor. That is engaging the specific claim, not merely the topic; whether the distinction is sound is a Rigor/Veracity matter, not an Acuity one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: "the cumulative impact of $9.5 million in expiring funding on Māori broadcasting capability" (and Willie Jackson's "keep delivering zero budgets at Budget time")

acuity.statement: There was mention of the Māori news service. Actually, the funder of that service and the decision maker of that service—for the Opposition member who asked that question—is not the Minister for Māori Development. It is the funding authority, and they are set up to do that job.
acuity.explanation: Identifies the specific question put by an earlier speaker and answers it on its own terms by disputing the premise that the decision was the Minister's to make. The response is unmistakably shaped by what was asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "I wonder if the Minister for Māori Development can answer how it reflects on his record that the nation has lost its national Māori news service"

acuity.statement: Clearly, the Minister is confused about his role after that terrible explanation about the state of Māori broadcasting. Somebody needs to inform the Minister that as the Minister of Māori Broadcasting as well as the Minister of Māori Development, his brief is not just te reo Māori.
acuity.explanation: Fastens on the particular framing the Minister had just used — an answer built around te reo — and argues it mistakes the scope of his portfolio. Not a mere reference to the previous speaker: the point only exists because of how Potaka answered.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "the Crown, have a very active duty to protect and tautoko te reo Māori" — his answer framed almost wholly around te reo Māori

acuity.statement: His brief, I agree, is not about telling TMP what to do—of course he doesn’t tell TMP what to do. His brief is to advocate for TMP, which he is not doing.
acuity.explanation: Concedes the exact point the Minister made about not directing Te Māngai Pāho and then disputes the inference drawn from it, substituting advocacy as the duty at issue. Accepting part and contesting the rest is the strongest form of engagement with the argument just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I should be telling Te Māngai Pāho how much money they should give to each and every individual Māori radio station. That is not my role—it’s not."

acuity.statement: The Minister has just responded on a few things that I want to put some questions to him on. He talked about the Government currently having a strong economy. I think that the experience of Pacific communities all around Aotearoa New Zealand would beg to differ with you, Minister.
acuity.explanation: Opens by naming the specific economic framing the Minister had just advanced and contests it directly, disputing the premise rather than changing the subject; the speech would read differently had Goldsmith not made the economic case. Engagement is pointable and squarely on the prior claim, though it answers the framing with lived experience rather than the Minister's fiscal reasoning.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It is not sustainable for us, as a country, to carry on as we were because big deficits have extremely large debt" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: I do hear the comments around “Actually, we can outsource it.” Well, I don’t know about that. I think that some things need to be foundational and some things need to be part of the core part of how the ministry functions, and so that’s one question that I would like the Minister to elaborate on.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's consolidation argument — that functions are better held inside the wider Government programme than replicated separately — and resists it on a specific ground, that cultural capability is foundational to the Ministry rather than contractable out. Engages the reasoning, not just the topic; falls short of 1.0 because it is paired with prepared material on the Samoan citizenship bill that would have been delivered regardless.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "why do you have a different group replicating a programme that is across Government, handled by the Ministry of Social Development?" — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.statement: I thank the Minister for mentioning Māori education. That's where I'll focus my question. Cuts to Māori education programmes, including Māori resource teachers and kaupapa Māori pathways, have been widely reported. Kura and wharekura in Tāmaki-makau-rau have raised concerns that these changes will reduce access to specialist support for their ākonga. What assurances can the Minister give that Māori-medium learners in Tāmaki-makau-rau will not experience a decline in support or outcomes as a result of these reductions?
acuity.explanation: Takes the education strand the Minister had just volunteered and turns it against his claim that reductions were offset by better-supported portfolios, naming the specific cuts (Māori resource teachers, kaupapa Māori pathways) and asking what assurance he can give. The engagement is pointable and the opening sentence explicitly hinges on what he said; it then moves into prepared multi-part questions on economic development and trades training that his turn did not raise, so it is a strong partial rather than a full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I think that, yes, some portfolios have had a reduction in funding, and we acknowledge that, but other portfolios—that are absolutely dedicated to the health, wealth, and wellbeing of Māori and all New Zealanders—have been supported more" and his claim about Māori school attendance.

acuity.statement: My question is about Māori economy and employment. Māori unemployment has risen from 6.8 percent to 10 percent, and the employment rate has fallen from 64.7 percent to 60.7 percent—both statistically significant. Name one Te Puni Kōkiri initiative in 2024-25 that has moved either number, with evidence.
acuity.explanation: Clearly prepared material on the matter under debate (the Te Puni Kōkiri vote), carrying its own statistics and its own demand. It does not take up the Minister's specific claims about added funding for Māori wardens or the Welfare League, nor anything in the preceding Te Pāti Māori questions; it would have read identically whatever they had said, beyond being pitched at the same portfolio. The demand for an initiative that moved the numbers gestures at his delivery claim, which puts it at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tama Potaka: "I'm happy to report again, if you didn't see it already, that we gave additional support to those organisations. Isn't that great? Isn't that good mahi?" — a loose gesture at his claim that Te Puni Kōkiri spending is delivering, but it engages no particular claim he or Oriini Kaipara made.

acuity.statement: What I will say is this: none of us want to see, OK, a deterioration in the Māori economy and the New Zealand economy, but these are the consequences that hailed from the economic terrorism of the previous administration. The investments that Māori development have made, the investments in fast-track approvals, many of which are actually Māori-owned and led—the fast track is actually benefiting a whole range of Māori organisations to generate employment.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the question put to him: he concedes the deterioration in the Māori economy that Dansey's figures described, attributes it to the previous government, and offers fast-track approvals as the investment generating Māori employment. That is a response to the topic and to the premise, but not to the specific demand — no Te Puni Kōkiri initiative is named and no evidence of movement in the unemployment or employment rate is supplied, and he then moves to prepared material on property developments and Waikato-Tainui. acuity.responding_to: Georgie Dansey: "Name one Te Puni Kōkiri initiative in 2024-25 that has moved either number, with evidence."

acuity.responding_to: It’s not a little, particular programme that’s going to fix it; what fixes unemployment is economic growth. — Paul Goldsmith

acuity.responding_to: The other question, Minister, is: why cut an initiative that was actually working? — Jenny Salesa

acuity.responding_to: Hamish Campbell: "They talk about the harm; they did nothing, for six years, about dealing with the harm of online gambling."
