acuity.statement: Removing red tape isn’t just about one step or one action; it’s about layers and layers of removal of unnecessary compliance, things that cost New Zealand businesses every day. acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan spoke about why the two AMLCFT bills went to different select committees, the removal of the term "risk management system" from new section 26(1), and the committee's decision to add censures while retaining formal warnings — this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.responding_to: "This bill is another step in removing unnecessary red tape. It’s about making it easier to do business, reducing compliance costs" — Carl Bates

acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific drafting point made in the preceding turn — the novel term 'risk management system' and the committee's decision to strike it — restates what the problem was and endorses the fix as streamlining. His wider speech is visibly built on the earlier turn (same-day committees, the Lafarge/Holcim case, the Regulations Review Committee), and would have to change if the previous speaker had argued something else. Short of 1.0 because he largely relays and agrees rather than testing or extending the reasoning.

acuity.responding_to: "submitters mentioned, rightly, that this particular term doesn’t appear anywhere else in the legislation... we have decided to remove that particular term “risk management system”" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.responding_to: 'Because our focus has been on working families, and that’s what we’ve delivered through in-work family tax credits.' — Christopher Luxon

acuity.statement: How did the maths acceleration trial boost achievement?
acuity.explanation: Picks up the trial the previous answer had just reported on and asks for the mechanism behind the results quoted, so it follows on from the content rather than ignoring it — but it engages the topic rather than any specific claim, and reads as the scheduled next step in a prepared sequence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: 'Participants in round two also made up two years’ worth of progress across four key foundational areas in 12 weeks.' — Erica Stanford

acuity.statement: The bill has been introduced within a broader policy landscape where obligations to Te Tiriti are being undermined, narrowed, and erased. The flow-on effect of this approach is that the bill does not address, nor does it provide a targeted assessment of, impacts on Māori, despite clear evidence and advocacy by justice experts since the He Whaipaanga Hou report in 1988.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive NZ First speech defending the bill as balanced and necessary to protect communities. The speech is prepared Te Pāti Māori material on Te Tiriti obligations and disproportionate Māori imprisonment; it neither accepts nor contests Costello's balance claim, and would read identically had Costello said something else. It is squarely on the bill under debate, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band's floor rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hon Casey Costello argued that "This is a balanced piece of legislation" which strikes a balance between protecting corrections officers and the rights of designated prisoners, and this statement does not take that balance argument up at any point.

acuity.statement: I thought that the Minister made a very levelled and very fair contribution in his opening remarks on the legislation. I really want to talk about the substantive amendment in the bill, which is going to establish a really clear statutory basis for the safe, lawful, and humane management of a really small group of prisoners who pose an extreme risk to the Department of Corrections, who manage our prisons, and they are prisoners whom the bill refers to as designated-management prisoners—the DMPs.
acuity.explanation: Immediately follows a detailed Treaty-based critique and engages none of it — no answer on active protection, on Wai 3060, or on disproportionate impact. The praise is directed backwards past that speech to the Minister's opening, and the rest is a prepared description of the DMP regime that would be word-identical whatever preceded it. On-topic prepared material, so bottom band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke argued immediately before that the bill "fails to recognise that the Crown must take positive steps to protect Māori" and that the new powers are "likely to have a disproportionate effect on Māori", and this statement does not take either claim up.

acuity.statement: Now, we understand the operational realities here. Staff must have lawful tools to manage genuine threats, but segregation is one of the most serious powers that are available inside a prison. It can have profound consequences for mental health and rehabilitation, and so Labour will be looking carefully at whether these powers are sufficiently targeted and whether they are applied consistently. We’re also keen to ensure that we do not disproportionately impact particular groups, including Māori, Pasifika, and prisoners with mental health needs, who are already overrepresented in the prison system.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the preceding Te Pāti Māori speech — that the expanded segregation powers will fall disproportionately on Māori — and converts it into a specific select committee test on targeting and consistency of application. It does not engage her Te Tiriti or Wai 3060 argument and otherwise proceeds through prepared Labour material clause by clause, so this is partial engagement rather than a full taking-up.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke: "the use of the new powers proposed under this bill is likely to have a disproportionate effect on Māori within the prison system and their whānau on the outside".

acuity.statement: The Minister has covered this all very well, and I’m really pleased with where this bill has got to. Ultimately, we are in a changing environment, and we need to change the law to suit. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, structured speech posing specific questions about thresholds, resourcing and oversight, and answers none of them. The content is generic commendation plus a claim that a changing environment requires changed law, which would be identical whoever had spoken before. It names the bill, so it is on the matter under debate, but engagement is nil.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Rosewarne immediately before set out three tests — "is it workable, is it properly resourced, and are the safeguards strong enough?" — and questioned whether the designation thresholds and independent oversight are adequate; this statement does not take up any of them.

acuity.statement: At the end of the day—actually, the minimum is 10 hours, and 14 is the aspiration, but of course we know that in Corrections, when resources are strained, as they very much are at the current time, aspirations are rarely achieved.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the exact figures the previous Labour speaker welcomed, corrects his own slip back to them, and does something with them: qualifies the "good move" verdict by arguing that under strained Corrections resourcing the aspirational 14 hours will not be met. He also takes up Rosewarne's designation-threshold concern. It stops short of 1.0 because much of the surrounding speech is his own prepared Pāremoremo/Ombudsman material rather than engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Rosewarne: "Having this bill set out a minimum of 10 hours of meaningful human contact over 14 days, with an aspirational target of 14 hours a week, is a good move".

acuity.statement: This bill has had very wide support across the House, and I also add my support. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: The observation that the bill has had wide support is a gesture at the debate just heard, which lifts it off the floor, but no argument from any preceding speaker is engaged — not Webb's point about administrative discretion, not Maipi-Clarke's Treaty critique. It is a commendation that would stand unchanged whatever had been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hon Dr Duncan Webb argued immediately before that the Pāremoremo regime had been governed by administrative order rather than a clear legal framework and that the designation test may not be right; this statement does not take that up, it only observes that support has been wide.

acuity.statement: I think the accountability question one is straightforward. Along with what the member has outlined, decisions by officials and elected representatives are always subject to judicial review—so if there’s anything that the local boards, councils are doing which would fall foul of natural justice, for example, or the empowering provisions of statute under which they are enabled to make those decisions, those decisions are reviewable through judicial review.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Utikere put to him — which accountability mechanisms apply to local board transport decisions — expressly acknowledges the options the member listed, and adds a further one (judicial review) with the grounds on which it would bite. The answer would be different had Utikere asked something else. Short of 1.0 because it addresses only the accountability question and leaves the 'longstanding ambiguity' and local-autonomy balance questions untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "are there other accountability mechanisms that exist that either the public, the community, or the elected members could avail themselves of"

acuity.statement: This clause 4 is really a lot of the impact of this bill, because it changes the status of local boards under the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009 and gives them much greater power. We need to really understand from the Minister what his policy programme is to make sure that Aucklanders have the right kind of say in local transport decisions if they’re being made at the local board level.
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — the clauses devolving transport decisions to local boards — but it engages no part of the answer that immediately preceded it. Meager had just offered judicial review as the accountability backstop; Williams neither accepts, tests nor disputes that, and instead opens her own prepared line of questioning on the legal status of local boards. The opening would read identically whatever the Minister had just said, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager answered that local board and council decisions are reviewable through judicial review, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: In terms of the crux of the question, local boards make decisions as though they are the local authority. They act as Auckland Council.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question Williams posed — whether local boards will be playing the role of a local authority — with a direct yes, then grounds it in the clause and section she had been reading from. He also picks up her own 'lady in the office' formulation earlier in the same turn. The reply is entirely contingent on what she asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "are they playing the role of a local authority? Have we got the empowering legislation right so that they can make decisions as if they are the local authority?"

acuity.statement: But to hear from the Minister that judicial review is the option that’s available to people as a form of accountability, that is extremely concerning.
acuity.explanation: Directly rebuts the specific mechanism the Minister had just offered, and does something with it: argues judicial review is unfamiliar and expensive for ordinary constituents, notes it was not raised before the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, and presses for clarification. Disagreement aimed at the content of the prior answer is the strongest evidence of engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "those decisions are reviewable through judicial review"

acuity.statement: In terms of the difference or the removal of the term “allocated to” and replacement with “conferred on”, my understanding is that’s just essentially a technical drafting change to make it very clear that the local boards must undertake their conferred responsibilities and they may exercise any of the conferred powers under clauses 47A to 47D. I’m advised that it’s a drafting reason rather than any particular change in power.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the answer the preceding turn asked for — the distinction between 'allocated' and 'conferred' in clauses 7 and 8 — and states whether any substantive change in power follows from it. Earlier in the same turn he also corrects Utikere's characterisation of his judicial review answer, explaining it was offered on top of the mechanisms the member himself listed rather than instead of them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "So, what is basically the difference there between what is allocated and conferred?"

acuity.statement: I want to ask the Minister to confirm what he said. I think he has said that local boards act as if they are the local authority in setting of the rules such as truck parking. That would be a change in the position that it is currently.
acuity.explanation: Repeats the Minister's answer back in order to test it, then draws out its consequences: the delegation structure under the Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004, the status of the Vehicle Use and Parking Bylaw 2025, and whether neighbouring local boards could set divergent truck-parking rules. She even registers his non-verbal reaction and presses him to confirm. The turn could not exist without the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: James Meager: "local boards make decisions as though they are the local authority. They act as Auckland Council."

acuity.statement: Under the existing statute, local boards are able to make decisions as if they are the governing body where they are allocated those decisions and those powers. So, the bill itself, as far as I can tell, doesn’t actually outline which decisions should or should not be made by local boards.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question Williams put — whether his change makes local boards synonymous with the local authority — and answers it on its own terms, explaining that the allocation is the council's under section 16 and that new subparagraph (4) only preserves an existing ability. The reply would read differently had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "is what he has said about local authorities and local wards being synonymous because of his change, at his new clause 7(4)(b), the case for all of these rules, and how will they interact with the national rules?"

acuity.statement: The Eden Park precinct belongs in Part 2, but my understanding is the streets that surround that will be in this part. They are part of the same things that Arena Williams is talking about because they are the streets that the local board will have determination over.
acuity.explanation: She explicitly hooks her questions onto the strand of the debate Williams opened (local board determination over streets) and applies it to a concrete case, but she does not engage the Minister's just-given answer; from there she moves into her own prepared questions on the Eden Park precinct, parking spillover and conflicts of interest.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "what is being done by new section 12 is a further devolution to local boards" — White picks up the devolution-of-street-control strand but not Meager's immediately preceding point about allocation under section 16.

acuity.statement: Then just on the questions of conflicts of interests, in the same clause 14, at new section *40(a), there’s a conflicts of interest section, which states that Schedule 3 of the Act applies to the Auckland Regional Transport Committee. When any conflicts do arise, both Schedule 3 applies but also the existing policies and procedures that the Auckland Council would have for managing conflicts generally would also apply.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of White's strands in turn — pointing her to new section 48 and the roading classification framework for which streets local boards control, then to the conflicts-of-interest provision she asked about and the council's own policies. The content is determined by what she asked, not by prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Helen White: "what happens when you have people with a conflict of interest in terms of determining what happens to a local street?"

acuity.statement: Has the Minister managed, through his new section 4B, to include infringement powers as something that Aucklanders can have a say on through their local boards?
acuity.explanation: Squarely on the matter under debate — devolution of powers to Auckland local boards — and gestures at the Minister ("As the Minister will know"), but it engages no part of the answer that immediately preceded it, opening instead a new and separately prepared line on parking infringement fees.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just answered Helen White on the roading classification framework under new section 48 and on the conflicts-of-interest provision, and this statement takes up neither; it opens a fresh strand on infringement fees under clause 5.

acuity.statement: I’m a bit surprised to hear some of the questions coming from the Opposition, because those particular things that I’ve been hearing are things that could have been traversed, but were not traversed, at select committee. I am a bit concerned about those questions, but the question that I want to pursue is, as Cam Luxton has raised in his amendment, the issue of co-design and consultation with “Māori”—it’s not “iwi”; the word is “Māori”—and the practicality of that.
acuity.explanation: Foster follows James Meager's answer on why the bill will not prescribe a 'green list or a red list' of backgrounds for appointments. Foster does not take up that reasoning at all: he comments on the fact that questions are being asked rather than on their content, then opens a separate line of his own on the practicality of consulting Māori in the design of the 30-year transport plan. The speech is squarely about the bill under committee consideration and gestures at the debate around it (the Opposition's questions, Luxton's amendment, the select committee report-back), so it is not wholly detached — but it would read identically whatever Meager had just said about appointments, which puts it in the prepared-material-on-topic band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager said "we’re not going to be outlining in the statute a green list or a red list of which particular background or profession you should or should not have when entering this process", and this statement does not take that argument up — it raises a different clause about consultation with Māori in the 30-year plan.

acuity.statement: I would like to ask a question that’s very practical and comes from a meeting I had with my constituents who live around Eden Park. And that is: what is the Eden Park precinct?
acuity.explanation: White follows a substantive turn by Meager on how the bill's undefined terms should be interpreted. Her question is squarely on the bill under committee consideration and shares the theme of definitional vagueness, but it engages no part of Meager's reasoning — it is a constituency-sourced question she would have put whatever he had said. Prepared material on the right subject, with a gesture at the debate's definitional theme.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager argued that the bill's terms are "both clear enough to point the committee in the direction of meeting those objectives" and that interpretation can be settled by the courts; this statement raises a separate definitional gap about the Eden Park precinct without taking up that argument.

acuity.statement: To clarify: Auckland Council will define the Eden Park precinct area when it develops the Auckland roading classification framework.
acuity.explanation: This takes the exact question just put to him and supplies the missing piece: who defines the precinct, by what instrument, and the safeguard on it. Had White asked a different question about the bill, this answer would have had to be different, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what is the Eden Park precinct?" — and "if there is no such definition, how will it be defined" — Helen White

acuity.statement: A question for you, Minister, is: are you comfortable that that select committee change is kind of the right balance, that the mayor is still required to consult, as opposed to just the mayor making those determinations by themselves?
acuity.explanation: Utikere takes up the precise guardrail Meager had just cited in answer to the "whim of the mayor" concern and presses on whether that consultation requirement is calibrated correctly. That is genuine engagement with a preceding turn's content, though it is one strand of an otherwise prepared run of separate questions on remuneration and standing orders, and it engages nothing in Watts's immediately preceding answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the mayor must consult the governing body before making an appointment" — James Meager, offering new section 38F(3)(a) as a guardrail against a rogue mayor

acuity.statement: Just in regards to the questions on the process, there absolutely is the expectation that it is a joint process shared between the mayor and the Minister, and “joint” is what it says on the tin.
acuity.explanation: He answers the specific question about whether the mayor and Minister are equal parts of the chairperson appointment, and in his next breath the select committee question. But he leaves the remuneration differential and the standing orders interaction untouched and pivots to the legislation's intent, so this is partial engagement with what was put to him rather than a full answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is it the Minister’s view that those are two equal parts of that particular equation" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: I want to check with the Minister regarding clear information in paragraph (c) and the reasonable opportunity in paragraph (d). How would seniors be captured in a lot of this?
acuity.explanation: The questions are closely tied to the clauses before the committee, so this is on the matter under debate, but it engages no part of the preceding turn — it is a prepared set of consultation questions that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Watts had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on the joint mayor–Minister appointment process and on being comfortable with the select committee's recommendation, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I wasn’t looking to take another call, but the answer from the previous Minister in the chair, the Hon James Meager, leaves a lot to be desired.
acuity.explanation: This call exists only because of Meager's answer and points precisely at it — the response to Amendment Paper 568 — so it is clearly prompted by what preceded. But in what is on the record here it supplies only an evaluation of that answer's adequacy, not engagement with its content, which keeps it short of a genuine partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I can’t answer that directly; all I can appoint to is a couple of things" — James Meager, on Luxton's question about the use of the word "Māori" in the bill

acuity.statement: One of the interesting things that the Minister referred to was multi-modal representation, potentially—rail representation, and the like. Now, the Auckland Regional Transport Committee that this bill establishes will have a mix of voting members and non-voting members, and the non-voting members are limited in number, to a total of three, and that’s contained in sections 38D, E, and F.
acuity.explanation: Foster's immediately preceding turn pressed the coalition-agreement/equal-citizenship objection and asked the Minister why he was not supporting the amendment. Utikere engages none of that; he opens his own prepared line on non-voting membership and standing orders. There is a gesture at the debate — a glance back at the Minister's earlier remark on multi-modal representation — so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero. His speech would read identically had Foster said something else about the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued that the bill's Māori-contribution provision sits awkwardly with the coalition agreements' equal-citizenship commitments, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Actually, it’s quite practically impossible to say whether something applies if another piece of law does or does not pass. This bill applies for the Auckland Regional Transport Committee to adopt a set of standing orders for the conduct of its meetings and those of its subcommittees. If the subsequent piece of law that the member Tangi Utikere referred to passes and overrides those standing orders, and provides a consistent set of standing orders, then it overrides those standing orders.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific interaction Utikere raised — new section 41D's standing-orders requirement against the Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill — and resolves it on its own terms, naming the member and the clause. The answer could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument; had Utikere asked about non-voting membership instead, this turn would have to change. Not 1.0 only because the engagement resolves into a restatement of the conditional rather than drawing out a further consequence.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Will a consistent set of standing orders override this provision, or will this provision stand and, effectively, trump any form of consistent set of standing orders that the bill that I mentioned would actually present?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Much has been said by this Government about localism and much has been said about this bill giving Auckland the say over transport that Auckland wants, but when I actually look at the voting members, it has potential for a tie with no tiebreaker in that there are three appointed by the Minister, three appointed by the mayor—and we understand that already that power of the mayor is quite different from other councils around the country—and then they’ve got to agree on the chairperson. I’m interested in what happens if there is a radically different either central government or local government.
acuity.explanation: Opens a fresh strand on membership, tie-breaking and the Infrastructure Commission with no engagement of the standing-orders exchange immediately before it. It is squarely on the bill under debate and flags the inconsistencies she wants teased out, which keeps it above the floor, but the content is indifferent to what preceded it — the only back-reference is a vague "as was referred to earlier" about the Government policy statement, which engages no claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just answered Tangi Utikere on whether a later bill's consistent standing orders would override new section 41D, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’d encourage the member, if she would like this committee to see some action before November, that we should hurry along and get this bill passed into law as quickly as possible. But in regard to her question, I’ll just refer to clause 14 again and the provisions around new section 38D, which outlines the membership—which the member referred to—which is the chairperson, and then three members appointed by the Minister and three members appointed by the mayor.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question put — turning to new sections 38D, 38E, 38G and 39A and quoting the removal powers for the chairperson, ministerial appointees and mayoral appointees — and then names and meets her underlying concern about politicisation of appointments rather than ignoring it. The turn even picks up her aside about the committee not getting much done before November. Short of 1.0 because her second question, on the Infrastructure Commission's input, is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "At what point are there opportunities to replace those people? Do they all get replaced at once, is there opportunity, perhaps, to change the chair earlier than their term would otherwise dictate" — Celia Wade-Brown

acuity.statement: Minister, is this plan a different sort of instrument to the Government policy statement (GPS)? Is it a planning instrument? Does it give rise to secondary legislation? What is it, and why is the Auckland Regional Transport Committee tasked with preparing the plan but its objectives are set by Government?
acuity.explanation: Williams moves to her own prepared set of questions on the 30-year plan without engaging the appointments answer immediately before her. She does gesture at the debate's thread — crediting her colleague Tangi Utikere's earlier canvassing and referring back to the Minister's answer on her Part 1 questions — which lifts it off the floor, but nothing in the content of the preceding turn is taken up or tested.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: James Meager had just explained the removal provisions in new section 39A and defended the appointments process to Celia Wade-Brown, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’ll just take the point around congestion into account: it would surprise me if anyone could interpret “safe and rapid movement of people and goods” as anything other than addressing issues around congestion. Of course, it’s wider than just addressing congestion; it could take into account distance of people from where they live to where they get to work or to main transport hubs or to critical infrastructure.
acuity.explanation: Engages Williams' proposed amendment directly and argues it is already covered by the existing objective in new section 42(3)(b), rather than brushing it aside. The wider turn also works through her other specific questions in order — whether the plan is secondary legislation, where it sits against the long-term plan and the GPS, and why objectives are fixed in primary legislation. Delete her turn and substitute a different critique and this speech would have to be rewritten, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read “reducing congestion” as one of the objectives of that plan" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: In light of those questions about new section 43B and the principles of what the Auckland Regional Transport Committee must take into account, it’s interesting—there’s another part of my Amendment Paper 568 that the Minister has had two calls on now from two different parties in the Chamber and hasn’t yet addressed, so I’m hoping he does take this opportunity to address it.
acuity.explanation: Luxton is listening to the exchange — he tracks that the Minister has now had two calls from two parties without reaching his Amendment Paper 568, and he revives the definitional point Andy Foster made about what "Māori" means in the bill. But he engages the omission in the Minister's answers rather than their content: nothing in Meager's reasoning about the section 42(3) objectives or congestion is tested. Partial engagement with the debate's thread, pointable, and short of a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’ll just take the point around congestion into account" and the Minister's survey of the new section 42(3) objectives — James Meager

acuity.statement: I had some questions that are related to the topics that have previously been discussed, but I just wanted to ask the Minister: in defining “productivity and economic growth” under new section 43A in new Subpart 2—I’m just wondering how that will be accounted for. I think we can all agree that productivity and economic growth might be useful if it leads to higher living standards and less waste. However, I guess the key question about a transport plan is: how do we know it’s delivering on these objectives, and what’s the definition or measure that we’re using to measure productivity?
acuity.explanation: Takes one strand of what the Minister had just put up — his list of the primary objectives the Government sets for the plan — and presses on how "productivity and economic growth" would actually be measured, which is a real engagement with his defence of setting objectives centrally. Her later remark on half the members being ministerial appointees also pushes against his expressed faith in the appointment process. But she does not take up Luxton's immediately preceding point at all, and most of the turn is her own prepared material on disabled access and devolution, so this is partial rather than full responsiveness.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which are, of course, productivity, economic growth, safe and rapid movement of people and goods, and efficient asset management" — James Meager

acuity.statement: Yes, in regards to new section 48A, inserted by clause 14, on page 28 of the bill, the five-year term is appropriate for all of the new transport arrangements to be bedded in Auckland.
acuity.explanation: Utikere asked directly whether the five-year term is still appropriate and, if not, why not. Watts takes up that exact question, names the provision it sits in (new section 48A, clause 14, page 28), affirms the five years and gives the reason — bedding in the new transport arrangements. The answer would be different had a different question been put, and he goes on in the same turn to answer two further questions put earlier by Lawrence Xu-Nan and by Utikere, each located by section and page.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Is the five years still appropriate, and, if not, why not?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: Yes, I do have confidence that they are going to work their way through this process in an appropriate manner when dealing with the HR matters. Actually, Auckland Council has already released a transition plan in regard to how it’s going to manage the risks related to this mechanism, so that will cover the questions in regard to the schedules.
acuity.explanation: Utikere had asked for assurance that staff would be protected and that there was Government confidence the entities could manage the transition, and had referred to the schedules setting out the transition process. Watts answers both strands in order: he states the confidence that was asked for, and meets the schedules point by pointing to Auckland Council's already-released transition plan. Not a full 1.0 because the confidence assertion is given without being argued out, but the engagement with what was just said is squarely pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "there’s confidence from the Government that the entities involved will be able to manage that transition smoothly" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: In regards to the question here around the broad term “Māori” used in the bill, the term “Māori” is intentionally used in the bill as an inclusive term, given that there are 19 iwi groups within the Auckland area, and obviously a significant number in that context.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the precise question Luxton (and Xu-Nan) had just put — what entity "Māori" denotes in this part — and answers it directly with a stated rationale (inclusiveness across 19 Auckland iwi) plus the statutory precedents. The answer would be different had the preceding question been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "We’ve got public and we’ve got Māori without a definition of whether that’s individuals, iwi, what sort of entity we’re talking about."

acuity.statement: My first question, though, is can he explain why he has allowed significant straying from what he’s written at clause 1 that it will provide for public transport—that seems clear—but then at clause 2 any other transport functions are something that can be delegated to it?
acuity.explanation: Substantive, detailed, and squarely about the bill under committee consideration, but it engages no part of the exchange it follows; the questions would read identically whatever the Minister had just said. Scored 0.3 rather than lower because it is addressed to the Minister in the same committee stage and stays on the matter under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just answered on why the undefined term “Māori” is used in the bill, and this statement does not take any part of that up — it opens a fresh line on the transport CCO.

Still within the debate on the same bill, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This is a very common practice about commencement dates, and it avoids situations where ... the bill may not be passed by that specific date" — James Meager. The statement acknowledges the answer but takes up no part of its content.

acuity.statement: Yes, I’m very comfortable. The name of the bill is the Regulatory Systems (Transport) Amendment Bill, because it amends parts of the transport and regulatory system.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question asked and gives the reason the title is apt, directly addressing Utikere's point about calling it what is on the tin. Terse and thin on detail, but that is a specificity matter; as responsiveness it is squarely aimed at the question just put.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "is he comfortable that this is the appropriate name for this bill?" — Tangi Utikere

acuity.statement: That was an awful lot of exuberance for a Government bill that was mainly designed and drafted by the Auckland Council itself. But, nevertheless, you've got to take credit where you can get some, I suppose, if you're this Government.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific claim Watts had just made — that the delivery on this bill belongs to the Government side — and disputes it with a counter-claim about who actually drafted the bill, i.e. she engages the credit-claim rather than merely naming him. It is only a partial engagement, because after this opening she turns to prepared third-reading material on the bill's merits and the select committee process, so the rest of the speech would have read much the same whatever Watts had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: "delivery is happening on this side. What's good for Auckland is good for New Zealand. I'm very pleased to commend this bill."

acuity.statement: Today is a good day for Auckland, because once this bill becomes law, this bill becomes an Act that restores democracy, accountability, and local responsiveness for Auckland Transport decisions. After 16 long years, it restores democracy by ensuring that elected people are accountable for transport decisions.
acuity.explanation: The speech follows a substantive Opposition turn that both credited Auckland Council with the drafting and set out what the select committee changed, and engages neither strand. It is prepared praise for the bill — correct subject matter, so not a zero, but it would be word-for-word identical had McLellan said something entirely different, and the only acknowledgement of others is a closing list of thanks rather than engagement with an argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tracey McLellan argued the bill was mainly designed and drafted by Auckland Council, and that it was improved by the select committee process into a more workable and balanced piece of legislation, and this statement does not take any of that up.

acuity.statement: Throughout the select committee process, Māori voices were very clear. Mana whenua, Māori organisations, local boards, and community groups all raised concerns. They told us that the bill as introduced did not adequately reflect the Te Tiriti principles.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: Andy Foster's preceding turn made claims about the Auditor-General missing infrastructure accounting, the infrastructure deficit and the need for long-term thinking and a working infrastructure funding system. Kaipara's contribution is prepared material on the bill under debate and takes up no strand of Foster's argument — it would read identically whatever he had said, so it sits in the 0.1-0.3 band, with 0.2 reflecting that it is squarely on the matter before the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster spoke about the Auditor-General and the infrastructure funding system ("the Auditor-General should have picked that up—absolutely") and this statement does not take it up.

It engages that strand rather than the whole argument, and then moves to prepared material on Canterbury funding, so it is a partial engagement rather than a full one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "There is still no guaranteed Māori representation at the governance level" — Oriini Kaipara
