acuity.explanation: Follows Davidson's specific argument that the bill hands effective control to two unelected-appointing figures (the Minister of Transport and the Mayor) and risks diverting transport funding from other regions. Watts asserts the bill restores democratic accountability without engaging either point — notably not the charge that the committee will contain ministerially appointed non-elected members. The speech is on the subject of the debate but indifferent to what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Davidson argued the Minister appoints three unelected voting members and that an Auckland-bespoke solution would starve Canterbury and the South Island of funding; this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: I’m not going to add to that last performance, other than saying with this anti -money-laundering third reading that it exactly exemplifies what this Government is all about: reducing business compliance costs, improving regulatory effectiveness and efficiency, continuing regulatory compliance with related international obligations, and providing sufficient funding for the regulatory system, and, of course, one single supervisor.
acuity.explanation: Brewer follows a substantive turn by Davidson that raised a specific definitional question about "dwellinghouse" and the power of entry, and takes up none of it. The only connection to the preceding speech is a dig at its length — a mere reference, which the rubric explicitly says is not engagement. What follows is prepared framing of the Government's general objectives and a commendation of the bill; it would read identically whatever Davidson had argued. There is a gesture at the debate (the bill and its single-supervisor model), so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "seeking clarification on what a dwellinghouse was" — Reuben Davidson. Brewer refers to "that last performance" but engages no part of Davidson's point about the definition of "dwellinghouse" in new section 133A.

acuity.statement: The other thing I just want to highlight, the red tape was often highlighted, like in previous readings. Now, anti - money-laundering and the countering financing of terrorism and the legislation behind it, is not red tape; it’s designed there to protect people, it’s designed there to protect our most vulnerable in our communities, and so it really needs some significant attention.
acuity.explanation: This directly contests the compliance-burden framing Brewer had just used, re-characterising the regime as protective rather than as red tape, and so does something with the preceding argument rather than merely naming it. Disagreement of this kind is strong evidence of having listened. Not a 1.0 because the rebuttal answers the framing in general terms, attributing it to "previous readings" as much as to the speaker immediately before, rather than taking up a specific claim or figure from Brewer's call.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "reducing business compliance costs, improving regulatory effectiveness and efficiency" — Cameron Brewer, who had just framed the bills as a compliance-cost reduction.

acuity.statement: The reason that these are good is that they both reduce the burden of administration on businesses and those who are trying to legitimately raise capital or other financing, while still protecting and detecting criminal activities.
acuity.explanation: Rosewarne had just disputed precisely the burden-reduction framing, and Weenink asserts it again without engaging that objection. The trailing clause about "still protecting and detecting criminal activities" is a gesture towards the protective purpose at issue, which lifts this off the floor, but no part of the preceding reasoning is taken up or answered. The sentence is prepared material on the correct subject and would be unchanged had Rosewarne argued something else about the bills.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it’s not red tape; it’s designed there to protect people" — Dan Rosewarne. Weenink restates the administrative-burden case and does not take up his argument that the regime is protective rather than compliance overhead.

acuity.statement: It’s also important to note that the legislation kind of specifies that only a portion of the costs will come from levies, whereas there’s a baseline understanding that the public interest aspect will still be funded publicly and by budgetary implications as part of, I guess, Vote Internal Affairs.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan's speech is largely prepared material walking the two bills clause by clause, but this passage takes up one strand of Webb's immediately preceding objection — that a public-interest cost is being loaded onto banks and lawyers — and answers it by noting levies fund only part of the cost with the public-interest share still appropriated. He does not name Webb or engage his retail-crime analogy, and he returns straight to prepared material, so this is partial engagement rather than a direct rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "why should you tax financiers for addressing financial crime?" — Webb argued the levy is a tax on a narrow sector for a public-interest function.

acuity.statement: Essentially, what this bill does is it strengthens the laws around anti - money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism. It does this by simplifying the system, by reducing red tape and unnecessary burdens on businesses—which is very important to us in the National Party—and still making sure that authorities are given better and practical tools to recognise risks and tackle crime.
acuity.explanation: A short prepared commendation that would read identically whoever had spoken before it and whatever they had said. It is on the right subject — the substance of the two bills — and glances at the Minister's own earlier speech, but engages no part of the arguments actually made by the preceding speakers, including Webb's objection to the very 'burdens on businesses' framing she adopts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Duncan Webb argued the levy taxes a narrow sector for a public-interest function and that the DIA transition needs forensic expertise migrated from the FMA, and Lawrence Xu-Nan raised stored value instruments and RBNZ/FMA dissent; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: The important component which I think is worth mentioning is the concept of the single supervisor. As has been mentioned, this is not about weakening our response; it is actually clarifying our response.
acuity.explanation: The 'as has been mentioned' is not a mere name-check: she takes up the live worry in the debate that collapsing three supervisors to one loosens the regime, and answers it on its own terms by distinguishing weakening from clarifying and arguing for a risk-proportionate rather than blanket response. It engages the strand rather than any specific claim or figure, and the rest of the speech is prepared party framing, so a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "the worst possible outcome would be that we change the rules and people with nefarious intent will spot the changes" — and Xu-Nan's note of "a lot of disagreement or dissent from the RBNZ as well as the FMA" about losing the supervisor role.

acuity.statement: I think one of the members from the Labour Party talked about how money-laundering could happen, used to happen, and probably still happens around real estate agents, as well. That was an important part to make and important to alert the Minister that, actually, this is also one of those areas of expertise that experience should be migrated over into that single supervisor role, as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes a specific point made by a member on the other side of the House, endorses it, and does something further with it — converting it into a recommendation that real-estate supervision expertise be migrated into the single supervisor. The speech would have to change if that point had not been made. Marked short of the top because the engagement is with a strand carried over from the committee stage rather than with the precise claim in the immediately preceding turn, and the surrounding speech is a prepared survey of the bills.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "imposing it on the businesses like banks and lawyers and real estate agents" — the Labour point about real estate as a money-laundering channel.

acuity.statement: These bills taken together address a serious concern for New Zealand. That is why it’s great to have all parties in this Parliament vote in favour of this bill.
acuity.explanation: A two-sentence commendation that engages no argument made by any preceding speaker. The observation that all parties support the bill is a gesture at the state of the debate rather than engagement with its content, which keeps it just above the floor; the speech is otherwise indifferent to what it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Teanau Tuiono had just urged the Minister to make subsidiary-company financing of terrorism an area of future work and to migrate real-estate expertise into the single supervisor, and this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: As you would have gathered from previous contributions in the House from this side, we do support this bill, and that is around the introduction of a single supervisor for the anti - money-laundering and countering the financing of terrorism. We do also, though, think that it’s very important not to confuse this as an issue of cutting red tape and at the same time losing some of the very vital tools that we have to address organised crime.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the part of the Government case he agrees with — the single supervisor — and disputes the framing the two preceding Government speakers used, arguing that red-tape reduction must not be conflated with giving up enforcement tools. It takes up their actual language and turns it, so the speech would be different had they framed the bill another way. Short of 1.0 because he does not engage a specific claim or figure and much of the rest of the contribution is his own prepared account of the committee stage.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rima Nakhle: "by reducing red tape and unnecessary burdens on businesses—which is very important to us in the National Party" (echoed by Casey Costello's case for the single supervisor).

acuity.statement: I stand today to raise the alarm on this coalition Government’s ram raid of conservation in Aotearoa, on the inheritance of our mokopuna. The bill touches on unresolved issues championed by Sir Tumu with regard to the Tongariro National Park—regardless of the Minister’s speech on toilet cleaning.
acuity.explanation: Andy Foster's immediately preceding turn made specific claims — that the disposals and swap process is not unilateral and sets out an extensive process, and that he awaits submissions. Waititi takes up none of that. His speech is prepared material on the bill's Treaty-settlement consequences, and would read identically whatever Foster had said; the one gesture outside his own text is a passing swipe at an earlier ministerial speech not at the argument just made. On the right subject, engaging no part of the preceding argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster said the disposals and swap process is "not unilateral; there is a process which is set out there and it’s quite an extensive process" and that he looks forward to submissions, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It’s out of date, and it is time for change. This bill will bring greater clarity, it will improve how decisions are made, and it will make it easier to get things done on DOC land.
acuity.explanation: Waititi had just argued at length that the bill forces iwi to relitigate full-and-final Treaty settlements and waters down section 4 of the Conservation Act. Wedd's speech answers none of it — not even to dismiss it — and is a self-contained case for modernisation and efficiency that would be word-for-word identical whoever had preceded her. It is at least about the bill under debate, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Rawiri Waititi argued that "iwi will have to relitigate the Crown’s commitment to uphold their Treaty settlements" and attacked the changes to section 4 of the Conservation Act; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: But what this bill does is an entire paradigm shift. It’s not what we’re expecting when we hear speeches from the other side saying, “Oh, this is just about efficiency and modernisation.” No—this is a paradigm shift.
acuity.explanation: This lifts the exact framing Wedd had just used — that the bill is about modernising an outdated system and managing conservation land more efficiently — concedes the premise that the Act needs work, and then disputes the characterisation, naming the three provisions she says exceed it (purpose changed to enable development, amenity areas, new section 4A). The speech would have had to be written differently had the previous speaker made a different argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "The Conservation Amendment Bill is about modernising an outdated system so that conservation land can be managed more efficiently."

acuity.statement: Let’s just go to a couple of core principles of the Bluegreens: “economic growth and improving the environment can and must go hand in hand”, and “New Zealanders have a unique birthright to access and enjoy our special places”. Well, guess what—all of that also comes at a price and a cost. By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
acuity.explanation: He answers the strand of Brooking's attack aimed at Bluegreens members directly, naming himself as co-chair and offering the Bluegreens principles plus a funding rationale for commercial activity as the reply. But he engages only that strand: Brooking's substantive objections — that amenity areas would admit accommodation and restaurants, and that new section 4A waters 'give effect to' down to a procedural checklist — go untouched, and he returns to prepared material about toilets and visitor charging. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, hence mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Shame on anybody across the aisle there who says that they are “blue-greens”, because this is diminishing every piece of the conservation estate and those settlements." — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific argument McCallum had just made, accepts the premise (charging visitors) and disputes the conclusion by attaching a condition on where the revenue goes, turning his own justification against the commercial-development provisions. The sentence could not have been delivered unchanged had the previous speaker argued something else, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: One of the areas that I’m keen to look at—and I think it’s a great amendment—is the ability to charge international visitors. One of the most often-made comments I get from international visitors who come and visit me is that they can’t believe how much free stuff there is in New Zealand, and this is one of them here.
acuity.explanation: On the right subject — visitor charging is exactly what the preceding speaker had just discussed — but it engages no part of her argument. She had already conceded the charging principle and put the contested question as where the revenue goes; he argues for the conceded point as though it were still in dispute. Prepared material that happens to land on the same topic, so the low band rather than the mid band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Jo Luxton had just said she does not oppose charging tourists provided the money funds tracks and species protection rather than restaurants and wine bars, and this statement advocates visitor charging without taking up that condition or disputing it.

acuity.statement: We’ll just bring back a little bit of common sense. Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
acuity.explanation: Abel's turn made specific charges — that the merger dilutes the environment ministry as submitters warned, that $200 million now subsidises fossil fuels, and that the merger weakens Crown-Māori obligations under Te Tiriti. Wedd takes up none of them. Her opening gestures at the preceding speech ("bring back a little bit of common sense") and counter-asserts at the level of the topic that development and environmental protection are compatible, then delivers prepared material describing MCERT and the RMA framework. Substitute any other anti-merger argument for Abel's and this speech would be word-for-word the same, so it sits in the low band; the gesture at the debate puts it at 0.3 rather than 0.1.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Steve Abel: "This Government, in their one term, will go down in history as the most environmentally destructive Government of New Zealand."

acuity.statement: It’s really interesting that the chair of the Environment Committee thinks it’s common sense to disestablish the environment ministry. At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense. Thankfully, most of the 588 people who submitted on this bill don’t agree, and, today, I will go through some of their reasons for that.
acuity.explanation: Takes the immediately preceding speaker's own framing — that the bill is common sense — identifies her as the chair of the committee that heard the bill, and turns the claim against her twice over: against the environmental conditions she is legislating into, and against the 588 submitters she heard. She then builds the rest of the speech on those submissions, which is the promise made in the last sentence. Had Wedd argued something else, this opening would have had to change, which is the deciding test. Not a bare reference-and-pivot: the "common sense" claim is the thing being contested. Short of 1.0 only because the rebuttal answers the claim by assertion about the state of the environment rather than engaging her specific proposition that development and protection can be achieved together.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Catherine Wedd: "This is good, common-sense legislation." (also "We’ll just bring back a little bit of common sense.")

acuity.statement: Oh, the bill is simple; not just little. Disestablishing a Government department that is part of our environmental institutional infrastructure is not a simple thing, and I would remind those members to think about the people who are involved in these workplaces, as well.
acuity.explanation: She takes the government members' claim that the bill is short and simple, accepts the correction of the word, and then directly contests the claim's substance — that disestablishing a department is not a simple act. The passage could not have been delivered had the interjection not been made; it is shaped entirely by it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill." (with Cameron Luxton's correction "No, he said “simple”.")

acuity.statement: I think what’s astounding in all of that is we’re hearing from Government members right now who were part of those select committee hearings that the significance of this bill and the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment is absolutely lost on them.
acuity.explanation: She picks up one strand of what immediately preceded her — the government interjections minimising the bill during the previous speech — and uses it as evidence that members did not absorb the submissions. But she engages the framing rather than any specific claim, and the bulk of the speech is prepared material (Cabinet paper, Hayward evidence, hearing times) that would have run unchanged whatever preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill." — the interjections made during Rachel Brooking's preceding turn

acuity.statement: The Environment Committee did hear quite a few submissions—two hours and 45 minutes, the previous speaker Lan Pham said—and I believe that these have been properly addressed here. The Secretary for the Environment will now be required to report annually on the performance of their Environment Act functions, and that report will sit inside a new ministry, which will be created and will report to this House.
acuity.explanation: He adopts the previous speaker's own figure and turns it against her conclusion, then supplies the specific answer to the reporting-requirement concern raised earlier in the debate (an annual report on Environment Act functions). The reply is visibly built on what was said rather than around it; whether the answer is adequate is a separate question from whether it engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings" — and Rachel Brooking: "we don’t know what the reporting requirements are"

acuity.statement: Look, we know there were many submitters who were fearful and worried about the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, and fair enough—it is what we know. This is a bold change, and so we hear them.
acuity.explanation: He acknowledges the submitter evidence that dominated the preceding Green speech and concedes its force in part, which is a real engagement with the topic and not merely a mention. But he does not take up the claim itself — that submissions were unanimously opposed — and moves straight to prepared New Zealand First material on Auckland amalgamation and spatial planning that would read identically after any opposing speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lan Pham: "we had not one credible submission actually in support of this"

acuity.statement: What we’ve been seeing month after month, week after week, and hour after hour is the continual eroding of the protection of our taiao, and I heard the speaker before me talk about what it means in an urban sense. It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
acuity.explanation: She names the preceding speaker's integration-and-urban-planning argument and rejects its implicit premise, that the choice is between urban integration and environmental protection. That is a genuine engagement with one strand. The remainder of the speech — seabed mining litigation, Te Tiriti, iwi settlements — is prepared material that does not take up anything Wilson argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David Wilson: "This is about integrated and spatial planning" and his account of Aucklanders "roving around different ministries"

acuity.statement: Well, 40 years on, this Government, dedicated to the war on nature, is blowing up the Ministry for the Environment, and we should not be surprised, because they have done everything, in every legislative realm, to diminish, to weaken, and to undermine environmental protection.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the bill, but it is indifferent to what precedes it: a prepared historical narrative of the ministry's 1986 founding and a general charge about the Government's legislative record. Luxton had put the direct challenge that a separate bureaucracy is not the same as protection, and this does not engage it; the speech would be word-for-word identical whichever member had spoken before.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued the bill is an attack on Te Tiriti and on iwi settlements, and Cameron Luxton argued that "a stand-alone ministry does not make a wetland"; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: This bill is really quite simple. It’s about taking the environment ministry and putting it into another ministry. Nothing’s disappearing. There’s no drama. Cheer up; the sun is shining. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition turn in the same second-reading debate, so it is eligible. It is on the matter under debate and offers a counter-framing ("nothing's disappearing", "no drama") that glances at Russell's "backtrack on the basics" characterisation, but it engages no part of her actual case — the 15 February introduction, the 19 February first reading, the under-two-week submission window, or the committee chair's decision. Substituting a different environment-focused critique would not have changed a word of this reply, which places it in the 0.1–0.3 band; 0.3 because there is at least a gesture at the debate rather than none.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "Instead, we’ve had a rushed process with just a very few days of submissions—getting the nuisance of the environment out of the way." — Hamilton gestures at her tone ("that was so depressing") and at the general charge of drama, but takes up none of her argument about the truncated select committee process or the submission deadline.

acuity.statement: During the select committee process—yes—there were a lot of submissions there that gave us lots of advice. One of the amendments that came from that was to strengthen the feedback from the Secretary for the Environment, who will hand the ultimate responsibility for this new ministry back to Parliament. We have inserted a new clause, and it’s requiring the secretary to report annually to ensure that he’s reporting on the performance of their function, as is required under the Environment Act.
acuity.explanation: MacLeod follows Rosewarne's specific attack on clause 9 and institutional independence with an evidently prepared account of the bill's scope and the select committee's work. It is squarely on the matter under debate, and the reporting-clause point brushes against the accountability theme, but nothing in the speech would change had Rosewarne argued something different about the bill. That is prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, not engagement with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Rosewarne argued that clause 9 collapses the ministry into a single statutory office so that "A secretary answers directly to the Minister, who controls their appointment and their performance reviews", and this speech does not take that up — it describes a new annual reporting clause as prepared select-committee material without addressing the independence argument at all.

acuity.statement: This Government has no commitment to the environment. If I look at what this bill is doing, it is removing our precious Ministry for the Environment and diluting all its powers by mixing them into a mega-ministry, where the focus on the environment will be lost. It’s a disgrace.
acuity.explanation: Russell's speech is on the bill under debate and flatly opposes the characterisation MacLeod had just offered, so there is a gesture at the preceding turn. But she engages none of its content — not the select committee process, not the strengthened reporting requirement — and the speech proceeds into a prepared catalogue of the Government's climate record that would have been delivered word for word whoever had spoken before her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David MacLeod said "This bill is actually quite a small bill—it’s only eight pages long" and described the select committee's new annual reporting clause; Russell contradicts the small-and-tidy framing in general terms but does not take up the page count, the committee amendment, or the reporting clause.

acuity.statement: Well, I don’t believe it would bring the system into disrepute. I think that the system would be stronger and our society would be stronger if we were prepared to accept responsibility for the actions of a State that were utterly criminal.
acuity.explanation: Mooney's justification for the stricter test was public confidence — 'to ensure that we retain confidence in the system, from all New Zealanders'. White engages that premise head-on and denies it, arguing public confidence would instead be raised by treating all State-abuse survivors alike. This is a direct rebuttal of the preceding speaker's reasoning rather than a pivot away from it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Joseph Mooney: 'This is about maintaining faith in the system from all New Zealanders, which is critical to ensuring that this is an enduring process.'

acuity.statement: I think, just to get back to the bill, the bill will ensure some clarity to continue in the process and recognise a person’s abuse in State care, as well as offering an alternative to litigation if they so choose, including one of three options: the financial payment, an apology, or counselling or other support, as appropriate.
acuity.explanation: White had just made a specific case — the 2 percent excluded are the most damaged, the State keeps the withheld money, a select committee submitter was left in despair, and the apology is therefore partial. Kirkpatrick's contribution is prepared material on the right subject: thanks to survivors and the committee, praise for colleagues' 'measured response', and a summary of what the bill offers. Naming Mooney and Costello is a reference, not engagement, and none of White's claims is taken up; the speech would read the same whatever the previous speaker had argued. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.1 only because it gestures at the dispute in the House.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Helen White argued the 2 percent exclusion means the State keeps the money and the apology is a limited, conditional one, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: It was a Labour Government. The Greens were not actually in Government with Labour. New Zealand First was, but Greens have never been in a coalition with Labour.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Foster's interjection directly and corrects the factual premise inside it — that the Greens were part of the government responsible for the ferry/wharf project. The speech would be different had Foster not made that claim; it is a point-by-point correction rather than a pivot to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "This is the problem: reds and greens can't deliver anything."

acuity.statement: I have been addressing the bill, and I’ve been talking about all the rats and mice, the infringement notices and the amendments to the Land Transport Act, the amendments to the Maritime Transport Act, the amendments to the Land Transport Management Act, “Part 5 Amendments to Railways Act 2005”, amendments to the Road User Charges Act 2012, and “Part 7 Miscellaneous amendments”.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific challenge put to her — that she was not addressing the bill — by enumerating the parts of the bill she has covered. The content is wholly determined by the challenge it follows; a different objection would have required a different answer.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Todd Stephenson: "Address the bill, then."

acuity.statement: ACT supports this bill. It’s an omnibus bill and it fixes transport legislation that would otherwise be holding New Zealand businesses and workers back. It provides clarity about transport service licensing.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the right subject. Court follows a speech whose central argument was that the bill is insufficient — no coastal fleet, no fuel economy standards, no demand pricing — and engages none of it; his only acknowledgement of the previous speaker is a quip about missing her energy, which is a reference, not engagement. The passage would read identically whatever Genter had argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter argued the bill "is far from sufficient to deal with the fuel crisis we’re currently facing" and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I just was sort of contemplating the conversation that’s been going on here in the House about how, you know, we’ve kind of missed a trick, possibly, during the committee of the whole House, about the name of the bill, because it seems to me that for some people it’s the sort of digital ID, whether it’s the digital ID for the vehicle or a digital ID for the person, or whether it’s a New Zealand Post extinction bill—because clearly if Simon keeps on losing his various certificates but doesn’t have to have them sent through the mail, clearly it will do New Zealand Post’s business no good whatsoever.
acuity.explanation: Foster takes up the specific scenario Court had just been arguing about — Simon losing his documents and not needing hard copies sent through the mail — and draws out a consequence of it (the effect on NZ Post's business), rather than reading prepared material. It is a light extension rather than a rebuttal of the argument's substance, so it engages one strand of what preceded it; the speech would have been different had Court's exchange gone another way.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Court: "if they do lose their phone, they can go down to the phone shop" — Court's exchange about losing documents/licences and having them replaced rather than posted.

acuity.statement: This bill is just another example of the Government getting on with fixing the basics while preparing for the future. This bill addresses a broad range of regulatory issues across our land transport, maritime, and aviation sectors. Like other speakers mentioned, there’s nothing fishy here, but this is exactly the point.
acuity.explanation: Follows Mike Davidson's substantive Greens contribution, which made two pointed arguments (that vehicle emissions kill more people than crashes and nothing is being done about it, and that the bill is welcome housekeeping but falls far short of transport transformation). Cheung takes up neither. The only nod to what preceded is a glancing 'Like other speakers mentioned, there's nothing fishy here', which repeats an earlier joke rather than engaging any claim; the rest is prepared government framing ('fixing the basics and building the future') that would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before. A gesture at the debate without engagement sits at the bottom band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "Like, yes, we would love to see a lot more transformation in transport, but at the same time we need to make sure we do these important housekeeping matters as well." — Cheung does not take up the transformation argument or the emissions claim.

acuity.statement: As has been noted, it’s certainly not transformative, and I note my colleague Andy Foster from New Zealand First’s comment, pleading almost: “Can we please stick to what’s in the bill and not what’s not in the bill?”, but life doesn’t quite work like that. Sometimes, when you are considering or ruminating or evaluating anything, the devil is in the detail, and what is missing or what could have been there is, you know, a potential for a lost opportunity.
acuity.explanation: Takes a specific procedural argument made earlier in the debate — that members should confine themselves to the bill's contents — quotes it, and rebuts it directly with a counter-principle about opportunity cost and what is omitted, then proceeds to act on that rebuttal by listing the omissions (affordability, emissions reduction, public transport). The speech would have to change if that plea had not been made. Disagreement engaged on its own terms is high acuity; the quality of the reasoning and the fact that it criticises other parties' choices are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster, quoted by McLellan in the chamber: "Can we please stick to what’s in the bill and not what’s not in the bill?"

acuity.statement: When we talk about strengthening safety and enforcement, as has been mentioned, it certainly gives the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) the authority to close unsafe highways, and I concur. I think it was Tangi Utikere who said that—I think most people would be a little bit bewildered to note that NZTA didn’t previously have the authority to be able to do something.
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific point made earlier in the debate — the highway-closure power, raised by Mike Davidson in the immediately preceding Greens turn and attributed by McLellan to Tangi Utikere — names it, agrees, and adds something to it (the observation that the absence of the power until now is itself surprising, and that the change is overdue). That is more than a mere reference, but it is agreement that extends a point rather than engagement with a contested argument, and she then returns to a prepared clause-by-clause walk-through.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "it’s also good to see that Waka Kotahi has the ability to close parts of the State highways network if it’s necessary to protect public safety."

acuity.statement: He maha ngā whāinga o te tukanga o te kerēme. Akenepea ko te whāinga tuatahi ko te whakapūāwai o te reo Māori puta noa i te motu nei. Nā reira ka kōrero au i te reo Māori anake i tēnei ata.
acuity.explanation: Fleming follows Jackson in the same third-reading debate but engages no part of Jackson's argument. His speech responds to the morning's mihi whakatau kaikōrero (the iwi's first and second speakers) rather than to the preceding member, and is otherwise prepared material on the settlement process. On topic, but it would read identically whatever Jackson had said — a gesture at the occasion, not at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willie Jackson spoke about the forecourt confrontation, the collective negotiation model and the inadequacy of the settlement quantum, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: It’s a start and I think it opens the door, but again, as colleagues have already shared in this House around the building of that bridge and the connection and the desire for the ongoing enduring relationship, the relationship that can span across generations and see honourable kāwanatanga meet mana ki te mana with you as hapū, iwi, marae, iwi kāinga, ahi kā.
acuity.explanation: There is a gesture at what has gone before — she picks up the shared bridge/relationship theme and attributes it to colleagues — but she engages no specific claim any of them made. Fleming's actual argument, that the Crown cannot revitalise a community and only the community can, is not taken up, affirmed or disputed. Generalised acknowledgement of "colleagues" is a reference, not an engagement, so this sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Greg Fleming: "ko te tino tūmanako o tēnei tukanga kia whakapapa, kia whakanui i tō koutou raukaha, tō koutou āheinga" (the true hope of this process is to empower and celebrate your capacity and capability).

acuity.statement: I thank you for, as many other speakers have said, making the compromise of what Treaty settlements are—the huge compromise; Hūhana Lyndon said the 1 or 2 percent of what it’s worth; well, in fact, it’s probably a lot less than that, to tell the truth.
acuity.explanation: He takes the specific figure the immediately preceding speaker put into the debate, names her, and does something with it — correcting it in the direction of her own case by saying the real proportion is lower still. The sentence could not have been written without having heard Lyndon's turn, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because he adjusts her number by impression ("probably", "to tell the truth") rather than supplying a competing figure or reasoning. Whether his revised estimate is accurate is a separate question and is not what is scored here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hūhana Lyndon: "our people are so gracious in accepting the 1 to 2 cents in the dollar for the immense loss for the people of Hauraki".

acuity.statement: I want to start by acknowledging my colleague Willie Jackson’s speech about the time that we stood out on the forecourt quite a number of years ago. It was really disconcerting. It was such a traumatic moment for us all—for you, and for us. That was a moment that actually started well over 150 years ago when rights were taken away from you.
acuity.explanation: She takes up the specific episode Jackson raised earlier in the debate and draws out its consequence — recasting the forecourt confrontation as something caused by the Crown's determinations 150 years earlier rather than, as Jackson had it, by what the settlement process does to Māori. That is engagement that adds to the preceding argument rather than restating it, and the passage would have to change if Jackson had spoken about something else. Short of 1.0 because she extends the point rather than testing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "putting iwi against iwi, hapū against hapū, whanaunga against whanaunga, and never, never more exemplified than that day we had out on the forecourt."

acuity.statement: People will say that this is the end of the process, and, as I’ve just heard from across the House, this is actually the new beginning.
acuity.explanation: She picks up the formulation the preceding speaker had just used, marks it as his ("as I’ve just heard from across the House"), adopts it against the alternative framing she sets up, and then builds the rest of her speech around it. That is taking a strand of the previous turn and doing something with it, across the benches. It is agreement rather than rebuttal, and the engagement is with a framing rather than a contestable claim, so it falls short of the top of the scale — but it is clearly responsive, not prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: David MacLeod: "I look forward to this getting Royal assent, but it is just the beginning—it is just the beginning of the new phase of where we’re going to."

acuity.statement: Yes, we’ve placed these three third readings in one third reading because, as Willie Jackson said, this is how desperate we are to get along with things. So we are. We’re desperate for our guests and your whānau to get along with things.
acuity.explanation: She quotes Jackson accurately but inverts his sense: his "desperate" described iwi accepting an inadequate quantum to get the process over with, and she repurposes it as the House's eagerness to deliver for the guests. Repeating a member's words back and pivoting away from what they meant is not responsiveness — nothing in Jackson's actual claim, that the redress does not compensate for the loss, is accepted, disputed or answered. It is on the debate's subject, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willie Jackson: "So that’s how desperate we are in terms of getting on with things, and so the challenges remain for our Hauraki collective and the different hapū, different iwi, to find a way to utilise the pūtea—which does not at all compensate for the loss".

acuity.statement: Other speakers have spoken to it never being enough, and I tautoko that: it’s never enough, but it’s a start.
acuity.explanation: She identifies a specific strand running through the preceding turns — that the settlement can never be adequate — endorses it, and qualifies it with "but it’s a start". That is a pointable engagement with content rather than a bare nod, so it clears the unresponsive band. It stays mid-scale because it engages a theme attributed to "other speakers" generally rather than any one member's argument, and she adds no reasoning to it before returning to her own prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Jan Tinetti: "but it never will make up for that hurt and that mamae that you have suffered for so many years" — the same strand also put by David MacLeod ("The monetary recompense is a pittance, really") and Hūhana Lyndon.

acuity.statement: The member over there is asking for our solution. It was quite interesting to hear from the Minister a really superficial discussion about sugar-rush economics. Where did you get that key line? Where did you get that key line? Actually, one of Labour’s solutions—which if the Minister actually read it properly; quite clearly he’s reading with a bit of difficulty—access to capital is one of the reasons why New Zealand’s productivity is lagging. What is Labour’s solution to that? The New Zealand future fund—that’s what it’s about.
acuity.explanation: McCallum interjects demanding Labour's alternative, and Edmonds takes the question up directly rather than ignoring it: she names the problem she says the solution addresses (access to capital as a drag on productivity), names the policy (the New Zealand future fund), and cites Ireland and Carney's Canada as precedents. The passage would not exist in this form had the interjection not been made, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 because part of the stretch pivots to a jibe about the Minister's reading rather than engaging the challenge itself — and the low civility of that jibe and the thinness of the Ireland/Canada analogy are scored elsewhere, not here.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "What’s your solution?" — Grant McCallum

acuity.statement: Yet this Government advances reforms that weaken environmental protections and sideline Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations in environmental law. Chris Bishop confirmed Cabinet agreed not to include a Treaty clause in the replacement legislation—imagine that, removing Te Tiriti from the laws governing the whenua itself in a country founded upon Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
acuity.explanation: Kaipara follows a substantive Green turn in the same debate, but her speech engages none of Abel's argument — not the Mike Smith case, not comity, not the ETS/methane exemption point. It is prepared material on the matter under debate (environmental protection and the RMA replacement bills), directed at ministers rather than at the previous speaker. She touches the Treaty theme Abel also raised, but asserts her own point rather than taking up his, so this sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band: the speech would read word-for-word the same had Abel argued something quite different about the environment.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Steve Abel, in the immediately preceding turn, argued that "Minister Goldsmith has promised to kill the Mike Smith case currently before the courts" and set out the principle of comity, and this statement does not take any part of that up.

acuity.statement: While I applaud the bipartisanship that’s being expressed tonight, I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed.
acuity.explanation: Leary takes up the cross-party willingness-to-act theme that Butterick and earlier speakers put forward and tests it against a bill this House has just passed, arguing its definitions miss exactly the harms being described tonight. That is a real engagement with one strand of the preceding argument — the Government's claimed readiness to protect children online — rather than a mere reference to it. It is partial rather than full: she does not take up Butterick's specific case about educating parents who never grew up with the technology, and the bulk of the speech (the Annabelle Daza account, the platform-design material) is prepared material that would have been delivered whoever preceded her.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Butterick: "I’m really pleased that, as a Government, we’re actually prepared to help our parents as well, because they do need help, and we are prepared to act."

acuity.statement: I welcome this report which recommends that the Government should consider restricting social media for under-16s, saying it is time to be a fast follower and follow other countries around the world which have already moved to ban social media for under-16s. There is a global movement, and we should not be left behind.
acuity.explanation: Leary had just put a pointed challenge to the bipartisan harm-reduction consensus, naming a specific bill and a specific failure of its definitions. Wedd's speech instead celebrates the consensus and advances prepared material on her member's bill and the Australian ban. It is squarely on the matter under debate, which keeps it above zero, but it would read identically had Leary said something else entirely, and the one gesture outward ("It's hard enough, as we've heard, for adults to stop") picks up a stray remark rather than any argument. Scored only on engagement — the substance of the case for a ban is not what this attribute measures.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Ingrid Leary argued that the online gambling bill just passed by this House has archaic definitions and expands a competitive gaming market reaching young people on the same devices, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Finally, to the young people themselves, I believe that we need to have a little bit of faith in our youth sometimes. They are actually smart and they understand the potential harm online, and they have the resilience to navigate those challenges.
acuity.explanation: Cheung's trust-the-young-people point sits in tension with Wedd's case for a statutory ban built on children's vulnerability, so there is a gesture at the live question in the debate. But he never engages her argument: he does not dispute the Australian evidence she cited, the vulnerability premise, or the guardrails analogy, and the passage is delivered as the fourth item in a prepared walk-through of the report's themes. A gesture at the debate without engaging any part of the preceding argument sits at the top of the unpointable band, not at a half.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Catherine Wedd argued that a legislated social media age for under-16s is needed because children are more vulnerable than adults to addictive design, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: And yet I’m addicted to my phone. I think if all politicians across the House here were to be quite honest, we would probably—like, you’re waiting somewhere; there’s no such thing as waiting without looking at your phone, whether it’s at the doctor’s or even the supermarket, when you’re waiting at the checkout. That is by design.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the specific strand of the immediately preceding speech — that the pull of the phone is designed, not accidental — and extends it from Nimon's parenting anecdote to the whole House, including herself. Partial rather than full engagement: she develops one thread of Nimon's argument and then moves to her own prepared material on the children's monitoring group and the Greens' position, without taking up Nimon's call for empowered regulators.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Katie Nimon: "The world wants me to think it's a toy so that I play with it all the time, so it makes me more accessible, and they make it look fun and all colourful" — the claim that the device is deliberately engineered to feel like a toy.

acuity.statement: After all, we accept common-sense protections around risks for children in the physical world: think about things like how we require seat belts in cars, we fence swimming pools, and we regulate harmful products like alcohol. The online environment should not be exempt from the same common-sense thinking simply because it is digital.
acuity.explanation: The speech is squarely on the matter under debate and endorses the under-16 restriction Davidson had just argued against, but it engages no part of her reasoning — neither the punishment framing nor the privacy/age-verification objection. The seat belts and pool fencing analogy is prepared material that would read identically whatever the previous speaker had said; it asserts the opposite conclusion rather than contesting her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Marama Davidson argued immediately before that an under-16 ban "is punishing young people for a platform that should instead be held accountable" and would "require, in effect, a breaching of privacy", and this statement does not take either objection up.

acuity.statement: The report recommends an independent regulator so that it’s safer and social media companies could be held responsible for the harm that they cause. These are really important recommendations that need serious consideration. All of them should be seriously considered, and we shouldn’t be looking at simply an age limit.
acuity.explanation: Disputes the direction the immediately preceding speaker had just backed, arguing the age limit should not be the answer and naming the regulator recommendation as the alternative; she also takes up his reference to The Worst Children's Library with her own account of it. Not a full 1.0 because she does not engage McCallum's actual case for age restrictions (the physical-world analogy or the parental-empowerment finding) — she counters the conclusion and otherwise delivers her own committee material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "I would like to acknowledge my colleague Catherine Wedd and the work she has done in this space through her member's bill on restricting social media for under-16-year-olds" — his endorsement of an age restriction as the headline response.

acuity.statement: And yes, as has been mentioned across the House, adults are not immune to that either. As other members have said, they’re addicted to social media, well, I admit that I have suffered that addiction, as well.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of the earlier turns — the cross-House admission of adult addiction — and folds it into her own account, which shows she was listening. But it is a concession in passing rather than engagement: the substance of her speech is prepared material on algorithmic amplification and transparency that does not respond to the arguments immediately before her, including Prime's case against an age-limit-only approach.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Marama Davidson: "I don’t even know how to use that chat PG, CP—chat thingy. And yet I’m addicted to my phone." — the earlier admission that the addiction reaches adults and politicians too.

acuity.statement: One of the things I did last year was—and the Hon Willow-Jean Prime has just talked about it: we bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way.
acuity.explanation: Picks up a specific point from an earlier speaker in the debate and supplies information it left open — who brought the exhibit to Parliament and why it was done cross-party — so the passage would have to change if that account had not been given. It falls short of a full score because it adds adjacent fact rather than engaging an argument, and nothing in it responds to Weenink's immediately preceding case on algorithmic transparency.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: "I want to acknowledge those who put this library together and who also brought it to Parliament and hope that many of you had the opportunity to see it."

acuity.statement: I want to congratulate the Governance and Administration Committee for this piece of work: 23 Acts—it’s an omnibus bill—10 minor changes to the Acts, and unanimous agreement in select committee for all of those changes. So with that sort of support from across the House, we should keep this moving.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's preceding turn made two substantive points — that the FENZ funding model itself may be unsustainable, and that serious out-of-scope issues raised in submissions (combat sports, the HART Act tissue case) must be carried forward. Reti takes up neither. His speech is on the matter under debate but is wholly prepared commendation: it would read word-for-word the same whatever Davidson had argued, so it sits in the unresponsive band with a gesture at the debate (the unanimity of the committee).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the question that should be asked is whether the current way that FENZ is funded is actually sustainable" — Mike Davidson (who also argued out-of-scope submissions must be progressed, not left on paper)

acuity.statement: It is largely technical, and as Mike Davidson said, 23 Acts are affected, but there are some issues which are not entirely technical, and there’s also—I think this is good work by the select committee, because we’ve identified a number of areas where, in fact, we were outside of the scope of the bill, but we’ve said that, actually, more work needs to be done on those.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's central worry was that matters ruled out of scope are noted and then dropped. Foster takes that exact strand up, accepts the framing that the bill is largely technical but disputes that it is only technical, and answers the worry directly with what the committee did about the out-of-scope items — then goes on to work through combat sports (Davidson's own example), the HART Act and the Public Records Act exemption. Delete Davidson's turn and this passage would have to change, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 only because he does not engage Davidson's second argument, on whether the FENZ levy model is sustainable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "It’s a shame if it just stops there on a piece of paper to say, “Oh, well, that’s out of scope.”" — Mike Davidson

acuity.statement: As much as I enjoyed the member’s speech, I will make mine very short. The bill is a modernisation bill. It is bringing us to a digitalised driver’s licence, which I look forward to. I commend this bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Garcia follows a substantive speech from Rosewarne covering digital licences, hard-copy licences for overseas travel, and new enforcement powers, and engages none of it. The nod to "the member's speech" is a courtesy, not engagement — the remainder would read identically whatever Rosewarne had said, though it is at least on the bill under debate, so it sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Rosewarne: "Going to the electronic drivers’ licences is very good for security, but, bear in mind, the hard-copy drivers’ licences might still be very important if you’re travelling overseas." Garcia gestures at Rosewarne's speech but takes up no part of it.

acuity.statement: Labour supports this bill as it’s a set of technical but meaningful improvements that modernise our transport laws and reduce inefficiencies across the system. This is a practical piece of legislation that closes regulatory gaps, strengthens enforcement, and brings New Zealand into better alignment with international transport and labour standards.
acuity.explanation: Two members had already spoken on the bill, including Rosewarne's point about hard-copy licences being retained for overseas use — which Dansey later covers independently without acknowledging he raised it. The speech opens as prepared material on the right subject, with no gesture at anything said before it, so it is on-topic and unresponsive. (Its quality as a contribution is a separate question from responsiveness.)
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paulo Garcia said "The bill is a modernisation bill" and Dan Rosewarne argued hard-copy licences remain necessary for overseas travel; this statement takes up neither, opening prepared material instead.

acuity.statement: Planes, trains, and automobiles—it’s a great bill. It’s taking the licences of old, as Dan Rosewarne talked about and which I remember, to become a new one, and now we have the optionality of it being digital. I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Hamilton gestures at the debate by naming Rosewarne's old-licences material and agreeing with it, which is a reference rather than engagement — nothing is done with the point. More tellingly, the immediately preceding speaker argued the bill is "a small step" that fails on affordability, emissions and public transport, and even named Hamilton as a supporter of trains; he answers only with congratulations on her first ten-minute call and leaves the critique untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dan Rosewarne: "The bill also covers the old drivers’ licences—and we all remember the old ones." Hamilton names the point but only restates it.

acuity.statement: It was great to hear the submissions on this bill in the glorious Governance and Administration Committee. There’s a lot of bits I’d like to touch on. There are some good changes I think the committee made, like the change to the Boxing and Wrestling Act, delaying that date so that there is time for regulations to be brought in.
acuity.explanation: Costley picks up the one change Belich had just acknowledged (the Boxing and Wrestling Act delay) and adds the reason for it — time for regulations — and later glances at her HART Act point with "we had some heartfelt examples for that". But he engages neither of her actual arguments (that the embryo-storage provisions are out of date, and that the fix was ruled out of scope), and the bulk of the turn moves to his own prepared material on the Public Records Act overseas exemption, which she never raised. That is one strand taken up and then a return to prepared content: a partial engagement, not a rebuttal or a correction.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I just wanted to acknowledge the quick change on the Boxing and Wrestling Act—that we did get an extension for that too" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: This bill is amending 23 different Acts. It’s time we got this through, just like the changes that the previous speaker, Jan Tinetti, spoke about—particularly in the lottery space. I’m not going to hold it up any further. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows Tinetti's substantive turn and gestures at it, naming her and the lottery changes she spent much of her speech on. But it engages no part of her content — not her argument that the omnibus received adequate scrutiny, not the research link she cited between youth Lotto purchase and later gambling harm, not the drafting change from "an instant game" to "a New Zealand lottery". A bare reference plus a commendation; substituting a different speech on the same bill would not have changed a word of it beyond the name. Sits in the 0.1–0.3 band, at 0.3 because there is a genuine gesture at the debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the amendments to the purchasing of Lotto tickets" — Jan Tinetti

acuity.statement: As other speakers from our Labour side of the House have attested, this is a bill that we do support. I didn’t have the opportunity to be there through the select committee process, but it’s been great to hear from those who were on the Governance and Administration Committee about the submissions that stuck out for them, but also the specific points that they wanted to address.
acuity.explanation: Eligible: two substantive turns by other members (Tinetti, Rutherford) precede it. But the acknowledgment is content-free — it names no submission, no argument and no point made by anyone, and the prepared material that follows (the $4.2 billion gambling cost, the 1993 Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act, information sharing with international law enforcement) is indifferent to what was said before it. Had Tinetti argued the opposite about the select committee's scrutiny, this speech reads identically. Scored low for unresponsiveness only; the quality of his own reasoning and the precision of his figures are other attributes' business.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Jan Tinetti argued at length that the departmental report shows the omnibus "went under" a high level of scrutiny, and this statement does not take that up — it only notes generically that colleagues spoke about submissions

acuity.statement: The first is the democracy angle of things, and one of our serious concerns is that this bill—and consistent with how this Government has gone on with their treatment of submissions—has basically just ignored the public feedback.

I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Twyford's immediately preceding turn made a specific argument: that a first reading cannot establish whether the bill balances innovation against environmental and public-health risk, and that select committee scrutiny with expert evidence is what must test the proponents' claims. They’re happy to trot out a short, succinct comms line, which I’ve heard several times before, but they don’t want to talk about how we get the balance between quality and price right, and how we progress a bill like this so that we can ensure that we are managing the risks but also getting the opportunities that we need in New Zealand for a vital sector of our economy.
acuity.explanation: Davidson takes up the strand of Kirkpatrick's preceding turn — the barrier-reduction/competitiveness case — accepts its premise that the bill is about the competitive edge, and disputes it as incomplete, naming the brevity and sloganeering of the speech he just heard and the specific gap he says it left (how the balance between risk and opportunity is actually struck). Partial engagement: the critique is pointable and would be invalid had Kirkpatrick made a detailed case instead, but it answers the topic and the manner of her contribution rather than the content of a specific claim, and the bulk of what follows is prepared.

acuity.responding_to: Dana Kirkpatrick: "We are about reducing unnecessary barriers, in this Government. We want to get Government out of the way so our country can grow our productive sector, increase the value of our exports, and get ahead."
