acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: “Why don’t they go and prune kiwifruit?”

acuity.statement: When it comes to the welfare changes, once again we have a Government that refuses to acknowledge that under no Government over the past hundred-plus years has there been enough jobs for every unemployed person out there.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the strand of the preceding Labour speech that the jobs do not exist and generalises it into a structural claim, then issues a testable challenge to the Minister. It engages the topic and one strand of the prior argument rather than any specific claim in it, and the rest of the contribution is prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: “when the member knows those jobs do not exist”

acuity.statement: Listening to that previous speech, clearly it shows that they don’t respect taxpayers’ contributions, that people work really, really hard to make in the form of tax.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speech and then pivots immediately to prepared framing about taxpayers; none of the content of that speech (jobs availability, the 68 percent figure, the officials' advice) is engaged. A mere reference, not a response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: “this Government’s priorities are to punch down on those who need our support” — the content of the speech is not taken up

acuity.statement: I hear members on the other side, the Opposition, saying that this is a very harsh approach, and I would say to these members that a policy should not be judged by how much we are spending but it should be judged on the basis of how targeted it is.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Opposition's characterisation of the bill as harsh and answers it with a competing criterion for judging the policy. It engages the thrust of the preceding criticisms rather than any particular figure or claim within them.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: “The changes in this bill will leave thousands of families worse off and, potentially, in hardship”

acuity.statement: As the Minister on my right here correctly said during another speech, those opportunities, especially in our primary industries and our orchards—there are an abundance of jobs there and opportunities.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the central factual premise of the two preceding Opposition speeches — that the jobs do not exist — but does so by citing the Minister rather than by engaging the evidence offered against it (the RNZ reporting, the fifteen advertised jobs). Partial engagement with the specific claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Willow-Jean Prime: “when the member knows those jobs do not exist”

acuity.statement: Introducing a parental assistance test for 16- to 19-year-olds seeking jobseeker support assumes that all rangatahi have parents who can support them, that every home is safe, and that every whānau has spare money.
acuity.explanation: Attacks the premise of the case Parmar and Arbuckle had just made for the parental assistance test — that family support is there to be drawn on — by naming the assumptions it rests on. It engages their reasoning rather than merely restating opposition to the bill, though it does not take up their specific carve-out for families who cannot support a young person.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Parmjeet Parmar: “People should not expect that welfare should support them when they have the support available from their family.”

acuity.statement: What I think that the Opposition has forgotten in debating this bill is that there’s a thing called the student allowance and there’s a thing called training and there is a thing called responsibility and accountability.
acuity.explanation: Answers the general Opposition contention that young people are being left without support by pointing to alternative supports, which is on the argument's topic, but leaves the specific points just made by Kaipara — unsafe homes, parents on benefits, the repeal of fees-free — untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Oriini Kaipara: “If this Government truly wanted more rangatahi in education, then why repeal fees-free?”

acuity.statement: I just remember, when there was the last election on, how much talk there was of how people could expect support from a National Government: they were going to get a better life.
acuity.explanation: Follows Kirkpatrick's claim that the Government is here to help with a gesture at National's election promises, but engages none of the substance she offered — the student allowance, the minimum-wage earnings figure, training. A glance at the preceding turn before turning to prepared material on the median income.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Dana Kirkpatrick: “We are here to help but we want young people to aspire to work or training” — the student allowance and earnings points are not taken up

acuity.statement: As we heard from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb, the standard period is six months, but it allows for that minimum four, which means we can open the submissions and, normally, proportionally the submissions will be open for four weeks, as opposed to what we’re seeing currently with three weeks.
acuity.explanation: Takes the six-month default that Webb had just argued for and does something concrete with it: uses it as the benchmark against which his own amendment (four months, 20 September) is calibrated, and derives a consequence — a four-week rather than three-week submission period. It is a partial engagement rather than a full one: Xu-Nan opens by saying he wants to raise what his colleagues 'haven’t quite touched on', and most of his speech is independent procedural material on sitting weeks, scrutiny week and Standing Orders 193/195/196 that would have been delivered whatever Webb had said. But the amendment itself is anchored in Webb's premise, so the speech would have to change if the preceding argument had been different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: 'there is a reason why six months is the default period and why many times there’s a request for extensions of time on that six months'

acuity.statement: I agree with the comments that were made by the member, Lawrence Xu-Nan, about the—while not ideal—reduction from the default six months down to his proposed amendment four months. If we can’t convince the Government to go with the default six months, then we would support the member’s amendment to at least extend it out to four months for all the reasons that he gave.
acuity.explanation: Engages the specific proposal just put — Xu-Nan's amendment substituting 20 September for 20 August — accepts his characterisation of it as a non-ideal fallback, states a conditional position on it, and then supplies additional reasons in support (the thin consultation in the regulatory impact statement, the stakeholders who would need to divert capacity to submit). This is more than a mere reference or polite agreement: she adopts his reasoning and extends it, so the speech is clearly shaped by what preceded it. Short of 1.0 because she does not test or dispute any strand of his procedural argument, and the bulk of her contribution is her own stakeholder-by-stakeholder case rather than work on his.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'The reason I proposed 20 September 2026 is it allows for that minimum four-month select committee period.'

acuity.statement: First of all, she made the argument that because this was well signalled in advance, it justifies having a three-month report-back date, and I don’t think that actually stacks up.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific justification Upston had just offered — that the measure was well-signalled in Budget 2025 so the compressed report-back is acceptable — names it as an argument and disputes its logic directly, then develops the counter (if it was signalled early, the bill could have been introduced early enough for proper scrutiny). The speech would be different had Upston given a different reason.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "This was well-signalled. It was in Budget 2025, and so young people and their families have had a long time to get used to this expectation."

acuity.statement: Again, I don’t think this goes against the idea that working families are working hard or otherwise; this speaks to the fact that because working families are working so hard, we’re actually restricting their ability to constructively engage on this.
acuity.explanation: Engages McCallum's interjected claim that extended hours and urgency are simply 'working hard' by accepting the premise about hard work and turning it into the opposite conclusion — that long working hours are precisely why compressed submission slots exclude people. Directly shaped by what was said from across the House rather than merely naming the interjector.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Grant McCallum: "Working hard." (and earlier "It’s called working hard.")

acuity.statement: The Minister simply said this is urgent, which I must say is barely an excuse. It’s usual for a Minister to give somewhat more substantive reasons, so I think it’s entirely appropriate that we do kind of interrogate exactly what those reasons are.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the actual justification Upston gave for the truncated report-back — urgency — and attacks it as insufficient, inviting a government member to supply more. The remark depends on what Upston said; a different justification from her would require a different opening.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "We want more for young people; it is urgent."

acuity.statement: As the member Ricardo Menéndez March pointed out, we’ve got Budget urgency coming up, we’ve got extended sittings, so when you think of the next step, which is that initial briefing—now, first of all, the first thing to note is that officials now have less time to prepare that initial briefing.
acuity.explanation: Adopts the preceding speaker's point about Budget week and extended sitting hours and draws out a further consequence he had not made — that officials' time to prepare the initial briefing is also compressed. That is engagement that builds on the content of the prior turn rather than a mere citation of it, though it extends rather than contests the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "in those three months we’ve got scrutiny week and we’ve got Budget week"

acuity.statement: So this is quite a substantive argument around this amendment, because the issue is, really, where is that line? The history of abuse and the severity of it is something that the Minister in the chair, Erica Stanford, has already made a line call about, with regard to torture. So where’s that line, and should it be something that an intelligent person takes into account rather than it’s either in or it’s completely out?
acuity.explanation: White follows a substantive turn by Prime about consultation and the select committee timetable, but engages none of it; she opens a fresh line on where the severity threshold in clause 20 should sit. It is squarely on the bill under debate and she later picks up one of Prime's amendments, so this is prepared material on the right subject rather than a non-sequitur — but her speech would read the same whatever Prime had just argued.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Willow-Jean Prime argued the consultation was confined to Government departments and that a truncated three-month select committee process is unfair, and this statement does not take that up — White moves to the substance of clause 20 and later to Prime's separate clause 21A amendment.

acuity.statement: The nature of the redress officer’s decision means that a judicial review is a more appropriate form of challenge than an appeal. Again, coming back to this matter of fact, an appeal is suitable when the decision involves making a finding of fact and that in the application of the law to the facts as found on appeal, a decision can be found to be right or wrong in fact or law. A judicial review is more appropriate for evaluating decisions such as those that are to be made by a redress officer where the issue is about the reasonableness of the decision rather than the weight that it is right or wrong.
acuity.explanation: Stanford takes the specific amendment White pressed her on and gives the reason for declining it: that the redress officer's decision turns on reasonableness rather than findings of fact, which makes judicial review the fitted remedy and an appeal the wrong one. She also answers White's clause 20 point about where the severity line sits. The speech is shaped by what White asked and would have had to change had White raised a different objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "So can I have an answer to whether the Minister is prepared to accept that amendment by the Hon Willow-Jean Prime?" — Helen White, who argued that clause 21A's right of appeal to the District Court "seems to me to be quite relevant in terms of allowing an appeal".

acuity.statement: At risk of repeating myself, we’ve already been over this part and explained the fact that these changes were made in the Social Services and Community Committee. Because of the feedback that was given, the select committee made these changes in order to protect the individual—the privacy of the people who are going through the system. As I’ve already said, there will only be a very, very, very small number of people who will go through this process, and if you start talking about the reasons for your decisions, they are potentially going to be identifiable.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific strand Carter pressed — why the reporting clause does not require the reasons behind individual redress decisions — and supplies a substantive counter-rationale (identifiability of a very small applicant cohort, and the select committee's privacy-versus-information balance). The speech would have been different had Carter raised a different objection. It falls short of 1.0 because it does not engage her distinct question about what advice was given on public confidence beyond transparency, instead closing with "We're traversing old ground."
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "that doesn’t really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied"

acuity.statement: I’m sure the Minister will appreciate the need for flexibility around whether submissions are written or sometimes could be oral submissions. I’m keen to understand her expectation of how that will be delivered and the duty of care on the redress officer to ensure that the format of the submissions are the most appropriate to determine a fair—to achieve justice, really.
acuity.explanation: Eligible (substantive turns by Carter and Stanford precede it in the same committee-stage debate on the same bill), but it engages no part of the preceding exchange about clause 22 reporting and privacy. It is a self-contained prepared question on a different clause, and would read identically whatever Stanford had just said. Scored 0.2 rather than 0.0 because it is squarely on the bill under consideration and invites a ministerial response.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford explained that the select committee removed much of the reporting detail to protect applicants' privacy because reasons for decisions could identify a very small cohort, and this statement does not take that up — it opens a fresh line on clause 20C(1)(b) and subclause (2).

acuity.statement: In terms of the tabled amendment, we won’t be supporting it. All statutory powers have to be consistent with the purpose of the Act, so there is no need to add this amendment.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the actual content of Andersen's amendment — which sought to remove the requirement that the Secretary's rules be consistent with the Act — and answers it with a reason (statutory powers must already be consistent with the Act's purpose, so the clause is redundant). It engages the amendment squarely, though it leaves the broader 'why is top-down better' question untouched, so not a full 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "Removing the part that requires that these rules must be consistent with this Act would allow the Secretary for Education to create rules that take into account specific circumstances."

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister just mentioned before in terms of the ideas to get students to school, which I agree with. I completely agree, but when we’re looking at this section, basically, only the secretary is able to allow for the exclusion of a student under the age of 16, under section 82, but there is nothing in section 82 that specifies that the secretary must first be satisfied that the board of a State school or a sponsor has excluded a student aged under 16 years after all possible intervention under section 81 has been exhausted.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's stated objective of getting students into school, concedes it, and turns it into a specific pressure point on section 82 — so one strand of the preceding turn is genuinely engaged. But the bulk is prepared amendment material he says he intended to move to regardless, so partial rather than full engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "It is this Government’s intention to make sure that young people are turning up to school so that they can learn and be at Curriculum and live the life that they deserve."

acuity.statement: In relation to the question about work experience and the member’s tabled amendment, this is a longstanding section of the Act. It’s not something we’ve looked at. It gets into employment law, so we’re not accepting the amendment.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question asked — why a student on work experience cannot be paid and why the 'entitle'/'require' amendment is refused — and gives the reason (longstanding provision, cuts into employment law). The reply exists only because of the question just put; it would be different had he asked something else. Short of 1.0 because it does not engage the substance of why the provision reads as it does.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "I want to know the overall rationale for why, if a student is getting work experience, they cannot be paid."

acuity.statement: As Lawrence Xu-Nan has already stated, this part of the bill allows the Minister herself to determine what students are to be taught and how they are to be assessed. That goes quite far beyond the current Act and, essentially, allows the Minister to give directions.
acuity.explanation: Directly contradicts the claim the Minister had just made — that ministerial curriculum power has existed since 1989 and 'nothing is changing' — by asserting the clause goes beyond the current Act. That is engagement with the specific assertion, but she offers nothing against the 1989 point itself and then proceeds into her prepared case on the four amendments, so it sits mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "there has always been in the Education Act—for a very long time; since 1989, I think—the ability of the Minister to issue curriculum statements. That’s not changing."

acuity.statement: Firstly, the member is 100 percent, entirely wrong. It has always been, since 1989, the ability of the Minister to set and revoke and amend curriculum statements. Nothing is changing, and it was exactly the same, in fact, when the previous Minister of Education, Minister Chris Hipkins, gazetted the new history curriculum in exactly the same manner.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific factual claim just made — that clause 9 goes beyond the current Act in giving the Minister power over curriculum — and corrects it with a dated counter-claim plus a concrete precedent from the previous Minister. The speech could not have been delivered against a different preceding argument. Scored on engagement only; whether the correction is true is a veracity matter, and the tone is a civility matter.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "That goes quite far beyond the current Act and, essentially, allows the Minister to give directions."

acuity.statement: I think, as part of the review process, what’s really missing—like the previous speaker Hon Ginny Andersen has said—is when the secretary reviews the national Curriculum, nothing in here states that they actually need to consult with the sector or take the experience of the sector on board.
acuity.explanation: Still within the same committee debate, so eligible, but it engages no part of the exchange immediately before it — the Minister's 1989 rebuttal and her complaint about personal remarks go entirely untaken-up. The nod to Andersen is a bare name-reference to an earlier theme, not engagement with a claim, and the material on Amendment Paper 617 would have read identically whatever had just been said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford rebutted Ginny Andersen's claim about ministerial curriculum powers, saying "It has always been, since 1989, the ability of the Minister to set and revoke and amend curriculum statements", and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Just in relation to the first part of that contribution around schools of serious concern: it is a judgment call by the chief review officer. They are they education expert, and I expect it to be focused on educational quality, and all of the things that the member mentioned in her contribution will be taken into account. I would make the point that the Education Review Office (ERO) already do this. They already label schools with “of serious concern”.
acuity.explanation: Stanford's turn directly takes up the preceding speech: Andersen asked what would trigger the 'serious concern' designation (attendance, NCEA results, staffing, finances) and argued the bill leaves it undefined and subjective. Stanford names who makes the call (the chief review officer), says the criteria Andersen listed will be taken into account, and disputes the novelty of the power by pointing out ERO already applies the label — a rebuttal of the premise rather than a pivot. She then goes on to engage Andersen's equity strand too, conceding that schools of serious concern are often in impoverished communities but drawing the opposite conclusion. Short of 1.0 only because she never addresses Andersen's specific request about the charter-school conversion amendments and section 212G(1). The speech would have had to be different had Andersen argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "I want to know from the Minister, will attendance issues trigger an intervention?"

acuity.statement: The other point I would like to make before getting on to my tabled amendments is that in Amendment Paper 583, which was tabled yesterday, there are a number of changes there that did not go through select committee.
acuity.explanation: The immediately preceding substantive turn was Stanford's argument that section 127 and the NZSPA provisions already place a Treaty duty on school boards mirroring the Crown's. Andersen takes up no part of that reasoning — she neither contests the reading of section 127 nor the claim that the duty sits with the Minister and the Crown — and instead opens new ground on the process defect in Amendment Paper 583 before moving to her own amendments. The material is squarely about the bill under consideration, so it is not wholly unresponsive to the debate, but this sentence would read identically whatever Stanford had just argued, which places it in the prepared-material band rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Erica Stanford spoke about the duties section 127 places on school boards to support the Crown's Treaty of Waitangi responsibilities, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: I want to start with clause 20. I understand some of the rationale from the Associate Minister regarding the ability to have multi-school contracts, but what I’m unclear with in this section is what material, then, does the authorisation board need to be able to determine that a particular sponsor is able to operate a multi-school contract in Aotearoa New Zealand, to know that they’re going to be successful, before approving one? Surely, wouldn’t it be better to allow a sponsor to start one school and wait for a little while to make sure it is successful before opening the path to have multiple schools?
acuity.explanation: Seymour's immediately preceding turn argued that charter schools' accountability lies in the loss of contract and that bureaucratic controls and a vote back to State status are unnecessary. Xu-Nan takes up none of that reasoning; he announces he is going back to sections he skipped and works through his own prepared questions on clauses 20, 22 and 34. The gesture at 'some of the rationale from the Associate Minister' on multi-school contracts refers to earlier material, not to the argument just made, so this sits in the on-topic-but-unengaged band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: David Seymour argued that the loss of a charter school's contract is itself 'a very big accountability' and that allowing schools to 'flip-flop back and forth' adds nothing, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: The idea that perhaps an operator of a multi-school charter would first have to operate one school—they are actually different activities. If they’re capable of operating one school, that is something that we test with the usual test: do they have community support, do they have a good educational plan, do they have a financially viable plan, do they have educational knowledge, do they have good people on their team? That’s the criteria for operating a school. There are separate criteria for having a multi-school charter, and if you have passed one test, you still have to pass the other.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific proposal just put by Xu-Nan — that a sponsor should have to run one school successfully before being allowed a multi-school contract — and rebuts its reasoning directly, by distinguishing the two authorisation tests and drawing out why staggering them would be pointless. The speech would have to be different if Xu-Nan had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Surely, wouldn’t it be better to allow a sponsor to start one school and wait for a little while to make sure it is successful before opening the path to have multiple schools?" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Just to quickly round out the Debbie Francis report, it was not a report that was commissioned by the Government; it was commissioned by the Teaching Council governance board themselves, in light of protected disclosures and what they saw and the concerns that they had in the operations of the Teaching Council.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific thing Xu-Nan asked — how the Debbie Francis report came to be — by supplying who commissioned it and why, which also bears on his complaint about terms of reference. Short of 1.0 because it leaves the methodology and 'independent review' strands of his question untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I want to just check in terms of, I guess, the process of how that report came to be." — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: Yes, and Chlöe Swarbrick says they were on the roof two weeks ago—that is absolutely true. But they were down and they were safe. They weren’t up there for days, creating a media spectacle and getting bribed with KFC. It also happens far less frequently because of the upgrades to security that the Minister has made.
acuity.explanation: Swarbrick interjects a specific factual counter-example against Seymour's claim that Oranga Tamariki rooftop incidents have been dealt with. He takes up that exact claim, concedes it is true, then disputes what follows from it (duration, frequency, security upgrades). The reply would be different word-for-word had she said anything else, which is the deciding test. Scored on engagement only — the quality of the inference and the jibe at her belong to other attributes.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "They were on the roof two weeks ago." — Chlöe Swarbrick

acuity.statement: Mr Speaker, I am charged up because earlier this week, I was at the Electrify Queenstown conference, where we heard the ambition, we heard the hunger, we heard the enthusiasm to power our nation on renewable electrons.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Hipkins in the same debate, but opens with prepared material on an unrelated subject — a renewable-energy conference and electrification. Nothing in the speech turns on what Hipkins argued about public service job cuts; it would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before and whatever they had said. There is a faint sense it belongs to the same wide-ranging debate, so not a flat 0.0, but no strand of the preceding argument is engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Chris Hipkins spoke at length about public sector headcount reductions and the specific agencies whose staff would be cut ("A quarter of all of the target agency staff will have to be cut in order to meet the target that the Government have set"), and this statement does not take any part of it up.

acuity.statement: Well, of course Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori oppose moves to make the public sector more efficient and to get value for taxpayers’ money. They think the public purse is Hermione Granger’s bag, a bottomless fund—you just keep pulling what you need out of it.
acuity.explanation: The preceding substantive turn was Scott Willis's attack on the Government's energy record — no energy strategy, cancelled battery project, 65,000 more households unable to keep warm. Brown takes up none of it, not even the topic, and opens on public-sector efficiency instead. There is a bare gesture at the opposition parties as a bloc, which names targets rather than engaging any claim, so this sits at the bottom of the unresponsive band; it reads as prepared material that would have been delivered word-for-word whatever Willis had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "everyone has said that we need a national energy strategy" — Scott Willis (the preceding turn, on the refusal of a national energy strategy, fuel poverty and energy hardship statistics)

acuity.statement: Wow! You know they’re in trouble when they spend four out of their five minutes in the general debate talking about the Labour Party. I just want to thank the honourable member Simeon Brown because, in this day and age, it’s very difficult to communicate policy announcements, given all of the platforms that people listen to, but he did a fantastic job of selling and re-announcing our three free GP visits.
acuity.explanation: This is squarely aimed at the turn just delivered and names the specific policy Brown attacked, but it does nothing with the content of the attack: it answers neither the $300,000-earner point nor the claim that the policy amounts to a nationwide triage service. Quoting an opponent's subject back in order to score a meta-point about how much of his speech was about Labour is a reference, not an engagement, so it belongs in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Let’s talk about their three free doctor visits, which, of course, Mr Hipkins is travelling up and down the country trying to explain to New Zealanders why people earning over $300,000 a year need a free doctors visit." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: We have heard senior Ministers in this House and through the public talking about job losses, dismissing the importance, the urgency, and the stress that that causes. We had Minister Bishop in the House yesterday, answering questions and saying that this is what happens—you lose jobs, and you go and get another job—as if the jobs are just there to be picked up.
acuity.explanation: This takes up one real strand of Brown's argument — the "no one likes job losses, but" framing — and contests it directly, arguing that the dismissal assumes other jobs exist. It is partial engagement: she leaves his actual figures (47,250 to 65,700, front-line versus administrative growth) untouched and widens the target to ministers generally, including Bishop and Willis, rather than the speaker she followed, then returns to prepared material about her own 1990s experience.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Of course, no one likes job losses, but here are some home truths: under Labour, the number of public servants increased from 47,250 to 65,700." — Simeon Brown

acuity.statement: It’s also been mentioned that we’re doing changes to the Public Service. Yes, there is concern around the number of public servants who over the next few years won’t be further employed, because we do need to get the numbers down. But what we don’t hear about quite so much from the other side is that during the six years when Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins were running the country, they increased the number by around 19,000.
acuity.explanation: Goldsmith concedes the point Sepuloni had just pressed — that there is real concern about public servants losing work — and then answers it with a counter-figure, the roughly 19,000 added under the previous Government. That is genuine engagement with one strand of her argument. It is half-marks rather than full because it answers the scale of the headcount rather than her actual claim about how the losses are being treated, and because the surrounding speech is prepared law-and-order material that would have been identical whoever preceded him.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’ve had Nicola Willis in the media, talking about the 8,700 jobs that she intends to cut from the public sector almost gleefully" — Carmel Sepuloni

acuity.statement: In 1984, the incoming Labour and Roger Douglas Government launched a neoliberal experiment on New Zealand, which was continued by Ruth Richardson in 1990. This was just after the Bob Hawke - Keating Government got to Government in Australia and began the incremental change.
acuity.explanation: The turn immediately before it made several arguable claims, including a specific case against a capital gains tax drawn from Australia. Peters engages none of them and instead delivers a prepared case for buying back the BNZ, arguing against critics outside the House rather than the member he follows. The speech would be word-for-word identical whoever had spoken before and could have been given in a different debate on a different day, which is the definition of the floor of this scale.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Paul Goldsmith spoke about reducing victims of crime, gang membership, stalking legislation, name suppression, public-sector headcount and a capital gains tax, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m going to take my five minutes of general debate time not to talk about the Labour Party, because I just sort of think that actually it’s a really good opportunity to talk about ACT’s achievements.
acuity.explanation: McKee follows a substantive Labour turn on Budget-driven public service redundancies and expressly declines to engage any part of it, pivoting to a prepared recital of ACT's law-and-order record. The reference to "the Labour Party" is a naming, not an engagement; later lines ("We have abolished Labour's prisoner reduction targets", "We reject the soft-on-crime ideology of the Opposition") engage nothing Belich said. The speech is at least a contribution to the same general debate and is about matters of government policy, so it sits at the top of the unresponsive band rather than at zero, but there is no strand of the preceding argument taken up.
acuity.subject: speaker

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I think there are a couple of technical questions that we should consider, as well." — Tim Costley, who raised the CCO status of ports, their listed-company structure, commercial sensitivity and the extension to power companies

acuity.statement: That’s why I disagree when the Minister of Finance says that the Rt Hon Winston Peters is very, very confused. I absolutely do not agree with that, because the Rt Hon Winston Peters is very clear what he’s up to.

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "Tell us about the Future Fund."

acuity.statement: We are operating in a world that’s increasingly uncertain, with global instability, a fragile economy, and a persistently high cost of living. In the face of all of these conditions, I would like to draw the public’s attention to a number of facts.

acuity.responding_to: Paulo Garcia: "We are operating in a world that’s increasingly uncertain, with global instability, a fragile economy, and a persistently high cost of living."

acuity.statement: One of the things we’ve heard as part of our ports inquiry is around port charges, how those port charges get applied, and the size of those port charges. acuity.explanation: Luxton's central argument was that ports are competitive traders, not monopolies, and so should not face LGOIMA. The speech would have to change if the preceding turn had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "This is not the sort of thing that a trading company that is competing with other trading companies—being other ports—needs to be accountable to in the same way that a monopoly like a local government organisation must be."

acuity.explanation: Concedes the compliance-burden strand of the preceding turn rather than ignoring it, and supplies his own grounds for it (serial requests, local government experience), while disputing the conclusion by still supporting the bill to select committee. Partial acceptance of the argument just made is genuine engagement, though he does not test Luxton's specific commercial-sensitivity claim.

acuity.responding_to: Cameron Luxton: "This is not a place that needs more compliance. They have enough going on already."

acuity.statement: I think that the bill that my colleague has before the House at the moment just adds further to the issues that are looked at in the committee, so I agree with Mr Foster that this is, I guess, well timed in that it could be considered alongside the work that the committee is doing.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one identifiable strand of the preceding turn — Foster's point that the bill's timing dovetails with the ports inquiry — and endorses it explicitly, so the engagement is pointable. But it is the easiest strand, it engages none of the opposing case put earlier, and the speech then moves to prepared material about the Palmerston North inland port.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "We think it might actually add some value to the ports inquiry, because we’ll be concluding that roughly about the same kind of time."

acuity.statement: This bill speaks to accountability, transparency, and community interests, which are all values we support. I guess the question is whether the bill is the right way to achieve this, or whether it’s maybe too blunt for what’s quite a complex system.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the case Utikere had just put — that the bill is a modest transparency measure that would not burden ports — and concedes the goal while disputing the mechanism, then goes on to name the specific overlap (Port Companies Act 1988, duplicated governance structures) that answers Utikere's claim. It engages the argument's substance rather than merely the topic, though the concession-then-pivot to prepared party reasons keeps it short of a direct rebuttal of Utikere's point about the withholding thresholds.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "This is not about additional work; it’s not about sort of uncovering these mass issues that are arising in port companies; but it is actually about providing a level of transparency and accountability."

acuity.statement: I just want to respond to some of the criticisms brought up by the other side. The first is that any concerns around how this bill will operate, that can be teased out at select committee. That is the purpose of a select committee, and I want to acknowledge New Zealand First for pointing out some of the things they believe need to be addressed at a select committee. That is the role of a select committee; so that’s where this bill needs to go.

The speech would have to be rewritten if the preceding contribution had opposed the bill on different grounds, which is the test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Shane Reti: "whether it’s maybe too blunt for what’s quite a complex system"

acuity.statement: There are certain things that cannot actually be answered, and often you see redacted documents that actually shows that, you know, it protects our privacy or free and frank conversations that Ministers might actually have with the Government officials. acuity.explanation: Picks up the one strand Boyack had just pressed — that the existing withholding grounds under LGOIMA/OIA make the transparency concern manageable — and acknowledges those grounds exist, but then turns it into a general characterisation of the other side's position rather than answering Boyack's point that those same grounds could be written in for ports. acuity.responding_to: Rachel Boyack: "there are reasons, under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act—just like there are under the Official Information Act—to withhold information"

acuity.statement: A couple of speakers have talked about the problem definition, and what I’m asking for, through this bill, is transparency and the ability to look at a possible national port strategy that would have a more complementary strategy for ports within New Zealand. acuity.responding_to: Melissa Lee: "this is supposed to be a solution looking for problem, because I have not heard that side of the House telling us why we actually need to change the Act"

acuity.explanation: Follows Nakhle's sponsor speech and takes up two strands of it: her hope that the bill reaches a select committee (he names which committee and why the Public Finance Act made Finance and Expenditure arguable) and her opening point that the funding is currently lawful, which he restates as it being "scary" that the bill is needed at all. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "hopefully we will be going through a select committee process" — Rima Nakhle (who also opened with "What’s even more shameful... is the fact that this is legal, right now, in New Zealand.")

Partial engagement, then prepared text.

Kaipara engages that premise head-on from a different framework — te reo has no such differentiation, and the whakataukī 'he tangata' 'doesn't say, nor define, a man or a woman' — which is a direct answer to the definitional claim just made. One strand engaged squarely.

acuity.responding_to: Karen Chhour: 'that men and women are biologically different—not socially different, not stereotypically different, but biologically different' — Kaipara answers the claim that man and woman are fixed definable categories.

Partial engagement, so mid-band.

acuity.responding_to: "I don’t want to prolong this debate because this debate does hurt" — Glen Bennett

Partial engagement with the topic rather than with the claim.

acuity.statement: That’s why I will be asking for advisers from the Public Service Commission to see if they can come and give us that perspective. I think it is a useful perspective to consider.

acuity.responding_to: Lemauga Lydia Sosene: "I am interested in just hearing from the public what they think, because it’s one thing to deal with Government agencies; it’s different to deal with people from diverse backgrounds."

Not a full rebuttal of a reasoned case, but the speech plainly would differ had the previous turn not raised it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "There are options available to the Government, and it’s, again, just a little bit peculiar that they haven’t decided to exercise that."

acuity.explanation: Takes the local-government-reform uncertainty raised by the earlier speakers, attaches it to a named clause (the Commissioner must consult Local Government New Zealand), and turns it the other way — from a select-committee issue to be ironed out into a reason to withhold support. Clearly shaped by what preceded it.

acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "The issue that we would have at the moment is just the uncertainty that might present itself as a result of a process that’s currently under way without that particular process being concluded."

We’ll probably do more consultation on doing this than we will on changing the local government boundaries, I might say, as Tangi Utikere has just said. Now, I do note that many councils want change, but they’re a little worried about the rate and the way in which it’s being proposed at the moment.
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand about local government's role and unease, names the member who raised it, and does something with it — contrasts the consultation this bill mandates against the consultation on the reforms themselves. Part engagement, part prepared material on agency boundaries.

acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "There is a little bit of unease around where the role of local government might sit within the context of the member’s bill."

acuity.statement: It’s really clear what the problem is to solve here; the problem definition: it’s Government agencies administratively being able to use different territorial and regional boundaries. That’s the problem we’re trying to solve. It’s really simple.
acuity.explanation: Answers the preceding speaker's central objection on its own chosen ground — Foster's "problem definition" framing — by stating the problem the bill addresses. Directly aimed at the argument just made rather than at its author.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "this to some degree feels like a solution which is looking for a problem"

acuity.statement: I’d make the point that there are many things that come through members’ bills that, for one reason or another, are not Government orders of the day, and that relates to a number of things including the attention that a private member’s bill can bring in a busy legislative agenda, the resources that a private member’s bill can bring, as well. I don’t find this at all unusual that a quality proposition like this should come through as a member’s bill.
acuity.explanation: Rebuts the objection made by two earlier speakers that this should have been done by Ministers rather than by legislation, giving reasons why a member's bill is an appropriate vehicle. The passage exists only because of what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Mike Davidson: "It is a shame that we’re having to use legislation to actually do this when it could have been done without it"

acuity.statement: It is interesting to hear others speaking against it in relation to cost. I would assume—and it would be good to know in select committee and to have that through the member’s submission on this—that the objective in due course would be to reduce cost, and that would be the basis of us supporting this and also supporting the greater alignment of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the cost strand of the opposing speeches and offers a counter-expectation, but engages the topic rather than the specific argument — Foster's claim was about restructuring every agency's organisational form, which is not addressed — and then returns to the party's position.

acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "It is not a cost-free one as I will come to very, very shortly."

acuity.statement: I am unsure, because I never actually got to work out how much what I was working on was going to cost, and I have to take the member’s word that this actually doesn’t really have a financial cost to it.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the cost question the preceding speakers pressed, but nothing is engaged — she declines to examine it and defers to the member. The surrounding speech is prepared, anecdotal material about her own near-identical bill that would read identically whatever had been said before it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Andy Foster: "what is the scale of the problem, and then what is the cost of fixing that problem?"

acuity.statement: A lot of the points have been traversed already by colleagues, in terms of trying to get efficiency for better regional services, and it doesn’t just exist in that part of the North Island; it’s actually even in Auckland, and my colleague just spoke earlier on the difficulties of the various Government agency boundaries and the confusion with local government boundaries.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the preceding speaker's misaligned-boundaries experience and extends its reach to Auckland, which is a real if slight addition. Beyond that it acknowledges the debate generically ("traversed already by colleagues") and moves to prepared support, engaging none of the objections raised against the bill.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Melissa Lee: "sometimes you don’t just deal with one policing district; you’re having to engage with three or four, because the boundary actually means that the police boundary is different to the electorate boundary"

acuity.statement: I think we actually have a responsibility in this House to debate and discuss these issues with respect, with facts, and actually not with rhetoric and create scaremongering or other things that could cause distress.
acuity.explanation: Stephenson follows Carter's substantive first-reading speech in the same debate, so he is eligible. He gestures at what preceded him by characterising the tone of the debate as rhetoric and scaremongering, but he takes up no part of Carter's actual argument — nothing on the absence of consultation, the 13 August submission deadline, captions for select committee hearings, or the pay equity/Uber pattern she alleged. The speech would be essentially unchanged had Carter made a different criticism of the bill, which places it in the 0.1-0.3 band; 0.3 rather than 0.1 because the reference to rhetoric is at least aimed at the preceding contribution.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This Minister has been consistent in targeting disabled people and the systemic erosion of disabled people's rights" — Kahurangi Carter

acuity.statement: Just like you did last night on Jenny Marcroft’s bill?
acuity.explanation: This takes up the specific proposition Stephenson had just advanced — that members owe the House respectful, fact-based debate — and turns it directly on him by citing his own conduct the previous night on a named bill. It is pointed at the content of the claim just made rather than at the topic in general, and it could not have been said after a different preceding remark. Not 1.0 only because it asserts the inconsistency without developing it. Scored for engagement alone; whether the charge is true or courteous is not acuity's question.
acuity.subject: speaker
