acuity.responding_to: "My question to the Minister is: does she have an update on the review that Internal Affairs—oh, sorry, I think it was the Ministry for Culture and Heritage" — Camilla Belich

acuity.statement: Yes, I thank the select committee for their scrutiny of these particular provisions. It’s very important work, and I do believe that the committee have ended up in the right area, and I also support the changes that the select committee has made to the question of whether there’s going to be any form of education for the change. Lotto will be updating their terms and conditions and providing updated information to retailers as well, but I do also just want to caution that it is quite a minor issue, and when talking with Lotto about how many young people are out there buying these products, they didn’t say it was a massive issue.
acuity.explanation: Takes up both of the specific things Belich put to her — whether she is content with the transitional change, and whether retailers will be told — and supplies the concrete answer that Lotto will update terms and conditions and brief retailers. The reply would be different had Belich asked something else; it falls just short of 1.0 because she then moves to her own framing of the issue's scale rather than engaging Belich's point about aligning the commencement date with the draw date.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Camilla Belich: "is there going to be any public education or training or any note that’s sent out to lottery retailers about this change in policy, with terms and conditions updated?"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you, Minister, for your response. I do want to just follow up on, I guess, the divide we created when it comes to looking at instant games versus lottery for under-18s.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of the Minister's answer — the age divide between Lotto product types she had just described — and presses it on instant games, so the engagement is pointable. But it does not contest her claim that the change is a minor alignment issue, and moves on to prepared harm-reduction questions about Instant Kiwi and loot boxes that are not drawn from what she said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Brooke van Velden: "some of Lotto’s products are accessible for anyone of any age and some Lotto products are restricted to those over the age of 18"

acuity.statement: I’m happy to take this contribution. I think I can alleviate the member’s concerns quite quickly. Instant games are already illegal for under-18s. This law change brings everything in line for the twice weekly draws to be also illegal for under-18s, and so to the previous contribution I made, this is simply an alignment issue. Things like Loot and things online are outside the scope of this bill.
acuity.explanation: Corrects the factual premise of the question put to her — that instant games are open to under-18s — and in doing so dissolves the "divide" Xu-Nan posited, then disposes of his second question by placing loot boxes and online products outside the bill's scope. The answer is wholly shaped by what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "will they be able to be purchased by under-18-year-olds? That is my first question."

acuity.statement: So this is very much a functionary outcome of transitioning those powers and oversights from the Commerce Commission to the FMA, and then that includes adding CCCFA to the definition on financial markets legislation. So as far as a catch-all and everything else, this—clause 51—is all about ensuring that the FMA has the tools required to get the job done.
acuity.explanation: Williams asked what he considered in excluding particular people — back-office assurance staff, repossession agents — from the clause 61 definition of those captured. He answers about the breadth of clause 51's FMA coverage and the Commerce Commission transfer, which glances at the question of 'how far the net is cast' but takes up none of the specific categories she said were excluded, and never addresses clause 61 at all. A gesture at the matter under debate rather than engagement with the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: 'Minister, really welcome your assurance on how far you intended to cast the net there.'

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. That is helpful. Moving on to clause 64—I’m at the top of page 35.
acuity.explanation: Acknowledges the Minister's answer as helpful and then proceeds to the next prepared clause without taking up any part of what he said — she does not test whether clause 51's 'catch-all' actually answers her clause 61 point, accept it, or dispute it. A courteous gesture at the exchange, not engagement with its content; the words would be the same whatever he had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: 'this—clause 51—is all about ensuring that the FMA has the tools required to get the job done'

acuity.statement: I suppose if we go back to the guiding principle of the fact that this regime will fall under the auspices of the Financial Markets Authority (FMA)—as will all the wider remit of consumer credit and its oversight—and the FMA, with its expanding remit, will have a renewed energy and focus on these issues. If there are issues—which there are—that continue, particularly in vulnerable communities, the member and the House can take comfort that the FMA will take on this remit and these responsibilities with renewed vigour and with a big mandate.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the strand Williams actually raised — future oversight of mobile traders in vulnerable communities — and answers it with the FMA's expanding remit. But he does not engage her specific point about why the provision singling out mobile traders was removed, nor her evidence that neighbourhood lenders have replaced them. Topic engaged; the specific claim only in part.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "how has he considered the need for regulation like this in the future?" — asked about the removal of clause 51(1)(c) covering mobile traders

acuity.statement: It’s also helpful to hear the Minister’s intention to continue to monitor that with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA), and I have also heard them express their interest in meeting with not only mobile traders but to use their new powers under this Act to be able to take proactive investigations.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's FMA-monitoring answer specifically and adds corroborating information of her own about the FMA's stated intention to use proactive investigation powers, before turning to new prepared material on clause 51(2). Engages one strand of what was just said rather than testing it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "the FMA will take on this remit and these responsibilities with renewed vigour and with a big mandate"

acuity.statement: The primary question was, I think, why this bill doesn’t further improve protections. There are protections already in the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, and, as the member has indicated, the regulation of “buy now, pay later” has only taken effect since September 2024, and so the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) and, eventually, the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) will continue to monitor.
acuity.explanation: Restates the question he takes himself to have been asked and answers it with the existing CCCFA protections and the September 2024 regulation, confirming the October 2022 Cabinet paper she cited. He engages the protections strand but leaves her actual definitional question — whether clause 51(2) should capture buy now, pay later — unaddressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "whether his definition of consumer credit contract go far enough to enable Parliament to have a view on whether that is a consumer credit contract"

acuity.statement: Minister, are you aware that consumer harm following the September 2024 regulation that you’ve roof-rinsed shows that hardship has continued to increase for users of “buy now, pay later”, and the level of consumer protection provided by the September 2024 regulation has been criticised by financial mentors in that it deals with the most significant harm that was caused, but it’s contributing further to consumers facing financial hardship and overcommitment?
acuity.explanation: Takes the exact assurance just given — that the September 2024 regulation has it covered — and turns it against itself with the financial mentors' finding that hardship has risen under that same regulation. The question only exists because of what he said immediately before; substitute a different answer and this intervention would have to change.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "“buy now, pay later” is regulated. It is under watch, and it will continue to be under a close watch"

acuity.statement: Just reflecting on the “buy now, pay later” issues that the member Arena Williams has rightly raised, they are not explicitly mapped out in this piece of legislation. That terminology is not part of this statute, but, as I’ve said, she and the committee can take every assurance that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment—and it’s soon to be the Financial Markets Authority, as well—will continue to monitor their practices very closely.
acuity.explanation: Answers the inclusion question literally — the term is not in the statute — which does engage what she asked. But the two questions she flagged, the affordability exemption and whether he has built a moat around two favoured providers, are passed over for a repeated monitoring assurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "if they were explicitly included in your new clause 51(2) as operators who are offering a consumer credit contract, then we would do away with that unfairness in the system"

acuity.statement: As far as the obligation on lenders, there remain plenty of obligations on lenders around the affordability to the borrower, and they are also supported in the non-binding guidance that is the Responsible Lending Code, but we do not believe that regulations as such should tell lenders how they should meet this obligation in every case.
acuity.explanation: This does take up her affordability-assessment proposal and gives a reason for refusing it — that regulation should not prescribe how lenders meet the obligation. It engages the principle behind her ask without engaging her evidence that the exemption is itself producing the harm.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "“buy now, pay later” providers can choose to be exempt from the obligation to undertake affordability assessments"

acuity.statement: As has been established, mobile traders are subject to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA), and that oversight that took effect about 18 months ago continues. Strengthening up that piece of legislation is not part of this, but, in saying that, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) already has a statutory duty to provide advice on the CCCFA as part of its regulatory stewardship.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the alternative regulatory mechanism she expressly asked him to name — the CCCFA plus MBIE's stewardship duty and its role as statutory monitor of the FMA — which is a direct answer to the lacuna question. It does not reach the non-credit conduct and pricing side of her question about the 2016-17 period.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Is it now a complete lacuna where we have mobile traders who are trading without credit licences and do not have any oversight"

acuity.statement: He said mobile traders are subject to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA). That’s right insofar as they offer credit contracts, but my question is: this provision before it was amended seemed to say that they were still subject to licensing arrangements for their businesses and then they had some supervisor who was responsible for their conduct.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's proposition in part and disputes its scope precisely — that CCCFA coverage only bites where a credit contract is offered, which leaves the licensing and supervision question she asked unanswered. This is the preceding answer taken apart on its own terms.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "mobile traders are subject to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA), and that oversight that took effect about 18 months ago continues"

acuity.statement: Just to reiterate, mobile traders continue to be subject to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act, and they will also be part of the licensing regime of the Financial Markets Authority (FMA), as well, given that they will be treated formally as lenders.
acuity.explanation: Meets the correction she made by adding the licensing point her objection turned on — that mobile traders will fall within the FMA licensing regime as lenders. He leaves her further question about what other services he intends to exempt under new section 389(4A) untouched, and finishes on general assurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "this provision before it was amended seemed to say that they were still subject to licensing arrangements for their businesses"

acuity.statement: Just on the title, this is a piece of legislation from 2003, the principal piece of legislation that has remained with its full title through successive Governments as the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Bill through three major overhauls by successive Governments. The name has always remained the same, and it will continue to. On the commencement, 1 July, as the most effective commencement date, was nominated by the Commerce Commission and the Financial Markets Authority as the most pragmatic commencement date—1 July 2026. Let's get on with it.
acuity.explanation: Williams' speech had two strands: a satirical renaming of the bill over its "buy now, pay later" provisions, and a substantive argument that the bill excludes BNPL providers from the CCCFA's default-fee limits, making New Zealand an outlier. Brewer takes up the title strand squarely and does something with it — the 2003 Act has carried the same full title through three overhauls — and answers the commencement clause with the regulators' nominated date. But he leaves the default-fee and household-debt argument entirely untouched, having first characterised the whole speech as "relitigation" of Part 1. One strand engaged, the substance pivoted away from, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "I am not suggesting that this bill will be called the “Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance (Buy Now, Pay Later - Free Ride) Amendment Bill”."

acuity.statement: Those lenders that the member raised in clause 70 as we near this other amendments section, those that are certified now by the Commerce Commission will be granted an FMA licence. So that comes across, and FMA is engaging the sector already and has been for some weeks and months as this transition has had some inevitability about it and they are helping lenders with that transition. But their certification comes across the Commerce Commission to the FMA.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific question put to him about what happens to existing Commerce Commission certifications and supplies the substantive answer — they carry across as FMA licences, with the FMA already engaging the sector. Not a full 1.0 because he leaves two strands of her question untouched (the notification mechanism for small operators, and whether this is dealt with in regulations), and he opens by pivoting to a prepared warning about car financing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "for those holders of licensing arrangements with another regulator who falls under the ambit now of FMA, what is the status of the licences?"

acuity.statement: As my colleague noted, this is the title and commencement, and it is the time to stand back and say what this bill actually does and how can we give it a title which appropriately and accurately reflects that. Certainly, the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Bill is not a particularly descriptive title.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the preceding speaker's device — that the bill's title should be renamed to describe what it really does — and carries it forward into his own tabled renaming amendments and the debt-forgiveness argument underlying it. The speech would be different had she not made the renaming argument. Short of 1.0 because it extends a colleague's line rather than engaging a contested claim, and much of what follows is prepared material on the rule of law.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "This is why we should rename the bill “Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance (Forgiveness of ANZ-ASB)”"

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. Speaking to the amendments on the Table, I want to further invite the Minister to consider the title “Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance (Buy Now, Pay Later) Amendment Bill”.
acuity.explanation: Engages the strand of the preceding turn — the tabled title amendments — and adds a further one, so it is not indifferent to what came before. But it takes up none of the content of Webb's argument (retrospectivity, unfiled claims, the rule of law) and moves instead to her own separate rationale about the 2022 'buy now, pay later' decisions.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "My suggestion that I’ve tabled is that clause 1 be deleted and replaced with “This Act is the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance (Letting Big Banks Off the Hook) Act”"

acuity.statement: What’s the difference between Green MP Wade-Brown’s accommodation or McAnulty from Labour’s accommodation as opposed to yours? What is the difference? The answer is none.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific charge just made about accommodation entitlements and does something with it — naming Green and Labour members' own accommodation arrangements to deny any distinction. The intervention would be different had Menéndez March raised a different line of attack, so engagement with the actual claim is close. (The inference is a tu quoque and the manner is pointed, but those belong to Rigor and Civility, not here.) Marked down from 1.0 because it rebuts the premise by assertion rather than engaging the entitlement rules the question invoked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ricardo Menéndez March: "while Ministers are still able to claim $1,000 a week in ministerial entitlements for a property they already own mortgage-free"

acuity.statement: I’d invite the member to look at the screeds of economic evidence that’s been conducted by Governments, both red and blue, in the past and of all different stripes by academic economists and others that indicates that the accommodation supplement, whilst not perfect, is a form of income support that goes to people in relation to their housing costs.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up Swarbrick's interjected claim about the incidence of the accommodation supplement and disputes it on its own ground — that the evidence characterises it as income support to tenants rather than a transfer to landlords. Pointable and squarely aimed, so well above the prepared-material band. Not 1.0 because he answers by gesturing at unnamed 'screeds of economic evidence' rather than engaging the incidence argument itself, and he does not address her second point that he had previously said the same thing.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Chlöe Swarbrick: "You know it’s a subsidy for landlords, Bish!"

acuity.statement: Well, it’s NZ Music Month and tomorrow is the New Zealand music awards. I am very happy to cede the crown of the worst New Zealand music performance of all time to Dr Ayesha Verrall.
acuity.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer immediately preceded him with a substantive case for a wealth tax — that the money sits in property portfolios, capital gains and trust structures, and that the Government chooses not to touch it. Bishop takes up no part of it: no reply on tax, on wealth, on who the Government protects. He opens on music month and Ayesha Verrall's weekend performance and proceeds to three prepared set-pieces about Labour's conference, the Future Fund and Hipkins. Substituting any other wealth-tax argument before him would not change a word of this speech, and it could have been delivered on a different day in a different debate. It stays above 0.0 only because a general debate has no fixed subject, so prepared material is nominally within the item.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Debbie Ngarewa-Packer argued that the money for a wealth tax exists and 'is sitting in property portfolios and capital gains and trust structures designed specifically to keep it out of reach of the public good', and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Never mind Lil Nas X and Billy Ray Cyrus’ “Old Town Road”, can Siri play “Obsessed” by Mariah Carey, please. Again, for the third week in a row—the third week in a row—the night before your Budget—the night before your Budget—all the National Party has been talking about is the Labour Party.
acuity.explanation: She clearly heard the speech she follows: she picks up Bishop's music-awards framing and turns it back on him, and she answers the shape of his contribution — that a Government minister on Budget eve spent his whole slot on the Opposition. That is engagement with one strand of the preceding turn rather than with its substance: she rebuts none of his three specific charges (the leaked regional-conference tape, the Future Fund details withheld until after the election, Hipkins on policy detail), and moves on to prepared material about the Minister of Finance's State housing remarks. Partial engagement that can be pointed at, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Labour Party are ducking the tough issues" — Chris Bishop, whose entire preceding speech was devoted to three events said to reveal Labour's attitude.

acuity.statement: Balancing our books by tinkering with superannuation seems to be endorsed even by the Opposition, who spent the last five minutes championing about how they were going to stand up for the underdog. Yet, they have, at the same time, said that, yes, they’ll have a conversation about adjusting the superannuation. Just yesterday in question time, with faux indignation, they said, “What about the pensioners?”, because of the adjustments to housing subsidies.
acuity.explanation: Costello follows Edmonds and takes up one identifiable strand of her speech — her advocacy for pensioners hit by the housing-subsidy/rent change, and her posture of standing up for the underdog — and turns it into a charge of inconsistency with Labour's openness to adjusting superannuation. But she does not engage Edmonds' actual argument (Budget winners and losers, interest deductibility, pay equity, public service job losses); the bulk of the speech is prepared material defending superannuation, a subject Edmonds never raised in the preceding turn. Partial, pointable engagement before returning to prepared material.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "86,000 households will have their rent increased by $30, and 30,000 of those households are pensioners" — Barbara Edmonds (and her closing claim that Labour "will choose differently" for the lowest paid)

acuity.statement: Barbara Edmonds, in her speech just before, put it quite truthfully, I thought, when she said New Zealanders will have a choice on 7 November. They will have a choice. The reality is that elections are meant to be a choice, a contest of ideas—a contest of ideas, not a contest of secrets. It seems like the Labour Party is wanting to have a contest of secrets.
acuity.explanation: Brown names the preceding speaker and lifts her actual closing line, which is more than a generic gesture at the debate, so this is not bottom-band. But he does nothing with her argument: he repeats her words back in order to pivot to a prepared attack on Labour's lack of released policy, and leaves untouched every substantive claim she made (interest deductibility, the heated-tobacco excise cut, the 86,000 households facing higher rent, pay equity). Quoting an opponent as a springboard is engagement with the topic, not with the content of the claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "This November, New Zealand will have a choice too." — Barbara Edmonds

acuity.statement: I find it quite disgusting that the Government thinks it’s so crack-up making these dry jokes over and over again about, whatever, ducks, horses, when just last week—I mean, where do we start with all of the announcements that they made to punch down on the most vulnerable people in our society?
acuity.explanation: She takes up the one thing that dominated Brown's turn — the duck/Billy Ray Cyrus mockery — and does something with it, contrasting the levity with the previous week's announcements, so the opening would have to change if Brown had made a different speech. But she engages no part of his substantive claims (tax, bills, the Budget) and from there delivers prepared material on public service job cuts, so this is partial engagement rather than a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simeon Brown: "Here she is, saying, 'I'm gonna take my duck to the old town pond, I'm gonna ride 'til I can't no more.' Is that what Labour's policy is?"

acuity.statement: Look, we hear a lot about the fact that there’s one more sleep—one more sleep until tomorrow, Budget day—and we will see if this Government has been listening to Kiwis all around the household.
acuity.explanation: The speech is on the running theme of the general debate (tomorrow's Budget and the cost of living) but is indifferent to what preceded it: it never touches Paul's public service argument, or Brown's claims about tax and bills, and would read word-for-word the same whoever had spoken before. Prepared material on the right subject.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Tamatha Paul argued that cutting around 9,000 public servants would degrade front-line services because departments are interdependent, and this statement does not take that up at any point.

acuity.statement: I can start off by saying that this is a Government that actually delivers for New Zealanders. It has only been one sleep since that stalking law has actually come into law—it’s only been one sleep, and already a 39-year-old man has been charged with stalking; allegedly stalking and harassing a woman getting off the bus.
acuity.explanation: The opening sentence is a direct contradiction of the proposition Utikere had just built his speech around, and she immediately offers evidence for it, so she is answering the topic he raised. But the evidence is law and order, while his specific claims were about fuel, food, power, rents and public transport fares — none of which she engages — so this is engagement with the topic rather than with the argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tangi Utikere: "Christopher Luxon and his Government promised to make things better and they have very clearly made things worse."

acuity.statement: I acknowledge the speech before me and give our thoughts and our prayers again to the whānau of our deceased and the many victims of stalking and those who have passed.
acuity.explanation: A gesture at the preceding turn — she names Farzana and acknowledges the speech — but she engages no part of Lee's argument that the stalking law shows the Government delivering, and immediately turns to prepared material on fast-track consenting and donations. Polite acknowledgement that takes up no content sits in the low band, not at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Melissa Lee: "I’m thinking of Farzana Yaqubi, a 21-year-old law student, resident of West Auckland."

acuity.statement: I just want to talk for a few minutes about something that is very important to Kiwis and that is health and our healthcare system.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the general debate's Budget theme, delivered without reference to anything said before it. It engages neither Lyndon's fast-track and donations charge nor the earlier public service arguments, and would be identical whoever had spoken previously.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Hūhana Lyndon argued that the McCallum Brothers' Bream Bay sand-mining application is being advanced through fast track despite donor ties and no proven regional benefit, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: We’ve got a great Budget coming up tomorrow, but I want to talk about something that’s already been announced and that, certainly, for my part of the world, is very good news.
acuity.explanation: On the debate's subject (the coming Budget and announcements already made) but wholly indifferent to the preceding turns: no claim by any earlier speaker, government or opposition, is engaged, and the speech would be unchanged had a different member spoken.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Todd Stephenson spoke about pre-Budget health announcements and ACT's coalition health achievements, and this statement moves to wilding pines without taking any of it up.

acuity.statement: Now, it’s Budget eve, and tomorrow we’ll hear the final Budget from Nicola Willis and this failed coalition Government. A Government that promised to fix the cost of living; they haven’t just failed, they have, in fact, made it worse.
acuity.explanation: The assertion that the Government has made the cost of living worse is a bare counter-claim, not engagement: it does not touch Smith's wilding pines case, Stephenson's health announcements, or Lee's law-and-order evidence. The AI and public service material that follows is prepared and could have been delivered after any preceding speech.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Stuart Smith argued for the wilding pine funding in the Leatham and Branch valleys and for his local government member's bill, and this statement does not take either up.

acuity.statement: As I’ve already said publicly, future changes to legislation will go through a process, and all of the affected groups will be part of those discussions.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the second strand of Andersen's question — whether other affected groups will be consulted — and answers it, but leaves her first and more pressed question (why the amendments were not made in the committee stage the previous night, and why a recommittal was needed) entirely untouched. Partial engagement, pointable but incomplete.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ginny Andersen: "I’m interested to know if the Minister would be prepared to have discussions, as she did with the home-schooling representatives, with other groups who are also impacted by the amendments"

acuity.statement: The Minister has already mentioned that there is a subsequent education bill that’s currently in draft. Would that be an appropriate time to consider more broadly—and I’m not saying that the Minister doesn’t have the ability to do things—and to be able to consider some of those changes and allow for the public to actually hear or for us to get public submissions on the other changes that haven’t had time to consult? I want to check with the Minister if there’s anything else that she thinks should be removed.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's assurance that future changes will 'go through a process' and presses it to a specific vehicle — the draft education bill — asking whether that is where the unconsulted parts of Amendment Paper 583 should go. The question would have to change if the Minister had said something else, so it is genuinely responsive, though it also carries prepared material on the Teaching Council and the peak body.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "future changes to legislation will go through a process, and all of the affected groups will be part of those discussions"

acuity.statement: At that point in time, as I’ve already explained in the House today—from that point, to get it into this bill, given that I have serious concerns about child safety, we had to go like the clappers, and I’ve already said that there wasn’t time for consultation. It’s not about new information, as the speaker has suggested, it’s about additional complexities that we didn’t expect, which is why we will take this back to a full process.
acuity.explanation: Directly corrects the premise of the preceding question: Xu-Nan characterised the climb-down as the Minister changing her mind 'in light of new evidence and new information', and she disputes that specific framing and substitutes her own account (unexpected complexity plus a late ministry options paper). This is engagement with the content of the claim, not a reference to the speaker.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "we are seeing that the Minister is willing to change her mind in light of new evidence and new information"

acuity.statement: I want to check, has the Minister then, at this stage, rather than making legislative changes—because one of the other things that we have heard, for example from the National Council of Home Educators New Zealand, is that changes could already be possible under the current legislative framework without having to make additional changes.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's child-safety rationale and then turns it against her conclusion: if the concern is real, existing powers over the stipend and exemption declarations could address it without urgent legislation. That is engaging the reasoning just offered rather than restating a prepared objection.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Erica Stanford: "given that I have serious concerns about child safety, we had to go like the clappers"

acuity.statement: Look, the advice that I’ve had is that that is not possible. And of course, the whole purpose of this is to remove this part of the bill so that we can then go through a full process and work with the Home Schooling NZ association on their views.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question just put — whether the Ministry could act under the existing framework — with a direct 'not possible' on advice, and then connects it to the purpose of the removal. Squarely on the claim raised, though it supplies no detail about the advice itself (a specificity matter, not an acuity one).
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "changes could already be possible under the current legislative framework without having to make additional changes"

acuity.statement: Can the Minister indicate whether there will be an opportunity for consultation and also for select committee submissions to occur if it’s resubmitted under that bill, given the fact that that was bypassed in this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Builds on the Minister's own earlier indication that the home-schooling provisions will reappear in a second bill and tests what 'a full process' will actually include, which is a real engagement with what was said. acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Francisco Hernandez asked why the bill was brought under urgency instead of going through a normal select committee process, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Nothing says centrepiece Budget legislation more than the chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, Ryan Hamilton, taking a two-second call on the first piece of legislation that has come to the House.
acuity.explanation: Fastens directly onto the turn immediately before hers — Hamilton's one-sentence call — and turns it into her argument that Government members will not defend their own Budget bill. Had Hamilton made a substantive case for the bill, this opening could not have been given. Scored on engagement only; that the engagement is mocking does not lower it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I look forward to deliberating further in committee of the whole House" — Ryan Hamilton

acuity.statement: Now, obviously my colleague Cushla Tangaere-Manuel is going to have many questions on behalf of the people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti because a point she makes very well, there may be that—and Cameron Luxton can claim—so produce can get out of the East Coast. But the problem she highlights is there’s no funding for the roading to get that produce to the airports to get it out of the East Coast.
acuity.explanation: Picks up Luxton's specific claim — that the aircraft leasing change will let Ikaroa-Rāwhiti producers get their produce to the world — and attacks its premise by pointing to the missing roading to reach the airports. The rebuttal is shaped entirely by what Luxton claimed and would have to change if he had argued something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "where they will now be able to get their produce to the world" — Cameron Luxton

acuity.statement: To the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Megan Woods, who just sat down: it’s coming; the fringe benefit tax legislation is coming later this year. Watch this space.
acuity.explanation: Woods's turn repeatedly asked why the announced fringe benefit tax changes were absent from the bill and when that legislation would arrive. Bidois names her and supplies a direct answer to exactly that question — the FBT bill is coming later this year. The reply would be different, or unnecessary, had Woods not raised the FBT omission, which is the deciding test. It is thin on detail (no date, no mechanism), but that is a specificity matter, not responsiveness; the engagement is squarely on the point just made.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: "The question we will have for the Minister is: what is the timeline? We don't know when that legislation is coming."

acuity.statement: Once again, I reiterate that I am shocked that this is the first matter of business for this Government while whānau across Aotearoa are struggling.
acuity.explanation: Eligible — two substantive turns with content (Woods's questions about urgency, select committee scrutiny and the missing FBT and bank levy provisions; Bidois's assertion that the changes are sensible and that FBT legislation is coming) precede this one in the same debate. The speech is on the matter under debate: it works through the aviation lease provision, the Working for Families change and the overpayment-debt risk, and states a position on supporting the bill to committee stage. But it engages no part of what either previous speaker argued — it neither tests Bidois's claim about the FBT timeline nor picks up Woods's select-committee or consultation point. Echoing the word "hodgepodge" repeats a term without engaging its content. Prepared material on the right subject with a gesture at the debate, so 0.3 rather than lower; the one apparent rejoinder ("The member opposite wants to talk about all the amazing produce getting out of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti") answers a turn not present in this window and cannot be credited.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Dan Bidois spoke immediately before, saying the bill "makes practical and sensible changes to our tax system" and that the fringe benefit tax legislation "is coming later this year", and this statement does not take either claim up.

acuity.statement: Just in regards to clauses 64 and 65 of the regulatory impact statement around shareholder loans, yeah, the member is right. The option that we went with was the option five around taxing shareholder loans six months after the lending company is removed from the register. Option six was more record-keeping.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Xu-Nan's specific point about the regulatory impact statement's preferred combination of options five and six, concedes the member is right, and explains why only option five was carried into the bill (simplicity of compliance). Not a full 1.0 because Xu-Nan's second question — how Inland Revenue will reach the ~4,500 companies removed from the register each year — is left untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Can I check with the Minister what happened to option six, which is improving record-keeping" — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: You have said that this clause, this mechanism is to increase productivity, so what I’d like the Minister to explain is: am I right in summarising it as for these loans that are under $200,000—only those ones—you have this by inserting a removal date, six months being a normal number in these tax laws, then what happens is it falls away and you don’t have the burden of extra administration? Is that where the productivity is coming from or is it somewhere else? When he gives an answer—and I’ve got another question—if he can just go up a level in explanation about how this clause is productive, I think that would be helpful.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the Minister's just-given answer — the six-month taxing mechanism and its compliance rationale — by restating it back for confirmation and asking him to raise the level of explanation to the productivity claim. It responds to the character and substance of the preceding answer, but does not take up the option five / option six point that answer was actually about, and then moves to her own prepared second question on clause 4.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "keeping it really simple, for low compliance, you just simply make it taxable after six months" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: We’ve just been talking about the principal of the loan, but often these loans from companies to shareholders, directors, associated parties are low- or no-interest loans, so I’m just trying to think through what happens in that circumstance. I guess if the shareholder gets a no-interest loan, that’s a considerable concession in itself, so how is that sort of interest discount treated? As the financial arrangement comes to an end, does the interest foregone by the company in the meantime get loaded on to the loan, which then gets taxed in the hands of the shareholder or something like that?
acuity.explanation: Explicitly builds on the mechanism just described ("We've just been talking about the principal of the loan") and draws out a consequence the Minister's answer left open — whether forgone interest on a concessionary loan is captured when the arrangement ends. The speech could not have been given without the preceding exchange about taxing the loan principal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the option five around taxing shareholder loans six months after the lending company is removed from the register" — Simon Watts

acuity.statement: What the member’s referring to there is not subject to this legislation. But going back to the member Rachel Brooking’s question around sort of stepping back and linkage to productivity, the major problem here is that when companies are providing loans to their directors, then that, in effect, is income going from the company to the director. If that loan is never repaid, then that income and the tax on that income is never crystallised. As a result, that is a loss to the broader system.
acuity.explanation: Answers two distinct preceding questions in turn: rules Russell's interest-forgone point outside the bill, then supplies exactly the higher-level account Brooking asked for, explaining the untaxed-income problem the clause is meant to crystallise. Short of 1.0 only because Russell's question is dismissed without explanation of why it falls outside the legislation.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "if he can just go up a level in explanation about how this clause is productive" — Rachel Brooking

acuity.statement: The Minister of Revenue said the reason we didn’t go down the donor-controlled charities route was because it’s complex. Complexity in the tax law has never stopped anything, Minister, but be that as it may.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's own stated reason and rebuts it directly — that complexity has never been a bar in tax law — before putting her question. This is engagement with the content of the reason given, not a mere reference to it. Marked down slightly because the answer she rebuts is not itself in the window, so the uptake is auditable only through her own quotation of it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: The Minister of Revenue's stated reason for not pursuing the donor-controlled charities route — that it is complex (Simon Watts; the answer itself falls in a gap in this window, but she quotes it before rebutting it)

acuity.statement: My second question is around the amount of entitlement ceiling in options 2, 3, and 4. I note that there is 4,500, 15,000, and then 100,000. It seems to be quite a broad gap between option 3 and option 4, and I just want to check if the Minister has tested with officials on any of the range between 15,000 and 100,000 in terms of additional balance that will both provide tax integrity and those of fiscal sustainability.
acuity.explanation: He returns to his own prepared thread — "I've remembered my second question now" — and engages no part of the urgency argument that immediately preceded him. The material is squarely on the bill and its regulatory impact statement, so it is not wholly adrift, but the speech would be word-for-word identical whatever the previous speaker had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell had just argued the measure does not take effect until 1 April 2027 and asked why it was taken under Budget urgency when the annual rates bill was a suitable vehicle, and this statement does not take that up at all.

acuity.statement: Now, moving on to clause 5, the first question I have—I know that the Hon Dr Deborah Russell has a lot of questions around corporate tax, and I always learn a lot through her in a lot of these tax debates as a result, as well as the Minister, who, really, in the past has been incredibly helpful and informative in terms of our questions.
acuity.explanation: Names the previous speaker warmly but engages no part of her argument or question: he moves straight to his own prepared question on the application date in clause 5(3). A mere reference, not engagement, though it is squarely on the clause under debate.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell asked 'just how much revenue does the Government expect that it will get in because of this measure?' and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: The question from Dr Deborah Russell on clause 5 in regards to the money involved—$146 million over the forecast period.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly the figure the preceding speaker asked for, identifying the question and answering it. The turn would be different had she asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: 'just how much revenue does the Government expect that it will get in because of this measure?'

acuity.statement: Covering both that answer to clause 4 and a brief question about clause 5—the Minister of Revenue has just said there in his response that the reason to not require these foreign companies that own aeroplanes to pay tax is because already some of those countries don’t pay the tax.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-delivered justification, restates it, registers his disagreement with the restatement ('He's shaking his head') and presses for the distinction and the fiscal cost. Directly built on the preceding turn's content.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'what we’re doing here is fixing an inconsistency between countries that have a double tax agreement with New Zealand and those countries that do not'

acuity.statement: I’m happy to answer that, and Lawrence Xu-Nan asked a similar question. The 4 December 2025 application date is the date on which the consultation paper was released, and, therefore, in effect, by applying that date, it mitigates any structuring opportunities or people looking to make changes to take advantage of the fact that as of that date, it was made public. That’s why that date has been selected.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand of the preceding turn — the rationale for the 4 December 2025 trigger date — with a specific reason, but leaves the rest of that turn (the difference between treaty and non-treaty countries, the tax forgone, who requested the change) untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Rachel Brooking: 'noting my Green colleague’s question about that date, 4 December 2025'

acuity.statement: Thank you, Minister. That’s very sensible. I think that’s a really sensible reason for a date, then. I know that my colleagues have a lot of questions on this clause as well. I just want to focus on one other question at this stage, and this is to do with clause 5(1).
acuity.explanation: Takes up the answer just given and resolves it — accepting the structuring rationale as sufficient answer to his own earlier question — then turns to a fresh line of questioning. Partial engagement: the acceptance is pointable but nothing in the answer is examined.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'The 4 December 2025 application date is the date on which the consultation paper was released'

acuity.statement: The option that the Government has decided to proceed with in this legislation is option five, which is tax shareholders on outstanding loans six months after the company is removed from the register. We can see that it did not score well for minimising complexity or compliance costs; on fact, it scored as being worse than the status quo in terms of that criteria.
acuity.explanation: Prepared material on the clause under debate, worked up from the regulatory impact statement. It engages no part of the preceding turns — neither the Minister's date rationale nor her Green colleague's six-month questions — and would read identically whatever had just been said about clause 5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just explained why the 4 December 2025 application date was chosen, and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: Nevertheless, just as the possibility of tax structuring was opened up the moment that the discussion document went out, the possibility of tax structuring might also have been raised from that quite targeted consultation with private sector firms.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the Minister's reasoning for the application date and draws out its consequence against him: if publication creates a structuring window, so did the earlier targeted consultation in September 2025. The argument exists only because of what he said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'it mitigates any structuring opportunities or people looking to make changes to take advantage of the fact that as of that date, it was made public'

acuity.statement: In regards to Lawrence Xu-Nan’s question around the six-month time period, again, in regards to clause 5: is six months a common period? Yes, six months is a common period. It allows for reinstatement to register. Also, this period is used because generally we’ve had feedback from submitters that that’s appropriate. The question around what happens if the company is reinstated after the six months: the loan becomes taxable income.
acuity.explanation: Answers both of the specific questions put earlier about the six-month window — whether it is standard practice and what happens on late reinstatement — squarely and in order. Marked down because the immediately preceding request for assurance about the targeted consultation is not engaged.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'is that a common period of time that’s already in existence?'

acuity.statement: My understanding is that a loan is a financial arrangement and that the $200,000 threshold that my colleague Dr Woods referred to is to do with whether a financial arrangement is treated on a cash basis or treated on an accrual basis.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the unanswered financial-arrangement question from an earlier turn and advances it — supplying her own reading of what the $200,000 threshold governs and asking the Minister to confirm or correct it. Pointable engagement with a specific prior claim.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Megan Woods: 'whether or not this change brings the loan under financial arrangement rules ... Does that mean then that loans under $200,000—which is the threshold financial arrangement—are not going to be affected?'

acuity.statement: Yeah, so the member is correct that loans under $200,000 are not affected by this new rule. Sorry, loans under $200,000 are—my apologies—affected by the new rule.
acuity.explanation: Addresses the threshold question put to him directly, confirming the member's reading and then correcting himself mid-answer. Engagement with the specific claim is unmistakable; the self-contradiction is a clarity problem, not an attention one.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: 'So that would capture all the loans below $200,000 quite easily, but what about the loans that are over $200,000?'

acuity.statement: I just want to clarify, Minister, because I think you stumbled over your words slightly. Loans under $200,000 are captured?
acuity.explanation: Catches the mis-speak in the answer just given and puts the point back as a single closed question to settle it. Impossible to have produced without listening to the exact wording of the preceding turn.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'Sorry, loans under $200,000 are—my apologies—affected by the new rule.'

acuity.statement: I wanted to check this is to do with the exemption of income and this has come down to the family scheme income. I do want to draw the Minister’s attention to clause 27(2). As the previous speaker, the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, pointed out, there are five Acts being referred to.
acuity.explanation: Takes up Russell's observation about the set of Acts moved in and out of Schedule 3, clause 5(2) and develops it into a specific question about why those five Acts were chosen; engages one strand of her question (the identity and effect of the listed Acts) rather than her central question about the impact on borrowers, and much of the turn is his own prepared analysis of the Arbitration and Pitcairn Trials Acts.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "There’s a whole set of Acts that are referred to—the Arbitration (International Investment Disputes) Act, the Consular Privileges and Immunities Act, the Pitcairn Trials Act—which can be taken in and out of Schedule 3, clause 5(2)."

acuity.statement: In summary, what you are seeing play through here is that the Student Loan Scheme uses the concept of adjusted net income in that legislation, and by repealing Schedule 38—which is what we’re doing in this bill—it means that certain income under other listed Acts, such as the Pitcairn Trials Act and other items that have been noted by the member, will not apply for Working for Families. However, these Acts are still relevant to the Student Loan Scheme Act, and so we are simply, by doing this, moving the relevant provisions out of the tax Act and putting them into the student loan legislation.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific puzzle Xu-Nan raised — why obscure statutes such as the Pitcairn Trials Act appear in a tax bill — by explaining the Schedule 38 repeal and the relocation of the provisions into the student loan legislation. The answer would have been different had the preceding speaker asked something else. Short of 1.0 only because it leaves Xu-Nan's separate point about a public/Gazette notification requirement for the Order in Council untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "Even more peculiar is the Pitcairn Trials Act." / "How is that in any way related to an income exemption from tax?"

acuity.statement: I guess my question to the Minister of Revenue is a really short one: in terms of the decision of this Government to do away with the third-year fees-free, is that encapsulated in this piece of legislation, or is it in fact part of the delegation of the Minister of Education to the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC)?
acuity.explanation: Stays on the part of the bill under debate and gestures at the administrative/student loan framing the Minister had just described, but engages no part of the Minister's actual answer about Schedule 38 and family scheme income; instead it opens a fresh line about fees-free and TEC delegation that would have read the same whatever the Minister had said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing specific: Simon Watts had just explained that repealing Schedule 38 means those Acts no longer apply for Working for Families, and this statement does not take that up — it only shares the subject of the student loan provisions.

acuity.statement: The aspects that we are discussing here relate to Working for Families. There is no interaction with the points that the members have noted; they are out of scope. We’re talking about the Working for Families portion.
acuity.explanation: Squarely addresses the question just put — it denies the premise that the fees-free/TEC financial power interfaces with this part of the bill — so the reply is shaped by what Webb asked. It engages the question rather than its reasoning, and supplies nothing further, which keeps it below the top band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Duncan Webb: "If the Minister could explain where that financial power comes from and the interface with the tax Act, that would be really good."

acuity.statement: I rise on behalf of ACT to speak on the taxation bill. This is a small but important bill which supports our overall Budget that was delivered yesterday. We’re going to return the Budget to surplus, we’re cutting waste, and we’re investing in what Kiwis care about, and I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive attack on the Government's Budget direction and engages none of it. The content is a party-position formula about surplus, waste and investment that would read word-for-word the same whatever Genter had said; it is at least on the bill under debate, so not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter had just argued "the Luxon Government has no plan and no vision for the future" and listed mining, asset sales and the super-rich, and this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: I’m speaking on behalf of New Zealand First to commend this bill to the House. We really, really want to pay a compliment to our National Party colleagues. We’ve heard a lot about the philanthropic sector that’s struggling and may or may not have considered the Active Investor Plus criteria being added to that one.
acuity.explanation: Prepared commendation plus thanks to a coalition partner. It gestures at the philanthropic sector generally but engages no claim, argument or figure from either preceding turn, and nothing in it depends on what was just said.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Julie Anne Genter attacked the Government for having "no plan and no vision for the future" and Todd Stephenson claimed the bill returns the Budget to surplus; this statement takes up neither.

acuity.statement: We’ve heard members opposite talking about how they’re getting back to surplus, but what they don’t mention is that they’re only getting back to surplus on a fake measure that the finance Minister has developed, a measure that’s actually not been done before, the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses measure, which artificially excludes liabilities from ACC, which doesn’t really make sense if you think about it.
acuity.explanation: Takes the specific claim made two turns earlier — that the Budget returns to surplus — and does something with it, naming the accounting measure (OBEGAL excluding ACC) he says the surplus depends on and why he thinks it is illegitimate. The passage could not stand if the preceding Government speakers had not made the surplus claim. Marked down from 1.0 only because it arrives at the end of a largely prepared philosophical speech that leaves Wilson's and Stephenson's other points untouched.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We’re going to return the Budget to surplus, we’re cutting waste" — Todd Stephenson

acuity.statement: I’m so inspired after that rant by Julie Anne Genter about looking for jobs. Well, the Budget promotes 220,000 new jobs over the forecast period, and for every $1 billion of capital expenditure, it’s estimated there will be 4,500 jobs, so hurrah to that! I commend the bill to the House.
acuity.explanation: Picks up one strand of Genter's attack — jobs — and answers it with specific figures rather than merely naming her as a target, so the turn would have to change if she had argued something else. It is only a partial engagement: it answers the topic she raised rather than her actual argument about mining, asset sales and workers, and then closes with a formula.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Luxon Government has no plan and no vision for the future" — Julie Anne Genter (whose speech he characterises as being about looking for jobs)

acuity.statement: It is indeed a privilege to follow after the most substantive contribution we’ve heard from a Government backbencher in this entire debate. Ryan, well done! You made 12 seconds.
acuity.explanation: A reference to the preceding turn that engages none of its content: Hamilton offered jobs figures and Hernandez a specific challenge to the surplus measure, and she takes up neither, mocking only how long Hamilton spoke before moving to prepared material on tax measures missing from the bill. On the matter under debate, with a gesture at the previous speaker, but the speech would be unchanged had he argued something different.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the Budget promotes 220,000 new jobs over the forecast period" — Ryan Hamilton; she engages only the brevity of his speech, not the claim

acuity.statement: As per what I’ve said before, I have just a couple of quick questions. The first one to the Minister is this: in the regulatory impact statement, I can’t see anything at this stage on the overseas pensions bit, as well as the superannuation bit that we see in clause 10. Would the Minister just quickly point me to where in the regulatory impact statement I would find any information on that?
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive turn by Russell probing the advice behind counting income equalisation accounts in family scheme income, but engages no part of it and instead opens a fresh line of prepared questions about the regulatory impact statement. On the bill under debate, so not 0.0, but there is no gesture at what preceded it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Deborah Russell said 'I’d like to know what advice the Minister received around that' about income equalisation accounts and tax structuring, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: Just in regard to the overseas pensions question that was raised before, the overseas pensions are excluded from the family scheme income, which affects the Working for Families tax credits. There is a fiscal implication for that, of around $3 million over the forecast period.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific gap Xu-Nan named and supplies substance on it, including a fiscal figure, and addresses the earlier strand about different types of pensions. Short of 1.0 because the actual request — a pointer to where this appears in the regulatory impact statement — is declined; the topic is engaged, the precise ask is not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'I can’t see anything at this stage on the overseas pensions bit, as well as the superannuation bit that we see in clause 10.'

acuity.statement: No, actually, thank you, Minister; that is already incredibly helpful. I want to check with the Minister again, very quickly, on clause 10, because it also relates to the superannuation scheme and pensioners. Does that mean that the superannuation scheme is exempt from calculations for the family scheme income as well—that’s the domestic superannuation scheme?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's answer about overseas pensions and draws out its consequence, testing whether the same exclusion runs to the domestic superannuation scheme. The question could not have been asked without having listened to the answer just given.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'the overseas pensions are excluded from the family scheme income, which affects the Working for Families tax credits.'

acuity.statement: Yes, I mean, I’m sure we are, by increasing the de minimis, providing more flexibility for families—acknowledging this is a complex and difficult area. More de minimis gives some more optionality and more flexibility in there and, at one level, more fairness in the context of complying.
acuity.explanation: Answers Russell's fairness framing directly in its own terms ('I’m sure we are'), but shifts the ground to the de minimis increase rather than engaging her actual point about excluded income creating unfairness between neighbouring households. One strand taken up, then a move to prepared material on the de minimis and Orders in Council.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: 'If we are excluding some income that a particular household is getting, is that fair to the household next door, and so on?'

acuity.statement: The final question I have—thank you, Minister, for your explanation—I do see in paragraph 16 of the regulatory impact statement where it talks about increasing the de minimis from $5,000 to $8,000, due to inflation. Has the Minister considered increasing it even further than that—for example, to $10,000?
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's own justification — that a bigger de minimis means more flexibility and fairness — and presses its logical consequence by asking why the threshold was not lifted further. The question is shaped by the answer it follows, not merely adjacent to it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'More de minimis gives some more optionality and more flexibility in there and, at one level, more fairness in the context of complying.'

acuity.statement: Yes, and I answered that before. It was fiscally not within the bounds we had available.
acuity.explanation: Answers the precise question put — yes it was considered, and the reason it was rejected — in two clauses with no deflection. Brevity and vagueness about the fiscal numbers are a specificity matter, not a responsiveness one; on engagement this is squarely aimed at the question asked.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: 'Has the Minister considered increasing it even further than that—for example, to $10,000?'

acuity.statement: I wonder if the Minister could please explain the reasoning behind that, because it’s quite an interesting thing to do within a tax Act—to step away from the tax residents rules. Could he tell us why this is a more appropriate way to go when it comes to determining the eligibility for Working for Families tax credits?
acuity.explanation: Moves to the residence conditions block with prepared material; nothing in it turns on the exchange it follows. It is squarely on the bill under debate, which keeps it out of the 0.0 band, but it would read identically whatever the Minister had just said about the de minimis.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Simon Watts had just said of the de minimis that 'It was fiscally not within the bounds we had available', and this statement does not take that up.

acuity.statement: I’m happy to do so. The basic premise here is that the residence requirements that we’re putting in place ensure that Working for Families is only paid to families who are living in New Zealand. That is therefore to help them with the costs related to raising their children. These rules are difficult for some customers to understand and therefore for IRD to apply.
acuity.explanation: Supplies the reasoning Russell asked for — the residence-in-New-Zealand premise and the administrability problem IRD observed — so the answer is shaped by the question. It stops short of 1.0 because her specific point, that a tax Act would ordinarily use tax residence rather than a separate residency test, is not itself addressed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: 'Could he tell us why this is a more appropriate way to go when it comes to determining the eligibility for Working for Families tax credits?'

acuity.statement: There are some quite detailed definitions and scenarios, actually, given in the commentary on the bill, and I think they’re very useful. They do go through a number of reasons why people could be away. In developing these certain 42 days and the 42-day requirements and an absence of more than that, I just wondered whether or not this was a period of time that the Minister chose to align with other requirements in other pieces of legislation around physical residency in terms of the ability to receive pensions or other transfers within the welfare system and whether that was something the Minister took into account when reaching these definitions.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the limit the Minister had just defended as 'reasonable', accepts part of his case about reasons for absence, and tests the unexamined element — where the 42-day figure came from and whether it was aligned to residency tests elsewhere in the welfare system. Clearly built on the answer it follows.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Simon Watts: 'hence we’ve put a limit on the amount of time that you are able to be outside of New Zealand before the Government stops paying this.'

acuity.statement: Yes, the Minister did take into account those factors. We also considered a wide range of reasons why individuals do need to leave New Zealand, such as seeking medical care and attention overseas, and other complexities in regard to serious illness and injury, etc. We did a wide range of assessment around that and we landed on this, also taking into account the precedent.

acuity.responding_to: "this is a bill that is in no way connected to the real lives of ordinary New Zealanders" and "Even a few days at select committee would have allowed us to tease out some of the problems" — Megan Woods

acuity.responding_to: "The concern is that charitable giving in New Zealand might, like many New Zealanders, pack its bags and head to Australia." — Megan Woods

On the deciding test it is indifferent to what it follows, so 0.2 — low because nothing in the preceding argument is taken up, not because it is brief or because she is a Minister speaking last.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Camilla Belich spoke about the Boxing and Wrestling Act review and the risk that the boxing and wrestling community has no regulation from 1 April 2028 if the review is not completed, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Mike Davidson argued 'have we created legislation that is leaving a lot of people exposed in the event of an earthquake?' and criticised the use of urgency, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.responding_to: "It’s still very, very concerning that we’re actually using urgency for this housekeeping matter." — Mike Davidson

acuity.responding_to: "It was around the meaning of a dwelling." — Mike Davidson

acuity.responding_to: nothing: Andy Foster argued the Public Records Act exemption for overseas deployments was inappropriate, and this statement does not take it up.

acuity.responding_to: Ingrid Leary: "do not be fooled, if you are watching at home, into thinking this is about efficiency and this is about taxpayer value for money"

acuity.responding_to: "the Treaty principles of active protection and equity may not be satisfied" — Ingrid Leary, who put a series of RIS-based questions on Māori consultation, disabled people's review time frames and the disclosure statement

acuity.explanation: Directly concedes the part of Upston's answer that is true (ADM is not new, reviews are already mandatory) and isolates what her answer did not address — the extension of ADM and the transparency of its use — then converts that into two specific, answerable questions on client notification and appeal rights. The speech would have to be different had Upston not rested her defence on "nothing changes"; it engages the content of that claim rather than merely naming her.

acuity.responding_to: "All this is doing is automating some of the process associated with it." — Louise Upston, who argued nothing changes in the welfare system's principles or settings and that members opposite are imagining myths

acuity.statement: Now, the Minister keeps mentioning the current uses of automated decision-making to justify giving carte blanche approval for ADM to be used just more broadly, but something that the Minister hasn't really engaged with is giving us assurances or a direction or an intent on what else in the future she would plan to use ADM for.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the Minister's immediately preceding defence of the ADM provisions and turns it against her: he accepts that current uses are being cited, identifies that as the whole of her justification, and presses on the gap it leaves — future uses the statutory standard would authorise. The question only makes sense as a reply to what she just said; a different defence of the clause would have required a different question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Hon Louise Upston: "That is why the bill strengthens the ADM standard by making it a statutory requirement, and the standard must consider bias, discrimination, legal and policy considerations, fraud considerations, transparency, human oversight, and compliance and assurance."

acuity.statement: To the comment around the jobseeker benefit and whether this will help: absolutely, because it will help ensure front-line staff can spend their time having meaningful conversations with job seekers, as opposed to comparing a medical certificate to the last one, when you can get technology to do that for you.

acuity.responding_to: Priyanca Radhakrishnan: "I also want to ask the Minister what the criteria is to determine the appropriateness of the health practitioner."

acuity.explanation: Quotes the Minister's own answer and works from it — treats "relevant agencies" as an admission that Whaikaha was included and presses for the next step, the content of that advice; then interrogates the Minister's ADM answer by asking what "no change" to a medical certificate actually means (a word, a copy-paste, a change in diagnosis). Scored mid-band rather than high because the specific answer she takes up sits outside the immediately preceding turn in this stretch.

Both are Upston answers from the question cycle, though the immediately preceding Upston turn in this window addressed the medical certificate requirements and the Privacy Act rather than consultation.

So the speech would have been different had Carter not asked. It stops short of 1.0 because the central questions put to her (what advice those disability organisations gave, what safeguards they recommended, what "no change" to a certificate means) are not taken up at all, and the reply restates "ADM is already in place" instead.

acuity.responding_to: Kahurangi Carter: "Please tell us which agencies have been consulted with. I am specifically asking around disabled people"

Well, you would expect that of any health professional, and so I can’t understand, then, how someone could be ruled in or ruled out.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's answer accurately and then does something with it: shows the stated criterion cannot do the work claimed, because registration and privacy compliance are universal among health professionals and so cannot distinguish a practitioner who is ruled in from one ruled out. The speech is unintelligible without the preceding answer, which is the test for the top of the band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "How to determine who a health assessor could be—clearly, registered with the Medical Council to ensure appropriate checks and balances."

As I said, I think the real opportunity here is that front-line staff get the opportunity to have higher-quality conversations with their clients if this kind of routine decision-making is taken care of by automation.
acuity.explanation: Engages the second of Sepuloni's two questions — why the authorisation goes beyond legitimising existing ADM practice — with an actual reason (technology advances, so more routine decisions can be automated, freeing front-line staff). One strand engaged, the other dropped.

acuity.responding_to: Carmel Sepuloni: "why have we got in front of us a broad new statutory authorisation?"

My colleague the Hon Carmel Sepuloni raised it, because it’s about why the powers go further, but it’s not only that; it is why those broadened powers are being relegated to regulation, which comes up later on and we’ll have a lot of questions about.

But the bulk of the turn is prepared legal material on clause 7, the overridden sections, the LDAC guidelines and CREEDNZ that would have been delivered whatever the Minister had just said, and the strand taken up was raised by her own colleague rather than by the preceding speaker.

acuity.responding_to: Louise Upston: "The members to my left are trying to dream up something very different from that."

acuity.explanation: Restates and answers the two specific questions put in the preceding turns — whether the ADM expansion mirrors Australia, and what in the standard would prevent a Robodebt-type outcome — rather than delivering prepared material.
