acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Now, I can understand why domestic consumers are not required to provide the information." — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: In regards to the certainty of their supply, we’re not aware of any concerns in that regard. However, we do know that the pure economics of gas versus electricity mean that many consumers are transitioning off gas and on to electricity because it is cheaper, if they have ability to do so.
acuity.explanation: Squarely addresses the specific thing Russell asked for — whether households can be reassured about continuity of gas supply — and answers it directly, then draws out the practical consequence she raised about which appliance to install.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "existing domestic household consumers of gas could do with some reassurance as to whether or not they will continue to get gas supply" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Yeah, with respect, on this side of the House, we’re not into slipping and sliding around amendments. The amendment the member’s proposing, in my view, is out of scope because this bill is putting in place regulation-making powers. What the member is trying to do is put in the detail of what those regulations would be, and that would be for the Government to determine.
acuity.explanation: Engages the actual amendment just moved, gives a reason for rejecting it, and even picks up the mover's own word ("slid in there"). The reply would be different had a different amendment been proposed.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a proposal that I hope the Minister can respond to, that I would hope that the Minister would accept that this could be adopted—slid in there" — Scott Willis

acuity.statement: Just in regards to the question on clause 4, new section 56AA(1)(a)(i) to (vii), and questions in regards to prioritising and other aspects and whether that list is representative of the priority in which Government will look at what that list represents as the scope of the areas in which the regulation-making powers will be within, it will be for Cabinet and the Government, subsequent to this law passing, to put in place the detail of what those regulations are and work their way through that.
acuity.explanation: Correctly identifies the question that was put — whether the order of the list signals prioritisation — and engages it to the extent of explaining where the decision will be made, but does not take up the substance of how the choices will be weighed. Topic engaged, specific claim not.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "In making the choices around regulation, how will the prioritisation be carried out by the Minister?" — Megan Woods

acuity.statement: That is why I say that we have been sold a lemon here, because we were sold a bill that was going to be about transparency and yet the real effect of it is that it will keep a lot of the information out of the public sector while giving the Government and Ministers lots of privileged commercial information.
acuity.explanation: Davidson's preceding turn framed the bill as addressing gaps in gas market information and announced Labour would support it. Leary speaks to the same matter under debate — what information the bill will actually make available — but takes up no part of Davidson's actual argument: she neither accepts nor disputes his account of the information gaps, nor his support for the bill, and instead delivers her own prepared line of attack on regulatory capture and the unmade regulations. The one engagement she points at ("We didn't hear a satisfactory response to that from the question from the Hon Dr Megan Woods") is with a turn outside this stretch of debate. Her speech would read identically had Davidson said something else on the same bill, so this sits in the on-topic-but-unresponsive band rather than at a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Reuben Davidson: "The problem that this bill is setting out to solve is that the current state of information has gaps."

acuity.statement: Secondly, when Labour passed this in 2019, we recognised that this retrospectivity clause was a bit untidy. It was a promise made, and, today, it’s a promise delivered.
acuity.explanation: Xu-Nan's immediately preceding turn made retrospectivity his central complaint — that the Government entertained it, that it was removed at select committee, and that members never got to question the Minister about the sequence. Hamilton picks up that same strand and gives it a competing account: the retrospectivity clause dates from Labour's 2019 law, was always untidy, and fixing it was a promise now delivered. That is one strand of the preceding argument taken up, and it is pointable. But he engages only the topic of retrospectivity, not Xu-Nan's actual claim about what entertaining it signalled or the absence of scrutiny, and the rest of the turn is prepared congratulation of the Minister. Partial engagement, not a rebuttal.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Lawrence Xu-Nan: "even the fact that the Government parties have entertained the retrospectivity signals the priority of the National Government"

acuity.statement: Someone on the other side shouted out “Heaps!”. I think there are a number of examples of bills—very important bills; some even just in the last week in this Budget urgency—that have progressed through all stages without even getting near a select committee.
acuity.explanation: Davidson is interrupted mid-sentence by Hamilton's interjection asserting that heaps of this Government's bills do get proper select committee scrutiny, and he turns straight round on it: he names the interjection, contests its substance, and supplies counter-examples — bills from the previous week's Budget urgency that passed all stages without reaching a committee. The speech would have had to change had Hamilton interjected something else or stayed silent, which is the deciding test. Marked down from the top only because the counter-examples are gestured at rather than named, and because he engages the heckle rather than Hamilton's substantive speech about the 2019 retrospectivity clause. Scored for engagement alone: whether the counter-examples are accurate or precise is not this attribute's question.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Ryan Hamilton: "Heaps! Heaps! Heaps do."

acuity.statement: The Minister across the other side says, “You haven’t added much”. Sorry, not the Minister but the member; sorry for my false advertising—the member on the other side who claims that I haven’t added much should compare the contribution I’ve made in resharing three of the 1,500 submissions, the majority of which are opposed to this piece of legislation, to the contributions made by his colleagues in this House for this piece of legislation that they believe is so important that it has to be moved through in Budget urgency on a Saturday, and yet they will speak for five or eight or 12 seconds on the bill in order to move it through.
acuity.explanation: Davidson takes up Uffindell's interjection directly, quotes its specific claim that he has added little value, and does something with it: he contests the comparison by setting his own summary of three submissions against the five-to-twelve-second speeches of Uffindell's colleagues. Delete the interjection and this passage could not stand as written, which is the deciding test. Not a full 1.0 only because the rebuttal shifts from whether his contribution had value to whether the other bench's was worse, rather than engaging the value standard itself.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "You haven’t added much value to this." — Sam Uffindell

acuity.statement: Oh, Mr Speaker, it’s a great day. We’re going to get this legislation passed. I commend it to the House.
acuity.explanation: Follows a substantive opposition speech in the same third-reading debate but engages none of its content. It gestures at the matter under debate (passing this legislation) and nothing more; it would have been word-for-word identical whatever Dansey had argued, so it sits at the bottom of the 0.1-0.3 band rather than at 0.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Georgie Dansey argued the bill moves away from strong consumer protection and towards weaker accountability for lenders, and that an individual is no match for a huge corporation; this statement does not take any of it up.

acuity.statement: The power imbalance that Georgie Dansey just mentioned is absolutely real. People assume that the lenders and the banks have all the power and, somehow, they must be wrong—they must have got their calculations wrong.
acuity.explanation: Takes up a specific strand of the immediately preceding Labour speech by name — Dansey's power-imbalance argument — and does something with it, supplying a concrete borrower example and the $3,000/$10,000 figures as evidence that the imbalance is real. Not 1.0 because much of the surrounding speech is prepared material on clause 47 and the 2015 disclosure regime rather than engagement with what was just said, but the engagement is clearly pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "that huge power imbalance that exists between large corporations and everyday people trying to live their lives" — Georgie Dansey

acuity.statement: It is my privilege to speak to commend the third reading of this bill. But before I commend it to the House, I have to say happy birthday to Minister Mike Butterick. I commend the bill to the House in building the future.
acuity.explanation: Follows a long, substantive opposition speech making specific claims about clause 47 and the disclosure regime, and engages none of them. Beyond naming the third reading it is indifferent to what preceded it — the same words could have followed any speaker saying anything.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cushla Tangaere-Manuel argued that clause 47 lets lenders avoid penalties for technical breaches on pre-existing loans and that this is a major risk for consumers; this statement does not take it up.

acuity.statement: This is where this side of the House looks forward to asking those hard questions during the committee of the whole House stage, because this bill also puts more power into the hands of the Minister. The Minister can set the terms for reviews and appoint a reviewer. So we just need to make sure that these reviews are genuinely independent.
acuity.explanation: Russell's preceding turn made the independence of reviewers and boards its central point, and flagged scrutiny at committee of the whole House. Rosewarne picks up exactly that strand — ministerial power to set review terms and appoint the reviewer, and the need for genuine independence — and the committee stage commitment. But he does not do anything with Russell's specific difficulty (finding people expert in financial services yet not involved in it); most of the speech around this is prepared material on car dealers and fine print that would be unchanged whoever spoke before. Partial engagement, pointable.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "We did some work on the independence of reviewers and the independence of the various boards and things that are involved in this" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: I was going to commend the member Dan Rosewarne for his contribution, and then he brought up the Crusaders, and it went down very quickly from there. But it’s good to see some collegiality across the House. We’re a Government focused on fixing the basics and building the future.
acuity.explanation: This refers to the previous speaker, but only to his rugby aside, not to any part of his argument about ministerial power over reviews or the independence of dispute resolution schemes. It then pivots to generic government messaging that could be delivered in any debate. A mere reference to the preceding turn, not engagement with its content, so it sits in the low band rather than at 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Last night, the Crusaders beat the Hurricanes 47-14; it was a fantastic win, so I thought I’d put that in" — Dan Rosewarne

acuity.statement: As we’ve heard through the contributions this afternoon and from the Finance and Expenditure Committee and previously in the first reading, the aim of this legislation is around improving outcomes for consumers. Now, does it go far enough? Well, maybe not, but it is what it is; it is where it is, and that’s why we are going to support it, because if it is about improving outcomes for consumers, then we are in, because we want to stand up for people in our communities and make sure that they’re looked after.
acuity.explanation: Bennett gestures at the earlier contributions and restates the same overall assessment Russell reached — the bill does not go far enough but is worth supporting — without taking up any specific claim or argument from the preceding turns, including Rutherford's immediately before him. He then moves to his own prepared constituency anecdote. A gesture at the debate on the right subject, so 0.3 rather than 0.5.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "a piece of legislation that, perhaps, is not quite as full as we would have liked, but nevertheless, it is worth supporting" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Did you not hear the start of my story, Mr Bates? Again, the reality is it isn’t actually funny; it’s not being silly, because it actually is—and they were examples in my own neighbourhood of the fact that they bought into the dream.
acuity.explanation: Bennett takes up Bates's interjection directly: he points out the interjection ignores what he had already set out (the dealers came doorknocking in his community), and rejects the implication that the example is trivial. The reply would not exist, and would read differently, had Bates said something else. Engagement with the specific point put to him, though it answers by reasserting his premise rather than fully unpacking it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "Why didn’t you buy your car locally?" — Carl Bates

acuity.statement: I think it’s important because it will be a recurring theme, and I’m not going to repeat it, and that’s around the call for scheme consolidation—i.e., why have we got four dispute resolution schemes and not one? I thought I’d deal with that and then I won’t be repeating myself for the rest of the afternoon and evening.
acuity.explanation: Identifies and takes up one strand of Williams' question — the case for consolidating the four schemes into one — and signals he will address it, but engages it only as a general theme rather than her specific sections 56-58 transitional-entity proposal, and leaves her section 52 compensation question untouched. Partial engagement that you can point at.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "Financial mentors have been making the case over many years for consolidating into either a single scheme or two schemes."

acuity.statement: As far as the Minister’s appointment of the reviewer and whether that should then be reviewed, well, I’m reliably informed that at least the key findings of each review will form each scheme’s annual report at the end of each year. And you’re right, it’s put in statute here: “The Minister may appoint as the reviewer any person who, in the Minister’s opinion, has the appropriate knowledge, skills, and experience to carry out the review.” So, yes, that does take some ministerial judgment, but as we have seen across parliaments, most Ministers, when they are appointing the people with the right expertise to oversee an independent review, get it right.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the specific provision Williams put to him — the Minister's power to appoint the reviewer and whether it needs a safeguard — quotes the clause she referred to, and answers with the annual-report disclosure plus a defence of ministerial judgment. He engages the substance rather than pivoting, but he does not take up her second, distinct question about appointing a consumer advocate or FinCap as default reviewer, so the engagement is strong on one strand and absent on the other.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Arena Williams: "is he sure, then, that his appointment provisions should not have an extra part there which says the Minister may appoint, as the reviewer, any person who is not a member of another scheme within the system?"

acuity.statement: I think the Minister has actually answered some of our questions already around review, etc.—my questions are quite separate. The Minister mentioned, multiple times, the fact that the Minister now gets to determine the framework, which I think is a great idea, but I just want to get a better understanding from the Minister of some of the potential questions around what that framework would look like.
acuity.explanation: He registers what the Minister has just said and picks up one strand of it — the Minister's claim to set the framework but not the outcomes — and uses it as the hook for his questions, so the opening would have to change if Brewer had argued differently. But he explicitly flags that his questions are separate and then moves into prepared material (timing, spot checks, NZQA-style categories, tiered fees) that does not engage the Minister's actual answer about scheme-commissioned versus Minister-directed reviews.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Cameron Brewer: "rather than ministerial oversight, to be able to set the framework but not the outcomes"

acuity.statement: He pointed to the ability for the Minister to oversee the schemes. This is written into not this bill but the principal Act, I think, at section 80.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's just-given assurance that he and his officials will keep monitoring the schemes, locates the actual statutory source of that power (s 80 of the principal Act), notes its limit (four schemes, not the system as a whole) and presses a specific follow-up about regulator oversight. The turn would have to be different had Brewer said something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I promise the member that the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and his officials will continue to monitor the schemes" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: What I was referring to there is pretty much what the Finance and Expenditure Committee suggested I do. That is, I’m not bequeathing myself statutory powers to conduct some oversight, but the select committee asks the Minister, in their report, for the Minister to undertake further analysis of cost-benefits and risks, broad stakeholder consultation, and, potentially, a wider review of the primary Act.
acuity.explanation: Engages one strand — he corrects her characterisation that he has given himself new oversight powers and locates what he meant in the select committee's recommendations. But the actual question put (did he take advice on whole-of-system regulator oversight, as under the Australian framework) is not taken up at all, and the turn closes on generic prepared material about all legislation being under review.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "which he’s given himself new powers to do" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: But I want to check with the Minister, because I wasn’t part of the Finance and Expenditure Committee for this. This particular clause has interesting wording, which is whether the requirements prescribed “(if any)” are complied with.
acuity.explanation: On the right subject — the clauses of the bill under committee examination — but it engages no part of the exchange that immediately precedes it about ministerial oversight powers and the select committee's recommendations. The questions would read identically had the preceding turn said anything else; the mention of not having sat on the committee is a gesture, not an engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer said he is "not bequeathing myself statutory powers to conduct some oversight" and would undertake the further analysis the committee asked for, and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: Just before we get too much further into the discussion on this bill, I am going to set that challenge for the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs that I signalled was going to come to him in my second reading speech.
acuity.explanation: Avowedly prepared material — a challenge flagged in an earlier speech and delivered regardless of what has since been said. It is squarely on the bill, so not a zero, but it takes up no part of Xu-Nan's clause 4 drafting question or the Minister's preceding answer on oversight.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Lawrence Xu-Nan asked what "(if any)" refers to in section 79(1)(caa) and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: We’ve got the Banking Ombudsman Scheme. Of course, providers that can choose that scheme—it takes into effect most banks. The Insurance & Financial Services Ombudsman—that takes insurers and credit providers under its wing. The Financial Services Complaints Limited—well, that encases lenders and financial advisers. The Financial Dispute Resolution Service—well, that also takes into consideration lenders and financial advisers.
acuity.explanation: Supplies exactly what the previous speaker asked for, scheme by scheme in the order she named them, and in listing two schemes as covering the same lenders and advisers he answers her 'where do they overlap' limb as well. Falls short of 1.0 only because the 'how do they differ' limb is left implicit.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I’d like the Minister to clarify the schemes" — Deborah Russell

acuity.statement: Firstly, I want to clarify with him whether it is, in fact, an error that there’s not a deletion of section 67A of the original Act. Section 67A is the provision which deals with mobile traders and other parts of the credit contracts system.
acuity.explanation: Opens a new line of committee questioning and engages nothing in the Minister's immediately preceding answer identifying the four schemes; the explicit "I'll move on" acknowledges the previous exchange without taking up its content. On topic, hence not a zero.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: nothing: Cameron Brewer had just listed which providers each of the four schemes covers and this statement does not take it up

acuity.statement: I just want to go back to the previous question and take it from the top, as far as why are we replacing scheme-commissioned independent reviews with Minister-directed independent reviews, which must occur every five years. It’s a very good question.
acuity.explanation: Returns to one strand of the questions put — the rationale for Minister-directed reviews, and later the terms-of-reference interaction between 67B and 67C that Williams said did not make sense. But the specific questions asked (whether the missing repeal of s 67A is an oversight, and what happened to the three-month timeliness requirement) go unanswered, and much of the turn is general assurance.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "doesn’t seem to make sense in light of new section 67C" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: This clause says, essentially, “enough of that”. Reviews will now be driven centrally under a standard approach that should make outcomes easier to compare and easier for the public to understand. But at the same time, it does shift power away from the schemes themselves and towards the Minister.
acuity.explanation: Accepts the consistency rationale the Minister had just offered for replacing scheme-commissioned reviews, then draws out its consequence — centralising the reviews moves power to the Minister, so independence must be secured some other way — and turns that into two questions. Engagement with the argument's logic rather than its detail, so short of 1.0.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "we are confident that they will be more robust, more consistent, and genuinely independent reviews, and removing duplication" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: As I understand it from the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs’ helpful response before, the interaction between 67B and 67C is that the consultation must happen before the review is entered into—those terms of reference must happen. Perhaps the reason why he has phrased this as “The notice may provide for the manner in which the review [happens]” is because there is clearly going to be an understanding between the agency, the Minister, and the complaints scheme. I think that’s fine.
acuity.explanation: Restates the Minister's answer accurately, concedes the part of it that resolves her earlier drafting objection, and then identifies the cost that follows from it — a notice that need say nothing beyond 'on the terms we agreed' loses transparency for aggrieved consumers. Classic accept-part-and-dispute-the-rest.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "the terms of reference is something that we work with the Minister and the scheme on together" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: Each of these dispute resolution schemes are publishing annual reports, I’m accurately informed. Each of these annual reports—like annual reports are having to reflect on their previous year’s operations and results—will be publicly releasing the key findings of those Minister-directed independent reviews, and so there will be a level of scrutiny there.
acuity.explanation: Answers the specific question asked — where the public assurance comes from if the terms of reference need not be public — by pointing to annual publication of review findings, and then to the statutory prescription of the review process. He does not engage the FinCap net promoter evidence or the consumer-experience measures she said the terms of reference need not contain.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "when the terms of reference are agreed, they don’t have to be public" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: I know that the Minister talked about how consolidation was not in scope of the bill, but I wonder whether clause 7—and what is in clause 7—would be used to initiate a review on whether there should be more than one approved scheme.
acuity.explanation: Takes the Minister's repeated scope answer and presses on it from a different direction: granting that an amendment to consolidate is out of scope, the review power the bill does create could still be pointed at the number of schemes. That is doing something with the claim rather than restating it.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "let’s not forget the issue of consolidation is outside the policy intent of this bill" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: Look, this is the last time I’ll canvass this, but the member did raise some good points as far as clause 7, and could there be a structural reform within the rounds of that? Clause 7 very much talks about the framework for reviews and, as I’ve touched on from the outset, a potential structural review of the system—i.e., perhaps a consolidation of four dispute resolution schemes down to one—is outside the policy intent of this legislation.
acuity.explanation: Names and answers the question actually put — whether clause 7's review power could reach the number of schemes — and later in the turn addresses the funding question too. But two of the three questions recapped to him (safeguards against a 'jobs for mates' reviewer appointment, and whether a reviewer's agreement must be obtained) are not taken up at all.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "I wonder if the Minister intends to use the provisions in clause 7 for the reviews to include whether there should be more than one approved scheme?" — Ricardo Menéndez March

acuity.statement: Just to further explore the answer from the Minister that we’ve just had now around making things publicly available on the website—and this is new section 67F(2) “The person responsible for a scheme must, within 5 working days after giving the notice to the Minister, publish the following on an Internet”—which was lower case, struck out, and replaced with “Internet” with a capital “I”—site that is publicly available”. There are a few questions about this.
acuity.explanation: Takes up the publication strand of the Minister's immediately preceding answer about schemes publishing notices and reports, and pushes it into the drafting of new section 67F(2). It engages the topic the Minister had just addressed rather than any specific claim he made, and then moves into his own prepared questions about the words "Internet site" and "at all reasonable times", so this is partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "The schemes will be published. They publish the fact that there’s been notice given, and they also publish the report received." — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair. I just have, for me, one final question on clause 12, new section 79AAA. This is in relation to the letter that was sent to the select committee from the Regulations Review Committee, and this is to do with the breadth of clause 12, which talks about a “failure to comply” with the requirements of section 79(1)(caa).
acuity.explanation: Follows Arena Williams on the same provision and takes up one strand of what she raised — the validity consequences of clause 12's non-invalidation rule — but approaches it from the Regulations Review Committee letter rather than engaging her specific proposition that section 79AAA should also point back to section 67B. Partial engagement with the matter she put, not with her argument.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "should the validity point point back to his new section 67B, inserted by clause 7?" — Arena Williams

acuity.statement: The failure to comply issue that he’s raised, the rationale for section 79AAA here is that it protects consumers from legal uncertainty and prevents technical challenges to past decisions. It mirrors section 34 of the Crown Entities Act 2004, does not remove consequences, and scheme approval can still be withdrawn under clause 5.
acuity.explanation: Answers precisely the question just put — what the repercussion is if there is a failure to comply when nothing is invalidated — by naming the rationale, the analogous provision it is modelled on, and the consequence that survives (withdrawal of scheme approval under clause 5). The answer would have been different had Xu-Nan asked something else.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "what then is the repercussion if there was a failure to apply? Because it doesn’t invalidate anything." — Lawrence Xu-Nan

acuity.statement: I can hear the Minister saying that he has made the requirements more stringent, but he hasn’t included some key consumer provisions which were available to him in two pieces of legislation that he is responsible for and he could have used as models.
acuity.explanation: Picks up the Minister's own consumer-protection justification for the clause and turns it against him, conceding the stringency point while disputing that the consumer provisions he could have modelled were used. It is aimed at what he said rather than merely naming him, though the rebuttal is asserted rather than worked through against his specific wording.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "it protects consumers from legal uncertainty and prevents technical challenges to past decisions" — Cameron Brewer

acuity.statement: The previous speaker talks about the urgency and the process and calling all of this a farce. Yet, his own party has put up hundreds of amendments over the last couple of days that have wasted the time of this House.
acuity.explanation: Takes up McAnulty's immediately preceding complaint about urgency and process being a sham, but answers the topic rather than the claim: it does not address whether the bills were urgent or whether Arena Williams' amendments were good-faith consumer-protection improvements, instead pivoting to Labour's own use of amendments. A pointable but partial engagement, so mid-band rather than high.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Kieran McAnulty: "Instead, we're here under a fake urgency, all for a PR show, all to save face" — and his claim that good-faith amendments were not being considered.

acuity.statement: Before I turn my attention to the bill, I do want to address the matter of urgency and when it is used, and why we have put so many amendments in. That is a Government that has abused urgency; that have used it excessively; that it has decided it can just put the House into urgency for no reason whatsoever; that has, on this Budget emergency move, included bills that have been sitting on the agenda for months since the last Budget.
acuity.explanation: Directly takes up the specific charge Rutherford had just made — that Labour's hundreds of amendments wasted the House's time — names it as the thing she will answer, and supplies a reason (the amendments are a response to urgency being abused on bills that have sat on the Order Paper since the last Budget). This speech would have had to be different had Rutherford not made that charge, which is the deciding test.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Tom Rutherford: "his own party has put up hundreds of amendments over the last couple of days that have wasted the time of this House".

acuity.statement: I am very glad that the Opposition is joining us to support the bill to fix the basics for New Zealanders, in making sure that we are building the future.
acuity.explanation: Registers that the previous speaker indicated Labour's support, which is a glance at her turn, but engages none of its content — nothing on the claimed lost opportunity to amalgamate the four schemes, the call for the Minister to begin reviews before the election, or the criticism of the Minister's committee answers. A gesture at the debate rather than a partial engagement.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: Deborah Russell: "On the whole, this is a bill we can support." — the rest of her argument (amalgamating the schemes, starting the ministerial reviews) is not taken up.

acuity.statement: This is an improvement because the problem with that unlimited number is that we simply get out of control. This is what we heard in select committee from Fisher & Paykel in particular, if I recall correctly.
acuity.explanation: Brooking's turn pressed for concrete examples of the mischief caused by over-broad divisional applications under the 1953 Act. Willis takes up that strand — he restates the unlimited-divisionals problem and supplies a named instance from select committee evidence (Fisher & Paykel) — so this part of the speech would read differently had Brooking not asked for examples. But he engages only one strand of her turn (he does not take up her retrospectivity concern or her question about where the new novelty line falls) before moving to prepared material on science funding, which is indifferent to what preceded it. Partial engagement, so mid-band.
acuity.subject: speaker
acuity.responding_to: "can the Minister, can the other side give us examples of where the mischief is going to be stopped" — Rachel Brooking, in the immediately preceding turn, which also set out the 1953-Act divisional-application problem and questioned the use of Budget urgency.

acuity.statement: Look, I think it’s pretty—you know, there’s nothing strange about the process this bill’s gone through. It’s had a full select committee. The only difference is we’re sitting here on a Saturday night, and I don’t think New Zealand taxpayers would actually mind that we’re sitting here on a Saturday night, getting good value for money.
acuity.explanation: Takes up one strand of Willis's turn — the complaint about the bill being rushed through under Budget urgency on a Saturday — and answers it directly by pointing to the completed select committee process. It leaves Willis's main argument (that defunding science undermines the bill) untouched and returns to prepared praise of the bill, so this is partial engagement rather than full.
acuity.subject: speaker
